# Five-Dimensional Vaidya Black Holes as High-Frequency Limits of Vacuum Spacetimes

### Large data, T² symmetry, and settling to Schwarzschild–Tangherlini

**Matthew Lach** · Independent Researcher · November 2026

## Abstract

Huneau and Luk proved that generic, small-data, polarized U(1)-symmetric solutions of the Einstein–null dust system with
angularly separated dusts are weak limits of vacuum solutions on a fixed time interval, in an elliptic gauge in which
smallness is needed even for local existence. We prove a five-dimensional counterpart on a large background. For vacuum
metrics with a T² isometry and both reflections, the Einstein equations reduce exactly to 2+1 gravity coupled to two
free waves with the flat, positive-definite target (3/2) dψ² + 2 dω². The background is five-dimensional Vaidya, a black
hole of mass μ0 grown by an ingoing shell, on a domain from before the shell reaches the hole to the surface, inside or
on the horizon, where the curvature reaches a fixed scale l5. For every amplitude A > 0 and every smooth compactly
supported envelope env, with no smallness of either, we construct T²-symmetric vacuum metrics g_λ on that domain, of
wavelength λ ≤ λ0, with |g_λ − g0| ≤ Cλ, ∂g_λ bounded and ∂g_λ → ∂g0 weakly but not strongly, where g0 is Vaidya with
dμ/dv = (2/9) A² env², the null dust of Isaacson's flux. The proof uses the wave-map gauge relative to the limit, an
approximate solution of every order whose powers of λ beat every nonlinear term, a phase-shift identity for the one
large coefficient of the linear problem, and the constraints solved outward in r as a parabolic–hyperbolic system. When
μ0 > √72 l5², the outgoing expansion of the round spheres has one zero on each column crossing the horizon, converging
to it at O(λ), and after the shell every sphere's mass is the limit's to O(λ²). Solutions with the same properties are
also constructed from the waves' free data at past null infinity, where they obey the five-dimensional Bondi mass law:
their Bondi mass is μ(v) + O(λ) during the shell and the limit's final mass μ_end plus (2/9) λ² A² ∫ env'² + O(λ³)
after it. Outside the black hole, the development of a continuation of the data of g_λ beyond a ball settles in the
class to Schwarzschild–Tangherlini, and the developments of perturbations without symmetry that are small in Hintz's
data class settle to slowly rotating Myers–Perry black holes; the proof carries Hintz's proof of the nonlinear stability
of Kerr into five dimensions in full, with linear stability in the gauge of the nonlinear problem as its linearisation.
Further, the development of the continued data also reaches inside the black hole after the shell, up to the curvature
boundary; the development of g_λ's own data settles without gluing, in a class wider by half-integer orders; the
construction extends to two crossing null dusts and to restricted massless Vlasov limits; the constants are stated as
far as they are explicit, among them an upper bound for λ0 at a numerical point and, at a parameter point outside the set
on which settling is proved, for one admissible choice of the weights, orders and inner products and the index sets as
the proofs construct them, 1.2497 × 10²⁴ < d < 1.57157 × 10⁵⁰ for the loss d with which the settling proof applies the
Nash–Moser theorem; at equality, μ0 = √72 l5², timelike curves of g_λ cross the boundary in a layer whose width tends to
zero with λ; and at the physical wavelength 10 l5 there is no separation of scales, existence holding where the solution
is the seed.

# Part I. Introduction and statements

## 1. Introduction

### 1.1 Burnett's problem

Burnett's problem [Bur89] concerns families of vacuum metrics whose derivatives converge only weakly. Huneau and
Luk state it as follows ([HL18], p. 1; their footnote omitted): "On a fixed manifold, consider a one-parameter family of
Lorentzian metrics g_λ for λ ∈ (0, λ_0], λ_0 ∈ R which satisfies the Einstein vacuum equations
R_μν(g_λ) = 0. (1.1) Assume moreover that there exists a metric g_0 such that as λ → 0, • g_λ converges to g_0
uniformly on compact sets; and • the derivatives of g_λ converges weakly in L² to the derivatives of g_0. Due to the
nonlinearity of the equations, it can happen that the limiting metric g_0 is a solution to the Einstein equations which
is not vacuum". Burnett's own assumptions, as Luk and Rodnianski print them ([LR20], p. 3, their (1.3)), are
"|g_n − g_∞| ≤ λ_n, |∂g_n| ≤ C, |∂²g_n| ≤ Cλ_n^(−1)". The direct question asks which limits occur; the reverse asks
whether a given Einstein–matter solution is such a limit.

### 1.2 The theorem of Huneau and Luk

Huneau and Luk work with metrics ([HL18], pp. 2–3) "⁽⁴⁾g = e^(−2φ) g + e^(2φ) (dx³)²", for which "Einstein vacuum
equations R(⁽⁴⁾g)_μν = 0 are equivalent to the following system for (g, φ): □_g φ = 0, R_μν(g) = 2∂_μφ ∂_νφ. (1.3)"
Their main theorem reads ([HL18], p. 10; their footnotes 11 and 12 omitted, and the two column vectors of (4.1)
printed in a row with ";"):

> **Theorem 4.2 (Main theorem).** Let k ≥ 10, −1/2 < δ < 0, R > 0 and A be a finite set. Given an admissible free
> initial data set (φ̇, ∇φ, F̆_A, u_A)↾Σ_0 such that
> • |∇u_A↾Σ_0| > 1/2;
> • u_A↾Σ_0 is angularly separated;
> • (Smallness condition) ‖∇u_A − c⃗_A‖_(H^11_δ) + ‖φ̇‖_(H^10) + ‖∇φ‖_(H^10) + ‖F̆_A‖_(H^10) ≤ ε;
> • (Genericity condition on initial data) there exists a point p ∈ R² such that ((∂_1φ_0)↾Σ_0; (∂_1φ̇_0)↾Σ_0)(p)
> and ((∂_2φ_0)↾Σ_0; (∂_2φ̇_0)↾Σ_0)(p) are linearly independent. (4.1)
>
> Then, there exists ε_0 > 0 such that if ε < ε_0, a unique solution (g_0, φ_0, (F_0)_A, (u_0)_A) to (1.4) arising
> from the given admissible free initial data set exists on a time interval [0, 1], and there exists a one-parameter
> family of solutions (g_λ, φ_λ) to (1.3) for λ ∈ (0, λ_0) (for some λ_0 ∈ R sufficiently small), which are all
> defined on the time interval [0, 1], such that (g_λ, φ_λ) → (g_0, φ_0) uniformly on compact sets and
> (∂g_λ, ∂φ_λ) ⇀ (∂g_0, ∂φ_0) weakly in L² with ∂g_λ, ∂φ_λ ∈ L^∞_loc uniformly.

Here (1.4) is the Einstein–null dust system with |A| families ([HL18], p. 3), the admissible free data are posed on a
maximal slice of R² and solved for in an elliptic gauge ([HL18], pp. 8–9, Definition 3.2 and Theorem 3.3), and angular
separation is [HL18] Definition 4.1, p. 10. Their review states where the smallness comes from and names the
large-data problem ([HL24], p. 28): "Notice that in the U(1) setting, because of our use of an elliptic gauge,
smallness is required even for local existence of smooth solution. It would be interesting to carry out these
constructions without smallness assumptions: Problem 8.6. Construct local high-frequency solutions as in Sections 5, 6
and 7.2 but such that the limiting solution is far away from Minkowski spacetime."

### 1.3 What is proved

We prove the counterpart of Theorem 4.2 of [HL18] in five dimensions, for one family of null dust, on a background
that is far from Minkowski: a black hole growing by an ingoing shell, on a fixed domain that reaches inside the horizon
to the surface where the limit's curvature reaches a fixed scale (Theorem 3.1). It is an instance of Problem 8.6 in a
five-dimensional symmetry class, not an answer to Problem 8.6 as posed, which concerns four dimensions. Solutions with
the same properties are also constructed from the waves' free data at past null infinity (Theorem 3.7),
and at past null infinity they obey the five-dimensional Bondi mass law with the prescribed radiation field
(Theorem 3.8).

Beyond that domain, and outside the black hole, we prove that in the class the development of a continuation of their
data beyond a ball about the hole settles at late times to five-dimensional Tangherlini of a nearby mass, and that the
developments of their perturbations without symmetry that are small in Hintz's data class settle to slowly rotating
Myers–Perry black holes (Theorem 3.9). The route is Hintz's proof of the nonlinear stability of Kerr [Hin26],
carried into five dimensions: every input that depends on the dimension is established at Tangherlini, the class removes
his boosts, rotations and their gauge modifications, and without it they are restored, with the inputs at every nearby
Myers–Perry parameter proved by perturbation from Tangherlini, in the manner of [HHV21], and the charges by which the
gluing at large radius matches the Myers–Perry family determined. The proof is written out in full in spacetime
dimension n + 1 = 5: his stability paper, the parts of his companion papers [Hin26a, Hin26c, Hin23a] that the route
uses, and the gluing of [CD03], part by part, from statements of those papers that hold in every dimension. We also
prove that the development of g_λ's own data settles, with no gluing, in a class wider by half-integer orders, and the
linear solution's settling in a Regge–Wheeler-type gauge and in harmonic gauge; and we prove the two-dust and
restricted-Vlasov counterparts, state the constants, and state the scope.

The two theorems share their architecture. Both reduce the vacuum equations in the symmetry class to 2+1 gravity
coupled to free waves with a flat, positive-definite target (Proposition 2.3; [HL18] (1.3)); both build an
approximate solution by geometric optics and correct it on a fixed interval; both conclude with uniform convergence of
the metric and weak, not strong, convergence of its derivatives (in Huneau and Luk, of the 3+1 metric; their reduced
metric's derivatives converge uniformly, [HL18] Remark 4.3, p. 10), the defect being null dust. They differ in what is
large: Huneau and Luk allow any finite number of angularly separated dusts on a small background; we allow one dust on
a large one, and the amplitude of the waves is not small either.

### 1.4 Why five dimensions and a black hole

In five dimensions the T² class is the natural analogue of polarized U(1): the two rotations of R⁴ = R² × R² commute,
the two reflections make the Killing fields hypersurface orthogonal and mutually orthogonal, and the reduction is
exact (Proposition 2.3). Unlike Huneau and Luk's translation, each rotation has an axis, where the reduced system
degenerates; the proof therefore never uses the reduced system and works in five-dimensional Cartesian coordinates, in
which the axes are regular points. Five-dimensional Vaidya is the simplest large solution of the limiting system: its
mass grows by exactly the averaged energy of the waves, and it carries a horizon. The domain ends where the curvature
reaches a fixed scale l5, x_K := l5² √𝒦 = 1 with 𝒦 the Kretschmann scalar; that surface lies inside the horizon, or on
it at equality, and is spacelike when μ0 > √72 l5² (Proposition 3.3), so the domain is the domain of
dependence of its data and nothing inside it is excised. The solution is constructed on a compact set Ω reaching a
fixed distance inside that surface, and nothing in Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 3.8 is
claimed beyond Ω and the past domain; Theorem 3.9 concerns the exterior of the black hole after the shell. Nothing
in the paper involves an inner or Cauchy horizon.

### 1.5 Relation to Huneau and Luk, Touati, and Luk and Rodnianski

Point by point; HL is [HL18], T is [Tou23a], LR is [LR20], and "here" is this paper.

- *Dimension and symmetry.* HL: 3+1, polarized U(1), a translation with no axis. T: 3+1, none. LR: 3+1, none. Here:
  4+1, T² with both reflections, rotations with two axes.
- *Reduced system.* HL: 2+1 gravity with one free wave φ, their (1.3). T, LR: none. Here: 2+1 gravity with two free
  waves on the target (3/2) dψ² + 2 dω² (Proposition 2.3), identified, and not used in the proof.
- *Gauge.* HL: elliptic (maximal slices, conformally flat). T: generalised wave. LR: double null. Here: the wave-map
  gauge relative to the limit g0.
- *Background.* HL: small, near Minkowski (the smallness condition of Theorem 4.2). T: small, his (2.9), with an
  asymptotically planar phase, his (2.10). LR: large and angularly regular, on a double null domain short in one null
  direction (u̲* ≤ ε, ε depending on the bound C of the data, their Theorem 1.9). Here: five-dimensional Vaidya with
  a black hole; no smallness of μ0, A or env.
- *Dusts.* HL: any finite number, angularly separated, with generic data. T: one. LR: two, measure-valued; their
  reverse statement, the counterpart of Huneau and Luk's theorem, is their Corollary 1.14, local. Here: one.
- *Data.* HL: admissible free data on a maximal slice. T: the conformal method of [Tou23b]. LR: characteristic.
  Here: Cauchy data on Σ_τ0, the constraints solved outward in r.
- *Domain.* HL: [0, 1] × R². T: [0, 1] × R³. LR: [0, u*] × [0, u̲*] × S². Here: Ω ⊃ D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}, through the
  horizon to a spacelike boundary.
- *What closes the estimates.* HL: the smallness ε. T: the smallness ε, with λ ≤ λ0 as well ([Tou23a] Proposition
  7.1, p. 13). LR: angular regularity on a domain short in one null direction. Here: powers of λ, with the
  approximant carried to any order.
- *The derivative loss.* HL: elliptic estimates for the metric. T: a null foliation and a Fourier cut-off. LR:
  angular regularity. Here: the phase-shift identity, the exact commutator (2.6) and a compact mollifier.
- *Conclusion.* HL: uniform convergence, weak L² convergence of derivatives, ∂ in L^∞ uniformly. T: g_λ = g0 +
  λ g(1) + … in generalised wave gauge. LR: C⁰ and weak W^(1,2). Here: uniform at O(λ), ∂g bounded, weak L².

*What carries over.* The reduction to a 2+1 system with free waves on a flat, positive-definite target, which here is
two copies of Huneau and Luk's scalar (Proposition 2.3); the geometric-optics construction around an eikonal phase
of the limit; the weak limit as null dust with Isaacson's flux [Isa68b]; the time interval fixed in advance.

*What changes.* One more dimension; a T²-mirror class whose orbits degenerate on two axes, so that the reduced system
cannot be used there; a large black-hole background in place of small data, so that the trapped region and a spacelike
inner boundary are inside the domain; Cauchy data before the shell reaches the hole, and by Theorem 3.7
data at past null infinity, which none of the three poses, rather than on a maximal slice or characteristic
hypersurfaces; one family of dust, not many.

*What the proof needs beyond theirs.* (1) An approximant of every order (Theorem 4.11), so that the nonlinear
terms are beaten by λ and only a linear estimate on the large background must be uniform; (2) the phase-shift identity
of Chapter 6, which removes the one large coefficient of that linear problem; (3) the exact commutator
(2.6) on five-dimensional Vaidya, in which the mass drops out; (4) a compactly supported mollifier adapted
to a domain with boundary, in place of a Fourier projector (Chapter 5); (5) a domain inside the horizon whose
time lines are spacelike, handled by changing only the independent variables to lines along a timelike vector field
(Chapter 6); (6) the constraints solved as a parabolic–hyperbolic evolution in r with no smallness and
no data imposed far out (Chapter 7); (7) a gauge hierarchy making D vanish to every order (Chapter 7).

### 1.6 Scope

Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 3.8 are made on D_T, on Ω and on the past domain of
Theorem 3.7, the last two bounded inside by r = a, a fixed distance inside x_K = 1; beyond them
Theorem 3.9 is stated outside the black hole, and, with its inner radius taken as half the radius of the curvature
boundary after the shell, its development also reaches inside the black hole after the shell, up to that boundary
(Proposition 43.2). Below the inner boundary the theorems are not silent: the boundary sits at the curvature scale l5,
which is arbitrary, and a smaller l5 puts every point with r > 0 and v ≤ v_end + T inside D_T, since r_q(v) = (√72 μ(v)
l5²)^(1/4) tends to 0 with l5, the constants then depending on l5; at r = 0 the limit itself is singular, its
Kretschmann scalar being 72 μ²/r⁸ (Proposition 2.5). The thresholds λ0, λ1 and δ exist by the proofs and are not
evaluated; Proposition 56.8 bounds λ0 above at a numerical point, and Chapter 49 states where the explicit
evaluation of λ1 and δ stops and bounds the loss d with which the proof of Theorem 3.9 applies the Nash–Moser
theorem at a point of the gauge and damping parameters outside the set on which that theorem is proved: there
d > 1.2497 × 10²⁴ at every admissible choice of the weights, for the index sets as the proofs construct them, and
d < 1.57157 × 10⁵⁰ at one admissible choice of the weights, orders and inner products (Theorem 49.59). A
high-frequency theorem, whose expansion parameter is the wavelength over the curvature length, does not apply at a
prescribed wavelength of 10 l5; there existence holds where the solution is the seed (Theorem 57.18). Chapter 58
collects these statements.

### 1.7 Organisation of the paper

Part I sets up the class, the background, the domain, the gauge and the waves (Chapter 2) and states
the theorems (Chapter 3).

Part II builds the approximate solution to every order by a two-scale expansion around the phase v
(Chapter 4).

Part III proves existence on Ω with remainder estimates uniform in λ: the inequalities on the slices
(Chapter 5), the linear structure, the phase-shift identity and the bootstrap (Chapter 6), and
the exact data, the constraints being solved outward in r (Chapter 7).

Part IV proves the statements on the boundary, the spheres' horizon and the mean mass
(Chapter 8), the construction from past null infinity (Chapter 9) and the Bondi mass law
(Chapter 10).

The stability theory of five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini occupies five parts: the spectral family on bundles
(Part V), analysis on the compactified spacetime (Part VI), the Myers–Perry family and
the linear theory at low energy (Part VII), forward solutions and their asymptotics
(Part VIII), and the exterior, the nonlinear theorem, gluing and linear stability
(Part IX).

Part X proves Theorem 3.9 (Chapter 41) and then treats the solutions after the shell and
the reach of the theorem (Chapter 42), the interior after the shell (Chapter 43), the settling of g_λ's
own data (Chapter 44), and the linear solution in a Regge–Wheeler-type gauge (Chapter 45) and in harmonic
gauge (Chapter 46, Chapter 47).

Part XI gives explicit resolvent bounds on five-dimensional Tangherlini (Chapter 48) and what
the proof of Theorem 3.9 makes explicit (Chapter 49).

Part XII treats two crossing dusts (Chapter 50), the class Einstein–null-dust system
(Chapter 51), restricted massless Vlasov limits (Chapter 52), localised data and the sign of the charge
(Chapter 53), the boundary at equality (Chapter 54, Chapter 55), the threshold λ0 at a
numerical point (Chapter 56), the prescribed wavelength 10 l5 (Chapter 57) and the scope (Chapter 58).

Appendix A states the results of the literature that the proofs use, each cited with its number and
page where the cited work gives them; Appendix B prints the coefficients of the explicit polynomials, approximants
and enclosures that the proofs use.

## 2. Setting

This chapter fixes the symmetry class, the background, the domain, the gauge, the profiles and their norms, and the
waves. Every identity is derived in full.

### 2.1 The class and the reduction

Let g5 be a Lorentzian metric on a five-manifold, invariant under an effective T² action and under both reflections
of its orbits. Invariance under each reflection removes the cross terms, so locally

    g5 = g3 + e^(2A) dφ1² + e^(2B) dφ2²,    (2.1)

with g3 a Lorentzian metric and A, B functions on the three-dimensional orbit space. On R⁴ = R² × R² we write
G := O(2) × O(2), acting by the rotations of the two planes and the reflections x2 ↦ −x2, x4 ↦ −x4; the class is the
class of G-invariant metrics, and we call it the T²-mirror class.

**Lemma 2.1** (Ricci tensor of the class). Let a, b, … be indices on the orbit space, ∇ and □ the
connection and wave operator of g3, and write R11, R22 for the φ1φ1 and φ2φ2 components of Ric[g5]. Then

    Ric[g5]_ab = Ric[g3]_ab − ∇_a∇_b A − ∂_aA ∂_bA − ∇_a∇_b B − ∂_aB ∂_bB,
    R11 = −e^(2A) (□A + |dA|² + ⟨dA, dB⟩),      R22 = −e^(2B) (□B + |dB|² + ⟨dA, dB⟩),

with |·| and ⟨·,·⟩ taken in g3, and the components Ric[g5]_(aφi) and Ric[g5]_(φ1φ2) vanish identically.

*Proof.* The mixed components vanish because the reflection φi ↦ −φi is an isometry of g5 that changes the sign of
every component with exactly one index φi. Since A and B do not depend on φ1, φ2, the Christoffel symbols of g5 are
those of g3 on the orbit space together with

    Γ^a_(φ1φ1) = −e^(2A) ∇^aA,   Γ^(φ1)_(aφ1) = ∂_aA,   Γ^a_(φ2φ2) = −e^(2B) ∇^aB,   Γ^(φ2)_(aφ2) = ∂_aB,

all others vanishing. We use R_bd = ∂_μΓ^μ_bd − ∂_dΓ^μ_bμ + Γ^μ_μνΓ^ν_bd − Γ^μ_dνΓ^ν_bμ. For b, d on the orbit
space, Γ^μ_bμ = Γ^a_ba + ∂_bA + ∂_bB and Γ^μ_μe = Γ^a_ae + ∂_eA + ∂_eB, while the φ-indices add to Γ^μ_dνΓ^ν_bμ
exactly ∂_dA ∂_bA + ∂_dB ∂_bB. Hence R_bd = Ric[g3]_bd − ∂_b∂_dA + Γ^e_bd ∂_eA − ∂_b∂_dB + Γ^e_bd ∂_eB − ∂_bA ∂_dA −
∂_bB ∂_dB, which is the first formula. For R11, the terms are ∂_aΓ^a_(φ1φ1) = −∂_a(e^(2A)∇^aA), then
Γ^μ_μaΓ^a_(φ1φ1) = −(Γ^b_ba + ∂_aA + ∂_aB) e^(2A)∇^aA, and Γ^μ_(φ1ν)Γ^ν_(φ1μ) = 2 Γ^(φ1)_(φ1a)Γ^a_(φ1φ1) =
−2 e^(2A)|dA|²; the term ∂_(φ1)Γ^μ_(φ1μ) is zero. Summing,
R11 = −e^(2A)(2|dA|² + ∇_a∇^aA + |dA|² + ⟨dA, dB⟩ − 2|dA|²), which is the second formula; R22 is the same with A
and B exchanged. ∎

**Lemma 2.2** (conformal change in three dimensions). Let g be a metric on a three-manifold, ψ a
function and h := e^(2ψ) g. Then, with ∇ and □ those of g,

    Ric[h] = Ric[g] − ∇∇ψ + dψ ⊗ dψ − (□ψ + |dψ|²) g,      □_h u = e^(−2ψ) (□u + ⟨dψ, du⟩).

*Proof.* Let m be the dimension. The difference of the connections is C^a_bc = δ^a_b ∂_cψ + δ^a_c ∂_bψ − g_bc ∇^aψ,
and Ric[h]_bc − Ric[g]_bc = ∇_aC^a_bc − ∇_cC^a_ba + C^a_adC^d_bc − C^a_cdC^d_ba. Here C^a_ba = m ∂_bψ, so
∇_aC^a_bc = 2∇_b∇_cψ − g_bc □ψ, ∇_cC^a_ba = m ∇_b∇_cψ and C^a_adC^d_bc = m (2 ∂_bψ∂_cψ − g_bc|dψ|²). Expanding
the nine products in C^a_cdC^d_ba gives (m + 2) ∂_bψ∂_cψ − 2 g_bc|dψ|². Altogether

    Ric[h] − Ric[g] = −(m − 2)(∇∇ψ − dψ ⊗ dψ) − (□ψ + (m − 2)|dψ|²) g.

For the wave operator, □_h u = h^(bc)(∇_b∇_c u − C^a_bc ∂_a u) = e^(−2ψ)(□u + (m − 2)⟨dψ, du⟩), because
g^(bc)C^a_bc = (2 − m)∇^aψ. Put m = 3. ∎

**Proposition 2.3** (the reduction). Put ψ := A + B, ω := (B − A)/2 and h := e^(2ψ) g3. Then

    Ric[h]_ab = Ric[g5]_ab + (3/2) ∂_aψ ∂_bψ + 2 ∂_aω ∂_bω + (e^(−2A) R11 + e^(−2B) R22) (g3)_ab,
    e^(2ψ) □_h ψ = −(e^(−2A) R11 + e^(−2B) R22),      e^(2ψ) □_h ω = (e^(−2A) R11 − e^(−2B) R22)/2.

Hence g5 is vacuum if and only if

    Ric[h] = (3/2) dψ² + 2 dω²,      □_h ψ = 0,      □_h ω = 0.    (2.2)

*Proof.* By Lemma 2.1, e^(−2A) R11 + e^(−2B) R22 = −(□ψ + |dψ|²), since |dA|² + |dB|² +
2⟨dA, dB⟩ = |dψ|²; and e^(−2A) R11 − e^(−2B) R22 = □(B − A) + ⟨d(B − A), dψ⟩ = 2(□ω + ⟨dψ, dω⟩). Since A = (ψ − 2ω)/2 and
B = (ψ + 2ω)/2, dA ⊗ dA + dB ⊗ dB = (1/2) dψ ⊗ dψ + 2 dω ⊗ dω, so Lemma 2.1 reads
Ric[g3] = Ric[g5] + ∇∇ψ + (1/2) dψ² + 2 dω². By Lemma 2.2,

    Ric[h] = Ric[g5] + ∇∇ψ + (1/2) dψ² + 2 dω² − ∇∇ψ + dψ² − (□ψ + |dψ|²) g3,

which is the first formula, and e^(2ψ) □_h u = □u + ⟨dψ, du⟩ gives the other two. If g5 is vacuum, all three
right-hand sides reduce to (3/2) dψ² + 2 dω² and 0. Conversely, if (3/2) dψ² + 2 dω² = Ric[h] and both waves vanish,
then e^(−2A) R11 ± e^(−2B) R22 = 0, so R11 = R22 = 0, then Ric[g5]_ab = 0, and the mixed components vanish by
Lemma 2.1. ∎

With ψ̃ := (√3/2) ψ, (2.2) reads Ric[h] = 2 (dψ̃² + dω²), □_h ψ̃ = □_h ω = 0: Huneau and Luk's system [HL18]
(1.3), quoted in Chapter 1, with the scalar φ replaced by the pair (ψ̃, ω), whose target is the flat Euclidean
plane.

### 2.2 The background

We use coordinates X = (τ, x) ∈ R × R⁴, r = |x|, x̂ = x/r, v := τ + r, and on R⁴ the coordinates

    x1 + i x2 = r cos ϑ e^(iφ1),      x3 + i x4 = r sin ϑ e^(iφ2),      ϑ ∈ [0, π/2],

in which the flat metric is dr² + r² (dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2²), c := cos ϑ, s := sin ϑ. The polar angle is ϑ; the
letter θ is reserved for the phase. The T² action rotates the planes (x1, x2) and (x3, x4); its axes {c = 0} and
{s = 0} are regular points of R⁴, and every tensor below is an array of Cartesian components. Let

    g0 := η + (μ(v)/r²) dv ⊗ dv,   g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − (μ/r²) L0 ⊗ L0,   L0 := ∂_τ − x̂·∂_x,   det g0 = −1,    (2.3)

with μ smooth and nondecreasing, μ = μ0 > 0 for v ≤ v_start and μ constant for v ≥ v_end; we write
μ_end := μ(v_end). The inverse and the determinant hold because dv = dτ + x̂·dx satisfies η⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0 and
η⁻¹dv = −L0: for a rank-one change by a covector null for η, the inverse changes by the opposite rank-one term and
the determinant does not change. We write □̃ := g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b acting on each Cartesian component, and ∂_r := x̂·∂_x.

In the coordinates (v, r, ϑ, φ1, φ2), with γ := dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2² the round metric of S³, the background is

    g0 = −f dv² + 2 dv dr + r² γ,      f := 1 − μ(v)/r²,    (2.4)

since −(dv − dr)² + dr² = −dv² + 2 dv dr. Its inverse has g^(vv) = 0, g^(vr) = 1, g^(rr) = f, g^(ij) = r⁻² γ^(ij)
on S³.

**Lemma 2.4** (curvature of the (v, r) form). Let f = f(v, r) be any smooth function and
g = −f dv² + 2 dv dr + r² γ, with i, j, k, l indices on S³. The nonzero Christoffel symbols are

    Γ^v_vv = f_r/2,  Γ^r_vv = (f f_r − f_v)/2,  Γ^r_vr = −f_r/2,  Γ^v_ij = −r γ_ij,  Γ^r_ij = −r f γ_ij,
    Γ^i_rj = δ^i_j / r,  Γ^i_jk = Γ[γ]^i_jk,

and the nonzero components of the Riemann tensor, up to its symmetries, are

    R_vrvr = f_rr/2,   R_vivj = (r/2)(f f_r − f_v) γ_ij,   R_virj = −(r/2) f_r γ_ij,
    R_ijkl = r² (1 − f)(γ_ik γ_jl − γ_il γ_jk).

Consequently

    Ric_vv = (f/2)(f_rr + 3 f_r/r) − 3 f_v/(2r),   Ric_vr = −(1/2)(f_rr + 3 f_r/r),   Ric_rr = 0,
    Ric_ij = (2(1 − f) − r f_r) γ_ij,   Ric_vi = Ric_ri = 0,

and the Kretschmann scalar 𝒦 is

    𝒦 = R_abcd R^abcd = f_rr² + 6 f_r²/r² + 12 (1 − f)²/r⁴,    (2.5)

in which f_v does not appear.

*Proof.* The Christoffel symbols follow from Γ_(c,ab) = (∂_a g_bc + ∂_b g_ac − ∂_c g_ab)/2 and the inverse above:
the only nonzero lowered symbols with no index on S³ are Γ_(r,vv) = f_r/2, Γ_(v,vv) = −f_v/2 and Γ_(v,vr) = −f_r/2,
and those with indices on S³ are Γ_(r,ij) = −r γ_ij, Γ_(j,ri) = r γ_ij and Γ[r² γ]_(k,ij); raising with g^(vr) = 1,
g^(rr) = f, g^(ij) = r⁻² γ^(ij) gives the list.

The isometries of γ act on g by isometries fixing v and r, and the isotropy group of a point of S³ is O(3), acting on
its tangent space; it contains reflections. An O(3)-invariant tensor on R³ of odd rank vanishes, and one of rank two
is a multiple of the metric. So, with A, B, C ∈ {v, r}, every component with an odd number of indices on S³ vanishes,
R_ABij vanishes (it is a multiple of γ_ij and antisymmetric in i, j), R_AiBj = r S_AB γ_ij for some S_AB, and the
components with four indices on S³ are determined by R^i_jkl, computed below. We use
R^a_bcd = ∂_cΓ^a_bd − ∂_dΓ^a_bc + Γ^a_ceΓ^e_bd − Γ^a_deΓ^e_bc and R_abcd = g_ae R^e_bcd.
Since Γ^v_rr = Γ^v_vr = Γ^r_rr = 0 and Γ^v_re = 0 for every e,

    R^v_rvr = 0,   R^r_rvr = −∂_rΓ^r_vr − Γ^r_rvΓ^v_vr = f_rr/2,   so R_vrvr = g_vr R^r_rvr = f_rr/2.

For the mixed components,

    R^v_irj = ∂_rΓ^v_ij − Γ^v_jkΓ^k_ir = −γ_ij + γ_ij = 0,
    R^r_irj = ∂_rΓ^r_ij + Γ^r_rvΓ^v_ij − Γ^r_jkΓ^k_ir = −(f + r f_r) γ_ij + (r f_r/2) γ_ij + f γ_ij = −(r/2) f_r γ_ij,
    R^v_ivj = Γ^v_vvΓ^v_ij = −(r/2) f_r γ_ij,
    R^r_ivj = ∂_vΓ^r_ij + Γ^r_vvΓ^v_ij + Γ^r_vrΓ^r_ij = (−r f_v − (r/2)(f f_r − f_v) + (r/2) f f_r) γ_ij
            = −(r/2) f_v γ_ij,

so R_virj = g_vr R^r_irj = −(r/2) f_r γ_ij, R_rirj = g_rv R^v_irj = 0, and R_vivj = g_vv R^v_ivj + g_vr R^r_ivj =
(r/2)(f f_r − f_v) γ_ij. On the spheres, the only
Christoffel symbols with an upper index on S³ and a lower index v or r are Γ^i_rj = δ^i_j/r, so

    R^i_jkl = R[γ]^i_jkl + Γ^i_krΓ^r_jl − Γ^i_lrΓ^r_jk = (δ^i_k γ_jl − δ^i_l γ_jk) − f (δ^i_k γ_jl − δ^i_l γ_jk),

using R[γ]^i_jkl = δ^i_k γ_jl − δ^i_l γ_jk on the unit sphere; lowering with r² γ gives R_ijkl. The Ricci components
are the contractions Ric_bd = g^(ac) R_abcd, with g^(vv) = 0, g^(vr) = 1, g^(rr) = f; for instance
Ric_vv = f R_rvrv + r⁻² γ^(ij) R_ivjv = (f/2) f_rr + (3/(2r))(f f_r − f_v), and
Ric_ij = g^(vr)(R_virj + R_rivj) + r⁻² γ^(kl) R_kilj = −r f_r γ_ij + 2(1 − f) γ_ij.

For 𝒦, group the components by their index pairs. The pair (vr) contributes 4 R_vrvr R^vrvr; raising the
antisymmetric pair (vr) with the (v, r) block of g⁻¹, [[0, 1], [1, f]], multiplies by its determinant −1, twice, so
the contribution is 4 (f_rr/2)² = f_rr². The components R_AiBj, A, B ∈ {v, r}, are r S_AB γ_ij with
S_vv = (f f_r − f_v)/2, S_vr = S_rv = −f_r/2 and S_rr = 0. Counting the four orderings of each pair, they contribute
4 r² r⁻⁴ (γ^(ij)γ_ij) tr((g2⁻¹ S)²), g2⁻¹ the (v, r) block of the inverse. Now

    g2⁻¹ S = [[0, 1], [1, f]] [[S_vv, S_vr], [S_vr, 0]] = [[S_vr, 0], [S_vv + f S_vr, S_vr]]

is triangular, so tr((g2⁻¹ S)²) = 2 S_vr² = f_r²/2, and S_vv, the only entry that contains f_v, drops out. With
γ^(ij)γ_ij = 3 this gives 6 f_r²/r². The components R_ijkl are those of a three-sphere of radius r times the
factor 1 − f, and contribute (1 − f)² r⁻⁴ · 2·3·2 = 12 (1 − f)²/r⁴. There are no other nonzero components. ∎

**Proposition 2.5** (the background).
(a) g0 is five-dimensional Vaidya: Ric(g0) = (3 μ'(v)/(2 r³)) dv ⊗ dv, and its (τ, r) block has determinant −1.
(b) The Kretschmann scalar is 𝒦 = 72 μ(v)²/r⁸, also where μ' ≠ 0; the round spheres {v, r = const} have exactly
one apparent horizon, r = √μ(v).
(c) ℓ := g0⁻¹ dv = −L0 is null and geodesic, with L0(v) = 0, L0(τ) = 1, L0(r) = −1; the phase v is an exact eikonal
of g0 and its level sets are the ingoing null cones.
(d) g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r², g0⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − μ/r², g0⁻¹(dr, dτ) = μ/r², g0⁻¹(d(v + τ), d(v + τ)) =
−3 − μ/r²; the slices {τ = const} are spacelike everywhere, and the lines of constant x are spacelike where r² < μ.
(e) For every function u,

    [L0, □̃] u = (2/r)(□̃ u + (∂_τ + ∂_r) L0 u) − (3/r²) ∂_r u,    (2.6)

the mass dropping out.
(f) H0^ρ := g0^(ab) Γ[g0]^ρ_ab = (−μ/r³, μ x^i/r⁴), smooth on r > 0.

*Proof.* (a) In the form (2.4), f = 1 − μ/r², so f_v = −μ'/r², f_r = 2μ/r³ and f_rr = −6μ/r⁴. Then
f_rr + 3 f_r/r = 0 and 2(1 − f) − r f_r = 0, so by Lemma 2.4 the only nonzero Ricci component is
Ric_vv = −3 f_v/(2r) = 3μ'/(2r³). In the coordinates (τ, r) the block is [[−1 + m, m], [m, 1 + m]], m := μ/r², of
determinant (m − 1)(m + 1) − m² = −1.

(b) By (2.5), 𝒦 = 36 μ²/r⁸ + 6 · 4μ²/r⁸ + 12 μ²/r⁸ = 72 μ²/r⁸, for every μ(v). For the spheres
S_(v,r) := {v, r = const}, the null normals lie in the span of ∂_v and ∂_r of the (v, r) form; ∂_r is null, and
n⁺ := ∂_v + (f/2) ∂_r is null. We time-orient g0 by dτ, which is timelike by (d): a causal vector Y is future directed
when dτ(Y) > 0. In Cartesian terms ∂_r of the (v, r) form is ℓ = −∂_τ + x̂·∂_x = −L0, and ∂_v is ∂_τ; so −∂_r = L0 is
future directed, since L0(τ) = 1, and n⁺ is future directed, since dτ(n⁺) = 1 − f/2 = (1 + μ/r²)/2 > 0. The expansion
of a normal N of S_(v,r) is (3/r) N(r), so the future ingoing normal −∂_r has expansion −3/r and the future outgoing
normal n⁺ has expansion 3f/(2r). Normalised by n(τ) = 1, that is divided by dτ(n⁺) = (1 + μ/r²)/2, the outgoing
expansion is

    θ⁺ = (2r²/(r² + μ)) · 3(1 − μ/r²)/(2r),

whose one zero, r = √μ, is simple; the spheres with r < √μ are trapped and those with r > √μ untrapped.

(c) η⁻¹dv = −∂_τ + x̂·∂_x = −L0, and L0(v) = 0, so ℓ = η⁻¹dv − (μ/r²) L0(v) L0 = −L0. Then
g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = dv(ℓ) = −L0(v) = 0: v is an exact eikonal. A gradient field of a function whose gradient is null
is geodesic: ℓ^a ∇_a ∇_b v = ℓ^a ∇_b ∇_a v = (1/2) ∂_b (g0⁻¹(dv, dv)) = 0. The values L0(τ) = 1 and
L0(r) = −x̂·x̂ = −1 are immediate.

(d) Contract g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − (μ/r²) L0 ⊗ L0 with L0(τ) = 1, L0(r) = −1, L0(v + τ) = 1; for instance
η⁻¹(2dτ + dr, 2dτ + dr) = −4 + 1. The covector dτ is timelike, so the slices are spacelike, and
g0(∂_τ, ∂_τ) = −1 + μ/r² because dv(∂_τ) = 1.

(e) Write g0^(ab) = η^(ab) − m L0^a L0^b, m = μ/r². Then

    [L0, □̃] u = (L0 g0^(ab)) ∂_a∂_b u − 2 g0^(ab) (∂_a L0^c) ∂_b∂_c u − g0^(ab) (∂_a∂_b L0^c) ∂_c u.

First, L0(L0^c) = 0, since L0^i = −x^i/r and x̂^j ∂_j(x^i/r) = 0; and L0(m) = μ'(v) L0(v)/r² + 2μ/r³ = 2μ/r³.
So L0 g0^(ab) = −(2μ/r³) L0^a L0^b, and L0^a L0^b ∂_a∂_b u = L0 L0 u. Second, ∂_j L0^i = −(δ_ij − x̂_i x̂_j)/r and
L0^j ∂_j L0^i = 0, so g0^(ab)(∂_a L0^c) ∂_b∂_c u = −(1/r)(Δu − ∂_r²u), Δ the flat Laplacian of R⁴, using
x̂_i x̂_j ∂_i∂_j u = ∂_r² u. Third, L0^a L0^b ∂_a∂_b L0^c = L0(L0(L0^c)) = 0, and in R⁴, Δ(x^i/r) = −3 x^i/r³, so
g0^(ab) ∂_a∂_b L0^i = 3 x^i/r³. Hence

    [L0, □̃] u = −(2μ/r³) L0 L0 u + (2/r)(Δu − ∂_r² u) − (3/r²) ∂_r u.

On the other side, □̃ u = −∂_τ² u + Δu − m L0 L0 u and (∂_τ + ∂_r)(∂_τ − ∂_r) u = ∂_τ² u − ∂_r² u, so
(2/r)(□̃ u + (∂_τ + ∂_r) L0 u) = (2/r)(Δu − ∂_r² u) − (2μ/r³) L0 L0 u, which is the same.

(f) Since det g0 = −1, g0^(ab) Γ[g0]^ρ_ab = −∂_a g0^(aρ) = ∂_a(m L0^a L0^ρ) = L0^ρ ∂_a(m L0^a), because
m L0^a ∂_a L0^ρ = m L0(L0^ρ) = 0 by the proof of (e). With
∂_i μ(v) = μ' x̂_i, ∂_a(m L0^a) = μ'/r² − μ'/r² − μ ∂_i(x^i/r³) = −μ/r³, because ∂_i(x^i/r³) = 4/r³ − 3/r³ in R⁴.
So H0^ρ = −(μ/r³) L0^ρ. ∎

The identity (2.6) is the five-dimensional form of Touati's commutator lemma ([Tou23a] Lemma 3.1, p. 21,
which bounds [L0, □]f by ∂L0 f, □f and ∂f); here it is an exact identity.

### 2.3 The curvature boundary and the domain

Fix a length l5 > 0 and put x_K := l5² √𝒦. By Proposition 2.5 (b), the surface x_K = 1 is r = r_q(v),

    r_q(v) := (√72 μ(v) l5²)^(1/4),

and r_q ≤ √μ, so that it lies inside or on the horizon, exactly when r_q⁴ = √72 μ l5² ≤ μ², that is when
μ ≥ √72 l5². The seed condition is μ0 ≥ √72 l5². Fix T > 0 and let

    D_T := { v ≤ v_end + T,  r ≥ r_q(v) },    (2.7)

the region from past null infinity to the curvature boundary, up to the time T after the shell has passed. Put
V := v_end + T and q0 := (√72 μ0 l5²)^(1/4), the value of r_q for v ≤ v_start, so q0 ≤ √μ0. Fix 0 < δ0 < q0,
a := q0 − δ0, τ0 with v_start − τ0 > √μ0 + 1 (on the slice {τ = τ0} the shell lies outside the seed's horizon: the
slice is before the shell reaches the hole), and τ_end := max_(v ≤ V) (v − r_q(v)). Let

    Ω := { τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ_end,  |x| ≥ a,  v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ V + 1 },    (2.8)

and Σ_τ := Ω ∩ {τ} = A(τ) := { a ≤ |x| ≤ b(τ) }, b(τ) := V + 1 − τ + (τ_end − τ). Ω is bounded by Σ_τ0, Σ_τ_end,
the inner sphere r = a and the outer surface {v + τ = V + 1 + τ_end}.

**Lemma 2.6** (the domain). (a) Each Σ_τ is spacelike: g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r².
(b) {r = a} is spacelike and r decreases along future causal curves near it: g0⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − μ/r² ≤
1 − μ0/a² < 0 and g0⁻¹(dr, dτ) = μ/r² > 0.
(c) {v + τ = const} is spacelike and v + τ increases along future causal curves: g0⁻¹(d(v + τ), d(v + τ)) =
−2 − (1 + μ/r²) < 0, g0⁻¹(dv, dτ) = −1.
(d) L0 is future null with L0(τ) = 1, L0(v) = 0, L0(r) = −1; the integral curve of L0 through any point of Ω,
followed to the past, stays in Ω and meets Σ_τ0.
(e) There is ε1 > 0 such that for every Lorentzian g with |g − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω, J⁻(p; g) ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} lies in Ω for
every p in Ω, Σ_τ and the two lateral boundaries stay spacelike for g, and L0 is transverse to Σ_τ for every metric,
since L0(τ) = 1.
(f) b(τ) − a ≥ 1 + δ0, b ≤ b(τ0), and D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} lies in Ω.

*Proof.* (a)–(c) are the contractions of g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − (μ/r²) L0 ⊗ L0 with L0(τ) = 1, L0(r) = −1, L0(v) = 0:
g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r², g0⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − μ/r², g0⁻¹(dr, dτ) = 0 − (μ/r²)(−1)(1), and g0⁻¹(dv, ·) = ℓ = −L0.
For (b): at r = a < q0 ≤ √μ0 ≤ √μ, dr and dτ are timelike with g0⁻¹(dr, dτ) > 0, so grad r lies in the cone
opposite to grad τ, which is past directed; hence grad r is future directed and dr(Y) = g0(grad r, Y) < 0 for future
causal Y. (c): dv(Y) = −g0(L0, Y) ≥ 0 and dτ(Y) > 0 for future causal Y. (d): along −L0, τ decreases, r increases
and v is fixed, so r ≥ a and v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ V + 1 are kept. (e): the strict inequalities in (a)–(c) and
L0(τ) = 1 are open conditions in g on the compact set Ω; a past causal curve from p cannot cross {r = a} or
{v + τ = const} outward, by (b) and (c), nor Σ_τ_end. (f): b decreases in τ, and b(τ_end) = V + 1 − τ_end =
min_(v ≤ V) (V − v + r_q(v)) + 1 ≥ q0 + 1; a point of D_T has v ≤ V, r ≥ r_q(v) ≥ q0 > a and τ = v − r ≤
v − r_q(v) ≤ τ_end, hence also v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ v ≤ V < V + 1. ∎

So every part of the boundary of Ω other than Σ_τ0 is spacelike with Ω to its past, and Ω is a domain of dependence
of Σ_τ0, for g0 and for every Lorentzian metric within ε1 of g0.

### 2.4 The gauge

The gauge is the wave-map gauge relative to g0 itself. For a Lorentzian metric g put

    D^ρ(g) := g^(ab) (Γ[g]^ρ_ab − Γ[g0]^ρ_ab),
    Ric^H(g)_mn := Ric(g)_mn − (1/2)(g_mρ ∇̂_n D^ρ + g_nρ ∇̂_m D^ρ)
                 = −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b g_mn + Q_mn(X; g)(∂g, ∂g),    (2.9)

∇̂ the connection of g0. In n + 1 dimensions, with H = D and D̂ = ∇̂, Choquet-Bruhat, Chruściel and Martín-García
give ([CBCM10] (2.7)–(2.9), p. 8) "R_(αβ) = R^(H)_(αβ) + 1/2 (g_(αλ) D̂_β H^λ + g_(βλ) D̂_α H^λ)" and
"R^(H)_(αβ) = −1/2 g^(λμ) D̂_λ D̂_μ g_(αβ) + f̂[g, D̂g]_(αβ)", with f̂ "independent of the second derivatives of g".
In the coordinates of Section 2.2, D̂_a D̂_b g − ∂_a ∂_b g is Γ[g0] and its first derivatives times (g, ∂g),
which gives the second line of (2.9): Q is a quadratic polynomial in ∂g, with a linear and a constant part, whose
coefficients are rational in g and smooth in X through Γ[g0] and its first derivatives, hence smooth on r > 0; the
trace g0^(ab) Γ[g0]^ρ_ab is H0 of Proposition 2.5 (f). Second derivatives of g enter (2.9) only through
−(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b g.

D is a vector field and Ric^H a tensor, built from g and g0 alone, so both are invariant under the isometries of g0,
which include O(4) acting on x and so contain G, and they may be computed in any coordinates. D(g0) = 0, so Ric^H(g0) =
Ric(g0), which is not zero; this is why Q needs a constant part. Ric^H(g) = 0 is a quasilinear wave system, and a
solution with D = 0 is vacuum.

### 2.5 Profiles and scaled norms

A *profile* is a smooth function or tensor f(X, θ) on Ω × S¹, S¹ = R/2πZ; we write [f](X) := f(X, v(X)/λ), and
⟨f⟩ for its θ-mean. The variable θ is the phase. For a function or tensor f on Σ_τ, with ∂^j all spacetime coordinate
derivatives of order j and ‖·‖ the flat L²(Σ_τ) norm, the λ-scaled norm is

    |f|_j := Σ_(i≤j) λ^i ‖∂^i f‖.    (2.10)

Chain rule: ∂_a [f] = λ⁻¹ (∂_a v)[∂_θ f] + [∂_a f], so |[f]|_j ≤ C_j sup_(i≤j) |∂^i_(X,θ) f|_(L^∞): the oscillation
costs nothing in the scaled norms; and ‖∂^i [f]‖_(L^∞) ≤ C λ^(−i).

For pointwise bounds on symmetric 2-tensors of Cartesian components, |·| is the Euclidean operator norm (the largest
absolute eigenvalue); for arrays of higher rank (|∂w|, |∂g|), |·| is the Frobenius norm, and ‖·‖ always integrates the
Euclidean sum of squares. Any other norm on arrays changes only constants.

The eigenvalues of g0 are explicit. In Cartesian components g0 = η + m U Uᵀ, with U the array of dv, |U|² = 2 and
m := μ/r². On the orthogonal complement of the span of (1, 0) and (0, x̂), g0 is the identity, and on that span it is
the matrix [[−1 + m, m], [m, 1 + m]], whose eigenvalues are m ± (m² + 1)^(1/2). So the eigenvalues of g0 are 1 (three
times), m + (m² + 1)^(1/2) and m − (m² + 1)^(1/2) < 0.

**Lemma 2.7** (the margins of the boundaries). Restricted to ker dτ, to ker dr on {r = a}, and to
ker d(v + τ), the form g0 has least eigenvalues, relative to the Euclidean inner product on each subspace,

    1,      min(1, μ/a² − 1),      min(1, (3 + μ/r²)/5).

Hence Lemma 2.6 (e) holds for every ε1 ≤ 3/5 with ε1 < μ0/a² − 1, and every Lorentzian g with |g − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω
is time-oriented by dτ. Where μ = μ0 on {r = a}, the Lorentzian metric g := g0 − (μ0/a² − 1) dτ ⊗ dτ
has |g − g0| = μ0/a² − 1 and makes {r = a} null.

*Proof.* On ker dτ, vectors (0, Y′), g0 = |Y′|² + (μ/r²)(x̂·Y′)², with eigenvalues 1 (three times) and 1 + μ/r². On
ker dr at r = a, vectors (Y⁰, Y′) with x̂·Y′ = 0, g0 = −(Y⁰)² + |Y′|² + (μ/a²)(Y⁰)² = (μ/a² − 1)(Y⁰)² + |Y′|². On
ker d(v + τ) = ker(2dτ + dr), write Y′ = Y′⊥ + s x̂ with x̂·Y′⊥ = 0; then Y⁰ = −s/2 and

    g0 = −s²/4 + |Y′⊥|² + s² + (μ/r²)(s/2)² = |Y′⊥|² + s² (3 + μ/r²)/4,

while the Euclidean norm squared of (Y⁰, Y′) is |Y′⊥|² + (5/4) s²; the ratio on the s-direction is (3 + μ/r²)/5 ≥ 3/5.

Let g be Lorentzian with |g − g0| ≤ ε on Ω, where ε ≤ 3/5 and ε < μ0/a² − 1, and put g₋ := g0 − ε I, I the
Euclidean identity. Then g ≥ g₋ as quadratic forms. The eigenvalues of g₋ are 1 − ε (three times),
m + (m² + 1)^(1/2) − ε > 0 and m − (m² + 1)^(1/2) − ε < 0, so g₋ is Lorentzian, and its nonzero causal vectors form
two convex cones, each the negative of the other. Subtracting ε I lowers each restricted eigenvalue by exactly ε, so
g₋ restricted to ker dτ, to ker dr at r = a and to ker d(v + τ) has least eigenvalues 1 − ε, min(1, μ/a² − 1) − ε and
min(1, (3 + μ/r²)/5) − ε, all positive: the first because ε ≤ 3/5 < 1; the second because moreover μ ≥ μ0, μ being
nondecreasing, and ε < μ0/a² − 1; the last because (3 + μ/r²)/5 > 3/5 ≥ ε. So dτ, dr (at r = a) and d(v + τ)
vanish on no nonzero g₋-causal vector, and each has one sign on each of the two cones. Every g0-causal vector is
g₋-causal, since g₋ ≤ g0; so the cone that contains the future causal vectors of g0 has dτ > 0, dr < 0 at r = a and
d(v + τ) > 0, by Lemma 2.6 (a)–(c). Every g-causal vector is g₋-causal, since g ≥ g₋. Hence dτ vanishes on no
nonzero g-causal vector, so g is time-oriented by dτ, and its future causal vectors, a convex set on which dτ > 0, lie
in that cone. So for g the hypersurfaces Σ_τ, {r = a} and {v + τ = const} are spacelike, g being bounded below by g₋,
which is positive definite on the three kernels; and along future causal curves of g, τ and v + τ increase and, at
r = a, r decreases. These are the properties (a)–(c) that the proof of Lemma 2.6 (e) uses, so (e) holds for g.

For the last claim, g0 − α dτ ⊗ dτ, α > 0, agrees with g0 on the four-dimensional subspace ker dτ, where g0 is
positive definite, and is ≤ g0, so it has exactly one negative eigenvalue and no zero one, and |α dτ ⊗ dτ| = α; on
ker dr at r = a it is ((μ0/a² − 1) − α)(Y⁰)² + |Y′|² where μ = μ0, degenerate at α = μ0/a² − 1. Such points exist: on
Σ_τ0, v = τ0 + a < v_start at r = a. ∎

Lemma 2.6 (e) is not the only requirement on ε1. The energy inequality of Chapter 5 needs ε1 < s0, where

    s0 := inf over Ω of g0's least absolute eigenvalue = (m*² + 1)^(1/2) − m*,   m* := sup_Ω μ/r² ≤ μ_end/a²,

since, by the eigenvalues of g0 found above, its least absolute eigenvalue at a point is (m² + 1)^(1/2) − m, which
decreases in m.

**Lemma 2.8** (Lorentzian metrics near g0). Every symmetric g̃ with |g̃ − g0| ≤ ε1 < s0 on Ω is
Lorentzian with |g̃⁻¹| ≤ (s0 − ε1)⁻¹. For ε1 ≥ s0, at a point of Ω where μ/r² = m*, there are Lorentzian forms g̃
with |g̃ − g0| ≤ ε1 and |g̃⁻¹| arbitrarily large.

*Proof.* Every eigenvalue of g0 has absolute value at least s0, so |g̃ x| ≥ |g0 x| − |(g̃ − g0) x| ≥ (s0 − ε1)|x|,
which bounds |g̃⁻¹|. Moreover x·g̃ x ≥ (s0 − ε1)|x|² on the four-dimensional span of g0's eigenvectors with positive
eigenvalues, while e·g̃ e ≤ −s0 + ε1 < 0 for the unit eigenvector e of its negative eigenvalue; so g̃ has exactly one
negative eigenvalue, since a second non-positive direction would meet that span. This is Weyl's inequality in the case
used. For ε1 ≥ s0, at a point where m = m* (there is one, Ω being compact), let e be the unit eigenvector of g0 with
eigenvalue −s0 and put g̃_t := g0 + t s0 e eᵀ for t ∈ [0, 1): g̃_t is Lorentzian, within s0 ≤ ε1 of g0, and its
eigenvalue −(1 − t) s0 tends to 0, so |g̃_t⁻¹| is unbounded. ∎

Since μ/a² > 1 on {r = a}, s0 < 2^(1/2) − 1 < 3/5. From here on ε1 is one fixed number with

    0 < ε1 < min(s0, μ0/a² − 1),

so that both Lemma 2.7 and Lemma 2.8 apply to it.

At the numerical point of Chapter 56 (μ0 = 1, l5 = 1/10, a = δ0 = q0/2, A = 1, [v_start, v_end] = [1/2, 7/2],
∫ env² = 105/128, T = 1, τ0 = −2) the three thresholds are as follows. They use the envelope only through its support
and ∫ env², so they hold for every env ∈ C_c^∞([1/2, 7/2]) with ∫ env² = 105/128, an envelope that Theorem 3.1
admits (a nonzero smooth function supported in [1/2, 7/2], multiplied by a suitable constant, is one).

(i) μ0/a² − 1 > 12, so every ε1 ≤ 3/5 serves for Lemma 2.6 (e) there: q0⁸ = 72 μ0² l5⁴ = 9/1250, so
μ0/a² = 4/q0² = 4 (1250/9)^(1/4), and 1250/9 > 28561/256 = (13/4)⁴ gives μ0/a² > 13.

(ii) No ε1 ≥ 0.6013096 serves for Lemma 2.6 (e) there. On the outer boundary v = V + 1 + τ_end − τ ≥ V + 1 > v_end,
so μ = μ_end there, and r ≤ b(τ0), with equality at its corner with Σ_τ0; so the least value of (3 + μ/r²)/5 on it is
ε_out := (3 + μ_end/b(τ0)²)/5, attained at the corner. Here μ_end = 1 + (2/9)(105/128) = 227/192 and V = 9/2. With
q_end := (√72 μ_end l5²)^(1/4), the value of r_q at v = V, one has τ_end ≥ V − q_end, so b(τ0) = V + 1 + τ_end − 2τ0 ≥
14 − q_end. Since q_end⁸ = 72 μ_end² l5⁴ = 51529/5120000 = 0.0100642… is less than 0.5628⁸ = 0.0100654…,
q_end < 0.5628, b(τ0) > 13.4372 and ε_out < (3 + (227/192)/13.4372²)/5 = 0.60130959… < 0.6013096. Now let
ν := (1, −2x̂)/√5, a Euclidean unit vector field, ν ⊗ ν the tensor of Cartesian components ν_a ν_b, and
g := g0 − ε_out ν ⊗ ν, so that |g − g0| = ε_out. The vector ν lies in ker d(v + τ), being the case s = −2/√5 of the
proof of Lemma 2.7, so g0(ν, ν) = (3 + m)/5, and g0(ν, (0, Y′⊥)) = 0 when x̂·Y′⊥ = 0. In the Euclidean orthonormal
basis of ker d(v + τ) formed by ν and three vectors (0, Y′⊥), g0 is diag((3 + m)/5, 1, 1, 1) and g is
diag((3 + m)/5 − ε_out, 1, 1, 1), which at the corner is diag(0, 1, 1, 1): the outer boundary is null for g there. And
g is Lorentzian on Ω. In the plane of the τ- and x̂-directions the Cartesian block of g0 is [[−1 + m, m], [m, 1 + m]],
with inverse [[−1 − m, m], [m, 1 − m]], so νᵀ g0⁻¹ ν = (3 − 9m)/5, and the rank-one determinant formula with
det g0 = −1 gives det g = det g0 (1 − ε_out νᵀ g0⁻¹ ν) = −(1 − ε_out (3 − 9m)/5) < 0, since ε_out < 1 and m > 0.
Since g is the identity on the three directions (0, Y′⊥), it has at least three positive eigenvalues, and, its
determinant being negative, exactly one negative one. So (e) fails for every ε1 ≥ ε_out, in particular for every
ε1 ≥ 0.6013096.

(iii) s0 lies between 0.030768559 and 0.030768560, so there ε1 < 0.0308. On the inner sphere of Σ_τ_end,
v = τ_end + a ≥ V − q_end + a > v_end, as V − v_end = 1 > q_end, so μ = μ_end there and m* = μ_end/a² =
(227/48)(1250/9)^(1/4). Since s0 = (m*² + 1)^(1/2) − m* is the positive root of s² + 2m* s = 1, a number x > 0 lies
below s0 exactly when x² + 2m* x < 1, that is when (24(1 − x²)/(227 x))⁴ > 1250/9 = 138.88888…; at x = 0.030768559 the
left side is 138.88889948…, larger, and at x = 0.030768560 it is 138.88888139…, smaller.

### 2.6 The waves and their average

The waves are two polarizations a quarter turn apart, with amplitude A > 0, envelope env ∈ C_c^∞([v_start, v_end]),
angular profile

    h(ζ) := √(2/(1 + ζ²)),      ζ := cos 2ϑ,      c² = (1 + ζ)/2,      s² = (1 − ζ)/2,

on the orbit space, and phase v/λ. As profiles,

    F := λ A env(v) h(ζ) sin θ,      G := λ A env(v) h(ζ) cos θ,

and at past null infinity their free data are [F] and [G]. The leading wave is the profile

    λ W_TT := 2 r^(1/2) (c² p1 dφ1² + s² p2 dφ2² − (p1 + p2) dϑ²),
    p1 := (2c² G − s² F)/3,      p2 := (2s² F − c² G)/3.    (2.11)

**Lemma 2.9** (the leading wave). (a) In Cartesian components,

    λ W_TT = 2 r^(−3/2) ( G (x1 dx2 − x2 dx1)²/r² + F (x3 dx4 − x4 dx3)²/r²
                          − ((c² G + s² F)/3) (|dx|² − (x̂·dx)²) ),

with c² = (x1² + x2²)/r², s² = (x3² + x4²)/r², ζ = c² − s². In particular W_TT is smooth on {r > 0} × S¹, both axes
included, and |W_TT| ≤ C A env r^(−3/2).
(b) W_TT has no dτ component and W_TT(L0, ·) = 0, so W_TT(ℓ, ·) = 0; it has no dv or dr component in the (v, r)
coordinates, and tr_(g0) W_TT = 0: the wave is transverse to ℓ and traceless on the spheres.
(c) Its g0-norm is |W_TT|²_(g0) = 8 r⁻³ λ⁻² (p1² + p1 p2 + p2²).

*Proof.* (a) Since γ = dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2²,

    c² p1 dφ1² + s² p2 dφ2² − (p1 + p2) dϑ² = c²(2p1 + p2) dφ1² + s²(p1 + 2p2) dφ2² − (p1 + p2) γ,

and 2p1 + p2 = c² G, p1 + 2p2 = s² F, p1 + p2 = (c² G + s² F)/3. With ρ1² := x1² + x2² = r² c², ρ1² dφ1 =
x1 dx2 − x2 dx1, so r² c⁴ dφ1² = c² ρ1² dφ1² = (x1 dx2 − x2 dx1)²/r², and likewise r² s⁴ dφ2² = (x3 dx4 − x4 dx3)²/r²;
and r² γ = |dx|² − (x̂·dx)². This gives the formula. Each term is smooth on r > 0: c², s² and ζ are, h is smooth on
[−1, 1], env(v) is smooth with v = τ + r, and the quadratic forms in dx have coefficients bounded by r² (for instance
the Euclidean norm of (x1 dx2 − x2 dx1)² is ρ1² ≤ r²). (b) No term contains dτ. Contracting with x̂ gives
(x1 x2 − x2 x1)/r = 0 in the first two forms and x̂·dx − x̂·dx = 0 in the third, so W_TT(L0, ·) = 0. Since
g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − (μ/r²) L0 ⊗ L0 and W_TT(L0, L0) = 0, the g0-trace is the Euclidean trace of the spatial array, which is
2 r^(−3/2) λ⁻¹ (G c² + F s² − (c² G + s² F)) = 0, the traces of the three forms being ρ1²/r² = c², s² and 4 − 1 = 3.
(c) In the frame dϑ, c dφ1, s dφ2, orthonormal for γ, the bracket of (2.11) is diagonal with entries −(p1 + p2),
p1, p2; on the spheres of radius r, with g0 = r² γ there and W_TT transverse, the norm squared is
4 r λ⁻² r⁻⁴ (p1² + p2² + (p1 + p2)²) = 8 r⁻³ λ⁻² (p1² + p1 p2 + p2²). ∎

The next lemma computes the mean of the leading equation of the two-scale expansion of Chapter 4. For a
profile k, |k|²_(g0) := g0^(ac) g0^(bd) k_ab k_cd.

**Lemma 2.10** (the averaged leading equation). Let g1, …, g_N be profiles, bounded with all their
derivatives on Ω × S¹, and g := g0 + λ[g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j]. Suppose (g1 − ⟨g1⟩)(ℓ, ·) = 0. Then, for λ small,
Ric^H(g) = [R⁽⁰⁾] + λ[R⁽¹⁾] + …, with no term of order λ⁻¹, and the θ-mean of the λ⁰ coefficient is

    ⟨R⁽⁰⁾⟩ = ( 3μ'/(2r³) − (1/4) ⟨|∂_θ g1|²_(g0)⟩ ) dv ⊗ dv.    (2.12)

*Proof.* Write k := ∂_θ g1, so k(ℓ, ·) = ∂_θ(g1(ℓ, ·)) = ∂_θ(⟨g1⟩(ℓ, ·)) = 0, and v_a := ∂_a v, so ℓ^a = g0^(ab) v_b
and v_a ℓ^a = 0. Let C := Γ[g] − Γ[g0], a tensor, so that

    Ric(g)_ab = Ric(g0)_ab + ∇̂_ρ C^ρ_ab − ∇̂_b C^ρ_aρ + C^ρ_ρσ C^σ_ab − C^ρ_bσ C^σ_aρ,
    C^ρ_ab = (1/2) g^(ρσ) (∇̂_a δg_bσ + ∇̂_b δg_aσ − ∇̂_σ δg_ab),   δg := g − g0.

By the chain rule, ∇̂_a [u] = λ⁻¹ v_a [∂_θ u] + [∇̂_a u], and g⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ + O(λ), so C = [C⁽⁰⁾] + λ[C⁽¹⁾] + … with

    C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab = (1/2)(v_a k_b^ρ + v_b k_a^ρ − ℓ^ρ k_ab),

indices raised by g0. Every term of C⁽⁰⁾ is linear in k, and ⟨k⟩ = 0, so ⟨C⁽⁰⁾⟩ = 0. Using k(ℓ, ·) = 0 and
v·ℓ = 0: v_ρ C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab = 0, C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ρσ = (1/2) v_σ tr k, and so C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ρσ C⁽⁰⁾σ_ab = (1/2) tr k · v_σ C⁽⁰⁾σ_ab = 0.
Expanding C⁽⁰⁾ρ_bσ C⁽⁰⁾σ_aρ into nine products, every product but v_b v_a k_σ^ρ k_ρ^σ contains k(ℓ, ·) or v·ℓ, so

    C⁽⁰⁾ρ_bσ C⁽⁰⁾σ_aρ = (1/4) v_a v_b |k|²_(g0).

The λ⁰ coefficient of ∇̂_ρ C^ρ_ab − ∇̂_b C^ρ_aρ is v_ρ ∂_θ C⁽¹⁾ρ_ab − v_b ∂_θ C⁽¹⁾ρ_aρ + ∇̂_ρ C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab −
∇̂_b C⁽⁰⁾ρ_aρ; the first two terms are θ-derivatives of profiles and the last two are linear in k with coefficients
independent of θ, so all four have θ-mean zero. The λ⁰ coefficient of C C is C⁽⁰⁾C⁽⁰⁾. Hence the θ-mean of the λ⁰
coefficient of Ric(g) is Ric(g0) − (1/4)⟨|k|²⟩ dv ⊗ dv, and its λ⁻¹ coefficient is v_ρ ∂_θ C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab −
v_b ∂_θ C⁽⁰⁾ρ_aρ = −(1/2) v_a v_b ∂_θ tr k.

For the gauge term, D = g^(ab) C^ρ_ab = [D⁽⁰⁾] + λ[D⁽¹⁾] + … with D⁽⁰⁾ρ = g0^(ab) C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab = k(ℓ)^ρ −
(1/2) ℓ^ρ tr k = −(1/2) ℓ^ρ tr k. The λ⁻¹ coefficient of −(1/2)(g_mρ ∇̂_n D^ρ + g_nρ ∇̂_m D^ρ) is
−(1/2)(v_m v_n + v_n v_m)(−1/2) ∂_θ tr k = (1/2) v_m v_n ∂_θ tr k, which cancels that of Ric(g). Its λ⁰ coefficient
is −(1/2) of the symmetrisation of

    g0_mρ (v_n ∂_θ D⁽¹⁾ρ + ∇̂_n D⁽⁰⁾ρ) + g1_mρ v_n ∂_θ D⁽⁰⁾ρ.

The first two terms have θ-mean zero as before. In the third, g1_mρ ℓ^ρ = g1(m, ℓ) = ⟨g1⟩(m, ℓ) does not depend on θ,
so ⟨g1_mρ ∂_θ D⁽⁰⁾ρ⟩ = −(1/2) ⟨g1⟩(m, ℓ) ⟨∂_θ² tr g1⟩ = 0. The gauge term has θ-mean zero at order λ⁰. With
Ric(g0) = (3μ'/(2r³)) dv ⊗ dv from Proposition 2.5 (a), this is (2.12). ∎

**Proposition 2.11** (the limit). Let g1 be a profile whose oscillating part g1 − ⟨g1⟩ is W_TT, evaluated at
a phase θ + κ(X), plus χ dv ⊗ dv, with κ a function of X and χ a profile. Then ⟨∂_θ g1⟩ = 0,

    ⟨|∂_θ g1|²_(g0)⟩ = (4/3) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴) r⁻³,      h² (c⁴ + s⁴) = 1,    (2.13)

and the θ-mean of the leading equation vanishes exactly when μ' = (2/9) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴), that is, when

    dμ/dv = (2/9) A² env².    (2.14)

The averaged stress of the waves is round, and it is a multiple of dv ⊗ dv: the defect is null dust along dv.

*Proof.* (dv ⊗ dv)(ℓ, ·) = dv(ℓ) dv = 0 and its g0-trace is g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0, so by Lemma 2.9 (b) the
oscillating part is transverse to ℓ and Lemma 2.10 applies. Moreover ⟨W_TT, dv ⊗ dv⟩_(g0) = W_TT(ℓ, ℓ) = 0
and |dv ⊗ dv|²_(g0) = g0⁻¹(dv, dv)² = 0, so χ does not contribute to |∂_θ g1|², and a phase shift does not change a
θ-mean. Since ∂_θ F = G and ∂_θ G = −F, Lemma 2.9 (c) gives |∂_θ W_TT|² = 8 r⁻³ (q1² + q1 q2 + q2²) with

    q1 := λ⁻¹ ∂_θ p1 = −(2c² F̂ + s² Ĝ)/3,      q2 := λ⁻¹ ∂_θ p2 = (c² F̂ + 2s² Ĝ)/3,

F̂ := â sin θ, Ĝ := â cos θ, â := A env h. With ⟨F̂²⟩ = ⟨Ĝ²⟩ = â²/2 and ⟨F̂ Ĝ⟩ = 0,

    ⟨q1²⟩ = (4c⁴ + s⁴) â²/18,   ⟨q2²⟩ = (c⁴ + 4s⁴) â²/18,   ⟨q1 q2⟩ = −(2c⁴ + 2s⁴) â²/18,

so ⟨q1² + q1 q2 + q2²⟩ = (c⁴ + s⁴) â²/6 and ⟨|∂_θ W_TT|²⟩ = (4/3) â² (c⁴ + s⁴) r⁻³. Next,
c⁴ + s⁴ = ((1 + ζ)² + (1 − ζ)²)/4 = (1 + ζ²)/2, so h² (c⁴ + s⁴) = 1. By (2.12) the mean of the leading
equation is (3μ'/(2r³) − (1/3) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴) r⁻³) dv ⊗ dv, which vanishes exactly when
μ' = (2/9) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴), that is (2.14). ∎

This is Isaacson's effective stress as a five-dimensional null dust along dv ([Isa68a], [Isa68b]). The quadratic form
q1² + q1 q2 + q2² of the proof is positive definite: 4(q1² + q1 q2 + q2²) = (2q1 + q2)² + 3q2².

The same structure holds exactly, with no expansion in λ, in the Bondi-type variables of Theorem 3.8. Let
β, W, U, P1, P2 be smooth functions of (v, r, ϑ), put y = (y¹, y², y³) := (ϑ, φ1, φ2), U^k := (U, 0, 0),

    ξ^k := dy^k − U^k dv,      γ_P := diag(e^(−2(P1+P2)), c² e^(2P1), s² e^(2P2)),
    g := −e^(2β) W dv² + 2 e^(2β) dv dr + r² (γ_P)_kl ξ^k ξ^l,    (2.15)

which is the form (3.3). We regard each component of Ric(g) in the coordinates (v, r, y) as a function of
the derivatives of β, W, U, P1, P2 at a point, and call ∂_vP1 and ∂_vP2 the rates; the other derivatives, among them
∂_v²P_i and ∂_r∂_vP_i, are separate variables.

**Lemma 2.12** (the rates in Bondi-type variables). With S := diag(−∂_vP1 − ∂_vP2, ∂_vP1, ∂_vP2),

    Ric(g)_ab = R̊_ab + L_ab − δ^v_a δ^v_b tr(S²),      tr(S²) = 2((∂_vP1)² + ∂_vP1 ∂_vP2 + (∂_vP2)²),    (2.16)

where R̊_ab does not involve the rates and L_ab is linear in them. So the part of R_vv quadratic in the rates is
−2((∂_vP1)² + ∂_vP1 ∂_vP2 + (∂_vP2)²), and no other component of the Ricci tensor contains a product of two rates.

*Proof.* Step 1 (the inverse metric). In the coframe (dv, dr, ξ^k), with dual frame (e_v, ∂_r, ∂_k), e_v := ∂_v +
U^k ∂_k, the metric is block diagonal: [[−e^(2β) W, e^(2β)], [e^(2β), 0]] on (dv, dr) and r² γ_P on (ξ^k). Inverting
each block,

    g⁻¹ = e^(−2β)(e_v ⊗ ∂_r + ∂_r ⊗ e_v) + e^(−2β) W ∂_r ⊗ ∂_r + r⁻² γ_P^(kl) ∂_k ⊗ ∂_l.

Since dv(e_v) = 1, ξ^k(e_v) = U^k − U^k = 0, ξ^k(∂_r) = 0 and ξ^k(∂_l) = δ^k_l, this gives

    g^(av) = e^(−2β) δ^a_r,      g^(ad) ξ^k_d = r⁻² γ_P^(kl) δ^a_l,    (2.17)

where ξ^k_d are the components of ξ^k: ξ^k_v = −U^k, ξ^k_r = 0, ξ^k_l = δ^k_l.

Step 2 (where the rates enter). The functions P_i enter g only through γ_P, and (γ_P)_kl ξ^k_a ξ^l_b is the only part of
g_ab that contains them. Since γ_P is diagonal, ∂_v γ_P = 2 γ_P S, and det γ_P = c² s² does not depend on v, so tr S = 0.
Hence the rates enter the first derivatives of g only through ∂_v g_ab, whose part containing them is

    2 r² 𝒮_ab,      𝒮_ab := (γ_P S)_kl ξ^k_a ξ^l_b,    (2.18)

and the derivatives ∂_r g, ∂_y g do not contain them. A second derivative of g contains a rate only through ∂_v∂_v γ_P =
2(∂_v γ_P) S + 2γ_P ∂_v S = 4γ_P S² + 2γ_P ∂_v S and ∂_c∂_v γ_P = 2(∂_c γ_P) S + 2γ_P ∂_c S for c ≠ v, where ∂_v S and
∂_c S consist of second derivatives of P_i and contain no rate.

Step 3 (the Christoffel symbols). Since Γ^a_bc = (1/2) g^(ad)(∂_b g_dc + ∂_c g_db − ∂_d g_bc) is linear in the first
derivatives of g, with coefficients g⁻¹ free of rates, Γ = Γ̊ + Σ with Γ̊ free of rates and Σ the part linear in them:

    Σ^a_bc = r² ( g^(ad)(δ^v_b 𝒮_dc + δ^v_c 𝒮_db) − g^(av) 𝒮_bc ).

By (2.17), g^(ad) 𝒮_dc = δ^a_l r⁻² γ_P^(lk)(γ_P S)_km ξ^m_c = r⁻² δ^a_l S^l_m ξ^m_c, so

    Σ^v_bc = 0,      Σ^r_bc = −e^(−2β) r² 𝒮_bc,      Σ^l_bc = S^l_m (δ^v_b ξ^m_c + δ^v_c ξ^m_b).    (2.19)

Since ξ^m_r = 0, every Σ with a lower index r vanishes: Σ^d_ar = Σ^d_ra = 0 for all a, d. The traces vanish:
Σ^c_ac = Σ^r_ar + Σ^l_al = 0 + δ^v_a S^l_l = δ^v_a tr S = 0.

Step 4 (the Ricci tensor). We use R_ab = ∂_cΓ^c_ab − ∂_bΓ^c_ac + Γ^c_cdΓ^d_ab − Γ^c_bdΓ^d_ac. A product of two
rates can arise in three ways only.
(i) From ∂_cΓ̊: Γ̊ is a function of rate-free quantities, so a single derivative of it contains each rate at most
linearly, by Step 2.
(ii) From ∂_cΣ^c_ab − ∂_bΣ^c_ac: by Step 3, Σ^v_ab = 0 and Σ^c_ac = 0 for every value of the fields, so these terms
are ∂_rΣ^r_ab + ∂_lΣ^l_ab, in which no derivative is taken in v; by Step 2 they are linear in the rates.
(iii) From the products: Γ̊Γ̊ is free of rates and Γ̊Σ is linear in them, so the quadratic part is
Σ^c_cdΣ^d_ab − Σ^c_bdΣ^d_ac. The first term vanishes because Σ^c_cd = 0.
In the second, Σ^v = 0 and Σ^d_ar = 0 leave only c = l and d = m on S³:

    Σ^c_bdΣ^d_ac = Σ^l_bm Σ^m_al = (δ^v_b S^l_m)(δ^v_a S^m_l) = δ^v_a δ^v_b tr(S²),

by (2.19) with ξ^k_m = δ^k_m. Finally tr(S²) = (∂_vP1 + ∂_vP2)² + (∂_vP1)² + (∂_vP2)² =
2((∂_vP1)² + ∂_vP1 ∂_vP2 + (∂_vP2)²). ∎

At leading order in λ this is (2.12): the linearised angular perturbation
r²(−2(P1 + P2) dϑ² + 2c² P1 dφ1² + 2s² P2 dφ2²) has v-derivative of g0-norm squared
4((∂_vP1 + ∂_vP2)² + (∂_vP1)² + (∂_vP2)²) = 4 tr(S²), and −1/4 of it is −tr(S²).

## 3. The theorems

This chapter states the four theorems and the three propositions that complete the first, shows how the first follows
from the approximant, the data and the uniform existence theorem, and lists the further results with the chapters
that prove them. The notation is that of Chapter 2. The order of the approximant is K, and the
Kretschmann scalar is 𝒦.

### 3.1 The construction on the domain

**Theorem 3.1** (the five-dimensional counterpart). Let l5 > 0, μ0 ≥ √72 l5², A > 0 and
env ∈ C_c^∞([v_start, v_end]), and let g0 be the Vaidya metric (2.3) with
μ(v) = μ0 + (2/9) A² ∫_(−∞)^v env². Fix T > 0, τ0 with v_start − τ0 > √μ0 + 1, and K ≥ 6. There are λ0 > 0 and
C, depending on (l5, μ0, A, env, T, τ0, K) and the inner radius a of Ω, and not on λ, such that for every
λ ∈ (0, λ0] there is a smooth Lorentzian metric g_λ on Ω ⊃ D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} with:

1. *Vacuum and symmetry.* Ric(g_λ) = 0 on Ω, and g_λ is invariant under the T² action and both reflections.
2. *Data.* On Σ_τ0, the Cauchy data of g_λ satisfy the vacuum constraints exactly, equal the data of the seed
   (five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini of mass μ0) on r < v_start − τ0, and differ from those of an
   approximate solution g_app (Theorem 4.11) by O(λ^K) in the λ-scaled data norm: with w := g_λ − g_app
   and k = 6,

       Data(w) := ‖w‖ + Σ_(1≤j≤k+1) λ^(j−1) ‖∂_x^j w‖ + Σ_(j≤k) λ^j ‖∂_x^j ∂_τ w‖ ≤ C λ^K   on Σ_τ0;

   the leading oscillation of g_app is the waves of Section 2.6.
3. *The remainder.* g_λ = g_app + w with |w| ≤ C λ^(K−3) and |∂w| ≤ C λ^(K−4) on Ω, where
   g_app = g0 + λ [g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j], N = K + 3, with smooth profiles g_j(X, θ), 2π-periodic in θ, evaluated
   at θ = v/λ.
4. *Convergence.* |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ and |∂g_λ| ≤ C on Ω; ∂g_λ − ∂g0 = dv ⊗ [∂_θ g1] + O(λ), so ∂g_λ → ∂g0 weakly
   in L²(Ω), and not strongly wherever env ≠ 0: the phase mean of ∂_θ g1 is 0 and that of its g0-norm squared is
   (4/3) A² env² r⁻³. The limit g0 satisfies Ric(g0) = (3 μ'/(2 r³)) dv ⊗ dv with (2.14): it is not vacuum
   but Einstein–null dust with one family.
5. *Gauge and uniqueness.* D(g_λ) = 0 on Ω, and g_λ is the only C² solution g of Ric^H(g) = 0 on Ω with the data
   of g_λ on Σ_τ0 and |g − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω, ε1 the number fixed in Section 2.5.
6. *The spheres' horizon.* If μ0 > √72 l5² and λ ≤ λ_H (Proposition 3.4), the outgoing expansion of the spheres
   {v, r = const} has at most one zero on each column (v and the angles fixed), exactly one within C λ of √μ(v) on the
   columns that reach across it, the spheres with r ≤ √μ(v) − C λ being trapped and those with r ≥ √μ(v) + C λ
   untrapped: no inner zero, and the zero converges to √μ at O(λ) (Proposition 3.4).
7. *Mean mass.* For every sphere S_(v,r) in D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}, its Hawking mass satisfies |M[S](g_λ) − μ(v)| ≤ C λ²
   before and after the shell (v ≤ v_start or v ≥ v_end), and ≤ C λ within it (Proposition 3.5).

The construction fixes some constants explicitly: the order of the energy is k = 6, the approximant used has N = K + 3
stages, λ ≤ λ_Ω := min(1, δ0)/10 with δ0 = q0 − a as in Section 2.3 (a condition the construction imposes, not a
bound below which the theorem holds: that is λ0), and the data are solved in H^s(S³) with s > 3/2 + 4 (Chapter 7). λ0
and C are not evaluated; Proposition 56.8 bounds λ0 above at a numerical point. Every constant of the approximant's own
estimates is independent of λ, because its profiles are (Theorem 4.11). The waves are high-frequency on all of
D_T once λ < l5/10: on D_T, x_K = l5² √𝒦 ≤ 1, so the curvature length 𝒦^(−1/4) is at least l5, and λ 𝒦^(1/4) ≤
λ/l5 < 1/10.

**Remark 3.2** (the regularity of the envelope). The hypothesis env ∈ C_c^∞ is used as it
stands: Definition 4.3 asks every profile to be bounded with all its derivatives, and g_λ and the profiles are
smooth. For a fixed K the estimates use only finitely many derivatives of env; their number is not determined here. An
envelope of finite smoothness is not covered. The profile sin⁴(π(v − 1/2)/3) on [1/2, 7/2], extended by zero, which
the numerical observations of Remark 10.13 and Remark 44.5 use, is C³ and not C⁴, its fourth
derivative jumping by 8π⁴/27 at both ends; the proof applies to it for no K ≥ 6, since already Step 4 of the
proof of Theorem 6.1 takes six derivatives of the coefficient C of (6.2), which
contains second derivatives of g1, and the oscillating part of g1 contains the wave W_TT, which is proportional to env,
and a term χ dv ⊗ dv proportional to env² (Theorem 4.11, (2.11), (4.9)), so that eight
derivatives of env enter its bounds. The numerical point at which Proposition 56.8 bounds λ0 has
[v_start, v_end] = [1/2, 7/2] and the smooth envelope

    env_C(v) := c β((2v − 4)/3),     β(y) := cos¹²(πy/2) exp(−y²/(1 − y²)) for |y| < 1,  β(y) := 0 for |y| ≥ 1,

with c > 0 fixed by ∫ env_C² = 105/128, which is also ∫ sin⁸(π(v − 1/2)/3) dv over [1/2, 7/2]; then
1.3240867 < c < 1.3240879 (Lemma 56.3 (b)).

**Proposition 3.3** (the boundary). On x_K = 1, with Φ := r − r_q(v),

    g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) = 1 − √(μ/(√72 l5²)) − r_q μ'/(2 μ),    (3.1)

so, μ being at least μ0 ≥ √72 l5² throughout, the boundary is spacelike for g0 wherever μ > √72 l5² or μ' > 0, and
every future causal curve that meets it leaves D_T there and does not return. If μ0 > √72 l5² the margin is uniform,
g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) ≤ −δ_b with δ_b := √(μ0/(√72 l5²)) − 1 > 0, and for g_λ the margin is −δ_b + C λ ≤ −δ_b/2 once
C λ ≤ δ_b/2. If μ0 = √72 l5² exactly, the boundary is the seed's horizon, and null for g_λ, on {v ≤ inf supp env};
after the shell starts it is spacelike for g_λ outside a layer whose width tends to 0 with λ (Chapter 54),
and inside that layer, for λ small, every column has points where it is timelike for g_λ, so the no-return property
stated above for μ0 > √72 l5² fails at equality (Theorem 54.26, Corollary 54.27, Theorem 55.22).

The proof is in Chapter 8.

**Proposition 3.4** (one zero per column of the spheres' outgoing expansion). Let μ0 ≥ √72 l5²,
K ≥ 6, and let θ⁺_λ(v, r, x̂) be the outgoing null expansion, for g_λ, of the sphere
S_(v,r) := {τ = v − r, |x| = r} at its point x̂ ∈ S³. There are λ_H ∈ (0, λ0] and C, δ1, δ2 > 0 such that for
λ ≤ λ_H: on every column (v and x̂ fixed, r varying, within D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}) θ⁺_λ has at most one zero, positive
above it and negative below; if μ0 > √72 l5², on the columns with √μ(v) ≤ v − τ0 − δ1 it has exactly one,
R_λ(v, x̂), with |R_λ − √μ(v)| ≤ C λ, and the spheres with r ≤ √μ(v) − C λ are trapped, those with
r ≥ √μ(v) + C λ untrapped (C twice the constant that places the zero, so that the spheres at distance C λ are
strictly trapped); if μ0 = √72 l5², the same holds on the columns with μ(v) ≥ μ0 + δ2 and √μ(v) ≤ v − τ0 − δ1.

The proof is in Chapter 8. The statement concerns the round family {v, r = const}: the per-column zero set
is not itself a marginally trapped surface.

For a 3-sphere S with future null normals n⁺, n⁻ and expansions θ⁺, θ⁻, let

    M[S](g) := R² (1 + (R²/9) ⟨Θ⟩),   R := (Area(S)/(2π²))^(1/3),   Θ := 2 θ⁺ θ⁻ / (−g(n⁺, n⁻)),    (3.2)

with ⟨·⟩ the mean over S: the five-dimensional Hawking mass. Θ does not depend on the normalisation of n⁺ and n⁻.
For g0 and S = S_(v,r), Area = 2π² r³, so R = r; with n⁺ = ∂_v + (f/2) ∂_r and n⁻ = −∂_r in the form
(2.4), θ⁺ = 3f/(2r), θ⁻ = −3/r and g0(n⁺, n⁻) = −1 (Proposition 2.5 (b)), so Θ = −9f/r² and
M[S_(v,r)](g0) = r² (1 − f) = μ(v).

**Proposition 3.5** (the mean mass). For K ≥ 6 and λ ≤ λ0, |M[S_(v,r)](g_λ) − μ(v)| ≤ C λ²
wherever v ≤ v_start or v ≥ v_end, and ≤ C λ for v_start < v < v_end.

The proof is in Chapter 8; it rests on a quarter-turn symmetry of the two polarizations, under which the first
mean correction of the approximant is odd while the mass is invariant, so that the mass does not see it. The mean of the
mass aspect at past null infinity is a different quantity from the Hawking mass of the spheres of the domain;
Theorem 3.8 treats it.

### 3.2 How the first theorem follows

Theorem 3.1 is the conjunction of three theorems: the approximant to every order (Theorem 4.11, proved in
Chapter 4), exact data within O(λ^K) of it (Theorem 7.1, proved in Chapter 7), and existence on Ω
with remainder estimates uniform in λ (Theorem 6.1, proved in Chapter 6), together with
Proposition 3.4 and Proposition 3.5.

**Lemma 3.6** (the gauge propagates). Let g be a C³ Lorentzian metric on Ω, within ε1 of g0,
with Ric^H(g) = 0, and suppose D(g) = 0 on Σ_τ0 and the Cauchy data of g on Σ_τ0 satisfy the vacuum constraints.
Then D(g) = 0 on Ω, and g is vacuum.

*Proof.* Write C := Γ[g] − Γ[g0], ∇ for the connection of g, and D_m := g_mρ D^ρ. Since ∇̂_n D^ρ = ∇_n D^ρ −
C^ρ_nσ D^σ, the equation Ric^H(g) = 0 reads

    Ric(g)_mn = (1/2)(∇_m D_n + ∇_n D_m) + L_mn,      L_mn := −(1/2)(g_mρ C^ρ_nσ + g_nρ C^ρ_mσ) D^σ,

with L linear in D and free of its derivatives. The contracted Bianchi identity ∇^m(Ric_mn − (1/2) g_mn R) = 0, with
R = ∇_m D^m + tr L, gives

    (1/2) □_g D_n + (1/2)(∇^m ∇_n D_m − ∇_n ∇^m D_m) + ∇^m (L_mn − (1/2) g_mn tr L) = 0,

and ∇^m ∇_n D_m − ∇_n ∇^m D_m = Ric(g)_nσ D^σ. Substituting the expression for Ric(g) once more, D solves a linear
homogeneous system −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b D = f, with f linear in (D, ∂D) and coefficients bounded on Ω.

On Σ_τ0, D = 0, so its derivatives tangent to Σ_τ0 vanish there, and ∇̂_b D^ρ = n_b ∂_τ D^ρ with n := dτ. Hence
Ric(g)_ab = (1/2)(n_a Y_b + n_b Y_a) there, Y_a := g_aρ ∂_τ D^ρ. With N := g⁻¹ n, the scalar curvature is
R = Y(N), and the Einstein tensor contracted with N is

    G(N, ·) = (1/2)(n(N) Y + Y(N) n) − (1/2) Y(N) n = (1/2) g⁻¹(n, n) Y.

The vacuum constraints are G(N, ·) = 0 on Σ_τ0, and g⁻¹(n, n) < 0 by Lemma 2.6 (e), so Y = 0: D and ∂_τ D vanish
on Σ_τ0. The energy inequality of Chapter 5, applied to this system on Ω, with Gronwall's lemma, gives D = 0
on Ω; then Ric(g) = 0. ∎

*Proof of Theorem 3.1.* Let g_app be the approximant of Theorem 4.11 with N = K + 3 stages and the stage data of
Lemma 7.4, which make its Cauchy data satisfy the constraints and D = 0 to order N − 2, and let the data on
Σ_τ0 be those of Theorem 7.1, which satisfy the constraints exactly, carry D = 0, equal the seed's data on
r < v_start − τ0 and are within C λ^K of g_app's in the norm of item 2. Theorem 6.1 gives, for λ ≤ λ0,
the solution g_λ of Ric^H(g) = 0 on Ω with these data, unique among C² solutions with these data and |g − g0| ≤ ε1 on
Ω, together with the bounds of items 3 and 4 on w = g_λ − g_app and |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ, |∂g_λ| ≤ C. Taking λ0 so small
that C λ0 ≤ ε1, g_λ is within ε1 of g0, hence Lorentzian by Lemma 2.8 (ε1 < s0), and it is smooth by
Theorem 6.1, the data of Theorem 7.1 being smooth; so Lemma 3.6 gives D(g_λ) = 0 and
Ric(g_λ) = 0. λ0 and C depend only on (l5, μ0, A, env, T, τ0, K) and a, through Ω, the profiles, the smallness
threshold of Theorem 7.1, C_R and C_D, the constants of (E3) (Definition 4.3) and of (E4)
(Theorem 6.1), and, for items 6 and 7, the constants of Proposition 3.4 and Proposition 3.5. By
Lemma 2.6 (f), D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} lies in Ω.

Symmetry. Let ι be an element of G = O(2) × O(2), acting on x by an orthogonal matrix and fixing τ. It preserves r,
v, η and dv, hence g0, Ω and Σ_τ0. Ric^H and D are built from g and g0 alone, so ι*g_λ solves Ric^H(ι*g_λ) = 0; its
data are ι* of the data of Theorem 7.1, which are invariant under G (Chapter 7); and ι acts on Cartesian arrays by
an orthogonal matrix, which preserves the Euclidean operator norm, so |ι*g_λ − g0| = |g_λ − g0| ≤ ε1. By the
uniqueness of item 5, ι*g_λ = g_λ. This is item 1.

Weak convergence. For a profile f and a test function u ∈ C_c^∞ in the interior of Ω, write f = Σ_n f_n(X) e^(inθ); the
coefficients decay faster than any power of n, uniformly with their X-derivatives. Since ∂_τ v = 1, for n ≠ 0,

    ∫ u f_n e^(inv/λ) = (λ/(in)) ∫ u f_n ∂_τ e^(inv/λ) = −(λ/(in)) ∫ ∂_τ(u f_n) e^(inv/λ) = O(λ/|n|),

so ∫ u [f] → ∫ u ⟨f⟩, and, [f] being bounded, [f] → ⟨f⟩ weakly in L²(Ω). By Theorem 4.11 the oscillating part of
g1 is W_TT at a shifted phase plus a term χ dv ⊗ dv, so Proposition 2.11 gives ⟨∂_θ g1⟩ = 0 and ⟨|∂_θ g1|²_(g0)⟩ = (4/3)
A² env² r⁻³. Hence dv ⊗ [∂_θ g1] → 0 weakly, which with item 3 is the weak convergence of item 4. Applying the same
limit to the profile |dv ⊗ ∂_θ g1|², the Euclidean square of the array, shows that ‖dv ⊗ [∂_θ g1]‖²_(L²(U)) tends to ∫_U
⟨|dv ⊗ ∂_θ g1|²⟩ for every open U ⊂ Ω, which is positive where env ≠ 0, because ∂_θ g1 is not zero there: the mean of
its g0-norm squared is positive. So the convergence is not strong wherever env ≠ 0. The formula for Ric(g0) is
Proposition 2.5 (a).

Items 2, 3 and 5 are those of Theorem 7.1 and Theorem 6.1; items 6 and 7 are Proposition 3.4 and
Proposition 3.5. ∎

### 3.3 The construction from past null infinity

**Theorem 3.7** (the construction from past null infinity). Let the waves at past null infinity
be the free data [F], [G] of Section 2.6, on the background of Theorem 3.1. For every K ≥ 6 there is λ_P > 0
such that for 0 < λ ≤ λ_P there is a smooth vacuum metric g_λ, in the wave-map gauge relative to g0, on Ω together
with a past domain P: the region τ ≤ τ0, r ≥ a, below the outer boundary v + (1/2)(1 + τ0 − τ)^(−1/4) = V_P, where
V_P := V + 1 + (τ_end − τ0) + 1/2; this boundary is spacelike and meets Σ_τ0 where the outer boundary of Ω does, so
that P and Ω share the slice Σ_τ0 (Chapter 9). It satisfies:

1. g_λ = g0 for v ≤ v_start: before the shell, the black hole exactly;
2. its radiation field at past null infinity is the prescribed one: at every fixed v < V_P and x̂,
   r^(3/2)(g_λ − g0 − λ[W_TT]) → 0 as r → ∞, at every λ;
3. on P, |g_λ − g_app| ≤ C λ^(K−3) t^(−2) and |∂(g_λ − g_app)| ≤ C λ^(K−4) t^(−2), with t = 1 + τ0 − τ and g_app
   the approximant built from past null infinity (Theorem 9.10);
4. on Ω, the conclusions of Theorem 6.1 hold (items 1 and 3–5 of Theorem 3.1), with the data on Σ_τ0
   now the trace of g_λ itself; and items 6–7 of Theorem 3.1 hold for these solutions too (Proposition 9.13);
5. g_λ is T² × Z2 × Z2-invariant, and unique among solutions g of Ric^H(g) = 0 on P with g = g0 on P ∩ {v ≤ v_start}
   whose difference from g_app is, with its first derivatives, at most ε_U t^(−3/2) for a small ε_U > 0 (within the
   margin of the past domain fixed in Chapter 9), and whose energy on the slices tends to zero at past
   null infinity.

So the counterpart holds with the waves' own free data at past null infinity, and the constraints need not be solved
on this route (Theorem 7.1 is the other route).

The proof is in Chapter 9; it runs as follows. Before the shell the solution is the black hole: the
region v ≤ v_start is a past set for the black hole's cones, and the data there are the black hole's. Near past null
infinity every stage of the approximant is solved with nothing coming in. Each stage has an explicit leading term in r
and a remainder half a power of r better, and no forcing term of the stages falls off like r^(−5/2), the rate that would
produce a logarithm. So the residual decays like r^(−3), and the remainder can be estimated with the rotations as
commutators, which gain t^(−3/2) in Sobolev's inequality. The past is split at t = λ^(−2). Before the split, the one
large coefficient of the linearised problem (Chapter 6) integrates in time to a constant, and no
decomposition is needed. After it, the decomposition of Chapter 6 runs over an interval of length
λ^(−2). There the transport of its auxiliary field loses a logarithm per unit of log t, which weights (T/t)^β0 absorb
at a cost λ^(−2β0); β0 does not depend on the order of the approximant, so a higher order pays it. The mollifier's
commutator with the wave operator is, apart from decaying terms, an exact derivative along the generators, and is
absorbed into the auxiliary field. The limit is vacuum because the gauge field of the approximant decays at past null
infinity, so its energy tends to zero there and the gauge field vanishes.

### 3.4 The Bondi mass law at past null infinity

**Theorem 3.8** (the Bondi mass at past null infinity). Let g_λ be the metric of
Theorem 3.7, 0 < λ ≤ λ_P. Near past null infinity it admits Bondi coordinates
(v_B, r_B, ϑ_B, φ1, φ2) — v_B null with v_B − v → 0 at past null infinity, ϑ_B constant along the generators, r_B the
areal radius — in which

    g_λ = −e^(2β) W dv_B² + 2 e^(2β) dv_B dr_B + r_B² [e^(−2(P1+P2)) (dϑ_B − U dv_B)² + cos²ϑ_B e^(2P1) dφ1²
          + sin²ϑ_B e^(2P2) dφ2²],    (3.3)

with P1, P2, β, U, W − 1 expanded in r_B^(−1/2) to order r_B^(−3) with o(r_B^(−3)) remainders, coefficients smooth in
(v_B, ϑ_B) and, for v_B ≤ v_start, those of g0: all zero except W − 1 = −μ0 r_B^(−2). In it:

1. P_i = r_B^(−3/2) p_i + O(r_B^(−5/2)), with p1 = (2c² G − s² F)/3 and p2 = (2s² F − c² G)/3 as in (2.11),
   c = cos ϑ_B, s = sin ϑ_B and the free data F, G of Section 2.6 at phase v_B/λ (the radiation field of
   Theorem 3.7, item 2); the r_B^(−2) coefficients vanish;
2. W = 1 + r_B^(−3/2) V1 − r_B^(−2) M + O(r_B^(−5/2)), with V1 a divergence on S³ and the mass aspect M obeying,
   pointwise, the five-dimensional Bondi law of [TTS09] (28), time-reversed,

       ∂_v M = (4/3)((∂_v p1)² + ∂_v p1 ∂_v p2 + (∂_v p2)²),    (3.4)

   with M = μ0 for v_B ≤ v_start;
3. the Bondi mass μ_B(v) := ⟨M(v, ·)⟩, the mean over S³, therefore obeys, exactly,

       μ_B' = (2/9) A² [env² + λ² env'² + (1 − π/2)(−(1/2)(env² − λ² env'²) sin(2v/λ) + λ env env' cos(2v/λ))],
    (3.5)

   the sphere mean of the flux of the radiation field: μ_B is μ(v) + O(λ) while the shell passes, and
   μ(v_end) + (2/9) λ² A² ∫ env'² + O(λ³) after it;
4. the Hawking mass M[S] ((3.2)) of the Bondi spheres S = {v_B, r_B = const} tends to μ_B(v_B) as
   r_B → ∞.

This is the mean mass at past null infinity, the sphere mean of the Bondi mass aspect.

The proof is in Chapter 10; it runs as follows. At fixed λ the far region of Theorem 3.7 is a
neighbourhood of past null infinity, and there the remainder g_λ − g_app solves a wave equation whose forcing decays
like r^(−3): subtracting its leading term, which is explicit, and estimating the rest with the energy of that far region
gains half a power of r at each step, so g_λ − g0 has an asymptotic expansion in r^(−1/2) to any order, with the
radiation field as its leading term (Lemma 10.2, Proposition 10.4). The derivatives along the
ingoing generators of the remainders gain a full order, because the wave equation is a transport along the outgoing
generators for them, and those generators reach the seed region, where everything vanishes, after a bounded parameter
length. The Bondi coordinates are then built from the null geodesics of g_λ asymptotic to the ingoing generators of the
background, in the manner of the eikonal function of [HL21] at future null infinity: v_B is constant on the null
hypersurfaces they sweep, and its eikonal equation, a transport along those generators with a forcing term that decays
like r^(−2) because the first-order wave is transverse to them, gives its expansion; the angular coordinates are the
generators' asymptotic angles, and the areal radius is algebraic. In the Bondi form the vacuum equations are a hierarchy
in r_B^(−1/2), the one of [TTS09] in five dimensions, solved in the class with every coefficient from the first order
general: the radial equations kill every coefficient below the waves' and fix β, U and V1, the traceless angular
equation at order r^(−1) makes the r_B^(−2) coefficients of P constant in v, which the seed sets to zero, and R_vv at
order r^(−3) is (3.4) plus a divergence that vanishes with them. The mass law integrates from the seed; its
sphere mean is (3.5).

### 3.5 Settling to Schwarzschild–Tangherlini

The domain of Theorem 3.1 ends at the time T after the shell. Settling for all later times concerns the exterior of
the black hole, the nonlinear stability theory of five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini set up in
Part V to Part IX: Hintz's initial surface, his data class, the time function t*,
the exterior and its spatially compact subsets, the slowly rotating Myers–Perry black holes [MP86], and the parameters
named below are defined there.

**Theorem 3.9** (settling). Fix l5, μ0, A, env and τ0 as in Theorem 3.1, set the stability theory up
about the Tangherlini metric of mass μ_end, that is at b₀ = (μ_end, 0), and fix its inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, (1/2)√μ_end]
and ℓ0 ∈ (3, 4); let ε_K be the decay parameter chosen in that theory (Theorem 38.24, step (4), with the data class
(38.15) of this ℓ0 at step (3)). It satisfies
0 < ε_K < ε_+ < min(δ_♯, ε_ind, ℓ_I − 3, 1/4) for some ε_+ and some ℓ_I ∈ (3, ℓ0) admissible in row d2 of
Section 38.6, δ_♯ = (1 − e_Υ) γ_Υ and ε_ind the index distance ((32.27), (25.10)), such that no
parameter exponent z at timelike infinity (an element of the set Λ of Definition 33.1, discrete and fixed before
these constants) has real part in (3, 3 + ε_+] (the condition (G⁺), Definition 34.11); and none has real part in
(2, 2 + ε_K] ∪ (3, 3 + ε_K], nor do z + d_c0, z + d_c1 have real part in (2, 2 + ε_K], and ε_K < ε_Υ (the gap (G),
Definition 33.3), d_c0, d_c1 ∈ (0, 1) being the offsets of the two class roots of Definition 32.30 and ε_Υ the
constant fixed by the indicial roots of the gauge operator □^Υ (Section 23.13). Chapter 38 collects these
conditions with the other choices of parameters. Fix ε ∈ (0, ε_K). There are a choice of the order α of row w2 and of
steps (5)–(6) of Theorem 38.24, a radius R and the enlarged domain Ω′ of Lemma 41.4, depending only on ε and
r_♭, such that the following holds for the solutions g_λ of Theorem 3.1 on Ω′, with K = d_1 + 14, d_1 the regularity
of Theorem 38.22 at that choice: for every ε_m > 0 there are λ1 > 0 and δ > 0, depending moreover on ε_m, such
that for λ ≤ λ1:
