(i) (in the class) the data of g_λ on Hintz's initial surface Σ^IVP within {r ≤ R}, continued G-equivariantly to
exact Tangherlini data on {r ≥ 4R} (Proposition 39.17, Corollary 39.19), have a G-invariant vacuum development, with
the same data as g_λ on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ R}, which settles to five-dimensional Tangherlini of a mass m′
with |m′ − μ_end| < ε_m: its difference from that metric is O(t*^(−2−ε)) in spatially compact subsets of the exterior;

(ii) (without symmetry) every smooth vacuum data set on Σ^IVP whose difference from the data of (i) lies in Hintz's
data class — polyhomogeneous at spatial infinity, with terms of orders r^(−2) and r^(−3) in the metric and r^(−3) and
r^(−4) in the second fundamental form, and conormal remainders in r^(−ℓ0) H_b^∞ and r^(−ℓ0−1) H_b^∞ — and has norm less
than δ in that class has a vacuum development that, its initial slice moved by a cut-off Lorentz boost and a cut-off
translation, each below ε_m (the slice φ_(−S,−S⁰)⁻¹(Σ^IVP) = φ_S(ψ_(S⁰)(Σ^IVP)) of Theorem 38.22, with
φ_(S,S⁰) := ψ_(S⁰) ∘ φ_S as in (38.1) and |S|, |S⁰| < ε_m), settles at the same rate to a Myers–Perry
black hole of mass m′ with |m′ − μ_end| < ε_m and spin below ε_m.

Theorem 3.9 is proved in Chapter 41, from the stability theory of Part V to
Part IX, which is Hintz's proof of the nonlinear stability of Kerr [Hin26] carried into spacetime
dimension n + 1 = 5 and written out in full. Gluing a perturbation far out to a translated, rotated and boosted
Myers–Perry metric replaces its data near infinity, on which the solution near the hole at late times depends; so (ii)
is stated for perturbations in Hintz's own data class, where his theorem applies without gluing, and Chapter 42
determines which decaying perturbations it reaches, directly or through gluing. The rate holds for every ε < ε_K.

The linear statement is proved with it, as the nonlinear theorem's linearisation at the Tangherlini data
(Theorem 40.4, Corollary 40.5). Every solution of the linearised constraint equations in Hintz's data class has
a linearised vacuum development in his generalised wave gauge. Up to the data of a linearised boost and a linearised
translation, Lie derivatives of the Tangherlini metric along their generators, it takes those data, and where the
late-time cut-off is 1 it differs from a linearised Myers–Perry metric by O(t*^(−2−ε)) in spatially compact subsets of
the exterior, for each ε < ε_K, the order α of row w2 being chosen for ε. In the class the boost and the translation
vanish and the Myers–Perry change is a change of mass alone. A linearised vacuum solution given in another gauge, with
the same data up to those of a linearised diffeomorphism and given on the whole future of the initial surface outside
r = r_♭, smooth up to that surface, differs from this one there by a linearised diffeomorphism L_X g, X unique up to
Killing fields (Theorem 40.12, Corollary 40.13).

### 3.6 Further results

The remaining chapters prove the following; each is stated in full where it is proved.

- *After the shell.* On {v > v_end} every oscillating profile of the approximant vanishes, the estimate of
  Theorem 6.1 holds at every order of derivatives, and the data near the hole are small in every norm
  Theorem 3.9 uses; equivariant gluing matches the mass alone. The perturbations to which Theorem 3.9 (ii)
  applies, directly or through gluing uniformly in the gluing radius, are exactly those small in Hintz's class
  (Chapter 42).
- *Beyond the boundary.* With r_♭ := ½(√72 μ_end l5²)^(1/4), half the radius of the curvature boundary after the shell,
  the development of Theorem 3.9 (i) also reaches inside the black hole after the shell, up to that boundary
  (Proposition 43.2). Glued to g_λ, taken just before Σ^IVP, along the part of Σ^IVP between r_♭ and R, where the two
  induce the same data, it forms one smooth vacuum spacetime, for λ small; and the two developments of those data have a
  maximal common globally hyperbolic development that contains a neighbourhood of that part, how far it reaches being
  left open (Lemma 43.5). The development of g_λ's own data settles, with no gluing, in a data class
  wider than (ii)'s by half-integer orders, for every λ below a threshold and with no exceptional set
  (Theorem 44.1).
- *The linear solution in two gauges.* In a Regge–Wheeler-type gauge the gauge vector is explicit, and the
  perturbation settles to the change of mass on each region r ≤ R, the horizon included, at the linear rate with two
  derivatives lost (Theorem 45.7). In the harmonic gauge a representative exists on the whole domain, induces
  the given data and settles on each region r_♭ < r ≤ R′, the horizon included, to ṁK* + cℒ_(W*)g: the gauge-fixed
  change of mass ṁK*, ṁ being the mass change of the perturbation, plus a multiple of the pure-gauge solution
  ℒ_(W*)g of an explicit stationary one-form W*. The rate is t*^(−min(p_0,3/2)+ε) for every ε > 0, where
  p_0 > 1/2 + 2γ_Υ is the supremum of the orders of decay at spatial infinity of the data of the one-form Z′_0 for
  which ṁK* + ℒ_(Z′_0)g is the spherically symmetric part of the representative, γ_Υ is a parameter of the gauge of
  the stability theory, and c is fixed by the horizon charge of Z′_0 and the Killing part of its data
  (Theorem 47.30).
- *The constants of Theorem 3.9.* The loss d with which the Nash–Moser step is applied, at least the loss that
  the proof assigns to the tame estimates, and its regularity N_NM = 21d + 6, with explicit lower bounds at a
  parameter point that lies outside the proved set (Theorem 49.32) and, there, explicit upper bounds for d and N_NM
  at one admissible choice of the weights, orders and inner products (Theorem 49.59); through the lower bounds,
  upper bounds for δ and for the modulus of the initial family at 2δ (and λ1 < δ); explicit resolvent bounds on
  five-dimensional Tangherlini (Chapter 48); and where explicit evaluation of λ1 and δ stops
  (Chapter 49).
- *More families.* Two crossing radial null dusts, one ingoing and one outgoing, with the background, the
  approximant, the uniform estimate and the data (Theorem 50.2); Cauchy stability of the class
  Einstein–null-dust system, without smallness, on compact domains of the type of Ω, for caustic-free dusts, the axes
  included where the lateral boundaries meeting them are adapted to the dust (Theorem 51.31); restricted
  massless Vlasov limits, for fields that are caustic-free families of dusts meeting the hypotheses stated there, as
  weak limits of class vacuum metrics along odd numbers of dusts (Theorem 52.10), also with the two radial dusts of
  Theorem 50.2 added to a small field, as weak limits on domains of the type of Ω inside the adapted domain of
  Corollary 51.32, not on the whole of that domain (Corollary 52.50); and exactly localised vacuum data
  near the initial data of an explicit two-dust background of Theorem 50.2 (Section 53.10.1): on a vacuum band
  of the initial slice (a shell {R1 < r < R2} whose closure lies where the background is vacuum), data equal to the
  background's outside a compact subset of the band and vacuum in the band, whose first-order part in a small
  amplitude is a perturbation of
  the metric that is not a gauge perturbation. On every vacuum band that meets the inside of the apparent horizon such
  data exist for small amplitude, while on vacuum bands outside it the sign of their charge at second order excludes
  them for small amplitude when the first-order part is T² × Z2 × Z2-invariant (Theorem 53.30).
- *The boundary at equality.* If μ0 = √72 l5², the curvature boundary is spacelike for g_λ away from a layer at the
  start of the shell, where timelike curves of g_λ cross it (Theorem 54.26, Corollary 54.27), and at the very edge of
  the layer the character of the boundary is decided column by column for envelopes with the edge hypotheses of
  Definition 55.1, among them env_C (Theorem 55.22, Corollary 55.29).
- *Physical wavelengths.* An upper bound for λ0 at a numerical point, and an approximate value, which is not proved, of
  the first stage's mean correction there (Proposition 56.8, Remark 56.9); at the prescribed wavelength 10 l5
  there is no separation of scales, and existence holds where the solution is the seed (Theorem 57.18).

Chapter 58 collects what is claimed and what is not.

# Part II. The approximant

## 4. The two-scale expansion and the approximant

This chapter constructs, for every number of stages N, a metric g_app that solves the reduced equations Ric^H = 0 up to
an error of order λ^(N−1) in the scaled norms. Its leading oscillation is the pair of waves of
(2.11), shifted in phase and completed by a second harmonic along dv ⊗ dv, and its mean at leading
order is the five-dimensional Vaidya metric g0 with the mass law (2.14). The construction is the
two-scale expansion of geometric optics, carried to every order: each order is a linear hyperbolic system with smooth
coefficients for a mean correction, a phase correction and the next oscillating profile. The uniform existence theorem
Theorem 6.1 takes g_app as its input, in the form fixed by Definition 4.3.

Throughout, the background g0, the phase v, the null geodesic generator ℓ = g0⁻¹dv = −L0, the operator □̃ := g0^(ab)
∂_a ∂_b acting componentwise and the commutator identity (2.6) for [L0, □̃] are those of Proposition 2.5; the
gauge field D and the reduced Ricci tensor Ric^H are those of Section 2.4; Ω, its slices Σ_τ, τ0 and
τ_end are those of Section 2.3; and profiles f(X, θ) on Ω × S¹, their evaluation [f](X) = f(X, v(X)/λ),
their θ-mean ⟨f⟩ and the scaled norms |f|_j are those of Section 2.5 and
(2.10). Tensors are arrays of components in the Cartesian coordinates X = (τ, x) unless
another chart is named.

### 4.1 Two-scale operators

Let u be a smooth function on Ω, a phase. For a profile f write [f]_u(X) := f(X, u(X)/λ), so that [f]_v = [f]. The chain
rule gives

    ∂_a [f]_u = [∂^u_a f]_u,        ∂^u_a := ∂_a + λ⁻¹ (∂_a u) ∂_θ.    (4.1)

In the coordinates X the reduced Ricci tensor is an expression

    Ric^H(g)_mn = F_mn(X, g, ∂g, ∂²g),

polynomial in g, g⁻¹, ∂g and ∂²g, whose explicit dependence on X is through the Christoffel symbols of g0 and their first
derivatives Section 2.4; second derivatives of g enter it only through −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b g_mn.

**Definition 4.1** (The two-scale operator.) For a profile G of symmetric 2-tensors with det G ≠ 0, the
two-scale operator is

    R_u[G](X, θ) := F(X, G, ∂^u G, ∂^u ∂^u G)(X, θ),

that is, Ric^H with g replaced by G and every derivative ∂_a by ∂^u_a. We write R := R_v.

By (4.1), Ric^H([G]_u) = [R_u[G]]_u. The operator R_u[G] is a polynomial in λ⁻¹ whose coefficients
are built from G and its X- and θ-derivatives, from g0 and its derivatives at X, and from the derivatives of u; it
contains θ only through G.

**Lemma 4.2** (Equivariance under shifts of the phase.) (a) For every profile G and every
constant c,

    R[G(·, · + c)](X, θ) = R[G](X, θ + c).    (4.2)

(b) If Φ is a smooth function on Ω, possibly depending on λ, and u = v + λΦ, then for each λ R[G(·, · + Φ)](X, θ) =
R_u[G](X, θ + Φ(X)).

*Proof.* (b) contains (a): for Φ = c, ∂u = ∂v, so R_u = R. For a profile f put f_Φ(X, θ) := f(X, θ + Φ(X)). Then

    ∂^v_a f_Φ = (∂_a f + (∂_a Φ) ∂_θ f + λ⁻¹ (∂_a v) ∂_θ f)(X, θ + Φ(X)) = (∂^u_a f)_Φ,

since ∂_a u = ∂_a v + λ ∂_a Φ. Applied to the profile ∂^u_b f, the same identity gives ∂^v_a ∂^v_b f_Φ = (∂^u_a ∂^u_b
f)_Φ. So R[G_Φ](X, θ) = F(X, G_Φ, ∂^v G_Φ, ∂^v ∂^v G_Φ) = F(X, G, ∂^u G, ∂^u ∂^u G)(X, θ + Φ(X)) = R_u[G](X, θ + Φ(X)),
because the explicit dependence of F on X does not involve θ. ∎

Let G = g0 + λ g1 + Σ_(j≥2) λ^j g_j be a finite sum of profiles bounded with all their derivatives. Then R[G] is a
polynomial in λ⁻¹ and, through G⁻¹, a smooth function of λ near 0 with profile coefficients, and we write its expansion

    R[G] = λ⁻¹ R^(−1) + R^(0) + λ R^(1) + … .    (4.3)

The term of order λ⁻¹ is

    R^(−1) = −(1/2) g0⁻¹(dv, dv) ∂_θ² g1 = 0.

Indeed ∂^v_a ∂^v_b (λ g1) = λ⁻¹ (∂_a v)(∂_b v) ∂_θ² g1 + O(1), and every other term of Ric^H contains at most first
derivatives, while ∂^v G = O(1); and g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0 because dv is null for g0 Proposition 2.5.

### 4.2 Approximants

**Definition 4.3** (Approximant.) Let N ≥ 1, K and k be integers. An approximant with N stages is a metric

    g_app = g0 + λ [g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j],    (4.4)

with profiles g_j such that every derivative ∂^i_(X,θ) g_j is bounded on Ω × S¹ independently of λ. It is of order K at
regularity k if it has the following three properties.

- (E1) *Transversality of the wave*: (g1 − ⟨g1⟩)(ℓ, ·) = 0 for all (X, θ). The mean ⟨g1⟩ is unrestricted.
- (E2) *The leading equation*: the coefficient R^(0)(X, θ) of λ⁰ in the two-scale expansion
  (4.3) of Ric^H(g_app), that is of R[g0 + λ g1 + Σ_(j≥2) λ^j g_j], vanishes identically in
  (X, θ).
- (E3) *The residual*: |Ric^H(g_app)|_k (τ) ≤ C_R λ^K for every τ ∈ [τ0, τ_end], with C_R independent of λ.

### 4.3 The leading coefficient

The leading coefficient R^(0) of a wave on g0 has a closed form once the wave is transverse to ℓ and traceless.

**Lemma 4.4** (The leading coefficient.) Let W be a profile of symmetric 2-tensors with W(ℓ, ·) =
0 and tr W := g0^(ab) W_ab = 0 at every (X, θ). Then the two-scale expansion of R[g0 + λ W] has R^(−1) = 0 and

    R^(0) = Ric(g0) − ∇_ℓ ∂_θ W − (1/2)(□_(g0) v) ∂_θ W − (1/4) |∂_θ W|² dv ⊗ dv,    (4.5)

where ∇ is the Levi-Civita connection of g0 acting on W at fixed θ, □_(g0) the wave operator of g0 on functions,
and |∂_θ W|² := g0^(ac) g0^(bd) ∂_θ W_ab ∂_θ W_cd.

*Proof.* We compute with profiles. The formulas below for Ric(g), C, D and S are polynomial identities in the 2-jet of h
:= g − g0 at a point, with coefficients from the 2-jet of g0, and they hold for every symmetric array of second
derivatives. The two-scale derivative ∂^v_a := ∂_a + λ⁻¹ v_a ∂_θ satisfies ∂^v_a ∂^v_b = ∂^v_b ∂^v_a, and ∂_a [F] =
[∂^v_a F] in every chart, since v is a scalar. So the identities hold for profiles, with ∂_a replaced by ∂^v_a and the
covariant derivative of g0 by ∇^v_a := ∇_a + λ⁻¹ v_a ∂_θ, where ∇_a acts at fixed θ; R[g0 + λ W] is Ric^H(g0 + λ W)
computed in this way, in any chart, and we identify the coefficients of the powers of λ, which are profiles. Write ∂ :=
∂_θ and v_a := ∂_a v, raise and lower indices with g0, so that ℓ^a = g0^(ab) v_b, and put h := λ W, g := g0 + h. The
hypotheses give, at every (X, θ),

    W_ab ℓ^b = 0,   ∂W_ab ℓ^b = 0,   ℓ^a v_a = 0,   g0^(ab) W_ab = 0,   g0^(ab) ∂W_ab = 0.

The tensor C := Γ[g] − Γ[g0] satisfies

    C^c_ab = (1/2) g^(cd) (∇_a h_bd + ∇_b h_ad − ∇_d h_ab),
    Ric(g)_ab = Ric(g0)_ab + ∇_c C^c_ab − ∇_b C^c_ac + C^c_cd C^d_ab − C^c_bd C^d_ac,

and the gauge field is D^ρ = g^(ab) C^ρ_ab, so that Ric^H(g)_mn = Ric(g)_mn − S_mn with S_mn := (1/2)(g_mρ ∇_n D^ρ + g_nρ
∇_m D^ρ) Section 2.4, with ∇ read as ∇^v. Now ∇^v_a h = v_a ∂W + λ ∇_a W, and g⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − λ W^♯ + O(λ²) with W^♯ :=
g0⁻¹ W g0⁻¹. So C = C_0 + λ C_1 + O(λ²) with the profiles

    C_0^c_ab = (1/2)(v_a ∂W_b^c + v_b ∂W_a^c − ℓ^c ∂W_ab),
    C_1^c_ab = (1/2)(∇_a W_b^c + ∇_b W_a^c − ∇^c W_ab) − (1/2) W^(cd) (v_a ∂W_bd + v_b ∂W_ad − v_d ∂W_ab).

Their traces are C_0^c_ac = (1/2) v_a g0^(cd) ∂W_cd = 0 and, writing W·∂W := W^(cd) ∂W_cd and using g0^(cd) ∇_a W_cd =
∇_a (tr W) = 0 and W^(cd) v_c = 0,

    C_1^c_ac = −(1/2) v_a W·∂W.

The gauge field. At order λ⁰, D is g0^(ab) C_0^ρ_ab = (1/2)(ℓ^b ∂W_b^ρ + ℓ^a ∂W_a^ρ − ℓ^ρ g0^(ab) ∂W_ab) = 0. At order λ,
D_1^ρ := g0^(ab) C_1^ρ_ab − W^(ab) C_0^ρ_ab. In the first term the linear part is (div W)^ρ − (1/2) ∇^ρ tr W = (div W)^ρ,
with (div W)_b := ∇^a W_ab, and the quadratic part is −(1/2) W^(ρd)(2 ℓ^b ∂W_bd − v_d g0^(ab) ∂W_ab) = 0; the second term
is −(1/2)(2 W^(ab) v_a ∂W_b^ρ − ℓ^ρ W·∂W) = (1/2) ℓ^ρ W·∂W. So D = λ D_1 + O(λ²) with

    D_1^ρ = (div W)^ρ + (1/2) ℓ^ρ W·∂W.

The order λ⁻¹. The only terms of size λ⁻¹ come from the derivatives of C_0 in phase: ∇^v_c C^c_ab − ∇^v_b C^c_ac
contains λ⁻¹ (v_c ∂C_0^c_ab − v_b ∂C_0^c_ac). Since C_0^c_ac = 0, this is λ⁻¹ v_c ∂C_0^c_ab = λ⁻¹ (1/2) ∂(v_a v_c
∂W_b^c + v_b v_c ∂W_a^c − v_c ℓ^c ∂W_ab) = 0, because v_c ∂W_b^c = ∂W_bc ℓ^c = 0. The products C C are O(1), and S = O(1)
because D = O(λ). So R^(−1) = 0.

The order λ⁰ of Ric(g) − Ric(g0) has four parts.

(i) From ∇^v_c C^c_ab: the term ∇_c C_0^c_ab and the phase derivative v_c ∂C_1^c_ab. First,

    ∇_c C_0^c_ab = (1/2)(∇_c v_a ∂W_b^c + ∇_c v_b ∂W_a^c + v_a ∇_c ∂W_b^c + v_b ∇_c ∂W_a^c − (∇_c ℓ^c) ∂W_ab
                   − ∇_ℓ ∂W_ab).

Second, v_c W^(cd) = 0 removes the quadratic part of C_1, and differentiating W_bd ℓ^d = 0 gives ℓ^d ∇_a W_bd = −W_bd
∇_a ℓ^d, so

    v_c ∂C_1^c_ab = (1/2)(−∂W_bd ∇_a ℓ^d − ∂W_ad ∇_b ℓ^d − ∇_ℓ ∂W_ab).

Since ℓ is the gradient of v, ∇_a ℓ^d = ∇^d ∇_a v, and so ∇_c v_a ∂W_b^c = ∂W_bd ∇^d ∇_a v = ∂W_bd ∇_a ℓ^d: these terms
cancel in pairs. With ∇_c ℓ^c = □_(g0) v the sum of (i) is

    −∇_ℓ ∂W_ab − (1/2)(□_(g0) v) ∂W_ab + (1/2)(v_a (div ∂W)_b + v_b (div ∂W)_a).

(ii) From −∇^v_b C^c_ac: −∇_b C_0^c_ac − v_b ∂C_1^c_ac = 0 + (1/2) v_a v_b ∂(W·∂W).

(iii) From C^c_cd C^d_ab: at order λ⁰ this is C_0^c_cd C_0^d_ab = 0.

(iv) From −C^c_bd C^d_ac: at order λ⁰ this is −C_0^c_bd C_0^d_ac. Of the nine products in

    (v_b ∂W_d^c + v_d ∂W_b^c − ℓ^c ∂W_bd)(v_a ∂W_c^d + v_c ∂W_a^d − ℓ^d ∂W_ac),

eight contain a contraction of ∂W with v or with ℓ, or the contraction v_c ℓ^c, and vanish; the ninth is v_a v_b ∂W_d^c
∂W_c^d = v_a v_b |∂W|². So (iv) is −(1/4) v_a v_b |∂W|².

The term S at order λ⁰. As D = λ D_1 + O(λ²), ∇^v_n D^ρ = v_n ∂D_1^ρ + O(λ), and g_mρ = (g0)_mρ + O(λ). So S has the
λ⁰ coefficient

    (1/2)(v_n ∂D_1m + v_m ∂D_1n) = (1/2)(v_n (div ∂W)_m + v_m (div ∂W)_n) + (1/2) v_m v_n ∂(W·∂W),

since ℓ lowered is v. Subtracting it from (i)–(iv), the divergence terms and the terms in ∂(W·∂W) cancel, and what
remains is (4.5). The parts of C and D of order λ² contribute at order λ only. ∎

### 4.4 Stage 0

Since (4.5) is tensorial we evaluate it in ingoing Eddington–Finkelstein coordinates (v, r, ϑ, φ1,
φ2), where x1 + i x2 = r cos ϑ e^(iφ1), x3 + i x4 = r sin ϑ e^(iφ2), ϑ ∈ [0, π/2], and c := cos ϑ, s := sin ϑ. With
τ = v − r the Minkowski metric is −dτ² + dr² + r² dΩ² = −dv² + 2 dv dr + r² dΩ², so

    g0 = −(1 − μ(v)/r²) dv² + 2 dv dr + r² (dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2²).    (4.6)

Its inverse has g0^(vv) = 0, g0^(vr) = 1, g0^(rr) = 1 − μ/r², no mixed component between (v, r) and the angles, and on
the angular coordinates A, B ∈ {ϑ, φ1, φ2} the inverse of the round metric of radius r. Hence ℓ = g0⁻¹dv = ∂_r, the
derivative at fixed (v, ϑ, φ1, φ2); it agrees with −L0 = −∂_τ + x̂·∂_x. The density is |det g0|^(1/2) = r³ c s, so

    □_(g0) v = (r³ c s)⁻¹ ∂_a (r³ c s g0^(ab) ∂_b v) = (r³ c s)⁻¹ ∂_r (r³ c s) = 3/r.

The Christoffel symbols with one lower index r are read from Γ^σ_(ra) = (1/2) g0^(σd)(∂_r g_da + ∂_a g_dr − ∂_d g_ra),
where g_vr = 1 and g_rr = g_rA = 0: for an angular index A, Γ^B_(rA) = r⁻¹ δ^B_A and Γ^v_(rA) = Γ^r_(rA) = 0; further
Γ^B_(rv) = Γ^B_(rr) = 0 and Γ^v_(ra) = (1/2) ∂_a g_rr = 0 for every a. Consequently ∇_ℓ dv = 0, and for a symmetric
tensor Y with only angular components, ∇_ℓ Y has only angular components, equal to

    (∇_ℓ Y)_AB = ∂_r Y_AB − (2/r) Y_AB.    (4.7)

The Ricci tensor of g0 is Ric(g0) = (3 μ'(v)/(2 r³)) dv ⊗ dv Proposition 2.5.

In these coordinates the leading wave W_TT of (2.11) reads, with y_i := r^(−3/2) p_i/λ,

    W_TT = 2 r² (−(y1 + y2) dϑ² + c² y1 dφ1² + s² y2 dφ2²),
    y1 = (α/3)(2 c² cos θ − s² sin θ),     y2 = (α/3)(2 s² sin θ − c² cos θ),     α := A env(v) h r^(−3/2),

with h = h(cos 2ϑ) of Section 2.6. The chart (v, r, ϑ, φ1, φ2) is singular on the axes c = 0 and s = 0. Every
identity below holds off the axes between tensors smooth on r > 0 (Lemma 2.9 (a), and the smoothness of χ shown
after Lemma 4.5), so it holds on the axes by continuity.

**Lemma 4.5** (Stage 0.) Let χ be a smooth function on Ω × S¹ and W := W_TT + χ dv ⊗ dv. Then:

(a) W(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr W = 0;

(b) R^(−1) = 0 in the two-scale expansion of R[g0 + λ W], and

    R^(0) = (3 μ'/(2 r³) − 2 ((∂_θ y1)² + ∂_θ y1 ∂_θ y2 + (∂_θ y2)²) − (∂_r + 3/(2r)) ∂_θ χ) dv ⊗ dv;    (4.8)

(c) the θ-mean of R^(0) vanishes in every component exactly when μ' = (2/9) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴), and h² (c⁴ + s⁴) = 1,
so exactly when μ' = (2/9) A² env²;

(d) with χ = 0, the oscillating part R^(0) − ⟨R^(0)⟩ is a second harmonic in θ (a combination of cos 2θ and sin 2θ) in
the vv component, and every other component of R^(0) vanishes;

(e) χ enters R^(0) only through the term −(∂_r + 3/(2r)) ∂_θ χ in the vv component.

*Proof.* (a) W_TT has only angular components and ℓ = ∂_r, so W_TT(ℓ, ·) = 0, and its trace is r⁻²(−2 r² (y1 + y2)) +
(r c)⁻²(2 r² c² y1) + (r s)⁻²(2 r² s² y2) = 0. For the second term, (dv ⊗ dv)(ℓ, ·) = dv(ℓ) dv = g0⁻¹(dv, dv) dv = 0, and
its trace is g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0.

(b) By (a), Lemma 4.4 applies and gives R^(−1) = 0 and R^(0) = Ric(g0) − ∇_ℓ ∂_θ W − (3/(2r)) ∂_θ W −
(1/4)|∂_θ W|² dv ⊗ dv. The angular components of ∂_θ W_TT are r^(1/2) times functions of (v, ϑ, θ), so by
(4.7) ∇_ℓ ∂_θ W_TT = (1/2 − 2) r⁻¹ ∂_θ W_TT, that is

    ∇_ℓ ∂_θ W_TT + (3/(2r)) ∂_θ W_TT = 0.

Since ∇_ℓ dv = 0, ∇_ℓ (∂_θ χ dv ⊗ dv) = (∂_r ∂_θ χ) dv ⊗ dv. For the quadratic term, the contraction of dv ⊗ dv with a
symmetric tensor Y is Y(ℓ, ℓ), so |∂_θ W|² = |∂_θ W_TT|² + 2 (∂_θ χ) ∂_θ W_TT(ℓ, ℓ) + (∂_θ χ)² g0⁻¹(dv, dv)² = |∂_θ
W_TT|². In the frame r⁻¹ ∂_ϑ, (r c)⁻¹ ∂_φ1, (r s)⁻¹ ∂_φ2, orthonormal for the round metric of radius r, ∂_θ W_TT is
diagonal with entries −2 ∂_θ(y1 + y2), 2 ∂_θ y1, 2 ∂_θ y2, so

    (1/4)|∂_θ W_TT|² = (∂_θ y1 + ∂_θ y2)² + (∂_θ y1)² + (∂_θ y2)² = 2 ((∂_θ y1)² + ∂_θ y1 ∂_θ y2 + (∂_θ y2)²).

With Ric(g0) = (3 μ'/(2 r³)) dv ⊗ dv this is (4.8).

(c) The χ term is a θ-derivative and has mean zero. By the formula for (1/4)|∂_θ W_TT|² in (b) and (2.13),
2 ⟨(∂_θ y1)² + ∂_θ y1 ∂_θ y2 + (∂_θ y2)²⟩ = (1/4) ⟨|∂_θ W_TT|²⟩ = (1/3) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴) r⁻³, so

    ⟨R^(0)⟩ = r⁻³ ((3/2) μ' − (1/3) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴)) dv ⊗ dv,

which vanishes exactly when μ' = (2/9) A² env² h² (c⁴ + s⁴); and h² (c⁴ + s⁴) = 1 by (2.13). This is
Proposition 2.11, here with the oscillating part of R^(0) in full.

(d) ∂_θ y1 and ∂_θ y2 are combinations of sin θ and cos θ, so the quadratic expression in (4.8) is a
combination of 1, cos 2θ and sin 2θ, and its oscillating part is a second harmonic. By (b) every component of R^(0)
other than vv vanishes.

(e) is read from (b). ∎

*The choice at stage 0.* Assume the mass law μ' = (2/9) A² env² (2.14). By Lemma 4.5,
R^(0) = (F_2 − (∂_r + 3/(2r)) ∂_θ χ) dv ⊗ dv with

    F_2 := −2 ((∂_θ y1)² + ∂_θ y1 ∂_θ y2 + (∂_θ y2)²) + (1/3) α² (c⁴ + s⁴),

the vv second harmonic of R^(0) at χ = 0. Let χ be the profile with zero θ-mean that vanishes on Σ_τ0 and solves the
transport

    (∂_r + 3/(2r)) ∂_θ χ = F_2    (4.9)

along ℓ = ∂_r: first ∂_θ χ, a second harmonic, is found by integrating along the integral curves of ℓ, which from every
point of Ω reach Σ_τ0 inside Ω Lemma 2.6 (d), and χ is its primitive in θ with zero mean. Then R^(0) ≡ 0
identically in (X, θ). The function χ is smooth on Ω × S¹, at the axes of the T² action included: ℓ has no angular
component, so the transport preserves smoothness on S³, and its right-hand side F_2 is built from g0 and W_TT, which is
smooth at both axes (Lemma 2.9 (a)); explicitly F_2 is r⁻³ env(v)² h² times a polynomial in sin θ, cos θ, c² =
(x1² + x2²)/r² and s² = (x3² + x4²)/r², with h² = 2/(1 + cos² 2ϑ) and cos 2ϑ = (x1² + x2² − x3² − x4²)/r², which is
smooth on r > 0.

### 4.5 The ansatz

The unknowns are the means m_j (j ≥ 1), the phases φ_j (j ≥ 1) and the oscillating profiles ĝ_j (j ≥ 2, of zero θ-mean).
With the mean metric ḡ := g0 + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j m_j, the phase u := v + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j φ_j, W := W_TT + χ dv ⊗ dv as in
Section 4.4, and

    G := ḡ + λ W + Σ_(j=2)^(N+1) λ^j ĝ_j(X, θ),        g_app := G(X, u/λ) = [G]_u,    (4.10)

we have Ric^H(g_app) = [R_u[G]]_u, and λ⁻¹ du = λ⁻¹ dv + Σ_j λ^(j−1) dφ_j. Expand R_u[G] = Σ_m λ^m ℛ^(m). The phase is
the eikonal of the mean metric to each order: in −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b (λ W), the terms in which both derivatives fall on
the phase sum to −(1/2) λ⁻¹ ḡ⁻¹(du, du) ∂_θ² W plus terms with an oscillating factor of g⁻¹, and

    ḡ⁻¹(du, du) = Σ_(j≥1) λ^j e_j,        e_j = 2 ℓ·dφ_j − m_j(ℓ, ℓ) − q_j,    (4.11)

with q_j a polynomial in (m_i, dφ_i), i < j: q_1 = 0 and q_2 = −(m1 m1)(ℓ, ℓ) − |dφ1|² + 2 m1(ℓ, dφ1), indices moved by
g0. Indeed ḡ⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − λ m1^♯ + λ² ((m1 m1)^♯ − m2^♯) + O(λ³), du = dv + λ dφ1 + λ² dφ2 + O(λ³) and g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0,
which gives e_1 = 2 ℓ·dφ1 − m1(ℓ, ℓ) and the stated q_2; the higher q_j are read off in the same way.

*Weights.* In the expansion of R_u[G] every monomial carries at most two derivatives. A derivative is ∂_X, of weight
0; λ⁻¹ (∂v) ∂_θ, of weight −1; or λ^(i−1) (∂φ_i) ∂_θ, of weight i − 1. The derivative ∂_θ acts only on oscillating
factors: W, of weight 1, and ĝ_i, of weight i. The mean m_i has weight i, and g0 weight 0; G⁻¹ is expanded in powers of
λ, its term of order λ^i having weight i. The order in λ of a monomial is the sum of the weights of its factors and its
derivatives.

**Definition 4.6** (The operator T̂.) Let G1 := g0 + λ (m1 + W) and u1 := v + λ φ1. For a
profile Y with zero θ-mean let T̂Y be the coefficient of λ⁰ in the two-scale expansion of

    (d/dε)|_(ε=0) R_(u1)[G1 + ε λ Y].

The coefficient of λ⁻¹ in this expansion is −(1/2) g0⁻¹(dv, dv) ∂_θ² Y = 0, so T̂ is the leading part of the linearised
two-scale operator at the first stage, applied to λY.

**Lemma 4.7** (Where each unknown first enters.) ℛ^(−1) = 0. ℛ^(0) is the coefficient of λ⁰ of R[g0 + λ W]
at (X, θ), minus (1/2) e_1 ∂_θ² W. For m ≥ 1,

    ℛ^(m) = T̂ ĝ_(m+1) − (1/2) e_(m+1) ∂_θ² W + 𝒲(m_m, φ_m) + 𝒴_m,    (4.12)

where 𝒲 is linear in m_m and in φ_m: in m_m to second order, its θ-mean part being −(1/2) □̃ m_m plus terms of first
order; in φ_m through dφ_m and □̃φ_m, the latter only as −(1/2)(□̃φ_m) ∂_θ W. 𝒴_m depends only on m_i, φ_i (i < m) and
ĝ_i (i ≤ m).

*Proof.* We count weights. A factor of stage m + 1 has weight m + 1 (ĝ_(m+1), m_(m+1)) or contributes the derivative λ^m
(∂φ_(m+1)) ∂_θ of weight m. In a monomial of order m containing ĝ_(m+1), the other factors and the derivatives therefore
have weights summing to −1. Every weight is at least 0 except that of λ⁻¹ (∂v) ∂_θ, and there are at most two
derivatives. Let n be the number of derivatives λ⁻¹ (∂v) ∂_θ in the monomial; then n ∈ {1, 2}, and the other factors and
derivatives have weights summing to n − 1. If n = 1, they all have weight 0, and the derivative λ⁻¹ (∂v) ∂_θ hits
ĝ_(m+1), since ∂_θ needs an oscillating factor and the only factor of weight 0 is g0. If n = 2, exactly one other factor
has weight 1 and every other factor and derivative weight 0; the two derivatives λ⁻¹ (∂v) ∂_θ both hit ĝ_(m+1), or one
hits ĝ_(m+1) and the other W, or both hit W while ĝ_(m+1) stands undifferentiated in g⁻¹ (the term (1/2) ĝ_(m+1)(ℓ, ℓ)
∂_θ² W). In every case ĝ_(m+1) appears linearly, since two such factors have weight at least 2(m + 1) − 2 > m, and the
other factors have weight at most 1: they are g0, v, W, m1 and φ1 (the derivative (∂φ1) ∂_θ having weight 0). These are
the factors of weight at most 1 of G1 and u1, and the same count applies to λ Y in R_(u1)[G1 + ε λ Y], which has weight
1; so these terms are T̂ ĝ_(m+1). A monomial of order m containing m_(m+1) or ∂φ_(m+1) has the remaining weights summing
to −1 or 0 respectively; they arise only in the phase contraction (4.11), where both derivatives of
λ W fall on the phase, and give −(1/2) e_(m+1) ∂_θ² W. Two factors among m_m and ∂φ_m have weights at least m − 1 each
(m_m has weight m, and the derivative λ^(m−1) (∂φ_m) ∂_θ weight m − 1), and every ∂_θ needs an oscillating factor, of
weight at least 1; so they reach order m only when m = 1, in the phase contraction, through the q_2 terms, which
(4.11) places in e_2. The second harmonic of W hit twice by λ⁻¹ (∂v) ∂_θ is contracted with ḡ⁻¹(dv,
dv), of weight at least 1, since g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0.

Apart from the q_2 terms, which (4.11) places in e_2, the stage-m unknowns m_m and φ_m therefore
appear linearly at order m. The mean m_m, of weight m, reaches order m undifferentiated in θ; its second derivatives
enter only through the principal term, as −(1/2) g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b m_m = −(1/2) □̃ m_m, the corrections to g⁻¹ having
positive weight, and its other terms carry at most one derivative of m_m. The phase φ_m enters only through the
derivative λ^(m−1) (∂φ_m) ∂_θ, of weight m − 1, which must act on an oscillating factor; at order m it appears through
dφ_m, or, when the second derivative of the principal term falls on ∂φ_m, as −(1/2) g0^(ab) (∂_a ∂_b φ_m) ∂_θ W =
−(1/2)(□̃φ_m) ∂_θ W; no other term of Ric^H contains a second derivative. At order m − 1 the stage-m unknowns appear only
in −(1/2) e_m ∂_θ² W and in −(1/2) g0⁻¹(dv, dv) ∂_θ² ĝ_(m+1) = 0, and at order m − 2 or lower not at all. This gives
the form of ℛ^(m) for m ≥ 1 and ℛ^(−1) = 0. At order 0, the terms containing m1 or φ1 are those of −(1/2) e_1 ∂_θ² W;
ĝ_2 enters order 0 only through −(1/2) g0⁻¹(dv, dv) ∂_θ² ĝ_2 = 0; the rest is the coefficient of λ⁰ of R[g0 + λ W].
At order −1 the only term is −(1/2) g0⁻¹(dv, dv) ∂_θ² W = 0. ∎

**Lemma 4.8** (The operator T̂.) If e_1 = 0, then on profiles Y of zero θ-mean

    T̂ Y = −(ℓ·∂_X) ∂_θ Y + ℳ Y,

with ℳ algebraic in X and of first order in θ, its coefficients smooth bounded profiles built from g0, its
derivatives, v and W alone. In particular, when e_1 = 0, T̂ does not depend on m1 or φ1.

*Proof.* We take the terms of R_(u1)[G1 + ε λ Y] linear in ε at order λ⁰. Here ∂^(u1)_a = ∂_a + λ⁻¹ v_a ∂_θ + (∂_a φ1)
∂_θ, so

    ∂^(u1)_a ∂^(u1)_b (λ Y) = λ⁻¹ v_a v_b ∂_θ² Y + v_a ∂_b ∂_θ Y + v_b ∂_a ∂_θ Y + (∂_a ∂_b v) ∂_θ Y
                    + (v_a ∂_b φ1 + v_b ∂_a φ1) ∂_θ² Y + O(λ),

and G1⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − λ (m1 + W)^♯ + O(λ²). The principal term −(1/2) G1^(ab) ∂^(u1)_a ∂^(u1)_b (λ Y) therefore contributes
at order λ⁰

    −(ℓ·∂_X) ∂_θ Y − (1/2)(□̃v) ∂_θ Y − (ℓ·dφ1) ∂_θ² Y + (1/2)(m1 + W)(ℓ, ℓ) ∂_θ² Y
        = −(ℓ·∂_X) ∂_θ Y − (1/2)(□̃v) ∂_θ Y − (1/2) e_1 ∂_θ² Y,

since W(ℓ, ℓ) = 0 and e_1 = 2 ℓ·dφ1 − m1(ℓ, ℓ). The variation of G⁻¹ in the principal term, −λ Y^♯ + O(λ²), meets
∂^(u1)_a ∂^(u1)_b G1 = λ⁻¹ v_a v_b ∂_θ² W + O(1) and gives (1/2) Y(ℓ, ℓ) ∂_θ² W. The remaining terms of Ric^H are of
first order in g Section 2.4; their variation contains ∂^(u1)(λ Y) = dv ⊗ ∂_θ Y + O(λ) times coefficients built from
G1, ∂^(u1) G1 and g0, bounded profiles whose parts of order λ⁰ are built from g0, ∂g0 and dv ⊗ ∂_θ W (m1 has zero
θ-derivative, and φ1 enters ∂^(u1) G1 only at order λ), and λ Y times bounded profiles, which is O(λ). So T̂ Y =
−(ℓ·∂_X) ∂_θ Y − (1/2) e_1 ∂_θ² Y + ℳ Y with ℳ Y := −(1/2)(□̃v) ∂_θ Y + (1/2) Y(ℓ, ℓ) ∂_θ² W + B·(dv ⊗ ∂_θ Y), B a
bounded profile built from g0, ∂g0, v and W. With e_1 = 0 this is the claim; m1 and φ1 entered only through e_1. ∎

**Lemma 4.9** (Linear wave equations on Ω.) Let d ≥ 1, and let B^a and C be smooth d × d matrices of
functions on Ω, smooth meaning that all their derivatives extend continuously to the boundary. For every smooth f on Ω
with values in ℝ^d and smooth u0, u1 on Σ_τ0 there is a unique smooth u on Ω with

    −(1/2) □̃ u + B^a ∂_a u + C u = f   on Ω,      u = u0  and  ∂_τ u = u1   on Σ_τ0.    (4.13)

*Proof.* Uniqueness. The difference w of two solutions solves −(1/2) □̃ w = −B^a ∂_a w − C w with zero data, so
Lemma 5.5 with g̃ = g0 gives ‖∂w(τ)‖ + ‖w(τ)‖ ≤ C ∫_(τ0)^τ (‖∂w(s)‖ + ‖w(s)‖) ds, and w = 0 by Gronwall's
inequality.

Existence. (i) The domain. Give the region {r > a/2} the metric g0 and the time orientation in which τ increases to
the future; it plays the role of the manifold M of Theorem A.2. Let S := {τ = τ0, r > a/2}, the whole
level set of τ in this region, which contains the annulus Σ_τ0 = A(τ0). Since g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r² < 0
(Proposition 2.5 (d)), τ is strictly increasing along future causal curves, so S is a smooth spacelike hypersurface
without boundary which every causal curve meets at most once: S is acausal. By Theorem A.2 its Cauchy
development D, the set of points of {r > a/2} through which every inextendible causal curve meets S, is open and
globally hyperbolic, with S as a Cauchy hypersurface. We show Ω ⊂ D. Let p ∈ Ω, and follow an inextendible causal
curve γ of {r > a/2} through p to the past. While τ ≥ τ0 along γ, γ stays in Ω, by Lemma 2.6 (e) applied to g0.
Suppose τ > τ0 along all of it. Parametrised by τ ∈ (τ*, τ(p)], τ* ≥ τ0, its velocity V has dτ(V) = 1. At the points
of the compact set Ω the causal vectors V with dτ(V) = 1 form a compact set: a sequence of them with Euclidean norms
tending to infinity would have, after normalisation, a causal limit V ≠ 0 with dτ(V) = 0, which the timelike covector
dτ excludes. So γ is Lipschitz in τ and converges, as τ decreases to τ*, to a point of Ω ⊂ {r > a/2}, and γ is
extendible, a contradiction. Hence γ reaches {τ = τ0}, at a point of Ω ∩ {τ = τ0} = Σ_τ0 ⊂ S, and p ∈ D. Ω is
connected and meets S, so it lies in the connected component of D that contains the connected set S. This component
is open and globally hyperbolic with Cauchy hypersurface S, since an inextendible causal curve in it is one of D; we
call it D again.

(ii) The extension. The interior of Ω is a bounded Lipschitz domain in ℝ⁵: near each point of its boundary it is
bounded by at most two of the hypersurfaces {τ = τ0}, {τ = τ_end}, {r = a} and {v + τ = V + 1 + τ_end}, which are
smooth and have linearly independent normals where two of them meet. Stein's operator of Theorem A.36,
applied to B^a, C and f, which lie in W^(k,∞) of the interior for every k, gives extensions to ℝ⁵ with bounded
derivatives of every order, hence smooth. Likewise extend u0 and u1 from the annulus Σ_τ0 to smooth functions on S.
Let ψ be a smooth function with compact support in D, equal to 1 on a neighbourhood of Ω, which exists since Ω is
compact and D open; multiply the extensions of f, u0 and u1 by ψ.

(iii) The solution. The operator P := −□̃ + 2 B^a ∂_a + 2 C = −g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b + 2 B^a ∂_a + 2 C acts on sections of
the trivial bundle D × ℝ^d and has the local form of Definition A.3, so P is normally hyperbolic for
g0, with principal symbol −g0⁻¹(ξ, ξ) id; (4.13), multiplied by 2, reads P u = 2 f. With n the future unit
normal of S and ∇ the connection of Theorem A.4, prescribing u and ∇_n u on S is equivalent to prescribing
u and ∂_τ u on S, since dτ(n) > 0 and the other terms of ∇_n u are tangential derivatives of u and multiples of u.
Theorem A.4 (5) therefore gives u ∈ C^∞(D) solving P u = 2 ψ f̃, f̃ the extension of f, with the data ψ ũ0,
ψ ũ1, the extensions of u0 and u1. On Ω the cut-off equals 1 and the extensions agree with B^a, C, f, u0 and u1, so u
restricted to Ω solves (4.13). ∎

**Lemma 4.10** (Each stage is a linear hyperbolic system.) Let m ≥ 1 and let everything of earlier stages
be given and smooth. Write the θ-mean of 𝒲(m_m, 0) as −(1/2) □̃ m_m + B̄·∂m_m + C̄ m_m, put 𝒲_φ(φ_m) := 𝒲(0, φ_m),
𝒮_m := −⟨𝒴_m⟩, and let Π_osc := 1 − ⟨·⟩ be the projection onto zero θ-mean. Impose e_m = 0, the θ-mean of
(4.12), and its oscillating part without the e_(m+1) term:

    (a) −(1/2) □̃ m_m + B̄·∂m_m + C̄ m_m = 𝒮_m − ⟨𝒲_φ(φ_m)⟩ − ⟨T̂ ĝ_(m+1)⟩,
    (b) L0 φ_m = −(1/2) m_m(ℓ, ℓ) − (1/2) q_m,
    (c) Π_osc T̂ ĝ_(m+1) = −Π_osc (𝒲(m_m, φ_m) + 𝒴_m),    (4.14)

with data (m_m, ∂_τ m_m), φ_m and ĝ_(m+1) on Σ_τ0. This system has a unique smooth solution on Ω.

*Proof.* Equation (b) is e_m = 0, since ℓ·dφ_m = −L0 φ_m. ⟨T̂ ĝ⟩ contains no X-derivative of ĝ, because the term −(ℓ·∂_X)
∂_θ ĝ of Lemma 4.8 has θ-mean zero; and ⟨𝒲_φ⟩ contains only dφ_m, because □̃φ_m multiplies ∂_θ W,
whose mean is zero. For Z := ∂_θ ĝ_(m+1), equation (c) is the transport

    −(ℓ·∂_X) Z + ℳ' Z = F

along ℓ, with ℳ' := Π_osc ℳ ∂_θ⁻¹ a bounded operator on smooth zero-mean profiles (Lemma 4.8; ∂_θ⁻¹
the zero-mean primitive): an ordinary differential equation along the integral curves of ℓ, which reach Σ_τ0 inside Ω
Lemma 2.6 (d). Its right-hand side contains □̃φ_m. Put Ψ_m := □̃φ_m. By the commutator identity for [L0, □̃]
(2.6) applied to (b), Ψ_m satisfies the transport

    L0 Ψ_m − (2/r) Ψ_m = −(1/2) □̃(m_m(ℓ, ℓ) + q_m) − (1/r)(∂_τ + ∂_r)(m_m(ℓ, ℓ) + q_m) − (3/r²) ∂_r φ_m,

and □̃(m_m(ℓ, ℓ)) = (□̃ m_m)(ℓ, ℓ) + first order, with □̃ m_m from (a): first order in (m_m, φ_m) and algebraic in
ĝ_(m+1). The datum of Ψ_m on Σ_τ0 is □̃φ_m computed from the data: φ_m is given there, ∂_τ φ_m = L0 φ_m + x̂·∂_x φ_m
with L0 φ_m from (b), and ∂_τ² φ_m follows from the τ-derivative of (b), which involves ∂_τ m_m on Σ_τ0. The system for
(m_m, φ_m, Ψ_m, Z) is then linear with smooth coefficients and closes without loss: m_m in H^(s+1), φ_m in H^(s+1),
Ψ_m and Z in H^s.

We solve it by Picard iteration on Ω. Given an iterate, the next one takes m_m from (a) by Lemma 4.9, with
the right-hand side evaluated at the given iterate, and φ_m, Ψ_m and Z from their transports, which are ordinary
differential equations with smooth coefficients along the integral curves of ℓ, solved from Σ_τ0 (Lemma 2.6 (d)).
Every iterate is smooth. The difference of two successive iterates solves the same linear system with zero data and
with the previous difference in its right-hand sides. For the profile Z, the statement and proof of Lemma 5.6
hold verbatim with L²(A(τ) × S¹) in place of L²(A(τ)) and with c := −ℳ', since −(ℓ·∂_X) = L0: at each X, c is a
bounded operator on the zero-mean functions in L²(S¹), bounded uniformly in X, and the largest eigenvalue of its
symmetric part is read as the supremum of ⟨z, c z⟩ over unit z. So the energy and transport estimates Lemma 5.5
and Lemma 5.6, in which λ plays no role, give for the sum e_n(τ) of the norms of the n-th difference, at the
regularities just stated, e_(n+1)(τ) ≤ C ∫_(τ0)^τ e_n(s) ds, hence e_n(τ) ≤ (C (τ − τ0))^n sup e_0 / n!. The iterates
converge and the limit solves the system; the same estimate, for zero data and zero right-hand side, gives uniqueness.
Ψ_m = □̃φ_m holds because, by (2.6) applied to (b), □̃φ_m solves the same transport as Ψ_m, so their
difference solves a homogeneous transport with zero data. Smooth data give smooth solutions, the iteration closing at
every s. ∎

### 4.6 The approximant

**Theorem 4.11** (The approximant to every order.) For every N ≥ 1 and every smooth choice of stage data
there are profiles g1, …, g_N, independent of λ, such that g_app = g0 + λ [g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j] is an approximant
with N stages of order K = N − 1 (Definition 4.3), at every regularity k, with C_R depending on k. Its oscillating
part of g1 is the wave W_TT of (2.11) with the second harmonic χ dv ⊗ dv of (4.9),
shifted in phase: g1 = m1 + W(X, θ + φ1(X)), W = W_TT + χ dv ⊗ dv. The background is g0 with μ' = (2/9) A² env².

Here the stage data are the data on Σ_τ0 of Lemma 4.10, (m_m, ∂_τ m_m), φ_m and ĝ_(m+1) for m = 1, …, N, each
smooth and ĝ_(m+1) of zero θ-mean.

*Proof.* Solve stage 0 (Section 4.4) and the stages m = 1, …, N (Lemma 4.10), with ĝ_(N+1) from stage
N. The unknowns φ_(N+1) and m_(N+1) are not included, so e_(N+1) = −q_(N+1) need not vanish; this is harmless, since
only ℛ^(m) with m ≤ N − 1 is used. By Lemma 4.7, ℛ^(m) = 0 for m ≤ N − 1: ℛ^(0) = 0 by the choice at stage 0
and e_1 = 0, and for 1 ≤ m ≤ N − 1 the mean and oscillating parts of (4.12) vanish by (4.14) and
e_(m+1) = 0. So R_u[G] = Σ_(m≥N) λ^m ℛ^(m) is λ^N times a profile bounded uniformly in λ, rational in λ through
G⁻¹. Since the scaled norm of an evaluated profile is bounded by the bounds of the profile and its derivatives, with no
loss for the oscillation Section 2.5, |Ric^H([G]_u)|_k ≤ C λ^N for every k.

Rewrite with the fixed phase v. With Ψ := Σ_(j≥2) λ^(j−2) φ_j, [G]_u(X) = G(X, v/λ + φ1 + λ Ψ). Expanding in λΨ by
Taylor's formula about θ + φ1 to order N gives profiles g_j(X, θ) independent of λ, with g1 = m1 + W(X, θ + φ1(X)), and a
remainder O(λ^(N+1)) in scaled norms. Ric^H contains at most two derivatives, each costing at most λ⁻¹ in the scaled
norms, so this remainder changes Ric^H by O(λ^(N−1)) in |·|_k.

(E1) holds because W is transverse (Lemma 4.5 (a)) and ⟨g1⟩ = m1. (E2) holds: by Lemma 4.2
(b) with Φ = φ1 + λΨ, the two-scale operator with the fixed phase satisfies R[G(·, · + Φ)](X, θ) = R_u[G](X, θ + Φ),
whose coefficient of λ⁰ is ℛ^(0)(X, θ + φ1) = 0, since ℛ^(−1) = 0. The coefficient R^(0) depends on the profiles only
through g1, because the coefficient of ∂_θ² g2 at that order is −(1/2) g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0, and the coefficient of λ in the
expansion of G(·, · + Φ) is g1; so R^(0) of g_app vanishes identically. (E3) holds with
K = N − 1. ∎

So the uniform existence theorem Theorem 6.1 applies to the approximant of any order, built from any smooth
stage data.

**Remark 4.12** Stage data for which the approximant's Cauchy data satisfy the constraints and the gauge
condition D = 0 to order N − 2 exist; they are chosen in Lemma 7.4, in the proof of Theorem 7.1.

# Part III. Uniform existence

## 5. Inequalities on the slices

This chapter collects the four estimates on the slices Σ_τ of Ω on which the uniform existence theorem
Theorem 6.1 rests: Sobolev and product inequalities in the scaled norms; a mollifier at scale λ that maps
functions on the annulus Σ_τ to functions on it, with the bounds of Bernstein and Friedrichs type; the energy inequality
for wave equations on Ω; and the estimate for transport along L0.

The domain Ω, its slices Σ_τ = A(τ) := {a ≤ |x| ≤ b(τ)} with outer radius b(τ), the numbers a, δ0, τ0 and τ_end, and the
properties of Ω under g0 and its small perturbations are those of Section 2.3, (2.8) and Lemma 2.6; the
scaled norms |f|_j = Σ_(i≤j) λ^i ‖∂^i f‖, with ‖·‖ the flat L²(Σ_τ) norm and ∂^i all spacetime coordinate derivatives of
order i, and the chain rule for profiles are those of Section 2.5 ((2.10)); and the numbers ε1 and s0
are those fixed in Section 2.5, after Lemma 2.8. All constants below depend on Ω, through a, b(τ0) and
δ0, and not on λ, and throughout

    0 < λ ≤ λ1 := min(1, δ0)/10.    (5.1)

The outer radius is b(τ) = V + 1 − τ + (τ_end − τ), so b' = −2, and b(τ) − a ≥ 1 + δ0 and b(τ) ≤ b(τ0) on [τ0, τ_end]
(Lemma 2.6 (f)).

### 5.1 Sobolev inequalities and products

**Lemma 5.1** (Sobolev inequality and products.) On A(τ),

    ‖f‖_(L^∞) ≤ C Σ_(i≤3) ‖∂_x^i f‖,     hence     ‖∂^i f‖_(L^∞) ≤ C λ^(−3−i) |f|_(i+3).    (5.2)

For k = 6, |f g|_k ≤ C λ⁻³ |f|_k |g|_k; and if m is a profile, |[m] f|_k ≤ C |f|_k.

*Proof.* The annuli A(τ) are images of the fixed annulus {a ≤ |x| ≤ a + 1 + δ0} under radial maps with derivatives of
all orders bounded uniformly in τ, since b(τ) − a ∈ [1 + δ0, b(τ0) − a]. So Sobolev's embedding of H³ into L^∞ in four
dimensions Theorem A.26 holds on A(τ) with a constant independent of τ. Applied to ∂^i f, and with λ ≤ 1,
it gives ‖∂^i f‖_(L^∞) ≤ C Σ_(j≤3) λ^(−i−j) λ^(i+j) ‖∂^(i+j) f‖ ≤ C λ^(−3−i) |f|_(i+3).

For products, expand λ^j ∂^j (f g) for j ≤ 6 by Leibniz's rule into terms λ^i ∂^i f · λ^(j−i) ∂^(j−i) g and put the
factor with at most three derivatives in L^∞. If i ≤ 3, then ‖λ^i ∂^i f‖_(L^∞) ≤ C λ⁻³ |f|_(i+3) ≤ C λ⁻³ |f|_6 by
(5.2), and ‖λ^(j−i) ∂^(j−i) g‖ ≤ |g|_6; if i ≥ 4, then j − i ≤ 2 and the roles are exchanged. For the last
claim, the chain rule for profiles in Section 2.5 gives ‖λ^i ∂^i [m]‖_(L^∞) ≤ C_i for every i, so each term λ^i ∂^i
[m] · λ^(j−i) ∂^(j−i) f of λ^j ∂^j ([m] f) is bounded in L² by C |f|_k. ∎

### 5.2 The mollifier

The decomposition of the remainder in the proof of Theorem 6.1 needs a smoothing operator at scale λ on
each slice. A Fourier multiplier supported in {|ξ| ≤ 1/λ}, as in [Tou23a, Section 3.2.3, p. 21], needs no boundary; on
the annulus A(τ) we use a compactly supported mollifier whose averaging ball is shifted 2λ inward near the outer sphere
and outward near the inner one, so that it maps functions on A(τ) to functions on A(τ).

**Lemma 5.2** (The shift profile.) Let L be the function on ℝ equal to 1 on (−∞, 7/20], to −1 on [13/20, ∞), and
linear on [7/20, 13/20], and let σ0 be its mollification with a smooth even nonnegative kernel of integral one supported
in [−1/120, 1/120], restricted to [0, 1]. Then σ0 is smooth and non-increasing, |σ0| ≤ 1, |σ0'| ≤ 20/3 ≤ 7, σ0 = 1 on
[0, 1/3] and σ0 = −1 on [2/3, 1].

*Proof.* σ0 is smooth as a mollification. Its derivative is the mollification of L', which equals −20/3 on (7/20, 13/20)
and 0 elsewhere; as the kernel is nonnegative with integral one, σ0' takes values in [−20/3, 0]. Likewise |σ0| ≤ 1
because |L| ≤ 1. For t ≤ 1/3 = 40/120 the window [t − 1/120, t + 1/120] lies in (−∞, 41/120] ⊂ (−∞, 7/20], where L = 1,
so σ0(t) = 1; for t ≥ 2/3 = 80/120 it lies in [79/120, ∞) ⊂ [13/20, ∞), where L = −1. ∎

For f on A(τ) put

    σ(τ, x) := σ0((|x| − a)/(b(τ) − a)),     Φ(x) := x + 2 λ σ(τ, x) x̂,

and fix ρ ∈ C_c^∞(B_1) with ρ ≥ 0 and ∫ ρ = 1. The mollifier is

    𝒫 f (x) := ∫ ρ(z) f(Φ(x) − λ z) dz          (spatial, at fixed τ).    (5.3)

**Lemma 5.3** (The shifted ball stays in the annulus.) For x ∈ A(τ), |z| ≤ 1 and t ∈ [0, 1], the point x +
t (Φ(x) − λ z − x) lies in A(τ), the segment from x to Φ(x) − λz has length at most 3λ, and Φ(x) − λz lies at distance
at least λ from the boundary of A(τ) near either sphere. The map Φ is a diffeomorphism of A(τ) onto its image, DΦ = I +
λ E with E bounded with all its derivatives, and the eigenvalues of DΦ lie in [3/10, 1] (radially) and in [2/5, 1 +
2λ1/a] (angularly). For t ∈ [0, 1] the map x ↦ x + t (Φ(x) − λz − x) has Jacobian eigenvalues at least 3/10 radially
and 2/5 angularly.

*Proof.* The length of the segment is |2λ σ x̂ − λ z| ≤ 2λ + λ = 3λ. Near the inner sphere, where |x| − a ≤ (b − a)/3,
σ = 1, and for t ∈ [0, 1]

    |x + t (2λ x̂ − λ z)| ≥ x̂·(x + t (2λ x̂ − λ z)) ≥ |x| + 2tλ − tλ = |x| + tλ,

so the segment stays outside the inner sphere and its end point Φ(x) − λz lies at least λ outside it; it stays inside
the outer sphere because |x| + 3λ ≤ a + (b − a)/3 + 3λ < b. Near the outer sphere, where |x| − a ≥ 2(b − a)/3, σ = −1,
and |x − t (2λ x̂ + λ z)| ≤ |x| − 2tλ + tλ = |x| − tλ, so the segment stays inside the outer sphere, its end point at
least λ inside it, and outside the inner sphere because |x| − 3λ ≥ a + 2(b − a)/3 − 3λ > a. In the middle third the
distance to the boundary is at least (b − a)/3 ≥ 1/3 > 3λ, which exceeds the length of the segment. So every point of
the segment lies in A(τ).

The map Φ is radial, r ↦ r + 2λ σ0((r − a)/(b − a)), so DΦ has the radial eigenvalue 1 + 2λ σ0'/(b − a) and three
angular eigenvalues 1 + 2λσ/r. Since λ/(b − a) ≤ λ1/(1 + δ0) ≤ 1/20 and σ0' ∈ [−7, 0] (Lemma 5.2), the radial one
lies in [1 − 14/20, 1] = [3/10, 1]. Since σ < 0 only where r − a > (b − a)/3 ≥ 1/3, so r > 1/3, and |σ| ≤ 1, the angular
ones are at least 1 − 2λ1/(1/3) ≥ 1 − 3/5 = 2/5, and at most 1 + 2λ1/a. A radial map whose radial and angular
eigenvalues are positive is a diffeomorphism onto its image, and DΦ − I = λ E with E built from σ0' , σ, r⁻¹ and their
derivatives, bounded with all derivatives. For the last claim, the Jacobian of x ↦ x + t (Φ(x) − λz − x) is (1 − t) I +
t DΦ, with the eigenvalues 1 + t (e − 1), e those of DΦ, which lie between 1 and e. ∎

**Lemma 5.4** (The mollifier.) For f on A(τ) and a smooth bounded function or profile m, with E1 and E2
bounded matrices of functions:

    (M1)   ‖𝒫 f‖ ≤ C ‖f‖;    (5.4)
    (M2)   ‖∂_x 𝒫 f‖ ≤ C λ⁻¹ ‖f‖;    (5.5)
    (M3)   ‖f − 𝒫 f‖ ≤ C λ ‖∂_x f‖;    (5.6)
    (M4)   ∂_x 𝒫 f = 𝒫(∂_x f) + λ E1 𝒫(∂_x f),   and   λ ‖𝒫 ∂_x f‖ ≤ C ‖f‖;    (5.7)
    (M5)   ‖[m, 𝒫] ∂_x f‖ ≤ C ‖∂_x m‖_∞ ‖f‖   and   ‖[m, 𝒫] f‖ ≤ C λ ‖∂_x m‖_∞ ‖f‖;    (5.8)
    (M6)   ∂_τ 𝒫 f = 𝒫(∂_τ f) + λ E2 𝒫(∂_x f).    (5.9)

Iterating, λ^j ‖∂^j 𝒫 f‖ ≤ C Σ_(i≤j) λ^i ‖∂^i f‖, and the same holds with 1 − 𝒫 in place of 𝒫.

*Proof.* (M1): for fixed z, x ↦ Φ(x) − λz maps A(τ) into itself with Jacobian bounded above and below uniformly in λ
(Lemma 5.3); changing variables in ‖f(Φ(·) − λz)‖ and integrating against ρ(z) gives (M1).

(M2): with y = Φ(x) − λz, 𝒫 f(x) = λ⁻⁴ ∫ ρ((Φ(x) − y)/λ) f(y) dy, and ∂_x falls on ρ, producing λ⁻¹ DΦ^T (∇ρ)((Φ(x) −
y)/λ); the bound follows as in (M1).

(M3): f(x) − f(Φ(x) − λz) is the integral of ∂_x f along the segment from x to Φ(x) − λz, of length at most 3λ, which
stays in A(τ) (Lemma 5.3). Writing the segment as x + t (Φ(x) − λz − x), t ∈ [0, 1], and changing variables x ↦
x + t (Φ(x) − λz − x), whose Jacobian has eigenvalues at least 3/10 radially and 2/5 angularly (Lemma 5.3), gives
the bound.

(M4): by the chain rule ∂_x [f(Φ(x) − λz)] = DΦ^T (∂f)(Φ(x) − λz) = (I + λ E^T)(∂f)(Φ(x) − λz), which integrated against
ρ(z) is the identity with E1 := E^T. Further (∂_j f)(Φ(x) − λz) = −λ⁻¹ ∂_(z_j) [f(Φ(x) − λz)], and integrating by parts
onto ρ gives 𝒫(∂_j f) = λ⁻¹ ∫ (∂_j ρ)(z) f(Φ(x) − λz) dz, so λ ‖𝒫 ∂_x f‖ ≤ C ‖f‖ as in (M1).

(M5) is Friedrichs' lemma in this form:

    [m, 𝒫] ∂_j f (x) = ∫ ρ(z) (m(x) − m(Φ(x) − λz)) (∂_j f)(Φ(x) − λz) dz.

Integrating by parts in z as in (M4), the factor λ⁻¹ meets either ∂_z of m(Φ(x) − λz), which is −λ (∂m)(Φ(x) − λz), or
m(x) − m(Φ(x) − λz), whose size is at most 3λ ‖∂_x m‖_∞ by the length of the segment. Both are O(λ ‖∂_x m‖_∞), and the
change of variables of (M1) gives the first bound. The second is the same without the integration by parts.

(M6): σ depends on τ through b(τ), with ∂_τ σ = −σ0' (|x| − a) b'/(b − a)², bounded since b' = −2 and b − a ≥ 1. So
∂_τ [f(τ, Φ(τ, x) − λz)] = (∂_τ f)(Φ(x) − λz) + 2λ (∂_τ σ) x̂·(∂_x f)(Φ(x) − λz); integrating against ρ gives (M6) with
E2 := 2 (∂_τ σ) x̂.

Higher derivatives follow by induction, each derivative of 𝒫 f being moved onto f by (M4) and (M6) at the cost of
bounded factors. ∎

### 5.3 The energy inequality

**Lemma 5.5** (Energy inequality.) Let g̃ be a Lorentzian metric on Ω with |g̃ − g0| ≤ ε1, ε1 the number fixed
after Lemma 2.8, so that Lemma 2.6 (e) applies to g̃ and |g̃⁻¹| ≤ (s0 − ε1)⁻¹ by
Lemma 2.8, and with ‖∂g̃‖_∞ ≤ Λ. Let u, a function or a Cartesian array, satisfy −(1/2) g̃^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b u =
f on Ω. Then for τ ∈ [τ0, τ_end],

    ‖∂u(τ)‖ + ‖u(τ)‖ ≤ C(Λ) (‖∂u(τ0)‖ + ‖u(τ0)‖ + ∫_(τ0)^τ ‖f(s)‖ ds).    (5.10)

*Proof.* Take the multiplier Y := −g̃⁻¹ dτ, future timelike by Lemma 2.6 (e), the energy current
J^a = T^a_b Y^b with T_ab = ∂_a u ∂_b u − (1/2) g̃_ab g̃(du, du), and apply the divergence theorem on Ω ∩ {τ0 ≤ s ≤ τ}
in the coordinate density. The flux through Σ_τ equals the flux through Σ_τ0, minus the fluxes through the lateral
boundaries, plus the bulk integral. The lateral boundaries are spacelike with Ω to their past
(Lemma 2.6 (b), (c), (e)), so their fluxes are nonnegative and are dropped. The fluxes through
Σ_τ are comparable to ‖∂u‖², by the dominant energy condition, since Y and the normal are uniformly timelike by
Lemma 2.6 (e) and |g̃⁻¹| ≤ (s0 − ε1)⁻¹. The bulk is bounded by C(Λ)(‖∂u‖² + ‖f‖ ‖∂u‖), since ∂g̃,
g̃⁻¹ and ∂Y = g̃⁻¹ (∂g̃) g̃⁻¹ dτ are bounded, the constant depending also on Ω and s0 − ε1. The norm ‖u‖ is added through
∂_τ ‖u‖² = 2 ⟨u, ∂_τ u⟩ plus the boundary term b'(τ) ∫_(|x|=b) |u|² ≤ 0. Gronwall's inequality concludes. ∎

### 5.4 The transport estimate

**Lemma 5.6** (Transport estimate.) Let L0 φ − c(X) φ = f on Ω, with φ a function or an array and c a
bounded function, or a bounded matrix acting on the components of φ. Then

    ‖φ(τ)‖ ≤ e^(C (τ − τ0)) (‖φ(τ0)‖ + ∫_(τ0)^τ ‖f(s)‖ ds),     C := max(0, sup_Ω (c − 3/(2r))),    (5.11)

where for a matrix c is read as the largest eigenvalue of its symmetric part. For example, c = 2/r gives C = 1/(2a),
since 2/r − 3/(2r) = 1/(2r) ≤ 1/(2a).

*Proof.* Since L0 = ∂_τ − x̂·∂_x, ∂_τ φ = L0 φ + x̂·∂_x φ. In ℝ⁴, div x̂ = Σ_i ∂_i (x_i/r) = 4/r − |x|²/r³ = 3/r, so the
divergence theorem on A(τ), with outer normal x̂ on {|x| = b} and −x̂ on {|x| = a}, gives

    ∫_(A(τ)) 2 φ x̂·∂_x φ = ∫_(A(τ)) x̂·∂_x (φ²) = ∫_(|x|=b) φ² − ∫_(|x|=a) φ² − ∫_(A(τ)) (3/r) φ².

The outer sphere moves with speed b', so

    ∂_τ ‖φ‖² = 2 ⟨φ, f + c φ⟩ − ∫ (3/r) φ² + (1 + b') ∫_(|x|=b) φ² − ∫_(|x|=a) φ²,

and 1 + b' = −1 < 0. As ⟨φ, c φ⟩ − ∫ (3/(2r)) φ² ≤ sup_Ω (c − 3/(2r)) ‖φ‖², this gives ∂_τ ‖φ‖² ≤ 2 ‖φ‖ ‖f‖ + 2 C
‖φ‖², hence ∂_τ ‖φ‖ ≤ ‖f‖ + C ‖φ‖, and Gronwall's inequality concludes. ∎

## 6. Uniform existence

This chapter proves the existence theorem on which the main theorem rests: given an approximate solution of high order
and Cauchy data close to it, the solution of the reduced equations exists on the fixed domain Ω for every small λ, and
its departure from the approximate solution obeys estimates uniform in λ. The proof turns on one decision. The
approximate solution is carried to high order K, so that the remainder is O(λ^K) and every nonlinear term is beaten by a
power of λ rather than by the size of the data. What then has to be uniform in λ is a linear estimate on the large
background. Its only coefficient of size 1/λ couples one scalar component of the remainder to the wave; that component's
own equation has no such coefficient; and the coupling is absorbed by a phase shift of the wave (Lemma 6.2).
This is the mechanism of [Tou23a, Section 3.2.3, p. 21], with a compactly supported mollifier adapted to the slices in
place of his Fourier cut-off.

Throughout, g0, L0 = ∂_τ − x̂·∂_x and □̃ := g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b (acting componentwise) are those of (2.3) and
Section 2.2, ℓ = g0⁻¹dv = −L0 is that of Proposition 2.5 (c), and (2.6) is the commutator identity
of Proposition 2.5 (e). D and Ric^H are the gauge vector and the reduced Ricci
tensor of (2.9), so that Ric^H(g) = −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b g + Q(X; g)(∂g, ∂g), with second derivatives of g
entering only through the first term. The domain Ω of (2.8), its slices Σ_τ = A(τ) = {a ≤ |x| ≤ b(τ)}, the times
τ0 < τ_end and the properties (a)–(f) of Ω are those of Lemma 2.6. Profiles f(X, θ) on Ω × S¹, their evaluations
[f](X) := f(X, v(X)/λ), their θ-means ⟨f⟩, the scaled norms |f|_j of (2.10) and the chain rule ∂_a [f] = λ⁻¹
(∂_a v) [∂_θ f] + [∂_a f] are those of Section 2.5. The number ε1, with 0 < ε1 < min(s0, μ0/a² − 1), is the one
fixed in Section 2.5, after Lemma 2.8: every g̃ with |g̃ − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω is Lorentzian with |g̃⁻¹| ≤
(s0 − ε1)⁻¹ (Lemma 2.8) and satisfies the conclusions of Lemma 2.6 (e) (Lemma 2.7). All
constants below depend on Ω and not on λ, and 0 < λ ≤ λ1
:= min(1, δ0)/10 ((5.1)). The inequalities on the slices used below are the Sobolev and product bounds of
Lemma 5.1, the compactly supported mollifier 𝒫 adapted to the annuli with its properties (M1)–(M6)
(Lemma 5.4), the energy inequality (5.10) of Lemma 5.5 for −(1/2) g̃^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b u = f with |g̃ −
g0| ≤ ε1, and the transport estimate (5.11) of Lemma 5.6 along L0.

### 6.1 The theorem

**Theorem 6.1** (Uniform existence.) Fix k = 6 and K ≥ 6. Let g_app be an approximant with N stages
of order K at regularity k (Definition 4.3): g_app is (4.4), with profiles g_j bounded with all their
derivatives independently of λ, and it satisfies (E1)–(E3) there, (E3) with the constant C_R. Suppose moreover:

- (E4) *The data*: g is a Cauchy datum on Σ_τ0 for Ric^H(g) = 0 with w := g − g_app satisfying

      Data(w) := ‖w‖ + Σ_(1≤j≤k+1) λ^(j−1) ‖∂_x^j w‖ + Σ_(j≤k) λ^j ‖∂_x^j ∂_τ w‖ ≤ C_D λ^K   on Σ_τ0.

Then there are λ0 > 0 and M, depending on Ω, k, K, C_R, C_D and the bounds on the profiles but not on λ, such that for 0
< λ ≤ λ0 the solution g of Ric^H(g) = 0 with these data exists on Ω, is unique there among C² solutions with |g − g0| ≤
ε1 on Ω, is smooth if the data are, and

    w = h + φ [∂_θ g1],     with     𝒩(τ) ≤ M λ^K   on [τ0, τ_end],    (6.1)

𝒩 the quantity (6.7) (energies of h, of φ and of □̃φ to order k, scaled). In particular ‖w(τ)‖ + ‖∂w(τ)‖ ≤ M
λ^(K−1), |w| ≤ M λ^(K−3) and |∂w| ≤ M λ^(K−4) on Ω, and |g − g0| ≤ C λ, |∂g| ≤ C.

The proof occupies the rest of the chapter: the linear structure in Section 6.2 and
Section 6.3, the bootstrap in Section 6.4, existence, continuation and uniqueness in
Section 6.5.

### 6.2 The linearisation and its one large coefficient

Let R = R_v be the two-scale operator of Definition 4.1, so that Ric^H([G]) = [R[G]] for a profile G; by
Lemma 4.2 (a) it satisfies the translation identity (4.2), R[G(·, · + c)](X, θ) =
R[G](X, θ + c) for every constant c.

For the profile of g_app, R has the expansion (4.3), R = λ⁻¹ R^(−1) + R^(0) + λ R^(1) + …, with
R^(−1) = −(1/2) g0⁻¹(dv, dv) ∂_θ² g1 = 0 because dv is null for g0 (as shown after (4.3)).

Let P(w) := (d/ds) Ric^H(g_app + s w) at s = 0. Then

    P(w) = −(1/2) g_app^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b w + (1/2) λ⁻¹ s(w) [∂_θ² g1] + B·∂w + C·w,  s(w) := w(ℓ, ℓ),    (6.2)

with B and C profiles (bounded with all X- and θ-derivatives; here C is a coefficient, not a constant). Indeed, expand
g_app⁻¹ to second order in the reduced equations. Second derivatives of g_app enter P only through (1/2) w^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b
g_app, where w^(ab) := g_app^(ac) g_app^(bd) w_cd, because second derivatives of g enter Ric^H(g) only through −(1/2)
g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b g. By the chain rule ∂_a ∂_b [λ g1] = λ⁻¹ ∂_a v ∂_b v [∂_θ² g1] + O(1), and w^(ab) ∂_a v ∂_b v = w(ℓ_app,
ℓ_app) with

    ℓ_app := g_app⁻¹ dv = ℓ − λ ⟨g1⟩(ℓ, ·)^♯ + O(λ²),

by (E1): the oscillating part of g1 drops out of the O(λ) term, since (g1 − ⟨g1⟩)(ℓ, ·) = 0. So w(ℓ_app, ℓ_app) = s(w) +
O(λ)|w|, and that difference times λ⁻¹ goes into C. All other terms are linear in w or ∂w with coefficients built from
g_app and ∂g_app, which are bounded.

For a profile Y, P([Y]) = [λ⁻¹ T Y + P_0 Y], with

    T Y = −(ℓ_app·∂_X ∂_θ Y) − (1/2)(g_app^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b v) ∂_θ Y + B·(dv ⊗ ∂_θ Y)
          + (1/2) Y(ℓ, ℓ) ∂_θ² g1 − (1/2) n1 ∂_θ² Y,

where λ n1 := g_app⁻¹(dv, dv) = −λ ⟨g1⟩(ℓ, ℓ) + O(λ²) by (E1): the λ⁻² part of the principal term, −(1/2) λ⁻²
g_app⁻¹(dv, dv) ∂_θ² Y, is of size λ⁻¹ and is kept in T. The coefficient (1/2) λ⁻¹ s(w) [∂_θ² g1] is the only one of
size λ⁻¹, and it couples the single scalar s = w(ℓ, ℓ) to the wave. This is the five-dimensional form of the quasilinear
coupling described in [Tou23a, Section 3.2.2, p. 20].

**Lemma 6.2** (The phase-shift identity.) Under (E2), T(∂_θ g1) = λ T1 with T1 a profile.

*Proof.* Differentiate (4.2) for G the profile of g_app at c = 0: the linearisation of R at G in the
direction ∂_θ G equals ∂_θ R[G]. Now ∂_θ G = λ ∂_θ g1 + λ² ∂_θ g2 + …, and P([Y]) = [D_G R[Y]], so the left side is λ⁻¹
T(λ ∂_θ g1 + λ² ∂_θ g2 + …) + P_0(λ ∂_θ g1 + …) = T(∂_θ g1) + O(λ). The right side is ∂_θ(λ⁻¹ R^(−1) + R^(0)) + O(λ) =
O(λ), since R^(−1) = 0 and R^(0) = 0 by (E2). Both sides are expansions in powers of λ with profile coefficients, the
remainders λ times bounded profiles. ∎

A constant shift of the phase is a symmetry of the leading equation, so its generator ∂_θ g1 is annihilated by the λ⁻¹
part of the linearised operator. This one line is the analytic content of Touati's transport and polarization conditions
at first order.

### 6.3 The decomposition and the regained derivative

Write G1 := [∂_θ g1] and G2 := [∂_θ² g1]. By (E1), G1(ℓ, ·) = G2(ℓ, ·) = 0; differentiating g1(ℓ, ·) − ⟨g1⟩(ℓ, ·) = 0,
also (∂_X ∂_θ g1)(ℓ, ℓ) = 0, and (∂_X ∂_X ∂_θ g1)(ℓ, ℓ) is bounded.

**Lemma 6.3** For φ(X) (independent of θ) and the metric g = g_app + w,

    −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b (φ G1) + B·∂(φ G1) + C·(φ G1)
        = −λ⁻¹ (ℓ_app·∂φ) G2 + λ⁻¹ φ [T(∂_θ g1)] − (1/2)(□̃_app φ) G1 + B1·∂φ + C1 φ + 𝒬_φ,    (6.3)

with □̃_app := g_app^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b, B1·∂φ and C1 φ with bounded profile coefficients, and 𝒬_φ collecting the terms with a
factor of w:

    |𝒬_φ| ≤ C |w| (λ⁻² |φ| + λ⁻¹ |∂φ| + |∂²φ|),

and likewise for derivatives, in scaled norms; the second derivatives ∂²φ in 𝒬_φ multiply G1 only.

*Proof.* Expand ∂_a ∂_b (φ G1) by the chain rule. The λ⁻² term carries g⁻¹(dv, dv) = g_app⁻¹(dv, dv) + O(|w|), whose
first part is λ n1 and belongs to φ T(∂_θ g1). The λ⁻¹ terms are the cross term −λ⁻¹ g^(ab) ∂_a φ ∂_b v G2, with g^(ab)
∂_b v = ℓ_app^a + O(|w|), and φ times the λ⁻¹ part of P(G1), which is φ T(∂_θ g1) by the definition of T. The second
derivatives of φ appear only as −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b φ G1 = −(1/2)(□̃_app φ) G1 + (a term with a factor w, multiplying
G1). The rest has bounded coefficients. ∎

Let s := s(w) and define φ by the transport

    L0 φ = −(1/2) 𝒫 s,      φ = 0 on Σ_τ0,    (6.4)

that is ℓ·∂φ = (1/2) 𝒫 s. It exists on Ω, because the integral curves of L0 followed to the past stay in Ω and meet Σ_τ0
(Lemma 2.6 (d)). Put h := w − φ G1. Then s(h) = s(w) = s, since G1(ℓ, ℓ) = 0. Write F := −Ric^H(g_app) and 𝒬(w) for
the terms of Ric^H(g_app + w) of second and higher order in (w, ∂w) other than the principal part. The equation
Ric^H(g_app + w) = 0 reads −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b w + (1/2) λ⁻¹ s G2 + B·∂w + C·w = F + 𝒬(w), and by (6.3),
(6.4) and Lemma 6.2 it becomes

    −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b h + B·∂h + C·h = F + 𝒬(w) − 𝒬_φ − (1/2) λ⁻¹ ((1 − 𝒫) s) G2
          + λ⁻¹ ((ℓ_app − ℓ)·∂φ) G2 − φ [T1] + (1/2)(□̃_app φ) G1 − B1·∂φ − C1 φ.    (6.5)

Indeed, the λ⁻¹ terms of (6.3) are −λ⁻¹ (ℓ_app·∂φ) G2 = −λ⁻¹ (ℓ·∂φ) G2 − λ⁻¹ ((ℓ_app − ℓ)·∂φ) G2 = −(1/2) λ⁻¹
(𝒫 s) G2 − λ⁻¹ ((ℓ_app − ℓ)·∂φ) G2 and λ⁻¹ φ [T(∂_θ g1)] = φ [T1]; subtracting from the equation for w leaves (1/2) λ⁻¹
s G2 − (1/2) λ⁻¹ (𝒫 s) G2 = (1/2) λ⁻¹ ((1 − 𝒫) s) G2 on the left, which is moved to the right.

Every coefficient on the right of (6.5) is a bounded profile. The one coefficient of size 1/λ left multiplies (1 −
𝒫) s, which is O(λ ∂s) by (M3), and |ℓ_app − ℓ| ≤ C λ. Two things remain: □̃_app φ has two derivatives of φ, and φ is
driven by s.

**Lemma 6.4** (The ℓℓ component.) The component s satisfies

    □̃ s = c1·∂h + c0·h + c2·∂φ + c3 φ − 2q F(ℓ, ℓ) − 2q 𝒬(w)(ℓ, ℓ) + 2q 𝒬_φ(ℓ, ℓ)
          + Σ_(b,i) c^(bi) (∂_b ∂_i h)(ℓ, ℓ),

where (∂_b ∂_i h)(ℓ, ℓ) := (∂_b ∂_i h_mn) ℓ^m ℓ^n, c0, …, c3 are bounded coefficients (profiles, and profiles times the
function q of the proof, which depends on w and so is not a profile; the terms 2 g0^(ab) ∂_a(ℓ ⊗ ℓ)·∂_b h and h·□̃(ℓ ⊗ ℓ)
carry no q), the sum runs over pairs with i spatial, |c^(bi)| ≤ C(λ + |w|) and |∂c^(bi)| ≤ C(1 + |∂w|), and 𝒬_φ(ℓ, ℓ)
contains no second derivative of φ. There is no coefficient of size 1/λ.

*Proof.* □̃ s = (□̃ h)(ℓ, ℓ) + 2 g0^(ab) ∂_a(ℓ ⊗ ℓ)·∂_b h + h·□̃(ℓ ⊗ ℓ). Write g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b = q g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b + Σ
c^(bi) ∂_b ∂_i with q := g0^(ττ)/g^(ττ); here g^(ττ) ≠ 0, since the slices stay spacelike for g (Lemma 2.6 (e)), and
c^(bi) = O(|g⁻¹ − g0⁻¹|) = O(λ + |w|); so (□̃ h)(ℓ, ℓ) = q (g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b h)(ℓ, ℓ) + Σ c^(bi) (∂_b ∂_i h)(ℓ, ℓ).
Contract (6.5) with ℓ ⊗ ℓ: G2(ℓ, ℓ) = G1(ℓ, ℓ) = 0 removes the 1/λ terms and the □̃_app φ term exactly; B1·∂φ and
C1 φ stay of first order; the second derivatives of φ in 𝒬_φ multiply G1 and also drop. ∎

**Lemma 6.5** (The commutator transport.) Ψ := □̃ φ satisfies

    L0 Ψ − (2/r) Ψ = −(1/2) □̃ 𝒫 s − (1/r)(∂_τ + ∂_r) 𝒫 s − (3/r²) ∂_r φ,    (6.6)

and □̃_app φ = Ψ + c^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b φ with |c| ≤ C λ. Every second derivative of φ is a combination, with bounded
coefficients, of L0 𝒫 s, ∂_x 𝒫 s, ∂φ and the spatial Hessian ∂_x² φ, which satisfies the transport

    L0(∂_x² φ) = −(1/2) ∂_x² 𝒫 s + (∂_x x̂) * ∂_x² φ + (∂_x² x̂) * ∂_x φ,

where * denotes contractions with bounded coefficients.

*Proof.* Apply (2.6) to φ: L0 Ψ = □̃ L0 φ + (2/r)(Ψ + (∂_τ + ∂_r) L0 φ) − (3/r²) ∂_r φ, and substitute L0
φ = −(1/2) 𝒫 s. Next, g_app⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ = O(λ) gives □̃_app φ − Ψ = c^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b φ with |c| ≤ C λ. For the second
derivatives, ∂_τ = L0 + x̂·∂_x, L0 L0 φ = −(1/2) L0 𝒫 s and L0 ∂_i φ = ∂_i L0 φ + (∂_i x̂^m) ∂_m φ; the commutator [L0,
∂_i] = (∂_i x̂^m) ∂_m involves spatial derivatives only, since the ∂_τ coefficient of L0 is the constant 1. Applying ∂_i
∂_j to L0 φ = −(1/2) 𝒫 s and commuting gives the transport of ∂_x² φ. ∎

### 6.4 The energy and the bootstrap

On [τ0, τ] (wherever the solution exists) put

    𝒩(τ) := Σ_(j≤k) λ^j ( ‖∂^j ∂h‖ + ‖∂^j Ψ‖ + ‖∂^j ∂φ‖ + λ ‖∂^j ∂_x² φ‖ ) + ‖h‖ + ‖φ‖.    (6.7)

*Proof of Theorem 6.1.* The proof is in eight steps; the first seven are an a priori bound, the eighth
gives existence.

**Step 1** (what 𝒩 controls). |w|_(k+1) ≤ C 𝒩. Indeed w = h + φ G1. For h, ‖h‖ ≤ 𝒩 and, for 1 ≤ i ≤ k + 1, λ^i ‖∂^i h‖ ≤
λ · λ^(i−1) ‖∂^(i−1) ∂h‖ ≤ 𝒩. For φ G1, the Leibniz rule writes λ^j ∂^j (φ G1) as a sum of λ^i ∂^i φ · λ^(j−i) ∂^(j−i)
G1, and λ^(j−i) |∂^(j−i) G1| ≤ C by the chain rule (each derivative of the evaluation costs at most λ⁻¹); moreover ‖φ‖ ≤
𝒩 and λ^i ‖∂^i φ‖ = λ · λ^(i−1) ‖∂^(i−1) ∂φ‖ ≤ λ 𝒩 for 1 ≤ i ≤ k + 1. Hence, by the Sobolev bound ‖∂^i f‖_(L^∞) ≤ C
λ^(−3−i) |f|_(i+3) of (5.2), ‖∂^i w‖_(L^∞) ≤ C λ^(−3−i) 𝒩 for i ≤ 4, and |∂w|_k ≤ λ⁻¹ |w|_(k+1) ≤ C λ⁻¹ 𝒩.

**Step 2** (data). φ = 0 on Σ_τ0, so h = w there. The derivatives of h, φ and Ψ on Σ_τ0 of order up to k + 1 in τ are
fixed by (6.4), (6.5) and the equation for w, whose coefficients obey the scaled bounds of the chain
rule; solving for ∂_τ² by induction gives 𝒩(τ0) ≤ C (Data(w) + C_R λ^K) ≤ C (C_D + C_R) λ^K. (On Σ_τ0, ∂_τ φ = −(1/2) 𝒫
s, and ∂_x 𝒫 s = 𝒫 ∂_x s + O(λ) 𝒫 ∂_x s by (M4): no 1/λ enters.)

**Step 3** (the bootstrap). Suppose 𝒩 ≤ 2 M λ^K on [τ0, τ*], with M to be fixed. Then by Step 1 |w| ≤ C M λ^(K−3)
and |∂w| ≤ C M λ^(K−4) ≤ C M λ², so for λ ≤ λ0(M) the metric g = g_app + w satisfies |g − g0| ≤ ε1 (so that the domain
lemma and the energy inequality apply to it) and |∂g| ≤ Λ with Λ independent of M.

**Step 4** (h). Apply ∂^α, |α| = j ≤ k, to (6.5), apply the energy inequality to each component, and multiply by
λ^j. The commutator [∂^α, g^(ab)] ∂_a ∂_b h has terms ∂^i g · ∂^(j−i+1) ∂h with i ≥ 1. With ‖∂^i g_app‖_∞ ≤ C λ^(1−i),
λ^j times each is at most C λ^(j−i+1) ‖∂^(j−i+1) ∂h‖ ≤ C 𝒩; the w part is at most C M λ^(K−4) 𝒩 (for i ≤ 4 with ∂^i w in
L^∞; for i ≥ 5 with ∂^i w in L² and the other factor in L^∞ by the Sobolev bound). The right side of (6.5):

- λ^j ‖∂^α F‖ ≤ C_R λ^K by (E3);
- B·∂h and C·h give C 𝒩 (profile coefficients cost λ⁻¹ per derivative, compensated by the weights);
- the term λ⁻¹ ((1 − 𝒫) s) G2 gives Σ_i λ^(i−1) ‖∂^i (1 − 𝒫) s‖ ≤ C Σ_i λ^i ‖∂^i ∂s‖ ≤ C 𝒩 by (M3), (M4), (M6);
- λ⁻¹ ((ℓ_app − ℓ)·∂φ) G2 and φ [T1] give C 𝒩;
- (1/2)(□̃_app φ) G1 = (1/2) Ψ G1 + (1/2)(c ∂²φ) G1 with |c| ≤ C λ, and by Lemma 6.5 λ ∂²φ is
  controlled by λ L0 𝒫 s, λ ∂_x 𝒫 s, λ ∂φ and λ ∂_x² φ, each at most C 𝒩 at every level j ≤ k (no Bernstein inequality
  is needed: λ^(j+1) ‖∂^j L0 𝒫 s‖ ≤ C λ^(j+1) ‖∂^j ∂s‖ by (M4), (M6));
- B1·∂φ and C1 φ give C 𝒩;
- the nonlinear terms 𝒬(w) and 𝒬_φ are at most C λ⁻⁵ 𝒩² + C λ⁻³ 𝒩² by the product bound and Step 1 (the worst is
  quadratic in ∂w: |∂w ∂w|_k ≤ C λ⁻³ |∂w|_k² ≤ C λ⁻⁵ 𝒩²), hence at most C M² λ^(2K−5) ≤ C M² λ^(K+1), as K ≥ 6.

So

    Σ_(j≤k) λ^j ‖∂^j ∂h(τ)‖ + ‖h(τ)‖ ≤ C ( 𝒩(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^(τ) (𝒩 + C_R λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1)) ).

**Step 5** (φ). Apply ∂^α to (6.4): L0 ∂^α φ = −(1/2) ∂^α 𝒫 s + [L0, ∂^α] φ, where [L0, ∂^α] has smooth
λ-independent coefficients and involves derivatives of φ of lower or equal order; λ^j ‖∂^α 𝒫 s‖ ≤ C Σ_(i≤j) λ^i ‖∂^i s‖
≤ C 𝒩 by (M1), (M4), (M6). The same holds for ∂φ (with ∂𝒫 s ≤ C 𝒫 ∂s). For λ ∂_x² φ use the transport of
Lemma 6.5: λ^(j+1) ‖∂^α ∂_x² 𝒫 s‖ = λ^(j+1) ‖∂_x 𝒫(∂^α ∂_x s)‖ + (commutators) ≤ C λ^j ‖∂^j ∂s‖, by
the Bernstein bound (M2) in the one spatial derivative. The transport estimate then bounds the φ-part of 𝒩(τ) by C
(𝒩(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^(τ) 𝒩) (∂_τ φ does not vanish on Σ_τ0).

**Step 6** (Ψ). Apply ∂^α to (6.6) and the transport estimate (with c = 2/r ≤ 2/a). Write □̃ 𝒫 s = 𝒫 □̃ s + [□̃,
𝒫] s. By Lemma 6.4, □̃ s is of first order in (h, φ) up to F, the nonlinear terms and Σ c^(bi) (∂_b ∂_i h)(ℓ, ℓ).
For the last, the contraction with ℓ ⊗ ℓ is understood below; differentiating ℓ ⊗ ℓ adds terms c ∂h ∂(ℓ ⊗ ℓ), of first
order with the small coefficient c. Then 𝒫(c ∂_b ∂_i h) = 𝒫 ∂_i(c ∂_b h) − 𝒫((∂_i c) ∂_b h) and ‖𝒫 ∂_i f‖ ≤ C λ⁻¹ ‖f‖
by (M2), (M4), with |c| ≤ C(λ + |w|):
at most C ‖∂h‖ at level 0, and at level j

    λ^j ‖∂^α 𝒫 ∂_i (c ∂h)‖ ≤ C λ^(j−1) Σ_i ‖∂^i c‖_∞ ‖∂^(j−i) ∂h‖ ≤ C 𝒩,

since ‖∂^i c‖_∞ ≤ C λ^(1−i) (for the w-part of c only for i ≤ 4; for i ≥ 5 its ∂^i w is in L² and the other factor in
L^∞ by the Sobolev bound, as in Step 4; the restriction to i ≤ 4 applies likewise to c0, …, c3 through q). For the
commutator, [g0^(ab), 𝒫] ∂_a ∂_b s with at least one spatial index is bounded by C ‖∂s‖ by (M5). The ττ term is
rewritten with

    ∂_τ² s = (□̃ s − 2 g0^(τi) ∂_τ ∂_i s − g0^(ij) ∂_i ∂_j s)/g0^(ττ),      g0^(ττ) = −1 − μ/r²,

after which (M5) applies to the spatial terms. In □̃ s (Lemma 6.4) the first-order terms gain the factor λ of
(M5)'s second form, and the terms c^(bi) ∂_b ∂_i h are written ∂_i(c ∂_b h) − (∂_i c) ∂_b h, so that (M5)'s first form
bounds them by C ‖c ∂h‖ + C ‖∂c‖_∞ ‖∂h‖ ≤ C 𝒩 (at level j likewise; applying the second form to them would cost a
derivative at j = k). The terms of g0^(ab)(∂_a ∂_b 𝒫 − 𝒫 ∂_a ∂_b) s carry, by (M4) and (M6), a factor λ and a spatial
derivative inside 𝒫, so they are at most C ‖∂s‖ by (M4); likewise at level j. The other terms of (6.6) are of
first order in 𝒫 s and φ. So the Ψ-part of 𝒩(τ) is at most C (𝒩(τ0) + ∫ (𝒩 + C_R λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1))).

**Step 7** (closing). Steps 4–6 give

    𝒩(τ) ≤ C2 ( 𝒩(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^(τ) 𝒩 + (τ_end − τ0)(C_R λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1)) ),

with C2 independent of M and λ. Gronwall's lemma and Step 2 give 𝒩(τ) ≤ C3 ((C_D + 1 + C_R) λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1)), with C3
:= C2 e^(C2 (τ_end − τ0)) (1 + τ_end − τ0) C. Take M := C3 (C_D + 1 + C_R) + 1 and λ0 so small that C3 C M² λ0 ≤ 1 and
Step 3 holds. Then 𝒩 ≤ (M − 1) λ^K + λ^K = M λ^K < 2 M λ^K on [τ0, τ*], which improves the bootstrap assumption. 𝒩 is
continuous in τ for a smooth solution, so the set of τ* for which the assumption holds is open and closed in the
interval of existence.

### 6.5 Existence, continuation and uniqueness

**Step 8** (existence and continuation). The local theory needs the time lines timelike as well as the slices spacelike.
[AO14, Theorem 1.1, p. 2] (Theorem A.10), for the divergence-form equation ∂_μ(A^(μν)(u) ∂_ν u) = F on
[0, T] × R^n, asks in its hypothesis (1.3) that c_A⁻¹ |ξ|² ≤ A^(ij) ξ_i ξ_j ≤ c_A |ξ|² and A^(00) ≤ −c_A′ for all (u,
ξ), with constants c_A, c_A′ > 0 (named γ and κ there); and in the first-order form the eigenvalue 0 of the symbol
meets a characteristic speed wherever g^(ij) ξ_i ξ_j = 0, against [DS23, (A4)], which asks that the distinct
eigenvalues of the symbol never meet. In the coordinates (τ, x) this fails on part of Ω: g0^(ij) ξ_i ξ_j = |ξ|²
− (μ/r²)(x̂·ξ)² < 0 for radial ξ where r² < μ, and Ω reaches r = a < √μ0. So the local theorems are applied in other
coordinates, in four steps. The results used are the following; 𝒰 denotes an open set of states.

- [DS23, Theorem 2.4] (Theorem A.6): let the system ∂_t u + A^i(t, x, u) ∂_i u = R(t, x, u) on the torus
  T^n satisfy (A1)–(A4) of [DS23] on 𝒰 (A^i and R smooth, each of their derivatives bounded by a continuous increasing
  function of |u|, uniformly in (t, x); A^i(t, x, u) ξ_i diagonalizable with real eigenvalues for ξ ≠ 0, its distinct
  eigenvalues continuously differentiable in (t, u) and continuous in (x, ξ), and never meeting), and let r > n/2 + 1.
  For every u0 ∈ H^r whose values lie at positive distance from the complement of 𝒰 there is T > 0, depending on ‖u0‖_r
  and that distance, such that the system has a unique solution u with u(0) = u0 in B([−T, T]) := C([−T, T]; C¹) ∩
  C¹([−T, T]; C⁰); moreover u ∈ C([−T, T]; H^r) ∩ C¹([−T, T]; H^(r−1)), with values in 𝒰.
- [DS23, Theorem 2.6] (Theorem A.7): under the same hypotheses, every solution u ∈ B([0, T]) with
  values in 𝒰 and u(0) ∈ H^r lies in C([0, T]; H^r) ∩ C¹([0, T]; H^(r−1)); and for the supremum T* of the T for which
  such a solution exists on [0, T], exactly one of the following holds: T* = ∞; the distance of the values from the
  complement of 𝒰 has infimum 0 on [0, T*); the norm of u in B([0, T]) tends to infinity as T tends to T*.
- [LY22, Theorem 26] (Theorem A.35): for a bounded smooth domain in R^n and a bounded neighbourhood of its
  closure there is one extension operator, bounded from W^(m,p) of the domain to the W^(m,p) functions with compact
  support in the neighbourhood, and from C^m of the domain to C^m functions with compact support there, for every
  integer m ≥ 0 and 0 < p ≤ ∞; in particular it maps smooth functions to smooth functions.
- [SY21, Sections 1 and 2.1] (Theorem A.36): a bounded Lipschitz domain in R^n has one extension operator
  (Stein's), bounded from W^(m,p) of the domain to W^(m,p)(R^n) for every integer m ≥ 0 and 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞.

(i) *The coefficients.* On Ω the system for w is Ric^H(g_app + w) = 0, relative to g0, and the profiles of g_app are
defined on Ω × S¹. Extend them to R⁵ × S¹ by one universal extension operator acting in X, the same for every order
(Stein's, for the bounded Lipschitz domain Ω, a convex polygon in (τ, r) times S³; [SY21, Sections 1, 2.1],
Theorem A.36): g_app extends smoothly with bounded derivatives of every order, for all τ, and is unchanged
on Ω. Put R2 := b(τ0) + 1. On {a/4 ≤ r ≤ R2 + 1}, at every τ, the extended g_app still has spacelike slices for λ small.
Indeed the extended profiles are bounded, so |g_app − g0| ≤ C λ there. The slices of g0 have the induced metric δ +
(μ/r²) dr² ≥ δ, g0 = η + (μ/r²) dv ⊗ dv has |g0| ≤ 1 + 2μ_end/r² ≤ 1 + 32 μ_end/a² (|dv|² = 2 in the Euclidean norm),
and det g0 = −1 ((2.3)). Put Θ := 2 + 32 μ_end/a² and λ_ext := 1/(10 C Θ⁴), which depends only on C, a and
μ_end, and let λ ≤ λ_ext, so that C λ ≤ 1/(10 Θ⁴) ≤ 1/160. On that region the extended g_app then has induced metric at
least (1 − C λ) δ ≥ δ/2 on every Σ_τ, |g_app| ≤ |g0| + C λ ≤ Θ, and determinant at most −1/2. For the determinant: det
g_app − det g0 is the sum over i = 1, …, 5 of the determinants of the matrices whose first i − 1 columns are those of
g0, whose i-th column is that of g_app − g0 and whose other columns are those of g_app, since the determinant is linear
in each column; a column has Euclidean length at most the operator norm, so by Hadamard's inequality each of these five
determinants is at most Θ⁴ |g_app − g0| ≤ Θ⁴ C λ in absolute value, and |det g_app + 1| ≤ 5 Θ⁴ C λ ≤ 1/2. A symmetric
form that is positive definite on a hyperplane has at least four positive eigenvalues, and with negative determinant the
fifth is negative: g_app is Lorentzian with every Σ_τ spacelike there, and its lapse ν, shift and spatial metric γ
relative to τ are defined. They are bounded uniformly in τ: δ/2 ≤ γ ≤ Θ, so 1/16 ≤ det γ ≤ Θ⁴; and det g_app = −ν² det
γ, so ν² = −det g_app/det γ lies between 1/(2 Θ⁴) and 16 Θ⁵, Hadamard's inequality giving |det g_app| ≤ Θ⁵. We take λ0 ≤
λ_ext. Outside a neighbourhood U of Ω in {a/2 < r < R2}, replace g_app and g0 by g_ext and g0_ext, obtained by
interpolating lapse, shift and spatial metric (relative to τ) convexly to (1, 0, δ) on {r ≤ a/4} and on {r ≥ R2 + 1}.
Every such combination is a Lorentzian metric with each Σ_τ spacelike: a convex combination of positive lapses is
positive and a convex combination of positive definite spatial metrics is positive definite, and a metric −ν² dτ² + γ_ij
(dx^i + β^i dτ)(dx^j + β^j dτ) with ν > 0 and γ positive definite is Lorentzian with dτ timelike. So the system keeps
its form, with coefficients smooth in X and equal to Minkowski's outside a compact set in x; on U nothing changes.

(ii) *The coordinates.* Write g_ext = −ν² dτ² + γ_ij (dx^i + β^i dτ)(dx^j + β^j dτ), with lapse ν, shift β_ext = β^i ∂_i
and spatial metric γ. The lapse is a convex combination of that of g_app, at least (2 Θ⁴)^(−1/2) by (i), and of 1, so ν
≥ ν_min := (2 Θ⁴)^(−1/2) > 0, as Θ ≥ 2. Put Z := ∂_τ − β_ext. Then Z(τ) = 1 and, since dx^i(Z) + β^i dτ(Z) = −β^i +
β^i = 0,

    g_ext(Z, Z) = −ν² ≤ −ν_min² < 0;

and Z = ∂_τ outside a compact set. Put X = (τ, Φ_Z(τ, y)), Φ_Z the flow of Z from τ0. The slices are unchanged and ∂_τ
at fixed y is Z. For a vector Y tangent to a slice, g_ext(Z, Y) = g_ext(∂_τ, Y) − γ(β, Y) = γ(β, Y) − γ(β, Y) = 0,
because g_ext(∂_τ, ∂_i) = γ_ij β^j. So in (τ, y) the metric g_ext has zero shift, g_ext = −ν² dτ² + γ̃_ab dy^a dy^b with
γ̃ the spatial metric in the coordinates y, and its inverse has g_ext^(00) = −ν⁻², g_ext^(0a) = 0 and g_ext^(ab) =
γ̃^(ab), the inverse spatial metric, uniformly positive definite. Only the independent variables change: the unknowns
stay the Cartesian arrays of the coordinates (τ, x), the principal part stays −(1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b with g^(ab)
transformed as a tensor, and the system stays quasilinear with coefficients smooth in (τ, y).

(iii) *The cut-off.* Let ϒ be a smooth map of the components, the identity on |w| ≤ ε2/2 and with values in |w| ≤ ε2,
with ε2 so small that every metric within ε2 of g_ext keeps the conditions g^(00) ≤ −c_0 and g^(ab) ξ_a ξ_b ≥ c_0 |ξ|²
with a fixed constant c_0 > 0 in (τ, y). Put ϒ(w) for w in the coefficients and lower-order terms. The modified system
agrees with the original where |w| ≤ ε2/2, which holds on Ω once C M λ0^(K−3) ≤ ε2/2 (|w| ≤ C M λ^(K−3), Step 3; c_0 and
ε2 depend only on Θ and on bounds for DΦ_Z and its inverse, which do not depend on λ since |∂g_app| ≤ C). The
coefficients and the forcing term are taken at time τ̄(τ), τ̄ smooth, equal to τ on [τ0 − 1, τ_end + 1] and constant
outside [τ0 − 2, τ_end + 2]: the coordinates of (ii) degenerate as |τ| grows (the flow lines of Z pile up where β_ext
vanishes), and [DS23, (A1)] asks for bounds uniform in t; on [τ0, τ_end] nothing changes. The coefficients and the
forcing term equal Minkowski's outside a compact set in y, so the system is posed on a torus T⁴_L of large period L.

Write the modified system as −(1/2) g^(μν) ∂_μ ∂_ν w = F̃(τ, y, w, ∂w), with μ, ν running over (τ, y) and a, b, c below
over y alone. In V := (w, u_0, u_a), with u_0 := ∂_τ w and u_a := ∂_(y^a) w, it is the first-order system

    ∂_τ w = u_0,
    −g^(00) ∂_τ u_0 − 2 g^(0a) ∂_a u_0 − g^(ab) ∂_a u_b = 2 F̃(τ, y, w, u),
    g^(ab) ∂_τ u_b − g^(ab) ∂_b u_0 = 0,

the second line being the equation with the first derivatives of w replaced by (u_0, u_b). Its coefficient of ∂_τ is
A⁰ = diag(1, −g^(00), g^(ab)) (acting on each of the fifteen components of w), symmetric and positive definite, and its
coefficient of ∂_c is

    A^c = [[0, 0, 0], [0, −2 g^(0c), −g^(cb)], [0, −g^(ac), 0]]

in the blocks (w, u_0, u_b), symmetric. So the system is symmetric hyperbolic. Its eigenvalues ζ, defined by A^c ξ_c V =
ζ A⁰ V for ξ ≠ 0, are as follows. If ζ ≠ 0, the last rows give u_b = −(ξ_b/ζ) u_0, the first gives w = 0, and the second
gives

    g^(00) ζ² − 2 g^(0c) ξ_c ζ + g^(ab) ξ_a ξ_b = 0,

whose two roots ζ_− < 0 < ζ_+ are real with product g^(ab) ξ_a ξ_b/g^(00) < 0. If ζ = 0, then u_0 = 0 and g^(ab) ξ_a
u_b = 0, with w free: a space of dimension four for each component. So (A⁰)⁻¹ A^c ξ_c is diagonalizable with the real
eigenvalues ζ_− < 0 < ζ_+ and 0, which never meet; ζ_± are simple roots of a quadratic with smooth coefficients and 0 is
constant, so all three are smooth in (τ, y, V, ξ) for ξ ≠ 0, more than (A4) of [DS23] (Theorem A.6) asks,
and the system satisfies (A1)–(A4) of [DS23] with 𝒰 the whole state space, the cut-off keeping the coefficients defined
for every value of w. The complement of 𝒰 is empty, so the conditions on the distance to it in [DS23, Theorems 2.4 and
2.6] hold for every datum, and T depends on the H^r norm of the datum alone. The relation u_a = ∂_a w propagates, since
∂_τ(u_a − ∂_a w) = ∂_a(u_0 − ∂_τ w) = 0.

(iv) *The restarts.* At τ_i extend the data from Σ_(τ_i) ∩ Ω = A(τ_i) to R⁴, in x, and compose with Φ_Z(τ_i, ·) to pass
to y, with bounds uniform in τ_i. For the extension let A_* := {a ≤ |x| ≤ a + 1 + δ0}, d_* := a(1 + δ0)/(2(b(τ0) −
a)), U_* := {a − d_* < |x| < a + 1 + δ0 + d_*}, and E_* the operator of [LY22, Theorem 26] for the smooth annulus A_*
and its neighbourhood U_*. The radial map

    ψ_τ(x) := (a + (|x| − a)(b(τ) − a)/(1 + δ0)) x̂

maps A_* onto A(τ), and U_* diffeomorphically onto a neighbourhood of A(τ): since 1 + δ0 ≤ b(τ) − a ≤ b(τ0) − a
