(Lemma 2.6 (f)), the factor (b(τ) − a)/(1 + δ0) lies in [1, a/(2 d_*)], so the radius stays at least a/2 on U_*.
Put E_τ f := E_*(f ∘ ψ_τ) ∘ ψ_τ⁻¹ on ψ_τ(U_*) and E_τ f := 0 elsewhere. Composition with a diffeomorphism ψ between
bounded open sets is bounded on H^m, with a constant depending only on m, on bounds for the derivatives of ψ of orders
1 to m and on a bound for the Jacobian determinant of ψ⁻¹: by the chain rule ∂^α(u ∘ ψ) is a sum of terms (∂^β u) ∘ ψ,
1 ≤ |β| ≤ |α|, times polynomials in the derivatives of ψ of orders at most |α|, and ∫ |v ∘ ψ|² = ∫ |v|² |det Dψ⁻¹|.
For ψ_τ on U_* and ψ_τ⁻¹ on ψ_τ(U_*) these bounds are uniform in τ. So E_τ f = f on A(τ), E_τ is bounded from
H^m(A(τ)) to H^m(R⁴) for every m uniformly in τ, its values are supported in the fixed ball {|x| ≤ b(τ0) + a}, and it
maps smooth functions to smooth functions. The flow Φ_Z(τ_i, ·) is a diffeomorphism of R⁴ equal to the identity outside
a compact set, and its derivatives of positive order and those of its inverse are bounded uniformly for τ_i ∈ [τ0,
τ_end]; by [LY22, Lemma 27] (Theorem A.35) composition with it, after multiplication by a smooth compactly
supported function equal to 1 on that ball, is bounded on every H^m(R⁴), and the chain-rule bound above makes the
constants uniform in τ_i.

[DS23, Theorem 2.4] with r = k > 4/2 + 1 (k = 6) gives a solution on [τ_i, τ_i + δ], δ depending only on the norm of
the data, which Steps 1 and 7 bound for each fixed λ (|w|_(k+1) ≤ C 𝒩 ≤ C M λ^K). The data are smooth, so they lie in
H^r for every r ≥ k, and the hypotheses (A1)–(A4) do not depend on r. By the first clause of [DS23, Theorem 2.6],
applied at each r ≥ k on [τ_i, τ_i + δ], the solution lies in C([τ_i, τ_i + δ]; H^r) for every r. By Sobolev's
embedding on the torus every spatial derivative of V is then continuous; the system, solved for ∂_τ V with A⁰
invertible, expresses ∂_τ V through V and its spatial derivatives with coefficients smooth in (τ, y, V), and
differentiating it expresses every derivative of V in the same way. So the solution is smooth. On Ω ∩ {τ_i ≤ τ ≤ τ_i +
δ} it solves the original system while |w| ≤ ε2/2.

It is the only C² solution there with the data on Σ_(τ_i) ∩ Ω and |g − g0| ≤ ε1, the class in which the energy
inequality applies; the solution here is in it by Step 3, and so is its image under an isometry of g0, which fixes g0
and acts on Cartesian arrays by an orthogonal matrix. For let g_(1) := g_app + w1 and g_(2) := g_app + w2 be two such.
Then

    −(1/2) g_(1)^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b (w1 − w2) = (1/2)(g_(1)^(ab) − g_(2)^(ab)) ∂_a ∂_b w2 + F(X, w1, ∂w1) − F(X, w2, ∂w2) =: f,

where F(X, w, ∂w) := −Ric^H(g_app + w) − (1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b w, g = g_app + w, contains no second derivative of w (and
F(X, 0, 0) = F). Then ‖f‖ ≤ C (‖w1 − w2‖ + ‖∂(w1 − w2)‖), because ∂²w2 is bounded and |g_(i)⁻¹| ≤ (s0 − ε1)⁻¹. The
energy inequality from τ_i and Gronwall's lemma give w1 = w2. This is the finite speed of propagation the proof uses,
obtained from the energy inequality with no further input, and the same argument, run from τ0 over all of Ω, gives the
uniqueness stated in the theorem. With Step 7 the bootstrap continues, so the solution exists on all of Ω with
(6.1).

Finally the bounds after (6.1). By Step 1, |w|_(k+1) ≤ C 𝒩 ≤ C M λ^K, so ‖w‖ ≤ C M λ^K and ‖∂w‖ ≤
λ⁻¹ |w|_(k+1) ≤ C M λ^(K−1); |w| ≤ C λ⁻³ 𝒩 ≤ C M λ^(K−3) and |∂w| ≤ C λ⁻⁴ 𝒩 ≤ C M λ^(K−4) (M renamed to absorb C).
Then |g − g0| ≤ |λ [g1] + Σ_(j≥2) λ^j [g_j]| + |w| ≤ C λ, and |∂g| ≤ |∂g_app| + |∂w| ≤ C, since ∂[λ g1] = dv ⊗ [∂_θ g1] +
λ [∂_X g1] is bounded. ∎

### 6.6 The theorem at every order

The proof fixes k = 6. Some uses of the theorem need the remainder small in H^d for a large d.

**Remark 6.6** Theorem 6.1 holds at every order k ≥ 6 with K ≥ 6: with 𝒩_k the quantity
(6.7) at order k, 𝒩_k(τ) ≤ M_k λ^K on [τ0, τ_end], given (E3) and (E4) at order k. The inputs hold at every
order for the approximant of Theorem 4.11 with the data of Theorem 7.1, and the remainder is O(λ) in H^d once k
≥ d and K ≥ d + 1.

*Proof.* (a) *Where k = 6 enters.* Step 1: the scaled Sobolev bound ‖∂^i w‖_∞ ≤ C λ^(−3−i) 𝒩 needs i + 3 ≤ k + 1, so i ≤
4 at k = 6 and i ≤ k − 2 in general. Step 4: the commutator terms ∂^i g · ∂^(j−i+1) ∂h are split with ∂^i w in L^∞ for i
≤ 4 and in L² for i ≥ 5, the other factor then of order j − i + 1 ≤ 2 in L^∞; at order k the split is at k − 2, the L^∞
factor needing at most 2 + 1 + 3 ≤ k + 1 derivatives of 𝒩's quantities. The nonlinear terms use |∂w ∂w|_k ≤ C
λ⁻³ |∂w|_k², the scaled product bound |f g|_k ≤ C_k λ⁻³ |f|_k |g|_k on the slices, in four space dimensions, which holds
at every k ≥ 3. Indeed, expand λ^j ∂^j (f g), j ≤ k, by Leibniz's rule into terms λ^i ∂^i f · λ^(j−i) ∂^(j−i) g. If i =
0, then ‖f‖_(L^∞) ≤ C λ⁻³ |f|_3 ≤ C λ⁻³ |f|_k by (5.2) and ‖λ^j ∂^j g‖ ≤ |g|_k; if i = j, the same holds with f
and g exchanged. If 1 ≤ i ≤ j − 1, both factors are put in L⁴. By Theorem A.28 ([BH17, Theorem 7.27,
p. 56]), on a nonempty bounded open subset of R^n with Lipschitz boundary W^(s,p) embeds in W^(t,q) whenever 1 ≤ p, q <
∞, 0 ≤ t ≤ s and s − n/p ≥ t − n/q; with s = 1, p = 2, t = 0, q = 4 and n = 4 this gives ‖u‖_(L⁴) ≤ C (‖u‖ + ‖∂_x u‖) on
the fixed annulus, and on every A(τ) with the same C by the radial maps of the proof of Lemma 5.1. Hence ‖λ^i ∂^i
f‖_(L⁴) ≤ C (λ^i ‖∂^i f‖ + λ^i ‖∂^(i+1) f‖) ≤ C λ⁻¹ |f|_(i+1) ≤ C λ⁻¹ |f|_k, since i + 1 ≤ j ≤ k, and likewise ‖λ^(j−i)
∂^(j−i) g‖_(L⁴) ≤ C λ⁻¹ |g|_k. By Hölder's inequality the term is at most C λ⁻² |f|_k |g|_k ≤ C λ⁻³ |f|_k |g|_k. Step 8:
[DS23, Theorem 2.4] with r = k > 4/2 + 1. Steps 2, 5, 6 and 7 do not use k = 6.

(b) *The closing.* The bootstrap closes when 2K − 5 ≥ K + 1 (Step 4's C M² λ^(2K−5) ≤ C M² λ^(K+1)), that is when K ≥ 6,
whatever k is; the constants C, C2, M and λ0 then depend on k. So 𝒩_k(τ) ≤ M_k λ^K on [τ0, τ_end], given (E3) and (E4)
at order k.

(c) *The inputs at order k.* (E3) at order k: for the approximant of Theorem 4.11, the residual of G(X, u/λ)
((4.10)) is λ^N times a profile bounded with all its derivatives, and the passage to the fixed-phase form
(4.4), which is g_app, changes Ric^H by O(λ^(N−1)) in |·|_k (Section 4.6); so |Ric^H(g_app)|_k ≤
C_k λ^(N−1) for every k: the approximant of Theorem 4.11 is of order N − 1 at every regularity k, and with N =
K + 3 this is λ^(K+2) ≤ λ^K. (E4) at order k: Proposition 7.7
bounds the correction at every order, sup_r ‖∂_r^j U(r)‖_(H^s(S³)) ≤ C_(j,s) λ^(N−2−j), with λ0 independent of the
order, so Data(w) at order k is O(λ^(N−3)) = O(λ^K) with N = K + 3, as in the proof of Theorem 7.1.

(d) *Unscaled norms.* 𝒩_k ≤ M_k λ^K gives ‖∂^j ∂h‖ ≤ M_k λ^(K−j) for j ≤ k, and likewise for φ G1 by Step 1, so the
remainder is O(λ) in H^d once k ≥ d and K ≥ d + 1. ∎

## 7. The data

This chapter constructs the Cauchy data of the main theorem, which the proof of its items 1–5 in Section 3.2
uses. The data are posed on the slice Σ := Σ_τ0, before the shell reaches the hole, and no smallness of the background
is used. The approximate solution of Theorem 4.11, with suitable stage data, has data that satisfy the
constraints and the gauge condition D = 0 to high order (Section 7.3). The remaining error is removed
exactly by solving the constraints outward in r, as a parabolic–hyperbolic system, from a sphere inside the shell where
the approximant's data are the seed's exactly (Section 7.4). The data then coincide with the seed's on
Σ ∩ {r < v_start − τ0}.

Notation is that of Chapter 6. In addition, the ansatz (4.10), G = ḡ + λ W + Σ_(j=2)^(N+1) λ^j ĝ_j
with the mean metric ḡ = g0 + Σ_(j=1)^(N) λ^j m_j, the phase u = v + Σ_(j=1)^(N) λ^j φ_j and the approximant g_app = G(X,
u/λ) (in (E4), and so in Theorem 7.1, g_app is the fixed-phase form (4.4) instead; the two differ by
O(λ^(N+1)) in scaled norms, Section 4.6), the two-scale operator R_u of Definition 4.1 with the orders ℛ^(m)
of the expansion R_u[G] = Σ_m λ^m ℛ^(m), and the coefficients e_j = 2 ℓ·dφ_j − m_j(ℓ, ℓ) − q_j of ḡ⁻¹(du, du) = Σ_(j≥1)
λ^j e_j ((4.11)) are those of Chapter 4. Stage 0 is Lemma 4.5: the wave W = W_TT +
χ dv dv has W(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr_g0 W = 0, and χ vanishes on Σ_τ0 ((4.9)). Where each unknown first enters
the expansion is Lemma 4.7; the stage equations (a)–(c), each a linear hyperbolic system solved without loss,
are Lemma 4.10; and the passage from G(X, u/λ) to the fixed-phase form (4.4), with ℛ^(m) = 0 for m
≤ N − 1, is the proof of Theorem 4.11 (Section 4.6). The leading wave W_TT of (2.11) has no dv and
no dr component and is traceless on the spheres {τ, r = const} (Lemma 2.9 (b)).

### 7.1 The theorem

**Theorem 7.1** (Exact data.) Let K ≥ 6 and N := K + 3, and let g_app be the approximant of Theorem 4.11
with N stages and the stage data of Lemma 7.4, in its fixed-phase form (4.4). For λ small there is
a vacuum Cauchy datum (γ, κ) on Σ (the constraints hold exactly), with the gauge condition D = 0 imposed through ∂_τ g,
whose w := g − g_app satisfies (E4) of Theorem 6.1; it equals the seed's datum on Σ ∩ {r < v_start − τ0}.
The datum is smooth and invariant under the T² action and both reflections.

The proof is in Section 7.5.

### 7.2 Two identities

For a Lorentzian g put E := Ric^H(g) and

    S(D)_mn := (1/2)(g_(mρ) ∇̂_n D^ρ + g_(nρ) ∇̂_m D^ρ),

∇̂ the connection of g0, so that Ric(g) = E + S(D) by the definition (2.9) of Ric^H, and Gt(T) := T − (1/2)(tr_g
T) g.

(I1) The contracted Bianchi identity div_g Gt(Ric) = 0 reads

    B_g[D] := div_g Gt(S(D)) = −div_g Gt(E),    (7.1)

with B_g linear in D, of second order with principal part (1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b (acting on D with its index lowered by
g), and with other coefficients involving g, ∂g, g0 and the derivatives of g0, and no second derivative of g.

*Proof.* The identity is div_g Gt(E + S(D)) = 0. For the structure, put T^ρ_n := ∇̂_n D^ρ and T_(mn) := g_(mρ) T^ρ_n, so
that S(D)_mn = (1/2)(T_(mn) + T_(nm)). Since ∇g = 0 for the connection ∇ of g,

    (div_g S(D))_n = (1/2)(∇_ρ T^ρ_n + g_(nρ) g^(ab) ∇_a T^ρ_b),     tr_g S(D) = T^ρ_ρ = ∇̂_ρ D^ρ.

Each ∇_a T^ρ_b = ∂_a T^ρ_b + Γ[g] T − Γ[g] T, and ∂_a T^ρ_b = ∂_a ∂_b D^ρ + (∂Γ[g0]) D + Γ[g0] ∂D. So div_g Gt(S(D)) =
div_g S(D) − (1/2) d tr_g S(D) has coefficients built from g, ∂g (through Γ[g]) and g0 with its derivatives, and no
second derivative of g. Its second-order part is (1/2)(∂_ρ ∂_n D^ρ + g_(nρ) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b D^ρ) − (1/2) ∂_n ∂_ρ D^ρ =
(1/2) g_(nρ) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b D^ρ. ∎

(I2) On a slice {τ = const} with future unit normal n, the induced data (γ, κ) have the constraint map

    (J, ρ) = (2(−div κ + d tr κ), R − |κ|² + (tr κ)²)    (7.2)

of [CD03, (2.1), p. 4], with R the scalar curvature of γ; these are the constraint equations in every space dimension.
By the Gauss and Codazzi equations, (J, ρ) equals 2 G(n, ·), G := Gt(Ric): ρ is its n-component and J its tangential
components, up to the sign convention of κ. If D = 0 on the slice, its tangential derivatives vanish there, so ∂D = −n♭
⊗ Z there, with n♭ := g(n, ·) and Z := ∂_n D (indeed n♭(n) = −1, so ∂_n D = Z). At D = 0, ∇̂D = ∂D, so

    S(D) = −(1/2)(n♭ ⊗ Z♭ + Z♭ ⊗ n♭),     tr_g S(D) = −g(n, Z),

and Gt(S(D))(n, ·) = −(1/2)(n♭(n) Z♭ + g(Z, n) n♭) + (1/2) g(n, Z) n♭ = (1/2) Z♭. Hence on a slice where D = 0,

    2 G(n, ·) = 2 Gt(E)(n, ·) + Z♭,    (7.3)

and for a solution of Ric^H(g) = 0 with D = 0 on the slice the constraints hold there exactly when ∂_n D = 0 there.

*What the theorem asks.* Let (γ, κ) on Σ satisfy the constraints, and give g on Σ the lapse and shift of G(X, u/λ), the
spatial part γ, ∂_τ of the spatial part fixed by κ, and ∂_τ of the lapse and shift fixed by D(g) = 0 on Σ. The last
choice is possible because D is linear in ∂_τ g_(τ ·), with an invertible coefficient on a spacelike slice. Indeed, with
D_σ := g_(σρ) D^ρ = g^(ab) (∂_a g_(σb) − (1/2) ∂_σ g_(ab)) − g_(σρ) g^(ab) Γ[g0]^ρ_ab, the terms containing y_σ := ∂_τ
g_(στ) are g^(ττ) y_σ + δ^τ_σ g^(τj) y_j − (1/2) δ^τ_σ (g^(ττ) y_τ + 2 g^(τj) y_j): that is, (1/2) g^(ττ) y_τ in D_τ and
g^(ττ) y_j in D_j. The coefficient matrix is diag((1/2) g^(ττ), g^(ττ), …, g^(ττ)), of determinant (1/2) (g^(ττ))⁵ ≠ 0,
since g^(ττ) < 0 on a spacelike slice; at g0, g0^(ττ) = −(r² + μ)/r² and the determinant is −(r² + μ)⁵/(2 r¹⁰). Then (g,
∂_τ g) is a Cauchy datum for Ric^H = 0 with D = 0 on Σ and, by (7.3), ∂_τ D = 0 on Σ; D = 0 and
the constraints on Σ are the hypotheses of Lemma 3.6, which the proof of the main theorem uses. (E4)
asks that w := g − g_app be O(λ^K) in the scaled norm Data. So there are two steps: the approximant's data must satisfy
the constraints and D = 0 to high order (Section 7.3), and the error must be removed exactly with λ-uniform
bounds (Section 7.4).

**Remark 7.2** (The conformal method.) Touati constructs high-frequency data by the conformal method,
inverting the flat operators Δ_e and div_e L_e and closing each fixed point by the smallness of the background: the
contraction of [Tou23b, Section 5.4.2, p. 29] holds for ε small, under his assumption [Tou23b, (2.1)] that the
background data are within ε of the Euclidean data in weighted Sobolev norms ([Tou23b, Theorem 2.1]). Here the slice
passes through the hole, the background data are not close to Euclidean, and an elliptic method needs boundary data at
r = a as well as far out. The evolution in r used below needs neither: it is solved outward from a sphere inside the
shell, where the approximant's data are the seed's exactly, and nothing is imposed further out.

### 7.3 The approximant's data

D(g_app) has the two-scale form [D_u[G]]_u, D_u[G] = Σ_(m≥0) λ^m D^(m)(X, θ), as Ric^H does. (7.1) is an
identity of differential polynomials in g, and the operators ∂_a + λ⁻¹ (∂_a u) ∂_θ are commuting derivations, so
(7.1) holds order by order for the profiles; its right side at order j involves ℛ^(i), i ≤ j + 1, only.
These vanish for i ≤ N − 1. Moreover D^(0) = g0⁻¹(∂_θ W(ℓ, ·) − (1/2) dv tr ∂_θ W) = 0, since W(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr W = 0.

**Lemma 7.3** (The gauge hierarchy.) Let N ≥ 3 and suppose that on Σ

- (F1) D^(m)(X, θ) = 0 for all θ, m = 1, …, N − 1;
- (F2) ∂_τ ⟨D^(m)⟩ = 0, m = 1, …, N − 2.

Then D^(m) = 0 on Ω × S¹ for m ≤ N − 2, and ∂_θ D^(N−1) = 0. Hence |D(g_app)|_k ≤ C λ^(N−1) on every Σ_τ, and the
constraint map of g_app's data on Σ has scaled norm |·|_(k−1) ≤ C λ^(N−2).

*Proof.* In two-scale form the principal part of B_g on λ^m [Y]_u is

    λ^(m−2) (1/2) g⁻¹(du, du) ∂_θ² Y + λ^(m−1) (g⁻¹(du, ∂_X) + (1/2) □_g u + M) ∂_θ Y + λ^m (1/2) g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b Y,

where g⁻¹(du, du) = O(λ²) (ḡ⁻¹(du, du) = O(λ^(N+1)), and W(ℓ, ·) = 0; the leading part, −λ² ĝ_2(ℓ, ℓ), multiplies ∂_θ²
Y, which vanishes for the Y = D^(m) of the induction), g⁻¹(du, ∂_X) = ℓ·∂_X + O(λ), □_g u = □_(g0) v + O(λ), and M(X,
θ), from the coefficient Γ[g] of ∂D (of size ∂g = O(1)), is a bounded multiplication operator on profiles. Induction on
m = 0, …, N − 2 with the hypothesis: D^(j) = 0 for j < m and ∂_θ D^(m) = 0 (true at m = 0). At order m the oscillating
part of (7.1) is the transport

    (ℓ·∂_X + (1/2) □_(g0) v) Z + Π_osc(M Z) = (first order in ⟨D^(m)⟩)     for Z := ∂_θ D^(m+1),

Π_osc the projection onto zero θ-mean, and its mean is the linear wave equation (1/2) □_(g0) ⟨D^(m)⟩ + (first order)
⟨D^(m)⟩ + ⟨M Z⟩ = 0 (M depends on θ, so M Z has a mean part, which the wave equation carries; the order-m equation does
not depend on λ, so its wave operator is g0's). Every other term vanishes by the hypothesis or because it contains
ℛ^(i), i ≤ m + 1 ≤ N − 1. The data are zero: ⟨D^(m)⟩ by (F1), ∂_τ ⟨D^(m)⟩ by (F2), Z by (F1) at order m + 1. This linear
system for (⟨D^(m)⟩, Z) closes without loss exactly as the stage equations do (Lemma 4.10: the mean in
H^(s+1), Z in H^s; the energy inequality of Lemma 5.5 and the transport estimate of Lemma 5.6; the
transport curves reach Σ inside Ω by Lemma 2.6 (d)), so ⟨D^(m)⟩ = 0 and Z = 0: the hypothesis at m + 1. Then
D(g_app) = λ^(N−1) [D^(N−1)] + O(λ^N) with bounded profiles, and 2 G(g_app)(n, ·) = 2 Gt(E)(n, ·) + 2 Gt(S(D))(n, ·)
with S(D) of first order in D: the scaled norm of the second term is at most C λ⁻¹ λ^(N−1), and of the first at most C
λ^(N−1), by (E3). ∎

**Lemma 7.4** (The stage data.) For every N there are stage data for Theorem 4.11 satisfying (F1)
and (F2), all vanishing on Σ ∩ {r < v_start − τ0}. The stage data constructed in the proof are fixed by the seed, by N
and by the slice Σ (on which they are posed: τ0 enters through the data on Σ, the phase (τ0 + r)/λ there and the region
r < v_start − τ0); "the stage data of Lemma 7.4" means these, and not any others with the stated properties.

*Proof.* Stage 0: χ = 0 on Σ, as chosen in (4.9). Stage m = 1, …, N, everything of the earlier stages
given: put φ_m = 0 and (m_m)_(τ ·) = 0 on Σ. Stage N's data are not needed for (F1) and (F2), but they are fixed here,
so that every stage's data are smooth, invariant under T² and both reflections, and vanish on Σ ∩ {r < v_start − τ0}; at
m = N step (iii) below runs inside Theorem 4.11 of order N, since after stage N ℛ^(N) = −(1/2) e_(N+1) ∂_θ² W
with e_(N+1) = −q_(N+1) independent of θ. The unknowns left on Σ are γ_m and κ_m, the order-m means of the induced
metric and of the second fundamental form (γ_m is the spatial part of m_m, and, given γ_m, κ_m fixes ∂_τ of that spatial
part), ∂_τ (m_m)_(τ ·), and ĝ_(m+1).

(i) On Σ the oscillating part of D^(m), its index lowered by g0, is Pol(∂_θ ĝ_(m+1)) + Λ_m(γ_m) + (known), where

    Pol(Y) := Y(ℓ, ·) − (1/2) dv tr_(g0) Y

for symmetric 2-tensors Y, and Λ_m is algebraic: it collects the terms of the order-m oscillating part of D that are
linear in m_m or in ∂φ_m (bilinear with ∂_θ W, such as m_m(ℓ, ·) contracted with ∂_θ W, ⟨m_m, ∂_θ W⟩ ℓ and ∂_θ W(grad
φ_m, ·)), in which ∂_τ φ_m = −(1/2)(m_m(ℓ, ℓ) + q_m) by the stage equation (b) of Lemma 4.10 and the
tangential derivatives of φ_m vanish. Pol is onto at every point. Indeed, fix a null vector k with dv(k) = g0(ℓ, k) = 1,
put k♭ := g0(k, ·), and fix a covector ξ with ξ(ℓ) = 0 and g0⁻¹(ξ, ξ) = 1. For a covector β put

    Y_β := β ⊗ k♭ + k♭ ⊗ β − β(ℓ) k♭ ⊗ k♭ − 2 β(k) ξ ⊗ ξ.

Then Y_β(ℓ, ·) = β(ℓ) k♭ + β − β(ℓ) k♭ = β, using k♭(ℓ) = 1 and ξ(ℓ) = 0, and tr_(g0) Y_β = 2 β(k) − 0 − 2 β(k) = 0,
using g0⁻¹(k♭, k♭) = g0(k, k) = 0; so Pol(Y_β) = β. Put Pol⁺ := Pol^T (Pol Pol^T)⁻¹, the transposes taken in the
Euclidean structure of the Cartesian coordinates (τ, x); Pol Pol^T is invertible because Pol is onto, and that structure
is O(4)-invariant, so Pol⁺ commutes with the symmetries. Then ∂_θ ĝ_(m+1) := −Pol⁺(Λ_m(γ_m) + known) on Σ solves the
equation (the right side has zero θ-mean, and ĝ_(m+1) is its zero-mean antiderivative in θ), smoothly, pointwise and
linearly in γ_m.

(ii) The mean of D^(m) on Σ is linear in ∂_τ (m_m)_(τ ·), with the invertible coefficient of the gauge's data
(Section 7.2), plus terms in γ_m, κ_m and known quantities: it fixes ∂_τ (m_m)_(τ ·).

(iii) First, every first derivative of D^(j), j < m, vanishes on Σ. Solve stage m with any data: D^(j), j ≤ m − 1, does
not depend on the data of stage m, and ℛ^(i) = 0 for i ≤ m − 1 once stage m is solved (before it, ℛ^(m−1) = −(1/2) e_m
∂_θ² W, and stage m imposes e_m = 0; Lemma 4.7, Lemma 4.10). For m ≥ 3, Lemma 7.3 with
N := m applies (its hypotheses, (F1) at orders 1, …, m − 1 and (F2) at orders 1, …, m − 2, were arranged at the earlier
stages) and gives D^(j) = 0 on Ω for j ≤ m − 2 and ∂_θ D^(m−1) = 0; then the first derivatives of D^(m−1) on Σ vanish
too: the tangential ones by (F1), the normal one of the mean by (F2) at order m − 1, and the oscillating part is zero.
For m = 1, 2 the same holds directly: D^(0) = 0, and for m = 2 the order-0 transport, with ∂_θ D^(1) = 0 on Σ by (F1),
gives ∂_θ D^(1) = 0 on Ω, and the normal derivative of ⟨D^(1)⟩ vanishes on Σ by (F2) at order 1. The tangential
derivatives of D^(m) vanish by (F1), and the phase part λ⁻¹ (du) ∂_θ D^(m+1) of the derivatives has mean zero. So the
order-m mean of 2 G(g_app)(n, ·) on Σ is ∂_n ⟨D^(m)⟩, the order-m mean of (7.3), the E-part
having mean zero (after stage m, ℛ^(i) = 0 for i < m and ℛ^(m) = −(1/2) e_(m+1) ∂_θ² W, of mean zero): (F2) at order m
is the order-m mean of the constraint equations. That is

    𝔓(γ_m, κ_m) + B_m(γ_m) = S_m,

with 𝔓 the linearisation of the constraint map at the data of g0 on Σ [CD03, (2.2), p. 4], B_m algebraic in γ_m (the
means of the products of γ_m and of ĝ_(m+1) of (i) with the oscillating data), and S_m known. Solve it with γ_m = α_m dr
dr and κ_m = ϖ_m Π + q′_m ⊗ dr + dr ⊗ q′_m by Lemma 7.6 (B_m is a zeroth-order term of the kind allowed
there), from zero data at r = a. Its forcing terms vanish where the earlier stages' data and the waves do, so (α_m, ϖ_m,
q′_m) vanish on r < v_start − τ0, and they are smooth. ∎

### 7.4 The constraints as an evolution in r

On Σ use (r, ω), ω ∈ S³, a ≤ r ≤ b1 := b(τ0); a stays the inner radius of Ω. For data (γ, κ) on Σ put Π := γ − |dr|_γ⁻²
dr ⊗ dr; on vectors tangent to the spheres {r = const} Π is the induced metric, and Π(γ⁻¹dr, ·) = 0. For U := (α, ϖ, q),
with α and ϖ functions and q a covector with q(γ⁻¹dr) = 0 (so that q is fixed by its angular components q_A, and q_r =
−γ^(rA) q_A/γ^(rr)), put, as in [Rac16] (the lapse of the foliation by the spheres, and the mixed and trace parts of κ),

    γ_U := γ + α dr ⊗ dr,      κ_U := κ + ϖ Π + q ⊗ dr + dr ⊗ q.    (7.4)

Write 𝒞(γ, κ) := (J, ρ) for the constraint map (7.2). Note that γ_U and γ induce the same metric on
the spheres, and that γ_U⁻¹ = γ⁻¹ − c(α) γ⁻¹dr ⊗ γ⁻¹dr with c(α) := α/(1 + α γ^(rr)).

**Lemma 7.5** (The constraints as an evolution in r.) (a) The constraint map of (γ_U, κ_U) is
quasilinear in U: of second order in α with no ∂_r² α and no ∂_r of an angular derivative of α, of first order in (ϖ,
q), and α enters J to first order only. Its ρ-component,

    ρ = p ∂_r α − γ^(rr) Π^(AB) ∂_A ∂_B α + (first order in the angular derivatives of α) + (algebraic in U),
        p := (γ^(rr))^(3/2) H,    (7.5)

with γ^(rr), H and Π^(AB) evaluated at γ_U (H the mean curvature of the spheres with respect to the unit normal toward
increasing r, Π^(AB) the inverse of their induced metric), is parabolic in r where the spheres have positive mean
curvature. Its J-component is symmetric hyperbolic in (ϖ, q) with r as time. At the data of g0 on Σ, γ = (1 + μ/r²)
dr² + r² dΩ² with μ = μ(τ0 + r), so that γ^(rr) = r²/(r² + μ), γ^(rA) = 0, Π = r² dΩ² and H = 3/(r² + μ)^(1/2) > 0 for
all r, and

    ρ = (3 r³/(r² + μ)²) ∂_r α − (r² + μ)⁻¹ Δ_(S³) α + …,
    J_r = 6 ∂_r ϖ − 2 Π^(AB) ∂_A q_B + …,     J_A = −(2 r²/(r² + μ)) ∂_r q_A + 4 ∂_A ϖ + …;

the symmetrizer 𝒮 = diag(1, −(1/2) Π⁻¹), which depends on γ alone, gives 𝒮 A0 = diag(6, (r²/(r² + μ)) Π⁻¹) > 0 and 𝒮 A^B
symmetric for every angle B. In the class of fields of (r, ϑ) invariant under T² and both reflections (q = q_ϑ dϑ; the
components q_(φ1), q_(φ2) and J_(φ1), J_(φ2) vanish by the reflections) these equations are the whole system: J_r = 6
∂_r ϖ − (2/r²) ∂_ϑ q + …, J_ϑ = −(2 r²/(r² + μ)) ∂_r q + 4 ∂_ϑ ϖ + …, with 𝒮 = diag(1, −1/(2r²)), 𝒮 A0 = diag(6, 1/(r² +
μ)), 𝒮 A^ϑ = [[0, −2/r²], [−2/r², 0]], and real characteristic speeds c² = 2 (r² + μ)/(3 r⁴) > 0; the construction stays
in that class. For γ_rA small, as at the approximant's data (where γ_rA = O(λ²), by (b) below), and with q and Π read
as above, the symmetrizers still form a one-dimensional space, depending on γ alone; its generator, the matrix 𝒮 that
takes (J_r, J_A) to

    (J_r + (γ^(rA)/γ^(rr)) J_A,  −(1/2) Π^(AB) J_B),    (7.6)

has 𝒮 A0 = diag(6, γ_U^(rr) Π^(AB)) > 0 and 𝒮 A^C symmetric for every angle C. The smallness of γ_rA enters only the
uniqueness of the symmetrizer: for every Riemannian metric γ and every α with 1 + α γ^(rr) > 0, 𝒮 is invertible (it is
block triangular with diagonal blocks 1 and −(1/2) Π^(AB)), 𝒮 A0 > 0 and every 𝒮 A^C is symmetric, by the proof below,
and these are the properties of 𝒮 that Lemma 7.6 uses.

(b) At the approximant's data (the data on Σ of g_app built from the stage data of Lemma 7.4) the constraint
map of (γ_U, κ_U), as a function of U, has no coefficient of order 1/λ: the second derivatives of γ of order 1/λ enter
the coefficients of U only through the trace of W on the spheres, which vanishes, and the ∂_r κ_rr terms of div κ and d
tr κ cancel.

(c) The phase on Σ is (τ0 + r)/λ, so angular derivatives of every coefficient are bounded uniformly in λ. At the
approximant's data the order-0 parts of all principal coefficients equal the background's, so p, γ^(rr) Π^(AB) and 𝒮 A0
keep their signs for λ small; 𝒮 depends on γ alone, whose first derivatives are bounded uniformly in λ; and
Lemma 7.6 needs no ∂_r p. Lower-order coefficients may oscillate at O(1), and some do: the coefficient of
α in ρ contains the term |𝒜|²/ν² of the proof below, where the second fundamental form 𝒜 of the spheres has the
oscillating part (1/(2ν)) [∂_θ W_AB] of order one, so that it oscillates, with a nonzero θ-mean where the waves do not
vanish (such a mean is part of B_m in Lemma 7.4 (iii)); and the coefficient of ∂_C α in J_A contains −γ^(rr)
Π^(BC) κ_AB, where κ_AB has the oscillating part (1/2) n0(v) [∂_θ W_AB] of order one, n0 the future unit normal of g0
to Σ. Lemma 7.6 needs only their angular regularity.

*Proof.* (a), ρ. Write γ = ν² dr² + Π_AB (dω^A + σ^A dr)(dω^B + σ^B dr), with lapse ν > 0 and shift σ of the foliation
by the spheres; then γ^(rr) = ν⁻², and γ_U has the same Π and σ and the lapse ν_U with ν_U² = ν² + α. Let e_r := ν⁻¹(∂_r
− σ) be the unit normal, 𝒜 := (1/(2ν))(∂_r Π − 𝓛_σ Π) the second fundamental form of the spheres and H := tr_Π 𝒜.
The Gauss equation for the spheres, R = R_Π + 2 Ric(e_r, e_r) − H² + |𝒜|², and the Riccati equation along the normal
flow, Ric(e_r, e_r) = −∂_(e_r) H − |𝒜|² − ν⁻¹ Δ_Π ν, give

    R(γ) = R_Π − 2 ∂_(e_r) H − H² − |𝒜|² − 2 ν⁻¹ Δ_Π ν.

Replace ν by ν_U. In H = H̃/ν, H̃ := (1/2) Π^(AB)(∂_r Π_AB − (𝓛_σ Π)_AB) does not depend on α, so −2 ∂_(e_r) H ⊃ 2 ν⁻³
H̃ ∂_r ν = H̃ ν⁻⁴ ∂_r(ν²): the coefficient of ∂_r α is H ν⁻³ = (γ^(rr))^(3/2) H, evaluated at γ_U. The second
derivatives of α come from −2 ν_U⁻¹ Δ_Π ν_U = −ν_U⁻² Δ_Π α + (first order): −γ_U^(rr) Π^(AB) ∂_A ∂_B α, angular only.
R_Π, H², |𝒜|² and the σ-part of ∂_(e_r) H contain α algebraically or through its angular derivatives. The terms
−|κ_U|² + (tr κ_U)² contain U algebraically. This proves the form (7.5).

(a), J. Let γ be a Riemannian metric and 1 + α γ^(rr) > 0; the smallness of γ_rA is used only for the uniqueness
at the end. Put Π^(ij) := γ^(ik) γ^(jl) Π_kl and Π_i^k := γ^(kj) Π_ji. Since Π = γ − dr ⊗ dr/γ^(rr),
Π^(ij) = γ^(ij) − γ^(ri) γ^(rj)/γ^(rr), that is γ⁻¹ = Π^♯ + γ⁻¹dr ⊗ γ⁻¹dr/γ^(rr) with Π^♯ := (Π^(ij)); so Π^(rk) = 0, and
the angular block Π^(AB) = γ^(AB) − γ^(rA) γ^(rB)/γ^(rr) is the inverse of the angular block (γ_AB) of γ (the inverse of
a block of a matrix is the Schur complement of the complementary block of the inverse matrix), that is of the induced
metric of the spheres, as in the statement. In J = 2(−div_(γ_U) κ_U + d tr_(γ_U) κ_U) the derivatives of (ϖ, q) come from
κ_U − κ. Since Π(γ⁻¹dr, ·) = 0 and q(γ⁻¹dr) = 0, the formula for γ_U⁻¹ gives tr_(γ_U) Π = 3 and
tr_(γ_U)(q ⊗ dr + dr ⊗ q) = 0, so d tr_(γ_U) κ_U contains 3 dϖ. Further, γ_U^(jk) Π_ij ∂_k ϖ = Π_i^k ∂_k ϖ, γ_U⁻¹dr =
(1 + α γ^(rr))⁻¹ γ⁻¹dr, and γ_U^(jk) ∂_k q_j = Π^(AB) ∂_A q_B + (lower order), because (γ⁻¹dr)^j ∂_k q_j =
∂_k(q(γ⁻¹dr)) − q_j ∂_k (γ⁻¹dr)^j is of order zero and Π^(rk) = 0. So the principal part of J is

    J_i ≅ 2 (3 ∂_i ϖ − Π_i^k ∂_k ϖ − (1 + α γ^(rr))⁻¹ (γ⁻¹dr)^k ∂_k q_i − ∂_i r Π^(AB) ∂_A q_B).

Contracting with γ⁻¹dr, which Π annihilates, and using q(γ⁻¹dr) = 0 again, J_r + (γ^(rA)/γ^(rr)) J_A = J(γ⁻¹dr)/γ^(rr) ≅
6 ∂_r ϖ + 6 (γ^(rC)/γ^(rr)) ∂_C ϖ − 2 Π^(CB) ∂_C q_B. For the angular components, ∂_A r = 0 and Π_A^k ∂_k = ∂_A, so J_A
≅ 4 ∂_A ϖ − 2 (1 + α γ^(rr))⁻¹ (γ^(rr) ∂_r + γ^(rC) ∂_C) q_A, and −(1/2) Π^(AB) J_B ≅ −2 Π^(AC) ∂_C ϖ + (1 + α γ^(rr))⁻¹
Π^(AB)(γ^(rr) ∂_r + γ^(rC) ∂_C) q_B. Since (1 + α γ^(rr))⁻¹ γ^(rr) = γ_U^(rr), the matrix 𝒮 of (7.6)
makes the principal part of J, in (ϖ, q_B), equal to 𝒮 A0 ∂_r + 𝒮 A^C ∂_C with 𝒮 A0 = diag(6, γ_U^(rr) Π^(AB)), positive
definite, and

    𝒮 A^C = [[6 γ^(rC)/γ^(rr), −2 Π^(CB)], [−2 Π^(AC), (1 + α γ^(rr))⁻¹ γ^(rC) Π^(AB)]],

symmetric; at the data of g0, where γ^(rA) = 0 and α = 0, 𝒮 = diag(1, −(1/2) Π⁻¹). α enters J through γ_U⁻¹ and through
the connection of γ_U, so to first order. A symmetrizer is a matrix S with S A0 and every S A^C symmetric: linear
conditions on S, with coefficients continuous in γ and α. Where γ_rA = 0, in a frame orthonormal for Π, A0 = diag(6, −2
γ_U^(rr) I) and A^C has the row −2 e_C^T (the J_r-equation on q) and the column 4 e_C (the J_A-equations on ϖ), e_C the
C-th unit vector. Writing S = [[s, b^T], [c, D]], S A^C = [[4 b·e_C, −2 s e_C^T], [4 D e_C, −2 c e_C^T]] is symmetric
for C = 1, 2, 3 only if D = −(s/2) I and c = 0, and then S A0 = [[6 s, −2 γ_U^(rr) b^T], [0, s γ_U^(rr) I]] is symmetric
only if b = 0: S = s diag(1, −(1/2) I), a one-dimensional space. The dimension of the solution space of such a linear
system cannot increase under small changes of its coefficients, and the space contains 𝒮 ≠ 0; so for γ_rA small it is
one-dimensional, generated by 𝒮. At the data of g0, ν² = 1 + μ/r², σ = 0 and Π = r² dΩ²; the volume density is r² (r² +
μ)^(1/2) times that of the unit sphere and e_r = (r/(r² + μ)^(1/2)) ∂_r, so H = div e_r = (r² (r² + μ)^(1/2))⁻¹ ∂_r
(r³) = 3/(r² + μ)^(1/2), and p = (r²/(r² + μ))^(3/2) · 3/(r² + μ)^(1/2) = 3 r³/(r² + μ)². In the symmetric class the
speeds solve det(A^ϑ − c A0) = 0 with A0 = diag(6, −2 r²/(r² + μ)) and A^ϑ = [[0, −2/r²], [4, 0]]: −12 c² r²/(r² + μ) +
8/r² = 0.

(b) Write γ and κ for the data of g_app on Σ, and expand in λ. On Σ the phases φ_j vanish, the means m_j have (m_j)_(τ
·) = 0 and spatial part α_j dr dr, W_TT has only angular components and χ dv dv only (τ, r) components, so γ_rA = λ² (…)
and the profiles ĝ_j, j ≥ 2, carry the factor λ^j. A derivative of order k along Σ of a term λ^j [f] is O(λ^(j−k)) in
the radial direction and O(λ^j) in the angular ones, since ∂_r v = 1 and ∂_A v = 0 on Σ. Hence the second derivatives of
γ of order 1/λ are λ⁻¹ [∂_θ² W_ij] in ∂_r² γ_ij, and κ has an oscillating part κ̃ of order one, with ∂_k κ = λ⁻¹ δ_k^r
[∂_θ κ̃] + O(1). Here κ = (1/2)(𝓛_n g)|_Σ up to sign, n the unit normal; the order-one oscillating part of 𝓛_n(λ [g1])
is n0(v) [∂_θ W_ij] and that of g0(∂_i n, ∂_j) + g0(∂_i, ∂_j n) is ∂_i v [∂_θ n♭_(1)]_j + ∂_j v [∂_θ n♭_(1)]_i, where
n♭_(1) := g0(n_(1), ·) and n_(1) is the coefficient of λ in n, which is algebraic in g1: n^a = −g^(aτ)/(−g^(ττ))^(1/2).
Its angular components are combinations of (g1)_(Ab) g0^(bτ) and of g0(n0, ∂_A) = 0; the oscillating part W_(Ab) g0^(bτ)
vanishes, since W_TT has no τ or r component, (dv)_A = 0, and g0^(Bτ) = 0. So κ̃_rA = 0, κ̃_AB = (1/2) n0(v) [∂_θ W_AB]
up to sign, and κ̃_rr is some function.

In ρ, by the formula for R(γ_U) above with ν_U² = ν² + α, the coefficients of U involve second r-derivatives of γ only
through ∂_(e_r) H, that is through (1/(2 ν_U²)) Π^(AB) ∂_r² Π_AB and through ∂_r 𝓛_σ Π; the second is O(1), since σ =
O(λ²), and the order-1/λ part of the first is λ⁻¹ (1/(2 ν_U²)) Π0^(AB) [∂_θ² W_AB] = λ⁻¹ (1/(2 ν_U²)) [∂_θ² tr_(Π0) W] =
0, W being traceless on the spheres. Every other coefficient of ρ involves at most one r-derivative of γ (angular
derivatives cost nothing) and no derivative of κ, so it is O(1). In J, the coefficients of (ϖ, q) involve γ, Π, dr and
the connection of γ_U, so they are O(1); and α enters through the connection of γ_U (O(1) coefficients) and through
γ_U⁻¹ in the terms with ∂κ. These are, by the formula for γ_U⁻¹,

    2 c(α) ((γ⁻¹dr)^j (γ⁻¹dr)^k ∂_k κ_ij − ∂_i(κ(γ⁻¹dr, γ⁻¹dr))) + (terms with ∂c(α) or ∂γ⁻¹: O(1) coefficients),

whose order-1/λ part is λ⁻¹ 2 c(α) (γ0^(rr))² ([∂_θ κ̃_ir] − δ_i^r [∂_θ κ̃_rr]), since γ⁻¹dr = γ0^(rr) ∂_r + O(λ): it
vanishes for i = r, where the two ∂_r κ_rr terms cancel, and for i = A, where κ̃_Ar = 0. Were W to have a nonzero trace
on the spheres, the term −ν_U⁻² Π^(AB) ∂_r² Π_AB of −2 ∂_(e_r) H would give the coefficient of α in ρ the part λ⁻¹ ν⁻⁴
[∂_θ² tr_(Π0) W], of order 1/λ.

(c) The principal coefficients are γ^(rr), Π^(AB), γ^(rA) and p = (γ^(rr))^(3/2) H; the first three are algebraic in γ =
γ0 + O(λ), and H = (1/(2 ν)) Π^(AB)(∂_r Π_AB − (𝓛_σ Π)_AB) has the order-one oscillating part (1/(2 ν)) Π0^(AB) [∂_θ
W_AB] = 0, the rest being γ0's value plus O(λ). The coefficient of α in ρ contains, from −|𝒜|² with 𝒜 = (1/(2 ν_U))(∂_r Π
− 𝓛_σ Π), the term ∂_α(−(ν²/ν_U²)|𝒜|²) = |𝒜|²/ν² at α = 0, and the oscillating part of 𝒜 is (1/(2 ν)) [∂_θ W_AB], so
that |𝒜|²/ν² has the oscillating part (1/(4 ν⁴)) |[∂_θ W]|²_(Π0) − (its θ-mean), and the θ-mean
(1/(4 ν⁴)) ⟨|∂_θ W|²_(Π0)⟩, positive where the waves do not vanish. (|∂_θ W|² is not constant in θ: by the form
(2.11) of W_TT it is a positive multiple of c⁴ sin²θ + s⁴ cos²θ + c²s² sin θ cos θ, with c = cos ϑ and s = sin ϑ, a
quadratic form in (sin θ, cos θ) that is not a multiple of sin²θ + cos²θ.) The other terms of the coefficient quadratic
in the oscillation come from ∂_r H̃ in ∂_(e_r) H, whose quadratic part (1/2) ∂_r Π^(AB) ∂_r Π_AB + (1/2) Π^(AB) ∂_r² Π_AB
⊃ −(1/2) |[∂_θ W]|² − (1/2) [W^(AB) ∂_θ² W_AB] has θ-mean zero, and from H², which has no oscillating part of order one;
the κ-terms carry κ̃(γ⁻¹dr, ·) and tr κ̃, and κ̃_rA = 0, while tr_(Π0) κ̃_AB = 0 and κ̃_rr vanishes with χ on Σ. In J_A =
2(…), the term −γ^(jk) Γ(γ_U)^l_(jk) κ_lA of div κ_U contributes 2 γ^(jk) Γ(γ_U)^B_(jk) κ_BA ⊃ −γ^(rr) Π^(BC) κ_AB ∂_C α
(the part l = r carries κ_rA), from γ^(jk) Γ(γ_U)^B_(jk) ⊃ −(1/2) γ^(rr) Π^(BC) ∂_C α, while the other terms with ∂_C α
carry κ(γ⁻¹dr, γ⁻¹dr) δ_A^C or κ_Ar, whose oscillating parts are multiples of δ_A^C or zero; the oscillating part −γ^(rr)
Π^(BC) κ̃_AB is not a multiple of δ_A^C, W_TT being traceless, so it does not cancel. The remaining claims are
those of (a). ∎

**Lemma 7.6** (The linear evolution.) Consider on [a, b1] × S³, b1 > a, the linear system, with
coefficients measurable in r for which M_s below is finite,

    p ∂_r α − Δ_p α + b′·∂_S α + c α + e·(ϖ, q) = F_ρ,
    A0 ∂_r (ϖ, q) + A^B ∂_B (ϖ, q) + c′ (ϖ, q) + f ∂_r α + f′·∂_S α + c″ α = F_J,    (7.7)

with ∂_S the first-order angular derivatives, Δ_p a second-order angular operator, elliptic on each sphere with
ellipticity constant at least δ_e > 0, p ≥ p0 > 0, and an invertible symmetrizer 𝒮 with 𝒮 A0 ≥ A00 > 0 and 𝒮 A^B
symmetric, with zero data at r = a. For s > 3/2 + 2 there is a unique solution, and

    sup_r (‖α‖_(H^(s+1)) + ‖(ϖ, q)‖_(H^s)) + ‖α‖_(L² H^(s+2)) ≤ C (‖F_ρ‖_(L² H^s) + ‖F_J‖_(L² H^s)),

norms on the spheres S³, with C depending only on s, b1 − a, p0, δ_e, A00 and an upper bound for

    M_s := sup_r ‖(p, Δ_p, 𝒮, 𝒮 A0, 𝒮 A^B)‖_(H^(s+1)(S³)) + sup_r ‖(b′, c, e, c′, f, f′, c″)‖_(H^s(S³))
           + ∫_a^(b1) ‖∂_r (𝒮 A0)‖_(L^∞) dr,

and increasing in M_s; no other r-derivative of a coefficient enters. Write ‖U‖_(X_s) for the left side of the bound plus
‖∂_r α‖_(L² H^s). The bound is tame: at an index s″ > s, with ‖U‖_(s″; [a, r]) the left side at index s″ on [a, r] and
m_(s″)(r) the norms at index s″ of the coefficients at r (those of M_(s″), without the supremum),

    ‖U‖_(s″; [a, r]) ≤ C (‖F‖_(L²((a, r); H^(s″))) + ∫_a^r m_(s″)(r′) ω_s(r′) dr′ + ‖m_(s″) ω_∞‖_(L²(a, r))),

with C depending only on s″, M_s and the bounds above; ω_s square-integrable on (a, b1), its L² norm bounded by the
solution's X_s norm and ‖F‖_(L² H^(s−1)) (‖∂_r (ϖ, q)‖_(L^∞), a part of ω_s, contains F_J); and ω_∞ := ‖α‖_(W^(1,∞)) +
‖(ϖ, q)‖_(L^∞), bounded by C times the X_s norm. For the squared energy 𝒴 at index s″ (the parabolic energy at index s″ +
1 plus the hyperbolic one at index s″) the proof gives

    ∂_r 𝒴 + c0 ‖α‖²_(H^(s″+2)) ≤ ω_0 𝒴 + C ‖F‖²_(H^(s″)) + C m_(s″) ω_s 𝒴^(1/2) + C m_(s″)² ω_∞²,

with c0 > 0 the gain from the ellipticity of Δ_p after division by p, depending only on δ_e and M_s (also below, at index
s), and ω_0 := C (1 + ‖∂_r (𝒮 A0)‖_(L^∞)), integrable on (a, b1), with C as above; and integrating, taking the supremum
over [a, r], and Young's and Gronwall's lemmas give the bound.

The commutator and product estimates used are these. The Kato–Ponce inequality [GO13, p. 1] (Theorem A.32, for
Schwartz functions, extended at p = 2 to the compactly supported functions used here by Corollary A.33): for 1 <
p < ∞ and s > 0, ‖𝒥^s(f g) − f 𝒥^s g‖_(L^p) ≤ C (‖∇f‖_(L^∞) ‖𝒥^(s−1) g‖_(L^p) + ‖𝒥^s f‖_(L^p) ‖g‖_(L^∞)), 𝒥 := (1 −
Δ)^(1/2) on R^n. The Moser estimate [DS23, Remark 2.3(i)] (Remark A.8, for s > n/2 in n dimensions and Φ
satisfying (A2) of [DS23]): for a smooth function Φ of u, ‖Φ(u)‖_s ≤ C_I + F_I(‖u‖_∞) ‖u‖_s for u ∈ H^s, with C_I and F_I
depending on Φ. On S³ both follow from R³ through a finite atlas and a partition of unity, the Moser estimate for s >
3/2, which covers every index used here (s > 3/2 + 2).

*Proof.* Commute s angular derivatives, by the Killing fields X^I of the round S³, through (7.7); the
commutators are estimated in terms of M_s by the Moser and Kato–Ponce inequalities on S³. Parabolic energy:

    ∂_r (1/2) ‖α‖²_(H^(s+1)) + c0 ‖α‖²_(H^(s+2)) ≤ C (‖α‖²_(H^(s+1)) + ‖(ϖ, q)‖²_(H^s) + ‖F_ρ‖²_(H^s))

after dividing by p (its ∂_r is not needed: the equation is solved for ∂_r α). Hyperbolic energy, after applying 𝒮 to
the second equation:

    ∂_r ⟨(ϖ, q), 𝒮 A0 (ϖ, q)⟩_(H^s) ≤ C (1 + ‖∂_r (𝒮 A0)‖_(L^∞)) ‖(ϖ, q)‖²_(H^s)
                                       + C ‖(ϖ, q)‖_(H^s) (‖∂_r α‖_(H^s) + ‖α‖_(H^(s+1)) + ‖F_J‖_(H^s)),

the 𝒮 A^B terms integrating by parts on the closed spheres, and ‖∂_r α‖_(H^s) ≤ C (‖α‖_(H^(s+2)) + ‖(ϖ, q)‖_(H^s) +
‖F_ρ‖_(H^s)) from the first equation. Young's inequality and Gronwall's lemma (which needs ‖∂_r (𝒮 A0)‖_(L^∞) only
integrable in r) give the bound.

At an index s″ > s the same pairings, with the Moser and Kato–Ponce inequalities applied to the top norms of the
coefficients, give the differential inequality of the statement. Its last term comes from the parabolic equation. The
coefficients b′, c and e lie in H^(s″) only, so pairing the first equation at index s″ + 1 must move one derivative onto
α: |⟨α, c α⟩_(H^(s″+1))| ≤ ‖α‖_(H^(s″+2)) ‖c α‖_(H^(s″)), with ‖c α‖_(H^(s″)) ≤ C (‖c‖_(H^(s″)) ‖α‖_(L^∞) + ‖c‖_(L^∞)
‖α‖_(H^(s″))), and Young's inequality against the gain c0 ‖α‖²_(H^(s″+2)) leaves C m_(s″)² ‖α‖²_(L^∞); likewise b′·∂_S α,
with ‖α‖_(W^(1,∞)), and e·(ϖ, q), with ‖(ϖ, q)‖_(L^∞), which must be paired so in any case, (ϖ, q) lying in H^(s″) only.
The hyperbolic part needs no such term: it is paired at index s″, where C m_(s″) ω_s 𝒴^(1/2) suffices.

Existence, by the Faedo–Galerkin method. Let P_L be the L²(S³)-orthogonal projection onto the eigenfunctions of the
Laplacian with eigenvalue at most L(L + 2), and for the covector q onto those of the Hodge Laplacian on 1-forms. The
eigenspaces are SO(4)-invariant, so P_L commutes with the Laplacian and with the Lie derivative along every Killing
field, which is what X^I means on q. Solve the first equation for ∂_r α (dividing by p), and seek α_L and (ϖ, q)_L in the
range of P_L with ∂_r α_L = P_L[…] and P_L[𝒮 A0 ∂_r (ϖ, q)_L] = P_L[…] (the symmetrized second equation, ∂_r α_L in it),
with the data of the lemma projected by P_L. This is a linear system of ordinary differential equations in r for finitely
many coefficients, whose matrix P_L 𝒮 A0 P_L is positive definite on the range (𝒮 A0 > 0) and continuous in r, the other
coefficients and the forcing terms being integrable in r, so Picard iteration gives a unique absolutely continuous
solution on [a, b1]. The test functions of the argument above, X^(I*) X^I applied to α_L or to (ϖ, q)_L, lie in the range
of P_L, so the projection drops out of each tested equation (⟨P_L G, f⟩ = ⟨G, f⟩ for f in the range), and the energy
identities are those above, with one addition: the commutator [X^I, 𝒮 A0] ∂_r (ϖ, q)_L needs ‖∂_r (ϖ, q)_L‖_(H^(s−1)),
which testing the projected second equation with X^(I′*) X^(I′) ∂_r (ϖ, q)_L, |I′| = 0, …, s − 1 in turn, bounds by C
(‖(ϖ, q)_L‖_(H^s) + ‖∂_r α_L‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖F_J‖_(H^(s−1))) (𝒮 A0 > 0; the commutators are of lower order in I′). So the
bound holds for (α_L, (ϖ, q)_L) uniformly in L; a weak-* limit as L → ∞ solves (7.7) and obeys it.

Uniqueness follows from the energy estimate at index 0, applied to the difference of two solutions whose left side is
finite. For such a difference α lies in L² H^(s+2) with ∂_r α in L² H^s, and (ϖ, q) in L^∞ H^s with ∂_r (ϖ, q) in L²
H^(s−1), by the equations; so at index 0 every pairing of the two energy identities is defined and absolutely continuous
in r, which at index s it need not be. The index-0 estimate commutes no derivative and needs only the L^∞ and W^(1,∞)
norms of the coefficients and ∫ ‖∂_r (𝒮 A0)‖_(L^∞) dr, all bounded by M_s; with zero forcing and data it gives zero. ∎

**Proposition 7.7** (The exact correction.) Let the stage data be those of Lemma 7.4 with
N ≥ K + 3, and (γ, κ) the data of g_app on Σ. For λ ≤ λ0 there is U on Σ, U = 0 on r < v_start − τ0, with 𝒞(γ_U, κ_U) =
0 on Σ and sup_r ‖∂_r^j U(r)‖_(H^s(S³)) ≤ C_(j,s) λ^(N−2−j).

*Proof.* Write 𝒞(γ_U, κ_U) = 𝒞(γ, κ) + 𝔏 U + 𝒬(U), 𝔏 the linearisation (Lemma 7.5) and 𝒬 the
remainder, quadratic in (U, ∂U, ∂ ∂_S α), with coefficients involving at most two derivatives of γ and one of κ, hence
of size at most C λ⁻¹. 𝒞(γ, κ) = O(λ^(N−2)) with all its angular derivatives (its profiles vanish below order N − 2 by
Lemma 7.3, and angular derivatives of profiles cost nothing on Σ), and it vanishes on r < v_start − τ0.
(It is in fact O(λ^(N−1)) with all its angular derivatives: Lemma 7.3 gives ∂_θ D^(N−1) = 0, so the phase
part λ^(N−2) (du) ∂_θ D^(N−1) of ∂D(g_app) vanishes and ∂D = O(λ^(N−1)), while Ric^H(g_app) = O(λ^N). The order gained
is not used, and N ≥ K + 3 is kept.) The ρ-component is linear in ∂_r α and in the angular second derivatives of α, with
coefficients depending on α algebraically (the scalar curvature of γ + α dr dr contains no (∂_r α)²), and the
J-component is linear in ∂(ϖ, q) with coefficients depending on α algebraically. Recall

    ‖U‖_(X_s) = sup_r (‖α‖_(H^(s+1)) + ‖(ϖ, q)‖_(H^s)) + ‖α‖_(L² H^(s+2)) + ‖∂_r α‖_(L² H^s),

the left side of Lemma 7.6 with the ∂_r α the first equation gives.

Iterate: U_(i+1) solves, with zero data at r = a, the linear system (7.7) whose principal coefficients are
frozen at U_i, as is the whole coefficient f of ∂_r α in the J-equation, f(γ, κ; α, ϖ, q), evaluated at U_i and
multiplying ∂_r α_(i+1). (It depends on α and on (ϖ, q), so the terms q_ϑ ∂_r α and α ∂_r α of J's remainder are not
left among the forcing terms; in the contraction the extra forcing term (f(U_i) − f(U_(i−1))) ∂_r α_i is at most C
λ^(N−2) ‖U_i − U_(i−1)‖_(X_(s_1)) in L² H^(s_1).) Its forcing terms are −𝒞(γ, κ) and the remaining terms, at least
quadratic and evaluated at U_i. Fix s_1 > 3/2 + 4 and s := s_1 + 2. At U = 0 the coefficients are those of
Lemma 7.5; frozen at U_i they change by at most C λ⁻¹ ‖U_i‖_X, ∂_r α_i entering M_s only through ∫
‖∂_r (𝒮 A0)‖_(L^∞) dr ≤ C (1 + ‖U_i‖_(X_(s_1))). So while ‖U_i‖_(X_s) ≤ 2 C_0 λ^(N−2), the hypotheses of
Lemma 7.6 hold at the indices s_1 and s with constants independent of λ, for λ small and N ≥ 4.
Lemma 7.6 at index s keeps the iterates in the ball of radius 2 C_0 λ^(N−2) of X_s, and at index s_1
gives ‖U_(i+1) − U_i‖_(X_(s_1)) ≤ C λ^(N−3) ‖U_i − U_(i−1)‖_(X_(s_1)) (the difference of the frozen coefficients
multiplies U_i, estimated in the higher norm), a contraction. Bounded in X_s and contracting in X_(s_1), the iterates
converge to a solution in X_s; this is the scheme of Kato and Majda for quasilinear symmetric hyperbolic systems
(Remark A.11; [AO14, Section 4.1, p. 19], [DS23, Section 4], [AG22, p. 1]: boundedness in a high norm and
contraction in a low norm), and the parabolic component obeys the same estimates. Uniqueness holds in the ball of radius
2 C_0 λ^(N−2) of X_s, by the difference estimate.

U = 0 on r < v_start − τ0. There 𝒞(γ, κ) vanishes, and where U_i vanishes so do the quadratic terms at U_i; so for every
r1 < v_start − τ0 the system for U_(i+1) has zero forcing terms on [a, r1] and zero data at r = a, and
Lemma 7.6 on [a, r1], whose bound there involves the forcing terms on [a, r1] alone, gives U_(i+1) = 0 on
[a, r1]. By induction from U_0 = 0 every iterate, and so the limit, vanishes there. The r-derivatives follow from the
equations, each ∂_r of a coefficient costing at most λ⁻¹.

Smoothness (persistence of regularity). The coefficients and forcing terms of each step are smooth in the angles when
the previous iterate is, so by Lemma 7.6 at every index the iterates U_i are smooth, by induction. At an
index s″ > s the bound of Lemma 7.6 is linear in the top norms, those of the coefficients (functions of
α) entering linearly by the Moser and Kato–Ponce inequalities with factors depending only on the X_s bound. With ℰ_i(r)
the X_(s″) norm of U_i on [a, r] it reads

    ℰ_(i+1)(r) ≤ Ξ_0 + Ξ_1 (∫_a^r ℰ_i²)^(1/2),

with Ξ_1 uniform in i. Indeed, by the tame form of Lemma 7.6 the forcing terms enter in L² H^(s″), and
the weight built from ‖∂_r α_(i+1)‖_∞ and ‖∂_r (ϖ, q)_(i+1)‖_∞, bounded in L²(a, b1), enters through the Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality, ‖∂_r (𝒮 A0)‖_∞ entering Gronwall's exponent; a forcing term carrying ∂_r α_i would put ℰ_i(r) itself on the
right, which is why the coefficient of ∂_r α is frozen. The term ‖m_(s″) ω_∞‖_(L²(a, r)) of the tame bound changes
neither the rate of Ξ_0 nor the uniformity of Ξ_1: ω_∞ ≤ C ‖U_(i+1)‖_(X_(s_1)) ≤ C λ^(N−2) in the ball; the lower-order
coefficients b′, c, e, c′, f′, c″ are those of Lemma 7.5 at U = 0, independent of U and smooth in the
angles uniformly in λ; and the others are functions of U_i entering linearly and changing by C λ⁻¹ ‖U_i‖, so that m_(s″)
≤ C (1 + λ⁻¹ ℰ_i), and the term is at most C λ^(N−2) (b1 − a)^(1/2) + C λ^(N−3) (∫_a^r ℰ_i²)^(1/2): a part of Ξ_0
proportional to λ^(N−2) and a part of Ξ_1 at most C λ^(N−3) ≤ C, as N ≥ 4.

By induction, ℰ_i(r) ≤ Ξ_0 Σ_(k≥0) Ξ_1^k ((r − a)^k/k!)^(1/2) for every i, with no smallness. For ℰ_0 = 0 this holds,
and if it holds for ℰ_i, then Minkowski's inequality gives (∫_a^r ℰ_i²)^(1/2) ≤ Ξ_0 Σ_k Ξ_1^k (∫_a^r (r′ − a)^k/k!
dr′)^(1/2) = Ξ_0 Σ_k Ξ_1^k ((r − a)^(k+1)/(k + 1)!)^(1/2), so ℰ_(i+1)(r) ≤ Ξ_0 + Ξ_0 Σ_(k≥0) Ξ_1^(k+1) ((r −
a)^(k+1)/(k + 1)!)^(1/2), which is the claim for i + 1; the series converges by the ratio test. So the limit U lies in
X_(s″) for every s″. Ξ_0 is proportional to λ^(N−2) (the forcing term 𝒞(γ, κ) and the low norms are) and Ξ_1 is bounded
independently of λ, so ‖U‖_(X_(s″)) ≤ C_(s″) λ^(N−2) for every s″, which with the equations gives the stated rate at
every s and j. So U is smooth for λ ≤ λ0, λ0 independent of s″. Theorem 6.1 needs only k + 1 = 7
derivatives of the data in any case. ∎

**Remark 7.8** (Numerical observation.) On the data of the stage-0 approximant, in the class of fields of
(r, ϑ) invariant under T² and both reflections, the linear system of Lemma 7.6 was solved numerically by a
pseudo-spectral discretisation in the angle, marched in r, with a forcing term of size λ⁴ (the size λ^(N−2) at N = 6).
Over the last halving of λ, from 1/32 to 1/64, the suprema in r of norms of H² type of U, ∂_r U and ∂_r² U decreased as
λ^4.00, λ^3.99 and λ^3.00, within the rates λ^(N−2−j) of Proposition 7.7 (the first r-derivative costing
nothing). With a trace of the waves on the spheres put in, which creates a coefficient of order 1/λ
(Lemma 7.5 (b)), the first r-derivative cost a factor λ⁻¹. The iteration of the proof, principal
coefficients frozen, contracted with first ratios 6.8 × 10⁻³, 5.8 × 10⁻⁴ and 3.5 × 10⁻⁵ at λ = 1/8, 1/16 and 1/32. These
are floating-point observations, and no proof uses them.

### 7.5 Proof of the theorem

*Proof of Theorem 7.1.* Take the stage data of Lemma 7.4 with N := K + 3 and U of Proposition 7.7.
Put g on Σ: the spatial part γ + α dr dr, the lapse and shift of G(X, u/λ), ∂_τ of the spatial part fixed by κ + ϖ Π + q
⊗ dr + dr ⊗ q, and ∂_τ of the lapse and shift fixed by D(g) = 0 (as in Section 7.2, "What the theorem asks").
Then the constraints hold exactly (Proposition 7.7), D = 0, and, by (7.3), ∂_τ D = 0 on
Σ for the solution of Ric^H = 0 with these data.

For w := g − g_app on Σ, g_app the fixed-phase form of the statement: G(X, u/λ) and that form differ by O(λ^(N+1)) in
scaled norms (Section 4.6), within C λ^K since N + 1 > K, so it suffices to bound w′ := g − G(X, u/λ). The
spatial part of w′ and ∂_τ of it are U and combinations of U and its tangential derivatives. The components w′_(τ ·) do
not vanish but are algebraic in U: g and G(X, u/λ) have the same lapse and the same shift β, and their spatial parts
differ by α dr ⊗ dr, so w′_(τi) = α (dr)_i dr(β) and w′_(ττ) = α dr(β)², with β bounded with its derivatives in the
scaled norms. And ∂_τ w′_(τ ·) solves the linear relation D(g) − D(G(X, u/λ)) = −D(G(X, u/λ)) = O(λ^(N−1)) with
invertible coefficient. So, each derivative costing at most λ⁻¹, Data(w′) ≤ C λ⁻¹ λ^(N−2) = C λ^K, hence Data(w) ≤ C λ^K:
(E4). The data are smooth (Proposition 7.7) and invariant under T² and both reflections: the construction
commutes with the symmetries, by the uniqueness in Lemma 7.6, Proposition 7.7 and the stage
equations, Pol⁺ being equivariant. They equal the seed's data on Σ ∩ {r < v_start − τ0}. ∎

### 7.6 The main theorem, items 1–5

Items 1–5 of Theorem 3.1 follow from Theorem 4.11, Theorem 7.1 and Theorem 6.1 with
Lemma 3.6; the proof is in Section 3.2.

# Part IV. The horizon, the construction from past null infinity and the mass law

## 8. The boundary, the spheres' horizon and the mean mass

This chapter proves the three propositions of Theorem 3.1 that concern the geometry of the solutions g_λ: the
curvature boundary x_K = 1 is spacelike (Proposition 3.3), the outgoing expansion of the round spheres
has exactly one zero on each column, close to √μ (Proposition 3.4), and the Hawking mass of every round sphere is
μ(v) up to O(λ²) outside the shell (Proposition 3.5). Items 6 and 7 of Theorem 3.1 are the last two.

### 8.1 Notation and the facts used

Throughout, K ≥ 6, 0 < λ ≤ λ0, g_λ is the solution of Theorem 3.1 on Ω, g_app = g0 + λ[g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j] is
its approximant (Theorem 4.11) and w := g_λ − g_app. The profiles and the bracket [f](X) := f(X, v(X)/λ) are
those of Section 2.5. Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 6.1 gives, with M the constant of that
theorem,

    ‖∂^i w‖_∞ ≤ C M λ^(K−3−i),   i ≤ 4,   on Ω.    (8.1)

The first profile is g1 = m1 + W(X, θ + φ1(X)), where the mean m1 and the phase φ1 do not depend on θ, and
W = W_TT + χ dv², with W_TT the wave of (2.11) and χ its second harmonic ((4.9)). We use two
properties of W: W(ℓ, ·) = 0 (Lemma 4.5 (a)), and W_TT has no dτ, dr or dv component (Lemma 2.9 (b)).

On R⁴ we use r = |x|, and on S³ the angles (ϑ, ξ1, ξ2) given by x1 + i x2 = r cos ϑ e^(iξ1), x3 + i x4 = r sin ϑ e^(iξ2),
0 ≤ ϑ ≤ π/2. The round metric of S³ is dϑ² + cos²ϑ dξ1² + sin²ϑ dξ2², and ζ := cos 2ϑ. We write ξ1, ξ2 for the two
azimuths because φ1 is the first phase. In this chart

    g0 = −dτ² + dr² + r² (dϑ² + cos²ϑ dξ1² + sin²ϑ dξ2²) + (μ(v)/r²)(dτ + dr)²,

which is block diagonal between the (τ, r) plane and the sphere, and the wave of (2.11) reads

    λ W_TT = 2 r^(1/2) (cos²ϑ p1 dξ1² + sin²ϑ p2 dξ2² − (p1 + p2) dϑ²),
    p1 := (2 cos²ϑ G − sin²ϑ F)/3,   p2 := (2 sin²ϑ F − cos²ϑ G)/3,    (8.2)

with F := λ A env(v) h(ζ) sin θ, G := λ A env(v) h(ζ) cos θ and h(ζ) := √(2/(1 + ζ²)), at the phase θ.

For a sphere S_(v,r) := {τ = v − r, |x| = r} we write tr_S f := γ0^(AB) f_AB for the trace on S_(v,r), with γ0 the
metric g0 induces there, r² times the round metric. The covectors dτ and dr vanish on the tangent spaces of S_(v,r),
and so does dv = dτ + dr. It follows at once from (8.2) that

    tr_S W = 0   on every S_(v,r) and at every phase.    (8.3)

Indeed χ dv² vanishes on tangent vectors of the sphere, and tr_S W_TT = r⁻² · 2 r^(1/2) λ⁻¹ (cos²ϑ p1/cos²ϑ + sin²ϑ
p2/sin²ϑ − (p1 + p2)) = 0.

A *column* is the set of points of D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} with v and x̂ ∈ S³ fixed and r varying. Its points are
(τ, x) = (v − r, r x̂), so d/dr along a column is −∂_τ + x̂·∂_x = ℓ, and a column is an integral curve of ℓ. Since
ℓ(v) = 0, the derivative along a column of a bracket is

    (d/dr) [f] = [ℓ f],    (8.4)

with ℓ acting on X only: no factor λ⁻¹ appears. A column lies in {r_q(v) ≤ r ≤ v − τ0}.

### 8.2 The boundary

*Proof of Proposition 3.3.* Write m := μ/r². By Proposition 2.5 (d),
g0⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − m, g0⁻¹(dr, dτ) = m and g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − m; since dv = dτ + dr, also g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0,
g0⁻¹(dv, dr) = 1 and g0⁻¹(dv, dτ) = −1. On x_K = 1 put Φ := r − r_q(v), r_q = (√72 μ l5²)^(1/4). Then
dΦ = dr − r_q′ dv with r_q′ = r_q μ′/(4μ), and

    g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) = g0⁻¹(dr, dr) − 2 r_q′ g0⁻¹(dr, dv) + r_q′² g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 1 − m − 2 r_q′.

At r = r_q, m = μ/r_q² = μ/(√72 μ l5²)^(1/2) = √(μ/(√72 l5²)), and 2 r_q′ = r_q μ′/(2μ). This is the formula of
Proposition 3.3.

*Sign.* μ is nondecreasing, so μ′ ≥ 0, and μ ≥ μ0 ≥ √72 l5². The second term is therefore at most −1 and the third at
most 0. Where μ > √72 l5² the second term is below −1; where μ′ > 0 the third is negative. At such points dΦ is
timelike for g0, which is to say that the hypersurface {Φ = 0} is spacelike.

*Time orientation.* g0⁻¹(dΦ, dτ) = g0⁻¹(dr, dτ) − r_q′ g0⁻¹(dv, dτ) = m + r_q′ > 0. The covector dτ is timelike
(Lemma 2.6 (a)), and it is positive on future causal vectors because τ is a time function for the time orientation
of g0, in which L0, with L0(τ) = 1, is future directed. Where dΦ is timelike too, the two have positive
g0⁻¹-product and so lie in opposite halves of the cone of timelike covectors: dΦ(Z) < 0 for every future causal vector
Z there. In particular dΦ(Y) = −g0⁻¹(dΦ, dτ) < 0 for the future timelike Y := −g0⁻¹ dτ. By continuity of the cone, every
point of {Φ = 0} at which dΦ is timelike has a neighbourhood U and a c > 0 with dΦ(Z) ≤ −c dτ(Z) for every future causal
Z at points of U.

*No return.* A future causal curve γ has dτ(γ′) > 0, so it may be parametrized by τ. Suppose γ meets {Φ = 0} at γ(τ1),
a point where μ > √72 l5² or μ′ > 0. Along γ, v does not decrease (dv(Z) = −g0(L0, Z) ≥ 0 for future causal Z) and μ is
nondecreasing; so if μ(v) > √72 l5² at γ(τ1) it holds at every later point of γ, and if μ′ > 0 there, then μ(v) >
μ(v(γ(τ1))) ≥ √72 l5² at every later point with larger v, while the points with the same v satisfy μ′ > 0. Hence the
condition holds at every later point of γ on {Φ = 0}, and at each such point Φ ∘ γ is strictly decreasing near it, by
the inequality of the time orientation. So Φ ∘ γ < 0 immediately after τ1: γ leaves D_T = {r ≥ r_q(v)} ∩ {v ≤ v_end + T}
there. If γ(τ2) ∈ D_T for some τ2 > τ1, let τ3 be the infimum of the τ > τ1 with Φ(γ(τ)) ≥ 0. Then τ3 > τ1,
Φ(γ(τ3)) = 0 and Φ ∘ γ < 0 on (τ1, τ3), which contradicts the strict decrease of Φ ∘ γ near τ3. So γ does not return.

*The margin.* If μ0 > √72 l5², then 1 − √(μ/(√72 l5²)) ≤ 1 − √(μ0/(√72 l5²)) = −δ_b, with δ_b the number of
Proposition 3.3, and the third term is at most 0, so g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) ≤ −δ_b on the whole boundary. By item 4 of
Theorem 3.1, |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ on Ω; since g0⁻¹ is bounded on the compact Ω and inversion is
smooth, |g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹| ≤ C1 λ. The covector dΦ = dr − r_q′ dv is bounded on Ω, so

    g_λ⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) ≤ g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) + C λ ≤ −δ_b + C λ ≤ −δ_b/2      once C λ ≤ δ_b/2.

Moreover g_λ⁻¹(dΦ, dτ) ≥ m + r_q′ − C λ, and m ≥ μ0/r² is bounded below on Ω, so g_λ⁻¹(dΦ, dτ) > 0 for λ small.
The covector dτ is timelike for g_λ (Lemma 2.6 (e)), and g_λ is time oriented, as g0 is, so that dτ is positive
on its future causal vectors. The argument of the time orientation, with g_λ in place of g0, then gives at every point
of {Φ = 0} a neighbourhood U and a c > 0 with dΦ(Z) ≤ −c dτ(Z) for every future causal vector Z of g_λ at points of U.
The no-return argument for g0 used that v does not decrease along causal curves of g0, and only to carry the condition
μ > √72 l5² or μ′ > 0 from γ(τ1) to the later points of γ on {Φ = 0}. For g_λ no such step is needed: the margin
g_λ⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) ≤ −δ_b/2 holds at every point of the boundary, so the inequality dΦ(Z) ≤ −c dτ(Z) holds near every point
of {Φ = 0}, and the first-return argument applies to every future causal curve of g_λ as it stands.

*Equality.* If μ0 = √72 l5², then on {v ≤ inf supp env} μ = μ0 and μ′ = 0, so the formula gives g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) = 0,
and r_q = (√72 μ0 l5²)^(1/4) = (μ0²)^(1/4) = √μ0: the boundary is the seed's horizon r = √μ0, null for g0. That g_λ
equals g0 on that region, so that the boundary is null for g_λ there, and that after the shell starts the boundary is
spacelike for g_λ outside a layer whose width tends to 0 with λ, are proved in Chapter 54;
that for λ small every column of the layer has points where the boundary is timelike for g_λ, so that the no-return
property fails at equality, is Theorem 54.26, Corollary 54.27 and Theorem 55.22. ∎

**Remark 8.1** (The first-order term at the boundary.) Put ♯dΦ := g0⁻¹ dΦ. Expanding
g_app⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − λ g0⁻¹ [g1] g0⁻¹ + O(λ²),

    g_λ⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) = g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) − λ ([χ(·, θ + φ1)] + m1(♯dΦ, ♯dΦ)) + O(λ²) + O(|w|).

Indeed [g1](♯dΦ, ♯dΦ) = m1(♯dΦ, ♯dΦ) + [χ(·, θ + φ1)] (dv(♯dΦ))² + [W_TT(·, θ + φ1)](♯dΦ, ♯dΦ). Here dv(♯dΦ) =
g0⁻¹(dv, dr) − r_q′ g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 1. The covector dΦ lies in the span of dτ and dr, so ♯dΦ lies in the span of ∂_τ
and ∂_r, g0 being block diagonal; W_TT has only components on the sphere, so its value on ♯dΦ is 0. The wave W_TT
drops out exactly.

### 8.3 The expansions of the round spheres

**Lemma 8.2** (The round spheres of g0.) For the sphere S_(v,r) and g0, the future null normals with
n(τ) = 1 are

    n⁺ = ∂_τ + ((r² − μ)/(r² + μ)) ∂_r,      n⁻ = L0 = ∂_τ − ∂_r,    (8.5)

with expansions and inner product

    θ⁺ = 3 (r² − μ)/(r (r² + μ)),     θ⁻ = −3/r,     g0(n⁺, n⁻) = −2 r²/(r² + μ).    (8.6)

θ⁺ has one zero on (0, ∞), at r = √μ, where ∂_r θ⁺ = 3/μ. The area of S_(v,r) is 2π² r³, and M[S_(v,r)](g0) = μ(v)
for the mass M of Proposition 3.5.

*Proof.* Put m := μ/r². In the chart of Section 8.1, g0 restricted to the (τ, r) plane is
g_ττ = −1 + m, g_τr = m, g_rr = 1 + m, and the normal plane of S_(v,r) is spanned by ∂_τ and ∂_r. A vector
∂_τ + β ∂_r is null when −1 + m + 2 m β + (1 + m) β² = 0, whose roots are β = (1 − m)/(1 + m) and β = −1. The root
β = −1 gives L0, which points inward, and the other gives n⁺. Both have n(τ) = 1 > 0, and τ is a time function, so both
are future directed.

Since g0 is block diagonal with sphere part r² times the round metric, the second fundamental form of S_(v,r) along a
normal n is r n(r) times the round metric, and the expansion is θ_n = (r²)⁻¹ · 3 · r n(r) = 3 n(r)/r. So θ⁺ =
3(1 − m)/((1 + m) r) = 3(r² − μ)/(r(r² + μ)) and θ⁻ = 3 L0(r)/r = −3/r. Next, g0(n⁺, L0) = g_ττ + (β − 1) g_τr − β
g_rr = −1 − β = −2/(1 + m) = −2r²/(r² + μ). The numerator of θ⁺ vanishes on (0, ∞) only at r² = μ; there the derivative
falls on the numerator alone, ∂_r θ⁺ = 6r/(r · 2μ) = 3/μ.

The area is r³ times the volume 2π² of S³, so R = r. Then Θ = 2 θ⁺ θ⁻/(−g0(n⁺, n⁻)) = 2 · 3(1 − m)/((1 + m) r) ·
(−3/r) · (1 + m)/2 = −9(1 − m)/r², constant on the sphere, and M = r² (1 + (r²/9)(−9(1 − m)/r²)) = r² m = μ(v). ∎

The next lemma is the reason the oscillation is invisible to the spheres at leading order. It is stated for every
metric of the two-scale form of g_app, so that it applies to the solutions of Chapter 9 as well.

**Lemma 8.3** (The sphere quantities of a two-scale metric.) Let

    g = g0 + λ [g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j]

with profiles g_j bounded on Ω × S¹ with all their (X, θ)-derivatives, independently of λ, and with g1 = m1 + W(X, θ +
φ1(X)), where m1 and φ1 do not depend on θ, W(ℓ, ·) = 0, and tr_S W = 0 on every S_(v,r) at every phase. There are
λ* > 0 and C such that for 0 < λ ≤ λ* the following holds on every sphere S_(v,r) in Ω.

(a) The future null expansions of S_(v,r) for g, with normals normalized by n(τ) = 1, are

    θ^±(g) = θ^±(g0) + λ [Θ^±_1] + λ² E^±,    (8.7)

with profiles Θ^±_1 and functions E^± = e^±(X, v/λ, λ), where e^± is smooth in (X, θ, λ) and bounded with all its
X-derivatives, uniformly in λ ≤ λ*. No term of order λ⁻² or λ⁻¹ occurs, and none of order λ⁰ beyond g0's.

(b) The area element of S_(v,r), the inner product g(n⁺, n⁻) and the normals have expansions of the same form.

(c) Along a column, (d/dr)(θ^±(g) − θ^±(g0)) = O(λ), and the same holds for the quantities of (b).

*Proof.* The conormal plane of S_(v,r), the covectors that vanish on its tangent spaces, is spanned by dτ and dr at
every point with r > 0, the axes included. For a metric g near g0 let k^± := c^±(X, g)(dr + α^±(X, g) dτ) be its two
null covectors in that plane, with n^± := g⁻¹ k^± normalized by n^±(τ) = 1; for g near g0 the two null directions stay
distinct, so c^±, α^± are smooth functions of (X, g). Let Π_g^(ab) be the inverse of the metric g induces on the sphere,
pushed forward:

    Π_g = g⁻¹ + (n⁺ ⊗ n⁻ + n⁻ ⊗ n⁺)/(−g(n⁺, n⁻)),

smooth in (X, g); it annihilates k⁺ and k⁻, hence every covector of the conormal plane. The covector field k^± is, at
each point, the null conormal of the sphere S_(v,r) through that point, and the second fundamental form of S_(v,r)
along n^± is (∇k^±)(Y, Z) = Y^a Z^b (∂_a k^±_b − Γ[g]^c_(ab) k^±_c) on tangent vectors Y, Z. So, in Cartesian
coordinates,

    θ^±(g) = Π_g^(ab) (∂_a k^±_b − Γ[g]^c_(ab) k^±_c),     Γ[g]^c_(ab) = ½ g^(cd) (∂_a g_db + ∂_b g_da − ∂_d g_ab).
    (8.8)

The first term contains no derivative of g. The Cartesian components of dτ are constant and those of dr are ∂_b r, so

    ∂_a k^±_b = (∂_a c^±) (dr + α^± dτ)_b + c^± ∂_a ∂_b r + c^± (∂_a α^±) dτ_b.

The derivatives of c^± and α^± are where ∂g enters, and they multiply dr + α^± dτ and dτ, which Π_g annihilates. Hence

    Π_g^(ab) ∂_a k^±_b = c^±(X, g) Π_g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b r,

a smooth function of (X, g) on r > 0. So θ^±(g) is a smooth function of (X, g) plus a smooth function of (X, g) times
∂g: it is affine in ∂g. (In the polar chart of Section 8.1 the components of k^± along the sphere vanish
identically and the first term is absent; in Cartesian components it is not, and for the flat metric η, where Γ = 0,
it is the whole expansion ±3/r.)

Let ĝ(X, θ; λ) := g0 + λ g1 + Σ_(j≥2) λ^j g_j be the profile of g, so g = [ĝ]. By the chain rule of
Section 2.5, ∂_a g = λ⁻¹ (∂_a v) [∂_θ ĝ] + [∂_a ĝ]. The first term of (8.8) depends on g only
through its value, so it is c^±(X, [ĝ]) Π_[ĝ]^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b r, with no fast part. In Γ_(dab) the fast parts of ∂_a g_db
and ∂_b g_da carry the factor ∂_a v or ∂_b v, and Π_g^(ab) ∂_a v = 0 because dv lies in the conormal plane. Only the
fast part of −½ ∂_d g_ab survives, and it contributes ½ λ⁻¹ k^±_c g^(cd) ∂_d v Π_g^(ab) [∂_θ ĝ_ab] = ½ λ⁻¹ k^±(ℓ_g)
Π_g^(ab) [∂_θ ĝ_ab], with ℓ_g := g⁻¹ dv. Hence θ^±(g) = f^±(X, v/λ, λ) with

    f^±(X, θ, λ) := Θ^±_slow(X, ĝ, ∂_X ĝ) + ½ k^±(ℓ_ĝ) Π_ĝ^(ab) (∂_θ g1 + λ ∂_θ g2 + λ² ∂_θ g3 + …)_ab,

where Θ^±_slow(X, ĝ, ∂_X ĝ) := c^±(X, ĝ) Π_ĝ^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b r − Π_ĝ^(ab) Γ^c_(ab) k^±_c, with Γ formed from ĝ and ∂_X ĝ
in place of g and ∂g, and we used ∂_θ ĝ = λ ∂_θ g1 + λ² ∂_θ g2 + …, which cancels the factor λ⁻¹. The function f^± is
smooth in (X, θ, λ) for λ ≤ λ*, λ* small enough that ĝ stays near g0, and it is bounded with all its X- and
θ-derivatives. At λ = 0, ĝ = g0 and ∂_X ĝ = ∂g0, so the first term is the right side of (8.8) for g0,
which is θ^±(g0), and the second is ½ k^±_0(ℓ) γ0^(AB) ∂_θ (g1)_AB = ½ k^±_0(ℓ) ∂_θ tr_S g1. Now tr_S g1 = tr_S m1 +
tr_S W(X, θ + φ1), the first independent of θ and the second zero by hypothesis, so this term vanishes and
f^±(X, θ, 0) = θ^±(g0). Taylor's formula in λ with integral remainder gives f^± = θ^±(g0) + λ Θ^±_1 + λ² e^± with
Θ^±_1 := ∂_λ f^±(·, ·, 0) and e^± of the stated kind. This is (a).

The term c^± Π_g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b r is what distinguishes (8.8) from the polar formula, and it changes
none of these conclusions, because it contains no derivative of g: it produces no factor λ⁻¹, so it lies in Θ^±_slow
and leaves the fast term ½ λ⁻¹ k^±(ℓ_g) Π_g^(ab) [∂_θ ĝ_ab] as it is; at λ = 0 it is the corresponding term of
θ^±(g0); and it is part of the smooth function f^±, to which the argument of (c) below applies as to the rest.

The area element, g(n⁺, n⁻) and n^± are smooth functions of (X, g) alone, with no derivative of g, so the same Taylor
argument applies with no fast term at all: (b). For (c), along a column v is constant, so by (8.4)
the derivative of f(X, v/λ, λ) along it is (ℓ_X f)(X, v/λ, λ), bounded with no factor λ⁻¹; applied to λ Θ^±_1 + λ² e^±
it is O(λ). ∎

The first profile of g_app satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 8.3: W(ℓ, ·) = 0, and tr_S W = 0 by
(8.3). The remaining profiles are bounded with their derivatives by Theorem 4.11.

*Proof of Proposition 3.4.* Let λ ≤ λ0 and write θ⁺_λ := θ⁺(g_λ).

(i) The expansion as a function of the metric. By (8.8) and the identity after it, θ⁺(g) =
c⁺(X, g) Π_g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b r − Π_g^(ab) Γ[g]^c_(ab) k⁺_c: a smooth function of (X, g) plus a smooth function of (X, g)
times ∂g, so affine in ∂g. It is estimated in the Cartesian arrays, in which the axes are regular points.

(ii) The background. By Lemma 8.2, θ⁺(g0) = 3(r² − μ)/(r(r² + μ)). Since S_(v,r) lies in {v = const}, μ =
μ(v) enters only algebraically. Its one zero on (0, ∞) is r = √μ, simple, with ∂_r θ⁺(g0) = 3/μ there. The ingoing
expansion is −3/r < 0.

(iii) The approximant. By Lemma 8.3 applied to g = g_app, θ⁺(g_app) = θ⁺(g0) + λ [Θ⁺_1] + λ² E⁺, and
along every column

    |θ⁺(g_app) − θ⁺(g0)| + |(d/dr)(θ⁺(g_app) − θ⁺(g0))| ≤ C λ.

(iv) The remainder. Since θ⁺ is smooth in g and affine in ∂g, and ∂g_app and ∂g_λ are bounded, |θ⁺(g_λ) − θ⁺(g_app)|
≤ C (|w| + |∂w|). Its derivative along a column is at most C (|w| + |∂w| + |∂²w|): the derivative
falls on w, on ∂w, or on coefficients that are smooth functions of (X, g) at g_app or g_λ, times ∂g_app; these have
bounded derivatives along a column, since ℓ g_app and ℓ ∂g_app = dv ⊗ [ℓ ∂_θ g1] + O(1) are bounded, because
ℓ(v) = 0. By (8.1) both are at most C M λ^(K−5) ≤ C λ, as K ≥ 6. With (iii), along every column

    |θ⁺_λ − θ⁺(g0)| + |(d/dr)(θ⁺_λ − θ⁺(g0))| ≤ C3 λ.    (8.9)

The same two steps, with Lemma 8.3 (a) for θ⁻ and θ⁻(g0) = −3/r, give |θ⁻(g_λ) + 3/r| ≤ C3 λ on the
columns, C3 enlarged if necessary.

(v) The zero. The columns lie in the compact Ω, and r ≥ r_q(v) ≥ q0 > 0 on them. The difference
√μ − r_q = μ^(1/2) − b μ^(1/4), b := (√72 l5²)^(1/4), equals μ^(1/4)(μ^(1/4) − b) and has derivative
¼ μ^(−3/4)(2 μ^(1/4) − b) in μ, which is positive for μ > b⁴/16 = √72 l5²/16, in particular for μ ≥ μ0 ≥ √72 l5².
So √μ(v) − r_q(v) is at least its value at μ0, which is positive when μ0 > √72 l5². Put μ_max := μ(v_end).
Fix δ in (0, that value) such that ∂_r θ⁺(g0) ≥ 3/(2 μ_max) on |r − √μ(v)| ≤ δ (possible by continuity, since
∂_r θ⁺(g0) = 3/μ ≥ 3/μ_max at r = √μ), and let m_δ > 0 be the minimum of |θ⁺(g0)| on the compact rest of the columns.
Let r_max be the largest value of r on Ω, and let λ_H ≤ λ0 be such that C3 λ_H < min(m_δ, 3/(4 μ_max), 3/r_max) and
λ_H ≤ λ*. For λ ≤ λ_H, by (8.9), θ⁺_λ has no zero where |r − √μ| > δ, and on |r − √μ| ≤ δ its
r-derivative is at least 3/(2 μ_max) − C3 λ > 3/(4 μ_max), so it is strictly increasing there. Hence it has at most one
zero on each column, positive above it and negative below it.

If the column contains [√μ − δ, √μ + δ], which holds when √μ(v) ≤ v − τ0 − δ1 with δ1 := δ, then θ⁺_λ changes sign on
that interval (at r = √μ ± δ, |θ⁺(g0)| ≥ m_δ > C3 λ, so θ⁺_λ has the sign of θ⁺(g0), ± there), so it has exactly one
zero R_λ; since |θ⁺_λ(√μ)| ≤ C3 λ and the slope exceeds 3/(4 μ_max),

    |R_λ − √μ(v)| ≤ C′ λ,     C′ := C3/(3/(4 μ_max)).

Put C := 2 C′. On the band, for r ≤ √μ − C λ,

    θ⁺_λ(r) ≤ θ⁺_λ(√μ) − (3/(4 μ_max)) (√μ − r) ≤ C3 λ − 2 C3 λ < 0,

and likewise θ⁺_λ(r) ≥ C3 λ > 0 for r ≥ √μ + C λ. At distance C′ λ these bounds give only θ⁺_λ ≤ 0 and θ⁺_λ ≥ 0,
which is why C is taken to be twice C′. Off the band θ⁺_λ has the sign of θ⁺(g0). The ingoing expansion satisfies
θ⁻(g_λ) ≤ −3/r + C3 λ ≤ −3/r_max + C3 λ < 0 at every point of the columns, by the bound after
(8.9) and the choice of λ_H. So the spheres with r ≤ √μ − C λ are trapped, both future null
expansions being negative at every point, and those with r ≥ √μ + C λ are untrapped.

If μ0 = √72 l5², fix instead δ in (0, √μ_max − b μ_max^(1/4)) with the same band property. The argument for the zero and
the signs runs on the columns where √μ − r_q ≥ δ; by the monotonicity in μ shown above, this is μ(v) ≥ μ0 + δ2 for some
δ2 > 0. The first assertion uses only the monotonicity band and the absence of zeros off it, and holds on every column. ∎

**Remark 8.4** (The round family.) The zero set of θ⁺_λ on the columns is not a marginally trapped
surface: the statement concerns the round family {S_(v,r)}. Although ∂g_λ converges only weakly, the expansion of these
spheres does not see the oscillation at leading order, because the wave is traceless on them
((8.3)) and the phase v/λ is constant along each column ((8.4)).

**Remark 8.5** (Numerical observation.) A numerical evolution of the metric in the Bondi form
(3.3) from the free data of Section 2.6, with each quantity read on the same round spheres, agrees with
Proposition 3.4: the departure of the computed zero of θ⁺ from √μ halves when λ is halved, the successive ratios being
2.47, 2.26 and 2.14 at μ0/l5² = 100, and 2.26 and 2.14 at μ0/l5² = 1000. No proof in this paper uses this observation.

### 8.4 The Hawking mass and the quarter turn

For a spacelike 3-sphere S and a Lorentzian metric g near g0, let M[S](g) be the five-dimensional Hawking mass of
Proposition 3.5: M[S](g) := R²(1 + (R²/9)⟨Θ⟩), R := (Area(S)/(2π²))^(1/3), Θ := 2 θ⁺ θ⁻/(−g(n⁺, n⁻)), ⟨·⟩ the mean
over S. Θ does not depend on the normalization of n^±. M is natural: M[S](ψ* g) = M[ψ(S)](g) for every diffeomorphism
ψ and every g near g0, since every ingredient is defined by g and S alone. It is a smooth function of g and ∂g on S.

Let J be the linear map (τ, x1, x2, x3, x4) ↦ (τ, x3, x4, x1, x2), which exchanges the two planes of the T² action. In
the angles of Section 8.1 it is ϑ ↦ π/2 − ϑ, ξ1 ↔ ξ2. J lies in O(4) acting on x, so it fixes τ, r and v,
maps each S_(v,r) to itself, and is an isometry of g0 = η + (μ(v)/r²) dv², both terms being O(4)-invariant; J² is the
identity, and J_* ℓ = ℓ. For a family of profiles (g_j) put

    (S g)_j (X, θ) := (−1)^j (J* g_j)(X, 3π/2 − θ).    (8.10)

**Lemma 8.6** (The quarter-turn symmetry.) (a) For every family of profiles (g_j) with
g := g0 + Σ_j λ^j g_j, the sum g̃ := g0 + Σ_j λ^j (S g)_j has two-scale residual R[g̃](X, θ; λ) =
J* R[g](X, 3π/2 − θ; −λ). Its coefficient of λ^m is (−1)^m J* R^(m)(·, 3π/2 − ·), so S preserves (E1)–(E3) of
Definition 4.3 at every order: it preserves (E1), (E2) and the vanishing of each coefficient R^(m).

(b) The stage-0 wave is S-invariant: (J* W_TT)(X, 3π/2 − θ) = −W_TT(X, θ); so is χ, and so is W = W_TT + χ dv² at
weight 1.

(c) The profiles of the approximant of Theorem 4.11, with the stage data of Lemma 7.4, satisfy
S g = g:

    (J* g_j)(·, 3π/2 − ·) = (−1)^j g_j,   and for the means,   J* ⟨g_j⟩ = (−1)^j ⟨g_j⟩;   in particular J* m1 = −m1.

*Proof.* (a) The operator R[g] is Ric^H of (2.9) with every ∂_a replaced by D^λ_a := ∂_a + λ⁻¹ (∂_a v) ∂_θ
(Definition 4.1), and it contains no explicit θ. Let ρ(θ) := 3π/2 − θ. Since ∂_θ (f ∘ ρ) = −(∂_θ f) ∘ ρ, we have
D^λ_a (f ∘ ρ) = (D^(−λ)_a f) ∘ ρ, hence R[g ∘ ρ](·; λ) = R[g](·; −λ) ∘ ρ. Since J is linear in x and fixes v, D^λ
commutes with J*, and Ric^H(J* g) = J* Ric^H(g) for every metric g, because Ric^H is built from g and g0 alone and J is
an isometry of g0. So R[J* g] = J* R[g]. Now g̃ = J* g(·, ρ(·); −λ), because λ^j (S g)_j = (−λ)^j J* g_j ∘ ρ and
J* g0 = g0; combining the two identities gives the formula. Expanding in λ gives the coefficients. (E1) is preserved
because J_* ℓ = ℓ; (E2) and the vanishing of each R^(m) because R^(m) ↦ (−1)^m J* R^(m) ∘ ρ; and J preserves each slice
and its flat L² norms.

(b) Under ϑ ↦ π/2 − ϑ, cos ϑ and sin ϑ exchange, ζ ↦ −ζ and h(−ζ) = h(ζ). Under θ ↦ 3π/2 − θ, sin θ ↦ −cos θ and
cos θ ↦ −sin θ. So F(JX, 3π/2 − θ) = −G(X, θ) and G(JX, 3π/2 − θ) = −F(X, θ), and from (8.2)

    p1(JX, 3π/2 − θ) = (2 sin²ϑ (−F) − cos²ϑ (−G))/3 = −p2(X, θ),    p2(JX, 3π/2 − θ) = −p1(X, θ).

Pulling back by J exchanges dξ1² and dξ2² and fixes dϑ², so (J* W_TT)(X, 3π/2 − θ) = 2 r^(1/2) λ⁻¹ (cos²ϑ (−p1)
dξ1² + sin²ϑ (−p2) dξ2² − (−p1 − p2) dϑ²) = −W_TT(X, θ). The two polarizations being a quarter turn apart is what makes
this work: with one quadrature alone (G = 0), F(JX, 3π/2 − θ) = −λ A env h cos θ is not −F(X, θ), and the identity
fails.

χ is the solution with zero data of the transport (ℓ + 3/(2r)) ∂_θ χ = f along ℓ, f the dv² second harmonic of
R^(0)[g0 + λ W_TT] ((4.9)). By (a) at order 0 and the S-invariance of W_TT, f(JX, 3π/2 − θ) = f(X,
θ), as J* (dv ⊗ dv) = dv ⊗ dv. Put χ̃(X, θ) := −χ(JX, 3π/2 − θ). Then ∂_θ χ̃ = (∂_θ χ)(JX, 3π/2 − θ), the operator ℓ +
3/(2r) commutes with J, so χ̃ solves the same transport with the same zero data, and by uniqueness χ̃ = χ. Hence χ dv²
is S-invariant at weight 1, and so is W. By (a) applied to the S-invariant family g0 + λ W, its residual is S-odd at
order one: J* R^(1)[g0 + λ W](·, 3π/2 − ·) = −R^(1)[g0 + λ W], the mean part and the oscillating part alike.

(c) The unknowns of the ansatz (4.10) are the means m_j, the phases φ_j and the oscillating profiles ĝ_j,
with profile 𝒢(X, θ; λ) := g0 + Σ λ^j m_j + λ W + Σ λ^j ĝ_j(X, θ) and phase u = v + Σ λ^j φ_j. Let S act by

    m_j ↦ (−1)^j J* m_j,    φ_j ↦ (−1)^j J* φ_j,    ĝ_j ↦ (−1)^j J* ĝ_j(·, 3π/2 − ·).

The transformed phase is ũ(X; λ) = J* u(X; −λ), so λ⁻¹ dũ = −J*((−λ)⁻¹ du(−λ)), and the calculation of (a) with u in
place of v shows that the transformed unknowns solve the transformed stage equations. Every stage of
Lemma 4.10 and every choice of Lemma 7.4 (φ_m = 0 and (m_m)_(τ·) = 0 on Σ_τ0,
∂_θ ĝ_(m+1) given by an O(4)-equivariant right inverse, and the unique solutions of the linear problems there) is the
unique solution of a problem that S maps to itself. So each unknown is S-invariant, given that the earlier ones are:
the transformed unknowns solve the same problem and coincide with the originals by uniqueness. At j = 1 this is the
uniqueness of stage 1, whose unknowns (m1, φ1, ĝ2) solve a system that S maps to itself; it gives J* m1 = −m1 and,
through L0 φ1 = −½ m1(ℓ, ℓ) with zero data, J* φ1 = −φ1.

The rewriting with the fixed phase (in the proof of Theorem 4.11) commutes with S. There the profiles g_j are the
coefficients of 𝒢̂(X, θ; λ) := 𝒢(X, θ + φ1 + λΨ; λ), Ψ := Σ_(j≥2) λ^(j−2) φ_j. For the transformed unknowns φ̃1 = −J*
φ1 and λ Ψ̃(λ) = −J*((−λ) Ψ(−λ)), and their profile is 𝒢̃(X, θ′; λ) = J* 𝒢(X, 3π/2 − θ′; −λ), so their rewritten
profile is

    𝒢̃(X, θ + φ̃1 + λ Ψ̃(λ); λ) = J* 𝒢(X, 3π/2 − θ + φ1 + (−λ) Ψ(−λ); −λ) = J* 𝒢̂(X, 3π/2 − θ; −λ),

whose coefficient of λ^j is (−1)^j J* g_j(·, 3π/2 − ·) = (S g)_j. Hence S g = g. Taking the θ-mean, which the
reflection θ ↦ 3π/2 − θ preserves, gives J* ⟨g_j⟩ = (−1)^j ⟨g_j⟩, and ⟨g1⟩ = m1 since W has θ-mean zero. ∎

*Proof of Proposition 3.5.* *Outside the shell.* The oscillating profiles (W, χ, the ĝ_m and the phase terms of the
fixed-phase rewriting) vanish outside v_start < v < v_end: each solves a transport along ℓ, at fixed v, whose forcing
and data are supported there (Lemma 4.10, and step (i) of the proof of Lemma 7.4), the wave being
proportional to env. So for v outside that interval g_app = g0 + λ m1 + λ² E, with E bounded with its derivatives, and

    M[S_(v,r)](g_λ) = M[S_(v,r)](g0) + λ DM[m1] + O(λ²) + O(|w| + |∂w|),

with DM the derivative of M at g0 on S_(v,r). By Lemma 8.2, M[S_(v,r)](g0) = μ(v). DM is linear, and
naturality with J fixing g0 and S_(v,r) gives DM[J* m] = DM[m]: as g0 + ε J* m = J*(g0 + ε m),

    M[S](g0 + ε J* m) = M[J(S)](g0 + ε m) = M[S](g0 + ε m).

By Lemma 8.6 (c), DM[m1] = DM[J* m1] = −DM[m1], so DM[m1] = 0. The remainder is at most C λ^(K−4) ≤ C λ² by
(8.1). For v < v_start the means vanish too: their forcing terms and data on Σ_τ0 are supported in
v ≥ v_start, and v does not decrease along future causal curves of g0.

*Inside the shell.* By Lemma 8.3 (a)–(b) for g = g_app, θ^±, the area and g_app(n⁺, n⁻) are those of g0
up to O(λ): the wave enters at order λ⁰ only through the term ½ k^±(ℓ) ∂_θ tr_S g1 of the proof of that lemma, which
vanishes by (8.3). So M[S_(v,r)](g_app) − μ(v) = O(λ), and the remainder contributes C(|w| + |∂w|) ≤
C λ^(K−4).

*Larger λ.* The two steps above hold for λ ≤ λ*, with λ* that of Lemma 8.3, taken so small that the
Taylor expansion about g0 applies. For λ* < λ ≤ λ0 the bounds hold with a larger C. Indeed |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ ≤ ε1
and |∂g_λ| ≤ C on Ω (Theorem 6.1, λ0 being so small that C λ0 ≤ ε1), and ε1 < 3/5. Each S_(v,r) lies in a
slice Σ_τ, on whose tangent space ker dτ the form g0 has least eigenvalue 1 relative to the Euclidean inner product
(Lemma 2.7); so g_λ restricted to ker dτ has least eigenvalue at least 2/5, and the spheres are spacelike for g_λ.
The area element of the spheres and Θ = 2 θ⁺ θ⁻/(−g(n⁺, n⁻)), which M integrates, are continuous functions of
(X, g, ∂g) on the compact set where X ∈ Ω, |g − g0(X)| ≤ ε1 and |∂g| ≤ C; on it the sphere through X is spacelike, its
two null directions are distinct and −g(n⁺, n⁻) > 0. The radii r are bounded on Ω, so |M[S_(v,r)](g_λ)| ≤ C_M, and for
λ > λ*, |M[S_(v,r)](g_λ) − μ(v)| ≤ C_M + μ(v_end) ≤ (C_M + μ(v_end)) λ*⁻² λ², which is at most C λ² and so at most
C λ, as λ ≤ 1. ∎

The first mean m1 is driven by the following forcing. By Lemma 4.7, the coefficient of λ is ℛ^(1) =
T̂ ĝ2 − ½ e_2 ∂_θ² W + 𝒲(m1, φ1) + 𝒴_1. The term 𝒴_1 contains none of the unknowns of the stages, so it is the value of
ℛ^(1) with all of them set to zero, which is the coefficient R^(1) of λ in R[g0 + λ W]. The term −½ e_2 ∂_θ² W, which
contains m2 and φ2, is not part of 𝒴_1, but its θ-mean is zero: e_2 does not depend on θ ((4.11)),
and ∂_θ² W has θ-mean zero. So the forcing of the mean equation of stage 1 (Lemma 4.10 (a)) is
𝒮_1 = −⟨𝒴_1⟩ = −⟨R^(1)⟩.

**Lemma 8.7** (The forcing of the first mean.) Let W = W_TT + χ dv ⊗ dv with χ a profile of zero
θ-mean, and let R^(1) be the coefficient of λ in the two-scale expansion of R[g0 + λ W] (Definition 4.1). In the
coordinates (v, r, ϑ, ξ1, ξ2) of (2.4),

    ⟨R^(1)⟩ = −(4/9) A² env² h(ζ)² r⁻³ sin 2ϑ (dv ⊗ dϑ + dϑ ⊗ dv).    (8.11)

In particular ⟨R^(1)⟩ does not depend on χ.

*Proof.* Write v_a := ∂_a v, Ẇ := ∂_θ W and δg := λ[W], with indices raised by g0. Four facts are used. (W1) W(ℓ, ·) = 0
and tr W = 0 (Lemma 4.5 (a)). (W2) As mixed tensors W and Ẇ commute, and ⟨W Ẇ⟩ = 0. The term χ dv ⊗ dv
contributes nothing to W^ρ_c Ẇ^c_σ or Ẇ^ρ_c W^c_σ, since ℓ^c Ẇ_cσ = 0 and W_TT^(ρc) v_c = 0. W_TT and Ẇ_TT are diagonal
in the coordinates (ϑ, ξ1, ξ2), on which g0 is diagonal, so W Ẇ = ½ ∂_θ (W_TT W_TT). (W3) ⟨W⟩ = 0, since W_TT is a first
harmonic in θ and χ has zero mean. (W4) In the coordinates of (2.4), with f = 1 − μ/r² and ℓ = ∂_r, the
Christoffel symbols of g0 give ∇̂_v ℓ^r = −μ/r³, ∇̂_A ℓ^B = r⁻¹ δ^B_A for angular A, B, and ∇̂_a ℓ^c = 0 otherwise; so
∇̂_ℓ ℓ = 0. Since g0^(vc) = δ^c_r, the Hessian of v is ∇̂_a v_b = −Γ^v_ab = ½ ∂_r g0_ab, that is −(μ/r³) dv² + r γ, with
γ the round metric; so ∇̂_ℓ v = 0.

*The expansion.* As in the proof of Lemma 2.10, with C := Γ[g] − Γ[g0], Ric(g) = Ric(g0) + ∇̂_ρ C^ρ_ab − ∇̂_b
C^ρ_aρ + C^ρ_ρσ C^σ_ab − C^ρ_bσ C^σ_aρ, C^ρ_ab = ½ g^(ρσ)(∇̂_a δg_bσ + ∇̂_b δg_aσ − ∇̂_σ δg_ab) and D^ρ = g^(ab) C^ρ_ab.
With ∇̂_a [u] = λ⁻¹ v_a [∂_θ u] + [∇̂_a u] and g⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − λ W^♯ + O(λ²), C = [C⁽⁰⁾] + λ [C⁽¹⁾] + O(λ²), where
C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab = ½(v_a Ẇ_b^ρ + v_b Ẇ_a^ρ − ℓ^ρ Ẇ_ab) and
