    C⁽¹⁾ρ_ab = G^ρ_ab − ½ (v_a (WẆ)^ρ_b + v_b (WẆ)^ρ_a),      G^ρ_ab := ½ (∇̂_a W_b^ρ + ∇̂_b W_a^ρ − ∇̂^ρ W_ab);

the second term comes from −λ W^(ρσ) acting on C⁽⁰⁾, whose term in v_σ drops since W^(ρσ) v_σ = 0. By (W1),
C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ρb = 0, v_ρ C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab = 0 and g0^(ab) C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab = 0. By (W2) and (W3), ⟨C⁽¹⁾⟩ = 0.

*The Ricci part.* At order λ the derivative terms give λ⁻¹ v_ρ [∂_θ C⁽²⁾] and ∇̂ C⁽¹⁾, both of θ-mean zero. The products
give C⁽⁰⁾ C⁽¹⁾ + C⁽¹⁾ C⁽⁰⁾. In C^ρ_ρσ C^σ_ab the cross terms are C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ρσ C⁽¹⁾σ_ab, zero since C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ρσ = 0, and
C⁽¹⁾ρ_ρσ C⁽⁰⁾σ_ab. For the second, the trace of C⁽¹⁾ is C⁽¹⁾ρ_ρσ = −½ v_σ tr(WẆ), the trace C_1^c_ac = −½ v_a W·∂W
of Lemma 4.4: the G-part has trace G^ρ_ρσ = ½ ∂_σ tr W = 0, and v_ρ (WẆ)^ρ_σ = 0 by W(ℓ, ·) = 0. So
C⁽¹⁾ρ_ρσ C⁽⁰⁾σ_ab = −½ tr(WẆ) v_σ C⁽⁰⁾σ_ab = 0, as v_σ C⁽⁰⁾σ_ab = 0. In C^ρ_bσ C^σ_aρ the two cross terms are
transposes in (a, b). So the mean of the Ricci part is −2 times the symmetric part
of ⟨T⟩, T_ab := C⁽⁰⁾ρ_bσ C⁽¹⁾σ_aρ. By (W1), Ẇ^ρ_σ v_ρ = 0, (WẆ)^σ_ρ ℓ^ρ = 0 and v·ℓ = 0, so

    Ẇ^ρ_σ C⁽¹⁾σ_aρ = ½ Ẇ^(ρσ) ∇̂_a W_ρσ − ½ v_a tr(ẆWẆ),
    v_σ C⁽¹⁾σ_aρ = −½ (W_ρσ ∇̂_a ℓ^σ + W_aσ ∇̂_ρ ℓ^σ + (∇̂_ℓ W)_aρ),
    ℓ^ρ C⁽¹⁾σ_aρ = ½ (−W_ρ^σ ∇̂_a ℓ^ρ + (∇̂_ℓ W)_a^σ + W_aρ ∇̂^σ ℓ^ρ).

In the first line the terms of G with ∇̂_ρ and ∇̂^σ cancel by the symmetry of Ẇ^(ρσ); the others use W(ℓ, ·) = 0.
Inserting these into T_ab = ½ v_b Ẇ^ρ_σ C⁽¹⁾σ_aρ + ½ Ẇ^ρ_b v_σ C⁽¹⁾σ_aρ − ½ Ẇ_bσ ℓ^ρ C⁽¹⁾σ_aρ, the two terms with ∇̂_a ℓ
cancel (both are (ẆW)_bσ ∇̂_a ℓ^σ), and

    T_ab = ¼ v_b Ẇ^(ρσ) ∇̂_a W_ρσ − ¼ v_a v_b tr(ẆWẆ) − ½ Ẇ^ρ_b (∇̂_ℓ W)_aρ − ½ Ẇ^ρ_b W_aσ ∇̂_ρ ℓ^σ.

The terms with χ in the last two vanish: Ẇ^ρ_b with χ̇ ℓ^ρ v_b meets (∇̂_ℓ W)(ℓ, ·) = −W(∇̂_ℓ ℓ, ·) = 0 and ℓ^ρ ∇̂_ρ ℓ =
0; W_aσ = χ v_a v_σ meets v_σ ∇̂_ρ ℓ^σ = −(∇̂_ρ v)(ℓ) = 0 by (W4); and ∇̂_ℓ (χ v ⊗ v) = (ℓχ) v ⊗ v by (W4), which Ẇ_TT
annihilates. For W_TT, (∇̂_ℓ W_TT)_AB = ∂_r W_AB − (2/r) W_AB = −(3/(2r)) W_AB ((4.7), W_TT being
r^(1/2) times a function of (v, ϑ, θ)), and ∇̂_ρ ℓ^σ = r⁻¹ δ^σ_ρ on angular indices, so the last two terms are multiples
of (ẆW)_ba, of θ-mean zero by (W2). The term tr(ẆWẆ) involves W_TT only and is cubic in a first harmonic, so its mean
is zero. Hence the Ricci part has mean −¼ (v_a X_b + v_b X_a), with X_a := ⟨Ẇ^(ρσ) ∇̂_a W_ρσ⟩.

*The gauge part.* D⁽⁰⁾ = g0^(ab) C⁽⁰⁾ = 0, and D⁽¹⁾ = g0^(ab) C⁽¹⁾ρ_ab − W^(ab) C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab = (div W)^ρ + ½ ℓ^ρ W^(ab) Ẇ_ab,
with (div W)^ρ := g0^(ab) ∇̂_a W_b^ρ, by tr W = 0 and W^(ab) v_a = 0. The coefficient of λ in −½(g_aρ ∇̂_b D^ρ + g_bρ
∇̂_a D^ρ) is −½ times the symmetrization of g0_aρ (v_b ∂_θ D⁽²⁾ρ + ∇̂_b D⁽¹⁾ρ) + W_aρ v_b ∂_θ D⁽¹⁾ρ. The first two terms
have mean zero, as ⟨D⁽¹⁾⟩ = 0 by (W2) and (W3). In the third, W_aρ ℓ^ρ = 0 removes the ℓ-part of D⁽¹⁾. For W = χ v ⊗ v,
v_ρ (div Ẇ)^ρ = −Ẇ^(ab) ∇̂_a v_b = −r Ẇ_TT^(AB) γ_AB = −r⁻¹ tr_S Ẇ_TT = 0 by (W4), the χ̇-part dropping since (∇̂ v)(ℓ,
ℓ) = 0; and the χ̇-part of div Ẇ is (ℓχ̇ + χ̇ □_(g0) v) ℓ, which W_TT annihilates. So the gauge part has mean −½
(v_a V_b + v_b V_a), with V_a := ⟨(W_TT)_aρ (div Ẇ_TT)^ρ⟩. Altogether

    ⟨R^(1)⟩_ab = −¼ (v_a X_b + v_b X_a) − ½ (v_a V_b + v_b V_a).

*The evaluation.* By (8.2), W_TT = r^(1/2) ω with ω := −2P dϑ² + 2 cos²ϑ Q1 dξ1² + 2 sin²ϑ Q2 dξ2², where
Q_i := λ⁻¹ p_i and P := Q1 + Q2 are functions of (v, ϑ, θ). In X_a the Christoffel terms pair Ẇ^(ρσ) with W_cσ and have
mean zero by (W2), and the χ-terms vanish by (W1); so X_a = ⟨Ẇ^(ρσ) ∂_a W_ρσ⟩ = r⁻³ ⟨ω̇ · ∂_a ω⟩ for a = v, ϑ, with ·
the contraction by γ; X_r = (2r)⁻¹ ⟨Ẇ^(ρσ) W_ρσ⟩ = 0, and X_ξ1 = X_ξ2 = 0. Since ω = env · ω̃ with ω̃ independent of v,
ω̇ · ∂_v ω = ½ env env′ ∂_θ (ω̃ · ω̃), so X_v = 0. For angular c, the (v, r)-block contributes nothing to (div Ẇ_TT)_c
(Γ^D_vr = Γ^D_rr = 0, and Ẇ_TT has no v or r component), so (div Ẇ_TT)_c = r⁻² (div_γ Ẇ_TT)_c = r^(−3/2) (div_γ ω̇)_c,
div_γ the divergence on the unit S³; and V_a = r⁻³ ⟨ω_a^c (div_γ ω̇)_c⟩ for angular a, zero otherwise. ω does not depend
on ξ1, ξ2 and is diagonal, so (div_γ ω̇)_ξ1 = (div_γ ω̇)_ξ2 = 0. Every component therefore vanishes except
⟨R^(1)⟩_vϑ = −¼ X_ϑ − ½ V_ϑ.

Write c := cos ϑ, s := sin ϑ and κ_A := A env/3. By (8.2) each of Q1, Q2, P has the form
κ_A h (α cos θ + β sin θ), with (α, β) = (2c², −s²), (−c², 2s²) and (c², s²) respectively. For two such functions Q and
Q′, the second with coefficients (α′, β′), the terms with ∂_ϑ h cancel and

    ⟨∂_θ Q ∂_ϑ Q⟩ = ½ κ_A² h² (β ∂_ϑ α − α ∂_ϑ β),      ⟨Q ∂_θ Q′⟩ = ½ κ_A² h² (α β′ − β α′).

This gives ⟨∂_θ P ∂_ϑ P⟩ = −κ_A² h² c s, ⟨∂_θ Q_i ∂_ϑ Q_i⟩ = 2 κ_A² h² c s (i = 1, 2), ⟨P ∂_θ Q1⟩ = −(3/2) κ_A² h² c² s²
and ⟨P ∂_θ Q2⟩ = (3/2) κ_A² h² c² s². Now ω̇ · ∂_ϑ ω = 4 (∂_θ P ∂_ϑ P + ∂_θ Q1 ∂_ϑ Q1 + ∂_θ Q2 ∂_ϑ Q2) plus multiples of
Q_i ∂_θ Q_i, which have mean zero; so X_ϑ = 4 r⁻³ κ_A² h² c s (−1 + 2 + 2) = 12 κ_A² h² c s/r³. The divergence of a
diagonal tensor depending on ϑ alone is (div_γ T)_ϑ = (cs)⁻¹ ∂_ϑ(cs T_ϑϑ) − ½ (∂_ϑ γ_AB) T^(AB), which gives

    (div_γ ω̇)_ϑ = −2 ∂_ϑ ∂_θ P + (4 s/c − 2 c/s) ∂_θ Q1 + (2 s/c − 4 c/s) ∂_θ Q2.

With ω_ϑ^ϑ = −2P and ⟨P ∂_ϑ ∂_θ P⟩ = −⟨∂_θ P ∂_ϑ P⟩ = κ_A² h² c s,

    V_ϑ = r⁻³ (4 κ_A² h² c s + 3 κ_A² h² c² s² ((4 s/c − 2 c/s) − (2 s/c − 4 c/s))) = r⁻³ κ_A² h² (4 c s + 6 c s)
        = 10 κ_A² h² c s/r³.

So ⟨R^(1)⟩_vϑ = −(3 + 5) κ_A² h² c s/r³ = −(8/9) A² env² h² c s/r³ = −(4/9) A² env² h² sin 2ϑ/r³. ∎

**Remark 8.8** (What the mass sees.) By Lemma 8.7 the forcing −⟨R^(1)⟩ of the
mean equation of stage 1 is nonzero wherever env ≠ 0 off the axes, and it lies in the dv dϑ component. The phase φ1 and
the oscillating profile ĝ2 also enter that equation, ĝ2 through the mean of a product with ∂_θ W, so the forcing alone
does not decide whether m1 vanishes; nothing in the structure of the stage forces m1 = 0, and Proposition 3.5 does
not need to know whether it does, since it uses only J* m1 = −m1. The forcing term is odd under the quarter turn, as
Lemma 8.6 requires (J fixes dv and h(ζ)², maps sin 2ϑ to itself and dϑ to −dϑ), and a rotation-invariant
mass cannot see such a term. The quantity of Proposition 3.5 is the
Hawking mass of the spheres S_(v,r) of the domain. It is not the angular mean of the mass aspect at past null infinity,
which is a different quantity, governed by the mass law of Theorem 3.8.

## 9. The construction from past null infinity

This chapter proves Theorem 3.7: the waves are prescribed by their own free data at past null infinity,
the solution is constructed on a past domain P together with Ω, and the constraints are never solved. Before the shell
the solution is the black hole: the region v ≤ v_start is a past set for the black hole's cones, and the data there are
the black hole's. Near past null infinity every stage of the approximant is solved with nothing coming in. Each stage
has an explicit leading term in r and a remainder half a power of r better, and no forcing term of a stage falls off
like r^(−5/2), the rate that would produce a logarithm. So the residual decays like r^(−3), and the remainder is
estimated with the rotations as commutators, which gain t^(−3/2) in Sobolev's inequality. The past is split at
t = λ^(−2). Before the split, the one coefficient of size 1/λ integrates in time to a constant, and no decomposition is
needed. After it, the decomposition of the proof of Theorem 6.1 runs over an interval of length λ^(−2);
there the transport of its auxiliary field loses a logarithm per unit of log t, which weights (T_λ/t)^β0 absorb at a
cost λ^(−2β0), with β0 independent of the order of the approximant. The mollifier's commutator with the wave operator
is, apart from decaying terms, an exact derivative along the generators, and is absorbed into the auxiliary field. The
limit is vacuum because the gauge field of the approximant decays at past null infinity.

The notation is that of Chapter 8 and of Theorem 4.11: the seed of mass μ0, the amplitude A, the
envelope env, the wave W_TT with free data F, G at past null infinity (Section 2.6), the means m_j, phases φ_j
and oscillating profiles ĝ_j of the stages ((4.10)), and □̃ := g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b acting componentwise.

### 9.1 The past domain

Put t := 1 + τ0 − τ for τ ≤ τ0, write Σ̂_τ := {X : τ(X) = τ} for the whole level set of τ, so that the slice Σ_τ of
Section 2.3 is Σ̂_τ ∩ Ω for τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ_end; fix κ_P := 1/2, h_P(τ) := κ_P t^(−1/4), and
V_P := V + 1 + (τ_end − τ0) + κ_P, with V := v_end + T and τ_end as in Section 2.3, so that V_P − κ_P is the
largest v on Σ_τ0. Let

    P := { τ ≤ τ0,  |x| ≥ a,  v + h_P(τ) ≤ V_P },      P⁺ := P ∩ {v ≥ v_start},
    A_P(τ) := Σ̂_τ ∩ P⁺ = { r_in(τ) ≤ |x| ≤ r_out(τ) },   r_in := v_start − τ,   r_out := V_P − h_P(τ) − τ.
    (9.1)

**Lemma 9.1** (The past domain.) (a) Each Σ̂_τ is spacelike. (b) The outer boundary B := {v + h_P(τ) =
V_P} is spacelike, with Φ_B := v + h_P(τ),

    g0⁻¹(dΦ_B, dΦ_B) = −2 h_P′ − h_P′² (1 + μ/r²) ≤ −(κ_P/2) t^(−5/4),

and v + h_P(τ) increases along future causal curves, so P lies to the past of B. (c) Σ̂_τ0 ∩ P = Σ_τ0. (d) On P⁺,
t + a1 ≤ r ≤ t + a2 with a1 := v_start − τ0 − 1 > √μ0 and a2 := V_P − τ0 − 1, and the thickness r_out − r_in =
V_P − h_P − v_start lies in [d0, d1], d0 := V_P − κ_P − v_start ≥ 1, d1 := V_P − v_start. (e) L0 is tangent to the inner
boundary {v = v_start} of P⁺; the past integral curve of L0 through any point of P stays in P and runs to past null
infinity (v and x̂ fixed, r → ∞). (f) There is ε_P > 0 such that for every Lorentzian g on P with |g⁻¹ − g0⁻¹| ≤
ε_P t^(−5/4): B and the Σ̂_τ are spacelike for g with g⁻¹(dΦ_B, dΦ_B) ≤ −(κ_P/4) t^(−5/4); {r = a} is spacelike with r
decreasing along future causal curves; L0 is transverse to Σ̂_τ; and J⁻(p; g) ∩ {τ ≥ τ1} lies in P for every p in P and
τ1 ≤ τ(p).

*Proof.* (a) g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r² < 0 wherever r > 0, the contraction of Lemma 2.6 (a). (b) dΦ_B = dv +
h_P′ dτ, with h_P′ = dh_P/dτ = (κ_P/4) t^(−5/4) > 0 because dt/dτ = −1. By Proposition 2.5 (c)–(d), g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0,
g0⁻¹(dv, dτ) = −1 and g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r², so g0⁻¹(dΦ_B, dΦ_B) = −2h_P′ − h_P′²(1 + μ/r²) ≤ −2h_P′ = −(κ_P/2)
t^(−5/4). For a future causal Y, dv(Y) = −g0(L0, Y) ≥ 0 and dτ(Y) > 0, so dΦ_B(Y) > 0. (c) At τ0, h_P = κ_P and the
condition reads v ≤ V_P − κ_P. (d) On P⁺, r = v − τ = v − τ0 − 1 + t with v ∈ [v_start, V_P]; a1 > √μ0 because v_start −
τ0 > √μ0 + 1; and d0 ≥ 1 because V_P − κ_P = V + 1 + τ_end − τ0 ≥ v_start + 1. (e) Along −L0, v and x̂ are fixed, τ
decreases and h_P decreases, so v + h_P ≤ V_P is kept, r = v − τ grows without bound, and v ≥ v_start is kept. (f) The
inequalities of (a), (b) and of Lemma 2.6 (b) are strict, with a margin of at least (κ_P/2) t^(−5/4) in (b) and
fixed margins in (a) and in Lemma 2.6 (b), the latter holding at r = a < √μ0 whatever τ is; the causal claim follows
as in Lemma 2.6 (e). ∎

**Lemma 9.2** (The seed region.) Let g solve Ric^H(g) = 0 on P ∩ {τ1 ≤ τ ≤ τ2}, be C², satisfy the
margin of Lemma 9.1 (f), and agree with g0 on Σ̂_τ1 ∩ P ∩ {v ≤ v_start} together with its first τ-derivative.
Then g = g0 on P ∩ {τ1 ≤ τ ≤ τ2, v ≤ v_start}.

*Proof.* g0 is vacuum on {v ≤ v_start}, where μ is constant. For 0 < ε ≤ 1 let R_ε := P ∩ {τ ≥ τ1, v + ε h_P(τ) ≤
v_start}, and τ* the supremum of the τ′ ≤ τ2 with g = g0 on R_ε ∩ {τ ≤ τ′}. R_ε ∩ Σ̂_τ* is compact, g = g0 on it, and g
is continuous, so on a neighbourhood U of it |g⁻¹ − g0⁻¹| ≤ (εκ_P/8) t^(−5/4). There {v + ε h_P = v_start} is spacelike
for g and g0 with R_ε to its past (the calculation of Lemma 9.1 (b) with εκ_P in place of κ_P), and {r = a}
likewise (Lemma 9.1 (f)). The difference u := g − g0 solves −½ g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b u = f with |f| ≤ C(|u| + |∂u|),
since the principal part and Q of (2.9) are smooth in (g, ∂g) and ∂²g0 is bounded; u = ∂_τ u = 0 on
R_ε ∩ Σ̂_τ*, and the proof of Lemma 5.5 on R_ε ∩ {τ* ≤ τ ≤ τ* + δ}, δ small so that the region lies in U, gives
u = 0 there. So τ* = τ2. Letting ε → 0 covers {v < v_start}, and continuity covers v = v_start. ∎

### 9.2 Inequalities on the past slices

All constants below depend on P (through a, a1, a2, d0, d1, κ_P) and not on τ or λ, and 0 < λ ≤ min(λ1, d0/20) with
λ1 := min(1, δ0)/10 as in (5.1). With Ω_ab := x_a ∂_b − x_b ∂_a the rotations of R⁴, the scaled norms
on A_P(τ) are

    |f|_(j,P) := Σ_(i + |β| ≤ j) λ^i ‖∂^i Ω^β f‖,      ‖·‖ the flat L²(A_P(τ)),    (9.2)

∂^i the spacetime coordinate derivatives of order i. The rotations carry no weight: Ω_ab τ = 0 and Ω_ab r = 0, so
Ω_ab v = 0 and Ω [f] = [Ω f] costs no power of λ. They also commute with □̃: they commute with ∂_τ and with the flat
Laplacian, and with L0 = ∂_τ − x̂·∂_x and the function μ(v)/r², which are invariant under rotations; and L0 L0 u =
L0^a L0^b ∂_a ∂_b u, the Cartesian components (1, −x̂) of L0 being constant along L0. Hence [Ω_ab, □̃] = 0.

**Lemma 9.3** (Sobolev with rotations; Poincaré.) (a) ‖f‖_∞ ≤ C t^(−3/2) Σ_(i + |β| ≤ 3) ‖∂_r^i Ω^β
f‖ on A_P(τ), ∂_r = x̂·∂_x; hence ‖∂^i f‖_∞ ≤ C λ^(−3−i) t^(−3/2) |f|_(i+3,P). (b) If f = 0 on {r = r_in(τ)}, then
‖f‖ ≤ C ‖∂_r f‖.

*Proof.* (a) In polar coordinates A_P(τ) = [r_in, r_in + d] × S³ with d := r_out − r_in in [d0, d1]. Put r = r_in + d s,
s ∈ [0, 1]. Then ∂_r = d⁻¹ ∂_s with d⁻¹ ∈ [d1⁻¹, d0⁻¹] and dr = d ds, so the H³ norm on [r_in, r_in + d] × S³ with the
product metric dr² + (round metric) and the H³ norm in s on the fixed manifold [0, 1] × S³ bound each other with
constants depending only on d0 and d1. On [0, 1] × S³, H³ embeds in L^∞ ([BH17, Theorem 7.26] in charts), so H³ embeds
in L^∞ on [r_in, r_in + d] × S³ with a constant uniform for d in [d0, d1]. The covariant derivatives of S³ are bounded
by the rotations, |∇^k f| ≤ C Σ_(|β| ≤ k) |Ω^β f|, because the Ω_ab span every tangent space of S³ and their commutators
are rotations. And ∫ |·|² dr dω ≤ r_in⁻³ ∫ |·|² r³ dr dω ≤ t⁻³ ‖·‖², since r_in ≥ t by Lemma 9.1 (d). For the
scaled form apply this to ∂^i f and reorder, using [Ω_ab, ∂_c] = −δ_ac ∂_b + δ_bc ∂_a. (b) On each ray f(r) is the
integral of ∂_r f from r_in over a length at most d1, and r³ varies over the ray by a factor at most (1 + d1)³ since
r_in ≥ 1; Cauchy–Schwarz. ∎

**Lemma 9.4** (The mollifier on the past slices.) The mollifier (5.3), with
σ(τ, x) := σ0((|x| − r_in)/(r_out − r_in)) and ρ radial, satisfies (M1)–(M6) of Lemma 5.4 on A_P(τ)
for 0 < λ ≤ min(λ1, d0/20), with constants independent of τ, and commutes with the rotations, hence with T² and both
reflections.

*Proof.* The proof of Lemma 5.4 is local at the scale λ and uses only that the annulus has thickness
Δ := r_out − r_in at least d0 ≥ 1 and inner radius at least 1; that DΦ = I + λ E with E bounded with its derivatives
(E involves ∂σ, of size at most 7/d0, and ∂x̂, of size 1/r ≤ 1); that Φ is a diffeomorphism onto its image with
Jacobian bounded above and below uniformly in λ; and, for (M6), that ∂_τ r_in = −1 and ∂_τ r_out = −1 − h_P′ are
bounded. The Jacobian: Φ is radial, r ↦ r + 2λσ, so DΦ has the radial eigenvalue 1 + 2λ σ0′/Δ and the angular ones
1 + 2λσ/r. Since σ0 is non-increasing with |σ0′| ≤ 7, and λ/Δ ≤ λ/d0 ≤ 1/20, the radial eigenvalue lies in
[1 − 14/20, 1] = [3/10, 1]. Since |σ| ≤ 1, r ≥ r_in ≥ 1 and λ ≤ 1/10, |2λσ/r| ≤ 1/5, so the angular ones lie in
[4/5, 6/5]. The map Φ(x) = x + 2λσ x̂ and ρ are invariant under O(4), so 𝒫(f ∘ R) = (𝒫 f) ∘ R for R in O(4). ∎

**Lemma 9.5** (The mollifier's commutator with □̃.) Write 𝒫 = 𝒞 ∘ M, with M f := ρ_λ * f the
convolution (ρ_λ(y) := λ⁻⁴ ρ(y/λ)) and 𝒞 g := g ∘ Φ the radial shift. In the coordinates (τ, v, x̂), with Δ(τ) :=
r_out − r_in, 𝒞 is g(τ, v, x̂) ↦ g(τ, ψ(τ, v), x̂), where ψ(τ, v) = v + 2λ σ0((v − v_start)/Δ(τ)), since |x| − r_in =
v − v_start at fixed τ. Put

    X_f := 4λ σ_r 𝒞(∂_r M f),      σ_r := σ0′((v − v_start)/Δ)/Δ.    (9.3)

Then [□̃, 𝒫] f = −L0 X_f + R_f, and for j ≤ k, with Z ranging over 𝒵 := {λ∂_τ, λ∂_r, Ω_ab} (∂_r = x̂·∂_x),

    ‖Z^j X_f‖ ≤ C λ Σ_(i ≤ j) ‖Z^i ∂f‖,
    ‖Z^j R_f‖ ≤ C (t⁻¹ + h_P′) Σ_(i ≤ j) ‖Z^i ∂f‖ + ‖Z^j R′_f‖,

where R′_f collects the terms with two time derivatives of f, each with a factor at most C λ (μ r⁻³ + |μ′| r⁻²); for
f = s := w(ℓ, ℓ) these are rewritten through the equation of Lemma 6.4, as in Step 6 of the proof of
Theorem 6.1.

*Proof.* *The operator.* In the coordinates (τ, v, x̂), L0 is the coordinate field ∂/∂τ at fixed (v, x̂), and the
radial derivative ∂_r = x̂·∂_x at fixed τ is the coordinate field ∂/∂v at fixed (τ, x̂), while ∂_τ at fixed x is
L0 + ∂_r. The flat wave operator is −∂_τ² + ∂_r² + (3/r)∂_r + r⁻² Δ̊, with Δ̊ the Laplacian of the
unit S³, so it equals −(L0 + ∂_r)² + ∂_r² + (3/r)∂_r + r⁻² Δ̊ = −L0² − 2 ∂_r L0 + (3/r)∂_r + r⁻² Δ̊ (L0 and ∂_r are
coordinate fields and commute). With g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − (μ/r²) L0 ⊗ L0 and L0^a L0^b ∂_a ∂_b = L0²,

    □̃ = −(1 + μ/r²) L0² − 2 ∂_r L0 + (3/r) ∂_r + r⁻² Δ̊.

*The radial part.* Write □̃_rad for the first three terms, r = v − τ, and ψ_τ, ψ_v, ψ_ττ, ψ_τv for the partial
derivatives of the function ψ(τ, v). With 𝒞 g =
g(τ, ψ, x̂), the chain rule gives L0 𝒞 g = 𝒞 L0 g + ψ_τ 𝒞 ∂_r g, ∂_r 𝒞 g = ψ_v 𝒞 ∂_r g, and the second derivatives
likewise. Collecting terms,

    [□̃_rad, 𝒞] g = −L0(2(ψ_v − 1) 𝒞 ∂_r g) + (3ψ_v/r − 3/(ψ − τ)) 𝒞 ∂_r g − μ(v)(1/r² − 1/(ψ − τ)²) 𝒞 L0² g
                   + ((μ(ψ) − μ(v))/(ψ − τ)²) 𝒞 L0² g
                   − (1 + μ(v)/r²)(2 ψ_τ 𝒞 ∂_r L0 g + ψ_τ² 𝒞 ∂_r² g + ψ_ττ 𝒞 ∂_r g) − 2 ψ_τ 𝒞 ∂_r² g.

For ψ independent of τ the last line vanishes: then □̃_rad 𝒞 g − 𝒞 □̃_rad g = −(μ(v)/r² − μ(ψ)/(ψ − τ)²) 𝒞 L0² g −
2(ψ_v − 1) 𝒞 ∂_r L0 g + (3ψ_v/r − 3/(ψ − τ)) 𝒞 ∂_r g, and −2(ψ_v − 1) 𝒞 ∂_r L0 g = −L0(2(ψ_v − 1) 𝒞 ∂_r g) since L0
commutes with 𝒞 and with ψ_v. When ψ depends on τ, L0 𝒞 g and L0² 𝒞 g acquire the terms with ψ_τ and ψ_ττ, and writing
−2(ψ_v − 1) 𝒞 ∂_r L0 g as −L0(2(ψ_v − 1) 𝒞 ∂_r g) adds 2 ψ_τv 𝒞 ∂_r g + 2(ψ_v − 1) ψ_τ 𝒞 ∂_r² g; the terms with
ψ_τv cancel against those from −2 ∂_r L0 𝒞 g, and what remains is the last line. Here 2(ψ_v − 1) = 4λ σ_r, and

    ψ_τ = 2λ σ0′((v − v_start)/Δ) (v − v_start) h_P′/Δ²,

since Δ′ = −h_P′ by (9.1); as |v − v_start| ≤ Δ, |σ0′| ≤ 7 and h_P″ = (5/4) h_P′/t, both ψ_τ and ψ_ττ are
at most C λ h_P′. Moreover |ψ − v| ≤ 2λ, so |μ(ψ) − μ(v)| ≤ 2λ sup|μ′|, |1/r² − 1/(ψ − τ)²| ≤ C λ r⁻³
and |3ψ_v/r − 3/(ψ − τ)| ≤ C/r.

*The angular part.* Δ̊ acts on x̂ at fixed (τ, v) and commutes with 𝒞, so [r⁻² Δ̊, 𝒞] = (r⁻² − (ψ − τ)⁻²) 𝒞 Δ̊, of size
C λ r⁻³ times two rotations, that is C λ r⁻¹ times two derivatives.

*The convolution.* M commutes with the constant-coefficient part η^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b of □̃; with the rest, −(μ/r²) L0 L0,
it commutes up to terms with the factor λ |∂(μ x̂ x̂/r²)| ≤ C λ (μ r⁻³ + |μ′| r⁻²) ((M5) of Lemma 5.4).

*The bounds.* Apply the radial and angular identities to g = M f. A λ-weighted second spatial derivative of M f costs
no more than one derivative of f (Bernstein's inequality, (M2)). The term −L0(4λ σ_r 𝒞 ∂_r M f) is −L0 X_f, and
‖Z^j X_f‖ ≤ C λ Σ ‖Z^i ∂f‖ needs no decaying factor. Every other term carries a factor C/r ≤ C t⁻¹, or C λ h_P′ (the
last line, with two derivatives of M f, of which one is absorbed by the factor λ), or C λ (μ r⁻³ + |μ′| r⁻²) (the
terms with L0², which form R′_f). L0 commutes with λσ_r, 𝒞 and M up to factors C(h_P′ + r⁻¹): L0 σ_r = O(h_P′), the ψ_τ
terms above, and [x̂·∂_x, M] = O(λ r⁻¹) by (M5). The fields Z commute with these operators up to bounded operators of the
same order, which suffices, since every term of R_f already carries a decaying factor and the bound on X_f needs none.
Z commutes with L0 exactly (∂_τ at fixed x, ∂_r and Ω_ab do, and L0 = ∂_τ − ∂_r in the coordinates (τ, r, x̂)), so the
same holds at every order. ∎

So the part of [□̃, 𝒫] f with no decaying factor is an exact L0-derivative. On Ω the commutator has the same form,
harmlessly. On P it would force the transport of Ψ := □̃ φ (Lemma 6.5) by a term of size
‖∂s‖ with no decay; Proposition 9.12 removes it by transporting Ψ − ½ X_s in place of Ψ.

**Lemma 9.6** (Energy on P.) Let g̃ be a Lorentzian metric on P with the margin of Lemma 9.1
(f) and ‖∂g̃‖_∞ ≤ k(τ) on Σ̂_τ ∩ P⁺, and let u vanish on P ∩ {v ≤ v_start} and satisfy −½ g̃^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b u = f on
P ∩ {τ1 ≤ τ ≤ τ2}. Then for τ in [τ1, τ2]

    ‖∂u(τ)‖ ≤ C exp(C ∫_(τ1)^τ k) ( ‖∂u(τ1)‖ + ∫_(τ1)^τ ‖f‖ ),      ‖u(τ)‖ ≤ C ‖∂u(τ)‖.    (9.4)

*Proof.* The proof of Lemma 5.5 on P ∩ {τ1 ≤ s ≤ τ}. B has P to its past with a spacelike normal for g̃
(Lemma 9.1 (b), (f)), so its flux is nonnegative and is dropped. u vanishes near {r = a}. On P⁺ the slices
are uniformly spacelike and Y := −g̃⁻¹ dτ is uniformly timelike (g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r² with μ/r² bounded), so the
fluxes through Σ̂_τ are comparable to ‖∂u‖² with constants independent of τ. The bulk is at most C k ‖∂u‖² + ‖f‖ ‖∂u‖.
Gronwall's inequality gives the first bound, and Lemma 9.3 (b) the second. ∎

**Lemma 9.7** (Transport on P.) Let L0 ψ − (c0/r) ψ = f on P⁺ ∩ {τ1 ≤ τ ≤ τ2}, with c0 a constant,
and put γ := c0 − 3/2. With a₊ := a1 if γ > 0 and a₊ := a2 if γ ≤ 0,

    (t + a₊)^γ ‖ψ(τ)‖ ≤ (t1 + a₊)^γ ‖ψ(τ1)‖ + ∫_(τ1)^τ (t′ + a₊)^γ ‖f(τ′)‖ dτ′.    (9.5)

*Proof.* As in Lemma 5.6, ∂_τ ‖ψ‖² = 2⟨ψ, L0 ψ⟩ − ∫ (3/r) ψ² plus boundary terms. L0 is tangent to
{v = v_start}, so that face contributes nothing, and the outer face contributes −h_P′ ∫_(r = r_out) ψ² r³ dω ≤ 0. Hence
∂_τ ‖ψ‖² ≤ 2γ ∫ ψ²/r + 2⟨ψ, f⟩, and t + a1 ≤ r ≤ t + a2 (Lemma 9.1 (d)) gives ∂_τ ‖ψ‖ ≤ γ (t + a₊)⁻¹ ‖ψ‖ +
‖f‖. Since ∂_τ t = −1, ∂_τ ((t + a₊)^γ ‖ψ‖) ≤ (t + a₊)^γ ‖f‖. ∎

The transports used below have c0 = 0 (φ and its derivatives; γ = −3/2), c0 = 3/2 (the oscillating profiles; γ = 0)
and c0 = 2 (Ψ; γ = 1/2).

**Lemma 9.8** (Linear wave equations on P.) Let τ1 < τ0 and P_1 := P ∩ {τ ≥ τ1}, and let B^a
and C be smooth d × d matrices of functions on P_1, smooth up to its boundary. For every smooth f on P_1 with values in
ℝ^d and smooth u0, u1 on Σ̂_τ1 ∩ P there is a unique smooth u on P_1 with

    −½ □̃ u + B^a ∂_a u + C u = f   on P_1,      u = u0  and  ∂_τ u = u1   on Σ̂_τ1 ∩ P.

If f, u0 and u1 vanish where v ≤ v_start, then u vanishes on P_1 ∩ {v ≤ v_start}.

*Proof.* The proof of Lemma 4.9 runs with P_1 and Σ̂_τ1 ∩ P in place of Ω and Σ_τ0. It uses four properties of
the domain, and each holds here. (1) P_1 is compact and connected: on it τ1 ≤ τ ≤ τ0 and a ≤ |x| ≤ r_out(τ). (2) A
past inextendible causal curve of g0 through a point of P_1 stays in P_1 while τ ≥ τ1: this is Lemma 9.1 (f)
for g = g0. With (1), step (i) of that proof shows that P_1 lies in the Cauchy development of Σ̂_τ1 ∩ {|x| > a/2}.
(3) The interior of P_1 is a bounded Lipschitz domain, as step (ii) needs: near each boundary point it is bounded by at
most two of the smooth hypersurfaces Σ̂_τ1, Σ_τ0, {r = a} and B, and where two of them meet their conormals are linearly
independent, since any two of dτ, dr and dΦ_B = (1 + h_P′) dτ + dr are. B does not meet {r = a}: ∂_τ r_out =
−1 − h_P′ < 0, so r_out(τ) ≥ r_out(τ0) for τ ≤ τ0, and r_out(τ0) = b(τ0) by Lemma 9.1 (c), with
b(τ0) − a ≥ 1 + δ0 by Lemma 2.6 (f). (4) For uniqueness, the boundary pieces of P_1 other than Σ̂_τ1 ∩ P are
spacelike for g0 with P_1 to their past (Lemma 9.1 (a), (b) and Lemma 2.6 (b)), so in the energy
argument of Lemma 5.5 on P_1 their fluxes are nonnegative and are dropped.

For the vanishing, let 0 < ε ≤ 1, Φ_ε := v + ε h_P(τ) and R_ε := P_1 ∩ {Φ_ε ≤ v_start}. The calculation of
Lemma 9.1 (b) with ε κ_P in place of κ_P gives g0⁻¹(dΦ_ε, dΦ_ε) ≤ −(ε κ_P/2) t^(−5/4), and Φ_ε increases
along future causal curves of g0, so {Φ_ε = v_start} is spacelike with R_ε to its past. R_ε does not meet B, since on
it v < v_start ≤ V_P − κ_P − 1 < V_P − h_P(τ) (Lemma 9.1 (d)). The energy argument of Lemma 5.5 on
R_ε ∩ {τ ≤ τ′}, in which the fluxes through {Φ_ε = v_start} and {r = a} are nonnegative and are dropped, gives u = 0 on
R_ε, since f, u0 and u1 vanish there. Letting ε → 0 covers P_1 ∩ {v < v_start}, and continuity covers v = v_start. ∎

### 9.3 Decay classes and the approximant from past null infinity

On P⁺ we use the coordinates (v, r, x̂): ∂_v is the derivative at fixed (r, x̂), which is ∂_τ at fixed x, and ℓ is the
derivative at fixed (v, x̂), so that ℓ = −L0, ℓ(v) = 0, ℓ(r) = 1 and the radial derivative at fixed τ is ∂_v + ℓ.
Profiles are smooth on P × S¹ and vanish for v ≤ v_start, then to all orders at v = v_start, env being smooth.

- E_p: profiles f with |∂_X^α Ω^β ∂_θ^j f| ≤ C r^(−p) on P⁺ × S¹ for all α, β, j (∂_X the Cartesian derivatives).
- L_p ("a leading term"): f = r^(−p) F + f̃ with F(v, x̂, θ) smooth, bounded with all its derivatives and vanishing for
  v ≤ v_start, and f̃ in E_(p+1/2).
- O_p ("transported"): f in L_p whose remainder also has ℓ f̃ in E_(p+3/2); then ℓ f is in L_(p+1).

The L² norm on A_P(τ) of a profile of class E_q is at most C t^(3/2−q): by Lemma 9.1 (d) the annulus has
r ≥ t + a1 and thickness at most d1, so ∫ r^(−2q) r³ dr dω ≤ C t^(3−2q).

**Lemma 9.9** (The decay calculus.) (a) E_p E_q ⊂ E_(p+q) and L_p L_q ⊂ L_(p+q); ∂_X, Ω, ∂_θ and
∂_v preserve E_p and L_p.

(b) In (v, r, x̂), g0⁻¹(du, du′) = ∂_v u ℓu′ + ℓu ∂_v u′ + (1 − μ/r²) ℓu ℓu′ + r⁻² ⟨∂̊u, ∂̊u′⟩, with ∂̊ the
gradient on the unit S³; that is, g^vv = 0, g^vr = 1 and g^rr = 1 − μ/r². For every function,

    □̃ u = 2 ∂_v ℓ u + (3/r) ∂_v u + (1 − μ/r²) ℓ ℓ u + (3/r) ℓ u + r⁻² Δ̊ u.    (9.6)

(c) □̃(r^(−p) F) = (3 − 2p) r^(−p−1) ∂_v F + E_(p+2) for F as in L_p. At p = 3/2 the first term vanishes, so □̃ W_TT is
in E_(7/2); and □̃ maps O_p into L_(p+1). The Cartesian components of W_TT are r^(−3/2) F_W with F_W(v, x̂, θ) smooth, so
W_TT is in O_(3/2), a pure leading term, and (ℓ + 3/(2r)) W_TT = 0.

(d) If f = r^(−q) f_q + f̃ is in L_q with q > 5/2, and c is in E_(3/2) (a multiplication, or a bounded operator on
zero-mean functions of θ with coefficients in E_(3/2), as in Lemma 4.8), then the transport
(ℓ + 3/(2r) + c) Z = f has exactly one solution with r^(3/2) Z → 0 along every generator, and

    Z = −r^(1−q) f_q/(q − 5/2) + Z̃   is in O_(q−1).

At q = 5/2 a logarithm appears: (ℓ + 3/(2r))(r^(−3/2) log r · f_(5/2)) = r^(−5/2) f_(5/2).

*Proof.* (a) Leibniz's rule, with ∂_X = x̂ (∂_v + ℓ) + r⁻¹ (angular derivatives), whose coefficients have bounded
derivatives; ∂_X (r^(−p) F) = r^(−p) x̂ ∂_v F + E_(p+1).

(b) Since v = τ + r, η = −dτ² + dr² + r² dω² = −dv² + 2 dv dr + r² dω², and g0 = η + (μ/r²) dv² = −(1 − μ/r²) dv² +
2 dv dr + r² dω². The (v, r) block, with rows (−(1 − μ/r²), 1) and (1, 0), has determinant −1 and inverse with rows
(0, 1) and (1, 1 − μ/r²), which gives the inverse metric. For (9.6): □̃ is the flat wave operator
plus −(μ/r²) L0 L0 = −(μ/r²) ℓ ℓ (as in the proof of Lemma 9.5). The flat operator is −∂_τ² + ∂_r² +
(3/r) ∂_r + r⁻² Δ̊, and at fixed x̂, ∂_τ = ∂_v and the radial derivative at fixed τ is ∂_v + ℓ, so it equals −∂_v² +
(∂_v + ℓ)² + (3/r)(∂_v + ℓ) + r⁻² Δ̊ = 2 ∂_v ℓ + ℓℓ + (3/r)∂_v + (3/r)ℓ + r⁻² Δ̊, ∂_v and ℓ being coordinate fields.
Adding −(μ/r²) ℓℓ gives
(9.6).

(c) F does not depend on r at fixed (v, x̂), so ℓ F = 0 and ℓ(r^(−p) F) = −p r^(−p−1) F. In (9.6),
2 ∂_v ℓ (r^(−p) F) = −2p r^(−p−1) ∂_v F and (3/r) ∂_v (r^(−p) F) = 3 r^(−p−1) ∂_v F, which sum to (3 − 2p) r^(−p−1)
∂_v F; the other three terms are (1 − μ/r²) p(p + 1) r^(−p−2) F − 3p r^(−p−2) F + r^(−p−2) Δ̊F, in E_(p+2). On f̃ with
ℓ f̃ in E_(p+3/2) every term of (9.6) is in E_(p+3/2). For W_TT: in (8.2) write the
round coframe as r dϑ, r cos ϑ dξ1, r sin ϑ dξ2, whose Cartesian components depend on x̂ alone; then

    W_TT = r^(−3/2) · 2 λ⁻¹ (p1 (r cos ϑ dξ1)² + p2 (r sin ϑ dξ2)² − (p1 + p2)(r dϑ)²),

and λ⁻¹ p1, λ⁻¹ p2 are functions of (v, ϑ, θ). So r^(3/2) W_TT =: F_W does not depend on r, and it is smooth in
(v, x̂, θ), the axes included, because W_TT is smooth there (Lemma 2.9 (a)). Then (ℓ + 3/(2r)) W_TT =
−(3/2) r^(−5/2) F_W + (3/2) r^(−5/2) F_W = 0.

(d) Along a generator, with I(r) := −∫_r^∞ c, (r^(3/2) e^I Z)′ = r^(3/2) e^I f, and |I| ≤ C′ r^(−1/2); for an operator
c, e^I is the propagator of the linear ordinary differential equation along the generator, bounded since the integral of
the norm of c converges. So Z = −r^(−3/2) e^(−I) ∫_r^∞ r′^(3/2) e^(I(r′)) f dr′ is the solution, and every other
solution differs from it by r^(−3/2) e^(−I) times a function of (v, x̂, θ). For the leading term,
(ℓ + 3/(2r))(r^(1−q) A) = (1 − q + 3/2) r^(−q) A = (5/2 − q) r^(−q) A, which equals r^(−q) f_q for A = −f_q/(q − 5/2);
at q = 5/2 the same calculation with r^(−3/2) log r gives the logarithm. The remainder has forcing terms f̃ and −c Z in
E_(q+1/2), so the integral formula puts it in E_(q−1/2), and ℓ Z̃ = −(3/(2r)) Z̃ − c Z + f̃ is in E_(q+1/2). ∂_v, Ω and
∂_θ commute with ℓ and r, which gives the derivatives. ∎

**Theorem 9.10** (The approximant from past null infinity.) For every N the stages of
Theorem 4.11 have unique solutions on P with nothing coming in from past null infinity: the energy of each m_m
on A_P(τ) tends to zero as τ → −∞, and φ_m, χ and ĝ_(m+1) are the transport solutions of Lemma 9.9 (d)
that vanish there. They vanish for v ≤ v_start, are T² × Z2 × Z2-invariant, satisfy S g = g (Lemma 8.6),
and

    W_TT ∈ O_(3/2) (a pure leading term),  χ ∈ O_2,  m_m ∈ L_2,  φ_m ∈ L_1 with ℓφ_m ∈ L_2,  ĝ_(m+1) ∈ O_2.
    (9.7)

The approximant g_app built from them as in the proof of Theorem 4.11 satisfies (E1) and (E2) of
Definition 4.3 on P, and Ric^H(g_app) = λ^(N−1) [R_N] + λ^N [R′_N] with R_N, R′_N in E_3, uniformly for
0 < λ ≤ 1, so |Ric^H(g_app)|_(k,P) ≤ C_R λ^(N−1) t^(−3/2). On Ω the profiles continue as the solutions of
Lemma 4.10 with their own data on Σ_τ0, g_app is smooth on P ∪ Ω, and the conclusions of
Theorem 4.11 hold on Ω.

*Proof.* *The count.* Give the factors of (2.9) these classes: g0 − η in L_2 (a coefficient, not a
profile: it does not vanish for v ≤ v_start, and its class is used only through its bounds); Γ[g0] in E_2 (its μ′ part
is (μ′/(2r²)) ℓ dv dv) and H0^ρ := g0^(ab) Γ[g0]^ρ_(ab) in E_3; W_TT in O_(3/2); χ and ĝ_i in O_2; m_i in L_2; φ_i in L_1
with ℓφ_i in L_2.

*Claim:* for m ≥ 1, every monomial of the coefficient ℛ^(m) of λ^m (Lemma 4.7) that contains none of
m_m, φ_m, ĝ_(m+1) lies in L_3. A monomial of (2.9) has at most two derivatives; g⁻¹ is expanded about
g0⁻¹, each term of the expansion adding profile factors; the phase enters only through du = dv + Σ λ^j dφ_j acting on
an oscillating factor. (i) Two profile factors from {W, χ, ĝ_i, m_i} give L_3 at least (Lemma 9.9 (a)).
(ii) A factor dφ_i, in E_1 only, occurs as (∂_a φ_i) ∂_θ Y with Y oscillating. With a second profile factor besides Y
the monomial is in E_4. Without one, both derivatives sit on Y in the principal part, contracted by g0⁻¹, and the
monomial is one of g0⁻¹(dφ_i, dv) ∂_θ² Y = (ℓφ_i) ∂_θ² Y, g0⁻¹(dφ_i, dφ_j) ∂_θ² Y, g0⁻¹(dφ_i, d∂_θY) or (□̃ φ_i) ∂_θ Y.
By (9.6) the first is in L_2 L_(3/2); the second in L_3 L_(3/2), since g^vv = 0 and no product
∂_v φ_i ∂_v φ_j occurs; the third, ∂_v φ_i ℓ∂_θY + ℓφ_i ∂_v∂_θY + …, is in L_1 L_(5/2) + L_2 L_(3/2), since Y in O_p
gives ℓY in L_(p+1); and □̃ φ_i = 2 ∂_v ℓφ_i + (3/r) ∂_v φ_i + … is in L_2. Each is in L_(7/2). (iii) A monomial with
one profile factor and no dφ: the factor has weight j and carries derivatives of total weight m − j. If it is a mean
m_j, the only such terms are those of its own stage equation (j = m) and Γ[g0] times m_j (E_2 L_2). If it is
oscillating, two slow derivatives give □̃ Y (j = m; in L_3 by Lemma 9.9 (c), and in E_(7/2) for W_TT) and
one fast derivative gives the operator T̂ of Lemma 4.8 applied to Y (j = m + 1: the unknown
ĝ_(m+1)); two fast derivatives carry g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0. This proves the claim. The same count shows that the
coefficients with which the unknowns enter (a)–(c) of Lemma 4.10 are in E_2 for m_m and E_3 for dφ_m
in (a), E_(3/2) for ĝ_(m+1) in (a) (the mean of a product with ∂_θ W), and, in (c), E_(3/2) for m_m, Ψ_m := □̃ φ_m and
ℓφ_m, and E_(5/2) for ∂_v φ_m and r⁻¹ Ω φ_m (which multiply ℓ∂_θW or r⁻¹ Ω ∂_θW).

*Stage 0.* The identities of Lemma 4.5 hold pointwise wherever the profiles are defined. By Lemma 4.5
(b) and (d), with χ = 0 the oscillating part of R^(0) is F_2 dv ⊗ dv, with F_2 the second harmonic of
(4.9). F_2 is r⁻³ env² h² times a polynomial in sin θ, cos θ and the functions c², s² of x̂, so
F_2 = r⁻³ f3 with f3 a smooth function of (v, x̂, θ). So χ, the solution of (4.9) that vanishes at past
null infinity, is r⁻² times a function of (v, x̂, θ): since (ℓ + 3/(2r))(r⁻² a) = −½ r⁻³ a for a independent of r,
∂_θ χ = −2 r⁻² f3, by Lemma 9.9 (d) at q = 3 with no remainder. So χ is in O_2. It is smooth at the axes,
by the argument given with (4.9).

*Stage m ≥ 1.* Let the earlier stages be solved, in their classes. By the count, the forcing term of (a) is
𝒮_m = r⁻³ 𝒮_(m,3) + 𝒮̃_m with 𝒮̃_m in E_(7/2); the forcing term of (c) without the unknowns is r⁻³ K_(m,3) + E_(7/2);
and q_m is in L_3, each of its terms pairing two of m_i, dφ_i as in (ii). *Leading terms:* M_m := 2 ∫_(−∞)^v 𝒮_(m,3)
dv′, which vanishes for v ≤ v_start; m⁰ := r⁻² M_m; φ⁰ := −½ r⁻¹ M_m(ℓ, ℓ); ĝ⁰ := the leading term of
Lemma 9.9 (d) at q = 3 for the forcing r⁻³ K_(m,3). Then −½ □̃ m⁰ = −½ (3 − 4) r⁻³ ∂_v M_m + E_4 = r⁻³
𝒮_(m,3) + E_4 by Lemma 9.9 (c) at p = 2, and ℓφ⁰ = ½ r⁻² M_m(ℓ, ℓ) = ½ m⁰(ℓ, ℓ). So the remainders
(m̃, φ̃, ĝ̃) := (m_m − m⁰, φ_m − φ⁰, ĝ_(m+1) − ĝ⁰) solve the system (a)–(c) with every forcing term in E_(7/2): the
coefficients act on the leading terms through the classes of the count, and ℓφ̃ = ½ (m̃(ℓ, ℓ) + q_m) with q_m in E_3.

*Estimates.* For n large let P_n := P ∩ {τ ≥ τ_n}. The proof of Lemma 4.10 runs on P_n with three
replacements: Lemma 9.8 with τ1 = τ_n in place of Lemma 4.9, for the wave equation (a) at each
step of the iteration; the transports solved along the integral curves of L0 from Σ̂_(τ_n), which they meet inside P by
Lemma 9.1 (e); and Lemma 9.6 and Lemma 9.7 in place of Lemma 5.5 and
Lemma 5.6 for the convergence. It gives the solution of the stage system on P_n whose data on Σ̂_(τ_n) are the
leading terms. These data and the forcing terms of (a)–(c) vanish for v ≤ v_start, since each forcing term contains a
profile of an earlier stage; so every iterate vanishes there, by the last clause of Lemma 9.8 for (a) and
because the transports run at fixed v. Hence the differences of iterates and the solution vanish on P_n ∩ {v ≤ v_start},
as Lemma 9.6 requires. The remainders of this solution start at zero. Commute the system with ∂_X and Ω to an
order j0 (the classes are preserved), and let e(τ) be the energy of m̃ to that order, f(τ) the norms of ∂_v φ̃ and Ω φ̃,
p(τ) that of Ψ̃ := □̃ φ̃, and z(τ) that of Z̃ := ∂_θ ĝ̃ (zero mean, so ‖ĝ̃‖ ≤ ‖Z̃‖). The L² norm of an E_q-profile on
A_P(τ) is at most C t^(3/2−q), and Lemma 9.3 (b) bounds m̃ by e. Lemma 9.6 for (a),
Lemma 9.7 with c0 = 0 for ∂_v φ̃ and Ω φ̃ (L0 commutes with ∂_v and Ω), with c0 = 2 for Ψ̃ (the transport
of Lemma 6.5 with σ̃ := m̃(ℓ, ℓ) + q_m in place of 𝒫 s, □̃ σ̃ taken from (a), so that no derivative
is lost), and with c0 = 3/2 for Z̃ ((c) and Lemma 4.8) give, with every integral over (τ_n, τ),

    e ≤ C ∫ ( t⁻² e + t^(−3/2) z + t⁻³ f + t⁻² ),            t^(−3/2) f ≤ C ∫ t^(−3/2) ( e + t^(−3/2) ),
    t^(1/2) p ≤ C ∫ t^(1/2) ( t⁻¹ e + t⁻² f + t^(−3/2) (z + p) + t⁻² ),
    z ≤ C ∫ ( t^(−3/2) (z + e + p) + t^(−5/2) f + t⁻² ).    (9.8)

The bad terms of the forcing of Ψ̃, r⁻¹ (∂_τ + ∂_r) σ̃ and r⁻² ∂_r φ̃, are the t⁻¹ e and t⁻² f. Every kernel is
integrable at −∞, and the forcing terms give e, z ≤ A_e t⁻¹, f ≤ A_f and p ≤ A_p t⁻¹ uniformly in n, with the
constants taken in order. The quantities e and z are fed by f and p through kernels with an extra integrable power, so
for t ≥ T0, T0 large, (9.8) returns their bounds with a factor ½. The quantities f and p are fed by e
with kernels of size O(1): f ≤ (2/3) C sup t e and p ≤ 2C (A_e + A_f + 1) t⁻¹, so A_f := C′ A_e and A_p := C″(A_e +
A_f) close. And [1, T0] is a bounded interval, on which Gronwall's inequality applies.

As n → ∞ the solutions converge. The difference of the n-th and the n′-th solves the homogeneous system on P_n with
data on Σ̂_(τ_n) given by the n′-th remainders there, of sizes C t_n⁻¹ (for e, z, p) and O(1) (for f).
(9.8) without forcing keeps e and z of size C t_n⁻¹, p of size C t^(−1/2) t_n^(−1/2), and f,
transported with γ = −3/2, of size C (t/t_n)^(3/2) ≤ C t^(3/2) t_n^(−3/2); so the difference tends to zero on every
bounded part of P. The limit solves the stage system on P with the same bounds. A solution with nothing coming in is
unique, since the difference of two satisfies (9.8) without forcing, and its e, z, p and t^(−3/2) f tend
to zero at −∞, which is what Lemma 9.7 with γ = −3/2 needs for f.

*Classes.* Lemma 9.3 (a), with the bound of m̃ by e, turns e ≤ C t⁻¹ into m̃ in E_(5/2). Then σ̃ is in
E_(5/2); φ̃ = −½ ∫_r^∞ σ̃ dr′ is in E_(3/2), with ℓφ̃ in E_(5/2); Ψ̃ is in E_(5/2) by (9.6); the
forcing term of (c) is in E_(7/2); and ĝ̃ is in E_(5/2) with ℓĝ̃ in E_(7/2). For the last, the integral formula of
Lemma 9.9 (d) with no leading term gives |ĝ̃| ≤ C r^(−3/2) ∫_r^∞ r′^(3/2) r′^(−7/2) dr′ = C r^(−5/2),
likewise for the derivatives that commute with ℓ, and ℓĝ̃ = −(3/(2r)) ĝ̃ − c ĝ̃ + (forcing) is in E_(7/2). So
ĝ_(m+1) = ĝ⁰ + ĝ̃ is in O_2. This is (9.7) at stage m.

*The residual, the phase, the continuation.* The argument of the proof of Theorem 4.11 gives ℛ^(m) = 0
for m ≤ N − 1. The rest of the residual is λ^N times a sum of monomials of (2.9) with all factors known, each in
E_3 by the count; the expansion of g⁻¹ converges uniformly, since |g_app − g0| ≤ C λ r^(−3/2). Rewriting with the fixed
phase v (Taylor's formula in λ Σ_(j≥2) λ^(j−2) φ_j about θ + φ1) multiplies profiles by powers of φ_j, keeping every
product in its class, and costs λ^(N+1) in the metric and so λ^(N−1) in Ric^H: R_N is in E_3. The scaled norm follows
because ∂^i [f] costs λ^(−i) and Ω costs nothing, and the L² norm of an E_3 profile on A_P(τ) is at most C t^(−3/2).
(E1) holds (W_TT and χ dv dv are transverse to ℓ), and (E2) by stage 0. On Σ_τ0 (Lemma 9.1 (c)) the profiles'
data determine, by Lemma 4.10 on Ω, solutions there; the two solve the same smooth linear system and agree on
Σ_τ0 with all their τ-derivatives, each fixed by the system from the data, so together they are smooth on P ∪ Ω. The
stage system is equivariant under T² × Z2 × Z2 and under S of Lemma 8.6, the condition of nothing coming in
is invariant, and the solutions are unique, so they are invariant. ∎

### 9.4 The far and near regions

Let β0 be the number of Proposition 9.12, which does not depend on the order of the approximant. For K ≥ 6 take the
approximant of Theorem 9.10 with N := K + 4 + ⌈4β0⌉ stages and put K′ := N − 1 = K + 3 + ⌈4β0⌉, its order,
so that the residual F_R := −Ric^H(g_app) has |F_R|_(k,P) ≤ C_R λ^(K′) t^(−3/2), with k = 6. Put T_λ := λ⁻² and let τ_λ
be the time with t = T_λ; the *far region* is P ∩ {τ ≤ τ_λ}, the *near region* P ∩ {τ_λ ≤ τ ≤ τ0}.

*The coefficients on P.* By Theorem 9.10 and (6.2), on P⁺: the coefficients B and C
of the linearised operator are in E_(3/2), being built from g_app and ∂g_app, and ∂[λ g1] = dv [∂_θ g1] + λ [∂g1];
G1 := [∂_θ g1] and G2 := [∂_θ² g1] are in E_(3/2), and the slow derivative [ℓ ∂_θ g1] is in E_(5/2), since the
oscillating part W_TT(· + φ1) of g1 is in O_(3/2) up to L_(5/2); g_app⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ is in λ E_(3/2) and ℓ_app − ℓ in λ E_2.
The profile T1 of Lemma 6.2 is in E_3: it collects the λ¹ terms of the linearisation in the direction
∂_θ G, namely ∂_θ ℛ^(1) = 0, −P_0(∂_θ g1) and −T(∂_θ g2), and the count of Theorem 9.10 puts each in E_3.
For instance □̃(W_TT(· + φ1)) = □̃ W_TT + 2 g0⁻¹(dφ1, d∂_θ W_TT) + (□̃ φ1) ∂_θ W_TT + g0⁻¹(dφ1, dφ1) ∂_θ² W_TT, each in
E_(7/2), and ℓ + 3/(2r) annihilates W_TT and maps ĝ_2 into L_3. In the equation (6.5) for h
and in Lemma 6.3 the terms in φ therefore have these coefficients: E_(3/2) on ℓφ = ½ 𝒫 s and on Ψ;
E_(5/2) on ∂_v φ (in (9.6), g^vv = 0, so ∂_v φ pairs only with ℓ∂_θ g1, in E_(5/2), and ∂_v∂_θ g1
pairs with ℓφ) and on the angular derivatives r⁻¹ Ω φ (the angular block r⁻² ⟨∂̊φ, ∂̊∂_θ g1⟩ of
(9.6) is (r⁻¹ Ω φ) · (r⁻¹ Ω ∂_θ g1)); and E_3 on φ and on λ ∂_x² φ. The same holds for the ℓℓ
contraction of Lemma 6.4, in which the dφ terms of B1 vanish, since the oscillating part of g1 is transverse to ℓ
and ℓ depends on x̂ alone.

**Proposition 9.11** (The far region.) There are λ_F > 0 and M_F, independent of τ_n, such that for
0 < λ ≤ λ_F and every τ_n < τ_λ, the solution g_n of Ric^H(g_n) = 0 on P ∩ {τ ≥ τ_n} with g_n = g_app and ∂_τ g_n =
∂_τ g_app on Σ̂_(τ_n) exists on P ∩ {τ_n ≤ τ ≤ τ_λ}, equals g0 on {v ≤ v_start} there, and w_n := g_n − g_app satisfies

    E(τ) := Σ_(i + |β| ≤ k) λ^i ‖∂^i Ω^β ∂w_n‖ ≤ M_F λ^(K′) t^(−1/2).    (9.9)

*Proof.* Assume E ≤ 2 M_F λ^(K′) t^(−1/2). Lemma 9.3 gives |w_n| ≤ C M_F λ^(K′−3) t⁻² and |∂w_n| ≤
C M_F λ^(K′−4) t⁻², so g_n has the margin of Lemma 9.1 (f) (|g_app⁻¹ − g0⁻¹| ≤ C λ t^(−3/2)), and
Lemma 9.2 gives w_n = 0 on {v ≤ v_start}; also |∂g_n| ≤ C t^(−3/2). Apply λ^i ∂^i Ω^β to the equation
for w without the decomposition, −½ g_n^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b w + ½ λ⁻¹ s G2 + B·∂w + C·w = F_R + 𝒬(w), s := w(ℓ, ℓ), with 𝒬 the
nonlinear terms, as in the proof of Theorem 6.1 ((6.2)), and Lemma 9.6 with
k(τ) = C t^(−3/2):

(i) the term with coefficient 1/λ: λ⁻¹ |s G2|_k ≤ C λ⁻¹ t^(−3/2) E, by Lemma 9.3 (b) for the
undifferentiated s and [λ ∂G2] in E_(3/2);
(ii) B·∂w and C·w give C t^(−3/2) E;
(iii) the commutators [λ^i ∂^i Ω^β, g^(ab)] ∂_a ∂_b w are as in Step 4 of the proof of Theorem 6.1, with
λ^i ∂^i g_app in λ E_(3/2) for i ≥ 1; for the rotations, [Ω, □̃] = 0, and Ω and [Ω, ∂_a ∂_b], a combination of second
derivatives, act otherwise only through g⁻¹ − g0⁻¹, in λ E_(3/2) plus w; so they are at most C t^(−3/2) E;
(iv) the nonlinear terms are at most C λ⁻⁵ t^(−3/2) E², as in Step 4, with Lemma 9.3 (a) in place of
Lemma 5.1;
(v) |F_R|_(k,P) ≤ C_R λ^(K′) t^(−3/2).

On the far region t ≥ T_λ, so ∫ λ⁻¹ t^(−3/2) ≤ 2 λ⁻¹ T_λ^(−1/2) = 2: the coupling of size 1/λ integrates to a constant.
On Σ̂_(τ_n), w_n = ∂_τ w_n = 0, so every term of E(τ_n) with at most one τ-derivative of w_n vanishes; the others are
fixed by the equation, solved for ∂_τ² w_n as in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 6.1 (at the lowest order
∂_τ² w_n = −2 F_R/g_n^ττ there). A term λ^i ∂^i Ω^β ∂w_n with i ≥ 1 is thus λ^i times derivatives of order i − 1 of
F_R, so E(τ_n) ≤ C λ |F_R|_(k,P)(τ_n) ≤ C C_R λ^(K′+1) t_n^(−3/2), which is at most C_R λ^(K′) t^(−1/2) once C λ ≤ 1,
as t ≤ t_n. With ∫_t^∞ t′^(−3/2) dt′ = 2 t^(−1/2), Gronwall's inequality gives E(τ) ≤ C e^(6C) (3 C_R λ^(K′) +
C M_F² λ^(2K′−5)) t^(−1/2), which is at most M_F λ^(K′) t^(−1/2) for M_F := 4 C e^(6C) C_R + 1 and λ small, as
2K′ − 5 > K′. Existence and continuation are Step 8 of the proof of Theorem 6.1 on the bounded pieces
P ∩ {τ_i ≤ τ ≤ τ_i + δ}, whose slices are compact annuli of the kind used there. ∎

**Proposition 9.12** (The near region.) There are β0 ≥ 2, λ_N > 0 and M_N such that for 0 < λ ≤ λ_N the
solutions of Proposition 9.11 continue to P ∩ {τ_λ ≤ τ ≤ τ0}, with w_n = h + φ [∂_θ g1] as in
Section 6.3 (φ = 0 on Σ̂_(τ_λ)), and

    𝒩_P(τ) ≤ M_N λ^(K′) t^(−1/2) (T_λ/t)^β0      on [τ_λ, τ0].    (9.10)

Here 𝒩_P is the quantity 𝒩 of (6.7) with four changes: products of at most k − i rotations Ω_ab stand
beside ∂^i in the h-part; the parts in φ and Ψ are commuted with Z ∈ 𝒵 = {λ∂_τ, λ∂_r, Ω_ab}, which commute with L0
exactly, and the second derivatives of φ are taken as λ (∂_r² φ, r⁻¹ ∂_r Ω φ, r⁻² Ω² φ) (with ∂_τ = L0 + ∂_r and
L0 φ = −½ 𝒫 s these give every second derivative; at each order the norms are equivalent to the Cartesian ones, with
constants depending on k); the Ψ-part is that of Ψ′ := Ψ − ½ X_s (Lemma 9.5); and the factor t^(−1/2) of
(9.10) is t^(1/2) for the parts in φ. β0 depends only on the constants C of (9.12) below at
the orders j ≤ k, which are built from the bounds of g0, g1, g2, from P and from Lemma 9.3,
Lemma 9.4, Lemma 9.5, Lemma 9.6 and Lemma 9.7. The profiles g0, g1, g2
do not depend on N, since stage m of Theorem 9.10 is fixed by the stages before it; every term with a
profile g_j, j ≥ 3, carries a factor λ and is absorbed for λ ≤ λ_N. In particular 𝒩_P(τ0) ≤ M_N λ^(K′−2β0).

*Proof.* Run Steps 1–7 of the proof of Theorem 6.1 on [τ_λ, τ], with these changes.
Lemma 9.3–Lemma 9.7 replace Lemma 5.1, Lemma 5.4,
Lemma 5.5 and Lemma 5.6; the mollifier is that of Lemma 9.4; the
coefficients have the decay listed above; and the φ-quantities are transported from Σ̂_(τ_λ), where φ vanishes (h = w_n
there). Its Z-derivatives containing λ∂_τ, and Ψ′, do not vanish there, but with L0 φ = −½ 𝒫 s all are bounded by
C′ E(τ_λ), so 𝒩_P(τ_λ) ≤ C′ E(τ_λ) ≤ C′ M_F λ^(K′) T_λ^(−1/2) by (9.9), and each line below carries this
data term.

Write H for the h-part of 𝒩_P, Q′ for the Ψ′-part, and D0, D1, D2 for the parts ‖φ‖, the first derivatives
(∂_τ φ, ∂_r φ, r⁻¹ Ω φ) and the second derivatives of φ. Since Ψ = Ψ′ + ½ X_s and ‖Z^j X_s‖ ≤ C λ H by
Lemma 9.5, the Ψ-part is at most Q′ + C λ H. The transport of Ψ′ follows from that of Ψ
(Lemma 6.5) and Lemma 9.5:

    (L0 − 2/r) Ψ′ = −½ 𝒫 □̃ s − ½ R_s + r⁻¹ X_s − r⁻¹ (∂_τ + ∂_r) 𝒫 s − 3 r⁻² ∂_r φ,    (9.11)

in which the term ½ L0 X_s of −½ [□̃, 𝒫] s has been absorbed. With every integral over (τ_λ, τ), the initial values at
τ_λ of Lemma 9.7 being those of 𝒩_P(τ_λ) and included in the first term of each line:

    H ≤ C 𝒩_P(τ_λ) + C ∫ ( t^(−3/2) (H + Q′) + t^(−5/2) D1 + t⁻³ (D0 + D2) + λ^(K′) t^(−3/2) + R_nl ),
    t^(−1/2) (D0 + D1) ≤ C T_λ^(−1/2) 𝒩_P(τ_λ) + C ∫ t^(−1/2) H,
    t^(1/2) D2 ≤ C T_λ^(1/2) 𝒩_P(τ_λ) + C ∫ t^(1/2) H,
    t^(1/2) Q′ ≤ C T_λ^(1/2) 𝒩_P(τ_λ)
                 + C ∫ t^(1/2) ( t⁻¹ H + t⁻² D1 + t^(−3/2) (H + Q′) + t⁻³ (D0 + D2) + λ^(K′) t^(−3/2) + R_nl ),
    (9.12)

with R_nl the nonlinear terms. The first line is Step 4 with the coefficients above; ℓφ = ½ 𝒫 s is bounded by H
through Lemma 9.3 (b). The second is Step 5: Lemma 9.7 with c0 = 0 for φ, ∂_τ φ and ∂_r φ and
c0 = 1 for r⁻¹ Ω φ, with forcing −½ Z^j of 𝒫 s, ∂_τ 𝒫 s, ∂_r 𝒫 s and r⁻¹ Ω 𝒫 s, the last bounded at top order by
Bernstein's inequality in one r⁻¹ Ω; the parts with c0 = 0 satisfy the stronger bound with t^(−3/2). The third: the
transports of λ ∂_r² φ, λ r⁻¹ ∂_r Ω φ and λ r⁻² Ω² φ have c0 = 0, 1, 2, so Lemma 9.7 applies with
c0 ≤ 2, and their forcing, λ times the same derivatives of 𝒫 s, is bounded by Bernstein's inequality (M2) in one ∂_r or
one r⁻¹ Ω. The fourth is Lemma 9.7 with c0 = 2 for (9.11): Lemma 9.5
bounds R_s and r⁻¹ X_s by C (t⁻¹ + h_P′) H ≤ C t⁻¹ H, its terms R′_s being rewritten through Lemma 6.4 as
in Step 6; r⁻¹ (∂_τ + ∂_r) 𝒫 s and r⁻² ∂_r φ give t⁻¹ H and t⁻² D1; and 𝒫 □̃ s is bounded through
Lemma 6.4 with the coefficients above. Z commutes with L0, and [Z, r^(−c)] carries the factor r^(−c−1),
so every line holds at every order j ≤ k with c0 unchanged.

*The bootstrap.* Assume H, Q′ ≤ B t^(−1/2) (T_λ/t)^β and D0, D1, D2 ≤ B t^(1/2) (T_λ/t)^β on [τ_λ, τ], with
B := 8 C C′ (M_F + C_R + 1) λ^(K′), C the sum of the constants of each line of (9.12) and C′ ≥ 2. Two
integrals are used, for t ≤ T_λ and β > 1: for a > −β,

    ∫_t^(T_λ) t′^(−1−a) (T_λ/t′)^β dt′ ≤ T_λ^β ∫_t^∞ t′^(−1−a−β) dt′ = t^(−a) (T_λ/t)^β/(β + a),

and ∫_t^(T_λ) t′⁻¹ dt′ = log(T_λ/t) ≤ (T_λ/t)^β/β, since log x = β⁻¹ log x^β ≤ β⁻¹ x^β for x ≥ 1. Substituting the
assumed bounds, each integrand of (9.12), with the weight of its line, is B t′^(−1−a) (T_λ/t′)^β times a
constant, with the following exponents a:

- the H-line: t^(−3/2)(H + Q′) and t^(−5/2) D1 give a = 1, and t⁻³(D0 + D2) gives a = 3/2; the integrals are at most
  C B t⁻¹ (T_λ/t)^β/(β + 1), which is the bound of H times C t^(−1/2)/(β + 1);
- the D0/D1-line: t^(−1/2) H gives a = 0, so D0 + D1 ≤ (C/β) B t^(1/2) (T_λ/t)^β;
- the D2-line: t^(1/2) H gives a = −1, so D2 ≤ (C/(β − 1)) B t^(1/2) (T_λ/t)^β;
- the Q′-line: t^(1/2) t⁻¹ H and t^(1/2) t⁻² D1 give a = 0, so they contribute (C/β) B t^(−1/2) (T_λ/t)^β to Q′: this is
  the loss the split pays; t^(1/2) t^(−3/2)(H + Q′) gives a = 1/2 and t^(1/2) t⁻³(D0 + D2) gives a = 1, which carry an
  extra integrable power.

So every integral of a bootstrap quantity returns at most C/(β − 1) times the bound of its line. The data terms and the
forcing terms λ^(K′) t^(−3/2) together contribute at most B/8 times the bound of each line: 𝒩_P(τ_λ) ≤
C′ M_F λ^(K′) T_λ^(−1/2) and T_λ^(−1/2) ≤ t^(−1/2) for the H-line; t^(1/2) T_λ^(−1/2) 𝒩_P(τ_λ) ≤ C′ M_F λ^(K′) t^(1/2)
T_λ⁻¹ for the D0/D1-line; t^(−1/2) T_λ^(1/2) 𝒩_P(τ_λ) ≤ C′ M_F λ^(K′) t^(−1/2) for the D2- and Q′-lines; ∫ λ^(K′)
t′^(−3/2) ≤ 2 λ^(K′) t^(−1/2) in the H-line and ∫ t′^(1/2) λ^(K′) t′^(−3/2) = λ^(K′) log(T_λ/t) ≤ λ^(K′) (T_λ/t)^β/β in
the Q′-line; and C C′ M_F λ^(K′) + 2 C λ^(K′) ≤ B/8 since C′ ≥ 2.

The nonlinear terms are small. Every bootstrap quantity is at most B λ^(−2β) t^(1/2) ≤ B λ^(−2β−1), since (T_λ/t)^β ≤
T_λ^β = λ^(−2β) and t^(1/2) ≤ T_λ^(1/2) = λ⁻¹. So by Lemma 9.3 (a), R_nl ≤ C λ⁻⁵ t^(−3/2) (B λ^(−2β−1))².
Its contribution to the H-line is at most C B² λ^(−7−4β) ∫ t^(−3/2) ≤ 2 C B² λ^(−7−4β), and the bound of H is at least
B T_λ^(−1/2) = B λ; its contribution to t^(1/2) Q′ is at most C B² λ^(−7−4β) log T_λ ≤ C B² λ^(−8−4β), and the bound of
t^(1/2) Q′ is at least B. Both ratios are at most C B λ^(−8−4β), which is C″ λ^(K′−8−4β) since B is a constant times
λ^(K′). For β = β0, K′ = K + 3 + ⌈4β0⌉ ≥ 9 + 4β0, so the ratios are at most C″ λ and at most 1/8 for λ small.

Take β = β0 := max(2, 4C + 1), so that C/(β0 − 1) ≤ 1/4. Then each line returns at most (1/8 + 1/4 + 1/8) times its
bound: the bootstrap bounds improve to B/2. The margin of Lemma 9.1 (f) holds, by Lemma 9.3, as in
Proposition 9.11. At τ0, t = 1 and (T_λ/t)^β0 = λ^(−2β0), which gives 𝒩_P(τ0) ≤ M_N λ^(K′−2β0). ∎

### 9.5 Proof of the construction

The proof below gives, for every K ≥ 6, numbers λ_P > 0 and C and, for 0 < λ ≤ λ_P, a smooth vacuum metric g_λ on
P ∪ Ω in the wave-map gauge relative to g0, with g_app the approximant of Theorem 9.10 with
N = K + 4 + ⌈4β0⌉ stages, such that:

- (P-i) g_λ = g0 on (P ∪ Ω) ∩ {v ≤ v_start}: the seed, exactly;
- (P-ii) for every v < V_P and x̂, r^(3/2) (g_λ − g0 − λ [W_TT])(v − r, r x̂) → 0 as r → ∞, with [W_TT] taken at the
  phase v/λ;
- (P-iii) on P, |g_λ − g_app| ≤ C λ^(K−3) t⁻² and |∂(g_λ − g_app)| ≤ C λ^(K−4) t⁻²;
- (P-iv) on Ω, the conclusions of Theorem 6.1 with this K, the bound on 𝒩 included;
- (P-v) g_λ is invariant under T² × Z2 × Z2, and it is the only solution of Ric^H(g) = 0 on P with g = g0 on
  P ∩ {v ≤ v_start}, with |g − g_app| + |∂(g − g_app)| ≤ ε_U t^(−3/2), and with the energy of g − g_app on A_P(τ)
  tending to zero as τ → −∞; here ε_U > 0 is so small that this class lies in the margin of Lemma 9.1 (f),
  since |g_app − g0| ≤ C λ t^(−3/2) and t^(−3/2) ≤ t^(−5/4).

These are items 1, 2, 3, 5 and the first part of item 4 of Theorem 3.7; the second part of item 4 is
Proposition 9.13.

*Proof of Theorem 3.7.* *The solution on P ∪ Ω.* At τ0, Data(w_n), the norm of (E4) of
Theorem 6.1, satisfies Data(w_n) ≤ C λ⁻¹ 𝒩_P(τ0) ≤ C M_N λ^(K′−2β0−1), since the term ‖∂_x(φ G1)‖
contains λ⁻¹ ‖φ‖; and K′ − 2β0 − 1 = K + 2 + ⌈4β0⌉ − 2β0 ≥ K + 2. (E1)–(E3) hold on Ω by Theorem 9.10, so
Theorem 6.1 with this K continues g_n to Ω with its bound on 𝒩: (P-iv) for g_n.

*The limit.* For n′ > n, δ := g_n − g_n′ solves on P ∩ {τ ≥ τ_n} a linear system −½ g_n^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b δ = f with |f|
≤ C(λ) t^(−3/2) (|δ| + |∂δ|), whose coefficient involves ∂²g_n′, at most C λ⁻¹ t^(−3/2). Lemma 9.6 gives
‖∂δ(τ)‖ ≤ C(λ) ‖∂w_n′(τ_n)‖ ≤ C(λ) M_F λ^(K′) t_n^(−1/2), and Lemma 5.5 continues the bound to Ω. So g_n
converges, with the bounds of Proposition 9.11 and Proposition 9.12 and of Theorem 6.1, uniformly
with k − 5 derivatives on compact sets. The limit is smooth: for fixed λ the higher norms of g_n are bounded uniformly
in n by the linear energy estimates for the commuted equation, with constants depending on λ and the order, whose
kernels are C(λ) t^(−3/2) on the far region, which is integrable, and are taken over the bounded interval [τ_λ, τ0] on
the near region, with no decomposition needed for fixed λ; the limit does not depend on the order used, by the
uniqueness of (P-v). It solves Ric^H(g_λ) = 0 on P ∪ Ω, it satisfies the bounds of Theorem 6.1 on
Ω, |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ ≤ ε1 among them, and it equals g0 on P ∩ {v ≤ v_start}, since each g_n does, by Lemma 9.2
with the margin of Proposition 9.11 and Proposition 9.12.

*The seed region on Ω.* The proof of Lemma 9.2 runs on Ω from Σ_τ0, where g_λ agrees with g0 on {v ≤ v_start}
together with its first τ-derivative, g_λ being smooth on P ∪ Ω. In place of {v + ε h_P(τ) = v_start} it uses the
surfaces {v + ε(τ − τ0) = v_start}, 0 < ε ≤ 1, for which g0⁻¹(dv + ε dτ, dv + ε dτ) = −2ε − ε²(1 + μ/r²) < 0 by
Proposition 2.5 (d), while v + ε(τ − τ0) increases along future causal curves of g0. So near the points where g_λ = g0
these surfaces are spacelike for g_λ too, with {v + ε(τ − τ0) ≤ v_start} to their past, and the other boundary pieces of
Ω are spacelike for g_λ with Ω to their past (Lemma 2.6 (e)). Letting ε → 0 gives g_λ = g0 on Ω ∩ {v ≤ v_start}.
This is (P-i).

*The bounds (P-iii).* On the far region, (9.9) and Lemma 9.3 (a) give |w| ≤ C M_F λ^(K′−3) t⁻²
and |∂w| ≤ C M_F λ^(K′−4) t⁻². On the near region, (9.10) with (T_λ/t)^β0 ≤ λ^(−2β0) gives
H ≤ M_N λ^(K′−2β0) t^(−1/2) and D0 ≤ M_N λ^(K′−2β0) t^(1/2), so by Lemma 9.3 (a) |h| ≤ C λ^(K′−2β0−3) t⁻²
and |φ G1| ≤ C λ^(K′−2β0−3) t⁻¹ · t^(−3/2), with one more factor λ⁻¹ for the first derivatives. Since K′ − 2β0 ≥ K +
3 > K, this is (P-iii).

*The gauge.* D(g_λ) solves the homogeneous linear system of the proof of Lemma 3.6, whose coefficients
are built from g_λ, ∂g_λ and ∂²g_λ, and so are at most C(λ) t^(−3/2) on P⁺. D(g_λ) = D(g_app) + O(|w| + |∂w|), and
D(g_app) = Σ_(j≥1) λ^j [D_j] with D_j in E_2. Indeed, the λ⁰ part of D(g_app) comes from the fast derivative of λ[g1] in
g^(ab)(Γ[g] − Γ[g0])^ρ_(ab), and equals g0^(ρσ) (∂_θ g1)(ℓ, ·)_σ − ½ ℓ^ρ tr_(g0) ∂_θ g1; it vanishes by (E1) and tr
W_TT = 0, χ dv dv being transverse and traceless too. In the λ¹ part, the ∂_v-part of the slow divergence of W_TT is ∂_v
(W_TT(ℓ, ·)) = 0, since the Cartesian components of ℓ do not depend on v; the rest of it gains a power, as ℓ W_TT =
−(3/(2r)) W_TT and r⁻¹ Ω W_TT are in E_(5/2); and every other term is a product, or a derivative of a stage-j profile of
class E_2. An r⁻² amplitude on A_P(τ) has L² norm at most C (∫_(r_in)^(r_in+d1) r⁻⁴ r³ dr)^(1/2) ≤ C t^(−1/2); so the
energy of D(g_λ) on A_P(τ) is at most C t^(−1/2), and tends to zero as τ → −∞. Lemma 9.6, with the integrable
kernel C(λ) t^(−3/2), gives D(g_λ) = 0 on P. Then Ric(g_λ)_mn = Ric^H(g_λ)_mn + ½(g_mρ ∇̂_n D^ρ + g_nρ ∇̂_m D^ρ) = 0 on
P, Σ_τ0 included, so the Cauchy data of g_λ on Σ_τ0 satisfy the vacuum constraints, and D(g_λ) = 0 there. On Ω, g_λ is
smooth, solves Ric^H(g_λ) = 0 and is within ε1 of g0. These are the hypotheses of Lemma 3.6, which gives
D(g_λ) = 0 on Ω: g_λ is vacuum.

*The radiation field (P-ii).* g_λ − g0 − λ[W_TT] = w + λ[m1] + λ[χ dv dv] + λ([W_TT(· + φ1)] − [W_TT]) +
Σ_(j≥2) λ^j [g_j]. Here |w| ≤ C λ^(K−3) t⁻², m1 and χ are in L_2, W_TT(· + φ1) − W_TT is in L_1 L_(3/2), and every g_j
with j ≥ 2 is in E_2 (means, oscillating profiles and the Taylor terms φ_i^p ∂_θ^p W_TT of the fixed-phase rewriting).
Along v = const and x̂ = const, t and r grow together (r − t is bounded on P⁺), so r^(3/2) times the sum tends to zero
as r → ∞.

*Uniqueness and symmetry (P-v).* For a second solution g′ with g′ = g0 on P ∩
{v ≤ v_start}, |g′ − g_app| + |∂(g′ − g_app)| ≤ ε_U t^(−3/2) and energy of g′ − g_app tending to zero, δ := g_λ − g′
solves a linear system with coefficients at most C(λ) t^(−3/2) (they involve ∂²g_λ and ∂g′, both controlled), its energy
tends to zero at −∞, and Lemma 9.6 gives δ = 0 on P; the uniqueness of Step 8 of the proof of
Theorem 6.1 continues this to Ω. The data at past null infinity, g_app and the equation are invariant under
T² × Z2 × Z2, so g_λ is too, by this uniqueness. ∎

### 9.6 The horizon and the mean mass for these solutions

**Proposition 9.13** (Items 6 and 7 of Theorem 3.1 for the solutions of Theorem 3.7.)
Let g_λ be the solution of Theorem 3.7, K ≥ 6, λ ≤ λ_P. Then on D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}:
(a) if μ0 > √72 l5², the conclusions of Proposition 3.4 hold for g_λ, with λ_H and C of the same form;
(b) the conclusions of Proposition 3.5 hold for g_λ: |M[S_(v,r)](g_λ) − μ(v)| ≤ C λ² if v ≤ v_start or v ≥ v_end,
and ≤ C λ in between.

*Proof.* The proofs of Proposition 3.4 and Proposition 3.5 in Chapter 8 use four facts about the
solution, and none about how its data were obtained. We check each for the g_λ of Theorem 3.7, with
g_app the approximant of Theorem 9.10.

(1) *The remainder bounds:* g_λ = g_app + w on Ω with ‖∂^i w‖_∞ ≤ C M λ^(K−3−i) for i ≤ 4, as in
(8.1). These follow from Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 6.1 once the bound on 𝒩 of
that theorem holds for g_λ itself on Ω. It does: the w_n of Section 9.5 have Data(w_n) ≤ C M_N
λ^(K′−2β0−1) ≤ C λ^(K+2) uniformly in n, and g_n → g_λ on Σ_τ0, so Data(w_λ) ≤ liminf Data(w_n), since the bound is
uniform in n and the slice is compact, so that the derivatives up to order k + 1 converge weakly in L². Then
Theorem 6.1 applied to the trace of g_λ on Σ_τ0 gives a solution on Ω with the bound on 𝒩, which is g_λ
by the uniqueness on Ω (Step 8 of its proof).

(2) *The first stage:* g1 = m1 + W(X, θ + φ1) with W = W_TT + χ dv², W(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr W_TT = 0, m1 independent of θ.
The stages of Theorem 9.10 are those of Theorem 4.11 with nothing coming in, so W_TT is the same, and
χ is −2 r⁻² times a function of (v, x̂, θ), with no radiation at past null infinity (Theorem 9.10, stage 0).
So tr_S W = 0 on every sphere, as in (8.3), and Lemma 8.3 applies to this g_app: along
every column θ⁺(g_app) = θ⁺(g0) + λ [Θ⁺_1] + λ² E⁺, with no term of order λ⁻², λ⁻¹ or λ⁰ beyond g0's. The later stages
are smooth on P ∪ Ω, and so bounded with their X-derivatives on the compact Ω.

(3) *The support of the oscillating profiles:* the stages of Theorem 9.10 vanish for v ≤ v_start, and its
oscillating profiles are transport solutions along ℓ at fixed v with forcing supported in v_start < v < v_end
(Lemma 9.9 (d), and on Ω Lemma 4.10 (c) with the trace data on Σ_τ0), so they vanish for
v ≥ v_end, as in the proof of Proposition 3.5.

(4) *The symmetry:* the stages of Theorem 9.10 satisfy S g = g (Lemma 8.6): the stage system is
S-equivariant, the condition of nothing coming in is S-invariant, and the solutions are unique. So J* m1 = −m1.

With (1)–(4) the two proofs run verbatim. In the proof of Proposition 3.4, steps (i)–(ii) concern g0 and the
expansion as a function of the metric; (iii) is (2); (iv) is (1), giving C λ^(K−5) ≤ C λ; and (v) uses Ω, μ and r_q
only. In the proof of Proposition 3.5, outside the shell g_app = g0 + λ m1 + λ² E by (3), DM[m1] = 0 by (4) and
naturality, and the remainder is O(λ^(K−4)) by (1); inside the shell the wave enters M[S](g_app) at order λ⁰ only
through ½ k^±(ℓ) ∂_θ tr_S g1, which vanishes by (2), θ⁻, the area and g(n⁺, n⁻) carrying none
(Lemma 8.3); and for λ* < λ ≤ λ_P, λ* that of Lemma 8.3, its step for larger λ uses
only |g_λ − g0| ≤ ε1 and |∂g_λ| ≤ C on Ω, which are conclusions of Theorem 6.1 and hold for g_λ by (1). ∎

The columns of Proposition 3.4 are those of D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}. On P the columns continue below Σ_τ0, where (P-iii)
bounds g_λ − g_app and its first derivatives by C λ^(K−3) t⁻² and C λ^(K−4) t⁻², and the second derivatives that step
(iv) needs come from (9.9) and (9.10) with Lemma 9.3. So the same argument runs on
P ∩ {r ≤ R} for each R, with constants depending on R, θ⁺(g0) being of size 3/r far out. The statement above is on
D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}, as item 4 of Theorem 3.7 is.

### 9.7 The flux at past null infinity

By (P-ii) the radiation field of g_λ at past null infinity is λ[W_TT] exactly, at every λ: its two polarizations are
the free data F, G, with no correction at any order. Write P1(v, ϑ) := p1(v, ϑ, v/λ) and P2(v, ϑ) := p2(v, ϑ, v/λ) for
the polarizations of (8.2) at the phase v/λ, and

    a_s(v) := λ env(v) sin(v/λ),   a_c(v) := λ env(v) cos(v/λ),   D_s := a_s′,   D_c := a_c′,

so that F = A h(ζ) a_s and G = A h(ζ) a_c along the phase. The flux density is the quadratic form (4/3)((∂_v P1)² + ∂_v
P1 ∂_v P2 + (∂_v P2)²), whose phase mean at leading order is μ′ ((4.8), Proposition 2.11).

**Lemma 9.14** (The flux and its integral.) (a) The flux density is

    (4/3)((∂_v P1)² + ∂_v P1 ∂_v P2 + (∂_v P2)²) = (4/9) A² h(ζ)² (cos⁴ϑ D_c² + sin⁴ϑ D_s² − cos²ϑ sin²ϑ D_c D_s).

(b) Its mean over S³ is exactly

    (2/9) A² [ env² + λ² env′² + (1 − π/2) ( −½ (env² − λ² env′²) sin(2v/λ) + λ env env′ cos(2v/λ) ) ].    (9.13)

(c) Its integral in v from −∞ is

    μ(v) − μ0 + (2/9) λ² A² ∫_(−∞)^v env′² + (1 − π/2)(2/9) A² ( (λ/4) env² cos(2v/λ) + (λ²/4) env env′ sin(2v/λ) )
        + (1 − π/2)(2/9) A² (λ²/4) ∫_(−∞)^v (env′² − env env″) sin(2v′/λ) dv′,

and the last term is O(λ³).

*Proof.* (a) Write c := cos ϑ, s := sin ϑ. By (8.2), ∂_v P1 = A h (2c² D_c − s² D_s)/3 and ∂_v P2 =
A h (2s² D_s − c² D_c)/3. Put a := 2c² D_c − s² D_s and b := 2s² D_s − c² D_c. Then a + b = c² D_c + s² D_s and
ab = 5 c² s² D_c D_s − 2c⁴ D_c² − 2s⁴ D_s², so a² + ab + b² = (a + b)² − ab = 3(c⁴ D_c² + s⁴ D_s² − c² s² D_c D_s), and
(4/3)(A² h²/9)(a² + ab + b²) is the stated form.

(b) The volume form of S³ in the angles of Section 8.1 is cos ϑ sin ϑ dϑ dξ1 dξ2, and with z := cos 2ϑ,
dz = −4 sin ϑ cos ϑ dϑ, so the mean over S³ of a function of ϑ is ½ ∫_(−1)^1 dz. Here h² = 2/(1 + z²), c² = (1 + z)/2
and s² = (1 − z)/2, so

    h² c⁴ = ½ + z/(1 + z²),    h² s⁴ = ½ − z/(1 + z²),    h² c² s² = (1 − z²)/(2(1 + z²)) = 1/(1 + z²) − ½.

The odd parts integrate to zero, so ⟨h² c⁴⟩ = ⟨h² s⁴⟩ = ½, and ⟨h² c² s²⟩ = ½ (2 arctan 1 − 1) = π/4 − ½. The sphere
mean of (a) is therefore (4/9) A² (½ D_c² + ½ D_s² − (π/4 − ½) D_c D_s) = (2/9) A² (D_c² + D_s² + (1 − π/2) D_c D_s).
Finally D_c = λ env′ cos(v/λ) − env sin(v/λ) and D_s = λ env′ sin(v/λ) + env cos(v/λ), so D_c² + D_s² = env² +
λ² env′², and D_c D_s = ½ (λ² env′² − env²) sin(2v/λ) + λ env env′ cos(2v/λ). This is (9.13).

(c) The non-oscillating part integrates to (2/9) A² ∫ (env² + λ² env′²) = μ(v) − μ0 + (2/9) λ² A² ∫ env′², by
μ′ = (2/9) A² env². For the oscillating part, the derivative of (λ/4) env² cos(2v/λ) + (λ²/4) env env′ sin(2v/λ) is

    −½ env² sin(2v/λ) + λ env env′ cos(2v/λ) + (λ²/4)(env′² + env env″) sin(2v/λ),

and adding (λ²/4)(env′² − env env″) sin(2v/λ) gives −½ (env² − λ² env′²) sin(2v/λ) + λ env env′ cos(2v/λ), the
oscillating bracket of (9.13). One more integration by parts, with the antiderivative −(λ/2) cos(2v′/λ) of
sin(2v′/λ), shows that the last integral is O(λ³), env being smooth with compact support. ∎

Both boundary terms carry the factor 1 − π/2: the integrated flux is linear in the oscillating coefficient. While the
shell passes, the integrated flux oscillates about μ(v) − μ0 with amplitude (π/2 − 1)(λ/18) A² env², at twice the wave
frequency (π/2 − 1 ≈ 0.571). After the shell (env = env′ = 0) the integrated flux exceeds μ(v_end) − μ0 by exactly
(2/9) λ² A² ∫ env′² + O(λ³), which comes from the non-oscillating part. The phase mean of (9.13) is
μ′ + (2/9) λ² A² env′². The mass law that turns this flux into the Bondi mass of g_λ is Theorem 3.8.

## 10. Bondi coordinates and the mass law at past null infinity

This chapter proves Theorem 3.8: the solution g_λ of Theorem 3.7 admits Bondi coordinates near past
null infinity, and in them its mass aspect obeys the five-dimensional Bondi law. The law is due to Tanabe, Tanahashi and
Shiromizu [TTS09]. We derive it again in the class at hand, with every coefficient general from the first order on, so
that nothing in the proof is taken from [TTS09] except the comparison. What has to be shown is that g_λ has the
asymptotic expansion at past null infinity which the law needs, in Bondi coordinates built on g_λ itself, and what the
law then gives.

The argument has four steps. At fixed λ the far region of Theorem 3.7 is a neighbourhood of past null
infinity, and there the remainder g_λ − g_app solves a wave equation whose forcing decays like r^(−3). First, every
derivative of the remainder obeys the bound which the construction gives for the first few
(Section Section 10.2). Second, subtracting the explicit leading term of the forcing and estimating the rest
with the energy of the far region gains half a power of r; repeated, this gives an expansion of g_λ − g0 in powers of
r^(−1/2) to any order, with the radiation field as its leading term. The derivatives of the remainders along the ingoing
generators gain a full order, because for them the wave equation is a transport along the outgoing generators, and these
reach the seed region, where everything vanishes, after a bounded parameter length (Section Section 10.3).
Third, Bondi coordinates are built from the null geodesics of g_λ asymptotic to the ingoing generators of the
background, in the manner of the eikonal function of [HL21] at future null infinity (Section Section 10.4).
Fourth, in the Bondi form the vacuum equations are a hierarchy in r^(−1/2). Its radial equations kill every coefficient
below the waves' and fix the shift and the first correction of W; the traceless angular equation makes the r^(−2)
coefficients of the angular metric constant in v, which the seed sets to zero; and R_vv at order r^(−3) is the mass law
plus a divergence that then vanishes (Section Section 10.5).

Throughout the chapter λ is fixed, 0 < λ ≤ λ_P, and every constant may depend on λ.

### 10.1 The setting at fixed λ

We use the notation of Chapter 9 (Section 9.1, Section 9.3). X = (τ, x) ∈ R × R⁴,
r = |x|, x̂ = x/r, v = τ + r and t := 1 + τ0 − τ; P is the past domain (9.1) of Theorem 3.7,
P⁺ := P ∩ {v ≥ v_start}, Σ̂_τ := {X : τ(X) = τ} the whole level sets of τ (Section 9.1), and ‖·‖ the flat L²
norm on Σ̂_τ ∩ P⁺. The field ℓ := g0⁻¹ dv is null and tangent to the ingoing generators of the cones {v = const};
ℓf := df(ℓ), and on P⁺ we use the coordinates (v, r, x̂), in which ℓ = ∂_r and ∂_v is the derivative at fixed (r, x̂).
Ω_ab := x_a ∂_b − x_b ∂_a are the rotations of R⁴, and □̃ := g0^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b acts on Cartesian components. On S³ we use
the polar angle ϑ ∈ [0, π/2] and the angles φ1, φ2 of the two rotation planes, the round metric being
γ = dϑ² + cos²ϑ dφ1² + sin²ϑ dφ2².

For p ≥ 0, E_p is the class of tensors f on P⁺ (Cartesian components) that vanish for v ≤ v_start and
satisfy |∂_X^α Ω^β f| ≤ C r^(−p) for all α and β: the class E_p of Section 9.3, for functions of X at fixed
λ. An oscillating factor [f], the profile f taken at the phase v/λ, belongs to these classes like any other function,
since each derivative of [f] costs a factor λ^(−1), a constant at fixed λ. A coefficient that does not vanish for
v ≤ v_start, such as g0 − η or Γ[g0], is said to be in E_p when it obeys the same bounds. The classes multiply,
E_p E_q ⊂ E_(p+q), and E_p ⊂ E_q for p ≥ q, since r ≥ 1 on P⁺. On P⁺ the quantities t and r are comparable,
t + a1 ≤ r ≤ t + a2 (Lemma 9.1 (d)).

The *far region* is P ∩ {t ≥ T_λ}, T_λ := λ^(−2), as in Section 9.4. On it Theorem 3.7 and its
proof give

    u := g_λ − g0 = λ[W_TT] + u_1,       λ[W_TT] = r^(−3/2) G_3,    (10.1)

with u_1 in E_2 pointwise together with the Cartesian derivatives that the construction controls. The terms of u_1 are
m1, χ, the later stages, the Taylor terms of the phase and the remainder w := g_λ − g_app, as in the proof of item 2 of
Theorem 3.7 (Section 9.5), with the classes (9.7) and item 3 of
Theorem 3.7 for w. Here G_3(v, x̂) denotes the r^(3/2)-normalised Cartesian components of λW_TT at the
phase v/λ. The first-order wave λW_TT is (2.11), with the polarizations p1, p2 built there from the free data F, G
of Section 2.6 at the phase v/λ. In the orthonormal coframe (r dϑ, r cos ϑ dφ1, r sin ϑ dφ2) its components are
r^(−3/2) times −2(p1 + p2), 2p1 and 2p2, and the coframe has bounded Cartesian components with bounded derivatives along
x̂; so G_3 is smooth and bounded with all its derivatives, smooth at the axes (Lemma 2.9 (a)), and zero for
v ≤ v_start, where env vanishes. The construction controls finitely many derivatives of u_1: with the regularity index
k = 6 of Section 9.4, (9.9) and the Sobolev inequality with rotations, Lemma 9.3 (a), give
∂^i w ∈ E_2 for i ≤ 4, the higher norms bounded. The approximating solutions of the construction give every order at
fixed λ, uniformly; this is Lemma 10.2, which the induction of Section Section 10.3 consumes.

### 10.2 Every order at fixed λ

**Lemma 10.1** (The equation for u.) On P, −½ □̃ u = S(u) with

    S(u) := −Ric(g0) + ½ (g_λ^{ab} − g0^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b (g0 + u)
            − [ Q(X; g0 + u)(∂g0 + ∂u, ∂g0 + ∂u) − Q(X; g0)(∂g0, ∂g0) ].    (10.2)

At every order at which the derivatives of u are in E_(3/2), the terms of S have the following classes:
Ric(g0) = (3μ'/(2r³)) dv dv exactly (Proposition 2.5 (a)); g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ is in E_(3/2), ∂²g0 = O(r^(−2)) and ∂²u is in
E_(3/2); and the difference of the Q terms is quadratic in ∂u (in E_3) plus Γ[g0] times ∂u (in E_2 E_(3/2)). So S(u)
is in E_3 at those orders. The construction gives them for the first few orders (Section Section 10.1), and
Lemma 10.2 gives them at every order.

Proof. Ric^H(g_λ) = 0, since g_λ is vacuum and in the wave-map gauge, and Ric^H(g0) = Ric(g0) (Section 2.4); subtract
the two, using the form (2.9) of Ric^H for both. The classes are those of the count in the proof of
Theorem 9.10. ∎

**Lemma 10.2** (Every order at fixed λ.) Every Cartesian derivative ∂_X^α Ω^β u_1 is in E_2 on the
far region, with constants depending on λ and on the order.

Proof. Write g := g_λ = g0 + r^(−3/2) G_3 + u_1. By Lemma 10.1, u_1 = u − r^(−3/2) G_3 solves

    −½ g^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b u_1 = F_1 := S(u) − ½ (g^{ab} − g0^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b u_1 + ½ □̃ (r^(−3/2) G_3).    (10.3)

*The structure of F_1.* By (2.9), every Lorentzian g satisfies Ric^H(g) = −½ g^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b g +
Q(X; g)(∂g, ∂g), with Q a polynomial of degree two in ∂g whose coefficients are rational in g and smooth in X through
Γ[g0] and its first derivatives, and Ric^H(g0) = Ric(g0) (Section 2.4). Insert the definition
(10.2) of S into (10.3), use ∂_a ∂_b (g0 + u) = ∂_a ∂_b (g0 + r^(−3/2) G_3) + ∂_a ∂_b u_1, and
replace Ric(g0) by −½ g0^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b g0 + Q(X; g0)(∂g0, ∂g0). The terms in g0 alone cancel, and

    F_1 = ½ g^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b (g0 + r^(−3/2) G_3) − Q(X; g)(∂g, ∂g)
        = −Ric^H(g) − ½ g^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b u_1,    (10.4)

an identity in u_1: it holds for every symmetric u_1 that keeps g Lorentzian, not only for the solution. So F_1 contains
no second derivative of u_1. It is a smooth function F_1(X, u_1, ∂u_1), and F_1(X, 0, 0) = −Ric^H(g0 + r^(−3/2) G_3) is
in E_3 with all its derivatives: at u_1 = 0 the terms of S are those of Lemma 10.1 in G_3 and g0, all in
E_3, and the third term of (10.3) is in E_(7/2), because by Lemma 9.9 (c)
□̃(r^(−p) Z) = (3 − 2p) r^(−p−1) ∂_v Z + E_(p+2) for Z(v, x̂) smooth, bounded and vanishing for v ≤ v_start, whose first
term vanishes at p = 3/2.

Along g the partial derivatives of F_1 are as follows. The first is b := ∂F_1/∂(∂u_1). Only Q depends on ∂u_1, so b is
minus the derivative of Q(X; g)(∂g, ∂g) in ∂g. It is linear in ∂g = ∂g0 + ∂u, with coefficients rational in g and smooth
in X, and its part free of ∂g is built from Γ[g0], which is O(r^(−2)) like ∂g0. Since ∂u is in E_(3/2), b is in
E_(3/2). It is moreover of λ-order 0, that is, bounded by C t^(−3/2) with C independent of λ, because ∂u is. By the
two-scale chain rule ∂_a [f] = λ⁻¹ (∂_a v)[∂_θ f] + [∂_a f], the λ⁰ part of ∂(λ[W_TT]) is dv [∂_θ W_TT], in E_(3/2);
that of ∂(λ[χ dv dv]) is dv [∂_θ χ] dv dv, in E_2; with ϕ_1 the phase of the first stage (written so here because φ1
is an angle), that of the term ∂(λ[W_TT(· + ϕ_1)] − λ[W_TT]) of the phase shift is
dv ([∂_θ W_TT(· + ϕ_1)] − [∂_θ W_TT]), at most |ϕ_1| sup |∂_θ² W_TT| and so in E_1 E_(3/2) = E_(5/2), because ϕ_1 is in
L_1 ((9.7)); and every other term of ∂u is O(λ): the mean m1 does not oscillate, each later stage
λ^j[g_j], j ≥ 2, costs at most λ^(j−1), and ∂w is O(λ² t^(−2)) by item 3 of Theorem 3.7, proved as
(P-iii) in Section 9.5, since λ^(K−4) ≤ λ² for K ≥ 6. The second derivative is c := ∂F_1/∂u_1. In the direction U,
the derivative of g^{ab} is −(g⁻¹ U g⁻¹)^{ab}, so

    c U = −½ (g⁻¹ U g⁻¹)^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b (g0 + r^(−3/2) G_3) − (∂_g Q)(X; g)[U](∂g, ∂g).

The second term is O(r^(−2)|U|): it is quadratic in ∂g, or built from Γ[g0] and its derivatives, all O(r^(−2)) or
better. In the first, ∂_a ∂_b g0 = O(r^(−2)), and the chain rule, applied twice, gives

    ∂_a ∂_b (λ[W_TT]) = λ⁻¹ (∂_a v)(∂_b v)[∂_θ² W_TT] + (∂_a v)[∂_b ∂_θ W_TT] + (∂_b v)[∂_a ∂_θ W_TT]
                        + (∂_a ∂_b v)[∂_θ W_TT] + λ[∂_a ∂_b W_TT],

where ∂_b ∂_θ W_TT and ∂_a ∂_b W_TT are slow derivatives, taken at fixed θ before the phase is inserted. Contracting with
(g⁻¹ U g⁻¹)^{ab}, and writing ℓ_λ := g⁻¹ dv, the first term gives −½ λ⁻¹ U(ℓ_λ, ℓ_λ)[∂_θ² W_TT]. Since the Cartesian
components of W_TT are r^(−3/2) times smooth functions of (v, x̂, θ), the slow derivative [∂_b ∂_θ W_TT] is
(∂_b v)[∂_v ∂_θ W_TT] + E_(5/2), and the second and third terms give −U(ℓ_λ, ℓ_λ)[∂_v ∂_θ W_TT] + E_(5/2) U. The fourth
term gives E_(5/2) U: ∂_a ∂_b v = ∂_a ∂_b r is (δ_ij − x̂_i x̂_j)/r in the spatial indices i, j and zero otherwise, and
[∂_θ W_TT] is in E_(3/2). The last term gives E_(3/2) U. Hence

    c = −½ λ⁻¹ (·)(ℓ_λ, ℓ_λ)[∂_θ² W_TT] + E_(3/2),    (10.5)

whose E_(3/2) part contains −(·)(ℓ_λ, ℓ_λ)[∂_v ∂_θ W_TT], from the dependence of the envelope on v, and the E_(5/2)
terms.

*The induction.* We induct on the order. Let |γ| = j + 1, and suppose the lemma holds for the orders up to j. By
Leibniz's rule U := ∂^γ u_1 solves

    −½ g^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b U = f_γ := b·∂U + c U + R_γ
                         + ½ Σ_{γ' ≤ γ, |γ'| = 1} C(γ, γ') (∂^{γ'} g^{ab}) ∂^{γ−γ'} ∂_a ∂_b u_1,

with C(γ, γ') := γ!/(γ'! (γ − γ')!), where

    R_γ := ∂^γ F_1 − b·∂U − c U + ½ Σ_{γ' ≤ γ, |γ'| ≥ 2} C(γ, γ') (∂^{γ'} g^{ab}) ∂^{γ−γ'} ∂_a ∂_b u_1

contains derivatives of u_1 of order at most j + 1 only. Indeed, by the chain rule the only term of ∂^γ[F_1(X, u_1,
∂u_1)] that contains a derivative of u_1 of order j + 2 is b·∂^γ ∂u_1 = b·∂U: every other term distributes the |γ|
derivatives over X or over at least two factors. The terms of the second sum carry ∂^{γ−γ'} ∂² u_1, of order at most
j + 1. In f_γ, the term b·∂U is of the order this step estimates and is not known; the terms with |γ'| = 1 are of the
form (∂g) ∂U' with ∂g in E_(3/2) and U' in the same family {∂^δ u_1 : |δ| = j + 1}; and c U is one order lower. They
enter through f_γ into the energy inequality (9.4) of Lemma 9.6, before Gronwall's lemma, not
through its kernel. Since U vanishes on {v = v_start}, the Poincaré inequality Lemma 9.3 (b) gives
‖U‖ ≤ C ‖∂U‖, so

    ‖b·∂U‖ ≤ C t^(−3/2) ‖∂U‖,       ‖c U‖ ≤ C λ⁻¹ t^(−3/2) ‖U‖ ≤ C λ⁻¹ t^(−3/2) ‖∂U‖,

and ‖f_γ‖ ≤ C (1 + λ⁻¹) t^(−3/2) Σ_{|δ| = j + 1} ‖∂ ∂^δ u_1‖ + ‖R_γ‖. Summed over the family, Gronwall's lemma then
costs the factor exp(∫ C (1 + λ⁻¹) t^(−3/2) dt). Over the far region t ≥ λ^(−2) this integral is at most 2 C (1 + λ⁻¹)
λ = 2 C (1 + λ), so the factor is at most e^(2C(1 + λ)), free of λ. (With c U taken as a forcing term, through the
energies of the lower steps, the step also closes at fixed λ, at the cost of one factor λ⁻¹ per order.)

R_γ is the sum of ∂_X^γ F_1(X, 0, 0), the forcing free of u_1, which is in E_3, and of products of a derivative of g or
of the coefficients of F_1, of order at most j + 1, with derivatives of u_1 of order at most j + 1. We estimate each
product in L²(Σ̂_τ ∩ P⁺), with the factor of higher order in L² (the energies of the lower steps, at most C t^(−1/2)) and
the others in the supremum norm (in E_2 by the induction hypothesis, through the Sobolev inequality with rotations
Lemma 9.3 (a) for the orders it costs, and by the far-region bound (9.9) for u_1^n, below, at the
lowest orders). The term ∂_X^γ F_1(X, 0, 0), in E_3, has L² norm at most C t^(−3/2) on Σ̂_τ ∩ P⁺, whose volume is at most
C t³; each product has L² norm at most C t^(−2), a coefficient in E_(3/2) or a second factor of u_1 in E_2 times the L²
factor. So ‖R_γ‖ ≤ C(λ, j) t^(−3/2).

*The approximating solutions.* We do not apply the energy inequality on the region P⁺ ∩ {τ' ≤ τ}: that
region is unbounded toward past null infinity (Lemma 9.1 (e)), and the flux of ∂^γ u_1 through infinity
there is known to vanish only at the orders that Theorem 3.7 controls. We apply it instead to each
approximating solution g_n of Proposition 9.11. The metric g_n equals g0 on {v ≤ v_start} and solves the same
equations, so u_1^n := g_n − g0 − r^(−3/2) G_3 has the structure above:
Lemma 10.1 applies to it verbatim, with the far-region bound on g_n through the Sobolev inequality in
place of Theorem 3.7 at the lowest orders, uniformly in n. We use the region P ∩ {τ_n ≤ τ' ≤ τ}, where
the energy identity of the far-region bound itself holds. On Σ̂_(τ_n) the data of U_n := ∂^γ u_1^n are explicit:
w_n = g_n − g_app vanishes there with its first derivatives, its higher derivatives are those of the residual
Ric^H(g_app) of the approximant through the equation, and g_app − g0 − r^(−3/2) G_3 is explicit with all its
derivatives (Theorem 9.10, (9.7)). So ‖∂U_n(τ_n)‖ ≤ C(λ, j) t_n^(−1/2), with t_n ≥ t.

Let f_γ^n, b^n, c^n and R_γ^n be f_γ, b, c and R_γ with g_n and u_1^n in place of g_λ and u_1. Since
Lemma 10.1 applies to u_1^n verbatim, b^n and c^n obey the bounds on b and c above with the same constants.
Moreover ‖R_γ^n‖ ≤ C(λ, j) t^(−3/2) uniformly in n: ∂_X^γ F_1(X, 0, 0) does not depend on n, and every other factor of
R_γ^n is bounded by the induction hypothesis for u_1^n, which is uniform in n, with the far-region bound at the lowest
orders. The energy inequality (9.4) for U_n with forcing f_γ^n, summed over the family, and Gronwall's
lemma give

    Σ_{|γ| = j + 1} ‖∂U_n(τ)‖ ≤ C e^(2C(1 + λ)) Σ_{|γ| = j + 1} ( ‖∂U_n(τ_n)‖ + ∫_{τ_n}^{τ} ‖R_γ^n‖ dτ' ).

Since ‖∂U_n(τ_n)‖ ≤ C(λ, j) t_n^(−1/2) ≤ C(λ, j) t^(−1/2) and ∫_{τ_n}^{τ} t'^(−3/2) dτ' ≤ 2 t^(−1/2), we obtain
‖∂U_n(τ)‖ ≤ C(λ, j) t^(−1/2) at every order, uniformly in n.

*Supremum norm against L².* The bookkeeping closes at every order |γ|: the factor taken in the supremum norm has order at
most ⌊(|γ| + 2)/2⌋, the class E_2 is in hand pointwise to the order max(4, |γ| − 3) (the far-region bound with the
Sobolev inequality, for u_1^n, at the lowest orders, and the Sobolev inequality applied to the energies of the lower
steps for the rest, at the cost of three orders), and ⌊(|γ| + 2)/2⌋ ≤ max(4, |γ| − 3) for every |γ| ≥ 1. The Sobolev
inequality turns the energies of the next three orders into |∂^γ u_1^n| ≤ C(λ, j) t^(−3/2) t^(−1/2) = C(λ, j) t^(−2),
uniformly in n. Rotations Ω^β among the derivatives are treated the same way, with the rotation energies in the
Sobolev inequality and the commutator [Ω, g_n^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b] absorbed as in item (iii) of the proof of
Proposition 9.11. For a pure rotation γ the Leibniz term of R_γ with |γ'| = |γ| has the L² factor
‖Ω^γ u_1^n‖, which the energies of the lower steps bound only by C t^(1/2), since |Ω f| ≤ 2 r |∂f|; that product is then
C t^(−3/2), so ‖R_γ‖ ≤ C(λ, j) t^(−3/2) still holds; alternatively the term can enter the Gronwall family through the
Poincaré inequality, with kernel t^(−2). The remark on c U taken as a forcing term concerns Cartesian γ.

*The limit.* The bounds pass to the limit. By the proof of Theorem 3.7 (Section 9.5), g_n → g_λ
with k − 5 derivatives on compact sets, and the higher derivatives of u_1^n are bounded uniformly in n on each compact
set. By the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem a subsequence converges in every C^j, its limit is
∂^γ u_1, and the bound is inherited: ∂^γ u_1 is in E_2. ∎

### 10.3 The half-order gain and the expansion in r^(−1/2)

**Lemma 10.3** (One half-order.) Let q ∈ {3, 7/2, 4, …}, and let ũ be a symmetric tensor on the far
region, vanishing for v ≤ v_start, with every Cartesian derivative ∂_X^α Ω^β ũ in E_(q−1), solving
