    −½ g_λ^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b ũ = r^(−q) S_q + S̃,       S̃ ∈ E_(q+1/2) with all derivatives,    (10.6)

with S_q(v, x̂) smooth, bounded with all derivatives and vanishing for v ≤ v_start. Put
Y_q(v, x̂) := (2/(2q − 5)) ∫_{v_start}^{v} S_q dv'. Then ũ = r^(1−q) Y_q + ǔ with every Cartesian derivative of ǔ in
E_(q−1/2). If moreover, for some m ≥ 1 and every j < m,

    (H_m)    ℓ^j S̃ ∈ E_(q+1/2+j)   and   ℓ^j (g_λ − g0) ∈ E_(3/2+j),   each with all derivatives,

then ℓ^m ǔ is in E_(q−1/2+m) with all derivatives.

Proof. By Lemma 9.9 (c), −½ □̃(r^(1−q) Y_q) = −½ (3 − 2(q − 1)) r^(−q) ∂_v Y_q + E_(q+1) =
r^(−q) S_q + E_(q+1), and (g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹) ∂²(r^(1−q) Y_q) is in E_(3/2) E_(q−1) = E_(q+1/2). So
ǔ := ũ − r^(1−q) Y_q solves −½ g_λ^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b ǔ = S′ with S′ in E_(q+1/2) with all derivatives, vanishes for
v ≤ v_start, and has every derivative in E_(q−1).

*Energy.* The L² norm of an element of E_p on Σ̂_τ ∩ P⁺ is at most C t^(3/2 − p), the volume being at most C t³. Apply
Lemma 9.6 with g̃ = g_λ, which has the margin of Lemma 9.1 (f) on P by Theorem 3.7
and satisfies ‖∂g_λ‖_∞ ≤ C t^(−3/2) on P⁺, an integrable kernel, and with forcing S′, from τ1 → −∞. Since
‖∂ǔ(τ1)‖ ≤ C t1^(3/2 − (q−1)) → 0 because q > 5/2, and ‖S′(τ')‖ ≤ C t'^(3/2 − q − 1/2) = C t'^(1−q), we get
‖∂ǔ(τ)‖ ≤ C ∫_{−∞}^{τ} t'^(1−q) dτ' = C t^(2−q)/(q − 2). Commuting with ∂_X and Ω preserves the form of the equation.
[∂_X, g_λ^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b] = (∂_X g_λ^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b with ∂_X g_λ^{ab} in E_(3/2) produces a forcing in E_(q+1/2), by the
hypothesis on ǔ (its second derivatives are in E_(q−1)), within the bound t^(1−q) of S′. And [Ω, □̃] = 0: the rotations
are linear maps of R⁴ that preserve g0, and for such a map R, □̃(f ∘ R) = (□̃ f) ∘ R. So Ω commutes with
g_λ^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b = □̃ + (g_λ^{ab} − g0^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b up to (Ω(g_λ^{ab} − g0^{ab})) ∂_a ∂_b and
(g_λ^{ab} − g0^{ab}) [Ω, ∂_a ∂_b], where [Ω, ∂_a ∂_b] is a combination of second derivatives with constant
coefficients; since g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ is in E_(3/2) with all its derivatives, these too are forcings in E_(q+1/2), as for
∂_X. So every commuted energy is at most C t^(2−q). *Pointwise.* The Sobolev inequality with rotations and the
Poincaré inequality (ǔ = 0 on {v = v_start}), Lemma 9.3 (a) and (b),
give |∂_X^α Ω^β ǔ| ≤ C t^(−3/2) t^(2−q) = C t^(1/2 − q). That is E_(q−1/2), since t and r are comparable on P⁺.

*The ℓ-gain.* In the coordinates (v, r, x̂) the operator □̃ is (9.6) (Lemma 9.9 (b)),
with Δ̊ the Laplacian of the unit S³. With ψ := ℓǔ (ℓ acting on Cartesian components) the equation of ǔ becomes

    2 ∂_v ψ + (1 − μ/r²) ℓ ψ + (3/r) ψ = −2 S′ − (3/r) ∂_v ǔ − r^(−2) Δ̊ ǔ − (g_λ^{ab} − g0^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b ǔ =: f,
    (10.7)

with f in E_(q+1/2): its terms are in E_(q+1/2), E_(q+1/2), E_(q+3/2) and E_(3/2) E_(q−1/2). The operator
L₊ := 2 ∂_v + (1 − μ/r²) ℓ is the outgoing null direction of g0: in (v, r), L₊ = 2 ∂_v + (1 − μ/r²) ∂_r, while the
covariant components of g0 are g0_vv = −(1 − μ/r²), g0_vr = 1 and g0_rr = 0 ((2.4)), so
g0(L₊, L₊) = −4 (1 − μ/r²) + 4 (1 − μ/r²) = 0. So (10.7) is a transport along the outgoing
generators. Along one of them, parametrised by σ, dv/dσ = 2 and
dr/dσ = 1 − μ/r² ∈ (0, 1]. From a point (v, r) the generator therefore reaches {v = v_start}, where ψ = 0, after a
parameter length (v − v_start)/2 ≤ d1/2 (Lemma 9.1 (d)), at a radius r' ∈ [r − d1/2, r]. Integrating
(L₊ + 3/r) ψ = f along it gives |ψ(v, r)| ≤ e^(3 d1/(2 r')) (d1/2) sup |f| ≤ C r^(−q−1/2), the supremum taken over the
segment, which lies in the far region once r is large.

Derivatives commute through (10.7) up to terms of the same kind. Ω commutes with L₊ and with 3/r, since
it annihilates v, r and μ(v); so Ω^b ψ solves (10.7) with the forcing Ω^b f. ∂_v commutes up to [∂_v,
L₊] = −(μ'/r²) ℓ, and ℓψ is read off (10.7) itself, (1 − μ/r²) ℓψ = f − 2 ∂_v ψ − (3/r) ψ. So ∂_v^a Ω^b
ψ solves (10.7) with a term of order zero, O(r^(−2)) times ∂_v^a Ω^b ψ, moved to the left (over a
parameter length at most d1/2 it changes the integrating factor by a bounded factor), and a forcing in E_(q+1/2) by the
lower a. The ℓ-components of the derivatives of ψ are then read off (10.7) in the same way: ℓ^c ∂_v^a
Ω^b ψ is in E_(q+1/2) by induction on c, and every Cartesian derivative is a combination of ℓ, ∂_v and r⁻¹ Ω with
coefficients bounded with all their derivatives. So ℓǔ is in E_(q+1/2) with all derivatives. This is the case m = 1,
which needs nothing of (H_m), since f contains no ℓ-derivative of S′ or of g_λ.

For m ≥ 2, under (H_m), the equation of ℓ^m ǔ = ℓ^(m−1) ψ is (10.7) commuted m − 1 times with ℓ. Its
forcing is ℓ^(m−1) f plus the commutators [ℓ, L₊] = (2μ/r³) ℓ, [ℓ, 3/r] = −3/r² and
[ℓ, (g_λ^{ab} − g0^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b] = (ℓ (g_λ − g0)^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b applied to the lower ℓ^j ǔ, with one exception:
[ℓ^(m−1), L₊] ψ = 2 (m − 1)(μ/r³) ℓ^m ǔ plus terms in ℓ^j ǔ with j < m contains the unknown itself, not a lower term.
It is moved to the left, and the transport becomes (L₊ + 3/r + 2 (m − 1) μ/r³) ℓ^(m−1) ψ = (the rest), whose O(r^(−3))
coefficient changes the integrating factor by a bounded factor. Each term of ℓ^(m−1) f is in E_(q+1/2+m−1): ℓ^j S′ by
(H_m) (S′ is S̃ plus (g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹) ∂²(r^(1−q) Y_q) and □̃(r^(1−q) Y_q) − r^(−q) S_q, whose ℓ-derivatives gain by
(H_m) and explicitly), ℓ^j of (3/r) ∂_v ǔ and of r^(−2) Δ̊ ǔ by the gains already established for j < m, and
(ℓ^j (g_λ − g0)^{ab}) ∂² ℓ^(m−1−j) ǔ by (H_m) with those gains, E_(3/2+j) E_(q−1/2+m−1−j) = E_(q+m). The commutator terms
are of the same kind. So the transport gives ℓ^m ǔ in E_(q−1/2+m), and derivatives commute as before. ∎

**Proposition 10.4** (The expansion in r^(−1/2).) For every J ≥ 3 there are smooth tensors G_k(v, x̂),
k = 3, …, J, bounded with all derivatives, vanishing for v ≤ v_start and invariant under T² × Z2 × Z2, with G_3 as in
(10.1), such that on the far region

    u = Σ_{k=3}^{J} r^(−k/2) G_k + u_J,     ∂_X^α Ω^β ℓ^m u_J ∈ E_((J+1)/2 + m) for all α, β, m.    (10.8)

The G_k are determined inductively: G_k = (2/(k − 3)) ∫_{v_start}^{v} S_(k/2+1) dv' for k ≥ 4 (so G_4 = 2 ∫ S_3), where
r^(−q) S_q is the leading term of the forcing once the terms below it are known.

Proof. We induct on J with Lemma 10.3. For J = 3, u_3 := u_1 is in E_2 with all derivatives by
Lemma 10.2, and by Lemma 10.1 it solves
−½ g_λ^{ab} ∂_a ∂_b u_3 = S(u) − ½ (g_λ^{ab} − g0^{ab}) ∂_a ∂_b u_3 + ½ □̃(r^(−3/2) G_3) =: F_1. The second term is in
E_(7/2) (E_(3/2) E_2), the third in E_(7/2) by Lemma 9.9 (c), and S(u) is in E_3 with a leading term
r^(−3) determined by G_3 alone: −(3μ'/2) dv dv from Ric(g0), plus the terms of (10.2) quadratic in
∂(r^(−3/2) G_3) or of the form (r^(−3/2) G_3) ∂²(g0 + r^(−3/2) G_3), since every term containing u_3 is in E_(7/2)
(E_(3/2) E_2, or Γ[g0] times E_2). So (10.6) holds at q = 3, and Lemma 10.3 gives
u = r^(−3/2) G_3 + r^(−2) G_4 + u_4 with every derivative of u_4 in E_(5/2).

*The ℓ-gains at J = 3, by induction on m.* The case m = 1 needs no hypothesis: ℓu_4 is in E_3, hence
ℓu_1 = ℓ(r^(−2) G_4) + ℓu_4 is in E_3 and ℓ(g_λ − g0) = ℓ(r^(−3/2) G_3) + ℓu_1 is in E_(5/2), with all derivatives.
Suppose ℓ^j u_4 is in E_(5/2+j) for j < m. Then ℓ^j (g_λ − g0) is in E_(3/2+j) for j < m, and ℓ^j S̃ is in E_(7/2+j):
S̃ = F_1 − r^(−3) S_3 is a polynomial in g0, g_λ⁻¹, u, ∂u and ∂²u each of whose terms either is explicit (the terms in
G_3 and g0, whose ℓ-derivatives gain an order each because r^(−k) and the profiles do) or contains u_1 or a derivative
of it, on which ℓ^j gains j orders by the hypothesis, the other factors keeping their classes. So (H_m) holds, and
Lemma 10.3 gives ℓ^m u_4 in E_(5/2+m): (10.8) at J = 4.

*Stage J ≥ 4.* The remainder u_J has every ℓ-gain. So the forcing of u_J, a polynomial in (u, ∂u, ∂²u) with
coefficients smooth in (X, g) whose arguments are expanded to the previous order with remainders in E_((J+1)/2), has
the form r^(−q) S_q + S̃ with q = (J + 3)/2 and S̃ satisfying (H_m) for every m: every product with a remainder factor is
in E_(3/2 + (J+1)/2) = E_(q+1/2) or better and gains under ℓ. So the coefficient of r^(−q) is a polynomial in the G_k,
k ≤ J, and their derivatives, and Lemma 10.3 applies at every m. The invariance and the vanishing for
v ≤ v_start are inherited by the integrals from v_start. ∎

**Remark 10.5** The coefficients from G_4 on depend on λ, through the phase v/λ and the powers of λ of the
profiles, and Proposition 10.4 claims nothing uniform in λ. It is an asymptotic statement at past null infinity
at each fixed λ, which is all the mass law needs.

### 10.4 Bondi coordinates at past null infinity

**Lemma 10.6** (The ℓ-components.) G_3(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr G_3 = 0. Hence u(ℓ, ·) is in E_2, the trace tr_S u
on the spheres S_(v,r) is in E_2, g_λ^{vv} = −u(ℓ, ℓ) + E_3 is in E_2, and (g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹)(dv, ·) = −g0⁻¹ u(ℓ, ·) + E_3
is in E_2.

Proof. By Lemma 2.9 (b) the wave λW_TT of (2.11) has no dv or dr component and is traceless on the spheres,
so G_3(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr G_3 = tr_S G_3 = 0; the rest of u is u_1, in E_2. Then
g⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ u g0⁻¹ + O(u²) and g0⁻¹ dv = ℓ. ∎

We write the coordinate components of the G_k in the basis of (v, r, ϑ) as scalar coefficients,

    u_rr = Σ_k ς^k C_k,   u_vr = Σ_k ς^k B_k,   u_vv = Σ_k ς^k A_k,   u_(rϑ) = r Σ_k ς^k E_k,   u_(vϑ) = r Σ_k ς^k D_k,
    u_(ϑϑ) = r² Σ_k ς^k F_k,   u_(φ1φ1) = r² cos²ϑ Σ_k ς^k G_k,   u_(φ2φ2) = r² sin²ϑ Σ_k ς^k H_k,    (10.9)

with ς := r^(−1/2) and one power of r for each angular index, the classes being of orthonormal components. These
A_k, …, H_k are scalar functions of (v, ϑ), the subscript being the power of ς; they are not the classes E_p, the
tensors G_k of (10.8) or the free data F, G. By Lemma 10.6, A_3 = B_3 = C_3 = D_3 = E_3 = 0 and
F_3 + G_3 + H_3 = 0, and by (2.11), F_3 = −2(p1 + p2), G_3 = 2p1 and H_3 = 2p2. The other components of u
vanish, by the reflections φ1 ↦ −φ1 and φ2 ↦ −φ2.

**Proposition 10.7** (The Bondi chart.) There is T_M(λ) such that on the far region P ∩ {t ≥ T_M} the
functions

    v_B := v + ů,      ϑ_B := ϑ + ν,      r_B := r (1 + ρ)

exist with the following properties. (i) g_λ⁻¹(dv_B, dv_B) = 0, and ů → 0 along every generator of g0 as r → ∞.
(ii) g_λ⁻¹(dv_B, dϑ_B) = 0, and ν → 0 likewise. (iii) r_B is the areal radius: r_B⁶ cos²ϑ_B sin²ϑ_B is the determinant
of the metric induced on {v_B, r_B = const} in the coordinates (ϑ_B, φ1, φ2). (iv) They are invariant under
T² × Z2 × Z2 and equal (v, ϑ, r) for v ≤ v_start. With u expanded to order J by (10.8), they have
expansions in ς with coefficients smooth in (v, ϑ) and vanishing for v ≤ v_start,

    ů = Σ_{k=2}^{J−2} ς^k ů_k + E_((J−1)/2),     ν = Σ_{k=4}^{J−2} ς^k ν_k + E_((J−1)/2),
    ρ = Σ_{k=4}^{J−2} ς^k ρ_k + E_((J−1)/2),    (10.10)

whose first coefficients are

    ů_2 = −C_4/2,   ů_3 = −C_5/3,   ů_4 = −C_6/4 + C_4 ∂_v C_4/8,   ν_4 = −E_4/2 − ∂_ϑ C_4/4,
    ρ_4 = (F_4 + G_4 + H_4)/6 − (1/3) div(ν_4),       div f := (sin ϑ cos ϑ)⁻¹ ∂_ϑ (f sin ϑ cos ϑ),    (10.11)

and whose remainders gain an order under ℓ. In the chart (v_B, r_B, ϑ_B, φ1, φ2) the metric has the Bondi form
(3.3), its functions being given by the inverse components g^{v_B r_B} = e^(−2β), g^{r_B r_B} = e^(−2β) W,
g^{r_B ϑ_B} = e^(−2β) U, g^{ϑ_B ϑ_B} = 1/(r_B² S) with S := e^(−2(P1+P2)), g^{φ1 φ1} = 1/(r_B² cos²ϑ_B e^(2P1)) and
g^{φ2 φ2} = 1/(r_B² sin²ϑ_B e^(2P2)). The functions β, W, U, P1, P2 have expansions in ς_B := r_B^(−1/2) with
coefficients smooth in (v_B, ϑ_B), equal to those of g0 for v_B ≤ v_start (zero there, but for W − 1 = −μ0 ς_B⁴), to
order ς_B^(J−2), with remainders o(ς_B^(J−2)) that stay o(ς_B^(J−2)) under every (v_B, ϑ_B)-derivative and gain an
order under each r_B-derivative. Their first coefficients are

    e^(2P1) = 1 + 2 p1 ς_B³ + O(ς_B⁴),    e^(2P2) = 1 + 2 p2 ς_B³ + O(ς_B⁴),
    e^(−2β) = 1 − (∂_v C_4/2) ς_B² − (∂_v C_5/3) ς_B³ + O(ς_B⁴),    (10.12)

and W − 1 = O(ς_B²), U = O(ς_B⁴).

Proof. *(i) The null coordinate.* Write L := g_λ⁻¹ dv = ℓ + ε with ε := (g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹)(dv, ·), in E_2 by
Lemma 10.6. Since g_λ⁻¹(dv + dů, dv + dů) = g_λ^{vv} + 2 L(dů) + g_λ⁻¹(dů, dů), condition (i) is the eikonal
equation

    2 ℓ ů = −g_λ^{vv} − 2 ε(dů) − g_λ⁻¹(dů, dů) =: N[ů].    (10.13)

We build v_B by characteristics, not by iterating (10.13): an iteration in a norm of ů and ℓů loses a
derivative at each step through the term ε(dů). In g0 the generators of {v = v0} are the affinely parametrised null
geodesics y0(r) = (v0, r, x̂0), with ℓ = ∂_r their tangent and Γ[g0]^a_rr = 0. For each (v0, x̂0) let y be the null
geodesic of g_λ asymptotic to y0: y(r) = (v0 + ζ(r), r, x̂0 + ξ(r)), parametrised by r, solving
d²y^a/dr² + Γ[g_λ]^a_bc y'^b y'^c = κ_y y'^a with κ_y fixed by the r-component (y^r = r), and with ζ, ζ', ξ, ξ' → 0 as
r → ∞. Writing y' = ∂_r + η, the system is

    η' = −(Γ[g_λ] − Γ[g0])^a_rr − 2 Γ[g_λ]^a_rb η^b − Γ^a_bc η^b η^c + κ_y y'^a,

a Volterra system from r = ∞. Its forcing (Γ[g_λ] − Γ[g0])^v_rr = ½ g^{vd}(2 ∂_r u_(dr) − ∂_d u_rr) is in E_3 by
Lemma 10.6 and the ℓ-gain of u (g^{vr} = 1 + E_(3/2) multiplies ∂_r u_rr, in E_3; g^{vv}, in E_2, multiplies
E_2; and g^{vϑ} = −r⁻¹ u(ℓ, e_ϑ) + E_4, in E_3, multiplies 2 ∂_r u_(ϑr) − ∂_ϑ u_rr, in E_2). Its angular forcing is in
E_4 (g^{ϑϑ} = r^(−2)(1 + E_(3/2)) times ∂_r u_(ϑr) = r ∂_r u(e_ϑ, ℓ) + u(e_ϑ, ℓ), in E_2). Its linear part
−2 Γ[g0]^a_rb η^b vanishes for a = v (Γ[g0]^v_rb = 0 in the ingoing chart) and is −(2/r) ξ' for a = ϑ
(Γ[g0]^ϑ_rϑ = 1/r). This is not an integrable perturbation but the unperturbed operator of the angular equation,
ξ'' + (2/r) ξ' = E_4, which the integrating factor r² solves with ξ' in E_3 and ξ in E_2. The remaining coefficients are
Lipschitz in (ζ, ξ, ζ', ξ') in the weighted norms below, with constants integrable in r: ∂(Γ[g_λ] − Γ[g0]) is in
E_(3/2), and the terms quadratic in η, whose largest coefficient is Γ[g0]^v_ϑϑ = −r, are O(r^(−2)) times the norm.
κ_y = Γ^r_bc y'^b y'^c is in E_2 and multiplies η. So for r ≥ T_M the Picard iteration converges in the weighted
supremum norm r² |ζ'| + r |ζ| + r³ |ξ'| + r² |ξ| (a contraction for an ordinary differential equation, so no derivative
is lost). The solution depends smoothly on
(v0, x̂0), with derivatives of the same decay (the variational equations have the same structure), it is invariant, and
it is y0 for v0 ≤ v_start (there g_λ = g0 along the whole generator).

Each generator stays in P outward, so the system is posed where g_λ is defined. With h_P(τ) = κ_P t^(−1/4) the
function of (9.1), along y, d/dr (v + h_P(τ)) = ζ'(1 + h_P′) − h_P′, with τ = v − r (so dτ/dr = ζ' − 1)
and h_P′ = dh_P/dτ = h_P/(4t) = (κ_P/4) t^(−5/4) > 0. Moreover |ζ'| ≤ C r^(−2) < h_P′/2 and h_P′ < 1 once T_M is
large, t and r being comparable on P⁺. So v + h_P(τ) decreases outward along each generator while t increases, and the
ray of a generator from a point of P ∩ {t ≥ T_M} out to past null infinity lies in P ∩ {t ≥ T_M} and never meets the
outer boundary {v + h_P(τ) = V_P}. (To solve for every (v0, x̂0) at once, continue g_λ − g0 across that boundary by a
Seeley extension in v + h_P(τ), which keeps every class E_p; by this monotonicity neither the generator through a point
of P ∩ {t ≥ T_M} nor Φ⁻¹ there depends on the continuation, so Φ⁻¹, below, is defined on all of P ∩ {t ≥ T_M}.)

The map Φ: (v0, r, x̂0) ↦ y(r) is then a C¹-small perturbation of the identity for r ≥ T_M, a diffeomorphism onto a
neighbourhood of past null infinity, and N_(v0) := Φ({v0} × [T_M, ∞) × S³) is a null hypersurface. Indeed, along each y,
d/dr g_λ(y', y') = 2 κ_y g_λ(y', y'), so g_λ(y', y') e^(−2∫κ_y) is constant and equal to its limit g0(ℓ, ℓ) = 0 at
infinity (y is null). And for each Jacobi field X = ∂_(x̂0) y of the congruence, tangent to N_(v0) as y' is, d/dr
g_λ(y', X) = κ_y g_λ(y', X) + g_λ(y', ∇_X y') = κ_y g_λ(y', X) + ½ X g_λ(y', y') = κ_y g_λ(y', X), so g_λ(y', X)
e^(−∫κ_y) is constant along y and equal to its limit at infinity, which is 0: g_λ(y', X) = ∂_(x̂0) ζ + r² ξ' (1 +
∂_(x̂0) ξ) + r u(ℓ, e_ϑ) + smaller terms, with ∂_(x̂0) ζ, r² ξ' and r u(ℓ, e_ϑ) in E_1. (The transverse field ∂_(v0) y
is not needed, and it is not orthogonal to y': g0(ℓ, ∂_v) = 1.) Hence y' is normal to N_(v0), which is null. Put v_B :=
v0 ∘ Φ⁻¹, so that g_λ⁻¹(dv_B, dv_B) = 0, and ů := v_B − v = −ζ ∘ Φ⁻¹. Then ů is in E_1, with ℓů in E_2 (ℓů = −ζ' up to
Jacobian corrections in E_2) and all derivatives; it vanishes for v ≤ v_start and is invariant.

*Expansion of ů.* v_B satisfies (10.13) exactly, so ů = −½ ∫_r^∞ N[ů] dr' along the generators of g0. Insert
(10.8). The integrals of the powers of ς are powers of ς, the nonlinear terms at order ς^(k+2) involve
only ů_j with j < k, and the remainder of ů is the integral along the generator of a remainder, with ℓ of it the
integrand: this gives (10.10) for ů. Since ∂_r ς^k = −(k/2) ς^(k+2), the ς^(k+2) coefficient of the left side
2∂_r ů is −k ů_k, so the ς^(k+2) coefficient of the equation is −k ů_k plus known terms. The first ones are found as
follows. In the coordinates (v, r, ϑ), ℓ = ∂_r, g0^{vv} = 0, g0^{vr} = 1, g0^{rr} = 1 − μ/r² and g0^{ϑϑ} = r^(−2).
Expanding g⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ u g0⁻¹ + g0⁻¹ u g0⁻¹ u g0⁻¹ − …, the term quadratic in u of g^{vv} is
g0⁻¹(u(ℓ, ·), u(ℓ, ·)), built from u_rr, u_rv = O(ς⁴) and r⁻¹ u_(rϑ) = O(ς⁴), so it is O(ς⁸), and
−g_λ^{vv} = C_4 ς⁴ + C_5 ς⁵ + C_6 ς⁶ + O(ς⁷). The components of ε are ε^v = −u_rr, ε^r = −u_rv − (1 − μ/r²) u_rr and
ε^ϑ = −r^(−2) u_(rϑ), up to terms quadratic in u; with ů = O(ς²), ∂_v ů = O(ς²) and ∂_r ů = O(ς⁴),
2 ε(dů) = −2 C_4 ∂_v ů_2 ς⁶ + O(ς⁷), and g_λ⁻¹(dů, dů) = 2 ∂_v ů ∂_r ů + O(ς⁸) = −2 ů_2 ∂_v ů_2 ς⁶ + O(ς⁷). So

    N[ů] = C_4 ς⁴ + C_5 ς⁵ + (C_6 + 2 C_4 ∂_v ů_2 + 2 ů_2 ∂_v ů_2) ς⁶ + O(ς⁷),

and comparing with −Σ_k k ů_k ς^(k+2): ů_1 = 0, −2 ů_2 = C_4, −3 ů_3 = C_5, and
−4 ů_4 = C_6 + 2 C_4 ∂_v ů_2 + 2 ů_2 ∂_v ů_2 = C_6 − C_4 ∂_v C_4 + ½ C_4 ∂_v C_4 = C_6 − ½ C_4 ∂_v C_4. These are the
values in (10.11).

*(ii) The angular coordinate.* ϑ_B := x̂0 ∘ Φ⁻¹ (the angle of the generator of g0 to which y is asymptotic) is constant
along the generators of N_(v0), whose tangent is L_B := g_λ⁻¹ dv_B up to a factor (y' is the null normal of N_(v0)). So
L_B ϑ_B = 0, which is (ii), and ν = ϑ_B − ϑ = −ξ ∘ Φ⁻¹ is in E_2 with ℓν in E_3. With L_B = ℓ + ε + g_λ⁻¹ dů, the
transport L_B ϑ_B = 0 reads

    2 ℓ ν = −2 ε(dϑ) − 2 g_λ⁻¹(dů, dϑ) − 2 (ε + g_λ⁻¹ dů)(dν),

where ε(dϑ) = −r^(−2) u(∂_ϑ, ℓ) + E_4 = −r⁻¹ u(e_ϑ, ℓ) + E_4 is in E_3 (e_ϑ := r⁻¹ ∂_ϑ) and
g_λ⁻¹(dů, dϑ) = r^(−2) ∂_ϑ ů + E_4 is in E_3. So ν expands as in (10.10), the ς^(k+2) coefficient of the
equation being −k ν_k plus known terms. In terms of the coefficients, −2 ε(dϑ) = 2 Σ_k E_k ς^(k+2) + O(ς⁸),
−2 g_λ⁻¹(dů, dϑ) = −2 ∂_ϑ ů_2 ς⁶ + O(ς⁷), and the last term is O(ς⁸), since ν = O(ς⁴), ε = O(ς⁴) and dů = O(ς²). As
E_k = 0 for k ≤ 3 and ů_1 = 0, the coefficients ν_1, ν_2, ν_3 vanish, and at ς⁶, −4 ν_4 = 2 E_4 − 2 ∂_ϑ ů_2 =
2 E_4 + ∂_ϑ C_4: the value in (10.11).

*(iii) The areal radius.* Let J0 be the Jacobian of (v, r, ϑ) ↦ (v_B, r_B, ϑ_B). In a chart with
g^{v_B v_B} = g^{v_B ϑ_B} = 0 the covariant metric has g_(r_B r_B) = g_(r_B ϑ_B) = 0, so it has the form
(3.3) once r_B is areal, and its inverse determinant is −e^(−4β)/(r_B⁶ cos²ϑ_B sin²ϑ_B) with
e^(−2β) = g^{v_B r_B}; the inverse determinant transforms with (det J0)². So the areal condition is the equation

    r_B⁶ cos²ϑ_B sin²ϑ_B det(g_λ⁻¹) (det J0)² + (g^{v_B r_B})² = 0,    (10.14)

whose ς^k coefficient is 6 ρ_k plus known terms. The factor ∂_r r_B = 1 + ρ + r ∂_r ρ of (det J0)² cancels against
the same factor of (g^{v_B r_B})² = (g_λ⁻¹(dv_B, dr_B))², and exactly, not only at this order. With
g^{v_B v_B} = g^{v_B ϑ_B} = 0 the inverse determinant in the chart is −(g^{v_B r_B})²/det q, q the metric induced on
{v_B, r_B = const} in (ϑ_B, φ1, φ2), so (10.14) is (g^{v_B r_B})² (1 − r_B⁶ cos²ϑ_B sin²ϑ_B/det q) = 0. And q,
induced on a cross-section of the null hypersurface {v_B = const} in coordinates constant along its generators, has no
component along them, so it depends on the points of the cross-section and not on its tilt: no derivative of ρ enters,
and r_B⁶ contributes 6 ρ_k (the leading determinant being 1). The condition is therefore algebraic in ρ and solvable for
every k ≥ 1.

The first coefficients follow. Since q annihilates the generators, q(∂_(ϑ_B), ∂_(ϑ_B)) = g_λ(X, X) for any vector X
tangent to N_(v0) with dϑ_B(X) = 1 and dφ_i(X) = 0; take X at fixed r. From d(v + ů)(X) = 0 and dϑ_B(X) = 1,
X = (1 − ∂_ϑ ν + O(ς⁶)) ∂_ϑ − (∂_ϑ ů + O(ς⁴)) ∂_v. Since g_(vϑ) = r O(ς⁴) and g_vv = O(1), the terms of g_λ(X, X)
containing ∂_v are r² O(ς⁸), and g_λ(X, X) = r² (1 + F_3 ς³ + (F_4 − 2 ∂_ϑ ν_4) ς⁴ + O(ς⁵)). Likewise
g_λ(∂_(φ1), ∂_(φ1)) = r² cos²ϑ (1 + G_3 ς³ + G_4 ς⁴ + O(ς⁵)) and g_λ(∂_(φ2), ∂_(φ2)) = r² sin²ϑ (1 + H_3 ς³ + H_4 ς⁴ +
O(ς⁵)), the cross terms vanishing by the reflections, with cos²ϑ = cos²ϑ_B (1 + 2 ν_4 tan ϑ_B ς⁴ + O(ς⁵)) and
sin²ϑ = sin²ϑ_B (1 − 2 ν_4 cot ϑ_B ς⁴ + O(ς⁵)); the shifts of the arguments of the coefficients, by ů = O(ς²) and
ν = O(ς⁴), change F_3 ς³, G_3 ς³ and H_3 ς³ only at O(ς⁵). Since F_3 + G_3 + H_3 = 0,

    det q = r⁶ cos²ϑ_B sin²ϑ_B (1 + (F_4 + G_4 + H_4 − 2 ∂_ϑ ν_4 + 2 (tan ϑ − cot ϑ) ν_4) ς⁴ + O(ς⁵))
          = r⁶ cos²ϑ_B sin²ϑ_B (1 + (F_4 + G_4 + H_4 − 2 div(ν_4)) ς⁴ + O(ς⁵)),

because div f = ∂_ϑ f + (cot ϑ − tan ϑ) f. With r_B⁶ = r⁶ (1 + 6 ρ_4 ς⁴ + …) the areal condition gives ρ_k = 0 for k ≤ 3
and 6 ρ_4 = F_4 + G_4 + H_4 − 2 div(ν_4): ρ starts at ς⁴ with the value in (10.11), the trace of G_4 on the
sphere plus the Jacobian of the angular shift. The remainder of ρ is algebraic in those of (i)–(ii) and of u.

*(iv) The invariance and the Bondi functions.* The invariance and the values for v ≤ v_start are inherited from the
construction. The covariant components of (3.3) in (v_B, r_B, ϑ_B) are g_vv = −e^(2β) W + r_B² S U²,
g_vr = e^(2β), g_(vϑ) = −r_B² S U, g_(ϑϑ) = r_B² S and g_rr = g_(rϑ) = 0, and multiplying them with the stated inverse
components gives the identity; so the formulae for β, W, U, S, P1, P2 are the inversion of the (v_B, r_B, ϑ_B) block
of (3.3). To re-express them in (v_B, ϑ_B, ς_B), a coefficient f(v, ϑ) = f(v_B − ů, ϑ_B − ν) is expanded by
Taylor's formula, ů = O(ς²) and ν = O(ς⁴) shifting the coefficients by two and four half-orders, and
ς = ς_B (1 + ρ)^(1/2) by four. The expansion to order ς_B^(J−2) with remainders o(ς_B^(J−2)) follows, and the
r_B-gains of the remainders follow from the ℓ-gains of the ingredients (∂_(r_B) is a combination of ℓ and of E_2
multiples of ∂_v and ∂_ϑ). The (v_B, ϑ_B)-derivatives of the remainders stay o(ς_B^(J−2)), since the remainders lie in
the classes E_p with all their derivatives, and ∂_(v_B) and ∂_(ϑ_B) are combinations of ∂_v, ∂_ϑ and ℓ with
coefficients bounded with all their derivatives.

The first coefficients. e^(2P1) = 1/(r_B² cos²ϑ_B g^{11}) with g^{11} = g_λ^{11} unchanged, since φ1 is unchanged,
r_B/r = 1 + O(ς⁴) and ϑ_B − ϑ = O(ς⁴). By (10.9) and the reflections, g_λ^{11} = 1/g_(φ1φ1) =
r^(−2) cos^(−2)ϑ (1 − 2 p1 ς³ + O(ς⁴)), since G_3 = 2p1. So e^(2P1) = 1 + 2 p1 ς_B³ + O(ς_B⁴), the change from (v, ϑ, ς)
to (v_B, ϑ_B, ς_B) costing O(ς⁵); likewise e^(2P2) with H_3 = 2p2. Next, e^(−2β) = g^{v_B r_B} =
g_λ⁻¹(dv + dů, dr_B). Here g_λ^{vr} = 1 + E_2, since its correction −u_rv − (1 − μ/r²) u_rr is O(ς⁴);
g_λ⁻¹(dů, dr) = ∂_v ů + ℓů + O(ς⁶) with ℓů = O(ς⁴); and dr_B = (1 + O(ς⁴)) dr + O(ς²) dv + O(ς²) dϑ, whose dv- and
dϑ-parts enter only at ς⁶, because they meet g_λ^{vv} in E_2, g_λ^{vϑ} = O(r^(−3)), ℓů and r^(−2) ∂_ϑ ů. So
e^(−2β) = 1 + ∂_v ů + O(ς⁴) at the orders shown, and with (10.11),
e^(−2β) = 1 − (∂_v C_4/2) ς² − (∂_v C_5/3) ς³ + O(ς⁴), which is (10.12) in ς_B.

Finally W = e^(2β) g^{r_B r_B} and U = e^(2β) g^{r_B ϑ_B}. In g^{r_B r_B} = g_λ⁻¹(dr_B, dr_B), g_λ^{rr} = 1 − μ/r² +
O(ς⁴) = 1 + O(ς⁴), since its correction −u_vv − 2 (1 − μ/r²) u_rv − (1 − μ/r²)² u_rr is O(ς⁴), and the O(ς²) dv- and
dϑ-parts of dr_B meet g_λ^{rv} = 1 + E_2 and g_λ^{rϑ} = O(ς⁶); so g^{r_B r_B} = 1 + O(ς²), and W − 1 = O(ς²). In
g^{r_B ϑ_B} = g_λ⁻¹(dr_B, dϑ + dν), g_λ⁻¹(dr, dϑ + dν) = g_λ^{rϑ} + ∂_v ν + O(ς⁶) = O(ς⁴), while the dv- and
dϑ-parts of dr_B meet g_λ⁻¹(dv, dϑ_B) = O(ς⁶) and g_λ⁻¹(dϑ, dϑ_B) = r^(−2) (1 + O(ς³)); so U = O(ς⁴). In ς_B these are
W − 1 = O(ς_B²) and U = O(ς_B⁴). ∎

**Remark 10.8** Taking J = 8 in Proposition 10.4 gives the Bondi functions to order ς_B⁶ with
o(ς_B⁶) remainders, which is what Section Section 10.5 uses. The hierarchy there, run from ς¹, gives
β_1 = β_2 = β_3 = 0 for a vacuum metric. By (10.12) this means ∂_v C_4 = ∂_v C_5 = 0, and then
C_4 = C_5 = 0, since C_4 and C_5 are components of G_4 and G_5, which vanish for v ≤ v_start
(Proposition 10.4): the (ℓ, ℓ) component of g_λ − g0 is O(r^(−3)). This is a consequence, not an input:
Proposition 10.10 lets β start at ς¹.

### 10.5 The hierarchy at past null infinity

In this section (v, r, ϑ) are Bondi coordinates and the metric has the form (3.3) with the subscript B
dropped, with β, W, U, P1, P2 functions of (v, r, ϑ), S = e^(−2(P1+P2)) and ς = r^(−1/2). The metric of the spheres is
q_AB = r² (γ_P)_AB with γ_P := S dϑ² + cos²ϑ e^(2P1) dφ1² + sin²ϑ e^(2P2) dφ2², as in (2.15), whose
determinant is cos²ϑ sin²ϑ, that of γ; capital indices run over (ϑ, φ1, φ2), D is the Levi-Civita connection of γ,
div f = ∂_ϑ f + (cot ϑ − tan ϑ) f is the divergence on S³ of the field f ∂_ϑ, and Δ_P is the Laplacian of γ_P. The
inverse metric is that of Proposition 10.7, with g^{vv} = g^{vϑ} = 0, and √|det g| = e^(2β) r³ cos ϑ sin ϑ. We write
the Ricci tensor as

    R_ab = ∂_c Γ^c_ab − ∂_a ∂_b log √|det g| + Γ^c_ab ∂_c log √|det g| − Γ^c_ad Γ^d_bc.

**The Christoffel symbols with a lower index r.** Since g^{va} = e^(−2β) δ^a_r, Γ^v_rb = ½ e^(−2β) ∂_b g_rr = 0 for every
index b. Since g_rr = g_(rϑ) = 0, Γ^ϑ_rr = Γ^(φi)_rr = 0 and Γ^r_rr = 2 ∂_r β. By the reflections φi ↦ −φi,
Γ^r_(rφi) = Γ^ϑ_(rφi) = Γ^(φi)_(rϑ) = 0. The others that enter below are

    Γ^r_(rϑ) = ∂_ϑ β − ½ r² e^(−2β) S ∂_r U,     Γ^ϑ_(rϑ) = 1/r − ∂_r (P1 + P2),     Γ^(φi)_(r φi) = 1/r + ∂_r P_i,
    Γ^ϑ_(rv) = −(1/(2r²S)) ∂_r (r² S U) − e^(2β) ∂_ϑ β/(r² S),
    Γ^v_(ϑϑ) = −½ e^(−2β) ∂_r (r² S),    Γ^ϑ_(ϑϑ) = ½ ∂_ϑ log S + U Γ^v_(ϑϑ),
    Γ^(φ1)_(ϑ φ1) = ∂_ϑ P1 − tan ϑ,    Γ^(φ2)_(ϑ φ2) = ∂_ϑ P2 + cot ϑ,    (10.15)

each obtained from Γ^a_bc = ½ g^{ad} (∂_b g_dc + ∂_c g_db − ∂_d g_bc) with the components of Proposition 10.7.

**The radial components.** With log √|det g| = 2β + 3 log r + log(cos ϑ sin ϑ) and (10.15),

    R_rr = ∂_r(2 ∂_r β) − ∂_r²(2β + 3 log r) + 2 ∂_r β (2 ∂_r β + 3/r)
           − [ (2 ∂_r β)² + (1/r − ∂_r(P1 + P2))² + Σ_i (1/r + ∂_r P_i)² ],

and the terms in 1/r² and in (∂_r β)² cancel, as do the cross terms (2/r)(∂_r(P1 + P2) − ∂_r P1 − ∂_r P2), so

    R_rr = (6/r) ∂_r β − 2 ((∂_r P1)² + ∂_r P1 ∂_r P2 + (∂_r P2)²),    (10.16)

exactly. In the same way, R_(rϑ) is ∂_r Γ^r_(rϑ) + ∂_ϑ Γ^ϑ_(rϑ) − 2 ∂_r ∂_ϑ β + Γ^r_(rϑ) ∂_r log √|det g| + Γ^ϑ_(rϑ) ∂_ϑ
log √|det g| minus Γ^r_(ϑr) Γ^r_rr + Γ^ϑ_(ϑr) Γ^r_(rϑ) + Γ^v_(ϑϑ) Γ^ϑ_(rv) + Γ^ϑ_(ϑϑ) Γ^ϑ_(rϑ) + Σ_i Γ^(φi)_(ϑφi)
Γ^(φi)_(rφi); the other products vanish by the symbols listed. Collecting: the undifferentiated U cancels between
Γ^v_(ϑϑ) Γ^ϑ_(rv) and U Γ^v_(ϑϑ) Γ^ϑ_(rϑ), because Γ^ϑ_(rϑ) = ∂_r(r²S)/(2r²S); the terms in ∂_r U combine to −½ ∂_r(r²
e^(−2β) S ∂_r U) − (3/(2r)) r² e^(−2β) S ∂_r U; the terms in ∂_ϑ β combine to −∂_r ∂_ϑ β + (3/r) ∂_ϑ β; and the terms in
P alone give the last line below. So, exactly,

    R_(rϑ) = −(1/(2r³)) ∂_r (r⁵ e^(−2β) S ∂_r U) − r³ ∂_r (r^(−3) ∂_ϑ β) − ∂_r ∂_ϑ (P1 + P2)
             + tan ϑ (2 ∂_r P1 + ∂_r P2) − cot ϑ (∂_r P1 + 2 ∂_r P2)
             − (2 ∂_r P1 ∂_ϑ P1 + ∂_r P1 ∂_ϑ P2 + ∂_ϑ P1 ∂_r P2 + 2 ∂_r P2 ∂_ϑ P2).    (10.17)

**The case β = U = 0.** For the metric −W dv² + 2 dv dr + q_AB dx^A dx^B the nonzero Christoffel symbols are

    Γ^v_vv = ½ ∂_r W,   Γ^v_AB = −½ ∂_r q_AB,   Γ^r_vv = ½ (W ∂_r W − ∂_v W),   Γ^r_vr = −½ ∂_r W,
    Γ^r_vA = −½ ∂_A W,   Γ^r_AB = −½ (∂_v q_AB + W ∂_r q_AB),   Γ^A_vv = ½ q^{AB} ∂_B W,
    Γ^A_vB = ½ q^{AC} ∂_v q_CB,   Γ^A_rB = ½ q^{AC} ∂_r q_CB,   Γ^A_BC = Γ[q]^A_BC,    (10.18)

and √|det g| = r³ cos ϑ sin ϑ does not depend on v. Inserting them in the formula for R_ab,
R_vr = ∂_r Γ^r_vr + (3/r) Γ^r_vr − Γ^A_rB Γ^B_vA, R_vv = (r³ cos ϑ sin ϑ)⁻¹ ∂_c (r³ cos ϑ sin ϑ Γ^c_vv) − (Γ^v_vv)² −
(Γ^r_vr)² − Γ^A_vB Γ^B_vA, and, for R_AB, the terms with indices A, B, C only give the Ricci tensor R[q] of q on the
spheres, while the others are those of Γ^v_AB, Γ^r_AB, Γ^A_vB and Γ^A_rB. Since tr(γ_P⁻¹ ∂_v γ_P) = ∂_v log det γ_P = 0,
and γ_P⁻¹ ∂γ_P = diag(−2 ∂(P1 + P2), 2 ∂P1, 2 ∂P2), this gives

    R_vr = −½ ∂_r² W − (3/(2r)) ∂_r W − (2 ∂_r P1 ∂_v P1 + ∂_r P1 ∂_v P2 + ∂_v P1 ∂_r P2 + 2 ∂_r P2 ∂_v P2),
    R_vv = ½ W ∂_r² W + (3/(2r)) (W ∂_r W − ∂_v W) + (1/(2r²)) Δ_P W − 2 ((∂_v P1)² + ∂_v P1 ∂_v P2 + (∂_v P2)²),
    R_AB = R[q]_AB − ∂_v ∂_r q_AB − ½ ∂_r (W ∂_r q_AB) − (3/(2r)) (∂_v q_AB + W ∂_r q_AB)
           + ½ (∂_r q q⁻¹ ∂_v q + ∂_v q q⁻¹ ∂_r q + W ∂_r q q⁻¹ ∂_r q)_AB.    (10.19)

For instance −Γ^A_rB Γ^B_vA = −¼ tr(q⁻¹ ∂_r q q⁻¹ ∂_v q) = −¼ tr(γ_P⁻¹ ∂_r γ_P γ_P⁻¹ ∂_v γ_P), which is the last
term of R_vr. With W = 1 − μ/r² and P1 = P2 = 0, (10.19) gives R_vr = 0 and R_vv = 3μ'/(2r³), the Ricci
tensor of g0 (Proposition 2.5 (a)).

**The terms linear in U.** At the flat metric η_B := −dv² + 2 dv dr + r² γ (β = 0, W = 1, P1 = P2 = 0), let U^A have the
single component U^ϑ = U and U_A := γ_AB U^B. The Christoffel symbols linear in U are

    δΓ^v_vA = δΓ^r_vA = ½ ∂_r (r² U_A),   δΓ^r_rA = −½ r² ∂_r U_A,   δΓ^r_AB = −½ r² (D_A U_B + D_B U_A),
    δΓ^A_vv = −∂_v U^A,   δΓ^A_vr = −(1/(2r²)) ∂_r (r² U^A),   δΓ^C_AB = −r U^C γ_AB,    (10.20)

and the others vanish; U does not change det g. By Palatini's identity δR_ab = ∇̄_c δΓ^c_ab − ∇̄_b δΓ^c_ac, with ∇̄ the
connection of η_B and δΓ^c_ac = 0, the parts of R_ab linear in U at η_B are

    δR_vr = −(1/(2r²)) ∂_r (r² D_A U^A),     δR_vv = −D_A ∂_v U^A,
    δR_AB = −(1/(2r)) ∂_r (r³ (D_A U_B + D_B U_A)) − r γ_AB D_C U^C.    (10.21)

D_A U^A = div U, and δR_AB contains no derivative in v.

**Lemma 10.9** (Orders in the Bondi form.) Use the frame e_0 = ∂_v, e_1 = ∂_r, e_2 = r⁻¹ ∂_ϑ,
e_3 = (r cos ϑ)⁻¹ ∂_(φ1), e_4 = (r sin ϑ)⁻¹ ∂_(φ2), put Û := r U and y := (β, W − 1, Û, P1, P2).

(a) The components of the metric in this frame are smooth functions of y: g_00 = −e^(2β) W + S Û², g_01 = e^(2β),
g_02 = −S Û, g_22 = S, g_33 = e^(2P1), g_44 = e^(2P2), and the others vanish.

(b) Each frame component R_ij of the Ricci tensor is a finite sum of terms F(y) Π, with F smooth and Π one of
e_k e_l y_α, (e_k y_α)(e_l y_β), c e_k y_α, c c' or e_k c, where c, c' are structure coefficients of the frame,
[e_i, e_j] = c^k_ij e_k. Each structure coefficient is r⁻¹ times 1, tan ϑ or cot ϑ, so e_0 c = 0, e_1 c = −r⁻¹ c, and
e_2 c is r^(−2) times a function of ϑ. Give e_0 the weight 0, and e_1, e_2 and a structure coefficient the weight 2.

(c) In R_00 the terms of (b) whose two slots are both e_0 sum to −2((e_0 P1)² + e_0 P1 e_0 P2 + (e_0 P2)²); in every
other component they sum to 0.

(d) Consequently, if y_α has an expansion in ς starting at ς^(m_α), a term of R_ij whose factors from y are
y_(α1), …, y_(αn) and whose slots have total weight w has an expansion starting at ς^(m_(α1) + … + m_(αn) + w). In
particular a coefficient of R_ij at a given power of ς is determined by finitely many coefficients of the y_α, and
remainders o(ς⁶), which stay o(ς⁶) under e_0 and ∂_ϑ and gain two orders under e_1, enter only through o(·) terms.

Proof. (a) is (3.3), with the subscript B dropped, in the frame. (b) In a frame the connection coefficients
are Γ_kij = ½ (e_i g_jk + e_j g_ik − e_k g_ij) plus structure coefficients times components of g, each a sum of terms
with one slot, and R_ij = e_k Γ^k_ij − e_j Γ^k_ik + Γ Γ − Γ Γ − c Γ has exactly two slots in each term, since e_k
(F(y)) = F'(y) e_k y. The functions depend on (v, r, ϑ) only, so e_3 and e_4 act on them as zero. The structure
coefficients follow from [e_1, e_2] = −r⁻¹ e_2, [e_1, e_3] = −r⁻¹ e_3, [e_1, e_4] = −r⁻¹ e_4, [e_2, e_3] = r⁻¹ tan ϑ e_3,
[e_2, e_4] = −r⁻¹ cot ϑ e_4 and [e_0, e_i] = 0.

(c) Freeze (r, ϑ) = (r0, ϑ0) and let y(v) := y(v, r0, ϑ0). The terms with two slots e_0, evaluated at (v, r0, ϑ0), are
exactly the Ricci components of the metric g' := g_ij(y(v)) dx^i dx^j on R⁵ with coordinates (v, ϱ, z1, z2, z3), whose
coordinate frame has no structure coefficients and on which only e_0 = ∂_v acts. Now
g' = e^(2β) dv (2 dϱ − W dv) + S (dz1 − Û dv)² + e^(2P1) dz2² + e^(2P2) dz3², all functions of v. Put dσ := e^(2β) dv,
ϱ' := ϱ − ½ ∫ W e^(−2β) dσ and z1' := z1 − ∫ Û dv. Then g' = 2 dσ dϱ' + Σ_i e^(2Q_i) dz_i'² with
(Q_1, Q_2, Q_3) := (−(P1 + P2), P1, P2) as functions of σ. For this metric the nonzero Christoffel symbols are
Γ^(z_i)_(σ z_i) = dQ_i/dσ and Γ^(ϱ')_(z_i z_i) = −(dQ_i/dσ) e^(2Q_i), and √|det g'| = e^(ΣQ_i) = 1. The formula for
R_ab gives R_σσ = −Σ_i (d²Q_i/dσ² + (dQ_i/dσ)²) = −Σ_i (dQ_i/dσ)², and all its other components vanish: nothing depends
on ϱ', Γ^c_(ϱ'd) = 0, and in R_(z_i z_i) the only candidate, ∂_(ϱ') Γ^(ϱ')_(z_i z_i), is zero. As
dQ_i/dσ = e^(−2β) ∂_v Q_i, the Ricci tensor of g' is −Σ_i (∂_v Q_i)² dv² = −2((∂_v P1)² + ∂_v P1 ∂_v P2 + (∂_v P2)²) dv².

(d) e_0 = ∂_v preserves the order of an expansion with smooth coefficients, e_1 = ∂_r raises it by two
(∂_r ς^k = −(k/2) ς^(k+2), and the remainders gain by hypothesis), e_2 = r⁻¹ ∂_ϑ raises it by two (r⁻¹ = ς²), and so does
a structure coefficient; products add orders. ∎

Write R_ij = R_ij|_(β=U=0) + L_ij + H_ij, where L_ij collects the terms of degree one in (β, Û) with the other
components of y at their flat values (the parts linear in β and U at η_B) and H_ij the terms that contain β or Û together
with at least one further factor of y. By (c) the terms with two slots e_0 sum to a function of the P_i alone; so those
of L_ij and of H_ij sum to zero, and every remaining term of L_ij and H_ij has weight at least 2. The coordinate
components are R_vv = R_00, R_vr = R_01, R_rr = R_11, R_(rϑ) = r R_12 and R_AB = r² × (the frame components).

**Proposition 10.10** (The hierarchy at past null infinity.) Let a metric of the form
(3.3) with the subscript B dropped, with β, W, U, P1, P2 functions of (v, r, ϑ), be vacuum near past null
infinity. Let P1, P2, β, U and W − 1 have expansions in ς to order ς⁶, with coefficients smooth in (v, ϑ) and remainders
o(ς⁶) that stay o(ς⁶) under every (v, ϑ)-derivative and gain two ς-orders (one power of r) under each r-derivative, as in
Proposition 10.7; let P_i = O(ς³), and β, U, W − 1 = O(ς). Let p and q be the ς³ coefficients of P1 and P2, a1 and a2
their ς⁴ coefficients, and β_k, u_k, w_k the coefficients of β, U and W. Then, in order:

(0) from R_rr at ς⁵, ς⁶ and R_(rϑ) at ς¹, ς²: β_1 = β_2 = 0 and u_1 = u_2 = 0;

(i) from R_rr at ς⁷, …, ς¹⁰: β_3 = β_4 = β_5 = 0 and β_6 = −¼ (p² + pq + q²);

(ii) from R_(rϑ) at ς³, …, ς⁶: u_3 = u_4 = 0 and

    u_5 = (12/5)(p + q) tan ϑ − (8p + 16q)/(5 sin 2ϑ) − (4/5) ∂_ϑ (p + q),
    u_6 = 4 (a1 + a2) tan ϑ − (8 a1 + 16 a2)/(3 sin 2ϑ) − (4/3) ∂_ϑ (a1 + a2);

(iii) from R_vr at ς⁵, ς⁶, ς⁷: w_1 = w_2 = 0 and w_3 = −(2/3) div(u_5), so that ⟨w_3⟩ = 0;

(iv) from the traceless part of R_AB at ς²: ∂_v a1 = ∂_v a2 = 0;

(v) R_vv at ς⁵ is then an identity (the rate of (iii)), and at ς⁶ it is linear in ∂_v w_4 and reads

    ∂_v M = (4/3) ((∂_v p)² + ∂_v p ∂_v q + (∂_v q)²) + (2/3) div(∂_v u_6),       M := −w_4.    (10.22)

The coefficient at ς⁶ involves only p, q, a1, a2 and w_4, so remainders o(ς⁶) do not disturb it. With (iv), ∂_v u_6 = 0,
and (10.22) is, pointwise, the law (3.4) with (p1, p2) = (p, q).

Proof. We use ∂_r ς^k = −(k/2) ς^(k+2) throughout, and Lemma 10.9 (d) for the orders of the terms not
displayed.

*(0) and (i).* In (10.16), (6/r) ∂_r (β_k ς^k) = −3k β_k ς^(k+4), and ∂_r P_i = −(3/2) p_i ς⁵ + O(ς⁶), with
(p_1, p_2) = (p, q), so the second term is −(9/2)(p² + pq + q²) ς¹⁰ + O(ς¹¹). The coefficient of ς^(k+4) in R_rr is
therefore −3k β_k for k ≤ 5 and −18 β_6 − (9/2)(p² + pq + q²) for k = 6; vacuum gives β_1 = … = β_5 = 0 and
β_6 = −¼ (p² + pq + q²). In (10.17), e^(−2β) S = 1 − 2 β_1 ς + O(ς²) and
r⁵ e^(−2β) S ∂_r U = −½ u_1 ς^(−7) + (β_1 u_1 − u_2) ς^(−6) + O(ς^(−5)), so its first term is
(7/8) u_1 ς + (3/2)(u_2 − β_1 u_1) ς² + O(ς³); the second term is (7/2) ∂_ϑ β_1 ς³ + O(ς⁴), and the terms in P are O(ς⁵).
Vacuum gives u_1 = 0 and then u_2 = 0.

*(ii).* Now β = O(ς⁶), so the term of (10.17) in ∂_ϑ β is O(ς⁸), e^(−2β) − 1 = O(ς⁶) and S − 1 = O(ς³). For
U = Σ_{k≥3} u_k ς^k, −(1/(2r³)) ∂_r (r⁵ ∂_r U) = −Σ_k (k(k − 8)/8) u_k ς^k, while (S − 1) and e^(−2β) − 1 add terms of
order at least ς³ times the lowest order of U. The terms in P are, with ∂_r P_i = −(3/2) p_i ς⁵ − 2 a_i ς⁶ + O(ς⁷),
(3/2)(∂_ϑ(p + q) − tan ϑ (2p + q) + cot ϑ (p + 2q)) ς⁵ + 2 (∂_ϑ(a1 + a2) − tan ϑ (2a1 + a2) + cot ϑ (a1 + 2a2)) ς⁶ +
O(ς⁷), the quadratic ones being O(ς⁸). So R_(rϑ) is (15/8) u_3 ς³ + O(ς⁴), which gives u_3 = 0; then 2 u_4 ς⁴ + O(ς⁵),
which gives u_4 = 0; and then, U being O(ς⁵), the coefficients of ς⁵ and ς⁶ are

    (15/8) u_5 + (3/2)(∂_ϑ(p + q) − tan ϑ (2p + q) + cot ϑ (p + 2q)),
    (3/2) u_6 + 2 (∂_ϑ(a1 + a2) − tan ϑ (2a1 + a2) + cot ϑ (a1 + 2a2)).

Vacuum gives u_5 = (4/5)((2p + q) tan ϑ − (p + 2q) cot ϑ − ∂_ϑ(p + q)) and
u_6 = (4/3)((2a1 + a2) tan ϑ − (a1 + 2a2) cot ϑ − ∂_ϑ(a1 + a2)). These are the stated forms, by
1/sin 2ϑ = ½ (tan ϑ + cot ϑ).

*(iii).* By (10.19), R_vr|_(β=U=0) = −½ ∂_r² W − (3/(2r)) ∂_r W + O(ς⁸), the last term being a product of ∂_r
P_i and ∂_v P_j. For W − 1 = Σ_k w_k ς^k, −½ ∂_r² (ς^k) − (3/(2r)) ∂_r (ς^k) = (k(4 − k)/8) ς^(k+4). By
(10.21), L_vr has the part −(1/(2r²)) ∂_r (r² div U) = ¼ div(u_5) ς⁷ + O(ς⁸) linear in U, and its part linear
in β has weight at least 2 and so is O(ς⁸), β being O(ς⁶). The terms of H_vr contain β, of order 6, or Û, of order 3
since U = O(ς⁵), together with a factor of order 3 (P_i or Û) or of the order m of W − 1, and have weight at least 2:
they are O(ς^(5+m)) when m ≤ 3. With m = 1 the coefficient of ς⁵ is (3/8) w_1, so w_1 = 0; then m = 2 and the
coefficient of ς⁶ is ½ w_2, so w_2 = 0; then m = 3 and the coefficient of ς⁷ is (3/8) w_3 + ¼ div(u_5), so w_3 = −(2/3)
div(u_5). Its sphere mean vanishes, since ∫_0^(π/2) ∂_ϑ (f sin ϑ cos ϑ) dϑ = 0 for every smooth f.

*(iv).* Now W − 1, P_i and Û are O(ς³) and β is O(ς⁶), so H_AB and the part of L_AB linear in β have frame order at
least 8, that is, coordinate order at least ς⁴; by (10.21) the part linear in U has no derivative in v and
is O(ς³) in coordinates. In R_AB|_(β=U=0) from (10.19), write W = 1 + ω and γ_P = γ + k, so that q = r²(γ + k)
with k = diag(−2(P1 + P2), 2 cos²ϑ P1, 2 sin²ϑ P2) + O(ς⁶). The terms of degree two or more in (ω, k) have weight at
least 2 by Lemma 10.9 (c), hence frame order at least 8 and coordinate order at least ς⁴. R[q] = R[γ + k] =
2γ + O(ς³). In the rest, to first order: the constant terms give −2γ, cancelling 2γ; the terms in ω give −(r ∂_r ω +
2ω) γ_AB = Σ_m (m/2 − 2) w_m ς^m γ_AB, which is O(ς³) now that w_1 = w_2 = 0; the terms in k with a derivative in v
come from −∂_v ∂_r q, −(3/(2r)) ∂_v q and ½ (∂_r q q⁻¹ ∂_v q + ∂_v q q⁻¹ ∂_r q), and sum to −r² ∂_r ∂_v k − (3/2) r ∂_v
k = Σ_j ((j − 3)/2) ∂_v k_j ς^(j−2) for k = Σ_j k_j ς^j; and the terms in k without a derivative in v are O(ς³). So at
ς² the three angular components of R_AB are those of ½ ∂_v k_4, with k_4 = diag(−2(a1 + a2), 2 cos²ϑ a1, 2 sin²ϑ a2):
they are −∂_v(a1 + a2), cos²ϑ ∂_v a1 and sin²ϑ ∂_v a2, a traceless tensor. Vacuum gives ∂_v a1 = ∂_v a2 = 0.

*(v).* All of W − 1, P_i and Û are O(ς³) and β is O(ς⁶). So H_vv and the part of L_vv linear in β are O(ς⁸), and the
part linear in U is −div(∂_v U) = −div(∂_v u_5) ς⁵ − div(∂_v u_6) ς⁶ + o(ς⁶), by (10.21). In R_vv|_(β=U=0)
from (10.19), ½ W ∂_r² W, (3/(2r)) W ∂_r W and (1/(2r²)) Δ_P W are O(ς⁷), −(3/(2r)) ∂_v W = −(3/2) ∂_v w_3 ς⁵
− (3/2) ∂_v w_4 ς⁶ + O(ς⁷), and −2((∂_v P1)² + ∂_v P1 ∂_v P2 + (∂_v P2)²) = −2((∂_v p)² + ∂_v p ∂_v q + (∂_v q)²) ς⁶ +
O(ς⁷). Hence

    R_vv = −((3/2) ∂_v w_3 + div(∂_v u_5)) ς⁵
           − ((3/2) ∂_v w_4 + 2((∂_v p)² + ∂_v p ∂_v q + (∂_v q)²) + div(∂_v u_6)) ς⁶ + o(ς⁶).

The coefficient of ς⁵ vanishes identically by (iii). The coefficient of ς⁶ involves only p, q, a1, a2 (through u_6) and
w_4, and its vanishing is (10.22) with M = −w_4. With (iv), ∂_v u_6 = 0, since u_6 is linear in a1 and a2
with coefficients depending on ϑ alone. ∎

**Remark 10.11** (Comparison with [TTS09].) Tanabe, Tanahashi and Shiromizu write the five-dimensional Bondi
form as ds² = −(V e^B/r²) du² − 2 e^B du dr + r² h_AB (dx^A + U^A du)(dx^B + U^B du), with h_AB built from functions C1,
C2, C3, D1, D2, D3 and the areal condition r⁶ sin²θ cos²θ = det(g_AB) [TTS09, (2), (4), (5), p. 2]. For waves, C ~
r^(−3/2), and their equations give B = B1/r³ + O(r^(−7/2)) with B1 = −(C11² + C11 C21 + C21² + D11² + D21² + D31²)/8,
U^A = U_(A1)/r^(5/2) + O(1/r³), and V = r² + V1(u, x^A) r^(1/2) − M(u, x^A) + O(r^(−1/2)), with V1 minus two thirds of
the divergence of U_(A1) [TTS09, (20), (21), (25)–(27), pp. 3–4]. Their mass law reads

    "∂M(u, x^A)/∂u = −(1/3)((C_11,u)² + C_11,u C_21,u + (C_21,u)² + (D_11,u)² + (D_21,u)² + (D_31,u)²)"
                                                                                  [TTS09, (28), p. 4],

and "Eq. (28) represents mass loss rate by gravitational waves" [TTS09, p. 4]. The r^(−2) term A of C satisfies ∂A/∂u =
0 and vanishes for asymptotic flatness, by its value at spatial infinity [TTS09, (35), (36), p. 5]. In the class the
reflections give D1 = D2 = D3 = 0, and with u = −v, θ = π/2 − ϑ and (φ, ψ) = (φ1, φ2) their form is (3.3),
with the subscript B dropped, C1 = −2(P1 + P2), C2 = 2P1, C3 = 2P2, B = 2β, V/r² = W and U^θ = −U. So C11 = −2(p + q),
C21 = 2p, and B1 = −½(p² + pq + q²) = 2 β_6, as in (i); V1 = w_3, as in (iii); (35) is (iv); and (28) becomes
∂M/∂u = −(4/3)((∂_u p)² + ∂_u p ∂_u q + (∂_u q)²). The time reversal u = −v leaves the squares unchanged and reverses
the sign of the rate, which gives the law (3.4): an incoming flux raises the mass. Proposition 10.10
derives all of this in the form (3.3) itself, with every coefficient general from ς¹ on, and takes nothing
from [TTS09].

### 10.6 Proof of the mass law

Proof of Theorem 3.8. *The chart.* Proposition 10.7 with J = 8 gives, on the far region P ∩ {t ≥ T_M},
T_M = T_M(λ), Bondi coordinates (v_B, r_B, ϑ_B, φ1, φ2): v_B is null for g_λ, with v_B − v → 0 at past null infinity
along every generator of g0; ϑ_B is constant along the generators of {v_B = const}; r_B is the areal radius of the
spheres {v_B, r_B = const}; and g_λ has the form (3.3). In ς := r_B^(−1/2), the functions P1, P2, β, U and
W − 1 have expansions f = Σ_{k=1}^{6} ς^k f_k(v_B, ϑ_B) + o(ς⁶) whose coefficients are smooth, bounded with all their
derivatives, invariant under T² × Z2 × Z2 and equal to those of g0 for v_B ≤ v_start (zero there, but for
W − 1 = −μ0 ς⁴), and whose remainders have every (v_B, ϑ_B)-derivative o(ς⁶) and gain an order, one power of r_B and
two of ς, under each r_B-derivative; the remainders of Proposition 10.7 lie in classes E_p with all their
derivatives. This is the chart and the form of the metric that the theorem asserts. By Proposition 10.7,
P_i = O(ς³) and β = O(ς²) ((10.12)), W − 1 = O(ς²) and U = O(ς⁴); so β, U and W − 1 are O(ς), and
Proposition 10.10 applies to g_λ, which is vacuum.

*Item 1, the angular metric.* The ς³ coefficient of P_i is p_i, by the last part of Proposition 10.7; it is the
polarization of (2.11) at (v_B, ϑ_B) and the phase v_B/λ:

    p1 = (2 cos²ϑ_B G − sin²ϑ_B F)/3,    p2 = (2 sin²ϑ_B F − cos²ϑ_B G)/3,
    F = λ A env(v_B) h sin(v_B/λ),    G = λ A env(v_B) h cos(v_B/λ),    (10.23)

with h = h(cos 2ϑ_B) the angular profile of Section 2.6. The radiation field of Theorem 3.7 is this
statement in the wave-map gauge, and the change of chart preserves it. For the ς⁴ coefficients a_i: by
Proposition 10.10 (iv), ∂_v a_i = 0, and a_i = 0 for v_B ≤ v_start, where the metric is g0 (Proposition 10.7
(iv)); so a_i = 0. This is the argument of [TTS09] from spatial infinity, with the seed in its place.

*Item 2, the mass aspect.* By Proposition 10.10 (iii), W = 1 + ς³ V1 − ς⁴ M + O(ς⁵) with V1 := w_3 = −(2/3)
div(u_5), a divergence on S³, and by (v) with a_i = 0 the mass aspect obeys (3.4) pointwise. M = μ0 for
v_B ≤ v_start, since g_λ = g0 there: the Vaidya metric with μ = μ0, whose W is 1 − μ0 ς⁴.

*Item 3, the Bondi mass.* Let μ_B(v) := ⟨M(v, ·)⟩, the mean over S³. By (10.23), p_i(v_B, ϑ_B) is the
polarization P_i of Section 9.7 evaluated at (v_B, ϑ_B); there P_i is a function of (v, ϑ), the polarization of
(2.11) at the phase v/λ, not a Bondi function. So the density (4/3)((∂_v p1)² + ∂_v p1 ∂_v p2 + (∂_v p2)²) of
(3.4) is that of Lemma 9.14 (a) at (v_B, ϑ_B), and by Lemma 9.14 (b) its mean over S³,
taken in ϑ_B, is (3.5) exactly: μ_B' is the flux. We integrate from v_start, where μ_B = μ0 by item 2 and
env vanishes to all orders. By Lemma 9.14 (c), μ_B(v) is μ(v), plus (2/9) λ² A² ∫_{−∞}^{v} env'², plus two
boundary terms that carry the factor 1 − π/2, are O(λ) and vanish with env and env', plus O(λ³). So μ_B is μ(v) + O(λ)
while the shell passes, and after it μ_B = μ(v_end) + (2/9) λ² A² ∫ env'² + O(λ³).

*Item 4, the Hawking mass.* Let M[S] be the Hawking mass (3.2) of a Bondi sphere. Write (v, r, ϑ) for the
Bondi coordinates, the subscript B dropped, and let S = {v, r = const}. Since r is areal, Area(S) = 2π² r³ and R = r.
The future null normals of S are n⁻ = −∂_r and n⁺ = ∂_v + (W/2) ∂_r + U ∂_ϑ: by (3.3),
g(∂_r, ∂_r) = g(∂_r, ∂_ϑ) = 0, g(n⁺, ∂_ϑ) = g_(vϑ) + U g_(ϑϑ) = 0, and
g(n⁺, n⁺) = (−e^(2β) W + U² g_(ϑϑ)) + W e^(2β) − 2 U² g_(ϑϑ) + U² g_(ϑϑ) = 0, while g(n⁺, n⁻) = −e^(2β). The area form
of S is r³ cos ϑ sin ϑ dϑ dφ1 dφ2, independent of v, so θ⁻ = −3/r exactly and θ⁺ = 3W/(2r) + div U. So
Θ = −(9/r²) e^(−2β) (W + (2r/3) div U) and

    M[S] = r² (1 − ⟨e^(−2β) (W + (2r/3) div U)⟩).

With β = O(ς⁶), W = 1 + w_3 ς³ + w_4 ς⁴ + O(ς⁵), U = u_5 ς⁵ + u_6 ς⁶ + o(ς⁶) and r = ς^(−2),
e^(−2β)(W + (2r/3) div U) = 1 + (w_3 + (2/3) div u_5) ς³ + (w_4 + (2/3) div u_6) ς⁴ + o(ς⁴), and

    M[S] = −ς⁻¹ ⟨w_3 + (2/3) div u_5⟩ − ⟨w_4 + (2/3) div u_6⟩ + o(1).

The divergences have zero mean, so M[S] → ⟨−w_4⟩ = ⟨M⟩ = μ_B(v_B) as r_B → ∞. ∎

**Remark 10.12** (The aspect after the shell.) After the shell the aspect itself, not only its mean,
is independent of ϑ_B to O(λ³). With D_c, D_s of Section 9.7, write cos⁴ϑ D_c² + sin⁴ϑ D_s² as
½ (cos⁴ϑ + sin⁴ϑ)(env² + λ² env'²) + (sin⁴ϑ − cos⁴ϑ) O_1, where O_1 := ½ (env² − λ² env'²) cos(2v/λ) +
λ env env' sin(2v/λ). Since h² (cos⁴ϑ + sin⁴ϑ) = 1 ((2.13)), the density of Lemma 9.14 (a) is
(2/9) A² (env² + λ² env'²) plus ϑ-dependent multiples of O_1 and of D_c D_s. Both oscillate at twice the frequency of
the wave, and each is a v-derivative of terms that vanish with env and env', plus λ² times a smooth function times
cos(2v/λ) or sin(2v/λ), whose integral is O(λ³): for D_c D_s this is the identity in the proof of Lemma 9.14
(c), and O_1 = d/dv [ (λ/4) env² sin(2v/λ) − (λ²/4) env env' cos(2v/λ) ] + (λ²/4)(env env'' − env'²) cos(2v/λ). So for
v ≥ v_end, M(v, ϑ_B) = μ(v_end) + (2/9) λ² A² ∫ env'² + O(λ³) uniformly in ϑ_B, and any average of M over ϑ_B equals
μ_B to O(λ³) there; while the shell passes, M depends on ϑ_B at O(λ), and such an average need not equal μ_B.

**Remark 10.13** (Numerical observation.) The observation below was made with the profile
p(v) := sin⁴(π(v − ½)/3) on [½, 7/2], extended by zero, in place of the envelope. It is C³ and not C⁴ at v = ½ and
v = 7/2, where its fourth derivative jumps by 8π⁴/27, so it is not an envelope of Section 2.6, and neither
Theorem 3.8 nor Remark 10.12 is claimed for it. The coefficient of Remark 10.12
evaluated on it is (2/9) ∫ p'² = 5π²/108 = 0.45693…, since the substitution ξ = π(v − ½)/3 gives
∫ p'² = (16π/3) ∫_0^π sin⁶ξ cos²ξ dξ = (16π/3)(5π/16 − 35π/128) = 5π²/24. In a numerical integration of the vacuum
equations in the form (3.3) from the free data (10.23), with p in place of env, A = 1 and
the angle sampled at Chebyshev–Lobatto nodes in cos 2ϑ_B, the offset of the node-averaged aspect from μ after the shell,
divided by λ², was observed to be 0.4589, 0.4577, 0.4568 at λ = 0.05, 0.025, 0.0125 (μ0 = 100 l5²) and 0.4578, 0.4569 at
λ = 0.025, 0.0125 (μ0 = 1000 l5²), against 5π²/108 = 0.45693…, within 0.05 % at λ = 0.0125. A run at
λ = 0.00625 (μ0 = 100 l5²), on the grid of the run at λ = 0.0125, which is too coarse for that wavelength, gave 0.4535.
The values at 1000 l5² reproduce those at 100 l5² to about 10⁻⁴ and are not an independent check. No proof uses this
observation.

**Remark 10.14** (What is not claimed.) Proposition 10.4 claims no uniformity in λ of the expansion
beyond its leading term, which the mass law does not need. Nothing is claimed about future null infinity or the Bondi
mass there, which the domain does not reach.


# Part V. The stability theory, I: the spectral family on bundles

## 11. The spectral family at bounded nonzero frequencies

This chapter proves the Fredholm theory of the stationary spectral family on a trivial vector bundle over the exterior
of a black hole in dimension 4 + 1, at bounded real frequencies σ ≠ 0 and in the closed upper half plane near them. The
main result, Theorem 11.33, is [Hin26c, Theorem 9.5] in dimension 4 + 1, for operators on a trivial bundle of any
rank and for a constant regularity order (Remark 11.3). The spectral family is Fredholm between spaces of variable
decay order; its kernel and the annihilator of its range do not depend on the admissible orders; its index does not
depend on σ; its kernel elements are conormal at infinity with an explicit leading term; and its inverse, where it
exists, is regular in σ. Two changes are forced by the dimension: the term −(n − 1)/2 of the operator at infinity is
−3/2, and the weights 1 + S̄ and ρ^(1+S) of [Hin26c, (9.20)–(9.21)], which are their values at n = 3, are 3/2 + S̄ and
ρ^(3/2+S). A third change concerns the sign of a term in [Hin26c, (9.45)] (Lemma 11.20). Of the expansion
[Hin26c, (9.21)] the first step is proved (Theorem 11.33 (5)). Theorem 11.38 makes the constants uniform under
continuous perturbations of the operator.

The hypotheses (H1)–(H5) of Section 11.1.3 are stated for the spectral family alone; every later chapter that uses
these results instantiates them. Section 11.2 states the calculus. Section 11.3 proves the one positive commutator
lemma used throughout, with its regularisation. Section 11.4 proves the three radial point estimates and the
commutator lemma for b-regularity, Section 11.5 the elliptic and propagation estimates, and Section 11.6 the
estimates near an artificial boundary inside the horizon. Section 11.7 proves the theorem and Section 11.8 its
uniformity in the operator.

*Notation.* The stability theory, from Chapter 11 to Chapter 40, does not use the number N of stages of the
approximant, and it uses the wavelength λ of the main construction only where Chapter 39 applies the gluing to the data
of the solution g_λ (Corollary 39.19). Elsewhere in these chapters λ, with or without indices, and N denote other
objects (exponents, parameters, eigenvalues and orders among them), each defined by its chapter where it is introduced;
λ is also a tensor index, and λ_max and λ_min are the largest and the least eigenvalue.

### 11.1 Setting and hypotheses

#### 11.1.1 The space

Let ℝ̄⁴ be the radial compactification of ℝ⁴, with boundary ∂ℝ̄⁴ ≅ 𝕊³. Near it we use ρ = |x|⁻¹ and ω = x/|x| ∈ 𝕊³,
so that a neighbourhood of the boundary is [0, ρ₁)_ρ × 𝕊³_ω. Fix radii 0 < r₀ − 2δ₀ < r₀ < r₀ + δ₀ < r₂ < r_h and set

    X̄ := {x : |x| ≥ r₀} ∪ ∂ℝ̄⁴,     ∂X := ∂ℝ̄⁴,     ∂_♯X := {|x| = r₀},     X̃ := {|x| > r₀ − 2δ₀} ∪ ∂X.

Write r := |x|. The radius r_h is that of the horizon in (H3), and ∂_♯X is the artificial boundary. All operators below
are defined on X̃. Every function space on X̄ is built from a space on ℝ⁴ through the extendible and supported
constructions at ∂_♯X of Section 11.6.1, and every Schwartz kernel used has support in X̃ × X̃. The density is the
Euclidean one, |dx| = r³ dr dω = ρ⁻⁵ dρ dω near ∂X, where dω is the round density on 𝕊³.

The radii, and in particular the inner radius r₀ of the artificial boundary, are parameters. The results of this
chapter hold for every choice of them for which the hypotheses below hold, with constants that depend on the choice;
the cut-offs and dilations used near ∂_♯X (Section 11.6.1) are taken in proportion to r₀. The radii used for the
Myers–Perry metrics are fixed in Chapter 22.

The condition r₀ + δ₀ < r₂ costs nothing. Decreasing δ₀ shrinks X̃, on which (H1)–(H3) below continue to hold; it
leaves X̄ and every space below unchanged; and it only weakens (H4) and (H5): the region of (H4) on which G₀ is
Lorentzian shrinks, the set {r < r₀ − δ₀} that the curves of (H4) must reach grows, and the parameters at which they
reach it, bounded in (H5), can only decrease. So if (H1)–(H5) hold for radii with 0 < r₀ − 2δ₀ < r₀ < r₂ < r_h,
they still hold, and so does the ordering above, once δ₀ is replaced by min(δ₀, (r₂ − r₀)/2). The condition is used
in Corollary 11.31, where it makes room for the radii b′ < b″ in (r₀, r₂ − δ₀).

#### 11.1.2 The bundle

Let E := X̃ × ℂ^(N_E), N_E ≥ 1. The bundles of the later chapters are the restrictions to X̃ of the cotangent bundle
of a five-dimensional spacetime and its symmetric square, trivialised by dt_*, dx¹, …, dx⁴ and their symmetric
products, with N_E = 5 and N_E = 15; nothing below uses more than that E is trivial. Large numbers that bound the orders
of error terms, as in H^(−M), are written M, and 𝐌 := (M, M) (Section 11.3). A *fibre inner product* is
h(x)(v, w) = ⟨H(x)v, w⟩_(ℂ^(N_E)), where H ∈ C^∞(ℝ̄⁴; End ℂ^(N_E)) is Hermitian, smooth on the compactification (that is,
smooth in (ρ, ω) up to ρ = 0), and satisfies c Id ≤ H ≤ C Id with c > 0. Let L²_h := L²(ℝ⁴; ℂ^(N_E)) with the norm
‖u‖²_h = ∫ h(u, u) |dx|, which is equivalent to the standard one. For an operator A, A^(∗h) = H⁻¹A∗H is its formal
adjoint in L²_h, and A∗ its adjoint in the standard L². We write Re_h A := ½(A + A^(∗h)) and
Im_h A := (A − A^(∗h))/2i.

#### 11.1.3 The operator

Let ℂ ∋ σ ↦ P̂(σ) ∈ Diff²(X̃°; E) be of the form

    P̂(σ) = P̂(0) + σT + σ²P₂.    (11.1)

This is the form of the spectral family e^(iσt_*) P₀ e^(−iσt_*) of a t_*-translation-invariant second-order operator
P₀, with T = −i[P₀, t_*] and P₂ of order 0 (compare [Hin26c, (9.30)]). For an operator A, σ_m(A) or σ(A) denotes its
principal symbol, of order m; σ₀ and σ₁, written without an argument, are the real and imaginary parts of the spectral
parameter, σ = σ₀ + iσ₁. The hypotheses are these.

(H1) (*Principal symbol.*) σ_2(P̂(0)) = G₀ Id, where G₀ ∈ C^∞(T∗X̃°) is real, fibrewise quadratic and even in the
fibres, and σ_1(T) = τ₁ Id with τ₁ real and fibre-linear. P₂ = g₀₀ Id with g₀₀ a real function.

(H2) (*Structure at infinity*; [Hin26c, Definition 9.4 and (9.31)] at n = 4.) On {ρ < ρ₁},

    T = 2iρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S) − iQ,     P̂(0) = ρ²P^(0),     g₀₀ ∈ ρ²C^∞(ℝ̄⁴),    (11.2)

where S ∈ C^∞(ℝ̄⁴; End ℂ^(N_E)), Q ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b, and P^(0) ∈ Diff²_b with
P^(0) − ((ρD_ρ)² + Δ_(𝕊³)) Id ∈ Diff¹_b + ρ Diff²_b. All b-operators here have End ℂ^(N_E)-valued coefficients smooth on
the compactification, D = −i∂, and Δ_(𝕊³) ≥ 0 is the Laplacian of the round metric. The first equation in
(11.2) is the form that the term −(n − 1)/2 of [Hin26c, (9.31)] takes at n = 4. Set

    S̄ := inf_(p ∈ ∂X) min Re spec S(0, p)     ([Hin26c, (5.2)]).

(H3) (*The horizon*; [Hin26c, Section 9.2.1, (1)–(4)].) Let ℋ := {r = r_h}. ℛ₊ is one of the two components of
N∗ℋ ∖ o, and ℛ₋ := −ℛ₊; both lie in Σ₀ := {G₀ = 0}. Let ρ_∞ be positive, homogeneous of degree −1 and even near N∗ℋ.
The *future-directed rescaled Hamilton vector field* on Σ₀ is 𝖧 := ±ρ_∞H_(G₀) on the component Σ₀^± containing ℛ_±.
Then for each sign

    β₀ := ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞ > 0 on ∂ℛ_±,     β := inf_(∂ℛ_±) (∓β₀⁻¹ρ_∞τ₁) > 0,    (11.3)

and there is a quadratic defining function q_± of ∂ℛ_± in ∂Σ₀ with 𝖧q_± ≥ c q_± near ∂ℛ_±, for some c > 0. Here ∂(·)
denotes the boundary at fibre infinity, viewed in S∗X̃°. For the spectral family of a t_*-translation-invariant
operator, ∓ρ_∞τ₁ = 𝖧t_*, since τ₁ = −H_G t_* [Hin26c, (9.30)]; so the second condition is the condition β > 0 of
[Hin26c].

(H4) (*Dynamics at fibre infinity.*) ∂Σ₀ = ∂Σ₀⁺ ⊔ ∂Σ₀⁻ lies over {r ≤ r_e} for some r_e > r_h. Every maximal integral
curve of 𝖧 in ∂Σ₀ ∖ (∂ℛ₊ ∪ ∂ℛ₋) tends to ∂ℛ₊ ∪ ∂ℛ₋ as its parameter tends to −∞, and reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} at a
finite positive parameter. On {r₀ − 2δ₀ < r < r₂}, G₀ is a Lorentzian form (signature (1, 3)) on each fibre of T∗X̃,
dr is timelike for it (G₀(dr) < 0), and 𝖧r < 0 on ∂Σ₀ there: the future direction decreases r. (For a spectral family,
G₀ is g⁻¹ restricted to the annihilator of ∂_(t_*), and such a restriction of a Lorentzian form is Lorentzian wherever
it contains a timelike covector, as dr is inside the horizon.)

(H5) (*Uniformity data.*) P̂ may depend on a parameter b in a compact metric space ℬ, continuously into the
coefficient topology (every coefficient continuous in b into C^∞, and in the classes of (H2)). The objects ℋ, ρ_∞,
q_± and r_e in (H3)–(H4) may depend continuously on b, and the constants c, inf β₀ and β in (H3) and the lengths of
the curves in (H4) are bounded uniformly. Section 11.8 uses (H5).

**Remark 11.1** (On the hypotheses.) (a) By (H1) the principal symbol of P̂(σ), of order 2, is G₀ Id
for every σ. Since P̂(0) − P̂(0)^(∗h) has vanishing principal symbol, Im_h P̂(0) ∈ Diff¹, and near ∂X it lies in
ρ²Diff¹_b. Indeed P̂(0) ∈ ρ²Diff²_b by (11.2), adjoints preserve ρ²Diff²_b for the density ρ⁻⁵dρ dω (the
adjoint of a b-vector field is a b-operator), and the b-principal symbols cancel.

(b) By (H1), for σ ∈ ℂ,

    σ_1(Im_h P̂(σ)) = σ_1(Im_h P̂(0)) + (Im σ) τ₁ Id.    (11.4)

To see this, write Im_h(σT) = (σT − σ̄T^(∗h))/2i = (Re σ) Im_h T + (Im σ) Re_h T. Then Im_h T has order 0,
σ_1(Re_h T) = τ₁ Id, and σ²P₂ has order 0.

(c) (H3)–(H4) are the hypotheses of [Hin26c, Section 9.2.1] and the dynamics of [Hin26c, Section 9.1.1]. For the
operators of the later chapters, on the Schwarzschild–Tangherlini metric and the Myers–Perry metrics near it, the
dynamics in (H3)–(H4) is verified in Chapter 22, and the horizon threshold ϑ_ℋ of Section 11.1.4 is evaluated where
each operator is studied (Chapter 23, Chapter 24).

(d) P̂(σ)^(∗h) satisfies (H1)–(H4) as well, with τ₁, S and Q replaced by τ₁, −S^(∗h) and a suitable Q′, and with σ
replaced by σ̄. Only its principal symbol and its imaginary part enter below, and they are determined where they are
used.

#### 11.1.4 Orders and thresholds

The phase space is the scattering cotangent bundle ^(sc)T̄∗ℝ̄⁴, compactified in the fibres. Its boundary consists of
*fibre infinity*, ^(sc)S∗ℝ̄⁴, and the *boundary face* ^(sc)T̄∗_(∂X)ℝ̄⁴ over ∂X, meeting at a corner. Near ∂X we write
scattering covectors as ξ dr + r η, with ξ ∈ ℝ and η ∈ T∗𝕊³, so that (ρ, ω, ξ, η) are coordinates
([Hin26c, Section 9.2.2]; ξ and η are the ξ_sc and η_sc of [Hin26c]). For an h-self-adjoint endomorphism A, max spec A
and min spec A denote its largest and smallest eigenvalues.

**Definition 11.2** (Admissible orders.) An *order pair* is (s, 𝗋) with s ∈ ℝ a constant
(regularity; Remark 11.3) and 𝗋 ∈ C^∞(^(sc)T̄∗_(∂X)ℝ̄⁴) (decay), each extended smoothly to a neighbourhood of its
face. For real σ₀ ≠ 0 it is *admissible for* σ₀ with weight α₊ ∈ ℝ if:

(O1) s = s_c, a constant (Remark 11.3);

(O2) 𝗋 is constant near R_(σ₀,in) and near R_out (defined in (11.17)), and on the characteristic set Σ^∂_(σ₀)
of (11.18) it is monotone non-increasing along the future-directed flow (sgn(σ₀) 𝖧_(σ₀)𝗋 ≤ 0, in the notation
of Section 11.4.2);

(O3) the thresholds [Hin26c, (9.16a)–(9.16c)] hold with respect to some fibre inner products, chosen separately for
each radial set (Section 11.2.3):

    s_c > 1/2 + ϑ_ℋ,     𝗋 + α₊ > (−1 + ϑ_in)/2 at R_(σ₀,in),     𝗋 + α₊ < −1/2 + S̄ at R_out.    (11.5)

Here

    ϑ_ℋ := max_± sup_(∂ℛ_±) max spec(β₀⁻¹ p_(1,±)(0)),     p_(1,±)(σ) := ±ρ_∞ σ_1(Im_h P̂(σ)),

where p_(1,±)(σ) is an h-self-adjoint endomorphism; this is [Hin26c, (5.17)] (Remark 11.15). Next,

    ϑ_in := sup_(∂X) max spec(p_in − (S + S^(∗h))),     p_in := σ(ρ⁻¹ Im_h P̂(0))|_(ξ = −2, η = 0)

([Hin26c, (9.32), (9.38b)]; Proposition 11.18). For complex σ = σ₀ + iσ₁ the orders used are those for σ₀.

The spaces are those of [Hin26c, Theorem 9.5]:

    H̄^(s,𝗋) := H̄^(s,𝗋)_sc(X̄; E),     Ḣ^(s,𝗋) := Ḣ^(s,𝗋)_sc(X̄; E),

extendible, respectively supported, at ∂_♯X (Section 11.6.1), built componentwise from the scattering Sobolev spaces
of [HJS, Definition 10.2] on ℝ⁴ (constant regularity order, variable decay order).

**Remark 11.3** (Constant regularity order.) [Hin26c] lets the regularity order vary at fibre infinity over a
region {r > r_Γ}, r_Γ > r_e, where P̂(σ) is elliptic. The calculus of [HJS] used here takes the differential order
constant ([HJS, p. 77]: "we will take the differential order to be constant, and the spatial order to be variable"),
and every proof below uses only s ≡ s_c, so Theorem 11.33 is stated and proved for constant s. The semiclassical
calculus of Chapter 12 has variable orders in all three senses; with the semiclassical parameter equal to 1 it would
supply the elliptic estimate at a variable s over {r > r_Γ}, but no result of this chapter needs it.

### 11.2 The calculus

#### 11.2.1 The statements used

The following statements of [HJS] are used as black boxes. They are stated in [HJS] on ℝⁿ for every n, so they hold at
n = 4; page numbers are those printed in [HJS]. Every operator below has Schwartz kernel supported in X̃ × X̃, and
X̄ ⊂ ℝ̄⁴, so the calculus on ℝ⁴ is the calculus used.

(C1) (Composition, [HJS, (2.1), p. 9]; principal symbol, [HJS, pp. 49–50].) Ψ^(m,ℓ)_sc ∘ Ψ^(m′,ℓ′)_sc ⊂
Ψ^(m+m′,ℓ+ℓ′)_sc. By [HJS, Proposition 7.4], "A ∈ Ψ^(m,l)_sc(M) ⇒ A∗ ∈ Ψ^(m,l)_sc(M)", and
"σ_(m₁+m₂,l₁+l₂)(AB) = σ_(m₁,l₁)(A) σ_(m₂,l₂)(B)" [HJS, (7.29)], the principal symbol taking values in
S^(m,l)_sc/S^(m−1,l−1)_sc [HJS, Definition 7.2].

(C2) (Commutators, [HJS, Proposition 7.5, p. 50].) "[A, B] ∈ Ψ^(m₁+m₂−1,l₁+l₂−1)_sc(M) and
σ(i[A, B]) = {σ(A), σ(B)}", the Poisson bracket being H_p a, with the scattering Hamilton vector field of
[HJS, (7.34)].

(C3) (Boundedness, [HJS, Proposition 3.11 and Remark 3.12, p. 20].) "If A ∈ Ψ^(m,l)_sc, then, for all s, r ∈ ℝ, A maps
A : H^(s,r)_sc → H^(s−m,r−l)_sc … and does so boundedly"; and "Op(a), viewed as an element of
L(H^(s,r)_sc, H^(s−m,r−l)_sc), depends continuously on a". Since a ↦ Op(a) is linear and continuous from the Fréchet
space S^(m,l)_sc to a Banach space, it is bounded by one seminorm: a family bounded in Ψ^(m,l) is uniformly bounded
H^(s,r) → H^(s−m,r−l).

(C4) (Compactness, [HJS, Proposition 3.13, p. 20]; duality, [HJS, Proposition 3.7, p. 19].) "For any s, s′, r, r′,
with s < s′ and r < r′, the embedding H^(s′,r′)_sc ↪ H^(s,r)_sc is compact." The L² pairing identifies (H^(s,r)_sc)∗
with H^(−s,−r)_sc.

(C5) (Ellipticity, [HJS, Propositions 2.3, 4.9, 4.10 and 10.1, pp. 12, 27–29, 79].) "Every elliptic element of the
scattering calculus has a parametrix" (Proposition 2.3). There is a microlocal parametrix at a closed subset of the
elliptic set (Proposition 4.10: "AB − 1, BA − 1 have WF′_sc disjoint from p. This also applies with p replaced by any
closed subset"), also for variable orders (Proposition 10.1). Microlocality (Proposition 4.9):
"WF^(s,r)_sc(Au) ⊆ WF^(s+m,r+l)_sc(u) ∩ WF′_sc(A)".

(C6) (Variable orders, [HJS, Sections 10.1–10.3, pp. 77–80].) The symbol classes S^(m,l)_sc with l variable are defined
with the vector fields ⟨x⟩^(−δ)𝒱_b [HJS, (10.3)–(10.4)], so that "the logarithmic factor" in derivatives of
⟨x⟩^(l(x,ξ)) costs an arbitrary δ > 0; composition and the principal symbol are as in [HJS, Section 10.2]; and the
spaces [HJS, Definition 10.2 and Section 10.3] are independent of the choices and Hilbert, with Ψ^(m,l)_sc bounded on
them.

(C7) (Bundles, [HJS, Section 7.5, pp. 52–53].) "Ψ^(m,l)_sc(M; E, F) := C^∞(X; Hom(E, F)) ⊗ Ψ^(m,l)_sc(M) …
Equivalently, an element in Ψ^(m,l)_sc(M; E, F) is a matrix with entries in Ψ^(m,l)_sc(M)."

(C8) (A regularising family, [HJS, Lemma 12.5, p. 95].) T_t := χ(t⟨z⟩) Op(χ(⟨tζ⟩)) ∈ Ψ^(−∞,−∞)_sc, t ∈ (0, t₀], with
T_t → Id strongly on each H^(s,r)_sc; the proof of [HJS, Lemma 12.5] records "T_r being uniformly bounded in
Ψ^(0,0)_sc and T_r → Id in the operator topology of Ψ^(δ,δ)_sc".

In the interior, at fibre infinity, the scattering calculus restricted to kernels supported in a compact set is the
classical calculus, and the scattering principal symbol there is the classical one: over a compact set ⟨x⟩ is bounded
above and below, so the scattering estimates of order (m, ℓ) for symbols supported over it are the Kohn–Nirenberg
estimates of order m.

#### 11.2.2 Matrix-valued operators

Write Ψ^(m,ℓ) := Ψ^(m,ℓ)_sc(ℝ⁴; ℂ^(N_E)), the N_E × N_E matrices with entries in Ψ^(m,ℓ)_sc(ℝ⁴), by (C7), and
H^(s,𝗋) := (H^(s,𝗋)_sc)^(N_E). The principal symbol of A = (A_ij) is the matrix (σ(A_ij)).

**Lemma 11.4** (Matrix-valued operators.) (a) Ψ^(m,ℓ) ∘ Ψ^(m′,ℓ′) ⊂ Ψ^(m+m′,ℓ+ℓ′) and σ(AB) = σ(A)σ(B), a
matrix product.

(b) For a fibre inner product h, A^(∗h) ∈ Ψ^(m,ℓ) and σ(A^(∗h)) = σ(A)^(∗h) := H⁻¹σ(A)^†H.

(c) If A = ã Id with ã ∈ Ψ^(m,ℓ)_sc scalar, and B ∈ Ψ^(m′,ℓ′), then [A, B] ∈ Ψ^(m+m′−1,ℓ+ℓ′−1) and
σ(i[A, B]) = H_a σ(B), entrywise. If A ∈ Ψ^(m,ℓ) has scalar principal symbol a Id, and B has scalar principal symbol
b Id, then [A, B] ∈ Ψ^(m+m′−1,ℓ+ℓ′−1) and σ(i[A, B]) = (H_a b) Id. More generally, if A has scalar principal symbol,
then [A, B] ∈ Ψ^(m+m′−1,ℓ+ℓ′−1) for every B ∈ Ψ^(m′,ℓ′): write A = ã Id + A′ with A′ ∈ Ψ^(m−1,ℓ−1) and use the first
statement and (a). This is what is meant below when a commutator with an operator of scalar principal symbol lowers
both orders.

(d) The statements (C3)–(C6) and (C8) hold for Ψ^(m,ℓ) and H^(s,𝗋), with T_t Id in (C8), ellipticity meaning that the
principal symbol is invertible with inverse bounded in the inverse orders.

*Proof.* (a) (AB)_ij = Σ_k A_ik B_kj, with (C1) entrywise. (b) (A∗)_ij = (A_ji)∗, so σ(A∗) = σ(A)^† by (C1).
Multiplication by H or H⁻¹ lies in Ψ^(0,0): a function smooth on ℝ̄⁴ is a symbol of order (0, 0), its x-derivatives of
order k being O(⟨x⟩^(−k)). Then (a) gives (b). (c) [ã Id, B]_ij = [ã, B_ij], with (C2). For the second statement
write A = ã Id + A′ and B = b̃ Id + B′, with A′ ∈ Ψ^(m−1,ℓ−1) and B′ ∈ Ψ^(m′−1,ℓ′−1). Then
[A′, B′] ∈ Ψ^(m+m′−2,ℓ+ℓ′−2) by (a); [ã Id, B′] and [A′, b̃ Id] lie there by the first statement; and [ã, b̃] gives
H_a b. (d) Boundedness, compactness and duality are statements about each entry. For an elliptic A, take
B₀ := Op(σ(A)⁻¹χ) for a cut-off χ, and run the Neumann series of [HJS, Proposition 2.3] with matrices: AB₀ = Id − R₁,
R₁ ∈ Ψ^(−1,−1) by (a), and the asymptotic sum Σ_j R₁^j exists entrywise. The microlocal versions are identical. ∎

**Lemma 11.5** (Square roots.) Let 𝒦 be a compact set of h-self-adjoint endomorphisms with spectra in
[c, ∞), c > 0. Then Q ↦ Q^(1/2), the h-positive square root, is real-analytic on a neighbourhood of 𝒦 in
End ℂ^(N_E), with

    Q^(1/2) = (2πi)⁻¹ ∮_γ z^(1/2) (z − Q)⁻¹ dz,

γ a fixed contour in {Re z > 0} around [c/2, C]. Consequently, if q is an h-self-adjoint symbol in a bounded family in
S^(2μ,2ν) (possibly with variable orders), with q ≥ c⟨ξ⟩^(2μ)⟨x⟩^(2ν) on a set W of phase space, then on W, q^(1/2) is
an h-self-adjoint symbol, bounded in S^(μ,ν), and (q^(1/2))² = q.

*Proof.* The integral is Q^(1/2) for Q h-self-adjoint with spectrum inside γ: diagonalise Q in an h-orthonormal basis
and use Cauchy's formula. It is holomorphic in the entries of Q wherever γ avoids spec Q. For the symbols, set
Λ := ⟨ξ⟩^μ⟨x⟩^ν (or the variable-order elliptic weight of (C6)), so q^(1/2) = Λ(Λ⁻²q)^(1/2). Here Λ⁻²q is bounded in
S^(0,0) with values in a compact set of positive matrices; the chain rule gives the symbol estimates of (Λ⁻²q)^(1/2),
and the product rule those of q^(1/2). ∎

**Lemma 11.6** (Microlocal square root.) Let K = K^(∗h) ∈ Ψ^(2μ,2ν) have principal symbol k with
k ≥ c⟨ξ⟩^(2μ)⟨x⟩^(2ν) on a neighbourhood W of a closed set W₀ of the boundary of phase space. Then there is
L ∈ Ψ^(μ,ν) with WF′(K − L^(∗h)L) ∩ W₀ = ∅. The construction depends continuously on K, and so is uniform for bounded
families with a uniform c.

*Proof.* Let χ ∈ C^∞ equal 1 near W₀ with support in W. Set L₀ := Op(χk^(1/2)), by Lemma 11.5, and replace it by
(L₀ + L₀^(∗h))/2. Then K − L₀^(∗h)L₀ is h-self-adjoint, and by Lemma 11.4 it lies in Ψ^(2μ−1,2ν−1) microlocally
near W₀, with h-self-adjoint principal symbol k₁. Given L₀, …, L_(j−1) with
K − (Σ_(i<j) L_i)^(∗h)(Σ_(i<j) L_i) ∈ Ψ^(2μ−j,2ν−j) near W₀, of principal symbol k_j, solve
k^(1/2)l_j + l_j k^(1/2) = k_j for l_j. This Lyapunov equation has a unique solution, which is h-self-adjoint, given by

    l_j = ∫_0^∞ e^(−τk^(1/2)) k_j e^(−τk^(1/2)) dτ,

because k^(1/2) ≥ c^(1/2) on W; it lies in S^(μ−j,ν−j) by the chain rule. With L_j := Op(χl_j), the error drops one
order near W₀. Then L ∼ Σ_j L_j (asymptotic sum, (C1)). ∎

#### 11.2.3 Inner products near ∂X

**Lemma 11.7** (Adapted fibre inner products.) For every ε > 0 there is a fibre inner product h such that
½ min spec(S + S^(∗h)) ≥ S̄ − ε at every point of ∂X.

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 5.12] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* At one point p, let S(0, p) = V(D + J)V⁻¹ with D diagonal, Re D ≥ S̄ and J nilpotent upper triangular in
Jordan form. Let D_t := diag(1, t, t², …). Then D_t⁻¹(D + J)D_t = D + tJ, with ‖tJ‖ ≤ t. In the inner product
⟨u, v⟩_t := ⟨D_t⁻¹V⁻¹u, D_t⁻¹V⁻¹v⟩, S(0, p) is unitarily equivalent to D + tJ, so Re⟨Su, u⟩_t ≥ (S̄ − t)|u|²_t. Take
t = ε/2. The inequality Re h(Su, u) ≥ (S̄ − ε) h(u, u) is open in p, so it holds for this constant inner product on a
neighbourhood of p. It is also convex in h: if it holds for h₁, …, h_k, it holds for Σ χ_i h_i with χ_i ≥ 0 and
Σ χ_i = 1. Cover ∂X by finitely many such neighbourhoods, take a subordinate partition of unity, and extend the
resulting inner product smoothly to ℝ̄⁴. Since ½ min spec(S + S^(∗h)) = min_(h(u,u)=1) Re h(Su, u), this is the claim.
∎

Different estimates below use different fibre inner products. All L²_h norms are equivalent, so each estimate proved in
one inner product holds in any other with a changed constant. No single inner product needs to serve two radial sets.

### 11.3 The positive commutator lemma

Orders are pairs 𝐬 = (s, 𝗋), the decay order possibly variable (C6), with 𝟏 := (1, 1) and 𝐌 := (M, M). Inequalities
between orders hold componentwise and pointwise. For an operator family, *microsupported in K uniformly* means that the
full symbols are supported in the closed set K, modulo a family bounded in Ψ^(−∞,−∞). For a fibre inner product h and
P ∈ Ψ^𝐦, write

    P_R := Re_h P = ½(P + P^(∗h)),     P_I := Im_h P = (P − P^(∗h))/2i.

**Lemma 11.8** (One step.) Let P ∈ Ψ^𝐦, let 𝐬 be an order, 𝐤 := 𝐬 − ½(𝐦 − 𝟏), and κ ∈ (0, ½]. Let K₁ ⊂ U
with K₁ closed and U open in the boundary of phase space, and let G ∈ Ψ^(0,0) be elliptic on Ū. Suppose that for
ε ∈ (0, 1] there are the following.

(i) Ǎ_ε = Ǎ_ε^(∗h), bounded in Ψ^𝐤, in Ψ^(𝐤−κ𝟏) for each ε, and microsupported in K₁ uniformly.

(ii) For a sign ς ∈ {1, −1}, the operator C_ε := i[P_R, Ǎ_ε²] + Ǎ_ε²P_I + P_IǍ_ε² satisfies

    ςC_ε = −B_ε^(∗h)B_ε − F_ε + E_ε^(∗h)E_ε + J_εP + R_ε.    (11.6)

The operators in (11.6) are as follows. B_ε is bounded in Ψ^𝐬, lies in Ψ^(𝐬−κ𝟏) for each ε, and converges to
B₀ in Ψ^(𝐬+δ𝟏) for every δ > 0. Ǎ_ε = Z_εB_ε + Y_ε, with Z_ε bounded in Ψ^(−½(𝐦−𝟏)) and Y_ε bounded in Ψ^(𝐤−𝟏).
⟨F_εw, w⟩_h ≥ −C_F‖w‖²_(−𝐌) for every Schwartz w (F_ε is never paired with u itself, so it may have any order). E_ε
is bounded in Ψ^𝐬 and lies in Ψ^(𝐬−κ𝟏) for each ε, J_ε lies in Ψ^(2𝐬−𝐦), and R_ε in Ψ^(2𝐬−𝟏). All of these are
microsupported in K₁ uniformly, E_ε in a closed set K_E, and J_ε in a closed set K_J ⊂ Ell(P).

Let E ∈ Ψ^(0,0) be elliptic on K_E. Then there is C such that for every u ∈ H^(−𝐌) with Gu ∈ H^(𝐬−κ𝟏),
GPu ∈ H^(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) and Eu ∈ H^𝐬, we have B₀u ∈ L² and

    ‖B₀u‖² ≤ C(‖GPu‖²_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖Eu‖²_𝐬 + ‖Gu‖²_(𝐬−½𝟏) + ‖u‖²_(−𝐌)).    (11.7)

C depends only on C_F, on bounds for the families in their classes, and on finitely many seminorms of P, G and E.

*Proof.* Norms are those of L²_h and of H^𝐭 (any fixed choice, (C6)); C changes from line to line.

*Step 0: microlocalisation.* By (C5) there is Φ ∈ Ψ^(0,0) with WF′(Φ) ⊂ Ell(G) and
WF′(Id − Φ) ∩ (K₁ ∪ K_E ∪ K_J) = ∅. Let v := Φu. The microlocal parametrix of G gives

    ‖v‖_𝐭 ≤ C(‖Gu‖_𝐭 + ‖u‖_(−𝐌))  (𝐭 ≤ 𝐬 − κ𝟏),     ‖ΦPu‖_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) ≤ C(‖GPu‖_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)),

and Pv = ΦPu + [P, Φ]u. Here WF′([P, Φ]) ⊂ WF′(Id − Φ), which is disjoint from K₁. So if W_ε is any family bounded in
some Ψ^𝐭 and microsupported in K₁ uniformly, then W_ε[P, Φ] and W_ε(Id − Φ) are bounded in Ψ^(−∞,−∞) (by the
composition formula (C1): the product of the symbols vanishes, and the remainders are bounded by seminorms). In
particular

    ‖Ǎ_εPv‖_(½(𝟏−𝐦)+κ𝟏) ≤ C(‖GPu‖_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)),    (11.8)

because Ǎ_ε ∈ Ψ^(𝐤−κ𝟏) maps H^(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) to H^(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏−𝐤+κ𝟏) = H^(½(𝟏−𝐦)+κ𝟏). The bound (11.8) holds for
each ε > 0, with a constant that may depend on ε. Likewise Ǎ_εv ∈ H^(½(𝐦−𝟏)) for each ε > 0, as v ∈ H^(𝐬−κ𝟏). Both
pairings below are therefore of H^𝐭 with H^(𝐭′), 𝐭 + 𝐭′ ≥ 0, and are defined by (C4).

*Step 1: the pairing.* For ε > 0 and Schwartz w,

    ⟨C_εw, w⟩ = 2 Im⟨Ǎ_εPw, Ǎ_εw⟩.    (11.9)

This is algebra: 2 Im⟨Ǎ_εPw, Ǎ_εw⟩ = (1/i)⟨(Ǎ_ε²P − P^(∗h)Ǎ_ε²)w, w⟩, and
Ǎ²P − P^(∗h)Ǎ² = [Ǎ², P_R] + i(Ǎ²P_I + P_IǍ²). Let w_t := T_tv with T_t from (C8). We show that the right side of
(11.9) at w = w_t tends to its value at v; C_ε itself is never applied to v, since with an absorbing term of
top order it need not act on H^(𝐬−κ𝟏). As t → 0, w_t → v in H^(𝐬−κ𝟏), and Ǎ_εw_t → Ǎ_εv in H^(½(𝐦−𝟏)).

Write Pv = ΦPu + [P, Φ]u (Step 0), so that Ǎ_εPw_t = Ǎ_εT_tΦPu + Ǎ_εT_t[P, Φ]u + Ǎ_ε[P, T_t]v. (This avoids
[Ǎ_ε, T_t], which for a variable decay order is bounded only in ⋂_δ Ψ^(𝐤−κ𝟏−𝟏+(0,δ)) [HJS, p. 79].) The first term
tends to Ǎ_εΦPu in H^(½(𝟏−𝐦)+κ𝟏), since T_t → Id strongly on H^(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) and Ǎ_ε ∈ Ψ^(𝐤−κ𝟏) for the fixed ε. The
second is bounded in Ψ^(−∞,−∞) uniformly in t, as Ǎ_ε and [P, Φ] have disjoint microsupports and T_t is bounded in
Ψ^(0,0), and it tends to Ǎ_ε[P, Φ]u. In the third, [P, T_t] is bounded in Ψ^(𝐦−𝟏) and tends to 0 in Ψ^(𝐦−𝟏+δ𝟏)
(Lemma 11.4 (c); P has constant orders), so the term is bounded in H^(½(𝟏−𝐦)), since v ∈ H^(𝐬−κ𝟏), and tends to
0 as distributions, hence weakly in H^(½(𝟏−𝐦)). A weakly null sequence paired with a strongly convergent one
tends to 0. So ⟨Ǎ_εPw_t, Ǎ_εw_t⟩ → ⟨Ǎ_εPv, Ǎ_εv⟩.

*Step 2: the estimate.* By (11.6) and (11.9), for Schwartz w,

    ‖B_εw‖² ≤ −ς · 2 Im⟨Ǎ_εPw, Ǎ_εw⟩ + C_F‖w‖²_(−𝐌) + ‖E_εw‖² + ⟨J_εPw, w⟩ + ⟨R_εw, w⟩.

Take w = w_t := T_tv and let t → 0, with ε > 0 fixed. The left side tends to ‖B_εv‖², and ‖E_εw_t‖² to ‖E_εv‖², as
B_ε, E_ε ∈ Ψ^(𝐬−κ𝟏); ⟨R_εw_t, w_t⟩ → ⟨R_εv, v⟩, as R_ε ∈ Ψ^(2𝐬−𝟏) and 2κ ≤ 1; the first term converges by Step 1,
and the J-term by the splitting in (d) below. So the inequality holds with v in place of w, and F_ε has dropped out. We
bound each term uniformly in ε ∈ (0, 1].

(a) |⟨Ǎ_εPv, Ǎ_εv⟩| ≤ ‖Ǎ_εPv‖_(−½(𝐦−𝟏)) ‖Ǎ_εv‖_(½(𝐦−𝟏)). Since Ǎ_ε is bounded in Ψ^𝐤, Step 0 gives
‖Ǎ_εPv‖_(−½(𝐦−𝟏)) ≤ C(‖GPu‖_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)). Next,

    ‖Ǎ_εv‖_(½(𝐦−𝟏)) ≤ ‖Z_εB_εv‖_(½(𝐦−𝟏)) + ‖Y_εv‖_(½(𝐦−𝟏)) ≤ C‖B_εv‖ + C‖v‖_(𝐬−𝟏).

So twice the term is at most ½‖B_εv‖² + C(‖GPu‖²_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖v‖²_(𝐬−½𝟏) + ‖u‖²_(−𝐌)).

(b) C_F‖v‖²_(−𝐌) ≤ C‖u‖²_(−𝐌).

(c) E_εv = E_εu − E_ε(Id − Φ)u, and E_ε(Id − Φ) is bounded in Ψ^(−∞,−∞) (Step 0), so
‖E_εv‖ ≤ C(‖E_εu‖ + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)) ≤ C(‖Eu‖_𝐬 + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)), the last by the microlocal parametrix of E on K_E (the
commutator [E, Φ] is not residual, and is not used).

(d) Choose Φ_J ∈ Ψ^(0,0) microlocally the identity near K_J, with WF′(Φ_J) ⊂ Ell(P) and
WF′(Φ_J) ∩ WF′(Id − Φ) = ∅; this is possible as K_J is closed, lies in the open set Ell(P) and misses WF′(Id − Φ).
Then ⟨J_εPv, v⟩ = ⟨J_εPv, Φ_Jv⟩ plus a term bounded by C‖u‖²_(−𝐌), since (Id − Φ_J)^(∗h)J_ε is residual. The same
splitting at w_t gives the convergence used above, as Φ_JT_tv → Φ_Jv in H^(𝐬+κ𝟏) (the bound below puts Φ_Jv in
H^(𝐬+𝟏), and [Φ_J, T_t] is bounded in Ψ^(−1,−1) and tends to 0 strongly).
Then |⟨J_εPv, Φ_Jv⟩| ≤ ‖J_εPv‖_(−𝐬)‖Φ_Jv‖_𝐬, and the microlocal parametrix of P on WF′(Φ_J) gives
‖Φ_Jv‖_𝐬 ≤ C(‖ΦPu‖_(𝐬−𝐦) + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)).

(e) |⟨R_εv, v⟩| ≤ C‖v‖²_(𝐬−½𝟏), and ‖v‖_(𝐬−½𝟏) ≤ C(‖Gu‖_(𝐬−½𝟏) + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)).

Absorbing ½‖B_εv‖² and using Step 0,

    ‖B_εv‖² ≤ C(‖GPu‖²_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖Eu‖²_𝐬 + ‖Gu‖²_(𝐬−½𝟏) + ‖u‖²_(−𝐌))     for all ε ∈ (0, 1].

The left side is finite for each ε > 0 (as B_ε ∈ Ψ^(𝐬−κ𝟏)), so nothing is assumed about B₀v. The qualitative
hypothesis Gu ∈ H^(𝐬−κ𝟏) is used only for the limits t → 0 in Steps 1 and 2; the bound uses ‖Gu‖_(𝐬−½𝟏).

*Step 3: the limit.* B_εv is bounded in L² and tends to B₀v as distributions, since B_ε → B₀ in Ψ^(𝐬+δ𝟏). A weak
limit point in L² is therefore B₀v, with ‖B₀v‖ ≤ lim inf ‖B_εv‖. Finally B₀u = B₀v + B₀(Id − Φ)u, where
B₀(Id − Φ) ∈ Ψ^(−∞,−∞). ∎

**Lemma 11.9** (Iteration.) Let Γ be a closed subset of the boundary of phase space, U₀ an open
neighbourhood of it, and 𝐬₀ = 𝐬 − τ𝟏 with τ > 0 a constant. Suppose that for every κ ∈ (0, ½], every order
𝐬′ = 𝐬₀ + τ′𝟏 with κ ≤ τ′ ≤ τ, and every open U with Γ ⊂ U ⊂ U₀, the hypotheses of Lemma 11.8 hold with
(𝐬′, κ, U) for some closed K₁ ⊂ U. Suppose this holds with the E-terms microsupported in a closed set
K_E(U) ⊂ Ū₀ ∖ Γ (or with no E-term), and with B₀ elliptic on the closure of an open neighbourhood U′ of Γ. Let G be
elliptic on Ū₀. Then there are a neighbourhood U_* of Γ and a closed set K_E^∗ ⊂ Ū₀ ∖ Γ such that for every
E ∈ Ψ^(0,0) elliptic on K_E^∗, every B ∈ Ψ^(0,0) microsupported in U_* and every 𝐌,

    ‖Bu‖_𝐬 ≤ C(‖GPu‖_(𝐬−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖Eu‖_𝐬 + ‖Gu‖_(𝐬₀) + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)),    (11.10)

in the strong sense: if the right side is finite, so is the left.

*Proof.* Let J be an integer with J ≥ 4τ, let κ := τ/J ≤ ¼, and let 𝐬_j := 𝐬₀ + jκ𝟏, so that 𝐬_j − κ𝟏 = 𝐬_(j−1).
Construct U₀ ⊃ U₁ ⊃ … ⊃ U_J ⊃ Γ inductively, U_j being the U′ of the hypothesis for (𝐬_j, κ, U_(j−1)), with B₀^(j)
elliptic on Ū_j, and let K_E^∗ := ⋃_(j=1)^J K_E(U_(j−1)), a finite union of closed sets missing Γ (the sets move with
U, so one K_E need not serve every step). Let 𝒢₀ := G and, for j ≥ 1, let 𝒢_j ∈ Ψ^(0,0) be elliptic on Ū_j with
WF′(𝒢_j) ⊂ Ell(B₀^(j)), so that ‖𝒢_ju‖_(𝐬_j) ≤ C(‖B₀^(j)u‖ + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)) by (C5). Lemma 11.8 with
(𝐬_j, κ, U_(j−1), 𝒢_(j−1)) needs 𝒢_(j−1)u ∈ H^(𝐬_j−κ𝟏) = H^(𝐬_(j−1)) and gives

    ‖B₀^(j)u‖ ≤ C(‖𝒢_(j−1)Pu‖_(𝐬_j−𝐦+𝟏) + ‖Eu‖_(𝐬_j) + ‖𝒢_(j−1)u‖_(𝐬_(j−1)) + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)).

Here ‖𝒢_(j−1)Pu‖ ≤ C(‖GPu‖ + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)), since U_(j−1) ⊂ U₀, and ‖Eu‖_(𝐬_j) ≤ ‖Eu‖_𝐬. Inducting on j gives
(11.10) with U_* := U_J, using ‖Bu‖_𝐬 ≤ C(‖B₀^(J)u‖ + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)). The strong sense holds because the
qualitative hypothesis of each step, 𝒢_(j−1)u ∈ H^(𝐬_(j−1)), is the conclusion of the previous step. ∎

**Remark 11.10** (Logarithmic losses.) With variable orders, symbols of the commutants carry factors log ϱ
(C6). Suppose, in Lemma 11.8, that B_ε is only bounded in Ψ^(𝐬+δ𝟏) for every δ > 0, and R_ε only in
Ψ^(2𝐬−𝟏+δ𝟏), while the other hypotheses hold as stated, κ < ½, and B₀ has principal symbol bounded below by c > 0
times an elliptic weight of order 𝐬. Then the conclusion holds with the a priori term ‖Gu‖_(𝐬−κ𝟏). The proof is
unchanged, except that (e) is bounded by C‖v‖²_(𝐬−½𝟏+δ𝟏) ≤ C‖v‖²_(𝐬−κ𝟏) for δ ≤ ½ − κ, and
‖Bu‖_𝐬 ≤ C(‖B₀u‖ + ‖u‖_(−𝐌)) for B microsupported in Ell(B₀): b₀⁻¹ is bounded by the inverse weight, so it is a
symbol of order −𝐬 in the class of (C6). Lemma 11.9 holds with this variant, since its steps have κ ≤ ¼. For
