- (D2) if γ(0) ∈ Γ_u^♮, then as long as it stays in Γ(ε_Γ) backward in time it stays in Γ_u^♮, |φ_s^♮| decreases
  exponentially, and γ(t) → Γ as t → −∞ (the ω-limit points lie in Γ_u^♮ ∩ Γ_s^♮ = Γ);
- (D3) if γ(0) ∈ Γ_u^♮ ∖ Γ, then γ leaves Γ(ε_Γ) in finite forward time.

Combined with (H8) (a)–(b): a point of Σ_(z_0) near Γ not on Γ_u^♮ is not on the corresponding global set, so its
backward V-curve leaves Γ(ε_Γ) and tends to the radial sets.

#### 12.6.3 The lossless estimate

**Proposition 12.37** (Cf. [Hin26c, (9.83)].) Let 𝐏′ := 𝐏 + h𝐗 with 𝐗 = 𝐗(z) ∈ Ψ^0 microsupported near Γ
and continuous in z (as the X of Lemma 12.36), and let p′^♮ := p^♮ + ςσ(Im 𝐗(z_0)) (so that ςh⁻¹ Im 𝐏′ has symbol
p′^♮ − ℓq^♮ up to O(Im z)). Let γ ∈ ℝ with sup_(ϖ∈Γ) max spec(p′^♮(ϖ) − γq^♮(ϖ)) < 0. There are ν′ > 0 and, for every
neighbourhood U of Γ, operators B, E, G ∈ Ψ^0 microsupported in U, B elliptic at Γ, WF′_h(E) ∩ Γ_u^♮ = ∅, such that
for z ∈ z_0 + i[hγ, ν′] with Im z ≥ −ν′, h < h_0 and all M,

    ‖Bu‖ ≤ C(h⁻¹‖G𝐏′u‖ + ‖Eu‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)).    (12.39)

For 𝐗 = 0 the condition is γ > γ_+, with γ_+ of (12.4).

*Proof.* With χ_0 as in the proof of Lemma 12.29, let ψ_u := χ_0(M_1(φ_u^♮)²), ψ_s := χ_0(M_1(φ_s^♮)²),
ψ_Σ := χ_0(M_Σ G_(z_0)²) and ǎ := χ_(O′)ψ_uψ_sψ_Σ, with M_Σ ≥ M_1 ≥ M_0 large (M_0 ≥ 2ε_Γ^(−2)); by the cut-offs
paragraph of Section 12.6.2, supp ǎ ⊂ Γ(√(2/M_1)) (for M_Σ ≥ M_1), and χ_(O′) = 1 near supp ǎ. Compute
(12.37) with a = ǎ². First, with χ_0χ_0′ ≤ 0,

    Vψ_u² = 4M_1 χ_0χ_0′(M_1(φ_u^♮)²) φ_u^♮ (−ν_u^♮φ_u^♮ + j_u^♮G_(z_0)),
    Vψ_s² = 4M_1 χ_0χ_0′(M_1(φ_s^♮)²) φ_s^♮ (ν_s^♮φ_s^♮ + j_s^♮G_(z_0)).

On supp χ_0′(M_1(φ_u^♮)²) ∩ supp ψ_Σ we have (φ_u^♮)² ≥ M_1⁻¹ and G_(z_0)² ≤ 2M_Σ⁻¹,
so |j_u^♮G_(z_0)| ≤ ¼ν_min|φ_u^♮| once M_Σ ≥ CM_1; then Vψ_u² = e_u² ≥ 0 with
e_u := 2M_1^(1/2) χ_u |φ_u^♮| (ν_u^♮ − j_u^♮G_(z_0)/φ_u^♮)^(1/2), χ_u := √(−χ_0χ_0′)(M_1(φ_u^♮)²), smooth, and
likewise Vψ_s² = −f_s². The O((Im z)²) term of (12.37) changes these by at most
C(Im z)²M_1|φ| · |χ_0χ_0′|, which keeps the signs and smoothness for Im z ≤ ν′, ν′ small depending on M_1. The
derivative of ψ_Σ is supported where G_(z_0)² ≥ M_Σ⁻¹, where G_z is elliptic for ν′ small; it gives a term J𝐏′ as in
Lemma 12.29. Next, on supp ǎ,

    p′_z^♮ − ℓq^♮ = (p′_z^♮ − γq^♮) − (ℓ − γ)q^♮,

where p′_z^♮ := p′^♮ + ςσ(Im 𝐗(z) − Im 𝐗(z_0)) is the symbol at z. p′^♮ − γq^♮ ≤ −c Id there for M_1 large, by the
hypothesis and continuity, and p′_z^♮ − γq^♮ ≤ −(c/2) Id for Im z ≤ ν′, ν′ small depending on M_1; the symbol b below is
built from the symbol at z. So, with b := ǎ(−2(p′_z^♮ − γq^♮))^(1/2) (the positive square root of a positive definite
smooth matrix function, smooth),

    ςC = −B*B − F_s*F_s + E_u*E_u + J𝐏′ − 2(ℓ − γ)Ǎ ςϵ_♭𝒬 Ǎ + R,     R ∈ h^(1/2)Ψ^0,

where ςϵ_♭𝒬 = z_0𝒬 has principal symbol q^♮ ≥ β_Γ on supp ǎ; since 0 ≤ ℓ − γ ≤ 3h⁻¹, the paragraph on positivity
of absorbing terms in Section 12.3.3 makes 2(ℓ − γ)Ǎz_0𝒬Ǎ a term F of Lemma 12.19, with the double commutator in
R. Lemma 12.19 and Lemma 12.20, with Λ := Γ and the sets Γ(√(2/M_1)) for an increasing sequence of M_1 in
[M_0, 2M_0] (and M_Σ := CM_1), give (12.39) with E elliptic on the union of the sets supp e_u, which lie in
{(φ_u^♮)² ≥ M_0⁻¹ · ½} (as M_1 ≤ 2M_0) and so avoid Γ_u^♮. Here ν′ was chosen depending on M_1, hence on U; for
ν′(U) ≤ Im z ≤ ν′, ν′ the constant of Section 12.6.2, 𝐏′ is elliptic near Γ (Lemma 12.1 (d)) and
Proposition 12.22 gives (12.39) with the same operators, so the ν′ of the statement does not depend on U. ∎

#### 12.6.4 Defect measures with values in matrices

In this section and the next, h_j → 0 is a sequence, the u_j are ℂ^(N_E)-valued, and we drop j. U is an open
precompact set at finite frequencies over the interior of K_Γ. The family is *tempered on U* if
‖u‖_(−M_t) ≤ C h^(−M_t) for some M_t and sup ‖Gu‖ < ∞ for some G ∈ Ψ^0 elliptic on Ū.

**Lemma 12.38** (Cf. [Hin26c, Lemma 9.30], on E.) If (u_j) is tempered on U, a subsequence has a *defect
measure* on U: a positive semidefinite End(ℂ^(N_E))-valued Radon measure μ on U, such that
⟨Bu, u⟩ → ∫_U tr(b dμ) for every B ∈ Ψ^0 with WF′_h(B) a compact subset of U and principal symbol
b ∈ C_c^∞(U; End ℂ^(N_E)). Write ν := tr μ ≥ 0; then μ has a density dμ/dν with respect to ν, with dμ/dν ≥ 0 and
tr(dμ/dν) = 1 ν-almost everywhere, and for every Hermitian continuous p, tr(p dμ) ≤ max spec(p) dν.

*Proof.* (a) For B as stated, limsup |⟨Bu, u⟩| ≤ C_b := sup|b| · sup_Ū |g|^(−2) · sup ‖Gu‖², where the G of the
definition is taken scalar with principal symbol g, |g| ≥ c > 0 on Ū. As in [Hin26c, (9.87)–(9.88)], B = G*QG + R with
Q ∈ Ψ^0 of principal symbol q := b|g|^(−2) ∈ C_c^∞(U) (the construction of Proposition 12.14), so that R ∈ hΨ^0 is
microsupported in Ell_h(G) up to a term in h^∞Ψ^(−∞); then R = G*R′G + R″ with R′ ∈ hΨ^0 and R″ residual. By
Theorem 12.11, |⟨QGu, Gu⟩| ≤ (sup|q| + ϵ + Ch^(1/4))‖Gu‖² for every ϵ > 0,
and |⟨Ru, u⟩| ≤ Ch sup‖Gu‖² + C_M h^M ‖u‖²_(−M_t) = o(1) by temperedness.

(b) The value depends only on b: two such B with the same b differ by hΨ^0 plus residual terms, whose pairings tend to
0 by (a).

(c) A diagonal argument over a countable dense subset of C_c^∞(U; End ℂ^(N_E)) (dense in C_c in the supremum norm on
each compact set) gives a subsequence along which L(b) := lim ⟨Op_h(b)u, u⟩ exists for all b in that set, and by (a) L
extends to a linear functional on C_c(U; End ℂ^(N_E)), continuous for the supremum norm on each compact set. By the
Riesz representation theorem applied to each matrix entry, L(b) = ∫ tr(b dμ) for a matrix of complex Radon measures.

(d) Positivity: let b ≥ 0 with supp b ⊂ K_b ⋐ U, and j ∈ C_c^∞(U) scalar, 0 ≤ j ≤ 1, equal to 1 on K_b. For ϵ > 0,
b + ϵj² Id is positive definite on K_b and equal to ϵj² Id off K_b, so it is q_ϵ*q_ϵ with q_ϵ ∈ C_c^∞(U) (on K_b the
positive square root; off K_b, √ϵ j, which is smooth as j ≥ 0); then
Op_h(b) + ϵ Op_h(j)* Op_h(j) = Op_h(q_ϵ)* Op_h(q_ϵ) + hR′, so liminf ⟨Op_h(b)u, u⟩ ≥ −ϵ limsup ‖Op_h(j)u‖² ≥ −Cϵ.
Hence L(b) ≥ 0 for b ≥ 0; taking b = φvv* with φ ≥ 0 scalar and v ∈ ℂ^(N_E) shows v*μv ≥ 0, so μ is Hermitian and
positive semidefinite. Each entry is then absolutely continuous with respect to ν (|μ_ab| ≤ ν for a positive matrix
measure), which gives dμ/dν; and tr(p dμ/dν) ≤ max spec(p) tr(dμ/dν) as dμ/dν ≥ 0. ∎

**Lemma 12.39** (Cf. [Hin26c, Lemmas 9.31–9.32], on E.) Let (u_j) be tempered on U with defect measure μ, and
𝐏_j := 𝐏_(h_j,z_j) with Im z_j/h_j → η ∈ [0, ∞).

(a) If ‖G𝐏_ju_j‖ = o(1) with G elliptic on Ū, then supp μ ⊂ Σ_(z_0).

(b) For real scalar a ∈ C_c^∞(U), and Y ∈ Ψ^0 microsupported in U with WF′_h(I − Y) ∩ supp a = ∅,

    |∫_U (Va dν + 2a tr((p^♮ − ηq^♮) dμ))| ≤ 4 sup|a| limsup h⁻¹‖Y𝐏u‖ ‖Yu‖.    (12.40)

(c) The same holds with 𝐏 replaced by a self-adjoint Φ ∈ Ψ^0 with real scalar principal symbol φ, with Va replaced by
H_φ a and with p^♮ − ηq^♮ replaced by 0.

*Proof.* (a) For b ∈ C_c^∞(U) with supp b ∩ Σ_(z_0) = ∅, 𝐏_j is elliptic on supp b for j large, so
Op_h(b) = Q𝐏_j + R with Q bounded and R ∈ h^∞Ψ^(−∞) near supp b, and ∫ |b|² dν = lim ‖Op_h(b)u‖² = 0.

(b) With A = A* quantising a Id and WF′_h(A) ⊂ supp a, (12.14) gives (2/h) Im⟨𝐏u, Au⟩ = ⟨Cu, u⟩, and by
(12.37) the principal symbol of ςC is Va + 2a(p^♮ − ℓ_jq^♮) + O((Im z_j)²), which converges in C_c^∞ to
Va + 2a(p^♮ − ηq^♮); as ⟨Op_h(c_j − c)u, u⟩ → 0 when c_j → c uniformly (Lemma 12.38 (a)),
⟨ςCu, u⟩ → ∫ tr((Va + 2a(p^♮ − ηq^♮)) dμ), and tr(Va dμ) = Va dν for scalar a. The left side is bounded by
(2/h)(‖Y𝐏u‖ + O(h^∞))(‖AYu‖ + O(h^∞)) and ‖AYu‖ ≤ (sup|a| + ϵ + Ch^(1/4))‖Yu‖ by Theorem 12.11, with ϵ ≤ sup|a|.

(c) is the same argument with Im Φ = 0. ∎

#### 12.6.5 The estimate with loss one

**Proposition 12.40** (Cf. [Hin26c, Theorem 9.28] with loss one.) Let β > γ_− and U a neighbourhood of Γ.
There are B, E, G ∈ Ψ^0 microsupported in U, B elliptic at Γ, WF′_h(E) ∩ Γ_u^♮ = ∅, with: every backward V-curve from a
point of WF′_h(B) ∖ Γ_u^♮ reaches Ell_h(E) in finite time within Ell_h(G); Γ ∪ WF′_h(B) ⊂ Ell_h(G); and for
z ∈ z_0 + i[hβ, ν′], h < h_0,

    ‖Bu‖ ≤ C(h⁻²‖G𝐏u‖ + h⁻¹‖Eu‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)).    (12.41)

*Proof.* Fix γ > γ_+. For Im z ≥ hγ, (12.41) follows from (12.39). Choose B, E, G for the dynamics as
stated, with WF′_h(B) ⊂ Γ(ε_Γ)° ⊂ Ell_h(G); this is possible by (D1)–(D2). Suppose (12.41) fails for every C in
the range hβ ≤ Im z ≤ hγ. Then there are h_j → 0, z_j and u_j with

    ‖Bu‖ = 1,     ‖G𝐏u‖ = o(h²),     ‖Eu‖ = o(h),     h^M‖u‖_(−M) = o(1),    (12.42)

and after passing to a subsequence Im z_j/h_j → η ∈ [β, γ] and (u_j) has a defect measure μ on U_1, an open
neighbourhood of Γ with Ū_1 ⊂ Ell_h(B) (B itself shows that (u_j) is tempered on U_1, and h^M‖u‖_(−M) = o(1) gives the
bound on ‖u‖_(−M)). We use Proposition 12.25 and Corollary 12.26 (real principal type) for the 𝐏_j, with
constants uniform in j; for Im z_j < 0 they hold near Γ because ℓ_j is bounded, so ℓ_j𝒬 is a bounded term of the class
of 𝒫_1 over the compact set K_Γ, and the absorbing sign is not needed (Remark 12.27).

*Localisation.* For ϖ ∈ U_1 ∖ Γ_u^♮, the backward V-curve from ϖ reaches Ell_h(E) within Ell_h(G), so
Corollary 12.26 gives ‖B′u‖ ≤ C(h⁻¹‖G𝐏u‖ + ‖Eu‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)) = o(1) for B′ elliptic at ϖ; so ϖ ∉ supp μ. With
Lemma 12.39 (a), supp μ ⊂ Γ_u^♮ ∩ Σ_(z_0). By (D2), backward curves from Γ_u^♮ ∩ WF′_h(B) reach any neighbourhood
of Γ; so with E′ elliptic on Γ, ‖Bu‖ ≤ C(h⁻¹‖G𝐏u‖ + ‖Eu‖ + ‖E′u‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)), and it suffices to find such E′
with ‖E′u‖ → 0. Taking WF′_h(E′) ⊂ Γ(δ), ‖E′u‖² → ∫ |e′|² dν, and it suffices to show 𝗆(δ) = 0 for some δ > 0, where

    𝗆(x) := ν(Γ_u^♮ ∩ Γ(ε_Γ) ∩ {|φ_s^♮| < x}).

*Step 1: an auxiliary equation.* Let Φ, N_u, J_u ∈ Ψ^0 be self-adjoint quantisations of φ_u^♮ Id, ν_u^♮ Id,
j_u^♮ Id, cut off to U_1 and equal to the uncut quantisations modulo h^∞ near Γ(ε_Γ). By Theorem 12.8 and
(12.37) (the symbols being scalar, the commutator of the matrix-valued lower order part of 𝐏 with Φ is in h²Ψ),
ς(i/h)[𝐏, Φ] = −N_uΦ + J_u𝐏 + hR + R_away, with R ∈ Ψ^0 and R_away microsupported off Γ(ε_Γ), as Im z = O(h). Hence
f := 𝐏u gives

    (𝐏 − iςhN_u)Φu = (Φ − iςhJ_u)f − iςh²Ru + R′_away u.    (12.43)

The operator 𝐏′ := 𝐏 − iςhN_u is of the form of Proposition 12.37 with p′^♮ = p^♮ − ν_u^♮, and
sup_Γ max spec(p^♮ − βq^♮ − ν_u^♮) ≤ sup_Γ max spec(p_1^Γ − βq^♮) − ν_min < 0, because β > γ_− means
sup_Γ max spec(p_1^Γ − βq^♮) < ½ν_min. So Proposition 12.37 applies to 𝐏′ with γ := β, on a small neighbourhood of Γ,
with operators B_1, E_1, G_1. Its right side for Φu: h⁻¹‖G_1(…)‖ = O(h) by (12.42) and sup‖G_1u‖ < ∞;
‖E_1Φu‖ ≤ C‖E_1′u‖ + O(h^∞) with E_1′ microsupported off Γ_u^♮ near WF′_h(E_1), and ‖E_1′u‖ = o(h) by
Corollary 12.26 as in the localisation; the last term is O(h^∞). So ‖B_1Φu‖ = O(h).

*Step 2.* Fix δ_1 ∈ (0, ε_Γ) with Γ(δ_1) ⊂ U_1 ∩ Ell_h(B_1), possible as U_1 and Ell_h(B_1) are neighbourhoods of Γ.
In Steps 2–4, and in the definition of 𝗆, ε_Γ is replaced by δ_1, so that every function a below is supported in
U_1 ∩ Ell_h(B_1), where μ lives and Lemma 12.39 (c) applies. Lemma 12.39 (c) with Φ and Y a cut-off elliptic
where B_1 is gives, for real a ∈ C_c^∞(U_1 ∩ Ell_h(B_1)), |∫ H_(φ_u^♮) a dν| ≤ C_1 sup|a|, C_1 independent of a. Take
a := χ_(O′) a_0(φ_u^♮) a_1(φ_s^♮) ψ(G_(z_0)) with a_0, ψ ∈ C_c^∞((−δ_1, δ_1)) equal to 1 near 0, 0 ≤ a_0, ψ ≤ 1 (so
that a ≥ 0 in Step 3), and a_1(t) := Θ(t/δ)χ_c(t), where Θ is smooth, non-decreasing, Θ(s) = ∓1 for ±s ≤ −2,
Θ′ ≥ ½ on [−1, 1], and χ_c ∈ C_c^∞((−δ_1, δ_1)), 0 ≤ χ_c ≤ 1, equals 1 on [−δ_1/2, δ_1/2] with |χ_c′| ≤ 4/δ_1. Then |a|
≤ 1, and by the cut-offs paragraph of Section 12.6.2 a is supported in Γ(δ_1), with χ_(O′) = 1 near its support.
On supp ν ⊂ Γ_u^♮ ∩ Σ_(z_0), H_(φ_u^♮) a = a_1′(φ_s^♮){φ_u^♮, φ_s^♮} on O′ and H_(φ_u^♮) a = 0 off O′ (the other
terms contain H_(φ_u)φ_u = 0, or ψ′(G_(z_0)), which vanishes near Σ_(z_0)). Replace a_1 by ϵ_♭a_1, ϵ_♭ being the sign
of {φ_u^♮, φ_s^♮} on Γ(ε_Γ); the integrand is then a_1′(φ_s^♮)|{φ_u^♮, φ_s^♮}| on O′. For δ < δ_1/4, Θ′(t/δ) = 0
for |t| ≥ 2δ and χ_c = 1 on [−δ_1/2, δ_1/2], so a_1′ ≥ 1/(2δ) on [−δ, δ], a_1′ ≥ 0 on [−δ_1/2, δ_1/2],
and |a_1′| = |Θ(t/δ)χ_c′(t)| ≤ 4/δ_1 for δ_1/2 < |t| < δ_1. With c_Γ ≤ |{φ_u^♮, φ_s^♮}| ≤ C_Γ on Γ(δ_1) ⊂ Γ(ε_Γ), the
integral over {|φ_s^♮| < δ} is at least (c_Γ/(2δ))𝗆(δ), that over {δ ≤ |φ_s^♮| ≤ δ_1/2} is non-negative, and that
over {δ_1/2 < |φ_s^♮| < δ_1} is at least −(4C_Γ/δ_1)ν(Γ(δ_1)). So

    (c_Γ/(2δ)) 𝗆(δ) ≤ C_1 + (4C_Γ/δ_1) ν(Γ(δ_1)),     so     𝗆(δ) ≤ C_2 δ    (12.44)

with C_2 := (2/c_Γ)(C_1 + 4C_Γν(Γ(δ_1))/δ_1), independent of δ ∈ (0, δ_1/4); ν(Γ(δ_1)) is finite as Γ(δ_1) is a
compact subset of U_1.

*Step 3: propagation for logarithmic times.* Lemma 12.39 (b), with ‖G𝐏u‖ = o(h²), gives
∫(Va dν + 2a tr((p^♮ − ηq^♮) dμ)) = 0 for real a ∈ C_c^∞(U_1). Let p_η := max spec(p^♮ − ηq^♮), continuous;
for a ≥ 0 Lemma 12.38 gives ∫(Va + 2ap_η) dν ≥ 0. Since η ≥ β and q^♮ > 0, p_η ≤ max spec(p^♮ − βq^♮), and
β > γ_− gives sup_Γ p_η < ½ν_min; so we can fix κ′ with sup_(Γ(δ_1)) p_η^+/ν_s^♮ < κ′ < ½ (shrinking δ_1;
p_η^+ := max(p_η, 0)). Take a := χ_(O′) a_0(φ_u^♮) a_1(φ_s^♮) ψ(G_(z_0)) with a_0, ψ as before and
a_1(t) := |t|^(−2κ′) f(|t|), f ∈ C_c^∞((δ/2, δ_1)), f ≥ 0, f = 1 on [δ, δ_1/2], f′ ≤ 0 on [δ, ∞), |xf′(x)| ≤ 4 on
[δ/2, δ]. On supp ν, by (12.38), V|φ_s^♮|^(−2κ′) = −2κ′ν_s^♮|φ_s^♮|^(−2κ′), so

    Va + 2ap_η = ν_s^♮ |φ_s^♮|^(−2κ′) (−2(κ′ − p_η/ν_s^♮) f + |φ_s^♮| f′(|φ_s^♮|)).

This is ≤ 0 where |φ_s^♮| ≥ δ, ≤ −c_3 on {δ ≤ |φ_s^♮| ≤ δ_1/2} with c_3 > 0 independent of δ, and bounded by
Cδ^(−2κ′) on {δ/2 ≤ |φ_s^♮| ≤ δ}. Hence c_3(𝗆(δ_1/2) − 𝗆(δ)) ≤ Cδ^(−2κ′) 𝗆(δ).

*Step 4.* With (12.44), 𝗆(δ_1/2) ≤ (1 + Cδ^(−2κ′))C_2δ → 0 as δ → 0, since 2κ′ < 1. So 𝗆(δ_1/2) = 0,
contradicting ‖Bu‖ = 1 as explained. ∎

[Hin26c] writes the range in this proof as −β ≤ h⁻¹ Im z and p_z ≤ p_1 + 2ββ_Γ, while its theorem is stated for
Im(h⁻¹z) ≥ β. With the range η ≥ β the bound used is p_η ≤ max spec(p^♮ − βq^♮), and Steps 1 and 3 need exactly
sup_Γ max spec(p_1^Γ − βq^♮) < ½ν_min, which is the definition of β > γ_− in (12.4). When β < 0 this
involves the largest value of q^♮ on Γ, not the smallest, which is why (12.4) defines γ_± as these thresholds
and not through β_Γ alone (Remark 12.4). The steps and the use of {φ_u, φ_s} follow [Hin26c], which follows
[Dya16]; the matrix-valued measure enters only through tr and max spec (Lemma 12.38).

#### 12.6.6 Complex absorption

To interpolate between Proposition 12.37 and Proposition 12.40 we need an invertible problem depending holomorphically
on σ, equal to 𝐏 near Γ. As in [Hin26c] the absorbing operator is built by averaging a symbol in the time frequency,
which makes it entire in σ; here it is also written as W*W, so that its sign is exact. We write the construction for
z_0 = 1; for z_0 = −1, q̃_1 below is defined with −τ in place of τ, and the factor z_0 in (12.45) makes the
absorbing sign the right one.

Let χ_Υ ∈ C_c^∞((−1, 1)) equal 1 on [−½, ½] and Υ(σ) := (2π)⁻¹ ∫ e^(−iσs) χ_Υ(s) ds: Υ is entire,
∫_ℝ Υ(τ + iη) dτ = χ_Υ(0) = 1 for every η (shift of contour), and |∂^k Υ(τ + iη)| ≤ C_(k,M) ⟨τ⟩^(−M) e^(|η|)
(Paley–Wiener). Let q̃_0 ∈ C^∞(T*X̃°), 0 ≤ q̃_0 ≤ 1, with q̃_0 = 0 on Γ(ε_Γ/2) and q̃_0 = 1 off Γ(¾ε_Γ). Put

    a(x; τ, ζ) := (1 − χ_Υ(|(τ, ζ)|)) |(τ, ζ)| q̃_1(x; τ, ζ),
    q̃_1 := q̃_0(x, ζ/τ) if τ > 0 and (x, ζ/τ) ∈ Γ(ε_Γ),     q̃_1 := 1 otherwise.

q̃_1 is smooth and homogeneous of degree 0 on (τ, ζ) ≠ 0, because q̃_0 = 1 near the boundary of Γ(ε_Γ) and |ζ/τ| is
large near τ = 0, ζ ≠ 0; so a is a symbol of order 1 in (τ, ζ), homogeneous of degree 1 for |(τ, ζ)| ≥ 1. Let
a_♭(x; σ, ζ) := ∫ Υ(σ − τ) a(x; τ, ζ) dτ, entire in σ; for |Im σ| ≤ C, a_♭ − a(·; Re σ, ·) is a symbol of order 0 in
(Re σ, ζ), uniformly, by Taylor's formula in τ and ∫ Υ = 1. Let χ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ⁴), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, equal 1 near the base
projection of Γ(ε_Γ), and χ_1 ∈ C_c^∞ equal 1 on supp χ, both supported in the interior of K_Γ. With Op the standard
quantisation in x (dual variable ζ, σ a parameter), acting componentwise,

    Q̂_♭(σ) := χ_1 Op(a_♭(·; σ, ·)) χ_1,     Q̂(σ) := Q̂_♭(σ̄)* Q̂_♭(σ),
    P̂′(σ) := χP̂(σ)χ − iz_0(χQ̂(σ)χ + (1 − χ²)(σ² + Δ)),     P′_(h,z) := h² P̂′(z/h),    (12.45)

on ℝ⁴, Δ ≥ 0 the Euclidean Laplacian. All three terms are entire in σ (σ ↦ Q̂_♭(σ̄)* is holomorphic, being
antiholomorphic composed with the antilinear adjoint).

**Lemma 12.41** Let Re z = z_0 and Im z = hη, |η| ≤ C.

(a) W := hQ̂_♭(z/h) ∈ Ψ^((1,0,0)) has principal symbol w := χ_1² |(1, ζ)| q̃_0, and h²Q̂(z/h) = W*W + hR_W with
R_W ∈ Ψ^((1,0,0)).

(b) WF′_h(W) ∩ Γ(ε_Γ/3) = ∅; so P′_(h,z) − P_(h,z) is microlocally O(h^∞) near Γ(ε_Γ/3).

(c) P′_(h,z) is semiclassically elliptic, in the scattering sense on all of 𝒫, outside Γ(¾ε_Γ).

(d) Over {χ = 1}, h⁻¹ Im P′_(h,z) = h⁻¹ Im P_(h,z) − z_0h⁻¹W*W − z_0 Re R_W and
Re P′_(h,z) − Re P_(h,z) = z_0h Im R_W.

*Proof.* (a) For a symbol b of order l in (σ, ζ), h^l b(x; z/h, ζ/h) is a semiclassical symbol of order (l, 0, 0): its
ζ-derivatives of order k are h^(l−k)(∂^k b) at (z/h, ζ/h), bounded by C(|z|² + |ζ|²)^((l−k)/2). Hence
h(a_♭ − a)(x; z/h, ζ/h) ∈ hS^0, and h a(x; 1/h, ζ/h) = |(1, ζ)| q̃_1(x; 1, ζ) = |(1, ζ)| q̃_0(x, ζ) for h ≤ 1
(homogeneity), with q̃_0 := 1 off Γ(ε_Γ); and Op(b(x; σ, ζ)) = Op_h(b(x; σ, ζ/h)). hQ̂_♭(z̄/h) − W ∈ hΨ^0 since
a_♭(σ̄) − a_♭(σ) is of order 0; so h²Q̂ = W*W + hR_W with R_W := (h⁻¹(hQ̂_♭(z̄/h) − W))* W.

(b) If (x, ζ) ∈ Γ(ε_Γ/3) and |hτ − 1| ≤ ϵ, then (x, ζ/(hτ)) ∈ Γ(ε_Γ/2) for ϵ small (uniform continuity of φ_u, φ_s,
G_(z_0) on a compact set), so a(x; τ, ζ/h) = 0; the rest of the integral defining a_♭(x; 1/h + iη, ζ/h) is over |τ − 1/h|
≥ ϵ/h, where |Υ| ≤ C_M(h/ϵ)^M, and likewise for all derivatives. So the symbol of W is O(h^∞) in S^((1,0,0))
near Γ(ε_Γ/3), and so is R_W (which ends in W). Near the base projection of Γ(ε_Γ), χ = 1 and 1 − χ² = 0.

(c) The principal symbol of P′_(h,z) is χ²G_(z_0) − iz_0(1 + |ζ|²)(χ²q̃_0² + 1 − χ²), as χ_1 = 1 on supp χ and
z² = 1 + O(h). Its imaginary part vanishes only where χ = 1 and q̃_0 = 0, which is inside Γ(¾ε_Γ); at fibre infinity
q̃_0 = 1, and over ∂X, χ = 0 and the symbol is −iz_0(z² + |ζ|²).

(d) W*W is self-adjoint, and Im(−iX) = −Re X, Re(−iX) = Im X. ∎

By (d), in the region 0 < q̃_0 < 1, 𝐏′ ∈ {P′, P′*} has the structure of Proposition 12.25 with the additional term
−ϵ_♭z_0h⁻¹W*W in h⁻¹ Im 𝐏′ and a bounded addition to 𝒫_1; since ςϵ_♭z_0 = z_0² = 1, Remark 12.27 (b) applies, and
Proposition 12.25 holds for it.

**Lemma 12.42** (Three lines.) Let F be holomorphic near the rectangle ℛ := [a − L, a + L] + i[0, 1], with
values in a Hilbert space, ‖F‖ ≤ A on ℛ, ‖F‖ ≤ A_0 on {Im w = 0} and ‖F‖ ≤ A_1 on {Im w = 1}, where
0 < A_0, A_1 ≤ A. Then for |Re w − a| ≤ L/2 and y := Im w,

    ‖F(w)‖ ≤ A_0^(1−y) A_1^y exp(3Λ e^(−πL/4)),     Λ := log(A/min(A_0, A_1)).

*Proof.* u := log‖F‖ is subharmonic, as the supremum over unit vectors e of the subharmonic functions
log|⟨F, e⟩|, attained at each point, and upper semicontinuous. v := (1 − y) log A_0 + y log A_1 is harmonic, and so is
k(w) := cosh((π/2)(x − a)) cos((π/2)(y − ½))/cos(π/4), x := Re w; k ≥ 1 on ℛ and k ≥ cosh((π/2)L) on its vertical
sides. So u − v − Λk/cosh((π/2)L) ≤ 0 on ∂ℛ (u − v ≤ 0 on the horizontal sides and ≤ Λ on the vertical ones), hence on
ℛ by the maximum principle. For |x − a| ≤ L/2, k/cosh((π/2)L) ≤ √2 cosh((π/4)L)/cosh((π/2)L) ≤ 2√2 e^(−πL/4). ∎

**Proposition 12.43** (Cf. [Hin26c, Lemma 9.33].) Let γ_− < β < γ_+ < β′. There is h_0 such that for
z ∈ z_0 + i[hβ, hβ′] and h < h_0, P′_(h,z) : H_h^((2,0,0)) → L² is invertible, and

    ‖(P′_(h,z))⁻¹‖_(L²→L²) ≤ C h^(−1−(β′−Im(z/h))/(β′−β)).    (12.46)

Consequently, for every ϵ > 0 and z ∈ z_0 + i[h(γ_− + ϵ), h(γ_+ + ϵ)],
‖(P′_(h,z))⁻¹‖ ≤ C_ϵ h^(−1−δ_Γ(Im(z/h)−ϵ)).

*Proof.* (a) A priori estimates. Let 𝐏′ ∈ {P′, P′*}. Outside Γ(¾ε_Γ), Proposition 12.22 bounds u by
‖𝐏′u‖_(H_h^((−2,0,0))). In Γ(ε_Γ): a point of the characteristic set not on Γ_u^♮ has a backward V-curve that leaves
Γ(ε_Γ) (D1), crossing {0 < q̃_0 < 1} into {q̃_0 = 1}, where 𝐏′ is elliptic; Corollary 12.26 (with Remark 12.27)
propagates the elliptic bound along it. Near Γ, Proposition 12.40 applies, with all its operators microsupported in
Γ(ε_Γ/3), where 𝐏′ = 𝐏 modulo O(h^∞) (Lemma 12.41 (b)), its term ‖Eu‖ being bounded by the propagation just
described. Altogether, for z ∈ z_0 + i[hβ, hβ′],

    ‖u‖_(L²) ≤ C h⁻² ‖𝐏′u‖_(L²) + C h^M ‖u‖_(−M𝟏),    (12.47)

and with h⁻¹ in place of h⁻² at Im z = hβ′, using Proposition 12.37 there; the last term is absorbed for h < h_0.

(b) Invertibility. For fixed h, P′_(h,z) is elliptic in the scattering sense at fibre infinity and over ∂X
(Lemma 12.41 (c)), so it has a parametrix modulo an operator with symbol in S^(−M𝟏), M large, which is compact on
L²; so P′_(h,z) : H_h^((2,0,0)) → L² is Fredholm, and by (a) it and its adjoint are injective.

(c) Interpolation. In terms of σ = z/h, (a) gives ‖P̂′(σ)⁻¹‖_(L²→L²) ≤ C for Re σ ≥ h_0⁻¹ and Im σ ∈ [β, β′], and
≤ C|σ|⁻¹ on Im σ = β′ (here ‖P̂′(σ)u‖_(L²) = h⁻²‖P′_(h,z)u‖_(L²) with h := |Re σ|⁻¹; for z_0 = −1 use
Re σ ≤ −h_0⁻¹). For σ_0 ≥ h_0⁻¹ and f ∈ L², apply Lemma 12.42 to F(w) := P̂′(3σ_0 + iβ + (β′ − β)w)⁻¹f on
[−2σ_0/(β′ − β), 2σ_0/(β′ − β)] + i[0, 1], with A = A_0 = C‖f‖, A_1 = Cσ_0⁻¹‖f‖, L = 2σ_0/(β′ − β),
Λ = log σ_0; Λe^(−πL/4) → 0, so ‖P̂′(σ)⁻¹f‖ ≤ Cσ_0^(−(Im σ−β)/(β′−β))‖f‖ for Re σ ∈ [2σ_0, 4σ_0], with C independent
of σ_0. With |σ| ≤ 5σ_0 and
(P′_(h,z))⁻¹ = h⁻² P̂′(z/h)⁻¹ this is (12.46). For the consequence take β := γ_− + ϵ and β′ := γ_+ + ϵ; then
(β′ − η)/(β′ − β) = δ_Γ(η − ϵ) for η ∈ [β, β′]. ∎

#### 12.6.7 The precise loss

**Theorem 12.44** (Cf. [Hin26c, Theorem 9.28], on E.) Let β > γ_− and U a neighbourhood of Γ. There are
B, E, G ∈ Ψ^0 microsupported in U, with B elliptic at Γ, WF′_h(E) ∩ Γ_u^♮ = ∅, Γ ∪ WF′_h(B) ⊂ Ell_h(G), and every
backward V-curve from WF′_h(B) ∖ Γ_u^♮ reaching Ell_h(E) within Ell_h(G), such that for z ∈ z_0 + i[hβ, ν′], h < h_0,
ϵ > 0 and all M, with δ := δ_Γ(Im(z/h) − ϵ),

    ‖Bu‖ ≤ C_ϵ(h^(−1−δ)‖G𝐏u‖ + h^(−δ)‖Eu‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)).    (12.48)

*Proof.* For Im z ≥ h(γ_+ + ϵ) this is (12.39), with δ = 0; for Im z ∈ [hβ, h(γ_− + ϵ)] it is
(12.41), as then δ = 1. Let Im z ∈ [h(γ_− + ϵ), h(γ_+ + ϵ)]. We follow [HV16, Theorem 4.7] as recalled in
[Hin26c]; all operators have kernels supported over {χ = 1}². Fix c ∈ (0, ε_Γ/12). Choose B elliptic at Γ with
WF′_h(B) ⊂ Γ(c/2), and B^♯ ∈ Ψ^0 with WF′_h(B^♯) ⊂ Γ(c) and WF′_h(I − B^♯) ∩ Γ(3c/4) = ∅; Γ(c) ⊂ Γ(ε_Γ/3). Then
B(I − B^♯) is residual and, by Lemma 12.41 (b),

    Bu = B(P′_(h,z))⁻¹B^♯𝐏u + B(P′_(h,z))⁻¹[𝐏, B^♯]u + O(h^∞)‖u‖_(−M)

(for 𝐏 = P* use (P′*)⁻¹). The first term is bounded by C_ϵh^(−1−δ)(‖G𝐏u‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)) by Proposition 12.43. The
commutator is h times an operator microsupported in Γ(c) ∖ Γ(3c/4). Let X_u ∈ Ψ^0 be microsupported in
Γ(ε_Γ) ∩ {|φ_u^♮| < c/8}, with WF′_h(I − X_u) disjoint from Γ_u^♮ ∩ Γ(c), and such that backward V-curves from
WF′_h(I − X_u) ∩ Γ(c) reach Ell_h(E) ((D1), choosing E elliptic on Γ(ε_Γ) ∩ {|φ_u^♮| ≥ c/16}).

(i) By Corollary 12.26, ‖(I − X_u)[𝐏, B^♯]u‖ ≤ Ch(h⁻¹‖G𝐏u‖ + ‖Eu‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)), and Proposition 12.43 turns this
into a bound C_ϵh^(−δ)(h⁻¹‖G𝐏u‖ + ‖Eu‖ + h^M‖u‖_(−M)) for B(P′)⁻¹(I − X_u)[𝐏, B^♯]u.

(ii) f_u := X_u[𝐏, B^♯]u is microsupported in K_f := Γ(c) ∖ Γ(3c/4) ∩ {|φ_u^♮| < c/8}, where |φ_s^♮| ≥ 3c/4
or |G_(z_0)| ≥ 3c/4. Let W̃ := Op_h(w̃) Id with w̃ ∈ C_c^∞ real and scalar, w̃ ≠ 0 on Γ(c/4) and supp w̃ ⊂ Γ(c/2), and
Q̃ := W̃*W̃. Then every backward bicharacteristic of the characteristic set in Γ(ε_Γ) reaches Ell_h(Q̃) (if on Γ_u^♮,
by (D2)) or the region q̃_0 = 1, so the argument of part (a) of the proof of Proposition 12.43 (with −iz_0Q̃ as a
further absorbing term: Remark 12.27 (b) with ϵ_W := z_0 for P′, and with ϵ_W := −z_0 for the adjoint
P′* + iz_0Q̃, so ςϵ_W = 1 as in Section 12.6.6) gives ‖(P′ − iz_0Q̃)⁻¹‖ ≤ Ch⁻¹, and Lemma 12.45 applies to
P′ − iz_0Q̃. The factor z_0 in the absorbing term is needed: without it the absorbing sign is wrong for z_0 = −1. The
forward V-flowout of K_f ∩ Σ_(z_0) stays in {|φ_s^♮| ≥ 3c/4} while it remains in Γ(ε_Γ) (as |φ_s^♮| increases
forward), and the part of K_f off Σ_(z_0) is elliptic; so the flowout misses WF′_h(Q̃) ∪ WF′_h(B) ⊂ Γ(c/2). By
Lemma 12.45, Q̃(P′ − iz_0Q̃)⁻¹f_u and B(P′ − iz_0Q̃)⁻¹f_u are O(h^∞)‖u‖_(−M). Since
v := (P′)⁻¹f_u − (P′ − iz_0Q̃)⁻¹f_u satisfies P′v = −iz_0Q̃(P′ − iz_0Q̃)⁻¹f_u, Proposition 12.43 gives
‖v‖ ≤ C_Mh^M‖u‖_(−M); so ‖B(P′)⁻¹f_u‖ ≤ C_Mh^M‖u‖_(−M).

Summing (i) and (ii) gives (12.48). ∎

**Lemma 12.45** (Direction of propagation.) Let 𝐏″ be P′ − iz_0Q̃ (or its adjoint, with forward replaced by
backward) with ‖(𝐏″)⁻¹‖ ≤ Ch⁻¹. Let X ∈ Ψ^0 be microsupported in a compact K_X ⊂ T*X̃°, and let ϖ ∉ K_X not lie in the
closure of the forward V-flowout of K_X ∩ Σ_(z_0) inside Γ(ε_Γ). Then there is B_ϖ elliptic at ϖ with
‖B_ϖ(𝐏″)⁻¹Xf‖ ≤ C_Mh^M‖f‖_(−M𝟏).

*Proof.* If ϖ is in the elliptic set of 𝐏″, Proposition 12.14 gives ‖B_ϖw‖ ≤ C(‖G𝐏″w‖ + h^M‖w‖) with G microsupported
near ϖ, off K_X. Otherwise the backward V-curve from ϖ reaches the elliptic set of the absorption without meeting K_X,
and Corollary 12.26 gives ‖B_ϖw‖ ≤ C(h⁻¹‖G𝐏″w‖ + h^M‖w‖) with G microsupported near that curve, again off K_X. Take
w := (𝐏″)⁻¹Xf: G𝐏″w = GXf = O(h^∞) and ‖w‖ ≤ Ch⁻¹‖Xf‖. ∎

### 12.7 The artificial boundary

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 9.35], the semiclassical form of Section 11.6. [Hin26c] proves the energy estimate for
h⁻¹ Im z large and cites [Hin25a, Theorem 9.44] for bounded h⁻¹ Im z; here one argument covers every z with Im z ≥ 0, the
exponential weight in r of Proposition 11.29 supplying the positivity that the weight in t supplies there only for
h⁻¹ Im z large. The slab spaces H^s(Ω_(a,b))^(•,−) (supported at r = b, extendible at r = a) and H^s(Ω_(a,b))^(−,•) are
those of Section 11.6.1, with the semiclassical norms ‖u‖_(H_h^s) := ‖⟨hD⟩^s u‖; over the compact slabs used here the
decay order plays no role, and an admissible 𝖻 is constant (Section 12.1.4), so it enters only as the factor h^(−𝖻).

#### 12.7.1 The H¹_h estimate

On ℳ := ℝ_t × {r_0 − 2δ_0 < r < r_2} let g be the metric of (H6), time-oriented so that −∇t is future directed, and
□_g := −∇^μ∇_μ componentwise. dr has no dt-component, and g⁻¹(dr, dr) = G_0(dr) < 0 (H4), so dr is g-timelike; the
future direction decreases r, so X := ∇^g r is future directed timelike. For ℂ^(N_E)-valued u′ on ℳ let
T[u′](Y, Z) := Re(⟨Yu′, Zu′⟩ − ½g(Y, Z) g⁻¹(⟨du′, du′⟩)) and ^(Y)K[u′] := ½T[u′]^(μν)(ℒ_Y g)_μν. Lemma 11.28
holds on ℳ with the same proof: div_g(T[u′](W, ·)^♯) = −Re⟨□_g u′, Wu′⟩ + ^(W)K[u′], and
^(wX)K = w ^(X)K + T(∇w, X). For future causal Y, Z, T(Y, Z) ≥ 0, and on a compact set T[u′](X, X) ≥ c_0|du′|²_R for a
fixed Riemannian metric R on ℳ.

**Proposition 12.46** Let r_0 − 2δ_0 < a < b < r_2 and Z as in Section 12.4. There is C such that for
z ∈ Z, h ∈ (0, 1],

    ‖u‖_(H¹_h(Ω_(a,b))) ≤ C h⁻¹ ‖P_(h,z) u‖_(L²(Ω_(a,b))),     u ∈ H²(Ω_(a,b))^(•,−),    (12.49)

and ‖v‖_(H¹_h(Ω_(a,b))) ≤ C h⁻¹ ‖P_(h,z)^(*h) v‖_(L²(Ω_(a,b))) for v ∈ H²(Ω_(a,b))^(−,•). C depends on bounds for
the coefficients, on inf(−G_0(dr)) over the slab and on Z.

*Proof.* By density (Lemma 11.27 (c), and smooth approximation up to the extendible side) take u smooth on Ω̄_(a,b)
and vanishing near r = b. P_0 − □_g Id =: L_1 is first order with t-independent coefficients (Section 12.1.2), so
L̂_1(σ) = L̂_1(0) + σL̂_1′ with L̂_1′ a matrix function and |L̂_1(z/h)u| ≤ C(|du| + h⁻¹|u|). Let
u′(t, x) := e^(−izt/h) u(x) on D := [0, 1]_t × Ω_(a,b), so that □_g u′ = e^(−izt/h)(P̂(z/h) − L̂_1(z/h))u, and let
W := wX with w := e^(−2(Im z)t/h) e^(ℓr). Then

    ^(W)K[u′] = w(^(X)K[u′] + 2h⁻¹(Im z) T[u′](−∇t, X) + ℓ T[u′](X, X)) ≥ w(ℓc_0 − C_0)|du′|²_R,

using Im z ≥ 0, T(−∇t, X) ≥ 0 and |^(X)K| ≤ C_0|du′|²_R. Since du′ = e^(−izt/h)(du − ih⁻¹z u dt)
and |α + β dt|²_R ≥ c(|α|²_R + |β|²) for α without dt-component, w|du′|²_R ≥ c e^(ℓr)(|du|² + ¼h⁻²|u|²), a function of x
only. Apply the divergence theorem to J := T[u′](W, ·)^♯ on D. At r = b nothing contributes. At r = a the outward
conormal is −dr, and the flux is −∫ wT[u′](X, X) ≤ 0. At t = 1 and t = 0 the fluxes are −E(1) and E(0),
E(t) := ∫_({t}×Ω_(a,b)) T[u′](W, −∇t); as T[u′] carries the factor |e^(−izt/h)|² = e^(2(Im z)t/h), which w cancels,
and g is t-independent, E(1) = E(0). Hence

    ∫_D ^(W)K[u′] ≤ ∫_D Re⟨□_g u′, Wu′⟩,

and as Wu′ = we^(−izt/h)(Xu − ih⁻¹z(Xt)u) and the integrands are t-independent,

    c(ℓc_0 − C_0) ∫_Ω e^(ℓr)(|du|² + ¼h⁻²|u|²) ≤ C ∫_Ω e^(ℓr)(|P̂(z/h)u| + |du| + h⁻¹|u|)(|du| + h⁻¹|u|).

For ℓ large the terms without P̂ on the right are absorbed, and then
∫ e^(ℓr)(|du|² + h⁻²|u|²) ≤ Cℓ^(−2) ∫ e^(ℓr)|P̂(z/h)u|². With e^(ℓa) ≤ e^(ℓr) ≤ e^(ℓb) and P̂(z/h) = h⁻²P_(h,z),
multiplying by h² gives (12.49). For v: P_(h,z)^(*h) = h²P̂(z/h)^(*h), and P̂(σ)^(*h) is the spectral family at
σ̄ of the formal adjoint P_0^(*h) (with respect to dt dx and h), a stationary operator of the same form with principal
symbol G. Under t ↦ −t, with the time orientation reversed, it becomes a stationary operator of this form at the
spectral parameter −z̄/h, Im(−z̄) = Im z ≥ 0, for which −∇t is again future directed while −∇r is now future directed,
the future increasing r. The argument above with X replaced by −∇r, e^(ℓr) by e^(−ℓr), and the roles of r = a and
r = b exchanged gives the second estimate. ∎

#### 12.7.2 All orders

**Proposition 12.47** For every s ∈ ℝ and slab Ω_(a,b) with r_0 − δ_0 < a < b < r_2 − δ_0, uniformly for
z ∈ Z and h < h_0:

(i) ‖u‖_(H_h^s(Ω_(a,b))^(•,−)) ≤ C h⁻¹ ‖P_(h,z) u‖_(H_h^(s−1)(Ω_(a,b))^(•,−)) for u ∈ H^s(Ω_(a,b))^(•,−);

(ii) ‖v‖_(H_h^s(Ω_(a,b))^(−,•)) ≤ C h⁻¹ ‖P_(h,z)^(*h) v‖_(H_h^(s−1)(Ω_(a,b))^(−,•)) for v ∈ H^s(Ω_(a,b))^(−,•).

*Proof.* As in Proposition 11.30, with the semiclassical estimates in place of the fixed-frequency ones; we prove (i).
Fix a′ ∈ (r_0 − δ_0, a) and Ω′ := Ω_(a′,b).

*Uniqueness* at each fixed h is Proposition 11.30 (iii) at σ = z/h.

*Existence with bounds, s ≥ 0.* For f ∈ H_h^(s−1)(Ω′)^(•,−) ⊂ H_h^(−1)(Ω′)^(•,−) = (H¹_h(Ω′)^(−,•))*, the functional
P_(h,z)^(*h)φ ↦ ⟨f, φ⟩ on {P_(h,z)^(*h)φ : φ ∈ H²(Ω′)^(−,•)} ⊂ L² is bounded by
C h⁻¹‖f‖_(H_h^(−1)) ‖P_(h,z)^(*h)φ‖, by Proposition 12.46 for the adjoint. The Hahn–Banach and Riesz theorems give
w ∈ L²(Ω′) with ‖w‖ ≤ C h⁻¹‖f‖_(H_h^(−1)) and P_(h,z)w = f, the extension W of w by 0 beyond b satisfying
P_(h,z)W = F (the supported extension of f) on {r > a′}.

*Regularity.* (α) At each h. W is in L²(Ω′)^(•,−) and solves P_(h,z)W = f; by Proposition 11.30 (iii) at σ = z/h, at
the orders s and 0, the solution in H^s(Ω′)^(•,−) ⊂ L²(Ω′)^(•,−) is the unique one in L²(Ω′)^(•,−), so
W ∈ H^s(Ω′)^(•,−), and the estimates of Section 12.3 and Section 12.4 apply to its cut-offs by Lemma 12.17.

(β) Uniformly in h. Over {a′ < r < b + δ_0} every characteristic point of P_(h,z), at finite frequencies or at fibre
infinity, lies on a bicharacteristic along which r is strictly monotone: H_G r = 2g⁻¹(ν, dr) ≠ 0 for null ν ≠ 0, dr
being timelike; and for Im z > 0 there is no characteristic point at finite frequencies there (Lemma 12.1 (d);
Lemma 12.1 (e), stated for z_0 = ±1, holds for every real z ≠ 0 by homogeneity). Its backward direction (in the
sense of Proposition 12.25 for P) increases r and reaches {r > b}, where W = 0. Fix a″ ∈ (a′, a).
Corollary 12.28 at the order (s, 0, 0) with J ≥ 4s, finitely many times (compactness), with all its operators
microsupported over {r > a″}, and Proposition 12.22 off the characteristic set, give
‖W‖_(H_h^s({r>a})) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖F‖_(H_h^(s−1)) + ‖W‖_(L²)). (Corollary 12.26 itself would leave h^M‖GW‖_(H_h^s) with G
elliptic on a neighbourhood of the curves, which reaches below r = a, a term on a larger set than the left side
controls, and no enlargement of the cover absorbs it.) So ‖w‖_(H_h^s(Ω_(a,b))) ≤ C h⁻¹‖f‖_(H_h^(s−1)(Ω′)).

*Conclusion for s ≥ 0.* For u ∈ H^s(Ω_(a,b))^(•,−) extend Pu to f ∈ H_h^(s−1)(Ω′)^(•,−) with at most twice its norm,
solve as above, and use uniqueness on Ω_(a,b): w|_(Ω_(a,b)) = u.

*s < 0.* By (ii) for P^(*h) at the order 1 − s > 0, the duality argument of Proposition 11.30 with
(H_h^(1−s)(Ω′)^(−,•))* = H_h^(s−1)(Ω′)^(•,−) gives a solution w ∈ H_h^s(Ω′)^(•,−) with ‖w‖ ≤ C h⁻¹‖f‖; uniqueness
concludes. (ii) is the same with the ends exchanged. ∎

**Corollary 12.48** (The semiclassical form of Corollary 11.31.) Let b′, b″, χ, χ_1 be as in
Corollary 11.31. For z ∈ Z, h < h_0 and all s,

    ‖χu‖_(H̄_h^s) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖P_(h,z) u‖_(H̄_h^(s−1)({r_0<r<b″})) + ‖χ_1 u‖_(H_h^s)),     u ∈ H̄_h^s,    (12.50)

    ‖v|_(Ω_(r_0,b″))‖_(H_h^(1−s)(Ω_(r_0,b″))^(−,•))
        ≤ C h⁻¹ ‖(P_(h,z)^(*h) v)|_(Ω_(r_0,b″))‖_(H_h^(−s)(Ω_(r_0,b″))^(−,•)),     v ∈ Ḣ_h^(1−s).    (12.51)

*Proof.* P_(h,z)(χu) = χP_(h,z)u + [P_(h,z), χ]u and [P_(h,z), χ] = h · Diff¹_h is supported in supp dχ, so
h⁻¹‖[P_(h,z), χ]u‖_(H_h^(s−1)) ≤ C‖χ_1 u‖_(H_h^s). Apply Proposition 12.47 (i) on Ω_(r_0,b″); (12.51) is
Proposition 12.47 (ii). ∎

### 12.8 Proof of the high-energy theorem

Fix z_0, α_+, s and admissible 𝗋, 𝖻, and write 𝐨 := (s, 𝗋 + α_+, 𝖻),
𝐨′ := 𝐨 − 𝐦 + (1, 1, 0) = (s − 1, 𝗋 + α_+ + 1, 𝖻). The decay order of u is 𝗋 + α_+, and the thresholds of
Section 12.1.4 are conditions on it.

#### 12.8.1 Splitting off the artificial boundary

Choose r_0 < b′_0 < b′_1 < b′_2 < b′ < b″ < r_2 − δ_0 and χ, χ_1 as in Corollary 12.48 for b′, b″, and ψ ∈ C^∞ with
ψ = 0 on {r ≤ b′_0} and ψ = 1 on {r ≥ b′_1}. Over {r_0 − 2δ_0 < r < r_2} the bicharacteristics move strictly
monotonically in r, the future direction decreasing it (Section 12.7.2). So a backward bicharacteristic from a point
over {r ≥ b′_2} stays over {r ≥ b′_2}: it increases r while r < r_2, and it cannot re-enter {r < r_2}, which it could
only do with r decreasing backward. Every estimate of Section 12.4 to Section 12.6 used below at points over
{r ≥ b′_2} for the direct problem is therefore taken with all its operators microsupported over {r > b′_1}, where
ψ = 1 (each estimate is local near its curves, and its neighbourhoods are chosen inside {r > b′_1}); applied to ψu,
extended by 0 to ℝ⁴, it has GPψu = GPu modulo a residual term. The points over {r ≥ b′_1} could not be covered in
this way, since their estimates reach below b′_1.

#### 12.8.2 The direct estimate at k = 0

**Proposition 12.49** Let ϵ > 0.

(a) There are ν_1 > 0, h_0 and C such that for z ∈ z_0 + i[0, ν_1], h < h_0 and u ∈ H̄_h^𝐨 with
P_(h,z)u ∈ H̄_h^(𝐨′), with δ := δ_Γ(Im(z/h) − ϵ),

    ‖u‖_(H̄_h^𝐨) ≤ C h^(−1−δ) ‖P_(h,z) u‖_(H̄_h^(𝐨′)).    (12.52)

(b) For ν ≥ ν_1, (12.52) holds for z ∈ z_0 + i[ν_1, ν] with δ = 0.

(c) In the setting of Theorem 12.2 (2), (12.52) holds with δ = 0.

*Proof.* By Lemma 12.17 (applied to ψu, and on the slab by Lemma 11.27) it suffices to take u smooth up to
∂_♯X and Schwartz at ∂X, the constants being independent of the approximation.

(a) *The cover.* Let K_Σ := Σ_(z_0) ∩ {r ≥ b′_2} ⊂ 𝒫, compact. Each ϖ ∈ K_Σ is of one of the following kinds, by
(H8), (H4) at fibre infinity and Lemma 11.17 over ∂X.

- (R) ϖ ∈ ∂ℛ_+ ∪ ∂ℛ_− ∪ R_(z_0,in): Proposition 12.30 and Proposition 12.31 give a neighbourhood U_ϖ and
  ‖B_* u‖_𝐨 ≤ C(h⁻¹‖GPu‖_(𝐨′) + h^M‖Gu‖_𝐨 + ‖u‖_(−M𝟏)) for B_* microsupported in U_ϖ, with no a priori term; here
  s > ½ + ϑ_ℋ and 𝗋 + α_+ > ½(−1 + ϑ_in) at R_(z_0,in) are used.
- (A) ϖ is not of kind (R), not in Γ̄_u and not R_out: its backward curve tends to a set of kind (R) ((H8) (a)), so
  after finite time enters a neighbourhood U_* given by (R); on the segment, 𝖧_(z_0) ≠ 0, q̂_(z_0) ≠ 0
  (Lemma 12.1 (e), and Section 12.4.1 over ∂X away from R_out), and (12.22) holds by admissibility.
  Corollary 12.26 gives an estimate at ϖ with a priori term on a compact subset of U_*, which (R) bounds.
- (Γ) ϖ ∈ Γ: Theorem 12.44 (with β := ½γ_− < 0, so that Im z ≥ 0 ≥ hβ) gives an estimate near Γ with loss h^(−1−δ)
  and a priori term h^(−δ)‖Eu‖, E microsupported off Γ_u near Γ; the points of WF′_h(E) are off Γ̄_u by (H8) (b), so
  of kind (A), or elliptic.
- (U) ϖ ∈ Γ̄_u ∖ Γ: its backward curve tends to Γ, so for large negative times it lies on Γ_u ((H8) (b)) inside the
  neighbourhood given by (Γ); Corollary 12.26 from there.
- (O) ϖ = R_out: Proposition 12.33 with a priori term on a compact K_E ⊂ Ū_0 ∖ R_out, whose points are of kinds (A),
  (U) or elliptic (a backward curve from near R_out leaves every small neighbourhood of it, R_out being a sink); here
  𝗋 + α_+ < −½ + ½ inf min spec(S + S^(*h)) is used.

Each kind is used only after the kinds its a priori terms need, and the order (R), (A), (Γ), (U), (O) is acyclic. By
compactness, finitely many of these neighbourhoods cover K_Σ, and each estimate holds for z in a neighbourhood of z_0
(Corollary 12.26; Proposition 12.30, Proposition 12.31, Proposition 12.33 for all z in the sets stated;
Theorem 12.44 for z ∈ z_0 + i[hβ, ν′]). The complement in 𝒫|_({r≥b′_2}) of the union of the neighbourhoods is
compact and elliptic for P_(h,z_0), hence for P_(h,z), |z − z_0| small (Proposition 12.22). Take ν_1 so small that all
of this holds for z ∈ z_0 + i[0, ν_1]. For φ ∈ {1 − χ, χ_1}, both supported in {r > b′_2}, a microlocal partition of
unity Σ_j B_j = φ, modulo a residual operator, subordinate to the cover, and the chain of estimates give, with δ ≤ 1
and h^(−δ) · h⁻¹ ≤ h^(−1−δ),

    ‖φu‖_(H_h^𝐨) ≤ C(h^(−1−δ)‖Pu‖_(H̄_h^(𝐨′)) + h^M‖u‖_(H̄_h^𝐨) + ‖u‖_(H̄_h^(−M𝟏))).

*The artificial boundary.* By (12.50), ‖χu‖_(H̄_h^𝐨) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖Pu‖_(H̄_h^(𝐨′)) + ‖χ_1 u‖_(H_h^𝐨)), the orders
being constant there apart from s; the last term is the previous display with φ = χ_1, and
‖u‖ ≤ ‖χu‖ + ‖(1 − χ)u‖, the second by the previous display with φ = 1 − χ. Together, as h⁻¹ ≤ h^(−1−δ),

    ‖u‖_(H̄_h^𝐨) ≤ C(h^(−1−δ)‖Pu‖_(H̄_h^(𝐨′)) + h^M‖u‖_(H̄_h^𝐨) + ‖u‖_(H̄_h^(−M𝟏))).    (12.53)

*Absorption.* For M ≥ max(1, −s, −min(𝗋 + α_+), 1 − min 𝖻), since w_(−M𝟏)/w_𝐨 ≤ Ch,

    ‖u‖_(H̄_h^(−M𝟏)) ≤ C h‖u‖_(H̄_h^𝐨),    (12.54)

and h^M ≤ h; so for h < h_0 the last two terms of (12.53) are absorbed, which is (12.52).

(b) For Im z ≥ ν_1, P_(h,z) is elliptic at finite frequencies over X̃° (Lemma 12.1 (d)) and over ∂X except at
R_out (Section 12.4.1), uniformly for Im z ∈ [ν_1, ν] by compactness. The characteristic set over {r ≥ b′_2} is
∂Σ_0 ∪ R_out. On ∂Σ_0 the kinds are (R) at ∂ℛ_± and (A) along the curves of (H4); at R_out, kind (O), whose a priori
set K_E is now elliptic. No trapping estimate enters, so the chain gives (12.53) with δ = 0, and the
absorption step of (a) gives (12.52) with δ = 0.

(c) The same as (b), with Re z varying in [−2, 2]: at fibre infinity 𝖧_z does not depend on z, 𝖻 is constant, and only
the constancy of 𝗋 near R_out and the threshold there are used. ∎

#### 12.8.3 The adjoint estimate

**Proposition 12.50** In the settings of Proposition 12.49, for v ∈ Ḣ_h^(−𝐨′) with
P_(h,z)^(*h)v ∈ Ḣ_h^(−𝐨),

    ‖v‖_(Ḣ_h^(−𝐨′)) ≤ C h^(−1−δ) ‖P_(h,z)^(*h) v‖_(Ḣ_h^(−𝐨)).    (12.55)

*Proof.* The same argument for ϵ_♭ = −1: estimates propagate along the past field. The kinds without a priori term are
now R_out (the adjoint half of Proposition 12.33, above threshold at the order −𝗋 − α_+ − 1) and the artificial
boundary ((12.51), with nothing on the right but P^(*h)v); Γ is handled by Theorem 12.44 for P*, with a priori
term off Γ_u^♮ = Γ_s; ∂ℛ_± and R_(z_0,in) are sinks for the past field, handled by (12.28) and Proposition 12.31
with a priori terms on punctured neighbourhoods. By (H8), the forward (future) curve of a characteristic point not on
Γ̄_s tends to R_out or reaches {r < r_0 − δ_0}, and at fibre infinity reaches {r < r_0 − δ_0} (H4); so the chains
start at the sets without a priori term. The orders −𝐨′ satisfy the reversed monotonicity, −𝗋 and −𝖻 being
non-increasing along the past field. Near ∂_♯X, v restricted to Ω_(r_0,b″) is bounded by (12.51); beyond, the
microlocal estimates apply to (1 − χ)v, whose commutator term [P^(*h), χ]v is supported where (12.51) already
bounds v. ∎

*Proof of Theorem 12.2 (1) and (2).* By Proposition 12.49 and Proposition 12.50, as δ_Γ ≤ 1. For Im z ∈ [ν_1, ν]
and in (2) the loss is h⁻¹. ∎

#### 12.8.4 Invertibility

*Proof of Theorem 12.2 (3).* Let σ with Im σ ≥ 0 and |σ| ≥ C_0. If Im σ ≥ ν′|σ|, put h := |σ|⁻¹ and z := hσ,
so |z| = 1 and Im z ≥ ν′ (part (2)). Otherwise |Re σ| ≥ |σ|√(1 − ν′²) and Im σ < ν′|σ| ≤ 2ν′|Re σ|; put
h := |Re σ|⁻¹, z := hσ ∈ z_0 + i[0, 2ν′] with z_0 = sgn Re σ (part (1) with ν := 2ν′). In both cases h < h_0 for C_0
large. At this fixed h, H_h^𝐨 is the space H^(s,(𝗋+α_+)_h) of Chapter 11 with 𝗋_h(x, ξ) := 𝗋(x, hξ), up to an
equivalent norm (Section 12.2.3; h^(−𝖻(x,hξ)) is a symbol of order 0 at fixed h), and in the case of part (1) 𝗋_h is
admissible for Re σ in the sense of (O2)–(O3) of Definition 11.2 (the characteristic set over ∂X at σ in the
variable
ξ is that at z in ζ = hξ, and Section 12.1.4 asks more than (O2)); in the case of part (2) it is constant near R_out
with the threshold there, which is what Theorem 11.33 (2) asks, for every real part including 0. So 𝒳_σ and 𝒴_σ of
Theorem 11.33 are the spaces of (12.6), and (12.6) shows that P̂(σ) = h⁻²P_(h,z) is injective on
𝒳_σ and P̂(σ)^(*h) injective on 𝒴_σ*. By Theorem 11.33 (3), P̂(σ) is Fredholm, so it is invertible. ∎

#### 12.8.5 b-regularity

*Proof of Theorem 12.2 (4).* By the equivalence after (12.32), (12.7) is

    ‖u‖_(𝐨;k) ≤ C h^(−1−δ) ‖P_(h,z) u‖_(𝐨′;k)    (12.56)

for 𝐨 and 𝐨′ read on X̄ (the norm (12.32) with H̄ in place of H). Induction on k; k = 0 is (12.52). Let
k ≥ 1.

(i) Over {r ≤ b″}, the V's are smooth vector fields spanning TX̃ (there r > 0), so ‖χu‖_(𝐨;k) is equivalent to
‖χu‖_(H̄_h^(𝐨+(k,0,0))), and (12.50) at regularity s + k bounds it by
h⁻¹‖Pu‖_(H̄_h^(𝐨′+(k,0,0))) + ‖χ_1 u‖_(H_h^(𝐨+(k,0,0))), the first term being at most Ch⁻¹‖Pu‖_(𝐨′;k).

(ii) Away from R_out and the zero section: the symbols of the hV_j are ρ⁻¹ times the components of ζ in a frame
(Lemma 11.16), so Σ_(|α|=k) ((hV)^α)*(hV)^α is elliptic of order 2k(1, 1, 0) wherever |ζ| ≥ c > 0, including fibre
infinity; there ‖Bu‖_(𝐨;k) and ‖Bu‖_(𝐨+k(1,1,0)) bound each other modulo ‖B̃u‖_(𝐨;k−1) + ‖u‖_(−M𝟏), by
Proposition 12.14. At the zero section over X̃°, G_z(x, 0) = z²g_00 ≠ 0, so P is elliptic there, and every order is
controlled by ‖Pu‖ (Proposition 12.22); at finite frequencies over a compact set all orders are equivalent.

(iii) So the chain of Section 12.8.2 at the shifted order 𝐨_k := 𝐨 + k(1, 1, 0) bounds u microlocally on the cover
except near R_out, with ‖GPu‖_(𝐨_k−𝐦+(1,1,0)) ≤ C(‖Pu‖_(𝐨′;k) + ‖u‖_(−M𝟏)) for the G that occur (all microsupported
where (ii) applies). 𝐨_k satisfies every condition the chain uses away from R_out: s + k > ½ + ϑ_ℋ, 𝗋 + α_+ + k is
above the threshold at R_(z_0,in), and the monotonicity is unchanged by adding constants.

(iv) Near R_out, Proposition 12.35, whose term ‖E′u‖_(𝐨+k(1,1,0)) is supported on K_E, bounded by (iii).

(v) The error terms h^M‖Gu‖_(𝐨_k) and h^M‖Gu‖_(𝐨;k) are bounded by h^M‖u‖_(𝐨;k) and h^M‖Pu‖ by (ii), and absorbed for
h small; the terms ‖B̃u‖_(𝐨;k−1) are bounded by the induction hypothesis.

This gives (12.56), uniformly in the settings of (1) and (2). ∎

#### 12.8.6 Regularity in the spectral parameter

*Proof of Theorem 12.2 (5).* For σ as in (3), P̂(σ)⁻¹ is C^∞ in σ as a map between the spaces of Theorem 11.33 (6)
(holomorphic for Im σ > 0), and on the overlaps the inverses at different admissible orders agree, kernels and
cokernels being trivial for all of them. So ∂_σP̂⁻¹ = −P̂⁻¹(∂_σP̂)P̂⁻¹, and (σ∂_σ)^j P̂⁻¹ is a sum, with integer
coefficients, of products

    P̂⁻¹ 𝒯_(i_1) P̂⁻¹ ⋯ 𝒯_(i_l) P̂⁻¹,     𝒯_i := (σ∂_σ)^i P̂(σ) = σT + 2^i σ² g_00,
    i_1 + ⋯ + i_l = j,  1 ≤ l ≤ j.    (12.57)

By (H2), σT = 2iσρ(V_1 − 3/2 − S) − iσQ, so 𝒯_i = σρ𝒱 + σρc + σρ³ Diff¹_b + 2^i σ² g_00 with 𝒱 = 2iV_1 and c a
matrix function. Write ‖·‖_((s;k),𝗋;+) for (12.5) at decay order 𝗋 (and 𝖻 fixed), so that
‖u‖_((s;k),𝗋;+) ≍ h^(−k)‖u‖_((s,𝗋,𝖻);k), with h as in Theorem 12.2 (3), so that ½|σ| ≤ h⁻¹ ≤ |σ|. Then:

(a) 𝒯_i maps (s′; k′ + 1), 𝗋′ to (s′; k′), 𝗋′ + 1 with norm ≤ C|σ|, for all s′, k′ and decay orders 𝗋′: with
σ = zh⁻¹, σρV_1 = h⁻²zρ(hV_1), and ‖h⁻²ρ(hV_1)u‖_((s′,𝗋′+1,𝖻);k′) ≤ Ch⁻²‖u‖_((s′,𝗋′,𝖻);k′+1) (hV_1 is one of the
module operators of (12.32), and ρ raises the decay order by 1), so the norm is h^(−k′)h⁻²h^(k′+1) = h⁻¹; the
other terms are smaller or equal: σρc and σρ³ Diff¹_b likewise, and σ²g_00 = h⁻²z²g_00 with g_00 ∈ ρ²C^∞ raises the
decay order by 2 and costs h⁻² from (s′; k′), which is h⁻¹ from (s′; k′ + 1) as
‖·‖_((s′;k′+1);+) ≥ h⁻¹‖·‖_((s′;k′);+).

(b) P̂(σ)⁻¹ = h²P_(h,z)⁻¹ maps (s′ − 1; k′), 𝗋 + α_+ + 1 to (s′; k′), 𝗋 + α_+ with norm ≤ C|σ|^(−1+δ), for every
s′ ≥ s and k′, by (12.56) (s′ is admissible since s′ > ½ + ϑ_ℋ).

(c) (s′; k′ + 1); + embeds in (s′ + 1; k′); + with norm ≤ C: at fibre infinity the module operators are elliptic of
order (1, 1, 0) (as in (ii) of Section 12.8.5), which gives one order of regularity, and at finite frequencies the
regularity order is immaterial.

In a product (12.57) with l factors 𝒯, apply (b) l + 1 times, at the regularity orders s, s + 1, …, s + l, and
(a) l times, starting from f in (s − 1; k + j), after converting j − l module orders into regularity by (c) where
needed: each P̂⁻¹ raises the regularity by one, each 𝒯 lowers the module order by one and leaves the regularity, and
the target (s + j; k) is reached after j − l uses of (c). The norm is at most
C|σ|^((l+1)(−1+δ)+l) ≤ C|σ|^(−1+(j+1)δ), as l ≤ j and |σ| ≥ 1. This is (12.8). ∎

### 12.9 Uniformity in the operator

Let P̂ depend on b ∈ ℬ as in (H5)–(H8). Every constant above depends on finitely many seminorms of the symbols involved
and on finitely many lower bounds: ellipticity constants, β_*, c_1 and c_𝒯 in Lemma 12.29, the margins in the
thresholds, c_0 in Proposition 12.25, ν_min, β_Γ, c_Γ and the thresholds γ_± in Section 12.6, the lengths of the curves
in the chains of Section 12.8, and the constants of Proposition 12.46. Each depends continuously on b, by (H5)–(H8),
and the constructions (flow boxes by Lemma 12.23 with b among the parameters; the commutants; the absorbing
operator of Section 12.6.6, with Γ(δ) defined through φ_(u/s), which depend continuously on b) can be made with b in a
neighbourhood of each b_0; by compactness of ℬ, finitely many suffice. The two arguments by contradiction
(Proposition 12.40 and the absorption in part (a) of the proof of Proposition 12.43) are run with sequences
(h_j, z_j, b_j), b_j → b_∞ after passing to a subsequence, every operator of the argument (the B, E, G, the
quantisations Φ, N_u, J_u of Step 1 of the proof of Proposition 12.40, and the cut-offs) being built from the data of
b_j, which converge in C^∞ to those of b_∞ by (H5)–(H8). So (12.43) holds with remainders O(h) uniformly in j,
Lemma 12.39 holds with the limit symbols (its proof uses only their convergence in C_c^∞), and the dynamics
(D1)–(D3) of b_∞ give the contradiction. Quantising the symbols of the limit b_∞ instead would make (12.43) exact
only up to o(1). Hence Theorem 12.2 holds with constants uniform in b ∈ ℬ. As in Section 11.8, (H5)–(H8) are not
verified in this chapter; for the operators of the stability theory they are verified in Chapter 22 and the chapters
that treat each operator.

**Remark 12.51** (Comparison with [Hin26c, Section 9.3].) Besides the changes of statement in
Remark 12.4, the following points differ from [Hin26c]. (a) [Hin26c, Theorem 9.28] states that B is
semiclassically elliptic "at ∂ℛ_+"; the estimate is at the trapped set, and B is elliptic at Γ (Theorem 12.44). (b) In
the proof of [Hin26c, (9.83)] a constant is fixed in (inf_Γ p_1/(2β_Γ), γ); positivity of −2p_1 + 4β_Γγ_0 on Γ needs
γ_0 > sup_Γ p_1/(2β_Γ) = γ_+. Proposition 12.37 avoids the constant by writing p − ℓq = (p − γq) − (ℓ − γ)q. (c)
[Hin26c, Theorem 9.28 (2)] states the adjoint estimate for z ∈ 1 + i[−hβ, ν]. For β < 0 that range misses the real
axis, which the adjoint estimate at Im z = 0 in [Hin26c, (9.59)] needs. The symbol calculus gives the same threshold for
P* as for P (Section 12.6.2 defines p^♮ and q^♮ with the field of each, and (12.4) reads the same), so the
range z_0 + i[hβ, ν′] of Theorem 12.44 serves both. (d) The second step of the b-regular estimate at R_out in
[Hin26c, (9.77)] carries the diagonal term −2kihzρδ_(α,(k,0,…,0)) of [Hin26c, (9.45)], whose sign and index set differ
from those of the commutator computed in Lemma 11.20 (there the diagonal term is +2iα_1σρ, for every α with
α_1 ≥ 1; see Remark 11.21); Lemma 12.34 moves the term to the right side through Pu, as Lemma 11.20
does at fixed σ, and Proposition 12.35 then needs no sign of it. (e) [Hin26c, (3.35)] defines
H_(sc,h)^(s,𝗋,𝖻) = ρ^𝗋 h^𝖻 H_(sc,h)^s, which gives ‖u‖ = h^(−𝖻)‖⟨hD⟩^s(⟨x⟩^𝗋 u)‖ on ℝ^n, while the parenthesis
after it prints ⟨x⟩^(−𝗋)u; we use w_𝐨 = ⟨ζ⟩^s⟨x⟩^𝗋h^(−𝖻), as (3.35) does. (f) The method differs in these points: one
positive commutator scheme without regularisation, a priori estimates being proved for Schwartz functions and extended by
density (Section 12.3); propagation with flow boxes depending on z, the difference 𝖧_z − 𝖧_(Re z) absorbed by ℓ𝒬
(Proposition 12.25), in place of the three regimes of [Hin26c, Propositions 9.19, 9.22, 9.23]; one radial lemma for all
three radial sets (Lemma 12.29); at R_out the large imaginary part written as W*M̃W − g_00, non-negative exactly
(Lemma 12.32), which needs the remainder R_2 of [Hin26c, (9.49)] to be put into that form; matrix-valued defect
measures, entering through tr and max spec (Lemma 12.38); the complex absorption written as Q̂_♭(σ̄)*Q̂_♭(σ), entire
and of exact sign (Section 12.6.6); a three lines lemma with its proof (Lemma 12.42) in place of [DZ19, Lemma D.1];
and the energy estimate at the artificial boundary for every Im z ≥ 0 through an exponential weight in r
(Proposition 12.46), in place of [Hin25a, Theorem 9.44] for bounded h⁻¹ Im z.

## 13. The spectral family at zero and low frequencies

This chapter studies the spectral family P̂(σ) of Chapter 11 at σ = 0 and at small σ ≠ 0 with Im σ ≥ 0.
Theorem 13.11 is the Fredholm theory of the zero energy operator P̂(0) on weighted b-Sobolev spaces. Theorem 13.14
is that of the transition face normal operator N_tf(σ̂), the model of P̂(σ) in the regime |x| ∼ |σ|⁻¹.
Definition 13.15 defines tf-admissibility, Corollary 13.16 draws its consequences, and Proposition 13.20 verifies it for
asymptotically Minkowski operators, with the help of Hankel functions. Theorem 13.25 gives estimates for P̂(σ) and
for its augmentations by finite-rank terms, uniform as σ → 0, together with an estimate for the adjoint;
Corollary 13.27 deduces that P̂(0) has index 0. Theorem 13.29 makes all of this uniform in the operator.

These are [Hin26c, Theorem 9.36, Theorem 9.38, Corollary 9.39, Proposition 9.40, Theorem 9.41 with Remark 9.42,
Corollary 9.43] in dimension 4 + 1, for operators on a trivial bundle of any rank. The dimensional changes are these.
The shift of [Hin26c, Lemma 3.11] is n/2 = 2, so α + 3/2 becomes α + 2 in Theorems 9.36 and 9.41 and in Corollary 9.43
of [Hin26c], and H_b^(∞,β−3/2) becomes H_b^(∞,β−2). In [Hin26c, Section 9.5], which is stated for every n,
(n − 1)/2 = 3/2, n/2 = 2 and −n + 2 + β = −2 + β. The Bessel order in Proposition 9.40 is ℓ + 1 and its weights are
(0, 2). Theorem 13.25 carries an estimate for the adjoint that [Hin26c] does not state; the proof of Corollary 13.27
needs it, because the augmented operator used there has an index that is not known in advance (Section 13.8). The
smallness of |σ| in Theorem 13.25 may depend on the b-regularity order (Remark 13.28).

Every input is proved here or in Chapter 11–Chapter 12, from the classical facts of Section 13.2.1, the scattering
calculus of [HJS] as used in Chapter 11, and the facts about Hankel functions from [DLMF] stated in Section 13.5.2.
The radii r_0, δ_0, r_2, r_h of Section 11.1.1 enter only through the results of Chapter 11 cited here, under the
conditions that Chapter 11 places on them: the ordering of Section 11.1.1, and the conditions on the slab of
Corollary 11.31, which is used in Section 13.3 and Section 13.6.7. The radius R_∂ of Section 13.2.6 is chosen above
r_e + 1 whatever r_0 is. So every result below holds with the inner radius r_0 as a parameter, for every choice of the
radii that satisfies those conditions.

Section 13.1 fixes the setting and the hypotheses. Section 13.2 proves the b-analysis used at the two conic ends, at
infinity and at the origin of the transition face. Section 13.3 treats the zero energy operator, Section 13.4 the
transition face normal operator, Section 13.5 tf-admissibility and the asymptotically Minkowski case, Section 13.6
the low-energy estimates and the index, and Section 13.7 their uniformity in the operator.

*Notation.* As in Chapter 12, the rank of the bundle of Section 11.1.2 is N_E, and large integers that
bound orders of Sobolev spaces are written M. Δ := Δ_(𝕊³) ≥ 0 is the Laplacian of the round metric on 𝕊³. The variable
of the Mellin transform and of indicial families is ι ∈ ℂ, and an indicial root is a value of ι. Variable decay orders
are written 𝗋, as in Section 11.1.4, and r = |x|. For an operator A on 𝕊³ with End ℂ^(N_E)-valued coefficients (in
particular for an endomorphism-valued function), A^† denotes its adjoint for the standard inner product of ℂ^(N_E) and
the round density, and A^(*h) := H_0⁻¹ A^† H_0, with H_0 = H(0, ·) as in Section 13.1.1. The same conjugation by H_0,
with A^† the adjoint for |dx̂|, gives the adjoints of the transition face operators in Section 13.4. For operators on
X̃, A^(*h) is the h-adjoint H⁻¹A^†H of Section 13.1.1, with A^† the adjoint for |dx|.

### 13.1 Setting and hypotheses

#### 13.1.1 Data from the bounded-frequency theory

Everything of Section 11.1 is kept: X̄, ∂X, ∂_♯X, X̃, the trivial bundle E = X̃ × ℂ^(N_E), fibre inner products h
(with matrices H) and h-adjoints A^(*h) = H⁻¹A^†H, the family P̂(σ) = P̂(0) + σT + σ²P_2, the hypotheses (H1)–(H5),
the thresholds S̄, ϑ_ℋ, ϑ_in, the order pairs, and the spaces H̄^(s,𝗋), Ḣ^(s,𝗋), 𝒳_σ, 𝒴_σ, 𝒳_σ^* of
Theorem 11.33. By (11.1)–(11.2), on {ρ < ρ_1},

    P̂(σ) = 2iσρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S) + ρ²P⁽⁰⁾ − iσQ + σ²g_00,    (13.1)

which is [Hin26c, (9.4) and (5.10)] in dimension 4 + 1. Every b-differential operator with coefficients smooth up to
ρ = 0 can be written as a polynomial in ρ∂_ρ with coefficients that are operators on 𝕊³; for P⁽⁰⁾,

    P⁽⁰⁾ = Σ_(j=0)^2 A_j(ρ)(ρ∂_ρ)^j,     A_j ∈ C^∞([0, ρ_1); Diff^(2−j)(𝕊³; End ℂ^(N_E))).    (13.2)

By (H2), P⁽⁰⁾ − ((ρD_ρ)² + Δ) Id ∈ Diff_b^1 + ρ Diff_b^2, and the second summand vanishes at ρ = 0. So A_2(0) = −Id,
A_1(0) =: a ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; End ℂ^(N_E)) is of order 0, and A_0(0) = Δ Id + V + b with V ∈ Diff¹(𝕊³; End ℂ^(N_E)) of
order 1 and b ∈ C^∞. The *normal operator* and the *indicial family* are

    N(P⁽⁰⁾) := Σ_j A_j(0)(ρ∂_ρ)^j,     I(ι) := Σ_j A_j(0) ι^j = −ι² + aι + Δ + V + b,     ι ∈ ℂ.    (13.3)

Then N(P⁽⁰⁾)(ρ^ι v) = ρ^ι I(ι)v for v ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)), and P⁽⁰⁾ − N(P⁽⁰⁾) ∈ ρ Diff_b^2. We write S_0 := S(0, ·)
and H_0 := H(0, ·).

**Definition 13.1** (Indicial roots and gaps; [Hin26c, Definition 3.12].) The *indicial roots* of P̂(0) are
the points of

    spec_b := {ι ∈ ℂ : ker I(ι) ∩ C^∞(𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)) ≠ 0},

those of ρ⁻²P̂(0) = P⁽⁰⁾, as [Hin26c] defines them for ρ² Diff_b^2. An *indicial gap* is an open interval
(β_−, β_+) ⊂ ℝ, −∞ ≤ β_− < β_+ ≤ ∞, containing no Re ι with ι ∈ spec_b.

By Lemma 13.5 below, spec_b is discrete with finitely many points in each vertical strip, so every real number
that is not the real part of a root lies in an indicial gap ([Hin26c, Remark 3.13]).

#### 13.1.2 The hypotheses of this chapter

(G) (*The gap.*) α ∈ ℝ, and α + 2 lies in an indicial gap I = (β_−, β_+) of P̂(0).

(Z) (*Zero energy.*) P̂(0): 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 of (13.7) below is invertible.

(TF) (*Transition face.*) P̂ is tf-admissible with weight α + 2 (Definition 13.15).

The regularity order is a constant s > ½ + ϑ_ℋ throughout (Remark 11.3).

*Remarks.* (a) (G) is the hypothesis "α + 3/2 lies in an indicial gap" of [Hin26c] in dimension 4 + 1: by
Lemma 13.3 and Definition 13.9, H̄_b^(0,α) = ρ^α L²(|dx|) = ρ^(α+2) L²(μ_b) near ∂X, so the b-weight is α + 2
(the b-density μ_b and the b-weight are defined in Section 13.2.2).
(b) Which operators of the Einstein problem satisfy (G), (Z) and (TF), and with which weights, is established in the
chapters where those operators are studied (Chapter 23–Chapter 25); it is not repeated here. (c) Only (H1)–(H2) near
∂X enter Section 13.4 and Section 13.5; (H3)–(H4) enter through the interior estimates of Section 13.3 and the
low-energy argument of Section 13.6; (H5) enters in Section 13.7.

### 13.2 b-analysis at a conic end

#### 13.2.1 The classical facts used

(K1) *Fourier analysis on ℝ^m.* H^s(ℝ^m) := {w : ⟨ζ⟩^s ŵ ∈ L²}. Three facts, each proved here in a line. (i) For
φ ∈ 𝒮(ℝ^m), ‖φw‖_(H^s) ≤ (2π)^(−m) 2^(|s|/2) ‖⟨·⟩^(|s|) φ̂‖_(L¹) ‖w‖_(H^s), by Peetre's inequality
⟨ζ⟩^s ≤ 2^(|s|/2) ⟨ζ − η⟩^(|s|) ⟨η⟩^s and Young's inequality for the transform (2π)^(−m) φ̂ ∗ ŵ of φw; so the norm of
multiplication by φ is bounded by finitely many derivatives of φ, if φ is supported in a fixed compact set. (ii) For
κ > 0 the transform of w(κ·) is κ^(−m) ŵ(ζ/κ), so ‖w(κ·)‖_(H^s) ≤ κ^(−m/2) max(κ, κ⁻¹)^(|s|) ‖w‖_(H^s). (iii) For
s > d + m/2, sup_(|β|≤d) |∂^β w| ≤ (2π)^(−m) ‖⟨ζ⟩^(d−s)‖_(L²) ‖w‖_(H^s), by Cauchy–Schwarz on ŵ.

(K2) *Interior elliptic estimates, uniformly.* Let ℱ be a family of second-order operators on a neighbourhood Ω′ of a
compact set K ⊂ ℝ⁴, with End ℂ^(N_E)-valued coefficients bounded in C^∞(Ω̄′) and principal symbols p Id
with |p(x, ζ)| ≥ c|ζ|². For φ ∈ C_c^∞(int K), φ̃ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω′) equal to 1 near K, and all s and M, there is C with
‖φu‖_(H^s) ≤ C(‖φ̃Lu‖_(H^(s−2)) + ‖φ̃u‖_(H^(−M))) for all L ∈ ℱ. This is Proposition 11.24 over a compact set, where
the scattering calculus is the classical one (last paragraph of Section 11.2.1). The uniformity comes from the proof
of Proposition 11.24, whose construction depends continuously on the symbol: by Arzelà–Ascoli the closure of ℱ in the
coefficient topology is compact, the coefficients depend continuously on its points, and the ellipticity bound
persists.

(K3) *Rellich.* [HJS, Proposition 3.13]: for distributions supported in a fixed compact set and s′ > s, the inclusion
H^(s′) ↪ H^s is compact.

(K4) *The sphere.* L²(𝕊³) = ⊕_(ℓ≥0) ℋ_ℓ, with ℋ_ℓ the finite-dimensional spaces of spherical harmonics of degree ℓ,
on which Δ = ℓ(ℓ + 2). For integers m ≥ 0, ‖(1 + Δ)^(m/2) w‖_(L²) is equivalent to the H^m(𝕊³) norm, and H^(−m)(𝕊³)
is the dual of H^m(𝕊³). Distributional solutions of elliptic equations with smooth coefficients on 𝕊³ with smooth
right side are smooth. The decomposition into spherical harmonics, with the eigenvalues ℓ(ℓ + 2), is the classical
theory of spherical harmonics on 𝕊³ and is used as such; the other three facts are (K2) in charts, with a partition of
unity.

(K5) *Analytic Fredholm theorem* ([RS1, Theorem VI.14, p. 201]). If D ⊂ ℂ is open and connected, F: D → ℒ(ℋ) is
analytic with compact values on a Hilbert space ℋ, and Id + F(z_0) is invertible for one z_0 ∈ D, then (Id + F(z))⁻¹
exists for z off a discrete set 𝒮 ⊂ D, and is meromorphic on D with finite-rank residues.

(K6) *Plancherel on ℝ and Cauchy's theorem.* ℱ_t w(τ) := ∫ e^(−itτ) w(t) dt, so ‖ℱ_t w‖² = 2π‖w‖² for
L²(ℝ; ℋ)-valued w, ℋ a Hilbert space.

#### 13.2.2 Ends and dyadic pieces

An *end* is a neighbourhood of ∞ or of 0 in ℝ⁴, with *decay variable* ϱ := |x|⁻¹ (the end at ∞, where ϱ = ρ) or
ϱ := |x| (the end at 0, used at the face ztf in Section 13.4). Put t := −log ϱ, so t → +∞ at the end,
ω := x/|x| ∈ 𝕊³, and μ_b := |dϱ/ϱ dω| = |dt dω|. The b-vector fields are spanned over C_b^∞ (below) by
ϱ∂_ϱ = −∂_t and a fixed frame Z_1, …, Z_6 of vector fields on 𝕊³; they are dilation invariant.

Fix ψ ∈ C_c^∞((−1, 1)), 0 ≤ ψ ≤ 1, with Σ_(k∈ℤ) ψ(· − k) = 1 on ℝ, and put ψ_k := ψ(t − k),
A := {e⁻¹ < |y| < e}, and Φ_k the dilation of ℝ⁴ by e^k (end at ∞) or e^(−k) (end at 0), which maps A onto
{k − 1 < t < k + 1}. For a distribution v supported in {t > t_0} let v_k := (ψ_k v) ∘ Φ_k, supported in Ā.

**Definition 13.2** For s, c ∈ ℝ and v supported in {t > t_0},

    ‖v‖²_(H_(b,c)^s) := Σ_(k≥⌊t_0⌋) e^(2ck) ‖v_k‖²_(H^s(ℝ⁴)).

c is the *b-weight*: at s = 0 the norm is equivalent to ‖ϱ^(−c) v‖_(L²(μ_b)), because μ_b = |y|⁻⁴|dy| on A pulls back
under Φ_k to itself, ϱ^(−c) = e^(ct) lies between e^(c(k−1)) and e^(c(k+1)) on the k-th piece, and Σ_k ψ_k = 1 with at
most two pieces overlapping. C_b^∞ denotes the functions f with (ϱ∂_ϱ)^j Z^α f bounded for all j, α (equivalently,
f ∘ Φ_k bounded in C^∞ on a neighbourhood of Ā uniformly in k); it contains the functions smooth in (ϱ, ω) up to ϱ = 0.
Diff_b^m denotes the operators Σ_(j+|α|≤m) f_(jα) (ϱ∂_ϱ)^j Z^α with f_(jα) ∈ C_b^∞, End ℂ^(N_E)-valued.
𝒜^c := ϱ^c C_b^∞.

**Lemma 13.3** Let s, c ∈ ℝ; all distributions are supported in {t > t_0}.

(a) Another choice of ψ gives an equivalent norm.

(b) For f ∈ C_b^∞, ‖fv‖_(H_(b,c)^s) ≤ C‖v‖_(H_(b,c)^s), with C depending on finitely many seminorms of f; and
‖ϱ^γ v‖_(H_(b,c+γ)^s) and ‖v‖_(H_(b,c)^s) are equivalent.

(c) B ∈ Diff_b^m maps H_(b,c)^s to H_(b,c)^(s−m), with norm bounded by finitely many seminorms of its coefficients.

(d) The pairing ⟨v, w⟩_(μ_b) := ∫ ⟨v, w⟩_(ℂ^(N_E)) μ_b extends continuously to H_(b,c)^s × H_(b,−c)^(−s) and
identifies H_(b,−c)^(−s) with the dual of H_(b,c)^s; C_c^∞ is dense in both.

(e) For s′ > s and c′ > c the inclusion H_(b,c′)^(s′) ↪ H_(b,c)^s is compact.

(f) For s > d + 2, |(ϱ∂_ϱ)^j Z^α v| ≤ C ϱ^c ‖v‖_(H_(b,c)^s) for j + |α| ≤ d. Hence H_(b,c)^∞ := ∩_s H_(b,c)^s ⊂ 𝒜^c;
conversely 𝒜^c ⊂ H_(b,c−ϵ)^∞ for every ϵ > 0.

(g) For every k_0 ≥ 0 and M, ‖v‖_(H_(b,c−1)^s) ≤ e^(−k_0) ‖v‖_(H_(b,c)^s) + C_(k_0,M) ‖v‖_(H_(b,−M)^s).

(h) For integers m ≥ 0, ‖v‖²_(H_(b,c)^m) is equivalent to Σ_(j+|α|≤m) ‖e^(ct) ∂_t^j Z^α v‖²_(L²(μ_b)), and to
∫_ℝ ‖ℱ_t(e^(ct)v)(τ)‖²_(H_⟨τ⟩^m) dτ, where ‖w‖²_(H_μ^m) := ‖(1 + μ² + Δ)^(m/2) w‖²_(L²(𝕊³)). For m < 0 the second
equivalence holds with H_(b,c)^m normed as the dual of H_(b,−c)^(−m).

*Proof.* (a) For a second choice ψ′, (ψ′_k v) ∘ Φ_k = Σ_(|j−k|≤2) (ψ′_k ∘ Φ_k)(ψ_j v) ∘ Φ_k and
(ψ_j v) ∘ Φ_k = v_j ∘ (Φ_j⁻¹Φ_k), a dilation by e^(±(k−j)), |k − j| ≤ 2; (K1) (i)–(ii) bound each term by C‖v_j‖_(H^s),
uniformly, and the weights e^(2ck), e^(2cj) are comparable. (b) Let χ̃ ∈ C_c^∞({e⁻² < |y| < e²}) equal 1 near Ā. Then
(fv)_k = χ̃ (f ∘ Φ_k) v_k, and χ̃ (f ∘ Φ_k) is bounded in C_c^∞ uniformly in k, so (K1) (i) applies. For ϱ^γ,
ϱ^γ ∘ Φ_k = e^(−γk)|y|^(∓γ), and |y|^(∓γ) is smooth near Ā. (c) The operators ϱ∂_ϱ and Z_i commute with the
dilations, so (Bv)_k = Σ_(|j−k|≤1) (ψ_k ∘ Φ_k) B^(k)(v_j ∘ Φ_j⁻¹Φ_k), with B^(k) the operator with coefficients
f_(jα) ∘ Φ_k, bounded in C^∞ near Ā uniformly in k; a differential operator of order m with such coefficients maps
compactly supported elements of H^s to H^(s−m) boundedly, by (K1) (i) and ‖∂_i w‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ ‖w‖_(H^s). (d) Let
J: v ↦ (e^(ck) v_k)_k, an isometry of H_(b,c)^s into ℓ²(ℤ; H^s), and L: (w_k)_k ↦ Σ_k e^(−ck)(χ̃ w_k) ∘ Φ_k⁻¹. Then
LJ = Id (as χ̃ = 1 on the support of v_k and Σ_k ψ_k = 1), and L is bounded from ℓ²(H^s) to H_(b,c)^s by (a)–(b), as
each point lies in at most three supports. The pairing: ⟨v, w⟩_(μ_b) = Σ_k ⟨ψ_k v, w⟩_(μ_b) =
Σ_k ∫ ⟨v_k, (χ̃w) ∘ Φ_k⟩ |y|⁻⁴ dy, and ‖(χ̃w) ∘ Φ_k‖_(H^(−s)) ≤ C Σ_(|j−k|≤2) ‖w_j‖_(H^(−s)), so Cauchy–Schwarz
gives |⟨v, w⟩_(μ_b)| ≤ C‖v‖_(H_(b,c)^s) ‖w‖_(H_(b,−c)^(−s)). Conversely a bounded functional ℓ on H_(b,c)^s gives the
functional ℓ ∘ L on ℓ²(H^s), represented by (g_k) ∈ ℓ²(H^(−s)); then ℓ(v) = ℓ(LJv) = ⟨v, w⟩_(μ_b) with
w := Σ_k e^(ck)(|y|⁴ χ̃ g_k) ∘ Φ_k⁻¹, and ‖w‖_(H_(b,−c)^(−s)) ≤ C‖(g_k)‖ by the same estimate. Density: truncate the sum
over k and mollify each piece. (e) For k_1 ∈ ℕ, the pieces with k ≤ k_1 form a compact map by (K3); for the rest,
Σ_(k>k_1) e^(2ck) ‖v_k‖²_(H^s) ≤ e^(−2(c′−c)k_1) ‖v‖²_(H_(b,c′)^(s′)). A norm-limit of compact maps is compact. (f) (K1)
(iii) on each piece gives |∂_y^β v_k| ≤ C e^(−ck) ‖v‖, and on A the fields ϱ∂_ϱ, Z_i are combinations of ∂_(y_j) with
smooth coefficients, the same for every k; ϱ^c is comparable to e^(−ck) there. Conversely, for v ∈ 𝒜^c,
‖v_k‖_(H^m) ≤ C_m e^(−ck), and Σ_k e^(2(c−ϵ)k) e^(−2ck) < ∞. (g) Split the sum at k = k_0: for k ≥ k_0,
e^(2(c−1)k) ≤ e^(−2k_0) e^(2ck); the finitely many k < k_0 give e^(2(c−1)k) ≤ C_(k_0,M) e^(−2Mk). (h) On each piece,
‖w‖_(H^m(ℝ⁴)) is equivalent to Σ_(|β|≤m) ‖∂_y^β w‖_(L²), and on A the coordinate change y ↦ (t, ω) is a fixed
diffeomorphism, which with Leibniz's rule for ψ_k gives the first equivalence. For the second, by Plancherel in t (K6)
and (K4) on 𝕊³, Σ_(j+|α|≤m) ‖∂_t^j Z^α u‖² is equivalent to ∫ Σ_ℓ (1 + τ² + ℓ(ℓ + 2))^m ‖(ℱ_t u)_ℓ(τ)‖² dτ, where
(·)_ℓ is the projection to ℋ_ℓ, u := e^(ct)v and [∂_t, e^(ct)] = c e^(ct); and (1 + τ² + ν)^m is equivalent to
Σ_(j≤m) τ^(2j)(1 + ν)^(m−j) for ν ≥ 0. For m < 0 both sides are the dual norms of the case −m, by (d) and Plancherel. ∎

#### 13.2.3 The Mellin transform

For v supported in {t > t_0} with e^(c_0 t)v ∈ L²(μ_b) define the L²(𝕊³)-valued function

    (ℳv)(ι) := ∫_ℝ e^(ιt) v(t, ·) dt = ∫_0^∞ ϱ^(−ι) v dϱ/ϱ.

For Re ι < c_0 the integral converges absolutely (Cauchy–Schwarz with e^((Re ι − c_0)t) ∈ L²((t_0, ∞))), and ℳv is
holomorphic there. On the line Re ι = x ≤ c_0, ℳv(x + iτ) = ℱ_t(e^(xt)v)(−τ), so by (K6)

    ∫_ℝ ‖ℳv(x + iτ)‖² dτ = 2π‖e^(xt)v‖² ≤ 2π e^(2(x−c_0)t_0) ‖e^(c_0 t)v‖²,     x ≤ c_0,    (13.4)

the last bound because e^(xt) ≤ e^((x−c_0)t_0) e^(c_0 t) for t > t_0. As x ↑ c_0, e^(xt)v → e^(c_0 t)v in L² by
dominated convergence, so the values on Re ι = c_0 are the L² limits of those on nearby lines. Integration by parts
gives ℳ((ϱ∂_ϱ)v) = ℳ(−∂_t v) = ι ℳv, and operators on 𝕊³ commute with ℳ. By Lemma 13.3 (h), for integers m,

    ‖v‖²_(H_(b,c)^m)  is equivalent to  ∫_ℝ ‖ℳv(c + iτ)‖²_(H_⟨τ⟩^m) dτ.    (13.5)

**Lemma 13.4** (Moving the line.) Let v be supported in {t > t_0} with e^(c_0 t)v ∈ L², and suppose that
ℳv extends holomorphically from {Re ι < c_0} to {Re ι < c_1}, c_1 > c_0, with
Ξ := sup_(c_0≤x<c_1) ∫ ‖ℳv(x + iτ)‖² dτ < ∞. Then e^(c_1 t)v ∈ L² and ‖e^(c_1 t)v‖² ≤ Ξ/2π.

*Proof.* The extension is continuous on Re ι = c_0, so it agrees there with the L² limits above. Let
φ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ × 𝕊³) and Ψ(ι) := ∫ e^(−ιt) φ̄(t, ·) dt, which is entire, with ‖Ψ(x + iτ)‖_(L²(𝕊³)) ≤ C_X ⟨τ⟩⁻²
for |x| ≤ X (integrate by parts twice in t). Put g(ι) := ∫_(𝕊³) ℳv(ι) · Ψ(ι) dω, with a · b := Σ_k a_k b_k the bilinear
pairing on ℂ^(N_E); g is holomorphic on {Re ι < c_1}. For x ≤ c_0, Parseval for e^(xt)v and e^(−xt)φ gives
⟨v, φ⟩_(μ_b) = (2π)⁻¹ ∫_ℝ g(x + iτ) dτ. Fix x_0 < c_0 and x_1 ∈ [c_0, c_1). Then
∫_(x_0)^(x_1) ∫_ℝ |g(s + iT)| dT ds < ∞ by Cauchy–Schwarz, (13.4) and the definition of Ξ, so there are
T_j → +∞ and T′_j → −∞ with ∫_(x_0)^(x_1) |g(s + iT_j)| ds → 0, and likewise at T′_j. Cauchy's theorem on the
rectangles [x_0, x_1] × [T′_j, T_j] then gives ∫ g(x_1 + iτ) dτ = ∫ g(x_0 + iτ) dτ, so

    |⟨v, φ⟩_(μ_b)| ≤ (2π)⁻¹ (∫ ‖ℳv(x_1 + iτ)‖² dτ)^(1/2) (∫ ‖Ψ(x_1 + iτ)‖² dτ)^(1/2) ≤ (Ξ/2π)^(1/2) ‖e^(−x_1 t)φ‖,

by (K6) for Ψ(x_1 + iτ) = ℱ_t(e^(−x_1 t)φ̄)(τ). So ‖e^(x_1 t)v‖² ≤ Ξ/2π; let x_1 ↑ c_1 (monotone convergence on
{t > 0}, dominated convergence on {t_0 < t ≤ 0}). ∎

#### 13.2.4 The indicial family

**Lemma 13.5** Let J(ι) = −ι² + a_J ι + Δ + V_J + b_J, with a_J, b_J ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; End ℂ^(N_E)) and
V_J ∈ Diff¹(𝕊³; End ℂ^(N_E)), and let m be an integer.

(a) For X > 0 there is μ_X such that for |Re ι| ≤ X and |Im ι| ≥ μ_X, J(ι): H^m(𝕊³) → H^(m−2)(𝕊³) is invertible with
‖J(ι)⁻¹‖_(H_μ^(m−2) → H_μ^m) ≤ 2, where μ := Im ι.

(b) spec_J := {ι : ker J(ι) ∩ C^∞ ≠ 0} is discrete, with finitely many points in each strip {|Re ι| ≤ X}; off it
J(ι): H^m → H^(m−2) is invertible, and J⁻¹ is meromorphic on ℂ.

(c) If [x_0, x_1] ∩ Re spec_J = ∅, then sup{‖J(ι)⁻¹‖_(H_μ^(m−2) → H_μ^m) : x_0 ≤ Re ι ≤ x_1} < ∞, μ = Im ι.

*Proof.* (a) Write ι = x + iμ, so −ι² = μ² − x² − 2ixμ and J(ι) = (1 + μ² + Δ) + R with
R := −1 − x² − 2ixμ + a_J(x + iμ) + V_J + b_J. By (K4) and the spectral theorem, 1 + μ² + Δ is an isometry
H_μ^m → H_μ^(m−2), and ‖w‖_(H_μ^(m−j)) ≤ (1 + μ²)^(−j/2) ‖w‖_(H_μ^m) for j ≥ 0. Multiplication by a smooth function is
bounded on H_μ^k uniformly in μ, for every integer k: for k ≥ 0 because ‖w‖²_(H_μ^k) is equivalent, uniformly, to
Σ_(j≤k) μ^(2(k−j)) ‖w‖²_(H^j), by Leibniz's rule; for k < 0 by duality. Likewise V_J maps H_μ^k to H_μ^(k−1)
boundedly, uniformly in μ (for k ≥ 1 directly, for k ≤ 0 by duality with V_J^†). So

    ‖Rw‖_(H_μ^(m−2)) ≤ C(1 + |μ|) ‖w‖_(H_μ^(m−2)) + C‖w‖_(H_μ^(m−1)) ≤ C′(1 + |μ|)⁻¹ ‖w‖_(H_μ^m),

and a Neumann series inverts J(ι) with the stated bound once C′(1 + |μ|)⁻¹ ≤ ½. (b) J(ι) = (1 + Δ)(Id + F(ι)) on
H^m, with F(ι) := (1 + Δ)⁻¹(J(ι) − 1 − Δ) compact on H^m (it maps H^m to H^(m+1), and (K3)–(K4) give compactness on
𝕊³) and polynomial in ι. By (a), Id + F(ι) is invertible for some ι, so (K5) applies on D = ℂ. Id + F(ι) is Fredholm
of index 0, so it fails to be invertible exactly when it has a kernel; a kernel element of J(ι) in H^m is smooth by
(K4), so the exceptional set is spec_J for every m. In a strip it lies in {|Im ι| ≤ μ_X} by (a), a compact set, which
meets the discrete set in finitely many points. (c) On the part with |Im ι| ≥ μ_X, X := max(|x_0|, |x_1|), the bound is
2. The rest is compact, J⁻¹ is continuous there, and the μ-weighted norms are equivalent to the unweighted ones
for |μ| ≤ μ_X. ∎

For the end at ∞ the operator is P⁽⁰⁾, with ϱ∂_ϱ = ρ∂_ρ, and ℳ turns N(P⁽⁰⁾) into multiplication by I(ι), which has
the form of Lemma 13.5 with spec_I = spec_b.

#### 13.2.5 The model estimates

Let L = Σ_(j=0)^2 B_j(ϱ)(ϱ∂_ϱ)^j on {t > t_0}, with B_j ∈ C^∞([0, e^(−t_0)); Diff^(2−j)(𝕊³; End ℂ^(N_E))), and with
*normal operator* N(L) := Σ_j B_j(0)(ϱ∂_ϱ)^j, whose Mellin symbol J(ι) := Σ_j B_j(0) ι^j has the form of
Lemma 13.5. Then L ∈ Diff_b^2 and L − N(L) ∈ ϱ Diff_b^2. Assume that L is *b-elliptic*: in the coordinates
(t, ω) its principal symbol is p Id with |p| ≥ c|(τ, η)|² on {t > t_0}, uniformly. (For N(L) the principal symbol is
that of −∂_t² + Δ.) Cut-offs below are functions of t, with χ̃ = 1 near the support of χ.

**Lemma 13.6** (The b-elliptic estimate.) For all s, c and M there is C with

    ‖χv‖_(H_(b,c)^s) ≤ C(‖χ̃Lv‖_(H_(b,c)^(s−2)) + ‖χ̃v‖_(H_(b,c)^(−M))).

*Proof.* Under Φ_k the operator L becomes L^(k) on a neighbourhood of Ā, with coefficients bounded in C^∞ uniformly in
k and principal symbols elliptic with a uniform bound, as ϱ∂_ϱ and Z_i are dilation invariant and on A they are
combinations of ∂_(y_j) with fixed smooth coefficients. Apply (K2) to the family {L^(k)} and to v ∘ Φ_k itself, with
φ := (ψ_k χ) ∘ Φ_k and φ̃ equal to 1 near a compact neighbourhood of supp φ and supported in a fixed neighbourhood of
Ā where χ̃ ∘ Φ_k = 1. This is possible as χ̃ = 1 near supp χ, and only finitely many distinct pairs (φ, φ̃) are
needed, χ being constant outside a compact set of t. Then φ̃ (Lv) ∘ Φ_k = φ̃ (χ̃Lv) ∘ Φ_k, so
‖(ψ_k χ v) ∘ Φ_k‖_(H^s) is bounded by the pieces of χ̃Lv and of χ̃v on the neighbouring k, uniformly, and no commutator
with χ arises. Multiply by e^(2ck) and sum, using Lemma 13.3 (a)–(c). ∎

**Lemma 13.7** (The normal operator estimate; [Hin26c, (3.47)].) Let c ∉ Re spec_J and m ∈ ℤ. Then
‖v‖_(H_(b,c)^m) ≤ C‖N(L)v‖_(H_(b,c)^(m−2)) for v supported in {t > t_0}, and

    ‖χv‖_(H_(b,c)^m) ≤ C(‖χ̃Lv‖_(H_(b,c)^(m−2)) + ‖χ̃v‖_(H_(b,c−1)^m)).    (13.6)

*Proof.* By (13.5), Lemma 13.3 (h) and ℳ(N(L)v)(c + iτ) = J(c + iτ) ℳv(c + iτ), the first estimate is
Lemma 13.5 (c) with x_0 = x_1 = c. For (13.6) apply it to χv:
N(L)χv = χLv + [L, χ]v + (N(L) − L)χv. The commutator has coefficients supported in supp dχ, a compact set of t, where
all weights are equivalent; N(L) − L ∈ ϱ Diff_b^2 maps H_(b,c−1)^m to H_(b,c)^(m−2) by Lemma 13.3 (b)–(c). The
transform of Section 13.2.3 is defined for e^(c_0 t)v ∈ L²; so the first estimate is proved for v ∈ C_c^∞, whose
transform is entire, and extends by density (Lemma 13.3 (d)) to every v ∈ H_(b,c)^m supported in {t > t_0}, both
sides being continuous on H_(b,c)^m. This covers m < 0, where it is used. ∎

**Lemma 13.8** (Improving the weight.) Let (c_−, c_+) contain no real part of a point of spec_J, let
c ∈ (c_−, c_+), and suppose χ̃v ∈ H_(b,c)^∞ and χ̃Lv ∈ H_(b,c′)^∞ for every c′ < c_+. Then χv ∈ H_(b,c′)^∞ for every
c′ < c_+, so χv ∈ ∩_(c′<c_+) 𝒜^(c′).

*Proof.* Take nested cut-offs χ̃ = χ_0, χ_1, …, χ_p = χ, each equal to 1 near the support of the next. Suppose
χ_i v ∈ H_(b,c_i)^∞ with c_i ∈ (c_−, c_+), and fix x_1 < min(c_i + 1, c_+). Then

    f := N(L)χ_(i+1)v = χ_(i+1)Lv + [L, χ_(i+1)]v + (N(L) − L)χ_(i+1)v

lies in H_(b,c″)^∞ with c″ := min(c_i + 1, ½(x_1 + c_+)) > x_1: the first term by hypothesis, the second because it is
supported in a compact set of t inside {χ_i = 1}, the third by Lemma 13.3 (b)–(c). So ℳf is holomorphic on
{Re ι < c″} with line norms bounded by (13.4), and J(ι) ℳ(χ_(i+1)v)(ι) = ℳf(ι) for Re ι < c_i. The strip
{c_i − ϵ ≤ Re ι ≤ x′_1}, x_1 < x′_1 < c″, contains no root for ϵ small, so J⁻¹ℳf is holomorphic on its interior,
agrees with ℳ(χ_(i+1)v) near Re ι = c_i − ϵ, and has line norms bounded by Lemma 13.5 (c) and (13.4).
Lemma 13.4, with c_0 := c_i − ϵ and c_1 := x′_1, gives χ_(i+1)v ∈ H_(b,x_1)^0; Lemma 13.6 at the weight x_1,
with Lv ∈ H_(b,x_1)^∞ on the support of χ_(i+1), gives χ_(i+2)v ∈ H_(b,x_1)^∞. Each two steps raise the weight by any
amount less than min(1, c_+ − c_i), so finitely many reach every c′ < c_+. The last claim is Lemma 13.3 (f). ∎

#### 13.2.6 The spaces on X̄

Fix R_∂ > r_e + 1 so large that {r ≥ R_∂} ⊂ {ρ < ρ_1} and P⁽⁰⁾ is b-elliptic on {r ≥ ½R_∂} (possible by (H2), its
b-principal symbol being that of (ρD_ρ)² + Δ plus O(ρ)), and let χ_∂ = χ_∂(r) with χ_∂ = 0 on {r ≤ R_∂} and χ_∂ = 1
on {r ≥ 2R_∂}.

**Definition 13.9** (The spaces of [Hin26c, (3.72)] in dimension 4 + 1.) For s, a ∈ ℝ,

    ‖u‖²_(H̄_b^(s,a)) := ‖(1 − χ_∂)u‖²_(H̄^s) + ‖χ_∂ u‖²_(H_(b,a+2)^s),

with H̄^s extendible at ∂_♯X (Section 11.6.1) and H_(b,a+2)^s of Definition 13.2 at the end at ∞; Ḣ_b^(s,a) is
defined with Ḣ^s (supported at ∂_♯X) in the first term. H̄_b^((s;k),a) := H̄_b^(s+k,a) (for b-spaces, b-regularity is
regularity).

By Lemma 13.3, near ∂X the norm is that of ρ^a H_b^s(|dx|) = ρ^(a+2) H_b^s(μ_b), as |dx| = ρ⁻⁴μ_b; the b-weight is
a + 2. The space does not depend on R_∂ or χ_∂, up to equivalent norms.

**Lemma 13.10** (a) The L²(|dx|) pairing identifies the dual of H̄_b^(s,a) with Ḣ_b^(−s,−a).
(b) For s′ > s and a′ > a, the inclusion H̄_b^(s′,a′) ↪ H̄_b^(s,a) is compact.
(c) ([Hin26c, (3.72)] in dimension 4 + 1.) H̄_b^(d+3,a) ⊂ ρ^(a+2) C_b^d near ∂X; in particular
H̄_b^(∞,β−2) ⊂ 𝒜^β near ∂X, and 𝒜^β ⊂ H̄_b^(∞,β−2−ϵ) near ∂X for ϵ > 0.
(d) P̂(0) maps H̄_b^(s,a) to H̄_b^(s−2,a+2) and Ḣ_b^(s,a) to Ḣ_b^(s−2,a+2).

*Proof.* (a) Near ∂X, ⟨u, v⟩_(|dx|) = ⟨u, ρ⁻⁴v⟩_(μ_b), and v ↦ ρ⁻⁴v maps H_(b,−a+2)^(−s) (the b-weight of
Ḣ_b^(−s,−a)) onto H_(b,−a−2)^(−s), the dual of H_(b,a+2)^s (Lemma 13.3 (b), (d)); in the interior it is
Lemma 11.27 (b); glue with χ_∂. (b) Lemma 13.3 (e) and (K3). (c) Lemma 13.3 (f) with d + 3 > d + 2.
(d) Near ∂X, P̂(0) = ρ²P⁽⁰⁾, and Lemma 13.3 (b)–(c). ∎

### 13.3 The zero energy operator

With s and α as in Section 13.1.2 let

    𝒳_0 := {u ∈ H̄_b^(s,α) : P̂(0)u ∈ H̄_b^(s−1,α+2)},     𝒴_0 := H̄_b^(s−1,α+2),
    𝒳_0^* := {v ∈ Ḣ_b^(1−s,−α−2) : P̂(0)^(*h)v ∈ Ḣ_b^(−s,−α)},    (13.7)

Hilbert spaces with the graph norms; 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 is [Hin26c, (9.108)], and 𝒴_0^* = Ḣ_b^(1−s,−α−2) by
Lemma 13.10 (a).

**Theorem 13.11** (The zero energy operator.) Assume (H1)–(H4) and (G), with s > ½ + ϑ_ℋ constant.

(1) (*Fredholm estimates.*) For every M there is C with

    ‖u‖_(H̄_b^(s,α)) ≤ C(‖P̂(0)u‖_(H̄_b^(s−1,α+2)) + ‖u‖_(H̄_b^(−M,−M))),     u ∈ 𝒳_0,    (13.8)

    ‖v‖_(Ḣ_b^(1−s,−α−2)) ≤ C(‖P̂(0)^(*h)v‖_(Ḣ_b^(−s,−α)) + ‖v‖_(Ḣ_b^(−M,−M))),     v ∈ 𝒳_0^*.    (13.9)

P̂(0): 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 is Fredholm, and the annihilator of its range in 𝒴_0^* is ker_(𝒳_0^*) P̂(0)^(*h).

(2) (*Kernel.*) Every u ∈ H̄_b^(s,α) with P̂(0)u = 0 is smooth up to ∂_♯X and lies in 𝒜^β near ∂X for every
β < β_+.

(3) (*Independence.*) The kernel and the annihilator of the range depend neither on s > ½ + ϑ_ℋ nor on α with
α + 2 ∈ I; nor, therefore, does the index.

(4) (*Invertibility.*) If (Z) holds for one such pair (s, α), it holds for all, and then (13.8)–(13.9)
hold without their last terms.

This is [Hin26c, Theorem 9.36] in dimension 4 + 1, on E. The weight on P̂(0)^(*h)v in (13.9) is −α, the dual
of the weight α of the domain; [Hin26c, (9.107)] prints −α − 2 (see Section 13.8).

#### 13.3.1 Proof of (1)

*Proof of Theorem 13.11 (1).* *The interior.* Let χ, χ_1 and b′ < b″ be as in Corollary 11.31, χ_far := 1 − χ,
and φ_j ∈ C_c^∞({r < jR_∂}) equal to 1 on {r ≤ (j − 1)R_∂}, j = 3, 4, 5. Run the pieces (A), (B) and (F) of
Section 11.7.1 at σ = 0 for φ_3 χ_far u: Proposition 11.14 (1) at the horizon (σ = 0 lies in its compact sets
𝒟 ⊂ {Im σ ≥ 0}), Proposition 11.25 along the curves of (H4), which lie over {r ≤ r_e}, and Proposition 11.24 on the
rest of fibre infinity over {r < 3R_∂}; at finite frequencies over a compact set every operator of order −∞ is bounded
by ‖u‖_(H^(−M)) there. With (11.28) at σ = 0 for χu this gives, with s > s_0 > ½ + ϑ_ℋ,

    ‖(1 − χ_∂)u‖_(H̄^s) ≤ C(‖P̂(0)u‖_(H̄^(s−1)({r<4R_∂})) + ‖φ_4 u‖_(H̄^(s_0)) + ‖φ_4 u‖_(H̄^(−M))),

as 1 − χ_∂ = (1 − χ_∂)(χ + φ_3 χ_far). By (K3) and Ehrling's lemma,
‖φ_4 u‖_(H̄^(s_0)) ≤ δ‖φ_5 u‖_(H̄^s) + C_δ‖φ_5 u‖_(H̄^(−M)), and over {r < 5R_∂} the norms of H̄_b^(s,α) and H̄^s are
equivalent. So

    ‖(1 − χ_∂)u‖_(H̄^s) ≤ C‖P̂(0)u‖_(H̄_b^(s−1,α+2)) + Cδ‖u‖_(H̄_b^(s,α)) + C_δ‖u‖_(H̄_b^(−M,−M)).    (13.10)

*Near ∂X.* Let χ̃_∂ be supported in {r > ½R_∂} and equal to 1 near supp χ_∂. Lemma 13.6 for L = P⁽⁰⁾ at the
b-weight α + 2, with χ̃_∂P⁽⁰⁾u = χ̃_∂ρ⁻²P̂(0)u, gives

    ‖χ_∂ u‖_(H_(b,α+2)^s) ≤ C(‖P̂(0)u‖_(H̄_b^(s−2,α+2)) + ‖χ̃_∂ u‖_(H_(b,α+2)^(−M))),

the b-weight of H̄_b^(s−2,α+2) being α + 4 and Lemma 13.3 (b) moving ρ⁻². Choose M ∈ ℕ. By Lemma 13.7 at
c = α + 2 (not a real part of a root, by (G)), with cut-offs χ̃_∂ and χ̃′, and Lemma 13.3 (g),

    ‖χ̃_∂ u‖_(H_(b,α+2)^(−M)) ≤ C‖P̂(0)u‖_(H̄_b^(−M−2,α+2)) + Ce^(−k_0)‖χ̃′u‖_(H_(b,α+2)^(−M))
                                 + C_(k_0)‖χ̃′u‖_(H_(b,−M)^(−M)).

Here χ̃′ − χ̃_∂ has compact support in {r > ¼R_∂}, where all weights are equivalent, so
‖χ̃′u‖_(H_(b,α+2)^(−M)) ≤ ‖χ̃_∂ u‖_(H_(b,α+2)^(−M)) + C‖u‖_(H̄_b^(−M,−M)), and
‖χ̃′u‖_(H_(b,−M)^(−M)) ≤ C‖u‖_(H̄_b^(−M,−M)). Take k_0 with Ce^(−k_0) ≤ ½; the left side is finite because
u ∈ H̄_b^(s,α), so it absorbs the middle term. With (13.10), and δ small, this proves (13.8).

*The adjoint.* Let v ∈ 𝒳_0^*. In the interior run the adjoint chain of Section 11.7.1 at σ = 0 over {r < 4R_∂}:
(11.29) at the artificial boundary, which needs nothing but P̂(0)^(*h)v; (B*), Proposition 11.25 for
P̂(0)^(*h) with the backward field from there to the horizon; (A*), Proposition 11.14 (2), whose E-term lies in the
region of (B*); and (F). No a priori term arises. Near ∂X,

    ρ⁻²P̂(0)^(*h) = H⁻¹ ρ² (P⁽⁰⁾)^(†_b) ρ⁻² H,

where †_b denotes the adjoint for μ_b and the standard inner product. It is b-elliptic, with (ρ∂_ρ)^(†_b) = −ρ∂_ρ,
and its normal operator has the Mellin symbol

    I^♯(ι) := H_0⁻¹ I(2 − ῑ)^† H_0 = −ι² + (4 − a^(*h))ι + H_0⁻¹ΔH_0 + V^(*h) + b^(*h) + 2a^(*h) − 4,    (13.11)

which is of the form of Lemma 13.5, since H_0⁻¹ΔH_0 − Δ = H_0⁻¹[Δ, H_0] ∈ Diff¹(𝕊³; End ℂ^(N_E)) can be absorbed
into V^(*h); and spec_(I^♯) = {2 − μ̄ : μ ∈ spec_b}.

These facts are verified as follows. For an operator A, ⟨Au, v⟩_(|dx|) = ⟨Au, ρ⁻⁴v⟩_(μ_b) =
⟨u, ρ⁴A^(†_b)ρ⁻⁴v⟩_(|dx|), so the adjoint for |dx| = ρ⁻⁴μ_b is A^† = ρ⁴A^(†_b)ρ⁻⁴; for A = ρ²P⁽⁰⁾ this is
ρ⁴(P⁽⁰⁾)^(†_b)ρ⁻², and as A^(*h) = H⁻¹A^†H with ρ commuting with H, ρ⁻²P̂(0)^(*h) = H⁻¹ρ²(P⁽⁰⁾)^(†_b)ρ⁻²H. Its
