normal operator is H_0⁻¹ρ²N(P⁽⁰⁾)^(†_b)ρ⁻²H_0, and N(P⁽⁰⁾)^(†_b) = Σ_j (−ρ∂_ρ)^j A_j(0)^† = Σ_j A_j(0)^†(−ρ∂_ρ)^j,
the A_j(0) not depending on ρ. For w ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)),

    ρ² N(P⁽⁰⁾)^(†_b) ρ⁻² (ρ^ι w) = ρ^ι Σ_j A_j(0)^† (2 − ι)^j w = ρ^ι (Σ_j A_j(0)(2 − ῑ)^j)^† w = ρ^ι I(2 − ῑ)^† w,

which gives the first equality in (13.11). For the second, I(2 − ῑ) = −(2 − ῑ)² + a(2 − ῑ) + Δ + V + b, and
taking adjoints, with Δ self-adjoint and scalar factors conjugated,

    I(2 − ῑ)^† = −(2 − ι)² + (2 − ι)a^† + Δ + V^† + b^† = −ι² + (4 − a^†)ι + Δ + V^† + b^† + 2a^† − 4;

conjugation by H_0 turns a^†, V^†, b^† into a^(*h), V^(*h), b^(*h) and Δ into H_0⁻¹ΔH_0. Finally, by the proof of
Lemma 13.5 (b), I(κ): H^m → H^(m−2) is Fredholm of index 0 for every κ ∈ ℂ, so I(κ)^† has a nontrivial kernel
exactly when I(κ) has, that is, when κ ∈ spec_b (kernel elements being smooth by (K4)); with κ = 2 − ῑ this is
ι ∈ {2 − μ̄ : μ ∈ spec_b}. Thus conjugation by ρ^(±2) shifts the roots by 2, and the †_b-adjoint reflects them.

v has b-weight −α − 2 + 2 = −α, and −α ∉ Re spec_(I^♯) if and only if α + 2 ∉ Re spec_b, which (G) gives.
Lemma 13.6, Lemma 13.7 and Lemma 13.3 (g) for this operator, as above, give (13.9), the target
weight being −α: ρ⁻²P̂(0)^(*h)v ∈ H_(b,−α)^(−1−s) is P̂(0)^(*h)v in the b-weight −α + 2, which is that of
Ḣ_b^(−s,−α).

*Fredholm.* By Lemma 13.10 (b) the inclusion 𝒳_0 ↪ H̄_b^(−M,−M) is compact for M > max(−s, −α), so
(13.8) gives a finite-dimensional kernel and closed range (Peetre's lemma), and (13.9) does the same
for P̂(0)^(*h) on 𝒳_0^*. *Green's formula*: ⟨P̂(0)u, v⟩ = ⟨u, P̂(0)^(*h)v⟩ for u ∈ 𝒳_0, v ∈ 𝒳_0^*, with the
h-weighted L²(|dx|) pairings of Section 11.7.3. Split with χ_∂. For (1 − χ_∂)u it is the proof in Section 11.7.3.
Near ∂X, Lemma 13.6 gives χ_∂u ∈ H_(b,α+2)^(s+1) and χ̃_∂v ∈ H_(b,−α)^(2−s); both sides of the formula are
continuous in χ_∂u ∈ H_(b,α+2)^(s+1) for fixed v (Lemma 13.10 (a), (d)), and for χ_∂u ∈ C_c^∞ the formula is the
definition of P̂(0)^(*h)v as a distribution; Lemma 13.3 (d) gives the density. *Cokernel*: an element of 𝒴_0^*
annihilating the range annihilates P̂(0)C_c^∞(X̄°), so it solves P̂(0)^(*h)v = 0 and lies in 𝒳_0^*; conversely use
Green's formula. ∎

#### 13.3.2 Proof of (2)

*Proof of Theorem 13.11 (2).* Let u ∈ H̄_b^(s,α) with P̂(0)u = 0. In the interior the estimates of Section 13.3.1
hold in the strong sense (Remark 11.34: Proposition 11.14 (1), Proposition 11.24, Proposition 11.25 and
Corollary 11.31 do), with the a priori term at the horizon given by the order s of u, so u ∈ H̄^(s′) on {r < 3R_∂}
for every s′: u is smooth up to ∂_♯X. Near ∂X, Lemma 13.6 at every order gives χ_∂u ∈ H_(b,α+2)^∞, and
Lemma 13.8 for L = P⁽⁰⁾, with (c_−, c_+) = I and c = α + 2, gives χ_∂u ∈ 𝒜^β for every β < β_+. In [Hin26c]
this step is a contour shift through [Hin26c, (9.109)]; here it is done by Lemma 13.4 and Lemma 13.8. ∎

#### 13.3.3 Proof of (3) and (4)

*Proof of Theorem 13.11 (3) and (4).* *Kernel.* By (2), every kernel element u for (s, α) is smooth up to ∂_♯X and
in 𝒜^β near ∂X for all β < β_+; by Lemma 13.10 (c) it lies in H̄_b^(s′,α′) for every s′ and every α′ with
α′ + 2 < β_+, so it is a kernel element for every pair (s′, α′).

*Annihilator.* Let v ∈ ker_(𝒳_0^*) P̂(0)^(*h) for (s, α). Near ∂X, Lemma 13.6 gives χ̃_∂v ∈ H_(b,−α)^∞, and
Lemma 13.8 for ρ⁻²P̂(0)^(*h), whose gap containing −α is (2 − β_+, 2 − β_−), gives χ_∂v ∈ H_(b,c′)^∞ for every
c′ < 2 − β_−; this is the b-weight −α′ of Ḣ_b^(1−s′,−α′−2) whenever α′ + 2 > β_−. In the interior, the adjoint
estimates of Section 13.3.1 hold in the strong sense (Remark 11.34) at every order 1 − s′ with s′ > ½ + ϑ_ℋ: at the
horizon the adjoint estimate is below threshold and needs no a priori condition beyond v ∈ H^(−M), and (11.29)
and propagation hold at every order. So v is an annihilator for every pair (s′, α′).

So kernels and annihilators do not depend on the pair, and neither does the index. (4) follows: if one pair has
trivial kernel and annihilator, all do. Without the last terms: if ‖u_j‖_(H̄_b^(s,α)) = 1 and ‖P̂(0)u_j‖ → 0, then by
Lemma 13.10 (b) a subsequence converges in H̄_b^(−M,−M), by (13.8) it is Cauchy in 𝒳_0, and its limit is a
kernel element of norm 1, a contradiction; likewise for (13.9). ∎

**Remark 13.12** ([Hin26c, Remark 9.37].) [Hin26c] notes that the error term of (13.8) may be taken
at orders s^♭ < s and α^♭ < α with α^♭ + 2 in the same gap, and that the kernel is polyhomogeneous. Neither is used
below, and neither is proved here.

### 13.4 The transition face normal operator

#### 13.4.1 The face and the operator

The interior of the transition face is tf° := ℝ⁴_x̂ ∖ 0, with r̂ := |x̂|, ρ̂ := r̂⁻¹ and ω := x̂/r̂; tf is its
compactification at both ends, sctf at r̂ = ∞ and ztf at r̂ = 0, with ρ_sctf := ρ̂/(1 + ρ̂) = (1 + r̂)⁻¹ and
ρ_ztf := (1 + ρ̂)⁻¹ = r̂/(1 + r̂). Each end is an end in the sense of Section 13.2.2: sctf with ϱ = ρ̂, ztf with
ϱ = r̂. C_b^∞(tf) is the space of smooth functions on tf° with all b-derivatives (r̂∂_r̂, Z_i) bounded, and
𝒜^(a,b)(tf) := ρ_sctf^a ρ_ztf^b C_b^∞(tf). For σ̂ ∈ ℂ,

    N_tf(σ̂) := 2iσ̂ρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − 3/2 − S_0) + ρ̂² N(P⁽⁰⁾),    (13.12)

with ρ∂_ρ read as ρ̂∂_ρ̂ in N(P⁽⁰⁾); this is [Hin26c, (9.110)] in dimension 4 + 1. It is the spectral family of the
*model* P̂_mod(σ) := 2iσρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S_0) + ρ²N(P⁽⁰⁾) on ℝ⁴ ∖ 0, written in x̂. For ς > 0 let
(S_ς u)(x̂) := u(x̂/ς). Since ρ = ςρ̂ and ρ∂_ρ = ρ̂∂_ρ̂ under x̂ = ςx,

    S_ς P̂_mod(σ) S_ς⁻¹ = ς² N_tf(σ/ς),     ς > 0,    (13.13)

which is [Hin26c, (5.13)]: N_tf(σ̂) = ς⁻² S_ς P̂_mod(σ̂ς) S_ς⁻¹ for every ς.

*Structure.* (a) On {r̂ > 1}, N_tf(σ̂) is an operator of the form (13.1) at σ = σ̂, with S = S_0,
P⁽⁰⁾ = N(P⁽⁰⁾), Q = 0, g_00 = 0 and P_2 = 0, so it satisfies (H1)–(H2) on {ρ̂ < 1}. Its thresholds S̄ and ϑ_in,
computed with the fibre inner product H_0(ω) extended to be independent of ρ̂ (or the inner product of Lemma 11.7
frozen at ρ = 0), are those of P̂, because they depend only on the coefficients at ρ = 0: S̄ on S_0, and p_in on the
boundary symbol of ρ⁻¹ Im_h P̂(0) ∈ ρ Diff_b^1, which is that of the same expression for ρ²N(P⁽⁰⁾) and H_0, as
P⁽⁰⁾ − N(P⁽⁰⁾) ∈ ρ Diff_b^2 and H − H_0 ∈ ρC^∞. (b) On tf°, N_tf(σ̂) is elliptic at fibre infinity: its principal
symbol is ρ̂² times that of (ρ̂D_ρ̂)² + Δ, which is |ζ̂|² Id in x̂. (c) Near ztf, with ϱ = r̂ and ρ̂∂_ρ̂ = −ϱ∂_ϱ,

    r̂² N_tf(σ̂) = N(P⁽⁰⁾)|_(ρ∂_ρ → −ϱ∂_ϱ) + 2iσ̂r̂(−ϱ∂_ϱ − 3/2 − S_0),

an operator L as in Section 13.2.5 at the end at 0, b-elliptic on {r̂ < 2}, whose Mellin symbol is J(ι) = I(−ι),
with spec_J = −spec_b. Its adjoint for |dx̂| = r̂⁴μ_b and H_0 satisfies
r̂²N_tf(σ̂)^(*h) = H_0⁻¹ r̂⁻² L^(†_b) r̂² H_0, with Mellin symbol H_0⁻¹ I(ῑ + 2)^† H_0 and roots
{μ̄ − 2 : μ ∈ spec_b}: L^(†_b) has the roots {μ̄}, and conjugation by r̂^(∓2) shifts them by −2. Indeed, for the
density r̂⁴μ_b the adjoint of an operator A is r̂⁻⁴A^(†_b)r̂⁴, so (r̂⁻²L)^† = r̂⁻⁴L^(†_b)r̂² and
r̂²(r̂⁻²L)^† = r̂⁻²L^(†_b)r̂²; the normal operator of L^(†_b) is Σ_j B_j(0)^†(−ϱ∂_ϱ)^j, with symbol J(−ῑ)^†, and
conjugation by r̂² evaluates it at ι + 2, as in the derivation of (13.11), giving J(−ῑ − 2)^† = I(ῑ + 2)^†,
whose roots are found as there. This is the shift −n + 2 of [Hin26c] at n = 4.

#### 13.4.2 The spaces on the face

Let φ_∞ ∈ C^∞(tf) be a function of r̂ with φ_∞ = 0 on {r̂ ≤ 1} and φ_∞ = 1 on {r̂ ≥ 2}.

**Definition 13.13** ([Hin26c, (3.44)] in dimension 4 + 1.) For s, q ∈ ℝ, k ∈ ℕ_0 and a decay order 𝗋 on the
scattering phase space of ℝ⁴_x̂ (as in Section 11.1.4),

    ‖w‖²_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋,q))(tf)) := ‖φ_∞ w‖²_(H_sc^((s;k),𝗋)(ℝ⁴)) + ‖(1 − φ_∞)w‖²_(H_(b,q−2)^(s+k)),

with H_sc^((s;k),𝗋) the space of Section 11.4.6 (k further b-derivatives) and H_(b,q−2)^(s+k) the space of
Definition 13.2 at the end at 0. For k = 0 we write H_(sc,b)^(s,(𝗋,q))(tf).

Near ztf, ρ_ztf^q L²(|dx̂|) = r̂^(q−2) L²(μ_b) as |dx̂| = r̂⁴μ_b, so the b-weight is q − 2, and the norm is that of
ρ_sctf^𝗋 ρ_ztf^q H_(sc,b)^s(tf) for the Euclidean density, as in [Hin26c]. By [HJS, Propositions 3.7, 3.11 and 3.13,
Sections 10.1–10.3] and Lemma 13.3: the L²(|dx̂|) pairing identifies the dual of H_(sc,b)^(s,(𝗋,q)) with
H_(sc,b)^(−s,(−𝗋,−q)) (near ztf the pairing is ⟨w, r̂⁴v⟩_(μ_b), and v ↦ r̂⁴v maps the b-weight −q − 2 of the second
space onto −(q − 2), the dual of q − 2); the inclusion is compact when all three orders drop, the decay order by a
positive constant; and N_tf(σ̂) maps H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋,q)) to H_(sc,b;b)^((s−2;k),(𝗋,q−2)), by (a) and (c) of
Section 13.4.1 (near sctf it lies in Ψ_sc^(2,0), with commutators with b-vector fields of the same class).

#### 13.4.3 The theorem

*Orders.* Let J_± := {σ_0 : |σ_0 ∓ 1| < ¼}, and let 𝗋_± be the decay order of an order pair that is admissible, with
weight α_+, for every σ_0 ∈ J_± (Lemma 11.32 at σ_* = ±1, which concerns only the boundary face; its order is a
function of ξ and |η|², so it is invariant under rotations). Let Θ_± := {θ ∈ [0, π] : |e^(iθ) ∓ 1| ≤ ½}; for
θ ∈ Θ_±, ±cos θ = 1 − ½|e^(iθ) ∓ 1|² ≥ 7/8, so Re e^(iθ) ∈ J_±. For orders and q put

    𝒳_(tf,θ) := {w ∈ H_(sc,b)^(s,(𝗋+α_+,q)) : N_tf(e^(iθ))w ∈ 𝒴_(tf,θ)},     𝒴_(tf,θ) := H_(sc,b)^(s−2,(𝗋+α_++1,q−2)),

    𝒳_(tf,θ)^* := {w ∈ H_(sc,b)^(−s+2,(−𝗋−α_+−1,−q+2)) : N_tf(e^(iθ))^(*h)w ∈ H_(sc,b)^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−q))},

the adjoint taken for |dx̂| and H_0; 𝒳_(tf,θ) → 𝒴_(tf,θ) is [Hin26c, (9.112)].

**Theorem 13.14** (The transition face normal operator.) Assume (H1)–(H2). Let q ∈ ℝ with −q + 2 in an
indicial gap (β_−, β_+) of P̂(0), and let α_+, s, M ∈ ℝ.

(1) (*Fredholm estimates, I.*) For θ ∈ Θ_± and 𝗋 = 𝗋_± there is C, uniform in θ ∈ Θ_±, with

    ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(s,(𝗋+α_+,q))) ≤ C(‖N_tf(e^(iθ))w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(s−2,(𝗋+α_++1,q−2))) + ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−M,(−M,−M)))),
                                                                              w ∈ 𝒳_(tf,θ),    (13.14)

    ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−s+2,(−𝗋−α_+−1,−q+2)))
        ≤ C(‖N_tf(e^(iθ))^(*h)w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−q))) + ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−M,(−M,−M)))),
                                                                              w ∈ 𝒳_(tf,θ)^*.    (13.15)

(2) (*Fredholm estimates, II.*) Let I ⊂ (0, π) be compact and 𝗋 constant near R_out with 𝗋 + α_+ < −½ + S̄ there.
Then (13.14)–(13.15) hold uniformly for θ ∈ I.

(3) (*Fredholm property.*) In the settings of (1) and (2), N_tf(e^(iθ)): 𝒳_(tf,θ) → 𝒴_(tf,θ) is Fredholm, and the
annihilator of its range is ker_(𝒳_(tf,θ)^*) N_tf(e^(iθ))^(*h). The kernel and the annihilator depend neither on q
with −q + 2 ∈ (β_−, β_+), nor on s, nor on the orders allowed in (1)–(2); the index does not depend on θ ∈ [0, π]
either.

(4) (*Higher b-regularity.*) If w ∈ 𝒳_(tf,θ) and N_tf(e^(iθ))w ∈ H_(sc,b;b)^((s−2;k),(𝗋+α_++1,q−2)), then
w ∈ H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋+α_+,q)) and

    ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋+α_+,q)))
        ≤ C(‖N_tf(e^(iθ))w‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s−2;k),(𝗋+α_++1,q−2))) + ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(s,(𝗋+α_+,q)))).    (13.16)

In the settings of (1) and (2), C is uniform in θ.

(5) (*Kernel.*) In the settings of (1) and (2), every w ∈ ker_(𝒳_(tf,θ)) N_tf(e^(iθ)) lies in
𝒜^(3/2+S̄−ϵ,−β)(tf) for every ϵ > 0 and β ∈ (β_−, β_+). Conversely ∩_(ϵ>0) 𝒜^(3/2+S̄−ϵ,−β_−−ϵ)(tf) ⊂ 𝒳_(tf,θ).

This is [Hin26c, Theorem 9.38] in dimension 4 + 1, on E, with the sign in the definition of Θ_± that matches the orders
𝗋_± (Section 13.8). [Hin26c, Theorem 9.38 (5)] also states [Hin26c, (9.115)]: the annihilator lies in
e^(−2i/ρ_sctf) 𝒜^(a,−2+β)(tf) (at n = 4). Its proof conjugates the scattering calculus by e^(2ir̂), which lies outside
the results of [HJS] used in Chapter 11, and uses [Hin26c, (9.117)], whose printed proof omits a term
(Section 13.8). Nothing here uses [Hin26c, (9.115)]: tf-admissibility is stated in Section 13.5 on the spaces of
this theorem. [Hin26c, (9.115)] is not proved here.

#### 13.4.4 Proof

*Proof of Theorem 13.14.* *Near sctf, (1)–(2).* Let N^♭ be an operator on ℝ⁴ equal to N_tf(e^(iθ)) on {r̂ > ½} and
of the class of (a) of Section 13.4.1 on {ρ̂ < 2}. The estimates of Chapter 11 at the boundary face hold for it:
Lemma 11.16, Lemma 11.17, Proposition 11.18, Proposition 11.22 and the pieces (C), (D), (E), (F) of
Section 11.7.1 (with Section 11.7.2 for (2)) use only (H1)–(H2) on {ρ < ρ_1}, their commutants being microsupported
at the boundary face, and Proposition 11.24 is the elliptic estimate. Apply them to φ_∞w, which is supported in
{r̂ ≥ 1}: at fibre infinity everything is elliptic by (b), so the regularity loss is 2, and at the boundary face the
radial estimates gain one order of decay, as in (11.30). With θ ∈ Θ_± the orders 𝗋_± are admissible for
Re e^(iθ), uniformly (Theorem 11.33 (1), whose constants are uniform for σ_0 in compact subsets of J_± and
Im σ ∈ [0, 1]); for θ ∈ I ⊂ (0, π), Im e^(iθ) is bounded below and Theorem 11.33 (2) applies. The a priori term at
R_in is absorbed by Ehrling's lemma as in Section 11.7.1. This gives, with φ′ a cut-off to {½ < r̂ < 4} and the
commutator [N^♭, φ_∞] supported in {1 ≤ r̂ ≤ 2},

    ‖φ_∞w‖_(H_sc^(s,𝗋+α_+)) ≤ C(‖N_tf w‖_(𝒴_(tf,θ)) + ‖φ′w‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−M,(−M,−M)))).

*The interior.* (K2) on {¼ < r̂ < 8} bounds ‖φ′w‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ ‖φ′w‖_(H^s) by ‖N_tf w‖ there plus ‖w‖_(H^(−M)) there.

*Near ztf.* Lemma 13.6 for L = r̂²N_tf(e^(iθ)) at the b-weight q − 2 (with r̂⁻² moved by Lemma 13.3 (b), so
that N_tf w ∈ H_(b,q−4)^(s−2) is the weight q − 2 of the target) bounds ‖(1 − φ_∞)w‖_(H_(b,q−2)^s) by
‖N_tf w‖_(𝒴_(tf,θ)) plus ‖χ̃w‖_(H_(b,q−2)^(−M)), χ̃ a cut-off to {r̂ < 3}. Then Lemma 13.7 at c = q − 2 (M an
integer), which is not a real part of a root of J because −(q − 2) lies in the gap, and Lemma 13.3 (g) give

    ‖χ̃w‖_(H_(b,q−2)^(−M)) ≤ C‖N_tf w‖ + Ce^(−k_0)‖χ̃′w‖_(H_(b,q−2)^(−M)) + C_(k_0)‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−M,(−M,−M))),

and the middle term is absorbed as in Section 13.3.1. This is the improvement of the error term in [Hin26c] from
(−M, q) to (−M, q − 1) and then to (−M, −M). Summing gives (13.14).

*The adjoint.* The same, with the adjoint chain of Section 11.7.1 at the boundary face ((E*), (D*), (C*) and (F),
the a priori term at R_out absorbed as there), (K2) in the interior, and near ztf Lemma 13.6–Lemma 13.7 for
the normal operator of the adjoint, whose roots μ̄ − 2 avoid the real part −q (the b-weight of −q + 2) exactly when
−q + 2 avoids Re spec_b. This gives (13.15).

*(3).* The inclusion 𝒳_(tf,θ) ↪ H_(sc,b)^(−M,(−M,−M)) is compact for M large, so (13.14)–(13.15) give
the Fredholm property, by Peetre's lemma, as in Section 11.7.3. Green's formula ⟨N_tf w, v⟩ = ⟨w, N_tf^(*h)v⟩ holds
for w ∈ 𝒳_(tf,θ), v ∈ 𝒳_(tf,θ)^*: near sctf by the proof in Section 11.7.3 (with the regularising family T_t of
[HJS, Lemma 12.5], there being no artificial boundary); near ztf as in Section 13.3.1, by Lemma 13.6 and density
(Lemma 13.3 (d)). So the annihilator of the range is the kernel of the adjoint on 𝒳_(tf,θ)^*. *Independence.*
Kernel elements are independent of q, s and the orders by (5) and its converse. For the annihilator: near ztf,
Lemma 13.6 and Lemma 13.8 for the adjoint, with roots μ̄ − 2 and gap (β_− − 2, β_+ − 2) containing −q, put
v in H_(b,c′)^∞ for every c′ < β_+ − 2, which is the b-weight −q′ of 𝒳_(tf,θ)^* for every q′ > 2 − β_+; near sctf,
the strong forms of the adjoint estimates put it in the space of any other allowed order and any s (the independence
of the orders in Section 11.7.3). *The index in θ.* As for the local constancy of the index in Section 11.7.3: at
θ_* ∈ [0, π] fix orders allowed near θ_* (𝗋_± near Θ_±, a constant order of (2) in (0, π)), augment with E_01, E_10
built from C_c^∞(tf°), and run the contradiction argument with θ_j → θ_* using the uniform estimates
(13.14)–(13.15) and the compact inclusion. The index is locally constant, the kernels and annihilators
do not depend on the allowed orders, and [0, π] is connected.

*(4).* Near sctf, the proof of Theorem 11.33 (4), with Proposition 11.22 (3) and Lemma 11.23, applies to N^♭;
near ztf, b-regularity is regularity in H_(b,q−2), and Lemma 13.6 at the order s + k gives it; in the interior,
(K2). These steps depend on θ only through the constants of (1)–(2), so C is uniform in θ as there.

*(5).* Let w be in the kernel. Near sctf, the first paragraph of the proof of Theorem 11.33 (5) (Remark 11.34,
Theorem 11.33 (4) with f = 0, and Lemma 11.37 (b)) gives φ_∞w ∈ ρ_sctf^(3/2+S̄−ϵ) C_b^∞. In the interior w is
smooth by (K2). Near ztf, Lemma 13.6 gives χ̃w ∈ H_(b,q−2)^∞, and Lemma 13.8 with J = I(−·),
(c_−, c_+) = (−β_+, −β_−) ∋ q − 2 and Lw = 0 gives (1 − φ_∞)w ∈ 𝒜^(c′) near ztf for every c′ < −β_−, that is, in
ρ_ztf^(−β) C_b^∞ for every β > β_−. Conversely, for w ∈ ∩_ϵ 𝒜^(3/2+S̄−ϵ,−β_−−ϵ): near sctf, Lemma 11.37 (a) and
the mapping of 𝒜^a to 𝒜^(a+1) by N_tf there (the converse in Section 11.7.5) give membership in the sctf part of
𝒳_(tf,θ); near ztf, 𝒜^(−β_−−ϵ) ⊂ H_(b,−β_−−2ϵ)^∞ ⊂ H_(b,q−2)^s by Lemma 13.3 (f), as q − 2 < −β_−, and
N_tf w ∈ r̂⁻² 𝒜^(−β_−−ϵ) ⊂ H_(b,q−4)^(s−2) likewise. ∎

### 13.5 tf-admissibility

#### 13.5.1 The definition and its consequences

**Definition 13.15** (tf-admissibility in dimension 4 + 1.) P̂ is *tf-admissible with weight* β if (i) β lies
in an indicial gap (β_−, β_+) of P̂(0); and, with q := 2 − β, s and α_+ as in Theorem 13.14, and the orders of
Theorem 13.14 (1)–(2) (𝗋_± for θ ∈ Θ_±, a constant order as in (2) for θ ∈ (0, π)), (ii)
N_tf(e^(iθ)): 𝒳_(tf,θ) → 𝒴_(tf,θ) is injective for every θ ∈ [0, π], and (iii) N_tf(1)^(*h) is injective on
𝒳_(tf,0)^* (with 𝗋 = 𝗋_+). By Theorem 13.14 (3), (ii) and (iii) do not depend on the choices of s, α_+ and the
orders, nor on q with −q + 2 in the gap.

*Relation to [Hin26c, Definition 5.10]* (with the weight −n + 2 + β = −2 + β of [Hin26c, Corollary 9.39]). There, (ii)
is the triviality of the kernel of N_tf(e^(iθ)) on 𝒜^(a,−β)(tf) for every a, which implies (ii) here by Theorem 13.14
(5); and (iii) is its triviality on e^(−2i/ρ_sctf)𝒜^(a,−2+β)(tf) for every a, which implies (iii) here when [Hin26c,
(9.115)] holds. So the tf-admissibility of [Hin26c] implies this one, given [Hin26c, (9.115)], which is not proved here
(Section 13.4.3). Corollary 13.16 needs only Definition 13.15, and Proposition 13.20 verifies Definition 13.15 directly.

**Corollary 13.16** (Consequences of tf-admissibility.) Let P̂ be tf-admissible with weight
β_0 ∈ (β_−, β_+). Then:

(a) N_tf(e^(iθ)): 𝒳_(tf,θ) → 𝒴_(tf,θ) is invertible for every θ ∈ [0, π], every q ∈ (2 − β_+, 2 − β_−) and the
orders of Theorem 13.14 (1)–(2), and so is N_tf(e^(iθ))^(*h): 𝒳_(tf,θ)^* → H_(sc,b)^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−q)).

(b) Let Σ_+ := [0, π/4], Σ_m := [π/4, 3π/4] and Σ_− := [3π/4, π], with orders 𝗋_(Σ_±) := 𝗋_± and
𝗋_(Σ_m) := 𝗋_mid, a constant with 𝗋_mid + α_+ < −½ + S̄. For each sector Σ and k ∈ ℕ_0, uniformly in θ ∈ Σ, with
𝗋 := 𝗋_Σ,

    ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋+α_+,q))) ≤ C_k ‖N_tf(e^(iθ))w‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s−2;k),(𝗋+α_++1,q−2))),    (13.17)

    ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−s+2,(−𝗋−α_+−1,−q+2))) ≤ C ‖N_tf(e^(iθ))^(*h)w‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−q))).    (13.18)

(c) P̂ is tf-admissible with every weight in (β_−, β_+).

This is [Hin26c, Corollary 9.39] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (a) At θ = 0 the kernel is trivial by (ii) and the annihilator of the range by (iii) and Theorem 13.14 (3),
so the index there is 0, and by Theorem 13.14 (3) it is 0 for every θ and q. By (ii) and Theorem 13.14 (3) the
kernel is trivial for every θ and q, so the operator is invertible, and its adjoint, whose kernel is the annihilator of
the range, is injective with closed range of codimension equal to the dimension of the kernel, which is 0. (b) Each
sector is covered by the settings of Theorem 13.14: Σ_+ by (1) on Θ_+ = [0, θ_1], θ_1 := 2 arcsin ¼ < π/4, and by (2)
on [θ_1/2, π/4] with the order 𝗋_+, which is constant near R_out with the threshold there; Σ_− likewise; Σ_m by (2).
So (13.14) holds uniformly on Σ. If (13.17) failed at k = 0 there would be θ_j → θ_* ∈ Σ and w_j of
norm 1 with ‖N_tf(e^(iθ_j))w_j‖ → 0; by (13.14) and the compact inclusion a subsequence converges in
H^(−M,(−M,−M)) to some w ≠ 0 (as the left side of (13.14) is 1), with N_tf(e^(iθ_*))w = 0 as a distribution
and, by (13.14) at θ_* applied to differences, w ∈ 𝒳_(tf,θ_*); this contradicts (a). For k ≥ 1 combine
(13.16) with the case k = 0; (13.18) is the same argument with (13.15). (c) Let
β ∈ (β_−, β_+) and q := 2 − β. (i) holds, and (ii)–(iii) at q hold by (a). ∎

#### 13.5.2 Hankel functions

We use the following facts from [DLMF]. For Re ν > 0, as z → 0 ([DLMF, (10.7.7)]),

    H_ν^(1)(z) ∼ −H_ν^(2)(z) ∼ −(i/π) Γ(ν) (½z)^(−ν);

and, as |z| → ∞ in the closed sectors indicated, with δ > 0, a_0(ν) = 1 and φ_ν(z) := z − ½νπ − ¼π
([DLMF, (10.17.2), (10.17.5), (10.17.6)]),

    H_ν^(1)(z) ∼ (2/(πz))^(1/2) e^(iφ_ν(z)) Σ_(k=0)^∞ i^k a_k(ν) z^(−k),          −π + δ ≤ ph z ≤ 2π − δ,
    H_ν^(2)(z) ∼ (2/(πz))^(1/2) e^(−iφ_ν(z)) Σ_(k=0)^∞ (−i)^k a_k(ν) z^(−k),      −2π + δ ≤ ph z ≤ π − δ.

H_ν^(1) and H_ν^(2) are solutions of Bessel's equation z²w″ + zw′ + (z² − ν²)w = 0, holomorphic in ℂ ∖ (−∞, 0]
(their definition, [DLMF, Section 10.2 (ii)]).

**Lemma 13.17** (The radial equation.) Let ℓ ∈ ℕ_0, ν := ℓ + 1, σ̂ = e^(iθ), θ ∈ [0, π). (At θ = π,
σ̂² = 1 as at θ = 0, so the equation in (a) is that of θ = 0, and f_j denotes the function defined at θ = 0.)

(a) The solutions on (0, ∞) of

    −u″ − (3/r̂)u′ + (ℓ(ℓ + 2)/r̂²)u − σ̂²u = 0

are the combinations of f_j(r̂) := r̂⁻¹ H_ν^(j)(σ̂r̂), j = 1, 2, which are linearly independent.

(b) For θ = 0, g_1 := e^(−ir̂)f_1 and g_2 := e^(ir̂)f_2 satisfy, for r̂ ≥ 1 and every
k, |(r̂∂_r̂)^k(g_j − c_j r̂^(−3/2))| ≤ C_k r̂^(−5/2), with c_j := (2/π)^(1/2) e^(∓i(½νπ+¼π)) ≠ 0 (the upper sign for j =
1); in particular g_j ∈ 𝒜^(3/2) near sctf.

(c) For θ ∈ (0, π), |f_1(r̂)| ≤ Ce^(−r̂ sin θ) and |f_2(r̂)| ≥ c r̂^(−3/2) e^(r̂ sin θ) for r̂ ≥ R.

(d) As r̂ → 0, |f_j(r̂)| ≥ c r̂^(−2−ℓ).

*Proof.* (a) Put z := σ̂r̂ and u(r̂) = r̂⁻¹Z(σ̂r̂). Writing ′ for d/dr̂ on u and for d/dz on Z,

    u′ = −r̂⁻²Z + σ̂r̂⁻¹Z′,     u″ = 2r̂⁻³Z − 2σ̂r̂⁻²Z′ + σ̂²r̂⁻¹Z″,

so −u″ − (3/r̂)u′ = r̂⁻³Z − σ̂r̂⁻²Z′ − σ̂²r̂⁻¹Z″, and

    −u″ − (3/r̂)u′ + (ℓ(ℓ + 2)/r̂²)u − σ̂²u = −r̂⁻³(σ̂²r̂²Z″ + σ̂r̂Z′ + (σ̂²r̂² − 1 − ℓ(ℓ + 2))Z)
                                            = −r̂⁻³(z²Z″ + zZ′ + (z² − (ℓ + 1)²)Z),

as 1 + ℓ(ℓ + 2) = (ℓ + 1)². So u solves the equation if and only if Z solves Bessel's equation of order ν = ℓ + 1 on the
ray {σ̂r̂ : r̂ > 0}, which lies in ℂ ∖ (−∞, 0] for θ ∈ [0, π); in particular f_1 and f_2 are solutions. The equation is
of second order with smooth coefficients on (0, ∞), so its solutions form a two-dimensional space; f_1 and f_2 are
independent because on the ray ph z = θ their leading terms e^(±iz) in [DLMF, (10.17.5)–(10.17.6)] are, e^(2iz) not
tending to a constant. (b) The remainders after the first term in [DLMF, (10.17.5)–(10.17.6)] are O(|z|^(−3/2))
uniformly in closed subsectors; e^(∓iz) z^(1/2) H_ν^(j)(z) is holomorphic on {|ph z| < π/2}, and for real x ≥ 1 the disc
of radius x/2 about x lies in {|ph z| ≤ π/6}, so Cauchy's estimates give |x^k ∂_x^k(·)| ≤ C_k times the bound on the
disc, for the remainder of the expansion as well as for each term. As (r̂∂_r̂)^k is a combination of the r̂^i∂^i, i ≤ k,
this gives (b); the constant is that of the first term, r̂⁻¹(2/π)^(1/2) r̂^(−1/2) e^(∓i(½νπ+¼π)). (c) On the ray
z = e^(iθ)r̂, θ ∈ (0, π) fixed, [DLMF, (10.17.5)–(10.17.6)] apply, |e^(iz)| = e^(−r̂ sin θ)
and |e^(−iz)| = e^(r̂ sin θ). (d) [DLMF, (10.7.7)] with |z| = r̂ and Γ(ν) ≠ 0 gives |f_j(r̂)| = r̂⁻¹|H_ν^(j)(σ̂r̂)| ≥ c
r̂^(−1−ν) = c r̂^(−2−ℓ). ∎

**Lemma 13.18** (Spherical waves.) Let κ ∈ ℝ, g ∈ C^∞([1, ∞)) with |∂^k g| ≤ C_k r̂^(−γ−k),
Y ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)), χ_∞ a cut-off to {r̂ ≥ 2}, and v := χ_∞ e^(iκr̂) g(r̂) Y(ω). Then v ∈ H_sc^(m,l) for all m and
l < γ − 2, and Qv ∈ H_sc^(∞,∞) for every Q ∈ Ψ_sc^(0,0) microsupported, at the boundary face over sctf, away from
{ξ = κ, η = 0}.

*Proof.* Derivatives ∂_x̂ of v are bounded by C r̂^(−γ), so v ∈ H^(m,l) for l < γ − 2, as
∫^∞ r̂^(2l−2γ) r̂³ dr̂ < ∞. Let

    A := χ(D_r̂ − κ)^*(D_r̂ − κ)χ + Σ_i (χr̂⁻¹Z_i)^*(χr̂⁻¹Z_i) + (1 − χ²),

with χ a cut-off to {r̂ ≥ 1} equal to 1 near the support of χ_∞ and adjoints for |dx̂|: a scattering differential
operator of order (2, 0) whose principal symbol at the boundary face is (ξ − κ)² + |η|² (Lemma 11.16 (a): D_r̂ has
symbol ξ, and r̂⁻¹Z_i that of a component of η), and which is elliptic at fibre infinity. It is elliptic at the boundary
face off {ξ = κ, η = 0}. (D_r̂ − κ)(e^(iκr̂)gY) = e^(iκr̂)(D_r̂ g)Y and r̂⁻¹Z_i(e^(iκr̂)gY) = e^(iκr̂) r̂⁻¹ g Z_iY, and
(D_r̂ − κ)^* = D_r̂ − κ − 3i/r̂; so A^j v has the form of v with γ replaced by γ + 2j, plus a smooth compactly supported
term, and lies in H^(m,l) for l < γ + 2j − 2. The microlocal elliptic estimate ([HJS, Propositions 4.9 and 4.10]) for
A^j, elliptic of order (2j, 0) on WF′(Q), gives Qv ∈ H^(m,l) for l < γ + 2j − 2, for every j. ∎

#### 13.5.3 The asymptotically Minkowski case

**Lemma 13.19** (Frames.) Let Θ ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; GL(N_E, ℂ)). Replacing S_0, N(P⁽⁰⁾) and H_0 by Θ⁻¹S_0Θ,
Θ⁻¹N(P⁽⁰⁾)Θ and Θ^†H_0Θ (a change of frame of E that does not depend on ρ) preserves the class of (13.1) at
ρ = 0, the indicial roots, and tf-admissibility with each weight.

*Proof.* Θ(ω) commutes with ρ∂_ρ and ρ̂, so Θ⁻¹N_tfΘ is (13.12) for the new data, Θ⁻¹ΔΘ − Δ being of first
order on 𝕊³; I(ι) becomes Θ⁻¹I(ι)Θ. Multiplication by Θ and Θ⁻¹ is bounded on every space of Definition 13.13 (Θ is
homogeneous of degree 0, so a symbol of order (0, 0) near sctf, and in C_b^∞ near ztf), and the adjoint for Θ^†H_0Θ of
Θ⁻¹NΘ is Θ⁻¹N^(*h)Θ. So kernels correspond, on spaces that correspond. ∎

**Proposition 13.20** (The asymptotically Minkowski case.) Suppose that, in some frame Θ as in
Lemma 13.19, S_0 = 0, N(P⁽⁰⁾) = (−(ρ∂_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ) Id and H_0 = Id: the data of the wave operator of
4 + 1-dimensional Minkowski space acting componentwise, as for the scalar and the tensor wave operators in the
Cartesian frame dt, dx¹, …, dx⁴, and so for an asymptotically Minkowski operator whose data at ρ = 0 are these. Then
P̂ is tf-admissible with every weight β ∈ (0, 2).

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 9.40] in dimension 4 + 1, with Bessel order ℓ + 1 and weights (0, 2).

*Proof.* By Lemma 13.19 take Θ = Id, and as the data act componentwise take N_E = 1. *The roots.* On ℋ_ℓ,
I(ι) = −ι² + 2ι + ℓ(ℓ + 2) = −(ι + ℓ)(ι − ℓ − 2), since (ι + ℓ)(ι − ℓ − 2) = ι² − 2ι − ℓ(ℓ + 2). So
spec_b = {−ℓ, ℓ + 2 : ℓ ≥ 0}; every root has real part ≤ 0 or ≥ 2, and (0, 2) is an indicial gap.

*The operator.* N_tf(σ̂) = e^(−iσ̂r̂)(Δ_e − σ̂²)e^(iσ̂r̂), with Δ_e ≥ 0 the Euclidean Laplacian on ℝ⁴. Indeed, in polar
coordinates Δ_e = −∂_r̂² − (3/r̂)∂_r̂ + r̂⁻²Δ, and e^(−iσ̂r̂)∂_r̂ e^(iσ̂r̂) = ∂_r̂ + iσ̂, so

    e^(−iσ̂r̂) Δ_e e^(iσ̂r̂) = −(∂_r̂ + iσ̂)² − (3/r̂)(∂_r̂ + iσ̂) + r̂⁻²Δ = Δ_e − 2iσ̂(∂_r̂ + 3/(2r̂)) + σ̂²,

and e^(−iσ̂r̂)(Δ_e − σ̂²)e^(iσ̂r̂) = Δ_e − 2iσ̂(∂_r̂ + 3/(2r̂)). With ∂_r̂ = −ρ̂²∂_ρ̂,
−2iσ̂(∂_r̂ + 3/(2r̂)) = 2iσ̂ρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − 3/2); and as r̂²∂_r̂² = (r̂∂_r̂)² − r̂∂_r̂ and r̂∂_r̂ = −ρ̂∂_ρ̂,

    r̂²Δ_e = −(r̂∂_r̂)² − 2r̂∂_r̂ + Δ = −(ρ̂∂_ρ̂)² + 2ρ̂∂_ρ̂ + Δ,

so Δ_e = ρ̂²N(P⁽⁰⁾). This is (13.12) with S_0 = 0. N_tf(σ̂) commutes with rotations, so with the projections
Π_ℓ onto ℋ_ℓ in ω, which are averages of rotations against the character of ℋ_ℓ and so bounded on every space of
Definition 13.13 whose order 𝗋 is rotation-invariant (the rotations act isometrically on them, strongly continuously);
the orders 𝗋_± are, and 𝗋_mid is constant. For a distribution w on tf°, Π_ℓ w = Σ_m w_m(r̂) Y_m(ω), with (Y_m) an
orthonormal basis of ℋ_ℓ and w_m distributions on (0, ∞).

*(ii).* Let w ∈ ker_(𝒳_(tf,θ)) N_tf(e^(iθ)) and β ∈ (0, 2). By Theorem 13.14 (5) (with S̄ = 0),
w ∈ 𝒜^(3/2−ϵ,−β′)(tf) for all ϵ > 0 and β′ ∈ (0, 2); so are its components w_m, and u_m := e^(iσ̂r̂)w_m solves the
equation of Lemma 13.17 (a), weakly and hence classically, so u_m = a_1f_1 + a_2f_2 with constants a_1, a_2. If
θ ∈ (0, π), |u_m| ≤ Ce^(−r̂ sin θ) r̂⁻¹, so a_2 = 0 by Lemma 13.17 (c). If θ = 0, w_m = a_1g_1 + a_2e^(−2ir̂)g_2
with g_1, g_2 ∈ 𝒜^(3/2) (Lemma 13.17 (b)); then a_2e^(−2ir̂)g_2 = w_m − a_1g_1 is conormal, while
r̂∂_r̂(e^(−2ir̂)g_2) = e^(−2ir̂)(−2ir̂g_2 + r̂∂_r̂g_2) has size 2|c_2| r̂^(−1/2)(1 + o(1)), with |c_2| = (2/π)^(1/2), not
O(r̂^(−3/2+ϵ)); so a_2 = 0. If θ = π, σ̂² = 1 again, u_m = a_1f_1 + a_2f_2 with the f_j of θ = 0 (Lemma 13.17), and
w_m = e^(ir̂)u_m = a_1e^(2ir̂)g_1 + a_2g_2; the same argument gives a_1 = 0. In each case one coefficient remains, and
by Lemma 13.17 (d), |w_m| ≥ c r̂^(−2−ℓ) as r̂ → 0 unless it vanishes, while w_m = O(r̂^(−β′)) with
β′ < 2 ≤ 2 + ℓ. So w = 0.

*(iii).* Take s := 2 (allowed by Theorem 13.14 (3)), so that 𝒳_(tf,0)^* ⊂ H_(sc,b)^(0,(−𝗋_+−α_+−1,−q+2)),
q = 2 − β ∈ (0, 2). Here N_tf(1)^(*h) = N_tf(1), because e^(∓ir̂) are adjoint to each other and Δ_e − 1 is symmetric
for |dx̂|. Let v be in the kernel; then u := e^(ir̂)v solves (Δ_e − 1)u = 0, so

    Π_ℓ v = Σ_m (a_(1m) e^(−ir̂)f_1 + a_(2m) e^(−ir̂)f_2) Y_m = Σ_m (a_(1m) g_1 + a_(2m) e^(−2ir̂)g_2) Y_m,

with f_j at θ = 0. *At sctf.* Near R_out, the zero section, the decay order of 𝒳_(tf,0)^* is the constant
𝗋′_0 := −(𝗋_+ + α_+)(R_out) − 1 > −½, as 𝗋_+ + α_+ < −½ there (S̄ = 0). Let Q ∈ Ψ_sc^(0,0) be the identity
microlocally near the zero section over sctf and microsupported where that order is constant. By Lemma 13.18 with
κ = −2, Q(χ_∞e^(−2ir̂)g_2Y_m) ∈ H^(∞,∞); with κ = 0, (I − Q)(χ_∞g_1Y_m) ∈ H^(∞,∞). Since
Qχ_∞Π_ℓ v ∈ H^(0,𝗋′_0), it follows that χ_∞ Σ_m a_(1m) g_1Y_m ∈ H^(0,𝗋′_0), that is,
∫^∞ |g_1|² r̂^(2𝗋′_0) r̂³ dr̂ · Σ_m |a_(1m)|² < ∞. By Lemma 13.17 (b), |g_1| ≥ ½|c_1| r̂^(−3/2) for r̂ large, and
∫^∞ r̂^(2𝗋′_0) dr̂ = ∞ as 𝗋′_0 > −½. So all a_(1m) = 0. *At ztf.* Then Π_ℓ v = Σ_m a_(2m) e^(−ir̂)f_2Y_m, which by
Lemma 13.17 (d) has size at least c(Σ_m |a_(2m)|²)^(1/2) r̂^(−2−ℓ) as r̂ → 0, while 𝒳_(tf,0)^* has b-weight −q at
ztf: ∫_0 r̂^(2(q−2−ℓ)) dr̂/r̂ < ∞ would need q > 2 + ℓ, which is false as q < 2. So a_(2m) = 0, and v = 0. ∎

The proof is that of [Hin26c], run for (iii) on the spaces of Theorem 13.14; the condition (iii) of [Hin26c], on
e^(−2i/ρ_sctf)𝒜^(a,−2+β), is settled by the same argument. The interval (0, 2) is the indicial gap between the roots
0 and 2 of ℓ = 0.

**Remark 13.21** (The upper end is sharp.) In the setting of Proposition 13.20, P̂ is tf-admissible with no
weight β ≥ 2.

*Proof.* If β is the real part of a root, (i) of Definition 13.15 fails. Otherwise β lies in an indicial gap
(β_−, β_+), and β_− ≥ 2, as 2 is a root. As in the proof of Proposition 13.20 take Θ = Id and N_E = 1, so that
N_tf(1) = e^(−ir̂)(Δ_e − 1)e^(ir̂). Let q := 2 − β, let Y_0 ∈ ℋ_0 be a nonzero constant, let f_1, g_1 be the functions
of Lemma 13.17 at ℓ = 0 and θ = 0, and put w := g_1Y_0 = e^(−ir̂)f_1Y_0 ≠ 0. Then
N_tf(1)w = e^(−ir̂)(Δ_e − 1)(f_1Y_0) = 0 by Lemma 13.17 (a), and w ∈ 𝒜^(3/2) near sctf by Lemma 13.17 (b).
Near ztf, r̂²|w| = r̂|H_1^(1)(r̂)||Y_0| is bounded on (0, 2], by [DLMF, (10.7.7)] (H_1^(1)(z) ∼ −2i/(πz)) and continuity;
so ‖r̂^(−c)w‖_(L²(μ_b)) is finite on {r̂ < 2} for every c < −2, as ∫_0^2 r̂^(−2c−4) dr̂/r̂ < ∞. Since r̂²N_tf(1) is
b-elliptic there ((c) of Section 13.4.1), Lemma 13.6 and Lemma 13.3 (f) give w ∈ 𝒜^c near ztf for every
c < −2. As w is smooth on tf° and −β_− − ϵ ≤ −2 − ϵ, w ∈ ∩_(ϵ>0) 𝒜^(3/2−ϵ,−β_−−ϵ)(tf), which lies in 𝒳_(tf,0) by
the converse in Theorem 13.14 (5) (S̄ = 0). So N_tf(1) is not injective on 𝒳_(tf,0), and (ii) of Definition 13.15
fails. ∎

### 13.6 Low energies

For σ ≠ 0 with Im σ ≥ 0 write ς := |σ|, θ := arg σ ∈ [0, π] and σ̂ := σ/ς = e^(iθ). S_ς is the dilation of
Section 13.4.1, (S_ς w)(x̂) = w(x̂/ς), applied to functions supported in {ρ < ρ_1}, so that ρ̂ = ρ/ς and r̂ = ςr.
The spaces on tf are those of Definition 13.13, and φ_∞ is the cut-off of Section 13.4.2, which vanishes on
{ρ̂ ≥ 1}. ρ = 1/r is a function on all of X̄, and χ_∂ is that of Section 13.2.6.

#### 13.6.1 The spaces

**Definition 13.22** (The low-energy spaces.) Let s ∈ ℝ, k ∈ ℕ_0, 𝗋 a decay order as in Definition 13.13,
l, q ∈ ℝ and ς ∈ (0, 1]. For u on X̄, extendible at ∂_♯X, put

    ‖u‖²_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q),ς) := ς^(−2q) ‖(1 − χ_∂)u‖²_(H̄^(s+k))
                               + ς^(−2(l+2)) ‖S_ς(χ_∂ u)‖²_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋,q−l))),    (13.19)

and let ℋ_ς^((s;k),(𝗋,l,q)) be the space of those u for which it is finite; ℋ̇_ς^((s;k),(𝗋,l,q)) is defined with
Ḣ^(s+k) in the first term. k = 0 is omitted from the notation.

The three orders sit at the three faces of the low-energy picture: 𝗋 at sctf, as a function of the frequencies of tf;
l at tf; q at zf. Near zf the norm is a b-norm on X̄ with weight l − q, near tf it is the norm of tf with weight q − l
at ztf, and the powers of ς make the two agree where they overlap (Lemma 13.23 (a)). This is the form that
[Hin26c, (3.46)] gives the norm of H_((sc-b,ς);b)^((s;k),(𝗋,l,q)) near zf and near tf, at n = 4, with the power of ς
explained in Section 13.8; below, only Definition 13.22 is used, and no other description of these spaces is
claimed.

The dilation acts on frequencies by (ξ, η) ↦ (ξ/ς, η/ς): a scattering covector ξ dr + r η at x is ξ̂ dr̂ + r̂ η̂ at
x̂ = ςx, with ξ̂ = ξ/ς and η̂ = η/ς. For a decay order 𝗋 on the boundary face over sctf put

    𝗋_ς(ω, ξ, η) := 𝗋(ω, ξ/ς, η/ς),

an order on the boundary face over ∂X (the dilation of the fibres extends to their radial compactification).

**Lemma 13.23** Let s, k, 𝗋, l, q be as in Definition 13.22. There is ς_1 > 0 such that the following hold
for ς ∈ (0, ς_1], with constants independent of ς, and likewise for the dotted spaces.

(a) (*Near zf.*) If u is supported in {ρ ≥ ς}, then ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q),ς) is equivalent to ς^(−q)‖u‖_(H̄_b^(s+k,l−q)).
If u is supported in {ρ ≥ ρ_*} for a fixed ρ_* > 0, it is equivalent to ς^(−q)‖u‖_(H̄^(s+k)), with constants
depending on ρ_* (and ς ≤ ρ_*).

(b) (*Multipliers.*) Let φ ∈ C^∞([0, ∞)) be constant on [0, a] and on [Λ, ∞), 0 < a < Λ, and let
ρ_c ∈ (0, 1/(2R_∂)]. Multiplication by φ(ρ/ς) and by φ(ρ/ρ_c) is bounded on ℋ_ς^((s;k),(𝗋,l,q)), for
ς ≤ ς_1(a, Λ, ρ_c).

(c) (*Fixed ς.*) ℋ_ς^((s;k),(𝗋,l,q)) = H̄^((s;k),𝗋_ς) (Section 11.4.6), with equivalent norms (the constants
depending on ς); the weights l, q do not enter. If 𝗋 is admissible with weight α_+ for every σ_0 in a set
J ⊂ ℝ ∖ 0, then 𝗋_ς is admissible with weight α_+ for every σ_0 ∈ ςJ; and if 𝗋 is constant near R_out with
𝗋 + α_+ < −½ + S̄ there, so is 𝗋_ς.

(d) (*Orders.*) The norm increases with s, k and 𝗋. For η ∈ [0, 1]:
(d1) ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q−η),ς) ≤ ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q),ς);
(d2) if u is supported in {ρ ≥ ρ_*}, ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q−η),ς) ≤ C_(ρ_*) ς^η ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q),ς);
(d3) if u is supported in {ρ ≤ Λς}, ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q),ς) ≤ C_Λ ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋,l,q−η),ς).

(e) (*Trading b-regularity.*) For m ∈ ℕ_0, ‖u‖_((s+m;k),(𝗋,l,q),ς) ≤ C‖u‖_((s;k+m),(𝗋,l,q),ς).

*Proof.* Take ς_1 ≤ 1/(4R_∂), so that {ρ ≥ ς} contains supp(1 − χ_∂).

(a) S_ς(χ_∂u) is supported in {ρ̂ ≥ 1}, where φ_∞ = 0, so the second term of (13.19) is
ς^(−(l+2))‖S_ς(χ_∂u)‖_(H_(b,q−l−2)^(s+k)), with the b-space of Definition 13.2 at the end at 0 of tf, ϱ = r̂
(Definition 13.13; b-regularity is regularity there). Both this space and the b-space at the end at ∞ of X̄ (ϱ = ρ) are
spaces of functions on the cylinder (0, ∞)_r × 𝕊³, and S_ς is r ↦ ςr. In t := log r the two ends use
−log r̂ = −log ς − t and −log ρ = t: both families of charts Φ_k are dilations of ℝ⁴ (Section 13.2.2), so with
κ_ς := −log ς the k-th piece of S_ς(χ_∂u) at the end at 0 and the (⌊κ_ς⌋ − k)-th piece of χ_∂u at the end at ∞ are
the same function on A, up to the cut-off ψ(−log|y|) in place of ψ(log|y|) and a translate by the fractional part of
κ_ς (no inversion of charts occurs). By Lemma 13.3 (a), whose proof allows such reflected and translated
cut-offs and whose constants depend only on finitely many derivatives of the cut-offs and on their overlap, the two
norms agree up to constants independent of ς once the weights match. At order 0 they do:
‖r̂^(−(q−l−2)) S_ς w‖_(L²(μ_b)) = ς^(−(q−l−2)) ‖ρ^(q−l−2) w‖_(L²(μ_b)), as μ_b is dilation invariant. So the second
term is equivalent to ς^(−(l+2)) ς^(−(q−l−2)) ‖χ_∂u‖_(H_(b,l−q+2)^(s+k)) = ς^(−q) ‖χ_∂u‖_(H_(b,l−q+2)^(s+k)), and with
the first term this is ς^(−q) times the norm of Definition 13.9 with a = l − q. On {ρ ≥ ρ_*} the b-weights are bounded
above and below and H̄_b^(s+k,a) is H̄^(s+k) there.

(b) Both functions commute with χ_∂. On supp(1 − χ_∂) ⊂ {ρ ≥ 1/(2R_∂)}, φ(ρ/ς) = φ(Λ) once ς ≤ 1/(2R_∂Λ), and
φ(ρ/ρ_c) is a fixed smooth function. On tf, φ(ρ/ς) = φ(ρ̂), which is smooth on tf = [0, ∞]_ρ̂ × 𝕊³ and constant near
both ends, hence a multiplier of the sc-b;b spaces; and φ(ρ/ρ_c) = φ(ςρ̂/ρ_c) is constant on {ρ̂ ≤ 1} once ς ≤ aρ_c,
while (ρ̂∂_ρ̂)^j φ(ςρ̂/ρ_c) = ((t∂_t)^j φ)(ςρ̂/ρ_c) is bounded, so Lemma 13.3 (b) applies near ztf, uniformly in
ς.

(c) Away from ∂X both norms are that of H̄^(s+k). For fixed ς, S_ς(χ_∂u) is supported in {ρ̂ ≤ ρ_1/ς}, on which ρ_ztf
is bounded below, so near ztf the norm is that of H^(s+k) on a compact set and l, q only change constants. Near sctf,
for a scattering symbol a,

    S_ς Op(a) S_ς⁻¹ = Op(a_ς),     a_ς(x̂, ζ̂) := a(x̂/ς, ςζ̂),

exactly (substitute y = ŷ/ς and ζ = ςζ̂ in the oscillatory integral). If a is an elliptic symbol of order (s, 𝗋_ς),
then a_ς is one of order (s, 𝗋), as (x̂, ζ̂) ↦ (x̂/ς, ςζ̂) extends to a diffeomorphism of the compactified phase space.
So S_ς maps H_sc^(s,𝗋_ς) isomorphically onto H_sc^(s,𝗋) ([HJS, Definition 10.2]), and the same holds with k
b-derivatives, since S_ς ⟨x⟩D_x S_ς⁻¹ = ⟨x̂/ς⟩ ς D_x̂ lies in the span of the fields ⟨x̂⟩D_x̂ over C^∞(ℝ̄⁴). For
admissibility, let D_ς(ω, ξ, η) := (ω, ςξ, ςη) on the boundary face, so 𝗋_ς = 𝗋 ∘ D_ς⁻¹. With
G_(σ_0) = 2σ_0ξ + ξ² + |η|² (Lemma 11.16), G_(ςσ_0) ∘ D_ς = ς²G_(σ_0), so D_ς maps Σ^∂_(σ_0),
R_(σ_0,in) = {ξ = −2σ_0, η = 0} and R_out onto Σ^∂_(ςσ_0), R_(ςσ_0,in) and R_out; and in (11.15) each of
∂_ξp (ρ∂_ρ + η·∂_η), (η·∂_η p)∂_ξ and H_p^(𝕊³) scales so that (D_ς)_* 𝖵_(G_(σ_0)) = ς⁻¹ 𝖵_(G_(ςσ_0)). Hence (O2) of
Section 11.1.4 for 𝗋 at σ_0 is (O2) for 𝗋_ς at ςσ_0 (sgn ςσ_0 = sgn σ_0), and (O1), (O3) involve only the values at
the radial sets and quantities on ∂X.

(d) Monotonicity in s, k, 𝗋 holds for each term. (d1): ς^(η−q) ≤ ς^(−q), and the order q − η − l at ztf is weaker
than q − l. (d2) is (a). (d3): for ς < 1/(2R_∂Λ) the first term vanishes, and on {ρ̂ ≤ Λ}, ρ_ztf ≥ (1 + Λ)⁻¹.

(e) The first term and the part near ztf are norms of H^(s+k+m) on both sides. Near sctf it suffices, by induction, to
take m = 1 and show H^((s;k+1),𝗋) ⊂ H^((s+1;k),𝗋) (Section 11.4.6) on ℝ⁴_x̂, which does not involve ς. Let
V_j := ⟨x⟩D_(x_j) and w := V^β u, |β| ≤ k. Then w and every V_j w lie in H^(s,𝗋), since V_jV^β is a combination of
the V^γ, |γ| ≤ k + 1, with coefficients in C^∞(ℝ̄⁴). Off the zero section of the boundary face the system (V_j) is
elliptic in Ψ^(1,1) (proof of Lemma 11.23), so w ∈ H^(s+1,𝗋+1) ⊂ H^(s+1,𝗋) microlocally there ([HJS,
Propositions 2.3, 4.9 and 4.10]); near the zero section, at finite frequencies, B ∈ Ψ^(−∞,0) maps H^(s,𝗋) to
H^(s+1,𝗋). With the norms, this is the claim. ∎

#### 13.6.2 The model at tf

On {ρ < ρ_1} let

    P̂_mod(σ) := 2iσρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S_0) + ρ²N(P⁽⁰⁾),
    E_σ := P̂(σ) − P̂_mod(σ) = ρ²(P⁽⁰⁾ − N(P⁽⁰⁾)) − 2iσρ(S − S_0) − iσQ + σ²g_00,    (13.20)

by (13.1). By (13.13), S_ς P̂_mod(σ) S_ς⁻¹ = ς²N_tf(σ̂). Let H_0 also denote the matrix H(0, ω),
extended to {ρ < ρ_1} independently of ρ, and P̂_mod(σ)^(*h_0) the adjoint for |dx| and H_0. Since
‖S_ς w‖_(L²(|dx̂|)) = ς²‖w‖_(L²(|dx|)) and H_0 does not depend on ρ, S_ς P̂_mod(σ)^(*h_0) S_ς⁻¹ = ς²N_tf(σ̂)^(*h),
the adjoint of Theorem 13.14. Put E_σ^* := P̂(σ)^(*h) − P̂_mod(σ)^(*h_0).

**Lemma 13.24** (The model error.) Let s, k, 𝗋, q be given. There is C such that for ρ_c ∈ (0, ρ_1/2],
ς ∈ (0, 1], θ ∈ [0, π] and u supported in {ρ ≤ ρ_c},

    ς⁻² ‖S_ς E_σ u‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s−2;k),(𝗋+1,q−2))) ≤ C(ρ_c + ς) ‖S_ς u‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋,q))),    (13.21)

and (13.21) holds for E_σ^* with the orders (s, 𝗋, q) and (s − 2, 𝗋 + 1, q − 2) replaced by
(−s + 2, −𝗋 − 1, −q + 2) and (−s, −𝗋, −q).

*Proof.* Write P⁽⁰⁾ − N(P⁽⁰⁾) = ρB_1, S − S_0 = ρS_1, Q = ρ³Q̃ and g_00 = ρ²g̃, with B_1 ∈ Diff_b^2,
Q̃ ∈ Diff_b^1 and S_1, g̃ smooth (Section 13.1.1 and (H2)). Since ρ = ςρ̂, σ = ςσ̂ and ρ∂_ρ = ρ̂∂_ρ̂,

    ς⁻² S_ς E_σ S_ς⁻¹ = ρ̂²ρB_1 − 2iσ̂ρ̂ ρS_1 − iσ̂ρ̂ ρ²Q̃ + ς²σ̂²ρ̂²g̃,

where ρ stands for ςρ̂ and every coefficient is a smooth function of (ςρ̂, ω). Indeed, divided by ς², the four terms of
E_σ are ρ²·ρB_1/ς² = ρ̂²ρB_1, −2iσρ·ρS_1/ς² = −2iσ̂ρ̂ ρS_1, −iσρ³Q̃/ς² = −iσ̂ρ̂ ρ²Q̃ and σ²ρ²g̃/ς² = ς²σ̂²ρ̂²g̃.
A smooth function f has (ρ̂∂_ρ̂)^j ∂_ω^γ f(ςρ̂, ω) = ((ρ∂_ρ)^j ∂_ω^γ f)(ςρ̂, ω), bounded independently of ς, and on
{ρ̂ ≤ 2} its ρ̂-derivatives carry powers of ς; so the operators B_1, Q̃, S_1, g̃ lie in bounded sets of their classes,
both near ztf (b-operators) and near sctf (smooth up to ρ̂ = 0). Split S_ς u = φ_∞S_ς u + (1 − φ_∞)S_ς u, and note
that the operator is differential.

*Near sctf*, on {ρ̂ ≤ 2}, write ρ = ςρ̂: the four terms are ςρ̂ · ρ̂²B_1, ςρ̂ · (−2iσ̂ρ̂S_1), ς²ρ̂² · (−iσ̂ρ̂Q̃) and
ς²ρ̂² · σ̂²g̃. Near sctf ρ̂² Diff_b^2 ⊂ Diff_sc^2 and ρ̂ Diff_b^1 ⊂ Diff_sc^1, these classes map H_sc^((s;k),𝗋) to
H_sc^((s−2;k),𝗋) (Section 11.4.6: the commutators of ⟨x̂⟩D_x̂ with Diff_sc^(m,0) lie in Diff_sc^(m,0)), and each
factor ρ̂ raises the decay order by one. So this part is bounded by Cς.

*Near ztf*, on {ρ̂ ≥ ½}, the operator is ρ̂² times ρB_1 − 2iσ̂(ρ/ρ̂)S_1 − iσ̂(ρ²/ρ̂)Q̃ + ς²σ̂²g̃. On the support of u,
ρ ≤ ρ_c; replacing ρ by ρχ̃(ρ/ρ_c), with χ̃ = 1 on [0, 1] and 0 on [2, ∞), does not change the operator there, and
ρχ̃(ρ/ρ_c) has all b-derivatives bounded by Cρ_c. Also ρ/ρ̂ = ς. So the bracket is a b-operator of order 2 with
coefficients bounded by C(ρ_c + ς) in C_b^∞, which maps H_(b,q−2)^(s+k) to H_(b,q−2)^(s+k−2) with that norm
(Lemma 13.3 (c)), and ρ̂² maps the ztf order q to q − 2 (Lemma 13.3 (b)).

*The adjoint.* E_σ^* = E_σ^(*h) + (P̂_mod(σ)^(*h) − P̂_mod(σ)^(*h_0)). The adjoint of each term of (13.20)
for |dx| = ρ⁻⁵dρ dω and H is of the same form (ρ^a Diff_b^m is preserved, and σ becomes σ̄; Remark (a) of
Section 11.1.3). Writing H = H_0(I + ρK) with K smooth, and A := P̂_mod(σ),

    A^(*h) − A^(*h_0) = (I + ρK)⁻¹ A^(*h_0) (I + ρK) − A^(*h_0) = (I + ρK)⁻¹ [A^(*h_0), ρK],

where A^(*h_0) = −2iσ̄(ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S_0))^(*h_0) + (ρ²N(P⁽⁰⁾))^(*h_0). Here
[(ρ²N(P⁽⁰⁾))^(*h_0), ρK] ∈ ρ³ Diff_b^1 and [σ̄(ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S_0))^(*h_0), ρK] ∈ σ̄ρ²C^∞, the latter a
multiplication operator (ρ∂_ρ differentiates ρK, and S_0^(*h_0) and K need not commute). These have the forms of the
first two terms of (13.20), with σ̄ for σ. The two estimates above then hold with the dual orders. ∎

#### 13.6.3 The theorem

For σ ≠ 0 with Im σ ≥ 0 let Σ be a sector of Corollary 13.16 (b) containing arg σ (Σ_+ = [0, π/4], Σ_m, Σ_−;
either one at π/4 and 3π/4), and 𝗋 := 𝗋_Σ, with the weight α_+ of Corollary 13.16. Put

    𝒳_σ := {u ∈ ℋ_ς^(s,(𝗋+α_+,α,0)) : P̂(σ)u ∈ 𝒴_σ},     𝒴_σ := ℋ_ς^(s−1,(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,0)),
    𝒳_σ^* := {v ∈ ℋ̇_ς^(1−s,(−𝗋−α_+−1,−α−2,0)) : P̂(σ)^(*h)v ∈ ℋ̇_ς^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−α,0))}.    (13.22)

By Lemma 13.23 (c) these are, at each σ, the spaces 𝒳_σ, 𝒴_σ, 𝒳_σ^* of Theorem 11.33 with the decay order 𝗋_ς,
and Theorem 11.33 applies to them: for θ ∈ Θ_±, 𝗋_(±,ς) is admissible for Re σ = ς cos θ ∈ ςJ_± (Section 13.4.3),
and (1) of Theorem 11.33 applies; for θ ∈ (0, π), 𝗋_ς is constant near R_out with the threshold, Im σ > 0, and (2)
applies.

*Augmentations* ([Hin26c, Remark 9.42]). Let m_1, m_2 ∈ ℕ_0, ψ_1, …, ψ_(m_1), φ_1, …, φ_(m_2) ∈ C_c^∞(X°; E), with
X° := {r > r_0}, and

    𝒫(σ)(u, c) := (P̂(σ)u + Σ_i c_i ψ_i, (⟨u, φ_j⟩_h)_j),
    𝒫(σ)^*(v, d) := (P̂(σ)^(*h)v + Σ_j d_j φ_j, (⟨v, ψ_i⟩_h)_i),    (13.23)

with ⟨·, ·⟩_h the h-weighted L²(|dx|) pairing, on 𝒳_σ ⊕ ℂ^(m_1) → 𝒴_σ ⊕ ℂ^(m_2) and
𝒳_σ^* ⊕ ℂ^(m_2) → ℋ̇_ς^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−α,0)) ⊕ ℂ^(m_1). Norms on the sums add |c| and |d|. The case m_1 = m_2 = 0 is P̂(σ)
itself. In place of (Z) we then assume

(Z_𝒫) 𝒫(0): 𝒳_0 ⊕ ℂ^(m_1) → 𝒴_0 ⊕ ℂ^(m_2) is invertible,

with 𝒳_0, 𝒴_0 of (13.7); for m_1 = m_2 = 0 this is (Z).

**Theorem 13.25** (Uniform low-energy estimates.) Assume (H1)–(H4), (G), (Z_𝒫) and (TF), with
s > ½ + ϑ_ℋ constant, and let α_+ ∈ ℝ. There are c_k > 0, k ∈ ℕ_0, non-increasing in k, such that the following hold.

(1) (*Uniform estimates.*) For every k ∈ ℕ_0 there is C_k such that for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_k with Im σ ≥ 0, and
(u, c) ∈ 𝒳_σ ⊕ ℂ^(m_1) with 𝒫(σ)(u, c) = (f, e),

    ‖u‖_((s;k),(𝗋+α_+,α,0),ς) + |c| ≤ C_k(‖f‖_((s−1;k),(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,0),ς) + |e|),    (13.24)

in the strong sense: if the right side is finite, so is the left.

(2) (*The adjoint.*) There is C such that for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_0 with Im σ ≥ 0, and (v, d) ∈ 𝒳_σ^* ⊕ ℂ^(m_2) with
𝒫(σ)^*(v, d) = (g, b),

    ‖v‖_((1−s),(−𝗋−α_+−1,−α−2,0),ς) + |d| ≤ C(‖g‖_((−s),(−𝗋−α_+,−α,0),ς) + |b|).    (13.25)

(3) (*Invertibility.*) For 0 < |σ| ≤ c_0 with Im σ ≥ 0, 𝒫(σ): 𝒳_σ ⊕ ℂ^(m_1) → 𝒴_σ ⊕ ℂ^(m_2) is invertible.

(4) (*Derivatives in σ; m_1 = m_2 = 0.*) For j, k ∈ ℕ_0 there are c_(j,k) ∈ (0, c_0] and C such that for
0 < |σ| ≤ c_(j,k) with Im σ ≥ 0,

    ‖(σ∂_σ)^j P̂(σ)⁻¹ f‖_((s+j;k),(𝗋+α_+,α,0),ς) ≤ C‖f‖_((s−1;k+j),(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,0),ς).    (13.26)

Here (σ∂_σ)^j P̂(σ)⁻¹ is the derivative of Theorem 11.33 (6), defined on H̄^((s+ϵ−1;j),𝗋_ς+ϵ+α_++1) and extended to
the space on the right by (13.26).

(5) (*Other weights.*) (1)–(4) hold for every α with α + 2 ∈ (β_−, β_+), the gap of (G): there (Z) holds by
Theorem 13.11 (4), and (TF) with weight α + 2 by Corollary 13.16 (c).

This is [Hin26c, Theorem 9.41] in dimension 4 + 1, on E, with the augmentations of [Hin26c, Remark 9.42] and with the
adjoint estimate (2). (G) is the gap hypothesis of Section 13.1.2. (13.24) is [Hin26c, (9.119)] and
(13.26) is [Hin26c, (9.120)], on the spaces of Definition 13.22. Remark 13.28 lists what differs from
[Hin26c].

#### 13.6.4 Proof of (1)

*Proof of Theorem 13.25 (1).* Fix k. Constants C do not depend on ς, on θ, or on ρ_c below, unless written C_(ρ_c).
Let φ_z ∈ C^∞([0, ∞)) vanish on [0, 2] and equal 1 on [4, ∞), let χ_0 ∈ C^∞([0, ∞)) equal 1 on [0, ½] and vanish on
[1, ∞), and put

    χ_zf := φ_z(ρ/ς),     χ_tf := χ_0(ρ/ρ_c),     0 < ρ_c ≤ ρ_c^0 := min(1/(2R_∂), ρ_1/2, 1/(2R)),

where supp ψ_i ∪ supp φ_j ⊂ {r ≤ R}. Then χ_∂ = 1 on supp χ_tf, χ_tf ψ_i = 0 = χ_tf φ_j, and for ς ≤ ρ_c/8,
χ_zf = 1 on supp(1 − χ_tf) and on supp ψ_i ∪ supp φ_j. Write ‖·‖_(l,q) for ‖·‖_((s;k),(𝗋+α_+,l,q),ς) and ‖·‖′_(l,q)
for ‖·‖_((s−1;k),(𝗋+α_++1,l,q),ς).

*Finiteness.* Let 𝒫(σ)(u, c) = (f, e) with the right side of (13.24) finite. Then
P̂(σ)u = f − Σ c_iψ_i ∈ H̄^((s−1;k),𝗋_ς+α_++1), so u ∈ H̄^((s;k),𝗋_ς+α_+) by Theorem 11.33 (4), and
‖u‖_(α,0) < ∞ by Lemma 13.23 (c). This is what makes the absorptions below legitimate.

*Step 1 (zf).* For ς small, χ_zf u is supported in {ρ ≥ 2ς}, a compact subset of X̄ ∖ ∂X for fixed ς. Since
χ_zf ψ_i = ψ_i and P̂(0)u = f − Σ c_iψ_i − (σT + σ²P_2)u,

    P̂(0)(χ_zf u) + Σ c_iψ_i = χ_zf f − χ_zf(σT + σ²P_2)u + [P̂(0), χ_zf]u.

By the finiteness above and Lemma 13.23 (c), u ∈ H̄^(s+k) and f ∈ H̄^(s+k−1) on {ρ ≥ ς}, which contains the
supports of all these terms, and the operators on the right are of order at most 1. So χ_zf u ∈ H̄^(s+k) and
P̂(0)(χ_zf u) ∈ H̄^(s+k−1), both with compact support in X̄ ∖ ∂X, and (χ_zf u, c) ∈ 𝒳_0 ⊕ ℂ^(m_1) at the regularity
s + k. (Z_𝒫) holds at the regularity s + k as well: the kernel of 𝒫(0) there lies in the kernel at s, and the index of
𝒫(0), which is that of P̂(0) plus m_1 − m_2, does not depend on the regularity by Theorem 13.11 (3). So by
Lemma 13.23 (a), the bounded inverse of 𝒫(0) at s + k, and ⟨χ_zf u, φ_j⟩_h = ⟨u, φ_j⟩_h,

    ‖χ_zf u‖_(α,0) + |c| ≤ C‖χ_zf u‖_(H̄_b^(s+k,α)) + |c| ≤ C(‖P̂(0)(χ_zf u) + Σ c_iψ_i‖_(H̄_b^(s+k−1,α+2)) + |e|).

The terms of the identity above are bounded as follows.

(i) By Lemma 13.23 (a), (b), ‖χ_zf f‖_(H̄_b^(s+k−1,α+2)) ≤ C‖χ_zf f‖′_(α+2,0) ≤ C‖f‖′_(α+2,0).

(ii) Let χ′_zf := φ′(ρ/ς) with φ′ = 0 on [0, 1] and 1 on [2, ∞); it is 1 near supp χ_zf, so
χ_zf(σT + σ²P_2)u = χ_zf(σT + σ²P_2)χ′_zf u. On {ρ < ρ_1}, σT + σ²P_2 = σρB_T + σ²ρ²g̃ with
B_T := 2i(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S) − iρ⁻¹Q ∈ Diff_b^1 by (13.1); ρB_T maps H̄_b^(s+k,α+1) to H̄_b^(s+k−1,α+2), and
ρ² maps H̄_b^(s+k,α) ⊃ H̄_b^(s+k,α+1) to H̄_b^(s+k,α+2). On {ρ ≥ ρ_1/2}, σT + σ²P_2 is σ times a first-order operator.
So, by Lemma 13.23 (a) with q = −1 and then (b), (d1),

    ‖χ_zf(σT + σ²P_2)u‖_(H̄_b^(s+k−1,α+2)) ≤ Cς‖χ′_zf u‖_(H̄_b^(s+k,α+1)) ≤ C‖χ′_zf u‖_(α,−1) ≤ C‖u‖_(α,−η),
                                                                                              η ∈ (0, 1].

(iii) [P̂(0), χ_zf] = ρ²[P⁽⁰⁾, χ_zf] is ρ² times a first-order b-operator whose coefficients, made of b-derivatives of
φ_z(ρ/ς), are bounded in C_b^∞ independently of ς and supported in {2ς ≤ ρ ≤ 4ς}. With χ″_zf := φ″(ρ/ς),
φ″ ∈ C_c^∞((1, 8)) equal to 1 on [2, 4], Lemma 13.23 (a), (d3) and (b) give

    ‖[P̂(0), χ_zf]u‖_(H̄_b^(s+k−1,α+2)) ≤ C‖χ″_zf u‖_(H̄_b^(s+k,α)) ≤ C‖χ″_zf u‖_(α,0) ≤ C‖χ″_zf u‖_(α,−η)
                                       ≤ C‖u‖_(α,−η).

(iv) (1 − χ_zf)u is supported in {ρ ≤ 4ς}, so by (d3) and (b), ‖(1 − χ_zf)u‖_(α,0) ≤ C‖u‖_(α,−η).

Together, for every η ∈ (0, 1] ([Hin26c, (9.121)]),

    ‖u‖_(α,0) + |c| ≤ C(‖f‖′_(α+2,0) + |e| + ‖u‖_(α,−η)).    (13.27)

*Step 2 (tf).* By (G), fix η ∈ (0, 1] with β_− < α + 2 − η and α + 2 + η < β_+, and put q_η := −α − η, so that
2 − q_η = α + 2 + η lies in the gap and Corollary 13.16 (b) applies at q = q_η. Split u = χ_tf u + (1 − χ_tf)u.

(v) (1 − χ_tf)u is supported in {ρ ≥ ρ_c/2}, so by (d2) and (b), ‖(1 − χ_tf)u‖_(α,−η) ≤ C_(ρ_c) ς^η ‖u‖_(α,0).

(vi) Since χ_∂ = 1 on supp χ_tf, ‖χ_tf u‖_(α,−η) = ς^(−(α+2)) ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋+α_+,q_η))) with
w := S_ς(χ_tf u). By (13.17), with C_T its constant, uniform in θ ∈ Σ,

    ‖w‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s;k),(𝗋+α_+,q_η))) ≤ C_T ‖N_tf(σ̂)w‖_(H_(sc,b;b)^((s−2;k),(𝗋+α_++1,q_η−2))),
    ς²N_tf(σ̂)w = S_ς(χ_tf f + [P̂(σ), χ_tf]u − E_σ χ_tf u),

using (13.13), (13.20) and χ_tf ψ_i = 0. The three terms, multiplied by ς^(−(α+2)) ς⁻², are bounded as
follows.

The first gives the tf part of ‖χ_tf f‖_((s−2;k),(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,−η),ς) (the order at ztf is −η − (α + 2) = q_η − 2),
which by Lemma 13.23 (b), (d) is at most C‖f‖′_(α+2,0).

The second: [P̂(σ), χ_tf] is a first-order operator with coefficients supported in {ρ_c/2 ≤ ρ ≤ ρ_c} and bounded, with
their derivatives, by C_(ρ_c) for |σ| ≤ 1. As χ_∂ = 1 there, the term is the full norm
‖[P̂(σ), χ_tf]u‖_((s−2;k),(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,−η),ς), which by Lemma 13.23 (a) with q = −η is at most
C_(ρ_c) ς^η ‖χ̃u‖_(H̄^(s+k−1)), χ̃ a cut-off to {ρ_c/4 ≤ ρ ≤ 2ρ_c}, and so by (a) and (b) at most
C_(ρ_c) ς^η ‖u‖_(α,0).

The third, by Lemma 13.24, is at most C(ρ_c + ς) ς^(−(α+2)) ‖w‖.

Fix ρ_c ≤ ρ_c^0 with C_T Cρ_c ≤ ¼, and let ς ≤ ρ_c/8 with C_T Cς ≤ ¼. Then the third term is absorbed, ‖w‖ being
finite, and

    ‖u‖_(α,−η) ≤ C‖f‖′_(α+2,0) + C_(ρ_c) ς^η ‖u‖_(α,0).

Inserted in (13.27) this gives ‖u‖_(α,0) + |c| ≤ C(‖f‖′_(α+2,0) + |e|) + C′_(ρ_c) ς^η ‖u‖_(α,0), and for
ς ≤ c′_k with C′_(ρ_c)(c′_k)^η ≤ ½ the last term is absorbed. Put c_k := min(c_0^*, min_(k′≤k) c′_(k′)), with
c_0^* > 0 the threshold of the proof of (2) below, which does not depend on the c_k. The c_k are non-increasing in k,
and for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_k this is (13.24). ∎

The argument is that of [Hin26c]: the zero energy estimate near zf, the tf estimate [Hin26c, (9.118)] near tf, and
absorption through the factor ς^η; no symbolic estimate is used. One step differs: [Hin26c] absorbs the model error
P̂(σ) − ς²N_tf through its vanishing at tf, [Hin26c, (9.122)], and here it is absorbed through the factor ρ_c + ς of
Lemma 13.24, with ρ_c fixed small first.

#### 13.6.5 Proof of (2) and (3)

*Proof of Theorem 13.25 (2) and (3).* *(2).* The proof of (1) at k = 0 applies to (v, d) with
𝒫(σ)^*(v, d) = (g, b); ‖v‖_((1−s),(−𝗋−α_+−1,−α−2,0),ς) is finite as v ∈ 𝒳_σ^*. The changes are these.

In Step 1, in place of the bounded inverse of 𝒫(0): for v ∈ 𝒳_0^* and d ∈ ℂ^(m_2),

    ‖v‖_(Ḣ_b^(1−s,−α−2)) + |d| ≤ C‖𝒫(0)^*(v, d)‖_(Ḣ_b^(−s,−α) ⊕ ℂ^(m_1)).    (13.28)

Indeed 𝒫(0) is invertible, so its Banach adjoint is, and by Green's formula of Section 13.3.1,
⟨𝒫(0)(u, c), (v, d)⟩ = ⟨(u, c), 𝒫(0)^*(v, d)⟩ for u ∈ 𝒳_0; as ‖u‖_(𝒳_0) ≥ ‖u‖_(H̄_b^(s,α)) and Ḣ_b^(−s,−α) is the
dual of H̄_b^(s,α) (Lemma 13.10 (a)), the norm of the functional (u, c) ↦ ⟨𝒫(0)(u, c), (v, d)⟩ on
𝒳_0 ⊕ ℂ^(m_1) is at most the right side of (13.28), and ‖v‖_(Ḣ_b^(1−s,−α−2)) is the norm of v in 𝒴_0^*. The
terms (i)–(iv) are as before with P̂(0)^(*h), σ̄T^(*h) + σ̄²P_2 (and T^(*h) ∈ ρ Diff_b^1 near ∂X, P_2^(*h) = P_2) and
[P̂(0)^(*h), χ_zf] ∈ ρ² Diff_b^1, the weights being those of (13.25) and the regularity 1 − s, respectively −s.

In Step 2 the weight moves the other way. Put q_η^* := η − α; then 2 − q_η^* = α + 2 − η lies in the gap by the
choice of η, and ‖χ_tf v‖_((1−s),(−𝗋−α_+−1,−α−2,−η),ς) = ς^α ‖w^*‖_(H_(sc,b)^(1−s,(−𝗋−α_+−1,−q_η^*+2))) with
w^* := S_ς(χ_tf v), the order at ztf being −η + α + 2. (13.18) at q = q_η^* bounds the stronger norm
‖w^*‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−s+2,(−𝗋−α_+−1,−q_η^*+2))) by C_T ‖N_tf(σ̂)^(*h)w^*‖_(H_(sc,b)^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−q_η^*))), whose order at
ztf, α − η, is that of ℋ̇_ς^(−s,(−𝗋−α_+,−α,−η)), and where

    ς²N_tf(σ̂)^(*h)w^* = S_ς(χ_tf g + [P̂(σ)^(*h), χ_tf]v − E_σ^* χ_tf v)

(Section 13.6.2; χ_tf φ_j = 0). The term with E_σ^* is absorbed at the regularity 2 − s, by the adjoint form of
Lemma 13.24, and the regularity is then lowered to 1 − s. The absorption needs the H^(−s+2)-norm of w^* to be
finite, and it is: on a neighbourhood of supp χ_tf, P̂(σ)^(*h)v = g, as the φ_j vanish there, and P̂(σ)^(*h) is
elliptic at fibre infinity there, so Proposition 11.24 in its strong form (the left side is finite when the right side
is) gives v the regularity 2 − s there, with its decay orders.

The absorptions are those of the proof of (1) at k = 0, with C_T the constant of (13.18) and the constants of
(13.28), of the adjoint terms (i)–(iv) and of the adjoint form of Lemma 13.24 in place of theirs: ρ_c is
fixed with C_T Cρ_c ≤ ¼, then ς ≤ ρ_c/8 with C_T Cς ≤ ¼, and the last absorption needs C′_(ρ_c)ς^η ≤ ½. These hold for
0 < ς ≤ c_0^*, for some c_0^* > 0 determined by these constants alone. As c_0 ≤ c_0^* by its definition in the proof of
(1), this gives (13.25) for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_0.

*(3).* 𝒫(σ) is P̂(σ) ⊕ 0 plus an operator of finite rank, so it is Fredholm by Theorem 11.33 (3), and by
(13.24) at k = 0 it is injective. Let (v, d) ∈ 𝒴_σ^* ⊕ ℂ^(m_2) annihilate its range. Taking c = 0 and
u ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ⁴)|_X (which lies in 𝒳_σ), ⟨u, P̂(σ)^(*h)v + Σ_j d_jφ_j⟩_h = 0 by Lemma 11.27 (d), so
P̂(σ)^(*h)v = −Σ_j d_jφ_j as a supported distribution; this lies in Ḣ^(−s,−𝗋_ς−α_+), so v ∈ 𝒳_σ^* (with
𝒴_σ^* = ℋ̇_ς^(1−s,(−𝗋−α_+−1,−α−2,0)) at fixed ς, by Lemma 13.23 (c) and Lemma 11.27 (b)). Taking u = 0 gives
⟨v, ψ_i⟩_h = 0. So 𝒫(σ)^*(v, d) = 0, and (v, d) = 0 by (13.25). The range is closed and has trivial
annihilator, so 𝒫(σ) is onto. ∎

[Hin26c] derives the invertibility in its Theorem 9.41 from the injectivity given by [Hin26c, (9.119)] and the index 0
of [Hin26c, (9.18)]. That route is not available for an augmented operator, whose index is m_1 − m_2 plus that of P̂(σ);
that index is what Corollary 13.27 determines, and (2) is the uniform estimate its proof needs.

#### 13.6.6 Proof of (4) and (5)

**Lemma 13.26** ([Hin26c, proof of (9.120)].) For i ≥ 1, A_i := (σ∂_σ)^i P̂(σ) = σT + 2^i σ²P_2. For
s′, l, q ∈ ℝ and k′ ∈ ℕ_0 there is C with

    ‖A_i u‖_((s′;k′),(𝗋+1,l+2,q),ς) ≤ C‖u‖_((s′;k′+1),(𝗋,l,q),ς),     ς ∈ (0, ς_1].

*Proof.* The formula for A_i holds because (σ∂_σ)σ^m = mσ^m and P̂(0), T, P_2 do not depend on σ.
(1 − χ_∂)A_i u = A_i(1 − χ_∂)u + [A_i, χ_∂]u. A_i is σ times a first-order operator on supp(1 − χ_∂), and
[A_i, χ_∂] = σ[T, χ_∂] is of order 0 with coefficients supported in {R_∂ ≤ r ≤ 2R_∂}; with Lemma 13.23 (a) for
the latter, the first term of the left side is at most Cς times the right side. For the second,
χ_∂A_i u = A_i(χ_∂u) − [A_i, χ_∂]u, the commutator again handled by Lemma 13.23 (a). By (13.1), with
Q = ρ³Q̃ and g_00 = ρ²g̃,

    ς⁻² S_ς A_i S_ς⁻¹ = 2iσ̂ρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − 3/2 − S) − iσ̂ς²ρ̂³Q̃ + 2^i ς²σ̂²ρ̂²g̃,

with coefficients smooth in (ςρ̂, ω) as in Lemma 13.24: indeed, as ρ = ςρ̂, σ = ςσ̂ and ρ∂_ρ = ρ̂∂_ρ̂,
S_ς(σT)S_ς⁻¹ = ςσ̂(2iςρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − 3/2 − S) − iς³ρ̂³Q̃) and S_ς(σ²P_2)S_ς⁻¹ = ς⁴σ̂²ρ̂²g̃. Near sctf,
ρ̂∂_ρ̂ uses one b-derivative and each factor ρ̂ raises the decay order by one, so the operator maps
H_sc^((s′;k′+1),𝗋) to H_sc^((s′;k′),𝗋+1). Near ztf, ρ̂ = r̂⁻¹ lowers the b-weight by one, and
H_(b,c−1)^(s′+k′) ⊂ H_(b,c−2)^(s′+k′) there (r̂ ≤ 2); and ς²ρ̂³ = ρ̂² · ςρ with ρ ≤ ρ_1. So it maps the ztf order q − l
to q − l − 2, and ς^(−(l+4)) ‖S_ς A_i χ_∂u‖ ≤ C ς^(−(l+2)) ‖S_ς χ_∂u‖ in the norms of (13.19). ∎

*Proof of Theorem 13.25 (4).* Let R(σ) := P̂(σ)⁻¹, 0 < |σ| ≤ c_0, and fix σ_* there. By Theorem 11.33 (6), for f in
D := H̄^((s+ϵ−1;j),𝗋_(ς_*)+ϵ+α_++1), σ ↦ R(σ)f is j times differentiable near σ_* in
Z := H̄^((s−ϵ;0),𝗋_(ς_*)−ϵ+α_+), on which P̂(σ) is injective (its kernel does not depend on the admissible orders,
Theorem 11.33 (3), for ϵ below the margins). Applying (σ∂_σ)^i to P̂(σ)R(σ)f = f, with σ∂_σ a derivation,

    (σ∂_σ)^i R(σ)f = −R(σ) Σ_(i′<i) [i!/(i′!(i − i′)!)] A_(i−i′) (σ∂_σ)^(i′) R(σ)f,     1 ≤ i ≤ j,    (13.29)

at σ = σ_*, as soon as the sum lies in 𝒴_(σ_*) (then both sides are elements of Z with the same image under the
injective P̂(σ_*)). We show by induction on i that, for |σ_*| ≤ c_(j,k) := min_(i≤j) c_(k+j−i)(s + i), with
c_(k′)(s′) the constant of (1) at the regularity s′ (all hypotheses hold at every s′ ≥ s, (Z_𝒫) by
Theorem 13.11 (4)),

    ‖(σ∂_σ)^i R(σ_*)f‖_((s+i;k+j−i),(𝗋+α_+,α,0),ς_*) ≤ C‖f‖_((s−1;k+j),(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,0),ς_*).

The case i = 0 is (1) at the regularity s and b-order k + j. For i ≥ 1, by the induction hypothesis and
Lemma 13.26 the term i′ of the sum lies in ℋ_(ς_*)^((s+i′;k+j−i′−1),(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,0)), which by
Lemma 13.23 (e) lies in ℋ_(ς_*)^((s+i−1;k+j−i),(𝗋+α_++1,α+2,0)), as i′ ≤ i − 1; (1) at the regularity s + i and
b-order k + j − i then gives the bound. At i = j this is (13.26) for f ∈ D. D contains C_c^∞(ℝ⁴)|_X, which is
dense in H̄^((s−1;k+j),𝗋_(ς_*)+α_++1), and by (13.29) and the bounds the derivatives extend continuously; this
is the extension in (4), and it agrees with that of (11.35). ∎

*Proof of Theorem 13.25 (5).* For α′ with α′ + 2 ∈ (β_−, β_+), (Z) at α′ holds by Theorem 13.11 (4) and (TF) at
α′ + 2 by Corollary 13.16 (c). For an augmented operator, (Z_𝒫) at α′: the kernel of 𝒫(0) and the annihilator of its
range, which is the kernel of 𝒫(0)^* on 𝒳_0^* ⊕ ℂ^(m_2) (as in the proof of (3)), consist of the (u, c) with
P̂(0)u = −Σ c_iψ_i, respectively the (v, d) with P̂(0)^(*h)v = −Σ d_jφ_j, whose right sides vanish near ∂X; so the proof
of Theorem 13.11 (2)–(3) shows that they do not depend on α′, and 𝒫(0) stays invertible. The proof of (1)–(4) used
no other property of α. ∎

#### 13.6.7 The index at zero energy

**Corollary 13.27** (Index 0 at zero energy.) Assume (H1)–(H4), (G) and (TF), with s > ½ + ϑ_ℋ, and that
the index of P̂(σ): 𝒳_σ → 𝒴_σ at σ ≠ 0, Im σ ≥ 0, which does not depend on σ (Theorem 11.33 (3)), is 0; under the
hypotheses of Chapter 12 this is Theorem 12.2 (3). Then P̂(0): 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 has index 0.

This is [Hin26c, Corollary 9.43] in dimension 4 + 1, on E.

*Proof.* Let d_0 and d_1 be the dimensions of the kernel K of P̂(0) on 𝒳_0 and of W := ker_(𝒳_0^*) P̂(0)^(*h), the
annihilator of its range (Theorem 13.11 (1)). An element of K that vanishes on X° is 0, as extendible distributions
are restrictions to X°. An element w of W that vanishes on X° is supported on ∂_♯X, and then (11.29) of
Corollary 11.31 at σ = 0 gives w = 0 on a slab Ω_(r_0,b″), so w = 0. So the pairings with C_c^∞(X°; E) separate the
points of K and of W, and there are φ_1, …, φ_(d_0) and ψ_1, …, ψ_(d_1) in C_c^∞(X°; E) with (⟨k_a, φ_j⟩_h) and
(⟨ψ_i, w_b⟩_h) invertible, for bases (k_a) of K and (w_b) of W. With these, m_1 := d_1 and m_2 := d_0, 𝒫(0) of
(13.23) is invertible: if P̂(0)u + Σ c_iψ_i = 0 and ⟨u, φ_j⟩_h = 0 for all j, pairing with w_b gives c = 0,
then u ∈ K and u = 0; and given (f, e), choose c with f − Σ c_iψ_i annihilated by W, hence equal to P̂(0)u_0 (the range
is closed), and then k ∈ K with ⟨u_0 + k, φ_j⟩_h = e_j. So (Z_𝒫) holds, and Theorem 13.25 (3) gives that 𝒫(σ) is
invertible for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_0. Its index is that of P̂(σ) plus m_1 − m_2, that is d_1 − d_0, and it is 0. So
d_0 = d_1. ∎

The proof is that of [Hin26c], with Theorem 13.25 (2)–(3) supplying the invertibility of the augmented operator,
which injectivity alone does not give, and with the choice of ψ_i, φ_j in C_c^∞(X°; E) justified.

**Remark 13.28** (What differs from [Hin26c].) (a) The smallness c_k in Theorem 13.25 (1) may depend on k.
[Hin26c] removes the dependence by applying its Theorem 9.5 (4) for |σ| ∈ [δ_k, δ_0]. Here that would need
Theorem 11.33 (4) with constants uniform for σ in a compact set and the orders 𝗋_ς, which depend on |σ|;
Theorem 11.33 gives uniformity only for orders that depend on Re σ (Theorem 11.33 (1)). So Theorem 13.25 is
stated with c_k, and with c_(j,k) in (4). (b) [Hin26c] asserts the conclusions uniformly for α in compact subintervals
of the gap; Theorem 13.25 (5) is stated for each α, and the uniformity is not proved here. (c) Theorem 13.25 (4) is
stated for P̂(σ): for an augmented operator it would need the analogue of Theorem 11.33 (6), which is not proved in
Chapter 11. (d) The regularity order is constant (Remark 11.3).

### 13.7 Uniformity in the operator

**Theorem 13.29** (Uniformity in the operator.) Assume (H1)–(H5), and let b_* ∈ ℬ be such that (G), (Z_𝒫)
and (TF) hold for P̂^(b_*) with the weight α and fixed ψ_i, φ_j. Then:

(1) (G), (Z_𝒫) and (TF) hold for P̂^b, with the same α, for b near b_*;

(2) the constants in Theorem 13.11 (1), (4), Theorem 13.14 (1), (2), (4), Corollary 13.16 (b) and
Theorem 13.25 (1), (2), (4), and c_k, c_(j,k), can be chosen uniform for b near b_*;

(3) the index of P̂^b(0): 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 is locally constant in b.

*Proof.* (G): let [α + 2 − ϵ, α + 2 + ϵ] contain no real part of a root at b_*. By Lemma 13.5 (c),
I^(b_*)(ι)⁻¹ is bounded from H_μ^(m−2) to H_μ^m, μ = Im ι, uniformly on the strip |Re ι − α − 2| ≤ ϵ. The difference
I^b(ι) − I^(b_*)(ι) = (a^b − a^(b_*))ι + (V^b − V^(b_*)) + (b^b − b^(b_*)) has coefficients that tend to 0 in C^∞ as
b → b_*, by (H5), and maps H_μ^m to H_μ^(m−2) with norm at most ϵ_b(1 + |Re ι|) → 0 uniformly on the strip, as
⟨μ⟩‖v‖_(H_μ^(m−2)) ≤ ‖v‖_(H_μ^(m−1)) and as in the proof of Lemma 13.5 (a) for the first-order part. A Neumann
series gives that I^b(ι) is invertible on the strip, so α + 2 lies in a gap at b.

(2) for the estimates with error terms ((13.8)–(13.9), (13.14)–(13.16)): their constants
are produced by finitely many seminorms of the coefficients and by positivity margins, as in Theorem 11.38, and by
the bounds of J(ι)⁻¹ on the lines used in Lemma 13.7 (Lemma 13.8 is qualitative), which are uniform near b_*
by the Neumann series above; the coefficients depend continuously on b by (H5).

(Z_𝒫) and the estimates without error terms: suppose b_j → b_* and (u_j, c_j) have
‖u_j‖_(H̄_b^(s,α)) + |c_j| = 1 and 𝒫^(b_j)(0)(u_j, c_j) → 0. By (13.8), uniformly in j,
‖u_j‖_(H̄_b^(s,α)) ≤ C(‖𝒫^(b_j)(0)(u_j, c_j)‖ + |c_j| + ‖u_j‖_(H̄_b^(−M,−M))), so a subsequence converges weakly in
H̄_b^(s,α) and strongly in H̄_b^(−M,−M) (Lemma 13.10 (b)) to u, with c_j → c and (u, c) ≠ 0. Since
P̂^(b_j)(0)u_j → P̂^(b_*)(0)u in distributions, P̂^(b_*)(0)u = −Σ c_iψ_i, so u ∈ 𝒳_0 and 𝒫^(b_*)(0)(u, c) = 0,
contradicting (Z_𝒫) at b_*. So the estimate ‖u‖ + |c| ≤ C‖𝒫^b(0)(u, c)‖ holds uniformly near b_*. The same argument
with (13.9) for 𝒫^b(0)^* shows that its kernel, the annihilator of the range, is trivial near b_*, so 𝒫^b(0)
is onto.

(TF) and Corollary 13.16 (b): the proof of Corollary 13.16 (b) by contradiction runs with sequences
(θ_j, b_j) → (θ_*, b_*), using (13.14) uniformly and N_tf^(b_j)(e^(iθ_j))w_j → N_tf^(b_*)(e^(iθ_*))w in
distributions; at b_*, Corollary 13.16 (a) gives injectivity for every θ. The same argument with a sequence of kernel
elements shows that Definition 13.15 (ii) and (iii) hold near b_* (for (iii), with (13.15) and the adjoint for
H_0^b).

Theorem 13.25: its constants are those of Theorem 13.11 (4) (for 𝒫), of (13.17)–(13.18), and of
Lemma 13.23, Lemma 13.24 and Lemma 13.26, which are uniform by the above and by (H5); c_k and c_(j,k) are
chosen from them. (3): augment P̂^(b_*)(0) as in the proof of Corollary 13.27; by (1), 𝒫^b(0) is invertible near b_*,
so the index of P̂^b(0) is m_2 − m_1 there. ∎

(Z) and (TF) are therefore open conditions in the operator: once they hold for one member of a family satisfying
(H5), they hold for the nearby ones.

### 13.8 Remarks on [Hin26c]

The following points concern the text of [Hin26c]; pages are its printed pages. Remarks (3) and (5) correct misprints
in two statements, [Hin26c, (9.107)] and the condition on θ in [Hin26c, Theorem 9.38 (1)]: as printed, the first would
gain two orders of decay, and the second pairs 𝗋_+ with θ near π. Their intended forms are the ones proved here.
Remark (2) corrects a power in the norm equivalence [Hin26c, (3.46)], which cancels in the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem
9.41]. Remarks (1), (4) and (7) concern two signs that cancel, a term dropped in a proof whose conclusion holds as
printed, and slips of the pen. Remark (6) closes a gap in a proof. No result of [Hin26c] changes in substance.

(1) In [Hin26c, Section 3.2.3, p. 61] the Mellin transform is (ℳu)(σ) = ∫_0^∞ ρ^(iσ) u dρ/ρ, so ρ∂_ρ becomes −iσ and
the indicial roots are ι = −iσ at the poles of N(A, σ)⁻¹ ([Hin26c, Definition 3.12]). For u ∈ ρ^β L²(dρ/ρ) the
Plancherel line is then Im σ = β, while [Hin26c, Lemma 3.11] integrates over σ − i(α + 3/2), that is
Im σ = −(α + 3/2); and the proof of [Hin26c, (3.47)] uses that N(A, −iν + κ), κ ∈ ℝ, is invertible when ν lies in an
indicial gap, whereas the poles on that line are the roots with real part −ν. With both signs reversed the argument is
unchanged, and [Hin26c, (3.47)] holds as stated. Lemma 13.4 and Lemma 13.7 use ℳv(ι) = ∫ e^(ιt) v dt,
t = −log ϱ, for which the line of the b-weight c is Re ι = c.

(2) In [Hin26c, (3.46), p. 60] the second equivalence carries the factor |σ|^(3/2−l), from the relation
r²|dr dω| = (|σ|^(3/2))² r̂²|dr̂ dω|. With r̂ = r|σ|, r² dr = |σ|⁻³ r̂² dr̂, so the factor is |σ|^(−3/2) and the
power |σ|^(−3/2−l); in dimension 4 + 1, where r³ dr = ς⁻⁴ r̂³ dr̂, it is ς^(−2−l), as in (13.19). The power enters
both sides of the tf step of the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 9.41] and cancels there.

(3) [Hin26c, (9.107), p. 194] bounds ‖u^*‖ in Ḣ_b^(−s_0+1,−α−2) by the norm of the adjoint applied to u^* in
Ḣ_b^(−s_0,−α−2). The adjoint lies in ρ² Diff_b^2 and raises the weight by 2, and the space of its values is dual to
that of the domain, H̄_b^(s_0,α); the weight there is −α, as in (13.9).

(4) [Hin26c, (9.117), p. 196] gives the conjugated adjoint e^(2i/ρ̂)N_tf(1)^*e^(−2i/ρ̂), the adjoint taken for the
Euclidean density ρ̂^(−n)|dρ̂/ρ̂ dω| of ℝⁿ, the form −2iρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − (n − 1)/2 − S̃) + ρ̂²P̃⁽⁰⁾ of N_tf(−1). Its proof
expands −ρ̂²(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − n + 2 + 2iρ̂⁻¹)², the conjugate of the adjoint of −ρ̂²(ρ̂∂_ρ̂)², with the middle term
−2iρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − n + 1). Of the two cross products, (ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − n + 2)·2iρ̂⁻¹ = 2iρ̂⁻¹(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − n + 1) and
2iρ̂⁻¹(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − n + 2), only the first is kept; with both, the middle term is −2iρ̂(2ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − 2n + 3). The conclusion
stands. The adjoint of 2iρ̂·ρ̂∂_ρ̂ for that density is 2iρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ + 1 − n), which the conjugation turns into
2iρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ + 1 − n) − 4, and every other term of N_tf(1)^* conjugates to ρ̂ times an operator of order 0 on the
sphere plus an element of ρ̂² Diff_b^2. So the coefficient of ρ̂·ρ̂∂_ρ̂ is 2i − 4i = −2i (with the printed middle
term it would be 0), the constants −4 and 4 cancel, and the remaining terms enter S̃ and P̃⁽⁰⁾: [Hin26c, (9.117)]
holds as printed. It serves only [Hin26c, (9.115)], which is not used here (Section 13.4.3).

(5) [Hin26c, Theorem 9.38 (1), p. 195] takes θ with |e^(iθ) ± 1| ≤ ½ and 𝗋 = 𝗋_±. The orders 𝗋_± are those for
frequencies near ±1 ([Hin26c, Theorem 9.41] uses 𝗋_+ for arg σ ∈ [0, π/4]), so the condition is |e^(iθ) ∓ 1| ≤ ½, as
in Θ_± of Section 13.4.3.

(6) The proof of [Hin26c, Corollary 9.43, p. 200] augments P̂(0) by maps E_01: ℂ^(d_1) → C_c^∞(X°) and E_10:
𝒳_0 → ℂ^(d_0), applies [Hin26c, Theorem 9.41] to the augmented operator to obtain its invertibility at σ = iϵ, and
concludes d_0 = d_1 from the index 0 of [Hin26c, (9.18)]. The estimate [Hin26c, (9.119)] gives injectivity; for P̂(σ)
itself invertibility then follows from the index 0 of [Hin26c, (9.18)]. The augmented operator has index d_1 − d_0,
which is the quantity the corollary asserts to vanish, and injectivity gives only d_1 ≤ d_0; surjectivity needs an
estimate for the adjoint of the augmented operator, uniform as σ → 0, which [Hin26c] does not state. Theorem 13.25 (2)
is that estimate and (3) the invertibility, proved for augmented operators; with them Corollary 13.27 follows by the
argument of [Hin26c], and the statement of [Hin26c, Corollary 9.43] stands.

(7) In the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 9.41, p. 198] the zero energy step writes the error and target norms with tf orders
α_+ and α_+ + 2 where the orders are α and α + 2, as in [Hin26c, (9.121)] a few lines later. In [Hin26c, Theorem 9.38
(3), p. 195], N_tf(P_0, e^(iθ)u) stands for N_tf(P_0, e^(iθ))u.

Not proved in this chapter, and not used in it: [Hin26c, (9.115)] and the conjugation behind it (Section 13.4.3); the
improvements of [Hin26c, Remark 9.37] (Remark 13.12); and, in [Hin26c, Theorem 9.41], a smallness independent of k,
uniformity in α, and [Hin26c, (9.120)] for augmented operators (Remark 13.28). tf-admissibility is stated here on the
Fredholm spaces (Definition 13.15), which [Hin26c, Definition 5.10] implies given [Hin26c, (9.115)] (Section 13.5.1);
Proposition 13.20 verifies Definition 13.15 directly.

# Part VI. The stability theory, II: analysis on the compactified spacetime

## 14. The compactified spacetime, its calculi and the standard estimates

This chapter sets up the geometry and the microlocal analysis on which the forward problems of the following chapters
rest. It writes out [Hin26c, Sections 2 and 3] in dimension 4 + 1: the compactified spacetime M with its faces ι⁺
(future timelike infinity), ℐ⁺ (null infinity), K⁺ (the Kerr face) and I⁰ (spacelike infinity); its Lie algebras of
b-, 3b-, eb- and e3b-vector fields; the e3b-calculus; the Fourier transform near K⁺ and the Mellin transform at ι⁺;
supported and extendible spaces; functions and operators of finite regularity; and the elliptic and real principal type
estimates on e3b-spaces, with b-regularity and in tame form.

*What changes in dimension 4 + 1.* The spacetime is ℝ^(1+4) and the sphere of directions is 𝕊³, so every construction
of [Hin26c, Section 2] is repeated with 𝕊³ in place of 𝕊², and the proofs do not use the dimension. The dimension enters
through the volume density |dt dx| of the L²-spaces. Near ι⁺, |dt dx| = t_*⟨x⟩⁴ times a b-density, and t_*⁻¹⟨x⟩⁻⁴ is a
smooth positive multiple of x_I⁸ ρ_+⁵ ρ_K. So the weights (2(α_I + 3/2), α_+ + 2, α_K + 1/2) of [Hin26c, (3.57), Lemma
3.14 and Lemma 3.22] become (2(α_I + 2), α_+ + 5/2, α_K + 1/2) (Lemma 14.19, Lemma 14.20 and Lemma 14.33),
the weight α + 3/2 of [Hin26c, (3.72)] becomes α + 2 ((14.10)), and the line of the Mellin transform becomes
Im σ = α_+ + 5/2 (Lemma 14.20). The Sobolev embeddings H^(d+3) ⊂ C^d and H³ ⊂ L^∞ hold on ℝ⁵ as on ℝ⁴ (3 > 5/2),
so no regularity threshold changes.

*Organisation.* Section 14.1 and Section 14.2 construct the compactified spacetime and its Lie algebras of vector
fields, with the commutator lemmas behind b-regularity. Section 14.3 lists the results of the calculus of [Hin26d] that
are used. Section 14.4 sets up the e3b-calculus and its spaces, Section 14.5 and Section 14.6 the Fourier transform
near K⁺ and the Mellin transform at ι⁺, Section 14.7 supported and extendible spaces, and Section 14.8 L^∞-spaces,
operators of limited regularity and Sobolev embedding. Section 14.9 to Section 14.13 prove the two standard
estimates without b-regularity, for coefficients of finite regularity and variable orders: the elliptic estimate
(Theorem 14.43) and the real principal type propagation estimate (Theorem 14.49). Section 14.14 derives from
them the estimates with b-regularity and their tame versions.

*Notation.* Variable orders are written in sans-serif letters 𝗌, 𝗆, 𝗅, 𝗋, 𝖻, 𝗄, 𝗍, constant orders in italic; the
sans-serif 𝖧 is not an order but the rescaled Hamilton vector field of Section 14.13.1. ℝ̄^N is the
radial compactification of ℝ^N, g̸ the round metric on 𝕊³, and ⟨x⟩ = (1 + |x|²)^(1/2). The bundles of the various
structures are written ᵇT, ³ᵇT, ᵉᵇT, ᵉ³ᵇT, ˢᶜT, and their duals with a star. Constants C may change from line to line.

### 14.1 Compactifications

Write z = (t, x) ∈ ℝ^(1+4), x = rω, r = |x|, ω ∈ 𝕊³, ρ := r⁻¹, and fix r_0 > 0. In applications r_0 is the radius of
the artificial boundary inside the horizon (Section 11.1.1); nothing in this chapter depends on its value.

*Radial compactification.* For N ≥ 1, ℝ̄^N := (ℝ^N ⊔ [0, ∞)_ϱ × 𝕊^(N−1))/∼, with Z = Rϖ ∼ (ϱ, ϖ) = (R⁻¹, ϖ) for Z ≠ 0
[Hin26c, (2.1)]. A linear isomorphism L of ℝ^N extends to a diffeomorphism of ℝ̄^N: in the coordinates (ϱ, ϖ) near the
boundary, L(ϖ/ϱ) = |Lϖ| ϖ′/ϱ with ϖ′ = Lϖ/|Lϖ|, so L acts by (ϱ, ϖ) ↦ (ϱ/|Lϖ|, Lϖ/|Lϖ|), which is smooth with smooth
inverse since |Lϖ| is bounded above and below on 𝕊^(N−1).

**Definition 14.1** (The spatial manifold; [Hin26c, Definition 2.1] in dimension 4 + 1.) X̃ := ℝ̄⁴ and
X := {r ≥ r_0} ⊂ X̃, with boundary hypersurfaces ∂_♯X := {r = r_0} and ∂X := {ρ = 0}. This is the manifold X̄ of
Section 11.1.1.

**Definition 14.2** (Spacetime compactifications; [Hin26c, Definition 2.2].) Let k_± ∈ ∂ℝ̄^(1+4) be the
limit points of (±t, 0) as t → ∞ (in the projective coordinates 1/(±t), x/(±t) near k_±, k_± = {1/(±t) = 0,
x/(±t) = 0}), and let Y⁺ := {1/t = 0, (r − t)/t = 0} ⊂ ∂ℝ̄^(1+4), the light cone at future infinity, a smooth
submanifold diffeomorphic to 𝕊³.

(1) M̃_0 := [ℝ̄^(1+4); k_+, k_−], with boundary hypersurfaces sf (the lift of ∂ℝ̄^(1+4)) and K^± (the lifts of k_±).

(2) M̃_1 := [M̃_0; Y⁺], with boundary hypersurfaces ℐ⁺_1 (the front face), K^±, ι⁺_1 (the closure of {r/t ∈ (0, 1),
1/t = 0}) and I⁰_1 (the closure of {t/r < 1, 1/r = 0}); and M̃ := [M̃_1; ℐ⁺_1, 1/2], the square root blow-up of ℐ⁺_1
(a square root of a defining function of ℐ⁺_1 is declared a defining function of its lift). The boundary hypersurfaces
of M̃ are null infinity ℐ⁺, the Kerr faces K^± (the name is that of [Hin26c]; here they are the faces of the black hole
region), future timelike infinity ι⁺ and spacelike infinity I⁰, with (local) defining functions x_I, ρ_K, ρ_+, ρ_0;
ρ_I := x_I² is a defining function of ℐ⁺_1.

(3) M_0, M_1 and M are the closures of {r ≥ r_0} in M̃_0, M̃_1 and M̃.

**Definition 14.3** (Domains; [Hin26c, Definition 2.3].) Ω̃^♯ := cl_M̃ {t ≥ 0}, Ω^♯ := Ω̃^♯ ∩ M, and
Ω := cl_M {t − r ≥ 1}.

*Coordinates* [Hin26c, (2.8)–(2.12)]. Put t_* := t − r and v := (t − r)/r = ρ t_*.

(A) In M°: (t, x), (t, r, ω) or (t_*, r, ω).

(B) Near the interiors: of K⁺, (1/t, x) or (1/t_*, x); of ι⁺, (v, ρ_+ = 1/t_*, ω) or (v, 1/r, ω); of ℐ⁺,
(t − r, r^(−1/2), ω); of I⁰ ∩ {t ≥ 0}, ((r − t)/r, 1/r, ω).

(C) Near the corners: at I⁰ ∩ ℐ⁺ (where t − r < 2), ρ_0 = 1/(r − t + 2) and x_I = ((r − t + 2)/r)^(1/2); at ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺
(where t − r > 0), ρ_+ = 1/(t − r) and x_I = ((t − r)/r)^(1/2) = √v; at ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, ρ_+ = 1/r and ρ_K = r/t; always with
ω ∈ 𝕊³.

These are the projective coordinates of the blow-ups. For instance, near k_+ the functions s := 1/t and y := x/t are
coordinates on ℝ̄^(1+4), with k_+ = {s = 0, y = 0}; on [ℝ̄^(1+4); k_+] the projective coordinates (s, y/s) = (1/t, x)
cover the interior of the front face K⁺, and (|y|, s/|y|, y/|y|) = (r/t, 1/r, ω) cover its corner with sf. Near Y⁺ in
sf°, (1/r, (t − r)/r = v, ω) are coordinates and Y⁺ = {1/r = 0, v = 0}; the projective coordinates of [M̃_0; Y⁺] near
the corner of ℐ⁺_1 with ι⁺_1 are (v, 1/(rv) = 1/(t − r), ω), and the square root blow-up replaces v by x_I = √v. The
other charts are obtained in the same way.

The blow-down map realises ℐ⁺ as the total space of a fibration ℝ̄ → ℐ⁺ → Y⁺ = 𝕊³, the fibres having interiors
{t − r ∈ ℝ, r^(−1/2) = 0, ω = ω_0} [Hin26c, (2.13)].

*Explicit defining functions on Ω* [Hin26c, Remark 2.4]:

    x_I = (t_*/(t_* + r))^(1/2),     ρ_+ = (t_* + r)/(t_* r),     ρ_K = r/(t_* + r).    (14.1)

Indeed, on Ω, t_* ∼ ρ_+⁻¹ρ_K⁻¹, r ∼ x_I⁻²ρ_+⁻¹ and t_* + r ∼ x_I⁻²ρ_+⁻¹ρ_K⁻¹ (the quotients being positive and smooth),
and the stated expressions solve these relations.

### 14.2 Lie algebras of vector fields

This section introduces the Lie algebras of vector fields on the compactifications: the scattering and b-vector fields
(Section 14.2.1), the 3b-vector fields at K⁺ (Section 14.2.2), the edge-b-vector fields at ℐ⁺ (Section 14.2.3),
and the e3b-vector fields which combine the two (Section 14.2.4); then Hamiltonian vector fields
(Section 14.2.5) and the two product structures on which the normal operators are defined (Section 14.2.6).

#### 14.2.1 Scattering and b-structures
The scattering tangent bundle ˢᶜTℝ̄^N is ℝ̄^N × ℝ^N, identified with Tℝ^N over ℝ^N by (z, v) ↦ v^μ ∂_(z^μ), and
𝒱_sc(ℝ̄^N) := C^∞(ℝ̄^N; ˢᶜTℝ̄^N). In the projective chart ρ_1 = 1/z¹, ẑ^i = z^i/z¹ (z¹ > 0),
∂_(z¹) = ρ_1(−ρ_1∂_(ρ_1) − Σ_(i≥2) ẑ^i ∂_(ẑ^i)) and ∂_(z^i) = ρ_1 ∂_(ẑ^i); so 𝒱_sc(ℝ̄^N) = ρ𝒱_b(ℝ̄^N), with ρ a
boundary defining function, where 𝒱_b is the space of smooth vector fields tangent to the boundary, spanned by ∂_(z^μ)
and z^μ ∂_(z^ν). On a manifold with corners, 𝒱_b is the space of smooth vector fields tangent to every boundary
hypersurface. The Minkowski metric ḡ = −dt² + dx² lies in C^∞(ℝ̄^(1+4); S² ˢᶜT*ℝ̄^(1+4)). We write 𝒯 → M̃_0, M̃_1, M̃
for the pullback of ˢᶜTℝ̄^(1+4) along the blow-down maps [Hin26c, Definition 2.6]. 𝒱_b(M̃) and 𝒱_sc are Lie algebras,
and Diff^m_b, Diff^m_sc are the spaces of sums of up to m-fold compositions of their elements, with smooth coefficients.
For a boundary hypersurface H with a collar [0, ε)_(ρ_H) × H, the b-normal field ρ_H ∂_(ρ_H) is independent of the collar
modulo ρ_H 𝒱_b.

*Spanning sets* [Hin26c, Example 2.9]. Near (K⁺)° (coordinates ρ_K = 1/t, x): t∂_t = −ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) and ∂_x. Near K⁺ ∩ ι⁺
(ρ_+ = 1/r, ρ_K = r/t): −ρ_+∂_(ρ_+) = t∂_t + r∂_r, −ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) = t∂_t, and ∂_ω. Near ℐ⁺_1 ∩ ι⁺_1 (ρ_+ = 1/(t − r),
ρ_I = (t − r)/r): −ρ_+∂_(ρ_+) = t∂_t + r∂_r, ρ_I∂_(ρ_I) − ρ_+∂_(ρ_+) = (t − r)∂_t, and ∂_ω; one may use
−ρ_I∂_(ρ_I) = r(∂_t + ∂_r) in place of the first. On Ω, r∂_x and t_*∂_(t_*) form a global frame (in the coordinates
(t_*, x)). Each of these follows from the chain rule in the charts of Section 14.1.

#### 14.2.2 3b-structures
**Definition 14.4** ([Hin26c, Definition 2.10].) ³ᵇTM̃_0 := M̃_0 × ℝ⁵, identified with Tℝ^(1+4) over
ℝ^(1+4) by (z, v) ↦ v^μ ⟨x⟩ ∂_(z^μ) (over M_0 equivalently v^μ r∂_(z^μ)); 𝒱_3b(M̃_0) is its space of smooth sections, and
Diff^m_3b(M̃_0) the space of sums of up to m-fold compositions of its elements, with smooth coefficients.

The Minkowski metric is

    ḡ = r²(−(dt/r)² + (dr/r)² + g̸) ∈ r² C^∞(M̃_0; S² ³ᵇT*M̃_0),     ḡ⁻¹ = r⁻²(−(r∂_t)² + (r∂_r)² + g̸⁻¹)

[Hin26c, (2.20)]. Near K⁺ ∩ sf, with ρ_K = r/t and ρ_+ = 1/r, r∂_t = −ρ_K²∂_(ρ_K) and r∂_r = ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) − ρ_+∂_(ρ_+).
Hence 𝒱_3b ⊂ 𝒱_b and ρ_K𝒱_b ⊂ 𝒱_3b (as ρ_K t∂_t = r∂_t), and [r∂_r, r∂_t] = r∂_t shows that 𝒱_3b is a Lie algebra. The
map t ↦ −t exchanges K⁺ and K⁻, fixes t∂_t and changes the sign of r∂_t, so near K⁻ all of this holds with
ρ_K := r/|t|; below, ρ_K denotes a defining function of K⁺ ∪ K⁻ of this form near the corners with sf. A
b-vector field V lies in 𝒱_3b if and only if Vt ∈ tρ_K C^∞ near K⁺ ∪ K⁻ (the coefficient of t∂_t must lie in
