Since WF′(G_2) ⊂ Ell(G_3) ∩ Ell(L), (14.21) at k − 1 bounds ‖G_2u‖_((𝗌;k−1)) by
C(‖G_3Lu‖_((𝗌−m;k−1)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k−1))). Lemma 14.29 (c) bounds ‖G_3Lu‖ by
C(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m;k−1)) + ‖χ_*Lu‖_((−N−m;k−1))), and the last term is treated as before. Each step shows that the quantity
bounded is finite when the right side of (14.21) is: the step at k − 1 applied to V_ju has finite right side.
So V_jBu ∈ H^((𝗌;k−1)) for every j, that is, Bu ∈ H^((𝗌;k)), with (14.21). The constants depend on L through
‖𝐚‖_((d_0;k)), the constants at k − 1 and those of (L3). The step from k − 1 to k applies (L3), Lemma 14.31 and the
statement at k − 1 to operators G_1, G_2, G_3, [V_j, B], cut-offs χ_1, χ_* and a finite set 𝒫′ chosen anew at each k.
The d_0 of (L3) and of Lemma 14.31 depends only on the orders and not on these choices (Theorem 14.43,
Lemma 14.31), so the same d_0 serves at every k: d_0 does not depend on k. ∎

**Proposition 14.52** ([Hin26c, Proposition 3.24].) There is d_0 = d_0(m, 𝗌, N) such that the following
holds for all δ > 0, k ∈ ℕ_0 and operators on ℂ^(N′) of the form below; d_0 depends neither on k, δ, N′ and the finite
sets nor on B, E, G and χ, which enter only the constant. The operators are

    L = L_0 + L_1 + L_2,   L_0 ∈ Diff^m_e3b ⊗ Id,   L_1 ∈ C^((d_0;k),(2δ,δ,δ))_(e3b;b) 𝒫_m ⊗ Id,
    L_2 ∈ C^((d_0;k))_(e3b;b) 𝒫_(m−1) ⊗ End ℂ^(N′),    (14.22)

under the hypotheses of (L4) on ℓ, B, E, G and 𝗌. If χu ∈ H^((−N;k)), GLu ∈ H^((𝗌−m+1;k)) and Eu ∈ H^((𝗌;k)), then
Bu ∈ H^((𝗌;k)) and

    ‖Bu‖_(H^((𝗌;k))_(e3b;b))
       ≤ C(‖GLu‖_(H^((𝗌−m+1;k))_(e3b;b)) + ‖Eu‖_(H^((𝗌;k))_(e3b;b)) + ‖χu‖_(H^((−N;k))_(e3b;b))),    (14.23)

with C locally uniform for perturbations as in (L4), at the regularity (d_0; k).

*Proof.* Let d_0 be the largest of the numbers of (L4), of Lemma 14.31 (a) at (−N, m, N), and 2. Induction
on k; k = 0 is (L4). Let k ≥ 1. By Lemma 14.15, [L_0, V_j] = Σ_(l=0)^N A^0_(j,l)V_l with A^0_(j,l) ∈ C^∞_b
Ψ^(m−1)_e3b fixed operators; here [L_0, V_j] ∈ Diff^m_e3b, by (14.4). For L_1 = Σ a_qP_q,

    [a_qP_q, V_j] = a_q[P_q, V_j] − (V_ja_q)P_q = Σ_l (a_qA′_(qjl) − (V_ja_q)A″_(ql))V_l,

with A′_(qjl), A″_(ql) ∈ C^∞_b Ψ^(m−1)_e3b fixed (Lemma 14.15 for [P_q, V_j] and for P_q). Likewise for L_2, with
operators of order m − 2. Hence

    [L, V_j] = Σ_(l=0)^N A_(j,l)V_l,
    A_(j,l) ∈ C^∞_b Ψ^(m−1)_e3b + C^((d_0;k−1),(2δ,δ,δ))_(e3b;b) Ψ^(m−1)_e3b + C^((d_0;k−1))_(e3b;b) Ψ^(m−2)_e3b,

each in the span of a fixed finite set, with coefficient norms at most C times those of L at (d_0; k). Here
Lemma 14.15 is applied with ϵ := ϵ_ϑ, the room of (R1) of Section 14.8.3 for B, E and G. So, D bounding the
kernel ranges of the operators of 𝒫_m and 𝒫_(m−1), the fixed operators A^0_(j,l), A′_(qjl), A″_(ql), and those for L_2,
have kernel ranges at most D + ϵ_ϑ. Put u^((1)) := (V_ju)_(j=0)^N and f := Lu. Then LV_ju − Σ_l A_(j,l)V_lu = V_jf,
that is,

    L^((1))u^((1)) = f^((1)) := (V_jf)_(j=0)^N,     L^((1)) := (Lδ_(jl) − A_(j,l))_(j,l=0,…,N).

L^((1)) acts on ℂ^(N′(N+1)), and is of the form (14.22) at the regularity (d_0; k − 1). Its parts are
L_0 ⊗ Id and L_1 ⊗ Id, and a part of order m − 1 that collects L_2 ⊗ Id and the A_(j,l); the weighted coefficients lie
in the unweighted class by Lemma 14.27 (d). Its principal symbol is ℓ Id, so the hypotheses on ℓ, 𝖧 and 𝗌 are those
for L. Choose B_1 slightly larger than B, with WF′(B) ⊂ Ell(B_1), and E_1, G_1 slightly smaller than E, G, with
WF′(E_1) ⊂ Ell(E) and WF′(G_1) ⊂ Ell(G), such that the hypotheses hold for (B_1, E_1, G_1) (the beginning of
Section 14.14): auxiliary operators of (R1) for B, E and G. Put χ_1 := h_♭(χ) ((R3)). By (R1) and (R3), B_1, E_1 and
G_1 are carried by χ_1 with the margin D + 7ϵ_ϑ, which bounds the kernel ranges of the operators of L^((1)) and of
B_1, E_1, G_1. So the inductive hypothesis, (14.23) at k − 1 for L^((1)) with these operators and χ_1, gives

    ‖B_1u^((1))‖_((𝗌;k−1)) ≤ C(‖G_1f^((1))‖_((𝗌−m+1;k−1)) + ‖E_1u^((1))‖_((𝗌;k−1)) + ‖χ_1u^((1))‖_((−N;k−1))).

Here ‖G_1V_jf‖_((𝗌−m+1;k−1)) ≤ ‖G_1f‖_((𝗌−m+1;k)) + ‖[G_1, V_j]f‖_((𝗌−m+1;k−1)). Both terms are bounded by
C(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m+1;k)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k))), by Lemma 14.29 (c) and Lemma 14.31 (a) for the error term, as in
Proposition 14.51. Similarly ‖E_1V_ju‖_((𝗌;k−1)) ≤ C(‖Eu‖_((𝗌;k)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k))), by Lemma 14.29 (c), and
‖χ_1u^((1))‖_((−N;k−1)) ≤ C‖χu‖_((−N;k)), by (R3). On the left,
‖Bu‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C Σ_j (‖BV_ju‖_((𝗌;k−1)) + ‖[V_j, B]u‖_((𝗌;k−1))), and both are bounded by
C(‖B_1u^((1))‖_((𝗌;k−1)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k))). For both, Lemma 14.29 (c) applies with the cut-off χ_1 of (R3),
which carries B, [V_j, B] and B_1. For the first, WF′(B) ⊂ Ell(B_1), and
‖BV_ju‖_((𝗌;k−1)) ≤ C(‖B_1V_ju‖_((𝗌;k−1)) + ‖χ_1V_ju‖_((−N;k−1))), where ‖χ_1V_ju‖_((−N;k−1)) ≤ C‖χu‖_((−N;k)) by (R3).
For the second, the wave front set lies in that of B, the j = 0 component of u^((1)) is u, and ‖χ_1u‖_((−N;k−1)) ≤
C‖χu‖_((−N;k)) likewise. The finiteness statements follow as in Proposition 14.51. At each k the step applies the
statement at k − 1, and through it (L4), to a new system L^((1)), of rank N′(N + 1), with finite sets enlarged by the
A_(j,l), and to new operators B_1, E_1, G_1 and a new cut-off χ_1; it applies Lemma 14.31 (a) with a new cut-off
χ_*. The kernel ranges grow with the depth of the induction: L^((1)) has kernel ranges at most D + ϵ_ϑ, and the proof of
the statement at k − 1, applied to it, adds the room found there, so at depth j the ranges are at most
D + ϵ^(1) + ⋯ + ϵ^(j), with ϵ^(i) the room found at the i-th level. This growth is harmless, as no bound on the ranges is
fixed in advance. The statement at k − 1 holds for all admissible data, whatever bound their kernel ranges have; here it
is applied with the bound D + ϵ_ϑ, which the margin D + 7ϵ_ϑ of B_1, E_1 and G_1 covers, and its proof finds its room
anew in the carriers of B_1, E_1 and G_1 ((R1)). There are k levels, so all ranges stay finite. The truncations change
operators by residual ones and so change only constants. Neither index depends on these choices
(Theorem 14.49, Lemma 14.31), so d_0 does not depend on k. ∎

#### 14.14.3 Tame estimates

**Lemma 14.53** ([Hin26c, Lemma 3.25].) Let R be a ring, ad_A := [A, ·], and P, X_1, …, X_N ∈ R. Then

    [X_1⋯X_N, P] = Σ_(q=1)^N Σ_(i_1<⋯<i_q) (ad_(X_(i_1))⋯ad_(X_(i_q))P) ∏_(j∉{i_1,…,i_q}) X_j    (14.24)
                 = Σ_(q=1)^N (−1)^(q−1) Σ_(i_1<⋯<i_q) (∏_(j∉{i_1,…,i_q}) X_j)(ad_(X_(i_q))⋯ad_(X_(i_1))P),    (14.25)

the products taken in increasing order of j.

*Proof.* N = 1 is the definition. For (14.24), assume it for N and let X_(N+1) ∈ R. Then

    [X_1⋯X_(N+1), P] = [X_1⋯X_N, P]X_(N+1) + (ad_(X_(N+1))P)X_1⋯X_N + [X_1⋯X_N, ad_(X_(N+1))P],

because X_1⋯X_N Q = QX_1⋯X_N + [X_1⋯X_N, Q] with Q := ad_(X_(N+1))P. The inductive hypothesis applies to the first and
third terms. The first gives the terms of (14.24) for N + 1 whose index set omits N + 1. The second gives the
set {N + 1}. The third gives the sets containing N + 1 and some i_1 < ⋯ < i_q ≤ N, with ad_(X_(N+1)) innermost, as
(14.24) requires. Each subset occurs exactly once. For (14.25), assume it for the N elements
X_2, …, X_(N+1). Then

    [X_1⋯X_(N+1), P] = X_1[X_2⋯X_(N+1), P] + X_2⋯X_(N+1)(ad_(X_1)P) − [X_2⋯X_(N+1), ad_(X_1)P].

The first term gives the sets omitting 1, with X_1 first in the product. The second gives {1}. The third gives the sets
{1} ∪ S, with sign −(−1)^(|S|−1) = (−1)^|S| and with ad_(X_1) innermost. ∎

**Definition 14.54** (Notation; [Hin26c, Notation 3.26].) Fix a finite set 𝒱^♯ spanning 𝒱_b(M̃) over
C^∞(M̃), and the good spanning set V_1, …, V_N. D^j_b, resp. D^j_([b]), denotes the vector of all j-fold compositions of
elements of 𝒱^♯, resp. of the V_i, and D^(≤j) those of order at most j. Each component of D^j_b is a combination, with
coefficients in C^∞(M̃), of components of D^(≤j)_([b]), and conversely; the coefficients' derivatives produce terms of
lower order. All the norms below are therefore unchanged up to constants when D_b is replaced by D_([b]). By
Lemma 14.53, for |J| = q, schematically,

    [D^q_([b]), P] = Σ_(q′=1)^q (ad^(q′)_(D_([b]))P) D^(q−q′)_([b]) = Σ_(q′=1)^q D^(q−q′)_([b]) (ad^(q′)_(D_([b]))P).
    (14.26)

**Lemma 14.55** ([Hin26c, Lemma 3.27], with C³_b in the first term.) For a, b ∈ ℕ_0 there is C_(a,b) with

    ‖(D^a_bℓ)(D^b_bu)‖_(L²(M̃)) ≤ C_(a,b)(‖ℓ‖_(C³_b)‖u‖_(H^(a+b)_b) + ‖ℓ‖_(C^(a+b+3)_b)‖u‖_(H³_b)).

*Proof.* In each chart φ_α of Section 14.4.1, the b-vector fields are uniformly bounded combinations of the
coordinate vector fields of (−2, 2)⁵, and the density is a constant c_α times a uniformly smooth positive multiple
of |dx|. The coefficient Lie algebra is C^∞_b 𝒱_b ((S1)). Hence ‖v‖²_(L²) and ‖v‖²_(H^q_b) are equivalent, uniformly, to
Σ_α c_α‖χ(φ_α)_*v‖²_(L²(ℝ⁵)) and to the same sum with the H^q(ℝ⁵)-norms of χ̃(φ_α)_*v, χ̃ = 1 on supp χ. And
‖χ̃(φ_α)_*ℓ‖_(C^q) ≤ C‖ℓ‖_(C^q_b) uniformly. It therefore suffices to show, for f ∈ C^(K+3) and g ∈ H^K supported in
(−2, 2)⁵, K := a + b, and |β| ≤ a, |γ| ≤ b, that

    ‖∂^βf ∂^γg‖_(L²(ℝ⁵)) ≤ C(‖f‖_(C³)‖g‖_(H^K) + ‖f‖_(C^(K+3))‖g‖_(H³)),

and to sum over α (finite multiplicity). If |γ| < 3, the left side is at most ‖f‖_(C^K)‖g‖_(H²). If β = 0, it is at
most ‖f‖_(C⁰)‖g‖_(H^K). Otherwise |β| ≥ 1, |γ| ≥ 3 and K′ := |β| + |γ| ≥ 4. Sobolev embedding on ℝ⁵ (3 > 5/2) gives
‖∂^βf‖_(L^∞) ≤ C‖f‖_(H^(|β|+3)). On the Fourier side, Hölder's inequality gives
‖h‖_(H^((1−θ)t_0+θt_1)) ≤ ‖h‖^(1−θ)_(H^(t_0))‖h‖^θ_(H^(t_1)). With θ := |β|/K′ for f (t_0 = 3, t_1 = K′ + 3) and
θ′ := (|γ| − 3)/(K′ − 3) for g (t_0 = 3, t_1 = K′),

    ‖∂^βf ∂^γg‖_(L²) ≤ C ‖f‖^(1−θ)_(H³)‖f‖^θ_(H^(K′+3))‖g‖^(1−θ′)_(H³)‖g‖^(θ′)_(H^(K′)).

Now θ′ ≤ 1 − θ, as K′(|γ| − 3) ≤ |γ|(K′ − 3), and ‖g‖_(H³) ≤ ‖g‖_(H^(K′)). So
‖g‖^(1−θ′)_(H³)‖g‖^(θ′)_(H^(K′)) ≤ ‖g‖^θ_(H³)‖g‖^(1−θ)_(H^(K′)), and the right side is at most
C(‖f‖_(H³)‖g‖_(H^(K′)))^(1−θ)(‖f‖_(H^(K′+3))‖g‖_(H³))^θ ≤ C(‖f‖_(H³)‖g‖_(H^(K′)) + ‖f‖_(H^(K′+3))‖g‖_(H³)) by Young's
inequality. Finally ‖f‖_(H^q) ≤ C‖f‖_(C^q) for f supported in (−2, 2)⁵, and K′ ≤ K. ∎

[Hin26c] uses the Moser estimate in place of the interpolation above, with ‖ℓ‖_(C⁰_b) in the first term. The three
derivatives lost here are absorbed in the thresholds of Proposition 14.56.

**Proposition 14.56** ([Hin26c, Proposition 3.28].) Let 𝗌 and 𝗌_0 be variable orders,
s̄ := max(0, ⌈sup 𝗌⌉), s̲ := max(0, ⌈−inf 𝗌⌉) and s̲_0 := max(0, ⌈−inf 𝗌_0⌉). There are d_0, d̃ ∈ ℕ, depending only on 𝗌
and 𝗌_0, such that the following holds for all B, B^♯ ∈ C^∞_b Ψ⁰_e3b carried by χ with WF′(B) ⊂ Ell(B^♯). For all k
there is C_k, depending also on B, B^♯ and χ, such that, for
all 0 ≤ j ≤ k,

    ‖B(D^j_([b])ℓ)(D^(k−j)_([b])u)‖_(H^𝗌_e3b)
       ≤ C_k(‖ℓ‖_(C^((d_0;d̃))_(e3b;b))(‖B^♯u‖_(H^((𝗌;k))_(e3b;b)) + ‖χu‖_(H^((𝗌_0;k))_(e3b;b)))
             + ‖ℓ‖_(C^((d_0;k))_(e3b;b))(‖B^♯u‖_(H^((𝗌;d̃))_(e3b;b)) + ‖χu‖_(H^((𝗌_0;d̃))_(e3b;b)))).    (14.27)

One can take d_1 := s̄ + max(s̲, s̲_0) + 3, d̃ := d_1 + max(s̲, s̲_0) + 3, and d_0 the larger of the numbers of
Lemma 14.30 (a) at 𝗌 and (b) at (𝗌, 𝗌_0), which do not depend on B, B^♯ or the operators B_1, B_2 of the proof.

*Proof.* Choose auxiliary operators B_1, B_2 ((R1) of Section 14.8.3, for B and B^♯), carried by χ, with
WF′(I − B_1) ∩ WF′(B) = ∅, WF′(B_1) ⊂ Ell(B_2) and WF′(B_2) ⊂ Ell(B^♯). By Lemma 14.29 (c),
‖B_iv‖_((𝗌;q)) ≤ C(‖B^♯v‖_((𝗌;q)) + ‖χv‖_((𝗌_0;q))), taking N ≥ −inf 𝗌_0 there. It therefore suffices to prove
(14.27) with B_2 in place of B^♯. By the support convention, u may be replaced by χu.

*The case k = 0.* Bℓu = BℓB_1u + Bℓ(I − B_1)u. Lemma 14.30 (a) and the boundedness of B bound the first term by
C‖ℓ‖_(C^(d_0)_e3b)‖B_1u‖_(H^𝗌), and Lemma 14.30 (b), applied to the pair (B, B_1), bounds the second by
C‖ℓ‖_(C^(d_0)_e3b)‖χu‖_(H^(𝗌_0)).
Finally ‖B_1u‖_(H^𝗌) ≤ C(‖B_2u‖_(H^𝗌) + ‖χu‖_(H^(𝗌_0))).

*The case k ≤ d̃.* Apply the case k = 0 to D^jℓ and D^(k−j)u. By Lemma 14.27 (b),
‖D^jℓ‖_(C^(d_0)_e3b) ≤ C‖ℓ‖_(C^((d_0;j))) ≤ C‖ℓ‖_(C^((d_0;d̃))). By (14.26),
B_1D^(k−j) = Σ_q D^(k−j−q)(ad^q_(D_([b]))B_1), where ad^qB_1 ∈ C^∞_b Ψ⁰_e3b has wave front set in
WF′(B_1) ⊂ Ell(B_2) (Lemma 14.29 (a)). So, by Lemma 14.29 (c),

    ‖B_1D^(k−j)u‖_(H^𝗌) ≤ C(‖B_2u‖_((𝗌;k−j)) + ‖χu‖_((𝗌_0;k−j))).    (14.28)

Also ‖χD^(k−j)u‖_(H^(𝗌_0)) ≤ C‖χu‖_((𝗌_0;k−j)), as in Proposition 14.51. This is (14.27).

*The case k > d̃.* If j ≤ d̃, the argument just given bounds the left side by the first line of (14.27). If
j ≥ k − d̃, it bounds it by ‖D^jℓ‖_(C^(d_0)_e3b) ≤ C‖ℓ‖_(C^((d_0;k))) times ‖B_2u‖_((𝗌;d̃)) + ‖χu‖_((𝗌_0;d̃)), the
second line. Let d̃ < j < k − d̃. By Lemma 14.29 (d),
‖v‖_(H^𝗌_e3b) ≤ ‖v‖_(H^(s̄)_e3b) ≤ C‖v‖_(H^(s̄)_b) ≤ C Σ_(l≤s̄) ‖D^l_([b])v‖_(L²). By (14.26),
D^l_([b])B = Σ_(l′≤l) (ad^(l−l′)_(D_([b]))B)D^(l′)_([b]), with ad^(l−l′)B bounded on L². By the Leibniz rule,
D^(l′)((D^jℓ)(D^(k−j)u)) is a sum of terms (D^(j+l_1)ℓ)(D^(k−j+l_2)u), l_1 + l_2 = l′. So it suffices to bound, for
l_1 + l_2 ≤ s̄ and v ∈ {B_1u, (I − B_1)u},

    ‖(D^(j+l_1)ℓ)(D^(k−j+l_2)v)‖_(L²).    (14.29)

Apply Lemma 14.55 to D^(d_1)ℓ and D^(d_1)v, with a := j + l_1 − d_1 and b := k − j + l_2 − d_1. Both are
positive, since j > d̃ ≥ d_1 and k − j > d̃. Then a + b + d_1 = k + l_1 + l_2 − d_1 ≤ k + s̄ − d_1, and
(14.29) is at most

    C(‖ℓ‖_(C^(d_1+3)_b)‖v‖_(H^(k+s̄−d_1)_b) + ‖ℓ‖_(C^(k+s̄−d_1+3)_b)‖v‖_(H^(d_1+3)_b)).

Here ‖ℓ‖_(C^(d_1+3)_b) ≤ ‖ℓ‖_(C^((d_0;d̃))), as d_1 + 3 ≤ d̃, and ‖ℓ‖_(C^(k+s̄−d_1+3)_b) ≤ ‖ℓ‖_(C^((d_0;k))), as
d_1 ≥ s̄ + 3. For v = B_1u, Lemma 14.32 and Lemma 14.29 (c) give
‖B_1u‖_(H^(k+s̄−d_1)_b) ≤ C‖B_1u‖_((𝗌;k+s̄−d_1+s̲)) ≤ C(‖B_2u‖_((𝗌;k)) + ‖χu‖_((𝗌_0;k))), as d_1 ≥ s̄ + s̲. Likewise
‖B_1u‖_(H^(d_1+3)_b) ≤ C(‖B_2u‖_((𝗌;d̃)) + ‖χu‖_((𝗌_0;d̃))), as d_1 + 3 + s̲ ≤ d̃. For v = (I − B_1)u, the same with 𝗌_0
for 𝗌 and s̲_0 for s̲ gives ‖χu‖_((𝗌_0;k)) and ‖χu‖_((𝗌_0;d̃)), as I − B_1 is bounded on the mixed spaces. The products
are those of (14.27). ∎

**Corollary 14.57** (Tame bound for operators of limited regularity.) Let 𝒫 ⊂ C^∞_b Ψ^m_e3b be finite,
A ∈ C^((d_0;k))_(e3b;b) 𝒫 with a representation 𝐚, and χ′, χ cut-offs with χ′ carried by χ. With d_0 and d̃ of
Proposition 14.56 for 𝗌 = 𝗌_0 = 𝗍 − m, which depend only on 𝗍 and m (not on k, 𝒫, χ′ or χ), and with C_k depending on
𝒫, χ′ and χ,

    ‖χ′Au‖_((𝗍−m;k)) ≤ C_k(‖𝐚‖_((d_0;d̃))‖χu‖_((𝗍;k)) + ‖𝐚‖_((d_0;k))‖χu‖_((𝗍;d̃))).

*Proof.* Let χ‴ ∈ C^∞(M̃) carry χ′: χ′ = χ‴χ′χ‴, and χ = 1 within d_ℬ-distance D of supp χ‴, D bounding the kernel
ranges of the operators of 𝒫. Then χ‴²χ′ = χ′, so |χ‴| = 1 on supp χ′. Put χ″ := F″(|χ‴|²) and χ_c := F_c(|χ‴|²),
with F″, F_c ∈ C^∞(ℝ), F″ = 1 on [3/4, ∞), F″ = 0 on (−∞, 1/2], F_c = 1 on [1/4, ∞) and F_c = 0 on (−∞, 1/8]. Then
χ″ = 1 near supp χ′, χ_c = 1 near supp χ″, and supp χ_c ⊂ supp χ‴. By (14.6) and the Leibniz rule,
for |J| ≤ k, V^J(χ′a_qP_qu) is a sum of products (V^(J_0)χ′)(V^(J_1)a_q)(V^(J_2)P_qu), with J_0, J_1, J_2 complementary
subwords of J. Apply (14.27) with the cut-off χ_c in place of χ, to B := V^(J_0)χ′ and B^♯ := χ″, which are
multiplication operators carried by χ_c (as χ_c = 1 near supp χ″ ⊃ supp χ′) with WF′(B) ⊂ Ell(B^♯), to ℓ := a_q, to
P_qu in place of u, and to (|J_1|, |J_1| + |J_2|) in place of (j, k). Its error terms are ‖χ″P_qu‖_((𝗍−m;q′)) and
‖χ_cP_qu‖_((𝗍−m;q′)), with q′ = |J_1| + |J_2| ≤ k or q′ = d̃. As χ = 1 within D of supp χ_c ⊃ supp χ″, these are
‖χ″P_qχu‖_((𝗍−m;q′)) and ‖χ_cP_qχu‖_((𝗍−m;q′)), which are at most C‖χu‖_((𝗍;q′)) by Lemma 14.29 (a). The
coefficient norms are ‖a_q‖_((d_0;d̃)) and ‖a_q‖_((d_0;|J_1|+|J_2|)) ≤ ‖a_q‖_((d_0;k)). Summing over the finitely many
J and q gives the bound. ∎

**Proposition 14.58** ([Hin26c, Proposition 3.29].) Let 𝒫 ⊂ C^∞_b Ψ^m_e3b be finite. There are d_0, d ∈ ℕ,
depending only on 𝗌, m and N, such that the following holds for all k and L ∈ C^((d_0;d))_(e3b;b) 𝒫 with a
representation 𝐋. Let B, G be carried by
χ with WF′(B) ⊂ Ell(G) ∩ Ell(L). If 𝐋 is a representation at (d_0; k), then

    ‖Bu‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m;k)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k)) + ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;k))(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m;d)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;d)))),    (14.30)

with the finiteness statement of Proposition 14.51. C_k depends on L only through a bound for ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d)) and the
ellipticity margin of (L3), and so is locally uniform in C^((d_0;d))_(e3b;b) 𝒫 for all k at once.

*Proof.* Take d := d̃ + 1, with d_0 and d̃ those of Proposition 14.56 for (𝗌 − m, −N − m), enlarged to serve also
Proposition 14.51 and Corollary 14.57. All of these depend only on 𝗌, m and N. The induction below applies (L3),
Proposition 14.51, Proposition 14.56 and Corollary 14.57 to operators G_1, G_2, G_3 and cut-offs chosen anew at each
k; as their indices do not depend on these choices, d_0 and d do not depend on k. For k ≤ d, (14.30) is
Proposition 14.51, whose constant depends on
‖𝐋‖_((d_0;k)) ≤ ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d)). Let k > d and assume (14.30) at all orders below k, for all admissible B and G.
Choose G_1, G_2, G_3 as in Proposition 14.51, with WF′(G_3) ⊂ Ell(G) ∩ Ell(L), and let χ_1 := h_♭(χ) and χ_* be the
cut-offs of (R3) and (R2) of Section 14.8.3. For a word J of length k, (14.24) gives

    LV^Ju = V^JLu − Σ_(∅≠S⊂J) (ad_(V_S)L)V^(J∖S)u,    (14.31)

with ad_(V_S) the iterated commutator in the order of S and J ∖ S in its order. (L3), applied to V^Ju with G_1 and the
cut-off χ_1, which carries B and G_1, has a constant depending only on ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;0)):

    ‖BV^Ju‖_(H^𝗌) ≤ C(‖G_1V^JLu‖_(H^(𝗌−m)) + Σ_S ‖G_1(ad_(V_S)L)V^(J∖S)u‖_(H^(𝗌−m)) + ‖χ_1V^Ju‖_(H^(−N))).

*The left side.* ‖Bu‖_((𝗌;k)) is at most the sum of ‖Bu‖_((𝗌;k−1)) and the ‖V^JBu‖_(H^𝗌), |J| = k. By
(14.24), V^JB = BV^J + Σ_S (ad_(V_S)B)V^(J∖S). The operators ad_(V_S)B are carried by χ with wave front set in
that of B, and each term with S ≠ ∅ has at most k − 1 factors V. Moving them to the left by (14.25) bounds these
terms by finitely many ‖B′u‖_((𝗌;k−1)), with WF′(B′) ⊂ WF′(B). These, and ‖Bu‖_((𝗌;k−1)), are bounded by
(14.30) at k − 1, which is at most the right side of (14.30) at k.

*The first two terms on the right.* ‖χ_1V^Ju‖_(H^(−N)) ≤ C‖χu‖_((−N;k)), by (R3). By (14.26),
‖G_1V^JLu‖_(H^(𝗌−m)) ≤ ‖G_1Lu‖_((𝗌−m;k)) + Σ ‖G′Lu‖_((𝗌−m;k−1)), with WF′(G′) ⊂ WF′(G_1) and the kernel of G′ in that
of G_1. By Lemma 14.29 (c) both are at most C(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m;k)) + ‖χ_*Lu‖_((−N−m;k))). Corollary 14.57, with χ_* in
place of χ′ (χ_* is carried by χ, (R2)), bounds the error term tamely by
C_k(‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d̃))‖χu‖_((−N;k)) + ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;k))‖χu‖_((−N;d̃))).

*The commutator terms.* Let |S| = j ≥ 1. With L = Σ_q ℓ_qA_q, iterating ad_V(ℓA) = (Vℓ)A + ℓ ad_VA gives
ad_(V_S)L = Σ_q Σ_(S′⊂S) (V_(S′)ℓ_q)(ad_(V_(S∖S′))A_q). Here ad_(V_(S∖S′))A_q ∈ C^∞_b Ψ^m_e3b is fixed, by (S10). By
(14.25), (ad A_q)V^(J∖S) = Σ V^(J′)A′ with |J′| ≤ k − j and A′ ∈ C^∞_b Ψ^m_e3b fixed. So the terms to bound are
‖G_1(V_(S′)ℓ_q)V^(J′)(A′u)‖_(H^(𝗌−m)), with j′ := |S′| ≤ j and |J′| ≤ k − j ≤ k − 1. If j′ ≥ 1, write
V_(S′)ℓ_q = V_(S′_2)(V_(s_1)ℓ_q), with s_1 the last letter of S′ (the field applied first) and S′_2 the other letters,
and apply (14.27) with 𝗌 − m for 𝗌, −N − m for 𝗌_0, and the cut-off χ_* in place of χ. Use
(B, B^♯) = (G_1, G_2), which are carried by χ_* ((R2)), ℓ := V_(s_1)ℓ_q, A′u for u, and (j′ − 1, j′ − 1 + |J′|) for
(j, k). Note j′ − 1 + |J′| ≤ k − 1. The bound is

    C_k(‖V_(s_1)ℓ_q‖_((d_0;d̃))(‖G_2A′u‖_((𝗌−m;k−1)) + ‖χ_*A′u‖_((−N−m;k−1)))
        + ‖V_(s_1)ℓ_q‖_((d_0;k−1))(‖G_2A′u‖_((𝗌−m;d̃)) + ‖χ_*A′u‖_((−N−m;d̃)))).

Now ‖V_(s_1)ℓ_q‖_((d_0;d̃)) ≤ C‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d)) and ‖V_(s_1)ℓ_q‖_((d_0;k−1)) ≤ C‖𝐋‖_((d_0;k)) (Lemma 14.27 (b); this
is why d = d̃ + 1). Next, A′ is a commutator of an operator of 𝒫 with vector fields, so its kernel range is at most D,
and χ_*A′ = χ_*A′χ ((R2)): ‖χ_*A′u‖_((−N−m;q)) = ‖χ_*A′χu‖_((−N−m;q)) ≤ C‖χu‖_((−N;q)) by Lemma 14.29 (a). And
‖G_2A′u‖_((𝗌−m;q)) ≤ C(‖G_3u‖_((𝗌;q)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;q))) by Lemma 14.29 (c). By (14.30) at the order
k − 1, with G_3 in place of B, ‖G_3u‖_((𝗌;k−1)) is bounded by the right side of (14.30) at k. Its constant
depends only on ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d)), and its high norm ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;k−1)) multiplies low norms only. By Proposition 14.51 at the
order d̃ < d, ‖G_3u‖_((𝗌;d̃)) ≤ C(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m;d)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;d))). If j′ = 0, the coefficient is ℓ_q itself
and |J′| ≤ k − 1, and (14.27) with ℓ := ℓ_q and (0, |J′|) gives the same bounds, with ‖ℓ_q‖_((d_0;d̃)) and
‖ℓ_q‖_((d_0;k−1)). Collecting the terms gives (14.30). ([Hin26c] treats only the term with the most
derivatives on the coefficient; the others are bounded in the same way.) ∎

**Proposition 14.59** ([Hin26c, Proposition 3.30], with 𝗌 − m + 1.) There are d_0, d ∈ ℕ, depending only on
𝗌, m and N, such that the following holds for all δ > 0, all k, finite sets 𝒫_(m−j), j = 0, 1, and
L = L_0 + L_1 + L_2. Here L_0 ∈ Diff^m_e3b,
L_1 ∈ C^((d_0;d),(2δ,δ,δ))_(e3b;b) 𝒫_m and L_2 ∈ C^((d_0;d))_(e3b;b) 𝒫_(m−1), with representations 𝐋_1 and 𝐋_2, under
the hypotheses of (L4). If the representations are at (d_0; k), then

    ‖Bu‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m+1;k)) + ‖Eu‖_((𝗌;k)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k))
                       + ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;k))(‖GLu‖_((𝗌−m+1;d)) + ‖Eu‖_((𝗌;d)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;d)))),    (14.32)

with ‖𝐋‖ := ‖𝐋_1‖ + ‖𝐋_2‖. C_k depends on L only through bounds at (d_0; d), and is locally uniform for perturbations of
L_0, L_1, L_2 in Diff^m_e3b, C^((d_0;d),(2δ,δ,δ))_(e3b;b) 𝒫_m and C^((d_0;d))_(e3b;b) 𝒫_(m−1). ([Hin26c, (3.85)] prints
𝗌 − m for 𝗌 − m + 1 in both places; the real principal type estimate gives 𝗌 − m + 1, which the proof of [Hin26c,
Proposition 3.30] uses, and 𝗌 − m would be false, as propagation loses one derivative.)

*Proof.* Take d := d̃ + 2, with d_0 and d̃ of Proposition 14.56 for (𝗌 − m + 1, −N − m), enlarged to serve
Proposition 14.52 and Corollary 14.57. All of these depend only on 𝗌, m and N. The induction below applies (L4) to the
system L^((k)), whose rank (N + 1)^k N′ grows with k, and applies (L4), Proposition 14.52, Proposition 14.56 and
Corollary 14.57 to operators B_1, E_1, G_1, G_2, G_3 and cut-offs χ_1, χ_* chosen anew at each k. As their indices
depend on none of these,
d_0 and d do not depend on k. For k ≤ d, (14.32) is Proposition 14.52. Let k > d and assume
(14.32) below k. Let 𝒲_k be the set of words of length k in the letters 0, …, N, with V_0 = I, and put
u^((k)) := (V^αu)_(α∈𝒲_k). By (14.24), LV^αu = V^αLu − Σ_(S≠∅) (ad_(V_S)L)V^(α∖S)u. For |S| = 1, S = {i},
Lemma 14.15, with ϵ := ϵ_ϑ, the room of (R1) of Section 14.8.3 for B, E and G, and the calculation in the proof
of Proposition 14.52 give ad_(V_(α_i))L = Σ_ν L_(α_i,ν)V_ν. Here

    L_(α_i,ν) ∈ C^∞_b Ψ^(m−1)_e3b + C^((d_0;d−1),(2δ,δ,δ))_(e3b;b) Ψ^(m−1)_e3b + C^((d_0;d−1))_(e3b;b) Ψ^(m−2)_e3b,

in the span of a fixed finite set. Its coefficients carry at most one b-derivative of those of L, so their
C^(d_0)_e3b-norms are bounded by C‖𝐋‖_((d_0;1)). And V_νV^(α∖{i}) is again a word of length k. Hence

    L^((k))u^((k)) = f^((k)) + f̃^((k)),     f^((k)) := (V^αLu)_α,     f̃^((k)) := (−Σ_(|S|≥2) (ad_(V_S)L)V^(α∖S)u)_α,

where (L^((k))w)_α := Lw_α + Σ_i Σ_ν L_(α_i,ν)w_(ν·(α∖{i})). L^((k)) is a system of the form of (L4), built from
commutators of the fixed operators with the V_j. Its principal symbol is ℓ Id and its coefficients have
C^(d_0)-norms bounded by C‖𝐋‖_((d_0;1)). If D bounds the kernel ranges of the operators of 𝒫_m and 𝒫_(m−1), those of
its operators are at most D + ϵ_ϑ, once and for all: L^((k)) is built from the fixed L_(α_i,ν) at every k. Apply (L4)
to it, with the cut-off χ_1 := h_♭(χ) of (R3) and with operators chosen as follows. Let T be as at the
beginning of Section 14.14, and U ⊂ Ell(G) a neighbourhood of T on which 𝖧𝗌 ≤ 0. Apply (O) to U, giving U_T, K_E and
K_U, and again to U_T ∩ U in place of U, giving U′_T ⊂ U_T, K′_E and K′_U ⊂ U_T. Take B_1 with WF′(B) ⊂ Ell(B_1) and
WF′(B_1) ⊂ U′_T, E_1 elliptic on K′_E with WF′(E_1) ⊂ Ell(E), and G_1, G_2, G_3 microsupported in U_T, with G_1 elliptic
on K′_U ∪ WF′(B_1), WF′(G_1) ⊂ Ell(G_2) and WF′(G_2) ⊂ Ell(G_3), all auxiliary operators of (R1) for B, E and G. They
are carried by χ, and by χ_1 with the margin D + 7ϵ_ϑ, which bounds the kernel ranges of the operators of L^((k)). By
(O) the hypotheses of (L4) hold for (B_1, E_1, G_1), and for (G_2, E, G) and (G_3, E, G). (Taking G_1 slightly
smaller than G would not do: then WF′(G_3) contains T and may reach where the hypotheses fail.) The constant depends on k
through the size of the system, and on L only through low norms:

    ‖B_1u^((k))‖_(H^𝗌) ≤ C_k(‖G_1f^((k))‖_(H^(𝗌−m+1)) + ‖G_1f̃^((k))‖_(H^(𝗌−m+1)) + ‖E_1u^((k))‖_(H^𝗌)
                              + ‖χ_1u^((k))‖_(H^(−N))).

The left side controls ‖Bu‖_((𝗌;k)) up to terms ‖B′u‖_((𝗌;k−1)), WF′(B′) ⊂ WF′(B), which are bounded by
(14.32) at k − 1 (as in Proposition 14.58). The terms with f^((k)), E_1 and χ_1 are bounded as in
Proposition 14.58, the error term of G_1f^((k)) by Corollary 14.57. It remains to bound G_1f̃^((k)). Its terms are
G_1(ad_(V_S)L)V^(α∖S)u with |S| = j ≥ 2, so at most k − 2 factors V act on u.

For L_0, ad_(V_S)L_0 ∈ Diff^m_e3b is fixed, and by Lemma 14.29 (c) and (d),

    ‖G_1(ad_(V_S)L_0)V^(α∖S)u‖_(H^(𝗌−m+1)) ≤ C(‖G_2u‖_((𝗌+1;k−2)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k)))
                                           ≤ C(‖G_2u‖_((𝗌;k−1)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k))).    (14.33)

The second inequality is [Hin26c, (3.87)], here Lemma 14.29 (d). For L_1 and L_2,
ad_(V_S)(ℓA) = Σ_(S′⊂S) (V_(S′)ℓ)(ad_(V_(S∖S′))A) with A of order m or m − 1. Commute the fixed operator through the
V's by (14.25). If j′ := |S′| ≥ 2, apply (14.27) at the order 𝗌 − m + 1, with (B, B^♯) = (G_1, G_2),
the cut-off χ_* of (R2) in place of χ, ℓ replaced by V_(S″)ℓ, S″ the last two letters of S′ (the fields applied first),
and (j′ − 2, ·) for (j, ·). The coefficient norms are ‖ℓ‖_((d_0;d̃+2)) ≤ C‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d)) and ‖ℓ‖_((d_0;k)). The
u-norms are bounded by
‖G_2A′u‖_((𝗌−m+1;k−2)) ≤ C(‖G_3u‖_((𝗌+1;k−2)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k))) ≤ C(‖G_3u‖_((𝗌;k−1)) + ‖χu‖_((−N;k)))
(Lemma 14.29 (c), (d)), and the same at d̃; the error terms ‖χ_*A′u‖ are at most C‖χu‖, as in
Proposition 14.58. If j′ ≤ 1, the coefficient carries at most one derivative, and (14.27) with ℓ replaced by
V_(S′)ℓ and (0, ·) gives the same bounds, with ‖V_(S′)ℓ‖_((d_0;d̃)) ≤ C‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d)). Here ‖G_3u‖_((𝗌;k−1)), and
‖G_2u‖_((𝗌;k−1)) in (14.33), are bounded by (14.32) at k − 1 with G_3, resp. G_2, in place of B, for
which the hypotheses hold by the choice above. And ‖G_3u‖_((𝗌;d̃+1)) is bounded by Proposition 14.52 at the order
d̃ + 1 < d, with constant depending on ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;d)). This gives (14.32). The local uniformity follows from
that of (L4) and Proposition 14.52. ∎


## 15. Null-bicharacteristic dynamics, wave-type operators and trapping of perturbed metrics

This chapter studies the null-bicharacteristic flow of a stationary model in the e3b-phase space of the compactified
spacetime of Chapter 14, introduces the classes of wave-type operators on which the forward problem is posed, and
proves that the stable and unstable hypersurfaces of the trapped set persist under perturbations of the metric that
decay in time. It is [Hin26c, Sections 4–6] in dimension 4 + 1.

In [Hin26c] the stationary model is a subextremal Kerr metric, and its dynamics is computed from the explicit metric:
Carter's constant, the potential of the radial motion, the expansion rates, and Dyatlov's proof of r-normal
hyperbolicity. Here no explicit metric is used. The stationary model is any metric satisfying the hypotheses (H1)–(H8)
of Chapter 11 and Chapter 12 together with the hypotheses (K1)–(K4) of Section 15.1.1, and the dynamics is read off
from the spectral hypotheses, which describe the flow at each frequency. The link is Section 15.2: over the interior
of the Kerr face the 3b-phase space is the stationary phase space with the frequency σ as a conserved variable, and a
map Φ_(z₀) identifies the semiclassical phase space 𝒫 of Section 12.2.4 at frequency sign z₀ with the part of the
3b-cosphere bundle over K⁺ where z₀σ ≥ 0, flows included. Near ι⁺, ℐ⁺ and the corner ∂K⁺ the metric is Minkowski to
second order by (K1), and there the flows are solved in closed form (Section 15.3 and Section 15.7). The r-normal
hyperbolicity of the trapped set is the hypothesis (K3); for the Myers–Perry metrics near Tangherlini it is verified,
with the other dynamical hypotheses, in Chapter 22.

The operators are treated in Section 15.9–Section 15.13: stationary wave-type operators are exactly the operators
whose spectral families satisfy (H1), (H2) and (H6); admissibility at the trapped set, at the transition face and at the
radial sets fixes the thresholds; asymptotically stationary metrics come with a time function t^♭_* that is explicit;
and order functions monotone along the flow of every nearby metric are constructed. The persistence of the stable and
unstable hypersurfaces (Section 15.14–Section 15.16) is proved by a graph transform, quantitatively, from the
defining functions of the trapped set and the tangential growth bound of (K3).

The radii 0 < r₀ − 2δ₀ < r₀ < r₀ + δ₀ < r₂ < r_h are those of Section 11.1.1. Nothing in this chapter depends on them
beyond these inequalities: they enter as the domains of the hypotheses, and every constant chosen from them below (the
radius r^♮ and the constant c₁ of Lemma 15.35, the radius r_Γ of Section 15.13.2) is chosen by an inequality that a
smaller r₀ does not make harder. The inner radius r₀ is therefore a free parameter of every result of this chapter.

### 15.1 The stationary model

This section fixes the stationary model, its decay at infinity and the hypotheses on its dynamics that are not part of
the spectral theory, and describes the metric and its characteristic set on the compactifications of Chapter 14.

#### 15.1.1 The metric and the hypotheses

Let P̂, E, X̃ and g be as in Section 11.1 and Section 12.1.2, satisfying (H1)–(H8). Thus g is a Lorentzian metric of
signature (1, 4) on ℝ_(t_*) × X̃°, X̃° = {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}, with t_*-independent components, dt_* is past timelike, and
G(ζ) := g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) satisfies G(−σ dt_* + ζ) = G₀(ζ) + στ₁(ζ) + σ²g₀₀ for ζ ∈ T*X̃° ((12.1)). We write t_* for
the time function t of Section 12.1.2. Points (t_*, x) are identified with points of ℝ^(1+4) by t := t_* + r, as in
[Hin26c, p. 80], so that t_* = t − r is the function t_* of Section 14.1 and g becomes a metric on
M̃° ∩ {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}. The Minkowski metric is ḡ := −dt² + dx² = −dt_*² − 2 dt_* dr + r² g_(𝕊³), with g_(𝕊³) the round
metric on 𝕊³. The further hypotheses are these.

(K1) (*Decay.*) There is R > r₂ such that on {r > R} the components of g − ḡ in the frame dt_*, dx¹, …, dx⁴ lie in
ρ²C^∞(X̄), ρ = r⁻¹.

(K2) (*The spectral hypotheses.*) (H1)–(H8) hold for the spectral family P̂ of an operator whose principal symbol is G
(Section 12.1.2).

(K3) (*r-normal hyperbolicity.*) Let Γ = Γ₁ ⊂ Σ^♭₁ be the trapped set of (H7) for z₀ = 1, let
q₁ = 2g⁻¹(−dt_* + ζ, dt_*) as in Lemma 12.1, and let 𝖵 := q₁⁻¹ H_(G₁) on Σ^♭₁ near Γ, where
G₁(ζ) = G(−dt_* + ζ). Then Γ is eventually absolutely r-normally hyperbolic for every r for the flow of 𝖵 within Σ^♭₁,
in the sense of [HPS77, Definition 4]: there is a continuous splitting

    T_Γ Σ^♭₁ = TΓ ⊕ N̄^u ⊕ N̄^s    (15.1)

preserved by De^(s𝖵) for all s ∈ ℝ, and there are constants μ, C > 0 and, for every ϵ > 0, a constant C_ϵ,
with |De^(s𝖵) v| ≤ C e^(−μ|s|) |v| for v ∈ N̄^u, s ≤ 0, and for v ∈ N̄^s, s ≥ 0, and |De^(s𝖵) v| ≤ C_ϵ e^(ϵ|s|) |v| for
v ∈ TΓ, s ∈ ℝ. Here |·| is any fixed fibre metric.

(K4) (*Parameters.*) When P̂ depends on b ∈ ℬ as in (H5), so does g, and ρ⁻²(g − ḡ) is bounded in C^∞(X̄ ∩ {r ≥ R})
uniformly and continuously in b; the splitting (15.1) depends continuously on b, and μ, C, C_ϵ are uniform.

**Remark 15.1** (a) (K1) is [Hin26c, (4.4) and Lemma 4.4] in dimension 4 + 1, with the rate r⁻²
that the mass term of a five-dimensional metric gives; Kerr has r⁻¹. For the five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini
metric with mass parameter m, written with t_* = t − T(r), T′ = (1 + T̃)(1 − m r⁻²)⁻¹ and T̃ vanishing quadratically at
r⁻¹ = 0, the components of g − ḡ are m r⁻² (in dt_*²), −2T̃ (in dt_* dr) and −(2 + T̃)T̃(1 − m r⁻²)⁻¹ (in dr²), all in
ρ²C^∞. Unlike in four dimensions, no logarithm enters T. (b) (K3) is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.19], which is proved there
for Kerr from Carter's integrability. The splitting and the normal rates follow from (H7) as in the proof of parts
(1)–(2) of [Hin26c, Proposition 4.19]; the tangential bound is the substance of the hypothesis. (c) (K4) is
[Hin26c, Remark 4.25].

#### 15.1.2 The metric on the compactifications

**Lemma 15.2** (The metric on the compactifications.) dt_* is everywhere past timelike. Moreover:

(1) g ∈ C^∞(M; S²𝒯*) is non-degenerate on M ∩ {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}, and g − ḡ ∈ r⁻²C^∞(M; S²𝒯*) near ∂M, where 𝒯 is the
pullback of the scattering tangent bundle (Section 14.2.1).

(2) g ∈ ρ_sf⁻² C^∞(M₀; S² ³ᵇT*M₀) is non-degenerate, and ρ_sf²(g − ḡ) ∈ ρ_sf² C^∞(M₀; S² ³ᵇT*M₀).

(3) g ∈ ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² C^∞(M; S² ᵉ³ᵇT*M) is non-degenerate, and

    ρ₀²x_I²ρ₊²(g − ḡ) ∈ ρ₀²x_I²ρ₊² C^∞(M; S² ᵉ³ᵇT*M).    (15.2)

The same holds for the inverses: g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ ∈ r⁻²C^∞(M; S²𝒯), and
ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²(g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹) ∈ ρ₀²x_I²ρ₊² C^∞(M; S² ᵉ³ᵇTM).

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 4.4] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* dt_* is past timelike by (H6) (Section 12.1.2). (1) The components of g in the frame dt_*, dx are
t_*-independent and, by (K1), smooth functions on X̄; by Lemma 14.13 a t_*-independent function that is smooth on
X̄ is smooth on M₁, and the blow-down M → M₁ is smooth. The forms dt_* = dt − dr, dr = ω·dx and dx are smooth sections
of 𝒯* (with ω = x/|x| smooth on X̄ near ∂X). This gives (1); on {r ≤ R} there is nothing to prove, r⁻² being bounded
there. (2) By Definition 14.4, ³ᵇTM₀ is spanned by r∂_t, r∂_x over M₀, so 𝒯* = r ³ᵇT*M₀ and
C^∞(M₀; S²𝒯*) = r²C^∞(M₀; S² ³ᵇT*M₀) near sf. Hence g − ḡ ∈ C^∞(M₀; S² ³ᵇT*M₀), and r⁻¹ is a defining function of
sf. Non-degeneracy: ρ_sf² ḡ is non-degenerate (Section 14.2.2) and the perturbation vanishes at sf; over M₀°, g is
Lorentzian. (3) Near K⁺ away from ℐ⁺ this is (2), ρ₊ and ρ_sf being comparable there and x_I, ρ₀ positive. Near ℐ⁺,
Lemma 14.8 shows that C^∞(M; S²𝒯*), spanned by dt_*², dt_* dr, dr², dt_* r dω, dr r dω and r dω r dω, lies in
ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻⁴ρ₊⁻² C^∞(M; S² ᵉ³ᵇT*M), the worst term being dr² = x_I⁻² · x_I² dr². Near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, r = ρ₊⁻¹x_I⁻², and near
ℐ⁺ ∩ I⁰, r = ρ₀⁻¹x_I⁻² (Section 14.1). So r⁻² ∈ ρ₀²x_I⁴ρ₊² C^∞ near ℐ⁺, and g − ḡ ∈ C^∞(M; S² ᵉ³ᵇT*M) there,
which is (15.2). Non-degeneracy follows as in (2), with ρ₀²x_I²ρ₊² ḡ non-degenerate (Definition 14.11). The
inverses: ḡ has constant components in the frame dt, dx, so g⁻¹ = ḡ⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹hḡ⁻¹ + …, h := g − ḡ, converges for r
large, and its terms after the first lie in r⁻²C^∞(M; S²𝒯). In e3b-terms, 𝒯 ⊂ ρ₊ ᵉ³ᵇTM near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ by
∂_(t_*) = ρ₊(−ρ₊∂_(ρ₊) + ½x_I∂_(x_I)), ∂_r = −½ρ₊x_I² · x_I∂_(x_I) and r⁻¹∂_ω = ρ₊x_I · x_I∂_ω (Section 14.2.3),
and likewise with ρ₀ near ℐ⁺ ∩ I⁰; so g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ ∈ r⁻²ρ₀²ρ₊² C^∞(S² ᵉ³ᵇTM) = ρ₀⁴x_I⁴ρ₊⁴ C^∞ near ℐ⁺, and near K⁺
the same follows from (2). ∎

In [Hin26c, (4.9)] the factor on the right of (15.2) is ρ₀x_I²ρ₊; the gain is the rate r⁻² of (K1). Nothing
below needs more than the rate of [Hin26c], except that errors vanish to second order at ι⁺ and ∂K⁺, which shortens two
proofs.

#### 15.1.3 Characteristic sets

Following [Hin26c, (4.11)], put g⁻¹_(e3b) := ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² g⁻¹ and

    Σ := {ζ ∈ ᵉ³ᵇT*M ∖ o : g⁻¹_(e3b)(ζ, ζ) = 0} = Σ⁺ ⊔ Σ⁻,    (15.3)

where ζ ∈ Σ⁺ ∩ T*M° if and only if g⁻¹(ζ, ·) is a future directed null vector; Σ⁻ = −Σ⁺, and Σ^± are the closures in
ᵉ³ᵇT*M ∖ o. Their boundaries at fibre infinity are ∂Σ^± ⊂ ᵉ³ᵇS*M. Fix defining functions ρ_∞ of ᵉ³ᵇS*M and x_I, ρ₊ of
ℐ⁺, ι⁺, and put, as in [Hin26c, (4.71)],

    𝖧_G := ρ_∞ x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² H_G,    (15.4)

an e3b-vector field on ᵉ³ᵇT*_Ω M tangent to ᵉ³ᵇS*M; on Σ it equals ρ_∞ H_(x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²G). Near K⁺ it is, on Σ, a positive
smooth multiple of the rescaled 3b-fields of Section 15.2–Section 15.6, and near ℐ⁺ of the eb-field of
Section 15.7. Positive multiples of a vector field have the same integral curves up to an increasing
reparametrisation, and all statements below are invariant under such a change.

**Lemma 15.3** (Future covectors.) (a) For every ζ ∈ Σ⁺ ∩ T*M°, H_G t_* > 0. (b) There is R₁ ≥ R such that
∂_(t_*) is future directed timelike on {r ≥ R₁}; there, every −σ dt_* + ζ ∈ Σ⁺ has σ > 0. (c) For a null covector
ν = −σ dt_* + ζ over X̃°, ν ∈ Σ⁺ if and only if g⁻¹(ν, dt_*) > 0.

*Proof.* (c) −∇t_* is future directed timelike (Section 12.1.2), and a future directed null vector has negative inner
product with it; so ν^♯ is future directed if and only if g(ν^♯, −∇t_*) < 0, that is, g⁻¹(ν, dt_*) > 0. (a) At ν,
H_G t_* = 2g⁻¹(ν, dt_*); use (c). (b) By (K1), g(∂_(t_*), ∂_(t_*)) = −1 + O(r⁻²), so ∂_(t_*) is timelike for r large;
it is future directed, since g(∂_(t_*), −∇t_*) = −dt_*(∂_(t_*)) = −1. For ν ∈ Σ⁺ there, ν(∂_(t_*)) = g(ν^♯, ∂_(t_*))
< 0, and ν(∂_(t_*)) = −σ. ∎

By (c), in the notation of Lemma 12.1, Σ⁺ ∩ {σ = z₀} is the component Σ⁺_(z₀) = Σ_(z₀) ∩ {q_(z₀) > 0}, on which
the future field is +H_(G_(z₀)) (Section 12.1.3), and the future component of the characteristic set at fibre infinity
of T*X̃° is ∂Σ₀⁺, the one containing ∂ℛ₊, with future field +ρ_∞ H_(G₀) ((H3) and Lemma 12.1 (e)).

### 15.2 The Kerr face and the stationary phase space

Over the Kerr face K⁺ the Hamilton vector field of G preserves the frequency σ, and at each fixed σ it is the Hamilton
vector field of the stationary symbol. This section identifies the 3b-cosphere bundle over K⁺ with the compactified
phase spaces of Chapter 12, flows included.

#### 15.2.1 The 3b-phase space over K⁺

Over M₀ ∩ {r > r₀ − 2δ₀} write 3b-covectors as −σ dt_* + ζ, ζ ∈ T*X̃°. By Definition 14.4 the 3b-fibre coordinates
are r(−σ, ζ) in the frame dual to r∂_(t_*), r∂_x, so (σ, ζ) are fibre coordinates up to the positive factor r, smooth
over M₀°. Near (K⁺)°, with ρ_K := t_*⁻¹, the 3b-vector fields are spanned by ∂_(t_*) = −ρ_K²∂_(ρ_K) and ∂_x
(Section 14.2.2; [Hin26c, Section 6.1]).

**Lemma 15.4** (The field over K⁺.) The Hamilton vector field H_G on ³ᵇT*M₀ over {r > r₀ − 2δ₀} is tangent
to ³ᵇT*_(K⁺)M₀ and annihilates σ, and its restriction to ³ᵇT*_((K⁺)°)M₀ = ℝ_σ × T*X̃° is, at each fixed σ, the
Hamilton vector field of ζ ↦ G(−σ dt_* + ζ) on T*X̃°.

*Proof.* In canonical coordinates (t_*, x; τ, ζ), τ = −σ,
H_G = (∂_τ G)∂_(t_*) + (∂_ζ G)∂_x − (∂_(t_*)G)∂_τ − (∂_x G)∂_ζ. G is t_*-independent, so the ∂_τ-component vanishes
and H_G σ = 0, and ∂_(t_*) = −ρ_K²∂_(ρ_K) vanishes at ρ_K = 0. The remaining components are those of the Hamilton
field of G(τ, ·) on T*X̃° at fixed τ. ∎

#### 15.2.2 The identification

The 3b-cosphere bundle over K⁺ is ³ᵇS*_(K⁺)M₀ = K⁺ × 𝕊⁴: Definition 14.4 trivialises ³ᵇTM₀ globally, and
K⁺ ≅ ℝ̄⁴ (the radial compactification of ℝ⁴; Lemma 14.13), with boundary ∂K⁺ = K⁺ ∩ ι⁺, defined within K⁺ by
ρ₊ = r⁻¹. In the trivialisation the class of −σ dt_* + ζ is [σ : ζ] (homogeneous coordinates, up to positive
multiples), since the trivialisation differs from (σ, ζ) by the positive factor r and the smooth fibre-linear map from
dt to dt_* (dt = dt_* + ω·dx, smooth on X̄). Recall 𝒫 = ℝ̄⁴ × ℝ̄⁴ (Section 12.2.4), with fibre infinity
ℝ̄⁴ × ∂ℝ̄⁴ and the face over ∂X.

**Definition 15.5** For z₀ ∈ {1, −1}, Φ_(z₀) : 𝒫 → ³ᵇS*_(K⁺)M₀ is Φ_(z₀)(x, ζ) := (x, [z₀ : ζ]), the class
of the covector −z₀ dt_* + ζ, extended to fibre infinity by Φ_(z₀)(x, θ∞) := (x, [0 : θ]).

**Lemma 15.6** (a) Φ_(z₀) is a diffeomorphism of manifolds with corners onto
K⁺ × {[σ : ζ] : z₀σ ≥ 0}, mapping fibre infinity onto {σ = 0} and the face over ∂X onto the part over ∂K⁺.

(b) Put G_(3b) := r²G, which near sf is a smooth fibre-quadratic function on ³ᵇT*M₀ (Lemma 15.2 (2)), and let
ρ̃_∞ := r⁻¹(σ² + |ζ|²)^(−1/2), a defining function of 3b-fibre infinity over K⁺. Then
ρ̃_∞² G_(3b) ∘ Φ_(z₀) = a Ĝ_(z₀) with a smooth and positive on 𝒫 and Ĝ_(z₀) = ρ_∞² G_(z₀) as in Lemma 12.21. So
Φ_(z₀) maps Σ_(z₀) ⊂ 𝒫 onto the characteristic set of G_(3b) in K⁺ × {z₀σ ≥ 0}.

(c) On Σ_(z₀), (Φ_(z₀))_* 𝖧_(z₀) = a′ ρ̃_∞ H_(G_(3b)) with a′ smooth and positive, where 𝖧_(z₀) = μ⁻¹H_(G_(z₀)) is the
field of (12.19).

(d) Φ_(z₀) maps Σ⁺_(z₀) ∩ T*X̃° onto Σ⁺ ∩ ³ᵇT*_((K⁺)°) ∩ {z₀σ > 0} (classes), and ∂Σ₀⁺ onto Σ⁺ ∩ {σ = 0} at fibre
infinity. Over ∂K⁺, Σ⁺ lies in {σ > 0}, and Φ₁ maps Σ₁ ∩ {ρ = 0}, the characteristic set of (11.18) at
σ₀ = 1, onto it. Σ⁺ ∩ {σ ≤ 0} lies over {r < R₁}.

*Proof.* (a) ℝ̄⁴_ζ is diffeomorphic to the closed hemisphere {z₀σ ≥ 0} ⊂ 𝕊⁴ by ζ ↦ [z₀ : ζ]: this is the standard
model of the radial compactification, whose boundary {|ζ| = ∞} goes to the equator {σ = 0}, smoothly with smooth
inverse ([z₀ : ζ] = [z₀|ζ|⁻¹ : ζ/|ζ|] near the equator, and |ζ|⁻¹ is a boundary defining function of ℝ̄⁴). In the
base it is the identity of X̄ ≅ K⁺, which maps ∂X to ∂K⁺. (b) G_(3b)(−z₀ dt_* + ζ) = r²G_(z₀)(x, ζ) and
ρ̃_∞ = r⁻¹⟨ζ⟩⁻¹ at σ = ±1, so ρ̃_∞² G_(3b) = ⟨ζ⟩⁻² G_(z₀) = Ĝ_(z₀) with the choice ρ_∞ = ⟨ζ⟩⁻¹ of Chapter 12; for
another choice of ρ_∞ the quotient is smooth and positive. Both sides are homogeneous of degree 0 in (σ, ζ), so the
identity extends to fibre infinity and to the face over ∂X by continuity. (c) By the Leibniz rule,
H_(G_(3b)) = r²H_G + G H_(r²), and on the characteristic set G = 0, so H_(G_(3b)) = r²H_G there. H_G at a covector
with σ = z₀ is tangent to {σ = z₀} and, in the coordinates (x, ζ) there, is H_(G_(z₀)) (Lemma 15.4); and Φ_(z₀)
restricted to {σ = z₀} is the projection to the cosphere bundle. Since H_G is homogeneous of degree 1 in the fibre,
ρ̃_∞ H_(G_(3b)) descends to the cosphere bundle, and at points of Φ_(z₀)(Σ_(z₀) ∩ T*X̃°)

    ρ̃_∞ H_(G_(3b)) = r⁻¹⟨ζ⟩⁻¹ r² H_(G_(z₀)) = r⟨ζ⟩⁻¹ μ 𝖧_(z₀).

With μ = ⟨ζ⟩⟨x⟩⁻¹ (Lemma 12.21 (c): H_p ∈ μ ρ_∞^(2−k) 𝒱_b for order (k, 0)), a′ = ⟨x⟩r⁻¹, smooth and positive on
𝒫. The identity extends by continuity to the faces of 𝒫, both sides being smooth vector fields there
(Lemma 12.21 (c); Lemma 15.2 (2)). (d) The first two statements are Lemma 15.3 (c) and the paragraph
after it, with (H3) at fibre infinity. Over ∂K⁺, ρ₊ = 0 and G_(3b) is the Minkowski function
Ḡ_(3b) = −2σ_(3b)ξ_(3b) + ξ_(3b)² + |η_(3b)|² of Section 15.3.1, on whose characteristic set σ_(3b) < 0 on Σ⁺
([Hin26c, p. 81]: dt_* is past causal for ḡ), with σ_(3b) = −rσ (Section 15.3.1), so σ > 0. The last statement is
Lemma 15.3 (b). ∎

Hence the future 3b-flow over K⁺ splits into three invariant pieces: {σ > 0}, the image under Φ₁ of the future
component Σ^♭₁ = Σ⁺₁ of Section 12.1.5 together with its face over ∂X; {σ = 0}, the image of ∂Σ₀⁺ at fibre infinity;
and {σ < 0}, the image under Φ₋₁ of Σ⁺₋₁, which lies over {r < R₁}. On each, the rescaled future 3b-field is a positive
multiple of the future field of Chapter 11 and Chapter 12: +𝖧₁, +ρ_∞ H_(G₀), resp. +𝖧₋₁ (Lemma 15.6 (c),
Lemma 15.3 and the paragraph after it).

### 15.3 The 3b-dynamics near ∂K⁺ and over ι⁺

Near the corner ∂K⁺ = K⁺ ∩ ι⁺ and over ι⁺ the metric is Minkowski to second order, and the rescaled Hamilton vector
field is, up to an error vanishing to second order at ρ₊ = 0, an explicit field whose flow is solved in closed form.

#### 15.3.1 The Minkowski model

Near K⁺ ∩ ι⁺ use ρ_K := r/t_*, ρ₊ := r⁻¹ and ω. (In Section 15.2 and Section 15.4, ρ_K is t_*⁻¹, a defining
function of K⁺ away from ι⁺, and in Section 15.7 and Section 15.8, ρ₊ is t_*⁻¹, a defining function of ι⁺ near ℐ⁺;
the two meanings of each meet only over ι⁺, where both vanish.) Write 3b-covectors as

    ζ = σ_(3b) dt_*/r + ξ_(3b) dr/r + η_(3b),        η_(3b) ∈ T*𝕊³,    (15.5)

so that −σ dt_* + ξ dr + η has σ_(3b) = −rσ, ξ_(3b) = rξ, η_(3b) = η. In the scattering coordinates ξ dr + r η_sc of
Section 11.1.4, η_sc = r⁻¹η. The Minkowski function is

    Ḡ_(3b) := r² ḡ⁻¹(ζ, ζ) = −2σ_(3b)ξ_(3b) + ξ_(3b)² + |η_(3b)|²    (15.6)

([Hin26c, (4.13)], with |·| the round norm on 𝕊³; it follows from ḡ⁻¹ = −2∂_(t_*) ⊗_s ∂_r + ∂_r² + r⁻² g_(𝕊³)⁻¹). By
Lemma 15.2 (the inverses) and 𝒯 = r⁻¹ ³ᵇTM₀, g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ ∈ r⁻⁴C^∞(S² ³ᵇTM₀), so
G_(3b) − Ḡ_(3b) ∈ ρ₊² P^[2](³ᵇT*M₀) near K⁺ ∩ ι⁺, where G_(3b) := r²G and P^[2] denotes the fibrewise quadratic
polynomials with smooth coefficients. By (14.2), with r∂_(t_*) = −ρ_K²∂_(ρ_K) and
r∂_r = ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) − ρ₊∂_(ρ₊),

    H_(Ḡ_(3b)) = 2(ξ_(3b) − σ_(3b))(ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) − ρ₊∂_(ρ₊) + σ_(3b)∂_(σ_(3b))) + 2σ_(3b)ξ_(3b)∂_(ξ_(3b))
                 + 2ξ_(3b)ρ_K²∂_(ρ_K) + H_(|η_(3b)|²).

The error H_(G_(3b) − Ḡ_(3b)) lies in ρ₊² 𝒱_b(³ᵇT*M₀): for p = ρ₊²q, H_p = ρ₊²H_q + 2qρ₊H_(ρ₊), and
H_(ρ₊) = −((r∂_r)ρ₊)∂_(ξ_(3b)) = ρ₊∂_(ξ_(3b)) by (14.2).

Since Ḡ_(3b) = (ξ_(3b) − σ_(3b))² + |η_(3b)|² − σ_(3b)², σ_(3b) ≠ 0 on Σ over ι⁺, and σ_(3b) < 0 on Σ⁺ there
([Hin26c, p. 81]). Near ∂Σ⁺ over a neighbourhood of ι⁺ use

    ρ_∞ := −σ_(3b)⁻¹,        ξ̂ := ξ_(3b)/σ_(3b),        η̂ := η_(3b)/σ_(3b).    (15.7)

Then ρ_∞² Ḡ_(3b) = ξ̂² − 2ξ̂ + |η̂|², and 𝖧̄ := ρ_∞ H_(Ḡ_(3b)) satisfies, exactly,

    𝖧̄ρ_K = 2(1 − ξ̂)ρ_K − 2ξ̂ρ_K²,     𝖧̄ρ₊ = −2(1 − ξ̂)ρ₊,     𝖧̄ρ_∞ = −2(1 − ξ̂)ρ_∞,
    𝖧̄ξ̂ = −2(2 − ξ̂)ξ̂,     𝖧̄η̂ = −2(1 − ξ̂)η̂ + ∂_ω|η̂|²,     𝖧̄ω = −∂_(η̂)|η̂|²,    (15.8)

which is [Hin26c, (4.15)]. For instance H_(Ḡ_(3b))ξ_(3b) = 2σ_(3b)ξ_(3b) and
H_(Ḡ_(3b))σ_(3b) = 2(ξ_(3b) − σ_(3b))σ_(3b) give H_(Ḡ_(3b))ξ̂ = 2σ_(3b)ξ̂(2 − ξ̂), and ρ_∞ = −σ_(3b)⁻¹. The full
rescaled field 𝖧 := ρ_∞ H_(G_(3b)) is 𝖧̄ + 𝖧̃ with 𝖧̃ ∈ ρ₊²𝒱_b, tangent to ³ᵇS*M₀ and to the boundary faces. In
particular 𝖧̃ρ₊ ∈ ρ₊³C^∞ and 𝖧̃ρ_K ∈ ρ₊²ρ_K C^∞, and over ι⁺ the flow of 𝖧 is that of 𝖧̄. None of this depends on
the dimension.

**Definition 15.7** (The radial sets over ∂K⁺; [Hin26c, Definition 4.5].)
∂R_(∂K⁺,in) := {ρ_K = ρ₊ = 0, ξ̂ = 2, η̂ = 0} and ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) := {ρ_K = ρ₊ = 0, ξ̂ = 0, η̂ = 0}, subsets of ∂Σ⁺ over
∂K⁺. Their conic extensions are {ξ_(3b) = 2σ_(3b) < 0, η_(3b) = 0} and {ξ_(3b) = 0, σ_(3b) < 0, η_(3b) = 0} over ∂K⁺.

Under Φ₁ these are R_(1,in) and R_out of (11.17) at σ₀ = 1: there ξ = −2σ₀, η = 0, resp. ξ = 0, η = 0, and
ξ̂ = ξ_(3b)/σ_(3b) = −ξ/σ.

*Linearisation* ([Hin26c, (4.16)]). 𝖧 vanishes on both sets. On ∂Σ⁺, ξ̂ is near each of them a smooth function of
(ρ_K, ρ₊, η̂), and by (15.8) and the error bounds, the linearisation of 𝖧 on the conormal spaces is
dρ_K ↦ −2dρ_K, dρ₊ ↦ 2dρ₊, dη̂ ↦ 2dη̂ at ∂R_(∂K⁺,in), and dρ_K ↦ 2dρ_K, dρ₊ ↦ −2dρ₊, dη̂ ↦ −2dη̂ at ∂R_(∂K⁺,out)
(the term ∂_ω|η̂|² is quadratic in η̂, and 𝖧̃ vanishes to second order at ρ₊ = 0). Also ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞ = 2, resp. −2,
there.

#### 15.3.2 The flow over ι⁺ and over ∂K⁺ in closed form

**Lemma 15.8** (a) (*Over ∂K⁺.*) On ∂Σ⁺ over ∂K⁺, ξ̂ ∈ [0, 2], and every maximal integral curve of 𝖧 not
contained in ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) ∪ ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) is, after a shift of the parameter, ξ̂(s) = 2/(1 + e^(4s)), defined for all
s, tending to ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) as s → −∞ and to ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) as s → ∞.

(b) (*Over ι⁺.*) On ∂Σ⁺ over (ι⁺)°, use u := t_*/r = ρ_K⁻¹ ∈ (0, ∞). Along a maximal integral curve of 𝖧,

    ξ̂′ = −2(2 − ξ̂)ξ̂,        u′ = −2(1 − ξ̂)u + 2ξ̂,        |η̂|² = ξ̂(2 − ξ̂).    (15.9)

Exactly one of the following holds. (i) ξ̂ ≡ 0, η̂ ≡ 0, u = u₀e^(−2s): the curve lies in
∂W_out := {ρ₊ = 0, ξ̂ = 0, η̂ = 0}, tends to ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) (u → ∞) as s → −∞ and to ℐ⁺ (u → 0) as s → ∞. (ii) ξ̂ ≡ 2,
η̂ ≡ 0, u = Ae^(2s) − 2 with A > 0 and s > ½ log(2/A): the curve lies in ∂W_in := {ρ₊ = 0, ξ̂ = 2, η̂ = 0}, tends to
∂R_(∂K⁺,in) as s → ∞, and reaches u = 0 as s decreases to ½ log(2/A). (iii) After a shift of the parameter,
ξ̂ = 2/(1 + e^(4s)) and

    u = (C − e^(−2s))/cosh 2s,        C > 0,        s > −½ log C;    (15.10)

u → 0 both as s ↓ −½ log C and as s → ∞, and u has one interior maximum.

(c) The angular coordinates converge at each end of each curve in (a) and (b).

*Proof.* Over ι⁺, 𝖧 = 𝖧̄ and ρ_∞² G_(3b) = ξ̂² − 2ξ̂ + |η̂|² there, so on ∂Σ⁺, |η̂|² = ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) and ξ̂ ∈ [0, 2].
(15.9) is (15.8) with u = ρ_K⁻¹: u′ = −ρ_K⁻²ρ_K′ = −2(1 − ξ̂)u + 2ξ̂. The logistic equation for ξ̂
has the constant solutions 0, 2 and, on (0, 2), the solutions 2/(1 + e^(4(s − s₁))). (a) Over ∂K⁺ (ρ_K = ρ₊ = 0) only
ξ̂, η̂, ω move; ξ̂ ∈ {0, 2} forces η̂ = 0, a zero of 𝖧, so a non-constant curve has ξ̂ ∈ (0, 2). (b) Consider the
linear equation for u. If ξ̂ ≡ 0, u′ = −2u; if ξ̂ ≡ 2, u′ = 2u + 4. Otherwise, with ξ̂ = 2/(1 + e^(4s)),
1 − ξ̂ = tanh 2s, the homogeneous solution is exp(−2∫tanh 2s ds) = (cosh 2s)⁻¹, and p := −e^(−2s)/cosh 2s is a
particular solution: p′ and −2(1 − ξ̂)p + 2ξ̂ both equal 2/cosh² 2s, by cosh 2s + sinh 2s = e^(2s) and
2ξ̂ = 4/(1 + e^(4s)) = 2e^(−2s)/cosh 2s. So u = (C − e^(−2s))/cosh 2s, positive if and only if C > e^(−2s); C ≤ 0 is
excluded. In case (iii), u ∼ 2Ce^(−2s) → 0 as s → ∞, and u = 0 at s = −½ log C. As u > 0 on the open interval and
u → 0 at both ends, u has an interior maximum, unique by Lemma 15.9 (3) below. In cases (i) and (ii) the limits
are read off. (c) By (15.8), |ω′| ≤ 2|η̂| in the round metric, and |η̂|² = ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) decays exponentially at
each infinite end (ξ̂ ∼ 2e^(−4s) or 2 − ξ̂ ∼ 2e^(4s)) and is bounded on the finite ends, so ω converges. ∎

The finite end in (b) (ii) and (iii) is not a limit point in ᵉ³ᵇS*M: as u = x_I² → 0 the 3b-coordinates degenerate,
and the curve continues over ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ in the eb-coordinates of Section 15.7, where the end is reached only as the
eb-parameter tends to −∞ (Lemma 15.17).

#### 15.3.3 Convexity and invariant manifolds

**Lemma 15.9** The flow of 𝖧 on ∂Σ⁺ over K⁺ ∪ ι⁺ near ∂K⁺ has the following properties.

(1) (*Convexity in K⁺.*) There is ϵ > 0 such that over K⁺, if 𝖧ρ₊ = 0 and 0 < ρ₊ < ϵ, then 𝖧²ρ₊ < 0.

(2) (*Curves over K⁺.*) Let γ : I → ∂Σ⁺ be a maximal integral curve over K⁺, not contained in
∂R_(∂K⁺,in) ∪ ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), with ρ₊(γ(0)) < ϵ. If (d/ds)ρ₊(γ(s)) ≤ 0 at s = 0, then γ(s) → ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) as s → ∞; if
it is ≥ 0, then γ(s) → ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) as s → −∞.

(3) (*Convexity in ι⁺.*) Over ι⁺, if 𝖧ρ_K = 0 and ρ_K > 0, then 𝖧²ρ_K > 0.

(4) (*Invariant manifolds over ι⁺.*) ∂W_out is the unstable manifold of ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) and ∂W_in the stable manifold
of ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) over ι⁺ (Lemma 15.8 (b)). Their conic extensions are, within Σ⁺, the characteristic sets of r∂_r
and of 2r∂_(t_*) − r∂_r over ι⁺.

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 4.6] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (1) Over K⁺ (ρ_K = 0), 𝖧ρ₊ = −2(1 − ξ̂)ρ₊ + ρ₊³a with a smooth, by Section 15.3.1. So 𝖧ρ₊ = 0 with
ρ₊ > 0 gives 1 − ξ̂ = ½ρ₊²a, so ξ̂ = 1 + O(ρ₊²). Then

    𝖧²ρ₊ = 2ρ₊𝖧ξ̂ − 2(1 − ξ̂)𝖧ρ₊ + 𝖧(ρ₊³a) = 2ρ₊(−2(2 − ξ̂)ξ̂ + O(ρ₊²)) + O(ρ₊³) = −4ρ₊ + O(ρ₊³),

using 𝖧ρ₊ = 0 at the point and 𝖧̃ξ̂ = O(ρ₊²). This is negative for ρ₊ < ϵ, ϵ small.

(2) If ρ₊(γ(0)) = 0, γ lies over ∂K⁺ (the face is invariant, 𝖧ρ₊ ∈ ρ₊C^∞), and Lemma 15.8 (a) applies. Let
ρ₊(γ(0)) ∈ (0, ϵ) and f := ρ₊ ∘ γ, with f′(0) ≤ 0. Then f > 0 throughout, {ρ₊ = 0} being invariant. At any s with
f′(s) = 0 and f(s) < ϵ, f″(s) < 0 by (1). Hence f′ < 0 on (0, sup I): if f′(0) < 0, or f′(0) = 0 and then
f″(0) < 0, then f′ < 0 on some (0, δ); at a first zero s₁ > 0 of f′, f(s₁) < f(0) < ϵ, so f″(s₁) < 0, while f′ < 0
on (0, s₁) forces f″(s₁) ≥ 0. So f is strictly decreasing for s > 0, γ stays in the compact set {ρ₊ ≤ ϵ} ∩ ∂Σ⁺ over
K⁺, sup I = ∞, and f → L ∈ [0, ϵ). The ω-limit set Ω_γ is non-empty, compact and invariant, and ρ₊ = L on it. If
L > 0, the curve through a point of Ω_γ has ρ₊ ≡ L, so 𝖧ρ₊ = 𝖧²ρ₊ = 0 there, against (1). So L = 0. For s > 0,
𝖧ρ₊ < 0, that is 1 − ξ̂ > ½ρ₊²a, so ξ̂ ≤ 1 + Cϵ² along γ and on Ω_γ. Ω_γ lies over ∂K⁺, where the flow is that of
Lemma 15.8 (a). If Ω_γ contained a point with ξ̂ ∈ (0, 2), it would contain its backward orbit, on which ξ̂ → 2,
against ξ̂ ≤ 1 + Cϵ². So ξ̂ = 0, hence η̂ = 0, on Ω_γ: Ω_γ ⊂ ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), which is the claim. The case f′(0) ≥ 0 is
the same with −𝖧, for which (1) holds as well since (−𝖧)² = 𝖧², and with the roles of ξ̂ = 0 and ξ̂ = 2 exchanged.

(3) Over ι⁺, 𝖧 = 𝖧̄. If 𝖧ρ_K = 0, then 1 − ξ̂ = ξ̂ρ_K and

    𝖧²ρ_K = −2ρ_K(1 + ρ_K)𝖧ξ̂ + (2(1 − ξ̂) − 4ξ̂ρ_K)𝖧ρ_K = 4ρ_K(1 + ρ_K)ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) = 4ρ_K(1 + ρ_K)|η̂|².

If η̂ = 0, then ξ̂ ∈ {0, 2} and 𝖧ρ_K = 2ρ_K, resp. −2ρ_K − 4ρ_K², which is not zero for ρ_K > 0. So 𝖧²ρ_K > 0.

(4) By Lemma 15.8 (b), the curves over ι⁺ that tend to ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) as s → −∞ are those of (i), and those that
tend to ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) as s → ∞ are those of (ii). The conic extensions are {ξ_(3b) = 0, η_(3b) = 0, σ_(3b) < 0} and
{ξ_(3b) = 2σ_(3b), η_(3b) = 0, σ_(3b) < 0} over ι⁺. These are the intersections with Σ⁺ of the characteristic sets of
r∂_r and of 2r∂_(t_*) − r∂_r (on Σ, ξ_(3b) = 0 and ξ_(3b) = 2σ_(3b) each force η_(3b) = 0 by (15.6)), with
which a 3b-covector (15.5) pairs to ξ_(3b), resp. 2σ_(3b) − ξ_(3b). In the coordinates (t, r), t = t_* + r,
these fields are r(∂_t + ∂_r) and r(∂_t − ∂_r), the outgoing and incoming null fields of ḡ: ∂_t|_r = ∂_(t_*) and
∂_r|_t = ∂_r − ∂_(t_*). ∎

The uniqueness of the interior maximum of u in Lemma 15.8 (b) (iii) is (3): u = ρ_K⁻¹, and at a zero of 𝖧ρ_K,
𝖧²u = −ρ_K⁻²𝖧²ρ_K < 0, so every critical point of u is a strict local maximum, and there is at most one.

### 15.4 The horizon at K⁺

**Definition 15.10** (The horizon radial set; [Hin26c, Definition 4.8].)
R_(ℋ⁺) := {ρ_K = 0, σ = 0, ζ ∈ ℛ₊} ⊂ ³ᵇT*_((K⁺)°)M₀ ∖ o, with ℛ₊ the component of N*ℋ ∖ o of (H3), and ∂R_(ℋ⁺) is its
boundary at fibre infinity, which is Φ_(±1)(∂ℛ₊).

Near ∂R_(ℋ⁺) let ρ_∞ be the function of (H3), positive and homogeneous of degree −1 in ζ, put σ̂ := σρ_∞ and
𝖧 := ρ_∞H_G; on Σ this is a positive multiple of (15.4). As ζ ≠ 0 there, (x, [ζ], σ̂), [ζ] ∈ S*X̃°, are
coordinates on ³ᵇS*_((K⁺)°)M₀ near ∂R_(ℋ⁺), in which ∂R_(ℋ⁺) = {σ̂ = 0} × ∂ℛ₊.

**Lemma 15.11** Let q̃ be the function of Lemma 11.13 for ℛ = ℛ₊, regarded as a function of (x, [ζ]).
There are C_F, c > 0 and a neighbourhood W of ∂R_(ℋ⁺) in ³ᵇS*_((K⁺)°)M₀ such that F := q̃ + C_F σ̂² is a quadratic
defining function of ∂R_(ℋ⁺) and 𝖧F ≥ cF on W. At ∂R_(ℋ⁺),

    ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞ = β₀ > 0,        ρ_K⁻²𝖧ρ_K = ρ_∞τ₁ ≤ −ββ₀ < 0,    (15.11)

with β₀, β of (H3). So ∂R_(ℋ⁺) is a repeller for the flow within ³ᵇS*_((K⁺)°)M₀ (not only within ∂Σ⁺), ρ_∞ grows
along the flow near it, and ρ_K decays. This is [Hin26c, Lemma 4.9 and (4.28)].

*Proof.* For a function f(x, [ζ]), independent of σ and t_* and homogeneous of degree 0 in ζ, Lemma 15.4 and
G = G₀ + στ₁ + σ²g₀₀ give

    𝖧f = 𝖧₀f + σ̂ H_(τ₁)f + σ̂² ρ_∞⁻¹H_(g₀₀)f,        𝖧₀ := ρ_∞H_(G₀),    (15.12)

where H_(τ₁)f and ρ_∞⁻¹H_(g₀₀)f = −ρ_∞⁻¹(∂_x g₀₀)·∂_ζ f are homogeneous of degree 0 and smooth near ∂ℛ₊. 𝖧₀ is the
field of (H3), extended off Σ₀ by the same formula, as in Lemma 11.13, which gives 𝖧₀q̃ ≥ c′q̃ on a neighbourhood
of ∂ℛ₊ in S*X̃°. As q̃ is smooth and vanishes quadratically at ∂ℛ₊, with q̃ ≥ c″dist², |dq̃| ≤ Cq̃^(1/2), so |H_(τ₁)q̃|
≤ Cq̃^(1/2). Hence 𝖧q̃ ≥ c′q̃ − C|σ̂|q̃^(1/2) − Cσ̂² ≥ (c′/2)q̃ − C₁σ̂². Next, 𝖧σ = 0 (Lemma 15.4), so
𝖧σ̂ = σ̂ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞, and

    ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞ = H_Gρ_∞ = β₀ + σ̂ρ_∞⁻¹H_(τ₁)ρ_∞ + σ̂²ρ_∞⁻²H_(g₀₀)ρ_∞,        β₀ := ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧₀ρ_∞,

the last two coefficients being homogeneous of degree 0. By (H3), β₀ ≥ c_β > 0 near ∂ℛ₊ for some constant c_β, so on
{|σ̂| ≤ δ}, ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞ ≥ c_β/2 and 𝖧(σ̂²) ≥ c_βσ̂². With C_F ≥ 2(C₁ + 1)/c_β,

    𝖧F ≥ (c′/2)q̃ + (C_F c_β − C₁)σ̂² ≥ (c′/2)q̃ + (C_F c_β/2)σ̂² ≥ min(c′/2, c_β/2) F.

In the coordinates (x, [ζ], σ̂), q̃ is a quadratic defining function of ∂ℛ₊ in S*X̃° (Lemma 11.13), so F is one of
{σ̂ = 0} × ∂ℛ₊. For (15.11): at σ̂ = 0, ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞ = β₀. With τ := −σ the dual variable of t_*,
H_G t_* = ∂_τG = −τ₁ − 2σg₀₀, so 𝖧t_* = −ρ_∞τ₁ at σ = 0, and 𝖧ρ_K = −ρ_K²𝖧t_*. By (H3), −β₀⁻¹ρ_∞τ₁ ≥ β on ∂ℛ₊. ∎

In the Kerr coordinates of [Hin26c], F corresponds to σ̂₀² + ρ_∞²𝒞 of [Hin26c, Lemma 4.9].

### 15.5 The trapped set at K⁺

**Definition 15.12** (The trapped set at K⁺; [Hin26c, (4.63)].) ∂Γ_(K⁺) := Φ₁(Γ), with Γ = Γ₁ the trapped
set of (H7) at z₀ = 1, and ∂Γ̄^(u/s)_(K⁺) := Φ₁(Γ̄_(u/s)), with Γ̄_(u/s) ⊂ Σ^♭₁ the global backward and forward trapped
sets of (H8); Γ^(u/s)_(K⁺) := Φ₁(Γ_(u/s)) for the local sets of (H7) in O.

**Lemma 15.13** (a) ∂Γ_(K⁺) is a compact invariant subset of ∂Σ⁺ ∩ ³ᵇS*_((K⁺)°)M₀, lying over
{r₂ < r < ρ₁⁻¹} and in {σ > 0}: σ is positive, hence elliptic, there ([Hin26c, (4.64)]). (b) ∂Γ̄^(u/s)_(K⁺) are
invariant, and consist of the points whose integral curves tend to ∂Γ_(K⁺) backward, resp. forward. Near ∂Γ_(K⁺),
Γ^u_(K⁺) and Γ^s_(K⁺) are smooth hypersurfaces of ∂Σ⁺ ∩ {σ > 0}, tangent to the flow, meeting transversally in
∂Γ_(K⁺), and, after shrinking O, ∂Γ̄^(u/s)_(K⁺) ∩ Φ₁(O) = Γ^(u/s)_(K⁺). (c) No integral curve tends to ∂Γ_(K⁺) in both
directions unless it lies in ∂Γ_(K⁺). (d) Under Φ₁, the field 𝖵 of (K3) is the projection of H_G/(H_G t_*) at σ = 1,
so (K3) is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.19] for the stationary model, with the quotient by t_*-translations and fibre
dilations realised by the slice {σ = 1} of ³ᵇT*_((K⁺)°)M₀.

*Proof.* (a), (b): Φ₁ is a diffeomorphism onto its image which maps Σ⁺₁ = Σ^♭₁ into ∂Σ⁺ ∩ {σ > 0} and the future
field to a positive multiple of the future field (Lemma 15.6 (c), (d)); (H7) and (H8) (b) transfer, and
Γ ⊂ T*{r₂ < r < ρ₁⁻¹} is compact by (H7). (c) Let γ tend to ∂Γ_(K⁺) in both directions. Then
γ ⊂ ∂Γ̄^u_(K⁺) ∩ ∂Γ̄^s_(K⁺), and for |s| large γ(s) ∈ Φ₁(O), so γ(s) ∈ Γ^u_(K⁺) ∩ Γ^s_(K⁺) = ∂Γ_(K⁺) by (b) and (H7)
(Γ_u ∩ Γ_s = Γ within O). ∂Γ_(K⁺) is invariant, so γ ⊂ ∂Γ_(K⁺). (d) At σ = 1, H_G t_* = −τ₁ − 2g₀₀ = q₁ (proof of
Lemma 15.11; Lemma 12.1 (b)), and by Lemma 15.4 the restriction of H_G to {σ = 1} acts on (x, ζ) as
H_(G₁). ∎

### 15.6 The dynamics over the Kerr face

**Proposition 15.14** (Dynamics over the Kerr face.) Let γ : I → ∂Σ⁺ ∩ ³ᵇS*_(K⁺)M₀, over
{r > r₀ − 2δ₀}, be a maximal integral curve of the field (15.4), not contained in ∂R_(∂K⁺,in),
∂R_(∂K⁺,out), ∂R_(ℋ⁺) or ∂Γ_(K⁺). Then:

(1) as s increases, γ tends to ∂Γ_(K⁺) or to ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), or reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} at a finite parameter;

(2) as s → −∞, γ tends to ∂Γ_(K⁺), to ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) or to ∂R_(ℋ⁺);

(3) γ does not tend to ∂Γ_(K⁺) in both directions.

Moreover, γ tends to ∂Γ_(K⁺) forward (backward) if and only if it lies in ∂Γ̄^s_(K⁺) (∂Γ̄^u_(K⁺)); a curve over ∂K⁺
goes from ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) to ∂R_(∂K⁺,out); and a curve in {σ ≤ 0} goes from ∂R_(ℋ⁺) to {r < r₀ − δ₀}.

"Tends to A" means that every limit point lies in A; for a set A of fixed points this is the convergence of [Hin26c].
This is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.21] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* The sign of σ is constant along γ (Lemma 15.4, the rescaling being positive), and the faces ∂K⁺ and
(K⁺)° are invariant. A curve in a compact set has a non-empty, compact, connected and invariant ω-limit set, and
likewise α-limit set; so "tends to A ∪ B", with A and B disjoint compact sets, means "tends to A or tends to B".

*σ > 0.* By Lemma 15.6, γ = Φ₁ ∘ γ̃ up to an increasing reparametrisation, with γ̃ a maximal integral curve of the
future field 𝖧₁ in Σ⁺₁ = Σ^♭₁, finite or over ∂X. Over ∂X (that is, γ over ∂K⁺), Lemma 11.17 at σ₀ = 1, or
Lemma 15.8 (a), gives the claim. Otherwise γ̃ lies in Σ₁ ∩ T*{r > r₀ − 2δ₀}, and (H8) (a) applies. If
γ̃ ⊄ Γ̄_u, it tends backward to ∂ℛ₊ ∪ ∂ℛ₋ or to R_(1,in); not to ∂ℛ₋, since at fibre infinity q̂₁ = −ρ_∞τ₁ is negative
near ∂ℛ₋ by (H3), while q₁ > 0 along γ̃. Under Φ₁, ∂ℛ₊ is ∂R_(ℋ⁺) and R_(1,in) is ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) (Definition 15.7). If
γ̃ ⊄ Γ̄_s, it tends forward to R_out, which is ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), or reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀}. If γ̃ ⊂ Γ̄_u (resp. Γ̄_s), it
tends to Γ backward (forward), by the definition of these sets. (3) is Lemma 15.13 (c).

*σ = 0.* γ lies in Φ_(±1)(∂Σ₀⁺) at fibre infinity of the stationary phase space, with the future field +ρ_∞H_(G₀) up to
a positive factor (Lemma 15.6). By (H4) it tends backward to ∂ℛ₊ ∪ ∂ℛ₋, hence to ∂ℛ₊, the components ∂Σ₀^± being
disjoint, compact and invariant; and it reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} forward at a finite parameter.

*σ < 0.* γ = Φ₋₁ ∘ γ̃ with γ̃ a maximal integral curve of the future field in Σ⁺₋₁, which lies over {r < R₁}
(Lemma 15.6 (d)), so its limit points are not over ∂X. Γ₋₁ ⊂ Σ^♭₋₁ = Σ⁻₋₁, and q₋₁ ≤ −2β_Γ on Γ₋₁, with β_Γ the
constant of (Γ.4) (q^Γ = −q₋₁ ≥ 2β_Γ there), hence q₋₁ < 0 near Γ₋₁, while q₋₁ > 0 on γ̃; so γ̃ lies in neither Γ̄_u nor
Γ̄_s. By (H8) (a), γ̃ tends backward to ∂ℛ₊ (not to ∂ℛ₋, as before, nor to R_(−1,in), which lies over ∂X), and reaches
{r < r₀ − δ₀} forward (not R_out, over ∂X). ∎

### 15.7 The eb-dynamics near ℐ⁺

Near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ use ρ₊ = t_*⁻¹, x_I = (t_*/r)^(1/2) and ω (Section 14.1) and eb-covectors
σ_(eb) dρ₊/ρ₊ + ξ_(eb) dx_I/x_I + η_(eb) dω/x_I (Definition 14.7), and put G_(eb) := x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²G. Since
dρ₊/ρ₊ = −ρ₊ dt_* and dx_I/x_I = ½ρ₊(dt_* − x_I² dr), the covector is
ν = ρ₊(½ξ_(eb) − σ_(eb)) dt_* − ½ρ₊x_I²ξ_(eb) dr + x_I⁻¹η_(eb) dω, and ḡ⁻¹(ν, ν) = −2ν_(t_*)ν_r + ν_r² + r⁻²|ν_ω|²
with r⁻² = ρ₊²x_I⁴ gives

    Ḡ_(eb) = ½ξ_(eb)(ξ_(eb) − 2σ_(eb)) + |η_(eb)|² + ¼x_I²ξ_(eb)².    (15.13)

This is the inverse of the form of ḡ near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ of Section 14.2.3, whose angular term is g_(𝕊³)/(2x_I²). By
Lemma 15.2 (the inverses), G_(eb) − Ḡ_(eb) ∈ x_I²ρ₊² P^[2](ᵉᵇT*M), so

    G_(eb) ≡ G⁰_(eb) := ½ξ_(eb)(ξ_(eb) − 2σ_(eb)) + |η_(eb)|²        modulo x_I² P^[2],

and as H_(x_I) = −x_I∂_(ξ_(eb)) by (14.3), H_(G_(eb)) ≡ H_(G⁰_(eb)) modulo x_I²𝒱_eb(ᵉᵇT*M), where, by
(14.3),

    H_(G⁰_(eb)) = −ξ_(eb)ρ₊∂_(ρ₊) + (ξ_(eb) − σ_(eb))(x_I∂_(x_I) + η_(eb)∂_(η_(eb))) − 2|η_(eb)|²∂_(ξ_(eb))
                  + x_I H_(|η_(eb)|²)    (15.14)

([Hin26c, p. 96], here on T*𝕊³).

*The sign of σ_(eb).* σ_(eb) = ν(ρ₊∂_(ρ₊)), and at fixed x_I, ρ₊∂_(ρ₊) = −(t_*∂_(t_*) + r∂_r) = −(t∂_t + r∂_r). The
vector field V := t∂_t + r∂_r has ḡ(V, V) = −t_*² − 2t_*r, and by (K1), |g(V, V) − ḡ(V, V)|
≤ Cr⁻²(t_* + r)² ≤ ½(t_*² + 2t_*r) on Ω ∩ {r ≥ R₂} for R₂ large (t_* ≥ 1). So V is timelike there,
and future directed: g(V, −∇t_*) = −dt_*(V) = −t_* < 0. For ν ∈ Σ⁺ over M° there, ν(V) < 0, so σ_(eb) = −ν(V) > 0; on
Σ over ℐ⁺, σ_(eb) = 0 would force ½ξ_(eb)² + |η_(eb)|² = 0, so σ_(eb) > 0 on Σ⁺ near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ ([Hin26c, p. 96]). Put

    ρ_∞ := σ_(eb)⁻¹,     ξ̂ := ξ_(eb)/σ_(eb),     η̂ := η_(eb)/σ_(eb),     𝖧 := ρ_∞H_(G_(eb)).    (15.15)

Then ρ_∞²G⁰_(eb) = ½ξ̂(ξ̂ − 2) + |η̂|², and 𝖧⁰ := ρ_∞H_(G⁰_(eb)) satisfies, exactly (H_(G⁰_(eb))σ_(eb) = 0),

    𝖧⁰ρ₊ = −ξ̂ρ₊,     𝖧⁰x_I = (ξ̂ − 1)x_I,     𝖧⁰ρ_∞ = 0,     𝖧⁰ξ̂ = −2|η̂|²,
    𝖧⁰η̂ = (ξ̂ − 1)η̂ − x_I∂_ω|η̂|²,    (15.16)

which is [Hin26c, (4.67)]; 𝖧 − 𝖧⁰ ∈ x_I²𝒱_eb, tangent to ᵉᵇS*M.

**Definition 15.15** (The radial sets at ℐ⁺; [Hin26c, Definition 4.22].)
∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) := {x_I = 0, ξ̂ = 0, η̂ = 0} over ℐ⁺ (all ρ₊), and ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) := {ρ₊ = 0, x_I = 0, ξ̂ = 2, η̂ = 0} over
ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺; their conic extensions lie in {σ_(eb) > 0}.

By (15.16), with ξ̂ a function of (ρ₊, x_I, η̂) on ∂Σ⁺ near each set, the linearisation of 𝖧 is
dx_I ↦ −dx_I, dη̂ ↦ −dη̂ at ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), and dρ₊ ↦ −2dρ₊, dx_I ↦ dx_I, dη̂ ↦ dη̂ at ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) ([Hin26c, (4.69)]);
the error vanishes to second order at x_I = 0. So the first set is a sink transversally to its ρ₊-fibres, and the
second a saddle.

**Lemma 15.16** (1) (*Over ℐ⁺.*) On ∂Σ⁺ over ℐ⁺, ξ̂ ∈ [0, 2] and |η̂|² = ½ξ̂(2 − ξ̂), and along integral
curves

    ξ̂′ = −ξ̂(2 − ξ̂),        ρ₊′ = −ξ̂ρ₊.    (15.17)

A maximal integral curve over ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω not contained in ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) ∪ ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) is one of the following.
(i) ξ̂ = 2/(1 + e^(2s)), ρ₊ = A(1 + e^(−2s)) with 0 < A < 1: forward it tends to ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) (at ρ₊ = A), backward it
reaches {t_* = 1} at a finite parameter. (ii) The same with A = 0, over ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺: from ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) to ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out).
(iii) ξ̂ ≡ 2, η̂ ≡ 0, ρ₊ = ρ₊(0)e^(−2s), ρ₊(0) > 0: forward it tends to ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+), backward it reaches {t_* = 1}.

(2) (*Convexity in ι⁺.*) Over ι⁺, if 𝖧x_I = 0 and x_I > 0, then 𝖧²x_I < 0.

(3) (*Invariant manifolds.*) ∂W_(ℐ⁺) := {ξ̂ = 2, η̂ = 0} over ℐ⁺ is the stable manifold of ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) within ∂Σ⁺
over ℐ⁺; in the present coordinates, ∂W_out of Lemma 15.9 (4) is {ρ₊ = 0, ξ̂ = 0, η̂ = 0}.

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 4.23] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (1) Over ℐ⁺, 𝖧 = 𝖧⁰ and ρ_∞²G_(eb) = ½ξ̂(ξ̂ − 2) + |η̂|², so on ∂Σ⁺, |η̂|² = ½ξ̂(2 − ξ̂), and
(15.16) gives (15.17). If ξ̂(0) ∈ {0, 2} then η̂ = 0; ξ̂ ≡ 0 gives a point of ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), and ξ̂ ≡ 2
gives (iii) or, at ρ₊ = 0, a point of ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+). Otherwise ξ̂ = 2/(1 + e^(2s)) after a shift,
ρ₊′/ρ₊ = −2/(1 + e^(2s)), and ρ₊ = A(1 + e^(−2s)). On Ω, ρ₊ ≤ 1, so A < 1 if A > 0, and ρ₊ increases as s decreases
and reaches 1 at a finite parameter. The angular coordinates do not move: |ω′| ≤ 2x_I|η̂| = 0 over ℐ⁺. The limits of
ξ̂, η̂ and ρ₊ are read off. (2) Over (ι⁺)°, x_I² = u = ρ_K⁻¹, and by Lemma 15.17 below 𝖧 is a positive multiple
c𝖧^(3b) of the field of Section 15.3 on Σ. At a zero of 𝖧x_I, 𝖧^(3b)ρ_K = 0, and
𝖧²x_I = c²(𝖧^(3b))²x_I = −½c²ρ_K^(−3/2)(𝖧^(3b))²ρ_K < 0 by Lemma 15.9 (3). (3) ∂W_(ℐ⁺) is invariant by
(15.17) and consists of the curves (iii) and the points of ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+); curves over ℐ⁺ with ξ̂ ≠ 2 tend to
∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) by (1). The last statement is Lemma 15.17 at ξ̂_(3b) = 0. ∎

**Lemma 15.17** (3b and eb over ι⁺.) Over (ι⁺)°, with u = x_I² = t_*/r and the 3b-coordinates
(15.5), (15.7), σ_(eb) = −σ_(3b)(u + ξ̂_(3b)), ξ_(eb) = −2ξ_(3b) and η_(eb) = x_Iη_(3b); hence

    ξ̂_(eb) = 2ξ̂_(3b)/(u + ξ̂_(3b)),     η̂_(eb) = −x_Iη̂_(3b)/(u + ξ̂_(3b)),     𝖧 = (u/(u + ξ̂_(3b))) 𝖧^(3b) on Σ,
    (15.18)

with 𝖧^(3b) := −σ_(3b)⁻¹H_(G_(3b)) as in Section 15.3. Consequently, in Lemma 15.8 (b), the curves (ii) and (iii)
tend to ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) as the eb-parameter tends to −∞, and the curves (i) and (iii) tend to ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) as s → ∞.

*Proof.* The identity −σ dt_* + ξ dr + η = σ_(3b) dt_*/r + ξ_(3b) dr/r + η_(3b) and the formula for ν above give
σ_(eb) = σt_* − ξr = −σ_(3b)u − ξ_(3b), ξ_(eb) = −2ξr = −2ξ_(3b) and η_(eb) = x_Iη_(3b). On Σ⁺ over ι⁺, σ_(3b) < 0 and
ξ̂_(3b) ∈ [0, 2], so u + ξ̂_(3b) > 0. Also G_(eb) = x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²G = rt_*G = uG_(3b), so H_(G_(eb)) = uH_(G_(3b)) on Σ,
and σ_(eb)⁻¹ = −σ_(3b)⁻¹(u + ξ̂_(3b))⁻¹. For the limits: in (ii) and (iii) the 3b-parameter reaches the end s₀ with
u → 0 and ξ̂_(3b) → ξ̂₀ ∈ (0, 2]; by (15.9), u′ = 2ξ̂₀ + O(u) there, so u ∼ 2ξ̂₀(s − s₀), and the eb-parameter
∫(u + ξ̂_(3b))u⁻¹ ds diverges to −∞; along the way ξ̂_(eb) → 2 and η̂_(eb) → 0 by (15.18), and ω converges
(Lemma 15.8 (c)): the limit lies in ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+). As s → ∞ in (iii), ξ̂_(3b) ∼ 2e^(−4s), |η̂_(3b)| ∼ 2e^(−2s) and
u ∼ 2Ce^(−2s), so ξ̂_(eb) ∼ (2/C)e^(−2s) → 0 and |η̂_(eb)| ≲ e^(−s) → 0; in (i), ξ̂_(3b) = 0 and ξ̂_(eb) = η̂_(eb) = 0
while u → 0. In both cases ρ₊ = 0 and x_I → 0: the limit lies in ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out). ∎

### 15.8 The global dynamics in e3b-phase space

**Proposition 15.18** (Curves over the boundary.) Let γ be a maximal integral curve of (15.4) in
∂Σ⁺ over ∂M̃ ∩ Ω ∩ {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}, that is, over (ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω) ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺. Say that γ is of type (A, B) if it tends to A
backward (or reaches A at a finite parameter, for A = {t_* = 1}) and to B forward (or reaches B, for
B = {r < r₀ − δ₀}). Write R^K_(in/out) := ∂R_(∂K⁺,in/out), R^I_in := ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+), R^I_out := ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out),
R_ℋ := ∂R_(ℋ⁺), Γ_K := ∂Γ_(K⁺) and r₋ := {r < r₀ − δ₀}. Then γ lies in one of ∂R_(ℋ⁺), ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+),
∂R_(∂K⁺,in), ∂Γ_(K⁺), ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), or it is of one of the following types.

| over | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| (ℐ⁺)° ∩ Ω | {t_* = 1} | R^I_in, R^I_out |
| ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ | R^I_in | R^I_out |
| (ι⁺)° | R^I_in | R^K_in, R^I_out |
| (ι⁺)° | R^K_out | R^I_out |
| ∂K⁺ | R^K_in | R^K_out |
| (K⁺)° | R_ℋ, R^K_in | r₋, Γ_K, R^K_out |
| (K⁺)° | Γ_K | r₋, R^K_out |

In the order {t_* = 1}, ∂R_(ℋ⁺), ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+), ∂R_(∂K⁺,in), ∂Γ_(K⁺), ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), {r < r₀ − δ₀}, ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), every
curve goes from an earlier set to a later one, as in [Hin26c, Figure 4.3]; with Proposition 15.19 this holds for every
curve over Ω. This is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.24] in dimension 4 + 1, for the curves over the boundary.

*Proof.* The field (15.4) is a b-vector field on ᵉ³ᵇS*M, so it is tangent to every boundary hypersurface, and
each open stratum of the boundary is invariant: (ℐ⁺)°, ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, (ι⁺)°, ∂K⁺ = K⁺ ∩ ι⁺ and (K⁺)° (within Ω). Over (K⁺)°
and ∂K⁺ the claim is Proposition 15.14. Over (ι⁺)° it is Lemma 15.8 (b), with the ends at u = 0 identified by
Lemma 15.17; case (i) of Lemma 15.8 (b) is the fourth row, cases (ii) and (iii) the third. Over ℐ⁺ it is
Lemma 15.16 (1). ∎

**Proposition 15.19** (Curves over the interior.) Let γ be a maximal integral curve of (15.4) in
∂Σ⁺ over M° ∩ Ω ∩ {r > r₀ − δ₀}, extended maximally within {r > r₀ − 2δ₀} ∩ Ω. Then γ reaches {t_* = 1} backward at
a finite parameter, and forward either reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} at a finite parameter or tends to the e3b-cosphere bundle
over (ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω) ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺: over ι⁺ ∪ K⁺ if t_* → ∞ along γ, over ℐ⁺ otherwise. This is [Hin26c, Proposition 6.1] for
the stationary model.

*Proof.* On ∂Σ⁺ over M°, ρ_∞H_G t_* = 2ρ_∞g⁻¹(ν, dt_*) > 0 for the null covectors ν there (Lemma 15.3 (c)), so
(15.4) increases t_*, at a rate bounded below by a positive constant on compact subsets of ∂Σ⁺ over
M° ∩ {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}. On {r < r₂}, H_G r = 2g⁻¹(ν, dr) < 0 for future null ν, as dr is future timelike there ((H4) and
Section 12.1.2: ∇r is future timelike, so ν(∇r) < 0); so backward r increases while r < r₂, and γ cannot leave
through {r = r₀ − 2δ₀} backward. The faces at infinity are invariant, so γ is defined until it reaches {t_* = 1} or
{r < r₀ − δ₀}.

*Forward.* If t_* → ∞, every limit point lies over {t_* = ∞} ∩ Ω = ι⁺ ∪ K⁺. If t_* stays bounded and γ does not reach
{r < r₀ − δ₀}, then sup I = ∞, and a limit point p over M° would be visited infinitely often, each visit to a fixed
small neighbourhood of p lasting a parameter time bounded below (the field is bounded) and increasing t_* by a fixed
amount: so t_* → ∞, a contradiction. The limit points therefore lie over ∂M̃ at finite t_* ≥ 1, which within Ω is ℐ⁺.

*Backward.* Suppose that γ does not reach {t_* = 1}; then inf I = −∞ and t_* ↓ L ≥ 1. As above, no limit point lies
over M°, so the α-limit set 𝒜 lies over ℐ⁺ ∩ {t_* = L}; it is non-empty, compact and invariant, and ρ₊ = L⁻¹ on it.
A curve in 𝒜 has ρ₊ constant, hence ξ̂ = 0 by (15.17) (ρ₊ > 0), hence η̂ = 0: 𝒜 ⊂ ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out). Near
∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), 𝖧x_I = (ξ̂ − 1)x_I + O(x_I³) ≤ −½x_I, so on a tail (−∞, s₁] of γ the function x_I ∘ γ > 0 increases as s
decreases and cannot tend to 0, a contradiction. ∎

**Remark 15.20** The sets of Proposition 15.18 and Proposition 15.19 that depend on the stationary model are
∂R_(ℋ⁺), through ℛ₊, and ∂Γ_(K⁺), through Γ. Under (H5), extended to (H6)–(H8) in Section 12.1.5, and (K4), both
depend continuously on the parameter b, with the constants of Lemma 15.11 and of (K3) uniform; the radial sets
over ∂K⁺ and ℐ⁺ do not depend on b. This is [Hin26c, Remark 4.25].

### 15.9 Stationary wave-type operators

This section and the four that follow are [Hin26c, Sections 5–6] in dimension 4 + 1, except [Hin26c, Proposition 6.3],
which is Proposition 15.55. The definitions are restated at n = 4: the constant 1 of [Hin26c, (5.1a)] becomes
3/2 = (n − 1)/2, the weight α_sf + 3/2 of the tf-admissibility of [Hin26c] becomes α_sf + 2, and the stationary model
is that of Section 15.1, a metric satisfying (K1)–(K4) together with (H1)–(H8), in place of Kerr. [Hin26c,
Proposition 6.4], which [Hin26c] proves by reference to the construction of [Hin23c, Lemma 5.8 and Appendix C], is
proved by that construction, written out in the coordinates of Section 15.3 and Section 15.7 and with the error
terms of the present class.

#### 15.9.1 The class

Throughout, g is the stationary metric of Section 15.1.1, which satisfies (K1)–(K4), E_X := X̃ × ℂ^(N_E) is the trivial
bundle of Section 11.1.2, and E := π_X^*E_X is its pullback along π_X(t_*, x) := x. Sections of E are ℂ^(N_E)-valued
functions, and ∂_(t_*) and ρ∂_ρ act componentwise; the connection of [Hin26c, Remark 5.3], needed for non-trivial
bundles, is not needed here. We write G(ζ) := g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) and ρ := r⁻¹, and ρ₁ is that of Section 11.1.1. The density
is |dt_* dx| = |dt dx|, the Euclidean density of Section 11.1.1 times |dt_*|, and for a fibre inner product h
(Section 11.1.2), A^(*h) and Im_h A := (A − A^(*h))/2i are taken with respect to it.

**Definition 15.21** (Stationary wave-type operators; [Hin26c, Definition 5.1] at n = 4.) A
t_*-translation-invariant P₀ ∈ Diff²(ℝ_(t_*) × X̃°; E) is a *stationary wave-type operator* (for g) if (1)
σ₂(P₀) = G Id, and (2) on {ρ < ρ₁},

    P₀ = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S) + P̂₀(0) + Q∂_(t_*) − g₀₀∂_(t_*)²,    (15.19)

with g₀₀ := g⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) and, all t_*-independent, P̂₀(0) ∈ ρ²Diff²_b(X̄; E), S ∈ C^∞(X̄; End ℂ^(N_E)) and
Q ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b(X̄; E). Put ([Hin26c, (5.2)])

    S̄ := inf_(p∈∂X) min Re spec S(p).

**Remark 15.22** (a) g₀₀ ∈ ρ²C^∞(X̄) by (K1): ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = 0, and the components of
g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ in the frame ∂_(t_*), ∂_x lie in ρ²C^∞(X̄) (Lemma 15.2, the inverses). (b) The representation
(15.19) is not unique: a zeroth-order term may be moved between 2ρS∂_(t_*) and Q∂_(t_*) ([Hin26c, Remark 5.2]).
But S|_(∂X) is determined by P₀. Indeed, if (S, Q) and (S′, Q′) both represent P₀, the parts linear in σ of the spectral
families (Lemma 15.23) give 2ρ(S − S′) = −(Q − Q′); the left side is of order 0, so Q − Q′ is a multiplication by
an element of ρ³C^∞, and S − S′ ∈ ρ²C^∞.

**Lemma 15.23** (The spectral family; [Hin26c, (5.10)].) Let P₀ be a stationary wave-type operator. Then
P̂(σ) := e^(iσt_*)P₀e^(−iσt_*) = P̂₀(0) + σT + σ²g₀₀ with T := 2iρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S) − iQ on {ρ < ρ₁}, and P̂ satisfies
(H1) and (H2) of Section 11.1.3 and (H6) of Section 12.1.2, with this g. Conversely, if a family
P̂(σ) = P̂(0) + σT + σ²P₂ satisfies (H1), (H2) and (H6), then P₀ := P̂(0) + T i∂_(t_*) − P₂∂_(t_*)²
(Section 12.1.2) is a stationary wave-type operator for the metric of (H6).

*Proof.* e^(iσt_*)∂_(t_*)e^(−iσt_*) = ∂_(t_*) − iσ acts as −iσ on t_*-independent sections, which gives the form and T;
and P₀ = P̂(0) + T i∂_(t_*) − g₀₀∂_(t_*)². The principal symbol of P₀ at −σ dt_* + ζ is
σ₂(P̂(0))(ζ) + σ σ₁(T)(ζ) + σ²g₀₀, as σ₁(i∂_(t_*))(−σ dt_* + ζ) = i · i · (−σ) = σ. By (12.1),
G(−σ dt_* + ζ) = G₀(ζ) + στ₁(ζ) + σ²g₀₀, so condition (1) of Definition 15.21 is equivalent to the three identities of
(H1) (σ₂(P̂(0)) = G₀ Id, σ₁(T) = τ₁ Id, P₂ = g₀₀ Id), the parts of different degree in σ being separate. (H2): the
first two equations of (11.2) are the form of T and P̂(0) = ρ²P^(0) with P^(0) ∈ Diff²_b, and g₀₀ ∈ ρ²C^∞ is
Remark 15.22 (a). For the normalisation of P^(0), write spatial covectors as
ξ dr + η = ξ_b dρ/ρ + η, so ξ_b = −rξ; then σ₂(ρ²((ρD_ρ)² + Δ_(𝕊³))) = ρ²(ξ_b² + |η|²) = ξ² + r⁻²|η|² = ḡ⁻¹(ζ, ζ)
for ζ = ξ dr + η. The components of ζ in the frame dt_*, dx are bounded by C(|ξ| + r⁻¹|η|), so by
Remark 15.22 (a), G₀(ζ) − ḡ⁻¹(ζ, ζ) ∈ ρ² · ρ²P^[2](ᵇT*X̄), P^[2] the fibrewise quadratic polynomials
with smooth coefficients. Hence σ₂(P^(0)) − (ξ_b² + |η|²) ∈ ρ²P^[2], and
P^(0) − ((ρD_ρ)² + Δ_(𝕊³))Id ∈ Diff¹_b + ρ²Diff²_b. (H6) is a hypothesis on g, which (K2) includes. The converse
reads the same identities backwards: the form of T in (H2) gives (15.19). ∎

So the stationary wave-type operators for g are the operators whose spectral families satisfy (H1), (H2) and (H6), and
(K2) asks (H3)–(H5) and (H7)–(H8) of them in addition.

#### 15.9.2 Tensor wave operators

**Lemma 15.24** (Tensor wave operators; [Hin26c, Example 5.4] at n = 4.) Identify (p, q)-tensors on ℝ^(1+4)
with ℂ^(N_E)-valued functions, N_E = 5^(p+q), by the coordinate frame of (t_*, x¹, …, x⁴) (for 1-forms, the frame dt_*,
dx^i of Section 11.1.2). Let ∇ be the Levi-Civita connection of g and □_g^((p,q)) := −g^(μν)∇_μ∇_ν. Then □_g^((p,q)) is
a stationary wave-type operator for g with S = 0, so S̄ = 0, and

    (□_g^((p,q)))^∧(0) − (□_ḡ^((p,q)))^∧(0) ∈ ρ⁴Diff²_b(X̄; E),    (15.20)

where ^∧(0) denotes the spectral family at σ = 0. For the scalar operator,

    □_ḡ = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2) + ρ²(−(ρ∂_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ_(𝕊³)).    (15.21)

*Proof.* (15.21): □_ḡ = ∂_t² − ∂_r² − 3r⁻¹∂_r + r⁻²Δ_(𝕊³) (Δ_(𝕊³) ≥ 0). In (t_*, r), ∂_t = ∂_(t_*) and
∂_r|_t = ∂_r − ∂_(t_*), so □_ḡ = 2∂_(t_*)∂_r + 3r⁻¹∂_(t_*) − ∂_r² − 3r⁻¹∂_r + r⁻²Δ_(𝕊³); with ∂_r = −ρ(ρ∂_ρ),
2∂_(t_*)∂_r + 3ρ∂_(t_*) = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2), and
−∂_r² − 3r⁻¹∂_r = −r⁻²((r∂_r)² + 2r∂_r) = ρ²(−(ρ∂_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ).

In the coordinates z = (t_*, x), ḡ = −dt_*² − 2ω_i dt_* dx^i + (δ_(ij) − ω_iω_j)dx^i dx^j, ω := x/|x|, from
dt = dt_* + ω_i dx^i. Write D_j := ∂_(x^j)|_(t_*); as D_j = ω_j∂_r + r⁻¹Y_j with Y_j smooth vector fields on 𝕊³,
D_j ∈ ρ𝒱_b(X̄), and D_j maps ρ^kC^∞(X̄) into ρ^(k+1)C^∞(X̄). The metric components of ḡ are functions of ω
(homogeneous of degree 0), so the Christoffel symbols Γ̄ lie in ρC^∞(X̄), and by (K1) and Lemma 15.2 those of g
satisfy Γ − Γ̄ ∈ ρ³C^∞ on {ρ < ρ₁} (on the compact set {R⁻¹ ≤ ρ ≤ ρ₁}, if it is non-empty, every smooth function lies
in ρ^kC^∞ for every k, so the restriction r > R in (K1) costs nothing), and g^(μν) − ḡ^(μν) ∈ ρ²C^∞. In the frame,
∇_μ = ∂_μ + A_μ on the tensor indices, A_μ linear in Γ, and

    □_g^((p,q)) = −g^(μν)((∂_μ + A_μ)(∂_ν + A_ν) − Γ^λ_(μν)(∂_λ + A_λ)).

The terms without A form the scalar operator □_g acting componentwise.

*The model.* For ḡ, ω^μΓ̄_(κμν) = 0 for all κ, ν, where ω^μ∂_μ = ∂_r (ω⁰ := 0). In
Γ̄_(κμν) = ½(∂_μḡ_(κν) + ∂_νḡ_(κμ) − ∂_κḡ_(μν)), the first term gives ω^μ∂_μḡ_(κν) = 0, the components being
homogeneous of degree 0 in x. For the others, ω^μḡ_(κμ) = −δ_(κ0) is constant, so ω^μ∂_νḡ_(κμ) = −T_(κν) with
T_(κν) := (∂_νω^μ)ḡ_(κμ), which is r⁻¹(δ_(κν) − ω_κω_ν) for spatial κ, ν and 0 otherwise, as
∂_νω^μ = r⁻¹(δ^μ_ν − ω_νω^μ); likewise ω^μ∂_κḡ_(μν) = −T_(νκ). T is symmetric, so
ω^μΓ̄_(κμν) = ½(−T_(κν) + T_(νκ)) = 0. Hence ω^μĀ_μ = 0. The ∂_(t_*)-coefficient of −2ḡ^(μν)Ā_μ∂_ν is
−2ḡ^(μt_*)Ā_μ = 2ω^iĀ_i = 0, since ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = 0 and ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dx^i) = −ω^i. The remaining terms with Ā are
−2ḡ^(μj)Ā_μD_j ∈ ρ²Diff¹_b and zeroth-order terms in ρ²C^∞. So □_ḡ^((p,q)) is (15.21) componentwise plus an
element of ρ²Diff¹_b, which is (15.19) with S = 0, Q = 0 and g₀₀ = 0.

*The difference.* □_g^((p,q)) − □_ḡ^((p,q)) is a sum of −(g^(μν) − ḡ^(μν))∂_μ∂_ν; of first-order terms B^λ∂_λ with
B^λ ∈ ρ³C^∞ (from (g − ḡ)⁻¹Γ̄, ḡ⁻¹(Γ − Γ̄), (g − ḡ)⁻¹A and ḡ⁻¹(A − Ā), where (g − ḡ)⁻¹ stands for g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹); and of
zeroth-order terms in ρ⁴C^∞. With ∂_μ ∈ {∂_(t_*), D_j}: the ∂_(t_*)²-term is
−(g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹)(dt_*, dt_*)∂_(t_*)² = −g₀₀∂_(t_*)²; the mixed terms ρ²C^∞ · ∂_(t_*)D_j lie in ρ³Diff¹_b ∂_(t_*);
B^(t_*)∂_(t_*) ∈ ρ³C^∞∂_(t_*); together they form Q∂_(t_*) with Q ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b. The spatial terms lie in
ρ²(ρ𝒱_b)² + ρ³ρ𝒱_b + ρ⁴C^∞ ⊂ ρ⁴Diff²_b, which gives (15.20). Finally σ₂ = G Id holds for every connection
Laplacian. ∎

In [Hin26c, Example 5.4], S ∈ ρC^∞ and the remainder in (15.20) has the weight ρ³; both come from the rate r⁻¹
of Kerr, and the rate r⁻² of (K1) gives S = 0 and ρ⁴.

#### 15.9.3 P₀ on the compactifications

**Lemma 15.25** ([Hin26c, Lemma 5.7] at n = 4.) Let P₀ be a stationary wave-type operator.
(a) P₀ ∈ ⟨x⟩⁻²Diff²_(3b)(M̃₀; E) over {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}. (b) On Ω, P₀ ∈ x_I²ρ₊²Diff²_(e3b)(M; E). (c) Near ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω, in
the coordinates ρ₊ = t_*⁻¹ ∈ (0, 1], x_I = (t_*/r)^(1/2), ω of Section 14.1,

    2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²P₀ ≡ −(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2S)(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ₊∂_(ρ₊)) + 2x_I²Δ_(𝕊³)    mod x_I Diff²_(eb).    (15.22)

The weight ρ₀² of [Hin26c, Lemma 5.7] is omitted: Ω does not meet I⁰, and ρ₀ is bounded below on it (Section 14.1).

*Proof.* (a) ³ᵇTM̃₀ is spanned by ⟨x⟩∂_t, ⟨x⟩∂_(x^i) (Definition 14.4). Near K⁺ away from sf, ⟨x⟩ is bounded above
and below, and P₀ is a t_*-independent differential operator with smooth coefficients in x, a combination of products
of ∂_(t_*) = ∂_t and ∂_(x^i)|_(t_*) = ∂_(x^i)|_t + ω^i∂_t. Near sf, r∂_(t_*), r∂_r = −ρ∂_ρ and ∂_ω are 3b-vector
fields, so 𝒱_b(X̄) ⊂ 𝒱_(3b) and ρ²Diff²_b(X̄) ⊂ r⁻²Diff²_(3b). In (15.19),
∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S) = r⁻²(r∂_(t_*))(−r∂_r − 3/2 − S), Q∂_(t_*) ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b · r⁻¹(r∂_(t_*)) ⊂ r⁻⁴Diff²_(3b) and
g₀₀∂_(t_*)² ∈ ρ²r⁻²(r∂_(t_*))². (b), (c) Away from ℐ⁺, (b) is (a), x_I being bounded below there and ρ₊ comparable to
⟨x⟩⁻¹ near K⁺ ∩ ι⁺. Near ℐ⁺, by Section 14.2.3, ∂_(t_*) = ρ₊(−ρ₊∂_(ρ₊) + ½x_I∂_(x_I)) and
∂_r = −½ρ₊x_I² · x_I∂_(x_I), and ρ = ρ₊x_I². Hence

    ρ∂_(t_*) = ½x_I²ρ₊²(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ₊∂_(ρ₊)),     ρ∂_ρ = −r∂_r = ½x_I∂_(x_I),     ρ²∂_ω = x_I³ρ₊² · x_I∂_ω,

each in x_I²ρ₊²𝒱_eb or better ([Hin26c, (5.6)]). As ∂_(t_*) commutes with ρ, the first term of (15.19) is
