−2(ρ∂_(t_*))(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S) = −½x_I²ρ₊²A(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2S) with A := x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ₊∂_(ρ₊). Since Aρ = 2ρ − 2ρ = 0,
A commutes with S, a function of (ρ, ω), and A(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2S) = (x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2S)A. Next, P̂₀(0) = ρ²P^(0)
with P^(0) ≡ (ρD_ρ)² + Δ_(𝕊³) modulo Diff¹_b + ρDiff²_b (Lemma 15.23):
2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²ρ²Δ_(𝕊³) = 2x_I²Δ_(𝕊³), while 2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²ρ²(ρD_ρ)² = −½x_I²(x_I∂_(x_I))², and
2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²ρ²Diff¹_b = 2x_I²Diff¹_b(X̄) ⊂ x_I Diff¹_(eb) (as x_I²∂_ω = x_I · x_I∂_ω), and likewise
2x_I²ρDiff²_b(X̄) ⊂ x_I²Diff²_(eb). Finally 2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²Q∂_(t_*) ∈ x_I³ρ₊²Diff²_(eb) and
2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²g₀₀∂_(t_*)² ∈ x_I²ρ₊²Diff²_(eb). This is (15.22), uniformly on {ρ₊ ≤ 1}, and
x_I²Δ_(𝕊³) ∈ Diff²_(eb) gives (b) near ℐ⁺. ∎

The constant 3 in (15.22) is the 2 of the factor 2(1 + S) of [Hin26c, (5.7)], at n = 4.

### 15.10 Admissibility of the stationary model

Admissibility collects the conditions under which the forward problem for P₀ is solved in Chapter 19: a threshold at
the trapped set, tf-admissibility at the transition face, thresholds at the radial sets, and the solvability estimate
(15.24).

#### 15.10.1 Trapping

**Definition 15.26** (Trapping admissibility; [Hin26c, Definition 5.8] at n = 4.) P₀ is *trapping
admissible* if, for z₀ = 1 and z₀ = −1, (Γ.4) of Section 12.1.5 holds with γ₋ < 0: there is a fibre inner product
h_Γ over Γ_(z₀) with sup_(Γ_(z₀)) λ_max(p₁^Γ) < ½ν_min. It is *strongly trapping admissible* if, for each z₀ and every
ϵ > 0, there is such an h_Γ with sup_(Γ_(z₀)) λ_max(p₁^Γ) < ϵ.

**Lemma 15.27** (a) Under (K2), P₀ is trapping admissible. (b) At a point −σ dt_* + ζ with σ > 0 and
(x, ζ/σ) ∈ Γ₁, and with ρ_∞ := σ⁻¹, ρ_∞σ₁(Im_h P₀)(−σ dt_* + ζ) = p₁(1)(x, ζ/σ), with p₁ as in Lemma 12.1. So
the case z₀ = 1 of Definition 15.26 is the condition [Hin26c, (5.8)] at the stationary extension of Γ₁, with Im taken
for the density |dt_* dx| and the inner product h_Γ extended to be stationary and homogeneous of degree 0.

*Proof.* (a) (H7) assumes γ₋ < 0 in (Γ.4). (b) The density |dt_* dx| is t_*-invariant, so
(T i∂_(t_*))^(*h) = i∂_(t_*)T^(*h), and i∂_(t_*) commutes with T^(*h); hence Im_h(T i∂_(t_*)) = (Im_h T) i∂_(t_*),
while g₀₀∂_(t_*)² is h-symmetric. So σ₁(Im_h P₀)(−σ dt_* + ζ) = σ₁(Im_h P̂(0))(ζ) + σ σ₀(Im_h T), homogeneous of
degree 1 in (σ, ζ); at σ = 1 it is p₁(1)(ζ) by Lemma 12.1 (b). ∎

[Hin26c, (5.9)], a conjugation by an elliptic operator realising [Hin26c, (5.8)] for a fixed inner product
([Hin17, Proposition 3.12]), corresponds to Lemma 12.36: for h_Γ on phase space, Section 12.6 conjugates by
Q = Op_h(b̃^(1/2)) near Γ and carries its estimates back. [Hin26c, (5.8)] uses the density |dg|. A change of density by
a smooth factor f changes Im P₀ by a first-order term with principal symbol ½f⁻¹H_G f, so the two conditions need not
coincide pointwise; Definition 15.26 is the one that the trapping estimate of Chapter 12 uses.

#### 15.10.2 The transition face

**Definition 15.28** (tf-admissibility; [Hin26c, Definition 5.10] at n = 4.) P₀ is *tf-admissible with
weight* β if its spectral family is tf-admissible with weight β in the sense of Definition 13.15.

By Corollary 13.16 (c), tf-admissibility with one weight in an indicial gap implies it for every weight in that gap.
Section 13.5.1 relates Definition 15.28 to [Hin26c, Definition 5.10].

#### 15.10.3 Orders

Over K⁺ the phase space is the 3b-cosphere bundle of the stationary model, ³ᵇS*M̃₀ (Section 15.2), and
t_*-translations act on it. On ∂Σ^± the future field is ±𝖧, with 𝖧 the field (15.4). The radial sets
∂R_(ℋ⁺) and ∂R_(∂K⁺,in/out) are those of Definition 15.10 and Definition 15.7. For a fibre inner product h on E_X,

    ϑ_out := inf_(R^K_out) λ_min(−ρ_∞σ¹_(3b)(r² Im_h P₀)),     ϑ^(3b)_in := sup_(R^K_in) λ_max(ρ_∞σ¹_(3b)(r² Im_h P₀)),
    (15.23)

with R^K_(in/out) := ∂R_(∂K⁺,in/out) (Proposition 15.18) and ρ_∞ := −σ_(3b)⁻¹ ([Hin26c, (5.18)] and after). Here
r² Im_h P₀ ∈ Diff¹_(3b) near sf by Lemma 15.25 (a), as its principal symbol of order 2 vanishes, and its
principal symbol σ¹_(3b)(r² Im_h P₀) is an h-self-adjoint endomorphism, homogeneous of degree 1 in the fibres. The
threshold ϑ_ℋ is that of (11.5) at the horizon: ∂R_(ℋ⁺) lies in {σ = 0}, where
σ₁(Im_h P₀) = σ₁(Im_h P̂(0)) by the identity in the proof of Lemma 15.27.

**Definition 15.29** (Stationary admissible orders; [Hin26c, Definition 5.11] at n = 4.) A
t_*-translation-invariant 𝗌 ∈ C^∞(³ᵇS*M̃₀), over {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}, is *stationary-P₀-admissible with weights* α_sf,
α_K *and margin* η ≥ 0 if:

(1) (*Monotonicity.*) ±𝖧𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ^±: 𝗌 is non-increasing along the future flow.

(2) (*Evenness.*) 𝗌(−ζ) = 𝗌(ζ).

(3) (*Black hole and trapping.*) 𝗌 is constant over {r ≤ r_Γ}, for some r_Γ > r_h with Γ_(±1) ⊂ T*{r < r_Γ}.

(4) (*Horizon.*) 𝗌 is constant near ∂R_(ℋ⁺), and 𝗌 > ½ + ϑ_ℋ + η there.

(5) (*Outgoing radial set.*) 𝗌 is constant near ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), and 𝗌 + α_sf < ½(−1 + ϑ_out) + α_K − η there.

(6) (*Incoming radial set.*) 𝗌 is constant near ∂R_(∂K⁺,in), and 𝗌 + α_sf > ½(−1 + ϑ^(3b)_in) + α_K + η there.

Each threshold is computed in a fibre inner product chosen for its radial set.

**Lemma 15.30** (Inner products adapted to S.) Let S ∈ C^∞(X̄; End ℂ^(N_E)) and ϵ > 0. There is a fibre inner
product h on E_X with λ_min(½(S + S^(*h))) ≥ S̄ − ϵ on ∂X. For every fibre inner product,
inf_(∂X) λ_min(½(S + S^(*h))) ≤ S̄. This is [Hin23c, Proposition B.1].

*Proof.* For p ∈ ∂X write S(p) = A(D + N)A⁻¹ in Jordan form, D diagonal and N with entries 0 or 1 on the first
superdiagonal. With Λ := diag(1, δ⁻¹, …, δ^(1−N_E)), ΛNΛ⁻¹ = δN. Put h_p(v, w) := ⟨ΛA⁻¹v, ΛA⁻¹w⟩_(ℂ^(N_E)); for
u := ΛA⁻¹v, Re h_p(S(p)v, v) = Re⟨(D + δN)u, u⟩ ≥ (min Re spec S(p) − δ)|u|² ≥ (S̄ − δ)h_p(v, v). As
λ_min(½(S + S^(*h))) = min_(h(v,v)=1) Re h(Sv, v), the constant inner product h_p gives λ_min ≥ S̄ − 2δ on a
neighbourhood U_p of p, by continuity of (q, v) ↦ Re h_p(S(q)v, v) on {h_p(v, v) = 1}. Take a finite cover of ∂X by
such U_(p_k), a subordinate partition of unity χ_k on a neighbourhood of ∂X, and h := Σ_k χ_k h_(p_k) there, extended
to X̄ by a convex combination with a fixed inner product away from ∂X. Then
Re h(Sv, v) = Σ_k χ_k Re h_(p_k)(Sv, v) ≥ (S̄ − 2δ)h(v, v) on ∂X; take δ := ϵ/2. Conversely, the eigenvalues of S(p)
depend continuously on p, so S̄ is attained: S(p_*)v = μv with Re μ = S̄. Then Re h(S(p_*)v, v) = S̄ h(v, v) for
every h. ∎

**Lemma 15.31** ([Hin26c, Lemma 5.12] at n = 4.) For every fibre inner product h,
ϑ_out = 2 inf_(∂X) λ_min(½(S + S^(*h))) ≤ 2S̄, and for the h of Lemma 15.30, ϑ_out ≥ 2S̄ − 2ϵ. Moreover
ϑ^(3b)_in = ϑ_in, the threshold of (11.5) at R_in.

*Proof.* Use the 3b-covectors (15.5), σ_(3b) dt_*/r + ξ_(3b) dr/r + η_(3b), so that σ₁(r∂_(t_*)) = iσ_(3b),
σ₁(r∂_r) = iξ_(3b), and −σ dt_* + ξ dr + η has σ_(3b) = −rσ, ξ_(3b) = rξ. We compute σ¹_(3b)(r² Im_h P₀) at sf term by
term in (15.19).

(i) −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2) is symmetric for |dt_* dx| = ρ⁻⁵|dt_* dρ dω|: (ρ∂_ρ)* = −ρ∂_ρ + 4 for ρ⁻⁵dρ and
∂_(t_*)* = −∂_(t_*), so (∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c))* = −(−ρ∂_ρ + 4 − c)ρ∂_(t_*) = ∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3 + c), which equals
∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c) exactly for c = 3/2. With h, the adjoint acquires terms H⁻¹[·, H]. As H is t_*-independent and
ρ∂_ρH ∈ ρC^∞, they lie in ρ · ρ ∂_(t_*)C^∞ ⊂ r⁻³Diff¹_(3b), which vanish at sf after the factor r².

(ii) 2∂_(t_*)ρS = 2ρS∂_(t_*) has Im_h = (1/i)ρ(S + S^(*h))∂_(t_*), as (2ρS∂_(t_*))^(*h) = −2ρS^(*h)∂_(t_*). Its symbol
at −σ dt_* + ζ is (1/i)ρ(S + S^(*h))(−iσ) = −ρσ(S + S^(*h)) = ρ²σ_(3b)(S + S^(*h)), so r² times it is
σ_(3b)(S + S^(*h)), and ∓ρ_∞ times that is ±(S + S^(*h)).

(iii) r² Im_h P̂₀(0) ∈ Diff¹_b(X̄) (the remark after (H5) in Section 11.1.3). Its 3b-principal symbol is that of a
spatial operator, linear in (ξ_(3b), η_(3b)). At ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), where ξ_(3b) = η_(3b) = 0, it vanishes. At
∂R_(∂K⁺,in), where ξ_(3b) = 2σ_(3b) and η_(3b) = 0, write the scattering symbol of
ρ⁻¹Im_h P̂₀(0) ∈ ρDiff¹_b = Diff¹_sc at ∂X, at ξ dr, as ξa; then σ(r² Im_h P̂₀(0))(ξ dr) = rξa = ξ_(3b)a at sf, and
ρ_∞ξ_(3b)a = −ξ̂a = −2a, which is p_in = σ(ρ⁻¹Im_h P̂(0))|_(ξ=−2, η=0) of (11.5).

(iv) Q∂_(t_*), g₀₀∂_(t_*)² ∈ r⁻⁴Diff²_(3b) (Lemma 15.25), so r² Im_h of them lies in r⁻²Diff¹_(3b) and vanishes at
sf.

Hence −ρ_∞σ¹_(3b)(r² Im_h P₀) = S + S^(*h) at ∂R_(∂K⁺,out), whose base is all of ∂K⁺ ∩ sf ≅ ∂X, and
ρ_∞σ¹_(3b)(r² Im_h P₀) = p_in − (S + S^(*h)) at ∂R_(∂K⁺,in). The first gives ϑ_out by Lemma 15.30, the second
ϑ^(3b)_in = sup λ_max(p_in − (S + S^(*h))) = ϑ_in. ∎

So the thresholds of Definition 15.29 at ∂K⁺ are those of (11.5) and Section 12.1.4 written in 3b-terms:
½(−1 + ϑ_out) ≈ −½ + S̄ and ½(−1 + ϑ_in).

#### 15.10.4 The spaces and ℵ-admissibility

For an order 𝗌, k ∈ ℕ₀ and weights, H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf,α_K))_(3b;b)(Ω; E)^(•,−) is the space of Section 14.7 (the
restrictions to {r > r₀} of elements of the weighted mixed 3b-space supported in {t_* ≥ 1}), with local defining
functions ρ_sf = r⁻¹ and ρ_K = r/(t_* + r) on Ω ([Hin26c, (5.21)]). On Ω, r∂_x and t_*∂_(t_*) form a global frame of
𝒱_b (Section 14.2.1), so b-regularity is tested by (t_*∂_(t_*))^j(r∂_x)^α.

**Definition 15.32** (ℵ-admissibility; [Hin26c, Definition 5.13] at n = 4.) Let ℵ, δ ≥ 0 and α_sf ∈ ℝ. P₀
is *ℵ-admissible with sf-weight α_sf and sf-loss δ* if, for every stationary-P₀-admissible order 𝗌 with weights α_sf,
−ℵ and margin 0: (1) P₀ is trapping admissible; (2) P₀ is tf-admissible with weight α_sf + 2; (3) for every k ∈ ℕ₀
and f ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)(Ω; E)^(•,−), the forward solution of P₀u = f lies in
H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf−δ,−ℵ))_(3b;b)(Ω; E)^(•,−), with

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf−δ,−ℵ))_(3b;b)) ≤ C_k ‖P₀u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)).    (15.24)

The relaxed version with margin d_ℵ ≥ 0 ([Hin26c, Remark 5.14]) asks (1)–(2) for orders with margin d_ℵ and (3) with
𝗌 − d_ℵ in place of 𝗌 on the left.

The weight in (2) is the weight α_sf + 3/2 of [Hin26c] at n = 4. Near ∂X, |dx| = ρ⁻⁵dρ dω = ρ⁻⁴μ_b, with μ_b := ρ⁻¹dρ dω
the b-density, so ρ^α L²(|dx|) = ρ^(α+2)L²(μ_b) near ∂X: the spatial weight α of an L²(|dx|)-based space is the b-weight
α + 2 at n = 4 (that is, α + n/2; see Section 13.1.2). In particular α_sf + 2 lies in an indicial gap of P̂₀(0). For
the scalar wave operator the gap is (0, 2), the indicial roots of (15.21) at ℓ = 0 being 0 and 2, so α_sf ∈ (−2,
0), where [Hin26c] has (−3/2, −1/2).

### 15.11 Asymptotically stationary metrics and wave-type operators

From here on the stationary metric of Section 15.9 is written g₀, and G₀(ζ) := g₀⁻¹(ζ, ζ) on spacetime covectors (on
spatial covectors, G₀ of Section 11.1.3 is its restriction). On Ω we use the e3b-structure of Section 14.2.4, the
weight w_(α) = x_I^(2α_I)ρ₊^(α₊)ρ_K^(α_K) and the spaces C^((d₀;k),(·))_(e3b;b) of Definition 14.26, for sections of a
bundle in a fixed smooth frame.

**Definition 15.33** (Asymptotically stationary metrics; [Hin26c, Definition 5.15] at n = 4.) Let
ℓ_I ∈ [0, ½], ℓ₊ ∈ [0, 1], ℓ_K ≥ 0 and d₀, k ∈ ℕ₀. Put

    𝒢̃^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) := x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω; S² ᵉ³ᵇT*_Ω M),
    𝒢^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) := g₀ + 𝒢̃^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b),

with the norm ‖h‖ := ‖x_I²ρ₊²h‖ of C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) on the first, equivalent by Lemma 14.27
(c) to the norm of C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I−2,ℓ₊−2,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b), which is the same space, and the induced metric on the second.
Subscripts are dropped for d₀ = 0 ("e3b") or k = 0 ("b").

**Remark 15.34** (a) g₀ − ḡ ∈ x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² C^(∞,(2,2,0))(Ω; S² ᵉ³ᵇT*_Ω M) by (15.2), as ρ₀ is
bounded below on Ω, so g₀ − ḡ lies in 𝒢̃^(∞,(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,0)) for all admissible ℓ_I, ℓ₊; for Kerr the weights are
(1, 0, 0) ([Hin26c, Remark 5.17]). (b) If h ∈ 𝒢̃^(0,(0,0,0))_(e3b) has small norm, then x_I²ρ₊²(g₀ + h) is a
non-degenerate section of S² ᵉ³ᵇT*_Ω M of Lorentzian signature, and g₀ + h is a Lorentzian metric on Ω°. Indeed
x_I²ρ₊²g₀ is non-degenerate of signature (1, 4) and continuous up to the boundary on the compact closure of Ω in
ᵉ³ᵇT*M (Lemma 15.2 (3)), so its inverse is bounded, and x_I²ρ₊²h is small in C⁰. g₀ + h is time-oriented by
Lemma 15.35, which makes dt^♭_* past timelike when h is small in 𝒢̃^(0,(2ℓ_I,0,0)), ℓ_I > 0.

**Lemma 15.35** (The time function; [Hin26c, Lemma 5.16] at n = 4.) Let ℓ := ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½] and
r^♮ := ½(r₀ + r₂). There are ϵ_G > 0, C′ ∈ (0, 1), r′₀ > r₂ and t^♭_* ∈ C^∞(Ω°) with

(a) t^♭_* = t_*(1 − (t_*/r)^ℓ) where t_*/r is small;

(b) C′t_* ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t_*;

(c) t^♭_* = C′t_* + C′r′₀ for r ≤ r′₀ − 1;

such that for every g = g₀ + h with ‖h‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(2ℓ,0,0))_(e3b)) < ϵ_G: (1) dr is future timelike for g on
{r₀ ≤ r ≤ r^♮}; (2) dt^♭_* is past timelike for g on Ω°.

*Proof.* *Bounds on g⁻¹.* Fix c_V > 0 so small that the description of Lemma 14.8 used below holds on {x_I < c_V}.
By that lemma, on {x_I < c_V} the covectors x_I⁻¹dt_*, x_I dr and r dω span ρ₊⁻¹x_I⁻¹C^∞(ᵉᵇT*), so the pointwise dual
vectors x_I∂_(t_*), x_I⁻¹∂_r, r⁻¹∂_ω span ρ₊x_I C^∞(ᵉᵇT), and the symmetric products

    ρ_I∂_(t_*)²,   ∂_(t_*) ⊗_s ∂_r,   x_I∂_(t_*) ⊗_s r⁻¹∂_ω,   ρ_I⁻¹∂_r²,   x_I⁻¹∂_r ⊗_s r⁻¹∂_ω,
    r⁻¹∂_ω ⊗_s r⁻¹∂_ω,        ρ_I := x_I² = t_*/r,

span x_I²ρ₊² C^∞(S² ᵉᵇT). As x_I²ρ₊²g₀ has a bounded inverse, g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹ (by a Neumann series) lies in
x_I²ρ₊² · x_I^(2ℓ) C⁰(S² ᵉ³ᵇT) with norm ≤ C‖h‖; and g₀⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ ∈ x_I⁴ρ₊⁴C^∞(S² ᵉ³ᵇT) (Lemma 15.2, the
inverses). Since ρ₊ ≤ 1 on Ω, the coefficients of g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ in the basis above are bounded by
C₁(ϵ_G + ρ_I^(1−ℓ))ρ_I^ℓ. Away from ℐ⁺, where x_I is bounded below, the same membership gives |(g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹)(α, α)|
≤ Cϵ_G(|α_t| + |α_r| + r⁻¹|α_ω|)² for α = α_t dt + α_r dr + α_ω: near K⁺ ∩ ι⁺ the 3b-vectors r∂_t,
r∂_x span ³ᵇT and x_I²ρ₊² ∼ r⁻² there; near K⁺ away from sf, ∂_t, ∂_x span it and x_I, ρ₊ are bounded below; near
ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ with x_I ≥ c, dt and dr evaluated on the eb-frame are O(t + r) = O(ρ₊⁻¹x_I⁻²).

*The function near ℐ⁺.* With ρ := ρ_I and F₁(ρ) := 1 − ρ^ℓ, d(t_*F₁(ρ_I)) = A dt_* + B dr with A = 1 − (1 + ℓ)ρ^ℓ and
B = ℓρ^(ℓ+1), as dρ_I = ρ_I(dt_*/t_* − dr/r). Since ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = 0, ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dr) = −1 and ḡ⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1, the
covector A dt_* + B dr has ḡ⁻¹-square −2AB + B², and −2AB ≤ −2ℓρ^(ℓ+1)(1 − 2ρ^ℓ) as 1 + ℓ ≤ 2. The basis elements
evaluated on (A dt_* + B dr)^(⊗2) give ρA², O(|AB|), 0, ρ⁻¹B², 0, 0, all at most ρ in size for ρ ≤ 1. So

    g⁻¹(d(t_*F₁), d(t_*F₁)) ≤ −2ℓρ^(ℓ+1)(1 − 2ρ^ℓ) + ρ^(2ℓ+2) + C₂(ϵ_G + ρ^(1−ℓ))ρ^(ℓ+1) ≤ −ℓρ^(ℓ+1)

for ρ ≤ ρ_a and ϵ_G ≤ ϵ_a, with ρ_a < c_V² and ρ_a, ϵ_a small depending on ℓ and C₂ (the error is of the order of the
main term, which is why ϵ_G must be small). This is timelike. It is past directed: V := t∂_t + r∂_r is future timelike
for g on {r ≥ R₂} ∩ Ω. For g₀ this is Section 15.7, with |g₀(V, V)| ≥ ½(t_*² + 2t_*r). For g: where x_I < c_V, we
have |h(V, V)| ≤ Cϵ_G x_I^(2ℓ) r t_* ≤ Cϵ_G|g₀(V, V)|. Where x_I ≥ c_V, the same membership of h, in the frames listed
above, gives |h(V, V)| ≤ Cϵ_G(t_* + r)², with C depending on c_V; there r ≤ c_V⁻²t_*, so
½(t_*² + 2t_*r) ≥ c_V²(1 + 2c_V²)⁻¹(t_* + r)², and again |h(V, V)| ≤ Cϵ_G|g₀(V, V)|. The orientation is continuous
along g₀ + τh, so V is future timelike for g once ϵ_G is small. Moreover d(t_*F₁)(V) = At_* + Br > 0, as Vt_* = t_* and
Vr = r; a timelike covector that is positive on a future timelike vector is past timelike.

*The function away from ℐ⁺.* dt = dt_* + dr has ḡ⁻¹(dt, dt) = −1, |(g₀⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹)(dt, dt)| ≤ Cr⁻² by (K1),
and |(g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹)(dt, dt)| ≤ Cϵ_G where x_I ≥ c, by the bounds above. So g⁻¹(dt, dt) ≤ −½ on {r ≥ r′₀ − 1, x_I ≥ c} for
r′₀ large and ϵ_G small, and dt is past timelike there (dt(V) = t > 0, V being future timelike as r′₀ − 1 ≥ R₂). On
{r₀ ≤ r ≤ r′₀ + 1}, g₀⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = g₀₀ ≤ −c₀ < 0 by (H6) and compactness, so g⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) ≤ −½c₀ for ϵ_G
small, and dt_* is past timelike there, for g₀ by (H6) and for g by continuity.

*Gluing.* Fix C large (below), C′ := (1 − C^(−ℓ))/(1 + C) and F₂(ρ) := C′(1 + ρ⁻¹), so that
t_*F₂(ρ_I) = C′(t_* + r) = C′t and F₁ = F₂ at ρ = 1/C. The function φ(ρ) := F₂(ρ) − F₁(ρ) satisfies φ(1/C) = 0 and
φ′(ρ) = −C′ρ⁻² + ℓρ^(ℓ−1) < 0 on (0, 2/C] for C large (as C′ ≥ (4C)⁻¹ and ℓρ^(ℓ+1) ≤ ℓ(2/C)^(ℓ+1)), and
F₁/F₂ ≥ 3/2 at ρ = 2/C. Moreover F₁/F₂ is increasing on (0, 2/C] for C large, since
(F₁/F₂)′ = C′ρ⁻²(1 − (1 + ℓ)ρ^ℓ − ℓρ^(ℓ+1))/F₂² and (1 + ℓ)ρ^ℓ + ℓρ^(ℓ+1) ≤ 2(2/C)^ℓ < 1 there. As F₁ vanishes at
ρ = 1, log F₁ is used only on (0, 2/C]. Let m_κ be smooth, even and convex, with m_κ(y) = |y| for |y| ≥ κ, and
M(a, b) := ½(a + b − m_κ(a − b)), a smooth minimum: M = min(a, b) when |a − b| ≥ κ, and ∂_aM, ∂_bM ∈ [0, 1] with
∂_aM + ∂_bM = 1. Let κ ≤ ¼ be small, and let ρ₋ < 1/C < ρ⁺ < 2/C be the points where F₂/F₁ = e^κ, resp.
F₁/F₂ = e^κ; they exist and are unique, as F₁/F₂ increases on (0, 2/C] from 0 through 1 at ρ = 1/C to at least
3/2 > e^κ. Put

    F := exp M(log F₁, log F₂) on (0, 2/C],        F := F₂ on [ρ⁺, ∞);

the two agree on [ρ⁺, 2/C], where log F₁ − log F₂ ≥ κ, so F is smooth on (0, ∞), F = F₁ on (0, ρ₋] and F = F₂ on
[ρ⁺, ∞), and F′/F = θF₁′/F₁ + (1 − θ)F₂′/F₂ with θ ∈ [0, 1] (θ = 0 on [ρ⁺, ∞)). Hence

    d(t_*F(ρ_I)) = F[(1 + ρF′/F)dt_* − ρ²(F′/F)dr] = F[θ d(t_*F₁)/F₁ + (1 − θ) d(t_*F₂)/F₂],

a positive combination of two past timelike covectors, hence past timelike, wherever both are. On the transition
interval [ρ₋, ρ⁺], with κ so small that ρ₋ ≥ 1/(2C), d(t_*F₁) is past timelike as ρ⁺ ≤ 2/C ≤ ρ_a, and d(t_*F₂) = C′dt
is past timelike by the previous paragraph with c := (2C)^(−1/2) (so that x_I = ρ_I^(1/2) ≥ c) and ϵ_G small depending
on C. So d(t_*F(ρ_I)) is past timelike on {r ≥ r′₀ + 1}: it is d(t_*F₁) where ρ_I ≤ ρ₋, C′dt where ρ_I ≥ ρ⁺ (there
x_I ≥ c), and the combination above on [ρ₋, ρ⁺]. Let R̃(r) be a smooth maximum of r and r′₀, equal to r′₀ for
r ≤ r′₀ − 1 and to r for r ≥ r′₀ + 1, with R̃′ ∈ [0, 1]. Define

    t^♭_* := C′(t_* + R̃(r)) on {r ≤ Ct_*/2},        t^♭_* := t_*F(t_*/r) on {r ≥ r′₀ + 1}.

For C > 2(r′₀ + 1) and t_* ≥ 1 the overlap {r′₀ + 1 ≤ r ≤ Ct_*/2} is where both are defined, and there both equal
C′(t_* + r), as ρ_I ≥ 2/C > ρ⁺ gives F = F₂. On {r ≤ Ct_*/2}, dt^♭_* = C′((1 − R̃′)dt_* + R̃′dt), a positive
combination of dt_* (past timelike for r ≤ r′₀ + 1) and dt (past timelike for r ≥ r′₀ − 1, x_I ≥ c, as ρ_I ≥ 2/C
there). On {r ≥ r′₀ + 1}, dt^♭_* = d(t_*F(ρ_I)) is past timelike, as just shown. This proves (2), and (a), (c) hold by
construction. (b): t_*F₁ ∈ [(1 − C^(−ℓ))t_*, t_*] for ρ ≤ 1/C, and t_*F₂ = C′t_*(1 + ρ⁻¹) ∈ [C′t_*, (1 − C^(−ℓ))t_*]
for ρ ≥ 1/C, so C′ ≤ F ≤ 1 on (0, ρ₋] and on [ρ⁺, ∞). A smooth convex even m_κ equal to |y| for |y| ≥ κ
satisfies |y| ≤ m_κ ≤ κ on [−κ, κ], so e^(−κ/2)min(F₁, F₂) ≤ F ≤ min(F₁, F₂) on (0, 2/C]; on the transition interval
min(F₁, F₂) ≥ C′(1 + C/2) (for C large, F₁ ≥ ½ there, and C′(1 + C/2) ≤ ½ as C^ℓ ≤ 2 + C for ℓ ≤ 1), and
e^(−1/8)(1 + C/2) ≥ 1, so C′ ≤ F ≤ 1 there too. And C′(t_* + R̃) ≤ C′(t_* + r′₀ + r) ≤ t_* where r ≤ Ct_*/2 and
r′₀ ≤ C/2. (1): g₀⁻¹(dr, dr) = G₀(dr) < 0 on {r₀ − 2δ₀ < r < r₂} by (H4), so G₀(dr) ≤ −c₁ < 0 on the compact set
{r₀ ≤ r ≤ r^♮}; the perturbation is O(ϵ_G) there, and dr is future timelike for g₀ (∇r is future timelike,
Section 12.1.2) and for g by continuity. ∎

By (b), Ω_* := cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1} ⊂ Ω ([Hin26c, (6.2)]).

**Definition 15.36** (Admissible operators; [Hin26c, Definition 5.18] at n = 4.) Let ℵ, δ ≥ 0 and
ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½], ℓ₊ > δ, ℓ_K > ℵ ([Hin26c, (5.23)]). Let P₀ be ℵ-admissible with sf-weight α_sf and sf-loss δ. An
operator P ∈ Diff²(Ω°; E) is *admissible* (relative to P₀) *of class* ((d₀;k), (2ℓ_I, ℓ₊, ℓ_K)) if:

(1) σ₂(P) = G Id, G(ζ) = g⁻¹(ζ, ζ), for some g ∈ 𝒢^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b);

(2) with a cut-off χ_I = χ_I(x_I), equal to 1 near 0 and supported in {x_I < 1}, there are

    p₀, p̃₁ ∈ ρ₊^(ℓ₊)C^(k+d₀)_b(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω; End ℂ^(N_E))    (15.25)

(extended to supp χ_I independently of x_I) with

    P̃ := P − [P₀ + χ_I ½x_I²ρ₊²(2p̃₁(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ₊∂_(ρ₊)) + p₀)]
         ∈ x_I²ρ₊² C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) Diff²_(e3b)(Ω; E);    (15.26)

(3) there is a splitting ℂ^(N_E) = ⊕_(j=1)^J E_j, over ∂X, in which p₁ := S|_(∂X) + p̃₁ is lower triangular with diagonal
blocks of real spectrum, and p₀ is strictly lower triangular.

P is *weakly admissible* if only ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½], ℓ₊ > 0 and ℓ_K > 0 are assumed ([Hin26c, (5.26)]).

Here S|_(∂X) is pulled back to ℐ⁺ along its fibration over ∂X ≅ Y⁺ (Section 14.1), and the operators in
(15.26) are those of Section 14.8.2 with coefficients in the stated space.

**Lemma 15.37** ([Hin26c, (5.27)] at n = 4.) For P as in Definition 15.36, near ℐ⁺ ∩ {ρ₊ ≤ 1},

    2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²P − [−(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2p₁)(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ₊∂_(ρ₊)) + 2x_I²Δ_(𝕊³) + p₀]
        ∈ C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,0))_(eb;b) Diff²_(eb).    (15.27)

The characteristic exponents of x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2p₁ are 3 + 2μ, μ ∈ spec p₁ (2(1 + μ) in [Hin26c]).

*Proof.* Where χ_I = 1,
2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²P = 2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²P₀ + 2p̃₁(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ₊∂_(ρ₊)) + p₀ + 2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²P̃. Insert (15.22);
S − S|_(∂X) ∈ ρC^∞ = x_I²ρ₊C^∞, so replacing S by S|_(∂X) costs x_I Diff¹_(eb), and
−(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2S|_(∂X))A + 2p̃₁A = −(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2p₁)A with A = x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ₊∂_(ρ₊). The remainders are
x_I Diff²_(eb) ⊂ C^(∞,(2ℓ_I,0))Diff²_(eb) (as 2ℓ_I ≤ 1) and
2x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²P̃ ∈ x_I^(2ℓ_I)ρ₊^(ℓ₊)C^((d₀;k))_(e3b;b) Diff²_(eb) (near ℐ⁺ the e3b- and eb-structures agree). ∎

**Definition 15.38** ([Hin26c, Definition 5.20].) p̄₁ := inf_(p∈ℐ⁺) min Re spec p₁(p).

The lower bounds on ℓ₊ and ℓ_K in [Hin26c, (5.23)] matter only when estimates for P are closed with the mapping
properties of P₀ ([Hin26c, Remark 5.21]); the regularity of p₀, p̃₁ in (15.25) follows [Hin26c, Remark 5.22].

**Definition 15.39** ([Hin26c, Definition 5.23].) ‖P − P₀‖_((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K)) is the sum of the norms of
p₀, p̃₁ in (15.25) and of a representation of P̃ in (15.26) (Section 14.8.2); on Ω′ ⊂ Ω the suprema
are taken over Ω′.

**Lemma 15.40** ‖g − g₀‖_(𝒢̃^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b)) ≤ C‖P − P₀‖_((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K)) when the
right side is small, and likewise on subsets.

*Proof.* The bracket in (15.26) has the principal symbol of P₀, the χ_I-terms being of first order. So
G − G₀ = σ₂(P̃), and g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹ ∈ x_I²ρ₊²C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b)(S² ᵉ³ᵇT) with norm ≤ C‖P̃‖. Then
g − g₀ = −g₀(g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹)g₀ + …, a convergent Neumann series in x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b), by
Lemma 14.27 (c)–(d). ∎

### 15.12 The global dynamics of perturbed metrics

Fix ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½], ℓ₊ ∈ (0, 1], ℓ_K > 0 ([Hin26c, (6.1)]) and d₀ ≥ 2, and consider

    g = g₀ + h,      h ∈ 𝒢̃^(d₀,(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b)(Ω_*),      ‖h‖ < ϵ_G ≤ 1,    (15.28)

with ϵ_G at most that of Lemma 15.35. Write w := x_I^(2ℓ_I)ρ₊^(ℓ₊)ρ_K^(ℓ_K), G(ζ) := g⁻¹(ζ, ζ),
G_(e3b) := x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²G and, with ρ_∞ a defining function of fibre infinity,

    𝖧_G := ρ_∞H_(G_(e3b)),    (15.29)

which on the characteristic set equals ρ_∞x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²H_G, the field (15.4) ([Hin26c, (6.4b)]). Put
Σ := {G_(e3b) = 0} ⊂ ᵉ³ᵇT*_(Ω_*)M ∖ o; Σ⁺ is the closure of the set of null covectors ν over Ω_*° with
g⁻¹(ν, dt^♭_*) > 0, that is, with ν^♯ future directed, as dt^♭_* is past timelike (Lemma 15.35); and Σ⁻ := −Σ⁺.

**Lemma 15.41** (a) G_(e3b) − G_(0,e3b) ∈ ϵ_G w C^(d₀) P^[2](ᵉ³ᵇT*_(Ω_*)M), and 𝖧_G − 𝖧_(G₀) is a
C^(d₀−1) b-vector field on ᵉ³ᵇT̄*_(Ω_*)M in ϵ_G w C^(d₀−1)𝒱_b, tangent to fibre infinity. In particular Σ and 𝖧_G agree
with those of g₀ over Ω_* ∩ ∂M, and 𝖧_G is C¹, so its integral curves are unique. (b) Σ⁺ ∩ Σ⁻ = ∅, and Σ^± agree with
those of g₀ over ∂M.

*Proof.* (a) g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹ ∈ x_I²ρ₊²ϵ_G w C^(d₀)(S² ᵉ³ᵇT) (Neumann series, as in the proof of Lemma 15.40), which is
the first statement. For p ∈ wC^(d₀)P^[2], H_p is a first-order e3b-differential operator applied to p
(Section 14.2.5); b-vector fields preserve wC⁰, so H_p ∈ wC^(d₀−1)𝒱_b(ᵉ³ᵇT*M), and ρ_∞H_p is tangent to fibre
infinity by homogeneity. w vanishes on ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺ as ℓ_I, ℓ₊, ℓ_K > 0. (b) Over Ω_*° a nonzero null covector is not
orthogonal to the timelike dt^♭_*. Over ∂M, use (a) and Section 15.1.3. ∎

**Proposition 15.42** (Global dynamics of perturbed metrics; [Hin26c, Proposition 6.1] at n = 4.) Let
γ : I → ∂Σ⁺ be a maximal integral curve of 𝖧_G over Ω_* ∩ {r ≥ r₀}. Then either γ lies over
(Ω_* ∩ ℐ⁺) ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺, where it is an integral curve of 𝖧_(G₀) and is described by Proposition 15.18; or γ reaches
{t^♭_* = 1} backward at a finite parameter, and forward either reaches {r = r₀} at a finite parameter, where
𝖧_G r < 0, or tends to ᵉ³ᵇS*M over (Ω_* ∩ ℐ⁺) ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺.

*Proof.* The boundary faces are invariant, as 𝖧_G is a b-vector field; over them 𝖧_G = 𝖧_(G₀) (Lemma 15.41). Let
γ lie over M°. At ν ∈ Σ⁺ over M°, H_G t^♭_* = 2g⁻¹(ν, dt^♭_*) > 0, and 𝖧_G t^♭_* is bounded below by a positive
constant on each compact subset of ∂Σ⁺ over Ω_* ∩ M°, by continuity.

*Forward.* If t^♭_* ∘ γ is unbounded, its limit points lie over {t^♭_* = ∞} ∩ Ω_* = ι⁺ ∪ K⁺. Otherwise, either γ reaches
{r = r₀}, or sup I = ∞ and a limit point over M° would be visited infinitely often, each visit to a fixed small
neighbourhood lasting a parameter time bounded below and raising t^♭_* by a fixed amount, so t^♭_* → ∞; hence the limit
points lie over ∂M at bounded t_*, which in Ω_* is ℐ⁺. At {r = r₀}, H_G r = 2g⁻¹(ν, dr) < 0 for future null ν, as dr
is future timelike there (Lemma 15.35 (1)), so γ leaves {r ≥ r₀} there.

*Backward.* Suppose that γ does not reach {t^♭_* = 1}. As 𝖧_G r < 0 at {r = r₀}, r increases backward there, so γ
does not leave through {r = r₀} backward. Then inf I = −∞ and t^♭_* ∘ γ ↓ L ≥ 1, and as before the α-limit set 𝒜 lies
over ℐ⁺ ∩ {t^♭_* = L}. Over ℐ⁺, t^♭_* = t_* by Lemma 15.35 (a), so ρ₊ = L⁻¹ on 𝒜. 𝒜 is non-empty, compact and
invariant under 𝖧_(G₀), and every curve in it has ρ₊ constant, so by (15.17) ξ̂ = 0 and then η̂ = 0:
𝒜 ⊂ ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out). Near ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), by (15.16) and Lemma 15.41 (a),
σ_(eb)⁻¹H_(G_(eb))x_I = (ξ̂ − 1)x_I + O(x_I^(1+2ℓ_I)) ≤ −½x_I for x_I small (with σ_(eb) > 0 on Σ⁺ there,
Lemma 15.45 below, for ϵ_G small). So on a tail (−∞, s₁], x_I ∘ γ > 0 increases as s decreases and cannot tend
to 0, a contradiction. ∎

The backward statement for g₀ is Proposition 15.19, and the argument carries over by Lemma 15.41.

### 15.13 Order functions

**Proposition 15.43** (Order functions; [Hin26c, Proposition 6.4] at n = 4.) Let P₀ be a stationary
wave-type operator for g₀, η ≥ 0 and α₊, α_K ∈ ℝ, and let ℓ_I, ℓ₊, ℓ_K be as in Section 15.12. There are
𝗌 ∈ C^∞(ᵉ³ᵇS*_Ω M) and ϵ_G > 0 such that:

(1) 𝗌 over K⁺, identified with a t_*-translation-invariant function on ³ᵇS*M̃₀ (over K⁺ the e3b- and 3b-cosphere
bundles agree), is stationary-P₀-admissible with margin η and α_sf = α₊;

(2) for every g = g₀ + h with ‖h‖_(𝒢̃^(1,(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b)(Ω)) < ϵ_G, ±𝖧_G𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ^± over Ω_*;

(3) 𝗌 is invariant under the dilations (t_*, r, ω) ↦ (at_*, ar, ω), a > 0, in a neighbourhood of
ι⁺ ∩ {r/t_* ∈ [1, 10]};

(4) (1) holds also for every stationary wave-type operator P₁ near P₀ (coefficients close in C¹), and (1)–(2) hold for
the stationary models of nearby parameters b ((K4));

(5) 𝗌 is constant near ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) and near ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) (Definition 15.15).

**Definition 15.44** ([Hin26c, Definition 6.5].) Order functions with (1)–(5) of Proposition 15.43 are
*admissible* for P₀ with weights α₊, α_K and margin η.

Item (5) is part of [Hin23c, Lemma 5.8 (3)]; it is included because the radial estimates at ℐ⁺ in Chapter 16 use it.
The proof of Proposition 15.43 occupies Section 15.13.1 (the characteristic set near ℐ⁺ and ι⁺, for every g as in (2))
and Section 15.13.2 (the construction).

#### 15.13.1 The characteristic set near ℐ⁺ and near ι⁺

*Near ℐ⁺.* Let Ω_I := Ω ∩ {x_I ≤ ϵ_I}, with the eb-coordinates of Section 15.7: ρ₊ = t_*⁻¹ ∈ (0, 1],
x_I = (t_*/r)^(1/2), covectors ν = σ_(eb) dρ₊/ρ₊ + ξ_(eb) dx_I/x_I + η_(eb)
dω/x_I, |ν|_(eb)² := σ_(eb)² + ξ_(eb)² + |η_(eb)|² and G_(eb) := x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²G. Let Ḡ_(eb) be (15.13) and
G⁰_(eb) := ½ξ_(eb)(ξ_(eb) − 2σ_(eb)) + |η_(eb)|². For g as in Proposition 15.43 (2), with ϵ_G ≤ 1, Section 15.7 and
Lemma 15.41 (a) at d₀ = 1 (its first assertion holds verbatim at d₀ = 1 and over Ω, its proof being the Neumann
series) give

    G_(eb) − G⁰_(eb) = ¼x_I²ξ_(eb)² + (G_(eb) − Ḡ_(eb)) ∈ x_I^(2ℓ_I) C¹ P^[2],    (15.30)

with norm bounded independently of g, as x_I² ≤ x_I^(2ℓ_I) and ρ₊ ≤ 1.

*Near ι⁺.* Let Ω_ι := Ω ∩ {ρ_K ≤ C_ι, ϱ ≤ ϵ_ι}, with the 3b-coordinates of Section 15.3: ρ_K := r/t_*, ϱ := r⁻¹,
ν = σ_(3b) dt_*/r + ξ_(3b) dr/r + η_(3b), |ν|_(3b)² := σ_(3b)² + ξ_(3b)² + |η_(3b)|², G_(3b) := r²G, and Ḡ_(3b) of
(15.6). (In Section 15.3, ρ₊ stands for ϱ.) On Ω_ι, x_I² = ρ_K⁻¹ ≥ C_ι⁻¹, so the e3b-defining function of ι⁺
is comparable to ϱ, and Section 15.3 and Lemma 15.41 (a) give

    G_(3b) − Ḡ_(3b) ∈ w_ι C¹ P^[2],        w_ι := ϱ^(ℓ₊),    (15.31)

with norm bounded in terms of C_ι, as ϱ² ≤ ϱ^(ℓ₊) and ρ_K^(ℓ_K)x_I^(2ℓ_I) is bounded on Ω.

**Lemma 15.45** For ϵ_I small, ϵ_ι small (depending on C_ι), and every g as in Proposition 15.43 (2) with
ϵ_G ≤ ϵ₁ small: on Σ over Ω_I, |σ_(eb)| ≥ 0.3|ν|_(eb), and σ_(eb) > 0 on Σ⁺; on Σ over
Ω_ι, |σ_(3b)| ≥ 0.3|ν|_(3b), and σ_(3b) < 0 on Σ⁺.

*Proof.* 2Ḡ_(eb) = (ξ_(eb) − σ_(eb))² − σ_(eb)² + 2|η_(eb)|² + ½x_I²ξ_(eb)². If |σ_(eb)| < 0.3|ν|_(eb), then
(ξ − σ)² ≥ ½ξ² − σ² (omitting the subscripts) gives
2Ḡ_(eb) ≥ ½(|ν|² − σ²) − 2σ² ≥ (½ − 2.5 · 0.09)|ν|² > ¼|ν|², while |2G_(eb) − 2Ḡ_(eb)| ≤ Cϵ_I^(2ℓ_I)|ν|² < ¼|ν|² by
(15.30) for ϵ_I small: so G_(eb) ≠ 0. The 3b case is the same, with
Ḡ_(3b) = (ξ_(3b) − σ_(3b))² + |η_(3b)|² − σ_(3b)² and (15.31).

*Signs.* σ_(eb) = ν(ρ₊∂_(ρ₊)) = −ν(V) with V := t∂_t + r∂_r (Section 15.7). On Ω_I, r = t_*x_I⁻² ≥ ϵ_I⁻² ≥ R₂, so V
is future timelike for g₀, and also for g: V = −ρ₊∂_(ρ₊) ∈ 𝒱_eb and h ∈ x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²ϵ_G x_I^(2ℓ_I)C⁰(S² ᵉᵇT*)
give |h(V, V)| ≤ Cϵ_G x_I^(2ℓ_I)x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² = Cϵ_G x_I^(2ℓ_I) r t_*, small against |g₀(V, V)| ≥ ½(t_*² + 2t_*r), and the
orientation is continuous along g₀ + τh. For ν ∈ Σ⁺ over M°, ν(V) = g(ν^♯, V) < 0, so σ_(eb) > 0, and by the first part
and continuity also over ∂M. Likewise σ_(3b) = rν(∂_(t_*)), and ∂_(t_*) is future timelike for g₀ on {r ≥ R₁}
(Lemma 15.3 (b)) and for g, as |h(∂_(t_*), ∂_(t_*))| ≤ Cϵ_G on Ω_ι (r∂_(t_*) is a 3b-vector field and
x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² ∼ r² there). ∎

On Σ⁺ over Ω_I put ξ̂ := ξ_(eb)/σ_(eb), η̂ := η_(eb)/σ_(eb) and 𝖧^(eb) := σ_(eb)⁻¹H_(G_(eb)); over Ω_ι put
ξ̂_(3b) := ξ_(3b)/σ_(3b), η̂_(3b) := η_(3b)/σ_(3b) and 𝖧^(3b) := −σ_(3b)⁻¹H_(G_(3b)). On Σ⁺ each is a positive
multiple of 𝖧_G, as G_(eb) and G_(3b) are positive multiples of G_(e3b) there (x_I being bounded below on Ω_ι); signs of
derivatives along them agree with those along 𝖧_G. By Lemma 15.45, |ξ̂| + |η̂| ≤ 7 on Σ over Ω_I, and likewise in
the 3b-coordinates over Ω_ι.

**Lemma 15.46** (Near ℐ⁺.) For ϵ_I small, on Σ⁺ over Ω_I ∩ {|ξ̂| ≤ ½}: (a) ξ̂ ≥ −1/8 and |η̂|² ≤ 3/2; (b)
𝖧^(eb)ξ̂ ≤ −¼ where ξ̂ ∈ [¼, ½]; (c) 𝖧^(eb)x_I ≤ −¼x_I.

*Proof.* By (15.30), 𝖧^(eb) = 𝖧⁰ + 𝖧^e with 𝖧⁰ := σ_(eb)⁻¹H_(G⁰_(eb)), given exactly by (15.16), and
𝖧^e := σ_(eb)⁻¹H_(G_(eb) − G⁰_(eb)). By (14.3), 𝖧^e applied to ξ̂ is O(x_I^(2ℓ_I)) and applied to x_I is
(∂_(ξ_(eb))(G_(eb) − G⁰_(eb)))σ_(eb)⁻¹x_I = O(x_I^(1+2ℓ_I)), uniformly where |ξ̂| + |η̂| ≤ 7. On Σ,
σ_(eb)⁻²G_(eb) = 0 gives |η̂|² = ½ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) + E with |E| ≤ C₃ϵ_I^(2ℓ_I). (a) For ξ̂ ∈ [−½, −1/8),
½ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) ≤ −1/8, so |η̂|² < 0 once C₃ϵ_I^(2ℓ_I) < 1/8, which is impossible; and for |ξ̂| ≤
½, |η̂|² ≤ 3/8 + C₃ϵ_I^(2ℓ_I) ≤ 3/2. (b) For ξ̂ ∈ [¼, ½], |η̂|² ≥ 7/32 − C₃ϵ_I^(2ℓ_I) ≥ 3/16, and
𝖧⁰ξ̂ = −2|η̂|² ≤ −3/8. (c) 𝖧⁰x_I = (ξ̂ − 1)x_I ≤ −½x_I. The errors are absorbed for ϵ_I small. ∎

**Lemma 15.47** (Near ι⁺; [Hin23c, (C.8)–(C.9)].) Put f_T := ϱ⁻¹(1 − ξ̂_(3b)) and f_W := −ξ̂_(3b). Let
δ ∈ (0, 1] (in this lemma and in Section 15.13.2, a parameter of the construction, not the sf-loss of
Definition 15.32). For ϵ_ι small depending on δ and C_ι, on Σ⁺ over Ω_ι ∩ {|ξ̂_(3b)| ≤ δ/2}: (a) 𝖧^(3b)f_T ≥ ϱ⁻¹;
(b) ξ̂_(3b) ≥ −δ/8, |η̂_(3b)|² ≥ |ξ̂_(3b)| − δ/8 and |η̂_(3b)|² ≤ 3δ; (c) 𝖧^(3b)f_W ≥ δ/8 where
ξ̂_(3b) ∈ [δ/4, δ/2].

*Proof.* Write 𝖧^(3b) = 𝖧̄ + 𝖧^e, with 𝖧̄ := −σ_(3b)⁻¹H_(Ḡ_(3b)) given exactly by (15.8) (with ρ₊ = ϱ) and
𝖧^e := −σ_(3b)⁻¹H_(G_(3b) − Ḡ_(3b)), which by (15.31) is a b-vector field with coefficients O(w_ι); it maps ϱ
into ϱO(w_ι) and ξ̂_(3b) into O(w_ι). We write ξ̂ for ξ̂_(3b) and η̂ for η̂_(3b). (a) By (15.8),
𝖧̄ϱ⁻¹ = 2(1 − ξ̂)ϱ⁻¹ and 𝖧̄ξ̂ = −2(2 − ξ̂)ξ̂, so

    𝖧̄f_T = 2ϱ⁻¹((1 − ξ̂)² + (2 − ξ̂)ξ̂) = 2ϱ⁻¹

exactly; and |𝖧^e f_T| ≤ Cϱ⁻¹w_ι, so 𝖧^(3b)f_T ≥ (2 − Cϵ_ι^(ℓ₊))ϱ⁻¹ ≥ ϱ⁻¹. (b) On Σ,
σ_(3b)⁻²G_(3b) = ξ̂² − 2ξ̂ + |η̂|² + O(w_ι) = 0, so |η̂|² = ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) + E with |E| ≤ Cϵ_ι^(ℓ₊) ≤ δ/16. For
ξ̂ ∈ [−δ/2, −δ/8), ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) ≤ 2ξ̂ < −δ/4, which is impossible. For ξ̂ ∈ [0, δ/2], ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) ≥ ξ̂; for ξ̂
∈ [−δ/8, 0), |η̂|² ≥ 0 ≥ |ξ̂| − δ/8. And ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) ≤ 3|ξ̂| for |ξ̂| ≤ ½, so |η̂|² ≤ 3|ξ̂| + δ/16 ≤ 3δ. (c) For ξ̂ ∈
[δ/4, δ/2], 𝖧̄f_W = 2(2 − ξ̂)ξ̂ ≥ 2ξ̂ ≥ δ/2, so 𝖧^(3b)f_W ≥ δ/2 − Cϵ_ι^(ℓ₊) ≥ δ/8. ∎

#### 15.13.2 The construction

*Proof of Proposition 15.43.* Fix the following functions, all with values in [0, 1]: φ ∈ C^∞_c((−½, ½)) even, with
φ = 1 on [−¼, ¼] and φ′ ≤ 0 on [0, ∞); ψ ∈ C^∞_c((−3, 3)) with ψ = 1 on [−2, 2]; ψ̃ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) with ψ̃ = 0 on (−∞, 4],
ψ̃ = 1 on [5, ∞) and ψ̃′ ≥ 0; ψ₀ ∈ C^∞([0, ∞)) with ψ₀ = 1 on [0, ½ϵ_I], ψ₀ = 0 on [ϵ_I, ∞) and ψ₀′ ≤ 0; and
Ψ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) with Ψ = 0 on (−∞, 0.04] and Ψ = 1 on [0.09, ∞). Choose, in this order: ϵ_I (Lemma 15.45 and
Lemma 15.46, and ϵ_I² < 1/10, used in (3)); C_ι := 8ϵ_I⁻²; δ := ϵ_I²/32; and ϵ_ι (Lemma 15.45 and
Lemma 15.47) so small that also 1/(ϵ_ιδ) > r_Γ for some r_Γ as in Definition 15.29 (3), and 1/(ϵ_ιδ) > r_h + 1.
Define

    χ_I := φ(ξ̂) ψ(|η̂|²) Ψ(σ_(eb)²/|ν|_(eb)²),
    χ_ι := φ(f_W/δ) ψ̃(ϵ_ιδ f_T) ψ(|η̂_(3b)|²/(2δ)) Ψ(σ_(3b)²/|ν|_(3b)²),
    χ := ψ₀(x_I)χ_I + (1 − ψ₀(x_I))χ_ι,        𝗌 := s_in − (s_in − s_out)χ,    (15.32)

with constants s_out ≤ s_in chosen below.

*Smoothness.* χ_I is smooth on ᵉᵇS* over {x_I < ϵ_I} ⊃ supp ψ₀(x_I), the ratios being smooth where Ψ ≠ 0, that is,
where |σ_(eb)| ≥ 0.2|ν|_(eb). χ_ι is a function of t_*, r and the 3b-fibre coordinates, which are smooth on ³ᵇS* away
from ℐ⁺; on supp(1 − ψ₀(x_I)), x_I ≥ ½ϵ_I, so ρ_K = x_I⁻² ≤ 4ϵ_I⁻² < C_ι. Where φ(f_W/δ) ≠ 0, |ξ̂_(3b)| < δ/2 ≤ ½, so
ϵ_ιδf_T ≥ ½ϵ_ιδϱ⁻¹ → ∞ as ϱ → 0, and ψ̃(ϵ_ιδf_T) = 1 near ϱ = 0. Where ψ̃(ϵ_ιδf_T) ≠ 0 as well, f_T > 4/(ϵ_ιδ) and
ϱ = (1 − ξ̂_(3b))/f_T < (5/16)ϵ_ιδ, inside Ω_ι. Near a point with ϱ = 0 and |ξ̂_(3b)| ≥ δ/2, φ(f_W/δ) vanishes on a
neighbourhood, supp φ being a compact subset of (−½, ½). So (1 − ψ₀)χ_ι is smooth and supported in
Ω_ι ∩ {ϱ < ϵ_ιδ}, and χ ∈ C^∞(ᵉ³ᵇS*_Ω M), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1. Every factor is even under ν ↦ −ν.

*Monotonicity.* Let g be as in (2) with ϵ_G ≤ ϵ₁, and work on ∂Σ⁺. On Σ over Ω_I ∩ supp φ(ξ̂), |η̂|² ≤ 3/2
and |σ_(eb)| ≥ 0.3|ν|_(eb) (Lemma 15.45 and Lemma 15.46), so ψ(|η̂|²) = 1 and Ψ = 1 on a neighbourhood of these
points in ∂Σ⁺, and 𝖧χ_I = φ′(ξ̂)𝖧ξ̂ there. Where φ′(ξ̂) ≠ 0, |ξ̂| ∈ [¼, ½], so ξ̂ ∈ [¼, ½] by Lemma 15.46 (a),
φ′ ≤ 0 and 𝖧^(eb)ξ̂ < 0 (Lemma 15.46 (b)): 𝖧χ_I ≥ 0. Likewise on Σ over Ω_ι the factors ψ and Ψ of χ_ι equal 1
near supp φ(f_W/δ) (Lemma 15.47 (b): |η̂_(3b)|²/(2δ) ≤ 3/2), and

    𝖧^(3b)χ_ι = δ⁻¹φ′(f_W/δ)ψ̃ 𝖧^(3b)f_W + ϵ_ιδ φ ψ̃′ 𝖧^(3b)f_T.

Where φ′(f_W/δ) ≠ 0, |ξ̂_(3b)| ∈ [δ/4, δ/2], hence ξ̂_(3b) ∈ [δ/4, δ/2] (Lemma 15.47 (b)), so
f_W/δ ∈ [−½, −¼], where φ′ ≥ 0, and 𝖧^(3b)f_W > 0 (Lemma 15.47 (c)). The second term is ≥ 0 by
Lemma 15.47 (a). So 𝖧χ_ι ≥ 0 on ∂Σ⁺ over supp(1 − ψ₀).

*Gluing.* 𝖧χ = ψ₀𝖧χ_I + (1 − ψ₀)𝖧χ_ι + ψ₀′(x_I)(𝖧x_I)(χ_I − χ_ι), and the last term lives on
U := {½ϵ_I ≤ x_I ≤ ϵ_I}. Two facts hold on ∂Σ⁺ over U.

(U1) Where χ_ι ≠ 0, χ_I = 1. Indeed there |ξ̂_(3b)| < δ/2 = ϵ_I²/64 and u := x_I² = t_*/r ∈ [¼ϵ_I², ϵ_I²]. The two
systems of fibre coordinates are related by σ_(eb) = −σ_(3b)(u + ξ̂_(3b)), ξ_(eb) = −2ξ_(3b) and η_(eb) = x_Iη_(3b),
an identity of coordinates proved in Lemma 15.17 that holds wherever both are defined. So
ξ̂ = 2ξ̂_(3b)/(u + ξ̂_(3b)), and u + ξ̂_(3b) ≥ ϵ_I²/8 gives |ξ̂| ≤ ¼: φ(ξ̂) = 1, and ψ = Ψ = 1 as before.

(U2) Where χ_I ≠ 0, 𝖧x_I < 0: there |ξ̂| < ½, and Lemma 15.46 (c) applies.

Where χ_I = 0, (U1) gives χ_ι = 0 and the last term vanishes. Where χ_I > 0, ψ₀′𝖧x_I ≥ 0 by (U2), and χ_I − χ_ι ≥ 0,
since either χ_ι = 0 or χ_I = 1 ≥ χ_ι. Hence 𝖧χ ≥ 0 on ∂Σ⁺, and 𝖧𝗌 = −(s_in − s_out)𝖧χ ≤ 0. On ∂Σ⁻: the antipodal map
A : ν ↦ −ν maps Σ⁺ onto Σ⁻, G is even, so H_G and 𝖧_G are odd (A_*𝖧_G = −𝖧_G), and 𝗌 ∘ A = 𝗌; hence
𝖧_G𝗌(Aν) = −𝖧_G𝗌(ν) ≥ 0, which is −𝖧_G𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ⁻. This proves (2), with ϵ_G := ϵ₁; the case h = 0 restricted to K⁺
is Definition 15.29 (1).

*Values.* Over K⁺, x_I = (t_*/r)^(1/2) = ∞, so ψ₀(x_I) = 0 and χ = χ_ι, a function of ϱ and the 3b-fibre coordinates,
hence t_*-translation-invariant there; it vanishes over {ϱ ≥ ϵ_ιδ}, a set containing {r ≤ r_Γ} and a neighbourhood of
the horizon: 𝗌 = s_in there. Near ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) (ξ̂_(3b) = 2), φ(f_W/δ) = 0, so 𝗌 = s_in. Near
∂R_(∂K⁺,out) = {ρ_K = ϱ = 0, ξ̂_(3b) = 0, η̂_(3b) = 0}: φ(f_W/δ) = 1 for |ξ̂_(3b)| ≤ δ/4, ψ̃ = 1 for ϱ small, ψ = 1 for
η̂_(3b) small, and Ψ = 1 as |σ_(3b)| = |ν|_(3b) at the set: 𝗌 = s_out on a neighbourhood. Near ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) (x_I = 0,
ξ̂ = 0, η̂ = 0), ψ₀ = 1 and χ_I = 1: 𝗌 = s_out. Near ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) (ξ̂ = 2), ψ₀ = 1 and χ_I = 0: 𝗌 = s_in. Choose

    s_in > max(½ + ϑ_ℋ + η, ½(−1 + ϑ^(3b)_in) + α_K + η − α₊) + 1,
    s_out < min(s_in, ½(−1 + ϑ_out) + α_K − η − α₊) − 1,

each threshold in a fibre inner product chosen for its radial set (for ϑ_out, that of Lemma 15.30). Then, with
𝗌 := s_in over {r₀ − 2δ₀ < r < r₀} (where nothing else is defined), (1)–(6) of Definition 15.29 hold, which is (1),
and (5) holds.

*(3).* In a neighbourhood of ι⁺ ∩ {ρ_K ∈ [1, 10]}, x_I² = ρ_K⁻¹ ≥ 1/10 > ϵ_I², so ψ₀(x_I) = 0, and ϱ is small, so
ψ̃(ϵ_ιδf_T) = 1 on supp φ(f_W/δ): χ = φ(−ξ̂_(3b)/δ)ψ(|η̂_(3b)|²/(2δ))Ψ(σ_(3b)²/|ν|_(3b)²) there. The 3b-covectors
dt_*/r, dr/r and dω are invariant under the dilations, and so are the ratios of their coefficients and |ν|_(3b)² (with
the round metric on 𝕊³).

*(4).* The thresholds ϑ_ℋ, ϑ^(3b)_in and ϑ_out are extreme eigenvalues of endomorphisms depending continuously on the
coefficients, over compact sets, so they move by less than 1 for P₁ near P₀ (with fixed inner products), and the
margins of 1 above keep (4)–(6) of Definition 15.29. Conditions (1)–(3) of that definition do not depend on the
operator beyond its metric. For nearby parameters b, the stationary metrics satisfy (K1) with uniform constants (K4),
so (15.30), (15.31) and Lemma 15.45–Lemma 15.47 hold uniformly; the horizon radius and Γ
vary continuously (Remark 15.20), so {ϱ ≥ ϵ_ιδ} still contains them after shrinking ϵ_ι. ∎

**Remark 15.48** [Hin23c, Appendix C] also multiplies χ_I by a localisation χ_t in a time function,
with a further small parameter ρ_(+,lo), because its error term in 𝖧x_I is Cρ₊^(ℓ₊)x_I. Here the error carries
x_I^(2ℓ_I) by (15.30) (the rate x_I² of the stationary part, Section 15.7, and the weight x_I^(2ℓ_I) of the
perturbation), so Lemma 15.46 (c) holds at all ρ₊ ≤ 1 and χ_t is not needed. [Hin26c, p. 114] refers to that
construction and adds that only the dynamics over ι⁺ matter; the construction above confirms this, the trapped set and
the horizon lying where 𝗌 is constant.

### 15.14 The persistence theorem

For a metric that decays in time to the stationary model, the null-bicharacteristic flow is tangent to hypersurfaces
that are close to the stable and unstable manifolds of the stationary trapped set and converge to them
(Proposition 15.55; [Hin26c, Proposition 6.3] in dimension 4 + 1). This section states the theorem on decaying
perturbations of a flow with normally hyperbolic trapping from which this follows. It is proved quantitatively, from
the defining functions of (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) with their exact equations (Γ.2) and the tangential growth bound of (K3).

**Theorem 15.49** (Persistence of the stable and unstable hypersurfaces.) Let Y be a smooth manifold with a
Riemannian metric, V₀ a smooth vector field on Y, Γ ⊂ Y a compact smooth submanifold, O ⊂ Y an open neighbourhood of Γ
with compact closure, and φ_u, φ_s, ν_u, ν_s ∈ C^∞(Ō) real, such that:

(i) Γ = {φ_u = φ_s = 0} ∩ O, and dφ_u, dφ_s are linearly independent at every point of Γ;

(ii) V₀φ_u = −ν_uφ_u and V₀φ_s = ν_sφ_s on O, with ν_u, ν_s ≥ ν > 0 on O;

(iii) Γ is invariant under the flow of V₀, and for every ε > 0 there is C_ε with |De^(sV₀)v| ≤ C_ε e^(ε|s|)|v| for
v ∈ TΓ, s ∈ ℝ.

Let k ≥ 2, ℓ > 0, T₀ ≥ 1 and ρ(t) := t^(−ℓ). Then there are a neighbourhood O′ ⊂ O of Γ, ϵ₀ > 0 and C such that the
following holds for every vector field Ṽ on [T₀, ∞) × O, tangent to the slices {t} × O, of class C^k in (t, y) jointly,
with

    ‖Ṽ‖ := sup_(t≥T₀) ρ(t)⁻¹ ‖Ṽ‖_(C^k([t,t+1]×O)) ≤ ϵ ≤ ϵ₀.    (15.33)

The vector field V := ∂_t + V₀ + Ṽ is tangent to the hypersurfaces

    W^u := {φ_u + ψ_u = 0},        W^s := {φ_s + ψ_s = 0}        of [T₀, ∞) × O′,    (15.34)

where ψ_u ∈ C^k, ψ_s ∈ C^(k−1), |∂^αψ_u(t, y)| ≤ Cϵρ(t) for |α| ≤ k and |∂^αψ_s(t, y)| ≤ Cϵρ(t) for |α| ≤ k − 1,
derivatives in (t, y) in fixed charts. W^u meets {t = T₀} in {φ_u = 0}. The constants O′, ϵ₀ and C depend only on k,
ℓ, ν, C_ε for ε := ν/(2k), the C^(k+1)-norms of V₀, φ_u, φ_s, ν_u, ν_s on O in a fixed finite atlas, and the choices
of Section 15.15.1; they depend neither on T₀ nor on Ṽ.

C^k-norms on [t, t + 1] × O are taken in the charts of a fixed finite atlas of a neighbourhood of Ō, in which the
metric is uniformly comparable to the Euclidean one.

**Remark 15.50** (a) (iii) is the tangential half of r-normal hyperbolicity for every r
([HPS77, Definition 4]); the normal half is (ii), in which the normal dynamics is linear in φ_u, φ_s. No invariant
splitting of T_ΓY is used. (b) W^s is the analogue of the stable manifold and is determined by V; W^u, the analogue of
the unstable manifold, depends on its initial slice, here {φ_u = 0} at t = T₀ ([Hin21, footnote 1]). In the
application, with time running forward, W^u is the backward-trapped hypersurface and W^s the forward-trapped one.

### 15.15 Proof of the persistence theorem

*Proof of Theorem 15.49.* The proof is a graph transform. The hypersurfaces have codimension one and (ii) gives the
normal dynamics in closed form, so each step of the transform solves one scalar equation by monotonicity; the
tangential dynamics enters only through the norm of a time-T map, which is made small against the normal rates by
taking T large. The proof occupies Section 15.15.1–Section 15.15.6.

#### 15.15.1 Coordinates

Let π : O₁ → Γ be a smooth retraction of a neighbourhood O₁ ⊂ O of Γ (π|_Γ = id; for instance the projection of a
tubular neighbourhood), and Ψ₀ := (π, φ_u, φ_s) : O₁ → Γ × ℝ².

*Ψ₀ is a local diffeomorphism near Γ.* At p ∈ Γ, ker dφ_u ∩ ker dφ_s has codimension 2 by (i) and contains T_pΓ (as
φ_(u/s) = 0 on Γ), which has codimension 2; so they are equal. If dΨ₀(v) = 0, then v ∈ T_pΓ and dπ(v) = v = 0.
*It is injective near Γ.* Otherwise there are p_n ≠ q_n with Ψ₀(p_n) = Ψ₀(q_n) and dist(p_n, Γ), dist(q_n, Γ) → 0;
for a subsequence p_n → p and q_n → q in Γ, and Ψ₀(p) = Ψ₀(q) gives p = q (Ψ₀(p) = (p, 0, 0) on Γ), contradicting
injectivity near p (inverse function theorem). So Ψ₀ is a diffeomorphism from a neighbourhood of Γ onto an open set
containing Γ × {0}, hence, Γ being compact, containing Γ × [−δ₁, δ₁]² for some δ₁ > 0. Put
O₂ := Ψ₀⁻¹(Γ × (−δ₁, δ₁)²).

In the coordinates (y, a, b) := Ψ₀ on O₂, by (ii),

    V₀ = Y₀(y, a, b) − ν_u(y, a, b) a ∂_a + ν_s(y, a, b) b ∂_b,    (15.35)

with Y₀ tangent to Γ (the y-component) and Y₀(·, 0, 0) = V₀|_Γ, and Ṽ = (Ỹ, Ã, B̃) with C^k-norms bounded by Cϵρ(t).
Fix a finite atlas of Γ, charts κ_i : U_i → ℝ^m, compact sets 𝒬_i ⊂ U_i whose interiors cover Γ and a Lebesgue number
d_L > 0 of the cover of Γ by these interiors (every ball of radius d_L in Γ lies in some 𝒬_i), and let C_at ≥ 1 bound
the factor by which the norm of a linear map between tangent spaces of Γ × ℝ² can change when its domain and its
codomain are read in two of the charts. For functions on Γ × I, I an interval, ‖D^j f‖_∞ is the supremum over i and
over 𝒬_i × I of the j-th derivatives in the chart κ_i × id.

#### 15.15.2 Time-T maps

Let Φ⁰_τ be the time-τ map of V₀ and, for t ≥ T₀, let Φ_(t,τ) be the spatial part of the time-τ map of V from the
slice {t} (τ of either sign). By (15.35), along an integral curve of V₀ in O₂,
a(τ) = a(0)exp(−∫₀^τ ν_u) and b(τ) = b(0)exp(∫₀^τ ν_s); so for τ ≥ 0

    Φ⁰_τ(y, a, b) = (f_τ(y, a, b), a m^u_τ(y, a, b), b m^s_τ(y, a, b)),     m^u_τ ≤ e^(−ντ),     m^s_τ ≥ e^(ντ),
    (15.36)

with m^(u/s)_τ ∈ [e^(−C_ντ), e^(C_ντ)], C_ν := sup_O(ν_u + ν_s), as long as the curve stays in O₂; and similarly for
τ ≤ 0 with the roles of a and b exchanged.

Fix T ≥ 1, to be chosen below, and then δ ∈ (0, ¼δ₁] with e^(2C_νT)δ ≤ ¼δ₁, and put B := Γ × [−δ, δ]². For ϵ₀ small
(depending on T and δ), Φ_(t,τ) is defined on B for |τ| ≤ 2T with t + τ ≥ T₀, with values in
Γ × (−½δ₁, ½δ₁)², and:

(T1) {|a| ≤ δ} is forward invariant and {|b| ≤ δ} backward invariant for V within O₂: (d/dτ)|a| ≤ −ν|a| + |Ã| < 0
at |a| = δ when Cϵ₀ < νδ, and likewise for b backward.

(T2) ‖Φ_(t,τ) − Φ⁰_τ‖_(C^k) ≤ C_Tϵρ(t) on B, derivatives in (t, τ, y, a, b) (for ∂_τ:
∂_τ(Φ_(t,τ) − Φ⁰_τ) = V₀(Φ_(t,τ)) − V₀(Φ⁰_τ) + Ṽ, which is O(ϵρ)), and ‖Φ_(t,τ)‖_(C^k) ≤ C_T. This is Grönwall's
inequality for the equation and its variational equations up to order k, whose inhomogeneous terms are Ṽ and its
derivatives at the times between t and t + τ. By (15.33) these are at most ϵρ(s) on each window [s, s + 1]
with s ≥ min(t, t + τ) ≥ T₀ ≥ 1, and ρ(s) ≤ ρ(min(t, t + τ)) ≤ (1 + 2T)^ℓρ(t), because t/(t + τ) ≤ 1 + 2T when τ < 0
and t + τ ≥ 1; the factor (1 + 2T)^ℓ and the number 4T + 1 of windows go into C_T.

(T3) (*The tangential rate.*) With ε := ν/(2k), |Df_τ(y, 0, 0)|_(T_yΓ)| ≤ C_ε e^(ε|τ|) by (iii), as f_τ(·, 0, 0) is the
flow of V₀|_Γ.

(T4) (*The cross terms.*) |∂_a f_τ(y, 0, 0)| ≤ C_*C_ε e^(ετ) for τ ≥ 0, and |∂_b f_τ(y, 0, 0)| ≤ C_*C_ε e^(ε|τ|) for
τ ≤ 0, with C_* := ν⁻¹ sup|∂_(a,b)Y₀|. Indeed, linearising (15.35) at (y, 0, 0) in the direction ∂_a gives
δb ≡ 0, δa(σ) = m^u_σ(y, 0, 0) ≤ e^(−νσ) and δy′ = D_yY₀ δy + ∂_aY₀ δa, so δy(τ) = ∫₀^τ J(τ, σ)∂_aY₀ δa(σ) dσ with
J(τ, σ) = De^((τ−σ)V₀)|_(TΓ) at f_σ(y, 0, 0), bounded by C_ε e^(ε(τ−σ)); hence |δy(τ)| ≤ C_ε sup|∂_aY₀| ∫₀^τ
e^(ε(τ−σ)−νσ) dσ ≤ C_*C_ε e^(ετ). Backward, b contracts and the same estimate applies.

(T5) On B, every first derivative of Φ⁰_τ differs from its value at (y, 0, 0) by at most C_Tδ; and ∂_y(am^u_τ),
∂_b(am^u_τ), ∂_y(bm^s_τ) and ∂_a(bm^s_τ) are O(C_Tδ) on B, carrying the factor a or b.

Let Λ_τ := C_at(C_* + 2)C_ε e^(ε|τ|). By (T3)–(T5) and (T2), for 0 ≤ τ ≤ 2T the block D_((y,a))(Φ_y, Φ_a) of DΦ_(t,τ)
has norm at most Λ_τ + C_T(δ + ϵ₀) in the chart norms (|(v, s)| := |v| + |s|), and for −2T ≤ τ ≤ 0 the block
D_((y,b))(Φ_y, Φ_b) likewise. We use C_T for constants depending on T and the data, and fix T so large that

    e^(−νT)(2Λ_T)^k(1 + 2T)^ℓ ≤ ¼,    (15.37)

which is possible as kε = ν/2 < ν; then δ as above, small also against C_T where stated; and finally ϵ₀ small
against δ and C_T.

#### 15.15.3 One step of the graph transform

For t ≥ T₀ and τ ∈ [0, 2T] let Φ := Φ_(t,τ), and B_a := Γ × [−δ, δ]_a. For β : B_a → ℝ with |β| ≤ ¼δ and
Lip β ≤ θ₀ := δ (in the chart norms) define 𝒮_Φβ : B_a → ℝ by

    Φ_b(y, a, 𝒮_Φβ(y, a)) = β(Φ_y(y, a, 𝒮_Φβ(y, a)), Φ_a(y, a, 𝒮_Φβ(y, a))):    (15.38)

graph(𝒮_Φβ) is the set of points of B that Φ maps into graph(β).

**Lemma 15.51** (One step.) For (y, a) ∈ B_a, (15.38) has exactly one solution b ∈ [−δ, δ], and:

(G1) |𝒮_Φβ| ≤ e^(−ντ)(|β|_∞ + C_Tϵρ(t));

(G2) |𝒮_Φβ − 𝒮_Φβ̃|_∞ ≤ e^(−ντ)(1 − 3C_Tδ)⁻¹|β − β̃|_∞ for two such β, β̃;

(G3) if β ∈ C^k and ‖D^jβ‖_∞ ≤ M_jϵρ(t) for 0 ≤ j ≤ k (the case j = 0 included), then 𝒮_Φβ ∈ C^k and, for
1 ≤ i ≤ k,

    ‖D^i𝒮_Φβ‖_∞ ≤ e^(−ντ)(1 − 3C_Tδ)⁻¹(2Λ_τ)^i‖D^iβ‖_∞ + C(T, M₀, …, M_(i−1)) ϵρ(t).    (15.39)

*Proof.* Fix (y, a) and put h(b) := Φ_b(y, a, b) − β(Φ_y, Φ_a)(y, a, b). By (T1) the point (Φ_y, Φ_a) lies in B_a, so
h is defined on [−δ, δ]. By (15.36), (T2) and (T5),
∂_bΦ_b = m^s_τ + b ∂_bm^s_τ + O(C_Tϵρ) ≥ e^(ντ)(1 − C_Tδ) − C_Tϵ₀, and |∂_b(Φ_y, Φ_a)| ≤ C_T with
Lip β ≤ θ₀ = δ, so h′(b) ≥ e^(ντ)(1 − C_Tδ) − C_Tϵ₀ − C_Tδ ≥ e^(ντ)(1 − 3C_Tδ) > 0, as e^(ντ) ≥ 1 and ϵ₀ ≤ δ. At
b = ±δ, ±Φ_b ≥ δm^s_τ(1 − C_Tδ) − C_Tϵρ ≥ ¾δ > |β|, so h changes sign: it has a unique zero. (G1): at the zero,
b m^s_τ(y, a, b) = β(⋯) − (Φ_b − Φ⁰_(τ,b)), and m^s_τ ≥ e^(ντ). (G2): with b and b̃ the two zeros,
h(b̃) = h(b̃) − h̃(b̃) = −(β − β̃)(⋯), so |b − b̃| ≤ |β − β̃|_∞/inf h′. (G3): 𝒮_Φβ ∈ C^k by the implicit function
theorem, H(w, b) := Φ_b(w, b) − β((Φ_y, Φ_a)(w, b)), w = (y, a), being C^k with ∂_bH ≥ e^(ντ)(1 − 3C_Tδ). Fix
p ∈ 𝒬_i × [−δ, δ]; as (Φ_y, Φ_a) has Lipschitz constant at most 2Λ_τ, it maps the ball of radius d_L/(2Λ_(2T)) about p
into a ball of radius d_L, whose projection to Γ lies in some 𝒬_l, hence, by (T1), into 𝒬_l × [−δ, δ], where the
derivatives of β in the chart κ_l × id are bounded by the norms ‖D^jβ‖_∞. Differentiate H(w, 𝒮_Φβ(w)) = 0 i times at
p in the charts i and l. For i = 1 the result is ∂_bH · D𝒮_Φβ = Dβ · D_w(Φ_y, Φ_a) − D_wΦ_b, and for i ≥ 2 it is

    ∂_bH · D^i𝒮_Φβ = D^iβ[(D_w(Φ_y, Φ_a) + ∂_b(Φ_y, Φ_a)D𝒮_Φβ)^(⊗i)] + R_i,

the term Dβ · ∂_b(Φ_y, Φ_a)D^i𝒮_Φβ being part of ∂_bH · D^i𝒮_Φβ. Here R_i (and −D_wΦ_b at i = 1) is a sum of products
of derivatives of order ≤ i of β and of order ≤ i − 1 of 𝒮_Φβ, and of derivatives of order ≤ i of Φ (bounded by
C_T). Every product in R_i contains a factor O(ϵρ(t)): either D^jβ with j ≥ 1; or D^j𝒮_Φβ with 1 ≤ j ≤ i − 1, bounded
inductively; or a pure w-derivative of Φ_b, which is b D^j_w m^s_τ + D^j_w(Φ_b − Φ⁰_(τ,b)) at b = 𝒮_Φβ = O(ϵρ) by
(G1) and (T2). In the leading term, |D_w(Φ_y, Φ_a)| ≤ Λ_τ + C_T(δ + ϵ₀)
and |∂_b(Φ_y, Φ_a)D𝒮_Φβ| ≤ C_T · Cϵ₀, together at most 2Λ_τ. Dividing by ∂_bH gives (15.39). ∎

*The backward step.* For τ ∈ [0, 2T] and t ≥ T₀ + τ let Φ⁻ := Φ_(t,−τ), the map back to the slice t − τ, and
B_b := Γ × [−δ, δ]_b. For α : B_b → ℝ with |α| ≤ ¼δ and Lip α ≤ θ₀, define 𝒰_(Φ⁻)α by
Φ⁻_a(y, 𝒰α(y, b), b) = α(Φ⁻_y, Φ⁻_b)(y, 𝒰α(y, b), b): graph(𝒰α) is the set of points of B that the backward map sends
into graph(α), which is the image of graph(α) under the forward map, within B. Lemma 15.51 holds verbatim for
𝒰, with (a, b) exchanged, Φ replaced by Φ⁻, and with ρ(t) as it stands in (G1) and (15.39), the factor
(1 + 2T)^ℓ for the backward window being part of C_T in (T2): backward, a is multiplied by (m^u)⁻¹ ≥ e^(ντ), {|b| ≤ δ}
is invariant by (T1), and the block D_((y,b))(Φ⁻_y, Φ⁻_b) is bounded by Λ_τ + C_T(δ + ϵ₀) by (T3)–(T5).

#### 15.15.4 The stable hypersurface

Let t_j := T₀ + jT, j ≥ 0, and 𝒮_j := 𝒮_(Φ_(t_j,T)). Choose M₀ := 2C_T and then, inductively,
M_i ≥ 2C(T, M₀, …, M_(i−1)), 1 ≤ i ≤ k, and let ϵ₀ be so small that M₀ϵ₀ ≤ ¼δ and M₁ϵ₀ ≤ θ₀. Let 𝔅 be the set of
sequences β = (β_j)_(j≥0) of C^k functions on B_a with ‖D^iβ_j‖_∞ ≤ M_iϵρ(t_j) for 0 ≤ i ≤ k, and put
(ℱβ)_j := 𝒮_jβ_(j+1).

*ℱ maps 𝔅 into itself.* As ρ(t_(j+1)) ≤ ρ(t_j), (G1)
gives |𝒮_jβ_(j+1)| ≤ e^(−νT)(M₀ + C_T)ϵρ(t_j) ≤ M₀ϵρ(t_j), and (15.39) with (15.37) gives
‖D^i𝒮_jβ_(j+1)‖_∞ ≤ ½M_iϵρ(t_j) + C(T, M₀, …, M_(i−1))ϵρ(t_j) ≤ M_iϵρ(t_j).

*ℱ is a contraction* for d(β, β̃) := sup_j ρ(t_j)⁻¹|β_j − β̃_j|_∞, by (G2) and ρ(t_j)⁻¹ ≤ ρ(t_(j+1))⁻¹, with factor
e^(−νT)(1 − 3C_Tδ)⁻¹ ≤ ½.

So β^(n) := ℱ^n(0) ∈ 𝔅 is Cauchy for d, and β^(n)_j → β_j uniformly. Bounded in C^k on the compact set B_a, the
D^(k−1)β^(n)_j are equicontinuous, so (Arzelà–Ascoli) every subsequence has a further subsequence converging in C^(k−1),
necessarily to β_j: β^(n)_j → β_j in C^(k−1), ‖D^iβ_j‖_∞ ≤ M_iϵρ(t_j) for i ≤ k − 1, and D^(k−1)β_j is Lipschitz with
constant ≤ CM_kϵρ(t_j). By (G2), ℱ is continuous for d on sequences with |β_j| ≤ ¼δ and Lip β_j ≤ θ₀, so ℱβ = β:
β_j = 𝒮_jβ_(j+1) for all j.

*All times.* For t ∈ [t_j, t_(j+1)] put β(t, ·) := 𝒮_(Φ_(t,t_(j+1)−t))β_(j+1); at t = t_(j+1) (Φ = id) this is
β_(j+1), and at t = t_j it is 𝒮_jβ_(j+1) = β_j. For t ∈ [t_(j−1), t_j], by the cocycle property
Φ_(t,t_(j+1)−t) = Φ_(t_j,T) ∘ Φ_(t,t_j−t) and uniqueness in Lemma 15.51 (applied with τ = t_(j+1) − t ≤ 2T, and
with (T1)), 𝒮_(Φ_(t,t_j−t))β_j = 𝒮_(Φ_(t,t_(j+1)−t))β_(j+1): a point is mapped into graph(β_j) at time t_j if and only if
it is mapped into graph(β_(j+1)) at time t_(j+1). So on [t_(j−1), t_(j+1)], β(t, ·) is given by the single equation

    H(t, w, b) := Φ_(t,t_(j+1)−t,b)(w, b) − β_(j+1)(Φ_(t,t_(j+1)−t,ya)(w, b)) = 0,

with H ∈ C^(k−1) in (t, w, b) (the flow map from time t to t_(j+1) is C^k in (t, w, b), and β_(j+1) ∈ C^(k−1)) and
∂_bH ≥ ½. By the implicit function theorem, β ∈ C^(k−1)([t_(j−1), t_(j+1)] × B_a), and differentiating the equation as
in (G3) bounds its derivatives of order ≤ k − 1 by Cϵρ(t_(j−1)) ≤ C(1 + 2T)^ℓϵρ(t). Hence
β ∈ C^(k−1)([T₀, ∞) × B_a) with |∂^αβ| ≤ Cϵρ(t) for |α| ≤ k − 1.

*Tangency.* Let W^s := {(t, y, a, b) : b = β(t, y, a)} ⊂ [T₀, ∞) × B, a C^(k−1) hypersurface. If (t, x) ∈ W^s with
t ∈ [t_(j−1), t_(j+1)), then for small σ > 0, Φ_(t+σ,t_(j+1)−t−σ)(Φ_(t,σ)(x)) = Φ_(t,t_(j+1)−t)(x) ∈ graph(β_(j+1)),
and Φ_(t,σ)(x) ∈ B by (T1) and |b| ≤ Cϵ₀ < δ along W^s; so Φ_(t,σ)(x) ∈ W^s(t + σ), and the integral curve of V through
(t, x) stays in W^s for small forward times. Hence V is tangent to W^s.

#### 15.15.5 The unstable hypersurface

Put α₀ := 0 on B_b and α_(j+1) := 𝒰_(Φ_(t_(j+1),−T))α_j: graph(α_(j+1)) is the image of graph(α_j) under Φ_(t_j,T),
within B. With M′₀ := 2C_T(1 + 2T)^ℓ and M′_i ≥ 2C(T, M′₀, …, M′_(i−1))(1 + 2T)^ℓ, and ϵ₀ so small that also
M′₀ϵ₀ ≤ ¼δ and M′₁ϵ₀ ≤ θ₀, so that Lemma 15.51 applies to each α_j, induction on j gives
‖D^iα_j‖_∞ ≤ M′_iϵρ(t_j) for i ≤ k: by the backward form of (G1) and (15.39), with
ρ(t_j) ≤ (1 + T)^ℓρ(t_(j+1)) and (15.37),

    ‖D^iα_(j+1)‖_∞ ≤ e^(−νT)(2Λ_T)^i(1 − 3C_Tδ)⁻¹M′_iϵρ(t_j) + Cϵρ(t_j) ≤ ½M′_iϵρ(t_(j+1)) + ½M′_iϵρ(t_(j+1)).

No limit is taken, and α_j ∈ C^k. For t ∈ [t_j, t_(j+1)] put α(t, ·) := 𝒰_(Φ_(t,−(t−t_j)))α_j, whose graph is the
image of graph(α_j) under Φ_(t_j,t−t_j); on [t_j, t_(j+2)] the same formula with α_j holds by the cocycle property, so
α ∈ C^k([T₀, ∞) × B_b) by the implicit function theorem (now with C^k data), with |∂^αα| ≤ Cϵρ(t) for |α| ≤ k. The
set W^u := {a = α(t, y, b)} is a union of forward orbit segments of V starting on {t = T₀, a = 0}, within B; so V is
tangent to it, as in Section 15.15.4.

#### 15.15.6 The defining functions

Let O′ := Ψ₀⁻¹(Γ × (−δ, δ)²) and, for (t, x) ∈ [T₀, ∞) × O′,

    ψ_s(t, x) := −β(t, π(x), φ_u(x)),        ψ_u(t, x) := −α(t, π(x), φ_s(x)).

Then {φ_s + ψ_s = 0} = W^s and {φ_u + ψ_u = 0} = W^u in [T₀, ∞) × O′, and the bounds follow by the chain rule, π and
φ_(u/s) being smooth. W^u ∩ {t = T₀} = {φ_u = 0} as α(T₀, ·) = α₀ = 0. The constants depend only on the quantities
listed in Theorem 15.49. ∎

### 15.16 The stable and unstable hypersurfaces of perturbed metrics

This section applies Theorem 15.49 to the null-bicharacteristic flow of a metric g = g₀ + h that decays in time to
the stationary model g₀ of Section 15.11: the perturbed characteristic set near the trapped set is written as a graph
over the stationary one, the flow is pulled back to it, and the theorem gives the hypersurfaces.

#### 15.16.1 The stationary data

Let Γ := Γ₁ ⊂ Σ^♭₁ ⊂ T*X̃° be the trapped set of (H7) at z₀ = 1, with O, φ_u, φ_s, ν_u, ν_s as there, let
q₁ = 2g₀⁻¹(−dt_* + ζ, dt_*) (Lemma 12.1 and (K3)), and let 𝖵 := q₁⁻¹H_(G₁) on Σ^♭₁ near Γ, where
G₁(x, ζ) := G₀(−dt_* + ζ) and G₀(ν) = g₀⁻¹(ν, ν). By (Γ.3), dG₁ ≠ 0 near Γ, so Y := Σ^♭₁ ∩ O₀, for a small
neighbourhood O₀ of Γ, is a smooth hypersurface of T*X̃°; q₁ ≥ 2β_Γ > 0 on Γ by (Γ.4), hence q₁ ≥ β_Γ on O₀. Wherever
injectivity on (−c, c) × Y is used below, Y is replaced by a relatively compact open neighbourhood of Γ in it.

**Lemma 15.52** Y, V₀ := 𝖵, Γ and the restrictions to Y of φ_u, φ_s and of ν_u/q₁, ν_s/q₁ satisfy
(i)–(iii) of Theorem 15.49, after shrinking O₀, with ν := ν_min/(4 sup_(O₀) q₁); and the constants are uniform in
the parameter b of (H5) and (K4).

*Proof.* (ii): (Γ.2) gives H_(G₁)φ_u = −ν_uφ_u and H_(G₁)φ_s = ν_sφ_s on Σ^♭₁ ∩ O, so 𝖵φ_u = −(ν_u/q₁)φ_u and
𝖵φ_s = (ν_s/q₁)φ_s; and ν_(u/s) ≥ ½ν_min near Γ by continuity. (i): Γ = Γ_u ∩ Γ_s within O by (Γ.1). Suppose that at
p ∈ Γ, a dφ_u + b dφ_s vanishes on T_pY for some (a, b) ≠ 0; as T_pY = ker dG₁, a dφ_u + b dφ_s = c dG₁ at p. The
Poisson bracket with φ_s gives a{φ_u, φ_s} = c{G₁, φ_s} = c H_(G₁)φ_s = c ν_sφ_s = 0 at p, so a = 0 by (Γ.3); with φ_u,
likewise b = 0. (iii): Γ is invariant, 𝖵 being tangent to Γ_u and Γ_s (Γ.1); the bound is the tangential part of (K3)
for 𝖵. Uniformity: (H5), extended to (H6)–(H8) in Section 12.1.5, and (K4) give continuity in b of Γ, φ_(u/s),
ν_(u/s) and q₁ into C^∞, and uniform ν_min, β_Γ and C_ε; the choices of Section 15.15.1 can then be made uniformly for
b near any b₀, and ℬ is compact. ∎

#### 15.16.2 The slice and the projected flow

Let T_♭ := 2/C′, with C′ of Lemma 15.35, and let [r_(Γ,−), r_(Γ,+)] ⊂ (r₂, ρ₁⁻¹) contain the projection of Γ. By
Lemma 15.35 (b), Ω_* ⊃ {t_* ≥ 1/C′}, a neighbourhood of {t_* ≥ T_♭} on which g is defined with its d₀
derivatives, so what is stated below for t_* > T_♭ holds on the closed set where t_* ≥ T_♭, as Theorem 15.49
requires. Over D := {t_* > T_♭, r_(Γ,−) < r < r_(Γ,+)}, near (K⁺)°, the e3b-structure is spanned by ∂_(t_*), ∂_x
(Section 14.2.2 and Section 15.2.1), and ᵉ³ᵇT*_D M = T*D with covectors −σ dt_* + ζ. On {σ > 0} use the slice
coordinates (t_*, x, z), z := ζ/σ, which identify {σ > 0} ∩ ᵉ³ᵇS*_D M with (T_♭, ∞) × T*{r_(Γ,−) < r < r_(Γ,+)}; at
ρ_K = t_*⁻¹ = 0 this is the map Φ₁ of Definition 15.5. Let g = g₀ + h with h ∈ 𝒢̃^(d₀,(0,0,ℓ_K))_(e3b), d₀ ≥ 3,
ℓ_K > 0 and ‖h‖ ≤ ϵ. Over D, x_I and ρ₊ are bounded above and below and ρ_K ∼ t_*⁻¹, so the components of
g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹ in the frame ∂_(t_*), ∂_x have derivatives of order ≤ d₀ along ∂_(t_*), ∂_x bounded by Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K)
(Neumann series, Lemma 14.27). Put

    p₁(t_*, x, z) := G(t_*, x; −dt_* + z),        g̃ := p₁ − G₁ = (g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹)(−dt_* + z, −dt_* + z),    (15.40)

so g̃ is quadratic in z, with |∂^αg̃| ≤ Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K), |α| ≤ d₀, on compact z-sets.

**Lemma 15.53** (The projected field.) For p := G (homogeneous of degree 2 on T*D), σ⁻¹H_p descends to
{σ > 0} ∩ ᵉ³ᵇS*_D M, and in the slice coordinates

    Ŵ := σ⁻¹H_p = (z·∂_zp₁ − 2p₁)∂_(t_*) + ∂_zp₁·∂_x − ∂_xp₁·∂_z − (∂_(t_*)p₁) z·∂_z.    (15.41)

Ŵ is tangent to {p₁ = 0}, and on {p₁ = 0} it is a positive multiple of the field 𝖧_G of (15.29).

*Proof.* With τ := −σ, p = τ²p₁(t_*, x, −ζ/τ), so ∂_τp = σ(z·∂_zp₁ − 2p₁), ∂_ζp = σ∂_zp₁, ∂_(t_*)p = σ²∂_(t_*)p₁ and
∂_xp = σ²∂_xp₁; and for f = f(t_*, x, z), ∂_τf = σ⁻¹z·∂_zf and ∂_ζf = σ⁻¹∂_zf. Inserting these into
H_p = ∂_τp ∂_(t_*) + ∂_ζp·∂_x − ∂_(t_*)p ∂_τ − ∂_xp·∂_ζ gives (15.41). Next, Ŵp₁ = −2p₁∂_(t_*)p₁, which
vanishes on {p₁ = 0}. On the characteristic set, 𝖧_G = ρ_∞H_(G_(e3b)) = ρ_∞fH_G with f = x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² > 0, so
𝖧_G = ρ_∞fσŴ. ∎

For g = g₀, (15.41) on {G₁ = 0} is q₁∂_(t_*) + H_(G₁), as z·∂_zG₁ = q₁ there (Lemma 15.13 (d)): the
stationary field of Section 15.2.

#### 15.16.3 Graphing the perturbed characteristic set

Let N be a smooth vector field on a neighbourhood O_N of Γ in T*X̃° with NG₁ = 1 there (N := ∇G₁/|∇G₁|² for a
Riemannian metric, as dG₁ ≠ 0). After shrinking, Ψ̂₀(f, w) := e^(fN)(w) is a diffeomorphism from (−c, c) × Y onto a
neighbourhood of Y, and G₁(e^(fN)w) = f, as (d/df)G₁(e^(fN)w) = (NG₁)(e^(fN)w) = 1. Write w(x, z) and f(x, z) for the
inverse.

**Lemma 15.54** (The graph.) For ϵ small there is F ∈ C^(d₀)((T_♭, ∞) × Y) with |∂^αF| ≤ Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K)
for |α| ≤ d₀ and {p₁(t_*, ·) = 0} ∩ Ψ̂₀((−c, c) × Y) = {e^(F(t_*,w)N)w : w ∈ Y}. The map
Ψ̂(t_*, f, w) := (t_*, e^((f+F(t_*,w))N)w) is a C^(d₀) diffeomorphism onto a neighbourhood of the perturbed
characteristic set near Γ, with ‖Ψ̂ − Ψ̂₀‖_(C^(d₀)) ≤ Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K) (where Ψ̂₀(t_*, f, w) := (t_*, e^(fN)w)), and it maps
{f = 0} onto the perturbed characteristic set.

*Proof.* At e^(fN)w, p₁ = f + g̃(t_*, e^(fN)w). The map f ↦ −g̃(t_*, e^(fN)w) sends [−c/2, c/2] into itself and has
Lipschitz constant sup|Ng̃| ≤ Cϵ < 1, so it has a unique fixed point F(t_*, w), with |F| ≤ Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K). Since
∂_f(f + g̃(t_*, e^(fN)w)) = 1 + Ng̃ ≥ ½, F ∈ C^(d₀) by the implicit function theorem, and each derivative of order ≤ d₀
of the identity F + g̃(t_*, e^(FN)w) = 0 expresses ∂^αF through derivatives of g̃, each O(ϵt_*^(−ℓ_K)), and lower
derivatives of F. Ψ̂ is then C^(d₀)-close to Ψ̂₀, hence a diffeomorphism near f = 0. ∎

Near Γ, Ŵt_* = z·∂_zp₁ − 2p₁, which is ≥ ½β_Γ near Γ for ϵ small: at ϵ = 0 it is exactly q₁, as
z·∂_zG₁ = 2g₀⁻¹(−dt_* + z, z) = 2G₁ + q₁. Put V^h := Ŵ/(Ŵt_*), a C^(d₀−1) vector field near (T_♭, ∞) × Γ with
V^ht_* = 1, tangent to {p₁ = 0} (Lemma 15.53), and V⁰ := Ŵ₀/(Ŵ₀t_*) = ∂_(t_*) + H_(G₁)/q₁ for g₀ (where
∂_(t_*)G₁ = 0). By (15.40) and (15.41), V^h − V⁰ has coefficients with derivatives of order ≤ d₀ − 1
bounded by Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K). Let V := Ψ̂^*V^h restricted to {f = 0} = (T_♭, ∞) × Y, which is tangent to it since V^h is
tangent to the characteristic set; Vt_* = 1, as Ψ̂ preserves t_*. As Ψ̂₀^*V⁰ restricted to {f = 0} is
∂_(t_*) + q₁⁻¹H_(G₁) = ∂_(t_*) + 𝖵, and Ψ̂ − Ψ̂₀ and V^h − V⁰ are O(ϵt_*^(−ℓ_K)) in C^(d₀), resp. C^(d₀−1),

    V = ∂_(t_*) + 𝖵 + Ṽ,     Ṽ(t_*, ·) tangent to Y,     |∂^αṼ| ≤ Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K),  |α| ≤ d₀ − 1.    (15.42)

#### 15.16.4 The statement

**Proposition 15.55** (The stable and unstable hypersurfaces; [Hin26c, Proposition 6.3] at n = 4.) Let
d₀ ≥ 3, ℓ_K > 0 and g = g₀ + h with h ∈ 𝒢̃^(d₀,(0,0,ℓ_K))_(e3b) of sufficiently small norm ϵ. With T_♭ of
Section 15.16.2, let ∂Γ₀ := {t_* > T_♭} × Γ in the slice coordinates (the stationary extension of ∂Γ_(K⁺),
Definition 15.12), and U a small neighbourhood of it in ᵉ³ᵇS*_D M. There are functions φ₀^(u/s) ∈ C^∞(U),
independent of t_*, with φ₀^(u/s) = φ_(u/s)(x, z) on the stationary characteristic set, and φ̃^u ∈ C^(d₀−1)(U),
φ̃^s ∈ C^(d₀−2)(U), with

    |∂^αφ̃^u| ≤ Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K)  (|α| ≤ d₀ − 1),        |∂^αφ̃^s| ≤ Cϵt_*^(−ℓ_K)  (|α| ≤ d₀ − 2),

derivatives along ∂_(t_*), ∂_x and the fibres, such that, with φ^(u/s) := φ₀^(u/s) + φ̃^(u/s), the field 𝖧_G is tangent
to Γ^(u/s) := ∂Σ⁺ ∩ U ∩ (φ^(u/s))⁻¹(0). There is ϵ₂ > 0 such that, for ϵ ≤ ϵ₂, sup t_*^(ℓ_K)|∂^αφ̃^(u/s)| ≤ 1 over the
stated ranges of α. The same holds, with uniform constants, for the stationary models of parameters b near b₀ ((K4)).

*Proof.* By Lemma 15.52 and (15.42), Theorem 15.49 applies on Y with V₀ = 𝖵, k := d₀ − 1 ≥ 2,
ℓ := ℓ_K and T₀ := T_♭ (the metric is defined on Ω_* by (15.28), and Ω_* ⊃ {t_* ≥ T_♭} because t^♭_* ≥ C′t_*
by Lemma 15.35 (b)). It gives ψ_u ∈ C^(d₀−1) and ψ_s ∈ C^(d₀−2) on (T_♭, ∞) × O′ with V tangent to
W^(u/s) = {φ_(u/s) + ψ_(u/s) = 0}. For (t_*, x, z) in U, write (x, z) = e^(fN)w (w = w(x, z) ∈ Y) and put

    φ₀^(u/s)(x, z) := φ_(u/s)(w(x, z)),        φ̃^(u/s)(t_*, x, z) := ψ_(u/s)(t_*, w(x, z)),

extended homogeneously of degree 0 in (σ, ζ). On the perturbed characteristic set, (x, z) = e^(F(t_*,w)N)w
(Lemma 15.54) and w(x, z) = w, so φ^(u/s)(t_*, x, z) = (φ_(u/s) + ψ_(u/s))(t_*, w), and
Γ^(u/s) = Ψ̂({f = 0} ∩ W^(u/s)). Since V is tangent to W^(u/s), V^h = Ψ̂_*V is tangent to Ψ̂(W^(u/s)); and Ŵ and 𝖧_G
are positive multiples of V^h on the characteristic set (Lemma 15.53 and Ŵt_* > 0). The bounds follow by the
chain rule, w(x, z) being smooth and t_*-independent. Uniformity follows from Lemma 15.52 and the explicit
dependence of the constants in Theorem 15.49. ∎

**Remark 15.56** (a) φ₀^(u/s) agrees with φ_(u/s) of (H7) on the stationary characteristic
set; off it the two may differ, which is immaterial for Γ^(u/s). (b) The intersections of Γ^(u/s) with the stationary
face {t_* = ∞} are the sets Γ^(u/s)_(K⁺) of Definition 15.12 (within U), as φ̃^(u/s) → 0; for U small, they coincide
with ∂Γ̄^(u/s)_(K⁺) within U, by Lemma 15.13 (b). (c) W^u at t_* = T_♭ is the stationary unstable hypersurface;
[Hin26c, p. 113] makes the same choice at its slice {ρ_K = 1} ("Γ^u = ⋃_(s≥0) e^(sV)(Γ^u₀ ∩ {ρ_K = 1})"). The slice is
immaterial in the sequel: Chapter 16 uses Γ^(u/s) only where ρ_K is small.

### 15.17 Remarks on [Hin26c] and [Hin21]

The following points compare this chapter with the texts it writes out in dimension 4 + 1.

- *The stationary model.* The arguments of [Hin26c, Lemmas 4.1–4.3, 4.7, 4.10–4.18 and Proposition 4.19] from the
  explicit Kerr metric are replaced by the hypotheses (H3), (H4), (H7), (H8) and (K3), from which Section 15.2
  recovers the dynamics over the Kerr face. [Hin26c, Lemma 4.20] serves in [Hin26c] only to prove part (3) of [Hin26c,
  Proposition 4.19] from the Carter flow, and is not needed here, (K3) being assumed for 𝖵 itself. The first row of
  [Hin26c, (4.72)], the curves over M°, is replaced by Proposition 15.19, the form that [Hin26c] states as its
  Proposition 6.1 and uses later ([Hin26c, p. 111]).
- *Rates.* (K1) has r⁻² where Kerr has r⁻¹, and no logarithm enters the hyperboloidal time. Accordingly
  (15.2) has ρ₀²x_I²ρ₊² for ρ₀x_I²ρ₊, H_(G_(3b)) − H_(Ḡ_(3b)) ∈ ρ₊²𝒱_b where [Hin26c] has ρ₊,
  G_(eb) − Ḡ_(eb) ∈ x_I²ρ₊²P^[2], S = 0 in Lemma 15.24, and the remainder of (15.20) carries ρ⁴. Nothing
  uses more than the rates of [Hin26c], except the shortened proofs of Lemma 15.9 (1)–(2).
- *The constants at n = 4.* The 1 of [Hin26c, (5.1a)] is 3/2; the factor 2(1 + S) of [Hin26c, (5.7)] is 3 + 2S; the
  characteristic exponents 2(1 + μ) are 3 + 2μ; the tf-weight α_sf + 3/2 is α_sf + 2; the sf-weights (−3/2, −1/2) of the
  scalar wave operator are (−2, 0). The symmetry of −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c) for the density ρ^(−n−1)dρ forces
  c = (n − 1)/2, and with it Lemma 15.31.
- *Misprints in [Hin26c].* In the proof of [Hin26c, Lemma 4.6 (2)], ρ₊ ∘ γ is strictly decreasing for s > 0 (a critical
  point is a strict local maximum), where the text says "strictly increasing"; the argument is otherwise as in
  Lemma 15.9 (2), which also shows why ρ₊ → 0. In [Hin26c, Lemma 4.6 (4)], the conic extension of {ξ̂_(3b) = 2} is
  {ξ_(3b) = 2σ_(3b)}, printed as ξ_(3b) = −2σ_(3b), and within Σ⁺ it is the characteristic set of 2r∂_(t_*) − r∂_r =
  r(∂_t − ∂_r), printed as r∂_(t_*) − 2r∂_r; the (t, r)-form r(∂_t − ∂_r) given there is the right one. [Hin26c, (4.18)]
  has the factor −2 in place of −4; only the sign is used. The angular coefficient 1 in G⁰_(eb) ((15.13)) comes
  from the angular term g_(𝕊³)/(2x_I²) of ḡ near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ (Section 14.2.3); the term g_(𝕊³)/x_I² printed in
  [Hin26c, (2.27)] would give ½|η_(eb)|², and [Hin26c, (4.67)] agrees with the former. [Hin26c, Definition 5.15] gives
  x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ₊,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) the norm of C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I+2,ℓ₊+2,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b); under the convention of
  [Hin26c, Definition 3.19] (Definition 14.26) the factor x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻² lowers both weights by 2, so the norm is that of
  C^((d₀;k),(2ℓ_I−2,ℓ₊−2,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) (Definition 15.33). On [Hin26c, p. 107], after Definition 5.15, the section
  x_I⁻²ρ₊⁻²(g_(m,a) + h) should read x_I²ρ₊²(g_(m,a) + h) (Remark 15.34 (b)). [Hin26c, Definition 5.11 (1)]
  says "monotonically non-decreasing along the future null-bicharacteristic flow", which contradicts its own condition
  ±H_G𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ^± and [Hin26c, Section 6.2]: the order is non-increasing, high at the radial sets that the future flow
  leaves and low at those it approaches (Definition 15.29 (1)). In [Hin26c, (6.5)], a covector ζ ∈ Σ lies in Σ⁺ if and
  only if g⁻¹(ζ, dt^♭_*) > 0, not ≤ 0, since dt^♭_* is past timelike.
- *Proofs written out.* [Hin26c, Lemma 5.16] takes "a smoothing" of a piecewise function; a smoothing preserves
  timelikeness only if its differential stays in the past cone, and Lemma 15.35 glues by a smooth minimum in log,
  taken only where t_*/r ≤ 2/C since 1 − (t_*/r)^ℓ vanishes at r = t_*, and a smooth maximum in r, whose differentials
  are convex combinations of those of the pieces; the comparison of the pieces at r = Ct_* is the inequality φ′ < 0
  there. The backward statement of [Hin26c, Proposition 6.1] is proved in Proposition 15.42 by the repulsion of
  ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) in x_I backward. [Hin26c, Proposition 6.4] is proved by the construction it cites (Section 15.13.2), with
  item (5) added and the localisation χ_t of [Hin23c] unnecessary in this class; the bound on the characteristic set
  stated as [Hin23c, (C.1)] is replaced by Lemma 15.45.
- *Changes of statement.* Definition 15.26 takes the threshold of trapping admissibility from (Γ.4), for the density of
  Chapter 11, in place of [Hin26c, (5.8)] for |dg|, and realises [Hin26c, (5.9)] as Lemma 12.36;
  Definition 15.28 is the tf-admissibility of Definition 13.15. Proposition 15.42 is stated over {r ≥ r₀}, where the
  perturbation is defined, with "reaches {r = r₀}" for "crosses {r = m}".
- *The persistence of the trapped hypersurfaces.* The proof of [Hin26c, Proposition 6.3] rests on
  [Hin21, Theorem 2.6]. That theorem is stated for a closed manifold, a C^∞ invariant splitting (the relaxation to
  continuous splittings is [Hin21, footnote 8]) and a fixed perturbation, and the uniformity in the perturbation that
  [Hin26c] asserts is a reading of its proof. Theorem 15.49 proves what is needed directly, with explicit
  dependence of the constants, from (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) and the tangential half of (K3), so the continuous splitting of (K3) is
  enough and is not used. [Hin26c] states φ̃^(u/s) ∈ C^(d₀−1,ℓ_K)_cu on all of the cosphere bundle over D; here
  φ̃^u ∈ C^(d₀−1) and φ̃^s ∈ C^(d₀−2), on a neighbourhood U of ∂Γ₀: the stable hypersurface is obtained as a limit and
  loses one derivative. d₀ is a free parameter, taken large wherever Proposition 15.55 is used (Chapter 16), and only
  a neighbourhood of the trapped set enters the trapping estimates. The graphing of the characteristic set on
  [Hin26c, p. 113] is Lemma 15.54, with the projected field computed in Lemma 15.53; the space ℝ⁵ there is
  the five-dimensional characteristic set of Kerr at fibre infinity over (K⁺)°, which at n = 4 is seven-dimensional.

## 16. Global microlocal regularity

This chapter proves the global regularity estimate for wave-type operators on the compactified spacetime: a
distribution supported to the future of an initial hypersurface is controlled in a weighted edge-3b Sobolev space by its
image under the operator, at the cost of one derivative, which the trapped set takes. It is [Hin26c, Section 7] in
dimension 4 + 1. The first half (Section 16.1–Section 16.5) proves the estimate without b-regularity: the radial
point estimates at the horizon, over ∂K⁺ and at ℐ⁺, the estimate at the trapped set with its loss, and their
combination along the null-bicharacteristic flow of Chapter 15. The second half (Section 16.6–Section 16.12) adds k
degrees of b-regularity, by commuting b-vector fields through the operator, and proves the estimate also in a form tame
in k.

*Method.* Every estimate here is a positive commutator estimate. Section 14.12 provides the machinery with coefficients
of finite regularity: one step with a regulariser (Lemma 14.44) and the iteration in the order
(Lemma 14.45). Two additions are made in Section 16.2: a term JL in the commutator inequality, which a cut-off
to the characteristic set produces (Lemma 16.4), and bounds of microlocal norms through symbols
(Lemma 16.7, Lemma 16.8), with which the norms produced by different commutators are compared. With these,
each radial estimate is a calculation of symbols at a radial set of Chapter 15. Weights and fibre inner products enter
through the subprincipal symbol of a conjugated operator (Lemma 16.1), and the thresholds are those of
Section 15.10.3 and (11.5). At ℐ⁺ the subprincipal symbol is calculated in Lemma 16.12, which is [Hin26c,
(7.22)] in dimension 4 + 1: the constant 3 = n − 1 of Lemma 15.37 is exactly the one that makes the leading part of
the operator symmetric for |dt dx|. [Hin26c] quotes its estimate at the trapped set from [Hin21, Theorem 3.9], whose
proof writes out the regularisation of its first step and sketches that of the others. Section 16.4 proves that
estimate in full in the present calculus, from the hypersurfaces of Proposition 15.55: an equation with damping for
the unstable defining function, two quantitative propagation estimates, and their combination, all with one regulariser
and by induction on the order in half steps.

*Notation.* Orders that may vary on phase space are written in sans-serif (𝗌, 𝗍); an order written s, s_0 or s′ is a
constant. For a matrix 𝔞 that is self-adjoint for some fibre inner product, max spec 𝔞 is its largest eigenvalue. N′
is a fixed integer with N′ ≥ −inf 𝗌_0 for every order 𝗌_0 (or s_0) of an a priori term below (N′ = 13 for the operator of
Theorem 29.17 at the orders of Lemma 49.10); every a priori term ‖χu‖_(−N′) below is with respect to it (such
terms are written ‖χu‖_(−N) in Chapter 14), and N_E is the rank of the bundle E = ℂ^(N_E) of Section 15.9.1. ϕ^u, ϕ^s
and ϕ_u, ϕ_s denote the defining functions of hypersurfaces at the trapped set that Chapter 12 and Chapter 15 write
φ^(u/s), φ_(u/s); here φ_ε is the regulariser of Section 16.2. β_0 is the constant of (H3) at the horizon
((11.3), (15.11)); the constant ½ min_Γ |q_(z_0)| > 0 of condition (Γ.4) of (H7) at the trapped set is
β_Γ, as in Chapter 12 and Chapter 15.

### 16.1 The setting and the global estimate

#### 16.1.1 The operators

g_0 is the stationary metric of Section 15.1.1, which satisfies (K1)–(K4) together with the hypotheses (H1)–(H8) of
Section 11.1.3, Section 12.1.2 and Section 12.1.5, and P_0 is a stationary wave-type operator for g_0
(Definition 15.21). The radii r_0 − 2δ_0 < r_0 < r_0 + δ_0 < r_2 < r_h that enter those hypotheses are arbitrary, subject
to the hypotheses: nothing below uses their values, and the radii chosen from them below (r_1, r_1⁺, r^♮) are chosen
again with them. Fix ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½], ℓ_+ ∈ (0, 1] and ℓ_K > 0. P is a weakly admissible wave-type operator relative to P_0
of class ((d_0; 0), (2ℓ_I, ℓ_+, ℓ_K)) (Definition 15.36), and ε_P := ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;0),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))
(Definition 15.39). Only ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½], ℓ_+ > 0, ℓ_K > 0 are used: the conditions [Hin26c, (5.23)] play no part in
microlocal regularity ([Hin26c, p. 115]). The bound ℓ_+ ≤ 1 is no restriction: as ρ_+ is bounded on Ω, ρ_+^(ℓ_+−1) is
bounded with its b-derivatives for ℓ_+ > 1, so a class with ℓ_+ > 1 lies in the class with ℓ_+ = 1, with norm at most
a constant times its own. Of Definition 15.36, only conditions (1) and (2) are used, together with
Definition 15.38 and Definition 15.39; condition (3), the triangular structure of p_1 and p_0, is not assumed anywhere in
this chapter. Indeed p_1 and p_0 enter only through (15.25)–(15.26) and Lemma 15.37, which follows
from (2); through p̄_1; and through fibre inner products built by Jordan scalings at points, continuity and a partition
of unity, as in Lemma 15.30, which need no triangular structure. Below, "weakly admissible" and "of class" are
meant in this sense. The metric g = g_0 + h of P has ‖h‖ ≤ Cε_P (Lemma 15.40). So, for ε_P
small, the time function t_*^♭ of Lemma 15.35 and the domain Ω_* := cl_M{t_*^♭ ≥ 1} (Section 15.11), the global
dynamics of Section 15.12 and the hypersurfaces of Proposition 15.55 are available (the norm of h in
𝒢̃^(d_0,(0,0,ℓ_K))_e3b is at most a constant times ε_P). Over ℐ⁺, t_*^♭ = t_* (Lemma 15.35 (a)). d_0 is taken large
where needed, depending only on the orders.

Put W := x_I² ρ_+² and L := W⁻¹P. By Lemma 15.25 (b) and (15.26), L = L_0 + L_1 + L_2 is of the form of
Section 14.13.1 with m = 2: L_0 is the scalar part of W⁻¹P_0, L_1 the second-order part of W⁻¹P̃, whose coefficients
lie in C^(d_0,(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_e3b, and L_2 is of first order. L_2 contains the first-order part of W⁻¹P_0, the terms
χ_I (p̃_1 (x_I ∂_(x_I) − 2ρ_+ ∂_(ρ_+)) + ½ p_0) of (15.26), whose coefficients need not decay at ℐ⁺, and the
rest of W⁻¹P̃. The principal symbol of L is ℓ := W⁻¹G = G_e3b, real and scalar, and 𝖧 := ρ_∞ H_ℓ is the field 𝖧_G of
(15.29).

Near a set O where another positive weight W′ has W/W′ and W′/W smooth with bounded e3b-derivatives, we use L′ :=
W′⁻¹P = (W/W′) L in place of L. For G microsupported over O, ‖G L′u‖_𝗍 and ‖G Lu‖_𝗍 then differ by lower-order terms
only. We take W′ = 1 near the horizon and the trapped set, over (K⁺)°, where W is smooth and positive; W′ = ρ_+² = r⁻²
near ∂K⁺, where x_I is smooth and positive; and W′ = W near ℐ⁺. The rescaled fields ρ H_(W′⁻¹G) are then those of
Chapter 15: ρ_∞ H_G with ρ_∞ of (H3) near the horizon (Section 15.4), σ⁻¹ H_G near the trapped set
(Section 15.5), −σ_3b⁻¹ H_(G_3b) near ∂K⁺ ((15.7), (15.8)), and σ_eb⁻¹ H_(G_eb) near ℐ⁺
((15.15), (15.16)).

#### 16.1.2 Weights, inner products and the conjugated operator

For weights (α_I, α_+, α_K) put w := x_I^(2α_I) ρ_+^(α_+) ρ_K^(α_K); then H^(𝗌,(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_e3b = w H^𝗌_e3b, with
H^𝗌_e3b based on L²(|dt dx|) (Section 14.4.2). Near ∂K⁺ we use ρ_K = r/t_* and ρ_+ = r⁻¹, near (K⁺)° ρ_K = t_*⁻¹,
and near ℐ⁺ ρ_+ = t_*⁻¹ (Section 15.3.1). A fibre inner product h on ℂ^(N_E) over a set O, smooth with bounded
e3b-derivatives, is written h(v, v′) = ⟨A⁻¹v, A⁻¹v′⟩ with A := 𝖦^(−1/2), 𝖦 the Gram matrix of h. Adjoints and Im_h are
taken for |dt dx| (Section 15.9.1).

**Lemma 16.1** (The conjugated operator.) Let W′ be a weight as in Section 16.1.1 on O, L′ := W′⁻¹P,
ℓ′ := W′⁻¹G, and L″ := A⁻¹w⁻¹L′wA. (a) L″ is of the form of Section 14.13.1 on O, with principal symbol ℓ′ and
coefficient norms bounded by those of L′ times constants depending only on w and A. (b) σ_1(Im L″) = A⁻¹(σ_1(Im_h L′)
− H_ℓ′ log w) A, where Im is taken for the standard inner product. (c) σ_1(Im_h L′) = W′⁻¹ σ_1(Im_h P) − ½ H_ℓ′ log W′.
Hence, for any positive ρ homogeneous of degree −1, with 𝖧′ := ρ H_ℓ′ and 𝔭′ := ρ W′⁻¹ σ_1(Im_h P),

    ρ σ_1(Im L″) = A⁻¹ (𝔭′ − ½ 𝖧′ log W′ − 𝖧′ log w) A.    (16.1)

*Proof.* (a) w⁻¹Vw = V + V(log w) for a vector field V, and for V ∈ 𝒱_e3b ⊂ 𝒱_b, V log w is smooth with bounded
e3b-derivatives, w being a product of powers of boundary defining functions; likewise for A. So the coefficients of L″
are those of L′ multiplied and differentiated as stated, and its second-order part is that of L′. (b) w⁻¹L′w = L′ +
w⁻¹[L′, w], and [L′, w] is of first order with principal symbol −i H_ℓ′ w; so w⁻¹L′w = L′ − iX modulo order 0, with X
of real principal symbol H_ℓ′ log w. As w is real and scalar, (w⁻¹L′w)^(*h) = w L′^(*h) w⁻¹ = L′^(*h) + iX′ modulo
order 0, with σ(X′) = H_ℓ′ log w, since σ([L′^(*h), w⁻¹]) = −i H_ℓ′ w⁻¹ = i w⁻² H_ℓ′ w. Hence σ_1(Im_h(w⁻¹L′w)) =
σ_1(Im_h L′) − H_ℓ′ log w. Next, for any operator M, M^(*h) = 𝖦⁻¹M*𝖦 with 𝖦 = A^(−*) A⁻¹, so A⁻¹ M^(*h) A = A* M*
A^(−*) = (A⁻¹MA)*, and Im(A⁻¹MA) = A⁻¹ (Im_h M) A exactly. (c) Im_h(fP) = f Im_h P − (1/(2i)) [P^(*h), f] for a real
function f, and σ([P^(*h), f]) = −i H_G f, so σ_1(Im_h(fP)) = f σ_1(Im_h P) + ½ H_G f. With f = W′⁻¹, ½ H_G W′⁻¹ =
−½ W′⁻¹ H_G log W′, and W′⁻¹ H_G log W′ = H_ℓ′ log W′ exactly, as H_ℓ′ = W′⁻¹ H_G + G H_(W′⁻¹) and the Hamilton field
of a function of the base annihilates functions of the base. (16.1) follows on multiplying by ρ. ∎

The estimates for L″ on ũ := A⁻¹w⁻¹u in unweighted spaces are estimates for u in the weighted spaces: for B ∈
C_b^∞Ψ^0_e3b, w⁻¹Bw and A⁻¹BA differ from B by operators of order −1 ((S11) of Section 14.3, and
Proposition 14.40), and A⁻¹w⁻¹W′⁻¹Pu = L″ũ.

#### 16.1.3 The radial sets and the standing choices

On ∂Σ⁺ the future field is 𝖧, on ∂Σ⁻ it is −𝖧 (Section 15.10.3). We use the sets of Chapter 15: the horizon radial
set ∂R_(ℋ⁺) (Definition 15.10), the radial sets ∂R_(∂K⁺,in/out) over ∂K⁺ (Definition 15.7), ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+) and
∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) (Definition 15.15), the trapped set ∂Γ_(K⁺) and the stable and unstable sets Γ^(u/s)_(K⁺), ∂Γ̄^(u/s)_(K⁺)
(Definition 15.12), and ∂W_(in/out) over ι⁺ (Lemma 15.8, Lemma 15.9). By Lemma 15.41, the
characteristic set and 𝖧 of P agree with those of P_0 over ∂M, and near it 𝖧_G − 𝖧_(G_0) ∈ ε_P w C^(d_0−1) 𝒱_b with
w = x_I^(2ℓ_I) ρ_+^(ℓ_+) ρ_K^(ℓ_K).

Fix, as in [Hin26c, (7.1)–(7.2)], radii r_0 < r_1 < r_1⁺ < r^♮, with r^♮ = ½(r_0 + r_2) of Lemma 15.35, so that
