At the radial set ∂R_(ℋ⁺) the vector field 𝖧 on the cosphere bundle vanishes, so ρ̃⁻¹𝖧ρ̃ = ρ⁻¹𝖧ρ +
(ρ̃/ρ)⁻¹𝖧(ρ̃/ρ) = ρ⁻¹𝖧ρ = β_0 there ((15.11), as in the proof of Proposition 16.9), ρ̃/ρ being homogeneous of
degree 0. This gives (16.43) on ∂Σ⁺, where ς = 1; on ∂Σ⁻ the quantity (H_G ξ_0)/ξ_0 is odd (H_G ξ_0 even, ξ_0
odd), the future field is −𝖧, whose ρ⁻¹(−𝖧)ρ is β_0, so ρ⁻¹𝖧ρ = −β_0 there, and ς = −1 restores (16.43). The
threshold of Proposition 16.9 for L^(k) is then sup max spec(β_0⁻¹(𝔭 − j_α β_0)) ≤ ϑ_ℋ, in the inner product h^(⊕𝒲_k). ∎

The non-positive sign in (16.43) is the red shift: commuting with ∂_r lowers the threshold, so the minimal
regularity s_0 > ½ + ϑ_ℋ of Proposition 16.9 does not rise with k.

**Proposition 16.27** (The horizon with b-regularity.) Let s > s_0 > ½ + ϑ_ℋ and k ∈ ℕ_0. There are B, E,
G with the properties (1)–(4) of Proposition 16.9 such that for all α_K ∈ ℝ and χ̃ as there

    ‖Bu‖_((s;k),α_K) ≤ C_k (‖GPu‖_((s−1;k),α_K) + ‖Eu‖_((s;k),α_K) + ‖χ̃u‖_((s_0;k),α_K)),    (16.44)

in the strong sense, uniformly for P = P_0 and P of class ((d_0; k), (0, 0, ℓ_K)) near K⁺ with ε_(P,k) small, d_0
depending only on s, s_0; and the tame estimate (16.40) holds, with d depending only on s, s_0 and C_k on P
only through ε_(P,d).

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 7.17] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* Lemma 16.21–Lemma 16.23 with 𝔩 = 0 and Lemma 16.26. ∎

### 16.10 Over ∂K⁺

Near ∂K⁺ use ρ_K := r/t_*, ρ_+ := r⁻¹, ω (Section 15.3.1), W′ = ρ_+² and L := ρ_+⁻²P, as in Proposition 16.10 and
Proposition 16.11. The family is 𝒳_K := (t_* ∂_(t_*), I), and U_0 is a small neighbourhood of ∂R_(∂K⁺,in) or of
∂R_(∂K⁺,out).

**Lemma 16.28** (Commutators over ∂K⁺.) (a) (M) holds with i_0 = 1, w = ρ_K: 𝒱_b near ∂K⁺ is spanned by
𝒱_3b and t_* ∂_(t_*) (Corollary 14.6), and t_* ∂_(t_*) is a commutator field (Lemma 14.5), and ρ_K t_*
∂_(t_*) = r ∂_(t_*) ∈ 𝒱_3b has principal symbol a non-zero multiple of σ_3b, which is elliptic at both radial sets
(σ_3b < 0 there, Definition 15.7). (b) (C) holds on U_0, with Q_11 of class 𝒬^1_1 whose coefficients carry a factor
ρ_K or ρ_K^(ℓ_K), so (16.41) holds with equality at both radial sets, which lie over K⁺.

This is [Hin26c, Lemmas 7.19–7.20] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (b) Write L = Σ_l p_l A_l with A_l ∈ Diff²_3b fixed and independent of t_*, p^♯_l the coefficients of
ρ_+⁻²P_0, independent of t_* in the coordinates (t_*, r, ω), and p̃_l ∈ ρ_+^(ℓ_+) ρ_K^(ℓ_K) C^((d_0;k))_(3b;b), the
coefficients of ρ_+⁻²(P − P_0) (Definition 15.36). t_* ∂_(t_*) commutes with ρ_+ and annihilates p^♯_l.
Lemma 14.5 gives [X_1, A_l] = ρ_K A^♭_l X_1 + ρ_K A^♯_l, as in Lemma 16.26. Let Q_K ∈ C_b^∞Ψ^(−1)_3b be a
microlocal parametrix of ρ_K X_1 on Ū_0, I = Q_K ρ_K X_1 + R_K. Then

    [L, X_1] = −Σ_l (p_l ρ_K A^♭_l + ((X_1 p̃_l) A_l + p_l ρ_K A^♯_l) Q_K ρ_K) X_1
               − Σ_l ((X_1 p̃_l) A_l + p_l ρ_K A^♯_l) R_K,

which is (C) with Q_11 the first sum and R_1 the second; the factors ρ_K, ρ_K^(ℓ_K) appear in every coefficient of
Q_11. ∎

**Proposition 16.29** (The radial sets over ∂K⁺ with b-regularity.) Proposition 16.10 and
Proposition 16.11 hold with H^((𝗍;k))_(e3b;b) in place of H^𝗍_e3b, with their thresholds (16.11) and
(16.13) unchanged, in the strong sense, uniformly for P with ε_(P,k) small, and in the tame form
(16.40).

This is the analogue of [Hin26c, Propositions 7.6–7.7] in [Hin26c, Section 7.2.3], in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* Lemma 16.21–Lemma 16.23 with 𝔩 = 0 and Lemma 16.28. The threshold (16.13) at
∂R_(∂K⁺,out) is an upper bound on the order, which every order of the iteration in Lemma 16.21 meets, as there the
order s is fixed and only k increases. ∎

### 16.11 The trapped set

Over D near ∂Γ_0 (Section 16.4) use (t_*, x), ρ_K = t_*⁻¹, W′ = 1, L = P. The family is 𝒳_Γ := (t_* ∂_(t_*), I),
and U_0 is a small neighbourhood of the component of ∂Γ_(K⁺) over ∂Σ⁺ or ∂Σ⁻; on it σ ≠ 0 (Lemma 15.13 (a)).

**Lemma 16.30** (Commutators at the trapped set.) (a) (M) holds with i_0 = 1, w = ρ_K: t_* ∂_(t_*) is a
commutator field (Lemma 14.5), and ρ_K t_* ∂_(t_*) = ∂_(t_*), whose principal symbol is a non-zero multiple of σ,
elliptic on Ū_0. (b) (C) holds with Q_11 decaying at K⁺, and (C2) holds with Q^(2) of order 0. So (16.41)
holds with equality at ∂Γ_(K⁺).

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 7.21] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (b) (C): as in Lemma 16.28, with L = P = Σ_l p_l A_l, A_l ∈ Diff²_3b (cusp operators over D) independent
of t_*, p^♯_l independent of t_* and p̃_l ∈ ρ_K^(ℓ_K) C^((d_0;k))_(3b;b), and Q_K a microlocal parametrix of ∂_(t_*) on
Ū_0. (C2): from the formula for [L, X_1],

    [X_1, [X_1, L]] = Σ_l ((X_1² p̃_l) A_l + (X_1 p̃_l)[X_1, A_l] + (X_1 p_l) ρ_K (A^♭_l X_1 + A^♯_l)
                      − p_l ρ_K (A^♭_l X_1 + A^♯_l) + p_l ρ_K ([X_1, A^♭_l] X_1 + [X_1, A^♯_l])),

using X_1 ρ_K = −ρ_K. By Lemma 14.5 again, [X_1, A^♭_l] and [X_1, A^♯_l] are of the form ρ_K(·)X_1 + ρ_K(·), and
[X_1, A_l] = ρ_K A^♭_l X_1 + ρ_K A^♯_l. So every term is a second-order operator D, or a first-order operator D′
followed by X_1 (the terms p_l ρ_K² c X_1 X_1, c smooth, from p_l ρ_K [X_1, A^♭_l] X_1 are already of the form Q^(2)
X_1 X_1 with Q^(2) of order 0), with coefficients in ρ_K C^∞ + ρ_K^(ℓ_K) C^((d_0;k−2))_(3b;b). Let Q′ ∈ C_b^∞Ψ^(−2)_3b
be a microlocal parametrix of (ρ_K X_1)² = ∂_(t_*)² on Ū_0, I = Q′(ρ_K X_1)² + R′, and note (ρ_K X_1)² = ρ_K² X_1² −
ρ_K² X_1. Then

    D = (DQ′ρ_K²) X_1 X_1 − (DQ′ρ_K²) X_1 X_J + DR′,       D′X_1 = (D′Q_K ρ_K) X_1 X_1 + D′R_K X_1,

with DQ′ρ_K² and D′Q_K ρ_K of order 0 and class 𝒬^0_2, DR′ of class 𝒬^2_2, and D′R_K X_1 of the form R″X_1 with R″ :=
D′R_K of class 𝒬^1_2, both microsupported off Ū_0. This is (C2). ∎

**Proposition 16.31** (The trapped set with b-regularity.) There are B, E, G with the properties (1)–(4) of
Proposition 16.17 such that for all s > s_0, k ∈ ℕ_0, α_K ∈ ℝ and χ̃ as there

    ‖Bu‖_((s;k),α_K) ≤ C_k (‖GPu‖_((s;k),α_K) + ‖Eu‖_((s+1;k),α_K) + ‖χ̃u‖_((s_0;k),α_K)),    (16.45)

in the strong sense, uniformly for P = P_0 and P of class ((d_0; k), (0, 0, ℓ_K)) with ε_(P,k) small, d_0 depending
only on s, s_0; and the tame estimate (16.40) holds.

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 7.22] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* Lemma 16.21–Lemma 16.23 with 𝔩 = 1 and Lemma 16.30. Lemma 16.23 gives (E_1) from
Proposition 16.17 for the systems L^(k), whose first-order part differs from P ⊗ Id by terms decaying at K⁺, so that
the condition ϑ_Γ < ½ν_min at ∂Γ_(K⁺) is that of P. ∎

### 16.12 Proof of the global estimate with b-regularity

*Proof of Theorem 16.18.* For k = 0, (16.31) is Theorem 16.2. Let k ∈ ℕ, let u be as in
Theorem 16.18, and for q ∈ ℕ_0 write

    ℛ_q := ‖Pu‖_((𝗌;q),(2α_I+2,α_++2,α_K)) + ‖u‖_((𝗌_0;q),(2α_I,α_+,α_K)),

the norms being those of (16.31) on Ω_*, so that the right side of (16.31) is ℛ_k and that of
(16.32) is ℛ_k + ε_(P,k) ℛ_d. As in Section 16.5, u and Pu, extended by zero, are supported in {t_*^♭ ≥ 1};
below ‖·‖_(𝗍;k) carries the weights of u, and Pu is measured with the weights of (16.31), which is the measure
of Lu = W⁻¹Pu with the weights of u. We say u is *controlled at order* (𝗍; k) on an open set V ⊂ ᵉ³ᵇS*M if ‖Bu‖_(𝗍;k)
≤ C_k ℛ_k, in the strong sense, for every B ∈ C_b^∞Ψ^0_e3b carried by χ with WF′(B) ⊂ V; and *tamely controlled* if
moreover, for every P as in the second half of Theorem 16.18, ‖Bu‖_(𝗍;k) ≤ C_k(ℛ_k + ε_(P,k) ℛ_d), with C_k
depending on P only through a bound for ε_(P,d).

The proof is that of Section 16.5, step for step, with each estimate replaced by its version with b-regularity. The
flow is that of P, unchanged, so the backward curves are those used there; only the estimates change. The replacements
are these.

(P0_k) *Elliptic estimate.* Off the characteristic set, Proposition 14.51 with m = 2 controls u at every order (𝗍; k)
with 𝗍 ≤ 𝗌 + 1, and its tame version, Proposition 14.58, tamely.

(P1_k) *Propagation.* Proposition 14.52, and its tame version Proposition 14.59, replace Theorem 14.49 in (P1) of
Section 16.5. Their hypotheses on the flow, on the orders and on B, E, G are those of Theorem 14.49, which (P1)
uses, and they give: control at order (𝗍; k) on V gives control at order (𝗍; k) at every ϖ whose backward 𝖧-curve
enters V in finite time, provided 𝖧𝗍 ≤ 0 along it and Pu is in H^((𝗍−1;k)) near it. The weights are put into the
operator as for k = 0 (Section 16.1.2): the conjugation by a weight w adds to L terms whose coefficients are those of
L times the functions w⁻¹Vw and w⁻¹VV′w, V, V′ ∈ 𝒱_e3b, which are smooth with smooth b-derivatives
(Section 16.6), so the conjugated operator has the form (14.22) at the regularity (d_0; k).

(P2), (P3) are unchanged: as u = 0 in {t_*^♭ < 1}, u is controlled there at every order (𝗍; k).

(R_k) *Radial sets and the trapped set.* Proposition 16.9, Proposition 16.10, Proposition 16.11, Proposition 16.13,
Proposition 16.14 and Proposition 16.17 are replaced by Proposition 16.27, Proposition 16.29, Proposition 16.29,
Proposition 16.25, Proposition 16.25 and Proposition 16.31. Each is used with the orders of Section 16.5, which
are constant near the set, with the threshold conditions there, and with operators B, E, G having the properties
(1)–(4) of the proposition it replaces. The thresholds do not change with k: at the horizon by Lemma 16.26 (c),
elsewhere by Lemma 16.24 (d), Lemma 16.28 (b) and Lemma 16.30 (b).

*Step 1: finite times.* Let t^♯ and 𝒱_out be as in Step 1 of Section 16.5. Along the backward curves used there,
(P1_k) at order (𝗌 + 1; k), with Pu ∈ H^((𝗌;k)), and (P2) control u at order (𝗌 + 1; k) near every compact subset of
∂Σ⁺ over Ω_* ∩ {t_*^♭ ≤ t^♯} disjoint from 𝒱_out.

*Step 2: the horizon and ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+).* Proposition 16.27 and Proposition 16.25 (for Proposition 16.13), with the
orders (𝗌 + 1, 𝗌_0), 𝗌_0 > ½ + ϑ_ℋ near ∂R_(ℋ⁺) and (16.15) from (16.3). Their E have property (4),
so they lie at finite times, away from K⁺, resp. ι⁺, and operator wave front sets in small neighbourhoods of the two
sets, the second away from ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out); this is what Step 2 of Section 16.5 uses. So Step 1 bounds ‖Eu‖_(𝗌+1;k), and
u is controlled at order (𝗌 + 1; k) on neighbourhoods V_ℋ of ∂R_(ℋ⁺) and V_I of ∂R_(ℐ⁺,in,+).

*Step 3: ∂R_(∂K⁺,in).* Proposition 16.29 (for Proposition 16.10), with the orders (𝗌 + 1, 𝗌_0) and (16.11).
Its E has property (4) and operator wave front set in a small neighbourhood of ∂R_(∂K⁺,in); the backward curves from it
are those of Step 3 of Section 16.5, which reach {t_*^♭ < 1} or enter V_I. (P1_k) at order (𝗌 + 1; k) and (P2) bound
‖Eu‖_(𝗌+1;k), and u is controlled at order (𝗌 + 1; k) on a neighbourhood V_K of ∂R_(∂K⁺,in).

*Step 4: the trapped set.* Proposition 16.31 with the orders (𝗌, 𝗌_0), U_Γ small and Pu ∈ H^((𝗌;k)). Its E has
WF′(E) ∩ Γ^u_(K⁺) = ∅, and by Step 4 of Section 16.5 the backward curves from WF′(E) ∩ ∂Σ⁺ reach {t_*^♭ < 1} or
enter V_ℋ ∪ V_K in locally bounded times. (P1_k) at order (𝗌 + 1; k) and (P2) bound ‖Eu‖_(𝗌+1;k), and u is controlled
at order (𝗌; k) on a neighbourhood V_Γ of ∂Γ_(K⁺).

*Step 5: ∂R_(∂K⁺,out).* Proposition 16.29 (for Proposition 16.11), with the orders (𝗌, 𝗌_0) and (16.13) at
the order 𝗌. Its E has WF′(E) ∩ ∂W_out = ∅, and by Step 5 of Section 16.5 the backward curves from it enter V_ℋ ∪
V_K ∪ V_Γ ∪ V_I or reach {t_*^♭ < 1}. (P1_k) at order (𝗌; k) bounds ‖Eu‖_(𝗌;k), and u is controlled at order (𝗌; k)
on a neighbourhood V_(K,out) of ∂R_(∂K⁺,out).

*Step 6: ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out).* Proposition 16.25 (for Proposition 16.14), with t_(*,−) := ½, the orders (𝗌, 𝗌_0) and
(16.17) from (16.3). By its property (4), WF′(E) ∩ ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) lies over {t_*^♭ ≤ ½}, where u = 0,
and (P2) controls u at every order near it. The rest of WF′(E) lies in a punctured neighbourhood of ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), from
which, by Step 6 of Section 16.5, the backward curves reach {t_* = 1} or {t_*^♭ < 1} or enter V_I ∪ V_(K,out).
(P1_k) at order (𝗌; k) bounds ‖Eu‖_(𝗌;k), and u is controlled at order (𝗌; k) on a neighbourhood V_(I,out) of
∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) ∩ {t_*^♭ ≥ ½}.

*Conclusion.* As in Section 16.5, every point of ∂Σ⁺ over supp χ has a neighbourhood on which u is controlled at
order (𝗌; k), by Step 1 or Step 6, or by (P1_k) at order (𝗌; k) from one of the sets of Steps 2–6 or from {t_*^♭ < 1};
the same holds on ∂Σ⁻ with the antipodal sets, for which Section 16.8–Section 16.11 prove the same estimates.
Finitely many such B, with (P0_k) off Σ, are jointly elliptic over supp χ, and Lemma 14.29 (c) at (𝗌; k), with
‖χu‖_(−N′;k) ≤ ‖u‖_(𝗌_0;k), gives (16.31), in the strong sense.

*Uniformity.* Each estimate used holds uniformly for P with ε_(P,k) small: Proposition 16.25, Proposition 16.27,
Proposition 16.29 and Proposition 16.31, and Proposition 14.51–Proposition 14.52, whose constants are locally
uniform at the regularity (d_0; k). The backward segments are those of Section 16.5, whose persistence under
perturbation is shown there. d_0 is the largest of the numbers required by the steps at the orders 𝗌_0, 𝗌 and 𝗌 + 1
and by Lemma 16.21–Lemma 16.23, and it does not depend on k. With Remark 16.3, which applies here
because the constants of Section 16.8–Section 16.11 depend on the model only through finitely many norms of its
coefficients and through the dynamical constants of Chapter 15, this proves (16.31).

*The tame estimate (16.32).* Let d be the largest of the numbers d of Lemma 16.22 for the families and
orders of Steps 2–6 and of Proposition 14.58–Proposition 14.59 at the orders 𝗌 + 1 and 𝗌. A tame estimate proved with
some d′ ≤ d holds with d, as ℛ_(d′) ≤ ℛ_d and ε_(P,d′) ≤ ε_(P,d). If ε_(P,d) is small, then P is of class ((d_0; d),
…) and ε_(P,q) ≤ ε_(P,d) for q ≤ d, so for k ≤ d (16.32) follows from (16.31). Let k > d. Run Steps
1–6 and the conclusion with the tame versions: (P0_k) and (P1_k) with Proposition 14.58 and Proposition 14.59, and
(R_k) with (16.40). Each turns tame control on the sets where its E lies into tame control on a neighbourhood
of its own set. In its right side, the terms at k are at most C_k(ℛ_k + ε_(P,k) ℛ_d), by tame control, and those at d
at most C_d ℛ_d, by Steps 1–6 run at k = d without the tame versions, which control u on each E-set at the orders used
there (among them (𝗌 + 1; d)), with a constant depending on P only through ε_(P,d) ((16.31) at d bounds only
the order 𝗌). The coefficient norm that multiplies the terms at d is ε_(P,k) in (16.40); in
Proposition 14.58–Proposition 14.59 it is ‖𝐋‖_((d_0;k)), which is at most C′_k + Cε_(P,k) with C′_k depending only on
P_0, and the part C′_k C_d ℛ_d ≤ C′_k C_d ℛ_k joins the terms at k. The constants of those propositions depend on L
only through bounds at (d_0; d), that is, through ε_(P,d). Lemma 14.29 (c) has no coefficients of limited
regularity, so the conclusion is linear in the bounds of the steps. This gives (16.32), with C_k depending on
P only through a bound for ε_(P,d). ∎

### 16.13 Remarks on [Hin26c, Section 7]

The statements above differ from those of [Hin26c, Section 7] at the following places; each difference is accounted
for in the proofs given here.

(1) In [Hin26c, Proposition 7.9] the time cut-offs ψ_− = η(𝔐(t_(*,−) − t_*)) and ψ_+ = η(𝔐(t_* − t_(*,+))) have their
arguments reversed: with η = 0 on (−∞, −½] and η = 1 on [0, ∞) they equal 1 before t_(*,−) and after t_(*,+). Its
property (4), WF′(E) ∩ ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) = ∅, does not hold as stated, as the term e_− lies on ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) near t_* =
t_(*,−); Proposition 16.14 (4) restricts it to {t_*^♭ ≤ t_(*,−) − ¼}. For finite t_(*,+) the proof there needs H_G t_*
≥ 0 on the support of the commutant, for the symbol b_+ to be real. The cut-off to the characteristic set localises only
to a neighbourhood of it, and off it, at x_I = 0, 𝖧t_*^♭ = t_* ξ̂ takes negative values, as ξ̂ < 0 occurs there.
Proposition 16.14 is therefore stated for t_(*,+) = ∞ only. The case of finite t_(*,+) serves in Step 1 of the proof of
[Hin26c, Proposition 7.1], and Section 16.5 does without it: finite times are controlled away from ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out), and
Step 6 controls all of it at once.

(2) In the proof of [Hin26c, Proposition 7.9] the equality −4|η̂|²ξ̂ = −4(2 − ξ̂)ξ̂² should read −4|η̂|²ξ̂ = −2(2 −
ξ̂)ξ̂², as |η̂|² = ½ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) on the characteristic set; and in [Hin26c, (7.21)] the middle expression −2|η̂|²(ξ̂ − 2)
should read −4|η̂|²(ξ̂ − 2). In both, the final inequality, ≤ −q resp. ≥ q, holds as printed (Proposition 16.13,
Proposition 16.14).

(3) In the proofs of [Hin26c, Propositions 7.17 and 7.22], the inclusions H^((s+1;k−2))_(3b;b) ⊂ H^((s;k−1))_(3b;b)
([Hin26c, (7.57)]) and H^((s+2;k−3))_(cu;b) ⊂ H^((s;k−1))_(cu;b) are false as inclusions. For k = 2 the first reads
H^(s+1)_3b ⊂ H^((s;1))_(3b;b), and over (K⁺)°, where ∂_(t_*) and ∂_x are 3b-vector fields and t_* ∂_(t_*) is a
b-vector field, v := a(x) b(t_*) e^(it_*) t_*^(−α_K−1), with a ∈ C_c^∞ and b a cut-off to {t_* ≥ 2}, lies in
H^(∞,α_K)_3b, while t_* ∂_(t_*) v = i a b e^(it_*) t_*^(−α_K) + (terms in H^(∞,α_K)_3b) lies in no H^(s,α_K)_3b, its
restrictions to the slabs {T ≤ t_* ≤ T + 1} having norms bounded below. What the arguments use is the estimate
‖v‖_(s+1;k−2) ≤ C‖v‖_(s;k−1), the reverse inclusion, which holds ((F1) of Section 16.6); Lemma 16.21 and
Lemma 16.22 use it in this direction.

(4) [Hin26c, (7.28)] prints the weights (2α_I + 2, α_+ + 2, α_K) on the last norm of u, ‖u‖_(s_0;d). The proof gives
the weights of u in [Hin26c, (7.27)], (2α_I, α_+, α_K), and (16.32) states them. The printed weights demand
more decay of u, which an application with u at the weights of [Hin26c, (7.27)] does not supply.

(5) [Hin26c, Section 7.2] writes X⃗^α = X_1^(α_1) ⋯ X_(J−1)^(α_(J−1)) for multi-indices α and expands [X⃗^α, P] by
[Hin26c, Lemma 3.25] (which is Lemma 14.53) as Σ_(β+γ=α) c_(βγ) (ad^β_X⃗ P) X⃗^γ ([Hin26c, (7.37), (7.43),
(7.61)]). Near ℐ⁺ the fields do not commute: the rotation fields, and in dimension 3 + 1 also [X_1, X_2] ∈ x_I C^∞
([Hin26c, (7.31)]). The expansion (7.37) is exact even so, as deleting positions from an ordered power leaves an
ordered power. But X_j X⃗^γ is not X⃗^(γ+e_j), and the argument there needs it to read Q_(ij) X_j X⃗^γ u as a component
of u^(k); so that system closes only modulo reordering commutators, which lie in the span of the family and can be
absorbed. With words (Section 16.7) the expansion (F2) is exact and the commuted system closes without reordering.
At the horizon, over ∂K⁺ and at the trapped set the fields commute, and words and multi-indices agree up to counting,
with the coupling (16.35), whose horizon coupling is diagonal.

(6) [Hin26c, Section 7.2] applies its Propositions 7.4, 7.6–7.9 and 7.10 to the commuted equations, operators with
off-diagonal first-order terms; for the radial point estimates it refers to its Remark 7.5, and for the trapping
estimate it gives no argument. Lemma 16.23 proves the estimates for such systems under the sign condition
(16.41), and Section 16.8–Section 16.11 verify that condition; at the trapped set this rests on the form
of the proof of Proposition 16.17, in which the operator enters only through its principal symbol, through 𝔭 and
through one commutator.

(7) [Hin26c, Section 6] states the regularity C^(d_0−1,ℓ_K)_cu for the perturbed stable and unstable hypersurfaces.
Section 16.4 uses only ϕ^u ∈ C^(d_0−1) and ϕ^s ∈ C^(d_0−2) (Proposition 15.55), and chooses d_0 accordingly.

## 17. Energy estimates, solvability on slabs, the black hole interior and the global estimate

This chapter proves, in spatial dimension n = 4, the results of [Hin26c, Section 8, pp. 141–157]: solvability of
forward problems on bounded time slabs, with energy estimates, on edge Sobolev spaces with and without b-regularity and
tame in it ([Hin26c, Lemma 8.1, Propositions 8.3, 8.6 and 8.9]); the same in the black hole interior, with r as the
time function ([Hin26c, Lemma 8.10, Propositions 8.11–8.13]); and the global estimate [Hin26c, Theorem 8.14], which
joins these to the microlocal estimate of Chapter 16. The dimension enters through the normal form of the operator at
ℐ⁺ (Lemma 17.1) and through the current of the multiplier (Lemma 17.7); the threshold α < −1/2 + p̄_1 is
the same as in dimension 3 + 1.

The energy estimates are proved with a vector field multiplier. Near ℐ⁺ the multiplier is a weighted edge vector field
whose deformation tensor is positive in the time derivative only through the threshold of the weight; the other
derivatives come from an exponential weight in time. Every first-order term of the operator is kept as a pointwise
quadratic form in the first derivatives, and every zeroth-order term is absorbed by a Poincaré inequality with the
exponential weight. So the fibre inner product need only make Re p_1 large; it need not also make Im p_1 and p_0 small,
as [Hin26c, (8.4)] asks. Solvability at all orders follows from the energy estimates for P and for its adjoint, by
duality, and from microlocal regularity on slabs. That regularity needs the radial estimates at the outgoing radial set
over ℐ⁺, localised in time, for P and for P*. [Hin26c] takes the first from its Proposition 7.9 with a finite final
time, whose proof uses H_G t_* ≥ 0 on the support of the commutant, and this fails off the characteristic set (the
paragraph after Proposition 16.14); the second it leaves to the reader. Section 17.3.1 proves both, with a time
cut-off in the function t_* − κ x_I^(2ℓ_I), which is monotone along the flow on a full neighbourhood of the radial set
up to a multiple of the principal symbol.

*Organisation.* Section 17.1: slabs and spaces, the operator near ℐ⁺, extensions of the operator, duality.
Section 17.2: the energy estimates. Section 17.3: the localised radial estimates, regularity on slabs,
solvability. Section 17.4: b-regularity and the tame estimates. Section 17.5: the black hole interior.
Section 17.6: the global estimate.

*Standing notation.* The notation is that of Chapter 14, Chapter 15 and Chapter 16: the compactified spacetime M with
its faces ι⁺, ℐ⁺ and K⁺; the b-, e3b- and eb-structures; the spaces H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_(e3b;b) of
(14.6), with their supported and extendible versions (Section 14.7); the model operator P_0, the quantity
p̄_1 of Definition 15.38, the time function t^♭_* and the domains Ω and Ω_* of Lemma 15.35; and the radial
estimates of Section 16.3. An estimate holds *in the strong sense* if, whenever its right side is finite, so is its
left side, and the estimate holds. The operators act on sections of the trivial bundle ℂ^(N_E) of Section 11.1; b-vector
fields act on them componentwise, and a fibre inner product is a smooth family of Hermitian inner products on the fibre.
The radii r_0 − 2δ_0 < r_0 < r_0 + δ_0 < r_2 < r_h are those of Section 11.1. They are parameters: every constant chosen
below from them is chosen by an inequality that a smaller inner radius r_0 does not make harder to satisfy (for instance
the bound (ε_ι δ)⁻¹ > r_h + 1 in Section 17.3.2), so every result of this chapter holds at every inner radius r_0 for
which the hypotheses (H1)–(H8) of Section 11.1, Section 12.1.2 and Section 12.1.5, and (K1)–(K4) of
Section 15.1.1, hold.

### 17.1 Setting

#### 17.1.1 Slabs and spaces

Ω, Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1} and the time function t^♭_* are those of Lemma 15.35; below t^♭ := t^♭_*, and t_* = t − r
is the coordinate of Definition 14.3. P is weakly admissible of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) relative to P_0 in the
following sense: conditions (1) and (2) of Definition 15.36 hold, with the weights of a weakly admissible operator, and
condition (3), the triangular structure of p_1 and p_0, is not assumed. No proof in this chapter uses condition (3)
(Section 17.1.3), nor do the results of Chapter 16 cited here (Section 16.1.1, Section 16.6); throughout the
chapter "of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))" and "weakly admissible" are meant in this sense. We take

    ε_P := ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;0),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))

small, so that the metric g of P satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 15.35: dt^♭ is past timelike on Ω°, and dr is
future timelike on {r_0 ≤ r ≤ r^♮}, where r^♮ = (r_0 + r_2)/2. For 1 ≤ T_0 < T_1 < ∞ the **slab** is

    Ω_(T_0,T_1) := Ω_* ∩ {T_0 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T_1}.

For 1 − η_0 ≤ T_0 < 1 the slab is defined in the same way in the region Ω⁻_* of Lemma 17.2 (iv), with P^ext in
place of P. In M° its boundary consists of the *initial face* {t^♭ = T_0} and the *final faces* {t^♭ = T_1} and
{r = r_0}, which are spacelike: their conormals dt^♭ and dr are timelike, and future directed causal vectors point out of
the slab at the final faces and into it at the initial face. Its closure meets ∂M only in ℐ⁺ ∩ {T_0 ≤ t_* ≤ T_1}, as
t^♭ = t_* on ℐ⁺ (Lemma 15.35 (a)).

Near ℐ⁺ at finite times we use (t_*, x_I, ω) with x_I := r^(−1/2) (Definition 14.3 (B)); it differs from the
x_I = (t_*/r)^(1/2) of Section 15.7 by the factor t_*^(1/2), which is smooth and positive at finite times. The edge
vector fields are spanned by ∂_(t_*), x_I∂_(x_I) and x_I∂_ω, and the b-vector fields by ∂_(t_*), x_I∂_(x_I) and ∂_ω; at
finite times the e3b- and eb-structures are the edge structure, and ρ_+, ρ_K are smooth and positive. We write

    H^(𝗌,2α)_e := H^(𝗌,(2α,0,0))_(e3b),        H^((𝗌;k),2α)_(e;b) := H^((𝗌;k),(2α,0,0))_(e3b;b)

(Section 14.4 and (14.6)), with the L²-density |dg|. Near ℐ⁺, |dg| is a smooth positive multiple of
r³|dt_* dr dω| = 2x_I^(−8)|dt_* (dx_I/x_I) dω|.

For a slab Ω′ = Ω_(T_0,T_1) put

    U′ := Ω° ∩ {t^♭ < T_1, r > r_0},     V′ := Ω° ∩ {t^♭ > T_0},     F′ := Ω ∩ {t^♭ ≤ T_1, r ≥ r_0},

and define, with quotient norms,

    H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) := {u|_(U′) : u ∈ H^(𝗌,2α)_e, supp u ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ T_0}},
    H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω′)^(−,•) := {v|_(V′) : v ∈ H^(𝗌,2α)_e, supp v ⊂ F′},

and H^((𝗌;k),2α)(Ω′)^(•,−), H^((𝗌;k),2α)(Ω′)^(−,•) likewise. The first are distributions supported at the initial face
and extendible at the final ones, the spaces of forward problems; the second the reverse, the spaces of backward
problems. We call D(Ω′) the set of restrictions to U′ of functions in C_c^∞(M°) supported in {t^♭ > T_0}, and D_*(Ω′)
the set of restrictions to V′ of functions in C_c^∞(M°) supported in {t^♭ < T_1, r > r_0}.

#### 17.1.2 The operator near ℐ⁺

**Lemma 17.1** (The normal form near ℐ⁺.) Near ℐ⁺ at finite times, in (t_*, x_I = r^(−1/2), ω),

    P − (1/2) x_I² [−2(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2p_1)∂_(t_*) + 2x_I² Δ_(𝕊³) + t_*⁻¹ p_0]
        ∈ x_I² C^((d_0;k),2ℓ_I)_(e;b) Diff²_e,    (17.1)

with p_0 and p_1 := S|_(∂X) + p̃_1 as in Definition 15.36, and Δ_(𝕊³) ≥ 0 the Laplacian of the round sphere. Hence,
for covectors ζ = ζ_(t_*) dt_* + ξ dx_I/x_I + η, G(ζ) ≡ x_I²(ξ ζ_(t_*) + x_I²|η|²) modulo x_I^(2+2ℓ_I) times a quadratic
form in (ζ_(t_*), ξ, x_I η); that is, g⁻¹ ≡ x_I²(x_I∂_(x_I) ⊗_s ∂_(t_*) + x_I² g̸⁻¹), with
a ⊗_s b := (a ⊗ b + b ⊗ a)/2 and g̸ the round metric.

This is [Hin26c, (8.3)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* In the coordinates ρ_+ = t_*⁻¹, x′_I := (t_*/r)^(1/2) = t_*^(1/2) x_I of Lemma 15.37, x′_I∂_(x′_I) at
fixed ρ_+ is −2r∂_r = x_I∂_(x_I) at fixed t_*, and x′_I∂_(x′_I) − 2ρ_+∂_(ρ_+) = 2t_*∂_(t_*) at fixed r. As
x′_I^(−2) ρ_+^(−2) = t_* x_I^(−2) and x′_I² = t_* x_I², (15.27) reads

    2t_* x_I^(−2) P ≡ −2t_*(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3 − 2p_1)∂_(t_*) + 2t_* x_I² Δ_(𝕊³) + p_0,

as t_* commutes with x_I∂_(x_I) and with multiplication by p_1. Multiply by x_I²/(2t_*); the remainder class becomes
x_I² C^((d_0;k),2ℓ_I)_(e;b) Diff²_e, t_* being bounded above and below. For the principal symbol,
σ(x_I∂_(x_I)) = iξ and σ(∂_(t_*)) = iζ_(t_*). As a check of the signs: for Minkowski space, with
□ = −∂_t² + ∂_r² + (3/r)∂_r + r⁻² Δ_lap and ∂_r|_t = ∂_r|_(t_*) − ∂_(t_*), ∂_r|_(t_*) = −(1/2) x_I² x_I∂_(x_I), one
finds

    −□ = x_I² (−(x_I∂_(x_I) − 3)∂_(t_*) − x_I² Δ_lap) + O(x_I⁴) Diff²_e,

which is (17.1) with p_0 = p_1 = 0 and Δ_(𝕊³) = −Δ_lap. ∎

In dimension 3 + 1 the bracket of (17.1) reads −2(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2(1 + p_1))∂_(t_*) + 2x_I² Δ̸ + p_0
[Hin26c, (8.3)]: the constant 3 = n − 1 here is 2 there, and p_0 stands where the normal form gives t_*⁻¹p_0. At bounded
times t_*⁻¹ is a bounded positive factor, and zeroth-order terms are absorbed by the Poincaré inequality
(Lemma 17.6), so nothing below depends on it.

#### 17.1.3 The fibre inner product

Let δ′ > 0. As in Lemma 15.30 (and the proof of Proposition 16.14) there is a smooth fibre inner product
h_I = ⟨A_I⁻¹·, A_I⁻¹·⟩ over a neighbourhood of cl(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω), extended independently of x_I, with

    Re_(h_I) p_1 ≥ p̄_1 − δ′     on cl(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω).    (17.2)

It is built by Jordan scalings of p_1 at single points, continuity and a smooth partition of unity: at each point x of
the compact set cl(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω) a Jordan scaling gives an inner product h_x with Re_(h_x) p_1(x) ≥ p̄_1 − δ′/2, by continuity
Re_(h_x) p_1 ≥ p̄_1 − δ′ near x, and the condition Re h(p_1 v, v) ≥ (p̄_1 − δ′) h(v, v) for all v is linear in h, so it
passes to a convex combination of such inner products. No triangular structure of p_1 is used.

Of the data p_0, p_1 at ℐ⁺, the proofs below use only (17.2), and that only through the positivity of
4 Re_(h_I) p_1 − 2 − 4α at ℐ⁺ (and so near ℐ⁺, p_1 and h_I being independent of x_I): with δ′ := (p̄_1 − 1/2 − α)/4,
(17.2) gives 4 Re_(h_I) p_1 − 2 − 4α ≥ 12δ′ (as used in Lemma 17.8), and ≥ 8δ′ where it holds with 2δ′
in place of δ′ (as used on the extended slabs of Proposition 17.10 and in Proposition 17.12). The other terms enter
without any smallness. In Lemma 17.8 every
first-order term other than 2x_I² p_1^A ∂_(t_*) of (17.5), and the part of that term carrying Im p_1, which
enters only through a cross term with x_I∂_(x_I), is kept as a pointwise quadratic form in the edge derivatives and
absorbed by the exponential weight in time; the zeroth-order terms, among them the one carrying p_0, are absorbed by the
Poincaré inequality Lemma 17.6. The commuted systems of Section 17.4 have the same p_1 ((17.11) and the
paragraph after it). So the fibre inner product need not make Im_h p_1 or p_0 small, as [Hin26c, (8.4)] requires
(|Im_h p_1| < ε and ‖p_0‖_h < ε), and the block-diagonal inner product by which [Hin26c] obtains that smallness from
condition (3) of Definition 15.36 is not used.

#### 17.1.4 Extensions of the operator

The microlocal estimates of Section 17.3 are applied on a neighbourhood of a slab, beyond its final faces, and, for
T_0 = 1, below its initial face, where P is not given.

**Lemma 17.2** (Extension; [Hin26c, Lemma 8.5 and the paragraph after it].) There are r^♯ ∈ (r_0 − δ_0, r_0)
and an operator P^ext on {r ≥ r^♯} ∩ {t_* ≥ 1/2} such that:

(i) P^ext = P on Ω;

(ii) P^ext − P_0 has coefficients bounded in the norms of P − P_0, in C^((d_0;k)) with the weights of Definition 15.36,
by a constant times those of P − P_0;

(iii) near ℐ⁺, P^ext has the form (17.1) with the data p_0, p̃_1 extended to t_* ∈ [1/2, 1], and
(17.2) holds for t_* ∈ [1 − η_0, 1] with 2δ′ in place of δ′, for some η_0 > 0;

(iv) t^♭ extends to {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ 1/2}, and for ε_P small there is δ_♮ > 0 such that, after shrinking η_0 (we take
η_0 ≤ 1/2): dt^♭ is past timelike for the metric of P^ext on the region Ω⁻_*, the union of {t^♭ ≥ 1, r ≥ r^♯} and of
the collar {1 − η_0 ≤ t^♭ ≤ 1} below its face {t^♭ = 1} (in the collar coordinates of Section 17.1.5), which lies in
{t_* > 1/2}; and dr is future timelike on Ω⁻_* ∩ {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮}.

*Proof.* Write P_0 and P − P_0 in a fixed frame as sums of coefficients times fixed operators Id, ∂_(z^μ),
∂_(z^μ)∂_(z^ν), z = (t_*, x), as in the paragraph after [Hin26c, Lemma 8.5]; those of P_0 are independent of t_*.
Extend each coefficient across {r = r_0} by Seeley's extension operator E_0 (see the proof of Lemma 17.3 (b)) in
the variable r − r_0, with (t_*, ω) as parameters, and across {t_* = 1} by E_0 in t_*, with (r, ω), resp. (x_I, ω) near
ℐ⁺, as parameters. Seeley's operator preserves C^((d_0;k))-regularity and weights in the parameters, which gives (ii),
and acts on the data p_0, p̃_1 of (15.25)–(15.26) in Definition 15.36 in the same way, which gives the
form in (iii). The extended p_1 is continuous in t_* and equals p_1 at t_* = 1, so (17.2) persists with 2δ′ on
[1 − η_0, 1]. The extension of P_0 in r keeps it stationary.

(iv) t^♭ is not extended by E_0: Seeley's extension of a function is not given by the function's own formula, which is
what is used below. On {t_* ≥ 1/2} it is defined by the gluing formulae of the proof of Lemma 15.35, with the
constant C there taken ≥ 4(r′_0 + 1), so that the overlap {r′_0 + 1 ≤ r ≤ C t_*/2} of the regions being glued is
non-empty for every t_* ≥ 1/2; the formulae make sense for t_* > 0. In particular t^♭ = t_*(1 − (t_*/r)^(ℓ_I)) near ℐ⁺
(Lemma 15.35 (a)) and t^♭ = C′(t_* + r′_0) for r ≤ r′_0 − 1 (Lemma 15.35 (c)), on all of {t_* ≥ 1/2}.

*dr.* By Lemma 15.35 (1) with h = 0, dr is future timelike for g_0 on {r_0 ≤ r ≤ r^♮}; g_0 is stationary and the
range of x is compact, so by continuity this holds on {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮} for r^♯ close to r_0 and δ_♮ small, and for
the extended metric, which differs from g_0 by O(ε_P) there.

*dt^♭.* For r ≤ r′_0 − 1, dt^♭ = C′dt_*, and dt_* is past timelike for g_0 there (by hypothesis (H6) of
Section 12.1.2, as in the proof of Lemma 15.35), hence for the extended metric, by stationarity and continuity
down to r^♯. Near ℐ⁺ the proof of Lemma 15.35 bounds g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ in the basis used there by
C(ε_P + ρ_I^(1−ℓ_I)) ρ_I^(ℓ_I), using ρ_+ ≤ 1 only to bound powers of ρ_+; for t_* ≥ 1/2, ρ_+ ≤ 2, and the argument
applies with larger constants. On the rest of {t^♭ ≤ T}, namely {x_I ≥ c, r ≥ r′_0 − 1}, which is compact at bounded
t_* (and t_* ≤ T/C′ on {t^♭ ≤ T} ∩ Ω by Lemma 15.35 (b)), dt^♭ is past timelike on Ω_* with a margin, hence on a
neighbourhood, by continuity.

*The collar.* Near the face {t^♭ = 1}, which lies in {t_* ≥ 1} by Lemma 15.35 (b), dt^♭ is past timelike, so the
field Z/(−Z t^♭) of Section 17.1.5 is defined there; its flow from the face for times at most η_0 sweeps the collar,
which for η_0 small lies in the neighbourhood just obtained and in {t_* > 1/2}: near ℐ⁺ the flow is translation in t_*
by at most 2η_0, and elsewhere at bounded times it stays in a compact set. ∎

#### 17.1.5 Duality

*A collar.* There is a vector field Z on a neighbourhood of Ω⁻_* ∩ {t^♭ ≤ T_1 + 2}, an edge vector field, equal to
−∂_(t_*) near ℐ⁺, with Z t^♭ ≤ −c < 0 and, near {r = r_0}, Z r ≥ c. Take Z := −χ_I ∂_(t_*) + (1 − χ_I)∇t^♭, with
χ_I = χ_I(r) equal to 1 for r ≥ R and to 0 for r ≤ R − 1, R large. Near ℐ⁺,
∂_(t_*) t^♭ = 1 − (1 + ℓ_I)(t_*/r)^(ℓ_I) ≥ 1/2 by Lemma 15.35 (a). On {r ≤ R}, ∇t^♭ is past timelike
(Lemma 15.35 (2) and Lemma 17.2 (iv)), so Z t^♭ = g⁻¹(dt^♭, dt^♭) < 0 there, with a negative bound on the
compact part at bounded times, and (∇t^♭) r = g⁻¹(dt^♭, dr) > 0 near r = r_0, dr being future timelike. Near ℐ⁺ the
flow Φ_τ of Z is translation in t_*, which preserves the edge structure and the weight, and the density up to a smooth
positive factor bounded with its derivatives at bounded times; elsewhere it is a smooth flow on a compact set. So
(Φ_τ)_* is bounded on H^(m,2α)_e, m ∈ ℕ_0, uniformly for |τ| ≤ τ_0, and strongly continuous at τ = 0, by the chain rule
and the density of C_c^∞.

As Z and Φ_τ are defined only near Ω⁻_* ∩ {t^♭ ≤ T_1 + 2}, in Lemma 17.3 below (Φ_(±τ))_* is applied only after
multiplication by a cut-off χ_Z, a function of t^♭ equal to 1 on {T_0 − η_0/4 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T_1 + 1} and supported in
{T_0 − η_0/2 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T_1 + 2} (there T_0 ≥ 1 − η_0/2). This changes neither the pairings, as the supports of the two
factors meet only where χ_Z = 1, nor the restrictions to U′ and V′. The level sets of t^♭ near {t^♭ = T}, with the flow
lines of Z/(−Z t^♭), give collar coordinates (t^♭, y) in which Z/(−Z t^♭) = −∂_(t^♭); near ℐ⁺, y = (x_I, ω), and in
(t^♭, x_I, ω) the edge vector fields are spanned by ∂_(t^♭), x_I∂_(x_I) and x_I∂_ω, as
t^♭ − t_* = −t_*^(1+ℓ_I) x_I^(2ℓ_I) has bounded edge derivatives.

**Lemma 17.3** (Pairing, duality and density.) Let Ω′ = Ω_(T_0,T_1) with T_0 ≥ 1 − η_0/2, α ∈ ℝ and
m ∈ ℤ; the weights are 2α on u and −2α on v.

(a) (*Separation.*) Let u ∈ H^(m,2α)_e and v ∈ H^(−m,−2α)_e with supp u ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ T_0}. If supp v ⊂ {t^♭ ≤ T_0}, or if
supp v ⊂ F′ and u|_(U′) = 0, then ⟨u, v⟩ = 0. Hence the pairing of u|_(U′) ∈ H^(m,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) with
v|_(V′) ∈ H^(−m,−2α)(Ω′)^(−,•), taken with extensions supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, resp. F′, is well defined, and
bounded by C times the product of the quotient norms.

(b) (*Duality.*) If m ≥ 0, every bounded functional Λ on H^(m,2α)(Ω′)^(−,•) is Λ = ⟨·, u⟩ for some
u ∈ H^(−m,−2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) with ‖u‖ ≤ C‖Λ‖.

(c) (*Density.*) If m ≥ 0, D(Ω′) is dense in H^(m,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) and D_*(Ω′) is dense in H^(m,2α)(Ω′)^(−,•); likewise
for the mixed spaces of order (m;k).

*Proof.* (a) The pairing is that of Lemma 14.21, bounded on H^m × H^(−m). In the first case, (Φ_(−τ))_* u is
supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0 + cτ} for τ > 0 small, as −Z increases t^♭, so ⟨(Φ_(−τ))_* u, v⟩ = 0, and
(Φ_(−τ))_* u → u in H^(m,2α)_e as τ ↓ 0 (for m < 0, (Φ_τ)_* is the transpose of (Φ_(−τ))_* on H^(−m), bounded
uniformly, and converges on the dense set C_c^∞). In the second case, (Φ_τ)_* v is supported, within
{t^♭ ≥ T_0 − η_0/2}, in U′, as Z points into F′ across {t^♭ = T_1} and {r = r_0} there; u vanishes on U′ and on
{t^♭ < T_0}, so ⟨u, (Φ_τ)_* v⟩ = 0, and τ ↓ 0 gives the claim. For the pairing, two extensions of u|_(U′) supported
in {t^♭ ≥ T_0} differ by an element vanishing on U′, and two extensions of v|_(V′) supported in F′ by an element
supported in {t^♭ ≤ T_0}; the bound follows by taking minimal extensions.

(b) Let E_0 be Seeley's extension operator across {t^♭ = T_0}, as in [Hin26c, Lemma 8.5], in the collar coordinates:
E_0 w := w on {t^♭ > T_0} and

    (E_0 w)(T_0 − τ, y) := Σ_(l≥0) c_l (χ w)(T_0 + τ/ε_l, y)     for τ > 0,

where ε_l = 3^(−l), sin(πs/2) = Σ_l c_l s^l (so that Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(−j) < ∞ and Σ_l c_l ε_l^(−j) = (−1)^j for all
j ∈ ℕ_0), and χ = χ(t^♭ − T_0) is a cut-off equal to 1 near 0 and supported in [0, η_0/2). It maps H̄^(m,2α)(V′)
boundedly into H^(m,2α)_e: the reflection acts in t^♭ only, commutes with x_I∂_(x_I) and x_I∂_ω in the collar
coordinates near ℐ⁺, matches all t^♭-derivatives at t^♭ = T_0, and after j derivatives in t^♭ is bounded on L² by
Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(1/2−j). E_0 w is supported in {t^♭ > T_0 − η_0/2}, within Ω⁻_*. It preserves support in F′: on a
collar line r increases as t^♭ decreases (near {r = r_0}, as Z r > 0 there), so if (T_0 − τ, y) has r < r_0, so has
(T_0 + τ/ε_l, y). Hence on H^(m,2α)(Ω′)^(−,•) the quotient norm and the norm of H̄^(m,2α)(V′) are equivalent. Given Λ,
extend it by the Hahn–Banach theorem to H̄^(m,2α)(V′) with comparable norm. By Lemma 14.23 and its proof (the case
of functionals on extendible spaces), there is ũ ∈ Ḣ^(−m,−2α)(V̄′), ‖ũ‖ ≤ C‖Λ‖, with Λ(y) = ⟨ỹ, ũ⟩ for every
extension ỹ ∈ H^(m,2α)_e of y. Take ỹ supported in F′; then u := ũ|_(U′) represents Λ in the pairing of (a).

(c) Given v supported in F′, (Φ_τ)_* v → v as τ ↓ 0, and for small τ > 0 its part in {t^♭ > T_0 − η_0/2} is
supported in {t^♭ < T_1, r > r_0}; the part in {t^♭ ≤ T_0 − η_0/2} does not affect the restriction to V′. Then
multiply by 1 − χ_0(x_I/δ), χ_0 a cut-off equal to 1 near 0, which converges strongly to the identity as δ → 0 (by
dominated convergence; the derivatives (x_I∂_(x_I))^j (x_I∂_ω)^β ∂_(t_*)^i of χ_0(x_I/δ) are bounded uniformly in δ),
and mollify on the resulting compact set. For D(Ω′) use Φ_(−τ), which moves supports into {t^♭ > T_0}. For the mixed
spaces the same holds, as the operations commute with b-vector fields up to terms bounded on these spaces. ∎

The equivalence of the quotient norm on H^(m,2α)(Ω′)^(−,•) with the norm on the slab, proved in (b), is what the
duality step of [Hin26c, Proposition 8.3] uses.

### 17.2 Energy estimates

#### 17.2.1 Three identities

For a C¹ Lorentzian metric g, a real C¹ vector field X and real covectors ζ put

    K_X(ζ) := (1/2) (H_G(ζ(X)) − (div_g X) G(ζ)),        T(V,W)(ζ) := ζ(V) ζ(W) − (1/2) g(V,W) G(ζ),

with G(ζ) = g⁻¹(ζ, ζ). For u with values in the fibre, K_X(du) and T(V,W)(du) are the corresponding Hermitian forms in
du (sums over the real and imaginary parts of the components in a unitary frame). In coordinates
K_X(ζ) = (∇_μ X_ν) ζ^μ ζ^ν − (1/2)(div_g X) G(ζ), as

    H_G(X^ν ζ_ν) = 2 g^(μγ) ζ_γ (∂_μ X^ν) ζ_ν − (∂_κ g^(μν)) X^κ ζ_μ ζ_ν,
    2 ζ^μ ζ_ν Γ^ν_(μκ) = ζ^μ ζ^γ ∂_κ g_(γμ) = −(∂_κ g^(μν)) ζ_μ ζ_ν.

P_□ := −□_g acts componentwise; σ_2(P_□) = G.

**Lemma 17.4** (Energy identity.) Let O be a region whose boundary in M° consists of finitely many C¹
hypersurfaces {φ_j = 0} meeting transversally, with O = {φ_j > 0 for all j} near them, and let X be a real C¹ vector
field. For u ∈ C²(Ō) with values in the fibre and with compact support in Ō,

    2 Re ∫_O ⟨P_□ u, Xu⟩ |dg| = ∫_O 2K_X(du) |dg| + Σ_j ∫ 2T(X, ∇φ_j)(du) δ(φ_j) |dg|.    (17.3)

For f ∈ C¹ real, K_(fX) = f K_X + 2T(X, (1/2)∇f), that is,
K_(fX)(ζ) = f K_X(ζ) + ζ(X) g⁻¹(df, ζ) − (1/2)(Xf) G(ζ).

*Proof.* For a real component a of u, with J := −(Xa)∇a + (1/2) G(da) X,

    div J = −(Xa) □a − (∇_μ X_ν) ∇^μ a ∇^ν a − (1/2) X(G(da)) + (1/2) X(G(da)) + (1/2)(div X) G(da),

using ∇^μ a ∇_μ(X^ν ∇_ν a) = (∇_μ X_ν) ∇^μ a ∇^ν a + (1/2) X(G(da)). So (−□a)(Xa) = div J + K_X(da). Integrate over O:
∫ div(1_O J) |dg| = 0 and div(1_O J) = 1_O div J + Σ_j δ(φ_j) J(dφ_j) (the divergence theorem on the Lipschitz domain
O), and −J(dφ_j) = (Xa) da(∇φ_j) − (1/2)(Xφ_j) G(da) = T(X, ∇φ_j)(da). Sum over the real and imaginary parts of all
components. The formula for K_(fX) follows from H_G(f ζ(X)) = f H_G(ζ(X)) + ζ(X) H_G f, H_G f = 2g⁻¹(df, ζ) and
div(fX) = f div X + Xf. ∎

**Lemma 17.5** (Dominant energy.) If V and W are both future causal, or both past causal, then
T(V,W)(ζ) ≥ 0 for all real ζ. If V is timelike, T(V,V)(ζ) ≥ c|ζ|² with c > 0 depending continuously on V and on a
Riemannian norm.

*Proof.* T is bilinear in (V, W), so the past case follows from the future one. Let Z := ζ^♯ and
Y := g(Z,V) Z − (1/2) g(Z,Z) V. Then T(V,W)(ζ) = g(Y,W), g(Y,Y) = (1/4) g(Z,Z)² g(V,V) ≤ 0, and
g(Y,V) = T(V,V)(ζ). In an orthonormal frame with V a positive multiple of e_0 (if V is timelike),
T(V,V)(ζ) = (1/2)|V|²(Z_0² + |Z_⊥|²), which is the second claim; if V is null, T(V,V)(ζ) = g(Z,V)² ≥ 0. So Y is causal
or zero, with g(Y,V) ≥ 0, hence past causal or zero, and g(Y,W) ≥ 0 for W future causal. In the remaining case,
g(Y,V) = 0 with V null, g(Z,V)² = T(V,V)(ζ) = 0, so Y = −(1/2) g(Z,Z) V; and Z ⊥ V with V null forces Z spacelike or
parallel to V, so g(Z,Z) ≥ 0, and Y is a non-positive multiple of V, again past causal or zero. ∎

**Lemma 17.6** (Poincaré inequality with an exponential weight.) Let O be as in Lemma 17.4, Y a C¹
vector field and τ a C¹ function with Yτ = 1 and |div_g Y| ≤ C_0 on O, w > 0 a C¹ weight with |Y log w| ≤ C_1, and
Φ ≥ C_0 + C_1. Let u ∈ C¹(Ō) have compact support in Ō and vanish near the part of every boundary face {φ_j = 0} where
Yφ_j > 0. Then

    ∫_O e^(−2Φτ) w |u|² |dg| ≤ 4Φ⁻² ∫_O e^(−2Φτ) w |Yu|² |dg|.    (17.4)

*Proof.* With Y_Φ := e^(−2Φτ) w Y,

    div(|u|² Y_Φ) = e^(−2Φτ) w Y|u|² + e^(−2Φτ) w (div Y + Y log w − 2Φ) |u|².

Integrating as in Lemma 17.4, ∫_O div(|u|² Y_Φ) |dg| = −Σ_j ∫ δ(φ_j) |u|² Y_Φ φ_j |dg| ≥ 0, as u = 0 near the
faces with Yφ_j > 0. With |Y|u|²| ≤ 2|u||Yu| and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality,

    (2Φ − C_0 − C_1) ∫ e^(−2Φτ) w |u|² ≤ 2 (∫ e^(−2Φτ) w |u|²)^(1/2) (∫ e^(−2Φτ) w |Yu|²)^(1/2),

which gives (17.4), as 2Φ − C_0 − C_1 ≥ Φ. ∎

With Y replaced by −Y and τ by −τ this is the inequality for the reverse direction:
∫ e^(2Φτ) w |u|² ≤ 4Φ⁻² ∫ e^(2Φτ) w |Yu|² when u vanishes near the faces with Yφ_j < 0.

#### 17.2.2 The multiplier near ℐ⁺

Near ℐ⁺ at finite times put, for β ∈ ℝ,

    X_0^(β) := x_I^(−4β−2) (∂_(t_*) − x_I∂_(x_I)) = r^(2β+1) (∂_(t_*) + 2r∂_r).

For covectors write ζ = ζ_(t_*) dt_* + ξ dx_I/x_I + η and η̂ := x_I η, so that ζ(∂_(t_*)), ζ(x_I∂_(x_I)) and η̂ are the
components of ζ on the edge frame, and |η̂|² = x_I² |η|²_(g̸).

**Lemma 17.7** (The current of the multiplier.) For the Minkowski metric ḡ = −dt_*² − 2dt_* dr + r² g̸,

    K_(X_0^(β))(ζ) = x_I^(−4β) [−(2β+1) ζ_(t_*)² − 3 ζ_(t_*) ξ − (2β+3)|η̂|²
                                 + x_I² ((2β−1)/4 · ξ² − (2β+1)/2 · ζ_(t_*) ξ)],
    T(X_0^(β), −∇t_*)(ζ) = (1/2) x_I^(−4β) (ξ² + |η̂|² + (1/4) x_I² ξ²).

For the metric g of P, the two sides change by x_I^(−4β) O(x_I^(2ℓ_I)) (ζ_(t_*)² + ξ² + |η̂|²), uniformly for ε_P ≤ 1,
with d_0 ≥ 2.

This is [Hin26c, (8.10)] in dimension 4 + 1. In dimension 3 + 1 the cross term −3ζ_(t_*)ξ is −2ζ_(t_*)ξ and the angular
coefficient −(2β+3) is −2(β+1); the coefficient −(2β+1) of ζ_(t_*)², which carries the threshold, is the same in both
dimensions, so the threshold of Lemma 17.8 is the same as there. The cross term is absorbed whatever its size.

*Proof.* With ⊗_s as in Lemma 17.1, ḡ⁻¹ = −2 ∂_(t_*) ⊗_s ∂_r + ∂_r ⊗ ∂_r + r⁻² g̸⁻¹, so in (t_*, r, ω)

    G(ζ) = −2 ζ_(t_*) ζ_r + ζ_r² + r⁻² |η|²,

and div_ḡ Y = r⁻³ ∂_μ(r³ Y^μ) for Y = Y^(t_*) ∂_(t_*) + Y^r ∂_r. Put c := 2β + 1 and X := r^c (∂_(t_*) + 2r∂_r). Then
ζ(X) = r^c (ζ_(t_*) + 2r ζ_r), which does not depend on t_*, ω or η, so

    H_G(ζ(X)) = ∂_(ζ_r)G · ∂_r(ζ(X)) − ∂_r G · ∂_(ζ_r)(ζ(X)),

with ∂_(ζ_r)G = −2ζ_(t_*) + 2ζ_r, ∂_r G = −2r⁻³|η|², ∂_r(ζ(X)) = r^(c−1)(c ζ_(t_*) + 2(c+1) r ζ_r) and
∂_(ζ_r)(ζ(X)) = 2r^(c+1); and div X = r⁻³ ∂_r(2r^(c+4)) = 2(c+4) r^c. So

    2K_X = r^(c−1) [(−2ζ_(t_*) + 2ζ_r)(c ζ_(t_*) + 2(c+1) r ζ_r) + 4r⁻¹|η|²]
           − 2(c+4) r^c (−2ζ_(t_*) ζ_r + ζ_r² + r⁻² |η|²).

Insert ζ_r = −ξ/(2r) (as dr = −2r dx_I/x_I) and |η|² = r|η̂|², and use r^(c−1) = x_I^(−4β) and r⁻¹ = x_I². The terms
are, after division by r^(c−1):

- ζ_(t_*)²: from the first product, −2c.
- ζ_(t_*)ξ: the first product gives ζ_(t_*)ζ_r(2c − 4(c+1)r) = ζ_(t_*)ξ(2(c+1) − c x_I²), and the second term gives
  4(c+4) r ζ_(t_*) ζ_r = −2(c+4) ζ_(t_*) ξ; the sum is −6 − c x_I².
- |η̂|²: 4 from the first bracket and −2(c+4) from the second term; the sum is −2c − 4.
- ξ²: the first product gives 4(c+1) r ζ_r² = (c+1) x_I² ξ², and the second term gives
  −2(c+4) r ζ_r² = −(c+4)/2 · x_I² ξ²; the sum is (c−2)/2 · x_I².

Halving gives K, with −c = −(2β+1), −3 − (c/2) x_I² = −3 − (2β+1)/2 · x_I², −c − 2 = −(2β+3) and
(c−2)/4 = (2β−1)/4. For T: ζ(X_0^(β)) = r^c(ζ_(t_*) + 2rζ_r) = r^c(ζ_(t_*) − ξ),
ζ(−∇t_*) = −ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, ζ) = ζ_r = −ξ/(2r), and ḡ(X_0^(β), −∇t_*) = −dt_*(X_0^(β)) = −r^c; so

    T = r^c (ζ_(t_*) − ξ)(−ξ/(2r)) + (1/2) r^c (−2ζ_(t_*)ζ_r + ζ_r² + r⁻²|η|²)
      = r^(c−1) (−(1/2)ζ_(t_*)ξ + (1/2)ξ²) + r^(c−1) ((1/2)ζ_(t_*)ξ + (1/8) r⁻¹ ξ² + (1/2)|η̂|²),

which is (1/2) r^(c−1)(ξ² + |η̂|² + (1/4) r⁻¹ ξ²), the ζ_(t_*)ξ terms cancelling. For g: by Lemma 17.1 and
(15.30), g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ is x_I^(2+2ℓ_I) times a quadratic form in (ζ_(t_*), ξ, η̂) with coefficients bounded in
C^(d_0−1)_e, and |dg|/|dḡ| − 1 ∈ x_I^(2ℓ_I) C^(d_0−1)_e; K and T involve these and one edge derivative of them. ∎

**Lemma 17.8** (Energy estimate near ℐ⁺.) Let α < −1/2 + p̄_1 and Ω′ = Ω_(T_0,T_1), T_0 ≥ 1; put
t′ := t_* + r^(ℓ_I/2). There are δ_I > 0 and T_2, with Ω′ ∩ {t′ ≥ T_2} ⊂ {x_I ≤ δ_I}, and C, such that:

(i) for u ∈ D(Ω′) supported in {x_I ≤ δ_I}, ‖u‖_(H^(1,2α)(Ω′)) ≤ C ‖Pu‖_(H^(0,2α+2)(Ω′));

(ii) for v ∈ C^∞(Ω̄′ ∩ {t′ ≥ T_2}) vanishing near {t^♭ = T_1} and near ℐ⁺,
‖v‖_(H^(1,−2α−2)(Ω′∩{t′≥T_2})) ≤ C ‖P*v‖_(H^(0,−2α)(Ω′∩{t′≥T_2})).

Here H^(1,2β)(O) and H^(0,2β)(O) denote the norms

    (∫_O x_I^(−4β) (|u|² + |∂_(t_*)u|² + |x_I∂_(x_I)u|² + |x_I∂_ω u|²) |dg|)^(1/2),     (∫_O x_I^(−4β) |u|² |dg|)^(1/2),

and P* is the adjoint for |dg| and the fibre inner product h_I of (17.2). C is uniform for ε_P small, with
d_0 = 2.

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 8.1] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* *The level sets of t′.* With α′ := ℓ_I/2, dt′ = dt_* + α′ r^(α′−1) dr has
ḡ⁻¹(dt′, dt′) = −2α′ r^(α′−1) + α′² r^(2α′−2). The proof of Lemma 15.35 bounds the coefficients of g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ in
its basis by C(ε_P + ρ_I^(1−ℓ_I)) ρ_I^(ℓ_I), ρ_I = t_*/r; the basis evaluated on (dt′)^(⊗2) gives ρ_I, O(r^(α′−1)), 0,
ρ_I⁻¹ α′² r^(2α′−2), 0, 0, all at most C r^(α′−1) · r^(α′) at bounded t_*. So g⁻¹(dt′, dt′) ≤ −α′ r^(α′−1) for r ≥ R_0,
as ρ_I^(ℓ_I) r^(α′) = O(r^(−ℓ_I/2)). Moreover dt′(V) = t_* + α′ r^(α′) > 0 for the future timelike V = t∂_t + r∂_r of
the proof of Lemma 15.35, so dt′ is past timelike there, and t′ increases along future causal curves. As t_* is
bounded on Ω′, Ω′ ∩ {t′ ≥ T_2} ⊂ {x_I ≤ δ_I} for T_2 large.

*Conjugation.* Put v_♭ := A_I⁻¹ u and P̃ := A_I⁻¹ P A_I. As A_I is independent of x_I, P̃ − P is of first order: the
commutator [x_I² x_I∂_(x_I) ∂_(t_*), A_I] is x_I² (∂_(t_*)A_I) x_I∂_(x_I), the commutator with x_I⁴ Δ_(𝕊³) is x_I³ times
a first-order edge operator, and the rest is of order 0 with coefficient O(x_I²). By Lemma 17.1, with P_□ for g
satisfying (17.1) with p_0 = p_1 = 0 (its difference from −□_ḡ comes from g − ḡ), near ℐ⁺

    P̃ = P_□ + 2x_I² p_1^A ∂_(t_*) + x_I² b x_I∂_(x_I) + R_1 + R_0,        p_1^A := A_I⁻¹ p_1 A_I,    (17.5)

with b bounded, R_1 a first-order edge operator with coefficients O(x_I^(2+2ℓ_I)) (of class C^(d_0−1)_e), and R_0 of
order 0 with coefficient O(x_I²). By (17.2), Re p_1^A = A_I⁻¹ (Re_(h_I) p_1) A_I, so
⟨Re p_1^A w, w⟩ = h_I(Re_(h_I) p_1 A_I w, A_I w) ≥ (p̄_1 − δ′)|w|²; take δ′ := (p̄_1 − 1/2 − α)/4.

*(i).* Let X := e^(−2Φt_*) X_0^(α), future timelike near ℐ⁺: ḡ(X_0^(α), X_0^(α)) = r^(2c)(−1 − 4r), c = 2α + 1, which
dominates the change O(x_I^(2ℓ_I)) r^(2c+1) from g − ḡ. Apply Lemma 17.4 on O := Ω′. Its faces near supp u are
{t^♭ = T_0}, where v_♭ = 0, and {t^♭ = T_1}, with φ = T_1 − t^♭ and ∇φ = −∇t^♭ future timelike, so the boundary term is
≥ 0 by Lemma 17.5. So

    2 Re ∫ ⟨P̃ v_♭, X v_♭⟩ ≥ ∫ 2K_X(dv_♭) + 2 Re ∫ ⟨(P̃ − P_□) v_♭, X v_♭⟩.

By Lemma 17.4 and Lemma 17.7, K_X = e^(−2Φt_*) (K_(X_0^(α)) + 2Φ T(X_0^(α), −∇t_*)). Write
τ_0 := |∂_(t_*) v_♭|, τ_1 := |x_I∂_(x_I) v_♭| and τ_2 := |x_I∂_ω v_♭|. Pointwise, after division by
e^(−2Φt_*) x_I^(−4α), the integrand on the right is at least

    (−2(2α+1) + 4(p̄_1 − δ′)) τ_0² − C_1 τ_0 τ_1 − C_1 τ_1² + 2Φ(τ_1² + τ_2²) − 2(2α+3)_+ τ_2²
        − C_2 (1 + Φ)(δ^(2ℓ_I) + δ²)(τ_0² + τ_1² + τ_2²) − C_2 |v_♭| (τ_0 + τ_1 + τ_2)

on {x_I ≤ δ}: the first term is 4⟨Re p_1^A ∂_(t_*) v_♭, ∂_(t_*) v_♭⟩ plus the ζ_(t_*)² part of 2K_(X_0^(α)); C_1 bounds
the cross terms −6 Re⟨∂_(t_*) v_♭, x_I∂_(x_I) v_♭⟩, −4 Re⟨p_1^A ∂_(t_*) v_♭, x_I∂_(x_I) v_♭⟩ and those of b; C_2 bounds
the x_I²-terms of Lemma 17.7, the change from ḡ to g, and R_1, R_0. The first coefficient is
a := −2(2α+1) + 4(p̄_1 − δ′) = 16δ′ − 4δ′ = 12δ′ > 0. Use C_1 τ_0 τ_1 ≤ (a/4) τ_0² + (C_1²/a) τ_1² and
C_2 |v_♭| τ_j ≤ (a/16) τ_j² + (4C_2²/a) |v_♭|², and Lemma 17.6 with Y = ∂_(t_*), τ = t_*, w = x_I^(−4α) (as
∂_(t_*)φ > 0 only at the initial face, where v_♭ = 0, and |div_g ∂_(t_*)| ≤ C_0), which gives
∫ e^(−2Φt_*) x_I^(−4α) |v_♭|² ≤ 4Φ⁻² ∫ e^(−2Φt_*) x_I^(−4α) τ_0². Choose Φ large, then δ ≤ δ_I small depending on Φ, to
get

    2 Re ∫ ⟨P̃ v_♭, X v_♭⟩ ≥ ∫ e^(−2Φt_*) x_I^(−4α) ((a/4) τ_0² + (Φ/4)(τ_1² + τ_2²)) |dg|
                          ≥ c ‖e^(−Φt_*) v_♭‖²_(H^(1,2α)).

The left side is at most

    2 ∫ e^(−2Φt_*) x_I^(−4α−2) |P̃ v_♭| (τ_0 + τ_1) ≤ (c/2) ‖e^(−Φt_*) v_♭‖²_(H^(1,2α))
                                                  + C ‖e^(−Φt_*) P̃ v_♭‖²_(H^(0,2α+2)).

As t_* is bounded on Ω′ and A_I, A_I⁻¹ are bounded with bounded derivatives, (i) follows.

*(ii).* Let β := −α − 1, O := Ω′ ∩ {t′ ≥ T_2}, w_♭ := A_I⁻¹ v and X_* := −e^(2Φt_*) X_0^(β), which is past timelike.
P̃* is the standard adjoint of P̃, and A_I⁻¹ P* A_I = P̃* (the proof of Lemma 16.1). P_□ is symmetric for |dg|. So

    P̃* = P_□ − 2x_I² (p_1^A)* ∂_(t_*) − x_I² b* x_I∂_(x_I) + R_1′ + R_0′,

with R_1′, R_0′ as before ((x_I∂_(x_I))* = −x_I∂_(x_I) + 8 + O(x_I^(2ℓ_I)) for |dg|). Apply Lemma 17.4 on O with
the multiplier X_*: the faces with w_♭ ≠ 0 nearby are {t^♭ = T_0} and {t′ = T_2}, with ∇φ = ∇t^♭, resp. ∇t′, past
timelike, so the boundary terms 2T(X_*, ∇φ)(dw_♭) are ≥ 0 by Lemma 17.5 (both vectors past causal). By
Lemma 17.4, K_(X_*) = e^(2Φt_*) (−K_(X_0^(β)) + 2Φ T(X_0^(β), −∇t_*)). The ζ_(t_*)² coefficient of −2K_(X_0^(β))
is 2(2β+1) = −2(2α+1), and the term 2 Re⟨−2x_I² (p_1^A)* ∂_(t_*) w_♭, X_* w_♭⟩ contributes
4⟨Re p_1^A ∂_(t_*) w_♭, ∂_(t_*) w_♭⟩, so the coefficient is again a. The rest is as in (i), with Lemma 17.6 in the
reverse direction (w_♭ = 0 near {t^♭ = T_1}, the only face of O with ∂_(t_*)φ < 0). ∎

**Lemma 17.9** (Energy estimate on a compact region.) Let Ω′ and t′ be as in Lemma 17.8, T ≥ T_2 and
O_T := Ω′ ∩ {t′ ≤ T}, which is compact. There is C such that ‖u‖_(H¹(O_T)) ≤ C ‖Pu‖_(L²(O_T)) for u ∈ C^∞(Ō_T)
vanishing near {t^♭ = T_0}, and ‖v‖_(H¹(O_T)) ≤ C ‖P*v‖_(L²(O_T)) for v ∈ C^∞(Ō_T) vanishing near {t^♭ = T_1},
{r = r_0} and {t′ = T}; uniformly for ε_P small, with d_0 = 2.

*Proof.* Let Y_♭ := −∇t^♭, which is future timelike and of class C^(d_0−1), Ŷ_♭ := Y_♭/(Y_♭ t^♭), and
X := e^(−2Φt^♭) Y_♭. By Lemma 17.4, K_X = e^(−2Φt^♭)(K_(Y_♭) + 2Φ T(Y_♭, Y_♭)), and by Lemma 17.5 and
compactness, T(Y_♭, Y_♭)(ζ) ≥ c|ζ|² on Ō_T. The faces with u ≠ 0 nearby are {t^♭ = T_1}, {r = r_0} and {t′ = T}, with
∇φ equal to −∇t^♭, ∇r and −∇t′, all future timelike (Lemma 15.35 and Lemma 17.8); the boundary terms are
≥ 0 by Lemma 17.5. The first- and zeroth-order terms of P − P_□ contribute at most
C e^(−2Φt^♭)(|du|² + |u||du|), and Lemma 17.6 with Y = Ŷ_♭ and τ = t^♭ bounds ∫ e^(−2Φt^♭)|u|² by
4Φ⁻² ∫ e^(−2Φt^♭)|Ŷ_♭ u|², the only face with Ŷ_♭ φ > 0 being the initial one. For Φ large this gives the first
estimate, as in Lemma 17.8. For P* use −e^(2Φt^♭) Y_♭ and the reverse inequality of Lemma 17.6. ∎

**Proposition 17.10** (Energy estimates on slabs.) Let α < −1/2 + p̄_1 and Ω′ = Ω_(T_0,T_1), T_0 ≥ 1. There
is C, uniform for ε_P small with d_0 = 2, such that for u ∈ D(Ω′) and v ∈ D_*(Ω′)

    ‖u‖_(H^(1,2α)(Ω′)) ≤ C ‖Pu‖_(H^(0,2α+2)(Ω′)),     ‖v‖_(H^(1,−2α−2)(Ω′)) ≤ C ‖P*v‖_(H^(0,−2α)(Ω′)).    (17.6)

The same holds on Ω′ ∩ {t′ ≤ T} for T ≥ T_2, with {t′ = T} a further final face, and for P^ext on the slabs
{T_0 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T_1, r ≥ r^♯} of Lemma 17.2, T_0 ≥ 1 − η_0.

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 8.1 and (8.23)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* Let χ = χ(t′) equal 1 for t′ ≤ T_2 and 0 for t′ ≥ T_2 + 1. For u: ‖χu‖_(H¹) ≤ C‖u‖_(H¹(O_(T_2+1))) ≤ C‖Pu‖ by
Lemma 17.9, the weights being bounded on O_(T_2+1). (1 − χ)u ∈ D(Ω′) is supported in {x_I ≤ δ_I}, so by
Lemma 17.8 (i), ‖(1 − χ)u‖_(H^(1,2α)) ≤ C(‖Pu‖ + ‖[P, χ]u‖_(H^(0,2α+2))), and [P, χ]u is supported in O_(T_2+1)
with norm at most C‖u‖_(H¹(O_(T_2+1))). For v, in the reverse order: Lemma 17.8 (ii) bounds v on
Ω′ ∩ {t′ ≥ T_2}, which contains the support of [P*, χ]v; then Lemma 17.9 applied to χv, which vanishes near
{t′ = T_2 + 1}, bounds χv. On the extended slabs the proofs apply verbatim, by Lemma 17.2 (iii)–(iv), with
(17.2) holding at 2δ′, so that the coefficient of Lemma 17.8 is a = −2(2α+1) + 4(p̄_1 − 2δ′) = 8δ′ in
place of 12δ′. ∎

### 17.3 Solvability on slabs

Throughout, α < −1/2 + p̄_1, and h is a fibre inner product equal to h_I of (17.2) near ℐ⁺ (patched with the
standard one by a partition of unity; the conditions are convex in the Gram matrix). P* is the adjoint of P (or of
P^ext) for |dg| and h. Changing the density from |dt dx| (Section 15.9.1) to |dg| = μ|dt dx| adds to σ_1(Im_h P) the
term (1/2) H_G log μ, which vanishes at the radial sets, where 𝖧 = 0; so the thresholds below are those of Chapter 16.
R := ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) is the outgoing radial set over ℐ⁺, and R_([a,b]) := R ∩ {a ≤ t_* ≤ b}.

#### 17.3.1 Radial estimates at ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out) localised in time

We use the eb-coordinates of Section 15.7 near ℐ⁺: ρ_+ = t_*⁻¹, x′_I = (t_*/r)^(1/2), ρ := σ_eb⁻¹, ξ̂, η̂,
ℓ := G_eb = x′_I^(−2) ρ_+^(−2) G and 𝖧 := ρ H_ℓ ((15.15)), as in Proposition 16.13 and Proposition 16.14. For
κ > 0 put

    F := t_* − κ x′_I^(2ℓ_I).

x′_I^(2ℓ_I) has bounded eb-derivatives of every order, so functions of F are admissible factors of a commutant.

**Lemma 17.11** (A time function adapted to R.) Let t̄ > 1. There are κ, x_0 > 0 and C, depending on t̄,
such that on U_F := {|ξ̂| ≤ 1/2, x′_I ≤ x_0, 1/2 ≤ t_* ≤ t̄} in ^(eb)S*M, for P with ε_P ≤ 1,

    𝖧F = h_F − t_* ρ² ℓ,     h_F = t_* ((1/2) ξ̂² + |η̂|² + (1/4) x′_I² ξ̂²) + x′_I^(2ℓ_I) h̃_F,     h̃_F ≥ (1/2) κ ℓ_I,
    (17.7)

with h̃_F of class C^(d_0−2) with bounded eb-derivatives.

*Proof.* In eb-coordinates σ_eb is dual to ρ_+∂_(ρ_+), so H_ℓ ρ_+ = ρ_+ ∂_(σ_eb) ℓ and 𝖧t_* = −t_* ρ ∂_(σ_eb) ℓ. For
Ḡ_eb = (1/2) ξ(ξ − 2σ) + |η|² + (1/4) x′_I² ξ² ((15.13)), −∂_σ Ḡ_eb = ξ, and
ρ² Ḡ_eb = (1/2) ξ̂(ξ̂ − 2) + |η̂|² + (1/4) x′_I² ξ̂², so

    ξ̂ = (1/2) ξ̂² + |η̂|² + (1/4) x′_I² ξ̂² − ρ² Ḡ_eb.

Put d := ℓ − Ḡ_eb; by (15.30) and Lemma 15.41 (a), d ∈ x′_I^(2ℓ_I) C^(d_0−1) P^[2], with norm bounded for
ε_P ≤ 1. Hence

    𝖧t_* = t_* ((1/2) ξ̂² + |η̂|² + (1/4) x′_I² ξ̂²) − t_* ρ² ℓ + t_* (ρ² d − ρ ∂_σ d),

and the last term is x′_I^(2ℓ_I) times a function bounded by C_d t_* on the cosphere bundle. By (15.16) and
(15.30), x′_I⁻¹ 𝖧x′_I = ξ̂ − 1 + O(x′_I^(2ℓ_I)), so 𝖧(x′_I^(2ℓ_I)) = 2ℓ_I x′_I^(2ℓ_I)(ξ̂ − 1 + O(x′_I^(2ℓ_I))).
Therefore (17.7) holds with

    h̃_F = 2κℓ_I (1 − ξ̂) + t_* x′_I^(−2ℓ_I) (ρ² d − ρ ∂_σ d) + κ O(x′_I^(2ℓ_I)),

and h̃_F ≥ κℓ_I − C_d t̄ − Cκ x_0^(2ℓ_I) ≥ (1/2) κℓ_I on U_F for κ := 4C_d t̄/ℓ_I and x_0 small. ∎

So 𝖧F is, up to a multiple of ℓ, a sum of squares of symbols on a full neighbourhood of R at bounded times, on and off
the characteristic set: h_F = Σ_i c_i² with c_i among (t_*/2)^(1/2) ξ̂, t_*^(1/2) η̂_j, (1/2) t_*^(1/2) x′_I ξ̂ and
x′_I^(ℓ_I) h̃_F^(1/2). For t^♭ in place of F this fails: at x_I = 0, 𝖧t^♭ = t_* ξ̂, which is negative off the
characteristic set near R (the paragraph after Proposition 16.14).

**Proposition 17.12** (Localised radial estimates at R.) Let t_− < t_+ and ω_0 ∈ (0, 1] with
t_− − ω_0 ≥ 1/2, let s > s_0 be constants, and suppose (17.2) holds with 2δ′ in place of δ′ on
R_([t_−−ω_0, t_++ω_0]) (for P^ext below t_* = 1, Lemma 17.2 (iii)). There are B, E, E_±, G ∈ C_b^∞Ψ⁰_(e3b) such
that

(1) their operator wave front sets lie in any given neighbourhood of R_([t_−−ω_0, t_++ω_0]);

(2) their Schwartz kernels lie in 𝒦 × 𝒦 for any given compact neighbourhood 𝒦 of ℐ⁺ ∩ {t_− − ω_0 ≤ t_* ≤ t_+ + ω_0};

(3) B is elliptic at R_([t_−,t_+]);

(4) WF′(E_−) ⊂ {t_* ≤ t_−}, WF′(E_+) ⊂ {t_* ≥ t_+}, and WF′(E) ∩ R = ∅;

and such that, in the strong sense and uniformly for ε_P small,

    ‖Bu‖_(s,2α) ≤ C (‖GPu‖_(s−1,2α+2) + ‖E_−u‖_(s,2α) + ‖Eu‖_(s,2α) + ‖χ̃u‖_(s_0,2α)),    (17.8)

    ‖Bv‖_(s,−2α−2) ≤ C (‖GP*v‖_(s−1,−2α) + ‖E_+v‖_(s,−2α−2) + ‖χ̃v‖_(s_0,−2α−2)),    (17.9)

with χ̃ as in Proposition 16.14 and the norms of H^(·,(2β,0))_(e3b) near ℐ⁺ at finite times.

(17.8) is the sink estimate of Proposition 16.14 localised to t_* ≤ t_+, with no error term at late times;
(17.9) is the estimate for the adjoint at R, which is then a radial source, propagating backward in time. In
the proof of [Hin26c, Proposition 8.3] the first is taken from [Hin26c, Proposition 7.9] with a finite final time, and
the second is left to the reader.

*Proof.* We follow the pattern of Section 16.3 at R, with W′ := x′_I² ρ_+², ρ and 𝖧 as above, A := A_I the frame of
h_I, and the weight w := x′_I^(2α) for (17.8), w* := x′_I^(2α*) with α* := −α − 1 for (17.9). Take
t̄ := t_+ + 2 in Lemma 17.11, and fix x_1 ∈ (0, x_0] with κ x_1^(2ℓ_I) ≤ ω_0/8.

*The sets of the iteration.* Lemma 16.5 needs, for every open U between a compact set Γ and a fixed
neighbourhood U_0 of it, a commutant supported in U and E-sets in U ∖ Γ. We take T_− := t_− − ω_0/4,
T_+ := t_+ + ω_0/4, and Γ := R_([T_−,t_+]) for (17.8), Γ := R_([t_−,T_+]) for (17.9); both are compact
and contain R_([t_−,t_+]). U_0 is an open neighbourhood of Γ inside the neighbourhood of (1) and inside
{x′_I < x_1, |ξ̂| < 1/2, 1/2 < t_* < t̄}, and so small that Q_ε ≥ 4δ′ on it (see below).
Given U with Γ ⊂ U ⊂ U_0, take λ ∈ (0, ω_0/4], and let the commutant be ǎ = ρ^(−s+1/2) Ψ χ_∞ with

    Ψ := ψ(𝔐_Σ ρ²ℓ) ψ(𝔐_R q) ψ(𝔐 x′_I) ψ_−(F) ψ_+(F),        q := ξ̂² + |η̂|²,
    ψ_−(F) := η_t((F − T_−)/λ),   ψ_+(F) := η_t((t_+ − F)/λ)        for (17.8),
    ψ_−(F) := η_t((F − t_−)/λ),   ψ_+(F) := η_t((T_+ − F)/λ)        for (17.9),

η_t as in Proposition 16.14. As η_t = 0 on (−∞, −1/2], η_t = 1 on [−1/4, ∞) and η_t′ ≠ 0 only on (−1/2, −1/4), the
time factors equal 1 on Γ and vanish unless T_− − λ/2 ≤ F ≤ t_+ + λ/2, resp. t_− − λ/2 ≤ F ≤ T_+ + λ/2. For
𝔐_R ≥ 4 and 𝔐 ≥ x_1⁻¹, on supp ψ(𝔐_R q) ψ(𝔐 x′_I) we have |ξ̂| ≤ 1/2, x′_I ≤ x_1 and
0 ≤ t_* − F = κ x′_I^(2ℓ_I) ≤ ω_0/8, so that supp Ψ lies in U_F ∩ {t_− − 3ω_0/8 ≤ t_* ≤ t_+ + ω_0/2}, which is compact.
On R, q = x′_I = 0, F = t_* and ℓ = 0, R lying in the characteristic set; so Ψ = 1 on Γ ⊃ R_([t_−,t_+]). The closed sets
supp ψ(𝔐_Σ ρ²ℓ) ψ(𝔐_R q) ψ(𝔐 x′_I) ψ_−(F) ψ_+(F) at fibre infinity decrease, as λ → 0 and 𝔐_Σ, 𝔐_R, 𝔐 → ∞, to the
set where x′_I = 0, q = 0, ℓ = 0 and T_− ≤ t_* ≤ t_+ (resp. t_− ≤ t_* ≤ T_+), which is Γ: at x′_I = 0 over ℐ⁺ the
characteristic set is |η̂|² = (1/2) ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) (Lemma 15.16 (1)), and q = 0 there is R. By compactness, for λ
small and 𝔐_Σ, 𝔐_R, 𝔐 large, supp Ψ lies in U near fibre infinity. In (16.9), which is used below, ℓ_I
denotes, as there, the principal symbol of the imaginary part of the conjugated operator, not the decay order at ℐ⁺.

*(17.8), with ς = 1.* (16.9) gives
H_ℓ(ǎ_ε²) + 2ǎ_ε² ℓ_I = ρ^(−2s) φ_ε² (−Ψ² Q_ε + 𝖧(Ψ²)), and at R, as in Proposition 16.14,

    Q_ε = 4A⁻¹(Re_(h_I) p_1)A − 2 − 4α ≥ 4(p̄_1 − 2δ′) − 2 − 4α = 8δ′,

by (17.2) with 2δ′, as 4(p̄_1 − 1/2 − α) = 16δ′; by continuity Q_ε ≥ 4δ′ on U_0 when U_0 is small. The
factors ψ(𝔐_Σ ρ²ℓ), ψ(𝔐_R q) and ψ(𝔐 x′_I) contribute as in Proposition 16.14: j_ε ℓ, and +e*e terms supported in
{q ≥ (2𝔐_R)⁻¹} ∪ {x′_I ≥ (2𝔐)⁻¹}, which give E. For the time factors, by the chain rule and (17.7),

    𝖧(ψ_−(F)²) = (2/λ) ψ_− η_t′((F − T_−)/λ) (h_F − t_* ρ² ℓ),
    𝖧(ψ_+(F)²) = −(2/λ) ψ_+ η_t′((t_+ − F)/λ) (h_F − t_* ρ² ℓ).

The part with t_* ρ² ℓ is of the form j_ε ℓ (Lemma 16.4). The part with h_F = Σ_i c_i² is, up to its sign,
Σ_i ((2/λ)^(1/2) (ψ_± η_t′)^(1/2) c_i)², a finite sum of squares of symbols, since (η_t η_t′)^(1/2) is smooth. For
ψ_+ it enters with the sign −: a term −b′*b′, so no error term arises at late times. For ψ_− it enters with the sign +:
a term +e_−*e_−, supported where η_t′((F − T_−)/λ) ≠ 0, so where T_− − λ/2 < F < T_− − λ/4, and hence, on supp Ψ,
t_* < T_− − λ/4 + ω_0/8 < t_− − ω_0/8; this gives E_−. The localiser φ_E of the pattern (6) is taken supported, near
fibre infinity, in U ∩ ({q ≥ (4𝔐_R)⁻¹} ∪ {x′_I ≥ (4𝔐)⁻¹} ∪ {T_− − 3λ/4 ≤ F ≤ T_− − λ/8}). The first two sets are
closed and miss R, where q = x′_I = 0. On the third, t_* ≤ F + ω_0/8 ≤ t_− − ω_0/8 − λ/8 within U_0, and on R it
meets only t_* ≤ T_− − λ/8 < T_−. So the set of (6) misses Γ, as Lemma 16.5 requires, and its union over the
finitely many U of the iteration is the union of a closed set missing R and a closed set in {t_* ≤ t_− − ω_0/8}. Let
E be elliptic on the first with WF′(E) ∩ R = ∅, and E_− the quantisation of a symbol supported in {t_* ≤ t_−} and
elliptic on the second; this is (4). The operator E*E + E_−*E_− is elliptic on the union, so it may serve as the E
of Lemma 16.5, and ‖(E*E + E_−*E_−)u‖_(s,2α) ≤ C(‖Eu‖_(s,2α) + ‖E_−u‖_(s,2α)). Then
Lemma 16.4–Lemma 16.6 give (17.8).

*(17.9), with ς = −1.* For P* the conjugated operator has 𝔭′_(P*) = −𝔭′ (Lemma 16.1, as
Im_h P* = −Im_h P), so (16.9) gives

    −(H_ℓ(ǎ_ε²) + 2ǎ_ε² ℓ_(I,P*)) = ρ^(−2s) φ_ε² (−Ψ² Q*_ε − 𝖧(Ψ²)),
    Q*_ε := −(2s_ε − 1) ρ⁻¹𝖧ρ − 2A⁻¹(𝔭′ + (1/2) 𝖧 log W′ + 𝖧 log w*)A.

At R, ρ⁻¹𝖧ρ = 0, 𝔭′ = −2 Re_(h_I) p_1 (Lemma 16.12), 𝖧 log W′ = 2x′_I⁻¹ 𝖧x′_I + 2ρ_+⁻¹ 𝖧ρ_+ = −2 and
𝖧 log w* = −2α* = 2α + 2 ((15.16)). So Q*_ε = 4A⁻¹(Re_(h_I) p_1)A + 2 − 4α − 4, the same quantity as Q_ε in
(17.8), and positive; near R the term with ρ⁻¹𝖧ρ is small, as in Section 16.3. Now the localisers enter
with the opposite sign. As 𝖧q ≤ −q and 𝖧x′_I ≤ −x′_I/2 near R (Proposition 16.14), the factors ψ(𝔐_R q) and
ψ(𝔐 x′_I) give −b′*b′ terms: for −𝖧 the set R is a radial source, and no error term arises from them.
ψ(𝔐_Σ ρ²ℓ) gives j_ε ℓ. Of the time factors, ψ_− gives −b′*b′ and ψ_+ gives +e_+*e_+, supported where
T_+ + λ/4 < F < T_+ + λ/2, hence in {t_* > t_+ + ω_0/4}, as t_* ≥ F; this is E_+. The localiser φ_E is taken
supported, near fibre infinity, in U ∩ {T_+ + λ/8 ≤ F ≤ T_+ + 3λ/4}, which lies in {t_* > t_+} and meets R only where
t_* > T_+, so misses Γ. E_+ is the quantisation of a symbol supported in {t_* > t_+} and elliptic on the union of these
sets over the finitely many U of the iteration, a closed subset of {t_* ≥ t_+ + ω_0/4}; this is (4).
Lemma 16.4–Lemma 16.6 hold with ς = −1, as Lemma 14.44, on which they rest, allows either sign; with
E_+ as the E of Lemma 16.5 they give (17.9).

Both estimates use the operator only through the pattern, so they hold for P^ext near {t_* ≤ 1}, and for systems
P ⊗ Id − Q with Q of first order whose principal symbol vanishes at R, as in Lemma 16.23. The constants depend on
P through finitely many coefficient norms and the margins, which are uniform for ε_P small. ∎

#### 17.3.2 Regularity on slabs

Below, 𝗌 is a **slab order**: 𝗌 ∈ C^∞(^(e3b)S*M) with ±𝖧𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ^± over the region considered, and 𝗌 constant
near R. Admissible order functions (Definition 15.44) are slab orders over Ω_*, by Proposition 15.43 (2) and (5); so
are constants.

*The order on the extension region.* Proposition 15.43 (2) concerns Ω_* only, while Lemma 17.13 (a) at T_0 = 1
propagates through the collar {1 − η_0/2 < t^♭ < 1}, part of which lies in {t_* < 1}, and over {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r_0}. There
the admissible order is extended by its own formula (15.32): 𝗌 = s_in − (s_in − s_out)χ, with
χ = ψ_0(x_I) χ_I + (1 − ψ_0(x_I)) χ_ι. The second term is supported in

    Ω_ι ∩ {ϱ < ε_ι δ} ⊂ {r > (ε_ι δ)⁻¹, t_* ≥ r/C_ι}

(Section 15.13.2, with ϱ = r⁻¹ and ρ_K = r/t_* ≤ C_ι on Ω_ι), which, after decreasing ε_ι so that (C_ι ε_ι δ)⁻¹ > 1,
meets neither {t_* ≤ 1} nor {r ≤ r_0} (as (ε_ι δ)⁻¹ > r_h + 1). The factor χ_I is a function of the eb-fibre variables
ξ̂, |η̂|² and σ_eb²/|ν|²_eb alone, defined and invariant under translation in t_* for t_* ≥ 1/2. So on {t_* ≥ 1/2}
outside Ω_*, 𝗌 = s_in − (s_in − s_out) ψ_0(x_I) χ_I, which is s_in where x_I ≥ ε_I (in particular over
{r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r_0} at these times). It is a slab order there: where it is constant, trivially; near ℐ⁺,
±𝖧(ψ_0(x_I) χ_I) ≥ 0 on ∂Σ^± by the monotonicity argument of Section 15.13.2 (ψ_0′ ≤ 0 with 𝖧x_I ≤ −x_I/4, and
φ′(ξ̂) 𝖧ξ̂ ≥ 0), which uses only Lemma 15.45 and Lemma 15.46 near ℐ⁺. Their proofs use only the bounds
𝖧^eb − 𝖧^0 = O(x_I^(2ℓ_I)) on ξ̂ and O(x_I^(1+2ℓ_I)) on x_I, uniformly in t_*, which Lemma 17.2 (ii) provides for
P^ext on {t_* ≥ 1/2}, the coefficients of P^ext − P_0 being small there in the norms of Definition 15.36. "Slab order"
in Proposition 17.14, Proposition 17.17, Proposition 17.19 and Theorem 17.26 refers to this extension.

Two slabs Ω_1 ⊂ Ω_2 are **nested with room δ > 0** if they have the same initial face and each final face of Ω_1 lies
at distance at least δ (in t^♭, resp. in r) inside Ω_2. Typical choices are Ω_1 = Ω_(T_0,T_1) and

    Ω_2 = Ω^♯_(T_0,T_1) := {T_0 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T_1 + 1, r ≥ r^♯}

with P^ext; or Ω_1 = Ω_(T_0,T_1−δ) ∩ {r ≥ r_0 + δ} and Ω_2 = Ω_(T_0,T_1). The spaces, Lemma 17.3,
Lemma 17.8, Lemma 17.9 and Proposition 17.10 hold for these domains with the same proofs, {r = r_0 + δ} and
{r = r^♯} being spacelike final faces (Lemma 17.2 (iv)).

**Lemma 17.13** (Regularity on slabs.) (a) Let Ω_1 ⊂ Ω_2 be nested with room δ, with initial face
{t^♭ = T_0}, T_0 ≥ 1 − η_0/2, let 𝗌_0 < 𝗌 be slab orders, and let u ∈ H^(𝗌_0,2α)(Ω_2)^(•,−) with
Pu ∈ H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)(Ω_2)^(•,−) (P^ext where defined). Then u|_(Ω_1) ∈ H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω_1)^(•,−) and

    ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω_1)^(•,−)) ≤ C (‖Pu‖_(H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)(Ω_2)^(•,−)) + ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌_0,2α)(Ω_2)^(•,−))).

(b) Let Ω_1 = Ω_(T_0,T_1) ⊂ Ω_3 := Ω_(T_0−δ,T_1) (the same final faces; T_0 − δ ≥ 1 − η_0), let s_0 < s be constants,
and let v ∈ H^(s_0,−2α−2)(Ω_3)^(−,•) with P*v ∈ H^(s−1,−2α)(Ω_3)^(−,•). Then v|_(Ω_1) ∈ H^(s,−2α−2)(Ω_1)^(−,•), with the
corresponding estimate.

The constants are uniform for ε_P small, with d_0 depending only on the orders.

*Proof.* (a) Let ũ be an extension of u supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, and f ∈ H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)_e the minimal extension of Pu.
Let U_2 be the union of the interior of Ω_2 relative to its final faces and of {t^♭ < T_0}, near the slab. On U_2,
Pũ = f: U_2 is the open set to which the spaces of Ω_2 restrict, and this is what Pu ∈ H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)(Ω_2)^(•,−) means. So
for operators with Schwartz kernels in U_2 × U_2 the microlocal estimates below see Pũ only through f. Let ω_0 be as
below; fix a cut-off χ_1 equal to 1 near Ω_1 and supported in U_2 ∩ {t^♭ > T_0 − ω_0/2}, and let all operators be
carried by such cut-offs. We control ũ microlocally at order 𝗌 at every point of ^(e3b)S*M over supp χ_1 (a compact
set in the compactified bundle).

Off the characteristic set we use the elliptic estimate (Theorem 14.43). On it over M°: by Proposition 15.42 and
Lemma 17.2 (iv), the backward curve reaches {t^♭ < T_0}, where ũ = 0, in finite time, and stays in
{r > r_0 − δ}, as dr is future timelike near {r = r_0}, so that r cannot decrease along a backward curve there.
Propagation (Theorem 14.49, at the order 𝗌, with 𝖧𝗌 ≤ 0) controls ũ there. Over ℐ⁺ off R: the curves of
Lemma 15.16 (1) (i), (iii) reach {t_* < T_0} backward (below t_* = 1 the flow over ℐ⁺ is still given by
(15.17), the normal form of P^ext being that of P_0 there); propagation applies as before. At
R_([T_0, T_1+δ/2]) we use Proposition 17.12, (17.8), with

    t_− := T_0 − ω_0/2,     t_+ := T_1 + δ/2,     ω_0 := min(δ/2, η_0/4),

at the constant value of 𝗌 near R. Its E_− quantises e_−, whose symbol is supported in {t_* ≤ t_−} (proof of
Proposition 17.12), and its Schwartz kernel lies in 𝒦 × 𝒦, which does not place it in {t^♭ < T_0}². So quantise e_−
with Schwartz kernel within ω_0/8 of the diagonal in t_*, as for E_+ in (b); this changes E_− by an operator of order −∞
with kernel in 𝒦 × 𝒦, which the low-order term of (17.8) absorbs, and the kernel then lies in
{t_* ≤ t_− + ω_0/8}². Taking 𝒦 so small that t^♭ = t_* − t_*^(1+ℓ_I) x_I^(2ℓ_I) ≤ t_* on it (Lemma 15.35 (a),
Lemma 17.2 (iv)), and as t_− + ω_0/8 = T_0 − 3ω_0/8, the kernel lies in {t^♭ ≤ T_0 − 3ω_0/8}², where ũ = 0, so
E_−ũ = 0. Its E is microsupported in a punctured neighbourhood of R at times in [t_− − ω_0, t_+ + ω_0], from whose
points the backward curves reach {t^♭ < T_0}, as above; by compactness of WF′(E) and the local boundedness of the
entrance times (Section 14.14.1, (O)), propagation bounds ‖Eũ‖_𝗌. The finitely many operators so obtained are
jointly elliptic over supp χ_1, and Lemma 14.29 (c) gives

    ‖χ_1 ũ‖_(𝗌,2α) ≤ C (‖χ_1′ f‖_(𝗌−1,2α+2) + ‖χ_1′ ũ‖_(𝗌_0,2α)).

χ_1 ũ is an extension of u|_(Ω_1) supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, and χ_1′f, χ_1′ũ depend only on Pu and u (the cut-off χ_1′
being supported in U_2), with norms at most C times the quotient norms. This is (a), in the strong sense, since each
estimate used holds in it.

(b) The same with −𝖧. Let ṽ be an extension of v supported in F_3 := Ω ∩ {t^♭ ≤ T_1, r ≥ r_0}; P*ṽ is controlled on
the set V_3 formed by the interior of Ω_3 relative to its initial face, together with {t^♭ > T_1} ∪ {r < r_0}, where
ṽ = 0. Propagation for the backward problem is propagation for −P*, whose rescaled Hamilton field is −𝖧; it applies to
constant orders. Every forward curve from a point of the characteristic set over Ω_1 either reaches
{t^♭ > T_1} ∪ {r < r_0} in finite time, or enters any given neighbourhood of R_([T_0,T_1]). Indeed t^♭ increases along
it; if it stays in the slab, its ω-limit set is non-empty, compact and invariant; a point of it over M° would have its
orbit in the limit set with t^♭ strictly increasing there, against t^♭ being constant (equal to lim t^♭) on the limit
set; so the limit set lies over ℐ⁺ at the time t_∞ := lim t^♭ ∈ [T_0, T_1], where 𝖧t_* = t_* ξ̂ = 0, so ξ̂ = 0
and |η̂|² = (1/2) ξ̂(2 − ξ̂) = 0: it lies in R. Over ℐ⁺ the curves (iii) of Lemma 15.16 reach {t_* > T_1} and the
curves (i) tend to R. At R_([T_0−δ/2, T_1]) use (17.9) with t_− := T_0 − δ/2 and t_+ := T_1 + ω_0/2 (ω_0 as in
(a)). Its E_+ quantises e_+, whose symbol is supported in {t_* > t_+} (proof of Proposition 17.12), and its Schwartz
kernel lies in 𝒦 × 𝒦. Neither places the kernel in {t^♭ > T_1}: the operator wave front set does not locate a kernel,
and 𝒦 covers ℐ⁺ ∩ {t_− − ω_0 ≤ t_* ≤ t_+ + ω_0}. So quantise e_+ with Schwartz kernel within ω_0/8 of the diagonal in
t_*, as is done for E after Proposition 16.14; this changes E_+ by an operator of order −∞ with kernel in 𝒦 × 𝒦,
which the low-order term of (17.9) absorbs, and the kernel now lies in (𝒦 ∩ {t_* > t_+ − ω_0/8})². 𝒦 is any
compact neighbourhood of a compact part of ℐ⁺, where x_I = 0, so we take it so small that
t_*^(1+ℓ_I) x_I^(2ℓ_I) < ω_0/4 on 𝒦. Then on 𝒦 ∩ {t_* > t_+ − ω_0/8},

    t^♭ = t_* − t_*^(1+ℓ_I) x_I^(2ℓ_I) > T_1 + ω_0/8,

where ṽ = 0, so E_+ṽ = 0. Conclude as in (a). ∎

#### 17.3.3 Solvability

**Proposition 17.14** (Solvability of forward problems on slabs.) Let α < −1/2 + p̄_1, Ω′ = Ω_(T_0,T_1) with
T_0 ≥ 1 (P^ext below t^♭ = 1), and 𝗌 a slab order. There are d_0, depending only on 𝗌 (and, in (i), on s′), and C,
uniform for ε_P small, such that:

(i) (*uniqueness*) if u ∈ H^(s′,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) for some s′ ∈ ℝ and Pu = 0, then u = 0;

(ii) (*existence*) for every f ∈ H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)(Ω′)^(•,−) there is u ∈ H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) with Pu = f and

    ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−)) ≤ C ‖f‖_(H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)(Ω′)^(•,−)).    (17.10)

The same holds for P* and backward problems on H^(s,−2α−2)(Ω′)^(−,•), s constant, and for the systems of
Section 17.4 and of Proposition 17.12.

This is [Hin26c, Corollary 8.2 and Proposition 8.3] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (i) For δ > 0 small let Ω_δ := Ω_(T_0,T_1−δ) ∩ {r ≥ r_0 + δ}, nested in Ω′ with room δ. By Lemma 17.13
(a) at the constant orders s′ < m′, u|_(Ω_δ) ∈ H^(m′,2α)(Ω_δ)^(•,−) for every m′ > s′, hence
u|_(Ω_δ) ∈ H^(2,2α)(Ω_δ)^(•,−). By Lemma 17.3 (c), D(Ω_δ) is dense in H^(2,2α)(Ω_δ)^(•,−); both sides of the
first estimate (17.6) on Ω_δ are continuous in that norm (P maps it to H^(0,2α+2), whose quotient norm is the
L²-norm on the slab). So ‖u‖_(H^(1,2α)(Ω_δ)) ≤ C‖Pu‖ = 0, and u = 0 on Ω_δ for every δ.

(ii) *Step 1: weak solutions in L².* Let Ω^♯ := Ω^♯_(T_0,T_1) and let f^♯ be the restriction to Ω^♯ of the minimal
extension of f in H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)_e; assume first inf 𝗌 ≥ 0, so that f^♯ ∈ H^(−1,2α+2)(Ω^♯)^(•,−) with norm ≤ C‖f‖. For
v ∈ D_*(Ω^♯), by Lemma 17.3 (a),

    |⟨f^♯, v⟩| ≤ C ‖f‖ ‖v‖_(H^(1,−2α−2)(Ω^♯)^(−,•)) ≤ C′ ‖f‖ ‖v‖_(H^(1,−2α−2)(Ω^♯)) ≤ C″ ‖f‖ ‖P*v‖_(H^(0,−2α)(Ω^♯)),

the second inequality by Seeley's extension E_0 of Lemma 17.3 (b), which is bounded from the slab norm, and the
third by (17.6) for the adjoint of P^ext on Ω^♯. So P*v ↦ ⟨f^♯, v⟩ is a bounded functional on P*D_*(Ω^♯) in
the L²-norm. By the Hahn–Banach theorem and the Riesz representation theorem there is u^♯ ∈ H^(0,2α)(Ω^♯), with
‖u^♯‖ ≤ C‖f‖ and ⟨u^♯, P*v⟩ = ⟨f^♯, v⟩ for v ∈ D_*(Ω^♯). Extended by zero, u^♯ is supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, and for
v ∈ D_* (a test function on M) ⟨Pu^♯, v⟩ = ⟨u^♯, P*v⟩. So Pu^♯ and f^♯ agree on D_*(Ω^♯), which contains the
C_c^∞-functions supported in {t^♭ < T_1 + 1, r > r^♯}: Pu^♯ = f^♯ on Ω^♯.

*Step 2: regularity.* Lemma 17.13 (a) with Ω′ ⊂ Ω^♯ (room 1, resp. r_0 − r^♯) and 𝗌_0 := min(0, inf 𝗌) − 1 gives
u := u^♯|_(Ω′) ∈ H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) and (17.10). By (i) it is the solution.

*Step 3: the backward problem at nonnegative orders.* The same argument applies with the roles exchanged. For
g ∈ H^(m_1−1,−2α)(Ω′)^(−,•), m_1 ≥ 1 an integer, let Ω_3 := Ω_(T_0−δ,T_1) (with P^ext if T_0 − δ < 1; δ := η_0/2) and
let g_3 be the restriction of the minimal extension, in L². For u ∈ D(Ω_3),

    |⟨u, g_3⟩| ≤ ‖u‖_(H^(0,2α)) ‖g_3‖ ≤ C ‖Pu‖_(H^(0,2α+2)) ‖g‖

by (17.6) on Ω_3, the H⁰ quotient norm being the L²-norm, so that no extension operator is needed. The
Hahn–Banach theorem gives v_3 ∈ H^(0,−2α−2)(Ω_3) with P*v_3 = g_3 (by the density of D(Ω_3), Lemma 17.3 (c)), and
Lemma 17.13 (b) gives S_* g := v_3|_(Ω′) ∈ H^(m_1,−2α−2)(Ω′)^(−,•) with ‖S_* g‖ ≤ C‖g‖. Uniqueness for the backward
problem is (i) with the roles exchanged. So S_* is the solution operator, and S_* P*v = v for v ∈ D_*(Ω′).

*Step 4: negative orders.* Let inf 𝗌 < 0 and m ∈ ℕ with −m < inf 𝗌 − 1. Work on Ω^♯ with
f^♯ ∈ H^(−m−1,2α+2)(Ω^♯)^(•,−). For g ∈ H^(m,−2α)(Ω^♯)^(−,•) put Λ(g) := ⟨f^♯, S_* g⟩, with S_* of Step 3 on Ω^♯ (at
the order m_1 = m + 1); |Λ(g)| ≤ C‖f‖‖g‖. By Lemma 17.3 (b) (at m, on Ω^♯) there is
u^♯ ∈ H^(−m,2α)(Ω^♯)^(•,−), ‖u^♯‖ ≤ C‖f‖, with ⟨u^♯, g⟩ = Λ(g). For v ∈ D_*(Ω^♯),

    ⟨Pu^♯, v⟩ = ⟨u^♯, P*v⟩ = ⟨f^♯, S_* P*v⟩ = ⟨f^♯, v⟩,

so Pu^♯ = f^♯ as in Step 1. Step 2 with 𝗌_0 := −m concludes.

The constants depend on P through finitely many coefficient norms and the structural margins (the timelike conditions,
the threshold, the dynamics), uniformly for ε_P small; for the systems of Section 17.4 the same margins hold, the
coupling being of first order with principal symbol vanishing at R and not entering the threshold of Lemma 17.8
(it decays at ℐ⁺). ∎

[Hin26c] proves the step 𝗌 ≥ 1 with its Proposition 7.9 for a finite final time, a case whose proof fails off the
characteristic set (the paragraph after Proposition 16.14); Proposition 17.12 replaces it. [Hin26c, Corollary 8.2]
constructs the H¹-solution by smoothing the coefficients, quoting finite-time solvability of wave equations with smooth
coefficients and passing to a weak limit, and asserts its uniqueness, which [Hin26c, (8.5)], proved for u ∈ H², gives
for solutions in H¹ only after a density argument. Steps 1–3 construct the solution by duality from the energy
estimates for P and P* instead, and (i) proves uniqueness in every H^(s′) by regularity on nested slabs
(Lemma 17.13) and the energy estimate on the dense class (Lemma 17.3 (c)).

### 17.4 b-regularity on slabs, and the tame estimates

#### 17.4.1 Operators on slab spaces

**Lemma 17.15** (Operators, products and words on slab spaces.) Let Ω′ be a slab of Section 17.3 (or of
Section 17.5), 𝗌 an order function and k ∈ ℕ_0; the spaces are those of Section 17.1.1 with any weight.

(a) A differential operator Q of order m whose coefficients, in a fixed frame (products of ∂_(t_*), x_I∂_(x_I) and
x_I∂_ω near ℐ⁺, of coordinate fields elsewhere), lie in C^((d_0;k))_(e;b) on a neighbourhood of Ω′ maps
H^((𝗌;k))(Ω′)^(•,−) to H^((𝗌−m;k))(Ω′)^(•,−), and H^((𝗌;k))(Ω′)^(−,•) to H^((𝗌−m;k))(Ω′)^(−,•), with norm at most C_k
times the coefficient norms; d_0 depends only on 𝗌 and m.

(b) (*Tame products, with room.*) Let Ω′ ⊂ Ω″ be nested with room δ. There are d_0 and d̃, depending only on 𝗌, such
that for all k, 0 ≤ j ≤ k, ℓ ∈ C^((d_0;k))_(e;b) near Ω″ and w ∈ H^((𝗌;k))(Ω″)^(•,−),

    ‖(D^j_([b]) ℓ)(D^(k−j)_([b]) w)‖_(H^𝗌(Ω′)^(•,−))
        ≤ C_k (‖ℓ‖_((d_0;d̃)) ‖w‖_(H^((𝗌;k))(Ω″)^(•,−)) + ‖ℓ‖_((d_0;k)) ‖w‖_(H^((𝗌;d̃))(Ω″)^(•,−))),

with D^j_([b]) as in Definition 14.54 and C_k depending also on δ.

(c) (*Norms through words, with room.*) Let 𝒳 = (X_1, …, X_J), X_J = I, be b-differential operators of order 1
spanning 𝒱_b over a neighbourhood of Ω″, and for a word γ = (γ_1, …, γ_q) ∈ {1, …, J}^q put X^γ := X_(γ_1) ⋯ X_(γ_q)
and |γ| := q. Then ‖X^γ w‖_(H^𝗌(Ω″)^(•,−)) ≤ C ‖w‖_(H^((𝗌;|γ|))(Ω″)^(•,−)), and, for Ω′ ⊂ Ω″ nested with room,

    ‖w‖_(H^((𝗌;k))(Ω′)^(•,−)) ≤ C_k Σ_(|γ|≤k) ‖X^γ w‖_(H^𝗌(Ω″)^(•,−)).

This is [Hin26c, Lemmas 8.7–8.8] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (a) Extend the coefficients by Seeley's operator across the final faces of Ω′ (in t^♭, resp. r, with the other
coordinates as parameters, and successively near the corner, where dt^♭ and dr are independent), as in
Lemma 17.2. The extension is bounded on C^((d_0;k))_(e;b) for all d_0 and k ([Hin26c, Lemma 8.5 (2)], whose proof
is that of Lemma 17.3 (b) with suprema in place of L²-norms: the reflection commutes with the tangential fields,
and j derivatives in the normal variable cost Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(−j)). Call the extended operator Q^♯. If w̃ extends w and
