is supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, then χQ^♯w̃ extends Qw, for a cut-off χ equal to 1 near Ω′, and is supported there;
Lemma 14.31 (a) bounds it. Take the infimum over w̃. The case (−,•) is the same with the initial face.

(b) Let χ_3 be a cut-off equal to 1 near Ω′, supported in the union of {t^♭ < T_0} and of the interior of Ω″ relative to
its final faces, with bounded b-derivatives. For w ∈ H^((𝗌;k))(Ω″)^(•,−) the distribution z := χ_3 w̃ does not depend
on the extension w̃ supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, as all such extensions agree where χ_3 ≠ 0. So, taking w̃ minimal for the
norm of order (𝗌;i), ‖z‖_((𝗌;i)) ≤ C_i ‖w‖_(H^((𝗌;i))(Ω″)^(•,−)) for every i, with the same z (Lemma 14.29 (a) for
multiplication by χ_3). z extends w|_(Ω′). Let ℓ^♯ be the Seeley extension of ℓ, and χ_1, χ_2 cut-offs equal to 1 near
Ω′ with χ_2 = 1 near supp χ_1 and χ_3 = 1 near supp χ_2. Then χ_1 (D^j_([b]) ℓ^♯)(D^(k−j)_([b]) z) extends
(D^j_([b]) ℓ)(D^(k−j)_([b]) w), and Proposition 14.56 with B = χ_1 and B^♯ = χ_2 bounds its H^𝗌-norm by the right
side, the terms with ‖χz‖_((𝗌_0;·)) being bounded by those with 𝗌.

(c) The first bound holds as X^γ w̃ extends X^γ w. For the second, with z as in (b), ‖z‖_((𝗌;k)) is equivalent to
Σ_(|γ|≤k) ‖X^γ z‖_𝗌 ((14.6) and Definition 14.54: two spanning sets give equivalent norms), and by the Leibniz
rule for words X^γ z is a sum of terms χ′ X^β w̃ with |β| ≤ |γ| and χ′ a b-derivative of χ_3, supported where χ_3 is;
each such term is independent of the extension, and its H^𝗌-norm is at most C ‖X^β w‖_(H^𝗌(Ω″)^(•,−)). ∎

[Hin26c, Lemma 8.8 (3)] proves (b) on Ω′ itself, with a crude bound in the middle range of j through the extension
operator of its Lemma 8.7 on integer b-Sobolev spaces, and notes in its footnote 64 that no single extension operator
respects all variable orders. With room, the cut-off χ_3 is such an operator. Room is always available below, as every
slab sits inside a larger one on which P (or P^ext) is given.

#### 17.4.2 The commuted system on slabs

On {r ≥ r^♯} ∩ {1/2 ≤ t_* ≤ t̄} let

    𝒳_sl := (V_1, V_2, Ω_12, …, Ω_34, I),        V_1 := 2t_* ∂_(t_*),     V_2 := x_I∂_(x_I) = −2r∂_r,

with Ω_ab the rotation fields of 𝕊³, as in Section 16.8. It spans 𝒱_b there: near ℐ⁺ the b-vector fields are spanned
by ∂_(t_*), x_I∂_(x_I) and ∂_ω; elsewhere, as r ≥ r^♯ > 0 and t_* ≥ 1/2, ∂_(t_*) = (2t_*)⁻¹ V_1, ∂_r = −(2r)⁻¹ V_2, and
the Ω_ab span the tangent fields of the spheres. Put W := x_I² t_*⁻¹, which near ℐ⁺ is the weight x′_I² ρ_+² of
Section 16.8, and L := W⁻¹P.

**Lemma 17.16** (The commutators on slabs.) For P of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)), the family 𝒳_sl
satisfies condition (C) of Section 16.7 on the region above with R_i = 0: [L, X_i] = Σ_j Q_ij X_j, where Q_ij is
the sum of an operator of order 0 with bounded coefficients and a first-order edge operator whose coefficients lie in
C^((d_0;k−1))_(e;b) and, near ℐ⁺, in x_I C^∞ + x_I^(2ℓ_I) C^((d_0;k−1))_(e;b).

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 7.12] on slabs.

*Proof.* Near ℐ⁺ this is Lemma 16.24 (b), whose proof uses only Lemma 15.37 near ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω, which holds at
finite times. Away from ℐ⁺, [L, X_i] is a second-order operator with coefficients in C^((d_0;k−1)), as X_i
differentiates the coefficients once; writing each coordinate field as Σ_j c_j X_j with smooth c_j gives the form
Σ_j Q_ij X_j, the first-order part of [L, X_i] going into Q_iJ X_J. Patch the two representations with a partition of
unity in x_I. ∎

Consequently, by Lemma 16.19 with 𝔩 = 0 (no loss of derivatives, the case of the radial sets) and with
R_i = 0, for u on a slab and f := Pu the words u^(j) := (X^γ u)_(γ∈𝒲_j) satisfy

    P^(j) u^(j) = W (X^γ(W⁻¹ f))_γ + W f̃^(j),        P^(j) := W L^(j) = P ⊗ Id − W Q^(j),    (17.11)

with Q^(j) the coupling of (16.34) and f̃^(j)_γ = −Σ_(|S|≥2) (ad_(X_S) L) X^(γ∖S) u, the sum over sets S of
positions in γ, X^(γ∖S) the word with those letters deleted, and ad_(X_S) the iterated commutator. P^(j) acts on
(ℂ^(N_E))^(𝒲_j). It has the principal symbol of P; its first-order coupling W Q^(j) has coefficients
O(x_I^(2+min(1,2ℓ_I))) near ℐ⁺, so its normal form at ℐ⁺, (17.1), has the same p_1 as P ⊗ Id (its
zeroth-order part, of size O(x_I²), changes p_0, which is never used), and its principal symbol of order 1 vanishes at
R. So P^(j) satisfies everything Section 17.2 and Section 17.3 use, with the same margins, and Proposition 17.14
holds for it (by the last paragraph of its proof), with constants depending on finitely many coefficient norms of
W Q^(j), which carry at most one b-derivative of those of P (Lemma 16.19). As
X^γ(W⁻¹f) = W⁻¹ Π_i (X_(γ_i) + c_(γ_i)) f with constants c_i = −X_i log W ∈ {2, −2, 0}, the first term on the right of
(17.11) is a word in shifted fields applied to f.

**Proposition 17.17** (b-regularity on slabs.) Let α < −1/2 + p̄_1, Ω′ = Ω_(T_0,T_1) with T_0 ≥ 1, 𝗌 a slab
order and k ∈ ℕ_0. There is d_0, depending only on 𝗌, such that for P of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) with
‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) small, the forward solution of Pu = f satisfies

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),2α)(Ω′)^(•,−)) ≤ C_k ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;k),2α+2)(Ω′)^(•,−)),    (17.12)

uniformly for such P.

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 8.6] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* Let Ω″ := Ω^♯_(T_0,T_1), nested around Ω′ with room; let f″ be the restriction to Ω″ of the minimal
extension of f in H^((𝗌−1;k),2α+2)_e, and u″ the forward solution on Ω″ of P^ext u″ = f″ (Proposition 17.14). By
uniqueness u″|_(Ω′) = u. We show by induction on j ≤ k that

    Σ_(|γ|≤j) ‖X^γ u″‖_(H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω″)^(•,−)) ≤ C_j ‖f″‖_(H^((𝗌−1;j),2α+2)(Ω″)^(•,−)).    (17.13)

j = 0 is (17.10). Let j ≥ 1. Each b-vector field maps H^(𝗍,2β)_e into H^(𝗍−1,2β−1)_e (as ∂_ω = x_I⁻¹ x_I∂_ω),
and by (17.13) at j − 1 every word of length j − 1 applied to u″ lies in H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω″)^(•,−), so a priori
u″^(j) ∈ H^(𝗌−1,2α−1)(Ω″)^(•,−). The threshold holds also for the weight α − 1/2, so by Proposition 17.14 (i) for P^(j)
at that weight and at s′ = inf 𝗌 − 1, u″^(j) is the forward solution of (17.11), which by Proposition 17.14 (ii)
at the weight α lies in H^(𝗌,2α)(Ω″)^(•,−), with norm at most C times that of the right side of
(17.11) in H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)(Ω″)^(•,−). The first term of the right side has norm at most C‖f″‖_((𝗌−1;j)), by
Lemma 17.15 (c). For f̃^(j), let |S| = q ≥ 2. W ad_(X_S) L is a second-order edge operator with coefficients in
C^((d_0;j−q))_(e;b), as each commutator with an element of 𝒳_sl preserves Diff²_e (Lemma 14.9 near ℐ⁺) and
differentiates the coefficients once, and W(ad_(X_S) L)W⁻¹ differs from it by lower order. Every edge vector field is a
combination of the X_i with bounded coefficients (x_I∂_ω = x_I · ∂_ω), so W ad_(X_S) L = Σ_i A_i X_i with A_i
first-order edge operators with C^((d_0;j−q)) coefficients, and by Lemma 17.15 (a)

    ‖W (ad_(X_S) L) X^(γ∖S) u″‖_(H^(𝗌−1,2α+2)) ≤ C Σ_i ‖X_i X^(γ∖S) u″‖_(H^(𝗌,2α)),

a sum over words of length j − q + 1 ≤ j − 1, bounded by (17.13) at j − 1. This proves (17.13) at j, the
order staying 𝗌 and the uniqueness being used at s′ = inf 𝗌 − 1 for every j and at inf 𝗌 for u″|_(Ω′) = u, so that
d_0 depends only on 𝗌. Finally, by Lemma 17.15 (c) with room, ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k))(Ω′)) ≤ C_k Σ_(|γ|≤k) ‖X^γ u″‖_(H^𝗌(Ω″))
≤ C_k ‖f″‖ ≤ C_k ‖f‖. ∎

*The extension in the tame estimates.* A tame bound controls a low and a high b-regularity of one function at once, so
its proof needs one extension of the right-hand side f across the final faces of the slab that is nearly minimal for
the norms of every order (𝗌 − 1; j) at once; the minimal extension used in the proof of Proposition 17.17 is minimal
for one norm only. Across {r = r_0}, where Ω_* ends and no room is available, and across the final face {r = a} of the
r-slabs of Section 17.5, Lemma 17.18 below provides one when the order 𝗌 − 1 of the right-hand side is
constant near the face with value a nonnegative integer there, that is, when 𝗌 is a positive integer there. Across the
time-final face {t^♭ = T_1}, which meets ℐ⁺, where an order need not be constant, no such extension is constructed (no
single extension operator respects all variable orders, [Hin26c, footnote 64]); the tame estimate on a slab is
therefore stated for a right-hand side given on the larger slab Ω_(T_0,T_1+1), and a cut-off in t^♭ provides the
extension there. Wherever the tame estimates are applied, in the proof of Theorem 17.26 below and in
Lemma 19.25 and Proposition 19.28, the right-hand side is the restriction of one given on Ω_*; in the last two
the orders are those of Lemma 19.19, which are constant near {r ≤ r_0} with values at least 2 there.

**Lemma 17.18** (A simultaneous extension across an r-face.) Let 𝗍 be an order function, m ∈ ℕ_0 and
κ_0 > 0, and let Ω′_+ be one of the following, with r-face {r = c} and final time T_+:

(S) a slab Ω_(T_0,T_+) with T_0 ≥ 1 and T_+ ≥ T_0 + 1, with c := r_0 and the spaces of Section 17.1.1 at a weight
2β, that is, at the weights (2β, 0, 0);

(K) an r-slab Ω^K_([c,b]) of Section 17.5.1 with T_0 ≥ 1 − η_0/2 and r^♯ < c < b ≤ r^♮, with T_+ := ∞ and the spaces
of Section 17.5.1 at a weight β, that is, at the weights (0, 0, β).

Write H^((𝗍;j))(Ω′_+)^(•,−) for the space of forward problems on Ω′_+ of order (𝗍;j) at that weight, and
H^((𝗍;j))_(e3b;b) for the space at those weights on M. Suppose that 𝗍 = m over

    𝒰 := {T_0 − κ_0 < t^♭ < T_+ + κ_0, c − κ_0 < r < c + κ_0},

a subset of the region {t_* ≥ 1/2, r ≥ r^♯} on which t^♭ is defined (Lemma 17.2 (iv)). Then there is a linear
map ℰ on H^((𝗍;0))(Ω′_+)^(•,−) such that for every u in it:

(i) ℰu ∈ H^((𝗍;0))_(e3b;b) is supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, and in case (K) in {t^♭ ≥ T_0, r ≤ b};

(ii) ℰu = u on {t^♭ < T_+ − 1/2, r > c};

(iii) for every j ∈ ℕ_0, in the strong sense and with C_j independent of u,

    ‖ℰu‖_(H^((𝗍;j))_(e3b;b)) ≤ C_j ‖u‖_(H^((𝗍;j))(Ω′_+)^(•,−)).

*Proof.* *Choices.* Decreasing κ_0, we may assume κ_0 ≤ η_0/4, c − κ_0 > r^♯ and c + κ_0 < r^♮ (in case (S),
r^♯ < r_0 < r^♮); as η_0 ≤ 1/2 (Lemma 17.2 (iv)), T_0 − κ_0 ≥ 1/2. Fix κ ∈ (0, κ_0/3], in case (K) with c + 2κ ≤ b.
Let ψ = ψ(r) equal 1 for r ≤ c + κ and 0 for r ≥ c + 2κ; ψ_− = ψ_−(r)
equal 1 for r ≥ c and 0 for r ≤ c − κ; and χ_+ = χ_+(t^♭) equal 1 on (−∞, T_+ − 1/2] and 0 on [T_+ − 1/4, ∞), with
χ_+ ≡ 1 if T_+ = ∞. These have bounded b-derivatives: ψ and ψ_− are smooth functions of x on a bounded range of r, and
χ_+ varies only where t_* ≤ T_+/C′ (Lemma 15.35 (b)), at bounded times, where t^♭ has bounded b-derivatives.

*Coordinates.* Let W := {t_* ≥ 1/2, r^♯ ≤ r < r^♮}. With the constant C ≥ 4(r′_0 + 1) of the proof of
Lemma 17.2 (iv), r < r^♮ < r′_0 ≤ Ct_*/2 − 1 on W, so the gluing formula of the proof of Lemma 15.35 gives

    t^♭ = C′(t_* + R̃(r))     on W,

with R̃ smooth, R̃′ ∈ [0, 1] and r′_0 ≤ R̃ ≤ r′_0 + 1 on W. So (t^♭, r, ω) are coordinates on W, with
t_* = t^♭/C′ − R̃(r). As C′ < (1 + C)⁻¹ ≤ 1/5, C′R̃ < 1/4 < (1 − C′)t_*, that is, t^♭ < t_* on W. Hence 𝒰 ⊂ W lies in
{t_* > T_0 − κ_0} ⊂ {t_* > 1/2} and is open in M. As r ∈ (r^♯, r^♮) on 𝒰, its closure meets ∂M at most in (K⁺)°,
where x_I and ρ_+ are smooth and positive, ρ_K = t_*⁻¹, the e3b-vector fields are spanned by ∂_(t_*), ∂_x and the
b-vector fields by t_*∂_(t_*), ∂_x (Section 17.5.1); in M° both structures are the standard one. As r is bounded
above and below on 𝒰, ∂_x and the fields ∂_r, Ω_12, …, Ω_34 (the rotation fields of Section 17.4.2) span the same
module over functions of x with bounded derivatives; and

    ∂_(t_*) = C′∂_(t^♭),     ∂_r|_(t_*) = ∂_r|_(t^♭) + C′R̃′ ∂_(t^♭),     t_*∂_(t_*) = 𝔮 t^♭∂_(t^♭),

with 𝔮 := C′t_*/t^♭ = t_*/(t_* + R̃). The functions 𝔮, 𝔮⁻¹ = 1 + R̃ t_*⁻¹ and C′R̃′/t^♭ have bounded b-derivatives. So on
𝒰 the e3b-vector fields are spanned by ∂_(t^♭), ∂_r and the Ω_ab, and the b-vector fields by t^♭∂_(t^♭), ∂_r and the
Ω_ab, with coefficients in C^∞_b. The weight function of the spaces, x_I^(2β) in case (S) and ρ_K^β in case (K), is
(t^♭)^(−e) times a function bounded above and below with bounded b-derivatives, where e := 0 in case (S) (t^♭ being
bounded on 𝒰) and e := β in case (K) (as ρ_K = t_*⁻¹ = C′𝔮⁻¹(t^♭)⁻¹). The density |dg| is a smooth positive multiple
of |dt_* dx| = r³ |dt_* dr dω| = (r³/C′) |dt^♭ dr dω| (Section 17.5.1 near K⁺).

*Differential norms.* Let 𝒦 := {T_0 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T_+, c − 2κ ≤ r ≤ c + 2κ}. For v supported in 𝒦 and j ∈ ℕ_0 put

    D_(m,j)(v) := Σ_(i+q≤j) Σ_(p+q′≤m) ‖(t^♭)^e (t^♭∂_(t^♭))^i Y^q ∂^p_(t^♭) Y^(q′) v‖_(L²(|dt^♭ dr dω|)),

where Y^q runs over the products of q fields among ∂_r and the Ω_ab. Then ‖v‖_(H^((𝗍;j))_(e3b;b)) and D_(m,j)(v) are
equivalent on such v, with constants depending on m and j. Indeed, let φ := φ_1(t^♭) φ_2(r), with φ_1 equal to 1 on
[T_0 − κ_0/3, T_+ + κ_0/3] and supported in (T_0 − 2κ_0/3, T_+ + 2κ_0/3), and φ_2 equal to 1 on [c − 5κ/2, c + 5κ/2]
and supported in (c − κ_0, c + κ_0). Then φ ∈ C^∞_b, supp φ ⊂ 𝒰 and φ = 1 near 𝒦. By Lemma 19.20 (with U := 𝒰,
and 𝗍 against the constant m both ways), whose proof uses only Chapter 14, the norms of orders (𝗍;j) and (m;j) are
equivalent on such v: we take ν ≥ max(0, −inf 𝗍) in that lemma, so that −ν ≤ m and −ν ≤ 𝗍, and its terms of order
(−ν;j) are bounded by either side.
As m ∈ ℕ_0, the norm of order (m;j) is equivalent on such v to D_(m,j)(v): by (14.6) it is the sum of the
H^m_e3b-norms of up to j b-derivatives of v, and on 𝒰 the spanning set used there may be replaced by t^♭∂_(t^♭), ∂_r
and the Ω_ab; in each scaled chart of (S3) of Section 14.3 the H^m(ℝ⁵)-norm is the sum of the L²-norms of up to m
derivatives, and on 𝒰 the scaled coordinate fields and ∂_(t^♭), ∂_r, Ω_ab span the e3b-vector fields over C^∞_b;
derivatives falling on coefficients, on the partition functions of (S3) and on the weight, and the reordering of the
factors, give terms of the same form with fewer derivatives; and the weight and the density are as above.

*The reflection.* Let c_l and ε_l = 3^(−l) be the constants of Lemma 17.3 (b), so that Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(−q) < ∞
and Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^q = 1 for q ∈ ℕ_0. For z on {r > c} supported in 𝒦 put ℰ_c z := z on {r > c} and

    (ℰ_c z)(t^♭, r, ω) := Σ_l c_l z(t^♭, c + (c − r)/ε_l, ω),     r < c.

As (c − r)/ε_l ≥ c − r, ℰ_c z vanishes for r < c − 2κ, so it is supported in 𝒦. ℰ_c commutes with ∂_(t^♭),
t^♭∂_(t^♭), the Ω_ab and multiplication by functions of t^♭. On {r < c}, a product of these fields containing q_r
factors ∂_r, applied to ℰ_c z, is Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^(q_r) times the same product applied to z, evaluated at
(t^♭, c + (c − r)/ε_l, ω); by the substitution r ↦ c + (c − r)/ε_l, the L²-norm on {r < c} of each such term is ε_l^(1/2)
times the L²-norm on {r > c} of the product applied to z. For z smooth up to {r = c}, the derivatives of every order of
ℰ_c z match across {r = c}, as Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^q = 1, so its distributional derivatives carry no term supported on
{r = c}. Hence, with D⁺_(m,j) denoting D_(m,j) with the integrals taken over {r > c},

    D_(m,j)(ℰ_c z) ≤ (1 + Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(1/2−m−j)) D⁺_(m,j)(z),

first for such z and then, by density, for every z with D⁺_(m,j)(z) < ∞.

*The map.* For u ∈ H^((𝗍;0))(Ω′_+)^(•,−) let ũ be an extension of u with the support required in the definition of
the space ({t^♭ ≥ T_0}, in case (K) {t^♭ ≥ T_0, r ≤ b}), and put

    ℰu := χ_+ (1 − ψ) ũ + ℰ_c(χ_+ ψ u).

Two such extensions differ by a distribution supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_+} ∪ {r ≤ c}, near which χ_+(1 − ψ) vanishes, so
the first term does not depend on ũ. In the second, χ_+ψu, extended by zero, is a distribution on {r > c} supported in
{T_0 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T_+ − 1/4, r ≤ c + 2κ} ⊂ 𝒦. So ℰ is well defined and linear. (i): the first term is supported in supp ũ,
the second in 𝒦 ∩ {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, which lies in {r ≤ c + 2κ} ⊂ {r ≤ b} in case (K). (ii): on {t^♭ < T_+ − 1/2, r > c},
χ_+ = 1 and ℰu = (1 − ψ)u + ψu = u.

(iii) For every j and every extension ũ as above with finite norm of order (𝗍;j),
‖χ_+(1 − ψ)ũ‖_((𝗍;j)) ≤ C_j ‖ũ‖_((𝗍;j)) (Lemma 14.29 (a)); the left side does not depend on ũ, so it is at most
C_j ‖u‖_(H^((𝗍;j))(Ω′_+)^(•,−)). For the second term, ψ_−ψχ_+ũ is supported in 𝒦 and equals χ_+ψu on {r > c}, so by
the equivalence of norms and Lemma 14.29 (a)

    D⁺_(m,j)(χ_+ψu) ≤ D_(m,j)(ψ_−ψχ_+ũ) ≤ C ‖ψ_−ψχ_+ũ‖_((𝗍;j)) ≤ C_j ‖ũ‖_((𝗍;j)),

and the infimum over ũ, taken for each j separately, bounds D⁺_(m,j)(χ_+ψu) by C_j ‖u‖_(H^((𝗍;j))(Ω′_+)^(•,−)). As
ℰ_c(χ_+ψu) is supported in 𝒦, ‖ℰ_c(χ_+ψu)‖_((𝗍;j)) ≤ C D_(m,j)(ℰ_c(χ_+ψu)) ≤ C D⁺_(m,j)(χ_+ψu). Each step holds
whenever its right side is finite, which gives (iii) in the strong sense. ∎

The construction is the one by which Lemma 19.21 extends functions on Ω_* across {r = r_0}. On a slab the cut-off
χ_+ makes the first term independent of the extension beyond the time-final face, where the extensions of u are not
unique; ℰu then agrees with u only up to t^♭ = T_+ − 1/2, which is why the tame estimate below takes its right-hand
side on a slab one unit of time longer.

**Proposition 17.19** (Tame estimates on slabs.) In the setting of Proposition 17.17, let 𝗌 be constant
over {t_* ≥ 1/2, r^♯ ≤ r < r_0 + κ_0} for some κ_0 > 0, with value a positive integer there, and put
Ω′_+ := Ω_(T_0,T_1+1). There is d ∈ ℕ, depending only on 𝗌, such that for all k, all P of class
((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) with ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) small and all f ∈ H^((𝗌−1;k),2α+2)(Ω′_+)^(•,−), the
forward solution u on Ω′ of Pu = f (that is, of Pu = f|_(Ω′)) satisfies

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),2α)(Ω′)^(•,−))
        ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;k),2α+2)(Ω′_+)^(•,−)) + ε_(P,k) ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;d),2α+2)(Ω′_+)^(•,−))),    (17.14)

with ε_(P,k) := ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)), which may be taken over a neighbourhood of Ω′, and C_k depending on P
only through a bound for ε_(P,d).

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 8.9] in dimension 4 + 1, with the right-hand side given on a slab one unit of time longer
than Ω′. [Hin26c] states it for "s ∈ ℕ an admissible order function"; the proof uses only what Proposition 17.17 uses,
together with Lemma 17.18.

*Proof.* Let d̃ and the regularity of Proposition 14.56 be those of Lemma 17.15 (b) at the orders 𝗌 + 1 and
𝗌 − 1, and d := d̃ + 3. An extension of f supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0} also extends f|_(Ω′), so the norms of f|_(Ω′) on Ω′
are at most those of f on Ω′_+. For k ≤ d, (17.14) therefore follows from (17.12), whose constant
depends on ε_(P,k) ≤ ε_(P,d). For k > d, let Ω″ := Ω^♯_(T_0,T_1) and u″ be as in the proof of Proposition 17.17, with
f″ := (ℰf)|_(Ω″) in place of the minimal extension, ℰ the extension of Lemma 17.18 (S) for the slab Ω′_+,
the order 𝗍 := 𝗌 − 1 and the weight 2α + 2 (its hypothesis holds with κ_0 replaced by min(κ_0, r_0 − r^♯)). As ℰf is
supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0} and equals f on {t^♭ < T_1 + 1/2, r > r_0}, f″ = f on Ω′, so u″|_(Ω′) = u by uniqueness,
and, for every j at once,

    ‖f″‖_(H^((𝗌−1;j),2α+2)(Ω″)^(•,−)) ≤ ‖ℰf‖_(H^((𝗌−1;j),2α+2)_(e;b)) ≤ C_j ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;j),2α+2)(Ω′_+)^(•,−)).

Run the induction of Proposition 17.17 on nested slabs

    Ω′ ⊂ Ω_(2k) ⊂ Ω_(2k−1) ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ Ω_(0) = Ω″,

with room 2^(−i−2) min(1, r_0 − r^♯) between Ω_(i) and Ω_(i−1), two slabs per step: step j proves the bound
(17.13) on Ω_(2j) in the tame form C_j(‖f″‖_((𝗌−1;j)) + ε_(P,j) ‖f″‖_((𝗌−1;d))). The coefficients of P^(j) carry
at most one b-derivative of those of P, so the constant of Proposition 17.14 for P^(j) depends on ε_(P,d) only. In
f̃^(j) write L = L_0 + (L − L_0), L_0 the operator of P_0. The terms of L_0, and those of L − L_0 in which at most 2
b-derivatives fall on the coefficients, are bounded as in Proposition 17.17 by norms of u″ with at most j − 1 words, on
Ω_(2j−2), with constants depending on ε_(P,2); by the induction hypothesis they are tame. In the others, q′ ≥ 3
b-derivatives fall on a coefficient p of P − P_0. As in Lemma 16.22 (b) and [Hin26c, (7.55)–(7.56)], commute the
second-order factor to the front; it remains to bound

    ‖(D^(q′)_([b]) D^(≤2)_e p)(D^(j−q)_([b]) u″)‖_(H^(𝗌+1)(Ω_(2j))),     q′ ≤ q.

Lemma 17.15 (b) on Ω_(2j) ⊂ Ω_(2j−1), with D²_([b]) D^(≤2)_e p in the place of ℓ and (q′ − 2, j − q + q′ − 2) in the
place of (j, k), bounds it by

    C_j (‖p‖_((d_1+2;d̃+2)) ‖u″‖_((𝗌+1;j−2)) + ‖p‖_((d_1+2;j)) ‖u″‖_((𝗌+1;d̃)))

on Ω_(2j−1), with d_1 the regularity of Lemma 17.15 (b) and d_0 ≥ d_1 + 2. Here ‖u″‖_((𝗌+1;j−2)) ≤ C‖u″‖_((𝗌;j−1))
on Ω_(2j−1) (Lemma 14.29 (d), on slab spaces by taking extensions), which Lemma 17.15 (c) bounds by the words
of length at most j − 1 on the larger slab Ω_(2j−2), tame by step j − 1;
‖u″‖_((𝗌+1;d̃)) ≤ C‖u″‖_((𝗌;d̃+1)) ≤ C‖f″‖_((𝗌−1;d̃+1)) by (17.12) at d̃ + 1 < d; and
‖p‖_((d_1+2;d̃+2)) ≤ Cε_(P,d), ‖p‖_((d_1+2;j)) ≤ Cε_(P,j). The finitely many nested slabs used for a given k make C_k
depend on k only. Conclude with Lemma 17.15 (c) and the bound on f″. ∎

### 17.5 The black hole interior

The region {r_0 ≤ r ≤ r^♮} at late times is unbounded in time: its closure meets K⁺. There dr is timelike, and −r
serves as a time function. The estimates of Section 17.2–Section 17.4 hold there with −r in place of t^♭, with no
radial set and no threshold; this is [Hin26c, Section 8.2] in dimension 4 + 1.

#### 17.5.1 r-slabs

By Lemma 17.2 (iv) there is δ_♮ > 0 such that dr is future timelike for the metric of P^ext on
{r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮} ∩ {t^♭ ≥ 1 − η_0}. For T_0 ≥ 1 − η_0/2 and r^♯ ≤ a < b ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮ the **r-slab** is

    Ω^K_([a,b]) := {t^♭ ≥ T_0, a ≤ r ≤ b},

with T_0 understood and P^ext in place of P where P is not given. Its faces in M° are {t^♭ = T_0} and {r = b}, which are
initial, and {r = a}, which is final: future causal vectors point into it across the first two and out of it across the
last, as ∇t^♭ is past and ∇r future timelike, and dt^♭, dr are independent where the faces meet. Its closure meets ∂M
only in K⁺ ∩ {a ≤ r ≤ b}. There, in the coordinates (ρ_K = t_*⁻¹, x), the e3b-vector fields are spanned by
∂_(t_*) = −ρ_K² ∂_(ρ_K) and ∂_x, and the b-vector fields by t_*∂_(t_*) and ∂_x (Section 14.1; [Hin26c] calls these
spaces cusp spaces). Only the weight at K⁺ matters, and near the r-slabs we write

    H^(𝗌,α_K)_K := H^(𝗌,(0,0,α_K))_(e3b),        H^((𝗌;k),α_K)_K := H^((𝗌;k),(0,0,α_K))_(e3b;b),

with the density |dg|, a smooth positive multiple of |dt_* dx| there. So ‖u‖_(H^(1,α_K)_K) is equivalent to the
L²-norm of t_*^(α_K)(|u| + |∂_(t_*)u| + |∂_x u|). [Hin26c] glosses the left side of its (8.38) as controlling
t_*^(−α_K) u; with its multiplier ρ_K^(−2α_K)∇r and (8.39) the norm is that of ρ_K^(α_K) L², which controls
t_*^(α_K) u = ρ_K^(−α_K) u.

Let U^K := M° ∩ {r > a}, V^K := M° ∩ {t^♭ > T_0, r < b} and U^K_0 := M° ∩ {a < r < b}, and define, with quotient norms,

    H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−) := {u|_(U^K) : u ∈ H^(𝗌,α_K)_K, supp u ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ T_0, r ≤ b}},
    H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(−,•) := {v|_(V^K) : v ∈ H^(𝗌,α_K)_K, supp v ⊂ {r ≥ a}},
    H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•    := {u|_(U^K_0) : u ∈ H^(𝗌,α_K)_K, supp u ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ T_0}},

and the mixed spaces of order (𝗌;k) likewise. The first are the spaces of forward problems, the second those of backward
problems; the third is supported at {t^♭ = T_0} only and extendible at both r-faces, the space of the continuation
estimates. D(Ω^K_([a,b])) is the set of restrictions to U^K of functions in C_c^∞(M°) supported in
{t^♭ > T_0, r < b}, and D_*(Ω^K_([a,b])) that of restrictions to V^K of functions in C_c^∞(M°) supported in {r > a}.
Both consist of functions vanishing near K⁺.

Lemma 17.3 holds for r-slabs, with these changes in its proof. The collar field is Z := ∇t^♭:
Z t^♭ = G(dt^♭) < 0, and Z r = g⁻¹(dt^♭, dr) > 0, as ∇t^♭ is past and ∇r future timelike. Near K⁺, Z is a stationary
vector field in (t_*, x) plus one with coefficients O(ρ_K^(ℓ_K)), so its flow changes t_* by a bounded amount in bounded
time and is bounded on H^(m,α_K)_K, uniformly for bounded times, and strongly continuous. −Z moves supports in
{t^♭ ≥ T_0, r ≤ b} into {t^♭ > T_0, r < b}, and Z moves supports in {r ≥ a} into {r > a}. Seeley's operator is applied
first across {r = b} in the variable r, with (t_*, ω) as parameters, and then across {t^♭ = T_0} in the collar
coordinates of Z, with collar width η_0/2; along a collar line r increases as t^♭ decreases, so the extension of a
function vanishing on {r < a} vanishes there. For density, one cuts off also at large times by 1 − χ_0(t_*/T),
T → ∞, whose derivative along ∂_(t_*) is O(T⁻¹) and along ∂_x is zero.

#### 17.5.2 Energy estimates

**Lemma 17.20** (Energy estimates on r-slabs.) Let α_K ∈ ℝ and Ω^K := Ω^K_([a,b]). There is C, uniform for
ε_P small with d_0 = 2 (the norm of P − P_0 with the weights (0, 0, ℓ_K) suffices), such that

    ‖u‖_(H^(1,α_K)(Ω^K)) ≤ C ‖Pu‖_(H^(0,α_K)(Ω^K)),          u ∈ D(Ω^K),
    ‖v‖_(H^(1,−α_K)(Ω^K)) ≤ C ‖P*v‖_(H^(0,−α_K)(Ω^K)),       v ∈ D_*(Ω^K).    (17.15)

Here H^(1,β)(Ω^K) and H^(0,β)(Ω^K) are the L²(Ω^K, |dg|)-norms of t_*^β(|u| + |∂_(t_*)u| + |∂_x u|) and of t_*^β u,
and P* is the adjoint for |dg| and a fixed smooth fibre inner product h_K. The same holds on Ω^K ∩ {t^♭ ≤ T_1}, with
{t^♭ = T_1} a further final face.

This is [Hin26c, Lemma 8.10] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* Let w := t_*^(2α_K) = ρ_K^(−2α_K), Y_r := ∇r/|G(dr)|, which is future timelike with Y_r(−r) = 1,
and |ζ|² := ζ_(t_*)² + |ζ_x|² for covectors ζ = ζ_(t_*) dt_* + ζ_x dx. On the r-slab, by stationarity of g_0, compactness
in x and the decay of g − g_0, there are constants, uniform for ε_P small with d_0 = 2, with: |div_g Y_r| ≤ C_0
and |Y_r log w| = 2|α_K| |Y_r t_*|/t_* ≤ C_1; T(∇r, ∇r)(ζ) ≥ c_r |ζ|², by Lemma 17.5;
and |K_(w^(±1)∇r)(ζ)| ≤ C_3 w^(±1) |ζ|², by the formula for K_(fX) in Lemma 17.4, as |∇w| ≤ Cw and ∇r has bounded
first derivatives. P − P_□ is of first order with bounded coefficients in the frame ∂_(t_*), ∂_x, so for any vector
field X with |X| ≤ C_X f, |2 Re⟨(P − P_□)u, Xu⟩| ≤ C_4 f (|du|² + |u||du|), with C_4 depending on C_X and h_K only.

*Forward.* Let X := e^(2Φr) w ∇r, which is future timelike. By Lemma 17.4,

    K_X = e^(2Φr) (K_(w∇r) + 2Φ w T(∇r, ∇r)) ≥ e^(2Φr) w (2Φ c_r − C_3) |ζ|².

Apply (17.3) on O := Ω^K to u ∈ D(Ω^K), which has compact support in Ō. The only face near which u ≠ 0 is
{r = a} (and {t^♭ = T_1}), where ∇φ = ∇r (resp. −∇t^♭) is future timelike; with X future timelike the boundary term is
≥ 0 by Lemma 17.5. So

    ∫ e^(2Φr) w (4Φ c_r − 2C_3 − C_4) |du|² ≤ 2 Re ∫ ⟨Pu, Xu⟩ + C_4 ∫ e^(2Φr) w |u||du|
                                          ≤ C_5 ∫ e^(2Φr) w |Pu||du| + C_4 ∫ e^(2Φr) w |u||du|.

Lemma 17.6 with Y = Y_r, τ := −r, the weight w and Φ ≥ C_0 + C_1 applies, as u vanishes near the faces with
Y_r φ > 0, namely {t^♭ = T_0} (Y_r φ = dt^♭(Y_r) > 0) and {r = b} (Y_r φ = −dr(Y_r) = 1); it gives

    ∫ e^(2Φr) w |u|² ≤ 4Φ⁻² ∫ e^(2Φr) w |Y_r u|² ≤ C_6 Φ⁻² ∫ e^(2Φr) w |du|².

With the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality the last term above is at most C_4 C_6^(1/2) Φ⁻¹ ∫ e^(2Φr) w |du|², and
C_5 |Pu||du| ≤ Φ c_r |du|² + C_5² (4Φ c_r)⁻¹ |Pu|². Fix Φ large: ∫ e^(2Φr) w |du|² ≤ C ∫ e^(2Φr) w |Pu|². As e^(2Φr)
lies between e^(2Φa) and e^(2Φb), this and the Poincaré inequality give the first estimate (17.15).

*Backward.* Let X_* := −e^(−2Φr) w⁻¹ ∇r, which is past timelike. By Lemma 17.4,

    K_(X_*) = e^(−2Φr) (−K_(w⁻¹∇r) + 2Φ w⁻¹ T(∇r, ∇r)) ≥ e^(−2Φr) w⁻¹ (2Φ c_r − C_3) |ζ|².

For v ∈ D_*(Ω^K) the faces near which v ≠ 0 are {t^♭ = T_0} and {r = b}, with ∇φ = ∇t^♭, resp. −∇r, past timelike, so
the boundary terms 2T(X_*, ∇φ)(dv) are ≥ 0 by Lemma 17.5. P* = P_□ + (P* − P_□), with P* − P_□ of first order
with bounded coefficients. Lemma 17.6 in the reverse direction, with the weight w⁻¹, applies, as v vanishes near
{r = a} (and {t^♭ = T_1}), the only faces with Y_r φ < 0. The rest is as before. ∎

#### 17.5.3 Solvability, uniqueness and continuation

A **slab order on an r-slab** is 𝗌 ∈ C^∞(^(e3b)S*M) with ±𝖧𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ^± over it. Admissible order functions are slab
orders on the r-slabs inside Ω_*, by Proposition 15.43 (2); so are constants.

**Lemma 17.21** (The flow in the interior.) There is c > 0 such that, over
{r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮} ∩ {t^♭ ≥ 1 − η_0}, up to K⁺ and for ε_P small, 𝖧r ≤ −c on ∂Σ^+ and 𝖧r ≥ c on ∂Σ^−. So r
decreases strictly along the future field, at a rate bounded below, and there is no radial set and no trapping there.

*Proof.* 𝖧 = ρH_G with ρ a positive defining function of fibre infinity, homogeneous of degree −1, and
H_G r = 2g⁻¹(ζ, dr). On ∂Σ^+ the future field is 𝖧 (Section 15.10.3): the projection of H_G there, 2g⁻¹(ζ, ·), is
future null, so g⁻¹(ζ, dr) = g(ζ^♯, ∇r) < 0, ∇r being future timelike. On ∂Σ^− the signs reverse. ρ g⁻¹(ζ, dr) is
homogeneous of degree 0 and continuous on the compactified cosphere bundle over the closure of the region, up to K⁺,
where it is that of the stationary metric g_0; it does not vanish on the characteristic set, which is compact. ∎

**Lemma 17.22** (Regularity on r-slabs.) (a) Let r^♯ ≤ a′ < a < b < r^♮ + δ_♮,
Ω_1 := Ω^K_([a,b]) ⊂ Ω_2 := Ω^K_([a′,b]), let 𝗌_0 < 𝗌 be slab orders, and let u ∈ H^(𝗌_0,α_K)(Ω_2)^(•,−) with
Pu ∈ H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω_2)^(•,−). Then u|_(Ω_1) ∈ H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω_1)^(•,−) and

    ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω_1)^(•,−)) ≤ C (‖Pu‖_(H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω_2)^(•,−)) + ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌_0,α_K)(Ω_2)^(•,−))).

(b) Let δ > 0 with T_0 − δ ≥ 1 − η_0 and b + δ ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮, let Ω_3 be the r-slab {t^♭ ≥ T_0 − δ, a ≤ r ≤ b + δ},
let s_0 < s be constants, and let v ∈ H^(s_0,−α_K)(Ω_3)^(−,•) with P*v ∈ H^(s−1,−α_K)(Ω_3)^(−,•). Then
v|_(Ω_1) ∈ H^(s,−α_K)(Ω_1)^(−,•), with the corresponding estimate.

Both hold for systems P ⊗ Id − Q, Q of first order, with constants depending on finitely many coefficient norms; they
are uniform for ε_P small, with d_0 depending only on the orders.

*Proof.* (a) Let ũ be an extension of u supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0, r ≤ b} and f one of Pu; that Pu lies in
H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω_2)^(•,−) means Pũ = f on U_2 := M° ∩ {r > a′}, which contains the region outside the initial faces. Let
χ_1 be a cut-off equal to 1 near Ω_1 and supported in {r > (a + a′)/2}, and carry all operators by such cut-offs. Off
the characteristic set use the elliptic estimate (Theorem 14.43). On it, by Lemma 17.21, the backward curve
from any point over supp χ_1 has r increasing at a rate at least c, so within parameter time (b − a′ + 1)/c it reaches
{r > b} or, earlier, {t^♭ < T_0}, where ũ = 0, staying in {r > (a + a′)/2}; this holds also over K⁺. Propagation
(Theorem 14.49, at the order 𝗌, with 𝖧𝗌 ≤ 0 along the future field) controls ũ at every such point. Finitely many
of these operators are jointly elliptic over supp χ_1, and Lemma 14.29 (c) gives

    ‖χ_1 ũ‖_𝗌 ≤ C (‖χ_1′ f‖_(𝗌−1) + ‖χ_1′ ũ‖_(𝗌_0))

with χ_1′ supported in U_2, which is (a) after taking infima over the extensions.

(b) The same with the future field: let ṽ extend v with support in {r ≥ a}; P*ṽ is controlled on
V_3 := M° ∩ {t^♭ > T_0 − δ, r < b + δ}; forward curves from points over Ω_1 reach {r < a}, where ṽ = 0, within bounded
time, staying in V_3, as t^♭ increases and r decreases along them. Propagation for −P* applies to constant orders. For
systems the principal symbol is scalar and the coupling of lower order, which the elliptic and real principal type
estimates allow. ∎

**Proposition 17.23** (Solvability, uniqueness and continuation on r-slabs.) Let α_K ∈ ℝ,
T_0 ≥ 1 − η_0/2, r^♯ < a < b ≤ r^♮, and 𝗌 a slab order. There are d_0, depending only on 𝗌 (and, in (i) and (iii), on
s′), and C, uniform for ε_P small, such that:

(i) (*uniqueness*) if u ∈ H^(s′,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−) for some s′ ∈ ℝ and Pu = 0, then u = 0;

(ii) (*existence*) for every f ∈ H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−) there is u ∈ H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−) with Pu = f
and

    ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−)) ≤ C ‖f‖_(H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−));    (17.16)

(iii) (*continuation*) for a < a⁺ < b, every u ∈ H^(s′,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•, s′ ∈ ℝ, with
Pu ∈ H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^• satisfies, in the strong sense,

    ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•)
        ≤ C (‖Pu‖_(H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•) + ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a⁺,b]))^•)).    (17.17)

The same holds for P* and backward problems at constant orders, and for systems P ⊗ Id − Q with Q of first order.

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 8.11 and (8.40)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (i) and (ii) are proved as Proposition 17.14, with Lemma 17.20 in place of (17.6),
Lemma 17.22 in place of Lemma 17.13, and the r-slab form of Lemma 17.3. For (i),
Ω_δ := Ω^K_([a+δ,b]), and D(Ω_δ) is dense in H^(2,α_K)(Ω_δ)^(•,−). For Step 1 of (ii), Ω^♯ := Ω^K_([a−δ_1,b]),
δ_1 := min(1, a − r^♯), with P^ext; for Step 3, Ω_3 := {t^♭ ≥ T_0 − δ, a ≤ r ≤ b + δ} with δ := min(η_0/2, δ_♮), so
that b + δ ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮, and the backward estimate (17.15) on Ω_3. There is no threshold, so the weight is any
α_K, and P does not shift it.

(iii) Let δ_2 := (b − a⁺)/4 and χ = χ(r) equal 1 for r ≤ a⁺ + δ_2 and 0 for r ≥ b − δ_2. If ũ extends u with support
in {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, then χũ is supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0, r ≤ b − δ_2}, so v := χu ∈ H^(s′,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−), and
Pv = g := χPu + [P, χ]u. [P, χ] is a first-order operator with coefficients supported in {a⁺ + δ_2 ≤ r ≤ b − δ_2}, so
by Lemma 17.15 (a), with a cut-off,

    ‖g‖_(H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−))
        ≤ C (‖Pu‖_(H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•) + ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω^K_([a⁺,b]))^•)).

By (i), v is the solution of (ii) with f := g, so ‖v‖_𝗌 ≤ C‖g‖_(𝗌−1), and in the strong sense, as (ii) produces a
solution in H^𝗌 whenever g ∈ H^(𝗌−1). As u = v on {r ≤ a⁺ + δ_2}, a partition of unity in r gives (17.17). ∎

#### 17.5.4 b-regularity and the tame estimates

On {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮} ∩ {t_* ≥ 1/2}, with x = (x¹, …, x⁴) the Cartesian coordinates of Definition 14.3 (A), let

    𝒳_K := (V_1, …, V_5, I),        V_1 := t_* ∂_(t_*),     V_(1+j) := ∂_(x^j)  (j = 1, …, 4),

acting componentwise in a fixed trivialisation of the bundle. The V_i commute. They span 𝒱_b near the closures of the
r-slabs, as near (K⁺)° the b-vector fields are spanned by t_*∂_(t_*) and ∂_x and in M° by all vector fields; and every
e3b-vector field there is a combination of the V_i with bounded coefficients, as ∂_(t_*) = t_*⁻¹ V_1 with t_* ≥ 1/2.

**Lemma 17.24** (The commutators in the interior.) For P of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)), 𝒳_K satisfies
condition (C) of Section 16.7 there, with W = 1 and R_i = 0: [P, X_i] = Σ_j Q_ij X_j, with Q_ij first-order
e3b-operators whose coefficients lie in C^((d_0;k−1))_(e3b;b) (a stationary part plus a part O(ρ_K^(ℓ_K))).

This is [Hin26c, (8.41)–(8.42)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* In (t_*, x) write P = Σ a^(μν) ∂_μ ∂_ν + Σ b^μ ∂_μ + c, the coefficients of P_0 independent of t_* and smooth,
those of P − P_0 in ρ_K^(ℓ_K) C^((d_0;k))_(e3b;b) near K⁺ (Definition 15.36). [P, ∂_(x^j)] has the coefficients
differentiated by −∂_(x^j); [P, t_*∂_(t_*)] = [P, t_*]∂_(t_*) − (t_*∂_(t_*) applied to the coefficients), with
[P, t_*] = 2 Σ_ν a^(t_* ν) ∂_ν + b^(t_*). In both cases a second-order operator in ∂_(t_*), ∂_x results, with
coefficients in C^((d_0;k−1))_(e3b;b), as V_i is a b-vector field. Write each second-order term ∂_μ ∂_ν as
∂_μ ∘ Σ_j c_(νj) V_j with c_(νj) ∈ {0, 1, t_*⁻¹}; this is Σ_j Q_ij V_j with Q_ij of first order. [P, I] = 0. ∎

By Lemma 16.19 with 𝔩 = 0 and R_i = 0, as in (17.11), for u on an
r-slab and f := Pu the words u^(j) := (X^γ u)_(γ∈𝒲_j) satisfy

    P^(j) u^(j) = (X^γ f)_γ + f̃^(j),     P^(j) := P ⊗ Id − Q^(j),
    f̃^(j)_γ = −Σ_(|S|≥2) (ad_(X_S) P) X^(γ∖S) u.    (17.18)

P^(j) is a system with scalar principal part and first-order coupling, whose coefficients carry at most one
b-derivative of those of P; Lemma 17.20, Lemma 17.21, Lemma 17.22 and Proposition 17.23 hold for it,
with no condition on the coupling, as on r-slabs every first-order term is absorbed by the factor Φ in
Lemma 17.20.

**Proposition 17.25** (b-regularity and tame estimates in the interior.) Let α_K, T_0 and
r^♯ < a < a⁺ < b ≤ r^♮ be as in Proposition 17.23, 𝗌 a slab order and s′ ∈ ℝ.

(a) There is d_0, depending only on 𝗌 and s′, such that for all k ∈ ℕ_0 and P of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) with
ε_(P,k) small, every u ∈ H^((s′;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^• with f := Pu satisfies, in the strong sense,

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•)
        ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•) + ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a⁺,b]))^•)).    (17.19)

(b) If 𝗌 is constant over {t^♭ > T_0 − κ_0, a − κ_0 < r < a + κ_0} for some κ_0 > 0, with value a positive integer
there, there is d ∈ ℕ, depending only on 𝗌, such that for all k and P of that class with ε_(P,d) small,

    ‖u‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k (‖f‖_((𝗌−1;k)) + ‖u‖^([a⁺,b])_((𝗌;k))
                       + ε_(P,k) (‖f‖_((𝗌−1;d)) + ‖u‖^([a⁺,b])_((𝗌;d)))),    (17.20)

with the spaces of (17.19), the superscript marking the norm on Ω^K_([a⁺,b]), and C_k depending on P only
through a bound for ε_(P,d). Here ε_(P,k) may be the norm of P − P_0 over Ω^K_([a,b]) alone: on the room below
{r = a} used in the proof, P is replaced by the operator whose coefficients are the Seeley extensions across {r = a}
of those on Ω^K_([a,b]) (as in Lemma 17.2), which agrees with P on the r-slab.

This is [Hin26c, Propositions 8.12 and 8.13] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* (a) *Reduction to a forward problem.* With χ and δ_2 as in the proof of Proposition 17.23 (iii), v := χu lies
in H^((s′;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−) and solves Pv = g := χf + [P, χ]u, and by Lemma 17.15 (a)

    ‖g‖_(H^((𝗌−1;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−))
        ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^•) + ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),α_K)(Ω^K_([a⁺,b]))^•)).    (17.21)

As u = v on {r ≤ a⁺ + δ_2}, it suffices to bound ‖v‖_((𝗌;k)) by C_k ‖g‖_((𝗌−1;k)).

*Induction.* Let Ω″ := Ω^K_([a−δ_1,b]), δ_1 := (1/2) min(1, a − r^♯), let g″ be the restriction to Ω″ of the minimal
extension of g, and let v″ be the forward solution of Pv″ = g″ on Ω″ (Proposition 17.23 (ii)); by uniqueness
v″|_(Ω^K_([a,b])) = v. We show by induction on j ≤ k that

    Σ_(|γ|≤j) ‖X^γ v″‖_(H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω″)^(•,−)) ≤ C_j ‖g″‖_(H^((𝗌−1;j),α_K)(Ω″)^(•,−)).    (17.22)

j = 0 is (17.16). Let j ≥ 1. A b-vector field maps H^(𝗍,β)_K into H^(𝗍−1,β−1)_K, as t_*∂_(t_*) = ρ_K⁻¹ ∂_(t_*),
and by (17.22) at j − 1 every word of length j − 1 applied to v″ lies in H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω″)^(•,−), so a priori
v″^(j) ∈ H^(𝗌−1,α_K−1)(Ω″)^(•,−). By Proposition 17.23 (i) for P^(j) at the weight α_K − 1, with inf 𝗌 − 1 for its s′,
v″^(j) is the forward solution of (17.18), which by Proposition 17.23 (ii) at the weight α_K lies in
H^(𝗌,α_K)(Ω″)^(•,−), with norm at most C times that of the right side of (17.18) in
H^(𝗌−1,α_K)(Ω″)^(•,−). By Lemma 17.15 (c), ‖X^γ g″‖_(𝗌−1) ≤ C ‖g″‖_((𝗌−1;j)). For |S| = q ≥ 2, ad_(X_S) P is a
second-order e3b-operator with coefficients in C^((d_0;k−q))_(e3b;b), as each commutator with a V_i differentiates the
coefficients once (Lemma 17.24); so it is Σ_i A_i X_i with A_i first-order e3b-operators, and by
Lemma 17.15 (a) ‖(ad_(X_S) P) X^(γ∖S) v″‖_(𝗌−1) ≤ C Σ_i ‖X_i X^(γ∖S) v″‖_𝗌, a sum over words of length
j − q + 1 ≤ j − 1, bounded by (17.22) at j − 1. This proves (17.22), the uniqueness being used at the
orders min(s′, inf 𝗌) and inf 𝗌 − 1 only, so that d_0 depends only on 𝗌 and s′. By Lemma 17.15 (c) with room,
‖v‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k Σ_(|γ|≤k) ‖X^γ v″‖_𝗌 ≤ C_k ‖g‖_((𝗌−1;k)). Each step holds in the strong sense, so
(17.19) does.

(b) As in Proposition 17.19, with 𝒳_K, W = 1, nested r-slabs

    Ω^K_([a,b]) ⊂ Ω_(2k) ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ Ω_(0) = Ω″

with room 2^(−i−2) δ_1 at the final face, two per step as there, and d := d̃ + 3. The right-hand side is
g″ := (ℰg)|_(Ω″) in place of the minimal extension, with ℰ the extension of Lemma 17.18 (K) for the r-slab
Ω^K_([a,b]), the order 𝗍 := 𝗌 − 1 and the weight α_K. As ℰg is supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0, r ≤ b} and equals g on
{r > a}, v″|_(Ω^K_([a,b])) = v by uniqueness, and ‖g″‖_(H^((𝗌−1;j),α_K)(Ω″)^(•,−)) ≤
C_j ‖g‖_(H^((𝗌−1;j),α_K)(Ω^K_([a,b]))^(•,−)) for every j at once. The one new term is [P, χ]u in (17.21). Its
coefficients are χ′ times those of P, which are stationary smooth ones plus O(ε_(P,k)) in C^((d_0;k)); by
Lemma 17.15 (b), whose proof applies verbatim to the spaces H(·)^• with room at both r-faces, here
{a⁺ + δ_2 ≤ r ≤ b − δ_2} inside Ω^K_([a⁺,b]),

    ‖[P, χ]u‖_((𝗌−1;k)) ≤ C_k (‖u‖^([a⁺,b])_((𝗌;k)) + ε_(P,k) ‖u‖^([a⁺,b])_((𝗌;d̃))),

the stationary part contributing ‖u‖_((𝗌;d̃)) ≤ ‖u‖_((𝗌;k)) for k ≥ d̃. The induction then gives (17.20), the
norms of g at order (𝗌 − 1; d) being bounded by (17.21) at k = d. ∎

[Hin26c] states its Propositions 8.11–8.13 for constant orders ("We do not need variable orders in this part", its
footnote 66), and its Theorem 8.14 applies them with the admissible order functions, which need not be constant on
r⁻¹([m, r^♮]). Here they are proved for slab orders (Lemma 17.22 at the variable order, Proposition 17.23 (ii) by
the scheme of Proposition 17.14), and admissible orders are slab orders by Proposition 15.43 (2).

### 17.6 The global estimate

**Theorem 17.26** (The global estimate.) Let the weights satisfy

    α_I < −1/2 + p̄_1,        α_+ < α_I − 1/2,        α_K ∈ ℝ

((16.3)), and let 𝗌_0 < 𝗌 be order functions admissible for P_0 with weights α_+, α_K and margin 0
(Definition 15.44). For every k ∈ ℕ_0 there is C_k such that

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−))
        ≤ C_k (‖Pu‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I+2,α_++2,α_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−))
               + ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌_0;k),(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−)))    (17.23)

for P = P_0, in the strong sense, and for every weakly admissible P of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) (conditions (1)
and (2) of Definition 15.36, as in Section 17.1.1) with ε_(P,k)
small, with C_k uniform; d_0 depends only on 𝗌_0 and 𝗌. Moreover, if 𝗌 and 𝗌_0 are constant over
{t_* ≥ 1/2, r^♯ ≤ r < r_0 + κ_0} for some κ_0 > 0, with values there a positive integer and a nonnegative integer
respectively, there is d ∈ ℕ such that for every k and every P of that class with ε_(P,d) small,

    ‖u‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k (‖Pu‖_((𝗌;k)) + ‖u‖_((𝗌_0;k)) + ε_(P,k) (‖Pu‖_((𝗌;d)) + ‖u‖_((𝗌_0;d)))),    (17.24)

with the spaces and weights of (17.23), ε_(P,k) := ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) over Ω_*, and C_k depending
on P only through a bound for ε_(P,d). Both hold uniformly when P_0 is replaced by the stationary models of nearby
parameters, or perturbed within the stationary wave-type operators.

This is [Hin26c, Theorem 8.14] in dimension 4 + 1. [Hin26c] assumes only the first condition on the weights; the second,
α_+ < α_I − 1/2, is the threshold at the incoming radial set over ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, where the quantity 4(α_I − α_+ − 1/2) must
be positive (Proposition 16.13; [Hin26c, (7.19)]), and [Hin26c, Proposition 7.11], invoked in its proof, assumes it. It
does not involve the orders. [Hin26c] prints its tame estimate (8.46) with the weights (2α_I, α_+, α_K) on Pu, where
(8.45) and [Hin26c, Proposition 7.11] have (2α_I + 2, α_+ + 2, α_K); as printed it would bound u by a weaker norm of Pu
than (8.45) does, which is not what the proof gives. (17.24) carries the weights of (17.23).

*Proof.* Let f := Pu, and assume the right side of (17.23) finite; then u ∈ H^((𝗌_0;k)), and u is the forward
solution of Pu = f on every slab and r-slab below, by Proposition 17.14 (i) and Proposition 17.23 (i).

*A partition of unity.* Let χ and r_1^+ be the cut-off and the radius of (16.2): r_0 < r_1 < r_1^+ < r^♮, χ = 0
on (t^♭)⁻¹([1, 2]) ∪ r⁻¹([r_0, r_1]) and χ = 1 on {t^♭ ≥ 3} ∩ {r ≥ r_1^+}. Let ψ_t ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, 7/2] and
0 on [4, ∞), and ψ_r ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, r_1^+ + δ_3] and 0 on [r^♮ − δ_3, ∞), δ_3 := (r^♮ − r_1^+)/4. Put

    φ_A := ψ_t(t^♭),     φ_C := (1 − ψ_t(t^♭)) ψ_r(r),     φ_B := (1 − ψ_t(t^♭))(1 − ψ_r(r)).

They are smooth on M with bounded b-derivatives (ψ_r(r) = 0 near ι⁺ and ℐ⁺, and r is smooth near (K⁺)°), and
φ_A + φ_B + φ_C = 1. φ_A is supported in {t^♭ ≤ 4}; φ_B in {t^♭ ≥ 7/2, r ≥ r_1^+ + δ_3}, where χ = 1; φ_C in
{t^♭ ≥ 7/2, r ≤ r^♮ − δ_3}. Let Ω_(1,5) be the slab of Section 17.1.1 and Ω^K := Ω^K_([r_0,r^♮]) the r-slab with
T_0 = 1, which is Ω_* ∩ {r ≤ r^♮}. On Ω_(1,5), ρ_+ and ρ_K are bounded above and below, and the spaces of
(17.23) restrict to those of Section 17.1.1 with the weight 2α_I; on Ω^K, ρ_I and ρ_+ are, and they restrict
to those of Section 17.5.1 with the weight α_K. An extension of u|_(Ω_(1,5)) supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}, multiplied by
φ_A, extends φ_A u; likewise for Ω^K and φ_C. As multiplication by the φ's is bounded (Lemma 14.29 (a)),

    ‖u‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C (‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),2α_I)(Ω_(1,5))^(•,−)) + ‖χu‖_((𝗌;k)) + ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),α_K)(Ω^K)^•)).    (17.25)

*(A) Finite times.* 𝗌 is a slab order (Section 17.3.2). By Proposition 17.17 on Ω_(1,5), with P^ext below t^♭ = 1,

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),2α_I)(Ω_(1,5))^(•,−)) ≤ C_k ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;k),2α_I+2)(Ω_(1,5))^(•,−)) ≤ C_k ‖f‖_((𝗌;k)).

[Hin26c] applies its Propositions 8.6 and 8.9 "on a t_*-interval [1, 4]", below the range T_0 ≥ inf_Ω t_* + 1 = 2 in
which they are stated, the margin giving room below the initial face for its extension argument; Lemma 17.2
extends P below t^♭ = 1, and Lemma 17.3 uses a collar of width η_0/2, so the slabs with T_0 ≥ 1 are covered.

*(B) Away from the initial surface and the interior.* Theorem 16.18, (16.31):
‖χu‖_((𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k (‖f‖_((𝗌;k)) + ‖u‖_((𝗌_0;k))).

*(C) The interior.* 𝗌 is a slab order on Ω^K (Section 17.5.3). Proposition 17.25 (a) at s′ := inf 𝗌_0, with a := r_0,
a⁺ := r_1^+ and b := r^♮, gives

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),α_K)(Ω^K)^•) ≤ C_k (‖f‖_((𝗌−1;k)) + ‖u‖^([r_1^+,r^♮])_((𝗌;k))).

On Ω^K_([r_1^+,r^♮]), u = ψ_t(t^♭)u + (1 − ψ_t(t^♭))χu, as χ = 1 on {t^♭ ≥ 7/2, r ≥ r_1^+}; so the last norm is at most
C times the sum of the first two norms on the right of (17.25), which (A) and (B) bound.

Inserting (A)–(C) in (17.25) gives (17.23), and in the strong sense, as each of (A)–(C) holds in it.
For (17.24) use Proposition 17.19, (16.32) and Proposition 17.25 (b) instead, whose hypotheses on 𝗌
hold by assumption (for Proposition 17.25 (b) with a := r_0, T_0 = 1 and κ_0 replaced by min(κ_0, r_0 − r^♯)). In
(A), Proposition 17.19 on Ω_(1,5) bounds u by the norms of f on Ω_(1,6); f is the restriction of Pu, given on all of
Ω_*, and on Ω_(1,6), as on Ω_(1,5), ρ_+ and ρ_K are bounded above and below, so for every j its norm there of order
(𝗌 − 1; j) is at most C_j times the norm of Pu of order (𝗌; j) on Ω_*. The term ε_(P,k) ‖u‖^([r_1^+,r^♮])_((𝗌;d)) of
(17.20) is bounded by (A) and (B) at k = d, with constants depending on ε_(P,d) only. d_0 and d are the largest
of those of the three pieces. Uniformity in P_0: the constants of Section 17.2–Section 17.5 depend on P_0 through
finitely many coefficient norms and the margins of Lemma 15.35, of (17.2) and of the dynamics of
Chapter 15, which are uniform as in Remark 16.3; so are those of (B). ∎

## 18. The normal operator at future timelike infinity

This chapter studies the normal operator of a stationary wave-type operator P_0 at future timelike infinity ι⁺, and its
Mellin-transformed family N⁰(σ), in dimension 4 + 1. It writes out the part of [Hin26c, Section 10.1] that precedes the
forward problem: the ι⁺-normal operator and its family ([Hin26c, Definition 10.3 and Lemma 10.5]); the estimates and
invertibility of N⁰(σ) at high frequencies, without and with b-regularity ([Hin26c, Proposition 10.6 (2) and Lemma
10.7]); and at bounded frequencies ([Hin26c, Proposition 10.6 (1) and Lemmas 10.9–10.10]). The forward problems for
N_(ι⁺)(P_0), for the modified operator P_+ and for P_0 on e3b-spaces, which rest on these results, are solved in
Chapter 19. Section 18.1.4 proves in addition a uniqueness lemma for hyperbolic equations with smooth coefficients
(Lemma 18.4), and the functions monotone along causal curves that supply the compact sets it asks for
(Lemma 18.5); later chapters use both.

*What changes in dimension 4 + 1.* The dimension enters through the constant c := (n − 1)/2 of the normal form
(15.19), which is 3/2 here (Remark 18.2), and through the volume densities, which shift weights by
n/2 = 2 and (n + 1)/2 = 5/2 ((18.2)). Every threshold below is a sum of these, and each is evaluated at n =
4 where it occurs.

*Method.* The analysis at high frequencies is semiclassical, in the parameterised scaled bounded geometry calculus on ι⁺
of Section 14.6.2, whose properties from [Hin26d] are listed in Section 14.3. [Hin26c, Section 10.1.2] runs the
positive commutator arguments in that calculus briefly and leaves "the statements of standalone propagation estimates to
the reader". Here the positive commutator scheme of Chapter 12 is carried over to that calculus (Section 18.2); each
radial estimate then reduces to an evaluation of symbols at the radial set, which is written out. At bounded frequencies
the model at ℐ⁺ is handled with the parametrix of the 0-calculus with bounds [Hin23e, Theorem 3.4], used only through
the Fredholm property it gives on a compact manifold, and b-regularity is proved by difference quotients. Uniqueness for
second-order hyperbolic equations with smooth coefficients is taken from [BGP].

*Radii.* The radii 0 < r_0 < r^♮ := (r_0 + r_2)/2 < r_2 < r′_0 are those of Section 11.1.1 and Lemma 15.35.
Nothing in this chapter depends on their values beyond these inequalities; in particular every result holds for every
inner radius r_0 at which the hypotheses of Chapter 11 and Chapter 15 hold.

*Notation.* As in Chapter 12, the rank of the bundle is N_E, so that sections take values in ℂ^(N_E); the largest
eigenvalue of an endomorphism that is self-adjoint for a fibre inner product is written max spec; and large integers
bounding orders of Sobolev spaces are written M. The constant that multiplies the absorbing operator 𝒜 in the
decompositions of Section 18.2.2 is written ℓ, and the localisation constant of (D9) below is written δ_s. Variable
orders are written in sans-serif letters 𝗌, 𝖻, 𝗋, and multi-orders in bold letters 𝐨, 𝐞, 𝐦, 𝐤, 𝐭.

### 18.1 Setting

#### 18.1.1 Coordinates and weights

Throughout, n = 4, and c := 3/2 except where c is introduced as a level (Lemma 18.4, Lemma 18.5) or as
the weight at cf of an order (Section 18.2.1). Near (ι⁺)° we use τ := t_*⁻¹ and R := r/t_* (Lemma 14.14), so
that ρ = r⁻¹ = τ/R; we put v := R⁻¹ = t_*/r, and near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺

    x_I := R^(−1/2) = (t_*/r)^(1/2),

which is the x′_I of Section 15.7 and Chapter 16 (it differs from the x_I = r^(−1/2) of Section 17.1 by the factor
t_*^(1/2)). ι⁺ = [0, ∞]_R × 𝕊³, with boundary faces ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ = {R = 0} and ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ = {x_I = 0}; ρ_K := R/(1 + R) and x_I
(or (1 + R)^(−1/2)) are defining functions of them. In (t_*, r) and (τ, R),

    t_*∂_(t_*)|_r = −τ∂_τ − R∂_R,      r∂_r|_(t_*) = R∂_R = −½ x_I∂_(x_I),      ρ∂_ρ|_(t_*) = −R∂_R.    (18.1)

Indeed τ = 1/t_* and R = r/t_* give t_*∂_(t_*)τ = −τ and t_*∂_(t_*)R = −R at fixed r, and x_I = R^(−1/2) gives R∂_R = −½
x_I∂_(x_I).

*Weights.* Let μ_b be a smooth positive b-density on ι⁺, for instance |(dR/R) dg̸|, with g̸ the round metric of 𝕊³.
Since t = t_* + r and dx = r³ dr dg̸ on ℝ⁴, and t_* = τ⁻¹, r = Rτ⁻¹ give dt_* ∧ dr = −τ⁻³ dτ ∧ dR,

    |dt dx| = r³ |dt_* dr dg̸| = R³τ⁻⁶ |dτ dR dg̸| = R⁴τ⁻⁵ |dτ/τ| μ_b.    (18.2)

So L²(|dt dx|) = R⁻²τ^(5/2) L²(|dτ/τ| μ_b). Near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, R⁻² = x_I⁴ and τ is a defining function of ι⁺ comparable to
ρ_+; near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, R ∼ ρ_K and τ ∼ ρ_+ρ_K, so R⁻²τ^(5/2) ∼ ρ_+^(5/2)ρ_K^(1/2). This is Lemma 14.19 near ι⁺ (on the
support of a cut-off χ to cl{r ≥ 1, t_* ≥ 1}): H^(0,(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_e3b(|dt dx|) =
H^(0,(2(α_I+2),α_++5/2,α_K+1/2))_e3b(|dτ/τ| μ_b). As τ ∼ ρ_+ρ_K near ι⁺, the weights ρ_+^(α_++5/2)ρ_K^(α_K+1/2) are
τ^(α_++5/2)ρ_K^(α_K−α_+−2). So, with b-densities on [0, ∞)_τ × ι⁺, the weights of this chapter are

    γ_I := α_I + 2 at ℐ⁺,    γ_+ := α_+ + 5/2 at τ = 0,    γ_cf := −(α_+ + 2) at ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ (for α_K = 0).    (18.3)

In dimension 3 + 1, [Hin26c] has α_I + 3/2, α_+ + 2 and −(α_+ + 3/2). The weight α_sf + 2 with which P_0 is
tf-admissible (Definition 15.32 (2), with α_sf = α_+) is −γ_cf.

*Indicial gap.* (β_−, β_+) is the indicial gap of P̂_0(0) that contains −γ_cf = α_+ + 2 (Definition 15.28,
Definition 15.32 (2) and Definition 13.1). By Section 15.10.4, α_+ + 2 is the b-weight at ∂X that corresponds to the
spatial weight α_+ of an L²(|dx|)-based space in dimension 4.

*The Mellin transform.* In this chapter, as in [Hin26c, Section 10],

    (ℳu)(σ, ·) := ∫_0^∞ τ^(−iσ) u(τ, ·) dτ/τ,      ℳ(τ∂_τ u) = iσ ℳu.    (18.4)

This is the transform of Section 14.6.2 at −σ. For u = τ^γ w, (ℳu)(σ − iγ) = (ℳw)(σ) for real σ, as τ^(−i(σ−iγ))τ^γ =
τ^(−iσ): the Plancherel line of the weight τ^γ is Im σ = −γ (Lemma 14.20 with σ ↦ −σ; its line Im σ = +β_+ is for
τ^(iσ)).

#### 18.1.2 The normal operator at ι⁺

By Definition 15.21, on {ρ < ρ_1},

    P_0 = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c − S) + ρ²P⁽⁰⁾(ρ, ω, ρ∂_ρ, ∂_ω) + Q∂_(t_*) − g_00∂²_(t_*),    (18.5)

with S ∈ C^∞(X̄; End ℂ^(N_E)), P⁽⁰⁾ ∈ Diff²_b(X̄; E), P⁽⁰⁾ ≡ ((ρD_ρ)² + Δ_(𝕊³)) Id modulo Diff¹_b + ρ Diff²_b
(Lemma 15.23), Q ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b and g_00 ∈ ρ²C^∞(X̄). We write P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ρ∂_ρ, ∂_ω) for the operator whose
coefficients are those of P⁽⁰⁾ frozen at ρ = 0 (its normal operator at ∂X, N(P⁽⁰⁾) of (13.12)), and S_0 :=
S|_(∂X).

**Definition 18.1** (The ι⁺-normal operator; [Hin26c, Definition 10.3] in dimension 4 + 1.) The *ι⁺-normal
operator* of P_0 is N_(ι⁺)(P_0) := t_*⁻² N⁰ on (0, ∞)_τ × (ι⁺)°, with

    N⁰ := −2R⁻¹(τ∂_τ + R∂_R)(R∂_R + c + S_0) + R⁻²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω).    (18.6)

Its *Mellin-transformed family* is

    N⁰(σ) := −2R⁻¹(iσ + R∂_R)(R∂_R + c + S_0) + R⁻²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω)
           = x_I²[−½(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2iσ)(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2(c + S_0)) + x_I²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ½x_I∂_(x_I), ∂_ω)],    (18.7)

so that ℳ(N⁰u)(σ) = N⁰(σ)(ℳu)(σ) by (18.4).

The second form of (18.7) follows from R∂_R = −½x_I∂_(x_I) and R⁻¹ = x_I²: iσ + R∂_R = −½(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2iσ) and
R∂_R + c + S_0 = −½(x_I∂_(x_I) − 2(c + S_0)). [Hin26c, Definition 10.3] prints the factor t_*² in place of t_*⁻²; the
factor t_*⁻² is the one that its use in [Hin26c, Proposition 10.12] ("N⁰_(ι⁺)(P_0)u = t_*²f") and the homogeneity of
degree −2 require.

In (t_*, r, ω), by (18.1), τ∂_τ + R∂_R = −t_*∂_(t_*) and R⁻¹ = t_*/r, so

    N_(ι⁺)(P_0) = 2r⁻¹∂_(t_*)(r∂_r + c + S_0) + r⁻²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −r∂_r, ∂_ω):    (18.8)

the operator (18.5) with Q = 0, g_00 = 0 and its coefficients frozen at ρ = 0. It is invariant under
translations in t_*, homogeneous of degree −2 under (t_*, x) ↦ (at_*, ax), a > 0, and its principal symbol is the dual
metric function of the Minkowski metric ḡ: by Lemma 15.23, σ_2(ρ²P⁽⁰⁾) = ḡ⁻¹ on spatial covectors up to ρ²P^[2],
and σ_2(−2∂_(t_*)ρ ρ∂_ρ) = σ_2(2∂_(t_*)∂_r), which with the frozen part gives −2ζ_(t_*)ζ_r + ζ_r² + r⁻²|η|² = ḡ⁻¹(ζ, ζ)
(the proof of Lemma 17.7). In (τ, R) this is the dual metric

    g⁻¹_(ι⁺) = τ⁻²ḡ⁻¹ = 2R⁻¹(τ∂_τ + R∂_R) ⊗_s R∂_R + R⁻²((R∂_R)² + g̸⁻¹),    (18.9)

with a ⊗_s b := ½(a ⊗ b + b ⊗ a), and d(log τ) = −dt_*/t_* is null for it, as dt_* is for ḡ.

**Remark 18.2** (The constant c.) For the wave operator of Minkowski space, P_0 = −□_ḡ Id on ℝ^(1+4),
(18.8) holds exactly with S_0 = 0, and it shows where c = 3/2 comes from. In (t_*, r, ω), ḡ = −dt_*² − 2dt_*
dr + r²g̸, so ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = 0, ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dr) = −1, ḡ⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1, and |det ḡ|^(1/2) = r³ |det g̸|^(1/2). With
Δ_(𝕊³) ≥ 0 the Laplacian of g̸,

    −□_ḡ = 2∂_(t_*)∂_r + 3r⁻¹∂_(t_*) − ∂_r² − 3r⁻¹∂_r + r⁻²Δ_(𝕊³)
         = 2r⁻¹∂_(t_*)(r∂_r + 3/2) + r⁻²(−(r∂_r)² − 2r∂_r + Δ_(𝕊³)),

since r²(∂_r² + 3r⁻¹∂_r) = (r∂_r)² − r∂_r + 3r∂_r. With ρ∂_ρ = −r∂_r the last bracket is (ρD_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ_(𝕊³). So
−□_ḡ is (18.8) with c = 3/2, S_0 = 0 and P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ρ∂_ρ, ∂_ω) = (ρD_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ_(𝕊³), whose principal part
is that of Lemma 15.23; as its coefficients do not depend on ρ and Q = 0, g_00 = 0, N_(ι⁺)(−□_ḡ) = −□_ḡ. In
dimension n + 1 the same steps give 3 ↦ n − 1, so c = (n − 1)/2, and the term (n − 2)ρ∂_ρ; c = 1 in dimension 3 + 1.

**Lemma 18.3** ([Hin26c, Lemma 10.5] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let χ ∈ C^∞(M) equal 1 near ι⁺, supported in a
small collar of ι⁺. Then

    χN_(ι⁺)(P_0) ∈ x_I²ρ_+²Diff²_e3b(M),    χ(P_0 − N_(ι⁺)(P_0)) ∈ x_I²ρ_+³Diff²_e3b(M).    (18.10)

*Proof.* The first membership is checked as in Lemma 15.25 (b), which uses of P_0 only the form (18.5),
and N_(ι⁺)(P_0) has that form. For the second, t_*²(P_0 − N_(ι⁺)(P_0)) = t_*²P_0 − N⁰, and by (18.1),
t_*²·(−2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c − S_0)) and t_*²ρ²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ρ∂_ρ, ∂_ω) are the two terms of (18.6): ∂_(t_*) =
−τ(τ∂_τ + R∂_R), which commutes with ρ = τ/R, and ρ∂_ρ = −R∂_R, so −2ρ∂_(t_*)(ρ∂_ρ − c − S_0) = −2τ²R⁻¹(τ∂_τ +
R∂_R)(R∂_R + c + S_0), and t_*²ρ² = R⁻². The remaining terms are, near ℐ⁺ with x_I = v^(1/2): (i) −2t_*²∂_(t_*)ρ(S_0 −
S), the difference of the S-terms of (18.5) and (18.8), with S − S_0 ∈ ρC^∞, so that ρ(S_0 − S) ∈
ρ²C^∞ and, ρ² = τ²R⁻² being annihilated by τ∂_τ + R∂_R, it is of the form τR⁻²(τ∂_τ + R∂_R)·C^∞, which vanishes at τ = 0
and to order R⁻² = x_I⁴ at ℐ⁺; (ii) t_*²ρ²(P⁽⁰⁾(ρ, ·) − P⁽⁰⁾(0, ·)) ∈ t_*²ρ³Diff²_b(X̄), of the schematic form
τR⁻³(R∂_R, ∂_ω)^(≤2), hence x_I⁴τ(x_I∂_(x_I), x_I∂_ω)^(≤2), as R⁻³∂_ω² = x_I⁴(x_I∂_ω)²; (iii) t_*²Q∂_(t_*) ∈
t_*²ρ³Diff¹_b(X̄)∂_(t_*), of the form τ²R⁻³(τ∂_τ + R∂_R)(R∂_R, ∂_ω)^(≤1); (iv) t_*²g_00∂²_(t_*), g_00 ∈ ρ²C^∞, of the
form τ²R⁻²(τ∂_τ + R∂_R)^(≤2). Each lies in τx_I⁴Diff² of the fields τ∂_τ, x_I∂_(x_I), x_I∂_ω near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, and in
τDiff²_b near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, where R ≤ C. Multiplying by t_*⁻² = τ² and using τ ∼ ρ_+ near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ and τ ∼ ρ_+ρ_K near ι⁺ ∩
K⁺, together with the e3b-spanning sets of Section 14.2.4, gives (18.10). The powers of ρ in (i)–(iv) do not
depend on n. ∎

#### 18.1.3 The family on ι⁺ and its semiclassical rescaling

By (18.7), N⁰(σ) ∈ x_I²ρ_K⁻²Diff²_(0,b)(ι⁺): near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ it is R⁻² times a b-differential operator in (R, ω),
and near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ it is x_I² times a 0-differential operator in the fields x_I∂_(x_I), x_I∂_ω (Section 14.6.2:
C^∞_b𝒱_(0,b)(ι⁺)). Its 0,b-principal symbol is, with 0-covectors ξ_0 dx_I/x_I + η_0 dω/x_I,

    x_I²(½ξ_0² + |η_0|² + ¼x_I²ξ_0²) Id,    (18.11)

since −½(x_I∂_(x_I))² ↦ ½ξ_0² and x_I²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ½x_I∂_(x_I), ∂_ω) ↦ x_I²(¼ξ_0²) + |η_0|² (Δ_(𝕊³) ≥ 0); near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ the
b-principal symbol is R⁻² times that of (RD_R)² + Δ_(𝕊³) plus the term −2R⁻¹(R∂_R)² ↦ 2R⁻¹ξ_b², positive definite. So
N⁰(σ) is elliptic in the 0,b-sense, for every σ ∈ ℂ.

For h ∈ (0, 1] and z ∈ ℂ with |z| ∈ [½, 2] put

    P_(ι,h,z) := h²N⁰(h⁻¹z)
               = x_I²[−½(hx_I∂_(x_I) − 2iz)(hx_I∂_(x_I) − 2h(c + S_0))
                      + h²x_I²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ½x_I∂_(x_I), ∂_ω)]    (18.12)
               = −2R⁻¹(iz + hR∂_R)(hR∂_R + h(c + S_0)) + h²R⁻²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω).    (18.13)

It is a family in the semiclassical 0- and cone calculus on ι⁺_(0ħ,cħ) of Section 14.6.2, of differential order 2,
with weights x_I² at the face over ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ and ρ_cf⁻² at cf, and orders 0 at sf and tf ([Hin26c, (3.55a)–(3.55b)]). Near
ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ we use semiclassical 0-covectors ξ dx_I/(hx_I) + η dω/(hx_I), and near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ semiclassical cone covectors ξ_cħ
((h + R)/h)(dR/R) + ((h + R)/h)η_cħ; over sf (h = 0) near cf these are ξ_cħ dR/h + (R/h)η_cħ. The principal symbol at sf
is

    G_(ι,z) = x_I²[½(ξ − 2z)ξ + |η|² + ¼x_I²ξ²] = 2(z + Rξ_cħ)ξ_cħ + ξ_cħ² + |η_cħ|²,    (18.14)

from (18.12) with hx_I∂_(x_I) ↦ iξ, hx_I∂_ω ↦ iη, and from (18.13) with hR∂_R ↦ iRξ_cħ, h∂_ω ↦ iRη_cħ
over sf: −2R⁻¹(iz + iRξ_cħ)(iRξ_cħ) = 2(z + Rξ_cħ)ξ_cħ and h²R⁻²((RD_R)² + Δ) ↦ ξ_cħ² + |η_cħ|². The term ¼x_I²ξ², which
[Hin26c, (10.21)] omits, vanishes at ℐ⁺ and changes none of the conclusions drawn there. At fibre infinity of the
semiclassical phase space the symbol is that of (18.11), positive definite, so the semiclassical characteristic
set is a compact subset of the face sf over ι⁺, away from fibre infinity ([Hin26c, Section 10.1.1]).

*Real z.* For z = ±1 the characteristic set and the flow over sf are the pull-back of Proposition 15.18 ([Hin26c,
Proposition 4.24]) along the identification of the semiclassical phase space with the e3b-phase space over ι⁺ at the
time frequency ∓1 ([Hin26c, Section 10.1.1]). Its radial sets are

    R_(ℐ⁺,±1,in) := {x_I = 0, ξ = ±2, η = 0},              R_(ℐ⁺,out) := {x_I = 0, ξ = 0, η = 0},
    R_(cf,±1,in) := {R = 0, ξ_cħ = ∓2, η_cħ = 0},    R_(cf,out) := {R = 0, ξ_cħ = 0, η_cħ = 0},    (18.15)

all over sf. At z = 1: on {x_I = 0}, G_(ι,1)/x_I² = ½(ξ − 1)² − ½ + |η|²; its Hamilton field in the coordinates (x_I, ω;
ξ, η) is

    𝖧_I := H_(x_I⁻²G_(ι,1)) = (ξ − 1)(x_I∂_(x_I) + η·∂_η) − 2|η|²∂_ξ + x_I H_(|η|²)
           at x_I = 0 to first order,    (18.16)

with H_(|η|²) = 2η·∂_ω at the centre of normal coordinates ([Hin26c, Section 10.1.2]; the evaluation is that of
(15.16) at the time frequency −1). It vanishes exactly at R_(ℐ⁺,1,in) and R_(ℐ⁺,out) on the characteristic set
over {x_I = 0}, where ξ(ξ − 2) = −2|η|². Near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, with ĥ := h/R, the field of G_(ι,1) in the covectors ξ_cħ dR/h +
η_cħ R dω/h is ([Hin26c, Section 10.1.2], by the change of variables)

    𝖧_cf := ĥ((2(1 + 2R)ξ_cħ + 2)(R∂_R − η_cħ·∂_(η_cħ)) + 2(|η_cħ|² − Rξ_cħ²)∂_(ξ_cħ) + H_(|η_cħ|²)).    (18.17)

Up to the factor ĥ, it vanishes over {R = 0} on the characteristic set exactly at R_(cf,1,in) and R_(cf,out). The future
flow has the types (A, B) (A the α-limit set, B the ω-limit set): A = R_(ℐ⁺,±1,in) and B = R_(ℐ⁺,out) or R_(cf,±1,in);
A = R_(cf,±1,in) and B = R_(cf,out); A = R_(cf,out) and B = R_(ℐ⁺,out) (Proposition 15.18, the entries over ι⁺, pulled
back). R_(ℐ⁺,±1,in) is a source, R_(ℐ⁺,out) a sink, and R_(cf,±1,in), R_(cf,out) are saddles: the stable manifold of
R_(cf,±1,in) lies over R > 0 (the curves from R_(ℐ⁺,±1,in)), its unstable manifold over R = 0, which is the stable
manifold of R_(cf,out), whose unstable manifold lies over R > 0 (the curves to R_(ℐ⁺,out)).

*Complex z.* If Im z ≠ 0, Im G_(ι,z) = 2(Im z)ξ_cħ (resp. −x_I²(Im z)ξ) vanishes only where ξ_cħ = 0, and then Re
G_(ι,z) = |η_cħ|² forces η_cħ = 0; likewise in the 0-variables. So the characteristic set is the zero section over sf,
and the flow of the Hamilton field of Re(z⁻¹G_(ι,z)) on it, 2ĥR∂_R = 2h∂_R near R = 0 and −x_I∂_(x_I) near x_I = 0 (up
to positive factors), runs from R_(cf,out), now a source, to the sink R_(ℐ⁺,out) ([Hin26c, (10.22) and Figure 10.1]).

*Orders.* Let 𝗌 be an order function admissible for P_0 with weights α_+, 0 and margin 0 (Definition 15.44). As in
[Hin26c, Section 10.1.1] (by pull-back along the identifications above) it induces a differential order 𝗌_(0,b) on
^(0,b)S*ι⁺, a differential order 𝗌_(0ħ,cħ) at fibre infinity of the semiclassical phase space, and semiclassical orders
𝖻_± on the face sf for σ → ±∞ ([Hin26c, (10.12)–(10.13)]). By Proposition 15.43 and Definition 15.29, pulled back: 𝖻_±
is non-increasing along the future flow over sf, constant near the radial sets (18.15), and

    𝖻_± + α_+ > ½(−1 + ϑ_in) at R_(cf,±1,in),    𝖻_± + α_+ < −½ + S̄ at R_(cf,out),    (18.18)

with the fibre inner products chosen as in Definition 15.29 and Lemma 15.31 (up to any margin): these are
Definition 15.29 (5)–(6) with α_sf = α_+ and α_K = 0, as the 3b-regularity order at the radial sets over ∂K⁺ is the
semiclassical order here ([Hin26c, (10.28) and after]).

#### 18.1.4 Uniqueness for hyperbolic equations with smooth coefficients

Several steps of Chapter 19 and of the later chapters show that a solution of a wave equation vanishes, or identify two
solutions, on regions of M° or of Minkowski space ℝ^(1+4) where the operator has smooth coefficients. They use one
statement, proved here from [BGP]. A *time function* on a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold X is τ ∈ C^∞(X) with dτ past
timelike; then dτ(V) > 0 for every future directed causal V, so τ is strictly increasing along future directed causal
curves. J⁻_X(p) is the set of points reached from p by past directed causal curves in X, together with p ([BGP, p. 18]).

**Lemma 18.4** (Uniqueness of solutions supported to the future.) Let X be a time-oriented Lorentzian
manifold with metric g, P a second-order operator with smooth coefficients on a vector bundle over X with principal
symbol g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id, τ a time function on X and c ∈ ℝ. Assume that for every p ∈ X with τ(p) > c there is a compact set
L_p ⊂ X containing J⁻_X(p) ∩ {τ ≥ c}. If w ∈ 𝒟′(X), Pw = 0 and supp w ⊂ {τ > c}, then w = 0.

*Proof.* We use the following from [BGP], whose pages are cited from its arXiv version 1. Theorem 3.1.1 (p. 68): on a
connected time-oriented Lorentzian manifold with no causal loops, a closed causal relation and a finite continuous time
separation, a distribution with past or future compact support solving Pu = 0, P normally hyperbolic, vanishes. Remark
3.1.3 (p. 72): these assumptions hold on globally hyperbolic manifolds. Definition 1.3.8 (p. 23): global hyperbolicity
is strong causality with J⁺(p) ∩ J⁻(q) compact for all p, q. A set A is past compact if A ∩ J⁻(p) is compact for every
p, and a curve is inextendible if no piecewise C¹ reparametrisation extends continuously to an end point (p. 18). The
Cauchy development D(S) of S is the set of points through which every inextendible causal curve meets S (Definition
1.3.5, p. 22), and the causal future of a Cauchy hypersurface is past compact (p. 22). Lemma A.5.9 (p. 176): for an
acausal hypersurface S, D(S) is an open, causally compatible, globally hyperbolic subset; and S is a Cauchy hypersurface
of D(S) (the end of the proof of Lemma A.5.9, p. 176). P or −P is normally hyperbolic in the sense of [BGP, Section
1.5], its principal part being ∓ the d'Alembertian of g, and Pw = 0 if and only if −Pw = 0. Working on each connected
component, we may assume X connected.

If {τ > c} is empty there is nothing to prove. Let p ∈ X with τ(p) > c, and γ a past directed causal curve from p, past
inextendible in X, along which τ > c. Then γ ⊂ L_p. τ is strictly monotone along γ, so it is a piecewise C¹ parameter on
γ, in which, the curve being run towards the future, the tangent lies in {V causal : dτ(V) = 1} over L_p; this set is
compact, as a sequence in it with |V_j|_k → ∞, k a Riemannian metric, would have a normalised limit V, causal
with |V|_k = 1 and dτ(V) = 0. So γ is Lipschitz in τ for the distance of k, and as τ decreases to inf_γ τ it converges in
the compact set L_p: γ extends continuously to its past end point, a contradiction. Hence τ reaches c along every past
inextendible causal curve from p, and every inextendible causal curve through p meets S := {τ = c}, a smooth
hypersurface (dτ ≠ 0) which is acausal (τ is strictly increasing along causal curves). So {τ > c} ⊂ D := D(S).

D is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy hypersurface S. A point q ∈ D with τ(q) > c lies in J⁺_D(S): an inextendible
timelike curve in D through q (the maximal integral curve of −∇τ, which has no zeros) meets S, where τ = c < τ(q), so in
the past of q. Hence supp(w|_D) ⊂ J⁺_D(S), and for x ∈ D, supp(w|_D) ∩ J⁻_D(x) is a closed subset of the compact set
J⁺_D(S) ∩ J⁻_D(x) (J⁻_D(x) is closed, as the causal relation of the globally hyperbolic D is closed, [BGP, Remark
3.1.3]): supp(w|_D) is past compact. On each connected component D_1 of D, which is open and globally hyperbolic (a
causal curve in D starting in D_1 stays in D_1, so the causal sets of D_1 are those of D), [BGP, Theorem 3.1.1] with
[BGP, Remark 3.1.3] gives w = 0. So w vanishes on D ⊃ {τ > c} ⊃ supp w, and w = 0. ∎

The compact sets L_p are produced by functions that are monotone along causal curves. Let Ḡ be the dual Minkowski metric
and G_0 that of g_0, time-oriented so that dt_* is past timelike (Lemma 15.2); let r′_0, C′, C and R̃ be as in
Lemma 15.35 and its proof (R̃ a smooth maximum of r and r′_0, equal to r′_0 for r ≤ r′_0 − 1 and to r for r ≥
r′_0 + 1, with R̃′ ∈ [0, 1]; C ≥ 4 by the proof of Lemma 17.2 (iv)), and t^♭_* the time function of
Lemma 15.35. For a smooth θ with values in [0, 1] put G_θ := (1 − θ)G_0 + θḠ on a region where it is Lorentzian.

**Lemma 18.5** (Monotone functions.) Along future directed causal curves of G_θ:

(a) if θ = 0 on {r ≤ r′_0 + 1}: t_* is non-decreasing; B := t_* + R̃(r) is a time function; and on {r_0 ≤ r ≤ r^♮}, r is
strictly decreasing, so that a past directed causal curve from a point p with r(p) > r_0 stays in {r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)}.
Consequently, let X be an open set on which G_θ is defined and Lorentzian, τ′ a time function on X with τ′ ≤ t_* on X, c
∈ ℝ, and p ∈ X with τ′(p) > c and r(p) > r_0. Then J⁻_X(p) ∩ {τ′ ≥ c} lies in

    L_p := {q ∈ X : c ≤ τ′(q) ≤ τ′(p), t_*(q) ≤ t_*(p), B(q) ≤ B(p), r(q) ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)},    (18.19)

on which c ≤ t_* ≤ t_*(p) and min(r(p), r^♮) ≤ r ≤ max(r′_0 + 1, B(p) − c). If the closure of L_p lies in X, then L_p is
compact, and it is a set as in Lemma 18.4 for τ := τ′ at p. If moreover C′t_* ≤ τ′ on X ∩ {τ′ ≥ c}, as holds for
τ′ = t^♭_* where it is a time function (C′t_* ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t_* by Lemma 15.35 (b)) and for τ′ = t_* when c ≥ 0, then
t_*(q) ≤ τ′(q)/C′ ≤ τ′(p)/C′ wherever c ≤ τ′(q) ≤ τ′(p), and the condition t_*(q) ≤ t_*(p) may be dropped: the set

    L′_p := {q ∈ X : c ≤ τ′(q) ≤ τ′(p), B(q) ≤ B(p), r(q) ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)} ⊃ L_p    (18.20)

also contains J⁻_X(p) ∩ {τ′ ≥ c}; on it c ≤ t_* ≤ τ′(p)/C′ and min(r(p), r^♮) ≤ r ≤ max(r′_0 + 1, B(p) − c); and if
its closure lies in X, then L′_p is compact and is a set as in Lemma 18.4 for τ := τ′ at p;

(b) if θ = χ(R) with χ as in Definition 19.5, on {t_* > t_1}, where t_1 ≥ r′_0 + 1 is so large that G_χ is Lorentzian
there: t_* is non-decreasing, t = t_* + r is a time function, and so is t^♭_+, defined as C′t on {r ≤ ½Ct_*} and as
t^♭_* on {r ≥ r′_0 + 1}, with C′t_* ≤ t^♭_+ ≤ t_*;

(c) if θ = 1, on ℝ^(1+4): t is a time function, and t_* = t − r and t + r are non-decreasing.

*Proof.* At a point, the past causal cones C_0 of G_0 and C̄ of Ḡ are closed convex cones, so C_0 ∩ C̄ is convex and G_θ
≤ 0 on it. In (a) and (b), θ ∈ (0, 1) only on {r ≥ r′_0 + 1}, and there dt is past timelike for Ḡ and for G_0: by
Lemma 15.2 (1), g_0⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ ∈ r⁻²C^∞(M; S²𝒯), so G_0(dt) ≤ −1 + Cr⁻² < 0 for r′_0 large, as in the proof of
Lemma 15.35. So (C_0 ∩ C̄) ∖ 0, connected and containing the G_θ-timelike dt, lies in the past causal cone of G_θ;
we orient G_θ by it (by dt_* where θ = 0, by dt where θ = 1). A covector in C_0 ∩ C̄ is then ≥ 0 on future causal
vectors of G_θ, and > 0 if it is timelike for G_0 where θ < 1 and for Ḡ where θ > 0. dt_* lies in C_0 ∩ C̄: it is past
timelike for G_0 (Lemma 15.2), and null for Ḡ with dt_*(V) = V^t − V^r ≥ 0 for Ḡ-future causal V. This gives the
claims on t_*.

(a) dB = (1 − R̃′)dt_* + R̃′dt is past timelike for G_0 everywhere (R̃′ > 0 only on {r ≥ r′_0 − 1}, where dt is) and
equals dt where θ > 0; so B is a time function. θ = 0 on {r_0 ≤ r ≤ r^♮} (r^♮ < r_2 < r′_0), where dr is future timelike
for g_0 (Lemma 15.35 (1) with h = 0), so dr(V) < 0 for future causal V: followed towards the past, r increases
while it lies in (r_0, r^♮], and so cannot pass below min(r(p), r^♮).

For the sets: let q ∈ J⁻_X(p) with τ′(q) ≥ c, reached by a past directed causal curve γ in X from p. Along γ, run
towards the past, τ′ and B decrease, t_* does not increase and r stays ≥ min(r(p), r^♮); so c ≤ τ′(q) ≤ τ′(p), t_*(q) ≤
t_*(p), B(q) ≤ B(p) and r(q) ≥ min(r(p), r^♮), that is q ∈ L_p. On L_p, t_* ≥ τ′ ≥ c; so R̃(r) = B − t_* ≤ B(p) − c, and
as R̃(r) = r for r ≥ r′_0 + 1, r ≤ max(r′_0 + 1, B(p) − c). The closure of L_p in the spacetime therefore lies in the
compact set {c ≤ t_* ≤ t_*(p), min(r(p), r^♮) ≤ r ≤ max(r′_0 + 1, B(p) − c)}; if it lies in X, the four conditions,
which are closed in X, hold on it, so it equals L_p, and L_p is compact. If C′t_* ≤ τ′ on X ∩ {τ′ ≥ c}, then on L′_p,
c ≤ τ′ ≤ t_* ≤ τ′/C′ ≤ τ′(p)/C′ and, as before, R̃(r) = B − t_* ≤ B(p) − c; so the closure of L′_p lies in the compact
set {c ≤ t_* ≤ τ′(p)/C′, min(r(p), r^♮) ≤ r ≤ max(r′_0 + 1, B(p) − c)}, and the same argument, with three closed
conditions, shows that L′_p is compact when its closure lies in X.

(b) Where θ ∈ (0, 1), 1 < R < 2, so r > t_* > t_1 ≥ r′_0 + 1; where R ≤ 1, G_χ = Ḡ; where R ≥ 2, G_χ = G_0. So dt is
past timelike for G_χ. On {r′_0 + 1 ≤ r ≤ ½Ct_*}, t^♭_* = C′(t_* + R̃(r)) = C′t (the proof of Lemma 15.35), so the
two definitions of t^♭_+ agree, and the two sets cover {t_* > t_1}. On {r ≤ ½Ct_*}, dt^♭_+ = C′dt; on {r ≥ ½Ct_*} ⊂ {R ≥
2}, G_χ = G_0 and dt^♭_+ = dt^♭_* is past timelike by Lemma 15.35 (2) with h = 0. On {r ≤ ½Ct_*}, C′t_* ≤ C′t ≤
C′(1 + ½C)t_* ≤ t_* (the proof of Lemma 15.35 (b)); on the rest, Lemma 15.35 (b).

(c) For Ḡ-future causal V, V^t ≥ |V^x| ≥ |V^r| (where r is differentiable along the curve, which is almost everywhere),
so dt(V) > 0 and (dt ∓ dr)(V) ≥ 0. ∎
### 18.2 The semiclassical calculus on ι⁺, and the positive commutator scheme

[Hin26c, Section 10.1.2] runs positive commutator arguments in the semiclassical 0- and cone calculus on ι⁺ and
"leave[s] the statements of standalone propagation estimates to the reader". This section supplies them. The calculus is
a parameterised scaled b.g. calculus (Section 14.3); the positive commutator scheme of Section 12.2–Section 12.5,
proved there for the semiclassical scattering calculus on ℝⁿ, uses of its calculus only a short list of properties, and
each holds here. The one structural difference is that remainders gain only at the semiclassical face sf and in the
differential order, not at the faces 0f, cf, tf; the dictionary (D1)–(D9) below records what changes.

#### 18.2.1 The space, the calculus and the orders

ι⁺_ħ := ι⁺_(0ħ,cħ) = [[0, 1)_h × ι⁺; {0} × (ι⁺ ∩ K⁺)] (Section 14.6.2) has four boundary hypersurfaces: sf, the lift
of {h = 0}; tf, the front face; cf, the lift of [0, 1) × (ι⁺ ∩ K⁺); and 0f, the lift of [0, 1) × (ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺). With ρ_K =
R/(1 + R) as in Section 18.1.1 we use the defining functions

    ρ_sf := h/(h + ρ_K),    ρ_tf := h + ρ_K,    ρ_cf := ρ_K/(h + ρ_K),    ρ_0f := (1 + R)^(−1/2).    (18.21)

ρ_0f = x_I(1 + x_I²)^(−1/2) near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺. Near sf ∩ tf the functions ĥ := h/R and R are local defining functions of sf
and tf, and ρ_sf/ĥ = (R/ρ_K)·(1 + ĥR/ρ_K)⁻¹ is smooth and positive, equal to 1 at ĥ = R = 0; near sf ∩ 0f, h and x_I
are, and ρ_sf/h, ρ_0f/x_I are smooth and positive, equal to 1 at h = x_I = 0. The face sf is a copy of ι⁺: the centre
{0} × (ι⁺ ∩ K⁺) of the blow-up is a boundary hypersurface of {0} × ι⁺, and blowing one up does not change a manifold
with corners.

*The structure.* By Section 14.6.2 ([Hin26c, Section 3.2.4]), for h ∈ (0, 1] the semiclassical 0- and cone structure
is the parameterised scaled b.g. structure (S7) of Section 14.3 on (ι⁺)°, with the cells U_(2,jk±), U_(3,jk±) of
Section 14.6.2 (and finitely many cells covering a compact subset of (ι⁺)°), the coefficient Lie algebra C^∞_b𝒱_b(ι⁺),
which does not depend on h, and the scalings (1 + ρ_K|σ|)⁻¹, resp. (⟨σ⟩⁻¹, x_I⟨σ⟩⁻¹) at |σ| = h⁻¹: up to factors bounded
above and below, h/(h + 2^(−j)) in every direction on U_(2,jk±), h in x_I and 2^(−j)h in ω on U_(3,jk±), and h on the
interior cells. Its operator Lie algebra 𝒱_ħ is spanned over C^∞_b(ι⁺), uniformly in h, by (h/(h + ρ_K))ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) and
(h/(h + ρ_K))∂_ω near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, by hx_I∂_(x_I) and hx_I∂_ω near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, and by h𝒱(ι⁺) in between.

**Lemma 18.6** (a) The scaling weight ρ̄ of this structure ((S1) of Section 14.3) satisfies C⁻¹ρ_sf ≤ ρ̄ ≤
Cρ_sf with C independent of h. (b) For a, c, l ∈ ℝ, ρ_0f^a ρ_cf^c ρ_tf^l and ρ_sf are weights in the sense of (S2),
uniformly in h. (c) P_(ι,h,z) ∈ ρ_0f²ρ_cf⁻²Diff²_(𝒱_ħ), with coefficients affine in z and bounded uniformly for |z| ≤ 2
and h ∈ (0, 1].

*Proof.* (a) On U_(2,jk±), ρ_K ∈ (2^(−j−2), 2^(−j+2)), so h/(h + 2^(−j)) and ρ_sf agree up to a factor in [¼, 4]. On
U_(3,jk±) the largest scaling is h, and ρ_K ∈ [½, 1] there, so h ≤ 2ρ_sf ≤ 2h; likewise on the interior cells. (b) Note
ρ_cf = ρ_K/(h + ρ_K) ∈ [0, 1]. Then ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) log ρ_tf = ρ_cf, ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) log ρ_cf = 1 − ρ_cf, ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) log ρ_sf =
−ρ_cf and ρ_K∂_(ρ_K)ρ_cf = ρ_cf(1 − ρ_cf), so every derivative of the logarithms of these functions along C^∞_b𝒱_b(ι⁺)
is a polynomial in ρ_cf with coefficients bounded uniformly in h; log ρ_0f is log x_I plus a smooth function near ℐ⁺,
and x_I∂_(x_I) log x_I = 1. So Ww/w ∈ C^∞_uni uniformly for each of these w and every W in the coefficient Lie algebra.
(c) Near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ (where we may use R in place of ρ_K, the two being smooth multiples of each other) put V_1 := (h/(h +
R))R∂_R and V_ω := (h/(h + R))∂_ω. Then hR∂_R = (h + R)V_1, R⁻¹(h + R) = ρ_cf⁻¹ and R⁻¹h = ρ_sfρ_cf⁻¹ up to smooth
positive factors, and V_1(h + R) = ρ_sfR; so in (18.13), R⁻¹(iz + hR∂_R) ∈ ρ_cf⁻¹Diff¹_(𝒱_ħ), hR∂_R + h(c +
S_0) ∈ Diff¹_(𝒱_ħ) and h²R⁻²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω) ∈ ρ_cf⁻²Diff²_(𝒱_ħ). Near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, (18.12) is x_I² times a
polynomial of degree 2 in hx_I∂_(x_I), hx_I∂_ω with coefficients bounded uniformly (h²x_I²(x_I∂_(x_I))² =
x_I²(hx_I∂_(x_I))², h²x_I²∂_ω² = (hx_I∂_ω)², h²x_I²∂_ω = hx_I·hx_I∂_ω). ∎

*Orders and spaces.* An *order* is 𝐨 = (𝗌; a, c, l; 𝖻): a, c, l ∈ ℝ are the weights at 0f, cf and tf, and 𝗌 (the
differential order) and 𝖻 (the order at sf) are smooth functions on the fibre-radially compactified phase space
^(0ħ,cħ)T̄*ι⁺_ħ of the structure, variable orders in the sense of (S8). Put

    w_𝐨 := ⟨ζ⟩^𝗌 ρ_0f^(−a) ρ_cf^(−c) ρ_tf^(−l) ρ_sf^(−𝖻),    𝐞 := (1; 0, 0, 0; 1),    𝐞_1 := (1; 0, 0, 0; 0),
    𝐦 := (2; −2, 2, 0; 0),    (18.22)

⟨ζ⟩ the fibre weight of the structure. Ψ^𝐨 is the class of (S4)–(S5) and (S8) with the weight
ρ_0f^(−a)ρ_cf^(−c)ρ_tf^(−l), differential order 𝗌 and decay order 𝖻 at the scaling weight ρ̄ ≍ ρ_sf (Lemma 18.6),
acting on ℂ^(N_E)-valued functions componentwise, and taken in the subalgebra of (S10); S^𝐨 is its symbol class. H^𝐨 :=
ρ_0f^a ρ_cf^c ρ_tf^l ρ_sf^𝖻 H^𝗌_ħ, with norm ‖·‖_𝐨, is the space H^(𝗌,(a,c,l,𝖻))_(0ħ,cħ,h)(ι⁺) of Section 14.6.2 and
[Hin26c, (3.56)], with L² := L²(ι⁺, μ_b; ℂ^(N_E)) for the b-density μ_b of Section 18.1.1 and a fibre inner product 𝔢
on ℂ^(N_E), smooth on ι⁺; adjoints A* and the parts Re A := ½(A + A*), Im A := (1/2i)(A − A*) are taken in this L². By
Lemma 18.6 (c), P_(ι,h,z) ∈ Ψ^𝐦. Orders are compared componentwise; 𝐨 − K𝐞 lowers the differential and sf orders
by K and keeps the weights. For fixed h > 0, H^𝐨 is the space H^(𝗌,(a,c))_(0,b)(ι⁺) with an h-dependent equivalent norm
([Hin26c, after (10.31)]): ρ_sf and ρ_tf are then bounded above and below, and ρ_cf ≍ ρ_K.

*Phase space.* 𝒫_ι := ^(0ħ,cħ)T̄*_(sf)ι⁺_ħ ∪ ^(0ħ,cħ)S*ι⁺_ħ is the fibre-compactified phase space over sf together with
fibre infinity over all of ι⁺_ħ; it is compact. The part over sf is a manifold with corners whose boundary hypersurfaces
are fibre infinity, F_I (over sf ∩ 0f = {x_I = 0}) and F_K (over sf ∩ tf = {R = 0}); F_I ∩ F_K = ∅. On it we use the
semiclassical 0-covectors ξ dx_I/(hx_I) + η dω/(hx_I) near F_I and the semiclassical cone covectors of Section 18.1.3
near F_K, over sf ξ_cħ dR/h + η_cħ R dω/h. WF′(A) and Ell(A) ⊂ 𝒫_ι are defined as in Definition 12.13, with S^(−K𝐞) in
place of S^(−M𝟏): ϖ ∉ WF′(A) if the symbol of A lies in S^(−K𝐞) on a neighbourhood of ϖ in ^(0ħ,cħ)T̄*ι⁺_ħ for every K.
The principal symbol of A ∈ Ψ^𝐨 is its symbol modulo S^(𝐨−(1−ϵ)𝐞), ϵ > 0 small (S8); over sf at finite frequencies it is
determined by its restriction to 𝒫_ι, as a symbol w_𝐨a with a smooth and vanishing at sf lies in S^(𝐨−(0;0,0,0;1)),
which at finite frequencies is S^(𝐨−𝐞).

**Lemma 18.7** (The calculus.) Uniformly for h ∈ (0, 1]:

(a) A ∈ Ψ^(𝐨′) maps H^𝐨 → H^(𝐨−𝐨′) with norm bounded by a seminorm of A.

(b) Ψ^𝐨Ψ^(𝐨′) ⊂ Ψ^(𝐨+𝐨′) with multiplicative principal symbols; (Ψ^𝐨)* ⊂ Ψ^𝐨, the principal symbol of A* being the
𝔢-adjoint of that of A; and if A ∈ Ψ^𝐨, B ∈ Ψ^(𝐨′) have scalar principal symbols, A − Op(a Id) ∈ Ψ^(𝐨−(1−ϵ)𝐞) and B −
Op(b Id) ∈ Ψ^(𝐨′−(1−ϵ)𝐞), then i[A, B] − Op(H_a b Id) ∈ Ψ^(𝐨+𝐨′−(2−2ϵ)𝐞), where H_a is the Hamilton field of the
canonical symplectic form of T*(ι⁺)° and H_a b ∈ S^(𝐨+𝐨′−(1−ϵ)𝐞).

(c) (Elliptic estimate.) If A ∈ Ψ^(𝐦′), B, G ∈ Ψ⁰ and WF′(B) ⊂ Ell(A) ∩ Ell(G), then ‖Bu‖_𝐨 ≤ C(‖GAu‖_(𝐨−𝐦′) +
‖u‖_(𝐨−K𝐞)) for every K.

(d) Lemma 12.6 holds for the classes S^𝐨, with the gains (|β|, |α|, 0) of its (d) replaced by |β|𝐞_1 for fibre
derivatives and 0 for derivatives along the coefficient Lie algebra; a smooth function of finitely many symbols in S⁰,
defined on a neighbourhood of the closure of their joint range, lies in S⁰.

(e) Lemma 12.16 holds with L_h replaced by L := 1 + log⟨ζ⟩ + log ρ_sf⁻¹.
