### 18.5 Bounded frequencies

This section proves [Hin26c, Proposition 10.6 (1)] and [Hin26c, Lemmas 10.9–10.10].

#### 18.5.1 The statement

Throughout this section γ_I < 3/2 + S̄, γ_cf = −(α_+ + 2), and (β_−, β_+) is the indicial gap of P̂_0(0) that contains
−γ_cf (Section 18.1.1). We write I(ζ) := P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ζ, ∂_ω), ζ ∈ ℂ, for the Mellin symbol of P̂_0(0) at ∂X, and spec_b
for the set of ζ at which I(ζ) is not invertible on 𝕊³ (Section 13.1 and Section 13.2.5); so (β_−, β_+) ∩ Re spec_b =
∅. For an order 𝗌 (a real number or a variable order on ^(0,b)S*ι⁺) and k ∈ ℕ_0 put

    𝒳^𝗌_k := H^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I,γ_cf))_(0,b;b)(ι⁺),      𝒴^𝗌_k := H^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_cf−2))_(0,b;b)(ι⁺),
    𝒳^𝗌 := 𝒳^𝗌_0,      𝒴^𝗌 := 𝒴^𝗌_0,    (18.48)

with the b-density μ_b of Section 18.1.1 (Section 14.6.2). The index k counts b-derivatives along W_1 = R∂_R and
W_(1+a) = Z_a, a = 1, …, 6, the rotation fields of 𝕊³ (Section 18.4.1), which span the b-vector fields of ι⁺ over
C^∞(ι⁺). By (18.7), N⁰(σ) ∈ x_I²ρ_K⁻²Diff²_(0,b)(ι⁺), and its commutators with the W_i are of the same class
(the proof of Lemma 18.22); so N⁰(σ) : 𝒳^𝗌_k → 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k is bounded.

**Proposition 18.24** ([Hin26c, Proposition 10.6 (1)] in dimension 4 + 1.) For every order 𝗌, every k ∈ ℕ_0
and every σ ∈ ℂ with Im σ > −γ_I,

    N⁰(σ) : 𝒳^𝗌_k → 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k    (18.49)

is Fredholm of index 0. If moreover Im σ > −1 − β_+, it is invertible.

The dimension enters only through c = 3/2. The upper bound γ_I < c + S̄ (1 + S̄ in dimension 3 + 1) is the upper end of
the weight interval I_σ = (−2 Im σ, 2(c + S̄)) of the 0-normal operator at ℐ⁺ (Lemma 18.28), whose lower end gives
Im σ > −γ_I in every dimension, as 2γ_I ∈ I_σ means exactly −γ_I < Im σ and γ_I < c + S̄. The bound −1 − β_+ comes from
the one-dimensional Fourier transform in v of Lemma 18.32, whose shifts by 1 ((18.59) and
(18.60)) are those of that transform, also in every dimension.

**Remark 18.25** (Relation to [Hin26c].) [Hin26c] builds a local left parametrix at ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ from [Hin23e,
Theorem 1.5], which assumes a boundary spectrum independent of the boundary point, and uses the structure of its
Schwartz kernel for b-regularity. Here the parametrix is that of [Hin23e, Theorem 3.4] (the 0-calculus with bounds,
which needs no such constancy), used only through the Fredholm property it gives on a compact manifold
(Lemma 18.29), and b-regularity is proved by difference quotients as in Lemma 18.22. The positivity argument
of [Hin26c] for the reduced normal operator is replaced by the asymptotics of modified Bessel functions
(Lemma 18.28), and the bound on the Fourier transform that [Hin26c, (10.41)] quotes from [Hin23d, Lemma 2.25] is
proved (Lemma 18.31). The proof of [Hin26c, Lemma 10.10] asks "1 + Im σ < β_+"; the condition its argument uses,
and its statement asserts, is −1 − Im σ < β_+.

#### 18.5.2 Two general facts

**Lemma 18.26** (Fredholm estimates with a weak remainder.) Let T : X → Y be a Fredholm operator between
Banach spaces and j : X → W a continuous injective linear map into a Banach space W. Then there is C with ‖x‖_X ≤
C(‖Tx‖_Y + ‖jx‖_W) for all x ∈ X.

*Proof.* Let e_1, …, e_m be a basis of ker T. Since j is injective, je_1, …, je_m are linearly independent in W, and the
Hahn–Banach theorem gives ℓ_1, …, ℓ_m ∈ W* with ℓ_i(je_k) = δ_(ik). Then Πx := Σ_i ℓ_i(jx)e_i is a continuous projection
of X onto ker T, with ‖Πx‖_X ≤ C‖jx‖_W. T is injective on the closed subspace ker Π, and T(ker Π) = T(X) is closed, so
by the open mapping theorem ‖x′‖_X ≤ C‖Tx′‖_Y for x′ ∈ ker Π. Apply this to x′ := x − Πx, for which Tx′ = Tx, and add
‖Πx‖_X. ∎

**Lemma 18.27** (Compact inclusions.) Let 𝗌′ < 𝗌 (orders with sup(𝗌′ − 𝗌) < 0), a′ < a and c′ < c. Then
H^(𝗌,(a,c))_(0,b)(ι⁺) ↪ H^(𝗌′,(a′,c′))_(0,b)(ι⁺) is compact. The same holds for x^aH^𝗌_0(X̂) ↪ x^(a′)H^(𝗌′)_0(X̂) on the
compact manifold X̂ of Section 18.5.3.

*Proof.* Let χ ∈ C^∞([0, ∞)) vanish on [0, 1] and equal 1 on [2, ∞), and for ϵ ∈ (0, ¼) let χ_ϵ := χ(x_I/ϵ)χ(ρ_K/ϵ). Its
0,b-derivatives are bounded uniformly in ϵ (x_I∂_(x_I) and ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) of χ(·/ϵ) are (tχ′)(·/ϵ)). With w :=
x_I^(−a)ρ_K^(−c)u, x_I^(−a′)ρ_K^(−c′)(1 − χ_ϵ)u = f_ϵw, f_ϵ := (1 − χ_ϵ)x_I^(a−a′)ρ_K^(c−c′), and every C^∞_b-seminorm
of f_ϵ is at most C(2ϵ)^δ, δ := min(a − a′, c − c′), because 1 − χ_ϵ is supported where x_I ≤ 2ϵ or ρ_K ≤ 2ϵ and x_I,
ρ_K ≤ 1 on ι⁺ (after normalising the defining functions). Multiplication by f_ϵ is bounded on H^(𝗌′)_(0,b) with norm
bounded by finitely many such seminorms ((S5)–(S6) of Section 14.3), so ‖(1 − χ_ϵ)u‖_(H^(𝗌′,(a′,c′))) ≤
Cϵ^δ‖u‖_(H^(𝗌,(a,c))). And u ↦ χ_ϵu maps into distributions supported in a fixed compact subset of (ι⁺)°, where all
these norms are the standard ones, so it is compact by Rellich's theorem. The inclusion is the norm limit of compact
operators as ϵ → 0. On X̂ the same argument with χ(x/ϵ). ∎

#### 18.5.3 The model at ℐ⁺

Near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ use (x, ω) := (x_I, ω) ∈ [0, 4) × 𝕊³, which covers {R > 1/16}. By (18.7),

    L_σ := x⁻²N⁰(σ) = −½(x∂_x − 2iσ)(x∂_x − 2(c + S_0)) + x²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ½x∂_x, ∂_ω) ∈ Diff²_0    (18.50)

there, with 0-principal symbol (½ + ¼x²)ξ_0² + |η_0|² (Section 18.1.3), positive definite.

*The compact model.* Let X̂ := {y ∈ ℝ⁴ : |y| ≤ 8}, and identify {4 < |y| ≤ 8} with [0, 4)_x × 𝕊³ by x = 8 − |y|, ω =
y/|y|; so ∂X̂ = {x = 0}, and X̂ is a compact manifold with boundary of dimension 4. Let χ_3 ∈ C^∞_c([0, 4)) equal 1 on
[0, 3], read as a function on X̂ vanishing on {|y| ≤ 4}, and put

    P̂ := χ_3L_σ + (1 − χ_3)Δ_(ℝ⁴) ∈ Diff²_0(X̂; ℂ^(N_E)).    (18.51)

Its principal symbol is a convex combination of positive definite forms, so P̂ is 0-elliptic, and P̂ = L_σ on {x < 3}.
Fix a smooth positive density ν_0 on X̂° equal to x⁻⁴|dx dω| on {x < 4} (a 0-density) and put μ_b := x³ν_0 there (a
b-density, a constant multiple of that of ι⁺, as |dR/R| = 2|dx/x|). The spaces x^αH^m_0(X̂) are taken with μ_b. Near ∂X̂
they coincide with the 0,b-spaces of ι⁺ near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺ (Section 14.6.2, the cells U_(3,jk±)), and with the spaces of
[Hin23e, Section 3.1, p. 31] (the pages of [Hin23e] cited in this chapter are those of its arXiv version 1) under the
identification g ↦ gν_0^(1/2) of functions with 0-half-densities: as ∫|x^(−α)g|²μ_b = ∫|x^(−α+3/2)g|²ν_0, x^αL²(μ_b)
corresponds to x^(α−3/2)L²(X̂, ⁰Ω^(1/2)), which is the space of [Hin23e, (3.23), p. 31] at the weight α (with n − 1 = 3,
n = dim X̂); and for integer m both families of norms are equivalent to
Σ_(|γ|≤m)‖x^(−α)V^γu‖_(L²(μ_b)) over products of the 0-fields x∂_x, xZ_a (elliptic regularity in either calculus),
negative orders being the duals. Under this identification P̂ is an operator on 0-half-densities with the coefficients
[Hin23e, (1.3)] it has on functions. Only integer orders are used in this section's appeals to X̂.

*Full ellipticity* ([Hin23e, (1.3)–(1.5), (1.7) and Definition 1.2, pp. 4–5]). Near a boundary point (0, y_0), in local
coordinates, a 0-differential operator of order m on 0-half-densities is P = Σ_(j+|β|≤m) a_(jβ)(x, y)(xD_x)^j(xD_y)^β.
Its reduced normal operator at y_0 is N̂(P, y_0, η̂) = Σ_(j+|β|≤m) a_(jβ)(0, y_0)(tD_t)^j(tη̂)^β on [0, ∞)_t, η̂ a unit
covector; its indicial family is I(P, y_0, σ′) := Σ_(j≤m) a_(j0)(0, y_0)σ′^j, and Spec_b(P, y_0) is the set of (z, k) ∈
ℂ × ℕ_0 such that I(P, y_0, σ′)⁻¹ has a pole at σ′ = −iz of order at least k + 1. For P with elliptic principal symbol
and α ∈ ℝ, N̂(P, y_0, η̂) is *invertible at the weight α* if (1) α ≠ Re z for all (z, k) ∈ Spec_b(P, y_0); (2) if u ∈
t^αL²([0, ∞], |dt/t|) solves N̂(P, y_0, η̂)u = 0, then u = 0; (3) if v ∈ t^(−α)L²([0, ∞], |dt/t|) solves N̂(P, y_0,
η̂)*v = 0, then v = 0, the adjoint being taken with respect to |dt/t|. P is *fully elliptic at the weight α* if this
holds for all y_0 and η̂.

**Lemma 18.28** (The reduced normal operator.) Let σ ∈ ℂ, ω_0 ∈ 𝕊³ and α ∈ I_σ := (−2 Im σ, 2(c + S̄)). Then
P̂ is fully elliptic at the weight α in the sense of [Hin23e, Definition 1.2], at every boundary point.

*Proof.* In normal coordinates y on 𝕊³ centred at ω_0, write P̂ near (0, ω_0) in the form [Hin23e, (1.3)]. The
coefficients of the terms with |β| ≤ 1 or with factors (x∂_x)^jx² vanish at x = 0, except those of the first term of
(18.50): x²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ½x∂_x, ∂_ω) equals g^(ij)(y)(xD_(y_i))(xD_(y_j)) plus terms with a factor x, because
P⁽⁰⁾(0, ·) − ((ρD_ρ)² + Δ_(𝕊³)) Id ∈ Diff¹_b (Lemma 15.23) and x²∂_ω = x·x∂_ω, x²(x∂_x) = x·x(x∂_x). So [Hin23e,
(1.4)–(1.5)] give the reduced normal operator

    N̂(P̂, ω_0, η̂) = −½(t∂_t − 2iσ)(t∂_t − 2(c + S_*)) + κ²t²,      S_* := S_0(ω_0),  κ² := g^(ij)(ω_0)η̂_iη̂_j > 0.

(1) The indicial operator is the first term, and det[−½(z − 2iσ)(z − 2(c + S_*))] = 0 exactly for z = 2iσ and z ∈ 2(c +
spec S_*), with real parts −2 Im σ and 2(c + Re d) ≥ 2(c + S̄), d ∈ spec S_* (S̄ as in (11.2)). With the
convention of [Hin23e] (xD_x ↦ σ′, poles at σ′ = −iz) these are the points of Spec_b, and none has real part α.

(2) Let u ∈ t^αL²((0, ∞), |dt/t|; ℂ^(N_E)) with N̂u = 0; u is smooth, the equation being a regular linear ODE on (0, ∞).
Choose a unitary U with U⁻¹S_*U upper triangular, with diagonal entries d_1, …, d_(N_E). The components u_(N_E),
u_(N_E−1), … of U⁻¹u satisfy, in this order, scalar equations −½(t∂_t − 2iσ)(t∂_t − 2μ)u_i + κ²t²u_i = f_i, μ := c +
d_i, where f_i is a combination of the (t∂_t − 2iσ)u_j, j > i; so by induction it suffices that the scalar equation with
f = 0 has no nonzero solution in t^αL². Put u = t^pw, p := iσ + μ. Since (t∂_t − 2iσ)(t∂_t − 2μ)t^p = t^p(t∂_t + ν)(t∂_t
− ν) with ν := μ − iσ (as p − 2iσ = μ − iσ = ν and p − 2μ = −ν), the equation becomes ((t∂_t)² − ν² − 2κ²t²)w = 0, which
in s := √2κt is the modified Bessel equation s²w″ + sw′ − (s² + ν²)w = 0 ([DLMF, (10.25.1)]). Here Re ν = Re μ + Im σ,
and w ∈ t^aL²(|dt/t|) with a := α + Im σ − Re μ; α < 2(c + S̄) ≤ 2 Re μ gives a < Re ν, and α > −2 Im σ gives a > −Re ν.
So Re ν > |a| ≥ 0. The solutions are w = AI_ν(s) + BK_ν(s): the Wronskian is 𝒲{K_ν, I_ν}(s) = 1/s ([DLMF, (10.28.2)]),
so this is the general solution for every ν. As s → ∞, I_ν(s) = (2πs)^(−1/2)e^s(1 + O(s⁻¹)) and K_ν(s) =
(π/(2s))^(1/2)e^(−s)(1 + O(s⁻¹)) ([DLMF, (10.40.1)–(10.40.2)]), so w ∈ t^aL² near ∞ forces A = 0. As s → 0, for Re ν >
0, K_ν(s) ∼ ½Γ(ν)(s/2)^(−ν) ([DLMF, (10.30.2)]), and Γ(ν) ≠ 0; so |w| ≥ c|B|s^(−Re ν) near 0, which lies in
s^aL²(|ds/s|) near 0 only if −Re ν > a. Hence B = 0.

(3) The adjoint for |dt/t| and the standard Hermitian form is N̂* = −½(t∂_t + 2(c + S_*^*))(t∂_t − 2iσ̄) + κ²t², as
(t∂_t)* = −t∂_t. In the same basis U⁻¹S_*^*U is lower triangular with diagonal d̄_i, so the components are solved in the
order 1, 2, …, and the scalar equation −½(t∂_t + 2μ̄)(t∂_t − 2iσ̄)v = −κ²t²v becomes, with v = t^pw, p := iσ̄ − μ̄, the
modified Bessel equation of order ν̄, Re ν̄ = Re ν. Now v ∈ t^(−α)L² gives w ∈ t^(−a)L², as Re p = Im σ − Re μ, and |−a|
< Re ν̄; the argument of (2) gives v = 0. ∎

**Lemma 18.29** (The model's Fredholm property.) Let Im σ > −γ_I. (a) For every m ∈ ℤ, P̂ : x^(2γ_I)H^m_0(X̂)
→ x^(2γ_I)H^(m−2)_0(X̂) is Fredholm, and so is the formal adjoint P̂* (for μ_b and the standard Hermitian form) :
x^(−2γ_I)H^(2−m)_0(X̂) → x^(−2γ_I)H^(−m)_0(X̂). (b) For m ∈ ℤ, M′ ∈ ℕ, β < 2γ_I and β′ < −2γ_I there is C with

    ‖w‖_(x^(2γ_I)H^m_0) ≤ C(‖P̂w‖_(x^(2γ_I)H^(m−2)_0) + ‖w‖_(x^βH^(−M′)_0)),
    ‖w‖_(x^(−2γ_I)H^(2−m)_0) ≤ C(‖P̂*w‖_(x^(−2γ_I)H^(−m)_0) + ‖w‖_(x^(β′)H^(−M′)_0)).    (18.52)

*Proof.* (a) 2γ_I ∈ I_σ: 2γ_I > −2 Im σ by assumption and 2γ_I < 2(c + S̄). Choose α_0 < 2γ_I < α_1 and ϵ > 0 with [α_0
− ϵ, α_1 + ϵ] ⊂ I_σ. By Lemma 18.28, P̂ is fully elliptic at every weight there. [Hin23e, Theorem 3.4, p. 33]
states: for α_0 < α_1 and P ∈ Ψ^m_0(X, ⁰Ω^(1/2)) fully elliptic at all weights in [α_0 − ϵ, α_1 + ϵ] for some small ϵ >
0, there exist Q, Q′ ∈ Ψ^(−m)_0 + Ψ_0^(−∞,(α_1,−α_0+(n−1))) + Ψ^(−∞,(α_1,−α_0+(n−1))) with PQ = I − R and Q′P = I − R′,
R ∈ Ψ^(−∞,(∞,−α_0+(n−1))) and R′ ∈ Ψ^(−∞,(α_1,∞)), n = dim X. Here n = dim X̂ = 4, so n − 1 = 3, and we obtain Q, Q′ ∈
Ψ^(−2)_0 + Ψ_0^(−∞,(α_1,3−α_0)) + Ψ^(−∞,(α_1,3−α_0)) with P̂Q = I − R, Q′P̂ = I − R′, R ∈ Ψ^(−∞,(∞,3−α_0)) and R′ ∈
Ψ^(−∞,(α_1,∞)) (fully residual operators on X̂²). Put α := 2γ_I. A Schwartz kernel kπ_L*ν_0^(1/2)π_R*ν_0^(1/2) acts on
functions by g ↦ ∫k(·, z′)g(z′)ν_0(z′), so T_(α_L,α_R) := x^(−α_L)Tx^(α_R) has the kernel κ := x^(−α_L)k x′^(α_R−3)
against μ_b(z′).

(i) *Fully residual kernels.* If |k| ≤ Cx^ax′^b on X̂² with a > α_L and b > 3 − α_R, then ∫|κ|μ_b(z′) ≤
Cx^(a−α_L)∫x′^(b+α_R−3)μ_b(z′) ≤ C and ∫|κ|μ_b(z) ≤ Cx′^(b+α_R−3)∫x^(a−α_L)μ_b(z) ≤ C, as ∫_0 x^δ dx/x < ∞ for δ > 0; by
Schur's test T_(α_L,α_R) is bounded on L²(μ_b).

(ii) *Kernels on the 0-double space.* Let k satisfy |k| ≤ Cρ_lb^aρ_rb^b on X̂²_0 with a > α, b > 3 − α and α_L = α_R =
α. Near the boundary diagonal, in coordinates (x, y, x′, y′), ρ_lb ∼ x/r and ρ_rb ∼ x′/r, r := x + x′ + |y − y′|. For
fixed z = (x, y) substitute z′ = (xs, y + xY): μ_b(z′) = x³s⁻¹ds dY, r = x(1 + s + |Y|), and ∫|κ|μ_b(z′) ≤ C∫_0^∞∫_(ℝ³)
s^(α+b−4)(1 + s + |Y|)^(−a−b)dY ds; the Y-integral is C(1 + s)^(3−a−b) (as a + b > 3), and ∫_0 s^(α+b−4)ds < ∞ (as α +
b > 3), ∫^∞ s^(α−a−1)ds < ∞ (as a > α). For fixed z′ substitute z = (x′s, y′ + x′Y): μ_b(z) = x′³s⁻¹ds dY, and
∫|κ|μ_b(z) ≤ C∫s^(a−α−1)(1 + s + |Y|)^(−a−b)dY ds < ∞, as a > α and α + b > 3. Away from the boundary diagonal |k| ≤
Cx^ax′^b, which is covered by (i). So T_(α,α) is bounded.

With a = α_1 and b = 3 − α_0, (i) and (ii) bound the residual parts of Q and Q′ on x^αL²(μ_b). Their kernels are
conormal: by the definition of these classes in [Hin23e, Section 2, p. 9], a kernel of Ψ_0^(−∞,(α_lb,α_rb)) stays
bounded by Cρ_lb^(α_lb)ρ_rb^(α_rb) after any number of smooth vector fields on X̂²_0 tangent to lb and rb are applied to
it, and a fully residual kernel likewise on X̂², with the vector fields tangent to its two boundary hypersurfaces.
The 0-fields of the left factor lift to X̂²_0 as smooth vector fields tangent to ff and rb and vanishing at lb ([MM87,
Lemma (5.10), p. 284], where lb is the top face and rb the bottom face), and those of the right factor, by the symmetry
of X̂²_0 that exchanges the factors, as smooth vector fields tangent to ff and lb and vanishing at rb; on X̂² the
0-fields of either factor are tangent to both boundary hypersurfaces. So the same bounds hold after applying them on
either side, and these parts map x^αH^(m−2)_0 to x^αH^m_0 for every integer m. The part in Ψ^(−2)_0 maps x^αH^(m−2)_0 to
x^αH^m_0 as well, for every integer m and every real α, by the boundedness of the small 0-calculus on weighted 0-Sobolev
spaces. Read on functions through g ↦ gν_0^(1/2), this part is a matrix of operators of Ψ^(−2)_0(X̂) in the sense of
[Usu26] (Theorem A.41 (5)); near ∂X̂ the density μ_b is x⁻¹|dx dω|, so L²(μ_b) is the space L²_b of
Theorem A.41 (2); and Corollary A.42, at the order −2 and with its k equal to m, bounds each
entry from x^αH^(m−2)_0 to x^αH^m_0 (for m ≥ 2 this is [Usu26, Theorem 5.20 (1), p. 119] itself). The proof of
[Hin23e, Corollary 3.3, pp. 31–32] uses this in the same way. By (i) with α_R = α and α < α_L < α_1, R′ maps x^αH^m_0
boundedly into x^(α_L)H^(m+1)_0, which embeds compactly in x^αH^m_0
(Lemma 18.27); likewise R (a = ∞, b = 3 − α_0 > 3 − α) is compact on x^αH^(m−2)_0. So Q′P̂ = I − R′ and P̂Q = I − R
make P̂ Fredholm at the weight α = 2γ_I: finite-dimensional kernel and closed range from the first, finite codimension
from the second. This is [Hin23e, Corollary 3.6, p. 34] at α = 2γ_I, whose proof [Hin23e]
leaves to the reader. Under the L²(μ_b) pairing the duals of x^(2γ_I)H^m_0 and x^(2γ_I)H^(m−2)_0 are x^(−2γ_I)H^(−m)_0
and x^(−2γ_I)H^(2−m)_0 (Lemma 14.21), and the Banach adjoint of P̂ acts on them as the formal adjoint P̂* (test
against C^∞_c(X̂°), which is dense). The adjoint of a Fredholm operator is Fredholm.

(b) Lemma 18.26 with the injections x^(2γ_I)H^m_0 ↪ x^βH^(−M′)_0 and x^(−2γ_I)H^(2−m)_0 ↪ x^(β′)H^(−M′)_0. ∎

#### 18.5.4 The Fredholm property

Under the L²(μ_b) pairing (Lemma 14.21), (𝒳^𝗌)* = H^(−𝗌,(−2γ_I,−γ_cf))_(0,b) and (𝒴^(𝗌−2))* =
H^(2−𝗌,(−2γ_I−2,2−γ_cf))_(0,b); N⁰(σ)* denotes the formal adjoint for μ_b and the standard Hermitian form on ℂ^(N_E),
which is the Banach adjoint of (18.49) at k = 0 on these spaces.

**Lemma 18.30** ([Hin26c, Lemma 10.9] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let Im σ > −γ_I, let 𝗌 be an order and M ∈ ℕ with
M > sup|𝗌| + 1. Put 𝒵_M := H^(−M,(2γ_I−1,γ_cf−1))_(0,b) and 𝒵*_M := H^(−M,(−2γ_I−3,1−γ_cf))_(0,b).

(a) There is C with

    ‖u‖_(𝒳^𝗌) ≤ C(‖N⁰(σ)u‖_(𝒴^(𝗌−2)) + ‖u‖_(𝒵_M)),    u ∈ 𝒳^𝗌,    (18.53)

    ‖v‖_((𝒴^(𝗌−2))*) ≤ C(‖N⁰(σ)*v‖_((𝒳^𝗌)*) + ‖v‖_(𝒵*_M)),    v ∈ (𝒴^(𝗌−2))*,    (18.54)

and the inclusions 𝒳^𝗌 ↪ 𝒵_M and (𝒴^(𝗌−2))* ↪ 𝒵*_M are compact.

(b) N⁰(σ) : 𝒳^𝗌 → 𝒴^(𝗌−2) is Fredholm of index 0.

(c) If u ∈ 𝒳^𝗌 and N⁰(σ)u ∈ 𝒴^(𝗌′−2)_k with 𝗌′ ≥ 𝗌 and k ∈ ℕ_0, then u ∈ 𝒳^(𝗌′)_k.

*Proof.* (a) *Step 1: the elliptic estimate.* N⁰(σ) is elliptic in x_I²ρ_K⁻²Diff²_(0,b) (Section 18.1.3), so
microlocal elliptic regularity in the calculus of the structure of Section 14.6.2 ((S5) of Section 14.3, with (S8)
for variable orders, and B = I) gives, as in Lemma 14.29 (c),

    ‖u‖_(𝒳^𝗌) ≤ C(‖N⁰(σ)u‖_(𝒴^(𝗌−2)) + ‖u‖_(𝒳^(−M)))    (18.55)

(the remainder of (S5) is bounded by ‖u‖_(𝒳^(−M))). Let χ ∈ C^∞_c([0, 2)) equal 1 on [0, 1], read as χ(R), and χ_1(x_I)
the same function of x_I. Since 1 − χ(R) is supported in {R ≥ 1} = {x_I ≤ 1}, where χ_1(x_I) = 1, ‖u‖_(𝒳^(−M)) ≤
‖χ(R)u‖_(𝒳^(−M)) + C‖χ_1(x_I)u‖_(𝒳^(−M)).

*Step 2: near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺.* There the 0,b-structure is the b-structure of the end ϱ = R, t = −log R, in the sense of
Section 13.2.2 (Section 14.6.2, the cells U_(2,jk±)), and ‖χu‖_(𝒳^(−M)) ∼ ‖χu‖_(H^(−M)_(b,γ_cf)). The operator L_K :=
R²N⁰(σ) = −2R(iσ + R∂_R)(R∂_R + c + S_0) + P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω) is of the form of Section 13.2.5 on {R < 4}, with B_j
polynomial in R, normal operator P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω), Mellin symbol J(ζ) = I(−ζ) and spec_J = −spec_b, as for the
operator at ztf in Section 13.4.1 (c); and it is b-elliptic, its principal symbol in (t, ω) being (1 + 2R)τ_t² + |η|²,
τ_t the covector dual to t. As −γ_cf ∈ (β_−, β_+), γ_cf ∉ Re spec_J, and Lemma 13.7 ((13.6)) with m = −M
and the weight γ_cf in the place of its c gives, with χ̃ ∈ C^∞_c([0, 3)) equal to 1 on [0, 2],

    ‖χu‖_(H^(−M)_(b,γ_cf)) ≤ C(‖χ̃L_Ku‖_(H^(−M−2)_(b,γ_cf)) + ‖χ̃u‖_(H^(−M)_(b,γ_cf−1)))
                         ≤ C(‖N⁰(σ)u‖_(𝒴^(𝗌−2)) + ‖u‖_(𝒵_M)),

since R² moves the weight γ_cf − 2 of 𝒴 to γ_cf and −M − 2 ≤ 𝗌 − 2.

*Step 3: near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺.* χ_1u is supported in {x < 2} and lies in x^(2γ_I)H^(−M)_0(X̂), transplanted. On {x < 3}, P̂ =
L_σ = x⁻²N⁰(σ), so P̂(χ_1u) = x⁻²(χ_1N⁰(σ)u + [N⁰(σ), χ_1]u), the commutator being a first-order operator with
coefficients supported in {1 ≤ x_I ≤ 2}, a compact subset of (ι⁺)°. Lemma 18.29 (b) with m = −M, M′ = M and β =
2γ_I − 1 gives

    ‖χ_1u‖_(𝒳^(−M)) ≤ C(‖χ_1N⁰(σ)u‖_(𝒴^(−M−2)) + ‖u‖_(H^(−M−1)({1≤x_I≤2})) + ‖χ_1u‖_(𝒵_M))
                    ≤ C(‖N⁰(σ)u‖_(𝒴^(𝗌−2)) + ‖u‖_(𝒵_M)),

using that on a compact subset of (ι⁺)° all weights are equivalent.

Steps 1–3 give (18.53). For (18.54) the same three steps apply to N⁰(σ)*, which is elliptic with the
same (real, scalar) principal symbol. Near K⁺: N⁰(σ)* = L_K*R⁻², and w := R⁻²v has the b-weight −γ_cf when v has 2 −
γ_cf. L_K* (for μ_b = |(dR/R) dω|, under which (R∂_R)* = −R∂_R) is of the same form, with Mellin symbol J(−ζ̄)*, so
spec_(J*) is the complex conjugate of spec_b, and −γ_cf ∉ Re spec_b; Lemma 13.7 at c = −γ_cf applies (as Chapter 13
applies it to adjoints in Section 13.3.1 and Section 13.4.4), with remainder ‖χ̃R⁻²v‖_(H^(−M)_(b,−γ_cf−1)) =
‖χ̃v‖_(H^(−M)_(b,1−γ_cf)). Near ℐ⁺: N⁰(σ)* = L_σ*x², and w := x²v lies in x^(−2γ_I)H_0 when v lies in x^(−2γ_I−2)H_0;
the second estimate of (18.52) with m = M + 2 (so 2 − m = −M) and β′ = −2γ_I − 1 gives the remainder
‖χ_1x²v‖_(x^(−2γ_I−1)H^(−M)_0) ∼ ‖χ_1v‖_(x^(−2γ_I−3)H^(−M)_0), which is the weight of 𝒵*_M.

The inclusions are compact by Lemma 18.27: every weight drops by 1, and the orders drop from 𝗌, resp. 2 − 𝗌, to −M,
below both as M > sup|𝗌| + 1.

(b) By (18.53) and the compact inclusion, N⁰(σ) has finite-dimensional kernel and closed range (Peetre's lemma,
as in Section 11.7.3). By (18.54), the kernel of N⁰(σ)* on (𝒴^(𝗌−2))*, which is the annihilator of the range,
is finite-dimensional. So (18.49) is Fredholm at k = 0. *Index.* The kernel does not depend on 𝗌: if N⁰(σ)u = 0
with u ∈ 𝒳^𝗌, then u ∈ 𝒳^(𝗌′) for every 𝗌′ by (c); likewise the kernel of the adjoint, by the same elliptic regularity
for N⁰(σ)*. So the index does not depend on 𝗌, and we may take 𝗌 constant. For σ, σ′ in the half-plane {Im σ > −γ_I},
N⁰(σ) − N⁰(σ′) = −2i(σ − σ′)R⁻¹(R∂_R + c + S_0), which maps 𝒳^𝗌 → 𝒴^(𝗌−2) with norm at most C|σ − σ′| (R⁻¹ is x_I² near
ℐ⁺, and near K⁺ it changes the weight γ_cf to γ_cf − 1, which is stronger than γ_cf − 2). So σ ↦ N⁰(σ) is continuous
into the Fredholm operators on the connected half-plane, and the index is constant there. At σ = i/h, with h small,
Proposition 18.12 (with z = i ∈ 𝒵^i, any γ_+ < γ_I, and the constant fibre order 𝗌) gives invertibility on these spaces.
So the index is 0.

(c) The elliptic parametrix of Lemma 14.29 (b), whose proof uses only (S5) and applies verbatim to the structure of
Section 14.6.2 with B = I, gives I = QN⁰(σ) + R_J with Q of order −2 (weights x_I⁻²ρ_K²) and R_J of order −J; so u =
QN⁰(σ)u + R_Ju ∈ 𝒳^(min(𝗌′,𝗌+J)), and, repeating, u ∈ 𝒳^(𝗌′). For k ≥ 1 put s_1 := inf 𝗌′, a constant; then u ∈ 𝒳^(s_1)
and N⁰(σ)u ∈ 𝒴^(s_1−2)_k. *b-regularity at the constant order s_1.* Argue by induction on k exactly as in the proof of
Lemma 18.22, with (18.53) at the order s_1 (and M > |s_1| + 2) in place of (18.29). The dilations
D_κ, κ ∈ [½, 2], and the rotations act boundedly and uniformly on 𝒳^(s_1), 𝒴^(s_1−2) and 𝒵_M (constant orders; the
weights x_I^aρ_K^c and μ_b change by factors bounded above and below). G_θN⁰(σ)G_θ⁻¹ is e^(−θ)(−2R⁻¹(iσ + R∂_R)(R∂_R +
c + S_0)) + e^(−2θ)R⁻²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω) for dilations and the transported operator for rotations, so the
commutators [T_θ, N⁰(σ)] and their iterates are uniformly bounded 𝒳^(s_1) → 𝒴^(s_1−2) after composition with G_θ. In the
inductive step T^α_θu is an average of transported copies of W^(α_1)T^(α′)_(θ′)u with T^(α′)_(θ′)u bounded in 𝒳^(s_1),
hence bounded in H^(s_1−1,(2γ_I−1,γ_cf))_(0,b) ⊂ 𝒵_M, because a b-field maps 𝒳^(s_1) there (Z_a = x_I⁻¹·x_IZ_a near ℐ⁺).
So (18.53) bounds T^α_θu in 𝒳^(s_1), and a weak limit point as θ → 0 is W^αu; thus u ∈ 𝒳^(s_1)_k. *The order
𝗌′.* For |α| ≤ k, [W^α, N⁰(σ)] = Σ_(|β|<|α|) A_(αβ)W^β with A_(αβ) ∈ x_I²ρ_K⁻²Diff²_(0,b), as each [W_i, N⁰(σ)] is of
that class and the b-fields normalise the 0,b-fields ([∂_ω, x_I∂_ω] ∈ x_I𝒱(𝕊³), [x_I∂_(x_I), x_I∂_ω] = x_I∂_ω). By
induction on |α|, N⁰(σ)W^αu = W^αN⁰(σ)u − Σ A_(αβ)W^βu ∈ 𝒴^(𝗌′−2) and W^αu ∈ 𝒳^(s_1), so the elliptic regularity just
proved puts W^αu in 𝒳^(𝗌′). ∎

#### 18.5.5 The kernel

**Lemma 18.31** (The Fourier transform of conormal functions.) Let a > −1, b ∈ ℝ, and let f ∈ C^∞((0, ∞)_v ×
𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)) satisfy, for all j and α, |(v∂_v)^j∂^α_ωf| ≤ C_(jα)v^a on {v ≤ 2} and ≤ C_(jα)v^(−b) on {v ≥ ½}. Let f^♯ be
its extension by 0 to v ≤ 0, a tempered distribution on ℝ × 𝕊³, and f̂(r̂, ω) := (ℱf^♯)(r̂, ω) = ∫e^(ir̂v)f^♯(v, ω) dv.
Then f̂ is smooth on {r̂ ≠ 0}, and for every ϵ > 0, j and α,

    |(r̂∂_r̂)^j∂^α_ωf̂(r̂, ω)| ≤ C(1 + |r̂|)^(−1−a)(|r̂|/(1 + |r̂|))^(min(b−1,0)−ϵ),    r̂ ≠ 0.    (18.56)

*Proof.* Let ψ ∈ C^∞_c((½, 2)) with Σ_(l∈ℤ) ψ(2^(−l)v) = 1 for v > 0, and f_l := ψ(2^(−l)v)f. Then f^♯ = Σ_l f_l in 𝒮′
(f^♯ is locally integrable, as a > −1, and polynomially bounded; dominated convergence). On supp f_l, v ∼ 2^l, and as
∂_v^m = v^(−m)p_m(v∂_v) for a polynomial p_m, |∂_v^m∂^α_ωf_l| ≤ C2^(−lm)M_l with M_l := 2^(la) for l ≤ 0 and 2^(−lb) for
l ≥ 0. Hence |∂^α_ωℱf_l(r̂)| ≤ ∫|∂^α_ωf_l| dv ≤ C2^lM_l and, integrating by parts m times, ≤ C|r̂|^(−m)2^(l(1−m))M_l;
so |∂^α_ωℱf_l(r̂)| ≤ C2^lM_l min(1, (2^l|r̂|)^(−m)). Since ℱ(∂_v(vg)) = −r̂∂_r̂ℱg (ℱ∂_v = −ir̂ℱ, ℱv = −i∂_r̂ℱ),
(r̂∂_r̂)^jℱf_l = ℱ((−v∂_v − 1)^jf_l), and (v∂_v + 1)^jf_l is a sum of terms of the same dyadic form with the same
bounds; so the bound holds for (r̂∂_r̂)^j∂^α_ωℱf_l too. Fix r̂ ≠ 0 and K ∈ ℤ with 2^(−K) ≤ |r̂| < 2^(1−K), and take m >
max(1 + a, 1 − b). If |r̂| ≥ 1 (K ≤ 0): Σ_(l≤K) 2^(l(1+a)) ≤ C2^(K(1+a)); Σ_(K<l≤0) 2^(l(1+a))(2^l|r̂|)^(−m) ≤
C|r̂|^(−m)2^(K(1+a−m)); Σ_(l>0) 2^(l(1−b))(2^l|r̂|)^(−m) ≤ C|r̂|^(−m); all are ≤ C|r̂|^(−1−a). If |r̂| < 1 (K ≥ 1):
Σ_(l≤0) 2^(l(1+a)) ≤ C; Σ_(0<l≤K) 2^(l(1−b)) ≤ C(1 + 2^(K(1−b)) + K) ≤ C|r̂|^(min(b−1,0)−ϵ); Σ_(l>K)
2^(l(1−b))(2^l|r̂|)^(−m) ≤ C|r̂|^(−m)2^(K(1−b−m)) ≤ C|r̂|^(b−1), which is ≤ C|r̂|^(min(b−1,0)). So Σ_l ℱf_l converges
with all these derivatives locally uniformly on {r̂ ≠ 0}, to a smooth function satisfying (18.56), which is f̂
there because ℱ is continuous on 𝒮′. ∎

The proof uses a > −1 only, for the local integrability of f^♯ and the sums Σ_(l≤K) 2^(l(1+a)), and Proposition 26.14
uses the lemma so. Lemma 18.31 is the bound [Hin26c, (10.41)], which [Hin26c] quotes from [Hin23d, Lemma 2.25]; it
is one-dimensional in v, the sphere being a parameter, and so does not depend on n.

**Lemma 18.32** ([Hin26c, Lemma 10.10] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let Im σ > −γ_I and Im σ > −1 − β_+. Then N⁰(σ)
has trivial kernel on 𝒳^𝗌.

*Proof.* Let N⁰(σ)u = 0, u ∈ 𝒳^𝗌. By Lemma 18.30 (c), u ∈ 𝒳^(s′)_k for all s′ and k; so ρ_0f^(−2γ_I)ρ_K^(−γ_cf)W^αu
∈ L²(μ_b) for every product W^α of b-fields (the weights commute with b-fields up to bounded factors; the weight at ℐ⁺
of the spaces is the bounded defining function ρ_0f = (1 + R)^(−1/2), which near ℐ⁺ is x_I times a smooth positive
function), and Sobolev embedding on the unit cells of the b-structure of ι⁺ (dimension 4; as in the proof of
Lemma 11.37 (b)) gives u ∈ ρ_0f^(2γ_I)ρ_K^(γ_cf)C^∞_b(ι⁺). In v := R⁻¹ ∈ [0, ∞], ρ_0f² = v/(1 + v) and ρ_K = (1 +
v)⁻¹, so u ∈ v^(γ_I)(1 + v)^(−γ_I−γ_cf)C^∞_b, and the b-fields are spanned by v∂_v = −R∂_R and the Z_a. So u_0 :=
v^(−iσ)u satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 18.31 with

    a := γ_I + Im σ > 0,    b := γ_cf − Im σ,    (18.57)

as |v^(−iσ)| = v^(Im σ) and v∂_v(v^(−iσ)g) = v^(−iσ)(v∂_v − iσ)g.

*The operator in v.* Conjugation by R^(iσ) replaces R∂_R by R∂_R − iσ, as R^(iσ)R∂_R(R^(−iσ)g) = (R∂_R − iσ)g. So
R^(iσ)R²N⁰(σ)R^(−iσ) = −2R(R∂_R)(R∂_R − iσ + c + S_0) + P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −R∂_R + iσ, ∂_ω), the factor iσ + R∂_R of
(18.7) becoming R∂_R. With R∂_R = −v∂_v and R(R∂_R) = R²∂_R = −∂_v,

    N¹(σ) := R^(iσ)R²N⁰(σ)R^(−iσ) = −2∂_v(v∂_v + iσ − c − S_0) + P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, v∂_v + iσ, ∂_ω)    (18.58)

([Hin26c, before (10.39)], with c = 1 there), and N¹(σ)u_0 = R^(iσ)R²N⁰(σ)u = 0 on {v > 0}. Let u^♯ be the extension of
u_0 by 0 to v ≤ 0. Then N¹(σ)u^♯ = 0 on ℝ × 𝕊³: for φ ∈ C^∞_c(ℝ × 𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)), ⟨u^♯, N¹(σ)^tφ⟩ = lim_(ϵ↓0) ∫_(v>ϵ)
u_0·N¹(σ)^tφ dv dω, and Green's formula on {v > ϵ} turns this into ∫_(v>ϵ)(N¹(σ)u_0)·φ + B_ϵ = B_ϵ, where B_ϵ is an
integral over {ϵ} × 𝕊³ of products of (v∂_v)^l∂^γ_ωu_0, l ≤ 1, |γ| ≤ 2, with derivatives of φ, with bounded coefficients
(each v-integration by parts of ∂_v or of v∂_v leaves one boundary term, and the ω-integrations by parts none). So |B_ϵ|
≤ C_φϵ^a → 0. u^♯ is tempered, and ℱ(∂_vg) = −ir̂ℱg, ℱ(vg) = −i∂_r̂ℱg, hence ℱ(v∂_vg) = −i∂_r̂(−ir̂ℱg) = −(r̂∂_r̂ +
1)ℱg. As P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ·, ∂_ω) is a polynomial with coefficients that are operators on 𝕊³, which commute with ℱ, the
substitutions ∂_v ↦ −ir̂ and v∂_v ↦ −(r̂∂_r̂ + 1) in (18.58) give, for û := ℱu^♯ in 𝒮′(ℝ × 𝕊³),

    [2ir̂(−r̂∂_r̂ + iσ − (c + 1) − S_0) + P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, −r̂∂_r̂ − 1 + iσ, ∂_ω)]û = 0:    (18.59)

indeed −2(−ir̂)(−(r̂∂_r̂ + 1) + iσ − c − S_0) = 2ir̂(−r̂∂_r̂ + iσ − (c + 1) − S_0). This is [Hin26c, (10.40)], with iσ −
2 − S there (c = 1) and iσ − 5/2 − S_0 here.

*Reduction to the transition face.* For r̂ > 0 put w_±(r̂, ω) := û(±r̂, ω) and w^♭_± := r̂^(1−iσ)w_±. Conjugation by
r̂^(1−iσ) replaces r̂∂_r̂ by r̂∂_r̂ − 1 + iσ, and r̂ ↦ −r̂ changes the sign of the first term of (18.59) only;
under the replacement, −r̂∂_r̂ + iσ − (c + 1) − S_0 becomes −r̂∂_r̂ − c − S_0 and −r̂∂_r̂ − 1 + iσ becomes −r̂∂_r̂. So
on {r̂ > 0}, with ρ̂ := r̂⁻¹ (r̂∂_r̂ = −ρ̂∂_ρ̂) and after multiplication by ρ̂²,

    [±2iρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − c − S_0) + ρ̂²P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ρ̂∂_ρ̂, ∂_ω)]w^♭_± = N_tf(±1)w^♭_± = 0,    (18.60)

with N_tf of (13.12) (see (18.39)), on tf° = ℝ⁴_x̂ ∖ 0, x̂ = r̂ω. By Lemma 18.31 with
(18.57), |w_±| ≤ C(1 + r̂)^(−1−γ_I−Im σ)(r̂/(1 + r̂))^(min(γ_cf−Im σ−1,0)−ϵ), with the same bound for
(r̂∂_r̂)^jZ^αw_±; as |r̂^(1−iσ)| = r̂^(1+Im σ) = (1 + r̂)^(1+Im σ)(r̂/(1 + r̂))^(1+Im σ) is conormal,

    w^♭_± ∈ 𝒜^(γ_I,−β)(tf),    β := max(−γ_cf, −1 − Im σ) + ϵ,    (18.61)

in the notation of Section 13.4.1 (ρ_sctf = (1 + r̂)⁻¹, ρ_ztf = r̂/(1 + r̂)). Indeed the exponent at sctf is 1 + γ_I +
Im σ − (1 + Im σ) = γ_I, and at ztf it is min(γ_cf − Im σ − 1, 0) − ϵ + 1 + Im σ = min(γ_cf, 1 + Im σ) − ϵ = −β. Take
ϵ > 0 so small that β < β_+; this uses −γ_cf < β_+ and −1 − Im σ < β_+, the second hypothesis. Also β > −γ_cf > β_−.

*tf-admissibility.* Fix β* ∈ (β, β_+), q := 2 − β* ∈ (2 − β_+, 2 − β_−), and in the spaces of Section 13.4.3 take the
real parameter α_+ there equal to 0 and orders 𝗋_± admissible as there whose value near R_out, the zero section over
sctf, is below γ_I − 2: this is allowed, admissibility imposing only an upper bound at R_out (Lemma 11.32, as used
in the proof of Theorem 11.33 (5)). Then w^♭_+ ∈ 𝒳_(tf,0) and w^♭_− ∈ 𝒳_(tf,π): near sctf, φ_∞w^♭_± ∈ H^(s,𝗋_±)_sc for
every s by Lemma 11.37 (a) with a = γ_I, which concerns a neighbourhood of the boundary face of ℝ̄⁴ only (as in the
converse of Theorem 13.14 (5)); near ztf, (1 − φ_∞)w^♭_± ∈ 𝒜^(−β) ⊂ H^∞_(b,q−2) as q − 2 = −β* < −β (Lemma 13.3
(f)); in between w^♭_± is smooth; and N_tf(±1)w^♭_± = 0. P̂_0 is tf-admissible with the weight α_+ + 2 = −γ_cf ∈ (β_−,
β_+) (Definition 15.32 (2)), so by Corollary 13.16 (a), N_tf(e^(iθ)) : 𝒳_(tf,θ) → 𝒴_(tf,θ) is invertible at θ = 0 and
θ = π for these q and orders. Hence w^♭_± = 0, and û = 0 on {r̂ ≠ 0}.

*Conclusion.* For ψ ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)), g := ⟨û, ψ⟩_(𝕊³) ∈ 𝒮′(ℝ) is supported in {0}, hence a finite sum Σ_l c_lδ^((l));
so its inverse transform ⟨u^♯, ψ⟩_(𝕊³) is a polynomial in v. It vanishes on {v < 0}, so it vanishes identically. As ψ is
arbitrary, u^♯ = 0, and u = 0. ∎

#### 18.5.6 Proof of Proposition 5.1

*Proof of Proposition 18.24.* For k = 0, Lemma 18.30 (b) gives the Fredholm property with index 0, and if also Im
σ > −1 − β_+, Lemma 18.32 gives a trivial kernel, so (18.49) is invertible. Let k ≥ 1. By Lemma 18.30
(c) with N⁰(σ)u = 0, the kernel on 𝒳^𝗌_k is the kernel on 𝒳^𝗌; and by Lemma 18.30 (c), N⁰(σ)(𝒳^𝗌_k) = 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k ∩
N⁰(σ)(𝒳^𝗌), which is closed in 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k since the inclusion 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k ↪ 𝒴^(𝗌−2) is continuous. The map 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k →
𝒴^(𝗌−2)/N⁰(σ)(𝒳^𝗌) has exactly this kernel, and it is onto: its image is dense, as C^∞_c((ι⁺)°) ⊂ 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k is dense in
𝒴^(𝗌−2), and the quotient is finite-dimensional. So the cokernels at k and at 0 have the same dimension, (18.49)
is Fredholm of index 0, and it is invertible when the operator at k = 0 is. ∎

**Corollary 18.33** On {Im σ > max(−γ_I, −1 − β_+)}, σ ↦ N⁰(σ)⁻¹ ∈ ℒ(𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k, 𝒳^𝗌_k) is holomorphic.

*Proof.* N⁰(σ) = N⁰(σ_0) − 2i(σ − σ_0)R⁻¹(R∂_R + c + S_0) is affine in σ with values in ℒ(𝒳^𝗌_k, 𝒴^(𝗌−2)_k) (the second
term commutes with the W_i up to terms of its own class), and invertible there by Proposition 18.24; near each σ_0 the
inverse is the Neumann series Σ_(j≥0)((σ − σ_0)A)^jN⁰(σ_0)⁻¹, A := 2iN⁰(σ_0)⁻¹R⁻¹(R∂_R + c + S_0), convergent for |σ −
σ_0|‖A‖ < 1. ∎


## 19. Forward solutions on e3b-spaces and their tame estimates

This chapter solves forward problems on the compactified spacetime M. The first half concerns the stationary model
P_0. Its normal operator N_ι⁺(P_0) at future timelike infinity is inverted on edge-b-edge spaces by the Mellin
transform (Proposition 19.2); a modified operator P_+, equal to N_ι⁺(P_0) near the timelike curve of the spatial
origin and to P_0 near ℐ⁺, is inverted on the same spaces (Proposition 19.8); and the two are joined, with the
ℵ-admissibility of P_0 at K⁺, into forward solutions of P_0 on e3b-Sobolev spaces with decay at ι⁺ and the loss ℵ at
K⁺ (Theorem 19.12). The second half solves forward problems for admissible wave-type operators P, perturbations of
P_0 that decay at ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺, on b-Sobolev spaces, with estimates tame in the b-regularity (Theorem 19.14,
Corollary 19.15). These results are [Hin26c, Proposition 10.12, Proposition 10.14, Theorem 10.1] and [Hin26c, Theorem
11.1] in dimension 4 + 1. The dimension enters through the constant c := (n − 1)/2 = 3/2 of the normal form of P_0
(Definition 15.21) and through the densities, which shift weights by n/2 = 2 and by (n + 1)/2 = 5/2.

The notation is that of Chapter 14–Chapter 18. In particular n = 4, c = 3/2, τ = t_*⁻¹, R = r/t_*, x_I = R^(−1/2) near
ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, ρ_K = R/(1 + R), the weights γ_I, γ_+, γ_cf of (18.3), the Mellin transform ℳ of (18.4),
the ι⁺-normal operator N_ι⁺(P_0) = τ² N⁰ and its family N⁰(σ) of Definition 18.1, the semiclassical family P_(ι,h,z)
of (18.12), the parameter sets (18.27), the orders and spaces (18.28) and the norms
(18.43). Order functions are written in sans-serif type (𝗌, 𝗍, 𝖻). The defining function x_I of ℐ⁺ is
R^(−1/2) near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, r^(−1/2) at finite times (Section 19.1.3) and (t_*/(t_* + r))^(1/2) on Ω ((19.20));
where two of these are defined near ℐ⁺ they differ by a smooth positive factor, so the weighted spaces do not depend on
the choice. The radii 0 < r_0 − 2δ_0 < r_0 < r_0 + δ_0 < r_2 of the artificial boundary are parameters of the setting.
The constants chosen from r_0 below (T_+ in Definition 19.5, the set Ω_♮ and the constants of Lemma 19.19, the
width κ of Section 19.5.6) are chosen by inequalities that a smaller r_0 makes no harder, so every result holds for
each choice of the radii at which the hypotheses of Chapter 15 hold.

### 19.1 Forward solutions of the ι⁺-normal operator

This section is [Hin26c, Section 10.1.4] in dimension 4 + 1. Throughout Section 19.1–Section 19.3, P_0 is a
stationary wave-type operator as in Definition 15.21, in the setting of Section 17.1.1, with γ_I, γ_cf = −(α_+ + 2)
and (β_−, β_+) as in Section 18.5.

#### 19.1.1 Edge-b-edge spaces

On [0, ∞]_τ × ι⁺, τ = t_*⁻¹, we write ι⁺ for the face {0} × ι⁺, ℐ⁺ for [0, ∞] × (ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺), and cf := [0, ∞] × (ι⁺ ∩
K⁺), with defining functions ρ_+ = τ/(1 + τ) (or τ), x_I, and ρ_cf = R/(1 + R). The face cf = {R = 0} = {r = 0} is the
timelike curve of the spatial origin, at each time; it is not K⁺. The *ebe-vector fields* ([Hin26c, Definition 10.11])
are the b-vector fields of [0, ∞] × ι⁺ tangent to the fibres of ℐ⁺ → 𝕊³ and of cf → [0, ∞]_τ. With χ ∈ C_c^∞([0, 3))
equal to 1 on [0, 2] they are spanned over C^∞ by

    χ(R) R∂_R,   χ(R) Z_a,   χ(R) Rτ∂_τ,      χ(v) v∂_v,   χ(v) √v Z_a,   χ(v) τ∂_τ,      v = R⁻¹,    (19.1)

where Z_a, a = 1, …, 6, are the rotation fields Z_(ij) = x_i ∂_(x_j) − x_j ∂_(x_i), 1 ≤ i < j ≤ 4, of 𝕊³ ⊂ ℝ⁴, in
place of the coordinate fields ∂_ω of [Hin26c, (10.42)]. They span T𝕊³ at every point: for x ∈ 𝕊³ and w ∈ T_x𝕊³,

    Σ_(i<j) (x_i w_j − x_j w_i) Z_(ij)(x) = ½ Σ_(i,j) (x_i w_j − x_j w_i)(x_i e_j − x_j e_i) = |x|² w − (x·w) x = w,

since the summand is symmetric under the exchange of i and j and vanishes for i = j. By (18.6) and
N_ι⁺(P_0) = τ² N⁰ (Definition 18.1), with R⁻¹ τ∂_τ = R⁻² (Rτ∂_τ) and R⁻¹ R∂_R near cf, and by (18.7) near ℐ⁺,

    N_ι⁺(P_0) ∈ x_I² ρ_+² ρ_cf⁻² Diff²_ebe([0, ∞] × ι⁺),    (19.2)

which is [Hin26c, (10.43)]. The spaces of [Hin26c, (10.45)–(10.48)] are, in dimension 4 + 1,

    H^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)
        := x_I^(2γ_I) τ^(γ_+) ρ_cf^(γ_cf) H^((𝗌;k))_(ebe;b)((0, ∞)_τ × ι⁺; |dτ/τ| μ_b),    (19.3)

the Sobolev spaces of the product structure of Section 14.6.2 (cells: unit intervals in t = −log₂ τ times the cells
U_(2,jk±), U_(3,jk±) of ι⁺), with k further b-derivatives along τ∂_τ and the fields W_i of Section 18.4.1. The order
𝗌 may be variable, the weights are constant, and all densities are b-densities. Ḣ(… [0, τ_0] × ι⁺) denotes the subspace
of distributions supported in {τ ≤ τ_0}; there τ^(γ_+) and ρ_+^(γ_+) give equivalent norms. As in [Hin26c, footnote
99], ũ ∈ H^(𝗌,γ_cf)_(e,loc)((0, ∞)_τ × {R < R_0}) means that χũ ∈ H^(𝗌,(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_ebe for all χ ∈ C_c^∞((0, ∞) ×
{R < R_0}), the orders at ℐ⁺ and ι⁺ being irrelevant there.

*Orders.* As in [Hin26c, (10.12)], let 𝗌 be admissible for P_0 with weights α_+, 0 and margin 0 (Definition 15.44).
Its restriction to ᵉ³ᵇS*_ι⁺M, extended to be invariant under τ-dilations, is an order on ᵉᵇᵉS*((0, ∞) × ι⁺), again
written 𝗌 (the identification of the phase spaces over ι⁺ is [Hin26c, Section 10.1.1], with [Hin26c, (10.44)] near cf).
Its induced orders are those of Section 18.1.3: 𝗌_(0,b) at fibre infinity for bounded frequencies, and, for ±Re σ ≥ 1,
𝗌_(0ħ,cħ) at fibre infinity and 𝖻_± at sf.

**Lemma 19.1** (Plancherel.) For u in (19.3), with ℳ of (18.4) and
𝐨_± := (𝗌_(0ħ,cħ); 2γ_I, γ_cf, γ_cf; 𝖻_±),

    ‖u‖²_(H^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)) ∼ ∫_(−1)^1 ‖(ℳu)(ζ − iγ_+)‖²_(H^((𝗌_(0,b);k),(2γ_I,γ_cf))_(0,b;b)) dζ
                                         + Σ_± ∫_(±[1,∞)) ‖(ℳu)(ζ − iγ_+)‖²_(𝐨_±;k,+) dζ,    (19.4)

with h = |ζ|⁻¹ in the norm (18.43). This is [Hin26c, (10.47)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* This is the proof of Lemma 14.20 with b-densities throughout (so without the shifts of Lemma 14.19):
property (S9) of the calculus (Section 14.3) for the product structure, after writing u = τ^(γ_+) w, for which
(ℳu)(ζ − iγ_+) = (ℳw)(ζ) by (18.4). The weights x_I^(2γ_I) ρ_cf^(γ_cf) are functions on ι⁺ and pass through,
the weight at tf being that at cf (the spaces of Lemma 14.20). The b-field τ∂_τ becomes multiplication by iσ
(ℳ(τ∂_τ u) = iσ ℳu), bounded for |ζ| ≤ 1 and giving the factors |ζ|^j = h^(−j) of ‖·‖_(𝐨;k,+) for |ζ| ≥ 1; the spatial
b-fields commute with ℳ. For |ζ| ≥ 1 the spectral orders are 𝗌_(0ħ,cħ) at fibre infinity and the restriction of 𝗌 at
sf, which is 𝖻_± (Section 18.1.3); for |ζ| ≤ 1 the spectral structure is the 0,b-structure, in which only the fibre
order 𝗌_(0,b) enters. ∎

#### 19.1.2 The statement

**Proposition 19.2** (Forward solutions of the ι⁺-normal operator.) Let 𝗌 be as above, γ_I < 3/2 + S̄,
γ_+ < min(γ_I, 1 + β_+), γ_cf := −(α_+ + 2), τ_0 ∈ (0, 1] and k ∈ ℕ₀.

(1) (*Existence.*) For every f ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺) there is a unique
u ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺) with

    N_ι⁺(P_0) u = f,
    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)) ≤ C ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))_(ebe;b)),    (19.5)

C independent of τ_0 and f. Uniqueness holds in H^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)((0, ∞) × ι⁺).

(2) (*Strong uniqueness.*) Let ũ ∈ 𝒟′((0, ∞) × (ι⁺)°) be supported in {τ ≤ τ_0}, with N_ι⁺(P_0) ũ = 0 and ũ ∈
H^(𝗌,γ_cf)_(e,loc)((0, ∞) × {R < R_0}) for some R_0 > 0. Then ũ = 0.

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 10.12] in dimension 4 + 1. [Hin26c] states (1) with f of order 𝗌 − 2; its proof gives
𝗌 − 1 ([Hin26c, (10.50)]), which is also the order Proposition 19.8 feeds it. The loss of one order is the loss at the
radial sets over sf, where the semiclassical estimates (18.29) and (18.46) lose one power of h. The
conditions on γ_+ make the line Im σ = −γ_+ lie in the region of Proposition 18.24 where N⁰(σ) is invertible:
−γ_+ > −γ_I and −γ_+ > −1 − β_+.

#### 19.1.3 Solutions near ℐ⁺ at finite times

The proof of (2) needs control at ℐ⁺ of solutions with compactly supported right-hand sides. Near ℐ⁺ at finite times
we use (t_*, x_I, ω) with x_I = r^(−1/2), the edge fields ∂_(t_*), x_I∂_(x_I), x_I∂_ω, and the spaces H^(s,2γ)_e with
the b-density |dt_* (dx_I/x_I) dω|. On a finite t_*-range these are the spaces (19.3) near ℐ⁺: the ebe-fields
τ∂_τ, v∂_v, √v Z_a are combinations of the edge fields with bounded coefficients and conversely, and (t_*/r)^(1/2) and
r^(−1/2) differ by a smooth positive factor. In the notation of Chapter 17, with the metric density |dg| a smooth
positive multiple of x_I⁻⁸ |dt_* (dx_I/x_I) dω|, the weight 2α there is 2(α + 2) here (Lemma 14.19): x_I^(2α)
L²(|dg|) = x_I^(2(α+2)) L²(|dt_* (dx_I/x_I) dω|). So the threshold α < −1/2 + p̄_1 of Chapter 17, with p̄_1 = S̄ for P_0
and for the operators below (Definition 15.38; [Hin26c, Remark 10.2]), is γ < 3/2 + S̄.

The existence of solutions below uses one standard result on hyperbolic equations, Theorem A.5, in
the following case.

*The Cauchy problem* (Theorem A.5 on ℝ^(1+4) with the Minkowski metric). Let Q be a second-order
operator on ℂ^(N_E)-valued functions on ℝ^(1+4), with principal symbol Ḡ Id, Ḡ the dual metric function of the Minkowski
metric ḡ, and with smooth lower-order coefficients, and let t be the Minkowski time. For s ∈ ℤ, t_0 ∈ ℝ and
f ∈ H^(s−1)_loc(ℝ^(1+4)) with supp f ⊂ {t ≥ t_0} there is u ∈ H^(s)_loc(ℝ^(1+4)) with Qu = f and supp u ⊂ {t ≥ t_0}.

**Lemma 19.3** (Control at ℐ⁺ of the extension.) Let s′ ∈ ℤ, T ∈ ℝ, and g ∈ H^(s′−1)_c with support in
{T ≤ t_* ≤ T + 2, 2 ≤ r ≤ 3}. There is a unique u on {t_* < T + 2}, vanishing for t_* < T and for r < 1, with
N_ι⁺(P_0) u = g and u ∈ H^(s′)_loc; and for every χ ∈ C_c^∞((−∞, T + 2)) and γ < 3/2 + S̄, χ(t_*) u ∈ H^(s′,2γ)_e near
ℐ⁺.

*Proof.* *Existence and support.* By (18.8) the principal symbol of N_ι⁺(P_0) is the dual Minkowski metric Ḡ,
and its coefficients are smooth on {r > 0}. Let Ñ be a second-order operator on ℝ^(1+4) with smooth coefficients and
principal symbol Ḡ Id, equal to N_ι⁺(P_0) on {r > 1/2}, and let t = t_* + r be the Minkowski time. By the solvability
of the Cauchy problem above, with the Minkowski time t, there is ũ ∈ H^(s′)_loc(ℝ^(1+4)) with Ñũ = g vanishing on
{t < T + 2}, which contains no point of supp g. It vanishes on A_1 := {t_* < T} and on A_2 := {t_* + 2r < T + 4}.
Indeed, g = 0 on each (on supp g, t_* ≥ T and t_* + 2r ≥ T + 4); t_* and t + r = t_* + 2r are non-decreasing along
future causal curves (Lemma 18.5 (c)), so for p ∈ A_j the Minkowski causal past J⁻(p) lies in A_j, and J⁻(p) ∩
{t ≥ T + 1} is compact; and supp ũ ⊂ {t ≥ T + 2}. So Lemma 18.4 applies on A_j, with the time function t,
c := T + 1 and L_p := J⁻(p) ∩ {t ≥ T + 1}. Hence a point of supp ũ has t_* ≥ T and t_* + 2r ≥ T + 4, and if
t_* < T + 2 then r > 1. So u := ũ|_({t_*<T+2}) vanishes for t_* < T and for r < 1, and solves N_ι⁺(P_0) u = g (on
{r > 1/2}, Ñ = N_ι⁺(P_0); on {r < 1} both sides vanish). If u′ is another such solution, w := u − u′, extended by 0
across {r = 0}, solves Ñw = 0 on {t_* < T + 2} and vanishes on {t < T}, and Lemma 18.4 on {t_* < T + 2} with the
time function t, c := T − 1 and L_p := J⁻(p) ∩ {t ≥ T − 1} gives w = 0. In particular u does not depend on the choice
of Ñ.

*Control at ℐ⁺.* By t_*-translation invariance we may take T ≥ 8/C′, with C′ of Lemma 15.35 (b). By the
homogeneity of N_ι⁺(P_0) (Section 18.1.2), (D_Λ u)(t_*, x) := u(t_*/Λ, x/Λ) satisfies N_ι⁺(P_0) D_Λ u = Λ⁻² D_Λ g.
D_Λ preserves the spaces H^(s′,2γ)_e near ℐ⁺ at finite times: it maps the edge fields to constant multiples of
themselves and x_I^(2γ) to Λ^γ x_I^(2γ). So we may replace g by D_Λ g, supported in {T′ ≤ t_* ≤ T′ + 2Λ, 2Λ ≤ r ≤
3Λ}, T′ := ΛT, with Λ ≥ 1 to be chosen; ũ by D_Λ ũ; and Ñ by its rescaling Ñ_Λ, equal to N_ι⁺(P_0) on {r > Λ/2}. By
the support argument above, ũ vanishes on {t_* < T′} and on {t_* + 2r < T′ + 4Λ}. Let ψ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) vanish on (−∞, 1/2]
and equal 1 on [1, ∞), ψ̃ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, T + 2] and 0 on [T + 3, ∞), and on Ω put

    P_Λ := P_0 + ψ(r/Λ) ψ̃(t_*/Λ) (N_ι⁺(P_0) − P_0).

Both cut-offs are scaled with Λ, so their b-derivatives are bounded uniformly in Λ: t_*∂_(t_*) ψ̃(t_*/Λ) = (t_*/Λ)
ψ̃′(t_*/Λ) with t_*/Λ ≤ T + 3 on the support of ψ̃′, and likewise for ψ(r/Λ); an unscaled ψ̃(t_*) would have
b-derivatives of size Λ. The second term is supported in {r ≥ Λ/2, t_* ≤ (T + 3)Λ}, where ρ_K = r/(t_* + r) ≥
(2T + 7)⁻¹, uniformly in Λ ≥ 1 (T being fixed): near ℐ⁺ ∪ (ι⁺)°, away from K⁺. There the terms (i)–(iv) of the proof
of Lemma 18.3, times t_*⁻², are τ³R⁻² times polynomials of degree at most 2 in the e3b-fields τ∂_τ, x_I∂_(x_I),
x_I∂_ω (Section 14.2.4) with coefficients bounded with all their b-derivatives, uniformly in Λ; and τ³R⁻² = x_I² ρ_+²
(t_* + r)⁻¹ for the e3b defining functions x_I² = t_*/(t_* + r), ρ_+ = (t_* + r)/(t_* r) of Section 14.1, x_I² ρ_+²
being the normalisation of P_0 (Lemma 15.25 (b)). Let ℓ_I := 1/2, ℓ_+ ∈ [1/2, 1) ∩ (δ, 1) and ℓ_K := ℵ + 1, a
class of Definition 15.36 (which presupposes δ < 1). On the support, (t_* + r)⁻¹ ≤ x_I ρ_+^(ℓ_+) (t_* + r)^(−(1−ℓ_+)),
as ℓ_+ ≥ 1/2, and ρ_K is bounded below. So P_Λ is weakly admissible relative to P_0 (Definition 15.36, with p_0 =
p̃_1 = 0, p_1 = S|_(∂X) as for P_0) of class ((d_0;0),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) for every d_0, with ‖P_Λ − P_0‖ ≤ C_(d_0)
Λ^(−(1−ℓ_+)), and its metric g_Λ is in 𝒢 with ‖g_Λ − g_0‖ ≤ C Λ^(−(1−ℓ_+)). Fix Λ so large that Λ/2 ≥ r′_0 + 1 and
P_Λ satisfies the smallness hypotheses of Section 17.1.1. Then t^♭ is a time function for g_Λ (Lemma 15.35 (2)),
and Lemma 18.5 (a) applies to g_Λ, whose dual metric is G_0 + ψ(r/Λ) ψ̃(t_*/Λ)(Ḡ − G_0), the interpolating
function vanishing on {r ≤ Λ/2} ⊃ {r ≤ r′_0 + 1}.

Let T_0 := C′T′ ≥ 8 and T_1 := T′ + 2Λ. D_Λ g is supported in {t_* ≥ T′} ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ T_0} (Lemma 15.35 (b)) and
compactly in M°, so it lies in every weighted space on the slab Ω′ := Ω_(T_0,T_1), and Proposition 17.14 (ii), with the
constant (slab) order s′ and α := γ − 2 < −1/2 + S̄, gives the forward solution u_Λ ∈ H^(s′,2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) of P_Λ u_Λ =
D_Λ g. Let X := Ω° ∩ {t_* < T_1, t^♭ < T_1, r > r_0}, on which u_Λ is defined, and w := ũ − u_Λ on X. On X, P_Λ ũ =
D_Λ g: the open sets X ∩ {r > Λ} and X ∩ {t_* + 2r < T′ + 4Λ} cover X, as t_* < T′ + 2Λ on X; on the first, P_Λ =
N_ι⁺(P_0) = Ñ_Λ (ψ̃(t_*/Λ) = 1 there), and on the second ũ and D_Λ g both vanish. So P_Λ w = 0 on X, and supp w ⊂
{t^♭ ≥ T_0} (ũ vanishes on {t_* < T′} ⊃ {t^♭ < T_0}, and u_Λ by its space). For p ∈ X with t^♭(p) > c := T_0/2,
J⁻_X(p) ∩ {t^♭ ≥ c} lies in

    L_p := {c ≤ t^♭ ≤ t^♭(p),  t_* ≤ t_*(p),  B ≤ B(p),  r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)}

(Lemma 18.5 (a), and t^♭ is increasing), which is compact (B bounds r) and contained in X (t_* ≥ t^♭ ≥ c ≥ 4).
By Lemma 18.4 with the time function t^♭, w = 0: ũ = u_Λ on X. Near ℐ⁺, t^♭ ≤ t_*, so X contains a neighbourhood
of ℐ⁺ ∩ {1 < t_* < T′ + 2Λ}. Hence χ(t_*) ũ ∈ H^(s′,2γ)_e near ℐ⁺ for χ ∈ C_c^∞((−∞, T′ + 2Λ)) (with the weight shift
of Lemma 14.19), and undoing D_Λ gives the claim. ∎

#### 19.1.4 Proof of the existence statement

*Proof of Proposition 19.2 (1).* *The equation on the Mellin side.* By Definition 18.1, N_ι⁺(P_0) u = f is N⁰u =
τ⁻² f, and τ⁻² f lies in H^((𝗌−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_+,γ_cf−2))_(ebe;b) with the same norm as f in the space of
(19.5), the τ-weight being τ^(γ_+). For σ on the line Im σ = −γ_+, which lies in {Im σ > max(−γ_I, −1 − β_+)},
define

    (ℳu)(σ) := N⁰(σ)⁻¹ ℳ(τ⁻² f)(σ),    (19.6)

which is well defined by Corollary 18.33.

*Bounds on the line.* Write σ = ζ − iγ_+. (i) For |ζ| ≥ h_0⁻¹ put h := |ζ|⁻¹ and z := hσ = ±1 − ihγ_+ ∈ 𝒵^±_h. By
Proposition 18.21 (the second estimate of (18.46)) and P_(ι,h,z) = h² N⁰(σ),

    ‖(ℳu)(σ)‖_(𝐨_±;k,+) ≤ C_k ‖h² ℳ(τ⁻² f)(σ)‖_(Y_(𝐨_±);k,+)
                         = C_k ‖ℳ(τ⁻² f)(σ)‖_((𝗌_(0ħ,cħ)−2; 2γ_I+2, γ_cf−2, γ_cf−2; 𝖻_±−1);k,+),

since multiplication by h² = ρ_tf² ρ_sf² lowers the tf- and sf-orders by 2, and Y_𝐨 = H^((𝗌′−2; 2γ_I+2, γ_cf−2, γ_cf;
𝖻+1)) ((18.28)). The last norm is at most C times the norm with the fibre order 𝗌_(0ħ,cħ) − 1, which is the
spectral norm of Lemma 19.1 for the order 𝗌 − 1 and the weights (2γ_I + 2, γ_+, γ_cf − 2) of τ⁻² f: its sf-order
is 𝖻_± − 1, and its tf-order equals its cf-weight γ_cf − 2. (ii) For |ζ| ≤ h_0⁻¹, σ ↦ N⁰(σ)⁻¹ ∈ ℒ(𝒴^(𝗌_(0,b)−2)_k,
𝒳^(𝗌_(0,b))_k) is continuous (Corollary 18.33), hence bounded on this compact segment; for 1 ≤ |ζ| ≤ h_0⁻¹ the norms
‖·‖_(𝐨;k,+) at h = |ζ|⁻¹ ∈ [h_0, 1] are equivalent to the 0,b-norms uniformly (Section 18.2.1), and
𝒴^(𝗌_(0,b)−2)_k ⊃ H^((𝗌_(0,b)−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_cf−2))_(0,b;b) continuously. Squaring, integrating in ζ and using
(19.4) for u (at the order 𝗌) and for τ⁻² f (at the order 𝗌 − 1): the function u with Mellin transform
(19.6) on the line lies in H^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)((0, ∞) × ι⁺), and (19.5) holds. Since
ℳ(N⁰u)(σ) = N⁰(σ)(ℳu)(σ) = ℳ(τ⁻² f)(σ) on the line (by (18.7) for u ∈ C_c^∞, and by continuity), N⁰u = τ⁻² f.
Conversely, if N_ι⁺(P_0) u = 0 with u in this space, then N⁰(σ)(ℳu)(σ) = 0 for almost every σ on the line, so ℳu = 0
and u = 0: this is the uniqueness.

*Support (Paley–Wiener).* The solution map f ↦ u is bounded by (19.5). The functions f ∈ C_c^∞((0, τ_0) ×
(ι⁺)°) are dense in the space of (19.5) on [0, τ_0] × ι⁺: the dilations f ↦ f(Λ·, ·), Λ ↓ 1, are
translations in t, strongly continuous on (19.3) as 𝗌 is dilation-invariant, and move the support into
{τ ≤ τ_0/Λ}; then multiply approximations in C_c^∞((0, ∞) × (ι⁺)°) by a cut-off in τ equal to 1 on [0, τ_0/Λ] and
supported in [0, τ_0). As supp u ⊂ {τ ≤ τ_0} is a closed condition, it suffices to take f ∈ C_c^∞ with supp f ⊂
[τ_1, τ_−] × 𝒞, 0 < τ_1 < τ_− < τ_0, 𝒞 ⊂ (ι⁺)° compact. Then F(σ) := ℳ(τ⁻² f)(σ) ∈ C_c^∞(𝒞) is entire in σ, and for
Im σ ≥ −γ_+ and L ∈ ℕ₀, as ℳ((1 + (τD_τ)²)^L g) = (1 + σ²)^L ℳg and |τ^(−iσ)| = τ^(Im σ) ≤ max(τ_−^(Im σ),
τ_1^(−γ_+)) on the support,

    ‖F(σ)‖_(H^ν) ≤ C_(ν,L) |1 + σ²|^(−L) max(τ_−^(Im σ), τ_1^(−γ_+)).

Let φ ∈ C_c^∞((ι⁺)°). By Corollary 18.33, σ ↦ ⟨(ℳu)(σ), φ⟩, defined by (19.6) with N⁰(σ)⁻¹, is holomorphic
on {Im σ > max(−γ_I, −1 − β_+)} ⊃ {Im σ ≥ −γ_+}. There is ν_1 with

    |⟨(ℳu)(σ), φ⟩| ≤ C ⟨σ⟩^(ν_1) ‖F(σ)‖_(H^(ν_1)),      Im σ ≥ −γ_+.

Indeed, for |σ| ≥ √2 h_0⁻¹, σ = h⁻¹ z with z in one of the families (18.27) (Section 18.3.1), and
(18.29) bounds (ℳu)(σ) in H^𝐨 by h² F(σ) in Y_𝐨; on compact subsets of (ι⁺)° the semiclassical norms of H^𝐨
and Y_𝐨 are bounded above and below by standard Sobolev norms times powers of h (the orders are bounded, and the weights
are bounded above and below there), and ⟨(ℳu)(σ), φ⟩ only sees supp φ. For |σ| ≤ √2 h_0⁻¹, Im σ ≥ −γ_+, a compact
set, use the continuity of Corollary 18.33. Fix L with ν_1 − 2L < −1. By Mellin inversion, ⟨u(τ, ·), φ⟩ = (2π)⁻¹
∫_(Im σ = −γ) τ^(iσ) ⟨(ℳu)(σ), φ⟩ dσ for γ = γ_+. The integrand is holomorphic on {Im σ ≥ −γ_+} and
O(⟨σ⟩^(ν_1−2L)) uniformly on {|Re σ| ≥ 2} in each horizontal strip (|1 + σ²| ≥ |σ|²/2 there), so the contour may be
moved to Im σ = γ for every γ ≥ max(2, −γ_+). There |τ^(iσ)| = τ^(−γ), and for τ > τ_− the integral is at most
C (τ_−/τ)^γ → 0 as γ → ∞. So ⟨u(τ, ·), φ⟩ = 0 for τ > τ_−, for every φ: supp u ⊂ {τ ≤ τ_−}. ∎

#### 19.1.5 A support lemma, and the proof of strong uniqueness

*Fixed-σ transforms.* Let m ∈ ℤ and v ∈ H^(m,(a,b,c))_ebe with τ-support in a compact interval [τ_1, τ_2] ⊂ (0, ∞).
Then σ ↦ (ℳv)(σ) is entire with values in H^(m,(a,c))_(0,b)(ι⁺), and

    ‖(ℳv)(σ)‖_(H^(m,(a,c))_(0,b)) ≤ C ⟨σ⟩^(|m|) max(τ_1^(Im σ), τ_2^(Im σ)) ‖v‖_(H^(m,(a,b,c))_ebe).    (19.7)

Indeed, the spatial fields among (19.1) (R∂_R, Z_a near cf; v∂_v, √v Z_a near ℐ⁺) are the 0,b-fields of ι⁺ at
bounded frequency and commute with ℳ, while τ∂_τ and Rτ∂_τ become iσ and iσR. For m ≥ 0, (19.7) without the
factor ⟨σ⟩^(|m|) follows from the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in τ on [τ_1, τ_2]. For m < 0 write v = Σ_(|α|≤|m|)
V^α v_α with V^α products of the fields (19.1) and v_α ∈ H^(0,(a,b,c)) supported in a slightly larger compact
τ-interval, Σ ‖v_α‖ ≤ C‖v‖; the weights commute with the fields up to bounded factors.

*Comparison of norms at fixed h.* For constant orders and h ∈ (0, 1], the norms of H^((m;a,c,l;𝖻))_((0ħ,cħ,h)) and of
H^(m,(a,c))_(0,b) are equivalent with constants C h^(−ν) and C⁻¹ h^ν, ν depending on |m|, |a|, |c|, |l| and sup|𝖻|.
Indeed, the cells of the structure at parameter h are those of the 0,b-structure rescaled by factors in [h, 1] (the
scalings (1 + ρ_K|σ|)⁻¹, ⟨σ⟩⁻¹, x_I⟨σ⟩⁻¹ of Section 14.6.2 against 1, 1, x_I), and the weights ρ_cf^c ρ_tf^l ρ_sf^𝖻
differ from ρ_K^c by factors in [h^ν, h^(−ν)], as ρ_tf = h + ρ_K, ρ_sf = h/(h + ρ_K) and ρ_cf = ρ_K/(h + ρ_K)
(Section 18.2.1).

The support lemma below uses the Paley–Wiener–Schwartz theorem, Theorem A.47, in dimension one: *a
distribution u on ℝ with compact support in an interval [a, b] has an entire Fourier–Laplace transform û(ζ) =
∫ e^(−itζ) u(t) dt with |û(ζ)| ≤ C (1 + |ζ|)^ν e^(H(Im ζ)) for some C, ν, where H(η) := sup_(t∈[a,b]) tη is the
supporting function of [a, b]; conversely, an entire function with such a bound is the Fourier–Laplace transform of a
distribution supported in [a, b].*

**Lemma 19.4** (Support.) Let m ∈ ℤ, T > 0, and let w ∈ H^(m,(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_ebe have τ-support in a
compact subset of (0, ∞), with N_ι⁺(P_0) w ∈ H^(m−1,(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))_ebe supported in {t_* ≥ T}. Then w is
supported in {t_* ≥ T}.

*Proof.* Let f := N_ι⁺(P_0) w, so that N⁰w = τ⁻² f, and let supp w ⊂ {τ_1 ≤ τ ≤ τ_2}. W(σ) := (ℳw)(σ) and
F(σ) := ℳ(τ⁻² f)(σ) are entire, N⁰(σ) W(σ) = F(σ) by (18.7), and by (19.7), as τ ≤ T⁻¹ on supp f,

    ‖F(σ)‖_(H^(m−1,(2γ_I+2,γ_cf−2))_(0,b)) ≤ C ⟨σ⟩^(|m−1|) T^(−Im σ),      Im σ ≥ 0.

For Im σ ≥ −γ_+, W(σ) ∈ 𝒳^m, and Proposition 18.24 (invertibility on 𝒳^m; any order) gives W(σ) = N⁰(σ)⁻¹ F(σ). Let
φ ∈ C_c^∞((ι⁺)°) and η_0 := max(0, −γ_+). For |σ| ≥ √2 h_0⁻¹, Im σ ≥ η_0, write σ = h⁻¹ z with z in one of the families
(18.27) (Section 18.3.1). At this fixed h, W(σ) ∈ H^𝐨 with the fibre order m (any order is allowed there)
and the sf-orders of Section 18.3.1, and (18.29) gives ‖W(σ)‖_𝐨 ≤ C ‖h² F(σ)‖_(Y_𝐨); with the comparison of
norms and the compact support of φ in (ι⁺)°, |⟨W(σ), φ⟩| ≤ C h^(−ν) ‖F(σ)‖_(H^(m−1,(2γ_I+2,γ_cf−2))_(0,b)). On the
compact set {|σ| ≤ √2 h_0⁻¹, Im σ ≥ η_0} use the continuity of Corollary 18.33. Hence |⟨W(σ), φ⟩| ≤ C ⟨σ⟩^(ν_1)
T^(−Im σ) for Im σ ≥ η_0. In the strip 0 ≤ Im σ ≤ η_0, which is empty unless γ_+ < 0 and where the families
(18.27) and the invertibility are not available, (19.7) alone gives |⟨W(σ), φ⟩| ≤ C ⟨σ⟩^(|m|)
τ_2^(Im σ), and τ_2^(Im σ) and T^(−Im σ) are bounded above and below there. Taking ν_1 ≥ |m|,

    |⟨W(σ), φ⟩| ≤ C ⟨σ⟩^(ν_1) T^(−Im σ),      Im σ ≥ 0.

In t := −log τ, the Mellin transform (18.4) of the compactly supported distribution τ ↦ ⟨w(τ, ·), φ⟩ is its
Fourier transform ∫ e^(iσt) ⟨w, φ⟩ dt, as τ^(−iσ) = e^(iσt). It is entire and, the support lying in t ∈ [−log τ_2,
−log τ_1], it is bounded by C ⟨σ⟩^(ν_1) e^((log τ_1) Im σ) for Im σ ≤ 0 (|e^(iσt)| = e^(−t Im σ), largest at t =
−log τ_1). With the last bound for Im σ ≥ 0 it is bounded by C ⟨σ⟩^(ν_1) e^(H(Im σ)), H(η) := sup{−tη : t ∈ [log T,
−log τ_1]}; this is the supporting function of that interval for the transform σ ↦ û(−σ), û(ζ) = ∫ e^(−itζ) u dt. By
the Paley–Wiener–Schwartz theorem (Theorem A.47) the support lies in {t ≥ log T} = {t_* ≥ T}. As φ is
arbitrary, supp w ⊂ {t_* ≥ T}. ∎

*Proof of Proposition 19.2 (2).* The proof uses only the integer order s″ := ⌊inf 𝗌⌋, and not part (1).

*Reduction.* Work in (t_*, r, ω), in which N_ι := N_ι⁺(P_0) is (18.8): translation-invariant in t_* and
homogeneous under D_Λ (Section 19.1.3). ũ is a distribution on {t_* > 0, r > 0}, supported in {t_* ≥ τ_0⁻¹}, and on
{r < R_0 t_*} it lies locally in the edge space of order s″ with weight γ_cf at r = 0. Pick Λ ≥ 1 with Λτ_0⁻¹ ≥ 4R_0⁻¹,
replace ũ by D_Λ ũ (with the same properties, τ_0/Λ in place of τ_0, as {R < R_0} is D_Λ-invariant), and then translate
t_* by 1 − Λτ_0⁻¹. The new ũ solves N_ι ũ = 0 on {r > 0}, vanishes for t_* < 1, and on {t_* ≥ 1, r < 4}, which lies in
the old {R < R_0} because the old t_* is ≥ Λτ_0⁻¹ ≥ 4R_0⁻¹ there, it is locally of edge order s″ with weight γ_cf at
r = 0. We show ũ = 0 on {t_* < 2}. The same argument after a further translation by 1 (the properties persist, the
region {t_* ≥ 1, r < 4} moving into itself) then gives ũ = 0 on {t_* < j} for every j, so ũ = 0.

*The extension.* Let χ_(t_*) ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 near (−∞, 2] and 0 near [3, ∞), χ_r ∈ C_c^∞([0, 3)) equal 1 near
[0, 2], and χ^♭_(t_*) ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, 2] and supported in {χ_(t_*) = 1}. Then g := χ_(t_*)[N_ι, χ_r] ũ ∈
H^(s″−1)_c is supported in {1 ≤ t_* ≤ 3, 2 ≤ r ≤ 3}; let u_ext be the solution of N_ι u_ext = g on {t_* < 3} of
Lemma 19.3 (T = 1, s′ = s″), which vanishes where t_* + 2r < 5 (the support argument there) and satisfies
χ^♭_(t_*) u_ext ∈ H^(s″,2γ_I)_e near ℐ⁺. Put

    w := χ_(t_*) χ_r ũ − χ^♭_(t_*) u_ext,
    f := N_ι w = [N_ι, χ_(t_*)](χ_r ũ) + χ_(t_*)(1 − χ^♭_(t_*))[N_ι, χ_r] ũ − [N_ι, χ^♭_(t_*)] u_ext.

w is supported in {1 ≤ t_* ≤ 3}, that is τ ∈ [1/3, 1], and lies in H^(s″,(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_ebe (any τ-weight): near
r = 0 it is χ_(t_*) ũ, near ℐ⁺ it is −χ^♭_(t_*) u_ext, and in between it is in H^(s″)_loc. Each term of f is supported in
{2 ≤ t_* ≤ 3}, that is τ ∈ [1/3, 1/2], and f ∈ H^(s″−1,(2γ_I+2,γ_+,γ_cf−2))_ebe by (19.2) (the commutators are
first-order ebe-operators with the weights of N_ι, or better).

*Support.* By Lemma 19.4 with m = s″ and T = 2, w is supported in {t_* ≥ 2}.

*Conclusion.* On {t_* < 2}, χ_(t_*) = χ^♭_(t_*) = 1, so χ_r ũ = u_ext there, and u_ext = 0 where t_* + 2r < 5, which
contains {t_* < 2, r < 3/2}. Hence ũ = 0 on {t_* < 2, r < 3/2}. Let ū be ũ on X := {t_* < 2} ⊂ ℝ^(1+4), extended by 0
across {r = 0} and to {t_* ≤ 0}; as ũ vanishes on {t_* < 2, r < 3/2} and on {t_* < 1}, ū ∈ 𝒟′(X), and Ñū = 0 on X, with
Ñ of Lemma 19.3 (Ñ = N_ι on {r > 1/2}, and ū = 0 on {r < 3/2}). t is a time function for ḡ, supp ū ⊂ {t_* ≥ 1}
⊂ {t ≥ 1}, and for p ∈ X the Minkowski causal past J⁻(p) lies in X (t_* is non-decreasing along future causal curves,
Lemma 18.5 (c)) and meets {t ≥ 1/2} in a compact set. Lemma 18.4 with the time function t, c := 1/2 and
L_p := J⁻(p) ∩ {t ≥ 1/2} gives ū = 0, so ũ = 0 on {t_* < 2}. ∎

[Hin26c] proves part (2) by solving N_ι w′ = f with part (1) and comparing w with w′ by uniqueness. That needs f in the
space of part (1), with the variable admissible order 𝗌 near ℐ⁺, where the extension u_ext is controlled only at a
constant order; Lemma 19.4 avoids this, using only Proposition 18.24 at a constant order and the high-energy
estimate (18.29).

### 19.2 The modified operator P_+

This section is [Hin26c, Section 10.2] in dimension 4 + 1.

#### 19.2.1 Definition and structure

**Definition 19.5** (The modified operator.) Let χ ∈ C_c^∞([0, 2)), 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, equal 1 near [0, 1], and
write χ = χ(R). Let T_+ := max(2, 2r_0). On {t_* > T_+} × ι⁺, that is on (0, T_+⁻¹)_τ × ι⁺,

    P_+ := χ N_ι⁺(P_0) + (1 − χ) P_0.

On supp(1 − χ), R ≥ 1, so r = R t_* > T_+ ≥ 2r_0 lies in the domain of P_0 (Definition 15.21); N_ι⁺(P_0) is defined on
{r > 0} by (18.8). This is [Hin26c, Definition 10.13] in dimension 4 + 1; [Hin26c] takes {t_* > 1}, and T_+
only keeps the domain of P_0 in view.

**Lemma 19.6** (Structure of P_+.) (a) P_+ ∈ x_I² τ² ρ_cf⁻² Diff²_ebe([0, T_+⁻¹) × ι⁺).
(b) P_+ − N_ι⁺(P_0) ∈ x_I² τ³ ρ_cf⁻² Diff²_ebe: N_ι⁺(P_0) is the normal operator of P_+ at τ = 0 ([Hin26c, (10.51)]).
(c) P_+ is principally scalar with principal symbol G_χ := χḠ + (1 − χ)G_0, the dual metric function of g_χ⁻¹ := χḡ⁻¹ +
(1 − χ)g_0⁻¹, which is Lorentzian on {τ < τ_1} for some τ_1 > 0; dt_* is past causal for g_χ; and g_χ = ḡ on {R ≤ 1}.

*Proof.* (a) On {R < 1}, P_+ = N_ι⁺(P_0) and (19.2) applies. On {R > 1/2}, (τ, R, ω) ↦ (t_* = τ⁻¹, r = Rτ⁻¹,
ω) identifies [0, T_+⁻¹) × ι⁺ with a neighbourhood of ι⁺ ∩ {R > 1/2} in M, away from K⁺. There the ebe-fields
(19.1) are the e3b-fields (Section 14.2.4: b-fields over (ι⁺)°, eb-fields near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺), ρ_+ ∼ τ, and P_0 ∈
x_I² ρ_+² Diff²_e3b (Lemma 15.25 (b)), as is N_ι⁺(P_0) by Lemma 18.3. (b) P_+ − N_ι⁺(P_0) = (1 − χ)(P_0 −
N_ι⁺(P_0)) is supported in {R ≥ 1}, and (18.10) applies. (c) The principal symbols are Ḡ Id for N_ι⁺(P_0)
((18.8)–(18.9)) and G_0 Id for P_0 (Definition 15.21). By (15.2) of Lemma 15.2, for the
inverses, ρ_0⁻² x_I⁻² ρ_+⁻² (g_0⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹) ∈ ρ_0² x_I² ρ_+² C^∞(M; S² ᵉ³ᵇTM), and ρ_0, x_I are bounded below on
{1 ≤ R ≤ 2} near ι⁺. So on supp χ ∩ supp(1 − χ) ⊂ {1 ≤ R ≤ 2} the normalised difference x_I⁻² ρ_+⁻² (g_χ⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹) =
χ x_I⁻² ρ_+⁻² (ḡ⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹) is O(ρ_+²), and the convex combination is Lorentzian for τ small, as in Definition 15.33,
remark (b). In dimension 4 + 1 the relative decay of g_0 − ḡ at (ι⁺)° is ρ_+², the mass term being O(r⁻²). Finally
Ḡ(dt_*) = 0 (dt_* is null for ḡ, Section 18.1.2) and G_0(dt_*) < 0 with dt_* past directed on {r ≥ T_+}
(Lemma 15.2, [Hin26c, Lemma 4.4]), so G_χ(dt_*) ≤ 0, past directed. ∎

#### 19.2.2 Orders

Let 𝗌 be admissible for P_0 with weights α_+, 0 and margin 0 (Definition 15.44), and let it meet the lower thresholds
(4) and (6) of Definition 15.29 with margin 1. An order admissible with margin 1 does, and so does its sum with 1, which
has margin 0 at the upper threshold (5); Section 19.3 uses both. Let 𝗌_I be the τ-dilation-invariant extension of
𝗌|_(ᵉ³ᵇS*_ι⁺M) (Section 19.1.1), and

    𝗌′ := χ(R) 𝗌_I + (1 − χ(R)) 𝗌      on ᵉᵇᵉS*([0, T_+⁻¹) × ι⁺).    (19.8)

Fix η_1 > 0 so small that 𝗌_♭ := 𝗌 − 1 − η_1 is admissible with weights α_+, 0 and margin 0. This is possible: the
threshold conditions (4)–(6) of Definition 15.29 are strict inequalities for the constant values of 𝗌 near finitely
many radial sets, 𝗌 meets the lower ones (4), (6) with margin 1, and lowering 𝗌 only helps at the upper one (5); and
(1)–(3) of Definition 15.29 and (2)–(5) of Proposition 15.43 are unaffected by subtracting a constant. Let 𝗌_(♭,I) be
its τ-dilation-invariant extension.

**Lemma 19.7** (The orders near ι⁺.) There is τ_1 ∈ (0, T_+⁻¹), not larger than that of Lemma 19.6 (c)
and with τ_1⁻¹ at least the t_1 of Lemma 18.5 (b), such that on {τ ≤ τ_1}:

(a) 𝗌′ = 𝗌_I on {R ≤ 10}, 𝗌′ = 𝗌 on {R ≥ 1}, and 𝗌_(♭,I) + 1 ≤ 𝗌′.

(b) 𝗌′ is non-increasing along the future null-bicharacteristic flow of every principally scalar operator whose dual
metric is g⁻¹ = g_χ⁻¹ + k with k supported in {τ ≤ τ_1} ∩ {R ≥ 1} and small in the norm of Proposition 15.43 (2), or
with k = 0.

(c) 𝗌′ is constant near the radial sets R_(ℐ⁺,in,+), R_(ℐ⁺,out) (over ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺; Definition 15.15) and near R_(cf,in),
R_(cf,out), the τ-invariant extensions over cf of ∂R_(∂K⁺,in), ∂R_(∂K⁺,out) under the identification ᵉᵇᵉT*_(ι⁺∩cf) =
³ᵇT*_(ι⁺∩K⁺)M_0 of [Hin26c, (10.44)], and satisfies there the thresholds (5)–(6) of Definition 15.29 with α_sf = α_+,
α_K = 0, margin 0. The same holds for 𝗌_(♭,I) in place of 𝗌′ near R_(cf,in/out) and R_(ℐ⁺,in,+).

*Proof.* (a) By Proposition 15.43 (3), 𝗌 is invariant under (t_*, r, ω) ↦ (Λt_*, Λr, ω) on a neighbourhood of
ι⁺ ∩ {R ∈ [1, 10]}, which contains {τ ≤ τ_1, R ∈ [1, 10]} for τ_1 small; there 𝗌 = 𝗌_I, which gives the first two
claims (on {1 ≤ R ≤ 2}, 𝗌′ = χ𝗌 + (1 − χ)𝗌). For the third: on {R ≤ 10}, 𝗌_(♭,I) + 1 = 𝗌_I − η_1 < 𝗌_I = 𝗌′; on
{R ≥ 1}, 𝗌′ = 𝗌, and 𝗌 is uniformly continuous on the compact set ᵉᵇᵉS*_({τ ≤ T_+⁻¹/2, R ≥ 1}) (where it is a smooth
function on ᵉ³ᵇS*M) and equals 𝗌_I at τ = 0, so |𝗌 − 𝗌_I| ≤ η_1 there for τ_1 small, and 𝗌_(♭,I) + 1 = 𝗌_I − η_1 ≤ 𝗌.

(b) On {R ≤ 1} the metric is ḡ (also for g, as k vanishes there) and 𝗌′ = 𝗌_I. Ḡ and 𝗌_I are invariant under
τ-dilations, so the rescaled Hamilton derivative 𝖧_Ḡ 𝗌_I is dilation-invariant; at τ = 0 it equals 𝖧_(G_0) 𝗌 over ι⁺,
since N_ι⁺(P_0) is the normal operator of P_0 at ι⁺ and their principal symbols agree there (Lemma 18.3,
(18.10)), and ±𝖧_(G_0) 𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ^± (Definition 15.29 (1), Proposition 15.43 (2) with h = 0). Every point is a
limit of its dilates towards τ = 0, so ±𝖧_Ḡ 𝗌_I ≤ 0 everywhere. On {R ≥ 1}, 𝗌′ = 𝗌 by (a), and g⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹ = χ(ḡ⁻¹ −
g_0⁻¹) + k. Let ψ(τ/τ_1) be a cut-off in time (ψ = 1 on [0, 1], supported in [0, 2)) and φ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal to 0 on
(−∞, 1/2] and 1 on [3/4, ∞). The dual metric g_0⁻¹ + ψ(τ/τ_1) φ(R) (χ(ḡ⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹) + k) on Ω equals g⁻¹ on {τ ≤ τ_1,
R ≥ 3/4}, and its difference from g_0⁻¹ has norm in 𝒢̃^(1,(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) (ℓ_+ ≤ 1) at most C τ_1^(2−ℓ_+) plus that of k:
on its support R ≥ 1/2, so that ρ_+ ≤ 3τ and ρ_K ≥ 1/3, and on supp χ, where ρ_0 and x_I are bounded below, ḡ − g_0 has
relative decay ρ_0² x_I² ρ_+² ((15.2)). Without φ the modified metric would be ḡ near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, where it is not
close to g_0. For τ_1 and k small, Proposition 15.43 (2) gives ±𝖧_G 𝗌 ≤ 0 on ∂Σ^±.

(c) Near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, 𝗌′ = 𝗌, constant near those radial sets by Proposition 15.43 (5). Near cf, 𝗌′ = 𝗌_I, the
dilation-invariant extension of 𝗌 restricted to the phase space over ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ identified by [Hin26c, (10.44)]; 𝗌 is
constant near ∂R_(∂K⁺,in/out) with the thresholds (5)–(6) of Definition 15.29 (Proposition 15.43 (1)), and so is 𝗌_I
near their τ-invariant extensions, with the same values. For 𝗌_(♭,I) the same holds, by the choice of η_1. ∎

#### 19.2.3 The statement

Fix τ_0 ∈ (0, C′τ_1/2), with C′ < 1 of Lemma 15.35 (b), to be decreased in Section 19.2.6; then τ_0 < 1/4 and
τ_0 < C′/(1 + C′). Spaces are those of (19.3) on [0, τ_0] × ι⁺.

**Proposition 19.8** (Forward solutions of P_+.) Let 𝗌, 𝗌′ be as in Section 19.2.2. There is τ_0 ∈
(0, C′τ_1/2) such that, for all γ_I < 3/2 + S̄, γ_+ < min(γ_I, 1 + β_+), γ_cf := −(α_+ + 2) and k ∈ ℕ₀:

(1) (*Existence.*) For every f ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺) there is a forward solution
u ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺) of P_+ u = f, with ‖u‖ ≤ C‖f‖ in these norms.

(2) (*Strong uniqueness.*) If ũ ∈ 𝒟′((0, ∞) × (ι⁺)°) is supported in {τ ≤ τ_0}, P_+ ũ = 0, and ũ ∈
H^(𝗌′,γ_cf)_(e,loc)((0, ∞)_τ × {R < R_0}) for some R_0 > 0, then ũ = 0.

τ_0 depends on 𝗌 and P_0 only through Section 19.2.6; the dependence on the weights is only through the constants.
The hypotheses on (γ_I, γ_+) are those of Proposition 19.2. This is [Hin26c, Proposition 10.14] in dimension 4 + 1.

#### 19.2.4 Strong uniqueness

*Proof of Proposition 19.8 (2).* As for Proposition 19.2 (2), only the region near r = 0 is non-standard. Let
s″ := ⌊inf 𝗌′⌋ and μ := min(1, R_0τ_0⁻¹/3), and work in (t_*, r, ω). As τ_0 < 1/3, for t_* ≥ τ_0⁻¹ we have {r ≤ 3μ} ⊂
{R < 1}, where P_+ = N_ι := N_ι⁺(P_0), and {r < 3μ} ⊂ {r < R_0 t_*}, where the hypothesis gives ũ edge order s″ with
weight γ_cf at r = 0; no rescaling of P_+ is needed. N_ι is t_*-translation invariant and homogeneous, so
Lemma 19.3 holds with its lengths multiplied by μ (apply it to D_(1/μ) g and rescale, Ñ becoming Ñ_μ, equal to N_ι
on {r > μ/2}): for g ∈ H^(s′−1)_c supported in {T ≤ t_* ≤ T + 2μ, 2μ ≤ r ≤ 3μ} there is a unique u on {t_* < T + 2μ},
vanishing for t_* < T and where t_* + 2r < T + 4μ, with N_ι u = g and χ(t_*) u ∈ H^(s′,2γ)_e near ℐ⁺ for χ ∈
C_c^∞((−∞, T + 2μ)). Let t_(*,0) ≥ τ_0⁻¹ be such that ũ = 0 on {t_* < t_(*,0)}; t_(*,0) = τ_0⁻¹ is one, by the support
condition. We show ũ = 0 on {t_* < t_(*,0) + μ/2}; iterating in steps of μ/2 gives ũ = 0.

Let χ_r ∈ C_c^∞([0, 3μ)) equal 1 near [0, 2μ]. Then N_ι(χ_r ũ) = P_+(χ_r ũ) = [P_+, χ_r] ũ =: g on {t_* ≥ t_(*,0)},
with g supported in {2μ ≤ r ≤ 3μ} and in H^(s″−1)_loc. Let χ_g ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, t_(*,0) + μ] and 0 on
[t_(*,0) + 3μ/2, ∞), and let u_mid solve N_ι u_mid = −χ_g g on {t_* < t_(*,0) + 2μ} as above (T = t_(*,0), s′ = s″): it
vanishes for t_* < t_(*,0) and where t_* + 2r < t_(*,0) + 4μ, and is in H^(s″,2γ_I)_e near ℐ⁺ for t_* < t_(*,0) + 2μ.
Then N_ι(χ_r ũ + u_mid) = 0 on {t_* ≤ t_(*,0) + μ}. Let χ_(t_*) ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, t_(*,0) + μ/2] and 0 on
[t_(*,0) + μ, ∞), and w := χ_(t_*)(χ_r ũ + u_mid). w has compact τ-support, lies in H^(s″,(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_ebe (near
r = 0 by hypothesis, near ℐ⁺ by Lemma 19.3, in between H^(s″)_loc), and N_ι w = [N_ι, χ_(t_*)](χ_r ũ + u_mid) is
supported in {t_* ≥ t_(*,0) + μ/2}. By Lemma 19.4, w is supported in {t_* ≥ t_(*,0) + μ/2}. So on {t_* < t_(*,0) +
μ/2}, χ_r ũ = −u_mid, which vanishes where t_* + 2r < t_(*,0) + 4μ, in particular on {t_* < t_(*,0) + μ/2, r < 7μ/4};
hence ũ = 0 there.

On the rest of {t_* < t_(*,0) + μ/2} we use Lemma 18.4. Let X := {τ_1⁻¹ < t_* < t_(*,0) + μ/2}, in the
coordinates (t, x) of ℝ^(1+4), t = t_* + r; let ū be the distribution on X equal to ũ on {r > 0} and to 0 on
{r < 7μ/4}, which is consistent; and let P̃ be the operator equal to P_+ on {r > μ/2} and to Ñ_μ on {r < μ}, both being
N_ι on X ∩ {μ/2 < r < μ} ⊂ {R < 1}. P̃ has smooth coefficients and principal symbol G_χ (Lemma 19.6 (c); G_χ = Ḡ
on {R ≤ 1}), and P̃ū = 0 on X. By Lemma 18.5 (b) (τ_1⁻¹ ≥ t_1, Lemma 19.7), t_* is non-decreasing along
future causal curves of g_χ in X, and t and t^♭_+ are time functions, with C′t_* ≤ t^♭_+ ≤ t_*. supp ū ⊂ {t_* ≥
t_(*,0)} ⊂ {t^♭_+ ≥ C′t_(*,0)}. Take the time function t^♭_+ and c := C′t_(*,0)/2, which exceeds τ_1⁻¹, as t_(*,0) ≥
τ_0⁻¹ and τ_0 < C′τ_1/2. For p ∈ X with t^♭_+(p) > c, J⁻_X(p) ∩ {t^♭_+ ≥ c} lies in L_p := {c ≤ t^♭_+ ≤ t^♭_+(p),
t_* ≤ t_*(p), t ≤ t(p)}, which is compact (r ≤ t(p) − c there) and contained in X (t_* ≥ t^♭_+ ≥ c > τ_1⁻¹).
Lemma 18.4 gives ū = 0, so ũ = 0 on {t_* < t_(*,0) + μ/2}. ∎

#### 19.2.5 Finite-time solvability

**Lemma 19.9** (Forward solutions on finite intervals.) Let f be as in Proposition 19.8 (1) and T ≥ τ_0⁻¹.
There is a unique u on {τ_0⁻¹ ≤ t_* < T}, vanishing near t_* = τ_0⁻¹, with P_+ u = f there and ψ_T u ∈
Ḣ^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b) for every ψ_T ∈ C_c^∞((−∞, T)) (a function of t_*), with ‖ψ_T u‖ ≤ C_(T,ψ_T) ‖f‖.
The same holds for the operators P^ε_+ of Section 19.2.6, ε ∈ (0, τ_0], in place of P_+, with constants independent
of ε.

*Proof.* *Uniqueness* follows from Proposition 19.8 (2), proved above: the difference of two solutions, cut off by ψ_T
near t_* = T, solves P_+ v = 0 on {t_* < T′} for T′ < T, and the argument of Section 19.2.4 is local in time.

*Existence, one step.* Let t_(*,0) ≥ τ_0⁻¹ and f_0 ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))_(ebe;b), supported in {t_* ≥
t_(*,0)}. By Lemma 19.7 (a), 𝗌′ = 𝗌_I on {R ≤ 10}, so χf_0 ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌_I−1;k),(∞,γ_++2,γ_cf−2)), and
Proposition 19.2 (1) gives the forward solution u_cf of N_ι u_cf = χf_0, with χu_cf ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌_I;k),(∞,γ_+,γ_cf)). Let
χ^♭ = χ^♭(R) equal 1 near [0, 1], supported in χ⁻¹(1). As P_+ = N_ι on {χ = 1}°,

    f_1 := f_0 − P_+(χ^♭ u_cf) = (1 − χ^♭) f_0 − [N_ι, χ^♭](χ u_cf) ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,∞)),

supported in {R ≥ 1} ∩ {t_* ≥ t_(*,0)}, with norm ≤ C‖f_0‖. Next we solve P_+ u_mid = f_1 on {t_* ≤ 2t_(*,0)}. Let ψ,
ψ̃ ∈ C^∞(ℝ), ψ = 0 on (−∞, 1/2], ψ = 1 on [1, ∞), ψ̃ = 1 on (−∞, 2], ψ̃ = 0 on [3, ∞), and on Ω

    P_aux := P_0 + ψ(8r/t_(*,0)) ψ̃(t_*/t_(*,0)) (P_+ − P_0).

P_+ − P_0 = χ(N_ι − P_0) is supported in {R ≤ 2}. On the support of the cut-offs, r ≥ t_(*,0)/16 and t_* ≤ 3t_(*,0),
and as χ(R) = 0 for R ≥ 2, also t_* ≥ t_(*,0)/32; so the second term lives where ρ_+ ∼ t_(*,0)⁻¹ and R ∈ [1/48, 2],
near (ι⁺)°. There N_ι − P_0 ∈ x_I² ρ_+³ Diff²_e3b (Lemma 18.3) and the principal symbols differ by O(ρ_+²)
relative to G_0 ((15.2)); the cut-offs, functions of r/t_(*,0) and t_*/t_(*,0) with r ∼ t_* ∼ t_(*,0) on
their supports, have e3b-derivatives bounded uniformly in t_(*,0). Hence P_aux is weakly admissible relative to P_0
(Definition 15.36, p_0 = p̃_1 = 0) with ε_P ≤ C t_(*,0)^(−(1−ℓ_+)) (ℓ_+ < 1), and its metric is close to g_0; for
t_(*,0) large (that is, τ_0 small), the hypotheses of Section 17.1.1 and of Proposition 15.43 (2) hold for P_aux, so 𝗌
is a slab order for it. Let Ω′ = Ω_(T_0,T_1) be a slab containing {t_(*,0) ≤ t_* ≤ 2t_(*,0), r ≥ t_(*,0)/4} and with
f_1 supported in {t^♭ ≥ T_0} there. Then f_1 ∈ H^((𝗌−1;k),2α+2)(Ω′)^(•,−), α := γ_I − 2 < −1/2 + S̄ (𝗌′ = 𝗌 on
{R ≥ 1}, and the weight shift is Lemma 14.19, as in Section 19.1.3), and Proposition 17.17 gives the forward
solution u_aux ∈ H^((𝗌;k),2α)(Ω′)^(•,−) of P_aux u_aux = f_1, with norm ≤ C‖f_1‖.

*Support and order of u_aux.* u_aux vanishes on {t_* < 2t_(*,0), r < t_(*,0)/4}. To see this, note that the dual metric
of P_aux is G_0 + a(Ḡ − G_0) with a := ψ(8r/t_(*,0)) ψ̃(t_*/t_(*,0)) χ(R) ∈ [0, 1], supported in {r ≥ t_(*,0)/16}, so
Lemma 18.5 (a) applies to it for t_(*,0) ≥ 16(r′_0 + 1), and t^♭ is a time function for it (Lemma 15.35
(2)). Let ψ_Φ ∈ C^∞(ℝ), 0 ≤ ψ_Φ ≤ 1, vanish on (−∞, 1/32] and equal 1 on [1/16, ∞), and

    Θ := t_* + Φ(r),      Φ(r) := (19/10) ∫_0^r ψ_Φ(r′/t_(*,0)) dr′.

Θ is non-decreasing along future causal curves of g_aux for t_(*,0) large. Where ψ_Φ = 0, dΘ = dt_* (Lemma 18.5

G_0(dt_*) − Φ′(2 − Φ′) + C r⁻² Φ′(2 + Φ′) < 0 for r large, by Lemma 15.2 (dt_* is past timelike, and g_0⁻¹ −
ḡ⁻¹ ∈ r⁻² C^∞(M; S²𝒯)); dΘ, which deforms continuously to dt_* through such covectors, is past causal for G_0 and Ḡ,
hence for G_0 + a(Ḡ − G_0) (the cone argument of Lemma 18.5). For r ≥ t_(*,0)/16, Φ(r) = (19/10) r − κ t_(*,0)
with κ := (19/10) ∫_0^(1/16) (1 − ψ_Φ) ∈ [0, 19/160]. On supp f_1 ⊂ {R ≥ 1, t_* ≥ t_(*,0)}, r ≥ t_* ≥ t_(*,0), so
Θ ≥ (29/10 − κ) t_(*,0) =: a_Θ; on {t_* < 2t_(*,0), r < t_(*,0)/4}, Θ < (2 + 19/40 − κ) t_(*,0) < a_Θ. Let U′ be the
interior of the slab Ω′ (Section 17.1.1), on which u_aux is defined, and X := U′ ∩ {Θ < a_Θ}. Then P_aux u_aux = f_1 =
0 on X, and supp u_aux ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ T_0}, with T_0 > 2 (enlarging t_(*,0)). For p ∈ X with t^♭(p) > c := T_0/2, J⁻_X(p) ∩
{t^♭ ≥ c} lies in

    L_p := {c ≤ t^♭ ≤ t^♭(p),  Θ ≤ Θ(p),  B ≤ B(p),  r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)},

which is compact (B bounds t_* and r) and contained in X (t_* ≥ t^♭ ≥ c > 1). By Lemma 18.4, u_aux = 0 on X,
which contains U′ ∩ {t_* < 2t_(*,0), r < t_(*,0)/4}. So on {t_* < 2t_(*,0)}, u_aux solves P_+ u_aux = f_1, as P_aux =
P_+ on {t_* ≤ 2t_(*,0), r ≥ t_(*,0)/8}. Its order is 𝗌; on {R ≥ 1} that is 𝗌′. On {t_(*,0)/4 ≤ r, R ≤ 1, t_* ≤
2t_(*,0)}, an interior region where P_+ = N_ι has smooth coefficients, we upgrade to the order 𝗌′ by real principal
type propagation (Theorem 14.49; in the interior b-regularity is regularity, and the k b-derivatives are handled by
the commuted systems of Lemma 16.19 and Lemma 16.23): 𝗌′ is non-increasing along the future flow
(Lemma 19.7 (b)), P_+ u_aux = f_1 ∈ H^((𝗌′−1;k)), there are no radial points over the interior, and every backward
null bicharacteristic from a point of this region reaches, within {t_* ≤ 2t_(*,0)}, either {r < t_(*,0)/4} (where
u_aux = 0) or {R ≥ 1} (where it is of order 𝗌 = 𝗌′): radially outgoing ones keep t_* and decrease r backward, the
others leave every compact subset of {t_* ≥ t_(*,0)} backward. With χ_(t_*) equal to 1 for t_* ≤ 3t_(*,0)/2 and 0 for
t_* ≥ 2t_(*,0), u_mid := χ_(t_*) u_aux ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,∞,∞))_(ebe;b) with norm ≤ C_(t_(*,0)) ‖f_0‖ (near ℐ⁺ by
Lemma 14.19 and the identification of e3b- and ebe-spaces there), and

    f_2 := f_1 − P_+ u_mid = −[P_+, χ_(t_*)] u_aux

is supported in {t_* ≥ 3t_(*,0)/2}, with norm ≤ C_(t_(*,0)) ‖f_0‖ in the space of f_0. Thus χ^♭ u_cf + u_mid solves
P_+ u = f_0 on {t_* < 3t_(*,0)/2}, with an error f_2 supported in {t_* ≥ 3t_(*,0)/2}.

*Iteration.* Apply the step to f_2 with 3t_(*,0)/2 in place of t_(*,0), and so on; after j steps the sum of the partial
solutions solves P_+ u = f on {t_* < (3/2)^j τ_0⁻¹}, and (3/2)^j → ∞. The bounds follow step by step. The same argument
applies to P^ε_+ of Section 19.2.6, which equals N_ι on {R ≤ 1} and differs from P_+ only on {τ ≤ 2ε} by a term of
the class (19.10), so that P_aux built from it satisfies the same smallness uniformly in ε. ∎

#### 19.2.6 The a priori estimate, and the proof of existence

*Radial estimates at cf.* Near cf, by [Hin26c, (10.44)], the ebe-phase space over {τ = 0, R = 0} is the 3b-phase space
over ∂K⁺ = ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, and P_+ = N_ι is τ-dilation-invariant on {R < 1}. Its rescaled Hamilton field is the
dilation-invariant extension of 𝖧̄ over ∂K⁺ (Section 15.3), with radial sets R_(cf,in), R_(cf,out) over all of cf:
R_(cf,in) is a saddle whose stable manifold lies over {R > 0} (radially infalling null geodesics) and whose unstable
manifold lies over {R = 0}, which is the stable manifold of R_(cf,out), whose unstable manifold lies over {R > 0}
(radially outgoing null geodesics) ([Hin26c, p. 223]; Lemma 15.9 over ι⁺, extended by invariance). With τ̃ :=
(t_* + r)⁻¹ = τ/(1 + R), whose differential is timelike for ḡ, let ψ_+ ∈ C^∞([0, ∞)) equal 1 near [0, τ_2], vanish on
[2τ_2, ∞), be non-increasing, and have √(−ψ_+ψ′_+) smooth.

**Lemma 19.10** (Radial estimates at cf.) Let 𝗍 be an order on ᵉᵇᵉS*, τ-dilation-invariant and constant near
R_(cf,in) (resp. R_(cf,out)), with the threshold (16.11) of Proposition 16.10 (resp. (16.13) of
Proposition 16.11) there for α_K = 0. Then Proposition 16.10 and Proposition 16.11, and their b-regular versions
Proposition 16.29, hold for L = N_ι, P_+ or P^ε_+ near R_(cf,in) (resp. R_(cf,out)) over cf ∩ {τ ≤ τ_2}, with the
ebe-weights (γ_+, γ_cf) for (α_+, α_K) (via α_+ − α_K = −γ_cf − 2, Lemma 14.20), for u vanishing on {τ̃ ≥ τ_2}. In
place of condition (4) of Proposition 16.10: at R_(cf,in) the Schwartz kernel of E is supported away from cf; at
R_(cf,out), WF′(E) is disjoint from the unstable manifold of R_(cf,out) (the τ-invariant extension of ∂W_out =
{ξ̂ = 0, η̂ = 0}, over {R > 0}); in both cases there is an additional term microsupported over supp ψ′_+(τ̃), which
vanishes for such u. This is the estimate of [Hin26c, p. 223].

*Proof.* These are the proofs of Proposition 16.10 and Proposition 16.11 with Ψ := ψ(𝔐_R q) ψ_+(τ̃) ψ(𝔐ρ_cf) in place of
ψ(𝔐_R q) ψ(𝔐ρ_+) ψ(𝔐ρ_K). The quantities at the radial set are unchanged: 𝖧 is the dilation-invariant extension of 𝖧̄,
so ρ⁻¹𝖧ρ, 𝖧q and the imaginary part 𝔭′ (that of N_ι, which at R = 0 is that of P_0 at ∂K⁺, its coefficients being those
of P_0 frozen) take the values used there at every τ. The weight w = τ^(γ_+) ρ_cf^(γ_cf) = ρ_+^(α_+) ρ_K^(α_K)·(smooth
positive) under [Hin26c, (10.44)] gives the same contribution, τ being dilation-invariant (τ⁻¹𝖧τ = 0 at the radial set,
as ρ_+⁻¹𝖧ρ_+ + ρ_K⁻¹𝖧ρ_K = 2 − 2 there). The factor ψ(𝔐ρ_cf) plays the role of ψ(𝔐ρ_K), with the same signs. The factor
ψ_+(τ̃) replaces ψ(𝔐ρ_+): 𝖧(ψ_+²) = 2ψ_+ψ′_+ 𝖧τ̃, and on the future characteristic set 𝖧τ̃ ≤ 0 (τ̃ decreases along
future causal curves), so this is (√(−ψ_+ψ′_+))² · 2(−𝖧τ̃) ≥ 0, a term +e*e microsupported over supp ψ′_+(τ̃) ⊂ {τ̃ ≥
τ_2}, where u = 0. For P_+ and P^ε_+ on {R < 1} the operator is N_ι. ∎

**Lemma 19.11** (The symbolic estimate.) For τ_0 ≤ τ_2/2 small and every ε ∈ (0, τ_0], with C independent of
ε, every u ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌_(♭,I);k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺) with P^ε_+ u ∈
Ḣ^((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))_(ebe;b) lies in Ḣ^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b) and

    ‖u‖_((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))
        ≤ C (‖P^ε_+ u‖_((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2)) + ‖u‖_((𝗌_(♭,I);k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))).    (19.9)

Here P^ε_+ := χ_0(τ/ε) N_ι + (1 − χ_0(τ/ε)) P_+, with χ_0 ∈ C_c^∞([0, 2)) equal to 1 on [0, 1]. This is [Hin26c,
(10.54)–(10.55)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* P^ε_+ − P_+ = −χ_0(τ/ε)(P_+ − N_ι), and by Lemma 19.6 (b)

    {P^ε_+ − N_ι : ε ∈ (0, 1]} is bounded in x_I² τ³ ρ_cf⁻² C^∞_b Diff²_ebe,
    P^ε_+ → P_+ in x_I² τ² ρ_cf⁻² C^∞_b Diff²_ebe,    (19.10)

as χ_0(τ/ε) is bounded in C^∞_b([0, ∞)_τ) and τχ_0(τ/ε) = O(ε) there ([Hin26c, (10.56)]). The dual metric of P^ε_+ is
g_χ⁻¹ + k_ε, k_ε = χ_0(τ/ε)(1 − χ)(ḡ⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹), supported in {τ ≤ 2ε, R ≥ 1} and small; so Lemma 19.7 (b)
applies to it. Now combine, in the ebe-phase space over [0, τ_0] × ι⁺, the following estimates, each valid for P^ε_+
uniformly in ε, in the strong sense, with the orders 𝗌′ (target) and 𝗌_(♭,I) (a priori), and with k b-derivatives:

(i) elliptic estimates off the characteristic set of G_χ (Theorem 14.43);

(ii) real principal type propagation along the future flow (Theorem 14.49; with k b-derivatives through the
commuted systems of Lemma 16.19 and Lemma 16.23), using Lemma 19.7 (b);

(iii) at R_(ℐ⁺,in,+), the radial saddle estimate Proposition 16.13 (Proposition 16.25), where P^ε_+ = P_0 (on
{R ≥ 2}) up to a term vanishing at ι⁺ in the class allowed there, with control on its stable manifold from (ii) along
ℐ⁺ (Lemma 15.16 (3));

(iv) at R_(cf,in), Lemma 19.10 (in), with control on its stable manifold (over {R > 0}: radially infalling null
bicharacteristics, which come backward from {t_* < τ_0⁻¹} or, over ι⁺, from the unstable manifold of R_(ℐ⁺,in,+))
from (ii) and (iii);
