(v) at R_(cf,out), Lemma 19.10 (out);

(vi) at R_(ℐ⁺,out), the radial sink estimate Proposition 16.14 (Proposition 16.25).

The thresholds hold for 𝗌′ and 𝗌_(♭,I) by Lemma 19.7 (c) (at the incoming sets the a priori order 𝗌_(♭,I) is
above threshold, at the outgoing sets the target order 𝗌′ is below it), and with γ_I < 3/2 + S̄ at ℐ⁺ (Proposition 16.13
and Proposition 16.14 at the weight α_I = γ_I − 2). The flow over ι⁺ is that of Proposition 15.18 (pulled back by
τ-invariance near cf), and t_* is non-decreasing along the future flow (Lemma 19.6 (c)). So every point of the
characteristic set over [0, τ_0] × ι⁺ is reached, backward along the flow, either from {t_* < τ_0⁻¹}, where u = 0, or
from one of the radial sets, in the order (iii)–(vi) ([Hin26c, Figure 10.3]). The constants depend on finitely many
seminorms of P^ε_+ in the class of (19.10) and on the margins, so they are uniform in ε; τ_0 ≤ τ_2/2 makes the
ψ_+-terms of Lemma 19.10 vanish for u supported in {τ ≤ τ_0} (there τ̃ ≤ τ < τ_2). ∎

*Inversion of the normal operator.* For u as in Lemma 19.11, u ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌_(♭,I);k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf)) and

    N_ι u = P^ε_+ u − (P^ε_+ − N_ι) u,
    ‖(P^ε_+ − N_ι) u‖_((𝗌_(♭,I)−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2)) ≤ C ‖u‖_((𝗌_(♭,I)+1;k),(2γ_I,γ_+−1,γ_cf))

by (19.10) (the factor τ³ against τ² shifts the τ-weight by one). As 𝗌_(♭,I) is the dilation-invariant
extension of an order admissible with weights α_+, 0 and margin 0, the uniqueness and the estimate of
Proposition 19.2 (1) at the order 𝗌_(♭,I) give

    ‖u‖_((𝗌_(♭,I);k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf)) ≤ C ‖N_ι u‖_((𝗌_(♭,I)−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))
        ≤ C (‖P^ε_+ u‖_((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2)) + ‖u‖_((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+−1,γ_cf))),

using 𝗌_(♭,I) + 1 ≤ 𝗌′ (Lemma 19.7 (a)). With (19.9),

    ‖u‖_((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))
        ≤ C (‖P^ε_+ u‖_((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2)) + ‖u‖_((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+−1,γ_cf))).    (19.11)

*Absorption.* Multiplication by χ_0(τ/δ_1) maps H^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf)) to H^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+−1,γ_cf)) with norm ≤
Cδ_1, as it equals τχ_0(τ/δ_1) times the identity of weights, and τχ_0(τ/δ_1) = δ_1·(τ/δ_1)χ_0(τ/δ_1) has
C^∞_b-seminorms O(δ_1). Fix δ_1 with C·Cδ_1 ≤ 1/2 in (19.11). For ε < δ_1/2, P^ε_+ = P_+ on {τ ≥ δ_1}, and (1 −
χ_0(τ/δ_1))u is controlled by Lemma 19.9 for P^ε_+, with T := 2δ_1⁻¹ and ψ_T ∈ C_c^∞((−∞, T)) equal to 1 on (−∞,
δ_1⁻¹], with constants independent of ε: the support of 1 − χ_0(τ/δ_1) lies in {t_* ≤ δ_1⁻¹}, where ψ_T = 1 and u is the
finite-time solution by uniqueness. Hence, for u in the space of Lemma 19.11 and ε < δ_1/2,

    ‖u‖_(Ḣ^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b))
        ≤ C ‖P^ε_+ u‖_(Ḣ^((𝗌′−1;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,γ_cf−2))_(ebe;b)),    (19.12)

C independent of ε ([Hin26c, (10.58)]); the absorbed term is finite because Lemma 19.11 places u in the space of
order 𝗌′.

*Proof of Proposition 19.8 (1).* Let f be as in Proposition 19.8 (1) and ε < δ_1/2. Let u^ε_ini be the finite-time
solution of P^ε_+ u = f on {t_* < 2ε⁻¹} (Lemma 19.9 for P^ε_+), and χ_(ε/2) := χ_0(2τ/ε). As P^ε_+ = N_ι on
supp χ_(ε/2) ⊂ {τ ≤ ε},

    u^ε := (1 − χ_(ε/2)) u^ε_ini + N_ι⁻¹(χ_(ε/2) f + [N_ι, χ_(ε/2)] u^ε_ini),

with N_ι⁻¹ the forward solution operator of Proposition 19.2 (1), solves P^ε_+ u^ε = f ([Hin26c, (10.59)]): on
{τ ≤ ε}, P^ε_+ u^ε = N_ι((1 − χ_(ε/2)) u^ε_ini) + χ_(ε/2) f + [N_ι, χ_(ε/2)] u^ε_ini = (1 − χ_(ε/2)) f + χ_(ε/2) f, and
on {τ ≥ ε}, u^ε = u^ε_ini. Proposition 19.2 (1) is applied at the order 𝗌_I − η_1, the dilation-invariant extension of
𝗌 − η_1, which is admissible with margin 0: on {τ ≤ τ_1}, 𝗌′ ≥ 𝗌_I − η_1 by the proof of Lemma 19.7 (a), so the
right-hand side lies in its space. So u^ε ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌_I−η_1;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf)) ⊂ Ḣ^((𝗌_(♭,I);k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf)), and
Lemma 19.11 places u^ε in the space of order 𝗌′. By (19.12), ‖u^ε‖ ≤ C‖f‖ uniformly in ε. A subsequence
u^(ε_j), ε_j → 0, converges weakly to some u ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺) with ‖u‖ ≤ C‖f‖.
Since P^ε_+ = P_+ on {τ ≥ 2ε}, P_+ u = f on {τ > 2ε_j} for every j, hence on {τ > 0}. ∎

### 19.3 Forward solutions of P_0 on e3b-spaces

**Theorem 19.12** (Forward solutions of the stationary model.) Let P_0 be a stationary wave-type operator
(Definition 15.21), in the setting of Section 17.1.1, with Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭ ≥ 1} and its slabs Ω_(1,T). Let α_I,
α_+ ∈ ℝ with

    α_I < −1/2 + S̄,      α_+ < α_I − 1/2.    (19.13)

Assume that P_0 is ℵ-admissible with sf-weight α_+ and sf-loss δ (Definition 15.32), and let 𝗌 ∈ C^∞(ᵉ³ᵇS*M) be
admissible with weights α_+, −ℵ and margin 0, and with weights α_+, 0 and margin 1 (Definition 15.44). Let k ∈ ℕ₀ and
f ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I+2,α_++2,0))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*; E)^(•,−), the space of restrictions to {r > r_0} of elements supported in
{t^♭ ≥ 1}, with the quotient norm (Section 14.7). The *forward solution* of P_0 u = f on Ω_* is the distribution u on
Ω_*° ∩ {r > r_0} whose restriction to every slab Ω_(1,T) is the forward solution there of Proposition 17.14: the
restrictions of f lie in the slab spaces, the weights at ι⁺ and K⁺ being bounded above and below at bounded times, and
the solutions on two slabs agree on the smaller by Proposition 17.14 (i). Then there is C_k, independent of f, with

    ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*;E)^(•,−))
        ≤ C_k ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I+2,α_++2,0))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*;E)^(•,−)).    (19.14)

This is [Hin26c, Theorem 10.1] in dimension 4 + 1. [Hin26c] states it on Ω = {t_* ≥ 1}; it is stated and proved here
on Ω_*, where the slab theory of Chapter 17 lives and where Theorem 19.14 uses it.

The thresholds (19.13) are those of [Hin26c] at every n. In the b-density weights of (18.3) they read
γ_I = α_I + 2 < 3/2 + S̄ = c + S̄ and γ_+ = α_+ + 5/2 < γ_I. Indeed, in (τ, R, ω) with t_* = τ⁻¹ and r = Rτ⁻¹, the map
(τ, R) ↦ (t_*, r) has Jacobian determinant −τ⁻³, and |dx| = r³ |dr dω|, |dt dx| = |dt_* dx|; so

    |dt dx| = τ⁻³ (R/τ)³ |dτ dR dω| = R⁴ τ⁻⁵ |(dτ/τ)(dR/R) dω| = 2 x_I⁻⁸ τ⁻⁵ |(dτ/τ)(dx_I/x_I) dω|,

using R = x_I⁻² near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺. Hence x_I^(2α_I) τ^(α_+) L²(|dt dx|) = x_I^(2(α_I+2)) τ^(α_++5/2) L²(|(dτ/τ)(dx_I/x_I)
dω|): the shifts are n/2 = 2 at ℐ⁺ and (n + 1)/2 = 5/2 at ι⁺. So α_I < −1/2 + S̄ is γ_I < 3/2 + S̄, and α_+ < α_I − 1/2
is α_+ + 5/2 < α_I + 2, that is γ_+ < γ_I. [Hin26c, Remark 10.2] applies: for P = P_0, p_1 = S|_(∂X), so p̄_1 = S̄,
and (19.13) is the threshold (16.3) at ℐ⁺.

#### 19.3.1 The weights

With the metric density |dt dx| on Ω and the b-densities of Section 19.1.1, Lemma 14.19 identifies near ι⁺

    H^(0,(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_e3b(|dt dx|) = H^(0,(2(α_I+2),α_++5/2,α_K+1/2))_e3b(|dτ/τ| μ_b),

and, on functions supported away from K⁺ (near ℐ⁺ and (ι⁺)°), the e3b-spaces are the ebe-spaces of (19.3) with
the weights

    γ_I := α_I + 2,      γ_+ := α_+ + 5/2,      γ_cf := −(α_+ + 2)    (19.15)

(the orders transported by the identification of Lemma 19.6 (a); near ι⁺, τ ∼ ρ_+ on {R ≥ 1/2}). They satisfy the
hypotheses of Proposition 19.2 and Proposition 19.8: γ_I < 3/2 + S̄ and γ_+ < γ_I by (19.13); and γ_+ − 1/2 =
α_+ + 2 = −γ_cf lies in (β_−, β_+), as P_0 is tf-admissible with the weight α_+ + 2 (Definition 15.32 (2)), so γ_+ <
β_+ + 1/2 < 1 + β_+. The buffer 1/2 is explained in [Hin26c, footnote 100]: pointwise decay at ι⁺ is governed by the
resonances, excluded in Im σ > −1 − β_+ (Proposition 18.24), whereas the 3b-regularity order limits the decay
obtainable by Sobolev embedding.

#### 19.3.2 Proof

*Proof of Theorem 19.12.* *Step 0: late right-hand sides.* Let τ_0 be as in Proposition 19.8, for the orders 𝗌 and
𝗌 + 1 (both meet its hypotheses: 𝗌 + 1 is admissible with weights α_+, 0 and margin 0 and meets the lower thresholds
with margin 2, as 𝗌 has margin 1); τ_0 < C′τ_1/2 < C′/(1 + C′) (Section 19.2.3). Let T := τ_0⁻¹ and ψ_T ∈ C^∞(ℝ)
equal 1 on (−∞, T] and 0 on [T + 1, ∞), a function of t_*. 𝗌 + 1 is a slab order (Section 17.3.2: admissible orders
are, and adding a constant preserves the conditions), so Proposition 17.17, with P = P_0, the slab order 𝗌 + 1 and the
weight α_I < −1/2 + S̄, gives on the slab Ω_(1,T+2) the forward solution u_0 of P_0 u_0 = f, with

    ‖u_0‖_(H^((𝗌+1;k),2α_I)(Ω_(1,T+2))^(•,−)) ≤ C ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌;k),2α_I+2)(Ω_(1,T+2))^(•,−)) ≤ C ‖f‖,

the last norm that of (19.14): on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭ ≤ T + 2}, t_* ≤ (T + 2)/C′, so the weights at ι⁺ and K⁺ are bounded
above and below there. As t^♭ ≤ t_*, supp ψ_T ⊂ {t^♭ ≤ T + 1}, inside the slab, so ψ_T u_0, extended by 0, lies in the
spaces on Ω_* of order 𝗌 + 1 with any weights at ι⁺ and K⁺, with norm ≤ C‖f‖, and P_0(ψ_T u_0) = ψ_T f + [P_0, ψ_T]
u_0. So f_1 := f − P_0(ψ_T u_0) = (1 − ψ_T) f − [P_0, ψ_T] u_0 is supported in {t_* ≥ T}, and, [P_0, ψ_T] ∈ x_I² ρ_+²
Diff¹_e3b having coefficients supported in {T ≤ t_* ≤ T + 1}, ‖f_1‖ ≤ C‖f‖ in the space of (19.14). The forward
solution of P_0 u = f on Ω_* is ψ_T u_0 + u_1, u_1 that of P_0 u_1 = f_1 (on each slab, by Proposition 17.14 (i)). So it
suffices to prove (19.14) when supp f ⊂ {t_* ≥ τ_0⁻¹}, which we assume.

For j = 1, 2, 3, 4 let χ_j ∈ C_c^∞([0, j + 1)) equal 1 near [0, j], regarded as functions of R = r/t_* on Ω, with
χ_1 = χ of Definition 19.5.

*Step 1: a solution near ℐ⁺.* (1 − χ_2) f is supported in {R ≥ 2} and defines a function on [0, ∞)_τ × ι⁺ vanishing
near cf; by Section 19.3.1,

    (1 − χ_2) f ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌;k),(2γ_I+2,γ_++2,∞))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺),

with norm ≤ C‖f‖. Apply Proposition 19.8 (1) at the order 𝗌 + 1, for which (𝗌 + 1)′ = 𝗌′ + 1 equals 𝗌 + 1 on {R ≥ 1}
(Lemma 19.7 (a)), so that (1 − χ_2) f lies in the space of its right-hand side: the forward solution u_I of
P_+ u_I = (1 − χ_2) f satisfies

    u_I ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′+1;k),(2γ_I,γ_+,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺),      ‖u_I‖ ≤ C ‖f‖.    (19.16)

On supp(1 − χ_3) ⊂ {R ≥ 3}, P_0 = P_+ and χ_2 = 0, so

    f′ := f − P_0((1 − χ_3) u_I) = f − (1 − χ_3) f + [P_0, χ_3] u_I = χ_3 f + [P_0, χ_3] u_I.

f′ is supported in {R ≤ 4}, away from ℐ⁺, so it is a function on M̃_0 near ι⁺ ∪ K⁺. [P_0, χ_3] is a first-order
e3b-operator with the weight ρ_+² of P_0 (Lemma 15.25), supported in {3 ≤ R ≤ 4}, and u_I has order 𝗌 + 1 there;
so, with the identification of e3b- and 3b-spaces away from ℐ⁺,

    f′ ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(α_++2,0))_(3b;b)(Ω)^(•,−),      supp f′ ⊂ {t_* ≥ τ_0⁻¹, R ≤ 4},      ‖f′‖ ≤ C ‖f‖.    (19.17)

*Step 2: the solution with right-hand side f′.* f, supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1} ⊂ {t_* ≥ 1}, lies in the corresponding space
on Ω with no larger norm, the quotient there being over more extensions; so (19.17) holds on Ω. By
ℵ-admissibility (Definition 15.32 (3), (15.24)), for the order 𝗌, which over K⁺ is stationary-P_0-admissible
with weights α_+, −ℵ and margin 0 (Proposition 15.43 (1)), the forward solution u′ of P_0 u′ = f′ on Ω satisfies

    u′ ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(α_+−δ,−ℵ))_(3b;b)(Ω)^(•,−),      ‖u′‖ ≤ C ‖f′‖.    (19.18)

u′ is the restriction to {r > r_0} of a distribution ũ′ supported in {t_* ≥ 1}, and P_0 u′ = f′ on {r > r_0} as such
distributions. So on Y := {1/2 < t_* < τ_0⁻¹, r > r_0}, P_0 u′ = 0, and u′ = 0 on {t_* < 1}. t_* is a time function for
g_0 (Lemma 15.2), and for p ∈ Y, J⁻_Y(p) ∩ {t_* ≥ 3/4} lies in L_p := {3/4 ≤ t_* ≤ t_*(p), B ≤ B(p), r ≥
min(r(p), r^♮)} (Lemma 18.5 (a) for the metric g_0 itself), which is compact and contained in Y;
Lemma 18.4 with the time function t_* and c := 3/4 gives u′ = 0 on Y. Let φ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 0 on
(−∞, τ_0⁻¹ − 1] and 1 on [τ_0⁻¹, ∞), a function of t_*. Then φũ′ extends u′, is supported in {t_* ≥ τ_0⁻¹ − 1} ⊂
{t^♭ ≥ C′(τ_0⁻¹ − 1)} ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ 1}, as τ_0 < C′/(1 + C′), and has norm at most C‖ũ′‖. So u′ lies in
H^((𝗌;k),(α_+−δ,−ℵ))_(3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−), with ‖u′‖ ≤ C‖f′‖ there.

*Step 3: u′ near ℐ⁺.* We show that (1 − χ_4) u′, regarded on M, is e3b-regular near ℐ⁺. As (1 − χ_4) f′ = 0,

    P_0((1 − χ_4) u′) = −[P_0, χ_4] u′ =: f″,

supported in {4 ≤ R ≤ 5}, away from ℐ⁺ and from cf; on [0, ∞) × ι⁺, by (19.18) and Section 19.3.1 with
α_+ − δ for α_+,

    f″ ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌−1;k),(∞,γ_+−δ+2,∞))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺).

On supp(1 − χ_4) ⊂ {R ≥ 4}, P_0 = P_+. Let u″ be the forward solution of P_+ u″ = f″ given by Proposition 19.8 (1) at
the order 𝗌 and with γ_+ − δ in place of γ_+ (allowed, δ ≥ 0; 𝗌′ = 𝗌 on supp f″):

    u″ ∈ Ḣ^((𝗌′;k),(2γ_I,γ_+−δ,γ_cf))_(ebe;b)([0, τ_0] × ι⁺),      ‖u″‖ ≤ C ‖f″‖ ≤ C ‖f‖.

ũ := u″ − (1 − χ_4) u′, extended by 0 to {τ > τ_0}, is a distribution on (0, ∞) × (ι⁺)° supported in {τ ≤ τ_0} with
P_+ ũ = f″ − f″ = 0; near cf it equals u″, as (1 − χ_4) u′ vanishes on {R ≤ 4}, so ũ ∈ H^(𝗌′,γ_cf)_(e,loc)((0, ∞) ×
{R < 4}). By Proposition 19.8 (2), ũ = 0. Hence, as 𝗌′ = 𝗌 on {R ≥ 1} and by Section 19.3.1,

    (1 − χ_4) u′ = u″ ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I,α_+−δ,∞))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−),      ‖(1 − χ_4) u′‖ ≤ C ‖f‖.    (19.19)

*Step 4: conclusion.* On Ω_* ∩ {r > r_0}, P_0((1 − χ_3) u_I + u′) = (f − f′) + f′ = f. Both terms lie in the spaces on
Ω_*: (1 − χ_3) u_I by (19.16), its support lying in {t_* ≥ τ_0⁻¹} ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ 1}, and u′ by Step 2; their
restrictions to each slab Ω_(1,T′) lie in its slab spaces, the weights at ι⁺ and K⁺ being bounded above and below at
bounded times. By Proposition 17.14 (i) on each slab, their sum is the forward solution of P_0 u = f on Ω_*:

    u = (1 − χ_3) u_I + χ_4 u′ + (1 − χ_4) u′.

By (19.16), (1 − χ_3) u_I ∈ H^((𝗌+1;k),(2α_I,α_+,∞))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−) ⊂
H^((𝗌;k),(2α_I,α_+−δ,∞))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−) (𝗌′ + 1 = 𝗌 + 1 on {R ≥ 1}); by Step 2, χ_4 u′ ∈
H^((𝗌;k),(∞,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−), as χ_4 u′ is supported in {R ≤ 5}, away from ℐ⁺, where 3b- and e3b-spaces
agree; and (19.19) holds. The three bounds give (19.14). ∎

In the last display of the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 10.1] the term u′ carries the sign −; the sign is +, as above.

**Remark 19.13** (Relaxed ℵ-admissibility.) If P_0 is ℵ-admissible with margin d_ℵ (the relaxed version
after Definition 15.32), then (19.14) holds with 𝗌 − d_ℵ in place of 𝗌 on the left, when 𝗌 is admissible with
weights α_+, −ℵ and margin d_ℵ, and with weights α_+, 0 and margin 1 + d_ℵ. Indeed, ℵ-admissibility enters only
(19.18), which then gives the order 𝗌 − d_ℵ, and the loss persists through Steps 3–4 (Proposition 19.8 is
applied in Step 3 at the order 𝗌 − d_ℵ, which meets its hypotheses). This is [Hin26c, Remark 10.17] in dimension 4 + 1.

### 19.4 Forward solutions of admissible wave-type operators: setting and statement

The rest of the chapter is [Hin26c, Section 11] in dimension 4 + 1. The forward solution of Pu = f is the weak limit
of the forward solutions of operators P_ε that equal P up to a time of order ε⁻¹ and the stationary model P_0 after it.
The a priori estimate for P_ε, uniform in ε, joins the global estimate Theorem 17.26 to the forward solution estimate
Theorem 19.12 for P_0. The error (P_ε − P_0)u is small near ι⁺ ∪ K⁺, where the weights gain, and is controlled at
bounded times by the energy estimates on slabs of Chapter 17. Three points need care. The order function
is taken with margin 3 + δ + ℵ (Lemma 19.19); the cut-offs are functions of the time function t^♭ of
Lemma 15.35, whose level sets carry the slabs on which forward solutions are unique (Section 19.5.7); and the
tame bound on the error uses a single extension across the artificial boundary {r = r_0} that is bounded at every order
of b-regularity at once, constructed where the order function is a constant integer (Section 19.5.5,
Section 19.5.6).

#### 19.4.1 Domains, weights and spaces

P_0 is a stationary wave-type operator on the bundle E (Definition 15.21), in the setting of Section 16.1.1, with
S̄ = inf_(∂X) min Re spec S ([Hin26c, (5.2)]; Definition 15.38 with p̃_1 = 0). t^♭ := t^♭_* is the time function of
Lemma 15.35, defined on Ω° and, by Lemma 17.2 (iv), on {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ 1/2}, and

    Ω_* := cl_M{t^♭ ≥ 1} ⊂ Ω = cl_M{t_* ≥ 1, r ≥ r_0}

(Lemma 15.35 (b): C′t_* ≤ t^♭ ≤ t_*). For T > 1 the *slab* Ω_(1,T) := Ω_* ∩ {t^♭ ≤ T} is that of
Section 17.1.1. On Ω we use the defining functions of Section 14.1 (Lemma 14.33),

    x_I² = ρ_I = t_*/(t_* + r),    ρ_+ = (t_* + r)/(t_* r),    ρ_K = r/(t_* + r),    ρ_+ ρ_K = t_*⁻¹,    (19.20)

of ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺. The formulae define smooth positive functions on {r > 0, t_* > 0}, and we use them also on the
extension region {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r_0}. For an order function 𝗍, k ∈ ℕ₀ and weights, H^((𝗍;k),(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*;
E)^(•,−) is the space of restrictions to {r > r_0} of elements of H^((𝗍;k),(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_(e3b;b) (Section 14.4.2)
supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}, with the quotient norm (Section 14.7, Section 16.1.1). As in [Hin26c, (11.1)], the
*b-spaces* carry powers of ρ_I = x_I² at ℐ⁺:

    H^(k,(α_I,α_+,α_K))_b := ρ_I^(α_I) ρ_+^(α_+) ρ_K^(α_K) H^k_b = H^((0;k),(2α_I,α_+,α_K))_(e3b;b)    (19.21)

(Lemma 14.29 (d)), with the density |dt dx|, and H^(k,(α_I,α_+,α_K))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) likewise. On Ω, t_*∂_(t_*)
and r∂_x span 𝒱_b (Section 15.10.4). C^∞_b denotes the functions on a neighbourhood of Ω_* in M that are bounded with
all their b-derivatives. Multiplication by an element of C^∞_b is bounded on every H^((𝗍;k),w)_(e3b;b), with norm bounded
by finitely many of its C^∞_b-seminorms ((14.6) and the remark after it): the e3b-vector fields are
combinations of b-vector fields with smooth coefficients (Lemma 14.12), so b-smoothness gives uniform smoothness on
the e3b unit cells, and the b-derivatives of an element of C^∞_b lie in C^∞_b. By acting on extensions it is bounded on
the spaces (Ω_*)^(•,−). Powers ρ^a, a ≥ 0, of the functions (19.20) lie in C^∞_b.

#### 19.4.2 The statement

**Theorem 19.14** (Forward solutions of admissible operators, with tame estimates.) Let P_0 be ℵ-admissible
with sf-weight α_+ and sf-loss δ (Definition 15.32), let

    α_I < −1/2 + S̄,      α_+ < α_I − 1/2,    (19.22)

and let ℓ_I ∈ (0, 1/2], ℓ_+ ∈ (δ, 1], ℓ_K > ℵ. There are ε_0 > 0 and d ∈ ℕ such that the following holds for every
k ∈ ℕ₀ and every P admissible relative to P_0 of class ((0;k+d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) (Definition 15.36) with
‖P − P_0‖_((0;d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) < ε_0 (Definition 15.39, over Ω_*). For every

    f ∈ H^(k+d,(α_I+1,α_++2,0))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−)    (19.23)

there is exactly one u in ⋃_(s′ ≥ s_u, β_+, β_K ∈ ℝ) H^(s′,(2α_I,β_+,β_K))_e3b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) with Pu = f, the *forward
solution*; here s_u := inf 𝗌 − 2 for the order 𝗌 of Lemma 19.19, which depends only on P_0 and the weights. It
lies in H^(k,(α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−), and

    ‖u‖_(H^(k,(α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_b)
        ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(H^(k+d,(α_I+1,α_++2,0))_b)
               + ‖P − P_0‖_((0;k+d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) ‖f‖_(H^(d,(α_I+1,α_++2,0))_b)),    (19.24)

the norms over Ω_*, with C_k independent of P and f. For k ≥ 1 the map (P, f) ↦ u is continuous from the set of such P,
with the norm ‖P − P_0‖_((0;k+d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)), times the space (19.23), to
H^(k−1,(α_I−ς,α_+−δ−ς,−ℵ−ς))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−), for every ς > 0.

In the theorem, as throughout this chapter, "admissible" may be read as conditions (1) and (2) of Definition 15.36
alone: the proof does not use condition (3) (Lemma 19.16 and the convention after it). So the theorem applies to
every P with (1) and (2) of that class and the stated smallness. Only the restriction of P to Ω_*, over which the
smallness is measured, enters: the proof applies the results of Chapter 17, which concern an operator on Ω with its
norms over Ω, to the operator P^♭ of Lemma 19.17, which equals P on Ω_*, acts as P on the spaces of the
theorem, and has its norms over Ω bounded by those of P over Ω_*. So P may also be given on Ω_* only, with (1), (2) and
its norms over Ω_*; Pu then means P^♭u.

This is [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] in dimension 4 + 1. [Hin26c] states it with ℓ_+ > δ; the class of Definition 15.33 has
ℓ_+ ≤ 1. The conditions of [Hin26c] are those of (19.22), and the dimension enters through the densities
(Corollary 19.15) and through the indicial gap (Remark 19.33). In the theorem the time function t^♭ is built
with the exponent ℓ = ℓ_I, the weight of the class; Remark 19.34 allows any exponent in [ℓ_I, ½], under one
further smallness condition on the metric of P.

**Corollary 19.15** (The estimate with unweighted b-densities.) Put μ_b := |dt_* dx|/(t_* ⟨x⟩⁴), a smooth
positive b-density on M̃ near Ω̄ (Lemma 14.33), and

    b_I := α_I + 2,      b_+ := α_+ + 5/2.    (19.25)

Then (19.22) reads b_I < 3/2 + S̄ and b_+ < b_I, and P_0 is ℵ-admissible with sf-weight b_+ − 5/2. With μ_b,
(19.24) reads

    ‖u‖_(H^(k,(b_I,b_+−δ,−ℵ+1/2))_b(Ω_*,μ_b))
        ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(H^(k+d,(b_I+1,b_++2,1/2))_b(Ω_*,μ_b))
               + ‖P − P_0‖_((0;k+d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) ‖f‖_(H^(d,(b_I+1,b_++2,1/2))_b(Ω_*,μ_b))).    (19.26)

In terms of integrals, the square of the left side of (19.26) is equivalent to

    ∬_(Ω_*) |ρ_I^(−b_I) ρ_+^(−b_++δ) ρ_K^(ℵ−1/2) (t_*∂_(t_*), r∂_x)^(≤k) u|² dt_* dx/(t_* r⁴),

the power meaning all products of at most k of the fields, with the weights (19.20); the norms of f likewise.
This is [Hin26c, (11.6b)], with r⁴ for r³. Pointwise, for k ≥ 3, on Ω_* ∩ {r > r_0},

    |(t_*∂_(t_*), r∂_x)^(≤k−3) u|
        ≤ C_k (right side of (19.24)) ρ_I^(b_I) ρ_+^(b_+−δ) ρ_K^(−ℵ+1/2).    (19.27)

This is [Hin26c, (11.4)–(11.7)] in dimension 4 + 1; in dimension 3 + 1 [Hin26c] has b_I = α_I + 3/2, b_+ = α_+ + 2, the
density |dt_* dx|/(t_* r³) and the conditions b_I < 1 + S̄, b_+ < b_I.

#### 19.4.3 What is not proved in this chapter

Two further statements of [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] are not proved here: (a) is not used; (b) is proved later for the
stationary models that are used.

(a) [Hin26c] adds that, if the principal part of P is that of P_0, the theorem holds with Ω = cl_M{t_* ≥ 1} in place
of Ω_*, by local solvability between {t_* = 1} and {t^♭ = 1}. That region meets ℐ⁺ only at {t_* = 1}, where its two
boundary hypersurfaces meet, and the energy estimates of Chapter 17 are not proved on it. The later chapters do not use
the statement, as their operators are quasilinear (their principal parts vary).

(b) [Hin26c] allows P_0 to vary among small stationary perturbations of an ℵ-admissible P_1, and among the stationary
models of nearby parameters, with uniform constants. Theorem 17.26 is uniform in this sense (its last sentence), but
Theorem 19.12 and the ℵ-admissibility estimate (15.24) are proved, resp. assumed, for one P_0. Here P_0 is
fixed. For the stationary models 2L_b, b near b_0, which the later chapters use, the uniform version of
Theorem 19.12 is Theorem 29.23 and that of Theorem 19.14 is Theorem 29.24.

### 19.5 Preliminaries

Throughout, α_I, α_+, ℓ_I, ℓ_+, ℓ_K, ℵ and δ are as in Theorem 19.14, and

    δ′ := min(ℓ_+ − δ, ℓ_K − ℵ) > 0.    (19.28)

For an order function 𝗍 and k ∈ ℕ₀ we write, all over Ω_* with the spaces (Ω_*; E)^(•,−) of Section 19.4.1,

    X(𝗍;k) := H^((𝗍;k),(2α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_(e3b;b),        Y(𝗍;k) := H^((𝗍;k),(2α_I+2,α_++2,0))_(e3b;b),
    Y′(𝗍;k) := H^((𝗍;k),(2α_I+2,α_+−δ+2,−ℵ))_(e3b;b),   Z(𝗍;k) := H^((𝗍;k),(2α_I,α_+−ℓ_+,−ℓ_K))_(e3b;b).    (19.29)

As ρ_+, ρ_K are bounded on Ω, ‖·‖_(Y′) ≤ C‖·‖_Y and ‖·‖_Z ≤ C‖·‖_X (the weights of Y and X are the larger at every face,
δ < ℓ_+ and ℵ < ℓ_K). These are Hilbert spaces: each is a quotient of a closed subspace of a Hilbert space, the norm
((14.6)) being equivalent to the Hilbert norm of property (S3) of Section 14.3.

#### 19.5.1 The threshold for perturbations

**Lemma 19.16** (The threshold at ℐ⁺.) Let δ_S := (S̄ − 1/2 − α_I)/4 > 0. Let h_S be a fibre inner product
on E over ∂X such that the smallest eigenvalue of ½(S + S^(*h_S)) is at least S̄ − δ_S/2 on ∂X (Lemma 15.30),
pulled back to ℐ⁺ along its fibration over ∂X and extended independently of x_I, as the data of Definition 15.36 (2)
are. There is ε_1 > 0 with the following property. Let P be an operator with (1) and (2) of Definition 15.36, condition
(3) of Definition 15.36 not being assumed; put p_1 := S|_(∂X) + p̃_1 over ℐ⁺, with p̃_1 of (15.25) and S|_(∂X)
pulled back as in Definition 15.36; and let sup_(ℐ⁺∩Ω) |p̃_1|_(h_S) ≤ ε_1 (in particular, this holds if
‖P − P_0‖_((0;0),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) is small). Then for every α ≤ α_I:

(a) Re_(h_S) p_1 ≥ S̄ − δ_S on cl(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω), and the same holds for the extension P^ext of Lemma 17.2 on
t_* ∈ [1 − η_0, 1]; hence p̄_1 ≥ S̄ − δ_S and α < −1/2 + p̄_1;

(b) the results of Chapter 16 and Chapter 17 that assume the threshold α < −1/2 + p̄_1 at the weight α at ℐ⁺, namely
those resting on (16.3) and (16.17) and Lemma 17.8, Proposition 17.10, Proposition 17.12,
Proposition 17.14, Proposition 17.17, Proposition 17.19 and Theorem 17.26, hold for P, with constants depending on P
only through the norms named in them, h_S and δ_S.

*Proof.* (a) S|_(∂X) is independent of t_* and of x_I in the extension, so Re_(h_S) S ≥ S̄ − δ_S/2 on a neighbourhood
of cl(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω). As p_1 = S|_(∂X) + p̃_1, |Re_(h_S) p̃_1| ≤ |p̃_1|_(h_S), and the Seeley extension of
Lemma 17.2 multiplies sup norms by at most c_Σ := Σ_l |c_l|, ε_1 := δ_S/(2 + 2c_Σ) gives both claims. Every
eigenvalue μ of p_1 has an eigenvector v, and Re μ h_S(v, v) = Re h_S(p_1 v, v) ≥ (S̄ − δ_S) h_S(v, v); so p̄_1 ≥ S̄ −
δ_S, and p̄_1 − 1/2 − α ≥ S̄ − δ_S − 1/2 − α_I = 3δ_S > 0.

(b) These results are stated in Chapter 16 and Chapter 17 for operators with (1) and (2) of Definition 15.36,
condition (3) not being assumed: this is the standing hypothesis of Chapter 16 (Section 16.1.1, and Section 16.6
with b-regularity) and of Chapter 17 (Section 17.1.1), and Section 17.1.3 records how p_1 and p_0 enter the energy
estimates. So they hold for P, and it remains to show how their constants depend on the data of P at ℐ⁺. Their
proofs use p̄_1 only through a fibre inner product h_I with Re_(h_I) p_1 ≥ p̄_1 − δ′_I,
δ′_I := (p̄_1 − 1/2 − α)/4 (Proposition 16.14; (17.2), with Lemma 17.2 (iii) for 2δ′_I), and they use
that inequality only through its consequence

    4 Re_(h_I) p_1 − 2 − 4α ≥ 12δ′_I > 0    (19.30)

at the radial set R = ∂R_(ℐ⁺,out): in Proposition 16.14, where Q_ε ≥ 4(p̄_1 − δ′_I − 1/2 − α_I) = 12δ′_I; in
Lemma 17.8, where the coefficient of τ_0² is −2(2α + 1) + 4(p̄_1 − δ′_I) = 12δ′_I; and in Proposition 17.12, where
4A⁻¹(Re_(h_I) p_1)A − 2 − 4α ≥ 8δ′_I with 2δ′_I. The remaining first-order terms, Im p_1 and p_0, enter those proofs
without any smallness: they are kept as quadratic forms in the edge derivatives, absorbed by the exponential weight in
time, and p_0 by the Poincaré inequality (Section 17.1.3, Lemma 17.8). The commuted systems of Chapter 16 and
of Section 17.4 have the same p_1 ((17.11) and the paragraph after it), at the weights α − j/2 ≤ α. By (a),
h_S in place of h_I and δ_S in place of δ′_I satisfy (19.30) with 12δ_S, for every α ≤ α_I, so the proofs run
verbatim with (h_S, δ_S), and their constants depend on these instead of on (h_I, δ′_I). ∎

In [Hin26c], condition (3) of Definition 15.36, the triangular structure of p_1 and p_0, serves one purpose: a
block-diagonal fibre inner product making Im p_1 and p_0 small ([Hin26c, (8.4)]), a smallness which, as the proof of
(b) shows, is not used here.

Below, "admissible" for P and for the operators P_ε of Section 19.5.7 means (1) and (2) of Definition 15.36 together
with the smallness of Lemma 19.16, and every result of Chapter 16 or Chapter 17 is used in the sense of
Lemma 19.16 (b). Moreover, from here on P stands for the operator P^♭ of Lemma 19.17 built from the P of
Theorem 19.14, whose norms are taken over Ω_*. P^♭ is given on Ω; its norms over Ω are at most C_j times those of P
over Ω_*, with one representation at every j ((19.34)), and these factors enter the constants below;
and P^♭u = Pu for u in every space of Theorem 19.14, whose orders s′ ≥ s_u satisfy s′ ≥ 2 − d, as s_u ≥ −d′ − 2 and
d ≥ d′ + d″ with d″ = s_in ≥ 4 ((19.47), Lemma 19.19). So P^♭ has the forward solutions of P.

#### 19.5.2 The operator off Ω_*

Theorem 19.14 measures P − P_0 over Ω_*, while Chapter 17 works with an operator on Ω, its norms over Ω and its
extension from Ω (Lemma 17.2). The proof therefore replaces P on Ω ∖ Ω_* = Ω ∩ {t^♭ < 1}, a set of bounded times,
by an extension from Ω_*.

*Coordinates.* At fixed x, t^♭ is strictly increasing in t_* on {t_* ≥ ½, r ≥ r^♯}. Indeed t^♭ = C′(t_* + R̃(r)) on
{r ≤ Ct_*/2}; on {r ≥ r′_0 + 1}, the formula for d(t_*F(ρ_I)) in the proof of Lemma 15.35, with
d(t_*F₁) = A dt_* + B dr and d(t_*F₂) = C′(dt_* + dr), gives ∂_(t_*)t^♭ = F(θA/F₁ + (1 − θ)C′/F₂) > 0, as A > 0 where
θ > 0; and the two sets cover {t_* ≥ ½}, as C ≥ 4(r′_0 + 1) (Lemma 17.2 (iv)). As t^♭ ≥ C′t_*, (t^♭, x) are
coordinates on Ω, in which Ω_* = {t^♭ ≥ 1} and Ω ∖ Ω_* = {τ_1(x) ≤ t^♭ < 1}, τ_1(x) := t^♭|_(t_*=1). Put
Ω_2 := Ω ∩ {t_* ≤ 2/C′}, which contains Ω ∩ {t^♭ ≤ 2}. On Ω_2 the functions ∂_(t_*)t^♭, 1/∂_(t_*)t^♭ and V t^♭, for V a
b-vector field, lie in C^∞_b: near ℐ⁺, t^♭ = t_*(1 − (t_*/r)^ℓ) with (t_*/r)^ℓ conormal and ∂_(t_*)t^♭ ≥ ½ (as in the
proof of Lemma 19.22 (a)), and the rest of Ω_2 is compact. As ∂_(t_*) = (∂_(t_*)t^♭)∂_(t^♭), and a vector field
V = v^i(x)∂_(x^i) taken at fixed t_* is V taken at fixed t^♭ plus (V t^♭)∂_(t^♭), the b-vector fields over Ω_2 are
spanned over C^∞_b by ∂_(t^♭) and the r∂_(x^i), and the e3b-vector fields by ∂_(t^♭) and fields whose coefficients in
(t^♭, x) depend on x only: near ℐ⁺ the fields r∂_r = −½x_I∂_(x_I) and r^(−1/2)Z_(ij), which span the x_I∂_ω (with
x_I = r^(−1/2) as in Section 17.1.1, and the rotation fields Z_(ij) of Section 19.1.1), and the ∂_(x^i) elsewhere;
here and below, fields in x are taken at fixed t^♭. On Ω_2, x_I²(1 + r), ρ_+ and ρ_K are positive functions which,
with their inverses, lie in C^∞_b ((19.20), t_* lying in [1, 2/C′]); so each weight x_I^(2a)ρ_+^bρ_K^c is
(1 + r)^(−a) times a function of that kind.

*Seeley's operator in t^♭.* Let c_l, ε_l = 3^(−l) be the constants of Seeley's operator in the proof of
Lemma 17.3 (b), so that Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(−q) < ∞ and Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^q = 1 for q ∈ ℕ_0 (Section 19.5.6), and
c_Σ := Σ_l |c_l| as in the proof of Lemma 19.16; let χ_♭ ∈ C^∞(ℝ), 0 ≤ χ_♭ ≤ 1, equal 1 on [0, ¼] and 0 on
[½, ∞). For a function q on Ω_* put E_♭q := q on Ω_* and, in the coordinates (t^♭, x),

    (E_♭q)(1 − τ, x) := Σ_(l≥0) c_l χ_♭(τ/ε_l) q(1 + τ/ε_l, x)      on Ω ∖ Ω_*  (τ > 0).    (19.31)

E_♭q uses q only on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭ ≤ 3/2} ⊂ Ω_2, at the same x, and it commutes with multiplication by functions of x and
with vector fields in x whose coefficients depend on x only. At (1 − τ, x), ∂^j_(t^♭)E_♭q is
Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^j ∂^j_(τ′)(χ_♭(τ′) q(1 + τ′, x)) taken at τ′ = τ/ε_l; as χ_♭ = 1 near 0, it tends to ∂^j_(t^♭)q(1, x)
as τ ↓ 0, so E_♭q is C^j on Ω when q is C^j up to {t^♭ = 1}, and |∂^j_(t^♭)E_♭q| is at most Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(−j) times
the supremum over τ′ ∈ [0, ½] of |∂^j_(τ′)(χ_♭(τ′) q(1 + τ′, x))|. With the description of the b-vector fields and of
the weights on Ω_2, this gives, for every j and every weight w,

    ‖E_♭q‖_(C^((0;j),w)_b(Ω)) ≤ C_j ‖q‖_(C^((0;j),w)_b(Ω_*)),      |(E_♭q)(1 − τ, x)| ≤ c_Σ sup_(1≤t′≤3/2) |q(t′, x)|,
    (19.32)

with C_j depending only on j, w, t^♭ and χ_♭. For an operator Q = Σ_(|β|≤2) q_β ∂^β on Ω_*, ∂^β the derivatives in
the coordinates (t^♭, x), put E_♭Q := Σ_β (E_♭q_β)∂^β. If Q = Σ_γ q′_γ V^γ, the V^γ being products of at most two
vector fields whose coefficients in (t^♭, x) depend on x only, then E_♭Q = Σ_γ (E_♭q′_γ)V^γ, as E_♭ commutes with
multiplication by functions of x; and the principal symbol of E_♭Q is E_♭ applied to that of Q, at fixed components
of the covector in the coordinates (t^♭, x).

**Lemma 19.17** (The operator off Ω_*.) Let k ≥ 2, and let P be an operator on Ω_* with (1) and (2) of
Definition 15.36 there, of class ((0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)), with data p_0, p̃_1 on ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω_* = ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω (t^♭ = t_* on ℐ⁺),
with P̃ as in (15.26), and with ‖P − P_0‖_((0;0)), over Ω_*, small. Put P^♭ := P on Ω_* and

    P^♭ := P_0 + χ_I ½x_I²ρ_+²(2p̃_1 A + p_0) + E_♭P̃   on Ω ∖ Ω_*,   A := x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ_+∂_(ρ_+).    (19.33)

(a) P^♭ has (1) and (2) of Definition 15.36 on Ω, with the data p_0, p̃_1, and for every j ≤ k

    ‖P^♭ − P_0‖_((0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) ≤ C_j ‖P − P_0‖_((0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)),    (19.34)

the left side over Ω and the right over Ω_*, with C_j depending only on j, t^♭ and the weights. The representation of
P̃^♭ := P^♭ − P_0 − χ_I ½x_I²ρ_+²(2p̃_1A + p_0) built below is linear in that of P̃, so (19.34)
holds at every j with one representation.

(b) For a metric g′ write 𝗀′ for the matrix of x_I²ρ_+²g′ in a fixed e3b-frame, and |·| for the operator norm; let 𝗀,
𝗀^♭ and 𝗀_0 be those of the metrics g, g^♭ and g_0 of P, P^♭ and P_0. For every a ∈ [0, ½],

    sup_Ω x_I^(−2a)|(𝗀^♭)⁻¹ − 𝗀_0⁻¹| ≤ c_♭ sup_(Ω_*) x_I^(−2a)|𝗀⁻¹ − 𝗀_0⁻¹|,

with c_♭ ≥ 1 depending only on t^♭ and the frame.

(c) If P is given on Ω°, of class ((0;k)) there, then P^♭v = Pv on Ω° for every distribution v on Ω° supported in
{t^♭ ≥ 1} and lying in H^(s′)_loc, s′ ≥ 2 − k.

*Proof.* Ω ∖ Ω_* lies in Ω_2, as t_* ≤ t^♭/C′ < 1/C′ there.

(a) Let P̃ = Σ_j a_jP_j be the representation of Definition 15.39 (Definition 14.28), the set of the P_j enlarged, with
coefficients 0, by the products of at most two fields of a fixed finite set of e3b-vector fields spanning them over
C^∞(M̃). Let the V^γ be the products of at most two of ∂_(t^♭) and the fields above whose coefficients depend on x only
(the empty product being 1). By the description of the e3b-vector fields on Ω_2, there P_j = Σ_γ n_(jγ)V^γ and
V^γ = Σ_j m_(γj)P_j with n_(jγ) and m_(γj) in C^∞_b, the derivatives of C^∞_b-functions by e3b-vector fields lying in
C^∞_b. So P̃ = Σ_γ q′_γV^γ on Ω_* ∩ Ω_2, with q′_γ := Σ_j a_j n_(jγ), and E_♭P̃ = Σ_γ (E_♭q′_γ)V^γ. Let ψ ∈ C^∞(ℝ)
equal 0 on (−∞, 3/2] and 1 on [2, ∞); ψ(t^♭) ∈ C^∞_b by Lemma 19.22 (a). Then

    a^♭_j := ψ(t^♭) a_j + (1 − ψ(t^♭)) Σ_γ m_(γj) E_♭q′_γ

is a representation of P̃^♭ on Ω: on Ω_* it gives ψP̃ + (1 − ψ)Σ_γ q′_γV^γ = P̃, and on Ω ∖ Ω_*, where ψ = 0, it gives
Σ_γ (E_♭q′_γ)V^γ = E_♭P̃. The derivatives of order at most k of E_♭q′_γ are continuous across {t^♭ = 1}, so
(19.32), with the weight x_I²ρ_+² times that of the class, and Lemma 14.27 (c)–(d) for the products
with C^∞_b-functions give ‖a^♭_j‖_((0;j′)) ≤ C_(j′) max_i ‖a_i‖_((0;j′)) for j′ ≤ k. With the unchanged data p_0, p̃_1,
this is (2) and (19.34). For (1): the χ_I-term is of first order, so on Ω ∖ Ω_*
σ_2(P^♭) = G_0 + σ_2(E_♭P̃) = G_0 + E_♭(G − G_0). The metric g^♭ of P^♭ is therefore given there by
(g^♭)⁻¹ = g_0⁻¹ + E_♭(g⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹), E_♭ acting on the components in the coordinates (t^♭, x), or in any local frame whose
coefficients depend on x only. By (19.32), (g^♭)⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹ lies in
x_I²ρ_+²C^((0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω; S² ᵉ³ᵇT) with norm at most C_k times that of g⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹ over Ω_*, and the
Neumann series of the proof of Lemma 15.40 gives g^♭ ∈ 𝒢^((0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) on Ω, as
‖P − P_0‖_((0;0)) is small.

(b) On Ω ∖ Ω_*, in a local frame whose coefficients depend on x only, the components of (𝗀^♭)⁻¹ − 𝗀_0⁻¹, the matrix of
x_I⁻²ρ_+⁻²((g^♭)⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹), are x_I⁻²ρ_+⁻² times E_♭ of x_I²ρ_+² times those of 𝗀⁻¹ − 𝗀_0⁻¹. The second bound of
(19.32), the comparability on Ω_2 of x_I, ρ_+ and the weight x_I^(−2a) at (1 − τ, x) and at the points
(t′, x), t′ ∈ [1, 3/2], at which E_♭ evaluates, and the change to the fixed e3b-frame, by a matrix bounded on Ω_2 with
its inverse, give (b).

(c) In the coordinates (t^♭, x), P^♭ − P = Σ_(|β|≤2) q_β∂^β on Ω°, with q_β of class C^k vanishing on {t^♭ ≥ 1}, hence
with their derivatives of order at most k there. For φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω°), q_βφ vanishes on {t^♭ ≥ 1}; its translates
(q_βφ)(t^♭ + δ, x), δ > 0 small, have compact support in Ω° ∩ {t^♭ ≤ 1 − δ} and tend to q_βφ in C^k, hence in
H^k ⊂ H^(2−s′), as δ ↓ 0. As ∂^βv ∈ H^(s′−2)_loc is supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}, it pairs to 0 with each translate, so
⟨(P^♭ − P)v, φ⟩ = Σ_β ⟨∂^βv, q_βφ⟩ = 0. ∎

#### 19.5.3 Uniqueness

**Lemma 19.18** (Uniqueness on Ω_*.) Let P be P_0, or admissible with ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;0)) small
(Lemma 19.16, and the smallness of Proposition 17.14, d_0 depending on s′), and let α ≤ α_I and s′, β_+,
β_K ∈ ℝ. If u ∈ H^(s′,(2α,β_+,β_K))_e3b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) and Pu = 0, then u = 0. The same holds on a slab Ω_(1,T) for u
in its space H^(s′,2α)(Ω_(1,T))^(•,−) (Section 17.1.1).

*Proof.* The second claim is Proposition 17.14 (i), with Lemma 19.16 (b). For the first, let T > 2 and φ =
φ(t^♭) ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal to 1 on (−∞, T + 1] and to 0 on [T + 2, ∞). Then φ(t^♭) = φ̃(1/t^♭) with φ̃(y) := φ(1/y),
φ̃′ ∈ C_c^∞((0, ∞)), so φ(t^♭) ∈ C^∞_b by Lemma 19.22 (a) (with ε = 1; its proof uses nothing from this
section); the same holds for every function of t^♭ used below. If ũ extends u with support in {t^♭ ≥ 1}, then φũ is
supported in {1 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T + 2}, where t_* ≤ (T + 2)/C′, so ρ_+, ρ_K are bounded below there by (19.20), and
φũ ∈ H^(s′,(2α,0,0))_e3b. It extends u|_(Ω_(1,T)), which therefore lies in H^(s′,2α)(Ω_(1,T))^(•,−) and solves Pu = 0
there. So u = 0 on {t^♭ < T, r > r_0}, for every T. ∎

#### 19.5.4 The orders

Write T_ℋ := 1/2 + ϑ_ℋ, T_out := (−1 + ϑ_out)/2 and T_in := (−1 + ϑ^(3b)_in)/2 for the thresholds of
Definition 15.29, each in the fibre inner product chosen for its radial set. An order function is admissible for P_0
with weights a_+, a_K and margin η (Definition 15.44) if it has (2)–(5) of Proposition 15.43, which do not involve the
weights, and, near the three radial sets over K⁺,

    𝗍 > T_ℋ + η,      𝗍 + a_+ − a_K < T_out − η,      𝗍 + a_+ − a_K > T_in + η,    (19.35)

by (1)–(6) of Definition 15.29 with α_sf = a_+, α_K = a_K (the order being constant near each radial set).

**Lemma 19.19** (The orders.) Let m_0 := 3 + δ + ℵ. There is 𝗌 ∈ C^∞(ᵉ³ᵇS*_ΩM), admissible for P_0 with
weights α_+ − δ, −ℵ and margin m_0, and an integer s_in ≥ 4, such that 𝗌 = s_in over

    Ω_♮ := {t_* ≥ 1/2, r_0 − 2δ_0 < r ≤ r_0 + 4}    (19.36)

(with the extension of Section 17.3.2 below r = r_0), and 𝗌 ≤ s_in everywhere. Put 𝗌_0 := 𝗌 − 2. Then:

(a) 𝗌_0 < 𝗌 are admissible for P_0 with weights α_+ − δ, −ℵ and margin 0 (the hypothesis of Theorem 17.26 at the
weights α_+ − δ, −ℵ);

(b) 𝗌_0 and 𝗌 are each admissible for P_0 with weights α_+, −ℵ and margin 0, and with weights α_+, 0 and margin 1 (the
hypotheses of Theorem 19.12);

(c) 𝗌 and 𝗌 + 1 are slab orders (Section 17.3.2).

*Proof.* Proposition 15.43 with η := m_0 and the weights α_+ − δ, −ℵ is proved by the construction of Section 15.13.2,
𝗌 = s_in − (s_in − s_out)χ with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, in which s_in is any constant above a stated bound and the small constants
ε_I, ε_ι may be decreased before the others are chosen. Take s_in ∈ ℕ, s_in ≥ 4, and ε_I² < (2r_0 + 9)⁻¹,
(ε_ι δ_ι)⁻¹ > r_0 + 4, where δ_ι is the constant called δ in Section 15.13.2. Then 𝗌 ≤ s_in. On Ω_♮ ∩ {r ≥ r_0},
x_I² = t_*/(t_* + r) ≥ (1/2)/(1/2 + r_0 + 4) > ε_I², so ψ_0(x_I) = 0, and r < (ε_ι δ_ι)⁻¹, so χ_ι = 0 there (χ_ι is
supported in {ϱ < ε_ι δ_ι}, ϱ = r⁻¹); hence χ = 0 and 𝗌 = s_in. Below r = r_0, 𝗌 = s_in by its extension
(Section 15.13.2, the last lines of its definition of the values; Section 17.3.2).

(a), (b): (2)–(5) of Proposition 15.43 hold for 𝗌 − j, j ∈ ℤ, as for 𝗌 (a constant shift changes no derivative and no
constancy). For (19.35), let 𝗌 satisfy it with (a_+, a_K) = (α_+ − δ, −ℵ) and η = m_0. Then 𝗌 − j satisfies it
with weights (a′_+, a′_K) and the margins

    m_0 − j at ℋ⁺,      m_0 + j − (a′_+ − α_+ + δ) + (a′_K + ℵ) at R_out,
    m_0 − j + (a′_+ − α_+ + δ) − (a′_K + ℵ) at R_in.

For (a′_+, a′_K) = (α_+ − δ, −ℵ) these are m_0 − j, m_0 + j, m_0 − j, all ≥ 0 for j ∈ {0, 2}: this is (a). For
(α_+, −ℵ) they are m_0 − j, m_0 + j − δ = 3 + ℵ + j, m_0 − j + δ, all ≥ 0 for j ∈ {0, 2}. For (α_+, 0) they are m_0 −
j = 3 + δ + ℵ − j, m_0 + j − δ + ℵ = 3 + 2ℵ + j and m_0 − j + δ − ℵ = 3 + 2δ − j, all ≥ 1 for j ∈ {0, 2}: this is (b).

(c) Admissible order functions are slab orders, and 𝗌 + 1 has the same monotonicity and constancy (Section 17.3.2). ∎

The margin 2 + δ + max(1, ℵ) taken in the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] gives for 𝗌_0 the last margin
max(1, ℵ) − ℵ + 2δ, which is less than 1 when ℵ ≥ 1 and δ < 1/2; the margin m_0 = 3 + δ + ℵ suffices in every case.

Fix 𝗌, s_in and 𝗌_0 as in Lemma 19.19. Only 𝗌_0, 𝗌 and 𝗌 + 1 occur below; over Ω_♮ they equal the integers
s_in − 2 ≥ 2, s_in ≥ 4 and s_in + 1; in particular they are constant and positive integers near {r ≤ r_0}, which is the
hypothesis of the tame estimates (17.24) and (17.14).

#### 19.5.5 Variable orders that agree on a set

**Lemma 19.20** (Pseudolocality of the order.) Let 𝗍_1, 𝗍_2 be order functions (property (S8) of
Section 14.3) and U ⊂ M̃ open with 𝗍_1 = 𝗍_2 over U, and let 𝒞 ⊂ U be closed and φ ∈ C^∞_b with supp φ ⊂ U and φ = 1
near 𝒞. For every j ∈ ℕ₀, ν and weight w there is C with

    ‖v‖_(H^((𝗍_2;j),w)_(e3b;b)) ≤ C (‖v‖_(H^((𝗍_1;j),w)_(e3b;b)) + ‖v‖_(H^((−ν;j),w)_(e3b;b)))

for every v supported in 𝒞.

*Proof.* Weights are removed by conjugation ((14.6) and the remark after it). Let A_i ∈ Ψ^(𝗍_i)_e3b be
elliptic, so that ‖v‖_((𝗍_i;j)) is equivalent to ‖A_i v‖_((0;j)) + ‖v‖_((−ν;j)) ((S8); for the b-derivatives, (S10)
and Lemma 14.29 (a)). Let B ∈ Ψ^(−𝗍_1)_e3b with BA_1 = I − R, R ∈ Ψ^(−ν′)_e3b, ν′ large (the finite parametrix of
the proof of Lemma 14.21, at variable orders by (S8)). As v = φv,

    A_2 v = (A_2 φ B) A_1 v + A_2 φ R v.

Q := A_2 φ B ∈ Ψ^(𝗍_2−𝗍_1)_e3b has WF′(Q) ⊂ WF′(φ), over supp φ ((S5)). Let φ_1 ∈ C^∞_b with supp φ_1 ⊂ U and φ_1 = 1
near supp φ. Then (1 − φ_1)Q has empty operator wave front set, so it is residual; and φ_1 Q is the left quantization
multiplied by φ_1, whose symbol is φ_1 q with q the symbol of Q, of order 𝗍_2 − 𝗍_1 = 0 on supp φ_1, so φ_1 q ∈
⋂_δ S^0_(1−δ,δ) ((S8)), and φ_1 Q is bounded on H^((0;j)) ((S8), (S10)). Hence ‖A_2 v‖_((0;j)) ≤ C‖A_1 v‖_((0;j)) +
C‖v‖_((−ν;j)), A_2 φ R being of order sup 𝗍_2 − ν′ ≤ −ν. ∎

#### 19.5.6 An extension across {r = r_0} at every order of b-regularity

The quotient norm of H^((𝗍;k))(Ω_*)^(•,−) is attained by an extension that depends on k. A tame estimate bounds a low
and a high norm of one function, and so needs one extension that is nearly minimal for both. Away from {r = r_0} a
cut-off provides it (Lemma 17.15 (b)); at {r = r_0}, where Ω_* ends and no room is available, the following lemma
does.

Fix κ ∈ (0, 1/4] with r_0 − 2κ > r^♯ and r_0 + 4κ ≤ r^♮ (Lemma 17.2, (16.2)). On N_κ := {t_* > 1/2,
r_0 − 2κ < r < r_0 + 4κ}, t^♭ = C′(t_* + R̃(r)) with R̃ = r′_0 or R̃′ ∈ [0, 1] (Lemma 15.35 (c) and its proof;
Lemma 17.2 (iv)), so (t^♭, r, ω) are coordinates on N_κ, and C′t_* ≤ t^♭ ≤ t_* there. In them the e3b-vector
fields over N_κ are spanned by ∂_(t^♭), ∂_r, ∂_ω and the b-vector fields by t^♭∂_(t^♭), ∂_r, ∂_ω, with coefficients in
C^∞_b. Indeed, near K⁺ the e3b-fields are spanned by ∂_(t_*), ∂_x and the b-fields by t_*∂_(t_*), ∂_x
(Section 17.5.1), and ∂_(t_*) = C′∂_(t^♭), ∂_r|_(t_*) = ∂_r|_(t^♭) + C′R̃′∂_(t^♭), t_*∂_(t_*) = (C′t_*/t^♭)
t^♭∂_(t^♭), with C′t_*/t^♭ = t_*/(t_* + R̃) and C′R̃′/t^♭ in C^∞_b (b-derivatives in t^♭∂_(t^♭) of functions of t_*/t^♭
and of (t^♭)⁻¹ are bounded). On N_κ the weights x_I^(2a) ρ_+^b ρ_K^c are (t^♭)^(−c) times smooth positive functions with
bounded b-derivatives, and |dt dx| is a smooth positive multiple of |dt^♭ dr dω|.

Let c_l, ε_l = 3^(−l) be the constants of Seeley's operator in the proof of Lemma 17.3 (b): sin(πs/2) =
Σ_l c_l s^l, so that Σ_l |c_l| ε_l^(−q) < ∞ and Σ_l c_l ε_l^(−q) = sin(π3^q/2) = (−1)^q, that is Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^q = 1,
for all q ∈ ℕ₀. For w on {r > r_0} ∩ N_κ supported in {r < r_0 + 2κ} put ℰ_r w := w on {r > r_0} and

    (ℰ_r w)(t^♭, r, ω) := Σ_l c_l w(t^♭, r_0 + (r_0 − r)/ε_l, ω),      r < r_0,    (19.37)

which vanishes for r ≤ r_0 − 2κ.

**Lemma 19.21** (A simultaneous extension.) Let 𝗍 be an order function equal to a constant m ∈ ℕ₀ over Ω_♮
(as 𝗌 + j, j ≥ −s_in, is), and w a weight x_I^(2a) ρ_+^b ρ_K^c. There is a linear map ℰ, defined on
⋃_j H^((𝗍;j),w)(Ω_*; E)^(•,−), with ℰu supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}, ℰu = u on {r > r_0}, and, for every j ∈ ℕ₀,

    ‖ℰu‖_(H^((𝗍;j),w)_(e3b;b)) ≤ C_j ‖u‖_(H^((𝗍;j),w)(Ω_*;E)^(•,−)).    (19.38)

*Proof.* Let ψ = ψ(r) equal 1 for r ≤ r_0 + κ and 0 for r ≥ r_0 + 2κ, and ψ_− = ψ_−(r) equal 1 for r ≥ r_0 and 0 for
r ≤ r_0 − κ. For u with an extension ũ supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1} put

    ℰu := (1 − ψ) ũ + ℰ_r(ψu).

The first term does not depend on ũ: two extensions differ by a distribution supported in {r ≤ r_0}, where 1 − ψ = 0.
The second uses only u on {r > r_0}. So ℰ is well defined and linear, and ℰu = (1 − ψ)u + ψu = u on {r > r_0}.
Supports: (1 − ψ)ũ is supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}; ψu is supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1} ∩ N_κ (as t^♭ ≥ 1 implies t_* ≥ 1), and
ℰ_r acts at fixed t^♭, so ℰ_r(ψu) is supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1, r_0 − 2κ ≤ r ≤ r_0 + 2κ}.

*The first term.* ‖(1 − ψ)ũ‖_((𝗍;j),w) ≤ C_j ‖ũ‖_((𝗍;j),w) for every extension ũ; the left side being independent of
ũ, it is at most C_j ‖u‖_((𝗍;j),w), at every j at once.

*The second term.* For v supported in the set 𝒞_κ := {t^♭ ≥ 1, r_0 − 2κ ≤ r ≤ r_0 + 2κ}, compact in r,
Lemma 19.20 (with U the interior of Ω_♮, which contains 𝒞_κ with a neighbourhood φ as required, and 𝗍 against
the constant m, both ways) gives ‖v‖_((𝗍;j),w) ∼ ‖v‖_((m;j),w), the terms ‖v‖_((−ν;j)) being bounded by either side as
m ≥ 0 ≥ −ν. As m ∈ ℕ₀, the norm of (S3) is, on such v, equivalent to the differential norm

    D_(m,j)(v) := Σ_(i+|α|≤j) Σ_(p+|β|≤m) ‖(t^♭)^c (t^♭∂_(t^♭))^i ∂^α_(r,ω) ∂^p_(t^♭) ∂^β_(r,ω) v‖_(L²(|dt^♭ dr dω|)):

the H^m(ℝ⁵)-norm in each scaled chart is the sum of the L²-norms of up to m derivatives, the scaled coordinate fields and
the frame above span the same module over C^∞_b, the derivatives falling on the partition functions χ_α give
lower-order terms with bounded coefficients, and the weight and density are as described above (the mixed norm being
(14.6)). ℰ_r commutes with ∂_(t^♭), t^♭∂_(t^♭), ∂_ω and with multiplication by functions of t^♭; ∂_r^q ℰ_r w =
Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^q (∂_r^q w)(t^♭, r_0 + (r_0 − r)/ε_l, ω) on {r < r_0}, whose L²-norm there is at most Σ_l |c_l|
ε_l^(1/2−q) ‖∂_r^q w‖_(L²({r>r_0})); and for w smooth up to {r = r_0} the derivatives of ℰ_r w of every order match
across {r = r_0}, since Σ_l c_l (−ε_l⁻¹)^q = 1, so that ℰ_r w has no distributional jump terms there. By density of
such w in the norm D_(m,j) on {r > r_0},

    D_(m,j)(ℰ_r w) ≤ C_(m,j) D⁺_(m,j)(w),

D⁺_(m,j) denoting D_(m,j) with the integrals over {r > r_0}. For any extension ũ, ψ_−ψũ = ψu on {r > r_0} and ψ_−ψũ is
supported in 𝒞_κ, so

    D⁺_(m,j)(ψu) ≤ D_(m,j)(ψ_−ψũ) ≤ C ‖ψ_−ψũ‖_((m;j),w) ≤ C ‖ψ_−ψũ‖_((𝗍;j),w) ≤ C_j ‖ũ‖_((𝗍;j),w).

Taking the infimum over ũ at each j separately, and using ‖ℰ_r(ψu)‖_((𝗍;j),w) ≤ C ‖ℰ_r(ψu)‖_((m;j),w) ≤
C D_(m,j)(ℰ_r(ψu)), gives (19.38). ∎

The tame estimates (17.14) and (17.24) of Chapter 17 use this construction at the face {r = r_0}, at
every level of b-regularity at once, for right-hand sides whose order is constant and in ℕ₀ near {r ≤ r_0}.

#### 19.5.7 The family P_ε

Fix χ_0 ∈ C_c^∞([0, 2)) with 0 ≤ χ_0 ≤ 1 and χ_0 = 1 on [0, 3/2]. For ε ∈ (0, 1] put

    χ_ε := χ_0(1/(ε t^♭)),      χ̃_ε := 1 − χ_ε,      P_ε := χ_ε P_0 + χ̃_ε P = P_0 + χ̃_ε (P − P_0),    (19.39)

on {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ 1/2} (with P^ext of Lemma 17.2 for P there).

**Lemma 19.22** (The family.) (a) χ_ε = 0 on {t^♭ ≤ 1/(2ε)} and χ_ε = 1 on {t^♭ ≥ 2/(3ε)}. So P_ε = P on
{t^♭ < 1/(2ε)} and P_ε = P_0 on {t^♭ > 2/(3ε)}, open sets. Every function φ(1/(ε t^♭)) with φ ∈ C^∞(ℝ), φ′ ∈
C_c^∞((0, ∞)), lies in C^∞_b with seminorms bounded uniformly in ε ∈ (0, 1]; in particular χ_ε, χ̃_ε do.

(b) P_ε satisfies (1) and (2) of Definition 15.36, and for all d_0, j

    ‖P_ε − P_0‖_((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) ≤ C_j ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)),
    sup|p̃^ε_1| ≤ sup|p̃_1|,    (19.40)

with C_j independent of ε and P (and depending on d_0). In particular P_ε is admissible in the sense of
Section 19.5.1 when P is, with the same bounds.

*Proof.* (a) The first claims are 1/(εt^♭) ≥ 2, resp. ≤ 3/2. Let V be a b-vector field and ς := 1/(εt^♭); then Vς =
−ς V log t^♭. On {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ 1/2}, log t^♭ = log t_* + log(t^♭/t_*), log t_* = −log ρ_+ − log ρ_K by
(19.20), and t^♭/t_* ∈ [C′, 1] has bounded b-derivatives: near ℐ⁺ it is 1 − (t_*/r)^(ℓ_I) with (t_*/r)^(ℓ_I) =
(x_I²/(1 − x_I²))^(ℓ_I) conormal, in the transition region a smooth function of t_*/r on a compact range, and near K⁺ it
is C′(1 + R̃(r) ρ_+ρ_K) (Lemma 15.35 and its proof). So V log t^♭ ∈ C^∞_b, and by induction V_1 ⋯ V_q ς is ς times
an element of C^∞_b independent of ε. The b-derivatives of φ(ς) are sums of φ^((i))(ς) ς^i times such elements, i ≥ 1,
and φ^((i))(ς) ς^i is bounded as φ^((i)) has compact support in (0, ∞).

(b) *The metric.* σ_2(P_ε) = χ_ε G_0 + χ̃_ε G, so g_ε⁻¹ := g_0⁻¹ + χ̃_ε (g⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹), with g⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹ ∈ x_I² ρ_+²
C^((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) of norm ≤ C‖P − P_0‖ (proof of Lemma 15.40). By (a) and Lemma 14.27
(c)–(d), χ̃_ε (g⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹) has norm ≤ C_j ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;j)), and the Neumann series of Lemma 15.40 gives g_ε ∈
𝒢^((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) with ‖g_ε − g_0‖ ≤ C_j ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;j)): this is (1).

*The data at ℐ⁺.* On ℐ⁺, t^♭ = t_* (Lemma 15.35 (a)), and χ̃_ε|_(ℐ⁺) is bounded in C^∞_b(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω) uniformly in
ε. Put p^ε_0 := χ̃_ε|_(ℐ⁺) p_0 and p̃^ε_1 := χ̃_ε|_(ℐ⁺) p̃_1, in ρ_+^(ℓ_+) C^(j+d_0)_b(ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω) with norms ≤ C_j times
those of p_0, p̃_1; and |p̃^ε_1| ≤ |p̃_1| as 0 ≤ χ̃_ε ≤ 1. Let π be the projection of the product structure
[0, ε_π)_(x_I) × ℐ⁺ in which Definition 15.36 (2) extends the data independently of x_I; near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ it is compatible
with the corner, the coordinates on ℐ⁺ including ρ_+, so that ρ_+ ∘ π/ρ_+ is smooth and positive. Then

    P_ε − [P_0 + χ_I ½ x_I² ρ_+² (2p̃^ε_1 A + p^ε_0)] = χ̃_ε P̃ + χ_I ½ x_I² ρ_+² δ_ε (2p̃_1 A + p_0),
    δ_ε := χ̃_ε − χ̃_ε|_(ℐ⁺) ∘ π,    (19.41)

with A := x_I∂_(x_I) − 2ρ_+∂_(ρ_+) and P̃ as in (15.26). We show δ_ε ∈ x_I^(2ℓ_I) C^∞_b uniformly in ε. Let L :=
−log t^♭ and L_I := L|_(ℐ⁺) ∘ π. With ς_υ := ε⁻¹ e^(L_I + υ(L − L_I)), υ ∈ [0, 1],

    δ_ε = χ_0(ε⁻¹ e^(L_I)) − χ_0(ε⁻¹ e^L) = −(L − L_I) ∫_0^1 χ_0′(ς_υ) ς_υ dυ,

and the integral lies in C^∞_b uniformly in ε, by the argument of (a). Near ℐ⁺, −L = log t_* + log(1 − (t_*/r)^(ℓ_I));
the second term is (t_*/r)^(ℓ_I) times an element of C^∞_b, so it lies in x_I^(2ℓ_I) C^∞_b. The first is −log ρ_+ −
log(1 − x_I²) near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ (by (19.20), ρ_K = 1 − x_I²) and a smooth function at finite times; so log t_* −
(log t_*)|_(ℐ⁺) ∘ π is smooth (as log(ρ_+/ρ_+ ∘ π) is) and vanishes at x_I = 0, hence lies in x_I C^∞_b ⊂ x_I^(2ℓ_I)
C^∞_b, as 2ℓ_I ≤ 1. So δ_ε ∈ x_I^(2ℓ_I) C^∞_b uniformly. A is an e3b-vector field near ℐ⁺: it is a b-vector field
tangent to the fibres of ℐ⁺, the curves of constant ω (Definition 14.11). The extended p̃_1, p_0 lie in ρ_+^(ℓ_+)
C^((d_0;j))_(e3b;b) near ℐ⁺, b-regularity of order j + d_0 giving e3b-regularity of order d_0 and b-regularity of order
j (Lemma 14.12), and χ_I is supported where ρ_K is bounded below. By Lemma 14.27 (c)–(d), the right side of
(19.41) lies in x_I² ρ_+² C^((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) Diff²_e3b, with a representation of norm ≤ C_j
‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;j)): this is (2) and (19.40). ∎

Condition (3) of Definition 15.36 may fail for P_ε: the diagonal blocks of S|_(∂X) + χ̃_ε p̃_1 need not have real
spectrum when those of S|_(∂X) and S|_(∂X) + p̃_1 do. By Lemma 19.16 (b) it is not needed.

#### 19.5.8 Cut-offs, slabs and the weights at late times

**Lemma 19.23** (Cut-offs.) (a) Let T ≥ 2, φ ∈ C^∞_b with φ = 0 on {t^♭ ≥ T − 1}, and 𝗍, α, β_+, β_K
given. For u in the slab space H^((𝗍;k),2α)(Ω_(1,T); E)^(•,−), φu (extended by 0 to {t^♭ ≥ T}) lies in
H^((𝗍;k),(2α,β_+,β_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*; E)^(•,−), with norm at most C ‖u‖_(H^((𝗍;k),2α)(Ω_(1,T))^(•,−)), C depending on T, φ
and the orders and weights.

(b) For u ∈ H^((𝗍;k),(2α,β_+,β_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*; E)^(•,−), ‖u|_(Ω_(1,T))‖_(H^((𝗍;k),2α)(Ω_(1,T))^(•,−)) ≤ C_T
‖u‖_(H^((𝗍;k),(2α,β_+,β_K))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−)).

(c) For η ∈ (0, 1] let χ_η := χ_0(1/(η t^♭)) as in (19.39). Then ‖χ_η v‖ ≤ C‖v‖ in each of the spaces
(19.29), and

    ‖χ_η u‖_(Z(𝗍;k)) ≤ C_k η^(δ′) ‖u‖_(X(𝗍;k)),    (19.42)

with C, C_k independent of η.

*Proof.* (a) Let ṽ extend u, supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}, in H^((𝗍;k))_(e3b;b) with the weight x_I^(2α) only
(Section 17.1.1). Then φṽ is supported in {1 ≤ t^♭ ≤ T − 1}, where t_* ≤ (T − 1)/C′, so by (19.20)
ρ_+^(−β_+) ρ_K^(−β_K) φ lies in C^∞_b and φṽ lies in the weighted space with norm ≤ C‖ṽ‖. On {r > r_0}, φṽ = φu: the
difference of ṽ and any extension of u to Ω_* vanishes on {t^♭ < T, r > r_0}, and φ vanishes on a neighbourhood of
{t^♭ ≥ T}. Take the infimum over ṽ. (b) Multiply an extension by φ(t^♭) equal to 1 on {t^♭ ≤ T + 1} and 0 on {t^♭ ≥
T + 2}, as in Lemma 19.18. (c) The first claim is Lemma 19.22 (a). For (19.42): with the weights
(19.20), ‖v‖_(Z(𝗍;k)) = ‖m_Z v‖_(X(𝗍;k)) for m_Z := ρ_+^(ℓ_+−δ) ρ_K^(ℓ_K−ℵ), as the weights of Z and X differ by
these powers. On supp χ_η, t^♭ ≥ 1/(2η), and by (19.20), ρ_+ρ_K = t_*⁻¹,

    m_Z χ_η = η^(δ′) · ρ_+^(ℓ_+−δ−δ′) ρ_K^(ℓ_K−ℵ−δ′) · (η t_*)^(−δ′) χ_η.

The exponents are ≥ 0 by (19.28), so the middle factor is in C^∞_b; and (η t_*)^(−δ′) χ_η is in C^∞_b
uniformly in η: η t_* ≥ η t^♭ ≥ 1/2 on its support, V(η t_*)^(−δ′) = −δ′ (η t_*)^(−δ′) V log t_* with V log t_* ∈
C^∞_b, and χ_η is as in Lemma 19.22 (a). ∎

#### 19.5.9 The tame bound for P_ε − P_0 on Ω_*

By Definition 15.39 and Section 14.8.2, P − P_0 = χ_I ½ x_I² ρ_+² (2p̃_1 A + p_0) + P̃ with P̃ = x_I² ρ_+² Σ_q b_q Q_q,
Q_q in a fixed finite subset of Diff²_e3b and b_q ∈ C^((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b). Dropping the factor x_I^(2ℓ_I)
of the b_q (bounded) and dividing by ρ_K^(ℓ_K) on supp χ_I (where ρ_K is bounded below),

    P_ε − P_0 = x_I² ρ_+^(2+ℓ_+) ρ_K^(ℓ_K) Σ_q (χ̃_ε a_q) Q′_q,
    ‖χ̃_ε a_q‖_(C^((d_0;j))_(e3b;b)) ≤ C_j e_j,      e_j := ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)),    (19.43)

with Q′_q in a fixed finite subset of C^∞_b Diff²_e3b (the Q_q, χ_I A and χ_I), C_j independent of ε (Lemma 14.27
(c), Lemma 19.22 (a)).

**Lemma 19.24** (The tame bound.) Let 𝗍 be an order function equal to an integer m ≥ 2 over Ω_♮. There are
d_0 and d̃, depending only on 𝗍, such that for all k, ε and v ∈ Z(𝗍;k),

    ‖(P_ε − P_0)v‖_(Y(𝗍−2;k)) ≤ C_k (e_(d̃) ‖v‖_(Z(𝗍;k)) + e_k ‖v‖_(Z(𝗍;d̃))),
    ‖(P_ε − P_0)v‖_(Y(𝗍−2;k)) ≤ C_k e_k ‖v‖_(Z(𝗍;k)),    (19.44)

with e_j of (19.43) and C_k independent of ε and P.

*Proof.* Extend each a_q across {r = r_0} by Seeley's operator in r − r_0 (with (t_*, ω) as parameters), which is
bounded on C^((d_0;j))_(e3b;b) for every d_0, j at once (Lemma 17.2 (ii) and the proof of Lemma 17.15 (a)),
and multiply by ψ_Ω ∈ C^∞_b equal to 1 near {t^♭ ≥ 1, r ≥ r_0 − 2κ} and supported in {t_* > 1/2, r > r^♯}; call the
result a^♯_q, and A^♯ := x_I² ρ_+^(2+ℓ_+) ρ_K^(ℓ_K) Σ_q (χ̃_ε a^♯_q) Q′_q, an operator on M̃. With ℰ of
Lemma 19.21 for the weights of Z, A^♯ℰv is supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1} and equals (P_ε − P_0)v on {r > r_0}, so it is
an extension of it. The weight x_I² ρ_+^(2+ℓ_+) ρ_K^(ℓ_K) takes the weights (2α_I, α_+ − ℓ_+, −ℓ_K) of Z to (2α_I + 2,
α_+ + 2, 0), those of Y. Corollary 14.57, on M̃ with χ′ = χ = 1 and on weighted spaces ((14.6) and the remark
after it), with d_0, d̃ of Proposition 14.56 for the orders 𝗍 − 2, gives

    ‖A^♯ℰv‖_((𝗍−2;k)) ≤ C_k (max_q ‖χ̃_ε a^♯_q‖_((d_0;d̃)) ‖ℰv‖_((𝗍;k)) + max_q ‖χ̃_ε a^♯_q‖_((d_0;k)) ‖ℰv‖_((𝗍;d̃))),

the norms of ℰv with the weights of Z. By (19.38) at j = k and j = d̃ and by (19.43), this is the
first bound of (19.44). The second is the same with Lemma 14.31 (a) in place of Corollary 14.57 (no tame
structure being needed, any extension of v may be used). ∎

#### 19.5.10 Forward solutions of P_ε

**Lemma 19.25** (Forward solutions of the family.) Let k ∈ ℕ₀, ε ∈ (0, 1] and f ∈ Y(𝗌;k), and let P be
admissible, of class ((d_0;k),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) with ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;d)) below the threshold of Proposition 17.19 for the
slab order 𝗌 + 1 (d_0, d being its constants; by (19.40) the same then holds for P_ε). There is u_ε ∈ X(𝗌;k)
with P_ε u_ε = f; by Lemma 19.18 it is the forward solution.

*Proof.* Let T := 4/ε and χ′ := χ_(ε/4) = χ_0(4/(ε t^♭)), which is 0 on {t^♭ ≤ 2/ε} and 1 on {t^♭ ≥ 8/(3ε)}. By
Lemma 19.23 (b), f|_(Ω_(1,T+1)) ∈ H^((𝗌;k),2α_I+2)(Ω_(1,T+1))^(•,−). By Proposition 17.19 for P_ε at the slab
order 𝗌 + 1 (Lemma 19.19 (c), Lemma 19.22 (b); its smallness condition is on ‖P_ε − P_0‖_((d_0;d)) only),
with the right-hand side f given on the larger slab Ω_(1,T+1), the forward solution u_ini of P_ε u_ini = f on Ω_(1,T)
lies in H^((𝗌+1;k),2α_I)(Ω_(1,T))^(•,−). As 1 − χ′ = 0 on
{t^♭ ≥ T − 1}, Lemma 19.23 (a) puts (1 − χ′)u_ini in H^((𝗌+1;k),(2α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_(e3b;b)(Ω_*)^(•,−) ⊂ X(𝗌;k). The
commutator [P_0, χ′] = x_I² ρ_+² [L_0, χ′] (L_0 := x_I⁻² ρ_+⁻² P_0 ∈ Diff²_e3b on Ω, Lemma 15.25 (b)) is a
first-order e3b-operator whose coefficients are e3b-derivatives of χ′, in C^∞_b and supported in {2/ε ≤ t^♭ ≤
8/(3ε)}; by Lemma 19.23 (a) (with φ equal to 1 there and 0 on {t^♭ ≥ T − 1}),

    g := χ′f + [P_0, χ′] u_ini ∈ Y(𝗌;k),      supp g ⊂ {t^♭ ≥ 2/ε}.

By Theorem 19.12 at the order 𝗌 (Lemma 19.19 (b)), the forward solution v of P_0 v = g on Ω_* lies in X(𝗌;k).
On the slab Ω_(1,2/ε), P_0 v = g = 0, so v = 0 on {t^♭ < 2/ε} by Lemma 19.18. As P_ε − P_0 = χ̃_ε(P − P_0) has
coefficients vanishing on the open set {t^♭ > 2/(3ε)}, which contains supp v, P_ε v = P_0 v = g. On {t^♭ < T}, P_ε
u_ini = f, and [P_ε, χ′] = [P_0, χ′] as supp dχ′ ⊂ {t^♭ > 2/(3ε)}; so

    P_ε((1 − χ′)u_ini) = (1 − χ′)f − [P_0, χ′] u_ini,

and u_ε := (1 − χ′)u_ini + v ∈ X(𝗌;k) satisfies P_ε u_ε = f. ∎

### 19.6 Small b-regularity orders

This section is Step 1 of the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] in dimension 4 + 1.

#### 19.6.1 The constants

b-regularity controls e3b-regularity: as Diff^(d_0)_e3b ⊂ C^∞(M̃) Diff^(d_0)_b (Lemma 14.12) and by
Lemma 14.27 (a), ‖a‖_(C^((d_0;j))_(e3b;b)) ≤ C ‖a‖_(C^((0;j+d_0))_(e3b;b)), with weights; the data p_0, p̃_1 carry
j + d_0 b-derivatives in both classes. Hence, for P of class ((0;j+d_0),·),

    e_j = ‖P − P_0‖_((d_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) ≤ C ‖P − P_0‖_((0;j+d_0),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)).    (19.45)

Let d^E_0, d^E be the d_0 and d of Theorem 17.26 for (𝗌_0, 𝗌) at the weights α_+ − δ, −ℵ; d^S_0, d^S the largest of
those of Proposition 17.14, Proposition 17.17 and Proposition 17.19 for the slab orders 𝗌 and 𝗌 + 1; d^T_0, d̃ those
of Lemma 19.24 for 𝗍 = 𝗌; and d^U_0 the d_0 of Proposition 17.14 (i) at s′ = s_u := inf 𝗌 − 2. Put

    D_0 := max(d^E_0, d^S_0, d^T_0, d^U_0),      D_1 := max(d^E, d^S, d̃),
    e_j := ‖P − P_0‖_((D_0;j),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)),    (19.46)

    d := D_0 + D_1 + d′ + d″,      d′ := max(0, ⌈−inf 𝗌⌉),      d″ := s_in (= max(0, ⌈sup 𝗌⌉)).    (19.47)

Choose ε_0 > 0 so small that ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)) < ε_0, for the operator of Theorem 19.14 over Ω_*, makes e_j,
j ≤ D_1, for P^♭ over Ω ((19.34)), and hence (by (19.40)) the corresponding norms of every
P_ε, smaller than the thresholds of Lemma 19.16, of Lemma 15.35 (through
Lemma 15.40), of Theorem 17.26 at k ≤ D_1 and at d^E, of Proposition 17.14 and Proposition 17.17 at k ≤ D_1 and
Proposition 17.19 at d^S, and of Proposition 17.14 (i) at s′ = s_u (Lemma 19.18). Then e_(D_1) ≤ Cε_0 ≤ 1 for
every such P. All constants below depend on P only through ε_0, unless e_k appears explicitly.

#### 19.6.2 The uniform a priori estimate

**Proposition 19.26** (The uniform estimate.) For every k ≤ D_1 there are η_k ∈ (0, 1] and C_k such that
for every ε ∈ (0, η_k/8] and every u ∈ X(𝗌;k) with P_ε u ∈ Y(𝗌;k),

    ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k ‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;k)).    (19.48)

This is [Hin26c, (11.15)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* *(i) The global estimate.* By (17.23) of Theorem 17.26, for P_ε at the weights α_+ − δ, −ℵ with the
orders 𝗌_0 < 𝗌 (Lemma 19.19 (a); Lemma 19.16 and Lemma 19.22 (b) for the hypotheses on P_ε; [Hin26c,
(11.10)]),

    ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k (‖P_ε u‖_(Y′(𝗌;k)) + ‖u‖_(X(𝗌_0;k))) ≤ C_k (‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;k)) + ‖u‖_(X(𝗌_0;k))).    (19.49)

*(ii) Inversion of P_0.* By Lemma 19.24, second bound of (19.44) with 𝗍 = 𝗌, (P_ε − P_0)u ∈ Y(𝗌_0;k),
as u ∈ X(𝗌;k) ⊂ Z(𝗌;k) and 𝗌 − 2 = 𝗌_0. So P_0 u = P_ε u − (P_ε − P_0)u ∈ Y(𝗌_0;k). Let v be the forward solution of
P_0 v = P_0 u given by Theorem 19.12 at the order 𝗌_0 (Lemma 19.19 (b)); u − v ∈ X(𝗌_0;k) and P_0(u − v) = 0,
so u = v by Lemma 19.18, and ([Hin26c, (11.11)])

    ‖u‖_(X(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C_k ‖P_0 u‖_(Y(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C_k (‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;k)) + ‖(P_ε − P_0)u‖_(Y(𝗌_0;k))).    (19.50)

*(iii) The error near ι⁺ ∪ K⁺.* With χ_η of Lemma 19.23 (c), by (19.44) and (19.42) ([Hin26c,
(11.13)–(11.14)]),

    ‖(P_ε − P_0) χ_η u‖_(Y(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C_k e_k ‖χ_η u‖_(Z(𝗌;k)) ≤ C^((1))_k ε_0 η^(δ′) ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)),    (19.51)

with C^((1))_k independent of η and ε.

*(iv) The error at bounded times.* Let T_η := 2/η. 1 − χ_η vanishes on {t^♭ ≥ 2/(3η)} ⊃ {t^♭ ≥ T_η − 1}. For ε ≤ η/8,
1/(2ε) ≥ 4/η > T_η, so P_ε = P on Ω_(1,T_η) (Lemma 19.22 (a)), and u|_(Ω_(1,T_η)), which lies in the slab space by
Lemma 19.23 (b), is the forward solution of Pu = P_ε u there (Lemma 19.18). By (19.44),
Lemma 19.23 (a), Proposition 17.17 for P at the slab order 𝗌 ([Hin26c, Proposition 8.6]) and Lemma 19.23
(b),

    ‖(P_ε − P_0)(1 − χ_η)u‖_(Y(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C_k ‖(1 − χ_η)u‖_(Z(𝗌;k)) ≤ C_(k,η) ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;k),2α_I)(Ω_(1,T_η)))
        ≤ C_(k,η) ‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;k)).    (19.52)

*(v) Absorption.* Inserting (19.50)–(19.52) in (19.49),

    ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) ≤ C^((2))_k ε_0 η^(δ′) ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) + C_(k,η) ‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;k)),

C^((2))_k independent of η. Fix η_k ∈ (0, 1] with C^((2))_k ε_0 η_k^(δ′) ≤ 1/2. As ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) < ∞, it is absorbed. ∎

#### 19.6.3 The forward solution at small orders

**Proposition 19.27** (Existence at small orders.) Let k ≤ D_1 and f ∈ Y(𝗌;k). The forward solution u of
Pu = f exists, lies in X(𝗌;k), and ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k ‖f‖_(Y(𝗌;k)). This is [Hin26c, (11.16)–(11.17)] in dimension
4 + 1.

*Proof.* For ε ∈ (0, η_k/8] let u_ε ∈ X(𝗌;k) be the forward solution of P_ε u_ε = f (Lemma 19.25). By
(19.48), ‖u_ε‖_(X(𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k ‖f‖_(Y(𝗌;k)). X(𝗌;k) is a Hilbert space (Section 19.5), so a sequence
u_(ε_j), ε_j ↓ 0, converges weakly to some u ∈ X(𝗌;k), and ‖u‖ ≤ C_k ‖f‖ (weak lower semicontinuity of the Hilbert
norm, equivalent to the norm used). For φ ∈ C_c^∞(M° ∩ {r > r_0}), w ↦ ⟨w, φ⟩ is continuous on X(𝗌;k) (pair any
extension with φ; the result does not depend on the extension, Lemma 14.23). supp φ is compact in M°, so t^♭ is
bounded on it, and P_(ε_j)* φ = P* φ for j large (Lemma 19.22 (a)), P* the formal adjoint, whose coefficients
involve at most two derivatives of those of P (d ≥ 2). Hence

    ⟨u, P*φ⟩ = lim_j ⟨u_(ε_j), P_(ε_j)* φ⟩ = lim_j ⟨P_(ε_j) u_(ε_j), φ⟩ = ⟨f, φ⟩,

so Pu = f on {r > r_0}, both sides supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}. By Lemma 19.18, u is the forward solution. ∎

### 19.7 Large b-regularity orders and the tame estimate

This section is Step 2 of the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Proposition 19.28** (The tame a priori estimate.) For every k ∈ ℕ₀ there are η_k ∈ (0, 1] and C_k such
that for every ε ∈ (0, min(η_k, η_(D_1))/8], every P as in Theorem 19.14 and every u ∈ X(𝗌;k) with P_ε u ∈ Y(𝗌;k),

    ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k (‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;k)) + e_k ‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;D_1))),    (19.53)

with e_k of (19.46). This is [Hin26c, (11.19)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Proof.* For k ≤ D_1 this is (19.48). Let k > D_1, and write A_j := ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;j)), B_j := ‖P_ε u‖_(Y(𝗌;j));
A_k, B_k are finite. By Proposition 19.26 at D_1 (as ε ≤ η_(D_1)/8), A_j ≤ A_(D_1) ≤ C B_(D_1) for j ≤ D_1.

*(i) The tame global estimate.* By (17.24) of Theorem 17.26, for P_ε (its d = d^E ≤ D_1, and ‖P_ε −
P_0‖_((d^E_0;d^E)) small), with (19.40) and ‖·‖_(Y′) ≤ C‖·‖_Y,

    A_k ≤ C_k (B_k + ‖u‖_(X(𝗌_0;k)) + e_k (B_(D_1) + A_(D_1)))
        ≤ C_k (B_k + ‖u‖_(X(𝗌_0;k)) + e_k B_(D_1)).    (19.54)

*(ii) Inversion of P_0.* As in Proposition 19.26 (ii), ‖u‖_(X(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C_k (B_k + ‖(P_ε − P_0)u‖_(Y(𝗌_0;k))).

*(iii) The error, tamely.* With χ_η of Lemma 19.23 (c), the first bound of (19.44) (with e_(d̃) ≤
e_(D_1) ≤ Cε_0) and (19.42),

    ‖(P_ε − P_0) χ_η u‖_(Y(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C_k (ε_0 η^(δ′) A_k + e_k ‖χ_η u‖_(Z(𝗌;d̃)))
        ≤ C^((1))_k ε_0 η^(δ′) A_k + C_k e_k B_(D_1),

using ‖χ_η u‖_(Z(𝗌;d̃)) ≤ C A_(d̃) ≤ C B_(D_1). With T_η := 2/η as in Proposition 19.26 (iv), and Proposition 17.19
for P on Ω_(1,T_η) ([Hin26c, Proposition 8.9]) in place of Proposition 17.17, with the right-hand side Pu = P_ε u given
on the larger slab Ω_(1,T_η+1) (P_ε = P on {t^♭ < 1/(2ε)}, and 1/(2ε) ≥ 2T_η ≥ T_η + 2, as ε ≤ η/8 and η ≤ 1),

    ‖(1 − χ_η)u‖_(Z(𝗌;j)) ≤ C_(j,η) ‖u‖_(H^((𝗌;j),2α_I)(Ω_(1,T_η))) ≤ C_(j,η) (B_j + e_j B_(D_1))

for every j (Lemma 19.23, and ‖P_ε u‖_(H^((𝗌−1;d^S),2α_I+2)(Ω_(1,T_η+1))) ≤ C B_(D_1)); so, by
(19.44),

    ‖(P_ε − P_0)(1 − χ_η)u‖_(Y(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C_k (ε_0 ‖(1 − χ_η)u‖_(Z(𝗌;k)) + e_k ‖(1 − χ_η)u‖_(Z(𝗌;d̃)))
        ≤ C_(k,η) (B_k + e_k B_(D_1)).

*(iv) Absorption.* Collecting,

    A_k ≤ C^((2))_k ε_0 η^(δ′) A_k + C_(k,η) (B_k + e_k B_(D_1)),

with C^((2))_k independent of η; fix η_k with C^((2))_k ε_0 η_k^(δ′) ≤ 1/2 and absorb. ∎

**Proposition 19.29** (Existence with the tame bound.) For every k ∈ ℕ₀, every P as in Theorem 19.14
and every f ∈ Y(𝗌;k), the forward solution u of Pu = f lies in X(𝗌;k), and

    ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k)) ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(Y(𝗌;k)) + e_k ‖f‖_(Y(𝗌;D_1))).    (19.55)

*Proof.* As for Proposition 19.27, with Lemma 19.25 at the level k (which needs only the smallness of ‖P_ε −
P_0‖_((d^S_0;d^S))) and (19.53) for ε ≤ min(η_k, η_(D_1))/8; the right side of (19.53) with P_ε u_ε =
f does not depend on ε. ∎

### 19.8 Pure b-estimates, and the proofs of the theorem and its corollary

This section is Step 3 of the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] in dimension 4 + 1.

*The embeddings.* By Lemma 14.32, with weights, H^((𝗌;j+d′))_(e3b;b) ⊂ H^j_b, d′ = max(0, ⌈−inf 𝗌⌉). By
Lemma 14.29 (d), applied d″ times, and 𝗌 ≤ s_in = d″, H^(j+d″)_b = H^((0;j+d″))_(e3b;b) ⊂ H^((d″;j))_(e3b;b) ⊂
H^((𝗌;j))_(e3b;b), with weights. Both inclusions preserve supports, so they hold for the spaces (Ω_*)^(•,−) with the
same constants (an extension in the smaller space is one in the larger). With (19.21),

    ‖u‖_(H^(k,(α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_b(Ω_*)) ≤ C ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k+d′)),
    ‖f‖_(Y(𝗌;j)) ≤ C ‖f‖_(H^(j+d″,(α_I+1,α_++2,0))_b(Ω_*)).    (19.56)

*Proof of Theorem 19.14.* Let ε_0, d be as in (19.47) and Section 19.6.1, k ∈ ℕ₀, and P and f as in
the theorem. By (19.56), f ∈ Y(𝗌;k+d′), as k + d′ + d″ ≤ k + d. By Proposition 19.29 at the level k + d′ (for
which P is of class ((D_0;k+d′),·), as k + d′ + D_0 ≤ k + d), the forward solution u lies in X(𝗌;k+d′) and

    ‖u‖_(H^(k,(α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_b) ≤ C ‖u‖_(X(𝗌;k+d′)) ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(Y(𝗌;k+d′)) + e_(k+d′) ‖f‖_(Y(𝗌;D_1)))
        ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(H^(k+d)_b) + ‖P − P_0‖_((0;k+d)) ‖f‖_(H^d_b)),

the b-norms with the weights of (19.24), by (19.56) (D_1 + d″ ≤ d), (19.45) (k + d′ + D_0 ≤
k + d) and (19.34), the last bounding the norm of P^♭ over Ω by that of P over Ω_*. Uniqueness in the
stated class is Lemma 19.18 at s′ = s_u, whose smallness is among those fixing ε_0 (Section 19.6.1): an element
of the class lies in the space with s′ = s_u, and P, of class ((d^U_0;0),·) by (19.45) as k + d ≥ D_0 ≥ d^U_0,
acts on it as Proposition 17.14 (i) at s′ = s_u requires. Below s_u the smallness of Proposition 17.14 (i), whose d_0
depends on s′, is not implied by that of ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)), and Pu need not be defined; this is why the uniqueness class
is restricted to s′ ≥ s_u. The continuity is proved in Section 19.9. ∎

*Proof of Corollary 19.15.* By (19.20),

    x_I⁻⁸ ρ_+⁻⁵ ρ_K⁻¹ = ((t_* + r)/t_*)⁴ (t_* r/(t_* + r))⁵ ((t_* + r)/r) = t_* r⁴,

and |dt dx| = |dt_* dx| = t_* ⟨x⟩⁴ μ_b; so |dt dx| = c x_I⁻⁸ ρ_+⁻⁵ ρ_K⁻¹ μ_b near Ω with c = ⟨x⟩⁴/r⁴ smooth and positive
(the identity of the proof of Lemma 14.33). Hence L²(|dt dx|) = ρ_I² ρ_+^(5/2) ρ_K^(1/2) L²(μ_b) and
H^(k,(a_I,a_+,a_K))_b(|dt dx|) = H^(k,(a_I+2,a_++5/2,a_K+1/2))_b(μ_b) with equivalent norms (b-derivatives of the
weights being the weights times smooth functions). This turns (19.24) into (19.26); α_I < −1/2 + S̄ is
b_I < 3/2 + S̄, and α_+ < α_I − 1/2 is b_+ < b_I. Writing out the norms with the frame t_*∂_(t_*), r∂_x of 𝒱_b on Ω, and
⟨x⟩ ∼ r on Ω, gives the integrals. For (19.27), let ũ be an extension of u supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1}, of at
most twice the norm of u in the space on the left of (19.26); it reaches {r < r_0}, so (14.8), stated
for functions supported in Ω, does not apply to it, but the statement of Lemma 14.33 for the unweighted b-density
μ_b has no support condition. With d = k − 3 and the weights (2b_I, b_+ − δ, −ℵ + 1/2) it bounds the C^(k−3)_b-norm of
ũ with the weight x_I^(2b_I) ρ_+^(b_+−δ) ρ_K^(−ℵ+1/2) = ρ_I^(b_I) ρ_+^(b_+−δ) ρ_K^(−ℵ+1/2) by C times the norm of ũ in
H^(k,(b_I,b_+−δ,−ℵ+1/2))_b(M̃, μ_b), which is at most twice the left side of (19.26); restricting to
{r > r_0} gives (19.27). ∎

### 19.9 Continuous dependence

This section is Step 4 of the proof of [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Lemma 19.30** (Compactness.) Let k ≥ 1, w = (α_I, α_+, α_K), ς > 0 and w′ := (α_I − ς, α_+ − ς, α_K − ς).
The inclusion H^(k,w)_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) ↪ H^(k−1,w′)_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) is compact.

*Proof.* Extend w to the other boundary hypersurfaces of M̃ by the exponent 0, and let w″ be w lowered by ς at every
boundary hypersurface; near ℐ⁺ ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺ it is w′. The b-Sobolev spaces are those of the bounded geometry structure of
b-vector fields on M̃°, with the weights ρ^w as weight functions, and ρ^w/ρ^(w″) = ρ_tot^ς → 0 at infinity (ρ_tot a total
boundary defining function); so H^(k,w)_b(M̃) ↪ H^(k−1,w″)_b(M̃) is compact by (S3) of Section 14.3. Given a bounded
sequence u_j in H^(k,w)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−), take extensions ũ_j supported in {t^♭ ≥ 1} with ‖ũ_j‖ ≤ 2‖u_j‖. A subsequence
converges in H^(k−1,w″)_b(M̃). The closure of {t^♭ ≥ 1} meets ∂M̃ only in ℐ⁺ ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺ (Section 17.1.1); multiplying by
a cut-off in C^∞_b equal to 1 near {t^♭ ≥ 1, r ≥ r_0} and supported where w″ = w′, the restrictions converge in
H^(k−1,w′)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−). ∎

*Proof of the continuity in Theorem 19.14.* Let k ≥ 1, let P^((j)) → P and f^((j)) → f in the stated norms, with
‖P^((j)) − P_0‖_((0;d)) < ε_0 and ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)) < ε_0, and let u^((j)), u be the forward solutions. Write
X := X(𝗌;k+d′) and H := H^(k,(α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−).

*Bounds.* By the proof of Theorem 19.14 (Proposition 19.29 at the level k + d′, with (19.56) and
(19.45)), u^((j)) ∈ X and

    ‖u^((j))‖_X ≤ C_k (‖f^((j))‖_(H^(k+d)_b) + ‖P^((j)) − P_0‖_((0;k+d)) ‖f^((j))‖_(H^d_b)),

the b-norms with the weights of (19.24), with C_k independent of j, as the constants depend on the operator
only through ε_0 (Section 19.6.1). The right side is bounded in j, as f^((j)) converges in the space (19.23)
and ‖P^((j)) − P_0‖_((0;k+d)) ≤ ‖P^((j)) − P‖_((0;k+d)) + ‖P − P_0‖_((0;k+d)) is bounded. So the u^((j)) are bounded in
the Hilbert space X (Section 19.5).

*The limit equation.* Let a subsequence u^((j_m)) converge weakly in X to some ũ ∈ X. The inclusion X ⊂ H of
(19.56) is continuous, so u^((j_m)) ⇀ ũ also in H. Let φ ∈ C_c^∞(M° ∩ {r > r_0}). For ψ ∈ L² supported in
supp φ, w ↦ ⟨w, ψ⟩ is continuous on H (pair any extension with ψ; the weights are bounded above and below on supp φ,
which is compact in M°), and the u^((j)) are bounded in L² on supp φ. P^((j))* φ → P* φ in L², as the coefficients
converge in C² on supp φ (k + d ≥ 2). So

    ⟨ũ, P*φ⟩ = lim_m ⟨u^((j_m)), P^((j_m))* φ⟩ = lim_m ⟨f^((j_m)), φ⟩ = ⟨f, φ⟩,

and Pũ = f on {r > r_0}.

*Identification.* As 𝗌 ≥ inf 𝗌 > s_u = inf 𝗌 − 2,

    ũ ∈ X ⊂ H^(𝗌,(2α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_e3b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) ⊂ H^(s_u,(2α_I,α_+−δ,−ℵ))_e3b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−),

so ũ lies in the class in which Theorem 19.14 asserts uniqueness, and so does u. Both solve Pv = f, so ũ = u by that
uniqueness, which is Lemma 19.18 at s′ = s_u for P, whose smallness holds as ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)) < ε_0 (the proof
of Theorem 19.14).

*Convergence.* Every subsequence of (u^((j))) is bounded in X, so it has a further subsequence converging weakly in X,
and by what was just shown its limit is u. Hence u^((j)) ⇀ u in X, and so in H. By Lemma 19.30, the inclusion of
H in H^(k−1,(α_I−ς,α_+−δ−ς,−ℵ−ς))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) is compact, so u^((j)) → u in norm there (each subsequence has a
norm-convergent subsequence, whose limit is the weak limit u). ∎

### 19.10 Four remarks

**Remark 19.31** (Relaxed ℵ-admissibility.) Let P_0 be ℵ-admissible with margin d_ℵ ≥ 0 (the relaxed version
after Definition 15.32), and put d̄_ℵ := ⌈d_ℵ⌉ ∈ ℕ₀. Then Theorem 19.14 holds with d increased by d̄_ℵ, that is,
with d := D_0 + D_1 + d′ + d″ + d̄_ℵ in (19.47), the constants of Section 19.6.1 being taken for the orders
below, and those of the slab propositions (d^S_0, d^S) for the slab orders 𝗌 and 𝗌 + d̄_ℵ + 1.

Indeed, P_0 is then ℵ-admissible with margin d̄_ℵ: an order admissible with margin d̄_ℵ is admissible with margin d_ℵ,
so (1)–(2) of Definition 15.32 hold for it, and (3) bounds u at the order 𝗌 − d_ℵ, hence at the order 𝗌 − d̄_ℵ ≤ 𝗌 − d_ℵ.
The orders are shifted by the integer d̄_ℵ, and not by d_ℵ, because the tame estimates (17.24) and
(17.14) and the extension of Lemma 19.21 need orders that are constant integers near {r ≤ r_0}. Take 𝗌 as
in Lemma 19.19 with the margin m_0 + 2d̄_ℵ and with s_in ≥ 4 + d̄_ℵ (its proof allows every integer s_in above a
bound), and 𝗌_0 := 𝗌 − 2 − d̄_ℵ. Over Ω_♮ the orders 𝗌_0, 𝗌 − 2, 𝗌, 𝗌 + d̄_ℵ and 𝗌 + d̄_ℵ + 1 used below equal the
integers s_in − 2 − d̄_ℵ ≥ 2, s_in − 2, s_in, s_in + d̄_ℵ and s_in + d̄_ℵ + 1. The margins of Section 19.5.4 (with
m_0 + 2d̄_ℵ for m_0) show: 𝗌_0 < 𝗌 meet the hypotheses of Theorem 17.26; 𝗌 − 2 = 𝗌_0 + d̄_ℵ is admissible with
weights α_+, −ℵ and margin d̄_ℵ and with weights α_+, 0 and margin 1 + d̄_ℵ, so Remark 19.13 with margin d̄_ℵ gives
‖u‖_(X(𝗌_0;k)) ≤ C ‖P_0 u‖_(Y(𝗌−2;k)), which replaces (19.50), the error (P_ε − P_0)u lying in Y(𝗌 − 2;k) by
(19.44); and 𝗌 + d̄_ℵ is admissible with the same two pairs of weights and margins d̄_ℵ, 1 + d̄_ℵ (its upper
margin at R_out with weights α_+, 0 being m_0 + 2d̄_ℵ − d̄_ℵ − δ + ℵ ≥ 1 + d̄_ℵ), so Lemma 19.25 holds for
f ∈ Y(𝗌 + d̄_ℵ;k), with u_ini of order 𝗌 + d̄_ℵ + 1 and v ∈ X(𝗌;k) by Remark 19.13. The absorption in
Proposition 19.26 is unchanged, as 𝗌_0 + d̄_ℵ + 2 = 𝗌. In Section 19.8, f ∈ Y(𝗌 + d̄_ℵ;k+d′) needs
k + d′ + d″ + d̄_ℵ ≤ k + d, as 𝗌 + d̄_ℵ ≤ d″ + d̄_ℵ.

This is [Hin26c, Remark 11.2] in dimension 4 + 1. [Hin26c] raises the margin by d_ℵ only; the second shift is needed in
the existence step (Lemma 19.25, [Hin26c, (11.16)]), where Theorem 19.12 loses d_ℵ.

**Remark 19.32** (No loss of b-regularity.) The absorption in Proposition 19.26 and Proposition 19.28 uses
that Theorem 17.26 is lossless in the b-regularity: both u and P_ε u carry k b-derivatives. If it needed k + 1 on
P_ε u, the error (P_ε − P_0)χ_η u would be needed in Y(𝗌_0;k+1), which (19.44) bounds by u in Z(𝗌;k+1), and
(19.51) could not be absorbed. Once (19.24) holds, b-regularity alone describes the solution, which is
how the later chapters use it. This is [Hin26c, Remark 11.3].

**Remark 19.33** (The indicial gap.) (19.22) gives α_+ < α_I − 1/2 < −1 + S̄, and tf-admissibility
puts α_+ + 2 in the indicial gap (β_−, β_+) of P̂_0(0) (Definition 15.32 (2); in dimension 3 + 1 [Hin26c] has α_+ +
3/2). So Theorem 19.14 requires β_− < α_+ + 2 < 1 + S̄, in particular β_− < 1 + S̄ (the β_− < 1/2 + S̄ of [Hin26c,
Remark 11.4] in dimension 3 + 1). For the scalar wave operator, S = 0 and the gap is (0, 2) (Section 15.10.4), so α_+ ∈
(−2, −1) and α_I ∈ (α_+ + 1/2, −1/2): α_I = −1/2 − ε_I, α_+ = −1 − ε_+ with 0 < ε_I < ε_+ < 1. In dimension 3 + 1
[Hin26c, (12.7)] prints 0 < ε_+ < ε_I < 1/2, which contradicts α_+ < α_I − 1/2; with α_I = −1/2 − ε_I and α_+ = −1 −
ε_+ the condition is ε_+ > ε_I. This is [Hin26c, Remark 11.4] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Remark 19.34** (The exponent of the time function.) Let ℓ_♭ ∈ [ℓ_I, ½], and let t^♭ be the function of
Lemma 15.35 built for g_0 with ℓ = ℓ_♭ in place of ℓ_I, given on {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ ½} by the formulae of its proof
(Lemma 17.2 (iv)); let Ω_*, its slabs, the spaces of Section 19.4.1, the cut-offs of this chapter and the
operator P^♭ of Lemma 19.17 be built from this t^♭. Distances between metrics are measured in the norm of
(19.57) below, taken over the set named. Let ϵ_G > 0 be the threshold of Lemma 15.35 for g_0 and this t^♭,
taken so small that every metric g′ within ϵ_G of g_0 on a set U ⊂ {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ ½} has, at the points of U, the
properties (A) of the proof, with the r^♯, δ_♮ and η_0 of Lemma 17.2 (iv) depending only on g_0 and ℓ_♭; such ϵ_G
exists and depends only on g_0 and ℓ_♭, as the proof shows. There are K_♭ ≥ 1, depending only on t^♭ and on upper bounds
for x_I²ρ_+²g_0 and its inverse on {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ ½}, and η_♭ > 0, depending only on g_0 and ℓ_♭, such that
Theorem 19.14, also in the form of Remark 19.31, and Corollary 19.15 hold, with ε_0, d and C_k depending also
on ℓ_♭, for every P as there whose metric g satisfies in addition

    ‖g − g_0‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(2ℓ_♭,0,0))_(e3b)) < η_♭,    (19.57)

the norm being taken over Ω_* as in Theorem 19.14; the continuity statement holds on the set of such P. For
ℓ_♭ = ℓ_I, (19.57) follows from ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)) < ε_0 for ε_0 small (Lemma 15.40), and the remark is
the theorem. Moreover, the proof applies (A) only to g_0, to g on Ω_*, to metrics g′ within K_♭‖g − g_0‖ of g_0 on the
sets where they are used, ‖g − g_0‖ being taken over Ω_*, and to metrics g′ that the proof of Theorem 19.12 takes
within any prescribed distance of g_0; its other uses of t^♭ concern the function alone.

*Proof.* In Chapter 15–Chapter 19 and in Remark 20.5 the time function enters in two ways only, and ℓ_I is
otherwise the weight of the class.

(A) Through the timelike hypotheses of Lemma 15.35 and Lemma 17.2 (iv): for the metric g′ of an operator
considered, dt^♭ is past timelike at the points of Ω° ∪ Ω⁻_*, and dr is future timelike at those of
{r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮, t_* ≥ ½}, at which the operator is given. The settings of Section 15.12, of Chapter 16 and of
Section 17.1.1 ask this on Ω_* or on Ω, and Lemma 17.2 (iv) asks it on Ω⁻_* for P^ext; they obtain it from the
smallness of ε_P through Lemma 15.40 and Lemma 17.2 (ii), which gives it at the exponent ℓ_I only.

(B) Through the form of t^♭ given by Lemma 15.35 (a)–(c) and its proof, and through the constant C′ of (b).

*The threshold in (A).* The proof of Lemma 15.35 is pointwise: at a point it bounds g′⁻¹ − g_0⁻¹ by the norm of
g′ − g_0 at that point, and it orients g′ by continuity along g_0 + τ(g′ − g_0), τ ∈ [0, 1]. So its conclusions (1)
and (2) hold for g′ at every point of Ω at which g′ is within the threshold of that lemma of g_0, and so does (A) at
the points of Ω°. Three further facts give (A) elsewhere; each holds for every g′ within some ϵ′ > 0 of g_0, with ϵ′,
r^♯, δ_♮ and η_0 depending only on g_0 and ℓ_♭, and ϵ_G is taken at most ϵ′.

(A1) *Bounded radii.* On {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r′_0 + 1, t_* ≥ ½}, t^♭ = C′(t_* + R̃(r)), as C ≥ 4(r′_0 + 1), so
dt^♭ = C′((1 − R̃′)dt_* + R̃′dt) with dt = dt_* + dr. The proof of Lemma 15.35 gives g_0⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) ≤ −c_0 on
{r_0 ≤ r ≤ r′_0 + 1} ((H6)), g_0⁻¹(dt, dt) ≤ −½ on {r′_0 − 1 ≤ r ≤ r′_0 + 1} ((K1)) and g_0⁻¹(dr, dr) ≤ −c_1 on
{r_0 ≤ r ≤ r^♮} (its (1) with h = 0), with c_0, c_1 > 0, dt_* and dt past timelike and dr future timelike for g_0.
These are statements about the stationary g_0 on sets compact in x, so they hold at every t_*, and, with halved
constants, on {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r′_0 + 1} and on {r^♯ ≤ r ≤ r^♮ + δ_♮}, for r^♯ close to r_0 and δ_♮ small. On
{r ≤ r′_0 + 1} the factor x_I²ρ_+² and the weight are bounded above and below, so the norm bounds g′ − g_0 in supremum
in the frame dt_*, dx^i; for ϵ′ small the three bounds hold for g′ with the constants halved again, and dt_*, dt and dr
keep along g_0 + τ(g′ − g_0) the cones they have for g_0. So dt^♭, a positive combination of dt_* and, where R̃′ ≠ 0,
of dt, is past timelike for g′ there, and dr is future timelike.

(A2) *Near ℐ⁺.* With ρ := t_*/r (the ρ_I of the proof of Lemma 15.35), that proof bounds the coefficients of
g′⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ in its basis by C₁(ϵ + ρ^(1−ℓ_♭))ρ^(ℓ_♭), with ϵ the distance of g′ from g_0, using ρ_+ ≤ 1 only to bound
powers of ρ_+; as ρ_+ is bounded on {t_* ≥ ½}, the bound holds there with a constant C₁′ depending only on g_0, as in
the proof of Lemma 17.2 (iv). The estimate of the proof of Lemma 15.35 for g′⁻¹(d(t_*F₁), d(t_*F₁)) then
