*Proof.* (x∂_x − y∂_y)(x^z u) = x^z f; replacing (u, f, E, α) by (x^z u, x^z f, E + z, α + Re z) reduces to z = 0 with
α > β, which is where α + Re z > β is used.

*Step 1, at x = 0.* Let (w, ℓ), ℓ = k(E, w), with Re w = min Re E ≤ α, and x^w(log x)^ℓ v(y, q),
v ∈ H^(k,(F,β))_b([0, 2) × (−2, 2)^d), the corresponding term of f. By

    (x∂_x − y∂_y)(x^w(log x)^ℓ a(y, q)) = x^w(log x)^ℓ(w − y∂_y)a + ℓx^w(log x)^(ℓ−1)a,    (21.60)

the coefficient a of x^w(log x)^ℓ in u on {y ≥ ¾} (which exists by the a priori hypothesis) solves (w − y∂_y)a = v
there. Extend a to (0, 2) by solving this equation; (y∂_y − w)a = −v, and Lemma 21.33 in the variable y, whose
hypothesis β ≠ Re w is ours, gives a ∈ H^(k,(F∪̄{(w,0)},β))_b. Then ũ := u − χ(x)x^w(log x)^ℓ a satisfies the hypotheses
with E replaced by E ∖ {(w, ℓ)} at x = 0 and F by F ∪̄ {(w, 0)} at y = 0 (the cut-off contributes terms supported in
x ∈ [½, ¾], where the spaces of u and f have no condition at x = 0). Repeating over the finitely many (w, ℓ) ∈ E with
Re w ≤ α produces u₀ ∈ H^(k,E,(F∪̄E,β))_b near x = 0 with

    ũ := u − u₀:     (x∂_x − y∂_y)ũ =: f̃ ∈ H^(k,α,(E∪̄F,β))_b,     (1 − χ(y))ũ ∈ H^(k,α,∞)_b.    (21.61)

*Step 2, at y = 0.* For (w, ℓ), ℓ = k(E ∪̄ F, w), Re w ≤ β < α, let y^w(log y)^ℓ v(x, q), v ∈ H^(k,α)_b, be the term of
f̃. As (x∂_x − y∂_y)(y^w(log y)^ℓ a(x, q)) = y^w(log y)^ℓ(x∂_x − w)a − ℓy^w(log y)^(ℓ−1)a, Lemma 21.41
(Re w < α, empty index set at x = 0) gives a ∈ H^(k,α)_b with (x∂_x − w)a = v; subtract χ(y)y^w(log y)^ℓ a, descend in ℓ
and ascend in Re w. This produces ũ₀ ∈ H^(k,α,(E∪̄F,β))_b with (1 − χ(y))ũ₀ = 0 near y ≥ ¾ and u^♭ := ũ − ũ₀
satisfying

    (x∂_x − y∂_y)u^♭ =: f^♭ ∈ H^(k,α,β)_b,     (1 − χ(y))u^♭ ∈ H^(k,α,∞)_b.    (21.62)

*Step 3, the remainder.* It suffices to show u^♭ ∈ H^(k,α,β)_b, and to do so for k = 0: x∂_x, y∂_y, ∂_q commute with
x∂_x − y∂_y. With ψ ∈ C_c^∞([0, 1)) equal to 1 on [0, ¾],
(x∂_x − y∂_y)(ψ(y)u^♭) = ψf^♭ + yψ′(y)(1 − χ(y))u^♭ still lies in H^(0,α,β) and ψu^♭ vanishes near y = 1; and
(1 − ψ)u^♭ ∈ H^(0,α,∞). Multiplication by (xy)^(−α) commutes with x∂_x − y∂_y, so let α = 0 > β. Drop q. The solution
vanishing near y = 1 is, by integration along the characteristics xy = const,

    u^♭(x, y) = ∫_y^1 f^♭(xy/s, s) ds/s

(indeed x∂_x and y∂_y of the integral agree except for the boundary term −f^♭(x, y) from y∂_y). By Cauchy–Schwarz with
∫_y^1 s^β ds/s ≤ |β|⁻¹y^β, then t := xy/s at fixed (x, s) (so y ∈ (0, s) becomes t ∈ (0, x), dy/y = dt/t), and
∫_t^2 x^β dx/x ≤ |β|⁻¹t^β:

    ∬ y^(−2β)|u^♭|² (dx/x)(dy/y) ≤ |β|⁻¹ ∬ s^(−β) ∫_0^s y^(−β)|f^♭(xy/s, s)|² (dy/y)(ds/s)(dx/x)
        = |β|⁻¹ ∬ s^(−2β) ∫_0^x t^(−β)x^β |f^♭(t, s)|² (dt/t)(ds/s)(dx/x) ≤ |β|⁻² ∬ s^(−2β)|f^♭(t, s)|² (dt/t)(ds/s),

with x ranging over (0, 2). ∎

**Lemma 21.43** (A product of such operators.) Let z_1, …, z_p ∈ ℂ, repetitions allowed, and let Z be the
smallest index set with k(Z, z) ≥ #{j : z_j = z} − 1 for every z. Let E be an index set without logarithms
(k(E, w) = 0 for w ∈ π₁E), and suppose α + Re z_j > β and Re(w + z_j) ≠ β for all w ∈ π₁E and all j. If

    Pu = f ∈ H^(k,(E,α),(F,β))_b,     (1 − χ(2y))u ∈ H^(k+p,(E,α),∞)_b,     P := Π_(j=1)^p (x∂_x − y∂_y + z_j),
    (21.63)

then u ∈ H^(k,(E,α),((E+Z)∪̄F,β))_b, with E + Z the sum of Definition 21.31 (4).

For p = 1 this is Lemma 21.42 for log-free E (Z = {(z_1 + j, 0) : j ∈ ℕ₀} and E + Z = E + z_1). Iterating
Lemma 21.42 instead loses: once z and z + 1 both occur, the factor z + 1 meets the pair (z + 1, 0) that E + z has
put into the index set at y = 0 and returns (z + 1, 1), which (E + Z) ∪̄ F need not contain. The cure is to solve for
each coefficient in x at once.

*Proof.* Order the factors so that Re z_1 ≥ ⋯ ≥ Re z_p, and let G := (E + Z) ∪̄ F.

*Step 1, at x = 0, one coefficient at a time.* As E has no logarithms, (21.60) gives
P(x^w a(y, q)) = x^w Π_j(w + z_j − y∂_y)a exactly. For w ∈ π₁E with Re w ≤ α, let v_w ∈ H^(k,(F,β))_b be the
coefficient of x^w in f, and a_w that of u on {y ≥ 3/8}, which lies in H^(k+p) there by (21.63) and solves
Π_j(w + z_j − y∂_y)a_w = v_w there. Extend a_w to y ∈ (0, 2) as the solution of this ordinary differential equation (with
constant coefficients in log y, q a parameter). Put b_p := a_w and b_(i−1) := (w + z_i − y∂_y)b_i, so that b_0 = v_w and
(y∂_y − (w + z_i))b_i = −b_(i−1). Apply Lemma 21.33 in y for i = 1, …, p in this order: its hypothesis
β ≠ Re(w + z_i) is ours, and (1 − χ(y))b_i ∈ H^k because b_i is p − i derivatives of a_w on {y ≥ 3/8}. It gives
b_i ∈ H^(k,(G_i,β))_b with G_0 := F and G_i := G_(i−1) ∪̄ {(w + z_i, 0)} (Definition 21.31 (4)). The completion by
(21.49) at step i adds pairs only at w + z_i + j, j ≥ 1, whose real parts exceed those of every later
w + z_(i′). So no later raise meets a completion: the count at c is raised from k(F, c) once for each j with
w + z_j = c, to at most k(F, c) + k(Z + w, c) + 1 = k((Z + w) ∪̄ F, c), and a completion reaching c from c − j carries
at most the final count at c − j. By induction on Re c, G_p ⊂ (Z + w) ∪̄ F ⊂ G, the extended union being monotone in
each argument and Z + w ⊂ E + Z. Moreover (y∂_y)^i a_w, i ≤ p, is a linear combination of b_p, …, b_(p−i), so it too
lies in H^(k,(G,β))_b.

Let u₀ := Σ_w χ(x)x^w a_w, summed over w ∈ π₁E with Re w ≤ α; then u₀ ∈ H^(k,(E,α),(G,β))_b near x = 0, and
Pu₀ = Σ_w χ(x)x^w v_w + Σ_w [P, χ(x)](x^w a_w). Each commutator term is supported in x ∈ [½, ¾] and applies at most
p − 1 of the fields x∂_x, y∂_y to x^w a_w, so it lies in H^(k,∞,(G,β))_b by the last remark. Hence ũ := u − u₀
satisfies Pũ =: f̃ ∈ H^(k,α,(G,β))_b (f less its expansion at x = 0 lies in H^(k,α,(F,β))_b, and F ⊂ G), and
(1 − χ(2y))ũ ∈ H^(k+p,α,∞)_b, since the a_w are the coefficients of u on {y ≥ 3/8}, and on {¼ < y < 3/8}, where
1 − χ(2y) ≠ 0 too, the coefficient of u solves the same equation and equals a_w by uniqueness.

*Step 2, the factors one at a time with nothing at x = 0.* Put w̃_p := ũ and w̃_(i−1) := (x∂_x − y∂_y + z_i)w̃_i, so
that w̃_0 = f̃. For i = 1, …, p, Lemma 21.42 with the empty index set at x = 0 (its hypothesis on E is then void,
α + Re z_i > β is ours, and (1 − χ(y))w̃_i ∈ H^(k,α,∞)_b by the order k + p in (21.63)) gives
w̃_i ∈ H^(k,α,(∅∪̄G,β))_b = H^(k,α,(G,β))_b. So u = u₀ + w̃_p ∈ H^(k,(E,α),(G,β))_b. ∎

### 21.12 The Fourier transform with partial expansions

This section is [Hin26, Section 2.3] in dimension 4 + 1. In it ι names a boundary face, not an indicial root.

Let X := ℝ⁴_x (radially compactified), M := [ℝ̄_(t_*) × X̄; {±∞} × ∂X̄] with faces ℐ (the lift of ℝ̄ × ∂X̄), ι (the front
face) and K (the lift of ∂ℝ̄ × X̄), the b-densities |dt_*/⟨t_*⟩|, |dx/⟨x⟩⁴| and their product, and the spaces
H^(k,(E_I,β_I),(E_ι,β_ι),(E_K,β_K))_b(M) of Definition 21.31 (5) (orders and index sets at ℐ, ι, K, in this
order); the testing fields are compositions of ∂_(t_*), t_*∂_(t_*), ⟨x⟩∂_(x^j), j ≤ 4. These are the manifold and the
spaces of Section 20.8.1. At high frequencies H^(k,β,γ)_(b+)(±[½, ∞) × X) is the space of Section 20.8.1; at low
frequencies X^±_sc-b := [±[0, 1]_σ × X̄; {0} × ∂X̄] with faces scf, tf, zf, as in Section 20.8.1, carries the spaces
of Definition 21.31 (5) with partial expansions (index set (0, 0) at zf, coefficients in H_b(X), as in
(20.19)).

*The inputs in dimension 4 + 1.* The four statements [Hin26, (2.25a)–(2.26b)], called (T1)–(T4) here, are proved in
dimension 4 + 1 in Chapter 20:

(T1) ([Hin26, (2.25a)] and the matching statement of [Hin26, (2.25b)]): by Proposition 20.18 (1), for β_K ∈ (0, ∞) ∖ ℕ,
ε ∈ (0, 1), β_I ≥ β_ι − min(β_K, 1 − ε) and u ∈ H^(k+1,(β_I,β_ι,β_K))_b(M),
(ℱu)|_(±(0,1]) ∈ H^(k,(min(β_I,β_ι)−ε,β_ι−1,((0,0),β_K−1)))_b(X^±_sc-b), with the σ-Taylor coefficients of order
< β_K − 1 of the two signs equal.

(T2) ([Hin26, (2.25b)]): Proposition 20.18 (2), with the loss ℓ = ⌈(½ − min(β_K, β_ι − β_I))_+⌉.

(T3) ([Hin26, (2.26a)]): by Proposition 20.20 (1), with ℓ := ⌈(max(β_ι − β_scf, β_K) + ε − ½)_+⌉, if
v^± ∈ H^(k+ℓ,(β_scf,β_ι−1,((0,0),β_K−1)))_b(X^±_sc-b) have the same σ-Taylor coefficients, then
ℱ⁻¹v ∈ H^(k,(min(β_scf,β_ι)−ε,β_ι,β_K))_b(M), v := χ(σ)Σ_± 1_(±σ>0)v^±.

(T4) ([Hin26, (2.26b)]): Proposition 20.20 (2), whose high-frequency space carries the weight δ − 1 where that of
[Hin26] carries δ; the statement of [Hin26], with any δ, follows by renaming δ.

We also use, from the same proofs, that ℱ ∘ t_*∂_(t_*) = (−σ∂_σ − 1) ∘ ℱ (integration by parts:
∫ e^(iσt_*) t_*∂_(t_*)u = −∫(iσt_* + 1)e^(iσt_*)u, and ∂_σℱu = ℱ(it_*u)), and that ℱ commutes with operators in x. As
σ∂_σ commutes with 1_(±σ>0) and [σ∂_σ, χ(σ)] = σχ′(σ) is supported in ½ ≤ |σ| ≤ 1, we have, for v as in (T3) and any
z,

    ℱ⁻¹((σ∂_σ − (z − 1))w) = (−t_*∂_(t_*) − z)ℱ⁻¹w    (21.64)

for every tempered w, and (σ∂_σ − (z − 1))v = χ(σ)Σ_± 1_(±σ>0)(σ∂_σ − (z − 1))v^± + r with r supported in
½ ≤ |σ| ≤ 1. Such an r, if of class H^(k′,β_scf) there, has ℱ⁻¹r ∈ H^(k′−ℓ′,(β_scf−ε,J,J))_b(M) for every J, with a
loss ℓ′ = ℓ′(J) that grows with J (Proposition 20.20 (1)) and is finite for the finitely many J used, by (T3)
with the tf- and zf-weights taken arbitrarily large (r vanishes near tf and zf); we call such terms *harmless*.

**Lemma 21.44** ([Hin26, Lemma 2.24].) Let χ ∈ C_c^∞((−1, 1)) equal 1 near 0. The following are b-normal
vector fields: (1) −t_*∂_(t_*) at K; (2) −t_*∂_(t_*) − χ(r⁻¹)r∂_r at ι (defined as −t_*∂_(t_*) near r = 0);
(3) −χ(r⁻¹)r∂_r at ℐ; (4) σ∂_σ at zf; (5) σ∂_σ + χ(ρ)ρ∂_ρ at tf; (6) χ(ρ)ρ∂_ρ at scf; here r = |x|, ρ = |x|⁻¹,
ω = x/|x| ∈ 𝕊³.

*Proof.* In t_* > 1 let τ := t_*⁻¹, so −t_*∂_(t_*) = τ∂_τ. Near ι ∩ K: ρ_ι = ρ, ρ_K = τ/ρ; then τ∂_τ = ρ_K∂_(ρ_K)
and ρ∂_ρ = ρ_ι∂_(ρ_ι) − ρ_K∂_(ρ_K), so −t_*∂_(t_*) − r∂_r = τ∂_τ + ρ∂_ρ = ρ_ι∂_(ρ_ι), and near K° (coordinates τ, x)
−t_*∂_(t_*) = τ∂_τ with τ defining K. Near ι ∩ ℐ: ρ_ι = τ, ρ_I = ρ/τ; τ∂_τ = ρ_ι∂_(ρ_ι) − ρ_I∂_(ρ_I),
ρ∂_ρ = ρ_I∂_(ρ_I), so the field in (2) is ρ_ι∂_(ρ_ι) and −r∂_r = ρ_I∂_(ρ_I), and near ℐ° (coordinates t_*, ρ, ω)
−r∂_r = ρ∂_ρ. The same holds for t_* < −1. On X^±_sc-b near zf ∩ tf: ρ_zf = |σ|/ρ, ρ_tf = ρ, and
σ∂_σ = ρ_zf∂_(ρ_zf), ρ∂_ρ = ρ_tf∂_(ρ_tf) − ρ_zf∂_(ρ_zf), so σ∂_σ + ρ∂_ρ = ρ_tf∂_(ρ_tf); near zf°, σ∂_σ = ρ_zf∂_(ρ_zf)
with ρ_zf = |σ|. Near tf ∩ scf: ρ_scf = ρ/|σ|, ρ_tf = |σ|; ρ∂_ρ = ρ_scf∂_(ρ_scf) and
σ∂_σ = ρ_tf∂_(ρ_tf) − ρ_scf∂_(ρ_scf), so (5) is ρ_tf∂_(ρ_tf) there too, and (6) holds. In each case the field equals
the normal field of an adapted chart exactly, and the cut-offs act only away from the face. ∎

**Proposition 21.45** ([Hin26, Proposition 2.25] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let β_K ∈ (0, ∞) ∖ ℕ,
β_I, β_ι ∈ ℝ, and E_I, E_ι, E_K index sets with β_I, β_ι − 1 ∉ Re π₁E_I, β_ι ∉ Re π₁E_ι, β_K ∉ Re π₁E_K and
min Re E_K > 0.

(1) (Fourier transform.) Suppose

    β_I ≥ β_ι − β_K,     β_I > β_ι − min(1, min Re E_K).    (21.65)

Let ε > 0 be small and β̃_ι := min(β_ι, min Re E_ι − ε). There is l ∈ ℕ₀, depending only on the weights and index sets,
such that for u ∈ H^(k+l,(E_I,β_I),(E_ι,β_ι),(E_K,β_K))_b(M),

    (ℱu)|_(σ∈±[0,1]) ∈ H^(k, (E_I, min(β_I,β̃_ι)−ε), ((E_ι−1)∪̄E_I, β_ι−1), ((0,0)∪̄(E_K−1), β_K−1))_b(X^±_sc-b).
    (21.66)

(2) (Inverse Fourier transform.) Let χ ∈ C_c^∞((−1, 1)) equal 1 near [−½, ½], β_scf ∈ ℝ, and ε and β̃_ι as in (1).
There is l ∈ ℕ₀ such that if v^± ∈ H^(k+l, β_scf, (E_ι−1,β_ι−1), ((0,0)∪̄(E_K−1),β_K−1))_b(X^±_sc-b) satisfy, at zf,

    (σ∂_σ)^(ℓ_j+1)∂_σ^j v⁻ = (σ∂_σ)^(ℓ_j+1)∂_σ^j v⁺,     j = 0, …, ⌊β_K − 1⌋,     ℓ_j := k(E_K, j + 1),    (21.67)

then for v := χ(σ)Σ_± 1_(±σ>0)v^±,

    ℱ⁻¹v ∈ H^(k, min(β_scf,β̃_ι)−ε, (E_ι,β_ι), (E_K,β_K))_b(M).    (21.68)

The meaning of (21.67): by (σ∂_σ)∂_σ^j = ∂_σ^j(σ∂_σ − j), it says that the coefficient of σ^j in
(σ∂_σ − j)^(ℓ_j+1)v^±, which is log-free, is the same for both signs. The factor σ∂_σ − j occurs k(E_K, j + 1) + 1
times in R_zf below, as (z, m′) ∈ E_K with z − 1 = j.

*Proof.* We take ε so small, and decrease it if necessary, that none of min(β_I, β̃_ι) − ε,
β̃_K := min(β_K, min Re E_K − ε) and min Re E_ι − ε is an integer or the real part of an element of π₁E_I, π₁E_K
(finitely many conditions below any bound). We write E_(ι,≤) := {(z, m′) ∈ E_ι : Re z ≤ β_ι} and similarly E_(K,≤),
E_(I,≤).

*Part (1), E_I = ∅.* Then u ∈ H^(k+l,(β_I,β̃_ι,β̃_K))_b(M), and the hypotheses of (T1) hold for these weights:
β_I ≥ β̃_ι − β̃_K (if β̃_K = β_K by (21.65), and otherwise because
β_I > β_ι − min Re E_K ≥ β̃_ι − β̃_K − ε strictly, so for small ε), and β_I ≥ β̃_ι − (1 − ε) for small ε, as
β_I > β_ι − 1. They remain true when β̃_K is increased up to β_K or β̃_ι up to β_ι. So (T1) gives

    ℱu ∈ H^(k,(min(β_I,β̃_ι)−ε, β̃_ι−1, ((0,0),β̃_K−1)))_b(X^±_sc-b).    (21.69)

Let R_ι := Π_((z,m′)∈E_(ι,≤)) (−t_*∂_(t_*) − χ(r⁻¹)r∂_r − z). By the converse in Lemma 21.34 at ι
(Lemma 21.44 (2)) and (F1) at ℐ and K, R_ιu ∈ H^(k+l−|E_(ι,≤)|,(β_I,β_ι,β̃_K))_b, so for l large (T1) gives
ℱ(R_ιu) ∈ H^(k,(min(β_I,β_ι)−ε,β_ι−1,((0,0),β̃_K−1))). As ℱ(−t_*∂_(t_*)u) = (σ∂_σ + 1)ℱu and −r∂_r = ρ∂_ρ commutes
with ℱ, ℱ(R_ιu) = Π_(E_(ι,≤)) (σ∂_σ + χ(ρ)ρ∂_ρ − (z − 1))ℱu. Weakening its scf-weight to min(β_I, β̃_ι) − ε,
Lemma 21.34 at tf (Lemma 21.44 (5); its hypothesis is β_ι − 1 ∉ Re π₁(E_ι − 1); its a priori hypothesis
away from tf is (21.69)) gives

    ℱu ∈ H^(k,(min(β_I,β̃_ι)−ε, (E_ι−1,β_ι−1), ((0,0),β̃_K−1)))_b.    (21.70)

Now let R_K := Π_((z,m′)∈E_(K,≤)) (−t_*∂_(t_*) − z). By the converse in Lemma 21.34 at K (Lemma 21.44 (1))
and (F1), R_Ku ∈ H^(k+l−|E_(K,≤)|,(β_I,(E_ι,β_ι),β_K))_b, with the full weight β_K at K; (21.70) applied to it
(with β̃_K replaced by β_K, allowed above) gives

    Π_((z,m′)∈E_(K,≤)) (σ∂_σ − (z − 1)) ℱu = ℱ(R_Ku) ∈ H^(k,(min(β_I,β̃_ι)−ε, (E_ι−1,β_ι−1), ((0,0),β_K−1)))_b.

Apply in addition Π_(j≤⌊β_K−1⌋)(σ∂_σ − j), which annihilates the zf-terms of index set (0, 0) with real part ≤ β_K − 1,
so that the right side has empty index set at zf and weight β_K − 1; then integrate one factor at a time, in decreasing
order of real part as in Lemma 21.34, by Lemma 21.33 at zf (Lemma 21.44 (4); its hypotheses are
β_K − 1 ≠ j, true as β_K ∉ ℕ, and β_K − 1 ≠ Re(z − 1), true as β_K ∉ Re π₁E_K; the a priori hypothesis away from zf is
(21.70)). The index set obtained at zf is (0, 0) ∪̄ (E_K − 1) (below the weight β_K − 1): in this order each
exponent c is raised once per factor, from −1 to k((0, 0), c) + k(E_K − 1, c) + 1, and the completions by
(21.49) stay below that. Each one-factor step costs at most one derivative (as in Lemma 21.34),
absorbed in l. With (21.70) at tf and scf this is (21.66).

*Part (1), general E_I.* Let χ_K ∈ C^∞(M) equal 1 near K and 0 near ℐ. χ_Ku vanishes near ℐ, so it lies in the space
with E_I = ∅ and any ℐ-weight β′_I ≥ β_I; the case just proved, with β′_I so large that
min(β′_I, β̃_ι) = β̃_ι, gives (21.66) for it (its tf index set E_ι − 1 lies in (E_ι − 1) ∪̄ E_I). So assume u
vanishes near K; then E_K = ∅ and the K-weight is arbitrary: fix β_K ∉ ℕ, at least its given value (so
(21.65) persists), with β_K > β_ι + max(0, −min Re E_I), so that β_K − 1 + Re z > β_ι − 1 for every
z ∈ π₁E_I, as Lemma 21.43 needs. Let χ̃ ∈ C_c^∞(X) equal 1 on {|x| ≤ 8}. As u vanishes near K, χ̃u has compact
support in (t_*, x), so ℱ(χ̃u) is entire in σ with values in H^(k+l)_b of compact support in x: it lies in
H^(k+l,(∞,∞,((0,0),β_K−1)))_b(X^±_sc-b). Let R_I := Π_((z,m′)∈E_(I,≤)) (−χ(r⁻¹)r∂_r − z); by the converse in
Lemma 21.34 at ℐ (Lemma 21.44 (3)) and (F1), R_Iu ∈ H^(k+l−|E_(I,≤)|,(β_I,(E_ι,β_ι),β_K))_b, and the case
E_I = ∅ gives

    Π_((z,m′)∈E_(I,≤)) (χ(ρ)ρ∂_ρ − z) ℱu = ℱ(R_Iu) ∈ H^(k+l′, (min(β_I,β̃_ι)−ε, (E_ι−1,β_ι−1), ((0,0),β_K−1)))_b,

l′ := l − |E_(I,≤)| − l₀, l₀ the loss of the case E_I = ∅. Integrate from ρ ≥ 1/8, where ℱu = ℱ(χ̃u), towards ρ = 0.
Near zf, in ρ_zf = |σ|/ρ, ρ_tf = ρ, each factor ρ∂_ρ − z equals −(ρ_zf∂_(ρ_zf) − ρ_tf∂_(ρ_tf) + z), so the product is
± the operator of Lemma 21.43 with x = ρ_zf, y = ρ_tf, one z_j for each (z, m′) ∈ E_(I,≤) (so z occurs
k(E_I, z) + 1 times and Z is E_(I,≤) completed by (21.49), contained in E_I), (E, α) = ((0, 0), β_K − 1),
which has no logarithms, and (F, β) = (E_ι − 1, β_ι − 1). Its hypotheses hold: β_K − 1 + Re z > β_ι − 1 by the choice of
β_K; Re(w + z) ≠ β_ι − 1 for w ∈ ℕ₀, as β_ι − 1 ∉ Re π₁E_I and index sets are closed under adding ℕ₀; and on ρ ≥ ¼,
where 1 − χ(2ρ) ≠ 0, the a priori condition is ℱu = ℱ(χ̃u), of order k + l ≥ k + l′ + |E_(I,≤)|. As (0, 0) + Z = Z,
Lemma 21.43 gives the index sets ((0, 0), β_K − 1) at zf and (Z ∪̄ (E_ι − 1), β_ι − 1) ⊂
(E_I ∪̄ (E_ι − 1), β_ι − 1) at tf. Near scf, in ρ_scf = ρ/|σ|, ρ_tf = |σ|, ρ∂_ρ − z = ρ_scf∂_(ρ_scf) − z, and
Lemma 21.33 at scf, one factor at a time in decreasing order of Re z as in Lemma 21.34 (with min(β_I, β̃_ι) −
ε ≠ Re z by the choice of ε; the a priori condition on ρ_scf ≥ ½ holds in the zf chart, and the tf index set found there
is carried as the data at the other face), gives the index set (E_I, min(β_I, β̃_ι) − ε) there, the derivatives lost one
factor at a time absorbed in l. This is (21.66).

*Part (2), E_K = ∅.* Then (21.67) is the equality of the σ-Taylor coefficients of v^± of orders
≤ ⌊β_K − 1⌋ (as ℓ_j = −1), and v^± ∈ H^(k+l,(β_scf,β̃_ι−1,((0,0),β_K−1))), so (T3) gives

    u := ℱ⁻¹v ∈ H^(k+l−l₁,(β′_I,β̃_ι,β_K))_b(M),     β′_I := min(β_scf, β̃_ι) − ε,    (21.71)

l₁ the loss of (T3). Let R_tf := Π_((z,m′)∈E_(ι,≤)) (σ∂_σ + χ(ρ)ρ∂_ρ − (z − 1)). By the converse in
Lemma 21.34 at tf (Lemma 21.44 (5)), R_tf v^± ∈ H^(k+l−|E_(ι,≤)|,(β_scf,β_ι−1,((0,0),β_K−1)))_b, and the
σ-Taylor coefficients of R_tf v^± still agree: near zf, σ∂_σ multiplies the coefficient of σ^j by j and χ(ρ)ρ∂_ρ acts
on the coefficients in x, the same on both sides. By (21.64),
ℱ⁻¹(R_tf v) = Π(−t_*∂_(t_*) − χ(r⁻¹)r∂_r − z)u, while R_tf v equals χ(σ)Σ_± 1_(±σ>0)R_tf v^± up to harmless terms; so
(T3) gives

    Π_((z,m′)∈E_(ι,≤)) (−t_*∂_(t_*) − χ(r⁻¹)r∂_r − z) u ∈ H^(k+l−|E_(ι,≤)|−l₁,(β′_I,β_ι,β_K))_b(M),

and Lemma 21.34 at ι (Lemma 21.44 (2); β_ι ∉ Re π₁E_ι; a priori hypothesis (21.71)) gives
(21.68) with E_K = ∅.

*Part (2), general E_K.* Weakening the zf data to ((0, 0), β̃_K − 1) (the terms of E_K − 1, and their extended union
with (0, 0), have real part ≥ min Re E_K − 1 > β̃_K − 1) and using (21.67) for j ≤ ⌊β̃_K − 1⌋, where it is
the plain matching (as j + 1 < min Re E_K gives ℓ_j = −1), the case just proved gives
u ∈ H^(k+l−l₂,(β′_I,(E_ι,β_ι),β̃_K))_b(M). Let R_zf := Π_((z,m′)∈E_(K,≤)) (σ∂_σ − (z − 1)). It annihilates the zf-terms
of E_K − 1 below β_K − 1, so R_zf v^± ∈ H^(k+l−|E_(K,≤)|,(β_scf,(E_ι−1,β_ι−1),((0,0),β_K−1)))_b. Its coefficient of
σ^j, j ≤ ⌊β_K − 1⌋, is a nonzero constant (the product of j − (z − 1) over the factors with z − 1 ≠ j, the same for
both signs) times the coefficient of σ^j in (σ∂_σ − j)^(ℓ_j+1)v^±, so (21.67) is exactly the matching of the
Taylor coefficients of R_zf v^±. By (21.64) and the case E_K = ∅ (harmless terms aside),

    Π_((z,m′)∈E_(K,≤)) (−t_*∂_(t_*) − z) u = ℱ⁻¹(R_zf v) ∈ H^(k′,(β′_I,(E_ι,β_ι),β_K))_b(M),

and Lemma 21.34 at K (Lemma 21.44 (1); β_K ∉ Re π₁E_K) gives the index set (E_K, β_K) at K. With l the sum
of the losses met, this is (21.68). ∎

*Use in the following chapters.* Lemma 21.34 (testing) and Lemma 21.33 (integration) prove partial
expansions at the faces of M and X_sc-b; Lemma 21.35 and Lemma 21.36 give normal-operator expansions at sf,
where the indicial roots are those of Section 21.2.3; Lemma 21.40 and (21.58)–(21.59) give
the spectral families and the normal operator at sf of the stationary operators of Section 21.5;
Lemma 21.41–Lemma 21.43 integrate the transport operators at ι and ℐ; and Proposition 21.45 passes
between the time and the frequency sides. Every statement of Section 21.9–Section 21.12 is in b-densities, so the
numbers in the hypotheses (β_ι − 1, β_K − 1, (21.65)) are those of [Hin26]; the dimension enters only through
Proposition 20.18 and Proposition 20.20, which hold in dimension 4 + 1.

*Remarks on [Hin26, Sections 2.1–2.3].* Several statements above differ from their counterparts in [Hin26].
(1) [Hin26, (2.29)] uses ℓ = k(E_K, j) in place of ℓ_j = k(E_K, j + 1) in (21.67). The logarithmic terms of
v^± at σ^j come from (j + 1, ·) ∈ E_K, and R_zf contains σ∂_σ − j exactly k(E_K, j + 1) + 1 times; already for
E_K = (1, 0), where v^± carries a^± log|σ| at zf, the condition with ℓ = k(E_K, 0) = −1 at j = 0 asks v⁻ = v⁺ at zf,
which is meaningless for a logarithmically divergent function, while the proof needs a⁻ = a⁺. (2) In the proof of
[Hin26, Proposition 2.25 (2)] the zf-weight of R_zf v^± is β_K − 1, not β_K. (3) The commutator of σ∂_σ with χ(σ),
supported in ½ ≤ |σ| ≤ 1, is harmless ((21.64)). (4) The constant in Cauchy's formula in the proof of
Lemma 21.36 is ℓ!/(2πi). (5) [Hin26, Lemma 2.23] assumes α > β; the reduction to z = 0 needs α + Re z > β, and the
condition is necessary: for α + Re z < c < β, u := x^(−z)χ(xy)(xy)^c solves (x∂_x − y∂_y + z)u = 0, satisfies the a
priori condition with E = ∅, and is not in H^(k,α,β)_b, being y^c times a smooth nonvanishing function near y = 0,
x = ½. In Proposition 21.45 the weight β_K is free in the case where the condition is used (the function vanishes near
K) and is taken large enough. (6) For general E_I the proof of [Hin26, Proposition 2.25 (1)] integrates the factors of
R_I one at a time; once z and z + 1 both occur in E_(I,≤), the extended union returns (z + 1, 1), a logarithm the stated
index set need not contain. The stated set is right, and follows coefficient by coefficient in the zf variable
(Lemma 21.43). (7) The integrations in Lemma 21.34 are carried out in decreasing order of real part, on
which the result depends (for V(V − 1), integrating V first gives (1, 1)); and Lemma 21.35 and Lemma 21.36
reach the weight β only once the terms of F with real part β are solved first.

## 22. The dynamics of the Myers–Perry metrics near Tangherlini

This chapter verifies, for the Myers–Perry metrics g_b of Chapter 21 with b near the Schwarzschild–Tangherlini
parameter b₀ = (m₀, 0) and with the time function t_* of (21.30), the hypotheses on the metric that
Chapter 11, Chapter 12 and Chapter 15 leave open. They are: the radial structure of the horizon in (H3) and (H4)
(Section 11.1.3); the Lorentzian structure and the time function (H6) (Section 12.1.2); the normally hyperbolic
trapping (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) of (H7) and the global dynamics (H8) (Section 12.1.5); the decay (K1) and the r-normal
hyperbolicity (K3) of Section 15.1.1; and the uniformity in b that (H5), its extension in Section 12.1.5, and (K4)
ask. We write (Dyn) for all of them together. They concern the metric alone, and every operator whose principal symbol
is g_b⁻¹ ⊗ Id has them. The threshold in (H3) and the condition (Γ.4) of (H7) involve the subprincipal symbol; they are
hypotheses on the operator and are verified for each operator in Chapter 23, Chapter 24 and Chapter 25.

Section 22.2–Section 22.8 treat g_(b₀), five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini, where everything is explicit;
(H6) and (K1) are proved there for every b. Section 22.2 also proves three facts about the photon sphere and the
interior of Tangherlini (Proposition 22.3, Proposition 22.4, Proposition 22.5) that the theory of the
gauge potential operator uses as well. Section 22.9–Section 22.10 carry the horizon hypotheses to b near b₀; the
one new fact is that the horizon of g_b is a level set of the Kerr–Schild radius r_A, null by an exact identity.
Section 22.11–Section 22.16 treat the trapped set and the global dynamics near b₀. The tool is the separability
of the null geodesic flow of five-dimensional Myers–Perry, which holds in the Kerr–Schild coordinates of Chapter 21
written in spheroidal form; it plays the part of Carter's constant in [Hin26c, Section 4.2.3], and it gives the trapped
set and its stable and unstable hypersurfaces in closed form, smooth in b. Every object near b₀ is defined from A
directly, without an eigenframe of A, which is not continuous in A at A = 0 nor where the two spins have equal
modulus; frames are used only to compute.

The inner radius of the spacetime is a parameter r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁], and the radii of Section 11.1.1 are fixed in terms
of it in Definition 22.1. Every result of the chapter holds for every such r_♭, with constants that depend on it.

*Notation.* The black-hole mass is m, as in Chapter 15: b = (m, A), b₀ = (m₀, 0), R₁ = m₀^(1/2). Some letters keep
the meaning they have in Chapter 21 and carry a second one here, separated by context: H_(m,A) is the Kerr–Schild
function of Definition 21.15, while H_p is the Hamilton vector field of p, with H_p f = ∂_ζ p ∂_z f − ∂_z p ∂_ζ f;
F_A is the function of Definition 21.15, while F is the shift of a time function τ′ = τ − F(r); ψ is the profile of
t_* in Section 22.2–Section 22.8 and an azimuth in Section 22.11–Section 22.16; Φ is a momentum in
Section 22.11 and Φ_m the change of time of (21.27); E is a momentum, not a bundle; u := 1 − 2m r⁻² in
Section 22.5 and u := r² in Section 22.9 and Section 22.12; C is the squared angular momentum |η|²_g̸ at b₀
and, in estimates, a constant; q_± and q_(z₀) are the functions of (H3) and (Γ.4). The separation constant of
Section 22.11, which plays the part of Carter's constant, is written 𝔎, the letter 𝒦 being the Kretschmann scalar.
The Poisson bracket is {a, b} := H_a b. The polar angle on 𝕊³ is ϑ.

### 22.1 The radii

**Definition 22.1** (The radii and the parameters.) Let m₀ > 0, R₁ := m₀^(1/2) and the *inner radius*
r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] be as in Section 21.4, and let ℬ and b₀ := (m₀, 0) be the parameter set and the base point of
Definition 21.18. The radii of Section 11.1.1 are

    r₀ := r_♭,     δ₀ := min(R₁/16, r_♭/4),     r₂ := 7R₁/8,     r_e := 17R₁/16,    (22.1)

and r_h := R₁ is the radius of the horizon of g_(b₀). The *collar* is {r₀ − 2δ₀ ≤ |x| ≤ r₀}, and
X̃° = {|x| > r₀ − 2δ₀}. |b − b₀| denotes a fixed norm on ℝ × 𝔰𝔬(4), and every ball {|b − b₀| ≤ ε} used in this
chapter is taken with ε so small that it lies in ℬ. The time function is t_* := t − ψ(|x|) of (21.30), on
{|x| ≥ r₀ − 2δ₀}; a different lower limit in the integral defining ψ changes t_* by a constant, which changes none of
the statements below.

These radii are ordered:

    ½r_♭ ≤ r₀ − 2δ₀ < r₀ − δ₀ < r₀ < r₀ + δ₀ < r₂ < r_h < r_h + δ₀ ≤ r_e,

since δ₀ ≤ r_♭/4, r_♭ ≤ ½R₁ < 7R₁/8 and δ₀ ≤ R₁/16. Since χ_∞ = 0 on (−∞, 2R₁], ψ′ = 1 on [r₀ − 2δ₀, 2R₁]. For every
r_♭, r₀ = r_♭ is the inner radius of Section 21.4. At r_♭ = ½R₁ the radii are r₀ − 2δ₀ = 3R₁/8, r₀ − δ₀ = 7R₁/16,
r₀ = ½R₁, r₂ = 7R₁/8 and r_e = 17R₁/16. Every constant and every neighbourhood of b₀ chosen below may depend on r_♭;
nothing is claimed uniform in r_♭.

As r₀ − 2δ₀ ≥ ½r_♭, Lemma 21.19 applies on the whole of {|x| ≥ r₀ − 2δ₀}: for every b ∈ ℬ, g^KS_b is defined
there, smooth in (x, b), Lorentzian of signature (1, 4), with H_(m,A) > 0 and F_A ∈ (0, 1].

### 22.2 Schwarzschild–Tangherlini: coordinates and the spectral symbols

In Section 22.2–Section 22.8, b = b₀, and we write m := m₀, f := 1 − m r⁻², r_h := m^(1/2) = R₁,
r_ph := (2m)^(1/2) = √2 R₁ and g̸ for the round metric of 𝕊³. By (21.27) and Lemma 21.20,
g_(b₀) = Φ_m^* g^KS_(m,0), where Φ_m changes the time coordinate by a function of r = |x|, and
g^KS_(m,0) = η + m r⁻²(dt + dr)² (Proposition 21.17). With t_KS the time coordinate of g^KS_(m,0) and v := t_KS + r,

    g_(b₀) = −f dv² + 2 dv dr + r² g̸     on ℝ_v × {r > 0},    (22.2)

as a direct expansion shows: with H := m r⁻², −f dv² + 2 dv dr = −(1 − H) dt_KS² + 2H dt_KS dr + (1 + H) dr², and
this is η + H(dt_KS + dr)² − r²g̸. Every time function used here has the form τ = v − F(r) with F smooth: t_* is one,
since t_* − t_KS is a function of r ((21.27), (21.30)); and on {r > r_h} so is the static time
t_s := v − r_*, r_*′ = f⁻¹, in which g_(b₀) = −f dt_s² + f⁻¹ dr² + r² g̸.

*The symbols.* For a time function τ with dτ timelike, (12.1) defines G₀, τ₁ and g₀₀ by
G(−σ dτ + ζ) = G₀(ζ) + στ₁(ζ) + σ²g₀₀, with G := g⁻¹ and ζ ∈ T*X̃, and for z₀ ∈ {1, −1} we put
G_(z₀)(ζ) := G(−z₀ dτ + ζ). Write ζ = ξ dr + η with η ∈ T*𝕊³, and C := |η|²_g̸. From (22.2),
G^(vv) = 0, G^(vr) = 1, G^(rr) = f and G = r⁻²g̸⁻¹ on T*𝕊³; and dτ = dv − F′dr, so that −σ dτ + ζ =
−σ dv + (ξ + σF′) dr + η. Expanding,

    G₀ = fξ² + r⁻²C,     τ₁ = −2(1 − F′f)ξ,     g₀₀ = F′²f − 2F′,    (22.3)

    G^(F)_(z₀) = fξ² + r⁻²C − 2z₀(1 − F′f)ξ + F′²f − 2F′.

At F = 0 this is fξ² − 2z₀ξ + r⁻²C, regular for all r > 0. At F = r_*, on {r > r_h}, it is

    G^s := fξ² + r⁻²C − f⁻¹,    (22.4)

the static form, which does not depend on z₀ ∈ {1, −1}.

**Lemma 22.2** (Change of time function.) Let τ and τ′ = τ − F(r) be functions on a region U, and define
G_(z₀)(ζ) := G(−z₀ dτ + ζ) and G′_(z₀) likewise with τ′, whether or not the differentials are timelike.

(a) G′_(z₀)(ζ) = G_(z₀)(ζ + z₀ dF). The fibre translation T_F : (x, ζ) ↦ (x, ζ + z₀ dF(x)) is a symplectomorphism of
T*U that maps {G′_(z₀) = 0} onto {G_(z₀) = 0} and intertwines the Hamilton vector fields. It preserves fibre infinity
and C, and it moves ξ by z₀F′(r).

(b) If dτ and dτ′ are timelike with the same time orientation, T_F preserves the components Σ^±_(z₀) of
Lemma 12.1 (e), and so the future fields on corresponding components.

(c) At one covector ν = −z₀ dτ′ + ζ = −z₀ dτ + (ζ + z₀ dF), the functions q′_(z₀) := 2G(ν, dτ′) and
q_(z₀) := 2G(ν, dτ) satisfy q′_(z₀) = q_(z₀) − 2F′(r) G(ν, dr), and 2G(ν, dr) = H_(G_(z₀)) r. So q′_(z₀) = q_(z₀)
wherever H_(G_(z₀)) r = 0, in particular on an invariant set on which r is constant.

*Proof.* (a) −z₀ dτ′ + ζ = −z₀ dτ + ζ + z₀ dF. Translation by a closed 1-form is symplectic, and
G′_(z₀) = G_(z₀) ∘ T_F, so T_F maps Hamilton vector fields to Hamilton vector fields; no causal hypothesis enters.
(b) The covector is the same spacetime covector. For a null ν ≠ 0, G(ν, dτ) and G(ν, dτ′) are nonzero with the same
sign, since dτ and dτ′ are timelike with the same orientation. That sign fixes the component (Lemma 12.1 (e)).
(c) dτ′ = dτ − F′dr, and H_(G_(z₀)) r = ∂_ξ G_(z₀) = 2G(−z₀ dτ + ζ, dr). ∎

So every statement about the flow of G_(z₀) over a range of r may be proved in whichever coordinates are convenient
there: v near and inside the horizon, t_s on {r > r_h}, t_* near infinity. The components Σ^±_(z₀) are always those of
t_*; on {r > r_h} they are the same as those of t_s by (b), as dt_s and dt_* are co-oriented there:
G(dt_s, dt_*) = −f⁻¹ < 0. The differential of v is null (G^(vv) = 0), and v is used only as a symplectic chart, by (a).
Near ℋ, t_* = v − F with F′ > 0, since g₀₀ = F′²f − 2F′ < 0 at f = 0; so G(dv, dt_*) = −F′ < 0, dv lies in the closed
causal cone of dt_*, and q_v := 2G(ν, dv) = 2ξ has the sign of t_*'s q_(z₀) wherever it is nonzero. The future field
on Σ^±_(z₀) is ±H_(G_(z₀)) (Section 12.1.3). On {r > r_h}, in static variables, q_(z₀) = 2G(−z₀ dt_s + ζ, dt_s) =
2z₀f⁻¹, so only Σ^(z₀)_(z₀) occurs there, with future field 𝖧^♭ := z₀H_(G^s).

#### 22.2.1 The photon sphere and the interior

The next three propositions hold for five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini of any mass m > 0, with f, r_h and
r_ph as above. They are stated in the static variables of (22.4) outside the horizon and in the
ingoing chart (22.2) inside it. For functions of (r, ξ, C) and covectors ζ = −σ dt_s + ξ dr + η the Hamilton
vector field acts on functions of (r, ξ) as H_p = ∂_ξp ∂_r − ∂_rp ∂_ξ, C and σ being conserved by every Hamilton
vector field of a function of (r, ξ, C, σ).

**Proposition 22.3** (The radial potential and the interior.)

(a) On {r > r_h}, at points of {G^s = 0}, f²ξ² = 1 − CW with W := f r⁻².

(b) W′ = 2(2m − r²) r⁻⁵. On (r_h, ∞), W has exactly one critical point, a maximum W = (4m)⁻¹ at r² = 2m; W(r_h) = 0
and W → 0 as r → ∞.

(c) f is increasing on (0, ∞) and vanishes exactly at r_h. So g(∂_(t_s), ∂_(t_s)) = −f < 0 on {r > r_h}, and, in the
chart (22.2), g⁻¹(dr, dr) = f < 0 on {0 < r < r_h}: there dr is timelike.

(d) In the chart (22.2), g_(vr) = 1, −∂_r is a nowhere vanishing null vector field and g(∂_v, −∂_r) = −1.
For the time orientation in which ∂_v is future directed on {r > r_h}, −∂_r is future directed on all of {r > 0}, and
on {0 < r < r_h} the vector field g⁻¹(dr, ·) is future directed timelike, with dr(g⁻¹(dr, ·)) = f < 0: r decreases
along future causal curves there. The time orientation of Section 12.1.2, in which −∇t_* is future directed, is this
one.

*Proof.* (a) G^s = 0 means fξ² = f⁻¹ − r⁻²C; multiply by f. (b) W = r⁻² − m r⁻⁴, so W′ = −2r⁻³ + 4m r⁻⁵ =
2(2m − r²)r⁻⁵, which is positive on (r_h, r_ph) and negative on (r_ph, ∞). At r² = 2m, W = ½(2m)⁻¹ = (4m)⁻¹;
W(r_h) = 0 as f(r_h) = 0, and 0 < W < r⁻² for r > r_h. (c) f′ = 2m r⁻³ > 0, and f(r) = 0 iff r² = m. In the
static form g_(b₀) = −f dt_s² + f⁻¹ dr² + r² g̸ of Section 22.2, g_(t_s t_s) = −f. In the chart (22.2),
g⁻¹(dr, dr) = G^(rr) = f. (d) The coefficients are read off (22.2): g(∂_r, ∂_r) = 0 and g(∂_v, ∂_r) = 1.
On {r > r_h}, ∂_v is timelike (g(∂_v, ∂_v) = −f < 0), and a null vector with negative product with a future timelike
vector is future directed; −∂_r is null and nowhere zero on the connected chart, so it stays future directed by
continuity. On {0 < r < r_h},
X := g⁻¹(dr, ·) has g(X, X) = f < 0 and g(X, −∂_r) = dr(−∂_r) = −1 < 0, so X lies in the cone of −∂_r. A future
causal V then has dr(V) = g(X, V) < 0. Finally, on {r > r_h}, g(∂_v, −∇t_*) = −dt_*(∂_v) = −1 < 0 with −∇t_* future
timelike, so ∂_v is future directed in the orientation of Section 12.1.2. ∎

**Proposition 22.4** (The trapped set at frequency σ.) Let σ ∈ ℝ ∖ {0} and, on {r > r_h},
G(ζ) := g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) = fξ² + r⁻²C − σ²f⁻¹ for ζ = −σ dt_s + ξ dr + η.

(a) At points of {G = 0, ξ = 0}, H_G ξ = 2C(r² − 2m)/(f r⁵).

(b) The trapped set {ξ = 0, H_G ξ = 0} ∩ {G = 0} over {r > r_h} ([Hin26c, Definition 4.13]) is
{r² = 2m, ξ = 0, C = 4mσ²}, and C > 0 there.

(c) At every point of that set, dξ, d(H_G ξ) and dG are linearly independent.

(d) There H_G t_s = 2σ/f = 4σ, and the linearisation of the (r, ξ)-component of the vector field H_G/(H_G t_s), at
fixed C and σ, has the eigenvalues ±ν with ν := (2m)^(−1/2) = 1/r_ph.

*Proof.* We have H_G r = ∂_ξG = 2fξ and

    H_G ξ = −∂_r G = −f′ξ² + 2C r⁻³ − σ²f′f⁻²,     f′ = 2m r⁻³.    (22.5)

(a) At ξ = 0, G = 0 gives σ² = fC r⁻². Substituting, H_G ξ = C r⁻³(2 − r f′f⁻¹) = C(2f − r f′)/(f r³), and
2f − rf′ = 2 − 4m r⁻² = 2(r² − 2m)r⁻². (b) For r > r_h, f > 0, and C > 0 on {G = 0, ξ = 0} since σ ≠ 0 and
C = σ²r²f⁻¹. So H_G ξ = 0 there exactly when r² = 2m, where f = ½ and C = σ²·2m·2 = 4mσ². (c) Differentiating
(22.5) in r at fixed (ξ, C, σ),

    ∂_r(H_G ξ) = −f″ξ² − 6C r⁻⁴ − σ²(f″f⁻² − 2f′²f⁻³),     f″ = −6m r⁻⁴.

At r² = 2m, ξ = 0, C = 4mσ² = 2r²σ²: f = ½, f′ = r⁻¹, f″ = −3r⁻², so f″f⁻² = −12r⁻², 2f′²f⁻³ = 16r⁻², and
∂_r(H_G ξ) = −12σ²r⁻² + 28σ²r⁻² = 16σ²r⁻² ≠ 0. dξ has no dr component; dG has neither a dr nor a dξ component there,
as ∂_rG = −H_Gξ = 0 and ∂_ξG = 2fξ = 0, while ∂_C G = r⁻² ≠ 0. If a dξ + b d(H_Gξ) + c dG = 0, the dr component gives
b = 0, the dξ component a = 0, and then c = 0. (d) With ζ_t := −σ the dt_s-component of ζ, G contains −ζ_t²f⁻¹, so
H_G t_s = ∂_(ζ_t)G = −2ζ_t f⁻¹ = 2σf⁻¹ = 4σ at r² = 2m. The (r, ξ)-component of H_G, (2fξ, H_Gξ), vanishes at the set,
so the linearisation of the field divided by H_G t_s is the linearisation of (2fξ, H_Gξ) divided by 4σ. At fixed C and
σ that linearisation is δṙ = 2f δξ = δξ and δξ̇ = ∂_r(H_Gξ) δr = 16σ²r⁻² δr (the dξ-derivative of H_Gξ is −2f′ξ = 0),
with eigenvalues ±4|σ|r⁻¹. Divided by 4σ they are ±r_ph⁻¹. ∎

**Proposition 22.5** (The trapped set of the semiclassical family at z₀ = 1.) On {r > r_h} let
G₁ := G^s = fξ² + r⁻²C − f⁻¹ and Σ₁ := {G₁ = 0}.

(a) The only point (r, ξ, C) of Σ₁ over {r > r_h} at which H_(G₁) r = H_(G₁) ξ = 0 is r² = 2m, ξ = 0, C = 4m.

(b) Fix C = 4m. The linearisation at (r_ph, 0) of the (r, ξ)-component of H_(G₁) has the eigenvalues ±ν,
ν := 4(2m)^(−1/2). The functions φ_(s/u) := ξ ± (ν/(2f))(r − r_ph) vanish at (r_ph, 0), and their differentials there
are left eigenvectors: d(H_(G₁)φ_s) = ν dφ_s and d(H_(G₁)φ_u) = −ν dφ_u at (r_ph, 0). The same holds on Σ₁ near the
point, with C = r²(f⁻¹ − fξ²), whose differential in (r, ξ) vanishes there.

(c) {φ_u, φ_s} = ν/f = 2ν > 0 at (r_ph, 0), and ∂_C G₁ = r⁻² ≠ 0.

(d) With q₁ := 2g⁻¹(−dt_s + ζ, dt_s), ½q₁ = f⁻¹, which is 1/f(r_ph) = 2 at the point; for a time function t_s − F(r)
the value at the point is the same. So the constant β_Γ = ½ min_Γ |q₁| of (Γ.4) is 2, and ν/(4β_Γ) = (8m)^(−1/2), half
the rate (2m)^(−1/2) of Proposition 22.4 (d).

*Proof.* (a) H_(G₁) r = 2fξ vanishes for r > r_h only at ξ = 0; there G₁ = 0 gives C = r²f⁻¹, and
H_(G₁) ξ = −∂_rG₁ = −f′f⁻² + 2Cr⁻³ = (2f − rf′)/(f² r) = 2(r² − 2m)/(f² r³), which vanishes only at r² = 2m; then
C = 2m·2 = 4m. This is Proposition 22.4 (a)–(b) at σ = 1. (b) By Proposition 22.4 at σ = 1, the linearisation
is δṙ = δξ, δξ̇ = 16 r_ph⁻² δr, with eigenvalues ±4r_ph⁻¹ = ±ν. For a function φ vanishing at the zero p of a vector
field V, d(Vφ)_p = dφ_p ∘ DV_p. Here dφ_(s/u) = dξ ± ν dr at p, as f(r_ph) = ½ and (r − r_ph) vanishes at p.
The linearisation maps (δr, δξ) to (δξ, ν²δr), as 16r_ph⁻² = ν², and dξ ± ν dr applied to (δξ, ν²δr) gives
ν²δr ± νδξ = ±ν(δξ ± νδr). On Σ₁, ∂_ξC = −2r²fξ = 0 and
∂_rC = r(2f − rf′)f⁻² = 0 at p, so the linearisation on Σ₁ in the coordinates (r, ξ) is the one at fixed C.
(c) At p, ∂_ξφ_(s/u) = 1 and ∂_rφ_(s/u) = ±ν/(2f), the term with the derivative of f⁻¹ vanishing with r − r_ph. So
{φ_u, φ_s} = ∂_ξφ_u ∂_rφ_s − ∂_rφ_u ∂_ξφ_s = ν/(2f) + ν/(2f) = ν/f = 2ν. ∂_CG₁ = r⁻² by inspection. (d) In static
variables g⁻¹(dt_s, dt_s) = −f⁻¹ and g⁻¹(dt_s, dr) = 0 = g⁻¹(dt_s, η), so q₁ = 2·(−1)(−f⁻¹) = 2f⁻¹. For t_s − F(r),
Lemma 22.2 (c) gives the same value where H_(G₁) r = 0, in particular at p. Finally ν/8 = ½(2m)^(−1/2) =
(8m)^(−1/2). ∎

The functions φ_(s/u) of Proposition 22.5 are linearisations at Γ. The hypotheses (Γ.1)–(Γ.2) ask for exact
invariant hypersurfaces; for Tangherlini they are the two branches fξ = ±(1 − 2m r⁻²) of {C = 4m} ∩ Σ₁, with the
exact rates of (22.8) below.

### 22.3 The Lorentzian structure and the decay

**Lemma 22.6** ((H6) and (K1) for every b.) Let b = (m, A) ∈ ℬ, the parameter set of
Definition 21.18. With τ = t_*: g_b is a smooth Lorentzian metric of signature (1, 4) on
ℝ × {|x| ≥ r₀ − 2δ₀} (the closure of X̃°; (H6) uses X̃° = {r > r₀ − 2δ₀}) with t_*-independent components,
g₀₀ = g_b⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) < 0, and G₀, τ₁, g₀₀ given by (12.1). On {r > 3R₁} the components of g_b − ḡ in the
frame dt_*, dx^i lie in ρ²C^∞(X̄), uniformly and smoothly in b. So (H6), (K1) and the first clause of (K4) hold.

*Proof.* On {|x| ≤ 2R₁}, T_m of (21.27) is constant, so g_b is g^KS_b in a translated time coordinate, and
r₀ − 2δ₀ ≥ ½r_♭; so g_b is smooth and Lorentzian of signature (1, 4) there, smoothly in b, by Lemma 21.19.
On {|x| ≥ 2R₁}, g_b = Φ_m^* g^KS_b with Φ_m a diffeomorphism (Lemma 21.20 (c)), so g_b has the signature of
g^KS_b, which is (1, 4) by Lemma 21.19. On {|x| ≥ ½R₁}, Proposition 21.21 gives smoothness and
g_b − η ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞, smoothly in b. *The time function.* In the
coordinates (t_KS, x) = Φ_m(t, x), t_* = t − ψ(|x|) has differential dt_KS − β d|x| with β := ψ′ − T_m′ = 1 −
χ_∞(ρ)(8m₀ρ⁻² − 2m(ρ² − m)⁻¹), ρ := |x| ((21.27), (21.30)). Off supp χ_∞, in particular on [r₀ − 2δ₀,
2R₁], β = 1. On supp χ_∞ ⊂ [2R₁, ∞), ρ² ≥ 4m₀ and m < 3m₀/2, so (8m₀ − 2m)ρ² − 8m₀m > 20m₀² − 12m₀² > 0, the bracket is
positive and β < 1; and β ≥ 1 − 8m₀ρ⁻² ≥ −1, with equality only at ρ = 2R₁, where χ_∞ = 0. So β ∈ (−1, 1] on [r₀ − 2δ₀,
∞), as in the proof of Lemma 21.22 (a), and Lemma 21.16 (e), valid there by Lemma 21.19, makes
dt_* timelike: g₀₀ < 0. The components of g_b in the frame dt_*, dx^i do not depend on t_*, as t_* − t is a function
of |x|. The inequality t_* ≤ t of Lemma 21.22 (a) is not claimed on the collar, where ψ < 0.

*Decay.* Here ḡ is the Minkowski metric of Section 15.1.1 in t̄ := t_* + r, ḡ = −(dt_* + dr)² + dx², not
η = −dt² + dx². With t = t_* + ψ(|x|) ((21.30)),

    η − ḡ = −2(ψ′ − 1) dt_* dr + (1 − ψ′²) dr²,

and ψ′ − 1 = −8m₀|x|⁻² on {|x| ≥ 3R₁}, the same function for every b, so ψ′ − 1 and 1 − ψ′² lie in ρ²C^∞(X̄) there;
dr = x̂·dx with x̂ smooth on X̄ near ∂X. And g_b − η ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞ in the frame dt, dx^i, which differs from the frame
dt_*, dx^i by dt = dt_* + ψ′x̂·dx, smooth on X̄. Adding the two gives g_b − ḡ ∈ ρ²C^∞(X̄) in the frame dt_*, dx^i, and
smoothness in b is that of Proposition 21.21. ∎

### 22.4 The horizon

With the radii of Definition 22.1, let ℋ := {r = r_h}, ρ_∞ := |ξ|⁻¹ near N*ℋ, and ℛ_± := {r = r_h, η = 0, ±ξ > 0}.

**Proposition 22.7** ((H3) and (H4) at b₀.) With τ = t_*, (H3) holds at b₀ with
β₀ = f′(r_h) = 2m^(−1/2), β = 2/β₀ = m^(1/2), q_± := |η/ξ|²_g̸ restricted to ∂Σ₀, and c = β₀. (H4) holds with the
radii of Definition 22.1.

*Proof.* By (22.3), G₀ = fξ² + r⁻²C does not depend on F. Its Hamilton vector field is

    H_(G₀) = 2fξ ∂_r − (f′ξ² − 2r⁻³C) ∂_ξ + r⁻² H^(𝕊³)_C,    (22.6)

with H^(𝕊³)_C the geodesic spray of g̸, which preserves C. At fibre infinity, {G₀ = 0} requires f ≤ 0, and ξ ≠ 0
there. So ∂Σ₀ lies over {r ≤ r_h} ⊂ {r ≤ r_e}. It has the two components ±ξ > 0, it is invariant under the dilations,
and N*ℋ ∖ o ⊂ Σ₀. The future-directed rescaled field is 𝖧 := sgn(ξ) ρ_∞ H_(G₀): then 𝖧r = 2f < 0 for r < r_h, the
future direction decreasing r inside the horizon, as (H4) requires. On ∂ℛ_±,
𝖧ρ_∞ = sgn(ξ)|ξ|⁻¹(−f′ξ²) ∂_ξ|ξ|⁻¹ = f′|ξ|⁻¹, so β₀ = ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧ρ_∞ = f′(r_h) = 2m r_h⁻³ > 0. By (22.3),
τ₁ = −2ξ at r = r_h for every F, so ∓β₀⁻¹ρ_∞τ₁ = 2/β₀ on ∂ℛ_±, which gives β. On ∂Σ₀, |η/ξ|² = −fr², so
(ω, η̂ := η/ξ) are coordinates there with ∂ℛ_± = {η̂ = 0}, and q := |η̂|² is a quadratic defining function. As
H_(G₀)C = 0, (22.6) gives

    𝖧q = sgn(ξ)|ξ|⁻¹ · C · (−2ξ⁻³)(−f′ξ² + 2r⁻³C) = 2q (f′(r) − 2r⁻³q),

which is ≥ β₀q near ∂ℛ_±, where f′(r) → f′(r_h) and q → 0.

(H4): every maximal integral curve of 𝖧 in ∂Σ₀ ∖ ∂ℛ_± lies in {r < r_h}, where 𝖧r = 2f < 0. Backward, r increases,
is bounded by r_h, and converges to a zero of f, as ṙ = 2f; so r → r_h. On ∂Σ₀, q = −fr² → 0, so the curve tends to
∂ℛ_±. Forward, r decreases, and |ṙ| = 2|f(r(s))| ≥ 2|f(r(s₀))| > 0 for s ≥ s₀, as |f| increases as r decreases
below r_h; so the curve reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} at a finite parameter. On {r₀ − 2δ₀ < r < r₂}, f < 0: G₀ = fξ² + r⁻²C
is Lorentzian of signature (1, 3), G₀(dr) = f < 0, and 𝖧r < 0 on ∂Σ₀. ∎

This is [Hin26c, Section 9.2.1, (1)–(4)] for Tangherlini. At b₀ the flow on ∂ℛ_± is the fibre dilation alone; at
b ≠ b₀ the Killing field normal to the horizon is not ∂_t, the flow on N*ℋ moves the base point, and (H3), which asks
only for invariant radial sets with the stated rates, is proved by perturbation in Section 22.10.

### 22.5 The trapped set

On {r > r_h} we use static variables (Lemma 22.2). Put u(r) := 1 − 2m r⁻² and, near Γ and on
Σ^s := {G^s = 0},

    φ₁ := fξ − u,     φ₂ := fξ + u,     Γ := {r = r_ph, ξ = 0} ∩ Σ^s = {r = r_ph, ξ = 0, C = 4m}.    (22.7)

**Proposition 22.8** ((Γ.1)–(Γ.3) at b₀.) For z₀ ∈ {1, −1}, with the future field 𝖧^♭ = z₀H_(G^s) on
Σ^s:

(a) Γ is compact and invariant, and it lies in T*{r₂ < r < ρ₁⁻¹} for the ρ₁ of (H2) provided ρ₁⁻¹ > r_ph = √2 R₁, as
holds for the operators used, whose (H2) is set on {r > 3R₁};

(b) on Σ^s near Γ, exactly,

    𝖧^♭φ₁ = −ν₁φ₁,     𝖧^♭φ₂ = ν₂φ₂,     ν_(1,2) = 2z₀(r⁴ ± ξ(r² − m)(r² − 2m)) / (r³(r² − m)),    (22.8)

with ν₁ = ν₂ = 4z₀(2m)^(−1/2) on Γ;

(c) {φ₁, φ₂} = (2/m)^(1/2) > 0 on Γ, and dG^s ≠ 0 there.

So (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) hold. For z₀ = 1 take φ_u := φ₁ and φ_s := φ₂; for z₀ = −1 take φ_u := φ₂ and φ_s := −φ₁. Then
ν_min = 4(2m)^(−1/2) for both signs, and Γ_(u/s) = {φ_(u/s) = 0} ∩ Σ^s are the two branches of {C = 4m} ∩ Σ^s.

*Proof.* On Σ^s, C = r²(f⁻¹ − fξ²), so (fξ)² = 1 − CW with W := f r⁻² and C conserved, and W′ = 2(2m − r²) r⁻⁵
(Proposition 22.3). W has the single critical point r_ph on (r_h, ∞), a maximum W = (4m)⁻¹.

(a) 𝖧^♭r = 2z₀fξ vanishes on Γ, and 𝖧^♭ξ = −z₀∂_rG^s = −z₀(f′f⁻² + f′ξ² − 2C r⁻³) vanishes there by
Proposition 22.5 (a). C and the flow on 𝕊³ preserve Γ, and Γ ≅ {(ω, η) : |η|² = 4m} is compact. Finally
r₂ = 7R₁/8 < r_ph.

(b) On Σ^s, (fξ)² = 1 − CW, and 1 − 4mW = 1 − 4m r⁻² + 4m² r⁻⁴ = u². So (fξ)² − u² = (4m − C)W, and
{φ₁φ₂ = 0} ∩ Σ^s = {C = 4m} ∩ Σ^s. Each branch is a union of orbits, by the identities derived next. Write X := fξ
and H := H_(G^s), with Hr = 2fξ and Hξ = −∂_rG^s. Then

    H(fξ) = 2ff′ξ² − f(f′ξ² − 2C r⁻³ + f′f⁻²) = ff′ξ² + 2fC r⁻³ − f′f⁻¹,

and on Σ^s, 2fC r⁻³ = 2r⁻¹(1 − f²ξ²). Since f′ − 2f r⁻¹ = (4m − 2r²) r⁻³ = −2u r⁻¹ and
2r⁻¹ − f′f⁻¹ = 2(r²f − m)/(r³f) = 2u (rf)⁻¹ (as r²f = r² − m), this gives H(fξ) = 2u (rf)⁻¹(1 − X²). Moreover
1 − u² = (1 − u)(1 + u) = 4m f r⁻², and Hu = u′·2fξ = 8m r⁻³X. Hence

    H(fξ) = 8m u r⁻³ − 2u (rf)⁻¹ (X − u)(X + u),
    Hφ₁ = H(fξ) − Hu = −(X − u) (8m r⁻³ + 2u (rf)⁻¹ (X + u)),
    Hφ₂ = H(fξ) + Hu = (X + u) (8m r⁻³ − 2u (rf)⁻¹ (X − u)).

With rf = (r² − m) r⁻¹ and u = (r² − 2m) r⁻²,

    8m r⁻³ + 2u² (rf)⁻¹ = 2((r² − 2m)² + 4m(r² − m)) / (r³(r² − m)) = 2r⁴ / (r³(r² − m)),
    2u (rf)⁻¹ · fξ = 2uξ r⁻¹ = 2ξ(r² − m)(r² − 2m) / (r³(r² − m)),

so the two brackets are ν₁/z₀ and ν₂/z₀ of (22.8). Multiplying by z₀ gives (22.8) on Σ^s. On Γ,
ξ = 0 and r² = 2m, so ν₁ = ν₂ = 2z₀ r_ph (r_ph² − m)⁻¹ = 2z₀(2m)^(1/2) m⁻¹ = 4z₀(2m)^(−1/2), the rate of
Proposition 22.5 (b).

(c) {φ₁, φ₂} = ∂_ξφ₁ ∂_rφ₂ − ∂_rφ₁ ∂_ξφ₂ = f(f′ξ + u′) − (f′ξ − u′)f = 2fu′, which at r_ph is
2·½·4m r_ph⁻³ = (2/m)^(1/2). ∂_η G^s = 2r⁻²η^♯ ≠ 0, as |η|² = 4m. For z₀ = −1 the roles of φ₁ and φ₂ are exchanged,
and the sign of φ_s restores {φ_u, φ_s} = {φ₂, −φ₁} = {φ₁, φ₂} > 0 without changing (Γ.2). (Γ.1): φ₁ and φ₂ are
functions of (r, ξ) with dφ₁ ∧ dφ₂ = −2fu′ dr ∧ dξ ≠ 0 (u′ = 4m r⁻³), while on Γ, ∂_rG^s = ∂_ξG^s = 0, so dG^s ≠ 0
has no dr or dξ component there. So dφ₁, dφ₂ and dG^s are independent along Γ, and Γ_u, Γ_s are smooth hypersurfaces
of Σ^s near Γ, meeting transversally in Γ, to which 𝖧^♭ is tangent by (22.8). Γ, Γ_(u/s), the flow and
(Γ.1)–(Γ.3) transfer to t_* by Lemma 22.2 (a)–(b), and the function q of (Γ.4) on Γ by Lemma 22.2 (c). ∎

This is [Hin26c, (Γ.1)–(Γ.3)] for Tangherlini; for Kerr it is [Hin26c, Lemma 4.16].

### 22.6 r-normal hyperbolicity

**Proposition 22.9** ((K3) at b₀.) (K3) holds at b₀: Γ is eventually absolutely r-normally hyperbolic for
every r, for 𝖵 := q_(*,1)⁻¹ H_(G₁) on Σ^♭₁, with q_(*,1) and G₁ those of t_*.

*Proof.* First take the field of the static time, 𝖵_s := q_(s,1)⁻¹ H_(G^s), in static variables
(Lemma 22.2 (a)). Here q_(s,1) = 2f⁻¹, so 𝖵_s = (f/2) H_(G^s), and on Γ, 𝖵_s = ¼H_(G^s), as f(r_ph) = ½. Use the
coordinates (r, ξ, ω, η) on Σ^s, where C is determined by (r, ξ). On Γ the flow is ṙ = ξ̇ = 0, and (ω, η) moves by
¼r_ph⁻² H^(𝕊³)_C, the geodesic flow of the round 𝕊³ on the cosphere bundle {|η|² = 4m}, reparametrised by a constant.
Its orbits are periodic, so De^(s𝖵_s)|_(TΓ) is bounded uniformly in s, and the tangential bound of (K3) holds with
C_ϵ = C for every ϵ > 0. Normal directions: the linearisation of 𝖵_s at Γ is block triangular. The (δr, δξ)-block is
autonomous, with eigenvalues ±¼ν, ν = 4(2m)^(−1/2), by (22.8) at z₀ = 1: on ker dφ₂, tangent to Γ_s, dφ₁
decays forward at the rate ¼ν, and on ker dφ₁, tangent to Γ_u, dφ₂ decays backward. The (δω, δη)-block is driven by
(δr, δξ), through r and C, which enter the speed of the spray. As the homogeneous tangential solutions are bounded and
the normal ones grow or decay at the rate ¼ν ≠ 0, each normal eigensolution e^(±νs/4)v_± has a unique tangential
correction e^(±νs/4)w_±, obtained by solving the driven equation with the variation-of-constants integral over
(−∞, s] or [s, ∞). This gives the invariant splitting (15.1), with N̄^u and N̄^s spanned by these solutions,
continuous along Γ, and the rate μ = ¼ν of (K3).

*Transport by T_F.* Transported by T_F (Lemma 22.2 (a)), 𝖵 = a𝖵_s with a := q_(s,1)/q_(*,1), smooth and positive
near Γ, as both time differentials are timelike there, and a = 1 on Γ by Lemma 22.2 (c). Hence e^(s𝖵) = e^(s𝖵_s)
on the invariant set Γ, and along Γ, D(a𝖵_s) = D𝖵_s + 𝖵_s ⊗ da. Here 𝖵_s is tangent to Γ and da vanishes on TΓ, so
the added term maps the normal directions into TΓ and annihilates TΓ. The normal block, its rates and the homogeneous
tangential equation are unchanged, and the added driving term is absorbed by the same variation-of-constants step. ∎

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.19] for Tangherlini.

### 22.7 The global dynamics

On Σ^(z₀)_(z₀) the future integral curves of G_(z₀) project to future null geodesics of g_(b₀) with velocity
2z₀ν^♯, ν = −z₀ dτ + ζ, whose energy −g(2z₀ν^♯, ∂_t) = −2z₀ν(∂_t) = 2 is positive for both signs of z₀. On
Σ^(−z₀)_(z₀), which occurs only inside the horizon, the velocity is −2z₀ν^♯ and the energy −2, which is allowed there
since ∂_t is spacelike. C is the squared angular momentum. By Lemma 22.2 each statement below may be checked in
the time function named; ξ_s and ξ_* denote ξ in the t_s and in the t_* variables. Near infinity, t_* = t_s − F(r)
with F = t_s − t_* = r − r_* − T_m + ψ ((21.27), (21.30)), so that on {r ≥ 3R₁}

    F′ = 1 − f⁻¹ − T_m′ + ψ′ = 1 + m(r² − m)⁻¹ − 8m r⁻² = 1 + O(r⁻²),    (22.9)

and ξ_* = ξ_s − z₀F′ by Lemma 22.2 (a).

**Proposition 22.10** ((H8) at b₀.) (H8) (a) and (b) hold at b₀ for z₀ ∈ {1, −1}, with
Γ̄_u = {φ_u = 0} ∩ Σ^s ∩ {r > r_h}, Γ̄_s = {φ_s = 0} ∩ Σ^s ∩ {r > r_h}, and every neighbourhood O ⊂ {r > r_h} of Γ.

*Proof.* *Outside the horizon* (static variables). Along 𝖧^♭, ṙ = 2z₀fξ, C is conserved and (fξ)² = 1 − CW(r), so
the radial motion is that of a particle in the potential CW, which has a single maximum C/(4m) at r_ph and tends to 0
at r_h and at ∞ (Proposition 22.3). There are three cases.

- C < 4m: fξ ≠ 0 throughout, so r is strictly monotone.
- C > 4m: {CW > 1} is an interval (r′, r″) ∋ r_ph with r_h < r′. A curve stays in (r_h, r′] or in [r″, ∞), with
  exactly one turning point, where ξ = 0 and ξ̇ ≠ 0.
- C = 4m: the curve lies on Γ or on one of the four branches of {fξ = ±u}, along which r is monotone and tends to r_ph
  at one end.

In the first two cases the curve meets neither Γ̄_u nor Γ̄_s, and r tends, at each end, to r_h or to ∞. In the third,
the branches with φ_u = 0 are backward asymptotic to Γ and those with φ_s = 0 are forward asymptotic, by
(22.8). This identifies Γ̄_(u/s) outside the horizon. Inside the horizon no curve tends to Γ, as shown below.

*At infinity.* If r → ∞ forward, then (fξ_s)² → 1 and ṙ > 0 give ξ_s → z₀. By (22.9), ξ_* → 0;
and |η|/r = C^(1/2) r⁻¹ → 0, as C is conserved. So the curve converges in the scattering phase space (Section 11.4) to
{ξ_* = 0, η = 0} over ∂X, which is R_out ((11.17)). Backward with r → ∞, ξ_s → −z₀, so ξ_* → −2z₀ and
η/r → 0: the curve converges to R_(z₀,in) = {ξ_* = −2z₀, η = 0} over ∂X ((11.17)).

*At the horizon* (v variables, regular across r = r_h; v is a chart, and the components are those of t_*,
Section 22.2). On {G^(0)_(z₀) = 0}, fξ² − 2z₀ξ + r⁻²C = 0, with the roots ξ = (z₀ ± (1 − fC r⁻²)^(1/2))/f. One root
is regular at f = 0, where it tends to C/(2z₀r_h²); the other is ∼ 2z₀/f. A future null covector with
ν(∂_t) = −z₀ ≠ 0 is not a multiple of dr, so ν^♯ is not tangent to the null generator ∂_v of ℋ. At r = r_h,
g⁻¹(dr, ·) = ∂_v + f∂_r = ∂_v is future directed null (Proposition 22.3 (d)), so dr(γ̇) = g(∂_v, γ̇) < 0 for the
future causal velocity γ̇: on the regular root a curve crosses ℋ inward in finite parameter. Inside, dr is timelike
(G(dr) = f < 0) and ṙ < 0 strictly. On compact subsets of Σ_(z₀) ∩ {r₀ − δ₀ ≤ r ≤ r_h − ϵ}, compactified at fibre
infinity, ṙ is bounded above by a negative constant, including at fibre infinity by Proposition 22.7 (𝖧r = 2f). So
the curve reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} in finite parameter. On the singular root, which near ℋ is the component
Σ^(−z₀)_(z₀) inside and the outgoing branch outside, |ξ| → ∞ as r → r_h with C fixed. So η/ξ → 0 and the curve tends
backward to ∂ℛ₊ ∪ ∂ℛ₋, reaching r_h only asymptotically in the parameter of the rescaled field, ρ_∞ times the future
field. For the unrescaled future field, |ṙ| → 2 and the curve reaches fibre infinity at a finite parameter; (H8) is
read for the rescaled field, whose integral curves are the same up to parametrisation.

So every curve not in Γ̄_u tends backward to ∂ℛ_± or R_(z₀,in), and every curve not in Γ̄_s tends forward to R_out or
reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} in finite time.

*Uniformity on compact sets.* Let 𝖪 ⊂ Σ_(z₀) ∩ T*{r > r₀ − 2δ₀} be compact and disjoint from Γ̄_s. C is conserved,
and C ≤ C_𝖪 on 𝖪. For ϵ ∈ (0, ¼) and R large given C_𝖪, put 𝒜_out := {r > R, |ξ_*| < ϵ}. While z₀ξ_s > 0 and r > R:
𝖧^♭r = 2z₀fξ_s = 2(1 − Cf r⁻²)^(1/2) ≥ 1, and (fξ_s)² = 1 − Cf r⁻² gives z₀ξ_* = |ξ_s| − F′,
hence |ξ_*| ≤ c₁(C + 1) r⁻² and |η|/r = C^(1/2) r⁻¹, with c₁ depending only on m. Take R with c₁(C_𝖪 + 1) R⁻² < ϵ/2 and
F′ > ½ on {r > R}. A curve from 𝖪 that enters 𝒜_out has z₀ξ_s = z₀ξ_* + F′ > 0 there, and on the maximal parameter
interval after entry on which z₀ξ_s > 0, r increases (𝖧^♭r ≥ 1), so r > R persists and |ξ_*| < ϵ/2, hence
z₀ξ_s > ¼; that interval is therefore closed as well as open, and contains every later parameter. So the curve stays
in 𝒜_out, with r ≥ R + s at parameter s after entry, and converges to R_out at rates independent of its initial point.
For T > 0 let U_T be the set of points of 𝖪 whose forward curve enters 𝒜_out or {r < r₀ − δ₀} before parameter T. Each
U_T is open, as both target sets are open and the flow is continuous; the U_T increase with T; and they cover 𝖪 by the
pointwise statement, since a curve tending to R_out has r → ∞ and ξ_* → 0. So 𝖪 ⊂ U_T for one T, and the forward
convergence is uniform on 𝖪.

Backward, for 𝖪 disjoint from Γ̄_u, the same argument applies with 𝒜_in := {r > R, |ξ_* + 2z₀| < ϵ} for R_(z₀,in),
with R also so large that F′ < 3/2 on {r > R}: on 𝒜_in, z₀ξ_s = z₀(ξ_* + 2z₀) − 2 + F′ < −¼,
and |ξ_* + 2z₀| = ||ξ_s| − (2 − F′)| ≤ c₁(C + 1) r⁻²; and with 𝒰_H := {|r − r_h| < δ, ρ_∞ < δ′, C < C_𝖪 + 1} near the
horizon, where δ, δ′ are so small, given C_𝖪, that 𝒰_H meets only the singular root. 𝒰_H is backward invariant,
as |r − r_h| decreases backward on both of its branches and ρ_∞ with it, and on 𝒰_H, ρ_∞ ≤ c|f|
and |η/ξ| ≤ c C_𝖪^(1/2)|f|. In the rescaled parameter, |dr/ds| = ρ_∞|ṙ| = |f|(1 + O(C_𝖪 f)) on 𝒰_H,
and |f| = β₀|r − r_h|(1 + O(r − r_h)), so |r − r_h| decays backward exponentially at a rate close to β₀, uniformly on
𝒰_H. With the cover argument this makes the backward convergence to ∂ℛ_± and to R_(z₀,in) uniform on 𝖪.

(b) Γ̄_u is the union of Γ and the two branches of {φ_u = 0}, on each of which r is monotone. So
Γ̄_u ∩ O = {φ_u = 0} ∩ Σ^s ∩ O = Γ_u for every O ⊂ {r > r_h}, and likewise for Γ̄_s. ∎

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.24] and the paragraph after [Hin26c, (9.5)], for Tangherlini.

**Lemma 22.11** (An escape function.) On Σ^s, ℱ := (r² − 2m)ξ satisfies

    H_(G^s)ℱ = 2r(ξ²(r² − m)² + (r² − 2m)²) / (r² − m)²  ≥ 0,    (22.10)

with equality exactly on Γ.

*Proof.* For ℱ = a(r)ξ, H_(G^s)ℱ = a′·2fξ·ξ − a(f′ξ² − 2C r⁻³ + f′f⁻²). On Σ^s, 2C r⁻³ = 2r⁻¹(f⁻¹ − fξ²), so

    H_(G^s)ℱ = ξ²(2fa′ − a(f′ + 2f r⁻¹)) + a f⁻¹(2r⁻¹ − f′f⁻¹).

Here f′ + 2f r⁻¹ = 2r⁻¹, so the first term is 2ξ² r⁻²((r² − m)a′ − ra), using r²f = r² − m; and
2r⁻¹ − f′f⁻¹ = 2u(rf)⁻¹ (proof of Proposition 22.8), so the second is 2ua(rf²)⁻¹ = 2r(r² − 2m)(r² − m)⁻²a. At
a = r² − 2m, (r² − m)a′ − ra = 2r(r² − m) − r(r² − 2m) = r³, and (22.10) follows. It vanishes exactly when
ξ = 0 and r² = 2m, and on Σ^s these give C = r²f⁻¹ = 4m: the set Γ. ∎

Lemma 22.11 is not needed at b₀, where Proposition 22.10 uses the conserved C. At b ≠ b₀, where C is not
conserved, Section 22.15 uses the separation of Section 22.11 instead. Exactly, φ₂² − φ₁² = 4fξu, so
ℱ = (r²/(4f))(φ₂² − φ₁²); with the choices of Proposition 22.8, z₀ℱ = (r²/(4f))(φ_s² − φ_u²) for both signs of z₀,
while 𝖧^♭(z₀ℱ) = H_(G^s)ℱ ≥ 0.

### 22.8 The theorem at b₀

**Theorem 22.12** ((Dyn) at b₀.) For g_(b₀) with the time function t_* and the radii of Definition 22.1:
(H6) and (K1) hold (Lemma 22.6, for every b ∈ ℬ); the dynamical parts of (H3) and all of (H4) hold
(Proposition 22.7); (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) hold with ν_min = 4(2m₀)^(−1/2) (Proposition 22.8); on Γ, q_(z₀) is the same in t_*
as in t_s (Lemma 22.2 (c)), where it is 2z₀f(r_ph)⁻¹ = 4z₀, so q^Γ := z₀q_(z₀) = 4 on Γ and
β_Γ = ½ min_Γ |q_(z₀)| = 2; (K3) holds (Proposition 22.9); and (H8) holds (Proposition 22.10). These hold for every
operator with principal symbol G Id.

*Proof.* Each item is the result cited for it. ∎

**Remark 22.13** (Two constants β₀ and β_Γ.) The β₀ of (H3), f′(r_h) = 2m₀^(−1/2), is twice the surface
gravity; the β_Γ of (Γ.4), ½ min_Γ |q_(z₀)| = 1/f(r_ph) = 2, belongs to the trapped set. They are different quantities,
defined in Section 11.1.3 and Section 12.1.5.

### 22.9 The horizon near b₀

This section and the next carry the horizon hypotheses, the dynamical parts of (H3) and all of (H4), from b₀ to every
b near b₀, uniformly in b as (H5) asks. (H6), (K1) and the first clause of (K4) hold for every b ∈ ℬ by
Lemma 22.6. The one new fact is that the Myers–Perry horizon is the null hypersurface {r_A = r₊} of the
Kerr–Schild form (Lemma 22.15); it is proved by an exact identity. The rest is continuity on compact sets, after a
diffeomorphism that fixes the horizon (Lemma 22.16).

For b = (m, A) ∈ ℬ let s, p, r_A, Π, 𝖬, ℓ_A, F_A and H_(m,A) be as in Section 21.5.1, Lemma 21.14 and
Definition 21.15. In a frame in which A = aJ₁₂ + bJ₃₄ (here b is the second spin, not the parameter),
Π(r) = (r² + a²)(r² + b²), since s = a² + b² and p² = a²b² (Section 21.5.1). Let r₊(b) be the largest positive
root of

    Δ_b(r) := Π(r) − m r² = 0.    (22.11)

With u := r², Δ_b = u² + (s − m)u + p², whose discriminant is
(m − s)² − 4p² = (m − (|a| + |b|)²)(m − (|a| − |b|)²) ≥ (m − (|a| + |b|)²)² > 0 for every (m, A) ∈ ℬ, as
(|a| + |b|)² ≤ 4‖A‖² < m₀/100 < m there. So Δ_b has, as a polynomial in u, two simple real roots u₋ < u₊, with
u₊ + u₋ = m − s > 0 and u₊u₋ = p² ≥ 0. Hence r₊ = u₊^(1/2) is a simple zero of Δ_b; with r₋ := u₋^(1/2),

    Δ_b > 0 on (r₊, ∞),     Δ_b < 0 on (r₋, r₊),     r₋ ≤ ‖A‖ < r_♭/4, strictly for A ≠ 0,

the last because ‖A‖ < ε_♭R₁ ≤ r_♭/4 on ℬ (Definition 21.18), and because u₊ ≥ ½(m − s) and
m − s > ½m₀ − m₀/200 > 2‖A‖² (as s ≤ 2‖A‖² < m₀/200), so that u₋ = p²/u₊ ≤ 2‖A‖⁴/(m − s) (as p² = a²b² ≤ ‖A‖⁴),
which is less than ‖A‖² if A ≠ 0, while u₋ = 0 = ‖A‖² if A = 0. r₊ is smooth in (m, A) ∈ ℬ, as u₊ is a smooth
function of (m, s, p²) where the discriminant is positive, and s and p² are polynomials in A. At b₀,
Δ_(b₀) = r²(r² − m₀), r₊(b₀) = m₀^(1/2) = r_h and r₋(b₀) = 0.

**Lemma 22.14** (The spheroidal form of the radius.) Let A ∈ 𝔰𝔬(4), |x|² > s, r := r_A(x),
𝒟 := (r²I − A²)^(1/2), which is symmetric, positive definite and commutes with A, and ω := 𝒟⁻¹x. Then |ω| = 1, and
with

    ϱ² := r² + s + ωᵀA²ω    (22.12)

the following hold.

(a) Π(r) · xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x = ϱ², and ϱ² ≥ r² > 0.

(b) F_A = r² xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x; so Π(r)F_A = r²ϱ² and H_(m,A) = m/ϱ².

(c) The Euclidean gradient of r_A is ∇r_A = 𝒟⁻²x/(r xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x), so |∇r_A|² = Π(r)/(r²ϱ²), and ℓ_A(∇r_A) = 1.

(d) In a frame in which A = aJ₁₂ + bJ₃₄, and with ω = (sin ϑ e^(iφ), cos ϑ e^(iψ)) in ℂ² ≅ ℝ⁴,
x = ((r² + a²)^(1/2) sin ϑ e^(iφ), (r² + b²)^(1/2) cos ϑ e^(iψ)) and ϱ² = r² + a² cos²ϑ + b² sin²ϑ.

*Proof.* By Lemma 21.14 (a), (r²I − A²)𝖬(r) = Π(r)I, so 𝒟⁻² = 𝖬(r)/Π(r).
Then |ω|² = xᵀ𝒟⁻²x = xᵀ𝖬(r)x/Π(r) = 1, as Q(r, x) = Π(r) − xᵀ𝖬(r)x = 0 at r = r_A(x).
(a) xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x = ωᵀ𝒟⁻²ω = ωᵀ𝖬(r)ω/Π(r), and ωᵀ𝖬(r)ω = (r² + s)|ω|² + ωᵀA²ω = ϱ². In a frame,
sI + A² = diag(b², b², a², a²) ≥ 0, so ϱ² ≥ r².
(b) By Definition 21.15, F_A = 1 + xᵀA²𝖬²x/Π² = 1 + xᵀA²𝒟⁻⁴x = 1 + ωᵀA²𝒟⁻²ω, as 𝒟 commutes with A. So
F_A = ωᵀ(𝒟² + A²)𝒟⁻²ω = r² ωᵀ𝒟⁻²ω = r² xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x, and Π F_A = r²ϱ² by (a). Hence H_(m,A) = m r²/(Π F_A) = m/ϱ².
(c) The function φ_A(r, x) := xᵀ(r²I − A²)⁻¹x − 1 = −Q(r, x)/Π(r) has, for fixed x, the zeros of Q(·, x) in (0, ∞), so
r_A(x) is its only positive zero; and ∂_rφ_A = −2r xᵀ(r²I − A²)⁻²x < 0. By the implicit function theorem,
∇r_A = −∇_xφ_A/∂_rφ_A = 𝒟⁻²x/(r xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x), and |∇r_A|² = 1/(r² xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x) = Π/(r²ϱ²) by (a). The coefficient vector of ℓ_A
is 𝖬(rI + A)x/Π = 𝒟⁻²(rI + A)x, so

    ℓ_A(∇r_A) = xᵀ(rI − A)𝒟⁻⁴x/(r xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x) = 1,

since A𝒟⁻⁴ is antisymmetric (A is antisymmetric and commutes with the symmetric 𝒟⁻⁴), so xᵀA𝒟⁻⁴x = 0.
(d) In the frame, A² = −diag(a², a², b², b²), 𝒟 = diag((r² + a²)^(1/2), (r² + a²)^(1/2), (r² + b²)^(1/2),
(r² + b²)^(1/2)), s = a² + b² and ωᵀA²ω = −a² sin²ϑ − b² cos²ϑ. ∎

**Lemma 22.15** (The horizon is null.) For b = (m, A) ∈ ℬ, on {|x|² > s},

    (g^KS_(m,A))⁻¹(dr_A, dr_A) = Δ_b(r_A) / (r_A² ϱ²),    (22.13)

with ϱ² of (22.12). Hence ℋ_b := {r_A = r₊(b)} is a smooth null hypersurface invariant under ∂_t. dr_A is
spacelike on {r_A > r₊} and timelike on {r₋ < r_A < r₊}, where Δ_b < 0; the latter set contains
{|x| ≥ ½r_♭, r_A < r₊}.

*Proof.* By Lemma 21.16 (d), (g^KS_(m,A))⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − H_(m,A) k_A^♯ ⊗ k_A^♯ with k_A^♯ = −∂_t + ℓ_A^♯, ℓ_A^♯ the
Euclidean dual of ℓ_A. As r_A does not depend on t, dr_A(k_A^♯) = ℓ_A(∇r_A) = 1 by Lemma 22.14 (c), and
η⁻¹(dr_A, dr_A) = |∇r_A|². So, by Lemma 22.14 (b)–(c),

    (g^KS_(m,A))⁻¹(dr_A, dr_A) = |∇r_A|² − H_(m,A) = Π/(r_A²ϱ²) − m/ϱ² = (Π − m r_A²)/(r_A²ϱ²).

dr_A ≠ 0 everywhere by Lemma 22.14 (c), so ℋ_b is a smooth hypersurface; its conormal dr_A is null there, as
Δ_b(r₊) = 0, so ℋ_b is null. It is invariant under ∂_t, as g^KS_(m,A) has t-independent components and r_A does not
depend on t. The signs of Δ_b on (r₊, ∞) and on (r₋, r₊) are those found after (22.11), and ϱ² > 0. On
{|x| ≥ ½r_♭}, r_A² > 3‖A‖² ≥ r₋², by Lemma 21.19 and r₋ ≤ ‖A‖. ∎

(22.13) is the component g^(rr) of the Myers–Perry metric [MP86] in Boyer–Lindquist coordinates ([ER08]),
written in the Kerr–Schild coordinates of Chapter 21; the radius r_A of the Kerr–Schild form is the Boyer–Lindquist
radius. Nothing below uses the Boyer–Lindquist form.

**Lemma 22.16** (Fixing the horizon.) There are ε_H > 0 and diffeomorphisms Ψ_b of {|x| ≥ r₀ − 2δ₀},
for |b − b₀| < ε_H, smooth in (b, x), with Ψ_(b₀) = Id, Ψ_b = Id on {|x| ≤ 5R₁/8} and on {|x| ≥ 7R₁/4}, and
Ψ_b({|x| = r_h}) = ℋ_b. Its spacetime lift is (t, x) ↦ (t, Ψ_b(x)).

*Proof.* Let χ_H ∈ C_c^∞((5R₁/8, 7R₁/4)) equal 1 near [3R₁/4, 3R₁/2], an interval that contains r_h = R₁. Put

    r̃_b(x) := χ_H(|x|) (r_h/r₊(b)) r_A(x) + (1 − χ_H(|x|)) |x|.

Then r̃_(b₀) = |x|, as r_A = |x| at A = 0 (Lemma 21.14 (b)); r̃_b − |x| is supported in {|x| ∈ supp χ_H} and
tends to 0 in C^∞ as b → b₀; and ℋ_b = {r̃_b = r_h} near {|x| = r_h}. Define Ψ_b(x) := κ x̂, with κ = κ_b(x) > 0
solving r̃_b(κx̂) = |x|. As ∂_κ r̃_b(κx̂) = 1 + O(|b − b₀|), the map κ ↦ r̃_b(κx̂) is strictly increasing on
[r₀ − 2δ₀, ∞) and equal to κ off supp χ_H (in particular for κ ≤ 5R₁/8, which contains r₀ − 2δ₀, and for large κ),
so it is a bijection of [r₀ − 2δ₀, ∞); κ_b is defined globally and is smooth by the implicit function theorem, and
Ψ_b is a diffeomorphism. It is the identity where χ_H(|x|) = 0, and it maps {|x| = r_h} onto {r̃_b = r_h}, which is
ℋ_b: on {χ_H = 1}, {r̃_b = r_h} = {r_A = r₊}, and on the transition region,
where |x| ∈ (5R₁/8, 3R₁/4) ∪ (3R₁/2, 7R₁/4), r̃_b is C^∞-close to |x| and so differs from r_h = R₁. For b near b₀,
{r_A = r₊} lies in {χ_H = 1}, since r_A is close to |x| and r₊ to R₁. ∎

Where χ_H(|Ψ_b(x)|) = 1, in particular near {|x| = r_h}, the definition of Ψ_b gives Ψ_b^* r_A = (r₊(b)/r_h)|x|, so
Ψ_b^* dr_A = (r₊(b)/r_h) dr there.

Below, g̃_b := Ψ_b^* g_b, with the time function Ψ_b^* t_*; its differential Ψ_b^* dt_* is timelike for g̃_b. The
spectral families of g_b and g̃_b are conjugate: on the bundles of Section 11.1.2, trivialised by dt_*, dx^i, pulling
back by Ψ_b conjugates each operator by the smooth bundle map B_b taking the frame Ψ_b^* dt_*, Ψ_b^* dx^i to dt_*,
dx^i, smooth in b, with B_(b₀) = Id. The hypotheses (H1)–(H8) and (K1)–(K4) are invariant under this conjugation. The
scalar principal symbol is preserved. With the transported fibre inner product h′ := |det DΨ_b| B_b^*(h ∘ Ψ_b)B_b,
under which the pull-back by Ψ_b followed by B_b⁻¹ is an isometry from L²(|dy|; h) to L²(|dx|; h′), y = Ψ_b(x), the
h′-imaginary part of the conjugated operator is the conjugate of Im_h P, exactly; without the Jacobian it would acquire
the term ½H_G log|det DΨ_b|. h′ is a fibre inner product as in Section 11.1.2 (Hermitian, bounded above and below,
smooth in b), equal to h where Ψ_b = Id. So the subprincipal endomorphisms that enter the threshold of (H3) and
condition (Γ.4) (Section 11.1.4, Section 12.1.5) are conjugate, with the same spectra and thresholds. Ψ_b is the
identity on {|x| ≤ 5R₁/8} and on {|x| ≥ 7R₁/4}, so the artificial boundary, the extendible and supported spaces there,
(H2), (K1) and the structure at infinity are untouched, and smoothness in b gives norms equivalent uniformly in b. The
conjugated family is Ψ_b^* of the family that Chapter 23, Chapter 24 and Chapter 25 build from g_b, gauge 1-forms
included; where those chapters evaluate a threshold at N*ℋ_b in the coordinates of g_b (Lemma 23.7), that is
the threshold of the conjugated family at N*{r = r_h}. We write G̃_(0,b) and τ̃_(1,b) for the symbols of g̃_b, and keep
the radii of Definition 22.1, ρ_∞ = |ξ|⁻¹ and ℛ_± = {r = r_h, η = 0, ±ξ > 0}, which are fixed sets, independent of b.

### 22.10 (H3) and (H4) near b₀

**Lemma 22.17** For |b − b₀| < ε_H, N*{r = r_h} ∖ o ⊂ {G̃_(0,b) = 0}, and H_(G̃_(0,b)) is tangent to it.

*Proof.* The change of time Φ_m of (21.27) fixes x, so g_b⁻¹(dr_A, dr_A) = (g^KS_b)⁻¹(dr_A, dr_A), which
vanishes on ℋ_b by Lemma 22.15. By the remark after Lemma 22.16, for c ∈ ℝ, G̃_(0,b)(c dr) = c²
g̃_b⁻¹(dr, dr) = c²(r_h/r₊(b))² g_b⁻¹(dr_A, dr_A) ∘ Ψ_b = 0 on {r = r_h}. So the Lagrangian submanifold N*{r = r_h} lies
in the level set {G̃_(0,b) = 0}. For v tangent to it and Ω the symplectic form, Ω(H_(G̃_(0,b)), v) = dG̃_(0,b)(v) = 0, so
H_(G̃_(0,b)) lies in the symplectic orthogonal of the tangent space, which is the tangent space itself. ∎

**Proposition 22.18** ((H3) and (H4) near b₀.) There is ε₁ ∈ (0, ε_H] such that for |b − b₀| < ε₁, and so
on the compact ball |b − b₀| ≤ ½ε₁ (as (H5) asks for a compact parameter space), the dynamical conditions of (H3) and
all of (H4) hold for g̃_b with the radii of Definition 22.1, the sets ℛ_±, ρ_∞, and q_(±,b) := |η/ξ|²_g̸ restricted
to ∂Σ̃_(0,b). Moreover β₀(b) ≥ ½β₀(b₀), β(b) ≥ ½β(b₀), 𝖧_b q_(±,b) ≥ ½β₀(b₀) q_(±,b) near ∂ℛ_±, and the lengths in
(H4) are bounded, all uniformly in b. So the uniformity of (H5) holds for these data.

*Proof.* All symbols depend smoothly on b with values in C^∞, as Ψ_b does. By the first step of (H4) below,
∂Σ̃_(0,b) lies over {r < r_h + ½δ₀}. At b₀, on ∂Σ₀ (over r ≤ r_h), C/ξ² = −fr² = m₀ − r² ≤ m₀ − (r₀ − 2δ₀)² < ∞ on
[r₀ − 2δ₀, r_h], so |ξ| ≥ c|ζ| there; by compactness of S*{r₀ − 2δ₀ ≤ r ≤ r_h + ½δ₀} this persists for b near b₀. So
ξ ≠ 0 on ∂Σ̃_(0,b), sgn ξ splits it into two open and closed parts, and ρ_∞ = |ξ|⁻¹ and the future-directed rescaled
field 𝖧_b := sgn(ξ) ρ_∞ H_(G̃_(0,b)) are defined on all of it.

*(H3).* By Lemma 22.17, ∂ℛ_± are invariant compact sets for every b. β₀(b) = ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧_bρ_∞ and
∓β₀⁻¹ρ_∞τ̃_(1,b) are continuous functions on the fixed compact set ∂ℛ_±, continuous in b, and their infima at b₀ are
2m₀^(−1/2) and m₀^(1/2) (Proposition 22.7). So they are at least half of that for b near b₀. Next, dG̃_(0,b) ≠ 0 at
∂ℛ_± (at b₀, ∂_r(fξ²) ≠ 0 there), so near ∂ℛ_±, ∂Σ̃_(0,b) is a smooth hypersurface of S*X̃, a graph
r = r_b(ω, η̂) over the coordinates (ω, η̂ := η/ξ), smooth in b (implicit function theorem). In these coordinates
∂ℛ_± = {η̂ = 0} for every b, and q_(±,b) = |η̂|² is a quadratic defining function. 𝖧_b is tangent to {η̂ = 0}, so
𝖧_b q_(±,b) = Q_b(ω)(η̂, η̂) + O(|η̂|³), with the quadratic form Q_b continuous in b and the remainder uniform. At b₀,
Q_(b₀) = 2β₀(b₀)|η̂|² (Proposition 22.7: 𝖧q = 2q(f′ − 2r⁻³q)). So Q_b ≥ (3/2)β₀(b₀)|η̂|² for b near b₀, and
𝖧_b q_(±,b) ≥ ½β₀(b₀) q_(±,b) on {q_(±,b) < ϵ_q} for a fixed ϵ_q > 0.

*(H4).* At b₀, ∂Σ₀ lies over {r ≤ r_h}, and G̃_(0,b₀) ≥ c > 0 on S*{r_h + ½δ₀ ≤ r ≤ ρ₁⁻¹}. On {r ≥ ρ₁⁻¹},
G̃_(0,b) is elliptic uniformly for b near b₀: at b₀ it is fξ² + r⁻²C, g_b − g_(b₀) is small in ρ²C^∞
((21.29)), and Ψ_b = Id there. So for b near b₀, ∂Σ̃_(0,b) lies over {r < r_h + ½δ₀} ⊂ {r ≤ r_e}. On
{r₀ − 2δ₀ ≤ r ≤ r₂} the conditions "G̃_(0,b) is Lorentzian of signature (1, 3)", "G̃_(0,b)(dr) < 0" and "𝖧_b r < 0 on
∂Σ̃_(0,b)" are strict and hold at b₀ on a compact set, so they persist. For the flow, let U := {q_(±,b) < ϵ_q} near
∂ℛ_±. At b₀, ∂Σ₀ ∖ U lies over {r ≤ r_h − d₁} for some d₁ > 0 (q = −fr² there), where 𝖧r = 2f ≤ −c′. By continuity,
for b near b₀, ∂Σ̃_(0,b) ∖ U lies over {r ≤ r_h − ½d₁}, where 𝖧_b r ≤ −½c′. Let γ be a maximal curve of 𝖧_b in
∂Σ̃_(0,b) ∖ ∂ℛ_±. In U, q_(±,b) grows forward at the rate ≥ ½β₀(b₀), so γ leaves U forward in finite time. Since
𝖧_b q_(±,b) ≥ ½β₀(b₀) q_(±,b) > 0 on the closure of U, in particular on {q_(±,b) = ϵ_q}, the complement of U in
∂Σ̃_(0,b) is forward invariant, and γ does not re-enter U. Outside U, r decreases at the rate ≥ ½c′, so γ reaches
{r < r₀ − δ₀} within the time 2(r_h − r₀ + 2δ₀)/c′ after leaving U. Backward, r increases outside U, so γ enters U in
finite time. In U, q_(±,b) decreases exponentially backward, so γ(s) → ∂ℛ_± as s → −∞. The times are bounded uniformly
in b on compact sets of initial points away from ∂ℛ_±. ∎

This is the non-degenerate radial point structure at the conormal bundle of the event horizon that
[Hin26, Remark 1.4 (b)] describes, for the Myers–Perry metrics near Tangherlini.

### 22.11 Spheroidal coordinates and the separation

This section and the next five prove the remaining dynamical hypotheses for g_b, b near b₀: the normally hyperbolic
trapping (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) of (H7), the r-normal hyperbolicity (K3) with the uniformity (K4), and the global dynamics (H8),
with the uniformity of (H5) extended to them (Section 12.1.5). With Section 22.3 ((H6), (K1), and (Dyn) at b₀) and
Section 22.10 ((H3)–(H4) near b₀) this completes (Dyn) near b₀ (Theorem 22.30).

*Notation.* In these sections b is the parameter and, in a frame, the second spin; Ψ is a momentum in a frame and Ψ_b
the diffeomorphism of Lemma 22.16; β is the coefficient of Lemma 22.19 (c) and β₀ the rate of (H3); ψ is an
azimuth; and ℛ_c, 𝒮 are the functions of Lemma 22.23.

Let b = (m, A) ∈ ℬ with |b − b₀| small, and use the notation of Chapter 21: s = −½ tr(A²), Π(r) = r⁴ + sr² + p²,
Δ_b = Π − m r², r_A, ℓ_A and H_(m,A) (Lemma 21.14, Definition 21.15), and r₊(b), the largest root of Δ_b
((22.11)). On {|x| ≥ r₀ − 2δ₀}, which lies in {|x|² > s} by Lemma 21.19, write

    x = (r²I − A²)^(1/2) ω,     r > 0,     ω ∈ 𝕊³ ⊂ ℝ⁴.    (22.14)

By Lemma 22.14, r = r_A(x) and ω = (r_A²I − A²)^(−1/2)x; conversely, for x given by (22.14)
with |x|² > s, xᵀ(r²I − A²)⁻¹x = |ω|² = 1, so r is the unique positive zero of Q(·, x) (Lemma 21.14), r = r_A(x).
So (22.14) is a diffeomorphism (r, ω) ↦ x onto {|x|² > s}, smooth in A, with no frame chosen. Write
𝒟 := (r²I − A²)^(1/2). Differentiating 𝒟² = r²I − A², with 𝒟 and ∂_r𝒟 commuting (both are functions of A²),
∂_r𝒟 = r𝒟⁻¹; so dx = r𝒟⁻¹ω dr + 𝒟 dω, with ⟨r𝒟⁻¹ω, 𝒟 dω⟩ = r⟨ω, dω⟩ = 0 and |r𝒟⁻¹ω|² = r² xᵀ𝒟⁻⁴x = r²ϱ²/Π by
Lemma 22.14 (a). Hence

    |dx|² = (r²ϱ²/Π) dr² + ⟨(r²I − A²) dω, dω⟩,     ϱ² = r² + s + ωᵀA²ω,

with ϱ² of (22.12). Write a covector as ν = −E dt + p_r dr + η, η ∈ T*_ω𝕊³, with t the Kerr–Schild
time, |η|²_(𝕊³) its round norm and |η|²_(e,r) its norm for the second term of |dx|². Put Y_r := (r²I − A²)⁻¹A, which is
antisymmetric, so that Y_rω ∈ T_ω𝕊³; Ẽ := E + η(Y_rω); 𝒯 := |η|²_(𝕊³) − ϱ²|η|²_(e,r); and

    𝔄 := (Π/r²) p_r² − r²E² − 𝒯 − m(Ẽ + p_r)²,     𝔎 := |η|²_(𝕊³) − (s + ωᵀA²ω) E².    (22.15)

*A frame.* Rotating, A = aJ₁₂ + bJ₃₄ with J₁₂ = e₁e₂ᵀ − e₂e₁ᵀ and J₃₄ = e₃e₄ᵀ − e₄e₃ᵀ, and
ω = (sin ϑ e^(iφ), cos ϑ e^(iψ)). Put Φ := η(J₁₂ω) and Ψ := η(J₃₄ω), the generators of the two rotations; as
J₁₂ω = −∂_φ and J₃₄ω = −∂_ψ, they are minus the momenta conjugate to φ and ψ. Then ϱ² = r² + a² cos²ϑ + b² sin²ϑ and

    𝔎 = p_ϑ² + Φ²/sin²ϑ + Ψ²/cos²ϑ − (a² cos²ϑ + b² sin²ϑ) E²,     η(Y_rω) = aΦ/(r² + a²) + bΨ/(r² + b²),
    𝒯 = (a² − b²)(Φ²/(r² + a²) − Ψ²/(r² + b²)).    (22.16)

So 𝔄 depends on (r, p_r, E, Φ, Ψ) only, and 𝔎 on (ϑ, p_ϑ, E, Φ, Ψ) only. The frame is used only to compute; every
statement below is about the frame-free functions (22.15).

**Lemma 22.19** (Separation.) On T*(ℝ_t × {|x| ≥ r₀ − 2δ₀}), with 𝒢 := 𝔄 + 𝔎 and g_b written in the
Kerr–Schild time t (that is, g^KS_b):

(a) ϱ² g_b⁻¹(ν, ν) = 𝒢.

(b) E, 𝔎 and, in any frame, Φ and Ψ are constant along the flow of H_𝒢, and they Poisson-commute with each other.

(c) 𝔄 = αp_r² + 2βp_r + γ with α := Δ_b/r², β := −mẼ and γ := −r²E² − 𝒯 − mẼ². With p̃ := αp_r + β and the
*radial function* ℛ := β² − α(γ + 𝔎), α𝒢 = p̃² − ℛ.

(d) H_𝒢 r = 2p̃ and H_𝒢 p̃ = ∂_rℛ + (α′/α)(p̃² − ℛ), where ∂_r is taken at fixed (ω, η). In a frame, ℛ, α, β and p̃
depend on (ω, η) only through (Φ, Ψ, 𝔎), and H_𝒢 f = 0 for every function f of (E, Φ, Ψ, 𝔎).

*Proof.* (a) By Lemma 21.16 (d), g_b⁻¹ = η_M⁻¹ − H_(m,A) k_A^♯ ⊗ k_A^♯ with η_M := −dt² + dx² the Minkowski
metric and k_A^♯ = −∂_t + ℓ_A^♯. From the formula for |dx|², η_M⁻¹(ν, ν) = −E² + (Π/(r²ϱ²)) p_r² + |η|²_(e,r). The
coefficient vector of ℓ_A is 𝒟⁻²(rI + A)x = r𝒟⁻²x + 𝒟⁻¹Aω (Lemma 22.14). At fixed ω, ∂_r x = r𝒟⁻¹ω = r𝒟⁻²x,
and the vector 𝒟⁻¹Aω = 𝒟(Y_rω) is the image of Y_rω ∈ T_ω𝕊³ under (r, ω) ↦ x at fixed r. So ℓ_A^♯ = ∂_r + Y_rω in
the coordinates (r, ω), and ν(k_A^♯) = E + p_r + η(Y_rω) = Ẽ + p_r. By Lemma 22.14 (b), H_(m,A) = m/ϱ².
Hence

    ϱ² g_b⁻¹(ν, ν) = (Π/r²) p_r² − ϱ²E² + ϱ²|η|²_(e,r) − m(Ẽ + p_r)²,

and ϱ²E² = r²E² + (s + ωᵀA²ω)E² and ϱ²|η|²_(e,r) = |η|²_(𝕊³) − 𝒯 give (a).

*The frame formulas (22.16).* In the frame, r²I − A² = diag(r² + a², r² + a², r² + b², r² + b²) and
dω = (cos ϑ e^(iφ) dϑ + i sin ϑ e^(iφ) dφ, −sin ϑ e^(iψ) dϑ + i cos ϑ e^(iψ) dψ), so

    ⟨(r²I − A²) dω, dω⟩ = ϱ² dϑ² + (r² + a²) sin²ϑ dφ² + (r² + b²) cos²ϑ dψ²,

since (r² + a²) cos²ϑ + (r² + b²) sin²ϑ = ϱ². The round metric is dϑ² + sin²ϑ dφ² + cos²ϑ dψ². With p_φ = −Φ and
p_ψ = −Ψ, |η|²_(𝕊³) = p_ϑ² + Φ²/sin²ϑ + Ψ²/cos²ϑ and |η|²_(e,r) = p_ϑ²/ϱ² + Φ²/((r² + a²) sin²ϑ) +
Ψ²/((r² + b²) cos²ϑ). Writing ϱ² = r² + a² − (a² − b²) sin²ϑ in the second term and ϱ² = r² + b² + (a² − b²) cos²ϑ in
the third,

    ϱ²|η|²_(e,r) = |η|²_(𝕊³) − (a² − b²) Φ²/(r² + a²) + (a² − b²) Ψ²/(r² + b²),

which is the formula for 𝒯. Next, s + ωᵀA²ω = a² + b² − a² sin²ϑ − b² cos²ϑ = a² cos²ϑ + b² sin²ϑ gives 𝔎. Finally
(r²I − A²)⁻¹ is (r² + a²)⁻¹ on span(e₁, e₂) and (r² + b²)⁻¹ on span(e₃, e₄), which contain J₁₂ω and J₃₄ω, so
Y_rω = aJ₁₂ω/(r² + a²) + bJ₃₄ω/(r² + b²) and η(Y_rω) is as stated. The proof of (a) chose no frame; the frame enters
only these formulas.

(b) E is the momentum of the Killing field ∂_t. In a frame, where sin 2ϑ ≠ 0, the coordinates (t, r, ϑ, φ, ψ) and
their conjugate momenta (−E, p_r, p_ϑ, −Φ, −Ψ) are canonical, and by (22.16) 𝔄 and 𝔎 share only the momenta
E, Φ, Ψ, whose coordinates t, φ, ψ appear in neither. So {𝔄, 𝔎} = 0, hence {𝒢, 𝔎} = 0, and E, Φ, Ψ Poisson-commute
with 𝔄, 𝔎 and with each other. These identities hold on a dense open set and so everywhere, by continuity; E and 𝔎 are
defined without a frame.

(c) is algebra: Π/r² − m = Δ_b/r² = α, so 𝔄 = αp_r² − 2mẼp_r − r²E² − 𝒯 − mẼ², and
α𝔄 = (αp_r + β)² − β² + αγ. Adding α𝔎 gives α𝒢 = p̃² − ℛ.

(d) In a frame, 𝔎 does not involve (r, p_r), and α, β and p̃ are functions of (r, p_r, E, Φ, Ψ); so
H_𝒢 r = ∂_(p_r)𝒢 = ∂_(p_r)𝔄 = 2αp_r + 2β = 2p̃. Since E, Φ and Ψ are conserved, H_𝒢 p̃ = ∂_(p_r)𝒢 · ∂_r p̃ −
∂_r𝒢 · ∂_(p_r)p̃ = 2p̃ ∂_r p̃ − α ∂_r𝒢, with ∂_r at fixed (p_r, ϑ, p_ϑ, Φ, Ψ, E), that is at fixed (ω, η). From
𝒢 = α⁻¹(p̃² − ℛ), α∂_r𝒢 = −(α′/α)(p̃² − ℛ) + 2p̃ ∂_r p̃ − ∂_rℛ. Hence H_𝒢 p̃ = ∂_rℛ + (α′/α)(p̃² − ℛ). The last claim
is (b). ∎

So on the characteristic set Σ = {𝒢 = 0} over {r > r₊}, where α > 0, p̃² = ℛ(r), with ℛ evaluated at the constant
values of (E, Φ, Ψ, 𝔎) along the curve, and the pair (r, p̃) moves as a particle in the potential −ℛ:
H_𝒢 r = 2p̃, H_𝒢 p̃ = ∂_rℛ. For a covector ν = −z₀ dt + ζ as in Section 22.2, E = z₀; the Hamilton vector field of
G_(z₀) = ϱ⁻²𝒢 on Σ is ϱ⁻²H_𝒢, and the future field on Σ^±_(z₀) is ±ϱ⁻²H_𝒢. This is [Hin26c, (4.30)–(4.32)] and
Carter's constant, for Myers–Perry.

### 22.12 The radial function

Put Λ := 𝔎 + sE² = |η|²_(𝕊³) + E²|Aω|² ≥ |η|²_(𝕊³), using −ωᵀA²ω = |Aω|². In a frame, with u := r², the function
𝒫(u) := uΠℛ is

    𝒫 = m(ΠE + aΦ(u + b²) + bΨ(u + a²))² + Δ_b(uΠE² + (a² − b²)(Φ²(u + b²) − Ψ²(u + a²)) − 𝔎Π),    (22.17)

a polynomial of degree 5 in u whose coefficients are polynomials in (m, a, b, E, Φ, Ψ, Λ). Indeed, with α = Δ_b/u,
β = −mẼ and m + Δ_b/u = Π/u, ℛ = m²Ẽ² + (Δ_b/u)(uE² + 𝒯 + mẼ² − 𝔎) = mẼ²Π/u + (Δ_b/u)(uE² + 𝒯 − 𝔎); and
Π = (u + a²)(u + b²), so ΠẼ = ΠE + aΦ(u + b²) + bΨ(u + a²) and Π𝒯 = (a² − b²)(Φ²(u + b²) − Ψ²(u + a²)), by
(22.16). Multiplying by uΠ gives (22.17); its terms have degrees at most 4, 5, 3 and 4 in u, the
coefficient of u⁵ is E², and 𝔎 = Λ − (a² + b²)E². Then 𝒬(w) := w⁵𝒫(w⁻¹) is a polynomial in w with 𝒬(0) = E², and at
A = 0, where Π = u², Δ_b = u² − mu, Ẽ = E, 𝒯 = 0 and 𝔎 = Λ, 𝒫 = u⁵E² − Λu⁴ + mΛu³, so

    𝒬 = E² − Λw + mΛw².    (22.18)

ℛ(r) = r⁸𝒬(r⁻²)/Π(r), so ℛ and 𝒬(r⁻²) have the same sign and the same zeros, with multiplicity, as Π > 0. ℛ and 𝒬 are
homogeneous of degree 2 in (E, Φ, Ψ, Λ^(1/2)), so their signs and zeros depend only on the normalised values in

    𝔑 := {(E, Φ, Ψ, Λ) : E² + Λ/m₀ = 1, (|Φ| + |Ψ|)² ≤ Λ},

a compact set. Every covector with E ≠ 0 (as in every use below, where E = z₀) has its normalised values in 𝔑:
by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, |η|²_(𝕊³) ≥ Φ²/sin²ϑ + Ψ²/cos²ϑ ≥ (|Φ| + |Ψ|)², and Λ ≥ |η|²_(𝕊³).

**Lemma 22.20** (Convexity.) There is ε_R > 0 such that for |b − b₀| ≤ ε_R, in any frame, and every point
of 𝔑, on [0, 2/m₀]: if Λ ≥ m₀/6, then 𝒬″ ≥ m₀²/12; if Λ < m₀/6, then 𝒬 ≥ ½.

*Proof.* At A = 0 and |m − m₀| ≤ ½m₀, (22.18) gives 𝒬″ = 2mΛ ≥ m₀²/6 when Λ ≥ m₀/6, and
𝒬 ≥ E² − Λ/(4m) ≥ 5/6 − 1/12 = 3/4 when Λ < m₀/6. The coefficients of 𝒬 at (m, A) minus those at (m, 0) are
polynomials in (m, a, b, E, Φ, Ψ, Λ) vanishing at a = b = 0, hence bounded by C‖A‖ on the compact set
𝔑 × {|m − m₀| ≤ ½m₀}, with C independent of the frame, as |a|, |b| ≤ ‖A‖. So the difference is at most C′‖A‖ in
C²([0, 2/m₀]), which is below min(m₀²/12, ¼) for ‖A‖ small. ∎

**Remark 22.21** (Numerical observation.) Sampled at m = m₀ and ‖A‖ ≤ 0.02 m₀^(1/2) on the
face (|Φ| + |Ψ|)² = Λ of 𝔑, the two bounds of Lemma 22.20 were observed with minima of about 0.30 m₀² (for 𝒬″,
where Λ ≥ m₀/6) and 0.788 (for 𝒬, where Λ < m₀/6). No proof uses this; Lemma 22.20 rests on the perturbation
argument above.

**Corollary 22.22** (The radial structure.) Let ε_R also be so small that r₊(b)⁻² < 2/m₀, and
let |b − b₀| ≤ ε_R and E ≠ 0. Then on (r₊, ∞):

(a) ℛ > 0 near ∞, and {r > r₊ : ℛ(r) < 0} is an interval, possibly empty.

(b) A double zero r_c of ℛ in (r₊, ∞) has ∂_r²ℛ(r_c) > 0, and then ℛ > 0 on (r₊, ∞) ∖ {r_c}.

(c) For every δ > 0 there is ε(δ) ≤ ε_R such that for |b − b₀| ≤ ε(δ) every double zero has |r_c − (2m)^(1/2)| < δ
and |Λ − 4mE²| < δE².

*Proof.* In w = r⁻² ∈ (0, w₊), w₊ := r₊⁻², 𝒬(0) = E² > 0, and 𝒬 is either positive on [0, w₊] or strictly convex
there (Lemma 22.20, after normalising). A strictly convex function is negative on an interval and has a double
zero only at its minimum, with 𝒬″ > 0; it is then positive elsewhere. As ℛ = r⁸𝒬(r⁻²)/Π and dw/dr ≠ 0, this gives
(a) and (b), with ∂_r²ℛ(r_c) = (r_c⁸/Π) 𝒬″(w_c)(dw/dr)² > 0, the other terms vanishing with 𝒬(w_c) and 𝒬′(w_c).
(c) Suppose b_n → b₀ and normalised double zeros (π_n, w_n) ∈ 𝔑 × [0, 2/m₀] have a limit (π, w). By continuity it is a
double zero of (22.18) at m = m₀: E² − Λw(1 − m₀w) = 0 = −Λ(1 − 2m₀w). Λ = 0 would give E² = 1 and
𝒬(w) = 1, so w = 1/(2m₀) and Λ = 4m₀E². Compactness gives (c). ∎
