This is [Hin26c, Lemmas 4.11–4.12] near b₀. [Hin26c, Lemma 4.12] proves its convexity for all subextremal Kerr metrics;
here the convexity of 𝒬 in w = r⁻² is proved by perturbation from (22.18), which suffices near b₀.

### 22.13 The trapped set near b₀

Fix z₀ ∈ {1, −1}, so E = z₀ and E² = 1. Let I_Γ := ((1.2m₀)^(1/2), (3m₀)^(1/2)), which contains r_ph = (2m₀)^(1/2)
and lies in (r_h, 7R₁/4), and 𝒲 := {(ω, η) ∈ T*𝕊³ : 3m₀ < |η|²_(𝕊³) < 5m₀}.

**Lemma 22.23** (The critical radius.) There is ε_Γ ∈ (0, ε_R] such that for |b − b₀| < ε_Γ: ∂_r²ℛ > 0 on
Ī_Γ × 𝒲̄; ∂_rℛ(·; ω, η) has a unique zero r_c(ω, η) ∈ I_Γ; and with ℛ_c := ℛ(r_c) and 𝒮 := (ℛ − ℛ_c)/(r − r_c)², the
functions r_c, ℛ_c on 𝒲̄ and 𝒮 on Ī_Γ × 𝒲̄ are smooth in (b, ·), 𝒮 > 0, and dℛ_c ≠ 0 on
{ℛ_c = 0} ∩ 𝒲̄ ⊂ {3.5m₀ < |η|² < 4.5m₀}. In a frame they depend on (ω, η) only through (Φ, Ψ, 𝔎). At b₀, with
C = |η|²: r_c² = C/2, ℛ_c = C(m₀ − C/4) and 𝒮 = (r + r_c)².

*Proof.* At b₀, ℛ = r⁸𝒬(r⁻²)/r⁴ = r⁴ − C(r² − m₀) by (22.18) with Λ = C, so ∂_rℛ = 2r(2r² − C) vanishes at
r² = C/2 ∈ (1.5m₀, 2.5m₀), and ∂_r²ℛ = 12r² − 2C ≥ 14.4m₀ − 10m₀ > 0 on Ī_Γ × 𝒲̄. Then ℛ_c = C(m₀ − C/4) vanishes on
𝒲̄ only at C = 4m₀, where dℛ_c = (m₀ − C/2) dC = −m₀ dC ≠ 0, and ℛ − ℛ_c = r⁴ − Cr² + C²/4 = (r² − C/2)², so
𝒮 = (r² − r_c²)²/(r − r_c)² = (r + r_c)². ℛ is smooth in (b, r, ω, η) and Ī_Γ × 𝒲̄ is compact, so ℛ_b → ℛ_(b₀) in C³
there. Hence for b near b₀, ∂_r²ℛ > 0, ∂_rℛ has exactly one zero in I_Γ, smooth in (b, ω, η) by the implicit function
theorem, and the statements on ℛ_c persist. 𝒮 = ∫₀¹ (1 − τ) ∂_r²ℛ(r_c + τ(r − r_c)) dτ is smooth and positive. The
frame statement holds because it holds for ℛ (Lemma 22.19 (d)). ∎

On O := {(r, ω; p_r, η) : r ∈ I_Γ, (ω, η) ∈ 𝒲} define

    φ_± := p̃ ∓ (r − r_c)√𝒮,     T_Γ := ∂_r((r − r_c)√𝒮),     Γ_b := Σ_(z₀) ∩ {φ₊ = φ₋ = 0} ∩ O.    (22.19)

**Proposition 22.24** ((Γ.1)–(Γ.3) near b₀.) Let |b − b₀| < ε_Γ. In the variables of the Kerr–Schild
time:

(a) Γ_b = {r = r_c, p̃ = 0, ℛ_c = 0} ∩ O. It is a compact submanifold of codimension 2 of Σ_(z₀), invariant under the
flow, and Γ_(b₀) is the set Γ of (22.7).

(b) On Σ_(z₀) ∩ O, φ₊φ₋ = ℛ_c, and the future field 𝖧 := z₀ϱ⁻²H_𝒢 satisfies

    𝖧φ₊ = −2z₀ϱ⁻²T_Γ φ₊,     𝖧φ₋ = 2z₀ϱ⁻²T_Γ φ₋,    (22.20)

with T_Γ = √𝒮 > 0 on Γ_b.

(c) (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) hold with (φ_u, φ_s) := (φ₊, φ₋) for z₀ = 1 and (φ₋, −φ₊) for z₀ = −1, ν_u = ν_s = 2ϱ⁻²T_Γ, and
{φ_u, φ_s} = 2α√𝒮 > 0 on Γ_b. At b₀, ν_u = ν_s = 4(2m₀)^(−1/2) on Γ.

(d) The same holds for g̃_b with the time function Ψ_b^* t_*, after the fibre translation of Lemma 22.2 from t
to t_* and the cotangent lift of the diffeomorphism Ψ_b of Lemma 22.16. All the data are smooth in b with values in
C^∞, Γ̃_b ⊂ T*{r₂ < r < ρ₁⁻¹}, and ν_min(b), β_Γ(b) := ½ min_(Γ̃_b) |q_(z₀)| and max_(Γ̃_b) |q^Γ − 4| tend to
4(2m₀)^(−1/2), 2 and 0 as b → b₀.

*Proof.* (a) φ₊ = φ₋ = 0 means p̃ = 0 and (r − r_c)√𝒮 = 0, so r = r_c; on Σ, Lemma 22.19 (c) then gives
0 = p̃² − ℛ = −ℛ_c. Conversely, r = r_c, p̃ = 0 and ℛ_c = 0 give 𝒢 = α⁻¹(p̃² − ℛ) = 0. By Lemma 22.23, (ω, η)
ranges over the compact set {ℛ_c = 0} ∩ 𝒲̄, which lies inside 𝒲, and (r, p_r) is a smooth function of (ω, η) on it
(r = r_c, p_r = −β/α). So Γ_b is compact, and it is smooth of codimension 2 in Σ by (c) below. It is invariant: on Γ_b,
H_𝒢 r = 2p̃ = 0 and H_𝒢 p̃ = ∂_rℛ(r_c) = 0, while r_c and ℛ_c are constant along the flow (Lemma 22.19 (d)). At
b₀, p̃ = (r² − m₀)p_r − m₀E, and the static time t_s = t − F_s, F_s′ = m₀/(r² − m₀), moves p_r to ξ_s = p_r − z₀F_s′
(Lemma 22.2 (a)). So p̃ = (r² − m₀)ξ_s, and {r = r_ph, p̃ = 0, C = 4m₀} is the set of (22.7).

(b) On Σ ∩ O, φ₊φ₋ = p̃² − (r − r_c)²𝒮 = ℛ − (r − r_c)²𝒮 = ℛ_c. By Lemma 22.19 (d), on Σ: H_𝒢 r = 2p̃;
H_𝒢 p̃ = ∂_rℛ = 2(r − r_c)𝒮 + (r − r_c)²∂_r𝒮, as ℛ_c does not depend on r; and H_𝒢 annihilates r_c and ℛ_c and acts on
𝒮 through r only. Hence H_𝒢((r − r_c)√𝒮) = 2p̃ T_Γ. Since 2√𝒮 ∂_r√𝒮 = ∂_r𝒮,

    2(r − r_c)√𝒮 T_Γ = 2(r − r_c)𝒮 + (r − r_c)² ∂_r𝒮 = ∂_rℛ,

so H_𝒢 p̃ = 2(r − r_c)√𝒮 T_Γ, and H_𝒢φ_± = 2(r − r_c)√𝒮 T_Γ ∓ 2p̃ T_Γ = ∓2T_Γ(p̃ ∓ (r − r_c)√𝒮) = ∓2T_Γφ_±
exactly. Multiplying by z₀ϱ⁻² gives (22.20). On Γ_b, r = r_c, so T_Γ = √𝒮.

(c) (Γ.2) is (22.20), the sign choices making φ_u decay and φ_s grow along 𝖧; ν_(u/s) are smooth and positive
near Γ_b. For (Γ.1) and (Γ.3): at Γ_b, d𝒢 = α⁻¹(2p̃ dp̃ − dℛ) = −α⁻¹dℛ_c, as p̃ = 0, ∂_rℛ = 0, and
d_((ω,η))ℛ = dℛ_c at r = r_c (since ∂_rℛ(r_c) = 0). So dG_(z₀) = ϱ⁻²d𝒢 ≠ 0. At Γ_b, dφ_± = dp̃ ∓ √𝒮(dr − dr_c). Of
the three covectors dφ₊, dφ₋, dℛ_c, only dp̃ has a dp_r component (it is α ≠ 0), while r_c and ℛ_c are functions of
(ω, η), so dr_c and dℛ_c have neither a dp_r nor a dr component. If c₊ dφ₊ + c₋ dφ₋ + c₀ dℛ_c = 0, the dp_r component
gives (c₊ + c₋)α = 0, so c₋ = −c₊ and the dp̃ terms cancel, leaving −2c₊√𝒮(dr − dr_c) + c₀ dℛ_c = 0; its dr component
gives 2c₊√𝒮 = 0. So c₊ = c₋ = 0, and c₀ = 0 as dℛ_c ≠ 0; the three covectors are independent. Hence Γ_u and Γ_s
are smooth hypersurfaces of Σ near Γ_b, meeting transversally in Γ_b, and 𝖧 is tangent to both by (22.20).
For the bracket, {φ₊, φ₋} = 2{p̃, (r − r_c)√𝒮}, which at r = r_c is 2√𝒮({p̃, r} − {p̃, r_c}) = 2α√𝒮. Here
{p̃, r} = ∂_(p_r)p̃ = α, and {p̃, r_c} = 0 because, in a frame, p̃ is a function of (r, p_r, Φ, Ψ) and r_c of
(Φ, Ψ, 𝔎), which Poisson-commute (Lemma 22.19 (b)). α > 0 on I_Γ, as I_Γ ⊂ (r₊, ∞). For z₀ = −1,
{φ₋, −φ₊} = {φ₊, φ₋}. At b₀, ϱ² = r_ph² = 2m₀ and √𝒮 = 2r_ph on Γ, so ν = 4r_ph/(2m₀) = 4(2m₀)^(−1/2), the rate of
Proposition 22.8.

(d) dt and dt_* are timelike for g_b (Lemma 21.16 (e) with β = 0, valid by Lemma 21.19, and
Lemma 22.6). They are co-oriented: g_b⁻¹(dt, dt_*) cannot vanish where both are timelike, the region is
connected, and near infinity it is close to η_M⁻¹(dt, dt − d|x|) = −1. The difference t − t_* is a function of |x|
((21.27), (21.30)). So Lemma 22.2 (a)–(b) carries Γ_b, φ_(u/s), (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) and the future
field to t_*, and the cotangent lift of Ψ_b, a symplectomorphism intertwining the Hamilton vector fields, carries them
to g̃_b. Everything in (22.19) is built from frame-free functions smooth in (b, ·), and so are the two maps.
At b₀, Γ ⊂ {r = r_ph} and r₂ < r_ph < 3R₁ = ρ₁⁻¹; by continuity Γ̃_b stays in T*{r₂ < r < ρ₁⁻¹}. q_(z₀) is continuous
in b and the point, and on Γ_(b₀) it is 4z₀ in t_* (Theorem 22.12); so β_Γ(b) → 2 and q^Γ → 4 uniformly. In
particular, after shrinking O uniformly in b, z₀q_(z₀) > 0 on Σ_(z₀) ∩ O, so there Σ_(z₀) agrees with the set
Σ^♭_(z₀) = Σ^(z₀)_(z₀) = Σ_(z₀) ∩ {z₀q_(z₀) > 0} of (H7), and the Γ_(u/s) of (22.19) are those of (H7). For
the continuity in b that (H5) asks, φ_(u/s) are taken on a fixed neighbourhood of Γ̃_(b₀) contained in the transported
O_b for every b near b₀. ∎

This is [Hin26c, Lemmas 4.14–4.18 and Definitions 4.13, 4.15, 4.17] for Myers–Perry near Tangherlini. The separation
gives the separatrices in closed form, smooth in b; the persistence of normally hyperbolic manifolds would give them
only in C^k for each k, on neighbourhoods shrinking with k.

### 22.14 r-normal hyperbolicity near b₀

(K3) concerns z₀ = 1 and 𝖵 := q₁⁻¹H_(G₁) on Σ^♭₁ near Γ. Its tangential bound, for every ϵ > 0, is the substance;
[Hin26c, Proposition 4.19 (3)] proves it for Kerr from the integrable structure of the flow on the trapped set, and so
does this section, for the flow of 𝔎 on T*𝕊³. At b ≠ b₀ that flow is not periodic.

**Lemma 22.25** (The flow on Γ_b.) Let |b − b₀| < ε_Γ and z₀ = 1. The projection
π : (r, ω; p_r, η) ↦ (ω, η) restricts to a diffeomorphism of Γ_b onto Γ^𝕊_b := {ℛ_c = 0} ∩ 𝒲, and
π_*(H_𝒢|_(Γ_b)) = H_𝔥 on Γ^𝕊_b, where 𝔥 := 𝔎 + 𝔄(r_c, p_r^c; ·) on 𝒲 and p_r^c := −β(r_c)/α(r_c). In a frame, 𝔥 is
a smooth function of (𝔎, Φ, Ψ), so H_𝔥 = c₀H_𝔎 + c₁H_Φ + c₂H_Ψ, with c₀, c₁, c₂ the partial derivatives of that
function, constant along each orbit.

*Proof.* The inverse is (ω, η) ↦ (r_c, ω; p_r^c, η) (Proposition 22.24 (a)). The (ω, η)-components of
H_𝒢 = H_𝔄 + H_𝔎 are those of the Hamilton vector field on T*𝕊³ of 𝔎 + 𝔄(r, p_r; ·) with (r, p_r) frozen. This differs
from H_𝔥 by (∂_r𝔄)H_(r_c) + (∂_(p_r)𝔄)H_(p_r^c). On Γ_b, ∂_(p_r)𝔄 = 2p̃ = 0, and ∂_r𝔄 = −H_𝒢 p_r = 0, because
p_r = p_r^c there is a function of the conserved (Φ, Ψ, 𝔎) and Γ_b is invariant. In a frame, 𝔄(r, p_r; ·) depends on
(ω, η) through (Φ, Ψ), and r_c, p_r^c through (Φ, Ψ, 𝔎) (Lemma 22.23). The Hamilton vector fields of 𝔎, Φ and
Ψ commute (Lemma 22.19 (b)), so the c_i are constant along orbits. ∎

Let 𝒴 := {(ω, η) : 3m₀ ≤ 𝔎 ≤ 5m₀} ⊂ T*𝕊³ (with E² = 1), compact and invariant under H_𝔎, H_Φ and H_Ψ; for b near b₀
it contains Γ^𝕊_b. Fix any Riemannian metric on T*𝕊³ for the norms.

**Lemma 22.26** (The flow of 𝔎.) Let ‖A‖² ≤ m₀/100. For every p ∈ 𝒴 there is C_p
with |D_p e^(sH_𝔎) v| ≤ C_p(1 + |s|)|v| for all v and all s ∈ ℝ.

*Proof.* Work in a frame, with Ξ := (Ξ₀, Ξ₁, Ξ₂) := (𝔎, Φ, Ψ) and X₀ := H_𝔎, X₁ := H_Φ, X₂ := H_Ψ, which commute.
With Φ, Ψ fixed, write U(ϑ) := Φ²/sin²ϑ + Ψ²/cos²ϑ − a² + (a² − b²) sin²ϑ, so that 𝔎 = p_ϑ² + U (with E² = 1). Then

    U″ ≥ 2Φ²/sin²ϑ + 2Ψ²/cos²ϑ − 2|a² − b²|,    (22.21)

since (sin⁻²ϑ)″ = 2 sin⁻²ϑ + 6 cos²ϑ sin⁻⁴ϑ ≥ 2 sin⁻²ϑ, (cos⁻²ϑ)″ = 2 cos⁻²ϑ + 6 sin²ϑ cos⁻⁴ϑ ≥ 2 cos⁻²ϑ, and
(sin²ϑ)″ = 2 cos 2ϑ ≥ −2. On 𝒴, wherever p_ϑ = 0, Φ²/sin²ϑ + Ψ²/cos²ϑ = 𝔎 + a² − (a² − b²) sin²ϑ ≥ 3m₀ − 2‖A‖², so
U″ ≥ 6m₀ − 6‖A‖² > 0 there.

*The singular set.* Let Z := {p ∈ 𝒴 : dΞ₀, dΞ₁, dΞ₂ are dependent at p}. Where sin 2ϑ ≠ 0, (ϑ, φ, ψ) and their momenta
are canonical coordinates, dΦ and dΨ are independent, and d𝔎 = 2p_ϑ dp_ϑ + U′ dϑ + (…) dΦ + (…) dΨ. So p ∈ Z there
if and only if p_ϑ = 0 = U′(ϑ). If Φ = 0, then U′ = 2 sin ϑ cos ϑ (Ψ²/cos⁴ϑ + a² − b²) > 0, since
Ψ²/cos⁴ϑ ≥ Ψ²/cos²ϑ ≥ 3m₀ − 2‖A‖² > |a² − b²| there; likewise for Ψ = 0. So these points of Z have ΦΨ ≠ 0 and lie on
Z₁ := {p_ϑ = 0, ϑ = ϑ₀(Φ, Ψ)}, ϑ₀ a critical point of U: a family of invariant 2-tori, one for each (Φ, Ψ) and ϑ₀.
Near ω₁ = 0 use y := ω₁ ∈ ℂ ≅ ℝ², ω = (y, (1 − |y|²)^(1/2) e^(iψ)), with momenta (η_y, η_ψ). The round metric
is |dy|² + (y·dy)²/(1 − |y|²) + (1 − |y|²) dψ², whose inverse on the y-block is I − yyᵀ, and |y| = sin ϑ; so

    𝔎 = |η_y|² − (y·η_y)² + η_ψ²/(1 − |y|²) − a² + (a² − b²)|y|²,    (22.22)

Ψ = −η_ψ and Φ = −(y₁η₂ − y₂η₁). At y = 0, dΦ = −(η₂ dy₁ − η₁ dy₂), dΨ = −dη_ψ and d𝔎 = 2η_y·dη_y + 2η_ψ dη_ψ. These
are independent if η_y ≠ 0. If η_y = 0, the point lies on Z₂ := {y = 0, η_y = 0}, a family of invariant circles, one
for each η_ψ (by (22.22), ẏ = η̇_y = 0 there). The same holds near ω₂ = 0, with a, b and Φ, Ψ exchanged,
giving the family of circles Z₂′. So Z = Z₁ ∪ Z₂ ∪ Z₂′.

*The singular levels.* Every local maximum ϑ_m of U has U″(ϑ_m) ≤ 0. By (22.21),
Φ²/sin²ϑ_m + Ψ²/cos²ϑ_m ≤ |a² − b²| there, so U(ϑ_m) ≤ 2‖A‖² < 3m₀. Hence for ΦΨ ≠ 0 and k ∈ [3m₀, 5m₀], {U ≤ k} is an
interval, as U → ∞ at both ends and every local maximum lies below k. If k = U(ϑ₀) is a critical value, then
U″(ϑ₀) > 0, ϑ₀ is the unique minimum, and Ξ⁻¹(Ξ(p)) for p ∈ Z₁ is the torus through p. For p ∈ Z₂,
Ξ(p) = (Ψ₀² − a², 0, Ψ₀). A point with Φ = 0, Ψ = Ψ₀ and ϑ > 0 has 𝔎 ≥ U(ϑ), and
U(ϑ) − (Ψ₀² − a²) = Ψ₀² tan²ϑ + (a² − b²) sin²ϑ > 0 because Ψ₀² ≥ 3m₀ − ‖A‖² > |a² − b²|. So Ξ⁻¹(Ξ(p)) is the circle
of Z₂ through p; likewise for Z₂′. Consequently every fibre of Ξ that meets Z lies in Z, and for p ∈ 𝒴 ∖ Z the
connected component L of Ξ⁻¹(Ξ(p)) ∩ 𝒴 containing p is compact and disjoint from Z.

*Regular orbits.* Let p ∉ Z and let V be a compact neighbourhood of L in 𝒴 ∖ Z. On V the X_i are independent and span
⋂_j ker dΞ_j: each X_i annihilates every Ξ_j, and both spaces have dimension 3. Let Y_i := Σ_j (𝔊⁻¹)_ij ∇Ξ_j, with
𝔊_ij := ⟨∇Ξ_i, ∇Ξ_j⟩, so that dΞ_j(Y_i) = δ_ij; the X_i and Y_i form a bounded frame on V. Since dΞ_k is closed and
X₀Ξ_k = 0, dΞ_k([X₀, Y_i]) = X₀(dΞ_k(Y_i)) − Y_i(X₀Ξ_k) = 0, so [X₀, Y_i] = Σ_j d_ij X_j with d_ij bounded on V. Let
p_s := e^(sX₀)p. Then De^(sX₀) X_i(p) = X_i(p_s), and W_i(s) := De^(−sX₀) Y_i(p_s) satisfies
W_i′ = Σ_j d_ij(p_s) X_j(p), so De^(sX₀) Y_i(p) = Y_i(p_s) − Σ_j c_ij(s) X_j(p_s) with
c_ij(s) = ∫₀^s d_ij(p_(s′)) ds′, |c_ij| ≤ C|s|. Hence |D_p e^(sX₀)| ≤ C_p(1 + |s|).

*The tori Z₁.* On Z₁, sin 2ϑ₀ ≠ 0. Along the orbit the linearised equations, in the canonical coordinates, are
δΦ̇ = δΨ̇ = 0 and

    d/ds (δϑ, δp_ϑ) = (2δp_ϑ, −U″(ϑ₀) δϑ − ∂_Φ U′ δΦ − ∂_Ψ U′ δΨ),

with constant coefficients, and δφ̇, δψ̇ linear in (δϑ, δΦ, δΨ) with constant coefficients. As U″(ϑ₀) > 0 the matrix
of the (δϑ, δp_ϑ)-system is invertible with imaginary eigenvalues, so (δϑ, δp_ϑ) is bounded and (δφ, δψ) grows at most
linearly. *The circles Z₂, Z₂′.* By (22.22), the Hessian of 𝔎 at Z₂ has no terms mixing (y, η_y) with
(ψ, η_ψ), so the linearisation splits: δẏ = 2δη_y and δη̇_y = −2(Ψ₀² + a² − b²) δy, an oscillator since
Ψ₀² + a² − b² > 0; and δη̇_ψ = 0, δψ̇ = 2δη_ψ. So the growth is at most linear. ∎

The singular orbits are the 2-tori of Z₁ and the circles of Z₂ and Z₂′, where Kerr has its equatorial set; all are
elliptic near b₀.

**Lemma 22.27** (Reparametrisation; compare [Hin26c, Lemma 4.20].) Let V₁ be a smooth vector field, a > 0
smooth, V₂ := aV₁, and let the V₂-orbit of p lie in a compact set on which a, 1/a, |da| ≤ c_a.
If |D_p e^(sV₁)| ≤ c(1 + |s|)^k for s ∈ ℝ, then |D_p e^(sV₂)| ≤ c′(1 + |s|)^(k+1).

*Proof.* e^(sV₂)p = e^(τ(s)V₁)p with τ′ = a(e^(sV₂)p), τ(0) = 0, so |τ| ≤ c_a|s|. Then
D_p e^(sV₂) = D_p e^(τV₁) + V₁ ⊗ D_pτ, and ∂_s D_pτ = da(D_p e^(τV₁)) + (V₁a) D_pτ. Along the orbit,
V₁a = ∂_s log a(e^(sV₂)p), so ∂_s(D_pτ/a) = da(D_p e^(τV₁))/a
and |D_pτ(s)| ≤ c_a³ ∫₀^(|s|) c(1 + c_as′)^k ds′. As V₁ is bounded on the compact set, the bound follows. ∎

**Proposition 22.28** ((K3) and (K4) near b₀.) There is ε_K ∈ (0, ε_Γ) such that for |b − b₀| ≤ ε_K, (K3)
holds for g̃_b with Ψ_b^* t_*, and the splitting (15.1) and the constants μ, C, C_ϵ can be chosen continuous in
b and uniform, as (K4) asks.

*Proof.* *Tangential bound.* By Proposition 22.24 (d) it suffices to work in the Kerr–Schild variables of g_b. There,
on Σ^♭₁ near Γ_b, the field 𝖵 of t_*, transported by T_F, is aH_𝒢 with a := (ϱ²q_*)⁻¹, where q_* > 0 is the q₁ of t_*; a
is smooth and positive. Let p ∈ Γ_b. By Lemma 22.25, e^(sH_𝒢)|_(Γ_b) is conjugate by π to e^(sH_𝔥) = e^(sc₀X₀)
e^(sc₁X₁) e^(sc₂X₂), the c_i being constant along the orbit. Differentiating, D_(πp) e^(sH_𝔥) = De^(sc₀X₀) De^(sc₁X₁)
De^(sc₂X₂) + s Σ_i X_i ⊗ dc_i. Here e^(tX₁) and e^(tX₂) are cotangent lifts of rotations of 𝕊³ (by the frame's J₁₂ and
J₃₄), with derivatives bounded uniformly in t on 𝒴. Every b with |b − b₀| ≤ ε_K lies in ℬ (Definition 22.1), so
‖A‖² < m₀/400 and Lemma 22.26 applies; it enters at the rotated point e^(sc₁X₁) e^(sc₂X₂) πp; the rotations
commute with X₀ and have derivatives bounded on 𝒴, so its constant there is at most C·C_(πp).
Hence |D_p e^(sH_𝒢)|_(TΓ_b)| ≤ C_p(1 + |s|)², and by Lemma 22.27, |D_p e^(s𝖵)|_(TΓ_b)| ≤ C′_p(1 + |s|)³. Now let
ϵ > 0. Identify Γ_b with Γ_(b₀) smoothly in b by ι_b(ω, η) := (ω, κ_b(ω, η)η) on Γ^𝕊_(b₀), where κ_b, near 1, solves
ℛ_c(ω, κ_bη) = 0 with ℛ_c taken at b (Lemma 22.23: the radial derivative η·∂_ηℛ_c is −8m₀² ≠ 0 at b₀, from ℛ_c =
C(m₀ − C/4) at C = 4m₀), followed by π⁻¹. The set 𝒮_K := {(b, p) : |b − b₀| ≤ ε_K, p ∈ Γ_b} ≅ {|b − b₀| ≤ ε_K} × Γ_(b₀)
is compact. For each (b, p) ∈ 𝒮_K the polynomial bound gives T ≥ 1 with |D_p e^(±T𝖵_b)|_(TΓ_b)| ≤ e^(ϵT/2). By continuity
in (b, p), read through ι_b, the same T gives e^(ϵT) on a neighbourhood. Finitely many such neighbourhoods cover 𝒮_K,
with times T_j ≤ T_max. Composing the flow over successive times T_j chosen at the current point gives |D_p
e^(s𝖵_b)|_(TΓ_b)| ≤ C_ϵ e^(ϵ|s|) for all (b, p) ∈ 𝒮_K and s ∈ ℝ, with C_ϵ := sup{|De^(t𝖵_b)| : |t| ≤ T_max, (b, p) ∈
𝒮_K}.

*Splitting and normal rates.* On Γ_b, (22.20) gives 𝖵φ_s = (ν_s/q₁)φ_s and 𝖵φ_u = −(ν_u/q₁)φ_u, so
dφ_s(De^(s𝖵)v) = Θ_s dφ_s(v) for v ∈ TΓ_u|_(Γ_b), with Θ_s := exp ∫₀^s (ν_s/q₁)(e^(s′𝖵)p) ds′ ≥ e^(ν′s) for s ≥ 0.
Here ν′ := inf ν_s/q₁ > 0 is uniform in b. Fix ϵ := ν′/4. Let n_u be a smooth section of TΓ_u|_(Γ_b) with
dφ_s(n_u) = 1, which exists by transversality. Write De^(s𝖵) n_u(p) = Θ_s(p) n_u(e^(s𝖵)p) + w_s(p) with
w_s(p) ∈ TΓ_b. An invariant line N^u = span(n_u + h), h a section of TΓ_b, is a fixed point of
(𝒞_t h)(e^(t𝖵)p) := Θ_t(p)⁻¹(De^(t𝖵) h(p) + w_t(p)). For t so large that C_ϵ e^(ϵt) e^(−ν′t) ≤ ½, 𝒞_t is a
contraction on bounded continuous sections, uniformly in b. So h exists, is unique and continuous in (b, p), and
𝒞_s h = h for all s by uniqueness. On N^u, De^(s𝖵) is multiplication by Θ_s, so |De^(s𝖵)v| ≤ Ce^(−ν′|s|)|v| for
s ≤ 0. N^s ⊂ TΓ_s is the same with time reversed. TΓ_b, N^u and N^s span T_(Γ_b)Σ^♭₁: the dimensions are 5 + 1 + 1,
N^u ⊄ TΓ_s as dφ_s(n_u + h) = 1, and TΓ_u ∩ TΓ_s = TΓ_b. This is (15.1) with μ := ν′, continuous in b, with
uniform constants. ∎

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.19 and Lemma 4.20] for Myers–Perry near Tangherlini.

### 22.15 The global dynamics near b₀

**Proposition 22.29** ((H8) near b₀.) There is ε₈ ∈ (0, ε_K] such that for |b − b₀| ≤ ε₈ and
z₀ ∈ {1, −1}, (H8) (a) and (b) hold for g̃_b with Ψ_b^* t_*, the radii of Definition 22.1 and the trapped set of
Proposition 22.24, with Γ̄_(u/s) the global backward and forward trapped sets. The convergence in (a) is uniform on
compact sets of (b, initial point), as the extension of (H5) asks.

*Proof.* All the sets named in (H8) are carried by the cotangent lift of Ψ_b to the corresponding sets for g_b (∂ℛ_± to
the conormal of ℋ_b at fibre infinity), and Ψ_b is the identity on {|x| ≤ 5R₁/8} ⊃ {r < r₀ − δ₀} and on
{|x| ≥ 7R₁/4} (Lemma 22.16; r₀ − δ₀ < r_♭ ≤ ½R₁). So it suffices to prove (H8) for g_b, where the separation
holds. The time function only translates fibres (Lemma 22.2), so the projected curves, r, and the limits at fibre
infinity do not depend on it. Limits over ∂X are read in t_*. Write γ for a maximal integral curve of the future field
in Σ_(z₀) ∩ T*{r > r₀ − 2δ₀}, parametrised by the rescaled field near fibre infinity (Section 22.7).

*Outside the horizon.* On {r_A > r₊}, (r, p̃) moves with p̃² = ℛ(r), ṙ = ±2ϱ⁻²p̃ and (p̃)˙ = ±ϱ⁻²∂_rℛ
(Lemma 22.19 (d)), the conserved values of (Φ, Ψ, 𝔎) fixed. By Corollary 22.22, either ℛ has no double zero,
or it has exactly one, r_c, and then ℛ_c = 0. In the first case r is strictly monotone except at most at one simple
turning point, where p̃ = 0 ≠ ∂_rℛ. Indeed r cannot converge to a point r̄ > r₊: p̃² = ℛ(r̄) > 0 would keep |ṙ| bounded
below, and a simple zero is passed in finite time. So at each end r → r₊ or r → ∞, or the curve leaves {r_A > r₊}. In
the second case ℛ > 0 off r_c, the curve is Γ_b or lies on {φ₊φ₋ = 0}, and r is monotone, tending to r_c at one end
and to r₊ or ∞ at the other. By Corollary 22.22 (c), with ε₈ ≤ ε(δ) for a δ that places r_c in I_Γ and (ω, η) in 𝒲
(|η|²_(𝕊³) = Λ − |Aω|²E²), and Lemma 22.23 (uniqueness of r_c in I_Γ, with {ℛ_c = 0} ∩ 𝒲̄ ⊂ 𝒲), every double
zero lies in O, so these curves are exactly those through {φ_u = 0} ∩ Σ ∩ O (backward asymptotic to Γ_b) or
{φ_s = 0} ∩ Σ ∩ O (forward asymptotic), extended by the flow.

*At infinity.* As r → ∞, ℛ = r⁴E² + O(r²(1 + Λ)) and α = r² + O(1), so p_r = (p̃ − β)/α = sgn(p̃) + O((1 + Λ) r⁻²); and
r_A = |x|(1 + O(|x|⁻²)) (Lemma 21.14 (b)) gives ξ_t = p_r + O((1 + Λ^(1/2)) r⁻²) for the coefficient ξ_t of d|x|,
while |η|/r ≤ Λ^(1/2) r⁻¹. Forward with r → ∞, ṙ > 0 forces sgn p̃ = z₀, so ξ_t → z₀; and with t_* = t − F(|x|), F := t
− t_* a function of |x| with F′ = 1 + O(r⁻²) ((21.27), Lemma 21.20 (a), (21.30)), ξ_* = ξ_t −
z₀F′ → 0. Backward, ξ_* → −2z₀. The bounds are uniform for Λ ≤ Λ_𝖪, the bound of Λ on a compact set 𝖪 of initial points,
so the argument at infinity of Proposition 22.10 applies verbatim with C replaced by Λ. This gives convergence to R_out
and R_(z₀,in), and the absorbing sets 𝒜_out = {r > R, |ξ_*| < ϵ} and 𝒜_in = {r > R, |ξ_* + 2z₀| < ϵ}.

*Near the radial sets.* (H3), as proved in Proposition 22.18, gives 𝖧_b q ≥ ½β₀q on ∂Σ₀ ∩ {q < ϵ_q} near ∂ℛ_±
and ρ_∞⁻¹𝖧_bρ_∞ ≥ ½β₀ at ∂ℛ_±, with β₀ := β₀(b₀). By continuity there is a neighbourhood U_R of ∂ℛ_± in the
compactified Σ, with compact closure and the same for all b near b₀, on which 𝖧_b q ≥ ¼β₀q − cρ_∞ and
𝖧_bρ_∞ ≥ ¼β₀ρ_∞, with q extended as |η/ξ|². So L := q + (8c/β₀)ρ_∞ satisfies
𝖧_bL ≥ ¼β₀q + cρ_∞ ≥ ⅛β₀L on U_R. Shrinking it, take U_R with closure inside a neighbourhood with these properties, so
that what follows holds on the boundary of U_R too. L vanishes on ∂ℛ_± and is positive on the rest of U_R: ρ_∞ > 0 at
finite covectors, and at fibre infinity near ∂ℛ_±, q = |η̂|² vanishes only on ∂ℛ_± (Proposition 22.18: there ∂Σ₀ is a
graph over (ω, η̂) and ∂ℛ_± = {η̂ = 0}). Fix 0 < δ_L < min L over the boundary of U_R, and let 𝒰_L := {L < δ_L} ∩ U_R,
an open neighbourhood of ∂ℛ_±. Backward along a curve in U_R, L does not increase; so a curve in 𝒰_L never reaches
{L ≥ δ_L}, which contains the boundary of U_R, and it stays in 𝒰_L backward, with L decaying backward exponentially at
the uniform rate ⅛β₀.

*At the horizon.* ℋ_b is a null hypersurface (Lemma 22.15), and dr_A(w) < 0 for every future-directed causal w at
ℋ_b not tangent to its null generators. Indeed this set of w is connected, dr_A(w) vanishes on it only for w tangent to
the generators, and the sign is that at b₀ (Section 22.7), by continuity. The velocity of γ is a nonzero multiple of
ν^♯, and ν^♯ tangent to a generator would make ν a multiple of dr_A, so ν(∂_t) = 0, against E = z₀. So a curve meeting
ℋ_b at a finite covector crosses it inward, transversally, and by continuity each finite covector p₀ over ℋ_b has
δ, T > 0 such that the curve through any point within δ of p₀ is in {r_A < r₊} a parameter T later and in
{r_A > r₊} a parameter T earlier. Let γ stay in {r_A > r₊} on a forward or a backward half-line, with r → r₊ along
it, and let 𝓛 be its limit set at that end, in the compactified characteristic set: compact, invariant, over ℋ_b, and
approached by γ. 𝓛 contains no finite covector p₀: γ comes within δ of p₀ arbitrarily far along the half-line, and is
then in {r_A < r₊} a parameter T later, still on the half-line. So 𝓛 ⊂ ∂Σ₀. A point of ∂Σ₀ ∖ ∂ℛ_± reaches
{r < r_h − d₁} forward in finite time (Proposition 22.18, (H4)), which an invariant set over ℋ_b cannot contain; so
𝓛 ⊂ ∂ℛ_±, and γ lies in 𝒰_L near that end. Forward this is impossible: L > 0 along γ does not decrease forward in
𝒰_L, so it cannot tend to 0. Hence an exterior curve with r → r₊ forward leaves {r_A > r₊}, so meets ℋ_b and crosses
it inward; one with r → r₊ backward tends backward to ∂ℛ_±. Inside, read for g̃_b (Ψ_b carries {r < r_h} to the inside
of ℋ_b, Lemma 22.16): on {r₀ − 2δ₀ ≤ r < r_h}, dr is timelike for g̃_b. On {r ≤ r₂} this is part of (H4) in
Proposition 22.18. On {r₂ ≤ r < r_h}, for b near b₀, χ_H(|Ψ_b(x)|) = 1, so Ψ_b^* r_A = (r₊(b)/r_h)|x| (the remark after
Lemma 22.16) and g̃_b⁻¹(dr, dr) = (r_h/r₊(b))² (g^KS_b)⁻¹(dr_A, dr_A) ∘ Ψ_b, as in the proof of Lemma 22.17;
this is negative by Lemma 22.15, since there r₋ < r_A ∘ Ψ_b = (r₊(b)/r_h)r < r₊(b) (the paragraph after
(22.11)). So r decreases strictly along γ. On compact subsets of the compactified
Σ_(z₀) ∩ {r₀ − δ₀ ≤ r ≤ r₁}, r₁ < r_h, the rescaled ṙ is bounded above by a negative constant, so γ reaches
{r < r₀ − δ₀} in finite time. Backward, r increases strictly
along an interior curve. If the curve meets ℋ_b backward, it crossed it inward there, and its earlier part is an
exterior curve, treated above. Otherwise, with s₀ a parameter at which γ is inside, r → r̄ ≤ r_h as s → −∞. The case
r̄ < r_h is impossible: on the compact part of the compactified Σ_(z₀) over
{r(γ(s₀)) ≤ r ≤ r̄} ⊂ {r₀ − 2δ₀ ≤ r < r_h}, where dr is timelike, the rescaled ṙ is at most a negative constant −c, so
r would exceed r̄ within the backward parameter (r̄ − r(γ(s₀)))/c. If r̄ = r_h, a finite covector p₀ in the backward
limit set is impossible, since γ would be outside ℋ_b a parameter T before passing within δ of p₀, still on the
backward half-line; so the limit set lies in ∂Σ₀ over ℋ_b, hence in ∂ℛ_± as above, and γ tends backward to ∂ℛ_±.

*(a).* Combining: a curve not in Γ̄_u tends backward to ∂ℛ_± or R_(z₀,in), and a curve not in Γ̄_s tends forward to
R_out or reaches {r < r₀ − δ₀} in finite time. *Uniformity.* With the absorbing sets 𝒜_out, 𝒜_in, 𝒰_L (in which L
decays backward at the uniform rate) and {r < r₀ − δ₀}, the cover argument of Proposition 22.10 applies on compact
subsets of {(b, p)}: the set of (b, p) whose curve enters the relevant absorbing set before parameter T is open and
increases with T, and these sets cover by the pointwise statement.

*(b).* Within O, a point with φ_u = 0 has ℛ_c = 0 and lies on the branch on which r → r_c and p̃ → 0 backward, so its
curve tends to Γ_b backward. A point with φ_s = 0 ≠ φ_u moves away from r_c backward, and a point with ℛ_c ≠ 0 has no
double zero. So Γ̄_u ∩ O = {φ_u = 0} ∩ Σ ∩ O = Γ_u, and likewise for Γ̄_s. ∎

This is [Hin26c, Proposition 4.24] for Myers–Perry near Tangherlini.

### 22.16 The theorem near b₀

**Theorem 22.30** ((Dyn) near b₀.) There is ε_VI > 0 such that on the compact parameter set
ℬ_VI := {|b − b₀| ≤ ε_VI}, the metrics g̃_b = Ψ_b^* g_b with the time function Ψ_b^* t_* and the radii of
Definition 22.1 satisfy: the dynamical conditions of (H3), and (H4) (Proposition 22.18); (H6) and (K1)
(Lemma 22.6); (Γ.1)–(Γ.3), with ν_min → 4(2m₀)^(−1/2), β_Γ → 2 and q^Γ → 4 as b → b₀ (Proposition 22.24); (K3)
and (K4) (Proposition 22.28); and (H8) (Proposition 22.29). All the data depend continuously on b into C^∞, with the
constants uniform, as (H5), its extension in Section 12.1.5, and (K4) ask. These hold for every operator with
principal symbol g̃_b⁻¹ ⊗ Id. The operator hypotheses, the threshold in (H3) and condition (Γ.4), are verified in
Chapter 23, Chapter 24 and Chapter 25, read through Ψ_b (Section 22.9).

*Proof.* Take ε_VI := min(ε₁/2, ε₈), with ε₁ from Proposition 22.18 and ε₈ from Proposition 22.29; the results cited
hold on ℬ_VI. ∎

For every r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁], ℬ_VI ⊂ ℬ, as every ball of this chapter lies in ℬ (Definition 22.1); ε_VI and the
constants of the theorem depend on r_♭.

## 23. The gauge potential operator

This chapter studies the gauge potential wave operator □^Υ_b, a wave operator on 1-forms built from the Myers–Perry
metric g_b of Chapter 21 and a modification E^Υ of its divergence, for b near the Tangherlini parameter b_0. It proves,
in dimension 4 + 1, what [Hin26, Section 6] proves on Kerr (pp. 113–134): the structure of □^Υ_b as a stationary
wave-type operator (Lemma 23.1), its Minkowski model (Lemma 23.2), the indicial roots at zero energy
(Lemma 23.3), the threshold at the horizon and the bound at the trapped set (Section 23.5), invertibility of
the spectral family at high energies and mode stability away from zero frequency (Section 23.6), tf-admissibility
(Lemma 23.20), the kernel and cokernel at zero energy of the unmodified operator and mode stability of □^Υ_b on
the whole closed upper half plane (Section 23.9–Section 23.12), and the large zero energy states and the
generalised zero energy states of □^Υ_b (Section 23.13–Section 23.18). These are [Hin26, Lemmas 6.1, 6.3, 6.4,
6.6, 6.8, 6.10, 6.11, 6.13, 6.14, Propositions 6.5, 6.9, 6.12, 6.15, 6.18] in dimension 4 + 1.

The dimensional changes are these. The mass of g_b enters g_b − ḡ at |x|⁻² and its rotation at |x|⁻³, where those of
Kerr enter at |x|⁻¹ and |x|⁻²; so every comparison with Minkowski space gains a power of |x|⁻¹. The radial weight
ρ∂_ρ − 1 becomes ρ∂_ρ − 3/2, the trace weight of the modification is 2/3 = 2/(n − 1), and the harmonics are those of
𝕊³, which has six rotations and a tensor type. The indicial roots move: the gap of the unmodified operator at zero
energy is (0, 2), and that of □^Υ_b is (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) with ι^Υ_(s1,2) just above 2. Two inputs that [Hin26] takes
from [AHW24, Theorem 5.1] on Kerr, mode stability of the unmodified operator away from zero frequency and its kernel at
zero frequency, are proved here on five-dimensional Tangherlini, by ordinary differential equations whose potentials
are positive. The corrections to the boosts and to the time translation carry no logarithm.

Thirteen results of the main argument enter as inputs and are proved in this chapter, with every identity derived:
Proposition 23.23 (the zero energy data of the unmodified operator), Proposition 23.16 (the mode equations on
Tangherlini), Proposition 23.5 (the structure at infinity and the horizon threshold), Proposition 23.6 (the radial
structure at the incoming radial set), Proposition 23.19 (the transition face and the weights), Proposition 23.29
(the symmetries and the linearised Myers–Perry metrics), Proposition 23.31 and Proposition 23.32 (the model
generalised states and their root facts, with their counterparts in dimension 3 + 1). So are the trapping
identities Proposition 23.8, Proposition 23.9–Proposition 23.11 and Proposition 23.13;
Proposition 22.4, Proposition 22.5 and Proposition 22.3 are proved in Chapter 22.

*The dynamical hypotheses.* The theory of Chapter 11–Chapter 13 applies to operators on a trivial bundle satisfying
hypotheses (H1)–(H8), (G), (Z) and (TF). Some of these concern the metric alone: the radial structure of the horizon in
(H3) and (H4), the time function and the Lorentzian metric in (H6), the normally hyperbolic trapping (Γ.1)–(Γ.3) in
(H7), and the global dynamics (H8). We write (Dyn) for them. For g_b, b near b_0, they hold by Theorem 22.12 (at
b_0) and Theorem 22.30 (near b_0), for every operator with principal symbol G Id. This chapter proves the operator
hypotheses for □^Υ_b: (H1) and (H2) with the endomorphism S̄ (Section 23.2), the horizon threshold
(Section 23.5.1), the bound (Γ.4) at the trapped set (Section 23.5.2), the gap (G) (Section 23.4) and (TF)
(Section 23.7).

*The inner radius.* The radii 0 < r_0 − 2δ_0 < r_0 < r_0 + δ_0 < r_2 < r_h are those of Section 11.1.1. The only step
below the horizon, part (d) of the proof of Proposition 23.17 (repeated in Lemma 23.21), holds on (r_0, r_h) for
every r_0 ∈ (0, r_h); every other step reaches the inner boundary only through the theorems of Chapter 11–Chapter 13,
which hold with r_0 as a parameter. So every result of this chapter holds with the inner radius r_0 as a parameter.

*Notation.* b = (m, A) are the parameters of Section 21.5, b_0 = (m_0, 0), and g_m := g_((m,0)) is the
five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini metric of mass parameter m. On g_(b_0) we write f := 1 − m_0/r²,
r_h := m_0^(1/2), r := |x|, ρ := r⁻¹ near infinity, and x̂ := x/|x|. On 𝕊³, g_𝕊 is the round metric, and d_𝕊, δ_𝕊,
δ*_𝕊 and Δ_𝕊 ≥ 0 its differential, divergence, symmetric gradient and Laplacian, with the conventions of
Section 21.1, where they are written d, δ̸, δ̸* and Δ̸: Δ_𝕊 is the rough Laplacian, equal to δ_𝕊d_𝕊 on functions.
𝒮_l and 𝒱_l are the scalar and vector harmonics of degree l (Definition 21.3), and κ := l(l + 2) is the eigenvalue
of Δ_𝕊 on 𝒮_l. The variable of indicial families is ι ∈ ℂ, and an indicial root is a value of ι.
When we use the static chart of g_(b_0) we write t for its static time, so that g_(b_0) = −f dt² + f⁻¹dr² + r²g_𝕊 on
{r > r_h}; this t differs from the time of (21.30) by a function of r. The ingoing time is v := t + r_*, with
the tortoise coordinate r_* of Proposition 23.16 (v).

### 23.1 The operator

Let ℬ be the parameter set of Section 21.5, g_b the Myers–Perry metric of Proposition 21.21, t_* the time function
of (21.30), and E_Υ = (c_Υ, e_Υ, γ_Υ; c_(Υ,H), γ_(Υ,H)) as in Definition 21.28, with the trace weight 2/3.
As [Hin26, (6.1)] requires, the supports of c_(Υ,H) and of c_Υ on {|x| < 5R_1} are disjoint from a fixed neighbourhood
U_Γ of the projection of the trapped sets of all g_b, b ∈ ℬ; by (Dyn) these lie over a fixed compact subset of
{r_h < |x| < 5R_1} near |x|² = 2m_0 (Section 23.5.2). The *gauge potential wave operator* is

    □^Υ_b := □^Υ_(g_b,E_Υ) = 2δ_(g_b,E_Υ) G_(g_b) δ*_(g_b) = □_(g_b) + 2E^Υ_(g_b) G_(g_b) δ*_(g_b),    (23.1)

acting on 1-forms, with □_g := 2δ_g G_g δ*_g. On a Ricci-flat metric, □_g = dδ_g + δ_g d = ∇*∇, the Hodge and the
Bochner d'Alembertian (Proposition 23.16 (i)). Its spectral family is

    (□^Υ_b)^(σ) := e^(iσt_*) □^Υ_b e^(−iσt_*),

acting on stationary 1-forms on X, which we trivialise by dt_*, dx¹, …, dx⁴: the bundle E of Section 11.1 with
N_E = 5. We also write P̂_b(σ) for it when E_Υ is fixed.

### 23.2 Structure

The Minkowski model is ḡ := −(dt_* + d|x|)² + Σ_(i=1)^4 (dx^i)², Minkowski space in the time t̄ := t_* + |x|. Put
c̄ := |x|⁻¹ dt̄, Ē h := −γ_Υ(2ι_(ḡ⁻¹c̄) h − (2/3)(1 − e_Υ) c̄ tr_ḡ h) and □̄^Υ := 2(δ̄ + Ē)Ḡ δ̄*. In the coordinates
t_*, ρ, x̂ this is the Minkowski space of Section 21.2, with t_* = t̄ − r there.

**Lemma 23.1** (Structure; [Hin26, Lemma 6.1] in dimension 4 + 1.) (1) □^Υ_b is stationary with principal
symbol g_b⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id, and (□^Υ_b)^(σ) = P̂(0) + σT + σ²P_2 satisfies (H1) and the operator part of (H6) of
Section 11.1.3 with g = g_b and t = t_*: P_2 = g_b^00 Id with g_b^00 := g_b⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*), σ_1(T) = −2g_b⁻¹(dt_*, ·) Id,
and P̂(0) − □_(g_b) Id is of first order with t_*-independent coefficients.

(2) On {|x| > 0}, exactly,

    □̄^Υ = −2∂_(t_*) ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) + (□̄^Υ)^(0),    (23.2)

with S̄ and (□̄^Υ)^(0) ∈ ρ² Diff_b² given in Lemma 23.2, and no ∂_(t_*)² term.

(3) On {|x| > 3R_1},

    □^Υ_b = □̄^Υ − g_b^00 ∂_(t_*)² + Q_b ∂_(t_*) + R_b,     g_b^00 ∈ ρ²C^∞(X̄),  Q_b ∈ ρ³ Diff_b¹,  R_b ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b²,
    (23.3)

all stationary and smooth in b (and in e_Υ, γ_Υ). Hence (H2) holds with S := S̄ near infinity (in the Cartesian frame,
Θ⁻¹S̄Θ with Θ = Θ(x̂) the change from the null splitting (21.10); its spectrum is that of S̄), Q := Q_b,
P⁽⁰⁾ := ρ⁻²((□̄^Υ)^(0) + R_b), and P⁽⁰⁾ − ((ρD_ρ)² + Δ_𝕊) Id ∈ Diff_b¹ + ρ² Diff_b². The normal operator of P⁽⁰⁾ at
ρ = 0, its indicial roots, and S̄ do not depend on b.

*Proof.* (1) The terms 2E^Υ G δ* and the connection terms of □_(g_b) are of order at most 1, so the principal part is
−g_b^(μν) ∂_μ ∂_ν Id in the frame. Conjugating by e^(−iσt_*) replaces ∂_(t_*) by ∂_(t_*) − iσ; the σ² term is
−g_b^00 (−iσ)² = σ²g_b^00, and the principal symbol of the σ¹ coefficient is −2g_b⁻¹(dt_*, ζ), times the identity.
g_b^00 < 0 on X°, as dt_* is timelike (Lemma 21.22 (a)).

(2) By Lemma 21.8 (1) at ν = 3, □̄ = −2∂_(t_*) ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2) + ᵇ□̄(0), and by Lemma 23.2 below
2ĒḠδ̄* = 2∂_(t_*) ρS̄ + γ_Υ ρ²M_E; this is (23.2). The dual metric
ḡ⁻¹ = 2ρ∂_(t_*) ⊗_s ρ∂_ρ + ρ²((ρ∂_ρ)² + g_𝕊⁻¹) ((21.11)) has no ∂_(t_*) ⊗ ∂_(t_*) term, and ĒḠδ̄* is of
first order.

(3) *The metric.* By Proposition 21.21, g_b − η ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞ with η = −dt² + dx² in the time t of
(21.30), and t_* = t − ψ(|x|) with ψ′ = 1 − 8m_0|x|⁻² on {|x| ≥ 3R_1}. So
η − ḡ = −(ψ′ − 1) d|x| ⊗_s (2dt_* + (ψ′ + 1)d|x|) ∈ ρ²C^∞, and k := g_b − ḡ ∈ ρ²C^∞(X̄; S²) in the frame dt_*, dx^i,
stationary; likewise g_b⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ ∈ ρ²C^∞, and ḡ^00 = 0 gives g_b^00 ∈ ρ²C^∞. *Derivatives.* ∂_(t_*) annihilates
stationary coefficients and ∂_(x^i) ∈ ρ𝒱_b(X̄), so ∂_(x^i) maps ρ^a C^∞(X̄) to ρ^(a+1)C^∞(X̄). The coefficients of ḡ
are homogeneous of degree 0, so Γ(ḡ) ∈ ρC^∞, and Γ′ := Γ(g_b) − Γ(ḡ) ∈ ρ³C^∞. *The 1-form d'Alembertian.* □_g ω
written out in Christoffel symbols has second-order coefficients g^(μν), first-order coefficients bilinear in g⁻¹ and
Γ, and zeroth-order coefficients in g⁻¹∂Γ and g⁻¹ΓΓ. Hence □_(g_b) − □̄ has second-order coefficients in ρ²C^∞
(vanishing in the ∂_(t_*)∂_(t_*) slot except for g_b^00), first-order coefficients in ρ³C^∞ (from Γ′ and from
(g_b⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹)Γ(ḡ)) and zeroth-order coefficients in ρ⁴C^∞. *The modification.* Near infinity c_Υ = |x|⁻¹dt
(Definition 21.28) and c_Υ − c̄ = |x|⁻¹(ψ′ − 1)d|x| ∈ ρ³C^∞; with g_b⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ ∈ ρ² this gives
E^Υ_(g_b,∞) − Ē ∈ ρ³C^∞ (of order zero); G_(g_b) − Ḡ ∈ ρ²C^∞; δ*_(g_b) − δ̄* ∈ ρ³C^∞ (of order zero, by Γ′); and
E^Υ_(g_b,H) = 0 there. So 2E^Υ G δ* − 2ĒḠδ̄* is a sum of terms (zeroth-order ρ³ coefficients) times ∂, and of
zeroth-order terms in ρ⁴. *Sorting.* A Cartesian derivative is ∂_(t_*) or lies in ρ𝒱_b. Terms ρ²∂_(t_*)² form
−g_b^00 ∂_(t_*)²; terms ρ²∂_(t_*)∂_(x^i) and ρ³∂_(t_*) form Q_b ∂_(t_*) with Q_b ∈ ρ³ Diff_b¹; terms
ρ²∂_(x^i)∂_(x^j), ρ³∂_(x^i) and ρ⁴ form R_b ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b². Smoothness in b is that of g_b (Section 21.5). *(H2).*
By (2), the ∂_(t_*)-coefficient of □^Υ_b is −2ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) + Q_b, so T = 2iρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) − iQ_b. In the
Cartesian frame □̄ acts componentwise as the scalar operator (proof of Lemma 21.8), so
ᵇ□̄(0) = ρ²(−(ρ∂_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ_𝕊) Id there, and γ_Υ ρ²M_E ∈ ρ² Diff_b¹ after the change of frame Θ(x̂), which
commutes with ρ∂_ρ. With (ρD_ρ)² = −(ρ∂_ρ)² the last claim of (3) follows; the normal operator of P⁽⁰⁾ is that of
ρ⁻²(□̄^Υ)^(0), which does not involve b. ∎

On Kerr, g_b − ḡ ∈ ρC^∞, so that S − S̄ ∈ ρC^∞ and the zero energy operators differ by ρ³ Diff_b² [Hin26, (6.7)]. In
dimension 4 + 1 the mass enters at ρ², and each difference gains one power.

### 23.3 The Minkowski model

We use the splitting (21.10) of 1-forms: (ω_0, ω_1, ω_𝕊) is ω_0 dx̄⁰ + ω_1 dx̄¹ + rω_𝕊, with
x̄⁰ := t̄ + r and x̄¹ := t̄ − r = t_*; and (a, b, c, e′, f, q) is the symmetric 2-tensor
a(dx̄⁰)² + 2b dx̄⁰dx̄¹ + 2dx̄⁰ ⊗_s rc + e′(dx̄¹)² + 2dx̄¹ ⊗_s rf + r²q.

**Lemma 23.2** (The Minkowski model; [Hin26, Lemma 6.3] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ν ≥ 2 and m_ν := 2/ν,
the trace weight 2/(n − 1) of dimension n + 1 = ν + 2 (2/3 at ν = 3). In the splitting (21.10) for 𝕊^ν, with
D := ρ∂_ρ, e := e_Υ and γ := γ_Υ:

    c̄ = ρ(½, ½, 0),     ḡ⁻¹(c̄) = −ρ(∂_0 + ∂_1),

           ⎛ 2   2 − 2m_ν(1 − e)   0   0   0   ½m_ν(1 − e) tr ⎞
    Ē = γρ ⎜ 0   2 − 2m_ν(1 − e)   0   2   0   ½m_ν(1 − e) tr ⎟ ;
           ⎝ 0   0                 2   0   2   0              ⎠    (23.4)

                                        ⎛ 1 − e   0   0 ⎞
    2ĒḠδ̄* = 2∂_(t_*) ρS̄ + γρ²M_E,   S̄ = γ ⎜ 1 − e   2   0 ⎟ ,
                                        ⎝ 0       0   1 ⎠

          ⎛ −(1 + e)D + νe    −(1 − e)D − νe   −e δ_𝕊 ⎞
    M_E = ⎜ (1 − e)D + νe     (1 + e)D − νe    −e δ_𝕊 ⎟ ;
          ⎝ 2d_𝕊              2d_𝕊             0      ⎠    (23.5)

so that □̄^Υ = −2∂_(t_*) ρ(D − ν/2 − S̄) + (□̄^Υ)^(0) with

    (□̄^Υ)^(0) = ᵇ□̄(0) + γρ²M_E.    (23.6)

At ν = 2 these are [Hin26, (6.10)–(6.11)]. The spectrum of S̄ is γ(1 − e), 2γ and γ (with multiplicity ν) at every ν,
so min Re spec S̄ = γ min(1 − e, 1).

*Proof.* dt̄ = ½(dx̄⁰ + dx̄¹) and ḡ⁻¹(dt̄) = −∂_(t̄) = −(∂_0 + ∂_1) give the first two. For h = (a, b, c, e′, f, q),
ι_(ḡ⁻¹c̄)h = −ρ(a + b, b + e′, c + f) in the 1-form splitting, and tr h = −4b + tr q (Section 21.2), so
Ēh = −γ(2ιh − m_ν(1 − e)c̄ tr h) is (23.4). By Lemma 21.29, ĒḠh = −γ(2ι_(ḡ⁻¹c̄)h − e c̄ tr h), so

    2ĒḠh = 2γρ(2a + 2(1 − e)b + ½e tr q,  2(1 − e)b + 2e′ + ½e tr q,  2(c + f)).

Insert h = δ̄*ω from Lemma 21.8 (1): a = −½ρDω_0, b = ½∂_(t_*)ω_0 + ¼ρD(ω_0 − ω_1),
c = ρ(½d_𝕊ω_0 − ¼(D + 1)ω_𝕊), e′ = ∂_(t_*)ω_1 + ½ρDω_1, f = ½∂_(t_*)ω_𝕊 + ρ(½d_𝕊ω_1 + ¼(D + 1)ω_𝕊), and
tr q = ρ(ν(ω_0 − ω_1) − δ_𝕊ω_𝕊) (as tr g_𝕊 = ν and tr δ*_𝕊 = −δ_𝕊). The ∂_(t_*)-terms are
2γρ∂_(t_*)((1 − e)ω_0, (1 − e)ω_0 + 2ω_1, ω_𝕊), which is 2∂_(t_*)ρS̄ω. The rest is γρ² times: in the first row
−2Dω_0 + (1 − e)D(ω_0 − ω_1) + eν(ω_0 − ω_1) − eδ_𝕊ω_𝕊; in the second (1 − e)D(ω_0 − ω_1) + 2Dω_1 + eν(ω_0 − ω_1) −
eδ_𝕊ω_𝕊; in the third 2d_𝕊ω_0 + 2d_𝕊ω_1 (the (D + 1)ω_𝕊 terms of c and f cancel). This is M_E. With
Lemma 21.8 (1) for □̄ we get (23.6). S̄ is lower triangular with diagonal γ(1 − e), 2γ, γ. At ν = 2,
m_ν = 1, 2 − 2m_ν(1 − e) = 2e and ½m_ν = ½, which is [Hin26, (6.10)]; and ±νe = ±2e is [Hin26, (6.11)]. ∎

### 23.4 Indicial roots

Write z := 4e_Υγ_Υ², κ := l(l + 2) and, for l ≥ 1,

    s_(l,1) := (l + 1)² + z/2 − ((l + 1)² + z + z²/4)^(1/2),   s_(l,2) := (l + 1)² + z/2 + ((l + 1)² + z + z²/4)^(1/2),

    ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) := ½ + (¼ + s_(l,j))^(1/2)  (j = 1, 2),     ι^Υ_(s0,2) := ½ + (9/4 + z)^(1/2).    (23.7)

The type-wise indicial matrices are read off from (23.6), Lemma 21.8 (1) and the identities
Lemma 21.5. On a scalar type l 1-form (aS, bS, c d_𝕊S), S ∈ 𝒮_l, l ≥ 1, the operator ρ⁻²(□̄^Υ)^(0) acts on
ρ^ι(a, b, c) as ρ^ι N_sl(ι)(a, b, c), where, with p := −ι² + 2ι,

               ⎛ p + κ + 3/2 − γ((1 + e)ι − 3e)   −3/2 − γ((1 − e)ι + 3e)            −κ(1 + eγ) ⎞
    N_sl(ι) =  ⎜ −3/2 + γ((1 − e)ι + 3e)           p + κ + 3/2 + γ((1 + e)ι − 3e)    κ(1 − eγ)  ⎟ ,
               ⎝ −2 + 2γ                           2 + 2γ                            p + κ − 1  ⎠    (23.8)

with e := e_Υ and γ := γ_Υ. Indeed, by (21.20) the operator ᵇ□̄(0) contributes p + κ on the first two
components, p + κ − 2 on the third, and the matrix with rows (3/2, −3/2, −κ), (−3/2, 3/2, κ), (−2, 2, 1); and M_E acts
by δ_𝕊(c d_𝕊S) = cκS and d_𝕊(aS) = a d_𝕊S. The scalar type 0 matrix N_s0(ι) is the upper left 2 × 2 block of
N_sl(ι) at κ = 0, acting on (aS, bS), S constant. On a vector type l 1-form (0, 0, cV), V ∈ 𝒱_l, the operator is
multiplication by N_vl(ι) := p + κ: ᵇ□̄(0) gives −ι² + 2ι + (κ − 1) + 1 by Δ_𝕊V = (κ − 1)V (Lemma 21.5), and
M_E vanishes on it, as δ_𝕊V = 0 and its third column is zero.

**Lemma 23.3** (Indicial roots; [Hin26, Lemma 6.6 and (6.17)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let z ∈ [0, ½]. The
indicial roots of (□^Υ_b)^(0), which are those of (□̄^Υ)^(0), are, in the terminology of Definition 21.9:

s0: 1 − ι^Υ_(s0,2), 0, ι^Υ_(s0,2), 3;

sl, l ≥ 1: 1 − ι^Υ_(sl,l+2), 1 − ι^Υ_(sl,l+1), 1 − l, ι^Υ_(sl,l+1), ι^Υ_(sl,l+2), l + 3;

vl, l ≥ 1: −l, l + 2.

All are real and simple: each is a simple zero of the determinant of its type's indicial matrix, so the inverse of the
indicial family has at most simple poles. At z = 0, ι^Υ_(s0,2) = 2 and ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) = l + j, the roots of
Lemma 21.10 for 1-forms. For 0 < z ≤ ½,

    ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) ∈ (l + j, l + j + ¼),     ι^Υ_(s0,2) ∈ (2, 2 + z/3],     2 < ι^Υ_(s1,2) < min(ι^Υ_(s0,2), 3),
    (23.9)

and (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) is an indicial gap (at z = 0 the gap is (0, 2)). As z → 0, ι^Υ_(s0,2) = 2 + z/3 + O(z²),
ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) = l + 1 + lz/(2(l + 1)(2l + 1)) + O(z²) and ι^Υ_(sl,l+2) = l + 2 + (l + 2)z/(2(l + 1)(2l + 3)) + O(z²).
The s0 indicial solutions for the root 0 are spanned by dt̄, and the s1 ones, for each S ∈ 𝒮_1, by d(rS).

*Proof.* By Lemma 23.1 (3) the normal operator is that of the model. *The determinants.* Put
Q_l(s) := s² − (2 + 2κ + z)s + κ(κ + 1) + zκ. We show

    det N_s0(ι) = ι(ι − 3)(ι² − ι − 2 − z),   det N_sl(ι) = (l + 3 − ι)(l + ι − 1) Q_l(ι² − ι),
    N_vl(ι) = (ι + l)(l + 2 − ι).    (23.10)

The last is p + κ = −ι² + 2ι + l² + 2l. For s0, expanding the 2 × 2 determinant,

    det N_s0 = (p + 3/2)² − γ²((1 + e)ι − 3e)² − 9/4 + γ²((1 − e)ι + 3e)² = p(p + 3) − 4eγ²ι(ι − 3),

and p = −ι(ι − 2), p + 3 = −(ι − 3)(ι + 1), so det N_s0 = ι(ι − 3)((ι − 2)(ι + 1) − z). For sl, pass to the
coordinates u := a + b, w := a − b (the coefficients of dt̄ and dr) and take the sum and the difference of the first
two rows; this does not change the determinant (the row operation and the change of coordinates have determinants −2
and −½). With P := p + κ the matrix becomes

        ⎛ P         −2eγ(ι − 3)   −2eγκ ⎞
    M = ⎜ −2γι      P + 3         −2κ   ⎟ ,
        ⎝ 2γ        −2            P − 1 ⎠

acting on (u, w, c). Expanding along the first row and collecting the terms in γ²,

    det M = P((P + 3)(P − 1) − 4κ) + z(P(κ − ι² + 3ι) + ι² − 3ι − 3κ).

Now (P + 3)(P − 1) − 4κ = (P + 1)² − 4(l + 1)² = (P − 2l − 1)(P + 2l + 3), and P = −(ι − l − 2)(ι + l),
P − 2l − 1 = −(ι − l − 1)(ι + l − 1), P + 2l + 3 = −(ι − l − 3)(ι + l + 1). With s := ι² − ι one has
(ι − l − 1)(ι + l) = s − l(l + 1) and (ι − l − 2)(ι + l + 1) = s − (l + 1)(l + 2), so the first term is
(l + 3 − ι)(l + ι − 1)(s − l(l + 1))(s − (l + 1)(l + 2)). For the second, put Y := κ − ι² + 3ι; then P = Y − ι,
ι² − 3ι − 3κ = −Y − 2κ, (l + 3 − ι)(l + ι − 1) = Y + ι − 3 and κ − s = Y − 2ι. So the bracket of the second term
is PY − Y − 2κ = Y² − ιY − Y − 2κ, while (Y + ι − 3)(Y − 2ι) = Y² − ιY − 3Y − 2ι² + 6ι; their difference
2Y + 2ι² − 6ι − 2κ vanishes by the definition of Y. So the second term is z(l + 3 − ι)(l + ι − 1)(κ − s). Finally

    (s − l(l + 1))(s − (l + 1)(l + 2)) = s² − (2 + 2κ)s + κ(κ + 1),    (23.11)

since l(l + 1) + (l + 1)(l + 2) = 2(l + 1)² = 2 + 2κ and l(l + 1)²(l + 2) = κ(κ + 1); so Q_l(s) is
(s − l(l + 1))(s − (l + 1)(l + 2)) + z(κ − s), and (23.10) follows.

*The list.* The discriminant of Q_l is 4(l + 1)² + 4z + z² > 0 (as 1 + κ = (l + 1)²), so its roots are
s_(l,1) < s_(l,2), and ι² − ι = s gives ι = ½ ± (¼ + s)^(1/2); ι² − ι = 2 + z gives the s0 pair. This is the list.

*Bounds.* By (23.11), Q_l(l(l + 1)) = lz and Q_l((l + 1)(l + 2)) = −(l + 2)z. So for z > 0,
l(l + 1) < s_(l,1) < (l + 1)(l + 2) < s_(l,2), and as ι ↦ ι² − ι increases on ι > ½, ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) > l + 1 and
ι^Υ_(sl,l+2) > l + 2. For the upper bounds, ∂_z s_(l,j) ≤ ½ + (1 + z/2)/(2(l + 1)) ≤ 1 + z/4, so
s_(l,j) − s_(l,j)|_(z=0) ≤ z(1 + z/8), and ι − (l + j) ≤ (s − s|_(z=0))/(2(l + j) − 1) ≤ z(1 + z/8)/3 < ¼ for z ≤ ½;
similarly (9/4 + z)^(1/2) ≤ 3/2 + z/3. *The ordering.* ι^Υ_(s1,2) < ι^Υ_(s0,2) iff s_(1,1) < 2 + z, iff
2 − z/2 < (4 + z + z²/4)^(1/2), iff (squaring, z < 4) z > 0; ι^Υ_(s1,2) > 2 iff s_(1,1) > 2, iff
2 + z/2 > (4 + z + z²/4)^(1/2), iff z > 0; and ι^Υ_(s1,2) < 9/4 < 3. *The gap.* Every root in the list other than
ι^Υ_(s1,2) is ≤ 0 or ≥ min(ι^Υ_(s0,2), 3): the negative ones are 1 − ι ≤ −l, 1 − l ≤ 0 and −l; the positive ones are
3, ι^Υ_(s0,2), l + 3 ≥ 4, l + 2 ≥ 3, and ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) ≥ l + j ≥ 3 unless (l, j) = (1, 1). *Simplicity.* Within each
type the roots are distinct for z ∈ [0, ½] by the bounds (ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) < l + 5/4 < l + 2 ≤ ι^Υ_(sl,l+2) < l + 9/4 <
l + 3, and the negative ones likewise), so each is a simple zero of a polynomial determinant, and
N(ι)⁻¹ = adj N(ι)/det N(ι) has at most a simple pole there. *Expansions.* s_(l,1) = l(l + 1) + lz/(2(l + 1)) + O(z²),
s_(l,2) = (l + 1)(l + 2) + (l + 2)z/(2(l + 1)) + O(z²), and dι/ds = (2ι − 1)⁻¹. *Indicial solutions at 0.* dt̄ and
d(rS) are Killing 1-forms of the model (translations), homogeneous of degree 0, of types s0 and s1
(Lemma 21.11); □̄^Υ = 2(δ̄ + Ē)Ḡδ̄* annihilates them, and they are stationary, so they solve the indicial
equation at ι = 0; the root being simple, they span. ∎

On Kerr the s0 pair is ±(1 + 4eγ²)^(1/2), symmetric about 0, and the gap is (0, λ^Υ_(s1,1)) [Hin26, (6.17)]. In
dimension 4 + 1 the roots pair about different points: the roots of ι² − ι = s, the s0 pair and the ι^Υ_(sl,·) with
their partners 1 − ι, pair about ½; the vl roots −l, l + 2 about 1; the s0 roots 0, 3 about 3/2; and the sl roots
1 − l, l + 3 about 2. The index of ι^Υ_(sl,·) is shifted by one, and the gap is (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) with ι^Υ_(s1,2) just
above 2.

**Remark 23.4** (The trace weight.) If the trace weight 2/3 of Definition 21.28 is replaced by
1, then, as tr_g G_g h = −(3/2) tr_g h in dimension 5, ĒḠh = −γ(2ι_(ḡ⁻¹c̄)h − ½(3e − 1)c̄ tr h): every formula of
Lemma 23.2 and (23.10) holds with e replaced by (3e − 1)/2. In particular the spectrum of S̄ becomes
(3/2)(1 − e)γ, 2γ, γ, and the s0 root 2 of the unmodified operator moves to (1 + (9 − 8γ²(1 − 3e))^(1/2))/2, which
lies in (1, 2) when e < 1/3 and 0 < γ²(1 − 3e) < 1, inside the gap (0, 2). The weight 2/3 = 2/(n − 1) avoids this:
(2/(n − 1))(1 − (n + 1)/2) = −1 in every dimension n + 1, so that ĒḠ takes the same form −γ(2ι − e c̄ tr) as in
dimension 4 with the weight 1.

### 23.5 The subprincipal data

#### 23.5.1 The structure at infinity and the horizon threshold

On g_(b_0), in the ingoing chart (v, r, y), y = (y¹, y², y³) coordinates on 𝕊³, the metric is
g = −f dv² + 2dv dr + r²g_𝕊, so g^vv = 0, g^vr = 1, g^rr = f, g^(ra) = g^(va) = 0, and |dg| = r³|dv dr dg_𝕊|. Its
Christoffel symbols with a lower index v are, from g_vv = −f and g_vr = 1,

    Γ^v_vv = f′/2,   Γ^r_vv = ff′/2,   Γ^r_vr = −f′/2,   Γ^v_vr = 0,   Γ^λ_va = 0,    (23.12)

since Γ^λ_vν = ½g^(λκ)(∂_ν g_κv − ∂_κ g_vν) for the stationary metric, g_κv does not depend on the angles, and
g_va = 0. At r_h, f = 0 and f′(r_h) = 2m_0 r_h⁻³ = 2/r_h.

**Proposition 23.5** (Structure at infinity and the horizon threshold.)

(i) On 4 + 1 Minkowski space, in the time t_* = t̄ − r and the Cartesian frame (dt̄, dx^i), □̄^Υ is
−2∂_(t_*) ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) plus a stationary operator, with no ∂_(t_*)² term, and

    S̄ω = γ_Υ(ω + ω(∂_(t̄)) dt_* + e_Υ ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, ω) dt̄).

(ii) The spectrum of S̄ is γ_Υ(1 − e_Υ), 2γ_Υ, and γ_Υ on the three angular directions.

(iii) On g_(b_0), let c_H = c_v dv + c_r dr near r_h, E_H h := 2ι_(g⁻¹c_H) h − (2/3)c_H tr_g h, and γ_H ∈ ℝ. At
N*ℋ, that is at r = r_h and ζ = ξ dr, the subprincipal symbol of □_(g_(b_0)) + 2γ_H E_H G δ*, on half-densities
by |dg| and in the coordinate frame (dv, dr, dy^a), is iξf′(r_h)K, where

        ⎛ 1 + c_vγ_H r_h    0                    0               ⎞
    K = ⎜ c_rγ_H r_h        −1 + 2c_vγ_H r_h     0               ⎟ .
        ⎝ 0                 0                    c_vγ_H r_h Id_3 ⎠

(iv) On g_(b_0), with t the static time and t_* := t − r, g⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = −(2m_0ρ² − m_0²ρ⁴)/(1 − m_0ρ²), which
lies in ρ²C^∞; and g − ḡ = m_0ρ²dt² + m_0ρ²(1 − m_0ρ²)⁻¹dr² for ḡ := −dt² + dr² + r²g_𝕊, which is O(ρ²) in the frame
(dt, dr, r dx̂).

*Proof.* (i) The first part is (23.2). In the null splitting, dt_* = dx̄¹, dt̄ = ½(dx̄⁰ + dx̄¹),
ω(∂_(t̄)) = ω_0 + ω_1 (as ∂_(t̄) = ∂_0 + ∂_1), and ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, ω) = −2ω_0 by (21.11). So the right side is
γ_Υ((1 − e_Υ)ω_0, (1 − e_Υ)ω_0 + 2ω_1, ω_𝕊), which is S̄ω by (23.5); the expression does not depend on the
frame. (ii) is Lemma 23.2.

(iii) *The unmodified operator.* Let 𝔪 := r³|g_𝕊|^(1/2), so |dg| = 𝔪|dv dr dy|. For an operator P on ℂ⁵-valued
functions with scalar principal part −g^(αβ)∂_α∂_β, the subprincipal symbol on half-densities by |dg| is that of
P̃ := 𝔪^(1/2)P𝔪^(−1/2) on half-densities by |dv dr dy|, namely p̃_1 − (1/2i)Σ_j ∂_(x^j)∂_(ζ_j) p̃_2, p̃_k the
homogeneous parts of the full symbol of P̃. Since ∇_α∇_βω_ν = ∂_α(∂_βω_ν − Γ^μ_βν ω_μ) − Γ^κ_αβ ∇_κω_ν
− Γ^μ_αν ∇_βω_μ, in coordinates

    (□ω)_ν = □_0 ω_ν + 2g^(αβ)Γ^μ_(αν) ∂_β ω_μ + (terms without derivatives of ω),
    □_0 := −g^(αβ)∂_α∂_β + g^(αβ)Γ^κ_(αβ)∂_κ.

The scalar wave operator □_0 is formally self-adjoint for |dg| and has real coefficients; so 𝔪^(1/2)□_0𝔪^(−1/2) is
formally self-adjoint for |dv dr dy| and real, and its subprincipal symbol is both real and purely imaginary, hence
zero. Conjugation by 𝔪^(1/2) changes the term 2g^(αβ)Γ^μ_(αν)∂_β only by terms without derivatives. So the
subprincipal symbol of □ is the matrix u ↦ (2iζ^αΓ^μ_(αν)u_μ)_ν, ζ^α := g^(αβ)ζ_β. At N*ℋ, ζ^α = ξg^(αr), that is
ζ♯ = ξ∂_v, and by (23.12) the matrix is u ↦ (iξf′u_v, −iξf′u_r, 0) at r_h. *The modification.* By
Lemma 21.29, E_H G h = 2ι_(c_H♯) h, so 2γ_H E_H G δ*u = 4γ_H ι_(c_H♯) δ*u, whose first-order part is
2γ_H c^α(∂_α u_ν + ∂_ν u_α), c^α := g^(αβ)(c_H)_β. It has no second-order part, so it adds to the subprincipal symbol
its symbol 2iγ_H(g⁻¹(c_H, ζ)u_ν + ζ_ν g⁻¹(c_H, u)). At r_h and ζ = ξdr, g⁻¹(c_H, ζ) = ξc_v,
g⁻¹(c_H, u) = c_v u_r + c_r u_v and ζ_ν = ξδ^r_ν. So the total is
iξ((f′ + 2γ_H c_v)u_v, 2γ_H c_r u_v + (−f′ + 4γ_H c_v)u_r, 2γ_H c_v u_a), and dividing by f′(r_h) = 2/r_h gives K.

(iv) g⁻¹(dt − dr, dt − dr) = g^tt + g^rr = −f⁻¹ + f = −(1 − f)(1 + f)/f with 1 − f = m_0ρ² and 1 + f = 2 − m_0ρ²;
and g − ḡ = (1 − f)dt² + (f⁻¹ − 1)dr². ∎

At the incoming radial set R_(σ₀,in) of (11.17), the threshold ϑ_in of (11.5) is computed from the
endomorphism p_in − (S + S^(∗h)) at ∂X; the following proposition gives its structure.

**Proposition 23.6** (The radial structure at the incoming radial set.) (a) For c ∈ ℝ, the operator
ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c) on C_c^∞((0, ∞)) is formally skew-adjoint for the density ρ⁻⁵dρ, the radial factor of the Euclidean
density r³dr dx̂ of ℝ⁴, if and only if c = 3/2.

(b) On 4 + 1 Minkowski space write the first-order part of the zero energy operator (□̄^Υ)^(0), in the Cartesian
coordinates x and the frame of the splitting (21.10), as Σ_i C^i ∂_(x^i), and put A_w := r Σ_i x̂^i C^i, the
coefficient of ∂_r times r. Then

    A_w = −γ_Υ M_D,     M_D := ((−(1 + e_Υ), −(1 − e_Υ), 0), (1 − e_Υ, 1 + e_Υ, 0), (0, 0, 0)),

M_D being the coefficient of ρ∂_ρ in M_E of (23.5), and A_w + S̄ = ΞS̄Ξ, where Ξ exchanges the first two
components and fixes the third: Ξ is the reflection dr ↦ −dr of the radial direction, which exchanges dx̄⁰ = dt̄ + dr
and dx̄¹ = dt̄ − dr. Hence spec(A_w + S̄) = spec S̄ = {γ_Υ(1 − e_Υ), 2γ_Υ, γ_Υ}, and at γ_Υ = 0 both vanish.

(c) For P̂ = (□^Υ_b)^(σ) and every fibre inner product h smooth near ∂X, the endomorphisms of (11.5) satisfy
p_in − (S + S^(∗h)) = −2Re_h(A_w + S̄) at ∂X.

*Proof.* (a) For u, v ∈ C_c^∞((0, ∞)), ∫ρ²u′v̄ ρ⁻⁵dρ = ∫u′v̄ ρ⁻³dρ = ∫u(−ρ²v̄′ + 3ρv̄)ρ⁻⁵dρ, so the formal adjoint
of ρ²∂_ρ is −ρ²∂_ρ + 3ρ, and that of ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c) is −ρ(ρ∂_ρ − (3 − c)). It equals −ρ(ρ∂_ρ − c) if and only if
3 − c = c.

(b) By (23.6), (□̄^Υ)^(0) = ᵇ□̄(0) + γ_Υρ²M_E. In the Cartesian frame ᵇ□̄(0) is −Σ_i ∂²_(x^i) Id, as □̄
acts componentwise there (proof of Lemma 21.8); it has no first-order part. The splitting differs from the
Cartesian frame by a matrix Θ(x̂), homogeneous of degree 0, and conjugation by Θ adds the first-order part
−2Σ_i Θ⁻¹(∂_(x^i)Θ)∂_(x^i), whose radial contraction Σ_i x̂^iΘ⁻¹∂_(x^i)Θ = r⁻¹Θ⁻¹(r∂_rΘ) vanishes. In γ_Υρ²M_E the
operators d_𝕊 and δ_𝕊 differentiate along the spheres, so their Cartesian coefficients are tangential and do not enter
A_w; the remaining first-order part is γ_Υρ²M_D ρ∂_ρ = −γ_Υ ρ M_D ∂_r. So A_w = −γ_Υ M_D, and, with S̄ of
(23.5),

    A_w + S̄ = γ_Υ ((2, 1 − e_Υ, 0), (0, 1 − e_Υ, 0), (0, 0, 1)),

which is S̄ with its first two rows and its first two columns exchanged, that is ΞS̄Ξ. Conjugate matrices have the
same spectrum, and that of S̄ is Lemma 23.2.

(c) We compute in the frame of the splitting: the change Θ(x̂) to the Cartesian frame is homogeneous of degree 0,
commutes with ρ∂_ρ, and conjugates p_in, S, A_w and S̄ alike, h being carried along. Write D := ρ∂_ρ. By (b),
(23.6) and Lemma 21.8 (1), ρ⁻²(□̄^Υ)^(0) = −D² + (2 − A_w)D + B, where B collects the terms with
angular derivatives and those of order 0; and P̂(0) − (□̄^Υ)^(0) ∈ ρ⁴Diff_b² (Lemma 23.1 (3)), with real
scalar principal symbol, so its h-imaginary part lies in ρ⁴Diff_b¹. For the density ρ⁻⁵dρ dx̂ the formal adjoint of D
is −D + 4, as in (a); hence (ρ²D)^* = −ρ²D + 2ρ² and (ρ²D²)^* = ρ²(D² − 4D + 4), so ρ²(−D² + 2D) is formally
self-adjoint, and Im_h(−ρ²A_wD) = −(2i)⁻¹ρ²(A_w + A_w^(∗h))D + ρ²(order 0), up to terms in ρ³Diff_b¹ from the
derivatives of h along D. The h-adjoints of the terms of B have no D-term. So ρ⁻¹Im_h P̂(0) is
−(2i)⁻¹(A_w + A_w^(∗h))ρD plus terms with angular derivatives and terms vanishing at ρ = 0. As ρD = −∂_r has
scattering symbol −iξ at ξ dr, the symbol at ξ = −2, η = 0, ρ = 0 is p_in = −(A_w + A_w^(∗h)) = −2Re_h A_w. Since
S = S̄ at ∂X (Lemma 23.1 (3)), p_in − (S + S^(∗h)) = −2Re_h(A_w + S̄). ∎

**Lemma 23.7** (The threshold.) Let c_(Υ,H) = −½χ(r)dr near r_h, with χ = 1 near r_h (the choice of
Section 23.8). Then at b_0 the threshold quantity ϑ_ℋ of (11.5), computed in a suitable fibre inner
product, is 1 for every γ_(Υ,H), and the regularity condition s > ½ + ϑ_ℋ is s > 3/2. For every δ > 0 there is a
neighbourhood of b_0 (and of (e_Υ, γ_Υ, γ_(Υ,H)) in a compact set) on which ϑ_ℋ < 1 + δ in a fixed fibre inner
product.

*Proof.* Near r_h, E^Υ_(g,∞) vanishes and the horizon part of □^Υ_(b_0) is 2γ_(Υ,H)E_H G δ* with E_H as in
Proposition 23.5 (iii) and c_H = c_(Υ,H) (Definition 21.28). Here c_v = 0, so by Proposition 23.5 (iii) K has the
distinct eigenvalues 1, −1, 0, the last with a diagonal block; K is diagonalisable, and in the inner product making its
eigenvectors orthonormal its self-adjoint part is diagonal with largest eigenvalue 1. The normalisation of
(11.5), β_0⁻¹p_(1,±)(0) with p_(1,±) = ±ρ_∞σ_1(Im_h P̂), divides ξf′(r_h) by the red-shift rate β_0ρ_∞⁻¹,
which on Tangherlini is ξf′(r_h) up to the orientation sign that the ± removes; so ϑ_ℋ is the largest eigenvalue, 1.
The subprincipal symbol at N*ℋ_b and β_0 depend continuously on b (the horizon ℋ_b and its conormal bundle depend
smoothly on b, by (Dyn)), so the largest eigenvalue in the fixed inner product is continuous. ∎

On Kerr, [Hin26, footnote 71] gives the threshold 3/2 for γ_(Υ,H) = 0 and a value close to 3/2 for small γ_(Υ,H). In
dimension 4 + 1 it is the same at γ_(Υ,H) = 0, and for this c_(Υ,H) it is exactly 3/2 for every γ_(Υ,H).

#### 23.5.2 The trapped set

[Hin26, Lemma 6.4] proves that □^Υ_b is strongly trapping admissible ([Hin26c, Definition 5.8]: for every ϵ > 0 some
fibre inner product makes the skew part at the trapped set smaller than ϵ) at every subextremal Kerr parameter. The
theory of Chapter 12 does not use that property: Theorem 12.2 assumes (Γ.4), the condition γ_− < 0, that is
sup_Γ λ_max(p_1^Γ) < ½ν_min, and its losses are governed by δ_Γ ((12.4)). That condition is open, and we
prove it near b_0. We use the facts (a)–(d) below on Tangherlini. Those in (b) are proved in Chapter 22, and the others
are proved here.

On {r > r_h}, in the static chart, write a covector as ζ = −σ dt + ξ dr + η with η angular, and put
G(ζ) := g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) = −σ²f⁻¹ + fξ² + r⁻²C, where C := r²g⁻¹(η, η) = |η|²_(g_𝕊) is the Casimir of 𝕊³. H_G is the
Hamiltonian vector field of G, and π_*H_G = 2g⁻¹(ζ, ·) =: X, so X^t = 2σ/f, X^r = 2fξ and X^a = 2r⁻²g_𝕊^(ab)η_b. With
the g-orthonormal covectors w^(0) := f^(1/2)dt and w^(1) := f^(−1/2)dr (g⁻¹(w^(0), w^(0)) = −1), write
ζ = ζ_(0)w^(0) + ζ_(1)w^(1) + η, so that ζ_(0) = −σf^(−1/2) and ζ_(1) = ξf^(1/2). A section of π*T* over T*X is
u = u_ν(x, ζ)dx^ν, and ∇_(H_G)u := (H_G u_ν − X^λΓ^μ_(λν)u_μ)dx^ν is its covariant derivative ∇^(π*T*)_(H_G). For an
operator P on 1-forms with principal symbol G Id, the subprincipal operator in a frame is
S_sub(P) := −iH_G + σ_sub(P), σ_sub(P) being the matrix p̃_1 − (1/2i)Σ_j ∂_(x^j)∂_(ζ_j)p̃_2 of the proof of
Proposition 23.5 (iii). The static Christoffel symbols are Γ^t_tr = f′/(2f), Γ^r_tt = ff′/2, Γ^r_rr = −f′/(2f),
Γ^r_ab = −rf(g_𝕊)_ab, Γ^a_rb = r⁻¹δ^a_b and the Γ^a_bc of g_𝕊; the others vanish.

**Proposition 23.8** (The subprincipal operator; [Hin17, Proposition 4.1].) For every metric g, on
half-densities by |dg| and in a coordinate frame, □_g = 2δ_gG_gδ*_g has principal part G Id and
subprincipal symbol the matrix iΓ^μ_(αν)∂_(ζ_α)G. Equivalently, S_sub(□_g) = −i∇^(π*T*)_(H_G).

*Proof.* By Proposition 23.16 (i), □_g = ∇*∇ − Ric, and the Ricci term is of order zero. The proof of
Proposition 23.5 (iii) uses g only through the formal self-adjointness of the scalar wave operator for |dg|. It shows
that the subprincipal symbol of ∇*∇ is the matrix u ↦ (2iζ^αΓ^μ_(αν)u_μ)_ν, and 2ζ^α = ∂_(ζ_α)G. Then
−i∇_(H_G)u = (−iH_G u_ν + 2iζ^λΓ^μ_(λν)u_μ)dx^ν, which is S_sub(□_g)u. ∎

**Proposition 23.9** (A frame at the trapped set.) On g_(b_0), over {r > r_h}, H_G C = 0. On {G = 0}
the covectors

    e_0 := ζ,     e_1 := r(ζ_(1)w^(0) + ζ_(0)w^(1)),     e_2 := ½r²(ζ_(0)w^(0) + ζ_(1)w^(1) − η)

have the Gram matrix (g⁻¹(e_i, e_j)) = CJ with J := ((0, 0, −1), (0, 1, 0), (−1, 0, 0)), whose determinant is −C³. An
angular covector is g-orthogonal to e_0, e_1 and e_2 if and only if it is orthogonal to η.

*Proof.* C depends only on the angular variables and on η, and G = −σ²f⁻¹ + fξ² + r⁻²C. So H_G C = r⁻²{C, C} = 0,
because the Poisson bracket of C with functions of (r, ξ, σ) vanishes. Next, G = −ζ_(0)² + ζ_(1)² + r⁻²C, so on
{G = 0} we have ζ_(0)² − ζ_(1)² = r⁻²C. The entries of the Gram matrix are:

- g⁻¹(e_0, e_0) = G = 0;
- g⁻¹(e_0, e_1) = r(−ζ_(0)ζ_(1) + ζ_(1)ζ_(0)) = 0;
- g⁻¹(e_0, e_2) = ½r²(−ζ_(0)² + ζ_(1)² − r⁻²C) = −C;
- g⁻¹(e_1, e_1) = r²(ζ_(0)² − ζ_(1)²) = C;
- g⁻¹(e_1, e_2) = ½r³(−ζ_(1)ζ_(0) + ζ_(0)ζ_(1)) = 0;
- g⁻¹(e_2, e_2) = ¼r⁴G = 0.

det J = −1. For an angular covector θ, g⁻¹(θ, e_0) = g⁻¹(θ, η), g⁻¹(θ, e_1) = 0 and g⁻¹(θ, e_2) = −½r²g⁻¹(θ, η). ∎

**Proposition 23.10** (The connection on the frame.) On g_(b_0), over {r > r_h} ∩ {G = 0},

    ∇_(H_G)e_0 = 0,     ∇_(H_G)e_1 = −2σe_0,     ∇_(H_G)e_2 = −2σe_1.

*Proof.* We use H_G r = 2fξ, H_G σ = 0 and H_G ξ = −∂_r G = −σ²f′f⁻² − f′ξ² + 2r⁻³C.

*e_0.* (∇_(H_G)ζ)_ν = −∂_ν G − X^λΓ^μ_(λν)ζ_μ. Since ∂_ν g^(αβ) = −g^(αλ)Γ^β_(νλ) − g^(βλ)Γ^α_(νλ), we have
−∂_ν G = X^λΓ^μ_(νλ)ζ_μ. So ∇_(H_G)ζ = 0 everywhere; this is the geodesic equation.

*e_2.* Write ζ = ζ_tr + η with ζ_tr := −σ dt + ξ dr = ζ_(0)w^(0) + ζ_(1)w^(1). The components of ∇_(H_G)η are:

- (∇_(H_G)η)_t = 0;
- (∇_(H_G)η)_r = −X^aΓ^b_(ar)η_b = −2r⁻³C;
- (∇_(H_G)η)_a = −2r⁻¹fξη_a.

In the last, the remaining terms are r⁻² times those of the geodesic equation on 𝕊³, and they cancel as for e_0. So
∇_(H_G)ζ_tr = −∇_(H_G)η = 2r⁻³C dr + 2r⁻¹fξη. Now e_2 = r²ζ_tr − ½r²ζ and H_G(r²) = 4rfξ, so

    ∇_(H_G)e_2 = 4rfξζ_tr + r²∇_(H_G)ζ_tr − 2rfξζ = 2rfξζ_tr + 2r⁻¹C dr = −2σrfξ dt + 2r(fξ² + r⁻²C)dr.

On {G = 0}, fξ² + r⁻²C = σ²/f. Since e_1 = r(fξ dt − σf⁻¹dr), this is −2σe_1.

*e_1.* Write e_1 = a dt + b dr with a := rfξ and b := −rσ/f. Then

    (∇_(H_G)e_1)_t = H_G a − X^tΓ^r_tt b − X^rΓ^t_rt a,     (∇_(H_G)e_1)_r = H_G b − X^tΓ^t_tr a − X^rΓ^r_rr b,

and (∇_(H_G)e_1)_c = −X^aΓ^r_ac b = 2r⁻¹fbη_c = −2ση_c. For the first component,
H_G a = 2f²ξ² + rff′ξ² − rσ²f′/f + 2r⁻²fC, so (∇_(H_G)e_1)_t = 2f²ξ² + 2r⁻²fC = 2f(fξ² + r⁻²C), which is 2σ² on
{G = 0}. For the second, H_G b = −σ(2ξ − 2rf′ξ/f), so (∇_(H_G)e_1)_r = −2σξ + 2σrf′ξ/f − 2σrf′ξ/f = −2σξ. Hence
∇_(H_G)e_1 = 2σ²dt − 2σξ dr − 2ση = −2σζ. ∎

**Proposition 23.11** (A nilpotent endomorphism.) Let 𝔫 be the endomorphism of span{e_0, e_1, e_2} with
𝔫e_0 = 0, 𝔫e_1 = e_0 and 𝔫e_2 = e_1, and let ϵ > 0. For the inner product diag(1, ϵ⁻¹, ϵ⁻²) in the basis
(e_0, e_1, e_2)/C^(1/2), 𝔫 + 𝔫* has norm 2^(1/2)ϵ^(1/2). For diag(1, ϵ⁻², ϵ⁻⁴) its norm is 2^(1/2)ϵ.

*Proof.* The vectors e_0/C^(1/2), ϵ^(1/2)e_1/C^(1/2) and ϵe_2/C^(1/2) are orthonormal. In this basis 𝔫 has the entries
ϵ^(1/2), ϵ^(1/2) above the diagonal and zeros elsewhere. So 𝔫 + 𝔫* = ϵ^(1/2)B with B := ((0, 1, 0), (1, 0, 1),
(0, 1, 0)), whose eigenvalues are 0 and ±2^(1/2). For the second inner product the basis is e_0, ϵe_1, ϵ²e_2 (divided
by C^(1/2)), and the entries are ϵ, ϵ. ∎

**Remark 23.12** (The frame on Kerr.) [Hin26, (6.16c)] writes ∇_(H_G) on Kerr as H_G plus 2σ times
the shift e_1 ↦ e_0, e_2 ↦ e_1 in a frame e_0, …, e_3 whose fourth member it annihilates. In the conventions here
∇_(H_G)e_1 = −2σe_0 (Proposition 23.10); in the frame (e_0, −e_1, e_2) the relations take the form printed there,
and the matrix is nilpotent either way. For the inner product diag(1, ϵ⁻¹, ϵ⁻², ϵ⁻³) named in the proof of
[Hin26, Lemma 6.4] the norm of 𝔫 + 𝔫* is 2^(1/2)ϵ^(1/2) by the proof above, 𝔫 vanishing on e_3; the order O(ϵ)
stated there holds for the squared weights, which is why the second inner product of Proposition 23.11 is recorded.
Either norm tends to 0 with ϵ, which is all that Lemma 23.14 uses.

**Proposition 23.13** (The loss at the trapped set.) At a point of the trapped set Γ of
Proposition 22.5, where σ = 1 and C = 4m_0, ∇_(H_G) maps e_0 ↦ 0, e_1 ↦ −2e_0 and e_2 ↦ −2e_1. It preserves
𝒫 := span{e_0, e_1, e_2} and the g-orthogonal complement V_⊥ of 𝒫. With the inner product diag(1, ϵ⁻¹, ϵ⁻²) on 𝒫 in
the basis e_j/C^(1/2), and M the matrix of ∇_(H_G) on 𝒫 there, p_1 := −½(M + M*) has spectrum 0, ±(2ϵ)^(1/2). So
sup p_1/(2β_Γ) = (2ϵ)^(1/2)/4 and 2 sup p_1/ν = (m_0ϵ)^(1/2) there, with β_Γ = 2 and ν = 4(2m_0)^(−1/2) of
Proposition 22.5.

*Proof.* On Γ, G = 0, σ = 1 and C = 4m_0 > 0, so the frame is defined. By Proposition 23.10, 𝒫 is invariant. Since
H_G C = 0 (Proposition 23.9), the matrix of ∇_(H_G) in the basis e_j/C^(1/2) is M = −2𝔫. Because ∇ is metric,
V_⊥ is invariant as well. Then p_1 = 𝔫 + 𝔫*, whose spectrum is 0, ±(2ϵ)^(1/2) by the proof of Proposition 23.11.
Finally, (2ϵ)^(1/2)/(2 · 2) = (2ϵ)^(1/2)/4, and 2(2ϵ)^(1/2)(2m_0)^(1/2)/4 = (m_0ϵ)^(1/2). ∎

(a) The subprincipal operator of □_(g_(b_0)) on half-densities by |dg| is −i∇^(π*T*)_(H_G) (Proposition 23.8).

(b) The trapped set in the future characteristic set is {r² = 2m_0, ξ = 0}. At the value 1 of the semiclassical
parameter it is {r² = 2m_0, ξ = 0, C = 4m_0}. Its expansion rates are ±ν with ν = 4(2m_0)^(−1/2), and
{φ_u, φ_s} = ν/f > 0, dG_1 ≠ 0 and β_Γ = 1/f(r_ph) = 2 (Proposition 22.4, Proposition 22.5).

(c) On the characteristic set, the frame e_0, e_1, e_2 of Proposition 23.9 has Gram matrix CJ, and
∇_(H_G)e_0 = 0, ∇_(H_G)e_1 = −2σe_0 and ∇_(H_G)e_2 = −2σe_1 (Proposition 23.10). An angular covector is orthogonal
to all three if and only if it is orthogonal to η.

(d) In the inner product diag(1, ϵ_1⁻¹, ϵ_1⁻²) on span{e_0, e_1, e_2}/C^(1/2), the endomorphism p_1 = −½(M + M*), with
M the connection matrix of (c), has spectrum 0, ±(2ϵ_1)^(1/2) at σ = 1 (Proposition 23.11, Proposition 23.13).

**Lemma 23.14** (The trapped set; [Hin26, Lemma 6.4] in dimension 4 + 1, in the form Theorem 12.2
uses.) Assume (Dyn), with the trapped sets Γ_b (at z_0 = ±1) depending continuously on b and Γ_(b_0) as in (b). For
every ϵ > 0 there are a stationary fibre inner product h_Γ on π*T* over a neighbourhood of Γ_(b_0) in phase space,
homogeneous of degree 0 (it depends on the covector, as (H7) of Section 12.1.2 and Definition 15.26 allow,
Lemma 12.36 reducing it to a standard one), and a neighbourhood ℬ_ϵ of b_0, such that for b ∈ ℬ_ϵ and every E_Υ
as in Section 23.1, sup_(Γ_b) λ_max(p_1^Γ) < ϵ. In particular (Γ.4) holds with γ_− < 0 (take ϵ < ½ν_min), and
δ_Γ(0), which by (12.4) tends to 0 with γ_+, is as small as wished.

*Proof.* E^Υ vanishes over U_Γ ⊃ π(Γ_b) (Section 23.1), so p_1^Γ is that of □_(g_b). *At b_0.* Near Γ_(b_0),
where C > 0, split π*T* = 𝒫 ⊕ V_⊥ with 𝒫 := span{e_0, e_1, e_2} and V_⊥ its g-orthogonal complement, the angular
covectors orthogonal to η, by (c); g is positive definite on V_⊥. 𝒫 is ∇_(H_G)-invariant by (c), and as ∇ is metric,
so is V_⊥, on which ∇_(H_G) is g-skew. Take h_Γ := diag(1, ϵ_1⁻¹, ϵ_1⁻²) on 𝒫 in the frame e_j/C^(1/2), and g on
V_⊥; it is stationary and homogeneous of degree 0, as H_G C = 0 and C has degree 2. In these frames h_Γ is constant,
−iH_G is symmetric for the symplectic volume, and H_G σ = 0, so by (a) p_1^Γ is −½(M + M*) on 𝒫 and 0 on V_⊥, with
largest eigenvalue (2ϵ_1)^(1/2) by (d) at the point considered. The isometries of Tangherlini (time translations and
SO(4)) act transitively on Γ_(b_0) and preserve the construction of the frame, so this holds at every point. Choose
ϵ_1 with (2ϵ_1)^(1/2) < ϵ/2. *Near b_0.* Extend h_Γ to a stationary inner product on a neighbourhood of Γ_(b_0). The
endomorphism p_1 is built from the subprincipal symbol of □_(g_b) and h_Γ, continuous in b uniformly near Γ_(b_0),
and Γ_b → Γ_(b_0) by (Dyn); so sup_(Γ_b) λ_max(p_1^Γ) < ϵ for b near b_0. ν_min and β_Γ are continuous in b by (Dyn)
and positive at b_0. Two conventions enter. First, p_1^Γ is the endomorphism of Lemma 12.36 for this h_Γ, which
in the frame e_j/C^(1/2), where h_Γ is constant, is the h_Γ-imaginary part of the subprincipal operator. Second, (a) uses
half-densities by |dg|, while the adjoints of Chapter 11 are for |dx| = r³dr dx̂ and dt_*. On Tangherlini |dg| = |dt_*|
r³dr dx̂, so the two agree at b_0; near b_0 the change of density by f_b := |dg_b|/|dg_(b_0)| adds the scalar ½f_b⁻¹H_G
f_b = O(|b − b_0|) to p_1 (the remark after Lemma 15.27), which the continuity step absorbs. ∎

### 23.6 High energies and bounded frequencies

**Proposition 23.15** ([Hin26, Proposition 6.5] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (Dyn). Fix c_Υ and c_(Υ,H) as
in Section 23.1. There are C_0 and a neighbourhood ℬ′ of b_0 such that for b ∈ ℬ′ and (e_Υ, γ_Υ, γ_(Υ,H)) in a
fixed compact set, (□^Υ_b)^(σ): 𝒳_σ → 𝒴_σ (Theorem 11.33, orders as in Theorem 12.2 (3)) is invertible for
Im σ ≥ 0, |σ| ≥ C_0.

*Proof.* Lemma 23.1 gives (H1), (H2) and the operator part of (H6); Lemma 23.7 the threshold in (H3),
with s > 3/2 + δ; Lemma 23.14 (Γ.4) with γ_− < 0; (Dyn) the rest of (H3)–(H8); and the continuity in
(b, e_Υ, γ_Υ, γ_(Υ,H)) of every datum is (H5), extended as in Section 12.9. Theorem 12.2 (3) applies, with
constants uniform in the parameters by Section 12.9. ∎

Mode stability at bounded nonzero frequencies needs that of the unmodified operator at b_0, which [Hin26] takes from
[AHW24, Theorem 5.1] on Kerr. On five-dimensional Tangherlini it reduces to three ordinary differential equations, by
the following identities. Write □ := □_(g_(b_0)), and let fields be e^(−iσt) times stationary ones, σ ∈ ℂ, in the
static chart on {r > r_h}; Φ_* := dΦ/dr_* = fΦ′.

**Proposition 23.16** (The mode equations on Tangherlini.)

(i) For every metric, on 1-forms, 2δ_g G_g δ*_g = ∇*∇ − Ric and dδ_g + δ_g d = ∇*∇ + Ric. So on g_(b_0),
□ = dδ + δd = ∇*∇.

(ii) For u = r^(−3/2)Φ(r)S e^(−iσt), S ∈ 𝒮_l: −fr^(3/2)e^(iσt)(δdu)/S = f(fΦ′)′ + σ²Φ − V_0Φ, with
V_0 := (f/r²)(κ + 3/4 + 9m_0/(4r²)).

(iii) Let Y be a 1-form on 𝕊³, ψ := r^(−1/2)Φ(r)e^(−iσt) and A := ψY. Then δA = r⁻²ψ δ_𝕊Y,
(δdA)_t = iσr⁻²ψ δ_𝕊Y, (δdA)_r = −r⁻²(∂_rψ)δ_𝕊Y, and on angular vectors

    −fr^(1/2)e^(iσt)((δdA)_a − r⁻²ψ(δ_𝕊d_𝕊Y)_a) = (f(fΦ′)′ + σ²Φ − U_1Φ)Y_a,     U_1 := (f/r²)(−1/4 + 5m_0/(4r²)).

In particular, if Y is co-closed with δ_𝕊 d_𝕊 Y = ΛY, then δA = 0, and δdA = 0 if and only if
f(fΦ′)′ + σ²Φ − V_1Φ = 0, with V_1 := U_1 + Λf/r² = (f/r²)(Λ − 1/4 + 5m_0/(4r²)). For Y ∈ 𝒱_l, Λ = (l + 1)².

(iv) Let A = (a(r)S dt + b(r)S dr)e^(−iσt), S ∈ 𝒮_l; every scalar type 1-form (aS dt + bS dr + c d_𝕊S)e^(−iσt)
differs from one of this form by d(cS e^(−iσt)), which does not change dA. Write dA = F_tr S e^(−iσt) dt ∧ dr + …,
so that F_tr = −iσb − a′, and M := δdA = (M_t S dt + M_r S dr)e^(−iσt) + (angular part). Then W := r³F_tr satisfies

    R[W] := (fW′/r)′ − κW/r³ + σ²W/(rf) = (r²M_t)′ + iσr²M_r,

and fr^(1/2)R[r^(1/2)Φ] = f(fΦ′)′ + σ²Φ − V_2Φ with V_2 := (f/r²)(κ + 3/4 − 7m_0/(4r²)). Where F_tr = 0,
M_t = κa/r² and M_r = κb/r². At l = 0, M_r = −iσF_tr/f, and F_tr S dt ∧ dr is all of dA. For l ≥ 1 and every
solution of R[W] = 0, A(W) := (κr)⁻¹(−fW′S dt + iσf⁻¹WS dr)e^(−iσt) satisfies δdA(W) = 0 and r³F_tr = W.

(v) For r > r_h: V_0 > 0; V_1 > 0 when Λ ≥ 2; V_2 > 0 when κ ≥ 3, while at l = 0 V_2 is negative near r_h. The
tortoise coordinate r_* := r + ½r_h log((r − r_h)/(r + r_h)) has dr_*/dr = 1/f and
r_* = r − m_0/r − (m_0²/3)r⁻³ + O(r⁻⁵); f′(r_h)/2 = 1/r_h; and dι_Tω + ι_Tdω = −iσω for T = ∂_t and every
ω = e^(−iσt)ω_0, ω_0 stationary.

*Proof.* (i) With δω = −∇^μω_μ and δ*ω = ½(∇_μω_ν + ∇_νω_μ), tr δ*ω = −δω, so Gδ*ω = δ*ω + ½gδω and
2(δGδ*ω)_ν = −∇^μ∇_μω_ν − ∇^μ∇_νω_μ − ∇_ν δω. The Ricci identity gives
∇^μ∇_νω_μ = ∇_ν∇^μω_μ + Ric_ν^μ ω_μ = −∇_νδω + (Ric ω)_ν, so 2δGδ*ω = ∇*∇ω − Ric ω. Likewise
(δdω)_ν = −∇^μ(∇_μω_ν − ∇_νω_μ) = (∇*∇ω)_ν − (dδω)_ν + (Ric ω)_ν. g_(b_0) is Ricci-flat (Proposition 21.17).

(ii) On functions δdu = −|g|^(−1/2)∂_μ(|g|^(1/2)g^(μν)∂_νu) with |g|^(1/2) = r³|g_𝕊|^(1/2), g^tt = −1/f,
g^rr = f and g^(ab) = r⁻²g_𝕊^(ab); so for u = e^(−iσt)u_0(r)S, e^(iσt)δdu = (−σ²f⁻¹u_0 − r⁻³(r³fu_0′)′ + κr⁻²u_0)S.
With u_0 = r^(−3/2)Φ, r³f u_0′ = f(r^(3/2)Φ′ − (3/2)r^(1/2)Φ), and
r⁻³(r³fu_0′)′ = r^(−3/2)((fΦ′)′ − (3/2)r⁻¹f′Φ − (3/4)r⁻²fΦ). Multiplying by −fr^(3/2) gives the equation with
V_0 = f((3/2)r⁻¹f′ + (3/4)r⁻²f + κr⁻²), and (3/2)r⁻¹f′ = 3m_0r⁻⁴, (3/4)r⁻²f = (3/4)r⁻² − (3/4)m_0r⁻⁴.

(iii) δA = −r⁻³|g_𝕊|^(−1/2)∂_a(r|g_𝕊|^(1/2)g_𝕊^(ab)ψY_b) = r⁻²ψδ_𝕊Y. For the 2-form F := dA,
(δF)^ν = −|g|^(−1/2)∂_μ(|g|^(1/2)F^(μν)), with F_ta = ∂_tψ Y_a, F_ra = ∂_rψ Y_a and F_ab = ψ(d_𝕊Y)_ab. Here
F^(at) = (fr²)⁻¹∂_tψ Y^a and F^(ar) = −fr⁻²∂_rψ Y^a, with the index raised by g_𝕊, so (δF)^t = (fr²)⁻¹∂_tψ δ_𝕊Y and
(δF)^r = −fr⁻²∂_rψ δ_𝕊Y; lowering by g_tt = −f and g_rr = f⁻¹, and ∂_t = −iσ, gives (δdA)_t and (δdA)_r. The
angular component is

    (δF)_a = (f⁻¹∂_t²ψ − r⁻¹∂_r(rf∂_rψ))Y_a + r⁻²ψ(δ_𝕊d_𝕊Y)_a,

the last term from the angular divergence of F^(ab) = r⁻⁴ψ(d_𝕊Y)^(ab), lowered by g_ab = r²(g_𝕊)_ab. With
∂_t² = −σ² and r⁻¹(rf(r^(−1/2)Φ)′)′ = r^(−1/2)((fΦ′)′ − ½r⁻¹f′Φ + ¼r⁻²fΦ), multiplying the first term by
−fr^(1/2)e^(iσt) gives f(fΦ′)′ + σ²Φ − U_1Φ with U_1 = f(½r⁻¹f′ − ¼r⁻²f), and ½r⁻¹f′ = m_0r⁻⁴,
−¼r⁻²f = −¼r⁻² + ¼m_0r⁻⁴. If Y is co-closed with δ_𝕊d_𝕊Y = ΛY, the t- and r-components vanish, δA = 0, and the
angular component gives the equation with V_1 = U_1 + Λf/r². For Y ∈ 𝒱_l,
δ_𝕊d_𝕊Y = Δ_𝕊Y + 2Y on co-closed 1-forms of 𝕊³ (the Ricci identity on the unit 𝕊³, where Ric = 2g_𝕊), and
Δ_𝕊Y = (κ − 1)Y (Lemma 21.5); so Λ = κ + 1 = (l + 1)².

(iv) Up to the factor e^(−iσt), F_tr = −iσb − a′, F_at = a∂_aS, F_ar = b∂_aS and F_ab = 0. Then
F^(rt) = g^rr g^tt F_rt = F_tr and F^(at) = −(fr²)⁻¹a∇^a_𝕊S, so, using ∇_(𝕊,a)∇^a_𝕊S = −κS,
(δF)^t = (−r⁻³W′ − κa(fr²)⁻¹)S and M_t = −f(δF)^t/S = fW′r⁻³ + κar⁻². Similarly F^(tr) = −F_tr and
F^(ar) = fr⁻²b∇^a_𝕊S give (δF)^r = (−iσr⁻³W + κfbr⁻²)S, so M_r = f⁻¹(δF)^r/S = −iσW/(fr³) + κb/r². Hence

    (r²M_t)′ + iσr²M_r = (fW′/r)′ + κa′ + σ²W/(fr) + iσκb = (fW′/r)′ + σ²W/(rf) − κF_tr = R[W].

The two formulas give M_t = κa/r², M_r = κb/r² where W = 0, and M_r = −iσF_tr/f at κ = 0, where d_𝕊S = 0, so that
dA = F_tr S dt ∧ dr. Next, with W = r^(1/2)Φ, (fW′/r)′ = r^(−1/2)(fΦ′)′ + ½r^(−3/2)f′Φ − (3/4)r^(−5/2)fΦ, so
fr^(1/2)R[r^(1/2)Φ] = f(fΦ′)′ + σ²Φ − f(κr⁻² + (3/4)fr⁻² − ½f′r⁻¹)Φ, and (3/4)f − ½rf′ = 3/4 − (7/4)m_0r⁻².
Finally, for A(W), a = −fW′/(κr) and b = iσW/(κrf), so F_tr = σ²W/(κrf) + (fW′/r)′/κ = W/r³ when R[W] = 0;
M_t = M_r = 0 by the formulas above; and the angular component of δdA, which by the same calculation is
r⁻¹(iσra/f + (rfb)′)d_𝕊S, vanishes since iσra/f = −iσW′/κ and (rfb)′ = iσW′/κ.

(v) V_0 > 0 is clear; Λ − 1/4 > 0; and κ + 3/4 − (7/4)m_0/r² > κ − 1 ≥ 2 for κ ≥ 3, as m_0/r² < 1, while at κ = 0
and r = r_h the bracket is −1. dr_*/dr = 1 + ½r_h((r − r_h)⁻¹ − (r + r_h)⁻¹) = r²/(r² − m_0) = 1/f, and
log((1 − x)/(1 + x)) = −2x − (2/3)x³ + O(x⁵), x = r_h/r, gives the expansion. f′(r_h) = 2m_0r_h⁻³ = 2/r_h. The last
identity is Cartan's formula, as the Lie derivative along T is ∂_t in the static chart. ∎

The potentials are positive at l ≥ 1. They differ from those on four-dimensional Schwarzschild by the terms that 𝕊³
brings: 3/4 in V_0 and V_2, −1/4 in V_1, and 9/4, 5/4 and −7/4 times m_0/r². At l = 0 the Maxwell scalar potential is
negative near the horizon, and that sector is settled by the relation M_r = −iσF_tr/f, not by positivity.

**Proposition 23.17** (Mode stability of □ on Tangherlini away from zero frequency.) Assume (Dyn) at b_0.
For σ ≠ 0 with Im σ ≥ 0, □̂(σ): 𝒳_σ → 𝒴_σ is invertible.

*Proof.* By Theorem 11.33 (3) and Theorem 12.2 (3), which apply to □, the case E_Υ = 0 of
Section 23.2–Section 23.5, □̂(σ) is Fredholm of index 0, so it suffices to show injectivity. Let u ∈ 𝒳_σ with
□̂(σ)u = 0. By Theorem 11.33 (5) with S̄ = 0, u ∈ 𝒜^(3/2−ϵ)(X̄) for every ϵ > 0, smooth up to {|x| = r_0}, hence
across the horizon r = r_h > r_0, and conormal at infinity. Let ω := e^(−iσt_*)u, so □ω = 0.

*The class.* The time t_* of (21.30) is regular across the future horizon and outgoing at infinity:
t_* = v + F_H(r) near r_h with F_H smooth across r_h in the ingoing chart, and t_* = t − r_* + c′ + O(r⁻¹), with all
derivatives, as r → ∞ ((21.30) and Lemma 21.20 at A = 0). So in the static chart ω = e^(−iσt)ω_0
with ω_0 = e^(−iσr_*) × (smooth across r_h in (v, r)) near r_h and ω_0 = e^(iσr_*) × (conormal, O(r^(−3/2+ϵ))) near
infinity. In the static frame the coefficients a, b of Proposition 23.16 (iv) are singular at r_h (b = A_r + A_v/f);
the argument below uses only F_tr = F_vr and ω(∂_t) = ω(∂_v), which are smooth across r_h. Expanding in spherical
harmonics (Lemma 21.6; the projections act in the angles and preserve both properties, with bounds), every
component inherits them.

We use repeatedly the following fact. *If −Φ_** + VΦ = σ²Φ on (r_h, ∞) with V real, V = O(r⁻²) with all derivatives
at infinity and V = O(f) near r_h, Φ = e^(−iσr_*)h with h smooth at r_h, and Φ = e^(iσr_*)k with k conormal and
O(r^N) at infinity for some N, then Φ = 0, provided V > 0.* Indeed the solutions at infinity are
e^(±iσr_*)(1 + O(r⁻¹)) (Volterra iteration, V ∈ L¹(dr_*) at infinity); the given form excludes e^(−iσr_*), which is
e^(iσr_*)e^(−2iσr_*), and e^(−2iσr_*) grows exponentially if Im σ > 0 and is not conormal if σ ∈ ℝ ∖ 0; so
Φ = c e^(iσr_*)(1 + O(r⁻¹)). If Im σ > 0, Φ and Φ_* decay exponentially at both ends (r_* → ∓∞), and pairing with Φ̄
gives ∫(|Φ_*|² + V|Φ|²)dr_* = σ²∫|Φ|²dr_*; if Φ ≠ 0 the left side is positive, forcing σ² > 0, so σ real: a
contradiction. If σ is real, the Wronskian Im(Φ̄Φ_*) is constant; at r_h, Φ_* = −iσΦ + e^(−iσr_*)fh′ gives
−σ|h(r_h)|², and at infinity σ|c|²; so c = 0 and Φ = 0.

*(a) The scalar step.* δω solves δd(δω) = δ□ω = 0 by Proposition 23.16 (i). For each component r^(−3/2)ΦS of δω,
Proposition 23.16 (ii) gives −Φ_** + V_0Φ = σ²Φ (multiply by f), and the class holds with the extra factor r^(3/2)
(polynomial growth); so Φ = 0, and δω = 0.

*(b) The Maxwell step.* Then δdω = □ω − dδω = 0. The vector type components r^(−1/2)ΦY of ω, Y ∈ 𝒱_l, have
δ_𝕊d_𝕊Y = (l + 1)²Y with (l + 1)² ≥ 4, so Proposition 23.16 (iii) and the fact give Φ = 0. For the scalar type part
at l ≥ 1, W = r³F_tr solves R[W] = 0 by Proposition 23.16 (iv) (as M = 0), so Φ := r^(−1/2)W solves the equation
with V_2 > 0; F_tr dt ∧ dr = F_vr dv ∧ dr is a component of dω, so Φ is in the class, and Φ = 0. Then F_tr = 0 and
M = 0 give a = b = 0 in the gauge of Proposition 23.16 (iv), κ ≠ 0: that part of ω is a gradient. At l = 0,
M_r = −iσF_tr/f = 0 gives F_tr = 0, which is all of dω there. So dω = 0.

*(c) The gauge step.* By Proposition 23.16 (v) and dω = 0, ω = (i/σ)dφ with φ := ω(T), which is in the scalar class.
δdφ = −iσδω = 0, so φ = 0 by (a), and ω = 0 on {r > r_h}.

*(d) Inside the horizon.* So u = 0 on {r > r_h}. The horizon is null, so a Cauchy argument does not apply, and we use
the mode equations. Expand u in harmonics (Lemma 21.6): □̂(σ) commutes with the rotations, so the coefficients
of each component of fixed type and degree l form a vector U(r) (at most three functions on (r_0, ∞)), smooth across
r_h, vanishing on (r_h, ∞), which solves a system −fU″ + AU′ + BU = 0 with A, B smooth on (0, ∞). Indeed, in the
ingoing chart (v, r, y), regular across r_h, in which t_* − v is a function of r, g^vv = 0, g^vr = 1, g^rr = f and
g^(ra) = 0; conjugation by e^(−iσt_*) turns ∂_v into −iσ and ∂_r into ∂_r − iσ∂_r t_*, so the only second
r-derivative of □̂(σ) is −f∂_r², and on a harmonic component the angular derivatives are algebraic. Put
Y := (U, (r − r_h)U′). Since (r − r_h)/f = r²/(r + r_h),

    (r − r_h)Y′ = MY,     M = ⎛ 0                          1                     ⎞ ,
                              ⎝ r²(r − r_h)(r + r_h)⁻¹B    1 + r²(r + r_h)⁻¹A    ⎠

with M smooth on (0, ∞). For r_0 < r_1 < r < r_h and m_1 := max_([r_1,r_h]) ‖M‖, wherever Y ≠ 0,
(d/dr) log|Y|² = 2Re⟨Y, MY⟩/((r − r_h)|Y|²) ≥ −2m_1/(r_h − r), so if Y(r_1) ≠ 0 then |Y(r)|
≥ |Y(r_1)|((r_h − r)/(r_h − r_1))^(m_1) on [r_1, r_h) (the bound holds up to the first zero of Y after r_1, if
there is one, and by continuity keeps |Y| positive there, so there is none), which contradicts the vanishing of Y to
infinite order at r_h. So Y(r_1) = 0 for every r_1 ∈ (r_0, r_h), every component vanishes, and u = 0. ∎

**Proposition 23.18** ([Hin26, Proposition 6.9] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (Dyn). Let c_0 > 0. There are
ϵ > 0 and a neighbourhood ℬ″ of b_0 such that if |e_Υ|, |γ_Υ|, |γ_(Υ,H)| < ϵ and b ∈ ℬ″, then (□^Υ_b)^(σ) is
invertible for all σ with Im σ ≥ 0 and |σ| ≥ c_0.

*Proof.* Let 𝗉 := (b, e_Υ, γ_Υ, γ_(Υ,H)), a parameter in a compact set, with 𝗉_0 := (b_0, 0, 0, 0), at which the
operator is □. For |σ| ≥ C_0, Proposition 23.15 applies. The set K := {c_0 ≤ |σ| ≤ C_0, Im σ ≥ 0} is compact, and at
each σ ∈ K, □̂(σ) is invertible by Proposition 23.17. By Theorem 11.38 (invertibility is open in (σ, 𝗉), the
hypotheses holding uniformly by Section 23.2 and (Dyn)), each σ ∈ K has a neighbourhood U_σ and an ϵ_σ with
invertibility on U_σ × {|𝗉 − 𝗉_0| < ϵ_σ}; finitely many U_σ cover K. ∎

### 23.7 tf-admissibility
