The transition face of Section 13.4 sees the operator only at infinity. For the unmodified Minkowski operator its
model is the conjugated Helmholtz operator, componentwise.

**Proposition 23.19** (The transition face and the weights.) Let Δ_e := −Σ_(i=1)^4 ∂_(x^i)² on ℝ⁴.

(i) At γ_Υ = 0, □̄^Υ = □̄ acts componentwise in the Cartesian frame (dt̄, dx^i) on 4 + 1 Minkowski space, as the
scalar operator ∂_(t̄)² + Δ_e, and its spectral family (□̄)^(σ) = e^(iσt_*)□̄e^(−iσt_*), t_* = t̄ − r, satisfies
e^(iσr)(□̄)^(σ)e^(−iσr) = Δ_e − σ² on each component.

(ii) For l ∈ ℕ_0 the substitution u = r⁻¹w turns −u″ − (3/r)u′ + l(l + 2)r⁻²u − u = 0 into Bessel's equation
r²w″ + rw′ + (r² − (l + 1)²)w = 0 of order l + 1. The exponents of u at r = 0 are l and −(l + 2); in the variable
1/r they are −l and l + 2, the indicial roots of the scalar operator on degree l harmonics (Lemma 21.10), with
the gap (0, 2) at l = 0. As x → 0, x^(l+1)H^(1)_(l+1)(x) → −(i/π)Γ(l + 1)2^(l+1); as x → ∞,
e^(−ix)x^(1/2)H^(1)_(l+1)(x) → (2/π)^(1/2)e^(−i((l+1)π/2 + π/4)); and on the positive imaginary half-axis H^(1)_(l+1)
decays exponentially and H^(2)_(l+1) grows exponentially.

(iii) ρ^a lies in ρ^α L²(r³dr) near infinity if and only if a > α + 2: the shift between decay rates and b-weights
for the Euclidean density of ℝ⁴ is 2. On g_(b_0), with t the static time and t_* := t − r, ∂_σ²□̂(0) = 2g^00 Id, by
the argument of Lemma 23.1 (1) for this t_* (near infinity, where t − r is used), and
2g^00 W* = −4m_0ρ⁴dt + O(ρ⁵), with W* of (23.15). The time t − r_* of Proposition 23.23 (vi) differs from
t − r by O(ρ), and the two choices give the same ∂_σ□̂(0)W* up to O(ρ⁵).

*Proof.* (i) The Christoffel symbols of ḡ vanish in Cartesian coordinates, so □̄ = −ḡ^(μν)∂_μ∂_ν = ∂_(t̄)² + Δ_e on
each component. On stationary functions, e^(iσt_*)□̄e^(−iσt_*) = e^(−iσr)(e^(iσt̄)□̄e^(−iσt̄))e^(iσr) =
e^(−iσr)(Δ_e − σ²)e^(iσr). (ii) With u = w/r, −u″ − 3u′/r = −w″/r − w′/r² + w/r³; adding l(l + 2)w/r³ − w/r and
multiplying by −r³ gives r²w″ + rw′ − (1 + l(l + 2))w + r²w = 0, and 1 + l(l + 2) = (l + 1)². Bessel's equation of
order l + 1 has exponents ±(l + 1) at 0, so u has exponents l and −l − 2. The limits are [DLMF, (10.7.7)], whose
hypothesis Re ν > 0 holds as ν = l + 1, and [DLMF, (10.17.5)]; the behaviour on the imaginary axis is
[DLMF, (10.17.5)–(10.17.6)], which hold uniformly in the sectors −π + δ ≤ ph x ≤ 2π − δ and −2π + δ ≤ ph x ≤ π − δ
respectively, both containing ph x = 0 and ph x = π/2 (there e^(±ix) = e^(∓|x|)). These are
Theorem A.45 (2)–(3). (iii) ∫^∞ ρ^(2(a−α))r³dr = ∫^∞ r^(3−2(a−α))dr is finite if and only if a − α > 2. By
the argument of Lemma 23.1 (1), the σ² coefficient of e^(iσt_*)□e^(−iσt_*) is g⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) Id for every
stationary time function, here near infinity; by Proposition 23.5 (iv), g^00 = −2m_0ρ² + O(ρ⁴), and
W* = ρ²dt + r_hρ³f⁻¹dr, so 2g^00W* = −4m_0ρ⁴dt + O(ρ⁵). For the last claim put F := r − r_* = m_0/r + O(r⁻³)
(Proposition 23.16 (v)), so F′ = O(ρ²) and F″ = O(ρ³). As ∂_σ□̂(0) = −i[□, t_*] (proof of Proposition 23.23 (vi)), the
two choices differ by −i[□, F]W* = −i((□_0F)W* − 2∇_(∇F)W*), with □_0F = −r⁻³(r³fF′)′ = O(ρ³), ∇F = fF′∂_r = O(ρ²)∂_r,
W* = O(ρ²) and ∇_(∂_r)W* = O(ρ³) in the static frame (proof of Proposition 23.23 (vi)); this is O(ρ⁵). ∎

**Lemma 23.20** (tf-admissibility; [Hin26, Lemma 6.8] in dimension 4 + 1.) There is ϵ > 0 such that for e_Υ ∈
[0, ϵ), |γ_Υ| < ϵ, every γ_(Υ,H) and every b ∈ ℬ, the family σ ↦ (□^Υ_b)^(σ) is tf-admissible (Definition 13.15) with
every weight in the indicial gap (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) of Lemma 23.3 (with (0, 2) when e_Υγ_Υ² = 0).

*Proof.* The transition face operator N_tf(e^(iθ)) of Section 13.4 is built from the data of the operator at ρ = 0
only: S_0, the normal operator N(P⁽⁰⁾) and H_0. By Lemma 23.1 (3) these are the model's, independent of b and
of the horizon modification; so it suffices to consider □̄^Υ. *At γ_Υ = 0.* The model is □̄, which in the Cartesian
frame has S_0 = 0, N(P⁽⁰⁾) = (−(ρ∂_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ_𝕊) Id (Lemma 23.1 (3), Proposition 23.19 (i)) and, with the
standard inner product, H_0 = Id: by Proposition 13.20 it is tf-admissible with every weight in (0, 2). *Small γ_Υ.*
Fix the weight β = 1, which lies in the gap for all small parameters (Lemma 23.3), q = 2 − β, and orders s, α_+,
𝗋_± as in Theorem 13.14, admissible with margins at γ_Υ = 0; as S̄ = O(γ_Υ) (Lemma 23.2) and the thresholds
of (11.5) move continuously, they remain admissible for small parameters. The perturbation

    N^γ_tf − N^0_tf = −2ie^(iθ)ρ̂S̄ + γ_Υ ρ̂²M_E(ρ̂∂_ρ̂, ∂_x̂)

([Hin26, (6.18a)] with Lemma 23.2) is bounded from the space H_(sc,b)^(s,(𝗋+α_+,q)) of 𝒳_(tf,θ) into that of
𝒴_(tf,θ) with norm O(|γ_Υ|), uniformly in θ: near the end ρ̂ → 0, ρ̂ · (order 0) gains one order of decay and
ρ̂² Diff_b¹ = ρ̂ Diff_sc¹ gains one order of decay for one sc-derivative; near ρ̂ → ∞ the weights q and q − 2 allow the
factors ρ̂ and ρ̂². So 𝒳_(tf,θ) is the same space for all small γ_Υ, and by Corollary 13.16 (b) at γ_Υ = 0, uniformly
over the three sectors, ‖w‖ ≤ C‖N^0_tf w‖ ≤ C‖N^γ_tf w‖ + C′|γ_Υ|‖w‖; for C′|γ_Υ| ≤ ½ this gives injectivity of
N^γ_tf(e^(iθ)) for all θ ∈ [0, π], and the adjoint estimate (13.18) gives that of N^γ_tf(1)^(*h) in the same
way. So the family of □̄^Υ is tf-admissible with weight 1, and by Corollary 13.16 (c) with every weight in the gap.
The condition e_Υ ≥ 0 makes z ≥ 0, so that Lemma 23.3 describes the gap. ∎

### 23.8 The zero energy setting

The rest of the chapter concerns σ = 0 and its neighbourhood: [Hin26, Section 6.4 and Lemma 6.13] (pp. 119–125) in
dimension 4 + 1 here and in Section 23.9–Section 23.12, and [Hin26, Section 6.5] in Section 23.13 and after.
The kernel of the unmodified operator at zero energy is proved on Tangherlini from the mode equations of
Proposition 23.16, and its cokernel from a distributional identity at the horizon, with the index from Chapter 13. The
first step of the proof of mode stability (Proposition 23.24) is a Grushin problem with a fixed compactly supported
augmentation, to which Theorem 13.25 and Theorem 13.29 apply as proved; its Schur complement is computed from two
pairings alone, so the augmented estimate [Hin26, (6.27)] with a joint parameter, and the decay of
∂_σ□̂(0)ω_(0) that it needs [Hin26, footnote 69], are not used. The second step is carried out at every frequency at
once, around a base point at which invertibility is already known.

ℬ, g_b, t_*, ρ, E_Υ and □^Υ_b are as in Section 23.1, with c_(Υ,H) := −½χ(r)dr, χ ∈ C_c^∞, χ = 1 near r_h and
supp χ ∩ U_Γ = ∅. Write 𝗉 := (b, e_Υ, γ_Υ, γ_(Υ,H)), P̂_𝗉(σ) := (□^Υ_b)^(σ), 𝗉_0 := (b_0, 0, 0, 0) and
P̂ := P̂_(𝗉_0), the spectral family of □ = □_(g_(b_0)) = dδ + δd. On g_(b_0), in the ingoing chart,
g = −f dv² + 2dv dr + r²g_𝕊 and |dg| = r³|dv dr dg_𝕊|, and t_* − v is a smooth function of r near r_h
((21.30)).

*The spaces.* For σ ≠ 0, Im σ ≥ 0: 𝒳_σ, 𝒴_σ of (13.22) (those of Theorem 11.33 with the orders of
Theorem 12.2 (3)); at σ = 0: 𝒳_0, 𝒴_0 of (13.7), with the Euclidean density, so that the b-weight of
H̄_b^(s,α) is α + 2 (Section 13.1.2). By Section 23.2–Section 23.5, Section 23.7 and (Dyn), every P̂_𝗉, 𝗉 in
a compact neighbourhood 𝒦 of 𝗉_0 with e_Υ ≥ 0, satisfies (H1)–(H5) with ϑ_ℋ = 1 (Lemma 23.7), (G) for every α
with α + 2 ∈ (0, 2) (Lemma 23.3: (0, 2) lies in the gap (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)), which is (0, 2) when
e_Υγ_Υ² = 0), and (TF) (Lemma 23.20), and has index 0 at σ ≠ 0 (Theorem 12.2 (3) at high frequencies, as in
Proposition 23.15, and the constancy of the index, Theorem 11.33 (3), at bounded ones). We fix such an α and a
constant s > 5/2; by Theorem 13.11 (3)–(4) and Theorem 11.33 (3), kernels, annihilators of ranges and
invertibility do not depend on these choices.

*The horizon functional.* Let ω* := d(H(r − r_h)) = δ(r − r_h)dr, H the Heaviside function, a stationary
distributional 1-form supported on the horizon sphere, and

    ℓ(v) := ∫_X g⁻¹(v, ω*) |dg_X| = r_h³ ∫_(𝕊³) v(∂_(t_*))|_(r=r_h) dx̂,    (23.13)

where |dg| = |dt_*| ⊗ |dg_X|, so |dg_X| = r³|dr dx̂| near r_h, and g⁻¹(v, dr) = v(∇r) = v(∂_v + f∂_r) equals
v(∂_(t_*)) at r_h. ℓ is continuous on H^(s′) near the horizon sphere for s′ > ½ (the trace theorem), so on 𝒴_0 and
𝒴_σ, as s − 1 > ½. It is [Hin26]'s pairing with ω*_(0).

*The modified divergence at the horizon.* With the trace weight 2/3, E_H h := 2ι_(c♯_(Υ,H))h − (2/3)c_(Υ,H) tr_g h
([Hin26, (6.22)] with the weight 2/3), and since tr_g G_g h = −(3/2)tr_g h in dimension 5 (Lemma 21.29),

    E_H G_g = 2ι_(c♯_(Υ,H)),    (23.14)

as [Hin26]'s E_(H⁺,1)G = 2ι_(c♯) in dimension 4 with the weight 1. The horizon part of □^Υ_b is
2γ_(Υ,H)E_H G δ*.

### 23.9 Kernel and cokernel at zero energy

Let

    W* := r⁻²dt + r_h r⁻³f⁻¹dr = r⁻²dv − dr/(r(r + r_h)).    (23.15)

The two forms agree, as dt = dv − f⁻¹dr and f = (r − r_h)(r + r_h)/r². The second shows that W* is smooth on
{r > 0} in the ingoing chart, so on X̄ up to ∂_♯X; near infinity dt = dt_* + (f⁻¹ + O(r⁻²))dr with all derivatives
((21.30)), so W* ∈ 𝒜²(X̄; E), and W* ∈ H̄_b^(s,α) for α + 2 < 2. dW* = 2r⁻³dt ∧ dr, and δW* = 0:
δ(a(r)dt) = 0 for the static metric, and δ(b(r)dr) = −r⁻³(r³fb)′ vanishes for b = r_h r⁻³f⁻¹. δdW* = 0, because
r³F^(rt) is constant for F = 2r⁻³dt ∧ dr (F^(rt) = g^rr g^tt F_rt, g^rr g^tt = −1). So □W* = 0 on {r > r_h}, and on
{r > 0}, since the components of □W* in the ingoing chart are real-analytic in r. By Proposition 23.23 (iii), W* is
the only l = 0 element of the kernel that is smooth at the future horizon and decays.

**Lemma 23.21** (Kernel and cokernel; [Hin26, Lemma 6.10] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (Dyn) at b_0.
(1) For every stationary u that is smooth near the horizon sphere, ℓ(P̂(0)u) = 0. (2) ker_(𝒳_0) P̂(0) = span{W*}.
(3) The annihilator of the range of P̂(0): 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 is spanned by ℓ.

*Proof.* (1) *Symmetry.* For stationary smooth 1-forms u, w with w compactly supported in X°,
B(u, w) := ∫_X g⁻¹(u, w̄)|dg_X| satisfies B(□u, w) = B(u, □w). Indeed, let θ_1 ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ) with ∫θ_1 = 1 and
W := θ_1(t_*)w. As □ = −∇^μ∇_μ, two integrations by parts against the compactly supported W give
∫g⁻¹(□u, W̄)|dg| = ∫g⁻¹(u, □W̄)|dg|. The left side is B(□u, w). On the right,
□(θ_1w) = θ_1□w + (□_0θ_1)w − 2∇_(∇θ_1)w with □_0 = −∇^μ∇_μ on functions, and ∇θ_1 = θ_1′∇t_*,
□_0θ_1 = −θ_1″g⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) + θ_1′□_0t_*; the coefficients of θ_1′ and θ_1″ are stationary, and
∫θ_1′ = ∫θ_1″ = 0, so the right side is B(u, □w). By continuity the identity extends to w a stationary distribution
with compact support in X° (u smooth). *The identity.* Since □ = dδ + δd and δ² = 0, □d = dδd = d□_0 on functions,
as operators on distributions. In the ingoing chart H(r − r_h) is a v-independent distribution, and

    □_0 H(r − r_h) = −r⁻³∂_μ(r³g^(μr)δ(r − r_h)) = −r⁻³∂_r(r³f δ(r − r_h)) = 0,

as ∂_v annihilates it, g^(ar) = 0, and r³fδ(r − r_h) = r_h³f(r_h)δ(r − r_h) = 0. So □ω* = d□_0H(r − r_h) = 0, and
ℓ(□u) = B(□u, ω*) = B(u, □ω*) = 0; on stationary u, □u = P̂(0)u. Only u near the horizon sphere enters.

(2) W* ∈ 𝒳_0 and P̂(0)W* = 0, by the above. Conversely let u ∈ 𝒳_0 with P̂(0)u = 0. By Theorem 13.11 (2), with the
gap (0, 2), u is smooth up to ∂_♯X, hence across the horizon, and u ∈ 𝒜^β near ∂X for every β < 2; fix β ∈ (1, 2).
Let ω := u, a stationary 1-form, and work first on {r > r_h} in the static chart, expanding in harmonics
(Lemma 21.6; the projections act in the angles and preserve smoothness at r_h in the ingoing chart and the
conormal bounds at infinity). Three facts are used. The *scalar identity*: for a stationary function φ,
δdφ = −r⁻³(r³fφ′)′ + r⁻²Δ_𝕊φ, so a degree l component φ_l of a solution of δdφ = 0 solves (r³fφ_l′)′ = κrφ_l. The
*energy fact*: if −Φ_** + VΦ = 0 on (r_h, ∞), Φ_* = fΦ′, with V > 0 continuous, Φ of class C¹ in r up to r_h, and
Φ_*Φ̄ → 0 as r → ∞, then Φ = 0: integrating Φ̄ times the equation over r_* ∈ [r_*(r_1), r_*(R)] gives
∫(|Φ_*|² + V|Φ|²)dr_* = [Φ_*Φ̄], whose endpoint terms tend to 0 as r_1 → r_h (Φ_* = fΦ′ → 0) and R → ∞. The *mode
equations* Proposition 23.16 (iii)–(iv), which hold for every σ and are used at σ = 0.

*(a) The divergence.* φ := δω is a smooth stationary function in 𝒜^(β+1) near infinity, and
δdφ = δ(□ω − δdω) = 0. Multiplying (r³fφ_l′)′ = κrφ_l by φ̄_l and integrating over [r_1, R]:
[r³fφ_l′φ̄_l]_(r_1)^R = ∫_(r_1)^R (r³f|φ_l′|² + κr|φ_l|²)dr. As r_1 → r_h the bracket tends to 0 (f → 0, φ_l smooth
in r there); as R → ∞ it is O(R^(3−(β+2)−(β+1))) = O(R^(−2β)). So φ_l′ = 0 and κφ_l = 0; at l = 0, φ_0 is a decaying
constant. So δω = 0.

*(b) The field.* F := dω ∈ 𝒜^(β+1) and δF = □ω − dδω = 0. *Vector type.* A component r^(−1/2)Φ(r)Y of ω, Y ∈ 𝒱_l,
l ≥ 1, has δ_𝕊d_𝕊Y = ΛY with Λ = (l + 1)² ≥ 4; by Proposition 23.16 (iii) at σ = 0, −Φ_** + V_1Φ = 0 with V_1 > 0.
Φ is smooth in r at r_h (angular components are the same in the static and the ingoing chart), and since |Y| is r⁻¹
in the Euclidean metric, Φ = O(r^(3/2−β)) and Φ_* = O(r^(1/2−β)), so Φ_*Φ̄ = O(r^(2−2β)) → 0. The energy fact gives
Φ = 0. *Scalar type, l ≥ 1.* In the notation of Proposition 23.16 (iv), W := r³F_tr solves R[W] = (r²M_t)′ = 0
(M = δdω = 0), so Φ := r^(−1/2)W solves −Φ_** + V_2Φ = 0 with V_2 > 0 (κ ≥ 3, m_0/r² < 1). F_tr = F_vr is smooth at
r_h, and Φ = r^(5/2)F_tr = O(r^(3/2−β)), Φ_* = O(r^(1/2−β)); so Φ = 0, F_tr = 0, and with M = 0,
Proposition 23.16 (iv) gives a = b = 0, where (a, b) is the gauge-invariant pair of Proposition 23.16 (iv), defined
after subtracting d(cS); so this part of ω is d(cS) for a function c(r). *Scalar type, l = 0.* κ = 0 and
R[W] = (fW′/r)′ = 0, so fW′/r is constant; it vanishes at r_h, as W is smooth there; so W = q, a constant,
F_tr = qr⁻³, and the l = 0 part a(r)dt + b(r)dr of ω has −a′ = F_tr. Altogether dω = qr⁻³dt ∧ dr = (q/2)dW*.

*(c) The gauge.* ω′ := ω − (q/2)W* is smooth across r_h, in 𝒜^β near infinity, closed on {r > r_h}, and has
δω′ = 0. With T = ∂_t, Cartan's formula and stationarity give d(ω′(T)) = ℒ_Tω′ − ι_Tdω′ = 0, so ω′(T) is a
constant; it decays, so it is 0. {r > r_h} is simply connected, so ω′ = dφ with ∂_tφ = ω′(T) = 0; in the ingoing
chart ω′ has no dv component and its dr component ∂_rφ is smooth at r_h, so φ is smooth in (r, x̂) up to r_h.
dφ ∈ 𝒜^β gives a constant φ_∞ with φ − φ_∞ = O(r^(1−β)), and δdφ = 0. At l = 0, r³fφ_0′ is constant and vanishes at
r_h, so φ_0 is constant. At l ≥ 1, the equation (r³fφ_l′)′ = κrφ_l has at r = ∞ a regular singular point (in
ρ = 1/r: ρ²fφ_ρρ + ρ(ρf_ρ − f)φ_ρ − κφ = 0, f = 1 − m_0ρ²) with indicial equation ν² − 2ν − κ = 0, roots ν = l + 2
and ν = −l for φ ∼ ρ^ν; by Frobenius' theorem every solution is c_1ρ^(l+2)a_1(ρ) +
c_2(ρ^(−l)b_1(ρ) + c_3 log ρ ρ^(l+2)a_1(ρ)) with a_1, b_1 analytic and a_1(0) = b_1(0) = 1, and φ_l = O(ρ^(β−1)) forces
c_2 = 0. So φ_l = O(r^(−l−2)), φ_l′ = O(r^(−l−3)), and the energy identity of (a) gives φ_l = 0. So ω′ = 0 on {r > r_h}.

*(d) Inside the horizon.* u − (q/2)W* lies in ker P̂(0), is smooth on X̄ and vanishes on {r > r_h}; part (d) of the
proof of Proposition 23.17, which uses only these properties (at σ = 0), shows that it vanishes on {r_0 < r < r_h}.
So u = (q/2)W*.

(3) By (1) and density, ℓ(P̂(0)u) = 0 for u ∈ 𝒳_0: near the horizon sphere u ∈ H^s, smooth u_j → u in H^s there give
P̂(0)u_j → P̂(0)u in H^(s−2), and ℓ is continuous on H^(s−2) as s > 5/2. ℓ ≠ 0 on 𝒴_0 (for instance
ℓ(ζ_1(r)dt_*) = 2π²r_h³ for ζ_1 ∈ C_c^∞ with ζ_1(r_h) = 1). By Corollary 13.27, whose hypotheses hold by
Section 23.8, P̂(0): 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 has index 0, so by (2) the annihilator of its range (Theorem 13.11 (1)) is
one-dimensional, and it is spanned by ℓ. ∎

### 23.10 The pairings at the horizon

**Lemma 23.22** (The pairings; [Hin26, Lemma 6.11] in dimension 4 + 1.) (1) ℓ([□, t_*]W*) = 4π².
(2) With c_(Υ,H) = −½χ dr as in Section 23.8, ℓ(2E_H G δ*W*) = 4π². ([Hin26]'s values are 4π and a number in
(3π, 5π). In dimension 4 + 1 both are (n − 2)|𝕊^(n−1)| = 2 · 2π², and in dimension 3 + 1 the first is 1 · 4π.)

*Proof.* We compute in the ingoing chart at r = r_h, where ℓ(v) = r_h³∫_(𝕊³) v_v dx̂ by (23.13),
v_v := v(∂_v), and W*_v = r⁻², W*_r = −(r(r + r_h))⁻¹; the Christoffel symbols are (23.12).

(1) t_* − v = F(r) near r_h, and ℓ([□, F]W*) = ℓ(□(FW*)) − ℓ(F□W*) = 0 by Lemma 23.21 (1) and □W* = 0; so t_*
may be replaced by v. For a function φ, □(φw) = φ□w + (□_0φ)w − 2∇_(∇φ)w, so [□, v]W* = (□_0v)W* − 2∇_(∇v)W*, with
∇v = g^vr∂_r = ∂_r and □_0v = −r⁻³∂_r(r³g^rv) = −3/r. Further (∇_(∂_r)W*)_v = ∂_rW*_v − Γ^r_rv
W*_r = −2r⁻³ − f′/(2r(r + r_h)), which at r_h is −5/(2r_h³). So ([□, v]W*)_v(r_h) = −3/r_h³ + 5/r_h³ = 2/r_h³, and
ℓ = 2|𝕊³| = 4π².

(2) By (23.14), 2E_H G δ*W* = 4ι_(c♯)δ*W* with c := c_(Υ,H), and at r_h, c♯ = −½∇r = −½(∂_v + f∂_r) = −½∂_v.
So (4ι_(c♯)δ*W*)_v = −2(δ*W*)_vv, and (δ*W*)_vv = ∇_vW*_v = −Γ^v_vv W*_v − Γ^r_vv W*_r = −1/r_h³ at r_h. So
ℓ = r_h³ · (2/r_h³) · 2π² = 4π². ∎

The two lemmas so far carry the zero energy data that the argument below uses. We collect them, with the remaining
facts about the unmodified operator at zero energy.

**Proposition 23.23** (The zero energy data of the unmodified operator.) On 4 + 1 Minkowski space and on
g_(b_0):

(i) The indicial roots of (□^Υ_b)^(0) are the zeros of ι(ι − 3)(ι² − ι − 2 − z) (type s0),
(l + 3 − ι)(l + ι − 1)Q_l(ι² − ι) (type sl) and (ι + l)(l + 2 − ι) (type vl), z = 4e_Υγ_Υ², with Q_l as in the proof
of Lemma 23.3. At γ_Υ = 0 the gap is (0, 2). For every z > 0, 2 < ι^Υ_(s1,2) < ι^Υ_(s0,2), every root other
than ι^Υ_(s1,2) and ι^Υ_(s0,2) is ≤ 0 or ≥ 3, and (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) is an indicial gap.

(ii) For stationary 1-forms on {r > r_h} the dt part and the spatial part of □ decouple. A S dt, S ∈ 𝒮_l, satisfies
□(AS dt) = 0 if and only if (f/r)(r³A′)′ = κA. For l ≥ 1, ω = B(r)S dr + C(r)d_𝕊S satisfies □ω = 0 if and only if

    −(r³f²B′)′ + rf(κ + 3f)B − 2κfC = 0,     −κ(rfC′)′ − 2κfB + κ²r⁻¹C = 0,

the Euler–Lagrange equations of ∫(r³f²B′² + κrfC′² + Z(B, C))dr, with Z the quadratic form of the matrix
((rf(κ + 3f), −2κf), (−2κf, κ²/r)), whose determinant κ²f(κ − 1 + m_0/r²) is positive for r > r_h. For Y ∈ 𝒱_l,
V(r)Y satisfies □(VY) = 0 if and only if −(rfV′)′ + (l + 1)²r⁻¹V = 0.

(iii) At l = 0 the stationary solutions of □ω = 0 on {r > r_h} are A(r)dt + B(r)dr with A = a_0 + a_2r⁻² and
B = b_3r⁻³f⁻¹ + b_1rf⁻¹, constants a_0, a_2, b_1, b_3. Those that are smooth at the future horizon and decay at
infinity form span{W*}.

(iv) ℓ(P̂(0)u) = 0 for every stationary u smooth near the horizon sphere.

(v) ℓ([□, t_*]W*) = 4π², and δW* = 0. At r_h, ι_(∇r)δ*W* = −r_h⁻³(dv + (3/2)dr), and for c_H = c_v dv + c_r dr at r_h,
ℓ(2E_H G δ*W*) = −12π²c_v − 8π²c_r; so c_H = −½χ dr gives 4π², and for the inhomogeneity
𝔣(σ̂, γ̂) := −iσ̂[□, t_*]W* + 2γ̂E_H G δ*W*, ℓ(𝔣(σ̂, γ̂)) = 4π²(−iσ̂ + γ̂), which is nonzero for Im σ̂ ≥ 0, γ̂ ≥ 0, not
both zero.

(vi) With t the static time and t_* := t − r_*, in the static frame, ∂_σP̂(0)W* = −i[□, t_*]W* = ir⁻³dt + O(r⁻⁴). The
leading term is of order ρ³ because (ρ∂_ρ − 3/2)ρ² = ½ρ², where in dimension 3 + 1 the corresponding (ρ∂_ρ − 1)ρ
vanishes.

*Proof.* (i) The determinants are (23.10), whose derivation in the proof of Lemma 23.3 uses no bound
on e_Υ or γ_Υ. At γ_Υ = 0 they are those at z = 0, and the gap (0, 2) is Lemma 23.3. Let z > 0. The argument of
the paragraphs *The list* and *Bounds* of that proof does not use z ≤ ½: the discriminant of Q_l is positive,
Q_l(l(l + 1)) = lz > 0 > −(l + 2)z = Q_l((l + 1)(l + 2)) and Q_l is monic, so
l(l + 1) < s_(l,1) < (l + 1)(l + 2) < s_(l,2), and as ι ↦ ι² − ι increases on ι > ½,

    l + 1 < ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) < l + 2 < ι^Υ_(sl,l+2),     ι^Υ_(s0,2) = ½ + (9/4 + z)^(1/2) > 2.

So the roots are real, and those below ½ are 1 − ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) < −l, 1 − ι^Υ_(s0,2) < −1, 1 − l ≤ 0, −l and 0. The
others are 3, l + 3 ≥ 4, l + 2 ≥ 3, ι^Υ_(sl,l+2) > l + 2 ≥ 3, ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) > l + 1 ≥ 3 for l ≥ 2, and the two
roots ι^Υ_(s1,2) ∈ (2, 3) and ι^Υ_(s0,2) > 2. Finally ι^Υ_(s1,2) < ι^Υ_(s0,2) if and only if s_(1,1) < 2 + z, that is
2 − z/2 < (4 + z + z²/4)^(1/2); this holds trivially for z ≥ 4, and for 0 < z < 4 it is, after squaring,
4 − 2z + z²/4 < 4 + z + z²/4. So no root lies in (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)). (iv) is Lemma 23.21 (1).

(ii) The static metric is invariant under the reflection t ↦ −t, which maps dt to −dt and fixes dr and the angular
covectors; □ commutes with it, and a stationary 1-form is odd under it exactly when it is a multiple of dt. So □ maps
the dt part to the dt part and the spatial part to the spatial part. *The dt part.* δ(AS dt) = 0, and F := d(AS dt)
has F_rt = A′S, F_at = A∂_aS; as in the proof of Proposition 23.16 (iv), (δF)^t = r⁻³(r³A′)′S − κA(fr²)⁻¹S and the
other components vanish, so □(AS dt) = −f(δF)^t dt = (−fr⁻³(r³A′)′ + κr⁻²A)S dt. *The scalar spatial part.*
δω = φS with φ := −r⁻³(r³fB)′ + κr⁻²C, so dδω = φ′S dr + φ d_𝕊S; and dω = (C′ − B)dr ∧ d_𝕊S, whose divergence is,
as in the proof of Proposition 23.16 (iii)–(iv), δdω = −κr⁻²(C′ − B)S dr − r⁻¹(rf(C′ − B))′d_𝕊S. So □ω = E_B S
dr + E_C d_𝕊S with E_B := φ′ + κr⁻²(B − C′) and E_C := φ − r⁻¹(rf(C′ − B))′. In r³fE_B the C′ terms cancel, and
r³fE_B = −r³f(r⁻³(r³fB)′)′ + κrfB − 2κfC. Expanding with r⁻³(r³fB)′ = (fB)′ + 3fB/r and f²B′ = f(fB)′ − ff′B,

    −r³f(r⁻³(r³fB)′)′ + (r³f²B′)′ = (r³f′² + 3rf² − (r³ff′)′)B = 3rf²B,

since r³f′² = 4m_0²r⁻³ = (r³ff′)′ for f = 1 − m_0r⁻². So r³fE_B = −(r³f²B′)′ + rf(κ + 3f)B − 2κfC. Likewise
r⁻²(r³fB)′ = 2fB + (rfB)′ gives κrE_C = −κ(rfC′)′ + κ²r⁻¹C − 2κfB. The determinant is
κ²(f(κ + 3f) − 4f²) = κ²f(κ − f) = κ²f(κ − 1 + m_0r⁻²), positive as f > 0 and κ ≥ 3. *The vector part.* By the proof
of Proposition 23.16 (iii) at σ = 0, δ(VY) = 0 and δd(VY) = (−r⁻¹(rfV′)′ + (l + 1)²r⁻²V)Y.

(iii) At l = 0 the dt equation is (r³A′)′ = 0, so A = a_0 + a_2r⁻². The dr equation is φ′ = 0, so (r³fB)′ = c r³ for
a constant c, and r³fB = cr⁴/4 + b_3; this is the stated B with b_1 = c/4. In the ingoing chart
A dt + B dr = A dv + (B − A/f)dr, and B − A/f = (b_3r⁻³ + b_1r − a_0 − a_2r⁻²)/f. Decay at infinity forces
a_0 = b_1 = 0, and smoothness at r_h forces the numerator to vanish at r_h, that is b_3 = a_2r_h. So
A dt + B dr = a_2W*.

(v) The first value is Lemma 23.22 (1), and δW* = 0 is shown before Lemma 23.21. At r_h, ∇r = ∂_v, and
with (23.12), (δ*W*)_vv = −r_h⁻³ (proof of Lemma 23.22). Further ∇_rW*_v = −5/(2r_h³) at r_h (proof of
Lemma 23.22) and ∇_vW*_r = −Γ^r_vr W*_r − Γ^v_vr W*_v = (f′/2)W*_r = −1/(2r_h³), so (δ*W*)_rv = ½(∇_rW*_v +
∇_vW*_r) = −3/(2r_h³), and ι_(∇r)δ*W* = (δ*W*)_(v·) = −r_h⁻³(dv + (3/2)dr). By (23.14) and c_H♯ = c_v∂_r +
c_r∂_v at r_h, (2E_H G δ*W*)_v = 4(c_v(δ*W*)_rv + c_r(δ*W*)_vv) = −(6c_v + 4c_r)r_h⁻³, and ℓ multiplies by 2π²r_h³. The
value of ℓ(𝔣) then follows from (1) and the case c_v = 0, c_r = −½; and |−iσ̂ + γ̂|² = |σ̂|² + 2γ̂ Im σ̂ + γ̂² > 0.

(vi) In the static chart the nonzero Christoffel symbols with indices in {t, r} are Γ^t_tr = f′/(2f), Γ^r_tt = ff′/2
and Γ^r_rr = −f′/(2f), and W* has no angular component. ∇t_* = −f⁻¹∂_t − ∂_r and □_0t_* = −r⁻³∂_r(r³f · (−f⁻¹)) = 3/r.
With f′ = 2m_0r⁻³: (∇_tW*)_t = −Γ^r_tt W*_r = O(r⁻⁶), (∇_tW*)_r = −Γ^t_tr W*_t = O(r⁻⁵),
(∇_rW*)_t = −2r⁻³ − Γ^t_rt W*_t = −2r⁻³ + O(r⁻⁵), and (∇_rW*)_r = O(r⁻⁴). So
[□, t_*]W* = (3/r)W* + 2f⁻¹∇_tW* + 2∇_rW* has dt component 3r⁻³ − 4r⁻³ + O(r⁻⁵) and dr component O(r⁻⁴).
T = ∂_σP̂(0) = −i[□, t_*] because e^(iσt_*)□e^(−iσt_*) = □ − iσ[□, t_*] + O(σ²). For the last sentence, by
(23.2) at S̄ = 0 the ∂_(t_*) coefficient of □ near infinity is −2ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2) up to ρ³ Diff_b¹, applied to
the leading part ρ²dt of W*. ∎

### 23.11 Mode stability on the closed upper half plane

**Proposition 23.24** ([Hin26, Proposition 6.12] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (Dyn). There is ϵ_0 > 0
such that for every γ_(Υ,H) ∈ (0, ϵ_0] there are ϵ_1 > 0 and a neighbourhood ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)) of b_0 such that, for
b ∈ ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)), e_Υ ∈ [0, ϵ_1] and |γ_Υ| < ϵ_1, (□^Υ_b)^(σ) is invertible for every σ with Im σ ≥ 0: as a map
𝒳_σ → 𝒴_σ when σ ≠ 0, and when σ = 0 as a map 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 for every s > 3/2 and every α with
α + 2 ∈ (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)). In particular (□^Υ_b)^(0) has trivial kernel on 𝒜^ϵ(X̄; E) for every ϵ > 0.

*Proof. Step 1: the horizon modification alone, at b_0.* For γ ∈ [0, 1] let 𝗉_γ := (b_0, 0, 0, γ) and
P̂_γ := P̂_(𝗉_γ), so

    P̂_γ(σ) = P̂(σ) + 2γE_H G (δ*)^(σ),     (δ*)^(σ) = δ* + σδ*_1,     δ*_1w := −i dt_* ⊗_s w,

and P̂(σ) = P̂(0) + σT + σ²P_2 (Section 11.1) with T = ∂_σP̂(0) = −i[□, t_*] (as
e^(iσt_*)□e^(−iσt_*) = □ − iσ[□, t_*] + O(σ²)) and P_2 of order 0. Fix ψ, ϕ ∈ C_c^∞(X°; E) with ℓ(ψ) ≠ 0
(Lemma 23.21 (3)) and ⟨W*, ϕ⟩_h = 1, and let 𝒫_γ(σ) be the augmented operator of (13.23) with
m_1 = m_2 = 1,

    𝒫_γ(σ)(u, c) := (P̂_γ(σ)u + cψ, ⟨u, ϕ⟩_h).

*(Z_𝒫) at γ = 0.* 𝒫_0(0): 𝒳_0 ⊕ ℂ → 𝒴_0 ⊕ ℂ is invertible. If P̂(0)u + cψ = 0 and ⟨u, ϕ⟩_h = 0, applying ℓ gives
cℓ(ψ) = 0 (Lemma 23.21 (3)), so c = 0, u = kW* (Lemma 23.21 (2)) and k = ⟨u, ϕ⟩_h = 0. Given (f_1, e_1),
c := ℓ(f_1)/ℓ(ψ) makes f_1 − cψ annihilated by ℓ, so f_1 − cψ = P̂(0)u_0 (the range is closed and its annihilator is
spanned by ℓ), and u := u_0 + (e_1 − ⟨u_0, ϕ⟩_h)W* solves 𝒫_0(0)(u, c) = (f_1, e_1).

*Uniform low-energy theory.* The family γ ↦ P̂_γ, γ ∈ [0, 1], satisfies (H1)–(H5), (G) and (TF)
(Section 23.8; the horizon term is compactly supported in X°, so the normal operators at ∂X and at tf do not
depend on γ). By Theorem 13.29 at γ = 0 and Theorem 13.25, there are γ_1 ∈ (0, 1], c_0 > 0 and C such that for
γ ∈ [0, γ_1]: 𝒫_γ(σ) is invertible for |σ| ≤ c_0, Im σ ≥ 0 (σ = 0 by Theorem 13.29 (1), σ ≠ 0 by
Theorem 13.25 (3)); ‖(u, c)‖ ≤ C‖𝒫_γ(0)(u, c)‖ on 𝒳_0 ⊕ ℂ (proof of Theorem 13.29); and the estimate
(13.24) of Theorem 13.25 (1) with k = 0 holds with the constant C for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_0. Let

    (u_(σ,γ), c_(σ,γ)) := 𝒫_γ(σ)⁻¹(0, 1).

*The Schur complement.* If c_(σ,γ) ≠ 0, then P̂_γ(σ) is invertible (on 𝒳_σ → 𝒴_σ, or 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 at σ = 0). Write
(u, c) := (u_(σ,γ), c_(σ,γ)), so P̂_γ(σ)u = −cψ and ⟨u, ϕ⟩_h = 1. If P̂_γ(σ)w = 0, then
𝒫_γ(σ)(w, 0) = ⟨w, ϕ⟩_h(0, 1), so (w, 0) = ⟨w, ϕ⟩_h(u, c), whence ⟨w, ϕ⟩_h c = 0, ⟨w, ϕ⟩_h = 0 and w = 0. Given
f_1, let (w, d) := 𝒫_γ(σ)⁻¹(f_1, 0); then P̂_γ(σ)(w − (d/c)u) = f_1 − dψ + dψ = f_1.

*The expansion.* By Lemma 23.21 (1) and density, ℓ(P̂(0)v) = 0 for every v that is H^s near the horizon
sphere (s > 5/2), so applying ℓ to P̂_γ(σ)u + cψ = 0 gives, with u = u_(σ,γ),

    c_(σ,γ) ℓ(ψ) = −σℓ(Tu) − σ²ℓ(P_2u) − 2γℓ(E_H G δ*u) − 2γσℓ(E_H G δ*_1u).    (23.16)

*Claim:* as (σ, γ) → (0, 0) with |σ| ≤ c_0, Im σ ≥ 0 and γ ∈ [0, γ_1], c_(σ,γ) → 0 and u_(σ,γ) → W* in H^(s′)(K)
for every compact K ⊂ X° and s′ < s. Let (σ_j, γ_j) → (0, 0), and (u_j, c_j) the corresponding pairs; |c_j| ≤ C. Let
φ_1 ∈ C^∞([0, ∞)) vanish on [0, 1] and equal 1 on [2, ∞), and put w_j := φ_1(ρ/ς_j)u_j, ς_j := |σ_j| (and w_j := u_j
if σ_j = 0). By Lemma 13.23 (b) and (a) (with q = 0, l = α), w_j, supported in {ρ ≥ ς_j}, has
‖w_j‖_(H̄_b^(s,α)) ≤ C′‖u_j‖_(s,(𝗋+α_+,α,0),ς_j) ≤ C′C, uniformly in j. Pass to a subsequence with w_j ⇀ w weakly
in H̄_b^(s,α) and c_j → c. As w_j = u_j on {ρ > 2ς_j}, on each compact K′ ⊂ X° the u_j equal the w_j for large j and
are bounded in H^s(K′); so u_j → w in distributions on X̄ ∖ ∂X, and by Rellich's theorem u_j → w in H^(s′)(K). The
coefficients of P̂_γ(σ) depend polynomially on (σ, γ), so P̂(0)w + cψ = 0, whence w ∈ 𝒳_0, and
⟨w, ϕ⟩_h = lim⟨u_j, ϕ⟩_h = 1. So 𝒫_0(0)(w, c) = (0, 1), and (w, c) = (W*, 0). The limit does not depend on the
subsequence, which proves the claim.

Since ℓ involves only the values at the horizon sphere of Tu and E_H G δ*u, first-order operators, the claim with
s′ ∈ (3/2, s) gives ℓ(Tu_(σ,γ)) → ℓ(TW*) = −iℓ([□, t_*]W*) = −4π²i and
2ℓ(E_H G δ*u_(σ,γ)) → 2ℓ(E_H G δ*W*) = 4π² (Lemma 23.22), while ℓ(P_2u) and ℓ(E_H G δ*_1u) stay bounded. So
(23.16) reads

    c_(σ,γ) ℓ(ψ) = −4π²(−iσ + γ) + o(|σ| + γ).

For Im σ ≥ 0 and γ ≥ 0, |−iσ + γ|² = |σ|² + 2γ Im σ + γ² ≥ ½(|σ| + γ)². So there are c_1 ∈ (0, c_0] and
γ_2 ∈ (0, γ_1] with c_(σ,γ) ≠ 0 whenever |σ| ≤ c_1, γ ∈ [0, γ_2], Im σ ≥ 0 and (σ, γ) ≠ (0, 0). By the Schur
complement, *for γ ∈ (0, γ_2], P̂_γ(σ) is invertible for all |σ| ≤ c_1 with Im σ ≥ 0, σ = 0 included*; c_1 does not
depend on γ.

*Step 2: the whole family, at every frequency.* Let ϵ and ℬ″ be those of Proposition 23.18 for its c_0 := c_1, and
ϵ_0 := min(γ_2, ½ϵ). Fix γ ∈ (0, ϵ_0]. At 𝗉_γ, P̂_γ(σ) is invertible for every σ with Im σ ≥ 0: for |σ| ≤ c_1 by
Step 1, for |σ| ≥ c_1 by Proposition 23.18 (γ < ϵ, b_0 ∈ ℬ″). Now vary 𝗉 = (b, e_Υ, γ_Υ, γ) near 𝗉_γ, with
e_Υ ≥ 0. (i) *Low energies.* (Z) holds at 𝗉_γ, so by Theorem 13.29 (with m_1 = m_2 = 0 and base point 𝗉_γ) and
Theorem 13.25 (3) there are c_0(γ) > 0 and a neighbourhood N_1 of 𝗉_γ on which P̂_𝗉(0) is invertible and P̂_𝗉(σ) is
invertible for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_0(γ). (ii) *High energies.* By Proposition 23.15 there is C_0 with invertibility
for |σ| ≥ C_0 and all 𝗉 in 𝒦. (iii) *The compact middle.* On {c_0(γ) ≤ |σ| ≤ C_0, Im σ ≥ 0}, a compact set, P̂_(𝗉_γ)(σ)
is invertible at each point, and invertibility is open in (σ, 𝗉) (Theorem 11.38, as in the proof of
Proposition 23.18); finitely many neighbourhoods cover it, giving N_2. On N_1 ∩ N_2 ∩ 𝒦, which contains
ℬ(γ) × [0, ϵ_1] × (−ϵ_1, ϵ_1) × {γ} for some neighbourhood ℬ(γ) and some ϵ_1 > 0, invertibility holds for every σ. At
σ = 0 it holds for one pair (s, α), hence for all s > 3/2 and all α with α + 2 in the gap (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2))
(Theorem 13.11 (4)); for σ ≠ 0 the kernel and the annihilator of the range do not depend on the admissible orders
(Theorem 11.33 (3)).

*The kernel on 𝒜^ϵ.* 𝒜^ϵ(X̄; E) ⊂ H̄_b^(s,α) when α + 2 < ϵ: its elements are smooth up to ∂_♯X, and near ∂X they and
their b-derivatives are O(ρ^ϵ), which lies in ρ^(α+2)L²(μ_b) = H̄_b^(0,α) (Section 13.1.2); and
α + 2 ∈ (0, min(ϵ, ι^Υ_(s1,2))) is allowed. A kernel element there lies in 𝒳_0 and vanishes. ∎

*Remarks.* (a) [Hin26, Proposition 6.12] states triviality of the nullspace on 𝒜^α for every α also when σ ≠ 0.
That needs 𝒜^α ⊂ 𝒳_σ for suitable admissible orders, which Theorem 11.33 (5) gives only for the weight
3/2 + S̄ − ϵ; it is not used here. (b) The neighbourhood ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)) of b_0 depends on γ_(Υ,H), as ϵ_1 does in
[Hin26]. The later chapters fix γ_(Υ,H) once and then work near b_0.

### 23.12 The zero energy operator

**Lemma 23.25** ([Hin26, Lemma 6.13] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (Dyn), and let E_Υ and b be as in
Proposition 23.24. Use an unweighted b-density near ∂X to define L², so that H̄_b^(s,α) here is the space
H̄_b^(s,α−2) of Chapter 13. (1) For s > 3/2 and α ∈ (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)),
(□^Υ_b)^(0): {u ∈ H̄_b^(s,α) : (□^Υ_b)^(0)u ∈ H̄_b^(s−1,α+2)} → H̄_b^(s−1,α+2) is invertible. (2) If
f_1 ∈ 𝒜^(2+ℰ)(X̄; E) for an index set ℰ with min Re ℰ > 0, then (□^Υ_b)^(0)⁻¹f_1 ∈ 𝒜^(ℰ′)(X̄; E) for an index set
ℰ′ with min Re ℰ′ > 0.

*Proof.* (1) With α′ := α − 2, the map is 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 of (13.7) with the weight α′, α′ + 2 = α in the gap;
this is Proposition 23.24 at σ = 0. The threshold is 3/2 for every γ_(Υ,H) (Lemma 23.7).

(2) Fix α ∈ (0, min(min Re ℰ, ι^Υ_(s1,2))). Then f_1 ∈ H̄_b^(s−1,α+2) for every s (in b-densities
ρ^(2+z) ∈ H_b^(∞,α+2) near ∂X when Re z > α, and f_1 is smooth up to ∂_♯X). Let u_s be the inverse image given by
(1) for the regularity s. For s′ > s, u_(s′) lies in the domain for s and solves the same equation, so
u_(s′) = u_s =: u, and u ∈ ⋂_s H̄_b^(s,α): smooth up to ∂_♯X, and of class H_b^(∞,α) near ∂X. Near ∂X,
(□^Υ_b)^(0) = ρ²A with A := P⁽⁰⁾ an elliptic b-operator on the trivial bundle ((13.1)–(13.3)), and
χ_1Au = χ_1ρ⁻²f_1 ∈ 𝒜^ℰ ⊂ H_b^(∞,(ℰ,β)) for every β, χ_1 a cut-off near ∂X. Lemma 21.35 then gives
χ̃_1u ∈ H_b^(∞,(ℰ_β,β)) for every β ∉ Re spec_b(A), where the index set built there from E(α) (the boundary spectrum
with Re ι > α), ℰ and their shifts by ℕ_0 does not depend on β; call it ℰ′. So u ∈ 𝒜^(ℰ′), and
min Re ℰ′ ≥ min(α, min Re ℰ) > 0. Lemma 21.35 is stated for scalar operators; its proof uses A only through the
meromorphy of N(A, ι)⁻¹ with bounds on vertical strips, which hold for the matrix-valued indicial family
(13.3) by Lemma 13.5; so it applies verbatim on E. The same holds for Lemma 21.36. ∎

### 23.13 Zero energy states from the symmetries of Minkowski space

This section and the next two prove [Hin26, Sections 6.5.1–6.5.2] (pp. 125–134) in dimension 4 + 1: the comparison of
the operators of g_b with those of Minkowski space and of g_m, and the stationary and generalised zero energy states
of □^Υ_b. The mass of g_b enters at |x|⁻² and the rotation at |x|⁻³ ((21.29)), so every comparison of
[Hin26, Lemma 6.14] gains one power of ρ, and so do the corrections and the symmetric gradients built from it. The
correction to the boost then sits at ρ¹, which is no indicial root, so [Hin26, (6.31)]'s logarithm and the formal
solution lemma it needs do not occur; the corrections to the translations and rotations sit at ρ², which is an s1 root
when e_Υγ_Υ² = 0, so here the modification at infinity is used with e_Υ > 0 and γ_Υ ≠ 0.

*Setting.* ℬ, g_b (b = (m, A), A ∈ 𝔰𝔬(4)), t_*, ρ, the trivialisation by dt_*, dx¹, …, dx⁴ and the bundle E are as in
Section 23.1, and g_m := g_((m,0)). The model is ḡ = −dt̄² + dx², t̄ = t_* + |x|, with δ̄*, □̄^Υ as in
Section 23.2. Fix γ_(Υ,H) ∈ (0, ϵ_0] and then b ∈ ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)), e_Υ ∈ (0, ϵ_1] and 0 < |γ_Υ| < ϵ_1 as in
Proposition 23.24, so that

    z := 4e_Υγ_Υ² ∈ (0, ½],    (23.17)

and write □^Υ_b := □^Υ_(g_b,E_Υ). We take c_Υ and c_(Υ,H) invariant under the rotations of x
(c_Υ = ζ_∞(|x|)|x|⁻¹dt with ζ_∞ = 1 for large |x|, and c_(Υ,H) = −½χ(|x|)d|x|), which Definition 21.28 and
Section 23.8 allow. By Proposition 23.24 and Lemma 23.25, (□^Υ_b)^(0) is invertible on the b-spaces with
an unweighted b-density, for every s > 3/2 and every weight in the gap (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)), and maps 𝒜^(2+ℰ),
min Re ℰ > 0, into polyhomogeneous spaces. *All b-spaces from here on use an unweighted b-density near ∂X*, as
[Hin26, Section 6.5] does.

*Indicial roots.* By Lemma 23.3 the indicial roots of (□^Υ_b)^(0) do not depend on b or on the horizon
modification, and for 0 < z ≤ ½: at s0 they are 0, 3, ι^Υ_(s0,2) ∈ (2, 3) and 1 − ι^Υ_(s0,2); at s1 they are 0, 4,
ι^Υ_(s1,2) ∈ (2, ι^Υ_(s0,2)), a root in (3, 4), and the mirror images 1 − ι of the last two; at sl, l ≥ 2, and vl,
l ≥ 1, every
root is ≤ 0 or ≥ 3. In particular *neither 1 nor 2 is an indicial root, of any type*: the integer roots are 0, 3,
1 − l, l + 3, −l and l + 2, none of which is 1 or 2 for l ≥ 1, and by (23.9) the others lie strictly
between consecutive integers for 0 < z ≤ ½.

*The constant ε_Υ.* Let ℳ be the set of real numbers in [−10, 10] of the form Re ι + j, with j ∈ ℤ and ι an indicial
root of (□^Υ_b)^(0) with |Re ι| ≤ 10 (all the roots are real). The set ℳ is finite. Indeed, by Lemma 23.3 and
(23.9) the roots of type sl are ≤ 1 − l or ≥ l + 1, and those of type vl are −l and l + 2; so every root of
type sl or vl has |Re ι| ≥ l − 1, and only the type s0 and the types sl and vl with l ≤ 11 have roots
with |Re ι| ≤ 10. These are finitely many types with at most six roots each, and each root gives at most 21 points of ℳ.
Fix ε_Υ > 0 less than half the least distance between distinct points of ℳ. As 0 is a root, ℳ contains every integer
in [−10, 10]; so ε_Υ < ½, and ε_Υ < d(Re ι, ℤ) for every indicial root ι with Re ι ∉ ℤ and |Re ι| ≤ 10, as the integer
nearest to such a Re ι lies in [−10, 10]. The restriction to |Re ι| ≤ 10 cannot be dropped. For z > 0 the root
ι := ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) satisfies ι + l > 0 and

    (ι − l − 1)(ι + l) = ι² − ι − l(l + 1) = s_(l,1) − l(l + 1) = l + 1 + z/2 − ((l + 1)² + z + z²/4)^(1/2),

which lies in (0, z/2), as (l + 1 + z/2)² − ((l + 1)² + z + z²/4) = lz > 0; so ι > l + 1, ι + l > 2l + 1 and
0 < ι − l − 1 < z/(2(2l + 1)). Hence the numbers Re ι + j, taken over all roots, accumulate at every integer, and have
no least distance. The constant ε_Υ is fixed by the indicial roots of □^Υ_b alone; it is not the constant ε_ind of
(25.10), which is fixed by the indicial roots of the linearised gauge-fixed Einstein operator. ℰ_ind denotes
an index set with min Re ℰ_ind ≥ ε_Υ, which may change from line to line, and (k, 0) the index set
{(k + j, 0) : j ∈ ℕ_0}.

*The model symmetries* ([Hin26, (6.29)] in dimension 4 + 1). For S ∈ 𝒮_1, so |x|S = ξ · x for some ξ ∈ ℝ⁴, and
V ∈ 𝒱_1, so V = Σ_(i<j) c_ij(x^i dx^j − x^j dx^i) with c ∈ 𝔰𝔬(4) (the Euclidean duals of the rotation fields;
Definition 21.7),

    ω̄^(0)_s0 := ḡ(∂_(t_*), ·) = −dt̄,   ω̄^(0)_s1(S) := d(|x|S),   ω̆̄^((0),1)_s1(S) := |x|d(|x|S) − |x|S dt̄,
    ω̄^(−1)_v1(V) := V.    (23.18)

ω̄_s1(S) = ξ · dx is dual to a translation, B̄(S) := t_*ω̄_s1(S) + ω̆̄¹_s1(S) = t̄ d(ξ · x) − (ξ · x)dt̄ to a Lorentz
boost, and V to the rotation field R_V := ḡ⁻¹V = Σ c_ij(x^i∂_j − x^j∂_i) (the same vector field in the coordinates
(t̄, x) and (t_*, x), as R_V|x| = 0). All four are Killing 1-forms of ḡ, so δ̄* annihilates them and
□̄^Υ = 2δ̄_Ē Ḡδ̄* does too. Their components are smooth on X̄, of orders ρ⁰, ρ⁰, ρ⁻¹ and ρ⁻¹.

### 23.14 Comparison of operators

**Lemma 23.26** ([Hin26, Lemma 6.14] in dimension 4 + 1.) For b = (m, A) ∈ ℬ, near ∂X and on stationary
sections,

    (δ*_(g_b))^(0) ∈ ρ Diff_b¹,  (δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ̄*)^(0) ∈ ρ³ Diff_b⁰,  (δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ*_(g_m))^(0) ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b⁰,
    (23.19)
    (□^Υ_b)^(0) ∈ ρ² Diff_b²,   (□^Υ_b)^(0) − (□̄^Υ)^(0) ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b²,   (□^Υ_b)^(0) − (□^Υ_(g_m,E_Υ))^(0) ∈ ρ⁵ Diff_b²,
    (23.20)

and [□^Υ_b, t_*] ∈ ρ Diff_b¹, [□^Υ_b − □^Υ_(g_m,E_Υ), t_*] ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b¹ on stationary sections. ([Hin26] has ρ², ρ³
in the first line and ρ³, ρ⁴ in the second.)

*Proof.* Near ∂X the components of g_b, g_b⁻¹, ḡ and ḡ⁻¹ in the coordinates (t_*, x) are smooth functions on X̄
(functions of (ρ, x̂)), and

    g_b − ḡ ∈ ρ²C^∞,     g_b − g_m ∈ ρ³C^∞,    (23.21)

and the same for the inverses. Indeed (21.29) gives g_b − g_m ∈ |x|⁻³C^∞ and g_m − η ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞,
η = −dt² + dx² in the time t of (21.30), with the duals; by (21.30), t̄ = t + C′ − 8m_0|x|⁻¹ near
infinity, so ḡ − η = −16m_0|x|⁻²dt d|x| − 64m_0²|x|⁻⁴d|x|² ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞; and the frame change
dt = dt_* + (1 − 8m_0|x|⁻²)d|x| has coefficients smooth on X̄, so it preserves ρ^kC^∞. The Cartesian derivatives
∂_(x^i) lie in ρ Diff_b¹, and ∂_(t_*) annihilates stationary sections. Hence Γ(g) ∈ ρC^∞ for g = g_b, ḡ, and
g_1 − g_2 ∈ ρ^kC^∞ (with the inverses) implies Γ(g_1) − Γ(g_2) ∈ ρ^(k+1)C^∞. On stationary 1-forms
δ*_gω = ½(∂_μω_ν + ∂_νω_μ) − Γ^λ_μν ω_λ, whose first part does not depend on g: this gives (23.19) with
k = 2, 3. For (23.20): δ_g = −g^(μν)∇_μ lies in ρ Diff_b¹ with δ_(g_1) − δ_(g_2) ∈ ρ^(k+1) Diff_b¹;
G_(g_1) − G_(g_2) ∈ ρ^k Diff_b⁰; and near ∂X, E^Υ_g h = −γ_Υ(2ι_(g⁻¹c_Υ)h − (2/3)(1 − e_Υ)c_Υ tr_g h) with
c_Υ ∈ ρC^∞ (Definition 21.28; the horizon term is supported in {|x| < 5R_1}), so E^Υ_g ∈ ρ Diff_b⁰ and
E^Υ_(g_1) − E^Υ_(g_2) ∈ ρ^(k+1) Diff_b⁰; the model's Ē uses c̄ = |x|⁻¹dt̄, which differs from c_Υ by ρ³C^∞. Expanding
2(δ_1 + E_1)G_1δ*_1 − 2(δ_2 + E_2)G_2δ*_2 into terms each containing one difference gives ρ^(k+2) Diff_b², and
(□^Υ_b)^(0) ∈ ρ² Diff_b² in the same way. For the commutators: on stationary sections [□^Υ_g, t_*] is the first-order
operator obtained from the terms of □^Υ_g with one ∂_(t_*) (those with ∂_(t_*)² give 2∂_(t_*), which vanishes on
stationary sections); these are −2g^(t_*ν)∂_ν plus connection and E terms, so the same counting applies, with
g^(t_*ν) ∈ C^∞ and its differences in ρ^kC^∞; and Lemma 23.1 (2)–(3) gives
[□^Υ_b, t_*] = −2ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) + Q_b ∈ ρ Diff_b¹. ∎

**Lemma 23.27** (Smooth dependence on b.) Let α ∈ (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) and let b ↦ f_b be of class C^k from
ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)) into H̄_b^(s−1,α+2) for every s. Then b ↦ u_b := (□^Υ_b)^(0)⁻¹f_b is of class C^k into H̄_b^(s,α) for
every s, and its derivatives are the inverse images ∂_b u_b = (□^Υ_b)^(0)⁻¹(∂_b f_b − (∂_b(□^Υ_b)^(0))u_b) and their
iterates.

*Proof.* Write P_b := (□^Υ_b)^(0). As in the proof of Lemma 23.25 (2), u_b ∈ ⋂_s H̄_b^(s,α). The coefficients
of P_b depend smoothly on b in C^∞ (Proposition 21.21), so P_(b′) − P_b maps H̄_b^(s+1,α) to H̄_b^(s−1,α+2) with norm
O(|b′ − b|); and ‖P_(b′)⁻¹‖ from H̄_b^(s−1,α+2) to H̄_b^(s,α) is bounded for b′ near b, by Theorem 13.29 (2) (the
estimate without error term, uniform near a point where (Z) holds). So
u_(b′) − u_b = P_(b′)⁻¹((f_(b′) − f_b) − (P_(b′) − P_b)u_b) → 0 in H̄_b^(s,α); that is, b ↦ P_b⁻¹w is continuous for
every fixed w ∈ ⋂_s H̄_b^(s−1,α+2), uniformly on bounded sets of each H̄_b^(s−1,α+2). With u̇ := P_b⁻¹(ḟ − Ṗu_b),

    (u_(b+h) − u_b)/h − u̇ = P_(b+h)⁻¹((f_(b+h) − f_b)/h − ((P_(b+h) − P_b)/h)u_b) − P_b⁻¹(ḟ − Ṗu_b) → 0,

since the bracket converges in every H̄_b^(s−1,α+2) and P_(b+h)⁻¹ → P_b⁻¹ strongly there. Induction gives C^k. ∎

### 23.15 The states

**Proposition 23.28** ([Hin26, Proposition 6.15] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (Dyn), and let E_Υ and b be
as in Section 23.13. There are stationary 1-forms, linear in S ∈ 𝒮_1 and V ∈ 𝒱_1 and smooth in b,

    ω^(0)_(b,s0) := g_b(∂_(t_*), ·),   ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S),   ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S),   ω^(−1)_(b,v1)(V),    (23.22)

smooth on X, with components in ρ⁻¹C^∞(X̄) at most ([Hin26, footnote 72]), with

    ω^(0)_(b,s0) − ω̄^(0)_s0 ∈ ρ²C^∞,                ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) − ω̄^(0)_s1(S) ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)),
    ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S) − ω̆̄^((0),1)_s1(S) ∈ 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)),   ω^(−1)_(b,v1)(V) − V ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)),
    (23.23)

such that

    □^Υ_b ω^(0)_(b,s0) = 0,   □^Υ_b ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) = 0,   □^Υ_b(t_*ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) + ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S)) = 0,
    □^Υ_b ω^(−1)_(b,v1)(V) = 0.    (23.24)

(1) (*No logarithm.*) In place of [Hin26, (6.31)]: the correction to the boost has no logarithmic term;
c_(b,s1) = 0.

(2) (*Symmetric gradients.*) δ*_(g_b)ω^(0)_(b,s0) = 0, and

    h_(b,s1)(S) := δ*_(g_b)ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) ∈ 𝒜^((3,0)∪(3+ℰ_ind)),
    δ*_(g_b)(t_*ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) + ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S)) =: t_*h_(b,s1)(S) + h̆¹_(b,s1)(S),
    h̆¹_(b,s1)(S) ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)),     h_(b,v1)(V) := δ*_(g_b)ω^(−1)_(b,v1)(V) ∈ 𝒜^((3,0)∪(3+ℰ_ind));
    (23.25)

the ρ² leading term of h̆¹_(b,s1)(S) is of scalar type 1, given by the same S; and h_(b,s1)(S),
t_*h_(b,s1)(S) + h̆¹_(b,s1)(S) and h_(b,v1)(V) lie in the kernels of D_(g_b)Ric and of δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b).

(3) (*Killing rotations*, [Hin26, Remark 6.17].) If R_V is a Killing field of g_b, then
ω^(−1)_(b,v1)(V) = g_b(R_V, ·) and h_(b,v1)(V) = 0. At b = (m, 0) this holds for every V ∈ 𝒱_1: six independent
rotations, where Kerr has three.

*Proof.* Throughout, P_b := (□^Υ_b)^(0), and we use two facts. (F1) *If f_1 ∈ 𝒜^(2+ℱ) is smooth on X̄, ℱ an index set
with min Re ℱ = k ∈ {1, 2} and (k, 0) its only element with real part below k + ε_Υ, then
P_b⁻¹f_1 ∈ 𝒜^((k,0)∪(k+ℰ_ind)).* Indeed, by Lemma 23.25, u := P_b⁻¹f_1 ∈ ⋂_s H̄_b^(s,α) for every α < k in the
gap (as k ≤ 2 < ι^Υ_(s1,2)), and Lemma 21.35 with A = ρ⁻²P_b near ∂X ((13.1)) and
α ∈ (k − ε_Υ, k) gives u ∈ 𝒜^ℰ with ℰ generated by ℱ and the boundary spectrum above α; the latter has no point with
real part in (k − ε_Υ, k + ε_Υ) (no root at 1 or 2), so the only element of ℰ there is ℱ's (k, 0), without
logarithm. (F2) *For a Killing 1-form K of g_b, δ*_(g_b)K = 0, hence □^Υ_bK = 0; and for any stationary 1-form ω,
h := δ*_(g_b)ω satisfies D_(g_b)Ric(h) = ½ℒ_(ω♯)Ric(g_b) = 0 and δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b)h = ½□^Υ_bω; the same holds for
t_*ω + ω̆.*

*Time translation.* ∂_(t_*) is Killing for g_b, so (F2) gives □^Υ_bω_(b,s0) = 0 and δ*ω_(b,s0) = 0; and
ω_(b,s0) − ω̄_s0 = (g_b − ḡ)(∂_(t_*), ·) ∈ ρ²C^∞ by (23.21).

*Translations.* δ̄*ω̄_s1 = 0, so by (23.19)
δ*_(g_b)ω̄_s1 = ((δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ̄*)^(0))ω̄_s1 ∈ ρ³C^∞, and f_b := □^Υ_bω̄_s1 = 2δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b)δ*_(g_b)ω̄_s1
is smooth on X̄ and in ρ⁴C^∞ near ∂X (δ_(g_b) + E^Υ_(g_b,∞) ∈ ρ Diff_b¹ there), that is in 𝒜^(2+(2,0)). By (F1) with
k = 2, ω′_b := −P_b⁻¹f_b ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)), and ω_(b,s1) := ω̄_s1 + ω′_b solves
□^Υ_bω_(b,s1) = f_b + P_bω′_b = 0. Then h_(b,s1) = (δ*_(g_b))^(0)ω′_b + ((δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ̄*)^(0))ω̄_s1 lies in
ρ Diff_b¹ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)) + ρ³C^∞ ⊂ 𝒜^((3,0)∪(3+ℰ_ind)). f_b depends smoothly on b in ρ⁴C^∞, so
Lemma 23.27 gives smoothness in b.

*Boosts.* B̄ = t_*ω̄_s1 + ω̆̄¹_s1 is Killing for ḡ, so □̄^ΥB̄ = 0, and □̄^Υω̄_s1 = 0. Hence

    f̆_b := □^Υ_b(t_*ω_(b,s1) + ω̆̄¹_s1) = [□^Υ_b − □̄^Υ, t_*]ω̄_s1 + ((□^Υ_b)^(0) − (□̄^Υ)^(0))ω̆̄¹_s1
            + [□^Υ_b, t_*]ω′_b,    (23.26)

as the terms with a factor t_*, t_*(□^Υ_b − □̄^Υ)ω̄_s1 = t_*f_b and t_*□^Υ_bω′_b = −t_*f_b, cancel. By
Lemma 23.1 (3), near ∂X, □^Υ_b − □̄^Υ = −g_b^00∂_(t_*)² + Q_b∂_(t_*) + R_b with Q_b ∈ ρ³ Diff_b¹ and
R_b = (□^Υ_b)^(0) − (□̄^Υ)^(0) ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b² (also (23.20)); on stationary sections
[□^Υ_b − □̄^Υ, t_*] = Q_b. So the first term of (23.26) is Q_bω̄_s1 ∈ ρ³C^∞, the second
R_bω̆̄¹_s1 ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b²(ρ⁻¹C^∞) ⊂ ρ³C^∞, and the third, by Lemma 23.26, in
ρ Diff_b¹ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)) ⊂ 𝒜^((3,0)∪(3+ℰ_ind)). So f̆_b ∈ 𝒜^(2+((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind))), smooth on X̄, and by (F1) with
k = 1, ω̆′_b := −P_b⁻¹f̆_b ∈ 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)). Put ω̆_(b,s1) := ω̆̄¹_s1 + ω̆′_b; then
□^Υ_b(t_*ω_(b,s1) + ω̆_(b,s1)) = f̆_b + P_bω̆′_b = 0. No logarithm arises, since 1 is not an indicial root; this is
(1). Smoothness in b: f̆_b is smooth in b (Lemma 23.27 for ω′_b), and Lemma 23.27 again.

For (2): [δ*_g, t_*] = dt_* ⊗_s (·) for every metric, and δ̄*B̄ = 0 gives dt_* ⊗_s ω̄_s1 + (δ̄*)^(0)ω̆̄¹_s1 = 0. So

    h̆¹_(b,s1) = dt_* ⊗_s ω′_b + ((δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ̄*)^(0))ω̆̄¹_s1 + (δ*_(g_b))^(0)ω̆′_b
              ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)) + ρ³ Diff_b⁰(ρ⁻¹C^∞) + ρ Diff_b¹ 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)) ⊂ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)).

*Its leading term.* At b_S := (m, 0) the metric g_m, t_* and E_Υ are invariant under the rotations of x
(Section 23.13); the construction is linear and, by the uniqueness of the inverse images, equivariant, so
S ↦ h̆¹_(b_S,s1)(S) is an SO(4)-equivariant linear map from 𝒮_1, the representation ℝ⁴. The decomposition of
Lemma 21.6 is into SO(4)-invariant subspaces, and among the types only scalar type 1 contains ℝ⁴ (at each l
the scalar, vector and tensor types are, for SO(4), the representations of highest weights (l/2, l/2),
((l ± 1)/2, (l ∓ 1)/2) and ((l ± 2)/2, (l ∓ 2)/2), and ℝ⁴ is (½, ½)); so h̆¹_(b_S,s1)(S) is of scalar type 1, given
by S. For general b, by (23.20), f_b − f_(b_S) = (P_b − P_(b_S))ω̄_s1 ∈ ρ⁵C^∞, so
ω′_b − ω′_(b_S) = −P_b⁻¹((f_b − f_(b_S)) + (P_b − P_(b_S))ω′_(b_S)), whose argument lies in
ρ^(2+3)C^∞ + 𝒜^(2+(5,0)∪(5+ℰ_ind)), lies in H̄_b^(∞,α) for some α > 2 (Lemma 23.25, any
α ∈ (2, ι^Υ_(s1,2))). Then, term by term in (23.26),
f̆_b − f̆_(b_S) ∈ ρ⁴C^∞ + H̄_b^(∞,α+1) + 𝒜^((6,0)∪(6+ℰ_ind)) by Lemma 23.26 (the commutator bound and
R_b − R_(b_S) ∈ ρ⁵ Diff_b²), and ω̆′_b − ω̆′_(b_S) = −P_b⁻¹((f̆_b − f̆_(b_S)) + (P_b − P_(b_S))ω̆′_(b_S)) lies in
H̄_b^(∞,α″) for every α″ < 2 (Lemma 23.25), so that (δ*_(g_b))^(0) of it is O(ρ^(α″+1)), α″ ∈ (1, 2). So, in
the formula for h̆¹, the differences dt_* ⊗_s (ω′_b − ω′_(b_S)),
((δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ*_(g_m))^(0))ω̆̄¹_s1 ∈ ρ³C^∞, (δ*_(g_b))^(0)(ω̆′_b − ω̆′_(b_S)) and
((δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ*_(g_m))^(0))ω̆′_(b_S) ∈ ρ⁵C^∞ are all O(ρ^(2+ϵ)) for some ϵ > 0, and h̆¹_b and h̆¹_(b_S) have the
same ρ² term.

*Rotations.* g_m(R_V, ·) = V, since g_m = η + m|x|⁻²(dt − d|x|)² ((21.28)) and R_V t = R_V|x| = 0; and R_V is
Killing for the spherically symmetric g_m, so δ*_(g_m)V = 0. By (23.19),
δ*_(g_b)V = ((δ*_(g_b))^(0) − (δ*_(g_m))^(0))V ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b⁰(ρ⁻¹C^∞) ⊂ ρ³C^∞ near ∂X, smooth on X̄, so
f_b := □^Υ_bV ∈ 𝒜^(2+(2,0)), and (F1) gives ω′_b := −P_b⁻¹f_b ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)), smooth in b by
Lemma 23.27. ω_(b,v1)(V) := V + ω′_b solves (23.24), and
h_(b,v1)(V) = δ*_(g_b)V + (δ*_(g_b))^(0)ω′_b ∈ ρ³C^∞ + 𝒜^((3,0)∪(3+ℰ_ind)).

The kernel statements in (2) are (F2).

(3) If R_V is Killing for g_b, K := g_b(R_V, ·) has □^Υ_bK = 0 by (F2), and
K − V = (g_b − ḡ)(R_V, ·) ∈ ρ²C^∞ · ρ⁻¹ ⊂ ρC^∞ by (23.21). So ω_(b,v1)(V) − K ∈ 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)) is in
the kernel of P_b on H̄_b^(s,α) for α ∈ (0, 1), which is trivial (Lemma 23.25 (1)); so ω_(b,v1)(V) = K and
h_(b,v1)(V) = δ*K = 0. At b = (m, 0), K = V for every V by the above, and 𝒱_1 ≅ 𝔰𝔬(4) has dimension 6. ∎

*Remarks.* (a) *The decay rates* ([Hin26, Remark 6.16]). h_(b,s1) gains three powers over ω_(b,s1), not one, because
g_b is translation-invariant to two orders (g_b − ḡ ∈ ρ²C^∞); h_(b,v1) gains four powers over ω_(b,v1) because g_b is
spherically symmetric to three orders (g_b − g_m ∈ ρ³C^∞). (b) Which R_V are Killing for g_b depends on the rotation
A; at A = 0 all are, and (3) is used there.

The following proposition collects the facts about the symmetries, and about the linearised Myers–Perry metrics at
zero rotation, that this section and Chapter 25 use.

**Proposition 23.29** (Symmetries and linearised metrics on Tangherlini.) Let g = g_m.

(i) In the coordinates (t, x), t the static time, where the Christoffel symbols of η := −dt² + dx² vanish,
g − η ∈ ρ²C^∞ and Γ(g) ∈ ρ³C^∞ in Cartesian components. In the coordinates (t_*, x) of Section 23.13, where
Γ(ḡ) ∈ ρC^∞ does not vanish, g − ḡ ∈ ρ²C^∞ and Γ(g) − Γ(ḡ) ∈ ρ³C^∞. Hence (δ*_g)^(0) − (δ̄*)^(0) ∈ ρ³ Diff_b⁰ and
(□^Υ_g)^(0) − (□̄^Υ)^(0) ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b². The tortoise coordinate satisfies r_* − r → 0, with no logarithm.

(ii) δ*_g dx¹ ∈ ρ³C^∞ and □dx¹ = 2δGδ*dx¹ ∈ ρ⁴C^∞. The number 2 is an s1 root of (□^Υ_b)^(0) at z = 0 and not for
z > 0, where the s1 root near 2 is ι^Υ_(s1,2) = ½(1 + (17 + 2z − 2(z² + 4z + 16)^(1/2))^(1/2)) > 2.

(iii) For the boost B̄ = t̄ dx¹ − x¹dt̄, which is Killing for ḡ, δ*_gB̄ − t_*δ*_g dx¹ is stationary and lies in
ρ²C^∞, and the stationary residual □^Υ_gB̄ − t_*□^Υ_g dx¹ lies in ρ³C^∞. In the static time t,
δ*_g(t dx¹ − x¹dt) = t δ*_g dx¹ + K with K stationary and in ρ²C^∞. The number 1 is not an s1 root for z ≥ 0: the s1
determinant at ι = 1 is 3(12 + 3z).

(iv) Each of the six 1-forms x^i dx^j − x^j dx^i equals g(R, ·) for the rotation field R = ḡ⁻¹(x^i dx^j − x^j dx^i)
and is Killing for g; they are linearly independent, as are the four functions x^i/r on 𝕊³.

(v) h_m := ∂_m g and, for w := x¹dx² − x²dx¹, h_A := (m/r⁴)(dt ⊗ w + w ⊗ dt) (t the static time) solve
D_g Ric(h) = 0 and lie in ρ²C^∞ and ρ³C^∞. η_m := δ_(g,E)G_g h_m lies in ρ³C^∞ and is spherically symmetric. h_A is
trace-free with δ_g h_A = 0, so η_A := δ_(g,E)G_g h_A = E^Υ h_A = (2γ_Υ m/(fr⁵))w near infinity, of order ρ⁴ and of
vector type 1. The number 1 is not an s0 root and 2 is not a v1 root: the s0 determinant at ι = 1 is 2(2 + z), and the
v1 determinant at ι = 2 is 3.

(vi) The single-spin Myers–Perry metric in five dimensions [ER08, (32)–(33), p. 14],

    −dt² + (m/Σ)(dt − a sin²ϑ dφ)² + (Σ/Δ)dr² + Σdϑ² + (r² + a²)sin²ϑ dφ² + r²cos²ϑ dψ²,

Σ := r² + a²cos²ϑ, Δ := r² + a² − m, is Ricci-flat: it is the odd-dimensional Myers–Perry metric
[ER08, (42), (44), p. 16] in dimension 5 with the rotation parameters (a, 0), a vacuum solution by
Theorem A.23 [MP86]. At a = 0 it is g_m, in the coordinates
x¹ + ix² = r sin ϑ e^(iφ), x³ + ix⁴ = r cos ϑ e^(iψ) on the round 𝕊³; and ∂_a of it at a = 0 is −h_A, with
w = r²sin²ϑ dφ.

*Proof.* (i) In the static chart g − η = mρ²dt² + mρ²f⁻¹dr², f := 1 − mρ², with dr = x̂ · dx, which lies in ρ²C^∞
in Cartesian components; as Γ(η) = 0 there, and g_1 − g_2 ∈ ρ^kC^∞ implies Γ(g_1) − Γ(g_2) ∈ ρ^(k+1)C^∞ (proof of
Lemma 23.26), Γ(g) ∈ ρ³C^∞. In (t_*, x) the statements are (23.21) and the same implication, and the
two consequences are Lemma 23.26 at b = (m, 0). r_* − r = −m/r + O(r⁻³) by Proposition 23.16 (v) with m in
place of m_0. (ii) δ̄*dx¹ = 0, so δ*_g dx¹ = ((δ*_g)^(0) − (δ̄*)^(0))dx¹ ∈ ρ³C^∞, and 2δ_gG_g ∈ ρ Diff_b¹. The
s1 root is (23.7) at l = 1, since ½ + (¼ + s)^(1/2) = ½(1 + (1 + 4s)^(1/2)) and
1 + 4s_(1,1) = 17 + 2z − 2(z² + 4z + 16)^(1/2); at z = 0 it is 2, and for z > 0 it exceeds 2 by Lemma 23.3.
(iii) δ̄*B̄ = 0 gives dt_* ⊗_s dx¹ + (δ̄*)^(0)B̆ = 0 with B̆ := B̄ − t_*dx¹ stationary in ρ⁻¹C^∞, so
δ*_gB̄ − t_*δ*_g dx¹ = ((δ*_g)^(0) − (δ̄*)^(0))B̆ ∈ ρ²C^∞; the residual is the sum of the first two terms of
(23.26), in ρ³C^∞. In the static time, δ*_g(φω) = φδ*_gω + dφ ⊗_s ω gives
δ*_g(t dx¹ − x¹dt) = t δ*_g dx¹ − x¹δ*_g dt; in the static chart (δ*_g dt)_μν = −Γ^t_μν, whose only nonzero Cartesian
components are Γ^t_(ti) = Γ^t_(it) = x̂_i f′/(2f) ∈ ρ³C^∞ (f′ = 2mr⁻³), so K := −x¹δ*_g dt ∈ ρ²C^∞, and K is
stationary. At l = 1, ι = 1, (23.10) gives (3)(1)Q_1(0) = 3(κ(κ + 1) + zκ) with κ = 3.
(iv) g_m = η + (m/r²)(dt − dr)² ((21.28)) and R annihilates t and r, so g(R, ·) = η(R, ·), which is the
given form; R is Killing for every spherically symmetric metric. Independence: 𝔰𝔬(4) has dimension 6, and the
coordinate functions are independent. (v) g_m is Ricci-flat for every m, so D Ric(∂_m g) = 0; by (vi), h_A is minus
the derivative of a Ricci-flat family, so D Ric(h_A) = 0. The orders follow from (21.28) and
from |w| = O(r) in Cartesian components. η_m is spherically symmetric because g_m, c_Υ and E_Υ are, and its order follows
as in Lemma 23.26: δ_(g,E)G_g maps ρ²C^∞ into ρ³C^∞. For h_A: g^tφ = 0 and w is angular, so tr_g h_A = 0; for
the divergence of a symmetric tensor, ∇_μh^μ_ν = |g|^(−1/2)∂_μ(|g|^(1/2)h^μ_ν) − ½(∂_ν g_αβ)h^(αβ), where the last
term vanishes as h^(αβ) has only tφ components and g_tφ = 0 identically; h^φ_t = m/r⁴ and h^t_φ = −(m/(fr²))sin²ϑ do
not depend on t or φ, so δ_g h_A = 0. Then G_g h_A = h_A and
E^Υ h_A = −2γ_Υ ι_(g⁻¹c)h_A, as tr_g h_A = 0; for c = r⁻¹dt, g⁻¹c = −(fr)⁻¹∂_t, which gives (2γ_Υ m/(fr⁵))w. The
c_Υ = |x|⁻¹dt of Definition 21.28 is built with the time of (21.30), which differs from the static time by a
function of r; so c_Υ − r⁻¹dt is a multiple of dr, and as ι_(g⁻¹dr)h_A = f h_A(∂_r, ·) = 0 the result is the same for
c_Υ. The determinants are (23.10):
1 · (−2)(−2 − z) and (2 + 1)(3 − 2). (vi) At a = 0, Σ = r², Δ = r² − m = r²f, and the metric is
−f dt² + f⁻¹dr² + r²(dϑ² + sin²ϑ dφ² + cos²ϑ dψ²), the last bracket being the round metric of 𝕊³ in these
coordinates. ∂_a of (m/Σ)(dt − a sin²ϑ dφ)² at a = 0 is −(m/r²)sin²ϑ(dt ⊗ dφ + dφ ⊗ dt), and the other coefficients
have vanishing a-derivative at a = 0; with w = x¹dx² − x²dx¹ = r²sin²ϑ dφ this is −h_A. The metric [ER08, (42)] in
dimension 5, with rotation parameters (a, 0), direction cosines μ_1 = sin ϑ, μ_2 = cos ϑ, angles φ, ψ and mass parameter
m, has F = Σ/(r² + a²) and Π = r²(r² + a²) by [ER08, (44)], so mr²/(ΠF) = m/Σ and ΠF/(Π − mr²) = Σ/Δ; and, as
dμ_1 = cos ϑ dϑ and dμ_2 = −sin ϑ dϑ, (r² + a²)(dμ_1² + μ_1²dφ²) + r²(dμ_2² + μ_2²dψ²) is
Σdϑ² + (r² + a²)sin²ϑ dφ² + r²cos²ϑ dψ². So [ER08, (42)] is the displayed metric, which is Ricci-flat by
Theorem A.23. ∎

### 23.16 Generalised zero energy states: the setting

The generalised zero energy states of □^Υ_b are polynomials in t_* in its kernel, built on the time translation, the
translations and boosts, the rotations, and the indicial roots of (□^Υ_b)^(0) below −1, with their symmetric gradients
([Hin26, Proposition 6.18 and Remark 6.19] in dimension 4 + 1). The zero energy operator of g_b differs from
Minkowski's by ρ⁴ Diff_b² (Lemma 23.26), one power more than on Kerr, so the correction to the leading term of
every stationary state lies two orders below it instead of one. The leading terms are computed exactly on Minkowski
space, and part (1) carries no logarithm.

E_Υ, b, □^Υ_b, P_b := (□^Υ_b)^(0), the model ḡ, t̄ = t_* + |x|, □̄^Υ, the unweighted b-density and the 1-forms
ω^(0)_(b,s0), ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S), ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S), ω^(−1)_(b,v1)(V) are those of Section 23.13–Section 23.15,
with z = 4e_Υγ_Υ² ∈ (0, ½]. Near ∂X write

    □^Υ_b = A_0 + A_1∂_(t_*) + A_2∂_(t_*)²,   A_0 = P_b ∈ ρ² Diff_b²,   A_1 ∈ ρ Diff_b¹,   A_2 = −g_b^00 ∈ ρ²C^∞,
    (23.27)

and Ā_0, Ā_1 for the model (Ā_2 = 0). By Lemma 23.1 and Lemma 23.26, A_0 − Ā_0 ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b²,
A_1 − Ā_1 = Q_b ∈ ρ³ Diff_b¹, and A_0 − A_0^(m) ∈ ρ⁵ Diff_b², A_1 − A_1^(m) ∈ ρ⁴ Diff_b¹ against the non-rotating
g_m. Also

    δ*_(g_b) = (δ*_(g_b))^(0) + dt_* ⊗_s (·)∂_(t_*),     (δ*_(g_b))^(0) ∈ ρ Diff_b¹.    (23.28)

By (23.2) and Lemma 23.2, Ā_1 = ρN_1(ρ∂_ρ) with N_1(ι) := −2(ι − 3/2 − S̄), and Ā_0 = ρ²N_0(ρ∂_ρ)
with N_0 the indicial family of Section 23.4; so Ā_1(ρ^a w) = ρ^(a+1)N_1(a)w and Ā_0(ρ^a w) = ρ^(a+2)N_0(a)w for w
on 𝕊³.

*Generalised states.* For stationary 1-forms ω̆⁰ := ω, ω̆¹, …, ω̆^K and k ≤ K put
ω^(≤k) := Σ_(i=0)^k (k!/(k − i)!) t_*^(k−i) ω̆^i ([Hin26, (6.36a)]). The coefficient of t_*^(k−j) in □^Υ_b ω^(≤k) is
(k!/(k − j)!)(A_0ω̆^j + A_1ω̆^(j−1) + A_2ω̆^(j−2)) (ω̆^(−1) = ω̆^(−2) := 0), so

    ω^(≤k) ∈ ker □^Υ_b  (k ≤ K)  ⟺  A_0ω̆^j = −A_1ω̆^(j−1) − A_2ω̆^(j−2)  (0 ≤ j ≤ K).    (23.29)

(The proof of [Hin26, Proposition 6.18] prints A_0ω̆^(l−2) for A_2ω̆^(l−2) in this recursion.) By
(23.28), δ*_(g_b)ω^(≤k) = Σ_(j=0)^k (k!/(k − j)!) t_*^(k−j) h̆^j with

    h̆^j := (δ*_(g_b))^(0)ω̆^j + dt_* ⊗_s ω̆^(j−1),    (23.30)

so its constant coefficient is k! h̆^k; and δ*_(g_b)ω^(≤k) lies in ker D_(g_b)Ric ∩ ker δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b) whenever
ω^(≤k) ∈ ker □^Υ_b (fact (F2) in the proof of Proposition 23.28).

*Exponents.* ℳ, ε_Υ and ℰ_ind are those of Section 23.13; the indicial roots of P_b do not depend on b
(Lemma 23.3). Every exponent below lies in ℳ.

*Dimension 3 + 1.* The comparisons with [Hin26] in Proposition 23.31 (iv) and Proposition 23.32 use the model on
Minkowski space ℝ^(1+3): the splitting (21.10) for 𝕊², which is [Hin26, (2.37b)], Ē of Lemma 23.2 at
ν = 2, that is with the trace weight 1 and c̄ = r⁻¹dt̄, and ρ, t_*, t̄ as before. On 𝕊² we write κ := l(l + 1), and
d_𝕊, δ_𝕊 and Δ_𝕊 for the operators of the unit 𝕊², with the conventions of the notation above.

**Lemma 23.30** (The model in dimension 3 + 1.) Write e := e_Υ, γ := γ_Υ, z := 4eγ² and p := −ι² + ι.

(1) □̄^Υ = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 1 − S̄) + (□̄^Υ)^(0) with S̄ of Lemma 23.2, so N_1(ι) = −2(ι − 1 − S̄), which is
−2(ι − 1 − γ) on the angular components. On (aS, bS, c d_𝕊S), S ∈ 𝒮_l(𝕊²), l ≥ 1, the indicial family of (□̄^Υ)^(0)
is

               ⎛ p + κ + 1 − γ((1 + e)ι − 2e)   −1 − γ((1 − e)ι + 2e)          −κ(1 + eγ) ⎞
    N_sl(ι) =  ⎜ −1 + γ((1 − e)ι + 2e)          p + κ + 1 + γ((1 + e)ι − 2e)   κ(1 − eγ)  ⎟ ,
               ⎝ −2 + 2γ                        2 + 2γ                         p + κ      ⎠

N_s0(ι) is its upper left 2 × 2 block at κ = 0, and N_vl(ι) = p + κ = −(ι + l)(ι − l − 1). Entry by entry these are
the matrices of [Hin26, Lemma 6.6] (p. 117), and N_1 at v1 is that of [Hin26, p. 134].

(2) det N_s0(ι) = ι(ι − 2)(ι² − 1 − z) and det N_sl(ι) = (l + 2 − ι)(l + ι − 1)Q♮_l(ι²), where

    Q♮_l(s) := s² − (2κ + 1 + z)s + κ(κ + z) = (s − l²)(s − (l + 1)²) + z(κ − s).

(3) Let ι♮_(s0,1) := (1 + z)^(1/2), and ι♮_(sl,l) := s♮_1^(1/2), ι♮_(sl,l+1) := s♮_2^(1/2) with s♮_1 < s♮_2 the roots of
Q♮_l. For z ≥ 0 the roots are ±ι♮_(s0,1), 0 and 2 (s0); ±ι♮_(sl,l), ±ι♮_(sl,l+1), 1 − l and l + 2 (sl); −l and l + 1
(vl). At z = 0, ι♮_(s0,1) = 1 and ι♮_(sl,l+j) = l + j, and the sl roots −l − 1, −l, 1 − l, l, l + 1, l + 2 are distinct.
For 0 < z < 40/7, l < ι♮_(sl,l) < l + 1 < ι♮_(sl,l+1) < l + 2, and ι♮_(sl,l+j) = l + j + z/(2(2l + 1)) + O(z²) as z → 0.
These are the roots λ^Υ of [Hin26, Lemma 6.6], whose parameter e_Υγ_Υ² is z/4; the coefficient 1/(2(2l + 1)) of z is
the coefficient 2/(2l + 1) of z/4 in [Hin26, p. 117].

(4) Call class roots μ_s0 := −ι♮_(s0,1) (type s0, range K = 2), μ_(l,j) := −ι♮_(sl,l+j) (type sl, l = 1, 2, 3, j = 0, 1,
K = 2), 1 − l (type sl, 2 ≤ l ≤ 5, K = 5 − l) and −l (type vl, 2 ≤ l ≤ 4, K = 4 − l). For 0 < z < 3 each class root μ
of type τ is simple, and neither μ + 1 nor μ − k, 1 ≤ k ≤ K, is a root of type τ. At z = 3 this still holds for
μ_s0 = −2, while ι♮_(s0,1) = 2 is a double s0 root. At z = 0, μ_s0 + 1 = 0 is an s0 root, and at sl
μ_(l,0) − 1 = μ_(l,1), μ_(l,1) + 1 = μ_(l,0), μ_(l,0) + 1 = 1 − l and 1 − l − k = μ_(l,k−1) for k ≤ min(2, 5 − l);
at vl no such coincidence occurs for any z.

(5) At vl, N_0(−l − i) = −i(2l + i + 1) and N_1(−l − i + 1) = 2(l + i + γ), so the recursion
N_0(−l − i)w̄_i = −N_1(−l − i + 1)w̄_(i−1) gives w̄_i = k_iw̄_0 with k_0 = 1 and
k_i = k_(i−1)·2(l + i + γ)/(i(2l + i + 1)); at l = 1, k_1 = 1 + γ/2, as in [Hin26, p. 134].

*Proof.* (1) Lemma 21.8 (1) holds for every sphere dimension ν: the radial term is −2∂_(t_*)ρ(D − ν/2), the
scalar part of ᵇ□̄(0) is ρ²(−D² + (ν − 1)D + Δ_𝕊), and the entries ±3/2 of the matrix B₁ of that lemma become ±ν/2.
Lemma 23.2 holds for every ν with the trace weight 2/ν. At ν = 2 the radial term of □̄^Υ is
−2∂_(t_*)ρ(D − 1 − S̄). On sl 1-forms ᵇ□̄(0) contributes, as for (23.8), −ι² + ι + κ on the first two
components (Δ_𝕊S = κS), −ι² + ι + κ − 1 on the third (Δ_𝕊d_𝕊S = (κ − 1)d_𝕊S, (21.7) at ν = 2), and B₁ with
the rows (1, −1, −κ), (−1, 1, κ), (−2, 2, 1); and γρ²M_E contributes γ times the rows (−(1 + e)ι + 2e, −(1 − e)ι − 2e,
−eκ), ((1 − e)ι + 2e, (1 + e)ι − 2e, −eκ), (2, 2, 0). On vl, Δ_𝕊V = (κ − 1)V ((21.7)), the third diagonal
entry of B₁ is 1, and M_E vanishes.

(2) For s0, (p + 1)² − γ²((1 + e)ι − 2e)² − 1 + γ²((1 − e)ι + 2e)² = p(p + 2) − zι(ι − 2), and p = −ι(ι − 1),
p + 2 = −(ι − 2)(ι + 1). For sl, the change to (u, w, c) of the proof of Lemma 23.3 gives, with P := p + κ,

    M♮ = ((P, −2eγ(ι − 2), −2eγκ), (−2γι, P + 2, −2κ), (2γ, −2, P)),
    det M♮ = P(P² + 2P − 4κ) + z(P(κ − ι² + 2ι) − 2κ).

Here P² + 2P − 4κ = (P + 1)² − (2l + 1)² = (P − 2l)(P + 2l + 2), with P = −(ι − l − 1)(ι + l),
P − 2l = −(ι − l)(ι + l − 1) and P + 2l + 2 = −(ι − l − 2)(ι + l + 1); so with s := ι² the first term is
(l + 2 − ι)(l + ι − 1)(s − l²)(s − (l + 1)²). With Y := κ − ι² + 2ι one has P = Y − ι,
(l + 2 − ι)(l + ι − 1) = Y + ι − 2 and κ − s = Y − 2ι, and (Y − ι)Y − 2κ − (Y + ι − 2)(Y − 2ι) =
2Y + 2ι² − 4ι − 2κ = 0; so the second term is z(l + 2 − ι)(l + ι − 1)(κ − s). Finally l² + (l + 1)² = 2κ + 1 and
l²(l + 1)² = κ².

(3) The list follows from (2) and (1). For z ≥ 0 the discriminant of Q♮_l is (1 + z)² + 4κ > 0, and the sum
2κ + 1 + z and the product κ(κ + z) of its roots are positive. Q♮_l(l²) = zl, Q♮_l((l + 1)²) = −z(l + 1) and
Q♮_l((l + 2)²) = 4(l + 1)(2l + 3) − z(3l + 4), positive for z < 40/7 as 4(l + 1)(2l + 3)/(3l + 4) increases in l and
is 40/7 at l = 1. So l² < s♮_1 < (l + 1)² < s♮_2 < (l + 2)² for 0 < z < 40/7. With (Q♮_l)′(l²) = −(2l + 1) − z and
(Q♮_l)′((l + 1)²) = 2l + 1 − z, s♮_1 = l² + lz/(2l + 1) + O(z²) and s♮_2 = (l + 1)² + (l + 1)z/(2l + 1) + O(z²), which
give the expansions. [Hin26, Lemma 6.6] gives (λ^Υ_(sl,l+j))² = κ + ½ + 2eγ² ∓ (κ + (½ + 2eγ²)²)^(1/2), whose sum is
2κ + 1 + z and whose product is κ² + κz: the roots of Q♮_l.

(4) For 0 < z < 3, ι♮_(s0,1) ∈ (1, 2), so the s0 roots μ_s0 ∈ (−2, −1), 0, ι♮_(s0,1) and 2 are distinct, and
μ_s0 + 1 ∈ (−1, 0), μ_s0 − 1 ∈ (−3, −2) and μ_s0 − 2 ∈ (−4, −3) contain none of them. At sl, by (3),
μ_(l,1) < −l − 1 < μ_(l,0) < −l < 1 − l < ι♮_(sl,l) < l + 1 < ι♮_(sl,l+1) < l + 2, so the roots are simple.
μ_(l,0) + 1 ∈ (−l, 1 − l), μ_(l,0) − 2 ∈ (−l − 3, −l − 2), μ_(l,1) − 1 ∈ (−l − 3, −l − 2) and
μ_(l,1) − 2 ∈ (−l − 4, −l − 3) contain no sl root; μ_(l,0) − 1 ∈ (−l − 2, −l − 1) and μ_(l,1) + 1 ∈ (−l − 1, −l)
could only be μ_(l,1), respectively μ_(l,0), and either means ι♮_(sl,l+1) = ι♮_(sl,l) + 1. With x := ι♮_(sl,l), the
relations s♮_1 + s♮_2 = 2κ + 1 + z and s♮_1s♮_2 = κ(κ + z) then give x² + x = κ + z/2 and (x² + x)² = κ² + κz, so
z² = 0. For μ = 1 − l, the numbers μ + 1 = 2 − l and μ − k = 1 − l − k are integers other than 1 − l and l + 2, the
integer sl roots, and the other sl roots are not integers; for μ = −l (vl), 1 − l and −l − k differ from −l and l + 1.
At z = 3, ι♮_(s0,1) = 2 and det N_s0(ι) = ι(ι − 2)²(ι + 2): 2 is double, −2 is simple, and −1, −3, −4 are not roots.
At z = 0 the roots are integers and the coincidences are read off from (3).

(5) N_0(ι) = −(ι + l)(ι − l − 1) at ι = −l − i, and N_1(ι) = −2(ι − 1 − γ) at ι = −l − i + 1. ∎

*The model states.* The leading terms of the states are the following exact solutions on 4 + 1 Minkowski space, with
E_Υ at the trace weight 2/3 and c̄ = r⁻¹dt̄. We write e := e_Υ, γ := γ_Υ, and S ∈ 𝒮_1, V ∈ 𝒱_1 as in
(23.18); V = r²V_𝕊 with V_𝕊 a 1-form on the unit 𝕊³, so that V is (0, 0, ρ⁻¹V_𝕊) in the splitting.

**Proposition 23.31** (The model states of the symmetries.)

(i) With W̄ := |x|(−dt̄ + β_e d|x|) and β_e := (2 − e)/(4e), t_*ω̄^(0)_s0 + W̄ ∈ ker □̄^Υ. The tensor
h̄^(0)_s0 := δ̄*(t_*ω̄^(0)_s0 + W̄) = dt_* ⊗_s ω̄^(0)_s0 + (δ̄*)^(0)W̄ is stationary, homogeneous of degree 0, of scalar
type 0, and in the splitting (21.10)

    h̄^(0)_s0 = (16e)⁻¹(2 − 5e, −(2 + 3e), 0, 2 − 5e, 0, 4(2 − e)g_𝕊) ≠ 0;

it lies in the kernels of D_ḡRic and δ_(ḡ,Ē)Ḡ. On g_(b_0), with t the static time, t_* := t − r_*,
ω_s0 := g(∂_t, ·) = −f dt and E_Υ near infinity built from c := r⁻¹dt, the 1-form
□^Υ(t_*ω_s0) = 2δ_(g,E)G(dt_* ⊗_s ω_s0) is, on (dt, dr),

    (−f′ − 3f/r − 2(2 − e)γ/r,  f⁻¹(f′ + 2γ/r)) = ρ(2eγ − 4γ − 3, 2γ) + ρ³(m_0, 2m_0(γ + 1)) + O(ρ⁵),

with no ρ² term. For 0 < z < 4, none of −1, −2, −3, −4 is an s0 root of P_b; −1 is none for every z > 0, and −2 is one
at z = 4.

(ii) With B̆ := ω̆̄^((0),1)_s1(S) and W̄_2 := r²(a_2S dx̄⁰ + b_2S dx̄¹) + k_2r³dS,
(a_2, b_2, k_2) := (24e)⁻¹(4 − 7e, −(4 + 17e), (2/3)(25e − 4)), the polynomial
t_*²ω̄^(0)_s1(S) + 2t_*B̆ + 2W̄_2 lies in ker □̄^Υ. Its halved symmetric gradient
h̄²_s1(S) := dt_* ⊗_s B̆ + (δ̄*)^(0)W̄_2 is stationary, homogeneous of degree −1, of scalar type 1, nonzero for S ≠ 0
and every e > 0, and in both kernels. For 0 < z < 20/3, none of −2, −3, −4 is an s1 root of P_b; −2 is none for every
z > 0 and is one at z = 0, and −3 is one at z = 20/3.

(iii) t_*V + k_1|x|V ∈ ker □̄^Υ if and only if k_1 = 1 + 2γ/5. Then

    h̄¹_v1(V) := dt_* ⊗_s V + (δ̄*)^(0)(k_1|x|V) = (0, 0, ¼(1 + ⅖γ)ρ⁻¹V_𝕊, 0, ¼(1 − ⅖γ)ρ⁻¹V_𝕊, 0),    (23.31)

stationary and in both kernels. None of −2, −3, −4 is a v1 root, for every z.

(iv) (*Dimension 3 + 1.*) On 3 + 1 Minkowski space, with the trace weight 1, in the splitting (21.10) for
𝕊²: t_*ω̄^(0)_s0 + W̄ ∈ ker □̄^Υ with W̄ := |x|(−dt̄ + β_e d|x|), β_e := (2 − e)/(3e);
t_*²ω̄^(0)_s1(S) + 2t_*B̆ + 2W̄_2 ∈ ker □̄^Υ with W̄_2 as in (ii) and
(a_2, b_2, k_2) := (10e)⁻¹(2 − 3e, −(2 + 7e), 2(4e − 1)); and t_*V + k_1|x|V ∈ ker □̄^Υ if and only if k_1 = 1 + γ/2,
and then

    h̄¹_v1(V) := dt_* ⊗_s V + (δ̄*)^(0)(k_1|x|V) = (0, 0, ¼(1 + ½γ)ρ⁻¹V_𝕊, 0, ¼(1 − ½γ)ρ⁻¹V_𝕊, 0),

which is [Hin26, (6.40)]. In both dimensions dt_* ⊗_s ω̄^(0)_s0 has b = −¼, e′ = −½ and its other components 0, and
dt_* ⊗_s B̆ = (0, 0, 0, −ρ⁻¹S, ½ρ⁻¹d_𝕊S, 0), the values of [Hin26, pp. 132–133]. On Schwarzschild,
g = −f dt² + f⁻¹dr² + r²g_(𝕊²) with f = 1 − 2M/r, with t_* := t − r_* for a tortoise coordinate r_*, a function of r
with dr_*/dr = f⁻¹ on {r > 2M}, with c := r⁻¹dt and the trace weight 1, the 1-form □^Υ(t_*ω_s0), ω_s0 := −f dt, has
on (dt, dr) the ρ¹ term (2eγ − 4γ − 2, 2γ) and the ρ² term (2M, 2M(2γ + 1)).

(v) ι^Υ_(s1,2) = ½(1 + (17 + 2z − 2(z² + 4z + 16)^(1/2))^(1/2)) = 2 + z/12 + O(z²) and
ι^Υ_(s0,2) = ½(1 + (9 + 4z)^(1/2)) = 2 + z/3 + O(z²), and ι^Υ_(s1,2) < ι^Υ_(s0,2) for every z > 0. In particular 1 and
2 lie in the gap (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) for z > 0, and 2 is its end at z = 0.

*Proof.* For a stationary u, □̄^Υ(t_*u) = t_*□̄^Υu + Ā_1u, and Ā_1 = −2ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄). In the splitting we use the
coefficients (a, b, c) of a type s1 1-form (aS, bS, c d_𝕊S) and the matrices (23.8); write D := ρ∂_ρ.

(i) ω̄ := ω̄^(0)_s0 = −dt̄ = (−½, −½, 0) is Killing, so □̄^Υ(t_*ω̄ + W̄) = Ā_1ω̄ + Ā_0W̄. Here
S̄ω̄ = −½γ(1 − e, 3 − e, 0) and (D − 3/2)ω̄ = (¾, ¾, 0), so Ā_1ω̄ = −ρ(3/2 + γ(1 − e), 3/2 + γ(3 − e), 0). Since dt̄ =
½(dx̄⁰ + dx̄¹) and d|x| = ½(dx̄⁰ − dx̄¹), W̄ = ρ⁻¹w with w = ½(β_e − 1, −β_e − 1), and Ā_0W̄ = ρN_s0(−1)w with

    N_s0(−1) = ( −3/2 + γ(1 + 4e) , −3/2 + γ(1 − 4e) ; −3/2 + γ(4e − 1) , −3/2 − γ(1 + 4e) ).

So N_s0(−1)w = (3/2 + γ(4eβ_e − 1), 3/2 + γ(4eβ_e + 1)), which equals (3/2 + γ(1 − e), 3/2 + γ(3 − e)) exactly when
4eβ_e = 2 − e. By Lemma 21.8 (1), (δ̄*)^(0)(ρ⁻¹w) has a = ½w_0, b = −¼(w_0 − w_1), e′ = −½w_1, q = (w_0 − w_1)g_𝕊
and c = f = 0, and dt_* ⊗_s ω̄ = dx̄¹ ⊗_s ω̄ has b = −¼, e′ = −½; with w_0 − w_1 = β_e this gives the stated
components. h̄^(0)_s0 = δ̄*(t_*ω̄ + W̄) because δ̄*(t_*u) = t_*δ̄*u + dt_* ⊗_s u and δ̄*ω̄ = 0; it lies in the kernels by
fact (F2) of the proof of Proposition 23.28 for ḡ.

*The right side on Tangherlini.* We calculate for a static metric g = −f dt² + f⁻¹dr² + r²g_(𝕊^ν), at the trace
weight 2/ν, so that Lemma 21.29 gives E G h = −γ(2ι_(g⁻¹c)h − e c tr_g h) (its proof uses only
(2/ν)(1 − (ν + 2)/2) = −1). As ω_s0 is Killing, δ*(t_*ω_s0) = dt_* ⊗_s ω_s0 =: 𝔨, and dt_* = dt − f⁻¹dr gives
𝔨 = −f dt² + dt ⊗_s dr, so 𝔨_tt = −f, 𝔨_tr = ½, 𝔨_rr = 0 and tr_g 𝔨 = 1. Then G𝔨 = 𝔨 − ½g, and δ_g(G𝔨) = δ_g𝔨, as
δ_g g = 0. With
(δ𝔨)_ν = −|g|^(−1/2)∂_μ(|g|^(1/2)𝔨^μ_ν) + ½(∂_νg_αβ)𝔨^(αβ), |g|^(1/2) = r^ν|g_𝕊|^(1/2), 𝔨^r_t = f/2, 𝔨^t_t = 1,
𝔨^t_r = −(2f)⁻¹, 𝔨^r_r = 0, 𝔨^(tt) = −f⁻¹ and 𝔨^(tr) = −½, one finds (δ𝔨)_t = −r^(−ν)(r^νf/2)′ = −½(f′ + νf/r) and
(δ𝔨)_r = ½(∂_rg_tt)𝔨^(tt) = f′/(2f); the angular components vanish. Next g⁻¹c = −(rf)⁻¹∂_t, so
ι_(g⁻¹c)𝔨 = r⁻¹dt − (2rf)⁻¹dr and E G 𝔨 = −γ((2 − e)r⁻¹dt − (rf)⁻¹dr). So

    □^Υ(t_*ω_s0) = 2(δ𝔨 + EG𝔨) = −(f′ + νf/r + 2(2 − e)γ/r)dt + f⁻¹(f′ + 2γ/r)dr.

At ν = 3, f = 1 − m_0ρ² and f′ = 2m_0ρ³, the dt component is (2eγ − 4γ − 3)ρ + m_0ρ³ exactly, and the dr component is
(2γρ + 2m_0ρ³)(1 − m_0ρ²)⁻¹ = 2γρ + 2m_0(γ + 1)ρ³ + O(ρ⁵).

*Roots.* The s0 roots below 0 are 1 − ι^Υ_(s0,2) = ½ − (9/4 + z)^(1/2), which equals −k exactly when
z = (k + 2)(k − 1); for k = 1, 2, 3, 4 these are 0, 4, 10, 18. The other s0 roots 0, 3 and ι^Υ_(s0,2) are not
negative; so −1 is not an s0 root for z > 0.

(ii) By (23.29) with Ā_2 = 0, the polynomial lies in the kernel if Ā_0ω̄_s1 = 0, Ā_1ω̄_s1 + Ā_0B̆ = 0 and
Ā_1B̆ + Ā_0W̄_2 = 0. The first two hold since ω̄_s1 and the boost t_*ω̄_s1 + B̆ are Killing. In the splitting,
d(rS) = (½S, −½S, d_𝕊S), so B̆ = r d(rS) − rS dt̄ = ρ⁻¹(0, −S, d_𝕊S), with coefficients ρ⁻¹(0, −1, 1), and
S̄(0, −1, 1) = γ(0, −2, 1); so −Ā_1B̆ = 2(D − 3/2 − S̄)(0, −1, 1) = (0, 5 + 4γ, −5 − 2γ). W̄_2 = ρ⁻²(a_2, b_2, k_2) and
Ā_0W̄_2 = N_s1(−2)(a_2, b_2, k_2), where at l = 1 (κ = 3), N_s1(−2) = N⁰ + γN¹ with

    N⁰ = ( −7/2 , −3/2 , −3 ; −3/2 , −7/2 , 3 ; −2 , 2 , −6 ),
    N¹ = ( 2 + 5e , 2 − 5e , −3e ; 5e − 2 , −(2 + 5e) , −3e ; 2 , 2 , 0 ).

Multiplying out, N⁰(a_2, b_2, k_2) = (24e)⁻¹(0, 120e, −120e) = (0, 5, −5) and
N¹(a_2, b_2, k_2) = (24e)⁻¹(0, 96e, −48e) = (0, 4, −2). For instance the first entry of N⁰(a_2, b_2, k_2) is
(24e)⁻¹(−(7/2)(4 − 7e) + (3/2)(4 + 17e) − 2(25e − 4)) = 0, and the second entry of N¹(a_2, b_2, k_2) is
(24e)⁻¹((5e − 2)(4 − 7e) + (2 + 5e)(4 + 17e) − e(50e − 8)) = (24e)⁻¹ · 96e. So the third relation holds. By
(23.28) for ḡ, δ̄*(t_*²ω̄_s1 + 2t_*B̆ + 2W̄_2) = 2t_*δ̄*(t_*ω̄_s1 + B̆) + 2(dt_* ⊗_s B̆ + (δ̄*)^(0)W̄_2), and
the first term vanishes; so h̄²_s1 is stationary, and it lies in the kernels by (F2). Its f component, in the
coefficient of the splitting (21.10), is ½ρ⁻¹d_𝕊S from dt_* ⊗_s B̆ = dx̄¹ ⊗_s ρ⁻¹(−S dx̄¹ + r d_𝕊S), plus
ρ(½d_𝕊(ρ⁻²b_2S) + ¼(D + 1)(ρ⁻²k_2d_𝕊S)) = ρ⁻¹(½b_2 − ¼k_2)d_𝕊S from (δ̄*)^(0)W̄_2 (Lemma 21.8 (1)); in all

    (½ + ½b_2 − ¼k_2)ρ⁻¹d_𝕊S = (288e)⁻¹(144e − 6(4 + 17e) − (50e − 8))ρ⁻¹d_𝕊S = −((e + 2)/(36e))ρ⁻¹d_𝕊S,

which is nonzero for e > 0 and S ≠ 0. For the roots: the s1 roots other than 1 − ι^Υ_(s1,j) are 0, 4 and the
positive ι^Υ_(s1,j); and 1 − ι = −k exactly when ι² − ι = k(k + 1), that is when Q_1(k(k + 1)) = 0. With
Q_1(s) = s² − (8 + z)s + 12 + 3z, Q_1(6) = −3z, Q_1(12) = 60 − 9z and Q_1(20) = 252 − 17z; in particular Q_1(6) ≠ 0
for z > 0, so −2 is not an s1 root for z > 0.

(iii) V = ρ⁻¹(0, 0, V_𝕊) and |x|V = ρ⁻²(0, 0, V_𝕊). On v1, Ā_0(ρ^a(0, 0, V_𝕊)) = ρ^(a+2)(−a² + 2a + 3)(0, 0, V_𝕊) and
S̄ = γ on angular components, so Ā_0(k_1|x|V) = −5k_1(0, 0, V_𝕊) and Ā_1V = −2(−1 − 3/2 − γ)(0, 0,
V_𝕊) = (5 + 2γ)(0, 0, V_𝕊). The relation Ā_1V + Ā_0(k_1|x|V) = 0 holds exactly when k_1 = 1 + 2γ/5. By
Lemma 21.8 (1), (δ̄*)^(0)(ρ⁻²(0, 0, V_𝕊)) has c = −¼ρ(D + 1)ρ⁻²V_𝕊 = ¼ρ⁻¹V_𝕊, f = −¼ρ⁻¹V_𝕊 and
q = ρ⁻¹δ*_𝕊V_𝕊 = 0 (V_𝕊 is Killing on 𝕊³), and dt_* ⊗_s V has f = ½ρ⁻¹V_𝕊; with k_1 this is (23.31).
Stationarity and the kernels follow as in (ii). The v1 roots are −1 and 3.

(iv) The calculations of (i)–(iii) hold verbatim with the indicial families of Lemma 23.30 (1) and
N_1(ι) = −2(ι − 1 − S̄). (i): (D − 1)ω̄ = (½, ½, 0), so Ā_1ω̄ = −ρ(1 + γ(1 − e), 1 + γ(3 − e), 0), and

    N_s0(−1) = ( −1 + γ(1 + 3e) , −1 + γ(1 − 3e) ; −1 + γ(3e − 1) , −1 − γ(1 + 3e) ),

so N_s0(−1)w = (1 + γ(3eβ_e − 1), 1 + γ(3eβ_e + 1)), which is (1 + γ(1 − e), 1 + γ(3 − e)) exactly when
3eβ_e = 2 − e. (ii): −Ā_1B̆ = 2(D − 1 − S̄)(0, −1, 1) = (0, 4 + 4γ, −4 − 2γ), and at l = 1 (κ = 2),
N_s1(−2) = N⁰ + γN¹ with

    N⁰ = ( −3 , −1 , −2 ; −1 , −3 , 2 ; −2 , 2 , −4 ),
    N¹ = ( 2 + 4e , 2 − 4e , −2e ; 4e − 2 , −(2 + 4e) , −2e ; 2 , 2 , 0 );

multiplying out, N⁰(a_2, b_2, k_2) = (10e)⁻¹(0, 40e, −40e) = (0, 4, −4) and N¹(a_2, b_2, k_2) =
(10e)⁻¹(0, 40e, −20e) = (0, 4, −2). For instance the second entry of N¹(a_2, b_2, k_2) is
(10e)⁻¹((4e − 2)(2 − 3e) + (2 + 4e)(2 + 7e) − 2e(8e − 2)) = (10e)⁻¹ · 40e. (iii): Ā_0(ρ^a(0, 0, V_𝕊)) =
ρ^(a+2)(−a² + a + 2)(0, 0, V_𝕊) and Ā_1V = −2(−1 − 1 − γ)(0, 0, V_𝕊), so the relation is 4 + 2γ − 4k_1 = 0. The
components of h̄¹_v1 are those found in (iii), c = ¼k_1ρ⁻¹V_𝕊 and f = (½ − ¼k_1)ρ⁻¹V_𝕊, as δ̄* of
Lemma 21.8 (1) does not depend on ν; with k_1 = 1 + γ/2 this is [Hin26, (6.40)] (p. 130). The two products
are dt_* ⊗_s ω̄ = dx̄¹ ⊗_s (−½dx̄⁰ − ½dx̄¹) and dt_* ⊗_s B̆ = dx̄¹ ⊗_s ρ⁻¹(−S dx̄¹ + r d_𝕊S), which do not involve the
dimension; [Hin26, p. 132] prints the first as (0, −¼, −½, 0) in its s0 components (a, b, e, p). On Schwarzschild the
1-form is given by the formula of the proof of (i) at ν = 2 with f = 1 − 2Mρ and f′ = 2Mρ²: the dt component is
−2Mρ² − 2ρ(1 − 2Mρ) − 2(2 − e)γρ = (2eγ − 4γ − 2)ρ + 2Mρ², and the dr component is
(2Mρ² + 2γρ)(1 − 2Mρ)⁻¹ = 2γρ + 2M(2γ + 1)ρ² + O(ρ³).

(v) ½ + (¼ + s)^(1/2) = ½(1 + (1 + 4s)^(1/2)), and 1 + 4s_(1,1) = 17 + 2z − 2(z² + 4z + 16)^(1/2),
1 + 4(2 + z) = 9 + 4z. The expansions are those of Lemma 23.3. ι^Υ_(s1,2) < ι^Υ_(s0,2) if and only if
s_(1,1) < 2 + z, that is 2 − z/2 < (4 + z + z²/4)^(1/2), which holds for z ≥ 4 trivially and for 0 < z < 4 after
squaring. That (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2)) is an indicial gap for every z > 0 is Proposition 23.23 (i). ∎

**Proposition 23.32** (The classes without symmetry.) On 4 + 1 Minkowski space, for □̄^Υ:

(i) (*The indicial families.*) On the types s0, sl (l ≥ 1) and vl, Ā_2 = 0, Ā_0 = ρ²N_0(ρ∂_ρ) with det N_0 given by
(23.10), and Ā_1 = ρN_1(ρ∂_ρ) with N_1(ι) = −2(ι − 3/2 − S̄), S̄ independent of ι. At vl,
N_0(ι) = −(ι + l)(ι − l − 2) and N_1(ι) = −2(ι − 3/2 − γ_Υ). In dimension 3 + 1, N_0 is given by
Lemma 23.30 (1), the matrices of [Hin26, Lemma 6.6] entry by entry, N_1(ι) = −2(ι − 1 − S̄), and
N_1(ι) = −2(ι − 1 − γ_Υ) at v1.

(ii) (*The classes.*) For every l ≥ 1, Q_l(l(l + 1)) = lz, Q_l((l + 1)(l + 2)) = −(l + 2)z and
Q_l((l + 2)(l + 3)) = (l + 2)(8l + 12 − 3z). So for every z > 0 the negative sl roots other than 1 − l,
μ_(l,0) := 1 − ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) and μ_(l,1) := 1 − ι^Υ_(sl,l+2), satisfy −l − 1 < μ_(l,0) < −l and μ_(l,1) < −l − 1
(as in the proof of Proposition 23.23 (i)), and for 0 < z < 20/3 also μ_(l,1) > −l − 2. As z → 0,
μ_(l,0) = −l − lz/(2(l + 1)(2l + 1)) + O(z²) and μ_(l,1) = −l − 1 − (l + 2)z/(2(l + 1)(2l + 3)) + O(z²).
μ_s0 := 1 − ι^Υ_(s0,2) = ½(1 − (9 + 4z)^(1/2)) = −1 − z/3 + O(z²) lies in (−2, −1) for 0 < z < 4. The sl roots
1 − l and the vl roots −l are roots at every z. For 0 < z < 4 the roots ≤ 0 of each type are these, together with 0 at
s0. In dimension 3 + 1 the corresponding roots are −(1 + z)^(1/2), −ι♮_(sl,l) and −ι♮_(sl,l+1) of
Lemma 23.30 (3), which are [Hin26]'s −λ^Υ_(s0,1), −λ^Υ_(sl,l) and −λ^Υ_(sl,l+1), with first-order coefficient
1/(2(2l + 1)) in z, [Hin26]'s 2/(2l + 1) in its parameter z/4.

(iii) (*The symmetric gradient.*) N(δ̄*(0), ι) is injective on the types sl and vl for l ≥ 2 and every ι ∈ ℂ, on s0
and s1 for ι ≠ 0, and on v1 for ι ≠ −1. The same holds in dimension 3 + 1, where these families are
[Hin26, (2.46a)–(2.46c)] (Section 21.2.4).

(iv) (*No resonance.*) Let 0 < z < 4. Call a class root each of μ_s0 (type s0, range K = 2), μ_(l,0) and μ_(l,1)
(type sl, l = 1, 2, 3, K = 2), 1 − l (type sl, 2 ≤ l ≤ 5, K = 5 − l) and −l (type vl, 2 ≤ l ≤ 4, K = 4 − l). For each
class root μ of type τ, μ is a simple root of type τ, and neither μ + 2 nor μ − k, 1 ≤ k ≤ K, is a root of type τ.
The bound 4 is sharp: at z = 4, μ_s0 = −2 and μ_s0 + 2 = 0 is an s0 root. At z = 0 the classes meet at sl:
μ_(l,0) − 1 = μ_(l,1), μ_(l,1) + 2 = 1 − l, and 1 − l − k = μ_(l,k−1) for k ≤ min(2, 5 − l); never at vl. In
dimension 3 + 1 the statement holds for 0 < z < 3 with μ + 1 in place of μ + 2, and the bound 3 is not sharp for the
class roots: at z = 3 only the s0 root 2 becomes double (Lemma 23.30 (4)).

(v) (*The states.*) For each class root μ of type τ with a nonzero indicial solution ρ^μ w̄_0 of the model, the
recursion N_0(μ − i)w̄_i = −N_1(μ − i + 1)w̄_(i−1), 1 ≤ i ≤ K, has a unique solution of type τ, and
Σ_(i=0)^k (k!/(k − i)!) t_*^(k−i) ρ^(μ−i)w̄_i ∈ ker □̄^Υ for k ≤ K. At vl, w̄_i = k_i w̄_0 with k_0 = 1 and
k_i = k_(i−1)(2l + 2i + 1 + 2γ_Υ)/(i(2l + i + 2)); at l = 1, k_1 = 1 + 2γ_Υ/5. In dimension 3 + 1 the same holds for
0 < z < 3, with k_i = k_(i−1)·2(l + i + γ_Υ)/(i(2l + i + 1)) at vl and k_1 = 1 + γ_Υ/2 at l = 1.

(vi) (*The case e_Υ = 0.*) Let e_Υ = 0 and γ_Υ ≠ 0, so that z = 0, in dimension 4 + 1 or 3 + 1. (a) For l = 1, 2, 3
the first step of the recursion of (v) for the root μ_(l,0) = −l, N_0(−l − 1)w̄_1 = −N_1(−l)w̄_0, has no solution:
N_0(−l − 1) has rank 2 and the right side is not in its range. (b) For l = 2, 3, 4 the first step for the root 1 − l,
N_0(−l)w̄_1 = −N_1(1 − l)w̄_0, is solvable, and its solutions form a line w̄_1^p + βŵ, ŵ spanning ker N_0(−l). (c) For
l = 2, 3 the second step for the root 1 − l, N_0(−l − 1)w̄_2 = −N_1(−l)w̄_1, is solvable for exactly one value of β.

*Proof.* (i) is (23.2), Lemma 23.2 and Section 23.4; on vl, S̄ acts as γ_Υ and N_0 = p + κ.
(ii) By (23.11), Q_l(s) = (s − l(l + 1))(s − (l + 1)(l + 2)) + z(κ − s), and κ − l(l + 1) = l,
κ − (l + 1)(l + 2) = −(l + 2), κ − (l + 2)(l + 3) = −3(l + 2), while the product at (l + 2)(l + 3) is
(4l + 6) · 2(l + 2). Let z > 0. Q_l is a monic quadratic, positive at l(l + 1) and negative at (l + 1)(l + 2), so
its roots satisfy l(l + 1) < s_(l,1) < (l + 1)(l + 2) < s_(l,2), as in the proof of Proposition 23.23 (i); since
ι ↦ ι² − ι is increasing on ι > ½, l + 1 < ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) < l + 2 < ι^Υ_(sl,l+2), which gives −l − 1 < μ_(l,0) < −l and
μ_(l,1) < −l − 1. If moreover z < (8l + 12)/3, which holds when z < 20/3, then Q_l is positive at (l + 2)(l + 3),
a point above s_(l,1), and Q_l is negative between its roots; so (l + 2)(l + 3) > s_(l,2), ι^Υ_(sl,l+2) < l + 3 and
μ_(l,1) > −l − 2. The expansions and
μ_s0 are those of Lemma 23.3, and ½ − (9/4 + z)^(1/2) ∈ (−2, −1) for 0 < z < 4. The sentence on the roots ≤ 0
follows from the list of the roots below ½ in the proof of Proposition 23.23 (i), which holds for every z > 0.
(iii) is Lemma 21.11.
(iv) *Simplicity.* For 0 < z < 4 the roots of type s0 are μ_s0 ∈ (−2, −1), 0, ι^Υ_(s0,2) ∈ (2, 3) and 3, and those of
type sl are μ_(l,1) < −l − 1 < μ_(l,0) < −l < 1 − l < l + 1 < ι^Υ_(sl,l+1) < l + 2 < ι^Υ_(sl,l+2) < l + 3; they are
distinct, so each is a simple zero of the determinant (23.10), whose degree is their number. *μ_s0.* μ_s0 + 2
∈ (0, 1), μ_s0 − 1 ∈ (−3, −2) and μ_s0 − 2 ∈ (−4, −3) contain no s0 root. *μ_(l,0).* μ_(l,0) + 2 ∈ (−l + 1, −l + 2)
and μ_(l,0) − 2 ∈ (−l − 3, −l − 2) contain no sl root. μ_(l,0) − 1 ∈ (−l − 2, −l − 1) could only be μ_(l,1); but
μ_(l,0) − 1 = μ_(l,1) means ι_2 = ι_1 + 1 for ι_j := ι^Υ_(sl,l+j). Then s_(l,1) = ι_1² − ι_1 and
s_(l,2) = ι_1² + ι_1, and the relations s_(l,1) + s_(l,2) = 2 + 2κ + z and s_(l,1)s_(l,2) = κ(κ + 1) + zκ give
ι_1² = (l + 1)² + z/2 =: X and X(X − 1) = κ((l + 1)² + z); since X − 1 = κ + z/2, the difference of the two sides is
z/2 + z²/4, which vanishes only at z = 0 and z = −2. *μ_(l,1).* μ_(l,1) + 2 ∈ (−l, −l + 1), μ_(l,1) − 1 and
μ_(l,1) − 2 lie below −l − 2, and none of these intervals contains an sl root. *The integer classes.* For μ = 1 − l
