    d₁ = 2 + 10e + h((3 − e)κ + 7 + 51e) + h²((10 + 42e)κ + 10 + 8e)
         + h³((9 − 3e)κ² + (2 + 26e)κ + 14 − 6e) + 6h⁴(3κ² − 1),
    d₂ = h(3 − e) + h²(8 + 22e) + h³((9 − 3e)κ + 1 + 17e) + 18h⁴κ,
    d₃ = h³(3 − e) + 6h⁴.    (24.22)

For instance, in d₀ the terms of order e give −3e(κ − 3) + 3e(κ + 5) = 24e, those of order h give
(1 − e)(κ − 3) + κ + 3 + 21eκ − 9e = 2κ + 20eκ − 6e, and those of order h² give
−(κ − 3)(κ + 1) + (4 − e)κ² − (1 − 9e)κ + 3 − 6e = (3 − e)κ² + (1 + 9e)κ + 6 − 6e. For κ > 1 and 0 < e < 1/3 every
bracket in (24.22) is positive, so d₀, d₂, d₃ > 0 and d₁ > 2. If P(2 + iy; κ, h) = 0 with y ≠ 0, then
Φ(y²) = Ψ(y²) = 0, so −Φ(y²) − h(κ + y²)Ψ(y²) = 0, while d₀ + d₁y² + d₂y⁴ + d₃y⁶ ≥ d₁y² > 0. ∎

#### 24.4.2 The line Re ι = −1/(2h)

**Lemma 24.17** (The line Re ι = −1/(2h).) Let κ ≥ 0 and 0 < h ≤ 10⁻⁶. Then P(·; κ, h) has no root
with real part −1/(2h).

*Proof.* Put K := h²κ and F(σ) := h³P(σ/h; κ, h). Multiply the matrix (24.6) at v = 1/2 by h, put ι = σ/h and
κ = K/h², then multiply its third column by h and divide its third row by h. The determinant becomes F(σ), and the
matrix becomes, with 𝔪 := K − σ − σ²,

    Y := ( 𝔪 + 2h(σ + 1),   2σ − 4h,                                2K                 )
         ( 2e(σ + h),       𝔪 − σ + 2hσ + 4h + 3h² + e(σ + h),      −(1 + 2h)K         )
         ( −2e,             −(e + 2h),                              𝔪 + 2hσ + 3h − h² ).    (24.23)

A root ι of P(·; κ, h) with real part −1/(2h) gives the root σ = hι = −1/2 + iy of F = det Y, y real. On this line
𝔪 = K + 1/4 + y² is real, |σ|² = 1/4 + y² ≤ 𝔪 and K ≤ 𝔪. Put m := 𝔪^(1/2) ≥ 1/2; then |σ| ≤ m, K ≤ m², 1 ≤ 2m and
m ≤ 2m². Write Y = Y⁰ + Z, where Y⁰ is the upper triangular matrix with rows (𝔪, 2σ, 2K), (0, 𝔪 − σ, −K) and
(0, 0, 𝔪). Then

    det Y⁰ = 𝔪²(𝔪 − σ),     |det Y⁰| ≥ 𝔪² Re(𝔪 − σ) = m⁴(m² + 1/2) > m⁶.

The rows of Z are (2h(σ + 1), −4h, 0), (2e(σ + h), 2hσ + 4h + 3h² + e(σ + h), −2hK) and (−2e, −(e + 2h),
2hσ + 3h − h²). Let α_i and β_i be the sums of the moduli of the entries of row i of Y⁰ and of Z. With the bounds
above,

    α₁ ≤ m² + 2m + 2m² ≤ 7m²,     α₂ ≤ (m² + m) + m² ≤ 4m²,     α₃ = m²,
    β₁ ≤ 2h(m + 1) + 4h ≤ 14hm ≤ 28hm²,
    β₂ ≤ 2e(m + h) + (2hm + 4h + 3h² + e(m + h)) + 2hm² ≤ (6e + 22h + 12eh + 12h²)m² ≤ (6e + 23h)m²,
    β₃ ≤ 2e + (e + 2h) + (2hm + 3h + h²) ≤ (12e + 24h + 4h²)m² ≤ (12e + 25h)m²,

where 1 ≤ 4m² and m ≤ 2m² were used to bring every term to a multiple of m². The determinant is multilinear in the
rows, so det Y − det Y⁰ is the sum, over the seven nonempty sets S ⊂ {1, 2, 3}, of the determinants of the matrices
whose rows i ∈ S are those of Z and whose other rows are those of Y⁰. By Hadamard's inequality, and since the
Euclidean norm of a vector is at most the sum of the moduli of its entries, such a determinant has modulus at most
the product of β_i over i ∈ S and of α_i over i ∉ S. Hence, the expression in the middle being increasing in each α_i
and each β_i,

    |det Y − det Y⁰| ≤ (α₁ + β₁)(α₂ + β₂)(α₃ + β₃) − α₁α₂α₃ ≤ 28m⁶((1 + 4h)(1 + (6e + 23h)/4)(1 + 12e + 25h) − 1).

As e < 10⁻⁵ and h ≤ 10⁻⁶, the numbers 4h, (6e + 23h)/4 and 12e + 25h are below 1.5·10⁻⁴, and the right side is
below 28m⁶((1 + 1.5·10⁻⁴)³ − 1) < 0.02m⁶ < |det Y⁰|. So det Y ≠ 0 on the line Re σ = −1/2. ∎

#### 24.4.3 The count

**Lemma 24.18** (The limits as h → 0⁺.) Let l ≥ 1.

(a) The roots ι₊, ι₋ of Q_5 have real part greater than 2.

(b) The three numbers 1/τ_j of Lemma 24.5 (a) are real and less than −1/2.

*Proof.* (a) By (24.8) at v = 1/2,

    4Q_5(ι) = e(5(ι − 3)(ι + 1) − 3κ) − 2(ι − 2)(ι − 3) = (5e − 2)ι² + (10 − 10e)ι − 12 − 15e − 3eκ,

a quadratic with leading coefficient 5e − 2 < 0, and 4Q_5(2) = −e(15 + 3κ) < 0, 4Q_5(3) = −3eκ < 0. The midpoint of
its roots is μ := (5 − 5e)/(2 − 5e) = 5/2 + 15e/(4 − 10e), which lies in (5/2, 3) as 0 < e < 1/10. If the roots are
not real, their real part is μ. If they are real, Q_5 ≥ 0 exactly on the closed interval between them, which contains
μ and neither 2 nor 3, so it lies in (2, 3).

(b) The factor τ + 1 of (24.9) gives 1/τ = −1. The quadratic factor q(τ) := (5e − 2)τ² + (e − 3)τ − 1 has
q(−2) = 18e − 3 < 0, q(−1) = 4e > 0, q(−1/2) = 3e/4 > 0 and q(0) = −1 < 0; so its roots lie in (−2, −1) and
(−1/2, 0), and their reciprocals in (−1, −1/2) and (−∞, −2). ∎

**Proposition 24.19** (The scalar type l ≥ 1 for every h ∈ (0, 10⁻⁶].) Let l ≥ 1 and
0 < h ≤ 10⁻⁶. Counted with multiplicity, P_l has three roots with real part less than −1/(2h) ≤ −5·10⁵ and three
roots with real part at least 2. For l ≥ 2 the latter three have real part greater than 2. For l = 1 one of them is
ι = 2, a simple root, and the other two have real part greater than 2. In particular no root of P_l has real part in
[−1/(2h), 2), and the only root with real part 2 is ι = 2 at l = 1.

*Proof.* *The roots on the left.* On Ω₁ := [3, ∞) × (0, 10⁻⁶] ∋ (κ, h) consider F(σ) = h³P(σ/h; κ, h) = det Y of
(24.23). Its coefficients in σ are polynomials in K = h²κ and h, hence continuous on Ω₁; its leading coefficient
is −1, that of P being −h³; and its roots are the numbers hι, ι a root of P(·; κ, h), with the same multiplicities. By
Lemma 24.17 F has no root with real part −1/2, so by Lemma 24.15 with H = {Re σ < −1/2} the
number N_− of roots of P(·; κ, h) with real part less than −1/(2h) is the same at every point of Ω₁. At κ = 3, that is
l = 1, Lemma 24.5 (a) gives, as h → 0⁺, three roots with hι → 1/τ_j, which are less than −1/2 by
Lemma 24.18 (b), and three roots converging to finite limits, for which hι → 0. So N_− = 3 for small h,
hence N_− = 3 on all of Ω₁.

*Degrees l ≥ 2.* On Ω₂ := (3, ∞) × (0, 10⁻⁶] the polynomial P(·; κ, h) has leading coefficient −h³ ≠ 0 and, by
Lemma 24.16, no root with real part 2. By Lemma 24.15 with H = {Re ι > 2} the number N_+ of
its roots with real part greater than 2 is the same at every point of Ω₂, and we find it at κ = 8, that is l = 2, for
small h. By Lemma 24.5 (a), three roots of P_2 converge to the pairwise distinct numbers 2, ι₊, ι₋, and the
real parts of the other three tend to −∞. The roots converging to ι₊ and ι₋ have real part greater than 2 for small h,
by Lemma 24.18 (a). For the third, choose δ > 0 smaller than |ι₊ − 2| and |ι₋ − 2| and such that Q_5 < 0
on [2, 2 + δ], which is possible as Q_5(2) = −(15 + 3κ)e/4 < 0 (Lemma 24.4 (a)). For small h exactly one root ι_h
of P_2 lies in the disc |ι − 2| < δ; its complex conjugate is also a root in that disc, so ι_h is real. Now
P_2(2) = f₀ > 0 by Lemma 24.16 (a), while P_2(2 + δ/2) tends to 4(δ/2)Q_5(2 + δ/2) < 0 as h → 0⁺, by
(24.8). So for small h, P_2 has a root in (2, 2 + δ/2), which is ι_h, and ι_h > 2. Hence N_+ = 3, at every point
of Ω₂. As P(·; κ, h) has six roots and N_− = 3, no root lies in the strip −1/(2h) ≤ Re ι ≤ 2 when (κ, h) ∈ Ω₂, in
particular when κ = l(l + 2) with l ≥ 2.

*Degree l = 1.* P_1(2) = 0 for every h, so P_1 = (ι − 2)P̃_1 with P̃_1 a polynomial of degree 5 in ι, of leading
coefficient −h³, whose coefficients are polynomials in h. By Lemma 24.16, P̃_1(2 + iy) = P_1(2 + iy)/(iy) ≠ 0
for real y ≠ 0, and P̃_1(2) = ∂_ιP_1(2) = f₁ ≠ 0; so P̃_1 has no root with real part 2, and by
Lemma 24.15 with Ω = {3} × (0, 10⁻⁶] the number of its roots with real part greater than 2 does not
depend on h. As h → 0⁺, three roots of P_1 converge to the pairwise distinct numbers 2, ι₊, ι₋ and the real parts of
the other three tend to −∞ (Lemma 24.5 (a)). For small h exactly one root of P_1 lies in a small disc about
2, and ι = 2 is a root there; so the five roots of P̃_1 are the other five. Two of them converge to ι₊ and ι₋ and have
real part greater than 2 for small h (Lemma 24.18 (a)), and three have real parts tending to −∞. So P̃_1
has exactly two roots with real part greater than 2, for every h ∈ (0, 10⁻⁶]. Its roots with real part less than
−1/(2h) are those of P_1, three by the first part. So P̃_1 has no root with real part in [−1/(2h), 2], and the roots
of P_1 are ι = 2, simple as P̃_1(2) ≠ 0, two with real part greater than 2, and three with real part less than
−1/(2h). ∎

Since −1/(2h) ≤ −5·10⁵ < −100 and 2 > 19/10, Proposition 24.19 gives the part of Proposition 24.6 (i)–(ii)
that concerns the scalar types l ≥ 1. It holds at every h ∈ (0, 10⁻⁶] and every l ≥ 1, with no exceptional value of h;
as h_* ≤ 10⁻⁶, this includes every h ∈ 𝖧 of (24.4).

### 24.5 The inputs in dimension 4 + 1

**Lemma 24.20** (The fibre algebra; [Hin26a, Lemmas 3.3–3.8] in dimension 4 + 1.) On each fibre, with G(c) < 0,
B := g⁻¹ − (1 + e)G(c)⁻¹c♯ ⊗ c♯ is positive definite for e > 0, ℓ_(g,c,e)(ζ) of (24.10) is B-self-adjoint for
every ζ, and the characteristic polynomial of ½ℓ(ζ) is (ν − G(c)ζ_0)³ times the quadratic of [Hin26a, (3.8)], where
ζ = ζ_0 c + ζ′ with ζ′ ⊥ c. [Hin26a, Lemmas 3.3–3.8] hold in dimension 4 + 1 verbatim.

*Proof.* The three statements are Proposition 24.8 (i), with ⟨c, ζ⟩ = G(c)ζ_0. [Hin26a, Lemmas 3.3–3.8] are proved on a
single fibre from these three facts and from the splitting T* = ℝc ⊕ c^⊥, in which G(ζ) = G(c)ζ_0² + G(ζ′) and ℓ(ζ) has
the block form [Hin26a, (3.5)]. In dimension 4 + 1, c^⊥ has dimension 4 instead of 3, and the factor (ν − G(c)ζ_0)
appears to the third power instead of the second, which no step uses beyond its eigenvalue. ∎

**Lemma 24.21** (The structure at infinity; [Hin26a, (6.4)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Near ∂X, in t_*, ρ and
spherical coordinates,

    □^C_b = −2∂_(t_*) ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄^C − ρS̃) + P^C_b + Q∂_(t_*) + R∂²_(t_*),    (24.24)

with S̃ smooth, Q ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b, R ∈ ρ²C^∞, P^C_b ∈ ρ²Diff²_b, and S̄^C constant with spectrum
γ_C{2(1 − v_C), (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C), 1 − v_C (three times)}, all positive.

*Proof.* On 4 + 1 Minkowski space with c = |x|⁻¹(dt − v dr) this is Proposition 24.12 (i): the ∂_(t_*)∂_ρ-coefficient
is 2 Id, there is no ∂_(t_*) times a tangential derivative, and S̄^C is r/2 times the ∂_(t_*)-coefficient less
(n − 1)/2 = 3/2. The metric g_b differs from ḡ by ρ²C^∞ (Proposition 21.21), and c_C from the model's 1-form by
ρ³C^∞; the differences enter S̃, Q, R and P^C_b as in the proof of [Hin26a, (6.4)], by the same counting
(Section 24.1). ∎

**Lemma 24.22** (The indicial roots; [Hin26a, Theorem 4.9] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let h ∈ (0, 10⁻⁶] and b near
b₀.

(a) Every indicial root ι of P^C_b satisfies Re ι ∉ [−100, 19/10]; the only roots with real part in [−100, 2] are ι = 2
at scalar type 0 and at scalar type 1, each simple. At each type and degree as many roots have real part ≥ 2 as
< −100: three each at scalar type l ≥ 1, two each at scalar type 0, one each at vector type l ≥ 1. Each strip
{|Re ι| ≤ R} contains only finitely many roots, so the real parts accumulate only at ±∞.

(b) There is a countable set 𝖹₁ ⊂ (0, 10⁻⁶] such that for h ∉ 𝖹₁ the roots are simple and the remaining clauses of
Theorem 24.1 (3) hold.

*Proof.* The indicial family of P^C_b at ∂X is that of the Minkowski model with c = |x|⁻¹(dt − v_C d|x|), independent of
b: g_b − ḡ ∈ ρ²C^∞ and the deviation of c_C are of lower order (Lemma 24.21; [Hin26a, p. 29]: the indicial roots are
determined by the leading part as ρ → 0). In the decomposition into scalar and vector type harmonics of 𝕊³, the
indicial roots of type and degree l are, in the variable ι of Proposition 24.3 (ii) (the 1-form decaying like
ρ^ι = r^(−ι)), the roots of p_(v) and of P_l. (a) is Proposition 24.6.

(b) Fix l. Each condition is the non-vanishing at h of a polynomial in h, and we show that none of these polynomials
vanishes identically; then each fails for at most finitely many h, and 𝖹₁, the union over l and over the finitely
many conditions at each l, is countable. *Simplicity.* By Lemma 24.5, for all sufficiently small h > 0 the roots
of P_l, of C and of p_(v) are simple; so their discriminants, polynomials in h, do not vanish identically; and
ι = 2 is not a root of C (proof of Proposition 24.6). *Excluded points.* For a fixed real x, P_l(x) is a polynomial
in h with value 8v(x − 2)Q_5(x) at h = 0, and p_(v)(x) has value −2v(x − 3) at h = 0. For the scalar type the points
are x ∈ {1 − l, 3 − l, l + 3, l + 5} ∖ {2}: each satisfies x ≤ 1 or x ≥ 4 when l ≥ 1, so Q_5(x) < 0
(Lemma 24.4 (a)); at l = 0 the points are 1, 3, 5, and C(x)|_(h=0) = (5e − 2)x + 5e + 4 is 10e + 2, 20e − 2 and
30e − 6 there. For the vector type with l ≥ 2 the points 1 − l, 2 − l, l + 3, l + 4 differ from 3. *Real parts.* Let
k ∈ [3, 51] be an integer, and write P_l(k + iy) = A_k(y²) + iyB_k(y²) with A_k, B_k real polynomials. A non-real root
k + iy, y ≠ 0, makes y² a common root of A_k and B_k, so the resultant Res(A_k, B_k), a polynomial in h, vanishes.
Conversely, as P_l is real, a common root t of A_k and B_k gives P_l(k ± it^(1/2)) = 0: a conjugate pair with real
part k if t > 0, two real roots k ± |t|^(1/2), of sum 2k, if t < 0, and a double root at k if t = 0. So Res(A_k, B_k)
vanishes exactly when P_l has two roots, counted with multiplicity, of sum 2k. By Lemma 24.5, as h → 0⁺
the roots of P_l converge to 2, ι₊, ι₋ or have real parts tending to −∞. The limit sums are 2 + ι_± and
ι₊ + ι₋ = 5 + 1/13653 (Lemma 24.4 (b)); 2 + ι_± = 2k would make 2k − 2 ≥ 4 a real root of Q_5, which
Lemma 24.4 (a) excludes. So for small h > 0 no two roots have sum 2k and no root is double, and Res(A_k, B_k) does
not vanish identically. The same argument applies to C, whose finite limit root is (4 + 5e)/(2 − 5e), and p_(v) has real
roots only. ∎

**Lemma 24.23** (The 1-form; [Hin26a, Proposition 5.1] in dimension 4 + 1.) With the weights

    α_K := 1,     α_sf := −C_0 − 5/2,    (24.25)

w := ρ_sf^(α_sf+1)ρ_K^(α_K) and w′ := ρ_sf^(α_sf+1), c_C satisfies the conditions (1)–(6) of [Hin26a, Proposition 5.1]
on Tangherlini space g_(b₀), for some δ_r > 0 and with δ_sf = 1/100. In dimension 4 + 1, with r_c the radius of the
saddle (the r_0 of [Hin26a]) and r_♯ the inner radius (Section 24.6.1), these conditions are: (1) r c is past timelike on
{r ≥ r_♯}; (2) c = ½r_c⁻²(r_c dt − v(r − r_c) dr) on [r_c/2, 2r_c] and c = r⁻¹(dt − v dr) for r ≥ 3r_c; (3) the S of
(24.11) is positive definite on |r − r_c| ≤ (6/5)r_ce^(1/2)/v; (4) r²(−ℓ(dw/w) + S) is positive definite near the
corner ∂K⁺, on {ρ_sf ≤ 2δ_r, ρ_K ≤ 2δ_r}; (5) r²(−ℓ(dw′/w′) + S) is positive definite near the sink, on
{ρ_sf ≤ 2δ_r, |(r/t)/v − 1| ≤ 2δ_sf}; (6) −ℓ(−dr) is positive definite on [r_♯, r_c − r_ce^(1/2)/v] and −ℓ(dr) on
[r_c + r_ce^(1/2)/v, ∞), and on 𝗌𝖿 the two conditions of [Hin26a, (5.8)] hold: −r²ℓ(d(r/t)) is positive definite for
r/t ∈ [δ_r, v(1 − δ_sf)], and −r²ℓ(−d(r/t)) for r/t ∈ [v(1 + δ_sf), 10]. The conditions also hold on g_b for b near
b₀, with smaller δ_r and the same δ_sf, conditions (5)–(6) on 𝗌𝖿 not depending on b. The same holds with C_0 − 1 for
C_0 in (24.25), that is at α_sf = −C_0 − 3/2, for every C_0 ≥ 0: the conditions at 𝗌𝖿 are then
b_sf = −C_0 − 1/2 < b* and b_K = 1 > b_sf − b*.

*Proof.* (1)–(3) and (6) off 𝗌𝖿 are Proposition 24.10 (i)–(iii). (4)–(6) at 𝗌𝖿: the symbol T = r²(−ℓ(dw/w) + S)
depends only on ρ_K and the weights there; it is positive definite at ∂K⁺ iff b_K > b_sf − b* and at the sink iff
b_sf < b*, with b_K = α_K, b_sf = α_sf + 1 and b* = 0.99340731… (Proposition 24.10 (iv)). At (24.25),
b_sf = −C_0 − 3/2 and b_K = 1, and the characteristic polynomials at ∂K⁺ and at R_v have positive roots for every
C_0 ≥ 0; at C_0 = 100, T is positive definite on all of 𝗌𝖿 with ρ_K ≤ 10 (Proposition 24.13 (iv)). So (4) holds near
∂K⁺ by continuity, and (5) holds on |(r/t)/v − 1| ≤ 2δ_sf because T at the sink, b_K = 0, does not depend on ρ_K.
Off 𝗌𝖿, for ρ_sf ≤ 2δ_r, (4)–(5) hold by continuity, as Tangherlini space differs from its Minkowski model by ρ_sf C^∞
terms (Proposition 24.10 (a); [Hin26a, p. 39]). [Hin26a, (5.8)] holds outside an interval about v of half-width below
1/200, which gives the conditions (6) on 𝗌𝖿 with δ_sf = 1/100 (Proposition 24.10 (v)). For g_b: each condition is a
strict positivity of a continuous function of the metric on a compact set, or holds at 𝗌𝖿, where g_b and g_(b₀) have
the same 3sc model; so it persists for b near b₀. ∎

**Lemma 24.24** (The horizon threshold.) For b near b₀ and every h ∈ (0, 10⁻⁶], the threshold ϑ_ℋ of
Section 11.1 of the spectral family of □^C_b satisfies ½ + ϑ_ℋ < −C_0.

*Proof.* ϑ_ℋ is the maximum over the compact ∂ℛ_± of the top eigenvalue of β_0⁻¹p_(1,±)(0), self-adjoint for the fibre
inner product B of Lemma 24.20. By its definition p_(1,±)(0) = A_± − h⁻¹ℓ(±ρ_∞·), where A_± comes from 2δGδ* and is
free of h, and the h⁻¹-part is h⁻¹ρ_∞ times the damping symbol of L at the conormal covectors of the horizon. These are
future null, so Lemma 24.20 ([Hin26a, Lemma 3.5]) makes ℓ of them B-positive definite, so that −h⁻¹ℓ is
negative definite, the sign that damps.
So, by Weyl's inequality, ϑ_ℋ ≤ ϑ_0(b) − c(b)h⁻¹ with ϑ_0 and c > 0 continuous in b. At b₀,
ϑ_0 = 102401/640 and c = 102399/20480000, and ϑ_ℋ itself is −4995.83… at h = 10⁻⁶ (Proposition 24.14); the bound
ϑ_0 − ch⁻¹ is −4839.95… at h = 10⁻⁶. So ½ + ϑ_0(b) − c(b)h⁻¹ < −100 for b near b₀ and h ≤ 10⁻⁶, the margin at b₀ being
more than 4700. ∎

**Lemma 24.25** (The hypotheses of the spectral theory.) For b near b₀ and h ∈ (0, 10⁻⁶], the spectral family
of □^C_b satisfies (H1)–(H4) of Section 11.1 ((11.2)–(11.3)), and the gap condition (G) of
Chapter 13 for every α with α + 2 ∈ [−C_0, 2), with the gap I = (β_−, 2), β_− < −C_0.

*Proof.* (H1): the principal symbol of □^C_b is that of □_(g_b) ⊗ Id, as E^C has order 0 and 2δGδ* has the scalar
principal symbol g⁻¹(ζ, ζ); so σ₂(P̂(0)) = G_0 Id, σ₁(T) = τ₁ Id with τ₁ = −H_G t_*, and P₂ = g_00 Id. (H2):
Lemma 24.21, with S = S̄^C + ρS̃ and P^(0) := ρ⁻²P^C_b, whose principal part at ∂X is that of the Euclidean
Laplacian in b-form, the first-order terms of E^C (coefficients in ρC^∞) lying in Diff¹_b. (H3)–(H4) concern only G_0
and τ₁, that is g_b and t_*: apart from the threshold in (H3), which is Lemma 24.24, they are part of the dynamical
hypotheses (Dyn) on the metric alone, verified for g_b, b near b₀, in Chapter 22 (Chapter 23), and they hold for every
operator with principal part □_(g_b) ⊗ Id. (G): by Lemma 24.22 (a) and Lemma 13.3, the indicial roots
relevant to the weight α + 2 (Euclidean density) are the ι with Re ι = α + 2; none has real part in
[−100, 19/10] ∪ (19/10, 2), so (β_−, 2) with β_− := max{Re ι : Re ι < −100} < −100 ≤ −C_0 is a gap. The maximum
exists: some root ι₀ has Re ι₀ < −100, and the strip {Re ι₀ ≤ Re ι ≤ −100} contains only finitely many roots
(Lemma 24.22 (a)). ∎

### 24.6 Solvability on weighted 3b-spaces

This section proves [Hin26a, Theorem 5.2] in dimension 4 + 1 (Theorem 24.44) for the constraint propagation operator
on the Myers–Perry metrics, b near b₀, with the 1-form c_C, the constants (24.4) and the weights
(24.25). The theorem solves the forward problem and the initial value problem on weighted semiclassical
3b-Sobolev spaces, with the a priori estimate (24.30) and the adjoint estimate (24.31), for all h < h_0
with h_0 uniform in b. [Hin26a, Section 5.2] is a chain of semiclassical estimates, each an identity of symbols or a
pairing in which the dimension does not appear. Each is written out below in dimension 4 + 1, and every place where the
dimension enters is named: the compactification and the 3sc structure of the metric (Section 24.6.1), the volume
density (Lemma 24.28 (b)), the causal facts (Lemma 24.29), the fibre algebra (Lemma 24.30) and the 1-form
(Lemma 24.31). Three families of estimates that [Hin26a] uses without stating them, the propagation through the
interior of Ω in both directions, along 𝗌𝖿 between its critical sets and along K⁺ outward from the saddle, are stated
and proved in Proposition 24.39 and Proposition 24.40. We follow [Hin26a, pp. 12–17, 25–28, 37–39, 41–66].

#### 24.6.1 The setting

Throughout n = 4. The mass m₀, R₁ = m₀^(1/2), the parameter set ℬ and b₀ = (m₀, 0) are those of Section 21.5.1.
Let r_♯ := r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] be the inner radius of Chapter 21 (the inner radius of [Hin26a, Section 5]), r̂ := ¾R₁,
and r_c := 100R₁ the radius of the saddle point of c_C (the radius r_0 of [Hin26a]; the r_0 = 100 of
Proposition 24.10 at m = 1, rescaled). Let v := v_C = 1/2 and e := e_C = 1/102400. Every radius used below near the
inner boundary is placed relative to r_♯ and r̂: ε_X ≤ T_0r_♯/2 and ε_r := (r̂ − r_♯)/10 in Proposition 24.40,
r_1 := r_♯ + (2/10)(r̂ − r_♯) and r_2 := r_♯ + (2.75/10)(r̂ − r_♯) in Proposition 24.42, the transitions of the
cut-offs χ_(r,j) in [r_♯, r̂], and t_1 < ¼T_0r_♯ in Proposition 24.43. Nothing below is uniform in r_♯.

*Coordinates.* We work in the Kerr–Schild coordinates (t, x) of Section 21.5.1, with r := |x|. For b ∈ ℬ,
g := g^KS_b = η + H_b k_b ⊗ k_b is defined, smooth and Lorentzian with H_b > 0 on ℝ_t × {r ≥ ½r_♯}, smoothly in b,
and the condition of Lemma 21.16 (c) holds there (Lemma 21.19). The metric g_b of Section 21.5.1
is Φ_m*g with Φ_m(t, x) = (t − T_m(|x|), x), and Remark 24.45 transfers the results to it. The 1-form c := c_C of
Section 24.2 is given by its formula on {r ≥ ½r_♯}; below the smoothing, which lies in [¼r_c, ½r_c], it is a
positive multiple of dt + (v/2) dr. It is past timelike for g_(b₀) at every r > 0 (Proposition 24.10 (i), (b)), so for
g_b, b near b₀, on the compact set {½r_♯ ≤ r ≤ 3r_c}, by continuity; and for r ≥ 3r_c it is r⁻¹(dt − v dr), past
timelike for every g_b by Lemma 24.29 (a).

**Definition 24.26** (The compactification and the spaces; [Hin26a, Definitions 2.1, 2.2, 2.5, (2.2)–(2.3),
(2.10), (2.11), (5.19)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let M₀ := [ℝ̄^(1+4); k₊, k₋], where k_± are the poles of the radial
compactification at future and past timelike infinity. Let M^♭ := cl_(M₀)(M₀° ∖ cl({r < r_♯} ∪ {t < −½r})). Its faces
are the *Kerr face* K⁺ := M^♭ ∩ β⁻¹(k₊), the *side face* 𝗌𝖿 := ∂M^♭ ∩ (∂M₀ ∖ (K⁺)°), X_0 := cl{t = 0} and
Σ^♯ := cl{r = r_♯}; and the domain is Ω := cl{t ≥ 0} = {τ ≥ 0}, τ := t/r. (M^♭ is not the compactification M̃ of
Chapter 14.) M^♭ is covered by three charts:

- [r_♯, ∞)_r × [−½, ∞)_τ × 𝕊³;

- [0, r_♯⁻¹]_(ρ_sf) × [0, 2]_(ρ_K) × 𝕊³, with (t, r) = (ρ_sf⁻¹ρ_K⁻¹, ρ_sf⁻¹);

- [0, r_♯⁻¹]_(ρ_sf) × [−½, ∞)_τ × 𝕊³.

On {t > ½r} we use ρ_K = r/t and ρ_sf = 1/r. Further:

- 𝒯 and 𝒯* are the pullbacks of the scattering bundles of ℝ̄^(1+4) (the 3sc-bundles; dt, dx¹, …, dx⁴ is a frame of
𝒯*);

- 𝒱_3b(M^♭) is the C^∞(M^♭)-span of r∂_(z^μ), μ = 0, …, 4; with it come ³ᵇTM^♭, ³ᵇT*M^♭ (frame dz^μ/r) and
Diff^k_3b with weights; ∂_(z^μ) ∈ ρ_sf 𝒱_3b(M^♭) by [Hin26a, Section 2];

- the projection (t, x) ↦ x extends to a smooth map π : M^♭ → X̄_♯ := X̄ ∩ {r ≥ r_♯}, so π*C^∞(X̄_♯) ⊂ C^∞(M^♭).

The semiclassical 3b-pseudodifferential calculus Ψ_(3b,ħ)(M^♭) carries with it its principal symbols, the operator wave
front set WF′_(3b,ħ), the elliptic set Ell_(3b,ħ), elliptic parametrices, the sharp Gårding inequality and the Sobolev
spaces H^s_(3b,h); it exists in this dimension by Proposition 24.27. Write

    H^(s,(β_sf,β_K))_(3b,h) := ρ_sf^(β_sf) ρ_K^(β_K) H^s_(3b,h)(M^♭; 𝒯*)

([Hin26a, (5.19)]), normed with the density |dg| and the fibre inner product B of Lemma 24.30. On Ω there are three
kinds of space: H^(s,(·))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(•,−), restrictions to Ω° of elements with support in {t ≥ 0}, so supported at X_0
and extendible at Σ^♯; (·)^(−,•), extendible at X_0 and supported at Σ^♯; and H̄, extendible at both ([Hin26a,
Section 2.3]). In all of these constructions the dimension enters only as the number of coordinates.

**Proposition 24.27** (The calculus in every dimension.) The semiclassical 3b-calculus of [Hin26a,
Section 2.3] is constructed on ℝ_t × ℝ^(N−1)_x for every N ([Hin23d, pp. 3, 7, 10–12, and Proposition 5.10, p. 109],
N the spacetime dimension), as bounded geometry pseudodifferential operators in the sense of [Shu92] ([Hin23d, p. 12]),
and its bounded geometry construction is that of [Hin26d] for a smooth manifold of any dimension ([Hin26d, Definitions
1.3 and 1.9 and Section 3], with the 3b-algebra among its examples in every dimension, [Hin26d, p. 14, example (10)]).
At N = 5 it is the calculus of the compactification M^♭ of Definition 24.26, with fibres 𝕊³.

*Proof.* These are the cited results, stated there for every dimension. ∎

**Lemma 24.28** (The metric and the 1-form as 3sc-objects; [Hin26a, Lemmas 2.3–2.4, (2.12)–(2.14), Lemma 5.3]
in dimension 4 + 1.) For b ∈ ℬ:

(a) g ∈ C^∞(M^♭; S²𝒯*) is a stationary nondegenerate Lorentzian 3sc-metric, g⁻¹ ∈ C^∞(M^♭; S²𝒯), and g − η,
g⁻¹ − η⁻¹ lie in ρ_sf²C^∞, smoothly in b;

(b) |dg| = |dt dx| = r³|dt dr d𝑔̸| = r⁴|dτ dr d𝑔̸|, d𝑔̸ the round density of 𝕊³;

(c) the Christoffel symbols of g in (t, x) lie in ρ_sf C^∞(M^♭); so ∇ ∈ ρ_sf Diff¹_3b(M^♭; 𝒯^(p,q), 𝒯* ⊗ 𝒯^(p,q)),
□_g ∈ ρ_sf² Diff²_3b and δ*_g, δ_g ∈ ρ_sf Diff¹_3b;

(d) c ∈ ρ_sf C^∞(M^♭; 𝒯*) is stationary, h²□_g ∈ h²ρ_sf²Diff²_3b(M^♭; 𝒯*) and L_h := L_(g,c,e,h) ∈
hρ_sf²Diff¹_3b(M^♭; 𝒯*); the semiclassical 3b-principal symbol of P_h := h²□^C_b = h²□_g − iL_h is p = G − iℓ, with
G(ζ) = g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) and ℓ := ℓ_(g,c,e) of (24.10).

*Proof.* (a) In (t, x) the components of g do not depend on t, are smooth on {r ≥ ½r_♯}, and near infinity lie in
C^∞(X̄) with g − η ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞(X̄): this is Proposition 21.21 and its proof, which establishes the expansion for g^KS_b
first. The same holds for the inverse, η⁻¹ − H_b k_b♯ ⊗ k_b♯ (Lemma 21.16 (d)). Through π these components are
smooth functions on M^♭, and |x|⁻² = ρ_sf². In the frame dz^μ this gives g ∈ C^∞(M^♭; S²𝒯*), and likewise for g⁻¹.
Since k_b is η-null (Lemma 21.16 (a)), det(η + H_b k_b ⊗ k_b) = det η (1 + H_b η⁻¹(k_b, k_b)) = −1 identically,
so g is nondegenerate on all of M^♭. It is Lorentzian on M^♭: at finite points it is the metric itself, and at 𝗌𝖿 its
components are those of η. Smoothness in b is that of Section 21.5.1.

(b) det g = −1 in (t, x) gives |dg| = |dt dx|. Polar coordinates on ℝ⁴ give |dx| = r³|dr d𝑔̸|, and dt = r dτ + τ dr
gives |dt dr| = r|dτ dr|.

(c) Γ^κ_(μν) = ½g^(κλ)(∂_μg_(νλ) + ∂_νg_(μλ) − ∂_λg_(μν)), with g^(κλ) ∈ C^∞(M^♭) and ∂_μg_(νλ) ∈ ρ_sf C^∞(M^♭)
because ∂_(z^μ) ∈ ρ_sf 𝒱_3b. The rest is [Hin26a, (2.13)–(2.14)], with the same proof. (On Tangherlini space,
Γ ∈ mρ³C^∞ by Proposition 24.13 (i).)

(d) c is stationary and smooth on {r ≥ ½r_♯}, and equals r⁻¹(dt − v dr) for r ≥ 3r_c (Proposition 24.10 (b)). Its
components (r⁻¹, −vr⁻¹x̂) lie in |x|⁻¹C^∞(X̄), so c ∈ ρ_sf C^∞(M^♭; 𝒯*). By Section 24.2, the trace weight 2/3 gives
hG_gE^C the form of [Hin26a], so L_h = 4ih δ_g(c ⊗_s ·) + 2ihe dι_(c♯) is [Hin26a, (3.2)]. Now δ_g and d lie in
ρ_sf Diff¹_3b by (c), and multiplication by c or ι_(c♯) lies in ρ_sf C^∞; so L_h ∈ hρ_sf²Diff¹_3b. The principal
symbols are [Hin26a, Lemma 3.2], a pointwise identity free of the dimension (Proposition 24.8 (i)). ∎

**Lemma 24.29** (The causal facts; [Hin26a, p. 15] and the uses in [Hin26a, Propositions 5.6, 5.16] in
dimension 4 + 1.) Let T_0 := ½ and r̂ = ¾R₁. There is a neighbourhood U ⊂ ℬ of b₀ such that for b ∈ U:

(a) for every β ∈ (−1, 1], d(t − βr) is past timelike on {r ≥ ½r_♯}, with
g⁻¹(dt − β dr, dt − β dr) ≤ −(1 − β²); in particular dt and d(t ± κr), κ ∈ (0, 1), are past timelike, X_0 is
spacelike, and future timelike vectors point into Ω at X_0;

(b) r²g⁻¹(dτ, dτ) ≤ −¾ on τ⁻¹([0, T_0]); so dτ is past timelike for g_3b := ρ_sf²g there, uniformly up to 𝗌𝖿;

(c) on {½r_♯ ≤ r ≤ r̂}, dr is future timelike, with g⁻¹(dr, dr) ≤ −½; so Σ^♯ is spacelike, future timelike vectors
point out of Ω there, and −dr is past timelike;

(d) dρ_K/ρ_K² = −dt with ρ_K = t⁻¹ near (K⁺)°, and dρ_sf/ρ_sf² = −dr.

*Proof.* (a) The time orientation is the one in which dt is past timelike ([Hin26a, p. 14]). By Lemma 21.16 (e),
g⁻¹(dt − β dr, dt − β dr) = −(1 − β²) − H_b(1 + βr_A/|x|)² < 0 for β ∈ (−1, 1], wherever the condition of
Lemma 21.16 (c) holds, which is all of {r ≥ ½r_♯} (Lemma 21.19). The family s ↦ d(t − sβr), s ∈ [0, 1],
is timelike throughout and starts at dt, so it stays in the past cone. A future timelike V has dt(V) > 0, since dt is
past timelike.

(b) dτ = r⁻¹(dt − τ dr), so r²g⁻¹(dτ, dτ) is the quantity of (a) at β = τ ∈ [0, ½], at most −(1 − ¼). As
g_3b⁻¹ = r²g⁻¹, this is the claim; on Tangherlini space it is Proposition 24.13 (ii).

(c) At b₀, g⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − m₀r⁻² ≤ 1 − 16/9 on [½r_♯, r̂], its value at r̂, as smaller r make it more negative, and
g⁻¹(dr, dt) = m₀r⁻² > 0 (Proposition 24.13 (iii)). The second says that the timelike covectors dr and dt lie in opposite
cones, so dr is future timelike. Both strict inequalities hold on a compact set, and g⁻¹ is continuous in b there, so
they persist on a neighbourhood U of b₀. A future timelike V has dr(V) < 0, so V points out of {r ≥ r_♯}.

(d) is direct. ∎

**Lemma 24.30** (The fibre algebra and the subprincipal symbol; [Hin26a, Lemmas 3.3–3.9, Corollary 3.6] in
dimension 4 + 1.) At every point of M^♭, [Hin26a, Lemmas 3.3–3.8 and Corollary 3.6] hold for (g, c, e), with
B := g⁻¹ − (1 + e)G(c)⁻¹c♯ ⊗ c♯. The skew-adjoint part S := (2ih)⁻¹(L_h − L_h*), adjoint for |dg| and B, is the bundle
map of (24.11), which is [Hin26a, Lemma 3.9] in dimension 4 + 1. There is C > 0, uniform for b ∈ U, such that
C(ρ_sf⁻²ℓ(ζ))² + ρ_sf⁻²G(ζ) is B-positive definite for 0 ≠ ζ ∈ ³ᵇT*_Ω M^♭.

*Proof.* [Hin26a, Lemmas 3.3–3.8] are Lemma 24.20; [Hin26a, Corollary 3.6] follows from [Hin26a, Lemma 3.5] on
one fibre, as there. As (2ih)⁻¹(L_h − L_h*) = A + A* with
A = (2ih)⁻¹L_h, the formula for S is Proposition 24.8 (ii), proved there on a Lorentzian manifold of any dimension
with the adjoint taken for |dg| and B.
For the uniform C, note that ρ_sf⁻²G and ρ_sf⁻²ℓ are smooth homogeneous functions on ³ᵇT*M^♭ (Lemma 24.28 (a),
(d)), and B is continuous on the compact Ω, K⁺ and 𝗌𝖿 included. [Hin26a, Corollary 3.6] at each point and compactness
of the unit sphere bundle over Ω give one C ([Hin26a, p. 47]), and continuity in b gives it for b ∈ U, shrinking U. ∎

**Lemma 24.31** (The 1-form; [Hin26a, Proposition 5.1] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let (α_sf, α_K) = (−C_0 − 5/2, 1)
with C_0 ∈ [0, 100], the weights (24.25). Put w := ρ_sf^(α_sf+1)ρ_K^(α_K) and w′ := ρ_sf^(α_sf+1). Shrinking U,
there are δ_r ∈ (0, (4r_c)⁻¹) and δ_sf = 1/100 such that for b ∈ U, c satisfies the conditions (1)–(6) of
Lemma 24.23 ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.1] with r_c for r_0 and r_♯ for its inner radius). The positivity statements
(3)–(6) hold with lower bounds uniform in b ∈ U.

*Proof.* Lemma 24.23. Each positivity is a strict inequality for a continuous function of (b, point) on a compact
set, or holds at 𝗌𝖿, where every g, b ∈ U, has the 3sc model η (Lemma 24.28 (a)); so the lower bounds are uniform
after shrinking U and δ_r, keeping δ_sf. ∎

*Notation* ([Hin26a, (5.19)]). P_h = □_h − iL_h with □_h := h²□_g; ℓ, B and S are as above. ⟨·, ·⟩ is the
L²(M^♭, |dg|; 𝒯*)-pairing with B. Schwartz kernels of pseudodifferential operators are supported in Ω′ × Ω′,
Ω′ := Ω ∖ (X_0 ∪ Σ^♯). Σ ⊂ ³ᵇT*M^♭ is the closure of G⁻¹(0), the characteristic set of h²ρ_sf⁻²□_g;
∂Σ = ∂Σ₊ ⊔ ∂Σ₋ are its components at fibre infinity, the future and past light cones; o is the zero section. |·| is a
fixed fibre norm on ³ᵇT*M^♭. A *square root* below is always of a B-self-adjoint endomorphism field that is positive
semidefinite on the support in question, and it is smooth wherever the argument is a smooth function times a positive
definite field, or is positive definite; [Hin26a] arranges this through the cut-off conditions (∓χχ′)^(1/2) ∈ C^∞.

#### 24.6.2 Elliptic estimates and the characteristic set at fibre infinity

**Lemma 24.32** ([Hin26a, Lemma 5.4].) The semiclassical 3b-characteristic set of ρ_sf⁻²P_h is ∂Σ ∪ o.

*Proof.* ρ_sf⁻²G and ρ_sf⁻²ℓ are homogeneous of degrees 2 and 1 on the fibres (Lemma 24.28), so the symbol vanishes
on o. At finite ζ ≠ 0, p(ζ) is invertible by Lemma 24.30 ([Hin26a, Lemma 3.7]). At fibre infinity G is principal
and ℓ subprincipal, so the characteristic set there is ∂Σ. ∎

*Cut-offs.* With T := T_0 of Lemma 24.29 and r̂ for the radius r₊ of [Hin26a], let χ_(τ,j)(τ) and χ_(r,j)(r),
j = 0, 1, 2, be those of [Hin26a, (5.20)]: χ_(τ,j) = 0 for τ ≤ ((j + ¼)/10)T and χ_(τ,j) = 1 for τ ≥ ((j + ¾)/10)T;
χ_(r,j) = 0 for r ≤ r_♯ + ((j + ¼)/10)(r̂ − r_♯) and χ_(r,j) = 1 for r ≥ r_♯ + ((j + ¾)/10)(r̂ − r_♯); χ′_(•,j) ≥ 0 and
(χ_(•,j)χ′_(•,j))^(1/2) ∈ C^∞. So χ_(•,j) = 1 near supp χ_(•,j+1), supp dχ_(τ,j) ⊂ τ⁻¹([0, T_0)), and
supp dχ_(r,j) ⊂ r⁻¹([r_♯, r̂)).

**Proposition 24.33** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.5].) Let B_0, B_1 ∈ Ψ⁰_(3b,ħ)(M^♭) with
WF′_(3b,ħ)(B_j) ∩ (o ∪ ∂Σ) = ∅ and WF′_(3b,ħ)(B_0) ⊂ Ell_(3b,ħ)(B_1). Then for all s, N there is C with

    ‖B_0χ_(τ,2)χ_(r,2)ω‖_(H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h))
      ≤ C(‖B_1χ_(τ,1)χ_(r,1)P_hω‖_(H^(s−2,(α_sf+2,α_K))_(3b,h)) + h^N‖χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)ω‖_(H^(−N,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h))),

and the same for P_h*.

*Proof.* Put ω′ := χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)ω. Then χ_(τ,1)χ_(r,1)P_hω′ = χ_(τ,1)χ_(r,1)P_hω and
χ_(τ,2)χ_(r,2)ω = χ_(τ,2)χ_(r,2)ω′. By Lemma 24.32, ρ_sf⁻²P_h is elliptic on WF′(B_1). A microlocal parametrix in
the calculus of Definition 24.26 gives the estimate; the weights only add terms of lower order, since
w⁻¹[P_h, w] ∈ hρ_sf²Diff¹_3b for w = ρ_sf^β ρ_K^(β′). ∎

**Proposition 24.34** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.6].) Let B_0, B_1 ∈ Ψ⁰_(3b,ħ)(M^♭) be elliptic at ∂Σ over
supp(χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)), with WF′_(3b,ħ)(B_0) ∩ o = ∅ and WF′_(3b,ħ)(B_0) ⊂ Ell_(3b,ħ)(B_1). Then for all s, N there are
h_0 > 0 and C such that for h ∈ (0, h_0)

    ‖B_0χ_(τ,2)χ_(r,2)ω‖_(H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h)) ≤ C(‖B_1χ_(τ,1)χ_(r,1)P_hω‖_(H^(s−1,(α_sf+2,α_K))_(3b,h))
        + h^(1/2)‖B_1χ_(τ,0)(1 − χ_(τ,2))χ_(r,0)ω‖_(H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h))
        + h^N‖χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)ω‖_(H^(−N,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h))),    (24.26)

    ‖B_0χ_(τ,2)χ_(r,2)ω‖_(H^(−s+1,(−α_sf−2,−α_K))_(3b,h)) ≤ C(‖B_1χ_(τ,1)χ_(r,1)P_h*ω‖_(H^(−s,(−α_sf,−α_K))_(3b,h))
        + h^(1/2)‖B_1χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)(1 − χ_(r,2))ω‖_(H^(−s+1,(−α_sf−2,−α_K))_(3b,h))
        + h^N‖χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)ω‖_(H^(−N,(−α_sf−2,−α_K))_(3b,h))),    (24.27)

each in the strong sense: if the right side is finite, so is the left side, and the estimate holds. These are
[Hin26a, (5.21) and (5.22)]; the first is a forward, the second a backward propagation estimate.

*Proof.* We prove [Hin26a, (5.21)] for ω ∈ H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h); the strong sense follows by the standard
regularisation ([Hin26a, p. 45]). By Proposition 24.33 it suffices to work in an h-independent neighbourhood of ∂Σ_±;
replace ω by χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)ω. Let ρ̂ define fibre infinity, Ĝ := ρ̂²ρ_sf⁻²G, χ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ) equal to 1 near 0, and χ_±
localise near ∂Σ_±. Take the commutant [Hin26a, (5.24)],

    a := ρ_sf^(−α_sf−1) ρ_K^(−α_K) ρ̂^(−s+½) χ_± χ(𝔛ρ̂) χ(𝔛Ĝ) χ_(τ,1)χ_(r,1),

and a quantisation A = A* with WF′(A) = supp a. Then [Hin26a, (5.25)] holds:

    ∓Im⟨P_hω, A²ω⟩ = ⟨(±(Re L_h − Im □_h)A² ∓ (i/2)[P_h, A²])ω, ω⟩.

*The main term.* On supp a, for 𝔛 large, the covectors are close to future (for +), resp. past (for −) lightlike
covectors. c is past timelike (Lemma 24.31 (1)), so Lemma 24.30 ([Hin26a, Lemma 3.5]) makes ±ρ_sf⁻²ℓ positive
definite there, with a lower bound fixed by compactness. Im □_h ∈ h Diff¹_(3b,ħ) is semiclassically subprincipal, □_h
having real scalar principal symbol. This gives [Hin26a, (5.26)]: ±(Re L_h − Im □_h)A² = A(B̃_0*B̃_0 + c_0Λ*Λ)A + hE.

*The commutator and the cut-offs.* ∓(i/2)[P_h, A²] has principal symbol ∓aH_Ga at order h ([Hin26a, (5.27)]). In
[Hin26a, (5.29)] it is split as follows. Differentiation of χ_± and of χ(𝔛Ĝ) lands off the characteristic set, so these
terms are hAQP_h. Differentiation of χ(𝔛ρ̂) gives order −∞. Differentiation of the weights gives bounded multiples of
a², the term hAB̃_2A. Next, ∓χ_(τ,1)H_Gχ_(τ,1) = ∓χ_(τ,1)χ′_(τ,1)H_Gτ = −e_T², because H_Gτ = 2g⁻¹(ζ, dτ) is positive
at future and negative at past lightlike ζ over supp dχ_(τ,1) ⊂ τ⁻¹([0, T_0)), where dτ is past timelike
(Lemma 24.29 (b)). Finally ∓χ_(r,1)H_Gχ_(r,1) = +e_R², because H_Gr = 2g⁻¹(ζ, dr) is negative at future and
positive at past lightlike ζ over supp dχ_(r,1) ⊂ r⁻¹([r_♯, r̂)), where dr is future timelike (Lemma 24.29 (c)).

*Conclusion.* Cauchy–Schwarz on the left of [Hin26a, (5.25)] gives [Hin26a, (5.30)]. Drop ‖E_Rω‖², which has the sign
of the main term, and absorb h⟨B̃_2Aω, Aω⟩ ≤ Ch‖B̃_0Aω‖² + h^N‖ω‖². Iterate in h^(1/2) on the error term
h^(1/2)‖B̃′_0ω‖, whose wave front set lies near supp a. This proves [Hin26a, (5.21)]; the a priori term is h^(1/2)‖E_Tω‖,
supported over supp dχ_(τ,1).

For [Hin26a, (5.22)], P_h* = □_h* + iL_h* with □_h* − □_h ∈ hDiff¹ and L_h* − L_h ∈ hDiff⁰, and [Hin26a, (5.28)] has
main term ∓ρ_sf⁻²ℓ, now negative definite. The weights in a become (−α_sf − 2, −α_K). [Hin26a, (5.29)] holds for P_h*,
as only □_h*, with principal symbol G, entered it. Now −e_T² has the sign of the main term and e_R² needs the a priori
term. ∎

#### 24.6.3 The saddle point at r = r_c

By Lemma 24.30 there is C with C(ρ_sf⁻²ℓ)² + ρ_sf⁻²G > 0 on ³ᵇT*_Ω M^♭ ∖ o. As in [Hin26a, (5.31)–(5.32)], define

    𝓛_h := −i(1 + iCL_h*ρ_sf⁻²)P_h = −L_h + J − iQ ∈ ρ_sf²Diff³_(3b,ħ),    (24.28)

with J = h²J_0 + h³J_1, J_0 = Im □_g, J_1 = Ch⁻³Re(L_h*ρ_sf⁻²□_h), Q = h²Q_0 + h³Q_1,
Q_0 = h⁻²Re(□_h + CL_h*ρ_sf⁻²L_h) and Q_1 = −Ch⁻³Im(L_h*ρ_sf⁻²□_h). The memberships J_0 ∈ ρ²Diff¹_3b,
J_1 ∈ ρ²Diff³_3b, Q_0 ∈ ρ²Diff²_3b and Q_1 ∈ ρ²Diff²_3b follow from Lemma 24.28 (d) and the self-adjointness of ℓ.
1 + iCL_h*ρ_sf⁻² is semiclassically elliptic everywhere, its principal symbol 1 + iCρ⁻²ℓ being invertible (ℓ
self-adjoint). The symbol j of J is homogeneous of degree 3 and vanishes cubically at o. Near (K⁺)°, ρ_K := t⁻¹, and the
weight at 𝗌𝖿 and the differential order are dropped.

**Proposition 24.35** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.8].) Near K⁺ let ρ_K := t⁻¹; the weight at 𝗌𝖿 and the
differential order play no role here and are dropped. Put ε_c := r_ce^(1/2)/v. There is δ > 0 such that, with
K := {|r − r_c| ≤ (3/2)ε_c, ρ_K ≤ 4δ}, the following holds for every χ ∈ C^∞(M^♭) equal to 1 on K and supported in a
small neighbourhood of K, all B_0, B_1, E ∈ Ψ_(3b,ħ)(M^♭) with compact operator wave front sets and Schwartz kernels
supported in K × K, and all sufficiently small h > 0.

(1) If WF′(B_0) ⊂ {|r − r_c| ≤ (55/50)ε_c, ρ_K ≤ 2δ, |ζ| < 1}, Ell(E) ⊃ {|r − r_c| ≤ (60/50)ε_c, δ ≤ ρ_K ≤ 3δ, |ζ| < 1}
and Ell(B_1) ⊃ {|r − r_c| ≤ (60/50)ε_c, ρ_K ≤ 3δ, |ζ| < 2}, then for every N there is C with

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_hω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)L²) + ‖Eω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)L²) + h^N‖χω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)H^(−N)_(3b,h))).

(2) If B_0, B_1 are as in (1) and Ell(E) ⊃ {|r − r_c| ∈ [(55/50)ε_c, (60/50)ε_c], ρ_K ≤ 2δ, |ζ| < 1}, then

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_h*ω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) + ‖Eω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) + h^N‖χω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)H^(−N)_(3b,h))).

These are [Hin26a, (5.33) and (5.34)] with r_c for r_0; (1) propagates control forward into the saddle, (2) backward
out of it.

*Proof.* (1) By Proposition 24.33 and the ellipticity of 1 + iCL_h*ρ_sf⁻² it suffices to prove [Hin26a, (5.33)] with 𝓛_h
for P_h, near o. With χ_0, χ_K and ψ as in [Hin26a, (5.35)] (r_c for r_0), take the commutant [Hin26a, (5.36)],
a = ρ_K^(−α_K)ψ(r)χ_K(𝔛ρ_K)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|), and A = A*. The pairing is [Hin26a, (5.37)–(5.38)]:

    h⁻¹Im⟨𝓛_hω, A²ω⟩ = ⟨𝒞ω, ω⟩,     𝒞 = ((i/(2h))[−L_h + J, A²] − h⁻¹(Im L_h)A²) − h⁻¹AQA − (1/(2h))[A, [A, Q]].

The bracket has principal symbol aH_(−ℓ+j)a − Sa². As ℓ is linear in the fibre, H_(−ℓ)f = −ℓ(df) for a function f on
M^♭. This gives [Hin26a, (5.39)], aH_(−ℓ+j)a − Sa² = −c_0a² − b_0² − b_R² + e² + f, with b_0, b_R, e and f those of
[Hin26a, (5.40)–(5.43)]. Their square roots exist for the following reasons.

- b_0: S is positive definite on {|r − r_c| ≤ (6/5)r_c e^(1/2)/v} (Lemma 24.31 (3)), so S ≥ 2c_0 there;
ℓ(dρ_K/ρ_K²) = −ℓ(dt) and H_jρ_K⁻¹ are bounded on supp χ_0(𝔛|ζ|) and carry the factor ρ_K ≲ 𝔛⁻¹.

- b_R: on supp ψ′ ∩ {±(r − r_c) > 0}, −ℓ(±dr) ≥ 2c₁ (Lemma 24.31 (6)), and |H_jr| = O(|ζ|²) < c₁ on
supp χ_0(𝔛|ζ|) for 𝔛 large.

- e: dρ_K/ρ_K² = −dt is future timelike (Lemma 24.29 (d)), so ℓ(−dt) is positive definite (Lemma 24.30), and
−χ_Kχ′_K ≥ 0; e is supported away from ρ_K = 0.

- f is supported off o, where Proposition 24.33 applies.

For Q: Q_0 has the positive definite principal symbol G + Cρ_sf⁻²ℓ² (Lemma 24.30), so Q_0 = Θ*Θ + R with
R ∈ Ψ^(−∞)_3b, which is [Hin26a, (5.44)]; the symbol of h⁻¹h³Q_1 vanishes quadratically at o, so it is O(𝔛⁻²) on
supp a, which gives [Hin26a, (5.45)] by Gårding; and the double commutator lies in hΨ and gives [Hin26a, (5.46)].
Collecting, fix 𝔛 large and then h small to absorb ‖Aω‖². Then [Hin26a, (5.47)], with WF′(F) ⊂ Ell(𝓛_h), gives
[Hin26a, (5.48)], and finitely many iterations in h^(1/2) give [Hin26a, (5.33)], with δ := 𝔛⁻¹.

(2) Replace P_h* by 𝓛_h* = iP_h*(1 − iCρ_sf⁻²L_h) = −L_h* + J + iQ and take
a = ρ_K^(α_K)ψχ_K(𝔛ρ_K)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|). The main symbol is aH_(−ℓ+j)a + Sa² = c_0a² + b_0² + b_K² − e² + f with the b_0, b_K,
e, f of [Hin26a]. The same three facts give the square roots, now with b_K from the sign of −ℓ(dt) and e from
Lemma 24.31 (6) on supp ψ′. Q enters with a lower bound by [Hin26a, (5.44)–(5.45)], and the iteration is the same. ∎

#### 24.6.4 The saddle point at the corner ∂K⁺

From here on, ρ_K = r/t and ρ_sf = 1/r.

**Proposition 24.36** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.9].) Let (α_sf, α_K) and δ_r be those of Lemma 24.31.
There is δ ∈ (0, δ_r] such that, with K := {ρ_K ≤ 3δ_r, ρ_sf ≤ 3δ}, the following holds for χ, B_0, B_1 and E as in
Proposition 24.35 with this K, and all sufficiently small h > 0.

(1) If WF′(B_0) ⊂ {ρ_K ≤ (3/2)δ_r, ρ_sf ≤ (3/2)δ, |ζ| < 1}, Ell(E) ⊃ {ρ_K ≤ 2δ_r, (5/4)δ ≤ ρ_sf ≤ 2δ, |ζ| < 1} and
Ell(B_1) ⊃ {ρ_K ≤ 2δ_r, ρ_sf ≤ 2δ, |ζ| < 2}, then for every N there is C with

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)ρ_K^(α_K)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_hω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf+2)ρ_K^(α_K)L²) + ‖Eω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)ρ_K^(α_K)L²)
        + h^N‖χω‖_(H^(−N,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h))).

(2) If B_0, B_1 are as in (1) and Ell(E) ⊃ {(5/4)δ_r ≤ ρ_K ≤ 2δ_r, ρ_sf ≤ 2δ, |ζ| < 1}, then

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_h*ω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf)ρ_K^(−α_K)L²)
        + ‖Eω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) + h^N‖χω‖_(H^(−N,(−α_sf−2,−α_K))_(3b,h))).

These are [Hin26a, (5.51) and (5.52)].

*Proof.* (1) Replace P_h by 𝓛_h. With χ_sf, χ_K and χ_0 as in [Hin26a], take the commutant [Hin26a, (5.53)],
a = w⁻¹χ_sf(𝔛ρ_sf)χ_K(ρ_K)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|). Then 𝒞 ∈ ρ_sf^(−2α_sf)ρ_K^(−2α_K)Ψ_3b, and [Hin26a, (5.54)] holds:
aH_(−ℓ+j)a − Sa² = −c_0ρ_sf²a² − b_0² − b_sf² + e² + f, with the b_0, b_sf, e and f of [Hin26a]. Their square roots
exist for the following reasons.

- b_0: ρ_sf⁻²(−ℓ(dw/w) + S) is positive definite on {ρ_sf ≤ 2δ_r, ρ_K ≤ 2δ_r} (Lemma 24.31 (4)), with a fixed lower
bound; ρ_sf⁻²w⁻¹H_jw vanishes at o, since ρ_sf⁻²j vanishes cubically there.

- b_sf: on supp χ′_K, ρ_K ∈ [(5/4)δ_r, (3/2)δ_r), and Lemma 24.31 (6) on 𝗌𝖿 ∩ {r/t ∈ [δ_r, v(1 − δ_sf)]} gives
ρ_sf⁻²(−ℓ(dρ_K)) > 0 near 𝗌𝖿 for 𝔛 large.

- e: dρ_sf/ρ_sf² = −dr, and −ℓ(dr) is positive definite for r ≥ r_c + r_c e^(1/2)/v (Lemma 24.31 (6)); H_jr
vanishes at o.

e is supported away from 𝗌𝖿 and gives the a priori term. Estimating the left side by
c_0⁻¹h⁻²‖ρ_sf⁻¹A𝓛_hω‖² + ¼c_0‖ρ_sfAω‖² produces the weights of [Hin26a, (5.51)]. The rest is the proof of
Proposition 24.35, with δ := 𝔛⁻¹.

(2) Take a = wχ_sf(𝔛ρ_sf)χ_K(ρ_K)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|) and the pairing with 𝓛_h*. Then
aH_(−ℓ+j)a + Sa² = c_0ρ_sf²a² + b_0² + b_K² − e² + f, with the symbols of [Hin26a]. These are those of (1) with
−α_sf − 2 for α_sf; b_0 comes from Lemma 24.31 (4), and the a priori term from supp χ′_K. ∎

#### 24.6.5 The sink in 𝗌𝖿°

**Proposition 24.37** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.11].) Let α_sf, δ_r and δ_sf be those of Lemma 24.31;
the weight at K⁺ and the differential order are dropped, and s := r/t. There is δ ∈ (0, δ_r] such that, with
K := {|s/v − 1| ≤ 3δ_sf, ρ_sf ≤ 3δ}, the following holds for χ, B_0, B_1 and E as in Proposition 24.35 with this K,
and all sufficiently small h > 0.

(1) If WF′(B_0) ⊂ {|s/v − 1| ≤ (3/2)δ_sf, ρ_sf ≤ (3/2)δ, |ζ| < 1}, Ell(B_1) ⊃ {|s/v − 1| ≤ 2δ_sf, ρ_sf ≤ 2δ, |ζ| < 2} and
Ell(E) ⊃ {|s/v − 1| ≤ 2δ_sf, ρ_sf ≤ 2δ, |ζ| < 1} ∖ {|s/v − 1| ≤ (5/4)δ_sf, ρ_sf ≤ (5/4)δ}, then for
every N there is C with

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_hω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf+2)L²) + ‖Eω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)L²)
        + h^N‖χω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)H^(−N)_(3b,h))).

(2) If B_0, B_1 are as in (1), then

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_h*ω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf)L²) + h^N‖χω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)H^(−N)_(3b,h))).

These are [Hin26a, (5.55) and (5.56)], with the weight w′ = ρ_sf^(α_sf+1) in the commutant.

*Proof.* (1) The commutant is a = (w′)⁻¹χ_sf(𝔛ρ_sf)χ_R((r/t)/v − 1)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|), with χ_R supported in
(−2δ_sf, 2δ_sf) and equal to 1 on [−(5/4)δ_sf, (5/4)δ_sf]. Then [Hin26a, (5.57)] holds:
aH_(−ℓ+j)a − Sa² = −c_0ρ_sf²a² − b_0² + e₁² + e₂² + f. Their square roots exist for the following reasons.

- b_0: Lemma 24.31 (5), for 𝔛 large.

- e₁: dρ_sf/ρ_sf² = −dr, H_j(ρ_sf⁻¹) = H_jr, and Lemma 24.31 (6) for large r.

- e₂: on supp dχ_R, |(r/t)/v − 1| ∈ [(5/4)δ_sf, 2δ_sf], where the sign of −r²ℓ(d(r/t)) is that of χ′_R
(Lemma 24.31 (6) on the two sides of the sink).

e₁ and e₂ are supported away from {|(r/t)/v − 1| ≤ δ_sf, ρ_sf ≤ 𝔛⁻¹} and give ‖Eω‖. The rest is the proof of
Proposition 24.35.

(2) Take a = w′χ_sf(𝔛ρ_sf)χ_R((r/t)/v − 1)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|). Then aH_(−ℓ+j)a + Sa² = c_0ρ_sf²a² + b_0² + b₁² + b₂² + f. Every
term except f, which is elliptic, has the sign of the main term, by the same three facts. So [Hin26a, (5.56)] carries no
a priori term. ∎

#### 24.6.6 Propagation between the critical sets

**Proposition 24.38** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.12].) Near K⁺ let ρ_K := t⁻¹; the weight at 𝗌𝖿 and the
differential order are dropped. Let r_3 := r_c − (52/50)r_c e^(1/2)/v and r_4 := r_c − (51/50)r_c e^(1/2)/v, and fix
0 < t_1 < t_2 < t_3 and r_♯ < r_1 < r_2 < r_3. Let B_0, B_1, E ∈ Ψ_(3b,ħ)(M^♭) have compact operator wave front sets
and Schwartz kernels supported in K × K, K a compact subset of {r_♯ < r < r_c, ρ_K < ∞}, and let χ ∈ C^∞(M^♭) equal 1
on K.

(1) If WF′(B_0) ⊂ {ρ_K ≤ t_2⁻¹, r_1 < r < r_4, |ζ| < 1}, Ell(B_1) ⊃ {ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r_1 ≤ r ≤ r_4, |ζ| < 2} and
Ell(E) ⊃ {t_3⁻¹ ≤ ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r_1 ≤ r ≤ r_4, |ζ| < 1} ∪ {ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r_3 ≤ r ≤ r_4, |ζ| < 1}, then for every N
there is C with, for all sufficiently small h > 0,

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_hω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)L²) + ‖Eω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)L²) + h^N‖χω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)H^(−N)_(3b,h))).

(2) If B_0, B_1 are as in (1) and Ell(E) ⊃ {ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r_1 ≤ r ≤ r_2, |ζ| < 1}, then

    ‖B_0ω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_h*ω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) + ‖Eω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)L²) + h^N‖χω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)H^(−N)_(3b,h))).

These are [Hin26a, (5.58) and (5.59)]: (1) propagates control from the saddle towards the inner boundary, (2) from
the inner boundary towards the saddle.

*Proof.* (1) The commutant is a = ρ_K^(−α_K)χ₁(r − r_1)χ₂(r)χ_K(ρ_K)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|), where χ₁(x) = e^(−𝔛/x) for x > 0, so
χ₁′(x) = 𝔛x⁻²χ₁(x). Then [Hin26a, (5.60)] holds: aH_(−ℓ+j)a − Sa² = −a² − b_0² + e_R² + e_T² + f, with the b_0, e_R,
e_T and f of [Hin26a]. The square roots exist for the following reasons.

- b_0: on [r_1, r_4] ⊂ [r_♯, r_c − r_c e^(1/2)/v], −ℓ(−dr) is positive definite (Lemma 24.31 (6)), so
−𝔛(r − r_1)⁻²(−ℓ(dr) + H_jr) ≥ C for any fixed C once 𝔛 is large.

- e_R: χ₂ is decreasing and ℓ(dr) is positive definite there.

- e_T: dρ_K/ρ_K² = −dt is future timelike, so ℓ(−dt) > 0 (Lemma 24.29 (d), Lemma 24.30).

e_R (on supp χ₂′χ_K) and e_T (on supp χ₂χ′_K) give ‖Eω‖. The rest is as before.

(2) Take a = ρ_K^(α_K)χ₁(r_4 − r)χ̃₂(r)χ_K(ρ_K)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|), with χ̃₂ = 0 near (−∞, r_1] and 1 near [r_2, ∞). Then
aH_(−ℓ+j)a + Sa² = a² + b_0² + b_T² − e_R² + f, and the only a priori term is e_R, on supp χ̃₂′. ∎

[Hin26a, pp. 57–58] states the next propagation estimates as analogous to Proposition 24.38. They are stated and proved
here, both directions included, since the combination in Section 24.6.8 uses each.

**Proposition 24.39** (Propagation along K⁺ outward, and along 𝗌𝖿.) Let B_0, B_1, E ∈ Ψ_(3b,ħ) have compact
operator wave front sets in {|ζ| < 2} and Schwartz kernels supported in a compact set 𝒦 as specified, with χ = 1 on 𝒦.
Each item asserts an estimate (1) for P_h of the form [Hin26a, (5.58)] and an estimate (2) for P_h* of the form
[Hin26a, (5.59)]. In (b)–(c) the 𝗌𝖿-weight ρ_sf^(α_sf) (resp. ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)) is included, and P_hω carries two more
powers of ρ_sf as in [Hin26a, (5.55)].

(a) (*Along K⁺, r > r_c.*) Let r′_1 := r_c + (51/50)r_c e^(1/2)/v < r′_2 := r_c + (52/50)r_c e^(1/2)/v < r′_3 < r′_4 < ∞
and 0 < t_1 < t_2 < t_3, with ρ_K = t⁻¹. Let WF′(B_0) ⊂ {ρ_K ≤ t_2⁻¹, r′_1 < r < r′_4, |ζ| < 1},
Ell(B_1) ⊃ {ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r′_1 ≤ r ≤ r′_4, |ζ| < 2}, and in (1)

    Ell(E) ⊃ {t_3⁻¹ ≤ ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r′_1 ≤ r ≤ r′_4, |ζ| < 1} ∪ {ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r′_1 ≤ r ≤ r′_2, |ζ| < 1},

while in (2) Ell(E) ⊃ {ρ_K ≤ t_1⁻¹, r′_3 ≤ r ≤ r′_4, |ζ| < 1}.

(b) (*Along 𝗌𝖿, below the sink.*) Let s := r/t, δ_r ≤ s_1 < s_2 < s_3 < s_4 := v(1 − δ_sf) and δ′ > 0 small. Let
WF′(B_0) ⊂ {s_1 < s < s_4, ρ_sf ≤ δ′, |ζ| < 1} and Ell(B_1) ⊃ {s_1 ≤ s ≤ s_4, ρ_sf ≤ 2δ′, |ζ| < 2}. In (1),

    Ell(E) ⊃ {s_1 ≤ s ≤ s_2, ρ_sf ≤ 2δ′} ∪ {s_1 ≤ s ≤ s_4, δ′ ≤ ρ_sf ≤ 2δ′}

(intersected with |ζ| < 1), and in (2) Ell(E) ⊃ {s_3 ≤ s ≤ s_4, ρ_sf ≤ 2δ′, |ζ| < 1}.

(c) (*Along 𝗌𝖿, above the sink.*) The same as (b) with s_4 := v(1 + δ_sf) < s_3 < s_2 < s_1 ≤ 10 and the inequalities in
s reversed.

*Proof.* Each is the proof of Proposition 24.38 with a different escape function φ and, in (b)–(c), the 𝗌𝖿-cut-off and
weight of Proposition 24.37. The escape functions are φ = r in (a), φ = s in (b) and φ = −s in (c). Each satisfies
−ℓ(dφ) positive definite on the support in question, by Lemma 24.31 (6): −ℓ(dr) > 0 for r ≥ r_c + r_c e^(1/2)/v,
−r²ℓ(ds) > 0 on 𝗌𝖿 ∩ {s ∈ [δ_r, v(1 − δ_sf)]}, and −r²ℓ(−ds) > 0 on 𝗌𝖿 ∩ {s ∈ [v(1 + δ_sf), 10]}. The last two persist to
{ρ_sf ≤ 2δ′} for δ′ small, by continuity on the compact s-intervals. With φ_1 < φ_4 the values of φ at the two ends (in
(a) r′_1, r′_4; in (b) s_1, s_4; in (c) −s_1, −s_4), take in (1)

    a = W⁻¹χ₁(φ_4 − φ)χ̃₂(φ)χ_⋆χ_0(𝔛|ζ|),

with χ₁(x) = e^(−𝔛/x) as before, χ̃₂ = 0 near φ ≤ φ_1 and 1 near φ ≥ φ_2, and (W, χ_⋆) = (ρ_K^(α_K), χ_K(ρ_K)) in (a),
(W, χ_⋆) = (w′, χ_sf(ρ_sf/δ′)) in (b)–(c). The terms of aH_(−ℓ+j)a are signed as follows.

- *Main term.* H_(−ℓ)χ₁(φ_4 − φ) = −χ₁′(φ_4 − φ)(−ℓ(dφ)), which is negative definite with
χ₁′/χ₁ = 𝔛(φ_4 − φ)⁻² ≥ 𝔛(φ_4 − φ_1)⁻². For 𝔛 large it dominates S, the weight term W⁻¹H_(−ℓ)W and the j-terms. These
are bounded on supp a in the rescaled sense: ρ_sf⁻²S, ρ_sf⁻²ℓ(dw′/w′) and ρ_sf⁻²H_j of functions are bounded near 𝗌𝖿
(Lemma 24.28 (d)), and j = O(|ζ|³). This gives −a² − b_0².

- *χ̃₂.* H_(−ℓ)χ̃₂(φ) = χ̃₂′(−ℓ(dφ)) ≥ 0, of the opposite sign. It is supported near the start, where (1) assumes
control.

- *χ_⋆ in (a).* H_(−ℓ)χ_K(t⁻¹) = χ_K′ ℓ(dt) t⁻², with χ_K′ ≤ 0 and ℓ(dt) < 0 (dt past timelike), so it is ≥ 0; it is
supported at ρ_K ∈ [t_3⁻¹, t_1⁻¹], where (1) assumes control.

- *χ_⋆ in (b)–(c).* H_(−ℓ)χ_sf(ρ_sf/δ′) = δ′⁻¹χ_sf′ ρ_sf² ℓ(dr), with χ_sf′ ≤ 0 and ℓ(dr) < 0 for large r, so it is
≥ 0; it is supported at ρ_sf ∈ [δ′, 2δ′], where (1) assumes control.

Each positive term is the square of a smooth symbol by the cut-off conditions of the notation, and gives ‖Eω‖. The rest
is the proof of Proposition 24.35: 𝓛_h, the Q-terms [Hin26a, (5.44)–(5.46)], and the iteration.

In (2) the commutant is Wχ₁(φ − φ_1)χ̃₃(φ)χ_⋆χ_0, with χ̃₃ = 1 near φ ≤ φ_3 and 0 near φ ≥ φ_4. The main term
H_(−ℓ)χ₁(φ − φ_1) = χ₁′(−ℓ(dφ)) is now positive, the sign the adjoint pairing [Hin26a, (5.49)] needs. The χ_⋆-terms,
≥ 0, now have the sign of the main term. The χ̃₃-term, ≤ 0, needs control at the far end. ∎

**Proposition 24.40** (Propagation through the interior of Ω.) Weights play no role here, all supports being
compact in Ω ∖ (K⁺ ∪ 𝗌𝖿).

(1) (*Forward.*) Let κ ∈ (0, 1), φ := t + κr and T_2 > 0. Let 𝒟 := {t ≥ 0, φ ≤ T_2}, which is compact, and let
0 < ε_X ≤ T_0r_♯/2 and ε_r := (r̂ − r_♯)/10. Let WF′(B_0) ⊂ {φ < T_2 − ε, t > ε_X, r > r_♯ + ε_r, |ζ| < 1} for some
ε > 0, let B_1 be elliptic on 𝒟 ∩ {|ζ| ≤ 2} away from X_0 ∪ Σ^♯, and let
Ell(E) ⊃ {½ε_X ≤ t ≤ ε_X, φ ≤ T_2, |ζ| < 1}. Then

    ‖B_0ω‖_(L²) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖B_1P_hω‖_(L²) + ‖Eω‖_(L²) + h^N‖χω‖_(H^(−N)_(3b,h))).

Ell(E) lies in τ⁻¹([0, T_0]), since t ≤ ε_X and r ≥ r_♯ give τ ≤ T_0/2.

(2) (*Backward.*) Let κ := 1/9, 0 < t_1 < t_2 and c₁ > 0. Let 𝒟′ := {t_1 ≤ t ≤ t_2 + 1, t − κr ≥ −c₁}, which is
compact. Let WF′(B_0) ⊂ {2t_1 < t < t_2, t − κr > 0, r > r_♯ + ε_r, |ζ| < 1}, let B_1 be elliptic on 𝒟′ ∩ {|ζ| ≤ 2}
away from Σ^♯, and let

    Ell(E) ⊃ ({t_2 ≤ t ≤ t_2 + 1} ∪ {r_♯ + ½ε_r ≤ r ≤ r_♯ + ε_r}) ∩ 𝒟′ ∩ {|ζ| < 1}.

Then the same estimate holds for P_h*.

*Proof.* (1) dφ and dt are past timelike (Lemma 24.29 (a)), so −ℓ(dφ) and −ℓ(dt) are positive definite on 𝒟
(Lemma 24.30, [Hin26a, Lemma 3.5]), with a lower bound by compactness. On supp χ_r′ ⊂ [r_♯, r_♯ + ε_r],
−ℓ(−dr) > 0 (Lemma 24.31 (6), as r_♯ + ε_r < r_c − r_c e^(1/2)/v). Take a = χ₁(T_2 − φ)χ̃(t)χ_r(r)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|), with
χ̃ = 0 on t ≤ ½ε_X and 1 on t ≥ ε_X, and χ_r = 0 near r ≤ r_♯ + ½ε_r and 1 on r ≥ r_♯ + ε_r, both non-decreasing. The
terms of aH_(−ℓ+j)a are signed as follows: H_(−ℓ)χ₁(T_2 − φ) = −χ₁′(−ℓ(dφ)) is the negative main term, dominating S and
j for 𝔛 large; H_(−ℓ)χ̃(t) = χ̃′(−ℓ(dt)) ≥ 0 needs control on supp χ̃′ ⊂ Ell(E); and
H_(−ℓ)χ_r(r) = χ_r′(−ℓ(dr)) = −χ_r′(−ℓ(−dr)) ≤ 0 has the sign of the main term and is dropped. The rest is the proof of
Proposition 24.35. The supports avoid X_0 and Σ^♯, as the convention on Schwartz kernels requires.

(2) d(t − κr) is past timelike (Lemma 24.29 (a), β = κ). Take

    a = χ₁(t − t_1)χ_late(t)f(t − κr)χ_r(r)χ_0(𝔛|ζ|),

with χ_late non-increasing, 1 on t ≤ t_2 and 0 on t ≥ t_2 + 1, and f non-decreasing, 0 on (−∞, −c₁] and 1 on [0, ∞). In
the adjoint pairing [Hin26a, (5.49)] the main term must be positive. The terms are signed as follows:
H_(−ℓ)χ₁(t − t_1) = χ₁′(−ℓ(dt)) is positive and dominant; H_(−ℓ)f = f′(−ℓ(d(t − κr))) ≥ 0 has its sign and is dropped;
H_(−ℓ)χ_late = χ_late′(−ℓ(dt)) ≤ 0 needs control on {t_2 ≤ t ≤ t_2 + 1}; and H_(−ℓ)χ_r ≤ 0 needs control near Σ^♯. On
supp a, r ≤ (t + c₁)/κ and t ≤ t_2 + 1, so the support is compact, and χ₁(t − t_1) is bounded below on WF′(B_0). The rest
is as in (1), with 𝓛_h*. ∎

#### 24.6.7 Energy estimates

[Hin26a, Lemma 5.14] is stated for an arbitrary time-oriented Lorentzian vector space, and [Hin26a, Corollary 5.15] on
ℝ^(1+n) for every n and on n-dimensional manifolds of bounded geometry ([Hin26a, pp. 58–60]). Both are used as stated,
with n = 4. Near X_0 the bounded geometry is that of the τ-level sets, with preferred charts products of charts on 𝕊³
with dyadic intervals in r. Near Σ^♯ it is that of the r-level sets, with charts on 𝕊³ times unit intervals in t. The
data required to lie in a compact subset of C^∞(I × B_3) are g, B, a 3b-connection, ℓ and φ; they do so by
Lemma 24.28 (a), (c), (d), uniformly for b ∈ U. The hypothesis on ℓ, positive definite on future causal covectors,
is Lemma 24.30 ([Hin26a, Lemma 3.5]).

**Proposition 24.41** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.16] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let α_sf, α_K ∈ ℝ.

(1) (*Near X_0*; the weight at K⁺ is dropped.) There are h_0 > 0 and C such that for h ∈ (0, h_0) and every
ω ∈ ρ_sf^(α_sf)H²_(3b,h) vanishing for t < 0,

    ‖ω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)H¹_(3b,h)(τ⁻¹([0,T_0]))) ≤ Ch⁻¹‖P_hω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf+2)L²(τ⁻¹([0,T_0]))),

and for every ω ∈ ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)H²_(3b,h), without support condition,

    ‖ω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)H¹_(3b,h)(τ⁻¹([0,T_0/2])))
        ≤ C(h⁻¹‖P_h*ω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf)L²(τ⁻¹([0,T_0]))) + ‖ω‖_(ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)H¹_(3b,h)(τ⁻¹([T_0/2,T_0])))).

(2) (*Near Σ^♯*; the weight at 𝗌𝖿 is dropped.) Let r_♯ ≤ r_1 < r_2 < r_3 ≤ r̂. There are h_0 > 0 and C such that for
h ∈ (0, h_0) and every ω ∈ ρ_K^(α_K)H²_(3b,h) vanishing for t < 0,

    ‖ω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)H¹_(3b,h)(r⁻¹([r_1,r_2])))
        ≤ C(h⁻¹‖P_hω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)L²(r⁻¹([r_1,r_3]))) + ‖ω‖_(ρ_K^(α_K)H¹_(3b,h)(r⁻¹([r_2,r_3])))),

and for every ω ∈ ρ_K^(−α_K)H²_(3b,h) vanishing for r < r_1,

    ‖ω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)H¹_(3b,h)(r⁻¹([r_1,r_3]) ∩ {τ ≥ 0})) ≤ Ch⁻¹‖P_h*ω‖_(ρ_K^(−α_K)L²(r⁻¹([r_1,r_3]) ∩ {τ ≥ 0})).

These four estimates are [Hin26a, (5.66)–(5.69)], with T := T_0 and with the radii r_1 < r_2 < r_3 < r₊ of [Hin26a],
from its inner radius on, read as above; in the proofs the level sets of τ carry the density r⁴|dr d𝑔̸|, which
tensored with |dτ| is |dg|. Moreover, at fixed h, for ω ∈ ρ_sf^(α_sf)H̄²_3b without support condition,

    ‖ω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)H̄¹_3b(τ⁻¹([0,T_0]))) ≤ C_h(‖P_hω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf+2)L²(τ⁻¹([0,T_0])))
                                                + ‖(ω, r𝓛_(∂_t)ω)|_(X_0)‖_(ℋ_data)),    (24.29)

where ℋ_data := ρ_sf^(α_sf)H̄¹_b(X_0, r⁴|dr d𝑔̸|) ⊕ ρ_sf^(α_sf)H̄⁰_b(X_0, r⁴|dr d𝑔̸|).

*Proof.* [Hin26a, (5.66)]. Take the multiplier a²L_h with a = ρ_sf^(−α_sf−2)e^(−𝔛τ)H(T_0 − τ)H(r − r_♯) (H the
Heaviside function), and the pairing [Hin26a, (5.70)],
h⁻¹Im⟨P_hω, a²L_hω⟩ = ⟨𝒞ω, ω⟩ − h⁻¹‖aL_hω‖². The principal symbol of 𝒞 is aT_(G,da,ℓ) − a²E in the notation of
[Hin26a, (5.61)], since H_Ga = 2g⁻¹(ζ, da). This leads to the decomposition [Hin26a, (5.71)], whose derivation only
expands (i/2)(□_h*bL_h − L_h*b□_h) in local coordinates with b = a². Then a da is [Hin26a, (5.72)], and the weight
identity [Hin26a, (5.73)] holds: aT_(G,−da,ℓ) = ρ_sf⁴T_(ρ_sf⁻²G, −a da, ρ_sf⁻²ℓ), by bilinearity, free of the dimension.

−a da is past timelike for 𝔛 large, since dτ is past timelike with r²g⁻¹(dτ, dτ) ≤ −¾ (Lemma 24.29 (b)) and the
δ(r − r_♯)-part of −a da is a positive multiple of −dr, past timelike (Lemma 24.29 (c)). So [Hin26a, Corollary
5.15] is integrated over {r ≥ r_♯, 0 ≤ τ ≤ T_0} twice: with dτ and φ² = 𝔛a² + ρ_sf^(−2α_sf−4)e^(−2𝔛τ)δ(T_0 − τ), and
with −dr and φ² = ρ_sf^(−2α_sf−4)e^(−2𝔛τ)δ(r − r_♯). Here the level sets of τ carry r⁴|dr d𝑔̸|,
which tensored with |dτ| is |dg| (Lemma 24.28 (b)). This gives [Hin26a, (5.74)].

The other terms of [Hin26a, (5.71)] carry the total weight ρ_sf⁴ of ∇*T∇ and are bounded by [Hin26a, (5.75)] and its
companions. The left side of [Hin26a, (5.70)] is at least −½h⁻¹(‖aP_hω‖² + ‖aL_hω‖²), which gives [Hin26a, (5.76)].
The fundamental theorem of calculus for L_h, [Hin26a, (5.77)], uses Lemma 24.30 ([Hin26a, Lemma 3.5]) for the
future timelike covector ρ_sf a d(ρ_sf a). It gives the bulk term C𝔛ρ_sf⁴a² and the two positive δ-terms, hence
[Hin26a, (5.78)]. Adding [Hin26a, (5.76)] and (5.78) and absorbing for h small gives [Hin26a, (5.66)].

[Hin26a, (5.68)] follows by the same argument with a = ρ_K^(−α_K)e^(𝔛r)H(r − r_1), applied to χω (χ = 1 on r ≤ r_2,
0 on r ≥ r_3), as −dr is past timelike on [r_♯, r̂] (Lemma 24.29 (c)). [Hin26a, (5.67) and (5.69)] are the same
arguments for P_h* = □_h* + iL_h*, whose damping acts backwards, as in [Hin26a].

(24.29). Run the proof of [Hin26a, (5.66)] at fixed h with a multiplied by H(τ). The boundary τ = 0 then adds to
[Hin26a, (5.74) and (5.77)] the terms of the boundary τ = T_0 with the opposite sign. Each is a quadratic form in
(ω, ∂_τω)|_(τ=0) with bounded coefficients in the 3b frame, so it is bounded by
C‖(ω, r𝓛_(∂_t)ω)|_(X_0)‖²_(ℋ_data). Here ∂_τ = r∂_t at fixed (r, ω), and the weight matches by Lemma 24.28 (b):
ρ_sf^(α+½)H̄^k_b(X_0, r³|dr d𝑔̸|) = ρ_sf^α H̄^k_b(X_0, r⁴|dr d𝑔̸|). ∎

#### 24.6.8 Combination: [Hin26a, Theorem 5.2] in dimension 4 + 1

Fix (α_sf, α_K) as in Lemma 24.31 and b ∈ U.

**Proposition 24.42** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.17] in dimension 4 + 1.) For s ≥ 1 there are h_0 > 0 and C such
that for h ∈ (0, h_0) and ω ∈ H^(s+1,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(•,−),

    ‖ω‖_(H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(•,−)) ≤ Ch⁻¹‖P_hω‖_(H^(s−1,(α_sf+2,α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(•,−)).    (24.30)

*Proof.* Take s = 1 first. Every microlocal estimate below bounds ‖B_0ω‖ by h⁻¹‖B_1P_hω‖, an a priori term ‖Eω‖ and
h^N‖χω‖_(H^(−N)). Each step's a priori set lies in the elliptic sets of the B_0's of earlier steps, so the estimates
chain. The B_0's of all the steps together are elliptic on a neighbourhood of o over supp χ_(τ,2)χ_(r,2). The steps are:

(i) [Hin26a, (5.66)] on τ⁻¹([0, T_0]).

(ii) Proposition 24.33 and Proposition 24.34 off o; the a priori term of [Hin26a, (5.21)] lies in
τ⁻¹([0, (2.75/10)T_0]), covered by (i).

(iii) Proposition 24.40 (1) on every 𝒟, with κ = ½ and T_2 arbitrary, from (i). This covers o over every compact subset
of Ω ∖ (K⁺ ∪ 𝗌𝖿), since {t ≤ T′, r ≤ R′} ⊂ {φ < T′ + R′}.

(iv) Proposition 24.39 (c) along 𝗌𝖿 from s ∈ [5, 10], where τ ≤ 1/5 < T_0 and (i) applies, to s > v(1 + δ_sf). Its
interior a priori set {δ′ ≤ ρ_sf ≤ 2δ′} is compact in Ω° and covered by (iii).

(v) Proposition 24.35 (1) at r = r_c; its E lies at finite t ∈ [1/(3δ), 1/δ], covered by (iii).

(vi) Proposition 24.38 (1) towards r_♯, with r_1 := r_♯ + (2/10)(r̂ − r_♯) and t_1 ≥ δ⁻¹; its E is near r_c, by (v), or
at finite times, by (iii).

(vii) Proposition 24.39 (a) (1) outward to r′_4 := 2δ_0⁻¹, with r′_3 := δ_0⁻¹, where δ_0 is the δ of Proposition 24.36;
its E is near r_c, by (v), or at finite times, by (iii).

(viii) Proposition 24.36 (1) at ∂K⁺; its E lies at ρ_sf ∈ [(5/4)δ_0, 2δ_0], ρ_K ≤ 2δ_r, covered by (vii) where t is
large and by (iii) where t is finite.

(ix) Proposition 24.39 (b) (1) along 𝗌𝖿 from s ∈ [δ_r, (5/4)δ_r], by (viii), to s < v(1 − δ_sf), its interior part by
(iii); here 2δ′ ≤ δ_0, so that the start set lies in the B_0 of Proposition 24.36.

(x) Proposition 24.37 (1) at the sink, with its δ ≤ δ′/2. Its E lies at |s/v − 1| ∈ [(5/4)δ_sf, 2δ_sf], covered by (iv)
and (ix), or at ρ_sf ≥ (5/4)δ with r finite, covered by (iii).

Together this is the first form of [Hin26a, (5.80)]:

    ‖ω‖_(H^(1,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h)(τ⁻¹([0,T_0]))) + ‖χ_(τ,2)χ_(r,2)ω‖_(H^(1,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h))
      ≤ C(h⁻¹‖P_hω‖_(H^(0,(α_sf+2,α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(•,−)) + h^N‖χ_(τ,0)χ_(r,0)ω‖_(H^(−N,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h))).

Then [Hin26a, (5.68)] with r_1 = r_♯, r_2 := r_♯ + (2.75/10)(r̂ − r_♯) and r_3 := ½(r_2 + r̂) estimates ω on
r⁻¹([r_♯, r_2]) by the region just controlled. This gives [Hin26a, (5.80)], and absorbing the h^N term for h small gives
(24.30) at s = 1.

For s > 1, the energy estimates are the only step restricted to s = 1, and we extend and restrict, as in [Hin26a].
Extend f := P_hω to f̃ on Ω̃ := cl{t ≥ 0, r ≥ ¾r_♯} with the same quotient norm, and g, c as in Section 24.6.1. The
forward solution ω̃ ∈ H^(0,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω̃)^(•,−) exists with ‖ω̃‖ ≤ Ch⁻¹‖f̃‖_(H^(−1)), by Proposition 24.43 at
s′ = 1 on Ω̃ and duality. On Ω̃ the argument runs with two changes. Proposition 24.38 is used with r_1 ≥ r_♯, and the
transition of χ_r in Proposition 24.40 is placed in {r ≥ r_♯}, where c is the 1-form of Proposition 24.10 and
Lemma 24.31 (6) holds. On {¾r_♯ ≤ r ≤ r_3}, r_3 < r̂, the estimates [Hin26a, (5.68)–(5.69)] of
Proposition 24.41 are used, with ¾r_♯ for r_♯; they need only Lemma 24.29 (c) and Lemma 24.30, which hold on
{r ≥ ½r_♯}, where g is defined and c is past timelike (Section 24.6.1). Proposition 24.34 needs only
Lemma 24.29 (c) there. Moreover ω̃ = ω on Ω, by uniqueness of forward solutions: Σ^♯ is spacelike with future
timelike vectors pointing out, and X_0 is spacelike (Lemma 24.29 (a), (c)). The microlocal estimates of
Section 24.6.2–Section 24.6.6 hold for every s in the strong sense; near the zero section the order is irrelevant. They
apply to ω̃ on {r ≥ (7/8)r_♯}, where Σ^♯ is now interior. Near τ = 0 they propagate from τ < 0, where ω̃ = 0, by
Proposition 24.40 (1) and Proposition 24.34 with the cut-offs moved below τ = 0. Restriction to Ω gives
(24.30) for s ≥ 1. ∎

**Proposition 24.43** (The adjoint estimate [Hin26a, (5.81)] in dimension 4 + 1.) For s′ ≥ 1 there are h_0 > 0
and C such that for h ∈ (0, h_0),

    ‖ω′‖_(H^(s′,(−α_sf−2,−α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(−,•)) ≤ Ch⁻¹‖P_h*ω′‖_(H^(s′−1,(−α_sf,−α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(−,•)).    (24.31)

*Proof.* At s′ = 1 the estimates chain as follows, each later a priori set covered by earlier steps.

(i) Proposition 24.37 (2) at the sink, which has no a priori term.

(ii) Proposition 24.39 (b) (2) and (c) (2) along 𝗌𝖿 outward from the sink, to s ∈ [δ_r, v(1 − δ_sf)] and
[v(1 + δ_sf), 10]. Their a priori sets are at the sink, by (i), and their 𝗌𝖿-cut-off terms have the good sign. Here
2δ′ is at most the δ of the sink, and s_3 ≥ v(1 − (5/4)δ_sf).

(iii) Proposition 24.36 (2) at ∂K⁺; its E at ρ_K ∈ [(5/4)δ_r, 2δ_r] is covered by (ii).

(iv) Proposition 24.39 (a) (2) along K⁺ inward from r′_4 := 2δ_0⁻¹ to r′_1, with r′_3 := δ_0⁻¹ and δ_0 the δ of
Proposition 24.36; its E at [r′_3, r′_4], where ρ_sf ≤ δ_0, is covered by (iii). Here t_1 ≥ 2/(δ_0δ_r), so that
[r′_3, r′_4] at ρ_K = 1/t ≤ t_1⁻¹ lies in {r/t ≤ (5/4)δ_r}.

(v) [Hin26a, (5.69)] near Σ^♯, which has no a priori term on supported spaces.

(vi) Proposition 24.38 (2) from Σ^♯ towards r_c; its E near r_♯ is covered by (v).

(vii) Proposition 24.35 (2) at r_c; its E at |r − r_c| ∈ [55/50, 60/50]r_c e^(1/2)/v is covered by (iv) and (vi).

At this point a neighbourhood of o over {ρ_K ≤ ε₁} ∪ ({ρ_sf ≤ ε₁} ∩ {s ≤ 10}) ∪ {r ≤ r_♯ + ε_r} is controlled, for some
ε₁ > 0. Here ρ_K = r/(t + r) globally.

(viii) Proposition 24.40 (2) with κ = 1/9, t_1 < ¼T_0r_♯ and t_2 ≥ max(ε₁⁻², 10c₁). Its late set
{t_2 ≤ t ≤ t_2 + 1} ∩ 𝒟′ is covered by (i)–(vii): points there with r ≤ ε₁⁻¹ have ρ_K ≤ ε₁, and the others have
ρ_sf ≤ ε₁ and s = r/t ≤ (t + c₁)/(κt) ≤ 10 once t_2 ≥ 10c₁. Its set near Σ^♯ is covered by (v). It controls o over
{t ≥ 2t_1, t ≥ κr} up to t_2, which covers {τ ≥ κ} there; and κ = 1/9 < ¼ = ½T_0. A point with τ ≥ ½T_0 has
t ≥ ½T_0r_♯ > 2t_1.

(ix) Proposition 24.33 and Proposition 24.34 (the adjoint estimate [Hin26a, (5.22)]) off o; the a priori term is near
Σ^♯, by (v).

(x) [Hin26a, (5.67)] on τ⁻¹([0, ½T_0]), from τ⁻¹([½T_0, T_0]), which is covered by (ii) near 𝗌𝖿, by (viii) elsewhere,
and by (ix) off o.

Absorbing h^N gives (24.31) at s′ = 1. For s′ > 1, extend and restrict as in Proposition 24.42. ∎

**Theorem 24.44** ([Hin26a, Theorem 5.2] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let (α_sf, α_K) be as in Lemma 24.31 and
C₁ > 0. There is h_0 > 0, uniform for b ∈ U (Lemma 24.46), such that for h ∈ (0, h_0), s ∈ [−C₁, C₁] and b ∈ U:

(a) the forward problem □^C_bω = f ∈ H^(s−1,(α_sf+2,α_K))_3b(Ω)^(•,−) has a unique solution
ω ∈ H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))_3b(Ω)^(•,−), with the semiclassical bound ‖ω‖_(H^s_(3b,h)) ≤ Ch⁻¹‖h²f‖_(H^(s−1)_(3b,h)) in these
weights ([Hin26a, (5.18)]);

(b) the initial value problem

    □^C_bω = f ∈ ρ_sf^(α_sf+2)ρ_K^(α_K)H̄⁰_3b(Ω, |dg|),
    (ω, r𝓛_(∂_t)ω)|_(X_0) ∈ ρ_sf^(α_sf+½)H̄¹_b(X_0, r³|dr d𝑔̸|) ⊕ ρ_sf^(α_sf+½)H̄⁰_b(X_0, r³|dr d𝑔̸|)    (24.32)

has a unique solution ω ∈ ρ_sf^(α_sf)ρ_K^(α_K)H̄¹_3b(Ω, |dg|), the densities on X_0 being Euclidean;

(c) (24.30) and (24.31) hold for s, s′ ∈ [1, C₁ + 1] and h ∈ (0, h_0), with constants uniform for b ∈ U
(h_0 depending on C₁).

*Proof.* (c) is Proposition 24.42 and Proposition 24.43 with Lemma 24.46.

(a) *Existence for s ≤ 0.* Take s′ := 1 − s ≥ 1. For ω′ in H^(s′,(−α_sf−2,−α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(−,•), the functional
P_h*ω′ ↦ ⟨h²f, ω′⟩ is well defined and bounded by Ch⁻¹‖h²f‖‖P_h*ω′‖, by (24.31). The spaces
H^(s−1,(α_sf+2,α_K))(Ω)^(•,−) and H^(1−s,(−α_sf−2,−α_K))(Ω)^(−,•) are dual under ⟨·, ·⟩, and so are
H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))(Ω)^(•,−) and H^(−s,(−α_sf,−α_K))(Ω)^(−,•) ([Hin26a, Section 2.3]). So the Hahn–Banach theorem gives
ω ∈ H^(s,(α_sf,α_K))_(3b,h)(Ω)^(•,−) with P_hω = h²f and the bound [Hin26a, (5.18)]. *s > 0.* Higher regularity follows
by extension and restriction with the propagation estimates, as in Proposition 24.42. *Uniqueness*, for every
distribution ω on Ω supported in {t ≥ 0} with P_hω = 0, follows by the classical duality argument. For
φ ∈ C_c^∞(Ω°), the backward solution ψ of P_h*ψ = φ is smooth, with support in the causal past of supp φ. That set is
compact, since t decreases and |dr/dt| is bounded along causal curves. It is disjoint from Σ^♯: along past-directed
causal curves r increases inside {r ≤ r̂} (Lemma 24.29 (c)), so r stays above min(min_(supp φ) r, r̂). Pairing the
extension of ω by zero across X_0 with ψ gives ⟨ω, φ⟩ = ⟨P_hω, ψ⟩ = 0.

(b) By Lemma 24.28 (b) the data space is ℋ_data of (24.29), with the density r⁴|dr d𝑔̸| that tensors with
dτ to |dg|; the shift ½ does not depend on the dimension ([Hin26a, p. 65]). *Smooth data.* Take f and data smooth with
compact support in Ω° ∪ X_0°. The initial value problem then has a solution ω smooth on Ω ∖ (K⁺ ∪ 𝗌𝖿), for the
following reasons. □^C_b has scalar principal symbol G Id (Lemma 24.28 (d)). Every past-inextendible causal curve in
Ω° meets X_0: t decreases along it (Lemma 24.29 (a)), r increases along it inside {r ≤ r̂} (Lemma 24.29 (c)),
and |dr/dt| is bounded along causal curves, since g is a 3sc-metric. So the classical theory of the Cauchy problem for
linear wave equations with scalar principal symbol applies ([Hin26a, p. 42]). By finite speed of propagation, ω
vanishes on τ⁻¹([0, T_0]) near 𝗌𝖿, the speed being 1 + O(r⁻²) and T_0 < 1; so
ω ∈ ρ_sf^(α_sf)H̄²_3b(τ⁻¹([0, T_0])) and (24.29) applies. Let χ = χ(τ) equal 1 for τ ≥ ½T_0 and 0 for
τ ≤ ¼T_0. Then P_h(χω) = h²χf + [P_h, χ]ω ∈ H^(0,(α_sf+2,α_K))(Ω)^(•,−), with norm bounded by ‖f‖ and by
‖ω‖_(ρ^(α_sf)H̄¹(τ⁻¹([0,T_0]))). By the uniqueness in (a), which holds for distributions, χω is the forward solution,
so it lies in H^(1,(α_sf,α_K)). Using (24.29),

    ‖ω‖_(ρ_sf^(α_sf)ρ_K^(α_K)H̄¹_3b(Ω)) ≤ C(‖f‖ + ‖(ω, r𝓛_(∂_t)ω)|_(X_0)‖_(ℋ_data)).

*General data.* Approximate f and the data in their spaces by such smooth data. By this estimate the solutions converge
in ρ_sf^(α_sf)ρ_K^(α_K)H̄¹_3b(Ω). Near X_0 they also converge in
C([0, T_0]_τ; ρ_sf^(α_sf)H̄¹_b) ∩ C¹([0, T_0]_τ; ρ_sf^(α_sf)H̄⁰_b): the boundary term at τ = T of [Hin26a, (5.74) and
(5.77)], run at every T ∈ [0, T_0] in the proof of (24.29), bounds the norm of (ω, ∂_τω)|_(τ=T) by the right
side of (24.29). So the limit takes the data and solves (24.32). For uniqueness, let
ω ∈ ρ_sf^(α_sf)ρ_K^(α_K)H̄¹_3b(Ω) solve (24.32) with f = 0 and vanishing data. Its extension by zero across X_0
is a distribution supported in {t ≥ 0} with P_hω = 0, the vanishing data leaving no layer on X_0; so ω = 0 by the
uniqueness in (a). ∎

**Remark 24.45** (In the coordinates of Section 21.5.1.) There g_b = Φ_m*g, with
Φ_m(t, x) = (t − T_m(|x|), x) and T_m ∈ |x|⁻¹C^∞(X̄) near infinity (Lemma 21.20 (a)). Φ_m commutes with ∂_t and
acts on 1-forms by dt ↦ dt − T_m′ dr, where T_m′ ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞. Hence Φ_m intertwines □^C for (g, c_C) with □^C for
(g_b, Φ_m*c_C), and it preserves stationarity, 𝒜^γ(X̄; E), the weighted b-spaces on X̄, and integrals over
[0, ∞)_t × A for an annulus A, up to the shift by the bounded T_m. Theorem 24.53 uses Theorem 24.44 through this
intertwining, with its initial data at {t_KS = 0}.

#### 24.6.9 Uniformity in b

**Lemma 24.46** The constants C and the thresholds h_0 in Proposition 24.33–Proposition 24.43 and
Theorem 24.44 can be taken uniform for b ∈ U.

*Proof.* Every estimate above is proved from three kinds of input, each uniform on U: finitely many seminorms of the
coefficients of P_h as an element of h²ρ_sf²Diff²_3b + hρ_sf²Diff¹_3b in the frames r∂_(z^μ), which are continuous in b
(Lemma 24.28 (a), (d), and the smooth dependence of Section 21.5.1); the lower bounds in the positivity
statements, from Lemma 24.29 (exact in (a)–(b) for all b ∈ ℬ, by continuity in (c)), Lemma 24.30 (the
constant C and the margin of [Hin26a, Lemma 3.5] on compact sets) and Lemma 24.31 (uniform by its statement); and
the cut-offs, commutants and the parameters 𝔛, δ, δ′, t_j, r_j, κ, chosen from these bounds alone, hence independently
of b. The calculus estimates used (composition, elliptic parametrices, the sharp Gårding inequality, L²-boundedness)
have constants depending on finitely many seminorms of the symbols involved, which depend continuously on b. Each
absorption step needs h below a threshold determined by these quantities. So each h_0 and C is uniform on U, after
shrinking U to a compact neighbourhood. ∎

### 24.7 The transition face model

This section proves that □^C_b is tf-admissible with every weight in [−C_0, 2) (Theorem 24.1 (4)), through
[Hin26a, Theorem B.1] in dimension 4 + 1 (Theorem 24.52): the invertibility of the spectral family of the
dilation-invariant model on 4 + 1 Minkowski space, which is the transition face normal operator of □^C_b. The proof has
three steps, as in [Hin26a, Appendix B, pp. 85–98]: the Fredholm property and index 0 (Section 24.7.2), by radial
estimates and Melrose's relative index theorem, sector by sector on 𝕊³; solvability on edge-b spaces
(Section 24.7.3), by the arguments of Section 24.6; and the kernel argument of [Hin26a, Section B.4] (Section 24.7.4).
Section 24.9 identifies the spaces with those of Section 13.4 and verifies Definition 13.15.

#### 24.7.1 The model in dimension 4 + 1

Let v := 1/2, e := 1/102400, h ∈ (0, 10⁻⁶], γ_C = h⁻¹ and C_0 ∈ [3/2, 100]. On Minkowski space ℝ_t × ℝ⁴_x,
η = −dt² + dr² + r²𝑔̸, 𝑔̸ the round metric of 𝕊³. Let c := r⁻¹(dt − v dr) ([Hin26a, (B.1)]) and
□^C := 2δ_ηG_η(δ*_η + E^C), with E^C the modification of Section 24.2 (trace weight 2/3). As there,
h²□^C = 2h²δGδ* − iL_h with L_h = 4ihδ(c ⊗_s ·) + 2ihe dι_(c♯). Let M := [ℝ̄^(1+4); {r = 0}] ([Hin26a, (B.3)]), with
faces 𝗌𝖿 (the lift of ∂ℝ̄^(1+4)) and 𝖼𝖿 (the lift of {r = 0}). Let 𝒯* be the pullback of the scattering cotangent
bundle, with frame dt, dx¹, …, dx⁴. Let X := [ℝ̄⁴; {0}] = [0, ∞]_ρ × 𝕊³, ρ = r⁻¹, and 𝒯*_X := 𝒯*|_X. In t_* := t − r,
the spectral family is

    (□^C)^(σ) := e^(iσt_*) □^C e^(−iσt_*) on stationary sections,     σ ∈ ℂ ∖ 0, Im σ ≥ 0.    (24.33)

**Lemma 24.47** (The model's homogeneity, weights and thresholds.) (i) In the frame dt, dx^i and in
(t_*, x), the coefficient of every derivative of order k in □^C is homogeneous of degree k − 2 in x.

(ii) For real ι, r^ι lies in r^β L²(r³ dr) near r = 0 iff ι > β − 2. So if the indicial roots of (□^C)^(0) in ρ at
infinity avoid [−C_0, 2), those in r at the origin, which are their negatives, avoid (−2, C_0], and the root-free weights
at the origin are β ∈ (0, 2 + C_0].

(iii) The symbol T of Proposition 24.10 (iv) at ρ_K = 0 with d = 1 − α_cf is positive definite iff α_cf > 1 − b*; and
−½r²ℓ(dr/r) has characteristic polynomial (ν − v)³(ν² − (3 − e)vν + (2 − e)v² − e), whose roots are positive at
(v, e) = (1/2, 1/102400), and at e = 0 for every v > 0.

(iv) (α_sf, α_cf) = (−5/2, 5/2) satisfies α_sf < b* − 1 and α_cf > 1 − b*, and 2(α_sf + α_cf) = 0; ℓ = −½ satisfies
−½ − h⁻¹(1 − e)(1 + v) < ℓ < −½ + h⁻¹(1 − e)(1 − v) for every h > 0; β = 7/2 lies in (0, 2 + C_0] iff C_0 ≥ 3/2; and in
(τ = t/r, r) the density |dg| = r⁴|dt (dr/r) d𝑔̸| is r|dτ| times r³|dr d𝑔̸|.

(v) The free 1-form wave operator 2δGδ* = □_η has at the origin the indicial roots −3, −2 | 0, 1 in the scalar sector
l = 0, −l − 3, −l − 2, −l − 1 | l − 1, l, l + 1 in the scalar sector l ≥ 1, and −l − 2 | l in the vector sector, each
simple; the window of β − 2 between the two groups contains (−2, 0).

*Proof.* (i) η has constant components and vanishing Christoffel symbols in (t, x), so □_η = ∂_t² − Δ acts
componentwise, homogeneous of degree −2; the components of c are homogeneous of degree −1, those of ∇c of degree −2,
and by (24.5) every term of h⁻¹𝓛_c is a product of a component of c with a first derivative or of a component of
∇c with the identity. The change to t_* = t − r preserves the homogeneity, r being homogeneous of degree 1. (ii) ∫_0
r^(2ι−2β)r³ dr < ∞ iff 2ι − 2β + 4 > 0. By (i) and the inversion ρ = r⁻¹, the indicial roots at the origin are the
negatives of those at infinity. (iii) The first statement is Proposition 24.10 (iv) with b_sf − b_K = d. For the
second, with ζ = dr/r, ⟨c, ζ⟩ = −v r⁻², G(c) = −(1 − v²)r⁻², G(ζ) = r⁻²; by Proposition 24.8 (i), ½ℓ(ζ) has eigenvalue
−vr⁻² three times and on span{c, ζ} trace −(3 − e)vr⁻² and determinant (2(1 − e)v² − e(1 − v²))r⁻⁴; multiplying by −r²
gives (ν − v)³(ν² − (3 − e)vν + (2 − e)v² − e). At (1/2, 1/102400) the quadratic has positive sum (3 − e)/2 and
positive product (2 − e)/4 − e; at e = 0 its roots are v and 2v. (iv) is arithmetic, with b* ∈ (0.9934, 0.9935) and
dt = r dτ + τ dr. (v) On stationary sections □_η = −Δ componentwise in the frame dt, dx^i. A section of scalar type l
has its dt-component r^ιS, with −Δ(r^ιS) = 0 at leading order iff ι ∈ {l, −l − 2}, and its spatial part a 1-form whose
Cartesian components are, at each order r^ι, combinations of harmonics of degree l ± 1 (for l = 0, of degree 1 only),
with the roots ι ∈ {l − 1, −l − 1} and {l + 1, −l − 3}; a section of vector type has Cartesian components of degree l,
with roots {l, −l − 2}. These are simple, and each group of three (two at l = 0, one for the vector type) lies on one
side of (−2, 0). ∎

**Lemma 24.48** (The structure; [Hin26a, (B.7)–(B.12)] in dimension 4 + 1.)

(a) □^C is homogeneous of degree −2 under (t, x) ↦ (λt, λx), the components of a section being taken in the frame dt,
dx^i; so r²(□^C)^(0) ∈ Diff²_b(X; 𝒯*_X) is dilation invariant.

(b) In the splitting of 𝒯*_X by dr, dt_* = dt − dr and r dω,

    (□^C)^(σ) = 2iσρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − h⁻¹S̄) + (□^C)^(0),     (□^C)^(0) ∈ ρ²Diff²_b(X; 𝒯*_X),    (24.34)

where S̄ = M of Proposition 24.12 is constant and lower triangular with diagonal 2(1 − v), (1 − e)(1 − v) and
(1 − v)Id_(T*𝕊³); it is diagonalisable with spectrum {2(1 − v), (1 − e)(1 − v), 1 − v}, the last three times.

(c) (□^C)^(σ) ∈ ρ_b⁻²Diff²_(sc,b)(X; 𝒯*_X), with ρ_sc := ρ/(ρ + 1) and ρ_b := r/(r + 1). The b-principal symbol of
r²(□^C)^(σ) near r = 0 is ξ_b² + |η_b|², and the scattering principal symbol near ρ = 0 is
G_σ(ξ, η) = −2σξ + ξ² + |η|².

(d) (□^C)^(σ) is the transition face normal operator of □^C_b for every b near b₀: N_tf(σ̂) = (□^C)^(σ̂) in
(13.12), with S_0 = h⁻¹S̄ = S̄^C and N(P^(0)) the normal operator of ρ⁻²(□^C)^(0).

*Proof.* (a) is Lemma 24.47 (i). (b) The form (24.34) is (24.24) on the model, where S̃, Q and R
vanish (g = η and c exactly r⁻¹(dt − v dr); Proposition 24.12 (i)). The 3/2 = (n − 1)/2 is the shift that makes
i(ρ²∂_ρ − kρ) symmetric on L²(ρ⁻⁴dρ/ρ): integrating by parts, i(ρ²∂_ρ − kρ) has adjoint i(ρ²∂_ρ + (1 − a + k)ρ) on
L²(ρ^(−a)dρ/ρ), symmetric iff k = (a − 1)/2, and here a = 4. Diagonalisability: the 2 × 2 block has the distinct
eigenvalues 2(1 − v) ≠ (1 − e)(1 − v), and the angular block is scalar. (c) The memberships follow from
(24.34) and (a). The symbols are computed from ρ²(ρ∂_ρ)², ρ²Δ_(𝕊³) and 2iσρ²∂_ρ; the Diff¹_b-terms of (□^C)^(0)
are subprincipal at both ends. (d) (13.12) defines N_tf from the data of P̂ at ρ = 0, namely S_0 and N(P^(0)).
Lemma 24.21 gives these for □^C_b as S̄^C = h⁻¹S̄ and the normal operator of the model, independent of b
(g_b − η ∈ ρ²C^∞, and c_C minus the model's 1-form in ρ³C^∞, as in the proof of Lemma 24.22). The model's spectral
family is (24.34), so the two agree. t_* differs from the t − ψ(|x|) of Theorem 24.53 by a constant plus O(ρ),
which does not change the data at ρ = 0. ∎

*Spaces.* H^(s,(ℓ,β))_(sc,b) := ρ_sc^ℓ ρ_b^β H^s_(sc,b)(X; 𝒯*_X), with L² taken for the Euclidean density
r³|dr d𝑔̸| = ρ⁻⁴(dρ/ρ)|d𝑔̸| and a fibre inner product fixed below. ℓ may be a variable order on
^(sc)T*_(∂_sc X)X. Near r = 0, H^(s,β)_b(r³ dr) = H^(s,β−2)_b(dr/r): the b-weight is β − 2
(Lemma 24.47 (ii)). The radial sets over ρ = 0 for σ = ±1 are R_out := {ξ = η = 0} (the zero section) and
R_in := {ξ = 2σ, η = 0}, and for Im σ > 0 the characteristic set over ρ = 0 is R_out ([Hin26a, (B.15)–(B.18)], free of
the dimension).

**Definition 24.49** (Admissible orders; [Hin26a, (B.13)] in dimension 4 + 1.) (s, ℓ, β) is *admissible at σ*
if β ∈ (0, 2 + C_0], ℓ < −½ + h⁻¹(1 − e)(1 − v) at R_out, and, when σ = ±1, ℓ > −½ − h⁻¹(1 − e)(1 + v) at R_in, with ℓ
constant near R_in and R_out and non-increasing along σH_(G_σ).

#### 24.7.2 Fredholm property and index 0

**Proposition 24.50** ([Hin26a, Proposition B.2] in dimension 4 + 1.) For (s, ℓ, β) admissible at
σ ∈ e^(i[0,π]),

    (□^C)^(σ) : {ω ∈ H^(s,(ℓ,β))_(sc,b) : (□^C)^(σ)ω ∈ H^(s−2,(ℓ+1,β−2))_(sc,b)}
                  → H^(s−2,(ℓ+1,β−2))_(sc,b)    (24.35)

is Fredholm of index 0, and its nullspace and the annihilator of its range do not depend on the admissible (s, ℓ, β).
The estimate

    ‖ω‖_(H^(s,(ℓ,β))_(sc,b)) ≤ C(‖(□^C)^(σ)ω‖_(H^(s−2,(ℓ+1,β−2))_(sc,b)) + ‖ω‖_(H^(s_0,(ℓ_0,β_0))_(sc,b)))    (24.36)
