    N_sf(ϰ) := −2∂_v(v∂_v + ϰ − 3/2 − S̄) + L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ, ∂_ω).    (26.3)

It acts on sections over sf := ℝ_v × 𝕊³; we write R := v⁻¹ near v = +∞. Conjugation of the last display by ρ^ϰ
replaces ρ∂_ρ by ρ∂_ρ + ϰ, and ρ∂_ρ annihilates functions of (v, ω), so 2ρ⁻²L̄(ρ^ϰ u) = ρ^ϰ N_sf(ϰ)u for u = u(v, ω).

**Remark 26.2** (The scalar wave operator.) Let □ = ∂_t² − Δ_(ℝ⁴) on ℝ^(1+4), and write it in
(t_*, r, ω), t_* = t − r, r = |x|. Then ∂_t = ∂_(t_*) and ∂_r|_t = ∂_r|_(t_*) − ∂_(t_*), so

    □ = 2∂_(t_*)∂_r + 3r⁻¹∂_(t_*) − ∂_r² − 3r⁻¹∂_r + r⁻²Δ_(𝕊³)
      = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2) + ρ²(−(ρ∂_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ_(𝕊³)),

using ∂_r = −ρ(ρ∂_ρ) and r²∂_r² + 3r∂_r = (r∂_r)² + 2r∂_r with r∂_r = −ρ∂_ρ. This is (26.1) with S̄ = 0 and
L̃(0)(x) = −x² + 2x + Δ_(𝕊³), and ρ^(−2−ϰ)□ρ^ϰ = N_sf(ϰ) on functions of (v, ω). The constant 3/2 is (n − 1)/2 at
n = 4; in dimension 3 + 1 it is 1.

**Lemma 26.3** (Structure.) (a) The principal symbol of N_sf(ϰ) is p_2 Id, with

    p_2(v, ω; ξ, η) := v(v + 2)ξ² + |η|²

(ξ dual to v, |η| the round norm). So N_sf(ϰ) is elliptic over {v > 0} ∪ {v < −2}, and on {−2 < v < 0}, p_2 is the
dual of a Lorentzian metric for which dv is timelike.

(b) Near v = ∞, with R = v⁻¹,

    N_sf(ϰ) = 2R(R∂_R)(−R∂_R + ϰ − 3/2 − S̄) + L̃(0)(ω, ϰ − R∂_R, ∂_ω),    (26.4)

an operator L of the form of Section 13.2.5 at the end at 0 (ϱ = R), b-elliptic on {R < 2} (its b-principal symbol
is (1 + 2R)ζ² + |η|²), with normal operator L̃(0)(ω, ϰ − R∂_R, ∂_ω) and Mellin symbol

    J_ϰ(ζ) = L̃(0)(ω, ϰ − ζ, ∂_ω) = −ζ² + (2ϰ − a)ζ + Δ_(𝕊³) + V + (b + aϰ − ϰ²),    (26.5)

of the form of Lemma 13.5; ζ is the variable of the Mellin transform of Section 13.2.3. The roots of J_ϰ are
{ϰ − r}, r over the indicial roots of L̃(0).

(c) N_sf(ϰ) = R^(2+ϰ) N_ι⁺(ϰ) R^(−ϰ) on {v > 0}, with

    N_ι⁺(ϰ) = −2R⁻¹(R∂_R + ϰ)(R∂_R + 3/2 + S̄) + R⁻² L̃(0)(ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω),    (26.6)

which is [Hin26, (9.10)–(9.11)] at n = 4. N_ι⁺(ϰ) is the operator N⁰(σ) of (18.7) (Definition 18.1) for
P_0 = 2L_b, c = 3/2, S_0 = S̄ and P^(0)(0) = L̃(0), at σ = −iϰ.

(d) N_sf(ϰ) commutes with the Lie derivatives ℒ_Ω along the rotation fields Ω of 𝕊³ (acting on sections of
S²T*ℝ^(1+4)).

(e) [v∂_v, N_sf(ϰ)] = −N_sf(ϰ) + L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ, ∂_ω), and N_sf(ϰ + 1)∂_v = ∂_v N_sf(ϰ).

(f) N_sf(ϰ) − N_sf(ϰ′) = (ϰ − ϰ′)(−2∂_v − 2v∂_v + a − ϰ − ϰ′), a first-order operator polynomial in ϰ, ϰ′; near
v = ∞ it lies in Diff¹_b, as ∂_v = −R(R∂_R).

(g) Let ĝ := |x|⁻²ḡ on ℝ_T × sf, T := log |x|. Then

    ĝ⁻¹ = ∂_T² − 2(v + 1)∂_T∂_v + v(v + 2)∂_v² + g̸⁻¹,

g̸ the round metric; dT is spacelike, and dv is timelike exactly on {−2 < v < 0}. N_sf(ϰ) is the spectral family
e^(iσT) P_c e^(−iσT) at σ = −iϰ of the T-independent operator P_c := 2|x|²L̄, whose principal symbol at
−σ dT + ξ dv + η is ĝ⁻¹(−σ dT + ξ dv + η) = σ² + 2(v + 1)σξ + p_2, and P_c − □_ĝ Id is a first-order operator with
T-independent coefficients.

*Proof.* (a) The second-order part of (26.3) is −2∂_v v∂_v − (v∂_v)² + Δ_(𝕊³), whose principal symbol is
2vξ² + v²ξ² + |η|². It is positive definite where v(v + 2) > 0, and on {−2 < v < 0} it has one negative direction, with
p_2(dv) = v(v + 2) < 0.

(b) v∂_v = −R∂_R and ∂_v = −R²∂_R = −R(R∂_R), so −2∂_v(v∂_v + ϰ − 3/2 − S̄) = 2R(R∂_R)(−R∂_R + ϰ − 3/2 − S̄). The term
−2R(R∂_R)² has b-symbol 2Rζ², and −(R∂_R)² in L̃(0) gives ζ². On R^ζ, v∂_v + ϰ acts as ϰ − ζ, and expanding
(26.2) at x = ϰ − ζ gives (26.5); its roots are the ζ with ϰ − ζ an indicial root of L̃(0).

(c) Conjugating (26.4) by R^ϰ replaces R∂_R by R∂_R + ϰ: R^(−ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)R^ϰ =
−2R(R∂_R + ϰ)(R∂_R + 3/2 + S̄) + L̃(0)(ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω). Multiplying by R⁻² gives (26.6), which is
(18.7) with these data at iσ = ϰ.

(d) ḡ, t_*, |x|, dt̄ and d|x| are invariant under the rotations of the spatial factor, so L̄, built from them
((25.3), Section 23.2), commutes with ℒ_Ω; so does ρ, and ℒ_Ω preserves v.

(e) S̄ and the coefficients of L̃(0) do not depend on v, so v∂_v commutes with B := v∂_v + ϰ − 3/2 − S̄ and with
L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ, ∂_ω), and [v∂_v, ∂_v] = −∂_v gives [v∂_v, −2∂_vB] = 2∂_vB = −(N_sf(ϰ) − L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ, ∂_ω)).
For the second identity, ∂_v F(v∂_v) = F(v∂_v + 1)∂_v for every polynomial F, as ∂_v v∂_v = (v∂_v + 1)∂_v. So
∂_v N_sf(ϰ) = −2∂_v(v∂_v + 1 + ϰ − 3/2 − S̄)∂_v + L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ + 1, ∂_ω)∂_v = N_sf(ϰ + 1)∂_v.

(f) By (26.2) with x = v∂_v, L̃(0)(ω, x + ϰ, ∂_ω) − L̃(0)(ω, x + ϰ′, ∂_ω) = (ϰ − ϰ′)(−2x − ϰ − ϰ′ + a), and
the first terms of (26.3) differ by −2(ϰ − ϰ′)∂_v.

(g) With r := |x| = e^T and t = r(v + 1), dt = e^T((v + 1)dT + dv) and dr = e^T dT, so

    ĝ = r⁻²(−dt² + dr² + r²g̸) = −v(v + 2) dT² − 2(v + 1) dT dv − dv² + g̸.

The (T, v)-block has determinant −1, and inverting it gives the stated ĝ⁻¹. Then ĝ⁻¹(dT, dT) = 1 > 0 and
ĝ⁻¹(dv, dv) = v(v + 2), negative exactly on (−2, 0). Next, ρ^ϰ = e^(−ϰT) = e^(−iσT) for σ = −iϰ, so
N_sf(ϰ) = e^(iσT)P_c e^(−iσT) on T-independent sections by Definition 26.1. The operator 2L̄ is homogeneous of degree
−2 under the dilations ((26.1): S̄ is homogeneous of degree 0 and 2L̄̂(0) is ρ² times a dilation-invariant
operator), so P_c = 2|x|²L̄ is invariant under them, that is, its coefficients in (T, v, ω) do not depend on T; and its
principal symbol is |x|²ḡ⁻¹ = ĝ⁻¹, since 2L̄ is the wave operator of ḡ plus terms of order at most 1
((25.3)). The operator □_ĝ Id is T-independent with the same principal symbol, so P_c − □_ĝ Id is of first
order with T-independent coefficients. Finally
ĝ⁻¹(−σ dT + ξ dv + η) = σ² + 2(v + 1)σξ + v(v + 2)ξ² + |η|². ∎

At σ = −iϰ, Im σ = −Re ϰ. The region {v > 0} is where ∂_T is timelike for ĝ (inside the light cone of the origin);
{v = 0} is a Killing horizon of ∂_T; {v = −2} is past null infinity; and v = ∞ is the timelike line {x = 0}, a conic
singularity of the dilation-reduced space.

#### 26.1.2 The spaces

Let sf_(≥−1) := [−1, ∞]_v × 𝕊³, compactified at v = ∞ by R = v⁻¹, with the density

    μ_sf := |dv/(2 + v) dg̸|

of [Hin26, Proposition 9.2], smooth and positive on {v > −2} and a b-density at R = 0,
as |dv|/(2 + v) = |dR|/(R(1 + 2R)). Fix χ_∂ ∈ C^∞(ℝ_v) with χ_∂ = 0 on {v ≤ 2} and χ_∂ = 1 on {v ≥ 4}.

**Definition 26.4** ([Hin26, Definition 9.1] in dimension 4 + 1.) For s, μ ∈ ℝ, Ḣ^(s,μ)_b(sf_(≥−1)) is the
space of distributions u on ℝ_v × 𝕊³ supported in {v ≥ −1} with

    ‖u‖²_(Ḣ^(s,μ)_b) := ‖(1 − χ_∂)u‖²_(H^s) + ‖χ_∂u‖²_(H^s_(b,μ)) < ∞,    (26.7)

where H^s is the Sobolev space on (−2, 5) × 𝕊³ and H^s_(b,μ) is the space of Definition 13.2 at the end at 0 with
ϱ = R. At s = 0 the second norm is that of R^(−μ)L²(μ_sf), so near v = ∞, Ḣ^(s,μ)_b = ⟨v⟩^(−μ)H^s_b, as in [Hin26].
H̄^(s,μ)_b(sf_(≥−1)) is the space of restrictions to {v > −1} of such distributions without the support condition
(extendible at v = −1), with the quotient norm. For k ∈ ℕ_0, Ḣ^((s;k),μ)_(b;b) consists of the u ∈ Ḣ^(s,μ)_b with
(v∂_v)^j ℒ_Ω^α u ∈ Ḣ^(s,μ)_b for j + |α| ≤ k, where ℒ_Ω^α are the words of length |α| in the Lie derivatives along the
six rotation fields Ω_1, …, Ω_6 of 𝕊³; Ḣ^((s;∞),μ)_(b;b) is the intersection over k.

Since ℒ_Ω differs from Ω acting componentwise by a constant matrix, the same space results with componentwise Ω. On
compact subsets of {v ≠ 0}, v∂_v and the Ω_a span the vector fields, so there Ḣ^((s;k),μ)_(b;b) is H^(s+k); near R = 0
it is H^(s+k)_(b,μ) (Lemma 13.3 (h)).

*Duality and calculi.* With the pairing of L²(μ_sf) and a fibre inner product 𝔥 (below),
(Ḣ^(s,μ)_b)* = H̄^(−s,−μ)_b: near v = −1 by Lemma 11.27 (b), near R = 0 by Lemma 13.3 (d), glued with χ_∂. For
Re ϰ in a compact set, N_sf(ϰ): Ḣ^(s,μ)_b → Ḣ^(s−2,μ)_b is bounded (Lemma 13.3 (c) near R = 0, by
(26.4)). On {−3/2 < v < 5} we use the diffeomorphism (v, ω) ↦ x = e^v ω onto an annulus of ℝ⁴, so that the
pseudodifferential operators of Section 11.2 and the semiclassical ones of Section 12.2 with kernels supported there
act; the decay orders are then immaterial. Near R = 0 we use x = Rω, the end at 0 of Chapter 13.

**Lemma 26.5** (Fibre inner products.) For every δ > 0 there is a smooth fibre inner product 𝔥 on
𝕊³ × ℂ¹⁵, independent of v, with Re_𝔥 S̄ := ½(S̄ + S̄^(*𝔥)) ≥ −δ everywhere.

*Proof.* This is the construction in the proof of Corollary 25.12: at each ω, rescale a Jordan basis of S̄(ω) so
that the strict inequality holds at ω, hence near ω; the condition is convex in 𝔥, so a partition of unity on 𝕊³ glues
the local choices. It applies as min spec S̄ = 0. ∎

### 26.2 Fixed ϰ: the Fredholm property and b-regularity

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 9.2 (1) and (3)] in dimension 4 + 1.

#### 26.2.1 The dynamics and the radial set

Write ℛ_± := {v = 0, η = 0, ±ξ > 0} ⊂ T*sf ∖ o, the two halves of N*{v = 0} ∖ o, ∂ℛ_± for their images at fibre
infinity, Σ_0 := {p_2 = 0} at fibre infinity, ρ_∞ := |ξ|⁻¹ near ∂ℛ_±, η̂ := ρ_∞η, and 𝖧 := ±ρ_∞H_(p_2) near ∂ℛ_±,
the convention of Section 11.4.1.

**Lemma 26.6** (Dynamics at fibre infinity.) (a) Over {v ≥ 0}, Σ_0 = ∂ℛ_+ ∪ ∂ℛ_−; over {v > 0} and over
{v < −2}, Σ_0 = ∅.

(b) Near ∂ℛ_±, 𝖧ρ_∞ = β_0ρ_∞ with β_0 = 2(1 + v), 𝖧 vanishes on ∂ℛ_±, and q̃ := v² + |η̂|² is a quadratic defining
function of ∂ℛ_± at fibre infinity with

    𝖧q̃ = 4(v + 2)v² + 4(1 + v)|η̂|² ≥ 2q̃     on {|v| ≤ ½}.

So, in the sense of Section 11.4.1, ∂ℛ_± is a source, and the conclusion of Lemma 11.13 holds with q̃.

(c) Over {−2 < v < 0}, 𝖧v = 2v(v + 2) < 0 on Σ_0. Every integral curve of 𝖧 in Σ_0 over {−2 < v < 0} has v strictly
decreasing, tends to ∂ℛ_+ ∪ ∂ℛ_− in the backward direction, and reaches {v < −1} in the forward direction.

*Proof.* (a) Over v = 0, p_2 = |η|², so p_2 = 0 forces η = 0; over v > 0 and v < −2, p_2 is positive definite.

(b) p_2 is the sum of v(v + 2)ξ², a function of (v, ξ), and |η|², a function of (ω, η); so {p_2, |η|²} = 0 and

    H_(p_2) = 2v(v + 2)ξ∂_v − 2(v + 1)ξ²∂_ξ + H_(|η|²).

Near ∂ℛ_±, ± = sgn ξ, so ±ρ_∞ξ = 1 and ∂_ξρ_∞ = ∓ξ⁻². Hence 𝖧v = 2v(v + 2), 𝖧ρ_∞ = ±ρ_∞ · (−2(v + 1)ξ²)(∓ξ⁻²) =
2(v + 1)ρ_∞, 𝖧|η|² = 0, and 𝖧|η̂|² = 𝖧(ρ_∞²|η|²) = 2ρ_∞(𝖧ρ_∞)|η|² = 4(v + 1)|η̂|². This gives the formula for 𝖧q̃,
and on {|v| ≤ ½}, 4(v + 2) ≥ 6 and 4(1 + v) ≥ 2. In the coordinates (ρ_∞, v, ω, η̂) the ρ_∞-, v- and η̂-components of 𝖧
are 2(v + 1)ρ_∞, 2v(v + 2) and 2(v + 1)η̂ plus a term quadratic in η̂ (from the rescaled H_(|η|²)), and its
ω-component is linear in η̂; all vanish at ρ_∞ = 0, v = 0, η̂ = 0, that is on ∂ℛ_±.

(c) On Σ_0 over (−2, 0), ξ ≠ 0 (else η = 0 too), and 𝖧v = ±ρ_∞ · 2v(v + 2)ξ = 2v(v + 2). Backward, v increases and is
bounded by 0; if its limit were v_1 < 0, then 𝖧v ≤ −c < 0 near v_1 would contradict the boundedness of the backward
time. So v → 0, and then |η̂|² = −v(v + 2) → 0 on Σ_0, so the curve tends to {v = 0, η̂ = 0} = ∂ℛ_+ ∪ ∂ℛ_−. Forward,
𝖧v ≤ −c(v_0) < 0 on {v ≤ v_0}, v_0 < 0, so v reaches every value in (−2, v_0). ∎

**Lemma 26.7** (Radial estimate at the light cone.) Let 𝒟 ⊂ ℂ be compact, δ > 0, 𝔥 as in
Lemma 26.5, and 𝔐 a first-order differential operator on a neighbourhood of {v = 0}, with smooth coefficients,
whose principal symbol vanishes on ℛ_±, acting on ℂ¹⁵ ⊗ ℂ^m (the case 𝔐 = 0, m = 1 being N_sf(ϰ) itself). Put
N_𝔐 := N_sf(ϰ) ⊗ Id + 𝔐. Let U be a neighbourhood of ∂ℛ_±.

(1) (*Below threshold.*) Let s < 2 − δ − sup_𝒟 Re ϰ. There are B, G, E ∈ Ψ⁰, microsupported in U, with kernels
supported near {v = 0}, B elliptic at ∂ℛ_± and WF′(E) ∩ ∂ℛ_± = ∅, such that for ϰ ∈ 𝒟 and all M, in the strong
sense,

    ‖Bu‖_(H^s) ≤ C(‖GN_𝔐u‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖Eu‖_(H^s) + ‖u‖_(H^(−M))).    (26.8)

(2) (*Above threshold, the adjoint.*) Let s′ > s_0 > δ − 1 + sup_𝒟 Re ϰ. There are B, G as in (1) such that for
ϰ ∈ 𝒟, in the strong sense,

    ‖Bw‖_(H^(s′)) ≤ C(‖GN_𝔐^(*𝔥)w‖_(H^(s′−1)) + ‖Gw‖_(H^(s_0)) + ‖w‖_(H^(−M))),    (26.9)

the adjoint taken for L²(μ_sf) and 𝔥 (or for any other fibre inner product, as Proposition 11.14 notes).

*Proof.* The proof of Proposition 11.14 uses of the operator and of the hypotheses of Chapter 11 only: that the operator
is a differential operator with principal symbol G_0 Id, G_0 real; that ∂ℛ is a source, with 𝖧ρ_∞ = β_0ρ_∞ and
β_0 > 0; a quadratic defining function q̃ of ∂ℛ with 𝖧q̃ ≥ c′q̃ (the conclusion of Lemma 11.13); and the bound
(11.12), β_0⁻¹p_1 ≤ ϑ Id on ∂ℛ, where p_1 := ±ρ_∞σ_1(Im_𝔥(·)). Its kernels are compactly supported, so the decay
order is immaterial. Here G_0 = p_2 (Lemma 26.3 (a); 𝔐 is of first order), and Lemma 26.6 (b) shows that
∂ℛ_± is a source, with β_0 = 2(1 + v) and q̃. It remains to compute p_1 on ∂ℛ_±.

*The subprincipal symbol at the light cone.* The first-order terms of N_𝔐 are −2(ϰ − 3/2 − S̄)∂_v; the terms
a v∂_v, −2ϰ v∂_v and V of (26.2)–(26.3); 𝔐; and the first-order part of Im_𝔥 of the second-order
part D := −2∂_v v∂_v − (v∂_v)² + Δ_(𝕊³). The symbols of v∂_v, of V and of 𝔐 vanish on ℛ_± (where v = 0, resp. η = 0).
For D: the density μ_sf = m|dv dg̸|, m := (2 + v)⁻¹, and 𝔥 do not depend on v except through m. For an operator
Q = q_2(v)∂_v² + q_1(v)∂_v with real coefficients, its formal adjoint for m|dv| is m⁻¹Q^t m, Q^t the transpose
for |dv|, with second-order coefficient q_2 and first-order coefficient 2q_2′ + 2q_2m′/m − q_1. The (v, ∂_v)-part of D is
Q = −v(v + 2)∂_v² − (v + 2)∂_v, with 2q_2′ + 2q_2m′/m − q_1 = −4(v + 1) + 2v + (v + 2) = −(v + 2) = q_1; so the first-
order coefficient of D − D^(*𝔥) in ∂_v vanishes identically. And Δ_(𝕊³) − Δ_(𝕊³)^(*𝔥) = H⁻¹[H, Δ_(𝕊³)], 𝔥 = ⟨H·, ·⟩,
has symbol linear in η, which vanishes on ℛ_±. Finally, with A := ϰ − 3/2 − S̄, the principal symbols of −2A∂_v and of
its 𝔥-adjoint are −2iξA and 2iξA^(*𝔥), so σ_1(Im_𝔥(−2A∂_v)) = (2i)⁻¹(−2iξA − 2iξA^(*𝔥)) = −ξ(A + A^(*𝔥)). So on ℛ_±

    σ_1(Im_𝔥 N_𝔐) = ξ(3 + 2Re_𝔥 S̄ − 2Re ϰ),   p_1 = 3 + 2Re_𝔥 S̄ − 2Re ϰ,   β_0⁻¹p_1 = 3/2 + Re_𝔥 S̄ − Re ϰ,
    (26.10)

as ±ρ_∞ξ = 1 and β_0 = 2 at v = 0.

*(2).* For N_𝔐^(*𝔥), Re_𝔥 is the same and Im_𝔥 changes sign, so by Lemma 26.5
β_0⁻¹p_1(N_𝔐^(*𝔥)) = −(3/2 + Re_𝔥 S̄ − Re ϰ) ≤ (Re ϰ − 3/2 + δ) Id: this is the bound (11.12) with
ϑ := sup_𝒟 Re ϰ − 3/2 + δ. (No Im σ term enters: the proof uses (11.12) only through the lower bound
2β_0(s_0 − ½ − ϑ) of the commutator.) Proposition 11.14 (1) for N_𝔐^(*𝔥) gives (26.9) for s′ > s_0 > ½ + ϑ,
which is the stated condition.

*(1).* N_𝔐 = (N_𝔐^(*𝔥))^(*𝔥), and Proposition 11.14 (2), with N_𝔐^(*𝔥) in place of P̂(σ) and the ϑ just found, gives
(26.8) at every order 1 − s″ with s″ > ½ + ϑ, that is at every s < ½ − ϑ = 2 − δ − sup_𝒟 Re ϰ, with the
control operator E microsupported in supp ψ′(ς_R q̃), away from ∂ℛ_±. The iteration runs from −M with no threshold,
which is the strong sense. The constants are uniform for ϰ ∈ 𝒟, the symbols being polynomial in ϰ. ∎

In (1) the threshold is s < 2 + min spec S̄ − Re ϰ, up to δ. The derivation of [Hin26], from the characteristic
exponents 0 and 3/2 + α − ϰ, α ∈ spec S̄, of vN_sf(ϰ) at v = 0 (whose indicial operator there is
−2(v∂_v)(v∂_v + ϰ − 3/2 − S̄)) and from v_+^w ∈ H^(Re w + 1/2 − ε)_loc for every ε > 0, gives the same number.

#### 26.2.2 The artificial boundary and the hyperbolic region

**Lemma 26.8** (Slab estimates.) On the slabs Ω_(a,b) := {a < −v < b} × 𝕊³ with 0 < a < b < 2, the
statements of Proposition 11.29, Proposition 11.30 and Corollary 11.31 hold for L = N_sf(ϰ) and for L = N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥),
uniformly for ϰ in compact sets, with r := −v (so that the spaces H^s(Ω_(a,b))^(•,−), supported at r = b, are supported
at v = −b). In particular, with the cut-offs of Corollary 11.31 placed at r = ½ and r = ¼ (that is, at v = −½ and
v = −¼),

    ‖u|_({−1<v<−1/4})‖_(H^s) ≤ C‖N_sf(ϰ)u|_({−1<v<−1/4})‖_(H^(s−1)),     u ∈ Ḣ^s near {v = −1},    (26.11)

    ‖χw‖_(H̄^(1−s)) ≤ C(‖N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥)w‖_(H̄^(−s)({−1<v<−1/4})) + ‖χ_1w‖_(H^(1−s))),     w ∈ H̄^(1−s) near {v = −1},
    (26.12)

with χ = 1 on {v ≤ −½}, χ = 0 near {v ≥ −¼}, and χ_1 supported in {−½ < v < −¼} and equal to 1 near supp dχ.

*Proof.* The proofs of Proposition 11.29 and Proposition 11.30 use of L only: order 2, principal symbol G_0 Id with G_0
the dual of a Lorentzian metric 𝔤 on the slab for which dr is timelike; bounds for the coefficients and for
inf(−G_0(dr)); that L* is of the same form; and that the null bicharacteristics of G_0 move strictly monotonically in r
(Section 11.6.2 and (H4) of Section 11.1), used with Proposition 11.24 and Proposition 11.25. For N_sf(ϰ) on
{−2 < v < 0}: G_0 = p_2 is the dual of a Lorentzian metric with dv timelike, and
−p_2(dv) = −v(v + 2) ≥ min(a(2 − a), b(2 − b)) > 0 on the closure of Ω_(a,b) (Lemma 26.3 (a)); its adjoint has
the same principal symbol; and v is strictly monotone along the bicharacteristics there (Lemma 26.6 (c); at
finite frequencies likewise, as H_(p_2)v = 2v(v + 2)ξ ≠ 0 on {p_2 = 0} ∖ o). Time-orient 𝔤 so that v increases to
the future; then r = −v decreases to the future, as in Chapter 11. (26.11) is (11.29) with the roles of
L and L* exchanged (Proposition 11.30 (i) for the forward problem, with the support at r = 1), and (26.12) is
(11.28) (Proposition 11.30 (ii) applied to χw, the commutator [L, χ] being supported in supp dχ). ∎

#### 26.2.3 The Fredholm property

Fix ϰ ∈ ℂ, and call (s, μ) *admissible for* ϰ if

    s < 2 − Re ϰ,     μ ∈ (Re ϰ − 1, Re ϰ).    (26.13)

Then μ is not the real part of a root of J_ϰ ((26.5)): Re(ϰ − r) = μ would give Re r ∈ (0, 1), which
Proposition 25.6 (a) excludes. Put

    𝒳 := {u ∈ Ḣ^(s,μ)_b : N_sf(ϰ)u ∈ Ḣ^(s−1,μ)_b},     𝒴 := Ḣ^(s−1,μ)_b,
    𝒳* := {w ∈ H̄^(1−s,−μ)_b : N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥)w ∈ H̄^(−s,−μ)_b},    (26.14)

Hilbert spaces with the graph norms; 𝒴* = H̄^(1−s,−μ)_b. By Lemma 26.3 (f), 𝒳 is the same space for every ϰ′
near ϰ, with equivalent norms.

**Proposition 26.9** (The Fredholm property; [Hin26, Proposition 9.2 (1)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let (s, μ)
be admissible for ϰ, and μ_0 < μ.

(1) For every M there is C such that for u ∈ 𝒳 and w ∈ 𝒳*

    ‖u‖_(Ḣ^(s,μ)_b) ≤ C(‖N_sf(ϰ)u‖_(Ḣ^(s−1,μ)_b) + ‖u‖_(Ḣ^(−M,μ_0)_b)),    (26.15)

    ‖w‖_(H̄^(1−s,−μ)_b) ≤ C(‖N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥)w‖_(H̄^(−s,−μ)_b) + ‖w‖_(H̄^(−M,−μ−1)_b)),    (26.16)

uniformly for ϰ in a compact set on which (s, μ) stays admissible. (26.15) holds in the strong sense: if
u ∈ Ḣ^(−M,μ)_b has N_sf(ϰ)u ∈ Ḣ^(s−1,μ)_b, then u ∈ Ḣ^(s,μ)_b.

(2) N_sf(ϰ): 𝒳 → 𝒴 is Fredholm, and the annihilator of its range in 𝒴* is ker_(𝒳*) N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥).

(3) Its kernel and the annihilator of its range do not depend on the admissible pair (s, μ); nor, therefore, does its
index. Kernel elements lie in Ḣ^(s′,μ′)_b for every admissible (s′, μ′), are smooth on {v ≠ 0} and, near R = 0, lie in
𝒜^c for every c < Re ϰ. Elements of the annihilator are smooth on (−1, ∞) × 𝕊³ up to {v = −1}, and lie in 𝒜^c near
R = 0 for every c < 1 − Re ϰ.

*Proof.* (1) *Near v = −1.* (26.11) bounds u on {−1 < v < −¼} in H^s by N_sf(ϰ)u there, with no error term.

*The hyperbolic region and the light cone.* Let B_*, E be the operators of Lemma 26.7 (1) at ∂ℛ_+ ∪ ∂ℛ_−, with
U so small that the closed set K_E ⊃ WF′(E) lies over {−⅛ < v < ⅛}. Every point of K_E is either elliptic for p_2
(Lemma 26.6 (a), and p_2 ≠ 0 off Σ_0) or a point of Σ_0 over {v < 0}, whose forward 𝖧-curve reaches {v < −½}
by Lemma 26.6 (c) (v decreases along it). Along these curves, which have bounded length outside the neighbourhood
U_* of ∂ℛ_±, Proposition 11.25 applies at fibre infinity (the subprincipal part there is unrestricted and the order is
constant), with control from {v < −½}, where (26.11) applies. Finitely many such estimates, Proposition 11.24
off Σ_0, and compactness give ‖Eu‖_(H^s) ≤ C(‖N_sf(ϰ)u‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖φu‖_(H^(−M))), φ a cut-off to {v < 5}. With
(26.8), Proposition 11.24 on the rest of fibre infinity over {−1 ≤ v ≤ 5} (elliptic by Lemma 26.6 (a)
and (c), with the curves of Lemma 26.6 (c) for Σ_0 over {−1 < v < 0}), and the fact that at finite frequencies
over a compact set every operator of order −∞ is bounded by ‖u‖_(H^(−M)) there,

    ‖(1 − χ_∂)u‖_(H^s) ≤ C(‖N_sf(ϰ)u‖_(H^(s−1)({v<5})) + ‖φu‖_(H^(−M))).    (26.17)

*Near R = 0.* N_sf(ϰ) is of the form of Section 13.2.5 at the end at 0, b-elliptic (Lemma 26.3 (b)).
Lemma 13.6 at the b-weight μ gives ‖χ_∂u‖_(H^s_(b,μ)) ≤ C(‖χ̃_∂N_sf(ϰ)u‖_(H^(s−2)_(b,μ)) +
‖χ̃_∂u‖_(H^(−M)_(b,μ))), and Lemma 13.7 at c = μ (not the real part of a root of J_ϰ) with Lemma 13.3 (g),
exactly as in the proof of Theorem 13.11 (1) near ∂X, bounds the last term by
C‖N_sf(ϰ)u‖_(H^(−M−2)_(b,μ)) + C‖u‖_(Ḣ^(−M,μ_0)_b) plus a term that is absorbed. With (26.17) this is
(26.15); the overlap {2 < v < 5} is in the interior, where the norms agree.

*The adjoint.* For w ∈ 𝒳*: (26.12) near v = −1, its last term controlled by the estimates that follow on
{−½ < v < −¼}. Lemma 26.7 (2) at ∂ℛ_± at the order 1 − s, with s_0 ∈ (Re ϰ − 1 + δ, 1 − s) (δ small;
1 − s > Re ϰ − 1 is (26.13)); then Proposition 11.25 along the 𝖧-curves of Lemma 26.6 (c) forwards,
from a neighbourhood of ∂ℛ_± to {v < −½} (the adjoint chain of Section 11.7.1, the curves starting in the region
controlled by the radial estimate); and Proposition 11.24 elsewhere. The term ‖Gw‖_(H^(s_0)) is bounded by
δ′‖w‖_(H^(1−s)) + C_(δ′)‖w‖_(H^(−M)) on a compact set (Ehrling, as s_0 < 1 − s). Near R = 0, N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥) is
b-elliptic with Mellin symbol H_0⁻¹J_ϰ(−ζ̄)^†H_0 up to lower-order terms on 𝕊³, whose roots are
{−ζ̄ : ζ a root of J_ϰ}, for the b-density μ_sf (as (R∂_R)^† = −R∂_R; this is (13.11) without the shift by 2,
which there comes from the density |dx|); −μ is not the real part of one. Lemma 13.6, Lemma 13.7 and
Lemma 13.3 (g) give (26.16) as there.

(2) The inclusions Ḣ^(s,μ)_b ↪ Ḣ^(−M,μ_0)_b and H̄^(1−s,−μ)_b ↪ H̄^(−M,−μ−1)_b are compact for
−M < min(s, 1 − s) (Lemma 13.3 (e) at R = 0, Rellich on the compact remainder), so (26.15) and
(26.16) give finite-dimensional kernels and closed ranges. *Green's formula*
⟨N_sf(ϰ)u, w⟩ = ⟨u, N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥)w⟩ for u ∈ 𝒳 and w ∈ 𝒳*: split with χ_∂ and a cut-off near v = −1; near v = −1 it
is Lemma 11.27 (d) with the density of C_c^∞({v > −1}) in Ḣ^s (Lemma 11.27 (a)); near R = 0 it is the argument
of the proof of Theorem 13.11; in between, Friedrichs mollifiers J_ε serve: [N_sf(ϰ), J_ε] is bounded H^s → H^(s−1)
uniformly and tends to 0 strongly, so J_εu → u in 𝒳 locally. The cokernel is then the kernel of N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥) on 𝒳*,
as in the proof of Theorem 13.11.

(3) *Kernel.* Let u ∈ 𝒳 with N_sf(ϰ)u = 0. The estimates of (1) hold in the strong sense at every order
s′ < 2 − Re ϰ: (26.8) needs no a priori regularity beyond H^(−M), and the propagation estimates, the
elliptic estimates and (26.11) hold at every order. So u ∈ H^(s′) on {v < 5} for all such s′, and u ∈ H^∞ on
compact subsets of {v ≠ 0} (there the radial estimate is not needed: ellipticity on {v > 0}, propagation from
(26.11) on {v < 0}). Near R = 0, Lemma 13.6 at every order and Lemma 13.8, with
(c_−, c_+) := (Re ϰ − 1, Re ϰ) containing no real part of a root of J_ϰ and c = μ, give χ_∂u ∈ H^∞_(b,c′) for every
c′ < Re ϰ, so u ∈ 𝒜^(c′) there (Lemma 13.3 (f)). So u lies in the kernel for every admissible pair.
*Annihilator.* Let w ∈ 𝒳* with N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥)w = 0. Lemma 26.7 (2) in the strong sense at every order s′ ≥ 1 − s
(with the a priori order 1 − s above threshold), propagation and ellipticity give w ∈ H^∞ on (−1, ∞) × 𝕊³ away from
R = 0, and (26.12) at every order gives smoothness up to v = −1. Near R = 0, Lemma 13.8 for
N_sf(ϰ)^(*𝔥), whose root-free strip containing −μ is (−Re ϰ, 1 − Re ϰ), gives w ∈ H^∞_(b,c′) for every
c′ < 1 − Re ϰ, which contains the b-weight −μ′ of every admissible μ′. So w is an annihilator for every admissible pair.
∎

#### 26.2.4 b-regularity at the light cone

Let 𝒟^m be the operators Σ_(j+|α|≤m) c_(jα)(v, ω)(v∂_v)^j ℒ_Ω^α on (−½, 2) × 𝕊³, c_(jα) smooth matrix functions.
Since v∂_v commutes with each ℒ_Ω, [ℒ_(Ω_a), ℒ_(Ω_b)] is a combination of the ℒ_(Ω_c), and derivatives of the
coefficients are smooth, [𝒟^p, 𝒟^q] ⊂ 𝒟^(p+q−1) and 𝒟^p𝒟^q ⊂ 𝒟^(p+q). A *word* W^α is a product of |α| factors from
𝒢 := {v∂_v, ℒ_(Ω_1), …, ℒ_(Ω_6)}; every element of 𝒟^m is a combination of words of length at most m with smooth
coefficients on the left. For u supported in (−½, 2) × 𝕊³, u ∈ Ḣ^((s;k),μ)_(b;b) if and only if W^αu ∈ H^s
for |α| ≤ k; and then Du ∈ H^s for D ∈ 𝒟^k and Du ∈ H^(s−1) for D ∈ 𝒟^(k+1) (one factor being a first-order differential
operator).

**Lemma 26.10** (Commuting with the dilation and the rotations.) N_sf(ϰ)ℒ_Ω = ℒ_ΩN_sf(ϰ), and

    N_sf(ϰ)(v∂_v) = (v∂_v + 1)N_sf(ϰ) − 𝔐_1(v∂_v) − Σ_a 𝔐_aℒ_(Ω_a) − 𝔐_0,    (26.18)

with 𝔐_1, 𝔐_a, 𝔐_0 ∈ 𝒟¹ (on all of {v > −2}, with coefficients independent of v), the principal symbols of 𝔐_1 and
𝔐_a (as first-order differential operators) vanishing on N*{v = 0}.

*Proof.* The first identity is Lemma 26.3 (d). By Lemma 26.3 (e),
N_sf(ϰ)(v∂_vu) = (v∂_v + 1)N_sf(ϰ)u − L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ, ∂_ω)u. The six rotation fields Z_(ij) = x_i∂_(x_j) − x_j∂_(x_i)
of 𝕊³ ⊂ ℝ⁴ satisfy Δ_(𝕊³) = −Σ_a Ω_a² on functions. Write Ω_a = ℒ_(Ω_a) − A_a with constant matrices A_a (the Lie
derivative of the frame dt_*, dx¹, …, dx⁴ along a rotation is constant), and V = Σ_a V_aΩ_a + V_0 with V_a, V_0 smooth.
From −Ω_a² = −Ω_aℒ_(Ω_a) + Ω_aA_a and Ω_aA_a = A_aℒ_(Ω_a) − A_a², (26.2) gives

    L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ, ∂_ω)u = 𝔐_1(v∂_vu) + Σ_a 𝔐_a(ℒ_(Ω_a)u) + 𝔐_0u,

with 𝔐_1 := −v∂_v − 2ϰ + a, 𝔐_a := −Ω_a + A_a + V_a and 𝔐_0 := aϰ − ϰ² + b + V_0 − Σ_a(V_a + A_a)A_a. The principal
symbol of 𝔐_1 is −ivξ and that of 𝔐_a is −iη(Ω_a); both vanish on {v = 0, η = 0}. ∎

**Proposition 26.11** (Commuted equations.) For every word W^α, |α| = j ≥ 1, on (−½, 2) × 𝕊³,

    N_sf(ϰ)W^α = W̃^αN_sf(ϰ) − Σ_(|β|=j) 𝔐_(αβ)W^β − Σ_(|β|<j) 𝔐′_(αβ)W^β,    (26.19)

with W̃^α ∈ 𝒟^j, 𝔐_(αβ) ∈ 𝒟¹ with principal symbols vanishing on N*{v = 0}, and 𝔐′_(αβ) ∈ 𝒟^(j−|β|) a combination of
products D_1D_2 with D_1 ∈ 𝒟¹ and D_2 ∈ 𝒟^(j−1−|β|).

*Proof.* Induction on j. For j = 1 it is Lemma 26.10 (W̃ = v∂_v + 1 or ℒ_Ω; 𝔐′_(·,∅) = 𝔐_0, of the form D_1 with
D_2 = Id). Suppose (26.19) holds for α, and let W ∈ 𝒢. Then
N_sf(ϰ)WW^α = (W̃N_sf(ϰ) − Σ_(W′) 𝔐_(WW′)W′ − 𝔐_W)W^α, and
W̃N_sf(ϰ)W^α = W̃W̃^αN_sf(ϰ) − Σ_β W̃𝔐_(αβ)W^β − Σ_β W̃𝔐′_(αβ)W^β. Write
W̃𝔐_(αβ)W^β = 𝔐_(αβ)W̃W^β + [W̃, 𝔐_(αβ)]W^β. The first is 𝔐_(αβ) (with vanishing symbol) times WW^β (of length j + 1),
plus terms 𝔐_(αβ)cW^β of length j (as W̃ − W is a constant c), which are of the second kind with D_1 = c𝔐_(αβ) and
D_2 = Id ∈ 𝒟^((j+1)−1−j); the commutator lies in 𝒟¹ and multiplies W^β, |β| = j, a term of the same kind. For |β| < j
and 𝔐′_(αβ) = D_1D_2, W̃D_1D_2W^β = D_1(W̃D_2)W^β + [W̃, D_1]D_2W^β, with W̃D_2 ∈ 𝒟^(j−|β|) = 𝒟^((j+1)−1−|β|) and
[W̃, D_1] ∈ 𝒟¹: of the second kind for the length j + 1. 𝔐_(WW′)W′W^α is of the first kind (W′W^α of length j + 1), and
𝔐_WW^α is of the second kind (D_1 = 𝔐_W, D_2 = Id, |β| = j). ∎

**Proposition 26.12** (b-regularity at the light cone; [Hin26, Proposition 9.2 (3)] in dimension 4 + 1.)
Let (s, μ) be admissible for ϰ, k ∈ ℕ_0, and u ∈ Ḣ^(s,μ)_b with N_sf(ϰ)u ∈ Ḣ^((s−1;k),μ)_(b;b). Then
u ∈ Ḣ^((s;k),μ)_(b;b).

*Proof.* Put f := N_sf(ϰ)u. *Away from v = 0.* On {v < −¼}, f ∈ H^(s−1+k), and (26.11) and propagation at
order s + k give u ∈ H^(s+k) there (Proposition 26.9 (1) in the strong sense, which on {v < 0} uses no radial
estimate). On compact subsets of {v > 0}, ellipticity gives u ∈ H^(s+1+k)_loc; near R = 0, Lemma 13.6 gives
χ_∂u ∈ H^(s+k)_(b,μ). Each of these is the module regularity there (Section 26.1.2).

*Near v = 0.* Let χ ∈ C_c^∞((−½, 2)) equal 1 on [−¼, 1], and u_0 := χu. Then N_sf(ϰ)u_0 = χf + [N_sf(ϰ), χ]u, and
[N_sf(ϰ), χ]u is supported where u ∈ H^(s+k); so N_sf(ϰ)u_0 ∈ Ḣ^((s−1;k)), with support in (−½, 2) × 𝕊³. We show by
induction on j ≤ k that W^αu_0 ∈ H^s for |α| ≤ j. For j = 0 it is the hypothesis. Let it hold for j − 1, and let
U := (W^αu_0)_(|α|=j), a priori in H^(s−1) (one factor of each word is a first-order operator applied to
W^(α′)u_0 ∈ H^s). By (26.19),

    (N_sf(ϰ) ⊗ Id + 𝔐)U = F,     𝔐 := (𝔐_(αβ))_(|α|=|β|=j),
    F := (W̃^αN_sf(ϰ)u_0 − Σ_(|β|<j) 𝔐′_(αβ)W^βu_0)_α,

and F ∈ H^(s−1): W̃^αN_sf(ϰ)u_0 ∈ H^(s−1), as W̃^α ∈ 𝒟^j, j ≤ k, and N_sf(ϰ)u_0 ∈ Ḣ^((s−1;k)); and in each term
D_1D_2W^βu_0 of 𝔐′_(αβ)W^βu_0, D_2W^β ∈ 𝒟^(j−1), so D_2W^βu_0 ∈ H^s by the induction hypothesis (the remark before
Lemma 26.10, with k = j − 1), and D_1 ∈ 𝒟¹ maps H^s to H^(s−1). The operator N_sf(ϰ) ⊗ Id + 𝔐 satisfies
Lemma 26.7 (1) at ∂ℛ_±, with the threshold of N_sf(ϰ) (the symbol of 𝔐 vanishes there); along Σ_0 over
{−½ < v < 0}, Proposition 11.25 applies to it (principal symbol p_2 Id; 𝔐 enters the subprincipal part, on which no sign
is imposed), with control from {v < −¼}, where U ∈ H^s by the first step; and it is elliptic elsewhere over supp u_0.
The estimates in the strong sense, as in Proposition 26.9 (1), give U ∈ H^s. ∎

### 26.3 Injectivity for Re ϰ < 2

This section is the first half of [Hin26, Proposition 9.2 (2)] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Lemma 26.13** (Conormality at the light cone.) Let s ∈ ℝ with s − ½ ∉ ℤ, and let u ∈ H^s(ℝ × 𝕊³) be
supported in {v ≥ 0} near {v = 0}, with W^αu ∈ H^s near {v = 0} for every word W^α. Then for every α there is C
with |W^αu(v, ω)| ≤ C v^(s−½) on (0, 1) × 𝕊³.

*Proof.* Localise with a cut-off in v, which commutes with the rotations, and with v∂_v up to a smooth compactly
supported function. With the Fourier transform in v and the expansion in spherical harmonics (eigenvalues κ_k of
Δ_(𝕊³)), ‖u‖²_(H^s) = ∫ Σ_k (1 + ξ² + κ_k)^s |û_k(ξ)|² dξ ≥ ‖u‖²_(H^s(ℝ;L²(𝕊³))) for s ≥ 0, and the same applied to
Ω^γu, |γ| ≤ m, gives u ∈ H^s(ℝ; H^m(𝕊³)) for every m; likewise for each W^αu. Let ℋ := H^m(𝕊³) with m ≥ 2, so that
ℋ ⊂ C⁰(𝕊³). Write s = k_0 + ½ + a_1 with k_0 ∈ ℕ_0 and a_1 ∈ (0, 1). For g ∈ H^s(ℝ; ℋ), g^(k_0) ∈ H^(½+a_1)(ℝ; ℋ)
and ‖g^(k_0)(x) − g^(k_0)(y)‖_ℋ ≤ C|x − y|^(a_1)‖g‖_(H^s): by Fourier inversion and Cauchy–Schwarz this difference is
at most (2π)⁻¹‖⟨τ⟩^(½+a_1)(g^(k_0))^∧‖_(L²) times (∫ min(4, |x − y|²τ²)⟨τ⟩^(−1−2a_1) dτ)^(1/2), and the integral is at
most C|x − y|^(2a_1) (split at |τ| = |x − y|⁻¹; 0 < a_1 < 1); and g^(i), i ≤ k_0, are continuous. If g is supported in
{v ≥ 0}, then g^(i)(0) = 0 for i ≤ k_0, and Taylor's formula gives ‖g(v)‖_ℋ ≤ Cv^(k_0+a_1) = Cv^(s−½) for v ∈ (0, 1).
Applied to g = W^αu this proves the case s > ½. For s < 0 the first step uses (1 + ξ²)^s ≤ (1 + ξ² + κ_k)^s(1 + κ_k)^(−s)
instead, at the cost of ⌈−s⌉ more rotations.

*The case s < ½.* Let j ∈ ℕ with s + j > ½, and let I be the primitive in v vanishing on {v < 0}, cut off beyond the
support. It maps H^σ(ℝ; ℋ) to H^(σ+1)(ℝ; ℋ) for compactly supported elements, satisfies v∂_vI = I(v∂_v + 1), and
commutes with the rotations. So U := I^ju satisfies the hypotheses at order s + j, and the case s > ½ gives |W^αU|
≤ Cv^(s+j−½). On (0, 1), u = ∂_v^jU = v^(−j) ∏_(i=0)^(j−1)(v∂_v − i)U, and W^αv^(−j) = v^(−j)W^α_((−j)), where
W^α_((−j)) is W^α with every v∂_v replaced by v∂_v − j; so |W^αu| ≤ Cv^(s−½). The number of words this uses is counted
in Lemma 26.25. ∎

**Proposition 26.14** (Injectivity.) Let Re ϰ < 2 and (s, μ) be admissible for ϰ. Then N_sf(ϰ): 𝒳 → 𝒴 is
injective.

*Proof.* Let u ∈ 𝒳 with N_sf(ϰ)u = 0. By Proposition 26.9 (3) we may change (s, μ): take
s ∈ (max(−½, ½ − Re ϰ), 2 − Re ϰ), which is possible as Re ϰ < 2, with s − ½ ∉ ℤ, and μ ∈ (Re ϰ − 1, Re ϰ). Put
a_0 := s − ½ > −1, so that a_0 + Re ϰ > 0.

*Step 1: support and regularity.* By Proposition 26.12, u ∈ Ḣ^((s;∞),μ)_(b;b). On {−1 < v < 0}, u solves
N_sf(ϰ)u = 0, is supported in {v ≥ −1}, and v is a time function there; by the uniqueness step of Proposition 11.30 on
the slabs {−1 − ε′ < v < −ε} (Lemma 26.8), u = 0 on {v < −ε} for every ε > 0. So u is supported in {v ≥ 0}. It
is smooth on {v > 0} (by ellipticity), satisfies |W^αu| ≤ Cv^(a_0) on (0, 1) by Lemma 26.13,
and |W^αu| ≤ Cv^(−(Re ϰ−ε)) on {v ≥ ½} for every ε > 0 by Proposition 26.9 (3) (u ∈ 𝒜^(Re ϰ−ε) near R = 0, R = v⁻¹,
the b-fields being v∂_v = −R∂_R and the rotations).

*Step 2: the Fourier transform.* u is the extension by zero of u|_(v>0). Indeed, let φ be smooth with compact support
and χ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ) equal to 1 near 0. Then ⟨u, φχ(·/ε)⟩ → 0 as ε → 0, since ‖φχ(·/ε)‖_(H^(−s)) = O(ε^(min(½,½+s))) and
s > −½; and ⟨u, φ(1 − χ(·/ε))⟩ → ∫_(v>0) uφ by dominated convergence (|u| ≤ Cv^(a_0), a_0 > −1). So Lemma 18.31
applies to f := u|_(v>0), with a := a_0 and b := Re ϰ − ε. The equation holds
across v = 0 by hypothesis, so the step of the proof of Lemma 18.32 that establishes it there is not needed. So
û(r̂, ω) := ∫ e^(ir̂v)u dv is smooth on {r̂ ≠ 0}, with

    |(r̂∂_r̂)^j ∂_ω^α û| ≤ C(1 + |r̂|)^(−1−a_0) (|r̂|/(1 + |r̂|))^(min(Re ϰ−1−ε, 0)−ε).

By Lemma 26.3 (c), N_sf(ϰ) is the operator of (18.58) at iσ = ϰ, with c = 3/2, S_0 = S̄ and
P^(0)(0) = L̃(0). The transformed equation follows from ℱ(∂_vg) = −ir̂ℱg and ℱ(vg) = −i∂_r̂ℱg, which give
ℱ(v∂_vg) = −(r̂∂_r̂ + 1)ℱg: the equation N_sf(ϰ)u = 0 on ℝ × 𝕊³ becomes

    [2ir̂(−r̂∂_r̂ + ϰ − 5/2 − S̄) + L̃(0)(ω, −r̂∂_r̂ − 1 + ϰ, ∂_ω)]û = 0,

which is (18.59) at iσ = ϰ. For r̂ > 0 put w^♭_±(r̂, ω) := r̂^(1−ϰ)û(±r̂, ω). Conjugation by r̂^(1−ϰ) replaces
r̂∂_r̂ by r̂∂_r̂ + ϰ − 1, and r̂ ↦ −r̂ changes the sign of the first term only; so on {r̂ > 0}, with ρ̂ := r̂⁻¹
(r̂∂_r̂ = −ρ̂∂_ρ̂) and after multiplication by ρ̂²,

    [±2iρ̂(ρ̂∂_ρ̂ − 3/2 − S̄) + ρ̂²L̃(0)(ω, ρ̂∂_ρ̂, ∂_ω)]w^♭_± = N_tf(±1)w^♭_± = 0,

with N_tf of (13.12) for these data, which is the operator N_tf(L̂_b, ±1) of Section 25.7; this is
(18.60).

*Step 3: the weights.* As |r̂^(1−ϰ)| = r̂^(1−Re ϰ) is conormal,

    w^♭_± ∈ 𝒜^(a_0+Re ϰ, −β)(tf),     β := max(2ε, Re ϰ − 1 + 2ε),    (26.20)

in the notation of Chapter 13 (ρ_sctf first): at r̂ → ∞ the exponent is −1 − a_0 + 1 − Re ϰ, and at r̂ → 0 it is
1 − Re ϰ + min(Re ϰ − 1 − ε, 0) − ε ≥ −β. Take ε so small that β < 1, which is possible as Re ϰ < 2; then β ∈ (0, 1).

*Step 4: tf-admissibility.* By Proposition 25.11, L̂_b is tf-admissible with every weight in (0, 1]. Fix
β* ∈ (β, 1] and q := 2 − β*, and in the spaces of Section 13.4.3 take orders 𝗋_± admissible as there whose value
near R_out, the zero section over sctf, is below a_0 + Re ϰ − 2 (admissibility imposes only an upper bound there,
Lemma 11.32). Then w^♭_+ ∈ 𝒳_(tf,0) and w^♭_− ∈ 𝒳_(tf,π), exactly as in the proof of Lemma 18.32, with the
weight γ_I there replaced by a_0 + Re ϰ > 0: near sctf by Lemma 11.37 (a), near ztf as
𝒜^(−β) ⊂ H^∞_(b,q−2) (Lemma 13.3 (f)), and smooth in between. By Corollary 13.16 (a), N_tf(e^(iθ)) is invertible
on these spaces at θ = 0 and θ = π, so w^♭_± = 0 and û = 0 on {r̂ ≠ 0}.

*Step 5.* As at the end of the proof of Lemma 18.32: for ψ ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; ℂ¹⁵), ⟨û, ψ⟩ is supported in {0}, so ⟨u, ψ⟩
is a polynomial in v, vanishing for v < 0; so u = 0. ∎

In dimension 3 + 1, [Hin26, Proposition 9.2] obtains injectivity for Re ϰ < 1 + ε_ind; its bound comes from the
tf-weights, which there must lie in (0, ε_ind). At n = 4 the gap (0, 1] and the tf-admissibility on all of it leave as
the only constraint the tf-weight β < 1 of Step 3, that is Re ϰ < 2.

### 26.4 High frequencies: the semiclassical estimate

This section is [Hin26, (9.9)] in dimension 4 + 1.

#### 26.4.1 The family

Fix C_ϰ ≥ 1. For ϰ with |Re ϰ| ≤ C_ϰ and |Im ϰ| ≥ 1 put σ := −iϰ, h := |Im ϰ|⁻¹ and z := hσ = ±1 + iy, with
y = −h Re ϰ and ± = sgn Im ϰ; so z ∈ 𝒵_h := {±1 + iy : |y| ≤ C_ϰh} and ϰ = iz/h. As in [Hin26], let
R̃ ∈ C^∞((0, ∞)) with R̃(R) = R for R < ½, R̃ ≥ ½ on [½, 1] and R̃ = 1 for R ≥ 1, and put

    N_h := R̃^(−ϰ)R̃^(−2)N_sf(ϰ)R̃^ϰ,   P := P_(h,z) := h²N_h.    (26.21)

By Lemma 26.3 (c), on {R < ½}, P = h²N⁰(h⁻¹z) = P_(ι,h,z) of (18.12) for P_0 = 2L_b; on {R ≥ 1}
({v ≤ 1}), P = h²N_sf(ϰ). On {½ ≤ R ≤ 1} conjugation by R̃^ϰ = e^((iz/h) log R̃) is the semiclassical conjugation by
e^(iφ/h), φ := z log R̃: it translates the fibres by (Re z) d log R̃ and multiplies by R̃^(−Re ϰ), a smooth function
bounded above and below, with O(y/h) derivatives.

*The spaces.* On {R < ½} we use the spaces of Section 18.3.1, H^((𝗌′;·,γ_cf,γ_cf;𝖻)), for functions supported in
{R < ½} (the weight at 0f does not enter); on {v < 4}, the semiclassical Sobolev spaces H^(s,𝖻)_h of Section 12.2
(differential order s, constant, and semiclassical order 𝖻, a function on phase space), with supports at v = −1. With
a partition of unity in v these define ℋ_𝐨, 𝐨 := (s; γ_cf, γ_cf; 𝖻), and 𝒴_𝐨 := ℋ_((s−1;γ_cf−2,γ_cf;𝖻+1)); on
{¼ < R < 1} the spaces of Chapter 18 are the semiclassical ones of the interior (h𝒱(ι⁺), Section 18.2.1), so the two
descriptions agree there, uniformly in h. The differential order of the spaces of Chapter 18 is chosen equal to s on
{R > ¼}, which is allowed, P being elliptic at fibre infinity over {R < ½} (Section 18.3.1). The weight
γ_cf ∈ (−1, 0) is fixed, and α_+ := −γ_cf − 2, so that α_+ + 2 ∈ (0, 1) is a weight with which P_0 = 2L_b is
tf-admissible (Proposition 25.11).

For fixed h, ℋ_𝐨 is Ḣ^(s,γ_cf)_b with an equivalent norm (Section 18.2.1), and u ↦ R̃^ϰu maps it onto
Ḣ^(s,γ_cf+Re ϰ)_b (|R̃^ϰ| = R^(Re ϰ) near R = 0, and R∂_R R̃^(i Im ϰ) is bounded); with
N_sf(ϰ) = R̃^(2+ϰ)N_hR̃^(−ϰ), the weight of the target matches: (γ_cf − 2) + 2 + Re ϰ.

#### 26.4.2 Symbols and dynamics across the light cone

**Lemma 26.15** (Symbols and dynamics.) On {v < 4}:

(a) The principal symbol of P is p_z := (vξ + z)((v + 2)ξ + z) + |η|² on {R ≥ 1} ({v ≤ 1}), and on {½ ≤ R ≤ 1} the
transport of R̃⁻²p_z by the fibre translation of Section 26.4.1. With z = ±1 + iy,

    Re p_z = p_(±1) − y²,     Im p_z = 2y((v + 1)ξ ± 1),

so h⁻¹Im P is a semiclassical operator of first order with coefficients bounded by C_ϰ: in (12.3) the
coefficient ℓ of the term in 𝒬 may be taken to be 0 and every imaginary term is part of 𝒫_1 (Remark 12.27 (a), which
holds also at fibre infinity over this compact region, where ℓ𝒬 and 𝒫_1 have the same order).

(b) Let z_0 = 1 and p := p_1. With ξ̃ := −(v + 2)(vξ + 1),

    H_pξ̃ = 2(v + 1)(|η|² − p),     H_p|η|² = 0.

On Σ := {p = 0} (finite frequencies), ξ ≠ 0, and ξ̃ is non-decreasing along H_p over {v > −1}, strictly where η ≠ 0; on
Σ ∩ {η = 0}, ξ̃ ∈ {−2, 0}.

(c) Σ = Σ_+ ∪ Σ_−, ±ξ > 0. With w := v + 1, t := |ξ| and L := |η| (constant along the flow): Σ_+ ∩ {v ≥ −1 − δ_1}
lies over {v < 0} for small δ_1 > 0, with ξ ≥ −1/v over {−1 ≤ v < 0}, H_pv ≤ −2 on {−1 < v < 0} and H_pv < 0 over
[−1 − δ_1, −1]. Σ_− over {−1 − δ_1 ≤ v ≤ 0} has H_pv > 0 and

    t = [−w + (1 + L²(1 − w²))^(1/2)]/(1 − w²),

bounded by a constant depending on L (with the limit (1 + L²)/2 at v = 0). Over {v > 0}, Σ_− lies in
{1/(v + 2) ≤ t ≤ 1/v} ∩ {w² ≤ 1 + L⁻²}, so for L > 0 in {v ≤ v_max(L) := (1 + L⁻²)^(1/2) − 1}.

(d) Every maximal integral curve of H_p in Σ over {v < 4} is one of the following. (i) A curve in Σ_+, which tends to
∂ℛ_+ at fibre infinity backwards (with v ↑ 0 and t → ∞) and reaches {v < −1} forwards. (ii) A curve in Σ_− with
L > 0, which comes from {v < −1}, crosses {v = 0} at t = (1 + L²)/2, has one turning point of v, and tends to ∂ℛ_− at
fibre infinity forwards, with v ↓ 0 and t → ∞ (if v_max(L) ≥ 4, part of it lies in {R < ¼}, where the description of
Chapter 18 applies). (iii) The incoming ray {η = 0, ξ = −1/(v + 2)}, from {v < −1} to the cone point v → ∞ (in the
coordinates of Chapter 18 it tends to R_(cf,1,in)), and the outgoing ray {η = 0, ξ = −1/v} over {v > 0}, from the
cone point (R_(cf,out)) to ∂ℛ_−.

(e) In the coordinates of Chapter 18 over {R < ½} (R = v⁻¹ and, for z = 1, ξ_cħ = −v(vξ + 1), η_cħ = vη under the
conjugation), the symbol of P is (18.14), G_(ι,1) = v²p, and ξ̃ = (1 + 2R)ξ_cħ. With the field 𝖧 of
(18.37),

    𝖧ξ̃ = −2(1 + R)ξ_cħ(ξ̃ + 2) ≥ 0     on {G_(ι,1) = 0} over sf,

with equality only at ξ_cħ = 0 and at ξ̃ = −2. The future flow of Chapter 18 (its ς = +1) is the flow of H_p, up to a
positive factor.

(f) For z_0 = −1 everything holds after (ξ, η) ↦ (−ξ, −η), with the flow reversed, as
p_(−z)(v, ω; −ξ, −η) = p_z(v, ω; ξ, η) (the symmetry of Section 18.3.2).

*Proof.* (a) The semiclassical principal symbol of h²N_sf(iz/h) is obtained from (26.3) with h∂_v ↦ iξ,
hϰ = iz and h²Δ_(𝕊³) ↦ |η|², the terms carrying a further factor h dropping out:

    −2(iξ)(ivξ + iz) − (ivξ + iz)² + |η|² = 2ξ(vξ + z) + (vξ + z)² + |η|² = (vξ + z)((v + 2)ξ + z) + |η|².

The transport on {½ ≤ R ≤ 1} is that of the conjugation. With A := vξ ± 1 and B := (v + 2)ξ ± 1,
(A + iy)(B + iy) = AB − y² + iy(A + B), and A + B = 2((v + 1)ξ ± 1); here |y| ≤ C_ϰh.

(b) The function ξ̃ does not depend on (ω, η), so H_pξ̃ = ∂_ξp ∂_vξ̃ − ∂_vp ∂_ξξ̃, with

    ∂_ξp = 2(v(v + 2)ξ + v + 1),   ∂_vp = 2ξ((v + 1)ξ + 1),   ∂_vξ̃ = −(2(v + 1)ξ + 1),   ∂_ξξ̃ = −v(v + 2).

With w = v + 1 and v(v + 2) = w² − 1 this gives

    H_pξ̃ = −2((w² − 1)ξ + w)(2wξ + 1) + 2(w² − 1)ξ(wξ + 1) = −2w((w² − 1)ξ² + 2wξ + 1) = −2w(p − |η|²),

as p − |η|² = (vξ + 1)((v + 2)ξ + 1) = (w² − 1)ξ² + 2wξ + 1. H_p|η|² = {p, |η|²} = 0 as in Lemma 26.6 (b). If
ξ = 0 then p = 1 + |η|² > 0. On Σ, H_pξ̃ = 2(v + 1)|η|². With a := vξ + 1 and b := (v + 2)ξ + 1, p = ab + |η|², and
η = 0 forces a = 0 (ξ̃ = 0) or b = 0 (ξ = −1/(v + 2), a = 2/(v + 2), ξ̃ = −2).

(c) With k := wξ + 1 we have a = k − ξ, b = k + ξ, so p = k² − ξ² + |η|²; and H_pv = ∂_ξp = 2(v(v + 2)ξ + v + 1),
H_pξ = −∂_vp = −2ξk. On Σ_+ over {v ≥ −1}, k ≥ 1 and ξ² ≥ k² give ξ ≥ wξ + 1, so v < 0 and ξ ≥ −1/v, whence
v(v + 2)ξ ≤ −(v + 2) and H_pv ≤ −2 on {−1 < v < 0}; over {v < −1} the inequality v < 0 is trivial, and near v = −1
the same expression for H_pv is negative by continuity. On Σ_− (ξ = −t) over
[−1, 0], H_pv = 2(w + (1 − w²)t) > 0 (at w = 0 it is 2t > 0), and near v = −1 likewise by continuity; in these
variables p = 0 is (1 − w²)t² + 2wt − (1 + L²) = 0, whose positive root is the stated t (at w = 1 the equation is
2t = 1 + L²). Over v > 0: t ≥ |1 − wt| gives 1/(v + 2) ≤ t ≤ 1/v, and real roots of the same quadratic need
1 + L²(1 − w²) ≥ 0.

(d) Along a curve, L is constant and, by (b), ξ̃ is monotone. (i) and the first half of (ii) follow from the signs of
H_pv in (c). On Σ_− over {v > 0} with L > 0, the curve stays in the compact set {0 < v ≤ v_max(L)} while t stays
bounded, and ξ̃ increases strictly. It cannot stay in a compact subset of {v > 0} at bounded t for all time (there
H_pξ̃ ≥ c > 0, and ξ̃ is bounded), so it leaves through v → 0. There the only points of Σ_− are at t ≤ 1/v → ∞ with
a = 1 − vt → 0 (the branch near t = 1/(v + 2) lies over v < 0 backwards, by the sign of H_pv there, and is the
incoming part); in the rescaled coordinates (ρ_∞, v, η̂) = (t⁻¹, v, η/t) → (0, 0, 0), that is to ∂ℛ_−. The turning
point is unique: at a critical point of v over {v > 0}, ξ = −w/(w² − 1), so (v + 1)ξ + 1 = −1/(w² − 1),
H_pξ = −2ξ((v + 1)ξ + 1) = −2w/(w² − 1)², and

    H_p²v = 2(2(v + 1)ξ + 1)H_pv + 2v(v + 2)H_pξ = 2(w² − 1)H_pξ = −4(v + 1)/(v(v + 2)) < 0;

so every critical point is a strict maximum, and there is at most one. (iii) On {η = 0}, Σ is the two curves named; on
the first H_pv = 2 and on the second H_pv = −2; Section 18.1.3 identifies their limits at R = 0.

(e) The correspondence is the conjugation of Section 26.4.1 on {R < ½}, where R̃ = R and φ = log R = −log v at
z = 1, so dφ = −dv/v. The semiclassical conjugation by e^(iφ/h) evaluates symbols at the covector translated by dφ: the
covector ζ of h²N⁰ corresponds to the covector ξ = ζ_v − 1/v of P. The dR-component of ζ is −v²ζ_v = −v(vξ + 1), which
is ξ_cħ over sf, and η_cħ = R⁻¹η = vη. With a := vξ + 1, ξ_cħ = −va, and (18.14) at z = 1 gives

    G_(ι,1) = 2(1 + Rξ_cħ)ξ_cħ + ξ_cħ² + |η_cħ|² = 2va(a − 1) + v²a² + v²|η|² = v²p,

as v²p = v²a(a + 2(a − 1)/v) + v²|η|² (since (v + 2)ξ + 1 = a + 2ξ and ξ = (a − 1)/v). Also
ξ̃ = −(v + 2)(vξ + 1) = (1 + 2/v)ξ_cħ = (1 + 2R)ξ_cħ. The conjugation carries R⁻²p, that is v²p, to the symbol
G_(ι,1) of h²N⁰, and preserves the Hamilton field up to the factor v² > 0 on Σ. Finally, at ĥ = 0 and z = 1,
(18.37) gives, with ξ := ξ_cħ, η := η_cħ,

    𝖧ξ̃ = (2(1 + 2R)ξ + 2) · 2Rξ + 2(|η|² − Rξ²)(1 + 2R),

and on {G_(ι,1) = 0}, |η|² = −2ξ − (1 + 2R)ξ², so

    𝖧ξ̃ = 4R(1 + 2R)ξ² + 4Rξ − 2(1 + 2R)(2ξ + (1 + 3R)ξ²) = −2(1 + R)ξ((1 + 2R)ξ + 2) = −2(1 + R)ξ_cħ(ξ̃ + 2).

On {G_(ι,1) = 0} over sf, 2ξ_cħ + (1 + 2R)ξ_cħ² = −|η_cħ|² ≤ 0 gives −2/(1 + 2R) ≤ ξ_cħ ≤ 0, that is ξ_cħ ≤ 0 and
ξ̃ + 2 ≥ 0; so 𝖧ξ̃ ≥ 0, with equality only where ξ_cħ = 0 or ξ̃ = −2.

(f) Complex conjugation of the coefficients exchanges z_0 = 1 and z_0 = −1, and the symbol identity is immediate. ∎

The function ξ̃ is the escape function of the problem: it increases along every bicharacteristic that is not one of the
two rays through the cone point, and on those it is −2 and 0; through the cone point it rises from −2 to 0 along the
curves of the face F_K of Chapter 18.

**Lemma 26.16** (The semiclassical order.) Let b_in > b_out with b_in + α_+ > ½(−1 + ϑ_in) and
b_out + α_+ < −½ + S̄ − ε_0 (here S̄ = min spec S̄ = 0 and ε_0 > 0 is small), the thresholds (18.18) at
R_(cf,1,in) and R_(cf,out). Let f_1 ∈ C^∞(ℝ) be non-increasing with f_1 = 1 on (−∞, −2 + δ′] and f_1 = 0 on [−δ′, ∞);
f_2 ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ) with 0 ≤ f_2 ≤ 1, f_2 = 1 on [0, L_0²] and f_2 = 0 on [4L_0², ∞); ψ a smooth compactly supported function
on the finite-frequency semiclassical phase space over sf (including the faces of Chapter 18 over R = 0), with
0 ≤ ψ ≤ 1, equal to 1 on a neighbourhood of 𝒞 := Σ ∩ supp(f_1(ξ̃)f_2(|η|²)), which is compact; and g ∈ C^∞(ℝ)
non-increasing with g = 1 on (−∞, −¼] and g = 0 on [−⅛, ∞). Here ξ̃, |η|² and the functions below are defined in the
frame of N_sf over {v < 4}, pulled back to the frame of P on {½ ≤ R ≤ 1} by the fibre translation of
Section 26.4.1, and over {R < ½} expressed in the variables of Chapter 18 (Lemma 26.15 (e)). Put

    𝖻 := b_out + (b_in − b_out)(1 − (1 − g(v))(1 − Φ)),   Φ := ψ f_1(ξ̃) f_2(|η|²)   (z_0 = 1),    (26.22)

and its reflection for z_0 = −1. Then 𝖻 is smooth; it equals the constant b_in over {v ≤ −¼} at all frequencies;
it equals b_out near fibre infinity over {v ≥ −⅛} and near R_(cf,out); it equals b_in near R_(cf,1,in); and, on a
neighbourhood of Σ, it is non-increasing in the directions of propagation of Proposition 26.20. These are: along H_p
(the future flow of Chapter 18) on Σ_− and over {v > 0}; and in the direction of increasing v on Σ_+ over {v ≤ 0}
(backward along H_p) and at fibre infinity over {−1 < v < 0}. Its restriction to the face F_K of Chapter 18 is a decay
order admissible at σ_0 = ±1 with weight α_+ in the sense of Section 11.1.4, as Lemma 18.17 requires of the
restriction of its order to F_K.

*Proof.* *Compactness of 𝒞.* In the cone region Σ is compact over sf (Section 18.1.3: |ξ_cħ| and |η_cħ| are bounded
on {G_(ι,1) = 0}). Over {v ≤ 0}, f_1 ≠ 0 excludes Σ_+ (there a ≤ 0, so ξ̃ ≥ 0), and on Σ_− with L ≤ 2L_0,
Lemma 26.15 (c) bounds t. Over {0 < v ≤ 1}, on Σ_− write c := vt ∈ [0, 1], so a = 1 − c
and |η|² = t² − (1 − t − c)² = (1 − c)(2t − 1 + c); f_1(ξ̃) ≠ 0 gives (v + 2)(1 − c) ≥ δ′, so 1 − c ≥ δ′/3
and |η|² ≥ (δ′/3)(2t − 1), and f_2 ≠ 0 bounds t. Over {1 ≤ v < 4}, t ≤ 1/v ≤ 1.

*Values.* Near fibre infinity ψ = 0. Near R_(cf,out), ξ̃ = (1 + 2R)ξ_cħ is near 0, so f_1 = 0. Near R_(cf,1,in), ξ̃ is
near −2 and |η|² = R²|η_cħ|² is near 0, and ψ = 1, so 𝖻 = b_in.

*The factor g.* Over {v ≤ −¼}, g = 1 and 𝖻 = b_in. Over {v ≥ −⅛}, g = 0 and 𝖻 = b_out + (b_in − b_out)Φ, treated
below. Near fibre infinity Φ = 0 (ψ = 0), and on a neighbourhood of Σ_+ ∩ {v ≤ 0}, Φ = 0 (ξ̃ ≥ 0 there, so f_1 = 0 on
{ξ̃ > −δ′}); there 𝖻 = b_out + (b_in − b_out)g(v) is non-increasing in v. On a neighbourhood of Σ_− over
{−¼ < v < −⅛}, H_pv > 0 (Lemma 26.15 (c)), and

    H_p(1 − (1 − g)(1 − Φ)) = g′(v)(H_pv)(1 − Φ) + (1 − g)H_pΦ ≤ 0,

as g′ ≤ 0, 0 ≤ Φ ≤ 1 and H_pΦ ≤ 0 (below).

*Monotonicity of Φ.* H_pΦ = ψf_2f_1′(ξ̃)H_pξ̃ + f_1f_2H_pψ, as H_p|η|² = 0 identically on {v < 4}
(Lemma 26.15 (b)) and, in the cone region, {G_(ι,1), R²|η_cħ|²} = {v²p, |η|²} = 0 likewise. The second term
vanishes on a neighbourhood of Σ: supp dψ ∩ supp(f_1(ξ̃)f_2(|η|²)) is compact, as ψ has compact support, and does not
meet Σ, as ψ = 1 near 𝒞. For the first, f_1′ ≤ 0, and H_pξ̃ > 0 on
𝒞′ := Σ ∩ supp f_1′(ξ̃) ∩ supp f_2(|η|²), a compact set: over {v < 4} by Lemma 26.15 (b), as η ≠ 0 on 𝒞′
(there ξ̃ ∈ [−2 + δ′, −δ′], while ξ̃ ∈ {−2, 0} where η = 0); over the cone region by Lemma 26.15 (e), as
−ξ_cħ = −ξ̃/(1 + 2R) ≥ δ′/(1 + 2R) and ξ̃ + 2 ≥ δ′, so 𝖧ξ̃ ≥ 2δ′²/(1 + 2R). By continuity H_pξ̃ > 0 on a
neighbourhood O′ of 𝒞′. The compact set (supp ψ ∩ supp f_1′(ξ̃) ∩ supp f_2(|η|²)) ∖ O′ does not meet Σ, so on a
neighbourhood of Σ the first term is ≤ 0.

*The face F_K.* At R = 0, |η|² = 0, and on a neighbourhood of Σ ∩ F_K, ψ = 1, so
𝖻 = b_out + (b_in − b_out)f_1(ξ_cħ). This is non-increasing along the boundary flow on a neighbourhood of Σ ∩ F_K,
since at R = 0, 𝖧ξ_cħ = 2|η_cħ|² ≥ 0 everywhere ((18.37)), as (12.22) requires (g = 0 there); and it is
constant near R_in (ξ_cħ = −2) and R_out (ξ_cħ = 0), with the thresholds there, which are those of (18.18) at
F_K (the proof of Lemma 18.17). ∎

#### 26.4.3 The estimates

**Lemma 26.17** (The semiclassical radial estimate at the light cone.) Let δ > 0, the fibre inner product
of Lemma 26.5, s < 2 − δ − C_ϰ constant, and 𝖻 as in Lemma 26.16. For each sign there are neighbourhoods
U_* ⊂ U_0 of ∂ℛ_± at fibre infinity and a compact K_E ⊂ Ū_0 ∖ ∂ℛ_± such that, uniformly for z ∈ 𝒵_h and h < h_0, with
B_* microsupported in U_*, G elliptic on Ū_0, E′ elliptic on K_E, and all M:

    ‖B_*u‖_𝐨 ≤ C(h⁻¹‖GPu‖_(𝐨−(1,1,0)) + ‖E′u‖_𝐨 + h^M‖Gu‖_𝐨 + ‖u‖_(−M𝟏)),     𝐨 = (s, 𝖻),    (26.23)

    ‖B_*v‖_(𝐨*) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖GP^(*𝔥)v‖_(𝐨*−(1,1,0)) + h^M‖Gv‖_(𝐨*) + ‖v‖_(−M𝟏)),   𝐨* = (1 − s, 𝖻*),    (26.24)

for any 𝖻* constant near ∂ℛ_± (in the notation of Chapter 12 for orders, the decay order being immaterial).

*Proof.* We verify the hypotheses of Lemma 12.29 with F fibre infinity and Λ := ∂ℛ_±. (i): Re_𝔥P has principal
symbol p_(±1) up to terms of the class of 𝒫_1 (Lemma 26.15 (a)), and with μ := |ξ|, 𝖧^𝐏 := μ⁻¹H_(p_(±1))
vanishes on Λ (Lemma 26.6 (b): Λ consists of radial points of the homogeneous part, and at fibre infinity the
field is that of p_2). Take ς := −sgn ξ for P (ε_♭ = 1), so that ς𝖧^𝐏 = −𝖧 near Λ and β_ϱ = −β_0 = −2(1 + v): a
sink; and for P^(*𝔥) (ε_♭ = −1), ς := sgn ξ: a source. (ii): ℓ := 0, by Lemma 26.15 (a). (iii): g := ρ_∞²p_(±1)
and φ := q̃ of Lemma 26.6 (b); ς𝖧^𝐏φ = ∓𝖧q̃ + O(ρ_∞), which is (12.24) by Lemma 26.6 (b). (iv):
s is constant, and 𝖻 = b_out near fibre infinity (Lemma 26.16). (v): at fibre infinity
μ⁻¹p_1^𝐏 = sgn ξ (3 + 2Re_𝔥 S̄ − 2Re ϰ) by (26.10), with Re ϰ = −y/h: the term −2ϰh²∂_v = −2iz(h∂_v)
contributes 2(y/h)ξ = −2(Re ϰ)ξ to the symbol of h⁻¹Im_𝔥P and its large part Re z only to Re_𝔥P, the remaining terms
being as in Lemma 26.7. So for P, κ̃ = s − ½ and, at Λ (v = 0),

    𝒯 = 2(s − ½)(−2(1 + v)) + 2(3 + 2Re_𝔥 S̄ − 2Re ϰ) = 4(2 + Re_𝔥 S̄ − Re ϰ − s) ≥ 4(2 − δ − C_ϰ − s) > 0;

for P^(*𝔥) at 𝐨*, κ̃ = ½ − s and ε_♭ = −1, which gives the same condition, as in the proof of Proposition 12.30.
Lemma 12.29 gives (26.23) with the control term (the sink case) and (26.24) without it. ∎

**Lemma 26.18** (Semiclassical slab estimates.) Proposition 12.46, Proposition 12.47 and Corollary 12.48 hold
for P = h²N_sf(ϰ) on the slabs {a < −v < b}, 0 < a < b < 2, for z ∈ 𝒵_h and h < h_0, with r replaced by −v, t by T,
and g by ĝ of Lemma 26.3 (g). In particular, with the cut-offs of Lemma 26.8,

    ‖u‖_(H^s_h({−1<v<−1/4})) ≤ Ch⁻¹‖Pu‖_(H^(s−1)_h({−1<v<−1/4}))     (u supported in {v ≥ −1}),
    ‖χv‖_(H̄^(1−s)_h) ≤ C(h⁻¹‖P^(*𝔥)v‖_(H̄^(−s)_h) + ‖χ_1v‖_(H^(1−s)_h)).    (26.25)

*Proof.* By Lemma 26.3 (g), N_sf(ϰ) is the spectral family at σ = −iϰ = z/h of the stationary operator P_c on
ℝ_T × sf° with metric ĝ, with P_c − □_ĝ of first order with T-independent coefficients, and dv timelike on the slab.
The proof of Proposition 12.46 uses the hypotheses of Chapter 12 on the time function only through this, except at two
places. First, it uses Im z ≥ 0 and T[u′](−∇t, X) ≥ 0 to drop the term 2h⁻¹(Im z)T[u′](−∇t, X) of ^(W)K[u′]. Here ∇T
is spacelike, but |h⁻¹Im z| ≤ C_ϰ and |T[u′](∇T, X)| ≤ C|du′|²_R, so the term is bounded by C′|du′|²_R and is absorbed
by ℓT[u′](X, X) ≥ ℓc_0|du′|²_R for the weight parameter ℓ large. The flux identity E(1) = E(0) uses only the
T-independence. Second, the adjoint estimate is obtained there by t ↦ −t, to keep Im z ≥ 0; here the first argument
applies directly to P^(*𝔥), the spectral family at z̄/h of the formal adjoint of P_c (|Im z̄| ≤ C_ϰh), with the ends of
the slab exchanged (the backward case of Proposition 11.29, with the weight e^(−ℓr)) and X unchanged. The proof of
Proposition 12.47 uses Proposition 11.30 (iii) at fixed h (Lemma 26.8), the monotonicity of v along every
characteristic point over the slab, at finite frequencies and at fibre infinity (H_(Ĝ)v = 2ĝ⁻¹(ν, dv) ≠ 0 for ĝ-null
ν ≠ 0, dv being timelike), and Corollary 12.28, valid here by Remark 12.27 (a) (Lemma 26.15 (a)); it
does not use the statement for Im z > 0 that there is no characteristic point at finite frequencies, which serves there
only as an alternative. Corollary 12.48 follows as there. ∎

**Lemma 26.19** (The cone point.) On {R < ½}, Proposition 18.9, Proposition 18.10, Proposition 18.11 and
items (R3)–(R4) of Lemma 18.15 hold for P with z ∈ 𝒵_h and the order 𝖻 of Lemma 26.16, and Lemma 18.17
and Lemma 18.18 hold for u supported in {R < ½}, with the proofs given there and these changes: in (R3), for
0 < y ≤ C_ϰh the term −yQ_1 is put into 𝒫_1 as for y ≤ 0 (its contribution ϖ⁻¹(−y)σ(Q_1) = 2yξ_cħ(1 + ĥ)²R/h is
bounded by 2C_ϰR and vanishes at R = 0); in (R4) and in the propagation along o_sf, the term with 𝒜, whose coefficient
has modulus |Im z|/|z|² ≤ C_ϰh, is part of 𝒫_1 for either sign (its symbol vanishes at R_(cf,out)); and in step (4) of
the proof of Lemma 18.18, |Im z| ≤ C_ϰh replaces |Im z| ≤ γ_+h. The constants depend on C_ϰ.

*Proof.* The three places listed are the only ones where the proofs of Chapter 18 use the range of Im z near the cone
point; elsewhere they use it only at ℐ⁺ (the face F_I, items (R1)–(R2)), which does not occur here ([Hin26, footnote
86]). The order 𝖻 enters through (18.18) at R_(cf,1,in) and R_(cf,out), constancy near them, monotonicity along
the future flow, and its restriction to F_K in Lemma 18.17, all of which Lemma 26.16 provides. P_0 = 2L_b is
tf-admissible with the weight α_+ + 2 ∈ (0, 1) (Proposition 25.11), which is the hypothesis of Lemma 18.17. ∎

**Proposition 26.20** ([Hin26, (9.9)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let C_ϰ ≥ 1, δ > 0 small, s < 2 − δ − C_ϰ,
γ_cf ∈ (−1, 0), and 𝖻 as in Lemma 26.16. There are h_0 > 0 and C such that for h < h_0 and z ∈ 𝒵_h

    ‖u‖_𝐨 ≤ C‖Pu‖_(𝒴_𝐨),     u ∈ ℋ_𝐨, Pu ∈ 𝒴_𝐨,    (26.26)

the dual estimate holds for P^(*𝔥) on the dual spaces, and P: {u ∈ ℋ_𝐨 : Pu ∈ 𝒴_𝐨} → 𝒴_𝐨 is invertible.

*Proof.* *Step 1: the symbolic estimate.* We show ‖u‖_𝐨 ≤ C(‖Pu‖_(𝒴_𝐨) + ‖u‖_(𝐨_♭)),
𝐨_♭ := (−M; γ_cf, γ_cf; 𝖻 − ¼), first for u smooth and compactly supported in {v > −1} × 𝕊³ with R bounded below on
its support, then by density (Lemma 12.17 in {v < 4}, Lemma 18.7 (g) near the cone, Lemma 11.27 (a) at
v = −1). Cover the characteristic set, at finite frequencies over sf and at fibre infinity, by finitely many open sets
on which one of the following holds, in this order (for z_0 = 1; z_0 = −1 by Lemma 26.15 (f)).

(1) {v < −¼}: Lemma 26.18 at the constant semiclassical order 𝖻 = b_in there (Lemma 26.16), which controls
u there in h^(−b_in)H^s_h by h^(−1−b_in)‖Pu‖_(H^(s−1)_h), at all frequencies, with no error term.

(2) Points of Σ, at finite frequencies or at fibre infinity, over {−½ < v < 4}, that are reached from {v < −¼} along the
direction of propagation: forward along H_p on Σ_− and on the fibre-infinity part of Σ over {−1 < v < 0} with ξ < 0;
backward along H_p on Σ_+ and on the part with ξ > 0. Here Proposition 12.25 with Corollary 12.28 and
Remark 12.27 (a) (in either direction, as ℓ = 0) applies over {v < 4}, and Proposition 18.10 over {R < ¼} away from
the cone saddles, from (1); 𝖻 is non-increasing in these directions of propagation on a neighbourhood of Σ
(Lemma 26.16). By Lemma 26.15 (d) this covers: Σ_+ outside a neighbourhood of ∂ℛ_+; the curves (ii) up to
neighbourhoods of the cone saddles and of ∂ℛ_−; the incoming ray (iii) up to a neighbourhood of R_(cf,1,in); and fibre
infinity over {−1 < v < 0} outside neighbourhoods of ∂ℛ_±.

(3) Neighbourhoods of ∂ℛ_+ and ∂ℛ_−: (26.23), whose control sets K_E consist of elliptic points and of points
of Σ near ∂ℛ_± and off it, covered by (2) (on the curves (i) and (ii) and at fibre infinity) or by (6) below (on the
outgoing ray (iii) and the curves (ii) near it). For ∂ℛ_− this step is taken after (6).

(4) A neighbourhood U_3 of R_(cf,1,in), by (R3) (Lemma 26.19), whose K_E ⊂ {R ≥ δ_1} lies in the set covered by
(2) (the points of Σ near R_(cf,1,in) with R > 0 lie on curves (ii) or (iii) from {v < −1}; the others are elliptic).

(5) The curves in F_K from R_(cf,1,in) to R_(cf,out), by Proposition 18.10 from U_3; then a neighbourhood U_5 of
R_(cf,out) by (R4), whose control set K_E ⊂ {φ ≥ δ_2} consists of points of Σ ∩ F_K on these curves, of points of Σ
over R > 0 near them, which lie on curves (ii) and so are covered by (2) or by Proposition 18.10 once more from (4), and
of elliptic points. This is steps (3)–(5) of the proof of Lemma 18.16, with "curves from R_(ℐ⁺,1,in)" read as
"curves from {v < −1}".

(6) The outgoing ray (iii) and the curves (ii) near it, from U_5 to a neighbourhood of ∂ℛ_−: over {R < ½}
Proposition 18.10 (for P or for z⁻¹P, the term with 𝒜 being part of 𝒫_1), over {R > ¼} Proposition 12.25 with
Remark 12.27 (a); 𝖻 is non-increasing along them (Lemma 26.16), and equal to b_out near them away from the
cone.

(7) Elsewhere, the elliptic estimates (Proposition 12.14 in {v < 4}, Proposition 18.11 near the cone), at finite
frequencies off Σ, at fibre infinity over {v ≥ 0} off ∂ℛ_±, and at the fibre infinity of the cone calculus.

Each estimate has its term h⁻¹‖GPu‖ bounded by C‖Pu‖_(𝒴_𝐨) (in {v < 4} the differential order of 𝒴_𝐨 is s − 1 and
its semiclassical order 𝖻 + 1, which is h⁻¹ times the order 𝖻; near the cone, Section 18.3.4 (d)), its term
‖E′u‖_𝐨 by an earlier one, and its errors h^M‖Gu‖_𝐨 + ‖u‖_(−M𝟏) in {v < 4}, and ‖Gu‖_(𝐨−¼𝐞) near the cone, by
C‖u‖_(𝐨_♭) + Ch‖u‖_𝐨. A microlocal partition of unity gives the claim, the last term being absorbed for h small. The
constants are uniform in z ∈ 𝒵_h: each estimate is uniform on neighbourhoods of z_* ∈ {±1}, the dependence on y being
through 𝒫_1, with |y/h| ≤ C_ϰ.

*Step 2: the transition face.* Lemma 18.18 (Lemma 26.19) applied to χ_tf u, which is supported in
{R < Ch^(1/2)} ⊂ {R < ½}, with the commutator [P, χ_tf] estimated there, and on the support of 1 − χ_tf the bound
‖(1 − χ_tf)u‖_(𝐨_♭) ≤ Ch^(δ_♭)‖u‖_𝐨 of its proof, which in {v < 4} is the trivial bound for semiclassical orders
(ρ_sf ∼ h there), give ‖u‖_(𝐨_♭) ≤ C‖Pu‖_(𝒴_𝐨) + Ch^(δ_♭)‖u‖_𝐨, with 𝖻_♭ := 𝖻 − 2δ_♭ still satisfying the
conditions of Lemma 26.16. With Step 1, (26.26) follows for h small.

*Step 3: the adjoint.* The same steps apply to P^(*𝔥) on the dual spaces, with the directions of propagation reversed
and sources and sinks interchanged: (26.24) at ∂ℛ_±, this time without the control term; propagation backwards
along the curves (ii)–(iii) to the cone point and through it (Section 18.3.6, the adjoint, for (R3)–(R4) and F_K); on
Σ_+ and at fibre infinity, propagation from ∂ℛ_± to {v < −¼}; and near v = −1 the second estimate of (26.25),
whose term ‖χ_1v‖ lies over {−½ < v < −¼} and is controlled by the propagation just described. The dual semiclassical
order −𝖻 − 1 is non-increasing in these reversed directions, and is the constant −b_in − 1 over {v ≤ −¼}, where the
second estimate of (26.25) is used. Step 2 uses the second estimate of (18.40).

*Step 4: invertibility.* For fixed h < h_0, (26.26) gives injectivity and closed range, and the dual estimate
the triviality of the annihilator of the range (by the pairing ⟨Pu, v⟩ = ⟨u, P^(*𝔥)v⟩ for u in a dense set, as in
Section 18.3.6). ∎

### 26.5 The spectral family: the theorem

**Theorem 26.21** ([Hin26, Proposition 9.2] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (C1) of Section 25.5 and the
parameters of Proposition 25.11, and let ϰ ∈ ℂ and (s, μ) be admissible for ϰ ((26.13)).

(1) (*Fredholm property.*) N_sf(ϰ): 𝒳 → 𝒴 of (26.14) is Fredholm of index 0, with kernel and cokernel
independent of the admissible pair.

(2) (*Invertibility.*) It is invertible for Re ϰ < 2. For every C it is invertible for all but finitely many ϰ with
Re ϰ ≤ C, and the inverse is finite-meromorphic: in every vertical strip on which one admissible pair serves,
ϰ ↦ N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ ∈ ℒ(𝒴, 𝒳) is meromorphic with finite-rank principal parts (every Laurent coefficient of negative order
has finite rank), and for f in the targets of two admissible pairs the two inverses agree.

(3) (*b-regularity at the light cone.*) If u ∈ Ḣ^(s,μ)_b and N_sf(ϰ)u ∈ Ḣ^((s−1;k),μ)_(b;b), k ∈ ℕ_0, then
u ∈ Ḣ^((s;k),μ)_(b;b).

*Proof.* (3) is Proposition 26.12. (1): The Fredholm property and the independence are Proposition 26.9.

*Index.* Let ind(ϰ) be the index, which does not depend on the admissible pair. Near any ϰ_1, fix a pair admissible for
every ϰ in a disc D_1 around ϰ_1 (shrink the intervals of (26.13) by a margin). On D_1, 𝒳 is fixed
(Lemma 26.3 (f)) and ϰ ↦ N_sf(ϰ) ∈ ℒ(𝒳, 𝒴) is holomorphic (a polynomial), so ind is constant on D_1, hence
constant on ℂ. By Proposition 26.20 with C_ϰ := |Re ϰ_1| + 1, N_h is invertible on ℋ_𝐨 for |Im ϰ| large, and by
Section 26.4.1 N_sf(ϰ) is then invertible from {u ∈ Ḣ^(s′,γ_cf+Re ϰ)_b : N_sf(ϰ)u ∈ Ḣ^(s′−1,γ_cf+Re ϰ)_b}, an
admissible pair (s′ < 2 − δ − C_ϰ ≤ 2 − Re ϰ and γ_cf + Re ϰ ∈ (Re ϰ − 1, Re ϰ)). So ind = 0.

(2): For Re ϰ < 2 the kernel is trivial (Proposition 26.14) and the index is 0, so the operator is invertible.

*Meromorphy.* Let S be a vertical strip on which one admissible pair serves (its width is less than 1, by
(26.13)). On S the spaces 𝒳 and 𝒴 are fixed, and ϰ ↦ N_sf(ϰ) ∈ ℒ(𝒳, 𝒴) is a holomorphic family of Fredholm
operators of index 0. Near ϰ_1 ∈ S choose a finite-rank K_1: 𝒳 → 𝒴 with N_sf(ϰ_1) + K_1 invertible (the index is 0);
then N_sf(ϰ) + K_1 is invertible on a disc D_1 around ϰ_1, and there N_sf(ϰ) = (N_sf(ϰ) + K_1)(Id − F(ϰ)) with
F(ϰ) := (N_sf(ϰ) + K_1)⁻¹K_1, a holomorphic family of finite-rank operators on 𝒳. By (K5) of Section 13.2.1 (the
analytic Fredholm theorem, [RS1, Theorem VI.14]), on D_1 either Id − F(ϰ), and with it N_sf(ϰ), is invertible at no
point, or it is invertible off a discrete set, with a meromorphic inverse. In the second case every Laurent coefficient
of negative order of N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ has finite rank: since (Id − F)⁻¹ = Id + F(Id − F)⁻¹,

    N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ = (N_sf(ϰ) + K_1)⁻¹ + (N_sf(ϰ) + K_1)⁻¹K_1(Id − F(ϰ))⁻¹(N_sf(ϰ) + K_1)⁻¹,

the first term is holomorphic on D_1, and each Laurent coefficient of negative order of the second is a finite sum of
operators AK_1B, A a Taylor coefficient of (N_sf(ϰ) + K_1)⁻¹, whose ranges lie in the finite-dimensional spaces A(K_1𝒳).
The set of ϰ_1 ∈ S at which the second alternative holds is open, and so is its complement; S is connected and contains
points of invertibility (those with |Im ϰ| large, by Proposition 26.20), so the second alternative holds on all of S.

*Finiteness.* For 2 ≤ Re ϰ ≤ C, Proposition 26.20 with C_ϰ := C gives invertibility for |Im ϰ| ≥ Y_0; the set where
N_sf(ϰ) is not invertible is discrete, so it meets the compact set {2 ≤ Re ϰ ≤ C, |Im ϰ| ≤ Y_0} in finitely many points.

*Agreement.* If f ∈ 𝒴 ∩ 𝒴′ for two admissible pairs and ϰ is not a pole, the two solutions u, u′ both lie in the larger
domain (the spaces are nested in s and μ, and by (26.13) one may pass to the minimum of the two values of s
and of μ), where the kernel is trivial (Proposition 26.9 (3)); so u = u′. ∎

### 26.6 The ι⁺-normal operator: setting

This section and the next three are [Hin26, Definition 9.3, Proposition 9.4, Definition 9.6 and Remark 9.7] in
dimension 4 + 1 (pp. 169–172). They construct the inverse of the ι⁺-normal operator from that of the spectral family
(Theorem 26.21), describe its asymptotics at ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ (of radiation-field type, with exponents 3/2 plus the small
eigenvalues of S̄) and at K⁺ ∩ ι⁺ (polyhomogeneous, with an index set generated by the indicial roots of
Proposition 25.6), prove a version at finite regularity, and identify the boundary spectrum.

#### 26.6.1 The operator

We use the notation of Section 26.1: v ∈ ℝ, ω ∈ 𝕊³, R := v⁻¹ near v = ∞, N_sf(ϰ) of (26.3), the spaces of
Definition 26.4, and the admissible pairs of (26.13). Let ι⁺ := [0, ∞]_v × 𝕊³, a compact manifold with two
boundary hypersurfaces, ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ = {v = 0} and K⁺ ∩ ι⁺ = {R = 0}, which do not meet; their defining functions are
ρ_I := v/(1 + v) and ρ_K := R/(1 + R). On ι⁺ we use the unweighted b-density |dv/v dg̸| = |dR/R dg̸| and
H^(k,α_I,α_K)_b(ι⁺) := ρ_I^(α_I)ρ_K^(α_K)H^k_b(ι⁺) (Definition 21.31 (3)). Ċ^∞(ι⁺) is the
space of smooth sections vanishing to infinite order at ∂ι⁺. The *ι⁺-normal operator* ([Hin26, (9.10)–(9.11)] at
n = 4) is

    N_ι⁺(ϰ) := R^(−2−ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)R^ϰ = −2v(v∂_v − ϰ)(v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄) + v²L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v, ∂_ω)    (26.27)

on (0, ∞)_v × 𝕊³. This is (26.6) in the coordinate v. Indeed R^ϰ = v^(−ϰ) and v^ϰ(v∂_v)v^(−ϰ) = v∂_v − ϰ,
so with ∂_v = v⁻¹(v∂_v),

    v^ϰN_sf(ϰ)v^(−ϰ) = −2v⁻¹(v∂_v − ϰ)(v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄) + L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v, ∂_ω),

and R^(−2) = v². So on {0 < v < ∞}, N_ι⁺(ϰ)h = f is equivalent to

    (v∂_v − ϰ)(v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄)h = −(2v)⁻¹f + (v/2)L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v, ∂_ω)h,    (26.28)

which is [Hin26, (9.22)] at n = 4. Near R = 0, by (26.6),

    R²N_ι⁺(ϰ) = A_0 + RA_1,   A_0 := L̃(0)(ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω),   A_1 := −2(R∂_R + ϰ)(R∂_R + 3/2 + S̄).    (26.29)

Since R²N_ι⁺(ϰ) = R^(−ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)R^ϰ, it is b-elliptic at R = 0 (Lemma 26.3 (b); conjugation by R^ϰ preserves
b-ellipticity). Its indicial family is N(R²N_ι⁺(ϰ), ζ) = L̃(0)(ω, −ζ, ∂_ω), which does not depend on ϰ. So its boundary
spectrum is {−μ}, μ over the indicial roots of Proposition 25.6: those of L̂_b(0), whose b-normal operator at ∂X is
^bL̄(0) = ρ²L̃(0)(ω, ρ∂_ρ, ∂_ω).

#### 26.6.2 The endomorphism

**Lemma 26.22** (S̄ is semisimple.) Let γ_Υ < min(½s_C, ⅜), s_C := γ_C(1 − e_C)(1 − v_C). At every
ω ∈ 𝕊³, S̄(ω) is diagonalisable, with the eigenvalues of (25.6), which do not depend on ω. So
S̄ = Σ_(s∈σ_S) sΠ_s, σ_S := spec S̄, where the spectral projections Π_s are smooth on 𝕊³, Π_sΠ_(s′) = δ_(ss′)Π_s and
Σ_sΠ_s = Id.

*Proof.* The proof of Lemma 25.2 writes ρS̄ = UV, with U: T* ⊕ T* → S²T* and V: S²T* → T* ⊕ T*, and

    T_S := VU = [ ρS̄^C     0    ]
                [ V_2U_1   ρS̄^Υ ],

where S̄^C and S̄^Υ are the endomorphisms of the constraint propagation operator and of the gauge potential operator.
Both leave the angular covectors invariant and act on them as γ_C(1 − v_C), resp. γ_Υ, times the identity; and both
leave the span of dt_* and k := dt̄ + d|x| invariant, acting on it by triangular matrices with the diagonal entries
γ_C(1 − e_C)(1 − v_C) and 2γ_C(1 − v_C), resp. 2γ_Υ and γ_Υ(1 − e_Υ). As 0 < e_C, e_Υ, v_C < 1, the three eigenvalues of
each are distinct, so each is annihilated by a product of distinct linear factors and is diagonalisable. Their spectra
are disjoint, since spec S̄^Υ ⊂ (0, 2γ_Υ], spec S̄^C ⊂ [s_C, ∞) and 2γ_Υ < s_C. Let m_1 and m_2 be the minimal
polynomials of the diagonal blocks B_1 := ρS̄^C and B_2 := ρS̄^Υ of T_S. They have simple roots and no common root;
m_1(T_S) has first block row 0, and m_2(T_S) has second block column 0. So m_2(T_S)m_1(T_S) = 0, and T_S is
diagonalisable. All its eigenvalues are non-zero, so VU is invertible; let q be its minimal polynomial, so q(0) ≠ 0.
From (UV)^(j+1) = U(VU)^jV we get UV q(UV) = U q(VU) V = 0. Hence the minimal polynomial of UV divides t q(t), which has
simple roots, so UV and S̄ = ρ⁻¹UV are diagonalisable. Their eigenvalues are those of (25.6), independent of
ω. The projections are Π_s = ∏_(s′≠s)(S̄ − s′)/(s − s′), polynomials in S̄ with constant coefficients, hence
smooth. ∎

We write

    σ_Υ := {0, (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ, 2γ_Υ},   σ_C := γ_C{(1 − e_C)(1 − v_C), 1 − v_C, 2(1 − v_C)},   Π_C := Σ_(s∈σ_C)Π_s,
    (26.30)

so σ_S = σ_Υ ∪ σ_C, σ_Υ ⊂ [0, 2γ_Υ] ⊂ [0, ¾) and min σ_C = s_C. [Hin26] works in the splitting of its (5.27), where S̄
is lower triangular ([Hin26, (8.8)]) and one component carries two small exponents; in the eigenbasis each component
carries one, and the counterpart of that splitting at n = 4 is not needed here.

#### 26.6.3 Index sets

As in Definition 21.31 (4), (z, k) denotes the smallest index set containing (z, k), that is
{(z + j, l) : j ∈ ℕ_0, 0 ≤ l ≤ k}, π_1 denotes the projection of an index set to its exponents, and ∪̄ is the extended
union.

**Definition 26.23** ([Hin26, Definition 9.3] in dimension 4 + 1.) (1) (*Index sets at ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺.*)

    ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) := ⋃_(s∈σ_Υ)(3/2 + s, 0),   ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ) := ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) + 1,   ℰ_s := ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ) ∪ (3/2 + s, 0)
    (26.31)

for s ∈ σ_Υ.

(2) (*Function spaces.*) For an index set ℰ_K at K⁺ ∩ ι⁺ and ℓ_I ∈ ℝ, 𝒜^((⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),ℰ_K)(ι⁺) is the space of
sections h with Π_Ch ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ),ℓ_I),ℰ_K) and Π_sh ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ_s,ℓ_I),ℰ_K) for s ∈ σ_Υ. Here Definition 21.31 (5)
and (6) are used, with the index sets referring to {v = 0} and {R = 0}, in this order.
H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_K,ℓ_K))_b(ι⁺) is defined in the same way. The sets ℰ_(ι⁺,ℐ,01), ℰ_(ι⁺,ℐ,1/) and
ℰ_(ι⁺,ℐ,0/) of [Hin26] are the ℰ_s for s = (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ and 0, its ℰ_(ι⁺,ℐ,11) is the union of those for 2γ_Υ
and (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, and 3/2 replaces its 1 throughout.

(3) (*The index set at K⁺ ∩ ι⁺.*) Fix α ∈ (−1, 0) and put A := R²N_ι⁺(ϰ). ℰ_K is the index set ℰ = ⋃_jℰ_j of
Lemma 21.35 for A with F = ∅, that is

    ℰ_0 := ℰ(α),   ℰ_(j+1) := ℰ(α) ∪̄ (ℰ_j + 1),    (26.32)

where ℰ(α) is the smallest index set containing the (ζ, k) ∈ Spec_b(A) with Re ζ > α.

**Lemma 26.24** (The index set at K⁺.) (a) ℰ_K depends neither on ϰ nor on α ∈ (−1, 0).

(b) ℰ_K ⊂ {Re z ≥ 0} and ℰ_K ∩ {Re z = 0} = {(0, 0)}. The exponents of ℰ(α) in (0, 1) are
ι^Υ_(s0,2) − 2 ∈ (0, z_Υ/3] and ι^Υ_(s1,2) − 2 ∈ (0, ¼), so min Re(ℰ_K ∖ {(0, 0)}) > 0.

(c) All exponents of ℰ(α) with real part at most 101 are real.

*Proof.* (a) Spec_b(A) is determined by N(A, ζ) = L̃(0)(ω, −ζ, ∂_ω), which does not depend on ϰ
(Section 26.6.1). Its elements are the (−μ, k) with μ a root of Proposition 25.6 and k below the order of the
root. No root has real part in (0, 1] (Proposition 25.6 (a)), so Re(−μ) > α holds exactly when Re μ ≤ 0, for every
α ∈ (−1, 0).

(b), (c) The roots with Re μ ≤ 0 are those before the semicolons in Proposition 25.6. They are: 0 at s0 and s2;
the ι^C_(·,≪,·) − 1, with real part < −101 (Proposition 25.6 (d)); −l, 1 − l and 2 − l at the types listed; −1 at
s1 and v1; −2 − 2γ_Cv_C at v1; and 2 − ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) (j = 1, 2) and 2 − ι^Υ_(s0,2). By Lemma 23.3 the last are
real, with ι^Υ_(s0,2) ∈ (2, 2 + z_Υ/3] and ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) ∈ (l + j, l + j + ¼) for 0 < z_Υ ≤ ½, z_Υ = 4e_Υγ_Υ² being
the z of that lemma. So every root with Re μ ≤ 0 other than 0 has Re μ < 0. The root 0 occurs only at s0 and s2 and is
simple there (Proposition 25.6 (c)), giving (0, 0) only. The exponents −μ ∈ (0, 1) are ι^Υ_(s0,2) − 2 and
ι^Υ_(s1,2) − 2; the next ones are ≥ 1. The iterates ℰ_j + 1 only add points with real part ≥ 1. ∎

### 26.7 Two lemmas at the light cone

Words W^α and the modules 𝒟^m are those of Section 26.2.4 (products of v∂_v and the Lie derivatives ℒ_(Ω_a)).

**Lemma 26.25** (Conormality at the light cone, every order.) Let s ∈ ℝ with s − ½ ∉ ℤ. There is
m(s) ∈ ℕ such that the following holds for every k ∈ ℕ_0. Let u ∈ H^s(ℝ × 𝕊³) be supported in [0, M_0] × 𝕊³, with
W^βu ∈ H^s for |β| ≤ k + m(s). Then for |α| ≤ k

    |W^αu(v, ω)| ≤ C v^(s−½) Σ_(|β|≤k+m(s)) ‖W^βu‖_(H^s)   on (0, 1) × 𝕊³,    (26.33)

with C depending on s, k and M_0. In particular, if W^βu ∈ H^s for every word, then u is conormal at {v = 0⁺} with the
bound v^(s−½).

*Proof.* (i) *Values in ℋ := H²(𝕊³; ℂ^(N_E)) ⊂ C⁰.* Expand in spherical harmonics, with eigenvalues κ_j of Δ_(𝕊³). For
s ≥ 0, (1 + ξ² + κ_j)^s ≥ (1 + ξ²)^s. For s < 0, (1 + ξ²)^s ≤ (1 + ξ² + κ_j)^s(1 + κ_j)^(−s), since
(1 + ξ² + κ_j)/(1 + ξ²) ≤ 1 + κ_j. In both cases

    ‖g‖_(H^s(ℝ;H²(𝕊³))) ≤ C Σ_(|γ|≤2+⌈max(0,−s)⌉) ‖ℒ_Ω^γ g‖_(H^s).

This uses Δ_(𝕊³) = −Σ_aΩ_a² and Ω_a = ℒ_(Ω_a) − A_a with constant A_a (the proof of Lemma 26.10). So
W^αu ∈ H^s(ℝ; ℋ) for |α| ≤ k + m(s) − 2 − ⌈max(0, −s)⌉.

(ii) *s > ½.* The Taylor argument of the proof of Lemma 26.13, applied to g = W^αu ∈ H^s(ℝ; ℋ) supported in
{v ≥ 0}, gives ‖g(v)‖_ℋ ≤ Cv^(s−½)‖g‖_(H^s(ℝ;ℋ)) on (0, 1); this is (26.33).

(iii) *s < ½.* Let j ∈ ℕ with s + j > ½. For g ∈ H^σ(ℝ; ℋ) supported in [0, M_0′], let Ig be the distribution with
∂_vIg = g and Ig = 0 on {v < 0}, and let ψ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, M_0′ + ½] and 0 on [M_0′ + 1, ∞). Then:

(α) ψIg is supported in [0, M_0′ + 1], and ∂_v(ψIg) = g + ψ′c with c := ⟨g, 1⟩ ∈ ℋ, since Ig = c on {v ≥ M_0′}. Its
Fourier transform is entire and equals the transform of ∂_v(ψIg) divided by iξ. This gives
‖ψIg‖_(H^(σ+1)(ℝ;ℋ)) ≤ C‖g‖_(H^σ(ℝ;ℋ)): use the quotient for |ξ| ≥ 1, and for |ξ| ≤ 1 the maximum principle on the
complex unit disc with the Paley–Wiener bound for compactly supported elements of H^σ.

(β) v∂_vIg = I((v∂_v + 1)g) and ℒ_ΩIg = I(ℒ_Ωg), since both sides vanish on {v < 0} and have the same v-derivative
(∂_v(v∂_vIg) = g + v∂_vg). So W^α(ψIg) = ψI(W̃^αg) + r, where W̃^α is W^α with every v∂_v replaced by v∂_v + 1, and r
is supported in [M_0′ + ½, M_0′ + 1] and built from v^iψ^(i) and I(W^γg) with |γ| < |α|.

Applying (α)–(β) j times, U := ψ_jI ⋯ ψ_1Iu satisfies W^αU ∈ H^(s+j)(ℝ; ℋ) for the same α, with bounds. By (ii) at
order s + j (with s + j − ½ ∉ ℕ_0), ‖W^αU(v)‖_ℋ ≤ Cv^(s+j−½) on (0, 1). On (0, 1), where every ψ_i equals 1, we have
u = ∂_v^jU = v^(−j)∏_(i=0)^(j−1)(v∂_v − i)U. Also W^αv^(−j) = v^(−j)W^α_((−j)), with v∂_v shifted by −j. So W^αu is
v^(−j) times a combination of words of length at most |α| + j applied to U. This gives (26.33) with
m(s) := 2 + ⌈max(0, −s)⌉ + j. ∎

This is Lemma 26.13 with the number of words counted. It replaces the identifications [Hin26, (9.5) and (9.21)]
of supported and extendible Sobolev spaces with b-spaces, which [Hin26] takes from [Hin26c, Lemma 13.4]; as it holds
for every s ∉ ½ + ℤ and with the module regularity, the case distinction Re ϰ < 2 / Re ϰ > 1 of [Hin26] is not needed.

For an index set G and γ ∈ ℝ, 𝒜^((G,γ))([0, 1)_v × 𝕊³) consists of the sums

    Σ_((z,k)∈G, Re z<γ) v^z(log v)^k g_(z,k)(ω) + r,

with g_(z,k) smooth and |W^αr| ≤ C_αv^γ for all α. The statements below hold for all orders in open ranges, so this
L^∞-based version and the L²-based one of Definition 21.31 (5) can be used interchangeably
(H^(∞,γ)_b ⊂ 𝒜^γ ⊂ H^(∞,γ−δ)_b near {v = 0}).

**Lemma 26.26** (Integration at the light cone.) Let a ∈ ℂ, γ_0 < γ with γ ≠ Re a, G an index set with no
exponent of real part γ, and w on (0, 1) × 𝕊³ with |W^αw| ≤ C_αv^(γ_0) for all α. If (v∂_v − a)w = g ∈ 𝒜^((G,γ)), then
w ∈ 𝒜^((G ∪̄ {(a,0)}, γ)). If moreover Re a < γ_0 and a ∉ π_1G, then w ∈ 𝒜^((G,γ)). The same holds with H^(k,(G,γ))_b in
place of 𝒜^((G,γ)) and w ∈ ρ_I^(γ_0)H^k_b.

*Proof.* Since (v∂_v − a)(v^z(log v)^j) = (z − a)v^z(log v)^j + jv^z(log v)^(j−1), each term v^z(log v)^kφ of g has a
particular solution v^zP(log v)φ, where P is a polynomial of degree k if z ≠ a and of degree k + 1 if z = a.
Subtracting these leaves (v∂_v − a)w′ = r with |W^αr| ≤ C_αv^γ and w′ conormal. If Re a < γ, put
w″ := v^a∫_0^v t^(−a)r(t) dt/t; if Re a > γ, put w″ := −v^a∫_v^1 t^(−a)r(t) dt/t. In both cases |w″| ≤ Cv^γ. Also
v∂_vw″ = aw″ + r, and the rotations pass through the integral, so by induction |W^αw″| ≤ C_αv^γ. Then
(v∂_v − a)(w′ − w″) = 0, so w′ − w″ = c(ω)v^a, with c = v^(−a)(w′ − w″) at any fixed v, smooth in ω. If Re a > γ, cv^a
is of order γ. This proves the first claim. If Re a < γ_0 and a ∉ π_1G, the term cv^a is the only term of order v^a in
the expansion of w = O(v^(γ_0)), so c = 0. In the L² version the two integrals are bounded on ρ_I^γH^k_b by Hardy's
inequality: after the Mellin transform in v they are multiplication by (ζ − a)⁻¹ on the line Re ζ = γ. They commute
with the rotations and intertwine v∂_v, so the b-regularity is preserved. ∎

### 26.8 The inverse of the ι⁺-normal operator

**Theorem 26.27** ([Hin26, Proposition 9.4] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume the hypotheses of
Theorem 26.21 and γ_Υ < min(½s_C, ⅜) (the smallness 0 < γ_Υ ≪ 1 of [Hin26]). Let ϰ ∈ ℂ be such that N_sf(ϰ) is
invertible; by Theorem 26.21 this does not depend on the admissible pair. For f ∈ Ċ^∞(ι⁺; S²T*), extend R^(2+ϰ)f by
0 to {v ≤ 0} and set

    h := N_ι⁺(ϰ)⁻¹f := R^(−ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹(R^(2+ϰ)f)|_((0,∞)_v×𝕊³).    (26.34)

Then N_ι⁺(ϰ)h = f, and:

(1) (*Conormality and polyhomogeneity.*) For every ℓ_I < 3/2 + s_C and every ℓ < 5/2 + s_C, with ℰ_K of
Definition 26.23 (3),

    h ∈ 𝒜^((⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),ℰ_K)(ι⁺),     (v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄)h ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ),ℓ))([0, 1)_v × 𝕊³).    (26.35)

(2) (*Finite regularity.*) Let ℓ_I < 3/2 + s_C with ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ), and let ℓ_K > −1 with
ℓ_K ∉ Re π_1ℰ_K. For Re ϰ < ℓ_I there is d ∈ ℕ_0, depending only on Re ϰ, ℓ_I and the parameters, such that for every
k ∈ ℕ_0 the map f ↦ h extends to a continuous linear map

    N_ι⁺(ϰ)⁻¹: H^(k+d,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K−2)_b(ι⁺; S²T*) → H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_K,ℓ_K))_b(ι⁺; S²T*),    (26.36)

with (v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄)h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ),ℓ_I))_b([0, 1)_v × 𝕊³); the order here is ℓ_I and not ℓ_I + 1, as the
term −(2v)⁻¹f of (26.28) has order ℓ_I only. On {Re ϰ < ℓ_I}, (26.36) is finite-meromorphic in ϰ.
Its principal parts at poles do not depend on k, ℓ_I or ℓ_K, and their ranges lie in the space of (1).

*Proof.* *Step 0: h solves.* Let F := R^(2+ϰ)f, extended by 0. As f vanishes to infinite order at v = 0 and at R = 0,
F is smooth on ℝ_v × 𝕊³, supported in {v ≥ 0}, and O(R^∞) with all b-derivatives at R = 0. So F ∈ Ḣ^((s−1;∞),μ)_(b;b)
for every (s, μ). By Theorem 26.21 (2)–(3), h̃ := N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹F lies in Ḣ^((s;∞),μ)_(b;b) for every pair admissible
for ϰ, and the inverses agree. For 0 < a < 1, N_sf(ϰ)h̃ = 0 on {−1 < v < −a}, so Lemma 26.8 on the slab
Ω_(a,1), with the support at v = −1, gives h̃ = 0 there. Hence supp h̃ ⊂ {v ≥ 0} and h = v^ϰh̃|_(v>0). By
(26.27), N_ι⁺(ϰ)h = v^(2+ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)h̃ = v^(2+ϰ)F = f.

*Step 1: a priori bounds.* Fix ε ∈ (0, ¼) with 3/2 − Re ϰ − ε ∉ ℤ, and put s := 2 − Re ϰ − ε; then (s, μ) is
admissible for μ ∈ (Re ϰ − 1, Re ϰ). *At v = 0:* take χ ∈ C_c^∞((−1, 2)) equal to 1 on [−½, 3/2]. On supp χ the norm of
Ḣ^(s,μ)_b is that of H^s, so χh̃ satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 26.25 for every k.
Hence |W^αh̃| ≤ C_αv^(3/2−Re ϰ−ε) on (0, 1). Since W^αv^ϰ = v^ϰW^α_((ϰ)) (with v∂_v shifted by ϰ),

    |W^αh| ≤ C_αv^(3/2−ε)   on (0, 1) × 𝕊³.    (26.37)

*At R = 0:* R∂_R = −v∂_v and the rotations span the b-vector fields there. So h̃ ∈ R^μH^∞_b near R = 0
(Definition 26.4), and h = R^(−ϰ)h̃ ∈ R^αH^∞_b with α := μ − Re ϰ ∈ (−1, 0). Lemma 21.35 applies with
A := R²N_ι⁺(ϰ) (b-elliptic, Section 26.6.1), Ah = R²f ∈ Ċ^∞, F = ∅ and every β. It gives h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_K,β))_b near
R = 0 for every β ∉ Re spec_b(A); that is, h is polyhomogeneous at R = 0 with index set ℰ_K
(Lemma 26.24 (a)).

*Step 2: the expansion at v = 0 for Re ϰ < 3/2 − ε.* Π_s commutes with v∂_v and with S̄, so (26.28) gives,
for each s ∈ σ_S,

    (v∂_v − ϰ)(v∂_v − 3/2 − s)Π_sh = Π_sg,   g := −(2v)⁻¹f + (v/2)L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v, ∂_ω)h.    (26.38)

L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v, ∂_ω) is a combination of words with smooth coefficients (the proof of Lemma 26.10). Fix
ℓ_I < 3/2 + s_C with ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ); it suffices to prove (26.35) for such ℓ_I, since
𝒜^((ℰ,ℓ′)) ⊂ 𝒜^((ℰ,ℓ)) for ℓ < ℓ′. Let ϑ_j := min(3/2 − ε + j, ℓ_I), and write ℰ^C := ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ). We show by
induction that h ∈ 𝒜^((⟨ℰ^C⟩,ϑ_j)) at v = 0. For j = 0 this is (26.37), as min Re ℰ_s = 3/2 > ϑ_0.

For the step: ℰ^C and the ℰ_s lie in ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ), and words preserve 𝒜^((ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ),ϑ_j)). So
g ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C,ϑ_j+1)), the f-term vanishing to infinite order. Apply Lemma 26.26 to w_1 := (v∂_v − 3/2 − s)Π_sh,
which is O(v^(3/2−ε)) by (26.37), with a = ϰ. Here Re ϰ < 3/2 − ε (the γ_0 of Lemma 26.26) and
ϰ ∉ π_1ℰ^C (whose real parts are ≥ 5/2), so w_1 ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C,ϑ_(j+1))). Apply Lemma 26.26 again, to Π_sh with
