a = 3/2 + s. For s ∈ σ_Υ, 3/2 + s ∉ π_1ℰ^C = 5/2 + σ_Υ + ℕ_0, as |s − s′| ≤ 2γ_Υ < 1; so
Π_sh ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C ∪ (3/2+s,0), ϑ_(j+1))) = 𝒜^((ℰ_s,ϑ_(j+1))). For s ∈ σ_C, Re(3/2 + s) ≥ 3/2 + s_C > ℓ_I ≥ ϑ_(j+1), so
Π_sh ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C,ϑ_(j+1))). (Each use has ϑ_(j+1) ≠ Re a, since ε + s ∈ (0, 1) for s ∈ σ_Υ, and ℓ_I is chosen, as the
monotonicity allows, with ℓ_I ≠ Re ϰ, ℓ_I + 1 ≠ Re ϰ and ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ).) After finitely many steps
ϑ_j = ℓ_I. At that step g ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C,ℓ_I+1)), and the first application of Lemma 26.26 gives
(v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄)h = Σ_s w_1 ∈ 𝒜^((ℰ^C,ℓ_I+1)). With Step 1 this proves (1) for Re ϰ < 3/2 − ε, and so for
Re ϰ < 3/2.

*Step 3: general ϰ, no v^ϰ-terms.* Let 𝒫 be the set of poles of N_sf(·)⁻¹. It is closed and discrete, with finitely
many points in each half plane {Re ≤ C} (Theorem 26.21 (2)). Let Λ_0 := 𝒫 ∪ (3/2 + σ_S + ℕ_0), also closed and
discrete; so 𝒪 := ℂ ∖ Λ_0 is open and connected. For ν ∉ 𝒫 put h(ν) := N_ι⁺(ν)⁻¹f.

(a) *Holomorphy.* Let ν_0 ∉ 𝒫. Choose a disc D ∋ ν_0 disjoint from 𝒫, and a pair (s, μ) admissible for every ν ∈ D,
with s − ½ ∉ ℤ (as in the proof of Theorem 26.21). Let 𝒳_k := {u ∈ Ḣ^((s;k),μ)_(b;b) :
N_sf(ν)u ∈ Ḣ^((s−1;k),μ)_(b;b)} and 𝒴_k := Ḣ^((s−1;k),μ)_(b;b). The difference N_sf(ν) − N_sf(ν_0) is (ν − ν_0)
times −2∂_v plus a module element (Lemma 26.3 (f)). Since [v∂_v, ∂_v] = −∂_v, ∂_v commutes with the rotations,
and ∂_v = −R²∂_R at R = 0, this difference maps Ḣ^((s;k),μ)_(b;b) to 𝒴_k. So 𝒳_k does not depend on ν ∈ D. By
Theorem 26.21 (3), N_sf(ν): 𝒳_k → 𝒴_k is a holomorphic family of bijections, so ν ↦ N_sf(ν)⁻¹ ∈ ℒ(𝒴_k, 𝒳_k) is
holomorphic; so is ν ↦ R^(2+ν)f ∈ 𝒴_k. With Lemma 26.25, whose bound is linear in the norms,
ν ↦ v^(−(s−½))W^αh̃(ν) ∈ L^∞((0, 1) × 𝕊³) is holomorphic on D, and h(ν) = v^νh̃(ν).

(b) *The Mellin recursion.* Let χ ∈ C_c^∞([0, 1)) equal 1 on [0, ½], and ℳ(u)(ζ) := ∫_0^∞ v^(−ζ)u(v) dv/v. By (a),
shrinking D, (ν, ζ) ↦ ℳ(χh(ν))(ζ) is holomorphic on D × {Re ζ < 3/2 − 2ε_0} for some ε_0 > 0. We have
ℳ(v∂_vu) = ζℳ(u) and ℳ(vu)(ζ) = ℳ(u)(ζ − 1). Applying ℳ to (26.38) for χh(ν) gives

    (ζ − ν)(ζ − 3/2 − s)Π_sℳ(χh(ν))(ζ) = ½Π_sL̃(0)(ω, ζ − 1, ∂_ω)ℳ(χh(ν))(ζ − 1) + H_s(ν, ζ).    (26.39)

Here H_s is the transform of −χΠ_sf/(2v) and of the commutator of the operators in (26.38) with χ; apart from
the term vanishing to infinite order it is supported in [½, 1). So H_s is entire in ζ and holomorphic in ν ∈ D. By
induction on the strips {Re ζ < 3/2 − 2ε_0 + j}, (26.39) continues ℳ(χh(ν))(ζ) meromorphically to D × ℂ. Its
singularities lie on {ζ ∈ ν + ℕ_0} ∪ {ζ ∈ 3/2 + σ_S + ℕ_0}, and it decays rapidly as |Im ζ| → ∞ on vertical lines away
from them, since ℳ(χ(v∂_v)^Mh) = ζ^Mℳ(χh) plus terms supported in [½, 1). By Mellin inversion and the circle
integrals of Lemma 21.36, the expansion of χh(ν) at v = 0 is read off from the principal parts: a term
c v^z(log v)^k corresponds to the principal part −k! c (ζ − z)^(−k−1) at ζ = z, since
ℳ(χv^z)(ζ) = −(ζ − z)⁻¹ + (an entire function).

(c) *The v^ν-coefficient vanishes on 𝒪.* Let ν_0 ∈ 𝒪. Choose r ∈ (0, ½) smaller than the distance from ν_0 to
3/2 + σ_S + ℕ_0, and let |ν − ν_0| < r/2. Inside the circle ∂D_r(ν_0) := {|ζ − ν_0| = r}, the only singularity of
ℳ(χh(ν)) is at ζ = ν. It is at most simple: in (26.39) at ζ = ν, ℳ(χh(ν))(ν − 1) is finite, because
ν − 1 ∉ ν + ℕ_0 and ν − 1 ∉ 3/2 + σ_S + ℕ_0, as ν_0 ∈ 𝒪. So

    c(ν) := (2πi)⁻¹ ∮_(∂D_r(ν_0)) Π_sℳ(χh(ν))(ζ) dζ    (26.40)

is minus the coefficient of v^ν in Π_sh(ν), and is holomorphic in ν, the integrand being jointly holomorphic near the
circle. If Re ν < 3/2 − 2ε_0, then ℳ(χh(ν)) is holomorphic at ζ = ν, so c(ν) = 0. As 𝒪 is connected and c is
intrinsically the residue at ζ = ν, c ≡ 0 on 𝒪. Then (26.39) has no singularity at ζ = ν, and so none at
ζ ∈ ν + ℕ_0 either. For ϰ ∈ 𝒪 the induction of Step 2 therefore goes through with Re ϰ arbitrary: in
Lemma 26.26 with a = ϰ, the possible term c_1v^ϰ in w_1 equals (ϰ − 3/2 − s) times the v^ϰ-coefficient of Π_sh,
which is 0; and no logarithm arises at ϰ, as ϰ ∉ 3/2 + σ_S + ℕ_0 ⊃ π_1ℰ^C. So (1) holds for ϰ ∈ 𝒪.

*Step 4: ϰ ∈ (3/2 + σ_S + ℕ_0) ∖ 𝒫, no extra logarithms.* Choose r ∈ (0, ½) such that the closed disc D̄_r(ϰ) meets
Λ_0 only at ϰ, and let 0 < |ν − ϰ| < r/2. Then ν ∈ 𝒪, and by Step 3 the only singularity of Π_sℳ(χh(ν)) inside
∂D_r(ϰ) is at ζ = ϰ. Its order is at most some k_s for all such ν: at ζ = ϰ the recursion (26.39) involves ν
only through (ζ − ν)⁻¹, which is regular there. Its Laurent coefficient of order k_s is the coefficient of the generic
expansion of Π_sh(ν), of the form found in Step 3. The map (ν, ζ) ↦ ℳ(χh(ν))(ζ) is jointly holomorphic on
D_(r/2)(ϰ) × (a neighbourhood of ∂D_r(ϰ)), by (a)–(b): the singular sets ζ = ν and 3/2 + σ_S + ℕ_0 stay away from the
circle. So for every j ≥ 0

    ∮_(∂D_r(ϰ)) (ζ − ϰ)^jΠ_sℳ(χh(ν))(ζ) dζ → ∮_(∂D_r(ϰ)) (ζ − ϰ)^jΠ_sℳ(χh(ϰ))(ζ) dζ   (ν → ϰ).    (26.41)

For j ≥ k_s the left side vanishes, so the pole of Π_sℳ(χh(ϰ)) at ζ = ϰ has order at most k_s. With j = k_s − 1, its
leading Laurent coefficient is the limit of the generic ones. So Π_sh(ϰ) carries, at the exponent ϰ, no logarithm and
no component beyond those that Π_sh(ν) carries. For Re ϰ < ℓ_I (respectively < ℓ), ϰ ∈ 3/2 + σ_Υ + ℕ_0 =
π_1ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) (respectively also ϰ = 3/2 + s, s ∈ σ_C, for the second statement). At such ϰ the generic exponent
structure is that of (26.35), and the remaining exponents of the expansions are unaffected (Step 3). So (1)
holds at ϰ. Exponents with real part beyond the order of (26.35) do not enter.

*Step 5: finite regularity.* Let f ∈ H^(k+d,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K−2)_b(ι⁺) and Re ϰ < ℓ_I.

(i) *Near v = 0:* v^(−2−ϰ)f ∈ ρ_I^(ℓ_I−1−Re ϰ)H^(k+d)_b with ℓ_I − 1 − Re ϰ > −1, so it is in L¹ near v = 0 with values
in H^(k+d)(𝕊³). Its extension F by 0 lies in H^(−½−δ)(ℝ; H^(k+d)(𝕊³)) ⊂ H^(−½−δ)(ℝ × 𝕊³) (the inclusion as in
Lemma 26.25 (i), for negative order). Moreover v∂_vF is the extension of v∂_v(v^(−2−ϰ)f): the boundary term
vuφ at v = 0 vanishes because |u| ≤ Cv^(ℓ_I−1−Re ϰ), by b-Sobolev embedding in v.

(ii) *Near R = 0:* F ∈ R^(ℓ_K+Re ϰ)H^(k+d)_b. Choose δ > 0 and s := min(½, 2 − Re ϰ) − δ with s − ½ ∉ ℤ, and
μ ∈ (Re ϰ − 1, min(Re ϰ, ℓ_K + Re ϰ)), which is non-empty as ℓ_K > −1. Then (s, μ) is admissible, and
F ∈ Ḣ^((s−1;k+d),μ)_(b;b): near v = 0 by (i), as s − 1 ≤ −½ − δ and v∂_v and the rotations pass to the extension by 0;
near R = 0 as μ < ℓ_K + Re ϰ. So h̃ := N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹F ∈ Ḣ^((s;k+d),μ)_(b;b) (Theorem 26.21 (3)), vanishing on
{v < 0} as in Step 0.

(iii) *The expansion at v = 0:* Lemma 26.25 gives |W^αh| ≤ C‖f‖v^(Re ϰ+s−½) for |α| ≤ k + d − m(s), hence the
weighted L² bound with a loss δ in the weight. The induction of Step 2 then runs with the L² version of
Lemma 26.26. Each step loses two b-derivatives (through L̃(0)), and the number of steps is at most
⌈ℓ_I − Re ϰ⌉ + 2; this fixes d in terms of Re ϰ and ℓ_I. Here the f-term of g stops the expansion at ℓ_I. In the first
application of Lemma 26.26, this time with γ_0 = Re ϰ + s − ½ − δ < Re ϰ, terms c_ϰ(f)v^ϰ and, when
ϰ ∈ π_1ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ), c′_ϰ(f)v^ϰ log v may appear, with c_ϰ and c′_ϰ continuous linear functionals. By Steps 3–4, c′_ϰ(f)
and c_ϰ(f) vanish (or c_ϰ(f) is a coefficient permitted by (26.35), when ϰ ∈ π_1ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ)) for
f ∈ Ċ^∞(ι⁺). That space is dense, so the same holds for all f.

(iv) *At R = 0:* the proof of Lemma 21.35 applies at finite order. b-ellipticity gains two b-derivatives, and
the expansion terms have smooth coefficients (they come from residues of N(A, ·)⁻¹ and from RA_1, with F = ∅). It gives
h ∈ H^(k+d+2,(ℰ_K,ℓ_K))_b near R = 0, as ℓ_K ∉ Re π_1ℰ_K. This proves (26.36), and the statement on
(v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄)h is the last application of Lemma 26.26 in (iii), with γ = ℓ_I, for ϰ ∉ 𝒫.

*Meromorphy.* f ↦ F is holomorphic in ϰ, and ϰ ↦ N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ ∈ ℒ(𝒴_k, 𝒳_k) is finite-meromorphic (Theorem 26.21 (2),
and (a) above). Multiplication by v^ϰ is holomorphic into weights reduced by any δ > 0. The expansion coefficients of
(iii)–(iv) are holomorphic in ϰ as well, although the decomposition of Lemma 26.26 is not (its particular
solutions have poles where ϰ ∈ π_1G): each coefficient at an exponent z, Re z < ℓ_I, is (2πi)⁻¹∮(ζ − z)^jΠ_sℳ(χh(ϰ))(ζ)
dζ over a fixed small circle around z, and is holomorphic by the joint holomorphy of Step 3 (b), which for f in the
weighted space holds on {Re ζ < ℓ_I}: there H_s is the transform of −χΠ_sf/(2v) ∈ ρ_I^(ℓ_I)H_b and of terms supported in
[½, 1). The remainder, h minus the finite expansion, is holomorphic in the weaker weight in which h(ϰ) is, and bounded in
the ℓ_I-weighted space locally uniformly in ϰ, the constants of Steps 1–5 being built from N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ and fixed-circle
integrals. A locally bounded map g from an open subset of ℂ into a Banach space X such that x* ∘ g is holomorphic for
every x* in a subspace of X* that separates the points of X is holomorphic ([AN00, Theorem 3.1, p. 787]); applied with X
the ℓ_I-weighted space and the functionals of the larger space, this shows that the remainder is holomorphic in the
ℓ_I-weighted space. So (26.36) is finite-meromorphic on {Re ϰ < ℓ_I}. Its principal part at ϰ_0 is obtained by
expanding R^(±ϰ) about ϰ_0: its Laurent coefficients are finite combinations of R^(−ϰ_0)(log R)^iA_(−j)(log
R)^(i′)R^(2+ϰ_0), with A_(−j) those of N_sf⁻¹. These have finite rank and do not depend on (s, μ), as the inverses agree
(Theorem 26.21 (2)); so they do not depend on k, ℓ_I or ℓ_K. For f ∈ Ċ^∞(ι⁺), the coefficient of order j is
(2πi)⁻¹∮(ϰ − ϰ_0)^(j−1)N_ι⁺(ϰ)⁻¹f dϰ over a small circle in 𝒪. By (1), with expansion coefficients and remainders
continuous in ϰ on the circle, it lies in the space of (1). The coefficients have finite rank and Ċ^∞(ι⁺) is dense, so
their ranges lie there for all f. ∎

### 26.9 The boundary spectrum

**Definition 26.28** ([Hin26, Definition 9.6] in dimension 4 + 1.) spec_ι⁺(L̄) is the set of poles of
ϰ ↦ N_ι⁺(ϰ)⁻¹ acting on Ċ^∞(ι⁺; S²T*), that is, of the ϰ_0 at which ϰ ↦ N_ι⁺(ϰ)⁻¹f ∈ C^∞((0, ∞) × 𝕊³) fails to be
holomorphic for some f. Spec_ι⁺(L̄) is the set of pairs (ϰ, k) with ϰ a pole of order k + 1.

**Lemma 26.29** (a) spec_ι⁺(L̄) ⊂ 𝒫 ⊂ {Re z ≥ 2}, with finitely many points in every half plane
{Re z ≤ C}.

(b) For ℓ_I, ℓ_K as in Theorem 26.27 (2), Spec_ι⁺(L̄) ∩ {Re ϰ < ℓ_I} is the divisor of (26.36) on
H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K−2)_b.

(c) ([Hin26, Remark 9.7] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ϰ_0 ∈ 𝒫 ∖ spec_ι⁺(L̄), and suppose that the principal part of
N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ at ϰ_0 does not vanish on the extensions by 0 of Ċ^∞(ι⁺). Then ker N_sf(ϰ_0) contains a non-zero
distribution supported in {v = 0}. By Lemma 26.30 this forces ϰ_0 ∈ 5/2 + spec S̄ + ℕ_0.

*Proof.* (a) N_ι⁺(ϰ)⁻¹ = R^(−ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹R^(2+ϰ) is holomorphic off 𝒫 (Theorem 26.27), and
𝒫 ⊂ {Re ≥ 2} with finitely many points in each half plane, by Theorem 26.21 (2).

(b) Ċ^∞(ι⁺) is dense in H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K−2)_b (in its Fréchet topology). The Laurent coefficients of (26.36)
are continuous and of finite rank, and they agree with those on Ċ^∞, so the pole orders agree.

(c) Let N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ = Σ_(i=1)^m A_(−i)(ϰ − ϰ_0)^(−i) + (holomorphic), and let j be the largest i with A_(−i)F ≠ 0 for
some F in the extensions by 0 of Ċ^∞(ι⁺). Write R^(2+ϰ)f = Σ_i ((ϰ − ϰ_0)^i/i!)(log R)^iR^(2+ϰ_0)f, and use
(log R)^iR^(2+ϰ_0)f ∈ Ċ^∞(ι⁺). Then the coefficient of (ϰ − ϰ_0)^(−j) in R^(−ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹R^(2+ϰ)f is
R^(−ϰ_0)A_(−j)(R^(2+ϰ_0)f). As ϰ_0 ∉ spec_ι⁺(L̄), this vanishes on {v > 0}. Further
A_(−j)F = (2πi)⁻¹∮(ϰ − ϰ_0)^(j−1)N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹F dϰ is supported in {v ≥ 0} (Step 0 of the proof of Theorem 26.27),
so A_(−j)F is supported in {v = 0}. The coefficient of (ϰ − ϰ_0)^(−j) in N_sf(ϰ)N_sf(ϰ)⁻¹ = Id is
N_sf(ϰ_0)A_(−j) + ∂_ϰN_sf(ϰ_0)A_(−j−1) + ½∂_ϰ²N_sf(ϰ_0)A_(−j−2) = 0 (N_sf is quadratic in ϰ). Applied to such F, with
A_(−i)F = 0 for i > j, this gives N_sf(ϰ_0)A_(−j)F = 0. ∎

**Lemma 26.30** (Kernels supported at the light cone.) If 0 ≠ u ∈ ker N_sf(ϰ), in 𝒳 for an admissible
pair, is supported in {v = 0}, then ϰ ∈ 5/2 + spec S̄ + ℕ_0.

*Proof.* A distribution supported in {0} × 𝕊³ and lying in H^s is u = Σ_(i=0)^j δ^(i)(v) ⊗ a_i, with distributions
a_i on 𝕊³; take a_j ≠ 0. As distributions, vδ^(i) = −iδ^(i−1) (for ⟨vδ^(i), φ⟩ = (−1)^i(vφ)^(i)(0) = (−1)^i iφ^(i−1)(0)),
so v∂_vδ^(i) = vδ^(i+1) = −(i + 1)δ^(i), and every polynomial F satisfies F(v∂_v)δ^(i) = F(−i − 1)δ^(i). Hence, by
(26.3),

    N_sf(ϰ)(δ^(i) ⊗ a) = −2δ^(i+1) ⊗ (ϰ − i − 5/2 − S̄)a + δ^(i) ⊗ L̃(0)(ω, ϰ − i − 1, ∂_ω)a:    (26.42)

the first term is −2∂_v applied to (ϰ − i − 1 − 3/2 − S̄)(δ^(i) ⊗ a), and the second is L̃(0)(ω, v∂_v + ϰ, ∂_ω) at
v∂_v = −i − 1. The coefficient of δ^(j+1) in N_sf(ϰ)u = 0 is −2(ϰ − j − 5/2 − S̄)a_j = 0. By Lemma 26.22,
(ϰ − j − 5/2 − s)Π_sa_j = 0 for every s, and Π_sa_j ≠ 0 for some s; so ϰ = j + 5/2 + s. ∎

In dimension 3 + 1 the same argument gives 2 + spec S̄ + ℕ_0, which fits the observation of [Hin26] that its (9.5)
is available for Re ϰ < 2. Such poles are invisible on ι⁺ and belong to the radiation field ([BVW15, Remarks 7.5 and
8.2], as [Hin26] notes).

### 26.10 Formal solutions at K⁺: the window and its states

This section and the next three are [Hin26, Definitions 9.8 and 9.10, Propositions 9.9 and 9.11 and Corollary 9.12] in
dimension 4 + 1 (pp. 172–179). Theorem 26.39 describes the solutions of Theorem 26.27 at ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, term by
term, as formal solutions built from zero energy states. Theorem 26.42 grafts such a solution into spacetime as an
approximate solution of L_b on the Myers–Perry family, accurate at ι⁺ and at K⁺, and Corollary 26.44 does the same
for sources with logarithms in t_* and at ι⁺-resonances.

*The window.* [Hin26] expands at R = 0 up to R^(ℓ_K) with ℓ_K < 3 + ε_ind, which keeps the indicial roots in [−3, 0],
each with generalised companions to the orders of [Hin26, (9.32)]: it grafts at ι⁺-order ϰ = 1 ([Hin26, (10.15) and
(11.119a)]), and the remainder must then have K⁺-order ϰ + ℓ_K > 4. In dimension 4 + 1 the expansion is carried to
ℓ_K < ℓ_K^max ≤ 3 ((26.43)), and Theorem 26.39, Theorem 26.42 and Corollary 26.44 hold for every
ℓ_K < ℓ_K^max. No graft is made at ϰ = 1: the pure ι⁺-resonances have real part at least 2 (Theorem 26.21 (2)), and
for sources with expansions at ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺ no ι⁺-pole has real part below ϰ_♯ = 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ of (27.22)
(Corollary 27.27). Every application of Corollary 26.44 is made at Re ϰ_0 ≥ ϰ_♯ > 3/2, with the order
ℓ_K := ℓ_K(ϰ_0) chosen there, and checks ℓ_K(ϰ_0) < ℓ_K^max where it is made: ℓ_K(ϰ_0) ∈ (0, 1) in the proofs of
Proposition 31.21 and Proposition 31.27, ℓ_K(ϰ_0) < 3/2 in that of Lemma 32.27, and
ℓ_K(ϰ_0) ≤ 4 + ε_K − ϰ_♯ < 3 in that of Proposition 33.8, since ε_K < (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ = ϰ_♯ − 3/2 by
(32.27), and ℓ_K^max = 3 under (C5) below. The window (−3, 0] needs no zero energy state at −3, and every
state it needs is constructed in Chapter 23 and Chapter 25, with at least the companions required
(Definition 26.31).

Throughout this section and the next three we assume (Dyn), the dynamical hypotheses of Chapter 23, which hold for
g_b, b near b_0, by Theorem 22.12 and Theorem 22.30; the parameters of Proposition 25.11 with
γ_Υ < min(½s_C, ⅜) (Lemma 26.22); (C1) of Section 25.5; and (C2)–(C3) of Section 25.5 with
z_Υ = 4e_Υγ_Υ² outside the exceptional set Z_exc of Proposition 25.6 (e), so that every indicial root of L̂_b(0) is
simple. We fix

    ℓ_K^max := min(3, 2 + 2γ_Cv_C),    (26.43)

so that the vector type 1 root −2 − 2γ_Cv_C of Proposition 25.6 lies below the window; the other roots from □^C with
real part ≤ 0 lie below −101 (Proposition 25.6 (d)). Under the condition

(C5) γ_Cv_C ≥ ½,

ℓ_K^max = 3. The choice of parameters in Theorem 38.24 satisfies (C5), as there v_C = ½ and γ_C > 10⁶. Without
(C5) every statement below holds with ℓ_K^max = 2 + 2γ_Cv_C, which still serves every graft at
Re ϰ_0 > 2 − 2γ_Cv_C + ε_K used at a K⁺-weight at most 4 + ε_K.

For ℓ_K < ℓ_K^max let 𝒲(ℓ_K) be the set of indicial roots μ of L̂_b(0) (Proposition 25.6) with
−ℓ_K < Re μ ≤ 0. All are real (Lemma 26.24 (c)). For a root μ of type τ and degree l, let 𝒴_τ be the space of
harmonics of Section 21.1 that parametrises that type: 𝒮_l for scalar, 𝒱_l for vector and 𝒯_l for tensor types.

**Definition 26.31** (The roots of 𝒲(ℓ_K), ℓ_K < 3, and their states.) For each root μ in
the window we list its types; its origin in the factorisation (25.9); the state whose leading term spans
its indicial solutions (Lemma 26.32); the number m_0 of generalised companions constructed; and the number k_μ
used below.

(1) μ = 0, type s0: the gauge-invariant root −l of (25.9) at l = 0; the time translation h^(0)_(b,s0) of
Proposition 23.34 (1); m_0 = 3; k_μ = 2.

(2) μ = 0, type s2: the root −l + 1 of □^Υ at scalar type l = 2; Proposition 23.34 (4)–(7); m_0 = 3; k_μ = 2.

(3) μ = −1, type s1: the boosts; h^(≤k)_(b,s1) of Proposition 23.28 and Proposition 23.34 (2); m_0 = 4; k_μ = 3,
with the indexing of the s1 chain below.

(4) μ = −1, type v1: the rotations; h^(≤k)_(b,v1) of Proposition 23.28 and Proposition 23.34 (3); m_0 = 3; k_μ = 2,
with the indexing of the v1 chain below.

(5) μ = −1, types s3 and v2: the roots −l + 1 (l = 3) and −l (l = 2) of □^Υ; Proposition 23.34 (4)–(7); m_0 = 2
for each; k_μ = 1.

(6) μ = −2, types s4 and v3: the roots −l + 1 (l = 4) and −l (l = 3) of □^Υ; Proposition 23.34 (4)–(7); m_0 = 1
for each; k_μ = 0.

(7) μ = −2, types s2, v2 and t2: the gauge-invariant root −l of (25.9) at l = 2; the states h^(−2)_(b,τ) of
Proposition 25.37; m_0 = 0; k_μ = 0.

(8) μ = 2 − ι^Υ_(s0,2) ∈ [−z_Υ/3, 0), type s0: a class root; Proposition 23.34 (4)–(7); m_0 = 2; k_μ = 2.

(9) μ = 2 − ι^Υ_(s1,2) ∈ (−¼, 0), type s1: a class root; Proposition 23.34 (4)–(7); m_0 = 2; k_μ = 2.

(10) μ = 2 − ι^Υ_(s2,3) ∈ (−5/4, −1), type s2, and μ = 2 − ι^Υ_(s1,3) ∈ (−5/4, −1), type s1: class roots;
Proposition 23.34 (4)–(7); m_0 = 2; k_μ = 1.

(11) μ = 2 − ι^Υ_(s2,4) and μ = 2 − ι^Υ_(s3,4), in (−9/4, −2), types s2 and s3: class roots; Proposition 23.34
(4)–(7); m_0 = 2; k_μ = 0.

A root μ of L̂_b(0) in the rows from □^Υ is the root μ − 1 of the list of □^Υ in Proposition 23.34, and the state is
h^(μ)_b := δ*_(g_b)ω^(μ−1)_b, whose leading term δ̄*(0)ω̄ is of degree μ (Proposition 23.34 (4)–(7)). Only the rows
with −μ < ℓ_K are used.

*Completeness of the list.* The roots of Proposition 25.6 with real part in (−3, 0] are those listed and the
excluded ones. Excluded are the ι^C_(·,≪,·) − 1 (real part < −101); −2 − 2γ_Cv_C (below −ℓ_K^max); and −l, 2 − l,
1 − l and 2 − ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) with real part ≤ −3. With the ranges of Lemma 23.3,
ι^Υ_(sl,l+j) − 2 ∈ (l + j − 2, l + j − 7/4) is less than 3 only for l + j ≤ 4; and ι^Υ_(s0,2) − 2 ∈ (0, z_Υ/3].

**Lemma 26.32** (The indicial solutions are the leading terms of the states.) For every μ ∈ 𝒲(ℓ_K) and
every type τ at which μ is a root, the kernel of the indicial family N_τ(L̄̂(0), μ) on the type-τ sections of degree l
is {h̄_τ(Y) : Y ∈ 𝒴_τ}. Here h̄_τ(Y) is the ρ^μ-leading term of the state of Definition 26.31 (for s1 and v1 at
−1, of h̆²_(b,s1)(S) and h̆¹_(b,v1)(V)), and Y ↦ h̄_τ(Y) is injective.

*Proof.* On the type-τ sections given by a harmonic Y, the indicial family is a matrix polynomial in μ whose
determinant has μ as a simple zero (the hypothesis on z_Υ). So its kernel is one-dimensional for each Y in a basis of
𝒴_τ, and depends linearly on Y. The leading term h̄ = ρ^μφ(ω) of the state lies in the kernel. Indeed it satisfies
L̄̂(0)h̄ = 0: for the base of a chain this is the leading order of (26.44) at m = 0, since
L̂_b(0) − L̄̂(0) ∈ ρ⁴Diff²_b (Lemma 25.1 (3)); for s1 and v1 it is (26.47) at the first index of the
chain. As 2L̄̂(0) = ρ²L̃(0)(ω, ρ∂_ρ, ∂_ω) ((26.1)) is dilation invariant, this is N(L̄̂(0), μ)φ = 0. The
leading term is non-zero for Y ≠ 0: for the roots from □^Υ by (R5) of Section 23.16, as N(δ̄*(0), μ − 1) is
injective on these types at μ − 1 ∉ {0, −1}, or (at s0 and s2 with μ = 0) by Lemma 25.8; for the boosts and
rotations by Proposition 23.34 (2)–(3); and for the physical states by Proposition 25.37, whose leading terms span
the kernel. ∎

In particular, within the window the leading terms of the states of Proposition 23.34 span the kernels of the
indicial families of L̄̂(0).

### 26.11 Formal solutions

#### 26.11.1 Towers

Let L be a stationary operator of order at most 2 in ∂_(t_*). For stationary h and functions a of t_*,
L(a(t_*)h) = aL̂(0)h + a′[L, t_*]h + ½a″[[L, t_*], t_*]h: with L = L_0 + L_1∂_(t_*) + L_2∂_(t_*)², L_j stationary,
[L, t_*]h = L_1h and [[L, t_*], t_*] = 2L_2.

**Lemma 26.33** (Towers.) (a) For stationary h̆⁰, …, h̆^(m_0), the following are equivalent:
L(Σ_(i=0)^k (k!/(k − i)!)t_*^(k−i)h̆^i) = 0 for k = 0, …, m_0; and

    L̂(0)h̆^m + [L, t_*]h̆^(m−1) + ½[[L, t_*], t_*]h̆^(m−2) = 0,   m = 0, …, m_0    (26.44)

(with h̆^(−1) = h̆^(−2) = 0). (b) If (26.44) holds, then for k ≤ m_0 and every smooth a,

    L(Σ_(j=0)^k a^(j)(t_*)h̆^j) = a^(k+1)([L, t_*]h̆^k + ½[[L, t_*], t_*]h̆^(k−1)) + ½a^(k+2)[[L, t_*], t_*]h̆^k.
    (26.45)

*Proof.* (b) Expanding by the rule for L(ah), the coefficient of a^(m) is the left side of (26.44) for m ≤ k;
for m = k + 1, k + 2 it is what remains. (a) With a = t_*^k/k!, (26.45) shows that (26.44) implies
the polynomial identities. Conversely, by induction on k: the identity for k minus t_* times k times the one for k − 1
leaves the t_*⁰-coefficient, which is k! times the left side of (26.44) at m = k, plus terms that vanish by
(26.44) at smaller m. ∎

For L = L_b, Lemma 25.1 (3) gives near infinity

    [L_b, t_*] = −ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) − g_b^(00)∂_(t_*) + ½Q_b,   [[L_b, t_*], t_*] = −g_b^(00) ∈ ρ²C^∞,    (26.46)

and for L̄ ((26.1), which has no ∂_(t_*)² term), [L̄, t_*] = −ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) and [[L̄, t_*], t_*] = 0.
Indeed by (25.5), L_b = L̄ − ½g_b^(00)∂_(t_*)² + ½Q_b∂_(t_*) + ½R_b, and [∂_(t_*)², t_*] = 2∂_(t_*).

The states of Definition 26.31 satisfy (26.44) for L = L_b. Proposition 23.34 gives
ω^(≤k) ∈ ker □^Υ_b as polynomials in t_*, so δ*_(g_b)ω^(≤k) ∈ ker D_(g_b)Ric ∩ ker δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b) ⊂ ker L_b; here
D_(g_b)Ric(ℒ_Xg_b) = ℒ_XRic(g_b) = 0 and 2δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b)δ*_(g_b) = □^Υ_b. The physical states lie in ker L̂_b(0)
(m_0 = 0).

#### 26.11.2 The Minkowski formal solutions

This is [Hin26, Definition 9.8] in dimension 4 + 1. Let (h̆^i_b)_(i≤m_0) be a tower of Definition 26.31 for
L_b, with h̆^i_b ∈ 𝒜^((μ−i,0) ∪ (μ−i+ℰ_ind)), min Re ℰ_ind > 0, and with ρ^(μ−i)-leading terms h̄̆^i, homogeneous of
degree μ − i. For s1 and v1 the indexing of [Hin26] is used. The s1 tower is h_(b,s1) ∈ 𝒜^((3,0)∪…),
h̆¹_(b,s1) ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪…), then h̆^k_(b,s1) ∈ 𝒜^((−k+1,0)∪…) for k ≥ 2, and its homogeneous part starts at
h̄̆²_s1 =: h̄²_s1, of degree −1. The v1 tower is h_(b,v1) ∈ 𝒜^((3,0)∪…), then h̆^k_(b,v1) ∈ 𝒜^((−k,0)∪…) for k ≥ 1,
starting at h̄¹_v1, of degree −1 ((23.25), Proposition 23.34 (2)–(3)).

**Lemma 26.34** (The Minkowski towers.) The leading terms satisfy (26.44) for L̄:

    L̄̂(0)h̄̆^m + [L̄, t_*]h̄̆^(m−1) = 0,    (26.47)

for the s1 chain from m = 2 and for the v1 chain from m = 1 (the earlier terms being omitted).

*Proof.* Under the dilations (t_*, x) ↦ (st_*, sx), t_*^(k−i)h̆^i has leading degree k − μ for every i (for s1,
k − 1 for i ≥ 2 and k − 3 for i = 0, 1; for v1, k for i ≥ 1 and k − 3 for i = 0). L̄ is homogeneous of degree −2.
L_b − L̄ = −½g_b^(00)∂_(t_*)² + ½Q_b∂_(t_*) + ½R_b ((25.5)) lowers the degree by at least 2, and the
corrections h̆^i_b − χh̄̆^i lower it by min Re ℰ_ind > 0. So the top-degree part of
L_b(Σ (k!/(k − i)!)t_*^(k−i)h̆^i_b) = 0 is L̄(Σ (k!/(k − i)!)t_*^(k−i)h̄̆^i) = 0, over the indices of top degree.
Lemma 26.33 (a) for L̄, with [[L̄, t_*], t_*] = 0, gives (26.47). ∎

**Definition 26.35** ([Hin26, Definition 9.8] in dimension 4 + 1.) For a function a = a(t_*) (valued in 𝒴_τ
where the state is linear in Y) and k ≤ m_0,

    h̄^((μ),≤k)(a) := Σ_(j=0)^k a^(j)(t_*)h̄̆^((μ),j),   h̄^(≤k)_s1(a) := Σ_(j=2)^k h̄̆^j_s1(a^(j−2)),
    h̄^(≤k)_v1(a) := Σ_(j=1)^k h̄̆^j_v1(a^(j−1)).    (26.48)

**Lemma 26.36** ([Hin26, (9.28)–(9.31)] in dimension 4 + 1.) (a)
L̄h̄^((μ),≤k)(a) = a^(k+1)[L̄, t_*]h̄̆^((μ),k), and likewise for s1 (with a^(k−1) and h̄̆^k_s1) and for v1 (with a^(k)
and h̄̆^k_v1).

(b) For a = t_*^(−ϰ+μ) (for s1 and for v1, a = t_*^(−ϰ−1)), the tensor t_*^ϰh̄^((μ),≤k)(a) is independent of t_* in
the coordinates (t_*, R, ω), R = (ρt_*)⁻¹. It is a finite sum Σ_j c_jR^(−μ+j)φ_j(ω), without logarithms. Moreover

    t_*^ϰt_*²L̄(h̄^((μ),≤k)(t_*^(−ϰ+μ))) ∈ R^(−μ+k−1)C^∞([0, 1)_R × 𝕊³)    (26.49)

is independent of t_*. The same holds for s1 with R^(k−2), and for v1 with R^(k−1), in place of R^(−μ+k−1).

*Proof.* (a) is (26.45) for L̄, with [[L̄, t_*], t_*] = 0, by Lemma 26.34. (b) a^(j) = c_jt_*^(−ϰ+μ−j)
and h̄̆^j = ρ^(μ−j)φ_j(ω), so t_*^ϰa^(j)h̄̆^j = c_j(ρt_*)^(μ−j)φ_j = c_jR^(−μ+j)φ_j. By (a) and
[L̄, t_*] = −ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄), the left side of (26.49) is
t_*^(ϰ+2)c_(k+1)t_*^(−ϰ+μ−k−1)ρ^(1+μ−k)ψ(ω) = c_(k+1)(ρt_*)^(1+μ−k)ψ = c_(k+1)R^(k−1−μ)ψ. For s1,
a^(k−1) = ct_*^(−ϰ−k) and h̄̆^k_s1 has degree 1 − k, which gives R^(k−2); for v1, a^(k) = ct_*^(−ϰ−1−k) and degree −k
give R^(k−1). ∎

#### 26.11.3 The Myers–Perry formal solutions

This is [Hin26, Definition 9.10] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Definition 26.37** With the towers of Definition 26.31 for L_b,

    h^((μ),≤k)_b(a) := Σ_(j=0)^k a^(j)(t_*)h̆^((μ),j)_b,
    h^(≤k)_(b,s1)(a) := h_(b,s1)(a) + Σ_(j=1)^k h̆^j_(b,s1)(a^(j)),
    h^(≤k)_(b,v1)(a) := h_(b,v1)(a) + Σ_(j=1)^k h̆^j_(b,v1)(a^(j)).
    (26.50)

**Lemma 26.38** ([Hin26, (9.37)] in dimension 4 + 1.) L_bh^((μ),≤k)_b(a) is given by (26.45) with
h̆^j = h̆^((μ),j)_b, and likewise for s1 and v1. For a = t_*^(−ϰ+μ) it is, near K⁺ (at bounded r),
O(t_*^(−ϰ+μ−k−1)) with all stationary derivatives, that is of K⁺-order ϰ − μ + k + 1. For s1 with a = a_s1 of
(26.54) the order is ϰ + k, and for v1 with a = a_v1 it is ϰ + k + 1. With k = k_μ of
Definition 26.31, every one of these orders is at least ϰ + 3.

*Proof.* (26.45) and the tower property (Section 26.11.1). The coefficients [L_b, t_*]h̆^k_b and
[[L_b, t_*], t_*]h̆^(k−1)_b are stationary and smooth; a^(k+1) ∼ t_*^(−ϰ+μ−k−1), and for s1
a_s1^(k+1) ∼ t_*^(−ϰ−k), for v1 a_v1^(k+1) ∼ t_*^(−ϰ−k−1). The bound ϰ − μ + k_μ + 1 ≥ ϰ + 3 is k_μ ≥ 2 + μ, which the
k_μ of Definition 26.31 satisfy: k_μ = 2 + μ at the integer roots; at the class roots
μ ∈ (−¼, 0), (−5/4, −1), (−9/4, −2), k_μ = 2, 1, 0; for s1, k = 3 gives ϰ + 3; for v1, k = 2 gives ϰ + 3. ∎

### 26.12 The expansion at K⁺

**Theorem 26.39** ([Hin26, Proposition 9.9] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ϰ ∈ ℂ, k ∈ ℕ_0, ℓ_K < ℓ_K^max with
ℓ_K ≠ −Re μ for every root μ, and α ∈ (−1, 0). Suppose N_ι⁺(ϰ)u = f on [0, 1)_R × 𝕊³, with f ∈ H^(k,ℓ_K−2)_b and
u ∈ H^(k+2,α)_b (for the b-density |dR/R dg̸|). Then u = u_0 + ũ, ũ ∈ H^(k+2,ℓ_K)_b, with

    u_0 = Σ_(μ∈𝒲(ℓ_K)) Σ_τ t_*^ϰ h̄^((μ),≤k_μ)_τ(t_*^(−ϰ+μ)Y^((μ))_τ),    (26.51)

for suitable Y^((μ))_τ ∈ 𝒴_τ. The sum runs over the types of Definition 26.31 at which μ is a root. At μ = −1
the s1 and v1 terms are t_*^ϰh̄^(≤3)_s1(t_*^(−ϰ−1)S^((−1))_1) and t_*^ϰh̄^(≤2)_v1(t_*^(−ϰ−1)V^((−1))_1). Each term is a
t_*-independent function of (R, ω) (Lemma 26.36 (b)) and is free of logarithms. The coefficients Y^((μ))_τ are
continuous linear functionals of (u, f) in these spaces.

*Proof.* (26.51) is [Hin26, (9.32)] at n = 4, with the window 𝒲(ℓ_K) and the orders k_μ of
Definition 26.31. By (26.29), R²N_ι⁺(ϰ) = A_0 + RA_1 with A_0 = L̃(0)(ω, −R∂_R, ∂_ω) b-elliptic. So

    A_0u = R²f − RA_1u.    (26.52)

By Lemma 21.35 (its proof at finite order, as in Step 5 (iv) of the proof of Theorem 26.27),
u ∈ H^(k+2,(ℰ,ℓ_K))_b with ℰ generated by Spec_b(A_0) above α. So u is a finite sum of terms R^z(log R)^jc_(z,j)(ω),
Re z < ℓ_K, plus an element of H^(k+2,ℓ_K)_b. We remove the terms in order of increasing real part.

*The lowest term.* Suppose some coefficient is non-zero, and let z_0 be the least real part of an exponent present. In
(26.52) the right side has exponents of real part ≥ min(ℓ_K, z_0 + 1) > z_0. So the terms of A_0u at real part
z_0 vanish: for each z with Re z = z_0 and J the top power of log R, N(A_0, z)c_(z,J) = 0 and
N(A_0, z)c_(z,J−1) + J∂_zN(A_0, z)c_(z,J) = 0. Hence z = −μ for a root μ, which is real, so z = z_0. As μ is a simple
root, ∂_zN(A_0, z) maps ker N(A_0, z) injectively into a complement of the range of N(A_0, z). So Jc_(z,J) = 0, J = 0,
and c := c_(z,0) ∈ ker N(A_0, −μ) = ker N(L̄̂(0), μ). The kernel is finite-dimensional (A_0 is elliptic on 𝕊³) and
splits by type and harmonic. By Lemma 26.32, c = Σ_τ h̄_τ(Y_τ) with unique Y_τ ∈ 𝒴_τ, and μ ∈ 𝒲(ℓ_K) as z_0 < ℓ_K.

*Subtraction.* Let w := Σ_τ t_*^ϰh̄^((μ),≤k_μ)_τ(t_*^(−ϰ+μ)Y_τ), a function of (R, ω) (Lemma 26.36 (b)). Its
R^(−μ)-coefficient is c, since t_*^ϰa h̄̆⁰ = R^(−μ)h̄_τ(Y); for s1 and v1 the lowest terms are R¹h̄²_s1(S) and
R¹h̄¹_v1(V). Its other terms have exponents −μ + j, j ≥ 1. On t_*-independent functions w = w(R, ω),
2L̄(t_*^(−ϰ)w) = t_*^(−ϰ−2)N_ι⁺(ϰ)w ((26.6), Definition 26.1: t_*^(−ϰ)w = ρ^ϰ(R^ϰw)). By
(26.49),

    N_ι⁺(ϰ)w ∈ R^(−μ+k_μ−1)C^∞ ⊂ H^(∞,ℓ_K−2)_b     near R = 0,

as −μ + k_μ − 1 ≥ 1 > ℓ_K − 2 (Lemma 26.38); the same holds for s1 and v1, with R¹. So u′ := u − w satisfies the
hypotheses with f′ := f − N_ι⁺(ϰ)w, and has no term R^(−μ) of the types removed. Doing this for every type and root at
real part z_0, the least real part of an exponent of u′ exceeds z_0. By the first step, every new least exponent is −μ′
for a root μ′ with −μ′ ∈ (z_0, ℓ_K). There are finitely many such roots, so after finitely many steps no term remains,
and ũ := u − u_0 ∈ H^(k+2,ℓ_K)_b. Each Y_τ is read off from the coefficient c, which is a continuous functional of
(u, f) (the circle integrals of Lemma 21.36), and the subtractions are continuous. ∎

**Corollary 26.40** (The index set at K⁺.) In Theorem 26.27, below the order ℓ_K^max, the expansion of
h at R = 0 has no logarithms. Its exponents are −μ + j (μ ∈ 𝒲(ℓ_K), 0 ≤ j ≤ k_μ, with the conventions for s1 and v1).
So h ∈ 𝒜^((⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ^♭_K,ℓ_K)) for every ℓ_K < ℓ_K^max, with

    ℰ^♭_K := ⋃_(μ∈𝒲(ℓ_K^max)) ⋃_(j≤k_μ) (−μ + j, 0).

This is the counterpart at n = 4 of the index set ℰ_K of [Hin26].

*Proof.* Theorem 26.39 with f = R² times a function vanishing to infinite order, and u = h near R = 0. ∎

### 26.13 Grafting

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 9.11 and Corollary 9.12] in dimension 4 + 1. Let M be the compactified spacetime
of Section 21.4 ([Hin26, (3.3)]), with its faces ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺, and Ω := cl_M{t_* ≥ 1} ([Hin26, (9.38)]), with
t_* of (21.30): the domain of Definition 14.3, for this time function. The b-spaces on Ω
(Definition 21.31 (3)–(6)) carry three orders, listed for ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺, and the superscript (•,−) marks, as in
Section 21.10 and Section 14.7, the spaces of distributions supported at the initial face {t_* = 1} and extendible
at the other boundary hypersurfaces of Ω. Let χ_K ∈ C^∞(M) equal 1
near K⁺ and 0 near t_*⁻¹(1) ∪ ℐ⁺, and be a function of R alone near ι⁺. Let χ_ι := χ(t_*), with χ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal to 0
on (−∞, 1] and 1 on [2, ∞); it equals 1 near ι⁺ and is supported in Ω.

**Lemma 26.41** (2L̄ is the ι⁺-normal operator of 2L_b.) For w = w(R, ω) conormal on ι⁺ near {R > 0}
(equivalently w(v, ω), v = R⁻¹), on {|x| > 3R_1},

    2L_b(t_*^(−ϰ)w) = t_*^(−ϰ−2)N_ι⁺(ϰ)w + t_*^(−ϰ−4)v²Bw,    (26.53)

with B = B_0 + vB_1 + v²B_2, each B_i a second-order b-operator in (v∂_v, ∂_ω) whose coefficients are smooth functions
of (ρ, ω) = (v/t_*, ω); B_1 and B_2 come from Q_b and R_b.

*Proof.* 2L̄(t_*^(−ϰ)w) = t_*^(−ϰ−2)N_ι⁺(ϰ)w is the definition of N_ι⁺ ((26.27); Lemma 26.3 (c),
P_0 = 2L_b). For the rest use (25.5), stated for 2L_b, with
∂_(t_*)(t_*^(−ϰ)w(ρt_*)) = t_*^(−ϰ−1)(v∂_v − ϰ)w and ρ∂_ρ = v∂_v at fixed t_*. The term g_b^(00)∂_(t_*)² gives
ρ²t_*^(−ϰ−2)(…)w = t_*^(−ϰ−4)v²(…)w. The term Q_b∂_(t_*) gives ρ³t_*^(−ϰ−1)(…), and R_b gives ρ⁴(…); both are
t_*^(−ϰ−4)v² times v or v². ∎

**Theorem 26.42** ([Hin26, Proposition 9.11] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ϰ ∉ spec_ι⁺(L̄) with Re ϰ > 0. Let
ℓ_K < ℓ_K^max, with ℓ_K ≠ −Re μ for all roots and ℓ_K ∉ Re π_1ℰ_K. Let ℓ_I < 3/2 + s_C with
ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ), and Re ϰ < ℓ_I. Let f_+ ∈ H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K−2)_b(ι⁺; S²T*) and u_+ := N_ι⁺(ϰ)⁻¹(2f_+)
(Theorem 26.27 (2), extended holomorphically to ϰ ∉ spec_ι⁺(L̄)). Write u_+ = χ_K|_ι⁺u_0 + ũ by
Theorem 26.39, with ũ ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),ℓ_K)_b(ι⁺). Define

    a_s1(t_*) := t_*^(−ϰ+1)/(ϰ(ϰ − 1)) if ϰ ≠ 1,   a_s1(t_*) := −log t_* if ϰ = 1,   a_v1(t_*) := −t_*^(−ϰ)/ϰ,
    (26.54)

and let u_(b,0) be (26.51) with every Minkowski formal solution replaced by its Myers–Perry version
(Definition 26.37), at the same orders, and with the s1 and v1 terms h^(≤3)_(b,s1)(a_s1S^((−1))_1) and
h^(≤2)_(b,v1)(a_v1V^((−1))_1):

    u_(b,0) := h^(≤3)_(b,s1)(a_s1S^((−1))_1) + h^(≤2)_(b,v1)(a_v1V^((−1))_1)
               + Σ′_(μ,τ) h^((μ),≤k_μ)_(b,τ)(t_*^(−ϰ+μ)Y^((μ))_τ),
    (26.55)

the primed sum running over the other rows. Let u := χ_Ku_(b,0) + χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ)ũ. Then

    χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ−2)f_+ − L_bu ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ)+2, ℓ_I+1), ϰ+2+ℰ_ind, ϰ+ℓ_K)_b(Ω; S²T*)^(•,−)    (26.56)

for an index set ℰ_ind with min Re ℰ_ind > 0, depending only on L̄ and on whether ϰ = 1. Moreover
(t_*^ϰu)|_ι⁺ = u_+, and

    u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I), (ϰ,0)∪(ϰ+ℰ_ind), (ℰ^gr_K(ϰ),ℓ_K))_b(Ω)^(•,−),

where ℰ^gr_K(ϰ) contains the index sets of a_s1 and a_v1 and (z, 0) for every exponent z of t_*⁻¹ in
(26.55).

*Proof.* *The restriction.* At (ι⁺)°, ρ ∼ t_*⁻¹. The leading term at ρ = 0 of each Myers–Perry tensor is the Minkowski
one. So t_*^ϰh^((μ),≤k)_b(t_*^(−ϰ+μ)Y) → t_*^ϰh̄^((μ),≤k)(t_*^(−ϰ+μ)Y) at ι⁺, and the corrections are
O(t_*^(−min Re ℰ_ind)) there. In the s1 and v1 terms, h_(b,s1)(a_s1S), h̆¹_(b,s1)(a′_s1S) and h_(b,v1)(a_v1V) are of
size ρ³t_*^(−ϰ+1) (or ρ³log t_*), ρ²t_*^(−ϰ) and ρ³t_*^(−ϰ) ((23.25)); these are O(t_*^(−ϰ−2)) at (ι⁺)°.
The next terms reproduce the Minkowski ones: the coefficient of h̆²_(b,s1) is a″_s1S = t_*^(−ϰ−1)S, and that of
h̆¹_(b,v1) is a′_v1V = t_*^(−ϰ−1)V, as in Theorem 26.39. With χ_K|_ι⁺ and χ_ι = 1 near ι⁺,
(t_*^ϰu)|_ι⁺ = χ_Ku_0 + ũ = u_+.

*Away from K⁺.* Near ι⁺, u = t_*^(−ϰ)u_+ up to terms supported near K⁺. Lemma 26.41 gives
t_*^(−ϰ−2)f_+ − L_b(t_*^(−ϰ)u_+) = −½t_*^(−ϰ−4)v²Bu_+, as N_ι⁺(ϰ)u_+ = 2f_+. As u_+ ∈ 𝒜^((⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I)) at v = 0
(Theorem 26.27), v²Bu_+ has ℐ⁺-index set in ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) + 2 to order ℓ_I + 2. Its ι⁺-orders are ϰ + 4 + ℕ_0,
from the Taylor expansion of the coefficients in ρ = v/t_*. The commutator
[L_b, χ_ι] = χ′(t_*)[L_b, t_*] + ½χ″(t_*)[[L_b, t_*], t_*] is supported in {1 ≤ t_* ≤ 2}. By (26.46), at
fixed t_* (where ρ = v/t_* and ρ∂_ρ = v∂_v), its main part on t_*^(−ϰ)ũ is −χ′t_*^(−ϰ−1)v(v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄)ũ. Near ℐ⁺,
ũ = u_+, and (v∂_v − 3/2 − S̄)u_+ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ),ℓ_I))_b by Theorem 26.27 (2). So this part has ℐ⁺-index set
ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ) + 1 = ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) + 2 to order ℓ_I + 1, which is the order (26.56) asks. The other parts carry
ρ² = v²t_*⁻² or ρ³ and give ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) + 2 as well.

*Near K⁺.* Each term of (26.56) has K⁺-order at least ϰ + ℓ_K: χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ−2)f_+, as f_+ has weight ℓ_K − 2
at R = 0 and t_*^(−ϰ−2)R^(ℓ_K−2) = t_*^(−ϰ−ℓ_K)r^(ℓ_K−2); L_b(χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ)ũ), as ũ has weight ℓ_K, L_b is stationary,
and ∂_(t_*) only adds decay; [L_b, χ_K]u_(b,0), which is supported away from K⁺; and L_bu_(b,0) on supp χ_K, as by
Lemma 26.38 each term has K⁺-order at least ϰ + 3 > ϰ + ℓ_K.

*The ι⁺-order of the remainder near K⁺ ∩ ι⁺.* t_*^(ϰ+2)L_bu restricted to ι⁺ is ½N_ι⁺(ϰ)u_+ = f_+, by
Lemma 26.41 and (t_*^ϰu)|_ι⁺ = u_+. The Myers–Perry corrections in u_(b,0) and the terms of Lemma 26.41
contribute at ι⁺-orders in ϰ + 2 + ℰ_ind, with ℰ_ind collecting the index sets of the states of Chapter 23 and
Chapter 25, 2 + ℕ_0, and (2, 1) when ϰ = 1: the term h_(b,s1)(−log t_* S) has size ρ³log t_* = v³t_*⁻³log t_*. No
t_*-dependence of χ_K enters, as χ_K is a function of R near ι⁺. So the ι⁺-index set of the remainder is
ϰ + 2 + ℰ_ind. The membership of u follows term by term: t_*^(−ϰ)ũ, and (26.55), whose t_*-exponents are
those collected in ℰ^gr_K(ϰ). ∎

As in [Hin26], a right side of size O(t_*^(−ϰ−2)) can set the black hole in motion. The s1 term is a centre-of-mass
motion of size O(t_*^(−ϰ+1)), or O(log t_*) at ϰ = 1; at n = 4 there are four directions. In the v1 term, the summand
h_(b,v1)(a_v1V) is invisible at ι⁺ and is non-zero only for A ≠ 0 (Proposition 23.28 (3)), an O(|A|) change of the
rotation in 𝔰𝔬(4); the summand h̆¹_(b,v1)(a′_v1V) is visible there and reproduces h̄¹_v1. At n = 4 the boost and
rotation states decay one order faster than in dimension 3 + 1 (ρ³, ρ², ρ³ against ρ², ρ, ρ; (23.25)), so
their invisibility at ι⁺ holds with room.

**Remark 26.43** (The graft as a holomorphic family.) For fixed ε > 0 and ϰ near ϰ_0 ≠ 1 with
ϰ ∉ spec_ι⁺(L̄) (a_s1 has a pole at ϰ = 1), Theorem 26.42 defines Φ_(ι,b)(ϰ)f_+ := u and
F_(ι,b)(ϰ)f_+ := χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ−2)f_+ − L_bΦ_(ι,b)(ϰ)f_+ on H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K−2)_b(ι⁺). These are holomorphic in ϰ, with
values in H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),ϰ_0−ε,ϰ_0−1−ε)_b(Ω)^(•,−) and in
H^(∞,(ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ)+2,ℓ_I+1),ϰ_0+2+min Re ℰ_ind−ε,ϰ_0+ℓ_K−ε)_b(Ω)^(•,−) respectively ([Hin26, (9.42a)–(9.42b)]).
Holomorphy holds because f_+ ↦ u_+ is holomorphic (Theorem 26.27 (2)), the coefficients Y^((μ))_τ are continuous
functionals of u_+ (Theorem 26.39), t_*^(−ϰ), a_s1 and a_v1 are holomorphic in ϰ with values in these weighted
spaces, and the states do not depend on ϰ.

**Corollary 26.44** ([Hin26, Corollary 9.12] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let Re ϰ_0 > 1, and let l_0 be the order
of the pole of N_ι⁺(L̄, ·)⁻¹ at ϰ_0 (l_0 = 0 if ϰ_0 ∉ spec_ι⁺(L̄)). Let ℓ_K and ℓ_I be as in Theorem 26.42, with
Re ϰ_0 < ℓ_I. Let k ∈ ℕ_0 and

    f = Σ_(j≤k) χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ_0−2)(log t_*)^jf^((j))_+ + f′,

with f^((j))_+ ∈ ⋂_ε H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K−2−ε)_b(ι⁺) and f′ ∈ ⋂_ε H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,∞,ϰ_0+ℓ_K−ε)_b(Ω; S²T*)^(•,−). Then there
are u^((j))_(b,0) of the form (26.55), with ϰ_0 for ϰ and a factor (log t_*)^j in each argument, and
ũ^((j)) ∈ ⋂_ε H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),ℓ_K−ε)_b(ι⁺), j = 0, …, k + l_0, such that
u := Σ_j χ_Ku^((j))_(b,0) + χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ_0)(log t_*)^jũ^((j)) satisfies

    f − L_bu ∈ ⋂_(ε>0) H^(∞,(ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ)+2,ℓ_I+1), ϰ_0+2+ℰ_ind+(0,k+l_0), ϰ_0+ℓ_K−ε)_b(Ω; S²T*)^(•,−),
    (26.57)

and u ∈ ⋂_(ε>0) H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I), (ϰ_0,k+l_0)∪(ϰ_0+ℰ_ind+(0,k+l_0)), (ℰ^gr_K(ϰ_0)+(0,k+l_0),ℓ_K−ε))_b(Ω)^(•,−)
([Hin26, (9.43)]).

*Proof.* As in [Hin26]. The quasi-homogeneous part is
f − f′ = (2πi)⁻¹∮ Σ_j (−1)^j j! (ϰ − ϰ_0)^(−j−1)χ_ιt_*^(−ϰ−2)f^((j))_+ dϰ, over a small circle around ϰ_0 on which
ϰ ∉ spec_ι⁺(L̄). Put u := (2πi)⁻¹∮ Σ_j (−1)^j j! (ϰ − ϰ_0)^(−j−1)Φ_(ι,b)(ϰ)f^((j))_+ dϰ (Remark 26.43). Then
f − L_bu is f′ plus the same integral of F_(ι,b)(ϰ)f^((j))_+, of the stated orders by the holomorphy of
Remark 26.43. Expanding in t_* gives the polyhomogeneity: the power of log t_* is at most the order of the pole
of the integrand at ϰ_0 minus 1, that is k + l_0. ∎

### 26.14 Remarks on the comparison with [Hin26]

The following points concern [Hin26, Section 9.1] itself and are recorded for a reader comparing the two texts.
[Hin26, Proposition 9.11] does not state the hypothesis Re ϰ < ℓ_I, which its use of [Hin26, Proposition 9.4 (2)]
(finite decay at ℐ⁺) needs; [Hin26, Corollary 9.12] states it, and Theorem 26.42 assumes it. The statement of
[Hin26, (9.17)], (v∂_v − 1 − S̄)h ∈ 𝒜^(ℰ^tot+1) without an order, holds in dimension 4 + 1 up to the order
5/2 + s_C of (26.35); beyond it the large eigenvalues of S̄ enter through the coupling by L̃(0), as they do in
h beyond ℓ_I. The hypothesis of [Hin26, Corollary 9.12] also allows terms t_*^(−ϰ_0−2−j), j ≥ 1, which its proof does
not remove; the hypothesis of Corollary 26.44 excludes them. In the proof of Theorem 26.42, the step of [Hin26]
that bounds L_b − N_ι⁺(L_b) through the class of L_b and [Hin26, (9.17)] is replaced by the exact identity
(26.53), and [Hin26, (9.17)] enters only through the commutator with χ_ι, to the finite order of
(26.35). In Theorem 26.39 the ordering of the iteration in [Hin26] (the roots at s0 and s2 first) is
replaced by an induction on the least exponent present, which also shows that the expansion is free of logarithms
below ℓ_K^max. Finally, the expansion of the inverse of the ι⁺-normal operator at v^ϰ is controlled through the Mellin
recursion (26.39), which gives the joint meromorphy in (ϰ, ζ) used tacitly in [Hin26, (9.23)–(9.24)] and,
with (26.41), excludes logarithms of every order at v^ϰ.

## 27. Null infinity, resonant states and the transition face

This chapter studies the linearised gauge-fixed Einstein operator L_b of Chapter 25 near future null infinity and at
the transition face, for Myers–Perry parameters b near b₀, in three steps.

The first, Section 27.1–Section 27.5, concerns the exterior region near spatial and future null infinity. It
introduces corner coordinates there, the classes of metric perturbations with partial expansions at ℐ⁺, the structure
of the gauge-fixed operator at ℐ⁺ (Proposition 27.14) and its mapping properties on these classes
(Proposition 27.17, Corollary 27.18). This is [Hin26, Definitions 5.1–5.4 and 5.13, Remark 5.5, Proposition 5.11
with (5.40)–(5.41a), Proposition 5.14 and Corollary 5.15] (pp. 84–99) in dimension 4 + 1, with the parts of [Hin26,
Lemmas 5.6–5.8, Corollaries 5.9–5.10] that these use. [Hin26, Sections 5.4–5.7] (Lemma 5.16, Theorems 5.17, 5.21 and
5.23, Proposition 5.25) and the edge-b form (5.26b) that their energy estimates use are carried to dimension 4 + 1 in
Chapter 37.

The second, Section 27.6–Section 27.8, extends the inverse of the ι⁺-normal operator of Chapter 26 to sources
with partial expansions at ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, locates the incoming poles this creates (Corollary 27.27), and describes the
quasi-homogeneous solutions and resonant states at ι⁺ (Proposition 27.36). This is [Hin26, Section 9.1.3]
(pp. 180–186) in dimension 4 + 1: Lemmas 9.13–9.14, Proposition 9.15, Definition 9.16 with (9.49), Remark 9.17,
Corollary 9.18, Definition 9.19, Remark 9.20, Lemma 9.21, (9.54)–(9.55), Proposition 9.22 and Remarks 9.23–9.24.
[Hin26] uses this material only in its Section 12.

The third, Section 27.10–Section 27.14, is [Hin26, Section 9.2] (pp. 186–199) in dimension 4 + 1: the formal
solutions at the corner ztf of the transition face ((9.57)–(9.61), Definition 9.25), the expansion at r̂ = 0 of the
inverse of the tf-normal operator (Lemma 9.26, Remarks 9.27–9.28), the grafting of tf-solutions into the low-energy
space (Definition 9.29, (9.72), Proposition 9.30, Remarks 9.31–9.34) and its conormal version (Proposition 9.35).
[Hin26] uses these results from its Section 11.5 on.

Two further sections complete the chapter. Section 27.9, after the second step, collects in
Proposition 27.39 the operator at null infinity in dimension 4 + 1, entry by entry, and what it gives for the order at
which a radiative term at null infinity reaches future timelike infinity. Section 27.15, at the end, gives in
Proposition 27.59 the quantities through which the spatial dimension enters [Hin23a, Section 3], the energy estimates
near null and spatial infinity that Chapter 37 carries to dimension 4 + 1; Chapter 37 uses them.

The notation is that of Chapter 21–Chapter 26. In particular n = 4, D = 5; the family g_b, b = (m, A) ∈ ℬ, of
Section 21.5, with m₀, R₁ = m₀^(1/2), the compactification M and its faces I₀, ℐ⁺, ι⁺, K⁺ (Definition 21.12); the
gauge-fixed operator of Section 21.8; the linearised operator L_b and its Minkowski model L̄ of Chapter 25, with the
endomorphism S̄ of Lemma 25.1 and its spectrum (25.6); and the index sets and partially polyhomogeneous
spaces of Section 21.9. We write the spectral families of Chapter 25 with a hat: L̂_b(σ) := L_b^(σ) and
L̄̂(σ) := L̄^(σ), so that 2L̄̂(0) = (2L̄)^(0) and L̂_b(0) is the zero energy operator. No step of this chapter involves
the inner radius r₀ of the spaces of Chapter 11: the exterior region below is a neighbourhood of I₀ ∪ ℐ⁺ of radius at
least 4R₁, and the results at ι⁺ and at the transition face concern faces at infinity and meet the inner radius only
through the results of Chapter 25 and Chapter 26 that they use.

### 27.1 Hypotheses, the exterior region, and its coordinates

**Remark 27.1** (What dimension 4 + 1 changes at null infinity.) Three things change against [Hin26,
Section 5], and together they make the structure simpler.

(a) Radiation fields at null infinity decay like r^(−3/2), so the index sets at ℐ⁺ start at 3/2 where those of [Hin26]
start at 1 (as at ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, Definition 26.23).

(b) The mass of Myers–Perry enters at |x|⁻² (Proposition 21.21). At the corner I₀ ∩ ℐ⁺ it lies in the error class
ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞, so the leading part there is that of Minkowski space, where [Hin26] carries the Schwarzschild terms.

(c) The contributions of the perturbation to the operator, the terms A^h − A₀ and B^h of [Hin26, (5.28)], carry at least
ρ_I^(1/2) relative to the constant matrix A₀, where in [Hin26] they are of the same order. They join the error, at the
cost of the index set ℰ_I^tot in place of ℰ_I^C in its perturbation part. So the structure theorem
(Proposition 27.14) has a constant lower-triangular matrix Ā and no leading part depending on h. The coupling of the
radiation field of π̸₀h into π₁₁h through the (7, 6) entry of [Hin26, (5.28)] is half an order lower and lands in ℰ_I^C,
so π₁₁h carries no radiation field (Remark 27.19). The last index condition of [Hin26, Definition 5.3] is
strengthened to ℰ_I^tot + (ℰ_I^tot − 1) ⊂ ℰ_I^C (Definition 27.6), which needs γ_Υ < 1/4.

Throughout this chapter we use, besides the notation fixed above, the time functions t_* = t − ψ(|x|) and t_IVP
((21.30), Lemma 21.22), with t_* = t − |x| + C′ − 8m₀|x|⁻¹ on {|x| ≥ 3R₁}, and the gauge parameters of
Section 25.1, with, in addition,

    0 < γ_Υ < 1/4,     0 < e_Υ < 1.    (27.1)

(The conditions [Hin26, (5.42)], v_C < 1, 0 < e_C < 1, γ_C > 0, 0 < e_Υ < 1, γ_Υ > 0, hold under the choices of
Section 25.1.) Let η := −dt² + dx² in the coordinates of Section 21.4, and

    x⁰ := t + |x|,     x¹ := t − |x|,     ρ₀ := 1/(2 − x¹),     ρ_I := (2 − x¹)/|x|,    (27.2)

the last two being the coordinates (21.23) near I₀ ∩ ℐ⁺. (Here x⁰ is that of Minkowski space; the x⁰ of
(21.34) for g_m is t + |x| − T_m(|x|), and the two null frames differ by I + ρ²C^∞, Lemma 27.4.) Fix
T₀ := C′ + 1 − 2R₁ and set

    Ω_ext := cl_M{t_* ≤ T₀},     U := Ω_ext ∩ {|x| ≥ 4R₁}.    (27.3)

([Hin26, (5.1)] fixes T and shifts it to 1; the choice of T₀ only makes (27.2) global on U.) On U,
x¹ = t_* − C′ + 8m₀|x|⁻¹ ≤ T₀ − C′ + 2R₁ = 1, since m₀ = R₁².

**Lemma 27.2** (The corner coordinates.) (1) (ρ₀, ρ_I, ω), ω = x/|x|, are coordinates on all of U, smooth
up to I₀ and ℐ⁺: ρ₀ ∈ [0, 1], ρ₀ = 0 exactly at I₀, ρ_I = 0 exactly at ℐ⁺, and ρ₀ρ_I = |x|⁻¹. (2) With
X₀ := ρ₀∂_(ρ₀), X_I := ρ_I∂_(ρ_I) (at fixed ω and the other coordinate), exactly on U,

    ∂_(t_*)|_(ρ,ω) = ρ₀(X₀ − X_I),     ρ∂_ρ|_(t_*,ω) = X_I + 8m₀ρ₀²ρ_I(X₀ − X_I),     ρ := |x|⁻¹,    (27.4)

    ∂₀ = −½ρ₀ρ_I X_I,     ∂₁ = ρ₀(X₀ − X_I + ½ρ_I X_I),    (27.5)

with ∂₀, ∂₁ the coordinate fields of (x⁰, x¹, ω). In particular ∂_t, ∂_(x^i), ∂₀, ∂₁ and |x|⁻¹∂_ω lie in ρ₀𝒱_b(U), and
∂₀, |x|⁻¹∂_ω ∈ ρ₀ρ_I𝒱_b(U).

*Proof.* (1) (x¹, |x|) ↦ (ρ₀, ρ_I) is a diffeomorphism of {x¹ < 2, |x| > 0} onto (0, ∞)², with inverse x¹ = 2 −
ρ₀⁻¹, |x| = (ρ₀ρ_I)⁻¹. Near I₀ ∩ ℐ⁺ these are the coordinates (21.23). Near the interior of I₀, Section 21.4
uses (τ, ρ) = (t/|x|, |x|⁻¹) with τ ∈ [−½, 1 − δ]; there ρ_I = 1 − τ + 2ρ and ρ₀ = ρ/ρ_I, smooth with smooth inverse
ρ = ρ₀ρ_I, τ = 1 − ρ_I + 2ρ₀ρ_I, as ρ_I ≥ δ. Near the interior of ℐ⁺, Section 21.4 uses (t₀, ρ) = (x¹, |x|⁻¹); there
ρ₀ = (2 − t₀)⁻¹ and ρ_I = (2 − t₀)ρ, smooth with smooth inverse for t₀ ≤ 1. These charts cover a neighbourhood of
(I₀ ∪ ℐ⁺) ∩ Ω_ext, and U meets no other face at infinity (it meets Σ^past and {t_* = T₀}, where the spaces are
extendible).

(2) A vector field aX₀ + bX_I is determined by its action on two functions of (ρ₀, ρ_I). With
t_* = 2 − ρ₀⁻¹ + C′ − 8m₀ρ₀ρ_I and ρ = ρ₀ρ_I: X₀t_* = ρ₀⁻¹ − 8m₀ρ, X_I t_* = −8m₀ρ, X₀ρ = X_Iρ = ρ. So ρ₀(X₀ − X_I) maps
t_* ↦ 1, ρ ↦ 0; and X_I + α(X₀ − X_I) with α := 8m₀ρ₀²ρ_I maps ρ ↦ ρ and t_* ↦ −8m₀ρ + αρ₀⁻¹ = 0. For
(27.5): ∂₀|x| = ½, ∂₁|x| = −½, ∂₀x¹ = 0, ∂₁x¹ = 1; so ∂₀ρ₀ = 0, ∂₀ρ_I = −½ρ₀ρ_I², ∂₁ρ₀ = ρ₀²,
∂₁ρ_I = −ρ₀ρ_I + ½ρ₀ρ_I², which is (27.5). The memberships: ∂_t = ∂₀ + ∂₁, ∂_(|x|) = ∂₀ − ∂₁,
∂_(x^i) = ω^i∂_(|x|) + |x|⁻¹(…)∂_ω, and |x|⁻¹∂_ω = ρ₀ρ_I∂_ω with ∂_ω (at fixed ρ₀, ρ_I) a b-vector field. ∎

For the null coordinates of the Tangherlini metric of mass m ((21.34)–(21.35)), with ρ₀, ρ_I defined by
(27.2) from their x¹ and |x|, the same calculation with ∂₀|x| = f/2, ∂₁|x| = −f/2, f := 1 − m|x|⁻², gives
∂₀ = −(f/2)ρ₀ρ_I X_I and ∂₁ = ρ₀(X₀ − X_I + (f/2)ρ_I X_I); (27.5) is the case f = 1.

*The splitting.* On U, in the rescaled frame (dx⁰, dx¹, |x|e^a), e^a a local orthonormal coframe of 𝕊³, the splitting
[Hin26, (5.27)] reads

    S²T* = ⟨(dx⁰)²⟩ ⊕ (2dx⁰ ⊗_s |x|T*𝕊³) ⊕ ⟨|x|²g̸⟩ ⊕ ⟨2dx⁰dx¹⟩ ⊕ (2dx¹ ⊗_s |x|T*𝕊³)
           ⊕ |x|² ker tr̸ ⊕ ⟨(dx¹)²⟩,    (27.6)

of ranks 1 + 3 + 1 + 1 + 3 + 5 + 1 = 15: the splitting (21.37) for η, reordered. Here 2dx⁰dx¹ :=
dx⁰ ⊗ dx¹ + dx¹ ⊗ dx⁰ and 2dx^i ⊗_s w := dx^i ⊗ w + w ⊗ dx^i. A symmetric 2-tensor h has rescaled components
h₀₀ = h(∂₀, ∂₀), h_(0ā) (the tangential part of h(∂₀, ·)), h₀₁ = h(∂₀, ∂₁), h_(1ā), h₁₁ = h(∂₁, ∂₁) and h_(āb̄) (the
tangential block, in the frame |x|e^a), as in Section 21.6, and its *slot coordinates* are, in the order of
(27.6),

    (h₀₀, h_(0ā), ⅓tr̸h, h₀₁, h_(1ā), π̸₀h, h₁₁),     tr̸h := g̸^(ab)h_(āb̄),    (27.7)

the third being the coefficient of |x|²g̸. Each of these is the coefficient of the basis element of the corresponding
summand: for instance the element 2dx⁰dx¹ of the fourth summand has h₀₁ = 1, as dx⁰(∂₀) = dx¹(∂₁) = 1 and
dx⁰(∂₁) = dx¹(∂₀) = 0.

**Definition 27.3** ([Hin26, Definition 5.2] in dimension 4 + 1.) π_C h := (h₀₀, h_(0ā), tr̸h),
π₀₁h := h₀₁, π_(1/)h := h_(1ā), π̸₀h := h_(āb̄) − ⅓(tr̸h)g̸_(ab), π₁₁h := h₁₁. (The factor ⅓ replaces the ½ of [Hin26]:
π̸₀h is the trace-free part on 𝕊³.)

**Lemma 27.4** (Frames.) Three smooth frames of S²T* on U are used: the products of the Cartesian dt, dx^i;
those of dt_*, dx^i (Chapter 25); and the rescaled null frame of (27.6). Each is related to the next by a
smooth bundle map with smooth inverse, of the form F₀(ω)(I + ρ²C^∞(U)) with F₀ depending on ω alone.

*Proof.* dt_* = dt − ψ′(|x|)d|x| with ψ′ = 1 − 8m₀|x|⁻² on U, so dt_* = dx¹ + 8m₀|x|⁻²d|x|. Further d|x| = ω_i dx^i,
and |x|e^a is the orthonormal tangential projection of dx; both depend on ω alone. Finally dx⁰ = dt + d|x| and
dx¹ = dt − d|x|. ∎

So the spaces below, which are defined slot by slot in (27.6), do not depend on which of the null frames of
η, of g_m ((21.35)) or of ḡ (Chapter 25) is used: these differ by I + ρ²C^∞, and ρ² = ρ₀²ρ_I² moves the index
sets of a component by 2 at both faces, into ℰ_I^C (Lemma 27.7 (c)).

### 27.2 Function spaces, products

We use the notions of Section 21.9 without change: index sets, (z, k) for the smallest index set containing (z, k),
sums ℰ + ℱ, and the partially polyhomogeneous spaces H^(k,(ℰ₀,α₀),(ℰ_I,α_I))_b of [Hin26, Definition 2.8 and Notation
2.9], with the faces listed as I₀, ℐ⁺. On Ω_ext these are spaces of restrictions (extendible at {t_* = T₀}, Σ^past and
Σ^int), as [Hin26, (5.2)] has them; dim Ω_ext = 5. Sections of the summands of (27.6) are taken in local
trivialisations by e^a.

**Lemma 27.5** (Products.) Let Z be a manifold with corners of dimension d, compact or a relatively compact
domain in one, with boundary hypersurfaces H; let k > d/2, k′ ≥ k, u ∈ H^(k,(ℰ⃗,α⃗))_b(Z),
v ∈ H^(k′,(ℱ⃗,β⃗))_b(Z). Let γ_H ≤ α_H + β_H, γ_H < α_H + min Re ℱ_H and γ_H < β_H + min Re ℰ_H for every H
(min Re ∅ := +∞). Then uv ∈ H^(k,(ℰ⃗+ℱ⃗,γ⃗))_b(Z), and (u, v) ↦ uv is continuous.

*Proof.* (i) *No expansions.* H^k_b is H^k for a b-metric, which in logarithmic coordinates s_i = −log x_i near a corner
is uniformly equivalent to the Euclidean metric on a cover by unit cubes Q_m of bounded overlap. On one cube
‖fg‖_(H^k(Q)) ≤ C‖f‖_(H^k(Q))‖g‖_(H^(k′)(Q)) for k > d/2, k′ ≥ k (Sobolev embedding and the Leibniz rule), with C the
same for every cube. Summing, ‖fg‖²_(H^k) ≤ C² Σ_m ‖f‖²_(H^k(Q_m))‖g‖²_(H^(k′)(Q_m)) ≤ C′‖f‖²_(H^k)‖g‖²_(H^(k′)).
Weights multiply: ρ^α H^k_b · ρ^β H^(k′)_b ⊂ ρ^(α+β)H^k_b.

(ii) *Expansions.* Induct on the number of pairs (face, factor) at which a factor carries an expansion. Pick such a face
H and write, in a collar, u = χ Σ ρ_H^z (log ρ_H)^l u_((z,l)) + u′ (as in [Hin26, Definition 2.8, (2.3)]), and the same
for v (with no sum if v has none at H). The products of the sums give χ²ρ_H^(z+w)(log ρ_H)^(l+m)u_((z,l))v_((w,m))
(χ² − χ is supported where ρ_H ≥ ε/2 and goes to the remainder), with (z + w, l + m) ∈ ℰ_H + ℱ_H. The coefficient
u_((z,l))v_((w,m)) lies in the space on H that [Hin26, Definition 2.8] requires, by the lemma on H (dimension d − 1,
k > (d − 1)/2). Terms with Re(z + w) ≤ γ_H are kept; the others are ρ_H^(γ_H) times ρ_H^ε(log ρ_H)^(l+m), ε > 0, and go
to the remainder. A cross term χρ_H^z(log ρ_H)^l u_((z,l))v′ has weight Re z + β_H − ε′ at H for every ε′ > 0, which
exceeds γ_H by hypothesis, and fewer expansions, so the induction applies to it. The same holds for u′v and u′v′, the
last of weight α_H + β_H ≥ γ_H. Continuity follows from the same bounds. ∎

We use with it property (F1) of Section 21.9: a b-vector field maps H^(k,(ℰ⃗,α⃗))_b to H^(k−1,(ℰ⃗,α⃗))_b.
Multiplication by C^∞ preserves the spaces, as index sets are closed under + ℕ₀, and multiplication by ρ_H^c shifts ℰ_H
and α_H by c.

### 27.3 Metric perturbations

This section is [Hin26, Definitions 5.3–5.4, Remark 5.5] in dimension 4 + 1. Write

    σ_Υ := {0, (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ, 2γ_Υ} ⊂ [0, ½),

the eigenvalues of S̄ on the slots 4–7 (Lemma 25.2, Lemma 27.12).

**Definition 27.6** ([Hin26, Definition 5.3] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ℰ₀, ℰ_I^C ⊂ ℂ × ℕ₀ be index sets
such that

(1) min Re ℰ₀ > 0 and jℰ₀ ⊂ ℰ₀ for all j ∈ ℕ;

(2) min Re ℰ_I^C > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ;

(3) with

    ℰ_I^tot := ℰ_I^C ∪ ⋃_(s∈σ_Υ) (3/2 + s, 0),    (27.8)

ℰ_I^tot + (ℰ_I^tot − 1) ⊂ ℰ_I^C.

This strengthens the condition ℰ_I^C + (ℰ_I^tot − 1) ⊂ ℰ_I^C of [Hin26, Definition 5.3], and it implies the condition
jℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C, j ≥ 2, there (Lemma 27.7 (b)). It is needed for Proposition 27.17. Under the counterparts
of the conditions of [Hin26] alone, ℰ_I^C + (ℰ_I^tot − 1) ⊂ ℰ_I^C and jℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C for j ≥ 2, the conclusion of
Lemma 27.7 (b) fails. Indeed, let z₀ ∈ (3/2 + 2γ_Υ, 2) and let ℰ_I^C be the smallest index set containing (z₀, 0)
with these two properties. Every element it acquires beyond (z₀, 0) is z + j with z an element and j ≥ 1 (real part at
least z₀ + 1 > 2), or lies in ℰ_I^C + (ℰ_I^tot − 1) (real part at least z₀ + ½ > 2) or in jℰ_I^tot, j ≥ 2 (real part
at least 3). So (2, 0) ∉ ℰ_I^C, while
(3, 0) = 2(3/2, 0) ∈ 2ℰ_I^tot; and (3, 0) ∈ ℰ_I^C + 1 would need (2, 0) ∈ ℰ_I^C. Hence 2ℰ_I^tot ⊄ ℰ_I^C + 1.

Set

    ℰ_(I,01) := ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0),     ℰ_(I,1/) := ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + γ_Υ, 0),
    ℰ̸_(I,0) := ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2, 0),
    ℰ_(I,11) := ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0) ∪ (3/2 + 2γ_Υ, 0).    (27.9)

Let k ≥ 5, ℓ₀ > 0 and ℓ_I > 3/2. Then H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_ext) ⊂ H^(k,0,0)_b(Ω_ext; S²T*) is the space of
real symmetric 2-tensors h whose restriction to U satisfies

    π_C h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_I^C,ℓ_I))_b,     π₀₁h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_(I,01),ℓ_I))_b,
    π_(1/)h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_(I,1/),ℓ_I))_b,     π̸₀h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ̸_(I,0),ℓ_I))_b,
    π₁₁h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_(I,11),ℓ_I))_b.    (27.10)

If 0 < ℓ₀ < min Re ℰ₀ we write ℓ₀ for (ℰ₀, ℓ₀), and if 3/2 < ℓ_I < min Re ℰ_I^C we write (−, ℓ_I) for (⟨ℰ_I^C⟩, ℓ_I).

So π_C h decays strongly at ℐ⁺; π₀₁h and π_(1/)h decay like |x|^(−3/2−(1−e_Υ)γ_Υ) and |x|^(−3/2−γ_Υ); π̸₀h has a
radiation field at |x|^(−3/2); and π₁₁h carries the exponents 3/2 + 2γ_Υ (its own) and 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ (from π₀₁h
through the entry (7, 4) of Ā), but no radiation field, unlike the exponent 1 of [Hin26]
(Remark 27.19). The condition k ≥ 5 gives k − 2 > 5/2 = ½ dim Ω_ext, so Lemma 27.5 applies to
H^(k−2) factors.

**Lemma 27.7** (Consequences of Definition 27.6.) Under (27.1) and Definition 27.6:

(a) ℰ_I^C + ½ ⊂ ℰ_I^C and ℰ_I^tot + ½ ⊂ ℰ_I^C; so ℰ_I^C + 1, ℰ_I^tot + 1 ⊂ ℰ_I^C, and (2, 0), (3, 0) ⊂ ℰ_I^C.

(b) jℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C + (j − 1) for j ≥ 2; in particular 2ℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1.

(c) ℰ_I^tot + 2 ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1, and every component index set of (27.10) lies in ℰ_I^tot.

(d) The intersections of ℰ_(I,01), ℰ_(I,1/), ℰ̸_(I,0), ℰ_(I,11) with {Re z > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ} equal that of ℰ_I^C ([Hin26,
remark (iii) after Definition 5.3]).

(e) For every index set ℰ̃ with min Re ℰ̃ > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ there is a smallest ℰ_I^C ⊇ ℰ̃ satisfying (2)–(3) of
Definition 27.6 ([Hin26, remark (ii) after Definition 5.3]).

*Proof.* (a) (3/2, 0) ⊂ ℰ_I^tot, so ½ ∈ ℰ_I^tot − 1, and (3) gives
ℰ_I^C + ½ ⊂ ℰ_I^tot + (ℰ_I^tot − 1) ⊂ ℰ_I^C, and likewise ℰ_I^tot + ½ ⊂ ℰ_I^C. Iterating gives + 1.
(2, 0) = (3/2, 0) + (½, 0) and (3, 0) = 2(3/2, 0).

(b) 2ℰ_I^tot = (ℰ_I^tot + (ℰ_I^tot − 1)) + 1 ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1, using only (3); and
(j + 1)ℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C + (j − 1) + ℰ_I^tot = (ℰ_I^C + (ℰ_I^tot − 1)) + j ⊂ ℰ_I^C + j.

(c) From (a): ℰ_I^tot + 1 ⊂ ℰ_I^C. The component sets are unions of ℰ_I^C with some (3/2 + s, 0).

(d) The added sets are {3/2 + s + j}. For j = 0, 3/2 + s ≤ 3/2 + 2γ_Υ; for j ≥ 1,
3/2 + s + j ∈ ℰ_I^tot + 1 ⊂ ℰ_I^C by (a).

(e) Put Σ := ⋃_s (3/2 + s, 0), ℰ_((0)) := ℰ̃, and let ℰ_((m+1)) be the smallest index set containing ℰ_((m)) and
ℰ′_m + (ℰ′_m − 1), ℰ′_m := ℰ_((m)) ∪ Σ. Each new element has real part at least ½ more than an element it is built
from, and the generators in {Re z < C} are finitely many; so in each half plane {Re z < C} only finitely many elements
arise, after at most 2C steps, with bounded logarithmic orders. The union ℰ_I^C is an index set; it satisfies (3) by
construction, and (2) since new elements have real part at least 3/2 + ½ = 2 > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ by (27.1). Every
set satisfying (2)–(3) and containing ℰ̃ contains each ℰ_((m)). ∎

**Definition 27.8** ([Hin26, Definition 5.4] in dimension 4 + 1.) For ℰ₀ as in Definition 27.6 (1),
k ≥ 5, ℓ₀ > 0, ℓ_I > 3/2, H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨(3,0)⟩₀,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_ext) is the space of h with
π_C h, π₀₁h, π_(1/)h, π̸₀h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),((3,0),ℓ_I))_b and π₁₁h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),((2,0),ℓ_I))_b on U. By
Lemma 27.7 (a) it lies in H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b for every ℰ_I^C of Definition 27.6.

The class ⟨(2, 0)⟩₀ of [Hin26] has (1, 0) for π̸₀ and π₁₁. For π₁₁ that is the mass order, (2, 0) here. For π̸₀ it is the
radiation order; the class above contains no radiation field of π̸₀, and with (3/2, 0) in slot 6 the mapping property
(27.19) below would fail as soon as ℓ_I ≥ 5/2: the error term ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_b of (27.16) maps
ρ_I^(3/2) to ρ_I^(7/2), a term that (4, 0) does not contain and that does not lie in ρ_I^(ℓ_I+1)H^(k−2)_b, as
7/2 ≤ ℓ_I + 1. (For ℓ_I < 5/2 that term lies in the remainder; the backgrounds of Definition 27.9 and
Lemma 27.10 lie in the class with ℓ_I = ∞.) [Hin26] uses ⟨(2, 0)⟩₀ to subtract the radiation fields in
[Hin26, Theorem 5.21, Step 2] ((5.64), p. 104). In dimension 4 + 1 that subtraction is not needed (Remark 37.37).

**Definition 27.9** (The background class.) 𝒢 is the set of Lorentzian metrics g₀ on Ω_ext, smooth on M,
with

    g₀ − η ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞(U; S²T*),     π(g₀ − η) ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I³C^∞(U)     (π ∈ {π_C, π₀₁, π_(1/), π̸₀}),    (27.11)

equivalently g₀ − η ∈ H^(∞,(2,0),⟨(3,0)⟩₀,∞)_b(U) ([Hin26, footnote 55], in dimension 4 + 1 and with η in place of
g_m). Proposition 27.14 uses only the first condition; the second matters for perturbations measured from g_b.

**Lemma 27.10** ([Hin26, Remark 5.5] in dimension 4 + 1.) (1) g_b ∈ 𝒢 for every b ∈ ℬ. (2) For S ∈ 𝒮₁
small as in Lemma 21.27, φ_S^*g_b − g_b ∈ H^(∞,(2,0),⟨(3,0)⟩₀,∞)_b on U ∩ {χ_IVP(1 − χ_K) = 1}, so φ_S^*g_b
agrees there with an element of 𝒢.

*Proof.* (1) By Proposition 21.21, g_b − g_m ∈ |x|⁻³C^∞ = ρ₀³ρ_I³C^∞, and on {|x| ≥ 3R₁},
g_m − η = m|x|⁻²(dt − d|x|)² = mρ₀²ρ_I²(dx¹)², which has only the slot π₁₁. (2) By Lemma 21.27, there
φ_S^*g_b − g_b = |x|⁻²h_S(ω)(dx¹)² + ρ₀²ρ_I³C^∞, with h_S ∈ C^∞(𝕊³). ∎

Outside {χ_IVP(1 − χ_K) = 1} near I₀, φ_S is the flow of a cut-off boost, and φ_S^*η − η is of size O(1) there:
ℒ_(V(S))η = dχ ⊗_s X_w^♭, with dχ of size |x|⁻¹ and X_w^♭ of size |x|. So [Hin26, Remark 5.5] holds where φ_S is the
boost. [Hin26, Section 5.6] modifies the gauge near I₀ by a cut-off χ₀ ((5.76) there); this is carried to dimension
4 + 1 in Chapter 37.

### 27.4 The structure at null infinity

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 5.11 and (5.40)–(5.41a)] in dimension 4 + 1. The operator is that of
(21.48): for metrics g, g₀,

    L^(g,g₀) := L_(g,g₀) = ½□_g + E^C_(g₀)δ_gG_g + (δ^*_(g₀) − δ^*_g)δ_gG_g + R_g
                           + δ^*_(g₀,E_C)(C_(g,g₀) − Y_(g,g₀) + E^Υ_(g₀)G_(g₀)),    (27.12)

the derivative D₁|_((g,g₀))P of [Hin26], with L^(g_b,g_b) = L_b of (25.1).

**Lemma 27.11** (The background at the corner.) On U, in the frame of products of dt_*, dx^i,

    L_b = −ρ₀²ρ_I(X_I − 3/2 − S̄)(X₀ − X_I) + R̃_b,     R̃_b ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²Diff²_b(U; S²T*),    (27.13)

with S̄ the endomorphism of Lemma 25.1 (2), and R̃_b with coefficients in C^∞(U).

*Proof.* By (25.4)–(25.5), on {|x| > 3R₁},
2L_b = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) + 2L̄̂(0) − g_b^(00)∂²_(t_*) + Q_b∂_(t_*) + R_b, where 2L̄̂(0), the spectral
family of 2L̄ at σ = 0, is its stationary part, with 2L̄̂(0) ∈ ρ²Diff²_b, g_b^(00) ∈ ρ²C^∞(X̄), Q_b ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b,
R_b ∈ ρ⁴Diff²_b, all stationary b-operators on X̄: polynomials in ρ∂_ρ|_(t_*) and ∂_ω with coefficients in C^∞(X̄).
By (27.4)
these vector fields are b-vector fields on U (∂_ω at fixed t_*, ρ is ∂_ω at fixed ρ₀, ρ_I, as t_* and ρ do not depend on
ω), and ρ = ρ₀ρ_I, ∂_(t_*) = ρ₀(X₀ − X_I). So the last four terms lie in ρ₀²ρ_I²Diff²_b(U); for instance
g_b^(00)∂²_(t_*) ∈ ρ₀⁴ρ_I²Diff²_b. For the first, (X₀ − X_I)ρ = 0, so

    −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄)
        = −2ρ₀²ρ_I(X₀ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − S̄) − 2ρ₀²ρ_I(X₀ − X_I) 8m₀ρ₀²ρ_I(X₀ − X_I),

and the second term lies in ρ₀⁴ρ_I²Diff²_b. S̄ is homogeneous of degree 0, a function of ω in this frame, so it
commutes with X₀ − X_I. Halving gives (27.13). ∎

The leading part can be checked on radial functions on Minkowski space without Lemma 25.1. With □ = −tr ∇²,
u := x¹ and v := x⁰, a radial function f satisfies ½□f = ½(∂_t² − ∂²_(|x|) − 3|x|⁻¹∂_(|x|))f =
2∂_u∂_v f + (3/2)|x|⁻¹(∂_u − ∂_v)f, since ∂_t = ∂_u + ∂_v and ∂_(|x|) = ∂_v − ∂_u. By (27.5), with
X_Iρ₀ = 0, X_Iρ_I = ρ_I and |x|⁻¹ = ρ₀ρ_I,

    2∂_v∂_u = −ρ₀²ρ_I X_I(X₀ − X_I) − ½ρ₀²ρ_I X_I ρ_I X_I,
    (3/2)|x|⁻¹∂_u = (3/2)ρ₀²ρ_I(X₀ − X_I) + ¾ρ₀²ρ_I² X_I,     (3/2)|x|⁻¹∂_v = −¾ρ₀²ρ_I² X_I,

so ½□ = −ρ₀²ρ_I(X_I − 3/2)(X₀ − X_I) modulo ρ₀²ρ_I²Diff²_b with polynomial coefficients (X_I and X₀ − X_I commute).
With |x|⁻¹ in place of (3/2)|x|⁻¹, as for the radial wave operator in dimension 3 + 1, the same lines give 1 in place of
3/2, which is [Hin26, (5.40)].

**Lemma 27.12** (The matrix Ā.) In the rescaled null frame (dt_* + 2d|x|, dt_*, |x|e^a) of ḡ, the image of
the products of (dt_*, dx^i) under a map F₀(ω), S̄ has a constant matrix Ā; in the frame (27.6) of η its
matrix is Ā modulo ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ (Lemma 27.4). It is lower triangular, with diagonal

    2(1 − v_C)γ_C,  (1 − v_C)γ_C,  (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C,  (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ,  γ_Υ,  0,  2γ_Υ,    (27.14)

and off-diagonal entries exactly at (3, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3), (5, 2), (7, 3), (7, 4), with Ā₇₄ = 2(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ and
Ā₇₆ = 0. Each summand of (27.6) is mapped to summands of its own type.

*Proof.* *The frame.* The model metric of Section 25.2 is ḡ = −(dt_* + d|x|)² + Σ_i(dx^i)², the Minkowski metric
with time t̄ := t_* + |x|. Its null coordinates are x̄⁰ := t̄ + |x| and x̄¹ := t̄ − |x| = t_*, so dx̄⁰ = dt_* + 2d|x|,
dx̄¹ = dt_*, and ḡ = −½(dx̄⁰ ⊗ dx̄¹ + dx̄¹ ⊗ dx̄⁰) + |x|²g̸. Let ∂̄₀, ∂̄₁ be the dual null vectors and take the slot
coordinates (27.7) in the frame (dx̄⁰, dx̄¹, |x|e^a). So ḡ(∂̄₀, ∂̄₁) = −½, ḡ⁻¹(dx̄⁰, dx̄¹) = −2 and
ḡ⁻¹(dx̄⁰, dx̄⁰) = ḡ⁻¹(dx̄¹, dx̄¹) = 0. For a 1-form α write α = α₀dx̄⁰ + α₁dx̄¹ + α_T with α₀ = α(∂̄₀), α₁ = α(∂̄₁) and
α_T tangential; then ⟨α, β⟩ := ḡ⁻¹(α, β) = −2(α₀β₁ + α₁β₀) + α_T·β_T, and tr h = −4h₀₁ + tr̸h for a symmetric
2-tensor h. For a symmetric product, (α ⊗_s β)(∂̄_i, ∂̄_j) = ½(α_iβ_j + α_jβ_i).

*The ingredients.* By (25.4), ρS̄ = −Ē^C ι_X Ḡ + (dt_* ⊗_s ·)Ē^Υ Ḡ with X := ḡ⁻¹dt_*. Here X = −2∂̄₀ and
ι_Xḡ = dx̄¹. By Definition 21.28 and (21.45), with v := v_C, c̄_C = ρĉ and
ĉ := ½(1 − v)dx̄⁰ + ½(1 + v)dx̄¹, which is dt̄ − v d|x| in these coordinates,

    Ē^Cω = γ_Cρ(2ĉ ⊗_s ω − ⅔(1 − e_C)ḡ⟨ĉ, ω⟩),     Ē^ΥḠh = −γ_Υρ(2ι_Y h − e_Υ(tr h) dt̄),

with dt̄ = ½(dx̄⁰ + dx̄¹) and Y := ḡ⁻¹dt̄ = −∂̄₀ − ∂̄₁. Hence

    S̄h = −γ_C(2ĉ ⊗_s ω − ⅔(1 − e_C)ḡ⟨ĉ, ω⟩) − γ_Υ dx̄¹ ⊗_s β,
    ω := ι_XḠh = −2h(∂̄₀, ·) − ½(tr h)dx̄¹,     β := 2ι_Y h − e_Υ(tr h) dt̄.    (27.15)

In components, with h(∂̄₀, ·) = h₀₀dx̄⁰ + h₀₁dx̄¹ + h_(0ā),

    ω₀ = −2h₀₀,     ω₁ = −2h₀₁ − ½(−4h₀₁ + tr̸h) = −½tr̸h,     ω_T = −2h_(0ā),
    β₀ = −2(h₀₀ + h₀₁) − ½e_Υ tr h,     β₁ = −2(h₀₁ + h₁₁) − ½e_Υ tr h,     β_T = −2(h_(0ā) + h_(1ā)).

*The slots.* Put a := ½(1 − v), b := ½(1 + v) and s₃ := ⅓tr̸h, so ⟨ĉ, ω⟩ = −2(aω₁ + bω₀) and
aω₁ + bω₀ = −(3a/2)s₃ − 2b h₀₀. The tensor 2ĉ ⊗_s ω has no tangential block, and dx̄¹ ⊗_s β has components only at
(∂̄₀, ∂̄₁), (∂̄₁, ∂̄₁) and (∂̄₁, tangential), equal to ½β₀, β₁ and ½β_T. Reading off the slot coordinates of S̄h:

- slot 1: S̄h(∂̄₀, ∂̄₀) = −2aγ_Cω₀ = 2(1 − v)γ_C h₀₀;
- slot 2: the tangential part of S̄h(∂̄₀, ·) is −aγ_Cω_T = (1 − v)γ_C h_(0ā);
- slots 3 and 6: the tangential block is ⅔(1 − e_C)γ_C⟨ĉ, ω⟩|x|²g̸, a multiple of g̸, so slot 6 of S̄h vanishes and
  slot 3 is −(4/3)(1 − e_C)γ_C(aω₁ + bω₀) = (1 − e_C)(1 − v)γ_C s₃ + (4/3)(1 − e_C)(1 + v)γ_C h₀₀;
- slot 4: S̄h(∂̄₀, ∂̄₁) = −γ_C(aω₁ + bω₀)(1 − ⅔(1 − e_C)) − ½γ_Υβ₀, which with tr h = −4h₀₁ + 3s₃ is
  ((1 + 2e_C)(1 + v)γ_C/3 + γ_Υ)h₀₀ + ¼((1 + 2e_C)(1 − v)γ_C + 3e_Υγ_Υ)s₃ + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ h₀₁;
- slot 5: the tangential part of S̄h(∂̄₁, ·) is −bγ_Cω_T − ½γ_Υβ_T = ((1 + v)γ_C + γ_Υ)h_(0ā) + γ_Υ h_(1ā);
- slot 7: S̄h(∂̄₁, ∂̄₁) = −2bγ_Cω₁ − γ_Υβ₁ = (3/2)((1 + v)γ_C + e_Υγ_Υ)s₃ + 2(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ h₀₁ + 2γ_Υ h₁₁.

The coefficients are constants, so the matrix Ā of S̄ in this frame is constant. Slot j of S̄h involves only slots
i ≤ j of h, so Ā is lower triangular; its diagonal is (27.14), and its off-diagonal entries are the nonzero
coefficients above, at (3, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3), (5, 2), (7, 3) and (7, 4), with Ā₇₄ = 2(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ. The slot π̸₀h
enters no slot of S̄h, so Ā₇₆ = 0. The scalar slots 1, 3, 4, 7 are mapped into scalar slots, the vector slots 2, 5 into
vector slots, and slot 6 to 0. The diagonal is (25.6) with its multiplicities, as the triangular form
requires. The frame (dx̄⁰, dx̄¹, |x|e^a) is the image of the products of (dt_*, dx^i) under the map that fixes dt_* and
sends dx^i to its tangential part plus ω^i(dx̄⁰ − dx̄¹)/2, which depends on ω alone; and it differs from the frame of η
by I + ρ²C^∞ (Lemma 27.4). ∎

Independently of the calculation: S̄ commutes with the rotations of ℝ⁴, which preserve ḡ, t_*, c_C and c_Υ near
infinity (Definition 21.28), and (27.6) is rotation-equivariant. The stabiliser SO(3) of ω acts on the rank-1
summands trivially, on the two rank-3 summands by its standard representation, and on |x|²ker tr̸ by the irreducible
5-dimensional one. By Schur's lemma S̄ maps each summand to the summands of the same type by scalars, and these do not
depend on ω, as SO(4) acts transitively on 𝕊³.

The trace couplings (3, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3), (7, 3) differ from the values of [Hin26, (5.28)] in dimension 3 + 1
(Proposition 27.39 (1)); only the support of Ā enters below.

**Lemma 27.13** (Counting coefficients.) Let g, g′, g₀, g₀′ be Lorentzian metrics on U whose Cartesian
components are bounded with bounded inverses. In the Cartesian frame, L^(g,g₀) − L^(g′,g₀′) is a second-order operator
Σ a^(μν)∂_μ∂_ν + Σ b^μ∂_μ + c whose coefficients are sums of products of: polynomials in the components of g, g′, g₀,
g₀′ and their inverses; at most two factors from {∂g, ∂g′, ∂g₀, ∂g₀′, c_C, c_Υ, c_(Υ,H)}, or one second derivative of
one of the metrics or one derivative of a c; and at least one factor δ from {g − g′, g₀ − g₀′} or a Cartesian
derivative of it of order at most 2. Second-order coefficients contain no derivative; first-order ones at most one
derivative of order one or one c; and the δ factor counts towards these limits.

*Proof.* Each term of (27.12) is, in Cartesian coordinates, of the stated form for a single pair (g, g₀): □_g
has principal part −g^(μν)∂_μ∂_ν, first-order part with one Christoffel symbol and zeroth-order part with one derivative
of a Christoffel symbol or two of them; E^C_(g₀) and E^Υ_(g₀) contain one c and no derivative ((21.41),
(21.42)); δ_g, δ^*_g, δ^*_(g₀) are first order with one Christoffel symbol in the zeroth-order part; C_(g,g₀)
and Y_(g,g₀) are zeroth order with one first derivative of g or g₀ (Lemma 21.30); R_g is zeroth order with one
second derivative or two first derivatives. Each coefficient of (27.12) is a polynomial in g, g⁻¹, g₀, g₀⁻¹,
their derivatives and the c's. The difference of a polynomial expression at two arguments is a sum of terms each with
one difference factor, by ab − a′b′ = (a − a′)b + a′(b − b′) and g⁻¹ − g′⁻¹ = −g⁻¹(g − g′)g′⁻¹. ∎

**Proposition 27.14** ([Hin26, Proposition 5.11 and (5.41a)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let k ≥ 5, ℰ₀ as in
Definition 27.6 (1), ℓ₀ > 0, ℓ_I > 0, and let ℱ be an index set with min Re ℱ > 0 and 2ℱ ⊂ ℱ. Let g₁, g₀ ∈ 𝒢,
a₀, a_I > 0, and h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b(U; S²T*) ∩ H^(k,a₀,a_I)_b(U; S²T*) (every component), with
‖h‖_(H^(3,a₀,a_I)_b) < ε₀, where ε₀ > 0 is small depending on a₀, a_I and g₁, and not on k. Then g := g₁ + h
satisfies, on U, in the splitting (27.6),

    L^(g,g₀) ≡ −ρ₀²ρ_I(X_I − 3/2 − Ā)(X₀ − X_I)
               mod (ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ + H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b) Diff²_b(U; S²T*),    (27.16)

with L^(g,g₀) − L^(g₁,g₀) in the second class, its coefficients depending smoothly on h, as maps from
{h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b ∩ H^(k,a₀,a_I)_b : ‖h‖_(H^(3,a₀,a_I)_b) < ε₀} to H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b, and
vanishing at h = 0. In particular this holds with ℱ = ℰ_I^tot for h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b
(Lemma 27.7 (b)–(c)), and with ℱ = (2, 0) for h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨(3,0)⟩₀,ℓ_I)_b.

*Proof.* *The background.* By Lemma 27.11 and Lemma 27.4, conjugate by the frame change
F = F₀(ω)(I + E), E ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞. F₀ commutes with X₀ and X_I, so F₀⁻¹L_bF₀ has a leading part with F₀⁻¹S̄F₀ = Ā
(Lemma 27.12); and (I + E)⁻¹P(I + E) − P = (I + E)⁻¹[P, E], which for P ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I Diff²_b lies in
ρ₀⁴ρ_I³Diff¹_b, as 𝒱_b preserves ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞. So (27.16) holds for (g, g₀) = (g_b, g_b) with remainder in
ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_b.

*Counting.* Apply Lemma 27.13 to the difference of L^(g,g₀) and L_b, with the conversion to b-operators: every
Cartesian derivative lies in ρ₀𝒱_b(U) (Lemma 27.2); c_C, c_Υ ∈ |x|⁻¹C^∞ = ρ₀ρ_I C^∞ on U (Definition 21.28),
and c_(Υ,H) is supported in {|x| < 5R₁}, a compact subset of U away from I₀ ∪ ℐ⁺; the Cartesian components of g_b, g₁,
g₀ and their inverses are smooth on U, and their Cartesian derivatives lie in ρ₀C^∞. A term with second-order
derivatives is a∂_μ∂_ν ∈ aρ₀²Diff²_b; a first-order term has its b^μ containing one first derivative or one c, both in
ρ₀(·), times ∂_μ ∈ ρ₀𝒱_b; a zeroth-order term contains two such factors or one second derivative. So each term is ρ₀²
times a product of the δ factor, or of 𝒱_b-derivatives of it of order at most 2, with smooth bounded functions and with
other δ factors, applied through Diff²_b.

*The backgrounds.* For (g₁, g₀) against (g_b, g_b): δ ∈ {g₁ − g_b, g₀ − g_b} ⊂ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ (Definition 27.9,
Lemma 27.10 (1)), which 𝒱_b preserves; the terms lie in
ρ₀⁴ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_b ⊂ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_b.

*The perturbation.* For (g₁ + h, g₀) against (g₁, g₀): δ = h. Smallness enters only through g⁻¹, and only at the
order 3. Put A := −g₁⁻¹h, so that g = g₁(I − A), and G := g⁻¹ − g₁⁻¹; write ‖·‖_m for the norm of H^(m,a₀,a_I)_b(U).

Step 1 (order 3). By part (i) of the proof of Lemma 27.5 at the order 3 > 5/2, as ρ₀^(a₀)ρ_I^(a_I) is bounded
with its b-derivatives on U, ‖uv‖₃ ≤ C‖u‖₃‖v‖₃ with C depending on a₀ and a_I only; and multiplication by the
components of g₁⁻¹, smooth on U, is bounded. So ‖A^jg₁⁻¹‖₃ ≤ C(Cε₀)^j, and for Cε₀ < 1 the series Σ_(j≥1)A^jg₁⁻¹
converges in H^(3,a₀,a_I)_b; its sum is G, as (I − A)Σ_(j≥0)A^j = I. The Sobolev embedding on the cubes of that proof
gives sup|h| + sup|G| ≤ C‖h‖₃; so for ε₀ small, g is Lorentzian with bounded inverse, as Lemma 27.13 asks.

Step 2 (order k). Let 3 ≤ m < k and G ∈ H^(m,a₀,a_I)_b. For V ∈ 𝒱_b(U), V(g⁻¹) = −g⁻¹(Vg)g⁻¹ by Leibniz's rule (the
factors are bounded and lie in H³ locally), so

    VG = −g₁⁻¹(Vh)g₁⁻¹ − G(Vg₁ + Vh)g₁⁻¹ − g₁⁻¹(Vg₁ + Vh)G − G(Vg₁ + Vh)G.

The components of g₁⁻¹ and Vg₁ are smooth on U, and G, Vh ∈ H^(m,a₀,a_I)_b, as h ∈ H^(m+1,a₀,a_I)_b; so by part (i)
of the proof of Lemma 27.5 at the order m > 5/2, each term lies in H^(m,a₀,a_I)_b, with no smallness. Hence
G ∈ H^(m+1,a₀,a_I)_b (Definition 21.31 (3)), and by induction G ∈ H^(k,a₀,a_I)_b, with ‖G‖_k bounded by a
polynomial in ‖h‖_k.

Step 3 (expansions). For J ≥ 1, g⁻¹ = Σ_(j<J)A^jg₁⁻¹ + A^Jg⁻¹. By Lemma 27.5 with γ = (ℓ₀, ℓ_I) (the strict
inequalities hold, as min Re ℰ₀, min Re ℱ, ℓ₀, ℓ_I > 0), the term A^jg₁⁻¹, j ≥ 1, lies in
H^(k,(jℰ₀,ℓ₀),(jℱ,ℓ_I))_b ⊂ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b. By Step 2 and part (i) of the proof of Lemma 27.5,
A^Jg⁻¹ = A^Jg₁⁻¹ + A^JG lies in H^(k,Ja₀,Ja_I)_b, so in H^(k,ℓ₀,ℓ_I)_b for J so large that Ja₀ ≥ ℓ₀ and Ja_I ≥ ℓ_I,
and it adds no expansion term. So G ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b. Every coefficient of the difference is then ρ₀² times
an element of H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b (Lemma 27.5 with k − 2 > 5/2, and (F1)); that is, an element of
H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b. The frame change F preserves both classes.

Step 4 (dependence on h). Let X := H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b ∩ H^(k,a₀,a_I)_b, on which multiplication is continuous
(Lemma 27.5). By Steps 2–3, ‖G‖_X is bounded by a polynomial in ‖h‖_X. For h′ ∈ X with ‖h′‖₃ < ε₀ and
g′ := g₁ + h′, g′⁻¹ − g⁻¹ = −g′⁻¹(h′ − h)g⁻¹. So G is locally Lipschitz in h on {h ∈ X : ‖h‖₃ < ε₀}, with values in
X, and differentiable, with derivative ḣ ↦ −g⁻¹ḣg⁻¹, which is of the same form; by induction, G is smooth in h. The
coefficients of L^(g,g₀) − L^(g₁,g₀) are sums of products of G, of h and its b-derivatives of order at most 2, and of
smooth functions, each with a factor h or a b-derivative of h (Lemma 27.13); so they depend smoothly on h and
vanish at h = 0. ∎

The smallness is asked at the order 3 only, and ε₀ does not depend on k: Step 1 uses it for the inverse metric at that
order, and Steps 2–3 give the membership at the order k from the products of Lemma 27.5 without it. This form,
and the dependence on h, are proved here and are not taken from [Hin26].
Below, h is *small as in Proposition 27.14* if, for some a₀, a_I > 0 with h ∈ H^(k,a₀,a_I)_b,
‖h‖_(H^(3,a₀,a_I)_b) < ε₀ on the domain of h, with ε₀ depending only on a₀, a_I and g₁ (off U, so small that Step 1
applies there without weights). For h in the classes of Definition 27.6 or Definition 27.8 such a₀, a_I exist
(0 < a₀ < min(ℓ₀, min Re ℰ₀) and 0 < a_I < 3/2), and the condition does not involve k.

The form [Hin26, (5.26a)] of this statement in dimension 4 + 1 is
L^(g,g₀) ≡ (2|x|^(−3/2)∂₀|x|^(3/2) + |x|⁻¹Ā)∂₁ modulo the same class, by (27.5):
2∂₀∂₁ + (3/2)|x|⁻¹∂₁ ≡ −ρ₀²ρ_I(X_I − 3/2)(X₀ − X_I) and |x|⁻¹Ā∂₁ ≡ ρ₀²ρ_IĀ(X₀ − X_I).

**Remark 27.15** (The terms A^h, B^h of [Hin26], and [Hin26, Lemmas 5.6–5.8] in dimension 4 + 1.) [Hin26]
keeps A^h − A₀ ∈ C^∞ + H^(k−1,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_I^tot−1,ℓ_I−1))_b and B^h in the leading part because in dimension 3 + 1,
min Re(ℰ_I^tot − 1) = 0: they are of the same order as A₀. In dimension 4 + 1 the same classes have min Re = ½, and
Proposition 27.14 places them in the error, in the form ρ₀²ρ_I · ρ_I^(ℰ_I^tot−1) = ρ₀²ρ_I^(ℰ_I^tot). [Hin26, Lemmas
5.6–5.8 and Corollaries 5.9–5.10] calculate the entries of A^h, B^h and the edge-b form; in dimension 4 + 1 the b-form
needs only the memberships used in the proof above, which are their counterparts:
g⁻¹ − g₁⁻¹ ≡ −g₁⁻¹hg₁⁻¹ modulo H^(k,(2ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(2ℱ,ℓ_I))_b ([Hin26, (5.11)]); the Cartesian Christoffel symbols satisfy
Γ(g) − Γ(g₁) ∈ ρ₀H^(k−1,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b ([Hin26, (5.12)]); and
Riem(g) − Riem(g₁) ∈ ρ₀²H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b ([Hin26, Lemma 5.8]). The edge-b form (5.26b) is in Chapter 37. Taking
ℱ = ℰ_I^tot for every component discards the component structure (for instance the ∂₁² coefficient g^(11) is tied to
h₀₀, of index ℰ_I^C); the b-form does not need it, but (5.26b) and the energy estimates of Chapter 37 do. At the level
of tensors the drop by half an order is the counting of Lemma 27.13. For comparison, item (7) of
Proposition 27.59 gives four of the h-dependent entries (A(7, 1), B(7, 1), A(4, 7), B(4, 1)) of the closely related
operator of [Hin23a] in dimensions 3 + 1 and 4 + 1, and those of dimension 4 + 1 are r^(−1/2) times those of dimension
3 + 1; that operator omits the γ_Υ term, which carries one c and obeys the same counting.

### 27.5 Forward mapping

This section is [Hin26, Definition 5.13, Proposition 5.14, Corollary 5.15] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Definition 27.16** ([Hin26, Definition 5.13] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ℰ₀, ℰ_I^C be as in
Definition 27.6, k ≥ 3, ℓ₀ > 0, ℓ_I > 3/2.

(1) Set

    ℱ_(I,11) := 1 + (ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0)).    (27.17)

H^(k,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1)_b(Ω_ext) is the space of real symmetric 2-tensors f with, on U,
π_C f, π₀₁f, π_(1/)f, π̸₀f ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℰ_I^C+1,ℓ_I+1))_b and π₁₁f ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℱ_(I,11),ℓ_I+1))_b.

(2) If ℓ₀ < min Re ℰ₀ we write ℓ₀ + 2 for (ℰ₀ + 2, ℓ₀ + 2), and if ℓ_I < min Re ℰ_I^C we write (−′, ℓ_I + 1) for
(⟨ℰ_I^C + 1⟩′, ℓ_I + 1).

(3) H^(k,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),⟨(4,0)⟩′,ℓ_I+1)_b(Ω_ext) is the space of f with π_C f, π₀₁f, π_(1/)f, π̸₀f in ((4, 0), ℓ_I + 1)
and π₁₁f in ((3, 0), ℓ_I + 1) at ℐ⁺, and in (ℰ₀ + 2, ℓ₀ + 2) at I₀.

The set ℱ_(I,11) of [Hin26, (5.43)] also contains 1 + (1, 0), from the radiation field of π̸₀ through the h-dependent
(7, 6) entry of A^h. In dimension 4 + 1 that entry is part of the error of (27.16), and what it produces lies
in ℰ_I^C + 1 (Remark 27.19).

**Proposition 27.17** ([Hin26, Proposition 5.14] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let g = g₁ + h, g₁, g₀ ∈ 𝒢, with
h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_ext) small as in Proposition 27.14, k ≥ 5. Then

    L^(g,g₀) : H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_ext) → H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1)_b(Ω_ext)    (27.18)

continuously. If h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨(3,0)⟩₀,ℓ_I)_b (small), then

    L^(g,g₀) : H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨(3,0)⟩₀,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_ext) → H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),⟨(4,0)⟩′,ℓ_I+1)_b(Ω_ext).    (27.19)

*Proof.* Away from U the spaces impose nothing beyond H^k and H^(k−2), and L^(g,g₀) is a second-order operator with
coefficients in H^(k−2) (there h is small in H³, and Steps 1–2 of the proof of Proposition 27.14, without weights,
give g⁻¹ − g₁⁻¹ ∈ H^k); by property (F2) of Section 21.9 it suffices to work on U. Let ġ be in the domain of
(27.18). Every slot of ġ lies in H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_I^tot,ℓ_I))_b (Lemma 27.7 (c)). Split L^(g,g₀) by
(27.16) with ℱ = ℰ_I^tot.

*The C^∞ error.* ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_b maps ġ into H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℰ_I^tot+2,ℓ_I+2))_b in every slot, and
ℰ_I^tot + 2 ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1 ⊂ ℱ_(I,11) (Lemma 27.7 (c)).

*The perturbation.* H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℰ_I^tot,ℓ_I))_b Diff²_b maps ġ, by Lemma 27.5 and (F1), into
H^(k−2,(2ℰ₀+2,γ₀),(2ℰ_I^tot,γ_I))_b with γ₀ = ℓ₀ + 2 and γ_I = ℓ_I + 1. The strict inequalities of Lemma 27.5
hold: ℓ₀ + 2 < ℓ₀ + 2 + min Re ℰ₀; ℓ_I + 1 < ℓ_I + 3/2 = ℓ_I + min Re ℰ_I^tot; and ℓ_I + 1 < 2ℓ_I as ℓ_I > 3/2.
And 2ℰ₀ + 2 ⊂ ℰ₀ + 2, 2ℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1 (Lemma 27.7 (b)).

*The leading part.* u := (X₀ − X_I)ġ has the slot index sets of ġ (F1). Then w := (X_I − 3/2 − Ā)u has, in slot j,
(X_I − 3/2 − Ā_(jj))u_j − Σ_(i<j) Ā_(ji)u_i. In a slot with index set ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + s, 0) and Ā_(jj) = s, the term
