This section is [Hin26, Lemmas 10.10–10.11] in dimension 4 + 1. For |σ| ≤ c with σ ≠ 0 and Im σ ≥ 0 put
(Definition 28.7, Corollary 28.11)

    (û_(reg,1)(σ), b̂_1(σ), Ŝ_1(σ)) := L̃_b(σ)⁻¹(f̂(σ), 0, 0).    (28.21)

By (28.16), for these σ,

    L̂_b(σ)⁻¹ f̂(σ) = û_(reg,1)(σ) + ĝ^aug(σ)(b̂_1(σ)) + ĥ^aug(σ)(Ŝ_1(σ)).    (28.22)

*Properties.* By the formula in the proof of Theorem 28.10 (3), with e = 0,
(b̂_1, Ŝ_1) = Ξ(σ)⁻¹(⟨R(σ)f̂(σ), φ_(i′)⟩_h)_(i′), with R = L̂_b⁻¹ and Ξ(σ)_(i′i) = ⟨R(σ)F_i(σ), φ_(i′)⟩_h. R is
holomorphic in Im σ > 0 (Theorem 11.33 (6)), the columns F_i = f̂_ḃ, f̂_S are holomorphic there with values in every
H̄_b^(p,M) (Lemma 28.4 (d)), and f̂ is entire. So b̂_1, Ŝ_1 and
û_(reg,1) = R(σ)(f̂(σ) − Σ_i (b̂_1(σ), Ŝ_1(σ))_i F_i(σ)), with (b̂_1, Ŝ_1)_i the coefficient of the column F_i (paired
with any φ ∈ C_c^∞(X°)), are holomorphic in Im σ > 0, continuous down to [−c, c] ∖ 0 (Theorem 11.33 (6) at real
σ_*), and bounded uniformly by (28.15). Here any orders of Section 13.6 may be used, since these are
statements about pairings with test sections, which do not depend on the orders; and
‖f̂(σ)‖_((s_c;k),(𝗋+α_sf+2,α_sf+2,0),|σ|) is bounded for |σ| ≤ 1, as f̂(σ) is supported in a fixed compact subset of
X̄ ∖ ∂X (Lemma 13.23 (a)).

**Lemma 28.24** (The regular part.)
u_reg(t_*, ·) := (2π)⁻¹ ∫_(𝒞_−∪𝒞_0∪𝒞_+) e^(−iσt_*) χ(|σ|) û_(reg,1)(σ) dσ satisfies

    ‖u_reg‖_(H^((𝗌+1;k),(α_sf,0))_(3b;b)(M_0)) ≤ C‖f‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)(Ω)^(•,−)).    (28.23)

[Hin26] has 𝗌 on the left and 𝗌 − 1 on the right; here f is used at its regularity 𝗌, and the gain is the elliptic
one (Section 28.13).

*Proof.* As χ = 1 on [0, c/2] and the integrand is bounded near 0 and holomorphic inside 𝒞_0, Cauchy's theorem moves
𝒞_0 to [−c/2, c/2] (pairing with test sections; the small semicircle around 0 contributes o(1)). So
û_reg = χû_(reg,1) on ℝ, supported in [−c, c]. By Lemma 14.17 with the order 𝗌 + 1 and the weight α_sf, and
Lemma 14.18 (the norms of Definition 13.22),

    ‖u_reg‖² ∼ Σ_(j≤k) ∫_(−c)^c ‖(σ∂_σ)^j(χû_(reg,1))‖²_((s_c+1;k−j),(𝗋+1+α_sf,α_sf,0),|σ|) dσ.

By Lemma 28.19 (c) and Corollary 28.12, Theorem 28.10 (3) applies to L̃_b on Σ′ = Σ_0 ∩ ℝ with the orders
(s_c + 1, 𝗋 + 1) and α_+ = α = α_sf. By Leibniz and (28.12), for |σ| ≤ c,

    ‖(σ∂_σ)^j(χû_(reg,1))‖_((s_c+1;k−j),(𝗋+1+α_sf,α_sf,0),|σ|)
        ≤ C Σ_(j_2≤j) ‖(σ∂_σ)^(j_2) f̂(σ)‖_((s_c;k−j_2),(𝗋+1+α_sf+1,α_sf+2,0),|σ|),

where j_2 counts the derivatives that fall on f̂; each derivative that falls on L̃_b⁻¹ costs one order of b-regularity
of f̂. The decay order 𝗋 + α_sf + 2 and the regularity s_c are those of 𝗌 + α_sf + 2 and 𝗌, so by Lemma 14.17 with
the weight α_sf + 2 the integral is at most C‖f‖²_(H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)). ∎

**Lemma 28.25** (The coefficients.)

    Σ_(j≤k) ∫_(−c)^c (|(σ∂_σ)^j b̂_1(σ)|² + |(σ∂_σ)^j Ŝ_1(σ)|²) dσ ≤ C‖f‖²_(H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)(Ω)^(•,−)).

*Proof.* As for Lemma 28.24, with the moduli of the second and third components in (28.12). ∎

### 28.10 The singular part

This section is [Hin26, Lemma 10.12] in dimension 4 + 1. With ĝ^aug, ĥ^aug of (28.8) and
𝒞 := 𝒞_− ∪ 𝒞_0 ∪ 𝒞_+ put

    v_ġ(t_*, ·) := (2π)⁻¹ ∫_𝒞 e^(−iσt_*) χ(|σ|) ĝ^aug(σ)(b̂_1(σ)) dσ,
    v_h(t_*, ·) := (2π)⁻¹ ∫_𝒞 e^(−iσt_*) χ(|σ|) ĥ^aug(σ)(Ŝ_1(σ)) dσ.    (28.24)

By Lemma 28.22, (28.22) and χ(|σ|) = 1 on 𝒞_0,

    u = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing,     u_sing := v_ġ + v_h.    (28.25)

On 𝒞_0, |e^(−iσt_*)| = e^(t_* Im σ), so (28.24) grows at most like e^(ct_*/2); the poles of ĝ^aug and ĥ^aug
at 0 prevent moving 𝒞_0 to the real axis. Their t_*-derivatives do not have these poles.

**Lemma 28.26** (Bounds for derivatives.) For every p ∈ ℕ_0, with k and c as in Section 28.7,

    ∂_(t_*)v_ġ ∈ H^((p;k),(α_sf+1,0))_(3b;b)(M_0),     ∂²_(t_*)v_h ∈ H^((p;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)(M_0),    (28.26)

with norms at most C_p‖f‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)(Ω)^(•,−)).

[Hin26, (10.51)–(10.52)] have the sf-weights −½ − ϵ and ½ − ϵ and the regularity 𝗌 only, under the condition
𝗌′ + α′ < −½ at R_out. Here every constant regularity is allowed and no condition at R_out is needed, as the transforms
decay rapidly at scf.

*Proof.* *The transforms.* Differentiating (28.24) under the integral, ∂_(t_*) brings a factor −iσ, and by
(28.8), −iσĝ^aug(σ)(ḃ) = Ψ(σ, ·)ġ(ḃ) and

    −σ²ĥ^aug(σ)(S) = (Ψ − σ∂_σΨ)h(S) − iσΨ h̆(S),    (28.27)

with Ψ(σ, x) = ∫ e^(iσt_*)∂_(t_*)χ_K dt_*, entire in σ for each x (the support of ∂_(t_*)χ_K(·, x) is compact). So
∂_(t_*)v_ġ = (2π)⁻¹∫ e^(−iσt_*)χΨġ(b̂_1) dσ over the same contour, and the integrand is bounded near 0 and holomorphic
inside 𝒞_0; as in Lemma 28.24, 𝒞_0 moves to [−c/2, c/2], and ℱ(∂_(t_*)v_ġ) = χΨġ(b̂_1) on ℝ. Likewise
ℱ(∂²_(t_*)v_h) is χ times (28.27) at S = Ŝ_1.

*Uniform bounds.* For r ≥ 1, Ψ = Φ(σr) (Lemma 28.5 (b)), with Φ entire and |∂^j_ζΦ| ≤ C_(j,M)⟨ζ⟩^(−M) on
{Im ζ ≥ 0}. So, with ζ = σr,

    Ψġ = r⁻²Φ(ζ)(r²ġ),     −σ²ĥ^aug(σ)(S) = r⁻³((Φ(ζ) − ζΦ′(ζ))r³h − iζΦ(ζ)r²h̆),

where r²ġ, r³h and r²h̆ are bounded with all their b-derivatives (the weights are 2 or 3, 3 and 2; Section 28.1).
Each is r^(−q)G(σr, x) with q = 2, resp. 3, and G smooth with |(ζ∂_ζ)^j(r∂_r)^a∂_ω^βG| ≤ C⟨ζ⟩^(−M) for ζ real;
σ∂_σ acts as ζ∂_ζ. The proof of Lemma 28.4 (b), with r⁻³ replaced by r^(−q), gives
sup_(0<|σ|≤1) ‖(σ∂_σ)^j(·)‖_(H^(k′,(M,β_tf,0))_(b,|σ|)) < ∞ for every k′, M and β_tf < q, since the bound
ρ_tf^(q−β_tf) is square integrable for μ_b uniformly if and only if β_tf < q. For r ≤ 1, Ψ and its σ- and
x-derivatives are bounded uniformly for |σ| ≤ 1 (proof of Lemma 28.5 (d):
∂^j_σΨ = ∫ (it_*)^j e^(iσt_*)∂_(t_*)χ_K dt_*). By (20.27) with l + 4 = β_tf, for every constant order pair
and |σ| ≤ ς_1 (and c ≤ ς_1, Section 28.7),

    sup_(0<|σ|≤c) Σ_(j≤k) (‖(σ∂_σ)^j(Ψġ(e_i))‖_((p;k),(p+β′,β′,0),|σ|)
                            + ‖(σ∂_σ)^j(σ²ĥ^aug(σ)(e′_i))‖_((p;k),(p+β″,β″,0),|σ|)) < ∞

for basis elements e_i, e′_i, every p, β′ < 0 and β″ < 1. Take β′ := α_sf + 1 < 0 and β″ := α_sf + 2 < 1, by
(28.17).

*Inverse transform.* By Lemma 14.17 with the constant order p and the weight β′, and Leibniz,

    ‖∂_(t_*)v_ġ‖² ∼ Σ_(j≤k) ∫_(−c)^c ‖(σ∂_σ)^j(χΨġ(b̂_1))‖²_((p;k−j),(p+β′,β′,0),|σ|) dσ
                 ≤ C Σ_(j≤k) ∫_(−c)^c |(σ∂_σ)^j b̂_1|² dσ,

and Lemma 28.25 bounds the right side; likewise for ∂²_(t_*)v_h, with β″ and Ŝ_1. ∎

The same holds uniformly for b near b_0, by Remark 28.6, as β′ < 0 and β″ < 1 hold with room.

### 28.11 Integration in t_*

This section is [Hin26, Lemma 10.13] in dimension 4 + 1, for variable orders.

**Lemma 28.27** (Translation-invariant elliptic operators.) Let 𝗌 ∈ C^∞(³ᵇS*M̃_0) be
t_*-translation-invariant, d ∈ ℕ and ν_0 > 0. There are t_*-translation-invariant operators A ∈ Ψ̃^𝗌_3b, elliptic,
Q′ ∈ Ψ̃^(−𝗌)_3b and R ∈ Ψ̃^(−d)_3b with

    I = Q′A + R²,    (28.28)

whose Schwartz kernels are supported in {|t_* − t′_*| ≤ ν_0⟨x⟩, |x − x′| ≤ ν_0⟨x⟩}. They act on H^(𝗌′,(β,γ))_3b
with the orders shifted by their own, for all β and γ. (Only b-order k = 0 is claimed: for variable orders,
commutators with b-vector fields carry logarithmic factors, and Lemma 28.28 reduces to k = 0 first.)

*Proof.* In the frame ⟨x⟩∂_(t_*), ⟨x⟩∂_(x_i), which is t_*-invariant, a 3b covector has fibre coordinates ζ ∈ ℝ⁵, and
a t_*-translation-invariant function on the 3b-cotangent bundle is a function of (x, ζ); in particular 𝗌 = 𝗌(x, ζ). For
a symbol a(x, ζ) of variable order (in the symbol classes of Section 14.3) put, with ψ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ⁵) equal to 1 near
0 and supported in {|y| ≤ ν_1},

    Op(a)u(t_*, x) := (2π)⁻⁵ ∫ e^(i((t_*−t′_*)τ+(x−x′)·ξ)) ψ((t_* − t′_*, x − x′)/⟨x⟩)
                          × a(x, ⟨x⟩(τ, ξ)) u(t′_*, x′) dt′_* dx′ dτ dξ.

In a unit cell of the scaled bounded geometry ((S9) in Section 14.3; cells of size ⟨x_α⟩), after rescaling by ⟨x_α⟩,
this is the quantization with the cut-off of [Hin26d, (3.26)] (Section 14.8.3) of the symbol
a(x, (⟨x⟩/⟨x_α⟩)ζ̃), which lies in the same class, since ⟨x⟩/⟨x_α⟩ is bounded above and below with bounded scaled
derivatives; the cut-off is rescaled by the same factor. A change of cut-off changes the operator by one with smooth
kernel, supported within bounded cell distance and rapidly decaying in the scaled variables: a residual operator
localized near the diagonal. So Op(a) ∈ Ψ̃^(ord a)_3b, localized near the diagonal, with kernel range ν_1⟨x⟩. Its
kernel depends on (t_* − t′_*, x, x′), so Op(a) commutes with t_*-translations; compositions of such operators commute
with them and have kernel ranges that add. Take a := ⟨ζ⟩^𝗌, A := Op(a) and Q_0 := Op(a⁻¹). Then Q_0A = I − R_1 with
R_1 ∈ Ψ̃^(−(1−2δ))_3b translation-invariant (the calculus with variable orders loses δ > 0 in the remainder). With
d′(1 − 2δ) ≥ d, Q := Σ_(j<d′) R_1^j Q_0 gives QA = I − R_1^(d′) =: I − R, and I = QA + R = (Q + RQ)A + R², so
Q′ := Q + RQ. All of these are translation-invariant, with kernel range at most 4d′(1 + ν_1)ν_1⟨x⟩ ≤ ν_0⟨x⟩ for ν_1
small (compositions add ranges, with ⟨x′⟩ ≤ (1 + ν_1)⟨x⟩ on them). For the weights w = ρ_sf^β ρ_K^γ, w⁻¹Aw has kernel
K_A(z, z′)w(z′)/w(z), and on the support of the kernel w(z′)/w(z) is smooth and bounded with bounded scaled
derivatives, as the logarithmic 3b-derivatives of ρ_sf and ρ_K are bounded: an operator of the same class. ∎

**Lemma 28.28** ([Hin26, Lemma 10.13] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let 𝗌 be a t_*-translation-invariant 3b order,
constant over {r ≤ r_0 + δ_1} for some δ_1 ∈ (0, 1] (as the orders in 𝒪_c are, by Definition 15.29 (3): constant over
{r ≤ r_Γ}, r_Γ > r_2 > r_0), and let k ∈ ℕ_0, β ∈ ℝ and ℓ > ½. If u is a distribution on M_0° with

    u|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^((𝗌;k),(β−1,−ℓ))_(3b;b)(Ω_−),     ∂_(t_*)u ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(β,−ℓ+1))_(3b;b)(M_0),

then u ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(β−1,−ℓ))_(3b;b)(M_0), with norm at most C times the sum of those two norms. The density is |dt_*|
times any weighted b-density on X; a change of density is a shift of β.

*Proof.* *Cut-off.* Let χ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on [−¼, ∞) and 0 on (−∞, −½], and put u′ := χ(t_*/r)u. Then u − u′ is
supported in {t_* ≤ −r/4} ⊂ Ω_−, away from {t_* = 1}, so it lies in H^((𝗌;k),(β−1,−ℓ))_(3b;b)(M_0); χ(t_*/r) is
homogeneous of degree 0, a 3b multiplier; and ∂_(t_*)u′ = χ(t_*/r)∂_(t_*)u + r⁻¹χ′(t_*/r)u, whose last term is
supported in Ω_− away from {t_* = 1} and from K^±, and lies in H^((𝗌;k),(β,−ℓ+1))_(3b;b), as r⁻¹ = ρ_sf there. So we
may assume u = 0 for t_* ≤ −r/2, and then only ∂_(t_*)u =: f enters.

*b-regularity.* ∂_(t_*) and ⟨x⟩∂_x commute with ∂_(t_*), and ∂_(t_*)(t_*∂_(t_*)u) = t_*∂_(t_*)f + f, which preserves
the support condition; by induction it suffices to take k = 0.

*The case 𝗌 = 0.* Let r_1 > 0, c ≥ 0 and ν ∈ (0, 1), put t := t_* + r + c, and let v be a distribution on M̃_0,
supported in {r ≥ r_1}, with v = 0 for t ≤ νr and g := ∂_(t_*)v ∈ H^(0,(β,−ℓ+1))_3b. Then v ∈ H^(0,(β−1,−ℓ))_3b, with
norm at most C‖g‖, C depending on r_1, c and ν. Indeed, on {r ≥ r_1, t ≥ νr}, ρ_sf and ρ_K are r⁻¹ and r/t up to
bounded factors. As ∂_(t_*) commutes with powers of r we may take β = 0. Dropping the angular variables (the density
is |dt dr| after the shift of β), g = ρ_K^(1−ℓ)g_0 = r^(1−ℓ)t^(ℓ−1)g_0 with g_0 ∈ L²(|dt dr|), and
v(t, r) = ∫_(νr)^t g(t′, r) dt′. Fix a ∈ (−½, ℓ − 1), which is possible as ℓ > ½. Then

    ‖ρ_sf ρ_K^ℓ v‖² ≤ C ∫_(r_1)^∞ ∫_(νr)^∞ t^(−2ℓ) |∫_(νr)^t t′^(ℓ−1) g_0(t′, r) dt′|² dt dr
                   ≤ C ∫∫ t^(−2ℓ) (t^(2a+1)/(2a + 1)) ∫_(νr)^t t′^(2ℓ−2−2a) |g_0|² dt′ dt dr,

by Cauchy–Schwarz with t′^(ℓ−1) = t′^a · t′^(ℓ−1−a). Exchanging the integrals and using
∫_(t′)^∞ t^(−2ℓ+2a+1) dt = t′^(−2ℓ+2a+2)/(2ℓ − 2a − 2), the right side is at most
C‖g_0‖²_(L²) = C‖g‖²_(H^(0,(0,1−ℓ))_3b).
Nothing here depends on the dimension.

*Extension across {r = r_0}.* The spaces on M_0 are the restrictions to {r ≥ r_0} of the spaces on M̃_0, with the
quotient norms (Definition 14.22), 𝗌 being extended to M̃_0 by its constant value s_0 over {r < r_0}. Let F̃ be an
extension of f with ‖F̃‖_(H^(𝗌,(β,−ℓ+1))_3b(M̃_0)) ≤ 2‖f‖_(H^(𝗌,(β,−ℓ+1))_3b(M_0)), and put

    F := χ_1(r) χ_2(t_*/⟨x⟩) F̃,

where χ_1 ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equals 0 on (−∞, r_0/2] and 1 on [r_0, ∞), and χ_2 ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equals 0 on (−∞, −¾] and 1 on
[−½, ∞). Both factors are bounded together with all their derivatives along ⟨x⟩∂_(t_*) and ⟨x⟩∂_x (where a derivative
of χ_2(t_*/⟨x⟩) is nonzero, |t_*| ≤ ⟨x⟩), so multiplication by them is bounded on the 3b spaces ((S3), (S8) in
Section 14.3), and ‖F‖ ≤ C‖f‖. On {r > r_0}, F = f: there χ_1 = 1, and χ_2(t_*/⟨x⟩) ≠ 1 only where
t_* < −⟨x⟩/2 ≤ −r/2, where f vanishes. F is supported in {r ≥ r_0/2, t_* ≥ −¾⟨x⟩}. Let U be the primitive of F in t_*
that vanishes for t_* < −⟨x⟩ (the convolution in t_* with the Heaviside function). Then ∂_(t_*)U = F, U is supported
in {r ≥ r_0/2, t_* ≥ −¾⟨x⟩}, and U = u on {r > r_0}, as both are primitives of f there that vanish for t_* < −⟨x⟩.
Restriction to {r ≥ r_0} being bounded, it suffices to prove ‖U‖_(H^(𝗌,(β−1,−ℓ))_3b(M̃_0)) ≤ C‖F‖. No extension
operator is used: f is extended through the definition of the quotient norm, at its own order, and U is obtained by
integration in t_*.

*General 𝗌.* Take A, Q′ and R of Lemma 28.27 for the extended order, with d ≥ sup|𝗌| + |inf 𝗌| and
ν_0 ≤ min(1/16, r_0/8). Let z = (t_*, x) lie in supp K_A or in supp K_R, as a function of its first variable, with its
second variable z′ = (t′_*, x′) in supp U, and write r′ := |x′|. Then r ≥ r′ − ν_0⟨x⟩ ≥ r_0/2 − ν_0(1 + r), so
r ≥ r_0/3. And ⟨x′⟩ ≤ (1 + ν_0)⟨x⟩, so t_* ≥ −¾⟨x′⟩ − ν_0⟨x⟩ ≥ −(¾ + 2ν_0)(1 + r), and t := t_* + r + 1 satisfies
t ≥ (¼ − 2ν_0)(1 + r) > r/8. The operators are localized near the diagonal, hence act on all distributions, and
(28.28) holds on them. So AU and RU are supported in {r ≥ r_0/3} and vanish for t ≤ r/8, and
∂_(t_*)(AU) = AF lies in H^(0,(β,−ℓ+1))_3b and ∂_(t_*)(RU) = RF in H^(𝗌+d,(β,−ℓ+1))_3b ⊂ H^(0,(β,−ℓ+1))_3b. By the
case 𝗌 = 0 with r_1 = r_0/3, c = 1 and ν = 1/8, AU, RU ∈ H^(0,(β−1,−ℓ))_3b, and
U = Q′(AU) + R(RU) ∈ H^(𝗌,(β−1,−ℓ))_3b, with the estimate. ∎

[Hin26] proves the case 𝗌 = 0 and refers the rest to [Hin26c, Lemma 14.6], whose proof applies the case 𝗌 = 0 to Au.
This needs A translation-invariant, so that ∂_(t_*)Au = Af, and localized near the diagonal, so that Au keeps a support
condition; Lemma 28.27 supplies both, by a translation-invariant quantization in the calculus of Chapter 14.

### 28.12 Proof of the 2-admissibility

*Proof of Theorem 28.20.* Let f be as in Section 28.7, and u = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing as in
(28.25). Write ‖f‖ := ‖f‖_(H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)(Ω)^(•,−)).

(i) By Lemma 28.23 (with ϵ < ½) and Lemma 28.24, u_hi + u_reg ∈ H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf,0))_(3b;b)(M_0) with norm
at most C‖f‖, as α_sf < α_sf + 1 − 2ϵ and 𝗌 < 𝗌 + 1.

(ii) u = 0 for t_* < t_1, where t_1 > 1, so u_sing = −(u_hi + u_reg) on Ω_−:

    u_sing|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^((𝗌;k),(α_sf,0))_(3b;b)(Ω_−),     ∂_(t_*)u_sing|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^((𝗌−1;k),(α_sf+1,0))_(3b;b)(Ω_−).

(iii) By Lemma 28.26 with p ≥ sup 𝗌, ∂²_(t_*)u_sing = ∂_(t_*)(∂_(t_*)v_ġ) + ∂²_(t_*)v_h lies in
H^((𝗌−1;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b)(M_0).

(iv) Lemma 28.28 for ∂_(t_*)u_sing, with the order 𝗌 − 1, β = α_sf + 2 and ℓ = 1 (the data (ii) lie in
(α_sf + 1, 0) ⊂ (β − 1, −1)), gives ∂_(t_*)u_sing ∈ H^((𝗌−1;k),(α_sf+1,−1))_(3b;b)(M_0).

(v) Lemma 28.28 for u_sing, with 𝗌 − 1, β = α_sf + 1 and ℓ = 2 (the data (ii) lie in (α_sf, 0) ⊂ (β − 1, −2),
at the regularity 𝗌 ≥ 𝗌 − 1), gives u_sing ∈ H^((𝗌−1;k),(α_sf,−2))_(3b;b)(M_0).

(vi) So u ∈ H^((𝗌−1;k),(α_sf,−2))_(3b;b)(M_0) with norm at most C‖f‖, every bound being linear in ‖f‖. As u is
supported in Ω, this is (28.18). For general f, (28.18) follows by density and the uniqueness of
forward solutions (Proposition 17.14). ∎

Each step needed only the weights of (28.17): α_sf + 1 < 0 in (iii), through β′, and α_sf + 2 < 1, through
β″. In dimension 3 + 1 the same steps stop at β′ = −½ − ϵ, below α_sf + 1, and this is the loss in [Hin26, Theorem
10.1].

### 28.13 Remarks on [Hin26, Section 10]

The following points compare the argument of this chapter with that of [Hin26, Section 10].

(a) *The rows.* [Hin26, (10.6b)] does not make the augmented zero energy operator injective; Remark 28.9 gives a
choice of rows satisfying it for which [Hin26, Proposition 10.6] fails, and (28.9) is the condition the proof
uses.

(b) *The incoming threshold.* Definition 15.29 (6) with α_K = −2 and margin 1 gives 𝗌 + α_sf > ½(−1 + ϑ_in) − 1 at
the incoming radial set (ϑ^(3b)_in = ϑ_in by Lemma 15.31), while the spectral estimates for
u ∈ H^(𝗌,(α_sf,0))_3b need 𝗌 + α_sf > ½(−1 + ϑ_in) ((11.5), Section 12.1.4). [Hin26, Lemmas 10.9–10.10]
measure u_hi and u_reg at the weight α_sf and the regularity 𝗌, which the hypothesis does not cover where
𝗌 + α_sf ≤ ½(−1 + ϑ_in). [Hin26, Remark 10.2] checks only the outgoing radial set, where the condition of
Definition 15.29 (5) is 𝗌 + α_sf < ½(−1 + ϑ_out) + α_K − 1 = ½(−1 + ϑ_out) − 3; the remark states −½ − 1 there,
without α_K. Here u_hi is measured at the weight α_sf + 1 − 2ϵ, with ϵ below the margin (Lemma 28.23), and
u_reg at the regularity 𝗌 + 1 (Lemma 28.24); both use the margin, and nothing is lost in Theorem 28.20.

(c) *The neighbourhood of b_0.* The high-energy estimate with k orders of b-regularity needs (k + 1)δ_Γ(−ϵ′) ≤ 1 for some
ϵ′ > 0 (Lemma 28.23). Proposition 25.3 gives strong trapping admissibility at b_0, and, near b_0, the smallness
of δ_Γ(0) only on a neighbourhood that shrinks as the bound decreases. [Hin26] states its Theorem 10.1 for b near b_0
with its Proposition 8.3 (strong trapping admissibility near b_0 in dimension 3 + 1). Theorem 28.20 is therefore
stated on the sets ℬ_k, and Remark 28.21 gives one neighbourhood for every k.

(d) *The class of orders.* 𝒪_c adds to Definition 15.29 the conditions (C1)–(C3), under which the induced spectral
orders satisfy the hypotheses of Chapter 11–Chapter 13: a constant regularity order ((O1) of Definition 11.2
and Remark 11.3; Chapter 13), the constancy of the semiclassical order over {r ≤ r_2 − δ_0}, and the monotonicity
on a neighbourhood of the characteristic set (Section 12.1.4; [Hin26c, footnote 78]). [Hin26] applies
[Hin26c, Theorems 9.16 and 9.41] to the induced orders without stating these conditions.

(e) *Bounded frequencies.* On c/2 ≤ |σ| ≤ C_0, [Hin26] cites only [Hin26c, Theorem 9.16 (5)], a high-energy
statement; here Theorem 11.33 (6) and (11.35), with the invertibility of Corollary 28.13, cover them
(Lemma 28.23).

(f) *Variable orders in [Hin26, Lemma 10.13].* Its reduction to 𝗌 = 0 through [Hin26c, Lemma 14.6] needs an elliptic
operator that commutes with ∂_(t_*) and is localized near the diagonal, so that Au keeps a forward support condition,
for which the case 𝗌 = 0 is proved with t ≥ νr for any ν > 0; Lemma 28.27 constructs it.

# Part VIII. The stability theory, IV: forward solutions and their asymptotics

## 29. Forward solutions in the cone, uniformly near b₀; null infinity; almost linear bounds

This chapter solves the linearised gauge-fixed Einstein equation forward in time around the backgrounds of the
nonlinear iteration: a patched Myers–Perry metric g_(b₀,b,−S), equal to g_b near K⁺ and to a boosted g_(b₀) near
null infinity, plus a perturbation h that decays at ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺. It writes out [Hin26, Section 11 (opening) and
Sections 11.1–11.3] in dimension 4 + 1, together with the uniformity in the black hole parameter that [Hin26] uses
there.

Section 29.1–Section 29.5 define the classes of metric perturbations and of their sources, show that the
perturbations are e3b-perturbations of g_b, give the structure of L^(g,g_0) in the forward cone and its mapping
properties, prove that 2L^(g,g_0) is admissible relative to 2L_b in the sense of Definition 15.36, and obtain forward
solutions at b₀ (Theorem 29.17). Section 29.6–Section 29.11 prove the two inputs that the case b ≠ b₀
needs, on one fixed neighbourhood of b₀ and with constants uniform in b: strong trapping admissibility of 2L_b at every
b, which gives 2-admissibility for every order k of b-regularity (Proposition 29.19, Theorem 29.21), and the
forward solution theory of Chapter 19 uniformly over the stationary models 2L_b (Theorem 29.23,
Theorem 29.24). Forward solutions near b₀, continuous in b, follow (Corollary 29.25). Section 29.12–
Section 29.14 give the partial polyhomogeneity of solutions at ℐ⁺ and formal solutions there, and
Section 29.15–Section 29.19 improve the forward solutions at ι⁺ and K⁺ for sources with more decay
(Proposition 29.35).

*What changes in dimension 4 + 1.* (1) The contributions of the perturbation h to the operator at null infinity are
half an order lower than the constant matrix Ā of Lemma 27.12 (Proposition 27.14, Remark 27.15). So the
leading part of L^(g,g_0) at ℐ⁺ is that of L_b, 2L^(g,g_0) is admissible relative to 2L_b with p_0 = p̃_1 = 0, and the
restriction ℓ_I < 2γ_Υ of [Hin26, Lemma 11.5] disappears (Lemma 29.3). (2) At ι⁺ the differences of the
backgrounds (mass, rotation, cut-off boost) are of order 2, where [Hin26] has 1, and the curvature of the patched
background is of order 4, where [Hin26] has 3 (Lemma 29.11, Lemma 29.13). (3) The forward solutions have
sf-loss 0 and their weights at ℐ⁺ reach 3/2, the order of a radiation field (Theorem 29.17). (4) The trapping
bound holds at every b near b₀ with a frame built from the null geometry alone, and the ι⁺-normal operator of 2L_b
does not depend on b (Proposition 29.19, Lemma 29.22). (5) At ℐ⁺ the first exponent of a solution is 3/2, in
the slot π̸₀ only; π₁₁ u has no term at 3/2; and formal solutions remove one exceptional term,
5/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ in the 11-component, where [Hin26] removes two (Lemma 29.28, Proposition 29.29). (6) The
Fourier transforms of the cut-off zero energy states decay rapidly at scf and lie one order deeper at tf
(Lemma 29.34). So the singular part of the low-frequency resolvent does not limit the decay at ι⁺: forward
solutions keep the ι⁺-weight min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+) − ε at every K⁺-weight α_K − 2, α_K ∈ [1/2, 1), where [Hin26]
has α_K − ε (Proposition 29.35). The cap 3/2 is the transport of the radiation field's order from ℐ⁺; in dimension
3 + 1 it is 1.

*Notation and the inner radius.* The notation is that of Chapter 14–Chapter 20 and of Chapter 21, Chapter 23–
Chapter 28. The black hole parameters are b = (m, A), b₀ = (m₀, 0) and R₁ = m₀^(1/2). L_b is the
linearised gauge-fixed Einstein operator of Chapter 25, with the gauge modification E_Υ of Section 23.1 and the
constraint damping (c_C, e_C, γ_C) of Section 25.1 fixed there, and for metrics g, g_0, L^(g,g_0) is the
linearisation (27.12) of the gauge-fixed Einstein operator P(g, g_0) of (21.44) in g, so that
L^(g_b,g_b) = L_b. The radii r_0 − 2δ_0 < r_0 < r_0 + δ_0 < r_2 of the artificial boundary are those of
Definition 22.1, with r_0 = r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁], the inner radius of the spacetime of Chapter 21; then the artificial
boundary of the spaces of Chapter 14–Chapter 20 is the inner boundary of that spacetime. Every result of the chapter
holds for each such r_♭, with constants and neighbourhoods of b₀ that may depend on it. The slots of a symmetric 2-tensor
near ℐ⁺ are those of Definition 27.3, in the splitting (27.6): slots 1–3 form π_C, and slots 4, 5, 6, 7 are
π₀₁, π_(1/), π̸₀ and π₁₁. The eigenvalues of Ā ((27.14)) on the slots 6, 4, 5, 7 are the elements 0, (1 −
e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ, 2γ_Υ of the set σ_Υ of Section 27.3, and those on the slots 1–3 are the elements 2(1 − v_C)γ_C, (1 −
v_C)γ_C, (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C of the set σ_C of (26.30). The gauge parameters satisfy 0 < γ_Υ < 1/4,
0 < e_Υ < 1 ((27.1)) and (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C > 100 (Section 25.1). For an index set E, (E, ℓ) denotes
the expansion in E up to the weight ℓ, and E ∪̄ {(z, 0)} is the extended union of Lemma 21.33: E ∪ {(z, 0)} if
z ∉ π_1E, and E with the logarithmic order at z raised by one otherwise; ∪̄^m is that union taken m times.

### 29.1 The setting

This section is [Hin26, (11.1)–(11.11)] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Background.* For b near b₀ and S ∈ 𝒮_1 small, with the cut-offs χ_K and the boosts φ_S of Section 21.7, put

    g_(b₀,b,−S) := (1 − χ_K) φ_(−S)^* g_(b₀) + χ_K g_b    (29.1)

([Hin26, (11.1)]). The cut-offs are moreover taken with ([Hin26, (11.5)])

    supp χ^♭_K ⊂ χ_K⁻¹(1) ⊂ supp χ_K ⊂ (χ^♯_K)⁻¹(1) ⊂ supp χ^♯_K ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ 10},    (29.2)

a further condition of the same kind as those of Section 21.7 (supports in {t > T} with T large), and compatible
with them.

*Time function and domain.* t^♭_* is the function of Lemma 15.35 with ℓ = ½, built for g_(b₀) ([Hin26, (11.3)]),
and Ω_* := cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1} ⊂ Ω = cl_M{t_* ≥ 1} ([Hin26, (11.4)]). Near ℐ⁺, (t_*/r)^(1/2) is a smooth positive
multiple of the x_I of Section 29.2, so t^♭_*/t_* = 1 − (t_*/r)^(1/2) is smooth on M_(1/2) there (Lemma 15.35
(a)); Chapter 38 uses the exponent ½ for this reason.

*The class parameter.* A number ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½) is fixed once and for all. It is the e3b-weight at ℐ⁺ of the classes of
admissible operators of Theorem 29.17 and Theorem 29.24. The value ½ is excluded for it because
(29.13) fails there (see its proof); [Hin26] likewise takes ℓ_I < ½. In Theorem 19.14 the exponent of the
time function and the weight of the class are one number; here the exponent ½ exceeds ℓ_I, and the forward solution
theory of Chapter 19 is applied in the form of Remark 19.34, which allows this.

L²-based spaces on Ω_* use the unweighted b-density μ_b = |dt_* dx|/(t_*⟨x⟩⁴) of Corollary 19.15 ([Hin26] has
t_*⁻¹⟨x⟩⁻³|dt_* dx|), and weights are listed at (ℐ⁺, ι⁺, K⁺), with the defining functions ρ_I, ρ_+, ρ_K of
(21.23).

**Definition 29.1** (Metric perturbations and their sources; [Hin26, Definition 11.3] in dimension 4 + 1.)
Let ℰ_+ ⊂ ℂ × ℕ₀ be an index set with

    (2, 0) ∈ ℰ_+,      min Re ℰ_+ > 1,      jℰ_+ ⊂ ℰ_+  (j ∈ ℕ),    (29.3)

and let ℰ_I^C satisfy Definition 27.6 (2)–(3), with ℰ_I^tot, ℰ_(I,01), ℰ_(I,1/), ℰ̸_(I,0), ℰ_(I,11) and ℱ_(I,11)
as there ((27.8)–(27.9), (27.17)). Let ℓ_I, ℓ_+, ℓ_K ∈ ℝ.

(1) For k ≥ 5, H^(k,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+),ℓ_K)_b(Ω_*) is the space of real symmetric 2-tensors h whose slot
components near ℐ⁺ lie in H^(k,(ℰ,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+),ℓ_K)_b with ℰ = ℰ_I^C for π_C, ℰ_(I,01) for π₀₁, ℰ_(I,1/) for π_(1/),
ℰ̸_(I,0) for π̸₀ and ℰ_(I,11) for π₁₁ ((27.10) with ι⁺ in place of I⁰).

(2) For k ≥ 3, H^(k,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),(ℰ_++2,ℓ_++2),ℓ_K)_b(Ω_*) is the space of f with π_C f, π₀₁ f, π_(1/) f,
π̸₀ f in (ℰ_I^C + 1, ℓ_I + 1) and π₁₁ f in (ℱ_(I,11), ℓ_I + 1) at ℐ⁺, all in (ℰ_+ + 2, ℓ_+ + 2) at ι⁺, and of
weight ℓ_K at K⁺ (Definition 27.16).

(3) H^(k,(⟨(3,0)⟩₀,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+),ℰ_K)_b(Ω_*) is the class of Definition 27.8 at ℐ⁺ ((3, 0) for every slot but
π₁₁, (2, 0) for π₁₁), with (ℰ_+, ℓ_+) at ι⁺ and the index set ℰ_K at K⁺.

[Hin26] has (1, 0) ∈ ℰ_+ and min Re ℰ_+ ≥ 1: (1, 0) is the ι⁺-order of its background differences, which in dimension
4 + 1 is 2 (Lemma 29.11). The condition min Re ℰ_+ > 1 is what Lemma 29.3 and Proposition 29.12 use.
Later chapters may raise min Re ℰ_+; the exponent 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ that formal solutions at ℐ⁺ produce
(Proposition 29.29) lies above it.

*The class of perturbations.* With parameters a_I > 3/2, a_+ > 1, a_K > 2, put

    𝒳^k := H^(k,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,a_I),(ℰ_+,a_+),a_K)_b(Ω_*; S²T*).    (29.4)

[Hin26, (11.9)–(11.10)] fixes (a_I, a_+, a_K) = (3 + ε_I, 3 + ε_+, 2 + ε_K), with
0 < ε_K < ε_+ < min(ε_ind, ε_I) < 1, for the iteration of [Hin26, Sections 11.2–11.8]. This chapter uses only the
inequalities a_I > 3/2, a_+ > 1, a_K > 2, and, where a statement says so, upper bounds of the weights in terms of a_I
and a_+; the values are chosen where the iteration needs them, from Chapter 31 on.

### 29.2 The edge-3b class

This section is [Hin26, Lemma 11.5 and (11.12)–(11.14)] in dimension 4 + 1. On M_(1/2) (Definition 21.12) put
x_I := ρ_I^(1/2). Near ℐ⁺, with the null coordinates x⁰ = t + |x|, x¹ = t − |x| and r dω the rescaled angular
coframe, the tensors

    x_I²(dx⁰)²,  dx⁰ ⊗_s dx¹,  x_I dx⁰ ⊗_s r dω,  x_I⁻²(dx¹)²,  x_I⁻¹ dx¹ ⊗_s r dω,  r dω ⊗_s r dω    (29.5)

span x_I⁻²ρ_+⁻² C^∞(Ω_(*,1/2); S² ᵉ³ᵇT*M_(1/2)), and (29.5) with the factors of x_I dropped is a global
frame away from ℐ⁺ ([Hin26, (11.13)]).

**Lemma 29.2** (The frame.) (29.5) is a frame of x_I⁻²ρ_+⁻² C^∞(S² ᵉ³ᵇT*) over Ω_(*,1/2).

*Proof.* By Lemma 14.8, as used in the proof of Lemma 15.35, near ℐ⁺ the covectors e_1 := x_I⁻¹ dt_*,
e_2 := x_I dr and r dω span ρ_+⁻¹x_I⁻¹ C^∞(ᵉ³ᵇT*). With dt_* = dx¹ + O(|x|⁻²) d|x| (Lemma 27.4 and its proof)
and dr = d|x|, we have x_I⁻¹dx¹ = e_1 + O(ρ²x_I⁻²)e_2 and x_I dx⁰ = x_I²e_1 + 2e_2 + O(ρ²)e_2, an invertible smooth
change of frame (ρ = |x|⁻¹, and ρ²x_I⁻² = ρ_+²ρ_I ≤ 1). Symmetric products give (29.5). Away from ℐ⁺, x_I is
bounded below and the same products of dt, dx^i span; near K⁺ they span x_I⁻²ρ_+⁻² S² ᵉ³ᵇT* themselves, with no
rescaling by ⟨x⟩ (Section 15.13.1). ∎

**Lemma 29.3** (Perturbations are e3b-perturbations; [Hin26, Lemma 11.5] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let h ∈ 𝒳^k,
k ≥ 3. Then h ∈ 𝒢̃^(k−3,(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_b (Definition 15.33) for every

    ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½],      ℓ_+ ∈ (0, 1],      ℓ_K ∈ (0, a_K],    (29.6)

with ‖h‖_(𝒢̃^(k−3,(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_b) ≤ C‖h‖_(𝒳^k). [Hin26] needs ℓ_I < min(2γ_Υ, ½) and ℓ_+ < 1.

*Proof.* b-Sobolev embedding for μ_b (dim M = 5, three derivatives) gives, slot by slot, sup bounds with k − 3
b-derivatives: at ℐ⁺ by the least real part of the slot's index set (the expansion terms) or by a_I, whichever is
smaller; at ι⁺ by min(a_+, min Re ℰ_+) − ε > 1 ≥ ℓ_+ for ε small; at K⁺ by a_K ≥ ℓ_K. In powers of x_I the slot
components are: h_00, h_0ā, tr̸ h of order > 3 + 4γ_Υ; h_01 and h_11 of order ≥ 3 + 2(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ; h_1ā of order
≥ 3 + 2γ_Υ; π̸₀ h of order 3 (Definition 29.1 (1), (27.9)). The coefficients of h in the frame
(29.5) are x_I⁻²h_00, h_01, x_I⁻¹h_0ā, x_I²h_11, x_I h_1ā and h_āb̄, of x_I-orders at least 1 + 4γ_Υ, 3,
2 + 4γ_Υ, 5, 4 and 3, all ≥ 1 ≥ 2ℓ_I. These are the orders of the index sets; where a_I is smaller, a slot has
x_I-order 2a_I (less ε for logarithms), and the least coefficient order is then 2a_I − 2 − ε > 1, so the conclusion
stands. Away from ℐ⁺ the coefficients are the Cartesian components times bounded factors. So the coefficients lie in
C^(k−3,(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_b, which is the claim. ∎

In dimension 3 + 1 the coefficient x_I⁻²h_00 has order 4γ_Υ, which is the restriction ℓ_I < 2γ_Υ of [Hin26]; in
dimension 4 + 1 the extra power of x_I in the radiation order 3/2 removes it. As in [Hin26, footnote 103], ℓ_I denotes
two weights, which are not compared. It is an e3b-weight in Lemma 29.3, where it ranges over (0, ½], in
(29.13) and Corollary 29.16, where it ranges over (0, ½), and in Theorem 29.17 and Theorem 29.24,
where it is the class parameter fixed in Section 29.1; it is a b-weight at ℐ⁺ in Definition 29.1,
Proposition 29.12 and from Section 29.12 on. The exponent ½ of the time function t^♭_* is neither.

*Consequences.* Let g = g_(b₀,b,−S) + h. By Lemma 29.3 with ℓ_I = ½ and k = 3, ‖h‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) ≤
C‖h‖_(𝒳³), as ρ_+ and ρ_K are bounded on Ω_*; and g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_(b₀) is small in 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)
(Lemma 29.11 with the argument of Lemma 29.3; it vanishes at b = b₀, S = 0 and depends continuously on
(b, S)). So g − g_(b₀) = (g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_(b₀)) + h is small in 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b) when |b − b₀|, |S| and ‖h‖_(𝒳⁴)
are small, and then dt^♭_* is past timelike for g by Lemma 15.35 (2), with ℓ = ½ (Corollary 29.16 gives the
bound). By Lemma 29.3 and Lemma 29.11, such g lie in the class 𝒢^((0;k−3),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_(e3b;b) of
asymptotically stationary metrics of Definition 15.33, with g_b in place of g₀ (cf. [Hin26c, Definition 5.15]), for
ℓ_I, ℓ_+, ℓ_K as in (29.6). Smallness of h in H^(3,(1,0,0))_b makes x_I²ρ_+²g non-degenerate and Lorentzian
(Remark 15.34 (b)): by the coefficients in the proof of Lemma 29.3, the weight 1 at ℐ⁺ suffices
([Hin26, footnote 104]).

### 29.3 The structure in the forward cone

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 11.6 and Remark 11.7] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Coordinates.* On U⁺ := Ω_* ∩ {|x| ≥ 4R₁} put

    ρ_+ := 1/(t_* + 1),   ρ_I := (t_* + 1)/|x|,   ρ := |x|⁻¹ = ρ_+ρ_I,   X_+ := ρ_+∂_(ρ_+),   X_I := ρ_I∂_(ρ_I).
    (29.7)

With ω these are smooth coordinates near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, and there they are smooth positive multiples of the functions ρ_+,
ρ_I of (21.23) (by (21.23) and t_* = t − |x| + C′ − 8m₀|x|⁻¹ on {|x| ≥ 3R₁}); so they define the
same faces and the same b-structure.

**Lemma 29.4** (The vector fields.) On U⁺_C := U⁺ ∩ {ρ_I ≤ C}, C ≥ 1 fixed, exactly

    ∂_(t_*)|_(ρ,ω) = −ρ_+(X_+ − X_I),        ρ∂_ρ|_(t_*,ω) = X_I.    (29.8)

The Cartesian derivatives ∂_t, ∂_(x^i) lie in ρ_+𝒱_b(U⁺_C), and |x|⁻¹∂_ω ∈ ρ_+ρ_I𝒱_b(U⁺_C). Near K⁺ (ρ_I → ∞) the
functions (29.7) are not coordinates, and the weights there are those of (21.23); Lemma 29.5
and Proposition 29.6–Proposition 29.7 use this lemma near ℐ⁺ ∪ (ι⁺)° only, and the proof of Proposition 29.7
treats K⁺ separately.

*Proof.* At fixed ρ, ∂_(t_*)ρ_+ = −ρ_+² and ∂_(t_*)ρ_I = ρ = ρ_+ρ_I; at fixed t_*, ρ_+ is constant and ρ_I is a constant
multiple of ρ. This gives (29.8). Then ∂_t|_x = ∂_(t_*)|_x, and ∂_|x||_t = ∂_|x||_(t_*) − ψ′(|x|)∂_(t_*) with
∂_|x||_(t_*) = −ρ · ρ∂_ρ = −ρ_+ρ_I X_I and ψ′ bounded; finally ∂_(x^i) = ω^i∂_|x| + |x|⁻¹(·)∂_ω,
and |x|⁻¹∂_ω = ρ_+ρ_I∂_ω. ∎

**Lemma 29.5** (The background in the cone.) On U⁺ ∩ {ρ_I ≤ 1}, in the frame of products of dt_*, dx^i,

    L_b = ρ_+²ρ_I(X_+ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − S̄) + R̃_b,        R̃_b ∈ ρ_+²ρ_I² Diff²_b(U⁺; S²T*),    (29.9)

with S̄ of Lemma 25.1 (2) and R̃_b with coefficients smooth on U⁺.

*Proof.* This is the proof of Lemma 27.11 with (29.8) in place of (27.4). By
(25.4)–(25.5),

    2L_b = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) + (2L̄)^∧(0) − g_b^00 ∂²_(t_*) + Q_b∂_(t_*) + R_b,

where (2L̄)^∧(0) ∈ ρ²Diff²_b is the stationary part of the model 2L̄. The last four terms lie in ρ²Diff²_b with
ρ = ρ_+ρ_I, since ρ∂_ρ|_(t_*) and ∂_ω are b-vector fields on U⁺ and ∂_(t_*) ∈ ρ_+𝒱_b. The first is

    2ρ_+(X_+ − X_I)ρ_+ρ_I(X_I − 3/2 − S̄) = 2ρ_+²ρ_I(X_+ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − S̄),

as (X_+ − X_I)(ρ_+ρ_I) = 0 and S̄ depends on ω only. Halving gives (29.9). ∎

This is (27.13) with ρ_+ for ρ_0 and −(X_+ − X_I) for X_0 − X_I; [Hin26, (11.17a)] has 1 for 3/2 and the
h-dependent A^h, B^h.

*The background class in the cone.* 𝒢⁺ is the set of metrics g_0 on Ω_*, smooth on M, whose component matrix in the
frame dt_*, dx^i is non-degenerate of Lorentzian signature at every point of the compact set Ω_*, its boundary included,
with, on U⁺ ∩ {ρ_I ≤ 1}, g_0 − η ∈ ρ_+²ρ_I²C^∞ and π(g_0 − η) ∈ ρ_+²ρ_I³C^∞ for π ≠ π₁₁ (Definition 27.9 with ρ_+
for ρ_0). The components of g_0 ∈ 𝒢⁺, and by Cramer's rule those of g_0⁻¹, are smooth on a neighbourhood of Ω_* in M,
so they lie in C^∞_b. g_b lies in 𝒢⁺ for b near b₀: its components and inverse lie in C^∞(M) (Proposition 21.21),
and near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, g_b − η = (g_b − g_(b₀)) + (g_(b₀) − η) = m|x|⁻²(dx¹)² + |x|⁻³C^∞ (the proof of Lemma 29.11),
whose slot π₁₁ has order ρ_+²ρ_I² and whose other slots have order ρ_+³ρ_I³. g_(b₀,b,−S) lies in 𝒢⁺ by
Lemma 29.11.

**Proposition 29.6** (The leading part at ℐ⁺; [Hin26, Proposition 11.6 (1)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
g_1, g_0 ∈ 𝒢⁺, k ≥ 5, and h ∈ 𝒳^k with small H^(3,(1,0,0))_b-norm. Then g := g_1 + h satisfies, on U⁺ ∩ {ρ_I ≤ 1}, in
the splitting (27.6),

    L^(g,g_0) ≡ ρ_+²ρ_I(X_+ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − Ā)
        mod (ρ_+²ρ_I²C^∞ + H^(k−2,(ℰ_I^tot,a_I),(ℰ_++2,a_++2))_b) Diff²_b.    (29.10)

For h ∈ H^(k,(⟨(3,0)⟩₀,a_I),(ℰ_+,a_+),·)_b the same holds with (2, 0) in place of ℰ_I^tot.

*Proof.* This is the proof of Proposition 27.14 on U⁺, with Lemma 29.4–Lemma 29.5 in place of
Lemma 27.2 and Lemma 27.11, and with the expansion of g⁻¹ after Proposition 29.7 in place of Steps 1–3
of the part *The perturbation* there; both ask smallness at the order 3 only. The change of frame (Lemma 27.4,
with ρ² = ρ_+²ρ_I²) turns S̄ into Ā (Lemma 27.12). The backgrounds (g_1, g_0) differ from (g_b, g_b) by
ρ_+²ρ_I²C^∞, which with the two factors ρ_+ from the derivatives gives ρ_+⁴ρ_I²C^∞ Diff²_b. The perturbation, counted
as in Lemma 27.13 with Cartesian derivatives in ρ_+𝒱_b (Lemma 29.4) and c_C, c_Υ ∈ ρ_+ρ_I C^∞, gives
ρ_+² times H^(k−2)-functions of the index sets of h: ℰ_I^tot at ℐ⁺ (Lemma 27.7 (b)–(c)), and ℰ_+ at ι⁺
(jℰ_+ ⊂ ℰ_+ for the Taylor terms of g⁻¹, Lemma 27.5 with the weights (a_I, a_+)). ∎

So, as at I⁰ ∩ ℐ⁺, the leading part has the constant lower-triangular Ā and no h-dependent term. The terms A^h − A_0
and B^h of [Hin26] are part of the error, of ℐ⁺-order 3/2 against the leading order 1 (Proposition 27.14,
Remark 27.15). The edge-b form [Hin26, (11.17b)] is not needed: Corollary 29.16 uses (29.13) instead.

**Proposition 29.7** (The difference from L_b; [Hin26, Proposition 11.6 (2)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
g_0 = g_(b₀,b,−S), or more generally g_0 ∈ 𝒢⁺ with ([Hin26, (11.15a)–(11.15b)])

    g_0 − g_(b₀) ∈ H^(∞,(⟨(3,0)⟩₀,∞),((2,0),∞),(0,0))_b(Ω_*),      g_0 = g_b near K⁺,    (29.11)

let h ∈ 𝒳^k, k ≥ 5, with small H^(3,(1,0,0))_b-norm, and g := g_(b₀,b,−S) + h ([Hin26, (11.16)]). Then on Ω_*

    L^(g,g_0) − L_b ∈ H^(k−2,(ℰ_I^tot,a_I),(ℰ_++2,a_++2),a_K)_b Diff²_b(Ω_*; S²T*),    (29.12)

    2L^(g,g_0) − 2L_b ∈ x_I²ρ_+² H^(k−2,(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_b Diff²_(e3b)(Ω_*; S²T*),    (29.13)

for ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½), ℓ_+ ∈ (0, 1] and ℓ_K ∈ (0, a_K], the latter with norm bounded by C(|b − b₀| + |S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳^k)),
C depending on k, on ℓ_I and on an upper bound for ‖h‖_(𝒳^k).

[Hin26, (11.18a)–(11.18b)] carry in addition the term χ_Iρ_Iρ_+²((A^h − A_0)(ρ_I∂_(ρ_I) − ρ_+∂_(ρ_+)) + ρ_+⁻¹B^h),
which contains a term of leading order at ℐ⁺; in dimension 4 + 1 it is part of the error.

*Proof.* Write g − g_b = (g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b) + h, and g_0 − g_b. By Lemma 29.11 below, g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b is
supported where χ_K < 1, so away from K⁺, and lies in H^(∞,(⟨(3,0)⟩₀,∞),((2,0),∞),∞)_b ⊂ 𝒳^∞ (Definition 27.8 and
Lemma 27.7 (a); (2, 0) ∈ ℰ_+); the same holds for g_0 − g_b under (29.11). So both differences are of
the class of h, and Lemma 27.13 applies to L^(g,g_0) − L^(g_b,g_b) with δ in 𝒳^k. Cartesian derivatives lie in
ρ_+𝒱_b near ℐ⁺ ∪ ι⁺ (Lemma 29.4, and in the interior of ι⁺ by homogeneity) and in ρ_+𝒱_(3b) ⊂ ρ_+𝒱_b near K⁺
(as in [Hin26]); the counting gives ρ_+² times H^(k−2)-functions of the class of 𝒳^k, which is (29.12)
(ρ_+² shifts the data at ι⁺ by 2; at K⁺, ρ_+² is bounded and the weight is a_K).

For (29.13): near ℐ⁺, ∂_0 ∈ x_I²ρ_+𝒱_(e3b), ∂_1 ∈ ρ_+𝒱_(e3b) and |x|⁻¹∂_ω ∈ x_Iρ_+𝒱_(e3b) ([Hin26, (11.12)],
which does not depend on the dimension), so all Cartesian derivatives lie in ρ_+𝒱_(e3b). A coefficient c of the
counting carries a factor δ, or a b-derivative of order at most two of δ, whose slot components have x_I-order at
least 3 (the least slot order, 3/2 in ρ_I, that of the radiation term of π̸₀h, (3/2, 0) ∈ ℰ̸_(I,0)). So
c ∂∂ ∈ x_I²ρ_+² · x_I c′ Diff²_(e3b) with c′ := x_I⁻³c, and x_I c′ = x_I^(2ℓ_I) · x_I^(1−2ℓ_I)c′. Near ℐ⁺ the factor
x_I⁻³δ is a sum of expansion terms ρ_I^(z−3/2)(log ρ_I)^j a_(z,j), with Re z ≥ 3/2, and of a remainder in
ρ_I^(a_I−3/2)H^k_b ⊂ H^k_b (a_I > 3/2); b-derivatives keep this form. Multiplied by x_I^(1−2ℓ_I) = ρ_I^(½−ℓ_I), an
expansion term becomes ρ_I^(z−1−ℓ_I)(log ρ_I)^j a_(z,j), with σ := Re(z − 1 − ℓ_I) ≥ ½ − ℓ_I > 0; such a term and its
b-derivatives, which are of the same form, lie in L²(μ_b) near ℐ⁺, as ∫_0^1 ρ_I^(2σ)|log ρ_I|^(2j) dρ_I/ρ_I < ∞
(μ_b is a b-density at ℐ⁺). The other factors of c lie in C^∞_b or in H^(k−2)_b ∩ L^∞ (further factors of δ and
their b-derivatives, and components of g⁻¹ − g_b⁻¹, by Lemma 29.9 as applied after it), so by
Lemma 29.8 (a) and (c), x_I^(1−2ℓ_I)c′ ∈ H^(k−2)_b near ℐ⁺, with norm at most C, depending on ℓ_I, times
the norms of the factors. Here ℓ_I < ½ is needed: the coefficient a_(3/2,0) of the radiation term of π̸₀h need not
vanish on ℐ⁺, and it enters c without further decay (for instance through the second derivatives of π̸₀h along ∂_1
in the curvature term); at ℓ_I = ½ the corresponding term of x_I^(1−2ℓ_I)c′ is a function of (t_*, ω) that is not
zero in general, and such a function is not in L²(μ_b) near ℐ⁺. At ι⁺ the factor has order > 1 ≥ ℓ_+, and at K⁺
order a_K ≥ ℓ_K. The b-regularity of the coefficients is k − 2, and the e3b-vector fields are b-vector fields on
M_(1/2). The norm bound is linear in the factors δ, whose norms add up to at most C(|b − b₀| + |S|) + ‖h‖; the other
factors are bounded in terms of an upper bound for ‖h‖_(𝒳^k). ∎

*Products on Ω_*.* For k ∈ ℕ₀, H^k_b(Ω_*) is the space of restrictions to the interior of Ω_* of elements of H^k_b(M̃)
for the density μ_b, with the quotient norm, and wH^k_b(Ω_*) := {u : w⁻¹u ∈ H^k_b(Ω_*)} for a weight
w = ρ_I^(w_I)ρ_+^(w_+)ρ_K^(w_K), w_I, w_+, w_K ∈ ℝ; likewise wL^∞. 𝒱_0 is a finite set of b-vector fields spanning the
b-vector fields over C^∞_b on Ω_* (t_*∂_(t_*) and the r∂_(x^i), Section 19.4.1). Corollary A.30 is stated
on ℝⁿ and on products ℝ^k × N with N closed; the next lemma carries its part (1) to these spaces, which have the faces
ℐ⁺, ι⁺, K⁺ at infinity in logarithmic coordinates and the boundary hypersurfaces {r = r_0} and {t^♭ = 1} across which
their elements are extended.

**Lemma 29.8** (Moser's product estimate on Ω_*.) Let k ∈ ℕ₀.

(a) There is C_k such that for u, v ∈ H^k_b(Ω_*) ∩ L^∞(Ω_*), uv ∈ H^k_b(Ω_*) and

    ‖uv‖_(H^k_b) ≤ C_k (‖u‖_(L^∞) ‖v‖_(H^k_b) + ‖u‖_(H^k_b) ‖v‖_(L^∞)).

Applied to w⁻¹u and w′⁻¹v, for weights w and w′, this bounds uv in ww′H^k_b(Ω_*). Applied r − 1 times, a product of
r factors in H^k_b(Ω_*) ∩ L^∞(Ω_*) is bounded in H^k_b by (1 + C_k)^(r−1) times the sum, over the factors, of the
H^k_b-norm of one factor times the L^∞-norms of the others.

(b) Let k ≥ 1. A function u ∈ L²(Ω_*, μ_b) lies in H^k_b(Ω_*) if and only if Vu ∈ H^(k−1)_b(Ω_*) for every V ∈ 𝒱_0,
the derivatives taken as distributions on the interior of Ω_*; and ‖u‖_(L²) + Σ_(V∈𝒱_0) ‖Vu‖_(H^(k−1)_b) is an
equivalent norm.

(c) Multiplication by an element of C^∞_b is bounded on H^k_b(Ω_*), and ‖u‖_(C^j_b) ≤ C‖u‖_(H^(j+3)_b) for j ∈ ℕ₀.

*Proof.* *Charts.* Near {t^♭ = 1} take the charts of Step 3 of the proof of Proposition 20.4 (for Ω_*,
Remark 20.5, with c_1 = 1/8 and, in (T2), ε = ½, the exponent of t^♭), which cover {|t^♭ − 1| ≤ c_1} and in
which t^♭ − 1 is the last coordinate and, at {r = r_0}, a defining function of {r = r_0} the first. Away from
{t^♭ = 1} take those of its Step 4 (b-cells in logarithmic coordinates near ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺, and charts onto orthants
at {r = r_0}) that are contained in
{t^♭ ≥ 1 + c_1/2}, refining its cells if necessary, which keeps the uniform bounds; as t^♭ has bounded b-derivatives
near ℐ⁺ at bounded t_* and {t^♭ ≥ 1 + c_1} contains a neighbourhood of ι⁺ ∪ K⁺ ((T3) of Remark 20.5), these
cover {t^♭ ≥ 1 + c_1}, and with the Step 3 charts they cover Ω_*. Restricted to Ω_*, each chart φ_α maps onto a
relatively open subset of an orthant ℝ⁵_q := [0, ∞)^q × ℝ^(5−q), q ≤ 2 (up to the order of the coordinates), whose
faces are the images of {r = r_0} and {t^♭ = 1}. As there, the family has finite multiplicity, in each chart the
b-vector fields and the coordinate fields span the same module over the functions uniformly bounded in C^∞, and μ_b is
the Lebesgue density times a function bounded above and below, uniformly in α. Let χ_α be a partition of unity of Ω_*
subordinate to the charts, and χ̃_α equal to 1 near supp χ_α, both uniformly bounded in C^∞ in the chart coordinates.
Let H̄^k(ℝ⁵_q) be the space of restrictions of H^k(ℝ⁵) to the interior of ℝ⁵_q, with the quotient norm, and E the
composition of Seeley's extension operators across the faces of ℝ⁵_q (Step 2 of that proof), bounded from H̄^k(ℝ⁵_q)
to H^k(ℝ⁵) for every k. E is also bounded on L^∞: on {x_i < 0} each of its factors is
Σ_l c_l (χf)(…, −x_i/ε_l, …), with the cut-off χ evaluated at the reflected point (the proof of Lemma 17.3 (b)),
so it multiplies sup norms by at most sup|χ| Σ_l |c_l| < ∞, as in the proof of Lemma 19.16. As in the paragraph
*Estimates* of the proof of Proposition 20.4, with {t^♭ = 1} as one more face of extension, ‖u‖_(H^k_b(Ω_*)) is
equivalent to

    N_k(u) := (Σ_α ‖(φ_α)_*(χ_α u)‖²_(H̄^k(ℝ⁵_q)))^(1/2),

and bounds the same sum with any family uniformly bounded in C^∞ and supported in the charts, χ̃_α for instance, in
place of χ_α: one inequality is (S3) of Section 14.3 applied to an extension of u of almost minimal norm, and for the
other Σ_α χ̃_α φ_α^* E((φ_α)_*(χ_α u)) is an extension of u of norm at most C N_k(u).

(a) For k = 0 this is ‖uv‖_(L²) ≤ ‖u‖_(L^∞)‖v‖_(L²). Let k ≥ 1, u_α := (φ_α)_*(χ̃_α u) and v_α := (φ_α)_*(χ_α v). As
χ̃_α = 1 on supp χ_α, (φ_α)_*(χ_α uv) is the restriction to ℝ⁵_q of (Eu_α)(Ev_α), and Eu_α, Ev_α lie in
H^k(ℝ⁵) ∩ L^∞(ℝ⁵), with sup-norms at most C‖u‖_(L^∞) and C‖v‖_(L^∞). Corollary A.30 (1) on ℝ⁵ gives

    ‖(φ_α)_*(χ_α uv)‖_(H̄^k(ℝ⁵_q)) ≤ C (‖u‖_(L^∞) ‖v_α‖_(H̄^k(ℝ⁵_q)) + ‖u_α‖_(H̄^k(ℝ⁵_q)) ‖v‖_(L^∞)),

with C independent of α. Squaring, summing over α and using the two bounds for N_k gives (a).

(b) Each V ∈ 𝒱_0 maps H^k_b to H^(k−1)_b ((S3)), which gives one direction and one inequality. Conversely let
u ∈ L² with Vu ∈ H^(k−1)_b for V ∈ 𝒱_0; by induction on k, u ∈ H^(k−1)_b. In a chart each coordinate field is
∂_i = Σ_(V∈𝒱_0) a_(iV) V with a_(iV) uniformly bounded in C^∞, so ∂_i(φ_α)_*(χ_α u) = (φ_α)_*((∂_iχ_α)u +
Σ_V χ_α a_(iV) Vu), whose H̄^(k−1)(ℝ⁵_q)-norms have square sum over α at most C(‖u‖_(H^(k−1)_b) +
Σ_V ‖Vu‖_(H^(k−1)_b))², by the bound above at the order k − 1. On the interior of an orthant, a function in L² whose
first derivatives lie in H̄^(k−1) lies in H̄^k, with norm at most C times the sum of those norms: the space defined by
distributional derivatives is that of restrictions, by the boundedness of E (the reduction in the proof of
Lemma 20.6). So N_k(u) is bounded as claimed.

(c) An element of C^∞_b is uniformly bounded in C^∞ in each chart, so the first claim follows from the Leibniz rule
and the equivalence above. The second is Lemma 14.33 for the density μ_b, applied to an extension of almost
minimal norm. ∎

*The inverse metric.* Components are taken in the frame of dt_*, dx^i, norms of matrices are operator norms, and the
norm of a tensor in a function space is the sum of those of its components.

**Lemma 29.9** (The inverse metric.) Let g_1 be a metric on Ω_* whose components and those of g_1⁻¹ lie
in C^∞_b, and let ϵ > 0 with ϵ sup|g_1⁻¹| ≤ ½. Let δ be a symmetric 2-tensor on Ω_* with components in C¹_b,
sup|δ| ≤ ϵ and ‖δ‖_(C¹_b) ≤ B. Then G := (g_1 + δ)⁻¹ exists, sup|G| ≤ 2 sup|g_1⁻¹|, and for every k ∈ ℕ₀ with
δ ∈ H^k_b(Ω_*),

    ‖G − g_1⁻¹‖_(H^k_b) ≤ C_k ‖δ‖_(H^k_b),

with C_k depending only on k, on B and on finitely many C^∞_b-seminorms of g_1 and g_1⁻¹.

*Proof.* As |g_1⁻¹δ| ≤ ½, g_1 + δ = g_1(I + g_1⁻¹δ) is invertible, G = (I + g_1⁻¹δ)⁻¹g_1⁻¹
with |(I + g_1⁻¹δ)⁻¹| ≤ 2, and G has components in C¹_b by Cramer's rule. So Ĝ := G − g_1⁻¹ satisfies
sup|Ĝ| ≤ 3 sup|g_1⁻¹|. We prove the bound by induction on k. For k = 0, Ĝ = −Gδg_1⁻¹ gives ‖Ĝ‖_(L²) ≤ C‖δ‖_(L²). Let
k ≥ 1 and δ ∈ H^k_b(Ω_*), and assume the bound at k − 1. For V ∈ 𝒱_0, VG = −G(V(g_1 + δ))G, as G is C¹; with
G = g_1⁻¹ + Ĝ,

    VĜ = −G(Vδ)G − Ĝ(Vg_1)g_1⁻¹ − g_1⁻¹(Vg_1)Ĝ − Ĝ(Vg_1)Ĝ.

Expanding G = g_1⁻¹ + Ĝ in the first term as well, VĜ is a sum of products of components of g_1⁻¹ and Vg_1, which lie
in C^∞_b, with one, two or three factors among the components of Ĝ and Vδ, at least one of them. By
Lemma 29.8 (c) and (a) at the order k − 1, each such product is bounded in H^(k−1)_b by C times the
H^(k−1)_b-norm of one of the factors among Ĝ, Vδ times the L^∞-norms of the others. These L^∞-norms are at most
3 sup|g_1⁻¹| and CB; and ‖Vδ‖_(H^(k−1)_b) ≤ C‖δ‖_(H^k_b), ‖Ĝ‖_(H^(k−1)_b) ≤ C_(k−1)‖δ‖_(H^(k−1)_b) ≤ C_(k−1)‖δ‖_(H^k_b).
Hence ‖VĜ‖_(H^(k−1)_b) ≤ C(1 + B)²(1 + C_(k−1))‖δ‖_(H^k_b), and Lemma 29.8 (b) gives Ĝ ∈ H^k_b(Ω_*) with
the bound at k. ∎

Smallness enters only through g⁻¹. In Proposition 29.7 apply Lemma 29.9 with g_1 := g_b, whose components and
inverse lie in C^∞(M) ⊂ C^∞_b (Proposition 21.21), and δ := g − g_b; in Proposition 29.6 apply it with the g_1 there,
whose components and inverse lie in C^∞_b by the definition of 𝒢⁺, and δ := h. By
Lemma 29.8 (c), sup|δ| is at most C(|b − b₀| + |S| + ‖h‖_(H^(3,(1,0,0))_b)) (Lemma 29.11; in
Proposition 29.6, C‖h‖_(H^(3,(1,0,0))_b)), which is at most ϵ when these are small, and ‖δ‖_(C¹_b) ≤ C‖δ‖_(H⁴_b). So
(g_1 + δ)⁻¹ − g_1⁻¹ lies in H^k_b with weights 0, with norm at most C_k‖δ‖_(H^k_b), C_k depending on an upper bound for
‖δ‖_(H⁴_b). Write

    (g_1 + δ)⁻¹ = Σ_(j≤N) (−g_1⁻¹δ)^j g_1⁻¹ + R_N,        R_N := (−g_1⁻¹δ)^(N+1)(g_1 + δ)⁻¹.

The factor (−g_1⁻¹δ)^(N+1) has N + 1 times the least orders of δ, which are positive at each face; so for N large, R_N
lies in H^k_b with weights beyond every weight in (29.10), (29.12) and (29.13)
(Lemma 29.8 (a) with weights, and (c)), and adds no expansion term. In Proposition 29.6, on U⁺ ∩ {ρ_I ≤ 1},
g_1⁻¹ − g_b⁻¹ = −g_1⁻¹(g_1 − g_b)g_b⁻¹ ∈ ρ_+²ρ_I²C^∞ is part of the background difference counted in its proof. The
Taylor terms are products, handled by Lemma 27.5. This is the counterpart on Ω_* of Steps 1–3 of the proof of
Proposition 27.14, with the tame bound of Lemma 29.9 in addition.

**Remark 29.10** ([Hin26, Remark 11.7] in dimension 4 + 1.) g_(b₀) + h and g_(b₀,b,0) + h differ near
(ι⁺)° by χ_K(g_b − g_(b₀)) ∈ ρ_+²C^∞, which is absorbed into h as (2, 0) ∈ ℰ_+. The same holds for the boost:
g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_(b₀,b,0) = (1 − χ_K)(φ_(−S)^* g_(b₀) − g_(b₀)) ∈ H^(∞,(⟨(3,0)⟩₀,∞),((2,0),∞),∞)_b
(Lemma 29.11). This is where the condition (2, 0) ∈ ℰ_+ of (29.3) is used.

**Lemma 29.11** (The background differences.) For |b − b₀| and |S| small, g_(b₀,b,−S) satisfies
(29.11) and lies in 𝒢⁺; g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b is supported in {χ_K < 1} and lies in
H^(∞,(⟨(3,0)⟩₀,∞),((2,0),∞),∞)_b(Ω_*), with seminorms O(|b − b₀| + |S|).

*Proof.* We have g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b = (1 − χ_K)(φ_(−S)^* g_(b₀) − g_(b₀)) + (1 − χ_K)(g_(b₀) − g_b). On
supp(1 − χ_K) ∩ Ω_*, χ_IVP = 1 and the flow of V(S) is the boost: this is the first alternative of Lemma 21.27,
with supp χ^♭_K ⊂ χ_K⁻¹(1); on its second alternative, {|x| < 6R₁}, the difference is smooth and supported in a
compact set away from the faces at infinity, as that alternative of Lemma 21.27 states, hence in the class. So
by (21.40), φ_(−S)^* g_(b₀) − g_(b₀) = |x|⁻²h_(−S)(ω)(dx¹)² + ρ_0²ρ_I³ρ_+² C^∞ with h_(−S) = O(|S|); and by
Proposition 21.21, g_(b₀) − g_b = (m₀ − m)|x|⁻²(dx¹)² + O(|b − b₀|)|x|⁻³C^∞ on {|x| ≥ 3R₁}. Near
ℐ⁺, |x|⁻²(dx¹)² is the slot π₁₁ at ρ_I-order 2 and ι⁺-order 2, and |x|⁻³ is of orders 3; in the interior of
ι⁺, |x|⁻² ∈ ρ_+²C^∞. This is the class stated, as 1 − χ_K is smooth on M. For (29.11): g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_(b₀) =
(g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b) + (g_b − g_(b₀)), the last term being independent of χ_K, smooth at K⁺ and of the same classes; and
g_(b₀,b,−S) = g_b on χ_K⁻¹(1), a neighbourhood of K⁺. 𝒢⁺: near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, g_(b₀,b,−S) = φ_(−S)^* g_(b₀), and
g_(b₀) − η = m₀|x|⁻²(dx¹)² has the slot π₁₁ only. Non-degeneracy: the components of g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b in the frame
dt_*, dx^i are bounded on Ω_* by O(|b − b₀| + |S|), by the class above and Lemma 29.8 (c), and those of
g_b⁻¹ are bounded there (Proposition 21.21); so for |b − b₀| and |S| small every g_b + τ(g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b),
τ ∈ [0, 1], has a non-degenerate component matrix at every point of Ω_*, and the signature, Lorentzian at τ = 0, is
the same at τ = 1. ∎

### 29.4 Forward mapping

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 11.8 and Corollary 11.9] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Proposition 29.12** (Forward mapping; [Hin26, Proposition 11.8] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let g_0 ∈ 𝒢⁺
satisfy (29.11), let h and g be as in Proposition 29.7, and let 3/2 < ℓ_I < a_I + ½,
0 < ℓ_+ < a_+ + min Re ℰ_+, ℓ_K ∈ ℝ and k ≥ 5. Then

    L^(g,g_0) : H^(k,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+),ℓ_K)_b(Ω_*) → H^(k−2,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),(ℰ_++2,ℓ_++2),ℓ_K)_b(Ω_*),
    (29.14)

and, if moreover ℓ_+ ≤ max(a_+, min Re ℰ_+), then for every ε > 0

    L^(g,g_0) − L_b : H^(k,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+),ℓ_K)_b
                          → H^(k−2,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),(2ℰ_++2,ℓ_++2+m_+−ε),ℓ_K+a_K)_b,
    m_+ := min(a_+, min Re ℰ_+).    (29.15)

[Hin26, (11.19)] has ℓ_+ + 3 − ε (m_+ = 1) and ℓ_K + 2 + ε_K (a_K = 2 + ε_K). The upper bounds on ℓ_I and ℓ_+ are
those of the products (Lemma 27.5): a coefficient of the error with no expansion beyond its ℐ⁺-weight a_I,
acting on the radiation term ρ_I^(3/2) of π̸₀ u, gives ρ_I^(a_I+3/2) times a function with no expansion, and likewise
at ι⁺. [Hin26, Proposition 11.8] is stated for all weights, but its products need the same restrictions (in dimension
3 + 1, ℓ_I < a_I and ℓ_+ < a_+ + min Re ℰ_+, and ℓ_+ ≤ max(a_+, min Re ℰ_+) for [Hin26, (11.19)]).
Corollary 29.14 (ℓ = a) lies inside this range, and the later chapters keep their weights in it.

*Proof.* (29.14). Near ℐ⁺ (on U⁺ ∩ {ρ_I ≤ 1}) this is the proof of Proposition 27.17, with
Proposition 29.6 in place of Proposition 27.14, ι⁺ in place of I⁰ and ℰ_+ in place of ℰ_0. The leading part
ρ_+²ρ_I(X_+ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − Ā) has the slot-by-slot effect established there: X_+ − X_I preserves index sets,
X_I − 3/2 − Ā_jj annihilates the exceptional terms, and the couplings of Ā act as there; the factor ρ_+²ρ_I shifts the
data by 2 at ι⁺ and by 1 at ℐ⁺. The C^∞ error gives ℰ_I^tot + 2 ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1 and ℰ_+ + 2. The perturbation error gives,
by Lemma 27.5, 2ℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1 at the weight ℓ_I + 1 and 2ℰ_+ + 2 ⊂ ℰ_+ + 2 at the weight ℓ_+ + 2. The
inequalities Lemma 27.5 asks are ℓ_I + 1 < ℓ_I + 3/2, ℓ_I + 1 < a_I + 3/2 (by the hypothesis ℓ_I < a_I + ½) and
ℓ_I + 1 ≤ a_I + ℓ_I; and ℓ_+ + 2 < ℓ_+ + 2 + min Re ℰ_+, ℓ_+ + 2 < a_+ + 2 + min Re ℰ_+ (by the hypothesis on ℓ_+) and
ℓ_+ + 2 ≤ a_+ + 2 + ℓ_+. Away from ℐ⁺, near ι⁺ ∪ K⁺: L_b ∈ ρ_+²Diff²_b near (ι⁺)° (Cartesian derivatives lie in
ρ_+𝒱_b) and L_b ∈ Diff²_b near K⁺, which gives (29.14) there, and L^(g,g_0) − L_b is handled by
(29.12) and Lemma 27.5.

(29.15). Only ι⁺ and K⁺ need an argument, as at ℐ⁺ (29.15) is (29.14). By
(29.12), the coefficients of L^(g,g_0) − L_b have the data (ℰ_+ + 2, a_+ + 2) at ι⁺ and the weight a_K at K⁺.
Lemma 27.5 gives the product index set 2ℰ_+ + 2 at the weight ℓ_+ + 2 + m_+ − ε, which is below each of
ℓ_+ + 2 + min Re ℰ_+, ℓ_+ + 2 + a_+ and a_+ + 2 + min Re ℰ_+ (the last because ℓ_+ + m_+ ≤ a_+ + min Re ℰ_+ when
ℓ_+ ≤ max(a_+, min Re ℰ_+)), and the weight ℓ_K + a_K at K⁺. ∎

**Lemma 29.13** (The curvature of the patched background.) For |b − b₀| and |S| small, Ric(g_(b₀,b,−S)) is
supported in supp χ_K ∩ supp(1 − χ_K) and lies in ρ_+⁴C^∞ near (ι⁺)°, with seminorms O(|b − b₀| + |S|).

*Proof.* g_1 := φ_(−S)^* g_(b₀) and g_2 := g_b are Ricci flat, so Ric(g_(b₀,b,−S)) vanishes on the interior of
χ_K⁻¹({0, 1}). So it is supported in supp χ_K ∩ supp(1 − χ_K), whose closure meets ∂M only in a compact subset of
(ι⁺)°: χ_K = 1 near K⁺ and χ_K = 0 near ℐ⁺, since χ^♭_K = 1 on {|x| < t/10, t > 60R₁} and supp χ^♯_K ⊂ {|x| < t/2}
(Section 21.7). Near (ι⁺)°, g_i − ḡ = k_i ∈ ρ_+²C^∞ (Lemma 29.11, and Lemma 21.26 for the pullback),
and Cartesian derivatives lie in ρ_+𝒱_b. With k := (1 − χ_K)k_1 + χ_K k_2, Ric(ḡ + k) = DRic(k) + Q(k), Q at least
quadratic, and Q(k) ∈ ρ_+⁶C^∞ (two factors k, two derivatives). Further DRic(k) = (1 − χ_K)DRic(k_1) +
χ_K DRic(k_2) + E, with DRic(k_i) = −Q(k_i) ∈ ρ_+⁶C^∞ and E the terms with a derivative on χ_K: ∂χ_K ∈ ρ_+C^∞ and
∂²χ_K ∈ ρ_+²C^∞ (χ_K is smooth on M), times ∂k_i ∈ ρ_+³C^∞ and k_i ∈ ρ_+²C^∞ respectively; so E ∈ ρ_+⁴C^∞. Where χ_K
is locally constant, E = 0 and the count gives ρ_+⁶. The size is linear in k_1 − k_2 (for k_1 = k_2 the patched metric
is Ricci flat), and k_1 − k_2 = O(|b − b₀| + |S|) by Lemma 29.11. ∎

In dimension 3 + 1 the same count gives ρ_+³, the order P(g_0, g_0) ∈ ρ_+³C^∞ of [Hin26].

**Corollary 29.14** (The gauge-fixed Einstein operator; [Hin26, Corollary 11.9] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
g_0 = g_(b₀,b,−S) with |b − b₀| and |S| small, and g = g_0 + h with h ∈ 𝒳^∞ of small H^(3,(1,0,0))_b-norm. Then

    P(g, g_0) = Ric(g) − δ^*_(g_0,E_C) Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g_0)
              ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,a_I+1),(ℰ_++2,a_++2),a_K)_b(Ω_*).    (29.16)

*Proof.* P(g_0, g_0) = Ric(g_0), as Υ^(E_Υ)(g_0, g_0) = 0 (the proof of Corollary 27.18). By Lemma 29.13 it
lies in ρ_+⁴C^∞, with support whose closure meets ∂M in a compact subset of (ι⁺)°, and (4, 0) ∈ ℰ_+ + 2 as
(2, 0) ∈ ℰ_+. And P(g, g_0) − P(g_0, g_0) = ∫_0^1 L^(g_0+sh,g_0)h ds, which lies in the space by Proposition 29.12
(with g_1 = g_0, uniformly in s), as in Corollary 27.18. ∎

### 29.5 Admissibility and forward solutions

This section is [Hin26, Corollary 11.10 and Theorem 11.12] in dimension 4 + 1.

#### 29.5.1 The orders

Theorem 28.20 holds for orders in its class 𝒪_c, the orders of Definition 15.29 with the conditions (C1)–(C3) of
Definition 28.18. The orders used by the forward solution theory of Chapter 19 are built by the construction of
Proposition 15.43 (Section 15.13.2: 𝗌 = s_in − (s_in − s_out)χ) and shifted by constants (Lemma 19.19 and
Remark 19.31). The next lemma shows that they lie in 𝒪_c, so that Theorem 28.20 supplies the
2-admissibility those results assume.

**Lemma 29.15** (The orders lie in 𝒪_c.) The order 𝗌 of Proposition 15.43, read over K⁺ as a
t_*-translation-invariant function (Proposition 15.43 (1)), satisfies (C1)–(C3) of Definition 28.18 with s_c = s_in;
and so does 𝗌 + c for every constant c.

*Proof.* Over K⁺, ψ_0(x_I) = 0 (x_I ≥ ϵ_I there), so 𝗌 = s_in − (s_in − s_out)χ_ι with

    χ_ι = φ(f_W/δ) ψ̃(ϵ_ιδ f_T) ψ(|η̂_(3b)|²/(2δ)) Ψ(σ_(3b)²/|ν|²_(3b))

on Ω_ι and χ_ι = 0 elsewhere ((15.32); the factor ψ̃ vanishes where ϵ_ιδ f_T ≤ 4, which holds near the inner
boundary of Ω_ι).

(C1): Ψ = 0 on (−∞, 0.04], so χ_ι = 0 on {σ_(3b)² ≤ 0.04|ν|²_(3b)} ⊃ {σ = 0}, and 𝗌 = s_in there.

(C2): on supp φ(f_W/δ), |ξ̂_(3b)| < δ/2, so f_T = r(1 − ξ̂_(3b)) < 2r, and ψ̃(ϵ_ιδ f_T) = 0 for r ≤ 2/(ϵ_ιδ); so
𝗌 = s_in over {r ≤ 2/(ϵ_ιδ)} ⊃ {r ≤ r_Γ}, the construction having chosen 1/(ϵ_ιδ) > r_Γ. (C2) is in any case implied
by Definition 15.29 (3), as noted after Definition 28.18.

(C3): −𝖧𝗌 = (s_in − s_out)𝖧χ_ι for the stationary G_0 (𝖧 = 𝖧^(3b) on Σ⁺, a positive multiple of 𝖧_(G_0)). On Σ⁺ over Ω_ι
the factors ψ and Ψ equal 1 (Lemma 15.45 and Lemma 15.47 (b): σ_(3b)² ≥ 0.09|ν|² and |η̂_(3b)|² ≤ 3δ < 4δ),
and 𝖧 applied to the other two factors is ≥ 0 (Lemma 15.47 (a), (c), with ψ̃′ ≥ 0, and φ′(f_W/δ) ≥ 0 where f_W ∈
[−δ/2, −δ/4], φ being even with φ′ ≤ 0 on [0, ∞); by Lemma 15.47 (b) the other branch ξ̂_(3b) < −δ/8 does not meet
Σ). Each of these holds with a margin off Σ. The proof of Lemma 15.45 shows |G_(3b)| > 0.0125|ν|²_(3b) where
σ_(3b)² < 0.09|ν|²_(3b), so Ψ = 1 on W_1 := {|G_(3b)| < 0.0125|ν|²_(3b)}. On W_2 := {|σ_(3b)⁻²G_(3b)| < δ/16} the
argument of Lemma 15.47 (b), with the error δ/16 + δ/16, still gives ξ̂_(3b) ≥ −δ/8 and |η̂_(3b)|² ≤ (3/2)δ + δ/8 <
4δ, so ψ = 1 there. Lemma 15.47 (a) and (c) are proved from (15.8) and (15.31) without using Σ
(𝖧̄f_T = 2ϱ⁻¹ and 𝖧̄f_W = 2(2 − ξ̂_(3b))ξ̂_(3b) wherever σ_(3b) ≠ 0), so they hold on W_1 ∩ Ω_ι ∩ {|ξ̂_(3b)| ≤ δ/2}. Any
other positive rescaling of the Hamilton field, or any other defining symbol of Σ (such as 𝖧^♮ of Section 12.1.4),
differs from 𝖧^(3b) by a positive factor and by terms vanishing on Σ, of size O(|σ_(3b)⁻²G_(3b)|) relative to the
margins δ/8 and ϱ⁻¹ of (a) and (c). So on a thinner neighbourhood W ⊂ W_1 ∩ W_2 of Σ the monotonicity 𝖧𝗌 ≤ 0 holds for
it too. On Σ⁻ the same holds by the evenness of the construction of Section 15.13.2 under the antipodal map. Outside
Ω_ι the order is constant. Constants added to 𝗌 change none of this. ∎

#### 29.5.2 Admissibility

**Corollary 29.16** (Admissibility relative to 2L_b; [Hin26, Corollary 11.10] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
g_0 = g_(b₀,b,−S) (or g_0 with (29.11)) and g := g_0 + h, h ∈ 𝒳^k, k ≥ 5, with small 𝒳⁵-norm. Then
P := 2L^(g,g_0) is admissible relative to P_0 := 2L_b of class ((0;k−5),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) (Definition 15.36) for every
ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½), ℓ_+ ∈ (0, 1] and ℓ_K ∈ (2, a_K], with p_0 = p̃_1 = 0, whenever P_0 is 2-admissible with sf-loss 0 and
margin 1 for the orders of 𝒪_c (Definition 28.18). By Theorem 28.20 this holds at b = b₀, and by
Theorem 29.21 at every b of the neighbourhood B̄_1 of Section 29.6, for every k. Moreover, for
g_0 = g_(b₀,b,−S) the metric g of P satisfies

    ‖g − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) ≤ ‖g_b − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) + C(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳³)),    (29.17)

and for g_0 with (29.11) the left side is at most ‖g_0 − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) + C‖h‖_(𝒳³), the
first term being at most a constant times a seminorm of g_0 − g_(b₀) in the class of (29.11). When the
right side is small, g therefore satisfies the hypothesis (19.57) of Remark 19.34 (at b = b₀) and that
of Theorem 29.24 (at b ∈ B̄_1), with ℓ_♭ = ½ and the time function t^♭_* of Section 29.1.

*Proof.* (1) σ_2(P) = G_g, with g − g_b = (g_0 − g_b) + h ∈ 𝒢̃^((0;k−3),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)) by Lemma 29.3 and
Lemma 29.11. (2) With p_0 = p̃_1 = 0, P̃ = P − P_0, which by (29.13) (ℓ_I < ½) and Sobolev embedding
(H^(k−2)_b ⊂ C^(k−5)_b, three derivatives for dim M = 5, Lemma 29.8 (c), the weight passing through) lies
in x_I²ρ_+² C^(k−5,(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K))_b Diff²_(e3b).
(3) p_1 = S|_(∂X), which in the splitting (27.6) is Ā, lower triangular with real diagonal
(Lemma 27.12), and p_0 = 0 is strictly lower triangular. The conditions ℓ_+ > δ = 0 and ℓ_K > ℵ = 2 of
Definition 15.36 hold.
(4) By (29.1), g − g_(b₀) = (1 − χ_K)(φ_(−S)^* g_(b₀) − g_(b₀)) + χ_K(g_b − g_(b₀)) + h. The first term is
g_(b₀,b₀,−S) − g_(b₀), which lies in H^(∞,(⟨(3,0)⟩₀,∞),((2,0),∞),∞)_b ⊂ 𝒳^∞ with seminorms O(|S|) (Lemma 29.11
at b = b₀, and the proof of Proposition 29.7); by Lemma 29.3 with ℓ_I = ½ and k = 3, its norm is at most
C|S|, ρ_+ and ρ_K being bounded on Ω_*. Multiplication by χ_K, which takes values in [0, 1], does not increase the norm
of the second term, as the norm is a weighted supremum of the coefficients in a fixed frame. The third term has norm at
most C‖h‖_(𝒳³), by Lemma 29.3 in the same way. For g_0 with (29.11), write
g − g_(b₀) = (g_0 − g_(b₀)) + h; the argument of Lemma 29.3 (b-Sobolev embedding, and the x_I-orders of the
coefficients in the frame (29.5), at least 1 for the index sets of (29.11) at ℐ⁺; at ι⁺ and K⁺ the
weight is 0) bounds the first term by a seminorm of g_0 − g_(b₀). ∎

[Hin26] has p̃_1 = (A^h − A_0)|_(ℐ⁺) and p_0 = 4ρ_+⁻¹B^h|_(ℐ⁺), of class ρ_+^(ℓ_+)C^(k−4)_b, and needs ℓ_+ ∈ (δ, 1)
and ℓ_I < min(2γ_Υ, ½). Here only ℓ_I < ½ remains, from (29.13).

#### 29.5.3 Forward solutions at b₀

**Theorem 29.17** (Forward solutions at b₀; [Hin26, Theorem 11.12] in dimension 4 + 1, at b₀.) Let
β_+ ∈ (½, 3/2) and β_I ∈ (β_+, 3/2). There are ε_0 > 0 and d ∈ ℕ such that for every k ∈ ℕ₀, every S ∈ 𝒮_1
with |S| < ε_0, every h ∈ 𝒳^(k+d) with ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) < ε_0, and every

    f ∈ H^(k+d,(β_I+1,β_++2,1/2))_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−),    (29.18)

the forward solution u of L^(g,g_0)u = f, g_0 := g_(b₀,b₀,−S), g := g_0 + h, satisfies

    u ∈ H^(k,(β_I,β_+,−3/2))_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−),
    ‖u‖_(H^(k,(β_I,β_+,−3/2))_b)
        ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(H^(k+d,(β_I+1,β_++2,1/2))_b) + ‖h‖_(𝒳^(k+d)) ‖f‖_(H^(d,(β_I+1,β_++2,1/2))_b)).    (29.19)

For k ≥ 1, u depends continuously on (S, h) in H^(k−1,(β_I−ς,β_+−ς,−3/2−ς))_b for every ς > 0. The densities are μ_b.

[Hin26] has β_+ ∈ (½, ½ + ε_ind), β_I ∈ (β_+, 1), an sf-loss δ > β_+ − ½ (so that u has the weight β_+ − δ), and b
near b₀. Here δ = 0, the window of β_+ is (½, 3/2), and β_I reaches 3/2, the order of the radiation field. [Hin26,
(11.23)] writes the K⁺-weights −2 for u and 0 for f where [Hin26, (11.22) and (11.21)] have −3/2 and ½; with μ_b
throughout, (29.19) uses the latter. Corollary 29.25 extends the theorem to every b near b₀, with
constants independent of b and continuity in b.

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 19.14 in the form of Corollary 19.15, with P_0 := 2L_(b₀), ℵ = 2, the sf-weight
α_+ := β_+ − 5/2 and α_I := β_I − 2, with Remark 19.31 for the relaxed admissibility with margin d_ℵ = 1
(d raised by 1), and with Remark 19.34 for ℓ_♭ = ½: the time function t^♭_* of Section 29.1 is that of
Lemma 15.35 built for g_(b₀), the metric of P_0, with the exponent ½ ≥ ℓ_I. Write ε′_0 for the ε_0 of
Theorem 19.14 in this form, the threshold for ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)), and η_♭ for that of (19.57). Its
hypotheses hold.

(i) P_0 is 2-admissible with sf-weight α_+, sf-loss 0 and margin 1, by Theorem 28.20 at b₀ for every k, as
α_+ + 2 = β_+ − ½ ∈ (0, 1), for the orders of Chapter 19, which lie in 𝒪_c by Lemma 29.15. (19.18), where
the admissibility enters (Remark 19.13), uses these orders over K⁺ with the weights α_+, −2 and margin 1, as
Definition 28.18 asks.

(ii) (19.22): α_I < −½ + S̄ = −½ (S̄ = 0, the least eigenvalue of Ā, (27.14)) is β_I < 3/2, and
α_+ < α_I − ½ is β_+ < β_I.

(iii) P = 2L^(g,g_0) is admissible relative to P_0 of class ((0;k+d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)), with the class parameter
ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½) of Section 29.1 and fixed ℓ_+ ∈ (0, 1] and ℓ_K ∈ (2, a_K], by Corollary 29.16 with h ∈ 𝒳^(k+d+5)
(d raised by 5), and ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)) ≤ C(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳^(d+5))) < ε′_0 for ε_0 small (Proposition 29.7,
(29.13)). Its metric g satisfies (19.57) with ℓ_♭ = ½: by (29.17) at b = b₀,
‖g − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) ≤ C(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳³)) < η_♭ for ε_0 small, as d ≥ 3. P is given on Ω_*, where h is,
and these norms are taken over Ω_*, which is all that Theorem 19.14 asks (the paragraph after it).

The tame form: for ‖h‖_(𝒳^(d+5)) small, ‖P − P_0‖_((0;k+d)) ≤ C_k(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳^(k+d+5))), with C_k independent of S
and h. By Sobolev embedding, as in Corollary 29.16 (2), the left side is at most C times the norm of the coefficients
of P − P_0 in the H^(k+d+3)_b-space of (29.13). By Lemma 27.13 with (g′, g_0′) = (g_(b₀), g_(b₀)), and
the counting of the proof of Proposition 29.7, each coefficient is a sum of products of functions in C^∞_b, of
components of g⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ and g_0⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹, and of b-derivatives of order at most two of δ := g − g_(b₀) and
δ_0 := g_0 − g_(b₀), each product containing a factor of the last kind, which carries the weight. By
Lemma 29.8 (a), with weights, and (c), each product is bounded in that space by C times the
H^(k+d+3)_b-norm of one factor times the L^∞-norms of the others. Lemma 29.9, with g_1 := g_(b₀), bounds
g⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ and g_0⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ pointwise, and in H^(k+d+3)_b by C‖δ‖_(H^(k+d+3)_b) and C‖δ_0‖_(H^(k+d+3)_b). The
L^∞-norms of the derivatives of δ and δ_0, with the weight on the factor that carries it, are at most
C(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳^(d+5))) by Lemma 29.8 (c), and their weighted H^(k+d+3)_b-norms at most
C(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳^(k+d+5))) (Lemma 29.11). These weighted norms are finite because ℓ_I < ½: at ℐ⁺ the factor
carrying the weight has x_I-order at least 3 and must carry x_I^(2+2ℓ_I), the factor x_I² of (29.13) times
x_I^(2ℓ_I), and the bound is that of the proof of (29.13), with C depending on ℓ_I. With (19.24) and
C_k|S| ‖f‖_(H^d) ≤ C_k‖f‖_(H^(k+d)), this is (29.19). The weights: Corollary 19.15 with
b_I = α_I + 2 = β_I, b_+ = α_+ + 5/2 = β_+, sf-loss 0, and the K⁺-weights ½ for f and −ℵ + ½ = −3/2 for u.

Continuity: the last statement of Theorem 19.14, in the form of Remark 19.34 (every P here satisfies
(19.57), by (iii)), P depending continuously on (S, h) in the norm of (29.13). Its coefficients are
the sums of products above, multilinear in their factors, so a difference of two of them is a sum of products in which
one factor is replaced by a difference. For the inverses,

    (g_1 + δ)⁻¹ − (g_1 + δ′)⁻¹ = −(g_1 + δ)⁻¹(δ − δ′)(g_1 + δ′)⁻¹,

and with g_1 := g_(b₀), (g_1 + δ)⁻¹ = g_1⁻¹ + Ĝ, (g_1 + δ′)⁻¹ = g_1⁻¹ + Ĝ′, the right side is a sum of products of
C^∞_b-functions with δ − δ′ and at most two factors among Ĝ, Ĝ′. By Lemma 29.8 (a), (c) and
Lemma 29.9 (for Ĝ, Ĝ′ in H^j_b ∩ L^∞), it is bounded in H^j_b by C‖δ − δ′‖_(H^j_b) for j ≥ 4 and δ, δ′ as in
Lemma 29.9, with C depending on upper bounds for ‖δ‖_(H^j_b) and ‖δ′‖_(H^j_b) (the L^∞-norm of δ − δ′ is
at most C‖δ − δ′‖_(H^j_b) by Lemma 29.8 (c)). ∎

**Remark 29.18** ([Hin26, Remark 11.13] in dimension 4 + 1.) As in [Hin26], rewriting
L_b u = f − (L^(g,g_0) − L_b)u and using (29.15), the tameness of (29.19) propagates through a fixed
finite number of such rewritings, with a total loss of b-regularity independent of k. This is used in the later
chapters, whose statements are written with k = ∞. Each rewriting uses (29.15), so the weights must lie in
the range of Proposition 29.12.

### 29.6 Uniformity near b₀: the setting

This section and Section 29.7–Section 29.11 prove, on one fixed neighbourhood of b₀ and with constants uniform
in b, the two inputs that Theorem 29.17 needs at b ≠ b₀: the 2-admissibility of 2L_b for every order k of
b-regularity, which is [Hin26, Proposition 8.3 and Theorem 10.1] near b₀, and the forward solution theory of
Theorem 19.12 and Theorem 19.14 uniformly over the stationary models 2L_b, which is [Hin26c, Theorems 10.1 and
11.1] for this family. Three facts make this possible. (1) Proposition 25.3 proves strong trapping admissibility at
b₀ from a frame built with the symmetry of Schwarzschild–Tangherlini; near b₀ it gives a bound ε only on a
neighbourhood that shrinks with ε. [Hin26, pp. 147–149] proves the bound at every Kerr parameter in Marck's tetrad.
Here the frame comes from the null geometry alone: along every null bicharacteristic e_0 := ζ/σ is parallel and the
filtration span e_0 ⊂ e_0^⊥ ⊂ T* is invariant, so in an adapted frame the connection is a rotation of the screen plus
a part that lowers a grading. The grading argument holds in such a frame at every b, with bounds uniform near b₀
(Proposition 29.19). (2) The model at ι⁺ does not see b (Lemma 29.22), so Section 18.1–Section 19.1,
which concern that operator alone, hold for every b with the same constants. (3) The rest is continuity and
compactness, as in Section 11.8, Section 12.9 and Remark 28.6.

*The parameters.* They are those of Section 28.1: the gauge modification E_Υ of Section 23.1 and the constraint
damping (c_C, e_C, γ_C) of Section 25.1, with e_C ∈ (0, 1) and γ_C > 0, and the dynamical hypotheses (Dyn) of
Chapter 22. ℬ is the neighbourhood of b₀ of Corollary 28.13, taken inside the parameter set of Definition 21.18,
on which Corollary 28.11–Corollary 28.12 hold uniformly. U_Γ is the fixed neighbourhood of the projections of the
trapped sets of Section 23.1, over which E^Υ = 0 for every b ∈ ℬ. As in Section 25.4 we take z_0 = 1 (the
operator has real coefficients, and z_0 = −1 is the conjugate case); then σ = 1 on Γ_b in the normalisation of
Chapter 12, and Γ_b lies in the future characteristic set over {|x| > r_h}.

The neighbourhoods are chosen in two steps. First fix an open B_1 ∋ b₀ whose closure B̄_1 is a compact subset of ℬ
such that for b ∈ B̄_1:

(B1) Γ_b lies over a fixed compact subset of U_Γ and in a fixed conic neighbourhood O of Γ_(b₀) in T*M ∖ o, on which
σ > 0 and which meets the characteristic set Σ_b of g_b only in its future component; O lies over U_Γ and is so small
that on it ζ and dt_* are independent and g_b⁻¹(dt_*, ζ) ≠ 0 (both hold on Σ_b, where a nonzero null covector is
independent of, and not orthogonal to, the timelike dt_* of (B2), hence near Γ_(b₀) for b near b₀); and (Γ.1)–(Γ.3)
of (H7) (Section 12.1.5) hold, with ν_min, β_Γ and sup_Γ q^Γ continuous in b and positive ((Dyn)).

(B2) dt_* is g_b-timelike over U_Γ (g_b^00 < 0 on X°, Lemma 21.22 (a)), and
‖g_b − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) < η_♭/2, the norm taken over {t_* ≥ ½, r ≥ r₀ − δ₀}, which contains Ω_* and the
region {r ≥ r^♯, t_* ≥ ½} of Lemma 17.2, with η_♭ fixed as follows. Let ϵ_G be the threshold of
Remark 19.34 for g_(b₀), the time function t^♭_* of Section 29.1 and ℓ_♭ = ½: that of Lemma 15.35 (2),
taken so small that it gives also the properties that Lemma 17.2 (iv) asks below Ω. Let K_♭ be the constant of
Remark 19.34 for ℓ_♭ = ½, this t^♭_* and stationary metrics g_0 with x_I²ρ_+²g_0 and its inverse bounded on
{t_* ≥ ½, r ≥ r₀ − δ₀} by twice the bounds of x_I²ρ_+²g_(b₀) and its inverse there; let η_♭ ≤ ϵ_G/(4K_♭ + 2) be so
small that every g_b with ‖g_b − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) < η_♭/2 over that set is such a metric, and that for such
g_0 the inversion identity of the proof of Remark 19.34 applies to the metrics of its (i)–(iii) whenever the
metric g there satisfies ‖g − g_0‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) < 3η_♭/2 over Ω_*. So η_♭ depends on g_(b₀) alone. The
condition holds for b near b₀: on {|x| ≥ 3R₁}, g_b − g_(b₀) = (m − m₀)|x|⁻²(dx¹)² + O(|b − b₀|)|x|⁻³C^∞ (the proof of
Lemma 29.11), of norm O(|b − b₀|) over Ω_* by the argument of Lemma 29.3, and so over {t_* ≥ ½}: below
Ω_*, at bounded t_*, the difference is stationary, and the weight and the frame at (t_*, x) are comparable to those at
the point of {t^♭_* = 1} with the same x; on {|x| ≤ 3R₁}, g_b is smooth in b and stationary, and x_I²ρ_+² is bounded
above and below there. By it the time function t^♭ := t^♭_* of Section 29.1, built from g_(b₀) with ℓ = ½, serves
every g_b, and Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭ ≥ 1} does not depend on b. Moreover, on the annulus {½r_♭ ≤ |x| ≤ 15R₁/16},
g_b⁻¹(dr, dr) ≤ −c and g_b⁻¹(dt, dr) > 0, with c := 31/450 independent of b; so dr is future timelike for g_b there.
This makes the inner boundary {r = r₀} spacelike at every b ∈ B̄_1, and r decreasing along future causal curves on the
collar {r₀ − 2δ₀ ≤ r ≤ r₀} and up to r₂ = 7R₁/8, with a margin uniform in b, as the energy estimates on slabs use at
each b (cf. (H4), and Lemma 15.35 (1), whose region {r₀ ≤ r ≤ r^♮} the annulus contains).

*The time orientation in (B2).* On {½r_♭ ≤ |x| ≤ 2R₁}, g_b is g^KS_b in a time coordinate translated by a constant
(Lemma 21.20 (c)), so by Lemma 21.16 (e), whose hypothesis holds there by Lemma 21.19, dt − β dr
is g_b-timelike for every β ∈ [0, 1]. On {r₀ − 2δ₀ ≤ |x| ≤ 2R₁}, where ψ′ = 1 (Definition 22.1),
dt_* = dt − dr; so the path β ↦ dt − β dr, β ∈ [0, 1], joins dt to dt_* through timelike covectors, and dt lies in
the cone of dt_*, which is the past cone of the time orientation of (H6) (Section 12.1.2, Lemma 22.6). As dt is
timelike on the connected set {½r_♭ ≤ |x| ≤ 2R₁}, it lies in one cone throughout; this extends the time orientation to
the annulus, with dt past timelike. Two timelike covectors lie in the same cone exactly when their g_b⁻¹-pairing is
negative; so the two inequalities say that dr is timelike and lies in the cone opposite to that of dt, that is, dr is
future timelike.

*The inequalities of (B2).* At b₀ they follow from (22.2): on {|x| ≤ 2R₁}, t − t_KS is constant, so
dt = dv − dr with v = t_KS + r, and g_(b₀)⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0, g_(b₀)⁻¹(dv, dr) = 1, g_(b₀)⁻¹(dr, dr) = f = 1 − m₀r⁻². So

    g_(b₀)⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − m₀r⁻² ≤ −31/225,      g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt, dr) = 1 − f = m₀r⁻² > 0      (½r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 15R₁/16),

as m₀r⁻² ≥ (16/15)² = 256/225 for r ≤ 15R₁/16. The components of g_b⁻¹ in the frame dt, dx^i do not depend on t and
are continuous in (x, b) on {|x| ≥ ½r_♭} (Lemma 21.19, with the inverse of Lemma 21.16 (d)), and the
annulus {½r_♭ ≤ |x| ≤ 15R₁/16} is compact; so for b near b₀ the second inequality persists and the first holds with
−31/225 replaced by −c = −31/450.

(B3) c_C is past timelike for g_b over U_Γ (Theorem 24.1 at b₀, and continuity over the closure of U_Γ, which is
compact modulo t_*-translations, all quantities being stationary).

(B4) The order 𝗌 of Proposition 15.43, built for 2L_(b₀), is admissible for 2L_b with the same weights and margin
(Proposition 15.43 (4)), and satisfies (C1)–(C3) of Definition 28.18 for 2L_b. At b₀ this is Lemma 29.15. At b,
(C1) and (C2) do not involve the metric. For (C3): Lemma 15.45 and Lemma 15.47 hold for every g of
Proposition 15.43 (2), whose item (4) includes the models 2L_b at nearby b, so the proof of Lemma 29.15 runs
verbatim with G_b, its margins (𝖧f_T ≥ ϱ⁻¹ against 2ϱ⁻¹, 𝖧f_W ≥ δ/8, and the gap ξ̂_(3b) < −δ/8 off Σ) being relative.

Section 29.7–Section 29.10 are stated and proved on B̄_1, with constants uniform there; their proofs use only
(B1)–(B4). Then fix an open B_* ∋ b₀ with B̄_* ⊂ B_1 and

(B5) |b − b₀| so small, for b ∈ B̄_*, that in Corollary 29.25 ‖P − 2L_b‖_((0;d)) < ε′_0, the ε_0 of
Theorem 29.24, for |S| and ‖h‖ small (Proposition 29.7, (29.13)).

This is the only condition on B_* in this chapter; Chapter 31 and Chapter 36 shrink B_* further. Theorem 29.23 and
Theorem 29.24 apply the slab estimates of Chapter 17 relative to 2L_b itself, so no condition on slabs enters (B5).
The choices are made in this order: η_♭ by g_(b₀) alone; B_1 by (B1)–(B4); the constants of
Section 29.7–Section 29.10, uniform on B̄_1; then B_* by (B5), which involves only the threshold ε′_0 of
Theorem 29.24. So nothing is circular, and every
statement of Section 29.7–Section 29.10 holds a fortiori on B̄_*.

Put f_b := |dg_b|/(|dt_*| |dx|), a smooth positive stationary function, smooth in b.

### 29.7 Strong trapping admissibility near b₀

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 8.3] on B̄_1, in dimension 4 + 1 and with a different frame. We use the following
result of [Hin17, Proposition 4.1, p. 20] (page of the arXiv version 1502.03183v2). Let (M, g) be a smooth manifold with
a metric g of arbitrary signature, let k ≥ 1, let T^kM := ⊗^k T*M carry the metric and the connection ∇ induced by g,
and let Δ_k := −tr ∇² ∈ Diff²(M; T^kM). Let G(x, ζ) := g⁻¹_x(ζ, ζ) on T*M, H_G its Hamilton vector field,
π : T*M ∖ o → M the projection and ∇^(π*T^kM) the pullback connection on π*T^kM. Then the subprincipal operator of Δ_k,
in the sense of [Hin17, Definition 3.8] for operators acting on bundle-valued half-densities, is

    S_sub(Δ_k) = −i∇^(π*T^kM)_(H_G) ∈ Diff¹(T*M ∖ o; π*T^kM).

We apply it on a subbundle E ⊂ T^kM preserved by ∇, here S²T*M ⊂ T²M. Then Δ_k maps sections of E to sections of E, and
∇^(π*T^kM) preserves π*E, on which it is the pullback connection ∇^(π*E). In a local frame of T^kM whose first members
span E, the matrix of Δ_k is block upper triangular. In a frame, [Hin17, Definition 3.8] defines
S_sub(Q) := σ_sub(Q) − iH_q for an operator Q with principal symbol q Id, σ_sub(Q) being the matrix of the subprincipal
symbols of the entries of Q (cf. Section 23.5.2). For Q = Δ_k that matrix is block upper triangular too, so the
subprincipal operator of Δ_k on E is the restriction of S_sub(Δ_k) to π*E; [Hin17, p. 26] restricts its results to such
subbundles in the same way. So the tensor wave operator □_g := Δ_k on E, taken on half-densities by |dg| as in
(25.7), satisfies iS_sub(□_g) = ∇^(π*E)_(H_G), in every dimension and for every metric.

**Proposition 29.19** (Strong trapping admissibility near b₀.) For η ∈ (0, 1] and b ∈ B̄_1 there is a
stationary fibre inner product h_(η,b) on π*S²T* over O, homogeneous of degree 0 and smooth in b, such that, with p_1^Γ
of (Γ.4) (Section 12.1.5) for 2L_b, the inner product h_(η,b) and the adjoints of Chapter 11 (for |dx| and dt_*),

    sup_(Γ_b) λ_max(p_1^Γ) ≤ Cη,    (29.20)

with C independent of η and b. In particular 2L_b is strongly trapping admissible (Definition 15.26; cf. [Hin26c,
Definition 5.8]) at every b ∈ B̄_1.

*Proof.* *Step 1: the subprincipal operator.* Over U_Γ, E^Υ = 0 and R_(g_b) has order 0, so (25.7) holds at
every b ∈ B̄_1, on half-densities by |dg_b|:

    iS_sub(2L_b) = ∇^(π*S²T*)_(H_G) + 2E^C_(g_b) σ_1(iδ_(g_b)) G_(g_b),

by [Hin17, Proposition 4.1] on S²T*, as recalled above, with σ_1(iδ_g)(ζ)h = ι_(g⁻¹ζ)h.

*Step 2: the frame.* On O put σ := −ζ(∂_(t_*)) and e_0 := ζ/σ: stationary, homogeneous of degree 0, null on Σ := Σ_b
and future directed there. As ∂_(t_*) is Killing, H_Gσ = 0; and ∇^(π*T*)_(H_G)ζ = 0, which is the geodesic equation
(the identity of Section 23.5.2 (c), which uses no property of the metric). So ∇_(H_G)e_0 = 0 on Σ ∩ O. Let
τ := dt_*, timelike by (B2). A timelike covector and a nonzero null covector are never g⁻¹-orthogonal, so with

    e_2 := aτ + a′e_0,        a := −1/g⁻¹(τ, e_0),        a′ := −a g⁻¹(τ, τ)/(2g⁻¹(τ, e_0)),

expansion with g⁻¹(e_0, e_0) = 0 gives g⁻¹(e_0, e_2) = −1 and g⁻¹(e_2, e_2) = a²g⁻¹(τ, τ) + 2aa′ g⁻¹(τ, e_0) = 0 on
Σ ∩ O; e_2 is stationary and homogeneous of degree 0. Let V := {e_0, e_2}^⊥, a bundle of rank 3 on which g⁻¹ is
