positive definite (the orthogonal complement of a Lorentzian plane). Every covector is ω = ω_0e_0 + ω_V + ω_2e_2 with
ω_V ∈ V, ω_2 = −g⁻¹(ω, e_0) and ω_0 = −g⁻¹(ω, e_2). As ∇ is metric and ∇_(H_G)e_0 = 0,

    (∇_(H_G)e_2)_2 = −H_G g⁻¹(e_2, e_0) = 0,        (∇_(H_G)e_2)_0 = −½H_G g⁻¹(e_2, e_2) = 0,

so w := ∇_(H_G)e_2 ∈ V; and for a section v of V, (∇_(H_G)v)_2 = −H_G g⁻¹(v, e_0) = 0, (∇_(H_G)v)_0 = g⁻¹(v, w), and
the V-part ∇^V v is g-skew. In a local frame (e_0, v_1, v_2, v_3, e_2) with (v_i) g⁻¹-orthonormal in V, therefore,

    ∇_(H_G) = H_G + σ(N_1 + Ω)  componentwise,    N_1e_0 = 0,  N_1v = σ⁻¹g⁻¹(v, w)e_0,  N_1e_2 = σ⁻¹w,    (29.21)

with Ω, the matrix of σ⁻¹∇^V in (v_i), skew; σ⁻¹w and Ω are homogeneous of degree 0, as H_G is of degree 1 and the
frame of degree 0. (At b₀ the frame of Section 23.5.2 (c), whose e_2 is not built from dt_*, has the same
structure; the comparison is not used.)

*Step 3: the grading.* Give e_0, V, e_2 the weights 0, 1, 2, and S²T* the induced weight wt, the weight of a symmetric
product being the sum of the weights of its factors. The dual frame vector E_2 satisfies g⁻¹e_0 = −E_2 (the pairings of
e_0 with e_0, V, e_2 are 0, 0, −1), so σ_1(iδ)(ζ) = ι_(g⁻¹ζ) = −σι_(E_2), and Step 1 reads, on components,

    iS_sub(2L_b) = H_G + σ(A + Ω),        A := N_1 + 2γ_C E^C_(c)(−ι_(E_2))G,    (29.22)

N_1 and Ω acting as derivations, and E^C_(c)ω := 2c_C ⊗_s ω − (2/3)(1 − e_C) g ⟨c_C, ω⟩ the map E^C_(g_b) of
(21.42) divided by γ_C, with ⟨·, ·⟩ := g⁻¹. We determine the part of A + Ω that preserves wt. Write
c_C = c_0e_0 + Σ_i c_i v_i + c_2e_2, so that c_2 = −g⁻¹(c_C, e_0), and e_ae_b := e_a ⊗_s e_b. The metric itself is

    g = −2e_0e_2 + T,        T := v_1² + v_2² + v_3²,

as the Gram matrix of g⁻¹ in (e_0, v_1, v_2, v_3, e_2) is its own inverse; in particular ι_(E_2)g = g(E_2, ·) = −e_0.

(a) N_1 maps e_0 to 0, V into span e_0 and e_2 into V; so as a derivation it lowers wt by exactly 1. Ω acts on V
alone, by skew maps, and preserves wt.

(b) As G = I − ½g tr, for h ∈ S²T*

    Jh := −ι_(E_2)Gh = −ι_(E_2)h − ½(tr h)e_0,

tr h being the g⁻¹-trace. ι_(E_2) removes a factor e_2 and so lowers wt by 2, and tr h vanishes on the parts of h of
weight ≠ 2, since g⁻¹ pairs e_0 only with e_2 and V only with V. So J maps the part of weight w of S²T* to the part of
weight w − 2 of T*.

(c) In E^C_(c), the component c_μe_μ of c_C raises wt by wt(e_μ) in the first term; in the second, ⟨e_μ, ω⟩ ≠ 0 only
for the part of ω of weight 2 − wt(e_μ), and g has weight 2, so it raises wt by wt(e_μ) as well. Hence
2γ_C E^C_(c) ∘ J changes wt by wt(e_μ) − 2 ≤ 0, with equality only for μ = 2.

So A + Ω does not raise wt, and its wt-preserving part is

    D := 2γ_C c_2 Φ + Ω,        Φh := 2e_2 ⊗_s Jh − (2/3)(1 − e_C) g ⟨e_2, Jh⟩,

where ⟨e_2, ω⟩ = −ω_0 is minus the e_0-coefficient of ω. On the monomials (v ∈ V, i ≠ j):

- e_0² and e_0v: ι_(E_2) vanishes on them and so does tr, so J = 0 and Φ = 0.
- e_0e_2: ι_(E_2)(e_0e_2) = ½e_0 and tr(e_0e_2) = g⁻¹(e_0, e_2) = −1, so J(e_0e_2) = −½e_0 + ½e_0 = 0 and Φ = 0.
- v_iv_j: ι_(E_2) and tr vanish, so Φ(v_iv_j) = 0.
- v_i²: ι_(E_2)v_i² = 0 and tr v_i² = 1, so J(v_i²) = −½e_0 and ⟨e_2, −½e_0⟩ = ½. Hence

      Φ(v_i²) = −e_0e_2 − (1/3)(1 − e_C)g = −(1/3)(1 + 2e_C)e_0e_2 − (1/3)(1 − e_C)T,

  by g = −2e_0e_2 + T. So Φ(T) = −(1 + 2e_C)e_0e_2 − (1 − e_C)T, and Φ(v_i² − v_j²) = 0.
- e_2v: ι_(E_2)(e_2v) = ½v and tr(e_2v) = 0, so J(e_2v) = −½v; ⟨e_2, v⟩ = 0, and Φ(e_2v) = −e_2v.
- e_2²: ι_(E_2)e_2² = e_2 and tr e_2² = 0, so J(e_2²) = −e_2; ⟨e_2, e_2⟩ = 0, and Φ(e_2²) = −2e_2².

Moreover Ω T = 2Σ_i v_i ⊗_s Ωv_i = 2Σ_(i,j) Ω_(ji) v_iv_j = 0, Ω being skew, and Ω maps the trace-free part S²_0V of
S²V into itself, the trace on S²V being invariant under the infinitesimal rotation Ω.

Refine wt to W := 2wt + s, with s = 1 on T and on S²_0V and s = 0 elsewhere. The seven pieces

    e_0²;   e_0 ⊗_s V;   e_0e_2;   ℝT;   S²_0V;   e_2 ⊗_s V;   e_2²

have W = 0, 2, 4, 5, 5, 6, 8; they are mutually orthogonal for the inner product of Step 4 below, and Ω maps each into
itself. By the list above, D maps each piece into itself except for the component of D(T) along e_0e_2, which goes from
W = 5 to W = 4. Every other part of A + Ω lowers wt by at least 1, by (a) and (c), and hence lowers W by at least
2 − 1 = 1. So

    A + Ω = D_= + D_<,

where D_< lowers W and D_= preserves each piece, and on the seven pieces, in the order above, D_= is Ω plus the scalars

    0,   0,   0,   −2(1 − e_C)γ_C c_2,   0,   −2γ_C c_2,   −4γ_C c_2.

This is the structure of Proposition 25.3, with N_1 in place of 2N, γ_C in place of γ, Ω in place of ϰR, and J
the map written ι there. The grading argument uses the frame only through four facts: g = −2e_0e_2 + Σ_i v_i²; the
weights; that the part of the connection that does not preserve wt lowers it; and that the wt-preserving part acts on V
by skew maps. All four hold here, as does g⁻¹e_0 = −E_2 with e_0 proportional to ζ. Finally c_2 = −g⁻¹(c_C, e_0) < 0:
c_C is past timelike (B3) and e_0 is future null, and a past and a future causal covector, not both null, have positive
g⁻¹-pairing. As e_C < 1, the scalars are ≥ 0.

*Step 4: the inner product.* Let ⟨·, ·⟩_0 be the inner product on π*S²T* induced by declaring e_0, v_1, v_2, v_3, e_2
orthonormal. It does not depend on the choice of (v_i), as O(V) acts unitarily, so it is defined on O, stationary,
homogeneous of degree 0 and smooth in b (the frame is built from g_b, ζ and dt_*); the seven pieces are orthogonal for
it, and Ω is skew for it. Put h⁰_(η,b) := Σ_P η^(−2W(P)) ⟨·_P, ·_P⟩_0 on Σ ∩ O, the sum over the pieces, and extend it
to O by the same formulas: e_0, e_2 (by the formulas for a and a′), V, the frame and the pieces are defined near Σ_b,
where span{e_0, e_2} = span{τ, e_0} stays Lorentzian and e_0, τ stay independent (on O, by (B1)–(B2)). This gives a
stationary inner product on O, homogeneous of degree 0 and smooth in b; p_1^Γ involves the inner product only on Γ_b
and through its derivative along H_G, which is tangent to Σ, so the extension does not enter. In an
h⁰_(η,b)-orthonormal frame a map lowering W by j ≥ 1 has its entries multiplied by η^j, so D_< is O(η), while D_= is
unchanged; h⁰_(η,b) is constant in the frame, so H_G is skew. By (29.22) and (12.35), on Γ_b,

    p_1^Γ = −½(D_= + D_=^*) + O(η),        −½(D_= + D_=^*) ≤ 0,

for half-densities by |dg_b|. The O(η) term is bounded by η times a polynomial in |σ⁻¹w|, γ_C and the components c_μ,
which are continuous on O and in b; as Γ_b ∩ {σ = 1} lies in a fixed compact subset of O modulo time translations (B1),
the bound is uniform on B̄_1.

*Step 5: the density.* The adjoints of Chapter 11 are for |dt_*| |dx|, and (29.22) is on half-densities
by |dg_b| = f_b |dt_*| |dx|. Put h_(η,b) := f_b h⁰_(η,b). Then ∫ h_(η,b)(u, v) |dt_*| |dx| = ∫ h⁰_(η,b)(u, v) |dg_b|, so
the two pairings agree, and with them the adjoints and p_1^Γ (p_1^Γ is an endomorphism, and a scalar factor in the inner
product changes neither its self-adjointness nor its eigenvalues). This replaces the scalar O(|b − b₀|) that
Lemma 23.14 and Proposition 25.3 carry for a fixed inner product. With Cη < ε, (29.20) gives strong
trapping admissibility. ∎

**Corollary 29.20** (δ_Γ uniformly small.) For every k ∈ ℕ₀ there are η_k ∈ (0, 1] and ε_k > 0 such that,
with h_Γ := h_(η_k,b) in (Γ.4), δ_Γ(0) < 1/(2(k + 1)) and δ_Γ(−ε) ≤ 1/(k + 1) for ε ∈ (0, ε_k] and every b ∈ B̄_1. So
B̄_1 ⊂ ℬ_k for every k, with ℬ_k of Section 28.6, the set of b ∈ ℬ at which (Γ.4) holds for 2L_b, for z_0 = ±1,
with δ_Γ(0) < 1/(2(k + 1)) (the case z_0 = −1 being the conjugate one, Section 29.6).

*Proof.* With f(η′) := sup_Γ λ_max(p_1^Γ − η′q^Γ) of (12.4), q^Γ ≥ 2β_Γ and (29.20) give
f(η′) ≤ Cη − 2β_Γη′ for η′ ≥ 0, so γ_+ ≤ Cη/(2β_Γ). f is Lipschitz with constant Q := sup_Γ q^Γ, and
f(γ_−) − f(γ_+) = ½ν_min, so γ_+ − γ_− ≥ ν_min/(2Q). Hence, by (12.4),

    δ_Γ(−ε) ≤ (γ_+ + ε)/(γ_+ − γ_−) ≤ (2Q/ν_min)(Cη/(2β_Γ) + ε),

and likewise δ_Γ(0) ≤ (2Q/ν_min)Cη/(2β_Γ). β_Γ, Q and ν_min are continuous and positive on the compact B̄_1 (B1).
Choose η_k and ε_k accordingly. ∎

For each k the inner product h_(η_k,b) is a different one. Theorem 12.2 is applied at each k separately (in the proof
of Lemma 28.23), so this is what it needs.

### 29.8 2-admissibility near b₀ for every order

This section is [Hin26, Theorem 10.1] near b₀, for every k.

**Theorem 29.21** (2-admissibility on B̄_1 for every k.) For every k ∈ ℕ₀, the order 𝗌 of (B4) and every
b ∈ B̄_1, the forward solution u of L_b u = f satisfies the estimate (28.18) of Theorem 28.20 with a
constant C_k independent of b. So 2L_b is 2-admissible with sf-weight α_sf, sf-loss 0 and margin 1
(Definition 15.32, relaxed, for these orders) at every b ∈ B̄_1, with constants uniform in b; and, by
Corollary 29.20, Theorem 28.20 holds at every b ∈ B̄_1, for every k.

*Proof.* Run the proof of Theorem 28.20 (Section 28.7–Section 28.12) at b ∈ B̄_1. Each constant is uniform,
as follows.

(i) Section 28.7: c is at most the c_(j,k′) of Theorem 28.10 (3) for j + k′ ≤ k, uniform near b₀ by
Corollary 28.11 (and Lemma 28.16 (b)). Lemma 28.22 has no constant; its high-energy input,
Theorem 12.2 (3), is uniform in b by Section 12.9.

(ii) Lemma 28.23 for |σ| ≥ C_0: Theorem 12.2 (5) at the orders of Lemma 28.19 (b), with
h_Γ := h_(η_k,b) of Corollary 29.20. By Section 12.9 its constants are uniform in b, given (H5)–(H8) continuously
in b ((Dyn)) and the inner product continuous in b; then the thresholds γ_± of Section 12.6 and c_Γ are continuous in
b. The condition (k + 1)δ ≤ 1 of that proof holds on B̄_1 by Corollary 29.20, for ε ≤ ε_k.

(iii) Lemma 28.23 for c/2 ≤ |σ| ≤ C_0: the argument by contradiction there, run with sequences
(σ_n, b_n) → (σ_*, b_*), b_* ∈ B̄_1. The estimates (11.30) and (11.32) of Theorem 11.33 hold uniformly
in b for these fixed orders (Theorem 11.38); the coefficients of L̂_(b_n)(σ_n) converge in C^∞ to those of
L̂_(b_*)(σ_*); and the limit is a nonzero element of the kernel of L̂_(b_*)(σ_*) on a space of admissible order. This
contradicts Corollary 28.13, as b_* ∈ ℬ. The inverse is then bounded uniformly and continuous in (σ, b)
(Theorem 11.38), which gives the σ∂_σ-derivatives as there.

(iv) Section 28.9 (Lemma 28.24–Lemma 28.25): Corollary 28.11–Corollary 28.12 and the bound
(28.15), uniform near b₀ (Remark 28.6 and the uniformity paragraph of the proof of Corollary 28.11).

(v) Section 28.10 (Lemma 28.26): uniform near b₀, by the last paragraph of Section 28.10
(Remark 28.6).

(vi) Section 28.11 (Lemma 28.27–Lemma 28.28): statements about t_*-translation-invariant elliptic
operators and integration in t_*, which do not involve b.

(vii) Section 28.12: the assembly, linear in the bounds above.

*Uniformity for every k on B̄_1.* The uniformity near b₀ that (i), (iv) and (v) cite (Corollary 28.11,
Remark 28.6, Lemma 28.16) comes from Theorem 13.29 (2), together with two arguments of the uniformity
paragraph of the proof of Corollary 28.11: the uniform inverse of Proposition 28.8 (by contradiction) and the
column bounds of Remark 28.6, both local in b. Theorem 13.29 gives constants uniform on a neighbourhood of a
parameter at which its hypotheses hold, and the neighbourhood may depend on k. Its hypotheses, (G), (Z_𝒫) and (TF) of
Chapter 13, and the invertibility in Proposition 28.8 and Corollary 28.13, are qualitative and hold at every
b ∈ B̄_1: (G) and (TF) by Section 28.1, the rest because ℬ is taken inside the neighbourhoods of Proposition 28.8
and Corollary 28.13. So for each k, Theorem 13.29 (2), with Proposition 28.8 and Remark 28.6 rerun at b_*,
gives uniform constants near each b_* ∈ B̄_1, and by compactness c_k and C_k are uniform on B̄_1.

For Definition 15.32: (1) is Proposition 29.19; (2), tf-admissibility with weight α_sf + 2, is Proposition 25.11,
which holds for every b near b₀ as the tf-normal operator does not depend on b; (3) is (28.18) at the orders of
(B4), which lie in 𝒪_c. ∎

### 29.9 Forward solutions of the stationary models, uniformly near b₀

This section is [Hin26c, Theorem 10.1] for the stationary models 2L_b, b ∈ B̄_1.

**Lemma 29.22** (The ι⁺-normal operator does not depend on b.) For b ∈ ℬ, in the normal form
(18.5) of P_0 = 2L_b on {|x| > 3R₁}: S = S̄, Q = Q_b, g_00 = g_b^00, and ρ²P⁽⁰⁾ = (2L̄)^∧(0) + R_b, so that
P⁽⁰⁾(0, ω, ρ∂_ρ, ∂_ω) is that of 2L̄. Hence N_(ι⁺)(2L_b) = N_(ι⁺)(2L̄), and N⁰(σ) ((18.7)) does not depend
on b.

*Proof.* By Lemma 25.1 (2)–(3), on {|x| > 3R₁}, 2L_b = 2L̄ − g_b^00∂²_(t_*) + Q_b∂_(t_*) + R_b, with
g_b^00 ∈ ρ²C^∞(X̄), Q_b ∈ ρ³Diff¹_b and R_b ∈ ρ⁴Diff²_b; and 2L̄ = −2∂_(t_*)ρ(ρ∂_ρ − 3/2 − S̄) + (2L̄)^∧(0) with
(2L̄)^∧(0) ∈ ρ²Diff²_b. Comparing with (18.5) (c = 3/2) gives the identifications. As ρ⁻²R_b ∈ ρ²Diff²_b
vanishes at ρ = 0, the frozen operator P⁽⁰⁾(0, ·) is (ρ⁻²(2L̄)^∧(0))|_(ρ=0). Definition 18.1 uses only S_0 = S|_(∂X)
and P⁽⁰⁾(0, ·). ∎

In dimension 3 + 1 the mass enters R_b at ρ³, and ρ⁻²R_b is of order ρ; in dimension 4 + 1 it is of order ρ². Either
way it vanishes at ρ = 0; what matters is that the remainder carries all the dependence on b.

**Theorem 29.23** (Theorem 19.12 uniformly near b₀.) Theorem 19.12, with Remark 19.13 (margin
1), holds for P_0 = 2L_b, b ∈ B̄_1, ℵ = 2, sf-loss 0, the order 𝗌 of (B4), and a constant C_k independent of b.

*Proof.* (a) *Section 18.1–Section 19.1.* They concern N_(ι⁺)(P_0): its Mellin family N⁰(σ) and the semiclassical
rescaling (Section 18.1.2–Section 18.1.3), the estimates of Proposition 18.12 and Proposition 18.24 and their
lemmas, and the forward problem for N_(ι⁺)(P_0) (Proposition 19.2). By Lemma 29.22 their statements do not
depend on b. The proof in Section 19.1.3 also uses P_0: it builds P_Λ := P_0 + ψ(r/Λ)ψ̃(t_*/Λ)(N_(ι⁺)(P_0) − P_0),
applies Proposition 17.14 to it with Λ chosen by smallness relative to P_0, and the orders of Section 19.1.1 are
admissible for P_0. So Section 19.1 is run with P_0 := 2L_(b₀) for every b, which is allowed as the statement of
Proposition 19.2 involves only N_(ι⁺)(P_0) = N_(ι⁺)(2L_(b₀)). The statement also involves the order of
Section 19.1.1, admissible for P_0; with P_0 := 2L_(b₀) this is the order 𝗌 of (B4), which Section 19.2.2 uses at
2L_b, so the substitution is consistent. The compactness and contradiction arguments of Section 18.3.5,
Section 18.4.2 and Section 18.5.4 concern N⁰ and N_tf, which do not depend on b. The uniqueness of
Section 18.1.4 (Lemma 18.4–Lemma 18.5) is qualitative and holds for every g_b, with t_* a time function
(Lemma 15.2).

(b) *Section 19.2.* P_+ = χN_(ι⁺)(P_0) + (1 − χ)P_0 (Definition 19.5), and P_+ − N_(ι⁺)(P_0) =
(1 − χ)(P_0 − N_(ι⁺)(P_0)) lies in x_I²τ³ρ_cf⁻² Diff²_ebe (Lemma 19.6 (b)), with seminorms continuous in b
(Lemma 25.1 (3): the coefficients are smooth in b). The τ_1 of Lemma 19.6 (c) is uniform, the normalised
difference there being O(ρ_+²) with constants continuous in b. By the remark after Proposition 19.8, τ_0 and the
constants depend on P_0 only through Section 19.2.6. Its estimates are the radial estimates at cf (Lemma 19.10,
whose quantities at the radial sets are those of N_(ι⁺)(P_0), independent of b by (a)), the radial estimates at ℐ⁺
(Proposition 16.13–Proposition 16.14), propagation estimates and the slab estimates of Chapter 17; and
τ_0 < ½C′τ_1 involves the C′ of Lemma 15.35. Their constants depend on finitely many seminorms of
P_+ − N_(ι⁺)(P_0) and of the orders, and on margins, all continuous in b. The one limit argument there (u^ε ⇀ u)
extracts a solution from an estimate that is already uniform. Strong uniqueness (Section 19.2.4) is qualitative.
Finite-time solvability (Section 19.2.5) applies Proposition 17.14 and Proposition 17.17 on slabs to operators weakly
admissible relative to P_0 = 2L_b itself, with ε_P ≤ C t_(*,0)^(−(1−ℓ_+)) (Lemma 19.9; C is a seminorm of
N_(ι⁺)(P_0) − P_0 in the class of Lemma 18.3, continuous in b by Lemma 25.1 (3)). The constants of
Chapter 17 depend on P_0 through finitely many coefficient norms and the structural margins (the timelike conditions,
the threshold, the dynamics), and are uniform for ε_P small (the last paragraph of the proof of Proposition 17.14, and
the proof of Proposition 17.17, which applies it). For P_0 = 2L_b these norms, which Section 19.2.5 bounds over all
its slabs at a fixed b, are seminorms of stationary coefficients smooth in b (Lemma 25.1 (3)), and the margins
are continuous and positive in b; so they are bounded, respectively bounded below, on the compact B̄_1, as no
perturbation of 2L_(b₀) is taken. What is uniform in b is the constant of each slab (those of Lemma 19.9 depend
on the step), and only finitely many steps enter (19.12) at T = 2δ⁻¹, so the bound is uniform. So
Proposition 19.8 holds with τ_0 and C uniform on B̄_1.

(c) *Section 19.3.* Step 0 of the proof in Section 19.3.2 uses Proposition 17.17 on a slab, uniform as in (b).
Steps 1 and 3 use Proposition 19.8, uniform by (b). Step 2 uses the 2-admissibility estimate (19.18), uniform
by Theorem 29.21, and Lemma 18.4–Lemma 18.5, which are qualitative. Step 4 sums the bounds. So
(19.14) holds with C_k independent of b. ∎

### 29.10 Forward solutions of admissible operators, uniformly near b₀

This section is [Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] uniformly over the family 2L_b.

**Theorem 29.24** (Theorem 19.14 uniformly near b₀.) Let α_I, α_+, ℓ_+, ℓ_K be as in
Theorem 19.14, with ℵ = 2, δ = 0 and the order 𝗌 of (B4), let ℓ_I ∈ (0, ½) be the class parameter of
Section 29.1, and let t^♭ and Ω_* be those of (B2), built for g_(b₀) with the exponent ½, and η_♭ the number of (B2).
There are ε_0 > 0 and d ∈ ℕ such that for every b ∈ B̄_1 the conclusions of Theorem 19.14 and Corollary 19.15
hold with P_0 := 2L_b (with Remark 19.31 for margin 1) for every P as there whose metric g satisfies in addition

    ‖g − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) < η_♭,    (29.23)

the norm taken over Ω_*, with ε_0, d and C_k independent of b. Moreover, for k ≥ 1: let b_j → b in B̄_1; let P_j be
admissible relative to 2L_(b_j) of class ((0;k+d),(2ℓ_I,ℓ_+,ℓ_K)), with ‖P_j − 2L_(b_j)‖_((0;d)) < ε_0, metric
satisfying (29.23) and ‖P_j − 2L_(b_j)‖_((0;k+d)) bounded, and with coefficients converging in C² on
compact subsets of M° ∩ {r > r_0} to those of P, admissible relative to 2L_b with ‖P − 2L_b‖_((0;d)) < ε_0 and metric
satisfying (29.23); and let f_j → f in (19.23). Then the forward solutions u_j of P_ju_j = f_j
converge to the forward solution u of Pu = f in H^(k−1,(α_I−ς,α_+−ς,−2−ς))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) for every ς > 0.

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 19.14 depends on P_0 only through the following inputs.

(i) Theorem 17.26 and Proposition 17.14, Proposition 17.17 and Proposition 17.19 (Section 19.6.1).
Theorem 17.26 is uniform over the stationary models of nearby parameters (its last sentence). The slab propositions
are applied relative to P_0 = 2L_b (Proposition 19.26 (iv) on Ω_(1,T_η), Lemma 19.25 on Ω_(1,4/ε), and
Proposition 17.19, which rests on Proposition 17.17), and are uniform on every slab as in the proof of
Theorem 29.23 (b).

(ii) The thresholds of Lemma 19.16 and Lemma 15.40, which are continuous in the coefficients, and the
hypothesis of Lemma 15.35 for the time function t^♭ of (B2), built for g_(b₀) with ℓ = ½. The proof of
Theorem 19.14 runs in the form of Remark 19.34 with g_0 := g_b and ℓ_♭ = ½, except that t^♭ is built for
g_(b₀). By the last statement of that remark, it applies (A) of the remark only to g_b, to g on Ω_*, to metrics g′
within K_♭‖g − g_b‖ of g_b on the sets where they are used, ‖g − g_b‖ being taken over Ω_*, and to metrics g′ within
ϵ_G/2 of g_b, the last by the choices of the proof of Theorem 19.12, which Theorem 29.23 makes uniformly on
B̄_1 (all distances in the norm of 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b), over the set named). All these sets lie in
{t_* ≥ ½, r ≥ r₀ − δ₀}. K_♭ is that of (B2), as x_I²ρ_+²g_b and its inverse are bounded there by twice the bounds at
b₀. By (B2) and (29.23), ‖g_b − g_(b₀)‖ < η_♭/2 over {t_* ≥ ½, r ≥ r₀ − δ₀}, and ‖g − g_(b₀)‖ < η_♭
and ‖g − g_b‖ < 3η_♭/2 over Ω_*; so g_b and g lie within η_♭ of g_(b₀), the metrics of the third kind within
(3K_♭ + 1)η_♭/2 < ϵ_G of g_(b₀), as η_♭ ≤ ϵ_G/(4K_♭ + 2), and those of the fourth kind within ϵ_G/2 + η_♭/2 < ϵ_G. So
(A) of Remark 19.34, for t^♭ and g_(b₀), holds for all of them, with the r^♯, δ_♮ and η_0 of that remark for
g_(b₀): the properties of Lemma 15.35 (1)–(2) on Ω, and those that Lemma 17.2 (iv) asks below Ω. The other
uses of t^♭ in that proof, (B) of Remark 19.34, concern the function alone.

(iii) The orders (Section 19.5.4), fixed by (B4).

(iv) Theorem 19.12 with Remark 19.13, uniform by Theorem 29.23.

(v) The 2-admissibility estimate (15.24), uniform by Theorem 29.21.

Every other constant depends on P only through ε_0 (the last sentence of Section 19.6.1) and the fixed η_♭. So
ε_0, d and C_k can be chosen independent of b ∈ B̄_1.

*Continuity.* We run the proof of Section 19.9 with P^((j)) := P_j relative to 2L_(b_j). Let u_j and u be the
forward solutions of P_j u_j = f_j and Pu = f, and write X := X(𝗌;k+d′) ((19.29) with δ = 0, ℵ = 2) and
H := H^(k,(α_I,α_+,−2))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−), with 𝗌 the order of (B4) and d′ := max(0, ⌈−inf 𝗌⌉). Neither depends on b.

*Bounds.* By the first part, the proof of Theorem 19.14 runs at every b ∈ B̄_1 with constants uniform there. So
Proposition 19.29 at the level k + d′, with (19.56) and (19.45), gives u_j ∈ X and

    ‖u_j‖_X ≤ C_k (‖f_j‖_(H^(k+d)_b) + ‖P_j − 2L_(b_j)‖_((0;k+d)) ‖f_j‖_(H^d_b)),

the b-norms with the weights of (19.24), with C_k independent of j: it depends on the operator only through
ε_0 (Section 19.6.1), and on 2L_(b_j) only through the inputs (i)–(v), which are uniform on B̄_1. The right side is
bounded in j, as f_j converges in (19.23) and ‖P_j − 2L_(b_j)‖_((0;k+d)) is bounded by hypothesis. So the u_j
are bounded in the Hilbert space X.

*The limit equation.* Let a subsequence u_(j_m) converge weakly in X to some ũ ∈ X. The inclusion X ⊂ H of
(19.56) is continuous, so u_(j_m) ⇀ ũ in H as well. For φ ∈ C_c^∞(M° ∩ {r > r_0}), the u_j are bounded in L²
on supp φ, and P_j^*φ → P^*φ in L², as the coefficients of P_j converge to those of P in C² on supp φ; so, as in
Section 19.9, ⟨ũ, P^*φ⟩ = lim_m ⟨u_(j_m), P_(j_m)^*φ⟩ = lim_m ⟨f_(j_m), φ⟩ = ⟨f, φ⟩, and Pũ = f on {r > r_0}.

*Identification.* As 𝗌 ≥ inf 𝗌 > s_u := inf 𝗌 − 2,

    ũ ∈ X ⊂ H^(𝗌,(2α_I,α_+,−2))_e3b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) ⊂ H^(s_u,(2α_I,α_+,−2))_e3b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−),

so ũ lies in the class in which Theorem 19.14 asserts uniqueness for P relative to 2L_b, and so does u. That
uniqueness is Lemma 19.18 at s′ = s_u for P relative to 2L_b, and it needs two smallness conditions. The first
is the threshold ε_1 of Lemma 19.16, uniform on B̄_1 by (ii). The second is the smallness of Proposition 17.14 (i)
at s′ = s_u relative to 2L_b, in the norm with the d_0 of that proposition. That d_0 depends only on 𝗌 and s′ (the
statement of Proposition 17.14), here 𝗌 and s_u, which (B4) fixes for every b ∈ B̄_1; it is the index
d^U_0 ≤ D_0 ≤ d, with D_0 the index of (19.46), so that norm is at most C‖P − 2L_b‖_((0;d))
((19.45)); and its smallness threshold is uniform on B̄_1 by (i). Both conditions are among those that fix
ε_0 (Section 19.6.1), so ‖P − 2L_b‖_((0;d)) < ε_0 gives them at the limit parameter b; the hypothesis of
Lemma 15.35 for the metric of P, which Lemma 19.18 also uses, is (29.23) for P, as in (ii).
Both ũ and u solve Pv = f, so ũ = u.

*Convergence.* Every subsequence of (u_j) is bounded in X, so it has a further subsequence converging weakly in X, and
by what was just shown its limit is u. Hence u_j ⇀ u in X, and so in H. By Lemma 19.30 (k ≥ 1), the inclusion of
H in H^(k−1,(α_I−ς,α_+−ς,−2−ς))_b(Ω_*; E)^(•,−) is compact, so u_j → u in norm there (each subsequence has a
norm-convergent subsequence, whose limit is the weak limit u). ∎

[Hin26c, Theorem 11.1] also allows P_0 near an admissible P_1 among all small stationary perturbations. That wider
statement is not proved here and is not used: the later chapters use only the family 2L_b, b ∈ B̄_*.

### 29.11 Forward solutions in the cone near b₀

**Corollary 29.25** (Forward solutions near b₀; [Hin26, Theorem 11.12] in dimension 4 + 1.)
Theorem 29.17 holds for every b ∈ B_* in place of b₀. With g_0 := g_(b₀,b,−S), g := g_0 + h and the forward
solution u of L^(g,g_0)u = f, (29.18)–(29.19) hold with ε_0, d and C_k independent of b. For k ≥ 1,
u depends continuously on (b, S, h) in H^(k−1,(β_I−ς,β_+−ς,−3/2−ς))_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−), for every ς > 0.

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 29.17, with P_0 := 2L_b and Theorem 29.24 in place of Theorem 19.14, so that
ε′_0 is the ε_0 of Theorem 29.24. Its hypothesis (i) is Theorem 29.21. (ii) is unchanged, as S̄ and Ā do not
depend on b. (iii) is Corollary 29.16, which is stated for g_0 = g_(b₀,b,−S) and P_0 = 2L_b and whose hypothesis holds
by Theorem 29.21, with ‖P − 2L_b‖_((0;d)) ≤ C(|b − b₀| + |S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳^(d+5))) by Proposition 29.7,
(29.13), below ε′_0 by (B5). The metric g of P satisfies (29.23), the additional hypothesis of
Theorem 29.24: by (29.17) and (B2), ‖g − g_(b₀)‖_(𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)) < η_♭/2 + C(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳³)),
over Ω_*, which is below η_♭ for |S| and ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) small (d ≥ 3), with C independent of b; no condition on b beyond
b ∈ B̄_1 enters.

*Continuity.* Let k ≥ 1. In the notation of the proof of Theorem 29.17, in which h ∈ 𝒳^(k+d+5), let (b_j, S_j, h_j) →
(b, S, h), with b_j, b ∈ B_*, S_j, S, h_j, h as in the statement and h_j → h in 𝒳^(k+d+5). Put g_(0,j) :=
g_(b₀,b_j,−S_j), g_j := g_(0,j) + h_j, P_j := 2L^(g_j,g_(0,j)) and P := 2L^(g,g_0), and let f_j := f. These satisfy the
hypotheses of the continuity statement of Theorem 29.24. By (iii) above, P_j is admissible relative to 2L_(b_j) of
the class that theorem asks, with ‖P_j − 2L_(b_j)‖_((0;d)) < ε′_0 by (B5) and its metric satisfying
(29.23) as just shown; and ‖P_j − 2L_(b_j)‖_((0;k+d)) is bounded in j
by Proposition 29.7, (29.13), as ‖h_j‖_(𝒳^(k+d+5)) is. The same holds for P relative to 2L_b; in particular
‖P − 2L_b‖_((0;d)) < ε′_0 by (B5), which is the smallness that the identification in the proof of Theorem 29.24
uses at the limit. The coefficients of P_j converge to those of P in C² on compact subsets of M° ∩ {r > r_0}. On such
a set g_(b₀,b,−S) depends smoothly on (b, S), as g_b is smooth in b (Proposition 21.21) and φ_(−S) = exp(V(−S)) is the
time-one flow of a vector field linear in S (Lemma 21.26); its difference from g_b lies in the class of
Lemma 29.11. And 2L^(g,g_0) depends continuously on h in the norm of (29.13) (its coefficients being the
sums of products of the tame form above, Lemma 29.8, Lemma 29.9, and, for the inverse,
(g_1 + δ)⁻¹ − (g_1 + δ′)⁻¹ = −(g_1 + δ)⁻¹(δ − δ′)(g_1 + δ′)⁻¹, bounded in H^j_b by C‖δ − δ′‖_(H^j_b) as at the end
of the proof of Theorem 29.17, here with g_1 := g_b), which controls the coefficients in C² on compact sets by
Sobolev embedding (three derivatives, dim M = 5). So the forward solutions converge in
H^(k−1,(α_I−ς,α_+−ς,−2−ς))_b, with α_I = β_I − 2 and α_+ = β_+ − 5/2, which with the density μ_b is
H^(k−1,(β_I−ς,β_+−ς,−3/2−ς))_b (Corollary 19.15). ∎

[Hin26, Theorem 11.12] states continuity in (b₀, b, S, h); here b₀ is fixed.

### 29.12 Null infinity: the setting and the structure

This section and the next two are [Hin26, Section 11.2] in dimension 4 + 1: the partial polyhomogeneity at ℐ⁺ of
solutions of L^(g,g_0)u = f without loss at ι⁺ ([Hin26, Proposition 11.14 and Lemma 11.15]), and formal solutions of
L_b u = f at ℐ⁺ ([Hin26, Proposition 11.16]). The leading part of the operator at ℐ⁺ is (X_+ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − Ā),
with the constant lower-triangular Ā, for the dynamical operator as for L_b (Proposition 29.6); the terms A^h, B^h
of [Hin26] and its h-dependent coupling (A^h)_(7,6) of the radiation field into the 11-component are half an order
lower and enter only through the error.

On the region U_I := [0, c_I]_(ρ_I) × [0, 1]_(ρ_+) × 𝕊³, with the coordinates (29.7) (so that
{ρ_+ = 1} = {t_* = 0}) and c_I ∈ (0, 1] small, weights are listed at (ℐ⁺, ι⁺) and none at K⁺, as in [Hin26].
L := L^(g,g_0) with g_0 := g_(b₀,b,−S), g := g_0 + h and h ∈ 𝒳^∞ small ((29.4), Proposition 29.7). All
functions below vanish for t_* ≤ 1, so the region {0 ≤ t_* ≤ 1}, where h is extended arbitrarily, plays no role.
Components are taken in the splitting (27.6), slots 1, …, 7. Section 25.1 takes
(1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C > 100. Put

    ℓ_I^max := 3/2 + (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C   (> 100),    (29.24)

the least indicial root of the π_C-slots. The weights at ℐ⁺ below reach min(a_I + ½, ℓ_I^max): a_I + ½ is the bound of
the products with the coefficients of the error, whose remainder has the weight a_I − 1, against the least exponent 3/2
of u ([Hin26] has ℓ_I ≤ 3 + ε_I, the same bound in dimension 3 + 1 with the least exponent 1); and ℓ_I^max keeps ℓ_I
below the roots of the π_C-slots, which [Hin26] states as 3 + ε_I < 1 + (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C.

**Lemma 29.26** (The structure; [Hin26, (11.26) and (11.34)] in dimension 4 + 1.) On U_I,

    ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²L = L_0 + L̃,        L_0 := (X_+ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − Ā),
    L̃ ∈ (ρ_I C^∞ + H^(∞,(ℰ_I^tot−1,a_I−1),(ℰ_+,a_+))_b) Diff²_b,    (29.25)

and for L_b the same holds with L̃ ∈ ρ_I Diff²_b (smooth coefficients). X_+ − X_I and X_I − 3/2 − Ā commute.

*Proof.* Divide (29.10) by ρ_Iρ_+², and for L_b use Lemma 29.5 with the change of frame of
Lemma 27.4. Ā is constant, and X_+, X_I commute. ∎

[Hin26] has L_0 = −(ρ_I∂_(ρ_I) − (I + A^h))(ρ_I∂_(ρ_I) − ρ_+∂_(ρ_+)) + ρ_+⁻¹B^h, with
L̃ ∈ (ρ_I C^∞ + H^(k−2,(ℰ_I^C−1,2+ε_I),(ℰ_+,3+ε_+))_b) Diff²_b, which gains min Re(ℰ_I^C − 1) > 2γ_Υ; here L̃ gains ½
(as min Re ℰ_I^tot = 3/2), and L_0 has constant coefficients.

*Integration tools.* We use Lemma 21.33 ([Hin26, Lemma 2.12]: the equation (x∂_x − z)u = f adds (z, 0) to the
index set when Re z ≤ α, for a weight α ≠ Re z), Lemma 21.41 ([Hin26, Lemma 2.22]) and Lemma 21.42
([Hin26, Lemma 2.23]: the equation (x∂_x − y∂_y + z)u = f, with α + Re z > β and an a priori bound near y = 1). Here
(x, y) = (ρ_I, ρ_+) when integrating forward from {ρ_+ = 1}, where u = 0, and (x, y) = (ρ_+, ρ_I) when integrating
backward from {ρ_I = c_I}. Slot j of L_0u is

    (L_0u)_j = (X_+ − X_I)((X_I − 3/2 − Ā_jj)u_j − Σ_(i<j) Ā_ji u_i),    (29.26)

the couplings being at (3, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3), (5, 2), (7, 3) and (7, 4) (Lemma 27.12).

### 29.13 Partial polyhomogeneity at null infinity

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 11.14 and Lemma 11.15] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Proposition 29.27** (Partial polyhomogeneity at ℐ⁺; [Hin26, Proposition 11.14] in dimension 4 + 1.)
Let ℰ_I^C and ℰ_+ be as in Definition 29.1. Let 3/2 < ℓ_I < min(a_I + ½, ℓ_I^max),
ℓ_+ < min(ℓ_I, a_+ + min Re ℰ_+), ℓ_+ ∉ Re π_1ℰ_+ ∪ Re π_1ℰ_I^tot and ℓ_I ∉ 3/2 + σ_Υ. Suppose that u and f vanish for
t_* ≤ 1, and

    Lu = f ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),(ℰ_++2,ℓ_++2))_b,      u ∈ H^(∞,α_I,(ℰ_+,ℓ_+))_b    (29.27)

for some α_I ∈ ℝ. Then u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+))_b.

[Hin26] asks ℓ_+ < ℓ_I ≤ 3 + ε_I, its 3 + ε_I being the product bound in dimension 3 + 1. Its exceptional roots
1 + σ_Υ (at most 1 + 2γ_Υ) can equal a small ℓ_I, which its statement does not exclude, and its roots 1 + σ_C of the
π_C-slots lie far above. The exclusions ℓ_I ∉ 3/2 + σ_Υ and ℓ_+ ∉ Re π_1ℰ_I^tot come from the conditions α ≠ Re z of
Lemma 21.33 and of Lemma 21.42.

**Lemma 29.28** (The expansion at ℐ⁺ away from ι⁺; [Hin26, Lemma 11.15] in dimension 4 + 1.) Under the
assumptions of Proposition 29.27, u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),α_+)_b for every
α_+ < min(α_I, 3/2, ℓ_+, min Re ℰ_+).

*Proof.* Reducing α_I if necessary, we may assume α_I < 3/2 and

    u ∈ H^(∞,α_I,α_+)_b.    (29.28)

*Step 1: the weight below 3/2.* Fix η ∈ (0, ½) with α_I + η < 3/2. By (29.25) and Lemma 27.5 (the
ℐ⁺-index set of the coefficient has min Re = ½ > η; at ι⁺, min Re ℰ_+ > 0), L̃u ∈ H^(∞,α_I+η,α_+)_b; and
ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²f ∈ H^(∞,α_I+η,α_+)_b, as its ℐ⁺-index sets ℰ_I^C and ℱ_(I,11) − 1 have min Re > 3/2 and its data at ι⁺
are (ℰ_+, ℓ_+) with α_+ < min(ℓ_+, min Re ℰ_+). So L_0u ∈ H^(∞,α_I+η,α_+)_b. In slot 1, by (29.26),
(X_I − 3/2 − s)w = (L_0u)_1 for w := (X_+ − X_I)u_1 and the eigenvalue s of the slot. Lemma 21.33 in ρ_I (with
3/2 + s > α_I + η, so that no term is added; the a priori hypothesis, on ρ_I near c_I, away from ℐ⁺, holds by
(29.28)) gives w ∈ H^(∞,α_I+η,α_+)_b. Then (X_I − X_+)u_1 = −w with u_1 = 0 near {ρ_+ = 1}, and
Lemma 21.42 with (x, y) = (ρ_I, ρ_+), z = 0, E = F = ∅ and α = α_I + η > β = α_+ gives
u_1 ∈ H^(∞,α_I+η,α_+)_b. In slot j > 1 the couplings (X_+ − X_I)Ā_ji u_i, i < j, already improved, go to the right,
and the same two steps apply, as every eigenvalue s satisfies 3/2 + s ≥ 3/2 > α_I + η. So (29.28) holds with
α_I + η in place of α_I, and iterating,

    u ∈ ⋂_(α_I<3/2) H^(∞,α_I,α_+)_b.    (29.29)

*Step 2: the first expansion term.* Let 0 < η < min((1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, ½), the least nonzero element of σ_Υ being
(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ (as 0 < e_Υ < 1). By (29.29) and (29.25), L̃u and ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²f lie in
H^(∞,3/2+η,α_+)_b. In the slots 1–5 and 7, whose eigenvalues exceed η, the two steps of Step 1 give membership at
3/2 + η (slot 7 by the couplings (7, 3) and (7, 4) from slots already improved; Ā_76 = 0). In slot 6 (π̸₀, eigenvalue
0), Lemma 21.33 adds (3/2, 0): (X_+ − X_I)π̸₀u ∈ H^(∞,((3/2,0),3/2+η),α_+)_b, and Lemma 21.42
(E = {(3/2, 0)}, α = 3/2 + η > α_+, 3/2 ≠ α_+) gives π̸₀u ∈ H^(∞,((3/2,0),3/2+η),α_+)_b, the terms it adds at ι⁺
lying above the weight α_+ < 3/2. So

    u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,α_I),α_+)_b        for every α_I < 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ,    (29.30)

with π̸₀u carrying (3/2, 0) and no other slot carrying an expansion term below the weight. In dimension 3 + 1, u_11
acquires (1, 0) here, from (A^h)_(7,6) acting on π̸₀u ([Hin26, (11.29)]); in dimension 4 + 1 that coupling is part of
L̃, and acting on (3/2, 0) it gives ℐ⁺-order ≥ 2 > 3/2 + η.

*Step 3: the full expansion.* Suppose (29.30) holds for some α_I, and let 0 < η < ½. Every slot of u has its
ℐ⁺-index set in ℰ_I^tot (Lemma 27.7 (c)), so by (29.25) and Lemma 27.5, with
(ℰ_I^tot − 1) + ℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C (Definition 27.6 (3)) and ℰ_I^tot + 1 ⊂ ℰ_I^C (Lemma 27.7 (a)),
L̃u ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_I^C,α′),α_+)_b with α′ := min(ℓ_I, α_I + η). The three inequalities of Lemma 27.5 hold:
α′ < α_I + ½; α′ ≤ α_I + a_I − 1, as a_I > 3/2; and α′ < (a_I − 1) + 3/2 = a_I + ½, the remainder of the coefficient at
the weight a_I − 1, which has no expansion, against the least exponent 3/2 of u. This last is where the hypothesis
ℓ_I < a_I + ½ enters. The term ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²f has the ℐ⁺-index sets ℰ_I^C (slots 1–6) and
ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0) (slot 7) at the weight ℓ_I. Here α′ is chosen off 3/2 + σ_Υ, by decreasing η (ℓ_I is
off it by hypothesis).

Slots 1–3: the eigenvalues s ∈ σ_C satisfy 3/2 + s ≥ ℓ_I^max > ℓ_I ≥ α′, so Lemma 21.33 adds nothing, and
(X_+ − X_I)u_j ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_I^C,α′),α_+)_b; Lemma 21.42 (E = ℰ_I^C, α′ > α_+, and α_+ ∉ Re π_1ℰ_I^C as α_+ < 3/2)
gives u_j ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_I^C,α′),α_+)_b, the index set it adds at ι⁺ lying above the weight α_+.

Slots 4, 5, 6: with the couplings (4, 1), (4, 3), (5, 2) from the slots 1–3 on the right, the eigenvalue
s ∈ {(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ, 0} adds (3/2 + s, 0), so u_01, π_(1/)u and π̸₀u lie in the classes of ℰ_(I,01), ℰ_(I,1/) and
ℰ̸_(I,0) at the weight α′.

Slot 7: the couplings (7, 3) (index set ℰ_I^C) and (7, 4) (index set ℰ_(I,01)), the term (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0) of
f, and, through L̃, the h-dependent couplings, which land in ℰ_I^C (above); with the eigenvalue 2γ_Υ,
Lemma 21.33 gives ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0) ∪ (3/2 + 2γ_Υ, 0) = ℰ_(I,11), as (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ ≠ 2γ_Υ.

So (29.30) holds with α′ in place of α_I, in the class of Definition 29.1 (1), and finitely many steps
reach ℓ_I. ∎

*Proof of Proposition 29.27.* *Step 1: the data at ι⁺, at a weaker ℐ⁺-weight.* Suppose that
u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,α_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+))_b for some α_I < ℓ_+ (or u ∈ H^(∞,α_I,(ℰ_+,ℓ_+))_b when α_I < 3/2; this holds for
the given α_I). By (29.25), L̃u has the ℐ⁺-weight α_I + η for η < ½, with some index set, and the data
(ℰ_+, ℓ_+) at ι⁺ (ℰ_+ + ℰ_+ ⊂ ℰ_+; the remainder of the product needs ℓ_+ < a_+ + min Re ℰ_+, the remainder of the
coefficient at the weight a_+ against the least exponent of u). Integrate L_0u = ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²f − L̃u slot by slot as in
Lemma 29.28, except that the hyperbolic field is integrated backward from {ρ_I = c_I}: Lemma 21.42 with
(x, y) = (ρ_+, ρ_I), the a priori bound near {ρ_I = c_I} being the hypothesis u ∈ H^(∞,·,(ℰ_+,ℓ_+)) there (away from
ℐ⁺), needs ℓ_+ > α_I + η (α + Re z > β) and α_I + η ∉ Re π_1ℰ_+; and in the slot-by-slot step Lemma 21.33 in
ρ_I needs α_I + η off 3/2 + spec Ā. Decrease η to ensure all three. This gives the data (ℰ_+, ℓ_+) at ι⁺, and ℐ⁺-index
sets that are extended unions with ℰ_+; but by Lemma 29.28 the ℐ⁺-expansion of u, which is determined by u away
from ι⁺, has exponents only in ⟨ℰ_I^C⟩ up to the weight ℓ_I, so the coefficients of all other terms vanish. Hence the
hypothesis holds with α_I + η, and finitely many steps give it for every α_I < ℓ_+.

*Step 2: both.* Integrate forward as in Lemma 29.28, from α_I < ℓ_+ close to ℓ_+ up to ℓ_I, keeping the data
(ℰ_+, ℓ_+) at ι⁺. In Lemma 21.42 with (x, y) = (ρ_I, ρ_+), the ℐ⁺-weight α_I + η of the right side exceeds ℓ_+
(α + Re z > β with β = ℓ_+), and ℓ_+ ∉ Re π_1 of the ℐ⁺-index sets, which lie in ℰ_I^tot (a hypothesis; these sets do
not depend on the weight); also ℓ_+ < ℓ_I and ℓ_+ ∉ Re π_1ℰ_+. The index sets at ι⁺ that it produces are extended
unions of ℰ_+ with ℐ⁺-index sets of components of u, but u has the index set ℰ_+ at ι⁺ by Step 1, so no other
exponent occurs. After finitely many steps, u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+))_b. ∎

### 29.14 Formal solutions at null infinity

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 11.16] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Proposition 29.29** (Formal solutions at ℐ⁺; [Hin26, Proposition 11.16] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ℰ_I^C
be as in Definition 29.1 and Ĕ_+ ⊂ ℂ × ℕ₀ an index set. Let ℓ̆_+ < ℓ_I < ℓ_I^max with ℓ_I > 3/2,
ℓ̆_+, ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ_I^C and ℓ̆_+, ℓ_I ≠ 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ. Let
f ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),(Ĕ_++2,ℓ̆_++2))_b vanish for t_* < 1. Then there are an index set ℰ^♯_+, depending only
on ℰ_I^C and Ĕ_+, and u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ^♯_+,ℓ̆_+))_b vanishing on {t_* < 1} ∪ {ρ_I > ½c_I}, with

    f − L_b u ∈ H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,(ℰ^♯_++2,ℓ̆_++2))_b(Ω_*; S²T*).    (29.31)

One can take ℰ^♯_+ = ⋃_(j≥1) ℰ^(♯,(j))_+, with

    ℰ^(♯,(1))_+ := Ĕ_+ ∪̄ {(3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0)},
    ℰ^(♯,(j+1))_+ := ℰ^(♯,(j))_+ ∪̄^(k(ℰ_I^C,z)+1) {(z, 0)}
                     for each z ∈ π_1ℰ_I^C with m_j ≤ Re z < m_j + 1,    (29.32)

m_j := min Re ℰ_I^C + j − 1 (only Re z ≤ ℓ_I matters), where k(ℰ_I^C, z) is the largest logarithmic order of ℰ_I^C
at z, and E ∪̄^m {(z, 0)} is the extended union of Lemma 21.33 taken m times: E ∪ {(z, m − 1)} if z ∉ π_1E, and
E with its logarithmic order at z raised by m otherwise. (The rounds of the proof take the windows [μ_j, μ_j + 1), with
μ_j ≥ m_j the least real part left; the union ℰ^♯_+ is the same.) If all the terms ρ_I^(z+1)(log ρ_I)^k of the
ℐ⁺-expansion of f vanish for Re z ≤ C_0, these z may be omitted from (29.32).

[Hin26, (11.33a)] has ℰ^(♯,(1))_+ = Ĕ_+ ∪ {(1, 0)} ∪ {(1 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0)} and windows j < Re z ≤ j + 1. The (1, 0)
comes from the radiation coupling of its Step 1, which dimension 4 + 1 does not have. Its windows rely on
min Re ℰ_I^C ∈ (1, 2) in dimension 3 + 1; (29.32) takes them from min Re ℰ_I^C upward in steps of 1, which is
what the induction uses. And [Hin26, (11.33a)–(11.33b)] write ∪ where Lemma 21.33 returns the extended union
E ∪̄ {(z, 0)}; the plain union understates the logarithmic orders at ι⁺ when Ĕ_+ meets 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ or π_1ℰ_I^C,
and the existence of ℰ^♯_+ is not affected.

*Proof.* By Lemma 29.26, ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²L_b = L_0 + L̃ with L̃ ∈ ρ_I Diff²_b. Let χ = χ(ρ_I) ∈ C^∞_c([0, ½c_I))
equal 1 near 0. By Definition 29.1 (2) ((27.17)), write

    f = χρ_I^(5/2+(1−e_Υ)γ_Υ) f^♭_11 (dx¹)² + f̃,      f^♭_11 ∈ H^(∞,(Ĕ_++2,ℓ̆_++2))_b(Ω_* ∩ ℐ⁺),
                                                     f̃ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_I^C+1,ℓ_I+1),(Ĕ_++2,ℓ̆_++2))_b,

the exceptional term of the 11-component: ℱ_(I,11) = 1 + (ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0)), and
z_1 := 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ < 3/2 + 2γ_Υ < min Re ℰ_I^C by Definition 27.6 (2), so the splitting is clean.

*Step 1: the exceptional term.* Try v := χρ_I^(z_1)u^♭(dx¹)² with u^♭ = u^♭(ρ_+, ω). On slot 7, the last,
X_I − 3/2 − Ā acts by z_1 − 3/2 − 2γ_Υ = −(1 + e_Υ)γ_Υ ≠ 0 (there is no slot below it), and
(X_+ − X_I)ρ_I^(z_1) = ρ_I^(z_1)(X_+ − z_1). So, where χ = 1,
L_0v = −(1 + e_Υ)γ_Υ ρ_I^(z_1)((X_+ − z_1)u^♭)(dx¹)², and the corresponding term of ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²f is
ρ_I^(z_1)ρ_+⁻²f^♭_11(dx¹)². Solve, on ℐ⁺,

    (X_+ − z_1)u^♭ = −((1 + e_Υ)γ_Υ)⁻¹ρ_+⁻²f^♭_11,        u^♭ = 0 near {ρ_+ = 1}.

Lemma 21.33 in ρ_+ (ℓ̆_+ ≠ z_1; the right side vanishes for t_* < 1, so the solution vanishing at ρ_+ = 1 does
too) gives u^♭ ∈ H^(∞,(Ĕ_+∪̄{(z_1,0)},ℓ̆_+))_b(Ω_* ∩ ℐ⁺). Then f − L_b v has no term ρ_I^(z_1+1) in slot 7: the
remainder from L̃ is ρ_I^(z_1+2) times H^∞-functions with the index set ℰ^(♯,(1))_+ + 2 at ι⁺, and
z_1 + 2 ∈ ℰ_I^tot + 2 ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1 (Lemma 27.7 (c)); the derivatives of χ are supported away from ℐ⁺. So f is
reduced to

    f ∈ H^(∞,(F_I+1,ℓ_I+1),(F_++2,ℓ̆_++2))_b,      F_I = ℰ_I^C,      F_+ = ℰ^(♯,(1))_+.    (29.33)

*Step 2: the remaining terms.* Given (29.33), let z ∈ π_1F_I with Re z < min Re F_I + 1 and Re z ≤ ℓ_I, let
k := k(F_I, z), and let χρ_I^(z+1)(log ρ_I)^k f^((z+1,k)) be the corresponding term of f, with
f^((z+1,k)) ∈ H^(∞,(F_++2,ℓ̆_++2))_b(Ω_* ∩ ℐ⁺; S²T*). As Re z > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ (Definition 27.6 (2)) and
Re z ≤ ℓ_I < ℓ_I^max, z ∉ 3/2 + spec Ā, so z − 3/2 − Ā is invertible. Let u^((z,k)) solve

    (z − 3/2 − Ā)(X_+ − z)u^((z,k)) = ρ_+⁻²f^((z+1,k)),        u^((z,k)) = 0 for t_* ≤ 1;

by Lemma 21.33 (ℓ̆_+ ≠ Re z), u^((z,k)) ∈ H^(∞,(F_+∪̄{(z,0)},ℓ̆_+))_b(Ω_* ∩ ℐ⁺). By (21.51) in ρ_I,

    L_0(ρ_I^z(log ρ_I)^k u^((z,k)))
        = ρ_I^z(log ρ_I)^k ρ_+⁻²f^((z+1,k)) + ρ_I^z Σ_(k′<k) (log ρ_I)^(k′) ρ_+⁻²f′^((z+1,k′)),

with explicit f′^((z+1,k′)) ∈ H^(∞,((F_+∪̄{(z,0)})+2,ℓ̆_++2))_b; and L̃ applied to it gives terms
ρ_I^(z+1+j)(log ρ_I)^(k″), j ≥ 1, k″ ≤ k, which lie in F_I + 1 at ℐ⁺ beyond the current window (z + j ∈ ℰ_I^C, as
ℰ_I^C + 1 ⊂ ℰ_I^C by Lemma 27.7 (a); L̃ has smooth coefficients, so the shifts are integers). Replacing f by
f − L_b(χρ_I^z(log ρ_I)^k u^((z,k))) replaces (F_I, F_+) by (F_I ∖ {(z, k)}, F_+ ∪̄ {(z, 0)}); repeating for
(z, k − 1), …, (z, 0) gives (F_I ∖ {(z, j)}_(j≤k), F_+ ∪̄^(k+1) {(z, 0)}), the logarithmic order at z rising by one at
each repetition through the extended union. Doing this for every such z (finitely many, by the construction of
Lemma 27.7 (e)) replaces F_I by {(z, k) ∈ F_I : Re z ≥ min Re F_I + 1} and F_+ by the next set of
(29.32). Finitely many rounds exhaust the terms with Re z ≤ ℓ_I, and the remainder has the ℐ⁺-weight ℓ_I + 1
with no expansion, which is (29.31). The terms of u vanish on {ρ_I > ½c_I} by the cut-off and on {t_* < 1}
by construction, and lie in the class of Definition 29.1 (1): their ℐ⁺-exponents are those of ℰ_I^C, and z_1 in
slot 7, with (z_1, 0) ∈ ℰ_(I,11). If the terms of f vanish for Re z ≤ C_0, the corresponding u^((z,k)) are 0. ∎

By (29.32), min Re ℰ^♯_+ = min(min Re Ĕ_+, 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ), since min Re ℰ_I^C > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ: when Ĕ_+
does not go lower, the index set at ι⁺ of the formal solution starts at 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ.

### 29.15 Almost linear bounds: the setting

This section and Section 29.16–Section 29.19 are [Hin26, Section 11.3] in dimension 4 + 1: the improvement of the
forward solutions of L^(g,g_0)u = f at ι⁺ and K⁺ for right sides with more decay there ([Hin26, Proposition 11.17]),
with the two integration lemmas it rests on ([Hin26, Lemmas 11.18 and 11.19]). The scheme is that of [Hin26]. The
forward solution of Theorem 29.17 is improved by rewriting L_b u = f − (L^(g,g_0) − L_b)u, solving away the terms
at null infinity (Proposition 29.29), splitting L_b⁻¹ by the Fourier transform in t_* into high, regular low and
singular low frequencies, integrating the singular part twice in t_*, and recovering the expansion at null infinity
(Proposition 29.27). The bookkeeping window of the iteration is (0, 1), the window of (28.1) inside the
indicial gap of L̂_b(0) (Proposition 25.6 (a)), where [Hin26] has (0, ε_ind). As in Theorem 29.17, everything in
these sections is at b = b₀; base points b near b₀ are treated in Proposition 30.5.

*The manifold.* X = {r ≥ r_0} as in Section 28.1, and M′ := [ℝ̄_(t_*) × X̄; {±∞} × ∂X̄], the manifold M of
Section 20.8.1 over X̄ (Remark 20.22; Section 21.12 in dimension 4 + 1). Its faces are I (the lift of
ℝ̄ × ∂X̄; its part in t_* > 0 is ℐ⁺), ι = ι⁺ ∪ ι⁻ (the front faces) and K = K⁺ ∪ K⁻ (the lifts of {±∞} × X̄), and it
has the artificial boundary {r = r_0}, at which all spaces are extendible. H^(k,β_I,β_ι,β_K)_b(M′), with index sets
where written, are the spaces of Section 21.12 for the b-density |dt_*/⟨t_*⟩| μ_b, μ_b = |dx|/⟨x⟩⁴; on Ω_* they are
the spaces of Section 29.1 (the last paragraph of Corollary 20.27). Put Ω_− := cl_(M′){t_* ≤ 1} and, for C > 0,
Ω_< := cl_(M′){t_* ≤ −Cr}, with H̄ for restrictions. X^±_(sc-b) and its spaces, with the faces scf, tf, zf and the
weights listed in that order, are those of Section 20.8.1 ((20.18)).

*Coordinates.* With r = |x|:

(a) near I ∩ ι⁺, on {t_* > 0}: ρ_I := t_*/r and ρ_+ := 1/t_* ([Hin26, (3.4e)]), and
t_*∂_(t_*) = ρ_I∂_(ρ_I) − ρ_+∂_(ρ_+);

(b) near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺: ρ_+ := 1/r and ρ_K := r/t_* ([Hin26, (3.4g)]), and near all of K⁺, ρ_K := ⟨x⟩/t_* with x ∈ X̄; in
both, t_*∂_(t_*) = −ρ_K∂_(ρ_K) at fixed x;

(c) near I ∩ ι⁻, on {t_* < 2}: ρ_0 := (2 − t_*)⁻¹ and ρ_I := (2 − t_*)/r, and
(2 − t_*)∂_(t_*) = ρ_0∂_(ρ_0) − ρ_I∂_(ρ_I).

Indeed, in (a), t_*∂_(t_*)ρ_I = ρ_I and t_*∂_(t_*)ρ_+ = −ρ_+; in (c), ∂_(t_*)ρ_0 = ρ_0² and ∂_(t_*)ρ_I = −1/r. The
chart [Hin26, (3.4c)] uses t_* + 2, whose field −(t_* + 2)∂_(t_*) vanishes at t_* = −2; (c) covers {t_* < 2} in one
chart. In all three, ∂_(t_*) ∈ ρ_ιρ_K 𝒱_b(M′) (ρ_ι, ρ_K defining functions of ι, K), so ∂_(t_*) raises the ι- and
K-weights by 1 and keeps the I-weight.

*The operator.* L_b := L_(b₀); g_0 := g_(b₀,b₀,−S), g := g_0 + h and L := L^(g,g_0), with |S| < ε_0, h ∈ 𝒳^∞
((29.4)) and ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) < ε_0, where ε_0 and d are those of Theorem 29.17. L̂_b(σ) is invertible for real
σ ≠ 0 (Corollary 28.13), and so is the augmented operator L̃_b(σ) of Definition 28.7 for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_k
(Corollary 28.11). ℓ_I^max is (29.24), and σ_Υ is the set of Section 27.3.

*The gap.* By Proposition 25.6 (a) no indicial root of L̂_b(0) has real part in (0, 1], so (0, 1) lies in its
indicial gap for μ_b; (28.1) takes its weight α with α + 2 ∈ (0, 1), and so do these sections.

### 29.16 Integration of ∂_(t_*)

**Lemma 29.30** (Integration of ∂_(t_*); [Hin26, Lemma 11.18] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let k ∈ ℕ₀,
β_I, β_ι, β_K ∈ ℝ with β_K ≠ 0, ℰ_K an index set, and C > 0.

(1) (*From t_* = 1.*) If u|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(k,β_I,β_ι,(ℰ_K,β_K))_b(Ω_−) and
∂_(t_*)u ∈ H^(k,β_I,β_ι+1,(ℰ_K+1,β_K+1))_b(M′), then for every ε > 0

    u ∈ H^(k,β_I,min(β_ι,β_I−ε),(ℰ_K∪̄{(0,0)},β_K))_b(M′).    (29.34)

(2) (*From t_* = −Cr.*) If u|_(Ω_<) ∈ H̄^(k,∞,β_ι,β_K)_b(Ω_<) and
(∂_(t_*)u)|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(k,β_I,β_ι+1,β_K+1)_b(Ω_−), then for every ε > 0

    u|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(k,min(β_I,β_ι−ε),β_ι,β_K)_b(Ω_−),    (29.35)

and likewise with (ℰ_K, β_K) and (ℰ_K + 1, β_K + 1) in place of β_K and β_K + 1.

As Ω_< ∩ I = ∅, the first weight on Ω_< is immaterial; the K⁻-weight in (29.35) is the a priori one, and the
content of (29.35) is the I-weight.

*Proof.* (1) *Near I ∩ ι⁺.* In the chart (a), with x := ρ_I/C′ and y := ρ_+/2 for a large C′, so that
{y ≥ ½} = {t_* ≤ 1} and {x < 2} covers {t_* < 2C′r}, the hypotheses read (x∂_x − y∂_y)u = t_*∂_(t_*)u ∈
H^(k,β_I,β_ι)_b (as t_* = ρ_+⁻¹ is a defining function of ι⁺ to the power −1 there) and u ∈ H^(k,β_I)_b on
{y ≥ ½}. Lemma 21.42 with z = 0, E = F = ∅, α := β_I and the target weight β := β′_ι := min(β_ι, β_I − ε) (so
that α > β and the right side lies in H^(k,α,β)_b) gives u ∈ H^(k,β_I,β′_ι)_b there. (The flow of x∂_x − y∂_y
preserves xy and increases x as y decreases, so the value at a point depends on the data at smaller x only; the end
x = 2 plays no role. Where the square [0, 2)² of the chart meets {r < r_0}, u is first extended across {r = r_0} by
the Seeley extension of Remark 20.22, which acts in the spatial variable and commutes with ∂_(t_*); the
characteristics being the sets {r = const}, nothing propagates across {r = r_0}.) This holds on every set
{t_* ≤ C′r}, that is, off any neighbourhood of K⁺.

*Near K⁺.* In the chart (b) with ρ_K = ⟨x⟩/t_* and x ∈ X̄, ρ_K∂_(ρ_K)u = −t_*∂_(t_*)u ∈ H^(k,(ℰ_K,β_K),β_ι)_b
(t_* = ⟨x⟩ρ_K⁻¹), and on {ρ_K ≥ ½}, a set of the previous kind, u has the ι⁺-weight β′_ι ≤ β_ι. Lemma 21.33 with
z = 0 (β_K ≠ 0) and H := X̄ (the ι⁺-face ∂X̄ carrying the weight β′_ι; its solution operators act in ρ_K alone and
commute with the extension at {r = r_0}) gives u ∈ H^(k,(ℰ_K∪̄{(0,0)},β_K),β′_ι)_b near K⁺. Away from I ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺ in
t_* ≥ 1 the set is compact, and u(t_*) = u(1) + ∫_1^(t_*) ∂_(t_*)u gives H^k there. With the hypothesis on Ω_− this is
(29.34).

(2) Ω_− ∖ Ω_< is covered by the chart (c) on {r ≥ R}, where ρ_I ≤ C + 2/R, and by the compact set
{r ≤ R, −CR ≤ t_* ≤ 1}, on which u(t_*) = u(−CR) + ∫_(−CR)^(t_*) ∂_(t_*)u gives the claim. In the chart (c), with
x := ρ_0 and y := ρ_I/C″, C″ > 2C, we have {y ≥ ½} ∩ {r ≥ R} ⊂ Ω_< for R large, and
(x∂_x − y∂_y)u = (2 − t_*)∂_(t_*)u ∈ H^(k,β_ι,β_I)_b (2 − t_* = ρ_0⁻¹ is a defining function of ι⁻ to the power −1).
Lemma 21.42 with z = 0, E = F = ∅, α := β_ι and the target weight min(β_I, β_ι − ε) < α at y = 0 gives
(29.35) near I. It is applied to ψ(r)u, ψ = 1 on [R, ∞) and ψ = 0 on [0, R/2], so that the square of the
chart meets only {r ≥ R/2}; ψ(r) commutes with ∂_(t_*) and changes nothing on {r ≥ R}. The K⁻-weight: near K⁻, Ω_−
lies in Ω_< for every constant. Index sets at K pass through unchanged. ∎

### 29.17 Integration with a moment condition

**Lemma 29.31** (Integration with a moment condition; [Hin26, Lemma 11.19] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
Ω_< := cl_(M′){t_* < −r} and β_I, β_ι, β_K ∈ ℝ with β_ι > β_I, β_K ≤ β_ι − β_I and β_K ∈ (−1, 1) ∖ {0}. Suppose
u|_(Ω_<) ∈ H̄^(k,∞,β_ι,β_K)_b(Ω_<), ℱu is supported in [−c_0, c_0] × X for some c_0 < ½, and

    ℱ(∂_(t_*)u)|_(±(0,1]) ∈ H^(k+ℓ,(β_I,β_ι,((0,0),β_K)))_b(X^±_(sc-b)),    (29.36)

with ℓ a k-independent integer depending on the weights, the restrictions to zf of the two signs agreeing when β_K > 0.
Then u ∈ H^(k,β_I,β_ι−ε,((0,0),β_K))_b(M′) for every ε > 0.

[Hin26] states β_K < 1, β_K ≠ 0. The condition β_K > −1 is needed for the application of Proposition 20.20 (1) below,
whose K-weight β_K + 1 must lie in (0, ∞) ∖ ℕ; it is implicit in [Hin26]. By Proposition 20.20 (1) alone,
(29.36) gives ∂_(t_*)u the I-weight β_I − ε, and Lemma 29.30 would then give u the ι-weight β_I − 2ε
only; the moment condition (29.39) below is what gives β_ι − ε. [Hin26] asks ℱu to be supported in
[−1, 1] × X. Its proof treats f_2 by Proposition 20.20 (1), whose cut-off is 1 only near [−½, ½], and f_1 by
Definition 20.13, which asks regularity across σ = ±1, where ℱf may jump. Support in [−c_0, c_0], c_0 < ½, meets
both, and the application in Section 29.19 has it.

*Proof.* Let χ = χ(t_*/r) equal 0 on (−∞, −3] and 1 on [−2, ∞), and f := ∂_(t_*)u. As ∂_(t_*)χ = r⁻¹χ′(t_*/r) is
supported in {−3r ≤ t_* ≤ −2r} ⊂ Ω_<, away from I and K,

    ∂_(t_*)(χu) = f′ + χf,        f′ := (∂_(t_*)χ)u ∈ H^(k,∞,β_ι+1,∞)_b(M′).    (29.37)

Let χ_scf ∈ C^∞_c([0, 2)) equal 1 on [0, 1], regarded as χ_scf(ρ/|σ|) on X^±_(sc-b), ρ = ⟨x⟩⁻¹ (1 near scf, 0 near
zf), and f_1 := ℱ⁻¹(χ_scf ℱf), f_2 := ℱ⁻¹((1 − χ_scf)ℱf). Since (1 − χ_scf)ℱf ∈
H^(k+ℓ,(∞,β_ι,((0,0),β_K)))_b (it vanishes near scf), Proposition 20.20 (1) (with the K-weight
β_K + 1 ∈ (0, 2) ∖ {1}; for ℓ large) gives

    f_2,  χf_2 ∈ H^(k,β_ι+1−ε,β_ι+1,β_K+1)_b(M′),    (29.38)

χ being bounded and conormal on M′. As χu = 0 for t_* ≤ −3r, χu = F′ + F_1 + F_2 with F′ := ∫_(−∞)^(t_*) f′ and
F_j := ∫_(−∞)^(t_*) χf_j.

*F′ and F_2.* F′ vanishes for t_* ≤ −3r. By Lemma 29.30 (2) with C = 3 and (29.37),
F′|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(k,β_ι−ε,β_ι,∞)_b, and Lemma 29.30 (1) (with a large nonzero K-weight) gives
F′ ∈ H^(k,β_ι−ε,β_ι−2ε,(0,0))_b(M′). Likewise, by (29.38), F_2|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(k,β_ι−ε,β_ι,∞)_b and
F_2 ∈ H^(k,β_ι−ε,β_ι−2ε,((0,0),β_K))_b(M′) (β_K ≠ 0).

*F_1.* As χ_scf vanishes near zf, ℱf_1 = χ_scf ℱf ∈ H^(k+ℓ,(β_I,β_ι,∞))_b. On its support, near tf ∩ scf,
ρ_scf = ρ/|σ| and ρ_tf = |σ| (the proof of Lemma 21.44), and near scf° ρ_scf ∼ ρ. Let γ := β_ι − β_I if this is
not an integer, and γ := β_ι − β_I − ε′ with 0 < ε′ < min(ε, 1 − β_K) if it is (then it is at least 1); so γ ∉ ℕ,
γ ≥ β_ι − β_I − ε and γ ≥ β_K. Then

    ℱf_1 = ρ^(β_I)|σ|^γ w,        w ∈ H^(k+ℓ)_b(±[0, 1]_σ × X̄; |dσ/σ| μ_b).

So the pair (ℱf_1|_((−∞,0)), ℱf_1|_((0,∞))) lies in the space X^(k′,γ) of Definition 20.13, with vanishing polynomial
part and with values in ρ^(β_I)H^(k″)_b(X̄, μ_b); and Proposition 20.14 (2) with β = γ + 1 ∉ ℕ, applied to V^αℱf_1 for
the b-vector fields V on X̄ (ℱ commutes with them), gives f_1 ∈ ρ^(β_I)⟨t_*⟩^(−γ−1)H^k_b(ℝ̄_(t_*) × X̄), in the
convention H^(k,β)_b(ℝ) = ⟨t_*⟩^(−β)H^k_b(ℝ, |dt_*/⟨t_*⟩|) of Definition 20.7; so does χf_1. As γ > 0, f_1(·, x) is
integrable in t_* (by Cauchy–Schwarz with ⟨t_*⟩^(−2γ−1)), and |ℱf_1(σ)| ≤ C|σ|^γ (by Sobolev embedding in log|σ|,
ℓ ≥ 1), so

    ∫_ℝ f_1(t_*, x) dt_* = ℱf_1(0, x) = 0.    (29.39)

*For t_* ≤ 1:* integrating χf_1 from −∞ (Lemma 21.33 in τ = |t_*|⁻¹, where t_*∂_(t_*) = −τ∂_τ, with the weight
γ > 0 and the solution vanishing at τ = 0) gives
F_1|_({t_*≤1}) ∈ ρ^(β_I)⟨t_*⟩^(−γ)H̄^k_b([−∞, 1] × X̄) = H̄^(k,β_I,β_I+γ,γ)_b(Ω_−): near I, ρ ∼ ρ_I; near ι⁻, ρ and
⟨t_*⟩⁻¹ are both ∼ ρ_ι; near K⁻, ⟨t_*⟩⁻¹ ∼ ρ_K; and the b-vector fields of ℝ̄ × X̄ lift to span those of M′.

*For t_* ≥ −1:* by (29.39),

    F_1(t_*) = −∫_(t_*)^∞ f_1(s) ds + F_3(t_*),        F_3(t_*) := ∫_(−∞)^(t_*) ((χ − 1)f_1)(s) ds.

The first term lies in ρ^(β_I)⟨t_*⟩^(−γ)H̄^k_b([−1, ∞] × X̄), which has the weights (β_I, β_I + γ, γ) at (I, ι⁺, K⁺), by
the same integration from +∞. (χ − 1)f_1 is supported in {t_* ≤ −2r}, so F_3|_(Ω_<) ∈ H̄^(k,∞,β_I+γ,γ)_b as above, and
∂_(t_*)F_3 = (χ − 1)f_1 ∈ H^(k,∞,β_I+γ+1,γ+1)_b(M′). Lemma 29.30 (2) (with C = 1) gives
F_3|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(k,β_I+γ−ε,β_I+γ,γ)_b, and Lemma 29.30 (1) (γ ≠ 0) gives
F_3 ∈ H^(k,β_I+γ−ε,β_I+γ−2ε,((0,0),γ))_b(M′). Altogether, as β_I + γ − ε ≥ β_I for ε small and β_I + γ ≥ β_ι − ε,
F_1 ∈ H^(k,β_I,β_ι−3ε,((0,0),γ))_b(M′).

*Conclusion.* χu = F′ + F_1 + F_2 ∈ H^(k,β_I,β_ι−3ε,((0,0),β_K))_b, as γ ≥ β_K. (1 − χ)u is supported in
{t_* ≤ −2r} ⊂ Ω_<, with the weights (∞, β_ι, β_K). Renaming ε gives the claim. ∎

### 29.18 The three frequency ranges

Fix k. Let c ∈ (0, ½] be at most ς_1 of Lemma 20.28, the c_(k′) of Corollary 28.11 and the c_(j,k′) of
Theorem 28.10 (3) for j + k′ ≤ k + ℓ_0, ℓ_0 being the losses below, and let χ ∈ C^∞_c([0, c)) equal 1 on
[0, c/2], as in Section 28.7. So c depends on k, and, through the weight α of (28.1) (Lemma 29.33),
on the step of Section 29.19 in which it is used. The memberships (29.47)–(29.51) below hold at
the order k for that c, the losses ℓ_0 being independent of k; u, u_I and u^♭ do not depend on c, so their memberships
hold at every order. H^∞ in (29.47)–(29.51) is to be read in this sense.

For f ∈ C^∞_c(Ω_*°), Lemma 28.22, (28.21)–(28.22) and (28.24)–(28.25)
give the forward solution of L_b u = f as u = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing, with ℱu_hi = (1 − χ(|σ|))L̂_b(σ)⁻¹f̂(σ) on ℝ,
ℱu_reg = χ(|σ|)û_(reg,1)(σ) on ℝ (the proof of Lemma 28.24), (û_(reg,1), b̂_1, Ŝ_1) := L̃_b(σ)⁻¹(f̂(σ), 0, 0),
and u_sing = v_ġ + v_h of (28.24)–(28.25), with (the proof of Lemma 28.26)

    ℱ(∂_(t_*)v_ġ) = χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(b̂_1(σ)),        ℱ(∂²_(t_*)v_h) = χ(|σ|)G_2(σ)(Ŝ_1(σ)),
    G_1(σ)(ḃ) := Ψ(σ, ·)ġ(ḃ),        G_2(σ)(S) := (Ψ − σ∂_σΨ)h(S) − iσΨh̆(S),    (29.40)

with Ψ of Lemma 28.5. The bounds below are linear in f, and the forward solution map is continuous
(Theorem 29.17 with h = 0, S = 0), so the decomposition and the bounds extend by density to the spaces stated. These
spaces are extendible at {r = r_0}, where C^∞_c(Ω_*°) is not dense: one approximates an extension of f across
{r = r_0}, vanishing for t_* < 1, by smooth compactly supported functions, for which the decomposition holds, and
restricts. The forward solution on {r ≥ r_0} depends on f there only, since {r = r_0} is spacelike with dr future
timelike (Lemma 15.35 (1)), so that r decreases along future causal curves. Chapter 28 uses the same convention.

**Lemma 29.32** (High and bounded frequencies; [Hin26, (11.44)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
f ∈ H^(∞,(β^f_I+1,β_ι+2,β_K))_b(Ω_*)^(•,−) with β_K ∈ (0, ∞) ∖ ℕ, β^f_I ≥ 3/2 and
β^f_I + 1 ≥ β_ι + 2 − min(β_K, 1 − ε_1) for some ε_1 ∈ (0, 1). Then u_hi ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−ε,N,N))_b(M′) for every N and
every ε > 0.

*Proof.* Let χ_(C_0) be the cut-off of Corollary 20.27 (1 on [−C_0, C_0], supported in [−C′_0, C′_0]). The piece
ℱ⁻¹((1 − χ_(C_0))L̂_b⁻¹f̂) lies in H^(∞,(β′_I,N,N))_b(M′) for every β′_I < min(β^f_I, 3/2 + S̄) = 3/2, by
Corollary 20.27 (with the hypotheses of Chapter 12 for 2L_(b₀), as in Section 28.8; S̄ = 0, as in the proof of
Theorem 29.17). The rest is w := (χ_(C_0) − χ(|σ|))L̂_b⁻¹f̂, supported in J := {c/2 ≤ |σ| ≤ C′_0}. By
Proposition 20.18 (1) and (2), whose hypotheses on the weights are those of the lemma, f̂ lies on ±(0, 1] in
H^(∞,(min(β^f_I+1,β_ι+2)−ε,β_ι+1,·))_b(X^±_(sc-b)), and on ±[½, ∞) in the high-frequency space with the scf-weight
β^f_I + 1. On functions supported in the compact set J, away from tf and zf, both norms are equivalent to that of
H̄^(∞,β)_b(J × X̄) of Corollary 20.24 (2), with β the scf-weight. So f̂|_J ∈ H̄^(∞,5/2−ε)_b(J × X̄), as β_ι + 2 ≥ 5/2
and β^f_I + 1 ≥ 5/2 (if β_ι < ½, use the weaker weight β_ι + 2 − ε in place of 5/2 − ε throughout; in the
applications β_ι > ½). Corollary 20.24 (2) with β_scf := 3/2 − ε < 3/2 + S̄ (L̂_b(σ) is invertible on J̄,
Corollary 28.13) gives w ∈ H̄^(∞,3/2−2ε)_b(J × X̄). With χ′ the cut-off of Proposition 20.20, χ′w is supported away
from tf and zf and lies in H^(∞,(3/2−2ε,N,N))_b(X^±_(sc-b)) for every N (and has no Taylor coefficients at 0), so
Proposition 20.20 (1) gives ℱ⁻¹(χ′w) ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−3ε,N,N))_b(M′); and (1 − χ′)w, supported in ±[½, C′_0], lies in the
high-frequency space with every σ-weight, so Proposition 20.20 (2) gives ℱ⁻¹((1 − χ′)w) ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−2ε,N,N))_b(M′).
Each step loses finitely many derivatives, depending on N; the space is H^∞. ∎

**Lemma 29.33** (Low frequencies; [Hin26c, Proposition 13.18] for L̃_b, [Hin26, (11.45)].) Let α be as in
(28.1), β_scf < 3/2, ε ∈ (0, 1), and β_tf, β_zf with β_tf − β_zf = α + 2. There is ℓ such that for
f̂ ∈ H^(k+ℓ,(β_scf+1,β_tf+2,β_zf))_b(X^±_(sc-b)) (over ±[0, c]) and (û, b̂, Ŝ)(σ) := L̃_b(σ)⁻¹(f̂(σ), 0, 0),

    û ∈ H^(k,(β_scf−ε,β_tf,β_zf))_b(X^±_(sc-b)),        b̂, Ŝ ∈ H^(k,β_zf)_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|),    (29.41)

with norms bounded by that of f̂.

*Proof.* This is the proof of Proposition 20.29, with Corollary 28.11 and Theorem 28.10 (3) for L̃_b in place of
Theorem 13.25 (4)–(5). Division by the scalar |σ|^(β_zf), which commutes with L̃_b(σ)⁻¹ (componentwise, L̃_b⁻¹ being
linear) and satisfies σ∂_σ|σ|^(β_zf) = β_zf|σ|^(β_zf), reduces to β_zf = 0, β_tf = α + 2. Take α_+ := 0,
𝗋_out := β_scf − 2 − ε/2, below the outgoing threshold −½ + S̄ = −½, and the orders of Section 13.6 built from it,
equal to 𝗋_out near the zero section over sctf (as the proof of Corollary 28.11 uses them). For 0 < |σ| ≤ c and
j ≤ k, Theorem 28.10 (3) (its estimate (28.12), as Lemma 28.24–Lemma 28.25 use it) bounds
‖(σ∂_σ)^j L̃_b⁻¹g‖ in ‖·‖_((s+j;m),(𝗋,α,0),ς), plus the moduli of the last two components, by
C‖g‖_((s−1;m+j),(𝗋+1,α+2,0),ς), ς = |σ|. (20.28) and (20.27) with l = α and ε/2 convert the left
side to H^(m−ℓ̃,(β_scf−ε,α+2,0))_(b,ς) and the right side to H^(m+j+ℓ_a,(β_scf+1,α+4,0))_(b,ς), as
𝗋_out + 2 − ε/2 = β_scf − ε and 𝗋_out + 3 + ε/2 = β_scf + 1. Leibniz' rule and integration in |dσ/σ| (the description of
the norm in Section 20.9.3) give (29.41), with ℓ := ℓ_a + ℓ̃; for the moduli,
∫ Σ_(j≤k) |(σ∂_σ)^j b̂|² |dσ/σ| is bounded the same way. ∎

**Lemma 29.34** (The cut-off states; [Hin26, (11.47)–(11.48)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let a ∈ ℝ,
b̂ ∈ H^(∞,a)_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|; 𝔟_ℂ) and Ŝ ∈ H^(∞,a)_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|; 𝒮_(1,ℂ)). Then for every N and ε > 0,

    χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(b̂(σ)) ∈ H^(∞,(N,a+2−ε,a))_b(X^±_(sc-b)),
    χ(|σ|)G_2(σ)(Ŝ(σ)) ∈ H^(∞,(N,a+3−ε,a))_b(X^±_(sc-b)).    (29.42)

[Hin26, (11.47)] has the orders (1 − ε, 1 − ε, ·) and (1 − ε, 2 − ε, ·) for the states before the cut-off, so that
[Hin26, (11.48)] has (1 − ε, a + 1 − ε, a) and (1 − ε, a + 2 − ε, a).

*Proof.* *Pointwise bounds.* By Section 28.1 the states ġ(ḃ) lie in 𝒜^q with q = 2 (for ṁ) or q = 3 (for Ȧ), and
h(S) ∈ 𝒜³, h̆(S) ∈ 𝒜². For r ≥ 1, Ψ = Φ(σr), Φ entire with |∂^j_ζΦ| ≤ C_(j,M)⟨ζ⟩^(−M) (Lemma 28.5 (b)),
σ∂_σΨ = ζΦ′(ζ) and r∂_rΨ = ζΦ′(ζ), ζ = σr. So G_1(ḃ) = Φ(ζ)ġ and
G_2(S) = (Φ − ζΦ′)(ζ)h − iζΦ(ζ) r⁻¹h̆, with r⁻¹h̆ ∈ 𝒜³. For r ≤ 1, Ψ and its σ- and x-derivatives are bounded
for |σ| ≤ 1 (Lemma 28.5 (d) and its proof). Hence, with q_1 := 2, q_2 := 3 and V any product of σ∂_σ and b-vector
fields on X̄, |VG_i| ≤ C_(V,M)⟨|σ|⟨x⟩⟩^(−M)⟨x⟩^(−q_i) on basis elements.

*Weights.* By Section 20.9.3 the norm of H^(K,β)_b(X^±_(sc-b)) is equivalent to

    (Σ_(K′≤K) ∫ ‖(σ∂_σ)^(K′)v(σ)‖²_(H^(K−K′,β)_(b,|σ|)) |dσ/σ|)^(1/2),

with ‖v‖_(H^(m,β)_(b,ς)) = ‖w_β(ς)⁻¹v‖_(H̄^m_b(X̄,μ_b)) and (the proof of Lemma 20.28)
w_β(ς) ∼ ς^(β_tf)W_β(ρ̂), ρ̂ := ⟨x⟩⁻¹/ς, W_β(ρ̂) = (ρ̂/(1 + ρ̂))^(β_scf)(1 + ρ̂)^(β_tf−β_zf), with bounded logarithmic
derivatives. Take β = (N, a + q_i − ε, a), so that β_tf − β_zf = q_i − ε. Where ς⟨x⟩ ≥ 1 (ρ̂ ≤ 1),
W_β⁻¹ ≤ C(ς⟨x⟩)^N, and with M = N + q_i, |W_β⁻¹VG_i| ≤ Cς^(q_i)(ς⟨x⟩)^(−2q_i), whose square is μ_b-integrable there
with integral ≤ Cς^(2q_i). Where ς⟨x⟩ ≤ 1, W_β⁻¹ ≤ C(ς⟨x⟩)^(q_i−ε), so |W_β⁻¹VG_i| ≤ Cς^(q_i−ε)⟨x⟩^(−ε), and
∫ ⟨x⟩^(−2ε) μ_b < ∞. So ‖W_β⁻¹VG_i(σ)‖_(L²(μ_b)) ≤ C|σ|^(q_i−ε), and by Leibniz' rule

    ‖χG_1(b̂)‖²_(H^(K,β)) ≤ C Σ_(K′≤K) ∫ |σ|^(−2(a+q_1−ε)) |σ|^(2(q_1−ε)) |(σ∂_σ)^(K′)b̂|² |dσ/σ| = C‖b̂‖²_(H^(K,a)_b),

and likewise for G_2. ∎

### 29.19 Almost linear bounds

**Proposition 29.35** (Almost linear bounds; [Hin26, Proposition 11.17] in dimension 4 + 1, at b₀.) Let
ℰ_I^C and ℰ_+ be as in Definition 29.1, L as in Section 29.15, and

    2 ≤ ℓ_I < min(a_I + ½, ℓ_I^max),        ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ_I^C,        ℓ_I ∉ 3/2 + σ_Υ.    (29.43)

Let α_K ∈ [½, 1), α_+ > α_K and β_+ < min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+). For
f ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α_++2,α_K)_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−), the forward solution u of Lu = f satisfies

    u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),β_+,α_K−2)_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−).    (29.44)

Moreover u depends continuously on (S, h) in the space (29.44) with every weight lowered by ς, for every
ς > 0.

[Hin26] has the ι⁺-weight α_K − ε and the ℐ⁺-weight 3 + ε_I. Its proof notes that the decay would be α_+ but for the
singular terms at σ = 0. In dimension 4 + 1 they do not limit it, and the cap is 3/2: the scf-weight of
Lemma 29.32 and Lemma 29.33, that is, the transport of the order of the radiation field from ℐ⁺; the
corresponding cap in [Hin26, pp. 232 and 238] is 1. The condition ℓ_I ≥ 2 serves Proposition 20.18 (1) in
Lemma 29.32 and in Step 2b, which needs ℓ_I + 1 ≥ γ_+ + 2 − α̃_K, that is ℓ_I ≥ 2 for ι⁺-weights up to 3/2;
the 3 + ε_I of [Hin26] meets it. The bound ℓ_I < a_I + ½ is the range of Proposition 29.12.

*Proof.* *Step 0: the start.* By Definition 27.6 (2), min Re ℰ_I^C > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ, so the ℐ⁺-exponents of f
(ℰ_I^C + 1, and ℱ_(I,11) ⊂ 1 + (ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0)) for π₁₁) have real parts > 5/2, and
f ∈ H^(∞,(5/2−ε,α_++2,α_K))_b. Fix β^(0)_+ ∈ (½, min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+)) and β^(0)_I ∈ (β^(0)_+, 3/2).
Theorem 29.17 (α_K ≥ ½) gives u ∈ H^(∞,(β^(0)_I,β^(0)_+,−3/2))_b. Proposition 29.27 with ℓ_+ := β^(0)_+ (which
is below min Re ℰ_+, so that (ℰ_+, ℓ_+) is the weight ℓ_+, and ℓ_+ < a_+ + min Re ℰ_+, a_+ > 0; ℓ_+ lies neither in
Re π_1ℰ_+ nor in Re π_1ℰ_I^tot, whose least real part is 3/2; and ℓ_+ < 3/2 < ℓ_I), f having the ι⁺-weight
α_+ + 2 ≥ ℓ_+ + 2, gives the expansion at ℐ⁺ near ℐ⁺; away from ℐ⁺ nothing changes. So

    u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I),β′_+,α′_K−2)_b    (29.45)

holds with (α′_K, β′_+) = (½, β^(0)_+).

*The iteration.* Suppose (29.45) holds with α′_K ∈ [½, α_K] and β′_+ ∈ (½, min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+)). Put
α̃_K := min(α′_K + a_K − 2, α_K) and fix

    γ_+ ∈ (α_K, min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+)),     ε > 0 with γ_+ < 3/2 − 5ε,  γ_+ − 4ε > max(½, α_K).    (29.46)

Then γ_+ − α̃_K ∈ (0, 1) (as α̃_K ≤ α_K < γ_+ < 3/2 ≤ α̃_K + 1) and γ_+ < α̃_K + 1 − ε.

*Step 1: the rewriting ([Hin26, (11.41)]).* By (29.15) of Proposition 29.12, whose hypotheses hold
(3/2 < ℓ_I < a_I + ½; 0 < β′_+ < min Re ℰ_+ ≤ max(a_+, min Re ℰ_+)), (L − L_b)u has the ℐ⁺-data
(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′, ℓ_I + 1), the ι⁺-weight β′_+ + 2 + m_+ − ε (with no expansion term, as β′_+ + m_+ < 2 min Re ℰ_+) and the
K⁺-weight α′_K − 2 + a_K. As β′_+ + m_+ − ε > ½ + 1 − ε > γ_+,

    L_b u = f′ := f − (L − L_b)u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ_I^C+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),γ_++2,α̃_K)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−).

*Step 2a: null infinity ([Hin26, (11.42)]).* Proposition 29.29 with Ĕ_+ := ∅ and ℓ̆_+ := γ_+ (γ_+ < 3/2 <
min Re ℰ_I^C and γ_+ ≠ 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ; ℓ_I by (29.43)) gives u_I, vanishing on
{t_* < 1} ∪ {ρ_I > ½c_I}, with the ℐ⁺-data (⟨ℰ_I^C⟩, ℓ_I) and the ι⁺-data (ℰ^♯_+, γ_+), which is the weight γ_+ as
min Re ℰ^♯_+ ≥ min(3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, min Re ℰ_I^C) > 3/2 ((29.32)); and
f^♭ := f′ − L_b u_I ∈ H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,γ_++2,α̃_K)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−), the K⁺-weight being unchanged as u_I is supported near ℐ⁺.
u^♭ := u − u_I vanishes for t_* < 1 and solves L_b u^♭ = f^♭, so it is the forward solution (Proposition 17.14).

*Step 2b: the Fourier transform ([Hin26, (11.43)–(11.52)]).* Decompose u^♭ = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing as in
Section 29.18, with f^♭ in place of f. Proposition 20.18 (1), with (β_I, β_ι, β_K) = (ℓ_I + 1, γ_+ + 2, α̃_K)
(α̃_K ∈ (0, 1), and ℓ_I + 1 ≥ γ_+ + 2 − min(α̃_K, 1 − ε_1) for ε_1 < 1 − α̃_K, as ℓ_I ≥ 2 > γ_+ + 1 − α̃_K), gives

    f̂^♭|_(±(0,1]) ∈ H^(∞,(min(ℓ_I+1,γ_++2)−ε,γ_++1,α̃_K−1))_b(X^±_(sc-b)),

the zf index set (0, 0) dropping as α̃_K − 1 < 0.

*High frequencies.* Lemma 29.32 (β^f_I = ℓ_I ≥ 3/2, β_ι = γ_+, β_K = α̃_K ∈ (0, 1); its weight condition is the
inequality ℓ_I + 1 ≥ γ_+ + 2 − min(α̃_K, 1 − ε_1) above) gives u_hi ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−ε,N,N))_b(M′).

*The regular part.* Lemma 29.33 with β_scf := 3/2 − ε, β_tf := γ_+ − 1, β_zf := α̃_K − 1
(α + 2 := γ_+ − α̃_K ∈ (0, 1); the space of the right side contains f̂^♭, as 5/2 − ε ≤ min(ℓ_I + 1, γ_+ + 2) − ε)
gives

    û_(reg,1) ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−2ε,γ_+−1,α̃_K−1))_b,        b̂_1, Ŝ_1 ∈ H^(∞,α̃_K−1)_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|).    (29.47)

χ(|σ|)û_(reg,1) is supported where the cut-off of Proposition 20.20 is 1 (c ≤ ½), and its Taylor condition is void
(K-weight α̃_K, α̃_K − 1 < 0); Proposition 20.20 (1) gives

    u_reg ∈ H^(∞,(γ_+−ε,γ_+,α̃_K))_b(M′).    (29.48)

*The singular part.* By (29.40), Lemma 29.34 with a = α̃_K − 1 and (29.47), and
ℱ(∂_(t_*)v) = −iσℱv, which raises the tf- and zf-weights by 1,

    ℱ(∂²_(t_*)u_sing) = −iσχG_1(b̂_1) + χG_2(Ŝ_1) ∈ H^(∞,(N,α̃_K+2−ε,α̃_K−1))_b(X^±_(sc-b)).    (29.49)

([Hin26, (11.49)] has (1 − ε, α̃_K + 1 − ε, α̃_K); the zf-weight that [Hin26, (11.48)] gives, and with which [Hin26,
Lemma 11.19] is then applied, is α̃_K − 1.) As u^♭ = 0 for t_* < 1, u_sing = −(u_hi + u_reg) there, so by
(29.48) and the bound for u_hi, with γ_+ < 3/2 − ε,

    u_sing|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(∞,γ_+−ε,γ_+,α̃_K)_b,        ∂_(t_*)u_sing|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(∞,γ_+−ε,γ_++1,α̃_K+1)_b.    (29.50)

*First integration.* Lemma 29.31 applies to v := ∂_(t_*)u_sing with β_I := 3/2, β_ι := γ_+ + 1 and
β_K := α̃_K − 1. Indeed β_ι > β_I (γ_+ > ½); β_K < 0 < β_ι − β_I; β_K ∈ [−½, 0); v|_(Ω_<) has the weights
(·, γ_+ + 1, α̃_K + 1), at least (∞, β_ι, β_K), by (29.50); ℱv is χ(|σ|) times the boundary value from
Im σ > 0 of a function holomorphic inside 𝒞_0 with at most a pole at 0 (Section 28.10), a distribution supported in
a compact subset of (−c, c), c ≤ ½, as Lemma 29.31 asks; and ℱ(∂_(t_*)v) is (29.49), whose tf-weight
α̃_K + 2 − ε is at least β_ι = γ_+ + 1 (as γ_+ < α̃_K + 1 − ε) and whose zf-weight is β_K, with no zf index term as
β_K < 0. So

    ∂_(t_*)u_sing ∈ H^(∞,3/2,γ_++1−ε,α̃_K−1)_b(M′).

([Hin26] takes β_ι = α̃_K + 1 − ε, from [Hin26, (11.49)] and the minimum min(α̃_+ + 1, α̃_K + 1 − ε) in [Hin26,
(11.50)]; here the tf-weight of (29.49) exceeds the a priori bound (29.50), which sets β_ι.)

*Second integration.* Lemma 29.30 (1) for u_sing with (β_I, β_ι, β_K) := (γ_+ − ε, γ_+ − ε, α̃_K − 2) and
ℰ_K = ∅ (α̃_K − 2 ≠ 0): the hypotheses are (29.50) and the last display (3/2 ≥ γ_+ − ε). So

    u_sing ∈ H^(∞,γ_+−ε,γ_+−2ε,α̃_K−2)_b(M′),    (29.51)

the term (0, 0) at K lying above the weight α̃_K − 2 < 0. With (29.48) and the bound for u_hi,
u^♭ ∈ H^(∞,γ_+−ε,γ_+−2ε,α̃_K−2)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−), and u = u^♭ + u_I has the same ι⁺- and K⁺-weights.

*Step 3: the expansion at ℐ⁺.* Proposition 29.27 with ℓ_+ := γ_+ − 2ε (below min Re ℰ_+ and a_+ + min Re ℰ_+, below
ℓ_I, and below min Re ℰ_I^tot = 3/2; f has the ι⁺-weight α_+ + 2 > ℓ_+ + 2; the a priori ℐ⁺-weight is γ_+ − ε) gives
(29.45) with (α̃_K, γ_+ − 2ε) in place of (α′_K, β′_+), again in the range of the iteration by
(29.46).

*Conclusion.* Each step raises α′_K by min(a_K − 2, α_K − α′_K), a_K > 2, so finitely many steps reach α′_K = α_K,
with the ι⁺-weight γ_+ − 2ε; given β_+ as in the proposition, choose γ_+ > β_+ + 2ε in (29.46). This is
(29.44). Each step loses finitely many b-derivatives, and the spaces are H^∞ in the sense of
Section 29.18: at each order k, with the c of that order.

*Continuity.* The maps of the scheme are linear in f and u; u_I, u_hi, u_reg and u_sing depend on f′ only, through maps
bounded between the spaces above (the construction of Proposition 29.29 by Lemma 21.33, and
Lemma 29.30, Lemma 29.31, Lemma 29.32–Lemma 29.34 with Proposition 20.18 (1) and
Proposition 20.20 (1), each with bounds). (S, h) enters in three ways. Through L − L_b, whose coefficients in
(29.12) depend continuously on (S, h) (Proposition 29.7 and the expansion of g⁻¹ after it), with the bound of
(29.15) uniform for (S, h) small. Through the start, which Theorem 29.17 gives continuously in (S, h) at
weights lowered by ς. And through Proposition 29.27 in Steps 0 and 3, whose proof is constructive (Lemma 21.33
and Lemma 21.42 with their bounds, the products by Lemma 27.5 with the coefficient norms of the operator),
so that its bound depends on L only through coefficient norms, which Proposition 29.7 bounds locally uniformly in
(S, h). (A closed graph argument would give a bound for each fixed L only.) So every constant of the scheme, and the
bound of u in (29.44) by f, is locally uniform in (S, h). For two parameters, L(u − u′) = (L′ − L)u′, with u′
bounded in (29.44) uniformly and (L′ − L)u′ small in the space of the right side of Step 1 at the lowered
weights; the bounds of the scheme for the difference give the claim, for ς below the room in (29.46). ∎

In dimension 4 + 1 the window needs no relaxation. [Hin26] relaxes the ι⁺-weight to α̃_+ ∈ (α̃_K, α̃_K + ε_ind) to stay
in the indicial gap at zero energy. Here the gap of L̂_b(0) contains (0, 1] (Proposition 25.6 (a)), the window (0, 1)
of (28.1) lies inside it, and γ_+ − α̃_K ∈ (0, 1) throughout (29.46).

## 30. The model at a base point near b₀

The linear theory of Chapter 29 is written at the base point b₀ = (m₀, 0), and in the chapters that follow it is written
at a base point whose black hole parameter b lies in a fixed neighbourhood ℬ_* of b₀. This chapter collects what that
requires, using nothing after Chapter 29: the statement at b of a result proved at b₀ (Definition 30.1); the model
objects at b, with bounds uniform in b (Lemma 30.2): the forward solutions, the ι⁺- and tf-normal operators and
the indicial roots, which do not depend on b, the zero energy states, towers and physical states at b, real and smooth in
b and equivariant under the antipodal map, the augmented low-energy theory, and the Killing time translation; the
rotation state at b (Lemma 30.4); and the results of Chapter 29 on null infinity and the almost linear bounds at
b, with constants uniform in b (Proposition 30.5). [Hin26] states its Sections 11.2–12 at base points with |b − b₀|
small; the results here are part of that statement in dimension 4 + 1.

*What changes in dimension 4 + 1.* At b₀ every rotation is Killing, and the rotation state h_(b₀,v1) vanishes. At a
rotating b only the rotations commuting with the spin are Killing, and h_(b,v1) is O(|b − b₀|) but not zero
(Section 24.12.2). Lemma 30.4 identifies it: h_(b,v1)(V) is the gauge-corrected linearised metric ġ_b(ḃ_V)
of a change ḃ_V of the black hole parameter, of size O(|b − b₀||V|); the boost part vanishes by the parity of the
states under x ↦ −x.

*Notation.* The notation is that of Chapter 21–Chapter 29. The black hole parameters are b = (m, A), with tangent space
𝔟 = ℝ ⊕ 𝔰𝔬(4), b₀ = (m₀, 0) and R₁ = m₀^(1/2), and |b − b₀| is the norm of Definition 22.1. We write ℬ_1 and ℬ_* for
the neighbourhoods B_1 and B_* of b₀ fixed in Section 29.6, ℬ̄_* ⊂ ℬ_1. Shrinking ℬ_*, we take it to be an open ball
about b₀. It is shrunk finitely many times, here and in the chapters that follow, each time to a smaller ball about b₀,
and every statement holds on the final ℬ_*. Here it is shrunk once, in Lemma 30.3, to radius at most 1/(2C_B), so
that the matrix B(b) of the rows (28.9) on the states satisfies |B(b)⁻¹| ≤ 2 on ℬ̄_*. The letter ε > 0 is
small. For the zero energy operator of the gauge potential operator we write P_b := (□^Υ_b)^(0) (Section 23.13), as in
Chapter 23; L̂_b(0) is the zero energy operator of L_b, L̃_b(0) its augmentation (Proposition 28.8), and the states
ġ_b(ḃ), h_b(S) = h_(b,s1)(S), h̆_b(S) and h_(b,v1)(V) are those of Section 28.1, Proposition 23.28 and
Proposition 25.26; ġ_b(ḃ) is the gauge-corrected state ġ^Υ_b(ḃ) of (25.17).

*The inner radius.* Every result of the chapter holds with the inner radius r₀ = r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] of Definition 22.1
as a parameter, with constants and neighbourhoods of b₀ that may depend on it. The chapter names no inner radius and
no fixed radius. It works on Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1} with the spaces of Chapter 14–Chapter 20, extendible at the inner
boundary, and with the results of Chapter 14–Chapter 29, which hold at every such r_♭. The neighbourhoods ℬ_1 and ℬ_*
are those chosen in Section 29.6 for the given r_♭.

**Definition 30.1** (Base points and the statement at b.) A *base point with black hole parameter b* is a
base point of the linear theory in the chapters that follow (a pair (h, S) or (h, p⃗), or a triple (h, p⃗, q)) whose
background equals g_b near K⁺; for (h, S), with h ∈ 𝒳^∞ small and S ∈ 𝒮_1 small, that background is g_(b₀,b,−S) of
(29.1). For
a statement of the linear theory made at the base points with parameter b₀, *the statement at b* is obtained as
follows: L_(b₀), g_(b₀) near K⁺, the states, towers and companions at b₀, and the index set ℰ_ind are replaced by those
at b; and derivatives in b are taken at b. At a rotating b the v1 terms of exponent of real part at most 2 need more
than this substitution; they are treated with the rotation rows.

### 30.1 The model at b

**Lemma 30.2** (The model objects at b.) For b ∈ ℬ̄_*, uniformly in b:

(P1) Theorem 29.17 holds at b, with continuity in (b, S, h) (Corollary 29.25), and so do Proposition 29.6,
Proposition 29.7, Proposition 29.12, Corollary 29.14, Corollary 29.16, Lemma 29.5 and Lemma 29.11,
which are stated for g_0 = g_(b₀,b,−S) of (29.1) with |b − b₀| small.

(P2) N_ι⁺(2L_b) = N_ι⁺(2L̄) (Lemma 29.22), so the boundary spectrum spec_ι⁺ (Definition 26.28),
Theorem 26.27 and the resonant states of Section 27.8 do not depend on b; Theorem 26.42 and
Corollary 26.44 are stated for general b (with the K⁺-towers of L_b); the tf-normal operator does not depend on b
(Lemma 27.40); and the indicial roots of Proposition 25.6 do not depend on b, the normal operator of L̂_b(0)
at ∂X being that of 2L̄ (Lemma 25.1 (3)).

(P3) The zero energy states of L_b listed in Section 26.10 and their companions, the 1-form towers of
Proposition 23.34, the physical states of Proposition 25.37 and ġ_b are chosen real and smooth in b, equal at b₀ to
those at b₀, with index sets in (μ − j) + ℰ_ind, ℰ_ind independent of b, and, except for ġ_b, with leading terms at ∂X
that do not depend on b. The leading terms of ġ_b may depend on b through the mass, and the linear theory uses the index
sets of ġ_b and its smoothness in b. The rotation state h_(b,v1) ∈ 𝒜³ is smooth in b and vanishes at b₀. The element −1
of SO(4), x ↦ −x on the spatial factor, is an isometry of every g_b: it commutes with the spin matrix, and the metric
(21.25) is even in x (Lemma 24.61 with O = −1). It preserves t_* = t − ψ(|x|) ((21.30)), the
radial functions ψ, ζ_∞ and χ, and the gauge 1-forms c_Υ = ζ_∞(|x|)|x|⁻¹dt and c_(Υ,H) = −½χ(|x|)d|x| of Section 23.13
and c_C of Section 24.2, a combination of dt and d|x| with coefficients that depend on |x| only. So it commutes with
L_b, □^Υ_b, P_b and L̂_b(0). The states are equivariant under it: h_b(S) is odd, ġ_b(ḃ) and h_(b,v1)(V) are even.

(P4) Corollary 28.11–Corollary 28.13 and Theorem 28.20 hold at b (Theorem 29.21 and the compactness
argument of its proof), and so do the other statements of Chapter 28 that the linear theory uses: Definition 28.1,
Definition 28.7, Lemma 28.3–Lemma 28.5, Proposition 28.8 and Theorem 28.10, which are stated for
b near b₀, and Lemma 28.22, (28.21)–(28.25) and Section 28.10. Theorem 29.21 reruns
Section 28.7–Section 28.12 at b, and its compactness argument covers Proposition 28.8. The states' bounds are
uniform in 𝒜^(q−δ) for every δ > 0 (Remark 28.6), a loss that the linear theory absorbs, each of its results
using its weights with room. The high-frequency loss is bounded at every order k at every b ∈ ℬ̄_1, with constants
independent of b: Proposition 29.19 holds with C independent of η and b, and Corollary 29.20 gives, for every k,
δ_Γ(0) < 1/(2(k + 1)) at every b ∈ ℬ̄_1. The propositions of Chapter 27 on the tf-normal operator and
Lemma 27.54 hold at b, their inputs being the tf-normal operator (P2), the zero energy states (P3) and
Chapter 28.

(P5) The time translation ∂_(t_*) is Killing for g_b, so every statement that uses only that the s0 gauge 1-form
ω^(0)_(b,s0) is Killing holds at b.

*Proof.* (P1), (P2) and (P4) are the cited statements. (P5): g_b is stationary.

*The choice in (P3).* The pure gauge states and their companions are δ*_(g_b)ω^(≤k)_b with ω^(≤k)_b ∈ ker □^Υ_b
polynomial in t_* and smooth in b (Proposition 23.34). By the remark closing Lemma 23.33 their leading terms
at ∂X are the Minkowski model solutions, which do not depend on b and which (R4) of Section 23.16 fixes uniquely, no
root lying at μ − k. The physical states at −2 are those of Proposition 25.37, smooth in b with the b-independent
leading term h̄_τ(Y). Composing each family with the inverse of the smooth invertible map Y ↦ (its leading
coefficient), normalised to be the identity at b₀, keeps everything at b₀ and makes the leading terms independent of
b. The corrections lie in 𝒜^((μ−j)+ℰ_ind) with ℰ_ind independent of b (Section 26.11, Proposition 23.34,
Proposition 25.37). The rotation state h_(b,v1)(V) = δ*_(g_b)ω^(−1)_(b,v1)(V) lies in 𝒜³ ((23.25)), is
smooth in b, and vanishes at b₀, where every rotation is Killing (Proposition 23.28 (3)). ġ_b = ġ^Υ_b is the
gauge-corrected derivative of the Myers–Perry family (Proposition 25.26), smooth in b; its leading term may depend on
b through the mass.

*Reality.* The reality in (P3) holds as at b₀: L_b, δ*_(g_b) and □_(g_b) are real, and Proposition 23.28,
Proposition 23.34, Proposition 25.37 and the normalisation by the leading coefficients are real constructions.
