*Parity.* The parity in (P3) follows from the constructions of the states. Write φ for the pullback by −1. P_b is
invertible on the b-spaces of decaying sections of Section 23.13 (weights in the gap (0, ι^Υ_(s1,2))), which φ
preserves. Since φ commutes with P_b, it commutes with P_b⁻¹ there, and it commutes with δ*_(g_b).
Proposition 23.28 builds

    ω_(b,s1)(S) = ω̄_s1(S) − P_b⁻¹□^Υ_b ω̄_s1(S)

from the Minkowski translation 1-form ω̄_s1(S), which is odd, and

    ω_(b,v1)(V) = V − P_b⁻¹□^Υ_b V

from the rotation 1-form V, which is even (the proof of Proposition 23.28). So ω_(b,s1)(S) and
h_b(S) = δ*_(g_b)ω_(b,s1)(S) are odd, and ω_(b,v1)(V) and h_(b,v1)(V) = δ*_(g_b)ω_(b,v1)(V) are even. φ fixes g_(b′)
for every b′, so ∂_b g_b(ḃ) is even; so are

    η_b(ḃ) = 2δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b)∂_b g_b(ḃ)     and     ω̇_b(ḃ) = −P_b⁻¹η_b(ḃ),

and so is ġ_b(ḃ) = ġ^Υ_b(ḃ) = ∂_b g_b(ḃ) + δ*_(g_b)ω̇_b(ḃ), the gauge-corrected state of (25.17)
(Proposition 25.26), which is what ġ_b means here, as in the basis of Section 28.1. The reparametrisation by the
leading coefficients in the choice above is linear in the parameter and keeps each family's parity. ∎

**Lemma 30.3** (The ball ℬ_*.) Fix the bases of 𝔟 and 𝒮_1 in which (28.9) is written, with the
Euclidean norms in these bases and the operator norm on matrices, and for b ∈ ℬ̄_* let

    B(b)(ḃ, S) := (⟨ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S), f*_1⟩, ⟨ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S), f*_2⟩),

with the rows f*_1, f*_2 of (28.9) and the pairing of Section 28.1 at b. Then B(b₀) = I, B(b) is real,
and B is of class C¹ in b, so C_B := sup_(ℬ̄_*)|∂_bB| is finite. After shrinking ℬ_* to a ball about b₀ of radius at
most 1/(2C_B),

    |B(b) − I| ≤ ½,     |B(b)⁻¹| ≤ 2     for every b ∈ ℬ̄_*.

In particular (ḃ, S) ↦ ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S) is injective for every b ∈ ℬ̄_*. If the same matrix B(b), in the same bases and
norms, is formed again later and its constant is taken as the supremum of |∂_bB| over the ball fixed here, that
supremum is at most C_B; so the condition that the radius be at most one over twice that supremum holds already, and
it shrinks ℬ_* no further. This is the case in the chapter that follows.

*Proof.* B(b₀) = I is (28.9). B(b) is real: the rows f*_1, f*_2 are real (Section 28.3 fixes them real),
g_b is real, and the states are real on real arguments ((P3)). The pairing ⟨u, f*_j⟩ = ∫_X ⟨u, f*_j⟩_(g_b)|dx| is an
integral over the compact set supp f*_1 ∪ supp f*_2 ⊂ X°, and g_b is smooth in b. The states are of class C¹ in b with
values in continuous sections over that set ((P3); Proposition 23.28 and Proposition 25.26 (3) construct them
smooth in b). So B is of class C¹, and C_B is finite, ℬ̄_* being compact. Shrinking ℬ_* does not increase C_B. The mean
value theorem along the segment from b₀ to b, which lies in the ball ℬ̄_*, gives |B(b) − I| ≤ C_B|b − b₀| ≤ ½, and the
Neumann series B(b)⁻¹ = Σ_(n≥0)(I − B(b))^n gives |B(b)⁻¹| ≤ Σ_(n≥0) 2^(−n) = 2. If ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S) = 0, then
B(b)(ḃ, S) = 0, so (ḃ, S) = 0. Finally, a supremum over the shrunk ball, a subset of the ball over which C_B was
taken, is at most C_B, so one over twice it is at least 1/(2C_B), which bounds the radius. ∎

**Lemma 30.4** (The rotation state at b.) For b ∈ ℬ̄_* and V ∈ 𝒱_1 there is ḃ_V ∈ 𝔟, linear in V,
with |ḃ_V| = O(|b − b₀||V|) and

    h_(b,v1)(V) = ġ_b(ḃ_V),     ker h_(b,v1) = {V : ḃ_V = 0}.

*Proof.* At b, h_(b,v1)(V) is δ*_(g_b) of a 1-form in ker □^Υ_b ((23.25)), so it lies in ker L̂_b(0) in the
space 𝒳_0 of Section 28.1, and it is O(|b − b₀||V|) (P3). That nullspace is eleven-dimensional, and ġ_b(ḃ), the
gauge-corrected state of (25.17), and h_b(S) span it (Proposition 25.30 (1) at the b-weight
α + 2 ∈ (0, 1)); they are independent by Lemma 30.3. So h_(b,v1)(V) = ġ_b(ḃ_V) + h_b(S_V), with
(ḃ_V, S_V) = B(b)⁻¹(⟨h_(b,v1)(V), f*_1⟩, ⟨h_(b,v1)(V), f*_2⟩), which is real for real V, B(b) being real
(Lemma 30.3) and h_(b,v1)(V) = δ*_(g_b)(V − P_b⁻¹□^Υ_b V) real for real V, the operators being real (the
proof of (P3)). As |B(b)⁻¹| ≤ 2 and the pairings are bounded by the supremum of h_(b,v1)(V) on the compact support of
the rows, |ḃ_V| + |S_V| = O(|b − b₀||V|). Moreover S_V = 0: the pullback by −1 fixes h_(b,v1)(V) and ġ_b(ḃ_V) and
reverses h_b(S_V) ((P3)), so h_b(S_V) = 0, and S_V = 0 by Lemma 30.3. So h_(b,v1)(V) = ġ_b(ḃ_V), and ker
h_(b,v1) = {V : ḃ_V = 0} by the injectivity in Lemma 30.3. ∎

### 30.2 Null infinity and the almost linear bounds at b

**Proposition 30.5** (Null infinity and the almost linear bounds at b.) Let b ∈ ℬ̄_*, let L_b be the
operator at b, and put g_0 := g_(b₀,b,−S), g := g_0 + h and L := L^(g,g_0), with |S| < ε_0, h ∈ 𝒳^∞ and ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) < ε_0,
where ε_0 and d are those of Corollary 29.25, independent of b. Then Lemma 29.26, Proposition 29.27,
Lemma 29.28, Proposition 29.29, Lemma 29.30, Lemma 29.31, Lemma 29.32–Lemma 29.34
and Proposition 29.35 hold with these L_b, g_0, g and L, and with the states ġ_b(ḃ), h_b(S), h̆_b(S) at b in place of
those at b₀, with constants and smallness conditions uniform in b ∈ ℬ̄_*. In particular, for ℓ_I with (29.43),
α_K ∈ [½, 1), α_+ > α_K, β_+ < min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+) and f as in Proposition 29.35, the forward solution u of
Lu = f lies in the space (29.44); and, at fixed b, u depends continuously on (S, h) in that space with every
weight lowered by ς, for every ς > 0.

*Proof.* The results on null infinity are stated for L = L^(g,g_0) with g_0 = g_(b₀,b,−S) (Section 29.12), with
Proposition 29.6 and Proposition 29.7 for general b ((P1)). The structure of L_b at ℐ⁺ is Lemma 29.5, which is
stated for L_b at every b, and S̄ and Ā do not depend on b ((P2), Lemma 29.22). The index sets ℰ^C_I, ℰ_+ and
ℰ^tot_I at ℐ⁺ and ι⁺ are data of the classes of Definition 29.1, fixed independently of b. So
Lemma 29.26–Proposition 29.29 hold at b, uniformly.

For the almost linear bounds, the steps of Section 29.15–Section 29.19 that use b₀ are supplied as follows.

- *The setting.* ε_0 and d are uniform in b ((P1)). X = {r ≥ r_0} is the same at every b, and Theorem 29.21 runs
  the second result of Chapter 28 on it for b ∈ ℬ̄_1 ((P4)). L̂_b(σ) is invertible for real σ ≠ 0
  (Corollary 28.13) and L̃_b(σ) for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_k (Corollary 28.11), with c_k uniform ((P4)). No indicial root of
  L̂_b(0) has real part in (0, 1] ((P2)), so the window (0, 1) is the same at every b.
- Lemma 29.30 and Lemma 29.31 use no property of the base point. In Section 29.18 the constants
  c ≤ c_k′ of Corollary 28.11 and c_(j,k′) of Theorem 28.10 (3) are those at b, uniform by (P4).
- *The three frequency ranges.* The Fourier transform in t_* uses only that g_b is stationary. The splitting
  u = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing of Lemma 28.22 and (28.21)–(28.25), with u_sing = ġ + h_s1,
  holds at b ((P4): Theorem 29.21 reruns Section 28.7–Section 28.12 at b), with ġ = ġ_b and
  h_s1 = h_(b,s1) the states at b ((P3), the derivative in b being taken at b). The forward map is continuous
  (Theorem 29.17 at b, (P1)). Lemma 29.32 and Lemma 29.33 use Corollary 20.27 with the hypotheses of
  Chapter 12 for 2L_b, which hold at b by (P4) (Theorem 29.21), and S̄ = 0, which does not depend on b ((P2),
  Lemma 29.22); Lemma 29.33 uses Corollary 28.11 and Theorem 28.10 (3) for L̃_b ((P4)). In
  Lemma 29.34, ġ_b(ḃ) ∈ 𝒜² (in the mass) and 𝒜³ (in the rotation), h_b(S) ∈ 𝒜³ and h̆_b(S) ∈ 𝒜², and the map
  Ψ of Lemma 28.5, are those at b ((P3)), the leading terms not depending on b; uniformly in b,
  Remark 28.6 gives these memberships in 𝒜^(q−δ), and the loss δ < ε is absorbed by the ε of (29.42).
- Proposition 29.35. Its start is Theorem 29.17 at b ((P1)). The K⁺-gain of (L − L_b)u in (29.15) holds
  with L_b the base point's operator, as g_0 = g_b near K⁺ (Lemma 29.11). Proposition 29.29 for L_b and
  Proposition 17.14 hold at every b. The holomorphy of F(v), with at most a pole at 0, is Section 28.10 at b
  ((P4)). The continuity in (S, h) is that of (P1) at fixed b.

Each supply is uniform on ℬ̄_*, which gives the uniform constants. ∎

## 31. The boost parameter, almost boundedness and the extraction of parameters

This chapter studies forward solutions of the linearised gauge-fixed Einstein operator at a base point near the
Schwarzschild–Tangherlini parameter b₀, for sources with more than one order of decay at K⁺, and reads off from them
the parameters of the linearised Myers–Perry family. It has three steps. First (Proposition 31.6), for sources of
K⁺-weight α_K ∈ (1, 3/2) the forward solution is a cut-off generalised zero energy state of the boosts,
χ^H_K h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ), plus a remainder of K⁺-weight α_K − 2 > −1; the vector Ṡ ∈ 𝒮_1 is the *boost parameter* of the
solution. Second (Section 31.4–Section 31.7), a correction term added to the operator lets a right-hand side
generate the boost term, and the map from the parameter of that term to the boost parameter of the forward solution is
invertible (Proposition 31.16, Proposition 31.19); so a forward solution with no boost term, growing at most like
t_*^(2−α_K) = o(t_*) in compact spatial sets, can be found (Corollary 31.20). Third, once the boost term is
eliminated, the forward solution has K⁺-weight α_K − 2 for every α_K < 2 (Proposition 31.21); and for sources with
a little more than t_*^(−2) decay at K⁺ it is a cut-off linearised Myers–Perry metric, plus a cut-off constant
centre-of-mass shift, plus a remainder that decays at K⁺ (Proposition 31.27). These are [Hin26, Proposition 11.20,
Proposition 11.30, (11.95), Proposition 11.32, Proposition 11.34] in dimension 4 + 1.

The scheme is that of [Hin26]. The dimension changes it in five places. The states decay one order faster, and the
correction terms carry no logarithm, so nothing has to be cancelled at ι⁺. The formal solution at null infinity has
ι⁺-exponents beginning at λ_♯ := 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, not at 1, so the step that removes a t_*^(−3) term at ι⁺ is not
needed below α_K = 3/2, and later it removes finitely many terms with no pole. The zero energy window is (0, 1), as
no indicial root of L̂_b(0) has real part in (0, 1]. The remainders keep the ι⁺-weight min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+) − ε
in place of 1 − ε; the cap 3/2 is the transport of the radiation order from ℐ⁺. And there is no logarithmic
centre-of-mass motion: the motions that the exponents at ι⁺ create decay at K⁺.

The chapter is written at a general base point b near b₀. The operator is taken at b and the corrections are tensors
built from b₀-objects. The one identity that is exact only at b₀, the boost identity Lemma 31.12, acquires an
error at b (Lemma 31.18), and the invertibility of the boost parameter map is proved at b by a direct bound
(Proposition 31.19). The rows of the augmented zero energy operator are normalised at b₀; at b their matrix on the
states is a perturbation of the identity (Lemma 31.1), and its inverse enters the row data
(Lemma 31.25).

### 31.1 The setting at a base point

The notation is that of Chapter 21–Chapter 29; n = 4 throughout. The black hole parameters are b = (m, A), with
tangent space 𝔟 := ℝ ⊕ 𝔰𝔬(4), and b₀ = (m₀, 0); R₁ = m₀^(1/2), and |b − b₀| is the norm of Definition 22.1. We
write ℬ_1 and ℬ_* for the open neighbourhoods B_1 and B_* of b₀ fixed in Section 29.6, B̄_* ⊂ B_1. Shrinking ℬ_*,
we take it to be an open ball about b₀. It is shrunk finitely many times below (Lemma 31.1,
Proposition 31.19), each time to a smaller ball about b₀, and every statement holds on the final ℬ_*; in particular
the segment from b₀ to each b ∈ ℬ̄_* lies in ℬ̄_*. 𝒮_1 is the space of the s1 parameters: S = S_w ∈ 𝒮_1
has |x|S = w · x with w ∈ ℝ⁴, so 𝒮_1 ≅ ℝ⁴.

*Spaces.* M, Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1}, the faces ℐ⁺, ι⁺, K⁺ with their defining functions ρ_I, ρ_+, ρ_K, and the
unweighted b-density μ_b are those of Section 29.1. Weights and index sets are listed at (ℐ⁺, ι⁺, K⁺); a single
number at a face is a plain weight there. H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+),ℓ_K)_b(Ω_*) and the spaces of
right-hand sides H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),(ℰ_++2,ℓ_++2),ℓ_K)_b(Ω_*) are those of Definition 29.1, with the
index sets ℰ_+ and ℰ^C_I there; the superscript (•, −) marks distributions supported in {t^♭_* ≥ 1} and extendible
at the artificial boundary. ℰ^tot_I, π_1 and the other index sets of Chapter 27 keep their meaning. The class of
perturbations is 𝒳^k of (29.4), with parameters a_I > 3/2, a_+ > 1, a_K > 2, and

    m_+ := min(a_+, min Re ℰ_+).

The constants γ_Υ, e_Υ, the set σ_Υ and ℓ_I^max are those of Chapter 29 and Section 29.12, and

    λ_♯ := 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ

is the exceptional exponent of Proposition 29.29; as 0 < γ_Υ < 1/4 ((27.1)), λ_♯ ∈ (3/2, 7/4). On the
spectral side, M′, Ω_− := cl_(M′){t_* ≤ 1}, Ω_<, the faces I, ι = ι⁺ ∪ ι⁻ and K = K⁺ ∪ K⁻ of M′, X̄ = {r ≥ r_0} and
the spaces on M′ are those of Section 29.15; H̄ denotes restrictions. X^±_(sc-b) over ±[0, c] is the space of
Section 20.8.1, with faces scf, tf, zf, weights listed in that order and the defining functions (20.18);
ρ = ⟨x⟩⁻¹, μ_X = |dx|/⟨x⟩⁴, r̂ := |σ|⟨x⟩, and χ_zf := χ_1(r̂) is the cut-off of Section 20.8.1, equal to 1 for
r̂ ≤ 1/8 and to 0 for r̂ ≥ 1/4. ℱ is the Fourier transform in t_*, under which ∂_(t_*) becomes −iσ.

*The inner radius.* Every result of the chapter holds with the inner radius r_0 = r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] of
Definition 22.1, the radius of the artificial boundary {r = r_0} at which every space is extendible, as a parameter;
constants and neighbourhoods of b₀ may depend on it. The chapter names no inner radius: the fixed radii it uses are
scale-free ({r ≤ 2}, {r ≥ 1}) or far out (|x| ≥ 5R₁, t ≥ 60R₁), and its weights are fixed at infinity and at K⁺.

*The operator at the base point.* A base point is a pair (h, S), with S ∈ 𝒮_1 small and h ∈ 𝒳^∞ small in 𝒳^d,
together with a black hole parameter b ∈ ℬ̄_*. Its background is

    g_(b₀,b,−S) = (1 − χ_K)φ*_(−S) g_(b₀) + χ_K g_b

of (29.1), equal to g_b near K⁺, and its operator is L^(g,g_0), g_0 := g_(b₀,b,−S), g := g_0 + h, where
L^(g,g_0) := D_1P(·, g_0) at g is the linearised gauge-fixed Einstein operator of Chapter 21. L_b := L^(g_b,g_b) is the
stationary model at b, and L̂_b(σ) = L_0 − iσL_1 − σ²L_2 its spectral family (Section 28.1). The following
properties of the base point are used.

(BP1) Lemma 29.11, Proposition 29.7, Proposition 29.12 and Corollary 29.16 are stated for the background
g_(b₀,b,−S) with |b − b₀| and |S| small: g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b lies in the class of h, vanishes near K⁺, and
L^(g,g_0) − L_b gains a_K at K⁺. Theorem 29.17 holds at every b ∈ ℬ̄_*, with constants uniform in b and with
continuity in (b, S, h) (Corollary 29.25).

(BP2) The models do not depend on b. N_ι⁺(2L_b) = N_ι⁺(2L̄) (Lemma 29.22), so the ι⁺-spectrum and
Theorem 26.27 are those at b₀, and Theorem 26.42 and Corollary 26.44 hold at b with the K⁺-towers of L_b.
The tf-normal operator does not depend on b (Lemma 27.40). The indicial roots of L̂_b(0) do not depend on b,
the normal operator of L̂_b(0) at ∂X̄ being that of 2L̄ (Lemma 25.1 (3)); by Proposition 25.6 (a) none of
them has real part in (0, 1], so (0, 1) lies in the indicial gap of L̂_b(0) for μ_b.

(BP3) The states at b are those of Section 28.1: for ḃ ∈ 𝔟 and S ∈ 𝒮_1, ġ_b(ḃ) is the gauge-corrected linearised
metric of (25.17), h_b(S) := h_(b,s1)(S) = δ*_(g_b) ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) and h̆_b(S) := h̆¹_(b,s1)(S), with the
1-forms ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S), ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S) of Proposition 23.28. They are stationary, linear in their arguments
and real on real arguments; their index sets at ∂X̄ are those at b₀, with ℰ_ind independent of b: ġ_b(ḃ) ∈ 𝒜²,
h_b(S) ∈ 𝒜^((3,0)∪(3+ℰ_ind)), h̆_b(S) ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)). They are of class C^k in b for every k, with values in
the b-Sobolev spaces in which Remark 28.6 takes them continuous: ġ_b(ḃ) by Proposition 25.26 (3); h_b(S) and
h̆_b(S) because their 1-forms are of class C^k in b (the construction of Proposition 23.28 with Lemma 23.27,
whose b-derivatives are inverse images of the same kind) and δ*_(g_b) has coefficients smooth in b. By the b-Sobolev
embedding H̄_b^(∞,a) ⊂ 𝒜^(a+2) of Remark 28.6, the states and their first derivatives in b are therefore
bounded in 𝒜^(q−δ), uniformly on ℬ̄_*, for every δ > 0, with q = 2 for ġ_b(1, 0) and h̆_b(S) and q = 3 for
ġ_b(0, Ȧ) and h_b(S); and, by Sobolev embedding on compact sets, they are of class C^k in b with values in C⁰(K) for
every compact K ⊂ X°. The loss δ is absorbed below, where every weight is used with room. The generalised state of
the boosts

    h^(≤1)_b(S) := t_* h_b(S) + h̆_b(S) = δ*_(g_b)(t_* ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) + ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S))

lies in the kernels of D_(g_b)Ric and of δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b) (Proposition 23.28 (2)), so L_b h^(≤1)_b(S) = 0; and
L_b ġ_b(ḃ) = 0. These results use the dynamical hypotheses (Dyn) of Chapter 23, which hold for b near b₀
(Chapter 22).

(BP4) The results of Chapter 28 that we use — Definition 28.1, Definition 28.7, Lemma 28.2–Lemma 28.5,
Proposition 28.8, Theorem 28.10 and Corollary 28.11–Corollary 28.13 — are stated for b near b₀ and hold on
ℬ̄_* with constants uniform in b, by Theorem 29.21. So do Proposition 27.58 and Lemma 27.54, whose inputs
are the tf-normal operator (BP2), the zero energy states (BP3) and Chapter 28.

(BP5) The rows f*_1, f*_2 of (28.9) are normalised at b₀. At b their matrix B(b) on the states is
invertible, with |B(b)⁻¹| ≤ 2, and (ḃ, S) ↦ ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S) is injective, uniformly in b (Lemma 31.1 and
Lemma 31.2 below).

The results of Chapter 29 that we use — Proposition 29.27, Proposition 29.29, Lemma 29.30,
Lemma 29.31, Lemma 29.32–Lemma 29.34 and Proposition 29.35 — are used at b: L_(b₀), g_(b₀) near
K⁺ and the states at b₀ are replaced by L_b, g_b and the states at b, and the background g_(b₀,b₀,−S) by
g_(b₀,b,−S). In this form they hold at every b ∈ ℬ̄_*, with constants and smallness conditions uniform in b, and with
the continuity of Proposition 29.35 in (S, h) at fixed b (Proposition 30.5).

**Lemma 31.1** (The rows at b.) Fix the bases of 𝔟 and 𝒮_1 in which (28.9) is written, with the
Euclidean norms in these bases and the operator norm on matrices, and a fibre norm |·| on S²T*X̄. Let
r(u) := (⟨u, f*_1⟩, ⟨u, f*_2⟩), with the pairing of Section 28.1 at b, and let 𝒦_0 := supp f*_1 ∪ supp f*_2, a
compact subset of X°. For b ∈ ℬ̄_* let

    B(b) : 𝔟_ℂ ⊕ 𝒮_(1,ℂ) → 𝔟_ℂ ⊕ 𝒮_(1,ℂ),        B(b)(ḃ, S) := r(ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S)),    (31.1)

the matrix of the rows on the states. Then B(b) is real and B(b₀) = I, and there are C_f and C_B such that, for every
b ∈ ℬ̄_* and every continuous u,

    |r(u)| ≤ C_f sup_(𝒦_0)|u|,        |B(b) − I| ≤ C_B|b − b₀|.

After shrinking ℬ_* to a ball of radius at most 1/(2C_B), |B(b) − I| ≤ 1/2, and

    |B(b)⁻¹| ≤ 2        for every b ∈ ℬ̄_*.

*Proof.* B(b₀) = I is (28.9), and B(b) is real, as the states are real on real arguments ((BP3)) and f*_j
and g_b are real. The pairing is ⟨u, f*_j⟩ = ∫_X ⟨u, f*_j⟩_(g_b) |dx| (Section 28.1), an integral over the compact
set supp f*_j, on which |⟨u, v⟩_(g_b)| ≤ C|u||v| with C uniform for b ∈ ℬ̄_*, g_b being smooth in b. So the first
bound holds with C_f := C(Σ_i ‖f*_(i)‖²_(L¹(|dx|)))^(1/2), the f*_(i) being the eleven components of f*_1 and f*_2 in
the fixed bases. The states and the fibre inner product of g_b are of class C¹ in b with values in C⁰(𝒦_0) ((BP3)),
so B(b) is of class C¹ in b, and C_B := sup_(ℬ̄_*)|∂_bB| is finite, ℬ̄_* being compact. The mean value theorem along
the segment from b₀ to b, which lies in the ball ℬ̄_*, gives |B(b) − I| ≤ C_B|b − b₀|. Shrinking ℬ_* does not
increase C_B, so on a ball of radius at most 1/(2C_B), |B(b) − I| ≤ 1/2, the Neumann series
B(b)⁻¹ = Σ_(n≥0)(I − B(b))^n converges, and |B(b)⁻¹| ≤ Σ_(n≥0) 2^(−n) = 2. ∎

**Lemma 31.2** (The states at b are determined on 𝒦_0.) Let 𝒦_0 and C_f be those of Lemma 31.1
and c := (2C_f)⁻¹. Then

    sup_(𝒦_0)|ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S)| ≥ c|(ḃ, S)|,        in particular        sup_(𝒦_0)|h_b(S)| ≥ c|S|,

for all b ∈ ℬ̄_*, ḃ ∈ 𝔟_ℂ and S ∈ 𝒮_(1,ℂ). So (ḃ, S) ↦ ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S) and S ↦ h_b(S) are injective, uniformly in
b, and h_b(Ṡ) determines Ṡ, with |Ṡ| ≤ c⁻¹ sup_(𝒦_0)|h_b(Ṡ)|.

*Proof.* By (31.1), (ḃ, S) = B(b)⁻¹r(ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S)), so by Lemma 31.1 |(ḃ, S)|
≤ 2|r(ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S))| ≤ 2C_f sup_(𝒦_0)|ġ_b(ḃ) + h_b(S)|. The second bound is the case ḃ = 0. ∎

### 31.2 Profiles at zero energy

This section and the next are [Hin26, Section 11.4.1] in dimension 4 + 1.

For γ_zf ∈ (0, 1), H^(k,(γ_scf,γ_tf,((0,0),γ_zf)))_b(X^±_(sc-b)) is the space of χ_zf v_0 + ũ with
v_0 ∈ H^(k,γ_tf)_b(X), its *zf-coefficient* (the same for both signs when so stated), and ũ ∈ H^(k,γ)_b(X^±_(sc-b))
(Section 20.8.1). Throughout, c ≤ 1/(8√5), so that χ_zf = 1 on {r ≤ 2} for |σ| ≤ c (there ⟨x⟩ ≤ √5, so
r̂ ≤ 1/8); and c is also below the k-independent bound of Section 31.3 (χ_zf = 1 on supp f*_j).

**Lemma 31.3** (Profiles independent of σ.) Let a ∈ ℝ, P ∈ ρ^p Diff^m_b(X̄) with smooth coefficients,
p ≥ 0, j ∈ ℕ₀, and u_0 ∈ H^(∞,a)_b(X). Then

(a) σ^j χ_zf P u_0 ∈ H^(∞,(∞,a+p+j,γ_zf))_b(X^±_(sc-b)) for every γ_zf < j;

(b) [P, χ_zf]u_0 (for m ≥ 1) and (χ′ − χ_zf)u_0, χ′ any other function of r̂ equal to 1 near 0 and with compact
support, lie in H^(∞,(∞,a+p,∞))_b, resp. H^(∞,(∞,a,∞))_b.

*Proof.* On supp χ_zf, |σ| ≤ ρ/4, so by (20.18) ρ_tf ∼ ρ, ρ_zf ∼ r̂ = |σ|/ρ and ρ_scf ∼ 1, and the weight is
w_γ ∼ ρ^(γ_tf−γ_zf) |σ|^(γ_zf). (a) By Fubini,

    ∬ |σ|^(2j) |Pu_0|² ρ^(−2(γ_tf−γ_zf)) |σ|^(−2γ_zf) 1_(|σ|≤ρ/4) |dσ/σ| μ_X = C ∫ |Pu_0|² ρ^(−2(γ_tf−j)) μ_X,

the inner integral ∫_0^(ρ/4) σ^(2(j−γ_zf)) dσ/σ = (ρ/4)^(2(j−γ_zf))/(2(j − γ_zf)) converging as γ_zf < j. This is
finite for γ_tf ≤ a + p + j, as Pu_0 ∈ H^(∞,a+p)_b(X). The fields σ∂_σ and ⟨x⟩∂_x fall on σ^j, on χ_zf (bounded
derivatives, Section 20.8.1) and on Pu_0, with the same bound. (b) The coefficients of [P, χ_zf] and of χ′ − χ_zf
are supported in r̂ ∈ [δ, δ⁻¹] for some δ ∈ (0, 1), a compact subset of the interior of tf, where w_γ ∼ ρ^(γ_tf).
Fubini with ∫_(δρ)^(ρ/δ) dσ/σ = 2 log δ⁻¹ bounds the norm by C‖ρ^(−γ_tf) · ‖_(L²(μ_X)) of terms of the form ρ^p times
b-derivatives of u_0, resp. of u_0 itself, finite for γ_tf ≤ a + p, resp. γ_tf ≤ a. ∎

**Lemma 31.4** (The augmented operator near zero energy; [Hin26, Lemma 11.21] in dimension 4 + 1.) For
u_0 ∈ H^(∞,a)_b(X) and |σ| ≤ c:

(a) (L̂_b(σ) − L̂_b(0))(χ_zf u_0) ∈ H^(∞,(∞,a+2,γ_zf))_b for every γ_zf < 1;

(b) for ḃ ∈ 𝔟, S ∈ 𝒮_1 and the columns f̂_ḃ, f̂_S of Definition 28.1 and Definition 28.7, f̂_ḃ(σ) − χ_zf f̂_ḃ(0)
and f̂_S(σ) − χ_zf f̂_S(0) lie in H^(∞,(N,3−ε,1−ε))_b(X^±_(sc-b)) for every N and ε > 0, and
f̂_ḃ(0), f̂_S(0) ∈ 𝒜³ ⊂ H^(∞,3−ε)_b(X).

[Hin26, (11.64)] has ρ_tf² ρ_zf Diff¹_b in (a) and, from [Hin26, Lemma 10.5], the tf-weight 2 + ε_ind − ε for the
columns. In dimension 4 + 1 the columns are one order better at tf, and the rows of L̃_b(σ) do not depend on σ
(Definition 28.7).

*Proof.* (a) L̂_b(σ) − L̂_b(0) = −iσL_1 − σ²L_2, with L_1 ∈ ρ Diff¹_b and L_2 ∈ ρ² C^∞ near ∂X̄ and with smooth
coefficients on compact sets (Section 28.1). Write L_1χ_zf = χ_zf L_1 + [L_1, χ_zf]. Lemma 31.3 (a) with
(p, j) = (1, 1) and (2, 2) puts σχ_zf L_1u_0 and σ²χ_zf L_2u_0 in the space stated, and Lemma 31.3 (b) gives
[L_1, χ_zf]u_0 ∈ H^(∞,(∞,a+1,∞))_b, which the factor σ, of tf-order 1 on the interior of tf, brings to a + 2.

(b) By Lemma 28.4 (a), f̂ = f̂_c + f̂_∞ with f̂_c entire in σ and supported in {r ≤ 2}, and f̂_∞ = r⁻³G(σr, x)
on {r ≥ 1}, with G entire and |(ζ∂_ζ)^j (r∂_r)^i ∂^β_ω G| ≤ C⟨ζ⟩^(−N) for Im ζ ≥ 0. For |σ| ≤ c, χ_zf = 1 on
{r ≤ 2}, so f̂_c(σ) − χ_zf f̂_c(0) = f̂_c(σ) − f̂_c(0) = O(|σ|) in C^∞, supported in {r ≤ 2}, where ρ_zf ∼ |σ|: this
gives the zf-weight 1 − ε and no condition at tf or scf. On {r ≥ 1}, H := G(σr, x) − χ_1(|σ|⟨x⟩)G(0, x)
satisfies |VH| ≤ C min(|σ|r, 1)⟨σr⟩^(−N) for products V of σ∂_σ, r∂_r, ∂_ω: G(ζ) − G(0) = O(|ζ|) where χ_1 = 1, G decays
rapidly where χ_1 = 0, and |σ|⟨x⟩ ∼ |σ|r in between. On {r̂ ≤ 1}, where w_γ ∼ ρ^(γ_tf−γ_zf) |σ|^(γ_zf), Fubini bounds
that part of the squared norm of r⁻³H by

    C ∫ ⟨x⟩^(−4+2(γ_tf−γ_zf)) ∫_0^(1/⟨x⟩) σ^(2−2γ_zf) (dσ/σ) μ_X = C′ ∫ ⟨x⟩^(2γ_tf−6) μ_X,

finite for γ_zf < 1 and γ_tf < 3. On {r̂ ≥ 1} the rapid decay in r̂ and r⁻³ ≤ (ρ_scf ρ_tf)³ give the bound, as in the
proof of Lemma 28.4 (b). f̂(0) ∈ 𝒜³ is Lemma 28.3. ∎

**Lemma 31.5** (The cut-off states near zero energy.) Let G_1, G_2 and the cut-off χ be those of
(29.40) and Section 29.18:

    G_1(σ)(ḃ) := Ψ(σ, ·) ġ_b(ḃ),      G_2(σ)(S) := (Ψ − σ∂_σΨ) h_b(S) − iσΨ h̆_b(S),

with Ψ of Lemma 28.5. For ḃ_0 ∈ 𝔟 and S_0 ∈ 𝒮_1,

    χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(ḃ_0) − χ_zf ġ_b(ḃ_0) ∈ H^(∞,(N,2−ε,1−ε))_b,     χ(|σ|)G_2(σ)(S_0) − χ_zf h_b(S_0) ∈ H^(∞,(N,3−ε,1−ε))_b

for every N and ε > 0; and ġ_b(ḃ_0) ∈ H^(∞,2−ε)_b(X), h_b(S_0) ∈ H^(∞,3−ε)_b(X).

*Proof.* As for Lemma 31.4 (b). For r ≥ 1, Ψ = Φ(σr) with Φ(0) = 1 (Lemma 28.5 (b)); so, with
ζ := σr,

    G_1(ḃ_0) − χ_zf ġ_b = (Φ(ζ) − χ_1(|σ|⟨x⟩)) ġ_b,
    G_2(S_0) − χ_zf h_b = ((Φ − ζΦ′)(ζ) − χ_1(|σ|⟨x⟩)) h_b − iζΦ(ζ) r⁻¹h̆_b,

both O(min(|ζ|, 1)⟨ζ⟩^(−N)) times states in 𝒜², resp. 𝒜³ ((BP3); r⁻¹h̆_b ∈ 𝒜³). For r ≤ 1, Ψ − 1 = O(|σ|) with its
derivatives (Lemma 28.5 (d) and its proof). And χ(|σ|) − 1 vanishes for |σ| ≤ c/2; on supp χ_zf the remaining
term is supported in a compact set of x away from tf and zf. The Fubini count of Lemma 31.4 (b), with ⟨x⟩⁻² in
place of ⟨x⟩⁻³ for G_1, gives γ_tf < 2 there. ∎

### 31.3 The boost parameter

Let h^(≤1)_b(S) = t_* h_b(S) + h̆_b(S) be the generalised state of the boosts at b ((BP3); [Hin26, (6.37), (6.32b)]),
and χ^H_K the cut-off of (28.2): smooth, vanishing for t_* ≤ 1 and for |x| ≥ t_*/2, and equal to 1 on
{t_* ≥ 2, |x| ≤ t_*/4}.

**Proposition 31.6** (The boost parameter; [Hin26, Proposition 11.20] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
b ∈ ℬ̄_* and L := L^(g,g_0), with g_0 := g_(b₀,b,−S), g := g_0 + h, |S| < ε_0, h ∈ 𝒳^∞ and ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) < ε_0, ε_0 and d
those of Theorem 29.17 at b ((BP1)). Let ℓ_I satisfy (29.43), α_K ∈ (1, min(a_K − 1, 3/2)) and α_+ > α_K.
For f ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α_++2,α_K)_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−), the forward solution of Lu = f is

    u = χ^H_K h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ) + ũ,     Ṡ ∈ 𝒮_1,
    ũ ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),β_+,α_K−2)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−)  for every β_+ < min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+),    (31.2)

with Ṡ and ũ depending continuously on f, uniformly in b ∈ ℬ̄_*.

Ṡ is determined by u: ũ has K⁺-weight α_K − 2 > −1, so h_b(Ṡ) is the coefficient of t_* in u at K⁺, and S ↦ h_b(S)
is injective (Lemma 31.2). [Hin26, (11.63)] has the ι⁺-weight 1 − ε and α_K ∈ (1, 1 + ε_K).

*Proof.* *Step 0* ([Hin26, (11.65)]). Fix α′_K ∈ [1/2, 1) with α′_K ≥ α_K − (a_K − 2), possible as α_K < a_K − 1,
and β′_+ ∈ (1, min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+)). Proposition 29.35, with α′_K for α_K (α_+ > α′_K), gives
u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),β′_+,α′_K−2)_b. (29.15) of Proposition 29.12 (3/2 < ℓ_I < a_I + 1/2,
β′_+ < min Re ℰ_+) gives (L − L_b)u the ι⁺-weight β′_+ + 2 + m_+ − ε > 4 (with no expansion term, as
β′_+ + m_+ < 2 min Re ℰ_+) and the K⁺-weight α′_K − 2 + a_K ≥ α_K. Fix

    α^♯_+ ∈ (α_K, min(α_+, λ_♯)),     α^♯_+ ≥ min(α_+, 3/2) − ε,    (31.3)

for a given small ε > 0. Then α^♯_+ ∈ (1, 7/4) ⊂ (1, 2), α^♯_+ − 1 ∈ (0, 1) and α^♯_+ − α_K ∈ (0, 1). So

    L_b u = f′ := f − (L − L_b)u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α^♯_++2,α_K)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−).

*Step 1* (null infinity; [Hin26, (11.66a)]). Proposition 29.29 with ℰ̆_+ := ∅ and ℓ̆_+ := α^♯_+ applies, as
α^♯_+ < λ_♯ < min Re ℰ^C_I (Definition 27.6 (2)), so α^♯_+ ∉ Re π_1ℰ^C_I and α^♯_+ ≠ λ_♯. It gives u_I, supported
near ℐ⁺ and vanishing for t_* < 1, with ι⁺-data (ℰ^♯_+, α^♯_+) and f′ − L_b u_I ∈
H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,(ℰ^♯_++2,α^♯_++2),α_K)_b. As min Re ℰ^♯_+ = λ_♯ > α^♯_+ ((29.32) with ℰ̆_+ = ∅; min Re ℰ^C_I is
larger), both are plain weights:

    u^♭ := u − u_I :     L_b u^♭ = f^♭ := f′ − L_b u_I ∈ H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,α^♯_++2,α_K)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−).

In [Hin26] the set ℰ^♯_+ contains (1, 0), which leaves a t_*^(−3) term at ι⁺ in f^♭, removed there by [Hin26,
Proposition 9.11] at λ = 1; in dimension 4 + 1 there is no such term. u^♭ vanishes for t_* < 1, so it is the forward
solution of L_b u^♭ = f^♭ (Proposition 17.14).

*Step 2* (the decomposition). As in Section 29.18, u^♭ = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing, with ℱu_hi =
(1 − χ(|σ|))L̂_b(σ)⁻¹ f̂^♭(σ), ℱu_reg = χ(|σ|)û_(reg,1)(σ), (û_(reg,1), b̂_1, Ŝ_1) := L̃_b(σ)⁻¹(f̂^♭(σ), 0, 0), and
u_sing = v_ġ + v_h with

    ℱ(∂_(t_*) v_ġ) = χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(b̂_1(σ)),        ℱ(∂²_(t_*) v_h) = χ(|σ|)G_2(σ)(Ŝ_1(σ))

((29.40)). The memberships (31.4)–(31.14) are read as there: at order k, with the c of
that order and of the weight α of (28.1) with α + 2 = α^♯_+ − α_K. The functions u, u_I, u^♭ and ũ and the
parameter Ṡ = S_0 (obtained from L̃_b(0)⁻¹) do not depend on c, so their memberships hold at every order.
Lemma 29.32 (β^f_I = ℓ_I, β_ι = α^♯_+, β_K = α_K ∈ (1, 2); ℓ_I + 1 ≥ α^♯_+ + 2 − (1 − ε_1), as ℓ_I ≥ 2) gives
u_hi ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−ε,N,N))_b(M′). Proposition 20.18 (1), with β_K = α_K ∈ (1, 2), gives

    f̂^♭|_(±(0,c]) ∈ H^(∞,(3−ε,α^♯_++1,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b(X^±_(sc-b))    (31.4)

(its scf-weight is min(ℓ_I + 1, α^♯_+ + 2) − ε ≥ 3 − ε), with zf-coefficient f̂^♭(0) = ∫ f^♭ dt_* ∈
H^(∞,α^♯_++1)_b(X), the same for both signs (f^♭(·, x) is integrable, its K⁺-weight being α_K > 1).

*Step 3.1* (zero energy; [Hin26, (11.68)–(11.70)]). By Proposition 28.8 at the weight α := α^♯_+ − 3, so that
α + 2 = α^♯_+ − 1 ∈ (0, 1) and 𝒴_0 = H̄^(s−1,α+2)_b has the μ_b-weight α^♯_+ + 1 (Section 20.9.1), at every
regularity s,

    (û_0, ḃ_0, S_0) := L̃_b(0)⁻¹(f̂^♭(0), 0, 0),     û_0 ∈ H^(∞,α^♯_+−1)_b(X),   ḃ_0 ∈ 𝔟,   S_0 ∈ 𝒮_1.    (31.5)

The rows of L̃_b(σ) do not depend on σ, and ⟨χ_zf û_0, f*_j⟩ = ⟨û_0, f*_j⟩ = 0 once c is so small that χ_zf = 1 on
supp f*_j; and χ_zf û_0 ∈ 𝒳_σ for σ ≠ 0, having compact support in x. So, for 0 < |σ| ≤ c,

    L̃_b(σ)(χ_zf û_0, ḃ_0, S_0) = (f̂^♭(σ) − f̂_2(σ), 0, 0),    (31.6)

    f̂_2 := (f̂^♭ − χ_zf f̂^♭(0)) − [L̂_b(0), χ_zf]û_0 − (L̂_b(σ) − L̂_b(0))(χ_zf û_0)
             − (f̂_(ḃ_0)(σ) − χ_zf f̂_(ḃ_0)(0)) − (f̂_(S_0)(σ) − χ_zf f̂_(S_0)(0)),

using L̂_b(0)û_0 + f̂_(ḃ_0)(0) + f̂_(S_0)(0) = f̂^♭(0), which is (31.5). The first term of f̂_2 lies in
H^(∞,(3−ε,α^♯_++1,α_K−1))_b by (31.4) and the definition of the space; the second in
H^(∞,(∞,α^♯_++1,∞))_b (Lemma 31.3 (b), p = 2, a = α^♯_+ − 1); the third in H^(∞,(∞,α^♯_++1,γ_zf))_b for every
γ_zf < 1 (Lemma 31.4 (a)); the last two in H^(∞,(N,3−ε,1−ε))_b (Lemma 31.4 (b)). As α^♯_+ < 2 − ε and
α_K − 1 < 1 − ε for ε small,

    f̂_2|_(±(0,c]) ∈ H^(∞,(5/2−ε,α^♯_++1,α_K−1))_b(X^±_(sc-b)).    (31.7)

*Step 3.2* (the rest; [Hin26, (11.71)]). By (31.6),

    (û_(reg,1), b̂_1, Ŝ_1) = (χ_zf û_0, ḃ_0, S_0) + L̃_b(σ)⁻¹(f̂_2(σ), 0, 0).

Lemma 29.33 with β_scf := 3/2 − ε, β_tf := α^♯_+ − 1, β_zf := α_K − 1 (α + 2 := α^♯_+ − α_K ∈ (0, 1)) applies
to (31.7), so

    û_(reg,1) ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−2ε,α^♯_+−1,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b,
    b̂_1 ∈ H^(∞,((0,0),α_K−1))_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|; 𝔟),      Ŝ_1 ∈ H^(∞,((0,0),α_K−1))_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|; 𝒮_1),
    (31.8)

with the coefficients û_0, ḃ_0, S_0 at σ = 0, the same for both signs (û_0 ∈ H^(∞,α^♯_+−1)_b(X) being the
zf-coefficient of the tf-weight α^♯_+ − 1). By Proposition 20.20 (1), applied to χ(|σ|)û_(reg,1), which is
supported where the cut-off of Proposition 20.20 is 1 as c ≤ 1/2, with β_K = α_K ∈ (1, 2) and the one Taylor
coefficient, of order 0 < α_K − 1, the same for the two signs,

    u_reg ∈ H^(∞,(min(3/2,α^♯_+)−3ε,α^♯_+,α_K))_b(M′).    (31.9)

*Step 3.3* (the singular part; [Hin26, (11.72)–(11.74)]). By (29.40), Lemma 31.5 and
Lemma 29.34 with a = α_K − 1, applied to b̂_1 − ḃ_0 and Ŝ_1 − S_0,

    ℱ(∂_(t_*) v_ġ) ∈ H^(∞,(N,2−ε,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b,     ℱ(∂²_(t_*) v_h) ∈ H^(∞,(N,3−ε,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b,

with zf-coefficients ġ_b(ḃ_0) and h_b(S_0): the tf-weights α_K + 1 − ε and α_K + 2 − ε of the remainders exceed 2 − ε
and 3 − ε, and 1 − ε > α_K − 1. Multiplication by −iσ takes the first to H^(∞,(N,3−ε,α_K−1))_b with zero
zf-coefficient (Lemma 31.3 (a) with j = 1 for σχ_zf ġ_b(ḃ_0); α_K − 1 < 1), so

    ℱ(∂²_(t_*) u_sing) ∈ H^(∞,(N,3−ε,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b(X^±_(sc-b)),   with zf-coefficient h_b(S_0) for both signs.
    (31.10)

This is [Hin26, (11.72a)–(11.72b)], with the tf-weight 3 − ε in place of 2 − ε. As u^♭ = 0 for t_* < 1,
u_sing = −(u_hi + u_reg) there, so by (31.9)

    u_sing|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(∞,min(3/2,α^♯_+)−3ε,α^♯_+,α_K)_b,
    ∂_(t_*)u_sing|_(Ω_−) ∈ H̄^(∞,min(3/2,α^♯_+)−3ε,α^♯_++1,α_K+1)_b,    (31.11)

∂_(t_*) raising the ι- and K-weights by 1 (Section 29.15).

*First integration.* Lemma 29.31 applies to v := ∂_(t_*)u_sing with β_I := 3/2, β_ι := α^♯_+ + 1 and
β_K := α_K − 1 ∈ (0, 1/2): β_ι > β_I; β_K ≤ β_ι − β_I = α^♯_+ − 1/2, as α^♯_+ > α_K; β_K ∈ (−1, 1) ∖ {0}; the
zf-restrictions of the two signs agree by (31.10); v|_(Ω_<) has weights at least (∞, β_ι, β_K) by
(31.11); ℱv is supported in a compact subset of (−c, c), c ≤ 1/2, as Lemma 29.31 asks (as in the
proof of Proposition 29.35); and the tf-weight 3 − ε of (31.10) is at least β_ι = α^♯_+ + 1. So

    ∂_(t_*)u_sing ∈ H^(∞,3/2,α^♯_++1−ε,((0,0),α_K−1))_b(M′).    (31.12)

*Second integration.* Lemma 29.30 (1) applies to u_sing with (β_I, β_ι, β_K) := (min(3/2, α^♯_+) − 3ε,
α^♯_+ − ε, α_K − 2) and ℰ_K := {(−1, 0)}, so that ℰ_K + 1 = {(0, 0)} (α_K − 2 ∈ (−1, −1/2) is not 0). Its hypotheses
are (31.11) (at K⁻ the weight α_K, with no expansion) and (31.12). So

    u_sing ∈ H^(∞,min(3/2,α^♯_+)−3ε,min(3/2,α^♯_+)−4ε,({(−1,0),(0,0)},α_K−2))_b(M′),    (31.13)

in which only (−1, 0) lies below the weight α_K − 2 ∈ (−1, −1/2): u_sing = t_* χ^H_K u_(K⁺) + O(α_K − 2) at K⁺, for
some u_(K⁺) on K⁺.

*Step 3.4* (the coefficient; [Hin26, (11.75)]). u_(K⁺) is the (0, 0)-coefficient of ∂_(t_*)u_sing at K⁺ in
(31.12), that is, lim_(t_*→∞) ∂_(t_*)u_sing(t_*, x). As ∂_(t_*)u_sing tends to 0 as t_* → −∞ (its
K⁻-weight is α_K + 1 > 0), and ∂²_(t_*)u_sing(·, x) is integrable (its K⁺-weight is α_K > 1 by (31.10) and
Proposition 20.20 (1), and ⟨t_*⟩^(−α_K) L²(dt_*/⟨t_*⟩) ⊂ L¹ for α_K > 1),

    u_(K⁺) = ∫_ℝ ∂²_(t_*)u_sing dt_* = ℱ(∂²_(t_*)u_sing)(0) = h_b(S_0)

by (31.10). So, with Ṡ := S_0 = Ŝ_1(0),

    u_sing − χ^H_K t_* h_b(Ṡ) ∈ H^(∞,min(3/2,α^♯_+)−3ε,min(3/2,α^♯_+)−4ε,α_K−2)_b(M′),    (31.14)

χ^H_K t_* h_b(Ṡ) itself being ρ_K⁻¹ρ_ι² times a bounded conormal function near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺ (h_b ∈ 𝒜³, and χ^H_K = 0 near
ℐ⁺), so of ι⁺-weight 2 − ε. Replacing t_* h_b by h^(≤1)_b = t_* h_b + h̆_b changes this by χ^H_K h̆_b(Ṡ), of weights
(∞, 2 − ε, −ε) (h̆_b ∈ 𝒜² is stationary), which lies within (31.14) as α_K − 2 < −ε. In [Hin26], (10.13)
identifies the total integral of ∂²_(t_*) applied to the augmented generalised state with h_(b,s1); here the augmented
state is χ^H_K h^(≤1)_b(S) (Definition 28.1), and G_2(0)(S) = Ψ(0, ·)h_b(S) = h_b(S) directly.

*Step 4* (null infinity). So u = χ^H_K h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ) + ũ with ũ := u_I + u_hi + u_reg + (u_sing − χ^H_K h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ)), of
ι⁺-weight ℓ′_+ := min(3/2, α^♯_+) − 4ε and K⁺-weight α_K − 2 (Steps 1–3; u_I is supported near ℐ⁺). Near ℐ⁺,
χ^H_K = 0, so Lũ = f there, and Proposition 29.27 with ℓ_+ := min(ℓ′_+, min Re ℰ_+ − ε) gives the ℐ⁺-data
(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I). Its hypotheses hold: ℓ_+ ∉ Re π_1ℰ_+, and lowering the a priori weight is free;
3/2 < ℓ_I < min(a_I + 1/2, ℓ_I^max) by (29.43); ℓ_+ < min(ℓ_I, a_+ + min Re ℰ_+); and ℓ_+ lies below
min Re ℰ_+, so that (ℰ_+, ℓ_+) is the weight ℓ_+, and below min Re ℰ^tot_I = 3/2. As α^♯_+ ≥ min(α_+, 3/2) − ε and
ε is arbitrary, (31.2) holds for every β_+ < min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+); Ṡ does not depend on these
choices, being determined by u.

*Continuity.* f′ depends continuously on f (Proposition 29.35 and (29.15)), and u_I, f̂^♭(0),
(û_0, ḃ_0, S_0), f̂_2, the pieces of Step 2 and the integrations are linear maps bounded between the spaces above (the
construction of Proposition 29.29, Proposition 28.8, Lemma 31.3–Lemma 31.5, Lemma 29.30,
Lemma 29.31, Lemma 29.32–Lemma 29.34, Proposition 20.18 (1) and Proposition 20.20 (1)). So
Ṡ = S_0 and ũ depend continuously on f; the ℐ⁺-data of Step 4 do so by the closed graph theorem, L being fixed, or
by the constructive bound of Proposition 29.27. Every input is uniform on ℬ̄_* by (BP1)–(BP5), and so are the bounds. ∎

### 31.4 Undoing the boost: the setting

Section 31.4–Section 31.7 are [Hin26, Section 11.4.2] in dimension 4 + 1. They construct the correction terms
that let a right-hand side generate the boost term of Proposition 31.6 ([Hin26, Definition 11.23, Lemma 11.24]),
the identity behind them ([Hin26, (11.76)–(11.78b)]), the augmented gauge-fixed Einstein operator ([Hin26, Definition
11.25]) and its linearisation in the boost parameter ([Hin26, Lemma 11.28]), and they eliminate the boosts ([Hin26,
Proposition 11.30, (11.95)]). Four things differ from [Hin26]. There are no logarithms: the correction h^(−1) has the
index set (2, 0) ∪ (2 + ℰ_ind) at ι⁺ and its linearised curvature (4, 0) ∪ (4 + ℰ_ind), with nothing to cancel,
where [Hin26, (11.82)] cancels a (3, 1)-coefficient. The parameter derivatives begin at order 4 at ι⁺, above every
weight that Proposition 31.6 uses, so the splitting of [Hin26, (11.86), Remark 11.29] and the special treatment of
(3, 0)-terms are not needed. The boosts of Section 21.7 are centred at t = 0 and the model states of
Proposition 23.28 at t̄ = 0, with t̄ − t → C′, a translation, so the generalised state is re-centred
(Lemma 31.8). And the augmented operator is taken in the form of [Hin26, Remark 11.27], so that its
linearisation is exactly the operator of Theorem 29.17 with a shifted perturbation.

*Cut-offs.* χ^♭_K, χ_K, χ^♯_K, χ_IVP, χ^♯_IVP and χ_r are the cut-offs of Section 21.7, with (29.2).
From here on χ_K is this cut-off: smooth on M, equal to 1 near K⁺ (on supp χ^♭_K ⊃ {|x| < t/10, t > 60R₁}) and to 0
near ℐ⁺ (supp χ_K ⊂ {|x| < t/2}), supported in {t^♭_* ≥ 10}, with Cartesian derivatives ∂χ_K ∈ ρ_+C^∞ near (ι⁺)°
(the proof of Lemma 29.13). χ^H_K := χ_+(t_*)χ_c(|x|/t_*) is the cut-off of (28.2), the one in
Proposition 31.6. Put

    𝒞 := supp χ_K ∩ supp(1 − χ_K),

whose closure meets ∂M only in a compact subset of (ι⁺)° (the proof of Lemma 29.13). Every derivative of χ_K
is supported in 𝒞, and χ^♭_K = 0 on 𝒞, as supp χ^♭_K ⊂ int χ_K⁻¹(1).

*Boosts.* For S = S_w ∈ 𝒮_1 let ω̄(S) := t d(|x|S) − |x|S dt = t w · dx − (w · x)dt, η := −dt² + dx²,
X_S := η⁻¹ω̄(S), Θ := χ_r(|x|)χ^♯_IVP(1 − χ^♭_K), V(S) := ½ΘX_S and φ_S := exp V(S) (Lemma 21.26). For the
fixed b ∈ ℬ̄_*, the background of the base point is

    g_S := g_(b₀,b,−S) = (1 − χ_K)φ*_(−S) g_(b₀) + χ_K g_b    (31.15)

((29.1)). Θ = 1 on 𝒞 ∩ {t ≥ T_1} for some T_1: there χ^♭_K = 0, |x| ≥ t/10 (so χ_r = 1 once t ≥ 60R₁),
and t_IVP = t − C″ > −|x|/10 (so χ^♯_IVP = 1). Put

    w(S) := g_(b₀)(X_S, ·) = g_(b₀)η⁻¹ω̄(S),        so that        g_(b₀)(V(S), ·) = ½Θ w(S).

*Conventions.* δ*_g is the symmetrised covariant derivative and δ_g h = −∇^κ h_(κμ) (Section 21.8), so
ℒ_X g = 2δ*_g(g(X, ·)); with a ⊗_s b := ½(a ⊗ b + b ⊗ a),

    [δ*_g, χ]ω = dχ ⊗_s ω,        [δ_g, χ]h = −ι_(g⁻¹dχ) h.    (31.16)

P(g, g_0), Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g_0), δ*_(g_0,E_C) and δ_(g_0,E_Υ) are those of Definition 21.28; L^(g,g_0) := D_1P(·, g_0) at
g, and L_b = L^(g_b,g_b) = D_(g_b)Ric + δ*_(g_b,E_C)δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b) ((21.48)). Three identities are used
throughout.

(i) Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g) = 0 for every g ((21.43)), so (D_1 + D_2)Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g) = 0 and P(g, g) = Ric(g).

(ii) D_1Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g) = −δ_(g,E_Υ)G_g. Indeed Υ⁰(g, g_0) = g g_0⁻¹δ_gG_g g_0 (Section 21.8), so by
(21.43) D_1Υ⁰(g, g)k = D(δ_gG_g)(k) g = −δ_gG_g k, as δ_gG_g g = 0 for every g; the E^Υ-term contributes
−E^Υ_g G_g k, which is (21.46) at g_0 = g.

(iii) If Ric(g) = 0, then D_gRic(ℒ_Y g) = ℒ_Y Ric(g) = 0 for every smooth vector field Y (differentiate
Ric(ψ_ε^* g) = ψ_ε^* Ric(g) along the flow ψ_ε of Y); in particular D_gRic ∘ δ*_g = 0.

*The boost states at b₀.* The corrections below are built from b₀-objects. By Proposition 23.28 at b₀, with
ω_s1(S) := ω^(0)_(b₀,s1)(S) and ω̆(S) := ω̆^((0),1)_(b₀,s1)(S), stationary and linear in S,

    ω_s1(S) − ω̄_s1(S) ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)),        ω̆(S) − ω̄̆_s1(S) ∈ 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)),

where ω̄_s1(S) = d(|x|S), ω̄̆_s1(S) = |x| d(|x|S) − |x|S dt̄ and t̄ = t_* + |x| are the Minkowski 1-forms of
Section 23.13. h(S) := δ*_(g_(b₀))ω_s1(S) ∈ 𝒜^((3,0)∪(3+ℰ_ind)), and

    h^(≤1)(S) = t_* h(S) + h̆(S) = δ*_(g_(b₀))(t_* ω_s1(S) + ω̆(S)),        h̆(S) ∈ 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)),

is the generalised state h^(≤1)_(b₀) of (BP3); h(S) and h^(≤1)(S) lie in the kernels of D_(g_(b₀))Ric and of
δ_(g_(b₀),E_Υ)G_(g_(b₀)). Near infinity t̄ = t + C′ − 8m₀|x|⁻¹ (Section 23.13, from (21.30)) and
g_(b₀) − η ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞ ((21.29), Proposition 21.21); C′ is that constant.

**Definition 31.7** (The re-centred states.) At b₀,

    ω^(≤1)_♮(S) := (t_* − C′)ω_s1(S) + ω̆(S),        h^(≤1)_♮(S) := δ*_(g_(b₀))ω^(≤1)_♮(S) = h^(≤1)(S) − C′h(S),

and at b ∈ ℬ̄_*, with the same constant C′,

    ω^(≤1)_(b,♮)(S) := (t_* − C′)ω^(0)_(b,s1)(S) + ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1)(S),
    h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(S) := δ*_(g_b)ω^(≤1)_(b,♮)(S) = h^(≤1)_b(S) − C′h_b(S).

Each lies in the kernels of D Ric and of δ_(E_Υ)G at its own metric, being a linear combination of the generalised
state and the state of (BP3). At b₀, h^(≤1)_(b₀,♮) = h^(≤1)_♮.

**Lemma 31.8** (The time origin.) (a) Near infinity,

    (t_* − C′)ω̄_s1(S) + ω̄̆_s1(S) − ω̄(S) = −8m₀|x|⁻¹(d(|x|S) + S d|x|) ∈ |x|⁻¹C^∞(X̄; T*).

(b) Let ℓ_I ∈ ℝ, β_+ < 2 and α_K < 2. If u = χ^H_K h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ) + ũ with ũ ∈
H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),β_+,α_K−2)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−), then u = χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ) + ũ′ with ũ′ in the same space, linear and
continuous in (Ṡ, ũ).

*Proof.* (a) As t_* = t̄ − |x|,

    (t_* − C′)d(|x|S) + |x| d(|x|S) − |x|S dt̄ − t d(|x|S) + |x|S dt = (t̄ − C′ − t)d(|x|S) − |x|S d(t̄ − t),

and t̄ − C′ − t = −8m₀|x|⁻¹, d(t̄ − t) = 8m₀|x|⁻²d|x|. The Cartesian components of |x|⁻¹d(|x|S) = |x|⁻¹w · dx and of
S d|x| lie in |x|⁻¹C^∞, resp. C^∞, homogeneous of degree −1, resp. 0.

(b) ũ′ := u − χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ) vanishes near {t^♭_* = 1}, as u does and χ_K = 0 for t^♭_* < 10, and

    ũ′ − ũ = (χ^H_K − χ_K)h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ) + C′χ_K h_b(Ṡ).

Both cut-offs are smooth on M, equal to 1 near K⁺ (χ^H_K = 1 on {|x| ≤ t_*/4, t_* ≥ 2}) and to 0 near ℐ⁺; so
χ^H_K − χ_K is supported in a set whose closure meets ∂M in a compact subset of (ι⁺)°. There |x| ∼ t_*, and functions
in 𝒜^ℰ(X̄) are in 𝒜^ℰ at ι⁺, ⟨x⟩⁻¹ being ρ_+ times a positive smooth function; so h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ) = t_* h_b(Ṡ) + h̆_b(Ṡ)
lies in 𝒜^((2,0)∪(2+ℰ_ind)) ((BP3)), hence in H^(∞,2−ε)_b at ι⁺, with no condition at ℐ⁺ or K⁺; the compact part is
smooth. And χ_K h_b(Ṡ) vanishes near ℐ⁺, is bounded and stationary near K⁺ (K⁺-weight −ε for every ε > 0, above
α_K − 2 < 0), and is O(⟨x⟩⁻³) with its b-derivatives near ι⁺ (ι⁺-weight 3 − ε). As β_+ < 2, both terms lie in the
space of ũ. ∎

### 31.5 The correction terms and the augmented operator

This section is [Hin26, (11.76)–(11.85)] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Definition 31.9** (The correction terms; [Hin26, Definition 11.23] in dimension 4 + 1.) For S ∈ 𝒮_1,

    h^(−1)(S) := −[δ*_(g_(b₀)), χ_K](ω^(≤1)_♮(S) − Θw(S)) = −dχ_K ⊗_s (ω^(≤1)_♮(S) − Θw(S)),
    ϑ^(−1)(S) := [δ_(g_(b₀),E_Υ)G_(g_(b₀)), χ_K]h^(≤1)_♮(S) = −ι_(g_(b₀)⁻¹dχ_K) G_(g_(b₀)) h^(≤1)_♮(S),
    ϑ_♯(S) := ϑ^(−1)(S) + D_1Υ^(E_Υ)(g_(b₀), g_(b₀))h^(−1)(S) = ϑ^(−1)(S) − δ_(g_(b₀),E_Υ)G_(g_(b₀))h^(−1)(S).

All three are linear in S, and they are the same tensors at every base point. In [Hin26] h^(−1) is built from
ω̄^((0),≤1)_s1 without the factor Θ. Here w(S) is the 1-form of the boost family of Section 21.7, so that
(31.19) below is exact, and Θ = 1 where it matters (Lemma 31.10); ϑ_♯ carries the counterterm of
[Hin26, Remark 11.27].

**Lemma 31.10** ([Hin26, Lemma 11.24] in dimension 4 + 1.) h^(−1)(S), ϑ^(−1)(S) and ϑ_♯(S) are supported
in 𝒞 and smooth, and, with 𝒢 := (2, 0) ∪ (2 + ℰ_ind), near (ι⁺)°

    h^(−1)(S) ∈ 𝒜^𝒢,      D_(g_0)Ric(h^(−1)(S)) ∈ 𝒜^(𝒢+2),      ϑ^(−1)(S), ϑ_♯(S) ∈ 𝒜^(𝒢+1),    (31.17)

for every metric g_0 smooth on M near (ι⁺)° with g_0 − η ∈ ρ_+C^∞ there; the seminorms are O(|S|).

*Proof.* Each is a differential expression with a factor dχ_K, so it is supported in 𝒞; it is smooth, as
ω^(≤1)_♮, w, Θ and h^(≤1)_♮ are. Near (ι⁺)°, on 𝒞 ∩ {t ≥ T_1}, Θ = 1 and |x| ≥ t/10, and, omitting S,

    ω^(≤1)_♮ − w = (t_* − C′)(ω_s1 − ω̄_s1) + (ω̆ − ω̄̆_s1) + ((t_* − C′)ω̄_s1 + ω̄̆_s1 − ω̄) + (η − g_(b₀))η⁻¹ω̄.

With t_* ∈ ρ_+⁻¹C^∞ there, the four terms lie in 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)), 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)), ρ_+C^∞
(Lemma 31.8 (a)) and ρ_+²C^∞ · ρ_+⁻¹C^∞ = ρ_+C^∞ (the components of ω̄ are tw and −w · x). So
ω^(≤1)_♮ − w ∈ 𝒜^((1,0)∪(1+ℰ_ind)), with no logarithm, and dχ_K ∈ ρ_+C^∞ gives h^(−1) ∈ 𝒜^𝒢. D_(g_0)Ric is a
second-order operator whose coefficients are smooth functions of g_0⁻¹, g_0 and its first two Cartesian derivatives,
and Cartesian derivatives lie in ρ_+𝒱_b, so D_(g_0)Ric ∈ ρ_+²Diff²_b with smooth coefficients near (ι⁺)°, and it maps
𝒜^𝒢 into 𝒜^(𝒢+2). h^(≤1)_♮ = (t_* − C′)h + h̆ ∈ 𝒜^𝒢 near (ι⁺)°, and ι_(g_(b₀)⁻¹dχ_K) has coefficients in ρ_+C^∞, so
ϑ^(−1) ∈ 𝒜^(𝒢+1). δ_(g_(b₀),E_Υ)G_(g_(b₀)) ∈ ρ_+Diff¹_b there: δ by the Cartesian count, and E^Υ_(g_(b₀)) has
coefficients c_Υ ∈ |x|⁻¹C^∞ and c_(Υ,H), which vanishes for |x| ≥ 5R₁ ((21.41)); so ϑ_♯ ∈ 𝒜^(𝒢+1). ∎

[Hin26, (11.79)–(11.81)] have the index sets (1, 1) ∪ (1 + ℰ_ind), (3, 0) ∪ (3 + ℰ_ind) and (2, 0) ∪ (2 + ℰ_ind),
and the middle membership there needs the vanishing of a (3, 1)-coefficient ([Hin26, (11.82)]). The absence of a
logarithm here comes from Proposition 23.28 (1).

**Definition 31.11** (The augmented operator; [Hin26, Definition 11.25] in dimension 4 + 1, in the form of
[Hin26, Remark 11.27].) For small S ∈ 𝒮_1, b ∈ ℬ̄_* and h ∈ 𝒳^∞ with small 𝒳^d-norm, with g_0 := g_(b₀,b,−S) and
g′ := g_0 + h^(−1)(S) + h, put

    P_1(h, S, b) := Ric(g′) − δ*_(g_0,E_C)(Υ^(E_Υ)(g′, g_0) − ϑ_♯(S)),     L_(h,S) := D_hP_1(·, S, b) at h.
    (31.18)

P_1(0, 0, b₀) = P(g_(b₀), g_(b₀)) = 0. For b ≠ b₀, P_1(0, 0, b) need not vanish on 𝒞, where the background
interpolates between g_(b₀) and g_b; the linear theory uses only D_hP_1 and D_SP_1. [Hin26, (11.83)] has
Υ^(E_Υ)(g_0 + h, g_0) and ϑ^(−1); [Hin26, Remark 11.27] notes that the present form makes the linearisation in h
exactly a gauge-fixed linearised Einstein operator (Lemma 31.13). With the form of [Hin26, (11.83)] one needs in
addition that D_(g′)Ric − D_(g_0+h)Ric is of the error class.

**Lemma 31.12** (The boost identity at b₀; [Hin26, (11.76)–(11.78b)] in dimension 4 + 1.) At b = b₀, for
Ṡ ∈ 𝒮_1,

    D_SP_1(0, S, b₀)|_(S=0)(Ṡ) = L_(b₀)(χ_K h^(≤1)_♮(Ṡ))
                               = −D_(g_(b₀))Ric([δ*_(g_(b₀)), χ_K]ω^(≤1)_♮(Ṡ)) + δ*_(g_(b₀),E_C)ϑ^(−1)(Ṡ).
    (31.19)

Its form at b ∈ ℬ̄_* is Lemma 31.18.

*Proof.* In this proof b = b₀, g_S = g_(b₀,b₀,−S), and δ*, D Ric, δ*_(E_C), δ_(E_Υ), G are taken at g_(b₀).
*The background.* s ↦ φ_(−sṠ) = exp(−sV(Ṡ)) is the flow of −V(Ṡ), so ∂_S φ*_(−S)g_(b₀)|_(S=0)(Ṡ) =
−ℒ_(V(Ṡ))g_(b₀) = −δ*(Θw(Ṡ)), and with (31.16)

    k′ := ∂_S g_S|_(S=0)(Ṡ) = −(1 − χ_K)δ*(Θw) = −δ*((1 − χ_K)Θw) − [δ*, χ_K](Θw).

*The curvature term.* At S = 0, g′ = g_(b₀) (h = 0 and h^(−1)(0) = 0), and ∂_S g′ = k′ + h^(−1)(Ṡ). By (iii),
D Ric(k′) = −D Ric([δ*, χ_K](Θw)), and adding D Ric(h^(−1)(Ṡ)) = −D Ric([δ*, χ_K](ω^(≤1)_♮ − Θw)) gives
∂_S Ric(g′) = −D Ric([δ*, χ_K]ω^(≤1)_♮(Ṡ)).

*The gauge term.* At S = 0 the bracket in (31.18) is Υ^(E_Υ)(g_(b₀), g_(b₀)) − 0 = 0, so only its
derivative counts. With D_jΥ := D_jΥ^(E_Υ)(g_(b₀), g_(b₀)), by (i) and the definition of ϑ_♯,

    D_1Υ(k′ + h^(−1)(Ṡ)) + D_2Υ(k′) − ϑ_♯(Ṡ) = D_1Υ h^(−1)(Ṡ) − ϑ^(−1)(Ṡ) − D_1Υ h^(−1)(Ṡ) = −ϑ^(−1)(Ṡ),

so the gauge term contributes +δ*_(E_C)ϑ^(−1)(Ṡ). This is the right side of (31.19).

*The left side.* h^(≤1)_♮ = δ*ω^(≤1)_♮ lies in both kernels, so with (31.16) and (iii),

    L_(b₀)(χ_K h^(≤1)_♮) = D Ric(δ*(χ_K ω^(≤1)_♮) − [δ*, χ_K]ω^(≤1)_♮)
                           + δ*_(E_C)(χ_K δ_(E_Υ)G h^(≤1)_♮ + [δ_(E_Υ)G, χ_K]h^(≤1)_♮),

which is −D Ric([δ*, χ_K]ω^(≤1)_♮) + δ*_(E_C)ϑ^(−1). ∎

As in [Hin26], (31.19) says that the right-hand side D_SP_1(0, 0, b₀)(Ṡ), supported in 𝒞, generates the
forward solution χ_K h^(≤1)_♮(Ṡ): the final black hole boosted along −Ṡ, without an initial boost.

**Lemma 31.13** (The linearisation in h; [Hin26, (11.84)–(11.85)] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume

    2 + ℰ_ind ⊂ ℰ_+.    (31.20)

(ℰ_ind is the index set of Proposition 23.28, independent of b by (BP3) and fixed once, so (31.20) is a
condition on ℰ_+.) Then h^(−1)(S) ∈ 𝒳^∞ with ‖h^(−1)(S)‖_(𝒳^k) ≤ C_k|S|, and, at b ∈ ℬ̄_*,

    L_(h,S) = L^(g′,g_0),       g′ = g_0 + h′,     h′ := h^(−1)(S) + h,     g_0 = g_S.

So for |S| and ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) small, L_(h,S) is the operator of Theorem 29.17 at b with (S, h′) in place of (S, h),
and Proposition 29.7, Proposition 29.12, Corollary 29.16, Theorem 29.17, Proposition 29.27,
Proposition 29.29, Proposition 29.35 and Proposition 31.6 hold for it, with their constants for (S, h′).

*Proof.* ϑ_♯(S) does not depend on h, so D_hP_1 = D_(g′)Ric − δ*_(g_0,E_C)D_1Υ^(E_Υ)(g′, g_0) = L^(g′,g_0)
((21.48)). By Lemma 31.10, h^(−1)(S) vanishes near ℐ⁺ and K⁺ and for t^♭_* < 10, is smooth, and near
(ι⁺)° lies in 𝒜^𝒢; 𝒢 ⊂ ℰ_+ by (2, 0) ∈ ℰ_+ ((29.3)) and (31.20), so h^(−1)(S) lies in
H^(∞,(ℰ_+,a_+))_b at ι⁺ for every a_+, with norms O(|S|). ∎

[Hin26] asks ℰ_+ ⊃ 1 + ℰ_ind and j(ℰ_+ ∪ (1, 1)) ⊂ ℰ_+ ∪ (1, 1) ([Hin26, (11.85)]), the latter for its logarithm; in
dimension 4 + 1, (31.20) and (29.3) suffice.

### 31.6 The linearisation in the boost parameter

This section is [Hin26, Lemma 11.28] in dimension 4 + 1. Let

    𝒦 := H^(∞,(⟨(3,0)⟩_0,∞),((2,0),∞),∞)_b(Ω_*),

the class of Lemma 29.11, contained in 𝒳^∞ (the proof of Proposition 29.7). By Lemma 29.11,
k_S := g_S − g_b ∈ 𝒦. Its proof rests on (21.40) of Lemma 21.27, with h_(S_w) smooth in w, and on the
pullbacks of Lemma 21.26, smooth in w; so S ↦ k_S ∈ 𝒦 is smooth, and k′ := ∂_S k_S(S′) = ∂_S g_S(S′) ∈ 𝒦 with
seminorms O(|S′|). k′ = −(1 − χ_K)∂_S(φ*_(−S)g_(b₀))(S′) does not depend on b, and it vanishes on int χ_K⁻¹(1), a
neighbourhood of K⁺.

**Lemma 31.14** (The derivative of the operator family.) Let |S| and ‖h‖_(𝒳⁵) be small, h ∈ 𝒳^k, k ≥ 5,
s ∈ [0, 1], S′ ∈ 𝒮_1, and L̇ := ∂_S[L^(g_S+sh, g_S)](S′), the derivative of the coefficients. Then L̇ vanishes near
K⁺, lies in the class (29.12), and for 3/2 < ℓ_I < a_I + 1/2, 0 < ℓ_+ ≤ max(a_+, min Re ℰ_+),
ℓ_+ < a_+ + min Re ℰ_+ and every ε > 0,

    L̇ : H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),(ℰ_+,ℓ_+),ℓ_K)_b → H^(k−2,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),(2ℰ_++2,ℓ_++2+m_+−ε),∞)_b,    (31.21)

with norm O(|S′|), uniformly in s.

*Proof.* g_S + sh − g_b = k_S + sh and g_S − g_b = k_S, both in 𝒳^k. In the proof of Proposition 29.7,
L^(g,g_0) − L_b is a sum of terms in which smooth functions of g⁻¹, g_0⁻¹ and of the background multiply Cartesian
derivatives, of total order two with the operator's own, of the differences g − g_b, g_0 − g_b
((21.46)–(21.48)), at least one factor in each term being a difference; Lemma 27.13 counts
them. L̇ is the sum of the same terms with one factor replaced by k′ or one of its derivatives (or g⁻¹ by
−g⁻¹k′g⁻¹), and k′ ∈ 𝒦 ⊂ 𝒳^∞ is counted as a difference. So L̇ lies in the class (29.12). Near ℐ⁺, in the
proof of (29.14) of Proposition 29.12, L^(g,g_0) is the leading part ρ_+²ρ_I(X_+ − X_I)(X_I − 3/2 − Ā),
which does not depend on (g, g_0), plus the C^∞ error of L_b, plus the perturbation error, in which the background
difference k_S ∈ 𝒦 ⊂ 𝒳^∞ is counted with h, as in the proof of Proposition 29.7. The first two do not depend on S.
L̇ is the S-derivative of the perturbation error, which is of the same kind, and the counts given there for the
perturbation error (2ℰ^tot_I ⊂ ℰ^C_I + 1 at the weight ℓ_I + 1, and 2ℰ_+ + 2 at the weight ℓ_+ + 2, by
Lemma 27.5) apply to it. Away from ℐ⁺, the count of (29.15), from (29.12) and
Lemma 27.5, gives the ι⁺-data; and L̇ = 0 near K⁺, as g_S = g_b there. Linearity in k′ gives the bound O(|S′|).
∎

**Lemma 31.15** ([Hin26, Lemma 11.28] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume (31.20). Let |S| and
‖h‖_(𝒳⁵) be small, h ∈ 𝒳^k, k ≥ 5, b ∈ ℬ̄_*, and f_(h,S)(S′) := D_SP_1(h, S, b)(S′), S′ ∈ 𝒮_1. Put

    ℰ̃_+ := 𝒢 ∪ (ℰ_+ + 𝒢),        𝒢 = (2, 0) ∪ (2 + ℰ_ind).    (31.22)

Then f_(h,S)(S′) is linear in S′ and vanishes on int χ_K⁻¹(1), a neighbourhood of K⁺; if h vanishes for t^♭_* < c,
c ≤ 10, so does f_(h,S)(S′); and for every ε > 0

    f_(h,S)(S′) ∈ H^(k−2,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,a_I+1),((ℰ̃_+∪2ℰ_+)+2, a_++2+min(2,m_+)−ε),∞)_b(Ω_*),    (31.23)

with norm O(|S′|), continuous in (h, S) with h ∈ 𝒳^k. In particular its ι⁺-weight is 4 − ε at worst. f_(0,0)(S′) is
supported in 𝒞, and at b = b₀ it is L_(b₀)(χ_K h^(≤1)_♮(S′)) (Lemma 31.12).

*Proof.* Write g_0 = g_S, g′ = g_0 + h^(−1)(S) + h, k′ = ∂_S g_S(S′), h^(−1)′ := h^(−1)(S′) and ϑ′ := ϑ_♯(S′), and
Υ := Υ^(E_Υ). Differentiating (31.18),

    f = D_(g′)Ric(k′ + h^(−1)′) − (∂_S δ*_(g_0,E_C))(Υ(g′, g_0) − ϑ_♯(S))
        − δ*_(g_0,E_C)(D_1Υ(g′, g_0)(k′ + h^(−1)′) + D_2Υ(g′, g_0)k′ − ϑ′).    (31.24)

Cover Ω_* by the open sets U_K := int χ_K⁻¹(1), U_I := int χ_K⁻¹(0), a neighbourhood U_ι of 𝒞 ∩ {t ≥ T_1} near
(ι⁺)° on which |x| ≥ t/20 and Θ = 1, and a set with compact closure in M°; multiplication by a subordinate partition
of unity of functions smooth on M preserves the spaces.

*On U_K:* g_0 = g_b, h^(−1)(S) = 0 and ϑ_♯(S) = 0 near each point, so P_1(h, S, b) does not depend on S, and f = 0.

*On U_I:* g_0 = φ*_(−S)g_(b₀) is Ricci flat and h^(−1), ϑ_♯ vanish, so by (i) P_1(h, S, b) = P(g_0 + h, g_0) =
P(g_0 + h, g_0) − P(g_0, g_0) = ∫_0^1 L^(g_0+sh, g_0)h ds, and

    f = ∫_0^1 L̇_s h ds,        L̇_s := ∂_S[L^(g_S+sh, g_S)](S′),

which vanishes where h vanishes on a neighbourhood. Lemma 31.14 with u = h and (ℓ_I, ℓ_+, ℓ_K) =
(a_I, a_+, a_K) (its hypotheses hold: 3/2 < a_I < a_I + 1/2, 0 < a_+ ≤ max(a_+, min Re ℰ_+) and
a_+ < a_+ + min Re ℰ_+) gives the ℐ⁺-data (⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′, a_I + 1) and the ι⁺-data (2ℰ_+ + 2, a_+ + 2 + m_+ − ε),
uniformly in s.

*On U_ι,* every term of (31.24) is counted near (ι⁺)°, where Cartesian derivatives lie in ρ_+𝒱_b. The
inputs: φ_(−S) is the exact boost on supp(1 − χ_K) near (ι⁺)° (the proof of Lemma 29.11), so
g_0 − η ∈ ρ_+²C^∞ and k′ ∈ ρ_+²C^∞, as g_(b₀) − η and g_b − η lie in |x|⁻²C^∞ and |x| ≥ t/20; h^(−1)(S),
h^(−1)′ ∈ 𝒜^𝒢 and ϑ_♯(S), ϑ′ ∈ 𝒜^(𝒢+1) (Lemma 31.10); and h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ_+,a_+))_b. So
g′ − η ∈ H^(k,(ℰ_+,a_+))_b (ρ_+²C^∞ ⊂ 𝒜^((2,0)), and (31.20)), and products stay in this class
(2ℰ_+ ⊂ ℰ_+). There are three counts, with 𝒜^𝒢 ⊂ 𝒜² (no logarithm at order 2), so that multiplication by an element
of 𝒜^𝒢 raises H_b-weights by 2.

(1) D_(g′)Ric ∈ ρ_+²(C^∞ + H^(k−2,(ℰ_+,a_+))_b)Diff²_b, applied to k′ + h^(−1)′ ∈ 𝒜^𝒢: the index set
(𝒢 + 2) ∪ (ℰ_+ + 𝒢 + 2) and the weight a_+ + 4.

(2) ∂_S δ*_(g_0,E_C) is of order zero with coefficients in ρ_+³C^∞: ∂_S Γ(g_0) involves g_0⁻¹∂k′ and k′∂g_0, and
∂_S E^C_(g_0) involves k′ and c_C ∈ |x|⁻¹C^∞ ((21.42)). Υ(g′, g_0) is a smooth function of g′, g_0 times
Γ(g′) − Γ(g_0), plus −E^Υ_(g_0)G_(g_0)(g′ − g_0), so with g′ − g_0 = h^(−1)(S) + h it lies in
H^(k−1,(ℰ_++1,a_++1))_b, as does ϑ_♯(S) (𝒢 + 1 ⊂ ℰ_+ + 1). The product: (ℰ_+ + 4, a_+ + 4).

(3) By (i), D_1Υ(g′, g_0)k′ + D_2Υ(g′, g_0)k′ = [(D_1 + D_2)Υ(g′, g_0) − (D_1 + D_2)Υ(g_0, g_0)]k′, a smooth function
of (g′, ∂g′) vanishing at g′ = g_0, hence, by Taylor's formula in g′, linear in (g′ − g_0, ∂(g′ − g_0)) with smooth
coefficients, applied to (k′, ∂k′), of total derivative order one (c_Υ counting as one): (ℰ_+ + 3, a_+ + 3). By the
definition of ϑ_♯,

    D_1Υ(g′, g_0)h^(−1)′ − ϑ′ = [D_1Υ(g′, g_0) − D_1Υ(g_(b₀), g_(b₀))]h^(−1)′ − ϑ^(−1)(S′),

which is linear in (g′ − g_(b₀), g_0 − g_(b₀)) and their first derivatives (both in H^(k,(ℰ_+,a_+))_b) times
ρ_+𝒜^𝒢, plus 𝒜^(𝒢+1): the index set (ℰ_+ + 𝒢 + 1) ∪ (𝒢 + 1) and the weight a_+ + 3. δ*_(g_0,E_C) ∈ ρ_+Diff¹_b
adds 1.

So on U_ι, f has the ι⁺-index set (𝒢 + 2) ∪ (ℰ_+ + 𝒢 + 2) ∪ (ℰ_+ + 4) = ℰ̃_+ + 2 (ℰ_+ + 4 ⊂ ℰ_+ + 𝒢 + 2, as
(2, 0) ∈ 𝒢) at the weight a_+ + 4, and no ℐ⁺ or K⁺ condition. On the compact part f lies in H^(k−2). Together these
give (31.23), with min Re(2ℰ_+ + 2) > 4, min Re(ℰ̃_+ + 2) = 4 and a_+ + 2 + min(2, m_+) > 4. Each term of
(31.24) and of ∫_0^1 L̇_s h ds is linear in S′ and a product of factors continuous in (h, S), with the
bounds of Lemma 27.5, so f is continuous in (h, S). If h = 0 for t^♭_* < c, c ≤ 10, then {t^♭_* < c} ⊂ U_I
(supp χ_K ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ 10}), and f = ∫_0^1 L̇_s h ds = 0 there. For h = 0, S = 0, f vanishes on U_K and on U_I, so it
is supported in 𝒞; at b₀ it is (31.19). ∎

[Hin26, (11.86)–(11.87)] split f into f¹, with the ι⁺-index set ℰ_+ + 3, and a term with ℰ̃_+ + 2 ∋ (3, 0)
supported where (1 − χ^♭_K)χ^♯_K ≠ 0, to keep (3, 0)-terms away from ℐ⁺ ([Hin26, Remark 11.29]). In dimension 4 + 1
the least exponent is 4 and the weight needed below is α_+ + 2 < 4, so no splitting is made. The finer index sets of
(31.23) are recorded for later use.

### 31.7 Elimination of boosts

This section is [Hin26, Proposition 11.30 and (11.95)] in dimension 4 + 1. Fix ℓ_I with (29.43), that is,
2 ≤ ℓ_I < min(a_I + 1/2, ℓ_I^max) and ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^C_I ∪ (3/2 + σ_Υ), and with ℓ_I ≤ a_I, which needs a_I ≥ 2; and
fix α_K ∈ (1, min(a_K − 1, 3/2)) and α_+ ∈ (α_K, 2). Proposition 31.6 needs ℓ_I ≥ 2, and the parameter derivative
has the ℐ⁺-weight a_I + 1; the choice a_I = 3 + ε_I of [Hin26] meets a_I ≥ 2. When the parameter b ∈ ℬ̄_* of the base
point is to be named, we write L_(h,S;b), f_(h,S;b), Ṡ_(h,S;b) and S^(−1)_(h,S;b) for the objects below.

**Proposition 31.16** (Elimination of boosts; [Hin26, Proposition 11.30] in dimension 4 + 1.) Assume
(31.20). There are d ∈ ℕ and ε_1 > 0 such that for b ∈ ℬ̄_*, |S| < ε_1 and h ∈ 𝒳^∞ vanishing near
{t^♭_* = 1} ([Hin26, (11.91)]) with ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) < ε_1:

(1) (*Asymptotics.*) For f ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α_++2,α_K)_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−), the forward solution of
L_(h,S)u = f is

    u = χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ(f)) + ũ,     Ṡ(f) ∈ 𝒮_1,
    ũ ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),β_+,α_K−2)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−)    for every β_+ < min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+),    (31.25)

with Ṡ(f) and ũ depending linearly and continuously on f.

(2) (*The boost parameter.*) The map S^(−1)_(h,S) ∈ ℒ(𝒮_1), S′ ↦ Ṡ(f_(h,S)(S′)), with f_(h,S) of Lemma 31.15
(which lies in the space of (1) by (31.23), as ℓ_I ≤ a_I and α_+ < 2), is invertible, with inverse of norm
at most 2.

We take d ∈ ℕ with

    d ≥ max(d_T, k_0 + 2, k_1 + d_T + 7),    (31.26)

where d_T is the d of Theorem 29.17 at b ((BP1)) and k_0, k_1 are the regularities of Lemma 31.17. The
first bound serves (1). For (2): Lemma 31.15 with k = d puts f_(h,S)(S′) in H^(d−2) ⊂ H^(k_0), the regularity
of the bound Lemma 31.17 (a); and the map Π_b of the proof of Lemma 31.17 needs the forward solutions,
and their dependence on (h, S), at the regularity k_1 + 2, which Theorem 29.17 and its continuity, through
(29.13), give with constants controlled by ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) once d ≥ k_1 + d_T + 7. The constants, d and
ε_1 do not depend on b ∈ ℬ̄_* (after the shrinking of ℬ_* in Proposition 31.19). (2) is proved in
Section 31.7.1, with the bound (31.29).

[Hin26, (11.92)] admits f = f¹ + (1 − χ^♭_K)f² with f² of ι⁺-index set (3, 0), and [Hin26, Remark 11.31] a further
f² with K⁺-weight 1 + ε_K; in dimension 4 + 1 both kinds of term have ι⁺-order 4 and lie in the space of (1). [Hin26,
(11.93)] has the ι⁺-weight 1 − ε and α_K ∈ (1, 1 + ε_K).

*Proof of (1).* Lemma 31.13 and Proposition 31.6 (its hypotheses: ℓ_I with (29.43),
α_K ∈ (1, min(a_K − 1, 3/2)), α_+ > α_K) give u = χ^H_K h^(≤1)_b(Ṡ) + ũ with ũ in the space of (31.25),
continuously in f, for ‖h′‖_(𝒳^d) and |S| small; Lemma 31.8 (b) (β_+ < 3/2 < 2, α_K < 2) gives
(31.25). Ṡ(f) is determined by u: ũ has K⁺-weight α_K − 2 > −1, so h_b(Ṡ) is the coefficient of t_* in u
at K⁺, and S ↦ h_b(S) is injective (Lemma 31.2). ∎

**Lemma 31.17** (The boost parameter depends continuously on the operator.) Write Ṡ_(h,S)(f) for the Ṡ(f)
of (31.25). There are k_0 ∈ ℕ and C such that, for b ∈ ℬ̄_* and (h, S) as in Proposition 31.16,

(a) |Ṡ_(h,S)(f)| ≤ C‖f‖_(H^(k_0,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α_++2,α_K)_b);

(b) if ℓ_I > 2, or if f vanishes near ℐ⁺, then for fixed f and b the map (h, S) ↦ Ṡ_(h,S)(f) is continuous, h in
the 𝒳^d-topology with d ≥ k_1 + d_T + 7 ((31.26)), d_T the d of Theorem 29.17 and k_1 below.

*Proof.* In the proof of Proposition 31.6 with L := L_(h,S), Ṡ = S_0 is obtained from f′ := f − (L − L_b)u alone:
u_I by the construction of Proposition 29.29 for L_b, f^♭ := f′ − L_b u_I, and S_0 the 𝒮_1-component of
L̃_b(0)⁻¹(f̂^♭(0), 0, 0) ((31.5)). So Ṡ = Π_b f′ with a linear map Π_b that depends on L_b only and is
bounded on H^(k_1,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α^♯_++2,α_K)_b for some k_1: the construction of Proposition 29.29 loses
finitely many derivatives, and so do Proposition 20.18 (1) and Proposition 28.8, which give f̂^♭(0) and
L̃_b(0)⁻¹. The bound of Π_b is uniform in b ∈ ℬ̄_* by (BP1) and (BP4). Moreover Ṡ is determined by u, so it does not
depend on the auxiliary weights (α′_K, β′_+, α^♯_+, ℓ_I) of that proof, which may therefore be taken with room:
α′_K > α_K − (a_K − 2) strictly and ℓ_I > 2 strictly, so that lowering the weights of u by a small ς > 0 keeps f′ in
a space on which some such Π_b is bounded. If ℓ_I = 2 and f vanishes near ℐ⁺, f lies in the space for any
ℓ″_I ∈ (2, min(a_I + 1/2, ℓ_I^max)) off the set excluded in (29.43), and the argument runs there; Ṡ is the
same, being determined by u.

(a) ‖f′‖ ≤ ‖f‖ + ‖(L − L_b)u‖ ≤ ‖f‖ + C‖u‖, by (29.15) with the coefficient bounds of Proposition 29.7,
uniform for small (S, h′); and ‖u‖ ≤ C‖f‖ in the space (29.44) of Proposition 29.35, whose constant is
locally uniform in (S, h′). With ‖h′‖_(𝒳^d) ≤ ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + C|S| (Lemma 31.13) this gives (a), k_0 being the
sum of the losses.

(b) For (h_1, S_1) near (h, S), let L_1 := L_(h_1,S_1) and u_1 its forward solution with right-hand side f. Then

    Ṡ_(h_1,S_1)(f) − Ṡ_(h,S)(f) = −Π_b((L_1 − L)u_1 + (L − L_b)(u_1 − u)),    (31.27)

as Π_b(f − (L_1 − L_b)u_1) − Π_b(f − (L − L_b)u) is this. The coefficients of L^(g,g_0) − L_b are polynomial in the
differences and their derivatives, with coefficients smooth in g⁻¹, g_0⁻¹ (the proof of Lemma 31.14), so
L_1 − L has coefficients in the class (29.12) of norm o(1) as (h_1, S_1) → (h, S) (h′_1 → h′ in 𝒳^d,
Lemma 31.10), and the bound (29.15) is linear in the coefficient norms (Lemma 27.5); u_1 is
bounded in (29.44) by the argument of (a). So (L_1 − L)u_1 → 0. The continuity in Proposition 29.35 gives
u_1 → u in (29.44) with the weights lowered by ς, at the regularity k_1 + 2 that Π_b needs once
d ≥ k_1 + d_T + 7 (the continuity in Theorem 29.17, through (29.13)); and (29.15) gives
(L − L_b)(u_1 − u) → 0 in the space of f′ with the weights lowered by ς, on which Π_b is bounded by the choice of
room. ∎

(b) is a continuity at fixed (h, S, b), and it is not used for Proposition 31.16 (2): the proof in
Section 31.7.1 is a direct bound, into which only the identity (31.27) enters.

#### 31.7.1 The boost parameter at b

Lemma 31.12 is an identity at b₀. It uses that g_(b₀) is Ricci flat in 𝒞 and that the correction and the
leading term are built from the same b₀-state. At b the background in 𝒞 interpolates between g_(b₀) and g_b, so the
identity acquires an error, and Proposition 31.16 (2) is proved by a bound that is uniform in b, not by continuity
at fixed b.

**Lemma 31.18** (The boost identity at b.) Let b ∈ ℬ̄_*, G := g_(b₀,b,0) = (1 − χ_K)g_(b₀) + χ_K g_b
((29.1)), P_1(h, S, b) as in (31.18), with g_0 := g_(b₀,b,−S), and
f_(0,0;b)(Ṡ) := D_SP_1(0, S, b)|_(S=0)(Ṡ). Let h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ) = δ*_(g_b)ω^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ) be the re-centred s1 state
at b (Definition 31.7; at b₀ it is h^(≤1)_♮). Then

    f_(0,0;b)(Ṡ) = L^(G,G)(χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ)) + E^S_b(Ṡ),    (31.28)

where E^S_b(Ṡ) is supported in 𝒞, vanishes at b = b₀, and, near (ι⁺)°, lies in 𝒜^(𝒢+2−δ) for every δ > 0,
𝒢 = (2, 0) ∪ (2 + ℰ_ind), with seminorms O(|b − b₀||Ṡ|) uniformly on ℬ̄_*.

*Proof.* *Support.* By (29.1), g_(b₀,b,−S) = (1 − χ_K)φ*_(−S)g_(b₀) + χ_K g_b, and the corrections h^(−1),
ϑ_♯ of Definition 31.9 are supported in 𝒞 (Lemma 31.10). In the interior of χ_K⁻¹(0),
g′ = g_0 = φ*_(−S)g_(b₀) is Ricci flat for every S, and Υ^(E_Υ)(g_0, g_0) = 0 by (i) of Section 31.4; so
P_1(0, S, b) = 0 there for all S, and f_(0,0;b) = 0. In the interior of χ_K⁻¹(1), g′ = g_0 = g_b does not depend on S,
so again f_(0,0;b) = 0. On both sets L^(G,G)(χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)) vanishes as well. On the first it vanishes trivially.
On the second it is L_b h^(≤1)_(b,♮), which is 0: h^(≤1)_(b,♮) = δ*_(g_b)ω^(≤1)_(b,♮) lies in ker D_(g_b)Ric by (iii),
and in ker δ_(g_b,E_Υ)G_(g_b) because ω^(≤1)_(b,♮) = (t_* − C′)ω^(0)_(b,s1) + ω̆^((0),1)_(b,s1) is a generalised zero
energy state of the gauge potential operator □^Υ_b ((23.24)), whose symmetric gradient lies in that kernel
by Proposition 23.28 (2). So E^S_b is supported in 𝒞.

*At b₀.* G = g_(b₀), L^(G,G) = L_(b₀) and h^(≤1)_(b₀,♮) = h^(≤1)_♮, so (31.28) with E^S_(b₀) = 0 is
(31.19).

*Size.* Every term of E^S_b(Ṡ) is linear in Ṡ and a smooth function of b on 𝒞. Its ingredients are
G − g_(b₀) = χ_K(g_b − g_(b₀)), which lies in |b − b₀|ρ_+²C^∞ near (ι⁺)° (on 𝒞, |x| ≥ t/10, and
g_b − g_(b₀) = O(|b − b₀||x|⁻²) with all Cartesian derivatives, Proposition 21.21); the state
h^(≤1)_(b,♮) = (t_* − C′)h_b + h̆_b, which near (ι⁺)° lies in 𝒜^(𝒢−δ) together with its first derivative in b,
uniformly on ℬ̄_* ((BP3): h_b, h̆_b and their b-derivatives are bounded in 𝒜^(3−δ), resp. 𝒜^(2−δ), by
Proposition 23.28 and Lemma 23.27 with the b-Sobolev embedding of Remark 28.6, and t_* ∈ ρ_+⁻¹C^∞
there); the b-independent corrections; and
k′ := ∂_S g_S(Ṡ) = −(1 − χ_K)δ*_(g_(b₀))(Θw(Ṡ)), which does not depend on b and lies in ρ_+²C^∞ near (ι⁺)° (the proof
of Lemma 31.15), and which enters because w itself has order ρ_+⁻¹. The count of Lemma 31.10, that
D_(g_0)Ric and δ*δG lie in ρ_+²Diff²_b near (ι⁺)°, takes 𝒜^(𝒢−δ) into 𝒜^(𝒢+2−δ), uniformly for b ∈ ℬ̄_*. So
∂_b E^S_b(Ṡ) is bounded there by C|Ṡ|, and E^S_b = E^S_b − E^S_(b₀) is O(|b − b₀||Ṡ|) by the mean value theorem along
the segment from b₀ to b, which lies in the ball ℬ̄_*. ∎

**Proposition 31.19** (Proposition 31.16 (2) and Corollary 31.20 at b.) In Proposition 31.16 (1)
at b ∈ ℬ̄_*, the leading term is built at b and Ṡ(f) is read from the coefficient h_b(Ṡ(f)) of t_* at K⁺, which
determines it by Lemma 31.2. There are C and a smallness of (h, S), uniform on ℬ̄_*, with

    |S^(−1)_(h,S;b) − id| ≤ C(‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + |S| + |b − b₀|).    (31.29)

So, after shrinking ℬ_* and the smallness of (h, S), S^(−1)_(h,S;b) is invertible with inverse of norm at most 2, and
Corollary 31.20 and Corollary 31.22 hold at b, with constants uniform in b.

*Proof.* At b, the map of Lemma 31.17 is Ṡ_(h,S;b)(f) = Π_b f′, with f′ := f − (L_(h,S;b) − L_b)u. Here Π_b is
built from the construction of Proposition 29.29 for L_b and from L̃_b(0)⁻¹ (Proposition 28.8 at b, (BP4)), and
its bound Lemma 31.17 (a) holds with C uniform in b, by (BP1) and (BP4). χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(S′) vanishes for
t^♭_* < 10, as supp χ_K ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ 10}. By Lemma 31.18 it is therefore the forward solution
(Proposition 17.14) of the operator L_(0,0;b) = L^(G,G) (Lemma 31.13 at h = 0, S = 0) with the right-hand side
f_(0,0;b)(S′) − E^S_b(S′), and it has the form (31.25) with Ṡ = S′ and ũ = 0. Hence, for S′ in a basis of
𝒮_1,

    S^(−1)_(h,S;b)(S′) − S′ = Ṡ_(h,S;b)(f_(h,S;b)(S′) − f_(0,0;b)(S′)) + (Ṡ_(h,S;b) − Ṡ_(0,0;b))(f_(0,0;b)(S′))
                              + Ṡ_(0,0;b)(E^S_b(S′)).

*The first term.* f_(h,S;b) := D_SP_1(h, S, b) depends smoothly on (h, S). The bounds of Lemma 31.15 hold for
small (h, S) and depend on b only through finitely many seminorms of g_(b₀,b,−S). The derivative of f_(h,S;b)(S′) in
h is ∂_S L_(h,S)(S′), where L_(h,S) = L^(g_S+h′,g_S) with h′ = h^(−1)(S) + h (Lemma 31.13): the operator L̇ of
Lemma 31.14 with h′ in place of sh, bounded by (31.21), plus the variation of the first metric slot
by h^(−1)(S′), which lies in 𝒳^∞ with norm O(|S′|) (Lemma 31.13) and is counted as a difference in the same
way. The derivative in S is bounded by the count of (31.24). With k = d in Lemma 31.15 and
d − 2 ≥ k_0 ((31.26)), ‖f_(h,S;b)(S′) − f_(0,0;b)(S′)‖ ≤ C(‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + |S|)|S′| in the norm of
Lemma 31.17 (a), and the first term is at most C(‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + |S|)|S′|.

*The second term.* By (31.27), with (h_1, S_1) := (h, S) and (0, 0) in place of (h, S), it is

    −Π_b((L_(h,S;b) − L_(0,0;b))u_(h,S) + (L_(0,0;b) − L_b)(u_(h,S) − u_(0,0))),

where u_(h,S), u_(0,0) are the forward solutions with the right-hand side f := f_(0,0;b)(S′), which vanishes near ℐ⁺
(it is supported in 𝒞). The coefficients of L_(h,S;b) − L_(0,0;b) lie in the class (29.12) with norm at most
C(‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + |S|): they are polynomial in the differences of the metrics, with coefficients smooth in their inverses
(the proofs of Lemma 31.14 and Lemma 31.13). So (29.15) gives
‖(L_(h,S;b) − L_(0,0;b))u_(h,S)‖ ≤ C(‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + |S|)‖f‖. Since L_(0,0;b)(u_(h,S) − u_(0,0)) =
−(L_(h,S;b) − L_(0,0;b))u_(h,S), Proposition 29.35, with the weights lowered by the room ς of the proof of
Lemma 31.17, gives ‖u_(h,S) − u_(0,0)‖ ≤ C(‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + |S|)‖f‖ at the regularity k_1 + 2 that Π_b needs, as
d ≥ k_1 + d_T + 7 ((31.26)), and (29.15) bounds the second summand in the same way. Π_b is bounded on the
space with that room, uniformly in b. So the second term is at most C(‖h‖_(𝒳^d) + |S|)|S′|.

*The third term.* By Lemma 31.18, E^S_b(S′) is supported in 𝒞. It vanishes near ℐ⁺ and K⁺, and its
ι⁺-order is at least 4 − δ > α_+ + 2 for δ < 2 − α_+, as α_+ < 2. So it lies in the space of Lemma 31.17 (a)
with norm at most C|b − b₀||S′|, and the third term is at most C|b − b₀||S′|.

This proves (31.29), and the Neumann series gives the inverse once the right side of (31.29) is
at most 1/2. The proofs of Corollary 31.20 and Corollary 31.22 use the invertibility alone, so they hold at
b. ∎

**Corollary 31.20** ([Hin26, (11.95)] in dimension 4 + 1.) For b ∈ ℬ̄_* and (h, S) and f as in
Proposition 31.16 (1), put S″ := (S^(−1)_(h,S))⁻¹Ṡ(f). The forward solution u of

    D_((h,S))P_1(·, ·, b)(u, S″) = L_(h,S)u + f_(h,S)(S″) = f    (31.30)

lies in H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),β_+,α_K−2)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−) for every β_+ < min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+); in compact spatial sets
it grows at most like t_*^(2−α_K) = o(t_*), by b-Sobolev embedding at K⁺.

*Proof.* f − f_(h,S)(S″) lies in the space of Proposition 31.16 (1) (Lemma 31.15), so
u = χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ) + ũ with Ṡ = Ṡ(f) − S^(−1)_(h,S)(S″) = 0 by linearity. ∎

[Hin26] then introduces P′(h, S, b) := P(χ_− h_(−S) + h, S, b) ([Hin26, (11.90)]), which carries the initial data,
and works with h vanishing for t_* < 1 ([Hin26, (11.91)]), restoring χ_− h_(−S) only at [Hin26, Definition 11.63,
Corollary 11.66]. The same is done here: every statement above is for h vanishing near {t^♭_* = 1}, and the initial
data enter with the augmented operators of Chapter 34.

### 31.8 Almost boundedness: the setting

This section and the next are [Hin26, Section 11.5] in dimension 4 + 1. Once the boost term is eliminated, the forward
solutions of the augmented linearised operator have K⁺-weight α_K − 2 for every α_K < 2: they grow at most like
t_*^(2−α_K) in compact spatial sets, almost boundedly ([Hin26, Proposition 11.32]). The proof improves the K⁺-weight
in steps, each a run of the argument of Proposition 31.6 with no boost term. In dimension 4 + 1 the exponents that
the formal solution at null infinity leaves at ι⁺ begin at λ_♯, not at 1, and the ι⁺-spectrum is empty below 2
(Lemma 26.29 (a)), so the step at ι⁺ solves away finitely many quasi-homogeneous terms with no pole. The zero
energy step needs neither [Hin26, Lemma 11.33] nor [Hin26, Proposition 9.30]: L̂_b(0) has no indicial root in (0, 1]
((BP2)), and the columns have tf-order 3 − ε (Lemma 31.4 (b)), so the relative tf–zf order stays in (2, 3).

L := L_(h,S) is the linearisation (31.18) of P_1 at (h, S, b), b ∈ ℬ̄_*, with h ∈ 𝒳^∞ vanishing near
{t^♭_* = 1}, ‖h‖_(𝒳^d) and |S| small, and

    2 + ℰ_ind ⊂ ℰ_+.    (31.31)

By Lemma 31.13, L = L^(g′,g_0) with g′ = g_S + h′ and h′ = h^(−1)(S) + h, so every result of Chapter 29 and of
Section 31.2–Section 31.3 holds for L. χ_K is the cut-off of Section 31.4 and h^(≤1)_(b,♮) the re-centred
state of Definition 31.7. Fix ℓ_I with (29.43),

    2 ≤ ℓ_I < min(a_I + 1/2, ℓ_I^max),        ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^C_I ∪ (3/2 + σ_Υ),    (31.32)

where ℓ_I^max = 3/2 + s_C and s_C = γ_C(1 − e_C)(1 − v_C) ((29.24), Lemma 26.22). For
f ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α_++2,α_K)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−) with 1 < α_K < min(a_K − 1, 3/2) and α_+ > α_K,
Proposition 31.16 (1) writes the forward solution of Lu = f as χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ(f)) + ũ. Section 31.7 assumes
ℓ_I ≤ a_I, but the proof of Proposition 31.16 (1) uses only (29.43) (only (2) uses ℓ_I ≤ a_I, through
(31.23)), so (1) holds under (31.32).

*Two inclusions of index sets.* (a) The ℐ⁺-index sets of the analysis at ι⁺ lie in those of Definition 29.1:

    ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) = ⋃_(s∈σ_Υ) (3/2 + s, 0) ⊂ ℰ^tot_I

((26.31), (27.8)), so ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ) = ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) + 1 ⊂ ℰ^tot_I + 1 ⊂ ℰ^C_I (Lemma 27.7
(a)). The index sets ℰ_s = ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ) ∪ (3/2 + s, 0) of Definition 26.23 (2) belong to the eigencomponents Π_s of S̄,
not to slots. In the constant frame of Chapter 27, which Section 26.6 uses, Ā is lower triangular; Π_((1−e_Υ)γ_Υ)
occupies the slots 4 and 7, Π_(γ_Υ) the slot 5, Π_0 the slot 6, Π_(2γ_Υ) the slot 7 and Π_C any slot; and the sets
(27.9) of those slots contain 3/2 + s for the matching s and ℰ^C_I, so they contain ℰ_s. So

    H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),·,·)_b ⊂ H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),·,·)_b.

(b) ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) + 2 ⊂ ℰ^tot_I + 2 ⊂ ℰ^C_I + 1, so H^(k,(ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ)+2,ℓ_I+1),·,·)_b ⊂
H^(k,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),·,·)_b (Definition 29.1 (2), ℱ_(I,11) ⊃ ℰ^C_I + 1), with no ρ_I^(z+1)-term for
Re z < 5/2.

### 31.9 Almost boundedness

**Proposition 31.21** (Almost boundedness; [Hin26, Proposition 11.32] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
1 < α_K < α_+ < 2 and f ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α_++2,α_K)_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−), and suppose that Ṡ(f) = 0
(Proposition 31.16 (1), for any admissible K⁺-weight there). Then the forward solution of Lu = f satisfies

    u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),β_+,α_K−2)_b(Ω_*; S²T*)^(•,−)      for every β_+ < min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+),
    (31.33)

continuously in f and uniformly in b ∈ ℬ̄_*. In compact spatial sets u grows at most like t_*^(2−α_K), and α_K may be
taken arbitrarily close to 2.

[Hin26, (11.96)–(11.97)] have the ι⁺-weight 1 − ε, the ℐ⁺-weight 3 + ε_I, and a second summand f_2 with the
ι⁺-index set ℰ̃_+ + 2 ∋ (3, 0) and K⁺-weight 2 − ε. In dimension 4 + 1 the corresponding terms have ι⁺-order 4
(Lemma 31.15), above α_+ + 2, so one class suffices.

**Corollary 31.22** (The remark after [Hin26, Proposition 11.32].) For f as in Proposition 31.21 but
with Ṡ(f) arbitrary, and ℓ_I ≤ a_I, the solution u of Corollary 31.20 (Lu + f_(h,S)(S″) = f with
S″ = (S^(−1)_(h,S))⁻¹Ṡ(f)) satisfies (31.33), at every b ∈ ℬ̄_* (Proposition 31.19).

*Proof.* f − f_(h,S)(S″) lies in the space of Proposition 31.21: f_(h,S)(S″) has the ℐ⁺-data
(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′, a_I + 1), the ι⁺-weight 4 − ε ≥ α_+ + 2, and vanishes near K⁺ (Lemma 31.15). Its boost parameter
is Ṡ(f) − S^(−1)_(h,S)(S″) = 0 (the proof of Corollary 31.20). ∎

*Proof of Proposition 31.21.* The proof raises the K⁺-weight in steps. Suppose that, for some α′_K ∈ (1, α_K] and
β′_+ ∈ (1, min(α_+, 3/2, min Re ℰ_+)),

    u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I),β′_+,α′_K−2)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−).    (31.34)

*Start.* Proposition 31.16 (1) with a K⁺-weight α′_K ∈ (1, min(a_K − 1, 3/2, α_K)) (the space of f for α_K lies in
that for α′_K) gives u = χ_K h^(≤1)_(b,♮)(Ṡ(f)) + ũ = ũ, so (31.34) holds.

*Step 0* ([Hin26, (11.98)–(11.100)]). (29.15) of Proposition 29.12 (3/2 < ℓ_I < a_I + 1/2;
β′_+ < min Re ℰ_+, so β′_+ ≤ max(a_+, min Re ℰ_+) and β′_+ < a_+ + min Re ℰ_+) gives (L − L_b)u the ℐ⁺-data
(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′, ℓ_I + 1), the ι⁺-weight β′_+ + 2 + m_+ − ε > 4 (as β′_+ > 1 and m_+ > 1; its index set 2ℰ_+ + 2 has real
parts > 4) and the K⁺-weight α′_K − 2 + a_K. Put α̃_K := min(α′_K + a_K − 2, α_K) ≥ α′_K, with equality only when
α′_K = α_K, and fix

    α^♯_+ ∈ (α̃_K, α_+),     α^♯_+ ∉ Re π_1ℰ^C_I ∪ Re π_1(ℰ^♯_+ + ℕ₀ℰ^ι_ind),     α^♯_+ ≥ min(α_+, 3/2) − ε
    (31.35)

for a given small ε > 0. Here ℰ^♯_+ is the index set of (29.32) with ℰ̆_+ = ∅, which contains λ_♯, and
ℰ^ι_ind is the index set of (26.56). Both are fixed in advance, and Step 2 creates only exponents in
ℰ^♯_+ + ℕ₀ℰ^ι_ind, so none at real part α^♯_+. Such α^♯_+ exist, as the excluded set is finite below 2. Then
α^♯_+ ∈ (1, 2), α^♯_+ − 1 ∈ (0, 1), α^♯_+ − α̃_K ∈ (0, 1), and

    L_b u = f′ := f − (L − L_b)u ∈ H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I+1⟩′,ℓ_I+1),α^♯_++2,α̃_K)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−).

*Step 1* (null infinity; [Hin26, (11.101)]). Proposition 29.29 with ℰ̆_+ := ∅ and ℓ̆_+ := α^♯_+ (α^♯_+ < 2 ≤ ℓ_I,
and (31.35)) gives u_I, vanishing on {t_* < 1} ∪ {ρ_I > ½c_I}, with the ℐ⁺-data (⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I) and the
ι⁺-data (ℰ^♯_+, α^♯_+), and

    f^♭_0 := f′ − L_b u_I ∈ H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,(ℰ^♯_++2,α^♯_++2),α̃_K)_b(Ω_*)^(•,−).

min Re ℰ^♯_+ = λ_♯ ((29.32) with ℰ̆_+ = ∅; min Re ℰ^C_I > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ > λ_♯). If α^♯_+ < λ_♯, f^♭_0 has the
plain ι⁺-weight α^♯_+ + 2 and Step 2 is void; this is the case of Proposition 31.6. Otherwise f^♭_0 has finitely
many ι⁺-expansion terms below α^♯_+ + 2,

    χ_ι t_*^(−λ−2)(log t_*)^k f^((λ,k))_+,        (λ, k) ∈ ℰ^♯_+,        λ_♯ ≤ Re λ < α^♯_+,    (31.36)

whose coefficients f^((λ,k))_+ ∈ H^(∞,ℓ_I+1)_b(ι⁺) come from L_b u_I (f′ has a plain ι⁺-weight) and so are supported
in {ρ_I ≤ ½c_I}, away from K⁺.

*Step 2* (ι⁺; [Hin26, (11.102)–(11.104)]). Write ε^ι_ind := min Re ℰ^ι_ind > 0. The λ_0 treated below lie in
ℰ^♯_+ + ℕ₀ℰ^ι_ind with Re λ_0 ∈ [λ_♯, α^♯_+); there are finitely many. As in [Hin26, (11.102)], we fix the K⁺-order
rather than the K⁺-weight: fix c_K ∈ (2, λ_♯ + 1) such that for each of these λ_0, ℓ_K(λ_0) := c_K − Re λ_0 is
neither −Re μ for a root μ of Section 26.10 nor in Re π_1ℰ_K (finitely many exclusions). Then
ℓ_K(λ_0) ∈ (c_K − 2, 1) ⊂ (0, 1), which is admissible in Theorem 26.27 (2) (ℓ_K > −1) and below
ℓ_K^max = min(3, 2 + 2γ_Cv_C) ≥ 2 ((26.43)). Let F be the current right-hand side, initially f^♭_0, and c_0
the least real part of its ι⁺-exponents below α^♯_+ + 2, minus 2.

For each λ_0 in the ι⁺-index set of F with Re λ_0 ∈ [c_0, c_0 + ε^ι_ind) (finitely many), with k the largest power
of the logarithm at λ_0, apply Corollary 26.44, with ℓ_K := ℓ_K(λ_0) and the remaining right-hand side 0, to the
terms of F at λ_0. Its hypotheses hold: Re λ_0 ≥ λ_♯ > 1; l_0 = 0, since spec_ι⁺(L̄) ⊂ {Re z ≥ 2}
(Lemma 26.29 (a)) and Re λ_0 < 2; ℓ_I < 3/2 + s_C and ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ) = 3/2 + σ_Υ + ℕ₀, by
(31.32) and as 5/2 + σ_Υ + ℕ₀ ⊂ Re π_1ℰ^C_I (Lemma 27.7 (a)), and Re λ_0 < 2 ≤ ℓ_I; and the
coefficients lie in H^(∞,ℓ_I+1,ℓ_K(λ_0)−2−ε)_b(ι⁺). Indeed, in the first round they come from L_b u_I and vanish near
K⁺; later, every term of F below α^♯_+ + 2 either vanishes near K⁺ or has K⁺-weight c_K − ε (see below), so its
coefficient at λ_0 has R-weight at least c_K − ε − Re λ_0 − 2 = ℓ_K(λ_0) − 2 − ε. Corollary 26.44 gives u_(λ_0),
vanishing for t_* < 1, with

    u_(λ_0) ∈ ⋂_(ε>0) H^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_(ι⁺,ℐ)⟩,ℓ_I),(λ_0,k)∪(λ_0+ℰ^ι_ind+(0,k)),(ℰ^gr_K(λ_0)+(0,k),ℓ_K(λ_0)−ε))_b,

and an error, the terms of F at λ_0 minus L_b u_(λ_0), in
H^(∞,(ℰ^tot_(ι⁺,ℐ)+2,ℓ_I+1),λ_0+2+ℰ^ι_ind+(0,k),λ_0+ℓ_K(λ_0)−ε)_b. Here min Re ℰ^gr_K(λ_0) ≥ Re λ_0 − 1. By the
definition in Theorem 26.42, ℰ^gr_K(λ_0) contains the index set of a_s1 ∼ t_*^(−λ_0+1) ((26.54)); the
others are that of a_v1 ∼ t_*^(−λ_0) and λ_0 − μ + j, j ≥ 0, for the roots μ ∈ 𝒲(ℓ_K(λ_0)), which have
−ℓ_K(λ_0) < Re μ ≤ 0 (Section 26.10). As ℓ_K(λ_0) < 1, −1 ∉ 𝒲(ℓ_K(λ_0)), so S^(−1)_1 = 0, the a_s1 and a_v1 terms
are absent, and the least exponent is in fact ≥ Re λ_0; the bound suffices. (If at a rotating b an a_v1 term is
present, the bottom of its v1 tower is a_v1 h_(b,v1), with h_(b,v1) ∈ 𝒜³ stationary (Proposition 23.28), of
K⁺-weight Re λ_0 − ε ≥ Re λ_0 − 1; so the bound holds at every b ∈ ℬ̄_*.) So u_(λ_0) has the K⁺-weight
min(Re λ_0 − 1, ℓ_K(λ_0)) − ε > 0 > α_K − 2 for ε < c_K − 2, and the error has the K⁺-weight
Re λ_0 + ℓ_K(λ_0) − ε = c_K − ε > 2 > α_K.

The ℐ⁺-expansion of the error is removed by Proposition 29.29 with ℰ̆_+ := λ_0 + ℰ^ι_ind + (0, k) and
ℓ̆_+ := α^♯_+. By inclusion (b) of Section 31.8 the error lies in its space, and its ℐ⁺-expansion has no
