the bound of (i) of Proposition 32.29 with (2) gives (36.5).

Along 𝒫_k ⊂ 𝒫_0, with F fixed, a change δW⃗ of the row coordinates therefore changes p⃗′_< (the motion coordinates and
the motions of ℳ_(α_1)) by δp⃗′_< = −p⃗′_(α_1)(D_(W⃗)P_5(δW⃗)), of size at most
C(‖h‖ + |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + ‖q‖ + |b − b₀|)|δW⃗|.

*The bound on A_k.* Let δW′ be a change of the new coordinates, those of higher rate being fixed, and let δp⃗′, δG′
and δu be the changes it causes along 𝒫_k. By the induction bound every coordinate changes by at most C|δW′|; in
particular the row coordinates change by δW⃗ with |δW⃗| ≤ C|δW′|, so, by the last paragraph, the motion coordinates
change by at most C(‖h‖ + |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + ‖q‖ + |b − b₀|)|δW′|. With δW′_ν the change of the row coordinate W′_ν for every
row ν ∈ 𝒩 ⊔ 𝒩_rot,

    δG′ = −f^S_(h,p⃗)(δS′) − f^b_(h,p⃗)(δb′) − f^(s1)_(h,p⃗)(δS^(0)′_1)
          − Σ_(ν∈𝒩⊔𝒩_rot) (r^ν_(h,p⃗) + E^ν_(h,p⃗))(δW′_ν) − Δ_q(δp⃗′) − R_q δu.

The motion terms are at most C(|δS′| + |δb′| + |δS^(0)′_1|) in ‖·‖_(𝒴,k+1), by their norms stated after the list at
the start of this step. By that list, the row terms are at most C(‖h‖ + |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + |b − b₀|)|δW′|, and Δ_q(δp⃗′)
and R_q δu at most C‖q‖|δW′|, with the induction bound for δu (Lemma 34.6 with w = β_k − 2, as
β_(k+1) < β_k + α − 4). So

    ‖δG′‖_(𝒴,k+1) ≤ C(‖h‖ + |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + ‖q‖ + |b − b₀|)|δW′|.

The change of C^(k+1) on the new rows is −δW′ + A_kδW′, where A_kδW′ is the tuple of the S^(h,p⃗,β_(k+1))_ν(δG′) and
A_(b,ν)(δG′). The forward solution of L_(h,p⃗)δu_0 = δG′ is δu_0 = δu + Σ_(𝒩⊔𝒩_rot) m_ν(δW′_ν), δW′_ν here the change
of every row coordinate, and δu_0 satisfies the hypothesis of Lemma 33.29 with w := min(β_k − 2, λ_♯ − 1), as
u_0 does (Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 34.9). So Lemma 36.7 gives

    |A_kδW′| ≤ C‖δG′‖_(𝒴,k+1) + C(‖h‖ + |p⃗|)‖δu_0‖_(w),     C uniform in b.

The last term does not vanish at (0, p⃗_b) when b ≠ b₀; it is bounded as follows. ‖δu‖_(w) ≤ C|δW′| by the induction
bound, as ‖·‖_(w) is bounded by a seminorm of 𝒵_(β_k) (w ≤ β_k − 2); and ‖m_ν(W)‖_(w) ≤ C|W| for every row, m_ν(W)
having K⁺-weight at least λ_♯ − 1 − ε ≥ w − ε, ι⁺-weight λ_♯ − ε and support away from ℐ⁺ (Lemma 32.32,
Lemma 36.4). So ‖δu_0‖_(w) ≤ C|δW′|, and, as |p⃗| ≤ |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + |p⃗_b| = |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + |b − b₀|,

    |A_k| ≤ C(‖h‖ + |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + ‖q‖ + |b − b₀|),     C uniform in b,

by the direct bound. At the levels below 3 the same direct bound applies: there, for ν = (s1, λ, j), C^(k+1)_ν is
the K⁺-coefficient S^(h,p⃗)_(λ,j)(G′) of u_0 := u + Σ_(𝒩⊔𝒩_rot) m_ν(W′_ν) given by Lemma 32.27, transferred to
P_4 as in Step 1 and applied from an admissible level α″ ∈ (2, 2 + w], whose hypothesis u_0 meets, minus W′_ν; and
‖δG′‖_(𝒴,k+1) has the bound above, the rows there being rows of (36.1) and the motion coordinates changing
as (36.5) gives. The bound of Lemma 32.27, C‖G′‖_(𝒴(β_(k+1))) + C(‖h‖ + |p⃗|)‖u_0‖_(α″),
uniform in b by (P1)–(P4), has the same form, and the estimate above holds with ‖·‖_(α″) in place of ‖·‖_(w).
At the base level the new coordinates are the motion parameters (S′, b′, S^(0)′_1), which enter G′ through f^S, f^b,
f^(s1) in full. There the level map is that of
Corollary 32.18, the composite of the maps of Lemma 32.15 and Lemma 32.17, and Proposition 32.14
bounds those directly, within C(‖h‖ + |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + |b − b₀|) of ±id, with ‖q‖ entering through Δ_q and R_q as above.
Their composite is block-triangular, not of the form −id + A_k; what the elimination uses is that its inverse is bounded
uniformly, which this gives. So |A_k| ≤ C(‖h‖ + |p⃗ − p⃗_b| + ‖q‖ + |b − b₀|) at every level above the base, the base
level's map has a uniformly bounded inverse, and the continuity statements that Step 3 of the proof of
Theorem 34.9 cites are not needed.

So −id + A_k is invertible for (h, p⃗, q) small, and 𝒫_(k+1) is a graph.

*The induction bound at k + 1.* At the point of 𝒫_k whose new coordinates are 0, C^(k+1) on the new rows is the tuple of
the S^(h,p⃗,β_(k+1))_ν(G′) and A_(b,ν)(G′). By Lemma 36.7 it is at most C‖G′‖_(𝒴,k+1) + C(‖h‖ + |p⃗|)‖u_0‖_(w)
(below 3, by Lemma 32.27, with ‖·‖_(α″) in place of ‖·‖_(w)), and by the induction bound at k this is at most
C(‖F‖ + |W⃗_free|): G′ is G̃ = F − Δ_q(p⃗′) − R_q u less the terms of the list and of f^S, f^b, f^(s1), and
u_0 = u + Σ_(𝒩⊔𝒩_rot) m_ν(W′_ν). As (−id + A_k)⁻¹ is bounded, the new coordinates on 𝒫_(k+1), and so all the
coordinates, are at most C(‖F‖ + |W⃗_free|), W⃗_free the coordinates of higher rate. On 𝒫_(k+1) every coefficient in
(36.4) vanishes, so u(p⃗′) = ũ. Like the coefficients, ũ is obtained from f′ := G′ − (L_(h,p⃗) − L_b)u_0 and
the W′_ν by maps linear and bounded uniformly in b, each level losing finitely many derivatives (the proofs of
Proposition 33.8, Proposition 33.15 and Lemma 33.16, at the level β_(k+1) as in Lemma 33.29; below
3 the bound on ũ of Lemma 32.27); and ‖f′‖_(𝒴,k+1) ≤ ‖G′‖_(𝒴,k+1) + C(‖h‖ + |p⃗|)‖u_0‖_(w) by the count of Step 0
of the proof of Lemma 33.16. So the induction bound holds at k + 1.

At k = K every row has rate below α − 2 (the rotation rows at b: Re λ ≤ 2 < α − 2), so 𝒫_K is one point p⃗′. It satisfies
(36.3), and u(p⃗′) ∈ 𝒵_α with no rotation-row content; by the induction bound, |p⃗′| ≤ C‖F‖ and the seminorms
of u(p⃗′) in 𝒵_α are at most C‖F‖, C uniform in b. The rest of the proof of Theorem 34.9, the splitting
u = h_(b,rem)(q′) + h′ by Theorem 33.24 at b (Corollary 33.33, with G := G′(p⃗′),
u_0 := u(p⃗′) + Σ_(𝒩⊔𝒩_rot) m_ν(W′_ν) and the W′_ν as the W_ν there), then applies. The three terms of the bound of
Corollary 33.33 are at most C‖F‖: ‖G′(p⃗′)‖_(𝒴,K) ≤ C‖F‖, by the terms of G′ and G̃ = F − Δ_q(p⃗′) − R_q u(p⃗′);
with w_0 := min(α − 2, λ_♯ − 1), ‖u_0‖_(w_0) ≤ ‖u(p⃗′)‖_(w_0) + C|p⃗′| ≤ C‖F‖, as w_0 < α − 2; and |W′_ν| ≤ |p⃗′| ≤ C‖F‖.
So the seminorms of q′ and h′ are at most C‖F‖, C uniform in b. The v1 coefficient of q′ has no term at ℳ_rot. p⃗′ is
affine in F, which enters through G̃ only, and linear since it vanishes at F = 0. Uniqueness: any p⃗″ satisfying
(36.3) with u(p⃗″) ∈ 𝒵_α lies in 𝒫_0 (the uniqueness in Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 34.9). Its
non-rotation coefficients vanish level by level by Lemma 36.3, since (36.3) removes the rotation
rows from (36.4). So p⃗″ ∈ 𝒫_K.

*At b₀.* Write W′^rot := (W′_ν)_(ν∈𝒩_rot). At b₀ the v1 coefficient of u = u_0 − Σ m_ν(W′_ν) at ℳ_rot is
A_(b₀)(G′) − W′^rot. The v1 pieces of u_0 are the construction's, with the coefficients A_(b₀)(G′)
(Proposition 36.5 at b₀). On 𝒫_K the coefficients of the rows of 𝒩 vanish, and the functional ℓ of Step 4′ of the
proof of Theorem 34.9, applied to u = u_0 − Σ m_ν(W′_ν), returns its v1 coefficient uniquely; by
Proposition 36.5 (c) and Definition 36.6 it is A_(b₀)(G′) − W′^rot, and m_ν(W), ν ∈ 𝒩_rot, has v1
coefficient a_ν W. So C^rot = 0 is (36.3) (with the sign of the derivative −id of Step 4′). The p⃗′ of
Theorem 34.9 satisfies the level conditions and (36.3), so it is the point 𝒫_K. ∎

**Remark 36.9** (Uniqueness at b.) At a rotating b, the p⃗′ of Proposition 36.8 is unique only
together with (36.3). The bottom of m_ν(W), ν ∈ 𝒩_rot, is a_ν h_(b,v1)(W) = a_ν(ġ_b(ḃ_W) + h_b(S_W)), with
coefficients O(|b − b₀||W|) (Lemma 30.4). The K⁺-expansion does not separate it from the b- and S-rows, so
the conditions u ∈ 𝒵_(β_k) alone are not shown to fix W′^rot. The results that use Proposition 36.8 use only the
constructed map F ↦ (p⃗′, q′, h′) and its uniqueness together with (36.3):

- Theorem 34.24 builds U′ from the constructed map; Remark 34.25 records that D_UΦ is not injective.
- A_b does not depend on the loss ε, being computed from ι⁺- and tf-data (Definition 36.6). So when F lies in a
  smaller class of right sides, which has the same ι⁺- and tf-data, a parameter found for F there that satisfies
  (36.3) and gives u ∈ 𝒵_α is the p⃗′ of Proposition 36.8, by that uniqueness.

### 36.3 The linear theory at b

**Theorem 36.10** (The linear theory at base points near b₀.) For base points with black hole parameter
b ∈ ℬ̄_*, the statements at b (Definition 30.1) of the following hold, the v1 terms of exponent of real part at most
2 being treated by Section 36.2, with constants and smallness conditions uniform in b:

- the results below level 3 (Lemma 29.26–Proposition 29.29, Lemma 29.30–Proposition 29.35,
  Lemma 31.3–Proposition 31.6, Definition 31.7–Corollary 31.20, Proposition 31.21,
  Corollary 31.22 and Lemma 31.23–Proposition 31.27), the backgrounds g_0 := g_(b₀,b₀,−S) of
  Section 29.15 and g_S of (31.15) becoming g_(b₀,b,−S), and the correction of the first kind staying
  the tensor built at b₀ ((P6)), with Proposition 31.16 (2), Corollary 31.20 and Corollary 31.22 in the form
  of Proposition 31.19;
- Lemma 32.4, Lemma 32.6, Lemma 32.8, Lemma 32.9, Lemma 32.10,
  Lemma 32.12, Lemma 32.15, Lemma 32.17, Definition 32.16 and Corollary 32.18:
  Lemma 32.6 being independent of b, Lemma 32.10 with p⃗ = (S, b − b₀, S^(0)_1) (its proof transfers,
  g_b being Ricci flat for every b and ġ_b given by (P3)), Lemma 32.8 in the form of Lemma 32.11,
  Lemma 32.12 at fixed b only, and Lemma 32.15, Lemma 32.17 and Corollary 32.18 in the form of
  Proposition 32.14;
- Proposition 32.29 and the lemmas it rests on (Lemma 32.20–Lemma 32.28), in the form of the direct
  bound of Proposition 36.8, with the base step by Proposition 32.14, Lemma 32.22 in the form
  (36.1), its rows being rows of the set 𝒩 of Section 32.10, and Proposition 32.29 (ii) and
  Lemma 32.28 at fixed b only;
- Section 32.11, with Lemma 32.34 and Lemma 32.36 (c) (r_(0,0) = 0) in the form (36.1)
  of Lemma 32.36 (e), and the identities (32.7) that Lemma 32.34 states for P_4 in the form
  (32.9) of Lemma 32.11, P_4 being P_2 on the directions of p⃗_≤0 at W = 0;
- Definition 33.1, Definition 33.3, Lemma 33.2, Lemma 33.4 (c) and Proposition 33.8;
- Proposition 33.15, Lemma 33.16 and Lemma 33.17 (stated at a fixed b),
  and Theorem 33.18 only inside Lemma 36.7 and Proposition 36.8: at a rotating b its parameter
  space lacks the rotation rows, and Proposition 36.8 with q = 0 is its form there;
- Lemma 33.22, Lemma 33.23 and Theorem 33.24, in the forms of Lemma 33.32 and
  Corollary 33.33;
- Proposition 33.28, Lemma 33.29 and Lemma 33.30 in the form of Lemma 36.7, and
  Proposition 33.31 only inside Proposition 36.8, as for Theorem 33.18;
- Definition 34.2 with (34.4), Lemma 34.5–Lemma 34.8, Remark 34.10 (2), and
  Theorem 34.9 in the form of Proposition 36.8 (unique among the p⃗′ with the assigned rotation
  coordinates);
- Lemma 34.17, Lemma 34.18, Lemma 34.19, Theorem 34.20 and Remark 34.21, as written, with
  the rows built at b₀ ((viii) below);
- Lemma 34.23, for the output of Proposition 36.8, and Theorem 34.24.

*Proof.* Chapter 31, Chapter 32 and Chapter 33 state and prove their results at a base point with parameter
b ∈ ℬ̄_*, with constants uniform in b: Chapter 31 from its own model at b, with Lemma 31.1 and
Lemma 31.2; Chapter 32 and Chapter 33 from (P1)–(P6), Lemma 30.3, Lemma 30.4,
Proposition 30.5, Lemma 36.3 and Section 36.2, and from the results at b of the chapters before
them (Lemma 31.2, Lemma 31.18 and Proposition 31.19 of Chapter 31 among them). The results of
Chapter 29 below level 3 hold at b by Proposition 30.5. The results of Chapter 34 stated at b₀ hold at b by
Proposition 36.8 and by the paragraph *The augmentation at b* below. Items (i)–(xi) record where a step proved at
b₀ uses a property of b₀ that a general b ∈ ℬ̄_* need not have, or an object built at b₀, and what replaces it at b.
The three steps that need more than a substitution are proved at b in Lemma 31.18 and Proposition 31.19,
Lemma 32.11 and Proposition 32.14, and Lemma 33.32 and Corollary 33.33.

(i) *The forward solutions.* The results listed solve with L^(g,g_0) at the base point through Theorem 29.17 and its
corollaries ((P1)). The splitting L_(h,p⃗) = L_(b₀) + (L_(h,p⃗) − L_(b₀)) near K⁺, used to move a perturbation into the
right-hand side (in Chapter 32 and Chapter 33, for instance in Step 0 of the proof of Theorem 33.24), becomes
L_(h,p⃗) = L_b + (L_(h,p⃗) − L_b). This has the same K⁺-gain, as g_0 = g_b near K⁺ (Lemma 29.11). The class
statement k_S ∈ 𝒦 of Chapter 31 reads k_S := g_(b₀,b,−S) − g_b ∈ 𝒦 at b, with differences taken from g_b; k′ := ∂_S k_S
is unchanged and vanishes near K⁺. At b, L_(h,S) := D_hP_1(·, S, b), and P_1(0, 0, b) need not vanish in 𝒞; the linear
theory uses only D_hP_1 and D_SP_1.

(ii) *The model at ι⁺ and at tf:* the results of Chapter 26 and Chapter 27, through (P2) and (P4).

(iii) *The states, towers and index sets.* The index sets of Proposition 23.28, Proposition 23.34,
Proposition 25.26 and Proposition 25.30, which Chapter 31 and Chapter 32 use, are independent of b ((P3)), so the
index sets ℰ_ind, ℰ_♯ and ℰ_+ serve at every b, and so does ℰ^♮ (Definition 33.26), built from ℰ_♯ and ℰ_ind. The
index set of the column terms ℰ_col (Definition 33.1, Lemma 33.9), which generates Λ and through it ℰ_par,
𝒩, ℰ_♯, ℰ^♮, (G) and admissibility, is the b-independent set

    ℰ_col = ({(0, 0), (1, 0)} ∪ ℰ_ind ∪ (1 + ℰ_ind)) + ℕ₀

of Lemma 33.9. There F = r⁴f with f = [L_b, χ_K]w, and at every b the states w have the index sets (2, 0) ∪
(2 + ℰ_ind) (ġ_b(1, 0) and h̆_b(S), and t_*h_b(S), as t_* = sr) and (3, 0) ∪ (3 + ℰ_ind) (ġ_b(0, Ȧ)) ((P3);
(25.18), (23.25)); the commutator gains 2, the factor r⁴ loses 4, and the smooth coefficients of the
L_k (Lemma 31.3 at b) add ℕ₀.

(iv) *The derivatives in b* (Corollary 32.18, Lemma 34.7 (c)) are taken at b: the b-column is ġ_b
((P3)). So is ġ = ∂_b g_b in Chapter 29 and Chapter 31, which enters through the columns and the singular part of
Chapter 28 ((P3), (P4)). The proof of Lemma 34.7 (c) is written for every b near b₀, and the use of
L̂_(b₀)(0)∂_b h_(b,v1) = 0 in Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 34.9 is replaced at b by the rates of the v1
coefficients of q, as Section 34.8 (1) shows.

(v) *The joint injectivity:* Lemma 33.5 and Corollary 33.6 hold at b by Lemma 36.3. Step 4′ of
the proof of Theorem 34.9 is not used at b, Proposition 36.8 replacing it. The injectivity of S ↦ h(S)
(Proposition 25.30 (1), proved at b₀ by symmetry), used in the proofs of Proposition 31.6, Proposition 31.16 and
Proposition 31.21, holds at b by Lemma 31.2.

(vi) *The v1 terms:* Section 32.10 (𝒲_v1 = 𝒱′ = 0, kept at every b), Lemma 33.4 and
Proposition 33.8, Lemma 33.12, Section 33.9, Lemma 33.22, Lemma 33.23 and
Theorem 33.24, and Definition 34.1, Definition 34.3 and Steps 2–3 and 4′ of the proof of
Theorem 34.9. These are Section 36.2: Proposition 36.5, Lemma 36.7, Proposition 36.8,
Lemma 33.32 and Corollary 33.33. At a rotating b, the rate of a v1 coefficient at z (Definition 34.1,
Lemma 34.7, and the construction of Section 34.5) is at least Re z, and Re z + 1 on ker h_(b,v1), the
rotations commuting with the spin; only the lower bound is used. The a_v1 term in the proof of Proposition 31.21 is
covered by Lemma 36.4: if present, its bottom a_ν h_(b,v1) has K⁺-weight Re λ₀ − ε ≥ Re λ₀ − 1, so the bound
used there survives.

(vii) *The time translation as a Killing field:* (P5).

(viii) *The data* (Chapter 34). The base points U of Chapter 34 map by Φ to (h, p⃗, q) with parameter b
(Theorem 34.20), and the proofs there use Theorem 34.9 and the maps of Section 34.5 at that base point,
by (i)–(vii). Section 34.5 builds its rows at b₀, and Lemma 34.17, Lemma 34.18, Lemma 34.19,
Theorem 34.20 and Remark 34.21 hold as written at b (Lemma 34.19, the log count, has b-independent
exponents, log orders and index sets by (iii)), with the rows m^(b₀)_ν, the towers T_(ψ,b) and the corrections at b₀:
the rule of (P6), rows at b, is not applied there, and the pure gauge of Remark 34.22 refers to g_(b₀). P_5 and
the coordinates W_ν do not depend on the convention (Section 34.8 (3)). Lemma 34.23, whose proof
applies L̃_(b₀)(0)⁻¹, holds for the output of Proposition 36.8: at b its roots are those of (P2),
Proposition 28.8 holds by (P4), and neither A_b, which reads only ι⁺-data and level-1 tf-data (Definition 36.6),
nor E^ν, a fixed tensor ((P6)), depends on η_2.

(ix) *The boost column:* Lemma 31.12, Proposition 31.16 (2), Corollary 31.20 and Corollary 31.22 at b are
Lemma 31.18 and Proposition 31.19.

(x) *The parameter columns:* Lemma 32.8 at b is Lemma 32.11, and Lemma 32.15,
Lemma 32.17, Corollary 32.18 and the base step of Proposition 32.29 at b are Proposition 32.14.

(xi) *The expansion:* Lemma 33.22, Lemma 33.23 and Theorem 33.24 at b are Lemma 33.32 and
Corollary 33.33.

*The augmentation at b.* The results of Chapter 34 stated at b₀ use b₀ only as follows, and each use is supplied at b.

- Section 34.1 and Definition 34.1–Definition 34.3: η_E = min Re ℰ_ind > 0, the inclusion
  ℰ_+ ⊃ (ℰ_♯ ∪ ℰ^♮) ∩ {Re < 3 + ε_+}, the sets ℰ^α_ψ and ℳ_rot are (iii) and (P3); the v1 rate Re z at a rotating b
  exceeds 2 + ε_K by (G), which does not depend on b; h_(b,rem), T_(ψ,b), h^(≤2)_(b,v1) and ġ_b are defined at b
  ((P3), (P6)); (34.3) is defined at every b, so (34.4) holds at b with h_(b,rem); at b,
  h_(b,rem)(q) is the χ_K u_exp of Theorem 33.24 at b, with the towers T_(ψ,b) (Corollary 33.33); the
  corrections of the rotation rows are those of Definition 32.31 at b₀ ((P6)); the rate of the rotation rows at b is
  Lemma 36.4, and they become new rows (Proposition 36.8); Theorem 33.18 is used only with the
  parameter in the non-rotation part of 𝒫, and v1 stays excluded from Corollary 33.6 at b (Lemma 30.4);
  and f^ν = L m_ν + r^ν acquires E^ν ((36.1)).
- Lemma 34.5 (a), (c) and Lemma 34.6: the index sets are (P3), with the loss of (P4) absorbed by the
  orders "−"; h_(b,rem)(q) is real ((P3)); L_b h^(≤1)_(b,s1)(S) is computed by the stationarity of L_b ((P5)) and the
  tower relations at b ((P3)).
- Lemma 34.7: in (a), the corrections h_ν are built at b₀ and supported in 𝒞 ((P6)); in (b), g_0 depends on S
  only off χ_K, and ∂_S g_p⃗ ∈ ρ²C^∞ by Lemma 32.4 at b; in (c), the derivative in b is taken at b, every
  coefficient of q having rate > 2 at every b ((iv)); ∂_b g_b has weight 2 (Section 28.1), Lemma 32.6 holds
  for every g_0, and the exponents of ∂_b h_(b,rem)(q) are those of Lemma 34.4 ((P3)).
- Lemma 34.8: the thresholds, the roots and the tf-propositions Proposition 27.55 and Proposition 27.58
  are (P2), (P4).
- Theorem 34.9: at b it is Proposition 36.8. Step 1 runs by (P1)–(P6) with E^ν ∈ 𝒴(α_1), and (iv) for the v1
  part; Step 2 by (P6) with E^ν; Corollary 33.6 by Lemma 36.3; Step 3 by the direct bound; Step 4′ is not
  used ((v)); the v1 coefficient of q′ has no exponent in ℳ_rot by Proposition 36.8 with the class of ũ in
  Lemma 36.7; and χ_K u_exp = h_(b,rem)(q′) with the towers T_(ψ,b) ((P6)). Remark 34.10 (2) does not
  involve b: the inputs at b use a_K only through strict inequalities.
- Lemma 34.23 and Theorem 34.24: Lemma 34.23 at b is as in (viii), its thresholds being on
  tf-exponents and so unaffected by the rate shift of Proposition 36.5 (b), and the absence of indicial roots in
  (0, 1) being (P2). Step 0 of the proof of Theorem 34.24 uses only the constructed map of Proposition 36.8
  (Remark 36.9); h_(b,rem)(q′) takes the place of h_(b₀,rem)(q′), and of the rows m_ν only the rows at λ₀ enter,
  whose λ₀-terms do not depend on b (Lemma 34.18); the order of [h′]_(λ₀) comes from u ∈ 𝒵_α
  (Proposition 36.8); the rates of q′ are below α (Proposition 36.8, Lemma 36.7), the v1 part with
  Re z ≤ 3 by (G⁺); the independent injective leading terms of distinct rows are those of Lemma 26.32 at the
  Minkowski model ((P2), (P3)); and the bounds of Proposition 36.8 are uniform in b.

*The constants.* Every constant above is a finite combination of constants of (P1)–(P4) and (P6), of Lemma 36.3,
of Lemma 36.4, Lemma 36.7, Lemma 31.18, Lemma 33.32 and Lemma 32.11, of
Proposition 31.19 and Proposition 32.14, and of the maps of Proposition 36.5, each uniform on ℬ̄_*. The
continuity statements (Proposition 32.29 (ii) and Lemma 32.28, Lemma 33.17, Lemma 33.30) enter
Lemma 36.7 at fixed b only and are not used for the bounds of the elimination. Lemma 31.17 (b) and
Lemma 32.12 are not used across b; the direct bounds of Proposition 31.19 and Proposition 32.14 replace
them. The smallness of the elimination, across b, comes from the direct bound of Step 3 of the proof of
Proposition 36.8, through (P6) and Definition 36.6. ℬ_* is the ball of radius at most 1/(2C_B) of
Lemma 30.3 and Lemma 31.1 (one ball: Lemma 31.1 takes its C_B as a supremum over the ball of
Lemma 30.3, which is at most the C_B there, so its condition on the radius holds already), inside condition (B5)
of Section 29.6, shrunk further so that the bound of Lemma 36.3 holds and the maps −id + A_k of
Proposition 36.8 are invertible on it. ∎

**Corollary 36.11** (The tame and exact forms at b.) For base points with black hole parameter b ∈ ℬ̄_*, the
statements at b (Definition 30.1) of the following hold, with constants, losses and smallness conditions uniform in
b:

- Theorem 35.7, Theorem 35.8 and Proposition 35.9, the solution maps that Theorem 35.7 estimates
  being, at a rotating b, those of Proposition 36.8 and Lemma 36.7;
- Proposition 35.20, Proposition 35.23, Proposition 35.26, Proposition 35.29, Proposition 35.31,
  Theorem 35.30, Theorem 35.32 and Corollary 35.33, Theorem 35.30 in the form of
  Proposition 36.8 at exact weights.

*Proof.* Chapter 35 states and proves these results at a base point with parameter b ∈ ℬ̄_*. Its proofs use, at b,
the model objects (P1)–(P6) (Lemma 30.2, Lemma 36.1), Lemma 36.3, Section 36.2,
Proposition 30.5, Corollary 29.25, Theorem 29.21, Proposition 29.19 and Corollary 29.20, the
results of Chapter 31–Chapter 33 at b (among them Proposition 31.19, Proposition 32.14, Lemma 33.32 and
Corollary 33.33), and the results of Chapter 34 at b, Section 34.8 (1)–(3). All of these hold on ℬ̄_*
with constants uniform in b: they are Theorem 36.10 and the statements its proof rests on, and
Theorem 29.21, Proposition 29.19 and Corollary 29.20 hold on ℬ̄_1 ⊃ ℬ̄_*, uniformly ((P4)). The following
records where a step of Chapter 35 uses a property of b₀ that a general b need not have, or an object built at b₀, and
what replaces it at b.

*The calculus, the classes and the inventory.* The tame calculus of Chapter 35 (Definition 35.1–Lemma 35.6)
has constants that depend on the base point through finitely many seminorms, continuous in b, so bounded on the
compact ℬ̄_*; the exact classes and the conditions (Ex1)–(Ex4) and (A_K) of Definition 35.13 do not involve b
((P2)–(P3): the exponents, roots and index sets are those at b₀), except that (Ex3), used also in (A_K), concerns the
K⁺-exponents at hand, among which at a rotating b are those of the v1 terms; (Ex3) at b is (Ex3) at b₀, by the
paragraph *(Ex3) at b* below. The solution maps of Chapter 29–Chapter 34 in Theorem 35.7 are read at b as in
Lemma 36.7 and Proposition 36.8; in particular, at a rotating b the map of Theorem 34.9 there is
the constructed map F ↦ (p⃗′, q′, h′) of Proposition 36.8 (Remark 36.9). The new objects enter the inventory
of Lemma 35.3 (c): A_b is bounded by a fixed low seminorm of the right side f′ = G − (L_(h,p⃗) − L_b)u, from
which it reads the ι⁺-data u_+ and the tf-data (Proposition 36.5), so by fixed low seminorms of G and of the
solution u (Definition 36.6); E^ν is bounded by C|b − b₀||W| in a fixed seminorm ((P6)); the rotation rows
enter −id + A_k as the other rows do; and d_* includes their orders.

*(Ex3) at b.* At a rotating b the K⁺-exponents at hand are those at b₀ together with: the exponents λ + j, λ ∈ π_1ℳ_rot,
j ∈ ℕ₀, of the bottoms a_ν h_(b,v1)(W) of the rotation rows and their shifts (Lemma 36.4, Proposition 36.5);
and the exponents z + j, j ∈ ℕ₀, of the v1 coefficients t_*^(−z) of q, whose rate is Re z at b and Re z + 1 at b₀
(Definition 34.1), with z ∈ π_1ℰ_♯ and 2 < Re z < 3 + ε_+ < 4. All of these lie in Λ (π_1ℰ_♯ ⊂ Λ, Section 33.9,
and Λ + 1 ⊂ Λ), so their real parts are at least λ_♯ (Lemma 33.2 (a)). Since λ_♯ ∈ Λ (Definition 33.1), also
λ_♯ + 1 ∈ Λ, with real part above 2, so (G) gives λ_♯ + 1 > 2 + ε_K. For i ∈ {0, 1, 2}, α − 2 + i ∈ (2 + i, 2 + i + ε_K],
as α ∈ (4, 4 + ε_K]. Let λ ∈ π_1ℳ_rot, so Re λ ≤ 2, and j ∈ ℕ₀. If j ≤ i, then Re(λ + j) ≤ 2 + i < α − 2 + i; if
j ≥ i + 1, then Re(λ + j) ≥ λ_♯ + i + 1 > 2 + i + ε_K ≥ α − 2 + i. So no λ + j has real part α − 2, α − 1 or α. For the
v1 coefficients of q: by (G) no element of Λ has real part in (2, 2 + ε_K] ∪ (3, 3 + ε_K], which contain α − 2 and α − 1;
and Re(z + j) = α forces j ≥ 1, as Re z < 4 < α, so z + j = (z + 1) + (j − 1) is an exponent at hand at b₀, where (Ex3)
holds. So (Ex3) at b is (Ex3) at b₀.

*The losses, the smallness and the exact weights.* In Lemma 35.3 (f), the loss at every order holds at b by
Proposition 29.19, uniformly on ℬ̄_1, so the neighbourhood of b₀ does not shrink with the order. The continuity of
Lemma 35.5 is read at b through Lemma 36.7 at (0, p⃗_b) and the direct bound of Proposition 36.8,
both in fixed seminorms, so d_* is unchanged; and Theorem 35.7 at b takes its smallness δ_𝔹 at most the radius
of the final ℬ_* (*The constants* in the proof of Theorem 36.10). Theorem 35.30 at b is
Proposition 36.8 at the exact weights, as its proof shows: E^ν is exact there, A_b does not depend on the loss
(Remark 36.9), and the errors of the identification of the rotation rows have room. That proof cites Step 3 of
the proof of Theorem 34.9 and its uniqueness, to identify the exact and the lossy solutions; at b, the
uniqueness of Proposition 36.8 together with (36.3) serves there (Remark 36.9), A_b being the
same on both classes. In the proof of Proposition 35.26 at b, the profiles of the level-3 towers are homogeneous of
degree d_ψ − j only in their leading parts, which do not depend on b ((P3)); the other terms are smaller by
min Re ℰ_ind (Section 33.9), so the profiles satisfy the bound |(r∂_r)^a ∂_ω^β p_j| ≲ r^(j−d_ψ) that
Lemma 35.27 (a) asks. Proposition 35.20 and Proposition 35.23 carry the rotation rows of
Proposition 36.5.

*The remaining results.* Theorem 35.8 and Theorem 35.32 apply Theorem 35.7, respectively
Theorem 35.30, at Φ(U), and then Steps 1–3 of the proof of Theorem 34.24, which hold at b with the rows built
at b₀ and with Lemma 34.23 for the output of Proposition 36.8 (item (viii) of the proof of
Theorem 36.10); the black hole parameter of U is that of Φ(U) (Definition 34.15, Theorem 34.20), so it lies
in ℬ_* for U small. Proposition 35.9 and Proposition 35.31 bound P_5 ∘ Φ through Theorem 34.20 and
(34.15), which hold at b by the same item, and through P_5(h, p⃗, q) = P_4(h + h_(b,rem)(q), p⃗), with
h_(b,rem) real and smooth in b ((P3)). Proposition 35.29 uses h_(b,rem)(q) at b, the stationarity of L_b ((P5)), the
tower relations at b ((P3)) and the rates of the coefficients of q, which exceed 2 + ε_K at every b
(Definition 34.1 and (G)). Corollary 35.33 composes the families of Lemma 35.3 and the results above at
fixed weights; so it holds at b, with constants uniform in b, as the exact classes do not involve b. ∎

**Corollary 36.12** (Right inverses at every base point.) Theorem 34.24 and its tame and exact forms
(Theorem 35.8, Corollary 35.33) hold at every base point U ∈ 𝒟^∞ small in 𝒟^d, a point of the data space of
Definition 34.15 whose black hole parameter, that of Φ(U) (Theorem 34.20), lies in ℬ_*, which the smallness of U in
𝒟^d ensures, with constants uniform in U; at a rotating b the right inverse is the one constructed by
Proposition 36.8. These are the right inverses that Theorem 20.1 (iii) asks for at every point of its
neighbourhood.

*Proof.* The black hole parameter of U is one of its components (Definition 34.15) and is that of Φ(U)
(Theorem 34.20), so b ∈ ℬ_* for U small in 𝒟^d. At such U, Theorem 34.24 holds in its statement at b by
Theorem 36.10, and Theorem 35.8 and Corollary 35.33 hold in their statements at b by Corollary 36.11,
with constants uniform in b; at a rotating b the solution map used in Step 0 of the proof of Theorem 34.24 is that
of Proposition 36.8 (Remark 36.9). ∎

# Part IX. The stability theory, V: exterior, nonlinear theorem, gluing, linear stability

## 37. The exterior region: estimates at infinity, the exterior solution, polyhomogeneity and boosts

This chapter solves the gauge-fixed Einstein equation near spatial infinity I₀ and future null infinity ℐ⁺, for small
data on the part of the initial surface Σ_IVP outside a large ball, and describes the solution there. It is [Hin26,
Sections 5.4–5.7] (Lemma 5.16, Theorem 5.17 with (5.52)–(5.53), Remarks 5.18 and 5.20, Theorem 5.21 with Remark 5.22,
Theorem 5.23 with the cut-off gauge (5.75)–(5.76), Remark 5.24, Proposition 5.25, Section 5.7.1, Remark 5.26 and
Example 5.27; pp. 99–113) in dimension 4 + 1, together with [Hin23a, Section 3] (pp. 9–32), on whose energy estimates
[Hin26, Theorem 5.17] rests, written out in dimension 4 + 1 for the gauge-fixed operator of Section 27.4.

Section 37.2 fixes the exterior domain Ω_(ext,r₀) and shows that its boundary hypersurfaces are spacelike for every
small perturbation of g_(b₀). Section 37.3–Section 37.7 are [Hin23a, Sections 3.1–3.2]: the edge-b structure at ℐ⁺,
the conjugated scalar wave operator, the basic energy estimate near ℐ⁺ (Proposition 37.8) and the b-energy estimate near
the interior of I₀ (Proposition 37.10). Section 37.8–Section 37.10 are [Hin23a, Sections 3.4–3.5] for the tensor
operator: its edge-b form (Proposition 37.13) and the energy estimate for the system with its tame form
(Proposition 37.16). Section 37.11–Section 37.14 are [Hin23a, Section 3.6]: the Cauchy problem near I₀ in both
directions, the linear exterior estimate with the sharp weight at ℐ⁺ (Theorem 37.27) and the nonlinear exterior
solution (Theorem 37.28). Section 37.15 states the result as [Hin26, Theorem 5.17] in dimension 4 + 1
(Theorem 37.30) and proves the propagation of the gauge condition and of the vacuum equation
(Proposition 37.32). Section 37.16 and Section 37.17 introduce the cut-off gauge of [Hin26, (5.76)] and show that
the estimates hold in it. Section 37.18 proves partial polyhomogeneity of the exterior solution (Theorem 37.36),
and Section 37.19–Section 37.21 treat boosted backgrounds and data (Theorem 37.39) and gauged Cauchy data
(Proposition 37.41).

*What dimension 4 + 1 changes.* (1) *Weights.* Radiation fields decay like |x|^(−3/2) (Remark 27.1 (a)), so
every weight at ℐ⁺ is shifted by ½: the condition 1 < ℓ^♭_I < min(ℓ^♭₀, 1 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 3/2) of [Hin26, (5.49)]
becomes (37.1). (2) *No subtraction.* [Hin26, Theorem 5.21, Step 2] measures h from g_(b₀) + h₀, h₀ carrying
the radiation fields of π̸₀h and π₁₁h, because in dimension 3 + 1 these enter the leading part of the operator at ℐ⁺.
In dimension 4 + 1 the leading part is the constant matrix Ā and all of the perturbation lies in the error
(Proposition 27.14); so the equation is integrated directly (Remark 37.37). (3) *Half steps.* The error gains ½
at ℐ⁺ in place of min(α_I − 1, (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ), so each step of the proof of Theorem 37.36 raises the weight at ℐ⁺
by any ν < ½. (4) *The index condition at I₀* is min Re ℰ₀ > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ, so that ℰ₀ ⊂ ℰ_I^C is compatible with
Definition 27.6 (2). (5) *The energy estimates.* The conjugation that removes the first-order term of the scalar wave
operator is by ρ^(3/2), the density is ρ₀⁵ρ_I⁴|dg|, and the conjugated operator carries ¾ with the spherical
Laplacian, which only increases the positive angular term of the energy identity. In the Minkowski null coordinates of
Section 27.1 the mass enters only through the error class, the first-order matrix of the conjugated tensor operator
at ℐ⁺ is the constant Ā, free of the perturbation, and its diagonal is nonnegative; so the sharp weights
α_I < min(α₀, 0) need no separate argument, the decay at ℐ⁺ is recovered in two integrations, and only the slot π̸₀
carries a radiation field. The estimate near the interior of I₀, for which [Hin23a] cites [HV20, Proposition 4.3], is
proved in Proposition 37.10. (6) *Boosts.* The past slab of Ω_(ext,r₀) has the slope 1/12, so that the cut-off boosts of
Section 21.7 are genuine boosts on all of it (Lemma 37.38); the time function differs from Boyer–Lindquist
time by a function smooth in |x|⁻¹, so the Cauchy data acquire no logarithms (Proposition 37.42); part (1) of
Theorem 37.39 needs the constraints, as the operator δ*_(g₀,E_C) is not natural under boosts; and the size of the
boost is made independent of r₀ by r₁ := 2r₀.

### 37.1 Notation and the inner radius

n = 4, D = 5. The notation is that of Chapter 21 and Chapter 27: the family g_b,
b = (m, A) ∈ ℬ, with b₀ = (m₀, 0) and R₁ = m₀^(1/2); the time functions t_* and t_IVP of Section 21.5, with
t_IVP = t − C″ on {|x| ≥ R₃} (Lemma 21.22 (b)); the gauge-fixed operator P(g, g₀) of (21.44) and its
linearisation L^(g,g₀) of (27.12), with the gauge parameters of Section 25.1 and (27.1), so
0 < γ_Υ < ¼, 0 < e_Υ < 1, 0 < e_C, v_C < 1 and (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C > 100; the coordinates (27.2), the
corner coordinates (ρ₀, ρ_I, ω) on U ((27.3), Lemma 27.2), X₀ := ρ₀∂_(ρ₀), X_I := ρ_I∂_(ρ_I),
ρ := ρ₀ρ_I = |x|⁻¹, and r := |x|; the splitting (27.6) with its slots 1–7 (Definition 27.3), the matrix Ā
of Lemma 27.12 with diagonal (27.14), the set σ_Υ = {0, (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ, 2γ_Υ}, the background class 𝒢
(Definition 27.9), and the partially polyhomogeneous spaces and classes of Section 27.2, Section 27.3 and
Section 27.5. Index sets and their operations are those of Definition 21.31. Unless stated otherwise the
weights at ℐ⁺ are powers of ρ_I, and the b-spaces are taken with the b-density, so that by b-Sobolev embedding (order
k > 5/2) a weight is the pointwise order. A vector field on 𝕊³ is written Θ. In this chapter r₀ is the exterior radius
of [Hin26, Lemma 5.16], not the radius of the artificial boundary of Section 11.1.1. The inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁]
of the spacetime (Section 21.4) enters this chapter only through the constants C′ of t_* and C″ of t_IVP near
infinity. Every result posed on the exterior domain or near infinity lives in {|x| ≥ r₀} with r₀ large and does not
reach the inner boundary. Proposition 37.41, Remark 37.40 and Remark 37.43 concern all of Σ_IVP, which
does reach it; but the proof of Proposition 37.41 is pointwise on Σ_IVP and uses only that g_(b₀) is smooth and dt_IVP
is timelike for g_(b₀) on {|x| ≥ r_♭} (Lemma 21.22 (b)). So every result of the chapter holds for each
r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁], with r₀ and the constants chosen after r_♭.

### 37.2 The exterior domain

This section is [Hin26, Lemma 5.16] in dimension 4 + 1. Fix weights

    ℓ^♭₀ > 3/2,     3/2 < ℓ^♭_I < min(ℓ^♭₀, 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 2).    (37.1)

So ℓ^♭_I < min Re ℰ_I^C for every ℰ_I^C of Definition 27.6, and H^(k,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b (Definition 27.6) consists
of the h with every slot in H^(k,ℓ^♭₀,ℓ^♭_I)_b except π̸₀h ∈ H^(k,ℓ^♭₀,((3/2,0),ℓ^♭_I))_b, which carries a radiation
field: the exponents 3/2 + s, s ∈ σ_Υ ∖ {0}, of the slots 4, 5 and 7 exceed ℓ^♭_I by (37.1) and
(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ ≤ γ_Υ ≤ 2γ_Υ.

**Lemma 37.1** (The spacetime domain; [Hin26, Lemma 5.16] in dimension 4 + 1.) For r₀ large let, with
r = |x|,

    Ω_(ext,r₀) := {−(r − r₀)/12 ≤ t_IVP ≤ 0} ∪ {0 ≤ t_IVP ≤ r + 2r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) − (r₀ + 2r₀^(1−ℓ^♭_I))},

with boundary hypersurfaces Σ_(past,r₀), Σ_(fut,r₀) (the first and the last level set) and
Σ_(IVP,r₀) := Ω_(ext,r₀) ∩ {t_IVP = 0}. There is R₀ > max(3R₁, R₃) such that for r₀ ≥ R₀ and every
h ∈ H^(3,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀)) with norm below 1 (the spaces (27.10), defined for k ≥ 5, extend
verbatim to k = 3), the three hypersurfaces are spacelike for g_(b₀) + h.

*Proof.* For r ≥ R₃, t_IVP = t − C″ (Lemma 21.22 (b)), and r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) → 0 as ℓ^♭_I > 1; so
Ω_(ext,r₀) ⊂ U ∩ {|x| ≥ r₀} ((27.3)) for r₀ large, and on it ρ₀ ≤ C/r₀: on Σ_(fut,r₀),
x¹ = t − r = −r₀ + 2r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) − 2r₀^(1−ℓ^♭_I) + O(1), and x¹ is smaller below it, so ρ₀ = (2 − x¹)⁻¹ ≤ C/r₀. By
Sobolev embedding (3 > 5/2) every slot of h is bounded by Cρ₀^(ℓ^♭₀)ρ_I^(ℓ^♭_I), except π̸₀h, which is bounded by
Cρ₀^(ℓ^♭₀)ρ_I^(3/2); and g_(b₀) − η ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ with its π_C, π₀₁, π_(1/), π̸₀ parts in ρ₀²ρ_I³C^∞
(Lemma 27.10 (1), Definition 27.9). Write δ := g_(b₀) + h − η, so
that |δ| ≤ C(ρ₀²ρ_I² + ρ₀^(ℓ^♭₀)ρ_I^(3/2)) in the frame of (27.6), which is small for r₀ large.

*Σ_(IVP,r₀) and Σ_(past,r₀).* dt is timelike for η, and so for η + δ when |δ| is small. In the coordinates (u, r) of
Minkowski space, u := t − r, η⁻¹ = −2∂_u∂_r + ∂_r² on du, dr, so ζ := d(t_IVP + (r − r₀)/12) = du + (13/12)dr has
η⁻¹(ζ, ζ) = −2 · 13/12 + (13/12)² = −143/144. (The calculation does not involve the dimension; any slope c ∈ (0, 1) in
place of 1/12 gives −2(1 + c) + (1 + c)² = (c + 1)(c − 1) < 0.) So ζ is timelike for η + δ too.

*Σ_(fut,r₀).* With x⁰ = t + r, x¹ = t − r, η = −dx⁰dx¹ (symmetric product), so η^(01) = −2,
η^(00) = η^(11) = 0, and dr = ½(dx⁰ − dx¹). For ℓ := ℓ^♭_I,

    ζ := d(t_IVP − r − 2r^(1−ℓ)) = (ℓ − 1)r^(−ℓ)dx⁰ + (1 − (ℓ − 1)r^(−ℓ))dx¹,

so η⁻¹(ζ, ζ) = −4(ℓ − 1)r^(−ℓ)(1 − (ℓ − 1)r^(−ℓ)), with r^(−ℓ) = ρ₀^ℓρ_I^ℓ. As ζ has no angular part,
(η + δ)⁻¹(ζ, ζ) − η⁻¹(ζ, ζ) = −η^(ia)η^(jb)δ_(ab)ζ_iζ_j + O(|δ|²), i, j, a, b ∈ {0, 1}. The coefficient of ζ₁² is
−4δ₀₀, of π_C-type, bounded by C(ρ₀²ρ_I³ + ρ₀^(ℓ^♭₀)ρ_I^(ℓ^♭_I)); that of ζ₀ζ₁ involves δ₀₁, bounded likewise; that of
ζ₀² involves δ₁₁, bounded by C(ρ₀²ρ_I² + ρ₀^(ℓ^♭₀)ρ_I^(ℓ^♭_I)) and multiplied by ζ₀² = O(ρ₀^(2ℓ)ρ_I^(2ℓ)); and
O(|δ|²) ≤ C(ρ₀⁴ρ_I⁴ + ρ₀^(2ℓ^♭₀)ρ_I³). Relative to ρ₀^ℓρ_I^ℓ these are at most
C(ρ₀^(2−ℓ)ρ_I^(3−ℓ) + ρ₀^(ℓ^♭₀−ℓ) + ρ₀^(2ℓ^♭₀−ℓ)ρ_I^(3−ℓ)), which tends to 0 as ρ₀ → 0, as ℓ < 2, ℓ < ℓ^♭₀ and ℓ < 3
((37.1)). As ρ₀ ≤ C/r₀ on Ω_(ext,r₀), for r₀ large (η + δ)⁻¹(ζ, ζ) ≤ −2(ℓ − 1)r^(−ℓ) < 0. ∎

The past slab of [Hin26, Lemma 5.16] has the slope ¼; the slope 1/12 keeps Ω_(ext,r₀) inside {t_IVP > −|x|/10}, where
χ_IVP = 1 (Section 21.7), so that the boosts of Section 37.19 are genuine boosts on all of it. [Hin26] uses its
Lemma 5.6 for the pointwise bounds; here the slots of h and of g_(b₀) − η give them directly, the mass entering at
ρ₀²ρ_I² in the slot π₁₁ only (Lemma 27.10).

*The radius R₀.* Enlarging R₀ keeps Lemma 37.1 true. We fix R₀ once, so that in addition R₀ ≥ 4|C″| + 4, the
function F₀ of Lemma 37.2 is increasing on [R₀, ∞), and every statement of this chapter made for r₀ large
(in Lemma 37.2, Remark 37.11, Lemma 37.20 (a), Lemma 37.24, Lemma 37.25 and Corollary 37.35)
holds for every r₀ ≥ R₀. Each of these asks r₀ above a bound depending only on b₀, the gauge parameters, ℓ^♭₀, ℓ^♭_I
and the constant c of Lemma 37.23, whose choice does not involve r₀ (it is the smallness of x_I in Proposition 37.8
and Proposition 37.16). From here on R₀ is this radius.

The causal structure of Ω_(ext,r₀) is that of a domain of dependence of Σ_(IVP,r₀). We record it in the form used for
uniqueness.

**Lemma 37.2** (Ω_(ext,r₀) is a Cauchy development.) Let r₀ ≥ R₀, let g₀ = g_(b₀), or g₀ ∈ 𝒢
with g₀ − g_(b₀) satisfying the pointwise bounds of the proof of Lemma 37.1, and let g := g₀ + h with h as in
Lemma 37.1 and smooth in the interior of Ω_(ext,r₀). Time-orient g by ∂_t. Then the interior Ω° of Ω_(ext,r₀) is
globally hyperbolic for g, and Σ° := Ω° ∩ {t_IVP = 0} is a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface of Ω°.

*Proof.* Write g = η + δ as in the proof of Lemma 37.1; |δ| is small on Ω_(ext,r₀) for r₀ large. For
c ∈ [−½, ½] the covector dt + c d|x| is timelike for η with η⁻¹-norm −(1 − c²) ≤ −¾ (the calculation of that proof, in
which the sign of c does not enter), hence timelike for g; ∂_t is timelike for g, and (dt + c d|x|)(∂_t) = 1 > 0. A
covector that is timelike for g and positive on one future timelike vector is positive on every future causal vector, the
future causal cone being connected. So t + c|x| is strictly increasing along future directed causal curves for every
such c; in particular t_IVP = t − C″ is, and |V|x|| < 2Vt for every future causal V. The same holds, by the proof of
Lemma 37.1, for φ₊ := t_IVP − F₀(|x|), F₀(r) := r + 2r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) − (r₀ + 2r₀^(1−ℓ^♭_I)), and for
φ₋ := t_IVP + (|x| − r₀)/12, whose differentials are the timelike covectors ζ there, each positive on ∂_t. As t_IVP is
strictly increasing along causal curves, Σ° is acausal in Ω°; it is spacelike by Lemma 37.1.

Let p ∈ Ω° with t_IVP(p) > 0 and γ a past inextendible causal curve in Ω° from p. If γ did not meet Σ°, then
t_IVP > 0 along γ (t_IVP is continuous along γ, and Ω° ∩ {t_IVP = 0} = Σ°); φ₊ ≤ φ₊(p) < 0 along γ;
and |x| ≤ |x(p)| + 2t_IVP(p) along γ; and |x| ≥ r₀ on Ω°. So γ would lie in the compact set
K := {0 ≤ t_IVP ≤ t_IVP(p), φ₊ ≤ φ₊(p), r₀ ≤ |x| ≤ |x(p)| + 2t_IVP(p)}, which lies in Ω°: at its points
F₀(|x|) > t_IVP ≥ 0, and F₀(r₀) = 0 with F₀ increasing on [r₀, ∞) (the choice of R₀), so |x| > r₀ and
−(|x| − r₀)/12 < 0 ≤ t_IVP < F₀(|x|). As in the proof of Lemma 18.4, t_IVP is strictly monotone
along γ and serves as a parameter in which the tangent lies in the compact set of causal vectors V over K with
dt_IVP(V) = 1; so γ extends continuously to its past end point in K ⊂ Ω°, against its inextendibility. Hence γ meets
Σ°. For p with t_IVP(p) < 0 the same argument, with future inextendible curves, φ₋ ≥ φ₋(p) > 0 in place of φ₊ and
the compact set {t_IVP(p) ≤ t_IVP ≤ 0, φ₋ ≥ φ₋(p), |x| ≤ |x(p)| + 2|t_IVP(p)|}, shows that every future inextendible
causal curve from p meets Σ°. Every inextendible causal curve through p contains a past (resp. future) inextendible
one from p. So Ω° is the Cauchy development of Σ° in Ω°, and Theorem A.2 gives the claim. ∎

### 37.3 The edge-b structure at null infinity

Section 37.3–Section 37.7 are [Hin23a, Sections 3.1–3.2] (pp. 9–17) in dimension 4 + 1, for the operator of
Section 27.4 on the exterior region of Section 27.1: the edge-b structure at ℐ⁺ ([Hin23a, Definitions 3.1–3.3,
Lemmas 3.6, 3.12–3.16, Corollary 3.14]), the basic energy estimate ([Hin23a, Proposition 3.17]), and the estimate near
the interior of I₀ for which [Hin23a] cites [HV20, Proposition 4.3]. The dimension enters through the quantities of
Proposition 27.59; here each is written into the proof.

*The region.* U, (ρ₀, ρ_I, ω), X₀ = ρ₀∂_(ρ₀), X_I = ρ_I∂_(ρ_I), the null coordinates x⁰ = t + |x|, x¹ = t − |x| and
ρ = ρ₀ρ_I = |x|⁻¹ are those of Section 27.1 (Lemma 27.2, (27.2)–(27.5)), with ω ∈ 𝕊³. Put
x_I := ρ_I^(1/2) and let M_♯ be U with the smooth structure in which (ρ₀, x_I, ω) are coordinates near ℐ⁺ ([Hin23a,
(3.6)], there with ρ₀ and x_I of the null coordinates of Schwarzschild space). The faces of M_♯ at infinity are
I₀ = {ρ₀ = 0} and ℐ⁺ = {x_I = 0}, and ℐ⁺ is fibred by (ρ₀, ω) ↦ ω over 𝕊³, with fibres the ρ₀-lines ([Hin23a,
Definition 3.7]).

*Edge-b objects* ([Hin23a, Definitions 3.1–3.4], stated on any manifold with two boundary hypersurfaces and a
fibration of one of them; no dimension enters). 𝒱_b(M_♯) is spanned over C^∞(M_♯) by X₀, X_I = ½x_I∂_(x_I) and the
vector fields on 𝕊³. 𝒱_(e,b)(M_♯) ⊂ 𝒱_b(M_♯), the vector fields whose restriction to ℐ⁺ is tangent to its fibres, is
spanned by X₀, X_I and x_IΘ, Θ ∈ 𝒱(𝕊³) ([Hin23a, (3.9)]). Diff^k_(e,b)(M_♯) consists of the sums of compositions of at
most k elements of 𝒱_(e,b)(M_♯) with C^∞ coefficients, and Diff^(m;k)_(e,b;b)(M_♯) := Diff^m_(e,b)(M_♯) · Diff^k_b(M_♯)
of the sums of compositions PQ with P ∈ Diff^m_(e,b), Q ∈ Diff^k_b; on sections of a bundle the coefficients are
smooth endomorphisms, and for a space ℱ of functions, ℱDiff^k_(e,b) denotes the operators with coefficients in ℱ. With
the b-density, H^k_(e,b)(M_♯) is the space of u ∈ L² with Pu ∈ L² for all P ∈ Diff^k_(e,b), and H^((m;k))_(e,b;b)(M_♯)
that of u with PQu ∈ L² for all P ∈ Diff^m_(e,b), Q ∈ Diff^k_b; the weighted spaces are
H^(k,(α₀,α₁))_(e,b) := ρ₀^(α₀)x_I^(α₁)H^k_(e,b) and H^((m;k),(α₀,α₁))_(e,b;b) := ρ₀^(α₀)x_I^(α₁)H^((m;k))_(e,b;b). The
b-spaces are those of Section 27.2: 𝒱_b and the b-density are the same in the coordinates ρ_I and x_I
(|dρ_I/ρ_I| = 2|dx_I/x_I|), and x_I^(2α) = ρ_I^α, so H^(k,(α₀,2α_I))_b in (ρ₀, x_I) is H^(k,α₀,α_I)_b of
Section 27.2 in (ρ₀, ρ_I). As dim M_♯ = 5,

    H^(s,(α₀,α₁))_b(M_♯) ↪ ρ₀^(α₀)x_I^(α₁)L^∞,     s > 5/2,    (37.2)

by the change of variables z₀ = log ρ₀, z₁ = log x_I, in which b-Sobolev spaces are uniformly local Sobolev spaces on
ℝ² × 𝕊³, and Sobolev embedding there; the order s = 3 serves in dimensions 3 + 1 and 4 + 1 (Proposition 27.59 (6)).

*The metric.* g_(b₀) is the Tangherlini metric, b₀ = (m₀, 0) (Section 21.5), in the coordinates of Chapter 21, and
η = −dx⁰dx¹ + |x|²g̸ is the Minkowski metric. On U the components of g_(b₀) − η in the rescaled null frame of
(27.6) lie in ρ²C^∞(U) (Lemma 27.10 (1), Lemma 27.4).

### 37.4 The frame as edge-b covectors

This section is [Hin23a, Lemmas 3.12–3.13, Corollary 3.14 and Remark 3.15] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Lemma 37.3** ([Hin23a, Lemma 3.13] in dimension 4 + 1.) For ω̸ ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; T*𝕊³),

    dx⁰ ∈ ρ₀⁻¹x_I⁻²C^∞(M_♯; ᵉᵇT*M_♯),     dx¹ ∈ ρ₀⁻¹C^∞(M_♯; ᵉᵇT*M_♯),     |x|ω̸ ∈ ρ₀⁻¹x_I⁻¹C^∞(M_♯; ᵉᵇT*M_♯),

where ᵉᵇTM_♯ is the bundle whose smooth sections are the elements of 𝒱_(e,b)(M_♯) and ᵉᵇT*M_♯ its dual; and the
products of the frame (27.6) have the orders of [Hin23a, (3.13)]: (dx⁰)² ∈ ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻⁴C^∞; dx⁰dx¹ and |x|²h̸,
for h̸ ∈ C^∞(𝕊³; S²T*𝕊³), in ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻²C^∞; dx⁰ ⊗_s |x|ω̸ ∈ ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻³C^∞; (dx¹)² ∈ ρ₀⁻²C^∞;
dx¹ ⊗_s |x|ω̸ ∈ ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻¹C^∞, as sections of S²ᵉᵇT*M_♯.

*Proof.* By (27.5), ∂₀ = −½ρ₀ρ_I X_I and ∂₁ = ρ₀(X₀ − X_I + ½ρ_I X_I), and |x|⁻¹e_a = ρ₀x_I · x_Ie_a for an
orthonormal frame e_a of 𝕊³. So (∂₀, ∂₁, |x|⁻¹e_a) = ρ₀DB(X₀, X_I, x_Ie_a) with D = diag(x_I², 1, x_I Id₃) and

    B = ( 0     −½            0   )
        ( 1     −1 + ½x_I²    0   )
        ( 0      0            Id₃ ),     det B = ½.

B is smooth and invertible up to x_I = 0, and (X₀, X_I, x_Ie_a) is a frame of ᵉᵇTM_♯. The dual coframe of
(∂₀, ∂₁, |x|⁻¹e_a) is (dx⁰, dx¹, |x|e^a). So (dx⁰, dx¹, |x|e^a) is ρ₀⁻¹D⁻¹(B⁻¹)ᵀ applied to the dual eb-coframe, which
gives the three memberships, and the products follow. ∎

**Corollary 37.4** ([Hin23a, Lemma 3.12 and Corollary 3.14] in dimension 4 + 1.)
g_(b₀) ∈ ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻²C^∞(M_♯; S²ᵉᵇT*M_♯) is nondegenerate of Lorentzian signature up to I₀ ∪ ℐ⁺, and

    ρ₀²x_I²g_(b₀) ≡ 2(dρ₀/ρ₀)² + 2(dρ₀/ρ₀) ⊗_s (dρ_I/ρ_I) + x_I⁻²g̸,
    ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻²g_(b₀)⁻¹ ≡ 2X_I ⊗_s (X₀ − X_I) + x_I²g̸⁻¹,

modulo x_IC^∞(M_♯; S²ᵉᵇT*M_♯), resp. x_IC^∞(M_♯; S²ᵉᵇTM_♯).

*Proof.* For η: dx¹ = ρ₀⁻¹dρ₀/ρ₀ and d|x| = −|x|(dρ₀/ρ₀ + dρ_I/ρ_I), from x¹ = 2 − ρ₀⁻¹ and |x| = (ρ₀ρ_I)⁻¹; with
dx⁰ = dx¹ + 2d|x|,

    ρ₀²ρ_Iη = 2(dρ₀/ρ₀)² + 2(dρ₀/ρ₀) ⊗_s (dρ_I/ρ_I) − ρ_I(dρ₀/ρ₀)² + ρ_I⁻¹g̸

exactly, and ρ_I⁻¹g̸ = x_I⁻²g̸ is a smooth eb-tensor (dω/x_I being an eb-covector). The dual statement for
η⁻¹ = −4∂₀ ⊗_s ∂₁ + |x|⁻²g̸⁻¹ follows from (27.5) in the same way, with the remainder x_I²X_I ⊗ X_I. By
Section 37.3, the components of g_(b₀) − η in the null frame are O(ρ²); by Lemma 37.3 the worst frame product,
(dx⁰)², lies in ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻⁴C^∞, and ρ² = ρ₀²x_I⁴. So g_(b₀) − η ∈ C^∞ = ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻² · ρ₀²x_I²C^∞, which lies in the
error class. Nondegeneracy and the signature follow from the leading form, which is that of η. ∎

**Remark 37.5** ([Hin23a, Remark 3.15].) As 𝒱_(e,b) is a Lie algebra and differentiation along it preserves
ρ₀^(ℓ₀)x_I^(ℓ_I)C^∞, the Koszul formula gives ∇^(g_(b₀)) ∈ Diff¹_(e,b) on eb-tensor bundles, and

    □_(g_(b₀)) ∈ ρ₀²x_I²Diff²_(e,b)(M_♯; ᵉᵇT^(p,q)M_♯)    (37.3)

([Hin23a, (3.14)]). Nothing here depends on the dimension.

### 37.5 The scalar wave operator

This section is [Hin23a, Lemma 3.16] and the density of [Hin23a, Proposition 3.17] in dimension 4 + 1. The
conjugation that removes the first-order term is by ρ^(3/2) = |x|^(−3/2), where in dimension 3 + 1 it is by ρ
(Proposition 27.59 (1)).

**Lemma 37.6** (The density.) μ_b := ρ₀⁵ρ_I⁴|dg_(b₀)| is a smooth positive b-density on M_♯. For η it is
exactly |(dρ₀/ρ₀)(dρ_I/ρ_I)dg̸|. The operator

    L := ρ_Iρ^(−7/2) □_(g_(b₀)) ρ^(3/2)    (37.4)

is formally self-adjoint on L²(M_♯; μ_b). ([Hin23a] has ρ₀⁴ρ_I³ and ρ_Iρ⁻³□ρ in dimension 3 + 1; Proposition 27.59
(2).)

*Proof.* |dη| = |x|³|dt d|x| dg̸| with t = x¹ + |x|, and |dx¹ ∧ d|x|| = ρ₀⁻²|x||dρ₀ ∧ dρ_I/ρ_I|, which is
ρ₀⁻¹|x||(dρ₀/ρ₀) ∧ (dρ_I/ρ_I)|. So |dη| = |x|⁴ρ₀⁻¹|(dρ₀/ρ₀)(dρ_I/ρ_I)dg̸| = ρ₀⁻⁵ρ_I⁻⁴|(dρ₀/ρ₀)(dρ_I/ρ_I)dg̸|, and
by Section 37.3 |dg_(b₀)| = |dη|(1 + O(ρ²)) with a smooth factor. For the self-adjointness,

    ⟨Lu, v⟩_(L²(μ_b)) = ∫(□ρ^(3/2)u) v ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)ρ₀⁵ρ_I⁴|dg| = ∫(□ρ^(3/2)u)(ρ^(3/2)v)|dg|,

as ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)ρ₀⁵ρ_I⁴ = ρ^(−7/2)ρ⁵ = ρ^(3/2), and □ is symmetric on L²(|dg|). ∎

**Lemma 37.7** (L as an eb-operator; commutators; [Hin23a, Lemma 3.16] in dimension 4 + 1.)
L ∈ Diff²_(e,b)(M_♯), and

    L = −2X_I(X₀ − X_I) + x_I²(Δ̸ + ¾) + L̃,     L̃ ∈ x_IDiff²_(e,b)(M_♯),    (37.5)

with Δ̸ = −tr̸∇̸² ≥ 0 the Laplacian of 𝕊³. For every vector field Θ on 𝕊³,

    [L, X₀],  [L, X_I],  [L, Θ] ∈ x_IDiff^(1;1)_(e,b;b)(M_♯).    (37.6)

*Proof.* *Minkowski space.* With □ = −tr∇², □_η = 4∂₀∂₁ − (3/|x|)∂_(|x|) + |x|⁻²Δ̸ on functions, and conjugation
by |x|^(−3/2) removes the first-order term:

    |x|^(3/2)□_η|x|^(−3/2) = 4∂₀∂₁ + |x|⁻²(Δ̸ + ¾),

the constant being (n − 1)(n − 3)/4 = ¾ (Proposition 27.59 (1); it is 0 in dimension 3 + 1). By (27.5) and
X_Iρ₀ = 0, X_Iρ_I = ρ_I,

    4∂₀∂₁ = −2ρ₀ρ_IX_I ρ₀(X₀ − X_I + ½ρ_IX_I) = −2ρ₀²ρ_IX_I(X₀ − X_I) − ρ₀²ρ_I²(X_I + 1)X_I.

Multiplying by ρ_Iρ⁻² = ρ₀⁻²ρ_I⁻¹ (with |x|⁻² = ρ₀²ρ_I²) gives

    L_η = −2X_I(X₀ − X_I) + x_I²(Δ̸ + ¾) − x_I²(X_I + 1)X_I,

and x_I²(X_I + 1)X_I ∈ x_I²Diff²_(e,b), X_I being an eb-vector field.

*The mass.* □_g modulo ρ₀²x_I³Diff²_(e,b) depends only on g modulo ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻¹C^∞(S²ᵉᵇT*), by (37.3) and the
Koszul formula. By the proof of Corollary 37.4, g_(b₀) − η ∈ ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻² · ρ₀²x_I²C^∞, which lies in that class.
Conjugation by ρ^(3/2) and multiplication by ρ_Iρ⁻² preserve the classes up to the factor ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻². So
L − L_η ∈ x_IDiff²_(e,b), which is (37.5).

*Commutators.* The argument of [Hin23a] uses only (37.5) and the structure of 𝒱_(e,b).

- [L, X₀] = [L̃, X₀] ∈ x_IDiff²_(e,b), as X₀ commutes with the leading part of (37.5) ([X₀, x_I²] = 0) and
  𝒱_(e,b) is a Lie algebra.
- [L, X_I] = −ρ_I(Δ̸ + ¾) + [L̃, X_I], as [x_I², X_I] = −x_I². Write Δ̸ = Σ_k Θ_(k,1)Θ_(k,2) + Θ_♭ + f, with the Θ's
  vector fields on 𝕊³ and f ∈ C^∞(𝕊³). As 𝒱(𝕊³) ⊂ x_I⁻¹𝒱_(e,b) ∩ 𝒱_b,

      ρ_I(Δ̸ + ¾) = x_I Σ_k (x_IΘ_(k,1))Θ_(k,2) + x_I(x_IΘ_♭) + x_I²(f + ¾) ∈ x_IDiff^(1;1)_(e,b;b)

  ([Hin23a, (3.18)]).
- [L, Θ] = ρ_I[Δ̸, Θ] + [L̃, Θ] ([Hin23a] prints the first commutator with the opposite sign, which does not matter
  here), and the first term lies in x_IDiff^(1;1)_(e,b;b) in the same way. For the second, lifts of vector fields on
  𝕊³ preserve the eb-classes: in coordinates, Θ = Σ_j Θ^j(y)∂_(y^j) and V = a⁰X₀ + a¹X_I + Σ_j a^j x_I∂_(y^j), and

      [Θ, V] = (Θa⁰)X₀ + (Θa¹)X_I + x_I Σ_j [Θ, a^j∂_(y^j)] ∈ 𝒱_(e,b)

  ([Hin23a, (3.19a)]). So [·, Θ] maps ρ₀^a x_I^b Diff²_(e,b) to itself for all weights a, b ([Hin23a, (3.19b)]),
  and [L̃, Θ] ∈ x_IDiff²_(e,b).

The term ¾x_I² commutes with X₀ and Θ, and [¾x_I², X_I] = −¾x_I² lies in x_IDiff⁰. ∎

### 37.6 The basic energy estimate near ℐ⁺

This section is [Hin23a, Proposition 3.17 and Remark 3.18] in dimension 4 + 1.

*Domains.* Let c_♯ > 0 be so small that, on {x_I < c_♯} ∩ {ρ₀ ≤ 1}:

- |x| = ρ₀⁻¹x_I⁻² > c_♯⁻² ≥ 4R₁, so that the part of the set in {t_* ≤ T₀} lies in U ((27.3); x¹ ≤ 1 alone
  does not give t_* ≤ T₀, as t_* = x¹ + C′ − 8m₀|x|⁻¹ there);
- the level sets of x_I are spacelike for g_(b₀);
- the multiplier V below is future timelike for g_(b₀).

This is possible. For η, dρ_I = |x|⁻¹(−½ρ_I dx⁰ − (1 − ½ρ_I)dx¹), so

    η⁻¹(dρ_I, dρ_I) = −2|x|⁻²ρ_I(1 − ½ρ_I) < 0     (ρ_I < 2)    (37.7)

([Hin23a, (3.8)], with η⁻¹(dx⁰, dx¹) = −2, η⁻¹(dx⁰, dx⁰) = η⁻¹(dx¹, dx¹) = 0). The correction from δ := g_(b₀) − η is
O(ρ²) relative to ρ_I|x|⁻²: η⁻¹dρ_I = |x|⁻¹((2 − ρ_I)∂₀ + ρ_I∂₁), and with δ_(ab) := δ(∂_a, ∂_b) as in the proof of
Lemma 37.1, δ₀₀, δ₀₁ ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I³C^∞ and δ₁₁ ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ (Definition 27.9, Lemma 27.10 (1)), so

    δ(η⁻¹dρ_I, η⁻¹dρ_I) = |x|⁻²((2 − ρ_I)²δ₀₀ + 2ρ_I(2 − ρ_I)δ₀₁ + ρ_I²δ₁₁) ∈ ρ_I|x|⁻² · ρ²C^∞,

and the terms quadratic in δ are smaller. So (37.7) persists for ρ = ρ₀x_I² small; this is the role of the bound
x̄_I ≤ 1/√(8m) of [Hin23a]. Here c_♯ is fixed by the three conditions above in the Minkowski coordinates of
Section 27.1; the bound of [Hin23a], stated in its tortoise coordinates (Proposition 27.59 (8)), is not used.

Let Ω ⊂ {x_I < c} ∩ {ρ₀ < 1} ∩ {t_* ≤ T₀}, c < c_♯, be open. Its boundary in the interior consists of two
hypersurfaces, each smooth or piecewise smooth (there is no boundary term at a corner of Σ_in, where u vanishes):
Σ_in, spacelike for g_(b₀), and Σ_fin, spacelike or null for g_(b₀), with Ω to the future of Σ_in and to the past of
Σ_fin. Every integral curve of X_I in Ω (at fixed ρ₀ and ω, with ρ_I decreasing) begins on Σ_in. The set
{x_I < c, ρ₀ < 1} of [Hin23a], with Σ_in = x_I⁻¹(c) and Σ_fin = ρ₀⁻¹(1), is an example once 1 is replaced by
ρ̄₀ := (1 + 2R₁)⁻¹: ρ₀ < ρ̄₀ means x¹ < 1 − 2R₁, which gives t_* < T₀. So is Ω_(ext,r₀) ∩ {x_I < c} ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0},
whose part of Σ_IVP and whose Σ_(fut,r₀) are spacelike (Lemma 37.1), together with the part of x_I⁻¹(c) in it
(a piecewise smooth Σ_in, with a corner where it meets Σ_IVP; Ω_(ext,r₀) ⊂ U by the proof of Lemma 37.1); an
outgoing ray at fixed x¹ enters it across Σ_IVP or x_I⁻¹(c).

**Proposition 37.8** (The energy estimate; [Hin23a, Proposition 3.17] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let Ω be as
above, k ∈ ℕ₀, and α₀, α_I ∈ ℝ with α_I < min(α₀, 0). Let f ∈ H^(k,(α₀,2α_I))_b(Ω) = ρ₀^(α₀)ρ_I^(α_I)H^k_b(Ω) vanish
near Σ_in. Then the forward solution u of Lu = f (vanishing Cauchy data on Σ_in) lies in
H^((1;k),(α₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)(Ω), and

    ‖u‖_(H^((1;k),(α₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)(Ω)) ≤ C‖f‖_(H^(k,(α₀,2α_I))_b(Ω)),    (37.8)

with C depending on k, α₀, α_I, c and the geometry of Σ_in, Σ_fin. Away from ℐ⁺ (on {x_I ≥ c/2}) the same holds with
H^(k+1)_b on the left.

*Proof.* *The multiplier* ([Hin23a, (3.22)]). Let

    W := w²V,     w := ρ₀^(−α₀)ρ_I^(−α_I),     V := X₀ − (1 + κ)X_I,     κ > 0.

V is future timelike: by (27.4)–(27.5), V = ρ₀⁻¹(∂_t + 2κρ_I⁻¹∂₀), a positive combination of the
future timelike ∂_t and the future null ∂₀ near ℐ⁺ for η, hence for g_(b₀) by Corollary 37.4. By the leading form of
Corollary 37.4, g_(b₀)(V, V) ≡ ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻²(2 − 2(1 + κ)) = −2κρ₀⁻²x_I⁻² modulo ρ₀⁻²x_I⁻¹C^∞, so V is uniformly timelike in
the eb-sense.

*The identity* ([Hin23a, (3.23)]). For u smooth with support as in the statement,

    2 Re⟨wLu, wVu⟩_(L²(Ω,μ_b)) = ⟨Qu, u⟩ + ℬ_fin(u),     Q := L*W + W*L = [L, W] − (div_(μ_b)W)L.

It is the integral over Ω of the pointwise identity 2 Re(w²Lu · Vū) = div_(μ_b)J + q(u) of the vector field method. As L
is real and formally self-adjoint (Lemma 37.6), L = −div_(μ_b)(G∇u) + V₀u with G its principal symbol and V₀ := L(1);
J is the energy current of W, including the potential term; and q(u), built from G, its derivative along W, ∇W,
div_(μ_b)W, V₀ and WV₀, is a quadratic form in u and its first derivatives with no products of u with its derivatives. We
write ⟨Qu, u⟩ for ∫_Ω q(u)μ_b, which is the pairing of Qu with u when u vanishes near Σ_fin, and ℬ_fin(u) for the flux of
J through Σ_fin. There is no boundary term at Σ_in, where u vanishes to second order, and none at I₀ ∪ ℐ⁺ in the
following approximation, which is needed as the forward solution is not known beforehand to lie in the weighted space.
Approximate f in H^(k,(α₀,2α_I))_b by f_j supported in {ρ₀ ≥ 1/j}. The forward solution u_j of Lu_j = f_j vanishes near
I₀, the causal future of supp f_j staying in {x¹ ≥ x¹_j} for some x¹_j, so away from spatial infinity. Apply the identity
to u_j on Ω_ε := Ω ∩ {x_I > ε}, whose added boundary {x_I = ε} is spacelike by (37.7), with Ω_ε to its past: it is
a further final boundary, with a boundary term of the same sign as ℬ_fin. The Poincaré inequality below does not depend
on where an X_I-curve ends. So the estimate holds for u_j on Ω_ε, uniformly in ε and j; let ε → 0, then j → ∞, the u_j
converging to u locally uniformly with their derivatives and the uniform bound passing to the limit. ℬ_fin(u) ≥ 0: it is
the flux through Σ_fin of the energy current of the future timelike W, and Σ_fin is spacelike or null with Ω to its past.
It also contains the potential term, a positive multiple of V₀|u|² with V₀ = L(1) = ¾x_I² + O(x_I³) > 0 (near I₀, ¾ρ_I),
of the same sign; so does the boundary term of the proof of Proposition 37.10.

*The bulk term.* Modulo ρ₀^(−2α₀)x_I^(−4α_I+1)Diff²_(e,b), L may be replaced by the leading part L₀ of (37.5), and
μ_b by μ̄_b := |(dρ₀/ρ₀)(dρ_I/ρ_I)dg̸| (Lemma 37.6). Accordingly q(u)μ_b differs from the bulk term q̄(u)μ̄_b of L₀
and μ̄_b by a quadratic form in u and V′u, V′ ∈ {X₀, X_I, x_IΘ}, with coefficients in w²x_IC^∞: the principal symbols of
L and L₀ differ by an element of x_IC^∞(M_♯; S²ᵉᵇTM_♯), V₀ − ¾x_I² ∈ x_I³C^∞, μ_b/μ̄_b ∈ 1 + ρ²C^∞, and
differentiation along eb-vector fields preserves these classes. For L₀ and μ̄_b, X₀ and X_I are skew-adjoint on
L²(μ̄_b), −div_(μ̄_b)W = −V(w²) = w²(2α₀ − 2(1 + κ)α_I), and, with c_A := 1 + 2(α₀ − α_I) + κ(1 − 2α_I) > 0,

    Q̄ := [L₀, W] − (div_(μ̄_b)W)L₀
       = 4|α_I|(X₀ − X_I)*w²(X₀ − X_I) + 4κ(α₀ − α_I)X_I*w²X_I + c_Ax_Iw(Δ̸ + ¾)wx_I    (37.9)

exactly. Indeed, put Y₀ := X₀ − X_I, so that L₀ = −2X_IY₀ + ρ_I(Δ̸ + ¾) and V = Y₀ − κX_I. The fields X_I, Y₀, V
commute with each other and with Δ̸, and X_Iw² = −2α_Iw², Y₀w² = −2(α₀ − α_I)w², Vρ_I = −(1 + κ)ρ_I. The angular part
of Q̄ is −w²(Vρ_I)(Δ̸ + ¾) + w²(2α₀ − 2(1 + κ)α_I)ρ_I(Δ̸ + ¾) = c_Aρ_Iw²(Δ̸ + ¾), which is the last term, as x_I and w
commute with Δ̸. The rest is

    [−2X_IY₀, w²V] − 2(2α₀ − 2(1 + κ)α_I)w²X_IY₀
        = −8α_I(α₀ − α_I)w²V + 4(α₀ − α_I)w²X_IV + 4α_Iw²Y₀V − 4(α₀ − (1 + κ)α_I)w²X_IY₀
        = w²(4α_IY₀² − 4κ(α₀ − α_I)X_I²) − 8α_I(α₀ − α_I)w²V,

the terms in X_IY₀ cancelling. On the other side, as X* = −X for X ∈ {X₀, X_I},
4|α_I|Y₀*w²Y₀ = 4α_IY₀w²Y₀ = 4α_Iw²Y₀² − 8α_I(α₀ − α_I)w²Y₀ and
4κ(α₀ − α_I)X_I*w²X_I = −4κ(α₀ − α_I)w²X_I² + 8κα_I(α₀ − α_I)w²X_I, whose first-order terms add up to
−8α_I(α₀ − α_I)w²V. Written with w² in front, as the identity is usually written, the right side of (37.9) would
be w²(4α_IY₀² − 4κ(α₀ − α_I)X_I² + c_Aρ_I(Δ̸ + ¾)); that form omits the first-order term −8α_I(α₀ − α_I)w²V, which
carries no factor x_I, so only the symmetric form is exact. Its principal symbol is that of [Hin23a, (3.25)] with
Δ̸ + ¾ in place of Δ̸, which is Proposition 27.59 (3) with q₄ = ¾ and κ in place of c.

So q̄(u) and

    4|α_I|w²|(X₀ − X_I)u|² + 4κ(α₀ − α_I)w²|X_Iu|² + c_Aρ_Iw²(|∇̸u|² + ¾|u|²)

are quadratic forms in u and its first derivatives without products of u with its derivatives, with the same operator
Q̄; such a form is determined by its operator, so the two are equal. As α_I < 0, κ > 0 and α₀ − α_I > 0, all
coefficients are positive, and with ‖wX₀u‖ ≤ ‖w(X₀ − X_I)u‖ + ‖wX_Iu‖ and |Θ_ju| ≤ C|∇̸u|,

    ∫_Ω q̄(u) μ̄_b ≥ c₀ Σ_(V′) ‖wV′u‖²_(L²_b),

the sum over V′ ∈ {X₀, X_I, x_IΘ_j}, with the Θ_j spanning T𝕊³. The constant ¾ only adds the term ¾c_Aρ_Iw²|u|² ≥ 0.

*Poincaré.* Along each integral curve of X_I in Ω, which begins on Σ_in where u = 0, with s := −log ρ_I and ρ₀ fixed,

    ∫ e^(2α_Is)|u|² ds ≤ α_I⁻² ∫ e^(2α_Is)|∂_s u|² ds     (α_I < 0),

by u(s) = ∫_(s₀)^s ∂_s u and Young's inequality for the kernel e^(α_I(s−s′)), s′ < s, of L¹-norm |α_I|⁻¹. The constant
does not depend on where the curve ends, so integrating in ρ₀ and ω gives ‖wu‖_(L²_b) ≤ C‖wX_Iu‖_(L²_b).

*Conclusion for k = 0.* On Ω ⊂ {x_I < c}, |∫_Ω(q(u)μ_b − q̄(u)μ̄_b)| ≤ Cc(Σ_(V′)‖wV′u‖²_(L²_b) + ‖wu‖²_(L²_b)), its
coefficients carrying the factor x_I < c. Cauchy–Schwarz on the left of the identity, ℬ_fin ≥ 0, the Poincaré
inequality and absorption for c small give ‖wu‖_(H¹_(e,b)) ≤ C‖wf‖_(L²_b), which is (37.8) for k = 0. Existence
of the forward solution, smooth in Ω, is standard for the wave equation with smooth coefficients on Ω.

*Higher b-regularity* (the induction of [Hin23a]). Let X₀, X₁ := X_I, X₂, …, X₇ be the six rotation fields of 𝕊³
(spanning T𝕊³ pointwise), and X₈ := 1. These span Diff¹_b over C^∞. By (37.6), [L, X_j] = Σ_l x_IP_(jl)X_l with
P_(jl) ∈ Diff¹_(e,b). Assume (37.8) at k. Applying it to L(X_ju) = X_jf + [L, X_j]u (the support condition is
preserved, the X_j being tangent to the faces and commuting with restriction to Σ_in up to terms vanishing there)
gives, with the weights,

    ‖X_ju‖_(H^((1;k))_(e,b;b)) ≤ C(‖X_jf‖_(H^k_b) + Σ_l ‖x_IX_lu‖_(H^((1;k))_(e,b;b))).

Summing over j, the last sum is absorbed for c small. This gives (37.8) at k + 1. The statement on
{x_I ≥ c/2} holds as 𝒱_(e,b) = 𝒱_b there, so (37.8) gives one b-derivative more. ∎

**Remark 37.9** ([Hin23a, Remark 3.18].) In the coordinates (t, |x|), modulo lower-order terms,
W = |x|^(2α_I)(2 − x¹)^(2(α₀−α_I))((2 − x¹)∂_t + κ|x|(∂_t + ∂_(|x|))).

### 37.7 The estimate near the interior of I₀

Near the interior of I₀, away from ℐ⁺, the coordinates of Section 21.4 are (τ, ρ) = (t/|x|, |x|⁻¹), with
τ ∈ [−½, 1 − δ] (the proof of Lemma 27.2), and ρ_I = 1 − τ + 2ρ ≥ δ. The following estimate takes the place of
[HV20, Proposition 4.3], which [Hin23a] cites.

**Proposition 37.10** (The b-energy estimate near I₀.) Let δ > 0 and
Ω₀ ⊂ {ρ ≤ ρ₁} ∩ {τ₀ ≤ τ ≤ 1 − δ} be open, with interior boundary consisting of {τ = τ₀} (initial) and a hypersurface
Σ_fin that is spacelike or null for g_(b₀) (final). Let k ∈ ℕ₀, α₀ ∈ ℝ, and let f ∈ ρ^(α₀)H^k_b(Ω₀) vanish near
{τ = τ₀}. Then for ρ₁ small the forward solution of Lu = f satisfies
‖u‖_(ρ^(α₀)H^(k+1)_b(Ω₀)) ≤ C‖f‖_(ρ^(α₀)H^k_b(Ω₀)).

*Proof.* In (τ, ρ, ω), ∂_t = ρ∂_τ and ∂_(|x|) = −ρ(τ∂_τ + ρ∂_ρ), so the coordinate fields of η are ρ times b-vector
fields. η⁻¹ is ρ² times a smooth nondegenerate Lorentzian b-metric G_b on {ρ ≤ ρ₁}:

    G_b = −∂_τ² + (τ∂_τ + ρ∂_ρ)² + g̸⁻¹.

G_b(dτ, dτ) = −(1 − τ²) < 0 for |τ| < 1, so τ is a b-time function there. g_(b₀)⁻¹ − η⁻¹ is O(ρ²) relative
(Section 37.3). So L = ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)□ρ^(3/2) lies in Diff²_b, with principal symbol ρ_IG_b up to O(ρ) and ρ_I ≥ δ.

Use the multiplier W₀ := w₀²V₀, with w₀ := ρ^(−α₀)e^(−Λτ) and V₀ := −G_b(dτ, ·), a future timelike b-vector field. In
the identity 2 Re⟨w₀Lu, w₀V₀u⟩ = ⟨Q₀u, u⟩ + ℬ_fin, the boundary term at Σ_fin is ≥ 0, as in the proof of
Proposition 37.8, and Q₀ = [L, W₀] − (div W₀)L. There is no boundary term at I₀ in the following approximation.
Approximate f in ρ^(α₀)H^k_b by f_j supported in {ρ ≥ 1/j}. As g_(b₀) − η is O(ρ²) relative, d|x| ≤ (1 + δ/4)dt along
future causal curves in Ω₀ for ρ₁ small; with t ≤ (1 − δ)|x| on Ω₀ and (1 + δ/4)(1 − δ) < 1,
the bound |x| ≤ |x₀| + (1 + δ/4)(t − t₀) along such a curve from (t₀, x₀) ∈ supp f_j keeps |x| bounded. So the forward
solution u_j of Lu_j = f_j vanishes near I₀, the identity holds for it, and the estimate passes to the limit j → ∞ as in
the proof of Proposition 37.8.

The term of Q₀ from differentiating e^(−2Λτ) is 2Λw₀² times the energy-momentum quadratic form of V₀ and dτ in ρ_IG_b.
It is positive definite in the b-gradient, as V₀ and −∇τ are future timelike (the dominant energy condition for the
scalar wave equation). The other terms are bounded by C(1 + |α₀|)w₀²|ᵇ∇u|² + Cw₀²|u|² with C independent of Λ.
The |u|² term is controlled by integrating ∂_τ from {τ = τ₀}, where u = 0, over the compact τ-interval. For Λ large this
gives the estimate for k = 0, with e^(±Λτ) bounded on [τ₀, 1 − δ].

Higher b-regularity follows by commuting ρ∂_ρ and the rotation fields: their commutators with L lie in Diff²_b and are
of first order in the commuted derivatives, since L is a b-operator. The induction closes on the compact τ-interval
with the same Λ-argument, the commutator terms entering as sources: the estimate for k = 0 has the form
‖w₀∇u‖ ≤ CΛ⁻¹‖w₀f‖, so these sources, of first order in the commuted derivatives, are absorbed for Λ large, and the
∂_τ²-terms of [L, ρ∂_ρ] are recovered from the equation. Commuting ∂_τ is not needed: a b-derivative transversal to the
level sets of τ is recovered from the equation, L being strictly hyperbolic with respect to τ. ∎

**Remark 37.11** (Gluing the estimates.) Proposition 37.8 near ℐ⁺ ∪ (I₀ ∩ ℐ⁺), Proposition 37.10 near the
interior of I₀, and the standard energy estimate on compact sets cover Ω_(ext,r₀) near infinity. The forward problem
is solved successively: on a region whose past boundary is Σ_IVP, then on the next region with the previous solution as
data. The data enter as sources after an extension of the Cauchy data, cut off near the initial surface, is
subtracted. The regions are ordered by domain of dependence (Lemma 18.4), as in [Hin23a, p. 16] ("cut and paste
energy estimates using domain of dependence properties"). Where two estimates apply the solutions agree, and the norms
are equivalent on the overlaps, each overlap lying away from the face that distinguishes the two calculi. Ω_(ext,r₀)
also contains the past slab {−(r − r₀)/12 ≤ t_IVP ≤ 0} (Lemma 37.1). There the solution is the backward one
from Σ_IVP, near the interior of I₀ (τ ∈ [−1/12 − ε, ε] for r₀ large), and the proof of Proposition 37.10, run backward
in time, gives it: it uses only the b-structure of L and that dτ is timelike on the τ-range, and Σ_(past,r₀) is
spacelike (Lemma 37.1). The backward problem is argued directly because t ↦ −t is not an isometry of the
gauge-fixed operator, whose E_C-term is odd in time. Lemma 37.24 writes this backward problem with the data, and
Proposition 37.16 and Theorem 37.27 give the estimate for the tensor operator, with weights at both faces.

### 37.8 The tensor operator: setting

Section 37.8–Section 37.10 carry [Hin23a, Sections 3.4–3.5] (Proposition 3.29, Lemmas 3.33–3.34, Proposition 3.32;
pp. 18–30) to the gauge-fixed operator of Section 27.4 in dimension 4 + 1, on the exterior region of
Section 27.1. Section 37.9 puts the conjugated operator in edge-b form; in dimension 4 + 1 its first-order matrix
is the constant Ā of Lemma 27.12, free of the perturbation h (Proposition 27.14, Remark 27.15).
Section 37.10 proves the energy estimate for the system, with its tame form and the sharp weights. [Hin23a,
Section 3.3] (metric perturbations, Lemmas 3.23–3.28) is Section 27.2–Section 27.5 in dimension 4 + 1, which we
use as they stand.

U, M_♯, x_I = ρ_I^(1/2), X₀, X_I, 𝒱_(e,b) and the spaces are those of Section 37.3, and the splitting
(27.6), its slots and Ā are those of Lemma 27.12. Let g₁, g₀ ∈ 𝒢 (Definition 27.9), k ≥ 5, and
h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b(U; S²T*) as in Proposition 27.14. That is: ℰ₀ as in Definition 27.6 (1),
min Re ℱ > 0, 2ℱ ⊂ ℱ, ℓ₀, ℓ_I > 0, and h small in H^(5,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b, the polyhomogeneous norm; the smallness is
at the order 5 for every k. It gives the smallness of Proposition 27.14, at the order 3, with
0 < a₀ < min(ℓ₀, min Re ℰ₀) and 0 < a_I < min(ℓ_I, min Re ℱ). (The coefficients ã below are ρ_I⁻¹ times terms in h,
whose size near ℐ⁺ the conormal norm H^(5,a₀,a_I)_b does not control when a_I < 1.) Assume moreover

    min Re ℱ > 1,     ℓ_I > 1,    (37.10)

which holds for ℱ = ℰ_I^tot (min Re ℰ_I^tot = 3/2, (27.8)) and every ℓ_I > 3/2, and for ℱ = (2, 0). Put
g := g₁ + h and

    L_g := 2ρ_Iρ^(−7/2) L^(g,g₀) ρ^(3/2),    (37.11)

with L^(g,g₀) the linearised gauge-fixed operator (27.12), whose principal part is ½□_g ⊗ Id. For the scalar
operator this is the L of (37.4) up to the factor 2: 2L^(g,g₀) has principal part □_g.

### 37.9 The operator in edge-b form

This section is [Hin23a, Proposition 3.29] for the operator of Section 27.4 in dimension 4 + 1 ([Hin26, (5.26b)]).

**Lemma 37.12** (Cartesian derivatives are ρ₀ times eb-vector fields.) On U, ∂_t, ∂_(x^i), ∂₀, ∂₁ lie in
ρ₀𝒱_(e,b)(M_♯), and |x|⁻¹∂_ω ∈ ρ₀x_I𝒱_(e,b)(M_♯).

*Proof.* By (27.5), ∂₀ = −½ρ₀ρ_IX_I and ∂₁ = ρ₀(X₀ − X_I + ½ρ_IX_I), with X₀, X_I ∈ 𝒱_(e,b).
And |x|⁻¹∂_ω = ρ₀x_I · x_I∂_ω, with x_I∂_ω ∈ 𝒱_(e,b). Finally ∂_t = ∂₀ + ∂₁ and
∂_(x^i) = ω^i(∂₀ − ∂₁) + |x|⁻¹(…)∂_ω, the dots smooth functions of ω. ∎

This refines Lemma 27.2, which places the same fields in ρ₀𝒱_b. The refinement is what the edge-b form needs:
angular second derivatives come with |x|⁻², hence with ρ₀²x_I² times eb-derivatives.

**Proposition 37.13** (The edge-b form.) Under the hypotheses of Section 37.8, on U, in the splitting
(27.6),

    L_g = −2(X_I − Ā)(X₀ − X_I) + x_I²Δ̸ + L̃_g,
    L̃_g ∈ (x_IC^∞(M_♯) + H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ−1,ℓ_I−1))_b) Diff²_(e,b)(M_♯; S²T*),    (37.12)

where Δ̸ = −g̸^(ab)∂_a∂_b acts on each slot, in local coordinates ω^a of 𝕊³. By (37.10) the coefficients of the
second class decay at ℐ⁺ at least like ρ_I^(γ−ε) for every ε > 0, γ := min(min Re ℱ − 1, ℓ_I − 1) > 0, and are small
in L^∞ near ℐ⁺ for h small. So L̃_g is small relative to the leading part near ℐ⁺, as [Hin23a, (3.29b)] is.

*Proof.* *The conjugation.* By Proposition 27.14,

    L^(g,g₀) = −ρ₀²ρ_I(X_I − 3/2 − Ā)(X₀ − X_I) + R,     R ∈ (ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ + H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b)Diff²_b.

As (X₀ − X_I)ρ = 0 and X_Iρ^(3/2) = (3/2)ρ^(3/2), ρ^(−3/2)(X_I − 3/2 − Ā)(X₀ − X_I)ρ^(3/2) = (X_I − Ā)(X₀ − X_I); and
2ρ_Iρ^(−7/2) · ρ₀²ρ_I · ρ^(3/2) = 2. So the leading part of (37.12) is the image of that of (27.16),
and L_g + 2(X_I − Ā)(X₀ − X_I) = 2ρ₀⁻²ρ_I⁻¹ρ^(−3/2)Rρ^(3/2). Conjugation by ρ^(3/2) preserves Diff_b and Diff_(e,b), as
ρ^(−3/2)Vρ^(3/2) = V + (3/2)V(log ρ) with V log ρ smooth for V ∈ 𝒱_b.

*The b-form remainder does not suffice.* ρ₀⁻²ρ_I⁻¹R lies in (ρ_IC^∞ + H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ−1,ℓ_I−1))_b)Diff²_b. But
Diff²_b ⊂ x_I⁻²Diff²_(e,b) only, ∂_ω being x_I⁻¹ times an eb-vector field. So we redo the count of the proof of
Proposition 27.14 with Lemma 37.12 in place of Lemma 27.2.

*The background part.* L^(g₁,g₀) differs from L_(b₀) := L^(g_(b₀),g_(b₀)) by terms with a factor g₁ − g_(b₀) or
g₀ − g_(b₀) in ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ (Definition 27.9, Lemma 27.10). By Lemma 27.13 and Lemma 37.12, these lie
in ρ₀² · ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_(e,b). After the prefactor 2ρ₀⁻²ρ_I⁻¹ this is ρ₀²ρ_IC^∞Diff²_(e,b) ⊂ x_I²Diff²_(e,b). For
L_(b₀) itself:

- its second-order part is ½□_(g_(b₀)) on each component in the frame, the principal symbol being scalar;
- its first-order part consists of the connection terms of the frame and the terms of E_C, E_Υ. These are Cartesian
  derivatives (in ρ₀𝒱_(e,b), Lemma 37.12) times coefficients in ρC^∞ = ρ₀ρ_IC^∞ (c_C, c_Υ and the Christoffel
  symbols of η in the frame are O(|x|⁻¹), Definition 21.28, Lemma 27.4), so they lie in
  ρ₀²ρ_IC^∞Diff¹_(e,b);
- its zeroth-order part lies in ρ²C^∞.

The calculation of Lemma 27.11 identifies the part of the first-order terms that is not O(x_I) relative: it is
ρ₀²ρ_IĀ(X₀ − X_I) (with the −3/2 of the scalar conjugation). So, after conjugation and the prefactor,

    L_(b₀,conj) = (2ρ_Iρ^(−7/2) ½□_(g_(b₀)) ρ^(3/2)) ⊗ Id + 2Ā(X₀ − X_I) + x_IC^∞Diff¹_(e,b) + x_I²C^∞.

The scalar term is the L of Lemma 37.7: −2X_I(X₀ − X_I) + x_I²(Δ̸ + ¾) modulo x_IDiff²_(e,b). Its first-order part
in Lemma 37.7 is that of the scalar wave operator, and it differs from that of the frame by the connection terms
just counted. ¾x_I² and x_IC^∞Diff¹_(e,b) (the angular connection terms) lie in x_IDiff¹_(e,b). So the background
part of (37.12) holds with L̃ in x_IC^∞Diff²_(e,b).

*The perturbation.* For (g₁ + h, g₀) against (g₁, g₀) the factor is δ = h. By Lemma 27.13 and Lemma 37.12,
each term is ρ₀² times a product of h or of 𝒱_b-derivatives of h of order at most 2 with smooth bounded functions,
applied through Diff²_(e,b) (Lemma 37.12 replaces ρ₀𝒱_b by ρ₀𝒱_(e,b) for the derivatives acting on u). By the
proof of Proposition 27.14 (Steps 1–3 of its part *The perturbation*, and Lemma 27.5 there), the coefficients
lie in ρ₀²H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b = H^(k−2,(ℰ₀+2,ℓ₀+2),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b. After the prefactor they lie in
H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ−1,ℓ_I−1))_b, multiplying Diff²_(e,b). The frame change of Lemma 27.4 preserves the classes, as
in the proof of Proposition 27.14.

*Smallness.* By (37.10) and the embedding (37.2) (order 3), elements of H^(3,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ−1,ℓ_I−1))_b are
bounded by Cρ₀^(min(min Re ℰ₀,ℓ₀)−ε)ρ_I^(γ−ε) times their norm, for every ε > 0, with γ as above. The coefficients of
the second class lie in this space (k − 2 ≥ 3), and their norm there tends to 0 with the norm of h in
H^(5,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b: they are products of the same kind as in Step 4 of the proof of Proposition 27.14, which
applies at k = 5. ∎

**Remark 37.14** (The terms A_g and B_g of [Hin23a].) In [Hin23a, (3.29a)] the h-dependent entries of A_g
and the term B_g are of the size of the leading part at ℐ⁺; in dimension 3 + 1 they are bounded there. In dimension
4 + 1 they carry an extra factor ρ_I^(1/2) (Proposition 27.59 (7), Remark 27.15) and lie in L̃_g. So the
first-order matrix of (37.12) is Ā, constant and lower triangular, with diagonal (27.14), all of whose
entries are ≥ 0:

    2(1 − v_C)γ_C,  (1 − v_C)γ_C,  (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C,  (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ,  γ_Υ,  0,  2γ_Υ.

The term A⁰_h of [Hin23a], for which its proof of Proposition 3.32 uses [Hin23a, Lemma 3.33], does not arise
(Proposition 27.14, Remark 27.15): all of the h-dependent first-order part is treated like the contribution of
L̃_g.

### 37.10 The energy estimate for the system

This section is [Hin23a, Proposition 3.32 and Lemmas 3.33–3.34] in dimension 4 + 1.

**Lemma 37.15** (A fibre inner product.) For every ε > 0 there is a constant positive definite inner product
⟨·, ·⟩_ε on the fibres of S²T*, in the frame (27.6), such that

    Ā = D + N_ε,     D = diag(d₁, …, d₇) ⊗ Id_slot,     |N_ε|_ε ≤ ε,

with the diagonal (27.14), d_j ≥ 0, and D self-adjoint for ⟨·, ·⟩_ε.

*Proof.* Take the slots of (27.6) orthogonal, each with its standard inner product multiplied by ε^(2j) on
slot j. Ā maps each slot to slots of the same type by scalars and is lower triangular (Lemma 27.12). An entry
Ā_(ji), i < j, which maps slot i to slot j, then has norm ε^(j−i)|Ā_(ji)| in the scaled norms. For ε ≤ 1 this is at
most ε max|Ā_(ji)|; rename ε. D is diagonal in an orthogonal splitting, so self-adjoint. ∎

**Proposition 37.16** (The energy estimate and its tame form; [Hin23a, Proposition 3.32] in dimension
4 + 1.) Let Ω, Σ_in, Σ_fin be as in Section 37.6, and α₀, α_I ∈ ℝ with α_I < min(α₀, 0). Let k ≥ 8 and 3 ≤ m ≤ k − 3,
and let h be as in Section 37.8, small in H^(8,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b. For f ∈ H^(m,(α₀,2α_I))_b(Ω; S²T*) vanishing near
Σ_in, the forward solution u of L_gu = f lies in H^((1;m),(α₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)(Ω; S²T*), and

    ‖u‖_(H^((1;m),(α₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)) ≤ C(‖f‖_(H^(m,(α₀,2α_I))_b)
                                           + ‖h‖_(H^(m+3,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b)‖f‖_(H^(3,(α₀,2α_I))_b)),    (37.13)

with C depending on m, k, α₀, α_I and the classes, not on f or h.

*Proof.* *The basic estimate.* Use the multiplier W = w²V of the proof of Proposition 37.8, V = X₀ − (1 + κ)X_I, with
κ > 0 to be fixed, the density μ̄_b, and the fibre inner product of Lemma 37.15. Then

    2 Re⟨wL_gu, wVu⟩ = ⟨Qu, u⟩ + ℬ_fin(u),     Q = [L_g, W] − (div W)L_g + (L_g* − L_g)W,

with ℬ_fin ≥ 0, as in Proposition 37.8. Write

    Y := w(X₀ − X_I)u,     Z := wX_Iu,     Vu = w⁻¹(Y − κZ).

The scalar part −2X_I(X₀ − X_I) + x_I²Δ̸ acts on each slot, and the fibre inner product is constant; so it gives the Q̄
of (37.9) with Δ̸ in place of Δ̸ + ¾, whose bulk term is, by the proof of Proposition 37.8,
4|α_I||Y|² + 4κ(α₀ − α_I)|Z|² + c_Aρ_Iw²|∇̸u|² (the ¾ of (37.9) only added a nonnegative term).

The first-order term 2Ā(X₀ − X_I) of (37.12) contributes, up to terms of order 0 in u and terms with a factor
x_I,

    4 Re⟨ĀY, Y − κZ⟩ = 4⟨DY, Y⟩ − 4κ Re⟨DY, Z⟩ + O(ε)(|Y|² + |Z|²).

On each slot, the quadratic form in (Y_j, Z_j) from the scalar part and this term is

    4(d_j − α_I)|Y_j|² − 4κd_j Re(Y_jZ̄_j) + 4κ(α₀ − α_I)|Z_j|².

It is positive definite if 4(d_j − α_I)(α₀ − α_I) > κd_j². As d_j ≥ 0, α_I < 0 and α₀ > α_I, this holds for κ > 0
small. Fix such κ, then ε small. The angular term c_Aρ_Iw²|∇̸u|² is nonnegative and bounds Σ_j|x_IwΘ_ju|²/C, so
⟨Qu, u⟩ controls ‖wu‖²_(H¹_(e,b)) modulo two terms: ‖wu‖²_(L²_b), which the Poincaré inequality of the proof of
Proposition 37.8 removes; and the contribution of L̃_g, whose coefficients are O(c^(γ′)) on {x_I < c} for every
γ′ < min(2 min Re ℱ − 2, 2ℓ_I − 2) by the smallness in Proposition 37.13, and which is absorbed for c small, as in
Proposition 37.8.

The term (L_g* − L_g)W is that of the first-order part, already counted, plus that of L̃_g. This gives

    ‖u‖_(H^(1,(α₀,2α_I))_(e,b)) ≤ C₀‖L_gu‖_(H^(0,(α₀,2α_I))_b),    (37.14)

with C₀ uniform for h small in H^(5,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b ([Hin23a, (3.53)]; the skew part needs ã ∈ W^(1,∞), so h ∈ H⁶,
which the hypothesis on H⁸ gives). Away from ℐ⁺, the argument of the proof of Proposition 37.10 applies to the system:
the principal part is scalar, and the first-order terms are bounded b-operators, absorbed by the exponential weight.
Remark 37.11 glues the pieces.

*Commuting.* With X₀, X₁ := X_I, the rotation fields X₂, …, X₇ of 𝕊³ (acting on the slots in the frame
(27.6), which they preserve, by the equivariance of Lemma 27.12) and X₈ := 1, apply (37.14) to
X_(j₁)⋯X_(j_l)u, l ≤ m. Lemma 37.18 gives ([Hin23a, (3.55)], with the weights (α₀, 2α_I) throughout)

    ‖u‖_(H^((1;m))_(e,b;b))
        ≤ C₀(‖L_gu‖_(H^m_b) + Σ_(1≤q≤l≤m) Σ ‖(ad_(X_(i₁))⋯ad_(X_(i_q))L_g) X_(j₁)⋯X_(j_(l−q))u‖_(H⁰_b)),    (37.15)

the inner sum over the indices. The commutators of the X_j with the leading part of (37.12) lie in
x_IDiff^(1;1)_(e,b;b): for the scalar part by Lemma 37.7; and Ā is constant and commutes with the X_j (X₀, X_I act
on the slot coordinates, and the rotations commute with Ā by the equivariance of Lemma 27.12). These terms are
absorbed for x_I small. For L̃_g = Σ_i(x_Ia_i + ã_i)P_i, with a_i ∈ C^∞, ã_i ∈ H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ−1,ℓ_I−1))_b and P_i
spanning Diff²_(e,b), the x_Ia_i-terms are absorbed. By Leibniz's rule the ã_i-terms are sums of products
(V₁⋯V_qã)(W′V′₁⋯V′_ru), q + r ≤ m + 1, with V_l, V′_l among the X_j and W′ an eb-vector field, up to smooth bounded
factors (the commutators of the X_j with P_i stay in Diff²_(e,b), as said below, and expanding smooth coefficients
produces only terms of this kind). For q = 0 such a product is bounded by
‖ã‖_(L^∞)‖u‖_(H^((1;m))) ≤ C‖ã‖_(H³)‖u‖_(H^((1;m))). For q ≥ 1, move W′ to the right of the V′_l: as [X_j, W′] is an
eb-vector field for each X_j, this costs only products of the same form with fewer V′_l. Put f := V_qã and g := W′u,
so that the remaining q − 1 derivatives fall on f and r ≤ m − q + 1 on g. We reduce to the estimate for products of
derivatives, Theorem A.31 (2) with s := m, through the charts of the proof of Lemma 37.17. Divide out the
weights, and extend f and g from Ω to M_♯ by the operator of that proof, which is bounded on H^m_b and on L^∞. Let φ_i
be the partition of unity and ψ_i the cut-offs of that proof, ψ_i = 1 near supp φ_i. The product
Π := (V₁⋯V_qã)(V′₁⋯V′_rW′u) is Σ_i φ_iΠ, and on supp φ_i it equals (V₁⋯V_(q−1)(ψ_if))(V′₁⋯V′_r(ψ_ig)). In the chart of
index i each V_l and each V′_l is a combination of the fields of 𝒱 (the two coordinate fields of ℝ² and the rotation
fields of 𝕊³) with coefficients bounded with all their derivatives; expanding the compositions by Leibniz's rule, φ_iΠ is
a finite sum of terms c(Q′(ψ_if))(Q″(ψ_ig)) with c bounded and Q′, Q″ compositions of at most q − 1 and at most r fields
of 𝒱, so of at most m fields in all. In the chart, Theorem A.31 (2) bounds each term in L² by
C(‖ψ_if‖_(L^∞)‖ψ_ig‖_(H^m) + ‖ψ_if‖_(H^m)‖ψ_ig‖_(L^∞)), and the chart comparison and the boundedness of multiplication by
ψ_i in the proof of Lemma 37.17 bound these norms by those of f and g. Summing over i gives

    ‖(V₁⋯V_qã)(V′₁⋯V′_rW′u)‖ ≤ C(‖V_qã‖_(L^∞)‖W′u‖_(H^m_b) + ‖V_qã‖_(H^m_b)‖W′u‖_(L^∞))
                              ≤ C(‖ã‖_(H⁴)‖u‖_(H^((1;m))) + ‖ã‖_(H^(m+1))‖u‖_(H^((1;3)))),

by (37.2) (H³_b ⊂ L^∞) and ‖W′u‖_(H^j_b) ≤ C‖u‖_(H^((1;j))), which holds by moving W′ to the left in the same way.
The first term is absorbed near ℐ⁺, the coefficients decaying at ℐ⁺; the second is bounded by ‖h‖_(H^(m+3)) times
