the bound of (37.13) at m = 3 for ‖u‖_(H^((1;3))), by ‖ã_i‖_(H^(m+1)) ≤ C‖h‖_(H^(m+3)) (the coefficients are
rational in at most two b-derivatives of h). Commutators of the X_j preserve Diff^k_(e,b): for X₀, X_I as eb-vector
fields, and for the rotations by the argument for (37.6) ([Hin23a, (3.19a)–(3.19b)]). This proves
(37.13). At m = 3 the constant depends on ‖h‖_(H⁸) ([Hin23a, (3.54)]). ∎

**Lemma 37.17** (Moser estimates on M_♯.) Let s ≥ 0 be an integer, and let Ω be M_♯ or a domain in it whose
boundary hypersurfaces in the interior are, in the charts of the proof, graphs over coordinate hyperplanes of functions
bounded with all their derivatives; the domains of this chapter on which the lemma is used are of this kind (Ω_c, Ω_N,
Ω⁺₁, Ω_(ext,r₀) and the parts cut from them by level sets of ρ_I, τ′ and t_IVP). For a, b on Ω with finite right side,

    ‖ab‖_(H^(s,(β₀+γ₀,β₁+γ₁))_b(Ω)) ≤ C(‖a‖_(ρ₀^(β₀)x_I^(β₁)L^∞)‖b‖_(H^(s,(γ₀,γ₁))_b(Ω))
                                        + ‖a‖_(H^(s,(β₀,β₁))_b(Ω))‖b‖_(ρ₀^(γ₀)x_I^(γ₁)L^∞)),

and for s ≥ 3 > 5/2 = ½ dim M_♯, H^s_b embeds in L^∞ ((37.2)). Every Sobolev order in this chapter is an integer.

*Proof.* Multiplication by ρ₀^(β₀)x_I^(β₁) maps H^s_b and L^∞ onto the weighted spaces, so we may take all weights 0.
For s = 0 the bound is ‖ab‖_(L²) ≤ ‖a‖_(L^∞)‖b‖_(L²); let s ≥ 1.

*On M_♯.* Cover M_♯ by finitely many charts: near I₀ ∩ ℐ⁺ the coordinates (z₀, z₁, ω), z₀ := log ρ₀, z₁ := log x_I;
near the interior of I₀, (log ρ, τ, ω); near the interior of ℐ⁺, (log ρ₀, log x_I, ω) with ρ₀ in a compact interval;
and a relatively compact part. In each chart the b-vector fields are combinations, with coefficients bounded with all
their derivatives, of the two coordinate fields of ℝ² and the rotation fields of 𝕊³, and conversely, and the b-density
is bounded above and below by the product measure. So for functions supported in a chart, extended by 0, the norm of
H^s_b is equivalent to that of H^s(ℝ² × 𝕊³) of Corollary A.30 (2), with k = 2, N = 𝕊³ and 𝒱 those fields.
Let φ_i be a partition of unity on M_♯ subordinate to the charts and ψ_i ∈ C^∞(M_♯) supported in them with ψ_i = 1
near supp φ_i; multiplication by these is bounded on H^s_b. Then ab = Σ_i(ψ_ia)(φ_ib), and Corollary A.30
(2) applied to each product gives the bound.

*On a domain Ω.* After a partition of unity in ω, a diffeomorphism that flattens the boundary hypersurfaces of Ω, with
its derivatives and those of its inverse bounded (composition with it is bounded on every W^(j,2) and on L^∞, by the
chain rule), makes Ω locally a half-space or, near an edge where two of them meet, a quadrant. The extension operator of
Theorem A.35 acts in the normal variable alone, the others being parameters, so its bounds hold fibrewise; it
is one operator bounded on every W^(j,2) and on L^∞. Applied in the normal variable of each hypersurface in turn, it
gives extensions Ea, Eb of a, b to M_♯ with ‖Ea‖_(H^s_b) ≤ C‖a‖_(H^s_b(Ω)), ‖Ea‖_(L^∞) ≤ C‖a‖_(L^∞(Ω)), and likewise for
b. As ab = (Ea)(Eb) on Ω, the bound on M_♯ gives the bound on Ω. ∎

**Lemma 37.18** ([Hin23a, Lemma 3.34], the commutator identity.) In any associative algebra, for
L, Z₁, …, Z_l, with ad_Z := [·, Z],

    [L, Z₁⋯Z_l] = Σ_(q=1)^l (−1)^(q−1) Σ_(i₁<⋯<i_q) (ad_(Z_(i₁))⋯ad_(Z_(i_q))L) Π_(j∉{i₁,…,i_q}) Z_j,

the products taken in increasing order of j.

*Proof.* Induction on l: [L, Z₁⋯Z_(l+1)] = [L, Z₁⋯Z_l]Z_(l+1) + [L, Z_(l+1)]Z₁⋯Z_l − [ad_(Z_(l+1))L, Z₁⋯Z_l], since
Z₁⋯Z_l[L, Z_(l+1)] = [L, Z_(l+1)]Z₁⋯Z_l − [ad_(Z_(l+1))L, Z₁⋯Z_l]; the induction hypothesis applied to the first and the
last term gives the formula for l + 1. ∎

**Remark 37.19** ([Hin23a, Lemma 3.33].) The tame product estimate of [Hin23a, Lemma 3.33], with the
Sobolev index d_(dim M−1), is used in [Hin23a] only for the term A⁰_h, which does not arise in dimension 4 + 1
(Remark 37.14). In dimension 4 + 1 its index is d₄ = 3 (Proposition 27.59 (6)).

### 37.11 Sharp decay: the setting

Section 37.11–Section 37.17 carry [Hin23a, Section 3.6] (Theorem 3.35, Corollary 3.36; pp. 30–32) to the gauge-fixed
operator of Section 27.4 in dimension 4 + 1 on the exterior domain Ω_(ext,r₀) of Lemma 37.1. They give the
linear estimate with its tame form (Theorem 37.27), the nonlinear solution (Theorem 37.28) and the backward
solution on the past slab (Lemma 37.24), and both in the cut-off gauge of Section 37.16 and for the
backgrounds of Remark 37.33 (2) (Corollary 37.35). Section 37.12 integrates the leading part along its two
families of curves; Section 37.13 proves the linear theorem in three steps: the Cauchy problem near the interior of I₀,
the energy estimate of Proposition 37.16 near ℐ⁺, and the recovery of the sharp weight at ℐ⁺; Section 37.14 applies
Theorem 20.1. In dimension 4 + 1 the recovery needs two integrations and no leading terms depending on h
(Remark 37.14), and only slot 6 carries a radiation field. Lemma 37.20, Lemma 37.21 and
Lemma 37.23 are stated so that the continuation of the solution near ℐ⁺ on a slab beyond Σ_(fut,r₀), which the
nonlinear theorem of Chapter 38 poses, can use them.

U, M_♯, x_I = ρ_I^(1/2), X₀, X_I, the edge-b and b-spaces and the weights are those of Section 37.3; the splitting
(27.6), its slots 1–7 and Ā are those of Lemma 27.12; L_g is (37.11). As in Section 37.3,
H^(k,(a₀,2a_I))_b = ρ₀^(a₀)ρ_I^(a_I)H^k_b, the weight at ℐ⁺ in this notation being written in powers of x_I; all other
weights at ℐ⁺ below are powers of ρ_I.

*Parameters.* ℓ^♭₀, ℓ^♭_I are as in (37.1), and

    β := ℓ^♭_I − 3/2 ∈ (0, ½),     β < d_* := min_(j≠6) Ā_(jj) = (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ.    (37.16)

The diagonal (27.14) is 2(1 − v_C)γ_C, (1 − v_C)γ_C, (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C, (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ, 0, 2γ_Υ; the
first three exceed 100 (Section 25.1: (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C > 100, 0 < e_C, v_C < 1), and
(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ ≤ γ_Υ ≤ 2γ_Υ; so d_* = (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, and β < d_* is the condition ℓ^♭_I < 3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ of
(37.1). By Lemma 27.12 the off-diagonal entries of Ā are at (3, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3), (5, 2), (7, 3) and
(7, 4): no row couples to slot 6, and row 6 has no off-diagonal entry.

*Conjugation.* For a symmetric 2-tensor ġ on U put u := ρ^(−3/2)ġ. Then

    L^(g,g₀)ġ = f   ⟺   L_gu = f_♭ := 2ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)f.    (37.17)

Multiplication by ρ^(±3/2) = ρ₀^(±3/2)ρ_I^(±3/2) and by ρ_I maps weighted b-Sobolev spaces isomorphically onto each
other with the weights shifted (b-derivatives of these functions are constant multiples of them). So
ġ ∈ H^(k,α₀,α_I)_b if and only if u ∈ H^(k,(α₀−3/2,2(α_I−3/2)))_b, and f ∈ H^(k,α₀+2,α_I+1)_b if and only if
f_♭ ∈ H^(k,(α₀−3/2,2(α_I−3/2)))_b. Put a₀ := α₀ − 3/2.

*The classes of Theorem 37.30 in these terms.* The forcing class H^(k,α₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b (Definition 27.16
(2)) has every slot in H^(k,α₀+2,ℓ^♭_I+1)_b near ℐ⁺: its index sets ℰ_I^C + 1 and ℱ_(I,11) have real parts above
ℓ^♭_I + 1 (by (37.1), and min Re ℱ_(I,11) ≥ 5/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ by (27.17)). So
f_♭ ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b in every slot. The solution class H^(k,α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b (Section 37.2) has every slot in
H^(k,α₀,ℓ^♭_I)_b except π̸₀ġ ∈ H^(k,α₀,((3/2,0),ℓ^♭_I))_b. In terms of u it is

    𝒴^k_(a₀)(Ω) := {u : u_j ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b (j ≠ 6),  u₆ = χ_Iu^((0)) + ũ₆,
                         u^((0)) ∈ H^(k,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_c),  ũ₆ ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b},    (37.18)

with χ_I := χ̂(ρ_I), χ̂ ∈ C_c^∞([0, c/2)) equal to 1 on [0, c/4], c the constant of Lemma 37.23 (so u^((0)) is used
only over Ω_c := Ω⁺ ∩ {ρ_I < c}, Ω⁺ as below; another such χ̂ gives an equivalent norm), and u^((0)) a function of
(ρ₀, ω) extended to be constant in ρ_I. Here ℐ⁺_c is the image of Ω_c under (ρ₀, ρ_I, ω) ↦ (ρ₀, ω), a domain in ℐ⁺
containing ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω̄_c and in general larger: an integral curve of X_I near Σ_(fut,r₀) leaves Ω⁺ through Σ_(fut,r₀) before
it reaches ℐ⁺. So the splitting u₆ = χ_Iu^((0)) + ũ₆ is determined by u over ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω̄_c, where ρ₀^(3/2)u^((0)) is the
radiation field of π̸₀ġ (the coefficient of ρ_I^(3/2)), and not elsewhere; the norm of 𝒴^k_(a₀) is therefore the infimum
over the splittings (Lemma 37.22). It is equivalent at each order to the norm of Definition 27.6: a
decomposition of an extension restricts to one of u, and conversely u^((0)) and ũ extend across the boundary of ℐ⁺_c and
across Σ_(fut,r₀) by the operator of the proof of Lemma 37.17. Away from U the classes impose only H^k.

*The operator.* Let g₀ ∈ 𝒢 (Definition 27.9) with Ric(g₀) = 0 and g₀ − g_(b₀) small in the sense of the pointwise
bounds of the proof of Lemma 37.1, or g₀ = g_(b₀); let h ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀); S²T*) and
g := g₀ + h. In the terms of Section 37.8, h ∈ H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ,ℓ_I))_b for every k, with ℰ₀ := ∅, ℓ₀ := ℓ^♭₀,
ℱ := ⋃_(j≥1)(3j/2, 0) and ℓ_I := ℓ^♭_I: ℱ + ℱ ⊂ ℱ, and (37.10) holds, as min Re ℱ = 3/2 and ℓ^♭_I > 3/2. So
Proposition 37.13 applies to L_g on U: in its coefficient class H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ−1,ℓ_I−1))_b the exponents at ℐ⁺ are at
least ½ and the weight is ℓ^♭_I − 1 > ½, so

    L̃_g = x_I Σ_i (a_i + ã_i)P_i,     a_i ∈ C^∞(M_♯),     ã_i ∈ x_I⁻¹H^(k−2,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℱ−1,ℓ_I−1))_b,
    P_i ∈ Diff²_(e,b),    (37.19)

with ã_i bounded (its expansion at ℐ⁺ starts at ρ_I⁰) and ‖ã_i‖_(H^j) ≤ C‖h‖_(H^(j+2)) in these classes (the proof of
Proposition 37.13: the coefficients are rational in h and in two b-derivatives of it, and the inverse metric obeys the
tame bound ‖g⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹‖_(H^j) ≤ C‖h‖_(H^j), C depending on a bound for ‖h‖_(H⁴), by the induction of the proof of
Lemma 29.9 with Lemma 37.17 in place of Lemma 29.8 (a), Definition 21.31 (3) in place of
its (b), and (37.2) for sup|h| and ‖h‖_(C¹_b) in its (c)). L denotes L^(g,g₀), or L^(χ₀)_(g,g₀) in Section 37.17.

*Domains.* Ω⁺ := Ω_(ext,r₀) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} and the past slab Ω⁻ := Ω_(ext,r₀) ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0}. For |x| ≥ R₃,
t_IVP = t − C″ (Lemma 21.22 (b)), and

    Ω⁺ = {0 ≤ t_IVP ≤ F₀(|x|)},     F₀(r) := r + 2r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) − (r₀ + 2r₀^(1−ℓ^♭_I)),    (37.20)

which is empty where r < r₀; Ω_(ext,r₀) ⊂ U ∩ {|x| ≥ r₀} (the proof of Lemma 37.1). Near the interior of I₀,
τ := t/|x| and ρ = |x|⁻¹ are the coordinates of Section 21.4, ρ_I = 1 − τ + 2ρ (Section 37.7), and
τ′ := t_IVP/|x| = τ − C″ρ.

### 37.12 The two families of curves

This section gives the integrations of [Hin23a, Theorem 3.35] along the integral curves of X_I and of X₀ − X_I.

**Lemma 37.20** (The curves.) Let c ∈ (0, ½] and r₀ ≥ R₀ (so r₀ ≥ 4|C″| + 4).

(a) {ρ_I = c} ∩ U = {t = (1 − c)|x| + 2} is spacelike for g_(b₀) near infinity, and {ρ_I < c} lies to its future.
Ω⁻ ⊂ {ρ_I ≥ ½}.

(b) Let p ∈ Ω⁺ with ρ_I(p) < c. The integral curve of X_I through p (at fixed ρ₀ and ω: the outgoing ray of η at fixed
x¹) and that of X₀ − X_I (at fixed |x| and ω), followed in the direction of increasing ρ_I, stay in Ω⁺ until they reach
{ρ_I = c}, which they do.

*Proof.* (a) ρ_I = (2 − x¹)/|x| = c if and only if t = (1 − c)|x| + 2. For η, ζ := dt − (1 − c)d|x| has
η⁻¹(ζ, ζ) = −1 + (1 − c)² < 0; the correction from g_(b₀) − η, O(|x|⁻²) in the frame (Lemma 27.4), does not
change the sign for |x| large. Along ∂_t, ρ_I decreases. On Ω⁻, t ≤ C″, so ρ_I ≥ (2 − C″ + |x|)/|x| ≥ ½ for |x| ≥ r₀.

(b) *The X_I-curve.* Along it x¹ = x¹_p is fixed and |x| decreases from |x|_p to r_c := (2 − x¹_p)/c, where ρ_I = c.
The upper condition of (37.20) is x¹ ≤ C″ − r₀ − 2r₀^(1−ℓ^♭_I) + 2|x|^(1−ℓ^♭_I), whose right side decreases
in |x| (ℓ^♭_I > 1); it holds at p, so at every smaller |x|. It gives x¹_p ≤ C″ − r₀ < 0. The lower condition is
x¹_p + |x| ≥ C″, and x¹_p + |x| decreases along the curve; at r_c, x¹_p + r_c = x¹_p(1 − c⁻¹) + 2c⁻¹ ≥ |x¹_p|
≥ r₀ − C″ > C″, as c⁻¹ − 1 ≥ 1. And r_c ≥ (2 + r₀ − C″)/c ≥ r₀. *The (X₀ − X_I)-curve.* Along it |x| = |x|_p and t
decreases to t_c := (1 − c)|x|_p + 2. The upper condition is monotone in t; the lower one holds at t_c, as
t_c − C″ ≥ ½|x|_p + 2 − C″ > 0. In both cases ρ_I increases to c along the curve. ∎

Both curves are integral curves of commuting b-vector fields: in the coordinates (ρ₀, ρ, ω), X_I = ρ∂_ρ at fixed ρ₀ and
X₀ − X_I = ρ₀∂_(ρ₀) at fixed ρ; X₀, X_I and the rotation fields of 𝕊³ commute with both.

**Lemma 37.21** (Integration.) Let c, r₀ be as in Lemma 37.20, Ω_c := Ω⁺ ∩ {ρ_I < c}, m ∈ ℕ₀, a₀, γ ∈ ℝ,
and let w ∈ H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b(Ω_c) vanish on {ρ_I > c/2}. Let v on Ω_c vanish on {ρ_I > c/2}.

(a) If (X_I − d)v = w with d > γ, then ‖v‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b) ≤ (d − γ)⁻¹‖w‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b).

(b) If X_Iv = w and γ > 0, then v = v^((0)) + ṽ on Ω_c, with v^((0)) a function of (ρ₀, ω) on ℐ⁺_c, the image of Ω_c
under (ρ₀, ρ_I, ω) ↦ (ρ₀, ω) (as after (37.18)), v^((0)) and ṽ given by one linear map of w, the same for
every m, and

    ‖v^((0))‖_(H^(m,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_c)) ≤ C(2γ)^(−1/2)c^γ‖w‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b),
    ‖ṽ‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b) ≤ Cγ⁻¹‖w‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b),

with C depending only on m and Ω_c. Over almost every point of ℐ⁺_c whose X_I-curve lies in Ω_c for all ρ_I < c, v^((0))
is the limit of v along that curve as ρ_I → 0.

(c) If (X₀ − X_I)v = w and a₀ > γ, then ‖v‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b) ≤ (a₀ − γ)⁻¹‖w‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b).

The norms are those of the b-density |(dρ₀/ρ₀)(dρ_I/ρ_I)dg̸|, equivalent to that of μ_b on Ω_c (Lemma 37.6).

*Proof.* (a), (b): in the coordinates (s, ρ₀, ω), s := log ρ_I, X_I = ∂_s, X₀ = ρ₀∂_(ρ₀) at fixed s, and the density
is ds (dρ₀/ρ₀) dg̸. By Lemma 37.20 (b), for p ∈ Ω_c the segment of its X_I-curve from p to s_c := log c lies in Ω_c,
and v = 0 near s_c. So v(s) = −∫_s^(s_c) e^(d(s−s′))w(s′) ds′. Hence

    e^(−γs)|v(s)| ≤ ∫_s^(s_c) e^(−(d−γ)(s′−s)) e^(−γs′)|w(s′)| ds′,

a convolution with a kernel of L¹-norm (d − γ)⁻¹; Young's inequality in s, then integration in (ρ₀, ω) with the weight
ρ₀^(−2a₀), gives (a) for m = 0.

For (b), d = 0, and the X_I-curve over a point of ℐ⁺_c may leave Ω_c through Σ_(fut,r₀) before it reaches ℐ⁺ (after
(37.18)), at a value of s that varies with the point; so we first extend w. Let Ω^♯_c be the set of the points
with (ρ₀, ω) ∈ ℐ⁺_c and ρ_I < c. It lies in M_♯ for r₀ large: over a point of ℐ⁺_c, x¹ ≤ C″ − r₀ + 2 by the upper
condition of (37.20) at a point of Ω_c (see the proof of Lemma 37.20), and |x| = (2 − x¹)/ρ_I ≥ 2(r₀ − C″)
for ρ_I < c ≤ ½. It contains the whole X_I-curve over each point of ℐ⁺_c. Let E be the extension operator of the proof
of Lemma 37.17 for Ω = Ω_c, one linear operator bounded on every H^j_b, and put
w_♯ := ρ₀^(a₀)ρ_I^γE(ρ₀^(−a₀)ρ_I^(−γ)w) on Ω^♯_c. Then w_♯ = w on Ω_c and
‖w_♯‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b(Ω^♯_c)) ≤ C‖w‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2γ))_b(Ω_c)), with C depending only on m and Ω_c. Put

    v^((0)) := −∫_(−∞)^(s_c) w_♯ ds′,     ṽ(s) := ∫_(−∞)^s w_♯ ds′     on Ω^♯_c.

At a point of Ω_c, v^((0)) + ṽ(s) = −∫_s^(s_c) w_♯ ds′ = −∫_s^(s_c) w ds′ = v(s), as the segment from s to s_c lies in
Ω_c. By Cauchy–Schwarz and as in (a),

    |v^((0))|² ≤ ∫_(−∞)^(s_c) e^(2γs′) ds′ · ∫ e^(−2γs′)|w_♯|² ds′ = (2γ)⁻¹c^(2γ)∫ e^(−2γs′)|w_♯|² ds′,
    e^(−γs)|ṽ(s)| ≤ ∫_(−∞)^s e^(−γ(s−s′))e^(−γs′)|w_♯(s′)| ds′,

the second a convolution with a kernel of L¹-norm γ⁻¹; integration in (ρ₀, ω) with the weight ρ₀^(−2a₀) gives (b) for
m = 0. Over a point of ℐ⁺_c whose curve lies in Ω_c for all ρ_I < c, w_♯ = w along it, and for almost every such point
∫ e^(−2γs′)|w|² ds′ is finite; then |ṽ(s)|² ≤ (2γ)⁻¹e^(2γs)∫ e^(−2γs′)|w|² ds′ by Cauchy–Schwarz on (−∞, s], so
v(s) = v^((0)) + ṽ(s) → v^((0)) as s → −∞. (c): in the coordinates (z, y, ω),
z := log ρ₀, y := log ρ, X₀ − X_I = ∂_z and log ρ_I = y − z, so the density is dz dy dg̸ and {ρ_I = c} is
{z = z_c(y) := y − log c}. By Lemma 37.20 (b), v(z, y) = ∫_(z_c(y))^z w(z′, y) dz′. The weight is
ρ₀^(−a₀)ρ_I^(−γ) = e^(−γy)e^(−(a₀−γ)z), and

    e^(−(a₀−γ)z)|v(z)| ≤ ∫_(z_c)^z e^(−(a₀−γ)(z−z′)) e^(−(a₀−γ)z′)|w(z′)| dz′,

a kernel of L¹-norm (a₀ − γ)⁻¹; Young's inequality in z gives (c) for m = 0.

*Derivatives.* Let V be one of X₀, X_I and the rotation fields. V commutes with X_I and with X₀ − X_I, and Vv vanishes
where v does; so in (a) and (c) Vv solves the same equation with Vw, and the bounds for m = 0 apply to it. (In (c),
differentiating the integral in y produces the boundary term w(z_c(y), y)∂_yz_c, which vanishes as w = 0 near
{ρ_I = c}.) Induction on m gives (a) and (c) for m ≥ 1, with the same constants. In (b) the limits of the integrals
defining v^((0)) and ṽ do not depend on (ρ₀, ω), so X₀ and the rotations, which act at fixed s, commute with them:
Vv^((0)) = −∫_(−∞)^(s_c) Vw_♯ ds′ and Vṽ(s) = ∫_(−∞)^s Vw_♯ ds′; and X_Iv^((0)) = 0, X_Iṽ = w_♯. Also X_I^jṽ(s) =
∫_(−∞)^s X_I^jw_♯ ds′ for j ≥ 1, as e^(−γs)w_♯ is bounded along almost every curve when m ≥ 1, so w_♯ → 0 as s → −∞. The
fields tangent to ℐ⁺ are X₀ and the rotations, so the bounds for m = 0, applied to every b-derivative of w_♯, give (b)
for every m, with the bound for w_♯ above. Without the extension, the lower limit would be the value of s at which the
curve leaves Ω_c, which depends on (ρ₀, ω), and its derivatives would enter those of v^((0)) and ṽ. ∎

**Lemma 37.22** (Decompositions.) For u ∈ 𝒴^k_(a₀)(Ω), Ω = Ω⁺ or Ω_(ext,r₀), so that Ω ∩ {ρ_I < c} =
Ω_c (Lemma 37.20 (a)), call a pair (u^((0)), ũ) with u^((0)) ∈ H^(k,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_c), ũ_j ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b in every slot
j, ũ₆ = u₆ − χ_Iu^((0)) and ũ_j = u_j for j ≠ 6, a *decomposition of order k* of u, and ‖u^((0))‖_(H^(k,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_c)) +
Σ_j‖ũ_j‖_(H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b) its norm of order k; the norm of u in 𝒴^k_(a₀)(Ω) is the infimum of the norms of its
decompositions of order k. Let y_* := C″ − r₀ − 2r₀^(1−ℓ^♭_I). Then ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω̄_c is the part of ℐ⁺ where x¹ ≤ y_*, and:

(a) two decompositions of u have the same u^((0)) almost everywhere on ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω̄_c;

(b) if (u^((0)), ũ) is a decomposition of u and z is smooth with compact support in ℐ⁺_c ∩ {x¹ > y_*}, then
(u^((0)) + z, ũ′) is a decomposition of u, where ũ′₆ := ũ₆ − χ_Iz and ũ′_j := ũ_j for j ≠ 6;

(c) if u lies in 𝒴^k_(a₀)(Ω) for every k, it has one decomposition whose norms of every order are finite.

*Proof.* On U, ρ_I = (2 − x¹)/|x| ((27.2)), and the upper condition of (37.20) reads
x¹ ≤ y_* + 2|x|^(1−ℓ^♭_I) (the proof of Lemma 37.20). Over a point of ℐ⁺ with x¹ ≤ y_* it holds at every |x|, and
the lower condition holds for ρ_I ≤ c, as in the proof of Lemma 37.20 (b); so the whole X_I-curve {0 < ρ_I < c}
over the point lies in Ω_c, and the point lies in Ω̄_c. Over a point with x¹ > y_*, the upper condition gives the
bound |x| ≤ ((x¹ − y_*)/2)^(−1/(ℓ^♭_I−1)) on Ω_c, so ρ_I is bounded below on Ω_c over a neighbourhood of the point,
which therefore is not in Ω̄_c. This proves the description of ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω̄_c.

(b) By the same bound, ρ_I ≥ c_z > 0 on Ω_c over the compact set supp z, and ρ₀ = 1/(2 − x¹) is bounded above and
below there. So χ_Iz, whose b-derivatives are bounded, is supported in a region of finite b-volume on which the weights
are bounded, and lies in H^(∞,(a₀,2β))_b(Ω_c); and u₆ = χ_I(u^((0)) + z) + ũ′₆.

(a) If (u^((0)), ũ) and (u′^((0)), ũ′) are decompositions of u, then z := u^((0)) − u′^((0)) satisfies
χ_Iz = ũ′₆ − ũ₆ ∈ H^(0,(a₀,2β))_b(Ω_c). In the coordinates (s, ρ₀, ω), s := log ρ_I, of the proof of Lemma 37.21,
the square of this norm is comparable to ∫(∫ e^(−2βs)|χ_Iz|² ds) ρ₀^(−2a₀)(dρ₀/ρ₀)dg̸, which is therefore finite. Over
a point with x¹ ≤ y_* the inner integral runs over (−∞, log c), on which χ_I = 1 for s ≤ log(c/4), and
∫_(−∞)^(log(c/4)) e^(−2βs) ds = ∞ as β > 0. So z = 0 at almost every such point.

(c) Let χ′ := χ̂′(ρ_I), χ̂′ ∈ C_c^∞([0, c/2)) equal to 1 on [0, c/8], and u′ := χ′u₆ on Ω_c, which vanishes on
{ρ_I > c/2}. If (u^((0)), ũ) is a decomposition of order k, then, as X_Iu^((0)) = 0,

    w′ := X_Iu′ = (X_Iχ′)u₆ + χ′(X_Iχ_I)u^((0)) + χ′X_Iũ₆,

where the first two terms are supported in {c/8 ≤ ρ_I ≤ c/2}, on which the weights at ℐ⁺ are bounded and u₆ and
u^((0)) lie in H^k_b; so w′ ∈ H^(k−1,(a₀,2β))_b(Ω_c) for every k, and it vanishes on {ρ_I > c/2}. Lemma 37.21 (b)
with γ := β, applied to u′ and w′, gives u′ = v^((0)) + ṽ, with v^((0)) and ṽ not depending on k, v^((0)) ∈
H^(k−1,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_c) and ṽ ∈ H^(k−1,(a₀,2β))_b for every k. Put ũ″₆ := u₆ − χ_Iv^((0)) on Ω, which is u₆ off Ω_c (χ_I = 0
there); on Ω_c it equals ṽ + (1 − χ_I)v^((0)) + (1 − χ′)u₆, whose last two terms are supported in {ρ_I ≥ c/8}, and ṽ +
(1 − χ_I)v^((0)) = u′ − χ_Iv^((0)) vanishes on {ρ_I > c/2}; so (v^((0)), ũ″), with ũ″_j := u_j for j ≠ 6, is a
decomposition with every norm finite. ∎

The estimates below bound the norm of a decomposition that they construct, linearly in the data, and so bound the norm
of u. Where a choice linear in u is needed, in the smoothing of the proof of Theorem 37.28, the decomposition is
carried with u.

### 37.13 The linear theorem

This section is [Hin23a, Theorem 3.35] with data, for the operator of Section 27.4, in dimension 4 + 1.

**Lemma 37.23** (The region of the radiation field.) Fix c ∈ (0, ½] so small that Proposition 37.16 holds on
Ω_c with Σ_in := {ρ_I = c} ∩ Ω⁺ and Σ_fin := Σ_(fut,r₀) ∩ {ρ_I < c}. These are admissible in Section 37.6.

*Proof.* Ω_c ⊂ Ω_(ext,r₀) ⊂ U and Ω_c ⊂ {x_I < c^(1/2)}; Σ_in is spacelike with Ω_c to its future (Lemma 37.20
(a)); Σ_fin is spacelike for g (Lemma 37.1); and every X_I-curve in Ω_c begins on Σ_in (Lemma 37.20 (b)). ∎

**Lemma 37.24** (The Cauchy problem near the interior of I₀, in both directions.) Let
Ω_N := Ω_(ext,r₀) ∩ {τ′ ≤ ¼}, which contains Ω⁻, and α ∈ ℝ, s ∈ ℕ₀. For h small in H⁵ with h ∈ H^(s+2),
f ∈ H^(s,α+2)_b(Ω_N) and data ġ_j ∈ H^(s+1−j,α)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀)), j = 0, 1, there is a unique ġ ∈ H^(s+1,α)_b(Ω_N) with
Lġ = f, ġ = ġ₀ and rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))ġ = ġ₁ on Σ_(IVP,r₀), and

    ‖ġ‖_(H^(s+1,α)_b(Ω_N)) ≤ C(‖f‖_(H^(s,α+2)_b) + ‖ġ₀‖_(H^(s+1,α)_b) + ‖ġ₁‖_(H^(s,α)_b))
        + C‖h‖_(H^(s+2))(‖f‖_(H^(4,α+2)_b) + ‖ġ₀‖_(H^(5,α)_b) + ‖ġ₁‖_(H^(4,α)_b)).    (37.21)

Here the weight at I₀ is a power of ρ; on Ω_N, ρ_I ≥ ½, so it is one of ρ₀. If moreover s ≤ 3 and h is bounded in
H⁸, then (37.21) holds without its last term, with C depending on that bound.

*Proof.* On Ω_N, τ′ ∈ [−1/12, ¼] (Lemma 37.1: t_IVP ≥ −(|x| − r₀)/12), so τ ∈ [−1/12 − ε, ¼ + ε] for r₀
large, inside the range of Proposition 37.10 with δ = ½. That proposition, for the system as in the proof of
Proposition 37.16 (the principal part is scalar, and the first-order terms are bounded b-operators, absorbed by the
exponential weight), and with τ replaced by τ′, applies here: τ′ is a smooth function near the interior of I₀ with
G_b(dτ′, dτ′) = G_b(dτ, dτ) + O(ρ) = τ² − 1 + O(ρ) < 0, and its proof uses only that dτ is uniformly timelike in the
b-sense on the τ-range and that L ∈ ρ²Diff²_b is a wave operator; for h ∈ H^(s₀) the change L − L_(b₀) lies in
ρ²(ρC^∞ + H^(s₀−2))Diff²_b (the coefficients of the perturbation are rational in h and two of its b-derivatives),
small for h small in H⁵ and g₀ − g_(b₀) small (Proposition 27.14, near the interior of I₀; Lemma 37.34 for
L^(χ₀)). Two changes are needed.

*Data.* Proposition 37.10 has vanishing data and f vanishing near the initial surface. With the data above, the energy
identity of its proof, on {0 ≤ τ′ ≤ τ′₁}, has in addition the flux through Σ_(IVP,r₀) = {τ′ = 0} of the energy current
of its multiplier, bounded by C(‖ġ₀‖²_(H^(1,α)_b) + ‖ġ₁‖²_(H^(0,α)_b)), as r∂_(t_IVP) = ∂_(τ′) modulo b-vector fields
tangent to {τ′ = 0} (with ρ∂_ρ at fixed τ′). The term on the left of the identity coming from f does not need f to
vanish there. This gives the case s = 0. For s ≥ 1, commute the b-vector fields tangent to {τ′ = 0}, ρ∂_ρ at fixed τ′
and the rotations: their commutators with L lie in ρ²Diff²_b (with coefficients in H^(s₀−3) for the perturbation), of
first order in the commuted fields, and their data are tangential derivatives of ġ₀, ġ₁ together with one normal
derivative, given at {τ′ = 0} by the data and the equation; the commutator terms enter as sources and are absorbed as
in the proof of Proposition 37.10. The normal derivatives ∂²_(τ′) are recovered from the equation, which is
non-characteristic at the level sets of τ′. The tame term comes from the Moser estimate (Lemma 37.17) for the
coefficients of the perturbation, which are rational in h and two of its b-derivatives.

*Low orders.* Let s ≤ 3 and h be bounded in H⁸; we use Leibniz's rule in place of the Moser estimate. A commutator
term of order s is a sum of products of a b-derivative of order at most s of a coefficient of L with a b-derivative of
order at most s + 1 of ġ. A b-derivative of order at most s of a coefficient of the perturbation is a polynomial in the
b-derivatives of h of order at most s + 2 ≤ 5, with smooth bounded factors (h is small, so the denominators are bounded
below). Each of these b-derivatives of h lies in H³_b, with norm at most ‖h‖_(H⁸), so in L^∞ by the embedding of
Lemma 37.17. Hence each commutator term is bounded by a constant depending only on the bound on h in H⁸ times
‖ġ‖_(H^(s+1,α)_b), and it is absorbed for Λ large as in the proof of Proposition 37.10, Λ now depending on that bound.
The normal derivatives that the equation gives at {τ′ = 0} are bounded by the data in the same way. So no norm of f or
of the data above those of the first term of (37.21) enters.

*Both directions.* On Ω⁺ ∩ Ω_N the solution is the forward one; on Ω⁻ it is the backward one, given by the same argument
run backward in time, which uses only the b-structure of L, that dτ′ is timelike, and that Σ_(past,r₀) is spacelike
(Lemma 37.1); the backward problem is argued directly as t ↦ −t is not an isometry of the gauge-fixed operator,
whose E_C-term is odd in time. Uniqueness: the estimate applied to the difference of two solutions, which has vanishing
data and forcing term. ∎

**Lemma 37.25** (The forward problem with growth at ℐ⁺; Remark 37.11 for the system.) Let
Ω⁺₁ := Ω⁺ ∩ {τ′ ≥ 1/16}, a₀ ∈ ℝ, α_I < min(a₀, 0), 3 ≤ m ≤ k_h − 3, k_h ≥ 8, with h ∈ H^(k_h) small in H⁸, and let
f_♭ ∈ H^(m,(a₀,2α_I))_b(Ω⁺₁) vanish on {τ′ < ⅛}. The forward solution u of L_gu = f_♭ on Ω⁺₁, vanishing on
{τ′ < ⅛}, satisfies

    ‖u‖_(H^(m+1,a₀)_b(Ω⁺₁∩{ρ_I>c/2})) + ‖u‖_(H^((1;m),(a₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)(Ω_c))
        ≤ C(‖f_♭‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2α_I))_b) + ‖h‖_(H^(m+3))‖f_♭‖_(H^(4,(a₀,2α_I))_b)).    (37.22)

For m = 3, (37.22) holds without its last term, with C depending on the bound on h in H⁸.

*Proof.* *Away from ℐ⁺.* Ω′ := Ω⁺₁ ∩ {ρ_I > c/4} lies in {1/16 ≤ τ′ ≤ 1 − c/8} for r₀ large (ρ_I = 1 − τ + 2ρ). Its
interior boundary consists of {τ′ = 1/16}, initial, and the piecewise smooth ({ρ_I = c/4} ∪ Σ_(fut,r₀)) ∩ Ω̄′,
spacelike (Lemma 37.20 (a), Lemma 37.1) with Ω′ to its past. Proposition 37.10, for the system and with
τ′, as in the proof of Lemma 37.24, gives u₁ on Ω′ with ‖u₁‖_(H^(m+1,a₀)_b) ≤ C(‖f_♭‖_(H^(m,a₀)_b) plus the tame
term), and for m = 3 without the tame term, by the part *Low orders* of that proof; on Ω′, ρ_I > c/4, so the weight at
ℐ⁺ does not matter. As the boundary to its future is spacelike, Ω′ is closed under the past within Ω⁺₁, and u₁ = u on
Ω′ (Lemma 18.4).

*Near ℐ⁺.* Let χ_c := χ̂_c(ρ_I) with χ̂_c = 1 on [c/2, ∞) and 0 on [0, c/4], and u₂ := u − χ_cu₁ on Ω_c. Then
u₂ = 0 on {ρ_I > c/2}, and

    L_gu₂ = f₃ := (1 − χ_c)f_♭ − [L_g, χ_c]u₁,

which vanishes on {ρ_I > c/2}, hence near Σ_in = {ρ_I = c}. The commutator is a first-order b-operator supported in
{c/4 ≤ ρ_I ≤ c/2}: [L_g, χ_c] = Σ_l c_lV_l + c₀, with V_l b-vector fields, c_l products of b-derivatives of χ_c with the
second-order coefficients of L_g, which are smooth functions of h, and c₀ involving also the first-order coefficients,
smooth functions of h and of its first b-derivatives. Each coefficient is its value at h = 0, smooth and bounded with
all its b-derivatives, plus a part c̃ that vanishes at h = 0, with ‖c̃_l‖_(H^j_b) ≤ C‖h‖_(H^j) and
‖c̃₀‖_(H^j_b) ≤ C‖h‖_(H^(j+1)) for every j, as for the coefficients ã_i ((37.19)), and with
‖c̃‖_(L^∞) ≤ C‖h‖_(H⁵) by the embedding of Lemma 37.17. On {ρ_I ≥ c/4} the weight at ℐ⁺ is immaterial, and
‖V_lu₁‖_(L^∞) + ‖u₁‖_(L^∞) ≤ C‖u₁‖_(H^(4,a₀)_b(Ω′)) with the weight a₀ divided out, by the same embedding. So
Lemma 37.17 with s := m, applied to each product c̃V_lu₁ and c̃₀u₁, gives

    ‖[L_g, χ_c]u₁‖_(H^(m,(a₀,2α_I))_b)
        ≤ C(‖u₁‖_(H^(m+1,a₀)_b(Ω′)) + ‖h‖_(H^(m+1))‖u₁‖_(H^(4,a₀)_b(Ω′))).    (37.23)

u₂ is the forward solution on Ω_c from Σ_in (uniqueness by Lemma 18.4), and Proposition 37.16 on Ω_c
(Lemma 37.23) gives ‖u₂‖_(H^((1;m),(a₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)) ≤ C(‖f₃‖_m + ‖h‖_(H^(m+3))‖f₃‖_3), where here and below
‖·‖_j is the norm of H^(j,(a₀,2α_I))_b, and that of H^(j,a₀)_b(Ω′) for u₁. The bound for u₁ above, at the order m and
at the order 3 (the latter without tame term, by the part *Low orders* of the proof of Lemma 37.24), gives
‖u₁‖_(m+1) ≤ C(‖f_♭‖_m + ‖h‖_(H^(m+2))‖f_♭‖_4) and ‖u₁‖_4 ≤ C‖f_♭‖_3. With (37.23) this gives

    ‖f₃‖_m ≤ C(‖f_♭‖_m + ‖u₁‖_(m+1) + ‖h‖_(H^(m+1))‖u₁‖_4) ≤ C(‖f_♭‖_m + ‖h‖_(H^(m+2))‖f_♭‖_4),
    ‖f₃‖_3 ≤ C(‖f_♭‖_3 + ‖u₁‖_4) ≤ C‖f_♭‖_3,

h being bounded in H⁸. Hence ‖u₂‖_(H^((1;m),(a₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)) ≤ C(‖f_♭‖_m + ‖h‖_(H^(m+3))‖f_♭‖_4), the second term of
(37.22); no product of two norms of h arises. For m = 3, the last term of (37.13) is
‖h‖_(H⁶)‖f₃‖_3 ≤ C‖f₃‖_3 ≤ C‖f_♭‖_3, and u₁ is bounded without tame term, so no tame term arises. ∎

**Lemma 37.26** (Interpolation.) For j ∈ ℕ₀ let (B^j, |·|_j) be Banach spaces with continuous
inclusions B^j ↪ B^i for j ≥ i along which the norms do not increase, B^∞ := ⋂_j B^j, and for θ > 1 let
S_θ : B^∞ → B^∞ be linear maps satisfying (20.1) for every v ∈ B^∞. For integers 0 ≤ s₀ ≤ s ≤ s₁ there is C
such that for every v ∈ B^∞

    |v|_s ≤ C|v|_(s₀)^(1−λ)|v|_(s₁)^λ,     λ := (s − s₀)/(s₁ − s₀) (λ := 0 if s₁ = s₀),    (37.24)

and for integers 0 ≤ s₀ ≤ q ≤ p there is C such that for every v ∈ B^∞

    |v|_p|v|_q ≤ C|v|_(s₀)|v|_(p+q−s₀),    (37.25)

C depending only on these integers and the constants C_(s,t) of (20.1). This applies to the spaces B^j of the
proof of Theorem 37.28, whose elements are the decompositions of Lemma 37.22 (after conjugation), with
their norms made monotone in j as in Remark 20.3, and to the smoothing operators of part (i) of that proof, which
act on each of the two components of a decomposition by the operator S̃_θ of Step 4 of the proof of Proposition 20.4;
their construction uses nothing of this section.

*Proof.* Let s₀ < s < s₁, the other cases being trivial, and v ≠ 0, so that |v|_(s₀) > 0. Put
R := |v|_(s₁)/|v|_(s₀), which is at least 1 as the norms are monotone. If R ≤ 2^(s₁−s₀), then

    |v|_s ≤ |v|_(s₁) = |v|_(s₁)^(1−λ)|v|_(s₁)^λ ≤ 2^(s₁−s₀)|v|_(s₀)^(1−λ)|v|_(s₁)^λ.

Otherwise θ := R^(1/(s₁−s₀)) > 2, and (20.1), with (s, t) := (s, s₀) for S_θv and (s, t) := (s, s₁) for
v − S_θv, gives

    |v|_s ≤ |S_θv|_s + |v − S_θv|_s ≤ C_(s,s₀)θ^(s−s₀)|v|_(s₀) + C_(s,s₁)θ^(s−s₁)|v|_(s₁)
        = (C_(s,s₀) + C_(s,s₁))|v|_(s₀)^(1−λ)|v|_(s₁)^λ,

as θ^(s−s₀) = R^λ and θ^(s−s₁) = R^(λ−1). For the product put n := p + q − s₀, so n ≥ p. If n = s₀, then p = q = s₀
and the claim is an identity. Otherwise (37.24) with s₁ := n, at s = p and at s = q, has the exponents
λ_p := (p − s₀)/(n − s₀) and λ_q := (q − s₀)/(n − s₀), and λ_p + λ_q = 1 as (p − s₀) + (q − s₀) = n − s₀. The product
of the two bounds is |v|_p|v|_q ≤ C|v|_(s₀)^(2−λ_p−λ_q)|v|_n^(λ_p+λ_q) = C|v|_(s₀)|v|_n. ∎

**Theorem 37.27** (The linear exterior estimate; [Hin23a, Theorem 3.35] in dimension 4 + 1, with [Hin26,
(5.52)–(5.53)].) Let α₀ > ℓ^♭_I, a₀ := α₀ − 3/2, k ∈ ℕ₀, d := 4, and let h be small in H^(8,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b. For
f ∈ H^(k+d,α₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀)) and ġ₀, ġ₁ ∈ H^(k+d,α₀)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) there is a
ġ ∈ H^(k,α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀)), unique in H^(max(k,1),α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b (the energy estimate needs H¹), with
Lġ = f, ġ|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = ġ₀ and rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))ġ|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = ġ₁; and with
N(f, ġ₀, ġ₁; j) := ‖f‖_(H^(j,α₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b) + ‖ġ₀‖_(H^(j,α₀)_b) + ‖ġ₁‖_(H^(j,α₀)_b),

    ‖ġ‖_(H^(k,α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b)
        ≤ C(N(f, ġ₀, ġ₁; k + d) + ‖h‖_(H^(k+d+3,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b)N(f, ġ₀, ġ₁; 8)),    (37.26)

with C depending on k, α₀, ℓ^♭_I, the parameters and the bound on h in H⁸, and not on h otherwise. Here the norms of h
in (37.26) and in that bound are those of one decomposition of ρ^(−3/2)h (Lemma 37.22, with
a₀ = ℓ^♭₀ − 3/2), the same at every order (one with every norm finite exists by part (c) of that lemma); and the left
side of (37.26) may be replaced by the norm of the decomposition of ġ that the proof constructs, which depends
linearly on (f, ġ₀, ġ₁). At α₀ = ℓ^♭₀ this is the tame form [Hin26, (5.52)] of
(37.34); (37.34) itself follows, with C depending on h.

*Proof.* *Step 1 (near Σ_IVP).* Lemma 37.24 with s := k + 3 and α := α₀ gives ġ_N on Ω_N, including the past
slab, bounded in H^(k+4,α₀)_b by (37.21).

*Step 2 (the forcing for the rest).* Let χ := χ̂_N(τ′), χ̂_N = 1 on (−∞, ⅛] and 0 on [¼, ∞). On Ω⁺, w := ġ − χġ_N must
satisfy

    Lw = f₂ := (1 − χ)f − [L, χ]ġ_N,     w = 0 on {τ′ < ⅛},

as ġ = ġ_N on Ω_N (uniqueness in Lemma 37.24). f₂ vanishes on {τ′ < ⅛}, and [L, χ] ∈ ρ²Diff¹_b is supported in
{⅛ ≤ τ′ ≤ ¼}, where ρ_I ≥ ½. The argument for (37.23), with χ in place of χ_c, L in place of L_g and the
factor ρ² of [L, χ] giving the weight α₀ + 2, gives

    ‖[L, χ]ġ_N‖_(H^(k+3,α₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b) ≤ C(‖ġ_N‖_(H^(k+4,α₀)_b) + ‖h‖_(H^(k+4))‖ġ_N‖_(H^(4,α₀)_b)).

Put u := ρ^(−3/2)w; then L_gu = f_(2,♭) := 2ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)f₂ ∈ H^(k+3,(a₀,2β))_b in every slot (Section 37.11).

*Step 3 (growth).* Fix ε := ¼(½ − β) > 0 and γ₀ := β − 1 + 2ε < 0; then γ₀ < min(a₀, 0), as a₀ > β > γ₀.
Lemma 37.25 with m := k + 3 and α_I := γ₀ gives u on Ω⁺₁, with (37.22), and u = 0 on {τ′ < ⅛}, so u is the
solution on Ω⁺. On Ω⁺ ∩ {ρ_I > c/2} this already bounds u in H^(k+4,a₀)_b, which is the claim there.

*Step 4 (the equation near ℐ⁺).* On Ω_c, with u₂ of the proof of Lemma 37.25, u₂ = 0 on {ρ_I > c/2} and, by
(37.12),

    (X_I − Ā)(X₀ − X_I)u₂ = F := −½(f₃ − x_I²Δ̸u₂ − L̃_gu₂).    (37.27)

*The gain.* Let j ≥ 2 and u₂ ∈ H^(j,(a₀,2γ))_b. Then x_I²Δ̸u₂ and L̃_gu₂ lie in H^(j−2,(a₀,2γ+1−2ε))_b. Indeed x_I²Δ̸
and x_Ia_iP_i carry the factor x_I and are of second order. For x_Iã_iP_iu₂ put b_i := P_iu₂, so that
‖b_i‖_(H^(j−2,(a₀,2γ))_b) ≤ C‖u₂‖_(H^(j,(a₀,2γ))_b). By (37.19), for every j′ ∈ ℕ₀,
ã_i ∈ H^(j′,(ℓ^♭₀,−2ε))_b ⊂ H^(j′,(0,−2ε))_b with norm at most C‖h‖_(H^(j′+2)) (its expansion at ℐ⁺ starts at ρ_I⁰,
which lies in every x_I^(−2ε)L²_b near ℐ⁺ but not in L²_b; and ρ₀ ≤ 1 on Ω_c). By the embedding of Lemma 37.17 (order
3, on Ω_c), ã_i ∈ x_I^(−2ε)L^∞ with norm at most C‖h‖_(H⁵). There are two cases.

(1) j ≥ 5. Then b_i ∈ H^(3,(a₀,2γ))_b, so b_i ∈ ρ₀^(a₀)x_I^(2γ)L^∞ with norm at most C‖u₂‖_(H^(5,(a₀,2γ))_b), by the same
embedding. Lemma 37.17 with s := j − 2, a := ã_i with the weights (0, −2ε) and b := b_i with the weights (a₀, 2γ),
followed by multiplication by x_I, gives

    ‖x_Iã_iP_iu₂‖_(H^(j−2,(a₀,2γ+1−2ε))_b)
        ≤ C(‖u₂‖_(H^(j,(a₀,2γ))_b) + ‖h‖_(H^j)‖u₂‖_(H^(5,(a₀,2γ))_b)),    (37.28)

the first term from ‖ã_i‖_(x_I^(−2ε)L^∞)‖b_i‖_(H^(j−2,(a₀,2γ))_b) and the second from
‖ã_i‖_(H^(j−2,(0,−2ε))_b)‖b_i‖_(ρ₀^(a₀)x_I^(2γ)L^∞).

(2) 2 ≤ j ≤ 4. Now b_i need not be bounded (j − 2 < 3), and we use Leibniz's rule, which puts at most j − 2 ≤ 2
derivatives on ã_i. Divide out the weights: ã_i = x_I^(−2ε)a′ and b_i = ρ₀^(a₀)x_I^(2γ)b′, so that the left side of
(37.28) is ‖a′b′‖_(H^(j−2)_b). Measure H^p_b by the L²_b-norms of the compositions of at most p of the fields
X₀, …, X₈ of the proof of Proposition 37.16, which span Diff¹_b over C^∞. For l ≤ 7, X_l obeys Leibniz's rule for the
product of a coefficient with a section, and X₈ = 1; so a composition Q of q of these fields maps a′b′ to a sum of at
most 2^q products (Q′a′)(Q″b′), with Q′ and Q″ compositions of q′ and q″ of the fields, q′ + q″ ≤ q. Hence

    ‖a′b′‖_(H^(j−2)_b) ≤ C max_(Q′) ‖Q′a′‖_(L^∞) ‖b′‖_(H^(j−2)_b),

the maximum over the compositions Q′ of at most j − 2 of the fields. For such Q′, as j − 2 ≤ 2, Q′a′ ∈ H³_b with norm
at most ‖a′‖_(H⁵_b) = ‖ã_i‖_(H^(5,(0,−2ε))_b) ≤ C‖h‖_(H⁷), so ‖Q′a′‖_(L^∞) ≤ C‖h‖_(H⁷) by the same embedding. Therefore

    ‖x_Iã_iP_iu₂‖_(H^(j−2,(a₀,2γ+1−2ε))_b) ≤ C‖h‖_(H⁷)‖u₂‖_(H^(j,(a₀,2γ))_b) ≤ C‖u₂‖_(H^(j,(a₀,2γ))_b),
    (37.29)

with C depending on the bound on h in H⁸, as (37.26) allows: at these orders there is no tame term.

With u₂ ∈ H^((1;m),(a₀,2γ))_(e,b;b) in place of H^(j,(a₀,2γ))_b the loss is one b-derivative instead of two, as
P_i ∈ Diff¹_(e,b)Diff¹_b and x_I²Δ̸ ∈ x_IDiff¹_(e,b)Diff¹_b: then b_i ∈ H^(m−1,(a₀,2γ))_b with norm at most
C‖u₂‖_(H^((1;m),(a₀,2γ))_(e,b;b)), and the two cases are m − 1 ≥ 3 and m − 1 ≤ 2. For m ≥ 4 the argument of (1)
gives (37.28) with j − 2, ‖u₂‖_(H^(j,(a₀,2γ))_b), ‖h‖_(H^j) and ‖u₂‖_(H^(5,(a₀,2γ))_b) replaced by m − 1,
‖u₂‖_(H^((1;m),(a₀,2γ))_(e,b;b)), ‖h‖_(H^(m+1)) and ‖u₂‖_(H^((1;4),(a₀,2γ))_(e,b;b)); for m ≤ 3 the argument of (2)
gives (37.29) with the same replacements. And f₃ ∈ H^(k+3,(a₀,2β))_b: f_(2,♭) is, and [L_g, χ_c]u₁ is
supported in {ρ_I ≥ c/4}.

*Step 5 (the integration, slot by slot).* Write (37.27) by slots. As Ā is lower triangular with the entries of
Section 37.11, for j ≠ 6

    (X_I − Ā_(jj))Y_j = F_j + Σ_(i<j, i≠6) Ā_(ji)Y_i,     Y_j := (X₀ − X_I)u_(2,j),    (37.30)

and, X_I and X₀ − X_I commuting, for slot 6

    (X₀ − X_I)Z₆ = F₆,     Z₆ := X_Iu_(2,6).    (37.31)

All of Y_j, Z₆, u₂, F vanish on {ρ_I > c/2}, so Lemma 37.21 applies; the solution of each equation vanishing there
is unique (it is an ordinary differential equation along curves that reach {ρ_I = c}, Lemma 37.20 (b)).

*First integration.* u₂ ∈ H^((1;k+3),(a₀,2γ₀))_(e,b;b) (Step 3), so by Step 4, F ∈ H^(k+2,(a₀,2γ₁))_b with
γ₁ := min(β, γ₀ + ½ − ε) = β − ½ + ε < 0. For j ≠ 6, in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, Lemma 37.21 (a) with
d = Ā_(jj) ≥ d_* > γ₁ gives Y_j ∈ H^(k+2,(a₀,2γ₁))_b, the right side of (37.30) lying there by induction; then
Lemma 37.21 (c), a₀ > γ₁, gives u_(2,j) ∈ H^(k+2,(a₀,2γ₁))_b. For slot 6, Lemma 37.21 (c) gives Z₆, and
Lemma 37.21 (a) with d = 0 > γ₁ gives u_(2,6) ∈ H^(k+2,(a₀,2γ₁))_b.

*Second integration.* Now u₂ ∈ H^(k+2,(a₀,2γ₁))_b, so by Step 4 (with two derivatives lost), F ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2γ₂))_b,
γ₂ := min(β, γ₁ + ½ − ε) = β. As in the first integration, with d_* > β ((37.16)) and a₀ > β,
u_(2,j) ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b for j ≠ 6. For slot 6, Z₆ ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b by Lemma 37.21 (c), and Lemma 37.21 (b),
β > 0, gives u_(2,6) = u^((0)) + ũ₆ with u^((0)) ∈ H^(k,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_c) and ũ₆ ∈ H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b.

*Step 6 (assembly).* On Ω_c, u = u₂ + χ_cu₁, with χ_cu₁ supported in {ρ_I ≥ c/4}; on Ω⁺ ∩ {ρ_I > c/2}, Step 3; on Ω_N,
Step 1. As χ_I = χ̂(ρ_I) vanishes for ρ_I ≥ c/2, u₆ − χ_Iu^((0)) = ũ₆ + (1 − χ_I)u^((0)) + χ_cu_(1,6) on Ω_c, and
(1 − χ_I)u^((0)) is supported in {ρ_I ≥ c/4} within Ω_c, where every weight at ℐ⁺ is equivalent. So u ∈ 𝒴^k_(a₀)(Ω⁺),
with the decomposition (Lemma 37.22) whose first component is u^((0)), linear in (f, ġ₀, ġ₁) as every
step is; that is, ġ = ρ^(3/2)u + χġ_N ∈ H^(k,α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b on Ω⁺ (Section 37.11), and on Ω⁻ by Step 1.

*The estimate.* Write |h|_j for the norm of order j of the decomposition of h fixed in the statement, made monotone in
j as in Remark 20.3, and N_j := N(f, ġ₀, ġ₁; j); let C depend only on k, α₀, ℓ^♭_I, the parameters and the bound
on h in H⁸, so that |h|_j ≤ C for j ≤ 8. For the other quantities ‖·‖_j is the norm of order j of the space in which
the step bounds them (H^(j,α₀)_b for ġ_N, H^(j,(a₀,2β))_b for f_(2,♭) and f₃, H^(j,a₀)_b(Ω′) for u₁), and
‖u₂‖_((1;m)) is the norm of u₂ in H^((1;m),(a₀,2γ₀))_(e,b;b). Each step is bounded by the previous ones. Each lower
norm is bounded by the same steps at a low order, where the tame factors are |h|_j with j ≤ 7, except
‖u₂‖_(H^(5,(a₀,2γ₁))_b), whose bound carries |h|_9 and is treated in the second integration.

- Step 1, by (37.21) at s = k + 3 (for k = 0, its clause for s ≤ 3):
  ‖ġ_N‖_(H^(k+4,α₀)_b) ≤ C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+5)N_5); at s = 3, ‖ġ_N‖_(H^(4,α₀)_b) ≤ CN_4.
- Step 2, by the bound for [L, χ]ġ_N: ‖f_(2,♭)‖_(H^(k+3,(a₀,2β))_b) ≤ C(N_(k+4) + ‖ġ_N‖_(k+4) + |h|_(k+4)‖ġ_N‖_4)
  ≤ C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+5)N_5); at k = 1, ‖f_(2,♭)‖_(H^(4,(a₀,2β))_b) ≤ CN_5.
- Step 3, by (37.22) at m = k + 3 (for k = 0, its clause for m = 3): ‖u₂‖_(H^((1;k+3),(a₀,2γ₀))_(e,b;b)), the
  norm of u in H^(k+4,a₀)_b(Ω⁺ ∩ {ρ_I > c/2}), and, by the proof of Lemma 37.25, those of u₁ in H^(k+4,a₀)_b(Ω′)
  and of f₃ in H^(k+3,(a₀,2β))_b are at most C(‖f_(2,♭)‖_(k+3) + |h|_(k+6)‖f_(2,♭)‖_4) ≤ C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+6)N_5); at
  k = 1, ‖u₂‖_(H^((1;4),(a₀,2γ₀))_(e,b;b)) ≤ CN_5.
- The first integration, by (37.28) in H^((1;m)) with m = k + 3 (for k = 0, (37.29)) and the
  constants of Lemma 37.21: ‖u₂‖_(H^(k+2,(a₀,2γ₁))_b) ≤ C(‖f₃‖_(k+2) + ‖u₂‖_((1;k+3)) + |h|_(k+4)‖u₂‖_((1;4)))
  ≤ C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+6)N_5). At k = 3 this is ‖u₂‖_(H^(5,(a₀,2γ₁))_b) ≤ C(N_7 + |h|_9N_5).
- The second integration, by (37.28) at j = k + 2 (for k ≤ 2, (37.29)) and Lemma 37.21: the
  norms of u_(2,j) (j ≠ 6), u^((0)) and ũ₆ in 𝒴^k_(a₀) are at most C(‖f₃‖_k + ‖u₂‖_(H^(k+2,(a₀,2γ₁))_b) + T), with
  T := 0 for k ≤ 2 and T := |h|_(k+2)‖u₂‖_(H^(5,(a₀,2γ₁))_b) ≤ C|h|_(k+2)(N_7 + |h|_9N_5) for k ≥ 3. For 3 ≤ k ≤ 6,
  as |h|_(k+2) ≤ C, T ≤ C(N_7 + |h|_9N_5) ≤ C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+7)N_5). For k ≥ 7, |h|_(k+2)N_7 ≤ |h|_(k+7)N_8, and
  (37.25) (Lemma 37.26 for the decompositions) with s₀ := 8, q := 9 and
  p := k + 2 ≥ 9 gives |h|_(k+2)|h|_9 ≤ C|h|_8|h|_(k+3) ≤ C|h|_(k+3); so T ≤ C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+7)N_8).

By Step 6, the norm of the decomposition of ġ constructed there, and so ‖ġ‖_(H^(k,α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b), is at most C times
the sum of these bounds, which is at most C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+7)N_8): this is (37.26).

*The estimate with C depending on h.* Let k ≥ 1. The lower norms in the tame terms are of orders 4, 5 and 4 for f, ġ₀
and ġ₁ in (37.21) at s = k + 3, of order 4 for ġ_N and for u₁ in the bounds for [L, χ]ġ_N and
(37.23), of order 4 for f_(2,♭) in (37.22) at m = k + 3, and of orders (1;4) and 5 for u₂ in
(37.28), which is used only at m ≥ 4 and j ≥ 5. Each is at most the order to which the same quantity is bounded
in the main term of its step: k + 4 for f, ġ₀, ġ₁, ġ_N and u₁, k + 3 for f_(2,♭), (1;m) and j for u₂. So every tame
term is at most C‖h‖_(H^(k+7,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) times the main terms, and the steps give (37.34) with C
depending on h. Let k = 0. Step 1 uses Lemma 37.24 at s = 3, Step 3 uses Lemma 37.25 at m = 3, and both
integrations of Step 5 use (37.29) (at m = 3 and j = 2); none of these has a tame term, h being bounded in
H⁸. So (37.34) holds at k = 0 too, with C depending on the bound on h in H⁸.

*Uniqueness.* Two solutions differ by one with vanishing data and forcing term; it vanishes on Ω_N by Lemma 37.24,
and on Ω⁺ as the forward solution with vanishing forcing term (Lemma 18.4). ∎

[Hin23a, Theorem 3.35] integrates π_(CΥ)u, then π̸₀u, then π₁₁u, and repeats, because in dimension 3 + 1 the radiation
field of π̸₀u enters the equation of π₁₁u through the h-dependent entry A̸₁₁ of [Hin23a] and through the second-order
error acting on π̸₀u, and π₁₁u has the size of the leading part. In dimension 4 + 1 both are in L̃_g, gaining
x_I^(1−2ε), and Ā₇₆ = 0: so all slots improve together, two integrations from the growth weight γ₀ suffice, with a loss
of d = 4 derivatives, and π₁₁ġ has no radiation field (Remark 27.19).

### 37.14 The nonlinear exterior solution

This section is [Hin23a, Corollary 3.36] in dimension 4 + 1, the nonlinear part of [Hin26, Theorem 5.17].

**Theorem 37.28** (The nonlinear exterior solution.) Let g₀ be as in Section 37.11, d := 7 and
N_NM := 21d + 6 = 153, the order of Theorem 20.1. There are ε₀ > 0 and, for every k and ε > 0, an ε₁ ∈ (0, ε₀] such
that for h₀, h₁ ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀); S²T*) with ‖h_j‖_(H^(N_NM,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₀ the problem

    P(g₀ + h, g₀) = 0 in Ω_(ext,r₀),     h = h₀,  rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h = h₁ on Σ_(IVP,r₀),    (37.32)

has a solution h ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀)) small in H^(3d) of this class, unique among the solutions small
in H^(8,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b, and ‖h_j‖_(H^(N_NM+k,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₁ gives ‖h‖_(H^(3d+k,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) < ε.

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 20.1 with d = 7 and:

- B^k := H^(k,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_c) × H^(k,ℓ^♭₀,ℓ^♭_I)_b(Ω_(ext,r₀); S²T*), a₀ := ℓ^♭₀ − 3/2, with the sum of the two norms. An
  element x = (v, h̃) is, after conjugation, a decomposition (Lemma 37.22) of the tensor h_x that equals
  h̃ + ρ^(3/2)χ_Iv in slot 6 and h̃ in the other slots: h_x ∈ H^(k,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀); S²T*), with norm in
  that class at most C|x|_k (Section 37.11). The map x ↦ h_x is linear. F^k := H^(k,ℓ^♭₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀))
  × H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀))². The norms are made monotone in k by Remark 20.3;
- trivial support classes: the subspaces B^k_η and F^∞_η of Theorem 20.1 all equal to B^k and F^∞, and η₀ := 1;
- Φ(x) := (P(g₀ + h_x, g₀), h_x|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) − h₀, rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h_x|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) − h₁) on the set {|x|_(3d) < δ}.

The unknown is the decomposition, not the tensor: a decomposition is not determined by h_x
(Lemma 37.22 (b)), and the smoothing operators must be linear.

*(i) Smoothing.* Componentwise: on v the operator S̃_θ of Step 4 of the proof of Proposition 20.4, which acts on
weighted b-Sobolev spaces without support conditions, built on ℐ⁺_c, and on h̃ the same operator built on Ω_(ext,r₀).
S_θ is linear and the norm of B^k is the sum of the two norms, so (20.1) holds; the support conditions are
vacuous.

*(ii) The map.* Write h := h_x. By Corollary 27.18 (with ℰ₀ = ∅, ℓ₀ = ℓ^♭₀, and ⟨ℰ_I^C⟩ at the weight ℓ^♭_I, which by
Definition 27.6 is the class (−, ℓ^♭_I) of h), P(g₀ + h, g₀) ∈ H^(k−2,ℓ^♭₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b for x ∈ B^k small in
B⁵, and by (27.21), Proposition 27.17 and the smooth dependence on h in Proposition 27.14 it is C² in x,
with Φ′(x)ẋ = (L^(g₀+h,g₀)h_ẋ, h_ẋ|_Σ, rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h_ẋ|_Σ) and Φ″ bilinear in two b-derivatives, with coefficients
rational in h and its first two b-derivatives. (20.2) and (20.3) follow from the Moser estimates
(Lemma 37.17, Lemma 27.5) applied to the components of x, the loss being 2 and the low norms of order at
most 5 ≤ d. The trace on Σ_(IVP,r₀) is bounded B^(k+1) → H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) (χ_I = 0 near Σ_(IVP,r₀)), which lies
within the loss d. The data enter the constants C_k of (20.3):
‖Φ(x)‖_k ≤ C^P_k(1 + |x|_(k+d)) + ‖h₀‖_(H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b) + ‖h₁‖_(H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b), with C^P_k depending only on g₀, k and δ.
For k ≤ N_NM and ‖h_j‖_(H^(N_NM,ℓ^♭₀)_b) ≤ 1 this is at most (C^P_k + 2)(1 + |x|_(k+d)); so we take
C_k := C^P_k + 2 for k ≤ N_NM, which does not depend on the data. For k > N_NM, C_k := C^P_k + ‖h₀‖_(H^k) + ‖h₁‖_(H^k)
is finite, as h_j ∈ H^∞, and does not enter the threshold of Theorem 20.1.
(Smallness in H^(2d) alone is not enough for this argument: the threshold of Theorem 20.1 depends on the C_k with
k ≤ N_NM.)

*(iii) Right inverses.* For x in the set above, Ψ(x)(f, ġ₀, ġ₁) is the decomposition of ġ that the proof of
Theorem 37.27 constructs, with α₀ := ℓ^♭₀ > ℓ^♭_I, for h := h_x with its decomposition x; it is linear in
(f, ġ₀, ġ₁), and h_(Ψ(x)F) = ġ. Then Φ′(x)Ψ(x) = id on F^∞, and (37.26), for these decompositions, gives
(20.4): |Ψ(x)F|_k ≤ C(‖F‖_(k+4) + |x|_(k+7)‖F‖₈) ≤ C(‖F‖_(k+d) + |x|_(k+d)‖F‖_(2d)) for k ≥ d, and 3d ≥ 8
gives the smallness that Theorem 37.27 asks. The support statement of (iii) is vacuous.

Φ(0) = (0, −h₀, −h₁), as P(g₀, g₀) = 0 (the proof of Corollary 27.18). Let ε_NM be the threshold of
Theorem 20.1 for d, δ, η₀ and the constants above, and ε₀ := min(1, ε_NM/2). If ‖h_j‖_(H^(N_NM,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₀, then
‖Φ(0)‖_(2d) ≤ ‖h₀‖_(H^(2d,ℓ^♭₀)_b) + ‖h₁‖_(H^(2d,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε_NM, and Theorem 20.1 gives x with |x|_(3d) < δ and
Φ(x) = 0; h := h_x solves (37.32), with norm below Cδ in H^(3d) of its class. *Higher norms.* For k ≥ 0 the
shifted scales |v|′_i := |v|_(i+k), ‖f‖′_i := ‖f‖_(i+k) satisfy (i)–(iii) with the same d: (20.1) and
(20.4) are invariant under the shift, and (20.3) holds on {|x|′_(3d) < δ′} ⊂ {|x|_(3d) < δ}, δ′ ≤ δ,
with constants depending on k; as above, those of order i ≤ N_NM do not depend on the data once
‖h_j‖_(H^(N_NM+k,ℓ^♭₀)_b) ≤ 1. So Theorem 20.1 for the shifted scales, with δ′ := min(δ, ε/C), gives ε₁ ∈ (0, ε₀]
such that data with ‖h_j‖_(H^(N_NM+k,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₁ have a solution h_x with |x|_(3d+k) < ε/C, so with norm below ε in
H^(3d+k) of its class; it is small in H⁸ of its class, so by uniqueness it is the h above.
*Uniqueness.* If h and h′ solve (37.32) and are small in H^(8,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b, then L̄(h − h′) = 0 with
vanishing data, where L̄ := ∫₀¹ L^(g₀+h′+s(h−h′),g₀) ds. Each L^(g₀+h_s,g₀) has the form (37.12) with the same
leading part, which does not depend on h, and a remainder in the class (37.19), uniformly in s; so L̄ has this
form too, and its principal part, an average of ½□_(g_s) with g_s close to g_(b₀), is a wave operator with the same
causal structure. Lemma 37.24 and Lemma 37.25 hold for L̄ (their proofs use only these properties), and the
difference vanishes. ∎

**Remark 37.29** (Constraints.) If the data of Theorem 37.28 satisfy the vacuum constraint equations and
the gauge condition on Σ_(IVP,r₀), the solution is Ricci flat and satisfies the gauge condition on Ω_(ext,r₀):
Remark 37.33 (1) applies to it as stated there.

### 37.15 The exterior solution

This section states [Hin26, (5.52)–(5.53) and Theorem 5.17] in dimension 4 + 1, and proves the propagation of the
gauge condition and of the vacuum equation that [Hin26, Remark 5.18] uses.

**Theorem 37.30** ([Hin26, Theorem 5.17] in dimension 4 + 1.) There is k₀ ∈ ℕ such that the following
holds. Let ℓ^♭₀, ℓ^♭_I be as in (37.1) and r₀ ≥ R₀, with R₀ as fixed after Lemma 37.1. There is
ε₀ > 0 such that for
h₀, h₁ ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀); S²T*) with ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₀,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₀, the problem

    P(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0 in Ω_(ext,r₀),     h = h₀,  rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h = h₁ on Σ_(IVP,r₀),    (37.33)

has a solution h ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀)), unique among the solutions of this class that are small in
H^(8,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b; and for every ε > 0 and k there are k₁ ≥ k₀ and ε₁ ∈ (0, ε₀] such that
‖h_j‖_(H^(k₁,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₁ gives ‖h‖_(H^(k,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) < ε. Moreover, for h ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b small in
H^(8,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b and every α₀ > ℓ^♭_I, d := 4, the solution of

    L^(g_(b₀)+h,g_(b₀))ġ = f ∈ H^(k+d,α₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b,     ġ|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = ġ₀,
    rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))ġ|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = ġ₁,     ġ₀, ġ₁ ∈ H^(k+d,α₀)_b,

satisfies

    ‖ġ‖_(H^(k,α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) ≤ C(‖f‖_(H^(k+d,α₀+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b) + ‖ġ₀‖_(H^(k+d,α₀)_b) + ‖ġ₁‖_(H^(k+d,α₀)_b)),
    (37.34)

with C depending on k, α₀, ℓ^♭_I and h; and the tame form of (37.34) at α₀ = ℓ^♭₀, [Hin26, (5.52)], is
(37.26).

Here (−′, ℓ^♭_I + 1) is the class of Definition 27.16 (2) with the index sets left out, as in [Hin26].

*Proof.* Theorem 37.28 with g₀ = g_(b₀) gives the solution, its uniqueness and the smallness, with k₀ := N_NM = 153
and k₁ := N_NM + k, as ‖h‖_(H^(k,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) ≤ ‖h‖_(H^(21+k,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) (21 = 3d for the d = 7 of
Theorem 37.28). Theorem 37.27 gives (37.34) and its tame form (37.26). ∎

[Hin26] derives its Theorem 5.17 from [Hin23a, Theorem 3.35 and Corollary 3.36] by a change of notation: the tame
estimate (5.52), a Nash–Moser scheme (by [SR89] there; here Theorem 20.1, which is [Hin26c, Theorem 12.4]), and the
radiation fields of π₁₁ġ and π̸₀ġ recovered by integrating the leading part. In dimension 4 + 1 the leading part is that
of (27.16), and only π̸₀ carries a radiation field (Remark 27.19). [Hin23a, Section 3] is written
out in dimension 4 + 1 in Section 37.3–Section 37.14, and Proposition 27.59 collects the places where the dimension
enters it.

The data and the gauge condition propagate by the second Bianchi identity. We first record the uniqueness statement for
linear wave equations that this uses.

**Lemma 37.31** (Uniqueness for the Cauchy problem.) Let X be a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold
with metric g and a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface S, and let P be a second-order operator with smooth
coefficients on a vector bundle over X, with principal symbol g⁻¹(ζ, ζ)Id. If v ∈ C²(X) solves Pv = 0 and v and all its
first derivatives vanish along S, then v = 0.

*Proof.* By Theorem A.1 (3) there is a Cauchy time function τ on X with S = τ⁻¹(0); its level sets are
spacelike Cauchy hypersurfaces (Theorem A.1 (2)). Let H be the Heaviside function and w := H(τ)v. In local
coordinates and a trivialisation, P = −g^(ij)∂_i∂_j + A^j∂_j + B; as v = 0 on S, ∂_j(H(τ)v) = H(τ)∂_jv, and as
∂_jv = 0 on S, ∂_i(H(τ)∂_jv) = H(τ)∂_i∂_jv, in the sense of distributions. So Pw = H(τ)Pv = 0 in 𝒟′(X), and
supp w ⊂ {τ ≥ 0}. For p ∈ X with τ(p) > −1, the set L_p := J⁻_X(p) ∩ J⁺_X(τ⁻¹(−1)) is compact
(Theorem A.1 (4) with K = {p}), and it contains J⁻_X(p) ∩ {τ ≥ −1}: through a point q with τ(q) ≥ −1 the
maximal integral curve of the gradient of τ, which is timelike, is an inextendible causal curve, so it meets the Cauchy
hypersurface τ⁻¹(−1), at a point where τ ≤ τ(q), that is, to the past of q. Lemma 18.4 with c = −1 gives w = 0,
so v = 0 on {τ ≥ 0}. With the time orientation of X reversed, X is globally hyperbolic with the same Cauchy
hypersurfaces, −τ is a Cauchy time function, and P is unchanged; the same argument applied to H(−τ)v gives v = 0 on
{τ ≤ 0}. ∎

**Proposition 37.32** (Propagation of the gauge condition and of the vacuum equation.) Let X be a globally
hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold with metric g and a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface S, with future unit normal n.
Let g₀ be a smooth Lorentzian metric on X, δ*_(g₀,E_C) = δ*_(g₀) + E^C_(g₀) the operator of (21.42) (with any
smooth 1-form c_C), and Υ a smooth 1-form on X with

    Ric(g) = δ*_(g₀,E_C)Υ     on X.    (37.35)

If Υ = 0 along S and the first and second fundamental forms of S satisfy the vacuum constraint equations, then Υ = 0
and Ric(g) = 0 on X. The dimension does not enter. In particular (37.35) holds with
Υ = Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g₀) when P(g, g₀) = 0 ((21.44)), and with Υ = Υ^(χ₀E_Υ)(g, g₀) when P^(χ₀)(g, g₀) = 0
((37.36)).

*Proof.* *The equation for Υ.* The contracted second Bianchi identity δ_gG_gRic(g) = 0 holds in every dimension.
Applying 2δ_gG_g to (37.35) gives QΥ = 0, with Q := 2δ_gG_gδ*_(g₀,E_C). For a 1-form ω, with
(δ_gu)_μ = −∇^κu_(κμ) and G_g = I − ½g tr_g,

    (2δ_gG_gδ*_gω)_μ = −∇^κ∇_κω_μ − ∇^κ∇_μω_κ + ∇_μ∇^κω_κ,

and by the Ricci identity ∇^κ∇_μω_κ − ∇_μ∇^κω_κ is of order zero in ω, linear in the curvature of g. The operator
δ*_(g₀,E_C) − δ*_g = (δ*_(g₀) − δ*_g) + E^C_(g₀) is of order zero. So Q = □_g + Q₁ with Q₁ of first order, and Q has
principal symbol g⁻¹(ζ, ζ)Id.

*The data of Υ.* Along S, Υ = 0, so its derivatives along S vanish, and there ∇Υ = −n♭ ⊗ Z with Z := ∇_nΥ,
n♭ := g(n, ·), g(n, n) = −1, where (∇Υ)(V, W) := (∇_VΥ)(W). The terms of order zero in δ*_(g₀,E_C)Υ vanish along S,
so there, with a ⊗_s b := ½(a ⊗ b + b ⊗ a),

    Ric(g) = δ*_gΥ = −n♭ ⊗_s Z,     G_gRic(g) = −n♭ ⊗_s Z + ½Z(n)g,

as tr_g(n♭ ⊗_s Z) = Z(n). For every vector Y, (G_gRic(g))(n, Y) = −½(n♭(n)Z(Y) + Z(n)g(n, Y)) + ½Z(n)g(n, Y) = ½Z(Y).
By the Gauss and Codazzi equations, the vacuum constraint equations for the first and second fundamental forms of S are
the equations (G_gRic(g))(n, ·) = 0 along S. So Z = 0, and all first derivatives of Υ vanish along S.

*Conclusion.* Lemma 37.31 with P = Q and v = Υ gives Υ = 0 on X, and then Ric(g) = 0 by
(37.35). ∎

**Remark 37.33** ([Hin26, Remarks 5.18 and 5.20] in dimension 4 + 1.) (1) Let h be the solution of
Theorem 37.30, and ĝ := g_(b₀) + h₀ + t_IVP r⁻¹h₁, with h₀, h₁ extended to be independent of t_IVP near
Σ_(IVP,r₀). If the first and second fundamental forms of Σ_(IVP,r₀) for ĝ satisfy the vacuum constraint equations and
Υ^(E_Υ)(ĝ, g_(b₀)) = 0 on Σ_(IVP,r₀), then Υ^(E_Υ)(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0 and Ric(g_(b₀) + h) = 0 on Ω_(ext,r₀).
Indeed g_(b₀) + h and ĝ agree on Σ_(IVP,r₀) with their first derivatives (h = h₀ and rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h = h₁ there), so
they have the same fundamental forms and the same Υ^(E_Υ) there; h is smooth in the interior Ω° of Ω_(ext,r₀); and Ω°
is globally hyperbolic with the spacelike Cauchy hypersurface Σ° (Lemma 37.2). Proposition 37.32 on Ω°
gives the claim there, and by continuity on Ω_(ext,r₀). The same argument applies in the cut-off gauge of
Section 37.16 and to the gauged data of Section 37.21 (Theorem 37.39). ([Hin26, Remark 5.18] prints
t_IVP r h₁; with h₁ = rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h as in (37.33) the factor is r⁻¹, as in [Hin26, Proposition 5.25 and
Section 5.7.1].)

(2) The structure (27.16) holds for every g₀ ∈ 𝒢 (Definition 27.9), and Corollary 27.18 needs only
Ric(g₀) = 0; so Theorem 37.30 holds for P(g₀ + h, g₀) = 0 with g₀ ∈ 𝒢 Ricci flat and g₀ − g_(b₀) small in the
sense of the pointwise bounds of the proof of Lemma 37.1: this is Theorem 37.28 and Theorem 37.27 for such
g₀. In particular it holds for g₀ = φ_S*g_(b₀) where Lemma 27.10 (2) applies; the cut-off region near I₀ is
treated in Section 37.19.

### 37.16 The cut-off gauge

This section is [Hin26, (5.75)–(5.76)] in dimension 4 + 1. Fix χ̌₀ ∈ C_c^∞((−¼, ¼)) equal to 1 on [−⅛, ⅛] ([Hin26]
prints [−⅛, −⅛]), and χ₀ := 1 − χ̌₀(t_IVP/r), extended by 1 where r is small relative to t_IVP. Near I₀ and ℐ⁺,
t_IVP/r is a smooth function on M (τ = t/|x| near the interior of I₀, Lemma 27.2), so χ₀ ∈ C^∞(M). It equals 0
on {|t_IVP| ≤ r/8} ⊃ Ω_(ext,r₀) ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0} and near Σ_IVP, and 1 on {t_IVP ≥ r/4}, a neighbourhood of
ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω_(ext,r₀) (there t_IVP/r → 1). Let

    Υ^(χ₀E_Υ)(g, g₀) := Υ⁰(g, g₀) − χ₀E^Υ_(g₀)G_(g₀)(g − g₀),
    P^(χ₀)(g, g₀) := Ric(g) − δ*_(g₀,E_C)Υ^(χ₀E_Υ)(g, g₀),    (37.36)

and L^(χ₀)_(g,g₀) the linearisation of P^(χ₀) in g. Υ⁰ is natural: for a diffeomorphism φ,

    φ*Υ⁰(g, g₀) = Υ⁰(φ*g, φ*g₀),    (37.37)

[Hin26, (5.75)], in any dimension, since ∇^(φ*g) = φ*∇^g and the trace is natural. The term E^Υ_(g₀)G_(g₀)(g − g₀)
is not natural in this sense when E^Υ is stationary relative to g_(b₀); this is why the cut-off is introduced.

**Lemma 37.34** (The structure in the cut-off gauge.) For g₀ ∈ 𝒢, Proposition 27.14, Proposition 27.17
and Corollary 27.18 hold for L^(χ₀) and P^(χ₀) in place of L and P.

*Proof.* L^(χ₀)_(g,g₀) − L_(g,g₀) = −δ*_(g₀,E_C)((1 − χ₀)E^Υ_(g₀)G_(g₀)(·)), as E^Υ_(g₀)G_(g₀)(g − g₀) is linear in
g − g₀. Its coefficients are those of the E^Υ-term of (27.12), which lie in ρ₀²C^∞Diff¹_b near I₀
(Definition 21.28: E^Υ_(g₀) is homogeneous of degree −1, and δ* is of degree −1 in |x|), times 1 − χ₀, which is
supported in {|t_IVP| < r/4}, a set on which ρ_I is bounded below. So the difference lies in
ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff¹_b, the error class of (27.16), and the leading part at ℐ⁺ is unchanged (χ₀ = 1 there). The
proofs of Proposition 27.17 and Corollary 27.18 use only (27.16) and P^(χ₀)(g₀, g₀) = 0, which holds as
Ric(g₀) = 0 and G_(g₀)(g₀ − g₀) = 0. ∎

### 37.17 The exterior estimates in the cut-off gauge

**Corollary 37.35** (The cut-off gauge.) Theorem 37.27, Theorem 37.28, Lemma 37.24 and
Lemma 37.25 hold with L^(χ₀)_(g,g₀) and P^(χ₀) of (37.36) in place of L^(g,g₀) and P, for every g₀ of
Section 37.11.

*Proof.* χ₀ = 1 − χ̌₀(t_IVP/r) equals 1 on {t_IVP ≥ r/4} (Section 37.16). On Ω_c, ρ_I < c ≤ ½ gives
t > (1 − c)|x| + 2, so t_IVP ≥ ¼|x| for |x| ≥ r₀ large, which suffices; so L^(χ₀) = L on Ω_c, and the edge-b
structure (Proposition 37.13), Proposition 37.16 and the integration of Section 37.13, which are used only on Ω_c, are
unchanged. Elsewhere only the b-structure enters (Proposition 37.10 in Lemma 37.24 and Lemma 37.25), and
L^(χ₀) − L ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff¹_b (the proof of Lemma 37.34), a first-order term of the class those proofs absorb.
In Theorem 37.28, Proposition 27.17 and Corollary 27.18 hold for L^(χ₀), P^(χ₀) by Lemma 37.34, and
P^(χ₀)(g₀, g₀) = 0 there. For g₀ ≠ g_(b₀): Section 37.8 is stated for g₁, g₀ ∈ 𝒢; the hypersurfaces Σ_(IVP,r₀),
Σ_(fut,r₀), Σ_(past,r₀) are spacelike for g₀ + h when g₀ − g_(b₀) is small as in Lemma 37.1 (its proof uses
only the size of g₀ + h − η in the frame); and Lemma 37.20 (a) persists likewise. ∎

So the change of gauge lies where only robust estimates are used, and the structure at ℐ⁺ is that of the original
gauge; this is the content of [Hin26]'s remark that the stationarity of E^Υ and the choice of c_Υ away from ℐ⁺ play
no role in its Theorems 5.17 and 5.21.

### 37.18 Partial polyhomogeneity

This section is [Hin26, Theorem 5.21 and Remark 5.22] (pp. 102–108) in dimension 4 + 1.

**Theorem 37.36** ([Hin26, Theorem 5.21] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ℰ₀ be an index set with
min Re ℰ₀ > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ and jℰ₀ ⊂ ℰ₀ for j ∈ ℕ. Let ℓ₀, ℓ_I > 3/2 with ℓ₀ ∉ Re π₁ℰ₀, ℓ_I < ℓ₀,
ℓ_I < 3/2 + (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C and ℓ_I ∉ 3/2 + σ_Υ. Let ℓ^♭₀ := 3/2 + ½(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ and
ℓ^♭_I := 3/2 + ¼(1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, which satisfy (37.1). There is an index set ℰ_I^C satisfying
Definition 27.6, with ℰ₀ ⊂ ℰ_I^C, such that: if h₀, h₁ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀); S²T*) satisfy the smallness of
Theorem 37.30, the solution h of (37.33) satisfies

    h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_(ext,r₀)),    (37.38)

and for every k and ε > 0 there are k₀ and ε₀ with

    ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₀,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b) < ε₀ (j = 0, 1)   ⟹   ‖h‖_(H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b) < ε.    (37.39)

As in [Hin26, Remark 5.22], smallness of ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₀,ℓ^♭₀)_b) does not make the coefficients of the expansions small,
which is why (37.39) is stated separately.

*Proof.* *Step 1 (the expansion at I₀).* Suppose h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,α₀),(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b for some α₀ ∈ [ℓ^♭₀, ℓ₀); for
α₀ = ℓ^♭₀ this is Theorem 37.30 (ℓ^♭₀ < min Re ℰ₀). As P(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0 and P(g_(b₀), g_(b₀)) = 0,

    L_(g_(b₀))h = −∫₀¹ (L_(g_(b₀)+sh,g_(b₀)) − L_(g_(b₀),g_(b₀)))h ds.    (37.40)

By Proposition 27.14, applied with g₁ = g₀ = g_(b₀) to h and to 0, the two operators have the same leading part and
the same C^∞ error (the part *The perturbation* of its proof), and their difference lies in
H^(∞,(ℰ₀+2,α₀+2),(ℰ_I^tot,ℓ^♭_I))_b Diff²_b on U (the perturbation part of (27.16), whose coefficients are
polynomial in sh and its first two derivatives, each term with a factor of h; Lemma 27.13), uniformly in s.
Acting on h, whose slots lie in H^(∞,(ℰ₀,α₀),(ℰ_I^tot,ℓ^♭_I))_b, it gives by Lemma 27.5 an element of
H^(∞,(ℰ₀+2,α₀+3),(2ℰ_I^tot,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b: at I₀ the index set is 2ℰ₀ + 2 ⊂ ℰ₀ + 2 and the weight
α₀ + 2 + min Re ℰ₀ > α₀ + 3 (as min Re ℰ₀ > 1); at ℐ⁺, 2ℰ_I^tot ⊂ ℰ_I^C + 1 (Lemma 27.7 (b)), at the weight
ℓ^♭_I + 3/2 > ℓ^♭_I + 1. Away from U the spaces impose only regularity. So h solves

    L_(g_(b₀))h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀+2,α₀+3),(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b,
    h|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = h₀,     rℒ_(∂_t)h|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = h₁ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b.    (37.41)

This is one order better at I₀ than Proposition 27.17 alone gives. ([Hin26] writes ℰ₀ + 3; the index set is ℰ₀ + 2,
the gain being in the weight, which is what the argument uses.) Lower α₀ slightly if needed so that
α₁ := min(α₀ + 1, ℓ₀) ∉ Re π₁ℰ₀. Let ℰ_(0,≤) := {(z, k) ∈ ℰ₀ : Re z ≤ α₁}, a finite set, p := |ℰ_(0,≤)|, and
R := Π_((z,k)∈ℰ_(0,≤))(X₀ − z) ∈ Diff^p_b. Then Rh ∈ H^(∞,α₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b (the converse part of Lemma 21.34),
and

    L_(g_(b₀))(Rh) = ρ₀²R(ρ₀⁻²L_(g_(b₀))h) + ρ₀²[ρ₀⁻²L_(g_(b₀)), R]h.

Index sets are closed under + ℕ₀, so ℰ₀ + j ⊂ ℰ₀. The first term: ρ₀⁻²L_(g_(b₀))h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,α₀+1),(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b by
(37.41), and R removes its expansion at I₀ up to α₁ ≤ α₀ + 1 (the converse part of Lemma 21.34), so the
first term lies in H^(∞,α₁+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b. For the second, by Lemma 27.11 and (37.42) below, A :=
ρ₀⁻²L_(g_(b₀)) = −ρ_I(X_I − 3/2 − Ā)(X₀ − X_I) + ρ₀⁻²R̃_b with ρ₀⁻²R̃_b ∈ ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_b, the leading part having
coefficients independent of ρ₀. X₀ commutes with X₀, X_I, ∂_ω, ρ_I and the constant Ā, and maps a ∈ C^∞ to X₀a ∈ ρ₀C^∞;
so R commutes with the leading part, and [A, R] = [ρ₀⁻²R̃_b, R] ∈ ρ₀ρ_I²Diff^(p+1)_b. (The cruder [A, R] ∈
ρ₀ρ_IDiff^(p+1)_b would not do: on the radiation field ρ_I^(3/2) of slot 6 it gives ρ_I^(5/2), below the weight ℓ^♭_I + 1
∈ (5/2, 3) of the target.) Split h = h_e + h_r, with h_e the terms of its expansion at I₀ with real part at most α₀
(those known) and h_r ∈ H^(∞,α₀) at I₀. Then Rh_e = 0, so [A, R]h_e = −RAh_e. At I₀, Ah_e has its expansion in ℰ₀ (smooth
coefficients only add ℕ₀), and R removes its terms up to α₁, leaving order > α₁. At ℐ⁺, Ah_e lies in (−′, ℓ^♭_I + 1): the
leading part sends the slots other than 6 from the weight ℓ^♭_I to ℓ^♭_I + 1 and annihilates the radiation field
ρ_I^(3/2)a of slot 6 (column 6 of Ā vanishes: Ā_(j6) = 0 for j < 6, Ā being lower triangular, and Ā₆₆ = Ā₇₆ = 0; so on it
X_I − 3/2 − Ā acts as X_I − 3/2, which commutes past X₀ − X_I), and ρ₀⁻²R̃_b gains ρ_I². And [A, R]h_r ∈ H^(∞,α₀+1) at
I₀, with α₀ + 1 ≥ α₁, and it has the weight at least 3/2 + 2 > ℓ^♭_I + 1 at ℐ⁺. So ρ₀²[A, R]h ∈
H^(∞,α₁+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b. The data of Rh lie in H^(∞,α₁)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₀)). Near I₀, X₀ = ρ∂_ρ + 2ρ∂_τ in the coordinates
(τ, ρ), so X₀τ′ = (2 − C″)ρ for τ′ = τ − C″ρ: X₀ is tangent to Σ_IVP = {τ′ = 0} only when C″ = 2, and in general these
data involve the normal derivatives ∂^j_(τ′)h on Σ_IVP. These are determined by h₀, h₁ and the equation, which is
non-characteristic on Σ_IVP, with coefficients in C^∞ + H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b (jℰ₀ ⊂ ℰ₀ for the nonlinear terms); so the jet of
h on Σ_IVP has its expansion at ∂Σ_IVP in ℰ₀ up to ℓ₀ ≥ α₁, and R removes its terms with real part at most α₁ (the
converse part of Lemma 21.34). (37.34) with h = 0 and α₀ replaced by α₁ > ℓ^♭_I gives Rh ∈
H^(∞,α₁,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b, and Lemma 21.34 gives h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,α₁),(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b. After finitely many steps, h ∈
H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b.

*Step 2 (the expansion at ℐ⁺).* Suppose h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,α_I)_b for some α_I ∈ [ℓ^♭_I, ℓ_I) and some ℰ_I^C of
Definition 27.6 with ℰ₀ ⊂ ℰ_I^C; Step 1 gives this for α_I = ℓ^♭_I, with any such ℰ_I^C (one exists:
Lemma 27.7 (e) applied to ℰ₀). By (37.40) and Proposition 27.14 on U,

    (X_I − 3/2 − Ā)(X₀ − X_I)h = f̃
        := ρ₀⁻²ρ_I⁻¹(R̃_bh + ∫₀¹ (L_(g_(b₀)+sh,g_(b₀)) − L_(g_(b₀)))h ds),    (37.42)

with R̃_b ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞Diff²_b ((27.16) at h = 0). The first term maps the slots of h, in (ℰ_I^tot, α_I) at ℐ⁺,
to (ℰ_I^tot + 1, α_I + 1) ⊂ (ℰ_I^C, α_I + 1) (Lemma 27.7 (a)). The second is ρ_I⁻¹ times a Diff²_b-operator
with coefficients in H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_I^tot,α_I))_b acting on h; by Lemma 27.5 it lies in
(ℰ_I^tot + ℰ_I^tot − 1, α_I + ν) ⊂ (ℰ_I^C, α_I + ν) for every ν < ½ (Definition 27.6 (3); the weight is
α_I + 3/2 − 1, with the strict inequality of Lemma 27.5). At I₀ both lie in (ℰ₀, ℓ₀). Fix ν ∈ (¼, ½) and put
α′ := min(α_I + ν, ℓ_I), as in [Hin26, Theorem 5.21, Step 2.6]; lower ν slightly if needed so that
α′ ∉ 3/2 + σ_Υ and α′ ∉ Re π₁ℰ₀ (which is not needed if α′ = ℓ_I, by the hypotheses). So

    f̃ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_I^C,α′))_b(U).    (37.43)

Write w := (X₀ − X_I)h; its slots have the index sets of those of h ((F1) of Section 21.9). By Lemma 27.12, Ā
is lower triangular with the diagonal (27.14), off-diagonal entries at (3, 1), (4, 1), (4, 3), (5, 2),
(7, 3), (7, 4), and Ā₇₆ = 0. We integrate slot by slot, in the order 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, putting the off-diagonal
terms on the right.

(i) *Slots 1–3 (π_Ch).* (X_I − 3/2 − Ā_(jj))w_j = f̃_j + Σ_(i<j) Ā_(ji)w_i, with
3/2 + Ā_(jj) ≥ 3/2 + (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C > ℓ_I ≥ α′ (1 − e_C < 1). By induction the right side lies in (ℰ_I^C, α′)
at ℐ⁺, and Lemma 21.33 (with α′ ≠ 3/2 + Ā_(jj); the new exponent 3/2 + Ā_(jj) lies above α′, so only the
conormal statement is affected) gives w_j ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ_I^C,α′))_b. Then (X₀ − X_I)h_j = w_j, and
Lemma 21.42 with z = 0 (ℓ₀ > α′, α′ ∉ Re π₁ℰ₀; away from ℐ⁺ there is nothing to show) gives
h_j ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),(ℰ₀∪̄ℰ_I^C,α′))_b.

(ii) *Slots 4–5 (π₀₁h, π_(1/)h).* The couplings (4, 1), (4, 3), (5, 2) bring w₁, w₂, w₃ ∈ (ℰ_I^C, α′).
Lemma 21.33 with z = 3/2 + Ā_(jj), Ā₄₄ = (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, Ā₅₅ = γ_Υ, gives w_j the index set
ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + Ā_(jj), 0), which is ℰ_(I,01), resp. ℰ_(I,1/) ((27.9)), at the weight α′; Lemma 21.42
then gives h_j the extended union with ℰ₀.

(iii) *Slot 6 (π̸₀h).* There is no coupling (Ā_(6i) = 0 for i < 6). Lemma 21.33 with z = 3/2 gives
ℰ̸_(I,0) = ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2, 0): the radiation field.

(iv) *Slot 7 (π₁₁h).* The couplings (7, 3) (from ℰ_I^C) and (7, 4) (from ℰ_(I,01)), and no (7, 6); Lemma 21.33
with z = 3/2 + 2γ_Υ gives ℰ_I^C ∪ (3/2 + (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, 0) ∪ (3/2 + 2γ_Υ, 0) = ℰ_(I,11). (If Ā₇₇ = 2γ_Υ equalled Ā₄₄,
the two exponents would coincide and Lemma 21.33 would give a logarithm, so that (27.9) would need
(3/2 + 2γ_Υ, 1); this happens only for e_Υ = −1, which 0 < e_Υ < 1 excludes.) No radiation field of π̸₀h reaches slot
7 (Remark 27.19).

Lemma 21.42 gives the extended union ℰ₀ ∪̄ (·) at ℐ⁺: where an exponent of the expansion at I₀ meets one at ℐ⁺,
the corner produces a logarithm. So, with ℰ′ the smallest index set containing ℰ₀ ∪̄ ℰ_I^C and satisfying
Definition 27.6 (it exists by Lemma 27.7 (e), as min Re(ℰ₀ ∪̄ ℰ_I^C) > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ; it contains ℰ₀), the slots
of h lie in the classes of (27.10) for ℰ′, at the weight α′ (for the slots 4, 5 and 7,
ℰ₀ ∪̄ ℰ_(I,j) ⊂ ℰ′_(I,j) by Lemma 27.7 (d), as min Re ℰ₀ > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ): h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ′⟩,α′)_b on U, and
off U trivially. This is [Hin26, Theorem 5.21, Step 2.6], with its ℰ_I^(C,new). Repeating with (α_I, ℰ_I^C) replaced
by (α′, ℰ′), ν > ¼, reaches ℓ_I after J ≤ 4(ℓ_I − ℓ^♭_I) + 1 repetitions, with index sets
ℰ^((0)) ⊂ ℰ^((1)) ⊂ ⋯ ⊂ ℰ^((J)); take ℰ_I^C := ℰ^((J)), with ℰ^((0)) the smallest index set of Definition 27.6
containing ℰ₀. As the number of repetitions and every step depend only on ℰ₀, ℓ₀, ℓ_I and the parameters, so does
ℰ_I^C. This is (37.38).

*Smallness, (37.39).* Each step is linear in the data of the previous one: the coefficients of the expansion
at I₀ are obtained from Rh, which (37.34) bounds by the data and the right side of (37.41); that
right side is quadratic in h, bounded in H^(k,α₀+3) by the norms of the previous step times the small
‖h‖_(H^(k+2,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))); and Lemma 21.33, Lemma 21.34 and Lemma 21.42 are bounded at every order.
At ℐ⁺ the coefficients are obtained by the integrations (i)–(iv), bounded likewise. Finitely many steps compose to
(37.39), with k₀ the sum of the losses plus that of Theorem 37.30. ∎

**Remark 37.37** (No subtraction of radiation fields.) In dimension 3 + 1 the entries A^h − A₀ and B^h of
[Hin26, (5.28)] are of the order of A₀ at ℐ⁺, so the radiation fields of π₁₁h and π̸₀h enter the leading part of the
operator; [Hin26, Theorem 5.21, Step 2] removes them by measuring h from g₀ = g_(b₀) + h₀, at the cost of the forcing
term P(g₀, g_(b₀)) ([Hin26, (5.64)], with the class ⟨(2, 0)⟩₀). In dimension 4 + 1 they are half an order lower
(Remark 27.1 (c)) and sit in the error of (37.42), whose index set ℰ_I^tot + ℰ_I^tot − 1 lies in
ℰ_I^C by Definition 27.6 (3). So the subtraction is not needed, and no class with (3/2, 0) in slot 6 is used as a
background.

### 37.19 The boosted background

Section 37.19–Section 37.21 are [Hin26, Sections 5.6–5.7] (Theorem 5.23 with the cut-off gauge (5.76), Remark
5.24, Proposition 5.25, Section 5.7.1, Remark 5.26 and Example 5.27; pp. 108–113) in dimension 4 + 1. The cut-off
boosts φ_S, S = S_w ∈ 𝒮₁, and the cut-offs χ_IVP, χ_K are those of Section 21.7, and |S| := |w|. The gauge 1-form
Υ⁰(g, g₀) and E^Υ_(g₀) are those of Section 21.8 ((21.41), (21.43)).

**Lemma 37.38** (The boosted Tangherlini metric on the exterior domain; [Hin26, Section 5.6, first
paragraph] in dimension 4 + 1.) There is ε_φ > 0 such that for S ∈ 𝒮₁ with |S| < ε_φ and r₁ ≥ R₀ + 1: φ_S*g_(b₀)
agrees on Ω_(ext,r₁) with an element of 𝒢 (Definition 27.9), it is Ricci flat, and φ_S*g_(b₀) − g_(b₀) satisfies
the pointwise bounds of the proof of Lemma 37.1. Hence Theorem 37.30 and Theorem 37.36 hold with
g_(b₀) replaced by g₀ = φ_S*g_(b₀) (Remark 37.33 (2); for Theorem 37.36, the same proof, with
Proposition 27.14 applied with g₁ = g₀ ∈ 𝒢).

*Proof.* On Ω_(ext,r₁), t_IVP ≥ −(r − r₁)/12 > −|x|/10, so χ_IVP = 1 there (Section 21.7); and
t_IVP ≤ r + 2r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) there, so t ≤ |x| + C, and χ_K = 0, as supp χ_K ⊂ {|x| < t/2} (χ^♯_K = 1 near supp χ_K). So
Ω_(ext,r₁) ⊂ {χ_IVP(1 − χ_K) = 1}, and Lemma 27.10 (2) with (21.40) gives
φ_S*g_(b₀) − g_(b₀) = |x|⁻²h_S(ω)(dx¹)² + ρ₀²ρ_I³C^∞ there for |S| small, with h_S smooth and O(|S|)
((21.39)). The first term has only the slot π₁₁ and lies in ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞, and g_(b₀) ∈ 𝒢 (Lemma 27.10
(1)); so φ_S*g_(b₀) satisfies (27.11) on Ω_(ext,r₁). Ric(φ_S*g_(b₀)) = φ_S*Ric(g_(b₀)) = 0. And
δ := φ_S*g_(b₀) + h − η obeys the pointwise bounds of the proof of Lemma 37.1 (the slots of φ_S*g_(b₀) − η are
those of g_(b₀) − η plus the term above in the slot π₁₁, Definition 27.9), so the hypersurfaces of Ω_(ext,r₁) stay
spacelike for |S| small. ∎

So the boost need only be genuine where the exterior problem is posed, and the slope 1/12 of Lemma 37.1
arranges it. The region where χ_IVP < 1 lies below Σ_(past,r₁) and plays no part.

### 37.20 Stability with boosted background and data

For h on Ω_(ext,r₀) and r₁ := 2r₀, put

    h_(S,0) := (φ_S*h)|_(Σ_(IVP,r₁)),     h_(S,1) := rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))(φ_S*h)|_(Σ_(IVP,r₁)),    (37.44)

defined for |S| < ε′_φ, with ε′_φ independent of r₀, as φ_S maps a neighbourhood of Σ_(IVP,r₁) into
{|t_IVP| < r/8} ∩ Ω_(ext,r₀): φ_S is the time-1 flow of a b-vector field, and near |x| = r it moves t_IVP by at most
C|S|r (Lemma 21.26, Lemma 21.27), while for r ≥ r₁ = 2r₀ the past slab of Ω_(ext,r₀) reaches down to
−(r − r₀)/12 ≤ −r/24; so C|S| < 1/24 suffices, for every r₀. ([Hin26] takes r₁ = r₀ + 1; then the slab reaches only to
−1/12 near |x| = r₁, while a boost moves t_IVP by about |S|r₁, so |S| would have to be below about 1/(12Cr₁), against
the bound depending only on b₀ and ℓ^♭ that [Hin26, Theorem 5.23] states.)

**Theorem 37.39** ([Hin26, Theorem 5.23] in dimension 4 + 1.) There are k₂ ∈ ℕ and ε₂ > 0 such that the
following holds. Let h₀, h₁ be data as in Theorem 37.36 with ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₂,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₂ (j = 0, 1), and let h be
the solution of

    P^(χ₀)(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0,     h|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = h₀,     rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h|_(Σ_(IVP,r₀)) = h₁    (37.45)

that Theorem 37.30 gives in the cut-off gauge (Corollary 37.35), which by its proof is small in H^(3d) of its
class for the d = 7 of Theorem 37.28. It lies in H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_(ext,r₀)) by Theorem 37.36, whose
proof holds for L^(χ₀) by Lemma 37.34, which leaves the leading part at ℐ⁺ unchanged and adds to the error of
(27.16) a term of that class. For S ∈ 𝒮₁ small, depending only on b₀, ℓ^♭₀ and ℓ^♭_I, the problem

    P^(χ₀)(φ_S*g_(b₀) + h_S, φ_S*g_(b₀)) = 0 in Ω_(ext,r₁),     h_S = h_(S,0),  rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h_S = h_(S,1) on Σ_(IVP,r₁)
    (37.46)

(Lemma 37.38) has a solution h_S ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_(ext,r₁)), unique among the solutions in
H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₁)) that are small in H^(8,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b. By the proof, k₂ = 2N_NM + 2 = 308, with
N_NM = 153 the order of Theorem 37.28. Then:

(1) h_S at S = 0 is h on Ω_(ext,r₁); and under the hypotheses of (3), h_S = φ_S*h on a neighbourhood in Ω_(ext,r₁) of
Σ°_(IVP,r₁) := Σ_(IVP,r₁) ∩ {|x| > r₁};

(2) h_S depends smoothly on S, in the sense of [Hin26, footnote 59]: it is C^l in S with values in
H^(k,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b for data of regularity depending on k and l;

(3) if h₀, h₁ induce data satisfying the vacuum constraint equations and Υ⁰(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0 at
Σ_(IVP,r₀), then Ric(φ_S*g_(b₀) + h_S) = 0 and Υ^(χ₀E_Υ)(φ_S*g_(b₀) + h_S, φ_S*g_(b₀)) = 0.

*Proof.* *The solution h_S.* For |S| < ε_φ, Lemma 37.38, Remark 37.33 (2) and Corollary 37.35 give
Theorem 37.30 on Ω_(ext,r₁) in the cut-off gauge with φ_S*g_(b₀) in place of g_(b₀). Its threshold ε₀ can be taken
equal to one ε_* > 0 for all |S| ≤ ½ε_φ. Indeed, the constants of Theorem 37.27 and Theorem 37.28 depend on the
background g₀ only through the pointwise bounds of the proof of Lemma 37.1 and through finitely many of the
seminorms that define 𝒢 (Definition 27.9), the C^∞-seminorms on Ω_(ext,r₁) of ρ₀⁻²ρ_I⁻²(g₀ − η) and of
ρ₀⁻²ρ_I⁻³π(g₀ − η): the coefficients of P^(χ₀) and of L^(χ₀) are smooth functions of g₀ and of its b-derivatives of
order at most two, and the leading part at ℐ⁺ does not depend on g₀ (Remark 37.33 (2)). For g₀ = φ_S*g_(b₀) these
seminorms depend continuously on S (the expansion of the proof of Lemma 37.38 is smooth in S, as used in the
proof of (2) below), so they are bounded for |S| ≤ ½ε_φ, and so are the constants C_k, C_(s,t) and δ of
Theorem 20.1 that fix ε₀.

Let |S| < ε′_φ, and let 𝒰 be a neighbourhood of Σ_(IVP,r₁) that φ_S maps into {|t_IVP| < r/8} ∩ Ω_(ext,r₀) (after
(37.44)). There ρ_I is bounded below, so the class of h there is H^(∞,ℓ^♭₀)_b. Pullback by φ_S is bounded from
H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b(φ_S(𝒰)) to H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b(𝒰), uniformly in S: φ_S is the time-1 flow of a b-vector field linear in S and
tangent to every boundary hypersurface (Lemma 21.26), so the b-derivatives of φ_S and of its inverse are bounded
uniformly, and ρ ∘ φ_S/ρ is bounded above and below. Near I₀, r∂_(t_IVP) = ∂_τ is a b-vector field, and the frame of
(27.6) does not depend on t; so rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP)) is a first-order b-differential operator near Σ_(IVP,r₁). The
restriction to Σ_(IVP,r₁) is bounded from H^(k+1,ℓ^♭₀)_b to H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₁)), as in the proof of Theorem 37.28
(ii). Hence, with C_* independent of S,

    ‖h_(S,j)‖_(H^(N_NM,ℓ^♭₀)_b(Σ_(IVP,r₁))) ≤ C_*‖h‖_(H^(N_NM+2,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r₀))),     j = 0, 1.

Let k₂ and ε₂ be the k₁ and ε₁ that the clause of Theorem 37.30 on higher norms, in the cut-off gauge, gives for
k := N_NM + 2 and ε := ε_*/C_*; by its proof, k₂ = N_NM + k = 2N_NM + 2. As k₂ is at least, and ε₂ at most, the k₀ and
ε₀ of Theorem 37.30 for g_(b₀) on Ω_(ext,r₀), data with ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₂,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₂ have the smallness that theorem
asks, so h exists, and the clause on higher norms applies to it. If ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₂,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₂, then
‖h‖_(H^(N_NM+2,ℓ^♭₀,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) < ε_*/C_*, so the data (37.44) have H^(N_NM,ℓ^♭₀)_b-norm below ε_*, and
Theorem 37.30 for the background φ_S*g_(b₀) gives h_S and its uniqueness, for |S| < min(½ε_φ, ε′_φ), a bound
depending only on b₀, ℓ^♭₀ and ℓ^♭_I. The data (37.44) lie in H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b(Σ_(IVP,r₁)): h is of that class
near Σ_(IVP,r₁) away from ℐ⁺, and pullback by φ_S preserves weighted, partially polyhomogeneous b-Sobolev spaces near
compact subsets of the interior of I₀ (φ_S is the flow of a b-vector field; [Hin26, after (5.77b)]). So
Theorem 37.36 for this background (Lemma 37.38) places h_S in H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀),⟨ℰ_I^C⟩,ℓ_I)_b(Ω_(ext,r₁)).

(1) For S = 0, φ_0 = id and (37.46) is (37.45) on Ω_(ext,r₁) ⊂ Ω_(ext,r₀). The restriction of h to
Ω_(ext,r₁) solves it and, like h_0, is small in H^(3d) of its class for the d = 7 of Theorem 37.28, hence in H⁸; so
h_0 = h there by the uniqueness. Now assume the hypotheses of (3), and let 𝒰 be as above, so that φ_S maps 𝒰 into
{|t_IVP| < r/8} ∩ Ω_(ext,r₀), where χ₀ = 0. Remark 37.33 (1) applies to h in the cut-off gauge (Proposition 37.32
with Υ = Υ^(χ₀E_Υ), whatever the term of order zero in the gauge; and Υ^(χ₀E_Υ) = Υ⁰ near Σ_(IVP,r₀), where χ₀ = 0):
Ric(g_(b₀) + h) = 0 and Υ^(χ₀E_Υ)(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0 on Ω_(ext,r₀), and on φ_S(𝒰), where χ₀ = 0,
Υ⁰(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0. Pulling back by φ_S, Ric(φ_S*g_(b₀) + φ_S*h) = φ_S*Ric(g_(b₀) + h) = 0 and, by
(37.37), Υ⁰(φ_S*g_(b₀) + φ_S*h, φ_S*g_(b₀)) = 0 on 𝒰, where χ₀ = 0 as well; so both terms of
P^(χ₀)(φ_S*g_(b₀) + φ_S*h, φ_S*g_(b₀)) vanish on 𝒰, and φ_S*h solves (37.46) there with the data
(37.44). The whole operator is not pulled back: δ*_(g₀,E_C) is not natural, E_C being built from the fixed
stationary 1-form c_C of Definition 21.28, which a boost does not preserve (φ_S*c_C ≠ c_C); so φ_S*h solves the
equation with φ_S*c_C, while (37.46) has c_C, and the two agree where Υ⁰ vanishes. Without the constraints
statement (1) is not proved here; [Hin26, Theorem 5.23 (1)] states it without them, but its proof pulls back the whole
operator. So v := h_S − φ_S*h satisfies L̄v = 0 on 𝒰 ∩ Ω_(ext,r₁) with vanishing Cauchy data on Σ_(IVP,r₁), where, with
g₀ := φ_S*g_(b₀) and g_s := g₀ + φ_S*h + sv, L̄ := ∫₀¹ L^(χ₀)_(g_s,g₀) ds. Each g_s is a convex combination of
φ_S*(g_(b₀) + h) and φ_S*g_(b₀) + h_S, so it is close to g_(b₀) in the frame of (27.6) for |S| and the data
small (Lemma 37.38); hence 2L̄ has principal symbol ḡ⁻¹(ζ, ζ)Id with ḡ⁻¹ := ∫₀¹ g_s⁻¹ ds, the inverse of a
Lorentzian metric ḡ for which dt_IVP is timelike. Let M := 𝒰 ∩ Ω°_(ext,r₁), the interior, time-oriented by ∂_t.
