t_IVP increases along future ḡ-causal curves in M, so Σ°_(IVP,r₁) ⊂ M is acausal, and its Cauchy development D in M
is open, globally hyperbolic and has Σ°_(IVP,r₁) as a Cauchy hypersurface (Theorem A.2). On D the
coefficients of L̄ are smooth and v and its first derivatives vanish on Σ°_(IVP,r₁), so Lemma 37.31 with
P = 2L̄ gives v = 0 on D, a neighbourhood of Σ°_(IVP,r₁) in Ω_(ext,r₁).

(2) The data (37.44) depend smoothly on S (differentiate (37.44)). Formally
ḣ := (d/ds)h_(S(s))|_(s=0), with S(0) = S₀ and Ṡ = S′(0), solves

    L^(χ₀)_(φ_(S₀)*g_(b₀)+h_(S₀), φ_(S₀)*g_(b₀))ḣ = −(d/ds)P^(χ₀)(φ_(S(s))*g_(b₀) + h_(S₀), φ_(S(s))*g_(b₀))|_(s=0),

with the differentiated data. Let D₁, D₂ denote the derivatives in the first and the second argument. As
P^(χ₀)(g₀, g₀) = 0 for every Ricci-flat g₀ (the proof of Lemma 37.34), in particular along φ_(S(s))*g_(b₀)
(Lemma 37.38), with g₀ := φ_(S₀)*g_(b₀) and ġ₀ := (d/ds)φ_(S(s))*g_(b₀)|_(s=0) the right side is

    −[(D₁ + D₂)P^(χ₀)(g₀ + h_(S₀), g₀) − (D₁ + D₂)P^(χ₀)(g₀, g₀)]ġ₀,

which carries a factor of h_(S₀) (Lemma 27.13); without this cancellation the index set at I₀ would be (4, 0),
which need not lie in ℰ₀ + 2 (for instance ℰ₀ = ∅, Remark 37.43). So it is a linear differential expression in
ġ₀, which lies in ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ with the slots of (27.11) on Ω_(ext,r₁) (differentiate the expansion of the proof
of Lemma 37.38 in S), applied with coefficients in the classes of Proposition 27.14; so it lies in the target
space of (27.18). The linear estimate (37.34), which holds for L^(χ₀) by Lemma 37.34 and
Corollary 37.35, and the proof of Theorem 37.36 give ḣ in the class of h_S; difference quotients converge to ḣ by
the same estimate applied to their difference with ḣ, and higher derivatives follow likewise, with the losses of
[Hin26, footnote 59].

(3) The metrics φ_S*g_(b₀) + h_S and φ_S*(g_(b₀) + h) have the same Cauchy data on Σ_(IVP,r₁) ((37.44),
(37.46)), hence the same first and second fundamental forms and the same Υ⁰ there, Υ⁰ involving the metric
and its first derivatives only; so (3) does not depend on (1). By the proof of (1), the Ricci tensor and Υ⁰ of
φ_S*(g_(b₀) + h) vanish on 𝒰 ⊃ Σ_(IVP,r₁). So the data of φ_S*g_(b₀) + h_S at Σ_(IVP,r₁) satisfy the constraints,
and Υ^(χ₀E_Υ) = Υ⁰ = 0 there (χ₀ = 0 near Σ_(IVP,r₁)). Remark 37.33 (1), with Remark 37.33 (2) for the
background φ_S*g_(b₀) and with Proposition 37.32 for the cut-off gauge, applied to (37.46), gives the
conclusions on Ω_(ext,r₁). ∎

**Remark 37.40** ([Hin26, Remark 5.24] in dimension 4 + 1.) If h₀ = h₁ = 0, then h_S = 0 by uniqueness,
and the metric is φ_S*g_(b₀). On all of Σ_IVP such data are compactly supported perturbations of the Myers–Perry data,
as gluing produces them ([CD03]; Chapter 39).

### 37.21 Gauged Cauchy data

**Proposition 37.41** ([Hin26, Proposition 5.25] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let ℰ₀ be an index set with
min Re ℰ₀ > 0 and jℰ₀ ⊂ ℰ₀ for j ∈ ℕ, and ℓ₀ > 0. The second fundamental form of Σ_IVP for a metric g is taken as in
Lemma 21.24: k(X, Y) := g(∇^g_Xν, Y) for X, Y tangent to Σ_IVP, with ν the future unit normal. Let
γ = γ_(b₀) + γ̃ and k = k_(b₀) + k̃ be symmetric 2-tensors on Σ_IVP, γ_(b₀) and k_(b₀) the first and second fundamental
forms of Σ_IVP for g_(b₀), with γ̃ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b(Σ_IVP; S²T*Σ_IVP), k̃ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀+1,ℓ₀+1))_b(Σ_IVP; S²T*Σ_IVP), and
γ̃ small in H³_b. There are h₀, h₁ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b(Σ_IVP; S²T*), depending continuously on (γ̃, k̃) and 0 at (0, 0),
such that for every spacetime metric g with (g − g_(b₀))|_(Σ_IVP) = h₀ and (rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))(g − g_(b₀)))|_(Σ_IVP) = h₁:
(1) the first and second fundamental forms of Σ_IVP for g are γ and k; (2) Υ⁰(g, g_(b₀)) = 0 at Σ_IVP.

*Proof.* We follow [Hin26], which follows [HV18b, Proposition 3.10] and [HV24, Theorem 4.2]; the dimension enters only
through the size of the frame. Near Σ_IVP write g_(b₀) = a dt_IVP² + 2dt_IVP ⊗_s b + γ_(b₀) and set h₀ := γ̃, extended
to S²T* by h₀(ν_(b₀), ·) := 0, so that g₀ := g_(b₀) + h₀ induces γ. Here ν_(b₀) is the future unit normal of Σ_IVP for
g_(b₀); as g₀(ν_(b₀), Y) = g_(b₀)(ν_(b₀), Y) = 0 for Y tangent to Σ_IVP and g₀(ν_(b₀), ν_(b₀)) = −1, it is also the
future unit normal ν₀ for g₀. We seek h₁ = rh̃₁ such that g := g₀ + t_IVP h̃₁ (still with unit normal ν₀ at Σ_IVP) has
second fundamental form k and Υ⁰(g, g_(b₀)) = 0 there. For X, Y tangent to Σ_IVP, g(ν, Y) = 0 along Σ_IVP, so
X(g(ν, Y)) = 0 gives k_g(X, Y) = −g(ν, ∇^g_XY) for the second fundamental form k_g of g with unit normal ν. As g = g₀
on Σ_IVP, with the same unit normal ν₀, k_g(X, Y) = −g₀(∇^g_XY, ν₀). As h₀(·, ν₀) = 0, g₀(Z, ν₀) = g_(b₀)(Z, ν_(b₀)) for
every vector Z, so

    g₀(∇^(g₀)_XY, ν₀) = −k_(b₀)(X, Y) + g₀((∇^(g₀)_X − ∇^(g_(b₀))_X)Y, ν₀),

as g_(b₀)(∇^(g_(b₀))_XY, ν_(b₀)) = −k_(b₀)(X, Y). Subtracting this from g₀(∇^g_XY, ν₀) = −k_(b₀)(X, Y) − k̃(X, Y),
which is k_g = k, gives the first of the two conditions; the second is Υ⁰(g, g_(b₀)) = 0 at Σ_IVP. They are the
conditions of [Hin26, (5.80) and (5.81)], written in the convention of Lemma 21.24 and with this choice of h₀:

    g₀((∇^g_X − ∇^(g₀)_X)Y, ν₀) = −k̃(X, Y) − g₀((∇^(g₀)_X − ∇^(g_(b₀))_X)Y, ν₀),
    tr_(g₀)(∇^g − ∇^(g₀)) = −tr_(g₀)(∇^(g₀) − ∇^(g_(b₀))).

Each x-derivative of h₀ gains a factor r⁻¹ (b-regularity), the Christoffel symbols of g_(b₀) are O(r⁻³) with all
b-derivatives in dimension 4 + 1 (Proposition 21.21: the mass enters at |x|⁻²), and ℰ₀ is closed under sums; so both
right sides lie in H^(∞,(ℰ₀+1,ℓ₀+1))_b. In a frame e₀ = ν₀, e₁, …, e₄, g₀-orthonormal and tangent to Σ_IVP for
i ≥ 1, at t_IVP = 0,

    2(Γ(g)_(λμν) − Γ(g₀)_(λμν)) = (t_IVP)_(;μ)(h̃₁)_(νλ) + (t_IVP)_(;ν)(h̃₁)_(μλ) − (t_IVP)_(;λ)(h̃₁)_(μν),

with e_it_IVP = 0 (i ≥ 1) and e₀t_IVP = ν_(b₀)t_IVP smooth and bounded away from 0. The first equation at
(e_i, e_j), i, j = 1, …, 4, reads −½(e₀t_IVP)(h̃₁)_(ij) = ⋯ and determines (h̃₁)_(ij); the e^j-component of the second
determines (h̃₁)_(0j); and its e⁰-component, −½(e₀t_IVP)(h̃₁)₀₀ = f₀ + ½(e₀t_IVP)(g₀)^(ij)(h̃₁)_(ij), with f₀ the
e⁰-component of its right side, determines (h̃₁)₀₀; all lie in H^(∞,(ℰ₀+1,ℓ₀+1))_b, linearly and continuously in the
data. So h₁ = rh̃₁ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b. ∎

These data enter Theorem 37.36 when min Re ℰ₀ > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ, ℓ₀ > 3/2 and ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₀,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₀ as in
Theorem 37.30 (k₀ = N_NM = 153), and they enter Theorem 37.39 when moreover ‖h_j‖_(H^(k₂,ℓ^♭₀)_b) < ε₂
(k₂ = 2N_NM + 2 = 308). Both smallness conditions hold for (γ̃, k̃) small in a suitable norm, by the continuity in
Proposition 37.41. If (γ, k) satisfy the constraints, the solutions are vacuum (Remark 37.33 (1),
Theorem 37.39 (3)).

**Proposition 37.42** (Data at Boyer–Lindquist time 0; [Hin26, Section 5.7.1 and Remark 5.26] in
dimension 4 + 1.) Let t_BL be the Boyer–Lindquist time of g_(b₀), Σ^BL := t_BL⁻¹(0) near spatial infinity, and
γ^BL_(b₀), k^BL_(b₀) the first and second fundamental forms of Σ^BL for g_(b₀), k as in Proposition 37.41. Let ℰ₀, ℓ₀
and ℓ^♭₀ be as in Theorem 37.36, δ ∈ (0, ¼] small, and let γ^BL = γ^BL_(b₀) + γ̃^BL and k^BL = k^BL_(b₀) + k̃^BL be
symmetric 2-tensors on Σ^BL ∩ {r > δ⁻¹} satisfying the vacuum constraint equations, with γ̃^BL ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b and
k̃^BL ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀+1,ℓ₀+1))_b. Let h^BL_0, h^BL_1 be the gauged Cauchy data on Σ^BL that the proof of Proposition 37.41
gives with t_BL in place of t_IVP, and assume them small in H^(N_NM,ℓ^♭₀)_b, N_NM = 153 as in
Theorem 37.28 (by the continuity in Proposition 37.41, this holds for (γ̃^BL, k̃^BL) small in a suitable norm).
Then the solution h of the gauge-fixed equation with Υ⁰,
Ric(g_(b₀) + h) − δ*_(g_(b₀),E_C)Υ⁰(g_(b₀) + h, g_(b₀)) = 0, with these data, on the domain of dependence D_δ of
Σ^BL ∩ {r > δ⁻¹} within the conic neighbourhood U_δ := {|t/r| < δ, r > δ⁻¹} of spatial infinity, induces on
Σ_IVP ∩ {r > r₀}, for r₀ large, data (h₀, h₁) in H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b: the index set is unchanged, and no index set
ℰ_log arises.

*Proof.* *The time functions.* On {|x| ≥ R₃}, t_IVP = t − C″ (Lemma 21.22 (b)), with t = t_KS + T_m the time of
(21.27) and T_m = 2m r⁻¹ + O(r⁻³) (Lemma 21.20 (a)). For the Tangherlini metric of mass m,
f = 1 − m r⁻², t_KS − t_BL = ∫ m r⁻²(1 − m r⁻²)⁻¹ dr = −m r⁻¹ − m²/(3r³) − ⋯, an odd series in r⁻¹; so
t − t_BL = m r⁻¹ + O(r⁻³), a smooth function of ρ = r⁻¹ near ρ = 0 (in dimension 3 + 1 the integral is 2m log r). So
τ_IVP := t_IVP/r = τ_BL + ρc(ρ) and τ_BL := t_BL/r = τ − ρc̃(ρ), with c and c̃ smooth.

*The solution.* As dτ_BL = dτ + O(ρ) in the b-sense, G_b(dτ_BL, dτ_BL) = τ² − 1 + O(ρ) < 0 on U_δ, and |τ| < ¼ there,
inside the range of Proposition 37.10. So Lemma 37.24 holds with τ′ replaced by τ_BL and Σ_(IVP,r₀) by
Σ^BL ∩ {r > δ⁻¹}, on D_δ: its proof uses only that the initial surface is a level set of a b-time function and the
b-structure of the operator, and U_δ itself has the timelike side {r = δ⁻¹}, so the problem is posed on D_δ. The
operator with Υ⁰ differs from L by a first-order term of the class absorbed there (the proof of Lemma 37.34 with
χ₀ = 0, ρ_I being bounded below on U_δ). With these estimates for the right inverses, Theorem 20.1 gives h on D_δ as
in the proof of Theorem 37.28 (d = 7, trivial support classes); this is the boost problem of [COM81], as in [Hin26].
Its partial polyhomogeneity h ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ₀,ℓ₀))_b(D_δ) follows as in Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 37.36, with
Lemma 37.24 in place of (37.34). On Σ_IVP, t is bounded, so Σ_IVP ∩ {r > r₀} ⊂ D_δ for r₀ large.

*The data.* Taylor expansion of a(τ_BL)ρ^z(log ρ)^k = a(τ_IVP − ρc(ρ))ρ^z(log ρ)^k in ρ gives the terms
ρ^(z+j)(log ρ)^k, j ∈ ℕ₀: the index set (z, k) + ℕ₀ ⊂ ℰ₀, with no new logarithm. ∎

So [Hin26, Remark 5.26] (logarithms from (2, 0) + ℰ_log) has no counterpart in dimension 4 + 1 from this mechanism;
logarithmic index sets enter the later chapters for other reasons (the analysis at ι⁺ and K⁺).

**Remark 37.43** ([Hin26, Example 5.27] in dimension 4 + 1.) (1) Data equal to the data of g_(b₀) outside a
compact set satisfy Proposition 37.41 with ℰ₀ = ∅ and every ℓ₀; gluing produces data equal outside a compact set to
those of a member of the family ([CD03] in dimension 4 + 1; Chapter 39). (2) The constructions by the conformal
method in [Hin26, Example 5.27 (2)–(3)] are stated in dimension 3 + 1; their counterparts in dimension 4 + 1 are not
used here.


## 38. The nonlinear stability theorem near Tangherlini, the parameters, and the symmetry class

This chapter proves the nonlinear stability of the five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini black hole g_(b₀),
b₀ = (m₀, 0), for initial data on the hypersurface Σ^IVP of Section 21.5.3 that are small in a weighted,
partially polyhomogeneous class (Theorem 38.22). This is [Hin26, Theorem 13.1] in dimension 4 + 1, assembled, as in
[Hin26, Section 13.1, pp. 318–323], from the linear theory of Chapter 21–Chapter 36 and the Nash–Moser theorem
Theorem 20.1. The proof has four steps: the parameters (Section 38.1), the solution up to a fixed level of the
time function, from the initial data (Section 38.2), the Nash–Moser iteration for the map Ψ (Section 38.3,
Section 38.4), and the propagation of the constraints (Section 38.5). Section 38.6 and Section 38.7 list
every condition that the stability theory places on its parameters and show that the conditions can be met together,
in an order with no circular threshold (Theorem 38.24). Section 38.8 and Section 38.9 restrict the theorem to
data invariant under G = O(2) × O(2): the development is then G-invariant and settles to a Tangherlini metric, without
boost or rotation (Proposition 38.27). Corollary 38.28 chooses the constants so that the final parameters lie within a
prescribed distance of b₀, and states the rate of settling on compact sets.

In dimension 4 + 1 the argument of [Hin26] needs four changes. (1) The initial family solves a gauge-fixed equation
whose gauge is cut off near the initial surface (Theorem 37.39), while the map Ψ uses the gauge of the forward
cone; the cut-off of Lemma 38.1 equals 1 on Ω_* and agrees with that of Theorem 37.39 on the exterior
domain. (2) The background of Chapter 32 is translated as well as boosted (Definition 32.3), so the initial family
is posed for a translation composed with a boost (Proposition 38.4). (3) The Nash–Moser theorem with support classes
asks for support conditions on every component of supported character (Section 38.4). (4) The right inverses of
Theorem 34.24 are formed for Ψ, in which the boost and translation directions carry the initial family
(Lemma 38.17). The region near null infinity that the initial family must
reach, a slab bounded in t_*, is solved together with the exterior problem and the compact region above the initial
surface, as one Cauchy problem with data on Σ^IVP alone (Section 38.2.3–Section 38.2.5); the compact region below it is
solved backward (Section 38.2.2); and the compact sets that the uniqueness lemma Lemma 18.4 asks for are
supplied near ℐ⁺ and near spatial infinity by Lemma 38.13 and Lemma 38.14.

*Notation and the inner radius.* The notation is that of Chapter 21–Chapter 36. b₀ = (m₀, 0), R₁ = m₀^(1/2), and the
inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] of Chapter 21 is a parameter: the spacetime M of (21.22) has the inner boundary
{|x| = r_♭}, and the radius r_0 of the artificial boundary of Chapter 14–Chapter 20 is r_♭ (Definition 22.1), as
in Chapter 29. Every result of this chapter holds for each such r_♭, with constants and neighbourhoods of b₀ that may
depend on it. C′ is the constant of (21.30), so that t_* = t − |x| + C′ − 8m₀|x|⁻¹ on {|x| ≥ 3R₁}, and C″ is
the constant value of ψ_IVP on [R₃, ∞) (Lemma 21.22 (b)), so that t_IVP = t − C″ on {|x| ≥ R₃}. The time function
t^♭_* is that of Lemma 15.35 with ℓ = ½, built with the constant C of the gluing in its proof, written C_g here,
taken ≥ max(4(r′_0 + 1), 32, 16R₁), r′_0 the radius of Lemma 15.35. Every condition that proof places on C_g is a
lower bound, so this is allowed; Lemma 17.2 (iv) takes C_g ≥ 4(r′_0 + 1), and Lemma 38.12 uses all three
bounds. The constant C′ of Lemma 15.35 (b) is written C_♭ ∈ (0, 1) here, to distinguish it from the constant of
(21.30). M_(1/2) is the space of Definition 21.12 on which ρ_I^(1/2) is
smooth. For S = S_w ∈ 𝒮_1 we write |S| := |w|. The boosts φ_S, S ∈ 𝒮_1, are those of Section 21.7 and the
translations ψ_(S⁰), S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1, those of Lemma 32.2; for S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1 put

    φ_(S,S⁰) := ψ_(S⁰) ∘ φ_S,     so that φ_(S,0) = φ_S.    (38.1)

Both factors are time-1 flows of b-vector fields, φ_(−S) = φ_S⁻¹ and ψ_(−S⁰) = ψ_(S⁰)⁻¹ (Lemma 21.26,
Lemma 32.2 (a)), so φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹ = φ_(−S) ∘ ψ_(−S⁰).

### 38.1 Setting

*The time functions.* t^♭_* is defined on {t_* ≥ ½} (Lemma 15.35, Lemma 17.2 (iv)), with
C_♭ t_* ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t_* there (Lemma 15.35 (b)); a sublevel set {t^♭_* ≤ c}, c ≥ 1, means the complement of
{t^♭_* > c}, which lies in {t_* > c}. Ω_* := cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1}. Put

    T̂ := 2/C_♭ ≥ 2,     T_ι := (T̂ + 2)/C_♭,     T_K := max(10, T_ι + 2),

so that {t^♭_* ≥ T̂} ⊂ Ω_*. Every level used below, the top of the region 𝒟 of Proposition 38.4 and the levels of the
support classes of Section 38.4, lies at t^♭_* ≥ T̂ ≥ 2. The cut-off χ_−, the region 𝒟 and the support classes are
defined by t^♭_*. Its differential is past timelike for every g_(b₀) + h with h small in 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b), on
{t_* > 1} by Lemma 15.35 (2), and on {t_* > ½}, for h small in that class on {t_* ≥ ½}, by Lemma 38.12; this
margin survives the perturbations used below. The timelike margin of dt_* near ℐ⁺ is only of order m₀r⁻², as
g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = −16m₀r⁻² + O(r⁻⁴) there, and a perturbation h₀₀ of order ρ_I^z, Re z < 2, can overturn it. t^♭_*
is smooth on M_(1/2) near ℐ⁺ (Lemma 15.35 (a)) and equals t_* on ℐ⁺.

*The cut-off χ_K and the background.* We take the cut-offs χ^♭_K, χ_K, χ^♯_K of Section 21.7 with the condition
(29.2) at the threshold T_K in place of 10, a condition of the same kind:

    supp χ_K ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ T_K};

so χ_K = 0 on {t_* < T_K}, as t^♭_* ≤ t_*. Every statement of Chapter 29–Chapter 36 holds with this threshold, the
supports only shrinking. The cut-offs being chosen consistently, the threshold 60R₁ of Section 21.7 at which
χ^♭_K = 1 on {|x| < t/10} is raised with T_K, as (29.2) presumes: there is T′ ≥ 60R₁ with χ^♭_K = 1 on
{|x| < t/10, t > T′}. g_(b₀,b,−S) is (29.1), and P_5 is the augmented operator (34.3); its
background at p⃗_(≤0) = (S, b − b₀, S^(0)_1) is the translated background of (32.4),

    g_(p⃗) = (1 − χ_K) φ_(−S,−S^(0)_1)^* g_(b₀) + χ_K g_b,

which is g_(b₀,b,−S) when S^(0)_1 = 0. Φ, the data space 𝒟, the class ℱ and 𝒳_J are those of Definition 34.15,
Definition 34.13 and Theorem 34.20, and 𝒟_ex, ℱ_ex, 𝒳_(J,ex), 𝒬_ex are the exact classes of Definition 35.11.
The data space is always written with a sub- or superscript (𝒟_ex, 𝒟^k_ex, 𝒟^∞_ex) below, so that 𝒟 alone denotes the
region of Proposition 38.4.

*The two time functions.* Put F(r) := t_IVP − t_* = ψ(r) − ψ_IVP(r). By Lemma 21.22 (b), ψ_IVP = ψ on [r_♭, 5R₁]
and 0 ≤ ψ_IVP′ ≤ ψ′ beyond, so F ≥ 0, F′ ≥ 0 and F = 0 on [r_♭, 5R₁]; so t_* ≤ t_IVP. For r ≥ R_5 := max(R₃, 3R₁),
ψ(r) = r − C′ + 8m₀r⁻¹ and ψ_IVP(r) = C″, so F(r) = r − C′ − C″ + 8m₀r⁻¹. As ψ_IVP ≥ 0, C″ ≥ 0. Let
R_6 := max(R_5, 2(|C′| + C″)); then

    F(r) ≥ r/4     for r ≥ R_6.    (38.2)

*Parameters* ([Hin26, Section 13.1, Step 1]). The constraint damping E_C has the constants of Theorem 24.1 fixed
in (24.4), with C_0 = 100: v_C = ½, e_C = 1/102400 and γ_C = h⁻¹, h ∈ 𝖧; as h < 10⁻⁶,
s_C := (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C > 100. The gauge modification E_Υ = (c_Υ, e_Υ, γ_Υ; c_(Υ,H), γ_(Υ,H)) has c_Υ and c_(Υ,H)
as in Section 23.1 and Lemma 23.22, and γ_(Υ,H), e_Υ, γ_Υ small enough for the mode stability of
Proposition 23.24 and the tf-admissibility of Proposition 25.11. The data index set ℰ_0 and the weight ℓ_0 satisfy
the hypotheses of Theorem 37.36:

    min Re ℰ_0 > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ,     jℰ_0 ⊂ ℰ_0 (j ∈ ℕ),     ℓ_0 > 3,     ℓ_0 ∉ Re π_1ℰ_0,

the bound ℓ_0 > 3 coming from (H4) of Section 33.2 (see row d1 of Section 38.6). ℰ^C_I and ℓ_I are then those
of Theorem 37.36. The weights ℓ_I, ε_+, ε_K and α of the cone are those of Chapter 29–Chapter 35, ℓ_I being the
b-weight at ℐ⁺ of Definition 29.1, not the class parameter of Section 29.1. The weights
3 + ε_0 and 1 + ε_0 of [Hin26] at spatial and null infinity are ℓ_0 and 3/2 + ε_0 here, in the normalisation of
Chapter 27, in which the weights at null infinity are shifted by ½ ((37.1)). Theorem 38.24 shows that all
the conditions can be met together.

*The cut-off χ_ι.* We take the cut-off χ_ι = χ(t_*) of Section 26.13 with χ = 0 on (−∞, T_ι] and χ = 1 on
[T_ι + 1, ∞). Then χ_ι = 0 on {t_* ≤ T_ι} ⊃ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2} (as C_♭t_* ≤ t^♭_*), and supp dχ_ι ⊂ {T_ι ≤ t_* ≤ T_ι + 1}
is disjoint from supp χ_K, as T_K > T_ι + 1. Section 26.13 uses χ_ι in the proof of Theorem 26.42 only through
χ_ι = 1 near ι⁺ and through the commutator of L_b with χ_ι, which is χ′(t_*) and χ″(t_*) times commutators of L_b with
t_* and so is supported where χ′(t_*) ≠ 0, a compact t_*-interval; Chapter 34 uses it in (34.11) and the results
built on it only as a real function of t_*, equal to 1 near ι⁺ and supported in Ω_*. Both hold for this choice, so it is
admissible, and the ι⁺-terms of Φ do not reach the region of the initial family.

### 38.2 The initial family

**Lemma 38.1** (The cut-off of the gauge.) Let χ_♮ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 0 on (−∞, ½] and 1 on [1, ∞), let χ_0
be the cut-off of Section 37.16, χ_0 = 1 − χ̌_0(t_IVP/r) with χ̌_0 ∈ C^∞_c((−¼, ¼)) equal to 1 on [−⅛, ⅛], and

    χ^♮_0 := 1 − (1 − χ_0)(1 − χ_♮(t_*)).    (38.3)

Then: (a) χ^♮_0 ∈ C^∞(M); (b) χ^♮_0 = 1 on {t_* ≥ 1} ⊃ Ω_*; (c) χ^♮_0 = χ_0 on {t_* ≤ ½}, and on Ω_(ext,r_1) for
r_1 ≥ R_6; (d) χ^♮_0 = 0 near Σ^IVP, and near φ(Σ^IVP) for φ = φ_(S,S⁰) and φ = φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹, |S| + |S⁰| small.

Here Ω_(ext,r_1) is the exterior domain of Lemma 37.1 at the radius r_1. The proof of (d) uses the following
bound on the boosts and translations.

**Lemma 38.2** (Boosts and translations move t_IVP and r by O((|S| + |S⁰|)r).) There is C such that
for S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1 with |S|, |S⁰| ≤ 1, for φ = φ_(S,S⁰) and φ = φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹, and for every p ∈ M,

    |t_IVP(φ(p)) − t_IVP(p)| ≤ C(|S| + |S⁰|) r(p),     |r(φ(p)) − r(p)| ≤ C(|S| + |S⁰|) r(p).

φ is the identity on {|x| ≤ 5R₁} and maps {|x| > 5R₁} into itself.

*Proof.* *Boosts.* φ_(S_w) is the time-1 flow of V(S_w) = ½χ_r(|x|)χ^♯_IVP(1 − χ^♭_K)X_w,
X_w = t w·∂_x + (w·x)∂_t (Lemma 21.26); φ_(−S) is that of V(S_(−w)) = −V(S_w). As 1 − χ^♭_K = 0 on
{|x| < t/10, t > T′} (Section 38.1), every point of supp V(S_w) has t ≤ 10|x| + T′. And t ≥ −½|x| on supp V(S_w):
there χ^♯_IVP ≠ 0, so t_IVP > −|x|/2 (Section 21.7), and t = t_IVP + ψ_IVP(|x|) ≥ t_IVP as ψ_IVP ≥ 0
(Lemma 21.22 (b)). So |t| ≤ 10|x| + T′ ≤ C|x| there, |x| ≥ r_♭ being bounded below. With X_w|x| = t S_w(x̂),
t_IVP = t − ψ_IVP(|x|), and
0 ≤ ψ_IVP′ ≤ ψ′ ≤ 1 on {|x| ≥ 5R₁} ⊃ supp V(S_w) (Lemma 21.22 (b); ψ′ = 1 − 8m₀|x|⁻² there),

    |V(S_w)|x|| ≤ ½|w||t| ≤ C|w||x|,     |V(S_w)t_IVP| = ½χ_rχ^♯_IVP(1 − χ^♭_K)|w·x − ψ_IVP′ t S_w(x̂)| ≤ C|w||x|

on M, the left sides vanishing off supp V(S_w). Along an integral curve γ(s), s ∈ [0, 1], of ±V(S_w),

    |d log|x(γ(s))|/ds| ≤ C|w|,  so  e^(−C|w|)|x(γ(0))| ≤ |x(γ(s))| ≤ e^(C|w|)|x(γ(0))|,
    |d t_IVP(γ(s))/ds| ≤ C|w||x(γ(s))| ≤ Ce^(C|w|)|w||x(γ(0))|.

Integrating over s ∈ [0, 1] gives both bounds for φ_(±S),
as e^(C|w|) − 1 ≤ C|w|e^C and 1 − e^(−C|w|) ≤ C|w| for |w| ≤ 1. *Translations.* ψ_(S⁰), S⁰ = S_w, is the time-1 flow
of V⁰(S⁰) = ½Θ w·∂_x, with Θ = χ_r(|x|)χ^♯_IVP(1 − χ^♭_K) ∈ [0, 1] (Lemma 32.2), and ψ_(−S⁰) is that of
−V⁰(S⁰). So |V⁰(S⁰)|x|| = ½Θ|w·x̂| ≤ ½|w| and |V⁰(S⁰)t_IVP| = ½Θψ_IVP′|w·x̂| ≤ ½|w|, as ψ_IVP′ ∈ [0, 1] on
supp Θ ⊂ {|x| ≥ 5R₁}. An integral curve of ±V⁰(S⁰) that moves starts and stays in {|x| > 5R₁} (below), so in time 1
it changes |x| and t_IVP by at most ½|w| ≤ |w||x(p)|/(10R₁); this gives both bounds for ψ_(±S⁰). *Composites.* For
φ_(S,S⁰) = ψ_(S⁰) ∘ φ_S and q := φ_S(p), r(q) ≤ (1 + C|S|)r(p) ≤ (1 + C)r(p), so

    |t_IVP(ψ_(S⁰)(q)) − t_IVP(p)|, |r(ψ_(S⁰)(q)) − r(p)| ≤ C|S⁰|r(q) + C|S|r(p) ≤ C′(|S| + |S⁰|)r(p);

likewise for φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹ = φ_(−S) ∘ ψ_(−S⁰). V(S_w) and V⁰(S⁰) vanish on {|x| ≤ 5R₁} (χ_r = 0 there), whose points
are fixed by the flows; by uniqueness of integral curves no curve starting in {|x| > 5R₁} reaches it. ∎

*Proof of Lemma 38.1.* (a) χ_0 ∈ C^∞(M) (Section 37.16). Near ℐ⁺, t_* is a smooth function on M
((21.30)); near I₀ and near the corner I₀ ∩ ℐ⁺, t_* → −∞, so χ_♮(t_*) = 0; near ι⁺ and K⁺, t_* → +∞, so
χ_♮(t_*) = 1. (b) There χ_♮(t_*) = 1, and t^♭_* ≤ t_*. (c) The first claim is clear. On
Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_* > ½}, r ≥ r_1 ≥ R_6, so t_IVP = t_* + F(r) > r/4 by (38.2), where χ_0 = 1
(Section 37.16); both cut-offs are 1 there. (d) On Σ^IVP, t_* = −F ≤ 0. Let ν_0 := min(¼, r_♭/8). On
{|t_IVP| < ν_0}, a neighbourhood of Σ^IVP, t_* ≤ t_IVP < ¼, so χ_♮(t_*) = 0; and |t_IVP| < r/8 as r ≥ r_♭, so
χ_0 = 0. Hence χ^♮_0 = 0 there. Let p be near φ(Σ^IVP), p = φ(q) with |t_IVP(q)| small. If r(p) ≥ R_6 + 1, then by
Lemma 38.2, applied to φ⁻¹ at p, |t_IVP(p)| ≤ |t_IVP(q)| + C(|S| + |S⁰|)r(p) < r(p)/8 for |S| + |S⁰|
and |t_IVP(q)| small, so χ_0(p) = 0, and t_*(p) = t_IVP(p) − F(r(p)) < r(p)/8 − r(p)/4 < 0, so χ_♮(t_*(p)) = 0. On
the compact set {r ≤ R_6 + 2} ∩ M, φ tends to the identity smoothly as (S, S⁰) → 0, so φ(Σ^IVP) ∩ {r ≤ R_6 + 1} lies
in {|t_IVP| < ν_0} for |S| + |S⁰| small, and χ^♮_0 = 0 there, as just shown. ∎

The exterior theory of Chapter 37 is stated for the boosts φ_S. It holds for φ_(S,S⁰), with the same proofs:

**Lemma 38.3** (The exterior theory for translated boosts.) Let S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1 be small.

(a) φ_(S,S⁰) is a diffeomorphism of M with the properties stated for φ_(S_w) in Lemma 21.26, smooth in
(S, S⁰), and the identity on {|x| ≤ 5R₁}.

(b) With 𝔥_S the function h_(S_w) of (21.39) (S = S_w), for every b near b₀,

    χ_IVP(1 − χ_K)(φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_b − (g_b + |x|⁻²𝔥_S(ω)(dx¹)²)) ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I³ρ_+²C^∞(M; S²T*),

smoothly in (S, S⁰).

(c) Lemma 37.38, Theorem 37.39 and Remark 37.40 hold with φ_(S,S⁰) in place of φ_S and |S| + |S⁰|
in place of |S|.

*Proof.* (a) φ_S and ψ_(S⁰) have these properties (Lemma 21.26, Lemma 32.2 (a)), and they persist under
composition. (b) is Lemma 32.4 (a), stated there for the composite ψ_(−S^(0)_1) ∘ φ_(−S) at every small pair
(−S, −S^(0)_1), hence for φ_(S,S⁰) at every small (S, S⁰); its leading term is that of φ_S. (c) The proof of
Lemma 37.38 uses of φ_S only (21.40) on Ω_(ext,r_1) ⊂ {χ_IVP(1 − χ_K) = 1} and the naturality of Ric,
and (b) is (21.40) for φ_(S,S⁰). The proof of Theorem 37.39 uses of φ_S: that near |x| = r it moves t_IVP
and r by at most C|S|r, so that it maps a neighbourhood of Σ_(IVP,r₁) into {|t_IVP| < r/8} ∩ Ω_(ext,r₀) (after
(37.44)), which Lemma 38.2 gives for φ_(S,S⁰) with C(|S| + |S⁰|); the naturality of Ric and of Υ⁰
((37.37)) under diffeomorphisms; that S ↦ φ_S^*g_(b₀) is smooth, with derivative in ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞ with the
slots of (27.11) on Ω_(ext,r_1), which (b), differentiated in (S, S⁰), gives; and that pull-back by the flow
of a b-vector field tangent to every boundary hypersurface preserves the weighted, partially polyhomogeneous b-Sobolev
spaces near compact subsets of the interior of I₀, which holds for both factors by (a); that pull-back by φ_S is
bounded on H^(k,ℓ^♭₀)_b near Σ_(IVP,r₁), uniformly in S, which holds for φ_(S,S⁰), each factor being the time-1 flow of
a b-vector field tangent to every boundary hypersurface and smooth in its parameter (Lemma 21.26,
Lemma 32.2); and that the C^∞-seminorms of φ_S^*g_(b₀) that define 𝒢 depend continuously on S, which (b) gives
for φ_(S,S⁰). Remark 37.40 is uniqueness. ∎

Let

    P^♮(g, g_0) := Ric(g) − δ*_(g_0,E_C) Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g, g_0),

(37.36) with χ^♮_0 in place of χ_0. Its linearisation in g at (g, g_0) is written L^(χ^♮_0)_(g,g_0).

**Proposition 38.4** (The initial family; [Hin26, (13.5) and (12.33)].) Let γ = γ_(b₀) + γ̃ and
k = k_(b₀) + k̃ be data on Σ^IVP satisfying the constraint equations, with γ̃ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b and
k̃ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b, small in H^(d_0) of these classes, where d_0 is the largest of the regularities that
Theorem 37.39 (with Theorem 37.36), Theorem 38.10 and the local theory on the compact set 𝔒⁻ of the proof
below ((N) of Section 38.2.2) ask of the data. Let h̊_0, h̊_1 be the Cauchy data of Proposition 37.41 for (γ, k).
For S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1 small let h⁰_(S,S⁰), h¹_(S,S⁰) be the pulled-back data (37.44) of these, with φ_(S,S⁰) in
place of φ_S, now on all of Σ^IVP. Let
N_ν := {t_IVP ≥ −ν(r)}, with ν smooth and non-decreasing, ν = 0 on [0, R_ν], R_ν := ½(r_♭ + 5R₁), ν > 0 on (R_ν, ∞),
0 ≤ ν′ ≤ 1/32, and ν(r) = r/64 for r ≥ 16R_8, where R_8 ≥ max(2r_1, 8, 5R₁) is fixed in Lemma 38.5. Such ν
exists, as 16R_8/64 ≤ (16R_8 − R_ν)/32; and ν(r) ≤ (r − R_ν)/32 ≤ r/32. So {t_IVP = −ν} is spacelike for g_(b₀) (see
below), N_ν = {t_IVP ≥ 0} near {r = r_♭}, and {r = r_♭} is an inflow boundary for a backward problem. Put

    𝒟 := N_ν ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3},     𝒟_(S,S⁰) := φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹({t_IVP ≥ 0}) ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}.

For |S| + |S⁰| small, 𝒟_(S,S⁰) ⊂ 𝒟, and φ_(S,S⁰) maps a neighbourhood of Σ^IVP ∪ φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹(Σ^IVP) in N_ν into N_ν. There
is a unique h_(S,S⁰) on 𝒟 with

    P^♮(φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) + h_(S,S⁰), φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀)) = 0,
    h_(S,S⁰) = h⁰_(S,S⁰),  r ℒ_(∂_(t_IVP)) h_(S,S⁰) = h¹_(S,S⁰)  on Σ^IVP,    (38.4)

and:

(1) h_(S,S⁰) = φ_(S,S⁰)^*h_0 on a neighbourhood of Σ^IVP ∪ φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹(Σ^IVP) in 𝒟, where h_0 := h_(0,0) on 𝒟, a
two-sided neighbourhood of Σ^IVP off {r ≤ R_ν}; on {r ≤ R_ν}, 𝒟 ends at Σ^IVP and φ_(S,S⁰) is the identity, so
φ_(S,S⁰)^*h_0 is defined there. Hence φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) + h_(S,S⁰) = φ_(S,S⁰)^*(g_(b₀) + h_0) there;

(2) Ric(φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) + h_(S,S⁰)) = 0 and Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) + h_(S,S⁰), φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀)) = 0 on 𝒟;
on 𝒟 ∩ Ω_* the gauge 1-form is Υ^(E_Υ) (Lemma 38.1 (b)), which is [Hin26, (12.33b)];

(3) on 𝒟 ∩ Ω_*, h_(S,S⁰) ∈ H̄^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I))_b (orders at ℐ⁺; the set is bounded in t_*); h_(S,S⁰) is C^l in
(S, S⁰) with values in each H^k of this class, for data of regularity depending on k and l (Theorem 37.39 (2)); and
for each k there are k′_k, s_k > 0 and a non-decreasing ω_k : [0, s_k] → [0, ∞) with ω_k(s) → 0 as s → 0 such that,
if ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+k′_k)) ≤ s_k,

    ‖h_(S,S⁰)‖_(H^(k+2)) + ‖∂_(S,S⁰)h_(S,S⁰)‖_(H^(k+2)) + ‖∂²_(S,S⁰)h_(S,S⁰)‖_(H^(k+2)) ≤ ω_k(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+k′_k))),

in the norms of this class, uniformly for |S| + |S⁰| small (the shift by 2 is the order of P_5, as Lemma 38.16
uses it). We take k′_k non-decreasing in k.

*The hypersurface {t_IVP = −ν} and the inclusions.* In the Kerr–Schild coordinates of Lemma 21.22,
t_IVP + ν = t − (ψ_IVP − ν)(|x|) has differential dt_KS − β′ d|x| with β′ = β_IVP − ν′, where β_IVP :=
ψ_IVP′ + 2χ_∞m₀/(|x|² − m₀) is the coefficient of t_IVP in the proof of Lemma 21.22. There β_IVP ≤ 1, β_IVP > 0
on [5R₁, ∞), and on [r_♭, 5R₁], where β_IVP = 1 − χ_∞(8m₀/ϱ² − 2m₀/(ϱ² − m₀)) (ϱ = |x|), either χ_∞ = 0 and
β_IVP = 1, or ϱ ≥ 2R₁ and 8m₀/ϱ² − 2m₀/(ϱ² − m₀) ≤ 6m₀/ϱ² ≤ 3/2, so β_IVP ≥ −½. As 0 ≤ ν′ ≤ 1/32,
β′ ∈ (−1, 1], and d(t_IVP + ν) is timelike for g_(b₀) by Lemma 21.16 (e) and Lemma 21.19: {t_IVP = −ν}
is spacelike. Near {r = r_♭}, ν = 0, and {r = r_♭} is spacelike with dr future timelike (Lemma 15.35 (1)), N_ν
lying to its past; past directed causal curves from points with r > r_♭ stay in {r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)}, so a backward
problem needs no data there. For the inclusions: φ := φ_(S,S⁰) and φ⁻¹ are the identity on {r ≤ 5R₁} and map
{r > 5R₁} into itself, where they move t_IVP and r by at most C(|S| + |S⁰|)r (Lemma 38.2); and
ν(r) ≥ c_ν r on [5R₁, ∞), with c_ν := min(ν(5R₁)/(16R_8), 1/64) > 0. Let C(|S| + |S⁰|) ≤ min(¼c_ν, ⅓). Then
φ⁻¹({t_IVP ≥ 0}) ⊂ N_ν: a point p of it with r(p) > 5R₁ has t_IVP(p) ≥ −¼c_ν r(p) > −ν(r(p)). In particular
𝒟_(S,S⁰) ⊂ 𝒟, and φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP) lies in W := N_ν ∩ {t_IVP > −⅓c_ν r}, a neighbourhood of Σ^IVP ∪ φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP) in N_ν. And
φ(W) ⊂ N_ν: for p ∈ W with r(p) > 5R₁, t_IVP(φ(p)) > −(⅓ + ¼)c_ν r(p) and r(φ(p)) ≥ ⅔r(p), so
t_IVP(φ(p)) > −c_ν r(φ(p)) ≥ −ν(r(φ(p))). (φ_(S,S⁰)⁻¹, not φ_(S,S⁰), appears in 𝒟_(S,S⁰): φ_(S,S⁰)^*h_0 at p needs
h_0 at φ_(S,S⁰)(p).)

#### 38.2.1 The cover of 𝒟

Let r_ext ≥ R_0 be the exterior radius at which Theorem 37.39 is applied, for φ_(S,S⁰) by
Lemma 38.3 (c) (R_0 that of Lemma 37.1), and r_1 := 2r_ext ≥ R_6, the radius of its
boosted problem; Ω_(ext,r_1), Σ^IVP_(r_1) := Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ Σ^IVP and its future
boundary Σ^fut_(r_1) = {t_IVP = r + 2r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) − (r_1 + 2r_1^(1−ℓ^♭_I))} are those of Lemma 37.1, with the
weights ℓ^♭_0, ℓ^♭_I of (37.1). Let

    R_8 ≥ max(2r_1, 8, 5R₁),     T″ := (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ + max(0, −C′) + 2,

and, with the chart (27.2) of Chapter 27 translated in t (g_(b₀) is stationary),

    ρ′_I := (T″ − x¹)/|x|     near infinity,     x¹ = t − |x|.

On 𝒟 near infinity t_* ≤ t^♭_*/C_♭ ≤ (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ (Lemma 15.35 (b)), so x¹ = t_* − C′ + 8m₀|x|⁻¹ ≤ T″ − 1 and
ρ′_I > 0 there. Fix c ∈ (0, ½] as in Lemma 37.23, and R_9 ≥ max(R_5, 4R₁, 4C″); decreasing c, which nothing chosen
before it depends on, we take c ≤ min(½, 1/R_9).

**Lemma 38.5** (The cover.) Put 𝒮 := 𝒟 ∩ {ρ′_I < c, r ≥ R_9} ∖ Ω_(ext,r_1) and
𝔒 := 𝒟 ∖ (Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝒮). Then:

(a) On 𝒟, ρ′_I < c forces |x| > 1/c ≥ R_9, so 𝒮 = 𝒟 ∩ {ρ′_I < c} ∖ Ω_(ext,r_1) has no side {r = R_9}; on {r ≥ R_9},
ρ′_I is defined and t_IVP = t − C″.

(b) 𝒟 ∩ {t_IVP < 0, r ≥ R_8} ⊂ Ω_(ext,r_1).

(c) 𝔒 is compact. Its boundary lies in the union of Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ R_ν}, {t_IVP = −ν}, Σ^fut_(r_1) ∩ {ρ′_I ≥ c},
Σ^past_(r_1), {ρ′_I = c}, {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3} and {r = r_♭}. These are spacelike, for g_(b₀) and for every metric C⁰-close
to it on 𝔒 whose difference from g_(b₀) is small in 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b); 𝔒 lies to the future of the first three and
to the past of the other four. So Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝔒 is closed under past causal curves within 𝒟. 𝔒 reaches below the
past slab of Ω_(ext,r_1) only for r slightly above r_1, where ν(r) > (r − r_1)/12.

(d) 𝒮 lies near the interior of ℐ⁺: x¹ is bounded on it. On 𝒮, t_IVP ≥ r/4.

(e) Put 𝒟^± := 𝒟 ∩ {±t_IVP ≥ 0}, 𝔒⁺ := 𝔒 ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} and

    𝔒⁻ := 𝒟⁻ ∩ {r − 2t_IVP ≤ 2R_8}.

Then 𝒟⁺ = (Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}) ∪ 𝔒⁺ ∪ 𝒮, and away from the faces at infinity its boundary lies in
Σ^IVP ∪ {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3} ∪ {r = r_♭}, with 𝒟⁺ to the future of the first and to the past of the other two; Σ^IVP ⊂ 𝒟⁺.
𝔒⁻ is compact, 𝔒 ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0} ⊂ 𝒟⁻ ∩ {r ≤ R_8} ⊂ 𝔒⁻, 𝒟⁻ ⊂ 𝔒⁻ ∪ Ω_(ext,r_1), and Σ^IVP ∩ 𝔒⁻ = Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ 2R_8}.
For g_(b₀) and every metric C⁰-close to it on 𝔒⁻, every future directed causal curve from a point of 𝔒⁻ that is future
inextendible in 𝒟⁻ stays in 𝔒⁻ and meets Σ^IVP: 𝔒⁻ is, for the reversed time orientation, the domain of dependence of
Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ 2R_8} within 𝒟⁻.

*Proof.* (a) As x¹ ≤ T″ − 1 on 𝒟, ρ′_I < c gives |x| > (T″ − x¹)/c ≥ 1/c ≥ R_9. For r ≥ R_9 ≥ R₃, t_IVP = t − C″.
(b) For r ≥ R_8 ≥ 2r_1, ν(r) ≤ r/32 ≤ (r − r_1)/12, so the points of 𝒟 there with t_IVP < 0 lie in the past slab
{−(r − r_1)/12 ≤ t_IVP ≤ 0} of Ω_(ext,r_1). (c) On 𝔒 near infinity, above Σ^fut_(r_1), t_IVP ≥ r + 2r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) −
(r_1 + 2r_1^(1−ℓ^♭_I)) and t_IVP = t − C″, so x¹ ≥ C″ − r_1 − 2 (as ℓ^♭_I > 1 and r_1 ≥ 1), and ρ′_I ≥ c,
so |x| ≤ (T″ + r_1 + 2 − C″)/c. With t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3, t_IVP ≥ −ν and (b) on 𝔒, 𝔒 is closed and bounded, hence
compact. Where ν = 0, that is on {r ≤ R_ν}, 𝒟 = {t_IVP ≥ 0} near Σ^IVP, so only there is Σ^IVP part of the boundary
of 𝔒.
{ρ′_I = c} is spacelike with {ρ′_I < c} to its future (Lemma 37.20 (a) in the translated chart); {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3}
is spacelike for the metrics named, dt^♭_* being past timelike (Lemma 15.35 (2)); {r = r_♭} is spacelike with dr
future timelike (Lemma 15.35 (1)); Σ^fut_(r_1) and Σ^past_(r_1) are spacelike (Lemma 37.1), with
Ω_(ext,r_1) to the past of the first and to the future of the second. For g_(b₀), dt_IVP is past timelike
(Lemma 21.22 (b)), so Σ^IVP is spacelike, and {t_IVP = −ν} is spacelike (after Proposition 38.4); on the
compact 𝔒 these persist for C⁰-close metrics. The points of 𝔒 with r ≥ r_1 and t_IVP < 0 lie below the past slab
{−(r − r_1)/12 ≤ t_IVP ≤ 0} of Ω_(ext,r_1), that is to the past of Σ^past_(r_1), and by (b) they have r < R_8. The
boundary that 𝒮 shares with Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝔒 lies in {ρ′_I = c} ∪ Σ^fut_(r_1), with 𝒮 to its future; so no past
directed causal curve enters 𝒮 from Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝔒. A point of 𝔒 with r ≥ r_1 below the past slab has
−ν(r) ≤ t_IVP < −(r − r_1)/12. (d) 𝒮 is disjoint from Ω_(ext,r_1) and lies near
infinity, so by (b) it lies in {t_IVP ≥ 0} ∖ Ω_(ext,r_1), above Σ^fut_(r_1); so x¹ ≥ C″ − r_1 − 2 as in (c), and
x¹ ≤ T″ − 1. ρ′_I < c ≤ ½ gives t > (1 − c)|x| + T″ ≥ ½|x| + T″, so t_IVP > ½|x| + T″ − C″ ≥ r/4, as r ≥ R_9 ≥ 4C″.
(e) By (d), 𝒮 ⊂ 𝒟⁺, and 𝒟 = (𝒟 ∩ Ω_(ext,r_1)) ∪ 𝔒 ∪ 𝒮. On Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, x¹ = t_IVP + C″ − r ≤ C″ − r_1,
as r^(1−ℓ^♭_I) ≤ r_1^(1−ℓ^♭_I) there, so t_* ≤ C″ + C′ − r_1 < 0 (r_1 ≥ R_6 ≥ 2(|C′| + C″)), and this set lies in 𝒟.
This gives the first claim. As N_ν ⊃ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, 𝒟⁺ is the set {t_IVP ≥ 0, t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3} of M, which gives its
boundary and Σ^IVP ⊂ 𝒟⁺; 𝒟⁺ lies to the past of {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3} and of {r = r_♭} as 𝔒 does in (c).
𝔒⁻ is closed, and on it t_IVP ≥ −ν(r) ≥ −r/32, so r ≤ 2R_8 + 2t_IVP ≤ 2R_8: 𝔒⁻ is
compact. On 𝒟⁻ ∩ {r ≤ R_8}, r − 2t_IVP ≤ r + 2ν(r) ≤ (17/16)R_8 < 2R_8. A point of 𝔒 with t_IVP ≤ 0 has r < r_1, or
r ≥ r_1 and (r − r_1)/12 ≤ ν(r) ≤ r/32, so r < 2r_1 ≤ R_8; and (b), with Σ^IVP_(r_1) ⊂ Ω_(ext,r_1), places the points
of 𝒟⁻ with r ≥ R_8 in Ω_(ext,r_1). This gives the inclusions; at t_IVP = 0 the definition of 𝔒⁻ reads r ≤ 2R_8. On
the face F := 𝒟⁻ ∩ {r − 2t_IVP = 2R_8}, r ≥ 2R_8 − r/16, so r ≥ (32/17)R_8 > R_8 ≥ max(R₃, 3R₁), and t_IVP = t − C″.
There, with u := m₀r⁻² ≤ 1/25, g_(b₀)⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − u(∂_t + ∂_r)^(⊗2) (Proposition 21.21), so
g_(b₀)⁻¹(dr − 2dt, dr − 2dt) = −3 − u < 0; and (dr − 2dt)(∂_t) = −2 < 0, where ∂_t is future timelike for g_(b₀)
(g_(b₀)(∂_t, ∂_t) = −1 + u < 0 and dt_IVP(∂_t) = 1 > 0, dt_IVP being past timelike, Lemma 21.22 (b)). A timelike
covector that is negative on one future timelike vector is negative on every future causal vector, so r − 2t_IVP
decreases strictly along future directed causal curves near F, for g_(b₀) and, with the margin on the compact F, for
every metric C⁰-close to it; likewise t_IVP + ν increases along them near {t_IVP = −ν}, which is spacelike with N_ν to
its future (Proposition 38.4), and t_IVP is a time function on 𝔒⁻ (dt_IVP is past timelike for g_(b₀) with a margin
on 𝔒⁻). Let γ be a future directed causal curve from p ∈ 𝔒⁻, future inextendible in 𝒟⁻. It cannot leave 𝔒⁻ through
{t_IVP = −ν} or through F; and it cannot stay in 𝔒⁻ ∖ Σ^IVP, as, parametrised by t_IVP, it would converge in the compact
𝔒⁻ and extend, as in the proof of Lemma 18.4. So it meets Σ^IVP ∩ 𝔒⁻. ∎

The slab 𝒮 is bounded by {ρ′_I = c} ∪ Σ^fut_(r_1) to the past and by {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3} to the future. Its points near
ℐ⁺ depend on all of Σ^IVP. So the forward problem is posed on all of 𝒟⁺ at once, with data on Σ^IVP only
(Section 38.2.3–Section 38.2.5): the hypersurfaces where 𝒮, 𝔒⁺ and Ω_(ext,r_1) meet lie inside 𝒟⁺ and carry no data. The
backward problem is posed on 𝔒⁻ (Section 38.2.2) and, near infinity, on the past slab of Ω_(ext,r_1).

#### 38.2.2 The local theory on compact sets

On the compact parts of 𝒟 (the set 𝔒⁻ of Lemma 38.5 (e), and a compact set Q ⊂ 𝒟⁺ containing 𝔒⁺ in the proof of
Theorem 38.9) the equations are solved by the local theory of quasilinear wave equations. The equation
(38.4) is, in the gauge's normal form, P^♮(g_0 + h, g_0) = ½□_(g_0+h)h plus a smooth function of (x, h, ∂h),
with g_0 = φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) and □ the operator of (21.47): its principal part is
½□_(g_0+h) ⊗ id = −½(g_0 + h)^(αβ)∂_α∂_β ⊗ id, with principal symbol ½(g_0 + h)⁻¹(ζ, ζ) times the identity (∂ → iζ),
and everything is smooth in the parameters (S, S⁰); h = 0 solves it for every value of the parameters, as
P^♮(g_0, g_0) = Ric(g_0) = 0. Its linearisations have the same principal part at h. Lemma 18.4 and
Lemma 37.31 are applied below to twice these operators, and to twice the operators δ_gG_gδ*_(g_0,E_C) of
the constraint propagation, whose principal symbol is then g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) times the identity.

Two statements are used, on a compact set 𝔒′ of one of two kinds, for the metric G of the equation: for the forward
problem, 𝔒′ ⊂ 𝒟⁺ and every past directed causal curve in 𝒟⁺ from a point of 𝔒′ stays in 𝔒′; for the backward problem,
𝔒′ ⊂ 𝒟⁻ and every future directed causal curve in 𝒟⁻ from a point of 𝔒′ stays in 𝔒′. In both, t_IVP is a time
function of G on 𝔒′, and Σ′ := Σ^IVP ∩ 𝔒′, which carries the data, is a compact domain with smooth boundary in
Σ^IVP. 𝔒⁻ is of the second kind (Lemma 38.5 (e)), and the set Q of the proof of Theorem 38.9 is of the
first. U is a fixed bounded open neighbourhood of 𝔒′ in {|x| > ½r_♭}, where g_(b₀) is defined (Lemma 21.19);
the coordinates are the (t, x) of Section 21.4; and on a domain H^k denotes the restrictions of H^k functions, with
the quotient norm.

(L) Let k ≥ 4, and let P := −½G^(αβ)∂_α∂_β + a^α∂_α + b act on symmetric 2-tensors, with smooth coefficients on U and
G a Lorentzian metric with |G − g_(b₀)| ≤ δ_L on U (in the components; δ_L > 0 is fixed in the proof), for which 𝔒′
is of its kind. For data (h₀, h₁) ∈ H^(k+1)(Σ′) × H^k(Σ′) and f ∈ H^k(𝔒′) there is a unique h ∈ H²(𝔒′) with Ph = f
on 𝔒′, h = h₀ and rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h = h₁ on Σ′. It lies in H^(k+1)(𝔒′), and

    ‖h‖_(H^(k+1)(𝔒′)) ≤ C_k N_k,     N_j := ‖h₀‖_(H^(j+1)(Σ′)) + ‖h₁‖_(H^j(Σ′)) + ‖f‖_(H^j(𝔒′)),

with C_k depending only on k, 𝔒′, U and a bound for the coefficients in C^k(U): the bound is uniform over a family of
such operators whose coefficients are bounded in C^k(U). Let moreover P_0 be a fixed operator of this kind, with
coefficients (g_(b₀)⁻¹, a_0, b_0), let c̃ := (G⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹, a − a_0, b − b_0), and let f be the restriction to 𝔒′ of
an element of H^k(U). Then

    ‖h‖_(H^(k+1)(𝔒′)) ≤ C(N^U_k + ‖c̃‖_(H^k(U)) N^U_4),    (38.5)

N^U_j being N_j with ‖f‖_(H^j(U)) in place of ‖f‖_(H^j(𝔒′)), and C depending only on k, 𝔒′, U, P_0 and a bound for
‖c̃‖_(C⁴(U)) + ‖c̃‖_(H⁵(U)); for k = 4 the last term is absent.

(N) (Cauchy stability) For the quasilinear equation, there is r_0 such that for data small in H^(r_0+1) × H^(r_0) and
(S, S⁰) small there is a unique solution on all of 𝔒′; it lies in H^(r+1)(𝔒′) for every r for which the data lie in
H^(r+1) × H^r, and it tends to 0 in H^(r+1)(𝔒′) as the data tend to 0 in H^(r+1) × H^r and (S, S⁰) tends to 0.

Both rest on [DS23, Theorems 2.4, 2.5 and 2.6] (Theorem A.6, Theorem A.9,
Theorem A.7). *The reduction.* Take τ := t_IVP as time and, on a neighbourhood of Ū, time lines
orthogonal to the levels of t_IVP for g_(b₀). The levels are spacelike and the time lines timelike for g_(b₀), with a
margin on Ū (Lemma 21.22 (b)); δ_L is so small that both keep half that margin for every metric within δ_L of
g_(b₀) in the components on Ū. As in Step 8 (i)–(iii) of Section 6.5, the equation is posed on a slab
X := I × 𝕋⁴, I a compact τ-interval containing the t_IVP-range of U, with the coefficients extended as follows: G⁻¹ as
G_ref⁻¹ + χ_U(G⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹), and (a, b) as (a_ref, b_ref) + χ_U(a − a_0, b − b_0), where G_ref, a_ref and b_ref are
fixed smooth extensions of g_(b₀), a_0 and b_0 from U to X (a_0 = b_0 = 0 if no P_0 is given), the levels of τ being
spacelike and the time lines timelike for G_ref (that is, G⁻¹(dτ, dτ) < 0 and G⁻¹ positive definite on the covectors
that vanish on the time lines: conditions convex in G⁻¹, which the extended G⁻¹ therefore keeps, with half the margin,
and which make it Lorentzian), and χ_U ∈ [0, 1] is a fixed cut-off, equal to 1 on a neighbourhood of 𝔒′ and supported
in U. Outside I the coefficients are taken constant in τ, as in Step 8 (iii). The forcing is replaced by
χ_Uf; the data are extended from the smooth domain Σ′ of Σ^IVP by the extension operator of Theorem A.35,
one operator bounded on every H^j, and then cut off in the same way. In V := (h, ∂_τh, ∂_yh), y the coordinates along
the levels of τ transported by the time lines, the equation becomes, as in Step 8 (iii),

    A⁰∂_τV + A^c∂_cV = BV + F,    (38.6)

with A⁰ = diag(1, −G^(ττ), G^(ab)) and A^c symmetric, both affine in the components of G⁻¹ in (τ, y), c_0 ≤ A⁰ ≤ c_0⁻¹
for some c_0 > 0, B affine in (G⁻¹, a, b) (the change to the coordinates (τ, y) adds first-order terms linear in G⁻¹),
and F = (0, 2f, 0); the relation between the last components of V and ∂_yh propagates. Divided by A⁰, it is a system
∂_τV + A^i∂_iV = B̃V + F̃ that satisfies (A1)–(A4) of [DS23]. The parameters
(S, S⁰) are adjoined as unknowns constant in τ, which adds the eigenvalue 0 that the symbol already has. [DS23] asks
r > N/2 + 1 = 3 for u ∈ H^r, r an integer, so r ≥ 4, which for h means data in H^(r+1) × H^r; this is why (L) is
stated for k ≥ 4. Finite speed of propagation, Lemma 18.4 with τ := ±t_IVP and the compact sets that the kind of
𝔒′ provides (𝔒′ together with a compact neighbourhood of Σ′ on its other side), shows that on 𝔒′ the solution depends
only on the data on Σ′ and on the forcing on 𝔒′, not on the extensions; and that it is unique among solutions in
H²(𝔒′), which, extended by 0 across Σ′, where their Cauchy data vanish, are solutions in the sense of distributions, as
in the proof of Proposition 38.4.

*(N).* Theorem A.6 at u₀ = 0, from a starting level t₀ of t_IVP, gives an interval [t₀ − T, t₀ + T] with
T > 0 depending on ‖u₀‖_r = 0 and on the structure only, so not on t₀, the bounds of (A1)–(A2) holding uniformly in
t_IVP. The solution 0 exists for all t_IVP and all parameters, and Theorem A.9 at it, on that interval,
shows that solutions with data near 0 at t₀ exist on [t₀ − T, t₀ + T] and tend to 0 in C([t₀ − T, t₀ + T]; H^r) as
the data tend to 0. Applied on successive intervals of length T, each time with the values of the solution at the end
of the previous one as data, finitely many to cover the t_IVP-range of 𝔒′ in both time directions, this gives (N)
with r_0 := 4, in C(I; H^r) for u; the higher regularity is Theorem A.7, and the spacetime norm on 𝔒′
follows from the equation, solved for the second time derivative, by induction on the number of time derivatives.

*(L).* For a linear equation, A^i = A^i(t, x) and R = B̃(t, x)u + F̃(t, x), with A^i, B̃ smooth and bounded with all
their derivatives, and F̃ the forcing; (A1)–(A4) hold on the whole state space ℝ^m, so the distance M̃ of
Theorem A.6 is infinite, and solutions scale with their data. Let I be the t_IVP-range of 𝔒′, enlarged by
1, and r ≥ 4.

(i) *The homogeneous system* (F̃ = 0). For σ ∈ ℝ, w(τ) := u(σ + τ) solves the system with coefficients A^i(σ + τ, x),
B̃(σ + τ, x); adjoin σ as an unknown constant in τ, as the parameters are. At the solution (0, σ₀),
Theorem A.6 gives an interval [−T(σ₀), T(σ₀)], and Theorem A.9 a δ(σ₀) > 0 such that data
(w₀, σ) with ‖w₀‖_r ≤ δ(σ₀) and |σ − σ₀| ≤ δ(σ₀) have solutions on that interval with ‖w(τ)‖_r ≤ 1. Covering I by
finitely many intervals (σ₀ − δ(σ₀), σ₀ + δ(σ₀)), and scaling, there are T₁ > 0 and K such that for every s ∈ I and
u₀ ∈ H^r the solution with u(s) = u₀ exists on [s − T₁, s + T₁] and satisfies ‖u(t)‖_r ≤ K‖u₀‖_r there. So the
solution operators 𝒰(t, s) exist for t, s ∈ I; they are linear, by uniqueness, satisfy 𝒰(t, s)𝒰(s, s′) = 𝒰(t, s′),
and are bounded on H^r by K^m, m the least integer ≥ |I|/T₁, uniformly in t, s ∈ I. By Theorem A.6,
t ↦ 𝒰(t, s)u₀ is continuous into H^r and C¹ into H^(r−1), with derivative 𝒜(t)𝒰(t, s)u₀, 𝒜(t) := −A^i∂_i + B̃; and
s ↦ 𝒰(t, s)u₀ is continuous into H^r, as 𝒰(t, s′)u₀ − 𝒰(t, s)u₀ = 𝒰(t, s′)(u₀ − 𝒰(s′, s)u₀) and the 𝒰(t, s′) are
uniformly bounded.

(ii) *Duhamel's formula.* Let u₀ and F̃ be smooth, and u the solution of Theorem A.6 with u(t₀) = u₀,
t₀ ∈ I; R = B̃u + F̃ satisfies (A2). On an interval J ⊂ I on which u exists, u ∈ C(J; H^(r+1)) ∩ C¹(J; H^r) for every r.
For fixed t, w(s) := 𝒰(t, s)u(s) satisfies w(s + ε) − w(s) = 𝒰(t, s + ε)(u(s + ε) − 𝒰(s + ε, s)u(s)), and in H^r
the bracket is εF̃(s) + o(ε), u and 𝒰(·, s)u(s) being C¹ into H^r with derivatives at s differing by F̃(s). With the
uniform bound and the continuity in s of (i), w has the continuous right derivative 𝒰(t, s)F̃(s) in H^r; a continuous
function with a continuous right derivative is continuously differentiable, so
u(t) = 𝒰(t, t₀)u₀ + ∫_(t₀)^t 𝒰(t, s)F̃(s) ds, and ‖u(t)‖_r ≤ K^m(‖u₀‖_r + ∫_I ‖F̃(s)‖_r ds) on J. This bounds u in
C(J; C¹) ∩ C¹(J; C), H^r lying in C¹ for r ≥ 4, so by Theorem A.7 u exists on all of I.

(iii) *Density.* For u₀ ∈ H^r and F̃ ∈ L¹(I; H^r), approximate by smooth ones. By (ii) the solutions converge in
C(I; H^r), and the limit solves the system in the sense of distributions, with the same bound.

(iv) *The spacetime norm, in tame form.* Let s ≥ 0 be an integer, the data and the forcing smooth, so that V is smooth
on X by (ii). The data are given at τ = 0, inside I; in what follows I stands for I ∩ {τ ≥ 0} =: [0, τ_1] and X for
[0, τ_1] × 𝕋⁴, and I ∩ {τ ≤ 0} is treated in the same way with τ replaced by −τ, the squared norms on I × 𝕋⁴ being the
sums of those on the two halves (V is smooth across τ = 0). Below ‖·‖_p is the norm of H^p(X), ‖·‖_(C^j) that of C^j(X),
and 𝔠 := (A⁰, A^c, B). Two facts on X are used: H³(X) ⊂ L^∞(X), and ‖v‖_p ≤ C‖v‖_(p₀)^(1−λ)‖v‖_(p₁)^λ for
p = (1 − λ)p₀ + λp₁, λ ∈ [0, 1]. On ℝ × 𝕋⁴, where ‖v‖_p is equivalent to (Σ_n ∫⟨(ξ, n)⟩^(2p)|v̂(ξ, n)|² dξ)^(1/2) by
Plancherel's theorem, the first holds as Σ_n ∫⟨(ξ, n)⟩^(−6) dξ < ∞ in dimension 5, and the second by Hölder's
inequality with the exponents 1/(1 − λ) and 1/λ; on X they follow through the extension operator of
Theorem A.35 in τ across both ends of I, one operator bounded on every H^p. So, for a coefficient e, a
function v and multi-indices γ, δ in (τ, y) with 5 ≤ |γ| ≤ s and |γ| + |δ| ≤ s + 1,

    ‖∂^γe ∂^δv‖_0 ≤ C‖e‖_(|γ|)‖v‖_(|δ|+3) ≤ C(‖e‖_5‖v‖_(s−1) + ‖e‖_s‖v‖_4):    (38.7)

with p := |γ| and q := s + 4 − p ≥ |δ| + 3, (p, q) = (1 − λ)(5, s − 1) + λ(s, 4) for λ := (p − 5)/(s − 5) (if s = 5,
then p = 5 and q = 4), so ‖e‖_p‖v‖_q ≤ C(‖e‖_5‖v‖_(s−1))^(1−λ)(‖e‖_s‖v‖_4)^λ, and x^(1−λ)y^λ ≤ x + y for x, y ≥ 0.

*The energy.* For a smooth solution v of A⁰∂_τv + A^c∂_cv = Bv + G on X and Λ > 0 put ‖v‖_Λ := ‖e^(−Λτ)v‖_0. As A^c
is symmetric, integration by parts on 𝕋⁴ gives, with the L²-pairing on the slices,
(d/dτ)⟨A⁰v, v⟩ = ⟨(∂_τA⁰ + ∂_cA^c)v, v⟩ + 2⟨Bv, v⟩ + 2⟨G, v⟩. Multiply by e^(−2Λτ), use ⟨A⁰v, v⟩ ≥ c_0‖v‖²_(L²(𝕋⁴)),
integrate over I and drop the non-negative term at τ_1: with K := ‖∂_τA⁰ + ∂_cA^c‖_(C⁰) + 2‖B‖_(C⁰),
(2Λc_0 − K)‖v‖²_Λ ≤ c_0⁻¹‖v(0)‖²_(L²(𝕋⁴)) + 2‖G‖_Λ‖v‖_Λ. So, for Λ ≥ K/c_0,

    ‖v‖_Λ ≤ 2c_0⁻¹(Λ^(−1/2)‖v(0)‖_(L²(𝕋⁴)) + Λ⁻¹‖G‖_Λ).    (38.8)

*Spatial derivatives.* For a multi-index α in y with |α| ≤ s, ∂_y^αV solves the system with G = ∂_y^αF + R_α,

    R_α := Σ_(0<γ≤α) (α choose γ)(∂_y^γB ∂_y^(α−γ)V − ∂_y^γA⁰ ∂_y^(α−γ)∂_τV − ∂_y^γA^c ∂_y^(α−γ)∂_cV).

Each term is a product ∂^γe ∂^δV with e an entry of 𝔠, 1 ≤ |γ| ≤ s, |γ| + |δ| ≤ s + 1 and |δ| ≤ s. In ‖·‖_Λ it is at
most ‖𝔠‖_(C⁴)‖∂^δV‖_Λ if |γ| ≤ 4, and at most the right side of (38.7) if |γ| ≥ 5, as e^(−Λτ) ≤ 1.
Put |||V|||_(s,Λ) := Σ_(|β|≤s)‖∂^βV‖_Λ, over all derivatives in (τ, y), and T_s := ‖𝔠‖_5‖V‖_(s−1) + ‖𝔠‖_s‖V‖_4 for
s ≥ 5, T_s := 0 for s ≤ 4. By (38.8), with C depending on s and c_0,

    Σ_(|α|≤s)‖∂_y^αV‖_Λ ≤ C(Λ^(−1/2)‖V(0)‖_(H^s(𝕋⁴)) + Λ⁻¹(‖F‖_s + ‖𝔠‖_(C⁴)|||V|||_(s,Λ) + T_s)).

*Time derivatives.* For j ≥ 1 and j + |α| ≤ s, ∂_τ^(j−1)∂_y^α applied to the system gives
A⁰∂_τ^j∂_y^αV = ∂_τ^(j−1)∂_y^α(−A^c∂_cV + BV + F) − [∂_τ^(j−1)∂_y^α, A⁰]∂_τV, and |A⁰v| ≥ c_0|v|. On the right,
A^c∂_τ^(j−1)∂_y^α∂_cV has j − 1 derivatives in τ, ∂_τ^(j−1)∂_y^αF is bounded by ‖F‖_(s−1), and the other terms are
products ∂^γe ∂^δV with |γ| + |δ| ≤ s and |δ| ≤ s − 1, at most ‖𝔠‖_(C⁴)|||V|||_(s−1,Λ) + CT_s in ‖·‖_Λ as before. By
induction on j,

    |||V|||_(s,Λ) ≤ C(Σ_(|α|≤s)‖∂_y^αV‖_Λ + ‖F‖_(s−1) + ‖𝔠‖_(C⁴)|||V|||_(s−1,Λ) + T_s),

C depending on s, c_0 and ‖𝔠‖_(C⁰). *Conclusion.* Insert the bound for the spatial derivatives, and take Λ ≥ K/c_0 so
large, depending on s, c_0 and a bound for ‖𝔠‖_(C⁴), that the term CΛ⁻¹‖𝔠‖_(C⁴)|||V|||_(s,Λ) is absorbed by the left
side. As e^(−Λτ_1) ≤ e^(−Λτ) ≤ 1 on I and |||V|||_(s−1,Λ) ≤ C‖V‖_(s−1), this gives
‖V‖_s ≤ C(‖V(0)‖_(H^s(𝕋⁴)) + ‖F‖_s + ‖V‖_(s−1) + T_s) for s ≥ 1, and ‖V‖_0 ≤ C(‖V(0)‖_(L²(𝕋⁴)) + ‖F‖_0) by
(38.8) with G = F; C depends only on s, |I|, c_0, a bound for ‖𝔠‖_(C⁴) and, for s ≥ 5, a bound for ‖𝔠‖_5.
With D_s := ‖V(0)‖_(H^s(𝕋⁴)), induction on s gives, as ‖𝔠‖_(s−1) ≤ ‖𝔠‖_s,

    ‖V‖_s ≤ C(D_s + ‖F‖_s)  (s ≤ 4),     ‖V‖_s ≤ C(D_s + ‖F‖_s + ‖𝔠‖_s(D_4 + ‖F‖_4))  (s ≥ 5).
    (38.9)

By (iii), and as the bound is linear in the data and the forcing, it holds for all data and forcing of these orders.

*Back to h.* h is a component of V and its first derivatives are the others, so ‖h‖_(H^(s+1)(X)) ≤ C‖V‖_s. V(0) is
given by the extended data through a fixed first-order relation (rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP)) and ∂_τ differ by the factor r and a
vector field tangent to Σ^IVP), so D_s ≤ C(‖h₀‖_(H^(s+1)(Σ′)) + ‖h₁‖_(H^s(Σ′))); ‖F‖_s ≤ C‖f‖_(H^s(U)), χ_Uf being
determined by f on U whatever extension of f is used to bound its norm; and 𝔠 is affine in the coefficients on X,
which are fixed smooth functions plus χ_Uc̃, so ‖𝔠‖_s ≤ C_s(1 + ‖c̃‖_(H^s(U))) and ‖𝔠‖_(C⁴) ≤ C(1 + ‖c̃‖_(C⁴(U))),
C_s depending on P_0. The restriction to 𝔒′ is bounded, (τ, y) and (t, x) being related by a fixed diffeomorphism. With
s := k this is (38.5), N^U_4 bounding D_4 + ‖F‖_4. For the first bound take a_0 = b_0 = 0, so that
‖c̃‖_(H^j(U)) ≤ C‖c̃‖_(C^j(U)), and extend f from 𝔒′ to U with H^k(U)-norm at most 2‖f‖_(H^k(𝔒′)); then N^U_4 ≤ N^U_k ≤
2N_k. [Hin26, p. 320] cites the same theory as "standard local well-posedness results".

**Lemma 38.6** (Gluing across spacelike hypersurfaces.) Let V be an open set of ℝ⁵ = {(x⁰, …, x⁴)},
V = A₁ ∪ A₂ with A₁, A₂ closed in V, Γ := A₁ ∩ A₂, and H_1, …, H_N smooth hypersurfaces in V with
Γ ⊂ H_1 ∪ ⋯ ∪ H_N. Let Γ_1 be the set of points p ∈ Γ that lie on exactly one H_j and have a neighbourhood W in which
Γ ∩ W = H_j ∩ W and A₁ ∩ W, A₂ ∩ W are the closures in W of the two sides of H_j; assume Γ_1 dense in Γ. Let m ≥ 2, and
let 𝒫(u) := −½G^(αβ)(x, u)∂_α∂_βu + F(x, u, ∂u) for u : V → ℝ^n, with G(x, ζ) a Lorentzian metric and F smooth in their
arguments. Let u_1, u_2 ∈ C^m(V; ℝ^n) satisfy 𝒫(u_i) = 0 on the interior of A_i, u_1 = u_2 and ∂u_1 = ∂u_2 on Γ, and let
each H_j be spacelike for G(·, u_1) at the points of Γ_1 ∩ H_j. Then the function u equal to u_i on A_i is well defined
and lies in C^m(V; ℝ^n), and ∂^βu = ∂^βu_i on A_i for |β| ≤ m. Linear equations are the case where G does not depend
on u and F is affine in (u, ∂u).

*Proof.* Put w := u_1 − u_2. (i) *Every derivative of w of order at most m vanishes on Γ.* Let p ∈ Γ_1, H := H_j and W
as in the hypothesis, and take coordinates (s, y) near p with H = {s = 0}. We show by induction on j ≤ m that every
derivative of w of order j vanishes on H near p; for j ≤ 1 this is the hypothesis. Let 2 ≤ j ≤ m, and let the claim
hold below j. A derivative ∂_y^a∂_s^l w of order j with l ≤ j − 1 is a tangential derivative of ∂_s^l w, which lies in
C^(m−l) and vanishes on H near p; so it vanishes there. ∂_s^(j−2)𝒫(u_i) is continuous on V and vanishes on the interior
of A_i, hence on its closure, which contains H near p. In ∂_s^(j−2)𝒫(u) the only term with j derivatives ∂_s on u is
−½G^(ss)(x, u)∂_s^ju, G^(ss) := G^(αβ)(ds)_α(ds)_β (the operator written in the coordinates (s, y), its first-order
terms joining F); each other term is a polynomial, with coefficients smooth in (x, u), in derivatives of u that are of
order at most j − 1 or of order j with at most j − 1 factors ∂_s, the derivatives that fall on G(x, u) or on F involving
those of u of order at most j − 1. On H near p these other terms agree for u_1 and u_2, by the induction hypothesis and
the previous remark, and G^(ss)(x, u_1) = G^(ss)(x, u_2) ≠ 0 there, as u_1 = u_2 on Γ and H is spacelike for G(·, u_1).
So ∂_s^ju_1 = ∂_s^ju_2 on H near p, which completes the induction. Every derivative of w of order at most m is continuous
and vanishes on Γ_1, which is dense in Γ; so it vanishes on Γ.

(ii) *Pasting.* For v ∈ C⁰(V) vanishing on Γ let v^Γ := v on A₁ and v^Γ := 0 on A₂. If v ∈ C¹(V) and ∂v vanishes on Γ,
then v^Γ ∈ C¹(V) with ∂(v^Γ) = (∂v)^Γ. Indeed V is the union of Γ and of the open sets V ∖ A₂ ⊂ A₁ and V ∖ A₁ ⊂ A₂, on
which v^Γ is v and 0. At p ∈ Γ, v(p) = 0 and ∂v(p) = 0, so |v^Γ(p′)| ≤ |v(p′)| = o(|p′ − p|) as p′ → p: v^Γ is
differentiable at p with derivative 0 = (∂v)^Γ(p). And (∂v)^Γ is continuous, its restrictions to the closed sets A₁ and
A₂, which cover V, being ∂v and 0, which agree on Γ. Applied to w and to its derivatives of order below m, by induction
on the order, this gives w^Γ ∈ C^m(V) with ∂^β(w^Γ) = (∂^βw)^Γ for |β| ≤ m. So u = u_2 + w^Γ, which is u_1 on A₁ and u_2
on A₂, lies in C^m(V). ∎

#### 38.2.3 The slab near null infinity: setting

This subsection and the next two solve the gauge-fixed equation forward on 𝒟⁺ = 𝒟 ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, from Σ^IVP, up to
{t^♭_* = T̂ + 3}, with its orders at ℐ⁺ on the slab 𝒮 of Lemma 38.5. The past boundary of 𝒮 contains the part of
Σ^fut_(r_1) near ℐ⁺, which reaches ℐ⁺ and is asymptotically null there; Cauchy data on it are avoided, and so are data
on the compact surface where 𝒮 meets 𝔒. The problem is posed on all of

    𝒟⁺ = (Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}) ∪ 𝔒⁺ ∪ 𝒮     (Lemma 38.5 (e)),

whose only data surface is Σ^IVP, which does not reach ℐ⁺. Near infinity 𝒟⁺ agrees with Ω^♮ ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, where

    Ω^♮ := Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝒮,

and there the argument of Theorem 37.27 and Theorem 37.28 applies, in the chart of Chapter 27 translated in t; on
the compact part the local theory of Section 38.2.2 applies; and the solution restricts to the forward exterior
solution on Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}. [Hin26, p. 321] covers this region in one sentence ("for globally small initial
data, h_S thus exists … on φ_S({t_IVP ≥ 0}) ∩ {t_* ≤ 2}").

Let T₀ := C′ + 1 − 2R₁ be the constant of (27.3), and put

    ρ′_0 := (T″ − x¹)⁻¹,     x′_I := (ρ′_I)^(1/2),     U″ := cl_M{t_* ≤ T₀ + T″ − 2} ∩ {|x| ≥ 4R₁},

(27.2)–(27.3) with 2 replaced by T″. On U″, x¹ = t_* − C′ + 8m₀|x|⁻¹ ≤ T₀ + T″ − 2 − C′ + 2R₁ =
T″ − 1, so ρ′_0 ≤ 1, and (ρ′_0, ρ′_I, ω) are coordinates near I₀ ∪ ℐ⁺. On U the ratios ρ′_0/ρ_0 = (2 − x¹)/(T″ − x¹)
and ρ′_I/ρ_I are smooth and positive up to I₀ and ℐ⁺, tending to 1 at I₀; so the weighted b- and edge-b spaces of the
two charts coincide on U, with equivalent norms (the fibration of ℐ⁺ by ω is the same). 𝒢″ denotes the class of
Definition 27.9 on U″ in the coordinates (ρ′_0, ρ′_I).

*The margin.* By (21.30), ψ(ϱ) = ϱ − r_♭ − ∫_(r_♭)^ϱ χ_∞(s)8m₀s⁻² ds, and for ϱ ≥ 3R₁, where χ_∞ = 1, the
integral is ∫_(r_♭)^∞ χ_∞(s)8m₀s⁻² ds − 8m₀/ϱ. So C′ = r_♭ + ∫_(r_♭)^∞ χ_∞(s)8m₀s⁻² ds ≥ ∫_(3R₁)^∞ 8m₀s⁻² ds = 8R₁/3,
as 0 ≤ χ_∞ ≤ 1 and m₀ = R₁². Hence C′ > 0, T″ = (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ + 2, and

    T₀ + T″ − 2 − (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ = C′ + 1 − 2R₁ ≥ 1 + 2R₁/3.

On 𝒮̄, |x| ≥ 1/c ≥ R_9 ≥ 4R₁ (Lemma 38.5 (a)) and t_* ≤ t^♭_*/C_♭ ≤ (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ (Lemma 15.35 (b)); so
𝒮̄ ⊂ U″, as Lemma 38.7 uses.

*Translation.* t ↦ t − (T″ − 2) is an isometry of g_(b₀) (stationary in the coordinates of Section 21.4) and of η,
and it maps the coordinates (27.2) and the frame (27.6) to those above. Section 27.1 and
Section 27.4 (Lemma 27.2, Lemma 27.4, Lemma 27.11–Lemma 27.13, Proposition 27.14) and
the results of Chapter 37 on the exterior region use the chart only through the form of η in it and through the bounds
of Lemma 27.4 for g_(b₀) − η, which are invariant under this map; so they hold on U″ in the translated chart, for
backgrounds in 𝒢″, with the same proofs.

**Lemma 38.7** (The background on the slab.) Let S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1 be small as in Lemma 21.27 and
Lemma 38.3. On a neighbourhood of 𝒮̄ in U″, φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) agrees with an element of 𝒢″; on
Ω_(ext,r_1) it is the background of Lemma 37.38 for φ_(S,S⁰) (Lemma 38.3 (c)).

*Proof.* On 𝒮, χ_IVP = 1, as t_IVP ≥ 0 > −|x|/10 (Section 21.7). And χ_K = 0 on 𝒮: supp χ_K lies in the interior
of {χ^♯_K = 1} ⊂ supp χ^♯_K ⊂ {|x| < t/2}, while on 𝒮, t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3 gives t_* ≤ (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ and so x¹ ≤ T″ − 1,
so t ≤ |x| + T″ < 2|x| near infinity, where 𝒮 lies. So Lemma 38.3 (b) gives near 𝒮̄

    φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) − g_(b₀) − |x|⁻² 𝔥_S(ω)(dx¹)² ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I³ρ_+² C^∞(M; S²T*),

with 𝔥_S the function h_(S_w) of (21.39); and g_(b₀) − η = m₀|x|⁻²(dx¹)² + |x|⁻³C^∞ on {|x| ≥ 3R₁}
(Lemma 27.10 (1) and its proof). On 𝒮, ρ₀, ρ′_0 and ρ_+ are bounded below and ρ_I/ρ′_I is smooth and positive,
so φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) − η ∈ (ρ′_0)²(ρ′_I)²C^∞ with only the slot π₁₁ at that order, (dx¹)² being of type π₁₁, and the
other slots in (ρ′_0)²(ρ′_I)³C^∞: this is (27.11) in the translated chart, and φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) is smooth on
M. On Ω_(ext,r_1) the statement is Lemma 38.3 (c). ∎

#### 38.2.4 The curves on Ω^♮

**Lemma 38.8** Let c_♮ ∈ (0, c/4] and r_ext large. (a) {ρ′_I = c_♮} = {t = (1 − c_♮)|x| + T″} is spacelike
near infinity, with {ρ′_I < c_♮} to its future. (b) For p ∈ Ω^♮ with ρ′_I(p) < c_♮, the integral curves of
X′_I := ρ′_I∂_(ρ′_I) and of X′_0 − X′_I through p (the outgoing ray at fixed x¹, and the curve of fixed |x|), followed
in the direction of increasing ρ′_I, stay in Ω^♮ until they reach {ρ′_I = c_♮}, which they do. (c) 𝔒 does not meet
{ρ′_I < c}, and Ω^♮ ∩ {ρ′_I < c} ⊂ {t_IVP ≥ 0}; so 𝒟⁺ ∩ {ρ′_I < c} = Ω^♮ ∩ {ρ′_I < c}.

*Proof.* (a) is Lemma 37.20 (a) in the translated chart. (c) On 𝒟, ρ′_I < c forces r > R_9 (Lemma 38.5 (a)),
and 𝒟 ∩ {ρ′_I < c, r ≥ R_9} lies in Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝒮 by the definition of 𝒮; so 𝔒 does not meet {ρ′_I < c}. On the
past slab of Ω_(ext,r_1) near infinity, t_IVP ≤ 0 gives t ≤ C″ and x¹ ≤ C″ − r, so ρ′_I ≥ (T″ − C″ + r)/r ≥ ¾ > c,
as T″ > 0 and r ≥ R_9 ≥ 4C″. With 𝒟⁺ = (Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}) ∪ 𝔒⁺ ∪ 𝒮 this gives the last claim. (b) By (c) and
Lemma 38.5 (e), near infinity Ω^♮ ∩ {ρ′_I < c} is the set {ρ′_I < c, t_IVP ≥ 0, t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3}: below
Σ^fut_(r_1) it is Ω_(ext,r_1), above it 𝒮. So it suffices that along the segment ρ′_I stays below c and t_IVP ≥ 0 and
t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3 persist. *The ray.* Along it x¹ = x¹_p, and |x| decreases to r_c := (T″ − x¹_p)/c_♮, where
ρ′_I = c_♮ < c. t_* = x¹ + C′ − 8m₀|x|⁻¹ decreases along it. So does t^♭_*, along this curve and the next: both are past
directed causal for g_(b₀) (the ray is g_(b₀)-null, as g_(b₀) = η + m₀|x|⁻²(dx¹)² there, Lemma 21.20 (b)), and
dt^♭_* is past timelike for g_(b₀) (Lemma 15.35 (2)). t_IVP = x¹ + |x| − C″ decreases too, and at r_c it is
x¹_p(1 − c_♮⁻¹) + T″c_♮⁻¹ − C″, which is ≥ |x¹_p|(c_♮⁻¹ − 1) + T″c_♮⁻¹ − C″ > 0 if x¹_p < 0, and
≥ T″ − 1 + c_♮⁻¹ − C″ > 0 if x¹_p ∈ [0, T″ − 1], for c_♮ small; and r_c = (T″ − x¹_p)/c_♮ ≥ 1/c_♮ ≥ 4/c ≥ 4R_9, as
T″ − x¹ ≥ 1 on 𝒟 and c ≤ 1/R_9, so the ray stays in {r ≥ R_9}. *The curve of fixed |x|.* t decreases to
t_c := (1 − c_♮)|x| + T″; t_* decreases; the curve may cross Σ^fut_(r_1) into Ω_(ext,r_1); and
t_IVP(t_c) ≥ ½|x| + T″ − C″ > 0; and ρ′_I < c_♮ along it, so it avoids 𝔒 by (c). ∎

*The constant c_♮ and the radiation field.* Let R_K be the largest value of r on the compact set 𝔒. Fix
c_♮ ≤ min(c/4, 4/(R_K + 2)) so small that Proposition 37.16 holds on Ω^♮_(c_♮) := Ω^♮ ∩ {ρ′_I < c_♮}, which is
𝒟⁺ ∩ {ρ′_I < c_♮} by Lemma 38.8 (c), in the translated chart, with Σ_in := {ρ′_I = c_♮} ∩ Ω^♮ and
Σ_fin := {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3} ∩ Ω^♮_(c_♮), as Lemma 37.23 fixes c; this is a smallness of x′_I, which involves no other
choice. Σ_in is spacelike with Ω^♮_(c_♮) to its future (Lemma 38.8 (a)); Σ_fin is spacelike for every g_0 + h of
Theorem 38.9 below, dt^♭_* being past timelike for every g_(b₀) + h′ with h′ small in 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b)
(Lemma 15.35 (2)); and every X′_I-curve in Ω^♮_(c_♮) begins on Σ_in (Lemma 38.8 (b)). Let ℐ⁺_♮ be the image
of Ω^♮_(c_♮) under (ρ′_0, ρ′_I, ω) ↦ (ρ′_0, ω): a domain of ℐ⁺ containing ℐ⁺ ∩ cl Ω^♮_(c_♮), and in general larger. Near
ℐ⁺, Ω^♮ ends at the future boundary {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3}, and t^♭_* = t_*(1 − (t_*/r)^(1/2)) increases along an
X′_I-curve at fixed x¹ towards ℐ⁺; so the curves through points with t^♭_* < T̂ + 3 < t_* leave Ω^♮ before they reach
ℐ⁺, through {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3}, at a value of ρ′_I that depends on (ρ′_0, ω).

Lemma 37.20 (b) is here Lemma 38.8 (b), and Lemma 37.21 holds on Ω^♮_(c_♮), in the translated chart, with
c_♮ in place of c and ℐ⁺_♮ in place of ℐ⁺_c, with the same proof. Its part (b) extends w, by the extension operator of
the proof of Lemma 37.17, to the set of the points over ℐ⁺_♮ with ρ′_I < c_♮, and both facts this uses hold here.
That set lies in U″. As U″ is closed, it suffices to take a point q of the set off ℐ⁺; let p be a point of Ω^♮_(c_♮) on
the X′_I-curve through q, which exists by the definition of ℐ⁺_♮. x¹ is constant along the curve and at most T″ − 1 on
𝒟, so x¹(q) = x¹(p) ≤ T″ − 1, and |x| = (T″ − x¹)/ρ′_I > 1/c_♮ ≥ 4/c ≥ 4R_9 ≥ 16R₁ at p and at q. Near infinity
t_*(p) ≤ t^♭_*(p)/C_♭ ≤ (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ (Lemma 15.35 (b)); so, with m₀ = R₁² and the margin of Section 38.2.3,
t_*(q) = x¹ + C′ − 8m₀|x_q|⁻¹ < t_*(p) + 8m₀|x_p|⁻¹ < (T̂ + 3)/C_♭ + R₁/2 < T₀ + T″ − 2, and q ∈ U″. And Ω^♮_(c_♮) is
a domain of the kind of Lemma 37.17: its boundary hypersurfaces in the interior are Σ_in, the coordinate
hypersurface {x′_I = c_♮^(1/2)}, and Σ_fin, which near ℐ⁺ is a graph {ρ′_0 = φ(x′_I, ω)} with φ smooth up to x′_I = 0,
as t^♭_* is smooth on M_(1/2) there with dt^♭_*|_(Tℐ⁺) = dt_*|_(Tℐ⁺) ≠ 0 (Section 38.1), and so bounded with all
its b-derivatives in the charts of that proof; Σ_fin stays away from I₀, t_* being bounded on it, and the two meet
transversally.

*The classes on 𝒟⁺.* Let χ_I := χ̂(ρ′_I), with χ̂ ∈ C_c^∞([0, c_♮/2)) equal to 1 on [0, c_♮/4], and
β := ℓ^♭_I − 3/2 as in Section 37.11. H^(k,α_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺) is the space of ġ on 𝒟⁺ for which u := ρ^(−3/2)ġ, in
the slots near infinity (in the translated chart over 𝒮), has a decomposition of order k as in
Lemma 37.22, with ℐ⁺_♮ and χ_I in place of ℐ⁺_c and χ̂(ρ_I): u^((0)) ∈ H^(k,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_♮),
a₀ := α_0 − 3/2, and ũ with every slot in H^(k,(a₀,2β))_b(𝒟⁺), this class imposing only H^k away from infinity. Its
norm is the infimum of the norms of the decompositions. The forcing classes H^(k,α+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b(𝒟⁺) are those of
Definition 27.16 (2), in the translated chart over 𝒮, restricted to 𝒟⁺; the data classes H^(k,α)_b(Σ^IVP) are the
weighted b-Sobolev spaces of Σ^IVP; and in the classes of Corollary 38.11 the coefficients of the expansion at ℐ⁺ are
functions on ℐ⁺_♮.

#### 38.2.5 The solution on 𝒟⁺

**Theorem 38.9** (The linear estimate on 𝒟⁺.) Let g_0 := φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) with |S| + |S⁰| small, or
g_0 := g_(b₀); h small in H^(10,ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺) (weights at ℐ⁺ in ρ′_I); L := L^(χ^♮_0)_(g_0+h,g_0);
α_0 > ℓ^♭_I, k ∈ ℕ with k ≥ 1, and d := 4. For f ∈ H^(k+d,α_0+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b(𝒟⁺) and data
ġ_0, ġ_1 ∈ H^(k+d,α_0)_b(Σ^IVP) there is a ġ ∈ H^(k,α_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺), unique in H^(max(k,2),α_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺),
with Lġ = f on 𝒟⁺, ġ = ġ_0 and r ℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))ġ = ġ_1 on Σ^IVP. (37.26) holds, its norms taken on 𝒟⁺ and on
Σ^IVP, with C depending on k, α_0, ℓ^♭_I, the parameters and the bound on h in H^10, and not on h otherwise; as in
Theorem 37.27, the norms of h are those of one decomposition of ρ^(−3/2)h, the same at every order (if h lies in
the class at every order, one with every norm finite exists, by the proof of Lemma 37.22 (c) with
Lemma 37.21 (b) on Ω^♮_(c_♮), Section 38.2.4), and the left side may be replaced by the norm of the decomposition of
ġ that the proof constructs, which is linear in (f, ġ_0, ġ_1). On Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, ġ depends only on f there
and on the data on Σ^IVP_(r_1).

*Proof.* As Theorem 37.27, with three changes. Its steps on Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, the forward part of Step 1 and
Steps 2–6, are taken with h extended across Σ^IVP_(r_1) to the past slab by the extension in the normal variable of the
proof of Lemma 37.17, which keeps h small in H^10 of the class; by Lemma 18.4 the forward solution does not
depend on the extension.

*The gauge.* On Ω_(ext,r_1), χ^♮_0 = χ_0 (Lemma 38.1 (c)); on 𝒮, χ^♮_0 = 1 = χ_0, as t_IVP ≥ r/4 there
(Lemma 38.5 (d)); so L = L^(χ_0) on Ω^♮ ∩ 𝒟⁺, and Corollary 37.35 applies there, χ_0 = 1 on Ω^♮_(c_♮)
(ρ′_I < c_♮ gives t_IVP ≥ r/4). On the compact part, L is an operator of the kind of (L) of Section 38.2.2: its
principal part is ½□_(g_0+h) ⊗ id, and its coefficients are smooth functions of the point, of (S, S⁰) and of h, ∂h and
∂²h, equal at (S, S⁰) = 0 and h = 0 to those of P_0 := L^(χ^♮_0)_(g_(b₀),g_(b₀)).

*The background.* g_0 ∈ 𝒢″ near 𝒮̄ by Lemma 38.7, and in the class of Lemma 37.38 on Ω_(ext,r_1)
(Lemma 38.3 (c)); it is Ricci flat, smooth on M, and C^∞-close to g_(b₀) on compact sets
when |S| + |S⁰| is small (Lemma 38.3 (a)).

*The regions.* c_♮, Σ_in and Σ_fin are those of Section 38.2.4. As T″ − x¹ ≥ 1 on 𝒟, ρ′_I ≥ 1/r ≥ c_♮/4 wherever ρ′_I
is defined on 𝒟 ∩ {r ≤ R_K + 2}. Let A be larger by 1 than the supremum of t_IVP + ½r on the bounded set
𝔒⁺ ∪ (𝒮 ∩ {ρ′_I ≥ c_♮/4}) ∪ (𝒟⁺ ∩ {r ≤ R_K + 2}), and put

    Q := (𝒟⁺ ∩ {t_IVP + ½r ≤ A}) ∖ {ρ′_I < c_♮/4},

the set {ρ′_I < c_♮/4} lying near infinity, where ρ′_I is defined (Lemma 38.5 (a)). Then:

(i) On Ω_N ∩ 𝒟⁺, near the interior of I₀: the forward part of Lemma 37.24, with the data on Σ^IVP_(r_1).

(ii) Away from ℐ⁺: on Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {τ′ ≥ 1/16} ∩ {ρ′_I > c_♮/4} (τ′ = t_IVP/|x| as in Section 37.11), the first step
of Lemma 37.25 (Proposition 37.10 for the system near the interior of I₀), unchanged; and on the compact set Q, (L)
of Section 38.2.2 for the forward problem, as follows.

*Q is of the first kind of Section 38.2.2.* Q is closed and lies in {r ≤ 2A}, so it is compact. It contains 𝔒⁺,
𝒮 ∩ {ρ′_I ≥ c_♮/4} and 𝒟⁺ ∩ {r ≤ R_K + 2}; and Σ^IVP ∩ Q = Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ 2A}, the annulus {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 2A} of Σ^IVP, as
ρ′_I ≥ ¾ on Σ^IVP where it is defined (t = C″ there, as in the proof of Lemma 38.8 (c)). Let γ be a past directed
causal curve of g_0 + h in 𝒟⁺ from p ∈ Q. It does not enter {ρ′_I < c_♮/4}, which lies to the future of the spacelike
{ρ′_I = c_♮/4} (Lemma 38.8 (a) with c_♮/4 in place of c_♮). While it lies in 𝔒⁺ ∪ 𝒮, it lies in Q. It enters
Ω_(ext,r_1) only through Σ^fut_(r_1), which has Ω_(ext,r_1) to its past (Lemma 37.1), at a point of the closure
of 𝔒⁺ ∪ (𝒮 ∩ {ρ′_I ≥ c_♮/4}), where t_IVP + ½r ≤ A − 1, and it does not cross Σ^fut_(r_1) back. Along future directed
causal curves in Ω_(ext,r_1), t_IVP + ½r increases, as |V|x|| < 2Vt for every future causal V (the proof of
Lemma 37.2). So t_IVP + ½r ≤ A on the rest of γ, and if p ∈ Ω_(ext,r_1) the same holds from p: γ stays
in Q. t_IVP is a time function of g_0 + h on Q: on Ω_(ext,r_1) by Lemma 37.2, and on the compact
(𝔒⁺ ∪ 𝒮) ∩ Q as dt_IVP is past timelike for g_(b₀) with a margin there, while g_0 + h − g_(b₀) is small in C⁰ there
(Sobolev embedding, 10 > 5/2).

*The bound on Q.* Extend h and f from 𝒟⁺ to a neighbourhood U of Q, as in Section 38.2.2, by an operator bounded on
every H^j and every C^j: near Q, 𝒟⁺ is a manifold with corners whose boundary hypersurfaces Σ^IVP, {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3}
and {r = r_♭} (Lemma 38.5 (e)) meet transversally, and the operator of Theorem A.35 applied in the
normal variable of each in turn, after flattening, as in the proof of Lemma 37.17, is such an extension. The
coefficients of L minus those of P_0 are c̃ = c̃_1 + c̃_2, c̃_1 smooth and depending only on (S, S⁰), and c̃_2 a smooth
function of the point, of (S, S⁰) and of h, ∂h, ∂²h that vanishes at h = 0; so ‖c̃‖_(H^j(U)) ≤ C_j(1 + ‖h‖_(H^(j+2)))
by the Moser estimate (Remark A.8, on a five-dimensional torus containing U); ‖c̃‖_(C⁴(U)) + ‖c̃‖_(H⁵(U)) is
bounded in terms of the bound on h in H^10 (Sobolev embedding, 10 > 6 + 5/2); and |g_0 + h − g_(b₀)| ≤ δ_L on U
for |S| + |S⁰| and h small. (L) at the order k + 3, which is at least 4 as k ≥ 1, with (38.5), gives
ġ ∈ H^(k+4)(Q) and, as N^U_(k+3) ≤ CN(f, ġ_0, ġ_1; k + 4) and N^U_4 ≤ CN(f, ġ_0, ġ_1; 5) ≤ CN(f, ġ_0, ġ_1; k + 4),

    ‖ġ‖_(H^(k+4)(Q)) ≤ C(N(f, ġ_0, ġ_1; k + 4) + ‖h‖_(H^(k+5))N(f, ġ_0, ġ_1; 5)),    (38.10)

without the last term for k = 1. This is the order the next step uses.

(iii) On Ω^♮_(c_♮), the second step of Lemma 37.25 and the steps of the proof of Theorem 37.27 near ℐ⁺, with c_♮
in place of c: the cut-off χ̂_(c_♮)(ρ′_I), Proposition 37.16, and the two integrations of Lemma 37.21 along the
curves of Lemma 38.8. The solution u₁ on {ρ′_I > c_♮/4} on which the commutator with χ̂_(c_♮)(ρ′_I) acts is given
by (ii): on Ω_(ext,r_1) by its first part, and on 𝒮 by Q. Nothing in these steps uses ρ′_0 beyond its role as a
coordinate; on 𝒮 it is bounded below, where the weight at I₀ is immaterial.

*Assembly.* Let O_1, O_2 and O_3 be the interiors relative to 𝒟⁺ of the closed sets Ω_N ∩ 𝒟⁺,
Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {τ′ ≥ 1/16, ρ′_I ≥ c_♮/4} and Q, and O_4 := Ω^♮_(c_♮), open in 𝒟⁺. They cover 𝒟⁺. A point of 𝒟⁺ with
r < R_K + 2 lies in O_3, as Q ⊃ 𝒟⁺ ∩ {r ≤ R_K + 2}. Let p ∈ 𝒟⁺ with r(p) ≥ R_K + 2, so p ∈ Ω^♮, and with
ρ′_I(p) ≥ c_♮, as otherwise p ∈ O_4. If p ∈ 𝒮 or p ∈ Σ^fut_(r_1), then t_IVP + ½r ≤ A − 1 at p, p lying in the closure
of 𝒮 ∩ {ρ′_I ≥ c_♮/4}, and ρ′_I > c_♮/4 near p; so a neighbourhood of p in 𝒟⁺ lies in Q, and p ∈ O_3. Otherwise a
neighbourhood of p in 𝒟⁺ lies in Ω_(ext,r_1), and p ∈ O_1 if τ′(p) < ¼, p ∈ O_2 if τ′(p) ≥ ¼. Where two of the
solutions of (i)–(iii) are defined they agree: on Q ∩ Ω_(ext,r_1), a compact set of the first kind (Q and
Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} are closed under past causal curves within 𝒟⁺, and its part of Σ^IVP is the annulus
{r_1 ≤ r ≤ 2A}), both solve the forward problem with the same data and forcing, and agree by the uniqueness clause of
(L); on the other overlaps as in Theorem 37.27. So they define one ġ on 𝒟⁺; and a partition of unity subordinate to
O_1, …, O_4, by functions of t_IVP, τ′, ρ′_I and r bounded with all their b-derivatives, bounds its norms by the sum of
those of the pieces. As the pieces overlap on open sets, no gluing across
a hypersurface is needed here (compare Lemma 38.6).

*The estimate.* The estimates compose as in *The estimate* of the proof of Theorem 37.27. (38.10) has the form
of the bound for u₁ there, C(N_(k+4) + |h|_(k+6)N_5), as ‖h‖_(H^(k+5)) ≤ |h|_(k+5) ≤ |h|_(k+6); its case k = 1 bounds the
low norm of u₁ on 𝒮 that the commutator bound (37.23) uses, by CN_5 ≤ CN_8; and it bounds ġ on Q, which
contains 𝒟⁺ ∩ {r ≤ R_K + 2}, where the class imposes H^k. The decomposition of ġ is that of Step 6 of the proof of
Theorem 37.27 on Ω^♮_(c_♮), u^((0)) coming from the second integration there, and ũ := u − χ_Iu^((0)) on 𝒟⁺. For k ≥ 7
that bookkeeping uses Lemma 37.26 for the norms of the decomposition of h; that lemma applies to the
spaces B^j of decompositions of the proof of Theorem 38.10, with the smoothing operators of its part (i), which are
linear, satisfy (20.1), and are built using nothing of this section. So (37.26) holds.

*Uniqueness.* Two solutions in H^(max(k,2),α_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺) differ by v with vanishing data and forcing. v = 0 on
Ω_N ∩ 𝒟⁺ by Lemma 37.24, on Q by the uniqueness clause of (L), v lying in H²(Q), and on the other regions by
Lemma 18.4, as in Theorem 37.27. Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} is closed under past causal curves within 𝒟⁺, with
past boundary Σ^IVP_(r_1); so by Lemma 18.4 ġ depends there only on f there and on the data on Σ^IVP_(r_1). The
case k = 0 is not needed: Theorem 38.10 uses the estimate for k ≥ d only, as (20.4) asks, and a bound in
H^(0,α_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b follows from the case k = 1. ∎

**Theorem 38.10** (The nonlinear solution on 𝒟⁺; [Hin26, p. 321].) Let g_0 be as in Theorem 38.9,
h_0, h_1 ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭_0)_b(Σ^IVP; S²T*), d := 7 and N_ex := 21d + 6 = 153, the regularity of Theorem 20.1 for this d.
There is ε_0 > 0 such that, if ‖h_j‖_(H^(N_ex,ℓ^♭_0)_b(Σ^IVP)) < ε_0, there is a unique h ∈ H^(∞,ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺),
small in H^(3d), with P^♮(g_0 + h, g_0) = 0 on 𝒟⁺, h = h_0 and r ℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h = h_1 on Σ^IVP. On
Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} it equals the solution of Theorem 37.28 (with Corollary 37.35, for the background g_0 and the
data restricted to Σ^IVP_(r_1)). For every k and ε > 0 there is ε_1 ∈ (0, ε_0] such that
‖h_j‖_(H^(N_ex+k,ℓ^♭_0)_b) < ε_1 gives ‖h‖_(H^(3d+k,ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b) < ε.

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 37.28 on 𝒟⁺, the unknown being a decomposition:
B^k := H^(k,a₀)_b(ℐ⁺_♮) × H^(k,ℓ^♭_0,ℓ^♭_I)_b(𝒟⁺; S²T*), a₀ := ℓ^♭_0 − 3/2, with the sum of the two norms, made monotone
in k by Remark 20.3. An element x = (v, h̃) is, after conjugation, a decomposition (Section 38.2.4) of the tensor h_x
that equals h̃ + ρ^(3/2)χ_Iv in slot 6 and h̃ in the other slots; x ↦ h_x is linear, and the norm of h_x in
H^(k,ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺) is at most C|x|_k. F^k := H^(k,ℓ^♭_0+2,(−′,ℓ^♭_I+1))_b(𝒟⁺) × H^(k,ℓ^♭_0)_b(Σ^IVP)², the
support classes are trivial, η_0 := 1, and
Φ(x) := (P^♮(g_0 + h_x, g_0), h_x|_(Σ^IVP) − h_0, rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))h_x|_(Σ^IVP) − h_1) on {|x|_(3d) < δ}.

(i) *Smoothing.* Componentwise: on v the operator S̃_θ of Step 4 of the proof of Proposition 20.4 built on ℐ⁺_♮, and on
h̃ the same operator built on 𝒟⁺, a compact manifold with corners in M_(1/2) whose boundary hypersurfaces are I₀ and ℐ⁺,
taken in ℋ_b, and Σ^IVP, {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3} and {r = r_♭} (Lemma 38.5 (e)), taken in ℋ̄; these meet transversally
(dt_IVP, dr and dt^♭_* are pairwise independent where the hypersurfaces meet, Σ^IVP stays away from ℐ⁺, and
{t^♭_* = T̂ + 3} meets ℐ⁺ transversally, Section 38.1), and the b-Sobolev spaces of M and of M_(1/2) coincide
(Section 38.4). S_θ is linear and the norm of B^k is the sum of the two norms, so (20.1) holds; the support
conditions are vacuous.

(ii) *The map.* Write h := h_x. Near infinity, P^♮ = P^(χ_0) on Ω^♮ ∩ 𝒟⁺ (as in the proof of Theorem 38.9), and
Corollary 27.18 holds for it by Lemma 37.34, near 𝒮 in the translated chart. On 𝒟⁺ ∩ {r ≤ R_K + 3},
P^♮(g_0 + h, g_0) is a smooth function of the point, of (S, S⁰) and of h, ∂h, ∂²h, which vanishes at h = 0
(P^♮(g_0, g_0) = Ric(g_0) = 0), and its first two derivatives in h are differential operators of order 2 whose
coefficients are functions of the same kind. So (20.2)–(20.3) hold as in part (ii) of the proof of
Theorem 37.28, applied to the components of x, with the loss 2 and low norms of order at most 5 ≤ d: near infinity by
the Moser estimates used there, and on the compact part by the Moser estimates on a five-dimensional torus containing an
extension of it (Remark A.8 for the compositions, Corollary A.30 (2) for the products). The trace
on Σ^IVP is bounded B^(k+1) → H^(k,ℓ^♭_0)_b(Σ^IVP) (χ_I = 0 near Σ^IVP). The data enter the map:
‖Φ(x)‖_k ≤ C′_k(1 + |x|_(k+d)) + Σ_j‖h_j‖_(H^(k,ℓ^♭_0)_b(Σ^IVP)), with C′_k independent of the data, so for k ≤ N_ex the
constants C_k of (20.3) are bounded independently of the data once these norms are at most 1 in H^(N_ex).

(iii) *Right inverses.* For x in the set above, Ψ(x)(f, ġ_0, ġ_1) is the decomposition of ġ that the proof of
Theorem 38.9 constructs, with α_0 := ℓ^♭_0, for h := h_x with its decomposition x; it is linear in (f, ġ_0, ġ_1),
h_(Ψ(x)F) = ġ, and (37.26) for these decompositions gives (20.4), as in part (iii) of the proof of
Theorem 37.28; 3d = 21 ≥ 10 gives the smallness of h that Theorem 38.9 asks.

The threshold of Theorem 20.1 depends on the constants up to the order N_ex only, so it is uniform, and ‖Φ(0)‖_(2d)
is below it for data small in H^(N_ex); the shifted scales of the proof of Theorem 37.28 give the higher norms in the
same way, with N_ex + k in place of N_ex; Theorem 20.1 gives x with |x|_(3d) < δ and Φ(x) = 0, and h := h_x.
*Uniqueness.* If h and h′ are two such solutions, small in H^(3d), then L̄(h − h′) = 0 with vanishing data,
L̄ := ∫_0^1 L^(χ^♮_0)_(g_0+h′+s(h−h′),g_0) ds. L̄ has the structure that the proof of Theorem 38.9 uses: near infinity
as in the uniqueness of Theorem 37.28, and on the compact part it is an operator of the kind of (L) of
Section 38.2.2; so Theorem 38.9 holds for L̄ with the same proof, and h = h′. On Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, which
is closed under past causal curves within 𝒟⁺ with past boundary Σ^IVP_(r_1), h and the solution of Theorem 37.28 with
the data restricted to Σ^IVP_(r_1) both solve the forward problem and are small in H⁸; their difference vanishes by the
forward parts of Lemma 37.24 and Lemma 37.25 for the averaged operator, as in the uniqueness of
Theorem 37.28. ∎

So the solution of Proposition 38.4 on 𝒟⁺ is that of Theorem 38.10; on 𝒟⁻ it is the backward solution on 𝔒⁻ and,
near infinity, the exterior solution on the past slab of Ω_(ext,r_1) (the proof of Proposition 38.4).

**Corollary 38.11** (The orders on the slab.) Under the hypotheses of Theorem 37.36 on the data, the
solution of Theorem 38.10 lies in H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0),⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I)_b(𝒟⁺), with the bound (37.39), the
coefficients of its expansion at ℐ⁺ being functions on ℐ⁺_♮ (Section 38.2.4); in particular h_(S,S⁰) has the orders
(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I) at ℐ⁺ on 𝒮, as Proposition 38.4 (3) states.

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 37.36 on 𝒟⁺, with Theorem 38.9 in place of the linear estimate
(37.34). Its Step 1 works at I₀, which 𝒟⁺ meets only within Ω_(ext,r_1); its Step 2 integrates, slot by
slot, along X_I and X_0 − X_I near ℐ⁺ (Lemma 21.33, Lemma 21.42), and on Ω^♮_(c_♮) the curves followed
backward reach {ρ′_I = c_♮}, where the solution is smooth (Lemma 38.8 (b)); away from ℐ⁺ there is nothing to show.
The structure (27.16) used there holds near 𝒮 by Lemma 38.7 and the translation. ∎

#### 38.2.6 Past causal curves near null infinity and near spatial infinity

The uniqueness lemma Lemma 18.4 asks, at each point p, for a compact set containing the part of the causal past of
p above a level of the time function. Near ℐ⁺ the levels of t^♭_* reach r = ∞, and near I₀ those of t_IVP do; so these
sets need a bound on r along past causal curves. Lemma 18.5 (a) bounds r by t_* + R̃(r), a time function of
g_(b₀) and of the combinations G_θ only: for h small in the class 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b) of Lemma 15.35 at ℓ = ½,
dt, and with it d(t_* + R̃), can
