be spacelike near ℐ⁺, as (g_(b₀)⁻¹ − η⁻¹)(dt, dt) = O(r⁻²) there while a perturbation of that class is larger. The next
two lemmas give the bounds for every metric of the classes used.

**Lemma 38.12** (The time function below Ω_*.) Let ℓ = ½, and let ε_G, C_♭, r′_0, r^♮ and t^♭_* be those of
Lemma 15.35 for g_0 = g_(b₀), built with the gluing constant C_g ≥ max(4(r′_0 + 1), 32, 16R₁) fixed at the start
of the chapter, with t^♭_* given on {t_* > 0} by the formulae of its proof (Lemma 17.2 (iv)).
Let Ω_(1/2) := cl_M{t_* ≥ ½}, with interior Ω°_(1/2), and let 𝒢̃_(1/2) be the class 𝒢̃^(0,(2ℓ,0,0))_(e3b) of
Definition 15.33 with Ω_(1/2) in place of Ω, with its norm. There are ε′_G ∈ (0, ε_G], C₁ and R_V such that for every
g = g_(b₀) + h with ‖h‖_(𝒢̃_(1/2)) < ε′_G:

(i) near ℐ⁺ on Ω_(1/2), with ρ := ρ_I = t_*/r, the coefficients of g⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ in the basis

    ρ∂²_(t_*),   ∂_(t_*) ⊗_s ∂_r,   x_I∂_(t_*) ⊗_s r⁻¹∂_ω,   ρ⁻¹∂²_r,   x_I⁻¹∂_r ⊗_s r⁻¹∂_ω,   r⁻¹∂_ω ⊗_s r⁻¹∂_ω

of the proof of Lemma 15.35 are at most C₁ε′_Gρ^ℓ, and those of g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ at most C₁(ε′_G + ρ^(1−ℓ))ρ^ℓ;

(ii) V := t∂_t + r∂_r is future timelike for g on Ω_(1/2) ∩ {r ≥ R_V};

(iii) dt^♭_* is past timelike for g on Ω°_(1/2), so t^♭_* is a time function of g there, and dt^♭_*(V) > 0 on
Ω°_(1/2) ∩ {r ≥ R_V};

(iv) dr is future timelike for g on Ω_(1/2) ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r^♮}.

The statements are pointwise, so they hold as well for h given only on an open subset of Ω_(1/2), and small there in
that norm, on that subset.

*Proof.* On Ω_(1/2) ∩ {t_* ≥ 1} ⊂ Ω (Ω = cl_M{t_* ≥ 1}, Definition 14.3) the statements are Lemma 15.35 and its
proof, the norm of h on Ω being at most its norm on Ω_(1/2). The proof of Lemma 15.35 is pointwise, and it is run
on Ω_(1/2) ∩ {t_* ≤ 1} as follows.

(i) The proof of Lemma 15.35 bounds the coefficients of g⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ by C‖h‖ρ^ℓ and those of g_(b₀)⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹
by Cρ, times powers of ρ_+, and uses ρ_+ ≤ 1 on Ω only to bound these powers. On Ω_(1/2), ρ_+ ≤ 2, as in the proof of
Lemma 17.2 (iv) (near ℐ⁺ ∩ ι⁺, ρ_+ = 1/t_*); so both bounds hold with a larger C₁. That proof uses them on
{ρ_I ≤ ρ_a}, ρ_a its constant, with 2/C_g ≤ ρ_a; they hold on the same set here.

(ii) As in the proof of Lemma 15.35 and in Section 15.7: ḡ(V, V) = −t_*² − 2t_*r, and
by (K1) |g_(b₀)(V, V) − ḡ(V, V)| ≤ C₂r⁻²(t_* + r)². For t_* ≥ ½ this is at most ½(t_*² + 2t_*r) once r ≥ 8C₂ and
r² ≥ 8C₂: if t_* ≤ r, the left side is at most 4C₂ and the right side at least t_*r ≥ r/2; if t_* > r, the left side is
at most 4C₂t_*²r⁻² and the right side at least ½t_*². Take R_V ≥ R₂ with R_V ≥ 8C₂ and R_V² ≥ 8C₂.
The bound |h(V, V)| ≤ Cε′_G|g_(b₀)(V, V)| of that proof uses, near ℐ⁺, the bound of (i), and where x_I ≥ c_V the
membership of h in its frames, both valid on Ω_(1/2); so V is timelike for g on Ω_(1/2) ∩ {r ≥ R_V} once ε′_G is small.
It is future directed for g_(b₀), as there, and so for g, the orientation being continuous along g_(b₀) + sh, s ∈ [0, 1].

(iii) Where t^♭_* = t_*F₁(ρ), dt^♭_* = d(t_*F₁) = A dt_* + B dr with A = 1 − (1 + ℓ)ρ^ℓ and B = ℓρ^(ℓ+1), as in the
proof of Lemma 15.35.

*The background near ℐ⁺.* Let Y := Ω_(1/2) ∩ {ρ_I ≤ 2/C_g}. On Y, ρ ≤ 2/C_g ≤ 1/16, so ρ^ℓ ≤ ¼, A ∈ [5/8, 1] and
0 < B ≤ ½ρ^(3/2) ≤ 1/128; and r = t_*/ρ ≥ C_g/4 ≥ max(r′_0 + 1, 4R₁), as t_* ≥ ½. So the exact forms of g_(b₀) and
t_* on {r ≥ 3R₁} apply on Y: in the coordinates (t, x) of Section 21.4 (t is not the t_* + r
of Lemma 15.35), g_(b₀)⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − u(∂_t + ∂_r)^(⊗2) with u := m₀r⁻² (Proposition 21.21), and
dt_* = dt − (1 − 8u)dr ((21.30)), so (∂_t + ∂_r)t_* = 8u and

    g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = −16u(1 − 2u)²,     g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt_*, dr) = −1 + 8u(1 − u),     g_(b₀)⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − u.

On Y, u ≤ 1/16, so the first is ≤ 0, the second ≤ −½ and the third ≤ 1. As A, B > 0,

    g_(b₀)⁻¹(d(t_*F₁), d(t_*F₁)) ≤ 2AB(−½) + B² = −B(A − B) ≤ −½B = −½ℓρ^(ℓ+1)     on Y,

at every t_* ≥ ½: the correction to ḡ⁻¹ that carries no factor B, the A²-term, has the sign of the main term. Also
g_(b₀)⁻¹(d(t_*F₁), dt_*) = A g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) + B g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt_*, dr) < 0, and dt_* is past timelike for g_(b₀)
(Lemma 15.2); two timelike covectors with negative product lie in the same cone, so d(t_*F₁) is past timelike
for g_(b₀) on Y.

*The perturbation near ℐ⁺.* On Y ∩ {ρ_I ≤ ρ_−}, where dt^♭_* = d(t_*F₁) (ρ_− < 1/C_g, and r ≥ r′_0 + 1 there), the
coefficients of g⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ in the basis of (i) are at most C₁ε′_Gρ^ℓ, and the six basis elements take on
α ⊗ α, α := dt^♭_*, the values ρA², at most 2AB in modulus, 0, ρ⁻¹B², 0 and 0, each at most ρ (2AB ≤ ρ^(3/2) and
ρ⁻¹B² = ¼ρ²). So |(g⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹)(α, α)| ≤ 3C₁ε′_Gρ^(ℓ+1) = 6C₁ε′_G B, and g⁻¹(α, α) ≤ −¼ℓρ^(ℓ+1) once
ε′_G ≤ 1/(24C₁). The same holds for g_(b₀) + sh, s ∈ [0, 1], so α is timelike for each of these metrics; it is past
timelike for g_(b₀), so it stays in the past cone along the path, which is the time orientation of g (as in (ii)).
So dt^♭_* is past timelike for g on Ω°_(1/2) ∩ {ρ_I ≤ ρ_−}.

*The rest.* The rest of Ω_(1/2) ∩ {t_* ≤ 1} is K := {½ ≤ t_* ≤ 1, ρ_I ≥ ρ_−} ∩ Ω_(1/2), which is compact (r ≤ t_*/ρ_−
there). On K, dt^♭_* is past timelike for g_(b₀). Indeed, by the formulae of the proof of Lemma 15.35, which cover
{t_* ≥ ½} as C_g ≥ 4(r′_0 + 1) (Lemma 17.2 (iv)), and with t := t_* + r there, dt^♭_* is C_♭dt_* on
{r ≤ r′_0 − 1}, a positive combination of dt_* and dt on {r ≤ C_g t_*/2}, and, on {r ≥ r′_0 + 1}, d(t_*F₁) where
ρ_I ≤ ρ_−, C_♭dt where ρ_I ≥ ρ⁺, and a positive combination of d(t_*F₁) and dt on [ρ_−, ρ⁺]. dt_* is past timelike for
g_(b₀) everywhere (Lemma 15.2), and so is dt on {r ≥ r′_0 − 1}. Indeed g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt, dt) ≤ −1 + C₂r⁻² < 0 there;
two timelike covectors have a non-zero product, so g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt, dt_*), a continuous function of x alone (dt, dt_* and
g_(b₀) being stationary), does not vanish on the connected set {|x| ≥ r′_0 − 1}, and it tends to η⁻¹(dt, dt − d|x|) = −1
as |x| → ∞; so it is negative, and dt lies in the past cone of dt_*. These are statements at a point that do not involve
t_*. d(t_*F₁) is past timelike for g_(b₀) on
Ω_(1/2) ∩ {ρ_I ≤ ρ⁺} ⊂ Y, by the first step, as ρ⁺ < 2/C_g. The past cone being convex, dt^♭_* is past timelike for
g_(b₀) at every point of K. By compactness, g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt^♭_*, dt^♭_*) ≤ −c_K < 0 on K, and, the norm bounding h in C⁰ on
K, g_s⁻¹(dt^♭_*, dt^♭_*) ≤ −½c_K for g_s := g_(b₀) + sh, s ∈ [0, 1], once ε′_G is small; as before dt^♭_* is past
timelike for g on K. Where dt^♭_* is past timelike and V is future timelike, dt^♭_*(V) > 0.

(iv) g_(b₀)⁻¹(dr, dr) ≤ −c_r < 0 on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r^♮} by (H4) and compactness of this range of r, at every t_*, as g_(b₀)
is stationary; dr is future timelike for g_(b₀) there, as in the proof of Lemma 15.35 (1), and on
Ω_(1/2) ∩ {t_* ≤ 1, r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r^♮}, a compact set, the perturbation is O(ε′_G). ∎

**Lemma 38.13** (The radius near ℐ⁺ along past causal curves.) Let ℓ = ½, ε′_G, C₁, R_V, r′_0, r^♮,
t^♭_*, Ω_(1/2) and 𝒢̃_(1/2) be those of Lemma 38.12, C_♭ the constant of Lemma 15.35 (b), and T ≥ ½; put
T_1 := T/C_♭ + 1. There is R_T < ∞, depending only on T and on the constants of Lemma 15.35, Lemma 38.12
and their proofs, such that for every g = g_(b₀) + h with ‖h‖_(𝒢̃_(1/2)) < ε′_G:

(a) on W_T := Ω°_(1/2) ∩ {t_* < T_1, r > R_T} the covector α := dt^♭_* + r⁻¹dr is past timelike for g, so
Ξ := t^♭_* + log r is a time function on W_T;

(b) if ½ < c < t^♭_*(p) ≤ T and γ is a past directed causal curve of g in Ω°_(1/2) from p along which t^♭_* ≥ c,
then r ≤ R_p := max(R_T, r(p)) e^(t^♭_*(p)−c) on γ;

(c) if moreover X ⊂ Ω°_(1/2) is open and contains L_p := {c ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t^♭_*(p), min(r(p), r^♮) ≤ r ≤ R_p}, then
L_p is compact and contains J⁻_X(p) ∩ {t^♭_* ≥ c}. These are the compact sets Lemma 18.4 asks for, with
τ := t^♭_*.

The proof is pointwise along the curves, so (a)–(c) hold as well for h given and small in that norm on an open
Y ⊂ Ω°_(1/2) only, with W_T ∩ Y in (a) and the curves and X in Y in (b)–(c).

*Proof.* (a) By Lemma 38.12 (i), near ℐ⁺ and with ρ := ρ_I = t_*/r, the coefficients of g⁻¹ − ḡ⁻¹ in the basis
displayed there are at most C₁(ε′_G + ρ^(1−ℓ))ρ^ℓ ≤ Cρ^ℓ for ρ ≤ 1, with C := max(1, C₁(ε′_G + 1));
ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dt_*) = 0, ḡ⁻¹(dt_*, dr) = −1 and ḡ⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1; on {ρ ≤ ρ_−, r ≥ r′_0 + 1}, t^♭_* = t_*F₁(ρ) and
dt^♭_* = A dt_* + B dr with A = 1 − (1 + ℓ)ρ^ℓ and B = ℓρ^(ℓ+1) (the coefficients of the proof of Lemma 15.35);
and V := t∂_t + r∂_r is future timelike for g on {r ≥ R_V}, with dt^♭_*(V) > 0 (Lemma 38.12 (ii)–(iii)). Let
x := ρ^ℓ, so ρ ≤ x ≤ 1 for ρ ≤ 1, and

    ρ_T := min(ρ_−, (37CT_1)^(−1/ℓ)),     R_T := max(R_V, r′_0 + 1, T_1/ρ_T).

On W_T, ρ < T_1/R_T ≤ ρ_T, so all of this applies, and x ≤ (37CT_1)⁻¹ ≤ 1/37. Then α = A dt_* + B′dr with
B′ := B + r⁻¹. As (1 + ℓ)x ≤ 3/74, A ∈ [½, 1]. As t_* ∈ (½, T_1) on W_T, r⁻¹ = ρ/t_* ∈ [ρ/T_1, 2ρ], and
B = ℓxρ ≤ ½ρ, so B′ ∈ [r⁻¹, (5/2)ρ]. The six basis elements take on α ⊗ α the values ρA², at most 2AB′ in modulus
(AB′ ≥ 0), 0, ρ⁻¹B′², 0 and 0. Hence

    g⁻¹(α, α) ≤ ḡ⁻¹(α, α) + Cx(ρA² + 2AB′ + ρ⁻¹B′²) = −2AB′ + B′² + Cx(ρA² + 2AB′ + ρ⁻¹B′²).

Each term is bounded as follows. −2AB′ ≤ −2A r⁻¹ ≤ −r⁻¹, as B′ ≥ r⁻¹ and A ≥ ½. B′² ≤ (25/4)ρ². And
ρA² + 2AB′ + ρ⁻¹B′² ≤ ρ + 5ρ + (25/4)ρ = (49/4)ρ. So

    g⁻¹(α, α) ≤ −r⁻¹ + (25/4)ρ² + (49/4)Cxρ ≤ −r⁻¹ + ((25/4) + (49/4)C)xρ ≤ −r⁻¹ + (37/2)Cxρ,

using ρ ≤ x and C ≥ 1. Finally ρ ≤ T_1 r⁻¹ (as r⁻¹ ≥ ρ/T_1), so

    g⁻¹(α, α) ≤ r⁻¹(−1 + (37/2)CT_1x) ≤ r⁻¹(−1 + ½) = −1/(2r).

So α is timelike, and α(V) = dt^♭_*(V) + 1 > 0, as dr(V) = r: a timelike covector positive on a future timelike vector
is past timelike. So Ξ, with dΞ = α, is a time function on W_T.

(b) t^♭_* is a time function of g on Ω°_(1/2) (Lemma 38.12 (iii)), so along γ, c ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t^♭_*(p) ≤ T, and
½ < t_* ≤ t^♭_*/C_♭ < T_1 (Lemma 15.35 (b)). Let R′_p := max(R_T, r(p)), suppose that r > R_p at γ(s_1), and let
s_0 := sup{s ≤ s_1 : r(γ(s)) ≤ R′_p}, which exists as r(γ(0)) = r(p). On (s_0, s_1], r > R′_p ≥ R_T, so γ lies in W_T
there and Ξ ∘ γ is non-increasing (dΞ = α is negative on past causal vectors); by continuity Ξ(γ(s_1)) ≤ Ξ(γ(s_0)),
and r(γ(s_0)) = R′_p. Hence log r(γ(s_1)) ≤ log R′_p + t^♭_*(γ(s_0)) − t^♭_*(γ(s_1)) ≤ log R′_p + t^♭_*(p) − c, that
is r(γ(s_1)) ≤ R_p, against the assumption. So r ≤ R_p on γ.

(c) For q ∈ J⁻_X(p) ∩ {t^♭_* ≥ c} let γ be a past directed causal curve in X from p to q. t^♭_* decreases along γ, so
c ≤ t^♭_*(q) ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t^♭_*(p) on it; r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮) on it, dr being future timelike for g on Ω_(1/2) ∩ {r ≤ r^♮}
(Lemma 38.12 (iv)), as in Lemma 18.5 (a); and r ≤ R_p by (b). So q ∈ L_p. L_p is closed, and on it
t_* ∈ [c, t^♭_*(p)/C_♭] and min(r(p), r^♮) ≤ r ≤ R_p, where r(p) (p ∈ X) and r^♮ lie in the range of r on M°; so L_p is
compact. ∎

**Lemma 38.14** (Uniqueness near spatial infinity for the initial family.) Let
g_(S,S⁰) := φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) + h_(S,S⁰) on 𝒟, where h_(S,S⁰) is given on 𝒟 ∩ Ω_(ext,r_1) by Theorem 37.39 for
φ_(S,S⁰) and on 𝒮 by Theorem 38.10, and is small in C⁰ on 𝔒, with |S| + |S⁰| and the data small. There is R ≥ R_5 such
that 𝒟 ∩ {r ≥ R} ⊂ Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝒮 and t_IVP = t − C″ there, and:

(a) on 𝒟 ∩ {r ≥ R}, every Cartesian component of g_(S,S⁰) − η is at most 1/20 in modulus, g_(S,S⁰)⁻¹(dt, dt) ≤ −½,
and |V^x| ≤ 2|V^t| for every g_(S,S⁰)-causal vector V; dt lies in the component of the timelike covectors of g_(S,S⁰)
that continues the past cone of η along η + s(g_(S,S⁰) − η), s ∈ [0, 1], and g_(S,S⁰) is time-oriented on 𝒟 as a small
deformation of g_(b₀), for which dt_IVP is past timelike (Lemma 21.22 (b)); so dt_IVP is past timelike for g_(S,S⁰)
on 𝒟;

(b) along causal curves of g_(S,S⁰) in {r ≥ R}, r + 2t_IVP does not increase towards the past and r − 2t_IVP does not
increase towards the future;

(c) along a past (future) directed causal curve of g_(S,S⁰) from p on which τ := t_IVP (τ := −t_IVP) stays ≥ c,

    r ≤ max(R, r(p)) + 2(τ(p) − c).

*Proof.* 𝔒 is compact, so for R above its radius 𝒟 ∩ {r ≥ R} lies in Ω_(ext,r_1) ∪ 𝒮 (Lemma 38.5), and
t_IVP = t − C″ for r ≥ R_5. There φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) agrees with an element of the class 𝒢 of Definition 27.9, so
φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀) − η ∈ ρ₀²ρ_I²C^∞: on Ω_(ext,r_1) by Lemma 37.38 for φ_(S,S⁰) (Lemma 38.3
(c)), and on 𝒮 by Lemma 38.7. And h_(S,S⁰) lies in the class H^(k,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0),⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I)_b of Definition 27.6,
k ≥ 5, with norm tending to 0 with ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(d_0)): on Ω_(ext,r_1) by Theorem 37.39 (2) with
Theorem 37.36, and on 𝒮 by Corollary 38.11. Its slot coordinates are bounded pointwise by that norm (Sobolev
embedding on the unit cubes of a b-metric, as in the proof of Lemma 27.5: k ≥ 5 > 5/2, and the weights ℓ_0 > 0,
ℓ_I > 3/2 and the real parts of the index sets are positive), and they are bounded multiples of its Cartesian components
(Lemma 27.4: the frames are related by F_0(ω)(I + ρ²C^∞)). So for R large and the data and |S| + |S⁰| small, each
Cartesian component of δ := g_(S,S⁰) − η is at most ε := 1/20 in modulus on 𝒟 ∩ {r ≥ R}.

Then, in the coordinates (t, x), with η = diag(−1, 1, 1, 1, 1), the matrix η⁻¹δ has entries ±δ_ij, so its maximum row-sum
norm is at most 5ε = ¼. The Neumann series g_(S,S⁰)⁻¹ = Σ_(k≥0)(−η⁻¹δ)^k η⁻¹
gives |(g_(S,S⁰)⁻¹ − η⁻¹)(dt, dt)| ≤ Σ_(k≥1)(5ε)^k = 5ε/(1 − 5ε) = ⅓, so g_(S,S⁰)⁻¹(dt, dt) ≤ −1 + ⅓ = −⅔ ≤ −½. The
same bound holds for η + sδ, s ∈ [0, 1], so dt stays timelike along that path, in the component that continues the past
cone of η. For V causal for g_(S,S⁰), η(V, V) ≤ −δ(V, V) ≤ Σ_(i,j)|δ_ij||V^i||V^j| ≤ ε(Σ_i|V^i|)² ≤ 5ε((V^t)² + |V^x|²),
by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in five variables; with η(V, V) = −(V^t)² + |V^x|² this
gives |V^x|² ≤ ((1 + 5ε)/(1 − 5ε))(V^t)² = (5/3)(V^t)², so |V^x| ≤ 2|V^t|.

On 𝒟 ∩ {r ≤ R}, dt_IVP is past timelike for g_(b₀) (Lemma 21.22 (b)), with a margin on this compact set, so also
for g_(S,S⁰), φ_(S,S⁰) tending to the identity there and h_(S,S⁰) being small in C⁰ there (on 𝔒⁻ by (N) of
Section 38.2.2, and on 𝒟⁺ by the smallness of the solution of Theorem 38.10 in H^(3d) of its class). This proves
(a), dt_IVP = dt on {r ≥ R}.

(b) For a past directed causal V in {r ≥ R}, dt(V) = V^t < 0 and dr(V) ≤ |V^x| ≤ −2V^t, so
d(r + 2t_IVP)(V) ≤ 0; likewise for future directed V, d(r − 2t_IVP)(V) ≤ |V^x| − 2V^t ≤ 0.

(c) Let γ be a past directed causal curve from p to q along which τ = t_IVP ≥ c, put R′ := max(R, r(p)), and let s_0
be the last parameter before q at which r ≤ R′ (it exists, as r(p) ≤ R′). Beyond s_0, γ lies in {r > R′} ⊂ {r ≥ R},
so by (b) r(q) + 2τ(q) ≤ r(γ(s_0)) + 2τ(γ(s_0)) ≤ R′ + 2τ(p), τ decreasing along γ. So
r(q) ≤ R′ + 2(τ(p) − τ(q)) ≤ R′ + 2(τ(p) − c). For future directed curves and τ = −t_IVP the same argument with
r − 2t_IVP applies. ∎

#### 38.2.7 Proof of the initial family

*Proof of Proposition 38.4.* By Lemma 38.5 (b) and (e), 𝒟 is the union of 𝒟 ∩ Ω_(ext,r_1), of 𝒟⁺ and of 𝔒⁻.
The solution is found on each, the three agree where two of them are defined, and they are glued across Σ^IVP. Write
φ := φ_(S,S⁰).

*Exterior.* By Lemma 38.1 (c), P^♮ = P^(χ_0) on Ω_(ext,r_1), so Theorem 37.39 for φ_(S,S⁰)
(Lemma 38.3 (c)), its h being the solution that Theorem 37.30 gives for the data h̊_0, h̊_1,
gives h_(S,S⁰) on Ω_(ext,r_1), smooth in (S, S⁰), with (2) there by its (3); its hypotheses (the constraints, and
Υ^0 = 0 at Σ^IVP) are Proposition 37.41 (1)–(2).

*Forward part.* On 𝒟⁺ the solution is that of Theorem 38.10 with the data h⁰_(S,S⁰), h¹_(S,S⁰) on Σ^IVP, which are
small in H^(N_ex) of their class when (γ̃, k̃) is small in H^(d_0), by the choice of d_0. On Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ 𝒟⁺ it equals
the exterior solution, which is the solution of Theorem 37.28 for the background φ^*g_(b₀) in the cut-off gauge (the
proof of Theorem 37.39), by the last clause of Theorem 38.10. It is the continuation near the interior of ℐ⁺ to
{t^♭_* = T̂ + 3}, small, with the orders (⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I) at ℐ⁺ (Corollary 38.11). On 𝒮, χ^♮_0 = 1, as t_IVP ≥ r/4
there (Lemma 38.5 (d)) and so χ_0 = 1.

*Backward part.* On 𝔒⁻, (38.4) is the quasilinear wave equation of Section 38.2.2, and 𝔒⁻ is a compact set
of the second kind there (Lemma 38.5 (e)). Its data on Σ^IVP ∩ 𝔒⁻ are small and smooth, and (N) gives h_(S,S⁰)
on 𝔒⁻, backward from Σ^IVP to {t_IVP = −ν}, small in every H^k when the data are small in H^(k+k′) for some k′. On
Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ 𝔒⁻, which lies in the past slab, it equals the exterior solution: the difference v of the two solves
L̄v = 0 with vanishing Cauchy data on Σ^IVP ∩ Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ 𝔒⁻, L̄ the average of the linearisations along the segment
between them (as in the uniqueness of *(1)* below), an operator of the kind of (L) of Section 38.2.2 for a metric
C⁰-close to g_(b₀); and Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ 𝔒⁻ is a compact set of the second kind for it, future directed causal curves in
𝒟⁻ from its points staying in 𝔒⁻ (Lemma 38.5 (e)) and in the past slab, which lies to the future of the
spacelike Σ^past_(r_1) (Lemma 37.1), while its part of Σ^IVP is the annulus {r_1 ≤ r ≤ 2R_8}. So v = 0 there by
the uniqueness clause of (L).

*Gluing.* 𝒟⁺ ∩ 𝔒⁻ = Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ 2R_8}, where the forward and the backward solutions have the same Cauchy data
h⁰_(S,S⁰), h¹_(S,S⁰). Every point of 𝒟 that does not lie on Σ^IVP ∩ {R_ν ≤ r ≤ r_1} has a neighbourhood in 𝒟 contained
in one of the three sets: in 𝒟⁺ if t_IVP > 0, or if t_IVP = 0 and r < R_ν (𝒟 ending at Σ^IVP there); in 𝔒⁻ if
t_IVP < 0 and r < R_8; and in Ω_(ext,r_1) if t_IVP = 0 and r > r_1, or if t_IVP < 0 and r ≥ R_8, as ν(r) < (r − r_1)/12
there. Let p ∈ Σ^IVP with R_ν ≤ r(p) ≤ r_1, and m ≥ 2. The forward solution lies in H^k of its class on 𝒟⁺ for every
k, a space of restrictions, so near p it is the restriction to {t_IVP ≥ 0} of a tensor u_1 of class C^m on a coordinate
ball V about p in M (Sobolev embedding, k > m + 5/2). The backward solution is, near p, the restriction of the solution
on the slab of the proof of (N), which is of class C^m and solves (38.4) near p below Σ^IVP, beyond 𝒟 as well
(the coefficients there are those of the equation, p lying in 𝔒⁻); let u_2 be it on V, V being small. u_1 and u_2 have
the same Cauchy data on Σ^IVP ∩ V, solve (38.4) on V ∩ {t_IVP > 0} and on V ∩ {t_IVP < 0}, and Σ^IVP is
spacelike for φ^*g_(b₀) + u_1. Lemma 38.6, with A₁ := V ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, A₂ := V ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0} and the one
hypersurface Σ^IVP ∩ V, every point of Γ = Σ^IVP ∩ V lying in Γ_1, shows that the tensor equal to u_i on A_i is C^m on V.
It equals h_(S,S⁰) on V ∩ 𝒟. As m is arbitrary, h_(S,S⁰) is smooth on 𝒟, up to its boundary.

*Uniqueness.* The solution on 𝒟 is unique: the difference of two solutions solves an equation L̄v = 0 as in the
uniqueness of *(1)* below, and vanishes by Lemma 18.4, with τ := t_IVP forward from Σ^IVP and τ := −t_IVP backward.
The compact sets that Lemma 18.4 asks for are bounded near infinity by Lemma 38.14 (c), and away from
infinity they lie in the compact sets 𝔒 and 𝔒⁻ or in the exterior and slab regions, closed under past causal curves
within 𝒟 (Lemma 38.5 (c)). In each use the solution (or the difference of two solutions) is extended by 0 across
Σ^IVP, where its Cauchy data vanish, so that it solves the equation across Σ^IVP and its support lies above a level c < 0
of τ, as Lemma 18.4 asks. For the forward problem, past causal curves from points of 𝒟 near Σ^IVP with r slightly
above R_ν reach {t_IVP = −ν} while t_IVP > c, as ν(r) → 0 when r ↓ R_ν; so the problem is posed on 𝒟° ∪ W_ν°, where, for
δ > 0 with |c| + δ < ½r_♭ and R′_ν > R_ν with ν(R′_ν) > |c| + δ,

    W_ν := {c − δ ≤ t_IVP ≤ 0,  r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′_ν} ⊂ M

(t ≥ t_IVP ≥ c − δ > −½|x| on W_ν). On W_ν, beyond 𝒟, the metric and the operator are extended smoothly from 𝒟, dt_IVP
keeping its margin on the compact W_ν, and the zero extension of the solution vanishes there. Where r ≥ R′_ν, 𝒟 contains
{t_IVP ≥ −ν(R′_ν)} ⊃ {t_IVP ≥ c − δ} near Σ^IVP, ν being non-decreasing; so past causal curves from 𝒟 along which
t_IVP ≥ c stay in 𝒟 ∪ W_ν, and the compact sets lie there.

*(2).* The argument of Theorem 37.39 (3) on 𝒟, h_(S,S⁰) being smooth on 𝒟 (*Gluing*). The data satisfy the
constraints and Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ) = Υ^0 = 0 at Σ^IVP (Lemma 38.1 (d); Proposition 37.41 (2)). With
g := φ^*g_(b₀) + h_(S,S⁰), g_0 := φ^*g_(b₀) and Υ := Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g, g_0), (38.4) reads Ric(g) = δ*_(g_0,E_C)Υ,
and the second Bianchi identity δ_gG_gRic(g) = 0 gives

    δ_gG_g δ*_(g_0,E_C) Υ = 0,

a wave equation for Υ: its principal symbol is that of δ_gG_gδ*_g, ½g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) times the identity, as
δ*_(g_0,E_C) − δ*_g is of order 0 (Definition 21.28). Its Cauchy data at Σ^IVP vanish: Υ = 0 there, and the
constraints give (G_g Ric(g))(ν, ·) = 0, that is (G_g δ*_(g_0,E_C)Υ)(ν, ·) = 0 there, which with Υ = 0 gives ∂_νΥ = 0
(Lemma 38.20 below). So Υ vanishes on 𝒟 by Lemma 18.4, with τ := t_IVP forward from Σ^IVP and, backward
to {t_IVP = −ν}, τ := −t_IVP, a time function for the reversed time orientation; the compact sets are those described
above, and for the backward problem they are bounded as follows. Past directed causal curves lose no r near the inner
boundary (by Lemma 15.35 (1)). Future directed causal curves lose r inside the horizon ({r ≤ r^♮}, where dr is
future timelike), and are bounded below in r by three facts: N_ν ∩ {t_IVP < 0} ⊂ {r > R_ν}, as ν = 0 on [0, R_ν];
t_IVP + ν increases along future causal curves, {t_IVP = −ν} being spacelike with N_ν to its future; and in a thin slab
{0 ≤ t_IVP ≤ t_1} above Σ^IVP the radial speed is bounded, |dr(V)| ≤ C_r dt_IVP(V) for future causal V, with C_r ≥ 2
depending on t_1 (dt_IVP being past timelike on the compact part of the slab, and |V^x| ≤ 2V^t near infinity by
Lemma 38.14 (a)). Fix t_1 := 1, the constant C_r for it, the level c < 0 and δ > 0
with |c| + δ < min(1, (R_ν − r_♭)/(2C_r)). The backward problem is posed on

    X := (N_ν ∩ {t_IVP < 0}) ∪ ({0 ≤ t_IVP ≤ |c| + δ} ∩ {r + 2C_r t_IVP ≥ R_ν}),

which future causal curves do not leave while t_IVP ≤ |c| + δ: they meet Σ^IVP from N_ν ∩ {t_IVP < 0} at r ≥ R_ν, and
d(r + 2C_r t_IVP)(V) ≥ C_r dt_IVP(V) > 0 along them. So r ≥ R_ν − 2C_r(|c| + δ) > r_♭ on X, which is closed, and
Lemma 18.4 is applied on X° with τ := −t_IVP at the level c, the slab being taken to |c| + δ so that the sets
L_p lie in X°; near infinity Lemma 38.14 (c) bounds r on them. The proof of Theorem 37.39 (3) uses no
property of the cut-off but its smoothness.

*(1).* The order is that of the proof of Theorem 37.39: first (S, S⁰) = (0, 0), which defines h_0 on 𝒟, a
two-sided neighbourhood of Σ^IVP off {r ≤ R_ν} (the backward part lying in N_ν; on {r ≤ R_ν} 𝒟 ends at Σ^IVP, which is
harmless as φ is the identity there); then (S, S⁰) ≠ (0, 0), which uses h_0 at φ(p) for p near Σ^IVP ∪ φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP).
The argument is that of the proof of Theorem 37.39 (1), made on all of 𝒟 at once.

*A band.* Let R be the radius of Lemma 38.14. dt_IVP is past timelike for g_(b₀) with a margin on the compact set
𝒟 ∩ {r ≤ R} (Lemma 21.22 (b)). Fix c′ ∈ (0, min(1/16, 1/(4R_6), ⅓c_ν)] (c_ν of the inclusions above) so small
that d(t_IVP − c′r) and d(t_IVP + c′r) are past timelike, with a margin, for g_(b₀) there. On {r ≥ R}, t_IVP = t − C″,
and for every metric g whose Cartesian components lie within 1/20 of those of η, g⁻¹(dt, dt) ≤ −⅔,
and |g⁻¹(dt, dr)|, |g⁻¹(dr, dr)| ≤ 2 (the Neumann series of the proof of Lemma 38.14 (a)), so
g⁻¹(dt ∓ c′dr, dt ∓ c′dr) ≤ −⅔ + 4c′ + 2c′² < 0, and dt ∓ c′dr lies in the cone of dt. Let
𝒰′ := 𝒟 ∩ {|t_IVP| < c′r}, a neighbourhood of Σ^IVP in 𝒟, and take C(|S| + |S⁰|) ≤ ¼c′ in Lemma 38.2,
besides the smallness of the statement.

*The cut-off vanishes.* Let 𝒪 := {|t_IVP| < 2c′r}. On 𝒪, |t_IVP| < r/8, so χ_0 = 0, and t_* < ½: for r ≥ R_6,
t_* = t_IVP − F < 2c′r − r/4 < 0 by (38.2), and for r < R_6, t_* ≤ t_IVP < 2c′R_6 ≤ ½. So χ^♮_0 = 0 on 𝒪. For
p ∈ 𝒰′, |t_IVP(φ(p))| < (5/4)c′r(p) ≤ (5/3)c′r(φ(p)), as r(φ(p)) ≥ ¾r(p) (Lemma 38.2); so φ(p) ∈ 𝒪. And
φ(p) ∈ N_ν, as 𝒰′ ⊂ W (c′ ≤ ⅓c_ν; the inclusions above), and t_*(φ(p)) < ½; so φ(p) ∈ 𝒟 ∩ 𝒪.

*φ^*h_0 solves the equation near the data surface.* By (2) at (0, 0), Ric(g_(b₀) + h_0) = 0 on 𝒟 and
Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g_(b₀) + h_0, g_(b₀)) = 0 on 𝒟, which on 𝒟 ∩ 𝒪 is Υ⁰(g_(b₀) + h_0, g_(b₀)) = 0. Pulling back by φ,
Ric(φ^*g_(b₀) + φ^*h_0) = φ^*Ric(g_(b₀) + h_0) = 0 and, by (37.37),
Υ⁰(φ^*g_(b₀) + φ^*h_0, φ^*g_(b₀)) = φ^*Υ⁰(g_(b₀) + h_0, g_(b₀)) = 0 on 𝒰′, where χ^♮_0 = 0 as well. So both terms of
P^♮(φ^*g_(b₀) + φ^*h_0, φ^*g_(b₀)) vanish on 𝒰′, and φ^*h_0 solves (38.4) there, with the data
h⁰_(S,S⁰), h¹_(S,S⁰) on Σ^IVP, by their definition. (The operator δ*_(g_0,E_C) is not pulled back, as in the proof
of Theorem 37.39 (1); it acts on a vanishing 1-form.)

*Uniqueness.* v := h_(S,S⁰) − φ^*h_0 solves L̄v = 0 on 𝒰′, L̄ := ∫_0^1 L^(χ^♮_0)_(g_s,g_0) ds with g_0 := φ^*g_(b₀)
and g_s := g_0 + φ^*h_0 + sv, and v and its first derivatives vanish on Σ^IVP. Each g_s is a convex combination of
φ^*(g_(b₀) + h_0) and φ^*g_(b₀) + h_(S,S⁰), so 2L̄ has principal symbol ğ⁻¹(ζ, ζ)Id, ğ⁻¹ := ∫_0^1 g_s⁻¹ ds, and ğ is a
Lorentzian metric, C⁰-close to g_(b₀) on 𝒰′ ∩ {r ≤ R} and with Cartesian components within 1/20 of those of η on
𝒰′ ∩ {r ≥ R}, as g_(S,S⁰) is in Lemma 38.14 (a), for |S| + |S⁰| and the data small. So (a)–(c) of
Lemma 38.14 hold for ğ, with the same proofs, and d(t_IVP − c′r), d(t_IVP + c′r) are past timelike for ğ on
𝒰′. Then v = 0 on 𝒰′ by Lemma 18.4, applied to 2L̄ as in the *(2)* paragraph, with 𝒰′ in place of 𝒟, the
constants there taken for ğ, and |c| + δ moreover below c′(R_ν − 2C_r(|c| + δ)) and below c′r_♭: forward from Σ^IVP with
τ := t_IVP, on (𝒰′ ∪ W_ν)° with W_ν of the *Uniqueness* paragraph above, which lies in {|t_IVP| < c′r}; and backward on
X ∩ 𝒰′ with τ := −t_IVP. The compact sets described there lie in 𝒰′ ∪ W_ν: along future causal curves of ğ,
t_IVP − c′r and t_IVP + c′r increase, so past curves from points with t_IVP < c′r keep t_IVP < c′r, and future curves
from points with t_IVP > −c′r keep t_IVP > −c′r; and the slab {0 ≤ t_IVP ≤ |c| + δ} ∩ X lies in {t_IVP < c′r}, as
r ≥ R_ν − 2C_r(|c| + δ) there. Finally φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP) ⊂ 𝒟 (the inclusions above) and |t_IVP| ≤ ¼c′r on it
(Lemma 38.2), so 𝒰′ is a neighbourhood of Σ^IVP ∪ φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP) in 𝒟, on which h_(S,S⁰) = φ^*h_0.

*(3).* 𝒟 ∩ Ω_* lies in 𝒟⁺, as t_IVP ≥ t_* ≥ t^♭_* ≥ 1 there. The orders at ℐ⁺ are Theorem 37.36 with
Theorem 37.39 (2) on the exterior part, for φ_(S,S⁰), and Corollary 38.11 on 𝒟⁺. *Derivatives in (S, S⁰).* The
data h^j_(S,S⁰) are smooth in (S, S⁰), being pull-backs of h_0 near Σ^IVP ∪ φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP) by φ_(S,S⁰), smooth in
(S, S⁰) (Lemma 38.3 (a)). With g_0 := φ^*g_(b₀) and ġ_0 its derivative in a direction of
(S, S⁰), the candidate derivative ḣ of h_(S,S⁰) in that direction solves on 𝒟⁺

    L^(χ^♮_0)_(g_0+h_(S,S⁰),g_0) ḣ = −[(D₁ + D₂)P^♮(g_0 + h_(S,S⁰), g_0) − (D₁ + D₂)P^♮(g_0, g_0)]ġ_0,

with the differentiated data, D₁ and D₂ the derivatives in the two arguments; the term (D₁ + D₂)P^♮(g_0, g_0)ġ_0 is 0,
as P^♮(g_0, g_0) = 0 for every (S, S⁰). The right side carries a factor of h_(S,S⁰) and lies in the forcing class, as
in the proof of Theorem 37.39 (2) near infinity (with Lemma 38.7 differentiated in (S, S⁰) over 𝒮), and
trivially on the compact part; so Theorem 38.9 gives ḣ in the class of h_(S,S⁰). The difference of a difference
quotient and ḣ solves L̄w = f_ε, L̄ the average of the linearisations along the segment between the two solutions, with
data and forcing tending to 0 with the increment; Theorem 38.9 holds for L̄ with the same proof, as in the
uniqueness of Theorem 38.10, with constants depending on L̄ only through bounds that are uniform here (on Q through
(L) of Section 38.2.2, whose constants depend on the coefficients only through bounds on finitely many of their
derivatives); so the difference quotients converge to ḣ. Higher derivatives follow likewise, with the losses of
[Hin26, footnote 59]. *The modulus.* ∂^j_(S,S⁰)h_(S,S⁰), j ≤ 2, solves the linearised equation with data
∂^j_(S,S⁰)(h⁰_(S,S⁰), h¹_(S,S⁰)), which are pull-backs of h_0 and its derivatives, and so small with h_0, and with the
term from varying the background, which carries a factor of h_(S,S⁰) and is small too; so Theorem 38.9 bounds it by
quantities that tend to 0 with the data. The sources give continuity at 0, not a linear bound: (37.39) and
the ε₁ clauses of Theorem 37.28 and Theorem 38.10 state that the solution tends to 0 as the data do, at a finite
loss of derivatives; uniformly in (S, S⁰) small, as the constants of these theorems depend on the background only
through bounds uniform for |S| + |S⁰| small (as in the proof of Theorem 37.39), and so do their thresholds. k′_k
collects the losses up to the order k + 2, and ω_k(s) is the supremum of the left side over the parameters and the data
with ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+k′_k)) ≤ s, finite for s ≤ s_k and tending to 0 with s. ∎

### 38.3 The map Ψ

**Definition 38.15** (The map Ψ; [Hin26, (12.34)].) Let χ_− ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, T̂ + 7/4] and 0 on
[T̂ + 2, ∞). For U ∈ 𝒟^∞_ex small, with boost component S and translation component S⁰ := S^(0)_1
(Definition 34.15),

    Ψ(U) := (χ_−(t^♭_*) h_(−S,−S⁰), 0, 0) + Φ(U).    (38.11)

The first component is defined on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2} ⊂ 𝒟_(−S,−S⁰), and extended by 0. For S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1 small put

    ĝ_(S,S⁰) := φ_(−S,−S⁰)^*g_(b₀),     G_(S,S⁰) := ĝ_(S,S⁰) + h_(−S,−S⁰),

so that g_(p⃗) = ĝ_(S,S⁰) where χ_K = 0, and G_(S,S⁰) = φ_(−S,−S⁰)^*(g_(b₀) + h_0) near φ_(−S,−S⁰)⁻¹(Σ^IVP)
(Proposition 38.4 (1)).

**Lemma 38.16** (Theorem 34.20 for Ψ; [Hin26, Lemma 12.7].) There are d and ε_0 > 0 such that for
U ∈ 𝒟^∞_ex with ‖U‖_(𝒟^d_ex) < ε_0:

(a) Ψ(U) − Φ(U) is supported in {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}, and P_5(Ψ(U)) = P_5(Φ(U)) on {t^♭_* > T̂ + 2};

(b) if the tail h̃ of U vanishes on {t^♭_* < c}, c ∈ [T̂, T̂ + 7/4], then P_5(Ψ(U)) = 0 on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < c};

(c) P_5(Ψ(U)) ∈ ℱ^∞_ex, and U ↦ P_5(Ψ(U)) satisfies Proposition 35.9 on the scales of Corollary 35.33, with
constants depending on the data through finitely many norms of (γ̃, k̃);

(d) P_5(Ψ(0)) is supported in {T̂ + 7/4 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}, and there is s_P > 0 such that ‖P_5(Ψ(0))‖_(ℱ^k_ex) ≤
C_kω_(k+3)(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+3+k′_(k+3)))) when ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+3+k′_(k+3))) ≤ min(s_(k+3), s_P), with k′_k, s_k and ω_k
of Proposition 38.4 (3).

Below, d is the d of Theorem 38.19, fixed in its proof (not the d = 7 of Chapter 37, whose N_NM is the N_ex of
Theorem 38.10 here), N_NM := 21d + 6 is the regularity of Theorem 20.1 for it, k″ := d + 3 + k′_(N_NM+d+3),
s_♭ := min(min_(k≤N_NM+d+3) s_k, s_P) and ω_♭ := max_(k≤N_NM+d+3) ω_k on [0, s_♭]. Let σ_0 > 0, independent of the
data, be such that Proposition 38.4 (3) holds for |S| + |S⁰| ≤ σ_0 at every order k: its proof asks the parameters
small only in conditions on the motions φ_(S,S⁰) and on the backgrounds φ_(S,S⁰)^*g_(b₀), which do not involve the
data and, these being smooth in (S, S⁰), hold on one ball at every order. For j ∈ ℕ₀ let

    Θ_j := sup_(|S|+|S⁰|≤σ_0) Σ_(l≤2) ‖∂^l_(S,S⁰) h_(S,S⁰)‖_(H^(j+5)),    (38.12)

the left side of Proposition 38.4 (3) at the order j + 3, in the norms of its class. Θ_j is finite, h_(S,S⁰) being
C² in (S, S⁰) with values in H^(j+5) by (3), the data lying in every H^k; it is non-decreasing in j; and by (3) at the
order j + 3,

    Θ_j ≤ ω_(j+3)(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(j+3+k′_(j+3))))     when ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(j+3+k′_(j+3))) ≤ s_(j+3).

The smallness constants use orders k ≤ N_NM only. Those of the map read the initial family through Θ_k, since a
product or a composition bounded by Lemma 20.6 (2)–(3) takes one factor at the order k + 3, as in (d); those of
the right inverses read it through Θ_(k+d) (Lemma 38.17), the loss d applying to the base point as to U. So the
data enter them at the orders up to N_NM + d + 3 + k′_(N_NM+d+3) = N_NM + k″. A bound needed at every order k (the
bound on e_S and e_(S⁰) in the proof of Lemma 38.17) carries k′_(k+3) and ω_(k+3).

*Proof.* Write ĝ := ĝ_(S,S⁰) and G := G_(S,S⁰), with S⁰ := S^(0)_1. On {t^♭_* < T̂ + 2}, χ_K = 0 (as T_K > T̂ + 2), so
g_(p⃗) = ĝ (Section 38.1). Also h_tot(p⃗) and ϑ_tot(p⃗) vanish there, being supported in 𝒞 ⊂ supp χ_K
(Lemma 32.6, Definition 32.33), and so does h_(b,rem)(q), which carries χ_K ((34.2)). By
(34.11), the metric component of Φ(U) is χ_ι Σ_λ u_λ + h̃ + χ_ι Σ_(λ₀) h_(λ₀), which is h̃ on
{t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}, as χ_ι = 0 there (Section 38.1). So on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < T̂ + 2},

    P_5(Ψ(U)) = P(ĝ + χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰) + h̃, ĝ),     P(g, g_0) := Ric(g) − δ*_(g_0,E_C)Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g_0)

((32.33), with g_0 = g_(p⃗) as in Definition 32.7).

(a) holds as χ_− = 0 on {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 2} and P_5 is a differential operator.

(b) On Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < c}, χ_− = 1 and h̃ = 0, so P_5(Ψ(U)) = P(G, ĝ). This is 0 − δ*0 = 0 by Proposition 38.4 (2)
with (−S, −S⁰), as Ω_* ⊂ {t_* ≥ 1}, where χ^♮_0 = 1.

(c) Near ℐ⁺ ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}, Corollary 27.18 applies with g_0 = ĝ (in 𝒢 by Lemma 38.3 (b),
as in Lemma 38.7; Ric(g_0) = 0) and h = χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰) + h̃, which has the orders (⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I) at ℐ⁺
(Proposition 38.4 (3), Definition 35.11). So P_5(Ψ(U)) has the orders (⟨ℰ^C_I + 1⟩′, ℓ_I + 1) of ℱ_ex there. On
{t^♭_* > T̂ + 2} it is P_5(Φ(U)) ∈ ℱ^∞_ex (Corollary 35.33). Supported character: for U whose tail vanishes on
{t^♭_* < T̂} (the class B^∞ of Section 38.4), P_5(Ψ(U)) vanishes there by (b); and on {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4},

    P_5(Ψ(U)) = ∫_0^1 L_(G+sh̃, ĝ) h̃ ds,

as P(G, ĝ) = 0; here L_(g,g_0) is the linearisation of P in its first argument. This is a differential operator applied
to h̃, which has supported character. The bounds of Proposition 35.9 hold for Φ. The added terms are
χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰), a fixed tensor smooth in the finite-dimensional (S, S⁰) (Proposition 38.4 (3)), and its products with
h̃ in P on the compact t^♭_*-range [1, T̂ + 2]. The tame bounds of Section 35.1 (with Lemma 20.6) bound them,
with constants depending on finitely many norms of h_(−S,−S⁰) and of its derivatives in (S, S⁰) of order at most 2.

(d) At U = 0, h̃ = 0 and S = S⁰ = 0, so P_5(Ψ(0)) = P(g_(b₀) + χ_−h_0, g_(b₀)) on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < T̂ + 2} by the display
above, and P_5(Ψ(0)) = P_5(Φ(0)) = P(g_(b₀), g_(b₀)) = 0 on {t^♭_* > T̂ + 2} by (a). On {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4} it is
P(g_(b₀) + h_0, g_(b₀)) = 0 by Proposition 38.4 (2). So it vanishes outside supp dχ_−, and it is a smooth function
of h_0 and its derivatives of order at most 2, vanishing at h_0 = 0, on the compact set supp dχ_−(t^♭_*); so, by
Lemma 20.6 (3) with d = 3 after a finite partition of unity, in the form for functions smooth also in the point
(the proof of Lemma 35.6), its ℱ^k_ex-norm is at most C_k‖h_0‖_(H^(k+5)) while ‖h_0‖_(H^5) is small. By
Proposition 38.4 (3) at the order 3, ‖h_0‖_(H^5) ≤ ω_3(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(3+k′_3))), which is that small once
‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(3+k′_3)) ≤ s_P for some s_P ∈ (0, s_3], as ω_3(s) → 0; and ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(3+k′_3)) ≤
‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+3+k′_(k+3))), k′_k being non-decreasing. At the order k + 3, Proposition 38.4 (3) bounds
‖h_0‖_(H^(k+5)) by ω_(k+3)(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+3+k′_(k+3)))). ∎

**Lemma 38.17** (Right inverses for Ψ; Theorem 34.24 for Ψ, [Hin26, Theorem 12.8, last paragraph].)
There are d and ε_0 ∈ (0, 1] such that for data with Θ_d < ε_0 ((38.12)) and U ∈ 𝒟^∞_ex with
‖U‖_(𝒟^d_ex) < ε_0 there is a linear map ℛ(U) : ℱ^∞_ex → 𝒟^∞_ex with D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)(ℛ(U)f) = f. It satisfies the tame
estimate (35.3) on the exact scales (Corollary 35.33) in the form

    ‖ℛ(U)f‖_(𝒟^k_ex) ≤ C_k (‖f‖_(ℱ^(k+d)_ex) + (‖U‖_(𝒟^(k+d)_ex) + Θ_(k+d)) ‖f‖_(ℱ^d_ex)),     k ∈ ℕ₀,    (38.13)

with C_k independent of U and of the data. If the tail h̃ of U and f vanish on {t^♭_* < c}, c ∈ [T̂, T̂ + 7/4], then so
does the tail h̃′ of ℛ(U)f.

*Proof.* Write S⁰ := S^(0)_1 for the translation component of U, and S′, S⁰′ for the boost and translation components
of U′. *The base point.* Ψ(U) = (h + χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰), p⃗, q) with (h, p⃗, q) = Φ(U). Its black hole parameter b lies in
ℬ_*, as |b − b₀| ≤ ‖U‖_(𝒟^d). Its metric component h + χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰) lies in the background class 𝒳^∞ of
(29.4), which has no support condition, and is small there (Proposition 38.4 (3)): for l ≤ 2, for
j ∈ ℕ₀ and for |S| + |S⁰| ≤ σ_0,

    ‖χ_−(t^♭_*) ∂^l_(S,S⁰)h_(−S,−S⁰)‖_(𝒳^(j+2)) ≤ C_j Θ_j,    (38.14)

with C_j depending only on χ_− and j, as multiplication by χ_−(t^♭_*) is bounded at every order on the class of
Proposition 38.4 (3) (the half-integer powers of ρ_I it adds at ℐ⁺ stay in the class, as in the proof of
Lemma 38.18), that class cut off by χ_−(t^♭_*) lies in 𝒳 with a bounded inclusion at every order, and the norms
are non-decreasing in the order. Theorem 34.9 (at a rotating b, through Proposition 36.8) and
Theorem 35.7 take the base point only through such a class and its smallness. The proof of Theorem 34.24
takes it only through these and through D_UΦ at U, which depends on U only through U_0 = (b − b₀, S, S⁰), as Φ is
affine in U_1 (Theorem 34.20).

*The boost and translation directions.* With H(S, S⁰) := h_(−S,−S⁰),
D_UΨ(U′) = D_UΦ(U′) + (χ_−(∂_S H(S′) + ∂_(S⁰) H(S⁰′)), 0, 0), so

    D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)(U′) = D_(Ψ(U))P_5(D_UΦ(U′)) + D_hP_5(Ψ(U))(χ_−(∂_S H(S′) + ∂_(S⁰) H(S⁰′))).

In the construction of the proof of Theorem 34.24, D_(Ψ(U))P_5(D_UΦ(U′)) enters (34.5) through
D_(p⃗)P_5(p⃗′). The boost component S′ enters there through its defect f^S_(h,p⃗)(S′), and the translation component
S⁰′ through its defect f^s1_(h,p⃗)(S⁰′) (Lemma 32.10; Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 34.9). Replace
these defects by

    f^S_Ψ(S′) := f^S_(h,p⃗)(S′) + e_S(S′),     f^s1_Ψ(S⁰′) := f^s1_(h,p⃗)(S⁰′) + e_(S⁰)(S⁰′),
    e_S(S′) := (D_(p⃗)P_5|_(Ψ(U)) − D_(p⃗)P_5|_(Φ(U)))(S′, 0, 0) + D_hP_5(Ψ(U))(χ_− ∂_S H(S′)),
    e_(S⁰)(S⁰′) := (D_(p⃗)P_5|_(Ψ(U)) − D_(p⃗)P_5|_(Φ(U)))(0, 0, S⁰′) + D_hP_5(Ψ(U))(χ_− ∂_(S⁰) H(S⁰′)),

the parameter directions written (S, b, S^(0)_1). e_S and e_(S⁰) are supported in Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}: the two base
points differ by χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰), and D_(p⃗)P_5 is local. On {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, e_S(S′) = f^S_Ψ(S′) − f^S_(h,p⃗)(S′)
and e_(S⁰)(S⁰′) = f^s1_Ψ(S⁰′) − f^s1_(h,p⃗)(S⁰′), and the four terms are O(h̃): f^S_Ψ and f^s1_Ψ are the derivatives
of U ↦ P_5(Ψ(U)) in the boost and translation directions, and f^S_(h,p⃗), f^s1_(h,p⃗) those of P_5 at Φ(U); where h̃
vanishes, P_5 vanishes identically in (S, S⁰) along both families (Lemma 38.16 (b) for Ψ; for Φ,
P(ĝ_(S,S⁰), ĝ_(S,S⁰)) = Ric(ĝ_(S,S⁰)) = 0, the other parameter terms being supported in supp χ_K), so the four
derivatives vanish there; in general each is an integral of h̃ as in Lemma 38.16 (c). So for U whose tail
vanishes on {t^♭_* < T̂}, e_S and e_(S⁰) vanish there, and they lie in ℱ^∞_ex, at ℐ⁺ by Corollary 27.18 as in
Lemma 38.16 (c). Their bounds are tame, e_S and e_(S⁰) involving h̃ through D_hP_5 at Ψ(U):

    ‖e_S(S′)‖_(ℱ^k_ex) + ‖e_(S⁰)(S⁰′)‖_(ℱ^k_ex)
        ≤ C_k (ω_(k+3)(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+3+k′_(k+3)))) + ω_♭(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″))) ‖U‖_(𝒟^(k+5)_ex)) (|S′| + |S⁰′|),

by Proposition 38.4 (3) at the order k + 3 and the tame bounds of Section 35.1, with Lemma 20.6 (2)–(3)
for the products of the coefficients, which carry h_(−S,−S⁰), with ∂_S H, ∂_(S⁰) H and h̃, when
‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(k+3+k′_(k+3))) ≤ min(s_(k+3), s_P) and ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″)) ≤ s_♭. The products read h_(−S,−S⁰) and
its derivatives in (S, S⁰) of order at most 2 in H^(k+5), and in H^5 at the low order 3 of Lemma 20.6 (2), where
Lemma 20.6 (3) asks them small; they read the tail h̃ of U, with its derivatives of order at most 2, in the same
way, in H^(k+5) and in H^5, which ‖U‖_(𝒟^(k+5)_ex) and ‖U‖_(𝒟^5_ex) bound (Definition 35.11), the term with h̃ at
the low order being absorbed in the first term of the display, as ‖U‖_(𝒟^5_ex) < 1. The two moduli enter only as
bounds, by Proposition 38.4 (3), for the norms of h_(−S,−S⁰): ω_(k+3)(…) for those in H^(k+5), and ω_♭(…) for those
in H^5, s_P giving their smallness there. The suprema of these norms over the parameters with |S| + |S⁰| ≤ σ_0 are Θ_k
((38.12)) and Θ_0. So, for ε_0 so small that Θ_0 < ε_0 and ‖U‖_(𝒟^5_ex) < ε_0 give the smallness in H^5 that
Lemma 20.6 (3) asks, the display holds at every order k with no condition on the data beyond Θ_d < ε_0 (as
Θ_0 ≤ Θ_d and ‖U‖_(𝒟^5_ex) ≤ ‖U‖_(𝒟^d_ex), d ≥ 5 by *The constants*), in the form

    ‖e_S(S′)‖_(ℱ^k_ex) + ‖e_(S⁰)(S⁰′)‖_(ℱ^k_ex) ≤ C_k (Θ_k + Θ_0 ‖U‖_(𝒟^(k+5)_ex)) (|S′| + |S⁰′|),

Θ_k being finite, as h_(S,S⁰) and its derivatives in (S, S⁰) lie in every H^(k+5) (Proposition 38.4 (3)). When
‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″)) ≤ s_♭, the first condition of the display with the moduli can fail only at orders
k > N_NM + d, as k + 3 + k′_(k+3) ≤ N_NM + k″ and s_♭ ≤ min(s_(k+3), s_P) for k ≤ N_NM + d.

So Theorem 34.9 at the base point Ψ(U), with the defects f^S_Ψ and f^s1_Ψ, is Theorem 34.9 with two
more terms e_S(S′) + e_(S⁰)(S⁰′) in the forcing G′ of Step 2 of its proof. They are linear in the finite-dimensional
(S′, S⁰′), and small with Θ_d and U in the fixed seminorm in which the proof of Lemma 35.5 asks such terms
small: with m its order, the display in its form with Θ_k and Θ_0 bounds them there by
C_m(Θ_m + Θ_0‖U‖_(𝒟^(m+5)_ex))(|S′| + |S⁰′|),
which is less than 2C_mε_0(|S′| + |S⁰′|), as Θ_m ≤ Θ_d < ε_0, Θ_0 < ε_0 ≤ 1 and ‖U‖_(𝒟^(m+5)_ex) ≤ ‖U‖_(𝒟^d_ex) < ε_0,
the d of the statement being at least m + 5 (*The constants*). They enter the maps A_k of Step 3 as Δ_q does
(Lemma 34.7), and they perturb Step 1 (the base level, where the parameters of low rate, among them S′ and
S⁰′, are determined) by terms of the same kind, small with them. So the elimination runs unchanged for ε_0 small, and
the construction of U′ in the proof of Theorem 34.24, Theorem 35.8 and Corollary 35.33 follow as for Φ.
At a rotating b, Corollary 36.12 provides them.

*The constants.* The proof of Lemma 35.2 uses of a background only that its norms are non-decreasing in the
order and below δ_𝔹 ≤ 1 at the order d_0. We apply it first to β̂ := (Ψ(U), Φ(U), (γ̃, k̃)), with
‖β̂‖_j := ‖Ψ(U)‖_j + ‖Φ(U)‖_j + Θ_j, and then, as the proof of Theorem 35.8 passes from the background Φ(U) to
U, to β^Ψ := (U, (γ̃, k̃)), with ‖β^Ψ‖_j := ‖U‖_(𝒟^j_ex) + Θ_j; both are non-decreasing in j. We take ε_0 ≤ σ_0/2, so
that the components S, S⁰ of U satisfy |S| + |S⁰| ≤ σ_0. By (i) and (ii) every family of the construction above is
tame in β̂, with the loss that it has in the background Φ(U) in the construction for Φ, and by (iii) the family that
Steps 1–3 subtract is tame in β^Ψ, with the loss that it has in U there; all have constants independent of U and of
the data:

(i) The families of Section 35.3 at the base point Ψ(U) are tame in Ψ(U), and so in β̂, as ‖Ψ(U)‖_j ≤ ‖β̂‖_j,
with constants that do not depend on the base point in the ball of Theorem 35.7. With d_Φ the loss of
U ↦ Φ(U) (Theorem 34.20, as in the proof of Theorem 35.8) and (38.14) at l = 0,

    ‖Ψ(U)‖_j ≤ ‖Φ(U)‖_j + ‖χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰)‖_(𝒳^j) ≤ C_j (‖U‖_(𝒟^(j+d_Φ)_ex) + Θ_j) ≤ C_j ‖β^Ψ‖_(j+d_Φ),

and so, as ‖Φ(U)‖_j ≤ C_j‖U‖_(𝒟^(j+d_Φ)_ex) and Θ_j ≤ ‖β^Ψ‖_j ≤ ‖β^Ψ‖_(j+d_Φ),

    ‖β̂‖_j ≤ C_j ‖β^Ψ‖_(j+d_Φ).

(ii) The first terms of e_S(S′) and e_(S⁰)(S⁰′) are D_(p⃗)P_5 at the base points Ψ(U) and Φ(U) in the directions of S′
and S⁰′, which Lemma 35.3 (b) bounds as it bounds the defects, in the spaces of its statement and at the
order j, by C_j(1 + ‖Ψ(U)‖_(j+d_BG) + ‖Φ(U)‖_(j+d_BG))(|S′| + |S⁰′|), d_BG ≤ d being the loss of its bound. Their
second terms are D_hP_5(Ψ(U)) = L_b + (D_hP_5(Ψ(U)) − L_b) applied to u := χ_−∂_S H(S′) or u := χ_−∂_(S⁰) H(S⁰′),
which L_b, of loss 2 (Lemma 35.2 (d)), and Lemma 35.3 (b) bound there by
C_j(‖u‖_(𝒳^(j+2)) + ‖Ψ(U)‖_(j+d_BG)‖u‖_(𝒳^(d_BG))). By (38.14) at l = 1, ‖u‖_(𝒳^(j+2)) ≤ C_jΘ_j(|S′| + |S⁰′|)
and ‖u‖_(𝒳^(d_BG)) ≤ ‖u‖_(𝒳^(d_BG+2)) ≤ CΘ_(d_BG)(|S′| + |S⁰′|), with Θ_(d_BG) ≤ Θ_d < 1. The four terms are bounded
one by one, at the orders of ℱ_ex at ℐ⁺ but without its support condition, as the terms at Ψ(U) need not vanish near
the initial face, while the sums e_S(S′), e_(S⁰)(S⁰′) have the supported character of ℱ_ex. The sums are supported in
{t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}, away from ι⁺ and K⁺, and at an integer order a section of supported character has the norm of its
zero extension, whose derivatives are its own extended by zero; so their norms in ℱ^j_ex are at most the sums of the
bounds of their terms. (The displays above pass from the terms of the products to e_S and e_(S⁰) in the same way.)
With Θ_j ≤ ‖β̂‖_j,

    ‖e_S(S′)‖_(ℱ^j_ex) + ‖e_(S⁰)(S⁰′)‖_(ℱ^j_ex) ≤ C_j (1 + ‖β̂‖_(j+d_BG)) (|S′| + |S⁰′|),

the form that Lemma 35.2 (c) asks of the finite-rank terms they add, with the loss d_BG that the defects
f^S_(h,p⃗), f^s1_(h,p⃗) have in the background Φ(U) in the construction for Φ; read in β^Ψ through (i), this is the loss
d_BG + d_Φ that they have in U. The defects themselves, which the construction keeps at Φ(U), are tame in Φ(U) with
the loss d_BG, and so in β̂, as ‖Φ(U)‖_j ≤ ‖β̂‖_j.

(iii) D_UΦ at U, which Steps 1–3 of the proof of Theorem 35.8 subtract, is tame in U (Remark 34.21), and
so in β^Ψ, as ‖U‖_(𝒟^j_ex) ≤ ‖β^Ψ‖_j.

So the proof of Theorem 35.7, run at the base point Ψ(U) with these families, gives (35.2) there with
its loss d_F (the d of (35.2)) and with ‖β̂‖_(k+d_F) in place of ‖h‖_(k+d_F) + |p⃗| + ‖q‖_(k+d_F): the
losses compose in β̂ as they compose in Φ(U) for Φ, the families of (i) keeping their losses and the terms of (ii)
being summands with the loss d_BG of the defects beside them (Lemma 35.2 (a)). Composed once with
‖β̂‖_j ≤ C_j‖β^Ψ‖_(j+d_Φ) of (i), as the proof of Theorem 35.8 composes with ‖Φ(U)‖_j ≤ C_j‖U‖_(𝒟^(j+d_Φ)_ex),
this has the form (35.1) in β^Ψ with the loss d_F + d_Φ, as it has in U for Φ. With (iii), the proof of
Theorem 35.8 then gives (35.3) with ‖β^Ψ‖_(k+d_R) in place of ‖U‖_(𝒟^(k+d_R)_ex), d_R the loss of
(35.3), that of the construction for Φ, and with constants independent of U and of the data. (Each family
taken in β^Ψ before composing would add d_Φ at every step of the composition.) The smallness that these proofs ask is
that of ‖β̂‖ at the order d_0 of Theorem 35.7, which (i) bounds by C‖β^Ψ‖_(d_0+d_Φ), and that of ‖β^Ψ‖ at the
order d′_0 at which the proof of Theorem 35.8 asks U small, d′_0 ≥ d_0 + d_Φ as that proof reads ‖Φ(U)‖_(d_0)
through ‖U‖_(𝒟^(d_0+d_Φ)_ex); the elimination asks the order m + 5 above, which is at most d′_0. Indeed m ≤ d_*, as
the proof of Lemma 35.5 bounds the background terms in that seminorm by Lemma 35.3 (b) at the order m,
which reads the background at an order at least m, and d_* is the largest of the orders so read; and
d′_0 ≥ d_0 + d_Φ ≥ d_* + 5, as d_0 = d_* + D (Lemma 35.5) with D at least the loss of the forward solution
operators, which is at least the 5 derivatives that Corollary 29.16 costs (Lemma 35.3 (a)). We take the d of
the statement at least d_R, d′_0 and d_BG. Then (38.13) holds with it, as the norms are non-decreasing in the
order, and
‖β^Ψ‖_j ≤ ‖U‖_(𝒟^d_ex) + Θ_d < 2ε_0 for j ≤ d, so the smallness holds for ε_0 small.

*Supports.* Let h̃ and f vanish on {t^♭_* < c}, c ∈ [T̂, T̂ + 7/4]. There χ_ι, χ_K and the corrections vanish, as in
Lemma 38.16, and χ_− = 1; so P_5 ∘ Ψ = Q(S, S⁰, h̃) := P(G_(S,S⁰) + h̃, ĝ_(S,S⁰)) there, Q being a differential
operator in h̃. As Q(S, S⁰, 0) = 0 for all small (S, S⁰) (Proposition 38.4 (2) with (−S, −S⁰)),
∂_(S,S⁰)Q(S, S⁰, 0) = 0; and as h̃ vanishes on the open set {t^♭_* < c}, there

    D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)(U′) = ∂_(S,S⁰)Q(S, S⁰, 0)(S′, S⁰′) + D_(h̃)Q(S, S⁰, 0)h̃′ = L_(G_(S,S⁰), ĝ_(S,S⁰)) h̃′;

the boost and translation components of U′ enter only through the first term, which vanishes. So
L_(G_(S,S⁰), ĝ_(S,S⁰)) h̃′ = f = 0 on {t^♭_* < c}. Within the construction, h̃′ is the remainder of the forward
solution there: the rows and towers are supported in supp χ_K, and the ι⁺-terms carry χ_ι. h̃′ has supported character
at {t^♭_* = 1} (the spaces of Definition 34.15), so, extended by 0, it solves L_(G_(S,S⁰), ĝ_(S,S⁰)) h̃′ = 0 on

    X := 𝒟°_(−S,−S⁰) ∩ {¾ < t^♭_* < c},

and Lemma 18.4 is applied on X with τ := t^♭_* at the level 7/8, below its support; t^♭_* is a time function of
G_(S,S⁰) on X by Lemma 38.12 (iii) on Y := X. Lemma 38.13 with G_(S,S⁰) in place of g, Y := X, its c equal
to 7/8 and T := T̂ + 2 gives the compact sets. Indeed L_p ⊂ X: 7/8 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t^♭_*(p) < c on L_p, and {t^♭_* > ¾}
lies in φ_(−S,−S⁰)⁻¹({t_IVP ≥ 0}), since on it t_IVP = t_* + F ≥ t^♭_* + F > ¾ + F, F ≥ r/4 for r ≥ R_6
((38.2)), while φ_(−S,−S⁰) moves t_IVP by at most C(|S| + |S⁰|)r and not at all on {r ≤ 5R₁}
(Lemma 38.2). G_(S,S⁰) lies in the class of Lemma 38.12 on X: on Ω_* as G_(S,S⁰) − g_(b₀) is small in
𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b) on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2} (Proposition 38.4 (3), Lemma 21.27,
Lemma 38.3 (b)); below Ω_* near ℐ⁺ by the same facts, h_(−S,−S⁰) having the orders of
Definition 27.6 on 𝒟 near infinity (Theorem 37.39 (2), Corollary 38.11); and on the compact rest by its
smallness in C⁰. So h̃′ = 0 on {t^♭_* < c}.

Without the hypothesis on h̃, D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)(U′) contains ∂_(S,S⁰)Q(S, S⁰, h̃)(S′, S⁰′), which need not vanish on
{t^♭_* < c}; so the support property holds only at base points whose tail vanishes below the level.
Theorem 20.1 (iii) asks it only there (Remark 20.2), and that is how Theorem 38.19 uses it. ∎

### 38.4 The Nash–Moser iteration

*The scales.* Let c_1 := ⅛ and c_0 := c_1/8 = 1/64 be the constants of Proposition 20.4 for t := t^♭_* − T̂ on
M_(1/2), with t := −1 where t_* < ½. (T1)–(T3) of Section 20.3.1 hold for this t as for t^♭_* − 1 in
Remark 20.5, the level only moving: t^♭_* is smooth on M_(1/2) with dt^♭_*|_(Tℐ⁺) = dt_*|_(Tℐ⁺) ≠ 0, the set
{|t| ≤ 2c_1} is bounded in t_* (t_* ≤ (T̂ + ¼)/C_♭ there) and lies in {t_* ≥ T̂ − ¼ ≥ 7/4}, so it meets neither ι⁺ nor
K⁺ nor {t_* = ½}, and on ℐ⁺, t^♭_* = t_* and t − t̄ ∈ ρ_I^(1/2)C^∞_b with
t̄ := t_* − T̂. The weighted b-Sobolev spaces on
M and on M_(1/2) coincide, their b-vector fields being the same. Fix χ_9 ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal to 0 on (−∞, 17/2] and 1 on
[9, ∞). For η ∈ [0, 1] and k ∈ ℕ₀ ∪ {∞} let

    B^k := {U ∈ 𝒟^k_ex : S_rem, b_rem, Y_(ψ,rem) supported in {t_* ≥ 8}, supp h̃ ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂}},
    B^k_η := {U ∈ B^k : supp h̃ ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + c_0η}, the q-tails supported in {t_* ≥ 8 + c_0η}},
    F^k := {f ∈ ℱ^k_ex : supp f ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂}},     F^∞_η := {f ∈ F^∞ : supp f ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + c_0η}},

with the norms of 𝒟^k_ex and ℱ^k_ex. Here the q-tails are the components S_rem, b_rem and Y_(ψ,rem), ψ ∈ ℛ′_0, of U
(Definition 34.15). B^k_η is closed in B^k (support conditions are closed), non-increasing in η, and B^k_0 = B^k;
F^k is closed in ℱ^k_ex.

**Lemma 38.18** (Smoothing on 𝒟_ex; [Hin26, Section 13.1, Step 3 (4)].) For θ > 1 there are linear maps
S_θ : B^∞_(θ^(−1/2)) → B^∞ with S_θ(B^∞_η) ⊂ B^∞_(η−θ^(−1/2)) for η ∈ [θ^(−1/2), 1], satisfying (20.1) with
constants independent of θ.

*Proof.* Componentwise: the norm of 𝒟^k_ex is the sum of the norms of the components (Definition 35.11), so
(20.1) for each component gives it for the sum.

*The finite-dimensional components* b − b₀, S, S^(0)_1 and u^0_λ: S_θ := id.

*f_λ:* a polynomial in z of bounded degree with coefficients in a partially polyhomogeneous b-Sobolev space on a compact
manifold with boundary, with no support condition. Smooth each expansion coefficient and the remainder by the operator
S̃_θ of Step 4 of the proof of Proposition 20.4, the smoothing on all of w H̄^0_b with no condition on supports, built
on the manifold carrying it; then reassemble.

*The q-tails* S_rem, b_rem, Y_(ψ,rem): weighted b-Sobolev functions of t_* ∈ [1, ∞]. Use Proposition 20.4 on the
one-dimensional manifold [1, ∞] with t := t_* − 8, for which (T1)–(T3) hold trivially (the set {|t| < 2c_1} lies in
the interior). This gives the support behaviour.

*h̃:* partially polyhomogeneous at ℐ⁺ with index set collection ⟨ℰ^C_I⟩ and remainder of order ℓ_I ((27.10),
in the splitting (27.6)). By the definition of these spaces, h̃ corresponds one to one to its expansion
coefficients a_(z,j) (functions on ℐ⁺ ∩ Ω_*) and its remainder, and the norm is the sum of their norms. Put

    S_θ h̃ := Σ_((z,j)) χ_I ρ_I^z (log ρ_I)^j E(S^ℐ_θ(a_(z,j))) + S_θ(h̃_rem).

Here S^ℐ_θ is Proposition 20.4 on ℐ⁺ with t|_ℐ⁺ (= t^♭_* − T̂ there), S_θ(h̃_rem) is Proposition 20.4 on M_(1/2) with
t = t^♭_* − T̂, and E(a) is the extension of a function a on ℐ⁺ that is constant along the fibres of a collar of ℐ⁺
which lie in the level sets of (t^♭_*, ω) on {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}, and along any b-smooth collar beyond. (t^♭_*, x_I, ω)
are smooth coordinates on M_(1/2) near ℐ⁺, so the fibres are smooth curves in M_(1/2) transversal to ℐ⁺, and a function
constant along them is smooth on M_(1/2): on M it is polyhomogeneous at ℐ⁺ with index set ½ℕ₀, without logarithms. So
passing from a smooth collar of M to this one changes χ_Iρ_I^z(log ρ_I)^jE(a) by terms ρ_I^(z+k/2)(log ρ_I)^j times
smooth functions, k ≥ 1. These stay in the class: each slot's index set ℰ_s in (27.10) is ℰ^C_I together with
points of ℰ^tot_I ((27.9)), so ℰ_s + ½ ⊂ ℰ^C_I ⊂ ℰ_s by Lemma 27.7 (a), logarithmic orders included.
The terms of order below ℓ_I join the expansion and the others the remainder, so the space and its norm are unchanged
up to equivalence. For U ∈ B_η the coefficients vanish on {t^♭_* < T̂ + c_0η} ∩ ℐ⁺, as h̃ does near it; so each term
χ_Iρ_I^z(log ρ_I)^jE(a_(z,j)), and hence the remainder, is supported in {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + c_0η}, the fibres preserving
t^♭_*. The operators of Proposition 20.4 preserve the support classes, and (20.1) holds for each piece by
(20.10). The collar follows the levels of the function that defines the classes, and that function has a robust
timelike margin; the cost is the half-integer powers just absorbed. ∎

**Theorem 38.19** (The solution of the gauge-fixed equation in the cone; [Hin26, Section 13.1, Step 3].)
There are d_1 and ε > 0 such that, if ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(d_1)) < ε, there is U ∈ B^∞_(1/2), small in 𝒟^(3d)_ex, with
P_5(Ψ(U)) = 0 on Ω_*. Its tail h̃ is supported in {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + ½c_0}.

*Proof.* Apply Theorem 20.1 with B^k, B^k_η, F^k and F^∞_η as above, η_0 := 1, d the largest of the d's of
Lemma 38.16, Lemma 38.17 and Proposition 35.9, and the map U ↦ P_5(Ψ(U)) on {U ∈ B^∞ : |U|_(3d) < δ}
in the role of the map of Theorem 20.1, with δ at most the ε_0 of Lemma 38.16 and Lemma 38.17 (a bound
in 𝒟^d_ex) and of Proposition 35.9 (a bound in 𝒟^(3d)_ex), as ‖U‖_(𝒟^d_ex) ≤ |U|_(3d).

*(i)* is Lemma 38.18.

*(ii)* For U ∈ B_η, η ≤ 1, the tail vanishes on {t^♭_* < T̂ + c_0η}, and T̂ + c_0η ≤ T̂ + 1/64 < T̂ + 7/4. So
P_5(Ψ(U)) ∈ F^∞_η by Lemma 38.16 (b)–(c). The map is twice differentiable in the sense of Theorem 20.1, with
(20.2)–(20.3), by Lemma 38.16 (c). Its q-tails enter only through h_(b,rem)(q), whose factor χ_K
vanishes on {t_* < 10} ((34.2), and T_K ≥ 10). They also enter through the iteration of Section 34.5,
whose sources involve them only through h_(b,rem)(q) (Theorem 34.20 (2)). So the map depends on the q-tails only
through their values on {t_* ≥ 10}.

*(iii)* For U in the domain put Ψ_NM(U) := Zℛ(U), the right inverse that Theorem 20.1 (iii) asks for, with ℛ(U)
from Lemma 38.17 and Z the multiplication of the q-tails by χ_9(t_*). By the last sentence of (ii),
D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)(ZU′) = D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)(U′), as χ_9 = 1 on {t_* ≥ 9}. So Ψ_NM(U) is a right inverse. Z is bounded on every
𝒟^k_ex (χ_9(t_*) is smooth and constant near t_* = ∞), so (20.4) holds by Lemma 38.17. As far as the
q-tails are concerned Z maps into B^∞_1: their support lies in {t_* ≥ 17/2} ⊂ {t_* ≥ 8 + c_0}. For U ∈ B_η in the
domain and f ∈ F_η, the tails of U and f vanish on {t^♭_* < T̂ + c_0η}, so the tail of ℛ(U)f does
(Lemma 38.17), and Ψ_NM(U)(F^∞_η) ⊂ B^∞_η; at η = 0 this says that Ψ_NM(U) maps F^∞ into B^∞. This is
Theorem 20.1 (iii), which asks the support property for u ∈ U ∩ B^∞_η only (Remark 20.2); the form
at every u in the domain does not hold here (the proof of Lemma 38.17).

*Smallness.* By Theorem 20.1, ε_NM depends only on d, δ, η_0 = 1, C_1, C_2, the C_k with d ≤ k ≤ N_NM and the
C_(s,t) with s, t ≤ N_NM. The d's are fixed by the proofs, and the C_(s,t) of Lemma 38.18 do not depend on the
data. Let θ_♭ ∈ (0, 1) be less than the ε_0 of Lemma 38.17 and than the smallness of h_(−S,−S⁰) in H^5 that
Lemma 20.6 (3) asks in (1) below. We show that the other constants depend on the data only through Θ_j,
j ≤ N_NM + d ((38.12)), and are bounded independently of the data once Θ_(N_NM+d) ≤ θ_♭.

(1) The C_k of (20.3) for d ≤ k ≤ N_NM, and C_1 and C_2, are the constants of Lemma 38.16 (c). Its
proof adds to Proposition 35.9 the terms χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰) and their products with h̃ in P, a smooth function of the
metric and of its derivatives of order at most 2, and bounds them as (d) is bounded, by Lemma 20.6 (2)–(3) with
d = 3, one factor at the order k + 3. So h_(−S,−S⁰) and its derivatives in (S, S⁰) of order at most 2 enter at the
order k in H^(k+5), through Θ_k ≤ Θ_(N_NM), and in H^5, through Θ_0, for the smallness that (3) asks; C_1 and C_2, with
the norms of 𝒟^(3d)_ex and ℱ^(2d)_ex, read them through Θ_(2d) ≤ Θ_(N_NM). In particular C_k ≥ ‖P_5(Ψ(0))‖_(ℱ^k_ex).

(2) The C_k of (20.4) for d ≤ k ≤ N_NM. By (38.13), with ‖f‖_(ℱ^d_ex) ≤ ‖f‖_(ℱ^(2d)_ex) ≤
‖f‖_(ℱ^(k+d)_ex) for k ≥ d and with the norm C_(Z,k) of Z on 𝒟^k_ex, which does not depend on the data,

    |Ψ_NM(U)f|_k ≤ C_(Z,k) C_k (1 + Θ_(k+d)) (‖f‖_(ℱ^(k+d)_ex) + |U|_(k+d) ‖f‖_(ℱ^(2d)_ex)),

and 1 + Θ_(k+d) ≤ 1 + Θ_(N_NM+d) ≤ 2.

(3) δ is at most the ε_0 of Lemma 38.16, Lemma 38.17 and Proposition 35.9, which the proofs fix; the
condition Θ_d < ε_0 of Lemma 38.17 holds, as Θ_d ≤ Θ_(N_NM+d) ≤ θ_♭.

So, once Θ_(N_NM+d) ≤ θ_♭, the hypotheses of Theorem 20.1 hold, the constants that its threshold reads are
independent of the data (the C_k with k > N_NM are finite, Θ_j being finite for every j, and may depend on the data),
and its threshold ε_NM > 0 does not depend on the data. By the display after (38.12) at j = N_NM + d,
Θ_(N_NM+d) ≤ ω_(N_NM+d+3)(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″))) ≤ ω_♭(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″))) when ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″)) ≤ s_♭,
as N_NM + k″ = N_NM + d + 3 + k′_(N_NM+d+3) and s_♭ ≤ s_(N_NM+d+3). Fix s_1 ∈ (0, s_♭] with ω_♭(s_1) ≤ θ_♭, which
exists as ω_♭(s) tends to 0 with s; then ε_NM is uniform for ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″)) ≤ s_1. Let
d_1 := max(d_0, N_NM + k″), with d_0 of Proposition 38.4. By Lemma 38.16 (d),
‖P_5(Ψ(0))‖_(ℱ^(2d)_ex) ≤ C_(2d)ω_(2d+3)(‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(2d+3+k′_(2d+3)))) for data of that norm at most
min(s_(2d+3), s_P), and 2d + 3 + k′_(2d+3) ≤ N_NM + k″ ≤ d_1, as 2d + 3 ≤ N_NM and k′_k is non-decreasing. Take
ε ∈ (0, s_1] with C_(2d)ω_(2d+3)(ε) < ε_NM, possible as ω_(2d+3)(s) tends to 0 with s, and so small that data with
‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(d_1)) < ε are small in H^(d_0) as Proposition 38.4 asks. For such data ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(H^(N_NM+k″)) < s_1
and, as s_1 ≤ s_♭ ≤ min(s_(2d+3), s_P), ‖P_5(Ψ(0))‖_(ℱ^(2d)_ex) < ε_NM. So Theorem 20.1 gives
U ∈ B^∞_(1/2) with |U|_(3d) < δ and P_5(Ψ(U)) = 0. ∎

### 38.5 Constraint propagation and the theorem

**Lemma 38.20** (The normal derivative; in any dimension.) Let g be a Lorentzian metric, Σ a spacelike
hypersurface with unit normal ν, κ a 1-form with κ|_Σ = 0, and δ*_(g_0,E_C) as in Definition 21.28. If
(G_g δ*_(g_0,E_C)κ)(ν, ·) = 0 on Σ, then ∂_νκ = 0 on Σ.

*Proof.* On Σ the tangential derivatives of κ vanish, and the zeroth-order part of δ*_(g_0,E_C) vanishes as κ = 0
(δ*_(g_0,E_C) − δ*_(g_0) and δ*_(g_0) − δ*_g are of order 0). So, as ∇_Y κ = −g(ν, Y)∂_νκ on Σ,
k := δ*_(g_0,E_C)κ = ½(ν^♭ ⊗ w + w ⊗ ν^♭) with w := −∂_νκ, ν^♭ := g(ν, ·), g(ν, ν) = −1. Then
tr_g k = g^(ab)ν_a w_b = w(ν), and (G_gk)(ν, X) = k(ν, X) − ½g(ν, X)w(ν). For X tangent to Σ:
k(ν, X) = ½(g(ν, ν)w(X) + w(ν)g(ν, X)) = −½w(X) and g(ν, X) = 0, so w(X) = 0. For X = ν: k(ν, ν) = −w(ν), so
(G_gk)(ν, ν) = −w(ν) + ½w(ν) = −½w(ν), and w(ν) = 0. So w = 0. ∎

**Proposition 38.21** (The metric and the constraints.) Let U be given by Theorem 38.19,
(h, p⃗, q) := Φ(U), S its boost, S⁰ := S^(0)_1 its translation and b its black hole parameter. Define

    g := g_(p⃗) + h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + χ_−(t^♭_*)h_(−S,−S⁰) + h     on Ω_*,
    g := ĝ_(S,S⁰) + h_(−S,−S⁰)                                            on 𝒟_(−S,−S⁰) ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + ¼c_0},

    κ := Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g_(p⃗)) − ϑ_tot(p⃗)          on Ω_*,
    κ := Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g, ĝ_(S,S⁰))              on 𝒟_(−S,−S⁰) ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + ¼c_0},

with ĝ_(S,S⁰) = φ_(−S,−S⁰)^*g_(b₀) of Definition 38.15. The two definitions agree on the overlap
Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + ¼c_0}, and Ric(g) = 0, κ = 0 on the union.

*Proof.* *Overlap.* There χ_K = 0, so g_(p⃗) = ĝ_(S,S⁰); h_tot, h_(b,rem) and ϑ_tot vanish; h = h̃ = 0 (the proof of
Lemma 38.16, and supp h̃ ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + ½c_0}); χ_− = 1; and χ^♮_0 = 1 (Lemma 38.1 (b)). So the two
lines of each definition coincide.

*The equation.* On Ω_*, P_5(Ψ(U)) = 0 reads Ric(g) − δ*_(g_0,E_C)κ = 0 with g_0 := g_(p⃗): this is (32.33)
with g′ = g, and (34.3), P_5(h′, p⃗, q) = P_4(h′ + h_(b,rem)(q), p⃗), with h′ := h + χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰). On the
second region, Ric(g) = 0 and κ = 0 by Proposition 38.4 (2) with (−S, −S⁰).

*Propagation.* On Ω_* the second Bianchi identity δ_gG_gRic(g) = 0 gives δ_gG_gδ*_(g_0,E_C)κ = 0. The operator
δ_gG_gδ*_(g_0,E_C) has the principal symbol of δ_gG_gδ*_g, which is ½g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) times the identity, as
δ*_(g_0,E_C) − δ*_g is of order 0. κ vanishes on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + ¼c_0}, which contains Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ 2}
(T̂ ≥ 2). Lemma 18.4 on Ω°_*, with τ := t^♭_* and c := 3/2, gives κ = 0. Its compact sets are those of
Lemma 38.13 (c), with Y := X := Ω°_*, c := 3/2 and T := t^♭_*(p): L_p ⊂ X, as t^♭_* ≥ c > 1 on it. The lemma
applies, g being a metric on Ω_* whose difference from g_(b₀) is small in 𝒢̃^(0,(1,0,0))_(e3b), by (B2) of
Section 29.6, Lemma 32.4 (a) for g_(p⃗), and the smallness of U and h_(−S,−S⁰); near the inner boundary,
past causal curves stay in {r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)} by Lemma 15.35 (1), as in Lemma 18.5 (a). So
Ric(g) = δ*_(g_0,E_C)0 = 0. ∎

[Hin26] propagates the constraints from φ_S(Σ^IVP), using Lemma 38.20 there. Here κ already
vanishes on an open slab of Ω_* (Proposition 38.4 (2)), and Lemma 38.20 enters only through the proof of
Proposition 38.4.

**Theorem 38.22** (Nonlinear stability near Tangherlini; [Hin26, Theorem 13.1] in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
b₀ = (m₀, 0), let the parameters be chosen as in Theorem 38.24, and let ℰ_0, ℓ_0 be as in Section 38.1. There
are ε > 0 and d_1 such that the following holds. Let (γ, k) be initial data on Σ^IVP satisfying the constraint
equations, with

    γ − γ_(b₀) ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b(Σ^IVP),     k − k_(b₀) ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b(Σ^IVP),

of norm < ε in H^(d_1) of these classes. Then there are a Myers–Perry parameter b ∈ ℬ_*, a boost parameter S ∈ 𝒮_1
and a translation parameter S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1, with |b − b₀|, |S| and |S⁰| small, and a Lorentzian metric g on
Ω_* ∪ 𝒟_(−S,−S⁰) with, for φ := φ_(−S,−S⁰) = ψ_(−S⁰) ∘ φ_(−S):

(1) Ric(g) = 0;

(2) g = φ^*(g_(b₀) + h_0) near φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP), so g induces on φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP) the data (φ|)^*(γ, k);

(3) on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 2},

    g = g_(p⃗) + h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + h,     (h, p⃗, q) = Φ(U),  U ∈ 𝒟^∞_ex,

with g_(p⃗) the translated background of (32.4), h ∈ 𝒳^∞_(J,ex) (orders (⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I) at ℐ⁺,
(ℰ_+, 3 + ε_+) at ι⁺, α at K⁺), q ∈ 𝒬_ex, and p⃗ with the components b − b₀, S, S⁰ of U (Theorem 34.20 (1)–(2));

(4) where χ_K = 1, g_(p⃗) = g_b, so g − g_b = h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + h there: g settles to the Myers–Perry metric
g_b at ι⁺ and K⁺ at the orders of these classes;

(5) the gauge condition κ = 0 of Proposition 38.21 holds on Ω_* ∪ 𝒟_(−S,−S⁰).

*Proof.* Theorem 38.19 and Proposition 38.21. (2) is Proposition 38.4 (1) with (−S, −S⁰): there
g = φ^*g_(b₀) + h_(−S,−S⁰) = φ^*(g_(b₀) + h_0). (3) holds as χ_− = 0 on {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 2}, with Corollary 35.33 for
the exact classes. (4) is (32.4). ∎

**Remark 38.23** ([Hin26, Remark 13.4 and Theorem 1.1].) (3) is [Hin26, Remark 13.4 (1)], with the
background translated as well as boosted: in dimension 4 + 1 the shift of the centre of mass is undone by translating
the exterior background (Definition 32.3), where [Hin26] uses a correction term (Chapter 32); so the data surface
of (2) is φ_(−S,−S⁰)⁻¹(Σ^IVP), translated as well as boosted. As in [Hin26], the slowest terms at ι⁺ come from
h_tot(p⃗), which is supported in 𝒞 (Lemma 32.6); in dimension 4 + 1 their orders are those of Chapter 32.
[Hin26] deduces its Theorem 1.1 by pulling back along a diffeomorphism of M that is the identity near
ℐ⁺ ∪ ι⁺ ∪ K⁺, which changes nothing above.

### 38.6 The parameters: the conditions

The stability theory leaves open the constraint damping gauge E_C, the gauge modification parameters E_Υ, the weights
at ℐ⁺, ι⁺ and K⁺, the data classes and the set of Myers–Perry parameters, and its results state conditions on them.
This section lists every such condition with the results that state or use it, and what its threshold depends on;
Theorem 38.24 shows that they can all be met, in an order in which each threshold depends only on choices already
made. m₀ > 0 is fixed and R₁ := m₀^(1/2). Conditions that only restate a choice made in another row are omitted. The
constants v_C, e_C, C_0 and γ_C of the damping are fixed once, in (24.4), at the point where Theorem 24.1
is proved, and no result varies them; every result that names them uses that point. The class parameter of
Section 29.1, the e3b-weight at ℐ⁺ of the admissible operators, is a number in (0, ½) fixed once and for all; it
carries no threshold and depends on no other choice. Chapter 29 writes it ℓ_I as well; in the rows below, ℓ_I is the
b-weight at ℐ⁺ of the data class of Theorem 37.36.

**c1.** (v_C, e_C, C_0) = (½, 1/102400, 100), the point at which Theorem 24.1 is proved ((24.4),
Section 38.1). Threshold: none.

**c2.** γ_C = h⁻¹, h ∈ 𝖧 = (0, h_*) ∖ 𝖹, h_* = min(10⁻⁶, h_0, h_tf), 𝖹 countable ((24.4), Lemma 24.22 (b),
Proposition 24.66 (ii)–(iii)). Threshold: c1.

**c3.** γ_C: (C1)–(C4), the clauses of Theorem 24.1 (3) after its first sentence: the indicial roots of □^C_b are
simple, avoid the listed sets, and are real where their real part is an integer in [3, 51] (used in Chapter 25).
Threshold: c1, c2.

**c4.** γ_C: (C5) γ_C v_C ≥ ½ (Section 33.2, Section 26.10), and s_C := (1 − e_C)(1 − v_C)γ_C > 100
(Section 25.1, Section 38.1). Both hold as γ_C > 10⁶. Threshold: c1.

**u1.** c_Υ, c_(Υ,H), c_C: the fixed 1-forms of Definition 21.28, in the radial forms the proofs use: c_Υ =
ζ(|x|)|x|⁻¹dt and c_(Υ,H) = −½χ(|x|)d|x| (Section 23.13, Lemma 23.7), and c_C of Section 24.2. Threshold:
c1.

**u2.** γ_(Υ,H) ∈ (0, ε_0], ε_0 that of Proposition 23.24. Threshold: none.

**u3.** e_Υ ∈ (0, min(ε_1, ε_L)), with ε_1 of Proposition 23.24 and ε_L of Lemma 23.20
(Proposition 25.11). Threshold: ε_1 on u2; ε_L on c1–c2.

**u4.** 0 < γ_Υ < min(ε_1, ε_L, γ_1, 3/8, ½s_C, ¼), with γ_1 of Proposition 25.11; ε_L contains the bound
C′|γ_Υ| ≤ ½ of the proof of Lemma 23.20 (Proposition 23.24, Section 26.10, (27.1),
(32.27)). Threshold: γ_1 on c1–c3 and u2–u3; ε_L on c1–c2.

**u5.** z_Υ := 4e_Υγ_Υ² ∈ (0, ½] ∖ 𝖹_exc, 𝖹_exc countable (Proposition 25.6 (e), Section 26.10). Threshold:
𝖹_exc on c1–c3; u3.

**b1.** b in the ball ℬ_VI of Theorem 22.30, on which (Dyn) holds. Threshold: none.

**b2.** b ∈ ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)) (Proposition 23.24); with the low-frequency radius c_0 of Corollary 28.12, written c_σ in this
section and the next to distinguish it from the constant c_0 of Section 38.4, b ∈ ℬ(c_σ) (Proposition 25.23) and in
the neighbourhood of Corollary 28.12–Corollary 28.13; and b near b₀ as Theorem 24.1, Proposition 25.11 and
Section 34.4 ask. Threshold: c1–c2, u1–u5.

**b3.** ℬ_*: open, with closure in ℬ_1, and (B5) of Section 29.6: ‖P − 2L_b‖_((0;d)) < ε_0 on ℬ̄_*. This is the only
condition on ℬ_* there; b4 shrinks it further. Threshold: b2, u1–u5.

**b4.** ℬ_*: shrunk so that the states at b are jointly injective (Lemma 36.3) and the maps −id + A_k of the
elimination are invertible at every base point (Theorem 36.10); both depend on the row set and on the levels up
to α. Threshold: b3, w1–w2, d1–d2.

**w1.** ε_+, ε_K: 0 < ε_K < ε_+ < min(δ_♯, ε_ind, ℓ_I − 3) and ε_+ < ¼ ((32.27), (H4) of
Section 33.2); (G⁺) (Definition 34.11) after decreasing ε_+, Λ containing π_1ℰ^C_I (Section 33.2), so
that it is fixed after rows d1–d2; the gap (G) of Definition 33.3 for ε_K and the condition ε_K < ε_Υ of

of (25.10), fixed by the indicial roots of L̂_b(0), with which the hypotheses of Proposition 27.58 are

the conclusion of Proposition 27.58 is stated. At the gauge parameters of Proposition 24.66, ε_ind ≤ δ_50 = 1.94137… ×
10⁻⁸ (Proposition 24.66 (iii), Proposition 25.6 (f); the value by Lemma 24.68), and δ_50 is the least distance
from ℤ among the non-integer entries of modulus at most 50 that do not depend on h; no proof uses its value.
Threshold: u1–u5, d1–d2.

**w2.** α: admissible (Definition 33.3), with (A_J) (Definition 34.12) and the exactness conditions (Ex3)–(Ex4) of
Definition 35.13, in (4 + ε_K − ε′_0, 4 + ε_K], where such α are dense (Definition 34.12, Lemma 35.14).
Threshold: w1, d1–d2 ((A_J) involves Λ).

**d1.** ℰ_0, ℓ_0: min Re ℰ_0 > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ, jℰ_0 ⊂ ℰ_0, ℓ_0 > 3 (so that row d2 is nonempty), ℓ_0 ∉ Re π_1ℰ_0
(Theorem 37.36, Section 38.1, (H4) of Section 33.2). Threshold: u4.

**d2.** ℓ_I: 3 < ℓ_I < min(ℓ_0, 3/2 + s_C), with row w1's ε_+ < ℓ_I − 3: Theorem 37.36 asks 3/2 < ℓ_I < ℓ_0, (H4)
asks ℓ_I > 3 + ε_+, and Theorem 38.22 uses one ℓ_I for both. ℓ_I avoids the exclusion sets of (H4), which are
discrete: for ℓ_I in a bounded interval, ℰ^C_I ranges over finitely many index sets (Theorem 37.36), and
ℓ_I ∉ Re π_1ℰ^C_I avoids their real parts; and ℓ_I ∉ 3/2 + σ_Υ, σ_Υ = {0, (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ, γ_Υ, 2γ_Υ} (Definition 27.6,
Proposition 29.29, Section 33.2). Threshold: c1–c2, u3–u4, d1.

**n1.** ε, d_1: the smallness and regularity of Theorem 38.22. Threshold: all the above.

### 38.7 The parameters: the choice

**Theorem 38.24** (The parameters can be chosen together.) The conditions of Section 38.6 can be met
together. Make the choices in this order; at each step the thresholds depend only on the choices before it:

(0) ℬ_VI := {|b − b₀| ≤ ε_VI} of Theorem 22.30. It depends on the metrics alone.

(1) (v_C, e_C, C_0) := (½, 1/102400, 100) and h ∈ 𝖧, γ_C := h⁻¹. Then Theorem 24.1 holds at these values
(Theorem 24.53 for (1)–(3), Theorem 24.55 for (4)), with (C1)–(C4) (row c3), and (C5) and s_C > 100 hold, as
γ_C > 10⁶.

(2) The gauge. ε_0 of Proposition 23.24 is uniform. Choose γ_(Υ,H) ∈ (0, ε_0]; this fixes ε_1 and ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)).
Choose e_Υ ∈ (0, min(ε_1, ε_L)); this fixes γ_1 of Proposition 25.11, which fixes all parameters but γ_Υ and
depends on the orders, hence on γ_C. 𝖹_exc is fixed by step (1). Choose γ_Υ in the interval of row u4 with
4e_Υγ_Υ² ∉ 𝖹_exc. This is possible because the interval is nonempty and open, while {γ > 0 : 4e_Υγ² ∈ 𝖹_exc} is
countable. Then z_Υ ∈ (0, ½], as γ_Υ < ¼ and e_Υ < 1. Proposition 23.18 (the invertibility of the spectral family
of □^Υ_b at |σ| ≥ c_σ) is then implied, for every c_σ and b ∈ ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)), by Proposition 23.24, which gives it for
every σ with Im σ ≥ 0; so it imposes no further condition.

(3) The data classes: ℰ_0 and ℓ_0 > 3 as in row d1, then ℓ_I in the interval (3, min(ℓ_0, 3/2 + s_C)) of row d2,
minus the four points 3/2 + σ_Υ and the exclusion sets of (H4). This fixes ℰ^C_I (Theorem 37.36) and Λ. In the
symmetry class, Section 38.8 takes ℰ_0 = {(j, 0) : j ≥ 2}, ℓ_0 ∈ (3, 4) and ℓ_I ∈ (3, ℓ_0) ((38.15)).

(4) The weights. δ_♯, ε_ind and ε_Υ, all positive, are fixed by step (2). Choose ε_+ < min(δ_♯, ε_ind, ¼, ℓ_I − 3),
decreased for (G⁺) and (Ex1)–(Ex2) (possible: no λ ∈ Λ has real part in (3, 3 + ε_+] for ε_+ small,
Definition 34.11, and (Ex2) excludes finitely many values in a bounded range, Lemma 35.14; (Ex2) involves
ℰ^tot_I and λ_♯, fixed by steps (2)–(3)); then ε_K, decreased for (G) and for the condition ε_K < ε_Υ of
Definition 33.3; then α as in row w2. (H4) holds as ε_+ < ℓ_I − 3, and decreasing ε_+ keeps rows d1–d2.

(5) The parameter set. The gauge being fixed, take c_σ of Corollary 28.12 (uniform near b₀), then ℬ(c_σ) of
Proposition 25.23, which fixes the modification parameters first and then allows every c_σ > 0. Let ℬ_* be an open
ball about b₀ whose closure lies in ℬ_VI, in every neighbourhood of row b2, and in ℬ_1, with (B5). These are finitely
many neighbourhoods of b₀, fixed by steps (0)–(4). Balls are taken in the norm |m − m₀| + |A|, |A| the Frobenius norm,
which is invariant under conjugation by O(4), so every parameter ball is O(4)-invariant (Lemma 38.26 uses this).
Section 29.6 imposes no lower bound on ℬ_*, so shrinking it is allowed. Every operator family of the stability
theory is then taken over ℬ̄_*, a compact set on which (Dyn) holds (step (0)), as (H5) and its extensions ask. Last,
ℬ_* is shrunk as row b4 asks, which depends on steps (3)–(4) only.

(6) ε and d_1 of Theorem 38.22, which depend on all of the above.

*Proof.* Each step's existence claim is the cited statement, read with the quantifiers it has; the last entry of each
row of Section 38.6 records that no threshold depends on a later choice. In step (2), the ε_0 of Proposition 23.24
is uniform, while its ε_1 and ℬ(γ_(Υ,H)) come after γ_(Υ,H), so the order γ_(Υ,H), e_Υ, γ_Υ meets it. The only
low-frequency radius that depends on the gauge is the c_σ of Corollary 28.12, and it is used only after the gauge is
fixed, through Proposition 25.23, whose neighbourhood is then chosen. In step (5), each neighbourhood of rows b2 and
b4 is open and contains b₀, so their intersection with ℬ_VI contains a ball. The ball of Theorem 22.30 depends on
no gauge parameter, as the dynamical hypotheses concern the metric alone (Section 22.2). (K3) holds for every ε
(Proposition 22.28), so ε_VI depends neither on the regularity d_0 of Theorem 15.49 nor on its order k. ∎

The invertibility of L̂_b(σ) for b ≠ b₀ and 0 < |σ| < c_σ, which Section 25.12 leaves open, holds for b near b₀ and
σ ∈ Σ_0, |σ| ≤ c_σ, by Corollary 28.12; its neighbourhood is one of row b2, so it holds on ℬ̄_*.

### 38.8 The symmetry class

*The group.* G := O(2) × O(2) acts on ℝ⁴ = ℝ² × ℝ² by the rotations of the planes (x¹, x²) and (x³, x⁴) and by the
reflections x² ↦ −x² and x⁴ ↦ −x⁴; on spacetime it acts by (t, x) ↦ (t, σx). Every element of O(4), acting so, is an
isometry of every g^KS_(m,0) and fixes every function of (t, |x|). The fixed spaces are

    (ℝ⁴)^G = 0,     𝔰𝔬(4)^G = 0.

Indeed, the torus T² = SO(2) × SO(2) fixes in ℝ⁴ only 0, and in 𝔰𝔬(4), acting by conjugation, exactly
span(W₁₂, W₃₄), the infinitesimal rotations of the two planes (T² is a maximal torus of SO(4), so its fixed subalgebra
is its own Lie algebra); and x² ↦ −x² reverses W₁₂ while fixing W₃₄, x⁴ ↦ −x⁴ reverses W₃₄ while fixing W₁₂.

*The data class.* In the class we take, in step (3) of Theorem 38.24,

    ℰ_0 := {(j, 0) : j ∈ ℕ, j ≥ 2},     ℓ_0 ∈ (3, 4),     ℓ_I ∈ (3, ℓ_0).    (38.15)

Row d1 holds: min Re ℰ_0 = 2 > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ, as γ_Υ < ¼ (step (2)); ℰ_0 is closed under sums and positive multiples; and
ℓ_0 > 3 with ℓ_0 ∉ ℕ, so ℓ_0 ∉ Re π_1ℰ_0. Row d2 holds for ℓ_I ∈ (3, min(ℓ_0, 3/2 + s_C)) = (3, ℓ_0), as s_C > 100,
off the discrete exclusion sets of row d2 and of (H4). Step (4) then takes ε_+ < ℓ_I − 3, so (H4) of
Section 33.2 holds. ε and d_1 are those of Theorem 38.22 (step (6)). For a pair (γ̃, k̃) of symmetric
2-tensors on Σ^IVP, ‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(d_1) denotes the norm in which Theorem 38.22 measures (γ − γ_(b₀), k − k_(b₀)):
the H^(d_1)-norm of H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b × H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b, and ∞ outside these spaces. The weights are those of the
b-density, so that a weight is the pointwise order (Section 37.1).

**Lemma 38.25** (What lies in the class.) Let ρ := |x|⁻¹, and let γ̃, k̃ be smooth symmetric 2-tensors on
Σ^IVP whose Cartesian components lie, on {r ≥ R′}, in ρ²C^∞ and ρ³C^∞ of the radial compactification. Then
‖(γ̃, k̃)‖_(d_1) is finite, and it is bounded by C_(R′) times the sum of the C^(d_1+3)-norms of the components on
{r ≤ 2R′} and finitely many C^∞-seminorms of ρ⁻²γ̃ and ρ⁻³k̃ on the compactified {r ≥ R′}.

*Proof.* Near ρ = 0, Taylor's formula in ρ writes a function of ρ²C^∞ as ρ²a₂(ω) + ρ³a₃(ω) + ρ⁴C^∞. The a_j are
smooth on 𝕊³, and the seminorms of the remainder are bounded by those of ρ⁻²γ̃. The exponents (2, 0) and (3, 0) lie in
ℰ_0 below ℓ_0, and ρ⁴C^∞ ⊂ ρ^(ℓ_0)H^∞_b, as ℓ_0 < 4. Likewise ρ³C^∞ = ρ³a₃ + ρ⁴a₄ + ρ⁵C^∞, with (3, 0) and (4, 0)
in ℰ_0 + 1 below ℓ_0 + 1 < 5. On {r ≤ 2R′} the weights are bounded above and below. ∎

### 38.9 The nonlinear theorem in the symmetry class

O(4) acts on M by (t, x) ↦ (t, σx) and on tensors by σ_* := (σ⁻¹)^*. On the components of 𝒟_ex (Definition 35.11,
Definition 34.15) it acts as follows: on b = (m, A) ∈ 𝔟 by (m, σAσ⁻¹); on 𝒮_1 ∋ S_w by S_w ↦ S_(σw); on the
coefficient spaces 𝒲_τ, 𝒴_ψ (spaces of harmonics on 𝕊³, 𝒮_1, and 𝒱′ = 0) by their representations; on 𝒱_1, the
rotations, the coefficient space of the rotation rows (Definition 34.3), by conjugation V ↦ σVσ⁻¹; and on the
tensor and function components (u^0_λ, f_λ, h̃, and the values of the q-tails) by σ_*.

**Lemma 38.26** (Naturality.) Make the following choices O(4)-equivariant.

(C1) *Cut-offs:* χ^♭_K, χ_K, χ^♯_K, χ_IVP, χ^♯_IVP and χ_r of Section 21.7, χ_∞ of (21.30), χ_ι and χ_9
(Section 38.1, Section 38.4), χ_− (Definition 38.15), the factor Θ = χ_rχ^♯_IVP(1 − χ^♭_K), and the cut-offs
inside t^♭_* (Lemma 15.35). Every set in their conditions (the values 0 and 1, the supports, and the nesting of
Section 21.7, each later function equal to 1 near the support of the earlier) is defined by
(t, t_*, t_IVP, t^♭_*, |x|), hence O(4)-invariant. So they are chosen directly, in nesting order, as smooth functions
of these and of |x|²: each is a cut-off between an invariant closed set and the interior of a larger invariant set. No
averaging is used; averaging separately could break the nesting.

(C2) *Gauge 1-forms:* c_Υ, c_(Υ,H), c_C (Definition 21.28, Section 24.1). They are stationary, lie in |x|⁻¹C^∞ or
are supported in {|x| < 5R₁}, and equal |x|⁻¹dt or |x|⁻¹(dt − v_C d|x|) for large |x|. The proofs use the forms
c_Υ = ζ(|x|)|x|⁻¹dt, c_(Υ,H) = −½χ(|x|)d|x| (Section 23.13) and c_C of Section 24.2 (that of Proposition 24.10,
whose coefficients are functions of r), which are O(4)-invariant; no averaging is needed.

(C3) *Linear maps given by existence statements:* ω_s1(S) and ω̆(S) (Proposition 23.28 at b₀, linear in S ∈ 𝒮_1);
the 1-form towers ω̆^i_τ(W), 0 ≤ i ≤ K_τ, of every type τ ∈ 𝒯 (Proposition 23.28 and Proposition 23.34 at b₀,
linear in W), for v1 as a map of all of 𝒱_1 and not only of 𝒲_v1 = 𝒱′ = 0, since the rotation rows use it there
(Definition 34.3); the proofs use these towers themselves, in the term dt_* ⊗_s ω̆^(K_τ)_τ of the rows m_ν and in
the corrections h_ν = −dχ_K ⊗_s ω_ν at every level (Section 32.11); the states and towers of the table of
Section 26.10, as linear maps of the coefficient spaces 𝒴_τ; and the solution operators 𝒮_(λ₀) of
Section 34.5. Each is a linear map L : V → 𝒯 from an O(4)-representation into tensors. Its conditions are affine
in L and O(4)-invariant: equations with natural operators of g_(b₀), asymptotic or support conditions at faces fixed by
O(4), and prescribed leading terms and right sides given by O(4)-equivariant data (for the towers the leading terms
d(|x|S) for s1, V and (1 + (2/5)γ_Υ)|x|V for v1, χ_∂W̄ for s0 and the model ω̄(Y) for s2, c0, c1,
Proposition 23.34), so that an average of solutions is a solution. So

    L^(O(4)) := ∫_(O(4)) σ_* ∘ L ∘ σ⁻¹ dσ

(Haar probability measure) meets them, with the same bounds. The 1-form towers are averaged once, and the towers of
the table of Section 26.10 at b₀ of the types of 𝒯 are taken as δ*_(g_(b₀)) of the averaged 1-forms, as they are
of the unaveraged ones; the pure-gauge rows outside 𝒯 are δ*-images of 1-forms that (C3) does not name, and the
physical rows are not δ*-images; both are averaged as the maps of 𝒴_τ. One averaged choice serves both names, as
δ*_(g_(b₀)) commutes with the average: δ*_g ω = ½ℒ_(g⁻¹ω) g, and for a diffeomorphism φ,
φ^*(ℒ_X g) = ℒ_(φ^*X)(φ^*g) and φ^*(g⁻¹ω) = (φ^*g)⁻¹(φ^*ω), so φ^*(δ*_g ω) = δ*_(φ^*g)(φ^*ω); every σ ∈ O(4) is an
isometry of g_(b₀), so σ_* δ*_(g_(b₀)) = δ*_(g_(b₀)) σ_*.

(C3′) *Families in b:* the towers and states at b used in h_(b,rem)(q), namely T_(ψ,b), h^(≤1)_(b,s1), h_(b,v1) and
h^(≤2)_(b,v1), chosen smooth in b by Lemma 34.4. Replace a family L_b by
