    L^(O(4))_b := ∫_(O(4)) σ_* ∘ L_(σ⁻¹·b) ∘ σ⁻¹ dσ.

Then σ_* ∘ L^(O(4))_b ∘ σ⁻¹ = L^(O(4))_(σ·b), and the average keeps the tower relations for L_b (natural, given (C2)),
smoothness in b, the b-independent leading terms, and the value at b₀ once (C3) is applied there. The parameter balls
are O(4)-invariant, being balls in the conjugation-invariant norm of step (5) of Theorem 38.24.

(C4) *The complement 𝒱′* of Section 32.10, which is 0 at b₀.

Then, for every closed subgroup G′ of O(4), every G′-invariant data (γ, k), every σ ∈ G′ and every small U ∈ 𝒟_ex,

    Φ(σ·U) = σ·Φ(U),     Ψ(σ·U) = σ_*Ψ(U),     P_5(Ψ(σ·U)) = σ_*P_5(Ψ(U)).

The averaged choices are admissible. Each object of (C3) and (C3′) is given by an existence statement, which asserts
that a choice with the conditions listed exists: Proposition 23.28 for ω_s1(S) and ω̆(S), Proposition 23.28 and
Proposition 23.34 for the 1-form towers, the table of Section 26.10 for the states and towers of the rows, the
step of Section 34.5 for the operators 𝒮_(λ₀), and Lemma 34.4 for the families in b. The results of
Chapter 23–Chapter 36 that use these objects take them as given by those statements, for any choice with the
conditions listed, and so hold for the averaged one. Four properties used there are not themselves linear conditions,
and each is kept; a use that takes a property from a construction rather than from the statement takes one of these. (i)
The s1 and v1 states are unique given their conditions (the zero energy operator is injective at the weights in the gap,
Proposition 23.28), so the average is the choice. (ii) The bijectivity of Lemma 26.32 is a statement about
leading terms, which are prescribed by O(4)-equivariant maps onto kernels split by harmonic, and which the average keeps.
(iii) The isotypic type of each construction is that of an equivariant map (Schur's lemma). (iv) Lemma 34.4
takes the leading terms at ∂X of the companions h̆^((μ),j)_(b,τ) from the construction of Proposition 23.34, not from
its statement, which lists only type τ leading terms: the tower relations fix the leading term of a companion only modulo
the indicial kernel, and the construction fixes the leading term of ω̆^((μ),k) at μ − k as the model solution ω̆̄^k. The
average keeps it. Its leading terms are of type τ, the average being O(4)-equivariant (Schur's lemma); they satisfy the
model recursion of that construction, Ā_0ω̆̄^k = −Ā_1ω̆̄^(k−1), which is linear and O(4)-invariant, the model being that
of g_(b₀); and as μ − k is no type τ root ((R4) of Section 23.16), the model recursion has exactly one type τ solution
at μ − k, by induction on k the model solution. So the averaged towers, and the companions built from them (through
δ*_(g_(b₀)), which commutes with the average), have the leading terms of the construction, at b₀ and, through (C3′), for
b near b₀.

*Proof.* By induction along the definitions; each object is natural, given (C1)–(C4) and (C3′).

- g_b = Φ_m^*g^KS_(m,A): Definition 21.15 builds r_A, ℓ_A and H_(m,A) from (m, A, x) by matrix operations, which are
  equivariant under x ↦ σx, A ↦ σAσ⁻¹; so σ_*g_((m,A)) = g_((m,σAσ⁻¹)). Φ_m and T_m are radial. So
  g_(b₀,σ·b,−σ·S) = σ_*g_(b₀,b,−S) ((29.1)) and g_(σ·p⃗) = σ_*g_(p⃗) ((32.4)), given the next
  item.

- φ_S = exp V(S_w), V(S_w) = ½ΘX_w, X_w = t w·∂_x + (w·x)∂_t (Lemma 21.26). So σ_*X_w = X_(σw) and
  σφ_(S_w)σ⁻¹ = φ_(S_(σw)); likewise for the translations ψ_(S_w) of (32.4), generated by ½Θ w·∂_x, so
  σφ_(S,S⁰)σ⁻¹ = φ_(σ·S,σ·S⁰) ((38.1)).

- t_* and t_IVP are functions of (t, |x|), and t^♭_* is a function of (t_*, r): C_♭(t_* + R̃(r)), t_*F₁(t_*/r) and
  their glued combinations (Lemma 15.35 and its proof), given (C1).

- E^Υ_(g_0), E^C_g, Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g_0) = Υ^0(g, g_0) − E^Υ_(g_0)G_(g_0)(g − g_0) and δ*_(g,E_C) (Definition 21.28) are
  natural in (g, g_0) and the forms of (C2). So are P, P_2–P_5 ((32.33), (34.3)) and P^♮,
  χ^♮_0 being a function of (t_IVP, |x|, t_*).

- ω̇_b(ḃ) = −(□̂^Υ_b(0))⁻¹η_b(ḃ) and ġ^Υ_b ((25.17)) are natural, the inverse being unique.
  w(S) = g_(b₀)(X_S, ·) is natural.

- h_tot and ϑ_tot (Definition 32.7, Definition 32.19, Definition 32.31, Definition 32.33) are built from χ_K,
  δ*_(g_(b₀)) and commutators with χ_K, the maps of (C3), w(S), Θ and functions of t_*. h_(b,rem)(q)
  (Definition 34.2) is χ_K times h^(≤1)_(b,s1), ġ_b and the towers of (C3′).

- Φ ((34.11)) is built from χ_ι, u_λ = u^0_λ + res_(z=λ)(t_*^(−z)N_(ι⁺)(z)⁻¹f_λ(z)), with N_(ι⁺) the normal
  operator of a natural operator, h̃, and the corrections h_(λ₀), given by the solution operators 𝒮_(λ₀) and the
  t_*^(−λ₀)-terms of rows and towers (Section 34.5).

- h_(S,S⁰) (Proposition 38.4) is the unique solution of (38.4) with data h⁰_(S,S⁰), h¹_(S,S⁰), the
  restrictions to Σ^IVP of the pull-backs by φ_(S,S⁰) of h_0, the solution with the data h̊_0, h̊_1 of
  Proposition 37.41. The proof of Proposition 37.41 builds these from (γ̃, k̃) and g_(b₀) by setting h̊_0 := γ̃ with
  h̊_0(ν_(b₀), ·) := 0, and by solving tensorial linear equations for the second datum, uniquely. So for G′-invariant
  data and σ ∈ G′, h̊_0, h̊_1 and h_0 are G′-invariant by uniqueness, h^j_(σ·S,σ·S⁰) = σ_*h^j_(S,S⁰), and
  h_(σ·S,σ·S⁰) = σ_*h_(S,S⁰) by uniqueness.

So Ψ(U) = (χ_−h_(−S,−S^(0)_1), 0, 0) + Φ(U) ((38.11)) and P_5 ∘ Ψ are equivariant. ∎

**Proposition 38.27** (Theorem 38.22 in the symmetry class; [Hin26, Theorem 13.1] in the class.) Make
the choices of Lemma 38.26 equivariant. If the data (γ, k) of Theorem 38.22 are G-invariant, and small for the
threshold ε^G_NM below, its conclusion holds with U fixed by G, b = (m′, 0), S = S⁰ = 0 and g G-invariant.

*Proof.* *The action.* G ⊂ O(4) acts on M by diffeomorphisms that are smooth on the compactification, preserve each
boundary hypersurface (the defining functions of (21.23) are functions of (t, |x|)), and fix t, t_*, t_IVP and
t^♭_*. So it preserves Σ^IVP, Ω_*, 𝒟, the classes B^k, B^k_η, F^k, F^∞_η of Section 38.4, and the collar of
Lemma 38.18. Its action on each 𝒟^k_ex and ℱ^k_ex is bounded uniformly in σ, G being compact and acting
smoothly. Replace each norm |·|_k by sup_(σ∈G)|σ·(·)|_k, an equivalent norm. Then G acts isometrically, and every
estimate used below holds with changed constants.

*Fixed spaces.* Let B^(k,G), B^(k,G)_η, F^(k,G) and F^(∞,G)_η be the G-fixed elements. They are closed, and
Π := ∫_G σ dσ (Haar probability measure) is a projection onto them of norm at most 1 that preserves every support
class.

*Theorem 20.1 on the fixed spaces.* (i) ΠS_θ, with S_θ of Lemma 38.18, maps B^(∞,G)_(θ^(−1/2)) into B^(∞,G) and
B^(∞,G)_η into B^(∞,G)_(η−θ^(−1/2)), and satisfies (20.1) with the constants of the G-sup norms: for
v ∈ B^(∞,G), v − ΠS_θv = Π(v − S_θv), and Π has norm at most 1. (ii) By Lemma 38.26, U ↦ P_5(Ψ(U)) maps the fixed
part of the domain of Theorem 38.19 into F^(∞,G), and B^(∞,G)_η into F^(∞,G)_η. Differentiability and
(20.2)–(20.3) hold by restriction. (iii) For U ∈ B^(∞,G), differentiating P_5(Ψ(σ·V)) = σ_*P_5(Ψ(V)) at
V = U gives D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ) ∘ σ = σ_* ∘ D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ), so D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ) commutes with Π. So Ψ^G_NM(U) := ΠΨ_NM(U) on F^(∞,G)
satisfies D_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)Ψ^G_NM(U)f = ΠD_U(P_5 ∘ Ψ)Ψ_NM(U)f = Πf = f, and it inherits (20.4). It maps F^(∞,G)_η
into B^(∞,G)_η for U in the domain of (ii) and in B^(∞,G)_η, which is what Theorem 20.1 (iii) asks. Indeed, for
such U and f ∈ F^(∞,G)_η ⊂ F^∞_η, Ψ_NM(U)f ∈ B^∞_η by (iii) of the proof of Theorem 38.19, which applies at
U ∈ B^∞_η, a base point whose tail vanishes below the level (Lemma 38.17); and Π preserves B^∞_η and maps it
into the fixed space. So Ψ^G_NM(U)f = ΠΨ_NM(U)f ∈ B^(∞,G)_η. Hence Theorem 20.1 holds on the fixed spaces, with
its own threshold ε^G_NM determined by the constants of the G-sup norms, and gives U ∈ B^(∞,G)_(1/2) with
P_5(Ψ(U)) = 0 on Ω_*.

*The metric.* Proposition 38.21 builds g from (h, p⃗, q) = Φ(U), h_(−S,−S^(0)_1) and g_(p⃗). By Lemma 38.26 every
ingredient is equivariant and U is fixed, so g is G-invariant. U_0 = (b − b₀, S, S^(0)_1) is fixed: 𝔟^G = ℝ × {0} and
𝒮_1^G = 0, 𝒮_1 being ℝ⁴ as a representation. So b = (m′, 0) and S = S^(0)_1 = 0, and Theorem 38.22 (1)–(5) hold
with these values. ∎

### 38.10 Small final parameters and the rate of settling

**Corollary 38.28** (Small final parameters; the rate on compact sets.) Make the choices of
Theorem 38.24 through the choice of ε_K in step (4). Let ε_m > 0 and ε_t ∈ (0, ε_K); take α in row w2 with
α > 4 + ε_t (possible: the α of row w2 are dense in (4 + ε_K − ε′_0, 4 + ε_K], and 4 + ε_t < 4 + ε_K), and finish
steps (5)–(6). Then there is ε = ε(ε_m, ε_t) > 0, with d_1 as in Theorem 38.22, such that for data as in
Theorem 38.22 of norm below ε:

(a) the conclusion of Theorem 38.22 holds with |b − b₀| < ε_m, |S| < ε_m and |S⁰| < ε_m;

(b) if the data are G-invariant, the conclusion of Proposition 38.27 holds, with |m′ − m₀| < ε_m;

(c) in either case, for every R′, ε′ > 0 and i, β there are C and T′ such that the Cartesian components of g − g_b, in
the coordinates (t, x) of Section 21.4, satisfy

    |(t_*∂_(t_*))^i ∂^β_x (g − g_b)| ≤ C t_*^(−(α−2)+ε′)     on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′},    (38.16)

where α − 2 > 2 + ε_K − ε′_0 > 2 (Definition 33.3) and α − 2 > 2 + ε_t; with ε′ := α − 4 − ε_t, g − g_b =
O(t_*^(−2−ε_t)) there.

*Proof.* (a) In the proof of Theorem 38.19, apply Theorem 20.1 with its radius δ replaced by min(δ, ε_m): its
hypotheses restrict to the smaller set, and its threshold then depends on ε_m. This gives Theorem 38.22
with |b − b₀| ≤ ‖U‖_(𝒟^d_ex) ≤ |U|_(3d) < ε_m and |S|, |S⁰| ≤ |U|_(3d) < ε_m, the black hole parameter, the boost and the
translation being components of U, for data of norm below some ε. (b) Take ε moreover below the threshold ε^G_NM of the
run of Theorem 20.1 in Proposition 38.27, with the radius min(δ, ε_m) there too, through the equivalence of the norms.

(c) Where χ_K = 1, g − g_b = h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + h (Theorem 38.22 (4)). h_tot(p⃗) is supported in 𝒞, whose
closure is disjoint from K⁺ (Lemma 32.6); so it vanishes on {r ≤ R′} for t_* large, as does 1 − χ_K.
h ∈ 𝒳^∞_(J,ex) has K⁺-order α, and h_(b,rem)(q) has K⁺-order (α − 2)− (Lemma 34.5 (a) at b₀; at b near b₀,
the rates of (34.1), which exceed α − 2, with Lemma 34.4). Near the interior of K⁺,
ρ_K = t₀⁻¹ with t₀ = t − |x| ((21.23)), comparable to t_* on {r ≤ R′}, and the b-vector fields there are
spanned by t_*∂_(t_*) and ∂_x. By b-Sobolev embedding for the b-density μ_b of Section 29.1, as in the proof of
Lemma 29.3 (a weight is then the pointwise order),
(t_*∂_(t_*))^i∂^β_x of a function of K⁺-order w− is O(t_*^(−w+ε′)) for every ε′ > 0. With w = α − 2 this is
(38.16). ∎

## 39. Gluing to the Myers–Perry family, and gluing in the symmetry class

This chapter proves [CD03, Theorem 8.1] in space dimension 4 for vacuum initial data whose Poincaré charges lie near
those of five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini. Smooth vacuum data on ℝ⁴ ∖ B that decay at a rate α ∈ (3/2, 2] are
glued, on an annulus Γ(R, 4R), to the data of a translated, rotated and boosted Myers–Perry metric, which they equal
for |x| ≥ 4R (Theorem 39.13). [CD03, Theorem 8.1, p. 35] is stated for three-dimensional data, and [CD03, Remark 8.2,
p. 36] names what is missing in higher dimensions: "The argument below carries over to any dimension, the only element
missing is an equivalent of Proposition F.1 for the family of translated, rotated, and boosted Myers-Perry metrics."
Near Tangherlini, which is the case needed here, this equivalent is Proposition 39.7 and Corollary 39.8. The proof
follows [CD03, Section 8.1], with three changes in dimension 4 + 1. First, the charges are defined and estimated
directly from a linear flux identity (Section 39.2); this replaces [CD03, Appendix E] and needs no parity condition,
since 2α > n − 1 = 3. Second, the exponentially weighted spaces of [CD03, Theorem 5.9] are used from the start, so the
glued data are smooth. Third, the powers of R are those of space dimension 4: R⁻² for the energy and the momentum, R⁻³
for the angular momentum and the centre of mass. Every result of [CD03] used here holds in every space dimension n ≥ 2
([CD03, p. 4]); each is stated exactly, here or in Appendix A. [CD03, Lemma 3.18] is proved again
(Lemma 39.12), and the continuity in the parameter that [CD03, Theorem 3.19] needs is proved as Lemma 39.11.

Section 39.5 runs the construction in the symmetry class of Section 2.1, G = O(2) × O(2), on the initial surface
Σ^IVP of Section 21.5.3 and with the Tangherlini data on that surface as the family (Proposition 39.17). The
obstruction is then one-dimensional and is matched by the mass alone, and the flux identity bounds the change of mass
by the size of the data's deviation on the annulus. Corollary 39.19 applies it to the data of the solution g_λ after
the shell; these are the data of item (i) of Theorem 3.9, proved in Chapter 41.

The continuity lemma Lemma 39.11 is stated on a general compact manifold with boundary and for a general smooth
background, with every hypothesis explicit (Section 39.4.1), and is then applied to the flat annulus.
Chapter 53 applies it to other data.

*The inner radius.* Nothing in this chapter reaches the inner region of the spacetime of Section 21.4. Section 39.3
uses the Myers–Perry family on {|x| ≥ 50R₁} only, and Section 39.5 takes data on Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ |x| ≤ 3R} and changes
them only on {R ≤ |x| ≤ 4R}. So every result holds for every inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] of Section 21.4.

*Notation.* n = 4 is the space dimension, except in Section 39.4.1, where n is general. As in [CD03], K denotes
the second fundamental form of an initial data set, and N a lapse or the function in a pair (Y, N); neither the
approximant's order nor its number of stages occurs in this chapter. The mass parameter of the Myers–Perry family is m,
as in Chapter 21; b₀ = (m₀, 0) and R₁ = m₀^(1/2). 𝔎 is the space of Killing initial data of flat space ((39.4)). A
pair (K, g) in the argument of a map of [CD03] is written u = (K, g). π_(g′) and π₀ always denote projections, and the
number π occurs only in the charges.

### 39.1 Initial data and the Killing initial data of flat space

ℝ⁴ carries Cartesian coordinates x, with r = |x|, x̂ = x/r, S_ϱ := {r = ϱ} with outward unit normal ν = x̂ and
Euclidean area element dS, and Γ(a, b) := {a < r < b}. Indices are raised and traced with δ unless a metric is named.
An *initial data set* is a pair (g, K) of a Riemannian metric and a symmetric 2-tensor. Its constraint map is
Theorem A.15 ([CD03, (2.1), p. 4]),

    J(K, g)_i := 2(−∇^j K_ij + ∇_i tr_g K),     ρ(K, g) := R(g) − |K|²_g + (tr_g K)²,    (39.1)

"the general relativistic constraint equations whatever the space-dimension n" ([CD03, p. 4]). The data are *vacuum*
where J = 0 and ρ = 0; this condition is invariant under K ↦ −K. For a Lorentzian metric
𝔤 = −N²dt² + g_ij(dxⁱ + βⁱdt)(dxʲ + βʲdt) the data on {t = 0} are g and

    K_ij := (1/(2N))(∂_t g_ij − D_iβ_j − D_jβ_i),    (39.2)

where D is the connection of g and β_i = 𝔤_0i; the Gauss–Codazzi equations make them vacuum when 𝔤 is Ricci-flat.

*Decay.* For α > 0, an integer j ≥ 1 and data on {r > R₀}, put

    |||(g, K)|||_(α,j) := sup_(r>R₀) ( Σ_(|γ|≤j) r^(α+|γ|)|∂^γ(g − δ)| + Σ_(|γ|≤j−1) r^(α+1+|γ|)|∂^γK| ),
    (39.3)

the components taken in Cartesian coordinates. This is the r^(−α)W^(j,∞)_r-asymptotic flatness of g, with
K ∈ r^(−α−1)W^(j−1,∞)_r, of [CD03, Section 7, (7.1)], at j = k + 4, k the order of the proof of Theorem 39.13.

*The Killing initial data of flat space.* Let 𝔎 be the space of pairs X = (Y, N) with Y a Killing field of (ℝ⁴, δ)
and N an affine function, and fix the basis

    e₀ := (0, 1),     e_l := (∂_l, 0),     e_ab := (W_ab x, 0),     e′_l := (0, x^l),    (39.4)

for 1 ≤ l ≤ 4 and 1 ≤ a < b ≤ 4, with W_ab := E_ab − E_ba and E_ab the matrix units (W_ab is the generator J_ab of
Section 21.5.1). So dim 𝔎 = 1 + 4 + 6 + 4 = 15 = (n + 1)(n + 2)/2. Each basis element X = (Y, N) is homogeneous of a
degree d(X), meaning that N(cx) = c^(d(X))N(x) and Yⁱ(cx) = c^(d(X))Yⁱ(x) for c > 0: the degree is 0 for e₀, e_l and
1 for e_ab, e′_l. The group O(4) acts on 𝔎 by push-forward under x ↦ Ox. As O(4)-representations, the four groups in
(39.4) are the trivial representation, the standard ℝ⁴, Λ²ℝ⁴ (with W ↦ OWOᵀ) and ℝ⁴.

We use the formal adjoint of the linearised constraint map in the form [CD03, (2.4), p. 5]: with P the linearisation
of (J, ρ) at (K, g) (Theorem A.15), "the formal L²-adjoint of P takes the form

    P*(Y, N) = ( 2(∇_(iY_j) − ∇^lY_l g_ij − K_ij N + tr K N g_ij),
                 ∇^lY_l K_ij − 2K^l_(i∇_j)Y_l + K^q_l∇_qY^l g_ij − ΔN g_ij + ∇_i∇_jN
                   + (∇^pK_lp g_ij − ∇_lK_ij)Y^l − N Ric(g)_ij + 2NK^l_iK_jl − 2N(tr K)K_ij )."

### 39.2 Killing initial data, the flux identity and the charges

**Lemma 39.1** (The Killing initial data.) Let 𝒪 ⊂ ℝ⁴ be open and connected. A smooth pair (Y, N) on 𝒪
satisfies P*_((0,δ))(Y, N) = 0 if and only if it is the restriction of an element of 𝔎.

*Proof.* At K = 0, g = δ, [CD03, (2.4)] gives P*(Y, N) = (2(∂_(iY_j) − (div Y)δ_ij), −ΔN δ_ij + ∂_i∂_jN). The trace of
the first component is 2(1 − n) div Y, so div Y = 0 and ∂_(iY_j) = 0. The trace of the second is (1 − n)ΔN, so ΔN = 0
and ∂_i∂_jN = 0, and N is affine on the connected 𝒪. For a Killing field, ∂_iY_j is antisymmetric, so
∂_k∂_iY_j = −∂_k∂_jY_i = −∂_j∂_kY_i = ∂_j∂_iY_k = ∂_i∂_jY_k = −∂_i∂_kY_j = −∂_k∂_iY_j, which therefore vanishes. So Y is
affine with antisymmetric linear part. The converse is immediate. ∎

**Lemma 39.2** (The flux identity.) Let X = (Y, N) ∈ 𝔎, let 𝒪 ⊂ ℝ⁴ be a bounded open set with smooth
boundary, and let (g, K) be data on cl 𝒪 with h := g − δ, |h| ≤ ½. Then

    ∫_𝒪 (YⁱJ_i + Nρ)(K, g) dμ_g = ∮_(∂𝒪) 𝔟_X(h, K) + ∫_𝒪 q_X dx,    (39.5)

    𝔟_X(h, K) := [N(∂_jh_ij − ∂_i tr h) − (∂_jN h_ij − ∂_iN tr h) − 2(YʲK_ij − Y_i tr K)] νⁱ dS,

where ν and dS are Euclidean, and q_X is a smooth function of (N, Y, h, ∂h, ∂²h, K, ∂K), linear in (N, Y), with

    |q_X| ≤ C(|N| + |Y|)(|h||∂²h| + |∂h|² + |h||∂K| + |∂h||K| + |K|²).    (39.6)

*Proof.* Write R(g) = g^ij(∂_kΓ^k_ij − ∂_jΓ^k_ki) + g^ij(Γ^k_klΓ^l_ij − Γ^k_jlΓ^l_ik), with Γ = ½g⁻¹∂h and
g⁻¹ = δ + O(|h|). Then R(g) = ∂_i∂_jh_ij − Δ tr h + ρ₂, where ρ₂ is a sum of terms (g⁻¹ − δ)∂²h, ∂(g⁻¹)∂h and
g⁻¹g⁻¹∂h ∂h. So |ρ₂| ≤ C(|h||∂²h| + |∂h|²), and the K-terms of ρ are bounded by C|K|². Likewise
J_i = −2(∂_jK_ij − ∂_i tr K) + J_(2,i) with |J₂| ≤ C(|h||∂K| + |∂h||K|), and dμ_g = (1 + O(|h|)) dx. So

    q_X := (YⁱJ_i + Nρ)(det g)^(1/2) − (−2Yⁱ(∂_jK_ij − ∂_i tr K) + N(∂_i∂_jh_ij − Δ tr h))

satisfies (39.6). For the linear part, integrate by parts:

    ∫_𝒪 N(∂_i∂_jh_ij − Δ tr h) = ∮ [N(∂_jh_ij − ∂_i tr h) − (∂_jN h_ij − ∂_iN tr h)]νⁱ
                                 + ∫ (∂_i∂_jN h_ij − ΔN tr h),

    ∫_𝒪 Yⁱ(∂_jK_ij − ∂_i tr K) = ∮ (YʲK_ij − Y_i tr K)νⁱ − ∫ (∂_jY_i K_ij − div Y tr K).

The last integrals vanish, because ∂∂N = 0, ∂_jY_i is antisymmetric, K is symmetric and div Y = 0. ∎

(39.5) is the identity of [CD03, (E.15)–(E.16) and (E.27), Appendix E] in linear form; it is all that is used.

**Proposition 39.3** (The charges.) Let (g, K) be vacuum data on {r > R₀} with |||(g, K)|||_(α,2) < ∞,
α > 3/2, and |g − δ| ≤ ½. For X in the basis (39.4), of degree d, the limit

    𝔔_X(g, K) := lim_(ϱ→∞) ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(g − δ, K)

exists, and

    |𝔔_X(g, K) − ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(g − δ, K)| ≤ C |||(g, K)|||²_(α,2) ϱ^(2+d−2α)     (ϱ > R₀),    (39.7)

with C depending only on α and R₀. Moreover:

(a) 𝔔_X is continuous on such data for the norm |||·|||_(α,2);

(b) for O ∈ O(4), 𝔔_X(O*(g, K)) = 𝔔_(O·X)(g, K), where O·X is the push-forward of X by x ↦ Ox.

*Proof.* Apply (39.5) on Γ(ϱ₁, ϱ₂), R₀ < ϱ₁ < ϱ₂, where J = ρ = 0:

    ∮_(S_(ϱ₂)) 𝔟_X − ∮_(S_(ϱ₁)) 𝔟_X = −∫_(Γ(ϱ₁,ϱ₂)) q_X dx.

By (39.3) every term of (39.6) is at most |||·|||² r^(−2α−2), and |N| + |Y| ≤ C(1 + r)^d. So the right side
is at most C|||·|||² ∫_(ϱ₁)^∞ r^(d−2α−2) r³ dr = C′|||·|||² ϱ₁^(2+d−2α), and 2 + d − 2α ≤ 3 − 2α < 0. So the flux is
Cauchy as ϱ → ∞, and (39.7) follows. (a): for two such data sets, |𝔔_X(1) − 𝔔_X(2)|
≤ |∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(h₁ − h₂, K₁ − K₂)| + Cϱ^(2+d−2α). Choose ϱ large, then the data close in C¹ on S_ϱ.
(b): 𝔟_X is built from δ, the radial normal and X, so a change of variables gives
∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(O*h, O*K) = ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_(O·X)(h, K), and S_ϱ is invariant. ∎

The normalisation is that of a linear flux. In ADM units (Newton's constant equal to one) the energy is 𝔔_(e₀)/16π and
the momentum −𝔔_(e_l)/16π, as −2(K − (tr K)δ) is −2 times the momentum density, and similarly for the others. Only 𝔔
is used below.

**Lemma 39.4** (Scaling.) For R > 0 and data (g, K) on Γ(R, 4R), define 𝒮_R(g, K) on Γ(1, 4) by
(𝒮_Rg)_ij(y) := g_ij(Ry) and (𝒮_RK)_ij(y) := R K_ij(Ry). Then (J, ρ)(𝒮_R(K, g))(y) = R²(J, ρ)(K, g)(Ry)
componentwise, and for X ∈ 𝔎 homogeneous of degree d,

    ∫_(Γ(1,4)) (YⁱJ_i + Nρ)(𝒮_R(K, g)) dμ_(𝒮_Rg) = R^(−2−d) ∫_(Γ(R,4R)) (YⁱJ_i + Nρ)(K, g) dμ_g.    (39.8)

*Proof.* With D_R(y) := Ry, 𝒮_Rg = R⁻²D_R*g and 𝒮_RK = R⁻¹D_R*K. The constraint map is natural under
diffeomorphisms. It satisfies ρ(c⁻¹K, c⁻²g) = c²ρ(K, g) and J(c⁻¹K, c⁻²g) = cJ(K, g), as g⁻¹ scales by c² and ∇ is
unchanged. As (D_R*J)_i(y) = RJ_i(Ry), both components scale by R². In (39.8) the left integrand at y is
R²(Yⁱ(y)J_i(Ry) + N(y)ρ(Ry))(det g(Ry))^(1/2), with Yⁱ(y) = R^(−d)Yⁱ(Ry) and N(y) = R^(−d)N(Ry), and dy = R⁻⁴dx. ∎

### 39.3 The Myers–Perry family and its charge map near Tangherlini

**Definition 39.5** For p = (m, A, w, c) with |m − m₀| < ½m₀, A ∈ 𝔰𝔬(4), w, c ∈ ℝ⁴ and ‖A‖, |w|, |c| < ε_P,
where ‖A‖ is the operator norm and ε_P ∈ (0, R₁] is fixed small below (Lemma 39.6), put:

- g^KS_(m,A), the Myers–Perry metric in Kerr–Schild form (Definition 21.15), on ℝ_t × {|x| ≥ 50R₁};
- Λ_w := exp(Σ_k w_kB_k), where B_k is the linear map of ℝ^(1+4) whose vector field is the boost
  Z_k := x^k∂_t + t∂_k;
- 𝒫_p(y) := Λ_w y + (0, c) and 𝔤_p := 𝒫_p*g^KS_(m,A);
- (g_p, K_p), the data (39.2) of 𝔤_p on {y⁰ = 0} ∩ {|y| > R_P}, with R_P := 100R₁ (not the gluing radius of
  Theorem 39.13).

Write p₀ := (m₀, 0, 0, 0). Writing A = Σ_(a<b) A_ab W_ab fixes the coordinates A_ab on 𝔰𝔬(4).

g^KS_(m,A) is defined, smooth in (x, m, A), Lorentzian and Ricci-flat on ℝ_t × {|x| ≥ 50R₁} for ‖A‖ < R₁. Indeed
−½ tr(A²) ≤ 2‖A‖² < 2R₁² < |x|², so r_A is defined there (Lemma 21.14 (b)), and
r_A² ≥ |x|² − ‖A‖² > 3‖A‖², so that ‖A‖²(r_A² + ‖A‖²) < (r_A²/3)(4r_A²/3) < r_A⁴, which is the condition of
Lemma 21.16 (c). The rest is the proof of Lemma 21.19 and Proposition 21.17.

**Lemma 39.6** (The family's data.) For ε_P small: (g_p, K_p) are smooth vacuum data on {|y| > R_P}, smooth in
(p, y); for every j, |||(g_p, K_p)|||_(2,j) ≤ C_j; and every p-derivative of (g_p − δ, K_p) obeys the bounds of
(39.3) with α = 2, uniformly in p.

*Proof.* g^KS_(m,A) − η = H_(m,A) k_A ⊗ k_A with H_(m,A) ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞(X̄) and k_A − dt = ℓ_A ∈ C^∞(X̄), smoothly in
(m, A): by Lemma 21.14 (b), r_A ∈ |x|(1 + |x|⁻²C^∞(X̄)), and by the proof of Proposition 21.21,
H_(m,A) ∈ m|x|⁻²(1 + |x|⁻²C^∞(X̄)) and the coefficient vector of ℓ_A lies in x̂ + |x|⁻¹Ax̂ + |x|⁻²C^∞(X̄) (with
Π = r_A⁴(1 + O(r_A⁻²)) and F_A = 1 + O(|x|⁻²)). So 𝔤 − η, 𝔤 := g^KS_(m,A), is independent of t and a classical symbol
of order −2 in x: |∂_x^γ(𝔤 − η)| ≤ C|x|^(−2−|γ|). 𝒫_p is affine with linear part near the identity. On {y⁰ = 0} the point
𝒫_p(0, y) has |x| ≥ ½|y| and |t| ≤ 2|w||y|, so 𝔤_p − η = 𝒫_p*(𝔤 − η) obeys the same symbol bounds on
{|y⁰| ≤ ½|y|}, smoothly in p together with all p-derivatives. There |𝔤_p − η| ≤ Cm₀R_P⁻² is small, so {y⁰ = 0} is
spacelike, N is bounded below, and (39.2) expresses (g_p, K_p) as smooth functions of (𝔤_p, ∂𝔤_p) on the slice,
vanishing at (η, 0). This gives the bounds. 𝔤_p is Ricci-flat (Proposition 21.17), so the data are vacuum. ∎

**Proposition 39.7** (The charge map near Tangherlini; the equivalent of [CD03, Proposition F.1].) The map

    𝔮 : p ↦ (𝔔_X(g_p, K_p))_X ∈ ℝ¹⁵

(X ranging over the basis (39.4)) is C¹. At every p = (m, 0, 0, 0) with |m − m₀| < ½m₀, in particular at p₀,
𝔮(p) = (6π²m, 0, …, 0) and D𝔮(p) is invertible, with the values below for m in place of m₀. In the bases (39.4)
and (m, w_k, A_ab, c_k) it is block lower triangular, with diagonal blocks

    ∂𝔔_(e₀)/∂m = 6π²,     (∂𝔔_(e_l)/∂w_k) = −6π²m₀I₄,     (∂𝔔_(e_ab)/∂A_(a′b′)) = −4π²m₀I₆,
    (∂𝔔_(e′_l)/∂c_k) = −6π²m₀I₄.    (39.9)

The block (∂𝔔_(e′_l)/∂w_k) is not needed, the other blocks off the diagonal vanish, and
det D𝔮(p) = 6π²(6π²m)⁸(4π²m)⁶.

*Proof.* *C¹.* For fixed ϱ, f_ϱ(p) := ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(g_p − δ, K_p) is C¹, with
∂_pf_ϱ = ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(∂_pg_p, ∂_pK_p), since 𝔟_X is linear. Differentiate in p the identity of the proof of
Proposition 39.3, which holds for every p. The difference of ∂_pf_ϱ at ϱ₂ and ϱ₁ is then −∫ ∂_p[q_X(g_p, K_p)] dx. As q_X
vanishes to second order in the jets, |∂_p[q_X]| ≤ C(1 + r)^d |jet(g_p − δ, K_p)| |jet ∂_p(g_p, K_p)| ≤ Cr^(d−6) by
Lemma 39.6. So ∂_pf_ϱ converges uniformly in p, at the rate ϱ^(d−2), and 𝔮 is C¹ with
D𝔮(p) = lim_ϱ ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(∂_p(g_p, K_p)).

*Equivariance.* For O ∈ O(4) let Õ(t, x) := (t, Ox). By Lemma 21.14, r_A(Ox) = r_(OᵀAO)(x),
since |Ox| = |x|, |AOx| = |OᵀAOx| and tr A², det A are invariant under conjugation. The other ingredients of
Definition 21.15 are covariant in the same way, so Õ*g^KS_(m,A) = g^KS_(m,OᵀAO). Also 𝒫_p ∘ Õ = Õ ∘ 𝒫_(p·O) with
p·O := (m, OᵀAO, Oᵀw, Oᵀc), and Õ preserves {y⁰ = 0}. So (g_(p·O), K_(p·O)) = O*(g_p, K_p), and Proposition 39.3 (b)
gives 𝔔_X(g_(p·O), K_(p·O)) = 𝔔_(O·X)(g_p, K_p). Fix m with |m − m₀| < ½m₀ and put p_m := (m, 0, 0, 0). As
p_m·O = p_m, D𝔮(p_m) intertwines the representations

    ℝ ⊕ Λ² ⊕ ℝ⁴ ⊕ ℝ⁴  (m, A, w, c)   ⟶   ℝ ⊕ ℝ⁴ ⊕ Λ² ⊕ ℝ⁴  (𝔔_(e₀), 𝔔_(e_l), 𝔔_(e_ab), 𝔔_(e′_l)),

the charges being linear functionals on 𝔎, whose representation is self-dual. The trivial representation, the
standard ℝ⁴ and Λ²ℝ⁴ of O(4) are real irreducible and pairwise non-isomorphic (dimensions 1, 4, 6), each with commutant
ℝ. For ℝ⁴ this holds already for SO(4). Λ² is the sum of the self-dual and anti-self-dual parts, each irreducible of
dimension 3 under SO(4) (acting through SO(3) × SO(3)); a reflection exchanges them, so no proper nonzero subspace is
O(4)-invariant. An SO(4)-equivariant endomorphism of Λ² is a ⊕ b on the two parts, and commuting with a reflection
forces a = b. By Schur's lemma D𝔮(p_m) is: a scalar c_E from m to 𝔔_(e₀); a scalar c_J times I₆ from A to (𝔔_(e_ab));
on the two copies of ℝ⁴, a matrix (a₁₁ a₁₂; a₂₁ a₂₂) ⊗ I₄ from (w, c) to (𝔔_(e_l), 𝔔_(e′_l)); and zero elsewhere.
Likewise 𝔮(p_m) is O(4)-invariant, so only its trivial component 𝔔_(e₀) can be nonzero.

*The base.* On {t = 0}, g^KS_(m,0) = η + H(dt + dr)² with H = mr⁻² (Proposition 21.17) has h₀ = H x̂ ⊗ x̂ exactly,
β₀ = H x̂, 𝔤₀₀ = −1 + H and N₀ = (1 + H)^(−1/2). Its second fundamental form K₀ = −N₀⁻¹D_(iβ_j) is O(mr⁻³) with
∂K₀ = O(mr⁻⁴). It is invariant under O(4), so K₀ = a(r) x̂ ⊗ x̂ + b(r)(δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂).

*c_E.* ∂_m h₀ = r⁻² x̂ ⊗ x̂, h_ij = m x_ix_j r⁻⁴. So ∂_jh_ij = m(n + 1 − 4)x_i r⁻⁴ = m x_i r⁻⁴ and
∂_i tr h = −2m x_i r⁻⁴, and 𝔟_(e₀) = 3m r⁻³ dS. Integrating over S_ϱ, of area 2π²ϱ³, gives 6π²m at every radius:
𝔔_(e₀)(g_((m,0,0,0)), K_((m,0,0,0))) = 6π²m and c_E = 6π². (In ADM units this is 3πm/8, the mass of
five-dimensional Tangherlini.)

*a₂₂ and a₁₂.* The translation in c_k changes the data to (h₀, K₀)(y + c), with derivative ∂_k(h₀, K₀). For
e′_l = (0, x^l): x^l∂_k(∂_jh_ij − ∂_i tr h)νⁱ = 3m x^l∂_k(x_i r⁻⁴)x̂_i = −9m x^lx_k r⁻⁵, and
−(δ_lj∂_kh_ij − δ_li∂_k tr h)νⁱ = −m(δ_lk r⁻³ − x_kx_l r⁻⁵). With ∫_(𝕊³) ω_kω_l = (π²/2)δ_kl the flux is
−(9/2)π²m δ_lk − (3/2)π²m δ_lk, so a₂₂ = −6π²m at every radius. For e_l the flux of ∂_kK₀ = O(r⁻⁴) is O(ϱ⁻¹), so
a₁₂ = 0.

*a₁₁.* ∂_(w_k)𝔤_p|_(p_m) = ℒ_(Z_k)𝔤 for 𝔤 := g^KS_(m,0). As ℒ_(Z_k)η = 0 and Z_k(H) = t∂_kH,
ℒ_(Z_k)(H k₀ ⊗ k₀) = t∂_kH k₀ ⊗ k₀ + H(ℒ_(Z_k)k₀ ⊗ k₀ + k₀ ⊗ ℒ_(Z_k)k₀), with k₀ = dt + dr, the 1-form k_A of
Definition 21.15 at A = 0, and ℒ_(Z_k)k₀ = d(x^k + t x̂_k) = dx^k + x̂_k dt + t dx̂_k. At t = 0 this gives

    δ𝔤₀₀ = 2H x̂_k,     δβ_i = H(x̂_kx̂_i + δ_ik),     δg_ij = H(δ_ik x̂_j + x̂_iδ_jk),
    ∂_tδg_ij = ∂_kH x̂_ix̂_j + H(∂_ix̂_k x̂_j + x̂_i ∂_jx̂_k).

Linearising (39.2), δK = −(δN/N₀)K₀ + (1/(2N₀))(∂_tδg − 2δ(D_(iβ_j))). Since δN = O(r⁻²), N₀ − 1 = O(r⁻²),
Γ₀δβ = O(r⁻⁵) and δΓ β₀ = O(r⁻⁵), this is δK_ij = ½(∂_tδg_ij − ∂_iδβ_j − ∂_jδβ_i) + O(r⁻⁵). The terms H∂x̂_k cancel.
With ∂_iH = −2Hx̂_i/r and ∂_ix̂_j = (δ_ij − x̂_ix̂_j)/r,

    δK_ij = (H/r)(2x̂_ix̂_jx̂_k + x̂_iδ_jk + x̂_jδ_ik − x̂_kδ_ij) + O(r⁻⁵),
    tr δK = (H/r)(4 − n)x̂_k + O(r⁻⁵) = O(r⁻⁵).

For e_l, 𝔟 = −2(δK_lj x̂_j − x̂_l tr δK) dS = −2mr⁻³(2x̂_lx̂_k + δ_lk) dS + O(r⁻⁵) dS, whose integral tends to
−2m(π² + 2π²)δ_lk. So a₁₁ = −6π²m; in ADM units the momentum per unit rapidity is the energy.

*c_J.* At A = 0, r_A = |x| + O(|A|²) and H_(m,A) = H + O(|A|²), as Π, F_A, tr A² and det A are even in A; and
ℓ_A = (r²I − A²)⁻¹(rI + A)x · dx = x̂ · dx + r⁻²(Ax) · dx + O(|A|²) (Lemma 21.14 (a): 𝖬/Π = (r²I − A²)⁻¹). So
the derivative in the direction A = W_ab is δ𝔤 = H(k₀ ⊗ ξ_A + ξ_A ⊗ k₀), ξ_A := r⁻²(Ax) · dx, ξ_A(x̂) = 0. Then
δ𝔤₀₀ = 0, δβ = Hξ_A = mr⁻⁴(Ax) · dx, δg = H(x̂ ⊗ ξ_A + ξ_A ⊗ x̂) and ∂_tδg = 0. Further
δ(N²) = −δ𝔤₀₀ + 2β₀ⁱδβ_i − β₀ⁱβ₀ʲδg_ij = 0, as β₀ ∥ x̂ ⊥ ξ_A. The remaining terms other than ∂δβ are O(r⁻⁶), so

    δK_ij = −∂_(iδβ_j) + O(r⁻⁶) = 2mr⁻⁶(x_i(Ax)_j + x_j(Ax)_i) + O(r⁻⁶),     tr δK = O(r⁻⁶).

For e_(a′b′) = (W′x, 0) with W′ := W_(a′b′), as (W′x) · x̂ = 0, 𝔟 = −2δK(W′x, x̂) dS =
−4mr⁻⁵(Ax) · (W′x) dS + O(r⁻⁵) dS. On S_ϱ, (Ax) · (W′x) = ϱ²(Aω) · (W′ω) and dS = ϱ³dω, so the integral tends to
−4m∫_(𝕊³) ωᵀAᵀW′ω dω = −2π²m tr(AᵀW′), using ∫ ω_iω_j = (π²/2)δ_ij. As tr(W_abᵀW_(a′b′)) = 2δ_aa′δ_bb′,
c_J = −4π²m; in ADM units the angular momentum is (πm/4)A_ab, two thirds of the mass per unit spin.

So D𝔮(p_m) is as stated, with m in place of m₀: c_E = 6π², a₁₁ = a₂₂ = −6π²m, a₁₂ = 0 and c_J = −4π²m. Its determinant
is c_E (a₁₁a₂₂ − a₁₂a₂₁)⁴ c_J⁶ = 6π²(6π²m)⁸(4π²m)⁶ ≠ 0. ∎

**Corollary 39.8** There are neighbourhoods U of p₀ and V of 𝔮(p₀) such that 𝔮 : U → V is a C¹
diffeomorphism (inverse function theorem). For Q ∈ V write p(Q) := 𝔮|_U⁻¹(Q); then p(Q) is continuous and the data
(g_(p(Q)), K_(p(Q))) have charge vector exactly Q.

**Remark 39.9** (Numerical observation.) Numerical quadrature on 𝕊³ of the charge fluxes of the fifteen
linearisations of the family at p₀, at a large radius, gives the 225 entries of D𝔮(p₀) as in Proposition 39.7, and gives
the block (∂𝔔_(e′_l)/∂w_k) zero to the accuracy of the quadrature. No proof uses this.

Proposition 39.7 is proved near Tangherlini only, which is the case the gluing needs; the global form of the equivalent
of [CD03, Proposition F.1] for the Myers–Perry family is not used. In ADM units its values are: energy 3πm/8, momentum
per unit rapidity equal to the energy, angular momentum πm/4 per unit spin, centre of mass shifted by the translation.

### 39.4 The gluing

#### 39.4.1 The solvability statement and its continuity in the background

The gluing solves the constraint equations on a compact annulus by [CD03, Theorem 5.9]. This subsection states what is
used of it, on a general compact manifold with boundary, and proves the continuity in the background that the gluing
needs (Lemma 39.11). Besides Theorem A.18, Theorem A.19, Theorem A.20
and Theorem A.21 we use the following statements of [CD03], which hold for every n ≥ 2.

- [CD03, (A.1), p. 58]: for smooth positive functions φ, ψ, H^k_(φ,ψ)(g) is "the space of H^k_loc functions or tensor
  fields such that the norm ‖u‖_(H^k_(φ,ψ)(g)) := (∫_M (Σ_(i=0)^k φ^(2i)|∇^(i)u|²_g)ψ² dμ_g)^(1/2) is finite";
  H̊^k_(φ,ψ) is "the closure in H^k_(φ,ψ) of the space of H^k functions or tensors which are compactly (up to a
  negligible set) supported in M"; L²_ψ := H̊⁰_(1,ψ); and W^(k,∞)_φ := {u ∈ W^(k,∞)_loc : φⁱ|∇^(i)u|_g ∈ L^∞}.
- [CD03, (2.9), p. 7]: "We define a map Φ by Φ(x, y) := (φx, φ²y)."
- [CD03, Lemma 2.6, p. 7]: "Let k ∈ ℤ. Suppose that g ∈ W^(k+3,∞)_loc and that Ric(g) ∈ φ⁻²W^(k+2,∞)_φ,
  K ∈ φ⁻¹W^(k+3,∞)_φ. If (A.2) holds with 0 ≤ i ≤ k + 2, then the linear operators
  ΦP* : H̊^(k+3)_(φ,ψ) × H̊^(k+4)_(φ,ψ) ⟶ H̊^(k+2)_(φ,ψ) × H̊^(k+2)_(φ,ψ), k ≥ −2,
  ψ⁻²PΦψ² : H̊^(k+2)_(φ,ψ) × H̊^(k+2)_(φ,ψ) ⟶ H̊^(k+1)_(φ,ψ) × H̊^k_(φ,ψ), k ≥ 0, are well defined, and bounded."
- [CD03, Proposition 3.3, p. 11]: "Under the hypotheses of Lemma 2.8 with (K, g) = (K₀, g₀), let 𝒦₀ be kernel of
  ΦP*₀ : H̊¹_(φ,ψ)(g₀) × H̊²_(φ,ψ)(g₀) ⟶ L²_ψ(g₀) × L²_ψ(g₀), and let 𝒦₀^(⊥g₀) be its L²_ψ(g₀) ⊕ L²_ψ(g₀)-orthogonal.
  …"; and, on the same page, "We denote by π_(𝒦₀^(⊥g)) the L²_ψ(g) projection onto 𝒦₀^(⊥g).", where 𝒦₀^(⊥g) is the
  L²_ψ(g) ⊕ L²_ψ(g)-orthogonal of 𝒦₀, g being the current metric. Theorem A.18, Theorem A.19
  and the equation (5.11) of Theorem A.21 are stated for this projection, on the space 𝒦₀^(⊥g), which
  moves with g.
- [CD03, (3.9), p. 13]: "L_(φ,ψ) := ψ⁻²PΦψ²ΦP*."
- [CD03, Definition 5.3, p. 22]: "Let k ∈ ℕ and let 𝒲 be a space of symmetric tensors on M. We shall say that g has an
  (𝒲, k)–behavior at ∂M if there exists a metric g_M̄ on M̄ of class C^k(M̄) such that g − g_M̄ ∈ 𝒲."

[CD03] identifies vector fields and 1-forms by the current metric g: P* at (K, g) lowers the index of Y with g
([CD03, (2.4)]), and the residual (J, ρ), whose first component is a 1-form, is projected onto 𝒦₀^(⊥g), a space of
pairs of a vector field and a function, and is paired with the Killing initial data ([CD03, (8.6)]), with the index of
J raised by g. We do the same.

*Setting.* Let 𝒜 be a compact manifold with boundary, of dimension n ≥ 2, and let u₀ = (K₀, g₀) be a symmetric
2-tensor and a Riemannian metric on 𝒜, both smooth up to ∂𝒜. Let x ∈ C^∞(𝒜) be a defining function of ∂𝒜 with
0 < x ≤ 1 on the interior 𝒜° that equals the g₀-distance to ∂𝒜 near ∂𝒜. Fix s > 0 and an integer k > n/2. The weighted
spaces are those of [CD03, (A.1)] on 𝒜, with φ := x², and we write ψ := e^(−s/x). For ε ∈ (0, ½] let 𝒩_ε be the set of
pairs u′ = (K′, g′) with

    ‖(K′ − K₀, g′ − g₀)‖_(x⁻²W^(k+3,∞)_(x²)(g₀) × W^(k+4,∞)_(x²)(g₀)) < ε;

in particular |g′ − g₀|_(g₀) < ε on 𝒜. The unknowns are pairs z = (Y, N) of a vector field and a function on 𝒜°. For
u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε their L²_ψ(g′) product is

    ⟨(Y, N), (Z, M)⟩_(L²_ψ(g′)) := ∫_𝒜 (g′(Y, Z) + NM) ψ² dμ_(g′),

and ♯_(g′)(V, f) := (g′⁻¹V, f) turns a pair of a 1-form and a function, such as a value of (J, ρ), into such a pair,
by raising the index with g′; ♭_(g′) := ♯_(g′)⁻¹. Let 𝒦₀ be the kernel of ΦP*_(u₀) on H̊¹_(x²,ψ)(g₀) × H̊²_(x²,ψ)(g₀),
as in [CD03, Proposition 3.3], with Φ(a, b) := (x²a, x⁴b). For u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε let 𝒦₀^(⊥g′) be the L²_ψ(g′)-orthogonal of
𝒦₀, and π_(g′) the L²_ψ(g′)-orthogonal projection onto 𝒦₀^(⊥g′), as on [CD03, p. 11]; put π₀ := π_(g₀). Put

    𝒴_(g′) := 𝒦₀^(⊥g′) ∩ (H̊^(k+3)_(x²,ψ) × H̊^(k+4)_(x²,ψ)),     𝒵̃ := H̊^(k+1)_(x²,ψ) × H̊^k_(x²,ψ),
    𝒵_(g′) := 𝒦₀^(⊥g′) ∩ 𝒵̃,     𝒴 := 𝒴_(g₀),     𝒵 := 𝒵_(g₀),
    𝒮 := H^(k+1)_(x²,e^(s/x)) × H^k_(x²,e^(s/x)),     𝒳 := x²H^(k+2)_(x²,e^(s/x)) × x⁴H^(k+2)_(x²,e^(s/x)),

the spaces of the unknowns, of the projected sources, of the sources (δJ, δρ) and of the solutions (δK, δg).

*The spaces.* All of them are built with g₀. For u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε the spaces built with g′ are the same, with norms equivalent
to these by constants independent of u′. Indeed, the difference D of the Levi-Civita connections of g′ and g₀ is a
tensor with x^(2i+2)|∇^(i)D|_(g₀) ≤ Cε for i ≤ k + 3; so φⁱ∇′^(i)u − φⁱ∇^(i)u is a sum of contractions of products of
factors φ^(j+1)∇^(j)D with one factor φ^l∇^(l)u, l < i; and |·|_(g′), dμ_(g′) are comparable to |·|_(g₀), dμ_(g₀)
(compare [CD03, (A.4)]). So the statements of [CD03], made in the spaces built with the current metric, hold in these.
Two further facts are used. First, multiplication by ψ² maps H^j_(x²,ψ) onto H^j_(x²,ψ⁻¹), with equivalent norms, as
φⁱψ^(∓2)∇^(i)(ψ^(±2)) is bounded for every i, each derivative of e^(±2s/x) bringing a factor of order x⁻²; so
e^(2s/x) = ψ⁻² maps 𝒮 isomorphically onto H^(k+1)_(x²,ψ) × H^k_(x²,ψ). Second, for φ = x² the closure H̊^j_(x²,ψ′) is
all of H^j_(x²,ψ′), for every positive weight ψ′. Let χ₁ ∈ C^∞(ℝ) vanish on (−∞, 1] and equal 1 on [2, ∞). For
u ∈ H^j_(x²,ψ′), χ₁(x/δ)u has compact support in 𝒜°, where the weights are bounded above and below, so it lies in H^j
there. It tends to u in H^j_(x²,ψ′) as δ → 0: the derivatives of the cut-off live on {δ ≤ x ≤ 2δ}, where
x^(2i)|∇^(i)(χ₁(x/δ))| ≤ C_iδⁱ, and the integrals of the weighted derivatives of u over {x ≤ 2δ} tend to zero. Hence
e^(2s/x) maps 𝒮 isomorphically onto 𝒵̃, and a pair smooth up to ∂𝒜 lies in H̊^j_(x²,ψ) for every j, its weighted
derivatives being bounded and ψ² integrable.

For u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε and z ∈ 𝒴 put ι_(u′) := π_(g′)|_𝒴 and

    T_(u′)z := e^(−2s/x)Φ²P*_(u′)ι_(u′)z,     Ψ(u′, z) := π₀♯_(g′)e^(2s/x){(J, ρ)(u′ + T_(u′)z) − (J, ρ)(u′)},
    (39.10)

with P*_(u′) the operator [CD03, (2.4)] at u′. So T_(u′)z is a field of the form e^(−2s/x)Φ²P*_(u′)(Y, N) in which
[CD03, Theorem 5.9] gives its solutions, with (Y, N) := ι_(u′)z ∈ 𝒴_(g′) (Lemma 39.10 (e)). The one further
hypothesis is:

(Fin) 𝒦₀ is finite-dimensional, with a basis (e_i)_(i∈I) of pairs smooth on 𝒜.

**Lemma 39.10** (The solvability statement.) In the setting above, with (Fin):

(a) The hypotheses of Theorem A.21 ([CD03, Theorem 5.9]) hold for g₀, K₀ and x. So there is ε > 0 such
that for u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε and every (δJ, δρ) ∈ 𝒮 of norm < ε there is (Y, N) ∈ 𝒴_(g′) for which
(δK, δg) := e^(−2s/x)Φ²P*_(u′)(Y, N) ∈ 𝒳 is close to zero and solves

    π_(g′)♯_(g′)e^(2s/x){(J, ρ)(K′ + δK, g′ + δg) − (J, ρ)(K′, g′)} = π_(g′)♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)(δJ, δρ),
    (39.11)

which is [CD03, (5.11)] at (K, g) = u′. For z ∈ 𝒴 and (δK, δg) := T_(u′)z, (39.11) holds if and only if

    Ψ(u′, z) = δf,     δf := π₀♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)(δJ, δρ) ∈ 𝒵;

and each (Y, N) ∈ 𝒴_(g′) is ι_(u′)z for exactly one z ∈ 𝒴, namely z = π₀(Y, N).

(b) Diminishing ε: if u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε is smooth on 𝒜, and (δJ, δρ) ∈ 𝒮 is smooth with compact support in 𝒜° and has norm less
than ε also in the norm of [CD03, Proposition 5.10] with t := s, then the solution (δK, δg) of (a) is smooth on 𝒜 and
extends smoothly by zero across ∂𝒜. If the support of (δJ, δρ) lies in a fixed compact set Ω_c ⊂ 𝒜°, that norm is at
most C(Ω_c)‖(δJ, δρ)‖_(C^(k+2)(𝒜)), with C(Ω_c) independent of u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε.

(c) 𝒳 ⊂ C²(𝒜), with ‖(δK, δg)‖_(C²(𝒜)) ≤ C‖(δK, δg)‖_𝒳.

(d) D_zΨ(u′, 0) = π₀L_(u′)ι_(u′), with L_(u′) := ♯_(g′)ψ⁻²P_(u′)Φψ²ΦP*_(u′), the operator L_(φ,ψ) of [CD03, (3.9)] at
u′. Diminishing ε, for every u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε, π_(g′)L_(u′) is an isomorphism 𝒴_(g′) → 𝒵_(g′) (Theorem A.18),
and D_zΨ(u′, 0) is an isomorphism 𝒴 → 𝒵 whose inverse has norm at most a constant C₁ independent of u′.

(e) For u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε let A_(g′) be the matrix (A_(g′))_(ij) := ⟨e_i, e_j⟩_(L²_ψ(g′)); it is symmetric and positive
definite, and

    π_(g′)v = v − Σ_(i,j∈I) (A_(g′)⁻¹)_(ij) ⟨v, e_j⟩_(L²_ψ(g′)) e_i.    (39.12)

The kernel of π_(g′) is 𝒦₀, and π₀π_(g′) = π₀, π_(g′)π₀ = π_(g′). π_(g′) maps 𝒵̃ and H̊^(k+3)_(x²,ψ) × H̊^(k+4)_(x²,ψ)
into themselves, and on each ‖π_(g′) − π_(g″)‖ ≤ C‖g′ − g″‖_(W^(k+4,∞)_(x²)(g₀)) for u′, u″ ∈ 𝒩_ε. The maps
ι_(u′) : 𝒴 → 𝒴_(g′) and π₀|_(𝒵_(g′)) : 𝒵_(g′) → 𝒵 are isomorphisms, with inverses π₀|_(𝒴_(g′)) and π_(g′)|_𝒵. These
four maps, and ♯_(g′) on 𝒵̃, have norms at most a constant independent of u′, and
‖♯_(g′) − ♯_(g″)‖_(𝒵̃→𝒵̃) ≤ C‖g′ − g″‖_(W^(k+4,∞)_(x²)(g₀)).

*Proof.* We prove (e) first.

(e) 𝒦₀ is finite-dimensional, hence closed, and the e_i lie in L²_ψ, being smooth up to ∂𝒜. A_(g′) is the Gram matrix
of the linearly independent e_i for the inner product of L²_ψ(g′), hence symmetric and positive definite. Let w be the
right side of (39.12). Then v − w ∈ 𝒦₀, and, all products being those of L²_ψ(g′),
⟨w, e_l⟩ = ⟨v, e_l⟩ − Σ_(i,j)(A_(g′))_(li)(A_(g′)⁻¹)_(ij)⟨v, e_j⟩ = 0 for every l. So w ∈ 𝒦₀^(⊥g′); as v − w lies in
𝒦₀, which is the L²_ψ(g′)-orthogonal of 𝒦₀^(⊥g′), w = π_(g′)v. By the formula, π_(g′)v = 0 only if v ∈ 𝒦₀; and for
v = e_l the sum is Σ_(i,j)(A_(g′)⁻¹)_(ij)(A_(g′))_(jl)e_i = e_l, so π_(g′)e_l = 0. Hence π_(g′)v = v − k with k ∈ 𝒦₀,
and π₀π_(g′)v = π₀v − π₀k = π₀v; likewise π_(g′)π₀ = π_(g′). The e_i lie in 𝒵̃ and in
H̊^(k+3)_(x²,ψ) × H̊^(k+4)_(x²,ψ) (*The spaces*), and |⟨v, e_j⟩_(L²_ψ(g′))| ≤ C‖v‖_(L²_ψ(g₀)), which is at most C times
either norm of v; so π_(g′) maps both spaces into themselves, with norm bounded independently of u′, as A_(g′) is within
Cε of A_(g₀). The integrand of ⟨v, e_j⟩_(L²_ψ(g′)) is a smooth function of the values of g′ times a bilinear expression
in v and e_j, so |⟨v, e_j⟩_(L²_ψ(g′)) − ⟨v, e_j⟩_(L²_ψ(g″))| ≤ C sup_𝒜|g′ − g″|_(g₀)‖v‖_(L²_ψ(g₀)); the same holds for
A_(g′) − A_(g″), hence for A_(g′)⁻¹ − A_(g″)⁻¹, and this gives the bound on π_(g′) − π_(g″), sup_𝒜|g′ − g″|_(g₀) being at
most the norm of W^(k+4,∞)_(x²)(g₀). For z ∈ 𝒴, ι_(u′)z lies in H̊^(k+3)_(x²,ψ) × H̊^(k+4)_(x²,ψ) and in 𝒦₀^(⊥g′), so in
𝒴_(g′); likewise π₀y ∈ 𝒴 for y ∈ 𝒴_(g′); and π₀ι_(u′)z = π₀π_(g′)z = π₀z = z, ι_(u′)π₀y = π_(g′)π₀y = π_(g′)y = y. The
same argument applies to π₀|_(𝒵_(g′)) and π_(g′)|_𝒵. Finally, ♯_(g′) multiplies the 1-form by g′⁻¹, and for
i ≤ k + 4, x^(2i)|∇^(i)(g′⁻¹ − g₀⁻¹)|_(g₀) ≤ Cε and x^(2i)|∇^(i)(g′⁻¹ − g″⁻¹)|_(g₀) ≤ C‖g′ − g″‖_(W^(k+4,∞)_(x²)(g₀));
by the Leibniz rule, multiplication by a tensor with bounded x^(2i)|∇^(i)·|_(g₀), i ≤ k + 1, is bounded on H̊^j_(x²,ψ),
j ≤ k + 1, by a multiple of these bounds.

(a) A metric smooth on 𝒜 has the (W^(k+4,∞)_(x²), k + 4)- and the (C^(k+4,α)_(x²,1), k + 5)-behaviour at ∂𝒜 of
[CD03, Definition 5.3], with g_M̄ := g₀. (5.10a) holds as Ric(g₀) is bounded on 𝒜, (5.10b) as ∇∇x is bounded near ∂𝒜,
and (5.10c) as K₀ and its derivatives are bounded. The ε and the solution are those of Theorem A.21. Its
(Y, N)-spaces are those of Theorem A.19 with ψ = e^(−s/x), as its solution
(δK, δg) = e^(−2s/x)Φ²P*(Y, N) = ψ²Φ²P*(Y, N) shows (*The spaces*). [CD03, Theorem 5.9] is obtained from
Theorem A.19 ([CD03, p. 26]), whose map (3.13) is defined on
𝒦₀^(⊥g′) ∩ (H̊^(k+3)_(x²,ψ) × H̊^(k+4)_(x²,ψ)) = 𝒴_(g′); so (Y, N) ∈ 𝒴_(g′). [CD03, (5.11)] at u′ is (39.11), the
index of J being raised with g′, as in [CD03]. By (e), the kernels of π_(g′) and of π₀ are both 𝒦₀. So (39.11)
says that

    v := ♯_(g′)e^(2s/x){(J, ρ)(u′ + (δK, δg)) − (J, ρ)(u′) − (δJ, δρ)} ∈ 𝒦₀;

for (δK, δg) = T_(u′)z, Ψ(u′, z) − δf = π₀v, so Ψ(u′, z) = δf says the same. δf lies in 𝒵, as e^(2s/x)(δJ, δρ) ∈ 𝒵̃
(*The spaces*) and by (e).
The last assertion is part of (e). "Close to zero" is the conclusion of [CD03, Theorem 5.9]; we use it in the form:
for every r > 0, diminishing ε, the solution has ‖(δK, δg)‖_𝒳 < r. [CD03] applies its existence theorems in this form,
with the solution bounded by a multiple of the norm of (δJ, δρ) ([CD03, (8.5)]), and Lemma 39.11 (c) proves that
bound for the solution it constructs.

(b) As k > n/2 is an integer, k ≥ k₀ := ⌊n/2⌋ + 1. The metric g₀ has the (C^(k+4,α)_(x²,1), k + 5)-behaviour and (5.10)
holds, by (a). As u′ is smooth on 𝒜, it lies in x⁻²C^(k+3,α)_(x²,1)(g₀) × C^(k+4,α)_(x²,1)(g₀), and the norm of 𝒩_ε
bounds the norm ‖(K′ − K₀, g′ − g₀)‖_(x⁻²W^(k₀+3,∞)_(x²)(g₀) × W^(k₀+4,∞)_(x²)(g₀)) of [CD03, Proposition 5.10], as
k₀ ≤ k. The condition of [CD03, Proposition 5.10] on (δJ, δρ), with t := s > 0, is assumed. So, ε being at most the ε
of [CD03, Proposition 5.10], the hypotheses of [CD03, Proposition 5.10] hold. A smooth pair with compact support in 𝒜°
lies in C^∞_(x²,e^(s/x))(g′), x being bounded below on its support, and u′ ∈ C^∞(𝒜) × C^∞(𝒜); so
[CD03, Corollary 5.11] (Theorem A.21) applies to the solution of (a). For the bound: on a neighbourhood
of Ω_c, x is bounded below, so the weights x², x⁻ⁿ and e^(s/x) are bounded above and below there, and the norm of
[CD03, Proposition 5.10] of a pair supported in Ω_c is at most C(Ω_c) times its C^(k₀+2) × C^(k₀+1)-norm, the covariant
derivatives being those of g′. These are at most C(Ω_c)‖(δJ, δρ)‖_(C^(k+2)(𝒜)), as k₀ ≤ k and the derivatives of g′ of
order at most k + 4 are bounded on Ω_c uniformly for u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε.

(c) x^(−4j)e^(−2s/x) is bounded on 𝒜°, so H^(k+2)_(x²,e^(s/x)) ⊂ H^(k+2)(𝒜), and H^(k+2)(𝒜) ⊂ C²(𝒜) by Sobolev's
inequality, as k + 2 > n/2 + 2; the factors x² and x⁴ are bounded.

(d) D_zΨ(u′, 0)z = π₀♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)P_(u′)(T_(u′)z) = π₀♯_(g′)ψ⁻²P_(u′)ψ²Φ²P*_(u′)ι_(u′)z = π₀L_(u′)ι_(u′)z, as Φ and
ψ² commute. The hypotheses of Theorem A.18 hold at u₀, with φ = x² and ψ = e^(−s/x):

- g₀ ∈ W^(k+4,∞)_loc, Ric(g₀) ∈ φ⁻²W^(k+2,∞)_φ(g₀) and K₀ ∈ φ⁻¹W^(k+3,∞)_φ(g₀), as g₀ and K₀ are smooth up to ∂𝒜 and
  x ≤ 1;
- (A.2) holds for every i: φ^(i−1)∇^(i)φ is a polynomial in x and the derivatives of x, and ψ⁻¹∇^(i)ψ is a sum of
  products of derivatives of s/x of total size at most Cx^(−2i), which φⁱ = x^(2i) compensates;
- the scaling property holds by [CD03, Lemma B.1] and the argument after it, [CD03, pp. 61–62], which treats φ = x²
  with the weights e^(±s/x) (see [CD03, p. 25]);
- inequality (3.4) holds for (Y, N) supported in a neighbourhood of ∂𝒜, whose complement is compact: there it is (5.12)
  and the display after it, [CD03, p. 26], obtained from [CD03, Corollary D.5 and Proposition C.4], with
  [CD03, Lemma 4.3], as (𝒜°, g₀, K₀, x) satisfies the asymptotic condition b) of [CD03, Definition 4.1] with
  U_i := {x > 1/i}, K₀, ∇K₀ and Ric(g₀) being bounded.

So, diminishing ε, for every u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε the map π_(g′)L_(u′) is an isomorphism 𝒴_(g′) → 𝒵_(g′) whose inverse has norm
bounded independently of u′; these are the spaces of Theorem A.18 at (K, g) = u′ (*The spaces*), and the
closeness there is in the norm of 𝒩_ε, as φ⁻¹ = x⁻². By (e), π₀ = π₀π_(g′), so

    D_zΨ(u′, 0) = (π₀|_(𝒵_(g′)))(π_(g′)L_(u′))ι_(u′),

a composition of three isomorphisms whose inverses have norms bounded independently of u′, by (e); its inverse is
π₀|_(𝒴_(g′))(π_(g′)L_(u′))⁻¹π_(g′)|_𝒵, of norm at most some C₁. ∎

**Lemma 39.11** (Continuity in the background.) In the setting above, with (Fin), let ε and C₁ be as in
Lemma 39.10. There are ε_c ∈ (0, ε] and r_c > 0 such that, with B the ball of radius r_c about zero in 𝒴:

(a) for u′ ∈ 𝒩_(ε_c) and z₁, z₂ ∈ B,

    ‖Ψ(u′, z₁) − Ψ(u′, z₂)‖_𝒵 ≥ (2C₁)⁻¹‖z₁ − z₂‖_𝒴;    (39.13)

in particular (39.11) has at most one solution (δK, δg) = T_(u′)z with z ∈ B;

(b) if z ∈ B solves (39.11) for (u′, (δJ, δρ)) and z̃ ∈ B for (ũ′, (δJ̃, δρ̃)), with u′, ũ′ ∈ 𝒩_(ε_c), then

    ‖z̃ − z‖_𝒴 ≤ 2C₁(‖δf̃ − δf‖_𝒵 + ‖Ψ(u′, z) − Ψ(ũ′, z)‖_𝒵),     δf̃ := π₀♯_(g̃′)e^(2s/x)(δJ̃, δρ̃),
    (39.14)

with δf as in Lemma 39.10 (a); both terms on the right tend to zero as (ũ′, (δJ̃, δρ̃)) tends to
(u′, (δJ, δρ)) in 𝒩_(ε_c) × 𝒮. So the solution with z ∈ B is unique and depends continuously on the background u′ and
the right side (δJ, δρ), and so does (δK, δg) = T_(u′)z in 𝒳;

(c) there are ε_s > 0 and C₅ such that for u′ ∈ 𝒩_(ε_c) and ‖(δJ, δρ)‖_𝒮 < ε_s, (39.11) has a solution
(δK, δg) = T_(u′)z with z ∈ B, and ‖z‖_𝒴 + ‖(δK, δg)‖_𝒳 ≤ C₅‖(δJ, δρ)‖_𝒮. Diminishing ε_c and ε_s, it is the
solution of Lemma 39.10 (a), so (b) of that lemma applies to it.

*Proof.* (a) By Lemma 39.10 (d), D_zΨ(u′, 0) is an isomorphism with inverse of norm at most C₁, independently of
u′. T_(u′) is bounded from 𝒴 to 𝒳, continuously in u′ in operator norm: so is e^(−2s/x)Φ²P*_(u′), its coefficients
being polynomial in the 2-jet of u′ and in g′⁻¹, and so is ι_(u′), by Lemma 39.10 (e). The constraint map is a
polynomial in the 2-jet of the data, with coefficients rational in the metric. The spaces H^(k+2)_(x²,e^(s/x)), with
k + 2 > n/2 + 1, embed in C¹(𝒜), and they are stable under products with each other and with W^(k+2,∞)_(x²)(𝒜), by
Sobolev's inequality on the balls B_p of centre p and radius x(p)²/2, on which x and e^(s/x) are comparable to their
values at p ([CD03, Appendix B, (B.2)–(B.3), pp. 61–62]). The space W^(k+2,∞)_(x²)(𝒜) contains C^(k+2)(𝒜) and the
coefficients built from u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε, each K′ and each Christoffel symbol of g′ entering with a factor x² supplied by the
factors x² and x⁴ of 𝒳, as in [CD03, Lemma 2.6]. So (u′, δu) ↦ (J, ρ)(u′ + δu) − (J, ρ)(u′) is C² from a neighbourhood
of zero in 𝒳 into 𝒮, with derivatives continuous in u′ and bounded uniformly. With
D_zΨ(u′, z) = π₀♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)D(J, ρ)(u′ + T_(u′)z)T_(u′), and e^(2s/x) : 𝒮 → 𝒵̃ bounded (*The spaces*), this gives a
constant C₃, independent of u′ ∈ 𝒩_ε for ε small (it includes the factors ‖π₀‖, ‖♯_(g′)‖ and ‖T_(u′)‖², bounded
uniformly), with

    ‖D_zΨ(u′, z₁) − D_zΨ(u′, z₂)‖ ≤ C₃‖z₁ − z₂‖

for z₁, z₂ in a ball about zero; this is hypothesis 3 of Theorem A.20, for the variable z. Take r_c
at most the radius of that ball and at most (2C₁C₃)⁻¹. For z₁, z₂ ∈ B, with z_θ := z₂ + θ(z₁ − z₂),

    Ψ(u′, z₁) − Ψ(u′, z₂) = D_zΨ(u′, 0)(z₁ − z₂) + ∫₀¹ (D_zΨ(u′, z_θ) − D_zΨ(u′, 0)) dθ (z₁ − z₂),

and ‖z_θ‖ ≤ max(‖z₁‖, ‖z₂‖), so

    ‖Ψ(u′, z₁) − Ψ(u′, z₂)‖ ≥ ‖D_zΨ(u′, 0)(z₁ − z₂)‖ − C₃ max(‖z₁‖, ‖z₂‖)‖z₁ − z₂‖ ≥ (2C₁)⁻¹‖z₁ − z₂‖.

By Lemma 39.10 (a), (δK, δg) = T_(u′)z solves (39.11) exactly when Ψ(u′, z) = δf; so two solutions with
z ∈ B have the same z.

(b) Ψ(ũ′, z̃) = δf̃ and Ψ(u′, z) = δf (Lemma 39.10 (a)), so by (a) at ũ′,

    ‖z̃ − z‖ ≤ 2C₁‖Ψ(ũ′, z̃) − Ψ(ũ′, z)‖ ≤ 2C₁(‖δf̃ − δf‖ + ‖Ψ(u′, z) − Ψ(ũ′, z)‖).

At fixed z, u′ ↦ T_(u′)z is continuous, the constraint map is continuous in the background and the datum by the same
product estimates, and ♯_(g′) is continuous in g′ (Lemma 39.10 (e)); so the last term tends to zero as ũ′ → u′.
As e^(2s/x) : 𝒮 → 𝒵̃ and π₀ are bounded and ♯_(g′) is continuous in g′, δf̃ → δf as
(ũ′, (δJ̃, δρ̃)) → (u′, (δJ, δρ)). The continuity of T_(u′)z in 𝒳 follows from that of z and of T_(u′).

(c) Apply Theorem A.20 with A := 𝒩_(ε_c), V_(u′) := 𝒴, W_(u′) := 𝒵, r := r_c and
f_(u′) := Ψ(u′, ·) on B. Hypothesis 1 holds by Lemma 39.10 (d), the inverse of D_zΨ(u′, 0) being a right
inverse of norm at most C₁. Hypothesis 3 is the bound with C₃ in the proof of (a). Hypothesis 2 follows from it: for
v, v + h ∈ B, B being convex,

    f_(u′)(v + h) − f_(u′)(v) − Df_(u′)(v)h = ∫₀¹ (Df_(u′)(v + θh) − Df_(u′)(v))h dθ,

of norm at most C₃‖h‖²/2. So there are ε_G and C_G such that for u′ ∈ 𝒩_(ε_c) and δf ∈ 𝒵 with ‖δf‖_𝒵 < ε_G there is
z ∈ B with Ψ(u′, z) − Ψ(u′, 0) = δf and ‖z‖_𝒴 ≤ C_G‖δf‖_𝒵; and Ψ(u′, 0) = 0. Take δf := π₀♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)(δJ, δρ). By
Lemma 39.10 (e) and *The spaces*, ‖δf‖_𝒵 ≤ C₆‖(δJ, δρ)‖_𝒮 with C₆ independent of u′. For
‖(δJ, δρ)‖_𝒮 < ε_s ≤ ε_G/C₆ this gives z ∈ B with Ψ(u′, z) = δf, that is, by Lemma 39.10 (a), a solution
(δK, δg) = T_(u′)z of (39.11), with ‖z‖_𝒴 ≤ C_GC₆‖(δJ, δρ)‖_𝒮 and ‖(δK, δg)‖_𝒳 ≤ ‖T_(u′)‖‖z‖_𝒴, ‖T_(u′)‖ being
bounded uniformly; this gives C₅.

Now let (δK_*, δg_*) = e^(−2s/x)Φ²P*_(u′)(Y, N), (Y, N) ∈ 𝒴_(g′), be the solution of Lemma 39.10 (a), and
z_* := π₀(Y, N), so that (δK_*, δg_*) = T_(u′)z_* and Ψ(u′, z_*) = δf (Lemma 39.10 (a)). As
D_zΨ(u′, 0) = π₀♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)D(J, ρ)(u′)T_(u′), the inverse bound of Lemma 39.10 (d) and the uniform bound on
the derivative of the constraint map in the proof of (a) give a constant C₄, independent of u′, with

    ‖z_*‖_𝒴 ≤ C₁‖D_zΨ(u′, 0)z_*‖_𝒵 ≤ C₁C₄‖T_(u′)z_*‖_𝒳.

Lemma 39.10 (a) uses "close to zero" in the form that, for every r > 0, the solution has 𝒳-norm below r once
the background and (δJ, δρ) are small enough. With r := r_c/(C₁C₄), diminishing ε_c and ε_s, which leaves r_c, C₁, C₃
and C₄ valid, gives ‖T_(u′)z_*‖_𝒳 < r_c/(C₁C₄). Then z_* ∈ B, and z_* = z by (a). ∎

**Lemma 39.12** ([CD03, Lemma 3.18, p. 19].) Let U′, V′ ⊂ ℝ^D be open, f : U′ → V′ a homeomorphism, and
f_R : U′ → ℝ^D, R ≥ R′, continuous maps with f_R → f uniformly on U′ as R → ∞. For every y ∈ V′ and every R large
there is v_R ∈ U′ with f_R(v_R) = y. If the closed ball B̄(y, r′) lies in V′, v_R can be taken in f⁻¹(B̄(y, r′)).

*Proof.* u_R := Id − f_R ∘ f⁻¹ tends to 0 uniformly on B̄(y, r′). Once max over B̄(y, r′) of |u_R| is at most r′, the
map z ↦ y + u_R(z) is continuous from B̄(y, r′) to itself and has a fixed point y_R by Brouwer's fixed point theorem.
Then v_R := f⁻¹(y_R) satisfies f_R(v_R) = y_R − u_R(y_R) = y. ∎

#### 39.4.2 The gluing theorem

**Theorem 39.13** ([CD03, Theorem 8.1 and Remark 8.4] in space dimension 4.) Let (g, K) be smooth vacuum data
on {r > R₀} ⊂ ℝ⁴ with |||(g, K)|||_(α,7) < ∞ for some α ∈ (3/2, 2], and with charge vector
𝔔⁰ := (𝔔_X(g, K))_X ∈ V. There is R_gl such that for every R ≥ R_gl there are p_R ∈ U and smooth vacuum data
(ĝ_R, K̂_R) on {r > R₀} that equal (g, K) on {r ≤ R} and (g_(p_R), K_(p_R)) on {r ≥ 4R}. Moreover 𝔮(p_R) → 𝔔⁰ as
R → ∞.

*Proof.* Enlarging R₀, |g − δ| ≤ ½ on {r > R₀}; this is assumed below. Fix k := 3, the least integer above n/2. The
proof has five steps.

*Step 1: the solvability statement on the annulus.* Apply Section 39.4.1 with 𝒜 := Γ̄(1, 4), a compact
manifold with boundary, n = 4, x ∈ C^∞(𝒜) a radial defining function of ∂𝒜 (a function of r) with 0 < x ≤ 1 in the
interior that equals the Euclidean distance to ∂𝒜 near it, u₀ := (0, δ), s := 1 and k = 3. Such an x exists, the
distance min(r − 1, 4 − r) being radial: take x := h(r) with h smooth, 0 < h ≤ 1 on (1, 4), h(r) = r − 1 near 1 and
h(r) = 4 − r near 4. Hypothesis (Fin) holds: 𝒦₀ is the restriction of 𝔎 to 𝒜, with the basis (39.4). Indeed, the
fifteen elements of 𝔎 are polynomials, bounded with all derivatives on 𝒜, and ψ² is integrable, so they lie in
H̊¹_(x²,ψ) × H̊²_(x²,ψ) (*The spaces* in Section 39.4.1), and P*_((0,δ)) annihilates them (Lemma 39.1); and
an element of the kernel of ΦP*_((0,δ)) is annihilated by P*_((0,δ)), Φ being multiplication by positive functions, so
it is smooth in 𝒜° by interior regularity and is one of them by Lemma 39.1, 𝒜° being connected. The elements of 𝔎
are polynomials, linearly independent on every open set. A pair (K′, g′) with
‖K′‖_(C^(k+3)(𝒜)) + ‖g′ − δ‖_(C^(k+4)(𝒜)) < ε lies in 𝒩_(Cε), as x ≤ 1, C depending only on x. So Lemma 39.10
and Lemma 39.11 apply: for such (K′, g′), ε small, and (δJ, δρ) ∈ 𝒮 of small norm, (39.11) has a solution
(δK, δg) = T_(u′)z, u′ := (K′, g′), with z ∈ B, unique there, continuous in
(u′, (δJ, δρ)), with ‖(δK, δg)‖_(C²(𝒜)) ≤ C‖(δJ, δρ)‖_𝒮 (Lemma 39.11 (c), Lemma 39.10 (c)); and when
(K′, g′) ∈ C^∞(𝒜) and (δJ, δρ) ∈ C^∞_c(𝒜°) is supported in Γ̄(2, 3) with C^(k+2)(𝒜)-norm small enough, (δK, δg) ∈ C^∞(𝒜)
and extends smoothly by zero across ∂𝒜 (Lemma 39.11 (c), and Lemma 39.10 (b) with Ω_c := Γ̄(2, 3)).

*Step 2: the approximate data.* Fix a radial χ ∈ C^∞(ℝ⁴) with 0 ≤ χ ≤ 1, χ = 1 for r ≤ 2 and χ = 0 for r ≥ 3. Let
B̄ ⊂ V be a closed ball about 𝔔⁰. For R ≥ max(2R₀, R_P) and Q ∈ B̄ put

    u_(Q,R) = (K_(Q,R), g_(Q,R)) := χ 𝒮_R(K, g) + (1 − χ) 𝒮_R(K_(p(Q)), g_(p(Q)))     on 𝒜.

Then:

(a) ‖K_(Q,R)‖_(C^(k+3)(𝒜)) + ‖g_(Q,R) − δ‖_(C^(k+4)(𝒜)) ≤ CR^(−α), uniformly for Q ∈ B̄, and Q ↦ u_(Q,R) is continuous
into C^(k+3) × C^(k+4)(𝒜). Indeed |∂^γ_y(𝒮_Rg − δ)(y)| = R^(|γ|)|∂^γ(g − δ)(Ry)| ≤ CR^(−α)
and |∂^γ𝒮_RK| ≤ CR^(−α) for |γ| ≤ k + 4 = 7 (resp. 6). The member's data obey the same bounds with α replaced by 2 ≥ α,
uniformly in p, and depend smoothly on p (Lemma 39.6), and p(Q) is continuous (Corollary 39.8).

(b) (J, ρ)(u_(Q,R)) is supported in Γ̄(2, 3), with C^(k+2)-norm at most CR^(−α). On Γ(1, 2) and Γ(3, 4) the data are
rescaled vacuum data, hence vacuum by Lemma 39.4. The constraint map is a smooth function of the 2-jet vanishing
at (0, δ).

By (b), (δJ, δρ) := −(J, ρ)(u_(Q,R)) is smooth and supported in Γ̄(2, 3) ⊂ 𝒜°, where x is bounded below, so its
weighted norms are at most C‖·‖_(C^(k+1)) ≤ CR^(−α); and its C^(k+2)-norm, which bounds the norm of
[CD03, Proposition 5.10] (Lemma 39.10 (b) with Ω_c := Γ̄(2, 3)), is at most CR^(−α) by (b). Let R_ε be such
that these bounds, and the bound of (a), are below the thresholds of Step 1 for R ≥ R_ε. For R ≥ R_ε, Step 1 gives a
smooth δu_(Q,R) on 𝒜 that extends by zero, with ‖δu_(Q,R)‖_(C²(𝒜)) ≤ CR^(−α), continuous in Q. Put
û_(Q,R) := u_(Q,R) + δu_(Q,R); by (39.11), with g′ := g_(Q,R), π_(g′)♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)(J, ρ)(û_(Q,R)) = 0.

*Step 3: the obstruction is a pairing.* By Lemma 39.10 (e), the kernel of π_(g′), g′ := g_(Q,R), is 𝒦₀. So
♯_(g′)e^(2s/x)(J, ρ)(û_(Q,R)) ∈ 𝒦₀, that is, on 𝒜°,

    (J, ρ)(û_(Q,R)) = e^(−2s/x) ♭_(g′) Σ_i κ_i e_i     for some κ ∈ ℝ¹⁵,

the e_i = (Y_i, N_i) being the basis (39.4): in Cartesian components J_a = e^(−2s/x) Σ_i κ_i g′_(ab)Y_iᵇ and
ρ = e^(−2s/x) Σ_i κ_iN_i. Let

    F_R(Q)_j := ∫_𝒜 (Y_jᵃJ_a + N_jρ)(û_(Q,R)) dμ_(ĝ_(Q,R)),

ĝ_(Q,R) the metric of û_(Q,R). Then F_R(Q) = 𝒢′κ with 𝒢′_(ji) := ∫_𝒜 (g′(Y_j, Y_i) + N_jN_i) e^(−2s/x) dμ_(ĝ). As in
[CD03, (8.6)], F_R pairs the residual with the Killing initial data themselves. As g′, ĝ → δ in C⁰(𝒜) uniformly on B̄,
𝒢′ → 𝒢, 𝒢_(ji) := ∫_𝒜 (Y_j · Y_i + N_jN_i) e^(−2s/x) dx, the Gram matrix, for a positive measure, of functions that are
linearly independent on every open set. So 𝒢 is positive definite, and there is R_𝒢 such that 𝒢′ is invertible for
R ≥ R_𝒢 and Q ∈ B̄. Then (J, ρ)(û_(Q,R)) = 0 if and only if κ = 0, if and only if F_R(Q) = 0. F_R is continuous on B̄,
its integrand depending continuously on û_(Q,R) in C²(𝒜).

*Step 4: the pairing's asymptotics.* Let 𝔵 = (K̂, ĝ) := 𝒮_R⁻¹û_(Q,R) on Γ(R, 4R). By Lemma 39.4 and then
(39.5),

    F_R(Q)_j = R^(−2−d_j) [ ∮_(S_(4R)) 𝔟_(e_j)(𝔵) − ∮_(S_R) 𝔟_(e_j)(𝔵) + ∫_(Γ(R,4R)) q_(e_j)(𝔵) dx ],     d_j := d(e_j).

Near S_(4R), 𝔵 is the member's data with all derivatives, since χ = 0 for r ≥ 3 and δu_(Q,R) vanishes to infinite
order at ∂𝒜. So (39.7) with α = 2 and Corollary 39.8 give ∮_(S_(4R)) 𝔟_(e_j) = Q_j + O(R^(d_j−2)), uniformly on B̄.
Near S_R, 𝔵 = (g, K), so ∮_(S_R) 𝔟_(e_j) = 𝔔⁰_j + O(R^(2+d_j−2α)). On Γ(R, 4R), unscaling the bounds of Step 2
gives |∂^γ(ĝ − δ)| ≤ CR^(−α−|γ|) (|γ| ≤ 2) and |∂^γK̂| ≤ CR^(−α−1−|γ|) (|γ| ≤ 1). With (39.6) and |e_j| ≤ CR^(d_j),
∫|q_(e_j)| ≤ CR^(d_j)R^(−2α−2)R⁴. As α ≤ 2, d_j − 2 ≤ 2 + d_j − 2α, so

    F̂_R(Q) := (R^(2+d_j)F_R(Q)_j)_j = Q − 𝔔⁰ + O(R^(3−2α))     uniformly on B̄,    (39.15)

and 3 − 2α < 0. (The power R^(−2−d_j) is R^(−(n−2)−d_j) at n = 4; [CD03, (8.7)] prints R⁻¹ for every charge at n = 3.)

*Step 5: conclusion.* Apply Lemma 39.12 with U′ the interior of B̄, f(Q) := Q − 𝔔⁰, f_R := F̂_R for
R ≥ R′ := max(2R₀, R_P, R_ε, R_𝒢), and y = 0. For every r′ > 0 below the radius of B̄ there is R(r′) ≥ R′ such that for
R ≥ R(r′) some Q_R with |Q_R − 𝔔⁰| ≤ r′ has F̂_R(Q_R) = 0; put R_gl := R(r′₀) for one such r′₀. Then F_R(Q_R) = 0 and,
by Step 3, as R ≥ R_𝒢, (J, ρ)(û_(Q_R,R)) = 0. Put p_R := p(Q_R), and let (ĝ_R, K̂_R) be (g, K) on {R₀ < r ≤ R},
𝒮_R⁻¹û_(Q_R,R) on Γ(R, 4R) and (g_(p_R), K_(p_R)) on {r ≥ 4R}. These are smooth, as χ is constant near ∂𝒜 and δu
extends smoothly by zero. They are vacuum everywhere, and ĝ_R is Riemannian, being C⁰-close to δ on Γ(R, 4R). Finally
𝔮(p_R) = Q_R. Choose Q_R for an admissible r′ = r′(R) ≤ 2 inf{r′ : R ≥ R(r′)} + R⁻¹, which exists as R ≥ R(r′₀), and
tends to 0 as R → ∞, since every r′ > 0 is admissible once R ≥ R(r′). Then 𝔮(p_R) → 𝔔⁰. ∎

**Remark 39.14** (What the settling theorem takes from Theorem 39.13.) The data (ĝ_R, K̂_R) equal, for
r ≥ 4R, the data that 𝔤_(p_R) = 𝒫_(p_R)*g^KS_(m,A) induces on {y⁰ = 0}. By uniqueness for the vacuum Cauchy problem,
their development contains the domain of dependence of {r > 4R} in 𝔤_(p_R): a Poincaré transform of a Myers–Perry
metric with parameters near b₀. The proof of Theorem 3.9 uses only the proof of Theorem 39.13, in the class form
Proposition 39.17, with Tangherlini members on Σ^IVP. The members of Definition 39.5 lie on the slices {y⁰ = 0} of
Kerr–Schild time. Far out, Σ^IVP is the graph {t_KS = f(|x|)}, f its height function, and the second fundamental form
K̃_p that the member 𝔤_p induces on the graph differs from the one on the slice by ∇²f + |x|⁻⁴C^∞(X̄), that is,
K̃_p − K_p = ∇²f + |x|⁻⁴C^∞(X̄) (Lemma 42.15 (d), whose base mass μ_end is m₀ here). By (a) and (b) of
the same lemma, the |x|⁻³ coefficient of K̃_p depends smoothly on p, through (m, w) only; at p₀, where 𝒫_(p₀) is the
identity, K̃_(p₀) = k^(m₀) = k_(b₀) by the definition in Section 39.5. So the |x|⁻³ coefficient of K_(p_R) − k_(b₀) is
within C|p_R − p₀| of that of −∇²f, which is −2m₀(δ − 3x̂ ⊗ x̂) (tr ∇²f = 2m₀|x|⁻³ + O(|x|⁻⁵)); so it is not zero,
U being small. So the glued data of Theorem 39.13 are not small in the data class (38.15) of Theorem 38.22
at any R. Gluing a decaying perturbation with smallness in that class takes the members on Σ^IVP (Chapter 42).

**Remark 39.15** ([CD03, Section 8.1] in space dimension 4.) [CD03, (8.1)] asks the parity condition (E.9)
so that the angular momentum and the centre of mass converge and so that the errors of [CD03, (8.6)] lie below the main
terms. In space dimension 4 with α > 3/2 both follow from the decay alone, since 2α > n − 1 = 3 (Proposition 39.3,
(39.15)). The members of Definition 39.5 are taken in Kerr–Schild form, where the shift is odd and of the same order
r⁻² as the metric, which (E.9) would exclude. The convergence rate of [CD03, (8.3)] is β = min(α, n − 2), printed as
min(α, 1), and the power of R in [CD03, (8.7)] is R^(−(n−2)−d). [CD03, Theorem 5.6] states s ≥ n − 2 where its proof
uses s ≥ n − 1, and [CD03, (8.5)] applies it with s = t − 1 where its solution space requires s = t + n − 2; the
exponentially weighted spaces of [CD03, Theorem 5.9], which [CD03] uses for smooth data, avoid both. [CD03, Theorem
3.19] applies [CD03, Lemma 3.18] to the maps of [CD03, (3.29)], which must be continuous in Q; this is
Lemma 39.11. Finally the projection of [CD03] is the L²_ψ-orthogonal projection, in the current metric, onto the
orthogonal of 𝒦₀ in that metric ([CD03, p. 11]). The obstruction it leaves is 𝒦₀ itself, and the unknowns lie in a
space that moves with the background; Lemma 39.10 (e) transports them to a fixed space, which Lemma 39.11
needs, and Step 3 pairs the residual with the Killing initial data themselves, as [CD03, (8.6)] does.

### 39.5 Gluing in the symmetry class

In this section b₀ = (m₀, 0), Σ^IVP is the hypersurface of Section 21.5.3, identified with X = cl{|x| ≥ r_♭} by
(t, x) ↦ x, and G = O(2) × O(2) acts on ℝ⁴ as in Section 2.1 and on spacetime by (t, x) ↦ (t, Ox), O ∈ G ⊂ O(4).
Every element of O(4), acting so, is an isometry of every g^KS_(m,0) and fixes every function of (t, |x|). The fixed
spaces are (ℝ⁴)^G = 0 and 𝔰𝔬(4)^G = 0: the torus T² ⊂ G fixes in ℝ⁴ only 0, and in 𝔰𝔬(4) exactly span(W₁₂, W₃₄),
while x₂ ↦ −x₂ reverses W₁₂ and x₄ ↦ −x₄ reverses W₃₄. So 𝔎^G = span(e₀).

For |x| ≥ R₃, Σ^IVP = {t = C″} (Lemma 21.22 (b)), that is {t_KS = f(|x|)} with f := C″ − T_(m₀)(|x|) in the
Kerr–Schild time t_KS = t − T_(m₀)(|x|) of (21.27). For m ∈ I_m := [¾m₀, (5/4)m₀], let (γ^m, k^m) be the data
that g^KS_(m,0) induces on this graph over {|x| > R₃}, as tensors on {|x| > R₃}. At m = m₀ they are (γ_(b₀), k_(b₀)) of
Lemma 21.24.

**Lemma 39.16** (Tangherlini on Σ^IVP.) (a) γ^m − δ ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞(X̄) and k^m ∈ |x|⁻³C^∞(X̄) on the
compactified {|x| > R₃}, smoothly in m ∈ I_m, and |x|²(γ^m − γ_(b₀)) and |x|³(k^m − k_(b₀)) have C^∞(X̄)-seminorms
O(|m − m₀|). In particular |||(γ^m, k^m)|||_(2,j) ((39.3)) is bounded for every j, uniformly in m. (b) (γ^m, k^m)
are vacuum and O(4)-invariant. (c) Their charges (Proposition 39.3) are 𝔔_(e₀) = 6π²m and 𝔔_X = 0 for X in the other
three groups of (39.4).

*Proof.* (a) g^KS_(m,0) − η = (m/r²) ℓ ⊗ ℓ with ℓ = dt_KS + x̂ · dx, independent of t_KS and a classical symbol of order
−2 in x, smoothly in m, and f′ ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞ near infinity (Lemma 21.20 (a)). The graph is spacelike for each
g^KS_(m,0), m ∈ I_m: its conormal is dt_KS − f′ d|x|, with f′ = −T′_(m₀) = 2χ_∞m₀/(|x|² − m₀) ∈ [0, ⅔]
((21.27); |x|² − m₀ ≥ 3m₀ on supp χ_∞), which is timelike by Lemma 21.16 (e). The induced metric
g_ij + 2g_(t(i)∂_(j)f + g_tt∂_if∂_jf and the second fundamental form ((39.2) for the graph) are smooth functions
of the components of g^KS_(m,0) at (f(x), x), which do not depend on the first argument, and of (∂f, ∂²f). They equal
(δ, 0) at g = η, f constant. This gives the symbol classes, and the m-derivatives are symbols of the same orders.
(b) g^KS_(m,0) is Ricci-flat (Proposition 21.17), and O(4) acts by its isometries, preserving the graph. (c) The
charges are limits of the fluxes ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X of (39.5). The flux integrand is natural for the Euclidean
structure, so on O(4)-invariant data X ↦ 𝔔_X is an O(4)-invariant linear form on 𝔎. It therefore vanishes on the
summands ℝ⁴, Λ²ℝ⁴, ℝ⁴, which are irreducible and nontrivial. 𝔟_(e₀) = (∂_jh_ij − ∂_i tr h)νⁱdS involves only
h = γ − δ. On the graph, γ^m_ij differs from the metric induced on {t_KS = 0} by 2g_(t(i)∂_(j)f + g_tt∂_if∂_jf = O(r⁻⁴),
with first derivatives O(r⁻⁵), as g_ti = (m/r²)x̂_i. So the two fluxes over S_ϱ differ by O(ϱ⁻²), and 𝔔_(e₀) is that of
{t_KS = 0}, which is 6π²m by the part *c_E* of the proof of Proposition 39.7, at p = (m, 0, 0, 0). ∎

**Proposition 39.17** (Gluing in the class; [CD03, Theorem 8.1] with G.) Fix k ≥ 3, the order of the
gluing. There are R_gl, ζ₀ and C such that for R ≥ max(R_gl, R₃) the following holds. Let (g, K) be G-invariant
smooth vacuum data on Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 3R} with

    ζ := sup_(R≤r≤3R) ( Σ_(|β|≤k+4) r^(2+|β|)|∂^β(g − γ^(m₀))| + Σ_(|β|≤k+3) r^(3+|β|)|∂^β(K − k^(m₀))| ) ≤ ζ₀.
    (39.16)

Then there are m with |m − m₀| ≤ Cζ, and G-invariant smooth vacuum data (ĝ, K̂) on Σ^IVP, equal to (g, K) on {r ≤ R}
and to (γ^m, k^m) on {r ≥ 4R}, with

    sup_(R≤r≤4R) ( Σ_(|β|≤k−1) r^(2+|β|)|∂^β(ĝ − γ^(m₀))| + Σ_(|β|≤k−2) r^(3+|β|)|∂^β(K̂ − k^(m₀))| ) ≤ Cζ.
    (39.17)

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 39.13, with k in place of 3 (Section 39.4.1 allows any integer k > n/2), and
seven changes.

(1) *The data used.* Steps 2–5 use (g, K) only on Γ(R, 3R) (in Step 2, χ = 0 for r ≥ 3), and through 𝔔⁰ in Step 4.
Replace 𝔔⁰ by the fluxes 𝔔⁰_R := (∮_(S_R) 𝔟_(e_j)(g − δ, K))_j; Step 4's term at S_R is then exactly 𝔔⁰_R.

(2) *The family.* Replace the members by (γ^m, k^m), m ∈ I_m. Lemma 39.16 (a) gives the bounds of Step 2 (a), with
α = 2, and continuity in m. The smallness of Step 1 holds for R ≥ R_gl: the rescaled u_(m,R) is within
C(m₀ + ζ₀)R⁻² of (0, δ) in C^(k+3) × C^(k+4)(𝒜), and so, by Step 2 (b), its constraint map is within C(m₀ + ζ₀)R⁻² of
zero in C^(k+2)(𝒜), which is also the smallness that Step 1 asks for smoothness.

(3) *Equivariance.* G acts on data on 𝒜 = Γ̄(1, 4) by pull-back, commuting with the rescaling 𝒮_R. For G-invariant
u′ = (K′, g′), the map Ψ(u′, ·) of (39.10) is G-equivariant. Indeed, the constraint map is natural; x and the
weights e^(±s/x), x² are radial (Step 1); ♯_(g′) commutes with G, as g′ is G-invariant; and π_(g′), π₀ and so ι_(u′)
commute with G, as 𝒦₀ = 𝔎|_𝒜 and the L²_ψ(g′) and L²_ψ(δ) inner products are G-invariant; so T_(u′) commutes with G,
P*_(u′) being natural. The norms of Step 1 are G-invariant, and so are 𝒴 and B. So the solution of (39.11) with z
in the ball B of Lemma 39.11 is unique, hence G-invariant when u′ and the right side are, and
û_(m,R) := u_(m,R) + δu_(m,R) is G-invariant.

(4) *A one-dimensional obstruction.* By Step 3, (J, ρ)(û_(m,R)) = e^(−2s/x) ♭_(g′) Σ_i κ_i e_i, which is G-invariant.
♭_(g′) and e^(−2s/x) are invertible and commute with G, so Σ_i κ_ie_i is G-invariant, that is, it lies in
𝔎^G = span(e₀), and κ_i = 0 for e_i ≠ e₀. Hence (J, ρ)(û_(m,R)) = 0 if and only if κ₀ = 0, if and only if
F_R(m)₀ = 𝒢′₀₀κ₀ = 0, where 𝒢′₀₀ = ∫_𝒜 e^(−2s/x) dμ_(ĝ) > 0 (Step 3, e₀ = (0, 1)).

(5) *A zero.* Step 4 at j = 0 with α = 2 gives F̂_R(m) := R²F_R(m)₀ = 6π²m − 𝔔⁰_(R,0) + O(R⁻¹), uniformly on I_m. By
(39.16) and Lemma 39.16, 𝔔⁰_(R,0) = 6π²m₀ + O(ζ) + O(R⁻²). So for R large and ζ₀ small,
F̂_R(¾m₀) < 0 < F̂_R((5/4)m₀). F̂_R is continuous (Step 3), so it has a zero m, by the intermediate value theorem in
place of Lemma 39.12.

(6) *The mass bound.* At m the data û are vacuum. Lemma 39.2 with X = e₀ on Γ(R, 4R), unscaled, gives

    ∮_(S_(4R)) 𝔟(γ^m, k^m) − ∮_(S_R) 𝔟(g, K) + ∫_(Γ(R,4R)) q_(e₀)(û) dx = 0.

The same lemma on Γ(4R, ϱ) for (γ^m, k^m), and on Γ(R, ϱ) for (γ^(m₀), k^(m₀)), with ϱ → ∞ (Lemma 39.16
(c); |q| ≤ Cr⁻⁶ is integrable), gives ∮_(S_(4R)) 𝔟(γ^m, k^m) = 6π²m + ∫_(r>4R) q(γ^m) and
∮_(S_R) 𝔟(γ^(m₀), k^(m₀)) = 6π²m₀ + ∫_(r>R) q(γ^(m₀)). By (39.16), ∮_(S_R) 𝔟(g, K) differs from the latter flux
by at most Cζ. Hence

    6π²(m − m₀) = ∫_(Γ(R,4R)) (q(γ^(m₀)) − q(û)) + ∫_(r>4R) (q(γ^(m₀)) − q(γ^m)) + O(ζ).

Write a := 𝒮_R(g, K) and b := 𝒮_R(γ^m, k^m); both are vacuum, and u_(m,R) = b + χ(a − b). The constraint map is smooth
near flat data and vanishes at b, and it involves two derivatives of the metric and one of the second fundamental form.
So the right side of Step 1, supported in Γ̄(2, 3), has
‖(J, ρ)(u_(m,R))‖_(C^(k+2)) ≤ C‖a − b‖_(C^(k+3) × C^(k+4)) ≤ C(ζ + |m − m₀|)R⁻², which bounds its norm in 𝒮 and that of
[CD03, Proposition 5.10]. By the bound of Step 1, δu_(m,R) is of the same size in H^(k+2)(𝒜) ⊂ C^(k−1)(𝒜). On 𝒜,
û_(m,R) − 𝒮_R(γ^(m₀), k^(m₀)) = χ(a − 𝒮_R(γ^(m₀), k^(m₀))) + (1 − χ)(b − 𝒮_R(γ^(m₀), k^(m₀))) + δu_(m,R); unscaled,
the difference û − (γ^(m₀), k^(m₀)), û := 𝒮_R⁻¹û_(m,R), has |h| ≤ C(ζ + |m − m₀|)R⁻², with each derivative, and K, a
further factor R⁻¹. Both û and (γ^(m₀), k^(m₀)) have |h| ≤ CR⁻² with the same scaling. q_(e₀) is a smooth function
of (h, ∂h, ∂²h, K, ∂K) vanishing to second order at 0 (the proof of Lemma 39.2), with the quadratic bound
(39.6). So |q(û) − q(γ^(m₀))| ≤ C(ζ + |m − m₀|)R⁻⁶ on
Γ(R, 4R), and |q(γ^m) − q(γ^(m₀))| ≤ C|m − m₀|r⁻⁶. Integrating, 6π²|m − m₀| ≤ C(ζ + |m − m₀|)R⁻² + Cζ,
so |m − m₀| ≤ Cζ for R large.

(7) *The bound (39.17) and the conclusion.* û − (γ^(m₀), k^(m₀)) is the sum of χ times the data's deviation,
(1 − χ)(γ^m − γ^(m₀), k^m − k^(m₀)) and δu. These are bounded in the norm of (39.17) by ζ, by C|m − m₀| ≤ Cζ
(Lemma 39.16 (a)), and by Cζ (from (6), rescaled). The glued data are smooth, vacuum and Riemannian as in Step 5 of
the proof of Theorem 39.13, and G-invariant by (3). ∎

**Remark 39.18** (The mass bound.) Proposition 39.17 adds to the proof of Theorem 39.13 the
equivariance of its Step 1, a one-dimensional obstruction, and the a priori bound |m − m₀| ≤ Cζ from the flux identity.
The bound makes the glued data close to Tangherlini, by a multiple of ζ, at a fixed gluing radius (by O(λ) in
Corollary 39.19), which the weighted norm of the data class (38.15) of Theorem 38.22 needs: a bump of
relative size R⁻¹ at radius R has, in that norm, size about R^(ℓ_0−3) (Remark 42.20), which grows with R,
ℓ_0 ∈ (3, 4) being the weight of the class.

**Corollary 39.19** (The data of item (i) of Theorem 3.9.) Let b₀ = (μ_end, 0), so that m₀ = μ_end. Let
k ≥ 3 and R ≥ max(R_gl, R₃), and let c₀ and Ω′ be as in Lemma 41.4. Take J = k + 5 in Lemma 41.3, and let
(g, K) be the data of g_λ on Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 4R}. Then (39.16) holds with ζ ≤ C_Rλ, and for λ small
Proposition 39.17 gives (γ_λ, k_λ) := (ĝ, K̂) and m_λ := m, with |m_λ − μ_end| ≤ C_Rλ. If k ≥ d_1 + 5, d_1 the order of
Theorem 38.22, then also ‖(γ_λ − γ_(b₀), k_λ − k_(b₀))‖_(d_1) ≤ C_Rλ, in the norm of the data class of
Theorem 38.22 ((38.15)).

*Proof.* The data a metric induces on a fixed spacelike slice are smooth functions of its components and their first
derivatives at the slice. By Lemma 41.4 the slice piece lies in Ω′_+, where the background g0 of Section 41.1
equals g_(b₀), so by Lemma 41.3 the data of g_λ differ from (γ_(b₀), k_(b₀)) = (γ^(μ_end), k^(μ_end)) by Cλ in
C^(k+4) there. With the
weights r^(2+|β|) ≤ (3R)^(k+6), ζ ≤ C_Rλ. The data are G-invariant (g_λ and Σ^IVP are, Lemma 41.3 and
Lemma 41.4) and vacuum. For the last claim apply Lemma 38.25 with R′ = 4R: on {r ≤ 8R} the deviation is
C_Rλ in C^(d_1+3), by Lemma 41.3, (39.17) and Lemma 39.16 (a), and on {r ≥ 4R} it is
(γ^m − γ_(b₀), k^m − k_(b₀)), whose seminorms are O(|m − μ_end|) = O(λ). ∎

## 40. Linear stability of five-dimensional Tangherlini, and the comparison of gauges

This chapter proves the linear stability of the five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini metric g_(b₀),
b₀ = (m₀, 0), in the gauge of the nonlinear problem of Chapter 38, and compares that gauge with every other. Every
solution (γ̇, k̇) of the linearised constraint equations in the data class of Theorem 38.22 has a linearised vacuum
development ġ in the generalised wave gauge of Proposition 38.21. Up to a linearised boost and translation, ġ induces
(γ̇, k̇), and where χ_K = 1 it differs from a linearised Myers–Perry metric ∂_b g_b(ḃ) by terms of K⁺-order (α − 2)−:
on spatially compact sets it is O(t_*^(−2−ε)) for each ε < ε_K, with α chosen for ε (Theorem 40.4). In the
symmetry class of Theorem 3.9, ḃ is a change of mass alone and the boost and the translation vanish
(Corollary 40.5). This is Theorem 3.9 one order down.

No new linear theory is needed. The linear solution is the derivative at zero data of the equation P_5(Ψ(U)) = 0 of
Chapter 38, solved directly: the linear Cauchy problem near Σ^IVP (Theorem 37.27, Theorem 38.9, (L) of
Section 38.2.2 and the proof of Theorem 37.36, each at h = 0), the right inverse of Lemma 38.17 at U = 0,
and the second Bianchi identity linearised at the Ricci-flat g_(b₀) in place of the nonlinear one. The Nash–Moser
theorem Theorem 20.1 gives existence and bounds but no differentiability of the nonlinear solution in the data, so
the linear solution is not obtained by differentiating the solution of Theorem 38.22. Being linear, nothing here
needs smallness.

Section 40.4–Section 40.6 compare ġ with a linearised vacuum solution given in another gauge. Every solution of
DRic = 0 on the future half of the Cauchy development, in {r > r_♭}, of a piece Σ_U of Σ^IVP, smooth up to Σ_U, whose
data agree with (γ̇, k̇) up to those of a linearised diffeomorphism, is ġ + ℒ_X g there for a vector field X, unique up
to Killing fields (Theorem 40.12, Corollary 40.13). So the linear stability of Theorem 40.4 holds in every gauge,
modulo a linearised diffeomorphism. The argument is the standard one: put the difference into the linearised harmonic
gauge by solving a linear wave equation for X, show that the result has vanishing Cauchy data, and conclude by
uniqueness for a linear wave equation. Its inputs beyond Section 40.1–Section 40.3 are chiefly the Cauchy problem
for normally hyperbolic operators on globally hyperbolic manifolds ([BGP]; Section A.1) and the pointwise
identities of Lemma 40.11. Nothing is asserted here about the size or decay of X (Remark 40.14). Linear
solutions in the Regge–Wheeler-type gauge of [KI03], whose gauge-invariant master quantities decay by [HKW18], and in
the harmonic gauge are treated in Chapter 45–Chapter 47, from the results of this chapter.

*The inner radius.* The inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] of Chapter 21, R₁ = m₀^(1/2), is a parameter, with the radii of
Definition 22.1; so r₀ = r_♭ and r^♮ = ½(r_♭ + r₂) < r₂ < R₁. Every result of the chapter holds for every such r_♭,
with constants depending on it. Besides results of earlier chapters stated for every such r_♭, the arguments of this
chapter use the inner radius directly only through: Lemma 21.19 (g_(b₀) is defined on {|x| ≥ ½r_♭});
Lemma 21.22 (the time functions; ψ_IVP(r_♭) = 0 by the proof of its (b)); Lemma 15.35 (1)–(2) at h = 0
(dr future timelike on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r^♮}, dt^♭_* past timelike); Lemma 18.5 (a) with r₀ = r_♭; Lemma 38.5
(c) (the boundary piece {r = r_♭} of 𝔒); the identity F = 0 on [r_♭, 5R₁] of Section 38.1, so that t_* = t_IVP
there; and the radius R_ν = ½(r_♭ + 5R₁) of Proposition 38.4. Each holds at r_♭. Lemma 15.35 is stated on
{t_* > 1}, but it is used below also near Σ^IVP, where t_* is near 0. At h = 0 its statement (1) concerns r only,
g_(b₀) being stationary, so it holds on all of {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r^♮}, at every t_*: this is the argument of
Lemma 38.12 (iv), and Proposition 22.3 (d) gives it as well, as r^♮ < R₁ = r_h.

*Notation.* g := g_(b₀). The future unit normal of Σ^IVP for g is written n; the letter ν is kept for the function
ν(r) of Proposition 38.4. For data on Σ^IVP, ‖(γ̇, k̇)‖_(H^k) is the norm of H^k of the classes
H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b × H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b, as in Theorem 38.22. G = O(2) × O(2) is the group of
Section 38.8; G_g k := k − ½g tr_g k is the trace reversal (Section 21.8).

### 40.1 Setting

Everything of Section 38.1 is kept: t_*, t_IVP, Σ^IVP := t_IVP⁻¹(0), t^♭_* and C_♭ (the constant C′ of
Lemma 15.35 (b)), T̂ = 2/C_♭, Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1}, the cut-offs χ_− (Definition 38.15), χ_K (with χ_K = 0
on {t^♭_* < T̂ + 2}) and χ_ι, E_C, E_Υ, ℰ_0, ℓ_0, ℰ^C_I, ℓ_I, the weights of the cone and α. The parameters are those
of Theorem 38.24, as in Theorem 3.9. A sublevel set {t^♭_* ≤ c} is the complement of {t^♭_* > c}, so that it
contains the points where t^♭_* is not defined. Also kept are χ^♮_0 and P^♮ of Lemma 38.1, and the region of
Proposition 38.4, which does not depend on the parameters,

    𝒟 = N_ν ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3},        N_ν = {t_IVP ≥ −ν(|x|)},

with ν = 0 on [0, R_ν] and ν > 0 on (R_ν, ∞), and its cover by Ω_(ext,r_1), the compact part 𝔒 and the slab 𝒮
(Lemma 38.5, with the same r_1, R_8, R_9, c, T″ and ρ′_I), with 𝒟^± := 𝒟 ∩ {±t_IVP ≥ 0} and the compact set 𝔒⁻
of its part (e). 𝒟 contains Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3}, as t_IVP ≥ t_* ≥ t^♭_* ≥ 1 there.

*Linearised operators.* For a symmetric 2-tensor k let DRic(k) := (d/ds) Ric(g + sk)|_(s=0), and let Υ̇(k), Υ̇^♮(k),
Υ̇⁰(k) be the derivatives at (g, g) in the first argument of Υ^(E_Υ), Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ) and Υ⁰ ((21.43),
(37.36), Lemma 38.1). As δ*_(g_0,E_C) depends on g_0 only,

    L := D_1P(g, g) = DRic − δ*_(g,E_C)Υ̇,        L^♮ := D_1P^♮(g, g) = DRic − δ*_(g,E_C)Υ̇^♮.    (40.1)

L is the operator L_g of (21.44), and L^♮ is the linearisation L^(χ^♮_0)_(g,g) of P^♮. On Ω_*, χ^♮_0 = 1
(Lemma 38.1 (b)), so L^♮ = L and Υ̇^♮ = Υ̇ there. Near Σ^IVP, χ^♮_0 = 0 (Lemma 38.1 (d)), so
Υ̇^♮ = Υ̇⁰ there. And Υ^(E_Υ)(g_0, g_0) = Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g_0, g_0) = 0 for every metric g_0, since Υ⁰(g_0, g_0) = 0 and the
E^Υ-term is linear in g − g_0 ((21.43), (37.36)). Lemma 18.4 asks for the principal symbol
g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id. L^♮ and the operator δ_gG_gδ*_(g,E_C) of the constraint propagation have the principal symbol
½g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id (the proof of Proposition 40.2); so wherever Lemma 18.4 is applied below to one of them, it is
applied to twice the operator, 2L^♮ or 2δ_gG_gδ*_(g,E_C), which has the same solutions.

*The constraints.* For a metric g̃ near Σ^IVP with future unit normal n_g̃, inducing the first and second fundamental
forms (γ, k), the Gauss and Codazzi equations write (G_g̃ Ric(g̃))(n_g̃, ·)|_(Σ^IVP) = 𝒞(γ, k), where 𝒞 is the
constraint map; it depends on g̃ only through (γ, k). Its vanishing is the constraint equations, as Proposition 38.4
uses them. Data (γ̇, k̇) satisfy the *linearised constraint equations* if D𝒞_((γ_(b₀),k_(b₀)))(γ̇, k̇) = 0.

*The boost and translation generators.* Let Θ := χ_r(|x|)χ^♯_IVP(1 − χ^♭_K) ∈ [0, 1] be the cut-off factor of
Lemma 21.26. The boosts are φ_S = exp V(S), with V(S_w) = ½ΘX_w linear in S = S_w ∈ 𝒮_1 (Lemma 21.26),
and the translations are ψ_(S⁰) = exp V⁰(S⁰), with V⁰(S_w) = ½Θ w·∂_x linear in S⁰ = S_w ∈ 𝒮_1
(Lemma 32.2). Both vector fields vanish where Θ = 0, so on {|x| ≤ 5R₁} and where χ^♭_K = 1. Their composite
is φ_(S,S⁰) = ψ_(S⁰) ∘ φ_S ((38.1)). For S′, S⁰′ ∈ 𝒮_1 put

    ġ_(S′) := (d/ds) φ*_(−sS′) g |_(s=0) = −ℒ_(V(S′)) g,
    ġ⁰_(S⁰′) := (d/ds) ψ*_(−sS⁰′) g |_(s=0) = −ℒ_(V⁰(S⁰′)) g,    (40.2)

linearised diffeomorphisms: φ_(−sS′) = exp(−sV(S′)) is the time-s flow of −V(S′), and likewise for ψ_(−sS⁰′). The
second is the derivative −δ*_g(Θw⁰(S⁰′)) of Chapter 32, as g(V⁰(S⁰′), ·) = ½Θw⁰(S⁰′) and ℒ_Xg = 2δ*_g(g(X, ·)). As
φ*_(−sS′,−sS⁰′)g = φ*_(−sS′)(ψ*_(−sS⁰′)g), by (38.1), is smooth in s and both flows are the identity at
s = 0,

    (d/ds) φ*_(−sS′,−sS⁰′) g |_(s=0) = ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′).

DRic(ġ_(S′)) = (d/ds) Ric(φ*_(−sS′)g)|_(s=0) = 0, Ric(φ*_(−sS′)g) = φ*_(−sS′)Ric(g) vanishing for every s, and
DRic(ġ⁰_(S⁰′)) = 0 likewise. Both tensors vanish on the interior of {Θ = 0}, which contains {|x| < 5R₁} and the
interior of {χ^♭_K = 1}, as V(S′) and V⁰(S⁰′) vanish there.

*The background.* The background of P_5 at p⃗_(≤0) = (S, b − b₀, S⁰) is the translated background of
(32.4) (Section 38.1),
