    g_(p⃗) = (1 − χ_K) φ*_(−S,−S⁰) g + χ_K g_b,

which is φ*_(−S,−S⁰)g where χ_K = 0 and g_b where χ_K = 1, and is smooth in p⃗ (Lemma 32.4 (a),
Lemma 38.3 (a)).

Put 𝒟′ := 𝒟 ∖ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 7/4}. Then Ω_* ∪ 𝒟 = Ω_* ∪ 𝒟′, as the points of 𝒟 with
t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 7/4 lie in Ω_*; and Ω_* ∩ 𝒟′ = Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, as 𝒟 contains Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3}.

### 40.2 The linear initial-value problem

**Lemma 40.1** (Linearised gauged Cauchy data; Proposition 37.41 linearised.) Let
γ̇ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b(Σ^IVP; S²T*Σ^IVP) and k̇ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b(Σ^IVP; S²T*Σ^IVP). There are
ḣ_0, ḣ_1 ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b(Σ^IVP; S²T*), linear in (γ̇, k̇), each seminorm bounded by finitely many of (γ̇, k̇), such
that every symmetric 2-tensor ḣ, smooth near Σ^IVP or on one side of it up to Σ^IVP, with ḣ|_(Σ^IVP) = ḣ_0 and
(rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))ḣ)|_(Σ^IVP) = ḣ_1 satisfies:

(1) the first and second fundamental forms of Σ^IVP for g + sḣ have the derivatives (γ̇, k̇) at s = 0;

(2) Υ̇⁰(ḣ) = 0 at Σ^IVP;

(3) if (γ̇, k̇) satisfy the linearised constraint equations, then (G_g DRic(ḣ))(n, ·) = 0 at Σ^IVP.

*Proof.* For |ε| small, Proposition 37.41 applies to (γ̃, k̃) := ε(γ̇, k̇) (γ̃ is small in H³_b, and
the constraints are not assumed there). It gives h_0(ε) = εγ̇, extended by h_0(n, ·) := 0, and h_1(ε) = r h̃_1(ε). Its
proof determines h̃_1(ε) at each point by linear algebraic equations, solved in the order (ij), (0j), (00), each step
dividing by a multiple of e_0 t_IVP, which is bounded away from 0. Their other coefficients (the frame, the normal n_0
of g + h_0, written ν₀ there, the Christoffel symbols of g + h_0) are smooth functions of h_0 and its first derivatives.
Their right sides are smooth in these and affine in k̃ (the proof of Proposition 37.41). So ε ↦ h_1(ε) is
smooth at each point, with h_1(0) = 0. Put ḣ_0 := γ̇, extended in the same way, and ḣ_1 := ∂_ε h_1(0). This is the same
construction with the two equations of that proof, for the second fundamental form and for Υ⁰, linearised at g. Their
right sides are linear in γ̇, its b-derivatives and k̇, with the coefficients of that proof. So they lie in
H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b by its count, and ḣ_1 ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b, linearly and with the stated bounds.

Given ḣ, extend it smoothly across Σ^IVP if it is given on one side only; (1)–(3) involve only its derivatives at
Σ^IVP. Fix χ ∈ C^∞_c(ℝ) equal to 1 near 0, and in the coordinates (t_IVP, x) put

    g_ε := g + εḣ + t_IVP χ(t_IVP) r⁻¹(h_1(ε) − εḣ_1),

the last bracket taken independent of t_IVP. Then (g_ε − g)|_(Σ^IVP) = εγ̇ = h_0(ε) and
(rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))(g_ε − g))|_(Σ^IVP) = εḣ_1 + h_1(ε) − εḣ_1 = h_1(ε). The conclusions of Proposition 37.41 are
identities at each point of Σ^IVP, derived pointwise in its proof. So they hold for g_ε near any compact piece of
Σ^IVP, where g_ε is Lorentzian for |ε| small. By its (1)–(2), g_ε induces (γ_(b₀) + εγ̇, k_(b₀) + εk̇) and
Υ⁰(g_ε, g) = 0 at Σ^IVP, for every small ε. The induced data and Υ⁰ at Σ^IVP are smooth functions of g_ε and its first
derivatives there, and the 1-jet of the last term at Σ^IVP is O(ε²) at each point: the term vanishes there, so do its
tangential derivatives, and its t_IVP-derivative is r⁻¹(h_1(ε) − εḣ_1) = O(ε²). So the 1-jet of g_ε at Σ^IVP has the
ε-derivative at ε = 0 of that of g + εḣ. Differentiating at ε = 0 gives (1) and (2).

(3) We use g + sḣ, not g_ε, since differentiating along g_ε would need the ε-derivative of its 2-jet. For |s| small
g + sḣ is Lorentzian near any compact piece of Σ^IVP, and there the Gauss and Codazzi equations give
(G_(g+sḣ) Ric(g + sḣ))(n_s, ·) = 𝒞(γ_s, k_s) at Σ^IVP, with (γ_s, k_s) the data g + sḣ induces and n_s its future unit
normal. Both sides are smooth in s. Differentiate at s = 0. On the left, the variations of G_(g+sḣ) and n_s multiply
Ric(g) = 0, leaving (G_g DRic(ḣ))(n, ·). On the right, (d/ds)(γ_s, k_s)|_(s=0) = (γ̇, k̇) by (1), so the derivative is
D𝒞(γ̇, k̇) = 0. ∎

**Proposition 40.2** (The linear initial solution; Proposition 38.4 linearised at zero data.) Let
(γ̇, k̇) be as in Lemma 40.1 and satisfy the linearised constraint equations. There is a unique ḣ on 𝒟, in the
classes named in the proof, with

    L^♮ḣ = 0,        ḣ = ḣ_0,   rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))ḣ = ḣ_1   on Σ^IVP,    (40.3)

and:

(1) Υ̇^♮(ḣ) = 0 and DRic(ḣ) = 0 on 𝒟; on 𝒟 ∩ Ω_*, Υ̇(ḣ) = 0;

(2) on 𝒟 ∩ Ω_*, ḣ ∈ H̄^(∞,(⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I))_b (orders at ℐ⁺; the set is bounded in t_*), and for each k there are k′ and
C_k with ‖ḣ‖_(H^k) ≤ C_k‖(γ̇, k̇)‖_(H^(k+k′)).

*Proof.* *The solution.* As in the proof of Proposition 38.4, 𝒟 is the union of 𝒟 ∩ Ω_(ext,r_1), of
𝒟⁺ = 𝒟 ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} and of the compact set 𝔒⁻ (Lemma 38.5 (b), (e)); the solution is found on each, the three
agree where two of them are defined, and they are glued across Σ^IVP. The linear theorems take the place of the
nonlinear ones. The data lie in H^(∞,ℓ^♭_0)_b, as ℓ^♭_0 < min Re ℰ_0 and ℓ^♭_0 < ℓ_0 (the first step of the proof of
Theorem 37.36).

- *Exterior.* On Ω_(ext,r_1) (the radius r₀ of Theorem 37.27 being r_1), L^♮ = L^(χ_0)_(g,g) (Lemma 38.1 (c)).
  Theorem 37.27 with Corollary 37.35, at h = 0 and α₀ = ℓ^♭_0, gives the unique
  ḣ ∈ H^(k,ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(Ω_(ext,r_1)) with these data, bounded by (37.26), whose tame term vanishes at
  h = 0. Lemma 37.24, which it uses, covers the past slab.

- *Forward part.* Theorem 38.9 with g_0 := g, h = 0, α_0 := ℓ^♭_0 and f = 0, with the data (ḣ_0, ḣ_1) on Σ^IVP,
  gives for every k ≥ 2 a solution ḣ ∈ H^(k,ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺), the same for every k by its uniqueness clause,
  bounded by (37.26), whose tame term vanishes at h = 0; on 𝒟⁺, L^♮ = L^(χ^♮_0)_(g,g). On
  Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} it equals the exterior solution: both solve the forward problem there with the data on
  Σ^IVP_(r_1), and their difference vanishes by the forward parts of Lemma 37.24 and Lemma 37.25, as in the
  uniqueness of Theorem 37.27 (the last clause of Theorem 38.9).

- *Backward part.* 𝔒⁻ is compact, and for the reversed time orientation it is the domain of dependence of
  Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ 2R_8} within 𝒟⁻ = 𝒟 ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0}: a compact set of the second kind of Section 38.2.2
  (Lemma 38.5 (e), which holds for g). L^♮ is a linear operator with smooth coefficients and principal part
  ½□_g ⊗ id = −½g^(αβ)∂_α∂_β ⊗ id, □_g as in (21.47), that is with principal symbol ½g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id
  (∂ → iζ): this is the normal form of the gauge of Section 38.2.2, at h = 0. Its only data are those on
  Σ^IVP ∩ 𝔒⁻. The linear local theory (L) of Section 38.2.2, with 𝔒′ := 𝔒⁻, then gives ḣ on 𝔒⁻, backward from
  Σ^IVP to {t_IVP = −ν}, unique in H²(𝔒⁻), and bounded in H^(k+1)(𝔒⁻) for every k ≥ 4 by finitely many norms of the
  data; uniqueness also follows from Lemma 18.4. On Ω_(ext,r_1) ∩ 𝔒⁻, which lies in the past slab, it equals
  the exterior solution, by the uniqueness clause of (L), as in the proof of Proposition 38.4 (*Backward part*).

*Gluing.* 𝒟⁺ ∩ 𝔒⁻ = Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ 2R_8}, where both solutions take the data, and each point of 𝒟 off
Σ^IVP ∩ {R_ν ≤ r ≤ r_1} has a neighbourhood in 𝒟 contained in one of the three sets, as in the proof of
Proposition 38.4 (*Gluing*). Near a point p of Σ^IVP with R_ν ≤ r(p) ≤ r_1 and for m ≥ 2, the forward solution is
the restriction to {t_IVP ≥ 0} of a C^m tensor u_1 on a small coordinate ball V about p (Sobolev embedding, its class
imposing H^k away from infinity for every k), and the backward one the restriction of the solution u_2 on the slab of
the proof of (L), which is C^m and solves L^♮u_2 = 0 below Σ^IVP near p, beyond 𝒟 as well. Lemma 38.6, for
the linear operator L^♮, with A₁ := V ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, A₂ := V ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0} and the one hypersurface Σ^IVP ∩ V,
spacelike for g, shows that ḣ is C^m on V ∩ 𝒟. So ḣ is smooth on 𝒟, up to its boundary.
*The uniqueness classes:* H^(max(k,1),ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b of Theorem 37.27 on Ω_(ext,r_1), that of Theorem 38.9 on
𝒟⁺, H^(max(k,2),ℓ^♭_0,(−,ℓ^♭_I))_b(𝒟⁺) (k ≥ 1), and H² on 𝔒⁻ ((L) of Section 38.2.2). Each is preserved by every
isometry of g that fixes t and |x|, the weights being functions of (t, |x|) ((21.23)) and ρ′_I a function of
(t, |x|) (Section 38.2.1).

*(2).* On Ω_(ext,r_1) this is the proof of Theorem 37.36 for L^(χ_0) (Lemma 37.34). There
L^(χ_0)_(g,g)ḣ = 0, with Lemma 37.34 giving the structure of Proposition 27.14 for L^(χ_0); so (37.41)
holds with right side 0 and (37.42) without its integral, and every step is linear in the data. Its
(37.39) becomes ‖ḣ‖_(H^(k,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0),⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I)_b) ≤ C_k‖(ḣ_0, ḣ_1)‖_(H^(k_0,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b), a linear map
continuous at 0 being bounded. On 𝒟⁺, the proof of Corollary 38.11 (the proof of Theorem 37.36 on 𝒟⁺, with
Theorem 38.9 at h = 0 in place of the linear estimate) gives the same, its only data being those on Σ^IVP;
𝒟 ∩ Ω_* lies in 𝒟⁺, as t_IVP ≥ t_* ≥ t^♭_* ≥ 1 there. Lemma 40.1 bounds (ḣ_0, ḣ_1) by (γ̇, k̇).

*(1).* This is the argument of Proposition 38.4 (2), linearised. Put η̇ := Υ̇^♮(ḣ). By (40.1) and
(40.3), DRic(ḣ) = δ*_(g,E_C)η̇. The second Bianchi identity δ_g̃ G_g̃ Ric(g̃) = 0 holds for every metric g̃.
Differentiated at the Ricci-flat g, the variation of δ_g̃ G_g̃ multiplies Ric(g) = 0, so δ_g G_g DRic(k) = 0 for
every k. Hence δ_g G_g δ*_(g,E_C)η̇ = 0 on 𝒟. This operator has the principal symbol of δ_g G_g δ*_g, which is
½g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) times the identity (Lemma 40.11 (a)), as δ*_(g,E_C) − δ*_g is of order 0 (Definition 21.28). At
Σ^IVP, η̇ = Υ̇⁰(ḣ) = 0 by Lemma 40.1 (2). Also (G_g δ*_(g,E_C)η̇)(n, ·) = (G_g DRic(ḣ))(n, ·) = 0 there by
Lemma 40.1 (3), so Lemma 38.20, with g for its metric, Σ^IVP for its Σ and n for its unit normal ν, gives
∂_nη̇ = 0. So the Cauchy data of η̇ vanish, and η̇ = 0 on 𝒟 by Lemma 18.4, forward and backward of
Σ^IVP, as in the proof of Proposition 38.4 (2). Then DRic(ḣ) = 0, and Υ̇ = Υ̇^♮ on Ω_*. ∎

### 40.3 The linear solution

**Lemma 40.3** (The source.) Let ḣ be given by Proposition 40.2. χ_−(t^♭_*)ḣ is defined on
Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2} ⊂ 𝒟; extend it by 0 to Ω_*, and put

    f := −L(χ_−(t^♭_*)ḣ)     on Ω_*.    (40.4)

Then f = −[L, χ_−(t^♭_*)]ḣ is supported in {T̂ + 7/4 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}, f ∈ ℱ^∞_ex, and
‖f‖_(ℱ^k_ex) ≤ C_k‖(γ̇, k̇)‖_(H^(k+k′_k)), with k′_k as in Lemma 38.16 (d).

*Proof.* On 𝒟 ∩ Ω_*, Lḣ = L^♮ḣ = 0 by (40.1) and (40.3). So L(χ_−ḣ) = [L, χ_−]ḣ, a first-order
operator applied to ḣ, with coefficients supported in supp dχ_−(t^♭_*) ⊂ {T̂ + 7/4 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2}. This set is
bounded in t_*, so f vanishes near ι⁺ and K⁺. It vanishes on {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, which gives the supported character
of ℱ_ex. Near ℐ⁺, χ_−ḣ has the orders (⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I) by Proposition 40.2 (2), as in Lemma 38.16 (c).
Proposition 27.17 with g_1 = g_0 = g and h = 0 then puts L(χ_−ḣ) in the orders (⟨ℰ^C_I + 1⟩′, ℓ_I + 1) of ℱ_ex
there, continuously, as Lemma 38.16 (c) uses Corollary 27.18. The bound follows from Proposition 40.2 (2). ∎

**Theorem 40.4** (Linear stability of Schwarzschild–Tangherlini in dimension 4 + 1.) Let
γ̇ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b(Σ^IVP) and k̇ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b(Σ^IVP) satisfy the linearised constraint equations at
(γ_(b₀), k_(b₀)). Then there are U′ ∈ 𝒟^∞_ex with components ḃ ∈ 𝔟, S′ ∈ 𝒮_1 (boost) and S⁰′ := S′^(0)_1 ∈ 𝒮_1
(translation) (Definition 34.15), and a symmetric 2-tensor ġ on Ω_* ∪ 𝒟, all linear in (γ̇, k̇), with:

(1) DRic(ġ) = 0 on Ω_* ∪ 𝒟;

(2) ġ = ḣ + ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) on 𝒟′ (Section 40.1), with ḣ of Proposition 40.2 and ġ_(S′), ġ⁰_(S⁰′) of
(40.2); so ġ − ġ_(S′) − ġ⁰_(S⁰′) induces the linearised data (γ̇, k̇) on Σ^IVP (Lemma 40.1 (1)), and
ġ induces them up to the data of the linearised diffeomorphism −ℒ_(V(S′)+V⁰(S⁰′))g;

(3) on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 2}, ġ = D_0𝔤(U′), the derivative at U = 0 of

    𝔤(U) := g_(p⃗) + h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + h,        (h, p⃗, q) = Φ(U),

with g_(p⃗) the translated background of (32.4) (Section 40.1): the metric of Theorem 38.22 (3); and
D_0Φ(U′) = (h′, p⃗′, q′) with h′ ∈ 𝒳^∞_(J,ex) and q′ ∈ 𝒬_ex (Proposition 35.31);

(4) where χ_K = 1,

    ġ − ∂_b g_b|_(b=b₀)(ḃ) = h_(b₀,rem)(q′) + h′.    (40.5)

So for every R′, ε′ > 0 and i, β there are C, k₁ and T′ with

    |(t_*∂_(t_*))^i ∂^β_x (ġ − ∂_b g_b|_(b₀)(ḃ))| ≤ C‖(γ̇, k̇)‖_(H^(k₁)) t_*^(−(α−2)+ε′)
                                                                  on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′};    (40.6)

and if, for a given ε_t < ε_K, α is chosen with α > 4 + ε_t, then ε′ := α − 4 − ε_t gives
ġ − ∂_b g_b(ḃ) = O(t_*^(−2−ε_t)) there. Such α exist, as ε_K does not depend on ε_t and the admissible α are dense in
(4 + ε_K − ε′_0, 4 + ε_K] (Definition 34.12, Lemma 35.14);

(5) the linearised gauge 1-form vanishes: on Ω_*,

    η̇ := Υ̇(ġ) + D_2Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g)(ġ_(p⃗′)) − Dϑ_tot(p⃗′) = 0,        ġ_(p⃗′) := D_0 g_(p⃗)(U′),

and on 𝒟′, Υ̇^♮(ġ) + D_2Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g, g)(ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′)) = 0. These are the derivatives of the two lines of the
gauge 1-form κ of Proposition 38.21: of Υ^(E_Υ)(𝔤(U) + k, g_(p⃗)) − ϑ_tot(p⃗) at (U, k) = (0, 0) in the direction
(U′, χ_−(t^♭_*)ḣ), and of Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(φ*_(−sS′,−sS⁰′)g + sḣ, φ*_(−sS′,−sS⁰′)g) at s = 0;

(6) |ḃ| + |S′| + |S⁰′| + ‖U′‖_(𝒟^k_ex) ≤ C_k‖(γ̇, k̇)‖_(H^(k+k′)).

*Proof.* *Step 1 (the right inverse at Tangherlini).* At zero data, h_(S,S⁰) = 0 for every (S, S⁰)
(Proposition 38.4 (3)), so Ψ = Φ ((38.11)). Lemma 38.17 at zero data and U = 0 gives a linear
ℛ : ℱ^∞_ex → 𝒟^∞_ex with D_0(P_5 ∘ Φ)(ℛf) = f, bounded by the tame estimate of Theorem 35.8 on the exact scales
(Corollary 35.33), which at U = 0 reads ‖ℛf‖_(𝒟^k_ex) ≤ C_k‖f‖_(ℱ^(k+d)_ex), d its loss. The tail of U = 0
vanishes everywhere, so the support clause of Lemma 38.17 applies with c := T̂ + 7/4: if f vanishes on
{t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, so does the tail of ℛf. Put U′ := ℛf with f of Lemma 40.3. Its tail h̃′ vanishes on
{t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, and (6) follows from Lemma 40.3.

*Step 2 (the equation in the cone).* For U small and a symmetric 2-tensor k on Ω_*, the equation of the proof of
Proposition 38.21 gives, with zero data,

    P_5(Φ(U) + (k, 0, 0)) = Ric(𝔤(U) + k) − δ*_(𝔤_0(U),E_C)(Υ^(E_Υ)(𝔤(U) + k, 𝔤_0(U)) − ϑ_tot(p⃗)),
                                                                                       𝔤_0(U) := g_(p⃗),

which is P_5(Ψ(U)) of Chapter 38 for k = χ_−h_(−S,−S⁰), S and S⁰ := S^(0)_1 the boost and translation components of U.
The right side is smooth in (U, k). Φ is smooth (Theorem 34.20; on the exact classes Proposition 35.31), g_(p⃗) is
smooth in p⃗ (Section 40.1; Lemma 32.4 (a)), and h_tot, ϑ_tot and h_(b,rem) are smooth in (p⃗, q)
(Definition 32.7, Definition 32.19, Definition 32.31, Definition 32.33, Definition 34.2). At
(U, k) = (0, 0) the metric is g and the gauge 1-form vanishes, so the variation of δ*_(𝔤_0(U),E_C) drops out.
Differentiating at (0, 0) in the direction (U′, χ_−ḣ) gives

    DRic(ġ) − δ*_(g,E_C)η̇ = D_0(P_5 ∘ Φ)(U′) + L(χ_−ḣ) = f − f = 0     on Ω_*,    (40.7)

with ġ := D_0𝔤(U′) + χ_−ḣ and η̇ as in (5). Here D_hP_5(0)(k) = Lk, since at U = 0 the right side is P(g + k, g).

*Step 3 (the initial part of the cone).* On Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, for every U: χ_K = 0, so
g_(p⃗) = φ*_(−S,−S⁰)g (Section 40.1), with S and S⁰ the boost and translation components of U; h_tot(p⃗) and
ϑ_tot(p⃗) vanish, being supported in supp χ_K (h_tot in 𝒞 ⊂ supp χ_K; Lemma 32.6 and the definitions cited in
Step 2), and h_(b,rem)(q) vanishes, carrying χ_K; and the metric component of Φ(U) is h̃, as χ_ι = 0 there (the proof
of Lemma 38.16). So there ġ_(p⃗′) = ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) (Section 40.1), Dϑ_tot(p⃗′) = 0,
D_0𝔤(U′) = ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) + h̃′ = ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) (Step 1) and χ_− = 1, whence

    ġ = ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) + ḣ,        η̇ = Υ̇(ḣ) + (D_1 + D_2)Υ^(E_Υ)(g, g)(ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′)) = 0.

The first term vanishes by Proposition 40.2 (1). The second is
(d/ds)Υ^(E_Υ)(φ*_(−sS′,−sS⁰′)g, φ*_(−sS′,−sS⁰′)g)|_(s=0), by the chain rule and Section 40.1, and this is 0, as
Υ^(E_Υ)(g_0, g_0) = 0 for every metric g_0 (Section 40.1).

*Step 4 (propagation).* By (40.7) and the linearised Bianchi identity (the proof of Proposition 40.2),
δ_gG_gδ*_(g,E_C)η̇ = 0 on Ω_*. η̇ vanishes on Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, which contains Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ 2} (T̂ ≥ 2).
Lemma 18.4 on Ω_*° with τ := t^♭_* and c := 3/2, as in the proof of Proposition 38.21, gives η̇ = 0. Its
hypotheses hold. dt^♭_* is past timelike for g (Lemma 15.35 (2) at h = 0), so t^♭_* is a time function on Ω_*°.
The compact sets are those of Lemma 18.5 (a) with θ = 0, which applies to g: along future causal curves of g,
t_* is non-decreasing and B := t_* + R̃(r) is a time function, and near the inner boundary past causal curves stay in
{r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)}, as dr is future timelike on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r^♮} (Lemma 15.35 (1) at h = 0). So for p ∈ Ω_*°
with t^♭_*(p) > c, J⁻_(Ω_*°)(p) ∩ {t^♭_* ≥ c} lies in

    L′_p := {c ≤ t^♭_* ≤ t^♭_*(p),  B ≤ B(p),  r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮)},

t^♭_* being a time function: this is the set L′_p of (18.20) (Lemma 18.5 (a)) with X := Ω_*°,
τ′ := t^♭_* (≤ t_*) and C′ := C_♭, which drops the condition t_* ≤ t_*(p) of (18.19) as C_♭t_* ≤ t^♭_*. L′_p is
compact, as B bounds r there (c ≤ t_* ≤ t^♭_*(p)/C_♭, R̃(r) ≤ B(p) − c, and R̃(r) = r for r ≥ r′_0 + 1), and it lies in
Ω_*°, as t^♭_* ≥ c > 1 and r ≥ min(r(p), r^♮) > r_♭ on it. (Lemma 38.13 (c) at h = 0 gives such sets as well.) So
DRic(ġ) = 0 on Ω_* by (40.7).

*Step 5 (the initial region).* On 𝒟′ put ġ := ḣ + ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′). DRic(ḣ) = 0 (Proposition 40.2 (1)) and
DRic(ġ_(S′)) = DRic(ġ⁰_(S⁰′)) = 0 (Section 40.1). The gauge 1-form of (5) on 𝒟′ is
Υ̇^♮(ḣ) + (D_1 + D_2)Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g, g)(ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′)) = 0 + 0, as in Step 3, Υ^(χ^♮_0E_Υ)(g_0, g_0) vanishing for
every metric g_0. On Ω_* ∩ 𝒟′ = Ω_* ∩ {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4} the two definitions of ġ agree (Step 3), and so do those of
the gauge 1-form, χ^♮_0 being 1 there. As Ω_* ∪ 𝒟′ = Ω_* ∪ 𝒟, this gives (1), (2) and (5).

*Step 6 ((3) and (4)).* On {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 2}, χ_− = 0, so ġ = D_0𝔤(U′); this is (3), with D_0Φ(U′) in the exact
classes by Proposition 35.31. Where χ_K = 1: g_(p⃗) = g_b for every p⃗ ((32.4)), so
ġ_(p⃗′) = D_0 g_(p⃗)(U′) = ∂_b g_b|_(b₀)(ḃ); h_tot(p⃗) vanishes for every p⃗, each of its terms carrying a factor dχ_K
(Definition 31.9, Definition 32.5, Definition 32.19, Definition 32.31), so its derivative vanishes;
h_(b,rem)(q) is linear in q for each b ((34.2)), so its derivative at (b₀, 0) in the direction (ḃ, q′) is
h_(b₀,rem)(q′); and the derivative of h is h′. This is (40.5).

*The rate.* This is the argument of Corollary 38.28 (c). On {r ≤ R′} and for t_* large, χ_K = 1, as supp(1 − χ_K) is
disjoint from a neighbourhood of K⁺ (Lemma 34.5 (c)). h′ has K⁺-order α−, and h_(b₀,rem)(q′) has K⁺-order
(α − 2)−, each seminorm bounded by one of q′ (Lemma 34.5 (a)). Near the interior of K⁺, ρ_K = t₀⁻¹ with
t₀ = t − |x| ((21.23), (21.34)), comparable to t_* on {r ≤ R′}, and the b-vector fields there are
spanned by t_*∂_(t_*) and ∂_x. By b-Sobolev embedding for the b-density μ_b of Section 29.1, as in the proof of
Lemma 29.3 (a weight is then the pointwise order), (t_*∂_(t_*))^i ∂^β_x of a function of K⁺-order w− is
O(t_*^(−w+ε′)), bounded by a seminorm of it. With w = α − 2, (6) and the tame bound for D_UΦ at U = 0
(Proposition 35.31), ‖D_0Φ(U′)‖_k ≤ C_k‖U′‖_(𝒟^(k+d)_ex), this is (40.6). The bound on α is the choice of
α in step (4) of Theorem 38.24 (row w2 of Section 38.6), made with α > 4 + ε_t. ∎

**Corollary 40.5** (In the class.) Let G act as in Section 38.8, and make the choices of Lemma 38.26
equivariant. If (γ̇, k̇) are G-invariant, Theorem 40.4 holds with U′ fixed by G, ḃ = (ṁ, 0), S′ = S⁰′ = 0 and ġ
G-invariant. So ġ = ḣ on 𝒟′, near Σ^IVP, and it induces (γ̇, k̇); and where χ_K = 1

    ġ − ṁ ∂_m g_((m,0))|_(m=m₀) = h_(b₀,rem)(q′) + h′,

with the rate (40.6): the perturbation settles to a change of mass alone, as O(t_*^(−2−ε_t)) on spatially
compact sets.

*Proof.* G acts on M fixing t, t_*, t_IVP, t^♭_* and |x|, so it preserves Σ^IVP, Ω_*, 𝒟 and the support classes. It
acts on 𝒟^k_ex and ℱ^k_ex boundedly, isometrically for the norms sup_(σ∈G)|σ · (·)|_k, and Π := ∫_G σ dσ projects
onto the fixed elements and preserves every support class (the proof of Proposition 38.27). The construction of
Lemma 40.1 is natural: it sets ḣ_0 := γ̇ with ḣ_0(n, ·) := 0 and solves tensorial linear equations for ḣ_1
uniquely, as Lemma 38.26 records for Proposition 37.41. So ḣ_0, ḣ_1 are G-invariant. L^♮ is natural, its
cut-offs being functions of (t_IVP, |x|) and t_* and its gauge 1-forms radial (Lemma 38.26 (C1)–(C2)). So σ_*ḣ
solves (40.3) for σ ∈ G, and ḣ is G-invariant by the uniqueness in Proposition 40.2, whose classes G
preserves. χ_− is a function of t^♭_*, so f is G-fixed. Differentiating P_5(Ψ(σ · U)) = σ_*P_5(Ψ(U))
(Lemma 38.26) at the fixed point U = 0, at zero data, gives D_0(P_5 ∘ Φ) ∘ σ = σ_* ∘ D_0(P_5 ∘ Φ). So U″ := Πℛf
satisfies D_0(P_5 ∘ Φ)(U″) = Πf = f. Its tail vanishes on {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, and it is bounded as in (6). Run Steps
2–6 of the proof of Theorem 40.4 with U″ in place of U′. U″_0 = (ḃ, S′, S⁰′) lies in
𝔟^G × 𝒮_1^G × 𝒮_1^G = (ℝ × {0}) × 0 × 0, as 𝔟 = ℝ × 𝔰𝔬(4), 𝒮_1 ≅ ℝ⁴ as a representation (for the boost and for the
translation components alike), and (ℝ⁴)^G = 0, 𝔰𝔬(4)^G = 0 (Section 38.8). So ġ_(S′) = ġ⁰_(S⁰′) = 0, and ġ is
G-invariant, every ingredient being equivariant and U″ fixed. ∎

**Remark 40.6** (What is and is not asserted.) (a) Theorem 40.4 has the form of Theorem 3.9: every
linearised data set in the class has a linearised vacuum development, in a fixed gauge, that settles at the stated
rate. By itself it does not assert that a given linearised solution in another gauge differs from ġ by a linearised
diffeomorphism. That comparison, on the future N⁺ of Σ^IVP in {r > r_♭}, is Theorem 40.12 and Corollary 40.13 below,
by a linear wave equation for the 1-form that generates the change of gauge; it is the linear counterpart of the
nonlinear comparison of Remark 41.5 (Lemma 43.5). Nothing in Section 40.2–Section 40.3
uses it. (b) The rate is that of the slowest term at K⁺, h_(b₀,rem)(q′), which carries the decaying tails of the
parameter and centre-of-mass motions ((34.2)).

### 40.4 The comparison of gauges: setting and conventions

This section and the next two compare the solution ġ of Theorem 40.4 with a linearised vacuum solution given in
another gauge, on the whole future of Σ^IVP in {r > r_♭}: the future half of the Cauchy development of
Σ^IVP ∩ {r > r_♭} (Lemma 40.10).

*The spacetime.* g := g_(b₀) on M_♭ := ℝ_t × {|x| ≥ r_♭}, in the coordinates (t, x) of Section 21.5
((21.27) defines g_(b₀) there, by Lemma 21.19), with interior M°_♭ := ℝ_t × {|x| > r_♭}. t_IVP is
the function of Lemma 21.22 (b), and Σ^IVP := t_IVP⁻¹(0). ν is the function of Proposition 38.4, smooth and
non-decreasing with ν = 0 on [0, R_ν], R_ν = ½(r_♭ + 5R₁), and ν > 0 on (R_ν, ∞); so ν ≥ 0, but ν is not positive
everywhere. N_ν = {t_IVP ≥ −ν(|x|)} is the set of Section 40.1. On {|x| ≤ R_ν}, then, N_ν ends at Σ^IVP, which is
there part of its boundary, and ġ is not defined to its past. So the comparison is posed in a region that extends past
Σ^IVP, where only g is used, and the tensors compared live on its future half. Put

    U^♯ := M°_♭ ∩ {t_IVP > −1},     Σ° := Σ^IVP ∩ M°_♭ ⊂ U^♯,     N⁺ := M°_♭ ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} ⊂ N_ν,

the inclusion as ν ≥ 0 (and t ≥ t_IVP ≥ 0 > −½|x| on N⁺, by Lemma 21.22 (b), so N⁺ lies in the spacetime M of
(21.22)). For an open U ⊂ U^♯ put Σ_U := Σ^IVP ∩ U and U_+ := U ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}.

*Smooth up to Σ_U.* U_+ is a manifold with boundary Σ_U, as dt_IVP ≠ 0. A tensor on U_+ is *smooth up to Σ_U* if it
is smooth on U ∩ {t_IVP > 0} and, in coordinates (t_IVP, y) near Σ_U, every derivative of its components extends
continuously to Σ_U. Such a tensor is the restriction to U_+ of a smooth tensor on an open neighbourhood of U_+ in U:
apply Seeley's extension operator (Theorem A.34) in each chart {t_IVP ≥ 0}, after a cut-off, and patch with a
partition of unity subordinate to a cover of Σ_U by such charts and to U ∩ {t_IVP > 0}.

**Lemma 40.7** (The domain of ġ.) Ω_* ∪ 𝒟 = N_ν. The tensor ġ of Theorem 40.4 is a smooth symmetric
2-tensor on the interior of N_ν, with DRic(ġ) = 0 there, and its restriction to N⁺ is smooth up to Σ°.

*Proof.* *The domain.* Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1} lies in N_ν, as t_IVP ≥ t_* ≥ t^♭_* there (Section 40.1;
Lemma 21.22, Lemma 15.35 (b)). A point of N_ν has either t^♭_* > T̂ + 3 ≥ 1, so lies in Ω_*, or lies in
𝒟 = N_ν ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3}, with the convention of Section 40.1 that this sublevel set contains the points where
t^♭_* is not defined. So Ω_* ∪ 𝒟 = N_ν, and DRic(ġ) = 0 there (Theorem 40.4 (1)).

*ḣ is smooth on the interior of 𝒟.* The proof of Proposition 40.2 (*Gluing*) shows that ḣ is smooth on 𝒟: on each
of 𝒟⁺, 𝔒⁻ and Ω_(ext,r_1), near each of its points in the interior of M, ḣ is for every k the restriction of a tensor
of class H^k on a neighbourhood (on 𝔒⁻ by (L) of Section 38.2.2, H^k(𝔒⁻) consisting of restrictions; on 𝒟⁺ and
Ω_(ext,r_1) because ḣ lies, for every k, in the classes of order k of Theorem 38.9 and Theorem 37.27, b-Sobolev
spaces of restrictions (Section 27.2), which near points of the interior of M are the spaces H^k), hence C^m there
for k > m + 5/2 by Sobolev embedding on ℝ⁵; each point of 𝒟 off Σ^IVP ∩ {R_ν ≤ r ≤ r_1} has a neighbourhood in 𝒟
contained in one of the three sets; and at the points of Σ^IVP ∩ {R_ν ≤ r ≤ r_1}, Lemma 38.6 applies with the
one hypersurface Σ^IVP.

*ġ is smooth on the interior of N_ν.* The interior of N_ν is covered by two open sets: its points with t^♭_* > 1,
which lie in the interior of Ω_*, and its points outside the closed set {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 7/4}, which lie in 𝒟′
(Section 40.1). On the second, ġ = ḣ + ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) (Theorem 40.4 (2)); ġ_(S′) and ġ⁰_(S⁰′) are smooth
((40.2)), and ḣ is smooth, as just shown. On the first, ġ = D_0𝔤(U′) + χ_−(t^♭_*)ḣ (Step 2 of the proof of
Theorem 40.4). χ_−(t^♭_*)ḣ is smooth there: its points with t^♭_* < T̂ + 3 are interior points of 𝒟, where ḣ is
smooth, and it vanishes on {t^♭_* > T̂ + 2}. The derivative of 𝔤 is

    D_0𝔤(U′) = ġ_(p⃗′) + D_(p⃗)h_tot(0)(p⃗′) + h_(b₀,rem)(q′) + h′,

h_(b,rem)(q) being linear in q and vanishing at q = 0 for every b ((34.2)). The first two terms are
smooth, g_(p⃗) and h_tot(p⃗) being smooth tensors depending smoothly on p⃗ (Section 40.1; the definitions cited in
Step 2 of that proof). As U′ ∈ 𝒟^∞_ex, h′ ∈ 𝒳^∞_(J,ex) and q′ ∈ 𝒬_ex (Proposition 35.31): h′ lies in a b-Sobolev
class of infinite order, and h_(b₀,rem)(q′) is χ_K times smooth tensors applied to the components of q′, functions of
t_* of infinite b-regularity ((34.1), (34.2)); both are smooth on the interior of M. So ġ is
smooth on the interior of N_ν.

*Up to Σ°.* Where ν > 0, Σ° lies in the interior of N_ν, where ġ is smooth. Where ν = 0, Σ° is part of the boundary
of N_ν. Such points have r ≤ R_ν < r_1: R_ν = ½(r_♭ + 5R₁) < 5R₁, and r_1 ≥ R_6 ≥ R₃ > 5R₁ (Section 38.1,
Section 38.2.1), as ψ′_IVP = ψ′ > 0 at 5R₁ and ψ′_IVP = 0 on [R₃, ∞) (the proof of Lemma 21.22 (b)). So of
the three sets on which Proposition 40.2 solves, only 𝒟⁺ reaches them off Σ^IVP: Ω_(ext,r_1) ⊂ {r ≥ r_1}, and
𝔒⁻ ⊂ 𝒟⁻ meets {r ≤ R_ν} only in Σ^IVP, as ν = 0 there. So a half-ball {t_IVP ≥ 0} about each such point lies in
𝒟⁺ ∩ {r < r_1}. There ġ = ḣ + ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) (Theorem 40.4 (2)); ġ_(S′) and ġ⁰_(S⁰′) vanish on {|x| < 5R₁},
which contains these points (Section 40.1), and ḣ is, for every k, of class H^k up to Σ^IVP on 𝒟⁺ ∩ {r ≤ r_1}, the
class of Theorem 38.9 imposing H^k away from infinity (Section 38.2.4). In a chart {t_IVP ≥ 0} near such a point,
H^k for every k gives every derivative continuous up to Σ°: after a cut-off, extend by the operator of
Theorem A.35, bounded on every W^(k,2) of a half-space, and apply Sobolev embedding on ℝ⁵. ∎

*Time orientation.* As in Lemma 15.2, dt_* is past timelike. dt_IVP is timelike for g on M_♭
(Lemma 21.22 (b)) and past timelike: both dt_* and dt_IVP are dt − φ′(|x|) d|x| with β := φ′ − T′_(m₀) in
(−1, 1] (the proof of Lemma 21.22), so are all their convex combinations, which are therefore timelike, and the
two covectors lie in the same cone. So t_IVP is a time function on M°_♭ in the sense of Section 18.1.4: it is
strictly increasing along future directed causal curves (the property [BGP, p. 24] records of a Cauchy time-function,
Theorem A.1 (2); t_IVP is not claimed to be one). Hence Σ° is a smooth spacelike hypersurface of M°_♭,
acausal in every open subset of M°_♭.

*Operators.* For a 1-form w and a symmetric 2-tensor k: (δ_g k)_μ := −∇^α k_αμ, G_g k := k − ½g tr_g k,
δ*_g w := ½(∇w + (∇w)^T), so that ℒ_X g = 2δ*_g X^♭, as in Section 21.8. DRic and Υ̇⁰, the derivative at (g, g)
in the first argument of Υ⁰, are as in Section 40.1, now on M_♭, Υ⁰ being defined pointwise by (21.43). By
Lemma 21.30 ((21.46) at g₀ = g, where C_(g,g) = 0 and Y_(g,g) = 0, as Υ⁰(g, g) = 0),

    Υ̇⁰(k) = −δ_g G_g k,

so −Υ̇⁰(k) is the linearised harmonic gauge 1-form. Put

    L⁰ := DRic − δ*_g Υ̇⁰ = DRic + δ*_g δ_g G_g,    (40.8)

the operator L of (40.1) with E_C = E_Υ = 0.

*Linearised data.* As in Lemma 40.1 (1): a symmetric 2-tensor k, defined near a piece of Σ^IVP or on one side of
it up to Σ^IVP, *induces* the linearised data (γ̇, K̇), the s-derivatives at s = 0 of the first and second fundamental
forms of Σ^IVP for g + sk, with K(X, Y) := g(∇_X n, Y), the convention of Lemma 21.24. They are linear in k and
depend only on its 1-jet at Σ^IVP; γ̇ is the restriction of k to TΣ^IVP. K is the second fundamental form, written
k_(b₀) for g in Section 40.1–Section 40.3, where k̇ denotes its variation; so the linearised data (γ̇, k̇) of
Theorem 40.4 are a pair (γ̇, K̇) in the present notation, and the tensor ḣ of Proposition 40.2 induces them
(Lemma 40.1 (1)).

*The Cauchy problem.* We use Theorem A.1, Theorem A.2, Definition A.3 and
Theorem A.4. The two operators to which they are applied below, 2L⁰ and 2δ_gG_gδ*_g, have in local
coordinates the principal part −g^(αβ)∂_α∂_β ⊗ id (Lemma 40.11 (a)), which is the local form that
Definition A.3 gives: they are normally hyperbolic as they stand. (With ∂ → iζ their principal symbol
is g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id; [BGP] writes the same symbol −⟨ξ, ξ⟩ with ∂ → ξ.) [BGP]'s globally hyperbolic manifolds are connected
(Theorem A.1 (1)). A Cauchy development below may have several connected components, and every statement
taken from [BGP] is applied on each component C, with Cauchy hypersurface S ∩ C: components of an open set are open and
closed in it, so an inextendible causal curve of C is one of D(S) and meets S, and it does so in C.

### 40.5 The Cauchy problem, and the domain

The proof of Lemma 40.9 uses two facts about slabs, which follow from Theorem A.1 and
Theorem A.2.

**Lemma 40.8** (Slabs.) Let (Y, g) be globally hyperbolic and S a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface.
There is a Cauchy time-function t on Y with S = t⁻¹(0) (Theorem A.1 (3)); its level sets are smooth
spacelike Cauchy hypersurfaces, and t is strictly increasing along future directed causal curves
(Theorem A.1 (2)). Then:

(a) for a ≤ b and a compact set C ⊂ Y, {a ≤ t ≤ b} ∩ J(C) is compact, where J(C) := J⁺(C) ∪ J⁻(C);

(b) for a < 0 < b, the open set Y_(a,b) := {a < t < b} is globally hyperbolic (on each component), and S is a smooth
spacelike Cauchy hypersurface of it.

*Proof.* (a) Let S_b := t⁻¹(b). A point q ∈ J⁺(C) with t(q) ≤ b lies in J⁻(S_b): the inextendible future directed
causal curves from q meet the Cauchy hypersurface S_b, and they do so to the future of q, t increasing along them. So
J⁺(C) ∩ {t ≤ b} ⊂ J⁺(C) ∩ J⁻(S_b), which is compact (Theorem A.1 (4)); intersecting with the closed set
{t ≥ a} keeps it compact. Likewise J⁻(C) ∩ {t ≥ a} lies in the compact set J⁻(C) ∩ J⁺(S_a).

(b) S is acausal in Y_(a,b), t being strictly increasing along causal curves. So the Cauchy development of S in
Y_(a,b) is open and globally hyperbolic, with Cauchy hypersurface S (Theorem A.2). It remains to show
that it is all of Y_(a,b): that every inextendible causal curve γ of Y_(a,b) meets S. Let p lie on γ, say with
t(p) ≥ 0 (the case t(p) ≤ 0 is symmetric). If t > 0 along the whole past half γ_− of γ from p, then γ_− lies in
J⁻(p) ∩ {0 ≤ t ≤ t(p)}, which is compact by (a). As in the proof of Lemma 18.4, t is then a parameter on γ_− in
which its tangent, normalised by dt = 1, ranges in a compact set over that compact set; so γ_− is Lipschitz in t and,
as t decreases to inf_(γ_−) t ∈ [0, t(p)], converges to an end point q with t(q) ∈ [0, b). Then q ∈ Y_(a,b), and γ is
extendible in Y_(a,b), a contradiction. So t takes the value 0 on γ_−, and γ meets S. ∎

**Lemma 40.9** ([BGP, Theorem 3.2.11] for data without compact support.) Let (Y, g) be globally hyperbolic,
S a smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface, n its future unit normal, and P a normally hyperbolic operator on a vector
bundle E, ∇ the connection on E with which Theorem A.4 (5) poses the data. For every u_0, u_1 ∈ C^∞(S; E)
and f ∈ C^∞(Y; E) there is a unique u ∈ C^∞(Y; E) with Pu = f, u|_S = u_0 and ∇_n u|_S = u_1. (In every use below
u_0 = 0, and then ∇_n u|_S does not depend on the connection.)

*Proof.* Uniqueness is Theorem A.4 (3). For existence, let t be the Cauchy time-function of
Lemma 40.8, with S = t⁻¹(0). Choose a locally finite partition of unity (φ_j) on S with compact supports, and a
locally finite partition of unity (ψ_i) on Y with compact supports, each supp ψ_i in a slab {a_i ≤ t ≤ a_i + 1}. By
Theorem A.4 (5) let u_j solve Pu_j = 0 with data (φ_ju_0, φ_ju_1), and v_i solve Pv_i = ψ_if with zero
data; then supp u_j ⊂ J(supp φ_j) and supp v_i ⊂ J(supp ψ_i).

- *Sources away from S.* If a_i > 0, then v_i = 0 on Y_(−R,a_i) for every R > 0: that slab is globally hyperbolic with
  Cauchy hypersurface S (Lemma 40.8 (b)), there Pv_i = 0, and v_i has zero data on S, so
  Theorem A.4 (3) applies on it. So v_i = 0 where t < a_i. Likewise, if a_i + 1 < 0, then v_i = 0 where
  t > a_i + 1. The remaining i have −1 ≤ a_i ≤ 0; the cases a_i = 0 and a_i + 1 = 0 are among them.

- *Local finiteness.* Let C ⊂ {−T ≤ t ≤ T} be compact. u_j ≠ 0 somewhere on C only if supp φ_j meets J(C) ∩ S, which is
  compact (Theorem A.1 (4)): finitely many j. If a_i > 0, v_i ≠ 0 somewhere on C only if a_i ≤ T and
  supp ψ_i meets {0 ≤ t ≤ T + 1} ∩ J(C), which is compact (Lemma 40.8 (a)): finitely many i. The case
  a_i + 1 < 0 is symmetric. If −1 ≤ a_i ≤ 0, then supp ψ_i ⊂ {−1 ≤ t ≤ 1} meets the compact set
  {−1 ≤ t ≤ 1} ∩ J(C): finitely many i.

So u := Σ_j u_j + Σ_i v_i is a locally finite sum of smooth sections, Pu = Σ_i ψ_if = f, u|_S = Σ_j φ_ju_0 = u_0 and
∇_n u|_S = u_1. ∎

**Lemma 40.10** (The domain.) For every open U ⊂ U^♯, D_U(Σ_U), the Cauchy development of Σ_U in U, is open and
globally hyperbolic (on each component, Section 40.4), with smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface Σ_U.
Ω^♯ := D_(U^♯)(Σ°) contains N⁺ = M°_♭ ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, so that Ω^♯_+ := Ω^♯ ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} = N⁺.

*Proof.* Σ_U is a smooth hypersurface of U, as dt_IVP ≠ 0, spacelike and acausal in U (Section 40.4).
Theorem A.2 gives the first assertion. Let p ∈ M°_♭ with t_IVP(p) ≥ 0; then p ∈ U^♯.

- *A compact set.* Along a past directed causal curve from p in M°_♭:
  - t_IVP decreases (Section 40.4), and t = t_IVP + ψ_IVP(|x|) with 0 ≤ ψ_IVP ≤ C₃ := max ψ_IVP, finite as ψ_IVP is
    constant on [R₃, ∞) (Lemma 21.22 (b) and its proof).
  - |x| stays ≥ min(|x(p)|, r^♮), r^♮ > r_♭: dr is future timelike for g on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r^♮} (Lemma 15.35 (1) at
    h = 0, which holds there at every t_*, g being stationary, as in Lemma 38.12 (iv); also
    Proposition 22.3 (d)), so r strictly increases towards the past there.
  - On {|x| ≥ 3R₁}, d(t + |x|) is past timelike. By Proposition 21.21, g⁻¹ = ḡ⁻¹ − m₀|x|⁻²(∂_t + ∂_|x|)^(⊗2) there,
    so g⁻¹(d(t + |x|), d(t + |x|)) = −4m₀|x|⁻² < 0. With dt_* = dt − ψ′ d|x|,
    g⁻¹(d(t + |x|), dt_*) = −1 − ψ′ − 2m₀|x|⁻²(1 − ψ′) < 0, as −1 < ψ′ < 1 there ((21.30): ψ′ = 1 − 8m₀ϱ⁻²
    for ϱ ≥ 3R₁). So d(t + |x|) and dt_* lie in the same cone, and t + |x| decreases towards the past there.

  Let q ∈ J⁻_(M°_♭)(p) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} with |x(q)| ≥ 3R₁, reached along a past directed causal curve from p. Its last
  segment in {|x| ≥ 3R₁} starts at p or at a point q_0 with |x(q_0)| = 3R₁ and t(q_0) ≤ t_IVP(p) + C₃, so

      t(q) + |x(q)| ≤ B_p := max(t(p) + |x(p)|, t_IVP(p) + C₃ + 3R₁).

  As t(q) ≥ t_IVP(q) ≥ 0, |x(q)| ≤ B_p. Hence

      J⁻_(M°_♭)(p) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} ⊂ L_p := {0 ≤ t_IVP ≤ t_IVP(p),  min(|x(p)|, r^♮) ≤ |x| ≤ max(B_p, 3R₁)},

  a compact subset of U^♯ (closed and bounded in (t, x), with t ∈ [0, t_IVP(p) + C₃]; |x| > r_♭ and t_IVP ≥ 0 > −1
  on it).

- *Every inextendible causal curve through p meets Σ°.* Let γ be one, in U^♯. If t_IVP > 0 along its whole past half,
  that half lies in L_p. As in the proof of Lemma 18.4, a past inextendible causal curve along which a time
  function is bounded below, and which lies in a compact set, extends continuously to a past end point: its tangent,
  normalised by dt_IVP = 1, ranges in a compact set over L_p, so the curve is Lipschitz in t_IVP and converges in
  L_p ⊂ U^♯. That contradicts inextendibility in U^♯. So t_IVP reaches 0 on γ, and γ meets Σ°, once by acausality.
  Hence p ∈ Ω^♯, and N⁺ ⊂ Ω^♯_+; the reverse inclusion holds as Ω^♯ ⊂ U^♯ ⊂ M°_♭. ∎

The region U^♯ reaches to t_IVP = −1 only so that Σ° lies inside it. Nothing below uses Ω^♯ ∩ {t_IVP < 0} beyond the
background g, the extension of Υ̇⁰(k) in Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 40.12, with that step's solution w and
field X := w^♯, which live on all of Ω′, and the extension by zero in its Step 3.

### 40.6 The comparison

**Lemma 40.11** (Pointwise identities.) At the Ricci-flat g:

(a) 2L⁰ and 2δ_gG_gδ*_g have principal part −g^(αβ)∂_α∂_β ⊗ id, so principal symbol g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id (∂ → iζ). In fact

    2L⁰k = −∇^α∇_α k + ([∇^λ, ∇_μ]k_λν + [∇^λ, ∇_ν]k_λμ)_(μν),        2δ_gG_gδ*_g w = −∇^α∇_α w,

where [∇^λ, ∇_μ]k_λν := ∇^λ∇_μk_λν − ∇_μ∇^λk_λν is of order zero, a contraction of the curvature with k.

(b) DRic(ℒ_X g) = 0 for every smooth vector field X.

(c) If k = 0 on Σ^IVP, then K̇ = ½(∇_n k)|_(TΣ^IVP).

(d) If k = 0 on Σ^IVP, then in an orthonormal frame (n, e_i) there, with k′ := ∇_n k:
−Υ̇⁰(k)(e_j) = k′(n, e_j) and −Υ̇⁰(k)(n) = ½k′(n, n) + ½Σ_i k′(e_i, e_i).

(e) If X = 0 on Σ^IVP and ∇_n X = Y there, then on Σ^IVP: (ℒ_Xg)(e_i, e_j) = 0, (ℒ_Xg)(n, e_j) = g(Y, e_j) and
(ℒ_Xg)(n, n) = 2g(Y, n). For k with k(e_i, e_j) = 0 on Σ^IVP, the vector field Y := Σ_j k(n, e_j)e_j − ½k(n, n)n on
Σ^IVP, that is Y^♭ = k(n, ·) + ½k(n, n)n^♭, gives ℒ_X g = k on Σ^IVP.

(f) If X = 0 on Σ^IVP, then ℒ_X g induces zero linearised data.

*Proof.* (a) The variation of the Christoffel symbols is Γ̇^κ_μν = ½g^κλ(∇_μk_λν + ∇_νk_λμ − ∇_λk_μν), and that of
the Ricci tensor is DRic(k)_μν = ∇_κΓ̇^κ_μν − ∇_νΓ̇^κ_κμ, with Γ̇^κ_κμ = ½∇_μ tr_g k. So

    DRic(k)_μν = ½(∇^λ∇_μk_λν + ∇^λ∇_νk_λμ − ∇^λ∇_λk_μν − ∇_μ∇_ν tr_g k).

−Υ̇⁰(k)_ν = (δ_gG_gk)_ν = −∇^λk_λν + ½∇_ν tr_g k (Section 40.4), so
(−δ*_gΥ̇⁰(k))_μν = −½(∇_μ∇^λk_λν + ∇_ν∇^λk_λμ) + ½∇_μ∇_ν tr_g k. Adding gives the formula for
2L⁰ = 2DRic − 2δ*_gΥ̇⁰. For a 1-form w, tr_g δ*_g w = ∇^λw_λ and

    (δ_gG_gδ*_g w)_ν = −½∇^λ∇_λw_ν − ½∇^λ∇_νw_λ + ½∇_ν∇^λw_λ = −½∇^λ∇_λw_ν − ½Ric_νλw^λ,

by the Ricci identity ∇^λ∇_νw_λ − ∇_ν∇^λw_λ = Ric_νλw^λ; at the Ricci-flat g the last term vanishes. A commutator of
two covariant derivatives acting on a tensor is a contraction of the curvature with it, of order zero. In local
coordinates ∇^α∇_α = g^(αβ)∂_α∂_β + (first order), the Christoffel symbols entering only at lower order. So both
operators have principal part −g^(αβ)∂_α∂_β, the local form of Definition A.3, and are normally
hyperbolic.

(b) Let φ_s be the local flow of X. Ric(φ*_sg) = φ*_s Ric(g) = 0, and (d/ds)φ*_sg|_(s=0) = ℒ_X g. Ric at a point is a
smooth function of the 2-jet of the metric there, and the 2-jet of φ*_sg is smooth in s; so the derivative at s = 0,
which is DRic(ℒ_X g), vanishes, pointwise.

(c) Let g_s := g + sk and n_s its future unit normal. As k = 0 on Σ^IVP, g_s = g at the points of Σ^IVP, so n_s = n
there for every s, and ṅ = 0. For X, Y tangent, K_s(X, Y) = g_s(∇^(g_s)_X n_s, Y), and its s-derivative at 0 is
k(∇_Xn, Y) + g(∇_Xṅ, Y) + g(C(X, n), Y), where C is the variation of the connection,

    g(C(X, Z), Y) = ½(∇_Xk(Z, Y) + ∇_Zk(X, Y) − ∇_Yk(X, Z)).

The first term vanishes as k = 0 on Σ^IVP, and the second as ṅ = 0 along Σ^IVP and X is tangent. As k = 0 on Σ^IVP,
its tangential covariant derivatives vanish there, ∇_Xk = ∇_Yk = 0. So K̇(X, Y) = g(C(X, n), Y) = ½(∇_nk)(X, Y).

(d) As k = 0 on Σ^IVP, ∇_(e_i)k = 0 there, and only normal derivatives survive. In the frame,
g⁻¹ = −n ⊗ n + Σ_i e_i ⊗ e_i, so the divergence is ∇^λk_λ· = −(∇_nk)(n, ·) + Σ_i(∇_(e_i)k)(e_i, ·) = −k′(n, ·);
and d tr_g k = tr_g ∇k vanishes on e_j, while (d tr_g k)(n) = tr_g k′ = −k′(n, n) + Σ_i k′(e_i, e_i). As
−Υ̇⁰(k) = −∇^λk_λ· + ½ d tr_g k, this gives −Υ̇⁰(k)(e_j) = k′(n, e_j), and
−Υ̇⁰(k)(n) = k′(n, n) + ½(−k′(n, n) + Σ_i k′(e_i, e_i)) = ½k′(n, n) + ½Σ_i k′(e_i, e_i).

(e) As X = 0 on Σ^IVP, its tangential covariant derivatives vanish there, ∇_(e_i)X = 0, and ∇_nX = Y. With
(ℒ_Xg)(a, b) = g(∇_aX, b) + g(a, ∇_bX) this gives the three values. For the given k, Y = Σ_j k(n, e_j)e_j − ½k(n, n)n
has g(Y, e_j) = k(n, e_j) and 2g(Y, n) = k(n, n), as g(n, n) = −1; so ℒ_X g = k at Σ^IVP, both vanishing on
(e_i, e_j). Since a covector ω equals Σ_j ω(e_j)e_j^♭ − ω(n)n^♭, Y^♭ = k(n, ·) + ½k(n, n)n^♭.

(f) Let φ_s be the flow of X, defined near any compact piece of Σ^IVP for |s| small. It fixes Σ^IVP pointwise, so φ_s
is an isometry from a neighbourhood of that piece with the metric φ*_sg to its image with the metric g, the identity
on Σ^IVP, and it preserves the future normal for |s| small, by continuity from s = 0. So φ*_sg induces exactly the
data (γ, K) of g on Σ^IVP, for every small s. The induced data are smooth functions of the 1-jet of the metric at
Σ^IVP, whose s-derivative at 0 is that of ℒ_X g. So the derivative of the data, which is the data induced by ℒ_X g,
vanishes. ∎

**Theorem 40.12** (Linearised vacuum solutions with gauge-equivalent data are gauge-equivalent.) Let U ⊂ U^♯
be open, Ω′ := D_U(Σ_U) and Ω′_+ := Ω′ ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}, a manifold with boundary Σ_U. Let k be a symmetric 2-tensor on
Ω′_+, smooth up to Σ_U (Section 40.4), with DRic(k) = 0, inducing on Σ_U the linearised data that ℒ_Z g induces, for a
vector field Z on a neighbourhood of Σ_U in Ω′_+, smooth up to Σ_U (Z = 0: zero data). Then there is a vector field X
on Ω′_+, smooth up to Σ_U, with

    k = ℒ_X g     on Ω′_+.

X is unique up to a Killing field of g on Ω′_+.

*Proof.* Ω′ is globally hyperbolic with smooth spacelike Cauchy hypersurface Σ_U (Lemma 40.10), and the data of a
tensor smooth up to Σ_U are defined from one side (the definition of linearised data in Section 40.4 allows this).
Uniqueness up to Killing fields is
ℒ_(X−X′)g = 0.

*Step 0 (zero data).* Let W = W̃ ∩ Ω′_+, W̃ open in Ω′, be the neighbourhood of Σ_U where Z is defined, and
ψ̃ ∈ C^∞(Ω′) equal to 1 near Σ_U with supp_(Ω′) ψ̃ ⊂ W̃ (smooth Urysohn: Σ_U is closed in Ω′); ψ := ψ̃|_(Ω′_+).
k_0 := k − ℒ_(ψZ)g has DRic(k_0) = 0 (Lemma 40.11 (b)), and it induces zero data: those of ℒ_(ψZ)g and ℒ_Zg agree,
as ψZ = Z near Σ_U. If k_0 = ℒ_(X_0)g, then k = ℒ_(X_0+ψZ)g. So we may assume Z = 0.

*Step 1 (the gauge vector field).* Zero data means k(e_i, e_j) = 0 on Σ_U (γ̇ = 0) and K̇ = 0. Let Y be the vector field
of Lemma 40.11 (e) on Σ_U, smooth, as Y^♭ = k(n, ·) + ½k(n, n)n^♭. Υ̇⁰(k) = −δ_gG_gk is a 1-form on Ω′_+, smooth up
to Σ_U. Let F be a smooth 1-form on Ω′ with F = −Υ̇⁰(k) on Ω′_+: Section 40.4 extends Υ̇⁰(k) to an open neighbourhood V
of Ω′_+ in Ω′, and a smooth function equal to 1 on the closed set Ω′_+ with support in V (smooth Urysohn) extends it by
0 beyond. By Lemma 40.9 on Ω′, with P := 2δ_gG_gδ*_g (Lemma 40.11 (a)), there is a smooth 1-form w on Ω′ with

    2δ_gG_gδ*_g w = F,        w|_(Σ_U) = 0,        ∇_n w|_(Σ_U) = Y^♭.

Put X := w^♯, a smooth vector field on Ω′; the theorem's X is its restriction to Ω′_+, and Lemma 40.11 (f) applies
to it as it stands. Then −Υ̇⁰(ℒ_X g) = δ_gG_g(2δ*_g w) = F = −Υ̇⁰(k) on Ω′_+, and X = 0, ∇_n X = Y on Σ_U.

*Step 2 (the difference has vanishing Cauchy data).* Let h := k − ℒ_X g.

- h = 0 on Σ_U, by Lemma 40.11 (e).

- h induces zero linearised data: k does by assumption, and ℒ_X g does by Lemma 40.11 (f). So by
  Lemma 40.11 (c), (∇_n h)(e_i, e_j) = 2K̇(e_i, e_j) = 0.

- Υ̇⁰(h) = 0 on Ω′_+ by Step 1. At Σ_U, Lemma 40.11 (d) with h′ := ∇_n h and h′(e_i, e_i) = 0 gives
  h′(n, e_j) = 0 and h′(n, n) = 0.

So h|_(Σ_U) = 0 and ∇_n h|_(Σ_U) = 0.

*Step 3 (it vanishes).* DRic(h) = DRic(k) − DRic(ℒ_X g) = 0 (Lemma 40.11 (b)), and Υ̇⁰(h) = 0, so L⁰h = 0 on Ω′_+
by (40.8); h is smooth up to Σ_U.

- *h vanishes to infinite order along Σ_U.* Work in coordinates (t_IVP, y) near a point of Σ_U. As h = 0 on Σ_U,
  ∇_n h = n^t ∂_(t_IVP) h there, with n^t := dt_IVP(n) > 0; so ∂_(t_IVP) h = 0 on Σ_U. Suppose ∂^j_(t_IVP) h = 0 on
  Σ_U for j < m, some m ≥ 2, so that every derivative of h of order below m vanishes there. By Lemma 40.11 (a),
  2L⁰ = −g⁻¹(dt_IVP, dt_IVP)∂²_(t_IVP) + R, with R of second order and at most first order in ∂_(t_IVP), and
  g⁻¹(dt_IVP, dt_IVP) < 0 as dt_IVP is timelike: Σ_U is noncharacteristic. Apply ∂^(m−2)_(t_IVP) to 2L⁰h = 0 and
  restrict to Σ_U. Every term but −g⁻¹(dt_IVP, dt_IVP)∂^m_(t_IVP)h is a derivative of h of order below m, or of order m
  with at most m − 1 derivatives in t_IVP (a tangential derivative of a vanishing normal one), so it vanishes; hence
  ∂^m_(t_IVP) h = 0 on Σ_U.

- *Extension by zero.* Put h̃ := h on Ω′_+ and h̃ := 0 on Ω′ ∩ {t_IVP < 0}. Every derivative of h tends to 0 at Σ_U,
  so h̃ is smooth on Ω′: each derivative of h̃ off Σ_U extends continuously by 0 across Σ_U, and a continuous function
  on Ω′ that is C¹ off the hypersurface Σ_U, with first derivatives extending continuously across it, is C¹ (the mean
  value theorem along curves transverse to Σ_U); induction on the order gives every C^j. L⁰h̃ is smooth and vanishes
  off Σ_U, so everywhere; and h̃|_(Σ_U) = 0, ∇_n h̃|_(Σ_U) = 0.

2L⁰ is normally hyperbolic (Lemma 40.11 (a)). Theorem A.4 (3) on Ω′, on each component, gives h̃ = 0,
so h = 0 on Ω′_+. ∎

**Corollary 40.13** (The solution of Theorem 40.4 in any gauge.) Let (γ̇, k̇), ġ, S′, S⁰′, ḃ and U′ be as
in Theorem 40.4, U ⊂ U^♯ open, Ω′ := D_U(Σ_U) and Ω′_+ := Ω′ ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} ⊂ N⁺ ⊂ N_ν. Let ġ′ be a symmetric
2-tensor on Ω′_+, smooth up to Σ_U, with DRic(ġ′) = 0, that induces on Σ_U the data (γ̇, k̇) plus those of ℒ_Z g, for
a vector field Z near Σ_U in Ω′_+, smooth up to Σ_U. Then

    ġ′ = ġ + ℒ_X g     on Ω′_+

for a vector field X on Ω′_+, smooth up to Σ_U. In particular, where χ_K = 1 in Ω′_+,

    ġ′ − ℒ_X g − ∂_b g_b|_(b=b₀)(ḃ) = h_(b₀,rem)(q′) + h′,

with q′ and h′ the components of D_0Φ(U′) = (h′, p⃗′, q′) named in Theorem 40.4 (3), as in (40.5). For
U = U^♯, Ω′_+ = N⁺ = M°_♭ ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} (Lemma 40.10). The region where (40.6) is stated has
t_IVP ≥ t_* ≥ T′ ≥ 0 ((40.6) holds with T′ enlarged, so we take T′ ≥ 0), so its part in {r > r_♭} lies in
N⁺, and there the remainder has the rate (40.6): every linearised vacuum solution with these data settles, up
to the linearised diffeomorphism ℒ_X g, to a linearised Myers–Perry metric, with X itself not controlled
(Remark 40.14 (b)). For a general open U this holds only on the part of that region which Ω′_+ contains.

*Proof.* ġ is smooth on the interior of N_ν with DRic(ġ) = 0, and its restriction to N⁺ ⊃ Ω′_+ is smooth up to Σ°
(Lemma 40.7). Near Σ^IVP in N_ν, ġ = ḣ + ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) with ġ_(S′) + ġ⁰_(S⁰′) = −ℒ_(V(S′)+V⁰(S⁰′))g
((40.2)): the set 𝒟′ = 𝒟 ∖ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂ + 7/4} of Theorem 40.4 (2) contains N_ν ∩ {t_IVP < T̂ + 7/4}, as
t^♭_* ≤ t_* ≤ t_IVP where t^♭_* is defined. ḣ induces (γ̇, k̇) (Lemma 40.1 (1), which allows a tensor given on
one side up to Σ^IVP, with the data of Proposition 40.2). The induced data being linear in the tensor and ℒ_Xg linear
in X, k := ġ′ − ġ is smooth up to Σ_U on Ω′_+, has DRic(k) = 0 there, and induces the data of
ℒ_(Z+V(S′)+V⁰(S⁰′))g, where Z + V(S′) + V⁰(S⁰′) is a vector field near Σ_U in Ω′_+, smooth up to Σ_U.
Theorem 40.12 gives k = ℒ_X g. The second display is (40.5) with ġ = ġ′ − ℒ_X g. ∎

**Remark 40.14** (What is and is not asserted.) (a) The statement is the linear counterpart of the nonlinear
comparison of Remark 41.5 (Lemma 43.5); it is proved here for the linearisation only.

(b) Nothing is asserted here about the size or decay of X. X solves a linear wave equation with right side
−Υ̇⁰(k) = δ_gG_gk and its own Cauchy data, and its behaviour at ℐ⁺ and K⁺ depends on the gauge of ġ′. A solution in the
Regge–Wheeler-type gauge or in the harmonic gauge with the same data, given on N⁺, the future of Σ^IVP in {r > r_♭}, and
smooth up to Σ°, is ġ + ℒ_X g there (Corollary 40.13 with U = U^♯), and so settles modulo ℒ_X g; the decay in those
gauges is the decay of ℒ_X g there. It is proved in the Regge–Wheeler-type gauge in Theorem 45.7, and for the
harmonic-gauge representative in Theorem 47.30.

(c) In the class, if U is G-invariant (for instance U = U^♯: G preserves t_IVP and |x|), so that Ω′ and Ω′_+ are
G-stable, the data (γ̇, k̇) are in the class of Corollary 40.5, and ġ′ is G-invariant, then X may be taken
G-invariant; Z's invariance is not needed, only k's is used. G is compact and acts by isometries of g (the proof of
Corollary 40.5); ġ is G-invariant by Corollary 40.5, so k = ġ′ − ġ is; and the Haar average
X_G := ∫_G σ_*X dσ has ℒ_(X_G)g = ∫_G σ_*(ℒ_X g) dσ = k.


# Part X. Settling at late times

## 41. The proof of the settling theorem

This chapter proves Theorem 3.9. The solutions g_λ of Theorem 3.1 live on a bounded domain Ω, which ends at the
time T after the shell. Settling concerns all later times, and it is proved with the nonlinear stability theory of
five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini of Part V to Part IX, which is posed on
Hintz's initial surface Σ^IVP (Section 21.5.3). The proof has three steps. First, after the shell the approximant
carries no oscillation (Lemma 41.2), so there g_λ lies within O(λ) of the Tangherlini metric of the final mass
μ_end in C^J, J = K − 4 (Lemma 41.3); and Ω can be enlarged so that it contains the part of Σ^IVP that is needed,
in coordinates in which the background is the Tangherlini metric g_(b₀), b₀ = (μ_end, 0), of the stability theory
(Lemma 41.4). The data of g_λ are read on Σ^IVP itself, so no Cauchy stability argument is used. Second, these
data are continued G-equivariantly to exact Tangherlini data far out, with only the mass to match (Corollary 39.19),
and their development settles to Tangherlini by the nonlinear stability theorem run in the symmetry class
(Proposition 38.27, Corollary 38.28): this is item (i). Third, every perturbation of those data that is small in
Hintz's data class has a development that settles to a Myers–Perry metric (Theorem 38.22): this is item (ii).
Theorem 41.1 states the result with all its quantifiers, and Theorem 3.9 is deduced from it at the end
of Section 41.3.

*The inner radius.* The inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] of Section 21.4, R₁ = μ_end^(1/2), is a parameter: the
spacetime M of (21.22) has the inner boundary {|x| = r_♭}, and every result of this chapter holds for each
such r_♭, with constants that may depend on it. The domain of Theorem 3.1 is enlarged inward, through its inner
constant alone, so that it reaches r ≥ a′ with a′ < ½r_♭, and forward through T′ (Lemma 41.4). r_♭ may be chosen
depending on μ_end, as in Chapter 43; every choice made in Section 41.3 comes after it.

*Notation.* The parameters l5, μ0 ≥ √72 l5², A, env and τ0 of Theorem 3.1 are fixed; its domain is a domain Ω′ of the
form (2.8), with constants T′, δ′_0 in place of T, δ0, which Lemma 41.4 chooses. As in Chapter 38, ε denotes
the smallness threshold of Corollary 38.28; the exponent of the rate, written ε in Theorem 3.9, is written ε_t
here. The integer J of Lemma 41.3 is unrelated to the index J of the class 𝒳^∞_(J,ex) of Theorem 38.22, and
the constant c₀ of Lemma 41.4 is a time shift.

### 41.1 The setting and the precise statement

*The main argument's side.* We use the coordinates (τ, x) of Section 2.2, with r = |x| and v = τ + r, and the
Vaidya background g0 = η + (μ(v)/r²) dv ⊗ dv of (2.3), where μ = μ_end for v ≥ v_end. As dv = dτ + dr,

    g0 = η + (μ_end/r²)(dτ + dr)²     on {v ≥ v_end},

which is the Kerr–Schild Tangherlini metric g^KS_(μ_end,0) of Definition 21.15, with Kerr–Schild time τ. A domain Ω′
of the form (2.8) has the τ0 of Theorem 3.1 and constants T′ > 0 and δ′_0 ∈ (0, q0): with a′ := q0 − δ′_0,
V′ := v_end + T′ and τ′_end := max_(v≤V′) (v − r_q(v)),

    Ω′ = {τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ′_end,  |x| ≥ a′,  v + (τ − τ′_end) ≤ V′ + 1}.

Theorem 3.1 holds on every such domain, its constants depending on it, and we put Ω′_+ := Ω′ ∩ {v ≥ v_end + 1}.

*The stability theory's side.* Put b₀ := (μ_end, 0), so that the mass m₀ of Chapter 21–Chapter 40 is μ_end and
R₁ = μ_end^(1/2). In the coordinates (t, x) of Section 21.4, g_(b₀) = Φ_(μ_end)^*g^KS_(μ_end,0), that is
t = t_KS + T_(μ_end)(|x|) with t_KS the Kerr–Schild time ((21.27)). The time functions t_* and
t_IVP = t − ψ_IVP(|x|), the initial surface Σ^IVP := t_IVP⁻¹(0), the radius R₃ beyond which ψ_IVP is constant and its
value C″ there are those of (21.30) and Lemma 21.22; (γ_(b₀), k_(b₀)) are the data that g_(b₀) induces
on Σ^IVP (Lemma 21.24). Ω_*, the region 𝒟 and its parts 𝒟_(S,S⁰), the cut-off χ_K, the cut-off Lorentz boosts
φ_S of Section 21.7 and the cut-off translations ψ_(S⁰) of Lemma 32.2, S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1, composed as
φ_(S,S⁰) := ψ_(S⁰) ∘ φ_S in (38.1), the parameter set ℬ_*, and the terms h_tot(p⃗) and h_(b,rem)(q) are
those of Section 38.1, Proposition 38.4 and Theorem 38.22. The parameters of the stability theory are chosen
by Theorem 38.24, with the data class (38.15) at its step (3):

    ℰ_0 = {(j, 0) : j ∈ ℕ, j ≥ 2},     ℓ_0 ∈ (3, 4),     ℓ_I ∈ (3, ℓ_0);

its steps (0)–(4), up to the choice of α with which step (4) ends, are made once, and fix ε_K, the number of row w1 of
Section 38.6. The order α of row w2 and steps (5)–(6) are chosen in the proof (Section 41.3), depending on the
exponent of the rate; with them the order d_1 and the norm ‖·‖_(d_1) of Section 38.8 are fixed. The group
G = O(2) × O(2) acts as in Section 38.8, and the choices of Lemma 38.26 are made O(4)-equivariant; they are
admissible choices of the stability theory, so Theorem 38.22 holds with them.

**Theorem 41.1** (Settling, precise form.) Let l5, μ0, A, env and τ0 be fixed and
b₀ = (μ_end, 0), as above; let r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁], and let steps (0)–(4) of Theorem 38.24, up to the choice of α, be
made as above. For every ε_t ∈ (0, ε_K) there are a choice of α in row w2 and of steps (5)–(6), R ≥ R₃ and a domain Ω′
of the form (2.8), depending on ε_t and r_♭ only, such that for every ε_m > 0 there are λ_1 > 0 and δ > 0,
depending moreover on ε_m, for which the following holds for 0 < λ ≤ λ_1. Here g_λ is the solution of Theorem 3.1 on
Ω′, built with K = d_1 + 14 and N = K + 3 stages, and Σ^IVP is placed in the coordinates (τ, x) by Lemma 41.4.

(i) *In the class.* There are G-invariant smooth vacuum data (γ_λ, k_λ) on Σ^IVP that equal the data of g_λ on
Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ R}, and on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≥ 4R} the data (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) that the Tangherlini metric g^KS_(m_λ,0) induces
there (Lemma 39.16), with

    |m_λ − μ_end| ≤ Cλ,     ‖(γ_λ − γ_(b₀), k_λ − k_(b₀))‖_(d_1) ≤ Cλ.

There are also m′ with |m′ − μ_end| < ε_m and a G-invariant metric g on Ω_* ∪ 𝒟_0 with Ric(g) = 0, inducing
(γ_λ, k_λ) on Σ^IVP, such that, where χ_K = 1,

    g − g_(m′,0) = h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + h,     h ∈ 𝒳^∞_(J,ex),  q ∈ 𝒬_ex,

the conclusions (3)–(4) of Theorem 38.22 with b = (m′, 0) and S = S⁰ = 0, where h_tot(p⃗) = 0 on the interior of
{χ_K = 1}. In particular, for every R′, ε′ > 0 and i, β there are C and T′ with

    |(t_*∂_(t_*))^i ∂^β_x (g − g_(m′,0))| ≤ C t_*^(−(α−2)+ε′)     on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′},    (41.1)

where α − 2 > 2 + ε_K − ε′_0 > 2 (row w2 of Section 38.6), α may be chosen as close to 4 + ε_K as desired, and
α > 4 + ε_t; so ε′ := α − 4 − ε_t gives g − g_(m′,0) = O(t_*^(−2−ε_t)) there. On Σ^IVP ∩ {r < R}, g and g_λ induce
the same data.

(ii) *Without symmetry.* Let (γ, k) be smooth vacuum data on Σ^IVP with

    (γ − γ_λ, k − k_λ) ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b × H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b,     ‖(γ − γ_λ, k − k_λ)‖_(d_1) < δ.

Then there are b ∈ ℬ_* with |b − b₀| < ε_m, S, S⁰ ∈ 𝒮_1 with |S|, |S⁰| < ε_m, and a metric g on
Ω_* ∪ 𝒟_(−S,−S⁰) with Ric(g) = 0 inducing (φ|)^*(γ, k) on φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP) = φ_S(ψ_(S⁰)(Σ^IVP)), φ := φ_(−S,−S⁰), such
that, where χ_K = 1, g − g_b = h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + h with the classes of (i), h_tot(p⃗) = 0 on the interior
of {χ_K = 1}, and (41.1) holds with g_b in place of g_(m′,0). So g settles to the Myers–Perry metric g_b at
the rates (41.1).

Here 𝒟_0 := 𝒟_(0,0) ⊂ 𝒟 is the region 𝒟_(S,S⁰) of Proposition 38.4 at S = S⁰ = 0, and |b − b₀| = |m − μ_end| + |A|
for b = (m, A), the norm of step (5) of Theorem 38.24. On the finite-dimensional space 𝔟 it is equivalent to the
norm ‖·‖_𝔟 of 𝔟 as a component of 𝒟_ex, in which Corollary 38.28 (a) bounds b − b₀; we fix C_𝔟 ≥ 1
with |b − b₀| ≤ C_𝔟‖b − b₀‖_𝔟, so that Corollary 38.28, applied with ε_m/C_𝔟 in place of ε_m, gives |b − b₀| < ε_m.
C depends on R and on the data of Theorem 3.1, not on λ.

### 41.2 The solution after the shell

After the shell the approximant of Theorem 4.11 carries no oscillation. We write it as in (4.10): the
profile G = ḡ + λW + Σ_(j=2)^(N+1) λ^j ĝ_j, with the mean metric ḡ = g0 + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j m_j, the phase
u = v + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j φ_j, the leading wave W = W_TT + χ dv ⊗ dv of Section 4.4 and the oscillating profiles
ĝ_j of zero θ-mean, and g_app = g0 + λ[g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j] its form with the fixed phase v.

**Lemma 41.2** (No oscillation after the shell.) Let Ω be a domain of the form (2.8), N ≥ 1, and
let g_app be the approximant of Theorem 4.11 on Ω with N stages and the stage data of Lemma 7.4. Put
Ω_> := Ω ∩ {v > v_end}. Then W and ĝ_2, …, ĝ_(N+1) vanish on Ω_> × S¹. Consequently, on Ω_>,

    g_app = g0 + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j m_j,     g0 = η + (μ_end/r²)(dτ + dr)²,

with m_j smooth on Ω and independent of λ; and if g = g_app + w is the solution of Theorem 6.1 with this
approximant, then w = h on Ω_>, h of (6.1).

*Proof.* Ω_> is relatively open in Ω, so a profile that vanishes on Ω_> × S¹ vanishes there with all its derivatives.
Let p ∈ Ω_>. The integral curve of ℓ = −L0 through p, followed to the past, stays in Ω and meets Σ_τ0
(Lemma 2.6 (d)); since L0(v) = 0, v is constant along it, so it stays in Ω_>. We call it the generator through p.

*The wave.* W_TT is proportional to env(v) ((2.11)), and env vanishes for v > v_end; so W_TT = 0 on Ω_>. The
second harmonic χ has zero θ-mean, vanishes on Σ_τ0 and solves (∂_r + 3/(2r))∂_θχ = F_2 ((4.9)), where
∂_r = ℓ in the coordinates (v, r, ϑ, φ1, φ2) and F_2 is quadratic in env(v) through y1, y2 and α (Section 4.4).
On a generator in Ω_>, F_2 = 0, so r^(3/2)∂_θχ is constant along it; it vanishes at the generator's point on Σ_τ0, so
∂_θχ = 0, and χ, of zero θ-mean, vanishes. So W = 0 on Ω_>.

*The oscillating profiles.* We use one observation twice. In the two-scale expansion of the reduced Ricci tensor and of
the gauge field, the dependence on θ enters only through W and the ĝ_j: g0, the means m_j and the phases φ_j do not
depend on θ, and a product of factors that do not depend on θ has zero oscillating part. So every term of the
oscillating part of an expression polynomial in the profiles and their derivatives contains W, some ĝ_j, or a
derivative of one of these.

We show by induction on m = 1, …, N that ĝ_(m+1) = 0 on Ω_> × S¹, given that W, ĝ_2, …, ĝ_m vanish there (for m = 1
this is the preceding step).

(a) The data. By Lemma 7.4 (i), on Σ_τ0 the oscillating part of the order-m coefficient D^(m) of the gauge
field, its index lowered by g0, is Pol(∂_θĝ_(m+1)) + Λ_m(γ_m) + (known), and the stage datum is
∂_θĝ_(m+1) := −Pol⁺(Λ_m(γ_m) + known), solved pointwise. The sum Λ_m(γ_m) + known does not contain ĝ_(m+1), and the
profiles of later stages are not defined at this stage; so by the observation each of its terms contains W, one of
ĝ_2, …, ĝ_m, or a derivative of one of these, and it vanishes on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_>. Pol⁺ acts pointwise, so ∂_θĝ_(m+1) = 0
on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_>, and ĝ_(m+1), of zero θ-mean, vanishes there.

(b) The transport. Stage 1 imposes e_1 = 0, so Lemma 4.8 gives T̂Y = −(ℓ·∂_X)∂_θY + ℳY, and
the equation (c) of Lemma 4.10 is, for Z := ∂_θĝ_(m+1), the transport

    −(ℓ·∂_X)Z + ℳ′Z = F,     F := −Π_osc(𝒲(m_m, φ_m) + 𝒴_m),

along ℓ, with ℳ′ = Π_osc ℳ ∂_θ⁻¹ a bounded operator on the zero-mean functions of θ, bounded uniformly on Ω. By
Lemma 4.7, 𝒲 is linear in (m_m, φ_m) and 𝒴_m depends only on m_i, φ_i (i < m) and ĝ_i (i ≤ m); neither
contains ĝ_(m+1). By the observation each term of F contains W, one of ĝ_2, …, ĝ_m, or a derivative of one of these,
so F = 0 on Ω_>. On a generator in Ω_>, parametrised by s, Z solves ℓ·∂_X Z = ℳ′Z,
so |(d/ds)‖Z‖²_(L²(S¹))| ≤ 2‖ℳ′‖ ‖Z‖²_(L²(S¹)); Z vanishes at the generator's point on Σ_τ0 by (a), and so, by Gronwall's
inequality, along the whole generator. Hence ∂_θĝ_(m+1) = 0 on Ω_>, and ĝ_(m+1) = 0 there. This completes the
induction.

*The approximant.* So G = ḡ on Ω_> × S¹, and G does not depend on θ there. The profiles g_j of Theorem 4.11 are
the coefficients of λ^j, j ≤ N, in the expansion of G(X, θ + φ1 + λΨ), Ψ = Σ_(j≥2) λ^(j−2) φ_j, by Taylor's formula in
λΨ about θ + φ1. At X ∈ Ω_> every θ-derivative of G vanishes, so the expansion is G(X, θ + φ1) = ḡ(X), without
remainder, and g_j = m_j for 1 ≤ j ≤ N (in particular g1 = m1 + W(X, θ + φ1) = m1). Hence g_app = ḡ on Ω_>. The means
m_j are smooth on Ω (Lemma 4.10) and, like every profile of Theorem 4.11, independent of λ. The formula
for g0 is the one displayed in Section 41.1. Finally ∂_θg1 = 0 on Ω_>, so w = h + φ[∂_θg1] = h there
((6.1)). ∎

**Lemma 41.3** (After the shell.) Let Ω′ be a domain of the form (2.8), with constants (T′, δ′_0) and
the τ0 of Theorem 3.1, and let J ≥ 2 be an integer. Put K := J + 4 and N := K + 3, and let g_λ be the solution of
Theorem 3.1 on Ω′ with these orders. There are C_J and λ_1 > 0, depending on Ω′ and J, such that for 0 < λ ≤ λ_1, on
Ω′_+ = Ω′ ∩ {v ≥ v_end + 1}, g_λ is G-invariant and vacuum, and its Cartesian components satisfy

    |∂^j(g_λ − g^KS_(μ_end,0))| ≤ C_J λ     (j ≤ J),    (41.2)

with ∂^j any j derivatives in (τ, x), and g^KS_(μ_end,0) = η + (μ_end/r²)(dτ + dr)².

*Proof.* *The order.* Theorem 3.1 builds g_λ by Theorem 6.1 from the approximant of Theorem 4.11
with N = K + 3 stages and the data of Theorem 7.1. By Remark 6.6 with its energy order k taken equal to
K ≥ 6, whose inputs (E3) and (E4) hold at every order for this approximant and these data, there are M and λ_1 > 0
such that 𝒩_K(τ) ≤ Mλ^K on [τ0, τ′_end] for 0 < λ ≤ λ_1, 𝒩_K being the quantity (6.7) at order k = K.
Since 𝒩_K contains ‖h‖ and λ^i‖∂^i∂h‖ for i ≤ K, the L²(Σ_τ) norms satisfy

    ‖h(τ)‖ ≤ Mλ^K,     ‖∂^i∂h(τ)‖ ≤ Mλ^(K−i)     (i ≤ K).

*After the shell.* Ω′_+ ⊂ Ω′ ∩ {v > v_end}, so by Lemma 41.2, on Ω′_+,

    g_λ − g^KS_(μ_end,0) = Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j m_j + h.

*Bounds.* By the Sobolev inequality (5.2) on the slices A(τ) of Ω′, with a constant independent of
τ, |∂^jh| ≤ C Σ_(i≤3) ‖∂_x^i ∂^jh‖ on A(τ). Let j ≤ K − 3. For j ≥ 1 the terms are bounded by
‖∂^(i+j−1)∂h‖ ≤ Mλ^(K−i−j+1) ≤ Mλ^(K−j−2), as i + j − 1 ≤ K; for j = 0 they are ‖h‖ ≤ Mλ^K and
‖∂^(i−1)∂h‖ ≤ Mλ^(K−i+1) ≤ Mλ^(K−2) (1 ≤ i ≤ 3). As λ ≤ 1, |∂^jh| ≤ C_Kλ^(K−j−3) on Ω′ for j ≤ K − 3. With K = J + 4
this is at most C_Kλ for j ≤ J. The derivatives of order at most J of Σ_j λ^j m_j are at most Cλ on the compact set
Ω′_+, the m_j being smooth and independent of λ. This gives (41.2). Finally Ric(g_λ) = 0 on Ω′, and g_λ is
invariant under the T² action and both reflections, which generate G (Theorem 3.1, item 1). ∎

**Lemma 41.4** (Placing Σ^IVP.) Let R ≥ R₃. There are c₀ ∈ ℝ and a domain Ω′ of the form (2.8), with
the τ0 of Theorem 3.1 and with a′ = q0 − δ′_0 < ½r_♭, such that in the chart

    (t, x) := (τ + T_(μ_end)(|x|) + c₀, x):

(a) g0 = g_(b₀) on Ω′ ∩ {v ≥ v_end, |x| ≥ r_♭};

(b) Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 4R} lies in the interior of Ω′_+.

The chart change commutes with G, and Σ^IVP is G-invariant.

*Proof.* (a) On {v ≥ v_end}, g0 = g^KS_(μ_end,0) in the coordinates (τ, x), by a formula valid for every r > 0 whose
coefficients do not depend on τ. In the chart, τ = t − T_(μ_end)(|x|) − c₀, so the map (t, x) ↦ (τ, x) is the map
Φ_(μ_end) of (21.27) followed by the translation τ ↦ τ − c₀, which preserves g^KS_(μ_end,0). So there
g0 = Φ_(μ_end)^*g^KS_(μ_end,0) = g_(b₀), which (21.27) defines on ℝ_t × {|x| ≥ ½r_♭}.

(b) On Σ^IVP, t = ψ_IVP(|x|), so τ = f_IVP(r) − c₀ with f_IVP := ψ_IVP − T_(μ_end), continuous on [r_♭, 4R]. Take

    c₀ := min_([r_♭,4R]) f_IVP − max(τ0 + 1, v_end + 2 − r_♭).

Then on Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 4R} we have τ ≥ τ0 + 1, v = τ + r ≥ v_end + 2, and τ ≤ τ_top := max_([r_♭,4R]) f_IVP − c₀.
Take δ′_0 ∈ (max(0, q0 − ½r_♭), q0), an interval that is nonempty as r_♭ > 0; then 0 < a′ < ½r_♭. Put
q_end := (√72 μ_end l5²)^(1/4); μ being nondecreasing, r_q(v) ≤ q_end for every v. Take T′ > 0 so large that
V′ = v_end + T′ ≥ τ_top + 2R + q_end + 1. Then τ′_end = max_(v≤V′) (v − r_q(v)) ≥ V′ − q_end ≥ τ_top + 1, and on
Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 4R}

    v + (τ − τ′_end) = 2τ + r − τ′_end ≤ 2τ_top + 4R + q_end − V′ < V′ + 1.

With τ0 < τ ≤ τ_top < τ′_end and r ≥ r_♭ > a′, every defining inequality of Ω′ holds strictly there, and
v ≥ v_end + 2 > v_end + 1. So these points lie in the interior of Ω′_+. Finally, T_(μ_end) and ψ_IVP are functions
of |x|, and G fixes τ, t and |x|. ∎

### 41.3 Proof of the theorem

*Proof of Theorem 41.1.* *The choices.* Let ε_t ∈ (0, ε_K). The parameters are chosen by Theorem 38.24
with (38.15) at its step (3), up to ε_K at its step (4); ε_K does not depend on ε_t. Take α > 4 + ε_t in row w2
and finish steps (5)–(6); this fixes the order d_1 of Theorem 38.22. These choices do not involve ε_m:
Corollary 38.28 takes the parameters so chosen, with d_1 as in Theorem 38.22, and ε_m enters only its threshold.
Then choose, in this order:

- k := d_1 + 5, the order of the gluing in Proposition 39.17;
- R ≥ max(R_gl, R₃), with R_gl of Proposition 39.17 at this k;
- c₀ and Ω′ by Lemma 41.4, and J := k + 5 in Lemma 41.3, so that g_λ is built on Ω′ with
  K = J + 4 = d_1 + 14.

Let ε_m > 0. Corollary 38.28, applied with ε_m/C_𝔟 in place of ε_m (C_𝔟 of Section 41.1), gives
ε = ε(ε_m, ε_t) > 0 such that its conclusions (a)–(c) hold for data of norm below ε; its part (b) contains the
threshold of the run of Theorem 20.1 in the symmetry class (Proposition 38.27). Take λ_1 > 0 so small that
Lemma 41.3 and Corollary 39.19 apply for λ ≤ λ_1, and C_Rλ_1 < ½ε, with C_R the constant of Corollary 39.19, and
put δ := ½ε. The choices of Lemma 41.4 depend on r_♭ through δ′_0, c₀ and T′. So R, Ω′ and K depend on ε_t and
r_♭ only; λ_1 and δ depend moreover on ε_m.

*(i).* Let 0 < λ ≤ λ_1. Corollary 39.19, with k = d_1 + 5 and the data of g_λ on Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 4R}, gives
G-invariant smooth vacuum data (γ_λ, k_λ) := (ĝ, K̂) and m_λ := m, equal to the data of g_λ on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ R} and to
(γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≥ 4R}, with |m_λ − μ_end| ≤ C_Rλ and

    ‖(γ_λ − γ_(b₀), k_λ − k_(b₀))‖_(d_1) ≤ C_Rλ < ½ε.

The differences lie in H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b × H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b, by Lemma 38.25 with R′ = 4R: beyond 4R they are
(γ^(m_λ) − γ_(b₀), k^(m_λ) − k_(b₀)), whose Cartesian components lie in ρ²C^∞ and ρ³C^∞ of the radial
compactification (Lemma 39.16 (a), with γ_(b₀) = γ^(μ_end) and k_(b₀) = k^(μ_end)). So Corollary 38.28 (b)
applies: Proposition 38.27 gives U fixed by G, b = (m′, 0) with |m′ − μ_end| < ε_m/C_𝔟 ≤ ε_m, S = S⁰ = 0, and a
G-invariant metric g with the conclusions (1)–(5) of Theorem 38.22. By (2) with S = S⁰ = 0, φ_(0,0) = ψ_0 ∘ φ_0
being the identity ((38.1)), g is defined on Ω_* ∪ 𝒟_0 and induces (γ_λ, k_λ) on Σ^IVP; on
Σ^IVP ∩ {r < R} these are the data of g_λ.

*The rate.* Where χ_K = 1, g − g_(m′,0) = h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q) + h, by (3)–(4) of Theorem 38.22 with
b = (m′, 0) and S = S⁰ = 0. Every term of h_tot(p⃗) carries a factor dχ_K: the terms are those of Definition 31.9,
Definition 32.5, Definition 32.19 and Definition 32.31, summed in Definition 32.7 and Definition 32.33 over
the rows and the rotation rows of Definition 34.3 (a rotation row has the terms that Definition 32.31 assigns to
the type v1), and each is −dχ_K ⊗_s ω for a 1-form ω. So h_tot(p⃗) vanishes on the interior of {χ_K = 1}.
Corollary 38.28 (c) gives (41.1), with α − 2 > 2 + ε_K − ε′_0 > 2 and α − 2 > 2 + ε_t. α was chosen with
α > 4 + ε_t among the admissible orders of row w2, which are dense in (4 + ε_K − ε′_0, 4 + ε_K]; so it may be taken as
close to 4 + ε_K as desired. With ε′ := α − 4 − ε_t > 0, (41.1) gives g − g_(m′,0) = O(t_*^(−2−ε_t)) on
{r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}.

*(ii).* The difference

    (γ − γ_(b₀), k − k_(b₀)) = (γ − γ_λ, k − k_λ) + (γ_λ − γ_(b₀), k_λ − k_(b₀))

lies in the class, with norm below δ + ½ε = ε. So Corollary 38.28 (a) applies: Theorem 38.22 holds with
‖b − b₀‖_𝔟 < ε_m/C_𝔟 and |S|, |S⁰| < ε_m/C_𝔟, hence |b − b₀| < ε_m and |S|, |S⁰| < ε_m, as C_𝔟 ≥ 1. By (2) of
Theorem 38.22, g induces (φ|)^*(γ, k) on φ⁻¹(Σ^IVP), φ := φ_(−S,−S⁰), and φ⁻¹ = φ_S ∘ ψ_(S⁰) ((38.1)).
The vanishing of h_tot(p⃗) on the interior of {χ_K = 1} holds as in (i), and Corollary 38.28 (c) gives (41.1)
with g_b in place of g_(m′,0). ∎

*Proof of Theorem 3.9.* *The parameters.* Theorem 3.9 fixes its quantities in the order of
Theorem 41.1: first l5, μ0, A, env and τ0, then b₀ = (μ_end, 0), about which the stability theory is set
up, and its inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁], R₁ = μ_end^(1/2), and then ℓ0 and ε_K. The number ℓ0 ∈ (3, 4) is the ℓ_0 of the
data class (38.15), and ε_K is the one chosen at step (4) of Theorem 38.24, with (38.15) at step (3).
With the ℓ_I ∈ (3, ℓ_0) chosen at step (3), which is admissible in row d2 of Section 38.6 (it avoids the discrete
exclusion sets of that row, Section 38.8), and the ε_+ chosen at step (4), ε_K satisfies the conditions that
Theorem 3.9 states, all of them conditions of row w1: 0 < ε_K < ε_+ < min(δ_♯, ε_ind, ℓ_I − 3, ¼), (G⁺) and (G).
Row w1 also asks the exactness conditions (Ex1)–(Ex2) of Definition 35.13, which Theorem 3.9 does not list;
step (4) imposes them on the ε_+ it chooses, together with the others. (Ex1) is (G⁺) with its closed endpoint, as
Theorem 3.9 states it. With the parameters so chosen, the hypotheses of Theorem 41.1 hold.

Let ε ∈ (0, ε_K) be the exponent of Theorem 3.9, put ε_t := ε, and apply Theorem 41.1. It gives
K = d_1 + 14, R and Ω′, which depend on ε_t and r_♭ only, and, for each ε_m > 0, λ_1 and δ, which depend moreover on
ε_m. The solutions g_λ of Theorem 3.9 are those of Theorem 3.1 on the enlarged domain Ω′ of Lemma 41.4,
built with K = d_1 + 14, d_1 the regularity of Theorem 38.22.

Item (i). The data of g_λ on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ R}, continued G-equivariantly to the exact Tangherlini data
(γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) on {r ≥ 4R}, are the data (γ_λ, k_λ) of Theorem 41.1 (i), constructed in
Corollary 39.19. Their development g is G-invariant and vacuum, induces the data of g_λ on the ball Σ^IVP ∩ {r < R},
and by (41.1) satisfies g − g_(m′,0) = O(t_*^(−2−ε_t)) on every set {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, where g_(m′,0)
is the Tangherlini metric of mass m′, |m′ − μ_end| < ε_m. Every spatially compact subset of the exterior of the black
hole lies in M ∩ {r ≤ R′} for some R′, and its points with t_* ≥ T′ lie in {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}.

Item (ii). The data class of (ii) in Theorem 3.9 is H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b × H^(∞,(ℰ_0+1,ℓ_0+1))_b with
(38.15): the elements of ℰ_0 below ℓ_0 give the polyhomogeneous terms of orders 2 and 3 in the metric, those of
ℰ_0 + 1 below ℓ_0 + 1 the terms of orders 3 and 4 in the second fundamental form, and the remainders have the weights
ℓ_0 and ℓ_0 + 1 (Section 38.8). For data in it, of norm below δ, Theorem 41.1 (ii) gives a vacuum
development g whose initial surface is the surface φ_(−S,−S⁰)⁻¹(Σ^IVP) = φ_S(ψ_(S⁰)(Σ^IVP)), φ_S the cut-off Lorentz
boost of Section 21.7 and ψ_(S⁰) the cut-off translation of Lemma 32.2, with |S|, |S⁰| < ε_m, and which
settles at the rate (41.1) to the Myers–Perry metric g_b, b = (m′, A), with |m′ − μ_end| + |A| = |b − b₀| < ε_m:
mass within ε_m of μ_end and spin below ε_m. ∎

### 41.4 Remarks on the statement

**Remark 41.5** (The development and g_λ.) The development g of Theorem 41.1 (i) and g_λ are
vacuum metrics that induce the same data on Σ^IVP ∩ {r < R}, in different gauges. Let Σ := Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ < r < R}.
That g_λ, near the hole just before Σ, and g, after Σ^IVP, glued along Σ by the identity, form one smooth vacuum
spacetime M_gl; and that the Cauchy developments of Σ in M_gl and, for g_λ, in a neighbourhood of the closure of Σ
have a maximal common globally hyperbolic development U, which contains a neighbourhood of Σ, with an isometric
embedding of U into the second that preserves the time orientation and is the identity on Σ, is
Lemma 43.5 of Chapter 43. How far U reaches into the future of Σ is not decided there.
Nothing in Theorem 41.1 or in its proof uses the lemma.

**Remark 41.6** (Perturbations and gluing.) Theorem 41.1 (ii) takes the perturbation in
the data class of Theorem 38.22, and not in a class of decaying data reached by gluing. Gluing a perturbation that
decays faster than r^(−3/2) far out to a translated, rotated and boosted Myers–Perry metric (Theorem 39.13) replaces
its data near infinity, and the solution near the black hole at late times depends on those data: K⁺ at late times is
not in the domain of dependence of any bounded part of the initial surface. So a settling statement reached by gluing
holds for the glued data, not for the perturbation. With (38.15) the data class has polyhomogeneous terms of
orders 2 and 3 at spatial infinity and a conormal remainder of order ℓ_0 ∈ (3 + ε_+, 4). By Lemma 38.25 it
contains every perturbation that is, outside a compact set, a classical symbol of order −2 (in the metric) and −3 (in
the second fundamental form), that is an element of ρ²C^∞, resp. ρ³C^∞, of the radial compactification, for instance
the data of a nearby translated, rotated and boosted Myers–Perry metric. So (ii) needs no gluing and no parity
condition; the gluing is used in (i) only, in its class form Proposition 39.17. For a merely decaying perturbation,
gluing gives only that it agrees on a large ball with one to which (ii) applies, and that statement is not made here.
Which decaying perturbations (ii) reaches, directly or through gluing, is determined in Chapter 42.

## 42. After the shell: the reach of the settling theorem

Theorem 3.1 holds on D_T for each fixed T. This chapter takes up what happens after the shell and how far the settling
theorem Theorem 3.9 reaches. Section 42.1 places the question: settling for all later times is the
nonlinear stability of five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini within the class, and the biaxial class in which that
stability is known meets the class only in spherical symmetry (Proposition 42.1).
Section 42.2 proves that every oscillating profile of the approximant vanishes after the shell, so that
there g_λ is Tangherlini of mass μ_end up to smooth corrections of order λ (Proposition 42.2).
Section 42.3 recalls how the data of g_λ near the hole are glued, in the class, to exact Tangherlini data
with only the mass to match, which gives the data of item (i) of Theorem 3.9.

Section 42.4 determines which perturbations of these data item (ii) reaches. A perturbation that decays like
r^(−a), with a > 3, lies in Hintz's class for the theorem run with ℓ0 ∈ (3, min(a, 4)) and is reached directly
(Proposition 42.7, Corollary 42.8). For 3/2 < a ≤ ℓ0 the rate does not decide. Agreement on
every ball with data to which (ii) applies, uniformly in the radius, is equivalent to membership in the class
(Proposition 42.9). At every such rate some pure-gauge perturbations lie outside the class, and every data
set in the class that agrees with them on {r < R} has norm at least of order R^(ℓ0−a) (Proposition 42.13).
Gluing to the translated, rotated and boosted Myers–Perry data on Hintz's own surface (Lemma 42.15) does
no worse than this order for every perturbation (Proposition 42.17, Corollary 42.19).
Theorem 42.21 collects the answer: the perturbations to which (ii) applies, directly or through gluing
uniformly in the gluing radius, are exactly those small in Hintz's class.

### 42.1 The question

Theorem 3.1 holds on D_T for each fixed T; the theorems of Huneau and Luk [HL18], of Touati [Tou23a] and of Luk and
Rodnianski [LR20] hold on a fixed interval too. Settling for all later v is the nonlinear stability of five-dimensional
Schwarzschild–Tangherlini within the class. Linear stability against every type of perturbation is known: Ishibashi and
Kodama "have shown that higher-dimensional Schwarzschild black holes are stable with respect to all tensorial types of
linear perturbations" ([IK03, p. 16]). Nonlinear asymptotic stability is known in a class of perturbations with more
symmetry: Holzegel proves "the non-linear asymptotic stability of the five-dimensional Schwarzschild metric under
biaxial vacuum perturbations", that is, "the evolution of (SU(2) × U(1))-symmetric vacuum perturbations of initial data
for the five-dimensional Schwarzschild metric finally converges in a suitable sense to a member of the Schwarzschild
family" ([Hol08, p. 1; Theorem 1.1, pp. 5–6]). In that class the vacuum equations reduce to a system of partial
differential equations in 1 + 1 dimensions ([Hol08, p. 4]); its metrics are ([Hol08, (22), p. 14])

    g = −Ω²(u, v) du dv + (1/4) r²(u, v) (e^(2B(u,v)) (σ1² + σ2²) + e^(−4B(u,v)) σ3²),    (42.1)

with σ1, σ2, σ3 a basis of left-invariant 1-forms on SU(2) = S³, normalised so that the round metric of S³ is
(1/4)(σ1² + σ2² + σ3²) ([Hol08, p. 14, footnote 25]); the squashing B vanishes for Schwarzschild–Tangherlini. That class
shares the torus T² of the T²-mirror class but not the reflections.

**Proposition 42.1** (The biaxial class meets the class only in spherical symmetry.) On S³ use the
coordinates of Section 2.2, x1 + i x2 = cos ϑ e^(iφ1), x3 + i x4 = sin ϑ e^(iφ2), with c = cos ϑ, s = sin ϑ, and
choose the left-invariant forms so that σ3 is dual to the generator of the diagonal action
(z1, z2) ↦ (e^(it) z1, e^(it) z2) of S³ ⊂ ℂ². Then, with η := c² dφ1 + s² dφ2,

    (1/4) σ3² = η²,      (1/4)(σ1² + σ2²) = dϑ² + c² s² (dφ1 − dφ2)²,    (42.2)

and the coefficient of dφ1 dφ2 in the quadratic form (1/4)(e^(2B)(σ1² + σ2²) + e^(−4B) σ3²) is

    2 c² s² (e^(−4B) − e^(2B)),    (42.3)

which vanishes at a point with c s ≠ 0 exactly when B = 0 there. Hence a metric (42.1) is of the
form (2.1) in these coordinates if and only if B ≡ 0, and then it is spherically symmetric.

*Proof.* Write S³ as SU(2) by (z1, z2) ↦ ((z1, −z̄2), (z2, z̄1)), the columns of the matrix. Right multiplication by
diag(e^(it), e^(−it)) multiplies the first column by e^(it), so the diagonal action is a right action and its generator
∂_φ1 + ∂_φ2 is a left-invariant vector field. For the metric (1/4)(σ1² + σ2² + σ3²) the frame X1, X2, X3 dual to σ1, σ2,
σ3 is orthogonal with |X_i| = 1/2; this metric is the round metric dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2². The field ∂_φ1 + ∂_φ2
has length (c² + s²)^(1/2) = 1, so it equals ±2X3, and its metric dual, η, equals ±σ3/2: both 1-forms vanish on the
orthogonal complement of X3, and they take the values 1 and ±1 on ∂_φ1 + ∂_φ2. This gives the first identity. For the
second,

    dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2² − η² = dϑ² + c²(1 − c²) dφ1² + s²(1 − s²) dφ2² − 2 c² s² dφ1 dφ2
                                 = dϑ² + c² s² (dφ1 − dφ2)²,

and the left side is (1/4)(σ1² + σ2²). Hence
(1/4)(e^(2B)(σ1² + σ2²) + e^(−4B) σ3²) = e^(2B)(dϑ² + c² s² (dφ1 − dφ2)²) + e^(−4B)(c² dφ1 + s² dφ2)², whose dφ1 dφ2
coefficient is −2 c² s² e^(2B) + 2 c² s² e^(−4B), which is (42.3). As e^(−4B) − e^(2B) is strictly
