decreasing in B and zero at B = 0, it vanishes exactly when B = 0. A metric (2.1) has no dφ1 dφ2 term. B is
a function of (u, v), so if B ≢ 0 the coefficient is nonzero on a whole orbit off the axes, and the metric is not of the
form (2.1). If B ≡ 0, (42.1) is −Ω² du dv + r² (dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2²), which is
spherically symmetric. ∎

The waves of Section 2.6 depend on the polar angle ϑ, so they lie outside the biaxial class in any case.

After the shell the oscillating profiles vanish (Proposition 42.2) and only the mean corrections remain: on
Ω ∩ {v > v_end}, g_λ differs from Tangherlini of the final mass μ_end by λ m1 + O(λ²), with its first derivatives.
Settling would therefore follow from the small-data stability of Tangherlini in the T²-mirror class, once the solution
is also constructed outside D_T. The first step is the stability theory of Part V to
Part IX, which gives Theorem 3.9. The second, continuing g_λ outside D_T, is replaced by a
gluing (Section 42.3). That the development of g_λ's own data settles, with no gluing, in a class wider
by half-integer orders, is Theorem 44.1.

### 42.2 No oscillation after the shell

We use the approximant of Theorem 4.11 with the stage data of Lemma 7.4, as Theorem 3.1 does, in the
notation of Section 4.5: the means m_j, the phases φ_j, the leading oscillation W = W_TT + χ dv ⊗ dv of
Section 4.4 and the oscillating profiles ĝ_j, 2 ≤ j ≤ N + 1, of zero θ-mean.

**Proposition 42.2** (After the shell.) Let g_λ and g_app be as in Theorem 3.1.

(a) On Ω ∩ {v > v_end}, W = 0 and ĝ_j = 0 for 2 ≤ j ≤ N + 1, so that there

    g_app = g0 + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j m_j,    (42.4)

with g0 = η + (μ_end/r²) dv ⊗ dv, five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini of mass μ_end, and the m_j smooth and
independent of λ. In the coordinates (t, x) := (τ, x), g0 = g^KS_(μ_end,0) of Definition 21.15 there.

(b) On Ω ∩ {v > v_end}, |g_λ − g0 − λ m1| ≤ C λ² and |∂(g_λ − g0 − λ m1)| ≤ C λ². If the energy estimate of
Theorem 3.1 is taken at order k ≥ d (Remark 6.6), with K ≥ d + 1, then g_λ − g0 is O(λ) in H^d of the
slices Σ_τ ∩ {v > v_end}.

(c) If T > r_q(μ_end) − a, a the inner radius of Ω (Section 2.3), then for every τ1 ∈ (v_end − a, τ_end] the whole
slice Σ_τ1 lies in {v > v_end}, and its inner sphere {r = a} lies inside the horizon {r = √μ_end} of g0.

*Proof.* (a) is Lemma 41.2. Its proof uses three facts. W_TT is proportional to the envelope, which vanishes
for v ≥ v_end, and the right-hand side of the transport (4.9) of χ is quadratic in it. Every term of the
oscillating part of an expression polynomial in the profiles contains W, some ĝ_j or a derivative of one, since a
product of factors that do not depend on θ has zero oscillating part; this applies to the stage data of
Lemma 7.4 (i) and to the right-hand side of the transport (c) of Lemma 4.10. And the transports run
along ℓ = −L0, whose integral curves keep v and reach Σ_τ0 inside Ω (Lemma 2.6 (d)). By induction on the stage,
every oscillating profile has zero data and zero right-hand side on Ω ∩ {v > v_end}, hence vanishes there. As
dv = dτ + d|x|, g0 = η + μ_end|x|⁻²(dτ + d|x|)² there, which is g^KS_(μ_end,0) of Definition 21.15 at A = 0
(Proposition 21.17) with t = τ.

(b) By Theorem 3.1 item 3, g_λ = g_app + w with |w| ≤ C λ^(K−3) and |∂w| ≤ C λ^(K−4) on Ω, and K ≥ 6. By (a),
g_λ − g0 − λ m1 = Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j m_j + w on Ω ∩ {v > v_end}, and the m_j are bounded with their first derivatives on the
compact set Ω. The statement at order k is Remark 6.6 (d) with (a).

(c) Write V = v_end + T and r_q(μ) := (√72 μ l5²)^(1/4). As μ(V) = μ_end,
τ_end = max_(v ≤ V)(v − r_q(v)) ≥ V − r_q(μ_end) = v_end + T − r_q(μ_end) > v_end − a, so the interval (v_end − a, τ_end]
is nonempty. For τ1 in it, Σ_τ1 = {a ≤ |x| ≤ b(τ1)} (Section 2.3), and there v = τ1 + r ≥ τ1 + a > v_end. Finally
a = q0 − δ0 < q0, the seed condition μ0 ≥ √72 l5² gives q0⁴ = √72 μ0 l5² ≤ μ0², that is q0 ≤ √μ0, and
μ_end = μ0 + (2/9) A² ∫ env² ≥ μ0, so a < √μ_end. ∎

With K and the order of Theorem 3.1 large enough for the number of derivatives needed, the data of g_λ near the hole
are therefore small in every norm the stability theory uses. The proof of Theorem 3.9 enlarges the domain of
Theorem 3.1 and places Hintz's initial surface Σ^IVP so that its part near the hole lies in the region after the shell
(Lemma 41.4); there g_λ is within O(λ) of g^KS_(μ_end,0) in every C^J (Lemma 41.3), and its data on Σ^IVP
are within O(λ) of those of Tangherlini of mass μ_end (Corollary 39.19).

### 42.3 Gluing in the class: only the mass is matched

Beyond a ball the data of g_λ on Σ^IVP are glued G-equivariantly to exact Tangherlini data on the same surface, by the
method of Chruściel and Delay [CD03] (Theorem 39.13, Proposition 39.17). The obstruction of that gluing is the space 𝔎 of
Killing initial data of flat space ((39.4)). On G-invariant data only its G-invariant part enters, and
𝔎^G = span(e₀), the Killing initial data of ∂_t (Section 39.5); so only the mass is matched. The antipodal map −I lies
in G, being the composition of the half-turns of the planes (x1, x2) and (x3, x4), so G-invariant data are invariant
under x ↦ −x; in space dimension 4 the gluing needs no parity condition at all (Remark 39.15). The flux identity
(39.5) at X = e₀ bounds the distance of the glued mass from μ_end by the size of the data's deviation on the
annulus: the flux of Tangherlini's data on the Kerr–Schild slices is 6π²m at every radius (the part *c_E* of the proof of
Proposition 39.7), and its charge on Σ^IVP is 6π²m (Lemma 39.16 (c)); the remainder q_(e₀) vanishes to second order at
flat data, and together these give the mass bound of step (6) of the proof of Proposition 39.17. So the glued data stay
O(λ)-close to Tangherlini in the weighted norm of the stability theory at a fixed gluing radius (Corollary 39.19,
Remark 39.18). The stability theorem, run on G-invariant spaces with its choices made equivariant
(Lemma 38.26), gives a G-invariant development whose final parameters, fixed by G, are a mass alone
(Proposition 38.27). These are the data and the development of item (i) of Theorem 3.9.

The glued data are not the data of a continuation of g_λ beyond the ball, and their development is not one. The
developments of two data sets that agree on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ R} agree on the domain of dependence of that set; the
statement of settling concerns late times near the hole, outside it.

### 42.4 Which perturbations the settling theorem reaches

In this section the letter a denotes an order of decay, not the inner radius of Ω.

*The data of (i).* Fix ℓ0 ∈ (3, 4), and let d_1 (Theorem 38.22), λ1, δ and the data (γ_λ, k_λ) of item (i) be those
of Theorem 3.9 and its proof run with this ℓ0, a fixed ε < ε_K and a fixed ε_m > 0, and fix λ ≤ λ1. By
Corollary 39.19, (γ_λ, k_λ) are G-invariant smooth vacuum data on Σ := Σ^IVP, equal to (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) on
Σ ∩ {r ≥ 4R_i}, where R_i is the gluing radius there, |m_λ − μ_end| ≤ C λ, and (γ^m, k^m) are the data that g^KS_(m,0)
induces on Σ far out (Section 39.5). We write b₀ = (μ_end, 0) and R₁ = μ_end^(1/2). For r ≥ R₃, Σ is the graph
{t_KS = f(|x|)} in the Kerr–Schild time of g^KS_(μ_end,0), with

    f := C″ − T_(μ_end)(|x|),      f′(r) = 2μ_end/(r² − μ_end)   (r ≥ 3R₁)    (42.5)

(Lemma 21.22 (b), (21.27)), and Σ is identified with {|x| > R₃} ⊂ ℝ⁴ there. We write r = |x|, ρ = r⁻¹,
ω = x/r ∈ 𝕊³ and |𝕊³| = 2π². Constants c, C may depend on λ, ℓ0, d_1, a and the data of (i), never on the radius R,
the size Ξ or the perturbation.

#### 42.4.1 The class and its norm

**Definition 42.3** (The norm.) Fix r_χ ≥ max(R₃, 4R_i) and χ_c ∈ C^∞(ℝ) with χ_c(r) = 0 for r ≤ r_χ
and χ_c(r) = 1 for r ≥ 2r_χ. Let 𝒜_d be the set of compositions of at most d of the b-vector fields r∂_r and
Ω_ij := x^i∂_j − x^j∂_i, the empty composition included. For w on {r > r_χ} put

    ‖w‖²_(H^(d,ℓ)_b) := Σ_(A∈𝒜_d) ∫_(r_χ)^∞ ∫_(𝕊³) r^(2ℓ) |Aw|² dω dr/r.

A symmetric 2-tensor u on Σ lies in ℋ^d_0 if u ∈ H^d(Σ ∩ {r ≤ 2r_χ}) and, on {r > r_χ}, in the frame ∂_(x^i),

    u_ij = χ_c(r) (ρ² u^((2))_ij(ω) + ρ³ u^((3))_ij(ω)) + ũ_ij,      u^((z))_ij ∈ H^d(𝕊³),   ũ_ij ∈ H^(d,ℓ0)_b.
    (42.6)

Its norm is
‖u‖_(ℋ^d_0) := Σ_(i,j)(‖u^((2))_ij‖_(H^d(𝕊³)) + ‖u^((3))_ij‖_(H^d(𝕊³)) + ‖ũ_ij‖_(H^(d,ℓ0)_b)) + ‖u‖_(H^d(Σ∩{r≤2r_χ})).
The space ℋ^d_1 is defined likewise with ρ³, ρ⁴ and the weight ℓ0 + 1. For pairs,
‖(u, v)‖_d := ‖u‖_(ℋ^d_0) + ‖v‖_(ℋ^d_1), and the *class* is ℋ^∞ := ⋂_d ℋ^d_0 × ℋ^d_1.

Near infinity the b-vector fields of the radial compactification are spanned by r∂_r = −ρ∂_ρ and the rotation fields
Ω_ij, and dr/r dω is a b-density, so 𝒜_d spans Diff^d_b there. The space ℋ^∞ is therefore the class
H^(∞,(ℰ0,ℓ0))_b × H^(∞,(ℰ0+1,ℓ0+1))_b of Definition 21.31 (5) with the index set ℰ0 = {(j, 0) : j ≥ 2} of
(38.15), whose exponents below ℓ0 are 2 and 3, and those of ℰ0 + 1 below ℓ0 + 1 are 3 and 4; and ‖·‖_(d_1) is a
norm in which Theorem 38.22 measures the data. Other choices of the cut-off, of the spanning set or of the sum over
components give the same spaces and equivalent norms. For the spanning set this is Definition 21.31 (3), and the
space does not depend on the defining function by Definition 21.31 (5). For the cut-off, let χ′_c have the
properties of χ_c. Then (χ_c − χ′_c)(ρ² b2 + ρ³ b3) is supported in {r_χ < r < 2r_χ}, where the weights are bounded,
and its norm in H^(d,ℓ0)_b is at most C(‖b2‖_(H^d(𝕊³)) + ‖b3‖_(H^d(𝕊³))), as r∂_r acts on the radial factor and the
Ω_ij are smooth vector fields on 𝕊³. So the difference of two expansions of u, one with each cut-off, puts
χ′_c(ρ²(u^((2)) − u′^((2))) + ρ³(u^((3)) − u′^((3)))) in H^(d,ℓ0)_b, and Lemma 42.4, whose proof uses
only large r, gives equal coefficients; ũ then changes by the term above, bounded by the coefficients' norms. For the
sum over components: they are finitely many. We read δ for this norm; an equivalent norm changes δ and the constants
below by fixed factors. Theorem 3.9 (ii) asks
(γ − γ_λ, k − k_λ) ∈ ℋ^∞ with ‖(γ − γ_λ, k − k_λ)‖_(d_1) < δ.

**Lemma 42.4** (The expansion is unique.) If b2, b3 ∈ L²(𝕊³) and χ_c
(ρ² b2 + ρ³ b3) ∈ H^(0,ℓ0)_b, then b2 = b3 = 0. So the coefficients u^((z)) are determined by u, the norm is well
defined, and ℋ^d_0, ℋ^d_1 are reflexive Banach spaces: each is a closed subspace of a product of Hilbert spaces
(the two descriptions agreeing on {r_χ < r < 2r_χ}), with an equivalent norm.

*Proof.* For almost every ω with b2(ω) ≠ 0, r^(2ℓ0) |r⁻² b2 + r⁻³ b3|² ≥ (1/2) r^(2ℓ0−4) |b2|² for r large, and
∫^∞ r^(2ℓ0−4) dr/r = ∞ as 2ℓ0 − 4 > 0. Where b2 = 0 ≠ b3, the same holds with the exponent 2ℓ0 − 6 > 0, as ℓ0 > 3. By
Fubini's theorem the weighted integral is infinite unless b2 = b3 = 0 almost everywhere. ∎

**Definition 42.5** (Perturbations of order a.) Let a > 3/2 and Ξ ∈ (0, 1]. A smooth vacuum data set
(γ, k) on Σ is a *perturbation of order a and size Ξ* if h := γ − γ_λ and κ := k − k_λ satisfy, in the coordinates x
of Σ,

    |∂^β h| ≤ Ξ ⟨r⟩^(−a−|β|),      |∂^β κ| ≤ Ξ ⟨r⟩^(−a−1−|β|)      (|β| ≤ d_1 + 6),    (42.7)

and the same bounds with some constant C_β in place of Ξ for every β (conormality). Nothing is assumed about
expansions: such a perturbation may or may not lie in the class.

**Definition 42.6** (The gluing statement.) For R ≥ 2r_χ let N^((d))_R(γ, k) be the infimum of
‖(γ′ − γ_λ, k′ − k_λ)‖_d over the smooth vacuum data (γ′, k′) on Σ with (γ′ − γ_λ, k′ − k_λ) ∈ ℋ^∞ and (γ′, k′) = (γ, k)
on Σ ∩ {r < R} (the infimum of the empty set being ∞). The statement "(γ, k) agrees on every large ball with data to
which Theorem 3.9 (ii) applies, with smallness uniform as R → ∞" is

(S) there are R₀ and M < δ with N^((d_1))_R(γ, k) ≤ M for every R ≥ R₀;

and (S_∞) is (S) together with sup_(R≥R₀) N^((d))_R(γ, k) < ∞ for every d.

#### 42.4.2 Above the threshold: a > ℓ0

**Proposition 42.7** (In the class without gluing.) Let a > ℓ0 and let (γ, k) be a perturbation of
order a and size Ξ. Then (h, κ) ∈ ℋ^∞, all its coefficients u^((z)) vanish, and

    ‖(h, κ)‖_(d_1) ≤ C_1 Ξ (1 + (a − ℓ0)^(−1/2)),    (42.8)

with C_1 depending only on d_1, r_χ and Definition 42.3. So if C_1 Ξ (1 + (a − ℓ0)^(−1/2)) < δ,
Theorem 3.9 (ii) applies to (γ, k) itself, and (S_∞) holds with (γ′, k′) = (γ, k) for every R.

*Proof.* Each of r∂_r = x^i∂_i and Ω_ij has coefficients linear in x. So a composition A ∈ 𝒜_d is
Σ_(|β|≤d) c_β ∂^β with c_β homogeneous polynomials of degree |β|, and |Ah| ≤ C Σ_(|β|≤d) r^(|β|) |∂^β h| ≤ C Ξ r^(−a)
on {r > r_χ} by (42.7), for d ≤ d_1 + 6. Take the coefficients zero, so ũ = h. Then

    ‖r^(ℓ0) A h‖²_(L²({r>r_χ}, dr/r dω)) ≤ C² Ξ² 2π² ∫_(r_χ)^∞ r^(2(ℓ0−a)) dr/r = C² Ξ² 2π² r_χ^(2(ℓ0−a)) / (2(a − ℓ0)).

For κ the weight is ℓ0 + 1 and the order a + 1, with the same integral. On {r ≤ 2r_χ}, ‖(h, κ)‖_(H^(d_1)) ≤ C Ξ by
(42.7). With C_β in place of Ξ the same argument gives every d, so (h, κ) ∈ ℋ^∞. ∎

**Corollary 42.8** (Every rate above 3.) Theorem 3.9 holds for every ℓ0 ∈ (3, 4), its
constants ε_K, λ1, δ and its data of (i) depending on ℓ0, which its statement fixes before them. Let a > 3 and run it
with ℓ0 ∈ (3, min(a, 4)). Then its item (ii) covers every perturbation of order a of its data of (i) with Ξ below
δ/(C_1(1 + (a − ℓ0)^(−1/2))), at the rate t*^(−2−ε) for every ε < ε_K, where ε_K < ℓ0 − 3 < a − 3.

*Proof.* Proposition 42.7 with that ℓ0. The bound ε_K < ℓ0 − 3 is the chain ε_K < ε_+ < ℓ_I − 3 with
ℓ_I < ℓ0 of Theorem 3.9. ∎

In four dimensions Hintz's theorem asks, "for structureless data", "O(r^(−3−ϵ0))-decay" ([Hin26, p. 2, footnote 1]);
Corollary 42.8 is the five-dimensional counterpart. The threshold is sharp: at a = ℓ0 the integral of
the proof is log(R/r_χ) on {r_χ < r < R}, and Proposition 42.13 gives perturbations of order ℓ0 outside the
class.

#### 42.4.3 The gluing statement is class membership

**Proposition 42.9** Let (γ, k) be smooth vacuum data on Σ, (h, κ) := (γ − γ_λ, k − k_λ), and
d ≥ 0.

(a) R ↦ N^((d))_R(γ, k) is nondecreasing. Its limit is at least ‖(h, κ)‖_d, read as ∞ when (h, κ) ∉ ℋ^d_0 × ℋ^d_1.

(b) If (h, κ) ∈ ℋ^∞, then N^((d))_R(γ, k) ≤ ‖(h, κ)‖_d for every R, so the limit equals ‖(h, κ)‖_d.

*Proof.* (a) Data equal to (γ, k) on {r < R′} are equal to it on {r < R} for R < R′, so the infimum over the smaller
set is larger. Let L := lim_R N^((d))_R < ∞. Choose R_n → ∞ and admissible (γ′_n, k′_n) with
u_n := (γ′_n − γ_λ, k′_n − k_λ) and ‖u_n‖_d ≤ L + 1/n. The space ℋ^d_0 × ℋ^d_1 is reflexive
(Lemma 42.4), so a subsequence converges weakly to some u, and ‖u‖_d ≤ L, the norm being convex and
continuous. For a compact K ⊂ Σ the restriction ℋ^d_0 × ℋ^d_1 → L²(K) is continuous, the weights being bounded on K,
so u_n|_K converges weakly to u|_K in L²(K). But u_n|_K = (h, κ)|_K once R_n > sup_K r. Hence u = (h, κ) on every
compact set, (h, κ) ∈ ℋ^d_0 × ℋ^d_1 and ‖(h, κ)‖_d ≤ L. (b) (γ, k) itself is admissible for every R. ∎

**Corollary 42.10** (S) implies (h, κ) ∈ ℋ^(d_1)_0 × ℋ^(d_1)_1 with ‖(h, κ)‖_(d_1) ≤ M < δ.
(S_∞) holds if and only if (h, κ) ∈ ℋ^∞ with ‖(h, κ)‖_(d_1) < δ, that is, if and only if Theorem 3.9 (ii)
applies to (γ, k) itself.

*Proof.* Proposition 42.9 (a) at d_1, and at every d for (S_∞); the converse is
Proposition 42.9 (b). ∎

So, whatever the decay rate, gluing uniformly in the radius gives nothing beyond (ii) applied directly.
Proposition 42.9 uses neither a decay rate nor the vacuum condition of the competitors, only the norm.

#### 42.4.4 The obstruction at every rate a ≤ ℓ0

**Lemma 42.11** (A positive distance.) Let q ∈ ℝ and let p1 ≠ p2 be real. On (1/2, 1) with the
measure ds/s, the functions s^q cos log s, s^q sin log s, s^(p1) and s^(p2) are linearly independent. Hence

    ϰ(q; p1, p2) := min_(ψ∈ℝ) dist_(L²((1/2,1), ds/s)) (s^q cos(log s + ψ), span(s^(p1), s^(p2))) > 0,

and ϰ² is the least eigenvalue of the Schur complement S = G11 − G12 G22⁻¹ G21 of the Gram matrix of the four
functions, block 1 being the pair (s^q cos log s, s^q sin log s). We write ϰ(a, ℓ0) := ϰ(ℓ0 − a; ℓ0 − 2, ℓ0 − 3).

*Proof.* With t = log s ∈ (−log 2, 0), a real relation c1 s^q cos log s + c2 s^q sin log s + c3 s^(p1) + c4 s^(p2) = 0
reads ((c1 − i c2)/2) e^((q+i)t) + ((c1 + i c2)/2) e^((q−i)t) + c3 e^(p1 t) + c4 e^(p2 t) = 0. The exponents q ± i,
p1, p2 are pairwise distinct, and the Wronskian of e^(z1 t), …, e^(z4 t) is e^((z1+⋯+z4)t) Π_(j<k)(z_k − z_j) ≠ 0, a
Vandermonde determinant; so all coefficients vanish. Now s^q cos(log s + ψ) = cos ψ s^q cos log s − sin ψ s^q sin log s
is a nonzero combination of the first two functions, hence not in the span of the last two. By least squares its
squared distance from that span is vᵀ S v with v = (cos ψ, −sin ψ), and S is positive definite because the Gram matrix
is. The minimum over the unit circle is the least eigenvalue of S. ∎

**Remark 42.12** (Numerical observation.) Evaluated by quadrature of the Gram matrix,
ϰ(5/2, 7/2) ≈ 7.655 × 10⁻⁴ and ϰ(7/2, 7/2) ≈ 1.737 × 10⁻³. The constant is small because the interval (1/2, 1) is
short in the variable log s. Quadrature also tests the lower bound in the proof of Proposition 42.13 (b),
with 𝔱, A_a and φ_a as there, on an instance: the model metric (1 + r⁻²) dr² + r² g_(𝕊³) (that is, α = r⁻² and
β = 0), Ξ = 10⁻², (a, ℓ0) = (5/2, 7/2) and (7/2, 7/2), and R = 10², 10³, 10⁴. In all six cases the distance D_R of
r^(ℓ0)𝔱 from span(r^(ℓ0−2), r^(ℓ0−3)) in L²((R/2, R), dr/r) gives a ratio D_R/(Ξ R^(ℓ0−a)) within a relative 10⁻² of
2A_a dist(s^(ℓ0−a) cos(log s + log R + φ_a), span(s^(ℓ0−2), s^(ℓ0−3))) and above 2A_a ϰ(a, ℓ0). No proof uses these
values; only the positivity of Lemma 42.11 is used.

**Proposition 42.13** (Perturbations outside the class.) Let 3/2 < a ≤ ℓ0. Put r_2 := 2r_χ, take
a cut-off χ_1(r) equal to 0 for r ≤ r_2 and to 1 for r ≥ 2r_2, and let

    ζ_a(r) := r^(1−a) cos log r,    φ_Ξ(r) := r + Ξ χ_1(r) ζ_a(r),    Ψ_Ξ(x) := φ_Ξ(|x|) x/|x|,
    (γ_Ξ, k_Ξ) := Ψ_Ξ*(γ_λ, k_λ).

(a) There is Ξ1 > 0 such that for 0 < Ξ ≤ Ξ1, Ψ_Ξ is an O(4)-equivariant diffeomorphism of Σ, the identity on
{r ≤ r_2}, and (γ_Ξ, k_Ξ) is G-invariant smooth vacuum data, isometric to (γ_λ, k_λ), and a perturbation of order a and
size C_P Ξ.

(b) There are R_ob ≥ 4r_2 and c_P := (2π²)^(1/2) A_a ϰ(a, ℓ0), with A_a := ((4 − a)² + 1)^(1/2), such that for
0 < Ξ ≤ Ξ1, R ≥ R_ob and every d,

    N^((d))_R(γ_Ξ, k_Ξ) ≥ c_P Ξ R^(ℓ0−a)   (a < ℓ0),      N^((d))_R(γ_Ξ, k_Ξ) ≥ c_P Ξ (log₂(R/R_ob))^(1/2)   (a = ℓ0).
    (42.9)

(c) Hence (S) fails for (γ_Ξ, k_Ξ) at every Ξ ∈ (0, Ξ1]. For a < ℓ0, once R > max(R_ob, (δ/(c_P Ξ))^(1/(ℓ0−a))), no
data in the class that agree with (γ_Ξ, k_Ξ) on {r < R} have norm ‖·‖_(d_1) < δ; for a = ℓ0, once
R > R_ob 2^((δ/(c_P Ξ))²).

*Proof.* (a) |∂_r^j(χ_1 ζ_a)| ≤ C_j r^(1−a−j), so φ_Ξ′ ≥ 1/2 for Ξ ≤ Ξ1′ := min(1, (2 sup|(χ_1 ζ_a)′|)⁻¹). Also
φ_Ξ(r) = r for r ≤ r_2 and φ_Ξ(r) → ∞, so φ_Ξ is an increasing bijection of [r_♭, ∞) (Σ is identified with
{|x| ≥ r_♭}, Section 39.5) and Ψ_Ξ a diffeomorphism, with inverse
x ↦ φ_Ξ⁻¹(|x|) x/|x|, commuting with O(4). The constraint map is natural under diffeomorphisms, so the pull-back is
vacuum. It is G-invariant, as (γ_λ, k_λ) is and G ⊂ O(4). On {r ≥ r_2} ⊂ {r ≥ 4R_i}, which Ψ_Ξ maps to itself, the data
are (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)), which are O(4)-invariant (Lemma 39.16 (b)). An O(4)-invariant symmetric 2-tensor is
A(r) x̂ ⊗ x̂ + B(r)(δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂): the stabiliser O(3) of x̂ acts irreducibly on x̂^⊥ and fixes no vector there, so an
invariant symmetric bilinear form has no x̂ ⊗ x̂^⊥ part and is a multiple of the identity on x̂^⊥. By
Lemma 39.16 (a), α := A − 1 and β := B − 1 lie in ρ²C^∞, and k^(m_λ) = Ã x̂ ⊗ x̂ + B̃(δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂) with
Ã, B̃ ∈ ρ³C^∞. Since A x̂ ⊗ x̂ + B(δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂) = A dr² + B r² g_(𝕊³), a radial map r ↦ φ(r) pulls it back to

    Ψ*(A x̂ ⊗ x̂ + B(δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂)) = A(φ) φ′² x̂ ⊗ x̂ + B(φ) (φ²/r²)(δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂).    (42.10)

Hence h = [A(φ_Ξ) φ_Ξ′² − A] x̂ ⊗ x̂ + [B(φ_Ξ) φ_Ξ²/r² − B](δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂) on {r ≥ r_2} and h = 0 inside, and likewise κ
with (Ã, B̃). Write A(φ) φ′² − A = (φ′² − 1) + (α(φ) − α) φ′² + α(φ′² − 1), with α(φ) − α = Ξ χ_1 ζ_a ∫_0^1
α′(r + sΞ χ_1 ζ_a) ds. The three terms are conormal, with constants times Ξ, of orders a, a + 2 and a + 2; the B terms
likewise, and the (Ã, B̃) terms are of order a + 3. The components x̂_i x̂_j lie in C^∞ of the radial compactification.
So, for Ξ ≤ Ξ1′, (42.7) holds with C_P Ξ in place of Ξ, C_P not depending on Ξ, and with C_β Ξ at
all orders. Put Ξ1 := min(Ξ1′, C_P⁻¹); then for 0 < Ξ ≤ Ξ1 the size C_P Ξ lies in (0, 1], as
Definition 42.5 requires.

(b) Let R ≥ 4r_2 and let (γ′, k′) be admissible for N^((d))_R. Write u := γ′ − γ_λ as in
(42.6), and Γ := {R/2 < r < R}, which lies in {χ_c = 1} ∩ {χ_1 = 1} ∩ {r < R}. On Γ, u = h, so
ũ_ij = h_ij − ρ² u^((2))_ij(ω) − ρ³ u^((3))_ij(ω), and

    ‖(u, ·)‖_d ≥ Σ_(i,j) ‖r^(ℓ0) ũ_ij‖_(L²(Γ)) ≥ ‖r^(ℓ0) Σ_i ũ_ii‖_(L²(Γ)),     Σ_i ũ_ii = 𝔱(r) − ρ² b2(ω) − ρ³ b3(ω),

with 𝔱 := tr_δ h, which is radial, and b_z := tr u^((z)). Integrating first in r at fixed ω,

    ‖r^(ℓ0)(𝔱 − ρ² b2 − ρ³ b3)‖_(L²(Γ, dr/r dω))
        ≥ (2π²)^(1/2) inf_(β2,β3∈ℝ) ‖r^(ℓ0)(𝔱 − β2 r⁻² − β3 r⁻³)‖_(L²((R/2,R), dr/r)).

On Γ, φ_Ξ = r + Ξ ζ_a. By (42.10), 𝔱 = (φ_Ξ′² − 1) + 3(φ_Ξ²/r² − 1) + e_αβ, where e_αβ collects the
α and β terms. With φ_Ξ′ = 1 + Ξ ζ_a′, ζ_a′ = r^(−a)((1 − a) cos log r − sin log r), and φ_Ξ/r = 1 + Ξ r^(−a) cos log r,

    𝔱 = 2Ξ r^(−a)((4 − a) cos log r − sin log r) + Ξ² (ζ_a′² + 3 ζ_a²/r²) + e_αβ.

As in (a), |e_αβ| ≤ C Ξ r^(−2−a). Since 4 − a > 0, (4 − a) cos t − sin t = A_a cos(t + φ_a) with
φ_a := arctan(1/(4 − a)), so 𝔱 = 2Ξ A_a r^(−a) cos(log r + φ_a) + e with |e| ≤ C_e(Ξ r^(−2−a) + Ξ² r^(−2a)). Substitute
r = Rs, so that dr/r = ds/s and r^(ℓ0) β_z r^(−z) = β_z R^(ℓ0−z) s^(ℓ0−z). The main term contributes

    inf_β ‖r^(ℓ0)(2Ξ A_a r^(−a) cos(log r + φ_a) − β2 r⁻² − β3 r⁻³)‖
        = 2Ξ A_a R^(ℓ0−a) dist(s^(ℓ0−a) cos(log s + log R + φ_a), span(s^(ℓ0−2), s^(ℓ0−3))) ≥ 2Ξ A_a ϰ(a, ℓ0) R^(ℓ0−a)

by Lemma 42.11. On (R/2, R), r^(ℓ0−2−a) ≤ 2^(2+a) R^(ℓ0−2−a) and r^(ℓ0−2a) ≤ 2^(2a) R^(ℓ0−2a), so
‖r^(ℓ0) e‖_(L²((R/2,R), dr/r)) ≤ (log 2)^(1/2) C_e (2^(2+a) Ξ R^(ℓ0−2−a) + 2^(2a) Ξ² R^(ℓ0−2a)). For R ≥ R_ob this is at
most Ξ A_a ϰ R^(ℓ0−a), uniformly in Ξ ≤ 1, since R⁻² and R^(−a) tend to 0. By the triangle inequality the infimum is at
least Ξ A_a ϰ R^(ℓ0−a), which gives (42.9) for a < ℓ0. For a = ℓ0, apply the same to the disjoint
annuli Γ_j := {2^(−j−1) R < r < 2^(−j) R} with 2^(−j) R ≥ R_ob. The coefficients b2, b3 are common to all of them, so the
square of the norm over their union is at least the sum of the squares of the separate infima, each at least
(c_P Ξ)², over ⌊log₂(R/R_ob)⌋ + 1 ≥ log₂(R/R_ob) annuli.

(c) follows from (42.9) at d = d_1: N^((d_1))_R ≥ δ in the stated ranges, and N^((d_1))_R → ∞. ∎

**Remark 42.14** (What the examples show.) The examples are pure gauge. Their maximal
developments are isometric to that of the data of (i), so the obstruction lies in the norm of Theorem 3.9 (ii),
which a diffeomorphism of the initial surface does not preserve, and not in the geometry; settling itself is not confined
to the class. The examples are radial, hence G-invariant: the obstruction persists in the symmetry class of (i).
Proposition 42.9 holds for every perturbation, gauge or not; the examples serve only to show that at every
rate a ≤ ℓ0 some vacuum perturbation lies outside the class. The function
R ↦ dist(s^(ℓ0−a) cos(log s + log R + φ_a), span(s^(ℓ0−2), s^(ℓ0−3))) in the proof is periodic in log R with period 2π,
with minimum ϰ(a, ℓ0).

#### 42.4.5 The Myers–Perry data on Hintz's surface, and the upper bound

We use the family of Definition 39.5 with base mass μ_end: for p = (m, A, w, c) in its range, 𝔤_p = 𝒫_p* g^KS_(m,A) with
𝒫_p(y) = Λ_w y + (0, c), in coordinates (y⁰, y) of ℝ^(1+4), and (g_p, K_p) are its data on the slice {y⁰ = 0}. Let
(g̃_p, K̃_p) be the data that 𝔤_p induces on the graph {y⁰ = f(|y|)} over {|y| > R_F}, f as in (42.5),
identified with Σ ∩ {r > R_F} by x = y. Write p_λ := (m_λ, 0, 0, 0), p₂ := (m, w) and Δp := p − p_λ. Let 𝔔_X be the
charges of Proposition 39.3, 𝔟_X and q_X those of Lemma 39.2, and d(X) the degree of X in the basis (39.4). A
Cartesian derivative gains a power of ρ near infinity: since r²∂_i = x_i r∂_r + Σ_j x_j Ω_ji,

    ∂_i = ρ (ω_i r∂_r + Σ_j ω_j Ω_ji),    (42.11)

and as ω_j ∈ C^∞ and r∂_r, Ω_ji preserve ρ^p C^∞ of the radial compactification, ∂_i maps ρ^p C^∞ into ρ^(p+1) C^∞.

**Lemma 42.15** (The Myers–Perry data on Hintz's surface.) For R_F large:

(a) (g̃_p, K̃_p) are smooth vacuum data; g̃_p − δ ∈ ρ²C^∞ and K̃_p ∈ ρ³C^∞ of the compactified {r ≥ R_F}, smoothly in p;
and (g̃_(p_λ), K̃_(p_λ)) = (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)).

(b) The ρ² coefficient of g̃_p and the ρ³ coefficient of K̃_p depend on p only through p₂. Hence
g̃_p − γ^(m_λ) = ρ² a2(p) + ρ³ a3(p) + ρ⁴ ℛ0(p), with |a2|_(C^m(𝕊³)) ≤ C_m |Δp₂|
and |a3|_(C^m(𝕊³)) + ‖ℛ0‖_(C^m) ≤ C_m |Δp|; the same holds for K̃_p − k^(m_λ) with ρ³, ρ⁴, ρ⁵.

(c) The charge map 𝔮̃(p) := (𝔔_X(g̃_p, K̃_p))_X is C¹ and D𝔮̃(p_λ) is invertible. Its degree-0 part
𝔮̃_0 := (𝔔_(e₀), 𝔔_(e_l)), the energy and momentum, depends only on p₂, and p₂ ↦ 𝔮̃_0 has invertible derivative at
(m_λ, 0). So there are r_U, r_V and L with |Δp| ≤ L |𝔮̃(p) − 𝔮̃(p_λ)| and |Δp₂| ≤ L |𝔮̃_0(p) − 𝔮̃_0(p_λ)|
for |Δp| < r_U; and 𝔮̃ maps {|Δp| < r_U} homeomorphically onto a set containing the ball of radius r_V about 𝔮̃(p_λ). We
write p(Q) for the inverse.

(d) The members of Definition 39.5 on the slices {y⁰ = 0} satisfy g̃_p − g_p ∈ ρ³C^∞ and

    K̃_p − K_p = ∇²f + ρ⁴C^∞,      tr ∇²f = 2μ_end r⁻³ + O(r⁻⁵),    (42.12)

∇²f the Euclidean Hessian. If w = 0, then g̃_p − g_p ∈ ρ⁴C^∞ and K̃_p − K_p − ∇²f ∈ ρ⁵C^∞, smoothly in (m, A, c).
In particular K_(p_λ) − k^(m_λ) = −∇²f + ρ⁵C^∞ has a ρ³ coefficient of size μ_end, which does not depend on any
perturbation.

*Proof.* (a) g^KS_(m,A) − η = H_(m,A) k_A ⊗ k_A is independent of t, with H_(m,A) ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞ and the coefficients of k_A
in C^∞ of the compactification, smoothly in (m, A) (proof of Proposition 21.21). The map 𝒫_p is affine, and on the
graph the spatial point of 𝒫_p(f(|y|), y) is x(y) = L_w y + f(|y|) b_w + c, where L_w, the spatial block of Λ_w, is
invertible and b_w ∈ ℝ⁴. As T_(μ_end) ∈ |x|⁻¹C^∞ (Lemma 21.20 (a)), f lies in C^∞ of the compactification near
infinity, so |x(y)|⁻¹ = |y|⁻¹ |L_w ŷ + |y|⁻¹(f b_w + c)|⁻¹ is ρ times a smooth positive function of (ρ, ŷ), and x̂(y) is
smooth in (ρ, ŷ): y ↦ x(y) extends to a diffeomorphism near the boundary of the compactification and preserves
ρ^j C^∞. The components of 𝔤_p − η are those of g^KS_(m,A) − η composed with 𝒫_p and multiplied by the constant matrix
Λ_w; so on the graph they lie in ρ²C^∞, and by (42.11) their first derivatives lie in ρ³C^∞, smoothly
in p. The data of the graph are smooth functions of 𝔤_p and ∂𝔤_p at the graph and of ∂f ∈ ρ²C^∞ and ∂²f ∈ ρ³C^∞
((42.5)): the induced metric is g̃_ij = G_ij + G_(0i) ∂_jf + G_(0j) ∂_if + G_00 ∂_if ∂_jf, with G := 𝔤_p,
and the second fundamental form, given by (39.2) in the coordinates (y⁰ − f(|y|), y), is linear in (∂G, ∂²f) with
coefficients smooth in (G, ∂f). They equal (δ, 0) at G = η and f constant. This gives g̃_p − δ ∈ ρ²C^∞ and
K̃_p ∈ ρ³C^∞. For R_F large the graph is spacelike, as its conormal dy⁰ − df has 𝔤_p⁻¹-norm −1 + O(ρ²), and 𝔤_p is
Ricci-flat (Proposition 21.17), so the data are vacuum. At p_λ, 𝒫_(p_λ) = id and the data are (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) by
definition (Section 39.5).

(b) g^KS_(m,A) − g^KS_(m,0) ∈ |x|⁻³C^∞, since H_(m,A) − H_(m,0) ∈ |x|⁻⁴C^∞ and ℓ_A − ℓ_0 ∈ |x|⁻¹C^∞
(proof of Proposition 21.21). A translation changes a function F ∈ ρ²C^∞ by F(x + c) − F(x) = c · ∫_0^1 ∂F(x + sc)
ds ∈ ρ³C^∞, by (42.11). So 𝔤_p − 𝔤_((m,0,w,0)) ∈ ρ³C^∞ on the graph, in the sense of (a). On the graph,
g̃ − δ = (G − η)_ij(f, y) + ρ⁴C^∞, as the terms G_(0i) ∂_jf and G_00 ∂_if ∂_jf lie in ρ⁴C^∞; and
(G − η)_ij(f, y) − (G − η)_ij(0, y) = f ∫_0^1 ∂_0 G_ij(sf, y) ds ∈ ρ³C^∞. So the ρ² coefficient of g̃_p is that of
(𝔤_((m,0,w,0)) − η)_ij(0, y), a function of p₂. The ρ³ coefficient of K̃_p is that of the part of K̃_p linear in
∂𝔤_((m,0,w,0)) plus that of ∇²f, which does not depend on p. The bounds follow by the mean value theorem in p, the
coefficients being smooth in p and equal at p_λ to those of (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)), with a2 a function of p₂.

(d) In the coordinates y′⁰ := y⁰ − f(|y|), y′ := y, the graph is {y′⁰ = 0}, and with G := 𝔤_p the new shift, metric and
lapse are β′ = β + G_00 ∂f = β − ∂f + ρ⁴C^∞, g′ − g ∈ ρ⁴C^∞ and N′ − N ∈ ρ⁴C^∞, at the same point, since G_00 + 1, G_(0i)
and G^(0i) lie in ρ²C^∞ and ∂f ∈ ρ²C^∞. The values on the graph are taken at (f, y) instead of (0, y), and
G(f, y) − G(0, y) = f ∂_0 G(0, y) + ρ⁴C^∞, where ∂_0 G_p = O(|w| ρ³). Inserting these in (39.2), the term
−D′_iβ′_j − D′_jβ′_i contributes 2∂_i∂_j f + ρ⁵C^∞, and 1/(2N′) = 1/2 + ρ²C^∞, which gives K̃_p − K_p = ∇²f + ρ⁴C^∞
and g̃_p − g_p ∈ ρ³C^∞. At w = 0, G_p does not depend on y⁰, there is no change of the point of evaluation, and so
g̃_p − g_p = g′ − g ∈ ρ⁴C^∞ and K̃_p − K_p − ∇²f ∈ ρ⁵C^∞, smoothly in (m, A, c); this is used in (c). For the trace:
f is radial, ∇²f = f″ x̂ ⊗ x̂ + (f′/r)(δ − x̂ ⊗ x̂), and by (42.5) f′ = 2μ_end r⁻² + 2μ_end² r⁻⁴ + O(r⁻⁶),
so tr ∇²f = f″ + 3f′/r = (−4μ_end + 6μ_end) r⁻³ + O(r⁻⁵). At p_λ, (g_(p_λ), K_(p_λ)) are the data of g^KS_(m_λ,0) on
{t_KS = 0}, and their difference from (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) is the case w = 0 of the above, with the sign of ∇²f reversed.

(c) C¹ and O(4)-equivariance follow as in the proof of Proposition 39.7, since (a) gives the bounds of Lemma 39.6 and
the graph is O(4)-invariant. By Schur's lemma, as there, D𝔮̃(p_λ) consists of scalars c̃_E (from m to 𝔔_(e₀)) and c̃_J
(from A to (𝔔_(e_ab)), times I₆), and a matrix (ã11 ã12; ã21 ã22) ⊗ I₄ from (w, c) to (𝔔_(e_l), 𝔔_(e′_l)), with zero
elsewhere. We compare with the charges 𝔮 of the members (g_p, K_p), for which Proposition 39.7 gives, at
p_λ = (m_λ, 0, 0, 0), c_E = 6π², a11 = a22 = −6π²m_λ, a12 = 0 and c_J = −4π²m_λ; p_λ is a base point of the range of
Definition 39.5, as m_λ lies in I_m = [¾μ_end, (5/4)μ_end] (Section 39.5), so |m_λ − μ_end| < ½μ_end.

The flux 𝔟_X is linear in the data, a degree-0 flux of a change in ρ³C^∞ of the metric or ρ⁴C^∞ of K tends to 0
(ρ⁴ · r³ → 0), and the term ∇²f carries no momentum at any radius: (∇²f − Δf δ)x̂ = −3(f′/r) x̂, which is odd. So by (d),
𝔮̃_0 = 𝔮_0 for every p. By the argument of (b) on {y⁰ = 0}, g_p − g_((m,0,w,0)) ∈ ρ³C^∞ and K_p − K_((m,0,w,0)) ∈ ρ⁴C^∞,
so 𝔮_0(p) = 𝔮_0(m, 0, w, 0): the energy and momentum depend only on p₂. Hence c̃_E = c_E, ã11 = a11 and ã12 = a12 = 0. At
w = 0 the differences of the graph's data from the slice's are ρ⁴C^∞ in the metric and ∇²f + ρ⁵C^∞ in K, smoothly in
(m, A, c), by (d). The term ∇²f does not depend on p and carries no angular momentum: for W antisymmetric, (Wx) · x̂ = 0,
so (Wx) · ∇²f · x̂ = f″ (Wx) · x̂ = 0, and the trace term of the flux vanishes too. The degree-1 fluxes of the A- and
c-derivatives of the rest tend to 0, as r · ρ⁵ · r³ → 0 and ρ⁴ · r³ → 0. So c̃_J = c_J and ã22 = a22, and det
D𝔮̃(p_λ) = c̃_E (ã11 ã22)⁴ c̃_J⁶ = 6π² (6π² m_λ)⁸ (4π² m_λ)⁶ ≠ 0. The p₂-block of D𝔮̃_0 is diag(c_E, a11 I₄), invertible.
The rest is the inverse function theorem. ∎

So, by Lemma 38.25, whose proof applies at every order, a smooth vacuum data set on Σ that agrees for r large with
the data (g̃_p, K̃_p) of a nearby translated, rotated and boosted Myers–Perry metric differs from (γ_λ, k_λ) by an
element of the class: the class contains these data on Hintz's own surface. On the slices {y⁰ = 0} of Definition 39.5 the
data (g_p, K_p) of the same metrics lie in the class too, as g_p − δ ∈ ρ²C^∞ and K_p ∈ ρ³C^∞ far out by (a) and (d) (∇²f
∈ ρ³C^∞), but not near (γ_λ, k_λ): by (d), already at p_λ the second fundamental form differs from k^(m_λ) by a fixed
term of order r⁻³, of size μ_end, so the members of Definition 39.5 are at a distance from (γ_λ, k_λ), in the norm of the
class, that no smallness of a perturbation removes. This is why the gluing below takes its family on Σ, as
Proposition 39.17 does in the class. That the mass and the boost are fixed by the energy and momentum alone (c) is what
makes the coefficient of ρ² of the glued data decay with R when a > 2 ((42.14) below).

**Lemma 42.16** (Charges.) (a) For a pair (h, K) of symmetric 2-tensors put
𝔪(h, K) := Σ_(|β|≤2) r^(|β|) |∂^β h| + Σ_(|β|≤1) r^(1+|β|) |∂^β K|. For data z_i = (δ + h_i, K_i), i = 1, 2, write
𝔪(z_i) := 𝔪(h_i, K_i) and z_1 − z_2 := (h_1 − h_2, K_1 − K_2). If |h_i| ≤ 1/2 and 𝔪(z_i) ≤ 1 for i = 1, 2, then

    |q_X(z_1) − q_X(z_2)| ≤ C (1 + r)^(d(X)) r⁻² (𝔪(z_1) + 𝔪(z_2)) 𝔪(z_1 − z_2).    (42.13)

(b) For a perturbation of order a and size Ξ, with Δ𝔔_X := 𝔔_X(γ, k) − 𝔮̃_X(p_λ): Δ𝔔_X = 0 if a > 2 + d(X),
and |Δ𝔔_X| ≤ C_1′ Ξ in every case.

*Proof.* (a) By the proof of Lemma 39.2, q_X is linear in (N, Y), with |N| + |Y| ≤ C(1 + r)^(d(X)). The scalar
curvature is g⁻¹g⁻¹∂²h + g⁻¹g⁻¹g⁻¹ ∂h ∂h, the K-terms of ρ are quadratic in K with coefficients smooth in h, J is
g⁻¹∂K + g⁻¹g⁻¹ ∂h K, and (det g)^(1/2) is smooth in h, where g⁻¹ is a smooth function of h on {|h| ≤ 1/2}.
Subtracting the linear part, q_X is a sum of terms c(h)·P, the factor N or Y included in c, with c smooth on
{|h| ≤ 1/2} and of size at most C(1 + r)^(d(X)) with its h-derivative, where either P is quadratic, one of ∂h ∂h,
∂h K, K K, or P is linear, ∂²h or ∂K, and then c(0) = 0. By the definition of 𝔪, |∂h|, |K| ≤ r⁻¹𝔪
and |∂²h|, |∂K| ≤ r⁻²𝔪. So a quadratic P has |P(z_1)| ≤ r⁻² 𝔪(z_1)² and, being
bilinear, |P(z_1) − P(z_2)| ≤ r⁻² (𝔪(z_1) + 𝔪(z_2)) 𝔪(z_1 − z_2); a linear P has |P(z_1)| ≤ r⁻² 𝔪(z_1)
and |P(z_1) − P(z_2)| ≤ r⁻² 𝔪(z_1 − z_2). The mean value theorem on the convex set {|h| ≤ 1/2}
gives |c(h_1) − c(h_2)| ≤ C(1 + r)^(d(X)) |h_1 − h_2| ≤ C(1 + r)^(d(X)) 𝔪(z_1 − z_2), and |c(h_2)| ≤ C(1 + r)^(d(X)),
or |c(h_2)| ≤ C(1 + r)^(d(X)) |h_2| ≤ C(1 + r)^(d(X)) 𝔪(z_2) when c(0) = 0. Now
c(h_1)P(z_1) − c(h_2)P(z_2) = (c(h_1) − c(h_2)) P(z_1) + c(h_2)(P(z_1) − P(z_2)). For a quadratic P the first term is
at most C(1 + r)^(d(X)) r⁻² 𝔪(z_1 − z_2) 𝔪(z_1)², which is at most C(1 + r)^(d(X)) r⁻² 𝔪(z_1 − z_2) 𝔪(z_1) as
𝔪(z_1) ≤ 1, and the second at most C(1 + r)^(d(X)) r⁻² (𝔪(z_1) + 𝔪(z_2)) 𝔪(z_1 − z_2). For a linear P the two terms
are at most C(1 + r)^(d(X)) r⁻² 𝔪(z_1 − z_2) 𝔪(z_1) and C(1 + r)^(d(X)) r⁻² 𝔪(z_2) 𝔪(z_1 − z_2). Summing over the
finitely many terms gives (42.13).

(b) 𝔔_X(γ, k) exists by Proposition 39.3 with α = min(a, 2) > 3/2: (γ_λ, k_λ) = (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) far out
(Lemma 39.16 (a)), and (h, κ) satisfies (42.7). Also 𝔮̃_X(p_λ) = 𝔔_X(γ_λ, k_λ), the two data sets
agreeing for r ≥ 4R_i. Write d_X := d(X). As 𝔟_X is linear, Δ𝔔_X = lim_ϱ ∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(h, κ),
and |∮_(S_ϱ) 𝔟_X(h, κ)| ≤ C Ξ ϱ^(2+d_X−a), which tends to 0 if a > 2 + d_X. In general, 𝔪(γ_λ − δ, k_λ) ≤ C r⁻²
and |γ_λ − δ| ≤ C r⁻² on {r ≥ r_χ}, as (γ_λ, k_λ) = (γ^(m_λ), k^(m_λ)) there, and 𝔪(h, κ) ≤ C Ξ r^(−a) and |h| ≤ Ξ r^(−a)
by (42.7). Take R_λ ≥ max(r_χ, R_F, 1) so large that, on {r ≥ R_λ}, |γ − δ|, |γ_λ − δ| ≤ ½ and
𝔪(γ − δ, k), 𝔪(γ_λ − δ, k_λ) ≤ 1; this is possible as 𝔪 is subadditive and Ξ ≤ 1, and R_λ does not depend on the
perturbation. Subtract the flux identity (39.5) for (γ_λ, k_λ) on Γ(R_λ, ϱ) from that for (γ, k); both are
vacuum, and both satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 39.2 and of (42.13) there. By
(42.13), |Δ𝔔_X| ≤ C Ξ R_λ^(2+d_X−a) + C Ξ ∫_(R_λ)^∞ r^(d_X−2)(r⁻² + Ξ r^(−a)) r^(−a) r³ dr. The
integrand is O(r^(d_X−1−a) + r^(d_X+1−2a)), and for d_X ∈ {0, 1} and a > 3/2 both exponents are below −1:
d_X − 1 − a ≤ −a < −1 and d_X + 1 − 2a ≤ 2 − 2a < −1. ∎

**Proposition 42.17** (Gluing to the Myers–Perry data on Hintz's surface, with the error.) Let
3/2 < a ≤ ℓ0 and k_g := d_1 + 2, the order of the gluing. There are R_G, Ξ0 and C with the following property. For every
perturbation (γ, k) of order a and size Ξ ≤ Ξ0, and every R ≥ R_G, there are p_R and smooth vacuum data (γ̂_R, k̂_R) on
Σ, equal to (γ, k) on {r ≤ R} and to (g̃_(p_R), K̃_(p_R)) on {r ≥ 4R}, with

    |Δp_(R,2)| ≤ C Ξ R^(min(0, 2−a)),      |Δp_R| ≤ C Ξ R^(min(0, 3−a)),    (42.14)

    sup_(R≤r≤4R) ( Σ_(|β|≤k_g−1) r^(|β|) |∂^β(γ̂_R − γ_λ)| + Σ_(|β|≤k_g−2) r^(1+|β|) |∂^β(k̂_R − k_λ)| ) ≤ C Ξ R^(−a).
    (42.15)

*Proof.* We follow the proof of Theorem 39.13, with k_g in place of 3 as in Proposition 39.17
(the solvability statement Lemma 39.10 allows every integer above n/2), the data being (γ, k) on
{r > max(R_F, r_χ)}, and we make six changes. By (42.7), |||(γ, k)|||_(min(a,2), k_g+4) < ∞
((39.3)), as k_g + 4 = d_1 + 6.

(1) *The family and the box.* The members (g̃_p, K̃_p) of Lemma 42.15 replace those of Definition 39.5:
its (a) gives the bounds of Lemma 39.6 and its (c) the inverse p(Q) of Corollary 39.8. In Step 2 let Q range over the
box 𝔅_R := {Q : |Q_X − 𝔮̃_X(p_λ)| ≤ r_X for every X}, with r_X := C_0 Ξ R^(min(0, 2+d(X)−a)) and C_0 := C_1′ + 1. Then
𝔅_R lies in the ball of radius r_V once √15 C_0 Ξ0 < r_V. The five degree-0 radii are C_0 Ξ R^(min(0,2−a)), and the ten
others C_0 Ξ R^(min(0,3−a)), the larger. So for Q ∈ 𝔅_R, Lemma 42.15 (c)
gives |Δp₂| ≤ √5 L C_0 Ξ R^(min(0,2−a)) and |Δp| ≤ √15 L C_0 Ξ R^(min(0,3−a)), where Δp := p(Q) − p_λ.

(2) *The constraint defect in relative form.* On 𝒜 = Γ̄(1, 4) write a_R := 𝒮_R(γ, k) and
b_Q := 𝒮_R(g̃_(p(Q)), K̃_(p(Q))), with 𝒮_R of Lemma 39.4. Both are vacuum, and the approximate data of Step 2 are
u_(Q,R) = b_Q + χ(a_R − b_Q). The constraint map is smooth near flat data and vanishes at b_Q, so
‖(J, ρ)(u_(Q,R))‖_(C^(k_g+1)) ≤ C ‖a_R − b_Q‖_(C^(k_g+3) × C^(k_g+4)) ≤ C 𝔢_R(Q), with

    𝔢_R(Q) := Ξ R^(−a) + |Δp₂| R⁻² + |Δp| R⁻³ ≤ C (1 + C_0) Ξ R^(−a).    (42.16)

Here we used the scaling ‖𝒮_R u‖_(C^m(𝒜)) ≤ C sup_(R≤r≤4R) Σ_(|β|≤m) r^(|β|) |∂^β u|
(one more power of r for the second fundamental form), the bounds (42.7) for a_R − 𝒮_R(γ_λ, k_λ), and
Lemma 42.15 (b) for b_Q − 𝒮_R(γ_λ, k_λ), as (g̃_(p_λ), K̃_(p_λ)) = (γ_λ, k_λ) on {r ≥ R}. The inequality
in (42.16) holds by (1): min(0, 2 − a) − 2 ≤ −a and min(0, 3 − a) − 3 ≤ −a. By the bound of Step 1 and
Lemma 39.11, ‖δu_(Q,R)‖_(C^(k_g−1)(𝒜)) ≤ C ‖δu_(Q,R)‖_(H^(k_g+2)(𝒜)) ≤ C 𝔢_R(Q), continuously in Q. So the unscaled
data 𝔵̂_Q := 𝒮_R⁻¹(u_(Q,R) + δu_(Q,R)) on Γ(R, 4R) satisfy the bound of (42.15) by C 𝔢_R(Q) against
(γ_λ, k_λ); they are the sum of χ times the deviation of the data, (1 − χ) times that of the member, and δu. The
hypotheses of Step 1 hold for R large, as u_(Q,R) is within C R⁻² + C Ξ R^(−a) of flat data.

(3) *Step 4 in relative form.* Lemma 39.4 and (39.5) give G_R(Q)_X := R^(2+d(X)) F_R(Q)_X = ∮_(S_(4R))
𝔟_X(𝔵̂_Q) − ∮_(S_R) 𝔟_X(𝔵̂_Q) + ∫_(Γ(R,4R)) q_X(𝔵̂_Q). Near S_(4R) the data are the member's, near S_R the
perturbation's. By the flux identity on the vacuum regions outside, ∮_(S_(4R)) 𝔟_X = Q_X + ∫_(r>4R) q_X(member) and
∮_(S_R) 𝔟_X = 𝔔_X(γ, k) + ∫_(r>R) q_X(γ, k). Subtracting the identity 0 = ∫_(r>4R) q_X − ∫_(r>R) q_X + ∫_(Γ(R,4R)) q_X
for (γ_λ, k_λ),

    G_R(Q)_X = Q_X − 𝔮̃_X(p_λ) − Δ𝔔_X + T_X(Q),

where T_X(Q) is the sum of ∫_(r>4R)[q_X(member) − q_X(γ_λ, k_λ)], −∫_(r>R)[q_X(γ, k) − q_X(γ_λ, k_λ)] and
∫_(Γ(R,4R))[q_X(𝔵̂_Q) − q_X(γ_λ, k_λ)]. The reference (γ_λ, k_λ) has 𝔪(γ_λ − δ, k_λ) ≤ C r⁻²
and |γ_λ − δ| ≤ C r⁻² on {r ≥ R}; the member differs from it by 𝔪(member − reference) ≤ C(|Δp₂| r⁻² + |Δp| r⁻³) on
{r ≥ 4R} (Lemma 42.15 (b)), the perturbation by 𝔪(h, κ) ≤ C Ξ r^(−a) on {r ≥ R}, and 𝔵̂_Q by C 𝔢_R on
the annulus, by (2). As |Δp| < r_U and Ξ ≤ 1, we take R_G so large that, on {r ≥ R}, the four data sets (the
reference, the member, (γ, k) and 𝔵̂_Q) satisfy the hypotheses of (42.13) and of Lemma 39.2
wherever they are used. By (42.13), with these bounds and d_X := d(X),

    |T_X(Q)| ≤ C R^(d_X) (|Δp₂| R⁻² + |Δp| R⁻³) + C Ξ (R^(d_X−a) + Ξ R^(d_X+2−2a)) + C R^(d_X) (𝔢_R + R² 𝔢_R²).

By (1) and (42.16), each term is C(1 + C_0)² Ξ times one of R^(d_X−2+min(0,2−a)),
R^(d_X−3+min(0,3−a)), R^(d_X−a) and R^(d_X+2−2a). Each of these exponents is strictly below E := min(0, 2 + d_X − a),
for d_X ∈ {0, 1} and 3/2 < a ≤ ℓ0 < 4. Indeed d_X − a < 0 and d_X − a < 2 + d_X − a; d_X + 2 − 2a < 0, as
2a > 3 ≥ d_X + 2, and d_X + 2 − 2a < 2 + d_X − a; d_X − 2 + min(0, 2 − a) ≤ d_X − 2 < 0 and ≤ d_X − a; and
d_X − 3 + min(0, 3 − a) ≤ d_X − 3 < 0 and ≤ d_X − a. So for R ≥ R_G, |T_X(Q)| ≤ Ξ R^E on 𝔅_R.

(4) *The charges.* By Lemma 42.16 (b), Δ𝔔_X = 0 if a > 2 + d(X), and |Δ𝔔_X| ≤ C_1′ Ξ otherwise.

(5) *A zero by Brouwer's fixed point theorem* (in place of Lemma 39.12). Let Θ(Q) := 𝔮̃(p_λ) + Δ𝔔 − T(Q). By (3) and
(4), |Θ_X(Q) − 𝔮̃_X(p_λ)| ≤ r_X on 𝔅_R: if a ≤ 2 + d_X this reads C_1′ Ξ + Ξ = C_0 Ξ, and if a > 2 + d_X it reads
0 + Ξ R^(2+d_X−a). Θ is continuous, by Step 3 of the proof of Theorem 39.13 and Lemma 39.11, and 𝔅_R is a product
of closed intervals, so Θ has a fixed point Q_R. Then G_R(Q_R) = 0, and by Step 3 the data u_(Q_R,R) + δu_(Q_R,R)
are vacuum.

(6) *Conclusion.* Step 5 of the proof of Theorem 39.13 gives the smooth vacuum data, with p_R := p(Q_R). Then
(42.14) is (1), and (42.15) is (2) with (42.16). ∎

**Remark 42.18** (Why the box does not shrink.) For a ≤ 2 + d(X) the charge difference Δ𝔔_X is O(Ξ) and
need not vanish, so the radius r_X cannot tend to 0 with R. For instance, with d(X) = 1, pull the data of (i) back by x ↦
x + χ_1(|x|) c for a small constant c ∈ ℝ⁴, χ_1 as in Proposition 42.13. This is a vacuum perturbation, pure
gauge, of order 3 = 2 + d(X): by (42.11), γ^(m_λ)(x + c) − γ^(m_λ)(x) ∈ ρ³C^∞. Its centre-of-mass charges
are Δ𝔔_(e′_l) = −6π² m_λ c_l + O(|c|²): they involve the metric only, the metric on Σ differs from that on the
Kerr–Schild slice by ρ⁴C^∞ (Lemma 42.15 (d) at w = 0), whose translation derivative contributes no
degree-1 flux, and the derivative of the slice charges at p_λ is a22 = −6π² m_λ (Proposition 39.7). This does not depend
on R, so a box of radius tending to 0 would exclude it. The same example lies in the class: its difference from (γ_λ,
k_λ) lies in ρ³C^∞ × ρ⁴C^∞ far out, so in ℋ^∞ by Lemma 38.25, whose proof applies at every order.

**Corollary 42.19** (The norm of the glued data.) In Proposition 42.17,
(γ̂_R − γ_λ, k̂_R − k_λ) ∈ ℋ^∞ and

    ‖(γ̂_R − γ_λ, k̂_R − k_λ)‖_(d_1) ≤ C Ξ (1 + R^(ℓ0−a))   (a < ℓ0),      ≤ C Ξ (1 + log R)^(1/2)   (a = ℓ0).
    (42.17)

So Theorem 3.9 (ii) applies to the glued data when C Ξ (1 + R^(ℓ0−a)) < δ. For a < ℓ0, as 1 + R^(ℓ0−a) ≤ 2R^(ℓ0−a)
for R ≥ 1, this holds for R_G ≤ R < (δ/(2CΞ))^(1/(ℓ0−a)), a range that is nonempty when 2CΞ R_G^(ℓ0−a) < δ; at a = ℓ0 it
holds for R ≥ R_G with log R < (δ/(CΞ))² − 1. For the perturbations of Proposition 42.13, to which
Proposition 42.17 applies when also C_P Ξ ≤ Ξ0, no data in the class that agree with them on {r < R} do better
than (42.9), so for them the order of the window is attained.

*Proof.* Membership: the data are smooth, and for r ≥ 4R the difference is
(g̃_(p_R) − γ^(m_λ), K̃_(p_R) − k^(m_λ)) ∈ ρ²C^∞ × ρ³C^∞ (Lemma 42.15 (a)), which lies in the class by
Lemma 38.25, whose proof applies at every order. For the norm let u := γ̂_R − γ_λ and use |Au| ≤ C Σ_(|β|≤d_1)
r^(|β|) |∂^β u| as in the proof of Proposition 42.7. The coefficients of u in (42.6) are
those of g̃_(p_R) − γ^(m_λ) (Lemma 42.4), namely a2(p_R) and a3(p_R), of size at most C|Δp_R| ≤ C Ξ
(Lemma 42.15 (b), (42.14)). The remainder ũ = u − χ_c(ρ² a2 + ρ³ a3) splits by region.

- r ≤ 2r_χ: u = h, of norm at most C Ξ.
- r_χ < r < R: ũ = h − χ_c(ρ² a2 + ρ³ a3). Its norm is at most C Ξ ‖r^(ℓ0−a)‖_(L²((r_χ,R), dr/r)) +
  C |Δp₂| ‖r^(ℓ0−2)‖ + C |Δp| ‖r^(ℓ0−3)‖, so at most C Ξ R^(ℓ0−a), or C Ξ (log R)^(1/2) at a = ℓ0, by
  (42.14), since min(0, 2 − a) + ℓ0 − 2 ≤ ℓ0 − a and min(0, 3 − a) + ℓ0 − 3 ≤ ℓ0 − a.
- R ≤ r ≤ 4R: |Aũ| ≤ C Ξ R^(−a) + C |Δp₂| R⁻² + C |Δp| R⁻³ ≤ C Ξ R^(−a), by (42.15) (k_g − 1 > d_1)
  and (42.16); so the norm there is at most C Ξ R^(ℓ0−a) (log 4)^(1/2).
- r ≥ 4R: ũ = ρ⁴ ℛ0(p_R), so the norm is at most C |Δp_R| (4R)^(ℓ0−4) (2(4 − ℓ0))^(−1/2) ≤ C Ξ.

The same holds for k̂_R − k_λ, with the weight ℓ0 + 1, the order a + 1 and the exponents 3 and 4. ∎

**Remark 42.20** (The cost of a bump.) The annulus term of Corollary 42.19 at a = 3 is
the cost of a bump of relative size R⁻¹ at radius R, read against the deviation of Tangherlini's data there
(μ r⁻² in the metric, μ r⁻³ in the second fundamental form): f_R := R⁻³ ψ(r/R) and k_R := R⁻⁴ ψ(r/R), ψ ∈ C_c^∞((0, ∞)).
With r = Rs,

    ‖r^(ℓ0) f_R‖²_(L²(dr/r dω)) = 2π² R^(2ℓ0−6) ∫_0^∞ s^(2ℓ0) ψ(s)² ds/s,

and the weight r^(ℓ0+1) on k_R gives the same power of R. As (r∂_r)^j (ψ(r/R)) = ((s∂_s)^j ψ)(r/R), every b-derivative
scales alike, so the bump has norm of order R^(ℓ0−3) in the class, which grows with R. This is the bound mentioned in
Remark 39.18. Proposition 42.13 supplies the matching lower bound, valid for every data set in the
class that agrees with the examples, and not only for the glued one.

#### 42.4.6 The reach of the settling theorem

**Theorem 42.21** (Which perturbations Theorem 3.9 (ii) reaches.) Fix ℓ0 ∈ (3, 4),
ε < ε_K, ε_m > 0, d_1, λ ≤ λ1, the data of (i) and δ as in Theorem 3.9, and let a > 3/2.

(i) If a > ℓ0, every perturbation of order a and size Ξ < δ/(C_1(1 + (a − ℓ0)^(−1/2))) lies in the class with
‖·‖_(d_1) < δ. So Theorem 3.9 (ii) applies to it directly, and (S) and (S_∞) hold with the perturbation itself as
the data on every ball. Over the admissible ℓ0 of Theorem 3.9, this covers every a > 3
(Corollary 42.8).

(ii) If 3/2 < a ≤ ℓ0, the decay rate does not decide. (S_∞) holds for a perturbation exactly when it lies in the class
with ‖·‖_(d_1) < δ, and (S) only if it lies in the class at regularity d_1 (Corollary 42.10). At every
such a and every Ξ ∈ (0, Ξ1], some perturbation of order a and size C_P Ξ fails (S): every data set in the class that
agrees with it on {r < R} has norm at least c_P Ξ R^(ℓ0−a), or c_P Ξ (log₂(R/R_ob))^(1/2) at a = ℓ0
(Proposition 42.13). The gluing of Proposition 42.17 does no worse than this order for every
perturbation of order a (Corollary 42.19), and attains it for these examples.

So the statement "Theorem 3.9 (ii) applies up to the gluing" is false for fixed Ξ and large R at every
a ∈ (3/2, ℓ0]; its form uniform in R is equivalent to (ii) applied directly; and the perturbations to which
Theorem 3.9 (ii) applies, directly or through gluing uniformly in R, are exactly those small in Hintz's class.

*Proof.* (i) is Proposition 42.7 with Corollary 42.8, and (ii) is
Corollary 42.10 with Proposition 42.13, Proposition 42.17 and
Corollary 42.19. ∎

That the rate does not decide below the threshold is seen from both sides. Perturbations of order a ≤ ℓ0 can lie in
the class: the translation pull-back of Remark 42.18 has order 3 and lies in it, and the glued data of
Corollary 42.19 have order 2 and lie in it. Others of the same orders lie outside it
(Proposition 42.13). Settling itself is not confined to the class, since the examples of
Proposition 42.13 have developments isometric to that of (i) (Remark 42.14). The
development of glued data is not the perturbation's: the two data sets differ on {r > R}, and the late-time solution
near the hole depends on them.

## 43. The interior after the shell

Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.7 and Theorem 3.8 are made on D_T, on Ω and on the past domain of
Theorem 3.7, whose inner boundary r = a lies a fixed distance inside x_K = 1; Theorem 3.9 is stated
outside the black hole. Two regions lie beyond. Inside x_K = 1, where the curvature exceeds the scale l5, nothing is
claimed. The second region is the interior after the time T: q_end ≤ r < μ_end^(1/2), v > v_end + T, below the event
horizon and above the curvature boundary, for all later times. This chapter shows that the development of
Theorem 3.9 (i) covers it. With the inner radius of the stability theory lowered below the curvature boundary,
the development is defined on all of {r ≥ q_end} to the future of its initial surface, for every final mass, its
constants then depending on that mass, and it settles there at the rate of Theorem 3.9 (Proposition 43.2).
Glued along the part of Σ^IVP between that inner radius and the gluing radius, where the two induce the same data, it
and g_λ form one vacuum spacetime for λ small, and the two developments of those data are isometric on their maximal
common globally hyperbolic development, which contains a neighbourhood of that part and whose reach is left open
(Lemma 43.5). The last section locates the first step towards the continuation of g_λ's own
data, the past domain of dependence of the far part of the initial surface (Lemma 43.9), and defines a
data class wider than that of Theorem 3.9 (ii) by half-integer orders (Definition 43.11), in which
Chapter 44 proves that the development of g_λ's own data settles.

*Notation.* b₀ := (μ_end, 0), so that the mass m₀ of the stability theory is μ_end and R₁ = μ_end^(1/2) = r_h, the radius
of the horizon of g_(b₀). q_end := (√72 μ_end l5²)^(1/4) is the radius of the curvature boundary x_K = 1 of the
background after the shell (Section 2.3); as μ_end ≥ μ0 ≥ √72 l5², q_end ≤ R₁. The inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁], the
spacetime M of (21.22), its coordinates (t, x), the functions T_m, ψ and ψ_IVP, the time functions t_* and
t_IVP, the initial surface Σ^IVP := t_IVP⁻¹(0) and the radius R₃ beyond which t_IVP = t − C″ are those of Chapter 21
((21.27), (21.30), Lemma 21.22). Since ψ_IVP = ψ on [r_♭, 5R₁] and ψ′ > 0 on [3R₁, ∞), R₃ ≥ 5R₁.
Ω_*, t^♭_* and T̂ are those of Section 38.1 and Proposition 38.4, and 𝒟_0 := 𝒟_(0,0) is the region 𝒟_(S,S⁰) of
Proposition 38.4 at (S, S⁰) = (0, 0); φ_(0,0) = ψ_0 ∘ φ_0 ((38.1)) is the identity, its factors being the
time-1 flows of the vector fields V(0) and V⁰(0) of Lemma 21.26 and Lemma 32.2 (a), which are zero, these
fields being linear in S. The domain Ω′ of the form (2.8) with constants (T′, δ′_0), a′ := q0 − δ′_0,
V′ := v_end + T′ and τ′_end := max_(v ≤ V′)(v − r_q(v)), the constant c₀ of the chart
(t, x) = (τ + T_(μ_end)(|x|) + c₀, x), which places Σ^IVP in the coordinates (τ, x) of Section 2.2, and the
gluing radius R ≥ R₃ are those of Lemma 41.4 and Theorem 41.1; Ω′_+ := Ω′ ∩ {v ≥ v_end + 1}.
G = O(2) × O(2) is the group of Section 38.8.

### 43.1 The development inside the black hole

On {|x| ≤ 2R₁}, χ_∞ = 0, so T_m is constant and ψ′ = 1 there: g_(b₀) is the Kerr–Schild Tangherlini metric
η + (μ_end/r²)(dt + dr)² translated in time, and dt_* = dt − dr. With f := 1 − μ_end/r², its inverse has
g⁻¹(dr, dr) = f, g⁻¹(dt, dr) = μ_end/r² and g⁻¹(dt, dt) = −1 − μ_end/r² (Lemma 21.16 (d)). Hence

    g⁻¹(dt − dr, dt − dr) = −1 − 3μ_end/r² + f = −4μ_end/r² < 0,

so the level sets of t_* are spacelike at every r ∈ (0, 2R₁]. The time orientation is the one in which dt_* is past
timelike; g⁻¹(dt, dt_*) = −1 − 2μ_end/r² < 0, so dt is past timelike too. On 0 < r < r_h, f < 0 and dr is timelike,
and g⁻¹(dt, dr) > 0 puts it in the cone opposite to dt: dr is future timelike, and r decreases along future causal
curves. At every inner radius r_♭ ≤ ½R₁,

    f(r_♭) = 1 − μ_end/r_♭² ≤ 1 − 4 = −3,

so the inner boundary {r = r_♭} of M is spacelike, for every final mass.

The stability theory is written for every inner radius r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] (Chapter 21, Definition 22.1, Chapter 24,
Chapter 38); in Chapter 24 the inner radius r_♯ of the analysis near the black hole is r_♭ (Section 24.6.1). One
explicit fact at small radii is the sign of the damping 1-form, which Proposition 24.10 gives at m = 1: (i) at every
r > 0, and (ii) on (0, 99.375], which ends just inside the saddle point r_0 = 100 of the 1-form. The next lemma writes
out the inequalities on the inner piece of the 1-form, all of them strict.

**Lemma 43.1** (The damping 1-form inside half the horizon radius.) Let m = 1, so that r_h = 1 (the
case μ_end = 1), let g and c be as in Proposition 24.10, and e its constant. On the piece 0 < r ≤ 50 of
(24.15), c = α(dt + ¼ dr) with α = 1/200, and for every r in (0, 50]

    g⁻¹(c, c) = α²(−3/2 + (9/16) f) < 0,    g⁻¹(c, dt) = α(−7/4 + (3/4) f) < −α,    g⁻¹(c, dr) = α(¼ + (3/4) r⁻²) > 0;

on 0 < r < r_h = 1, moreover, f e g⁻¹(c, c) + 2(1 − e) g⁻¹(c, dr)² > 0. These are (i) and (ii) of Proposition 24.10 on
(0, r_h/2], and ℓ(−dr) is negative definite there (Proposition 24.8 (i)). By scaling, the same holds at every mass.

*Proof.* With g^(tt) = −(2 − f), g^(tr) = 1 − f and g^(rr) = f, a form c = α(dt + b dr) has
α⁻²g⁻¹(c, c) = −2 + 2b + f(1 − b)², α⁻¹g⁻¹(c, dt) = −(2 − b) + f(1 − b) and α⁻¹g⁻¹(c, dr) = 1 − f + fb. At b = ¼
these are −3/2 + (9/16)f, −7/4 + (3/4)f and 1 − (3/4)f = ¼ + (3/4)r⁻². As f < 1, the first is below −3/2 + 9/16 < 0
and the second below −1; so c is timelike and in the cone of dt, which is past, and r c is past timelike. The third is
positive at every r > 0. On 0 < r < 1, f < 0, so f e g⁻¹(c, c) > 0, and 2(1 − e) g⁻¹(c, dr)² > 0. ∎

**Proposition 43.2** (The development reaches the curvature boundary inside the black hole.) Fix l5, μ0, A,
env and τ0 as in Theorem 3.9, take its inner radius to be

    r_♭ := ½ min(R₁, q_end) = ½ q_end,

and let its other constants be chosen, in its order, at this r_♭. Then for λ ≤ λ1 the G-invariant vacuum development g
of Theorem 3.9 (i) is defined on

    M ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} = {|x| ≥ r_♭, t_IVP ≥ 0} ⊃ {r ≥ q_end, t_IVP ≥ 0},

the whole coordinate region outside the curvature boundary x_K = 1 of the background after the shell, to the future of
Σ^IVP, for all later times. Its data on Σ^IVP differ from those of g_(b₀) by at most Cλ in the norm of
Theorem 38.22, and for every R′ and i, β there are C and T_1 with

    |(t_*∂_(t_*))^i ∂^β_x (g − g_(m′,0))| ≤ C t_*^(−2−ε)     on {q_end ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T_1},

m′ and ε being those of Theorem 3.9. This holds for every final mass μ_end; λ1, δ and the constants depend on
r_♭, hence on μ_end. The part {r_♭ ≤ r < q_end} of the domain lies beyond the curvature boundary.

*Proof.* *The inner radius.* r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] since q_end ≤ R₁, and Theorem 41.1 holds at every such
inner radius, its choices depending on r_♭ (Section 41.3); its g is the development of Theorem 3.9 (i). The
stability theory it rests on is written at every r_♭ ∈ (0, ½R₁] (Chapter 21, Definition 22.1, Chapter 24,
Chapter 38), the inner radius r_♯ of Section 24.6.1 being r_♭. The radius enters it through choices of small
constants, which exist at every r_♭ > 0 and depend on it, and through four facts at the inner radius, each of which
holds at r_♭: the Kerr–Schild family is defined on {|x| ≥ ½r_♭} (Lemma 21.19); ψ ≥ 0, and dt_* and dt_IVP
are timelike on {|x| ≥ r_♭} (Lemma 21.22); dr is future timelike inside the horizon for g_(b₀), as shown above,
and for b near b₀ uniformly on the compact {½r_♭ ≤ r ≤ ¾R₁}, by continuity in b (Lemma 24.29 (c)); and the damping
1-form has the signs of Proposition 24.10 (i)–(ii) for g_(b₀) on all of (0, r_h/2], which contains the collar down to
½r_♭ (Proposition 24.10, Lemma 43.1), and, the inequalities being strict there, for b near b₀ by
continuity in b: (i) on the compact {½r_♭ ≤ r ≤ ½r_h} (Section 24.6.1) and (ii) on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ ½r_h}
(Lemma 24.31). Lemma 41.4 takes δ′_0 in (max(0, q0 − ½r_♭), q0), which is not empty, so that
a′ = q0 − δ′_0 < ½r_♭; Theorem 3.1 holds on such an Ω′.

*The domain.* g is defined on Ω_* ∪ 𝒟_0 (Theorem 41.1 (i)). This set is M ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}. Indeed,
t^♭_* ≤ t_* ≤ t_IVP where t^♭_* is defined (Section 38.1), so Ω_* = cl_M{t^♭_* ≥ 1} lies in {t_IVP ≥ 1}; and a
point of M with t_IVP ≥ 0 lies in 𝒟_0 = {t_IVP ≥ 0} ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 2} or in {t^♭_* > T̂ + 2} ⊂ Ω_*. Since t_IVP ≤ t,
t_IVP ≥ 0 implies t ≥ 0 ≥ −½|x|, so M ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} = {|x| ≥ r_♭, t_IVP ≥ 0}. As r_♭ = ½q_end < q_end, it contains
{r ≥ q_end, t_IVP ≥ 0}.

*The data and the rate.* G-invariance, Ric(g) = 0 and the bound on the data are Theorem 41.1 (i), and the
rate is (41.1) with ε_t := ε, its threshold time written T_1 here, on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T_1}, which
contains {q_end ≤ r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T_1}. ∎

**Remark 43.3** (At the inner radius ½R₁.) With the inner radius ½R₁ the development already
covers {r ≥ q_end} exactly when q_end ≥ ½R₁, that is when

    μ_end ≤ 16√72 l5² ≈ 135.76 l5²:    (43.1)

q_end ≥ ½μ_end^(1/2) ⟺ √72 μ_end l5² ≥ μ_end²/16 ⟺ (43.1). At the numerical point of
Chapter 56 (μ0 = 1, l5 = 1/10, A = 1, ∫ env² = 105/128), (2.14) gives μ_end = 1 + (2/9)(105/128) =
227/192 ≈ 118.2 l5², and (43.1) holds with a margin of about 17.5 l5²: μ_end² = 51529/36864 < 1.4,
while 256 · 72 l5⁴ = 1.8432. For a seed μ0 = 1000 l5², μ_end ≥ μ0 > 16√72 l5² and (43.1) fails;
Proposition 43.2 covers both.

### 43.2 One spacetime across the common part of the initial surface

g is the development of the glued data (γ_λ, k_λ) of Theorem 3.9 (i), which equal the data of g_λ on
Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ R} and the data of the Tangherlini metric g^KS_(m_λ,0) on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≥ 4R} (Corollary 39.19,
Chapter 42). On Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ < r < R}, g and g_λ induce the same data, so near it they are vacuum
developments of the same data. Lemma 43.5 makes this precise, without deciding how far their
identification reaches; it makes g_λ, near the hole just before Σ^IVP, and g, after Σ^IVP, one vacuum spacetime. Its
proof compares g_λ with g_(b₀) on a neighbourhood of Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R}, which reaches below r_♭, outside the set
on which Lemma 41.4 (a) is stated. The next lemma gives that comparison; its part (a) is Lemma 41.4 (a) on a
larger set, and the proof of (a) there extends to it, its formula holding at every r > 0.

**Lemma 43.4** (The Tangherlini metric in the chart of Lemma 41.4.) In the chart
(t, x) = (τ + T_(μ_end)(|x|) + c₀, x) of Lemma 41.4:

(a) the Tangherlini metric g^KS_(μ_end,0) = η + (μ_end/r²)(dτ + dr)² of Lemma 41.3 is g_(b₀) on
ℝ_t × {|x| ≥ ½r_♭}, and g0 = g_(b₀) on {v ≥ v_end, |x| ≥ ½r_♭};

(b) with J := d_1 + 10, d_1 the order of Theorem 38.22, so that K = J + 4 = d_1 + 14 is the order of
Theorem 41.1, and with C_J and the threshold of Lemma 41.3 at this J, the threshold written λ_J here
to keep it apart from the threshold λ1 of Theorem 3.9, the components of g_λ − g_(b₀) in the chart are at most
25C_Jλ on Ω′_+ ∩ {|x| ≥ ½r_♭} for 0 < λ ≤ λ_J; and for every compact set Q ⊂ Ω′_+ ∩ {|x| ≥ ½r_♭} there are C_Q and
λ_Q > 0 such that the components of g_λ⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ in the chart are at most C_Qλ on Q for 0 < λ ≤ λ_Q.

*Proof.* (a) The map (t, x) ↦ (τ, x) is the map Φ_(μ_end)(t, x) = (t − T_(μ_end)(|x|), x) of (21.27)
followed by the translation τ ↦ τ − c₀. T_(μ_end) is smooth on [0, ∞) and constant on [0, 2R₁], so this is a
diffeomorphism of ℝ × (ℝ⁴ ∖ 0). The coefficients of g^KS_(μ_end,0) do not depend on τ, so the translation preserves it,
and in the chart g^KS_(μ_end,0) is Φ_(μ_end)*g^KS_(μ_end,0), which (21.27) defines as g_(b₀) on
ℝ_t × {|x| ≥ ½r_♭}. On {v ≥ v_end}, μ = μ_end, and g0 = η + (μ_end/r²) dv ⊗ dv with dv = dτ + dr ((2.3)),
which is g^KS_(μ_end,0) at every r > 0.

(b) By Lemma 41.3 with j = 0, the components of g_λ − g^KS_(μ_end,0) in the coordinates (τ, x) are at most C_Jλ
on Ω′_+ for 0 < λ ≤ λ_J. In the chart, dτ = dt − T′_(μ_end)(|x|) x̂ · dx and the dxⁱ are unchanged, and |T′_(μ_end)(ϱ)| =
2χ_∞(ϱ)μ_end/(ϱ² − μ_end) ≤ 2/3, as ϱ² ≥ 4μ_end on the support of χ_∞; so every entry of this change of
basis has absolute value at most 1, and a component in the chart is a sum of at most 25 components in (τ, x), each
multiplied by two such entries. With (a) this gives the first bound. On Q, g_(b₀)⁻¹ is continuous, so the operator norm
of its matrix is at most some B_Q. Let E be the matrix of g_λ − g_(b₀); its operator norm is at most 125C_Jλ, five
times its largest entry. For λ ≤ λ_Q := min(λ_J, (250C_JB_Q)⁻¹), g_(b₀)⁻¹E has operator norm at most ½, so
g_λ = g_(b₀)(I + g_(b₀)⁻¹E) is invertible, with g_λ⁻¹ of operator norm at most 2B_Q by the Neumann series, and
g_λ⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ = −g_λ⁻¹Eg_(b₀)⁻¹ has operator norm, and so components, at most C_Qλ with C_Q := 250C_JB_Q². ∎

**Lemma 43.5** (One vacuum spacetime.) Let Σ := Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ < r < R}, with the data (γ, k)
that g_λ and g both induce on it; in the chart of Lemma 41.4 Σ is one set for both metrics, and the sets A and B
below lie in the coordinate space ℝ × ℝ⁴ of that chart. Let λ ≤ λ1 be so small, depending on R and Ω′, that dt_IVP,
with ψ_IVP continued below r_♭ by ψ′_IVP = 1, is timelike for g_λ and in the cone of dτ on a connected open
neighbourhood of the closure Σ̄ in Ω′_+ (such λ exist, see the proof), and let V ⊂ Ω′_+ be such a neighbourhood,
time-oriented as on Ω′, so that dt_IVP is past timelike on V. Let D_V(Σ) be the Cauchy development of Σ in (V, g_λ)
(Theorem A.2), and put

    A := D_V(Σ) ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0}  with g_λ,     B := {|x| > r_♭, t_IVP > 0} ∪ Σ  with g.

B is the domain M ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} of g with the points of Σ^IVP ∖ Σ and of {|x| = r_♭} removed. B is time-oriented as
the development of its data on Σ^IVP, so that the unit normal of Σ pointing into B is future directed; this is the
orientation in which g induces k on Σ. A and B are manifolds with boundary, the boundary of each being Σ (see the
proof), and (i) glues them along the whole of it. The points of Σ^IVP ∖ Σ and of {|x| = r_♭} are left out of B
because the glued space would have boundary points there, and at the edge of Σ it would not be a manifold.

(i) The space M_gl := (A ⊔ B)/∼, gluing Σ ⊂ A to Σ ⊂ B by the identity, is a connected, smooth, Hausdorff,
time-oriented vacuum spacetime, equal to (A, g_λ) and (B, g) away from Σ. Σ is a smooth spacelike hypersurface of
M_gl, on which its metric induces (γ, k).

(ii) Σ is acausal in M_gl and in V, and its Cauchy developments D_(M_gl)(Σ) and D_V(Σ) are globally hyperbolic
developments of (Σ, γ, k) in the sense of [Sbi15, Definition 2.1] (Theorem A.14 (1)). Their maximal common
globally hyperbolic development U ⊂ D_(M_gl)(Σ) contains a neighbourhood of Σ; there is a time-orientation-preserving
isometric embedding j : U → D_V(Σ), the identity on Σ, so that on U the metric of M_gl and g_λ agree up to j; and the
two developments glued along U by j form one Hausdorff globally hyperbolic development of (Σ, γ, k).

*Proof.* *V exists.* Σ̄ = Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ R} is compact and connected, a graph over the closed shell
{r_♭ ≤ |x| ≤ R}, and lies in the interior of Ω′_+ (Lemma 41.4 (b)). dt_IVP is timelike for g_(b₀) on
{|x| ≥ ½r_♭}: on {|x| ≥ r_♭} by Lemma 21.22 (b), and on {½r_♭ ≤ |x| ≤ r_♭}, where ψ′_IVP = ψ′ = 1, as for t_*
after Lemma 21.22. In the Kerr–Schild coordinates, with τ = t_KS − c₀, dt_IVP = dt_KS − β dr with β ∈ (−1, 1],
and g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt_KS, dt_IVP) = −1 − H(1 + β) < 0, H = μ_end r⁻² (Lemma 21.16 (d)); so dt_IVP lies in the cone of
dτ. By compactness and continuity there are c_V, δ_V > 0 such that the closed coordinate δ_V-neighbourhood Q of Σ̄ lies
in the interior of Ω′_+ ∩ {|x| > ½r_♭}, and g_(b₀)⁻¹(dt_IVP, dt_IVP) and g_(b₀)⁻¹(dτ, dt_IVP) are at most −2c_V on Q.
Q is compact, so by Lemma 43.4 (b) the components of g_λ⁻¹ − g_(b₀)⁻¹ are at most C_Qλ on Q. So for
λ small, depending on c_V and Q and hence on R and Ω′, the two quantities, in which dt_IVP and dτ have components
bounded on Q, are at most −c_V for g_λ on Q. Let V be the open δ_V-neighbourhood of Σ̄; it is connected, the union of
balls each meeting the connected set Σ̄. So this V is one such neighbourhood as the statement asks for. On any such V,
dt_IVP is timelike for g_λ and in the cone of dτ, which is past: Ω′ is time-oriented by dτ, which is timelike for g_λ
(Lemma 2.6 (e) on Ω′, with item 4 of Theorem 3.1). So t_IVP increases strictly along future causal curves of
(V, g_λ).

*Σ in V.* Σ = V ∩ {r_♭ < |x| < R, t_IVP = 0} is an open subset of a level set of t_IVP, whose differential does not
vanish; so Σ is a smooth hypersurface of V, spacelike as dt_IVP is timelike, and acausal, as t_IVP increases strictly
along future causal curves. By Theorem A.2, D_V(Σ) is an open subset of V containing Σ, globally
hyperbolic, with Σ as a Cauchy hypersurface. Moreover D_V(Σ) ∩ {t_IVP = 0} = Σ: an inextendible causal curve through a
point p of D_V(Σ) meets Σ, and t_IVP increases strictly along it, so that if t_IVP(p) = 0 it meets Σ at p.

*A and B are manifolds with boundary Σ.* As D_V(Σ) is open in V and dt_IVP ≠ 0, A = D_V(Σ) ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0} is a
manifold with boundary D_V(Σ) ∩ {t_IVP = 0} = Σ, and A ∖ Σ = D_V(Σ) ∩ {t_IVP < 0} is open in V. B ∖ Σ =
{|x| > r_♭, t_IVP > 0} is open in ℝ × ℝ⁴. A point of Σ has an open neighbourhood N ⊂ {r_♭ < |x| < R}, on which
N ∩ {t_IVP = 0} = N ∩ Σ^IVP ⊂ Σ, so that B ∩ N = N ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0}; as dt_IVP ≠ 0, B is a manifold with boundary Σ. g is
smooth on B up to Σ, which is spacelike for it, γ being Riemannian. As A ⊂ {t_IVP ≤ 0} and B ⊂ {t_IVP ≥ 0},
A ∩ B = Σ.

*(i), the topology.* The inclusions of A and B into ℝ × ℝ⁴ agree on Σ, so they define a continuous injective map from
M_gl onto A ∪ B. It is open. Indeed, A = (A ∪ B) ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0} and B = (A ∪ B) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} are closed in A ∪ B; so if
S ⊂ A ∪ B meets A and B in relatively open sets, (A ∪ B) ∖ S is the union of the closed sets A ∖ S and B ∖ S, and S is
open in A ∪ B. We identify M_gl with A ∪ B by this homeomorphism. Then M_gl is Hausdorff and second countable, and
A ∖ Σ = M_gl ∩ {t_IVP < 0} and B ∖ Σ = M_gl ∩ {t_IVP > 0} are disjoint open subsets of it, covering M_gl ∖ Σ, which
carry the smooth structures of V and of ℝ × ℝ⁴ and the metrics g_λ and g. The smooth structure across Σ is the one
constructed next, not that of the coordinates (t, x): g_λ and g need not agree as matrices on Σ.

*(i), the charts at Σ.* Let n_λ and n be the future unit normals of Σ for g_λ and g. Then dt_IVP(n_λ) > 0, as dt_IVP
is past timelike for g_λ on V, and dt_IVP(n) > 0, as n points into B. In the chart, Σ is the graph t = ψ_IVP(|x|) over
the open shell {r_♭ < |x| < R}, so the coordinates x = (x¹, …, x⁴) of the chart, restricted to Σ, are coordinates on all
of Σ; every chart below uses them. Let p ∈ Σ, and let Π_0 be a neighbourhood of p in Σ. Near p, g is the restriction to
B of a smooth Lorentzian metric g̃ on an open set of ℝ × ℝ⁴, g being smooth up to Σ. The maps

    E_λ(s, x) := exp^(g_λ)_x(s n_λ),     Ẽ(s, x) := exp^(g̃)_x(s n)

are defined and smooth near (0, p) in ℝ × Π_0, and their differentials at (0, p) map (σ, ξ) ∈ ℝ × T_pΣ to σn_λ + ξ
and to σn + ξ, which are isomorphisms, n_λ and n being transverse to Σ. By the inverse function theorem there are an
open neighbourhood Π ⊂ Π_0 of p and s_0 > 0 such that E_λ and Ẽ map (−s_0, s_0) × Π diffeomorphically onto open sets
O_λ ⊂ D_V(Σ) and O ⊂ {r_♭ < |x| < R}, and such that ∂_s(t_IVP ∘ E_λ) > 0 and ∂_s(t_IVP ∘ Ẽ) > 0 there, these being
dt_IVP(n_λ) and dt_IVP(n) at s = 0. Since t_IVP vanishes at s = 0, t_IVP ∘ E_λ and t_IVP ∘ Ẽ have the sign of s. So
E_λ maps (−s_0, 0] × Π onto O_λ ∩ {t_IVP ≤ 0} = O_λ ∩ A, and Ẽ maps [0, s_0) × Π onto O ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} = O ∩ B, with
O ∩ Σ = Π. For 0 ≤ s < s_0 the g̃-geodesic σ ↦ Ẽ(σ, x), σ ∈ [0, s], lies in B, where g̃ = g; so Ẽ(s, x) =
E(s, x) := exp^g_x(s n) there, whatever the extension g̃. Put

    Φ_Π(s, x) := E_λ(s, x)  (−s_0 < s ≤ 0),     Φ_Π(s, x) := E(s, x)  (0 ≤ s < s_0),

both being x at s = 0. Φ_Π is a bijection from (−s_0, s_0) × Π onto W_Π := (O_λ ∩ A) ∪ (O ∩ B), which is open in
M_gl, since W_Π ∩ A = O_λ ∩ A and W_Π ∩ B = O ∩ B are open in A and in B. Φ_Π is continuous on the closed halves
{s ≤ 0} and {s ≥ 0}, and its inverse on the closed pieces W_Π ∩ A and W_Π ∩ B; so Φ_Π is a homeomorphism. On {s < 0}
and on {s > 0} it is a diffeomorphism onto the open subsets O_λ ∩ (A ∖ Σ) of A ∖ Σ and O ∩ (B ∖ Σ) of B ∖ Σ.

*(i), the smooth structure.* Two charts Φ_Π and Φ_Π′ of this kind are given by the same formulas where both are
defined, both using the coordinates x on Σ. Let (s, x) lie in the domain of Φ_Π′⁻¹ ∘ Φ_Π. If s ≠ 0, this map is smooth
near (s, x), as both charts are diffeomorphisms onto open subsets of A ∖ Σ, or both of B ∖ Σ, there. If s = 0, then
x ∈ Π ∩ Π′, and Φ_Π = Φ_Π′ on a neighbourhood N of (0, x) contained in both domains. Φ_Π′⁻¹ ∘ Φ_Π is continuous and
fixes (0, x), so it maps a smaller neighbourhood N′ ⊂ N into N, and for y ∈ N′, Φ_Π′(Φ_Π′⁻¹Φ_Π(y)) = Φ_Π(y) = Φ_Π′(y),
whence Φ_Π′⁻¹Φ_Π(y) = y, Φ_Π′ being injective. So the transition maps are smooth, and the charts Φ_Π, with the charts
of A ∖ Σ and of B ∖ Σ, form a smooth atlas of M_gl, a five-dimensional manifold without boundary. A ∖ Σ and B ∖ Σ are
open submanifolds of it, and Σ, which is {s = 0} in every chart Φ_Π, is a smooth embedded hypersurface.

*(i), the metric.* s ↦ E_λ(s, x) and s ↦ E(s, x) are geodesics of g_λ and of g with unit timelike tangent, equal to
n_λ and n at s = 0. So E_λ^*g_λ = −ds² + h^λ_s on (−s_0, 0] × Π and E^*g = −ds² + h_s on [0, s_0) × Π, with
Riemannian metrics h^λ_s and h_s on Π: along a unit timelike geodesic g(∂_s, ∂_s) = −1, and for a coordinate field ∂_i
of Π, ∂_s g(∂_s, ∂_i) = g(∂_s, ∇_(∂_s)∂_i) = g(∂_s, ∇_(∂_i)∂_s) = ½∂_i g(∂_s, ∂_s) = 0, with g(∂_s, ∂_i) = 0 at s = 0.
At s = 0, h^λ_0 = h_0 = γ, and ∂_s h^λ_0 = ∂_s h_0: ∂_s g(∂_i, ∂_j) = g(∇_(∂_i)∂_s, ∂_j) + g(∂_i, ∇_(∂_j)∂_s) is at
s = 0 twice the form (X, Y) ↦ g(∇_X ν, Y) on the tangent spaces of Σ, ν being the future unit normal, n_λ resp. n,
which ∂_s is at s = 0. The form is symmetric: for vector fields X, Y tangent to Σ, g(∇_X ν, Y) = −g(ν, ∇_X Y), and
∇_X Y − ∇_Y X = [X, Y] is tangent to Σ. It is the second fundamental form up to the sign of its convention, so it is
the same for both metrics, both inducing k. The metric −ds² + h_s has the Christoffel symbols Γ^s_ij = ½∂_s h_ij,
Γ^i_sj = ½h^ik ∂_s h_kj and Γ^i_jk those of h_s, the others vanishing; so the spatial components of its Ricci tensor are

    R_ij = ½∂_s²h_ij + Ric(h_s)_ij + ¼(h^kl ∂_s h_kl) ∂_s h_ij − ½h^kl ∂_s h_ik ∂_s h_jl.

Ric = 0 therefore reads ∂_s²h = F(h, ∂_s h, ∂_x h, ∂_x²h), with
F := −2 Ric(h) − ½(h^kl ∂_s h_kl) ∂_s h + (∂_s h)h⁻¹(∂_s h) a universal expression, polynomial in h⁻¹, h, ∂_s h and the
first and second x-derivatives of h. Differentiating m times in s makes ∂_s^(m+2)h at s = 0 a universal expression in the
∂_s^j h, j ≤ m + 1, and their x-derivatives. By induction on m, from h^λ_0 = h_0 and ∂_s h^λ_0 = ∂_s h_0, ∂_s^m h^λ and
∂_s^m h agree at s = 0 for every m, with all their x-derivatives. So H := h^λ on s ≤ 0 and h on s ≥ 0 has one-sided
partial derivatives of every order which agree at s = 0. By induction on the order, every partial derivative of H exists,
the one-sided difference quotients in s having the same limit at s = 0, and it is continuous; so H is C^∞. The metric
−ds² + H is then smooth on (−s_0, s_0) × Π, Ricci-flat on s ≠ 0, and so on s = 0 as well, Ric depending continuously
on two derivatives. As the transition maps between the Φ_Π are the identity near Σ, these metrics, g_λ on A ∖ Σ and g
on B ∖ Σ, form one smooth Ricci-flat Lorentzian metric g_gl on M_gl. On Σ = {s = 0} it induces the metric H_0 = γ, and
its form (X, Y) ↦ g_gl(∇_X ∂_s, Y) there is ½∂_s H_0 = ½∂_s h_0, the form of g; so it induces the second fundamental
form k, as g does.

*(i), time orientation and connectedness.* Along each geodesic s ↦ Φ_Π(s, x) the tangent ∂_s is timelike and
continuous, so it stays in the cone of its value n_λ, resp. n, at s = 0: ∂_s is future directed for g_λ on s < 0 and
for g on s > 0. The future cones of g_λ on A ∖ Σ, of g on B ∖ Σ and the cones of ∂_s on the sets W_Π therefore agree
where these sets overlap, and define a time orientation of g_gl, in which the unit normal ∂_s of Σ is future.
B ∖ Σ = {|x| > r_♭, t > ψ_IVP(|x|)} is connected, the region above the graph of a continuous function over the
connected set {|x| > r_♭} ⊂ ℝ⁴, and B lies in its closure; so B is connected. For A, and for later use: let S be an
acausal set in a time-oriented Lorentzian manifold N, p ∈ D_N(S), and c an inextendible future causal curve through p
meeting S at q, say with p before q (the other case is the same with past and future exchanged). Then every point y
of c between p and q lies in D_N(S). Indeed, for an inextendible causal curve c′ through y, the curve formed by c up to
y and the future half of c′ from y is causal, inextendible and passes through p, so it meets S; c meets S only at q,
S being acausal, and q follows y; so c′ meets S. In V, through a point p of A ∖ Σ passes an inextendible timelike
geodesic of g_λ, which meets Σ at a point q, after p as t_IVP(p) < 0 = t_IVP(q). Every point of it between p and q
lies in D_V(Σ) and has t_IVP ≤ 0, so it lies in A. So every point of A is joined to the connected set Σ in A, and A is
connected; M_gl = A ∪ B, with A ∩ B = Σ ≠ ∅, is connected. Every point of D_(M_gl)(Σ) and of D_V(Σ) is joined to Σ
within it in the same way, so these two sets are connected too.

*(ii).* In V, Σ is acausal (above). In M_gl, let c be a future causal curve with c(0) ∈ Σ. In each chart Φ_Π, ds is
timelike, as g_gl⁻¹(ds, ds) = −1, and past, as its metric dual is −∂_s; so s increases strictly along future causal
curves. So c lies in {s > 0} ⊂ B ∖ Σ just after the parameter 0, and if c meets Σ at a parameter σ₁ it lies in
{s < 0} ⊂ A ∖ Σ just before σ₁. Σ is closed in M_gl. If c met Σ again, let σ₁ be the first parameter after 0 at which
it does; then c((0, σ₁)) is a connected subset of (A ∖ Σ) ⊔ (B ∖ Σ) meeting both open sets, which is impossible. So Σ
is acausal in M_gl.

So Σ is an acausal smooth spacelike hypersurface in each of the connected time-oriented Lorentzian manifolds M_gl and V.
D_(M_gl)(Σ) and D_V(Σ) are open and globally hyperbolic, with Σ as a Cauchy hypersurface (Theorem A.2),
and connected (shown above). In the chart, Σ is the graph of a function over the shell {r_♭ < |x| < R} ⊂ ℝ⁴, which is
connected; γ is Riemannian; and (γ, k) satisfies the constraint equations, by the Gauss and Codazzi equations, both
metrics being vacuum. So (Σ, γ, k) is initial data in the sense of [Sbi15, p. 11], with d = 4, and both Cauchy
developments, with the inclusion of Σ, are globally hyperbolic developments of it [Sbi15, Definition 2.1]
(Theorem A.14 (1)): they are connected and time oriented, as [Sbi15] assumes of every Lorentzian manifold
(p. 10), vacuum, and induce (γ, k) on Σ with respect to the future normal, by (i) for M_gl. By [Sbi15, Theorem 2.6] they
have a common globally hyperbolic development, and by [Sbi15, Theorem 3.4] a maximal one (Theorem A.14 (3), (4)),
U ⊂ D_(M_gl)(Σ), with an isometric embedding j into D_V(Σ) that preserves the time orientation and the embedding of Σ
[Sbi15, Definitions 2.2 and 2.4] (Theorem A.14 (2)), so that j is the identity on Σ. U is open (the proof of
[Sbi15, Theorem 3.4]; Theorem A.14 (4)) and contains Σ, a Cauchy surface of U. By [Sbi15, Theorem 3.13] U has no
corresponding boundary points (Theorem A.14 (5)), and gluing the two developments along U by j gives a Hausdorff
globally hyperbolic development that extends both [Sbi15, Theorem 2.7 and its proof] (Theorem A.14 (3), (6)). ∎

**Remark 43.6** (What Lemma 43.5 says.)

- M_gl is one vacuum spacetime: g_λ just before Σ, near the hole, and g after Σ^IVP, everywhere in {r > r_♭}. Across
  Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≥ R} nothing is glued, since on R < r < 4R the glued data differ from those of g_λ.
- The identification of g with g_λ to the future of Σ holds on U, their maximal common globally hyperbolic development.
  How far U reaches into the future of Σ in each is not decided here.
- The side of g_λ is taken in V, where Σ is acausal by construction. Whether Σ is acausal in all of Ω′, which would
  enlarge the development on that side, is not decided here.
- At late times near the hole, the domain of dependence of no bounded part of Σ^IVP reaches. For g_(b₀): on
  {|x| ≤ 2R₁}, v = t_* + 2r + const, and the past ingoing null ray {v = v(p), x̂ = x̂(p)} from a point p near r = r_h
  meets Σ^IVP = {τ = F(r)} on r ≥ R₃ (see Lemma 43.7) at the radius where r + F(r) = v(p), which tends to
  infinity with t_*(p). So the interior covered by Proposition 43.2 belongs to a vacuum continuation of g_λ fixed by
  the gluing. It is not the continuation of g_λ's own data, since g_λ is constructed on the compact Ω′ only.

### 43.3 Towards the continuation of g_λ's own data

To continue g_λ's own data, g_λ would first have to be constructed on the whole of Σ^IVP, out to spatial infinity. The
region there lies after the shell (v > v_end), where g_λ is Tangherlini plus the means times powers of λ plus the
remainder of Lemma 41.3. Those data would then have to be shown to lie in a data class of Theorem 38.22, and
Proposition 38.27 with b = (m′, 0) and S = S⁰ = 0, applied to g_λ's own data, would give their development, with the
interior of Proposition 43.2 at late times; without the symmetry, Theorem 3.9 (ii) would. The first step needs
estimates on a domain reaching spatial infinity at the time of Σ^IVP; the construction from past null infinity
(Theorem 3.7) is the natural start. This section locates that step and fixes the data class.

Let P′ be the past domain (9.1) built with V′, τ′_end and a′ in place of V, τ_end and a, so that
V′_P := V′ + 1 + (τ′_end − τ0) + κ_P, with κ_P = ½ and h_P(τ) = κ_P t^(−1/4), t := 1 + τ0 − τ. The proof of
Lemma 41.4 chooses c₀ and T′ so that on Σ^IVP ∩ {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ 4R}

    τ ≥ τ0 + 1,   v ≥ v_end + 2,   τ ≤ τ_top,   and   V′ ≥ τ_top + 2R + q_end + 1,    (43.2)

τ_top a constant; then τ′_end ≥ V′ − q_end ≥ τ_top + 1, as r_q(v) ≤ q_end. Also a′ < ½r_♭ < 4R.

Two solutions carry the name g_λ here: that of Theorem 3.1 on Ω′, whose data Theorem 3.9 glues, and that of
Theorem 3.7 on P′ ∪ Ω′, which satisfies items 1 and 3–5 of Theorem 3.1 on Ω′ (item 4 of
Theorem 3.7). Lemma 43.7 (i) speaks of both; from Lemma 43.7 (ii) on, g_λ denotes
the solution of Theorem 3.7, whose own data this section continues.

**Lemma 43.7** (Where g_λ is defined.) (i) Theorem 3.1 gives g_λ on Ω′, and Theorem 3.7
gives its solution on P′ ∪ Ω′; both domains lie in {v ≤ V′_P}: on Ω′, v ≤ V′ + 1 + τ′_end − τ ≤ V′_P − κ_P, as
τ ≥ τ0; on P′, v ≤ V′_P − h_P(τ).

(ii) On r ≥ R₃, Σ^IVP = {τ = F(r)} with F(r) := C″ − c₀ − T_(μ_end)(r), and v = r + F(r) → ∞ along it as r → ∞. So
Σ^IVP ∩ {v > V′_P} is not empty and contains the whole end of Σ^IVP at spatial infinity, where neither solution gives
data; Theorem 3.9 (i) replaces the data there, beyond 4R, by those of g^KS_(m_λ,0).

*Proof.* (i) Ω′ = {τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ′_end, |x| ≥ a′, v + (τ − τ′_end) ≤ V′ + 1}, and V′_P − κ_P = V′ + 1 + τ′_end − τ0. P′
is {v + h_P(τ) ≤ V′_P} intersected with {τ ≤ τ0, |x| ≥ a′}. (ii) In the chart of Lemma 41.4, t = τ + T_(μ_end)(r) +
c₀, and Σ^IVP = {t = C″} on r ≥ R₃ (Lemma 21.22 (b)). T_(μ_end)(r) → 0 as r → ∞ (Lemma 21.20 (a)). ∎

**Remark 43.8** (Neither construction reaches further at a fixed λ.) The threshold of Theorem 3.1 on
Ω′ depends on T′. The constants of Theorem 3.7 depend on the past domain, through V′_P: the annuli
A_P(τ) have thickness up to d1 = V′_P − v_start and outer radius up to t + a2, a2 = V′_P − τ0 − 1
(Lemma 9.1 (d)); the Poincaré constant of Lemma 9.3 (b) grows with d1, r³ varying along a ray by a
factor up to (1 + d1)³; Lemma 9.7 carries the weight (t + a2)^γ when γ ≤ 0; and the decay classes E_p of
Section 9.3 are bounds whose constants are taken on the domain. The proofs give no threshold uniform in
V′_P. So at a fixed λ the data of either solution are available on a bounded part of Σ^IVP: on Σ^IVP ∩ {r ≤ 4R} for
λ small depending on R, which is what Corollary 39.19 uses for the solution of Theorem 3.1.

*The far part and its past domain of dependence.* At every point with r > 0,

    g0 = η + m dv dv,     g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − m L0 L0,     m := μ(v) r⁻²,     L0 = ∂_τ − x̂·∂_x

((2.3)). On {v ≥ v_end}, μ = μ_end, so m = μ_end r⁻² there, and g0 = g_(b₀) on {v ≥ v_end, |x| ≥ ½r_♭} in
the chart of Lemma 41.4 (Lemma 43.4 (a)). As μ is nondecreasing and equal to μ0 > 0 for v ≤ v_start, 0
< μ0 ≤ μ(v) ≤ μ_end at every v; and 4R ≥ 20R₁, as R ≥ R₃ ≥ 5R₁, with R₁² = μ_end. Hence on {r ≥ 4R}

    0 < m ≤ μ_end r⁻² ≤ μ_end/(400R₁²) = 1/400.

Every bound below that involves m uses only 0 ≤ m ≤ 1/400 on {r ≥ 4R}, and every identity below that involves m
contracts the display above at a point, so that no derivative of μ enters it. By Lemma 43.7 (ii) and
Lemma 21.20 (a), on r ≥ 4R

    F′(r) = 2μ_end/(r² − μ_end) ∈ (0, ¼],     F(r) − F(4R) ≤ T_(μ_end)(4R) = μ_end^(1/2) log((4R + R₁)/(4R − R₁)),
