   Lemma 37.25, away from ℐ⁺ by 3, and near ℐ⁺ the forward problem for u − χ_cu_1, the first-order b-commutator
   [L_□, χ_c] being supported in {c/4 ≤ ρ_I ≤ c/2}, by 2.
5. *The slab: Theorem 38.9 at □.* Of its three changes, the gauge cut-off is absent for □; the background is g
   itself (S = 0), for which Lemma 38.7 is the form of g − η of Lemma 27.10, and Lemma 46.21 holds in the
   translated chart, g being stationary; and the regions, whose curves (Lemma 38.8) are statements about g, t^♭_*,
   t_IVP and ρ′_I alone, are unchanged, with c_1 in place of c_♮, every condition on c_♮ in Section 38.2.4 being an
   upper bound. The compact part, the set Q of that proof (a compact set of the first kind of Section 38.2.2 for g,
   containing 𝔒⁺, 𝒮 ∩ {ρ′_I ≥ c_1/4} and 𝒟⁺ ∩ {r ≤ R_K + 2}, whose only data surface is Σ^IVP ∩ Q), uses the energy
   estimates for a linear wave equation with principal symbol g⁻¹(ζ, ζ) Id (Lemma 40.11 (a)) on that compact domain
   of dependence; on Ω^♮_(c_1), 2 applies with Σ_in = {ρ′_I = c_1} and Σ_fin = {t^♭_* = T̂ + 3}, spacelike for g.
   Uniqueness on each region is Lemma 18.4.
6. *What is not used.* The recovery of the sharp weight at ℐ⁺, Steps 4–6 of the proof of Theorem 37.27, integrates
   each slot along X_I and X₀ − X_I; with Ā = 0 every Cartesian component would be integrated as slot 6 is there. Only
   the estimate (46.15) is needed below. ∎

**Theorem 46.23** (The order of the gauge vector on the initial slab.) Let q_ḣ := min(min Re ℰ_0, ℓ_0), so
that q_ḣ > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ (min Re ℰ_0 > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ and ℓ_0 > 3, Section 38.1). For every β ∈ (0, δ_♯) and every p with

    ½ + β < p < min(3/2, q_ḣ − 1),

the Cartesian components of Z_1 of Proposition 46.20 and all their b-derivatives are O(ρ_I^p) near ℐ⁺ on
N⁺ ∩ {2 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ 3}, with constants bounded by finitely many norms of the data. The interval is not empty:
q_ḣ − 1 > ½ + 2γ_Υ ≥ ½ + 2δ_♯. With the weight ℓ^♭_0 = 3/2 + ½δ_♯ of Theorem 37.36 in place of q_ḣ the same holds
for β ∈ (0, ½δ_♯).

*Proof.* (1) *The forcing term on the past of the slab.* In the class S′ = S⁰′ = 0 (Corollary 40.5), so
ġ_(S′) = ġ⁰_(S⁰′) = 0, ġ = ḣ on 𝒟′ (Theorem 40.4 (2)) and Υ̇^♮(ġ) = 0 there (Theorem 40.4 (5)). As
Υ̇^♮ = Υ̇⁰ − χ^♮_0E^ΥG (the proof of Theorem 46.19 (ii)) and χ_K = 0 on {t^♭_* < T_K} with
T_K = max(10, T_ι + 2) ≥ T̂ + 4 (Section 38.1), F_Y = χ^♮_0E^ΥGḣ on N⁺ ∩ {t^♭_* < T̂ + 7/4}, which contains
{t^♭_* ≤ 7/2} as T̂ ≥ 2. Let χ_3 ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal 1 on (−∞, 3] and 0 on [7/2, ∞), and F_3 := χ_3(t^♭_*)F_Y, a smooth
1-form on 𝒟⁺. As dt^♭_* is past timelike (Section 38.1), N⁺ ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ 3} is closed under past causal curves in
N⁺; so the solution Z_3 of □Z_3 = F_3 on 𝒟⁺ with vanishing data equals Z_1 there (Lemma 18.4; the extension
across Σ° is immaterial by Lemma 46.4).

(2) *Support.* Near infinity on {τ′ < ⅛}, t_IVP < r/8 and t_* = t_IVP − F_s(r) ≤ r/8 − r/4 < 0 for r ≥ R_6, where
F_s(r) := t_IVP − t_* is the function of (38.2), so χ_♮(t_*) = 0, and χ_0 = 0 as χ̌_0(t_IVP/r) = 1; so χ^♮_0 = 0
((38.3)). And χ^♮_0 = 0 near Σ^IVP (Lemma 38.1 (d)). So F_3 vanishes near Σ^IVP and, near infinity, on
{τ′ < ⅛}. Proposition 46.22 does not ask this, but it places the I₀-tail of F_3 in {τ′ ≥ ⅛}, the region of
Lemma 37.25.

(3) *Weights.* On Ω_(ext,r_1) and 𝒮, ḣ ∈ H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0),⟨ℰ^C_I⟩,ℓ_I)_b (Proposition 40.2 (2) and its proof): conormal
with order q_ḣ − η at I₀ for every η > 0 and, at ℐ⁺, with the exponents of (27.9) slot by slot, above ℓ^♭_I
in every slot but π̸₀, which has 3/2. E^Υ_(g,∞) is |x|⁻¹ times coefficients smooth on M (Definition 21.28) and does not
see π̸₀ (the proof of Lemma 46.18); χ^♮_0 and χ_3(t^♭_*) are smooth on M near infinity (Lemma 38.1 (a);
t^♭_* is smooth near ℐ⁺, Section 38.1). So F_3 has I₀-order q_ḣ + 1 − η and ℐ⁺-order ℓ^♭_I + 1, and
f_♭ := ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)F_3 ∈ H^(m,(a₀,2α_I))_b for every m, every a₀ < q_ḣ − 5/2 and every α_I < ℓ^♭_I − 3/2, as
ρ_Iρ^(−7/2) = ρ₀^(−7/2)ρ_I^(−5/2) ((37.17)).

(4) *The estimate.* Fix a₀ < q_ḣ − 5/2 with p − 3/2 < a₀, and put α_I := p − 3/2; then α_I < min(a₀, 0) and
α_I < ℓ^♭_I − 3/2 (p < 3/2 < ℓ^♭_I), and Proposition 46.22 gives u = ρ^(−3/2)Z_3 ∈ H^((1;m),(a₀,2α_I))_(e,b;b)(Ω^♮_(c_1))
for every m. By b-Sobolev embedding ((37.2)), V^ju = O(ρ₀^(a₀)ρ_I^(α_I)) for b-vector fields V and j ≤ m − 3; as
Vρ^(3/2) ∈ ℂρ^(3/2) for V ∈ {X₀, X_I, rotations}, V^jZ_3 = O(ρ₀^(3/2+a₀)ρ_I^p). On the slab ρ₀ is bounded above and below
(Section 38.2.3), and away from ℐ⁺ there is nothing to show. The three conditions are: α_I > β − 1, that is p > ½ + β;
α_I < a₀, possible for some a₀ < q_ḣ − 5/2 exactly when p < q_ḣ − 1; and α_I < 0, that is p < 3/2. ∎

**Remark 46.24** (Where the two bounds on p come from.) This remark is a heuristic about the method,
and no proof uses it. The bound p < 3/2 is the condition α_I < 0 of the multiplier (Lemma 46.21 (e)), whose
threshold α_I = 0 is the indicial root ι = 0 of Lemma 46.21 (c), the radiation field, of ℐ⁺-order exactly 3/2;
it is not shown here whether Z_1 attains that order, the recovery of the sharp ℐ⁺-weight not being carried out for
□ (item 6 of the proof of Proposition 46.22). The bound p < q_ḣ − 1 is the condition α_I < a₀ of Proposition 46.22,
which the multiplier needs at the corner I₀ ∩ ℐ⁺ (Lemma 46.21 (e)); it ties the ℐ⁺-order to the I₀-order of the
forcing term, which is one above that of ḣ through the factor |x|⁻¹ of c_Υ (step (3) of the proof of
Theorem 46.23). Without that factor the same argument would give only p < q_ḣ − 2, which leaves no p > ½ + β when
q_ḣ ≤ 5/2 + β.

**Corollary 46.25** (Homogeneous solutions with data of compact support on Σ°.) Let Y be a 1-form on N⁺,
smooth up to Σ°, with □Y = 0, whose Cauchy data on Σ° have compact support. Then Q[Y] is constant, and on each
{r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, |Y − (Q[Y]/4π²)W*| ≤ Ct_*^(−1/2) with the derivatives of (46.10). Near ℐ⁺ on
N⁺ ∩ {t^♭_* ≤ T̂ + 3} the Cartesian components of Y and all their b-derivatives are O(ρ_I^p) for every p < 3/2.

*Proof.* Q[Y] is constant by (46.7). (1) *ℐ⁺.* Let Y_c be a smooth 1-form on N⁺ of compact support with Y's Cauchy
data on Σ°. Then Y − Y_c has vanishing data and □(Y − Y_c) = −□Y_c, which has compact support; so ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)□Y_c lies in
every weighted space, and Proposition 46.22 applies with every a₀. With a₀ > 0 and α_I = p − 3/2 < 0, the b-Sobolev
embedding of step (4) of the proof of Theorem 46.23 gives the order p; Y_c vanishes near infinity. (2) *The slab.* With
χ of Lemma 46.18, χ(t^♭_*)Y solves □(χ(t^♭_*)Y) = [□, χ(t^♭_*)]Y, supported in {2 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ 3} and meeting ∂M only at
ℐ⁺, of ℐ⁺-order p + 1 (the proof of Proposition 46.20). Fix β ∈ (0, 1) and p ∈ (½ + β, 3/2), and put b_+ := β + ½ and
b_I ∈ (b_+, p). This forcing term lies in H^(∞,(b_I+1,b_++2,1/2))_b(Ω_*, μ_b)^(•,−), the space of (19.23) in the
form of Corollary 19.15, whose conditions b_I < 3/2 + S̄ and b_+ < b_I hold for □ (S̄ = 0, Lemma 23.2 at
γ_Υ = 0); □ is 1-admissible with sf-weight b_+ − 5/2 = β − 2 (Theorem 46.11 (iii), as β ∈ (0, 1)), and
Theorem 19.14 gives its forward solution, which is χ(t^♭_*)Y by the uniqueness argument of the proof of
Proposition 46.20. (3) *Late times.* As in the proof of Theorem 46.19 (iii): χ′Y solves □(χ′Y) = [□, χ′]Y, a forcing
term supported in supp dχ′ and in the class of Theorem 46.11; Theorem 46.14 gives |χ′Y − c(t_*)W*| ≤ Ct_*^(−1/2), and
for large t_*, dχ′ = 0 near the horizon, so c is constant there, equal to Q[χ′Y]/4π² = Q[Y]/4π²
((46.7) and □Y = 0). ∎

The data must be taken on Σ°: a slice {t_* = t_0} reaches ℐ⁺, outgoing null rays from a compact set reach ℐ⁺ after a
bounded increment of t_*, and in 4 + 1 dimensions there is no Huygens principle, so a solution with data of compact
support on such a slice does not vanish near ℐ⁺ on later slices. Step (1) supplies the estimate at ℐ⁺ that the slab
needs.

**Corollary 46.26** (The harmonic gauge on all of N⁺.) With Z_1 of Proposition 46.20, Z := ṁχ_KW**_H + Z_1 and
ġ_H := ġ + ℒ_Zg on N⁺: ġ_H is G-invariant, DRic(ġ_H) = 0, Υ̇⁰(ġ_H) = 0 on all of N⁺, ġ_H = ġ on a neighbourhood of Σ°
(so ġ_H induces (γ̇, k̇) exactly), and on each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, with the derivatives of (46.10),

    |ġ_H − ṁK* − c_∞ℒ_(W*)g| ≤ Ct_*^(−1/2),        c_∞ := (4π²)⁻¹ ∫ ℓ(χ′J_h + [□, χ′]Z_1) dv,

the limit of a horizon charge. For a 1-form Y_h on N⁺, smooth up to Σ°, with □Y_h = 0 and Cauchy data of compact
support on Σ°, ġ_H + ℒ_(Y_h)g has the properties above with three changes: c_∞ + Q[Y_h]/4π² replaces c_∞; where
ġ_H equals ġ it equals ġ + ℒ_(Y_h)g, so it induces (γ̇, k̇) plus the data of ℒ_(Y_h)g; and it is G-invariant when Y_h
is. With the same three changes, (i)–(iii) of Theorem 46.19 hold for that theorem's representative plus ℒ_(Y_h)g.

*Proof.* Proposition 46.20, whose hypothesis is Theorem 46.23. Z_1 is G-invariant by the argument of
Proposition 46.5 (a). *Near Σ°.* χ_K = 0 there, and F_Y = χ^♮_0E^ΥGḣ (step (1) of the proof of Theorem 46.23)
vanishes on V ∩ N⁺ for a neighbourhood V of Σ° in U^♯ (Lemma 38.1 (d)); so Z_1, with vanishing data, vanishes
on D_V(Σ°) ∩ {t_IVP ≥ 0} by the argument of Lemma 46.4 on D_V(Σ°) (Lemma 40.10). The clause on Y_h is
Corollary 46.25, ℒ_(Y_h)g being linear in Y_h, and DRic(ℒ_(Y_h)g) = 0, Υ̇⁰(ℒ_(Y_h)g) = −□Y_h = 0; ℒ_(Y_h)g is
G-invariant when Y_h is. ∎

So every perturbation in the class has a representative in harmonic gauge on all of N⁺ that induces the given data
exactly, and its settling on compact sets is determined up to the constant c_∞: the explicit ṁK*, growing linearly
in v, plus the stationary c_∞ℒ_(W*)g, plus a decaying remainder.

### 46.11 The spherically symmetric sector

**Proposition 46.27** (The spherically symmetric sector in harmonic gauge.) Let ġ_H be a harmonic-gauge
solution of Proposition 46.5 (a), with gauge vector Z′.

(a) (*Exact form.*) (ġ_H)_0 = ṁK* + ℒ_(Z′_0)g, where Z′_0 is the l = 0 part of Z′, □Z′_0 = 0, and K* is the mass
change of Proposition 46.2 (iv) (c): smooth across the horizon, Υ̇⁰(K*) = 0, δm[K*] = 1, and K* − (v/2)ℒ_(W*)g
stationary. The choice Z′_0 = 0 is allowed, and then (ġ_H)_0 = ṁK* identically.

(b) (*Decaying gauge data.*) If Z′_0 has Cauchy data of compact support on Σ°, then on each
{r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, with the derivatives of (46.10),

    (ġ_H)_0 = ṁK* + cℒ_(W*)g + O(t_*^(−1/2)),        c = Q[Z′_0]/4π².

When ṁ ≠ 0 this grows linearly in v, and it is not the sum of a stationary tensor smooth at r_h and a term o(1).

(c) (*Non-decaying gauge data.*) Let F be as in Lemma 46.1, ψ = v + F, and

    Ξ := ψ² + K_Ξ(r),        K_Ξ′ := (r⁴/2 + r²r_h² − (3/2)r_h⁴ + 2r_h⁴ log(r/r_h))/(r(r² − r_h²)).

Then □_0Ξ = 0, dΞ is smooth across r_h, and S := K* − (4m₀)⁻¹ℒ_(dΞ)g is stationary, smooth across the horizon, with
Υ̇⁰(S) = 0 and δm[S] = 1; but S_vv → −1/m₀ as r → ∞. So ṁS is the l = 0 part of a harmonic-gauge solution, with
Z′_0 = −(ṁ/(4m₀))dΞ: stationary near the horizon, not decaying at infinity, and with a gauge vector that grows in v and
in r. The growth of the horizon charge (Theorem 46.6) is then carried by (ṁ/(2m₀))v(∂_v)^♭, a linearly growing time
translation, whose Lie derivative is stationary.

*Proof.* (a) (ġ_RW)_0 = ṁK_V (Theorem 45.7 (a)), W**_H is spherically symmetric, and □Z′_0 = 0 by
Proposition 46.5 (c); ṁK_V + ṁℒ_(W**_H)g = ṁK* by Proposition 46.2 (iv) (c), which gives the properties of K*.

(b) Z′_0 is smooth up to Σ°, with □Z′_0 = 0, so Corollary 46.25 applies; ℒ_(Z′_0)g − cℒ_(W*)g = ℒ_(Z′_0−cW*)g is
bounded by the derivatives of Z′_0 − cW*. By (46.6), ṁK* = (ṁv/2)ℒ_(W*)g + (stationary), with
ℒ_(W*)g ≠ 0.

(c) By Lemma 46.1, dψ = m₀W* − (∂_v)^♭ and □_0ψ = 0. So □_0(ψ²) = 2ψ□_0ψ − 2g⁻¹(dψ, dψ) = −2g⁻¹(dψ, dψ), and,
with dψ = dv + F′dr and P := −F′ = (r² + rr_h + r_h²)/(r(r + r_h)), for which fP = (r³ − r_h³)/r³,

    g⁻¹(dψ, dψ) = 2F′ + fF′² = P(fP − 2) = −P(r³ + r_h³)/r³ = −(r⁴ + r²r_h² + r_h⁴)/r⁴.

For a function of r, □_0K_Ξ = −r⁻³(r³fK_Ξ′)′, and r³fK_Ξ′ = r⁴/2 + r²r_h² − (3/2)r_h⁴ + 2r_h⁴ log(r/r_h), whose
derivative is 2(r⁴ + r²r_h² + r_h⁴)/r. So □_0Ξ = 2(r⁴ + r²r_h² + r_h⁴)/r⁴ − 2(r⁴ + r²r_h² + r_h⁴)/r⁴ = 0.
dΞ = 2ψdψ + K_Ξ′dr: ψ and dψ are smooth on {r > 0}, and the numerator of K_Ξ′ vanishes at r = r_h
(r_h⁴/2 + r_h⁴ − (3/2)r_h⁴ = 0), so K_Ξ′ is analytic on {r > 0}. *Stationarity.* ℒ_(dΞ)g = 2∇dΞ =
4dψ ⊗ dψ + 4ψ∇dψ + 2∇(K_Ξ′dr), and ∇dψ = ½ℒ_(dψ)g = ½m₀ℒ_(W*)g, (∂_v)^♭ being Killing. So

    (4m₀)⁻¹ℒ_(dΞ)g = m₀⁻¹dψ ⊗ dψ + ((v + F)/2)ℒ_(W*)g + (2m₀)⁻¹∇(K_Ξ′dr),

and by (46.6) the terms (v/2)ℒ_(W*)g cancel in S, which is therefore stationary and smooth across the horizon.
Υ̇⁰(S) = Υ̇⁰(K*) + (4m₀)⁻¹□dΞ = (4m₀)⁻¹d□_0Ξ = 0, as □ = dδ + δd commutes with d. δm[ℒ_(dΞ)g] = 0, dΞ being spherically
symmetric (Lemma 45.6 (a)), so δm[S] = 1. *S_vv.* For Y = a dv + b dr, (ℒ_Yg)_vv = 2∂_va − f′a − ff′b (the
symbols Γ^v_(vv) = f′/2 and Γ^r_(vv) = ff′/2). The v-dependent terms of S_vv cancel, S being stationary. As r → ∞,
f′ = 2m₀r⁻³, rA → ½, rB → −¼, F = −r + O(1), 1 + fF′ = r_h³r⁻³ and K_Ξ′ = r/2 + O(r⁻¹); so the stationary part of
(ℒ_(W**)g)_vv is r⁻² + O(r⁻⁴), that of (ℒ_(dΞ)g)_vv = 4 − 2f′ψ(1 + fF′) − ff′K_Ξ′ is 4 + O(r⁻²), and
S_vv = K̄_vv + (ℒ_(W**)g)_vv − (4m₀)⁻¹(ℒ_(dΞ)g)_vv = −1/m₀ + O(r⁻²). *The gauge vector.* By Proposition 46.5 (a), a
harmonic-gauge solution with Z′_0 = −(ṁ/(4m₀))dΞ exists, and its l = 0 part is ṁK* − (ṁ/(4m₀))ℒ_(dΞ)g = ṁS. The
growing part of −(ṁ/(4m₀))dΞ = −(ṁ/(2m₀))ψdψ − (ṁ/(4m₀))K_Ξ′dr is −(ṁ/2)vW* + (ṁ/(2m₀))v(∂_v)^♭. The first
cancels the growing part (ṁ/2)vW* of ṁW**; Q[dΞ] = 0, as δdΞ = □_0Ξ = 0 and d dΞ = 0; and by the argument in the
proof of Theorem 46.6, Q[(ṁ/(2m₀))v(∂_v)^♭] = 2π²ṁv, while ℒ_(v(∂_v)^♭)g = 2dv ⊗_s (∂_v)^♭ is stationary. ∎

So the growth of the spherically symmetric part is forced for perturbations whose gauge vector has decaying data, and
only for them; a statement of the final state in harmonic gauge carries that class.

### 46.12 The forward solution at positive K⁺-weight

The rate t_*^(−1/2) of Theorem 46.14 is what square integrability in time gives. For forcing terms with more decay
at K⁺ the forward solution of □ improves, by the argument of Proposition 29.35, which is shorter at □: □ is its own
stationary model, it has one zero-energy state W* ∈ 𝒜² with no generalised partner, and the forcing terms below have
ℐ⁺-weight at least 5/2.

*Setting.* X = {r ≥ r_♭}, and M′, its faces I, ι = ι⁺ ∪ ι⁻ and K = K⁺ ∪ K⁻, the spaces H^(k,(w_I,w_ι,w_K))_b(M′) for the
b-density |dt_*/⟨t_*⟩|μ_b, μ_b = |dx|/⟨x⟩⁴, which on Ω_* are those of Corollary 19.15, and X^±_(sc-b) with its faces
scf, tf, zf, are those of Section 29.15. P̂ and P̃ are those of Section 46.5.

*The dictionary.* Near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, with ρ_+ = 1/r and ρ_K = r/t_*, one has t_* = 1/(ρ_+ρ_K) and r = 1/ρ_+, so the
density |dt_* dx| = ρ_+^(−5)ρ_K^(−1)|(dρ_+/ρ_+)(dρ_K/ρ_K)dω| and L²(|dt_* dx|) = ρ_+^(5/2)ρ_K^(1/2)L²_b. So a 3b-weight
(β_sf, β_K) of Section 28.6 is the b-weight (β_sf + 5/2, β_K + ½), as Corollary 19.15 records. The forcing class
H^((𝗌;k),(α_sf+2,0))_(3b;b) of Theorem 46.11 is the b-class (γ_+ + 2, ½) with γ_+ := α_sf + 5/2, its window
α_sf + 2 ∈ (0, 1) is γ_+ − ½ ∈ (0, 1), and the K⁺-weight −1 of its solution is the b-weight −½. A conormal function
O(ρ_+^Aρ_K^B) lies in ρ_+^(w_ι)ρ_K^(w_K)L²_b near the corner if A > w_ι and B > w_K, and b-Sobolev embedding returns to
pointwise bounds; on compact r-sets ρ_K is comparable to t_*⁻¹, so the b-weight α_K at K⁺ is the rate t_*^(−α_K).

*The window.* On Cartesian components P̂(0) is −Δ up to ρ²-relative terms (Lemma 46.21 (a)), with indicial roots
−l and l + 2 on r^(−q)Y_l (l the degree of the spherical harmonic Y_l); a weight α of Section 28.1 is the
μ_b-weight α + 2, and the root-free interval around it is (0, 2), the gap of Section 46.5. The column f̂_*(0)
∈ 𝒜³ lies in 𝒴_0, of μ_b-weight α + 4, if and only if α + 2 < 1. So the window at □ is α + 2 ∈ (0, 1). At ℐ⁺ the
outgoing root is 3/2 (Lemma 46.21 (c)), the cap 3/2 + S̄ of Corollary 20.27 with S̄ = 0.

**Theorem 46.28** (Theorem 46.11 at positive K⁺-weight.) Let α_K ∈ [½, 1), γ_+ ∈ (α_K, 3/2),
w_I ≥ max(5/2, γ_+ + 2 − α_K) and

    f ∈ H^(∞,(w_I,γ_++2,α_K))_b(Ω_*; T*)^(•,−),    (46.16)

and let u be the forward solution of □u = f (Theorem 19.14 at P = P_0 = □). Then γ_+ − α_K ∈ (0, 1), and for every
ϵ ∈ (0, (3/2 − γ_+)/5]:

(i) u = u′ + u_sing with u′ ∈ H^(∞,(γ_+−ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′);

(ii) u_sing = β(t_*, r)W*, where for one B ∈ H^(∞,α_K)_b(ℝ) (Definition 20.7: ⟨t⟩^(α_K−½)∂_t^p(t∂_t)^qB ∈ L²(dt)),
∂_(t_*)β(·, r) = (∂_tχ^H_K)(·, r) ∗ B and β(·, r) − β(·, r′) = (χ^H_K(·, r) − χ^H_K(·, r′)) ∗ B;

(iii) u_sing, and so u, lies in H^(∞,(γ_+−ϵ,γ_+−ϵ,α_K−1))_b: one order is lost at K⁺ and none at ι⁺.

At each order k the norms are bounded by C_k times the norm of f in (46.16) at an order k + k′, k′ independent of
k; u′, u_sing and B depend on k through the constant c of Section 29.18, and u does not. At α_K = ½, for b-regular
forcing terms, (i)–(iii) are Theorem 46.11 (i)–(iii) in the b-form of the dictionary.

*Proof.* We follow the proof of Proposition 29.35 with the following changes.

1. *The operator.* There, L is a perturbation of L_b, removed by Step 1 and the iteration. Here L = L_b = □: Step 0,
   Step 1, the iteration and the continuity in (S, h) are void. P̂(σ) is invertible for real σ ≠ 0
   (Proposition 23.17), and P̃(σ) for 0 < |σ| ≤ c_k (Theorem 46.10). The window is the one above.
2. Lemma 29.30 and Lemma 29.31 involve no operator, and hold as stated.
3. *The decomposition* (Section 29.18). For f ∈ C_c^∞(Ω_*°), the proof of Theorem 46.11 gives
   u = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing with ℱu_hi = (1 − χ(|σ|))P̂(σ)⁻¹f̂, ℱu_reg = χ(|σ|)û_(reg,1),
   (û_(reg,1), b̂_1) := P̃(σ)⁻¹(f̂, 0) and ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing) = χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(b̂_1), G_1(σ)b := Ψ(σ, ·)bW*: the first member
   of (29.40), with no second (there is no generalised state). c is chosen as in Section 29.18, with the
   constants of Theorem 46.10. For the density argument, the forward solution map of Theorem 19.14 at
   P = P_0 = □ (with Remark 19.31 and the orders of Remark 46.12) is continuous from the space of
   Corollary 19.15 with b_+ := ½(½ + γ_+) and b_I := ½(b_+ + 3/2), which contains (46.16): ½ < b_+ < b_I < 3/2,
   b_+ ≤ γ_+, b_I + 1 < 5/2 ≤ w_I and α_K ≥ ½; and □ is 1-admissible with sf-weight b_+ − 5/2 by Theorem 46.11
   (iii), as b_+ − ½ ∈ (0, 1). The extension across {r = r_♭} is that of Section 29.18.
4. *High and bounded frequencies: Lemma 29.32.* Its inputs are Corollary 20.27, with the hypotheses of
   Chapter 12 for □ (the proof of Proposition 23.15 gives them on a compact set of parameters), Corollary 20.24, with
   the hypotheses of Chapter 11 (Section 46.5), invertibility on the compact frequency set J
   (Proposition 23.15, Proposition 23.17), and S̄ = 0. Its weight conditions at
   (β^f_I + 1, β_ι + 2, β_K) = (w_I, γ_+ + 2, α_K) are α_K ∈ (0, 1), β^f_I = w_I − 1 ≥ 3/2 and
   w_I ≥ γ_+ + 2 − min(α_K, 1 − ϵ_1), which holds with ϵ_1 := 1 − α_K. So u_hi ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−ϵ,𝔪,𝔪))_b(M′) for every 𝔪.
5. *The transform of f.* The condition of Proposition 20.18 (1) at the weights (w_I, γ_+ + 2, α_K) is
   w_I ≥ γ_+ + 2 − min(α_K, 1 − ϵ), and it holds: if α_K ≤ 1 − ϵ it is the hypothesis w_I ≥ γ_+ + 2 − α_K; otherwise it
   reads w_I ≥ γ_+ + 1 + ϵ, and γ_+ + 1 + ϵ ≤ γ_+ + 1 + (3/2 − γ_+)/5 = 13/10 + (4/5)γ_+ < 5/2 ≤ w_I, as γ_+ < 3/2. So
   Proposition 20.18 (1) gives f̂|_(±(0,1]) ∈ H^(∞,(min(w_I,γ_++2)−ϵ,γ_++1,α_K−1))_b(X^±_(sc-b)), the zf index set
   (0, 0) dropping as α_K − 1 < 0.
6. *Low frequencies: Lemma 29.33* with P̃ in place of L̃_b; its proof is that of Proposition 20.29 with
   Theorem 28.10 (3) and the estimate of Theorem 46.10, with the outgoing order β_scf − 2 − ϵ/2 below
   −½ + S̄ = −½. With β_scf := 3/2 − ϵ, β_tf := γ_+ − 1 and β_zf := α_K − 1, so that β_tf − β_zf = γ_+ − α_K ∈ (0, 1),
   and f̂ in the space of its right side (5/2 − ϵ ≤ min(w_I, γ_+ + 2) − ϵ):
   û_(reg,1) ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−2ϵ,γ_+−1,α_K−1))_b and b̂_1 ∈ H^(∞,α_K−1)_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|).
7. *The regular part.* Proposition 20.20 (1) at the K-weight α_K ∈ (0, 1), with a void Taylor condition, gives
   u_reg ∈ H^(∞,(γ_+−ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′). With 4 this is (i), u′ := u_hi + u_reg, as γ_+ < 3/2 − 2ϵ.
8. *The cut-off state: Lemma 29.34* with the one state W* ∈ 𝒜² (q_1 = 2) and Ψ of Lemma 28.5, which does
   not depend on the operator: χG_1(b̂_1) ∈ H^(∞,(𝔪,α_K+1−ϵ,α_K−1))_b(X^±_(sc-b)).
9. *The singular part: one integration.* Lemma 29.31 is applied once, to u_sing, with β_I := γ_+ − ϵ,
   β_ι := γ_+ and β_K := α_K − 1 ∈ [−½, 0). Its hypotheses: β_ι > β_I; β_K < 0 < β_ι − β_I; β_K ∈ (−1, 1) ∖ {0};
   ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing) = χG_1(b̂_1) is 8, whose tf-weight α_K + 1 − ϵ is at least γ_+ (as ϵ ≤ 3/2 − γ_+ and
   α_K + 1 ≥ 3/2) and whose zf-weight β_K < 0 carries no index term; on {t_* < −r}, u = 0, so
   u_sing = −(u_hi + u_reg) there, of weights at least (∞, β_ι, β_K) by 4 and 7; and ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing) is χ(|σ|) times
   the boundary value from Im σ > 0 of Ψb̂_1W* (the proof of Theorem 46.11), so ℱu_sing is supported in
   supp χ(|·|) ∪ {0}, a compact subset of (−c, c), c ≤ ½. Lemma 29.31 gives
   u_sing ∈ H^(∞,γ_+−ϵ,γ_+−ϵ,((0,0),α_K−1))_b(M′), the term (0, 0) lying above the weight α_K − 1 < 0: this is (iii).
   At □ the second integration of Proposition 29.35, which is needed there for the generalised state, does not occur.
10. *(ii).* B := ℱ⁻¹(χb̂_1). By 6, the pair (χb̂_1|_(σ<0), χb̂_1|_(σ>0)) lies in the space X^(k,α_K−1) of
   Definition 20.13 with no polynomial part (α_K − 1 < 0), and Proposition 20.14 (2) at the weight α_K ∈ (0, 1) gives
   B ∈ H^(k,α_K)_b(ℝ). The identities are those of Theorem 46.11 (ii), proved there from
   ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing) = χΨb̂_1W* without a weight.
11. *What is not used.* The formal solutions at ℐ⁺ (Step 2a of the proof of Proposition 29.35) are not needed, as
   w_I ≥ 5/2; a forcing term that reaches ℐ⁺ with a lower order is first localised to a cone, as in the proof of
   Theorem 46.19. The expansion at ℐ⁺ (Step 3 there) is not carried: (iii) states the plain weight γ_+ − ϵ. ∎

**Theorem 46.29** (Theorem 46.14 at K⁺-weight α_K.) Let f and u be as in Theorem 46.28 and R′ > r_♭. On
{r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ 8 max(R′, 1)}, with any number of derivatives in x and t_* (the constant depending on the number),

    |u − c_f(t_*)W*| ≤ C t_*^(−α_K)‖f‖,    (46.17)

with c_f of (46.10) and ‖f‖ a norm of (46.16). In particular: (a) if ℓ(f) = 0, u = O(t_*^(−α_K)); (b) if
∫_v^∞|ℓ(f)| ≤ C′v^(−κ′), then u = c_∞W* + O(t_*^(−min(α_K,κ′))).

*Proof.* The steps (1)–(5) of the proof of Theorem 46.14, with three replacements. In (2): |B(t)| ≤ C⟨t⟩^(−α_K)‖f‖, by
Lemma 46.13 with H = ℂ on [T/2, 4T], as ⟨t⟩^(α_K−½)B and ⟨t⟩^(α_K−½)t∂_tB in L²(dt) give
∫_(T/2)^(4T)(|B|² + |t∂_tB|²) dt ≤ CT^(1−2α_K); the kernels ∂_rχ^H_K, ∂_tχ^H_K and χ_(r,r_h) are supported in
[1, 4 max(R′, 1)], so for t_* ≥ 8 max(R′, 1) the convolutions sample B on [t_*/2, t_*] and are O(t_*^(−α_K)).
In (3): |Q[u′](v)| ≤ C‖u′(t_*)‖_(C¹(𝒰_h)) ≤ Ct_*^(−α_K)‖f‖, by b-Sobolev embedding of Theorem 46.28 (i) near K⁺.
In (5): u′ = O(t_*^(−α_K)) the same way, with its b-derivatives t_*∂_(t_*) and ∂_x; ∂_(t_*)β = ∂_tχ^H_K ∗ B, and
∂_(t_*)c_f = ℓ(f)/(4π²) is O(t_*^(−α_K)) by b-Sobolev embedding of f near K⁺. Density as in Theorem 46.14, by the
bounds of Theorem 46.28. ∎

At α_K = ½ this is the bound of Theorem 46.14, for b-regular forcing terms. In Chapter 47 this theorem
gives the faster rates of Theorem 46.19 (iii) and Corollary 46.26 (Corollary 47.27); its extension to K⁺-weights in
(1, 2), and past that window to (2, 3) for forcing terms of zero total charge, gives those of the gauge vectors of
Corollary 46.25, of Proposition 46.27 (b) and of the Y_h clauses (Corollary 47.6, Corollary 47.10,
Corollary 47.11), and the rate t_*^(−min(p_0,3/2)+ε), for every ε > 0, of the representative of
Corollary 46.26, p_0 being the supremum of the orders at spatial infinity of the data of its Z′_0
(Proposition 46.27 (a), Theorem 47.30).

## 47. The linear solution in harmonic gauge, II: the rate

Chapter 46 gave every perturbation in the class a representative ġ_H that is in harmonic gauge on all
of N⁺, induces the given data exactly, and settles on compact sets to ṁK* + c_∞ℒ_(W*)g at the rate t_*^(−1/2)
(Corollary 46.26). This chapter determines the rate. Two parts of ġ_H behave differently.

The spherically symmetric part is ṁK* + ℒ_(Z′_0)g exactly, with □Z′_0 = 0 (Proposition 47.13), so its rate is that of a
homogeneous solution of the 1-form wave operator, and is set by the decay of its Cauchy data at spatial infinity. We
carry the forward solution of □ to K⁺-weights in (1, 2) (Theorem 47.4, Theorem 47.5) and, for forcing terms of
zero total horizon charge, past that window to (2, 3) (Theorem 47.7). A homogeneous solution with data of order
p ∈ (½, 3/2) at spatial infinity then settles at t_*^(−α) for every α < p (Corollary 47.15), and one with data of
compact support settles with an exact t_*^(−2) term, which an explicit solution of charge 4π² exhibits: the
switched-on Coulomb field of flat 4 + 1 placed on Tangherlini (Lemma 47.8, Theorem 47.9, Corollary 47.10). In
the class the order is p_0 > ½ + 2γ_Υ, and p_0 = ∞ for data of compact support; for data that differ from a change
of mass only on a ball the rate is t_*^(−1+ε) (Corollary 47.16).

The part with l ≥ 2 sees no zero-energy state. On the 1-forms with no part of degree l ≤ 1 the zero-energy operator of
□ has the indicial gap (−1, 3), no kernel and no cokernel at the weights of that gap, and an admissible transition face,
so the low-energy theory of Chapter 13 holds there without augmentation, at negative weights too (Corollary 47.26).
The forward solution then decays as fast as the forcing term allows (Theorem 47.28), and the part with l ≥ 2 of
ġ_H settles at t_*^(−3/2−κ) for every κ < δ_♯ (Corollary 47.29), δ_♯ = (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ being the margin by which the
constraint damping makes the gauge forcing term decay along the forward cone (Proposition 46.17).

Together (Theorem 47.30): ġ_H settles to ṁK* + cℒ_(W*)g at t_*^(−min(p_0,3/2)+ε) for every ε > 0, at
t_*^(−1+ε) when the data differ from a change of mass only on a ball, and at t_*^(−3/2−κ), κ < δ_♯, for data of compact
support, whose spherically symmetric part then carries the exact term (m₀c/2)t_*^(−2)ℒ_(W*)g. The constant c, which
is the c_∞ of Corollary 46.26, is the horizon charge of Z′_0 over that of W*, corrected by the Killing part of the data
of Z′_0.

### 47.1 Setting

Everything of Section 46.1 and Section 46.12 is kept: g = g_(b₀) of mass m₀, r_h = m₀^(1/2), the ingoing
chart, the class, K̄ = r⁻²dv², K_V, the linear solution ġ, its mass change ṁ, h = ġ − ṁK_V and w = α − 2 > 2 + ε_t; □
on 1-forms and □_0 on functions; W*, the horizon functional ℓ of (46.2) and the horizon charge Q of
(46.3); W**, W**_H and K* of Proposition 46.2; P̂, P̃, f_*, φ_* and the spaces of Section 46.5; the
cut-offs χ_K and χ^H_K of Section 46.1, and the cone cut-off χ′ and the constant T_1 of Section 46.8; the
forcing term F_Y of Section 46.9 and J_h of (46.11); and M′, its faces I, ι = ι⁺ ∪ ι⁻ and K = K⁺ ∪ K⁻, the
spaces H^(k,(w_I,w_ι,w_K))_b(M′), X^±_(sc-b) with its faces scf, tf, zf, and the dictionary of Section 46.12,
by which a conormal function whose pointwise orders exceed the weights lies in the space.

*The gauge condition.* Υ̇⁰(k) = −δGk, and −Υ̇⁰(k) is the linearised harmonic gauge 1-form (Section 40.4). A symmetric
2-tensor k is in harmonic gauge if Υ̇⁰(k) = 0, and (46.1) reads Υ̇⁰(ℒ_Xg) = −□X. By Proposition 46.2 (iv)
(b)–(c), Υ̇⁰(K_V) = □W**_H and Υ̇⁰(K*) = 0.

*The form dψ.* dψ = m₀W* − (∂_v)^♭, ψ = v + F, is the closed 1-form of Lemma 46.1: □dψ = d□_0ψ = 0, and
ℒ_(dψ)g = m₀ℒ_(W*)g, as (∂_v)^♭ is Killing. dψ is stationary and bounded, and does not decay at infinity.

*Charges.* For a 1-form f on Ω_* in one of the spaces (46.16) (of Theorem 46.28), (47.2) and
(47.6) (below), c_f(t_*) := (4π²)⁻¹∫_(−∞)^(v_h(t_*)) ℓ(f) dv is its *running charge* ((46.10)), and
for the forward solution u of □u = f, Q[u](v_h(t_*)) = 4π²c_f(t_*) by (46.7), as u and f vanish at early
times. If f has K⁺-weight α_K > 1, as in (47.2) and (47.6), then f and its derivatives are
O(t_*^(−α_K)) on compact r-sets, by b-Sobolev embedding near K⁺ (Section 46.12); so f̂(0) := ∫f dt_* exists
there, and ∫ℓ(f) dv = ℓ(f̂(0)), as t_* − v is a function of r near r_h and ℓ evaluates at r = r_h. We call ∫ℓ(f) dv
the *total charge* of f; it is the limit of 4π²c_f(t_*) as t_* → ∞.

**Lemma 47.1** (Two horizon charges.) For functions β and φ of (v, r) near the horizon, with ∂_r taken at
fixed v,

    Q[βW*] = 4π²(β − r_h∂_rβ)|_(r=r_h),        Q[φ dψ] = −4π²r_h³∂_rφ|_(r=r_h).    (47.1)

*Proof.* The first is step (2) of the proof of Theorem 46.14. For the second, δ(φ dψ) = φ δdψ − g⁻¹(dφ, dψ) =
−g⁻¹(dφ, dψ), as δdψ = □_0ψ = 0. With dψ = dv + F′dr, g^(vv) = 0, g^(vr) = 1 and g^(rr) = f,
g⁻¹(dφ, dψ) = F′∂_vφ + (1 + fF′)∂_rφ, and 1 + fF′ = r_h³r⁻³, as fF′ = −(r − r_h)(r² + rr_h + r_h²)r⁻³. Also
d(φ dψ) = dφ ∧ dψ has the component (d(φ dψ))_(vr) = F′∂_vφ − ∂_rφ. So δ(φ dψ) + (d(φ dψ))_(vr) = −(1 + r_h³r⁻³)∂_rφ,
which is −2∂_rφ at r = r_h, and (46.3) gives Q[φ dψ] = r_h³ · 2π² · (−2∂_rφ). ∎

### 47.2 The forward solution at K⁺-weights in (1, 2)

Above the K⁺-weight 1 the transform of a forcing term has a Taylor term at zero frequency, f̂(0) = ∫f dt_*. The
augmented zero-energy operator inverts it at the weight α + 2 = γ_+ − 1, which lies in its window (0, 1) as long as
γ_+ < 2, and one integration in t_* recovers the solution. The spaces X^±_(sc-b), the cut-off χ_zf = χ_1(|σ|⟨x⟩) and
the constant c ≤ 1/(8√5) are those of Section 31.2, c being also so small that χ_zf = 1 on supp φ_*.
Lemma 31.3 involves no operator and holds as stated. Its two companions at □ are the following.

**Lemma 47.2** (Lemma 31.4 at □.) For u_0 ∈ H^(∞,a)_b(X) and |σ| ≤ c:

(a) (P̂(σ) − P̂(0))(χ_zf u_0) ∈ H^(∞,(∞,a+2,γ_zf))_b for every γ_zf < 1;

(b) f̂_*(σ) − χ_zf f̂_*(0) ∈ H^(∞,(𝔪,3−ε,1−ε))_b(X^±_(sc-b)) for every 𝔪 and ε > 0, and f̂_*(0) ∈ 𝒜³.

*Proof.* (a) P̂(σ) − P̂(0) = −iσL_1 − σ²L_2, with L_1 ∈ ρDiff¹_b and L_2 ∈ ρ²C^∞ near ∂X and with coefficients smooth
on compact sets (Section 46.5); the proof of Lemma 31.4 (a) uses of the operator only this. (b) By
Lemma 46.8 (c), Lemma 28.4 (a) holds for f̂_*: f̂_* = f̂_c + f̂_∞, with f̂_c entire in σ and supported in
{r ≤ 2}, and f̂_∞ = r⁻³G(σr, x) on {r ≥ 1}, G entire and rapidly decreasing for Im ζ ≥ 0. The proof of
Lemma 31.4 (b) uses only this. f̂_*(0) ∈ 𝒜³ is Lemma 46.8 (b). ∎

**Lemma 47.3** (Lemma 31.5 at □.) Put G_1(σ)b := Ψ(σ, ·)bW* for b ∈ ℂ, with Ψ of
Lemma 28.5, and let χ be the cut-off of Section 29.18. For b_0 ∈ ℂ,
χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(b_0) − χ_zf b_0W* ∈ H^(∞,(𝔪,2−ε,1−ε))_b for every 𝔪 and ε > 0, and W* ∈ H^(∞,2−ε)_b(X).

*Proof.* The proof of Lemma 31.5 for G_1 alone, with the state W* ∈ 𝒜² (Section 46.1) in place of
ġ_b(ḃ_0): for r ≥ 1, Ψ = Φ(σr) with Φ(0) = 1 (Lemma 28.5 (b)), so G_1(b_0) − χ_zf b_0W* =
(Φ(ζ) − χ_1(|σ|⟨x⟩))b_0W*, ζ = σr, is O(min(|ζ|, 1)⟨ζ⟩^(−𝔪)) times a state in 𝒜²; and the Fubini count of the proof of
Lemma 31.4 (b), with ⟨x⟩⁻² in place of ⟨x⟩⁻³, gives the tf-weight 2 − ε. There is no generalised state. ∎

**Theorem 47.4** (The forward solution at K⁺-weights in (1, 2).) Let α_K ∈ (1, 2), γ_+ ∈ (α_K, 2),
ϵ_1 ∈ (0, ½), w_I ≥ max(5/2, γ_+ + 1 + ϵ_1) and

    f ∈ H^(∞,(w_I,γ_++2,α_K))_b(Ω_*; T*)^(•,−),    (47.2)

with plain weights (no expansion at ℐ⁺), and let u be the forward solution of □u = f (Theorem 19.14 at
P = P_0 = □). Then for every ϵ ∈ (0, (2 − γ_+)/5]:

(i) u = u′ + u_sing with u′ ∈ H^(∞,(min(3/2,γ_+)−3ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′);

(ii) u_sing = β(t_*, r)W*, where ∂_(t_*)β(·, r) = (∂_tχ^H_K)(·, r) ∗ B and
β(·, r) − β(·, r′) = (χ^H_K(·, r) − χ^H_K(·, r′)) ∗ B for one B ∈ H^(k,α_K)_b(ℝ) (Definition 20.7), ∗ the
convolution in t_*, and ∫B = c_0 := (4π²)⁻¹∫ℓ(f) dv;

(iii) u − c_0χ^H_KW* ∈ H^(∞,(min(3/2,1+γ_+−α_K)−3ϵ,γ_+−2ϵ,α_K−1))_b(M′): at K⁺, u is c_0W* plus a term of weight
α_K − 1 > 0.

At each order k the norms are bounded by C_k times the norm of f in (47.2) at an order k + k′, with k′
independent of k. u′, u_sing and B depend on k through the constant c of Section 29.18; u and c_0 do not.

*Proof.* We follow the proof of Proposition 31.6, with L_b replaced by □ and L̃_b by P̃. Its Step 0 removes L − L_b
and is void, as L = L_b = □. Its Step 1 removes the terms of the forcing term at ℐ⁺; (47.2) has none, so
u^♭ = u and f^♭ = f.

*Step 2 (the decomposition).* u = u_hi + u_reg + u_sing as in step 3 of the proof of Theorem 46.28, with
ℱu_hi = (1 − χ(|σ|))P̂(σ)⁻¹f̂, ℱu_reg = χ(|σ|)û_(reg,1), (û_(reg,1), b̂_1) := P̃(σ)⁻¹(f̂, 0) and
ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing) = χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(b̂_1). Lemma 29.32 applies with (β^f_I + 1, β_ι + 2, β_K) =
(w_I, γ_+ + 2, α_K): β_K ∈ (1, 2) is not an integer, β^f_I = w_I − 1 ≥ 3/2, and β^f_I + 1 ≥ β_ι + 2 −
min(β_K, 1 − ϵ_1) reads w_I ≥ γ_+ + 1 + ϵ_1, as α_K > 1 − ϵ_1; its inputs at □ are those of step 4 of the proof of
Theorem 46.28. So u_hi ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−ϵ,𝔪,𝔪))_b(M′) for every 𝔪. Put ϵ_PP := min(ϵ, ϵ_1). Proposition 20.18 (1) with
β_K = α_K and with ϵ_PP for its ε, whose condition w_I ≥ γ_+ + 2 − min(α_K, 1 − ϵ_PP) = γ_+ + 1 + ϵ_PP holds, gives

    f̂|_(±(0,c]) ∈ H^(∞,(5/2−ϵ,γ_++1,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b(X^±_(sc-b)),    (47.3)

as min(w_I, γ_+ + 2) − ϵ_PP ≥ 5/2 − ϵ, with the zf-coefficient f̂(0) = ∫f dt_* ∈ H^(∞,γ_++1)_b(X), the same for both
signs (f(·, x) is integrable, its K⁺-weight being α_K > 1). For the density argument of step 3 of the proof of
Theorem 46.28, the forward solution map is continuous from the space of Corollary 19.15 with b_+ := 1 and
b_I := 5/4, which contains (47.2): ½ < b_+ < b_I < 3/2, b_+ ≤ γ_+, b_I + 1 ≤ w_I and α_K ≥ ½; and □ is
1-admissible with sf-weight b_+ − 5/2 by Theorem 46.11 (iii), as b_+ − ½ ∈ (0, 1).

*Step 3.1 (zero energy).* At the weight α := γ_+ − 3, α + 2 = γ_+ − 1 ∈ (0, 1), and 𝒴_0 has the μ_b-weight
α + 4 = γ_+ + 1, so f̂(0) ∈ 𝒴_0; the column f̂_*(0) ∈ 𝒜³ lies in 𝒴_0, as γ_+ + 1 < 3. By Proposition 46.9, at every
regularity, put

    (û_0, c_0) := P̃(0)⁻¹(f̂(0), 0),        û_0 ∈ H^(∞,γ_+−1)_b(X).

Apply ℓ to P̂(0)û_0 + c_0f̂_*(0) = f̂(0): ℓ ∘ P̂(0) = 0 on 𝒳_0, and ℓ(f̂_*(0)) = ℓ(L_1W*) = 4π² (the proof of
Proposition 46.9); so c_0 = ℓ(f̂(0))/4π² = (4π²)⁻¹∫ℓ(f) dv. For 0 < |σ| ≤ c, P̃(σ)(χ_zfû_0, c_0) =
(f̂(σ) − f̂_2(σ), 0), with

    f̂_2 := (f̂ − χ_zf f̂(0)) − [P̂(0), χ_zf]û_0 − (P̂(σ) − P̂(0))(χ_zfû_0) − c_0(f̂_*(σ) − χ_zf f̂_*(0)):

the row ⟨·, φ_*⟩_h does not depend on σ, ⟨χ_zfû_0, φ_*⟩_h = ⟨û_0, φ_*⟩_h = 0, and χ_zfû_0 ∈ 𝒳_σ for σ ≠ 0, having
compact support in x. The four terms lie in H^(∞,(5/2−ϵ,γ_++1,α_K−1))_b ((47.3) and the definition of the
space), H^(∞,(∞,γ_++1,∞))_b (Lemma 31.3 (b) with p = 2, P̂(0) ∈ ρ²Diff²_b, a = γ_+ − 1),
H^(∞,(∞,γ_++1,γ_zf))_b for every γ_zf < 1 (Lemma 47.2 (a) at a = γ_+ − 1), and H^(∞,(𝔪,3−ϵ,1−ϵ))_b
(Lemma 47.2 (b)). As γ_+ + 1 ≤ 3 − ϵ and α_K − 1 < 1 − ϵ (both by ϵ ≤ (2 − γ_+)/5 and α_K < γ_+),

    f̂_2|_(±(0,c]) ∈ H^(∞,(5/2−ϵ,γ_++1,α_K−1))_b(X^±_(sc-b)).

*Step 3.2 (the regular part).* (û_(reg,1), b̂_1) = (χ_zfû_0, c_0) + P̃(σ)⁻¹(f̂_2, 0). Lemma 29.33, with P̃ in
place of L̃_b as in step 6 of the proof of Theorem 46.28, applies with β_scf := 3/2 − ϵ, β_tf := γ_+ − 1,
β_zf := α_K − 1 and the window β_tf − β_zf = γ_+ − α_K ∈ (0, 1) (Theorem 46.10 at that weight). It gives

    û_(reg,1) ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−2ϵ,γ_+−1,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b,        b̂_1 ∈ H^(∞,((0,0),α_K−1))_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|),

with the coefficients û_0 and c_0 at σ = 0, the same for both signs. Proposition 20.20 (1) with β_K = α_K ∈ (1, 2),
applied to χ(|σ|)û_(reg,1) (supported where the cut-off of that proposition is 1, as c ≤ ½), with its one Taylor
coefficient û_0 ∈ H^(∞,γ_+−1)_b(X), of order 0 < α_K − 1, gives u_reg ∈ H^(∞,(min(3/2,γ_+)−3ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′). With
Step 2 this is (i), with u′ := u_hi + u_reg.

*Step 3.3 (the singular part: one integration).* By Lemma 47.3 for c_0, and by Lemma 29.34 with a = α_K − 1
for b̂_1 − c_0 (with the one state W* ∈ 𝒜², as in step 8 of the proof of Theorem 46.28), whose tf-weight α_K + 1 − ϵ
exceeds 2 − ϵ,

    ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing) = χ(|σ|)G_1(σ)(b̂_1) ∈ H^(∞,(𝔪,2−ϵ,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b,

with zf-coefficient c_0W*, the same for both signs. Lemma 29.31 applies once, to u_sing, with
β_I := 1 + γ_+ − α_K, β_ι := γ_+ and β_K := α_K − 1 ∈ (0, 1). Its hypotheses hold: β_ι > β_I, as α_K > 1;
β_K = β_ι − β_I; β_K ∈ (−1, 1) ∖ {0}; the zf-restrictions of the two signs agree; the tf-weight 2 − ϵ is at least γ_+,
as ϵ ≤ 2 − γ_+; on Ω_<, u_sing = −(u_hi + u_reg), since u = 0 for t_* < 1, with weights at least (∞, γ_+, α_K); and
ℱu_sing is supported in supp χ(|·|) ∪ {0}, a compact subset of (−c, c) with c ≤ ½ (step 9 of the proof of
Theorem 46.28). So

    u_sing ∈ H^(∞,(1+γ_+−α_K,γ_+−ϵ,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b(M′).

Its (0, 0)-coefficient at K⁺ is lim_(t_*→∞) u_sing = ∫∂_(t_*)u_sing dt_* = ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing)(0) = c_0W*, as
∂_(t_*)u_sing(·, x) is integrable, its K⁺-weight being α_K > 1. Near K⁺, χ^H_K = 1; near ℐ⁺, χ^H_K = 0; and
χ^H_KW* has the ι⁺-weight 2 − ϵ, W* ∈ 𝒜² being stationary. So u_sing − c_0χ^H_KW* has the weights
(1 + γ_+ − α_K, γ_+ − ϵ, α_K − 1), as γ_+ < 2; with (i) this is (iii), as 1 + γ_+ − α_K < γ_+.

*Step 3.4 (the coefficient B).* B := ℱ⁻¹(χb̂_1). The pair (χb̂_1|_(σ<0), χb̂_1|_(σ>0)) lies in X^(k,α_K−1) of
Definition 20.13, with polynomial part the constant c_0, of degree 0 < α_K − 1, the same for both signs.
Proposition 20.14 (2) with β = α_K ∈ (1, 2) gives B ∈ H^(k,α_K)_b(ℝ), and ∫B = (χb̂_1)(0) = c_0. The identities of (ii)
are those of Theorem 46.11 (ii), proved there from ℱ(∂_(t_*)u_sing) = χΨb̂_1W* without a weight. The dependence on k
is that of Theorem 46.28. ∎

The expansion at ℐ⁺, Step 4 of the proof of Proposition 31.6, is not needed for (i)–(iii). There is one state and
no generalised partner, so one integration in t_* suffices, and the term at K⁺ is the constant c_0W*. The ι⁺-weight
γ_+ may exceed 3/2; the cap γ_+ < 2 is the zero-energy inversion of Step 3.1, which needs the column f̂_*(0) ∈ 𝒜³ to
lie in 𝒴_0 at the μ_b-weight γ_+ + 1.

**Theorem 47.5** (The rate at K⁺-weights in (1, 2).) Let f and u be as in Theorem 47.4 and R′ > r_♭. On
{r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ 8 max(R′, 1)}, with every number of derivatives in x and t_* (the constant depending on the
number),

    |u − c_f(t_*)W*| ≤ C t_*^(−α_K)‖f‖,    (47.4)

with ‖f‖ a norm of (47.2). In particular, if ℓ(f) vanishes for large v, then u = c_∞W* + O(t_*^(−α_K)),
c_∞ := (4π²)⁻¹∫ℓ(f) dv.

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 46.29, with Theorem 47.4 (i)–(ii) in place of Theorem 46.28 (i)–(ii). By
Lemma 46.13 on [T/2, 4T], |B(t)| ≤ C⟨t⟩^(−α_K)‖f‖, as ⟨t⟩^(α_K−½)B and ⟨t⟩^(α_K−½)t∂_tB lie in L²(dt); the
kernels ∂_rχ^H_K, ∂_tχ^H_K and χ^H_K(·, r) − χ^H_K(·, r′) are supported in [1, 4 max(R′, 1)], so for
t_* ≥ 8 max(R′, 1) the convolutions sample B on [t_*/2, t_*]. u′ = O(t_*^(−α_K)) with its b-derivatives, by b-Sobolev
embedding near K⁺, where ρ_K is comparable to t_*⁻¹ on compact r-sets; so |Q[u′]| ≤ Ct_*^(−α_K)‖f‖, and
4π²β(t_*, r_h) = 4π²c_f + O(t_*^(−α_K)) as in step (4) of the proof of Theorem 46.14. ∂_(t_*)c_f = ℓ(f)/(4π²) is
O(t_*^(−α_K)) by b-Sobolev embedding of f near K⁺. ∎

### 47.3 Gauge vectors with compactly supported data

**Corollary 47.6** (The rate t_*^(−2+ε).) Let Y be a smooth 1-form on N⁺, smooth up to Σ°, with □Y = 0,
whose Cauchy data on Σ° have compact support. Then Q[Y] is constant, and for every ε > 0, on each
{r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′} and with every number of derivatives,

    |Y − (Q[Y]/4π²)W*| ≤ C_ε t_*^(−2+ε).    (47.5)

*Proof.* Q[Y] is constant by (46.7).

(1) *The cut-off.* Let 𝒞_Y ⊂ Σ° be the support of the data. Ω^♯ is globally hyperbolic on each component, with Cauchy
hypersurface Σ° (Lemma 40.10), and □ is normally hyperbolic (Lemma 40.11 (a)); so Theorem A.4 (5)
gives a smooth solution on Ω^♯ with the data of Y, supported in J(𝒞_Y), and by Lemma 40.9 and Lemma 46.4 Y is
its restriction to N⁺. So Y vanishes on N⁺ ∖ J⁺(𝒞_Y), a relatively open set containing Σ° ∖ 𝒞_Y. Take
χ_Y ∈ C_c^∞(M°_♭) equal to 1 on a neighbourhood of 𝒞_Y. Then U := (1 − χ_Y)Y vanishes on a neighbourhood of Σ° in N⁺:
near 𝒞_Y because χ_Y = 1, elsewhere because Y = 0. So F := □U = −[□, χ_Y]Y is smooth, supported in a compact subset of
N⁺, and vanishes near Σ°.

(2) *The forward problem.* Let T_a := min t_* on supp F. For p ∈ N⁺ with t_*(p) < T_a, the past of p in N⁺ lies in
{t_* < T_a}, dt_* being timelike (Lemma 21.22 (a)), and there □U = 0; U vanishes near Σ°, so U(p) = 0
(Lemma 40.9 on Ω^♯, Lemma 46.4). Extended by 0 across Σ°, U is smooth on M°_♭, vanishes on {t_* < T_a},
and solves □U = F. Let T̂ = 2/C_♭ be the constant of Section 40.1. g being stationary, the translate
U_T of U by T̂ − T_a in t_* solves □U_T = F_T, F_T the translate of F, and vanishes on {t_* < T̂}, which contains
{t^♭_* < 2} as C_♭t_* ≤ t^♭_* (Lemma 15.35 (b)). So U_T is the forward solution on Ω_* of □U_T = F_T
(Proposition 17.14), and F_T, smooth with compact support, lies in (47.2) for every α_K < 2, γ_+ < 2 and w_I.

(3) *The rate.* On compact r-sets at late times χ_Y = 0, so Y = U. Theorem 47.5 with α_K := 2 − ε and
γ_+ ∈ (α_K, 2), translated back, gives |U − c_F(t_*)W*| ≤ Ct_*^(−2+ε). Once χ_Y = 0 near the horizon,
c_F(t_*) = Q[U]/4π² = Q[Y]/4π², by (46.7) and U = 0 for t_* < T_a. ∎

The cut-off has compact support in spacetime, and this is what gives the rate: a cut-off in a cone, as in the proof of
Corollary 46.25, produces a forcing term whose ι⁺-weight is that of the forward solution of Theorem 19.14, below
3/2. The cut-off is admissible because Y vanishes near Σ° off the domain of influence of its data.

### 47.4 Past the window: forcing terms of zero total charge

The cap γ_+ < 2 of Theorem 47.4 is the column at order 0 in σ. A forcing term of zero total charge needs no column
there, and the column enters only at order 1, at the weight γ_+ − 2; so the window extends to K⁺-weights in (2, 3).
An explicit solution of charge 4π² then gives the t_*^(−2) term of every forcing term with enough decay at ℐ⁺.

**Theorem 47.7** (Past the window, for forcing terms of zero total charge.) Let α_K ∈ (2, 3),
γ_+ ∈ (α_K, 3), ϵ_1 ∈ (0, 3 − γ_+), w_I ≥ γ_+ + 1 + ϵ_1 and

    f ∈ H^(∞,(w_I,γ_++2,α_K))_b(Ω_*; T*)^(•,−),        ∫ℓ(f) dv = 0,    (47.6)

with plain weights, and let u be the forward solution of □u = f. Then for every ϵ ∈ (0, ϵ_1/3]:

(i) u = u′ + u_sing with u′ ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−3ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′);

(ii) u_sing = β(t_*, r)W* with ∂_(t_*)β(·, r) = (∂_tχ^H_K)(·, r) ∗ B and
β(·, r) − β(·, r′) = (χ^H_K(·, r) − χ^H_K(·, r′)) ∗ B, where B ∈ H^(k,α_K)_b(ℝ) and ∫B = 0;

(iii) on {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ 8 max(R′, 1)}, with every number of derivatives in x and
t_*, |u − c_f(t_*)W*| ≤ C t_*^(−α_K)‖f‖.

The dependence on k is that of Theorem 47.4.

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 47.4, with the following changes.

*Step 2.* Lemma 29.32 at (w_I, γ_+ + 2, α_K), α_K ∈ (2, 3) not an integer, gives u_hi ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−ϵ,𝔪,𝔪))_b; its
conditions are w_I − 1 ≥ 3/2 and w_I ≥ γ_+ + 1 + ϵ_1. Proposition 20.18 (1) at β_K = α_K, with ϵ_PP := min(ϵ, ϵ_1)
for its ε, gives

    f̂|_(±(0,c]) ∈ H^(∞,(5/2−ϵ,γ_++1,((0,0),(1,0),α_K−1)))_b(X^±_(sc-b)),

with the Taylor terms of orders 0 and 1: their coefficients are f̂(0) = ∫f dt_* ∈ H^(∞,γ_++1)_b(X) and
f̂_1 := i∫t_*f dt_* ∈ ⟨x⟩H^(∞,γ_++1)_b(X) ⊂ H^(∞,γ_+)_b(X), each the same for both signs. The density step is that of
Theorem 47.4.

*Step 3.1′ (zero energy at order 0, without the column).* Put β_tf := γ_+ − 1 ∈ (1, 2). At the b-weight β_tf, which
lies in the interval (0, 2) on which P̂ satisfies (G) (Section 23.8), P̂(0): 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 has kernel span{W*} and
range ker ℓ (Lemma 23.21 (2)–(3); by Theorem 13.11 (3)–(4), kernels and annihilators of ranges do not depend
on the weight within the gap). f̂(0) ∈ 𝒴_0, its μ_b-weight being β_tf + 2, and ℓ(f̂(0)) = ∫ℓ(f) dv = 0. So there is a
unique û_0 ∈ H^(∞,β_tf)_b(X) with P̂(0)û_0 = f̂(0) and ⟨û_0, φ_*⟩_h = 0 (the argument at every regularity s > 5/2). The
column is not used.

*Step 3.1″ (order 1).* Put g_1 := f̂_1 + iL_1û_0 ∈ H^(∞,β_tf+1)_b(X) (L_1 ∈ ρDiff¹_b). Proposition 46.9 at the weight
α + 2 := β_tf − 1 = γ_+ − 2 ∈ (0, 1), where 𝒴_0 has the μ_b-weight γ_+ < 3 and so contains g_1 and the column, gives
(û_1, b_1) := P̃(0)⁻¹(g_1, 0), with û_1 ∈ H^(∞,β_tf−1)_b(X), ⟨û_1, φ_*⟩_h = 0 and b_1 = ℓ(g_1)/4π².

*The remainder.* With P̂(σ) = P̂(0) − iσL_1 − σ²L_2, P̂(0)û_0 = f̂(0) and P̂(0)û_1 + b_1f̂_*(0) = g_1, expanding gives,
for 0 < |σ| ≤ c, P̃(σ)(χ_zf(û_0 + σû_1), σb_1) = (f̂(σ) − f̂_2(σ), 0), where

    f̂_2 := (f̂ − χ_zf(f̂(0) + σf̂_1)) − [P̂(0), χ_zf](û_0 + σû_1) + iσ[L_1, χ_zf]û_0 + σ²L_2χ_zfû_0
             + iσ²L_1χ_zfû_1 + σ³L_2χ_zfû_1 − σb_1(f̂_*(σ) − χ_zf f̂_*(0));

the row vanishes, as ⟨û_0, φ_*⟩_h = ⟨û_1, φ_*⟩_h = 0. The terms lie, in order: in H^(∞,(5/2−ϵ,γ_++1,α_K−1))_b
(Step 2); in H^(∞,(∞,γ_++1,∞))_b (Lemma 31.3 (b) with p = 2, at a = β_tf, and at a = β_tf − 1 with the factor
σ, which has tf-order 1 on supp dχ_zf); in the same space (Lemma 31.3 (b) with p = 1, and one factor σ); in
H^(∞,(∞,β_tf+4,γ_zf))_b (Lemma 31.3 (a) with p = j = 2); in H^(∞,(∞,β_tf+2,γ_zf))_b (Lemma 31.3 (a)
at a = β_tf − 1 with p = 1, j = 2, and (b) for the commutator [L_1, χ_zf]); in H^(∞,(∞,β_tf+4,γ_zf))_b
(Lemma 31.3 (a) with p = 2, j = 3), for every γ_zf < 2; and in H^(∞,(𝔪,4−ϵ,2−ϵ))_b (Lemma 47.2 (b) and
one factor σ, |σ| = ρ_tfρ_zf). As α_K − 1 < 2 − ϵ and β_tf + 2 = γ_+ + 1 ≤ 4 − ϵ (by ϵ ≤ ϵ_1/3 < 3 − γ_+),

    f̂_2|_(±(0,c]) ∈ H^(∞,(5/2−ϵ,γ_++1,α_K−1))_b(X^±_(sc-b)).

*Step 3.2.* Lemma 29.33 with P̃, whose β_zf is free and enters by division by |σ|^(β_zf), at
β_scf := 3/2 − ϵ, β_tf and β_zf := α_K − 1, with the window β_tf − β_zf = γ_+ − α_K ∈ (0, 1) (Theorem 46.10 there),
gives (û′, b̂′) := P̃(σ)⁻¹(f̂_2, 0) with û′ ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−2ϵ,β_tf,α_K−1))_b and
b̂′ ∈ H^(∞,α_K−1)_b(±(0, c], |dσ/σ|). So û_(reg,1) = χ_zf(û_0 + σû_1) + û′ and b̂_1 = σb_1 + b̂′.
Proposition 20.20 (1) at β_K = α_K applies with the two Taylor terms: their coefficients û_0 and û_1 are the same for
both signs, and v_0 = û_0 and v_1 = ⟨x⟩⁻¹û_1 lie in H^(∞,γ_+−1)_b(X), the tf-weight β_ι − 1 that it asks
(β_ι = γ_+). It gives u_reg ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−3ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′), as γ_+ > 3/2. With Step 2 this is (i).

*Step 3.4.* B := ℱ⁻¹(χb̂_1). The pair (χb̂_1|_(σ<0), χb̂_1|_(σ>0)) lies in X^(k,α_K−1) of Definition 20.13, with the
polynomial part b_1σ, of degree 1 < α_K − 1, the same for both signs. Proposition 20.14 (2) at β = α_K ∈ (2, 3)
gives B ∈ H^(k,α_K)_b(ℝ), and ∫B = (χb̂_1)(0) = 0. The identities of (ii) are those of Theorem 46.11 (ii).

*(iii)* is the proof of Theorem 47.5, with (i)–(ii): |B(t)| ≤ C⟨t⟩^(−α_K)‖f‖ by Lemma 46.13, the convolutions
sample B on [t_*/2, t_*], and u′ = O(t_*^(−α_K)) with its b-derivatives by b-Sobolev embedding near K⁺;
so |Q[u′]| ≤ Ct_*^(−α_K)‖f‖ and 4π²β(t_*, r_h) = 4π²c_f + O(t_*^(−α_K)). No integration with a moment condition
is needed, and no statement at K⁺ is made for u_sing itself. ∎

The caps here are γ_+ < 3, which the column at order 1 needs (û_0 is of order r⁻², and 𝒴_0 must contain f̂_*(0) at
the μ_b-weight γ_+), and α_K < 3, where the Taylor term of order 2 enters.

**Lemma 47.8** (An explicit solution of charge 4π².) For w > 0 and r > 0 put

    𝔨(w, r) := r⁻²((w + r)(w(w + 2r))^(−1/2) − 1),        𝔨(w, r) := 0  for w < 0,    (47.7)

so that a_0(t, r) := r⁻²H(t − r) + 𝔨(t − r, r) = tr⁻²(t² − r²)^(−1/2)H(t − r), H the Heaviside function. Let
R_T ≥ 3R₁, let 𝔥 ∈ C^∞([r_♭, ∞)) equal −2r for r ≤ R_T and −2r_*(r) for r ≥ 2R_T, r_* of Section 21.6, and put
T := v + 𝔥(r). On {r ≥ 2R_T}, v = x¹ + 2r_*, so T = x¹ = t − |x| ((21.34)); near infinity
t_* = x¹ + C′ − 8m₀|x|⁻¹ ((21.30)); and on {r ≤ 2R_T}, t_* − v and T − v are functions of r. So |T − t_*| is
bounded on {r ≥ r_♭}. Fix T_2 so large that {T ≥ T_2} ⊂ {t^♭_* ≥ T̂}, and χ_on ∈ C^∞(ℝ) equal to 0 on (−∞, T_2] and to
1 on [T_2 + 1, ∞). Put

    𝔞(T, r) := ∫χ_on′(s)𝔨(T − s, r) ds,        u_ex := χ_on(T)W* + 𝔞(T, r) dψ,        f_ex := □u_ex.

Then:

(a) u_ex is smooth on {r ≥ r_♭}, spherically symmetric, and vanishes on {T < T_2}. At m₀ = 0 it is a dt, with
a(T, r) := χ_on(T)r⁻² + 𝔞(T, r) = ∫χ_on′(s)a_0(t − s, r) ds: the flat field of a charge switched on along χ_on.

(b) f_ex has ℐ⁺-order 4, ι⁺-order 6 and K⁺-order 3, with b-regularity, and vanishes on {t^♭_* < T̂}. So it lies in the
space of (47.6), the condition on the charge aside, for every α_K < 3, γ_+ < 3 and w_I < 4, and in
(47.2) for every α_K < 2.

(c) At r = r_h, with ∂_r at fixed v, Q[u_ex](v) = 4π²(χ_on(T) − r_h∂_r(χ_on(T))) − 4π²r_h³∂_r𝔞. So
Q[u_ex] = 4π² + O(t_*^(−3)) at late times, and the total charge of f_ex is 4π².

(d) On compact r-sets at late times, with every derivative, u_ex − W* = 𝔞 dψ = ½t_*^(−2)dψ + O(t_*^(−3)).

*Proof.* *The flat field.* In the variables (t, r), for t > r > 0, a_0 = tr⁻²(t² − r²)^(−1/2) solves the radial wave
equation of ℝ^(1+4):

    (∂_t² − ∂_r² − (3/r)∂_r)a_0 = 0.

Indeed b_0 := ∂_ta_0 = −s^(−3/2), s := t² − r², and ∂_t²b_0 = 3s^(−5/2) − 15t²s^(−7/2), ∂_rb_0 = −3rs^(−5/2),
∂_r²b_0 = −3s^(−5/2) − 15r²s^(−7/2), so (∂_t² − ∂_r² − (3/r)∂_r)b_0 = 15s^(−5/2) − 15(t² − r²)s^(−7/2) = 0. The
operator has coefficients independent of t, so the left side for a_0 is a function of r alone. As t → ∞ at fixed r,
a_0 = r⁻²(1 − r²/t²)^(−1/2) tends to r⁻² with its r-derivatives while its t-derivatives tend to 0, and
(∂_r² + (3/r)∂_r)r⁻² = 0; so that function vanishes. In the variables (w, r) := (t − r, r) the operator is

    P := 2∂_w∂_r − ∂_r² − (3/r)∂_r + (3/r)∂_w,

as ∂_t = ∂_w and ∂_r|_t = ∂_r|_w − ∂_w; so Pa_0 = 0 on {w > 0}. Near w = 0, a_0 = w^(−1/2)g(w, r), with
g(w, r) := (w + r)r⁻²(w + 2r)^(−1/2) smooth on [0, ∞) × (0, ∞) and g(0, r) = 2^(−1/2)r^(−3/2); as
(2∂_r + 3/r)r^(−3/2) = 0, 𝔟 := (2∂_r + 3/r)a_0 = w^(−1/2)(2∂_r + 3/r)g is O(w^(1/2)) as w → 0+, locally uniformly in
r. Now a(T, r) = ∫_0^∞ χ_on′(T − w)a_0(w, r) dw, as χ_on(T) = ∫_0^∞ χ_on′(T − w) dw. The r-derivatives of a_0 are
w^(−1/2) times functions smooth up to w = 0, so they are locally integrable, uniformly for r in compact subsets of
(0, ∞); hence a is smooth on {r > 0}, and we may differentiate under the integral, the T-derivatives falling on χ_on′.
As χ_on″(T − w) = −∂_w(χ_on′(T − w)), an integration by parts on [ε, ∞) gives

    Pa(T, r) = lim_(ε→0) (χ_on′(T − ε)𝔟(ε, r) + ∫_ε^∞ χ_on′(T − w)(Pa_0)(w, r) dw) = 0,    (47.8)

since Pa_0 = ∂_w𝔟 − (∂_r² + (3/r)∂_r)a_0 = 0 on {w > 0} and 𝔟(ε, r) → 0.

*(a)* 𝔨(·, r) = a_0(·, r) − r⁻²H is smooth on {w > 0} and vanishes on {w < 0}, with the integrable singularity
w^(−1/2)g(0, r) at w = 0+, and its r-derivatives behave alike; so 𝔞 is smooth on {r > 0}, as a is. T, W* and dψ are
smooth on {r ≥ r_♭}, r_♭ > 0. χ_on(T) and 𝔞 vanish on {T < T_2}, as χ_on′(T − w)𝔨(w, r) ≠ 0 needs w > 0 and T − w ≥ T_2.
Everything is spherically symmetric. At m₀ = 0, r_h = 0, v = t + r and T = t − r; W* = r⁻²dv − r⁻²dr = r⁻²dt and,
as F′ = −1, dψ = dv − dr = dt; so u_ex = a dt.

*(b) Near infinity.* On {r ≥ 2R_T}, dv = dT + 2f⁻¹dr, so g = −f dT² − 2 dT dr + r²γ, and

    W* = r⁻²dT + dr/(r(r − r_h)),        dψ = dT + 𝔭(r) dr,        𝔭(r) := 1 + m₀/(r(r − r_h)).

For a spherically symmetric 1-form Y = A dT + B dr, the calculation of the proof of Lemma 46.1, with g^(TT) = 0,
g^(Tr) = −1 and g^(rr) = f, gives, for φ := δY and q := r³(dY)_(Tr),

    φ = ∂_TB + r⁻³∂_r(r³(A − fB)),        q = r³(∂_TB − ∂_rA),
    (□Y)_T = ∂_Tφ + r⁻³(f∂_rq − ∂_Tq),        (□Y)_r = ∂_rφ + r⁻³∂_rq,

and no angular components. For Y = u_ex, with χ := χ_on(T),

    φ = χ′/(r(r − r_h)) + 𝔭 ∂_T𝔞 − r_h³r⁻³∂_r𝔞,        q = 2χ + r²χ′/(r − r_h) + r³𝔭 ∂_T𝔞 − r³∂_r𝔞,

and substituting gives, for all functions χ of T and 𝔞 of (T, r), with a := χr⁻² + 𝔞,

    f_ex = (Pa) dψ + R_T dT + R_r dr,    (47.9)
    R_T = m₀r⁻²∂_r²𝔞 + 3m₀r⁻³∂_r𝔞 − 2m₀r⁻³𝔭 ∂_T𝔞 − 2m₀r⁻⁴(r − r_h)⁻¹χ′,
    R_r = m₀r⁻²𝔭 ∂_r²𝔞 + 3m₀(r² + rr_h − r_h²)r⁻⁴(r − r_h)⁻¹∂_r𝔞 − 2m₀(2r − r_h)r⁻²(r − r_h)⁻²∂_T𝔞
          − r_h(3r² − 2rr_h + r_h²)r⁻⁴(r − r_h)⁻²χ′,

with Pa = 2∂_T∂_ra − ∂_r²a − (3/r)∂_ra + (3/r)∂_Ta. By (47.8), Pa = 0, so f_ex = R_T dT + R_r dr there: every
term carries a factor m₀ or r_h, and no term has χ or 𝔞 undifferentiated.

*Orders at ℐ⁺.* 𝔨(w, r) = r⁻²𝔨_0(w/r) with 𝔨_0(ϱ) := (1 + ϱ)(ϱ(2 + ϱ))^(−1/2) − 1, and for 0 < ϱ < 2,
𝔨_0(ϱ) = (2ϱ)^(−1/2)Σ_(j≥0) c_jϱ^j − 1 with a convergent series, c_0 = 1. On the support of χ_on′(T − w),
0 < w ≤ T − T_2; so for T in a bounded set and r large, with every derivative,

    𝔞 = −χ_on(T)r⁻² + 2^(−1/2)Σ_(j≥0) c_j r^(−3/2−j)F_j(T),        F_j(T) := ∫_0^∞ χ_on′(T − w)w^(j−½) dw,

each F_j smooth. Hence ∂_T𝔞 = O(r^(−3/2)), ∂_r𝔞 = O(r^(−5/2)) and ∂_r²𝔞 = O(r^(−7/2)), and T∂_T and r∂_r preserve these
forms. In (47.9) the coefficients of ∂_r²𝔞 are O(r⁻²) and those of ∂_r𝔞 and ∂_T𝔞 are O(r⁻³); so these terms
have ℐ⁺-order at least 9/2. The χ_on′ terms are −2m₀r⁻⁵χ_on′(1 + O(r⁻¹)) and −3r_hr⁻⁴χ_on′(1 + O(r⁻¹)), of order 4,
supported in the slab {T_2 ≤ T ≤ T_2 + 1}. dT and dr are smooth combinations of the Cartesian frame there.

*Orders at ι⁺.* For T ≥ T_2 + 1, χ_on = 1, and f_ex = Σ_m c_m(r)D_m𝔞 on {r ≥ 2R_T}, with D_m ∈ {∂_T, ∂_r, ∂_r²}; by
(47.9) the coefficients have the leading powers r^(−p_m), p_m = 3, 3, 2, in both components, and their other
terms carry further powers of r⁻¹. D_m𝔞 = ∫χ_on′(s)(D_m𝔨)(T − s, r) ds, and with ϱ := w/r,

    ∂_w𝔨 = r⁻³𝔨_0′(ϱ),        ∂_r𝔨 = −r⁻³(2𝔨_0 + ϱ𝔨_0′)(ϱ),        ∂_r²𝔨 = r⁻⁴(6𝔨_0 + 6ϱ𝔨_0′ + ϱ²𝔨_0″)(ϱ):

D_m𝔨 = r^(−d_m)𝔨_m(ϱ) with d_m = 3, 3, 4. As ϱ → 0, by the series above, 𝔨_m(ϱ) = ϱ^(a_m)(𝔨_m⁰ + O(ϱ^(1/2))) with
(a_m) = (−3/2, −1/2, −1/2), and as ϱ → ∞, from 𝔨_0(ϱ) = ½ϱ⁻² − ϱ⁻³ + (15/8)ϱ⁻⁴ + O(ϱ⁻⁵), 𝔨_m(ϱ) = ϱ^(−b_m)(𝔨_m^∞ +
O(ϱ⁻¹)) with (b_m) = (3, 3, 4); both expansions are conormal, ϱ∂_ϱ preserving them. Near ι⁺ ∩ ℐ⁺, with ρ_+ ∼ T⁻¹ and
ρ_I ∼ ϱ = T/r, a term c_mD_m𝔨 is ρ_+^(p_m+d_m)ρ_I^(p_m+d_m+a_m) times a bounded conormal function; near ι⁺ ∩ K⁺, with
ρ_+ ∼ r⁻¹ and ρ_K ∼ ϱ⁻¹, it is ρ_+^(p_m+d_m)ρ_K^(b_m) times one. Here p_m + d_m = 6, p_m + d_m + a_m ≥ 9/2 and b_m ≥ 3.
The lower terms of c_m raise the orders, r∂_r and ϱ∂_ϱ preserve the forms, and the convolution with χ_on′ shifts T by
at most T_2 + 1. So f_ex has ι⁺-order 6, with ℐ⁺-order 9/2 and K⁺-order 3 at the corners.

*Near compact sets.* At late times χ_on(T) = 1 on {r ≤ 2R_T}, so u_ex = W* + 𝔞 dψ there and, as □W* = □dψ = 0 and
□ = −∇^α∇_α on 1-forms,

    f_ex = (□_0𝔞) dψ − 2∇_(∇𝔞) dψ,

every term carrying a derivative of 𝔞. From 𝔨_0(ϱ) = ½ϱ⁻² − ϱ⁻³ + O(ϱ⁻⁴), uniformly for r in compact sets,
𝔨 = ½w⁻² − rw⁻³ + O(w⁻⁴), ∂_w𝔨 = −w⁻³ + O(w⁻⁴), ∂_r𝔨 = −w⁻³ + O(w⁻⁴), and the second derivatives are O(w⁻⁴), each
w∂_w preserving the bounds. T − v is a function of r, so the derivatives of 𝔞 in (v, r) are O(T⁻³) there, with
b-regularity: f_ex has K⁺-order 3. The slab {T_2 ≤ T ≤ T_2 + 1} ∩ {r ≤ 2R_T} is compact.

f_ex is smooth and vanishes on {T < T_2}, which contains {t^♭_* < T̂}. With these orders the criterion of
Section 46.12 gives the memberships.

*(c)* By (47.1), Q[χ_on(T)W*] = 4π²(χ_on(T) − r_h∂_r(χ_on(T))) and Q[𝔞 dψ] = −4π²r_h³∂_r𝔞 at r = r_h, with ∂_r
at fixed v. As r_h < R_T, T = v − 2r near the horizon, so ∂_r(χ_on(T)) = −2χ_on′(T) vanishes at late times, and
∂_r𝔞|_v = ∂_r𝔞|_T − 2∂_T𝔞 = O(T⁻³). So Q[u_ex] = 4π² + O(t_*^(−3)). As u_ex = 0 for T < T_2, (46.7) gives
∫ℓ(f_ex) dv = lim_(v→∞) Q[u_ex](v) = 4π².

*(d)* On compact r-sets, 𝔨(w, r) = ½w⁻² + O(w⁻³) uniformly, with every derivative, and ∫χ_on′ = 1; so
𝔞 = ½T⁻² + O(T⁻³), and T − t_* is bounded there. ∎

The coefficient ½ is that of the flat field: at m₀ = 0 and fixed r, a_0 = r⁻²(1 − r²/t²)^(−1/2) = r⁻² + ½t⁻² + O(t⁻⁴),
and a_0 → r⁻² = 4π²G as t → ∞, G = (4π²|x|²)⁻¹ the Green function of −Δ on ℝ⁴. So a_0 is the field of the charge
4π²δ_0 switched on at t = 0, which in 4 + 1 dimensions approaches its static value at the rate t⁻².

**Theorem 47.9** (The t_*^(−2) term.) Let f satisfy (47.6) without the condition ∫ℓ(f) dv = 0, with
γ_+ < 3 and w_I < 4 (lowering weights is free), let c_0 := (4π²)⁻¹∫ℓ(f) dv, and let u be the forward solution of
□u = f. Then on each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, with every number of derivatives in x and t_*,

    u − c_f(t_*)W* = (c_0/2) t_*^(−2) dψ + O(t_*^(−α_K)),        dψ = m₀W* − (∂_v)^♭.    (47.10)

*Proof.* f′ := f − c_0f_ex lies in the space of (47.6) (Lemma 47.8 (b)) and has zero total charge
(Lemma 47.8 (c)). u − c_0u_ex is smooth, vanishes on {t^♭_* < 1} (u_ex vanishes on {t^♭_* < T̂}), and solves
□(u − c_0u_ex) = f′; so it is the forward solution of f′ (Proposition 17.14). Theorem 47.7 (iii) gives
u − c_0u_ex − c_(f′)(t_*)W* = O(t_*^(−α_K)). By (46.7), at v = v_h(t_*),
4π²c_(f′) = Q[u] − c_0Q[u_ex] = 4π²c_f − c_0Q[u_ex], and Q[u_ex] = 4π² + O(t_*^(−3)) (Lemma 47.8 (c)). So
u = c_fW* + c_0(u_ex − W*) + O(t_*^(−α_K)), and Lemma 47.8 (d) gives (47.10), as α_K < 3. ∎

**Corollary 47.10** (Gauge vectors with compactly supported data.) Let Y be a smooth 1-form on N⁺, smooth up
to Σ°, with □Y = 0, whose Cauchy data on Σ° have compact support, and let c := Q[Y]/4π². For every ε > 0, on each
{r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′} and with every number of derivatives,

    Y − cW* = (c/2) t_*^(−2) dψ + O(t_*^(−3+ε)),
    ℒ_Yg − cℒ_(W*)g = (m₀c/2) t_*^(−2) ℒ_(W*)g + O(t_*^(−3+ε)).    (47.11)

The second term is not o(t_*^(−2)) when c ≠ 0: ℒ_(W*)g ≠ 0, and (ℒ_(W*)g)_(vr) = −(7/24)r_h⁻³ at r = 2r_h. Both
identities hold, with the same c, when the data of Y on Σ° vanish outside a ball and need not vanish near {|x| = r_♭}.

*Proof.* The cut-off of the proof of Corollary 47.6, with its translation, gives U = Y on compact r-sets at late times,
U the forward solution of a smooth forcing term with compact support in spacetime; that forcing term lies in
(47.6) (without the condition on the charge) for every α_K < 3, γ_+ < 3 and w_I < 4, and its running charge is
constant, c_F = Q[U]/4π² = c, once the cut-off vanishes near the horizon. Theorem 47.9 with α_K := 3 − ε gives the
first identity. For the second, ℒ_(φ dψ)g = φℒ_(dψ)g + 2dφ ⊗_s dψ and ℒ_(dψ)g = m₀ℒ_(W*)g; with φ := (c/2)t_*^(−2),
dφ = O(t_*^(−3)). For the value: (ℒ_(W*)g)_(vr) = ∂_rW*_v + ∂_vW*_r − 2Γ^μ_(vr)W*_μ, and in the ingoing chart
Γ^v_(vr) = 0 and Γ^r_(vr) = −f′/2; so (ℒ_(W*)g)_(vr) = −2r⁻³ − f′/(r(r + r_h)), f′ = 2m₀r⁻³, which is
−¼r_h⁻³ − (1/24)r_h⁻³ at r = 2r_h.

*Data vanishing only outside a ball.* Fix r_1 ∈ (r_♭, r_h), put K := Σ° ∩ {|x| ≤ r_1}, let θ ∈ C^∞(Σ°) equal 1 on
{|x| ≤ ½(r_♭ + r_1)} and 0 on {|x| ≥ r_1}, and let Y_2 solve □Y_2 = 0 on N⁺ with (1 − θ) times the data of Y, which
have compact support in Σ° (Theorem A.4 (5) on Ω^♯, Lemma 40.10). The data of Y − Y_2 vanish on Σ° ∖ K.
A point of N⁺ ∖ J⁺(K) lies in the Cauchy development of Σ° ∖ K in Ω^♯, as a past inextendible causal curve from it
meets Σ°, and not in K; that development is globally hyperbolic with Cauchy hypersurface Σ° ∖ K
(Theorem A.2), so the argument of Lemma 46.4 there gives Y = Y_2 on N⁺ ∖ J⁺(K). On {r < r_h},
f < 0. A future causal vector X has X^v = −g(X, −∂_r) ≥ 0, −∂_r being future null (Proposition 22.3 (d)), and the
inequalities 0 ≥ g(X, X) ≥ |f|(X^v)² + 2X^vX^r give X^r ≤ −½|f|X^v (if X^v = 0, X is a negative multiple of ∂_r). So
along a future causal curve from K, r does not increase and v increases by at most 2(r_1 − r_♭)/|f(r_1)|; as v is
bounded on K and t_* − v is a smooth function of r on {r_♭ ≤ r ≤ r_1}, J⁺(K) ⊂ {r ≤ r_1, t_* ≤ T_K} for a constant
T_K. Hence Y = Y_2 on {r > r_1}, so Q[Y] = Q[Y_2], and on {t_* > T_K}: the identities for Y_2, with T′ > T_K, are
those for Y. ∎

**Corollary 47.11** (The rates of Chapter 46 for gauge vectors with compactly
supported data.) Let ε > 0; on each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, with every number of derivatives:

(a) for Y as in Corollary 46.25, Y − (Q[Y]/4π²)W* = (Q[Y]/8π²)t_*^(−2)dψ + O(t_*^(−3+ε));

(b) in Proposition 46.27 (b), with c = Q[Z′_0]/4π²,

    (ġ_H)_0 = ṁK* + cℒ_(W*)g + (m₀c/2)t_*^(−2)ℒ_(W*)g + O(t_*^(−3+ε));

(c) in the last clause of Corollary 46.26, ℒ_(Y_h)g − (Q[Y_h]/4π²)ℒ_(W*)g = (m₀Q[Y_h]/8π²)t_*^(−2)ℒ_(W*)g +
O(t_*^(−3+ε)); so ġ_H + ℒ_(Y_h)g settles to ṁK* + (c_∞ + Q[Y_h]/4π²)ℒ_(W*)g at the rate of ġ_H, for the
representative of Corollary 46.26 that of Theorem 47.30, whose c is c_∞, and for that of Theorem 46.19
that of Corollary 47.27.

*Proof.* (a) and (c) are Corollary 47.10 for Y and Y_h. (b): (ġ_H)_0 = ṁK* + ℒ_(Z′_0)g exactly
(Proposition 46.27 (a)), and Corollary 47.10 applies to Z′_0. ∎

### 47.5 The spherically symmetric part

The l = 0 part of a class tensor or 1-form is its SO(4)-average (Section 46.1); Υ̇⁰, □ and X ↦ ℒ_Xg commute
with it, the rotations being isometries of g. Recall X_RW and Y[h_0] of Theorem 45.7, with
h_0 := (ġ − ṁK_V)_0 = ℒ_(Y[h_0])g (Theorem 45.7 (a)) and X_(RW,0) = −Y[h_0]^♭.

**Lemma 47.12** (The spherically symmetric part of the gauge forcing term.) On N⁺ the l = 0 part of F_Y is

    F_(Y,0) = □(X_(RW,0) + ṁ(1 − χ_K)W**_H),        so        J_(h,0) = □X_(RW,0)  on {χ_K = 1}.

*Proof.* F_Y = Υ̇⁰(ġ) − ṁ□(χ_KW**_H) on N⁺ (Section 46.9), ġ = ġ_RW − ℒ_(X_RW)g and (ġ_RW)_0 = ṁK_V
(Theorem 45.7 (a)). Averaging, Υ̇⁰(ġ)_0 = ṁΥ̇⁰(K_V) + □X_(RW,0) = ṁ□W**_H + □X_(RW,0), so
F_(Y,0) = □X_(RW,0) + ṁ□((1 − χ_K)W**_H). On {χ_K = 1}, F_Y = J_h (Section 46.9). ∎

On the cone the spherically symmetric gauge forcing term is therefore □ of a radial 1-form, and X_(RW,0) =
O(t_*^(−(w−1)+ε′)) on compact sets (Theorem 45.7 (c)). The next proposition shows that this part never reaches
the l = 0 part of the representative.

**Proposition 47.13** (The spherically symmetric part is homogeneous.) Let ġ_H = ġ + ℒ_Zg be the
representative of Corollary 46.26, Z = ṁχ_KW**_H + Z_1, let Y_0 := Y[h_0]^♭ = −X_(RW,0), and put
Z′_0 := Z_0 + Y_0 − ṁW**_H. Then on N⁺

    (ġ_H)_0 = ṁK* + ℒ_(Z′_0)g,        □Z′_0 = 0,        Z′_0 = Y_0 − ṁW**_H  near Σ°.    (47.12)

For ġ_H + ℒ_(Y_h)g, the clause of Corollary 46.26, the same holds with Z′_0 + Y_(h,0) in place of Z′_0.

*Proof.* ġ_0 = ṁK_V + h_0 = ṁK_V + ℒ_(Y_0)g, and averaging commutes with X ↦ ℒ_Xg; so
(ġ_H)_0 = ṁK_V + ℒ_(Y_0+Z_0)g = ṁK* + ℒ_(Z′_0)g, as K* = K_V + ℒ_(W**_H)g (Proposition 46.2 (iv) (c)). Υ̇⁰(ġ_H) = 0
on N⁺ (Corollary 46.26), Υ̇⁰(K*) = 0 and Υ̇⁰(ℒ_Xg) = −□X; so □Z′_0 = −Υ̇⁰((ġ_H)_0) + ṁΥ̇⁰(K*) = 0. Near Σ°,
χ_K = 0 and Z_1 = 0 (the proof of Corollary 46.26), so Z = 0 there. For Y_h, □Y_h = 0 and (ℒ_(Y_h)g)_0 = ℒ_(Y_(h,0))g. ∎

The l = 0 part of Z_1 is −Y_0 + ṁ(1 − χ_K)W**_H + Z′_0: its slow piece −Y_0 cancels against the term ℒ_(Y_0)g of ġ,
and the l = 0 rate of ġ_H is the rate of Z′_0, a solution of □Z′_0 = 0 whose Cauchy data on Σ° are those of
Y_0 − ṁW**_H, fixed by the spherically symmetric part of the initial data. This is the statement
Proposition 46.5 (c) for this representative.

**Definition 47.14** (Data of order p.) Let n be the future unit normal of Σ^IVP. A 1-form Y on N⁺, smooth up
to Σ°, has *data of order p at spatial infinity* if there is a constant c′ such that, near infinity on Σ^IVP, the
Cartesian components of Y − c′(∂_t)^♭ and of ∇_n(Y − c′(∂_t)^♭) are conormal of orders p and p + 1 in |x|⁻¹. c′ is its
*Killing multiple*; it is unique when p > 0. Data that have compact support up to such a multiple have every order.

(∂_t)^♭ = (∂_v)^♭ is the Killing form, with □(∂_t)^♭ = 0, ℒ_((∂_t)^♭)g = 0 and Q[(∂_t)^♭] = 4π²m₀ (Lemma 46.3 (b)).

**Corollary 47.15** (Homogeneous solutions with data of order p.) Let □Y = 0 on N⁺, with Y smooth up to Σ° and
data of order p ∈ (½, 3/2), with Killing multiple c′. Then Q[Y] is constant, and for every α_K < p with α_K ≠ 1, on
each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′} and with every number of derivatives,

    |Y − c′(∂_t)^♭ − cW*| ≤ C t_*^(−α_K),        |ℒ_Yg − cℒ_(W*)g| ≤ C t_*^(−α_K),        c := (Q[Y] − 4π²m₀c′)/4π².

*Proof.* Q[Y] is constant by (46.7). Subtract c′(∂_t)^♭, a solution with Q[(∂_t)^♭] = 4π²m₀ and
ℒ_((∂_t)^♭)g = 0; so we may take c′ = 0, and then c = Q[Y]/4π². It suffices to take α_K ∈ [½, p) ∖ {1}. Put
δ := (p − α_K)/5 and

    γ_+ := α_K + δ,   b_+ := α_K + 2δ,   b_I := α_K + 3δ,   p_slab := α_K + 4δ,   β := b_+ − ½,
    α_I := p_slab − 3/2,

so that α_K < γ_+ < b_+ < b_I < p_slab < p < 3/2, β ∈ (0, 1) and α_I < 0. Let τ′ := t_IVP/|x|, as in step (2) of the
proof of Theorem 46.23, χ_d ∈ C_c^∞((−1/16, 1/16)) equal to 1 near 0, and Y_d := χ_d(τ′)(y_0 + t_IVP y_1) near
infinity, (y_0, y_1) the data of Y (y_1 the t_IVP-derivative), extended to a smooth 1-form on the set 𝒟⁺ of
Proposition 46.22 with the data of Y on Σ°. τ′ is a b-time function at I₀ for every weight (Lemma 46.21 (d)), so □Y_d
is conormal of I₀-order p + 2, and near infinity it is supported in {|τ′| ≤ 1/16}, away from ℐ⁺.

(1) *The initial slab.* Y − Y_d has vanishing data and solves □(Y − Y_d) = −□Y_d. As ρ_Iρ^(−7/2) = ρ₀^(−7/2)ρ_I^(−5/2)
((37.17)), ρ_Iρ^(−7/2)□Y_d lies in H^(m,(a₀,2α_I))_b for every m, every a₀ < p − 3/2 and every α_I. Fix
a₀ ∈ (α_I, p − 3/2), possible as p_slab < p. Proposition 46.22, with α_I < min(a₀, 0), and b-Sobolev embedding as in
step (4) of the proof of Theorem 46.23, give the Cartesian components of Y and all their b-derivatives the
ℐ⁺-order α_I + 3/2 = p_slab on N⁺ ∩ {2 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ 3}, Y_d vanishing near ℐ⁺.

(2) *The forward solution.* With χ of Lemma 46.18, χ(t^♭_*)Y solves □(χ(t^♭_*)Y) = [□, χ(t^♭_*)]Y, a forcing
term supported in {2 ≤ t^♭_* ≤ 3}, meeting ∂M only at ℐ⁺, of ℐ⁺-order p_slab + 1 (the proof of Proposition 46.20).
As b_I + 1 < p_slab + 1 and the slab meets neither ι⁺ nor K⁺, it lies in H^(∞,(b_I+1,b_++2,1/2))_b(Ω_*, μ_b)^(•,−)
(a conormal tensor whose pointwise orders exceed the weights lies in the space, the proof of Lemma 46.18), the
space of (19.23) in the form of Corollary 19.15. Its conditions b_I < 3/2 + S̄ and b_+ < b_I hold for □
(S̄ = 0, Lemma 23.2 at γ_Υ = 0), and □ is 1-admissible with sf-weight b_+ − 5/2 = β − 2 (Theorem 46.11
(iii), as β ∈ (0, 1)). So χ(t^♭_*)Y is its forward solution (Theorem 19.14; uniqueness as in the proof of
Proposition 46.20), and Corollary 19.15 gives χ(t^♭_*)Y ∈ H^(k,(b_I,b_+,−1/2))_b(Ω_*, μ_b) for every k.

(3) *The cone.* χ′Y is the forward solution of [□, χ′]Y. On the cone part {t_*/40 ≤ r ≤ t_*/20} of supp dχ′,
[□, χ′] ∈ ρ_+²Diff¹_b (the proof of Theorem 46.19 (iii)), and that cone stays away from K⁺ and ℐ⁺; the rest of
supp dχ′ is compact. So [□, χ′]Y ∈ H^(∞,(𝔪,b_++2,𝔪))_b for every 𝔪. If α_K < 1, it lies in (46.16) with
γ_+ ∈ (α_K, 3/2) and α_K ∈ [½, 1), as γ_+ < b_+; if α_K ∈ (1, 2), it lies in (47.2) with γ_+ ∈ (α_K, 2),
for any ϵ_1, the forcing term vanishing near ℐ⁺. Theorem 46.29, resp. Theorem 47.5,
gives |χ′Y − c_f(t_*)W*| ≤ Ct_*^(−α_K). At late times dχ′ = 0 near the horizon, so ℓ of the forcing term vanishes for
large v and c_f = Q[χ′Y]/4π² = Q[Y]/4π², constant. On compact r-sets at late times χ′Y = Y. The metric part:
ℒ_Yg − cℒ_(W*)g = ℒ_(Y−cW*)g, bounded by the derivatives of Y − cW*. ∎

At p = ½ the chain α_K < γ_+ < b_+ < b_I < p_slab < p is empty; for p ≥ 3/2 it stops at 3/2, the a priori ι⁺-weight
b_+ < 3/2 of the forward solution on the slab. For data of compact support Corollary 47.10 is better.

**Corollary 47.16** (The spherically symmetric rate.) Let ġ_H be the representative of Corollary 46.26 for
data (γ̇, k̇) in the class of Corollary 40.5, let q := min(min Re ℰ_0, ℓ_0, 2), so that q > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ
(Section 38.1: min Re ℰ_0 > 3/2 + 2γ_Υ and ℓ_0 > 3; and γ_Υ < ¼), and let c′ be the Killing multiple of the data of
Z′_0 ((47.12)) and c := (Q[Z′_0] − 4π²m₀c′)/4π².

(a) Z′_0 has data of order p for every p < q − 1. Let p_0 be the supremum of the orders of its data; so
p_0 ≥ q − 1 > ½ + 2γ_Υ > ½ + δ_♯. Then (ġ_H)_0 − ṁK* − cℒ_(W*)g = O(t_*^(−α)) on compact sets, with every derivative,
for every α < min(p_0, 3/2) with α ≠ 1. In particular the spherically symmetric part of every perturbation in the class
settles faster than t_*^(−1/2−δ_♯).

(b) Suppose that outside a ball (γ̇, k̇) are ṁ times the data of K_V, as for the data of Theorem 3.9, glued to
exact Tangherlini data beyond a ball (Chapter 42). Then Z′_0 = ṁZ^(V) + Z_c + c″(∂_t)^♭, where Z_c solves
□Z_c = 0 with data vanishing outside a ball, c″ is a constant, and Z^(V) is one solution of □Z^(V) = 0, independent of
the perturbation, with data of order exactly 1. So (ġ_H)_0 − ṁK* − cℒ_(W*)g = O(t_*^(−1+ε)) for every ε > 0. If
ṁ = 0, as for data with compact support, then the data of Z′_0 − c′(∂_t)^♭ vanish near infinity, so that p_0 = ∞, and

    (ġ_H)_0 − cℒ_(W*)g = (m₀c/2) t_*^(−2) ℒ_(W*)g + O(t_*^(−3+ε)).

*Proof.* (a) Near Σ°, Z′_0 = Y_0 − ṁW**_H ((47.12)). Y_0 = ζ(∂_v)^♭ + rH_L dv, with dζ = 𝔷 algebraic in h_0
and the first derivatives of H_L (Lemma 45.6 (b)). In the class S′ = S⁰′ = 0, so ġ_(S′) = ġ⁰_(S⁰′) = 0 and
ġ = ḣ on 𝒟′, near Σ° (Corollary 40.5, Theorem 40.4 (2)); the data ḣ_0 and ḣ_1 = rℒ_(∂_(t_IVP))ḣ of ḣ lie in
H^(∞,(ℰ_0,ℓ_0))_b(Σ^IVP) (Lemma 40.1); and K_V ∈ |x|⁻²C^∞ is stationary ((21.31)). So along Σ^IVP near
infinity the components of h_0 and of its normal derivative are conormal of every order below q, resp. q + 1. Hence 𝔷
is conormal of every order below q and rH_L of every order below q − 1; ζ has a limit ζ_∞ at infinity along Σ^IVP, with
ζ − ζ_∞ of every order below q − 1; and ∇Y_0 is of every order below q. So Y_0 has data of every order below q − 1,
with Killing multiple ζ_∞. W**_H has data of order 1 with no Killing part: near infinity on Σ^IVP = {t = C″}
(Lemma 21.24), v = |x| + O(1); from (46.5), A = 1/(2r) + O(r⁻²) and B = −1/(4r) + O(r⁻² log r);
dv = dt + ((2 − f)/f)d|x| ((21.35)) and W* = r⁻²dt + O(r⁻³)d|x|; and V = −(∂_mT_m)∂_t ((45.2)) with
T_m(|x|) = 2|x| − 2r_*, so ∂_mT_m = 2/|x| + O(|x|⁻³) and V^♭ = (2/|x|)dt + O(|x|⁻³). So

    W**_H = −dt/|x| + d|x|/(4|x|) + O(|x|⁻² log|x|),        ∂_tW**_H = ½W* = O(|x|⁻²),

with conormal components (A and B are analytic in r with logarithmic terms at infinity). As q − 1 ≤ 1, Z′_0 has data of
every order below q − 1, with Killing multiple c′ = ζ_∞; and q − 1 > ½ + 2γ_Υ ≥ ½ + 2δ_♯. Corollary 47.15 for Z′_0,
at every p < min(p_0, 3/2), with (47.12), gives the rate.

(b) The data (ḣ_0, ḣ_1) of Lemma 40.1 are determined at each point by linear algebraic equations in (γ̇, k̇) and
finitely many of their derivatives; so outside a ball they are ṁ times those of the initial solution ḣ^(V) of
Proposition 40.2 for the data of K_V, and ḣ − ṁḣ^(V) has data of compact support. (The data of K_V satisfy the
linearised constraint equations: they are the derivative in m at m₀ of the data of the vacuum metrics g_((m,0)).)
ḣ − ṁḣ^(V) solves L^♮(ḣ − ṁḣ^(V)) = 0, an equation whose principal part is ½□_g ⊗ id; so it vanishes on the Cauchy
development ℰ, in the interior of 𝒟, of the part of Σ° outside a large ball (Theorem A.2,
Theorem A.4 (3)). ḣ^(V) induces the data of K_V (Lemma 40.1 (1)), so k := ḣ^(V) − K_V induces zero
data; and DRic(k) = 0 on 𝒟, as DRic(ḣ^(V)) = 0 there (Proposition 40.2 (1)) and DRic(K_V) = 0 (Section 45.1).
By Theorem 40.12 and Step 1 of its proof (with Z = 0 and U := U^♯ ∩ {t_IVP < 1}, so that Ω′_+ ⊂ 𝒟), k = ℒ_(Y_V)g
near Σ°, with Y_V = 0 on Σ° and ∇_nY_V^♭ = k(n, ·) + ½k(n, n)n^♭ = −K_V(n, ·) − ½K_V(n, n)n^♭ there, as
ḣ^(V)(n, ·) = 0 on Σ^IVP (Lemma 40.1); averaging over SO(4), we take Y_V spherically symmetric. Near infinity on
Σ^IVP, K_V = |x|⁻²(dt − d|x|)² (Section 46.10), so ∇_nY_V is conormal of order 2: Y_V has data of order 1 and no
Killing part. On ℰ, h_0 = (ḣ − ṁK_V)_0 = ṁk = ℒ_(ṁY_V)g, so ℒ_(Y_0−ṁY_V)g = 0: Y_0 − ṁY_V is a spherically symmetric
Killing field on ℰ, whose orbit space is connected, so it equals c″(∂_v)^♭ (Lemma 45.6 (c)). Let Z^(V) be the
solution of □Z^(V) = 0 on N⁺ with the data of Y_V − W**_H on Σ° (Lemma 40.9, Lemma 46.4). Its data have order
1, and exactly 1: its value on Σ° near infinity is dt/|x| − d|x|/(4|x|) + O(|x|⁻² log|x|), and subtracting
c′(∂_t)^♭ = −c′dt + O(|x|⁻²) leaves a term of order 0 unless c′ = 0. Then Z_c := Z′_0 − ṁZ^(V) − c″(∂_t)^♭ solves
□Z_c = 0, and its data, those of Y_0 − ṁY_V − c″(∂_v)^♭ near Σ° ((47.12)), vanish outside a ball.
Corollary 47.15 for Z^(V) at every p < 1 and Corollary 47.10 for Z_c give the rate t_*^(−1+ε), the Killing part
dropping out of the metric.

*If ṁ = 0*, then ḣ vanishes on ℰ, and ġ = ḣ near Σ° (as in (a)); so h_0 = ġ_0 = 0 on a neighbourhood 𝒪 in N⁺ of the
part Σ°_ext of Σ° outside a large ball. On 𝒪, H_L = 0 and, as δm[h_0] = 0 (Theorem 45.7 (a)), the tensor h′ of
Lemma 45.6 (b) is h_0 = 0; so 𝔷 = 0, and Y_0 = ζ(∂_v)^♭ with ζ locally constant. Σ°_ext is connected and ζ tends
to ζ_∞ along it, so ζ = ζ_∞ and Y_0 = ζ_∞(∂_v)^♭ near Σ°_ext. As Z′_0 = Y_0 near Σ° ((47.12) with ṁ = 0),
Z′_0 − ζ_∞(∂_t)^♭ vanishes near Σ°_ext. Its data vanish near infinity, so they have every order, with Killing multiple
ζ_∞ (Definition 47.14): c′ = ζ_∞, p_0 = ∞ and c = (Q[Z′_0] − 4π²m₀ζ_∞)/4π². Corollary 47.10 applied to
Z′_0 − ζ_∞(∂_t)^♭, whose data vanish outside a ball, whose charge is 4π²c, as Q[(∂_t)^♭] = 4π²m₀, and whose metric
part is ℒ_(Z′_0)g = (ġ_H)_0 ((47.12)), gives the last display.

*Data with compact support have ṁ = 0:* ġ_0 = 0 near Σ° outside a ball, and δm[ġ_0] = ṁδm[K_V] + δm[h_0] = ṁ
(Lemma 45.6 (a), Theorem 45.7 (a)) is constant on the simply connected orbit space of the interior of N⁺
(Lemma 45.6 (b)); so ṁ = 0. ∎

### 47.6 The 1-forms with no part of degree l ≤ 1

On all 1-forms the window of Theorem 47.4 cannot be lowered: the indicial root 0 of the l = 0 forms bounds it from
below, and at negative weights the zero-energy kernel contains W* and (∂_v)^♭. On the 1-forms with no part of degree
l ≤ 1 neither obstruction occurs. This section proves the low-energy hypotheses (G), (Z) and (TF) of Section 13.1.2 on
that subspace, at every b-weight of (−1, 3).

*Setting.* As in Section 23.8 at 𝗉_0: P̂(σ) is the spectral family of □ = dδ + δd at b₀, with (H1)–(H5),
ϑ_ℋ = 1, index 0 at σ ≠ 0, and P̂(σ) invertible for every σ ≠ 0 with Im σ ≥ 0 (Proposition 23.17); the spaces 𝒳_0,
𝒴_0 and 𝒳^*_0 of (13.7), 𝒳_σ and 𝒴_σ of (13.22), the tf spaces of Section 13.4.3, a constant
s > 5/2, and the frame dt_*, dx¹, …, dx⁴ of Chapter 11, the *Cartesian frame*. On stationary 1-forms P̂(0) = □,
computed in the ingoing chart, as t_* − v is a function of r. A 1-form on {r = c} decomposes into its dt_* and dr
components and its angular part, and by Lemma 21.6 a 1-form is a sum of *scalar types of degree l*,
aS dt_* + bS dr + c dS with S ∈ 𝒮_l, l ≥ 0, and *vector types of degree l*, ϖY with Y ∈ 𝒱_l, l ≥ 1, the coefficients
functions of r (of (t_*, r) on spacetime). As dt_* = dv + (t_* − v)′dr, the scalar type aS dt_* + bS dr + c dS is
aS dv + (b + a(t_* − v)′)S dr + c dS, so the same types are written with dv in place of dt_*, as in Lemma 47.19.

**Definition 47.17** (The projections.) O(4) acts on X by x ↦ gx, isometries of g that fix t, r and t_*, and on
1-forms by T_gu := (g⁻¹)^*u; in the Cartesian frame (T_gu)(x) = A_gu(g⁻¹x) with the constant orthogonal matrix
A_g = diag(1, g). For an irreducible representation τ of SO(4) with character χ_τ put

    P_τ := dim τ ∫_(SO(4)) χ̄_τ(g) T_g dg        (Haar probability measure).

Let τ_0 be the trivial representation, τ_1 the standard one on ℂ⁴, and τ_± those on the self-dual and anti-self-dual
2-forms Λ²_±ℂ⁴, so that Λ²ℂ⁴ = τ_+ ⊕ τ_−. Put

    Π_(≥2) := 1 − P_(τ_0) − P_(τ_1) − P_(τ_+) − P_(τ_−),        Π_0 := P_(τ_0),        Π_G := ∫_G T_g dg,
    Π_cl := Π_G(1 − Π_0),

G = O(2) × O(2) the group of the class. Π_0 is the SO(4)-average, the l = 0 part of Section 46.1. Below Π is
either Π_(≥2) or Π_cl, and h, the index of the pairing ⟨·, ·⟩_h of Section 46.5 (not the tensor
h = ġ − ṁK_V), is an O(4)-invariant fibre inner product equal to the identity in the Cartesian frame at ∂X (average any
admissible choice over O(4)).

**Lemma 47.18** (The projections.)

(a) Π is a projection; it commutes with P̂(σ), P̂(σ)^(*h), multiplication by functions of r, ρ∂_ρ, the dilations S_ς of
Section 13.6, N(P⁽⁰⁾), I(ι), N_tf(σ̂) and its adjoint, and the Mellin transform of Section 13.2.3; and Π^(*h) = Π.

(b) Π and 1 − Π are bounded, uniformly in ς, on every space of Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (H̄^s, Ḣ^s, H^s_(b,c),
H̄^(s,a)_b, 𝒳_0, 𝒴_0, 𝒳^*_0, the scattering spaces with the decay orders of Section 13.4.3 and Section 13.6.1, the
spaces of Definition 13.13 and Definition 13.22, 𝒳_σ, 𝒴_σ, 𝒳^*_σ and the tf spaces), so ran Π is closed in each. On M′,
Π is bounded on every H^(k,(w_I,w_ι,w_K))_b and commutes with □, with the cut-offs that are functions of (t_*, r), and
with the forward solution operator of Theorem 19.14.

(c) ℓ ∘ Π = 0.

(d) For u ∈ ran Π, every component of u in the Cartesian frame has zero mean on every sphere {r = c}.

(e) ran Π_(≥2) lies in the closed span of the scalar and vector types of degrees l ≥ 2. ran Π_cl is the space of class
1-forms with no l = 0 part, and lies in the closed span of the scalar types of even degrees l ≥ 2.

*Proof.* (a) Each T_g, g ∈ O(4), commutes with the operators listed: x ↦ gx is an isometry of the metric fixing t_* and
r, it preserves |dx| and the Laplacian of 𝕊³, and h is invariant; the restrictions to ρ = 0, the Mellin transform in ρ
and the conjugation by e^(iσ̂r̂) that define N(P⁽⁰⁾), I(ι) and N_tf commute with maps that fix ρ and r̂. The averages
inherit this, a bounded operator commuting with a Bochner integral. P_τP_σ = δ_(τσ)P_τ is the orthogonality of the
characters of a compact group, for every strongly continuous representation; so Π_(≥2), one minus four mutually
orthogonal P_τ, is a projection. Conjugation by g ∈ O(4) maps P_τ to P_(τ^g), τ^g(h) := τ(g⁻¹hg); τ_0 and τ_1 are
invariant under it, and τ_+, τ_− are exchanged when det g = −1; so every T_g, g ∈ O(4), commutes with Π_(≥2) and with
Π_0. Hence Π_G commutes with Π_0, and Π_cl is a projection. T_g^(*h) = T_(g⁻¹), χ_τ(g⁻¹) = χ̄_τ(g) and the Haar measures
are inversion-invariant, so P_τ^(*h) = P_τ, Π_G^(*h) = Π_G, and Π^(*h) = Π.

(b) Let E be one of the spaces listed. On the b-Sobolev spaces the weights are functions of |x|, or of (t_*, r) on M′,
and T_g is an isometry. On the scattering spaces with variable decay order the norm is ‖Au‖ + ‖u‖_(−𝔪) for an elliptic
A of that order; T_g⁻¹AT_g is elliptic of the same order, which is a function of ξ and |η|², hence rotation- and
reflection-invariant (Section 13.4.3), and it depends continuously on g in the calculus; as O(4) is compact,
C_E := sup_g‖T_g‖_(E→E) < ∞. With this uniform bound, the density of C_c^∞ (or of Schwartz sections) gives the strong
continuity of g ↦ T_gu on E by an ε/3 argument. For a graph-norm space 𝒳 = {u ∈ H : Pu ∈ Y},
‖u‖_𝒳 = ‖u‖_H + ‖Pu‖_Y, with H and Y base spaces and P commuting with every T_g (by (a)), T_g𝒳 ⊂ 𝒳 with
‖T_g‖_𝒳 ≤ max(C_H, C_Y), and ‖T_gu − u‖_𝒳 = ‖T_gu − u‖_H + ‖T_g(Pu) − Pu‖_Y → 0 as g → e; this covers 𝒳_0, 𝒳_σ,
𝒳^*_0, 𝒳^*_σ and the tf domains. So each average is a Bochner integral of a continuous bounded E-valued function, with
‖P_τ‖ ≤ (dim τ)²C_E, ‖Π_G‖ ≤ C_E, ‖Π_(≥2)‖ ≤ 1 + (1 + 16 + 9 + 9)C_E and ‖Π_cl‖ ≤ C_E(1 + C_E); and S_ς commutes with
every T_g, so the bounds are uniform in ς. On M′ the weights are functions of (t_*, r), □ is natural under isometries,
and the forward solution is unique with an O(4)-invariant support condition, so it commutes with each T_g.

(c) ℓ(u) = r_h³∫_(𝕊³) u(∂_(t_*))|_(r=r_h) dω, and ∂_(t_*) and dω are O(4)-invariant; so ℓ = ℓ ∘ Π_0. Π_0Π_(≥2) = 0 by the
orthogonality of characters, and Π_0Π_cl = Π_GΠ_0(1 − Π_0) = 0.

(d) For Π_(≥2): the map u ↦ (∫_(𝕊³) u_μ(cω) dω)_μ, the means of the components in the Cartesian frame, is
SO(4)-equivariant into ℂ ⊕ ℂ⁴, on which SO(4) acts by τ_0 ⊕ τ_1. Equivariance gives 𝔐 ∘ P_τ = P_τ^♭ ∘ 𝔐, 𝔐 that map
and P_τ^♭ the projections on ℂ ⊕ ℂ⁴, and P_(τ_0)^♭ + P_(τ_1)^♭ = 1 there by the orthogonality of characters; so
𝔐 ∘ Π_(≥2) = 0. For Π_cl: G contains each reflection x_i ↦ −x_i, so the
spatial Cartesian components of a class 1-form are odd under it and have zero mean, and the mean of its time component
is the time component of its l = 0 part, which vanishes on ran Π_cl.

(e) The projections onto a type and a degree commute with every T_g, g ∈ O(4), as the isometries of 𝕊³ commute with
d, δ and the Laplacian and preserve 𝒮_l and 𝒱_l; so Π maps each type and degree into itself. The scalar type of degree
