0 is SO(4)-invariant, so it lies in ran P_(τ_0). On the scalar type of degree 1, SO(4) acts through 𝒮_1, the
restrictions of the linear functions ⟨a, x⟩/r (Lemma 21.4 (1)), by a ↦ ga, that is by τ_1. On 𝒱_1, the duals
of the Killing fields Ω_A, A ∈ 𝔰𝔬(4) (Lemma 21.4 (2)), it acts by T_gΩ_A^♭ = Ω_(gAg⁻¹)^♭, the adjoint
representation 𝔰𝔬(4) ≅ Λ²ℂ⁴ = τ_+ ⊕ τ_−. So Π_(≥2) vanishes on the types of degree ≤ 1, and the first claim follows from
Lemma 21.6. Π_G is the identity on class 1-forms and Π_cl u = u − Π_0u for them; a 1-form u with Π_cl u = u is
G-invariant and has Π_0u = Π_GΠ_0(1 − Π_0)u = 0. The class 1-forms are sums over even l of scalar types
(Lemma 45.2 (a), (c)), and those with no l = 0 part have l ≥ 2. ∎

**Lemma 47.19** ((G) on the subspace.)

(a) (*The radial systems.*) Let k_l² := l(l + 2), the κ of Proposition 23.16. On ω = aS dv + bS dr + c dS, S ∈ 𝒮_l, a, b,
c functions of r, P̂(0)ω = E_vS dv + E_rS dr + E_θ dS with

    r³E_v = −[r(r² − m₀)a″ + 3(r² − m₀)a′ − k_l²ra],
    r⁴E_r = −[r²(r² − m₀)b″ + (3r³ + m₀r)b′ − (k_l²r² + 3r² − 3m₀)b + 2k_l²rc − 3r²a],
    r³E_θ = −[r(r² − m₀)c″ + (r² + m₀)c′ − k_l²rc + 2r²a + 2(r² − m₀)b],    (47.13)

and δω = −r⁻³[(r³a)′ + (r³fb)′ − k_l²rc]S. On ω = ϖY, Y ∈ 𝒱_l, ϖ a function of r and Λ_l := (l + 1)²,
P̂(0)ω = −r⁻²[r(rfϖ′)′ − Λ_lϖ]Y. The types do not couple.

(b) (*The roots.*) In the Cartesian frame the indicial roots of the scalar type of degree l are
{−l − 1, −l, 1 − l, l + 1, l + 2, l + 3}, and those of the vector type of degree l are {−l, l + 2}.

(c) (*The gap.*) Let Π_∂ be the action of Π on C^∞(𝕊³; ℂ⁵), and spec^Π_b := {ι : ker I(ι) ∩ ran Π_∂ ≠ 0}. Then
spec^Π_b ⊂ (−∞, −1] ∪ [3, ∞), so (−1, 3) is an indicial gap of the restricted operator, for both projections and
uniformly in l: every scalar root of degree l ≥ 2 is ≤ 1 − l ≤ −1 or ≥ l + 1 ≥ 3, and every vector root of degree
l ≥ 2 is ≤ −l ≤ −2 or ≥ l + 2 ≥ 4. The ends −1 and 3 are roots of the scalar type of degree 2. On all 1-forms the roots
0 (of degree 0 and of the scalar type of degree 1) and 2 lie in (−1, 3), and the gaps there are (−1, 0), (0, 2) and
(2, 3).

*Proof.* (a) In the ingoing chart |det g|^(1/2) = r³γ^(1/2), g^(vv) = 0, g^(vr) = 1, g^(rr) = f, g^(ij) = r⁻²γ^(ij), and
Δ̂S = −k_l²S. So ω^v = bS, ω^r = (a + fb)S, ω^i = r⁻²cγ^(ij)∂_jS, and δω = −|det g|^(−1/2)∂_μ(|det g|^(1/2)ω^μ) is the
stated formula; write δω = 𝒹S. For F := dω, F_(vr) = −a′S, F_(vi) = −a∂_iS, F_(ri) = e∂_iS with e := c′ − b, and
F_(ij) = 0; raising, F^(vr) = a′S, F^(vi) = r⁻²eγ^(ij)∂_jS and F^(ri) = r⁻²(fe − a)γ^(ij)∂_jS. With
(δF)^ν = −|det g|^(−1/2)∂_μ(|det g|^(1/2)F^(μν)),

    (δF)^v = (r⁻³(r³a′)′ − k_l²r⁻²e)S,    (δF)^r = k_l²r⁻²(a − fe)S,    (δF)^i = −r⁻³(r(fe − a))′γ^(ij)∂_jS,

and lowering with g_(vv) = −f, g_(vr) = 1, g_(ij) = r²γ_(ij) gives (δF)_v = (−fr⁻³(r³a′)′ + k_l²r⁻²a)S, (δF)_r =
(r⁻³(r³a′)′ − k_l²r⁻²e)S and (δF)_i = r⁻¹(r(a − fe))′∂_iS. As P̂(0)ω = dδω + δdω on stationary ω, E_v = −fr⁻³(r³a′)′ +
k_l²r⁻²a, E_r = 𝒹′ + r⁻³(r³a′)′ − k_l²r⁻²e and E_θ = 𝒹 + r⁻¹(r(a − fe))′, which with r³f = r(r² − m₀) multiply out to
(47.13). For ϖY, δ(ϖY) = r⁻²ϖδ̸Y = 0, d(ϖY) has the components ϖ′Y_i and ϖ(d̸Y)_(ij), and the same calculation
gives (δd(ϖY))_v = (δd(ϖY))_r = 0 and the stated angular part, with δ̸d̸Y = Λ_lY (Lemma 21.4 (2)). Each formula
maps a type and degree to itself.

(b) This is Lemma 23.3 at z = 0, the parameter value γ_Υ = 0 at which the operator there is □: its roots of type
sl are 1 − (l + 2), 1 − (l + 1), 1 − l, l + 1, l + 2, l + 3, those of type vl are −l and l + 2, and those of type s0 are
−1, 0, 2, 3. (They are the roots −m and m + 2 of the Cartesian components of degree m ∈ {l − 1, l, l + 1}, resp. m = l,
under the flat Laplacian, Lemma 21.10.)

(c) I(ι) commutes with the rotations and with Π_∂ (Lemma 47.18 (a)), and preserves each type and degree, on which it
is the indicial family of that type. By Lemma 47.18 (e), an element of ker I(ι) ∩ ran Π_∂ is a sum of components of
types of degree l ≥ 2 (for Π_cl: scalar, of even degree), each in ker I(ι); so ι is a root of such a type, and (b)
gives the bounds. On all 1-forms the roots of types s0 and s1 are {−1, 0, 2, 3} and {−2, −1, 0, 2, 3, 4}, and of type v1
{−1, 3}. ∎

**Lemma 47.20** (No kernel at negative weights.) Let β ∈ (−1, 0) and let u be a stationary 1-form on X, smooth
up to ∂_♯X (so across the horizon), in 𝒜^β near ∂X (conormal, |u| = O(r^(−β)) in the Cartesian frame, with all its
b-derivatives), with P̂(0)u = 0, whose expansion in types and degrees (Lemma 21.6) has no component of degree
l ≤ 1 (for instance u ∈ ran Π, by Lemma 47.18 (e)). Then u = 0.

*Proof.* We follow the proof of Lemma 23.21 (2), with the growth at infinity excluded mode by mode. Expand u in
types and degrees (Lemma 21.6; the projections act in the angles and preserve smoothness at r_h in the ingoing
chart and the conormal bounds); only degrees l ≥ 2 occur. Let k_l² := l(l + 2) and ρ := 1/r.

*(a) The divergence.* φ := δu is smooth, stationary and in 𝒜^(β+1) near infinity, and δdφ = δ(P̂(0)u) = 0, as
δ□ = δdδ = □_0δ. Its degree-l component solves (r³fφ_l′)′ = k_l²rφ_l. At r = ∞ this equation has a regular singular point
with the indicial roots ρ^(l+2) and ρ^(−l) (the proof of Lemma 23.21 (2) (c)); φ_l = O(r^(−β−1)) with
β + 1 > 0 excludes ρ^(−l) for every l ≥ 0, so φ_l = O(r^(−l−2)) and φ_l′ = O(r^(−l−3)). On [r_1, R] ⊂ (r_h, ∞),
[r³fφ_l′φ̄_l]_(r_1)^R = ∫_(r_1)^R (r³f|φ_l′|² + k_l²r|φ_l|²) dr, and the bracket tends to 0 as r_1 → r_h (f → 0) and as
R → ∞. So φ_l = 0: δu = 0 on {r > r_h}.

*(b) The field.* F := du ∈ 𝒜^(β+1) has δF = P̂(0)u − dδu = 0 on {r > r_h}. *Vector type.* A component r^(−1/2)Φ(r)Y, Y ∈
𝒱_l, of u has −Φ_** + V_1Φ = 0 with V_1 > 0 (Proposition 23.16 (iii), (v) at σ = 0, Λ = (l + 1)² ≥ 9). Φ is smooth in r
at r_h, and Φ = O(r^(3/2−β)), as |Y| is r⁻¹ in the Euclidean metric. The equation has a regular singular point at r = ∞,
where r^(−1/2)Φ grows like r^(l+1) or decays like r^(−l−1), as V_1 = ((l + 1)² − ¼)r⁻² + O(r⁻⁴); as l + 1 > 1 − β, the
first is excluded, so Φ = O(r^(−l−1/2)) and Φ_* = fΦ′ = O(r^(−l−3/2)). The energy identity of the proof of
Lemma 23.21 (2), ∫(|Φ_*|² + V_1|Φ|²) dr_* = [Φ_*Φ̄], whose end terms vanish, gives Φ = 0. *Scalar type.* With W :=
r³F_tr, R[W] = (r²M_t)′ = 0 (M = δdu = 0), and Φ := r^(−1/2)W solves −Φ_** + V_2Φ = 0 with V_2 > 0 as k_l² ≥ 3
(Proposition 23.16 (iv)–(v), whose κ is k_l²). F_tr = F_vr is smooth at r_h, and W = O(r^(2−β)). R[W] = 0 has a regular
singular point at r = ∞, with the indicial roots W ∼ r^(l+2) and W ∼ r^(−l); as l + 2 > 2 − β, W = O(r^(−l)), so Φ =
O(r^(−l−1/2)), Φ_* = O(r^(−l−3/2)), and the energy identity gives Φ = 0. So F_tr = 0, and with M = 0 Proposition 23.16
(iv) gives a = b = 0 for the gauge-invariant pair there: each scalar component of u is d(c_lS) on {r > r_h}, for a
function c_l of r.

*(c) The gauge.* So u = Σ_(l≥2) d(c_lS_l) on {r > r_h}, and δu = 0 gives (r³fc_l′)′ = k_l²rc_l. c_l dS has size |c_l|/r
in the Cartesian frame, so c_l = O(r^(1−β)). At r = ∞ the indicial roots are r^l and r^(−l−2), and r^l is excluded as
l > 1 − β, which holds for l ≥ 2 as β > −1. So c_l = O(r^(−l−2)), and the energy identity of (a) gives c_l = 0. So
u = 0 on {r > r_h}.

*(d) Inside the horizon.* u is smooth across r_h, in ker P̂(0), and vanishes on {r > r_h}; part (d) of the proof of
Proposition 23.17, which uses only these properties (at σ = 0, as in Lemma 23.21 (2) (d)), gives u = 0 on
{r_♭ < r < r_h}. ∎

At degree l = 1, (c) fails: the solution r^l of the gauge equation is admitted by the weights of (−1, 0). The four
1-forms d(φ_1S), S ∈ 𝒮_1, lie in the kernel on all 1-forms at those weights, φ_1 being the solution of
(r³fφ′)′ = 3rφ that is smooth at r_h (where the equation has the double indicial root 0); it cannot decay, by the energy
identity of (a), so it grows like r. At degree 0, W* and (∂_v)^♭ lie in the kernel.

**Lemma 47.21** (Fredholm operators and commuting projections.) Let T : X → Y be a bounded Fredholm operator
between Banach spaces, and Π_X, Π_Y bounded projections with TΠ_X = Π_YT. Then T_1 := T|_(ran Π_X) : ran Π_X → ran Π_Y
and T_2 := T|_(ker Π_X) : ker Π_X → ker Π_Y are Fredholm, ind T = ind T_1 + ind T_2, ker T_1 = ker T ∩ ran Π_X and
ran T_1 = ran T ∩ ran Π_Y.

*Proof.* X = X_1 ⊕ X_2 and Y = Y_1 ⊕ Y_2 with X_1 = ran Π_X, X_2 = ker Π_X and likewise for Y, closed and complementary.
T maps X_i into Y_i, as TΠ_X = Π_YT; so T = T_1 ⊕ T_2 and ker T = ker T_1 ⊕ ker T_2, both finite-dimensional. If
y ∈ ran T ∩ Y_1, y = T_1x_1 + T_2x_2 with T_2x_2 ∈ Y_2, so T_2x_2 = 0 and y = T_1x_1: ran T_1 = ran T ∩ Y_1, which is
closed, and likewise ran T_2. Y_i/ran T_i → Y/ran T is injective, and Y/ran T ≅ Y_1/ran T_1 ⊕ Y_2/ran T_2; so the
cokernels are finite-dimensional and the indices add. ∎

**Proposition 47.22** ((Z) on the subspace.) For every α with α + 2 ∈ (−1, 0) ∪ (0, 2),
P̂(0) : 𝒳_0 ∩ ran Π → 𝒴_0 ∩ ran Π is invertible, at every regularity s > 5/2. By Theorem 47.25 (b) the same holds at
every α with α + 2 ∈ (−1, 3).

*Proof.* *Fredholm.* α + 2 lies in a gap of the full bundle, (−1, 0) or (0, 2) (Lemma 47.19 (c)), so
Theorem 13.11 (1) makes P̂(0) : 𝒳_0 → 𝒴_0 Fredholm. Π is bounded on 𝒴_0, and on 𝒳_0 with its graph norm, as
‖Πu‖ + ‖P̂(0)Πu‖ = ‖Πu‖ + ‖ΠP̂(0)u‖ ≤ C(‖u‖ + ‖P̂(0)u‖); and it commutes with P̂(0) (Lemma 47.18). By
Lemma 47.21 the restriction is Fredholm, with ker = ker P̂(0) ∩ ran Π.

*Kernel.* At α + 2 ∈ (0, 2) the kernel is span{W*} (Lemma 23.21 (2)), and ΠW* = 0, W* being SO(4)-invariant. At
α + 2 ∈ (−1, 0), a kernel element is smooth up to ∂_♯X and lies in 𝒜^β near ∂X for every β < 0 (Theorem 13.11 (2) at
the gap (−1, 0)), so Lemma 47.20 applies with some β ∈ (−1, 0), by Lemma 47.18 (e).

*Cokernel.* Let w be a bounded functional on 𝒴_0 ∩ ran Π that annihilates the restricted range, and v := w ∘ Π on
𝒴_0, so that v ∘ Π = v. v annihilates P̂(0)𝒳_0, as ΠP̂(0) = P̂(0)Π. At α + 2 ∈ (0, 2), v = cℓ (Lemma 23.21 (3)),
and v = v ∘ Π = cℓ ∘ Π = 0 (Lemma 47.18 (c)); so w = 0. At α + 2 ∈ (−1, 0): fix α′ with α′ + 2 ∈ (0, 2).
𝒳_0(α′) ⊂ 𝒳_0(α) and 𝒴_0(α′) ↪ 𝒴_0(α) continuously, so v|_(𝒴_0(α′)) annihilates P̂(0)𝒳_0(α′), hence equals cℓ there,
and so vanishes there, as v = v ∘ Π; so w vanishes on 𝒴_0(α′) ∩ ran Π. This is dense in 𝒴_0(α) ∩ ran Π: if d_n → y in
𝒴_0(α) with d_n smooth and vanishing for large r (Lemma 13.3 (d)), then Πd_n → Πy = y, and Πd_n is again smooth and
vanishes for large r, so lies in 𝒴_0(α′).

*Invertibility.* Kernel and cokernel are trivial at each s > 5/2 by the same arguments (Lemma 23.21 holds at each
such s, Section 23.8), and the inverse is bounded by the open mapping theorem. ∎

**Proposition 47.23** ((TF) on the subspace.) Let β ∈ (−1, 0) ∪ (0, 2). Then Definition 13.15 holds on ran Π
with the weight β: (i) β lies in the gap (−1, 3) of spec^Π_b; (ii) N_tf(e^(iθ)) is injective on 𝒳_(tf,θ) ∩ ran Π for
every θ ∈ [0, π]; (iii) N_tf(1)^(*h) is injective on 𝒳^*_(tf,0) ∩ ran Π. By Theorem 47.25 (b) the same holds for every
β ∈ (−1, 3).

*Proof.* (i) is Lemma 47.19 (c). The transition-face data of P̂ are those of the model: in the Cartesian frame
S_0 = 0, N(P⁽⁰⁾) = (−(ρ∂_ρ)² + 2ρ∂_ρ + Δ_(𝕊³))Id and H_0 = Id (the proof of Lemma 23.20 at γ_Υ = 0). So
N_tf(σ̂) = e^(−iσ̂r̂)(Δ_e − σ̂²)e^(iσ̂r̂) on each component (the proof of Proposition 13.20), and on the part of degree
ℓ in ω each component solves the equation of Lemma 13.17 (a). Π commutes with N_tf and with the projections Π_ℓ of
the proof of Proposition 13.20, and on ran Π every component has degrees ℓ ≥ 1 only (Lemma 47.18 (d)).

(ii) The argument of (ii) in the proof of Proposition 13.20, with Theorem 13.14 (5) applied at the gap of the full
bundle that contains β, (−1, 0) or (0, 2) (its part at sctf uses no gap): a kernel element lies in
𝒜^(3/2−ε,−β′)(tf) for every β′ in that gap, so its components are O(r̂^(−β′)) at ztf with β′ < 2. In each component and
degree ℓ ≥ 1 one Hankel coefficient remains, of size at least cr̂^(−2−ℓ) at ztf (Lemma 13.17 (d)) unless it
vanishes; as 2 + ℓ > β′, it vanishes.

(iii) The argument of (iii) in the proof of Proposition 13.20: at sctf the coefficients a_(1m) vanish, by the same
argument, which uses no gap; at ztf the remaining term has size at least cr̂^(−2−ℓ), while 𝒳^*_(tf,0) has the b-weight
−q there, q = 2 − β, so it would need ∫_0 r̂^(2(q−2−ℓ)) dr̂/r̂ < ∞, that is q > 2 + ℓ ≥ 3, which is false as β > −1. ∎

The argument of (iii) uses ℓ ≥ 1: at ℓ = 0 its condition at ztf, q > 2, holds for every β < 0.

Write P_Π(σ) for P̂(σ) on the spaces of Chapter 13 intersected with ran Π, and its adjoint on the dual spaces
intersected with ran Π (Π^(*h) = Π), and read (G) for spec^Π_b and Definition 13.15 on ran Π, as in Proposition 47.23.

**Lemma 47.24** (The Mellin families on the subspace.) Let J be one of the Mellin families of Chapter 13: I(ι)
(the end at infinity), I(−ι) (at ztf, Section 13.4.1), I^♯(ι) of (13.11), and the adjoint family of ztf,
H_0⁻¹I(ῑ + 2)^†H_0. Each commutes with Π_∂. Put spec^Π_J := {ι : ker J(ι) ∩ ran Π_∂ ≠ 0}. Then Lemma 13.5 (a)–(c)
hold for J restricted to ran Π_∂, with spec^Π_J in place of spec_J, and Lemma 13.7 and Lemma 13.8 hold for
every v with Πv = v, with spec_J replaced by spec^Π_J.

*Proof.* H_0 = Id is invariant, so the families commute with Π_∂ (Lemma 47.18 (a)). Fix m and put
E_m := ran Π_∂ ∩ H^m(𝕊³; ℂ⁵), closed in H^m as Π_∂ is bounded there (Lemma 47.18 (b)).

1. The proof of Lemma 13.5 (b) writes J(ι) = (1 + Δ)(Id + F(ι)) on H^m, with F(ι) compact and analytic in ι.
   Π_∂ commutes with J(ι) and with 1 + Δ (the rotations commute with the Laplacian), so with
   F(ι) = (1 + Δ)⁻¹J(ι) − Id, and F(ι)E_m ⊂ E_m.
2. The restriction of a compact operator to a closed invariant subspace is compact: the image of the unit ball of E_m
   lies in that of H^m, which is relatively compact, and in the closed set E_m.
3. 1 + Δ maps E_m injectively onto E_(m−2): for y ∈ E_(m−2), x := (1 + Δ)⁻¹y = (1 + Δ)⁻¹Π_∂y = Π_∂(1 + Δ)⁻¹y ∈ E_m.
   So it is an isomorphism, by the open mapping theorem.
4. So J(ι)|_(E_m) = (1 + Δ)|_(E_m) ∘ (Id + F(ι)|_(E_m)), and the second factor is Fredholm of index 0 (Riesz–Schauder),
   so the product is Fredholm of index 0 from E_m to E_(m−2).
5. The restricted family is analytic in ι, and invertible wherever J(ι) is invertible on H^m, as J(ι)⁻¹ commutes with
   Π_∂ and so maps E_(m−2) into E_m; such ι exist (Lemma 13.5 (a)). So Theorem A.44 applies on
   these Hilbert spaces: the restricted inverse is meromorphic, and its poles are where the restriction is not
   invertible, which, at index 0, is where it has a kernel, that is spec^Π_J.

Lemma 13.5 (a) holds for the restriction because the Neumann series of its proof stays in E_m, and (c) follows as
there. In Lemma 13.7 and Lemma 13.8 the Mellin transform of v = Πv takes values in ran Π_∂, the cut-offs are
functions of t, N(L) commutes with Π, and the proofs use J(ι)⁻¹ only on ℳv and ℳ(N(L)χv), both in ran Π_∂, where the
restricted inverse replaces it. ∎

**Theorem 47.25** (The low-energy theory on the subspace.) Let Π ∈ {Π_(≥2), Π_cl}.

(a) For every α with α + 2 ∈ (−1, 0) ∪ (0, 2), Theorem 13.11, Theorem 13.14 (at every q with −q + 2 in the same gap
of the full bundle), Corollary 13.16 (a)–(b) and Theorem 13.25 (1), (3) and (4) with m_1 = m_2 = 0 hold for P_Π,
with (Z) given by Proposition 47.22 and (TF) by Proposition 47.23.

(b) The same holds for every α with α + 2 ∈ (−1, 3), 0 included, and Proposition 47.22 and Proposition 47.23 hold there.

*Proof.* (a) *Restriction.* Every estimate of Chapter 13 for P̂(σ), its adjoint, N_tf and its adjoint
((13.8)–(13.9), (13.14)–(13.16), (13.21) and those of Theorem 11.33) holds for
every element of its space at the weights where it is proved, so for the elements of ran Π; at the weights of (a),
α + 2 and −q + 2 lie in gaps of the full bundle, where (G) holds for P̂. Fredholm properties pass to the restrictions
(Lemma 47.21), and the annihilator of a restricted range is the part in ran Π of the full one: if v ∈ ran Π
annihilates P_Π(𝒳 ∩ ran Π), it annihilates P̂𝒳, as ⟨P̂u, v⟩ = ⟨ΠP̂u, v⟩ = ⟨P̂Πu, v⟩. The statements on the regularity
of kernels (Theorem 13.11 (2), Theorem 13.14 (5)) restrict. Theorem 13.11 (4) for P_Π is Proposition 47.22.
Corollary 13.16 (a): by Proposition 47.23 (ii)–(iii) and Theorem 13.14 (3) restricted, the restricted N_tf(1) has index
0, the index is constant in θ (the local constancy argument of Theorem 13.14 (3) runs with its finite-rank
augmentations chosen in ran Π, which is possible as ΠC_c^∞(tf°) ⊂ C_c^∞(tf°) is dense in each restricted space), and
(ii) gives invertibility. Corollary 13.16 (b): the contradiction argument stays in ran Π, which is closed in
H^(−𝔪,(−𝔪,−𝔪))_(sc,b). Theorem 13.25 (1): Step 1 inverts P_Π(0) at the regularity s + k (Proposition 47.22 at that
regularity) on χ_zf u ∈ ran Π (χ_zf is a function of ρ); Step 2 applies (13.17) to S_ς(χ_tf u) ∈ ran Π at the
weight shifted by η ∈ (0, 1], η so small that α + 2 + η lies in the same gap of the full bundle (Corollary 13.16 (b)
restricted); Lemma 13.23, Lemma 13.24 and Theorem 11.33 (4) are estimates for all u. Theorem 13.25 (3):
P̂(σ) is invertible for σ ≠ 0, Im σ ≥ 0 (Proposition 23.17), and commutes with Π, so P_Π(σ) is. Theorem 13.25 (4):
its proof, with P̂(σ)⁻¹ restricted to ran Π, whose differentiability is Theorem 11.33 (6) restricted, and (1) at the
regularities s + i (Proposition 47.22 at each).

(b) *Transposition.* Every use of the gap in the proofs of Theorem 13.11, Theorem 13.14,
Corollary 13.16 and Theorem 13.25 is one of Lemma 13.5, Lemma 13.7 and Lemma 13.8 applied to an
element of ran Π: Lemma 13.7 at c = α + 2 to χ̃_∂u and at c = −α to the v of the adjoint (Section 13.3.1);
Lemma 13.8 for kernels and annihilators (Section 13.3.2–Section 13.3.3); Lemma 13.7–Lemma 13.8 at
ztf (Section 13.4.4); and the choice of η in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 13.25, now inside (−1, 3). By
Lemma 47.24 these hold on ran Π with (G) read for spec^Π_b, at every weight of (−1, 3) (Lemma 47.19 (c)); so the
proofs run on ran Π. Theorem 13.11 (3)–(4) restricted carries the invertibility of Proposition 47.22 from one weight
to every weight of (−1, 3); Theorem 13.14 (5) restricted gives Proposition 47.23 (ii) by the same argument at every
β ∈ (−1, 3), now with β′ < 3 ≤ 2 + ℓ; (iii) uses no gap; and Corollary 13.16 (c) restricted gives (TF) at every weight
of the gap. ∎

Part (a) is all that is used below: Theorem 47.28 works at weights in (−1, 0).

**Corollary 47.26** (The low-energy hypotheses on the subspace.) For P̂(σ) restricted to ran Π_cl (the class
1-forms with no l = 0 part) or to ran Π_(≥2), (G), (Z) and (TF) of Section 13.1.2 hold at every b-weight
α + 2 ∈ (−1, 3), in particular at every α + 2 ∈ (−1, 0]. Theorem 13.25 (4) holds there for P_Π, and so do
Proposition 20.29 and Lemma 29.33, with β_tf − β_zf = α + 2 and with û = P_Π(σ)⁻¹f̂ in place of
(û, b̂, Ŝ): no augmentation is needed.

*Proof.* Lemma 47.19 (c), Proposition 47.22, Proposition 47.23 and Theorem 47.25. The proof of
Proposition 20.29 uses of the operator only Theorem 13.25 (4) with m_1 = m_2 = 0 at its weight α, which
Theorem 13.25 (5) supplies when α is not the weight of the hypotheses, and Lemma 20.23, which involves no
operator. For P_Π, Theorem 47.25 states (4) at every α with α + 2 ∈ (−1, 3), so (5) is not needed; (2), the adjoint
estimate, is not used. The proof of Lemma 29.33 is that proof with the augmented estimates of Chapter 28 in place
of those of Chapter 13, which are no longer needed. ∎

### 47.7 The rate of the representative

The first improvement uses only Theorem 46.29: the forcing term of the gauge vector on the cone has the ι⁺-order
5/2 + δ_♯ less any η > 0 (Proposition 46.17), and the window γ_+ − α_K ∈ (0, 1) of Theorem 46.28 turns it into the
rate t_*^(−1/2−κ), κ < δ_♯. Its construction serves the part with l ≥ 2 below.

**Corollary 47.27** (The harmonic gauge at t_*^(−1/2−κ).) For every κ ∈ (0, δ_♯) there is C_κ, bounded by
finitely many norms of the data, such that on each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, with every number of derivatives,

    |ġ_H − ṁK* − c_∞ℒ_(W*)g| ≤ C_κ t_*^(−1/2−κ),    (47.14)

for ġ_H of Corollary 46.26 (on all of N⁺) and of Theorem 46.19 (on the late region), each with its c_∞.

*Proof.* Fix κ and put

    β := ½(κ + δ_♯),    η := ½(δ_♯ − β),    b_+ := ½ + β,    γ_+ := ½ + ½(κ + β),    α_K := ½ + κ.

Then κ < β < δ_♯ < ¼, and: α_K ∈ [½, 1); γ_+ − α_K = ¼(δ_♯ − κ) > 0 and γ_+ < 3/2; γ_+ + 2 < 5/2 + δ_♯ − η, as
δ_♯ − η = ½(δ_♯ + β) > ½(κ + β); and γ_+ < b_+, as b_+ − γ_+ = ½(β − κ) > 0.

*The full solution.* For Corollary 46.26: with Theorem 46.23 at this β (some p ∈ (½ + β, min(3/2, q_ḣ − 1))) and
b_I ∈ (b_+, p), Y := χ(t^♭_*)Z_1 is the forward solution on Ω_* of χ(t^♭_*)F_Y + [□, χ(t^♭_*)]Z_1, a forcing term in
the space of Lemma 46.18 (the proof of Proposition 46.20); and Corollary 19.15 gives
Y ∈ H^(k,(b_I,b_+,−1/2))_b(Ω_*, μ_b) for every k. For Theorem 46.19, Y is its own forward solution, with the same
weights (Lemma 46.18).

*Cone localisation.* χ′Y is the forward solution of f := χ′J_h + [□, χ′]Y (the proof of Theorem 46.19 (iii)). f
vanishes near ℐ⁺, as supp χ′ ⊂ {r ≤ t_*/20}, so (46.16) holds with every w_I. On supp χ′ ⊂ {χ_K = 1}, χ′J_h is
conormal of ι⁺-order ϰ_♯ + 1 − η = 5/2 + δ_♯ − η and of K⁺-order α − 2 − η = w − η > 2 + ε_t − η > 1
(Proposition 46.17 and its proof, Section 46.1); so it lies in (46.16), as γ_+ + 2 < 5/2 + δ_♯ − η and
α_K < 1. On the cone part {1/40 ≤ r/t_* ≤ 1/20} of supp dχ′, [□, χ′] ∈ ρ_+²Diff¹_b, and that cone stays away from K⁺
and ℐ⁺; the rest of supp dχ′ is compact. So [□, χ′]Y ∈ H^(∞,(𝔪,b_++2,𝔪))_b for every 𝔪, in (46.16) as
γ_+ < b_+.

*The rate.* Theorem 46.29 gives |χ′Y − c_f(t_*)W*| ≤ Ct_*^(−1/2−κ), with every derivative. For large t_*, χ′ = 1 near
the horizon, and ℓ(f) = ℓ(J_h) = ℓ(Υ̇⁰(h)) = O(v^(−w+ε′)) (Theorem 46.6), so c_f − c_∞ = O(t_*^(−(w−1)+ε′)), w − 1 > 1.
On compact r-sets at late times χ′ = χ(t^♭_*) = χ_K = 1, so Z_1 = χ′Y (for Theorem 46.19, Y = χ′Y), and
ġ_H − ṁK* − c_∞ℒ_(W*)g = h + ℒ_(Z_1−c_∞W*)g as K* = K_V + ℒ_(W**_H)g, with |h|_k = O(t_*^(−w+ε′)) ((45.3)). ∎

For the representative of Corollary 46.26 this is improved below: its spherically symmetric part is that of a
homogeneous solution (Corollary 47.16), and its part with l ≥ 2 sees no zero-energy state.

**Theorem 47.28** (Theorem 47.4 on the subspace, with the window in (−1, 0).) Let Π ∈ {Π_(≥2), Π_cl},
α_K ∈ (1, 2), γ_+ ∈ (max(½, α_K − 1), 1), ϵ_1 ∈ (0, ½), w_I ≥ max(5/2, γ_+ + 1 + ϵ_1), let
f ∈ H^(∞,(w_I,γ_++2,α_K))_b(Ω_*; T*)^(•,−) with plain weights and Πf = f, and let u be the forward solution of □u = f.
Then Πu = u, and for every small ϵ > 0

    u ∈ H^(∞,(γ_+−3ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′),     |u| ≤ C t_*^(−α_K)‖f‖  on {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ 8 max(R′, 1)},    (47.15)

with every number k of derivatives in x and t_*, ‖f‖ a norm of f in that space at an order k + k′, k′ independent
of k. There is no singular part and no W*.

*Proof.* Πu = u by Lemma 47.18 (b). We follow the proof of Theorem 47.4.

*The decomposition.* For f with Πf = f, (û_(reg,1), b̂_1) := P̃(σ)⁻¹(f̂, 0) has b̂_1 = 0 and
û_(reg,1) = P_Π(σ)⁻¹f̂ for 0 < |σ| ≤ c: Π_0 commutes with P̂(σ), fixes the column f̂_*(σ), the transform of the
SO(4)-invariant [□, χ^H_K]W*, and the row, φ_* and h being SO(4)-invariant, and kills f̂ (Π_0Π = 0); so
P̃(σ)(Π_0û_(reg,1), b̂_1) = (Π_0f̂, ⟨û_(reg,1), φ_*⟩_h) = (0, 0), whence Π_0û_(reg,1) = 0, b̂_1 = 0, and
P̂(σ)û_(reg,1) = f̂. Moreover Πû_(reg,1) = û_(reg,1): Π commutes with P̂(σ), Π^(*h) = Π (Lemma 47.18 (a)), and
Πφ_* = ΠΠ_0φ_* = 0, as ΠΠ_0 = 0 (the orthogonality of characters, and Π_G(1 − Π_0)Π_0 = 0); so
P̃(σ)(Πû_(reg,1), 0) = (ΠP̂(σ)û_(reg,1), ⟨û_(reg,1), Πφ_*⟩_h) = (Πf̂, 0) = (f̂, 0), and the invertibility of P̃(σ)
gives Πû_(reg,1) = û_(reg,1). As P_Π(σ) is invertible (Theorem 47.25 (a)), û_(reg,1) = P_Π(σ)⁻¹f̂. So u_sing = 0
and u = u_hi + u_reg, with c at most the constant c_k of Corollary 47.26 at the weight below.

*Step 2* is that of Theorem 47.4: Lemma 29.32 at (w_I, γ_+ + 2, α_K), whose conditions are w_I − 1 ≥ 3/2 and
w_I ≥ γ_+ + 1 + ϵ_1 (as α_K > 1 − ϵ_1), gives u_hi ∈ H^(∞,(3/2−ϵ,𝔪,𝔪))_b; and Proposition 20.18 (1) with ϵ_PP gives
f̂|_(±(0,c]) ∈ H^(∞,(min(w_I,γ_++2)−ϵ,γ_++1,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b, with f̂(0) = ∫f dt_* ∈ H^(∞,γ_++1)_b(X) ∩ ran Π. The
density step takes b_+ := ½(½ + γ_+) ∈ (½, γ_+) and b_I := ½(b_+ + 3/2) in Corollary 19.15: ½ < b_+ < b_I < 3/2, b_+
≤ γ_+, b_I + 1 < 5/2 ≤ w_I and α_K ≥ ½, and b_+ − ½ ∈ (0, 1).

*Step 3.1 (zero energy, without the column).* At α := γ_+ − 3, α + 2 = γ_+ − 1 ∈ (−1, 0), and 𝒴_0 has the μ_b-weight
γ_+ + 1, so f̂(0) ∈ 𝒴_0 ∩ ran Π and û_0 := P_Π(0)⁻¹f̂(0) ∈ H^(∞,γ_+−1)_b(X) (Proposition 47.22 at every regularity). With

    f̂_2 := (f̂ − χ_zf f̂(0)) − [P̂(0), χ_zf]û_0 − (P̂(σ) − P̂(0))(χ_zfû_0),

P̂(σ)(χ_zfû_0) = f̂ − f̂_2, and f̂_2 lies in H^(∞,(min(w_I,γ_++2)−ϵ,γ_++1,α_K−1))_b by Lemma 31.3 (b) and
Lemma 47.2 (a) at a = γ_+ − 1, as α_K − 1 < 1. The column term of Theorem 47.4 is absent.

*Step 3.2.* Corollary 47.26 (Lemma 29.33 for P_Π) applies at β_scf := 3/2 − ϵ, β_tf := γ_+ − 1,
β_zf := α_K − 1, with the window β_tf − β_zf = γ_+ − α_K ∈ (−1, 0); its forcing space asks the scf-weight
5/2 − ϵ ≤ min(w_I, γ_+ + 2) − ϵ, which is γ_+ ≥ ½. So û_(reg,1) = χ_zfû_0 + P_Π(σ)⁻¹f̂_2 lies in
H^(∞,(3/2−2ϵ,γ_+−1,((0,0),α_K−1)))_b with zf-coefficient û_0, the same for both signs. Proposition 20.20 (1) at
β_K = α_K ∈ (1, 2), with that one Taylor coefficient, v_0 = û_0 ∈ H^(∞,β_ι−1)_b(X), β_ι = γ_+, gives
u_reg ∈ H^(∞,(γ_+−ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′), as γ_+ < 3/2 − 2ϵ.

*The rate.* u = u_hi + u_reg ∈ H^(∞,(γ_+−3ϵ,γ_+,α_K))_b(M′), and b-Sobolev embedding near K⁺, where ρ_K is comparable
to t_*⁻¹ on compact r-sets, gives (47.15), as in the proof of Theorem 47.5 without u_sing. ∎

Where Theorem 47.4 needs γ_+ > α_K, the lower end 0 of the window being the indicial root of W* and of the
constants, here γ_+ − α_K > −1 suffices.

The *part with l ≥ 2* of a class tensor or 1-form k is k_(≥2) := k − k_0; class tensors and 1-forms carry only l = 0
and even l ≥ 2 (Lemma 45.2), and for a class 1-form Z, (ℒ_Zg)_(≥2) = ℒ_(Z_(≥2))g, as X ↦ ℒ_Xg commutes with the
SO(4)-average. For class 1-forms, Z_(≥2) = Π_cl Z.

**Corollary 47.29** (The part with l ≥ 2.) Let ġ_H be the representative of Corollary 46.26. For every
α < 3/2 + δ_♯, on each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′} and with every number of derivatives, (ġ_H)_(≥2) = O(t_*^(−α)), the
constant bounded by finitely many norms of the data.

*Proof.* It suffices to take α = α_K ∈ (1, 3/2 + δ_♯). Choose

    γ_+ ∈ (max(½, α_K − 1), ½ + δ_♯),        β ∈ (γ_+ − ½, δ_♯),        η ∈ (0, ½ + δ_♯ − γ_+),

possible as α_K − 1 < ½ + δ_♯; then γ_+ < ¾ < 1 and β > 0. As in the proof of Corollary 47.27 at this β, with
Theorem 46.23 (some p ∈ (½ + β, min(3/2, q_ḣ − 1)), which is nonempty as q_ḣ − 1 > ½ + 2γ_Υ), b_+ := ½ + β and
b_I ∈ (b_+, p): Y := χ(t^♭_*)Z_1 ∈ H^(k,(b_I,b_+,−1/2))_b(Ω_*, μ_b), and χ′Y is the forward solution of
f := χ′J_h + [□, χ′]Y. Put f_(≥2) := Π_cl f; its forward solution is Π_cl(χ′Y) (Lemma 47.18 (b)). f vanishes near
ℐ⁺, so every w_I is allowed. χ′J_h has ι⁺-order 5/2 + δ_♯ − η > γ_+ + 2 and K⁺-order w − η > α_K: Proposition 46.17
applies with some β′ ∈ (0, δ_♯ − η), which exists as η < ½ + δ_♯ − γ_+ < δ_♯; and w − η > 2 − ¼ > 3/2 + δ_♯ > α_K,
as w > 2 + ε_t and η < δ_♯ < ¼. [□, χ′]Y ∈ H^(∞,(𝔪,b_++2,𝔪))_b with b_+ > γ_+, and Π_cl preserves these classes
(Lemma 47.18 (b)). So f_(≥2) satisfies the hypotheses of Theorem 47.28 with Π = Π_cl, which gives
Π_cl(χ′Y) = O(t_*^(−α_K)) on compact sets, with every derivative. At late times on compact sets χ′ = χ(t^♭_*) = χ_K = 1,
so Z_(1,≥2) = Π_cl(χ′Y), and (ġ_H)_(≥2) = h_(≥2) + ℒ_(Z_(1,≥2))g, as ṁK_V and ℒ_(W**_H)g have no part with l ≥ 2;
and |h|_k = O(t_*^(−w+ε′)) ((45.3)). ∎

**Theorem 47.30** (The harmonic-gauge representative and its rate.) Let (γ̇, k̇) be data in the class of
Corollary 40.5, ġ its linear solution and ṁ its mass change, and let ġ_H = ġ + ℒ_Zg be the representative of
Corollary 46.26: G-invariant, DRic(ġ_H) = 0 and Υ̇⁰(ġ_H) = 0 on all of N⁺, and ġ_H = ġ near Σ°, so that ġ_H induces
(γ̇, k̇) exactly. Let Z′_0 be the 1-form of (47.12), with □Z′_0 = 0, c′ the Killing multiple of its data, p_0 the
supremum of the orders of its data (Definition 47.14), and

    c := (Q[Z′_0] − 4π²m₀c′)/4π².

Then c = c_∞, the constant of Corollary 46.26, and on each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}, with every number of
derivatives:

(a) ġ_H − ṁK* − cℒ_(W*)g = O(t_*^(−α)) for every α < min(p_0, 3/2), where p_0 ≥ q − 1 > ½ + 2γ_Υ, q of
Corollary 47.16. As γ_Υ ≥ δ_♯, this is faster than t_*^(−1/2−δ_♯) for every perturbation in the class.

(b) If outside a ball (γ̇, k̇) are ṁ times the data of K_V, as for the data of Theorem 3.9, then
ġ_H − ṁK* − cℒ_(W*)g = O(t_*^(−1+ε)) for every ε > 0.

(c) For data with compact support, ṁ = 0 and ġ_H − cℒ_(W*)g = O(t_*^(−3/2−κ)) for every κ < δ_♯, and the spherically
symmetric part is

    (ġ_H)_0 = cℒ_(W*)g + (m₀c/2) t_*^(−2) ℒ_(W*)g + O(t_*^(−3+ε))        for every ε > 0.

In every case the part with l ≥ 2 is O(t_*^(−3/2−κ)) for every κ < δ_♯. K* = K̄ + ℒ_(W**)g is the gauge-fixed mass
change of Proposition 46.2 (iv) (c), smooth across the horizon, with K* − (v/2)ℒ_(W*)g stationary: ṁK* grows linearly
in v.

*Proof.* In the class, ġ_H − ṁK* − cℒ_(W*)g = ((ġ_H)_0 − ṁK* − cℒ_(W*)g) + (ġ_H)_(≥2), as K* and ℒ_(W*)g are
spherically symmetric. The first term is Corollary 47.16 (a), (b) and its last display; the case α = 1 of (a) follows
from a slightly larger α when min(p_0, 3/2) > 1. The second is Corollary 47.29, whose exponent 3/2 + δ_♯ exceeds 3/2
and 1 and is below 2: so in (c) the rate of the sum is that of the part with l ≥ 2.

*c = c_∞.* Take R′ ≥ 2r_h and α ∈ (0, ½), possible in (a) as p_0 > ½. Subtracting the bound of Corollary 46.26 from
(a) gives (c − c_∞)ℒ_(W*)g = O(t_*^(−α)) on {r_♭ < r ≤ R′, t_* ≥ T′}. W* and g are stationary and spherically
symmetric, so the value of ℒ_(W*)g on (∂_v, ∂_r) is a function of r alone, and at r = 2r_h it is −(7/24)r_h⁻³
(Corollary 47.10). Along {r = 2r_h}, t_* − v is constant; letting t_* → ∞ there gives (7/24)r_h⁻³|c − c_∞| = 0. ∎

On each {r_♭ < r ≤ R′}, t_* − v and t_* − t are bounded, so the rates hold with v or t in place of t_*. Without decay of
the data of Z′_0 the growth ṁK* can be traded for a stationary term that does not decay at infinity
(Proposition 46.27 (c)).

# Part XI. Explicit constants

## 48. Explicit resolvent bounds on five-dimensional Tangherlini

The stability theory obtains its inverse bounds for the spectral families by Fredholm, compactness and contradiction
arguments, which give no number. This chapter makes the first of them explicit for one operator: the scalar wave
operator □ = δd on functions on five-dimensional Schwarzschild–Tangherlini, whose spectral family is invertible for
Im σ ≥ 0, σ ≠ 0 (Lemma 48.24), and whose mode equation, the one solved in step (a) of the proof of
Proposition 23.17, is an ordinary differential equation harmonic by harmonic. For each harmonic the resolvent,
cut off to an interval about the photon sphere, is bounded with explicit constants: off the real axis by self-adjointness
(Lemma 48.1); on the real axis first with a constant exponential in the harmonic's degree
(Proposition 48.4), then uniformly in the degree where the potential barrier covers the interval
(Proposition 48.7, Corollary 48.8) and where the frequency lies above the barrier
(Proposition 48.10); and then for every harmonic and every real frequency by multiplier identities of
Morawetz type (Lemma 48.12), with multipliers polynomial or rational in r⁻² whose weights are positive by
exact polynomial inequalities (Proposition 48.15, Proposition 48.16,
Proposition 48.20, Proposition 48.21). The same identities give one derivative
(Corollary 48.22), extend off the real axis (Lemma 48.17), apply to every master operator of
the 1-form wave operator and of the linearised Einstein operator (Proposition 48.28), and, with
multipliers adapted to the frequency, give a bound uniform in the degree on the band 3 ≤ |σ| ≤ 384 (Theorem 48.37,
Corollary 48.40).

The chapter then states the elementary operator facts by which bounds of this kind enter an inverse bound in the
function spaces of the stability theory: a parametrix gives a Fredholm estimate with an explicit constant
(Lemma 48.42), absorption and interpolation are explicit (Lemma 48.45, Lemma 48.46),
the rotation group splits the inverse into blocks (Lemma 48.25), and a complex absorbing potential reduces the
global inverse to a cut-off one (Lemma 48.47, Lemma 48.48). It ends with the scalar-type blocks of the
linearised gauge-fixed Einstein operator at zero energy, and with an obstruction to a good constant for them that comes
from the weight (Lemma 48.53).

### 48.1 The radial problem

Let m > 0, f := 1 − m/r² and r_h := m^(1/2). The tortoise coordinate r_* of Proposition 23.16 (v) has dr_*/dr = 1/f,
r_* → −∞ as r → r_h and r_* = r + O(r⁻¹) as r → ∞; we write u′ := du/dr_*. For S ∈ 𝒮_l, κ := l(l + 2) (so that
−Δ_(𝕊³)S = κS), and a function u of r_*, Proposition 23.16 (ii) gives, with □ = δd on functions,

    −fr^(3/2)e^(iσt)S⁻¹ □(r^(−3/2)u S e^(−iσt)) = u″ + σ²u − V_l u,
    V_l := f((κ + 3/4)/r² + 9m/(4r⁴)),    (48.1)

since f(fu_r)_r = u″. So □(r^(−3/2)uSe^(−iσt)) = gSe^(−iσt), with g a function of r, is the equation

    −u″ + V_l u − σ²u = F,     F := fr^(3/2)g.    (48.2)

V_l > 0 on r > r_h. As r_* → −∞, f and V_l decay like e^(2r_*/r_h), since f′(r_h)/2 = 1/r_h; as r_* → ∞,
V_l = (κ + 3/4)r_*⁻² + O(r_*⁻³). The integral of V_l in r_* is explicit:

    I_l := ∫_ℝ V_l dr_* = ∫_(r_h)^∞ ((κ + 3/4)/r² + 9m/(4r⁴)) dr = (κ + 3/2)/r_h.    (48.3)

*Solutions at the ends.* Let σ ∈ ℂ ∖ {0} with Im σ ≥ 0. V_l is integrable in r_* at both ends, so the Volterra
equations u(x) = e^(−iσx) + ∫_(−∞)^x σ⁻¹ sin(σ(x − x′))V_l(x′)u(x′) dx′ and
u(x) = e^(iσx) − ∫_x^∞ σ⁻¹ sin(σ(x − x′))V_l(x′)u(x′) dx′ have unique solutions by iteration, as in the fact stated
in the proof of Proposition 23.17. They define the solutions u_h and u_∞ of −u″ + (V_l − σ²)u = 0 with

    u_h e^(iσr_*) → 1,  u_h′ + iσu_h → 0 as r_* → −∞;     u_∞ e^(−iσr_*) → 1,  u_∞′ − iσu_∞ → 0 as r_* → ∞,

the second limit in each case from the differentiated Volterra equation, whose remainder is bounded by the tail of
∫|V_l|. For real σ the same Volterra equations with e^(iσx) at −∞ and e^(−iσx) at +∞ give a second solution at each
end; so at each end every solution is Ae^(−iσr_*) + Be^(iσr_*) + o(1), with derivative
−iσAe^(−iσr_*) + iσBe^(iσr_*) + o(1). A solution with u′ + iσu → 0 at −∞ is a multiple of u_h, and one with
u′ − iσu → 0 at ∞ a multiple of u_∞. For real σ this holds because u′ + iσu = 2iσBe^(iσr_*) + o(1) at −∞, so that
B = 0, and likewise at +∞. For Im σ > 0, let u′ + iσu → 0 at −∞. Then (e^(iσx)u)′ = e^(iσx)(u′ + iσu) and the
modulus e^(−x Im σ) of e^(iσx) give |u(x)| ≤ C(e^(x Im σ) + 1/Im σ) near −∞, so u is bounded there; as u_h → 0 and
u_h′ + iσu_h → 0 at −∞, the constant Wronskian u_hu′ − u_h′u = u_h(u′ + iσu) − u(u_h′ + iσu_h) tends to 0, hence
vanishes, and u is a multiple of u_h. The same argument with e^(−iσx) applies at +∞. In the spacetime,
e^(−iσt)u_h = e^(−iσ(t + r_*))(1 + o(1)) is the behaviour of a field smooth across the future horizon, and
e^(−iσt)u_∞ = e^(−iσ(t − r_*))(1 + o(1)) that of an outgoing one: these are the classes of *The class* in the proof of
Proposition 23.17.

*The resolvent.* H_l := −∂²_(r_*) + V_l, with domain H²(ℝ), is self-adjoint and nonnegative on L²(ℝ, dr_*), V_l being
bounded and nonnegative. For Im σ > 0, R_l(σ) := (H_l − σ²)⁻¹; then σ² ∉ [0, ∞). For real σ ≠ 0, R_l(σ) is the
outgoing resolvent of Proposition 48.4. Throughout, ‖·‖ is the norm of L²(ℝ, dr_*), I ⊂ ℝ an r_*-interval,
‖·‖_I the norm of L²(I, dr_*) and χ_I multiplication by the indicator function of I; for m = 1 we fix
I := {6/5 ≤ r ≤ 4}, whose length in r_* is Λ < 3.7436 (Section 48.6).

### 48.2 Off the real axis

**Lemma 48.1** (Off the real axis.) For Im σ > 0 and every l,

    ‖R_l(σ)‖_(L²→L²) ≤ 1/dist(σ², [0, ∞)),

which is 1/(2|Re σ| Im σ) when |Re σ| ≥ Im σ and 1/|σ|² when |Re σ| < Im σ.

*Proof.* H_l ≥ 0 is self-adjoint, so spec H_l ⊂ [0, ∞) and ‖(H_l − σ²)⁻¹‖ = 1/dist(σ², spec H_l) ≤
1/dist(σ², [0, ∞)). With σ² = (Re σ)² − (Im σ)² + 2i Re σ Im σ, the distance is |Im σ²| = 2|Re σ| Im σ if
Re σ² ≥ 0, that is |Re σ| ≥ Im σ, and |σ²| otherwise. ∎

This bound is uniform in l and degenerates as Im σ → 0, where the content of Lemma 48.24 lies.

### 48.3 The flux and the outgoing resolvent

From here on σ is real and nonzero.

**Lemma 48.2** (The flux.) Write u_h = A e^(−iσr_*) + B e^(iσr_*) + o(1) as r_* → ∞, with
u_h′ = −iσAe^(−iσr_*) + iσBe^(iσr_*) + o(1) (*Solutions at the ends* in Section 48.1). Then |A|² = 1 + |B|²,
and the Wronskian 𝒲 := u_h u_∞′ − u_h′ u_∞ equals 2iσA. In particular |𝒲| ≥ 2|σ|.

*Proof.* V_l is real, so Im(ūu′) is constant for every solution u. For u_h it is −σ at −∞, and −σ|A|² + σ|B|² at +∞,
the cross terms being real; so |A|² = 1 + |B|². 𝒲 is constant; at +∞, with u_∞ = e^(iσr_*)(1 + o(1)) and
u_∞′ = iσu_∞ + o(1),
𝒲 = (Ae^(−iσr_*) + Be^(iσr_*))iσe^(iσr_*) − (−iσAe^(−iσr_*) + iσBe^(iσr_*))e^(iσr_*) + o(1) = 2iσA. ∎

**Lemma 48.3** (Growth through the barrier.) For a solution u of −u″ + (V_l − σ²)u = 0 put
E_σ := |u′|² + σ²|u|². Then |E_σ′| ≤ (V_l/|σ|)E_σ. Hence

    |u_∞(x)|² ≤ 2 exp(|σ|⁻¹ ∫_x^∞ V_l dr_*),     |u_h(x)|² ≤ 2 exp(|σ|⁻¹ ∫_(−∞)^x V_l dr_*).

*Proof.* E_σ′ = 2Re(ū′u″) + 2σ²Re(ūu′) = 2(V_l − σ²)Re(ū′u) + 2σ²Re(ūu′) = 2V_l Re(ū′u), and
2|ū′u| ≤ |u′|²/|σ| + |σ||u|² = E_σ/|σ|. E_σ tends to 2σ² at the end where u is normalised (u_∞ at +∞, u_h at −∞), so
Gronwall's inequality from that end gives E_σ ≤ 2σ² exp(|σ|⁻¹∫V_l) over the interval between the end and x, and
σ²|u|² ≤ E_σ. ∎

**Proposition 48.4** (The outgoing resolvent.) Let σ be real and nonzero, and F ∈ L²(ℝ) vanish
outside a bounded set.

(a) There is exactly one solution u, with u and u′ locally absolutely continuous, of −u″ + (V_l − σ²)u = F almost
everywhere, that is a multiple of u_h near −∞ and of u_∞ near +∞. We write u =: R_l(σ)F. It satisfies
u − c_±e^(±iσr_*) → 0 and u′ ∓ iσu → 0 as r_* → ±∞, for constants c_±, and

    u(x) = ∫ k_l(x, x′) F(x′) dx′,     k_l(x, x′) := −u_h(min(x, x′)) u_∞(max(x, x′))/𝒲.    (48.4)

(b) |k_l(x, x′)| ≤ |σ|⁻¹ exp(I_l/(2|σ|)), with I_l of (48.3). So for an r_*-interval J of length
Λ_J, ‖χ_J R_l(σ) χ_J‖ ≤ (Λ_J/|σ|) exp(I_l/(2|σ|)).

*Proof.* (a) 𝒲 ≠ 0 by Lemma 48.2. Define u by (48.4), that is
u(x) = −𝒲⁻¹(u_∞(x)∫_(−∞)^x u_h F + u_h(x)∫_x^∞ u_∞ F). The integrals are finite, F having bounded support, and u is
locally absolutely continuous with u′ = −𝒲⁻¹(u_∞′(x)∫_(−∞)^x u_h F + u_h′(x)∫_x^∞ u_∞ F), the two terms from the
variable limits cancelling; u′ is locally absolutely continuous, and almost everywhere
u″ = (V_l − σ²)u − 𝒲⁻¹(u_∞′u_h − u_h′u_∞)F = (V_l − σ²)u − F. Left of the support of F, u is the multiple
−𝒲⁻¹(∫u_∞F)u_h of u_h, and right of it the multiple −𝒲⁻¹(∫u_hF)u_∞ of u_∞; this gives the limits, with
c_− and c_+ these coefficients. If two such solutions exist, their difference solves the homogeneous equation and is a
multiple of u_h and of u_∞, so it vanishes since 𝒲 ≠ 0.

(b) For x ≤ x′, Lemma 48.3 gives |u_h(x)||u_∞(x′)| ≤ 2 exp((2|σ|)⁻¹(∫_(−∞)^x V_l + ∫_(x′)^∞ V_l)) ≤
2 exp(I_l/(2|σ|)), as V_l ≥ 0, and |𝒲| ≥ 2|σ|. A kernel bounded by K on J × J defines an operator on L²(J) of norm at
most its Hilbert–Schmidt norm, KΛ_J. ∎

This is the injectivity of the scalar spectral family (Lemma 48.24) at real σ on {r > r_h}, harmonic by
harmonic, which step (a) of the proof of Proposition 23.17 proves, here with a constant obtained by inequalities
alone. The constant grows like exp(κ/(2|σ|r_h)): the bound |𝒲| ≥ 2|σ| ignores that 𝒲 = 2iσA carries the same
tunnelling factor through the barrier as the solutions.

### 48.4 Uniformly in the harmonic where the barrier covers the interval

Let σ > 0 (σ < 0 follows by complex conjugation, as V_l is real: R_l(−σ)F = conj(R_l(σ) conj F)), let I = [α, β] be an
r_*-interval, and for a solution u of the homogeneous equation write V_σ := V_l − σ² and n := |u|², so that
½n′ = Re(ūu′) and ½n″ = |u′|² + V_σ n.

**Lemma 48.5** (An energy monotone on each side of the barrier.) Put ℰ := |u′|² + (σ² − V_l)n. Then
ℰ′ = −V_l′n. So ℰ(u_h) ≤ 2σ² on every interval (−∞, x] on which V_l is nondecreasing, and ℰ(u_∞) ≤ 2σ² on every [x, ∞)
on which V_l is nonincreasing.

*Proof.* ℰ′ = 2Re(ū′u″) − V_l′n + (σ² − V_l)n′, and 2Re(ū′u″) = 2V_σ Re(ū′u) = −(σ² − V_l)n′. At the end where each is
normalised, u_h ~ e^(−iσr_*) and u_∞ ~ e^(iσr_*) together with their derivatives, and V_l → 0, so ℰ → 2σ² there; and ℰ
does not increase toward the barrier on the stated intervals. ∎

For m = 1 put g_l := (κ + 3/4)/r² + 9/(4r⁴), so that V_l = fg_l. Then −4g_l/r ≤ dg_l/dr ≤ −2g_l/r, and with
df/dr = 2/r³ and f = 1 − 1/r², dV_l/dr = g_l df/dr + f dg_l/dr satisfies

    (g_l/r³)(6 − 4r²) ≤ dV_l/dr ≤ (g_l/r³)(4 − 2r²):    (48.5)

V_l increases in r for r² < 3/2 and decreases for r² > 2, for every l.

**Lemma 48.6** (The signs at the ends of I.) Let x_1 < α and x_2 > β be points with
V_σ(x_1) = V_σ(x_2) = 0 and V_σ ≥ 0 on [x_1, x_2], with V_l nondecreasing on (−∞, x_1] and nonincreasing on [x_2, ∞).
Put A_− := ∫_(x_1)^α V_σ^(1/2) dr_*, A_+ := ∫_β^(x_2) V_σ^(1/2) dr_*, and for x < x_1 and x′ > x_2 with V_l(x) < σ² and
V_l(x′) < σ²,

    D_−(x) := (2σ²/(σ² − V_l(x)))^(1/2) + √2σ(x_1 − x),     D_+(x′) := (2σ²/(σ² − V_l(x′)))^(1/2) + √2σ(x′ − x_2).

Then ½n′(α) ≥ 2σA_− − √2σD_−(x) for u = u_h, and ½n′(β) ≤ √2σD_+(x′) − 2σA_+ for u = u_∞.

*Proof.* We treat u_h; u_∞ is the mirror image, with flux Im(ū_∞u_∞′) = +σ. n > 0 everywhere, since the flux
Im(ūu′) = −σ is not zero. On (−∞, x_1], σ² − V_l ≥ 0, and ℰ ≤ 2σ² (Lemma 48.5) gives |u′|² ≤ 2σ² and
(σ² − V_l)n ≤ 2σ²; so n(x)^(1/2) ≤ (2σ²/(σ² − V_l(x)))^(1/2), and |(n^(1/2))′| = |Re(ūu′)|/n^(1/2) ≤ |u′| ≤ √2σ, so
n(x_1)^(1/2) ≤ D_−(x). As V_l(x_1) = σ², |u′(x_1)|² = ℰ(x_1) ≤ 2σ², and |½n′(x_1)| ≤ n^(1/2)|u′| ≤ √2σD_−(x). On
[x_1, α], |u′| ≥ |Im(ūu′)|/|u| = σn^(−1/2), so ½n″ ≥ σ²/n + V_σ n ≥ 2σV_σ^(1/2). Integrating from x_1 to α gives the
claim. ∎

**Proposition 48.7** (Where the barrier covers the interval.) Suppose c_I := min_I V_σ > 0,
½n′(u_h)(α) ≥ 0 and ½n′(u_∞)(β) ≤ 0; for x_1, x_2 as in Lemma 48.6, the last two hold when
A_− ≥ D_−(x)/√2 and A_+ ≥ D_+(x′)/√2 for some x, x′ as there. Then ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I‖ ≤ 1/c_I.

*Proof.* For F ∈ L² vanishing off I, u := R_l(σ)F equals c_h u_h on (−∞, α] and c_∞u_∞ on [β, ∞)
(Proposition 48.4). Pairing −u″ + V_σ u = F with ū over I and taking real parts,

    ∫_I(|u′|² + V_σ|u|²) = Re∫_I Fū + |c_∞|² ½n′(u_∞)(β) − |c_h|² ½n′(u_h)(α) ≤ ‖F‖‖u‖_I,

and the left side is at least c_I‖u‖_I². ∎

**Corollary 48.8** (Closed form; m = 1, I = {6/5 ≤ r ≤ 4}.) Let a := κ + 3/4 and c := (15/16)a. If

(i) (15/256)a > σ² and (0.21/1.4641)a > σ² (the second follows from the first, as 0.21/1.4641 > 0.1434 > 15/256),

(ii) 0.32727(0.120523a − σ²)^(1/2) > (2 + 1.1248σ)/√2, and

(iii) c^(1/2) > 8σ and (√3/2)c^(1/2) log(c^(1/2)/(8σ)) > (2 + 0.79217(κ + 1)^(1/2))/√2,

then the hypotheses of Proposition 48.7 hold, and

    ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I‖ ≤ 1/((15/256)a − σ²) = (256/15)/(κ + 3/4 − (256/15)σ²).    (48.6)

Each of (i)–(iii), once true, stays true as l grows; so with l_0(σ) the least l at which they hold, the bound holds for
every l ≥ l_0(σ). It is asymptotically (256/15)/κ ≈ 17.07/κ.

*Proof.* (i) On I, y := 1/r² ∈ [1/16, 25/36] and f/r² = y(1 − y), whose least value there is at y = 1/16, namely 15/256.
As V_l ≥ af/r², min_I V_σ ≥ (15/256)a − σ² > 0. Also V_l(r = 1.1) ≥ af(1.1)/1.21 = (0.21/1.4641)a > σ², and V_l
increases on {r ≤ 1.1} by (48.5); so the point x_1 of Lemma 48.6, where V_l first reaches σ², lies
at r < 1.1. V_l has a single maximum (Proposition 48.10), so V_l ≥ min(V_l(1.1), V_l(4)) > σ² on
[1.1, 4], and the point x_2 beyond the maximum where V_l = σ² lies at r > 4, where V_l decreases. (ii) On [1.1, 1.2],
1/f ≥ 1/f(1.2) = 3.2727 and V_l ≥ af(1.1)/1.44 = 0.120523a, so A_− ≥ 0.32727(0.120523a − σ²)^(1/2). Take x where
V_l = σ²/2. On {r ≤ 1.1}, d log V_l/dr_* = f d log V_l/dr ≥ (6 − 4r²)/r³ ≥ 1.16/1.331 = 0.87152 by (48.5), so
x_1 − x ≤ log 2/0.87152 < 0.79534 and D_−(x) ≤ 2 + 1.1248σ. (iii) For r ≥ 4, 1/f ≥ 1 and V_l ≥ af/r² ≥ c/r²; on [4, ρ],
ρ := c^(1/2)/(2σ) > 4, σ² = c/(4ρ²) ≤ c/(4r²), so V_σ ≥ (3/4)c/r², and A_+ ≥ (√3/2)c^(1/2)∫_4^ρ dr/r =
(√3/2)c^(1/2) log(ρ/4). Take x′ where V_l = σ²/2. For r ≥ 4, |d log V_l/dr_*| ≥ (2/r)(1 − 2/r²) ≥ 1.75/r by
(48.5), and V_l ≤ (κ + 3/4)/r² + 9/(64r²) ≤ (κ + 1)/r², so r(x′) ≤ (2(κ + 1))^(1/2)/σ,
x′ − x_2 ≤ (log 2/1.75)r(x′) and D_+(x′) ≤ 2 + (2 log 2/1.75)(κ + 1)^(1/2) ≤ 2 + 0.79217(κ + 1)^(1/2). So (ii) and (iii)
give A_− ≥ D_−(x)/√2 and A_+ ≥ D_+(x′)/√2, and Proposition 48.7 applies with c_I ≥ (15/256)a − σ².

Monotonicity: the left sides of (i) and (ii) increase with a and their right sides do not depend on l. In (iii) the
first condition improves with a; dividing the second by a^(1/2), its left side becomes
(√3/2)(15/16)^(1/2) log(c^(1/2)/(8σ)), which increases with l, and its right side
(2a^(−1/2) + 0.79217((κ + 1)/a)^(1/2))/√2, which decreases. ∎

At σ = 3, (i)–(iii) hold at l = 50 (the proof of Corollary 48.22 (d) evaluates them), so
(48.6) holds for every l ≥ 50 at σ = 3, and, every condition being monotone in σ, for every
0 < |σ| ≤ 3.

**Remark 48.9** (Numerical observation.) The least degrees at which (i)–(iii) of
Corollary 48.8 hold are l_0 = 14, 19 and 50 at σ = 0.3, 1 and 3. Evaluating the hypotheses of
Proposition 48.7 directly by quadrature, with the points x, x′ optimised over samples, gives them already from
l = 3, 7 and 18. Against the cut-off norms of the resolvent computed from numerical solutions of the radial equation
(on I, with a discretised kernel of 161 points), the bound 1/c_I lies within a factor 2 of the computed norm (ratios 1.3
to 1.9): at σ = 0.3 and l = 8, 16, 32 the computed norms are 0.121, 0.0399, 0.0120 against 0.215, 0.0594, 0.0157; at
σ = 1, 0.139, 0.0415, 0.0122 against 0.267, 0.0628, 0.0159; at σ = 3 and l = 32, 0.0135 against 0.0182. No proof uses
these values.

### 48.5 Above the barrier

**Proposition 48.10** (Above the barrier.) Let m = 1. For every l, V_l, as a function of
r_*, has exactly one critical point, a maximum; write V_max := max V_l. If σ is real and σ² > V_max,
then |u_h|² ≤ 2σ²/(σ² − V_max) and |u_∞|² ≤ 2σ²/(σ² − V_max) everywhere. Hence, for every r_*-interval J of length Λ_J,

    ‖χ_J R_l(σ) χ_J‖ ≤ Λ_J|σ|/(σ² − V_max);

in particular ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I‖ ≤ Λ|σ|/(σ² − V_max).

*Proof.* With a := κ + 3/4, b := 9/4 and y := 1/r², V_l = (1 − y)(ay + by²) and r³ dV_l/dr = −2a + 4(a − b)y + 6by².
This convex quadratic in y is −2a < 0 at y = 0 and 2a + 2b > 0 at y = 1, so it changes sign exactly once on (0, 1):
V_l rises, then falls. Let σ > 0; σ < 0 follows by conjugation.

- Where V_l rises, ℰ(u_h) ≤ 2σ² by Lemma 48.5, and (σ² − V_l)n ≤ ℰ, so n ≤ 2σ²/(σ² − V_max) there.
- Where V_l falls, 𝒢 := ℰ/(σ² − V_l) satisfies 𝒢′ = V_l′|u′|²/(σ² − V_l)² ≤ 0, because ℰ′ = −V_l′n and
  ℰ − (σ² − V_l)n = |u′|². So 𝒢 does not exceed its value at the maximum, which is at most 2σ²/(σ² − V_max), and
  n ≤ 𝒢.
- The mirror argument, from +∞, gives the same bound for u_∞: where V_l rises, 𝒢 is nondecreasing in r_*.
- So |k_l| ≤ |u_h||u_∞|/|𝒲| ≤ (2σ²/(σ² − V_max))/(2σ) = σ/(σ² − V_max), by Lemma 48.2, and the
  Hilbert–Schmidt bound on J × J gives the estimate. ∎

Above the barrier the constant is polynomial; the exponential constant of Proposition 48.4 is needed, before
the multiplier bounds below, only for the harmonics with V_max ≥ σ² below l_0(σ). At σ = 3 these are 5 ≤ l < 50: for
12 ≤ l < 50, min_I V_σ > 0 and only the end signs of Lemma 48.6 are missing; for 5 ≤ l < 12 the barrier top
lies above σ² without covering I.

**Remark 48.11** (Numerical observation.) On I (Λ = 3.74), the cut-off norm computed from numerical
solutions of the radial equation (a discretised kernel of 161 points) lies below the bound of
Proposition 48.10: 1.89 ≤ 7.57 at σ = 1, l = 0, and 0.41, 0.42, 0.45, 0.51, 0.67 ≤ 1.32, 1.45, 1.72,
2.35, 4.44 at σ = 3, l = 0, …, 4. Between the two bounds, at σ = 3,
the computed norm is 0.672, 1.132, 0.983, 0.725, 0.287, 0.193, 0.0551 and 0.0225 at l = 4, 5, 6, 8, 11, 12, 17 and 25
(max V_l = 6.47, 9.22, 12.47, 20.47, 36.22, 42.47, 81.22, 169.22). It peaks at l = 5, the harmonic whose barrier top
lies nearest σ² = 9, is at most 1.132 for l ≤ 25, and falls like about 1/(l(l + 2)) beyond; where min_I V_σ > 0
(l ≥ 12) it lies below 1/min_I V_σ (1.116, 0.1002, 0.0327 at l = 12, 17, 25), also where the end-sign conditions of
Lemma 48.6 fail. For 5 ≤ l ≤ 11, max_I|u_h|² grows to 9.18 · 10¹³ while |𝒲|/(2σ) grows in step to
4.72 · 10⁶, and the kernel stays of order 1. At further frequencies the computed norms for l = 0, 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 are
4.75, 1.66, 0.79, 0.33, 0.12, 0.040, 0.012 at σ = 0.3 and 1.89, 3.00, 1.96, 0.55, 0.14, 0.042, 0.012 at σ = 1, while
the constant of Proposition 48.4 (b) is about 10⁶⁰ at (σ, l) = (0.3, 8). No proof uses these values.

### 48.6 The multiplier identity

From here on m = 1, so that f = 1 − 1/r², r_h = 1 and the photon sphere is r = √2. The bounds of the previous
sections are not uniform in the harmonic exactly where the barrier top of a harmonic lies near σ² and the barrier does
not cover I. A multiplier identity of Morawetz type covers every harmonic and every real σ ≠ 0. Every multiplier of
Section 48.6–Section 48.15 is a polynomial or a rational function of r⁻², every
weight there is (1 − r⁻²)r⁻³ times a rational function of r⁻², and every constant is obtained from exact rational
inequalities; the band (Section 48.16) also uses the algebraic multipliers Φ(νz). The coefficient lists that the
Bernstein bounds below use are in Section B.3.

Throughout, y := 1/r² ∈ (0, 1), z := 1 − 2y ∈ (−1, 1) and η(y) := (1 − y)y^(3/2) = (r² − 1)/r⁵. The tortoise coordinate
r_* has dr_*/dr = 1/f, and g′ := dg/dr_*. Since dy/dr = −2y^(3/2),

    d/dr_* = −2η(y) d/dy.    (48.7)

As r_* → −∞, y → 1 and 1 − y decays like e^(2r_*); as r_* → ∞, r_* = r + O(r⁻¹). The interval I := {6/5 ≤ r ≤ 4} is
{1/16 ≤ y ≤ 25/36} = {−7/18 ≤ z ≤ 7/8}. With r_* = r + ½ log((r − 1)/(r + 1)), its length is
Λ := 14/5 + ½ log(33/5) < 3.7436. We write ‖·‖ for the norm of L²(ℝ, dr_*) and ‖·‖_I for that of L²(I, dr_*).

For a potential V as below, a real σ ≠ 0 and F ∈ L²(ℝ) vanishing outside I, R(σ)F is the outgoing solution of
−u″ + (V − σ²)u = F. Its construction in Section 48.1 and Proposition 48.4 (a) uses of V_l only that it
is real, smooth and integrable in r_*: the solutions u_h and u_∞ come from the Volterra equations, and their Wronskian
is not zero by Lemma 48.2, whose proof uses only that V_l is real. So the construction applies verbatim to each V
below, and the proof of Lemma 48.12 recalls it. R_l(σ) is R(σ) for V = V_l, and ‖χ_I R(σ) χ_I‖ is the
norm of F ↦ χ_I R(σ)F on L²(I).

Since η_y = y^(1/2)(3/2 − 5y/2), η increases on [0, 3/5] and decreases on [3/5, 1]; so on an interval of y its least
value is attained at an end. We use η(1/16) = 15/1024, η(1/2) = 2^(−5/2), η(25/36) = 1375/7776 > 2^(−5/2) (as
32 · 1375² > 7776²) and max η = η(3/5) = 6√15/125 < 0.18591. At a rational r, η = (r² − 1)/r⁵ is rational.

The potentials. Put U := f/r² = (1 − y)y, Q := f/r⁴ = (1 − y)y² and V_(a,b) := aU + bQ = (1 − y)(ay + by²). With
κ := l(l + 2), the potentials V_0, V_1, V_2 of Proposition 23.16 at degree l, which we write V^□, V^v and V^s (those of
the scalar wave, of the vector-type and of the scalar-type 1-forms), are V_(κ+3/4,b) with b = 9/4, 5/4 and −7/4; so
V^□ = V_l. Those of Theorem 25.16 are V_T = V^□ and V_V = V_(κ+3/4,−27/4), and V_S = (1 − y)yQ_S/(16H²), with Q_S the
polynomial (25.16) at ς = y, p := κ − 3 and H := p + 6y, for l ≥ 2. Each of them is (1 − y)y times a rational
function of y bounded on [0, 1] (for V_S, H ≥ p > 0), so V and V′ = −2ηV_y are O(r⁻²) and O(r⁻³) as r_* → ∞ and
O(e^(2r_*)) as r_* → −∞: they are integrable and tend to 0 at ±∞.

**Lemma 48.12** (The multiplier identity.) Let V be a real smooth function on ℝ with V, V′ integrable
and V, V′ → 0 at ±∞. Let φ and q be real smooth functions on ℝ, φ bounded with limits φ(±∞) at ±∞, and φ′, φ″, φ‴, q,
q′, q″ integrable and tending to 0 at ±∞. Let σ ≠ 0 be real, F ∈ L²(ℝ) vanish outside I, and let u be a solution, with
u and u′ locally absolutely continuous, of −u″ + (V − σ²)u = F (almost everywhere), such that u − c_±e^(±iσr_*) → 0 and
u′ ∓ iσu → 0 as r_* → ±∞. Then, with integrals over ℝ,

    2∫(φ′ − q)|u′|² + ∫W|u|² + 2σ²∫q|u|² = Re∫F(2φū′ + (φ′ − 2q)ū) + 2σ²(φ(∞)|c_+|² − φ(−∞)|c_−|²),
    W := −φV′ − ½φ‴ + q″ − 2qV,    (48.8)

and σ(|c_+|² + |c_−|²) = −Im∫Fū. The outgoing solution R(σ)F is a solution of this kind.

Suppose moreover that φ′ − q ≥ 0, q ≥ 0 and W ≥ 0 on ℝ, and let m′ > 0, M′, w_I > 0, p_I and p_∞ satisfy
m′ ≤ φ′ − q, |φ′ − 2q| ≤ M′, w_I ≤ W and |φ| ≤ p_I on I, and p_∞ ≥ max(φ(∞), −φ(−∞), 0). Then X := ‖u′‖_I and
Y := ‖u‖_I satisfy

    Y ≤ B‖F‖,     B := ((2p_I²/m′ + (M′ + 2p_∞|σ|)²/w_I)/w_I)^(1/2);    (48.9)

for every B̃ with Y ≤ B̃‖F‖, X ≤ X(B̃)‖F‖ with X(B̃) := (p_I + (p_I² + 2m′(M′ + 2p_∞|σ|)B̃)^(1/2))/(2m′); and for every
decomposition W = W_0 + W_1 with W_0, W_1 ≥ 0 on ℝ, ∫_I W_1|u|² ≤ (2p_IX(B̃) + (M′ + 2p_∞|σ|)B̃)‖F‖². When |φ| ≤ 1 on
ℝ one may take p_I = p_∞ = 1; then B = ((2/m′ + (M′ + 2|σ|)²/w_I)/w_I)^(1/2) and
X(B̃) = (1 + (1 + 2m′(M′ + 2|σ|)B̃)^(1/2))/(2m′).

*Proof.* First, R(σ)F is a solution of this kind. Let u_h and u_∞ be the solutions of the homogeneous equation with
u_h − e^(−iσr_*) → 0 and u_h′ + iσu_h → 0 as r_* → −∞, and u_∞ − e^(iσr_*) → 0 and u_∞′ − iσu_∞ → 0 as r_* → ∞,
given by the Volterra equations of Section 48.1 with V in place of V_l, and let 𝒲 := u_hu_∞′ − u_h′u_∞ be their
Wronskian, a nonzero constant by Lemma 48.2, whose proof uses only that V is real. Then

    R(σ)F(x) = −𝒲⁻¹(u_∞(x)∫_(−∞)^x u_hF + u_h(x)∫_x^∞ u_∞F).

As F ∈ L² vanishes outside the bounded interval I and u_h, u_∞ are continuous, u_hF and u_∞F are integrable, and both
integrals are absolutely continuous in x. Differentiating, the two terms ±𝒲⁻¹u_∞u_hF cancel, so
u′ = −𝒲⁻¹(u_∞′∫_(−∞)^x u_hF + u_h′∫_x^∞ u_∞F), which is again absolutely continuous; differentiating once more,
u″ = (V − σ²)u − 𝒲⁻¹(u_hu_∞′ − u_h′u_∞)F = (V − σ²)u − F almost everywhere. To the right of I, u is a multiple of u_∞,
and to its left a multiple of u_h, which gives the stated behaviour at ±∞.

Now let u be any solution as in the statement. Since u and u′ are locally absolutely continuous and φ, q, V are smooth,
all the products below are locally absolutely continuous and the product rule holds for them almost everywhere. With
Re(u″ū) = ½(|u|²)″ − |u′|² and Re(u′ū) = ½(|u|²)′, one checks term by term, almost everywhere:

    Re(−u″ · 2φū′) = −(φ|u′|²)′ + φ′|u′|²,
    Re(−u″ · φ′ū) = −(φ′Re(u′ū))′ + φ′|u′|² + (½φ″|u|²)′ − ½φ‴|u|²,
    Re((V − σ²)u · 2φū′) = ((V − σ²)φ|u|²)′ − (φV′ + (V − σ²)φ′)|u|²,
    Re((V − σ²)u · φ′ū) = (V − σ²)φ′|u|²,
    Re((−u″ + (V − σ²)u) · (−2qū)) = (q(|u|²)′ − q′|u|²)′ + q″|u|² − 2q|u′|² − 2qV|u|² + 2σ²q|u|².

Adding, Re(F(2φū′ + (φ′ − 2q)ū)) = 2(φ′ − q)|u′|² + W|u|² + 2σ²q|u|² + E′ almost everywhere, where the locally
absolutely continuous function E is −φ|u′|² − φ′Re(u′ū) + ½φ″|u|² + (V − σ²)φ|u|² + q(|u|²)′ − q′|u|². The function u
is continuous with limits of modulus |c_±| at ±∞, and u′ continuous with limits of modulus |σc_±|; so both are bounded,
and every integral in (48.8) converges absolutely, as F vanishes outside I and φ′, φ‴, q, q″, V′ and qV are
integrable. Integrate over [−R, R] and let R → ∞: at ±∞, |u′|² → σ²|c_±|², |u|² → |c_±|², Re(u′ū) → 0, φ → φ(±∞) and
φ′, φ″, q, q′, V → 0, so E → −2σ²φ(±∞)|c_±|², and (48.8) follows. Next, almost everywhere,
Im(Fū) = −Im(u″ū) = −(Im(u′ū))′, and Im(u′ū) → ±σ|c_±|² at ±∞; integrating gives the flux identity.

Under the sign conditions every integrand on the left of (48.8) is nonnegative. Dropping the term with q and
restricting the other two to I, the left side is at least 2m′X² + w_IY². On the right, F vanishes outside I
and |φ| ≤ p_I on I, so the integral is at most ‖F‖(2p_IX + M′Y); and
2σ²(φ(∞)|c_+|² − φ(−∞)|c_−|²) ≤ 2σ²p_∞(|c_+|² + |c_−|²) = −2σp_∞Im∫Fū ≤ 2|σ|p_∞‖F‖Y. Hence, with
M_σ := M′ + 2p_∞|σ|,

    2m′X² + w_IY² ≤ ‖F‖(2p_IX + M_σY).    (48.10)

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, 2p_IX + M_σY ≤ (2p_I²/m′ + M_σ²/w_I)^(1/2)(2m′X² + w_IY²)^(1/2), so
(2m′X² + w_IY²)^(1/2) ≤ (2p_I²/m′ + M_σ²/w_I)^(1/2)‖F‖ and w_I^(1/2)Y ≤ (2m′X² + w_IY²)^(1/2), which is (48.9).
Dropping w_IY² in (48.10) and using Y ≤ B̃‖F‖ gives 2m′X² − 2p_I‖F‖X − M_σB̃‖F‖² ≤ 0, so X is at most the
positive root, X(B̃)‖F‖. Finally the left side of (48.8) is at least ∫_I W_1|u|², and the right side is at
most ‖F‖(2p_IX + M_σY) ≤ (2p_IX(B̃) + M_σB̃)‖F‖². When |φ| ≤ 1 on ℝ, also |φ(±∞)| ≤ 1, so p_I = p_∞ = 1 serve. ∎

For a multiplier φ = Θ(y) and a Lagrangian term q = ηg(y), (48.7) gives φ′ = −2ηΘ_y,
−½φ‴ = 4η(η(ηΘ_y)_y)_y, −φV′ = 2ηΘV_y and, with h := (3/2 − 5y/2)g + y(1 − y)g_y, q′ = −2(1 − y)y²h and
q″ = 4ηy((2 − 3y)h + y(1 − y)h_y). So W = ηG with

    G = 2ΘV_y + 4(η(ηΘ_y)_y)_y + 4y((2 − 3y)h + y(1 − y)h_y) − 2gV.    (48.11)

Every φ below is a polynomial or a rational function of y with no pole on [0, 1], and every q is η times a polynomial g.
Since ηη_y = (1 − y)y²(3 − 5y)/2 and η² = (1 − y)²y³ are polynomials, φ′, φ″, φ‴, q, q′, q″ are η or (1 − y)y² times
bounded functions; they are O(r⁻³) as r_* → ∞ and O(e^(2r_*)) as r_* → −∞, hence integrable and vanishing at ±∞.

### 48.7 The weight of the multiplier 1 − 2/r²

**Proposition 48.13** (The Morawetz weight of φ = 1 − 2/r².) Let φ := z = 1 − 2/r². Then φ is
increasing, φ → ±1 at ±∞, φ′ = 4η, and for q = 0 and V = V_(a,b) the weight of Lemma 48.12 is
W = ηP_(a,b)(z) with

    P_(a,b)(z) := 2 + (b/2 − 6)z + (2a + b − 6)z² + (10 − 3b/2)z³.    (48.12)

P_(a,b) is affine in b and nondecreasing in a, with ∂_aP_(a,b) = 2z², and ψ := −φU′ = 2ηz² ≥ 0. For the scalar wave at
harmonic l (a = κ + 3/4, b = 9/4) the weight is w_l := ηP_l with

    P_l(z) = P̄(z) + c_l z²,     P̄(z) := 2 − (39/8)z + (53/8)z³,     c_l := 2κ − 9/4,    (48.13)

so that w_l = w_1 + (κ − 3)ψ. In the variable y, P_1 = ½p with

    p(y) := 15 − 90y + 189y² − 106y³ = 15(1 − y)(1 − 3y)² + y(29y² − 36y + 15).    (48.14)

Hence w_l ≥ w_1 > 0 on ℝ for every l ≥ 1, and φ satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 48.12 with q = 0
for every V_(κ+3/4,9/4), l ≥ 1.

*Proof.* With Θ = 1 − 2y, Θ_y = −2 and ηΘ_y = −2η, so 4(η(ηΘ_y)_y)_y = −8(η_y² + ηη_yy). From η_y = (y^(1/2)/2)(3 − 5y)
and η_yy = (3/4)y^(−1/2)(1 − 5y), η_y² + ηη_yy = (y/4)((3 − 5y)² + 3(1 − y)(1 − 5y)) = y(10y² − 12y + 3). So by
(48.11), G = 2zV_y − 8y(10y² − 12y + 3). For V = V_(a,b), V_y = a(1 − 2y) + by(2 − 3y), and with
y = (1 − z)/2 one has y(2 − 3y) = (1 − z)(1 + 3z)/4 and 10y² − 12y + 3 = −½ + z + (5/2)z². Hence
2zV_y = 2az² + (b/2)(z + 2z² − 3z³) and −8y(10y² − 12y + 3) = −4(1 − z)(−½ + z + (5/2)z²) = 2 − 6z − 6z² + 10z³; the sum
is (48.12). U = V_(1,0) gives U_y = z, U′ = −2ηz and −φU′ = 2ηz². At a = κ + 3/4, b = 9/4 the coefficients
are 2, −39/8, 2κ − 9/4 and 53/8, which is (48.13); and c_l − c_1 = 2(κ − 3) gives w_l − w_1 = (κ − 3)ψ.
Substituting z = 1 − 2y in P_1 gives ½p, and expanding the right side of (48.14) gives p. Its first term
is nonnegative on [0, 1] and its second is positive on (0, 1], since 29y² − 36y + 15 has discriminant 1296 − 1740 < 0;
at y = 0, p = 15. So p > 0 on [0, 1], w_1 > 0 on ℝ, and w_l ≥ w_1 because κ ≥ 3 and ψ ≥ 0. φ is increasing as φ′ =
4η > 0, and |φ| < 1. ∎

**Lemma 48.14** (The weight on I.) Let l ≥ 1 and c := c_l. On I:

(i) for 6/5 ≤ r ≤ √2, w_l ≥ 2^(−3/2) = √2/4;

(ii) for √2 ≤ r ≤ 8/5, with e_0 := 1677/2048 and
d := e_0c − 9/16, w_l ≥ 2^(−5/2)(2 − (47/8)z + dz²); hence w_l is at least
2^(−5/2)(2 − 2209/(256d)) when d ≥ 94/7, and at least 2^(−5/2)(2 − 329/256 + 49d/1024) otherwise;

(iii) for 2 ≤ r ≤ 3, w_l ≥ 25/1944 + (392/19683)c; for 17/10 ≤ r ≤ 2, w_l ≥ 0.03658 + 0.012624c; and for
8/5 ≤ r ≤ 17/10, w_l ≥ 0.09213 + 0.0071190c;

(iv) for 3 ≤ r ≤ 4, w_l ≥ w_l(4) = (15/1024)(8899/4096 + (49/64)c).

Consequently min_I w_l ≥ ω_l, where ω_1 := 0.07388, ω_2 := 0.1860, ω_3 := 0.2847, ω_4 := 0.3122, ω_5 := 0.3257,
ω_l := 0.3335 for 6 ≤ l ≤ 19 and ω_l := 0.3514 for l ≥ 20.

*Proof.* Write A := ηP̄ and Z := ηz², so that w_l = A + cZ by (48.13), with c ≥ 15/4. P̄′(z) =
−39/8 + (159/8)z² vanishes on [0, 1] only at z_0 := (39/159)^(1/2) < 0.4953, and P̄(z_0) = 2 − (13/4)z_0 > 0.3902;
P̄ decreases on [0, z_0] and increases on [z_0, 1]. In the variable z, η = (1 + z)(1 − z)^(3/2)2^(−5/2) decreases on
[0, 7/8] (that is y ∈ [1/16, 1/2] ⊂ [0, 3/5]), and Z is unimodal on [0, 1], since
d log Z/dz = 1/(1 + z) − 3/(2(1 − z)) + 2/z is decreasing.

(i) Here z ∈ [−7/18, 0], so −(39/8)z = (39/8)|z|, cz² ≥ 0 and (53/8)z³ ≥ −(53/8)(49/324)|z| > −1.002|z|; thus P_l ≥ 2.
Also y ∈ [1/2, 25/36], where η ≥ min(η(1/2), η(25/36)) = 2^(−5/2). So w_l ≥ 2^(−3/2).

(ii) Here z ∈ [0, 7/32]. First, P_l ≥ Q_c := 2 − (39/8)z + cz², as (53/8)z³ ≥ 0, and Q_c > 0 because its
discriminant (39/8)² − 8c is negative for c ≥ 15/4. Second, (1 − z)^(1/2) ≥ (1 − z)(1 + z/2) on [0, 1]: with
t := (1 − z)^(1/2) ∈ [0, 1] this is 2 ≥ t(3 − t²), that is (t − 1)²(t + 2) ≥ 0. Hence
η ≥ 2^(−5/2)(1 + z)(1 − z)²(1 + z/2) ≥ 2^(−5/2)(1 − z/2 − 3z²/2) ≥ 0, the middle step dropping (z³ + z⁴)/2 ≥ 0.
Multiplying,

    w_l ≥ 2^(−5/2)(1 − z/2 − 3z²/2)Q_c = 2^(−5/2)(2 − (47/8)z + (c − 9/16)z² + (117/16)z³ − c(z/2 + 3z²/2)z²),

and z/2 + 3z²/2 ≤ 7/64 + 147/2048 = 1 − e_0 on [0, 7/32]. Dropping (117/16)z³ ≥ 0 gives the bound. Its minimum over
z ∈ [0, 7/32] is at z = 47/(16d) when that lies in [0, 7/32], that is d ≥ 94/7, and at z = 7/32 otherwise.

(iii) On 2 ≤ r ≤ 3, y ∈ [1/9, 1/4] and z ∈ [1/2, 7/9] ⊂ [z_0, 1]: η ≥ η(1/9) = 8/243 and P̄ ≥ P̄(1/2) = 25/64, so
A ≥ 25/1944; and Z ≥ min(Z at r = 3, Z at r = 2) = min(392/19683, 3/128). On 17/10 ≤ r ≤ 2, y ∈ [1/4, 100/289]:
η ≥ η(1/4) = 3/32 and P̄ ≥ P̄(z_0) > 0.3902, so A ≥ 0.03658; Z ≥ Z(17/10) = (189000/1419857)(89/289)² > 0.012624, as
Z(2) = 3/128 is larger. On 8/5 ≤ r ≤ 17/10, z ∈ [7/32, 89/289] ⊂ [0, z_0]: η ≥ η(17/10) = 189000/1419857 and
P̄ ≥ P̄(89/289) = 66831535/96550276, so A > 0.09213; Z ≥ Z(8/5) = (4875/32768)(49/1024) = 238875/33554432.

(iv) We show that A and Z increase with y on [1/16, 1/9], so that w_l, an increasing combination, does too. There
z ∈ [7/9, 7/8] ⊂ [z_0, 1], so P̄ decreases with y, and |dP̄/dy| = 2P̄′(z) = (159/4)z² − 39/4. Now
d log Z/dy = 3/(2y) − 1/(1 − y) − 4/(1 − 2y) ≥ 27/2 − 9/8 − 36/7 > 0, and
d log A/dy = 3/(2y) − 1/(1 − y) + (dP̄/dy)/P̄.
On y ∈ [1/16, 1/12] the last expression is at least 18 − 12/11 − (5295/256)/(3061/1728) > 5.2, using P̄(5/6) = 3061/1728
and (159/4)(7/8)² − 39/4 = 5295/256; on [1/12, 1/10] it is at least 15 − 10/9 − (857/48)/(373/250) > 1.9, using
P̄(4/5) = 373/250; on [1/10, 1/9] it is at least 27/2 − 9/8 − 15.69/P̄(7/9) > 0.53, using P̄(7/9) > 1.3254. Finally
η(1/16) = 15/1024, P̄(7/8) = 8899/4096 and (7/8)² = 49/64.

Evaluating (i)–(iv): at l = 1 and l = 2, (iv) gives 309885/4194304 > 0.07388 and 780285/4194304 > 0.1860, (ii) more
than 0.147 and 0.216, the three bounds of (iii) more than 0.0839 and 0.190, and (i) more than 0.3535. For
l = 3, 4, 5, 6 and 20, d ≥ 94/7, and the vertex value in (ii) exceeds 0.2847, 0.3122, 0.3257, 0.3335 and 0.3514; the
bounds of (iii) are at least 0.2896, 0.4178, 0.5744, 0.7595 and 6.33, and those of (iv) at least 0.3430, 0.5449, 0.7916,
1.083 and 9.87. As w_l is nondecreasing in l (Proposition 48.13), the bounds at l = 6 and l = 20 hold for every
larger l. ∎

**Proposition 48.15** (Morawetz bounds for every harmonic l ≥ 1.) For every l ≥ 1 and every
real σ ≠ 0,

    ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I‖ ≤ B_l(σ) := ((512/15 + (M′ + 2|σ|)²/ω_l)/ω_l)^(1/2),     M′ := 0.74362,

with ω_l of Lemma 48.14. At σ → 0, 1, 3 and 10 these are at most:

| l | B_l(0+) | B_l(1) | B_l(3) | B_l(10) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 23.74 | 42.91 | 93.78 | 281.60 |
| 2 | 14.13 | 20.03 | 38.71 | 112.35 |
| 3 | 11.26 | 14.59 | 26.10 | 73.68 |
| 4 | 10.73 | 13.66 | 24.00 | 67.27 |
| 5 | 10.49 | 13.26 | 23.10 | 64.51 |
| every l ≥ 6 | 10.36 | 13.04 | 22.62 | 63.02 |
| every l ≥ 20 | 10.09 | 12.58 | 21.58 | 59.85 |

### 48.9 Off the real axis with a multiplier

**Lemma 48.17** (Off the real axis.) Let V ≥ 0 be real, smooth and bounded, with V and V′ integrable
and tending to 0 at ±∞, and let φ and q satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 48.12 on φ and q, its sign
conditions φ′ − q ≥ 0, q ≥ 0 and W ≥ 0 on ℝ included, and |φ| ≤ 1 on ℝ; put max q := sup_ℝ q, and let m′, M′ and w_I
be constants as there. Let Im σ > 0,
F ∈ L²(ℝ) vanish outside I, and let u := (−∂²_(r_*) + V − σ²)⁻¹F be the solution in L²(ℝ). Then

    ‖u‖_I ≤ B⁺(σ)‖F‖,     B⁺(σ) := ((2/m′ + (M′ + 4|σ| + 2 max q)²/w_I)/w_I)^(1/2),

and the bounds of Lemma 48.12 for ‖u′‖_I and for ∫_I W_1|u|², with p_I = p_∞ = 1, hold with 2|σ|
replaced by 4|σ| + 2 max q. When q = 0, or when Re σ² ≥ 0, the term 2 max q may be dropped.
If instead |φ| ≤ p_φ on ℝ for a constant p_φ > 0, and the other hypotheses hold, then
‖u‖_I ≤ ((2p_φ²/m′ + (M′ + 4p_φ|σ| + 2 max q)²/w_I)/w_I)^(1/2)‖F‖.

*Proof.* Write σ² = a_σ + ib_σ. The operator −∂² + V is self-adjoint and nonnegative, so u ∈ H²(ℝ); off I, u solves
the homogeneous equation and lies in L², so near ±∞ it is a multiple of the solution that behaves like e^(±iσr_*),
which decays exponentially with its derivative. So every boundary term below vanishes and no flux term arises. Pair
−u″ + (V − a_σ)u − ib_σu = F with 2φū′ + (φ′ − 2q)ū and take real parts. The terms with V − a_σ give, by the
calculation in the proof of Lemma 48.12 with σ² replaced by a_σ, the integrand
2(φ′ − q)|u′|² + W|u|² + 2a_σq|u|² plus an exact derivative; the new term gives
Re(−ib_σu(2φū′ + (φ′ − 2q)ū)) = 2b_σφ Im(uū′). Integrating over ℝ,

    2∫(φ′ − q)|u′|² + ∫W|u|² + 2a_σ∫q|u|² = Re∫F(2φū′ + (φ′ − 2q)ū) − 2b_σ∫φ Im(uū′).

Integration by parts gives the energy identity ∫Fū = ‖u′‖² + ∫V|u|² − σ²‖u‖², norms over ℝ. Its imaginary part
gives |b_σ|‖u‖² ≤ ‖F‖‖u‖_I, and its real part, with V ≥ 0, ‖u′‖² ≤ ‖F‖‖u‖_I + a_+‖u‖², a_+ := max(a_σ, 0). As |φ| ≤ 1,

    |2b_σ∫φ Im(uū′)| ≤ 2|b_σ|‖u‖‖u′‖ ≤ 2|b_σ|‖u‖(‖F‖‖u‖_I)^(1/2) + 2|b_σ|a_+^(1/2)‖u‖²
                      ≤ 2(|b_σ|^(1/2) + a_+^(1/2))‖F‖‖u‖_I ≤ 4|σ|‖F‖‖u‖_I,

since |b_σ| = 2|Re σ| Im σ ≤ |σ|² and a_+^(1/2) ≤ |Re σ| ≤ |σ|. If a_σ ≥ 0 the term 2a_σ∫q|u|² is nonnegative and is
dropped; if a_σ < 0, the real part of the energy identity gives |a_σ|‖u‖² ≤ ‖F‖‖u‖_I, so
−2a_σ∫q|u|² ≤ 2 max q ‖F‖‖u‖_I, and this term is moved to the right. Then the left side is at least 2m′X² + w_IY²,
X := ‖u′‖_I, Y := ‖u‖_I, and, as |φ| ≤ 1 on I, the right side is at most ‖F‖(2X + (M′ + 4|σ| + 2 max q)Y); the rest is
the algebra of the proof of Lemma 48.12 with p_I = p_∞ = 1, with M′ + 4|σ| + 2 max q in place of
M′ + 2|σ|. For the last statement, φ/p_φ and q/p_φ satisfy the hypotheses with |φ/p_φ| ≤ 1; since W, φ′ − q and
φ′ − 2q are linear in (φ, q), their constants are m′/p_φ, M′/p_φ, w_I/p_φ and max q/p_φ, and the bound just proved for
them is the one stated. ∎

So the real-axis bounds are stable under Im σ > 0: B⁺ is continuous in σ and bounded on compact subsets of
{Im σ ≥ 0, σ ≠ 0}, and the degeneration of Lemma 48.1 as Im σ → 0 is not met. As Im σ → 0, B⁺ tends to the
constant with 4|σ|, not to the real-axis one: the factor 2 is the price of bounding the b_σ-term by norms over ℝ. The
lemma applies directly to the multiplier φ = z, which has |z| < 1, with q = 0 for l ≥ 1
(Proposition 48.15) and max q = 2√6/27 for l = 0 (Proposition 48.16), and in the scaled form,
with p_φ := sup_ℝ|φ|, to the multipliers of Proposition 48.28, as stated there.

### 48.10 Polynomial multipliers

**Lemma 48.18** (Bernstein lower bound.) Let p be a polynomial of degree at most n and α < β.
Write p(α + (β − α)t) = Σ_(j≤n) c_j t^j and b_k := Σ_(j≤k) (C(k, j)/C(n, j))c_j for 0 ≤ k ≤ n. Then
min_k b_k ≤ p ≤ max_k b_k on [α, β]; in particular |p| ≤ max_k |b_k| there.

*Proof.* Expanding t^j = t^j(t + (1 − t))^(n−j) by the binomial theorem gives
t^j = Σ_(k≥j) (C(k, j)/C(n, j))C(n, k)t^k(1 − t)^(n−k), as C(n − j, k − j)/C(n, k) = C(k, j)/C(n, j). So
p(α + (β − α)t) = Σ_k b_k C(n, k)t^k(1 − t)^(n−k), a combination of the b_k with nonnegative weights of sum 1 on
t ∈ [0, 1]. ∎

**Lemma 48.19** (The weight of a polynomial multiplier.) Let Θ be a real polynomial in z
and g a real polynomial in y, with g ≥ 0 and 4Θ_z(1 − 2y) − g(y) ≥ 0 for 0 ≤ y ≤ 1, and put φ := Θ(z) and q := ηg. Then
φ and q satisfy the hypotheses of Lemma 48.12 on φ and q, with φ(±∞) = Θ(±1); and q ≥ 0, φ′ = 4ηΘ_z,
φ′ − q = η(4Θ_z − g) ≥ 0 and φ′ − 2q = η(4Θ_z − 2g) on ℝ, the derivatives of Θ taken at z = 1 − 2y. For V = V_(a,b) or
V = V_S the weight of Lemma 48.12 is W = ηG with

    G = 2ΘV_y − 8y(10y² − 12y + 3)Θ_z + 24(1 − y)y²(3 − 5y)Θ_zz − 32(1 − y)²y³Θ_zzz
        + 4y((2 − 3y)h + y(1 − y)h_y) − 2gV,    (48.16)

with h as in (48.11). If g = 0 and Θ(0) = 0, then zΘ ≥ 0 on [−1, 1], and for V = V_(a,b) the polynomial
G is affine in b and nondecreasing in a, with ∂_aG = 2zΘ; the a-part of W is a(−φU′), with −φU′ = 2ηzΘ ≥ 0.

*Proof.* φ is smooth and bounded, and z → ±1 as r_* → ±∞, so φ(±∞) = Θ(±1). By the remark after
(48.11), φ′, φ″, φ‴, q, q′, q″ are integrable and tend to 0 at ±∞. With Θ_y = −2Θ_z,
(48.7) gives φ′ = 4ηΘ_z, and the identities for φ′ − q and φ′ − 2q follow. Next,
4(η(ηΘ_y)_y)_y = 4(η_y² + ηη_yy)Θ_y + 12ηη_yΘ_yy + 4η²Θ_yyy, since (η²)_y = 2ηη_y; substituting Θ_y = −2Θ_z,
Θ_yy = 4Θ_zz, Θ_yyy = −8Θ_zzz, η_y² + ηη_yy = y(10y² − 12y + 3) (proof of Proposition 48.13),
ηη_y = (1 − y)y²(3 − 5y)/2 and η² = (1 − y)²y³ gives the Θ-terms of (48.16); the others are those of
(48.11). If Θ(0) = 0 and Θ_z ≥ 0 on [−1, 1] (which holds when g = 0), Θ(z) has the sign of z. With
g = 0, G is linear in (a, b) up to an a- and b-free term, and the coefficient of a is 2ΘU_y = 2zΘ, since U_y = z;
−φU′ = 2ηΘU_y = 2ηzΘ. ∎

its range, and each bound is even in σ and increasing in |σ|, hence so is their least. For l ≥ 6, rows C6 and
Proposition 48.15 give bounds independent of l. The entries come from row A′ at l = 1; from row B′ at
l = 2, except at σ = 10, from row E; from Proposition 48.15 at l = 3 for σ → 0 and |σ| = 1/2, and from
row C3 otherwise; and from rows C4, C5 and C6 at l = 4, 5 and every l ≥ 6. At |σ| = 1/2 and 2 they evaluate
(48.9) with the constants of those rows, rounding up.

(ii) max V_(a,b) ≤ a max U + b max Q = a/4 + 4b/27 for a, b ≥ 0, since U = (1 − y)y ≤ 1/4 and Q = (1 − y)y² ≤ 4/27; at
l = 0 this is 3/16 + 1/3 = 25/48 < 1. For σ² > max V_0 the bound above the barrier, Proposition 48.10,
gives ‖χ_I R_0(σ) χ_I‖ ≤ Λ|σ|/(σ² − max V_0) ≤ Λ|σ|/(σ² − 25/48). As Λt/(t² − 25/48) decreases for t² > 25/48, its value
for |σ| ≥ 1 is at most Λ/(23/48) < 3.7436 · 48/23 < 7.8128. The entries at l = 0 are B_0(0+) and B_0(1/2) of
Proposition 48.16 and 3.7436|σ|/(σ² − 25/48) at |σ| = 1, 2, 3, 10, rounded up. ∎

At |σ| ≥ 3 the bound above the barrier also improves the entries for 1 ≤ l ≤ 4 (Proposition 48.29); the
estimates below use B*_l for l ≥ 1 because it is increasing in |σ|.

C_u < 568.55.

*Proof.* (a) and (b) are Lemma 48.12 with B̃ = B*_l, applied to φ = z with q = 0 for l ≥ 1 and to the
multiplier of Proposition 48.16 for l = 0, both with p_I = p_∞ = 1. In (a), W_1 := (κ − 3)ψ and W_0 := w_1 are
nonnegative (Proposition 48.13); so (κ − 3)∫_Iψ|u|² ≤ J_l‖F‖², and κ∫_Iψ|u|² ≤ A_l‖F‖² for l ≥ 2. At l = 1,
3‖u‖_I² ≤ 3(B*_1)²‖F‖². For l ≥ 6, B*_l is at most the line "every l ≥ 6" of Proposition 48.21, X_l and J_l
increase with B*_l, and κ/(κ − 3) decreases, so C_l ≤ C_6. In the table each entry is evaluated from the rounded entries
above it and rounded up. In (b), for 0 < |σ| ≤ 1, X_0 increases with |σ| and with B*_0 ≤ B_0 ≤ B_0(1) < 226.50, so

give X_0 ≤ (1 + (1 + (3315/32768)(6.3999)(7.8128))^(1/2))(32768/3315) < 34.22. At |σ| = 3, B*_0 < 1.3246 gives
X_0 < 23.36.

(c) *The harmonic components.* Let (S_(l,k))_k be an orthonormal basis of 𝒮_l ⊗ ℂ in L²(𝕊³), finite for each l, and
F_(l,k)(r_*) := ∫_(𝕊³) F(r_*, ω) conj(S_(l,k)(ω)) dω. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Fubini's theorem F_(l,k) lies
in L²(ℝ) and vanishes outside I, and F_l = Σ_k F_(l,k)S_(l,k). The S_(l,k), over all l and k, form an orthonormal basis
of L²(𝕊³), so by Parseval's identity for almost every r_* and integration in r_* (monotone convergence),
‖F‖² = Σ_l ‖F_l‖² and ‖F_l‖² = Σ_k ‖F_(l,k)‖². By definition u_l = Σ_k (R_l(σ)F_(l,k))S_(l,k), each R_l(σ)F_(l,k) a
solution as in Lemma 48.12, so u_l and ∂_(r_*)u_l = Σ_k (R_l(σ)F_(l,k))′S_(l,k) are defined on ℝ × 𝕊³,
and since the S_(l,k) are orthonormal for each fixed r_*,

    ‖u_l‖_I² = Σ_k ‖R_l(σ)F_(l,k)‖_I²,     ‖∂_(r_*)u_l‖_I² = Σ_k ‖(R_l(σ)F_(l,k))′‖_I²,
    ∫_I ψ|u_l|² = Σ_k ∫_I ψ|R_l(σ)F_(l,k)|².

*The bound for each harmonic.* Applying Proposition 48.21, (a) and (b) to each F_(l,k) and summing over k,
‖u_l‖_I ≤ B*_l‖F_l‖ and ‖∂_(r_*)u_l‖_I ≤ X_l‖F_l‖ for every l ≥ 0; for l ≥ 2, ‖∂_(r_*)u_l‖_I² + κ∫_Iψ|u_l|² ≤
(X_l² + A_l)‖F_l‖² = C_l²‖F_l‖²; at l = 1, ‖∂_(r_*)u_1‖_I² + 3‖u_1‖_I² ≤ (X_1² + 3(B*_1)²)‖F_1‖² = C_1²‖F_1‖²; and at
l = 0, where κ = 0, ‖∂_(r_*)u_0‖_I² ≤ X_0²‖F_0‖².

*The constants are uniform in l.* B*_l is increasing in |σ| (Proposition 48.21), and X_l, J_l, A_l and C_l
increase with |σ| and with B*_l; so for 0 < |σ| ≤ 3 each is at most its value at |σ| = 3, and C_l(σ) ≤ C_l(3) ≤ 179.26
for every l ≥ 1, by the table (for l ≥ 6, C_l ≤ C_6). Also X_0 ≤ 83.85 by (b). Moreover B*_l ≤ B_l(σ) ≤ B_1(σ) for
l ≥ 1, as ω_l ≥ ω_1 in Proposition 48.15, so b := max(B*_0(σ), B_1(σ)) and
x := max(X_0, X(B_1(σ))), with X(B̃) := (1 + (1 + 2m′(M′ + 2|σ|)B̃)^(1/2))/(2m′), the bound of
Lemma 48.12 with the constants of (a), bound B*_l and X_l for every l ≥ 0.

*Convergence.* For l ≠ l′ and almost every r_*, u_l(r_*, ·) ∈ 𝒮_l ⊗ ℂ and u_(l′)(r_*, ·) ∈ 𝒮_(l′) ⊗ ℂ are orthogonal
in L²(𝕊³), and so are ∂_(r_*)u_l(r_*, ·) and ∂_(r_*)u_(l′)(r_*, ·); integrating over I, the u_l are mutually orthogonal
in L²(I × 𝕊³), and so are the ∂_(r_*)u_l. Hence for every finite set L of harmonics
‖Σ_(l∈L) u_l‖_I² = Σ_(l∈L) ‖u_l‖_I² ≤ b² Σ_(l∈L) ‖F_l‖² and ‖Σ_(l∈L) ∂_(r_*)u_l‖_I² ≤ x² Σ_(l∈L) ‖F_l‖². As
Σ_l ‖F_l‖² = ‖F‖² < ∞, the partial sums of both series are Cauchy sequences in L²(I × 𝕊³), so both series converge
there; let v be the sum of the second. For a smooth function χ with compact support in the interior of I × 𝕊³, each
R_l(σ)F_(l,k) is absolutely continuous in r_*, so ∫u_l ∂_(r_*)χ = −∫(∂_(r_*)u_l)χ; summing over l and passing to the
limit in L² gives ∫u ∂_(r_*)χ = −∫vχ, that is ∂_(r_*)u = v weakly. By orthogonality and the continuity of the norm,
‖∂_(r_*)u‖_I² = Σ_l ‖∂_(r_*)u_l‖_I².

*The sum.* Adding the bounds for each harmonic,
‖∂_(r_*)u‖_I² + Σ_l κ∫_Iψ|u_l|² ≤ Σ_(l≥1) C_l²‖F_l‖² + X_0²‖F_0‖² ≤ max(sup_(l≥1) C_l, X_0)²‖F‖², and the maximum is at
most 179.26. At |σ| = 1/2, 1 and 2, B*_l ≤ B*_2 for l ≥ 2 (every bound that serves l = 2 in
Proposition 48.21 serves every l ≥ 2, and B_l ≤ B_2), so X_l ≤ X_2, J_l ≤ J_2 and, as κ/(κ − 3) decreases,
C_l ≤ C_2 for l ≥ 2. The same evaluation of (a) and (b) with the bounds of Proposition 48.21 at that σ gives
the values listed; they are evaluated from B*_1(1/2) < 30.4202, B*_1(1) < 41.46, B*_1(2) < 66.1908, B*_2(1/2) < 14.85,
B*_2(1) < 18.61, B*_2(2) < 27.88, B*_0(1/2) < 140.82, B*_0(1) < 7.8128 and B*_0(2) < 2.1521, the values of
Proposition 48.21 computed from the rows' constants; its table rounds them up to two decimals, which is too
coarse to reproduce C_1 at |σ| = 1/2 and 2 and X_0 at |σ| = 1 and 2.

(d) As in (c), for each l ≥ 1 and every B̃_l with ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I‖ ≤ B̃_l,
‖∂_(r_*)u_l‖_I² + κ‖u_l‖_I² ≤ (X(B̃_l)² + κB̃_l²)‖F_l‖², with X(B̃) as in (c); and
