#### 49.12.3 Null infinity and the Fourier steps

**Lemma 49.99** (The constructions at null infinity.) (a) Every application of Proposition 29.29 in the
constructions is charged at most 6. (b) An application of Proposition 29.27 with ℓ_+ < 3/2 whose a priori
ℐ⁺-weight α_I is at least −3/2 is charged at most 37 · 11 = 407. Every application below has α_I > ½.

*Proof.* (a) The operator of Proposition 29.29 is L_b, with ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²L_b = L_0 + L̃ fixed (Lemma 29.26).
Step 1 of its proof solves for u^♭ by Lemma 21.33 and a fixed scalar (charge 0) and subtracts L_b v (charge 2).
Step 2 treats the windows [m_j, m_j + 1), m_j = min Re ℰ^C_I + j − 1 = 1 + j (Proposition 49.69 (a): the least
exponent of ℰ^C_I is 2), with Re z ≤ ℓ_I < 3.5; so j ∈ {1, 2}. ℰ^C_I has logarithmic order 0 (Proposition 49.69 (a)),
so k(F_I, z) = 0 at every z, and each term is solved once, by (z − 3/2 − Ā)⁻¹ and Lemma 21.33 (charge 0); the
terms of one window are independent, as L̃ moves the exponents by positive integers, out of the window. Each window
passes f − L_b(Σ_z χρ_I^z u^((z,0))) to the next (charge 2). So a chain is charged at most 2 + 2 · 2 = 6.

(b) Each step of the proofs of Lemma 29.28 and Proposition 29.27 applies L̃ of L = L^(g,g_0) once (charge 11,
Lemma 49.97 (d)), the products ρ_I⁻¹ρ_+⁻²f and the integrations of Lemma 21.33 and Lemma 21.42
costing nothing; so it suffices to count the steps, with the increments of Definition 49.96 (d). Step 1 of the proof
of Lemma 29.28 is run until the weight exceeds 1 + η₂, η₂ < (1 − e_Υ)γ_Υ < 0.01 being the number of its Step 2
(Step 2 needs L̃u at the weight 3/2 + η₂, and L̃ gains any η′ < ½); from α_I ≥ −3/2 this takes at most
⌈2.51/0.4⌉ = 7 steps. Step 2 is one step. Step 3 goes from 3/2 + η₂ to ℓ_I < 3.5 in at most ⌈2/0.4⌉ = 5 steps.
Step 1 of the proof of Proposition 29.27 goes from α_I to below ℓ_+ < 3/2 in at most ⌈3/0.4⌉ = 8 steps, and its
Step 2 from there to ℓ_I in at most ⌈5/0.4⌉ = 13 steps. In all 7 + 1 + 5 + 8 + 13 = 34 ≤ 37 steps. At the
applications below the a priori ℐ⁺-weights are: β^(0)_I > ½ at the start of Proposition 29.35 (the weight of
Theorem 29.17), γ_+ − ε > ½ in its Step 3, and at least 1 − 5ε in Proposition 31.6, Proposition 31.27,
Lemma 32.27 and Proposition 33.15, whose remainders are sums of pieces of ℐ⁺-weight at least
min(3/2, α^♯_+) − 5ε > 1 − 5ε and of u_I, which has the ℐ⁺-data (⟨ℰ^C_I⟩, ℓ_I). ∎

**Lemma 49.100** (The Fourier steps of a level above 3.) Let β ∈ (3, α] be a level of Step 2 of the proof of
Theorem 34.9, and consider the proof of Proposition 33.15 at β (through Proposition 33.28 when β < 4).

(a) The application of Proposition 21.45 (1) in its Step 0 is charged at most 9 + N_ι.

(b) In the application of Proposition 21.45 (2) in its Step 7, n_ι = 0 and n_K ≤ N_ι + N_Λ, and it is charged at most
N_ι + N̄_Λ + 2.

(c) The inverse transforms of the column pieces in its Step 5 (Lemma 33.13) are charged at most 5 each.

*Proof.* (a) is Lemma 49.56 with Lemma 49.49 (with β_K = β − ε when β < 4): the charge is
1 + n_ι + 2⌊β − ε⌋ ≤ 1 + N_ι + 8. For a forcing in 𝒴^♮(β), Proposition 33.8 (c) and Lemma 33.27 (b) give
ℰ^♭ the hypothesis of Lemma 49.56.

(b) Step 7 applies Proposition 21.45 (2) on each half with β_scf = 3/2 − 3ε, the tf-data (E_tf, β′_+ − 1), so
E_ι = E_tf + 1 and β_ι = β′_+ < 3/2, and the zf-data ((0, 0) ∪̄ (E_K − 1), β − 3 − ε), so β_K = β − 2 − ε. By
(49.6) (2) its charge is n_ι + n_K + ℓ_F, where n_ι counts the pairs of E_tf of real part at most
β′_+ − 1 < ½, and n_K the pairs (d, m) of E_K − 1 with Re d ≤ β − 3 − ε < 1 + ε_K; E_tf and E_K − 1 are the smallest
index sets containing the tf-terms, resp. the zf-terms below these weights, of the pieces other than the columns with
constant coefficients.

*tf.* The pieces at zero energy are σ^jχ_zf û_j. By Lemma 33.10, û_0 has at ∂X the exponents of
(ℰ^♭ − 1) ∪ (1 + ℰ_col) ∪ (2, ·) and their ℕ₀-shifts, of real part at least 1, as ℰ^♭ ⊂ {Re ≥ 2} and ℰ_col ⊂ {Re ≥ 0}
(Lemma 33.9); for j ≥ 1, û_j has exponents of real part at least η_1 > 0 (Step 2), and the factor σ^j adds j at
tf. The pieces σ^ju_((α_0,k)) of Proposition 27.55 have tf-exponents in α_0 − 2 + j + ((0, 0) ∪ ℰ_ind) and, from the
term with G^exc_(s1), in 2 + j and α_0 + j with ℰ_ind added (Step 1.1 of the proof of Proposition 27.55), all of real
part at least 1 (level 1: Re α_0 ≥ 2; level 2: Re α_0 ≥ 1 + η_1; min Re ℰ_ind > 0). The pieces of level 3 and of the last
level are conormal at tf, of tf-weight above 2, and so are the column pieces with non-constant coefficients
(Lemma 29.34: tf-weight at least ℓ_3 + 2 − ε plus the powers of σ they carry). So E_tf ⊂ {Re ≥ 1} and n_ι = 0.

*zf.* By Step 5 (i), (ii) and (iv) of the proof of Proposition 33.15, and Lemma 33.12, the zf-terms of the
pieces are: terms of integer degree without log|σ| (the zero energy pieces, the column pieces and σ^jP_int); and, for
an application of Proposition 27.55 at a tf-exponent (α_0, k) at the level j ∈ {1, 2}, the terms
σ^jc_τ(σ)(−iσ)^ih̆^i_τ of degree α_0 − 3 + j + i (s1), α_0 − 2 + j + i (v1) and α_0 − 2 − μ + j + i (the other rows,
μ a root of the table of (27.44), Re μ ≤ 0), i ≥ 0, with logarithmic order at most k + 1 (the derivatives in
α_0 give log|σ| up to the power k, and a critical α_0 or β_μ one power more). At level 1, Re α_0 ∈ [2, 2 + η_1) and
α_0 ∈ Λ is the u-exponent; at level 2, Re α_0 ∈ [1 + η_1, 2 + η_2) and α_0 + 1 ∈ Λ is the u-exponent; and the
logarithmic order k at the tf-exponent is at most k̄ of the u-exponent (Lemma 33.2 (c),
Lemma 33.27 (b)). As Λ ∩ {Re ≤ 3 + ε_+} is real (Proposition 49.70) and meets (2, 2 + ε_K] in no point ((G)),
and as the roots of the table are real, and those with −1 < μ < 0 have −μ ≥ ε_ind > ε_K by (25.10)
(Section 27.10, (32.27)), a term of real part below
1 + ε_K is one of: at level 1, the s1 term with i = 0, of degree α_0 − 2; at level 1 with α_0 = 2, the s1 term with
i = 1, the v1 term with i = 0 and the terms of the rows with μ = 0 and i = 0, all of degree 1 = 3 − 2; at level 2, the
s1 term with i = 0, of degree α_0 − 1 = (α_0 + 1) − 2; and the integer degrees 0 = 2 − 2 and 1 = 3 − 2. So every pair
of E_K − 1 of real part below 1 + ε_K is (λ − 2, m) with λ ∈ Λ, 2 ≤ λ < 3 + ε_+, and m ≤ k̄(λ) + 1, where at degree 1
we use k̄(2) ≤ k̄(3) and 2, 3 ∈ Λ. The ℕ₀-shifts add nothing below 1 + ε_K except at the degree 0 + 1 = 1, as every other
degree has real part above ε_K. Hence, with λ_1 < ⋯ < λ_(N_Λ) as in Lemma 49.55 (c),

    n_K ≤ Σ_(i≤N_Λ) (k̄(λ_i) + 2) = N_Λ + 4N_Λ + 765,000,816 · N_Λ(N_Λ + 1)/2 ≤ N_Λ + N_ι

by the proof of Lemma 49.56. Finally ℓ_F = ⌈(max(β′_+ − 3/2 + 3ε, β − 2 − ε) + ε − ½)_+⌉ ≤ ⌈3/2 + ε_K⌉ = 2.

(c) By Lemma 33.13, these are Proposition 21.45 (2) with E_ι = E_K = ∅ and the weights 3/2 − ε at ι⁺ and at
most α at K⁺, so their charge is ℓ_F ≤ ⌈α + ε − ½⌉ = 4 (Lemma 49.98 (b)). ∎

#### 49.12.4 The level steps and the base

**Lemma 49.101** (The level steps.) Let 1 ≤ k ≤ K. (a) If β_k < 3, then c(β_k) ≤ 497. (b) If β_k > 3, then

    c(β_k) ≤ C_lev := 2N_ι + N̄_Λ + 529 = 214,558,790,360,052,785,818,485,009,600,000,520.    (49.47)

The same bounds hold at a rotating black hole parameter and for c^Ψ(β_k).

*Proof.* By Lemma 49.95 we add the charges of the applications of each step, the windows, the transition face
rounds, the applications of Proposition 27.55 at the levels 1 and 2 and the level-3 rounds being charged 0.

*The background terms of Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 34.9.* The forcing G′ of (34.8) is F minus
Δ_q(p⃗′), R_q u and the defects f^S(S′), f^b(b′), f^s1(S^(0)′_1) and r^ν(W′_ν); u_0 adds the rows m_ν(W′_ν). These are
summands, each a family of Lemma 49.97 (d) or a finite-rank map with such sections; so they are charged at most 11
beyond the steps that compute u and p⃗′, which are other steps of the chain. At a rotating b, Proposition 36.8 adds
the errors E^ν (charge 11) to the same sum and the coordinates A_b (charge 0); for ℛ(U), Lemma 38.17 adds the
sources e_S(S′) + e_(S⁰)(S⁰′) (charge 11) to it. In every case this sum is charged at most 11.

(a) The step is Lemma 32.27 at β_k. Its Step 0 applies (L − L_b)u (11). Steps 1–2 apply Proposition 29.29 (6,
Lemma 49.99 (a)) and L_b u_I (2), the windows being charged 0. Step 3 runs Steps 3–3.3 of the proof of
Proposition 31.27 with α − ε′ for α_K: Lemma 29.32 at β_ι = 2 − ε (30, Lemma 49.98 (e)),
Proposition 20.18 (1) (1), L̃_b(0)⁻¹ (1), the terms of f̂_2, which apply [L̂_b(0), χ_zf], L̂_b(σ) − L̂_b(0) and the
columns (2), the division by σ (0), Proposition 27.58 (9, Lemma 49.97 (f)), Lemma 31.26 (0), f̂_4 (2),
L̃_b(0)⁻¹ (1) and f̂_5 (2). Step 3.4′ runs its rounds (charged 0) and applies Lemma 29.33 at β_scf = 3/2 − 2ε (2,
Lemma 49.98 (d)); the row terms U^((i)), B^((i)), Σ^((i))_r of Lemma 31.25 are fixed sections
L̃_b(σ)⁻¹(0, E_k) times the coefficients of the row functional (0), and (32.24) is a sum; so is
(31.47) of Step 3.5′, whose row term (U_r, B_r, Σ_r) of Step 3.5 is of the same kind (0). Steps 4–5 of the
proof of Proposition 31.27 apply Proposition 20.20 (1) twice, at the output weights (3/2 − 4ε, 2 − 2ε, α_K − 1) and
(3 − 2ε, 3 − ε, α_K − 1) (5 each, Lemma 49.98 (b)), Lemma 31.5, Lemma 29.34 and
Lemma 29.30 (0). Steps 6–7 read coefficients (0). Step 8 applies Proposition 29.27 (407, Lemma 49.99
(b)). With the background terms,

    11 + 11 + 6 + 2 + (30 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 9 + 2 + 1 + 2) + 2 + (5 + 5) + 407 = 497.

(b) The step is Lemma 33.29 (at a rotating b Lemma 36.7, which adds the coordinates A_b, charge 0),
whose proof is that of Lemma 33.16. Its Step 0 applies (L − L_b)u (11). Steps 1–2 are Proposition 33.8 at
β_k: its Step 1 applies Proposition 29.29 (6) and L_b u⁽⁰⁾_I (2); its Step 2 is a window loop (0); the rows are read
by Lemma 33.4 (c) (0). Step 3 is Proposition 33.15 at β_k (through Proposition 33.28 when β_k < 4). Its
Step 0 applies Lemma 29.32 at β_ι = 3 + ε_+ − ε (30) and Proposition 21.45 (1) (9 + N_ι,
Lemma 49.100 (a)). Steps 1, 2 and 3 each apply Lemma 33.10 (9) and Lemma 33.11 (2), the
applications of Proposition 27.55 being charged 0. Step 4 applies, besides its rounds, Lemma 33.10 (9; only

tails by Lemma 33.7 (0) and transforms the column pieces back (5, in parallel, Lemma 49.100 (c)). Step 6

Proposition 29.27 (407). With the background terms,

    11 + 11 + 6 + 2 + 30 + (9 + N_ι) + 3 · (9 + 2) + (9 + 2 + 2) + 5 + (N_ι + N̄_Λ + 2) + 407
        = 2N_ι + N̄_Λ + 529,

and 2N_ι + N̄_Λ + 529 is the integer of (49.47). ∎

**Lemma 49.102** (The base.) c′_b ≤ 466 and c_b ≤ 469, also at a rotating black hole parameter and for ℛ(U).

*Proof.* *One step of Proposition 29.35.* Step 1 applies (L − L_b)u (11). Step 2a applies Proposition 29.29 (6) and
L_b u_I (2). Step 2b applies Proposition 20.18 (1) (1), Lemma 29.32 at β_ι = γ_+ > ½ (30), Lemma 29.33
at β_scf = 3/2 − ε (2), Proposition 20.20 (1) at the output weights (γ_+ − ε, γ_+, α̃_K) (at most 5),

Proposition 29.27 (407). So c′_b ≤ 11 + 6 + 2 + 1 + 30 + 2 + 5 + 2 + 407 = 466.

*One round of Proposition 31.21.* Step 0 applies (L − L_b)u (11). Step 1 applies Proposition 29.29 (6) and
L_b u_I (2). Step 2 is the window loop (0). Step 3 runs Steps 2–3 of the proof of Proposition 31.6:
Lemma 29.32 at β_ι = α^♯_+ > 1 (30), Proposition 20.18 (1) (1), L̃_b(0)⁻¹ (1), the terms of f̂_2 (2),
Lemma 29.33 at β_scf = 3/2 − ε (2), Proposition 20.20 (1) at the output weights
(min(3/2, α^♯_+) − 3ε, α^♯_+, α̃_K) (at most 5), Lemma 31.5, Lemma 29.34 and the multiplication by
−iσ (0), Lemma 29.31 (2) and Lemma 29.30 (0); the coefficient S_0 is read at no cost. Step 4 applies
Proposition 29.27 (407). So c_b ≤ 11 + 6 + 2 + 30 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 5 + 2 + 407 = 469.

At a rotating b the statements are those at b ((BP1)–(BP5), Proposition 30.5), with the same families; for ℛ(U)

#### 49.12.5 The remaining steps

c_0 contains, besides finitely many steps of the kinds above, the iterations of the top level and of one further base,
which the definition before Proposition 49.40 charges in full. We bound these first.

**Lemma 49.103** (Iterations charged in full.) Put R_b := 61,038,200,000,000 and

    I_lev := 16 · 1,470,302 + 3 + 3 · 3,000,004 + 5 · 6,847,261,001 = 34,268,829,852,
    I_base := 469 R_b + 466 (R_b + 1) + 16 · 1,470,302 · (R_b + 3)
            = 1,435,970,471,299,470,574,962.    (49.48)

(a) A level step at β ∈ (3, α] (Lemma 33.29 or Lemma 33.16 at β), with its window loop, its
applications of Proposition 27.55 at the levels 1 and 2 and its level-3 rounds charged as well, is charged at most
C_lev − 11 + I_lev along every chain.

(b) A base, that is, Proposition 32.29 at a level in (2, 3) for a background of K⁺-order above a♭_K, with all its
rounds of Proposition 31.21, steps of Proposition 29.35 and windows charged as well, is charged at most
B + I_base along every chain, where B is the sum of the charges of its other applications.

*Proof.* (a) Lemma 49.101 (b), without the 11 of the background terms of Theorem 34.9, bounds the other
applications. By Lemma 49.39 (e), Lemma 49.54 and Proposition 49.57, the window loop has at most 1,470,302
windows, each charged at most r_ι ≤ 16 (Lemma 49.38 (c), Lemma 49.53). By Lemma 49.39 (d)

#### 49.12.6 The bound

**Proposition 49.105** (The largest single-step loss.) At the computational point, with the index sets as
constructed and the choices of Definition 49.52 and Definition 49.96,

    c_* ≤ 6N_ι + 3N̄_Λ + 17,389,163,815,025,371,354,557,103,786
        = 643,676,388,469,322,172,480,826,383,357,103,759
        < C_* := 643,680,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 = 6.4368·10³⁵.    (49.50)

*Proof.* By Lemma 49.101 and Lemma 49.102, c(β_k), c^Ψ(β_k) ≤ max(497, C_lev) = C_lev and c_b, c^Ψ_b ≤ 469,
c′_b, c′^Ψ_b ≤ 466. By Lemma 49.104, c_0 and c^Ψ_0 are at most the right side of (49.49). With
C_lev = 2N_ι + N̄_Λ + 529, this is

    2 · 20,183 + 2 · 1,914 + 33 + 3C_lev + 3I_lev + 2X_12 + I_base + d_Φ + (N̄_Λ + 2)(d_Φ + 30)
        = 6N_ι + 3N̄_Λ + 1,587 + 44,227 + 102,806,489,556 + 102,492,973,325,715,479,993,544
          + 1,435,970,471,299,470,574,962 + 1,038,326,399,999,940 + 17,389,059,886,080,535,910,399,999,970,

with 3I_lev = 102,806,489,556, 2X_12 = 8k̄_max + 48 = 102,492,973,325,715,479,993,544 and
(N̄_Λ + 2)(d_Φ + 30) ≤ 16,747,200,000,001 · 1,038,326,399,999,970 = 17,389,059,886,080,535,910,399,999,970. The seven
numbers after 6N_ι + 3N̄_Λ add up to 17,389,163,815,025,371,354,557,103,786, and with
6N_ι = 643,676,371,080,158,357,455,404,787,199,999,976 and 3N̄_Λ = 50,241,599,999,997 the sum is the integer of
(49.50), which is less than C_*. This bound exceeds C_lev, 469 and 466, so it bounds c_*. ∎

**Remark 49.106** (What the bound counts.) Of the bound of (49.50), all but less than 1.74·10²⁸
is 6N_ι (C_* itself exceeds 6N_ι by less than 3.63·10³⁰): two counts of the logarithmic terms of Λ below 3 + ε_+ in
each of the three runs of the top level counted in the bound for c_0, each count being taken at the bound k̄(λ) of
Definition 33.1 for the logarithmic orders. The next term,
(N̄_Λ + 2)(d_Φ + 30) < 1.739·10²⁸, comes from Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 34.24, whose chain passes through
every exponent of Λ_* and composes the map Φ at each. A level step above 3 is charged at most C_lev ≈ C_*/3, and c_0
enters the second line of (49.24) once; bounding that line by K·C_lev + 469N_b + 466(N_b + 1) + C_*, with
K < 1.22077·10¹⁴ (Remark 49.41), instead of by M_c C_*, gives d_acc, d_R < 2.62·10⁴⁹ (Lemma 49.107). The
bound is crude in another way as well: n_ι and n_K count every pair (λ, k) with k ≤ k̄(λ), while the logarithmic
orders that the constructions produce are bounded in this paper only by k̄(λ).

#### 49.12.7 The smallness orders and the loss of the Nash–Moser step

The proof of Theorem 38.19 applies Theorem 20.1 with d the largest of the d's of Lemma 38.16,
Lemma 38.17 and Proposition 35.9. Each of these d's is at least the loss of the estimate of its result and at
least the orders at which its proof asks U small. For Lemma 38.17 one of these orders is the order d′_0 at which
the proof of Theorem 35.8 asks U small, and d′_0 ≥ d_0 + d_Φ with d_0 = d_* + D (*The constants* in the proof of
Lemma 38.17, and Lemma 35.5), where d_* is the order of the smallness conditions of
Chapter 29–Chapter 34 and D is the d of Theorem 35.7. This subsection sums the second line of (49.24)
level by level (Lemma 49.107), evaluates the orders of the smallness conditions and d_* (Lemma 49.108),
and bounds the d of Theorem 38.19 (Proposition 49.110).

Throughout, the point, the index sets and the choices are those of Theorem 49.59; N_ι, N̄_Λ, k̄_max, C_lev, R_b,
I_lev, I_base, X_12, T_11 and T_12 are the numbers of Section 49.12; d_T = 20,180 is the loss of Theorem 29.17 at
every b ∈ ℬ̄_* (Theorem 49.9, Corollary 49.25); ‖β‖_j = ‖h‖_(𝒳^j) + |p⃗| + ‖q‖_(𝒬^j) is the background norm of
Section 35.1; and

    K̄ := 122,076,389,376,829,     R_base := 20,183 + 1,914 + I_base = 1,435,970,471,299,470,597,059.

A *base* is Proposition 32.29, with its forward solution, at a level in (2, 3) that it reaches from its α_0 by one
level step without transition face round, for a background of K⁺-order at least a♭_K. The bases used are that of
Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 34.9 at α_1, at b also in Proposition 36.8; that of the proof of
Theorem 33.18 at the α′ of Definition 49.96 (f); and those of the proofs of Lemma 33.17 and
Lemma 33.30, whose admissible α′ we take below 2 + ε_g − 2ε, with one level step from an admissible
α_0 ∈ (2, α′), as those proofs and that of Proposition 32.29 allow. Each of these levels is below
τ_0 = 2 + ε_g − 2ε, so its level step has no transition face round ((6) of Step 1 in the proof of Lemma 49.104). By
Lemma 49.103 (b), with the count of Step 1 in the proof of Lemma 49.104, a base with all its rounds, steps
and windows charged is charged at most R_base along every chain.

**Lemma 49.107** (The single-step losses summed level by level.) The number K of the levels β_1, …, β_K of
Theorem 34.9 satisfies K ≤ K̄, and

    d_acc ≤ D_♭,     d_R ≤ D_♭,     D_♭ := D_e + K̄ C_lev + 469R_b + 466(R_b + 1) + C_*,
    D_♭ = 26,192,562,436,215,872,034,699,391,908,492,342,632,997,875,951,546 < 2.6193·10⁴⁹,    (49.51)

with D_e and C_* of Theorem 49.59.

*Proof.* *The levels.* At the choice of Definition 49.52, α_1 = β_0 < β_1 < ⋯ < β_K = α, and every spacing
β_(k+1) − β_k is at least Δβ_0 (Lemma 49.53); so KΔβ_0 ≤ α − α_1 < 2 + ε_K, as α ≤ 4 + ε_K and α_1 > 2.
With ε_K = 16,416·10⁻¹⁸ and Δβ_0 = 16,383,184,416·10⁻²⁴ ((49.31)), (2 + ε_K)/Δβ_0 is
2,000,000,000,000,016,416,000,000/16,383,184,416, and

    16,383,184,416 · 122,076,389,376,829 = 2,000,000,000,000,012,824,296,864,
    16,383,184,416 · 122,076,389,376,830 = 2,000,000,000,000,029,207,481,280;

so K < 122,076,389,376,830, that is, K ≤ K̄.

*The bound.* By Lemma 49.53 and Lemma 49.54, Proposition 49.40 holds with the T_2 and W of
(49.32), and its first line is less than D_e (Proposition 49.57). Its second line is
Σ_k c(β_k) + N_b c_b + (N_b + 1)c′_b + c_0. There every c(β_k) is at most max(497, C_lev) = C_lev (Lemma 49.101),
c_b ≤ 469 and c′_b ≤ 466 (Lemma 49.102), and c_0 is at most the integer of (49.50), which is less than C_*
(Lemma 49.104, Proposition 49.105). The number N_b of Lemma 49.39 (f) is at most 1/Δβ_0 + 1
((49.25)), and 16,383,184,416 · 61,038,194,688,415 > 10²⁴, so N_b < 61,038,194,688,416 < R_b. Hence
the second line is at most K̄C_lev + 469R_b + 466(R_b + 1) + C_*, and d_acc ≤ D_♭. By Lemma 49.58, d_R satisfies
(49.24) with the same first line and with c^Ψ(β_k), c^Ψ_b, c′^Ψ_b and c^Ψ_0 in place of c(β_k), c_b, c′_b and
c_0; these satisfy the same bounds (Lemma 49.101, Lemma 49.102, Lemma 49.104), so d_R ≤ D_♭.

*The integer.* K̄C_lev = 26,192,562,436,215,228,354,699,390,649,792,285,562,280,875,951,080, and
469R_b + 466(R_b + 1) = 28,626,915,800,000,000 + 28,443,801,200,000,466 = 57,070,717,000,000,466. Adding these,
D_e = 1,258,700,000,000,000,000,000,000 and C_* = 643,680,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000,000 gives the integer of
(49.51), whose leading digits are 2.619256. ∎

*Orders.* We say that a condition on the background β = (h, p⃗, q) has *order j* if it holds whenever ‖β‖_j is less than
one positive number and ‖β‖_(j+D) is less than another, D being the d of Theorem 35.7. As the norms are
non-decreasing in the order, a condition of order j has order j′ for every j′ ≥ j; and as d_0 = d_* + D
(Lemma 35.5), every condition of order at most d_* holds on the ball ‖β‖_(d_0) < δ_𝔹 of Theorem 35.7 once
δ_𝔹 is small. The bound at the order j + D is the one that the proof of Lemma 35.5 uses when it asks the
solutions u_j entering a comparison to be bounded at a fixed order.

**Lemma 49.108** (The orders of the smallness conditions.) At the computational point, with the index
sets as constructed and the choices of Definition 49.52 and Definition 49.96:

(a) the conditions of Theorem 29.17 and Corollary 29.25, at the backgrounds of Lemma 35.3 (a), have
order d_T + 3 = 20,183;

(b) in (31.26) one may take k_1 = 10 and k_0 = k̄_0 := 20,602 + 466R_b = 28,443,801,200,020,602, and so the d of
(31.26) equal to k̄_0 + 2; the conditions of Chapter 31 then have order k̄_0 + 2, and k̄_0 + 5 at the backgrounds
h + h_rem(q) + h_tot(p⃗);

(c) the conditions that Chapter 31, Chapter 32 and Proposition 32.29 place on the background of a base, at a base
point with parameter b ∈ ℬ̄_* included (Proposition 31.19, Proposition 32.14), have order 2R_base + 16;

(d) let the fixed seminorm of the forcing class of a level β of Theorem 34.9 (in Lemma 32.27,
Lemma 33.16, Lemma 33.29, Definition 36.6, Lemma 36.7 and Step 3 of the proof of
Proposition 36.8), and the seminorm in which the proof of Lemma 35.5 asks R_j → 0, be taken at the
regularity ρ at which the maps that read the coefficients from the forcing of the step are bounded. Then
ρ ≤ C_lev − 11 + I_lev at the levels, and ρ < T_12 in Steps 4′ and 4; and every condition of Steps 2–4′ of the proofs
of Theorem 34.9 and Proposition 36.8 has order ρ + 14, or ρ + R_base + 16 when it is read at a reference
point (0, p⃗_b) with b ≠ b₀;

(e) hence every condition named in the proof of Lemma 35.5 has order at most

    D_* := T_12 + 14 = 214,558,790,360,104,032,305,147,901,608,827,158 < 2.14559·10³⁵,    (49.52)

so the largest of these orders, d_*, satisfies d_* ≤ D_*, and the order m of the proof of Lemma 38.17
satisfies m + 14 ≤ d_*.

*Proof.* *Three facts.* (F1) Let A be one of the families of Lemma 35.3 (b), its sources and its operators
applied to a fixed section or to a solution, and let β, β′ be backgrounds with ‖β‖_14 and ‖β′‖_14 small. Then for
every k

    ‖(A_β − A_β′)u‖_k ≤ C_k ‖β − β′‖_(k+11) ‖u‖_(k+2),    (49.53)

with C_k depending only on upper bounds for ‖β‖_(k+14) and ‖β′‖_(k+14). Indeed, the proof of Proposition 49.48 writes
A_β = A′_(p⃗) + Σ_(|γ|≤2) Φ_γ(x, p⃗, w)D^γ_b with w = (h̃, D_bh̃, D²_bh̃), h̃ := h + h_tot(p⃗) + h_(b,rem)(q),
‖h̃‖_m ≤ C_m‖β‖_(m+3), A′_(p⃗) with coefficients smooth in (x, p⃗), and Φ_γ smooth with Φ_γ(x, p⃗, 0) = 0. The
coefficients of A′_(p⃗) − A′_(p⃗′) are O(|p⃗ − p⃗′|) with all their derivatives, and Φ_γ(x, p⃗, w) − Φ_γ(x, p⃗′, w′) is
the integral over the segment of ∂_(p⃗)Φ_γ·(p⃗ − p⃗′) + ∂_wΦ_γ·(w − w′). Here ∂_(p⃗)Φ_γ vanishes at w = 0, and ∂_wΦ_γ is
a function smooth in (x, p⃗) plus one vanishing at w = 0; so Lemma 20.6 (2)–(3) with d = 3 bound the difference at
the order j by C_j(‖w − w′‖_j + |p⃗ − p⃗′| + ‖w_s‖_(j+6)(‖w − w′‖_0 + |p⃗ − p⃗′|)), w_s on the segment. The product with
D^γ_bu is bounded by Lemma 20.6 (2), which reads the coefficient at the orders 3 and k + 3. As
‖w − w′‖_j ≤ C_j‖β − β′‖_(j+5), with C_j depending on a bound for ‖q′‖_(𝒬^(j+5)), as h_(b,rem)(q) is linear in q and
smooth in b and h_tot(p⃗) is smooth in p⃗, and ‖w_s‖_j ≤ C_j(‖β‖_(j+5) + ‖β′‖_(j+5)), this gives (49.53).
The weights and the coefficients at the faces are treated as in the proof of Proposition 49.48.

(F2) In each comparison below, a solution u of an earlier entry of Section 35.3 enters only through terms
(A_β − A_β′)u, at a rotating b also through (L_(b₀) − L_b)u, whose coefficients are O(|b − b₀|), and is needed at the
order ρ + 2, ρ the regularity of the seminorm. By the induction in the proof of Theorem 35.7, over the entries of
Section 35.3 in their order and, in Theorem 34.9, over its levels, the solution maps of the earlier entries
are tame with losses at most D. Their forcings are F, which lies in every order, and background sources times
finite-dimensional coordinates, of order-j norm at most C_j(1 + ‖β‖_(j+11)) per unit coordinate (Proposition 49.48). So
‖u‖_(ρ+2) is bounded by the data of the step once ‖β‖_(ρ+13+D) is bounded.

(F3) At b₀ and the background 0, L_(0,0) = L_(b₀) (Lemma 32.9 (a), Lemma 33.16), so the forcing
f′ = G − (L − L_b)u of Step 0 of the proofs of Lemma 32.27, Lemma 33.16 and Lemma 33.29 is G
itself, and the coefficients at (0, 0) are the maps that read them from the forcing, applied to G. With the seminorm at
the regularity ρ of (d), |S^(0,0)_ν(G)| ≤ C‖G‖_ρ.

*(a)* The proof of Theorem 29.17, in (iii), asks ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)) small for the d of Theorem 19.14, with
d + 5 = d_T, through ‖P − P_0‖_((0;d)) ≤ C(|S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳^(d_T))), and (29.17) asks |S| + ‖h‖_(𝒳³) small;
Corollary 29.25 adds |b − b₀|, a component of p⃗. At the backgrounds h̃ of Lemma 35.3 (a),
‖h̃‖_(𝒳^m) ≤ C_m‖β‖_m, and ‖h̃‖_(𝒳^m) ≤ C_m‖β‖_(m+3) at h + h_rem(q) + h_tot(p⃗). So these conditions are smallness of
‖β‖_(d_T+3), and d_T + 3 = 20,183 (Theorem 49.9, Corollary 49.25).

*(b)* *k_1.* The proof of Lemma 31.17 writes Ṡ = Π_bf′, with Π_bf′ the 𝒮_1-component of
L̃_b(0)⁻¹(f̂^♭(0), 0, 0), where f^♭ = f′ − L_bu_I and u_I is the construction of Proposition 29.29 for L_b applied to

### 49.13 The first constants of the linear theory

For the scalar wave operator on five-dimensional Tangherlini of mass 1, Chapter 48 gives explicit
constants: the resolvent cut off to I = {6/5 ≤ r ≤ 4} is bounded for every harmonic and every real 0 < |σ| ≤ 3
(Proposition 48.15, Proposition 48.16) and by 11.477 on 3 ≤ |σ| ≤ 384 (Theorem 48.37), with
the values of Proposition 48.38 at sampled frequencies; there the constant bounding the radial derivative is at
most 283.06 for every l ≥ 1 and 305.31 at l = 0, and 308.46 bounds the radial derivative together with the angular
derivatives weighted by ψ, the weight of Proposition 48.13, which vanishes at the photon sphere (unweighted at
l = 1), summed over the harmonics (Corollary 48.40). The same chapter makes explicit the factor of the
interpolation step of the high-energy inverses (Lemma 48.46: at most 1.002659 at b_0, the final black
hole, where κ_Γ = 2^(−3/2), with h_0 ≤ 1), replaces one of the inverse bounds by a parametrix
(Lemma 48.42), bounds the resolvent of every master operator behind the mode stability of the 1-form wave
operator and of the linearised operator at every harmonic and every real frequency, carried exactly to the
tensor-type and vector-type blocks (Proposition 48.28, Lemma 48.27), and writes out the
scalar-type blocks of the linearised operator at zero energy, with an upper bound for their least singular value that
obstructs a good constant at a weight next to an indicial root (Section 48.18, Lemma 48.53).

How far the upper bound of Theorem 48.37 lies above the norm can be measured from below, since a test function supported
in I is its own resolvent.

**Lemma 49.111** (Lower bounds by test functions.) Let σ be real and nonzero, l ≥ 0, and let
u ≠ 0 be a function of r_*, supported in I, with u and u′ absolutely continuous and u″ ∈ L². Put
F := −u″ + (V_l − σ²)u. Then F ≠ 0, R_l(σ)F = u, and

    ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I‖ ≥ ‖u‖/‖F‖.    (49.55)

*Proof.* F lies in L² and vanishes outside I, V_l being bounded on I. If F were 0, u would solve the homogeneous
equation and vanish on an interval, so u = 0. The function u solves −u″ + (V_l − σ²)u = F and vanishes near −∞ and
near +∞, where it is the zero multiple of u_h and of u_∞; by the uniqueness in Proposition 48.4 (a),
u = R_l(σ)F. As F = χ_IF and u = χ_Iu, ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I F‖ = ‖u‖, which gives (49.55). ∎

**Remark 49.112** (Numerical observation.) Polynomial test functions in the radial variable
on I, of degree up to 159 and vanishing to high order at the ends of I, evaluated in exact rational arithmetic with
the resolvent inverted exactly as in Lemma 49.111, give ‖χ_I R_l(σ) χ_I‖ ≥ 0.450, 0.250, 0.147, 0.0827,
0.0448 and 0.0241 at |σ| = 3, 6, 12, 24, 48 and 96, each at one harmonic; these are about 40 to 46 per cent of the
values of Remark 48.41. With them, the bounds of Proposition 48.38 would lie at most 19.8,
18.8, 40.8, 49.6, 67.5 and 93.5 times above the norm at these frequencies. The test functions are not printed here,
and no proof uses these values.

**Remark 49.113** (Numerical observation.) Three further constants of the linear theory at the
final black hole (mass 1, at rest) were evaluated, from exact identities with bounds in exact rational arithmetic and
certified enclosures, and are not proved in this paper: the zero-energy inverse bound of the scalar model, carried
into the low-energy norm of order 1 and weight −1 on the domain extended through the horizon, with constant 2.81; the
zero-energy inverse bound of the tensor-type blocks of the linearised gauge-fixed operator, at every harmonic and
through the horizon, with constant 3.94; and the data of the trapping estimate at the trapped set {r² = 2, ξ = 0}
(minimal expansion rate ν_min = 4·2^(−1/2), q^Γ = 4, β_Γ = 2), where, for the graded fibre inner products h_Γ(η)
of the trapping estimate of 2L_(b_0), the largest eigenvalue of the relevant symbol is η²(γ_C − 80·2^(1/2))²/(192γ_C)
to leading order in η, matched by enclosures at twelve points (γ_C = 10⁶, 10⁷, 10⁸; η = 10⁻¹, …, 10⁻⁴), so that the
estimate's condition needs η below about 16.48γ_C^(−1/2) and the condition number of h_Γ(η) is η^(−16). No proof uses
them.

**Remark 49.114** (Where explicit evaluation stops.) The values of λ1 and δ are not determined in this
paper; Proposition 49.33 bounds λ1 by δ, δ by a power of 2 that decreases with d, and the modulus at 2δ, and they are
positive by the proof of Theorem 3.9. Explicit values stop first upstream of every constant: the proof fixes the
gauge and damping parameters only below thresholds whose existence it proves (Theorem 38.24), and the cut-offs and
orders of its function spaces only up to admissibility, so explicit constants need those choices made with numbers, which
this chapter does only at a point outside the proved set: Definition 49.1 for the gauge and damping parameters, and
Definition 49.52 and Definition 49.96 for the weights, orders and inner products on which d depends. Among the inputs
that depend on those choices are the gauge reconstruction, the inverse of the absorbed problem in the norms of Chapter 11
(invertible by a Fredholm argument, Lemma 48.48, which gives no bound), and a lower bound, uniform in the
harmonic, for the least singular value of the scalar-type blocks at zero energy (Lemma 48.53 bounds it from
above). Four kinds of argument give a constant without a value: a compact error removed by injectivity, by contradiction
(the low-energy and Fredholm estimates of Chapter 11–Chapter 13 and their analogues later); uniformity in the spectral
parameter and in the black hole parameters near the final one, by sequences and compactness; the trapping estimate, by a
defect-measure argument by contradiction (Chapter 12), with the a priori constants built on it; and finite covers of
compact parameter sets. Bounds obtained from the closed graph, open mapping and uniform boundedness theorems, among them
the tame constants C_k of the membership statements (Lemma 35.2 (f)), also give no value until each is read off
from the explicit estimates behind the statement. The parametrix norms at ι⁺ are not given by the construction of the
parametrix, and the tame constants to the order N_NM, the Nash–Moser thresholds of the exterior and slab problems and the
constants of the gluing are not evaluated. This is a limit of the explicit evaluation, not of Theorem 3.9.

# Part XII. Further results

## 50. Two crossing null dusts

This chapter carries Theorem 3.1 over to two families of waves, one ingoing and one outgoing, whose high-frequency
limit is a solution of the Einstein equations with two crossing radial null dusts. Three things change. The background
is no longer explicit: it is the solution of a characteristic problem with explicit Vaidya data on two null cones, and it
carries a single dust everywhere except on a compact diamond where the two dusts cross (Proposition 50.6).
The approximant carries two phases, and the harmonics that mix them are removed at every order by division by a symbol
that is bounded away from zero, so that there are no small divisors (Lemma 50.14). The uniform estimate
needs one phase shift per family; the two phase shifts are coupled through bounded coefficients, and the coupling enters
at the top order of their second derivatives, which are therefore estimated together (Theorem 50.19). The
data, the spheres' horizon and the mean mass then follow as for one family.

Where an argument of Chapter 4, Chapter 6, Chapter 7 or Chapter 8 carries over word
for word we say so, and we write out what changes.

### 50.1 The data and the theorem

*Notation.* The background g0 of this chapter is a round double-null metric

    g0 = −2 e^(2σ) du dv + R² dΩ₃²,    (50.1)

with σ and R > 0 functions of (u, v) and dΩ₃² the round metric of S³, written in the angles (ϑ, φ1, φ2) of
Section 2.2. Since g0 is invariant under O(4) acting on S³, the point x := R x̂ ∈ R⁴, x̂ ∈ S³, is well defined,
and with a time function τ (fixed in Section 50.2) the pair X = (τ, x) is a chart in which tensors are
arrays of Cartesian components, as in Section 2.2. Two-phase profiles are smooth functions or tensors f(X, θ1, θ2)
on Ω₂ × T², 2π-periodic in each phase variable; we write [f](X) := f(X, v(X)/λ, u(X)/λ) and ⟨f⟩ for the mean over T².
The letter 𝔨, and 𝔧 beside it, is a family index, ranging over {in, out}; θ_in := θ1, θ_out := θ2, ϕ_in := v,
ϕ_out := u, F_𝔨 := ∂_(θ_𝔨) and ℓ_𝔨 := g0⁻¹ dϕ_𝔨. A harmonic e^(i(n1 θ1 + n2 θ2)) with n ≠ 0 is *pure* if n1 n2 = 0
and *mixed* if n1 n2 ≠ 0. The chain rule reads

    ∂_a [f] = λ⁻¹ (∂_a v) [F1 f] + λ⁻¹ (∂_a u) [F2 f] + [∂_a f],    (50.2)

so that, as in Section 2.5, |[f]|_j ≤ C_j sup_(i≤j) |∂^i_(X,θ) f|_(L^∞) in the scaled norms (2.10) and
‖∂^i [f]‖_(L^∞) ≤ C λ^(−i). The conformal factor is σ; the letter s is kept for the contractions s_𝔨(h) := h(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨)
of Section 50.5.

**Definition 50.1** (The two-dust data.) Let l5, μ0 ≥ √72 l5², A > 0, env ∈ C_c^∞([v_start, v_end]),
T > 0 and τ0 with v_start − τ0 > √μ0 + 1 be as in Theorem 3.1, and let q0, δ0 and a = q0 − δ0 be as in
Section 2.3. An outgoing family is given by A₂ > 0 and env₂ ∈ C_c^∞((u1, u2)). Put

    𝒜(v) := (1/3) A² env(v)²,      ℬ(u) := (1/3) A₂² env₂(u)²,      E₂ := (2/9) A₂² ∫ env₂².    (50.3)

The characteristic data of the background are explicit Vaidya data on two null cones, both in the past of Σ_τ0:

- on the ingoing cone 𝒞_in := {v = v0}, v0 < τ0 + a, before the shell: Tangherlini of mass μ0 (the seed) for u ≥ u2;
  across the packet [u1, u2] the outgoing Vaidya metric g = −(1 − m(u)/r²) du² − 2 du dr + r² dΩ₃², u its retarded
  time, with dm/du = −(2/9) A₂² env₂(u)², the mass law (2.14) for the outgoing wave; and Tangherlini of mass
  μ0 + E₂ for u ≤ u1. The packet lies where 𝒞_in is untrapped, r² > m;
- on the outgoing cone 𝒞_out := {u = u0}, u0 < u1, outside the packet: the ingoing Vaidya metric (2.4), v its
  advanced time, with dμ/dv = (2/9) A² env(v)² and μ = μ0 + E₂ before the shell.

On 𝒞_in the parameter u is the retarded time on {u ≤ u2}, continued smoothly and increasing inward, and affine on
{u ≥ u2 + 1}; on 𝒞_out the parameter v is the advanced time. These fix the double-null coordinates (u, v) of the
background, each constant on the null cones of the other family. The *ingoing waves* are the wave W_TT of (2.11)
with the phase variable θ1 in place of θ; the *outgoing waves* are the same tensor with A₂, env₂(u) and θ2 in place of
A, env(v) and θ. Both are written in the chart X, where |x| = R.

The outgoing waves are posed on Σ_τ0, not at past null infinity: traced to the past, their rays run inward, toward the
seed's past horizon.

The background, its domain Ω₂, the region D_T, the slice Σ_τ0 and the number ε1 are those of
Section 50.2 (Proposition 50.6, Lemma 50.8). The trace of the packet on Σ_τ0 is
the shell of the points of Σ_τ0 with u1 ≤ u ≤ u2; it is {r1 ≤ R ≤ r2} for numbers r1 < r2 (Proposition 50.6
(a)).

**Theorem 50.2** (Two crossing dusts.) Let the data be those of Definition 50.1, with the packet's
trace on Σ_τ0 placed between the seed's horizon and the shell, √μ0 < r1 < r2 < v_start − τ0, and the outer cone 𝒞_out
chosen as in Lemma 50.8, so that it meets {τ ≥ τ0} only where R > b(τ). Let g0 be the two-dust background
on the domain Ω₂ (Section 50.2). Fix K ≥ 6. There are λ0 > 0 and C, depending on the data, T, τ0, K and
a, and not on λ, such that for every λ ∈ (0, λ0] there is a smooth Lorentzian metric g_λ on Ω₂ ⊃ D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0},
invariant under the T² action and both reflections, with:

1. *Vacuum.* Ric(g_λ) = 0 on Ω₂.
2. *Data.* On Σ_τ0 the Cauchy data of g_λ satisfy the vacuum constraints exactly, equal the seed's on R < r1, and
   differ from those of the two-phase approximant g_app of Theorem 50.18, with N = K + 3 stages, by
   O(λ^K) in the norm Data of item 2 of Theorem 3.1.
3. *The remainder.* g_λ = g_app + w with |w| ≤ C λ^(K−3) and |∂w| ≤ C λ^(K−4) on Ω₂.
4. *Convergence.* |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ, |∂g_λ| ≤ C, and ∂g_λ − ∂g0 = dv ⊗ [F1 g1] + du ⊗ [F2 g1] + O(λ), so ∂g_λ → ∂g0
   weakly in L²(Ω₂), and not strongly wherever env or env₂ is nonzero. The limit is the two-null-dust background:

       Ric(g0) = (𝒜(v)/R³) dv ⊗ dv + (ℬ(u)/R³) du ⊗ du,    (50.4)

   the two families' Isaacson fluxes (50.3).
5. *Gauge and uniqueness.* D(g_λ) = 0 on Ω₂ (the gauge of Section 2.4, relative to the two-dust g0), and g_λ is the
   only C² solution g of Ric^H(g) = 0 on Ω₂ with the data of g_λ on Σ_τ0 and |g − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω₂.
6. *The spheres' horizon.* For a column (v and x̂ fixed, R varying, within D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}) let R_H(v) be the zero on
   the column of the outgoing expansion of the round spheres of g0, the radius at which R² = μ. There are λ_H ∈ (0, λ0]
   and C, δ1, δ2 > 0 such that for λ ≤ λ_H: on every column the outgoing expansion of the spheres S_(v,R) for g_λ has
   at most one zero, positive above it and negative below it; if μ0 > √72 l5², on every column with R_H(v) ≤ v − τ0 −
   δ1 it has exactly one, within C λ of R_H(v), the spheres with R ≤ R_H(v) − C λ being trapped and those with
   R ≥ R_H(v) + C λ untrapped; if μ0 = √72 l5², the same holds on the columns with R_H(v)² ≥ μ0 + δ2 and R_H(v) ≤ v −
   τ0 − δ1 (Proposition 50.27). No condition on where the outgoing packet lies is needed beyond those above.
7. *Mean mass.* For every sphere S_(v,R) in D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} at which neither family oscillates (v ∉ (v_start, v_end)
   and u ∉ (u1, u2)), its Hawking mass (3.2) satisfies |M[S](g_λ) − μ(S)| ≤ C λ², μ(S) the background's
   mass function there; elsewhere |M[S](g_λ) − μ(S)| ≤ C λ (Proposition 50.29).

The theorem is the conjunction of the background on the whole domain (Proposition 50.6,
Lemma 50.8), the approximant (Theorem 50.18), the uniform estimate
(Theorem 50.19), the data (Theorem 50.24), and Proposition 50.27 and
Proposition 50.29; it is assembled in Section 50.8.

**Remark 50.3** (Other placements of the packet.) The theorem does not treat data whose packet lies
outside the shell on Σ_τ0, for then the two families do not cross in the future of Σ_τ0, nor data whose packet lies
inside the seed's horizon: there the packet is trapped on 𝒞_in and the mass function increases inward across it, so
that the argument for the lower bound μ ≥ μ0 of Proposition 50.6 (b), on which the inner boundary of the
domain rests, does not apply; that case is not examined here.

### 50.2 The two-dust background

In this section g0 is a round double-null metric (50.1) on a region of the (u, v)-plane, and 𝒜(v),
ℬ(u) ≥ 0. The *two-null-dust equations* are (50.4), Ric(g0) = (𝒜/R³) dv ⊗ dv + (ℬ/R³) du ⊗ du: the right
side is the stress of two radial null dusts, one along ℓ_in = g0⁻¹ dv and one along ℓ_out = g0⁻¹ du, each trace-free
because dv and du are null. We time-orient g0 so that u and v increase to the future; the causal past of a point p in
a rectangle of the (u, v)-plane is J⁻(p) := {u ≤ u(p), v ≤ v(p)} there.

**Lemma 50.4** (The equations.) For a round double-null metric, with γ̂ the round metric of S³ and
A, B angular indices, the nonzero components of the Ricci tensor are

    Ric_uu = −(3/R)(R_uu − 2σ_u R_u),      Ric_vv = −(3/R)(R_vv − 2σ_v R_v),      Ric_uv = −2σ_uv − 3 R_uv/R,
    Ric_AB = 2 e^(−2σ) (R R_uv + e^(2σ) + 2 R_u R_v) γ̂_AB.

Hence g0 solves the two-null-dust equations exactly when the evolution equations

    R R_uv = −(e^(2σ) + 2 R_u R_v),      σ_uv = 3 (e^(2σ) + 2 R_u R_v)/(2R²)    (50.5)

and the two constraints

    C_u := R_uu − 2σ_u R_u + ℬ/(3R²) = 0,      C_v := R_vv − 2σ_v R_v + 𝒜/(3R²) = 0    (50.6)

hold. Modulo (50.5), ∂_v(R² C_u) = (1/3) ∂_v ℬ = 0 and ∂_u(R² C_v) = (1/3) ∂_u 𝒜 = 0. So data with
C_v = 0 on a cone {u = u0} and C_u = 0 on a cone {v = v0}, evolved by (50.5), give a solution of the
two-null-dust equations.

*Proof.* Write g0 = h + R² γ̂ with h := −2e^(2σ) du dv, so that h^(uv) = −e^(−2σ). The nonzero Christoffel symbols of
h are Γ^u_uu = 2σ_u and Γ^v_vv = 2σ_v; those of g0 are these, Γ^a_AB = −R ∇^a R γ̂_AB for a ∈ {u, v} (∇ the connection
of h), Γ^A_aB = (∂_a R/R) δ^A_B, and those of γ̂. With R_bd = ∂_cΓ^c_bd − ∂_dΓ^c_bc + Γ^c_ceΓ^e_bd − Γ^c_deΓ^e_bc, as
in the proof of Lemma 2.1, the trace Γ^A_bA = 3 ∂_b R/R contributes −∂_a(3 ∂_b R/R) + 3 Γ^c_ab ∂_c R/R −
Σ_(A,B) Γ^A_aB Γ^B_bA = −(3/R) ∇_a∇_b R to Ric_ab; the components Ric_aA vanish, the reflections of S³ that fix a
point being isometries; and the angular components are Ric_AB = (2 − R □_h R − 2 |dR|²_h) γ̂_AB, the 2 being the Ricci
curvature of the unit three-sphere. For h, ∇_u∇_u R = R_uu − 2σ_u R_u, ∇_v∇_v R = R_vv − 2σ_v R_v, ∇_u∇_v R = R_uv,
Ric[h]_uu = Ric[h]_vv = 0, Ric[h]_uv = −∂_v Γ^u_uu = −2σ_uv, □_h R = −2e^(−2σ) R_uv and |dR|²_h = −2e^(−2σ) R_u R_v.
This gives the four components. The angular equation is the first of (50.5); with it, Ric_uv = 0 is
σ_uv = −3 R_uv/(2R), the second; Ric_uu = ℬ/R³ is C_u = 0, and Ric_vv = 𝒜/R³ is C_v = 0.

For the propagation, put Y := R² (R_uu − 2σ_u R_u), so that R² C_u = Y + ℬ/3. Differentiating the first equation of
(50.5) in u gives R R_uuv = −2σ_u e^(2σ) − 2 R_uu R_v − 3 R_u R_uv, and σ_uv = −3 R_uv/(2R). Hence

    ∂_v Y = 2R R_v (R_uu − 2σ_u R_u) + R (R R_uuv) − 2R² σ_uv R_u − 2R² σ_u R_uv
          = −2R σ_u (e^(2σ) + 2 R_u R_v + R R_uv) = 0,

and ∂_v(R² C_u) = ∂_v ℬ/3 = 0, since ℬ depends on u alone. The identity for C_v is the same with u and v exchanged.
So R² C_u is constant along each line of constant u and vanishes where that line meets {v = v0}; likewise C_v. ∎

**Lemma 50.5** (Identities.) Let g0 solve the two-null-dust equations and put

    μ := R² (1 + 2 e^(−2σ) R_u R_v),      f := 1 − μ/R² = −2 e^(−2σ) R_u R_v = g0⁻¹(dR, dR),    (50.7)

the mass function. Then:

(i) μ_u = −(2/3) ℬ e^(−2σ) R_v and μ_v = −(2/3) 𝒜 e^(−2σ) R_u;
(ii) R_uv = −e^(2σ) μ/R³, σ_uv = (3/2) e^(2σ) μ/R⁴ and (R³)_uv = −3 R e^(2σ);
(iii) μ_uv = (2/9) 𝒜ℬ e^(−2σ)/R²;
(iv) (e^(−2σ) R_u)_u = −e^(−2σ) ℬ/(3R²) and (e^(−2σ) R_v)_v = −e^(−2σ) 𝒜/(3R²);
(v) where R_u < 0, (v̂, R) are coordinates for every increasing function v̂ of v, and with e^ψ := −e^(2σ)/(R_u v̂′),

        g0 = −e^(2ψ) f dv̂² + 2 e^ψ dv̂ dR + R² dΩ₃²,      ψ_u = ℬ/(3R² R_u),
        g0^(v̂v̂) = 0,      g0^(v̂R) = e^(−ψ),      g0^(RR) = f;    (50.8)
    where R_v > 0, for every increasing function ũ of u, with e^ψ̃ := e^(2σ)/(R_v ũ′), g0 = −e^(2ψ̃) f dũ² − 2 e^ψ̃ dũ dR
    + R² dΩ₃² and ψ̃_v = 𝒜/(3R² R_v);
(vi) the Kretschmann scalar is

        𝒦 = 72 μ²/R⁸ + (8/3) e^(−4σ) 𝒜ℬ/R⁶.    (50.9)

*Proof.* (i) Differentiating, μ_u = 2R R_u + 2e^(−2σ)(2R R_u² R_v − 2R² σ_u R_u R_v + R² R_uu R_v + R² R_u R_uv). By the
first equation of (50.5), R² R_u R_uv = −R R_u (e^(2σ) + 2 R_u R_v), so μ_u = 2e^(−2σ) R² R_v (R_uu −
2σ_u R_u), which is −(2/3) ℬ e^(−2σ) R_v by C_u = 0. The second identity is the same with u and v exchanged.
(ii) By (50.7), e^(2σ) + 2 R_u R_v = e^(2σ) μ/R², which turns (50.5) into the first two
identities; and (R³)_uv = 3R (R R_uv + 2 R_u R_v) = −3R e^(2σ).
(iv) is e^(−2σ) C_u = 0 and e^(−2σ) C_v = 0. (iii) Differentiate μ_v = −(2/3) 𝒜 e^(−2σ) R_u in u and use (iv).
(v) With dv = dv̂/v̂′ and du = (dR − R_v dv)/R_u,

    −2 e^(2σ) du dv = −(2 e^(2σ)/(R_u v̂′)) dR dv̂ + (2 e^(2σ) R_v/(R_u v̂′²)) dv̂² = 2 e^ψ dv̂ dR − e^(2ψ) f dv̂²,

because e^(2ψ) f = (e^(4σ)/(R_u² v̂′²))(−2e^(−2σ) R_u R_v). The (v̂, R) block [[−e^(2ψ) f, e^ψ], [e^ψ, 0]] has the
inverse [[0, e^(−ψ)], [e^(−ψ), f]]. Since v̂′ depends on v alone, ψ_u = 2σ_u − R_uu/R_u = −(R_uu − 2σ_u R_u)/R_u =
ℬ/(3R² R_u) by C_u = 0. The second form follows in the same way from du = dũ/ũ′ and dv = (dR − R_u du)/R_v, and
ψ̃_v = 2σ_v − R_vv/R_v = 𝒜/(3R² R_v) by C_v = 0.
(vi) For the warped product g0 = h + R² γ̂ the nonzero components of the Riemann tensor are, up to its symmetries,
R_abcd = K_h (h_ac h_bd − h_ad h_bc), R_aAbB = −R ∇_a∇_b R γ̂_AB and R_ABCD = R² (1 − |dR|²_h)(γ̂_AC γ̂_BD − γ̂_AD
γ̂_BC), with K_h the Gauss curvature of h; they follow from the Christoffel symbols of the proof of
Lemma 50.4 as in the proof of Lemma 2.4. Hence, counting the four orderings of the mixed
components and using γ̂^(AB) γ̂_AB = 3,

    𝒦 = 4 K_h² + 12 |∇∇R|²_h/R² + 12 (1 − |dR|²_h)²/R⁴.

Here Ric[h]_uv = K_h h_uv gives K_h = 2e^(−2σ) σ_uv = 3μ/R⁴ by (ii), 1 − |dR|²_h = μ/R², and, with ∇_u∇_u R = −ℬ/(3R²),
∇_v∇_v R = −𝒜/(3R²) and ∇_u∇_v R = −e^(2σ) μ/R³,

    |∇∇R|²_h = 2 (h^(uv))² ((∇_u∇_v R)² + ∇_u∇_u R ∇_v∇_v R) = 2 e^(−4σ) (e^(4σ) μ²/R⁶ + 𝒜ℬ/(9R⁴)).

So 𝒦 = 36 μ²/R⁸ + 24 μ²/R⁸ + (8/3) e^(−4σ) 𝒜ℬ/R⁶ + 12 μ²/R⁸. ∎

At ℬ = 0 these are the identities of Proposition 2.5: with v̂ = v and ψ = 0 the mass law μ_v = (2/3) 𝒜, and the
Kretschmann scalar 72 μ²/R⁸. One null dust has Ric_ab Ric^ab = 0; two crossing ones do not, and their term in 𝒦 is
nonnegative because 𝒜ℬ ≥ 0.

**Proposition 50.6** (The background on the whole domain.) Let the data be those of
Definition 50.1, fix V1 > 2(v_end + T) + 1 − τ0, and let Q := [u0, ∞) × [v0, V1] in the double-null coordinates
of Definition 50.1. There is a past set 𝒟 ⊂ Q, the development of the data, on which the characteristic problem
has exactly one smooth solution g0 of the two-null-dust equations, and:

(a) *Structure.* Where ℬ = 0 the background is an ingoing Vaidya metric, after reparametrising v, and where 𝒜 = 0 and
R_v > 0 an outgoing Vaidya metric, after reparametrising u. The two dusts cross only on the compact crossing diamond
Q× := [u1, u2] × [v_start, v_end]: off Q× one of 𝒜, ℬ vanishes. Off Q× the background is explicit from the data only
in {u ≤ u1}, where it is the ingoing Vaidya metric of the data on 𝒞_out with v its advanced time, and in
{v ≤ v_start}, where it is the outgoing Vaidya metric of the data on 𝒞_in; in {u ≥ u2} it is the ingoing
Vaidya metric with the mass function μ(u2, ·), and in {v ≥ v_end} its mass function is μ(·, v_end), an outgoing Vaidya
metric where R_v > 0; both mass functions are read from the solution on the edges of the diamond. On the slice Σ_τ0 of
Lemma 50.8 the Cauchy data are the seed's for R < r1, outgoing Vaidya on the packet r1 ≤ R ≤ r2,
Tangherlini of mass μ0 + E₂ between the packet and the shell, and, outside, those of the shell of Theorem 3.1 on a
Tangherlini metric of mass μ0 + E₂.

(b) *The mass bound.* μ ≥ μ0 on 𝒟.

(c) *The inner sphere.* R_u < 0 on 𝒟. On {R = a}, μ > a², so {R = a} is trapped (R_u, R_v < 0) and spacelike,
g0⁻¹(dR, dR) = 1 − μ/a² < 0, and R decreases along future causal curves crossing it. If R(p) ≥ a, then R ≥ min(R(p),
√μ0) ≥ a on J⁻(p).

(d) *Existence.* The set G := {p ∈ 𝒟 : R ≥ a on J⁻(p)} is closed in Q and its boundary in Q lies in {R = a}; the
background is smooth on G.

*Proof.* (c), first part. The corner (u0, v0) lies on the part of 𝒞_in where the data are Tangherlini of mass μ0 + E₂
and the cone is untrapped, and u increases inward along 𝒞_in, so R_u(u0, v0) < 0. Along 𝒞_out, μ ≥ μ0 + E₂ > 0 (the
data's mass function is nondecreasing), so ∂_v R_u = R_uv = −e^(2σ) μ/R³ < 0 there by Lemma 50.5 (ii),
and R_u(u0, ·) < 0. By Lemma 50.5 (iv), ∂_u(e^(−2σ) R_u) ≤ 0, so e^(−2σ) R_u ≤ e^(−2σ(u0, v)) R_u(u0,
v) < 0 wherever the solution exists.

(b) By Lemma 50.5 (iii), μ_uv ≥ 0, so μ(u, v) ≥ μ(u, v0) + μ(u0, v) − μ(u0, v0). The difference
μ(u0, v) − μ(u0, v0) = ∫ μ_v(u0, ·) is nonnegative, because μ_v = −(2/3) 𝒜 e^(−2σ) R_u ≥ 0 by (i) and R_u < 0. On 𝒞_in,
μ(·, v0) = m decreases from μ0 + E₂ to μ0 across the untrapped packet and equals μ0 inward of it. Hence μ ≥ μ0.

(c), the rest. Since a < q0 ≤ √μ0 (Section 2.3, μ0 ≥ √72 l5²), μ ≥ μ0 > a² on {R = a}, so f < 0 there, and as
f = −2e^(−2σ) R_u R_v with R_u < 0, also R_v < 0: both null expansions of the round spheres are negative, and dR is
timelike. Future causal vectors are combinations of ∂_u, ∂_v with nonnegative coefficients plus vectors tangent to the
spheres, so dR is negative on them. For the last claim let q = (u_q, v_q) ∈ J⁻(p). Since R_u < 0, R(q) ≥ R(u_p, v_q),
so it suffices to bound R(u_p, ·) on [v0, v_p]. Suppose R(u_p, v′) < min(R(p), √μ0) for some v′ < v_p. There R² < μ0 ≤
μ, so R_v < 0 as above. Let v″ be the supremum of the v ∈ [v′, v_p] such that R(u_p, ·) < min(R(p), √μ0) on [v′, v];
on [v′, v″] R(u_p, ·) decreases, so R(u_p, v″) ≤ R(u_p, v′) < min(R(p), √μ0), and continuity forces v″ = v_p, so that
R(p) < min(R(p), √μ0), a contradiction.

(a) By Lemma 50.5 (i) and (v), μ_u = 0 and ψ_u = 0 where ℬ = 0, so on {u ≤ u1} and on {u ≥ u2} μ and
ψ do not depend on u, and with dṽ := e^ψ dv̂ the form (50.8) becomes −f dṽ² + 2 dṽ dR +
R² dΩ₃², f = 1 − μ(ṽ)/R²: an ingoing Vaidya metric. On 𝒞_out the data are those of the ingoing Vaidya metric in its
advanced time v, for which e^ψ = 1 when v̂ = v, by comparison of (50.8) with (2.4); so ψ = 0 on
𝒞_out with v̂ = v, and on {u ≤ u1} the background is that ingoing Vaidya metric, with the mass function of the data. On
{u ≥ u2} it is ingoing Vaidya with ψ(u2, ·) and μ(u2, ·). The statements where 𝒜 = 0 and R_v > 0 follow in the same
way from the second form of (v), with ψ̃ = 0 on 𝒞_in ∩ {u ≤ u2} in the retarded time of the data. On {u ≤ u2,
v ≤ v_start}, R_v > 0. Indeed 𝒞_in ∩ {u ≤ u2} is untrapped (r² > m on the packet, and outward of it r is larger and m
constant), so f > 0 there, and with R_u < 0 this gives R_v > 0; and where 𝒜 = 0, C_v = 0 reads R_vv = 2σ_v R_v, so
that R_v(u, v) = R_v(u, v0) e^(2σ(u, v) − 2σ(u, v0)) keeps its sign. Where 𝒜 = ℬ = 0 the background is Tangherlini.
𝒜ℬ ≠ 0 only on Q×, which is compact.

On Σ_τ0, u is strictly decreasing outward: in the chart of Lemma 50.8, where v̂ = v and e^ψ = −e^(2σ)/R_u,
R_v = e^ψ f/2 ≤ 1/2, since f ≤ 1 and e^ψ ≤ 1 (ψ = 0 on 𝒞_out and ψ_u = ℬ/(3R² R_u) ≤ 0), so du(∂_R|_τ) =
(1 − R_v)/R_u < 0. Hence the points of Σ_τ0 with u ∈
[u1, u2] form a shell r1 ≤ R ≤ r2, with u > u2 inside it and u < u1 outside. The points of Σ_τ0 with R < v_start − τ0
have v = τ0 + R < v_start, where the background is the outgoing Vaidya metric of the data on 𝒞_in: Tangherlini of mass
μ0 for u > u2, outgoing Vaidya on the packet, Tangherlini of mass μ0 + E₂ for u < u1. Since r2 < v_start − τ0, the
points with R ≥ v_start − τ0 have u < u1, where the background is the ingoing Vaidya metric of the data on 𝒞_out, the
shell of Theorem 3.1 on a Tangherlini metric of mass μ0 + E₂.

(d) *The integral equations.* Put U := (R, σ, P, Q̄), 𝔉(U) := −(e^(2σ) + 2 P Q̄)/R, ℌ(U) := 3 (e^(2σ) + 2 P Q̄)/(2R²),
and for a function z on Q, D[z](u, v) := z(u0, v) + z(u, v0) − z(u0, v0). Consider

    P(u, v) = P(u, v0) + ∫_(v0)^v 𝔉(U)(u, v′) dv′,        Q̄(u, v) = Q̄(u0, v) + ∫_(u0)^u 𝔉(U)(u′, v) du′,
    R(u, v) = R(u0, v) + ∫_(u0)^u P(u′, v) du′,          σ(u, v) = D[σ](u, v) + ∫_(u0)^u ∫_(v0)^v ℌ(U),
    (50.10)

with the data P(·, v0) = ∂_u R(·, v0), Q̄(u0, ·) = ∂_v R(u0, ·), R(u0, ·) and σ on both cones, which satisfy C_u = 0 on
𝒞_in and C_v = 0 on 𝒞_out. A continuous solution solves (50.5): R_u = P by the third equation;
differentiating it in v, R_v(u, v) = ∂_v R(u0, v) + ∫ ∂_v P du′ = Q̄(u0, v) + ∫ 𝔉 du′ = Q̄(u, v); so R_uv = P_v = 𝔉, and
σ_uv = ℌ. The constraints (50.6) then hold by Lemma 50.4, propagated from the cones.

*A priori bounds.* Let S ⊂ Q be a past set on which a solution exists with R ≥ a′ > 0. With R_max := max_v R(u0, v)
and the identities of Lemma 50.5, at every point of S: (i) R³ = D[R³] − 3 ∫∫ R e^(2σ), and D[R³] ≤
R(u0, v)³ because R decreases along 𝒞_in, so R ≤ R_max and 3 ∫∫ R e^(2σ) ≤ R_max³ over every rectangle J⁻(p);
(ii) μ ≥ μ0 by (b); (iii) σ_uv ≥ 0, so σ ≥ D[σ] ≥ −S0, S0 := −min D[σ]; and on the part of S where u ≤ u_*, for a
number u_*: (iv) μ_uv ≤ (2/9) max(𝒜ℬ) e^(2S0)/a′², so μ ≤ M⁺ := max D[μ] + (2/9) max(𝒜ℬ) e^(2S0) (u_* − u0)(V1 − v0)/a′²;
(v) σ_uv = (3/2) e^(2σ) μ/R⁴ ≤ (3/2)(M⁺/a′⁵) R e^(2σ), so σ ≤ max D[σ] + (M⁺/(2a′⁵)) R_max³; (vi) |R_uv| = e^(2σ) μ/R³
is then bounded, and so are P and Q̄, by integrating R_uv from the cones. So |U| ≤ C_U there, with C_U depending on the
data, a′ and u_* only; each bound comes from the data, a′ and the bounds before it.

*Boundedness of the domain.* On 𝒞_in ∩ {u ≥ u2 + 1}, ℬ = 0 and u is affine, so σ_u = 0 there and C_u = 0 gives R_uu =
0: R_u(·, v0) is constant there, and R_u(·, v0) < 0 on the compact [u2, u2 + 1]; so R_u(·, v0) ≤ c0 < 0 on {u ≥ u2}.
R_uv = −e^(2σ) μ/R³ < 0 gives R_u ≤ c0 on {u ≥ u2} wherever the solution exists, so R ≤ R_max + c0 (u − u2) there, and
the set where R ≥ a′ lies in {u ≤ u_*(a′)}, u_*(a′) := u2 + (R_max − a′)/|c0|, for every a′ > 0.

*Existence.* Fix a′ ∈ (0, a), let C_U be the bound above for this a′ and u_* = u_*(a′), and let 𝔉♯, ℌ♯ be smooth,
globally Lipschitz in U, and equal to 𝔉, ℌ on {|U| ≤ 2C_U, R ≥ a′}. The map defined by the right sides of
(50.10) with 𝔉♯, ℌ♯ is a contraction in the norm sup_Q e^(−γ (u − u0 + v − v0)) |U| for γ large: each
single integral divides the Lipschitz constant by γ and the double one by γ², on the unbounded u-interval as well. So
it has one continuous fixed point Ũ on Q. Let Q_(a′) := {p ∈ Q : R̃ > a′ on J⁻(p)}, R̃ the first component of Ũ.
(1) Ũ solves the true equations on Q_(a′). For p ∈ Q_(a′), suppose |Ũ| ≥ 2C_U somewhere on the compact J⁻(p), and let q
be such a point with u + v least. On J⁻(q) ∖ {q}, |Ũ| < 2C_U and R̃ > a′, so Ũ solves the true equations there, the a
priori bounds give |Ũ| ≤ C_U there and, by continuity, at q: a contradiction. (2) Q_(a′) is a past set, open in Q, the
least of R̃ over J⁻(p) being continuous in p; the development 𝒟 := ∪_(a″>0) Q_(a″) is a past set carrying one smooth
solution, since two truncations agree where both solve the true equations, by the contraction. (3) For p ∈ 𝒟 with R(p) ≥
a, (c) applies on J⁻(p) ⊂ 𝒟 and gives R ≥ min(R(p), √μ0) ≥ a > a′ there, so p ∈ Q_(a′). (4) So G ⊂ Q_(a′), and G is
closed in Q, as G ⊂ Q_(a′) and R̃ is continuous there. At p ∈ ∂G the least of R over J⁻(p) is a, since otherwise a
neighbourhood of p would lie in G; so (c) at p gives min(R(p), √μ0) ≤ a < √μ0, that is R(p) = a: ∂G ⊂ {R = a}.

*Regularity.* Let U be the continuous solution on a past set. From (50.10), R_u = P and R_v = Q̄, P_v =
𝔉(U), Q̄_u = 𝔉(U), and σ_u, σ_v are continuous. For ∂_u P, the difference quotients δ_h P solve δ_h P(u, v) = δ_h P(u,
v0) + ∫_(v0)^v (a_h · δ_h(R, σ, Q̄) + b_h δ_h P) dv′, where a_h, b_h are the mean values of ∇𝔉 on the segments,
continuous and converging uniformly, and δ_h(R, σ, Q̄) → (P, σ_u, 𝔉) uniformly; Gronwall's lemma in v makes δ_h P
uniformly Cauchy, so ∂_u P exists and is continuous, and likewise ∂_v Q̄. So U ∈ C¹. The k-th derivatives solve linear
Volterra equations of the same form, with coefficients built from lower derivatives, so U ∈ C^∞ by induction, the data
being smooth. ∎

The double-null coordinates of Definition 50.1 are one normalisation among many. Data posed in another one define
the same background.

**Lemma 50.7** (Reparametrising the cones.) Let g0 be a round double-null metric
(50.1) on a region of the (u, v)-plane, and let ũ(u) and ṽ(v) be smooth with ũ′ > 0 and ṽ′ > 0. Then

    g0 = −2 e^(2σ̃) dũ dṽ + R² dΩ₃²,      σ̃ := σ − ½ ln(ũ′ ṽ′),

and g0 solves the two-null-dust equations with the fluxes 𝒜(v), ℬ(u) exactly when it solves them in the coordinates
(ũ, ṽ) with the fluxes 𝒜̃ := 𝒜/ṽ′² and ℬ̃ := ℬ/ũ′², read as functions of ṽ and of ũ. The constraints
(50.6) in (ũ, ṽ) are C̃_ũ = C_u/ũ′² and C̃_ṽ = C_v/ṽ′², and R, μ, f, e^(−4σ) 𝒜ℬ and, for a fixed
increasing function v̂ of v, ψ are the same functions in both coordinates. Moreover:

(a) the advanced time v of Definition 50.1 is, up to an additive constant, the increasing function v̂ of the
parameter of 𝒞_out with ψ = 0 on 𝒞_out, and the retarded time on 𝒞_in ∩ {u ≤ u2} is, up to an additive constant, the
increasing function of the parameter of 𝒞_in for which ψ̃ = 0 there, ψ̃ as in Lemma 50.5 (v);

(b) let characteristic data on 𝒞_in and 𝒞_out be given in parameters ũ, ṽ of the cones (R and σ̃ on both cones, 𝒜̃ and
ℬ̃) which, rewritten by these formulas in the normalisation of Definition 50.1, are the data of
Definition 50.1. Then the background g0 of Proposition 50.6, written in (ũ, ṽ), solves the
characteristic problem posed in (ũ, ṽ) on the development 𝒟, and it is the only solution there. Parts (b)–(d) of
Proposition 50.6 and Lemma 50.8 hold as stated: they concern g0, R, μ, the cones, the advanced
time v and the sets J⁻(p) = {u ≤ u(p), v ≤ v(p)}, none of which depends on the parametrisation, by (a) for v.

*Proof.* As dũ = ũ′ du and dṽ = ṽ′ dv, −2 e^(2σ̃) dũ dṽ = −2 e^(2σ̃) ũ′ ṽ′ du dv = −2 e^(2σ) du dv. Ric(g0) is a
tensor, and (𝒜/R³) dv ⊗ dv + (ℬ/R³) du ⊗ du = (𝒜̃/R³) dṽ ⊗ dṽ + (ℬ̃/R³) dũ ⊗ dũ. For the constraints, R_ũ = R_u/ũ′,
R_ũũ = R_uu/ũ′² − ũ″ R_u/ũ′³ and σ̃_ũ = σ_u/ũ′ − ũ″/(2ũ′²), so R_ũũ − 2σ̃_ũ R_ũ = (R_uu − 2σ_u R_u)/ũ′², while
ℬ̃/(3R²) = ℬ/(3R² ũ′²); the same calculation in ṽ gives C̃_ṽ. By (50.7), f = g0⁻¹(dR, dR) and
μ = R²(1 − f); by (50.8), e^ψ = g0(∂_v̂, ∂_R) in the coordinates (v̂, R, ϑ, φ1, φ2); these depend only on
g0, R and v̂. Finally e^(−4σ̃) 𝒜̃ℬ̃ = e^(−4σ) (ũ′ṽ′)² 𝒜ℬ/(ũ′ṽ′)².

(a) By the proof of Proposition 50.6 (a), ψ = 0 on 𝒞_out when v̂ is the advanced time, and ψ̃ = 0 on
𝒞_in ∩ {u ≤ u2} when the outgoing coordinate is the retarded time. Conversely, ψ = 0 on 𝒞_out means v̂′ = −e^(2σ)/R_u
along 𝒞_out, by the definition of ψ in Lemma 50.5 (v), which fixes v̂ up to a constant; likewise
ψ̃ = 0 fixes the outgoing coordinate on 𝒞_in ∩ {u ≤ u2} up to a constant.

(b) By the first part, g0 written in (ũ, ṽ) solves the two-null-dust equations with 𝒜̃, ℬ̃ and takes the given data.
Conversely, a solution of the problem posed in (ũ, ṽ) on 𝒟, written in the coordinates of
Definition 50.1, solves the problem of Proposition 50.6 there, by the first part, and so equals g0
by the uniqueness there. The rest is read off. ∎

**Lemma 50.8** (The domain.) Use the double-null coordinates of Definition 50.1, so that v̂ = v
in (50.8) and e^ψ = −e^(2σ)/R_u, and on G the chart X = (τ, x), τ := v − R, x := R x̂. Let r_q(m) :=
(√72 m l5²)^(1/4), V := v_end + T, and

    D_T := {p ∈ G : v ≤ V, R ≥ r_q(μ)},      r_q^♭(v) := min {r_q(μ(p)) : p ∈ D_T, v(p) = v},
    τ_end := max_(v ≤ V) (v − r_q^♭(v)),      b(τ) := V + 1 − τ + (τ_end − τ),
    Ω₂ := {p ∈ G : τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ_end, v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ V + 1},      Σ_τ := Ω₂ ∩ {τ},    (50.11)

the forms of (2.7) and (2.8) with the mass function at the point. The outer cone can be chosen so that
𝒞_out ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} ⊂ {R > b(τ)}, and we choose it so. Then Σ_τ = A(τ) := {a ≤ |x| ≤ b(τ)}, and:

(a) g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = 1 − μ/R² − 2e^(−ψ) ≤ −1 − μ/R²: each Σ_τ is spacelike;
(b) on {R = a}, g0⁻¹(dR, dR) = 1 − μ/a² < 0 and g0⁻¹(dR, dτ) = e^(−ψ) − 1 + μ/a² > 0;
(c) g0⁻¹(d(v + τ), d(v + τ)) = 1 − μ/R² − 4e^(−ψ) ≤ −3 − μ/R², and g0⁻¹(dv, dτ) = −e^(−ψ) < 0;
(d) the ingoing generators are the lines {v, x̂ = const}, integral curves of ℓ_in = −e^(−ψ) L0, L0 := ∂_τ − x̂·∂_x;
followed to the past they stay in Ω₂ and meet Σ_τ0; every past causal curve from a point of Ω₂ meets Σ_τ0 inside Ω₂,
and both generators ℓ_in and ℓ_out are transverse to every Σ_τ;
(e) there is ε1 with 0 < ε1 < s0, s0 the least over Ω₂ of the least absolute eigenvalue of g0, such that every
Lorentzian g with |g − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω₂ is time-oriented by dτ, J⁻(p; g) ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} ⊂ Ω₂ for every p ∈ Ω₂, and Σ_τ and
the two lateral boundaries stay spacelike for g; and every symmetric g̃ with |g̃ − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω₂ is Lorentzian
with |g̃⁻¹| ≤ (s0 − ε1)⁻¹;
(f) b(τ) − a ≥ 1 + δ0, b ≤ b(τ0), D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} ⊂ Ω₂, and D_T contains {p ∈ G : v ≤ V, 𝒦 ≤ l5⁻⁴}.

From here on ε1 is one fixed number as in (e).

*Proof.* The choice of the cone. In {u ≤ u1} the background is the ingoing Vaidya metric of the data on 𝒞_out
(Proposition 50.6 (a)), so replacing u0 by a smaller value, with the data of the same Vaidya metric on the
new cone and of Tangherlini of mass μ0 + E₂ on the added part of 𝒞_in, changes the background nowhere in {u ≥ u0}, by
the uniqueness in Proposition 50.6. Along an outgoing null ray of that Vaidya metric on which R² > μ_end :=
μ0 + E₂ + (2/9) A² ∫ env², the radius increases with τ (its radial speed f/(2 − f) is positive, Section 50.3)
while b decreases. So the condition holds once the cone meets Σ_τ0 at a radius above max(b(τ0), √μ_end).

The slices. By Proposition 50.6 (c), R_u < 0 on G, so (v, R) are coordinates there. ψ = 0 on 𝒞_out
(Proposition 50.6 (a)) and ψ_u = ℬ/(3R² R_u) ≤ 0, so ψ ≤ 0 on G. Along each ingoing ray {v = const}, R
decreases strictly inward from 𝒞_out, the point of the ray on 𝒞_out lies in G, and G is closed with boundary in {R = a};
so the ray lies in G until R = a, and G = {a ≤ R ≤ R(u0, v)} in the coordinates (v, R). On 𝒞_out, ψ = 0, so dR/dv =
R_v = f/2 ≤ 1/2 there, and R(u0, τ + R) − R is strictly decreasing in R. So {τ = const} ∩ G is an interval a ≤ R ≤
R_out(τ), R_out(τ) the radius at which the slice meets 𝒞_out or, if it reaches the edge {v = V1} of Q first, the radius
V1 − τ at which it does. For τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ_end, R_out(τ) > b(τ): in the first case by the choice of the cone, in the second
because b(τ) + τ = V + 1 + τ_end − τ ≤ V + 1 + τ_end − τ0 < 2V + 1 − τ0 < V1, as τ_end ≤ V − q0 (proof of (f) below) and
by the choice of V1 in Proposition 50.6. The third condition of (50.11) is R ≤ b(τ). So Σ_τ =
A(τ).

(a)–(c) are the contractions of the inverse in (50.8) with dτ = dv − dR and d(v + τ) = 2dv − dR, with
e^(−ψ) ≥ 1 and f = 1 − μ/R². As in the proof of Lemma 2.6, dτ is timelike and positive on future causal vectors; at
R = a, dR and dτ are timelike with positive product, so dR is negative on future causal vectors; and dv(Y) = g0(ℓ_in, Y)
≥ 0 for future causal Y, ℓ_in = −e^(−ψ) L0 being past directed, so v + τ increases to the future.

(d) In the chart, ∂_R at fixed v is −∂_τ + x̂·∂_x = −L0, so ℓ_in = g0^(vR) ∂_R = −e^(−ψ) L0. Along −L0, τ decreases, R
increases and v is fixed, so R ≥ a and v + τ − τ_end ≤ V + 1 are kept; the curve reaches τ = τ0 at R = v − τ0, and for p
∈ Ω₂, v(p) − τ0 ≤ V + 1 + τ_end − τ(p) − τ0 ≤ b(τ0). A past causal curve cannot cross {R = a} or {v + τ = const}
outward, by (b) and (c), nor Σ_τ_end; parametrised by τ, it is Lipschitz on the compact Ω₂ (as in the proof of
Lemma 4.9), so it reaches Σ_τ0 inside Ω₂. A null vector is never tangent to a spacelike hypersurface.

(e) The strict inequalities in (a)–(c), and the nondegeneracy of g0, are open conditions in g on the compact set Ω₂;
the proof of Lemma 2.6 (e) applies, and that of Lemma 2.8 for the bound on g̃⁻¹.

(f) By Proposition 50.6 (b), μ ≥ μ0, so r_q(μ) ≥ r_q(μ0) = q0 > a. A point of D_T has v ≤ V, R ≥ q0 and
τ = v − R ≤ v − r_q^♭(v) ≤ τ_end, hence v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ v < V + 1: it lies in Ω₂ if τ ≥ τ0. Further τ_end ≤ V − q0,
so b(τ) − a ≥ b(τ_end) − a = V + 1 − τ_end − a ≥ 1 + q0 − a = 1 + δ0, and b decreases. By (50.9)
and 𝒜ℬ ≥ 0, 𝒦 ≥ 72 μ²/R⁸, so 𝒦 ≤ l5⁻⁴ gives R⁸ ≥ 72 μ² l5⁴, that is R ≥ r_q(μ). ∎

So every part of the boundary of Ω₂ other than Σ_τ0 is spacelike with Ω₂ to its past, and Ω₂ is a domain of
dependence of Σ_τ0, for g0 and for every Lorentzian metric within ε1 of g0. Its slices are the annuli A(τ) of
Section 2.3, with the outer radius b(τ), b′ = −2, and the same bounds. Hence Lemma 5.1, the mollifier 𝒫 of
(5.3) with its properties (M1)–(M6) (Lemma 5.4), and the energy inequality Lemma 5.5 hold on Ω₂
verbatim; the last uses only that Σ_τ, {R = a} and the outer boundary are spacelike with Ω₂ to their past, and (e).

**Remark 50.9** (Numerical observation.) The characteristic problem of Proposition 50.6
was discretised for one choice of data, in the gauge e^(2σ) = 1/2 on both cones: corner mass 1.5 at R = 5, packet ℬ =
1.7 b(u; 5.7, 7.2) on 𝒞_in, shell 𝒜 = 3.6 b(v; 3, 4.5) on 𝒞_out with b a smooth bump, seed mass μ0 = 0.82211 and mass
3.6058 after the shell, on a rectangle that stops at v = 5. At 40, 80 and 160 steps per unit the discrete solutions
showed the structure of (a), the departures from a Vaidya metric off the diamond being 1.8 × 10⁻⁵, 5.2 × 10⁻³, 5.2 ×
10⁻³ and 2.2 × 10⁻⁴ in the four regions at 160 steps, each falling with the resolution; the mass bound (b) up to a
discretisation deficit falling at second order, −4.0 × 10⁻², −9.9 × 10⁻³ and −2.3 × 10⁻³ (with ℬ replaced by −ℬ the
deficit was −0.648 at both resolutions tried); the inner sphere trapped with μ − a² ≥ 0.332; and the diamond at R ≥
2.59, untrapped. On Σ_τ0, τ0 = −a + 0.02, the packet lay at R ∈ [1.861, 3.431], between the seed's horizon 0.907 and
the shell's inner edge 3.825. With T = 1 and δ0 = 0.05, the outgoing ray of {u ≤ u1} from R = 7.505 at v = 0 kept
R − b ≥ 0.9951 on [τ0, τ_end], the least value at τ0, while the cone through R = 5 at v = 0 met Σ_τ0 at R − b = −4.09.
Along the inner edge of the packet, R(u2, v) − √μ(u2, v) ≥ 0.6127 at the three resolutions; with the amplitude of the
shell raised to 16 the edge was trapped, the gap −0.617. For one other choice of the outgoing family's characteristic
data, a discretisation on a rectangle reaching its initial slice showed the constraint residuals converging at second
order away from the steep inner boundary, and the inner boundary trapped. No proof uses these observations.

### 50.3 The phases and the transports

From here on the background is that of Proposition 50.6 on Ω₂, in the double-null coordinates of
Definition 50.1 and the chart X = (τ, x) of Lemma 50.8. The ingoing phase is v, the advanced time
of the data on 𝒞_out (on Σ_τ0, v = τ0 + R), and the outgoing phase is u. Both are exact eikonals of g0, being
double-null coordinates: g0⁻¹(dv, dv) = g0⁻¹(du, du) = 0, while g0⁻¹(dv, du) = −e^(−2σ). The normalisation of u is any
λ-independent one; that of Definition 50.1 is fixed for definiteness. The generators are

    ℓ_in := g0⁻¹ dv = −e^(−2σ) ∂_u = −e^(−ψ) L0,      ℓ_out := g0⁻¹ du = −e^(−2σ) ∂_v,    (50.12)

the first form in the coordinates (u, v, ϑ, φ1, φ2) and the second in the chart X (Lemma 50.8 (d)): the
ingoing generator is the operator L0 of Section 2.2 up to the smooth bounded factor e^(−ψ).

The outgoing generator has a variable radial speed. In the coordinates (v, R) of (50.8) the second null
direction of the round spheres is ∂_v + y ∂_R, y := e^ψ f/2, since −e^(2ψ) f + 2 e^ψ y = 0. With ∂_v|_R = ∂_τ and
∂_R|_v = −∂_τ + x̂·∂_x it is (1 − y)(∂_τ + c_out x̂·∂_x), so

    ℓ_out = ℓ_out(τ) Z_out,      Z_out := ∂_τ + c_out x̂·∂_x,      c_out := y/(1 − y),      y = e^ψ f/2 ∈ (−∞, 1/2],
    (50.13)
with ℓ_out(τ) := dτ(ℓ_out). Here y ≤ 1/2 because e^ψ ≤ 1 and f ≤ 1, so c_out ∈ (−1, 1], and c_out < 0 exactly where f
< 0, that is where the spheres are trapped. In particular c_out(a) < 0 on {R = a} (Proposition 50.6 (c)).
Since a null vector is never tangent to a spacelike slice, ℓ_out(τ) ≠ 0, and on the compact Ω₂, |ℓ_out(τ)| ≥ c > 0.

**Lemma 50.10** (Transport along both generators.) Let c be a smooth function on Ω₂ and Z := ∂_τ +
c x̂·∂_x. For φ on A(τ), with the flat measures on A(τ) and on its boundary spheres,

    ∂_τ ‖φ‖² = 2 ⟨φ, Zφ⟩ + ∫_(A(τ)) div(c x̂) φ² + (b′ − c(b)) ∫_(|x|=b) φ² + c(a) ∫_(|x|=a) φ².
    (50.14)

For c = −1, Z = L0 and this is the identity of the proof of Lemma 5.6. For c = c_out, b′ − c_out(b) < −2 + 1 =
−1 and c_out(a) < 0, so both boundary terms are nonpositive, as for L0, and if Z_out φ − c′ φ = f, with c′ a bounded
function or matrix, then

    ‖φ(τ)‖ ≤ e^(C (τ − τ0)) (‖φ(τ0)‖ + ∫_(τ0)^τ ‖f(s)‖ ds),      C := max(0, sup_(Ω₂) (c′ + ½ div(c_out x̂))),

c′ read as the largest eigenvalue of its symmetric part when it is a matrix.

*Proof.* ∂_τ ‖φ‖² = 2⟨φ, ∂_τ φ⟩ + b′ ∫_(|x|=b) φ², and ∂_τ φ = Zφ − c x̂·∂_x φ. By the divergence theorem on A(τ), with
outer normal x̂ on {|x| = b} and −x̂ on {|x| = a}, −2 ∫ c φ x̂·∂_x φ = −∫ c x̂·∂_x(φ²) = −∫_(|x|=b) c φ² + ∫_(|x|=a) c
φ² + ∫ div(c x̂) φ². This is (50.14). With Zφ = c′ φ + f it gives ∂_τ ‖φ‖² ≤ 2 ‖φ‖ ‖f‖ + 2C ‖φ‖², hence
∂_τ ‖φ‖ ≤ ‖f‖ + C ‖φ‖, and Gronwall's lemma concludes. For c = −1, div(−x̂) = −3/r in R⁴. ∎

If the inner sphere were untrapped, c_out(a) would be positive and the boundary term at R = a would have the wrong sign:
the trapped inner sphere of Proposition 50.6 (c) is what both transports need.

**Lemma 50.11** (The commutator with a generator.) Let g0 be a round double-null metric
(50.1) and L_in := ℓ_in·∂ = −e^(−2σ) ∂_u. For every function f,

    [□_(g0), L_in] f = a_in □_(g0) f + M_in(L_in f) + N_in f,      a_in := 2 L_in(R)/R,
    M_in ξ := 4 e^(−4σ) σ_v ∂_u(e^(2σ) ξ) + 4 e^(−4σ) (R_u/R) ∂_v(e^(2σ) ξ),    (50.15)

with N_in a first-order operator with smooth coefficients; the mirror identity holds for L_out := ℓ_out·∂ = −e^(−2σ) ∂_v
with u and v exchanged. The same holds for □̃ := g0^(ab) ∂_a∂_b in the chart X, with another first-order N_in.

*Proof.* In the coordinates (u, v) and the angles,

    □_(g0) f = −e^(−2σ) (2 f_uv + 3 R⁻¹ (R_u f_v + R_v f_u)) + R⁻² Δ_(S³) f.

Put ρ := −e^(−2σ), so L_in = ρ ∂_u, and compute □(ρ f_u) − ρ ∂_u □f. The third derivatives cancel, as in any
commutator of a second-order with a first-order operator. Of the second derivatives, the terms in f_uv are
−2e^(−2σ) ρ_u f_uv − 2ρ ρ_u f_uv = 0, since ρ = −e^(−2σ); the terms 3R⁻¹(R_u f_uv + R_v f_uu) cancel between the two
sides; −2e^(−2σ) ρ_v f_uu = −4e^(−4σ) σ_v f_uu remains; and the angular part gives −ρ ∂_u(R⁻²) Δf = (2ρR_u/R) R⁻² Δf =
a_in R⁻² Δf, because the angular inverse metric R⁻² γ̂⁻¹ changes along ∂_u by a multiple of itself: the generator is
shear-free. Writing R⁻² Δf = □f + e^(−2σ)(2 f_uv + first order) gives a_in □f − 4e^(−4σ)(R_u/R) f_uv + first order. The
two remaining second derivatives, −4e^(−4σ) σ_v f_uu − 4e^(−4σ)(R_u/R) f_uv, carry the generator's index u; as f_u =
−e^(2σ) L_in f, they are M_in(L_in f). Finally □̃f = □_(g0) f + H0·∂f with H0^ρ := g0^(ab) Γ[g0]^ρ_ab smooth, and the
commutator of L_in with the first-order operator H0·∂ is of first order. ∎

So if ℓ_𝔨·dφ = ξ along a generator, then Ψ := □̃φ satisfies the transport

    L_𝔨 Ψ + a_𝔨 Ψ = □̃ξ − M_𝔨(ξ) − N_𝔨 φ,      𝔨 ∈ {in, out},    (50.16)

the form of (6.6): on Vaidya, ℓ_in = −L0, R = r and a_in = 2/r. The generators normalised by dτ are those of
Lemma 50.10: ℓ_𝔨 = ℓ_𝔨(τ) Z, ℓ_𝔨(τ) := dτ(ℓ_𝔨), with Z = L0 (c = −1, ℓ_in(τ) = −e^(−ψ)) for 𝔨 = in and
Z = Z_out (c = c_out) for 𝔨 = out. So Zφ = ξ/ℓ_𝔨(τ), that is ∂_τ φ = ξ/ℓ_𝔨(τ) − c x̂·∂_x φ; differentiating this once
more in x and in τ, and writing ∂_τ ξ = Zξ − c x̂·∂_x ξ, every second derivative of φ is a combination, with smooth
λ-independent coefficients, of L_𝔨 ξ, ∂_x ξ, ξ, dφ and the spatial Hessian ∂_x² φ. The Hessian satisfies

    Z(∂_j∂_k φ) = ∂_j∂_k (ξ/ℓ_𝔨(τ)) − ∂_j(c x̂^i) ∂_i∂_k φ − ∂_k(c x̂^i) ∂_i∂_j φ − ∂_j∂_k(c x̂^i) ∂_i φ,

since ∂_τ commutes with ∂_j: a transport along Z with the smooth λ-independent coefficients ∂_x(c x̂) and ∂_x²(c x̂).

### 50.4 The approximant

The two-scale operator with two phases is Ric^H with every ∂_a replaced by ∂_a + λ⁻¹ (∂_a v) F1 + λ⁻¹ (∂_a u) F2, as in
Definition 4.1; we write R[G] for it. It contains no explicit θ1, θ2, so

    R[G(·, · + c1, · + c2)](X, θ1, θ2) = R[G](X, θ1 + c1, θ2 + c2)    (50.17)

for all constants c1, c2, and the form (b) of Lemma 4.2, with phases u_𝔨 = ϕ_𝔨 + λ Φ_𝔨, holds with
the same proof. For a profile G = g0 + λ g1 + Σ_(j≥2) λ^j g_j we write R[G] = λ⁻¹ R^(−1) + R^(0) + λ R^(1) + ….

The waves are

    W_in := W_TT^in + χ_in dv ⊗ dv,      W_out := W_TT^out + χ_out du ⊗ du,    (50.18)

with W_TT^in, W_TT^out the ingoing and outgoing waves of Definition 50.1, and χ_in(X, θ1), χ_out(X, θ2) second
harmonics fixed below. Their Cartesian components are smooth on Ω₂ × T², the axes included (Lemma 2.9 (a)).

**Definition 50.12** (Two-phase approximant.) Let N ≥ 1, K and k be integers. A two-phase
approximant with N stages is a metric g_app = g0 + λ [g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j], with two-phase profiles g_j bounded with
all their (X, θ1, θ2)-derivatives independently of λ. It is of order K at regularity k if:

- (E1₂) g1 = ⟨g1⟩ + g1^in + g1^out, with g1^in a profile in (X, θ1) alone and g1^out in (X, θ2) alone, each of zero
  mean, and g1^in(ℓ_in, ·) = 0, g1^out(ℓ_out, ·) = 0;
- (E2₂) the coefficient R^(0) of λ⁰ in the two-scale expansion of Ric^H(g_app) vanishes identically in (X, θ1, θ2);
- (E3) |Ric^H(g_app)|_k (τ) ≤ C_R λ^K for every τ ∈ [τ0, τ_end], with C_R independent of λ.

**Lemma 50.13** (Stage 0 with two phases.) Let q be a two-phase profile and χ_in, χ_out smooth of
zero mean. In the two-scale expansion of R[g0 + λ (W_in + W_out) + λ² q]:

(a) R^(−1) = 0;
(b) R^(0) = R^(0)_in + R^(0)_out − Ric(g0) + R^(0)_× + e^(−2σ) F1F2 q, where R^(0)_𝔨 is the coefficient of λ⁰ of
R[g0 + λ W_𝔨], given by (4.5) with v replaced by ϕ_𝔨, and R^(0)_× is bilinear in (W_in, W_out)
and has only mixed harmonics;
(c) the mean of R^(0) is Ric(g0) − (𝒜/R³) dv ⊗ dv − (ℬ/R³) du ⊗ du, so it vanishes exactly when g0 solves the
two-null-dust equations with the fluxes (50.3);
(d) the pure harmonics (n, 0) of R^(0) vanish except in the component dv ⊗ dv, where they are those of
−(ℓ_in + ½ □_(g0) v) F1χ_in − ¼ (|F1 W_TT^in|²_(g0) − ⟨|F1 W_TT^in|²_(g0)⟩), the second term a second harmonic in θ1;
and likewise for (0, n) with du ⊗ du;
(e) on a mixed harmonic e^(i(n1 θ1 + n2 θ2)), q enters R^(0) as multiplication by −e^(−2σ) n1 n2, which does not vanish;
(f) the gauge field has D = O(λ), the coefficient of λ⁰ being Σ_𝔨 g0⁻¹(F_𝔨 W_𝔨(ℓ_𝔨, ·) − ½ dϕ_𝔨 tr_(g0) F_𝔨 W_𝔨) = 0.

Hence, with χ_in the solution of zero mean of

    (ℓ_in + ½ □_(g0) v) F1χ_in = −¼ (|F1 W_TT^in|²_(g0) − ⟨|F1 W_TT^in|²_(g0)⟩),      χ_in = 0 on Σ_τ0,
    (50.19)

χ_out the solution of the same transport along ℓ_out, with u, θ2 and W_TT^out, and q the profile of zero mean whose
mixed harmonics are the quotients of those of −R^(0)_× by −e^(−2σ) n1 n2, R^(0) ≡ 0. The transports are along the
generators, which reach Σ_τ0 inside Ω₂ (Lemma 50.8 (d)), and χ_in, χ_out are smooth on Ω₂ × S¹, the axes
included, as in Section 4.4.

*Proof.* (a) Second derivatives of g enter Ric^H only through −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b g (Section 2.4), and the other terms
contain at most first derivatives, which are O(1). The λ⁻¹ part of −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b (λ (W_in + W_out)) is
−½ λ⁻¹ Σ_(𝔧,𝔨) g0⁻¹(dϕ_𝔧, dϕ_𝔨) F_𝔧 F_𝔨 (W_in + W_out) = 0: g0⁻¹(dϕ_𝔨, dϕ_𝔨) = 0, and F1F2 (W_in + W_out) = 0.

(b) A term of order λ⁰ is linear in one W_𝔨 with at most one phase derivative, quadratic in the waves with two phase
derivatives, or linear in λ² q with two phase derivatives, the last only from the principal part, where it is
−½ g0^(ab) (2 ∂_a v ∂_b u) F1F2 q = e^(−2σ) F1F2 q, the terms with two derivatives in one phase vanishing as in (a). The
terms in which only W_𝔨 occurs are those of the expansion of R[g0 + λ W_𝔨]. The proof of Lemma 4.4
uses of g0 only that dϕ_𝔨 is null and of the wave only W_𝔨(ℓ_𝔨, ·) = 0 and tr_(g0) W_𝔨 = 0; both hold here, W_TT^𝔨
having only angular components and being traceless on the spheres (Lemma 2.9 (b)) and dϕ_𝔨 ⊗ dϕ_𝔨 being null and
transverse to ℓ_𝔨. So R^(0)_𝔨 is given by (4.5) with v replaced by ϕ_𝔨. The remaining terms are
products of a function of θ1 of zero mean with a function of θ2 of zero mean, which have only mixed harmonics.

(c) By (b), the mean of R^(0) is Ric(g0) − ¼ ⟨|F1 W_in|²⟩ dv ⊗ dv − ¼ ⟨|F2 W_out|²⟩ du ⊗ du, the other terms of
(4.5) being phase derivatives. As in the proof of Proposition 2.11, χ_𝔨 does not contribute, and the
calculation there, which uses only that g0 is R² times the round metric on the spheres, gives ⟨|F1 W_TT^in|²_(g0)⟩ =
(4/3) A² env² R⁻³ and ⟨|F2 W_TT^out|²_(g0)⟩ = (4/3) A₂² env₂² R⁻³ ((2.13)).

(d) The pure harmonics (n, 0) come from R^(0)_in alone. In the coordinates (u, v), ℓ_in = −e^(−2σ) ∂_u and □_(g0) v =
−3 e^(−2σ) R_u/R. The angular components of F1 W_TT^in are R^(1/2) times functions of (v, the angles, θ1), and
Γ^C_uA = (R_u/R) δ^C_A, while Γ^C_ua = 0 for a ∈ {u, v}; so ∇_(ℓ_in) F1 W_TT^in = −e^(−2σ)(½ − 2)(R_u/R) F1 W_TT^in and

    ∇_(ℓ_in) F1 W_TT^in + ½ (□_(g0) v) F1 W_TT^in = 0.

Since ∇_(ℓ_in) dv = 0, the χ_in term of (4.5) is −(ℓ_in + ½ □_(g0) v)(F1χ_in) dv ⊗ dv. The
quadratic term is −¼ |F1 W_TT^in|² dv ⊗ dv, the χ_in part dropping out of |F1 W_in|² as in the proof of
Lemma 4.5 (b), and its oscillating part is a second harmonic in θ1, as in Lemma 4.5 (d). This holds
for every χ_in of zero mean.

(e) e^(−2σ) F1F2 multiplies the harmonic (n1, n2) by e^(−2σ)(i n1)(i n2).

(f) D is computed as in the proof of Lemma 2.10: its coefficient of λ⁰ is g0^(ab) C⁽⁰⁾ρ_ab, with C⁽⁰⁾ now the
sum over 𝔨 of the terms with F_𝔨 W_𝔨 and dϕ_𝔨; it vanishes because W_𝔨(ℓ_𝔨, ·) = 0 and tr_(g0) W_𝔨 = 0. ∎

With χ_in = χ_out = 0 the mixed harmonics of R^(0) do not vanish: the two families interact at stage 0, and the
interaction is removed by q with no transport.

**Lemma 50.14** (No small divisors.) Let ḡ be a mean metric with ḡ − g0 = O(λ), and u_in, u_out
phases with u_in − v = O(λ), u_out − u = O(λ), ḡ⁻¹(du_𝔨, du_𝔨) = O(λ). A term λ^j q(X) e^(i(n1 u_in + n2 u_out)/λ) E of
the metric, E a constant symmetric array, first meets Ric^H at order j − 2, through −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b only, as
multiplication by the symbol

    ½ ḡ⁻¹(n1 du_in + n2 du_out, n1 du_in + n2 du_out) = −e^(−2σ) n1 n2 + λ 𝔮(n1, n2),    (50.20)

𝔮 a quadratic form in (n1, n2) with smooth bounded coefficients. The leading part vanishes exactly on the pure
harmonics, and on every mixed harmonic |e^(−2σ) n1 n2| ≥ e^(−2σ) ≥ min_(Ω₂) e^(−2σ) > 0. So the mixed harmonics are
solved by division with no small divisors, and the division loses no derivative; the part λ 𝔮 is of the next order. For
any two radial phases f(v) and h(u) in place of v and u the leading symbol is −e^(−2σ) f′ h′ n1 n2.

*Proof.* With Φ := (n1 u_in + n2 u_out)/λ, ∂_a∂_b e^(iΦ) = (−∂_aΦ ∂_bΦ + i ∂_a∂_bΦ) e^(iΦ), so the term of order λ^(j−2)
of −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b (λ^j q e^(iΦ) E) is ½ λ^(j−2) ḡ⁻¹(n1 du_in + n2 du_out, n1 du_in + n2 du_out) q e^(iΦ) E; every
other term of Ric^H has at most one derivative on the factor e^(iΦ) and is O(λ^(j−1)). Expanding, the symbol is
½ n1² ḡ⁻¹(du_in, du_in) + n1 n2 ḡ⁻¹(du_in, du_out) + ½ n2² ḡ⁻¹(du_out, du_out), and ḡ⁻¹(du_in, du_out) =
g0^(uv) + O(λ) = −e^(−2σ) + O(λ). For radial phases f(v), h(u), g0^(ab) ∂_a f ∂_b h = −e^(−2σ) f′ h′. ∎

In the (u, v)-plane the null cone of g0 is the pair of lines du = 0 and dv = 0, so every combination n1 dv + n2 du with
n1 n2 ≠ 0 is timelike or spacelike, with g0⁻¹-length bounded below. This is Touati's strong coherence condition
[Tou24, (1.18), p. 9], min |g0⁻¹(dz, dz)| ≥ c over the combinations z of the phases that occur, for all mixed
