combinations at once. Two ingoing phases would be resonant: their combinations are all null, and the symbol vanishes on
every harmonic.

**Remark 50.15** (The constant of the division.) The constant of Lemma 50.14 is
min_(Ω₂) e^(−2σ), which is positive on the compact Ω₂ but degenerates with the time spent inside the hole. With
e^(2σ) = −e^ψ R_u (Lemma 50.8), along a line of constant u, d(ln e^(−2σ))/dv = −ψ_v − R_uv/R_u = −ψ_v −
e^ψ μ/R³. In {u ≥ u2}, where ψ depends on v alone (Proposition 50.6 (a)), this gives on R ≥ a

    d(ln e^(−2σ))/dv ≥ −ψ′(v) − μ_max/a³,      μ_max := max_(Ω₂) μ,

an exponential lower bound for the constant in terms of the time spent in Ω₂ ∩ {u ≥ u2}. The constants of
Theorem 50.2 depend on it, which is harmless for a fixed T.

**Remark 50.16** (Numerical observation.) On the discrete background of
Remark 50.9, |g0⁻¹(dv, du)| = e^(−2σ), with v the advanced time on 𝒞_out and u normalised as there, had
least value 0.181, 0.138 and 0.148 off the trapped region (R² ≥ 1.5 μ) at 40, 80 and 160 steps per unit, stable to ten
per cent and not monotone in the resolution. Its least value over every cell, 0.131, 0.071 and 0.042, did not converge:
each finer grid reached further into the strip near R = a at late v, where the double-null grid thins. Integrated along
the outgoing rays of {u ≥ u2}, where ψ and μ depend on v alone, its values on R = a were 0.892, 0.446, 0.240, 0.134,
0.0758, 0.0434, 0.0266, 0.0212, 0.0183 and 0.0156 at v = 0.5, 1, 1.5, …, 4.5 and 4.9, agreeing with the grids at v = 0.5,
1, 1.5 to one per cent (the coefficients at 80 and 160 steps to two per cent), decreasing at a rate per unit v of 1.4,
falling to 1.1 by v = 3 and to 0.3–0.5 once the shell had raised the mass; the analytic rate of Remark 50.15
is μ_max/a³ ≈ 10.5 there. No proof uses these observations.

**Lemma 50.17** (The stages with two phases.) Let the unknowns be the means m_j (j ≥ 1), the phases
φ_j^in, φ_j^out (j ≥ 1) and the profiles ĝ_j(X, θ1, θ2) of zero mean (j ≥ 2). Put ḡ := g0 + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j m_j,
u_in := v + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j φ_j^in, u_out := u + Σ_(j=1)^N λ^j φ_j^out, W := W_in + W_out,

    G := ḡ + λ W + Σ_(j=2)^(N+1) λ^j ĝ_j(X, θ1, θ2),      g_app := G(X, u_in/λ, u_out/λ),    (50.21)

and expand R_u[G] = Σ_m λ^m ℛ^(m), R_u the two-scale operator with the phases u_in, u_out. Then

    ḡ⁻¹(du_𝔨, du_𝔨) = Σ_(j≥1) λ^j e_j^𝔨,      e_j^𝔨 = 2 ℓ_𝔨·dφ_j^𝔨 − m_j(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨) − q_j^𝔨,

with q_j^𝔨 a polynomial in (m_i, dφ_i^𝔨), i < j, as in (4.11), once per phase; and
ḡ⁻¹(du_in, du_out) = g0^(uv) + λ c_1 + O(λ²), c_1 := ℓ_in·dφ_1^out + ℓ_out·dφ_1^in − m1(ℓ_in, ℓ_out); the cross
contraction does not vanish for λ small, since g0^(uv) = −e^(−2σ).

(a) ℛ^(−1) = 0, and ℛ^(0) is the coefficient of λ⁰ of R[g0 + λ W + λ² ĝ_2] minus ½ Σ_𝔨 e_1^𝔨 F_𝔨² W_𝔨.
(b) For m ≥ 1,

    ℛ^(m) = T̂ ĝ_(m+1) + e^(−2σ) F1F2 ĝ_(m+2) − ½ Σ_𝔨 e_(m+1)^𝔨 F_𝔨² W_𝔨 + 𝒲(m_m, φ_m^in, φ_m^out) + 𝒴_m,
    (50.22)

where T̂ is linear and is applied to the pure harmonics of ĝ_(m+1) only (here and in (c), T̂ ĝ_(m+1) means T̂ applied
to the pure part of ĝ_(m+1)), and on profiles Y of the harmonics of θ_𝔨 alone Π_𝔨 T̂ Y = −(ℓ_𝔨·∂_X) F_𝔨 Y + Π_𝔨 ℳ Y, Π_𝔨
the projection onto those harmonics and ℳ algebraic in X and of first order in (θ1, θ2), with smooth bounded coefficients
built from g0, ϕ_in, ϕ_out and W; 𝒲 is as in Lemma 4.7, linear in m_m to second order, with mean part −½ □̃ m_m
plus terms of first order, and linear in φ_m^𝔨 through dφ_m^𝔨 and □̃φ_m^𝔨, the latter only as −½ (□̃φ_m^𝔨) F_𝔨 W_𝔨; and
𝒴_m depends only on the earlier stages, among them the mixed harmonics of ĝ_(m+1), fixed at stage m − 1. Only the mixed
harmonics of ĝ_(m+2) enter ℛ^(m).
(c) Each stage m ≥ 1 is the system

    (a′) −½ □̃ m_m + B̄·∂m_m + C̄ m_m = 𝒮_m − ⟨𝒲_φ⟩ − ⟨T̂ ĝ_(m+1)⟩,
    (b′) ℓ_𝔨·dφ_m^𝔨 = ½ m_m(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨) + ½ q_m^𝔨,      𝔨 ∈ {in, out},
    (c′) Π_𝔨 T̂ ĝ_(m+1) = −Π_𝔨 (𝒲 + 𝒴_m),      𝔨 ∈ {in, out},
    (d′) e^(−2σ) F1F2 ĝ_(m+2) = −Π_mix (𝒲 + 𝒴_m + T̂ ĝ_(m+1)),    (50.23)

with 𝒮_m := −⟨𝒴_m⟩, 𝒲_φ := 𝒲(0, φ_m^in, φ_m^out) and Π_mix the projection onto the mixed harmonics: a wave equation
for the mean, a transport along its own generator for each phase, a transport along its own generator for the pure
harmonics of each family, and a division for the mixed harmonics. Given everything of the earlier stages, smooth, it has
a unique smooth solution on Ω₂ with data (m_m, ∂_τ m_m), φ_m^in, φ_m^out and the pure harmonics of ĝ_(m+1) on Σ_τ0;
the mixed harmonics take no data.

*Proof.* The expansions of ḡ⁻¹(du_𝔨, du_𝔨) are those of (4.11) for each phase. For the cross
contraction, ḡ⁻¹ = g0⁻¹ − λ m1^♯ + O(λ²) and du_𝔨 = dϕ_𝔨 + λ dφ_1^𝔨 + O(λ²) give g0^(uv) + λ (ℓ_in·dφ_1^out +
ℓ_out·dφ_1^in − m1(ℓ_in, ℓ_out)) + O(λ²).

(a) and (b) follow from the weight count of the proof of Lemma 4.7, in which each phase derivative λ⁻¹ (∂ϕ_𝔨)
F_𝔨 has weight −1. A factor of stage m + 1 reaches order m in the ways listed there: the pure harmonics of ĝ_(m+1) hit by
one phase derivative of their own phase, which gives T̂ (a phase derivative of the other phase annihilates them); and
m_(m+1), dφ_(m+1)^𝔨 in the phase contractions, which give −½ e_(m+1)^𝔨 F_𝔨² W_𝔨. In addition, ĝ_(m+2) hit by two phase
derivatives reaches order m, through the principal part only, as −½ Σ_(𝔧,𝔨) g0⁻¹(dϕ_𝔧, dϕ_𝔨) F_𝔧 F_𝔨 ĝ_(m+2) =
e^(−2σ) F1F2 ĝ_(m+2) (Lemma 50.14); this vanishes on the pure harmonics. The mixed harmonics of
ĝ_(m+1) reach order m too, hit by one phase derivative, or by two through the cross contraction below; they were fixed
at stage m − 1 (by (d′), and at m = 1 by Lemma 50.13), and these terms, with their X-derivatives,
belong to 𝒴_m. The cross contraction ḡ⁻¹(du_in, du_out) = g0^(uv) + Σ_(j≥1) λ^j c_j contributes at order m the terms
−c_j F1F2 ĝ_(m+2−j), 1 ≤ j ≤ m, which have mixed harmonics only. For j < m they contain only the earlier stages and,
at j = 1, the mixed harmonics of ĝ_(m+1), and are part of 𝒴_m. For j = m, c_m is a linear function of (m_m, dφ_m^𝔨)
plus a polynomial in the earlier stages; the first part of −c_m F1F2 ĝ_2 belongs to 𝒲 and the second to 𝒴_m. At m = 1,
c_1 is linear in (m1, dφ_1^𝔨), and −c_1 F1F2 ĝ_2 belongs to 𝒲. T̂ is defined at G1 = g0 + λ (m1 + W) with the phases v +
λ φ_1^in and u + λ φ_1^out as in Definition 4.6, and its form on pure harmonics of θ_𝔨 is that of
Lemma 4.8, with ℓ_𝔨 and ϕ_𝔨: the principal term gives −(ℓ_𝔨·∂_X) F_𝔨 Y − ½ (□̃ϕ_𝔨) F_𝔨 Y − ½ e_1^𝔨
F_𝔨² Y, and e_1^𝔨 = 0. The products of such Y with the other family's wave, for instance ½ Y(ℓ_𝔧, ℓ_𝔧) F_𝔧² W_𝔧 with
𝔧 ≠ 𝔨, have mixed harmonics; they are the mixed part of T̂ ĝ_(m+1), which (d′) carries.

(c) (b′) is e_m^𝔨 = 0. The mean of (50.22) is (a′), its pure harmonics of θ_𝔨 are (c′), and its mixed
harmonics are (d′), which, by Lemma 50.14, is solved pointwise in X by division by −e^(−2σ) n1 n2.
⟨T̂ ĝ⟩ contains no X-derivative of ĝ and ⟨𝒲_φ⟩ only dφ_m^𝔨. For Ξ_𝔨 := F_𝔨 Π_𝔨 ĝ_(m+1), (c′) is the transport −(ℓ_𝔨·∂_X)
Ξ_𝔨 + ℳ′_𝔨 Ξ_𝔨 = (forcing) along ℓ_𝔨, with ℳ′_𝔨 a bounded operator on profiles of zero mean. Its forcing contains
□̃φ_m^𝔨, and Ψ_m^𝔨 := □̃φ_m^𝔨 satisfies the transport (50.16) along ℓ_𝔨 with ξ = ½ (m_m(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨) + q_m^𝔨),
whose □̃ξ contains □̃ m_m from (a′). The system for (m_m, φ_m^in, φ_m^out, Ψ_m^in, Ψ_m^out, Ξ_in, Ξ_out) is linear with
smooth coefficients and closes without loss, m_m and φ_m^𝔨 in H^(s+1), Ψ_m^𝔨 and Ξ_𝔨 in H^s, by the Picard iteration of
the proof of Lemma 4.10: the mean by Lemma 4.9 on Ω₂, the transports along ℓ_in by Lemma 5.6
(ℓ_in = −e^(−ψ) L0) and along ℓ_out by Lemma 50.10, both generators reaching Σ_τ0 inside Ω₂
(Lemma 50.8 (d)). Then (d′) gives the mixed harmonics of ĝ_(m+2), which involve one X-derivative of the
mixed harmonics of ĝ_(m+1) through 𝒴_m: one derivative per stage, harmless for smooth data and finitely many stages.

Lemma 4.9 holds on Ω₂ with the same proof. Besides the shape of Ω and Lemma 2.6 (e), that proof uses g0
on an open region containing Ω on which τ is a time function, {r > a/2} there. Here fix a′ ∈ (0, a), and let 𝒪 be the
connected component containing Ω₂ of the set of points of Q_(a′) with u > u0 and v0 < v < V1 at which g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) < 0; 𝒪
takes the place of {r > a/2}, and S := {τ = τ0} ∩ 𝒪 that of {τ = τ0, r > a/2}. 𝒪 is open and contains Ω₂. Indeed Q_(a′)
is open in Q and carries the smooth g0, with R > a′, so that the chart X is defined there, and G ⊂ Q_(a′) (proof of
Proposition 50.6 (d)), so Ω₂ ⊂ Q_(a′); on Ω₂, u > u0, as 𝒞_out ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} ⊂ {R > b(τ)}, and v0 < τ0 + a ≤ v =
τ + R ≤ V + 1 + τ_end − τ0 < V1 (proof of Lemma 50.8); and g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) ≤ −1 − μ/R² on Ω₂
(Lemma 50.8 (a)). On 𝒪, τ increases along future causal curves, since dτ is timelike on the connected set 𝒪
and positive on future causal vectors at the points of Ω₂ (proof of Lemma 50.8). So S is acausal, and the
argument of that proof, with Lemma 50.8 (d) and (e) in place of Lemma 2.6 (e), gives Ω₂ ⊂ D. ∎

**Theorem 50.18** (The approximant to every order, two phases.) For every N ≥ 1 and every smooth
choice of stage data there are two-phase profiles g1, …, g_N, independent of λ, such that g_app = g0 + λ [g1] +
Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j] is a two-phase approximant with N stages of order K = N − 1 at every regularity k
(Definition 50.12), with

    g1 = m1 + W_in(X, θ1 + φ_1^in(X)) + W_out(X, θ2 + φ_1^out(X)),

W_in and W_out as in (50.18) with χ_in, χ_out of (50.19), and the background g0 of
Proposition 50.6. The stage data are those of Lemma 50.17 (c) on Σ_τ0, for m = 1, …, N.

*Proof.* Solve stage 0 by Lemma 50.13, with ĝ_2's mixed harmonics the profile q there, and the stages
m = 1, …, N by Lemma 50.17 (c), keeping in (50.21) the pure harmonics of ĝ_(N+1) and the mixed
harmonics of ĝ_j for j ≤ N + 1. By Lemma 50.17 (a)–(b), ℛ^(m) = 0 for m ≤ N − 1, so R_u[G] is λ^N times a
profile bounded uniformly in λ. Rewriting with the fixed phases v and u, the Taylor expansion in λΦ_𝔨, Φ_𝔨 := Σ_(j≥2)
λ^(j−2) φ_j^𝔨, about θ_𝔨 + φ_1^𝔨, as in the proof of Theorem 4.11, gives profiles g_j(X, θ1, θ2) with the stated
g1 and a remainder that changes Ric^H by O(λ^(N−1)) in |·|_k. (E1₂) holds because W_𝔨(ℓ_𝔨, ·) = 0 and ⟨g1⟩ = m1. (E2₂)
holds by the two-phase form of Lemma 4.2 (b) with Φ_𝔨 = φ_1^𝔨 + λΦ_𝔨: the coefficient of λ⁰ of
R[G(·, · + Φ)] is R^(0) of g_app, and it equals ℛ^(0)(X, θ1 + φ_1^in, θ2 + φ_1^out) = 0, since ℛ^(−1) = 0. (E3) holds
with K = N − 1. ∎

Theorem 4.11 is the case W_out = 0.

### 50.5 The uniform estimate

Let g_app be a two-phase approximant (Definition 50.12), ℰ := −Ric^H(g_app), and

    ℓ_app^𝔨 := g_app⁻¹ dϕ_𝔨,   s_𝔨(w) := w(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨),   G1^𝔨 := [F_𝔨 g1],   G2^𝔨 := [F_𝔨² g1],
    Y_𝔨 := [F_𝔨 g1 + λ F_𝔨 g2],   ω_in := G1^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in),   ω_out := G1^in(ℓ_out, ℓ_out),
    □̃_app := g_app^(ab) ∂_a∂_b,   □̃ := g0^(ab) ∂_a∂_b,

for 𝔨 ∈ {in, out}, with g1, g2 the first two profiles of g_app. The remainder w is decomposed as

    w = h + φ_in Y_in + φ_out Y_out,    (50.24)

with φ_in(X), φ_out(X) fields fixed in Lemma 50.21, Ψ_𝔨 := □̃φ_𝔨, and the energy is

    𝒩₂(τ) := Σ_(j≤k) λ^j (‖∂^j ∂h‖ + Σ_𝔨 (‖∂^j Ψ_𝔨‖ + ‖∂^j ∂φ_𝔨‖ + λ ‖∂^j ∂_x² φ_𝔨‖)) + ‖h‖ + Σ_𝔨 ‖φ_𝔨‖,
    (50.25)

the norms those of Chapter 5 on the slices Σ_τ = A(τ) of Ω₂.

**Theorem 50.19** (Uniform existence with two phases.) Fix k = 6 and K ≥ 6. Let g_app be a two-phase
approximant with N stages of order K at regularity k, with the constant C_R in (E3), and let g be a Cauchy datum on Σ_τ0
for Ric^H(g) = 0 with w := g − g_app satisfying (E4) of Theorem 6.1, Data(w) ≤ C_D λ^K. There are λ0 > 0
and M, depending on Ω₂, k, K, C_R, C_D and the bounds on the profiles but not on λ, such that for 0 < λ ≤ λ0 the
solution g of Ric^H(g) = 0 with these data exists on Ω₂, is unique there among C² solutions with |g − g0| ≤ ε1 on Ω₂,
is smooth if the data are, and

    w = h + Σ_𝔨 φ_𝔨 Y_𝔨,      𝒩₂(τ) ≤ M λ^K   on [τ0, τ_end].    (50.26)

In particular |w| ≤ M λ^(K−3) and |∂w| ≤ M λ^(K−4) on Ω₂, |g − g0| ≤ C λ and |∂g| ≤ C.

With W_out = 0 this is Theorem 6.1, with φ_out = 0. The proof is that of Theorem 6.1 with
two phase shifts. We collect the structure of the linearisation, define the phase shifts, write the equation for h and
its ℓ_in ⊗ ℓ_in component, and then go through the eight steps.

**Lemma 50.20** (The linearisation with two phases.) Let P(w) := (d/ds) Ric^H(g_app + s w) at s = 0, and
for g := g_app + w let P_g be P with its principal part −½ g_app^(ab) ∂_a∂_b replaced by −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b, so that
Ric^H(g_app + w) = 0 reads P_g(w) = ℰ + 𝒬(w), 𝒬(w) the terms of second and higher order in (w, ∂w) other than the
principal part. Then:

(L1) P(w) = −½ g_app^(ab) ∂_a∂_b w + ½ λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 s_𝔨(w) G2^𝔨 + B·∂w + C·w, with B and C two-phase profiles: there is no
term of order λ⁻², and one of order λ⁻¹ for each family.

(L2) For φ(X),

    P_g(φ Y_𝔨) = φ [T1^𝔨] − λ⁻¹ (ℓ_app^𝔨·dφ) G2^𝔨 − ½ (□̃_app φ) G1^𝔨 − ½ λ (□̃_app φ) [F_𝔨 g2] + B1^𝔨·dφ + C1^𝔨 φ
                 + 𝒬_φ^𝔨,

with T1^𝔨, B1^𝔨, C1^𝔨 bounded two-phase profiles and |𝒬_φ^𝔨| ≤ C |w| (λ⁻² |φ| + λ⁻¹ |dφ| + |d²φ|), likewise for
derivatives in the scaled norms, the second derivatives of φ in 𝒬_φ^𝔨 multiplying Y_𝔨. The term of order λ⁻¹ contains
no derivative of φ along the other family's generator.

(L3) P(Y_𝔨) = [T1^𝔨], a bounded profile.

(L4) G1^in(ℓ_in, ·) = G2^in(ℓ_in, ·) = 0 and G1^out(ℓ_out, ·) = G2^out(ℓ_out, ·) = 0; ω_in and G2^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) are
bounded profiles in θ2 alone, ω_out and G2^in(ℓ_out, ℓ_out) in θ1 alone; |ℓ_app^𝔨 − ℓ_𝔨| ≤ C λ, so that
g_app⁻¹(dϕ_𝔨, dϕ_𝔨) = O(λ). For the approximant of Theorem 50.18, ω_in = e^(−4σ) [F2 χ_out] and
G2^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) = e^(−4σ) [F2² χ_out], at the phase θ2 + φ_1^out; the oscillating part of ℓ_app^in − ℓ_in at order
λ is λ e^(−2σ) [χ_out] ℓ_out; and

    g_app⁻¹(dv, dv) = −λ (m1(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + e^(−4σ) [χ_out]) + O(λ²),

with [χ_out] at the same phase: the other family's term χ_out du ⊗ du is not annihilated by ℓ_in. The mirror statements
hold with in and out exchanged.

(L5) With q := g0^(ττ)/g^(ττ) and c^(ab) := g0^(ab) − q g^(ab), c^(ττ) = 0 and

    c^(ab) = (g0^(ab) (g^(ττ) − g0^(ττ)) − g0^(ττ) (g^(ab) − g0^(ab)))/g^(ττ),

so |c| ≤ C |g⁻¹ − g0⁻¹| ≤ C (λ + |w|); g0^(ττ) ≤ −1 on Ω₂, so g^(ττ) ≤ −½ for |g − g0| small. For every h,
□̃ s_𝔨(h) = (□̃h)(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨) + 2 g0^(ab) ∂_a(ℓ_𝔨 ⊗ ℓ_𝔨)·∂_b h + h·□̃(ℓ_𝔨 ⊗ ℓ_𝔨).

(L6) If ℓ_𝔨·dφ_𝔨 = ½ 𝒫 s_𝔨(h), then Ψ_𝔨 satisfies L_𝔨 Ψ_𝔨 + a_𝔨 Ψ_𝔨 = ½ □̃ 𝒫 s_𝔨(h) − ½ M_𝔨(𝒫 s_𝔨(h)) − N_𝔨 φ_𝔨
((50.16)); every second derivative of φ_𝔨 is a bounded combination of L_𝔨 𝒫 s_𝔨(h), ∂_x 𝒫 s_𝔨(h),
𝒫 s_𝔨(h), dφ_𝔨 and ∂_x² φ_𝔨; and, with Z = L0 for 𝔨 = in and Z = Z_out for 𝔨 = out,

    Z(∂_x² φ_𝔨) = ½ ∂_x² (𝒫 s_𝔨(h)/ℓ_𝔨(τ)) + (bounded) ∂_x² φ_𝔨 + (bounded) ∂_x φ_𝔨,

the bounded coefficients smooth and independent of λ.

(L7) ℓ_in = −e^(−ψ) L0 and ℓ_out = ℓ_out(τ) Z_out ((50.12), (50.13)), |ℓ_out(τ)| ≥
c > 0 on Ω₂, and the transport estimates Lemma 5.6 and Lemma 50.10 hold for both, the boundary
terms having the sign they have for L0.

*Proof.* (L1) Second derivatives of g_app enter P only through ½ w^(ab) ∂_a∂_b g_app, w^(ab) := g_app^(ac) g_app^(bd)
w_cd, because second derivatives of g enter Ric^H(g) only through −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b g. By (50.2),
∂_a∂_b [λ g1] = λ⁻¹ Σ_(𝔧,𝔨) ∂_aϕ_𝔧 ∂_bϕ_𝔨 [F_𝔧 F_𝔨 g1] + O(1) = λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 ∂_aϕ_𝔨 ∂_bϕ_𝔨 [F_𝔨² g1] + O(1), because F1F2 g1 =
0 by (E1₂); and ∂_a∂_b [λ^j g_j] = O(1) for j ≥ 2. Further w^(ab) ∂_aϕ_𝔨 ∂_bϕ_𝔨 = w(ℓ_app^𝔨, ℓ_app^𝔨) = s_𝔨(w) +
O(λ) |w|, and that difference times λ⁻¹ goes into C. Every other term is linear in w or ∂w with coefficients built from
g_app and ∂g_app, which are bounded. This is the derivation of (6.2), once per phase.

(L2) In −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b(φ Y_𝔨) = −½ φ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b Y_𝔨 − g^(ab) ∂_aφ ∂_b Y_𝔨 − ½ (g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b φ) Y_𝔨 the first term
belongs to φ P_g(Y_𝔨). By (50.2), ∂_b Y_𝔨 = λ⁻¹ ∂_bϕ_𝔨 [F_𝔨² g1] + Σ_𝔧 ∂_bϕ_𝔧 [F_𝔧 F_𝔨 g2] + [∂_b(F_𝔨 g1 +
λ F_𝔨 g2)], the λ⁻¹ term with the other phase vanishing because F_𝔧 F_𝔨 g1 = 0 for 𝔧 ≠ 𝔨; so the second term is
−λ⁻¹ (g^(ab) ∂_aφ ∂_bϕ_𝔨) G2^𝔨 + B·dφ, and g^(ab) ∂_bϕ_𝔨 = (ℓ_app^𝔨)^a + O(|w|). In the third term g^(ab) = g_app^(ab) +
O(|w|), and Y_𝔨 = G1^𝔨 + λ [F_𝔨 g2]. The first-order terms of P_g give φ times their action on Y_𝔨 and terms in dφ. The
terms with a factor w form 𝒬_φ^𝔨, and the bounds follow, each derivative of Y_𝔨 costing λ⁻¹. Finally φ P_g(Y_𝔨) =
φ P(Y_𝔨) + O(|w| λ⁻² |φ|), and P(Y_𝔨) = [T1^𝔨] by (L3).

(L3) Let G be the profile of g_app. Differentiating (50.17) in c1 (for 𝔨 = in) or in c2 (for 𝔨 = out)
at c1 = c2 = 0, the linearisation of R at G in the direction F_𝔨 G equals F_𝔨 R[G]. On a profile Z, P([Z]) = [λ⁻² P_(−2)
Z + λ⁻¹ T Z + P_0 Z], where P_(−2) Z = −g0⁻¹(dv, du) F1F2 Z = e^(−2σ) F1F2 Z; the terms −½ λ⁻² g_app⁻¹(dϕ_𝔨, dϕ_𝔨)
F_𝔨² Z and −λ⁻² (g_app⁻¹(dv, du) − g0⁻¹(dv, du)) F1F2 Z are of order λ⁻¹, by (L4) and g_app − g0 = O(λ), and are kept
in T.
Since F_𝔨 G = λ F_𝔨 g1 + λ² F_𝔨 g2 + O(λ³) and P_(−2) F_𝔨 g1 = 0 by (E1₂), the left side is T F_𝔨 g1 + P_(−2) F_𝔨 g2 +
O(λ). The right side is F_𝔨(λ⁻¹ R^(−1) + R^(0)) + O(λ) = O(λ), since R^(−1) = −½ Σ_(𝔧,𝔨) g0⁻¹(dϕ_𝔧, dϕ_𝔨) F_𝔧 F_𝔨 g1 =
0 and R^(0) = 0 by (E2₂). So T F_𝔨 g1 + P_(−2) F_𝔨 g2 = O(λ), and P(Y_𝔨) = [λ⁻¹ (T F_𝔨 g1 + P_(−2) F_𝔨 g2) + P_0 F_𝔨 g1 +
T F_𝔨 g2 + λ P_0 F_𝔨 g2] is bounded. Without the term λ F_𝔨 g2 in Y_𝔨, the term λ⁻¹ P_(−2) F_𝔨 g2, which does not vanish
on the mixed harmonics of g2, would remain.

(L4) By (E1₂), G1^in = [F1 g1^in] and G2^in = [F1² g1^in] with g1^in(ℓ_in, ·) = 0, and they depend on θ1 alone; likewise
for out. For the approximant of Theorem 50.18, g1^out = W_out(X, θ2 + φ_1^out); W_TT^out has only
angular components, and (du ⊗ du)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) = g0⁻¹(du, dv)² = e^(−4σ). Next, ℓ_app^in − ℓ_in = (g_app⁻¹ − g0⁻¹) dv =
−λ g0⁻¹(g1(ℓ_in, ·)) + O(λ²), and g1(ℓ_in, ·) = m1(ℓ_in, ·) + [χ_out] du(ℓ_in) du = m1(ℓ_in, ·) − e^(−2σ) [χ_out] du;
in particular |ℓ_app^𝔨 − ℓ_𝔨| ≤ C λ, which holds for every two-phase approximant, g_app − g0 being O(λ). Contracting
with dv, as dv(ℓ_in) = 0 and du(ℓ_in) = −e^(−2σ), g_app⁻¹(dv, dv) = dv(ℓ_app^in) = −λ g1(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + O(λ²) =
−λ (m1(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + e^(−4σ) [χ_out]) + O(λ²).

(L5) c^(ττ) = g0^(ττ) − (g0^(ττ)/g^(ττ)) g^(ττ) = 0, and the formula for c^(ab) is algebra. g0^(ττ) ≤ −1 − μ/R² by
Lemma 50.8 (a). The last identity is the product rule.

(L6) is (50.16) with ξ = ½ 𝒫 s_𝔨(h), and the remarks after it. (L7) is Section 50.3. ∎

**Lemma 50.21** (The phase shifts.) Let w be smooth on Ω₂ ∩ {τ ≤ τ*}. The system

    ℓ_𝔨·dφ_𝔨 = ½ 𝒫 s_𝔨(h),      h := w − Σ_𝔧 φ_𝔧 Y_𝔧,      φ_𝔨 = 0 on Σ_τ0,      𝔨 ∈ {in, out},    (50.27)

has a unique solution (φ_in, φ_out) on Ω₂ ∩ {τ ≤ τ*}, and it is smooth.

*Proof.* Since s_𝔨(h) = s_𝔨(w) − Σ_𝔧 φ_𝔧 [Y_𝔧(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨)], with Y_out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) = ω_in + O(λ) and Y_in(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) =
O(λ) by (L4), and likewise for out, (50.27) is a linear system of two transports along transversal null
generators, L0 φ_in = −½ e^ψ 𝒫 s_in(h) and Z_out φ_out = ½ 𝒫 s_out(h)/ℓ_out(τ) by (L7), coupled through the maps φ ↦
½ 𝒫([Y_𝔧(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨)] φ), which are bounded on L²(A(τ)) by (M1). By Lemma 5.6 and Lemma 50.10, the
solution map of the two transports with zero data on a slab [τ1, τ1 + δ] is bounded from L¹ in τ to C in τ with values
in L²(A(τ)), so the map that takes (φ_in, φ_out) to the solutions with the sources computed from h is a contraction in
C([τ1, τ1 + δ]; L²(A(τ)))² for δ small independently of the data. Picard iteration on successive slabs gives a unique
solution on [τ0, τ*]. It is smooth, 𝒫 smoothing in x at fixed λ and (M6) giving the τ-derivatives. ∎

The estimates below use (50.27) through s_𝔨(h), which 𝒩₂ controls, the coupling being inside h. If the
phases were defined through s_𝔨(w) instead, their sources would contain 𝒫([Y_𝔧(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨)] φ_𝔧), with a coefficient that
oscillates at the mollifier's own scale, and λ^j ‖∂^j ∂ 𝒫(c φ_𝔧)‖ with every derivative on c costs λ⁻¹ ‖φ_𝔧‖ by (M2):
a power of λ would be lost.

**Lemma 50.22** (The equation for h.) With φ_𝔨 from (50.27) and h := w − Σ_𝔨 φ_𝔨 Y_𝔨, the
equation Ric^H(g_app + w) = 0 is

    −½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b h + B·dh + C·h = ℰ + 𝒬(w) − Σ_𝔨 𝒬_φ^𝔨 − ½ λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 ((1 − 𝒫) s_𝔨(h)) G2^𝔨
          + λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 ((ℓ_app^𝔨 − ℓ_𝔨)·dφ_𝔨) G2^𝔨 − Σ_𝔨 φ_𝔨 [T1^𝔨] + ½ Σ_𝔨 (□̃_app φ_𝔨) G1^𝔨
          + ½ λ Σ_𝔨 (□̃_app φ_𝔨) [F_𝔨 g2] − Σ_𝔨 (B1^𝔨·dφ_𝔨 + C1^𝔨 φ_𝔨).    (50.28)

Every coefficient on the right is a bounded profile, except the one of order λ⁻¹ of each family, which multiplies
(1 − 𝒫) s_𝔨(h) = O(λ ∂s_𝔨(h)) by (M3); and |ℓ_app^𝔨 − ℓ_𝔨| ≤ C λ.

*Proof.* Insert w = h + Σ_𝔨 φ_𝔨 Y_𝔨 in P_g(w) = ℰ + 𝒬(w) and use (L1) for P_g(h) and (L2) for P_g(φ_𝔨 Y_𝔨). The terms of
order λ⁻¹ are ½ λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 s_𝔨(h) G2^𝔨 − λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 (ℓ_app^𝔨·dφ_𝔨) G2^𝔨, and by (50.27), ℓ_𝔨·dφ_𝔨 = ½ 𝒫 s_𝔨(h),
so they are ½ λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 ((1 − 𝒫) s_𝔨(h)) G2^𝔨 − λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 ((ℓ_app^𝔨 − ℓ_𝔨)·dφ_𝔨) G2^𝔨. Move them and the terms of (L2) to
the right side. ∎

**Lemma 50.23** (The ℓ_in ⊗ ℓ_in component.) With s := s_in(h),

    □̃ s = c1·dh + c0·h + Σ_𝔨 (c2^𝔨·dφ_𝔨 + c3^𝔨 φ_𝔨) − q ω_in Ψ_out + q λ⁻¹ ((1 − 𝒫) s_out(h)) G2^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in)
          + Σ_𝔨 c4^(𝔨,ab) ∂_a∂_b φ_𝔨 − 2q ℰ(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) − 2q 𝒬(w)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + 2q Σ_𝔨 𝒬_φ^𝔨(ℓ_in, ℓ_in)
          + Σ_(b,i) c^(bi) (∂_b∂_i h)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in),    (50.29)

with c0, c1, c2^𝔨, c3^𝔨 bounded coefficients (profiles, and profiles times the function q of (L5)), ω_in and
G2^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) bounded profiles oscillating in θ2, |c4^𝔨| ≤ C λ, |c^(bi)| ≤ C (λ + |w|) and |∂c^(bi)| ≤ C (1 + |∂w|),
i spatial. 𝒬_φ^in(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) contains second derivatives of φ_in only with a factor λ |w|, and 𝒬_φ^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in)
contains |w| |∂² φ_out|. The only coefficient of order λ⁻¹ multiplies (1 − 𝒫) s_out(h), which is O(λ ∂s_out(h)) by (M3).
The mirror statement holds for s_out(h), with ℓ_out ⊗ ℓ_out, ω_out and Ψ_in.

*Proof.* By (L5), □̃ s = (□̃h)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + c1·dh + c0·h, ℓ_in being smooth and λ-independent, and (□̃h)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) =
q (g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b h)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + Σ c^(bi) (∂_b∂_i h)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + (first order), each term of c^(ab) ∂_a∂_b having a
spatial index because c^(ττ) = 0. By (50.28), (g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b h)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) is −2 times the contraction of its
right side minus B·dh − C·h. Contract with ℓ_in ⊗ ℓ_in using (L4). Family in: G1^in(ℓ_in, ·) = G2^in(ℓ_in, ·) = 0
removes its term of order λ⁻¹, its (ℓ_app^in − ℓ_in) term and ½ (□̃_app φ_in) G1^in exactly, and ½ λ (□̃_app φ_in) [F1
g2](ℓ_in, ℓ_in) is O(λ |∂² φ_in|). Family out: −½ λ⁻¹ ((1 − 𝒫) s_out(h)) G2^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) survives, and gives the term
with q λ⁻¹; λ⁻¹ ((ℓ_app^out − ℓ_out)·dφ_out) G2^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) is O(|dφ_out|), since |ℓ_app^out − ℓ_out| ≤ C λ;
½ (□̃_app φ_out) ω_in = ½ ω_in Ψ_out + O(λ |∂² φ_out|), because □̃_app − □̃ = c′^(ab) ∂_a∂_b with |c′| ≤ C λ; and
½ λ (□̃_app φ_out) [F2 g2](ℓ_in, ℓ_in) is O(λ |∂² φ_out|). The rest is of first order or part of 𝒬_φ^𝔨. In 𝒬_φ^𝔨 the
second derivatives of φ_𝔨 multiply Y_𝔨, and Y_in(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) = λ [F1 g2](ℓ_in, ℓ_in), Y_out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) = ω_in + O(λ).
So φ_in drops out at the top order, φ_out enters only through Ψ_out with the bounded coefficient −q ω_in, and no
coefficient of order λ⁻¹ remains other than the one stated. ∎

So s_in's equation has no large coefficient, and at the top order it is coupled to Ψ_out through a bounded profile
oscillating in θ2; the equation for s_out is the mirror image. This replaces Lemma 6.4.

*Proof of Theorem 50.19.* The proof follows the eight steps of the proof of Theorem 6.1, on Ω₂,
with 𝒩₂ for 𝒩, (50.28) for (6.5), (50.29) for Lemma 6.4, and (L6) for
Lemma 6.5. Every constant depends on Ω₂, k, K and the profiles, never on λ.

**Step 1** (what 𝒩₂ controls). λ^j ∂^j(φ_𝔨 Y_𝔨) is a sum of λ^i ∂^i φ_𝔨 times bounded profiles, and λ^i ‖∂^i φ_𝔨‖ ≤ λ 𝒩₂
for 1 ≤ i ≤ k + 1, ‖φ_𝔨‖ ≤ 𝒩₂. So, as in Step 1 there, |w|_(k+1) ≤ C 𝒩₂, ‖∂^i w‖_∞ ≤ C λ^(−3−i) 𝒩₂ for i ≤ 4, and |∂w|_k
≤ C λ⁻¹ 𝒩₂.

**Step 2** (data). φ_𝔨 = 0 on Σ_τ0, so h = w there, and the derivatives of φ_𝔨 tangent to Σ_τ0 vanish; so ∂_τ φ_𝔨 =
½ 𝒫 s_𝔨(h)/ℓ_𝔨(τ) there by (50.27), with no factor λ⁻¹, ℓ_in(τ) = −e^(−ψ) and |ℓ_out(τ)| ≥ c. The higher
τ-derivatives of h, φ_𝔨 and Ψ_𝔨 on Σ_τ0 follow from (50.27), (50.28) and the equation for w, as
there, and 𝒩₂(τ0) ≤ C (C_D + C_R) λ^K.

**Step 3** (the bootstrap). Suppose 𝒩₂ ≤ 2M λ^K on [τ0, τ*]. Then |w| ≤ C M λ^(K−3) and |∂w| ≤ C M λ^(K−4), so for
λ ≤ λ0(M), |g − g0| ≤ ε1: the conclusions of Lemma 50.8 (e) hold for g (Σ_τ and the lateral boundaries
spacelike, both generators transverse to Σ_τ), and |∂g| ≤ Λ with Λ independent of M.

**Step 4** (h). Apply ∂^α, |α| = j ≤ k, to (50.28), apply Lemma 5.5 to each component, and multiply by
λ^j. Term by term, with the exponent of λ each attains:

- (a) the commutator [∂^α, g^(ab)] ∂_a∂_b h: ‖∂^i g_app‖_∞ ≤ C λ^(1−i), so at most C 𝒩₂, and the w part at most
  C M λ^(K−4) 𝒩₂, with ∂^i w in L^∞ for i ≤ 4 and in L² for i ≥ 5, as in Step 4 there;
- (b) ℰ: at most C_R λ^K, by (E3);
- (c) B·dh and C·h: at most C 𝒩₂, a derivative on a profile costing λ⁻¹ and the weight paying for it;
- (d) ½ λ⁻¹ ((1 − 𝒫) s_𝔨(h)) G2^𝔨: Σ_i λ^(i−1) ‖∂^i (1 − 𝒫) s_𝔨‖ ≤ C Σ_i λ^i ‖∂^i ∂s_𝔨‖ ≤ C 𝒩₂, by (M3), (M4), (M6);
- (e) λ⁻¹ ((ℓ_app^𝔨 − ℓ_𝔨)·dφ_𝔨) G2^𝔨: ℓ_app^𝔨 − ℓ_𝔨 is λ times a profile, by (L4), so at most C 𝒩₂;
- (f) φ_𝔨 [T1^𝔨], B1^𝔨·dφ_𝔨 and C1^𝔨 φ_𝔨: at most C 𝒩₂;
- (g) ½ (□̃_app φ_𝔨) G1^𝔨 = ½ Ψ_𝔨 G1^𝔨 + ½ (c′^(ab) ∂_a∂_b φ_𝔨) G1^𝔨 with |c′| ≤ C λ: the first at most C 𝒩₂, both Ψ_𝔨
  being in 𝒩₂ at every level; the second by (L6), λ^(j+1) ‖∂^j ∂² φ_𝔨‖ ≤ C 𝒩₂, since λ^(j+1) ‖∂^j L_𝔨 𝒫 s_𝔨‖ ≤ C λ^(j+1)
  ‖∂^j ∂s_𝔨‖ by (M4), (M6) (no Bernstein inequality is needed here);
- (h) ½ λ (□̃_app φ_𝔨) [F_𝔨 g2] = λ (Ψ_𝔨 + O(λ) ∂² φ_𝔨) times a profile: at most C λ 𝒩₂;
- (i) 𝒬_φ^𝔨: at most C M λ^(K−5) 𝒩₂ ≤ C M λ 𝒩₂, as K ≥ 6, its part |w| |∂² φ_𝔨| at most C M λ^(K−4) 𝒩₂;
- (j) 𝒬(w): at most C λ⁻⁵ 𝒩₂² ≤ C M² λ^(2K−5) ≤ C M² λ^(K+1), as K ≥ 6, the worst term being quadratic in
  ∂w, |∂w ∂w|_k ≤ C λ⁻³ |∂w|_k², by the product bound of Lemma 5.1 at the top derivatives of w.

The g0 part of [∂^α, g^(ab)] and the commutator [∂_x², L_𝔨] of Step 5 have smooth λ-independent coefficients and are at
most C 𝒩₂. So

    Σ_(j≤k) λ^j ‖∂^j ∂h(τ)‖ + ‖h(τ)‖ ≤ C (𝒩₂(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^τ (𝒩₂ + C_R λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1))).

No term in (a)–(j) has a coefficient of order λ⁻¹ beyond (d), which (M3) pays for, and the two families enter (d)–(i)
once each.

**Step 5** (φ_in, φ_out). Each φ_𝔨 obeys its own transport (50.27) with right side ½ 𝒫 s_𝔨(h): L0 φ_in =
−½ e^ψ 𝒫 s_in(h), the transport (6.4) with the smooth bounded factor e^ψ, and Z_out φ_out =
½ 𝒫 s_out(h)/ℓ_out(τ). Apply ∂^α, |α| = j ≤ k: [L0, ∂^α] and [Z_out, ∂^α] have smooth λ-independent coefficients and
involve derivatives of φ_𝔨 of order at most j, and λ^j ‖∂^α ∂ 𝒫 s_𝔨‖ ≤ C λ^j ‖∂^(j+1) s_𝔨(h)‖ ≤ C 𝒩₂ by (M1), (M4),
(M6), s_𝔨(h) = h(ℓ_𝔨, ℓ_𝔨) with ℓ_𝔨 smooth. For λ ∂_x² φ_𝔨 use the transport of (L6), whose right side is
½ ∂_x² (𝒫 s_𝔨/ℓ_𝔨(τ)). Its top term ½ (∂_x² 𝒫 s_𝔨)/ℓ_𝔨(τ) takes the Bernstein bound (M2) on one spatial derivative:
λ^(j+1) ‖∂^j ∂_x² 𝒫 s_𝔨‖ ≤ C λ^j ‖∂^j ∂_x s_𝔨‖ ≤ C 𝒩₂; its other terms carry at most one derivative of 𝒫 s_𝔨, with
smooth λ-independent coefficients, and are at most C 𝒩₂ by (M1), (M4), (M6). Lemma 5.6 for φ_in
and Lemma 50.10 for φ_out bound the φ-part of 𝒩₂(τ) by C (𝒩₂(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^τ 𝒩₂). Without (M2) the
transport of ∂_x² φ_𝔨 would need k + 2 derivatives of s_𝔨.

**Step 6** (Ψ_in, Ψ_out). Apply ∂^α to the transport of (L6) for Ψ_in, along L_in = −e^(−ψ) L0 with the bounded
coefficient a_in, and Lemma 5.6. In ½ □̃ 𝒫 s_in = ½ 𝒫 □̃ s_in + ½ [□̃, 𝒫] s_in insert (50.29).

- (a) 𝒫 of the terms of (50.29): c1·dh, c0·h, c2^𝔨·dφ_𝔨 and c3^𝔨 φ_𝔨 give at most C 𝒩₂. The coupling:
  ‖𝒫(q ω_in Ψ_out)‖ ≤ C ‖Ψ_out‖ by (M1), and λ^j ‖∂^j 𝒫(q ω_in Ψ_out)‖ ≤ C Σ_(i≤j) λ^i ‖∂^i Ψ_out‖ ≤ C 𝒩₂, each
  derivative on the profile q ω_in costing λ⁻¹ and the weight paying for it. q λ⁻¹ ((1 − 𝒫) s_out) G2^out(ℓ_in, ℓ_in)
  is at most C 𝒩₂ by (M3); c4^𝔨 ∂² φ_𝔨 at most C 𝒩₂ by (L6); ℰ, 𝒬(w) and 𝒬_φ^𝔨 give C_R λ^K, C M² λ^(K+1) and
  C M λ^(K−5) 𝒩₂; and Σ c^(bi) ∂_b∂_i h, written 𝒫 ∂_i(c ∂_b h) − 𝒫((∂_i c) ∂_b h) with the Bernstein bound on the ∂_i,
  is at most C λ⁻¹ ‖c ∂h‖ + C ‖∂h‖ ≤ C 𝒩₂, as |c| ≤ C (λ + |w|); at level j only k + 1 derivatives of h occur, where
  taking the second derivatives directly would need k + 2.
- (b) [□̃, 𝒫] s_in: the terms with a spatial index are at most C ‖∂s_in‖ by the first form of (M5). The ττ term is
  rewritten through ∂_τ² s_in = (□̃ s_in − 2 g0^(τi) ∂_τ∂_i s_in − g0^(ij) ∂_i∂_j s_in)/g0^(ττ), g0^(ττ) ≤ −1, after
  which the second form of (M5) gains λ on every term of (50.29), the coupling included (at most C λ 𝒩₂),
  except Σ c^(bi) ∂_b∂_i h, which is written ∂_i(c ∂_b h) − (∂_i c) ∂_b h and bounded by the first form (the second
  form on them would cost a derivative at j = k, as in Step 6 there); and g0^(ab) (∂_a∂_b 𝒫 − 𝒫 ∂_a∂_b) s_in is at
  most C ‖∂s_in‖ by (M4), (M6).
- (c) −½ M_in(𝒫 s_in) and −N_in φ_in are of first order, at most C 𝒩₂.

So the Ψ_in-part of 𝒩₂(τ) is at most C (𝒩₂(τ0) + ∫ (𝒩₂ + C_R λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1))). The same holds for Ψ_out, along
Z_out with Lemma 50.10, whose right side contains 𝒫(q′ ω_out Ψ_in). The coupling enters through ∫ 𝒩₂: Ψ_in
and Ψ_out are estimated together, which is why both are in 𝒩₂. Treated as a generic second derivative of φ_out, the
coupling term would lose a power of λ.

**Step 7** (closing). Steps 4–6 give 𝒩₂(τ) ≤ C2 (𝒩₂(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^τ 𝒩₂ + (τ_end − τ0)(C_R λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1))), C2
independent of M and λ. Gronwall's lemma and Step 2 give 𝒩₂(τ) ≤ C3 ((C_D + 1 + C_R) λ^K + C M² λ^(K+1)). With M :=
C3 (C_D + 1 + C_R) + 1 and λ0 such that C3 C M² λ0 ≤ 1 and Step 3 holds, 𝒩₂ ≤ M λ^K < 2M λ^K, which improves the
bootstrap assumption. K ≥ 6 enters only in (i) and (j) of Step 4, through 2K − 5 ≥ K + 1 and K − 5 ≥ 1. 𝒩₂ is
continuous in τ for a smooth solution, so the set of τ* for which the assumption holds is open and closed in the
interval of existence.

**Step 8** (existence, continuation and uniqueness). This is Step 8 of the proof of Theorem 6.1 with Ω₂ in
place of Ω. Its part (i) uses of the background only that the extended approximant has spacelike slices {τ = const},
with lapse, shift and spatial metric bounded above and below, on a neighbourhood of the domain; here the profiles of
g_app, g0 among them, are extended from Ω₂ by Stein's operator (Theorem A.36), and by continuity and the
compactness of Ω₂ (Lemma 50.8 (a), (e)) this holds on a neighbourhood U of Ω₂ for λ small, with bounds
independent of λ. With a smooth cut-off equal to 1 on a smaller neighbourhood U′ of Ω₂ and supported in U, the lapse,
shift and spatial metric are interpolated convexly, inside U, between those of the extended approximant and (1, 0, δ),
as there, and equal (1, 0, δ) outside U; on U′ nothing changes. Parts (ii)–(iv) are unchanged, the slices being the
annuli A(τ) of Ω₂. Uniqueness among C² solutions with |g − g0| ≤ ε1 is
the energy argument there, and with Step 7 the bootstrap continues, so the solution exists on all of Ω₂ with
(50.26). The bounds after (50.26) follow from Step 1 as there: |w| ≤ C λ⁻³ 𝒩₂, |∂w| ≤
C λ⁻⁴ 𝒩₂, and |g − g0| ≤ |λ [g1] + Σ_(j≥2) λ^j [g_j]| + |w| ≤ C λ, |∂g| ≤ C, since ∂[λ g1] = dv ⊗ [F1 g1] + du ⊗ [F2
g1] + λ [∂_X g1] is bounded. ∎

### 50.6 The data

**Theorem 50.24** (Exact data with two families.) Let K ≥ 6 and N := K + 3, and let g_app be the
approximant of Theorem 50.18 with N stages and the stage data of Lemma 50.26, in its
fixed-phase form. For λ small there is a vacuum Cauchy datum on Σ_τ0, with the gauge condition D = 0 imposed through
∂_τ g, whose w := g − g_app satisfies (E4) of Theorem 6.1; it equals the seed's datum on Σ_τ0 ∩ {R < r1},
and it is smooth and invariant under the T² action and both reflections.

The proof is that of Theorem 7.1 on the two-dust slice, with the changes of the next two lemmas.

**Lemma 50.25** (The constraints on a round slice.) Let γ = G(R) dR² + R² γ̂ on [a, b1] × S³, G > 0,
and let κ be any symmetric 2-tensor invariant under O(4). With U = (α, ϖ, q) and (γ_U, κ_U) as in (7.4), the
linearisation at U = 0 of the constraint map of (γ_U, κ_U) has the principal part

    ρ ≅ (3/(R G²)) ∂_R α − (1/(G R²)) Δ_(S³) α,
    J_R ≅ 6 ∂_R ϖ − (2/R²) γ̂^(AB) ∂_A q_B,      J_A ≅ −(2/G) ∂_R q_A + 4 ∂_A ϖ,

with no ∂_R² α and no ∂_R∂_A α in ρ, and independent of κ. The coefficient of ∂_R α is (γ^(RR))^(3/2) H, H = 3/(R √G) >
0 the mean curvature of the spheres; the symmetrizer 𝒮 = diag(1, −½ Π⁻¹), Π = R² γ̂, gives 𝒮A0 = diag(6, G⁻¹ Π⁻¹) > 0
and 𝒮A^B symmetric for every angle B; and in the class of fields of (R, ϑ) invariant under T² and both reflections the
characteristic speeds satisfy c² = 2G/(3R²) > 0. At G = 1 + μ/R² these are the formulas of Lemma 7.5
(a). The slice Σ_τ0 of the two-dust background is such a slice, with G = e^ψ (2 − e^ψ f) ≥ e^ψ > 0.

*Proof.* The proof of Lemma 7.5 (a) is written for γ = ν² dr² + Π_AB (dω^A + σ^A dr)(dω^B + σ^B dr)
in general. Here ν² = G, the shift σ^A vanishes and Π = R² γ̂, so the second fundamental form of the spheres is (1/(2ν))
∂_R Π = (R/√G) γ̂, with trace H = 3/(R √G) with respect to Π. The coefficient of ∂_R α is (γ^(RR))^(3/2) H = G^(−3/2) ·
3/(R √G) = 3/(R G²), and the angular second derivatives of α are −γ^(RR) Π^(AB) ∂_A∂_B α = −(G R²)⁻¹ Δ_(S³) α; κ enters ρ
only through −|κ_U|² + (tr κ_U)², algebraically. The principal part of J there, at γ^(RA) = 0 and α = 0, is J_R ≅ 6 ∂_R ϖ
− 2 Π^(AB) ∂_A q_B and J_A ≅ 4 ∂_A ϖ − 2 γ^(RR) ∂_R q_A, and (7.6) at γ^(RA) = 0 is 𝒮 = diag(1, −½
Π⁻¹), with 𝒮A0 = diag(6, γ^(RR) Π^(AB)). In the class, A0 = diag(6, −2/G) and A^ϑ = [[0, −2/R²], [4, 0]] in (ϖ, q_ϑ), and
det(A^ϑ − c A0) = −12 c²/G + 8/R² vanishes at c² = 2G/(3R²). On Σ_τ0, dτ = 0 gives dv = dR, so by (50.8)
the induced metric is (2e^ψ − e^(2ψ) f) dR² + R² dΩ₃²; and 2 − e^ψ f ≥ 1, as e^ψ ≤ 1 and f ≤ 1. ∎

So the slice need not be a Vaidya slice: H > 0 holds on every round slice on which R is a coordinate.

**Lemma 50.26** (The gauge hierarchy and the stage data, two families.) (a) Lemma 7.3
holds for the approximant of Lemma 50.17 with N stages, with D^(m)(X, θ1, θ2) two-phase profiles, (F1)–(F2)
there for all (θ1, θ2), and its conclusion ∂_θ D^(N−1) = 0 read as: D^(N−1) does not depend on (θ1, θ2).

(b) For every N there are stage data for Theorem 50.18 satisfying (F1) and (F2) of
Lemma 7.3, all vanishing on Σ_τ0 ∩ {R < r1}; "the stage data of Lemma 50.26" means those
constructed in the proof. The mixed harmonics of every profile vanish off the diamond Q×, and in particular on a
neighbourhood of Σ_τ0.

*Proof.* (a) Let G be the profile of (50.21), with the phases u_in, u_out, and write D(g_app) =
[Σ_(m≥0) λ^m D^(m)] in this two-scale form. As in Section 7.3, (7.1) holds order by order for
the profiles, its right side at order j involving ℛ^(i), i ≤ j + 1, only; these vanish for i ≤ N − 1
(Lemma 50.17). In two-scale form the principal part ½ g^(ab) ∂_a∂_b of B_g ((7.1)) acts on a
term λ^m [Y] of D as

    λ^(m−2) ½ Σ_(𝔧,𝔨) G⁻¹(du_𝔧, du_𝔨) F_𝔧 F_𝔨 Y + λ^(m−1) Σ_𝔨 (G⁻¹(du_𝔨, ∂_X) + ½ □_G u_𝔨) F_𝔨 Y + λ^m ½ G^(ab) ∂_a∂_b Y,

and its other terms, of first order in D with bounded coefficients, as λ^(m−1) Σ_𝔨 𝔪_𝔨 F_𝔨 Y + O(λ^m), 𝔪_𝔨 bounded
multiplications by profiles. Here G⁻¹(du_𝔨, ∂_X) = ℓ_𝔨·∂_X + O(λ) and □_G u_𝔨 = □_(g0) ϕ_𝔨 + O(λ), the part
Σ_𝔧 dϕ_𝔧 ⊗ F_𝔧 W_𝔧 of order one of ∂G dropping out because each W_𝔧 is traceless with W_𝔧(ℓ_𝔧, ·) = 0. The contractions
of the phases are

    G⁻¹(du_in, du_in) = −λ e^(−4σ) χ_out(X, θ2) + O(λ²),      G⁻¹(du_out, du_out) = −λ e^(−4σ) χ_in(X, θ1) + O(λ²),
    G⁻¹(du_in, du_out) = g0^(uv) + λ c + O(λ²),      g0^(uv) = −e^(−2σ),

with c a bounded profile. Indeed G⁻¹ = ḡ⁻¹ − λ ḡ⁻¹ W ḡ⁻¹ + O(λ²), so G⁻¹(du_in, du_in) = ḡ⁻¹(du_in, du_in) −
λ W(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) + O(λ²); here ḡ⁻¹(du_in, du_in) = O(λ^(N+1)) by (b′) of (50.23), W_in(ℓ_in, ·) =
0, W_TT^out(ℓ_in, ·) = 0 as W_TT^out is angular, and χ_out (du ⊗ du)(ℓ_in, ℓ_in) = χ_out g0⁻¹(du, dv)² = e^(−4σ)
χ_out; likewise for out. This is the two-scale form of (L4) of Lemma 50.20: the other family's term χ_out du
⊗ du is not annihilated by ℓ_in, so G⁻¹(du_in, du_in) is of order λ, not λ². Hence:

(α) at order λ^(m−2) the principal part acts on Y as g0^(uv) F1F2 Y, the coefficients g0⁻¹(dϕ_𝔨, dϕ_𝔨) of F_𝔨²
vanishing: it multiplies the mixed harmonic (n1, n2) of Y by e^(−2σ) n1 n2, which does not vanish, and annihilates the
mean and the pure harmonics of Y;

(β) at order λ^(m−1), the principal part and the other terms of B_g act on Y as

    Σ_𝔨 (ℓ_𝔨·∂_X + ½ □_(g0) ϕ_𝔨 + 𝔪_𝔨) F_𝔨 Y + c F1F2 Y − ½ e^(−4σ) χ_out F1² Y − ½ e^(−4σ) χ_in F2² Y.

Every term of (β) contains a phase derivative of Y, so (β) vanishes on a Y that does not depend on (θ1, θ2). On a pure
harmonic Y of θ1, c F1F2 Y = 0 and F2² Y = 0, and −½ e^(−4σ) χ_out F1² Y is the product of a pure harmonic of θ1 with
the function χ_out of θ2, of zero mean, so it has mixed harmonics only; likewise on a pure harmonic of θ2.

Induct on m = 0, …, N − 2 with the hypothesis (H_m): D^(j) = 0 for j < m, D^(m) does not depend on (θ1, θ2), and the
mixed harmonics of D^(m+1) vanish. (H_0) holds: D^(0) = 0 by Lemma 50.13 (f), and at order −1 the only
term of (7.1) is, by (α), g0^(uv) F1F2 D^(1), its right side involving only ℛ^(−1) and ℛ^(0), which vanish;
so the mixed harmonics of D^(1) vanish. Assume (H_m). At order m the terms of the left side of (7.1) are:
from D^(m), only terms without phase derivatives, by (β), namely ½ □̃ ⟨D^(m)⟩ and terms of first order in ⟨D^(m)⟩ with
bounded profiles as coefficients; from D^(m+1), whose mixed harmonics vanish, by (β), Σ_𝔨 (ℓ_𝔨·∂_X + ½ □_(g0) ϕ_𝔨 + 𝔪_𝔨)
Ξ_𝔨 with Ξ_𝔨 := F_𝔨 Π_𝔨 D^(m+1), together with −½ e^(−4σ) χ_out F1 Ξ_in − ½ e^(−4σ) χ_in F2 Ξ_out, which has mixed
harmonics only; and from D^(m+2), by (α), g0^(uv) F1F2 D^(m+2), which has mixed harmonics only. The terms from D^(j),
for j ≥ m + 3, are of higher order. So the mean of the order-m equation is the linear wave equation for ⟨D^(m)⟩ of the
proof of Lemma 7.3, with the forcing Σ_𝔨 ⟨𝔪_𝔨 Ξ_𝔨⟩; its pure harmonics of θ_𝔨 are the transport

    (ℓ_𝔨·∂_X + ½ □_(g0) ϕ_𝔨) Ξ_𝔨 + Π_𝔨 Σ_𝔧 𝔪_𝔧 Ξ_𝔧 = (first order in ⟨D^(m)⟩)

along ℓ_𝔨, the two transports coupled through bounded multiplications; and its mixed harmonics are algebraic and give
the mixed harmonics of D^(m+2), divided by e^(−2σ) n1 n2, in terms of ⟨D^(m)⟩, the Ξ_𝔨 and their X-derivatives, the
terms −½ e^(−4σ) χ_out F1 Ξ_in and −½ e^(−4σ) χ_in F2 Ξ_out among them. The data of ⟨D^(m)⟩, ∂_τ⟨D^(m)⟩ and the Ξ_𝔨 are
zero by (F1)–(F2), so the system for (⟨D^(m)⟩, Ξ_in, Ξ_out), which closes as the stage equations do
(Lemma 50.17, both generators reaching Σ_τ0 inside Ω₂), gives ⟨D^(m)⟩ = 0 and Ξ_𝔨 = 0. Then D^(m) = 0, the
pure harmonics of D^(m+1) vanish, so that D^(m+1) does not depend on (θ1, θ2), and the mixed harmonics of D^(m+2)
vanish: (H_(m+1)). At m = N − 2 this gives D^(m) = 0 for m ≤ N − 2 and D^(N−1) independent of (θ1, θ2). The rest is the
proof of Lemma 7.3.

(b) Supports. The harmonics with n1 ≠ 0 of W_in, and those with n2 ≠ 0 of W_out, vanish where v ∉ (v_start, v_end),
respectively u ∉ (u1, u2). For every later profile the same holds by induction over the stages: a harmonic with n1 ≠ 0
of a forcing term contains a factor with such a harmonic, the pure harmonics of θ1 are transported along ℓ_in at fixed
v, the divisions are pointwise, and the data below are fixed pointwise on Σ_τ0 from such terms; likewise for n2 and u.
So every mixed harmonic vanishes off Q× = [u1, u2] × [v_start, v_end], which lies in the future of Σ_τ0, and the mixed
harmonics take no data.

The construction is that of the proof of Lemma 7.4. Stage 0: χ_in = χ_out = 0 on Σ_τ0 ((50.19)).
Stage m = 1, …, N: φ_m^in = φ_m^out = 0 and (m_m)_(τ ·) = 0 on Σ_τ0. (i) On Σ_τ0 the pure harmonics of θ_𝔨 of the
oscillating part of D^(m) are Pol_𝔨(F_𝔨 Π_𝔨 ĝ_(m+1)) + Λ_m^𝔨(γ_m) + (known), with Pol_𝔨(Y) := Y(ℓ_𝔨, ·) − ½ dϕ_𝔨 tr_(g0)
Y; Pol_𝔨 is onto at every point, by the construction of the proof of Lemma 7.4 with the null covector dϕ_𝔨 in
place of dv, and its right inverse Pol_𝔨⁺ = Pol_𝔨^T (Pol_𝔨 Pol_𝔨^T)⁻¹ commutes with the symmetries; so each family's
pure harmonics of ĝ_(m+1) are fixed as there, each on its own support. The mixed harmonics of D^(m) vanish on Σ_τ0 by
the supports. (ii) As there. (iii) As there, with Lemma 50.25 in place of Lemma 7.5 (a):
the order-m mean of the constraints is a linear radial problem on the two-dust slice, solved by Lemma 7.6
outward from R = a with zero data, through the packet and then the shell; its forcing terms vanish where the earlier
stages' data and both families' waves do, so on R < r1. ∎

*Proof of Theorem 50.24.* The proof in Section 7.5 applies, with Lemma 50.26 for
Lemma 7.3 and Lemma 7.4, and with Lemma 7.5 (a) at the data of g0 replaced by
Lemma 50.25. Lemma 7.5 (b) and (c) hold as stated, with the same proofs: they use of the
approximant's data only that on Σ_τ0 every phase is a function of R, so that phase derivatives are radial (here v = τ0 +
R and u is a function of R on the slice, Proposition 50.6 (a)); that the parts W_TT^𝔨 of the waves have only
angular components and are traceless on the spheres, and the other parts are multiples of dϕ_𝔨 ⊗ dϕ_𝔨, which on Σ_τ0 is a
multiple of dR ⊗ dR; that φ_j^𝔨 = 0 and (m_j)_(τ ·) = 0 there and γ_RA = O(λ²); that g0^(Aτ) = 0, g0 being round; and
that the mixed harmonics vanish on Σ_τ0. In particular, at the approximant's data the constraint map of (γ_U, κ_U) has no
coefficient of order λ⁻¹: the second derivatives of γ of order λ⁻¹, λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨 (∂_R ϕ_𝔨)² [F_𝔨² W_𝔨] in ∂_R² γ, enter the
coefficients of U in ρ only through the traces of the W_TT^𝔨 on the spheres, which vanish; and in J the derivatives of κ
of order λ⁻¹ enter only through κ̃_RA, κ̃ the order-one oscillating part of κ, which vanishes, and through the ∂_R κ_RR
terms of div κ and d tr κ, which cancel. This holds for any phases that are functions of R on the slice, null or not; and
the constraint map depends only on g and ∂_τ g on Σ_τ0, not on ∂_τ² of the phases, so the eikonal equation of the
outgoing phase is not used by the data. The principal coefficients at the approximant's data have the background's values
at order zero in every harmonic, H's oscillating part (1/(2ν)) Π0^(AB) Σ_𝔨 ∂_R ϕ_𝔨 [F_𝔨 W_𝔨,AB] vanishing.
Proposition 7.7 then holds on [a, b(τ0)] × S³ with its proof, U = 0 on R < r1, where the constraint map of (γ,
κ) and the forcing vanish. ∎

### 50.7 The spheres' horizon and the mean mass

**Proposition 50.27** (One zero per column, two families.) Let μ0 ≥ √72 l5² and K ≥ 6, and for a
column let θ⁺_λ(R) be the outgoing null expansion, for g_λ, of the sphere S_(v,R) = {τ = v − R, |x| = R} at its point
R x̂, and R_H(v) the radius on the column at which R² = μ. There are λ_H ∈ (0, λ0] and C, δ1, δ2 > 0, independent of λ,
such that for λ ≤ λ_H: (a) on every column θ⁺_λ has at most one zero, and θ⁺_λ > 0 above it, < 0 below it; and, if
μ0 > √72 l5², (b) on every column with R_H(v) ≤ v − τ0 − δ1 it has exactly one zero R_λ(v, x̂), and |R_λ − R_H(v)| ≤
C λ; (c) the spheres with R ≤ R_H(v) − C λ (within the domain) are trapped, both future null expansions being negative
at every point, and those with R ≥ R_H(v) + C λ are untrapped. If μ0 = √72 l5², (b)–(c) hold on the columns with
R_H(v)² ≥ μ0 + δ2. In particular there is no inner apparent horizon.

*Proof.* (i) The background. The spheres S_(v,R) are the spheres {u, v = const}. The expansion of a round sphere along a
normal N is 3 N(R)/R. The future null normals ∂_v and ∂_u, normalised by n(τ) = 1, are ∂_v/(1 − R_v) and ∂_u/(−R_u),
since dτ(∂_v) = 1 − R_v ≥ ½ and dτ(∂_u) = −R_u > 0; so

    θ⁺(g0) = 3 R_v/(R (1 − R_v)) = 3 e^ψ f/(R (2 − e^ψ f)),      θ⁻(g0) = −3/R,

using R_v = e^ψ f/2 (Section 50.3). On a column R decreases in u, and ∂_u R_v = R_uv = −e^(2σ) μ/R³ < 0
(Lemma 50.5 (ii)), so along the column ∂_R R_v = R_uv/R_u = e^ψ μ/R³ > 0: θ⁺(g0) has at most one zero
on each column, at R_v = 0, that is at f = 0, R = R_H(v), and there ∂_R θ⁺(g0) = 3 e^ψ μ/R⁴ = 3 e^ψ/μ ≥ 3 e^(min
ψ)/μ_max, min ψ and μ_max := max μ taken over Ω₂. The ingoing expansion is negative everywhere.

(ii) The approximant. The proof of Lemma 8.3 applies with two phases: the conormal plane of the spheres is
spanned by dτ and dR, which also span du and dv, so Π_g^(ab) ∂_a ϕ_𝔨 = 0, and the fast part of θ^±(g) is ½ λ⁻¹ Σ_𝔨
k^±(g⁻¹ dϕ_𝔨) Π_g^(ab) [F_𝔨 ĝ_ab]. Its λ⁰ coefficient is ½ Σ_𝔨 k^±_0(ℓ_𝔨) F_𝔨 tr_S g1 = 0, because tr_S W_𝔨 = 0 on
every sphere ((8.3) for W_TT^𝔨, and dϕ_𝔨 ⊗ dϕ_𝔨 vanishes on vectors tangent to the spheres). So
θ^±(g_app) = θ^±(g0) + λ [Th1^±] + λ² E^±, with Th1^± a two-phase profile and E^± = e^±(X, v/λ, u/λ, λ), e^± smooth and
bounded with all its derivatives. Along a column v is constant, but u is not: by (50.2) the derivative
along a column of λ [Th1⁺] is λ [∂_R Th1⁺] + (∂_R u) [F2 Th1⁺], which is O(1) unless Th1⁺ does not depend on θ2. It does
not ((iii) below). Then ∂_R(λ [Th1⁺]) = O(λ) and ∂_R(λ² E⁺) = λ² [∂_R e⁺] + λ (∂_R u) [F2 e⁺] = O(λ), so along every
column

    |θ⁺(g_app) − θ⁺(g0)| + |∂_R (θ⁺(g_app) − θ⁺(g0))| ≤ C λ,

and |θ⁻(g_app) + 3/R| ≤ C λ.

(iii) The coefficient Th1⁺ does not depend on θ2. Work in the coordinates (u, v, y), y = (ϑ, φ1, φ2), off the axes (the
identities below extend to the axes by continuity), where the spheres are {u, v = const} with induced metric γ_AB :=
g_AB, A, B angular, and put α := (det γ_AB)^(1/2). For a normal covector k = k_u du + k_v dv and n := g⁻¹ k,

    θ_k = −γ^(AB) Γ[g]^c_AB k_c = (n^u ∂_u + n^v ∂_v) ln α + ½ γ^(AB) n^C ∂_C g_AB − γ^(AB) n^d ∂_A g_dB,
    (50.30)

since γ^(AB) ∂_d g_AB = 2 ∂_d ln α for d ∈ {u, v}. The outgoing covector is k⁺ = c(g)(du + β dv), with β fixed by g⁻¹(k⁺,
k⁺) = 0 and c(g) < 0 by n(τ) = 1, g0⁻¹ du = −e^(−2σ) ∂_v being past directed; for g0, β = 0 and n0 = c0 g0⁻¹ du has no
angular component and n0^u = 0. The last two terms of (50.30) contain only angular derivatives of g, which
carry no phase derivative since ∂_A ϕ_𝔨 = 0. At order λ they are products of first-order quantities with g0-quantities;
as g0_dB = 0 for d ∈ {u, v}, n0^C = 0, the oscillating parts of g1 have no components g1_dB with d ∈ {u, v} (W_TT^𝔨 is
angular and χ_𝔨 dϕ_𝔨 ⊗ dϕ_𝔨 lies in the (u, v)-block), and the oscillating part of the λ-coefficient n1 of n has no
angular component, their coefficient of λ does not depend on (θ1, θ2). In the first term write ln α = ln α0 + λ a1 + λ²
a2 + O(λ³), with

    a1 = ½ tr_(γ0) G1 = ½ tr_S m1,      a2 = ½ tr_(γ0) G2 − ¼ |G1|²_(γ0),      G_j := (g_j)_AB,

tr_S W_𝔨 = 0 making a1 independent of (θ1, θ2). By (50.2), ∂_v [λ^j a_j] = λ^j [∂_v a_j] + λ^(j−1) [F1
a_j] and ∂_u [λ^j a_j] = λ^j [∂_u a_j] + λ^(j−1) [F2 a_j], so, with n = n0 + λ n1 + O(λ²) and n0^u = 0, the coefficient
of λ of the first term is n0^v [F1 a2] + n0^v [∂_v a1] + n1^v [∂_v ln α0] + n1^u [∂_u ln α0]. The λ-coefficient n1
depends on (θ1, θ2) only through g1(ℓ_out, ·) = m1(ℓ_out, ·) + [χ_in] dv(ℓ_out) dv, which enters β, c(g) and g⁻¹ at order
λ, and so only through θ1. Hence Th1⁺ depends on θ2 only through n0^v [F1 a2], that is through the mixed harmonics of a2
(F1 kills those of θ2 alone).

The mixed harmonics of a2 vanish. In the fixed-phase form, the mixed harmonics of G2 are those of ĝ_2 at the phases
θ1 + φ_1^in, θ2 + φ_1^out (the other parts of g2 are m2 and phase-shift terms φ_2^𝔨 F_𝔨 W_𝔨, which have no mixed
harmonics), and those of |G1|² are those of 2 ⟨W_TT^in, W_TT^out⟩_(γ0); so the mixed part of a2 is that of ã2 :=
½ tr_S ĝ_2 − ¼ |W_TT^in + W_TT^out|²_(γ0) at the shifted phases. We show that, for the stage-0 metric g0 + λ (W_in +
W_out) + λ² ĝ_2 of Lemma 50.13,

    γ0^(AB) R^(0)_AB = −2 g0^(uv) F1F2 ã2      on the mixed harmonics;    (50.31)

as R^(0) ≡ 0 and F1F2 multiplies the harmonic (n1, n2) by −n1 n2 ≠ 0, the mixed harmonics of ã2 then vanish. First,
Ric^H = Ric − S with S_AB = ½ (g_Aρ ∇̂_B D^ρ + g_Bρ ∇̂_A D^ρ), and D = O(λ) by Lemma 50.13 (f); the
derivatives in S_AB are angular, so they bring no factor λ⁻¹, and S_AB = O(λ). Ric has no term of order λ⁻¹ either, so
γ^(AB) Ric_AB has the λ⁰ coefficient γ0^(AB) R^(0)_AB. Second, a mixed harmonic of order λ⁰ comes only from terms with
two phase derivatives: bilinear in (W_in, W_out), or linear in λ² ĝ_2. The latter come from the
principal part alone and give e^(−2σ) F1F2 tr_S ĝ_2 = −2 g0^(uv) F1F2 (½ tr_S ĝ_2). The former are terms of Ric_AB with
two phase derivatives of g̃ := g0 + λ (W_in + W_out), and contain no angular derivative; Ric being at most quadratic in
first derivatives, they are those of the metric with the same components and the same derivatives in (u, v) at the
point and no dependence on y. The metric g̃ is block diagonal for the splitting into the (u, v)-block and the angular
block. For a metric h_ab(x) dx^a dx^b + γ_AB(x) dy^A dy^B, x = (u, v), whose components do not depend on y, the
Christoffel symbols are those of h, Γ^a_AB = −½ h^(ab) ∂_b γ_AB and Γ^A_aB = ½ γ^(AC) ∂_a γ_CB, so that

    Ric_AB = −½ □_h γ_AB − ¼ h^(ab) ∂_a ln det γ ∂_b γ_AB + ½ h^(ab) γ^(CD) ∂_a γ_AC ∂_b γ_BD,
    γ^(AB) Ric_AB = −α⁻¹ □_h α,      α = (det γ)^(1/2),    (50.32)

the trace following from γ^(AB) □_h γ_AB = □_h ln det γ + h^(ab) tr(γ⁻¹ ∂_a γ γ⁻¹ ∂_b γ); this is the trace identity of
colliding plane waves. For g̃, ln α = ln α0 + λ ½ tr_S W − ¼ λ² |W|²_(γ0) + O(λ³), and tr_S W = 0. In −α⁻¹ □_h α = −□_h
ln α − |d ln α|²_h, the terms of order λ⁰ with two phase derivatives come from −h0^(ab) ∂_a∂_b(−¼ λ² |W|²_(γ0)) alone
(d ln α = O(λ), and h − h0 = O(λ)), and their mixed part is −2 g0^(uv) F1F2(−¼ |W_TT^in + W_TT^out|²_(γ0)), the terms
with two derivatives in one phase being multiplied by g0^(uu) = g0^(vv) = 0. This gives (50.31).

(iv) The remainder. θ⁺(g) is a smooth function of (X, g) plus a smooth function of (X, g) times ∂g
(Lemma 8.3). So |θ⁺(g_λ) − θ⁺(g_app)| ≤ C (|w| + |∂w|), and its derivative along a column is at most C
(λ⁻¹ |w| + |∂w| + |∂²w|), the derivatives along a column of g_app and ∂g_app being at most C and C λ⁻¹. By
(8.1), which holds here by Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 50.19, both are at most C M
λ^(K−5) ≤ C λ, as K ≥ 6. With (ii), along every column |θ⁺_λ − θ⁺(g0)| + |∂_R(θ⁺_λ − θ⁺(g0))| ≤ C3 λ and |θ⁻(g_λ) + 3/R|
≤ C3 λ.

(v) The zero. This is (v) of the proof of Proposition 3.4, with R_H(v) in place of √μ(v), the lower bound 3 e^(min ψ)/
μ_max for ∂_R θ⁺(g0) at the zero in place of 3/μ_max, and the margin of the zero from the curvature boundary as follows.
At R = R_H, μ = R_H², so R_H⁴ − r_q(μ)⁴ = μ² − √72 μ l5² ≥ μ0 (μ0 − √72 l5²), which is positive when μ0 > √72 l5²; μ
being uniformly continuous on the compact Ω₂, there is δ > 0 such that the points of a column with |R − R_H| ≤ δ and
R ≤ v − τ0 lie in D_T. If μ0 = √72 l5², the same holds on the columns with R_H² ≥ μ0 + δ2. ∎

The statement concerns the round family {S_(v,R)}: its zero set on the columns is not itself a marginally trapped
surface. Although ∂g_λ converges only weakly, the expansions of these spheres do not see the oscillation at order λ⁰,
the waves being traceless on them; and at order λ the outgoing wave, which oscillates along the columns, does not enter
the outgoing expansion, because stage 0's division has removed the mixed harmonics of the angular trace.

**Lemma 50.28** (The quarter turn with two phases.) Let J be the map of Section 8.4, and
let S act on families of two-phase profiles by (S g)_j(X, θ1, θ2) := (−1)^j (J* g_j)(X, 3π/2 − θ1, 3π/2 − θ2).

(a) J is an isometry of every round double-null metric, fixing u, v and every sphere, with J_* ℓ_𝔨 = ℓ_𝔨; and
Lemma 8.6 (a) holds for two phases: the two-scale residual of g̃ := g0 + Σ_j λ^j (S g)_j is
R[g̃](X, θ1, θ2; λ) = J* R[g](X, 3π/2 − θ1, 3π/2 − θ2; −λ).
(b) W_in and W_out are S-invariant at weight 1, and the coefficient of λ in the expansion of R[g0 + λ W_𝔨] is S-odd.
(c) The mixed harmonics of ĝ_2 fixed in Lemma 50.13 are S-invariant at weight 2.
(d) The profiles of the approximant of Theorem 50.18, with the stage data of Lemma 50.26,
satisfy S g = g. In particular J* m1 = −m1.

*Proof.* (a) J is linear in x and lies in O(4), so it preserves R = |x|, τ, the round metric and hence g0, and every
function of (τ, R), u and v among them. The proof of Lemma 8.6 (a) applies with D^λ_a := ∂_a +
λ⁻¹ (∂_a v) F1 + λ⁻¹ (∂_a u) F2 and ρ(θ1, θ2) := (3π/2 − θ1, 3π/2 − θ2): D^λ_a(f ∘ ρ) = (D^(−λ)_a f) ∘ ρ, and J*
commutes with D^λ.
(b) The outgoing wave has the algebraic form (8.2) of the ingoing one, its two quadratures having A₂,
env₂(u) and θ2 in place of A, env(v) and θ, and J fixes u; so the calculation of Lemma 8.6 (b) gives
(J* W_TT^𝔨)(X, 3π/2 − θ_𝔨) = −W_TT^𝔨(X, θ_𝔨) for both families. χ_in and χ_out are S-invariant by the uniqueness of the
transports (50.19), which commute with J and whose forcing terms are S-even by (a) at order 0, as in
Lemma 8.6 (b). The last claim is (a) at order 1 for the S-invariant family g0 + λ W_𝔨.
(c) By (a), applied to the S-invariant family g0 + λ (W_in + W_out), J* R^(0)(X, 3π/2 − θ1, 3π/2 − θ2) = R^(0)(X, θ1,
θ2). The division by e^(−2σ) F1F2 commutes with J*, σ being O(4)-invariant, and with ρ, since F1F2 is invariant under ρ.
So the mixed harmonics of ĝ_2, the quotients of those of −R^(0) at ĝ_2 = 0, satisfy (J* ĝ_2)(X, 3π/2 − θ1, 3π/2 − θ2) =
ĝ_2(X, θ1, θ2).
(d) Every later stage of Lemma 50.17 (c) and every choice of Lemma 50.26 (the right inverses
Pol_𝔨⁺, which are O(4)-equivariant and act pointwise in (θ1, θ2), the division, and the data of the means and phases as
in Lemma 7.4) is the unique solution of a problem that S maps to itself, and the rewriting with the fixed phases
commutes with S. So the proof of Lemma 8.6 (c) applies and gives S g = g; taking the mean over T², J* m1 =
−m1. ∎

The base of the induction is (b) for both families and (c) for the interaction: with one quadrature alone in either
family, (b) fails for that family.

**Proposition 50.29** (The mean mass, two families.) For K ≥ 6 and λ ≤ λ0, and every sphere
S = S_(v,R) in D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}: if v ∉ (v_start, v_end) and u ∉ (u1, u2) on S, then |M[S](g_λ) − μ(S)| ≤ C λ², μ(S) the
mass function (50.7) on S; otherwise |M[S](g_λ) − μ(S)| ≤ C λ. Moreover M[S](g0) = μ(S) for every round
double-null metric.

*Proof.* For g0, with the future null normals n⁺ := e^(−2σ) ∂_v and n⁻ := e^(−2σ) ∂_u (Θ in (3.2) does not
depend on their normalisation), θ^± = 3 e^(−2σ) R_v/R and 3 e^(−2σ) R_u/R, and g0(n⁺, n⁻) = −e^(−2σ); so Θ = 18 e^(−2σ)
R_u R_v/R², the area is 2π² R³, and M[S](g0) = R² (1 + 2e^(−2σ) R_u R_v) = μ(S).

If v ∉ (v_start, v_end) and u ∉ (u1, u2) on S, every oscillating profile of g_app vanishes on S: the harmonics with
n1 ≠ 0 vanish where v ∉ (v_start, v_end) and those with n2 ≠ 0 where u ∉ (u1, u2) (Lemma 50.26 (b)),
and so do the phase-shift terms of the fixed-phase form, which carry the waves. So g_app = g0 + λ m1 + λ² E on S, and
M[S](g_λ) = μ(S) + λ DM[m1] + O(λ²) + O(|w| + |∂w|). By naturality DM[J* m] = DM[m], J fixing g0 and S, as in the
proof of Proposition 3.5; so DM[m1] = −DM[m1] = 0 by Lemma 50.28 (d), and the remainder is at most
C λ^(K−4) ≤ C λ². Elsewhere θ^± have no oscillation at order λ⁰ ((ii) of the proof of Proposition 50.27) and
the area none, tr_S W_𝔨 being zero, so M[S](g_app) − μ(S) = O(λ), and the remainder is at most C λ^(K−4). For λ beyond
the λ* of Lemma 8.3 the bounds hold with a larger C, as in the proof of Proposition 3.5. ∎

### 50.8 Proof of the theorem

*Proof of Theorem 50.2.* The background exists on Ω₂ ⊃ D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0} with the properties of
Proposition 50.6 and Lemma 50.8. Let g_app be the approximant of Theorem 50.18
with N = K + 3 stages and the stage data of Lemma 50.26, and let the data on Σ_τ0 be those of
Theorem 50.24, which satisfy the constraints exactly, carry D = 0, equal the seed's on R < r1, and are within
C λ^K of those of g_app. Theorem 50.19 gives, for λ ≤ λ0, the solution g_λ of Ric^H(g) = 0 on Ω₂ with these
data, unique among C² solutions with these data and |g − g0| ≤ ε1, smooth, with w = g_λ − g_app as in items 3 and 4.
Taking λ0 so small that C λ0 ≤ ε1, g_λ is Lorentzian by Lemma 50.8 (e). Lemma 3.6 holds on
Ω₂ with its proof, which uses of the domain only Lemma 2.6 (e) and the energy inequality, both of which hold on Ω₂
(Lemma 50.8); it gives D(g_λ) = 0 and Ric(g_λ) = 0. This is items 1, 2, 3 and 5.

Symmetry. Every element of G = O(2) × O(2), acting on x and fixing τ, lies in O(4), so it preserves R, u and v, hence
g0, Ω₂ and Σ_τ0, and the argument of Section 3.2 applies: by the uniqueness of item 5 and the invariance of the
data (Theorem 50.24), g_λ is invariant.

Convergence. For a two-phase profile f = Σ_n f_n(X) e^(i(n1 θ1 + n2 θ2)) and a test function ζ ∈ C_c^∞ in the interior of
Ω₂, let n ≠ 0 and Φ_n := n1 v + n2 u. If n1 ≠ 0, put Z := ℓ_out, so that Z(Φ_n) = n1 g0^(uv) = −n1 e^(−2σ); if n1 = 0,
put Z := ℓ_in, with Z(Φ_n) = −n2 e^(−2σ). Then e^(iΦ_n/λ) = (λ/(i Z(Φ_n))) Z(e^(iΦ_n/λ)), and integrating by parts,
∫ ζ f_n e^(iΦ_n/λ) = O(λ/|n1|) or O(λ/|n2|), with constants given by derivatives of ζ f_n, which decay faster than any
power of |n|. So ∫ ζ [f] → ∫ ζ ⟨f⟩, and [f] → ⟨f⟩ weakly in L²(Ω₂). Now ∂[λ g1] = dv ⊗ [F1 g1] + du ⊗ [F2 g1] + λ [∂_X
g1], ∂[λ^j g_j] = O(λ^(j−1)) for j ≥ 2, and |∂w| ≤ C λ^(K−4), which gives the formula of item 4; ⟨F_𝔨 g1⟩ = 0, so ∂g_λ →
∂g0 weakly. Applying the same limit to |dv ⊗ F1 g1 + du ⊗ F2 g1|², whose mean over T² is the sum of the means of the two
families' terms, the cross term having mean zero, shows that ‖dv ⊗ [F1 g1] + du ⊗ [F2 g1]‖²_(L²(U)) tends to a positive
limit on every open U on which env or env₂ is not identically zero: there the mean of |F_𝔨 W_TT^𝔨|²_(g0) is (4/3) A² env²
R⁻³, respectively (4/3) A₂² env₂² R⁻³ (Lemma 50.13 (c)). So the convergence is not strong there.
(50.4) is Lemma 50.13 (c) with Proposition 50.6; Lemma 50.5
(vi) gives the background's Kretschmann scalar.

Items 6 and 7 are Proposition 50.27 and Proposition 50.29. ∎

## 51. The class Einstein–null-dust system

Chapter 50 carries the main theorem over to two radial null dusts, one ingoing and one outgoing, on a round
background. This chapter asks what remains when the dusts and the background are not round. In the T²-mirror class of
Section 2.1 a null phase is an invariant function, and at the axes of the T² action its gradient is radial: two
families of one orientation are not angularly separated there (Proposition 51.3), and families with non-radial
phases make the background non-round (Lemma 51.2). Such a background is a solution of the class
Einstein–null-dust system, and its existence without smallness is the subject of the chapter.

The difficulty is one derivative. The density of a null dust is transported by the expansion of its phase, one
derivative below the metric, and the Raychaudhuri equation for the expansion holds the shear, again one derivative low.
In the class the null second fundamental form of every invariant null hypersurface is diagonal, with two of its three
entries of first order (Proposition 51.5). So off the axes each family's Raychaudhuri equation closes on its
expansion, and the Einstein–null-dust system, augmented by the expansions, is Cauchy-stable around any smooth
caustic-free solution whose dusts avoid the axes, with no smallness of the solution (Theorem 51.18).
At an axis one entry becomes a second derivative (Proposition 51.21). The quantity to be recovered there is the planar
shear, the trace-free part of the second fundamental form of the family's level sets in the slice, and elliptic
regularity of those level sets recovers it from the expansion with no loss (Lemma 51.27). With lateral
boundaries adapted to the dusts where they meet an axis, the system is then Cauchy-stable with the dusts at the axes
(Theorem 51.31), and the two-dust background of Chapter 50, which is round, carries every small
non-round perturbation on its whole adapted domain, provided its outgoing packet does not reach the inner sphere
(Corollary 51.32). The local theory needs Kato's iteration with a right side that is non-local in the planar
directions (Lemma 51.12, Theorem 51.13, Theorem 51.14, Corollary 51.15).

### 51.1 Null phases in the class

We use the coordinates X = (τ, x) of Section 2.2 and put ρ1 := |(x1, x2)| = r c and ρ2 := |(x3, x4)| = r s. The
T² action is generated by the Killing fields K1 := ∂_(φ1) = x1 ∂_2 − x2 ∂_1 and K2 := ∂_(φ2) = x3 ∂_4 − x4 ∂_3 of every
class metric. K1 vanishes on *axis 1*, {ρ1 = 0} = {c = 0}, and K2 on *axis 2*, {ρ2 = 0} = {s = 0}; we write
dist(x, axes) := min(ρ1, ρ2). The group G = O(2) × O(2) of Section 2.1 contains, in each plane, every rotation and
every reflection in a line through 0. A *phase in the class* is a smooth G-invariant function u with du ≠ 0 on an open
G-invariant set; its *rays* are the integral curves of g⁻¹du, and projected to the orbit space they lie in the quarter
plane {ρ1, ρ2 ≥ 0}, whose edges are the axes.

**Lemma 51.1** (Phases at the axes.) Let u be a phase in the class. At every point of axis 2 with
ρ1 > 0 the spatial gradient ∂_x u is a multiple of x̂, so du lies in span(dτ, dr); the same holds at axis 1. For g0 of
(2.3), a null radial covector α dτ + β dr is a multiple of dv or of the outgoing covector (1 − μ/r²) dτ −
(1 + μ/r²) dr. Hence at an axis point the gradient of a null phase in the class is parallel to dv or to that outgoing
covector.

*Proof.* Let x = (x1, x2, 0, 0) with ρ1 > 0. The rotations of the (x3, x4)-plane fix x and u, so they fix the
(x3, x4)-component of ∂_x u, which is therefore 0. The reflection of the (x1, x2)-plane in the line through (x1, x2)
fixes x and u, so the (x1, x2)-component of ∂_x u is fixed by it and is parallel to (x1, x2), that is, to x̂. For the
second claim, g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − (μ/r²) L0 ⊗ L0 with L0(τ) = 1 and L0(r) = −1 gives

    g0⁻¹(α dτ + β dr, α dτ + β dr) = −α² + β² − (μ/r²)(α − β)² = (β − α)((1 − μ/r²) β + (1 + μ/r²) α),

which vanishes exactly when β = α (a multiple of dv = dτ + dr) or when (1 − μ/r²) β + (1 + μ/r²) α = 0. ∎

**Lemma 51.2** (Non-radial phases.) Let α1, α2 > 0 with α1 ≠ α2, let E := {x ∈ R⁴ : ρ1²/α1² +
ρ2²/α2² ≤ 1}, and let d_E(x) be the Euclidean distance from x to E. Then w := τ + d_E is a phase in the class on
R × (R⁴ ∖ E), an exact eikonal of Minkowski space, η⁻¹(dw, dw) = 0, whose rays are the straight lines normal to ∂E, and:

(a) at every point of an axis, ∂_x d_E = x̂: the ray is radial;
(b) at a point off the axes, ∂_x d_E and x̂ lie in the plane spanned by e_I := (x1, x2, 0, 0)/ρ1 and e_II :=
(0, 0, x3, x4)/ρ2, and the angle β between them satisfies 0 < β < π/2;
(c) for a dust q dw ⊗ dw with q > 0 at a point off the axes, the restriction of q dw ⊗ dw to the tangent space of the
sphere {τ, |x| = r} through the point is q (∂_ϑ d_E)² dϑ ⊗ dϑ with ∂_ϑ d_E = ± r sin β ≠ 0; it is not a multiple of the
round metric, so q dw ⊗ dw is not the Ricci tensor of any metric invariant under O(4) near that point.

*Proof.* E is compact and convex, and its boundary {ρ1²/α1² + ρ2²/α2² = 1} is a smooth ellipsoid of R⁴, strictly
convex. For such a set the map (y, t) ↦ y + t n(y), y ∈ ∂E, t > 0, n the outer unit normal, is a diffeomorphism onto
R⁴ ∖ E. It is onto: every exterior point x has a nearest point π(x) ∈ ∂E, and x − π(x) is an outer normal there. It
is one-to-one: E lies on the inner side of the tangent hyperplane at each y ∈ ∂E, by convexity, so for x = y + t n(y)
and z ∈ E, |x − z|² = t² + |y − z|² − 2t ⟨n(y), z − y⟩ ≥ t² + |y − z|², and y is the unique nearest point of x. Its
differential is invertible because the derivative of n is the shape operator, positive definite for a strictly convex
boundary. In these coordinates d_E = t, so d_E is smooth, ∂_x d_E = n(π(x)) and |∂_x d_E| = 1; hence η⁻¹(dw, dw) =
−1 + |∂_x d_E|² = 0, and the rays of w are the normal lines. E is G-invariant, hence so is d_E.

(a) By Lemma 51.1, ∂_x d_E = ± x̂ at an axis point, and the sign is + since d_E increases along x̂: on
axis 2 the nearest point of E is α1 x̂ (respectively α2 x̂ on axis 1) and x lies beyond it.

(b) The argument of Lemma 51.1, applied in each plane, shows that the two components of ∂_x d_E are
parallel to e_I and e_II. In the basis (e_I, e_II) the point is (ρ1, ρ2) with ρ1, ρ2 > 0, and its nearest point on
the ellipse is y = (α1 cos t, α2 sin t) with 0 < t < π/2: changing the signs of the coordinates of a point of the
ellipse to those of (ρ1, ρ2) does not increase its distance, so 0 ≤ t ≤ π/2, and at t = 0 or π/2 the normal is
along a coordinate axis, so that the point y + d_E n would lie on an axis. The normal at y is n ∝ (α2 cos t, α1 sin
t). The polar angles of y and n are arctan((α2/α1) tan t) and arctan((α1/α2) tan t), which differ since α1 ≠ α2, and
both lie in (0, π/2). The point y + d_E n is a combination of y and n with positive coefficients, so its angle lies
strictly between theirs. Hence 0 < β < π/2.

(c) Since w is invariant, dw has no dφ_i components, and on the sphere dw = ∂_ϑ d_E dϑ. With x = r (c e_I + s e_II), ∂_ϑ
x = r (−s e_I + c e_II), a vector of length r orthogonal to x̂ in the plane of (b), so ∂_ϑ d_E = ∂_x d_E · ∂_ϑ x = ± r
sin β. The tangent space of the sphere is spanned by ∂_ϑ, ∂_(φ1), ∂_(φ2), on which q dw ⊗ dw has the single nonzero
entry q (∂_ϑ d_E)². For a metric invariant under O(4), whose isotropy group at a point of a sphere acts irreducibly on
the tangent space of the sphere, the restriction of every invariant symmetric tensor to that tangent space is a multiple
of the round metric dϑ² + c² dφ1² + s² dφ2², which has nonzero φφ entries. ∎

So families with non-radial phases carry a stress that is not round: their background is a G-invariant solution that
is not invariant under O(4), a problem on the three-dimensional orbit space with the axes as boundary. The next
proposition says which families are separated. For a mixed harmonic n1 v + n2 w the leading symbol is n1 n2 g⁻¹(dv,
dw), as in (50.20).

**Proposition 51.3** (Angular separation at the axes.)
(a) With v = τ + r and w of Lemma 51.2, η⁻¹(dv, dw) = −1 + cos β, which vanishes at the axes. At the
points at distance d > 0 from E, β/ϑ → |α1² − α2²|/(α2² + d α1) as the point approaches axis 2 (for α1 = 1/2, α2 =
1/3 and d = 3/2 the limit is 5/31), and near axis 1 the same holds with α1 and α2 exchanged
and ϑ replaced by π/2 − ϑ. Hence η⁻¹(dv, dw) = −β²/2 + O(β⁴) vanishes like ϑ² at the axes, the mixed symbol is a
small divisor there, and {v, w} is not angularly separated in the sense of [HL18, Definition 4.1, p. 10], "we say
that the set of eikonal functions {u_A}_(A∈A) is angularly separated if there exists η′ ∈ (0, 1) such that δ^(ij)
(∂_i u_A1)(∂_j u_A2) / (|∇u_A1||∇u_A2|) (t, x) < 1 − η′, ∀(t, x) ∈ I × R², ∀A1 ≠ A2": the quotient (∂_x v · ∂_x
w)/(|∂_x v| |∂_x w|) = cos β tends to 1 at the axes.
(b) The radial pair v and τ − r satisfies η⁻¹(dv, d(τ − r)) = −2 everywhere.
(c) Let u_A, u_B be null phases in the class for g0 of (2.3). At an axis point where both gradients are
parallel to dv, or both to the outgoing covector of Lemma 51.1, g0⁻¹(du_A, du_B) = 0, so the leading
symbol of every mixed harmonic of u_A and u_B vanishes there. Hence, for families whose densities do not vanish at the
axes, at most two are angularly separated in the class: at each axis point one ingoing and one outgoing.
(d) Phases f_A(v) that are functions of v alone are resonant: every combination Σ_A n_A f_A(v) has the null differential
(Σ_A n_A f_A′(v)) dv, so every harmonic has leading symbol 0, and such families form one family with a multi-frequency
profile.

*Proof.* (a) η⁻¹(dτ + dr, dτ + dd_E) = −1 + x̂·∂_x d_E = −1 + cos β, and β = 0 at the axes by Lemma 51.2
(a). In the plane of Lemma 51.2 (b) let the foot point be y(t) = (α1 cos t, α2 sin t) and the unit
normal n̂(t) = (α2 cos t, α1 sin t)/(α2² cos² t + α1² sin² t)^(1/2), so that y(t) = (α1, α2 t) + O(t²) and n̂(t) =
(1, (α1/α2) t) + O(t²) as t → 0. The point p(t) = y(t) + d n̂(t) = (α1 + d, (α2 + d α1/α2) t) + O(t²) has polar angle
ϑ = t (α2² + d α1)/(α2 (α1 + d)) + O(t²), and the ray's angle is arctan((α1/α2) tan t) = (α1/α2) t + O(t³). Hence β =
t |α1² − α2²|/(α2 (α1 + d)) + O(t²) and β/ϑ → |α1² − α2²|/(α2² + d α1); at α1 = 1/2, α2 = 1/3, d = 3/2 this is
(5/36)/(31/36). Near axis 1 exchange the roles of the two planes. Then cos β − 1 = −β²/2 + O(β⁴). Since ∂_x v = x̂ and
∂_x w = ∂_x d_E are unit vectors, the quotient of [HL18, Definition 4.1] is cos β.
(b) η⁻¹(dτ + dr, dτ − dr) = −1 − 1.
(c) Both gradients are multiples of one null covector, so their contraction is a multiple of its square, which is 0. If
both families have densities that do not vanish at an axis point, their separation would have to hold there. By
Lemma 51.1 the gradient of each phase at an axis point is a multiple of dv or of the outgoing covector; so
of three families with densities nonzero at an axis point, two have gradients that are multiples of the same covector
there, of the same sign when g⁻¹du_A and g⁻¹du_B have the same time orientation, and their quotient of [HL18, Definition
4.1] is 1 there. At most two families are therefore separated at each axis point, one with gradient a multiple of dv and
one with gradient a multiple of the outgoing covector.
(d) d(Σ n_A f_A(v)) = (Σ n_A f_A′) dv and g⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0. ∎

At an axis point the gradient of a phase u with g0⁻¹du future directed is a negative multiple of dv or of the outgoing
covector, at every r: g0⁻¹(dτ, dv) = −1 and g0⁻¹(dτ, (1 − μ/r²) dτ − (1 + μ/r²) dr) = −1 − μ/r² are negative, so g0⁻¹dv
and g0⁻¹ of the outgoing covector are past directed. The sign of du(∂_τ) is no normalisation, the dτ-component 1 − μ/r²
of the outgoing covector changing sign at r² = μ, which Ω reaches. So in (c) the quotient of [HL18, Definition 4.1]
equals 1 for two families of one orientation. With densities that vanish near the axes, separation is needed only on
the overlaps of the supports, and any finite number of separated families is possible, for instance non-radial phases
of different ellipsoids supported away from the axes.

### 51.2 The class Einstein–null-dust system

**Definition 51.4** (The class Einstein–null-dust system.) Let N_f ≥ 1 be an integer. A solution of the
Einstein–null-dust system with N_f families on an open set is a smooth Lorentzian metric g with smooth functions u_A and
q_A ≥ 0, A = 1, …, N_f, such that

    Ric(g) = Σ_A q_A du_A ⊗ du_A,      g⁻¹(du_A, du_A) = 0,      div_g(q_A g⁻¹du_A) = 0.    (51.1)

It is a *class solution* if g, every u_A and every q_A are invariant under G. We write T := Σ_A q_A du_A ⊗ du_A,
P_A := g⁻¹du_A and Θ_A := □_g u_A, the *expansion* of the family.

The last equation is the conservation law of the dust, P_A(q_A) = −Θ_A q_A. This is where a derivative is lost. Let an
energy control dg in H^k. The gradient du_A has the regularity of the geodesic flow of g, H^k; its second derivatives
obey a Riccati equation driven by the curvature and lie in H^(k−1); so Θ_A ∈ H^(k−1), the density q_A transported by
Θ_A lies in H^(k−1), T lies in H^(k−1), and the wave equation for g returns dg in H^(k−1) only. The loop g → du_A →
Θ_A → q_A → T → g loses one derivative. Carrying Θ_A as an unknown does not help by itself: the Raychaudhuri equation
P_A(Θ_A) = −|∇²u_A|² − Ric(P_A, P_A) (see the proof of Proposition 51.5 (c)) has the whole Hessian ∇²u_A on its
right side, again in H^(k−1). In the class, Proposition 51.5 shows that |∇²u_A|² is a function of Θ_A and of
first derivatives of u_A and g, away from the axes.

### 51.3 The class structure

Off the axes write a class metric as in (2.1), g = g3 + e^(2ψ1) dφ1² + e^(2ψ2) dφ2², with g3 the
orbit metric and ψ1, ψ2 the functions written A, B in (2.1) (here A and B index the families), so
that e^(2ψ_i) = g(K_i, K_i). For a phase u in the class put P := g⁻¹du,

    κ_i := g⁻¹(du, dψ_i) = P(ψ_i),      e_i := e^(−ψ_i) K_i      (i = 1, 2).

The curvature is R(X, Y) := ∇_X∇_Y − ∇_Y∇_X − ∇_[X,Y].

**Proposition 51.5** (The class structure.) Let g be a class metric and u a phase in the class, on an
open set off the axes, and let ∂_a be coordinate fields of the orbit space.

(a) ∇²u(∂_a, K_i) = 0, ∇²u(K1, K2) = 0 and ∇²u(K_i, K_i) = e^(2ψ_i) κ_i. Hence ∇_(K_i) P = κ_i K_i.

(b) At a point where g⁻¹(du, du) vanishes to first order, ∇²u(P, ·) = 0. For every null vector L̄ with g(P, L̄) = −1
the restriction χ of ∇²u to the screen {P, L̄}^⊥ satisfies tr χ = □_g u and |∇²u|²_g = |χ|². For L̄ tangent to the
orbit space the screen has an orthonormal frame (e_h, e1, e2) with e_h tangent to the orbit space, χ = diag(Θ_h, κ1, κ2)
with Θ_h := □_g u − κ1 − κ2, and

    |∇²u|²_g = (□_g u − κ1 − κ2)² + κ1² + κ2².    (51.2)

(c) If u is an eikonal, g⁻¹(du, du) = 0 on the open set, then with Θ := □_g u

    P(Θ) = −(Θ − κ1 − κ2)² − κ1² − κ2² − Ric(P, P).    (51.3)

For a class solution (51.1) and u = u_A, Ric(P_A, P_A) = Σ_B q_B g⁻¹(du_A, du_B)², and the right side of
(51.3) is a smooth function of Θ_A, of the du_B and q_B, and of g and dg (through κ_i, which holds
dψ_i): it holds no derivative of Θ_A or of du_A and no second derivative of g.

(d) If u is an eikonal, P is geodesic and

    P(κ_i) = ∇²ψ_i(P, P) = −κ_i² + g(R(P, e_i) P, e_i).    (51.4)

So the first-order character of κ_i is algebraic, through (a), and not dynamical: κ_i obeys its own Riccati equation,
driven by curvature. This is why it can degenerate, and at the axes it does (Proposition 51.21).

*Proof.* (a) By the proof of Lemma 2.1, the Christoffel symbols of g with an index φ_i are Γ^a_(φiφi) =
−e^(2ψ_i) ∇^a ψ_i (∇ of g3) and Γ^(φi)_(aφi) = ∂_a ψ_i, and all others with an index φ_i vanish. As u does not depend on
φ1, φ2: ∇²u(∂_a, ∂_(φi)) = −Γ^(φi)_(aφi) ∂_(φi) u = 0; ∇²u(∂_(φ1), ∂_(φ2)) = −Γ^μ_(φ1φ2) ∂_μ u = 0; and ∇²u(∂_(φi),
∂_(φi)) = −Γ^a_(φiφi) ∂_a u = e^(2ψ_i) g3^(ab) ∂_a u ∂_b ψ_i = e^(2ψ_i) κ_i, since neither du nor dψ_i has a dφ
component and g⁻¹ is block diagonal. Then g(∇_(K_i) P, X) = ∇²u(K_i, X) = κ_i g(K_i, X) for every X.

(b) Put ν := g⁻¹(du, du). As ∇g = 0, dν = 2 ∇²u(P, ·), so ν = 0 and dν = 0 at the point give ∇²u(P, ·) = 0. With
(e_α) an orthonormal frame of the screen, g⁻¹ = −P ⊗ L̄ − L̄ ⊗ P + Σ_α e_α ⊗ e_α. Contracting, □_g u = −2 ∇²u(P, L̄) +
Σ_α χ(e_α, e_α) = tr χ, and in |∇²u|² = g^(ac) g^(bd) ∇²u_ab ∇²u_cd every term with a factor P puts P into a slot of
∇²u and vanishes, leaving Σ_(α,β) χ(e_α, e_β)². The covector du has no dφ components, so P is tangent to the orbit
space, and g(P, K_i) = du(K_i) = 0. The orbit metric g3 is Lorentzian of dimension 3 and P is null for it; take L̄ null
in the orbit space with g(P, L̄) = −1 and e_h a unit vector of the orbit space orthogonal to P and L̄. Then (e_h, e1, e2)
is an orthonormal frame of the screen, by (a) χ(e_h, e_i) = 0, χ(e1, e2) = 0 and χ(e_i, e_i) = κ_i, and tr χ = □_g u
gives χ(e_h, e_h) = □_g u − κ1 − κ2. Summing the squares gives (51.2).

(c) Write u_a := ∂_a u. Then ½ □_g ν = ∇^b(u^a ∇_b u_a) = |∇²u|² + u^a ∇^b∇_b u_a, and ∇^b∇_b u_a = ∇^b∇_a u_b =
∇_a ∇^b u_b + Ric_ab u^b, by the commutation rule ∇_b∇_a X^b − ∇_a∇_b X^b = Ric_ab X^b. Hence

    ½ □_g ν = |∇²u|² + P(□_g u) + Ric(P, P).

If ν ≡ 0 the left side vanishes and P(Θ) = −|∇²u|² − Ric(P, P), which with (b) is (51.3). For a class
solution, Ric(P_A, P_A) = Σ_B q_B (du_B(P_A))² = Σ_B q_B g⁻¹(du_A, du_B)², and ψ_i = ½ log g(K_i, K_i) is a smooth
function of the metric's components off the axes.

(d) ν ≡ 0 gives ∇_P P = g⁻¹∇²u(P, ·) = ½ g⁻¹dν = 0. So P(κ_i) = P(P(ψ_i)) = ∇²ψ_i(P, P) + (∇_P P)(ψ_i) = ∇²ψ_i(P, P).
The flow of K_i preserves g and u, hence P, so [P, K_i] = 0 and ∇_P K_i = ∇_(K_i) P = κ_i K_i by (a). Then

    R(P, K_i) P = ∇_P ∇_(K_i) P − ∇_(K_i) ∇_P P − ∇_([P, K_i]) P = ∇_P (κ_i K_i) = (P(κ_i) + κ_i²) K_i,

and dividing g(R(P, K_i) P, K_i) by g(K_i, K_i) = e^(2ψ_i) gives the second equality. ∎

**Remark 51.6** (The 2 + 1 quotient of Huneau and Luk.) In the 2 + 1 quotient of Huneau and Luk the
null hypersurfaces have one-dimensional sections, so their null second fundamental form is a scalar without shear, and
the Raychaudhuri equation closes on it: "L_A(χ) + χ² = −R_(L_A L_A) = −(L_A ϕ)² − e^(−4ϕ)(L_A ϖ)²" [HL25, (6.31), p.
22], in their notation. Proposition 51.5 is the five-dimensional class version of that structure: the two torus
directions add principal curvatures of first order, and the one orbit direction carries the whole expansion. It holds
where the T² action is free. Their symmetry has no fixed points: φ and g are viewed as functions on I × R³ "which do not
depend on the variable x³" [HL18, p. 3, footnote 5]. Their local theory assumes "‖φ̇‖_(L∞) + ‖∇φ‖_(L∞) + max_A
‖F̆_A‖_(L∞) ≤ ε, (3.17)" [HL18, Theorem 3.3, p. 9], a smallness of the dust in L^∞, while "the smallness is not needed
for the higher norms" (p. 9); and in [HL25] "local existence in the elliptic gauge requires a smallness assumption" (p.
4). They use the Raychaudhuri equation for a gain in the wavelength: "To obtain this improvement, we use the
Raychaudhuri equation that χ_A satisfies" [HL25, pp. 4–5].

### 51.4 The augmented system

**Definition 51.7** (Admissible domains.) Let g̊ be a smooth G-invariant Lorentzian metric on a
neighbourhood of a compact set Ω ⊂ R × (R⁴ ∖ {0}). Ω is *admissible* for g̊ if Ω = ⋃_(τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ1) {τ} × Σ_τ, where
each Σ_τ is a G-invariant compact domain of R⁴ ∖ {0} with smooth boundary, the image of the annulus {1 ≤ |x| ≤ 2}
under a diffeomorphism ψ_τ of R⁴, smooth in (τ, x), equal to the identity outside a compact set, with every derivative
of positive order of ψ_τ and ψ_τ⁻¹ bounded uniformly in τ, and:

(a) dτ is timelike for g̊ on Ω, so every Σ_τ is spacelike;
(b) each lateral boundary component, the hypersurface swept by one component of ∂Σ_τ, is spacelike for g̊ with Ω to
its past: future causal vectors at its points do not point into Ω;
(c) there is ε1 > 0 such that (a) and (b) hold for every Lorentzian g with |g − g̊| ≤ ε1 on Ω; then J⁻(p; g) ∩
{τ ≥ τ0} ⊂ Ω for every p ∈ Ω, because a past causal curve cannot leave Ω through a lateral boundary or through Σ_(τ1).

The domain Ω of (2.8) is admissible for g0 by Lemma 2.6 (a)–(c), (e), and the domain Ω₂ of
(50.11) is admissible for the two-dust background by Lemma 50.8 (a)–(c), (e). The slices are
connected and simply connected, and the Sobolev inequality of Lemma 5.1 holds on them with a constant independent
of τ, by its proof. The energy inequality Lemma 5.5 holds on an admissible domain with g̊ in place of g0. Its proof
uses (a)–(c) for the derivative part; for the norm ‖u‖, whose boundary term there uses the annular slices, add |u|² Y to
the energy current J. In the coordinate density ∂_a(|u|² Y^a) = 2u Y(u) + |u|² ∂_a Y^a, bounded by C (|u| |∂u| + |u|²);
its flux through Σ_τ is ∫ |u|² dτ(Y), comparable to ‖u‖² since dτ(Y) = −g̃⁻¹(dτ, dτ) is bounded above and below; and its
flux through a lateral boundary component {F = 0}, with Ω ⊂ {F ≤ 0} and dF positive on future timelike vectors, is the
integral of |u|² dF(Y) times a positive density, nonnegative because Y is future timelike. So the energy ‖∂u‖² + ‖u‖²
obeys the same Gronwall inequality.

Let ů = (g̊, ů_A, q̊_A), A = 1, …, N_f, be a class solution on a neighbourhood of a domain Ω admissible for g̊, with
dů_A ≠ 0 on Ω. Replacing ů_A by −ů_A where needed (which changes nothing in (51.1)), every P̊_A := g̊⁻¹dů_A
is future directed: it is null and nonzero, hence never tangent to the spacelike Σ_τ, so its time orientation is
constant on the connected Ω. For a closed
set S ⊂ Σ_τ0 and a vector field P on Ω transverse to the slices, the *tube* of S is the union of the integral curves
of P in Ω through the points of S. Fix δ > 0, closed G-invariant sets S_A ⊂ Σ_τ0 containing supp q̊_A ∩ Σ_τ0 whose
tubes 𝒯̊_A for P̊_A lie at distance at least 2δ from the axes, and G-invariant cut-offs ζ_A ∈ C^∞, equal to 1 on a
neighbourhood of 𝒯̊_A and to 0 within distance δ of the axes. Put S̊_A := P̊_A(□_g̊ ů_A), a fixed smooth function on Ω.

The unknowns of the *augmented system* are a metric g and, for each family, a covector field p_A and functions Θ_A and
q_A; we put P_A := g⁻¹p_A, ψ_i := ½ log g(K_i, K_i) and κ_Ai := g⁻¹(p_A, dψ_i). The equations are

    (Aug1)   Ric^H(g) = Σ_A q_A p_A ⊗ p_A,    (51.5)
