    (Aug2)   P_A^b ∂_b p_(A,a) = P_A^b Γ[g]^c_(ba) p_(A,c),      that is, ∇_(P_A) p_A = 0,    (51.6)
    (Aug3)   P_A(Θ_A) = ζ_A S_A + (1 − ζ_A) S̊_A,    (51.7)
    (Aug4)   P_A(q_A) = −Θ_A q_A,    (51.8)

with S_A := −(Θ_A − κ_A1 − κ_A2)² − κ_A1² − κ_A2² − Σ_B q_B g⁻¹(p_A, p_B)², the right side of
(51.3), and Ric^H the reduced Ricci tensor of Section 2.4 relative to g̊ (g̊ in place of g0 in
(2.9)), with its gauge vector D(g). ζ_A S_A is smooth, since ζ_A vanishes near the axes.

**Proposition 51.8** (The augmented system.) Let (g, p_A, Θ_A, q_A) solve (Aug1)–(Aug4) on an open
set, and put ν_A := g⁻¹(p_A, p_A), Δ_A := Θ_A − div_g P_A and T := Σ_A q_A p_A ⊗ p_A.

(a) (Orders.) The right sides of (Aug2)–(Aug4) are smooth functions of (g, dg, p_B, Θ_B, q_B), and the lower-order
part of (Aug1) is a smooth function of (g, dg, p_B, q_B). So if an energy controls ∂^j of (dg, p_A, Θ_A, q_A) for j ≤ k,
every right side is controlled at order k, and the loop closes. Each of three variants loses one derivative: the
transport P_A(q_A) = −(div_g P_A) q_A in place of (Aug4), whose right side holds ∂p_A; the general Raychaudhuri right
side −|∇²u_A|², which holds ∂p_A; and S_A at an axis point, where κ_A2 is of the order of ∂p_A (Proposition 51.21 (b)).

(b) (The phase.) P_A(ν_A) = 2 g⁻¹(p_A, ∇_(P_A) p_A), ∇_(P_A) p_A = ½ dν_A + i_(P_A) dp_A, and ℒ_(P_A)(dp_A) =
d(i_(P_A) dp_A), with i_P ω := ω(P, ·). So under (Aug2) ν_A is constant along P_A, and where ν_A ≡ 0, dp_A is
Lie-transported along P_A.

(c) (The stress.) div_g T = Σ_A ((P_A(q_A) + q_A div_g P_A) p_A + q_A ∇_(P_A) p_A) and tr_g T = Σ_A q_A ν_A; under
(Aug2) and (Aug4), div_g T = −Σ_A Δ_A q_A p_A.

(d) (The expansion defect.) Where ζ_A = 1 and p_A = du_A with u_A an eikonal,

    P_A(Δ_A) = −Δ_A (Θ_A + div_g P_A − 2κ_A1 − 2κ_A2) − (T − Ric(g))(P_A, P_A).    (51.9)

(e) (The gauge.) Put B_g T := −div_g T + ½ d tr_g T = Σ_A Δ_A q_A p_A + ½ d(Σ_A q_A ν_A). The gauge vector D := D(g),
with D_m := g_mρ D^ρ, solves

    □_g D_n + Ric(g)_nσ D^σ + 2 ∇^m(L_mn − ½ g_mn tr L) = 2 (B_g T)_n,    (51.10)

with L the tensor of the proof of Lemma 3.6, linear in D and free of its derivatives; and
(T − Ric(g))(P_A, P_A) = −g(∇_(P_A) D, P_A) − L(P_A, P_A), linear in (D, ∂D).

(f) (Characteristics.) The symbol ξ ↦ ξ(P_A) of the transport P_A·∂ vanishes at ξ = p_A, where also g⁻¹(ξ, ξ) =
ν_A = 0 for an eikonal: the characteristic set of the transport meets the light cone along the conormal p_A. In a
first-order form with time τ, the speed P_A^i ξ_i/P_A^τ of the transport meets the speed 0 where P_A^i ξ_i = 0, and the
speed of another family on hyperplanes of ξ. So condition (A4) of [DS23] (Theorem A.6), that distinct
eigenvalues of the symbol never meet, fails for the augmented system.

*Proof.* (a) S_A is a polynomial in Θ_A, κ_Ai, q_B and g⁻¹(p_A, p_B), and κ_Ai = g⁻¹(p_A, dψ_i) holds dψ_i = ½ d g(K_i,
K_i)/g(K_i, K_i), a smooth function of (g, dg) where g(K_i, K_i) > 0, in particular on supp ζ_A; the right side of
(Aug2) holds Γ[g], of (Aug4) Θ_A q_A; and the lower-order part Q of Ric^H is a polynomial of degree two in dg, with
linear and constant parts, by (2.9). The three variants hold div_g P_A, |∇²u_A|² and ∂²u_A respectively, each one
derivative above p_A.

(b) P_A(ν_A) = 2 g^(ab) p_(A,a) ∇_(P_A) p_(A,b) since ∇g = 0. For a covector p, P^b ∇_b p_a = P^b ∇_a p_b + P^b
(∇_b p_a − ∇_a p_b) = ½ ∂_a (g^(bc) p_b p_c) + P^b (dp)_(ba), with (dp)_(ba) := ∂_b p_a − ∂_a p_b. Cartan's formula
ℒ_P = d i_P + i_P d and d(dp) = 0 give the third identity. Under (Aug2) the first gives P_A(ν_A) = 0; where ν_A ≡ 0, the
second gives i_(P_A) dp_A = 0, and then ℒ_(P_A)(dp_A) = 0.

(c) ∇^a(q p_a p_b) = P(q) p_b + q (∇^a p_a) p_b + q p_a ∇^a p_b, and p_a ∇^a p_b = (∇_P p)_b; tr_g T = Σ q_A
g⁻¹(p_A, p_A). Under (Aug2) and (Aug4), the coefficient of p_A is −Θ_A q_A + q_A div_g P_A = −Δ_A q_A.

(d) Put Θ̃ := div_g P_A = □_g u_A. Where ζ_A = 1, (Aug3) reads P_A(Θ_A) = −(Θ_A − κ1 − κ2)² − κ1² − κ2² − T(P_A, P_A),
since T(P_A, P_A) = Σ_B q_B (p_B(P_A))² = Σ_B q_B g⁻¹(p_A, p_B)² (κ_i := κ_Ai). (51.3) gives P_A(Θ̃) =
−(Θ̃ − κ1 − κ2)² − κ1² − κ2² − Ric(g)(P_A, P_A). Subtracting, P_A(Δ_A) = −(Θ_A − Θ̃)(Θ_A + Θ̃ − 2κ1 − 2κ2) − (T −
Ric(g))(P_A, P_A).

(e) As in the proof of Lemma 3.6, (Aug1) reads Ric(g) = T + ½(∇_m D_n + ∇_n D_m) + L_mn. Put E :=
Ric(g) − T. The contracted Bianchi identity gives ∇^m(E_mn − ½ g_mn tr E) = −∇^m(T_mn − ½ g_mn tr T) = (B_g T)_n, and
the left side is ½ □_g D_n + ½(∇^m∇_n D_m − ∇_n∇^m D_m) + ∇^m(L_mn − ½ g_mn tr L) with ∇^m∇_n D_m − ∇_n∇^m D_m =
Ric(g)_nσ D^σ. The last claim is the formula for Ric(g) contracted with P_A twice.

(f) ξ(P_A) = g⁻¹(p_A, ξ) vanishes at ξ = p_A. With time τ the transport reads P_A^τ (∂_τ + (P_A^i/P_A^τ) ∂_i), with
speed P_A^i ξ_i/P_A^τ in the direction ξ; the first-order form of the wave equation has the speed 0 among its
eigenvalues, as in Step 8 of Section 6.5. ∎

**Lemma 51.9** (Speeds on the two-dust background.) Let g0 be the two-dust background of
Proposition 50.6 in the chart (τ, R, angles) of Lemma 50.8, with v̂ = v, τ = v − R and ψ the
function of (50.8), and f = 1 − μ/R² of (50.7). At every point of Ω₂, every future causal
vector Y with dτ(Y) = 1 satisfies

    R² |Ω̇|² ≤ e^ψ/(2 − e^ψ f) ≤ 1,      dR(Y) ∈ [−1, e^ψ f/(2 − e^ψ f)] ⊂ [−1, 1],

where |Ω̇| is the length of the angular part of Y in the unit round metric; the upper end of the interval is negative
where f < 0, and 1 − e^ψ/(2 − e^ψ f) = (2 − e^ψ (1 + f))/(2 − e^ψ f).

*Proof.* Put E := e^ψ and x := dR(Y). On Ω₂, ψ ≤ 0 (proof of Lemma 50.8) and μ ≥ μ0 > 0
(Proposition 50.6 (b)), so 0 < E ≤ 1, f ≤ 1 and E f ≤ 1. By (50.8) with dv̂(Y) = 1 + x,

    g0(Y, Y) = −E² f (1 + x)² + 2E (1 + x) x + R² |Ω̇|²,

so Y is causal exactly when R² |Ω̇|² ≤ q(x) := E (1 + x)(E f (1 + x) − 2x). The quadratic q has leading coefficient
E (E f − 2) < 0 and roots x = −1 and x = E f/(2 − E f), so q ≥ 0 exactly between them; E f/(2 − E f) ≤ 1 because E f ≤ 1,
and it is negative where f < 0. Its maximum, at x* = −(1 − E f)/(2 − E f) where 1 + x* = 1/(2 − E f), is q(x*) =
(E² f + 2E (1 − E f))/(2 − E f)² = E/(2 − E f), and E/(2 − E f) ≤ 1 because E (1 + f) ≤ 2. ∎

**Lemma 51.10** (Transport along a causal field.) Let Ω be admissible for g̊, g a Lorentzian metric
with |g − g̊| ≤ ε1 on Ω, and P a C¹ vector field on Ω, future causal for g, with P(τ) ≥ c_P > 0 and |P| + |∂P| ≤ c_P⁻¹.
Let P(φ) − c φ = f on Ω, with φ a function or an array and c a bounded function or matrix. Then

    ‖φ(τ)‖ ≤ C (‖φ(τ0)‖ + ∫_(τ0)^τ ‖f(t)‖ dt),      ‖·‖ the flat L²(Σ_τ) norm,

with C depending on c_P, sup |c| and Ω.

*Proof.* In the coordinate density, ∂_a(φ² P^a) = 2φ (c φ + f) + φ² ∂_a P^a. Integrate over Ω ∩ {τ0 ≤ t ≤ τ}. The
flux through Σ_τ is ∫_(Σ_τ) P^τ φ², that through Σ_τ0 enters with the opposite sign, and that through a lateral
boundary component {F = 0}, with Ω ⊂ {F ≤ 0} and dF positive on future timelike vectors, is the integral of φ² dF(P)
times a positive density, which is nonnegative because P is future causal and the component is spacelike for g
(Definition 51.7 (c)). Dropping it, ∫_(Σ_τ) P^τ φ² ≤ ∫_(Σ_τ0) P^τ φ² + ∫ (2|φ||f| + C φ²), and c_P ≤ P^τ ≤
c_P⁻¹. Gronwall's inequality concludes. ∎

### 51.5 Kato's iteration with a non-local term

Let d ≥ 1, let s > d/2 + 1 be an integer, so s ≥ 2, and let A^0, A^1, …, A^d be smooth symmetric m × m matrix functions
of (t, x, u) ∈ [0, T0] × R^d × R^m with A^0 ≥ c0 I, c0 > 0, every derivative of which is bounded on [0, T0] × R^d ×
{|u| ≤ R} for every R. Norms without subscript and ⟨·, ·⟩ are those of L²(R^d). For an integer σ ≥ 0, H^σ := H^σ(R^d;
R^m) carries the norm (Σ_(|α|≤σ) ‖∂^α u‖²)^(1/2); for real σ ≥ 0 we also use the norm ‖(1 + |ξ|²)^(σ/2) û‖ of
(A.2), equivalent to the former for integer σ with constants depending on d and σ, and we write H^σ for
either. Hölder's inequality in ξ gives, for the norms of (A.2), 0 ≤ σ0 ≤ σ′ ≤ σ1 and σ′ = (1 − β) σ0 +
β σ1,

    ‖w‖_(H^(σ′)) ≤ ‖w‖_(H^(σ0))^(1−β) ‖w‖_(H^(σ1))^β,    (51.11)

and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, ∫ |ŵ| dξ ≤ ‖(1 + |ξ|²)^(σ/2) ŵ‖ ‖(1 + |ξ|²)^(−σ/2)‖, gives ‖w‖_(L^∞) ≤ C ‖w‖_(H^σ)
for σ > d/2 and ‖∂w‖_(L^∞) ≤ C ‖w‖_(H^σ) for σ > d/2 + 1. We fix C_S ≥ 1 with ‖w‖_(L^∞) ≤ C_S ‖w‖_(H^(s−1)) and
‖w‖_(W^(1,∞)) ≤ C_S ‖w‖_(H^s).

For an integer σ ≥ 0, a *bound of order σ* for a function Φ of (t, x, u), such as A^μ or a forcing term, is an
increasing function of R ≥ 0 that bounds |∂_t^a ∂_x^β ∂_u^γ Φ| on [0, T0] × R^d × {|u| ≤ R} for all a, β, γ with
a + |β| ≤ σ and |γ| ≤ σ. By ∂(A^0)⁻¹ = −(A^0)⁻¹ (∂A^0) (A^0)⁻¹, each such derivative of (A^0)⁻¹ is a sum of
products of (A^0)⁻¹ and of derivatives ∂_t^(a_i) ∂_x^(β_i) ∂_u^(γ_i) A^0 with Σ a_i = a, Σ β_i = β and Σ γ_i = γ;
as |(A^0)⁻¹| ≤ c0⁻¹, c0 and a bound of order σ for A^0 give one for (A^0)⁻¹. At the order s the constants of this section
depend on the coefficients and on local forcing terms only through bounds of order s and through sup_t ‖F(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^s)
(the paragraph after Remark 51.16).

*Mollifiers.* Let φ ∈ C_c^∞(R^d) be even and nonnegative with integral one, φ_ε(x) := ε^(−d) φ(x/ε) and J_ε u := φ_ε ∗ u.
J_ε is self-adjoint on L², commutes with every ∂^α, and does not increase the norms of L², L^∞ and H^σ; ‖∂_j J_ε u‖ ≤
‖∂_j φ‖_(L¹) ε⁻¹ ‖u‖ by Young's inequality; and since |φ̂(εξ) − 1| ≤ min(2, ε |ξ| ∫ |z| φ(z) dz) ≤ C (ε |ξ|)^β for
0 ≤ β ≤ 1, ‖J_ε u − u‖_(H^σ) ≤ C ε^β ‖u‖_(H^(σ+β)).

*Gronwall's inequality in the form used below.* If E ≥ 0 is Lipschitz on [0, T] and its upper right Dini derivative
satisfies D⁺E ≤ 2a E + 2b E^(1/2) with a ≥ 0 constant and b ≥ 0 integrable, then E(t)^(1/2) ≤ e^(at) (E(0)^(1/2) +
∫_0^t b). Indeed E is differentiable almost everywhere with E′ = D⁺E there, so for η > 0 the Lipschitz function
(E + η)^(1/2) has derivative at most a (E + η)^(1/2) + b almost everywhere; Gronwall's inequality for it, and η → 0,
give the bound.

**Lemma 51.11** (Products and compositions.) Let σ ≥ 1 be an integer, and let Φ be a smooth
function of (t, x, u) ∈ [0, T0] × R^d × R^m, with values in a space of matrices, every derivative of which is bounded
on [0, T0] × R^d × {|u| ≤ R} for every R. Constants C(·) are increasing functions of their argument R, depending only
on d, σ and a bound for |∂_x^β ∂_u^γ Φ| on [0, T0] × R^d × {|u| ≤ R}, |β| ≤ σ, |γ| ≤ σ.

(a) For f_1, …, f_ℓ ∈ H^σ ∩ L^∞ and multi-indices α_1, …, α_ℓ with |α_1| + … + |α_ℓ| ≤ σ, every component product
satisfies ‖∂^(α_1) f_1 ⋯ ∂^(α_ℓ) f_ℓ‖ ≤ C Σ_i ‖f_i‖_(H^σ) Π_(j≠i) ‖f_j‖_(L^∞), C depending on d, σ and ℓ.
(b) For u ∈ H^σ ∩ L^∞, Φ(t, ·, u) − Φ(t, ·, 0) ∈ H^σ and ‖Φ(t, ·, u) − Φ(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^σ) ≤ C(‖u‖_(L^∞)) ‖u‖_(H^σ).
(c) For u, y ∈ H^σ ∩ L^∞, ‖Φ(t, ·, u) y‖_(H^σ) ≤ C(‖u‖_(L^∞)) (‖y‖_(H^σ) + ‖u‖_(H^σ) ‖y‖_(L^∞)).
(d) For u ∈ H^σ ∩ W^(1,∞), y ∈ H^(σ−1) ∩ L^∞ and |α| ≤ σ, ‖[∂^α, Φ(t, ·, u)] y‖ ≤ C(‖u‖_(W^(1,∞))) (‖y‖_(H^(σ−1)) +
‖u‖_(H^σ) ‖y‖_(L^∞)).

The bounds hold uniformly in t, and in further parameters on which Φ depends smoothly over a compact set.

*Proof.* (a) Let k := |α_1| + … + |α_ℓ|. If k = 0 the product is at most ‖f_1‖ Π_(j≥2) ‖f_j‖_(L^∞). Let k ≥ 1 and let
the f_i first be real Schwartz functions. The proof of Theorem A.31 (1), at the order k in place of s, shows
max_(|γ|=j) ‖∂^γ f‖_(L^(2k/j)) ≤ (2k)^(j(k−j)/2) ‖f‖_(L^∞)^(1−j/k) ‖f‖_(H^k)^(j/k) for 0 ≤ j ≤ k. Hölder's inequality
with the exponents 2k/|α_i| (∞ where α_i = 0), whose reciprocals add to 1/2, gives ‖Π_i ∂^(α_i) f_i‖ ≤ C Π_i
‖f_i‖_(L^∞)^(1−c_i) ‖f_i‖_(H^k)^(c_i) with c_i := |α_i|/k, Σ_i c_i = 1. With X_i := ‖f_i‖_(H^k) Π_(j≠i) ‖f_j‖_(L^∞),
each ‖f_j‖_(L^∞) appears in Π_i X_i^(c_i) with the exponent Σ_(i≠j) c_i = 1 − c_j, so the right side is C Π_i
X_i^(c_i) ≤ C Σ_i c_i X_i, by the inequality between weighted geometric and arithmetic means; and ‖·‖_(H^k) ≤
‖·‖_(H^σ). For general f_i, take the Schwartz approximations of the proof of Corollary A.30 (1) (real when
f_i is, with L^∞ norms not increased, converging in H^σ); along a subsequence ∂^(α_i) of them converges almost
everywhere, and Fatou's lemma gives (a).
(b) Let u first be a Schwartz function. For 0 < |α| ≤ σ, by the chain rule ∂^α[Φ(t, x, u) − Φ(t, x, 0)] is
(∂_x^α Φ)(t, x, u) − (∂_x^α Φ)(t, x, 0) plus a sum, with coefficients depending on α, of terms (∂_x^β ∂_u^γ Φ)(t, x,
u) applied to ∂^(α_1) u, …, ∂^(α_ℓ) u, ℓ = |γ| ≥ 1, |β| + |α_1| + … + |α_ℓ| = |α|, every |α_i| ≥ 1. The first part is
at most sup |∂_u ∂_x^α Φ| |u| pointwise; in the others the coefficient is bounded by C(‖u‖_(L^∞)) and (a) bounds the
product by C ‖u‖_(H^σ) ‖u‖_(L^∞)^(ℓ−1); for α = 0, |Φ(t, x, u) − Φ(t, x, 0)| ≤ C(‖u‖_(L^∞)) |u|. For general u take
Schwartz u_n → u in H^σ with ‖u_n‖_(L^∞) ≤ ‖u‖_(L^∞); Φ(t, ·, u_n) − Φ(t, ·, 0) converges to Φ(t, ·, u) − Φ(t, ·, 0)
in L² and is bounded in H^σ, so the limit lies in H^σ with the same bound.
(c) By Leibniz's rule ∂^α(Φ(u) y) = Σ_(β≤α) (α choose β) ∂^(α−β)[Φ(u)] ∂^β y, and ∂^(α−β)[Φ(u)] is the sum of
terms of (b), including also ℓ = 0, (∂_x^(β′) Φ)(t, x, u). Terms with ℓ = 0 are bounded functions times ∂^β y; those
with ℓ ≥ 1 are bounded functions times products of derivatives of u and of y of total order at most σ, bounded by (a)
by C(‖u‖_(L^∞)) (‖u‖_(H^σ) ‖y‖_(L^∞) + ‖y‖_(H^σ)). The approximation is that of (b).
(d) [∂^α, Φ(u)] y = Σ_(0<β≤α) (α choose β) ∂^β[Φ(u)] ∂^(α−β) y. Choose a unit multi-index e ≤ β and write ∂^β[Φ(u)] =
∂^(β−e)[(∂_(x_e) Φ)(t, x, u) + (∂_u Φ)(t, x, u) ∂_e u]. Expanding as in (b) and writing every derivative of u of
order at least one as a derivative of some ∂_(e′) u, each term is a function bounded by C(‖u‖_(W^(1,∞))) times a
product of derivatives of the functions ∂_(e′) u and of y of total order at most |α| − 1 ≤ σ − 1. By (a) at the order
σ − 1 (for σ = 1 the products are bounded functions times y), with ‖∂u‖_(H^(σ−1)) ≤ ‖u‖_(H^σ) and ‖∂u‖_(L^∞) ≤
‖u‖_(W^(1,∞)), each is at most C(‖u‖_(W^(1,∞))) (‖y‖_(H^(σ−1)) + ‖u‖_(H^σ) ‖y‖_(L^∞)). For general u and y take
the approximations of (b); the commutators converge as distributions and are bounded in L², so the bound passes to the
limit, ‖∂u_n‖_(L^∞) ≤ ‖u‖_(W^(1,∞)) + o(1).
In (b)–(d), Φ enters only through derivatives ∂_x^β ∂_u^γ Φ with |β| ≤ σ and |γ| ≤ σ, evaluated at u or, in the
first part of (b), between 0 and u: the chain rule for ∂^α, |α| ≤ σ, produces |β| + |γ| ≤ |α| in (b) and (c), the
first part of (b) uses ∂_u ∂_x^α Φ, and in (d) the derivative ∂^β, |β| ≤ σ, falls on Φ(t, x, u) in the same way, so
that the constants depend on Φ only through a bound for these derivatives. ∎

The iteration below solves, at each step, a linear problem, and the energy inequalities it needs are proved first.

**Lemma 51.12** (The linear problem.) Let 0 < T ≤ T0, and let v map [0, T] into H^s with
‖v(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐 and ‖v(t) − v(t′)‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ 𝔐′ |t − t′| for t, t′ ∈ [0, T]. Put 𝐀^μ(t, x) := A^μ(t, x, v(t, x)),
E_σ(t; w) := Σ_(|α|≤σ) ⟨𝐀^0(t) ∂^α w, ∂^α w⟩ for w ∈ H^σ, and

    K := sup_t ‖v(t)‖_(W^(1,∞)) + sup_(t≠t′) ‖v(t) − v(t′)‖_(L^∞)/|t − t′| ≤ C_S (𝔐 + 𝔐′),

and consider

    𝐀^0 ∂_t w + 𝐀^j ∂_j w = f,      w(0) = w0.    (51.12)

(a) Every w ∈ C¹([0, T]; L²) with w(t) ∈ H¹ for every t that solves (51.12) with f ∈ C([0, T]; L²)
satisfies, for t ∈ [0, T],

    E_0(t; w)^(1/2) ≤ e^(C_0 t) (E_0(0; w)^(1/2) + c0^(−1/2) ∫_0^t ‖f‖),

with C_0 depending only on c0 and on bounds for A^μ and its first derivatives at |u| ≤ K. In particular such a
solution is unique.
(b) Let f ∈ C([0, T]; L²) with f(t) ∈ H^s for every t and sup_t ‖f(t)‖_(H^s) < ∞, and w0 ∈ H^s. Then
(51.12) has a solution w ∈ C¹([0, T]; L²) ∩ C([0, T]; H^(s−1)) with w(t) ∈ H^s for every t,

    ‖∂_t w(t)‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ C_1 (‖f(t)‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖w(t)‖_(H^s)),
    E_s(t; w)^(1/2) ≤ e^(C t) (E_s(0; w)^(1/2) + C ∫_0^t ‖f‖_(H^s)),

with C_1 depending on d, s, c0, 𝔐 and bounds of order s for the A^μ, and C on these and 𝔐′.
(c) The solution of (b) satisfies, with K_w := sup_t (‖∂_x w(t)‖_(L^∞) + ‖∂_t w(t)‖_(L^∞)),

    E_s(t; w)^(1/2) ≤ e^(C_* t) (E_s(0; w)^(1/2) + C_* ∫_0^t (‖f‖_(H^s) + K_w ‖v‖_(H^s))),

with C_* depending only on d, s, c0, K and bounds of order s for the A^μ, at R = K.

*Proof.* (1) *Coefficients.* For every t, ‖v(t)‖_(W^(1,∞)) ≤ C_S 𝔐, and |v(t, x) − v(t′, x)| ≤ C_S 𝔐′ |t − t′|; so the
pointwise bounds |𝐀^0(t, x) − 𝐀^0(t′, x)| ≤ L_0 |t − t′| and |∂_j 𝐀^j| ≤ L_1 hold, with L_0, L_1 depending on K and the
bounds of the first derivatives of the A^μ. The inverse (A^0)⁻¹ is smooth with derivatives bounded on bounded sets of u,
since A^0 ≥ c0 I and d(A⁻¹) = −A⁻¹ (dA) A⁻¹. By Lemma 51.11 (c) at σ = s − 1 and σ = s, with ‖y‖_(L^∞) ≤
C_S ‖y‖_(H^(s−1)), multiplication by 𝐀^μ(t) and by (𝐀^0(t))⁻¹ is bounded on H^(s−1) and on H^s, with norm at most C(𝔐);
and by Lemma 51.11 (d) at σ = s, for |α| ≤ s and y ∈ H^(s−1),

    ‖[∂^α, 𝐀^μ] y‖ ≤ C(K) (‖y‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖v‖_(H^s) ‖y‖_(L^∞)) ≤ C(𝔐) ‖y‖_(H^(s−1)).    (51.13)

Write 𝐀^μ(t) − 𝐀^μ(t′) = (t − t′) Ψ_1 + Ψ_2 (v(t) − v(t′)), with Ψ_1, Ψ_2 the integrals over η ∈ [0, 1] of ∂_t A^μ
and ∂_u A^μ at (t′ + η (t − t′), x, v(t′) + η (v(t) − v(t′))). By Lemma 51.11 (c) at σ = s − 1, for
these functions of (x, v(t), v(t′)), and Corollary A.30 (1), t ↦ 𝐀^μ(t) is Lipschitz from [0, T] to the
bounded operators on H^(s−1), with constant C(𝔐)(1 + 𝔐′); likewise (𝐀^0)⁻¹.
(2) *Regularised problem.* For 0 < ε ≤ 1 consider ∂_t w_ε = (𝐀^0)⁻¹ (f − J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε w_ε)), w_ε(0) = w0, in
H^(s−1). Its operator y ↦ (𝐀^0)⁻¹ J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε y) is bounded on H^(s−1), by (1) and ‖∂_j J_ε y‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ C ε⁻¹
‖y‖_(H^(s−1)), and Lipschitz in t; and t ↦ (𝐀^0)⁻¹ f is continuous into H^(s−1), since f is continuous into L² and
bounded in H^s, hence continuous into H^(s−1) by (51.11). Picard's iteration for linear ordinary
differential equations in a Banach space gives a unique solution w_ε ∈ C¹([0, T]; H^(s−1)). At every t its right side
lies in H^s with norm at most C_ε := C(𝔐)(sup_t ‖f(t)‖_(H^s) + ε⁻² sup_t ‖w_ε(t)‖_(H^(s−1))). So w_ε is Lipschitz into
H^s: for φ in the Schwartz class, ⟨w_ε(t) − w_ε(t′), (1 − Δ)^s φ⟩ = ∫_(t′)^t ⟨∂_t w_ε, (1 − Δ)^s φ⟩ is at most
C_ε |t − t′| ‖φ‖_(H^s), the norms being those of (A.2), and w0 ∈ H^s.
(3) *Uniform bounds.* Let |α| ≤ s and E^α(t) := ⟨𝐀^0(t) ∂^α w_ε, ∂^α w_ε⟩, which is Lipschitz in t by (2). As w_ε is
Lipschitz into H^s and continuously differentiable into H^(s−1), the difference quotients of ∂^α w_ε converge weakly in
L² to ∂^α ∂_t w_ε; with the pointwise Lipschitz bound of (1) and the symmetry of 𝐀^0 this gives D⁺E^α ≤ L_0 ‖∂^α
w_ε‖² + 2 ⟨𝐀^0 ∂^α ∂_t w_ε, ∂^α w_ε⟩. Apply ∂^α to the equation 𝐀^0 ∂_t w_ε = f − J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε w_ε), both sides of
which lie in H^s, and put y := ∂^α J_ε w_ε = J_ε ∂^α w_ε. As J_ε is self-adjoint and ⟨𝐀^j ∂_j y, y⟩ = −½ ⟨(∂_j 𝐀^j)
y, y⟩ (the matrices 𝐀^j are symmetric and Lipschitz, y ∈ H¹),

    2 ⟨𝐀^0 ∂^α ∂_t w_ε, ∂^α w_ε⟩ = 2 ⟨∂^α f − [∂^α, 𝐀^0] ∂_t w_ε, ∂^α w_ε⟩ + ⟨(∂_j 𝐀^j) y, y⟩
                                     − 2 ⟨[∂^α, 𝐀^j] ∂_j J_ε w_ε, y⟩.

By the equation and (1), ‖∂_t w_ε‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ C_1 (‖f‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖w_ε‖_(H^s)); with (51.13) and
‖y‖ ≤ ‖∂^α w_ε‖, the sum over |α| ≤ s gives D⁺E_s(t; w_ε) ≤ C (E_s(t; w_ε) + ‖f‖_(H^s) E_s(t; w_ε)^(1/2)), as E_s ≥
c0 ‖·‖²_(H^s). The function t ↦ ‖f(t)‖_(H^s) is lower semicontinuous, f being continuous into L², hence measurable;
Gronwall's inequality gives the bound of (b) for w_ε, uniformly in ε, since E_s(0; w_ε) = E_s(0; w0). For (c), use the
first form of (51.13), ‖∂_x J_ε w_ε‖_(L^∞) ≤ ‖∂_x w_ε‖_(L^∞), and the bound ‖∂_t w_ε‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤
C(K) (‖f‖_(H^(s−1)) + ‖w_ε‖_(H^s) + ‖v‖_(H^s) (‖∂_x w_ε‖_(L^∞) + ‖∂_t w_ε‖_(L^∞))), which follows from the equation
by Lemma 51.11 (c) at σ = s − 1, applied to 𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε w_ε and to (𝐀^0)⁻¹ (𝐀^0 ∂_t w_ε). This gives
D⁺E_s ≤ C_* (E_s + (‖f‖_(H^s) + K_(w_ε) ‖v‖_(H^s)) E_s^(1/2)) with K_(w_ε) defined as K_w, and the bound of (c) for w_ε.
(4) *Limit.* z := w_ε − w_(ε′) solves 𝐀^0 ∂_t z + J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε z) = r, z(0) = 0, with r := J_(ε′)(𝐀^j ∂_j
J_(ε′) w_(ε′)) − J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε w_(ε′)), and ‖r‖ ≤ C (ε + ε′) ‖w_(ε′)‖_(H²) ≤ C (ε + ε′), as s ≥ 2. The argument of (3)
at the order 0, where ⟨J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε z), z⟩ = −½ ⟨(∂_j 𝐀^j) J_ε z, J_ε z⟩, gives sup_t ‖z‖ ≤ C (ε + ε′). So w_ε → w
in C([0, T]; L²). At each t, w_ε(t) is bounded in H^s and converges in L², hence weakly in H^s; so w(t) ∈ H^s, and as
y ↦ E_s(t; y) is a continuous nonnegative quadratic form on H^s, hence weakly lower semicontinuous, the bound of (b)
holds for w. By (51.11), w_ε → w in C([0, T]; H^(s′)) for every s′ < s, in particular in
C([0, T]; H^(s−1)), and J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε w_ε) → 𝐀^j ∂_j w in C([0, T]; L²), by ‖J_ε g − g‖ ≤ C ε ‖g‖_(H¹). So ∂_t w_ε
converges in C([0, T]; L²) to (𝐀^0)⁻¹ (f − 𝐀^j ∂_j w), and w ∈ C¹([0, T]; L²) solves (51.12), with
the bound on ∂_t w by the equation. For (c), fix s′ with max(d/2 + 1, s − 1) < s′ < s and s″ with max(d/2, s − 2)
< s″ < s − 1. Then ‖∂_x(w_ε − w)‖_(L^∞) ≤ C ‖w_ε − w‖_(H^(s′)) → 0 uniformly in t, and ‖∂_t w_ε − ∂_t w‖_(L^∞) → 0
uniformly in t: ∂_t w − ∂_t w_ε is (𝐀^0)⁻¹ applied to J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j J_ε(w_ε − w)) + J_ε(𝐀^j ∂_j (J_ε w − w)) + (J_ε −
I) g, g := 𝐀^j ∂_j w, whose terms are bounded in L^∞ by C ‖∂_x(w_ε − w)‖_(L^∞), by C ‖J_ε w − w‖_(H^(s′)) ≤ C
ε^(s−s′) ‖w‖_(H^s), and by C ‖J_ε g − g‖_(H^(s″)) ≤ C ε^(s−1−s″) ‖g‖_(H^(s−1)). So K_(w_ε) → K_w, and the bound of (c)
passes to the limit as that of (b).
(5) *The order 0.* For w as in (a), E_0(t; w) is Lipschitz, and D⁺E_0 ≤ L_0 ‖w‖² + 2 ⟨𝐀^0 ∂_t w, w⟩ = L_0 ‖w‖² +
2 ⟨f, w⟩ + ⟨(∂_j 𝐀^j) w, w⟩, the integral of ∂_j ⟨𝐀^j w, w⟩, a function of W^(1,1)(R^d), being 0. With ‖w‖² ≤
E_0/c0 this is D⁺E_0 ≤ 2 C_0 E_0 + 2 c0^(−1/2) ‖f‖ E_0^(1/2), and Gronwall's inequality gives (a). ∎

The theorem below solves

    A^0(t, x, u) ∂_t u + A^j(t, x, u) ∂_j u = F(t, u),      u(0) = u0,    (51.14)

with a forcing term F that may be non-local, given on a ball about a reference path. Fix a reference path u_* ∈
C([0, T0]; H^(s+1)) ∩ C¹([0, T0]; H^s) and a radius ρ ∈ (0, ∞], and put 𝒟_ρ := {(t, u) : t ∈ [0, T0], u ∈ H^s,
‖u − u_*(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ ρ}; for ρ = ∞ take u_* := 0, so that 𝒟_∞ = [0, T0] × H^s. Let F map 𝒟_ρ to H^s with:

(F1) ‖F(t, u)‖_(H^s) ≤ C_F(𝔐) for (t, u) ∈ 𝒟_ρ with ‖u‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐;
(F2) ‖F(t, u) − F(t, v)‖ ≤ L(𝔐) ‖u − v‖ for (t, u), (t, v) ∈ 𝒟_ρ with ‖u‖_(H^s), ‖v‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐;
(F3) t ↦ F(t, u(t)) is continuous into L² whenever u ∈ C([0, T]; L²), (t, u(t)) ∈ 𝒟_ρ for every t, and
sup_t ‖u(t)‖_(H^s) < ∞;

C_F and L increasing. A *solution on [t1, t2]* is a u ∈ C¹([t1, t2]; L²) with u(t) ∈ H^s and (t, u(t)) ∈ 𝒟_ρ for every
t, and sup_t ‖u(t)‖_(H^s) < ∞, that satisfies the equation of (51.14). Let C_A bound |A^0| on [0, T0]
× R^d × {|u| ≤ C_S (sup_t ‖u_*(t)‖_(H^s) + ρ)}, and put η_ρ := ½ (c0/C_A)^(1/2) if ρ < ∞, η_∞ := 1.

The *domain version* concerns a compact set Ω = ⋃_(t∈[0,T0]) {t} × Σ_t ⊂ [0, T0] × R^d with Σ_t = ψ_t(Σ_⋆), where Σ_⋆
⊂ R^d is a compact domain with smooth boundary and the ψ_t are diffeomorphisms of R^d, smooth in (t, x), equal to the
identity outside a compact set, with every derivative of positive order of ψ_t and of ψ_t⁻¹ bounded uniformly in t. Its
lateral boundary is ⋃_t {t} × ∂Σ_t, with ν the outward conormal (positive on vectors pointing out of Ω) at its points.
It assumes, for a number r_b > 0:

(F4) for (t, u), (t, v) ∈ 𝒟_ρ with u = v on Σ_t, F(t, u) = F(t, v) on Σ_t; and ‖F(t, u) − F(t, v)‖_(L²(Σ_t)) ≤ L(𝔐)
‖u − v‖_(L²(Σ_t)) when moreover ‖u‖_(H^s), ‖v‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐;
(F5) the lateral boundary is spacelike for the system at the states within r_b of u_*: ν_t A^0(t, x, u) + ν_j A^j(t,
x, u) ≥ 0 at its points (t, x) for every u with |u − u_*(t, x)| ≤ r_b.

**Theorem 51.13** (Kato's iteration with a non-local term.) Assume (F1)–(F3).

(a) For every u0 ∈ H^s with ‖u0 − u_*(0)‖_(H^s) ≤ η_ρ ρ there are T* > 0, depending only on an upper bound for
‖u0‖_(H^s), on ρ and on u_*, and a unique solution on [0, T*] with u(0) = u0. If u is a solution on [0, T1] for every
T1 < T2 ≤ T0, with sup_(t<T2) ‖u(t)‖_(H^s) < ∞ and ‖u(t) − u_*(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ η_ρ ρ for t < T2, then u extends to a
solution on [0, T2], and beyond T2 if T2 < T0.
(b) (Domain version.) Assume (F4) and (F5). (i) Two solutions u, ũ on [t1, t2] with |u − u_*| ≤ r_b and |ũ − u_*| ≤
r_b on Ω, whose values at t1 agree on Σ_(t1), agree on Ω ∩ {t1 ≤ t ≤ t2}. (ii) Let C_S ρ ≤ r_b. There is C_E ≥ 1,
depending on Ω and s, such that for every u0 ∈ H^s(Σ_0) with ‖u0 − u_*(0)‖_(H^s(Σ_0)) ≤ η_ρ ρ/C_E the system has a
solution on Ω ∩ {t ≤ T*}, T* > 0 depending only on ρ, u_* and Ω: a function on Ω ∩ {t ≤ T*} equal near every time to
the restriction of a solution on an interval, with value u0 on Σ_0; by (i) it does not depend on the solutions used. It
extends to Ω ∩ {t ≤ T2} as long as ‖u(t) − u_*(t)‖_(H^s(Σ_t)) ≤ η_ρ ρ/C_E for t < T2.

*Proof.* (a) Let C_u bound |A^0| on [0, T0] × R^d × {|u| ≤ C_S ‖u0‖_(H^s)}, and put 𝔐² := 2 C_u ‖u0‖²_(H^s)/c0 + 1,
so that C_u ‖u0‖²_(H^s) < c0 𝔐², and 𝔐′ := C_1(𝔐)(C_F(𝔐) + 𝔐) + sup_t ‖∂_t u_*(t)‖_(H^(s−1)), C_1 the constant of
Lemma 51.12 (b). Put u^0(t) := u0 + u_*(t) − u_*(0) (so u^0 = u0 if ρ = ∞), and for n ≥ 0 let u^(n+1)
be the solution of Lemma 51.12 (b) with v := u^n, f := F(t, u^n) and w0 := u0:

    A^0(t, x, u^n) ∂_t u^(n+1) + A^j(t, x, u^n) ∂_j u^(n+1) = F(t, u^n),      u^(n+1)(0) = u0.

We show by induction that for T* small, depending only on the quantities named, every u^n satisfies: u^n ∈ C([0, T*];
L²), u^n(0) = u0, and for t, t′ ∈ [0, T*], ‖u^n(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐, ‖u^n(t) − u^n(t′)‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ 𝔐′ |t − t′| and
‖u^n(t) − u_*(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ ρ. For u^0 this holds once T* sup_t ‖∂_t u_*(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐 − ‖u0‖_(H^s), since ‖u0 −
u_*(0)‖_(H^s) ≤ ρ. Let it hold for u^n. Then f is defined, continuous into L² by (F3), and ‖f(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ C_F(𝔐) by
(F1), so u^(n+1) exists. *Boundedness.* E_s(0; u^(n+1)) ≤ C_u ‖u0‖²_(H^s), so by Lemma 51.12 (b), with
its constant C = C(𝔐, 𝔐′),

    c0^(1/2) ‖u^(n+1)(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ E_s(t; u^(n+1))^(1/2) ≤ e^(Ct) (C_u^(1/2) ‖u0‖_(H^s) + C t C_F(𝔐)) ≤ c0^(1/2) 𝔐

for t ≤ T* small. By the same lemma ‖∂_t u^(n+1)(t)‖_(H^(s−1)) ≤ C_1(𝔐)(C_F(𝔐) + 𝔐) ≤ 𝔐′, which gives the Lipschitz
bound into H^(s−1) by the duality argument of step (2) of that proof. If ρ < ∞, w := u^(n+1) − u_* solves the linear
problem with the same coefficients, with data u0 − u_*(0) and forcing term F(t, u^n) − 𝐀^0 ∂_t u_* − 𝐀^j ∂_j u_*,
continuous into L² and bounded in H^s by a constant K_* depending on 𝔐 and u_*; by Lemma 51.12 (a) w is
the solution of (b) there, and as C_u ≤ C_A and η_ρ = ½ (c0/C_A)^(1/2),

    ‖w(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ c0^(−1/2) e^(Ct) (C_A^(1/2) η_ρ ρ + C t K_*) = e^(Ct) (ρ/2 + c0^(−1/2) C t K_*) ≤ ρ

for t ≤ T* small. *Contraction.* For n ≥ 1, δ^(n+1) := u^(n+1) − u^n solves the linear problem with the coefficients at
u^n, data 0 and the forcing term

    −(A^0(t, x, u^n) − A^0(t, x, u^(n−1))) ∂_t u^n − (A^j(t, x, u^n) − A^j(t, x, u^(n−1))) ∂_j u^n + F(t, u^n) −
    F(t, u^(n−1)),

which is continuous into L² with norm at most (C(𝔐, 𝔐′) + L(𝔐)) ‖δ^n‖, since ‖∂_t u^n‖_(L^∞) ≤ C_S 𝔐′ and ‖∂_x
u^n‖_(L^∞) ≤ C_S 𝔐, and by (F2). Lemma 51.12 (a) gives sup_t ‖δ^(n+1)‖ ≤ c0^(−1) e^(C_0 T*) (C(𝔐, 𝔐′) +
L(𝔐)) T* sup_t ‖δ^n‖ ≤ ½ sup_t ‖δ^n‖ for T* small. *Limit.* So u^n → u in C([0, T*]; L²). For each t, u^n(t) is bounded
in H^s and converges in L², hence weakly in H^s, and the norms and the ball are weakly closed: ‖u(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐, ‖u(t) −
u_*(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ ρ, and u is Lipschitz into H^(s−1) with constant 𝔐′. By (51.11), u^n → u in C([0,
T*]; H^(s−1)), so ∂_x u^n → ∂_x u in C([0, T*]; L²) and A^μ(t, x, u^n) → A^μ(t, x, u) uniformly; by (F2), F(t, u^n) →
F(t, u) in C([0, T*]; L²). Passing to the limit in u^(n+1)(t) = u0 + ∫_0^t (A^0)⁻¹(u^n) (F(t′, u^n) − A^j(u^n) ∂_j
u^(n+1)) dt′ gives u(t) = u0 + ∫_0^t (A^0)⁻¹(u) (F(t′, u) − A^j(u) ∂_j u) dt′, with an integrand continuous into L²: u
is a solution on [0, T*]. *Uniqueness.* Let u, ũ be solutions on [0, T] with the same data. By its equation ‖∂_t
u(t)‖_(H^(s−1)) is bounded, so v := u satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 51.12, and z := u − ũ solves the
linear problem with coefficients at u, data 0 and forcing term F(t, u) − F(t, ũ) − (A^μ(u) − A^μ(ũ)) ∂_μ ũ (∂_0 := ∂_t),
continuous into L² with norm at most C ‖z‖, by (F2) and the bounds on ∂ũ. Part (a) of the lemma and Gronwall's
inequality give z = 0. *Continuation.* The hypotheses are unchanged under t ↦ t − t1 on [t1, T0]. With 𝔐_2 := sup_(t<T2)
‖u(t)‖_(H^s), the first part from the time t1 with data u(t1) gives a solution on [t1, t1 + T*(𝔐_2)], T*(𝔐_2) not
depending on t1; for t1 > T2 − T*(𝔐_2) it agrees with u on [t1, T2) by uniqueness, and the two together form a solution
on [0, min(t1 + T*(𝔐_2), T0)].

(b) (i) z := u − ũ lies in C¹([t1, t2]; L²) ∩ C([t1, t2]; H^(s−1)), by (51.11), so z and its first
derivatives lie in L² on Ω_t := Ω ∩ {t1 ≤ t′ ≤ t}, and z is bounded. The matrices 𝐀^μ := A^μ(t, x, u) are Lipschitz in
(t, x), u being Lipschitz in x, and in t into L^∞. On Ω, 𝐀^0 ∂_t z + 𝐀^j ∂_j z = g := F(t, u) − F(t, ũ) − (A^μ(u) −
A^μ(ũ)) ∂_μ ũ, and by (F4), ‖g(t)‖_(L²(Σ_t)) ≤ C ‖z(t)‖_(L²(Σ_t)). The field V^μ := ⟨𝐀^μ z, z⟩ (x^0 := t, here the
inner product of R^m) lies in W^(1,1)(Ω_t), with ∂_μ V^μ = ⟨(∂_μ 𝐀^μ) z, z⟩ + 2 ⟨g, z⟩ by the symmetry of the 𝐀^μ.
Ω_t is the image of [t1, t] × Σ_⋆ under (t′, y) ↦ (t′, ψ_(t′)(y)), a Lipschitz domain, on which the divergence theorem
holds for W^(1,1) fields, by the density of smooth fields and the continuity of the trace from W^(1,1)(Ω_t) to
L¹(∂Ω_t). It gives

    e(t) − e(t1) + ∫ ⟨(ν_μ 𝐀^μ) z, z⟩ |ν|⁻¹ dS = ∫_(t1)^t ∫_(Σ_(t′)) ∂_μ V^μ dx dt′,      e(t) := ∫_(Σ_t) ⟨𝐀^0 z, z⟩ dx,

the middle integral over the lateral boundary of Ω_t, ν the outward conormal and dS the Euclidean surface measure. By
(F5) at the states u, within r_b of u_*, it is nonnegative. As e ≥ c0 ‖z‖²_(L²(Σ_t)), e(t) ≤ e(t1) + C ∫_(t1)^t e,
and e(t1) = 0; so e = 0. (ii) Let E_⋆ be Stein's extension operator for Σ_⋆ (Theorem A.36), bounded from
H^σ(Σ_⋆) to H^σ(R^d) for 0 ≤ σ ≤ s + 1, and E_t g := E_⋆(g ∘ ψ_t) ∘ ψ_t⁻¹. Composition with ψ_t and with ψ_t⁻¹ is
bounded on H^σ uniformly in t, by the chain rule and the change of variables, as in Step 8 (iv) of
Section 6.5; so E_t g = g on Σ_t and the norms of E_t on H^σ, σ ≤ s + 1, are bounded uniformly in t. Let C_E
≥ 1 bound them for σ ≤ s. At a time t1 with ‖u(t1) − u_*(t1)‖_(H^s(Σ_(t1))) ≤ η_ρ ρ/C_E, the datum u_*(t1) + E_(t1)(u(t1)
− u_*(t1)) lies within η_ρ ρ of u_*(t1) in H^s, so (a) from the time t1 gives a solution on [t1, t1 + T*], T* depending
only on ρ, u_* and Ω, within ρ of u_* in H^s, hence within C_S ρ ≤ r_b pointwise. Starting at t1 = 0 with u(0) := u0,
and restarting at the times k T*/2, the restrictions to Ω agree where they overlap, by (i); this gives the solution on
Ω and its extension. ∎

[IT20, Theorem 1, p. 3] is the case A^0 = I and F = 0 of (a): "The equation (1.2) is locally well-posed in H^s in the
Hadamard sense for s > d/2 + 1", for ∂_t u = A^j(u) ∂_j u with "the m × m matrices A^j … symmetric" [IT20, p. 2]; it is
due to Kato [Kat75] ([IT20, p. 4]). Cauchy stability is part of well-posedness in Hadamard's sense: "for a solution u ∈
C([0, T]; H^s), small perturbations of the initial data u_0 yield solutions which are also defined in [0, T]"
[IT20, p. 2]. With a non-local forcing term over a given interval it needs a bound that is linear in the H^s norm.

**Theorem 51.14** (Cauchy stability.) Let ρ = ∞, and assume (F1)–(F3) and

(F1′) ‖F(t, u)‖_(H^s) ≤ C′(‖u‖_(W^(1,∞))) (1 + ‖u‖_(H^s)), C′ increasing.

(a) Let 0 < T ≤ T0 and let ū ∈ C¹([0, T]; L²), with ū(t) ∈ H^s for every t and sup_t ‖ū(t)‖_(H^s) < ∞, satisfy

    A^0(t, x, ū) ∂_t ū + A^j(t, x, ū) ∂_j ū = F(t, ū) + R,    (51.15)

where R ∈ C([0, T]; L²), R(t) ∈ H^s and ‖R(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ 1 for every t. There are ε0 > 0 and C such that, if ‖u0 −
ū(0)‖_(H^s) ≤ ε0 and sup_t ‖R(t)‖ ≤ ε0, the solution u of Theorem 51.13 with u(0) = u0 exists on [0, T], and

    sup_t ‖u − ū‖ ≤ C (‖u0 − ū(0)‖ + sup_t ‖R(t)‖),      sup_t ‖u‖_(H^s) ≤ C,
    sup_t ‖u − ū‖_(H^(s′)) ≤ C (‖u0 − ū(0)‖ + sup_t ‖R(t)‖)^(1−s′/s)      for d/2 + 1 < s′ < s.

ε0 and C depend only on d, s, s′, c0, T, sup_t ‖ū(t)‖_(H^s), K_ū := sup_t (‖ū(t)‖_(W^(1,∞)) + ‖∂_t ū(t)‖_(L^∞)),
the functions C_F, L and C′, and bounds of order s for the A^μ.
(b) (Domain version.) Let Ω be as in the domain version, and let ū, defined on Ω ∩ {t ≤ T}, satisfy the equation of
(51.14) there, with ū ∘ Ψ ∈ C([0, T]; H^(s+1)(Σ_⋆)) ∩ C¹([0, T]; H^s(Σ_⋆)), Ψ(t, y) := (t,
ψ_t(y)). Let (F4) and (F5) hold with u_* := ū_e, the extension defined in the proof. Then for data u0 on Σ_0 with ‖u0
− ū(0)‖_(H^s(Σ_0)) ≤ ε0 the system has a solution on Ω ∩ {t ≤ T}: the restriction to Ω of a solution on [0, T] of the
system with a forcing term equal to F on every Σ_t. It is the only such restriction within r_b of ū_e, and the
conclusions of (a) hold for it with R = 0 and every norm taken on Σ_t, the constants depending also on Ω. The
hypothesis on ū ∘ Ψ in (b) is stronger than continuity of ū into H^s(Σ_t); no result of this paper uses (b), and none
needs it for a ū with that weaker regularity.

With R = 0, (a) is the stability of an exact solution. If ū solves the system with coefficients Ā^μ and forcing term F̄,
it satisfies (51.15) with R := (A^μ(t, x, ū) − Ā^μ(t, x, ū)) ∂_μ ū − F(t, ū) + F̄(t, ū); so (a)
is also the stability under a perturbation of the coefficients and of the forcing term that is small in L² along ū and
bounded in H^s, the constants being uniform over a family of systems with uniform bounds.

*Proof.* (a) Let C_u bound |A^0| on [0, T0] × R^d × {|u| ≤ C_S (sup_t ‖ū(t)‖_(H^s) + 1)}, and let ε0 ≤ 1. K_ū is
finite: by (51.15), ‖∂_t ū(t)‖_(H^(s−1)) is bounded. Let u be the solution of Theorem 51.13
(a) with u(0) = u0 on its maximal interval [0, T_m) ∩ [0, T], and put q(t) := ‖u(t) − ū(t)‖_(W^(1,∞)) + ‖∂_t u(t) −
∂_t ū(t)‖_(L^∞). q is continuous: u and ū are continuous into H^(s′) for s′ < s by (51.11), and
H^(s′) ⊂ W^(1,∞) for s′ > d/2 + 1; and by their equations ∂_t u and ∂_t ū are continuous into L^∞, since F(t, u(t))
and R are continuous into L² and bounded in H^s, hence continuous into H^(s″) ⊂ L^∞ for d/2 < s″ < s. At t = 0, the
estimates of (3), with w(0) = u0 − ū(0), give q(0) ≤ ½ for ε0 small. Let T* be the supremum of the t < min(T_m, T)
with q ≤ 1 on [0, t]; we show q ≤ ½ on [0, T*) for ε0 small, which excludes T* < min(T_m, T), and T_m ≤ T.

(1) Put K := K_ū + 1. On [0, T*), sup (‖u‖_(W^(1,∞)) + ‖∂_t u‖_(L^∞)) ≤ K, and ‖ū‖_(W^(1,∞)) + ‖∂_t ū‖_(L^∞) ≤ K.
On [0, t] for t < T*, v := u satisfies the hypotheses of Lemma 51.12, ∂_t u being bounded in H^(s−1) by
its equation, and u solves the linear problem with f := F(t, u); by part (a) of the lemma it is the solution of (b), so
(c) and (F1′) give

    E_s(t; u)^(1/2) ≤ e^(C_* t) (E_s(0; u)^(1/2) + C_* ∫_0^t (C′(K)(1 + ‖u‖_(H^s)) + K ‖u‖_(H^s))),

with C_* = C_*(K). As ‖u‖_(H^s) ≤ c0^(−1/2) E_s^(1/2) and E_s(0; u) ≤ C_u (sup_t ‖ū(t)‖_(H^s) + 1)², Gronwall's
inequality gives ‖u(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ 𝔐 on [0, T*), with 𝔐 depending only on the quantities named.

(2) w := u − ū solves the linear problem with coefficients at u and forcing term f_w := F(t, u) − F(t, ū) − R −
(A^μ(u) − A^μ(ū)) ∂_μ ū, ∂_0 := ∂_t, and ‖f_w‖ ≤ L_1 ‖w‖ + ‖R‖, with L_1 := L(𝔐_1) + C(K) K_ū and 𝔐_1 := max(𝔐,
sup_t ‖ū(t)‖_(H^s)). Lemma 51.12 (a) and Gronwall's inequality give, with C_0 = C_0(K),

    ‖w(t)‖ ≤ C_2 δ,      δ := ‖w(0)‖ + sup_t ‖R‖,      C_2 := c0^(−1/2) e^(C_0 T) (C_u^(1/2) + c0^(−1/2) T) e^(b T),

with b := c0^(−1) L_1 e^(C_0 T), as E_0(0; w) ≤ C_u ‖w(0)‖² and ‖w‖ ≤ c0^(−1/2) E_0(t; w)^(1/2).

(3) By (51.11), for d/2 + 1 < s′ < s, ‖w‖_(W^(1,∞)) ≤ C ‖w‖_(H^(s′)) ≤ C (C_2 δ)^(1−s′/s)
(2𝔐_1)^(s′/s). By the two equations, 𝐀^0 ∂_t w = F(t, u) − F(t, ū) − R − 𝐀^j ∂_j w − (A^μ(u) − A^μ(ū)) ∂_μ ū, so
‖∂_t w‖_(L^∞) ≤ C(K)(‖F(t, u) − F(t, ū)‖_(L^∞) + ‖R‖_(L^∞) + (1 + K_ū) ‖w‖_(W^(1,∞))). For d/2 < s″ < s, by
(51.11), (F2) and (F1′),

    ‖F(t, u) − F(t, ū)‖_(L^∞) ≤ C ‖F(t, u) − F(t, ū)‖_(H^(s″)) ≤ C (L(𝔐_1) C_2 δ)^(1−s″/s) (2 C′(K)(1 + 𝔐_1))^(s″/s),

and ‖R‖_(L^∞) ≤ C ‖R‖^(1−s″/s) ‖R‖_(H^s)^(s″/s) ≤ C ε0^(1−s″/s). As δ ≤ 2ε0, q ≤ ½ on [0, T*) for ε0 small,
depending only on the quantities named.

(4) If T* < min(T_m, T), then q ≤ ½ at T* by continuity and q < 1 a little beyond, against the definition of T*. If
T_m ≤ T, then on [0, T_m) the bounds (1) and q ≤ ½ hold, so Theorem 51.13 (a) extends u beyond T_m, against its
maximality. So u exists on [0, T] and the bounds of (1)–(3) hold there; they are those stated.

(b) Put ū_e(t) := E_t(ū(t)) with E_t of the proof of Theorem 51.13 (b) (ii); by the assumption on ū ∘ Ψ, ū_e ∈
C([0, T]; H^(s+1)) ∩ C¹([0, T]; H^s), the time derivative falling on ψ_t and ψ_t⁻¹ costing one derivative in x. Let
R_e := A^0(t, x, ū_e) ∂_t ū_e + A^j(t, x, ū_e) ∂_j ū_e − F(t, ū_e), continuous into L² and bounded in H^s; by (F4),
R_e = 0 on Σ_t, where ū_e = ū. The system with forcing term F(t, u) + R_e(t) satisfies (F1′), (F1)–(F5) with the same
u_* := ū_e and agrees with the original on Ω, and ū_e solves it exactly. For data u0 on Σ_0, (a) applies to it with the
datum ū_e(0) + E_0(u0 − ū(0)), within C_E ‖u0 − ū(0)‖_(H^s(Σ_0)) of ū_e(0) in H^s and within C_E ‖u0 − ū(0)‖_(L²(Σ_0))
in L² (Stein's operator being bounded on L² as well). The solution stays within r_b of ū_e pointwise for ε0 small, by
the bound on ‖u − ū_e‖_(H^(s′)). The argument of Theorem 51.13 (b) (i) uses the equations on Ω only, where the
forcing terms of such systems agree with F, so it gives the uniqueness; and the norms on Σ_t are at most those on
R^d. ∎

**Corollary 51.15** (Closed leaves, perturbed coefficients.) Let n ≥ 1, let S^n be the unit sphere
of R^(n+1), W_ab := x_a ∂_b − x_b ∂_a (0 ≤ a < b ≤ n) the rotation fields, which are tangent to S^n and span its
tangent spaces, and H^σ(S^n) the space of u ∈ L²(S^n) with W_(a1b1) ⋯ W_(akbk) u ∈ L²(S^n) for k ≤ σ, normed as in
Corollary A.30 (2). Let s > (n + 1)/2 + 1 be an integer, T > 0, and A^0, A^(ab), F smooth functions of (t,
ω, u, π) ∈ [0, T] × S^n × R^m × R^q, A^0 and A^(ab) symmetric m × m matrices. Let P̄ : [0, T] × S^n → R^q and ū :
[0, T] × S^n → R^m be smooth, ū solving

    A^0(t, ω, u, P) ∂_t u + Σ_(a<b) A^(ab)(t, ω, u, P) W_ab u = F(t, ω, u, P)    (51.16)

with P = P̄, and let A^0 be positive definite at the points (t, ω, ū(t, ω), P̄(t, ω)). There is r̄ > 0 such that for
every r0 ∈ (0, r̄] there are ε0 > 0 and C such that, for every smooth P : [0, T] × S^n → R^q with ‖P − P̄‖_(C^s) ≤ ε0
(derivatives of order at most s in (t, ω)) and every u0 ∈ H^s(S^n) with ‖u0 − ū(0)‖_(H^s(S^n)) ≤ ε0:

(a) (51.16) has a solution u ∈ C¹([0, T] × S^n) with u(0) = u0, u(t) ∈ H^s(S^n), |u − ū| ≤ r0, and

    sup_t ‖u − ū‖_(L²(S^n)) ≤ C (‖u0 − ū(0)‖_(L²(S^n)) + ‖P − P̄‖_(C^0)),      sup_t ‖u(t)‖_(H^s(S^n)) ≤ C,
    sup |u − ū| ≤ C (‖u0 − ū(0)‖_(L²(S^n)) + ‖P − P̄‖_(C^0))^(1/(4s));

it is the only solution in C¹([0, T]; L²(S^n)) with u(t) ∈ H^s(S^n) for every t, sup_t ‖u(t)‖_(H^s(S^n)) < ∞ and |u −
ū| ≤ r0. So every map that carries such solutions with the datum u0 to such solutions with the datum u0 fixes u.
(b) If u0 is smooth, u is smooth on [0, T] × S^n.
(c) Let Ω ⊂ [0, T] × S^n be compact, with every Ω_t := Ω ∩ {t′ ≤ t} a Lipschitz domain whose boundary consists of the
base Ω ∩ {t′ = 0}, the slice Ω ∩ {t′ = t} and a lateral part, a finite union of smooth hypersurfaces at whose points
(t, ω) the outward conormal ν satisfies ν(∂_t) A^0 + Σ_(a<b) ν(W_ab) A^(ab) ≥ 0 at P̄(t, ω) and at every u with |u −
ū(t, ω)| ≤ r0. If P = P̄ on Ω and u0 = ū(0) on the base, then u = ū on Ω.

Every vector field Y = Y^K ∂_K tangent to S^n can be written Σ_(a<b) ⟨Y, W_ab⟩ W_ab, since Σ_(a<b) ⟨X, W_ab⟩ W_ab = |x|²
X − ⟨x, X⟩ x = X for X tangent to S^n at x; so a system ∂_t u + B^K ∂_K u + C = 0 on S^n with a symmetrizer H (H B^K
symmetric, H positive definite at ū) is of the form (51.16) with A^0 := H, A^(ab) := H B^K ⟨∂_K, W_ab⟩
and F := −H C.

*Proof.* (1) *A cut-off of the states.* By compactness there are r̄, ε1 > 0 and c0 > 0 with A^0(t, ω, u, π) ≥ 2c0 I
for |u − ū(t, ω)| ≤ 2r̄ and |π − P̄(t, ω)| ≤ ε1; let 0 < r0 ≤ r̄. Let ϒ be a smooth map of R^m with ϒ(w) = w for |w| ≤
r0 and |ϒ| ≤ 2r0, and let ε0 ≤ ε1; the constants below depend on r0. For w := u − ū the system reads, where |w| ≤ r0,

    B^0 ∂_t w + Σ_(a<b) B^(ab) W_ab w = G(t, ω, w),

with B^μ(t, ω, w) := A^μ(t, ω, ū + ϒ(w), P) (μ = 0 or μ = ab) and G := F(t, ω, ū + ϒ(w), P) − B^0 ∂_t ū − Σ B^(ab)
W_ab ū; B^0 ≥ 2c0 I for every w, and G(t, ω, 0) = 0 when P = P̄. So |G(t, ω, 0)| ≤ C ‖P − P̄‖_(C^0) and the C^s norm of
G(·, ·, 0) is at most C ‖P − P̄‖_(C^s). A derivative of the B^μ or of G of order at most s in (t, ω), and of any order
in w, holds derivatives of P of order at most s only, and ‖P‖_(C^s) ≤ ‖P̄‖_(C^s) + ε1; so these derivatives are
bounded on bounded sets of w uniformly in P.

(2) *The system on R^(n+1).* Let χ, χ_1 ∈ C_c^∞((1/2, 2)) take values in [0, 1] and equal 1 on [3/4, 4/3], and for x ≠ 0
put x̂ := x/|x|. On [0, T] × R^(n+1) let

    Ã^0 := χ(|x|) B^0(t, x̂, W) + (1 − χ(|x|)) I,      Ã^j := χ(|x|) Σ_(a<b) B^(ab)(t, x̂, W) (W_ab)^j(x),
    F̃ := χ(|x|) G(t, x̂, W),

(W_ab)^j the components of W_ab, linear in x; these are zero or the identity off {1/2 < |x| < 2}. They are smooth and
symmetric, Ã^0 ≥ min(2c0, 1) I, every derivative is bounded on bounded sets of W and, by (1), their bounds of order s
(in the sense of Section 51.5) are uniform in P, and F̃(t, x, 0) vanishes for |x| ∉ (1/2, 2). As the W_ab are
tangent to the spheres |x| = r and commute with dilations, the system Ã^0 ∂_t W + Ã^j ∂_j W = F̃ holds no derivative
across the spheres, and on each sphere |x| = r ∈ [3/4, 4/3], with W_r(t, ω) := W(t, rω), it is the system of (1) for W_r.
Its forcing term is local and satisfies (F1)–(F3) and (F1′) by Remark 51.16, and for P = P̄, W̄ := 0 solves
it; for general P, 0 satisfies (51.15) with R := −F̃(t, x, 0), ‖R(t)‖ ≤ C ‖P − P̄‖_(C^0) and
‖R(t)‖_(H^s) ≤ C ‖P − P̄‖_(C^s) ≤ 1.

(3) *Existence and bounds.* Put W(0, x) := χ_1(|x|) w0(x̂), w0 := u0 − ū(0). Since ∂_j = x̂_j ∂_r − |x|⁻² Σ_b x_b W_jb
(W_jb := −W_bj), ‖W(0)‖_(H^s(R^(n+1))) ≤ C ‖w0‖_(H^s(S^n)) and ‖W(0)‖ ≤ C ‖w0‖_(L²(S^n)). Theorem 51.14
(a) in R^(n+1), with s > (n + 1)/2 + 1, gives for ε0 small a solution W on [0, T] with sup_t ‖W‖ ≤ C (‖w0‖_(L²(S^n)) +
‖P − P̄‖_(C^0)) and sup_t ‖W‖_(H^s) ≤ C. Put s′ := s − 1/4, which exceeds (n + 1)/2 + 1, an integer larger than
(n + 1)/2 + 1 being larger by at least 1/2; then 1 − s′/s = 1/(4s), and the bound of that theorem in H^(s′) gives

    sup_t ‖W‖_(W^(1,∞)) ≤ C sup_t ‖W‖_(H^(s′)) ≤ C (‖w0‖_(L²(S^n)) + ‖P − P̄‖_(C^0))^(1/(4s)),

which is at most r0 for ε0 small. The constants are uniform in P: at the order s, those of
Theorem 51.14 depend on the coefficients and on the local forcing term F̃ only through bounds of order s
and through sup_t ‖F̃(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^s) (the paragraph after Remark 51.16), and by (1) and (2) these are
uniform in P, sup_t ‖F̃(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^s) being at most C ‖P − P̄‖_(C^s) ≤ 1. W lies in C([0, T]; C¹) by
(51.11), and ∂_t W is continuous by the equation; so W ∈ C¹([0, T] × R^(n+1)), and every W_r,
3/4 ≤ r ≤ 4/3, is a C¹ solution on [0, T] × S^n of the system of (1) with the datum w0. Two such solutions coincide:
their difference z satisfies the L² energy identity on S^n, in which ∫_(S^n) ⟨B^(ab) W_ab z, z⟩ = −½ ∫_(S^n) ⟨(W_ab
B^(ab)) z, z⟩ because the rotations preserve the measure of S^n, and Gronwall's inequality gives z = 0. So W(t, rω) =
W(t, ω) on the shell 3/4 ≤ |x| ≤ 4/3, and u := ū + W_1 solves (51.16), since |W_1| ≤ r0; and
sup |u − ū| = sup |W_1| ≤ sup_t ‖W‖_(W^(1,∞)). On the shell W_ab W(t, rω) = (W_ab W_1)(t, ω), and the W_ab have
bounded coefficients there; so the L² and H^s norms of W_1(t) on S^n are bounded by C times those of W(t) on R^(n+1).
This is (a) except uniqueness. *Uniqueness.* For two solutions in the class of (a), the H^s(S^n) norm bounds W_ab u in
H^(s−1)(S^n) ⊂ L^∞ (Theorem A.27, s − 1 > n/2, the norm of Corollary A.30 (2) being equivalent to
that of [BH17] by the chart comparison in its proof), and ∂_t u is bounded by the equation; the L² energy identity on S^n
for their difference, as above, gives uniqueness.

(4) *Smoothness.* If u0 is smooth, W(0) and the coefficients are smooth, and for every integer σ ≥ s, Theorem 51.13
(a) at the order σ gives a solution in H^σ, equal to W on its interval by uniqueness. While it exists,
Lemma 51.12 (c) at the order σ, with v := W, f := F̃(t, W), ‖F̃(t, W)‖_(H^σ) ≤ ‖F̃(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^σ) +
C(‖W‖_(L^∞)) ‖W‖_(H^σ) (Lemma 51.11 (b)) and K_W ≤ sup_([0,T]) (‖∂_x W‖_(L^∞) + ‖∂_t W‖_(L^∞)) < ∞, gives a
linear Gronwall inequality for ‖W(t)‖_(H^σ); so ‖W(t)‖_(H^σ) is bounded on [0, T] and, by the continuation in
Theorem 51.13 (a), W(t) ∈ H^σ for t ∈ [0, T]. By the equation ∂_t W is a smooth function of (t, x, W, ∂_x W), and
by induction ∂_t^k W is bounded in every H^σ; so W is smooth, and so is u.

(5) *Domain of influence.* z := u − ū satisfies on Ω, where P = P̄, B^0 ∂_t z + Σ B^(ab) W_ab z = g with |g| ≤ C |z|,
B^μ := A^μ(t, ω, u, P̄). The field (⟨B^0 z, z⟩, ⟨B^(ab) z, z⟩ W_ab) on [0, T] × S^n has divergence ⟨(∂_t B^0 + Σ W_ab
B^(ab)) z, z⟩ + 2 ⟨g, z⟩, the W_ab being divergence free; the divergence theorem on Ω_t, as in the proof of
Theorem 51.13 (b) (i), with the lateral terms nonnegative by the condition on ν at the states u, |u − ū| ≤ r0,
gives e(t) ≤ e(0) + C ∫_0^t e for e(t) := ∫_(Ω∩{t′=t}) ⟨B^0 z, z⟩, and e(0) = 0. ∎

**Remark 51.16** (Local forcing terms.) A forcing term F(t, x, u) that is a smooth function of (t, x,
u), every derivative of which is bounded on [0, T0] × R^d × {|u| ≤ R} for every R, with F(t, x, 0) = 0 for x outside a
fixed compact set, satisfies (F1)–(F3) with ρ = ∞, (F1′), and (F4) for every domain: by Lemma 51.11 (b),
‖F(t, u)‖_(H^s) ≤ ‖F(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^s) + C(‖u‖_(L^∞)) ‖u‖_(H^s), which gives (F1) and (F1′); |F(t, x, u) − F(t, x, v)| ≤
C |u − v| pointwise for |u|, |v| ≤ C_S 𝔐, which gives
(F2) and the bound of (F4); F(t, x, u) − F(t′, x, u) = (t − t′) ∫_0^1 ∂_t F(t′ + η (t − t′), x, u) dη, bounded in L² by
C |t − t′| (1 + ‖u‖), which with (F2) gives (F3); and locality is (F4).

*Which derivatives the constants use.* At the order σ, Lemma 51.11 uses Φ only through a bound of order
σ (the end of its proof). In Lemma 51.12 the coefficients enter through step (1) of the proof, the later
steps using its bounds: through Lemma 51.11 (c) and (d) at the orders s − 1 and s for A^μ and (A^0)⁻¹,
through Lemma 51.11 (c) at the order s − 1 for Ψ_1 and Ψ_2, which hold ∂_t A^μ and ∂_u A^μ under at
most s − 1 further derivatives in x and in u, and through L_0 and L_1, which hold first derivatives. The constants of
Theorem 51.13 and Theorem 51.14 are made from those of Lemma 51.12, from C_S and the
other Sobolev constants of this section, which depend only on d and the orders used, from sup |A^0|, sup |(A^0)⁻¹|,
sup |A^j| and sup |∂_u A^μ| on sets {|u| ≤ R}, and from C_F, L and C′; for a local forcing term the proof above obtains
these from Lemma 51.11 (b) at the order s, from sup |∂_u F| on such sets and from sup_t ‖F(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^s).
So at the order s these constants depend on the coefficients and on a local forcing term only through bounds of order s
and through sup_t ‖F(t, ·, 0)‖_(H^s).

**Remark 51.17** (Numerical observation.) For the scalar model u_t + (1 + u) u_x = −(1 − ∂_x²)⁻¹(u²)
on the line, whose right side is non-local, the iteration of Theorem 51.13 was run in floating point: the successive
differences sup_t ‖u^(n+1) − u^n‖_(L²) fell by ratios between 0.053 and 0.110, and the H² norms stayed at 2.40 within
5 %; with the right side 0.5 u_xx in its place, which violates (F1) and (F2), the H² norms grew from 2.07 to 230. For the
stability statement, the quotient ‖F(u)‖_(H²)/(‖u‖_(L^∞) ‖u‖_(H²)) stayed below 0.2629 on twenty random states, and on
[0, 1], inside the lifespan of the computed solution ū, sup_t ‖u_d − ū‖_(H²)/d was 12.46, 12.45, 12.45 for perturbations
of the data of size d = 4 × 10⁻³, 2 × 10⁻³, 10⁻³; on [0, 3], past the shock of ū, ‖ū‖_(H²) grew by a factor 420. No
proof uses these observations.

### 51.6 Cauchy stability off the axes

Keep the setting of Section 51.4. For a solution U = (g, p_A, Θ_A, q_A) of the augmented system put w :=
g − g̊, δp_A := p_A − dů_A, δΘ_A := Θ_A − □_g̊ ů_A and δq_A := q_A − q̊_A, and on Σ_τ

    𝒩_k(τ) := Σ_(j≤k) (‖∂^j ∂w‖ + Σ_A (‖∂^j δp_A‖ + ‖∂^j δΘ_A‖ + ‖∂^j δq_A‖)) + ‖w‖,    (51.17)

with ∂^j all spacetime coordinate derivatives of order j and ‖·‖ the flat L²(Σ_τ) norm. No wavelength enters: the
background does not oscillate.

A *datum* on Σ_τ0 is the Cauchy data (g, ∂_τ g) of a metric together with, for each family, functions u_A and q_A ≥ 0
on Σ_τ0, all smooth and G-invariant. From it, p_A on Σ_τ0 is the covector whose spatial part is ∂_x u_A and whose
τ-component is the root of g⁻¹(p_A, p_A) = 0 near that of dů_A, and Θ_A := □_g u_A on Σ_τ0, computed with the
τ-derivative of p_A that (Aug2) gives. The datum satisfies the *gauge condition* if D(g) = 0 on Σ_τ0, and the
*constraints* if (Ric(g) − ½ R(g) g − T + ½ (tr_g T) g)(n♯, ·) = 0 on Σ_τ0, n♯ := g⁻¹dτ, the constraints of Ric(g) = T
written in Cauchy data. It lies within ε of ů's if the expression (51.17) at τ0, with spatial derivatives
only and with ∂_τ w included among the first derivatives, is at most ε.

**Theorem 51.18** (Cauchy stability off the axes.) Fix an integer k ≥ 6, δ > 0 and N_f ≥ 1.
Let Ω be admissible for g̊ and ů = (g̊, ů_A, q̊_A) a class solution of (51.1) on a neighbourhood of Ω with

(H1) every ů_A smooth on Ω with dů_A ≠ 0 there (no caustic on Ω), and
(H2) closed G-invariant sets S_A ⊂ Σ_τ0 containing supp q̊_A ∩ Σ_τ0, whose tubes 𝒯̊_A for P̊_A lie at distance at
least 2δ from the axes.

Then there are ε, ε2 > 0 and C such that every datum on Σ_τ0 that satisfies the constraints and the gauge condition,
lies within ε of ů's, and has supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ⊂ S_A for every A, has a smooth G-invariant development on Ω solving
(51.1) in the gauge D(g) = 0 relative to g̊, with 𝒩_k ≤ C ε on [τ0, τ1], p_A = du_A and Θ_A = □_g u_A on
supp q_A, and supp q_A within C ε of 𝒯̊_A; and it is the only smooth G-invariant development on Ω in that gauge,
with that datum, whose norm 𝒩_(k−1), computed with p_A := du_A and Θ_A := □_g u_A, is at most ε2 on [τ0, τ1]. No
smallness of ů or of the families is assumed; ε, ε2 and C depend on ů, Ω, N_f, k and δ.

*Proof.* We follow the steps of Section 6.4 and Section 6.5.

*Step 1 (Sobolev).* On Σ_τ, ‖∂^i U − ∂^i ů‖_(L^∞) ≤ C 𝒩_k for the first-order variables U = (w, ∂w, δp_A, δΘ_A, δq_A)
and i ≤ k − 3, by the Sobolev inequality of Lemma 5.1 (with λ = 1). Products and compositions of the unknowns are
estimated in H^k(Σ_τ) by Moser's estimate and the composition estimate after a uniform extension
(Theorem A.36, Corollary A.30 (1), Lemma 51.11).

*Step 2 (data).* The τ-derivatives of every order of the unknowns on Σ_τ0 are fixed by (Aug1)–(Aug4), (Aug1) through
−½ g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b g with g^(ττ) ≠ 0, and 𝒩_k(τ0) ≤ C ε. The data of Θ_A are □_g u_A, those of q_A the densities.

*Step 3 (bootstrap).* Suppose 𝒩_k ≤ 2C_* ε on [τ0, τ*] ⊂ [τ0, τ1], with C_* fixed in Step 8. For ε small, |g − g̊| ≤
ε1 on Ω ∩ {τ ≤ τ*}, so (a)–(c) of Definition 51.7 hold for g; every P_A is null, future directed and transverse
to Σ_τ, with P_A(τ) bounded below; by (Aug4), q_A vanishes along every integral curve of P_A on which it vanishes
initially, so supp q_A lies in the tube 𝒯_A of S_A for P_A; the integral curves of P_A from S_A stay within C ε of
𝒯̊_A, by comparison of ordinary differential equations on the compact Ω, hence 𝒯_A ⊂ {ζ_A = 1}; and Θ_A stays
bounded.

*Step 4 (w).* Since ů solves (Aug1) with Ric^H(g̊) = Ric(g̊) (D(g̊) = 0), (2.9) gives −½ g^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b w =
½ (g^(ab) − g̊^(ab)) ∂_a ∂_b g̊ − Q(X; g)(∂g, ∂g) + Q(X; g̊)(∂g̊, ∂g̊) + T − T̊, with

    T − T̊ = Σ_A (δq_A p_A ⊗ p_A + q̊_A (δp_A ⊗ p_A + dů_A ⊗ δp_A)).

Apply ∂^α, |α| ≤ k, and the energy inequality Lemma 5.5 with g̊ in place of g0. The term ∂^α(T − T̊) is at most
C 𝒩_k in L², and the commutators [∂^α, g^(ab)] ∂_a ∂_b w and the quadratic terms give at most C 𝒩_k + C 𝒩_k².

*Step 5 (δp_A).* Apply ∂^α to (Aug2) minus its form for ů: P_A(∂^α δp_A) equals ∂^α of the terms P_A^b (Γ[g] −
Γ[g̊])^c_ba p_(A,c), Γ[g̊]^c_ba (P_A^b p_(A,c) − P̊_A^b ∂_c ů_A) and −(P_A − P̊_A)^b ∂_b ∂_a ů_A, plus the commutator
[∂^α, P_A·∂] δp_A, whose top term is (∂^α P_A)·∂ δp_A. All are at most C 𝒩_k + C 𝒩_k² in L². Lemma 51.10
applies: the lateral boundaries are spacelike with Ω to their past, so every future causal transport field leaves Ω
through them, and the boundary terms have the good sign for every family; on the two-dust background this is explicit in
Lemma 51.9. The angular part of P_A enters only the term ∂_a P^a of the bulk.

*Step 6 (δΘ_A).* Where ζ_A ≠ 0, ů satisfies (51.3) (Proposition 51.5 (c)), so S_A(ů) =
S̊_A there, and (Aug3) minus its form for ů reads

    P_A(δΘ_A) = ζ_A (S_A(U) − S_A(ů)) − (P_A − P̊_A)(□_g̊ ů_A).

On supp ζ_A, g(K_i, K_i) ≥ c δ², so S_A is a smooth function of (g, dg, p_B, Θ_A, q_B) there (Proposition 51.8
(a)), and ∂^α(ζ_A (S_A(U) − S_A(ů))) is at most C(δ) (𝒩_k + 𝒩_k²) in L², the constant carrying a factor δ^(−1−j) from
the j-th derivatives of 1/g(K_i, K_i). The other term and the commutator are bounded likewise, and
Lemma 51.10 applies.

*Step 7 (δq_A).* P_A(δq_A) = −δΘ_A q_A − (□_g̊ ů_A) δq_A − (P_A − P̊_A)(q̊_A), with every term at most C 𝒩_k after
∂^α, and Lemma 51.10 applies.

*Step 8 (closing).* Steps 4–7 give 𝒩_k(τ) ≤ C2 (𝒩_k(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^τ (𝒩_k + 𝒩_k²)). With 𝒩_k ≤ 2C_* ε ≤ 1, Gronwall's
inequality and Step 2 give 𝒩_k ≤ C3 ε on [τ0, τ*], C3 := C2 C e^(2C2 (τ1 − τ0)). Put C_* := C3; then 𝒩_k ≤ C_* ε <
2C_* ε for ε ≤ ε0, which improves the bootstrap. Only the perturbation is small.

*Step 9 (existence).* Extend the coefficients outside Ω as in Step 8 (i) of Section 6.5, to a background equal
to Minkowski space outside a compact set, with the families extended smoothly and cut off to vanish there (S̊_A and the
ζ_A likewise), and use the coordinates (τ, y) of Step 8 (ii) there, the cut-off of Step 8 (iii) there, and a cut-off on
p_A that keeps P_A^τ ≥ c > 0. In the unknowns U := (w, ∂_τ w, ∂_y w, δp_A, δΘ_A, δq_A), the differences from the
extended ů, the augmented system is then a quasilinear symmetric hyperbolic system on [τ0, τ1] × R⁴ of the form of
(51.14), with A^0 = diag(1, −g^(00), g^(ab)) on the wave block and P_A^τ on the transports, and with a
forcing term F(τ, y, U) that is a smooth function, every derivative bounded on bounded sets of U, with F(τ, y, 0) = 0
outside a compact set (the extended background solves the extended system there). By Remark 51.16 it
satisfies (F1)–(F4) and (F1′). (F5) holds at the states within some r_b of 0: on the wave block the boundary matrix at a
conormal ν is ν_0 on w and, on (u_0, u_b), the form −(g^(00) ν_0 + 2 g^(0c) ν_c) u_0² + ν_0 g^(ab) u_a u_b − 2 u_0
g^(cb) ν_c u_b; by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality for the positive definite g^(ab), it is nonnegative exactly when ν_0 ≥
0 and g⁻¹(ν, ν) ≤ 0, that is, where the boundary is spacelike or null with Ω to its past; on a transport it is ν(P_A),
nonnegative when P_A is future causal. At ů both hold strictly, by Definition 51.7 (a)–(b), so they hold at the
states within some r_b of it. By Proposition 51.8 (f) the theorem of [DS23] does not apply as stated.
Theorem 51.13 (b) (ii) with s = k, u_* := 0 and C_S ρ ≤ r_b gives the solution on Ω ∩ {τ ≤ τ0 + T*} and its
extension on Ω while ‖U(τ)‖_(H^k(Σ_τ)) ≤ η_ρ ρ/C_E; that norm is at most C 𝒩_k, so by Steps 3–8 the solution exists on Ω
with 𝒩_k ≤ C ε. On each interval of the restarts the solution on R⁴ is smooth, the datum being smooth, by the argument
of step (4) of the proof of Corollary 51.15 (Lemma 51.12 (c) at every order, with coefficients
bounded by 𝒩_k); so the solution is smooth. The system is invariant under G: g(K_i, K_i) is invariant, K_i is mapped to
± K_i, and ζ_A, S̊_A are invariant. So the image of the solution under an element of G solves the same system with the
same datum, and equals it on Ω by Theorem 51.13 (b) (i). *Uniqueness.* Let (g, u_A, q_A) be a smooth G-invariant
development on Ω in the gauge D(g) = 0, with the same datum and 𝒩_(k−1) ≤ ε2, computed with p_A := du_A and Θ_A := □_g
u_A. With p_A := du_A, (Aug1) and (Aug2) hold, since Ric^H(g) = Ric(g) = T and ∇_(P_A) du_A = ½ d g⁻¹(du_A, du_A) = 0.
Let Θ_A solve (Aug3) with the data □_g u_A on Σ_τ0. On the tube of supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0, which contains supp q_A and lies in
{ζ_A = 1} for ε2 small (as in Step 3), Θ_A and □_g u_A solve the same ordinary differential equation along P_A
(Proposition 51.5 (c)) with the same data, so they agree, and (Aug4) is the conservation law there; off it
q_A = 0. So the development gives a solution of the augmented system on Ω, within C ε2 of ů in 𝒩_(k−1) by the estimate of
Step 6 at the order k − 1. For ε2 small both it and the solution constructed lie within r_b of ů pointwise, and the
argument of Theorem 51.13 (b) (i), which uses the solutions on Ω only, at the order s = k − 1 > 3, shows that they
agree on Ω.

*Step 10 (constraints).* On Σ_τ0, ν_A = 0 by the choice of p_A, and P_A(ν_A) = 0 with P_A^τ ≠ 0 gives ∂_τ ν_A = 0
there, so dν_A = 0 on Σ_τ0. Then i_(P_A) dp_A = ∇_(P_A) p_A − ½ dν_A = 0 on Σ_τ0 (Proposition 51.8 (b)); the
spatial components of dp_A vanish there (p_A has spatial part ∂_x u_A), so dp_A = E_i dτ ∧ dx^i, and i_(P_A) dp_A = 0
with P_A^τ ≠ 0 gives E_i = 0: dp_A = 0 on Σ_τ0. Every point of Ω lies on an integral curve of P_A that meets Σ_τ0
inside Ω (Definition 51.7 (c)), so by Proposition 51.8 (b), ν_A ≡ 0 and dp_A ≡ 0 on Ω. Ω is simply
connected, so p_A = du_A with u_A an eikonal of g.

The gauge vector D vanishes on Σ_τ0, so, as in the proof of Lemma 3.6, Ric(g) − T = ½ (n ⊗ Y + Y ⊗ n)
there with n := dτ and Y_a := g_aρ ∂_τ D^ρ, and the constraints give ½ g⁻¹(n, n) Y = 0, so ∂_τ D = 0 on Σ_τ0. On Σ_τ0
also Δ_A = Θ_A − □_g u_A = 0. On the tube 𝒯_A ⊂ {ζ_A = 1}, Proposition 51.8 (d) and (e) give

    P_A(Δ_A) = −Δ_A (Θ_A + div_g P_A − 2κ_A1 − 2κ_A2) + g(∇_(P_A) D, P_A) + L(P_A, P_A),

and D solves (51.10) with B_g T = Σ_A Δ_A q_A p_A, since ν_A ≡ 0 and supp q_A ⊂ 𝒯_A. The quantity
‖∂D(τ)‖ + ‖D(τ)‖ + Σ_A ‖Δ_A‖_(L²(𝒯_A ∩ Σ_τ)) obeys a linear Gronwall inequality: for D by Lemma 5.5, and for Δ_A by
the argument of Lemma 51.10 on the tube, whose lateral boundary is ruled by integral curves of P_A, so that
the transport has no flux through it. Its value at τ0 is 0, so D = 0 and Δ_A = 0 on 𝒯_A. Hence Ric(g) = T, Θ_A =
□_g u_A on supp q_A, and (Aug4) is the conservation law div_g(q_A P_A) = 0 there: (g, u_A, q_A) solves
(51.1). ∎

**Corollary 51.19** (Non-round families on the seed.) Let g̊ be g0 of (2.3) with μ ≡ μ0
≥ √72 l5², the seed, on the domain Ω of (2.8), with q̊_A = 0, and let ů_A be finitely many phases in the class
that are eikonals of g̊, smooth with dů_A ≠ 0 on Ω, with closed sets S_A ⊂ Σ_τ0 whose tubes lie at distance at least 2δ
from the axes: for instance radial eikonals with S_A in an angular band {ϑ1 ≤ ϑ ≤ ϑ2}, 0 < ϑ1 < ϑ2 < π/2. Then every
datum satisfying the constraints and the gauge condition, within ε of ů's, with supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ⊂ S_A, has its non-round
Einstein–null-dust development on the whole of Ω, within C ε of the seed.

*Proof.* (H1) and (H2) hold, and Ω is admissible for g̊ by Lemma 2.6; apply Theorem 51.18. ∎

The corollary gives a large background, the seed, carrying any finite number of small non-round families supported away
from the axes, on the whole domain; the hole grows by O(ε), unlike the growing hole of Theorem 3.1. It assumes the data.
They are not constructed here: the outward radial solve of Chapter 7 is built for data depending on the wavelength, and
a small non-round dust density, with regularity at the axes for a solve that is parabolic in ϑ, is not examined here (the
symmetrizer of that solve exists on every slice, Lemma 52.26, and Chapter 52 carries the solve out for
its own data, with constants independent of λ, Proposition 52.28); data localised in an angle are the
subject of Chapter 53.

**Corollary 51.20** (Large data for a short time.) Let a datum on Σ_τ0 satisfy the constraints and the
gauge condition, with densities vanishing within 2δ of the axes, and let Ω be admissible for a smooth G-invariant metric
g̃ whose Cauchy data on Σ_τ0 are those of the datum. With g̃ in place of g̊ in the gauge of (Aug1), ζ_A equal to 1 on
the points at distance at least 2δ from the axes, S̊_A replaced by any fixed smooth function, and p_A on Σ_τ0 the root
of g⁻¹(p_A, p_A) = 0 with spatial part ∂_x u_A for which P_A is future directed, the augmented system has a solution on
Ω ∩ {τ ≤ τ0 + T}, T > 0 depending on the datum, which solves (51.1) as long as the tubes of the S_A := supp
q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 stay in {ζ_A = 1}.

*Proof.* Step 9, with g̃ in place of g̊ and the datum, constant in τ, as the reference path u_*, gives the solution for
a short time, during which g stays within ε1 of g̃ and the admissibility of Ω persists (Definition 51.7
(c)); Steps 4–8 bound it on a short interval, and Step 10 applies on the tubes. ∎

### 51.7 The axes

Near a point of axis 2 with ρ1 > 0 the circle of K1 acts freely, and a class metric is g = ĝ + e^(2ψ1) dφ1², with ĝ a
metric in the coordinates (τ, ρ1, x), x := (x3, x4), invariant under the rotations and reflections of x. We write
X^B ∈ {τ, ρ1}, ∂_3 := ∂_(x3), ∂_4 := ∂_(x4), and use the invariance under rotations of x to work at the points
x = (ρ2, 0), ρ2 ≥ 0. There the reflection x4 ↦ −x4 fixes the point, so ĝ(∂_B, ∂_4) = ĝ(∂_3, ∂_4) = 0 and ∂_4 u = 0 for
an invariant u. Along the ray ρ2 ↦ (ρ2, 0), the rotation by π, which maps (ρ2, 0) to (−ρ2, 0) and ∂_3, ∂_4 to −∂_3,
−∂_4, shows that ĝ(∂_B, ∂_3) and ∂_3 u are odd smooth functions of ρ2, and ĝ(∂_B, ∂_C), ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3), ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4) and
∂_B u even ones. At ρ2 = 0 every rotation fixes the point, so ĝ(∂_B, ∂_3) = 0 and ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3) = ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4) there. Put
a_⊥ := g(K2, K2)/ρ2², an invariant function equal to ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4) at (ρ2, 0), positive and even along the ray. By
Taylor's formula, an odd smooth function of ρ2 divided by ρ2, and an even one vanishing at 0 divided by ρ2², are smooth
and even; so at (ρ2, 0) the metric is

    ĝ = ĝ_BC dX^B dX^C + 2 (c_B dX^B)(x·dx) + a_⊥ |dx|² + b_⊥ (x·dx)²,    (51.18)

with ĝ_BC := ĝ(∂_B, ∂_C), c_B := ĝ(∂_B, ∂_3)/ρ2, a_⊥ and b_⊥ := (ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3) − ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4))/ρ2² smooth even
functions of ρ2.

**Proposition 51.21** (The torus curvature at the axis.) Let g be a class metric and u a phase in the class
near a point of axis 2 with ρ1 > 0, and work at the points (ρ2, 0).

(a) g(K2, K2) = a_⊥ ρ2², and ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3) − a_⊥ = b_⊥ ρ2² tends to 0 at the axis.
(b) κ2 = g⁻¹(du, dψ2) extends continuously to the axis, with the value

    κ2 = ∂_3²u/a_⊥ + γ^B ∂_B u + ĝ^(BC) ∂_B u ∂_C a_⊥/(2a_⊥),      γ^B := lim_(ρ2→0) ĝ^(3B)/ρ2,

there: on the axis κ2 holds a second derivative of u, while du = ∂_B u dX^B holds none. The curvature κ1 of the circle
that does not degenerate there holds no second derivative of u on the axis.
(c) Off the axis κ2 is a function of the 1-jets of u and g, and at (ρ2, 0) the coefficient of ∂_3 u in it is
1/(a_⊥ ρ2) + O(1).
(d) If moreover g⁻¹(du, du) = 0 near the point, then at (ρ2, 0) with ρ2 > 0, ∇²u(e2, e2) = κ2 and

    ∇²u(∂_3, ∂_3)/ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3) − κ2 = O(ρ2²):

the planar anisotropy vanishes to second order. On the axis the restriction of ∇²u to span(∂_3, ∂_4) is ½(Θ − κ1)
times that of ĝ, Θ := □_g u; so κ2 and Θ_h extend continuously to the axis with the value (Θ − κ1)/2, and the planar
shear σ := Θ_h − κ2 extends by 0. Off the axis, with χ of Proposition 51.5 (b),

    |χ|² = κ1² + ½ (Θ − κ1)² + ½ σ².    (51.19)

*Proof.* (a) At (ρ2, 0), K2 = ρ2 ∂_4, so g(K2, K2) = ρ2² ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4) = a_⊥ ρ2², and ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3) − ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4) = b_⊥ ρ2².
(b) ψ2 = ½ log a_⊥ + log ρ2, and at (ρ2, 0), dρ2 = dx3, so κ2 = ½ g⁻¹(du, d log a_⊥) + (ĝ^(3B) ∂_B u + ĝ^(33) ∂_3 u)/ρ2.
As ρ2 → 0: ĝ^(3B) is odd and ĝ^(3B)/ρ2 → γ^B; ∂_3 u is odd and ∂_3 u/ρ2 → ∂_3²u; at the axis ĝ is block diagonal with
ĝ(∂_i, ∂_j) = a_⊥ δ_ij, so ĝ^(33) → 1/a_⊥; and ∂_3 a_⊥ = O(ρ2), ∂_4 a_⊥ = 0. For κ1 = ½ g⁻¹(du, d log e^(2ψ1)), with
e^(2ψ1) smooth and positive near the point, the inverse metric is block diagonal at the axis and du holds no second
derivative.
(c) Off the axis ψ2 is smooth, so κ2 is a function of the 1-jets. In the formula of (b) the terms in ∂_3 u are
ĝ^(33) ∂_3 u/ρ2 and ½ ∂_3 u (ĝ^(33) ∂_3 + ĝ^(3B) ∂_B) log a_⊥ = ∂_3 u · O(ρ2), and ĝ^(33) − 1/a_⊥ is even and vanishes
at the axis, hence O(ρ2²).
(d) At (ρ2, 0), e2 = K2/|K2| = ∂_4/√a_⊥, and Proposition 51.5 (a) gives ∇²u(e2, e2) = κ2. Along the ray the
functions ∇²u(∂_3, ∂_3) and ∇²u(∂_4, ∂_4) are smooth and even, by the rotation by π, and equal at ρ2 = 0, where every
rotation fixes the point; so their difference is O(ρ2²), and so is that of ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3) and ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4). Hence
∇²u(∂_3, ∂_3)/ĝ(∂_3, ∂_3) − ∇²u(∂_4, ∂_4)/ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4) = O(ρ2²), the second quotient being κ2. On the axis, ∂_i u = 0
and ĝ(∂_B, ∂_i) = 0, so ∂_3, ∂_4 and K1 are orthogonal to P, and they span a screen of P. The argument of
Proposition 51.5 (a) for the free circle of K1 gives ∇²u(∂_i, K1) = 0 and ∇²u(K1, K1) = e^(2ψ1) κ1; the planar
block of ∇²u is invariant under the rotations of x, hence m ĝ|_plane for a number m; and the trace over the screen is
□_g u by the first part of Proposition 51.5 (b), which is pointwise and holds at the axis (its proof uses
only that P is null with ∇²u(P, ·) = 0 at the point, and the screen is {P, L̄}^⊥ for a null L̄ with g(P, L̄) = −1), so
Θ = κ1 + 2m and m = (Θ − κ1)/2. By continuity κ2 = ∇²u(∂_4, ∂_4)/ĝ(∂_4, ∂_4)
tends to m, and Θ_h = Θ − κ1 − κ2 tends to m. Finally (51.2) reads |χ|² = Θ_h² + κ1² + κ2², and Θ_h² +
κ2² = ½ (Θ_h + κ2)² + ½ (Θ_h − κ2)² with Θ_h + κ2 = Θ − κ1. ∎

So the order-zero structure of (51.3) holds at distance at least δ from the axes, with constants
growing like δ^(−1−j) at order j by (c), and fails at an axis, where by (b) κ2 is of the order of ∂du. By
(51.19) the one quantity that must be recovered there is the planar shear σ. The flat model shows that the map
du ↦ κ2 is unbounded and that σ is nevertheless recovered from the Laplacian with no loss.

**Proposition 51.22** (The flat model.) On R² with polar radius ρ, for a radial function u put κ :=
∂_ρ u/ρ, the flat κ2, and ℓ := Δu = ∂_ρ²u + ∂_ρ u/ρ.

(a) For u_ε := exp(−ρ²/ε²), ‖κ‖_(L²(R²))/‖∇u_ε‖_(L²(R²)) = √2/ε, and for every j ≥ 0 the quotient of the homogeneous
Ḣ^j seminorms of κ and ∇u_ε is ε⁻¹ times its value at ε = 1. So no bound ‖κ‖_(H^j) ≤ C ‖∇u‖_(H^j) holds near the axis.
For the rings u_ε := exp(−(ρ² − ρ0²)²/ε²), ρ0 > 0, smooth on R², the L² quotient is at most 1/ρ0 and tends to
1/ρ0 as ε → 0.
(b) For a radial Schwartz function u, put 𝒜ℓ(ρ) := ρ⁻² ∫_0^ρ t ℓ(t) dt and σ_pl := ∂_ρ²u − ∂_ρ u/ρ, the flat planar
shear. Then 𝒜ℓ = κ = ∫_0^1 t ℓ(t ·) dt, σ_pl = ℓ − 2𝒜ℓ, ‖σ_pl‖_(L²(R²)) = ‖ℓ‖_(L²(R²)), and ‖𝒜ℓ‖_(Ḣ^j) ≤
‖ℓ‖_(Ḣ^j)/(j + 1) for every j. For the Gaussians of (a), ‖𝒜ℓ‖_(L²) = ‖ℓ‖_(L²)/√2 at every ε.

*Proof.* (a) ∂_ρ u_ε = −(2ρ/ε²) u_ε, so κ = −(2/ε²) u_ε, and with ∫_0^∞ e^(−2ρ²/ε²) ρ dρ = ε²/4 and ∫_0^∞ ρ³
e^(−2ρ²/ε²) dρ = ε⁴/8, ‖κ‖² = 2π (4/ε⁴)(ε²/4) = 2π/ε² and ‖∇u_ε‖² = 2π (4/ε⁴)(ε⁴/8) = π. For the scaling, u_ε(x) =
u_1(x/ε), so ∂^β ∇u_ε = ε^(−1−|β|) (∂^β ∇u_1)(x/ε) and ∂^β κ_ε = ε^(−2−|β|) (∂^β κ_1)(x/ε), and in two dimensions
‖F(·/ε)‖_(L²) = ε ‖F‖_(L²); so every Ḣ^j quotient carries the factor ε⁻¹, and for ε small the top seminorms dominate
the H^j norms. For the rings, u_ε is a smooth function of ρ² = |x|², ∂_ρ u_ε = −(4ρ (ρ² − ρ0²)/ε²) u_ε and κ =
−(4 (ρ² − ρ0²)/ε²) u_ε is smooth. The quotient ‖κ‖²/‖∇u_ε‖² is ∫ (∂_ρ u_ε)² ρ⁻¹ dρ / ∫ (∂_ρ u_ε)² ρ dρ, and with t :=
ρ² − ρ0² the two integrals are (8/ε⁴) I_ε and (8/ε⁴)(ρ0² I_ε + R_ε), where I_ε := ∫_(−ρ0²)^∞ t² e^(−2t²/ε²) dt and R_ε :=
∫_(ρ0²)^∞ t³ e^(−2t²/ε²) dt, the odd integrand t³ e^(−2t²/ε²) cancelling on [−ρ0², ρ0²]. Here I_ε ≥ ∫_0^∞ t²
e^(−2t²/ε²) dt = √(2π) ε³/16 and R_ε = (ε²/8)(2ρ0⁴ + ε²) e^(−2ρ0⁴/ε²) ≥ 0. So the quotient I_ε/(ρ0² I_ε + R_ε) is at
most ρ0⁻², and as 0 ≤ R_ε/I_ε ≤ (2/(√(2π) ε))(2ρ0⁴ + ε²) e^(−2ρ0⁴/ε²) → 0, it tends to ρ0⁻².
(b) (ρ ∂_ρ u)′ = ρ ℓ, so ∫_0^ρ t ℓ(t) dt = ρ ∂_ρ u and 𝒜ℓ = κ; the substitution t ↦ ρt gives the dilation average; and ℓ
− 2𝒜ℓ = ∂_ρ²u − ∂_ρ u/ρ. With a := ∂_ρ²u and b := ∂_ρ u/ρ, ℓ² − σ_pl² = 4ab, and ∫_(R²) 4ab = 8π ∫_0^∞ ∂_ρ²u ∂_ρ u dρ =
4π [(∂_ρ u)²]_0^∞ = 0. For the seminorms, ∂^β(ℓ(t ·)) = t^|β| (∂^β ℓ)(t ·) and ‖F(t ·)‖_(L²(R²)) = t⁻¹ ‖F‖_(L²(R²)), so
Minkowski's integral inequality gives ‖∂^β 𝒜ℓ‖ ≤ ∫_0^1 t^|β| ‖∂^β ℓ‖ dt = ‖∂^β ℓ‖/(|β| + 1). For the Gaussians, ℓ =
(4/ε²)(ρ²/ε² − 1) u_ε, and with ρ² = ε² t, ‖ℓ‖² = 2π (16/ε⁴)(ε²/2) ∫_0^∞ (t − 1)² e^(−2t) dt = (16π/ε²)(1/4) = 4π/ε²,
twice ‖𝒜ℓ‖² = ‖κ‖² = 2π/ε². ∎

At an axis point the family's generator runs along the axis (Lemma 51.1), while the recovery of (b) is an
integral in ρ from the axis, across every generator: no transport along P_A supplies it, and it loses nothing, 𝒜 being
bounded on every Ḣ^j. The families concerned are those whose densities are nonzero at an axis, in particular the round
ingoing and outgoing dusts of Chapter 50, for which σ ≡ 0 on the round background and which every non-round
perturbation perturbs. The next section carries the recovery of (b) over to curved metrics.

### 51.8 The planar shear at an axis

Let Σ_τ be a slice with future unit normal n and second fundamental form K_Σ(X, Y) := g(∇_X n, Y), and M3 := Σ_τ ∩ {φ1 =
0} with the induced metric γ3. M3 is the fixed set in Σ_τ of the isometry φ1 ↦ −φ1, hence totally geodesic in Σ_τ, and
the gradient ∇_Σ u of an invariant u is tangent to it. For a phase u and a value c, the section S_c := {u = c} ∩ Σ_τ of
the null hypersurface {u = c} is transverse to its generator; near axis 2 its planar part is the *leaf* Σ_L := S_c ∩ M3,
a surface of revolution about the axis in M3. We write ∇_M3 and hess_M3 for γ3, and e_r for the unit tangent of Σ_L in
the meridional plane.

**Lemma 51.23** (The leaf and the null hypersurface.) (a) For X, Y tangent to M3 and every function u,

    ∇²u(X, Y) = hess_M3 u(X, Y) − n(u) K_Σ(X, Y).    (51.20)

(b) Let u be a phase in the class with g⁻¹(du, du) = 0 to first order, at a point off the axes with ∇_Σ u ≠ 0, and Θ :=
□_g u. The trace of ∇²u over TΣ_L is Θ − κ1. With k_L := hess_M3 u/|∇_M3 u| on TΣ_L, the second fundamental form of
Σ_L in M3 for the normal ν_L := ∇_M3 u/|∇_M3 u|, the restriction χ̸ of ∇²u to TΣ_L is χ̸ = |∇_M3 u| k_L − n(u) K_Σ, it is
diagonal in the frame (e_r, e2), χ̸(e2, e2) = κ2, χ̸(e_r, e_r) = Θ_h, and with k_r := k_L(e_r, e_r), k_φ := k_L(e2, e2),

    σ = |∇_M3 u| (k_r − k_φ) − n(u) (K_Σ(e_r, e_r) − K_Σ(e2, e2)),    (51.21)

and |χ̸ − ½ (tr χ̸) γ̸| = |σ|/√2, γ̸ the induced metric of Σ_L.
(c) k_φ = ν_L(log |K2|). So neither a curvature component nor the torsion of the null hypersurface enters σ.

*Proof.* (a) For X, Y tangent to Σ_τ, g(∇_X Y, n) = −g(Y, ∇_X n) = −K_Σ(X, Y) and g(n, n) = −1, so ∇_X Y = ∇^Σ_X Y +
K_Σ(X, Y) n and ∇²u(X, Y) = X(Y u) − (∇_X Y) u = hess_Σ u(X, Y) − n(u) K_Σ(X, Y); on TM3, hess_Σ u = hess_M3 u since
M3 is totally geodesic.
(b) TS_c = TΣ_L ⊕ R e1 orthogonally, e1 being normal to M3 and tangent to S_c. TS_c is spacelike, orthogonal to P (du
vanishes on it) and does not contain P (P is null), so it is a screen, and by Proposition 51.5 (b) the trace of
∇²u over it is Θ. By Proposition 51.5 (a), ∇²u(e1, e1) = κ1 and ∇²u(e1, TΣ_L) = 0, which gives the trace over
TΣ_L. On TΣ_L, hess_M3 u = |∇_M3 u| k_L, the second fundamental form of a level set, and |∇_M3 u| = |∇_Σ u|; with (a)
this is the formula for χ̸. The frame (e_r, e2) diagonalises k_L, K_Σ and ∇²u by the reflection φ2 ↦ −φ2, and χ̸(e2,
e2) = κ2 by Proposition 51.5 (a). The vectors e_r and e_h of Proposition 51.5 (b) are unit, orthogonal
to P and tangent to the orbit space; the vectors of the orbit space orthogonal to P form the plane span(P, e_h), so
e_r = ± e_h + c P, and ∇²u(P, ·) = 0 gives χ̸(e_r, e_r) = Θ_h. Then σ = χ̸(e_r, e_r) − χ̸(e2, e2), and a symmetric form
on a plane with eigenvalues x, y has trace-free part of norm |x − y|/√2.
(c) ν_L is invariant, so [K2, ν_L] = 0 and k_φ = |K2|⁻² γ3(∇_(K2) ν_L, K2) = |K2|⁻² γ3(∇_(ν_L) K2, K2) = |K2|⁻² ½
ν_L(|K2|²). ∎

**Lemma 51.24** (The leaf's equation.) Near a point of axis 2 use on M3 the coordinates (z, y) := (ρ1, x3,
x4), with r := |y| = ρ2 and φ := φ2.

(a) In the polar coordinates (z, r, φ), at the points y = (r, 0),

    γ3 = A3 dz² + 2 C3 r dz dr + (B3 + D3 r²) dr² + B3 r² dφ²,    (51.22)

with A3, B3, C3, D3 smooth functions of (z, r), even in r.

(b) Let u be a phase in the class with ∂_z u ≠ 0 at a point of the axis. Near it the leaves are graphs z = h(y) over a
disc 𝔻 centred on the axis, with h smooth and invariant. With F := z − h(y) and ν := ∇F/|∇F| (equal to ± ν_L), the
mean curvature H_L := div_γ3 ν of the leaf satisfies, in the Cartesian coordinates y,

    H_L = −|∇F|⁻¹ (γ3^(ij) − ν^i ν^j) ∂_i ∂_j h + b_L(y, h, ∂h),      i, j ∈ {1, 2},    (51.23)

with every coefficient evaluated at (h(y), y), and b_L := −|∇F|⁻¹ (γ3^(ab) − ν^a ν^b) Γ[γ3]^c_ab ∂_c F, a smooth
function of (y, h, ∂h) built from γ3 and its first derivatives. The matrix (γ3^(ij) − ν^i ν^j)_(i,j) is positive
definite, so (51.23) is a uniformly elliptic equation on 𝔻, the axis being an interior point.

(c) (Radial form.) For h a function of r put, at (h(r), r), det₂ := A3 (B3 + D3 r²) − C3² r² and N_L² := B3 + D3 r² +
2 C3 r h′ + A3 h′². Then H_L = a_L h″ + (terms free of h″) with a_L := −det₂^(1/2)/N_L³ < 0, and E_L := r H_L/a_L −
(r h′)′ holds no h″ and only first derivatives of A3, B3, C3, D3. The functions a_L and H_L are smooth and even in r,
E_L is smooth and odd, and

    r h′(r) = ∫_0^r (ρ H_L(ρ)/a_L(ρ) − E_L(ρ)) dρ,      σ_L := ½ (k_r − k_φ) = ½ H_L − k_φ,    (51.24)

with k_φ = ν^r/r + ½ ν(log B3) and ν^r = −(C3 r + A3 h′)/(det₂^(1/2) N_L), k_r, k_φ taken for the normal ν. Since
h′/r = r⁻² ∫_0^r (ρ H_L/a_L − E_L) dρ, k_φ and σ_L are given by H_L, h, h′ and the 1-jet of γ3 through an average over
[0, r]: the factor 1/r of κ2 (Proposition 51.21 (c)) is absorbed by the integral from the axis. In the flat case,
A3 = B3 = 1 and C3 = D3 = 0, linearised at h = 0, (51.24) is the recovery of
Proposition 51.22 (b).

*Proof.* (a) As for (51.18): at (z, r, 0) the reflection y2 ↦ −y2 kills the cross terms with dy2, the
rotation by π makes γ3(∂_z, ∂_(y1)) odd and the other components even in r, and the two diagonal planar components
agree at r = 0. Put A3 := γ3(∂_z, ∂_z), C3 := γ3(∂_z, ∂_(y1))/r, B3 := γ3(∂_(y2), ∂_(y2)) and D3 :=
(γ3(∂_(y1), ∂_(y1)) − B3)/r², and use dy1 = dr, r ∂_(y2) = ∂_φ at (r, 0).
(b) By Lemma 51.1, du = ∂_z u dz on the axis, and ∂_z u ≠ 0, so the implicit function theorem gives the
graphs; h is invariant because u is. Since ν is a unit field, H_L = |∇F|⁻¹ (γ3^(ab) − ν^a ν^b) ∇²F_ab with ∇²F_ab =
∂_a ∂_b F − Γ^c_ab ∂_c F, and ∂_a ∂_b F = −∂_i ∂_j h for a, b = i, j ∈ {y1, y2} and 0 otherwise. For ξ ∈ R² ∖ {0} and
ω := ξ_i dy^i, (γ3^(ab) − ν^a ν^b) ω_a ω_b = |ω|² − γ3⁻¹(ω, dF)²/|dF|², which is positive by the Cauchy–Schwarz
inequality, because ω, which has no dz component, is not parallel to dF = dz − ∂_i h dy^i. The bounds are uniform on a
compact disc.
(c) In (z, r, φ), √(det γ3) = r (B3 det₂)^(1/2), and the components of ∇F, F = z − h(r), are ((B3 + D3 r²) + C3 r
h′)/det₂ and −(C3 r + A3 h′)/det₂, with |∇F|² = N_L²/det₂. So ν^r = −(C3 r + A3 h′)/(det₂^(1/2) N_L), and in H_L = (det
γ3)^(−1/2) (∂_z((det γ3)^(1/2) ν^z) + ∂_r((det γ3)^(1/2) ν^r)), evaluated at z = h(r), h″ enters only through ∂_r ν^r,
with the coefficient

    ∂ν^r/∂h′ = (−A3 N_L² + (C3 r + A3 h′)²)/(det₂^(1/2) N_L³) = −det₂/(det₂^(1/2) N_L³) = −det₂^(1/2)/N_L³.

Every other term holds h′, r and A3, …, D3 with at most one derivative. As h′ is odd, r h′ and h′² are even, so N_L,
det₂ and a_L are smooth and even; H_L is a smooth invariant function on the leaf, so even in r; then r H_L/a_L and
(r h′)′ = h′ + r h″ are odd, so E_L is odd, and integrating (r h′)′ = r H_L/a_L − E_L from 0 gives
(51.24). By Lemma 51.23 (c) with |K2|² = B3 r², k_φ = ν(log r) + ½ ν(log B3) = ν^r/r +
½ ν(log B3), and k_r + k_φ = H_L. In the flat case, linearised at h = 0, H_L = −(h″ + h′/r) and E_L = 0. ∎

**Lemma 51.25** (The leaf equation is uniquely solvable.) In the coordinates of Lemma 51.24, let H
be a C¹ function of (z, r) near (z0, 0). There are r0 > 0 and C, depending on lower bounds for A3, B3 and det₂ near
(z0, 0), on bounds for A3, B3, C3, D3 and their derivatives of order at most two, and on bounds for H and its first
derivatives, such that (51.24), with H_L(ρ) := H(h(ρ), ρ) and a_L, E_L evaluated at (ρ, h(ρ),
h′(ρ)), has exactly one solution h ∈ C¹([0, r0]) with h(0) = z0; and |h′(r)| ≤ C r. For r > 0 the equation is the
regular ordinary differential equation (r h′)′ = r H_L/a_L − E_L, so the solution continues uniquely while it stays in
the chart.

*Proof.* Write a_L(r, z, p) and E_L(r, z, p) for the functions of Lemma 51.24 (c) with h := z and h′ := p; they
are smooth. By the proof of Lemma 51.24 (c), H_L = a_L h″ + ν^r/r + B̃ with B̃ smooth in (r, z, p), so E_L =
ν^r/a_L − p + r B̃/a_L, and at r = 0, where det₂ = A3 B3 and N_L² = B3 + A3 p², ν^r/a_L = (C3 r + A3 p) N_L²/det₂ = p +
A3 p³/B3; so E_L(0, z, p) = A3 p³/B3. Put G(r, z, p) := r H(z, r)/a_L(r, z, p) − E_L(r, z, p). Then G(0, z, p) = −A3
p³/B3, ∂_p G vanishes at r = p = 0, and on a neighbourhood of (0, z0, 0), |G(r, z, 0)| ≤ C_0 r, |∂_z G| ≤ C_1 and |∂_p
G| ≤ C_2 (r + |p|). A solution h ∈ C¹ has p := h′ continuous and r p(r) = ∫_0^r G(ρ, h(ρ), p(ρ)) dρ, so p(0) = G(0, z0,
p(0)) = −A3 p(0)³/B3, and p(0) = 0 as A3, B3 > 0. For δ_p, r0 > 0 put X := {p ∈ C([0, r0]) : sup |p| ≤ δ_p}, h_p(r) :=
z0 + ∫_0^r p, and 𝒯p(r) := r⁻¹ ∫_0^r G(ρ, h_p(ρ), p(ρ)) dρ, 𝒯p(0) := G(0, z0, p(0)). Then |𝒯p(r)| ≤ C_0 r/2 + C_2 (r0 +
δ_p) δ_p, and as |h_(p1)(ρ) − h_(p2)(ρ)| ≤ ρ sup |p1 − p2|, sup |𝒯p1 − 𝒯p2| ≤ (C_1 r0/2 + C_2 (r0 + δ_p)) sup |p1 − p2|.
For C_2 (r0 + δ_p) ≤ ¼, C_0 r0 ≤ δ_p and C_1 r0 ≤ ½, 𝒯 maps X to itself and is a contraction with constant ½. Its fixed
point p gives the solution h_p. Every C¹ solution has h′ ∈ X on some [0, r1], r1 ≤ r0, and equals h_p there, the same
contraction holding on [0, r1]; for r > 0 the equation is regular and Lipschitz in (h, h′), and the Picard–Lindelöf
theorem gives uniqueness on [r1, r0]. Finally q(r) := sup_([0,r]) |p| satisfies q(r) ≤ C_0 r/2 + q(r)/4, so |h′(r)| ≤
C_0 r. ∎

**Lemma 51.26** (Interior regularity in two variables.) Let L := a^(ij) ∂_i ∂_j + b^i ∂_i + c
on the disc 𝔻_(2δ) ⊂ R², with a^(ij) = a^(ji), b^i, c ∈ C^∞(𝔻̄_(2δ)) and a^(ij) ξ_i ξ_j ≥ c_a |ξ|², c_a > 0. Let j ≥ 0.
If w ∈ H¹(𝔻_(2δ)) and Lw = f ∈ H^j(𝔻_(2δ)) in the sense of distributions, then w ∈ H^(j+2)(𝔻_δ) and

    ‖w‖_(H^(j+2)(𝔻_δ)) ≤ C (‖f‖_(H^j(𝔻_(2δ))) + ‖w‖_(L²(𝔻_(2δ)))),

C depending only on δ, j, c_a, the C^(j+1) norms of the a^(ij) and the C^j norms of the b^i and c on 𝔻̄_(2δ); for
j = 0, only on δ, c_a, sup |a^(ij)|, sup |∂a^(ij)|, sup |b^i| and sup |c|, which are the quantities steps (i) and (ii)
of the proof use.

*Proof.* Write Lw = ∂_i(a^(ij) ∂_j w) + b̃^i ∂_i w + c w, b̃^i := b^i − ∂_j a^(ij), so that Lw = f means ∫ a^(ij) ∂_j w
∂_i φ = ∫ (b̃^i ∂_i w + c w − f) φ =: ∫ G φ for φ ∈ H¹_0. Let 𝔻′ ⊂ 𝔻″ be concentric discs between 𝔻_δ and 𝔻_(2δ), and ζ a
cut-off equal to 1 on 𝔻′ and supported in 𝔻″. (i) With φ = ζ² w, ellipticity and the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality give
c_a ‖ζ ∇w‖² ≤ C (‖ζ ∇w‖ + ‖w‖) ‖w‖ + C ‖ζ ∇w‖ ‖w‖ + ‖f‖ ‖w‖, so ‖∇w‖_(L²(𝔻′)) ≤ C (‖f‖ + ‖w‖) (norms on 𝔻_(2δ) when
unlabelled). (ii) For a unit vector e and small h ≠ 0 let ∂^e_h w(x) := (w(x + h e) − w(x))/h, and take φ := −∂^(−e)_h
(ζ² ∂^e_h w). Summation by parts moves the difference quotient onto a^(ij) ∂_j w, and ∂^e_h(a^(ij) ∂_j w) =
a^(ij)(· + he) ∂_j ∂^e_h w + (∂^e_h a^(ij)) ∂_j w. Ellipticity, ‖∂^(−e)_h ψ‖ ≤ ‖∇ψ‖ and ‖∂^e_h w‖_(L²(𝔻″)) ≤ ‖∇w‖ give
c_a ‖ζ ∇∂^e_h w‖² ≤ C (‖ζ ∇∂^e_h w‖ + ‖∇w‖)(‖∇w‖ + ‖G‖), so ‖ζ ∇∂^e_h w‖ ≤ C (‖f‖ + ‖w‖_(H¹)) uniformly in h. A weak
