limit h → 0 gives ∂_e ∇w ∈ L² with the same bound, and with (i) on a larger disc, ‖w‖_(H²(𝔻′)) ≤ C (‖f‖ + ‖w‖). (iii) For
j ≥ 1, the case j − 1 on a larger disc gives w ∈ H^(j+1), so ∂_e w ∈ H¹ there and L(∂_e w) = ∂_e f − (∂_e a^(ij)) ∂_i ∂_j
w − (∂_e b^i) ∂_i w − (∂_e c) w ∈ H^(j−1); the case j − 1 applied to ∂_e w gives ∂_e w ∈ H^(j+1) on a smaller disc.
Finitely many nested discs between 𝔻_δ and 𝔻_(2δ) conclude. ∎

On the slice, near a point p of axis 2 with ρ1(p) > 0, let 𝒰_δ := {x : |ρ1(x) − ρ1(p)| < δ, ρ2(x) < δ}, a
G-invariant neighbourhood of the orbit of p, for 0 < δ ≤ ρ1(p)/4.

**Lemma 51.27** (The planar shear at an axis.) Let g be a smooth class metric and u a phase in the
class with g⁻¹(du, du) = 0, near a point p of axis 2 with ρ1(p) > 0, and Θ := □_g u. Fix k ≥ 5. There is C, depending
on δ, on lower bounds for |∇_Σ u| and |∂_z u| on 𝒰_(2δ), on C² norms of g, on C¹ norms of u and on sup |Θ| over
𝒰_(2δ), such that

    ‖σ‖_(H^k(𝒰_δ)) ≤ C (‖Θ‖_(H^k(𝒰_(2δ))) + ‖dg‖_(H^k(𝒰_(2δ))) + ‖du‖_(H^k(𝒰_(2δ))) + 1),

H^k in all directions: along the axis, in the planes, and in τ through the equations. On the axis σ = 0 and κ2 =
(Θ − κ1)/2, and |χ̸ − ½ (tr χ̸) γ̸| = |σ|/√2 (Lemma 51.23 (b)).

*Proof.* (1) By Lemma 51.23 (b), tr χ̸ = |∇_M3 u| tr k_L − n(u) tr K_Σ, so on each leaf

    H_L = ± (Θ − κ1 + n(u) tr K_Σ|_(TΣ_L))/|∇_Σ u|,

the sign that of ∂_z u; κ1 is smooth near axis 2. So H_L ∈ H^k(𝒰_(2δ)) whenever Θ, dg and du are, by Moser's estimate.
(2) In the coordinates (z, y) of M3 the leaf is the graph z = h(y), and it solves (51.23), uniformly
elliptic on the disc with the axis interior, with b_L holding ∂γ3 only (Lemma 51.24 (b)).
(3) Freeze the coefficients of (51.23) at the solution and apply Lemma 51.26
with j = 0 to the derivatives ∂^β h along the disc, |β| ≤ k: ∂^β h solves the frozen equation with right side ∂^β(H_L
− b_L) minus the commutator of ∂^β with the frozen coefficients, bounded in L² by Moser's estimate
(Theorem A.31 (1), Lemma 51.11), and induction on |β| gives ‖h‖_(H^(k+2)(𝔻_δ)) ≤ C
(‖H_L‖_(H^k(𝔻_(2δ))) + ‖γ3‖_(H^(k+1)) + 1). The constant of that lemma at j = 0 needs sup |∂h| and sup |∂²h|. Here
∂h = −∂_y u/∂_z u is bounded by the C¹ norm of u, and the Hessian of the radial function h has the eigenvalues h″ and
h′/r. In the coordinates (z, r) of Lemma 51.24, √det γ3 = r (B3 det₂)^(1/2) and √det γ3 H_L = ∂_z(√det γ3
ν^z) + ∂_r(√det γ3 ν^r), so along z = h(r)

    (√det γ3 ν^r)(h(r), r) = ∫_0^r (√det γ3 H_L − ∂_z(√det γ3 ν^z) + h′ ∂_z(√det γ3 ν^r))|_(z=h(ρ)) dρ,

the left side vanishing at r = 0. The field ν depends on z only through the coefficients of γ3, so each term of the
integrand is O(ρ), with constants depending on sup |H_L|, sup |h′| and the 1-jet of γ3. Hence |ν^r| ≤ C r, so |h′| ≤ C
r by ν^r = −(C3 r + A3 h′)/(det₂^(1/2) N_L), and, as H_L = a_L h″ + ν^r/r + (terms in r, h′ and the 1-jet of γ3) by
the proof of Lemma 51.24 (c) with |a_L| bounded below, |h″| ≤ C. So sup |∂²h| is bounded by sup |H_L|, sup |∂h|
and the 1-jet of γ3: this is why C² norms of u are not needed.
(4) Derivatives across the leaves, in c = u, and in τ follow by differentiating the equation in c and in τ: each
derivative gives the same elliptic equation, linearised at h, for ∂_c h (or ∂_τ h), with a right side one order lower and
coefficients again of first order in γ3, and ∂_c (H_L(h(y), y)) = ∂_z H_L ∂_c h. The change of variables (z, y) ↔ (c, y)
has the Jacobian 1/∂_z u, in H^k. Induction on the number of transverse derivatives gives the bound in all directions.
(5) Then k_L ∈ H^k, and σ ∈ H^k by (51.21), whose last term is a smooth function of dg and of the leaf's
tangent. On the axis σ = 0 and κ2 = (Θ − κ1)/2 by Proposition 51.21 (d). ∎

The radial form (51.24) is step (3) in the radial variable: the bound appears directly, through the
Hardy-type averages of Proposition 51.22 (b).

**Lemma 51.28** (The planar shear of nearby solutions.) Let ů be a smooth class solution and,
near a point of axis 2, let h̊ be the leaves of ů_A. For U = (g, p_A, Θ_A, q_A) on a slice let the leaves of family A
be the graphs z = h(r) through the points of the axis near that point, each solving (51.24) with
H_L := H_L[Θ_A], the formula of step (1) of Lemma 51.27 with Θ_A in place of Θ and the spatial part of
p_A in place of ∇_Σ u; they exist and are unique by Lemma 51.25, and for U near ů they are C¹-close to the
leaves of ů and foliate a neighbourhood of the axis. Let σ[U] at a point be the planar shear (51.21) of
the leaf through it. Let k ≥ 6. There are a ball 𝔅 around ů in the norm 𝒩_k, a ball 𝔅′ ⊃ 𝔅 around ů in the norm
𝒩_(k−1), and C, such that:

(a) ‖∂^α(σ[U] − σ[ů])‖_(L²(𝒰_δ)) ≤ C 𝒩_k(U) for |α| ≤ k and U ∈ 𝔅;
(b) ‖σ[U] − σ[U′]‖_(L²(𝒰_δ)) ≤ C ‖U − U′‖_(L²(𝒰_(2δ))) for U, U′ ∈ 𝔅′, where U includes ∂g among its components.

The constants use C¹ norms of the phases and sup |Θ_A|, not C² norms of the phases. For a solution of the class system
with Θ_A = □_g u_A the leaves are the level sets of u_A near the axis, by Lemma 51.24 (c) and the uniqueness in
Lemma 51.25.

*Proof.* (a) The difference δh of the leaves solves L_ů δh = δH_L − (terms in δγ3 and its first derivatives) + Q(δh),
with L_ů the mean curvature operator of (51.23) linearised at h̊, smooth and uniformly elliptic on
the disc with the axis interior, and Q collecting the terms at least quadratic in (δh, ∂δh, ∂²δh), with smooth
coefficients. Lemma 51.26 with j = k, the quadratic terms absorbed on 𝔅, bounds δh in
H^(k+2) along the disc. Derivatives transverse to the disc commute with L_ů up to operators of lower order with smooth
coefficients, so ∂_⊥ δh obeys the same equation with a right side controlled by the previous step; induction on the
number of transverse derivatives gives (a) for all |α| ≤ k. The shift δc of the foliation enters as (∂_c σ[ů]) δc, the
derivative falling on ů.
(b) The same with Lemma 51.26 for j = 0 applied to the difference of the leaves of U and U′, on a
ball 𝔅′ small enough that L_U − L_ů is absorbed. The constant of that lemma at j = 0 holds the sup norms of the
coefficients of L_U and of their first derivatives, that is, of first and second derivatives of the leaves and of first
derivatives of g; on 𝔅′ these are bounded by the Sobolev inequality of Lemma 5.1 at the order k − 4 ≥ 2 and by the
bound of step (3) of Lemma 51.27. The shift of the foliation costs ∂_c σ, bounded on 𝔅′. The bound
needs the coefficients of L_U, which hold first derivatives of g, among the components of U. ∎

**Remark 51.29** (Numerical observation.) On a metric γ3 of the form (51.22) with
non-constant A3, B3, C3, D3, whose leaf z = 0 has mean curvature of order one, the leaves h_ε = ε² exp(−r²/ε²) for ε =
0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025 were compared with the leaf z = 0 on r < 1/2 with the weight r dr, in floating point. The
quotients ‖δσ_L‖/‖δH_L‖ were 0.49713, 0.49928, 0.49982, 0.49996, tending to the flat value 1/2, and ‖∂_r δσ_L‖/‖∂_r
δH_L‖ were 0.28615, 0.28813, 0.28854, 0.28864, near the flat Gaussian value 1/(2√3); the first-order quantity
‖δk_φ‖/‖h′‖ was 7.07, 14.14, 28.28, 56.57, growing like 1/ε. These are frozen-coefficient limits and show no loss at
orders 0 and 1 only. Integrating (51.24) from the axis with h′ = 0 there and H_L given recovered h′
within 4.1 × 10⁻¹¹ and σ_L within 8.0 × 10⁻¹⁰, while the flat equation h″ + h′/r = H_L in its place missed them by
0.146 and 2.91. No proof uses these observations.

### 51.9 Cauchy stability with the dusts at the axes

**Definition 51.30** (Adapted boundaries and the adapted domain.) Let Ω be admissible for g̊ and B a
lateral boundary component of Ω that meets an axis. B is *adapted* to the family A near the points where it meets an axis
if there are a G-invariant neighbourhood 𝒱_B of those points and a smooth function c_B with B ∩ Σ_τ
∩ 𝒱_B = {ů_A = c_B(τ)} ∩ Σ_τ ∩ 𝒱_B for every τ. Take 𝒱_B so small that, near each point of B on axis 2, it lies over the
disc {|y| < δ} on which the leaves of Lemma 51.28 are graphs z = h(y) in the coordinates (z, y) of
Lemma 51.24, and likewise near axis 1 with the two planes exchanged; then B ∩ Σ_τ ∩ 𝒱_B is a part of the leaf of
ů_A at the value c_B(τ). Let C_L and r_L be constants C and r0 of Lemma 51.25 valid, for every family, for the
leaves of ů and of the states near ů used below, so that |h(y) − h(0)| ≤ C_L |y|² for |y| ≤ r_L on each of them. Fix δ_B
∈ (0, δ/4] with 8 C_L δ_B ≤ 1 and 4δ_B ≤ r_L, and so small that, about each point p of B on the axes, the set 𝒰_(4δ_B)
defined before Lemma 51.27 lies in 𝒱_B and ∂_z ů_A ≠ 0 on it. Then B ∩ Σ_τ ∩ 𝒰_(4δ_B) is the graph over
{|y| < 4δ_B} of the leaf of ů through p, which lies within 16 C_L δ_B² ≤ 2δ_B of p in z, since that leaf is the level set
of ů_A through p (Lemma 51.28) and the level set meets each line of constant y in 𝒰_(4δ_B) at most
once; over the disc D_B := {|y| < 2δ_B} the graph lies within 4 C_L δ_B² ≤ δ_B/2 of p in z, hence in 𝒰_(2δ_B). Fix a
G-invariant cut-off χ_B supported in 𝒱_B and equal to 1 on the sets 𝒰_(2δ_B) about these points. The 𝒱_B of different
adapted components are taken disjoint, and disjoint from the other lateral boundary components.

A datum for the adapted domain is given on W_0 := ψ_τ0({1 − η0 ≤ |x| ≤ 2 + η0}), with η0 ∈ (0, ½] fixed so small that W_0
lies in R⁴ ∖ {0} and in the set on which ů is defined. It lies within ε of ů's if the expression (51.17) at
τ0, taken as in Section 51.6, is at most ε on W_0; the constraints and the gauge condition are required on Σ_τ0
∩ Ω_U, which depends only on the datum (below). Its phases are normalised by adding the constants that make u_A = ů_A at
a fixed point of Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω outside the 𝒱_B, where the map T_(τ0,U) below is the identity, so that the point lies in Σ_τ0
∩ Ω_U; the normalisation changes neither the development nor the augmented system, and then |u_A − ů_A| ≤ C ε on W_0,
since |d(u_A − ů_A)| ≤ C ε there by Lemma 5.1, whose proof applies to W_0, and the points of W_0, the image of an
annulus under ψ_τ0, are joined in it by paths of bounded length.

For a solution U of the augmented system near ů, the *axis phase* of family A is the function on the axes in 𝒱_B that is
constant along the integral curves of P_A, which run in the axis there (the argument of Lemma 51.1 applies
to the G-invariant covector p_A), with the values of the datum's u_A on Σ_τ0. Let z_B(τ) be the point of the axis, near
the point z̊_B(τ) of B ∩ Σ_τ there, at which the axis phase takes the value c_B(τ), the only one near z̊_B(τ): on the
axis the axis phase is the datum's phase, whose z-derivative is within C ε of ∂_z ů_A ≠ 0, composed with the flow of P_A
from τ to τ0 along the axis, an increasing map, and the bound below places such a point near z̊_B(τ). Let h_B be the leaf
of U through z_B(τ) and h̊_B the leaf of ů through z̊_B(τ), let d_B be the average over the rotations and reflections of
the y-plane of Stein's extension (Theorem A.36) to R² of the restriction of h_B − h̊_B to D_B, and put, on
Σ_τ,

    T_(τ,U)(x) := x + Σ_B χ_B(x) d_B(y) e(x),

the sum over the adapted components, with e := (x1, x2, 0, 0)/ρ1 and y := (x3, x4) near axis 2, e := (0, 0, x3, x4)/ρ2
and y := (x1, x2) near axis 1, so that T_(τ,U) adds χ_B d_B(y) to z and leaves y fixed. d_B is invariant and equal to h_B
− h̊_B on D_B: for y ∈ D_B and every rotation or reflection R of the y-plane, Ry ∈ D_B, where the extension is h_B
− h̊_B, a function of |y|, and the Haar measure of O(2) is invariant. The *adapted domain* of U is Ω_U := ⋃_τ {τ}
× T_(τ,U)(Σ_τ ∩ Ω), whose lateral boundary components are the *adapted boundaries* B_U := ⋃_τ T_(τ,U)(B ∩ Σ_τ) and the
components of Ω that are not adapted. For U = ů, T_(τ,U) is the identity and B_U = B. In the set 𝒰_(2δ_B) about z̊_B(τ),
where χ_B = 1 and d_B = h_B − h̊_B, B_U ∩ Σ_τ is the graph of h_B over D_B, the leaf of U through z_B(τ), and Ω_U lies on
one side of it: B ∩ Σ_τ ∩ 𝒰_(4δ_B) is the graph of h̊_B, with Ω on one side, and T_(τ,U) maps (h̊_B(y), y) to (h_B(y), y)
for y ∈ D_B, keeps y, is increasing in z and, for U near ů, moves points by at most δ_B/2 (by the bound below). For a
solution with p_A = du_A and Θ_A = □_g u_A this graph is the level set {u_A = c_B(τ)} ∩ Σ_τ there, by the last statement
of Lemma 51.28, the axis phase being u_A, which is constant along P_A = g⁻¹du_A. Elsewhere in 𝒱_B, B_U
∩ Σ_τ is not a leaf, and T_(τ,U) does not use the leaf there.

Let U be a solution of the augmented system on [τ0, τ] × R⁴ whose states lie in the ball 𝔅 of
Lemma 51.28, 𝒩_k(τ′) being the norm of the state at τ′. Every derivative of order at most k of T_(τ,U)
− id is bounded by C (sup_(τ′≤τ) 𝒩_k(τ′) + ε). Indeed, let δh(z0, y) be the difference of the leaves of U and of ů
through the axis point z0, for z0 in I := {|z0 − z̊_B(τ)| ≤ δ_B}; their graphs over D_B lie in 𝒰_δ about z̊_B(τ). The
proof of Lemma 51.28 (a), through its induction on the derivatives transverse to the disc, bounds
∂_(z0)^j δh, j ≤ 2, in L² over I with values in H^(k+2−j)(D_B) by C 𝒩_k(τ). So for |β| ≤ k, ∂_y^β δh lies in H² of (z0,
y) ∈ I × D_B with norm at most C 𝒩_k(τ), and Theorem A.26 in three variables (2 · 2 > 3) bounds it pointwise
by C 𝒩_k(τ): the leaves of U and of ů through one point of I differ in W^(k,∞)(D_B) by at most C 𝒩_k(τ). Next, on the
axis near z̊_B(τ) the axis phase is within C (sup_(τ′≤τ) 𝒩_k(τ′) + ε) of ů_A: the integral curves of P_A and of P̊_A in
the axis from one point stay within C sup_(τ′≤τ) 𝒩_k(τ′) of each other by Gronwall's inequality, and the data of the
phases differ by at most C ε on W_0. As ∂_z ů_A ≠ 0 on the axis, the intermediate value theorem gives z_B(τ),
with |z_B(τ) − z̊_B(τ)| ≤ C (sup_(τ′≤τ) 𝒩_k(τ′) + ε) ≤ δ_B, so z_B(τ) ∈ I. The leaves of ů depend smoothly on their axis
point; so h_B − h̊_B is at most C (sup_(τ′≤τ) 𝒩_k(τ′) + ε) in W^(k,∞)(D_B), and so is d_B in W^(k,∞)(R²): Stein's
operator is bounded on W^(k,∞) (Theorem A.36), a rotation or reflection of the y-plane changes that norm by
at most a factor depending on k, and the average keeps the bound. On supp χ_B, ρ1 (near axis 2) or ρ2 (near axis 1) is
bounded below, so χ_B, y and e have bounded derivatives of every order there, and T_(τ,U) − id = Σ_B χ_B d_B(y) e
satisfies the bound. So for U near ů, T_(τ,U) − id is small in W^(k,∞), and T_(τ,U) is a G-equivariant diffeomorphism of
R⁴, equal to the identity outside the 𝒱_B: G-equivariant, as χ_B and d_B(y) are invariant and e is equivariant;
injective, as |T_(τ,U)(x) − T_(τ,U)(x′)| ≥ |x − x′|/2; onto, the map x ↦ x′ − (T_(τ,U)(x) − x) being a contraction for
each x′; and of class C^(k−1), with bounded derivatives of order k and invertible differential. The same argument for the
τ-derivatives, which the proof of Lemma 51.28 (a) bounds as well, shows that B_U is a C¹-small
perturbation of B, so it stays spacelike with Ω_U to its past, these being open conditions; so (a) and (b) of
Definition 51.7 hold on Ω_U for the metric of U.

So T_(τ,U), and with it Ω_U ∩ {τ0 ≤ τ′ ≤ τ}, is determined by U on the closure of Ω_U ∩ {τ0 ≤ τ′ ≤ τ}: by its values
along the integral curves of P_A in the axes from Σ_τ0 to the points z_B(τ), and on the part of B_U over D_B, along which
(51.24) determines h_B. Indeed, let U′ be a second solution near ů for which T_(τ,U′) is defined,
given on a set that contains that closure and equal to U there. By the argument of (c) of Definition 51.7 for
Ω_U and the metric of U, and by continuity in the initial point, the integral curve of P_A from z_B(τ) runs backwards in
the closure of Ω_U until it meets Σ_τ0; P_A is that of U′ there, so it is also the integral curve of U′. The datum's
phase on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U is the same for both, being fixed by the spatial part of p_A there up to a constant, as Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U,
the image under the diffeomorphism T_(τ0,U) of the connected slice Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω (Definition 51.7), is connected, and
by its value at the point of the normalisation, which lies in Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U. So the axis phase
of U′ at z_B(τ) is c_B(τ), and z_B(τ) is the point of U′, as the axis phase of U′ is monotone along the axis near
z̊_B(τ). The graph of h_B over D_B lies in B_U ∩ Σ_τ, where U′ and U agree with their first derivatives; so h_B solves on
[0, 2δ_B) the equation (51.24) of U′ with h(0) = z_B(τ), and by the uniqueness in
Lemma 51.25 it is the leaf of U′ through z_B(τ) there. Hence U′ has the same d_B, and T_(τ,U′) = T_(τ,U). This
defines Ω_U also for U given only on the closure of Ω_U, z_B(τ) being then the point of the axis near z̊_B(τ) in the
closure of Ω_U ∩ Σ_τ at which the axis phase is c_B(τ), the only one by the monotonicity above; a solution on a domain is
*on its own adapted domain* if the domain is the Ω_U that it defines, and the argument above applies to such a U when the
lateral boundary of Ω_U is C¹-close to that of Ω. The bound above holds for such a U, with 𝒩_k(τ′), τ′ < τ, computed on
Σ_τ′ ∩ Ω_U as in (51.17), and 𝒩_k(τ) the norm of any state on Σ_τ in 𝔅 equal to U on Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U: the bound
on |z_B(τ) − z̊_B(τ)| uses the times before τ only through |P_A − P̊_A| along the integral curve from z_B(τ), at most C
sup_(τ′≤τ) 𝒩_k(τ′) by Step 1 of the proof of Theorem 51.18, and h_B is the leaf of the state over D_B,
by the uniqueness just used.

Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U = T_(τ0,U)(Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω) lies in W_0 for ε small, by the bound at τ0 with the datum's difference from ů's extended
from W_0 by Stein's operator of the annulus {1 − η0 ≤ |x| ≤ 2 + η0} transported by ψ_τ0, as the state there, and by the
above only the datum's values on it enter. If for every adapted B the datum's normalised phase u_A of the family to which
B is adapted equals c_B(τ0) on B ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ 𝒰_(2δ_B) about each point of B on the axes, then T_(τ0,U) is the identity.
Indeed the axis phase on Σ_τ0 is u_A, so z_B(τ0) = z̊_B(τ0). On Σ_τ0 the datum has Θ_A = □_g u_A, and dp_A = 0 and
dν_A = 0 by Step 10 of the proof of Theorem 51.18, so its leaves are the level sets of u_A, by the
last statement of Lemma 51.28, which concerns one slice; the level set {u_A = c_B(τ0)} meets 𝒰_(2δ_B)
in a graph over D_B, as ∂_z u_A ≠ 0 there, and that graph contains the graph of h̊_B; so h_B = h̊_B on D_B, and d_B = 0.
In that case a datum given on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω only, within ε of ů's there, may be used, extended to W_0 by the operator E_τ0 of
the proof of Theorem 51.13 (b) (ii) applied to its difference from ů's; by the above, the extension changes neither
the adapted domain nor the development, and a condition on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U is then one on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω, as Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U = Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω.

**Theorem 51.31** (Cauchy stability of the class Einstein–null-dust system.) The conclusion of
Theorem 51.18 holds, on the adapted domain, with (H2) replaced by

(H2′) closed G-invariant sets S_A ⊂ Σ_τ0 containing supp q̊_A ∩ Σ_τ0 such that, where a lateral boundary component B
of Ω meets an axis, the tubes 𝒯̊_(A′) meeting a neighbourhood of that point all belong to one family A = A(B), and B is
adapted to that family there (Definition 51.30) if there are such tubes.

The dusts may reach the axes. The datum is given on the set W_0 of Definition 51.30, or on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω where that
definition allows it, and in place of supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ⊂ S_A its densities satisfy supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U ⊂ T_(τ0,U)(S_A)
for every A, a condition on the first slice of the adapted domain, with Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U and T_(τ0,U) of Definition 51.30,
which depend only on the datum. When T_(τ0,U) is the identity, as for a datum on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω, it is the condition supp q_A
∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω ⊂ S_A of Theorem 51.18. The development lies on its own adapted domain, whose lateral
boundaries depend on the solution through u_A and stay spacelike with the domain to their past, these being open
conditions; the uniqueness is among the smooth G-invariant developments, each on its own adapted domain, in the gauge
D(g) = 0 relative to g̊ with 𝒩_(k−1) ≤ ε2. No smallness of ů or of the families is assumed; ε, ε2 and C depend on ů, Ω,
N_f, k and the constants of Lemma 51.27 and Lemma 51.28. Where no dust meets a point at
which a lateral boundary meets an axis, (H2′) puts no condition there.

*Proof.* The proof of Theorem 51.18 holds with the following changes.

*Step 3.* By (Aug4), supp q_A lies in the tube 𝒯_A, for P_A in Ω_U, of supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U, hence in that of
T_(τ0,U)(S_A). The points of T_(τ0,U)(S_A) lie within C ε of S_A, by the bound of Definition 51.30 at τ0 and Step 2,
so the integral curves of P_A from them stay within C ε of 𝒯̊_A, by comparison of ordinary differential equations as
there, and 𝒯_A ⊂ {ζ_A = 1} for ε small, ζ_A being the cut-off of Step 6 below, equal to 1 on a neighbourhood of 𝒯̊_A.

*Step 6, near an axis.* Write the right side of the Raychaudhuri equation of family A by (51.19) as

    S_A^ax := −κ_A1² − ½ (Θ_A − κ_A1)² − ½ σ_A[Θ_A]² − Σ_B q_B g⁻¹(p_A, p_B)²,

where σ_A[Θ_A] is the planar shear of the leaves of u_A defined from (p_A, Θ_A) as in Lemma 51.28. A
partition of unity in the slice joins S_A^ax near the axes to S_A of Theorem 51.18 away from them, so
for family A no cut-off ζ_A is needed at the axes. Lemma 51.28 (a) gives ‖∂^α(S_A^ax(U) − S_A^ax(ů))‖
≤ C 𝒩_k for |α| ≤ k. The leaves of another family A′ can cross an adapted boundary B at distance O(ε). So, for A′ ≠ A(B),
ζ_(A′) = 0 on the sets 𝒰_(r_B) about the points where B meets an axis, with r_B ∈ (0, δ_B] fixed (δ_B of
Definition 51.30), and still ζ_(A′) = 1 on a neighbourhood of 𝒯̊_(A′); this is possible because (H2′) puts no tube
of A′ near those points, which form a compact set. Every ζ_(A′) vanishes likewise near the points where a component that
is not adapted meets an axis, and in Step 10 the energy of Δ_(A′) is taken on a set inside {ζ_(A′) = 1} that is a union
of leaves of u_(A′). By (H2′) the leaves used at points of the domain lie in its closure. Take the partition of unity so
that, where ζ_A ≠ 0, S_A^ax is used only within distance δ_* of the axes, with δ_* ≤ min_B r_B fixed below. At a point x
where S_A^ax is used, ζ_A(x) ≠ 0 and |y(x)| < δ_*, and σ_A needs the leaf through x over the disc {|y| ≤ |y(x)|}
((51.24)), which lies within 2 C_L |y(x)|² ≤ δ_*/4 of x in z, as 8 C_L δ_* ≤ 8 C_L δ_B ≤ 1
(Definition 51.30). If x lies in the set 𝒰_(δ_B) about a point p where an adapted boundary B meets an axis, and
A = A(B), that part of the leaf runs in 𝒰_(2δ_B), where B_U is the graph of h_B over D_B and Ω_U lies on one side of it;
the leaves of family A(B) of U foliate a neighbourhood of the axis, B_U being one of them there, so the leaf, which
contains x, does not cross B_U and lies in the closure of Ω_U. Otherwise x lies at distance at least r_B in z from each
point p where an adapted boundary B meets an axis: if x is not in the set 𝒰_(δ_B) about p, because |y(x)| < δ_* ≤ δ_B; if
it is, then A ≠ A(B), and ζ_A(x) ≠ 0 puts x outside the set 𝒰_(r_B) about p while |y(x)| < r_B. As ζ_A(x) ≠ 0, x lies
also at a fixed distance from the points where the other components meet the axes. The lateral boundaries meet the set
{|y| < δ_*} only near the points where they meet the axes, and an adapted boundary B_U meets it, near such a point p, in
the graph of h_B over {|y| < δ_*}, which lies within C_L δ_*² + C ε of p in z (Definition 51.30). So, for δ_* small
and then ε small, in particular with 3 C_L δ_*² + C ε < r_B for every B, that part of the leaf, within 2 C_L δ_*² of x in
z, meets no lateral boundary, and it lies in Ω_U.

*Step 9.* Near the axes the right side of the augmented system is non-local in the planar directions, an integral from
the axis along each leaf. Extend the system as in Step 9 of Theorem 51.18, with the right side
S_A^ax near the axes for the families present there (Step 6) and ζ_A S_A away from them; the leaves are those of
Lemma 51.28, defined on each slice from (g, p_A, Θ_A) by (51.24) and
Lemma 51.25, so that p_A need not be closed for them to exist, and the right side at a time depends on the
unknowns at that time only. The cut-off on p_A keeps P_A^τ > 0, as before. In the unknowns U of that Step 9 the forcing
term is defined on a ball 𝒟_ρ about u_* := 0 in H^k, with ρ so small that the states of 𝒟_ρ lie in the balls 𝔅 and 𝔅′ of
Lemma 51.28 near the axes; it satisfies (F1) by Lemma 51.28 (a) and
Remark 51.16 for the local terms, (F2) by Lemma 51.28 (b) and Remark 51.16,
and (F3) by (F2) and its smoothness in τ. Theorem 51.13 (a) gives a solution on R⁴ for a short time, for data within
η_ρ ρ of 0 in H^k, and its continuation while ‖U(τ)‖_(H^k) ≤ η_ρ ρ.

*The adapted domain is a domain of dependence.* Fix θ0 ∈ (0, ¼]. Let Ũ be a solution on [τa, τb] × R⁴ with states in 𝒟_ρ,
and U a solution of the augmented system on its own adapted domain Ω_U up to the time τb (Definition 51.30), whose
lateral boundary is C¹-close to that of Ω, with 𝒩_(k−1) ≤ ρ on Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U and ‖T_(τ,U) − id‖_(W^(k−1,∞)) ≤ θ0 for τa ≤ τ
≤ τb, and with U = Ũ on Σ_(τa) ∩ Ω_U; by the bound of Definition 51.30, for ρ and ε small, U may for instance be
equal on Ω_U ∩ {τa ≤ τ ≤ τb} to a second solution on [τa, τb] × R⁴ with states in 𝒟_ρ. Then U = Ũ on Ω_U ∩ {τa ≤ τ ≤ τb}.
Indeed z := U − Ũ satisfies the energy identity of the proof of Theorem 51.13 (b) (i), at the order s = k − 1 > 3,
on Ω_U, whose lateral boundary is spacelike for the system at the states of U and Ũ, which lie within C ρ of those of ů
pointwise, for ρ small, as in Step 9 of Theorem 51.18, B_U being C¹-close to B; and the local parts of
the forcing terms differ by at most C |z| pointwise. Near the axes they differ by ½ (σ_A[Ũ]² − σ_A[U]²) times bounded
factors. On Σ_τ put Ŭ := Ũ + 𝔼 z, with 𝔼 the following extension operator from Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U to R⁴. In the coordinates of
Step 9, Σ_τ ∩ Ω = ψ_τ(Σ_⋆), with Σ_⋆ the annulus and ψ_τ a diffeomorphism of R⁴ whose derivatives of positive order, and
those of ψ_τ⁻¹, are bounded uniformly in τ, as in the proof of Theorem 51.13 (b) (ii). Put Φ := T_(τ,U) ∘ ψ_τ, with
T_(τ,U) of Definition 51.30 written in these coordinates, which maps Σ_⋆ onto Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U; let E_⋆ be Stein's
extension operator for Σ_⋆ (Theorem A.36), 𝔼_0 g := E_⋆(g ∘ Φ) ∘ Φ⁻¹ and 𝔼 g := ∫_G (𝔼_0(g ∘ γ)) ∘ γ⁻¹ dγ,
the integral for the Haar probability measure of G. Then 𝔼 g = g on Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U, which G preserves, and 𝔼 g is G-invariant
when g is. Let m be k − 1 or k, and ‖T_(τ,U) − id‖_(W^(m,∞)) ≤ θ0. The derivatives of Φ of orders 1 to m are then bounded
uniformly in τ and U; those of Φ⁻¹ are polynomials in the derivatives of Φ at Φ⁻¹ and in (DΦ)⁻¹ ∘ Φ⁻¹, which is bounded;
and the Jacobian determinants of Φ and Φ⁻¹ are bounded. So, by the chain-rule bound of Step 8 (iv) of
Section 6.5, composition with Φ and with Φ⁻¹ is bounded on H^σ, 0 ≤ σ ≤ m, uniformly in τ and U, and as G acts
by isometries of R⁴, 𝔼 is bounded from H^σ(Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U) to H^σ(R⁴), 0 ≤ σ ≤ m, uniformly in τ and U. Here m = k − 1. Then
Ŭ = U on Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U, and Ŭ ∈ 𝔅′ for ρ small, since ‖𝔼 z‖_(H^(k−1)) ≤ C ‖z‖_(H^(k−1)(Σ_τ∩Ω_U)) ≤ C ρ. At a point x ∈ Σ_τ
∩ Ω_U where σ_A is used the leaf of U through x comes from an axis point of Ω_U and lies in the closure of Ω_U, as Step 6
shows with ρ + ε in place of ε; by the uniqueness in Lemma 51.25 it is also the leaf of Ŭ through x. So
σ_A[Ŭ] = σ_A[U] on Σ_τ ∩ Ω_U, and by Lemma 51.28 (b)

    ‖σ_A[U] − σ_A[Ũ]‖_(L²(Σ_τ∩Ω_U∩𝒰_δ)) ≤ ‖σ_A[Ŭ] − σ_A[Ũ]‖_(L²(𝒰_δ)) ≤ C ‖𝔼 z‖_(L²(𝒰_(2δ))) ≤ C ‖z‖_(L²(Σ_τ∩Ω_U)).

So e(τ) := ∫_(Σ_τ∩Ω_U) ⟨A^0 z, z⟩ satisfies e(τ) ≤ e(τa) + C ∫_(τa)^τ e, and e(τa) = 0; hence z = 0 on Ω_U.

*Existence.* Restart as in the proof of Theorem 51.13 (b) (ii): at the times τ_i extend the data from Σ_(τ_i) ∩ Ω_U
by 𝔼, bounded on H^k uniformly, as ‖T_(τ_i,U) − id‖_(W^(k,∞)) ≤ C (ρ + ε) ≤ θ0 by Definition 51.30, the state on
Σ_(τ_i) being that of the solution on R⁴ of the previous interval (at τ0, the datum extended from W_0 as in
Definition 51.30), and solve on R⁴; by the domain of dependence the solutions agree on the adapted domain, which the
solution determines on its closure (Definition 51.30). The bootstrap of Steps 3–8, run on the adapted domain, keeps
𝒩_k ≤ C ε there, hence the extended data within η_ρ ρ of 0, so the solution exists on the whole adapted domain.

*Smoothness.* Let σ ≥ k be an integer. The proof of Lemma 51.28 (a), with
Lemma 51.26 at j = σ, the quadratic terms absorbed on 𝔅 and Moser's estimate for the terms of lower
order, gives ‖σ_A[U] − σ_A[ů]‖_(H^σ(𝒰_δ)) ≤ C_σ (1 + ‖U‖_(H^σ)) for U ∈ 𝔅 ∩ H^σ; with Lemma 51.11 (b) for
the local terms, ‖F(τ, U)‖_(H^σ) ≤ C_σ (1 + ‖U‖_(H^σ)) for U ∈ 𝒟_ρ ∩ H^σ. The proof of Theorem 51.13 (a) then runs
at the order σ with the ball 𝒟_ρ kept in H^k (the step *Boundedness* at the order σ, the others at the order k), and its
continuation holds while sup_τ ‖U(τ)‖_(H^σ) < ∞ and ‖U(τ)‖_(H^k) ≤ η_ρ ρ. On each interval of the restarts the extended
data lie in H^σ: the data are smooth on the slice by induction over the intervals, so are the leaves through the axis
points, by Lemma 51.26 at every order, hence d_B, Stein's operator being bounded on every W^(m,∞),
and T_(τ_i,U); and E_⋆ is bounded on every H^σ. So the solution in H^σ exists for a short time, equals the solution in
H^k by uniqueness, and Lemma 51.12 (c) at the order σ, with the bound on F(τ, U) in H^σ and K_U bounded by
the H^k bound, gives a linear Gronwall inequality for ‖U(τ)‖_(H^σ), so that it lies in H^σ on the whole interval. By the
equation, and by differentiating (51.24) in τ as in step (4) of the proof of
Lemma 51.27, every ∂_τ^j U is bounded in every H^σ, by induction on j. So the solution is smooth.

*Uniqueness.* A smooth G-invariant development in the gauge D(g) = 0 on its own adapted domain Ω′, with the same datum
and 𝒩_(k−1) ≤ ε2 ≤ ρ, gives a solution U′ of the augmented system there as in that Step 9, its Θ_A on the tubes being □_g
u_A and its σ_A that of its own leaves by Step 10 below. Let U be the solution constructed, and τ* the largest τ′ ∈ [τ0,
τ1] such that Ω′ and Ω_U coincide in {τ ≤ τ′} and U′ = U there. The set of these τ′ is closed, T_(τ,U′) and T_(τ,U) being
continuous in τ, and it contains τ0: U′ and U have the datum's values on Σ_τ0, so T_(τ0,U′) = T_(τ0,U) by
Definition 51.30. Suppose τ* < τ1. U′ is smooth up to the boundary of Ω′, so its points z_B(τ) and its leaves h_B
over D_B are smooth in τ and y, and, Stein's operator being linear and bounded on every W^(m,∞), τ ↦ T_(τ,U′) is
continuous into W^(k−1,∞), with its τ-derivative. For τ ≤ τ*, T_(τ,U′) = T_(τ,U) by Definition 51.30, as U′ and U
agree on the closure of Ω′ ∩ {τ′ ≤ τ}; this map is within C (ρ + ε) of the identity in W^(k,∞) by Definition 51.30,
and the lateral boundary of Ω′ is that of Ω_U up to τ*, C¹-close to that of Ω. So for τ* ≤ τ ≤ τ* + θ, θ > 0 small,
‖T_(τ,U′) − id‖_(W^(k−1,∞)) ≤ 2C (ρ + ε) ≤ θ0, and the lateral boundary of Ω′ stays C¹-close to that of Ω. The domain of
dependence on [τ*, τ* + θ], with U′ in place of U and Ũ the solution on R⁴ of an interval of the restarts that contains
[τ*, τ* + θ], equal to U′ on Σ_τ* ∩ Ω′, gives U′ = Ũ on Ω′ ∩ {τ* ≤ τ ≤ τ* + θ}. So U′ agrees on the closure of Ω′ ∩ {τ
≤ τ* + θ} with the solution constructed, which is U on Ω_U ∩ {τ ≤ τ*} and Ũ on [τ*, τ* + θ] × R⁴. The two adapted domains
coincide up to τ* + θ: by Definition 51.30, applied to the development, T_(τ,U′) is determined by U′ on the closure
of Ω′ ∩ {τ′ ≤ τ}, where the development and the solution constructed agree; so the transported phases on the axes agree
there, z_B(τ) is the same point for both, and by the uniqueness in Lemma 51.25 so is the leaf h_B over D_B, a
part of the development's adapted boundary. Hence U′ = U on Ω′ ∩ {τ ≤ τ* + θ} = Ω_U ∩ {τ ≤ τ* + θ}, against the choice of
τ*; so τ* = τ1. Invariance under G follows as before.

*Step 10.* (51.24) is uniquely solvable (Lemma 51.25), so on a solution with Θ_A = □_g
u_A it returns the true leaves of u_A, hence the true σ_A. So near an axis Δ_A = Θ_A − □_g u_A obeys

    P_A(Δ_A) = −½ Δ_A (Θ_A + div_g P_A − 2κ_A1) − ½ (σ_A[Θ_A]² − σ_A[□_g u_A]²) + g(∇_(P_A) D, P_A) + L(P_A, P_A).

Here σ_A[□_g u_A] is computed from U′ := U with Θ_A replaced by □_g u_A = div_g P_A. 𝒩_k(U) controls div_g P_A at the
order k − 1 only, so U′ lies in the ball 𝔅′ of Lemma 51.28 (b), which bounds the middle term on 𝒰_δ
by C ‖Δ_A‖_(L²(𝒰_(2δ))), the factor σ_A[Θ_A] + σ_A[□_g u_A] being bounded: the map of (51.24) from
H_L to σ_L is a Hardy-type average. Near an axis the energy of Δ_A is taken on 𝒯′_A, the tube for P_A of T_(τ0,U)(S_A)
∪ ({ρ2 ≤ δ1} ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U), δ1 > 0 fixed. The axis {ρ2 = 0}, the zero set of K2, is invariant under the flow of P_A,
since [P_A, K2] = 0; that flow being Lipschitz on the compact domain, ρ2 grows along it at most by a factor e^(L (τ
− τ0)), so for 2δ e^(L (τ1 − τ0)) ≤ δ1 every 𝒯′_A ∩ Σ_τ contains the points of {ρ2 < 2δ} near the axis, as the bound on
𝒰_δ needs. Its lateral boundary is ruled by integral curves of P_A, so the transport has no flux through it. With zero
data the energy of (D, Δ_A) obeys a linear Gronwall inequality, as before, so Δ_A = 0. ∎

**Corollary 51.32** (The two-dust background with non-round perturbations.) Let ů be the two-dust
background of Proposition 50.6 on Ω₂ (Lemma 50.8), with the ingoing family v, density 𝒜/R³,
and the outgoing family u, density ℬ/R³ ((50.4)), and assume that the outgoing packet does not reach
the inner sphere: {u1 ≤ u ≤ u2} ∩ Ω₂ ∩ {R = a} = ∅. Replace the lateral boundaries of Ω₂ by adapted ones:

- *inner:* the boundary B_U of Definition 51.30 for B = {R = a}, the ingoing family and c_B(τ) := τ + a, near the
axes the leaf {v_ε − τ = a} of the ingoing phase v_ε of the solution;
- *outer:* the boundary B_U for B = {R = b(τ)}, the outgoing family and c_B(τ) := U_b(τ), the value of the
background's outgoing phase on {R = b(τ)}, near the axes the leaf {u_ε = U_b(τ)} of the outgoing phase u_ε.

For the background both are the spheres {R = a} and {R = b(τ)} of Ω₂. Let S_in := {v_start − η ≤ v ≤ v_end + η} ∩ Σ_τ0
and S_out := {u1 − η ≤ u ≤ u2 + η} ∩ Σ_τ0 with 0 < η < 1 so small that {u1 − η ≤ u ≤ u2 + η} ∩ Ω₂ does not meet {R = a},
and let ů_A, A = 3, …, N_f, be further phases in the class, eikonals of ů without caustics on Ω₂, with q̊_A = 0 and sets
S_A whose tubes avoid neighbourhoods of the points where the lateral boundaries meet the axes. Then every datum on the
set W_0 of Definition 51.30 that satisfies the constraints and the gauge condition, lies within ε of ů's and has
supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_U ⊂ T_(τ0,U)(S_A) for every A (Ω_U and T_(τ0,U) as in Definition 51.30) has its
Einstein–null-dust development on the whole adapted domain, in the gauge D(g) = 0 relative to the metric of ů and unique
there as in Theorem 51.31, within C ε of ů. The datum may be non-round, and it carries the further families
with small densities. If in the sets 𝒰_(2δ_B) of Definition 51.30 its normalised ingoing phase is τ0 + a on {R = a}
and its normalised outgoing phase is U_b(τ0) on {R = b(τ0)}, then T_(τ0,U) is the identity, a datum on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂
suffices, and the condition on the supports reads supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂ ⊂ S_A (Definition 51.30).

*Proof.* v and u are double-null coordinates of ů, smooth on Ω₂ with dv, du ≠ 0 (Proposition 50.6), so (H1)
holds. On Σ_τ, v = τ + R, so {R = a} = {v − τ = a}; and u is constant on the spheres and strictly decreasing in R along
each slice, since du(∂_R|_τ) = (1 − R_v)/R_u with R_u < 0 (Proposition 50.6 (c)), and R_v = e^ψ f/2 ≤ 1/2:
the vector ∂_v at fixed u, which is ∂_v + R_v ∂_R in the chart (v, R) of (50.8), is null, so −e^(2ψ) f +
2 e^ψ R_v = 0, and e^ψ ≤ 1 (proof of Lemma 50.8) and f ≤ 1; so {R = b(τ)} ∩ Σ_τ = {u = U_b(τ)} ∩ Σ_τ. Both
boundaries are spacelike with Ω₂ to their past (Lemma 50.8 (b), (c)). The ingoing tube 𝒯̊_in = {v_start − η
≤ v ≤ v_end + η} ∩ Ω₂ stays away from the outer boundary, where v = V + 1 + τ_end − τ ≥ V + 1 > v_end + η by
(50.11); the outgoing tube 𝒯̊_out = {u1 − η ≤ u ≤ u2 + η} ∩ Ω₂ stays away from the inner one by the choice
of η; and the further tubes avoid both near the axes. So near the points where the inner boundary meets an axis only the
ingoing family has tubes, near those of the outer boundary at most the outgoing family, and (H2′) holds. Apply
Theorem 51.31. ∎

Whether the outgoing packet stays off the inner sphere is a property of the background that Proposition 50.6
does not decide; it is assumed here. Data for the corollary are any small invariant solutions of the constraints with
the stated supports; data equal to the background's outside the domain of influence, for the constraints solved with
the radius as time, of a compact set away from the axes are constructed in Chapter 53 on a slice bent from
Σ_τ0, and carried to Σ_τ0 by their development.

**Remark 51.33** (What the theorems do not give.) Theorem 51.31 constructs the background; the
high-frequency construction over a non-round background needs more. By Proposition 51.3, two families of one
orientation are not separated at an axis point, so beyond one ingoing and one outgoing family the further families must
have densities vanishing near the axes. For three or more families present at a point, pairwise separation is not
enough, since at the first stage combinations of three phases occur. The frequency hierarchy that replaces it, the
polarisation of the waves for a non-radial family, and the limits that carry massless Vlasov matter are taken up in
Chapter 52.

## 52. Restricted massless Vlasov limits

Theorem 50.2 realises two crossing radial null dusts as high-frequency limits of vacuum metrics of the T²-mirror
class. This chapter treats a continuum of null dusts, that is, massless Vlasov matter. In four dimensions, under a U(1)
symmetry and in an elliptic gauge, Huneau and Luk prove that high-frequency limits of vacuum metrics are solutions of the
Einstein–massless Vlasov system whose measure is restricted to the cotangent bundle of the quotient [HL19, p. 1; p. 13],
and that suitable small, localised, U(1)-symmetric solutions of that system are such limits [HL25, Theorem 1.1, p. 2].
Their construction approximates the Vlasov field by n null dusts, approximates each Einstein–n-dust solution by vacuum
metrics of frequency 1/λ large compared with n, and joins the two steps along a diagonal [HL25, pp. 3, 19]. Without
symmetry, the construction for finitely many dusts is not uniform in their number [Tou24, p. 4].

We prove the five-dimensional counterpart in the class, without smallness, for fields that stay off the axes. In
Section 52.1 we show that a high-frequency limit inside the class has no stress along the torus, so that a
massless Vlasov limit in the class is restricted: its momenta are tangent to the orbit space; if the limit is moreover
round, it is a two-dust solution of the kind of Theorem 50.2. In Section 52.2 we show that restricted
particles move on the null geodesics of the orbit space, and that those reaching an axis off the axial directions focus
there, so that the field of a smooth solution stays off the axes. Theorem 52.10 then states: every smooth class
Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov solution whose field is a caustic-free family of dusts labelled by initial direction
and off the axes, on a domain of the type (2.8) whose initial spheres have positive mean curvature, is a weak
limit of class vacuum metrics. The proof has the two steps of [HL25]. The n-dust approximants of the field are uniform
in n (Proposition 52.31); the high-frequency step is not, and the steps are joined along a diagonal. Four facts
make the high-frequency step work for every n in the class: frequencies 1, Λ, …, Λ^(n−1) remove every resonance among
three or more phases up to the order the scheme uses (Lemma 52.15); waves polarised along the torus leave
no term of order λ⁻¹, in the field equations or in the constraints (Lemma 52.18,
Lemma 52.21); the orbit space has no shear (Lemma 52.23); and the constraints,
whose coefficients oscillate in every direction of the initial slice, are solved with bounds uniform in λ in norms in
which each angular derivative carries the factor λ that the oscillation costs, except the first two of the metric
unknown (Proposition 52.28). Each label is an eikonal only near its tube, so every transport of a family
is cut off, or posed, near its tube (Lemma 52.30, Section 52.8). The section after the proof of
Theorem 52.10 shows that the hypotheses are open and that an explicit family on Tangherlini meets them
(Lemma 52.38, Proposition 52.40), and the last adds to a small field the two radial dusts of
Theorem 50.2, which reach the axes, on domains of the type (2.8) inside the adapted domain of
Corollary 51.32 (Corollary 52.50).

*Notation.* g5 is a metric of the T²-mirror class of Section 2.1. We write ψ1 := A and ψ2 := B for the functions of
(2.1), so that

    g5 = g3 + e^(2ψ1) dφ1² + e^(2ψ2) dφ2²,      ψ := ψ1 + ψ2,      ω := (ψ2 − ψ1)/2,    (52.1)

with ψ and ω those of Proposition 2.3. The orbit space Q carries the Lorentzian metric g3; a, b, c are its indices;
⟨·,·⟩, |·|², ∇ and □3 are taken in g3, and □5 is the wave operator of g5. An invariant function is a function on Q.
Since √|g5| = √|g3| e^ψ, for every invariant u

    □5 u = □3 u + ⟨dψ, du⟩.    (52.2)

In the chart X = (τ, x) of Section 2.2 we put ρ1² := x1² + x2² and ρ2² := x3² + x4², r := |x| and v := τ + r.
The axes are {ρ1 = 0} and {ρ2 = 0}, where one circle of the action degenerates; the distance to the axes is
min(ρ1, ρ2), the Euclidean distance of the chart. The orbit slice of Σ_τ is its quotient by T², with coordinates
(r, ϑ), ρ1 = r cos ϑ, ρ2 = r sin ϑ. Families of null dusts are indexed by A, B, C ∈ {1, …, n}, n being their number;
multi-indices are j ∈ ℤⁿ, with |j|₁ := Σ_A |j_A|. Labels are points α of the circle S¹ = ℝ/2πℤ, with its distance
d(α, α′). As in Theorem 50.2, the stress of a massless matter model is the tensor T with Ric(g5) = T; a null dust
is T = q du ⊗ du with u an eikonal (g5⁻¹(du, du) = 0) and q ≥ 0, and ℓ := g5⁻¹du is its generator. For an invariant
u, ℓ = g3⁻¹du.

### 52.1 Massless Vlasov limits in the class

**Definition 52.1** (Massless Vlasov fields and limits.) A massless Vlasov field on a Lorentzian manifold
assigns to each point x a finite positive Borel measure μ_x on the null covectors at x; its stress is T_x := ∫ p ⊗ p
dμ_x(p). A field on a metric of the class is *restricted* at x if μ_x is carried by the covectors with p(∂_(φ1)) =
p(∂_(φ2)) = 0, that is, by the null covectors of the orbit space. A *high-frequency limit in the class* is a C² metric
g0 of the class for which there are vacuum metrics g_i of the class with g_i → g0 uniformly and ∂g_i ⇀ ∂g0 weakly in L²
on compact sets. It is a *massless Vlasov limit* if Ric(g0) is the stress of a massless Vlasov field.

**Proposition 52.2** (Massless Vlasov limits in the class.) Let g0 be a high-frequency limit in the
class.

(a) Ric(g0) has no torus components: R11[g0] = R22[g0] = 0, and the components Ric(g0)(∂_a, ∂_(φi)) and
Ric(g0)(∂_(φ1), ∂_(φ2)) vanish.

(b) If g0 is a massless Vlasov limit, its field is restricted at every point.

(c) If moreover g0 is round (invariant under the action of O(4) on the spheres {τ, r = const} of the chart, as every
background of Theorem 50.2 is), then at every point with r > 0 the field is carried by the two radial null
directions, and in double-null coordinates (u, v) of the round metric, Ric(g0) = 𝔮_in dv ⊗ dv + 𝔮_out du ⊗ du with
𝔮_in, 𝔮_out ≥ 0: g0 is an Einstein–two-null-dust solution, with one ingoing and one outgoing radial dust.

*Proof.* (a) The mixed components vanish identically for every metric of the class (Lemma 2.1). Let U be a
compact set off the axes and put h := e^(2ψ) g3, as in Proposition 2.3. The functions ψi = ½ log g(∂_(φi), ∂_(φi))
and the components of h and of √|h| h⁻¹ are smooth functions of the components of g on U. Hence for the sequence g_i
they converge uniformly on U to those of g0, and their first derivatives, being smooth functions of the components times
first derivatives of the components, converge weakly in L²(U). Each g_i is vacuum, so by Proposition 2.3

    ∂_a(√|h[g_i]| h[g_i]^(ab) ∂_b ψ[g_i]) = 0,      ∂_a(√|h[g_i]| h[g_i]^(ab) ∂_b ω[g_i]) = 0

in the sense of distributions on U, where h[g_i], ψ[g_i], ω[g_i] are h, ψ, ω of g_i. The products √|h[g_i]| h[g_i]^(ab)
∂_b ψ[g_i] converge weakly in L²(U), a uniformly convergent factor times a weakly convergent one, so the identities pass
to the limit: ∂_a(√|h0| h0^(ab) ∂_b ψ0) = ∂_a(√|h0| h0^(ab) ∂_b ω0) = 0 in distributions, and classically since g0 is
C². That is □_(h0) ψ0 = □_(h0) ω0 = 0 on U, and by Proposition 2.3, e^(−2ψ1) R11 + e^(−2ψ2) R22 = −e^(2ψ) □_h ψ = 0
and e^(−2ψ1) R11 − e^(−2ψ2) R22 = 2 e^(2ψ) □_h ω = 0 for g0, so R11 = R22 = 0 off the axes, and on the axes by
continuity.

(b) By (a), ∫ p(∂_(φi))² dμ_x = R_(ii)[g0](x) = 0. A nonnegative continuous function with zero integral against a
positive measure vanishes on its support, so p(∂_(φ1)) = p(∂_(φ2)) = 0 on the support of μ_x.

(c) Let r(x) > 0, let S_x be the sphere {τ, r = const} through x and γ its induced metric. The isotropy group of O(4) at
x contains a copy of SO(3) acting on T_x S_x ≅ ℝ³ by rotations, irreducibly, and Ric(g0)_x is invariant under it. The
symmetric endomorphism γ⁻¹B of the restriction B of Ric(g0)_x to T_x S_x commutes with this action, so its eigenspaces
are invariant subspaces, hence 0 or T_x S_x: B = c γ. At least one of ∂_(φ1), ∂_(φ2) is a nonzero vector of T_x S_x,
and B vanishes on it by (a); so c = 0. Then ∫ p(e)² dμ_x = B(e, e) = 0 for every e ∈ T_x S_x, and as in (b) μ_x is
carried by the null covectors that vanish on T_x S_x. These form a Lorentzian plane, whose null covectors are the
multiples of dv and du; writing p = E dv or p = E du on the two lines, Ric(g0)_x = (∫ E² dμ_in) dv ⊗ dv + (∫ E² dμ_out)
du ⊗ du. Each dust is conserved: Ric(g0) is traceless, dv and du being null, so the contracted Bianchi identity gives
div Ric(g0) = 0; since ∇_(g0⁻¹dv) dv = ½ d(g0⁻¹(dv, dv)) = 0, div(𝔮_in dv ⊗ dv) = div(𝔮_in g0⁻¹dv) dv, and likewise for
du; as dv and du are independent, div(𝔮_in g0⁻¹dv) = div(𝔮_out g0⁻¹du) = 0, in the sense of distributions where the
densities are only continuous. ∎

So the round massless Vlasov limits in the class are Einstein–two-radial-null-dust solutions, and those with the
configuration of Theorem 50.2 (a seed, an ingoing shell and an outgoing packet between them on Σ_τ0) are realised
as limits by that theorem. The proposition does not say that every round limit has this configuration. Radial momenta
stay radial along radial geodesics, so for a round metric the Einstein–(radial) massless Vlasov system is the
Einstein–two-null-dust system.

**Remark 52.3** (Why the torus stress vanishes.) The proof of (a) uses only the divergence form
of the torus components of the Ricci tensor, the five-dimensional form of [HL19, p. 4]. In a two-scale expansion it reads
as follows. Let H^(ab) := √|h| h^(ab) = H0^(ab) + λ H1^(ab)(X, θ) and f = f0 + λ f1(X, θ) at the phase θ = u/λ, with
H0(du, du) = 0. With the two-scale derivative (4.1), the coefficient of λ⁻¹ in ∂_a(H^(ab) ∂_b f)
is H0^(ab) u_a u_b ∂_θ² f1 = 0, and its coefficient of λ⁰ is ∂_a(H0^(ab) ∂_b f0) + ∂_a(H0^(ab) u_b ∂_θ f1) + u_a ∂_θ
(H0^(ab) ∂_b f1 + H1^(ab) ∂_b f0 + H1^(ab) u_b ∂_θ f1), whose mean over θ is ∂_a(H0^(ab) ∂_b f0): every oscillating
contribution is a θ-derivative. For the operator h^(ab) ∂_a∂_b f, not in divergence form, with h = h0 + λ h1, the mean of
the coefficient of λ⁰ contains ⟨h1(du, du) ∂_θ² f1⟩ = −⟨∂_θ h1(du, du) ∂_θ f1⟩, nonzero in general. The quadratic term
(3/2) dψ ⊗ dψ of Ric[h] in (2.2) acquires the mean (3/2) ⟨(∂_θ ψ^(1))²⟩ du ⊗ du, λψ^(1) the oscillating part of
ψ: the stress of a limit lives on the orbit block.

### 52.2 The restricted system

**Lemma 52.4** (Restricted geodesics.) Off the axes the geodesic Hamiltonian of g5 is

    H(x, p) = ½ (g3^(ab) p_a p_b + e^(−2ψ1) p_(φ1)² + e^(−2ψ2) p_(φ2)²).

(a) p_(φ1) and p_(φ2) are constant along every geodesic.

(b) On {p_(φ1) = p_(φ2) = 0}, Hamilton's equations read ẋ^a = g3^(ab) p_b, ṗ_a = −½ ∂_a g3^(bc) p_b p_c, φ̇_i = 0: the
restricted null geodesics are the null geodesics of g3 at fixed angles. So the restricted fields form an invariant set
of the Vlasov equation of g5, on which it is the Vlasov equation of (Q, g3), and their stress T has T(∂_(φi), ·) = 0.
Off this set ṗ_a contains −½ p_(φi)² ∂_a e^(−2ψi), and the geodesics do not project to geodesics of g3.

(c) Let T be a symmetric tensor field of the class with T(∂_(φi), ·) = 0. Then, on orbit indices,
div_(g5) T = e^(−ψ) div_(g3)(e^ψ T). In particular a null dust T = q du ⊗ du with u an invariant eikonal satisfies
div_(g5) T = 0 if and only if

    ℓ(q) + q □5 u = 0,      equivalently      div_(g3)(e^ψ q ℓ) = 0,    (52.3)

and the orbit density e^ψ q is transported by ℓ with the expansion □3 u: ℓ(e^ψ q) + (□3 u) e^ψ q = 0.

*Proof.* (a) H does not depend on φ1, φ2. (b) is Hamilton's equations for H at p_φ = 0, and T(∂_(φi), ·) = ∫ p(∂_(φi)) p
dμ = 0. (c) Since T^(φi μ) = 0 and the components do not depend on the angles, (div_(g5) T)_b = |g5|^(−1/2)
∂_a(|g5|^(1/2) T^a_b) − ½ ∂_b (g5)_(cd) T^(cd), the second term having orbit indices only; with |g5|^(1/2) = |g3|^(1/2)
e^ψ this is e^(−ψ)(|g3|^(−1/2) ∂_a(|g3|^(1/2) e^ψ T^a_b) − ½ ∂_b (g3)_(cd) e^ψ T^(cd)) = e^(−ψ) (div_(g3)(e^ψ T))_b. For
the dust, ∇^μ(q ∂_μ u ∂_ν u) = div_(g5)(q ℓ) ∂_ν u + q ℓ^μ ∇_μ ∂_ν u, and ℓ^μ ∇_μ ∂_ν u = ½ ∂_ν(g5⁻¹(du, du)) = 0; as du
≠ 0, div_(g5) T = 0 is div_(g5)(q ℓ) = ℓ(q) + q □5 u = 0. By (52.2), ℓ(e^ψ q) = e^ψ(ℓ(q) + q ⟨dψ, du⟩) = −e^ψ
q □3 u, and div_(g3)(e^ψ q ℓ) = ℓ(e^ψ q) + e^ψ q □3 u. ∎

**Definition 52.5** (Fields in label form.) Let Ω be a domain of the type (2.8) for a metric g of
the class (its constants (τ0, τ_end, a, V) fixed and its sets defined by the coordinate functions τ, r, v). For a smooth
invariant function u on Ω the *rays* of u are the integral curves of g⁻¹du, and the *tube* of a compact set K ⊂ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω
for u is the set of points of Ω on the rays of u from K, each followed forward while it stays in Ω. A *restricted field
in label form* on Ω is a pair (F, u) of smooth invariant functions on Ω × S¹, F ≥ 0, with density q := F², such that
each u_α := u(·, α) is an eikonal of g on a neighbourhood of the tube D_α of supp q(·, α) ∩ Σ_τ0 for u_α, with g⁻¹du_α
future directed there, with stress

    T_V := ∫_(S¹) q(·, α) du_α ⊗ du_α dα,    (52.4)

and with every amplitude F(·, α) transported by

    2 ℓ_α(F) + (□5 u_α) F = 0,      ℓ_α := g⁻¹du_α,    (52.5)

and vanishing off D_α. The transport is (52.3) for q(·, α) = F(·, α)², as in [HL25, (1.2)]. Off a
neighbourhood of D_α the function u_α enters neither T_V nor (52.5), and nothing is assumed of it there:
a label is an eikonal only near its tube. Let β0(x, α) be the angle, in a frame of the orbit slice of Σ_τ0 orthonormal
for its induced metric, of the covector d(u_α|Σ_τ0)(x). The field is *labelled by initial direction* if for every x the
map α ↦ β0(x, α) is injective on the labels α with (x, α) ∈ supp q. T_V is the stress of the restricted field μ_x := ∫
q(x, α) δ_(du_α(x)) dα, and each label is a null dust. Replacing u_α by −u_α changes neither T_V nor
(52.5), so the time orientation of ℓ_α only fixes a sign. It fixes the *branch* of the eikonal equation
used below: given the restriction of u_α to Σ_τ0, of nonzero differential, the τ-derivative of u_α there is the root of
g⁻¹(du_α, du_α) = 0 for which g⁻¹du_α is future directed. (With 𝔫 the future unit normal of Σ_τ0, the two roots are
du_α(𝔫) = ±|d(u_α|Σ_τ0)|, and g⁻¹du_α is future directed exactly when du_α(𝔫) < 0.)

In [HL25, (1.2), p. 2] the labels are the initial directions themselves: u_α↾Σ0 = x¹ cos α + x² sin α, so β0 = α.

**Lemma 52.6** (The stress at an axis.) Let T be a smooth symmetric 2-tensor field on a
neighbourhood of a point x0 of the axis {ρ2 = 0}, invariant under the rotations of the (x3, x4)-plane and under x4 ↦
−x4. For ρ2 > 0 put e_ρ := ρ2⁻¹(x3 ∂_3 + x4 ∂_4) and e_φ := ρ2⁻¹(x3 ∂_4 − x4 ∂_3). Then T(e_ρ, e_φ) = 0 and

    T(e_ρ, e_ρ) − T(e_φ, e_φ) = O(ρ2²).

If T is the stress of a restricted field, T(e_φ, e_φ) = ρ2⁻² T(∂_(φ2), ∂_(φ2)) = 0, so T(e_ρ, e_ρ) = O(ρ2²), and at x0
the field's measure is carried by the covectors in span(dτ, dr): at an axis point the momenta of a restricted field with
smooth stress are radial.

*Proof.* At x with ρ2 > 0 let R be the reflection of the (x3, x4)-plane in the line through (x3, x4), the identity on the
other coordinates; it is a rotation composed with x4 ↦ −x4, it fixes x, and Re_ρ = e_ρ, Re_φ = −e_φ. So T(e_ρ, e_φ) =
T(Re_ρ, Re_φ) = −T(e_ρ, e_φ) = 0. Let T_(ij), i, j ∈ {3, 4}, be the planar block, a smooth function of y := (x3, x4) at
fixed other coordinates, and expand T_(ij)(y) = T_(ij)(0) + L_(ij)(y) + O(|y|²) with L linear. Invariance under the
rotations and the reflection makes T(0) commute with O(2) acting on ℝ², which is irreducible, so T(0) = c I. Invariance
under the rotation by π, y ↦ −y, gives T_(ij)(−y) = T_(ij)(y), so L(−y) = L(y) and L = 0. Hence T_(ij) = c δ_(ij) +
O(ρ2²), and T(e_ρ, e_ρ) − T(e_φ, e_φ) = (T_(ij) − c δ_(ij))(e_ρ^i e_ρ^j − e_φ^i e_φ^j) = O(ρ2²). For a restricted field
T(∂_(φ2), ∂_(φ2)) = 0 and ∂_(φ2) = ρ2 e_φ, so T(e_φ, e_φ) = 0, T(e_ρ, e_ρ) = O(ρ2²), and c = lim T(e_φ, e_φ) = 0; so
∫ p(∂_3)² dμ_(x0) = ∫ p(∂_4)² dμ_(x0) = 0. On the support p also vanishes on ∂_(φ1) = x1 ∂_2 − x2 ∂_1, and with ρ2 = 0,
ρ1 = r at x0, so p ∈ span(dτ, dr). ∎

**Remark 52.7** (Densities at an axis.) Let a restricted field near the axis {ρ2 = 0} have, at
distance ρ2, the density f(ρ2, β) dβ/(2π) on unit-energy momenta whose spatial part makes the angle β with the axis in
an orthonormal frame (e_axis, e_ρ) of the orbit slice, so that T(e_ρ, e_ρ) = (2π)⁻¹ ∫ f sin²β dβ. If f is continuous and
f(0, ·) does not vanish off {sin β = 0}, then T(e_ρ, e_ρ) has a positive limit at the axis, not O(ρ2²), and by
Lemma 52.6 the stress is not smooth. A density concentrating on the axial directions keeps the stress
of size ρ2²: for f = ρ2⁻¹(e^(−β²/ρ2²) + e^(−(|β|−π)²/ρ2²)) on (−π, π], the total density (2π)⁻¹ ∫ f dβ tends to π^(−1/2)
and T(e_ρ, e_ρ)/ρ2² tends to 1/(2√π), while ∂_β f is unbounded. Indeed, since sin²β = sin²(|β| − π), ρ2 ∫ f sin²β dβ is,
up to terms O(e^(−c/ρ2²)), the sum of two Gaussian integrals ∫ e^(−t²/ρ2²)(t² + O(t⁴)) dt = (√π/2) ρ2³ + O(ρ2⁵);
so T(e_ρ, e_ρ) = (2π)⁻¹ ρ2⁻¹ (√π ρ2³ + O(ρ2⁵)). So at an axis a restricted field with smooth stress is zero, or, in the
limit, two radial dusts along the axis.

**Lemma 52.8** (Invariant null phases at an axis.) Let u be an invariant function and x0 a point of
the axis {ρ2 = 0} with r(x0) > 0. Then du(x0) ∈ span(dτ, dr). If u is null at x0 and du(x0) ≠ 0, then du(x0) lies on
one of the two null lines of the Lorentzian plane span(dτ, dr) at x0, and two invariant null phases on the same line
have g⁻¹(du_A, du_B) = 0 at x0. So among the null dusts present at an axis point at most two, one on each line (one
ingoing and one outgoing), are pairwise separated.

*Proof.* The reflection x3 ↦ −x3 is a rotation by π composed with x4 ↦ −x4, so u is even in x3 and ∂_3 u = 0 on
{x3 = 0}; likewise ∂_4 u = 0 on {x4 = 0}. The rotation field x1 ∂_2 − x2 ∂_1 annihilates du. At x0 these give du(x0)
∈ span(dτ, x1 dx1 + x2 dx2) = span(dτ, dρ1), and dρ1 = dr there. The plane span(dτ, dr) contains the timelike dτ (the
slices are spacelike) and the null du(x0) ≠ 0, so g⁻¹ restricted to it is Lorentzian, and its null covectors form two
lines. Two covectors on one null line are proportional and null, so their product vanishes. ∎

**Proposition 52.9** (Restricted particles cannot reach an axis.) Let g5 be a C² metric of the
class near a point x0 of the axis {ρ2 = 0} with r(x0) > 0, and suppose that off the axes Ric(g5) = T := e^(−ψ) T3, where
T3 is the stress of a continuous density f ≥ 0 on the bundle of null directions of (Q, g3) transported by the null
geodesic flow of g3 (the Vlasov equation of (Q, g3), Lemma 52.4 (b) and (c)): X(f) + κ f = 0 along the
generator X of that flow, with κ a continuous function of g3 and its first derivatives. Then f vanishes on every null
direction whose g3-geodesic reaches x0 transversally to the axis.

*Proof.* Suppose that f > 0 at a null direction whose geodesic reaches x0 transversally. Let P be the fixed set {x2 =
x4 = 0} of the two reflections, a three-dimensional submanifold with coordinates (τ, x1, x3). It meets every orbit near
x0, at the points (τ, ±ρ1, ±ρ2). The Killing fields ∂_(φ1), ∂_(φ2) are along ∂_2, ∂_4 at the points of P and orthogonal
to P by the reflection symmetry, so on {x1 > 0, x3 > 0} the induced metric g_P of P is g3 in the coordinates (τ, ρ1,
ρ2) = (τ, x1, x3). As g5 is C², g_P is a C² Lorentzian metric on P, even in x3: g3 extends across the edge {ρ2 = 0} to
g_P, and the null geodesic flow of g3 extends to the flow of g_P, which is C¹, under which the geodesic reaching x0
transversally crosses {x3 = 0}. In the coordinates of P, κ is the same function of g_P and its first derivatives, so it
is continuous on the bundle of null directions of g_P over a neighbourhood of x0. Hence f, which equals its initial
value times exp(−∫κ) along each flow line, stays positive along the flow line of the given direction, and, by
continuity, f ≥ c1 > 0 on a neighbourhood U of the arriving direction at the points of the geodesic near x0. So T3(e0,
e0) ≥ ∫_U f (p(e0))² ≥ c2 > 0 there, for a timelike vector field e0. The Killing field ∂_(φ2) = x3 ∂_4 − x4 ∂_3 has, at
points of P, e^(2ψ2) = g5(∂_(φ2), ∂_(φ2)) = x3² (g5)_(44) = ρ2² (g5)_(44), with (g5)_(44) > 0, and e^(ψ1) is bounded
near x0 since ρ1(x0) = r(x0) > 0. So T(e0, e0) = e^(−ψ1−ψ2) T3(e0, e0) ≥ c/ρ2 at the points of the geodesic near x0,
with c > 0. But Ric(g5) is continuous near x0, so Ric(g5)(e0, e0) is bounded there: a contradiction. ∎

The mechanism is the focusing of a converging beam: in a flat plane, particles moving radially inward with speed v have
a density ϱ(ρ, t) solving ∂_t ϱ − v ρ⁻¹ ∂_ρ(ρ ϱ) = 0, so ρ ϱ(ρ, t) = (ρ + v t) ϱ0(ρ + v t) and ρ ϱ → v t ϱ0(v t) > 0 as
ρ → 0 once the beam has reached the centre; particles moving along the axis (v = 0) keep their density.

### 52.3 The theorem

Let Ω be a domain of the type (2.8), Ω = {τ0 ≤ τ ≤ τ_end, r ≥ a, v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ V + 1}, with Σ_τ := Ω ∩ {τ}
and its outer radius b(τ) := V + 1 − τ + (τ_end − τ). Let (g, F, u) be a smooth class solution on Ω of the
Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov system in label form, Ric(g) = T_V. For a compact set S ⊂ (Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω) × S¹ (points
and labels) put S_x := {α : (x, α) ∈ S}, S_α := {x : (x, α) ∈ S}, let D_α(S) be the tube of S_α for u_α
(Definition 52.5), and let 𝒟(S) be the set of the (x, α) with x ∈ D_α(S). We assume:

- (Ω) For g: each Σ_τ is spacelike; {r = a} is spacelike and r decreases along future causal curves near it;
  {v + τ = const} is spacelike and v + τ increases along future causal curves; every ray of u_α through a point of
  D_α(S), S the set of (V1), followed to the past, stays in Ω and meets Σ_τ0. These are (a)–(d) of Lemma 2.6, for
  g.
- (V1) F and u are smooth in (x, α), and there is a compact set S ⊂ (Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω) × S¹, each S_α invariant under T² and
  both reflections, whose interior int S, relative to (Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω) × S¹, contains supp q ∩ (Σ_τ0 × S¹), such that: u is an
  eikonal in each label, with ℓ_α future directed, on a neighbourhood 𝒲 of 𝒟(S) in Ω × S¹, that is
  g⁻¹(du_α, du_α)(x) = 0 for (x, α) ∈ 𝒲; for every x, α ↦ β0(x, α) is injective on S_x (the field is labelled by initial
  direction); ∂_α β0 ≥ b_* > 0 on S; and for (x0, α) ∈ S the point y_τ(x0) where the ray of u_α from x0 meets Σ_τ
  depends on x0 with Jacobian determinant ≥ J0 > 0 in the coordinates (r, ϑ) of the orbit slices, for every τ with
  y_τ(x0) in a neighbourhood of Ω̄ (no caustic).
- (V2) dist(D_α(S), axes) ≥ 2δ > 0 for every α.
- (V3) On Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω the spheres {r = const} have positive mean curvature.

The tube D_α of supp q(·, α) ∩ Σ_τ0 lies in D_α(S), and 𝒟(S) is compact, as in Remark 52.11. A neighbourhood of each
D_α(S) alone would not do: the cut-offs of Section 52.7 are smooth in (x, α), and they need the neighbourhood 𝒲
of (V1). (V3) is the first of the two signs of Lemma 7.5 (a); the second, 𝒮 A0 > 0 for the
symmetrizer 𝒮 of (7.6), holds on every slice (Lemma 52.26).

The invariance of the sections S_α costs nothing. If a compact S meets every other requirement of (V1) and (V2), so does
S^G := {(x, α) : (h x, α) ∈ S for every h ∈ G}, G = O(2) × O(2) the group generated by T² and the two reflections, and
its sections are invariant. Indeed S^G ⊂ S is compact; each condition of (V1) and (V2), and the clause of (Ω) on rays,
holds on a compact subset of S as on S; and supp q ∩ (Σ_τ0 × S¹) ⊂ int S^G, since this set is a union of orbits of G, q
being invariant, and an orbit G·(x, α) in it, compact and contained in the open set int S, has a neighbourhood whose
images under G lie in int S, so that this neighbourhood lies in S^G and the orbit in int S^G. The union of the images of
S under G would not do: two points of one orbit may carry different labels with the same initial direction, against the
injectivity in (V1).

**Theorem 52.10** (Restricted massless Vlasov limits.) Let (g, F, u) satisfy (Ω), (V1), (V2) and (V3). Then
there are smooth metrics g_i on Ω, invariant under T² and under both reflections, with Ric(g_i) = 0,

    g_i → g uniformly on Ω,      ∂g_i ⇀ ∂g weakly in L²(Ω).

The metric g_i is a vacuum approximation of the n_i-dust approximant of the field, along odd n_i → ∞.

No smallness of g or of the field is assumed. The properties (b) and (c) of Lemma 7.5, no
coefficient of order λ⁻¹ and unchanged principal coefficients, are properties of the approximant's data; they are proved
in Theorem 52.36 for torus-polarised waves and are not hypotheses. The hypotheses are open
(Lemma 52.38), and an explicit family on Tangherlini meets them (Proposition 52.40), so the theorem
covers a nonempty open set of solutions. The two radial dusts of Theorem 50.2, which reach the axes, can be added to
a small field, the weak limit then holding on domains of the type (2.8) inside the adapted domain of
Corollary 51.32 (Section 52.11, Corollary 52.50).

**Remark 52.11** ((V2) for smooth solutions.) Let (g, F, u) be smooth on Ω̄ and satisfy (Ω) and (V1), with S
disjoint from axes × S¹. Then (V2) holds for some δ > 0. Indeed, let x be a point of an axis, say {ρ2 = 0}, with
r(x) > 0. By Lemma 52.8, du_α(x) ∈ span(dτ, dr). The components of g⁻¹dτ and g⁻¹dr along ∂_3 are
g^(τ3) and (x1 g^(13) + x2 g^(23))/r at x, and those along ∂_4 are g^(τ4) and (x1 g^(14) + x2 g^(24))/r; g is invariant
under x3 ↦ −x3 (a rotation by π composed with x4 ↦ −x4) and under x4 ↦ −x4, so these components are odd in x3,
respectively x4, and vanish on the axis. So ℓ_α(x) is tangent to the axis, the axis is invariant under the flow of
ℓ_α, and by uniqueness of integral curves a ray that meets the axis lies in it at every parameter, its starting point
included. The rays start on S_α, off the axes, so the set 𝒟(S) = {(x, α) : x ∈ D_α(S)}, the image of the compact set of
(x0, α, τ) with (x0, α) ∈ S whose ray reaches Σ_τ inside Ω̄ under the continuous map (x0, α, τ) ↦ (y_τ(x0), α), is
compact and disjoint from the closed set axes × S¹, hence at positive distance from it.

**Remark 52.12** (What the hypotheses avoid.) Four obstructions are proved in this chapter, and the
theorem is built so that none applies. (O1) At an axis point every invariant null phase is radial, and two of one
orientation have vanishing mixed symbol (Lemma 52.8): the labels are kept off the axes, and only the
radial pair of Section 52.11, one dust on each null line, reaches them. (O2) Under a C² metric a continuous orbit
density carries no particle to an axis transversally: it would focus there (Proposition 52.9). (O3) Without a
hierarchy of frequencies, an antipodal pair and any third phase resonate exactly (Lemma 52.14): the
frequencies are 1, Λ, …, Λ^(n−1). (O4) A non-radial wave whose orbit part is a nonzero multiple of q̂ ⊗ q̂, q̂ the unit
covector of the orbit slice orthogonal to the phase's gradient, leaves a term of order λ⁻¹ in the constraints
(Lemma 52.21 (c)): the waves of the labels are torus-polarised; those of the radial pair have
an orbit part, a multiple of q̂ ⊗ q̂ on Σ_τ0, and leave no such term because their phases are radial there
(Lemma 52.44).

### 52.4 Separation and coherence of the labels

**Lemma 52.13** (The flow keeps the labels separated.) Assume (Ω), (V1) and (V2), and let S′ ⊂ int S
be compact. There is c0 > 0, depending on Ω, the field, S and S′ and not on any choice of labels, such that at every
point y ∈ D_α(S′) ∩ D_α′(S′)

    |g⁻¹(du_α, du_α′)(y)| ≥ c0 d(α, α′)².    (52.6)

*Proof.* Let ℬ be the bundle of null directions of g3 over the orbit slices of the Σ_τ, a circle bundle. On the orbit
slices off the axes fix a smooth frame (e1, e2) orthonormal for the slice metric (by the Gram–Schmidt process from
(∂_r, ∂_ϑ)), let 𝔫 be the future unit normal of the orbit slice in (Q, g3), and describe a null direction at y by the
angle β with which a covector k on it, with g3⁻¹k future directed, is written k(𝔫) = −E, k(e1) = E cos β, k(e2) =
E sin β, E > 0. For two such covectors at y,

    g⁻¹(k, k′) = −E E′ + E E′ cos(β − β′) = −2 E E′ sin²((β − β′)/2).    (52.7)

Let 𝔰(x0, α) := (x0, β0(x0, α)) on S, with values in ℬ over the orbit slice of Σ_τ0. It is injective, by (V1), and its
differential is triangular with determinant ∂_α β0 ≥ b_* > 0, so on int S it is an injective local diffeomorphism, hence
a diffeomorphism onto the open set 𝔰(int S). For τ ∈ [τ0, τ_end] and y in the orbit slice of Σ_τ ∩ Ω̄, let Ψ_τ(y, β) be
the point and direction in which the null geodesic of g3 through y with direction β, followed to the past, meets Σ_τ0.
It meets Σ_τ0 inside Ω̄: by (Ω) future causal curves leave Ω through its lateral boundaries, so a past causal curve from
Ω̄ does not; and τ is monotone along it. Ψ_τ is smooth, continuous in (τ, y, β), and a diffeomorphism onto its image,
its inverse being the future flow. By Lemma 52.4 (b) the rays of u_α are null geodesics of g3, with direction
that of du_α; so if the ray of u_α from x0 ∈ S_α passes through y ∈ Σ_τ, then Ψ_τ(y, β(y; α)) = 𝔰(x0, α), β(y; α) the
angle of du_α at y.

Let 𝔇 be the compact set of (x0, α, τ) with (x0, α) ∈ S whose ray reaches Σ_τ inside Ω̄, and Φ_τ(x0, α) :=
(y_τ(x0), β(y_τ(x0); α)) = Ψ_τ⁻¹(𝔰(x0, α)) on it. det DΦ_τ = det DΨ_τ⁻¹ · ∂_α β0 is positive, the flow Ψ_τ⁻¹ depending
continuously on τ and being the identity at τ0, so det DΦ_τ ≥ c_Φ > 0 on 𝔇. Write DΦ_τ in blocks, with A := ∂y/∂x0,
B := ∂y/∂α, C := ∂β/∂x0, D := ∂β/∂α; A is invertible by (V1), with 0 < det A ≤ C_A on 𝔇. At fixed y, inverting
x0 ↦ y_τ(x0) gives x0 = x0(y, α) with ∂_α x0 = −A⁻¹B, and the angle β(y; α) = β(x0(y, α), α) has

    ∂_α β(y; α) = D − C A⁻¹ B = det DΦ_τ / det A ≥ c1 := c_Φ/C_A,

the Schur complement.

Fix τ and y ∈ Σ_τ ∩ Ω̄. On the open set B_y := {β : Ψ_τ(y, β) ∈ 𝔰(int S)} put Λ_y(β) := the label of 𝔰⁻¹(Ψ_τ(y, β)),
a smooth function; if y ∈ D_α(S′), then β(y; α) ∈ B_y and Λ_y(β(y; α)) = α. At β ∈ B_y, with (x0, α″) :=
𝔰⁻¹(Ψ_τ(y, β)) ∈ int S, whose ray reaches y, so that (x0, α″, τ) ∈ 𝔇, Λ_y is the inverse of α ↦ β(y; α) near α″, and
0 < Λ_y′(β) = 1/∂_α β(y; α″) ≤ 1/c1. Since 𝔰(S′) is a compact subset of the open set 𝔰(int S) and Ψ is uniformly
continuous on a compact neighbourhood, inside its domain, of the compact set of the (τ, y, β) with Ψ_τ(y, β) ∈ 𝔰(S′)
(the rays from S′ stay 2δ from the axes), there is ρ0 > 0 such that for every τ, y ∈ Σ_τ ∩ Ω̄ and β with Ψ_τ(y, β)
∈ 𝔰(S′), the arc of the β″ with |β″ − β| ≤ ρ0 lies in B_y.

Let y ∈ D_α(S′) ∩ D_α′(S′), β := β(y; α), β′ := β(y; α′), and δβ ∈ [0, π] their distance on the circle. Let E_* > 0 be
the minimum of E = −du_α(𝔫) over the compact set of the (y, α) with y in the closure of D_α(S); it is positive since
du_α ≠ 0 is null with g⁻¹du_α future directed. By (52.7) and sin(t/2) ≥ t/π on [0, π], |g⁻¹(du_α,
du_α′)(y)| ≥ 2 E_*² sin²(δβ/2) ≥ 2 E_*² δβ²/π². If δβ ≥ ρ0, this is at least 2 E_*² ρ0²/π² ≥ (2 E_*² ρ0²/π⁴) d(α, α′)²,
as d(α, α′) ≤ π. If δβ < ρ0, the arc of length δβ from β to β′ lies in B_y, Λ_y maps its ends to α and α′, and Λ_y′ ≤
1/c1 on it, so d(α, α′) ≤ δβ/c1 and the bound is at least (2 E_*² c1²/π²) d(α, α′)². So (52.6) holds
with c0 := (2 E_*²/π²) min(c1², ρ0²/π²). The injectivity of β0(x, ·) is used in the definition of Λ_y, which needs 𝔰
injective. ∎

For the n labels α_A := 2πA/n, d(α_A, α_B) ≥ 2π/n, so the dusts sampled at them are pairwise separated with constant
c0 (2π/n)² on the overlaps of the tubes D_(α_A)(S′). This is the separation η′ ≳ 1/n² of [HL25, Lemma 4.15, p. 18]; for
n directions 2πA/n on the flat orbit space with unit energies the least mixed symbol is exactly 1 − cos(2π/n), and
n²(1 − cos(2π/n)) → 2π².

Pairwise separation is not enough for the scheme of Theorem 52.33. At stage m its residual carries the
harmonics e^(i j·θ) with |j|₁ ≤ m + 2, and a harmonic with two or more nonzero entries is removed by division by

    Q_j := g⁻¹(𝔎_j, 𝔎_j),      𝔎_j := Σ_A j_A ν_A du_A,    (52.8)

ν_A the frequency of family A.

**Lemma 52.14** (An exact resonance.) In 2+1-dimensional Minkowski space let k_a, k_b be future null
covectors of equal energy with antipodal spatial directions, and k_c any future null covector of that energy. Then
𝔎 := k_a + k_b − k_c is null. So with equal frequencies the mixed harmonic e^(i(θ_a + θ_b − θ_c)) is exactly resonant,
whatever the pairwise separations.

*Proof.* In an orthonormal frame, k_a = E(−1, e), k_b = E(−1, −e), k_c = E(−1, f), with e, f unit vectors. Then 𝔎 =
E(−1, −f), and g⁻¹(𝔎, 𝔎) = E²(−1 + 1) = 0. ∎

**Lemma 52.15** (Coherence under a hierarchy of frequencies.) Let k_1, …, k_n be covectors at a point
of a 2+1-dimensional Lorentzian space with g⁻¹(k_A, k_A) = 0, |g⁻¹(k_A, k_B)| ≥ c > 0 for A ≠ B, and |k_A| ≤ Ē in an
orthonormal frame. Let Λ > 1 and ν_A := Λ^(A−1). For every j ∈ ℤⁿ with at least two nonzero entries and |j|₁ ≤ m, let B1
and B2, B1 > B2, be its two largest indices with nonzero entries. Then

    |g⁻¹(𝔎_j, 𝔎_j)| ≥ 2 ν_B1 ν_B2 (c − m Ē²/Λ − m² Ē²/(2Λ)),      𝔎_j := Σ_A j_A ν_A k_A.    (52.9)

In particular every such combination is non-null, with this margin, once Λ > (m + m²/2) Ē²/c.

*Proof.* In the orthonormal frame |g⁻¹(k, k′)| ≤ |k| |k′|. Put 𝔎 := 𝔎_j = j_B1 ν_B1 k_B1 + V, V := Σ_(A ≠ B1) j_A ν_A
k_A. Since k_B1 is null, g⁻¹(𝔎, 𝔎) = 2 j_B1 ν_B1 g⁻¹(k_B1, V) + g⁻¹(V, V). Here g⁻¹(k_B1, V) = j_B2 ν_B2 g⁻¹(k_B1,
k_B2) + Σ_(A < B2) j_A ν_A g⁻¹(k_B1, k_A), and ν_A ≤ ν_B2/Λ for A < B2, so |g⁻¹(k_B1, V)| ≥ ν_B2 (c − m Ē²/Λ),
using |j_B2| ≥ 1 and Σ|j_A| ≤ m. Further |V| ≤ Σ_(A ≤ B2) |j_A| ν_A Ē ≤ m ν_B2 Ē, so |g⁻¹(V, V)| ≤ m² Ē² ν_B2² ≤ m² Ē²
ν_B1 ν_B2/Λ. With |j_B1| ≥ 1, |g⁻¹(𝔎, 𝔎)| ≥ 2 ν_B1 ν_B2 (c − m Ē²/Λ) − m² Ē² ν_B1 ν_B2/Λ, which is
(52.9). ∎

With c = c0 (2π/n)², Λ is of order n², as in the choice a_A = c n² a_(A−1) of [HL25, Lemma 4.16, p. 18]. The phases ν_A
u_A are eikonals, so the two-scale scheme is unchanged; the wave of family A carries the amplitude λ F_A/ν_A, so that its
derivatives are of the size of F_A ((52.11)).

**Remark 52.16** (Numerical observation.) On the orbit space of Tangherlini with μ = 1 and
labels in [−0.6, 0.6], the Schur formula of Lemma 52.13 agreed with shooting to 1.1 × 10⁻⁹, ∂_α β was at
least 0.798, and the least mixed symbol of adjacent labels divided by (Δα)² was 0.2923, 0.2926, 0.2927, 0.2927 at n = 8,
16, 32, 64. For the four labels 2πA/4 on flat 2+1 with the hierarchy, every Q_j with |j|₁ ≤ 5 satisfied
exactly |Q_j|/(ν_B1 ν_B2) ≥ 359/216. No proof uses these values.

### 52.5 Torus-polarised waves and the orbit space

A wave of a non-radial family cannot be the wave W_TT of Section 2.6, which is adapted to radial phases. We take
it on the torus.

**Definition 52.17** (Torus-polarised waves.) Let u be an invariant phase and ξ1, ξ2 invariant
functions. The *torus wave* of amplitudes (ξ1, ξ2) changes a class metric (52.1) by

    ψ_i ↦ ψ_i0 + λ ξ_i cos θ,      θ := u/λ,      g3 unchanged,

so that (g5)_(φiφi) = e^(2ψ_i0) e^(2λ ξ_i cos θ). It is *torus-polarised* if ξ2 = −ξ1 =: −ξ: it oscillates only in
ψ2 − ψ1, so that ψ is unchanged and ω ↦ ω − λ ξ cos θ.

**Lemma 52.18** (Torus waves in the field equations.) In the setting of Definition 52.17 put
Ξ := ξ1 + ξ2, ψ0 := ψ10 + ψ20 and E_i := −R_(ii)/(g5)_(φiφi). In the two-scale expansion in λ:

(a) the coefficient of λ⁻¹ in Ric(g5)_(ab) is Ξ cos θ ∂_a u ∂_b u, and Ric(g5)_(aφi) = Ric(g5)_(φ1φ2) = 0;

(b) the coefficient of λ⁻¹ in E_i is −ξ_i |du|² cos θ;

(c) the coefficient of sin θ in the part of order λ⁰ of E_i is −(2⟨dξ_i, du⟩ + ξ_i(□3 u + ⟨du, dψ0⟩) + Ξ ⟨dψ_i0, du⟩);

(d) the terms of order λ⁰ quadratic in the oscillation have mean −½(ξ1² + ξ2²) du ⊗ du in Ric(g5)_(ab), and, for u
null, mean zero in E_i.

Hence, for u null and ξ2 = −ξ1, the whole part of order λ⁻¹ of Ric(g5) vanishes with g3 unperturbed. If the
coefficients (c) vanish for i = 1, 2, as the vacuum equations at order λ⁰ require, their sum is the homogeneous
transport

    2 ℓ(Ξ) + Ξ (□5 u + ℓ(ψ0)) = 0,      ℓ := g3⁻¹du,    (52.10)

so Ξ = 0 on Σ_τ0 gives Ξ = 0 along every generator that reaches Σ_τ0: the torus polarisation is kept. The torus-polarised
wave of amplitude ξ contributes the mean ξ² du ⊗ du to the mean metric's Ricci tensor, so it realises every density
F² = ξ².

*Proof.* By Lemma 2.1, with A = ψ1 and B = ψ2,

    Ric(g5)_(ab) = Ric[g3]_(ab) − Σ_i (∇_a∇_b ψ_i + ∂_a ψ_i ∂_b ψ_i),      E_1 = □3 ψ1 + |dψ1|² + ⟨dψ1, dψ2⟩,

E_2 likewise, and the mixed components vanish. With the two-scale derivative, ∂_a ψ_i = ∂_a ψ_i0 + λ ∂_a ξ_i cos θ −
ξ_i sin θ ∂_a u. (a) Only ∇_a∇_b ψ_i has a term of order λ⁻¹, the fast derivative of −ξ_i sin θ ∂_a u, which is
−λ⁻¹ ξ_i cos θ ∂_a u ∂_b u; so the coefficient is (ξ1 + ξ2) cos θ ∂_a u ∂_b u. (b) In □3 ψ_i the same term traced is
−λ⁻¹ ξ_i cos θ |du|², and |dψ_i|², ⟨dψ1, dψ2⟩ are of order one. (c) In □3 ψ1 the terms of order λ⁰ in sin θ are
∇^a(λ ∂_a ξ1 cos θ) ⊃ −sin θ ⟨dξ1, du⟩ and ∇^a(−ξ1 sin θ ∂_a u) ⊃ −sin θ (⟨dξ1, du⟩ + ξ1 □3 u). In |dψ1|² they are
−2 ξ1 sin θ ⟨dψ10, du⟩, and in ⟨dψ1, dψ2⟩ they are −sin θ (ξ2 ⟨dψ10, du⟩ + ξ1 ⟨dψ20, du⟩). The sum is
−sin θ (2⟨dξ1, du⟩ + ξ1(□3 u + ⟨du, dψ0⟩) + Ξ ⟨dψ10, du⟩); E_2 is the same with the indices exchanged. (d) The fast
parts of ∂_a ψ_i ∂_b ψ_i are ξ_i² sin²θ ∂_a u ∂_b u, of mean ½ ξ_i² ∂_a u ∂_b u; in E_i the quadratic fast terms are
multiples of |du|². For the consequences: with u null and Ξ = 0, (a) and (b) vanish. Summing (c) over i gives
−(2 ℓ(Ξ) + Ξ(□3 u + 2 ℓ(ψ0))), and □3 u + ℓ(ψ0) = □5 u up to O(λ) by (52.2), which is
(52.10); a linear homogeneous transport along ℓ keeps zero data. For ξ1 = −ξ2 = ξ the mean in (d) is
−ξ² du ⊗ du, and the vacuum equation at order λ⁰, averaged, gives Ric of the mean metric equal to ξ² du ⊗ du. The other
terms of order λ⁰ are linear in an oscillating profile or are θ-derivatives, so they have mean zero. ∎

The quadratic term of (d) has, besides its mean, a second harmonic in θ, which no term of order λ² can remove (its
symbol vanishes on harmonics of the null phase u alone, Lemma 50.14); as for the waves of
Theorem 50.2 ((50.18)), it is removed by a gauge term of order λ along du ⊗ du, transported along the
generator. In the two-scale scheme the wave is the linear part of the torus-polarised wave plus that term.

**Definition 52.19** (The wave of a dust.) Let g0 be a class metric, u an invariant eikonal of g0 with ℓ :=
g0⁻¹du future directed, F ≥ 0 an invariant amplitude transported by (52.5) (with u in place of u_α),
and ν > 0 a frequency; put ξ := F/ν and k := ν du. The *wave* of the dust (u, F) at frequency ν is the profile in
(X, θ)

    W := 2 ξ cos θ (e^(2ψ1) dφ1² − e^(2ψ2) dφ2²) + χ k ⊗ k,      χ := ½ c sin 2θ,    (52.11)

where c solves ν (ℓ(c) + ½ (□5 u) c) = ξ² along the generators, with c = 0 on Σ_τ0. Its first term is the part of
order λ of the torus-polarised wave of amplitude ξ at the phase θ = ν u/λ; its second, χ k ⊗ k, is its *gauge part*,
which vanishes on Σ_τ0 with all its θ-derivatives.

**Lemma 52.20** (The wave of a dust at order λ⁰.) In the setting of Definition 52.19, W(ℓ, ·) = 0 and
tr_(g0) W = 0, and in the two-scale expansion of R[g0 + λ W] at the phase θ = ν u/λ (the reduced Ricci tensor relative to
g0, computed with ∂_a + λ⁻¹ ν ∂_a u ∂_θ), R^(−1) = 0 and

    R^(0) = Ric(g0) − F² du ⊗ du.    (52.12)

*Proof.* The first term of W has torus components only and ℓ is an orbit vector, and (k ⊗ k)(ℓ, ·) = ν² g0⁻¹(du, du)
du = 0; tr_(g0) W = 2 ξ cos θ (e^(−2ψ1) e^(2ψ1) − e^(−2ψ2) e^(2ψ2)) + χ g0⁻¹(k, k) = 0. The proof of
Lemma 4.4 uses of the background only that the phase is null and has gradient ℓ, and of the wave only
W(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr W = 0 (as in the proof of Lemma 50.13 (b)); applied with v replaced by ν u, dv by k
and ℓ by ν ℓ, it gives R^(−1) = 0 and

    R^(0) = Ric(g0) − ν ∇_ℓ ∂_θ W − ½ ν (□5 u) ∂_θ W − ¼ |∂_θ W|² k ⊗ k.

For the Killing field K_i := ∂_(φi), the Christoffel symbols of Lemma 2.1 give ∇_ℓ K_i = ∇_(K_i) ℓ = ℓ(ψi)
K_i (ℓ is invariant, so it commutes with K_i), hence ∇_ℓ K_i♭ = ℓ(ψi) K_i♭, and e^(2ψi) dφi² = e^(−2ψi) K_i♭ ⊗ K_i♭ has
∇_ℓ (e^(2ψi) dφi²) = (−2 ℓ(ψi) + 2 ℓ(ψi)) e^(−2ψi) K_i♭ ⊗ K_i♭ = 0. Also ∇_ℓ du = ½ d(g0⁻¹(du, du)) = 0. With T0 :=
e^(2ψ1) dφ1² − e^(2ψ2) dφ2², ∂_θ W = −2 ξ sin θ T0 + c cos 2θ k ⊗ k, so

    ν ∇_ℓ ∂_θ W + ½ ν (□5 u) ∂_θ W = −2 ν sin θ (ℓ(ξ) + ½ (□5 u) ξ) T0 + ν (ℓ(c) + ½ (□5 u) c) cos 2θ k ⊗ k
                                   = ξ² cos 2θ k ⊗ k,

the first term vanishing because ξ = F/ν is transported by (52.5), and the second by the choice of c.
Further |∂_θ W|² = 4 ξ² sin²θ |T0|² = 8 ξ² sin²θ, since |T0|² = e^(−4ψ1) e^(4ψ1) + e^(−4ψ2) e^(4ψ2) = 2, T0 and k ⊗ k
are orthogonal (T0(ν ℓ, ν ℓ) = 0) and |k ⊗ k|² = g0⁻¹(k, k)² = 0. So R^(0) = Ric(g0) − ξ² (cos 2θ + 2 sin²θ) k ⊗ k =
Ric(g0) − ξ² ν² du ⊗ du = Ric(g0) − F² du ⊗ du. ∎

The constraints on Σ_τ0 need the same cancellation, now for a phase that is not radial on a slice that is not round. On
Σ_τ0 write the data of a class metric as (γ, κ), the induced metric and the second fundamental form, and let Φ(γ, κ) :=
(ρ, J), ρ := R(γ) − |κ|² + (tr κ)², J := 2(−div κ + d tr κ), be the constraint map ((7.2)). Let the
data oscillate as

    γ = γ0 + λ W(x, θ) + O(λ²),      κ = κ0 + κ1(x, θ) + O(λ),      θ = u/λ,      p := d(u|Σ_τ0) ≠ 0,

with profiles 2π-periodic in θ, where O(λ²) and O(λ) stand for λ² and λ times profiles. Write W″ := ∂_θ² W and κ1′ :=
∂_θ κ1, raise indices and take contractions with γ0, and put ⟨h, p ⊗ W″p⟩ := h^(ij) p_i W″_(jk) p^k.

**Lemma 52.21** (The constraints' coefficient of order λ⁻¹.) (a) For slow h and k, the
coefficient of λ⁻¹ in the linearisation DΦ(γ, κ)[h, k] is

    dρ⁽⁻¹⁾ = −2 ⟨h, p ⊗ W″p⟩ + h(p, p) tr W″ + |p|² ⟨h, W″⟩,
    dJ_i⁽⁻¹⁾ = 2 (h^(jl) p_l κ1′_(ji) − p_i h^(jl) κ1′_(jl)).    (52.13)

It is linear in (W, κ1) and does not involve k. With n families present at once, γ = γ0 + λ Σ_A W_A(x, θ_A) + λ²(…)
and κ = κ0 + Σ_A κ1_A(x, θ_A) + λ(…), the coefficient of λ⁻¹ is the sum over A of (52.13)
for (W_A, κ1_A, p_A), and the second and mixed harmonics of order λ² in γ, of order λ in κ, enter at order λ⁰.

(b) For torus-polarised waves, W_A = 2 ξ_A cos θ_A (e^(2ψ10) dφ1² − e^(2ψ20) dφ2²) and κ1_A = z_A sin θ_A (e^(2ψ10)
dφ1² − e^(2ψ20) dφ2²), the part of order λ⁻¹ of Φ(γ + h, κ + k) vanishes for every slow h without torus components and
every slow k. In particular the corrections of Lemma 7.5, which change γ by multiples of dr ⊗ dr,
meet no coefficient of order λ⁻¹. More precisely, the terms of Φ(γ + h, κ + k) that carry a second derivative of a
λ W_A or a first derivative of a κ1_A, which are those of order λ⁻¹, are, at every point and for every h without torus
components and every k, slow or not, −λ⁻¹ Σ_A |p_A|² tr W_A″ in ρ and 2 λ⁻¹ Σ_A p_A tr κ1_A′ in J, |p_A|² taken with
the inverse of γ + h and the traces in the torus block of γ, which h does not change; these traces are O(λ), so the
terms are of order one.

(c) For a wave with an orbit part, W = cos θ (ζ q̂ ⊗ q̂ + W_T) with q̂ the γ0-unit covector of the orbit slice orthogonal
