covector of every family is within C_k n^(−k) in C¹ of the continuum's du_(α_A) on its tube 𝒰_A of int S_(α_A)
(written 𝒯_A in Proposition 52.31). Fix compact sets S′ and S″, with sections invariant under T² and both
reflections, with supp q ∩ (Σ_τ0 × S¹) ⊂ int S″, S″ ⊂ int S′ and S′ ⊂ int S (the points at distance at least ρ′,
respectively 2ρ′, from the complement of int S, for the distance of the chart and that of S¹, which G preserves, with ρ′
small, will do). Fix an odd n ≥ n0, enlarged if necessary, and check the setting of Section 52.8 for g^(n), with
S_A := S″_(α_A) and F_A := q_A^(1/2), and (i)–(iv). The tube 𝒱_A of S″_(α_A) for u_A is a compact subset of 𝒰_A, which
is relatively open in Ω, so u_A is an eikonal near 𝒱_A; it is extended to a smooth invariant function on Ω by a cut-off
equal to 1 near 𝒱_A and vanishing off 𝒰_A. F_A is transported, and vanishes off the tube of supp F_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ⊂ int
S″_(α_A), by Proposition 52.31 and (iii) below. Rays are compared as follows: the ray of u_A for g^(n) and that
of u_(α_A) for g from a point of S_(α_A) are null geodesics whose metrics differ by C_k n^(−k) in C¹ and whose initial
covectors, the future roots over the same spatial covector, differ by C_k n^(−k); so they stay within C n^(−k) of each
other while both are in Ω, and as both leave Ω transversally through its lateral boundary, every point of one in Ω is
within C n^(−k) of a point of the other in Ω. In particular 𝒱_A lies within C n^(−k) of D_(α_A)(S″) ⊂ D_(α_A)(S).

(i) (Ω) is a finite set of strict inequalities on the compact Ω̄, continuous in g in C¹, so it holds for g^(n) for n
large.

(ii′) Let y be a point where the supports of the families A and B of g^(n) overlap. By the comparison of rays, y is
within C n^(−k) of a point of D_(α_A)(S″), where u_(α_A) is an eikonal of g on a neighbourhood of uniform size by (V1);
so the ray of u_(α_A) for g through y, followed to the past, stays in Ω and meets Σ_τ0 within C n^(−k) of S″_(α_A), and
for n large y ∈ D_(α_A)(S′); likewise y ∈ D_(α_B)(S′). By Lemma 52.13 with S′, the modulus of the mixed
symbol g⁻¹(du_(α_A), du_(α_B))(y) is at least c0 (2π/n)², so |g^(n)⁻¹(du_A, du_B)(y)| ≥ c0 (2π/n)² − C_k n^(−k) ≥
½ c0 (2π/n)² for n large (k = 3). So c := ½ c0 (2π/n)², and Λ = Λ(n) is chosen as in (ii′).

(iii) The wave of each label is the wave W_A of Definition 52.19 of the dust (u_A, F_A) of g^(n) at frequency ν_A,
F_A² = q_A the density (F_A smooth, being transported by (52.5) from the smooth data (2π/n)^(1/2)
F(·, α_A)).

(iv) Every 𝒱_A lies within C n^(−k) of D_(α_A)(S), at distance at least 2δ from the axes by (V2), hence at distance at
least δ for n large.

(V3) holds for g^(n), being an open condition on the slice data (Lemma 52.38), which are within C_k n^(−k) of
those of g. So Theorem 52.33, Theorem 52.34 and Theorem 52.36 give vacuum metrics
g^(n)_λ on Ω, λ ≤ λ0(n), invariant under T² and both reflections (by uniqueness, the data being invariant), with

    |g^(n)_λ − g^(n)| ≤ C(n) λ,      ∂g^(n)_λ − ∂g^(n) = Σ_A ν_A du_A ⊗ [∂_(θ_A) W_A] + O(C(n) λ),

W_A the wave of family A at its phase θ_A = ν_A u_A/λ, of zero mean in θ_A, with |ν_A ∂_(θ_A) W_A| ≤ C(F_A + F_A²),
C independent of n and A. Indeed the torus part of ν_A ∂_(θ_A) W_A is −2 F_A sin θ_A T0, and its gauge part is
ν_A³ c_A cos 2θ_A du_A ⊗ du_A, where, by Definition 52.19, ℓ_A(ν_A³ c_A) + ½ (□5 u_A) ν_A³ c_A = F_A² with zero data;
since F_A² is transported along the same generator, F_A²(s′) = F_A²(s) exp(∫_(s′)^s □5 u_A), the solution is at most
C F_A² at each point, C depending only on bounds for □5 u_A and for the length of the generators in Ω, which are uniform
in n and A.

*The diagonal.* Fix a sequence (η_j) of smooth tensor fields with compact support in the interior of Ω, dense in L²(Ω).
For each odd n ≥ n0 choose λ_n ≤ λ0(n) such that:

1. C(n) λ_n ≤ 1/n;
2. |∫_Ω η_j · (∂g^(n)_(λ_n) − ∂g^(n))| ≤ 1/n for j ≤ n. This is possible since each harmonic's integral is O(λ) at fixed
   n, by non-stationary phase: du_A ≠ 0 on the support, so e^(i k ν_A u_A/λ) = (λ/(i k ν_A |du_A|²_E)) du_A·∂ e^(i k ν_A
   u_A/λ) with the Euclidean norm of the chart, and one integration by parts gains λ;
3. ‖Σ_A ν_A du_A ⊗ [∂_(θ_A) W_A]‖²_(L²) ≤ Σ_A ‖ν_A du_A ⊗ [∂_(θ_A) W_A]‖²_(L²) + 1. The cross terms of distinct families
   have the phases ν_A u_A ± ν_B u_B, with d(ν_A u_A ± ν_B u_B) ≠ 0, since du_A, du_B are null and not parallel on the
   overlaps by (ii′); they tend to zero as λ → 0 at fixed n, by non-stationary phase.

The diagonal terms are at most C Σ_A ∫ |du_A|²_E (F_A² + F_A⁴), and F_A² = (2π/n) q(·, α_A) + O(n^(−k)) on the tubes by
Proposition 52.31; so they are at most C Σ_A (2π/n) ∫ q(·, α_A) |du_(α_A)|²_E + C/n + O(n^(1−k)), and the sum is
a label quadrature of ∫∫ q |du_α|²_E dα, bounded independently of n by Lemma 52.29. Put g_i :=
g^(n_i)_(λ_(n_i)) along the odd n_i → ∞. Then:

- |g_i − g| ≤ |g^(n_i)_(λ_(n_i)) − g^(n_i)| + |g^(n_i) − g| ≤ 1/n_i + C_k n_i^(−k) → 0 uniformly on Ω;
- ‖∂g_i‖_(L²) ≤ ‖∂g^(n_i)‖_(L²) + (Σ_A ‖ν_A du_A ⊗ [∂_(θ_A) W_A]‖²_(L²) + 1)^(1/2) + 1, bounded independently of i;
- for each j and n_i ≥ j, |∫ η_j · (∂g_i − ∂g)| ≤ 1/n_i + |∫ η_j · (∂g^(n_i) − ∂g)| ≤ 1/n_i + C_k n_i^(−k) ‖η_j‖_(L¹),
  which tends to zero.

A sequence bounded in L² that converges against a dense set converges weakly: ∂g_i ⇀ ∂g in L²(Ω). Each g_i is vacuum,
smooth and invariant under T² and both reflections. ∎

The high-frequency step is not uniform in n: λ0(n), M(n) and C(n) depend on n, as the constants c^n n^n of
[HL25, p. 5, footnote 5] do. Only the background step is uniform (Proposition 52.31), which is what the diagonal
needs. No smallness threshold enters: the theorem is a large-data statement, its smallness at each n being λ alone.

### 52.10 Openness, stability and an explicit family

**Lemma 52.38** (The hypotheses are open.) Let (g, F, u) satisfy (Ω) and (V3), and let S ⊂ (Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω) × S¹
be compact (points and labels), each S_α invariant under T² and both reflections, with supp q ∩ (Σ_τ0 × S¹) ⊂ int S.
Suppose that on S and its tubes: u is an eikonal in each label, with ℓ_α future directed, on a neighbourhood in Ω × S¹
of 𝒟(S); the Jacobian of (V1) is at least J0 on the tubes D_α(S); ∂_α β0 ≥ b_* on S, and β0(x, ·) is injective on S_x;
and dist(D_α(S), axes) ≥ 2δ. Then there is a neighbourhood 𝒰 of (g, u|Σ_τ0, ∂u|Σ_τ0) in C² × C¹ with the following
property. Let (g′, F′, u′) be a solution whose metric on Ω and data lie in 𝒰, with supp q′ ∩ (Σ_τ0 × S¹) ⊂ int S, and
let u″_α be the eikonal of g′ with the data u′_α|Σ_τ0 and the future branch, on the points of Ω on its rays from a
neighbourhood of S_α. It is defined and smooth in (x, α) on a neighbourhood in Ω × S¹ of the set 𝒟′(S) of the (x, α)
with x in the tube D′_α(S) of S_α for u″_α, and it agrees with u′_α, with all derivatives, where q′(·, α) > 0. So
replacing u′ by χ u″ + (1 − χ) u′, χ a smooth invariant cut-off on Ω × S¹ equal to 1 near 𝒟′(S) and vanishing off the
domain of u″, changes neither T_V nor (52.5) (which holds where q′ > 0, hence on its closure, and
trivially elsewhere), and after this replacement (g′, F′, u′) satisfies (V1) on S with the margins J0/2 and b_*/2, and
(V2) with δ/2 in place of δ, that is dist(D′_α(S), axes) ≥ δ. (Ω) and (V3) are open in C² × C¹.

*Proof.* The tubes are the images of S under the flows of the rays of u″, which are null geodesics of g′ with initial
covectors given by ∂u′|Σ_τ0, the τ-component being the future root. The rays and their first variation (whose
determinant is the Jacobian) solve ordinary differential equations whose coefficients are the Christoffel symbols of g′
and their first derivatives, so by continuous dependence on coefficients and data they depend continuously on (g′, u′) in
C² × C¹, uniformly on the compact S × [τ0, τ_end]; β0 and ∂_α β0 depend continuously on u′|Σ_τ0 in C¹. The Jacobian, the
margin b_* and the distance to the axes are infima over compact sets of continuous positive functions, so on a
neighbourhood they hold halved, also on a fixed neighbourhood of S. Where the Jacobian is positive the rays from a
neighbourhood of S_α foliate a neighbourhood of D′_α(S), uniformly in α, so the eikonal u″_α of g′ with the data
u′_α|Σ_τ0 exists there (the method of characteristics), and it is smooth in (x, α), the rays depending smoothly on their
initial points and on α; this is why the margins are asked on S and not only on supp q, the tube of supp q′ lying inside
that of S. The label form's u′_α is an eikonal of g′ near the tube of supp q′(·, α) ∩ Σ_τ0 with the same data and
branch. So the ray of u′_α from a point x0 of that set is the null geodesic of g′ from x0 with the covector du′_α(x0) =
du″_α(x0), also the ray of u″_α from x0; along it both functions are constant, with the value u′_α(x0). Hence u′_α =
u″_α on that tube, which contains the open set where q′(·, α) > 0, and there all derivatives agree. Injectivity is
kept: if α_k ≠ α′_k in S_(x_k) had β0′_k(x_k, α_k) = β0′_k(x_k, α′_k) for perturbations tending to zero, a limit point
would give, by injectivity of β0(x, ·), α = α′, and then for k large α_k and α′_k lie in an interval on which
∂_α β0′_k ≥ b_*/2 > 0, a contradiction. (Ω) consists of strict inequalities between contractions of g⁻¹, continuous
in C⁰, and of the statement on generators, which holds for the tubes by their definition; (V3) consists of strict
inequalities between functions of the slice data and their first derivatives. ∎

**Proposition 52.39** (Cauchy stability of the restricted system off the axes.) Let (g̊, F̊, ů) be a
smooth class Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov solution on Ω in label form satisfying (Ω), (V1), (V2) and (V3), with
the compact set S of (V1); F̊ may vanish identically. Fix m ≥ 6. There are ε0 > 0, ε2 ∈ (0, ε1], ε1 the number of
Definition 51.7 (c) for g̊, and C such that every smooth datum D in label form near (g̊, F̊, ů), as defined
before Proposition 52.31, with d(D) ≤ ε0, has a smooth class development (g, F, u) on Ω, invariant under T² and
both reflections: a solution of the Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov system in label form with Ric^H(g) = T_V, the
gauge of Section 51.4 relative to g̊, with ‖g − g̊‖_(H^(m+1)) ≤ C d(D) on every Σ_τ, and with each u_α the
eikonal of g with the data u_D(·, α) on a neighbourhood in Ω × S¹ of the (x, α) with x in its tube D_α(S). Its metric
and field are unique: every such solution (g′, F′, u′) whose metric is within ε2 of g̊ in C² and whose data are those of
D has g′ = g and F′ = F, and u′_α = u_α on the tube of supp q(·, α) ∩ Σ_τ0, for every α. No smallness of the reference
is assumed.

*Proof.* *Existence.* For n ≥ n0 let g^(n) be the development of the n-dust datum D_n of D given by
Proposition 52.31, with (g̊, F̊, ů) as reference and k = 2: it exists on Ω and ‖g^(n) − g̊‖_(H^(m′+1)) ≤ C_(m′)
(d(D) + n⁻²) on every Σ_τ, for every m′ ≥ m and n ≥ n0(m′), with C_(m′) independent of n. The energy (51.17)
contains the τ-derivatives, so by Sobolev's inequality on the slices (Lemma 5.1, with λ = 1) the g^(n) are bounded
in C^j(Ω̄) for every j, uniformly in n, and by the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem and a diagonal argument a subsequence converges
in C^j(Ω̄) for every j to a smooth metric g, invariant under T² and both reflections, with ‖g − g̊‖_(H^(m+1)) ≤ C d(D) on
every Σ_τ. For α ∈ S¹ let u^(n)_α be the eikonal of g^(n) with the data u_D(·, α) (the future root), which exists on a
neighbourhood in Ω × S¹ of the (x, α) with x in its tube D^(n)_α(S) by the proof of Lemma 52.38, g^(n) being
C²-close to g̊ and u_D C¹-close to ů on Σ_τ0, and F^(n)_α the solution of (52.5) for g^(n) with the
data F_D(·, α), along the rays of u^(n)_α, vanishing off the tube of supp F_D(·, α); they are smooth in (x, α), with
derivatives bounded uniformly in n, the rays depending smoothly on g^(n) and on the data. For α = α_A, u^(n)_α agrees
on the tube 𝒯_A of int S_(α_A) with the eikonal u_A of the family A of g^(n), by the argument of the proof of
Lemma 52.38: both are eikonals of g^(n) there with the same data and the future branch, so they have the same
rays from int S_(α_A), along which both are constant. The density q_A, supported in 𝒯_A, solves
div(q_A g^(n)⁻¹du_A) = 0, that is ℓ_A(q_A) + (□5 u_A) q_A = 0 on 𝒯_A, ℓ_A := g^(n)⁻¹du_A, by (52.3): the
transport that (F^(n)_(α_A))² also solves there, by (52.5), along the same rays, with the data
F_D(·, α_A)², respectively (2π/n) F_D(·, α_A)² for q_A, both vanishing off the tube of supp F_D(·, α_A); so
q_A = (2π/n) (F^(n)_(α_A))². So, with h^(n)(x, α) := F^(n)_α(x)² du^(n)_α ⊗ du^(n)_α (zero off the tubes),
Ric(g^(n)) = (2π/n) Σ_A h^(n)(·, α_A). Along the subsequence the null geodesic flows of g^(n) converge with their
derivatives to that of g, so u^(n)_α → u_α and F^(n)_α → F_α in C¹, uniformly in α, where u_α is the eikonal of g with
the data u_D(·, α) on a neighbourhood of the (x, α) with x ∈ D_α(S), extended smoothly to Ω × S¹ by a cut-off as in
Lemma 52.38, and F_α solves (52.5) along its rays with the data F_D(·, α); and h^(n) →
h := F_α² du_α ⊗ du_α uniformly. The Riemann sum error is |(2π/n) Σ_A h^(n)(x, α_A) − ∫ h^(n)(x, α) dα| ≤ Σ_A
∫_(arc A) |h^(n)(x, α_A) − h^(n)(x, α)| dα ≤ 2π (2π/n) sup |∂_α h^(n)| → 0, the arc A being the set of α with
α_A − 2π/n ≤ α ≤ α_A. Hence Ric(g), the limit of Ric(g^(n)), is ∫_(S¹) h dα = T_V: (g, F, u) solves the
Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov system in label form, F_α vanishing off the tube of supp F_D(·, α), on which u_α is
an eikonal. The g^(n) solve Ric^H(g^(n)) = T^(n) in the gauge relative to g̊ (Lemma 52.30), so g does
in the limit, and its data are those of D, since the metric data of D_n differ from those of D by at most C n⁻²
(Proposition 52.28).

*Uniqueness.* Let (g_i, F_i, u_i), i = 1, 2, be two such solutions, q^i := F_i², and η := ε2 + ε0. By
Lemma 52.38, for η small, the eikonal û^i_α of g_i with the data u_D(·, α) and the future branch exists, smooth
in (x, α), on a neighbourhood of the (x, α) with x in its tube D^i_α(S), whose distance to the axes is at least δ, and
it agrees with u^i_α, with all derivatives, where q^i(·, α) > 0; q^i(·, α) is transported along its rays and vanishes
off the tube of supp F_D(·, α). So T^i_V = ∫ q^i(·, α) dû^i_α ⊗ dû^i_α dα, and we use û^i in place of u^i.

Fix a compact S′ with supp F_D ⊂ int S′ and S′ ⊂ int S, and put 𝒱_α := D^1_α(S′), the tube of S′_α for û^1_α. For η
small, 𝒱_α ⊂ D^2_α(S), and supp q^1(·, α) ∪ supp q^2(·, α) ⊂ 𝒱_α, for every α. Indeed, extend g_1, g_2 to a
neighbourhood of Ω, C²-close to an extension of g̊, and let y^i_τ and ẙ_τ map a point x0 near S_α to the point where the
null geodesic of g_i, respectively g̊, with the future covector over d(u_D(·, α)|Σ_τ0)(x0), respectively over
d(ů_α|Σ_τ0)(x0), meets Σ_τ, in the coordinates (r, ϑ) of the orbit slices. By the continuous dependence of the proof of
Lemma 52.38, ‖y^i_τ − ẙ_τ‖_(C¹) ≤ C η, uniformly in (α, τ), and by (V1) Dẙ_τ is invertible with |Dẙ_τ⁻¹| ≤ L
and is uniformly continuous. Let y ∈ 𝒱_α ∩ Σ_τ, y = y^1_τ(x0), x0 ∈ S′_α. Fix d > 0 such that the closed d-neighbourhood
of S′_α in the orbit slice lies in S_α and |Dẙ_τ(x) − Dẙ_τ(x0)| ≤ 1/(4L) for |x − x0| ≤ d. For η small, |Dy^2_τ(x) −
Dẙ_τ(x0)| ≤ 1/(2L) there, so the inverse function theorem gives y^2_τ(B(x0, d)) ⊃ B(y^2_τ(x0), d/(2L)), which contains
y once 2Cη < d/(2L). So y lies on the ray of û^2_α from a point of S_α, and that ray stays in Ω up to y, since a future
causal curve that leaves Ω through its lateral boundary does not return (Definition 51.7 (b)): y ∈ D^2_α(S).
The same argument with the solutions exchanged, and supp F_D(·, α) ⊂ int S′_α in place of S′_α ⊂ int S_α, gives
supp q^2(·, α) lies in the tube of supp F_D(·, α) for û^2_α, inside 𝒱_α; and supp q^1(·, α) lies in that for û^1_α,
inside 𝒱_α.

So both û^i_α are eikonals near 𝒱_α. On 𝒱_α put p^i := dû^i_α, P^i := g_i⁻¹p^i, Θ^i := □_(g_i) û^i_α and q^i_α :=
q^i(·, α), with differences δp_α, δΘ_α, δq_α, and let w := g_1 − g_2. On 𝒱_α, ∇_(P^i) p^i = 0 for g_i, the Raychaudhuri
equation (51.3) holds with Ric(g_i)(P^i, P^i) = ∫ q^i_β g_i⁻¹(p^i, dû^i_β)² dβ, in which dû^i_β
enters only on supp q^i_β ⊂ 𝒱_β, and P^i(q^i_α) = −Θ^i q^i_α. Subtracting, along P^1 on 𝒱_α,

    P^1(δp_(α,a)) = P^(1,b) (Γ[g_1] − Γ[g_2])^c_(ba) p^1_c + Γ[g_2]^c_(ba) (P^(1,b) p^1_c − P^(2,b) p^2_c)
                    − (P^1 − P^2)^b ∂_b p^2_a,
    P^1(δΘ_α) = S^1 − S^2 − (P^1 − P^2)(Θ^2),      P^1(δq_α) = −δΘ_α q^1_α − Θ^2 δq_α − (P^1 − P^2)(q^2_α),

S^i the right side of (51.3) for g_i. Pointwise, |P^1 − P^2| ≤ C (|w| + |δp_α|); the terms of
S^1 − S^2 other than the Ricci terms are at most C (|w| + |∂w| + |δp_α| + |δΘ_α|), 𝒱_α lying at distance at least δ
from the axes; and the Ricci terms differ by at most C (|w| + |δp_α|) + C ∫ (|δq_β| + 𝟙_(𝒱_β) |δp_β|) dβ. The
constants are uniform in α, the fields being smooth in (x, α). The metrics solve Ric^H(g_i) = T^i_V, so, as in Step 4 of
the proof of Theorem 51.18, −½ g_1^(ab) ∂_a∂_b w is the sum of terms at most C (|w| + |∂w|) and of
T^1_V − T^2_V = ∫ (δq_α p^1 ⊗ p^1 + q^2_α (δp_α ⊗ p^1 + p^2 ⊗ δp_α)) dα, whose integrand vanishes off 𝒱_α, so that its
L² norm on Σ_τ is at most C (∫ (‖δp_α‖² + ‖δq_α‖²)_(L²(𝒱_α ∩ Σ_τ)) dα)^(1/2) by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality on S¹.
Put

    𝒩̃(τ) := ‖∂w‖ + ‖w‖ + (∫_(S¹) (‖δp_α‖² + ‖δΘ_α‖² + ‖δq_α‖²)_(L²(𝒱_α ∩ Σ_τ)) dα)^(1/2).

The energy inequality Lemma 5.5 for w, with g̊ in place of g0, and for each α the argument of
Lemma 51.10 on 𝒱_α, along the future null P^1 — no flux through the part of the boundary of 𝒱_α ruled by its
integral curves, and a nonnegative flux through the lateral boundary of Ω — with the Minkowski inequality in α, give
𝒩̃(τ) ≤ C (𝒩̃(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^τ 𝒩̃). The two solutions have the same Cauchy data, completed by the gauge condition as in
the definition of D, so w = ∂w = 0 on Σ_τ0; and δp_α = δΘ_α = δq_α = 0 there, the p^i being the same roots over the
same spatial covectors, their τ-derivatives fixed by the geodesic equation, and q^i_α = F_D(·, α)². So 𝒩̃(τ0) = 0 and,
by Gronwall's lemma, 𝒩̃ ≡ 0: g_1 = g_2, and on 𝒱_α, q^1_α = q^2_α and dû^1_α = dû^2_α, so û^1_α = û^2_α, both being
constant along the common rays from S′_α with the values of u_D. As both q^i_α vanish off 𝒱_α, F_1 = F_2; and u^i_α =
û^i_α on the tube of supp F_D(·, α), the closure of the set where q^i(·, α) > 0. ∎

The explicit family is built on the orbit space of Tangherlini, where the eikonal equation separates. Let μ = 1, f :=
1 − 1/r², 𝔪 := 1/r², and let t := τ − κ(r) with κ′ = 𝔪/f be the static time on r > 1, so that g3 = −f dt² + f⁻¹dr² +
r² dϑ² there. For |α| < 0.7 put k(α) := 3 sin α and

    u_α := −t + k(α)(ϑ − π/4) + ∫_3^r f(s)⁻¹ (1 − f(s) k(α)²/s²)^(1/2) ds,      r > 1.    (52.29)

Since f/r² = (r² − 1)/r⁴ ≤ 1/4, with equality at r² = 2 only, and k² < 9 sin² 0.7 < 3.74 < 4, the square root is smooth
and positive on r > 1. We extend u to a smooth invariant function on Ω × S¹ that agrees with (52.29) on
{r ≥ 2} × [−0.65, 0.65]; only its values on a neighbourhood in Ω × S¹ of the (x, α) with x in the tubes of the set S
below, in r ≥ 2.64 and |α| ≤ 0.6, enter.

**Proposition 52.40** (The theorem is not vacuous.) Let g0 be Tangherlini of mass 1 in the chart of
Section 2.2 with μ ≡ 1, and Ω the domain with τ0 = 0, τ_end = 3, a = 4/5 and V = 5. Let F0 ≥ 0 be a smooth
function of (r, ϑ, α), not identically zero, supported in {|r − 3| ≤ 0.3, |ϑ − π/4| ≤ 0.15} × [−0.5, 0.5], and let the
labels be the eikonals (52.29). Then for every small ε > 0 the class Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov
solution with the field of amplitude ε F0 and labels u_α, its metric data those of g0 corrected by
Proposition 52.28 (λ = 1, no phases) to satisfy the constraints with the stress of the field, exists on Ω
and satisfies (Ω), (V1), (V2) and (V3). By Lemma 52.38, the solutions covered by Theorem 52.10 form a nonempty
open set.

*Proof.* *(Ω) and (V3) for g0.* With μ = 1 the contractions of Lemma 2.6 are g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − 1/r² < 0; at r = a,
g0⁻¹(dr, dr) = 1 − 25/16 = −9/16 < 0 and g0⁻¹(dr, dτ) = 25/16 > 0, so {r = a} is spacelike and r decreases along future
causal curves near it, as in the proof of Lemma 2.6 (b); g0⁻¹(d(v + τ), d(v + τ)) = −3 − 1/r² < 0, and v + τ
increases along future causal curves, as in Lemma 2.6 (c); and b(τ) = 9 − 2τ ≥ 3, so b(τ) − a ≥ 11/5. On Σ_0 the
data of g0 are γ = (1 + 1/r²) dr² + r² dΩ², and by Lemma 7.5 (a) the spheres have mean curvature
3/(r² + 1)^(1/2) > 0 and 𝒮 A0 = diag(6, 1/(r² + 1)) > 0. The statement of (Ω) on generators holds for the tubes by their
definition.

*The rays.* Put w := (1 − f k²/r²)^(1/2). Then −u_t²/f + f u_r² + u_ϑ²/r² = −1/f + (1 − f k²/r²)/f + k²/r² = 0, so u_α is
an eikonal for |α| < 0.7, and ℓ_α = g3⁻¹du_α has the components (1/f, w, k/r²) in (t, r, ϑ), future directed on r > 1.
Its rays solve
dt/ds = 1/f, dr/ds = w, dϑ/ds = k/r², and with dτ/dt = 1 + κ′ dr/dt = 1 + 𝔪 w,

    dr/dτ = ṙ(r) := f w/(1 + 𝔪 w),      dϑ/dτ = ϑ̇(r) := f k/(r² (1 + 𝔪 w)),

functions of r alone at fixed α. Let S̃ := {|r − 3| ≤ 0.36, |ϑ − π/4| ≤ 0.18} and S := S̃ × [−0.6, 0.6], so that supp
F0 ⊂ int S; S̃, defined by r and ϑ, is a union of orbits, so every S_α is invariant under T² and both reflections.
For |α| ≤ 0.6, |k| ≤ 3 sin 0.6 < 1.7, and for r ≥ 2.64, f k²/r² ≤ 2.89/6.9696 < 0.42, so w > 0.76, f > 0.856 and
𝔪 < 0.1435, and ṙ ≥ f w/(1 + 𝔪) > 0.56. ṙ is increasing in r on r² > 2: f increases, 𝔪 decreases, and f
k²/r² = k²(r² − 1)/r⁴ has derivative 2k²(2 − r²)/r⁵ < 0, so w increases and ṙ = f/(w⁻¹ + 𝔪) has an increasing numerator
and a decreasing positive denominator. On the rays from S̃, r ≥ 2.64 and r increases, and |ϑ̇| ≤ |k|/r² < 1.7/r².

*(V1).* In the coordinates (r, ϑ) the flow map from Σ_0 to Σ_τ is (r0, ϑ0) ↦ (R(τ; r0), ϑ0 + ∫_0^τ ϑ̇(R(s; r0)) ds),
with dR/dτ = ṙ(R), R(0; r0) = r0. Its Jacobian is ∂R/∂r0 = ṙ(R(τ; r0))/ṙ(r0), since both sides solve y′ = ṙ′(R) y with
y(0) = 1; as R ≥ r0 and ṙ increases, it is at least 1 =: J0. On Σ_0, t = −κ(r), so d(u_α|Σ_0) = (κ′ + ϕ′) dr + k dϑ
with κ′ + ϕ′ = (𝔪 + w)/f, ϕ the integral in (52.29). In the coframe ((1 + 𝔪)^(1/2) dr, r dϑ), orthonormal
for the orbit part (1 + 𝔪) dr² + r² dϑ² of γ, its angle β0 from the outward radial direction satisfies tan β0 =
𝔗(r, k) := k f (1 + 𝔪)^(1/2)/(r (𝔪 + w)). Since ∂_k w = −f k/(r² w),

    ∂_k 𝔗 = (f (1 + 𝔪)^(1/2)/r) ((𝔪 + w) + f k²/(r² w))/(𝔪 + w)² ≥ f/(r (1 + 𝔪)) = (r² − 1)/(r (r² + 1)),

which decreases on r² > 2 + √5 and is > 0.249 on [2.64, 3.36]. There |𝔗| ≤ 1.7 · 1.0694/(2.64 · 0.8485) < 0.82, since
𝔪 > 0.0885 there, so cos²β0 = (1 + 𝔗²)⁻¹ > 0.59; and dk/dα = 3 cos α ≥ 3 cos 0.6 > 2.47. Hence ∂_α β0 = cos²β0 ∂_k 𝔗
dk/dα > 0.59 · 0.249 · 2.47 > 0.36 =: b_* on S, and β0(x, ·) is increasing, so injective: the field is labelled by
initial direction. The tubes of S lie in r ≥ 2.64, so u is an eikonal in each label, with ℓ_α future directed, on the
neighbourhood ({r > 2} × (−0.65, 0.65)) ∩ (Ω × S¹) of 𝒟(S).

*(V2).* A ray from S̃ is in Ω only while r ≤ b(τ) = 9 − 2τ, and r ≥ 2.64 + 0.56 τ on it, so only for τ ≤ 6.36/2.56 <
2.49. Over that time |ϑ − ϑ0| ≤ ∫_0^2.49 1.7 (2.64 + 0.56 s)⁻² ds = (1.7/0.56)(1/2.64 − 1/4.0344) < 0.3975. So on the
tubes of S, ϑ ∈ [0.2078, π/2 − 0.2078], since π/4 − 0.18 − 0.3975 > 0.2078, and r ≥ 2.64; so ρ1 = r cos ϑ and ρ2 =
r sin ϑ are at least 2.64 sin 0.2078 > 0.54 > 0.53 =: 2δ.

*The solutions.* The reference (g0, 0, u), with the zero field and the labels u_α, is a smooth class solution in label
form satisfying (Ω), (V1) on S with J0 = 1 and b_* = 0.36, (V2) with 2δ = 0.53, and (V3), by the preceding steps. The
datum D_ε has the field ε F0, the labels u_α|Σ_0 with the future roots, and the metric data of g0 on Σ_0 corrected to
satisfy the constraints with the stress of the field: 𝔉(U) := 𝒞(γ_U, κ_U) − 𝒯_ε(·, α), 𝒯_ε the constraint stress of ∫ ε²
F0(·, α)² du_α ⊗ du_α dα, has the structure of Lemma 52.25 with λ = 1 and no phases, the signs by (V3) and
Lemma 52.26, and sup_r ‖𝔉(0)‖_(20) ≤ C ε², since the data of g0 satisfy the vacuum constraints; so
Proposition 52.28 with k = 20 gives a smooth invariant correction U with ‖U‖_(𝒴_20) ≤ C ε², which at
λ = 1 bounds U in C⁹. Indeed, by the induction in the data step of the proof of Proposition 52.31 with 2m = 20,
U is bounded in H^20(S³) and ∂_r^i U in H^(21−2i)(S³), 1 ≤ i ≤ 10, uniformly in r, and H^s(S³) ⊂ C^l(S³) for
s > l + 3/2; as 20 > 9 + 3/2 and 21 − 2i > (9 − i) + 3/2 for i ≤ 9, every ∂_r^i ∂_ω^l U with i + l ≤ 9 is bounded, and
the Cartesian derivatives of order at most 9 are combinations of these with bounded coefficients (r ≥ a > 0). So
d(D_ε) ≤ C ε, and Proposition 52.39 around (g0, 0,
u), with m = 6, gives for ε small the solution on Ω, with ‖g − g0‖_(H^7) ≤ C ε on every Σ_τ, hence, by Sobolev's
inequality on the slices and the equations for the τ-derivatives, C²-close to g0, and with eikonals C¹-close to u_α. By
Lemma 52.38, whose eikonals u″ are those of the solution, it satisfies (V1) with the margins J0/2 = 1/2 and
b_*/2 = 0.18 and (V2) with dist(D_α(S), axes) ≥ 0.265, and (Ω), (V3) by openness. ∎

**Remark 52.41** (Numerical observation.) For the family with data u_α = cos α ρ(r) + 3 sin α ϑ on
Σ_0, ρ′ = (1 + 1/r²)^(1/2), outgoing labels α ∈ [−0.5, 0.5] and ingoing labels α ∈ [π − 0.15, π + 0.15] (inside the
horizon when they leave Ω), and the density on the same ball, the margins were measured on a 9 × 9 grid of rays over the
ball enlarged by 20 %, with 81 labels per interval: J0 = 1.0000 and 0.8978, δ = 0.157 and 0.098, b_* = 0.909. A family
focused at distance 1 ahead had a Jacobian changing sign (least value −0.071); a wider ingoing interval [π − 0.5, π +
0.5] reached an axis inside the horizon, as Proposition 52.9 predicts, so (V2) is a real restriction; with
mass 1.02 and directions tilted by 0.02 sin 2ϑ, the margins were J0 = 1.0000 and 0.8471, δ = 0.152 and 0.072. No proof
uses these values.

### 52.11 Radial dusts reaching the axes

Theorem 52.10 keeps every label at distance at least 2δ from the axes, and by Lemma 52.8 at most two of
the dusts present at an axis point are separated, one on each null line. The background of Theorem 50.2 carries
such a pair, an ingoing and an outgoing radial dust, present at the axes. This section adds a small restricted field to
it. The pair is indexed by 𝔨 ∈ {in, out}, as in Chapter 50; its phases are written ϕ_𝔨 and its amplitudes F_𝔨, as
F_A is the amplitude of family A (F_𝔨 is not the phase derivative that Chapter 50 writes so). The labels are
localised as in Lemma 52.30 and Section 52.8; the pair is not, and its phases are eikonals on the
whole domain. Four things change. First, the waves of the pair cannot be torus-polarised. Near axis 2, e^(2ψ2) dφ2² is
a_⊥ times the form (x3 dx4 − x4 dx3)²/ρ2² (Proposition 51.21 (a)), which equals dx4² at the points (ρ2, 0) and dx3² at
the points (0, ρ2) of the (x3, x4)-plane and so has no limit at ρ2 = 0; a torus-polarised wave whose amplitude does not
vanish at the axis is not continuous there. The waves of the pair are polarised instead by tensors parallel along their
generators, smooth across the axes (Lemma 52.43). Second, such a wave has an orbit part, and it leaves no
term of order λ⁻¹ in the constraints because its phase is radial on Σ_τ0 and it is tangent to the spheres there
(Lemma 52.44); the data of the pair are chosen so. Third, the commutator of the wave operator with
a generator that reaches an axis has smooth coefficients there, because the planar shear of Proposition 51.21 vanishes
to second order at the axis (Lemma 52.45, Lemma 52.46). Fourth, the background is
constructed on the adapted domain of Corollary 51.32, uniformly in the number of dusts
(Proposition 52.49), and the high-frequency step runs on a domain of the type (2.8) inside it
(Proposition 52.47).

**Definition 52.42** (Waves with a parallel polarisation.) Let g0 be a class metric and u an
invariant eikonal of g0, both smooth across the axes, with ℓ := g0⁻¹du future directed, and let F, ν, ξ := F/ν, k := ν du
and c be as in Definition 52.19, except that F may take either sign (the proof of Lemma 52.20 uses no sign of
F). A *parallel polarisation* of u is a smooth G-invariant symmetric 2-tensor field 𝒵 on a neighbourhood of supp F with

    ∇_ℓ 𝒵 = 0,      𝒵(ℓ, ·) = 0,      tr_(g0) 𝒵 = 0,      |𝒵|²_(g0) = 2.

The *wave* of the dust (u, F) with the polarisation 𝒵 at frequency ν is the profile

    W := 2 ξ cos θ 𝒵 + χ k ⊗ k,      χ := ½ c sin 2θ,      θ := ν u/λ.

F vanishes on every generator on which it vanishes on Σ_τ0, and so does c, so W is smooth where g0 and u are. Off the
axes T0 := e^(2ψ1) dφ1² − e^(2ψ2) dφ2² is a parallel polarisation (proof of Lemma 52.20), and the wave with
𝒵 = T0 is that of Definition 52.19.

**Lemma 52.43** (Parallel polarisations.) Let Ω be a domain of the type (2.8), g0 a smooth
class metric on Ω and u a smooth invariant eikonal of g0 on Ω, with du ≠ 0 and ℓ := g0⁻¹du future directed, such that
every ray of u through a point of Ω, followed to the past, stays in Ω and meets Σ_τ0.

(a) Let 𝒵0 be a smooth G-invariant field on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω of symmetric bilinear forms on the tangent spaces of the
spacetime, with 𝒵0(ℓ, ·) = 0, tr_(g0) 𝒵0 = 0 and |𝒵0|²_(g0) = 2. Its parallel transport along the rays of u is a
parallel polarisation 𝒵 of u on Ω, smooth on Ω, the axes included, equal to 𝒵0 on Σ_τ0.

(b) The wave W of Definition 52.42 satisfies W(ℓ, ·) = 0 and tr_(g0) W = 0, and in the two-scale expansion of
R[g0 + λ W] at the phase θ = ν u/λ, R^(−1) = 0 and R^(0) = Ric(g0) − F² du ⊗ du.

(c) Put 𝔷 := (ρ1² − ρ2²)/r², let 𝔥(y) := sin(πy/3)/y, an entire function with 𝔥(0) = π/3, put P_⊥ := |dx|² −
(x̂·dx)², and

    𝒳 := −(2/√3) cos(π𝔷/3) P_⊥ + 4 𝔥(1 + 𝔷) (x1 dx2 − x2 dx1)²/r²
          + 4 𝔥(1 − 𝔷) (x3 dx4 − x4 dx3)²/r²      on R × (R⁴ ∖ {0}).    (52.30)

Let 𝕊_r := {τ0} × {|x| = r}, Π the metric g0 induces on 𝕊_r, 𝔭 the g0-orthogonal projection of the tangent spaces of
the spacetime at points of 𝕊_r onto T𝕊_r, and 𝒳̊ the Π-trace-free part of the restriction of 𝒳 to T𝕊_r. If u|Σ_τ0 is a
function of r and |𝒳̊|_Π > 0 on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω, then 𝒵0 := √2 |𝒳̊|_Π⁻¹ 𝒳̊(𝔭 ·, 𝔭 ·) satisfies the hypotheses of (a), and it
vanishes on every vector g0-orthogonal to the spheres 𝕊_r. If g0 is invariant under O(4) with area radius |x|, as the
backgrounds of Theorem 50.2 are in their chart, then 𝒵0 = 𝒳, and |𝒳̊|_Π ≥ 1 for every metric close enough to g0
in C⁰ on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω.

*Proof.* (a) Since ∇_ℓ ℓ = ½ d g0⁻¹(du, du) = 0, the rays are null geodesics. A null vector is never tangent to a
spacelike slice, so ℓ(τ) ≠ 0, and Z := ℓ/ℓ(τ) has τ as parameter along its integral curves. Let Φ(x0, t) be the point at
time τ0 + t of the integral curve of Z from x0 ∈ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω, defined while the curve stays in Ω. Φ is smooth, injective
(integral curves do not cross) and has invertible differential (Z is transverse to Σ_τ0), so it is a diffeomorphism onto
its image, which is Ω by hypothesis. Along t ↦ Φ(x0, t) let 𝒵 solve the linear system ∇_Z 𝒵 = 0, that is
d𝒵_ab/dt = Z^c (Γ^d_ca 𝒵_db + Γ^d_cb 𝒵_ad), with 𝒵 = 𝒵0(x0) at t = 0. Its coefficients are smooth in (x0, t), so 𝒵 is
smooth in (x0, t), hence on Ω, and ∇_ℓ 𝒵 = ℓ(τ) ∇_Z 𝒵 = 0. The covector 𝒵(ℓ, ·) satisfies
∇_ℓ (𝒵(ℓ, ·)) = (∇_ℓ 𝒵)(ℓ, ·) + 𝒵(∇_ℓ ℓ, ·) = 0 and vanishes on Σ_τ0, so it vanishes; ℓ(tr 𝒵) = tr ∇_ℓ 𝒵 = 0 and
ℓ(|𝒵|²) = 2 ⟨∇_ℓ 𝒵, 𝒵⟩ = 0, so tr 𝒵 = 0 and |𝒵|² = 2. An element of G is an isometry of g0 that fixes u, hence ℓ, and
maps Σ_τ0 to itself; it maps rays to rays and parallel fields along them to parallel fields, so 𝒵 is G-invariant, 𝒵0
being so, by uniqueness for the system. Nothing here refers to the orbit space: g0, u and 𝒵0 are smooth in the chart X,
the axes included, and so is 𝒵.

(b) The proof of Lemma 52.20 uses of T0 only ∇_ℓ T0 = 0, T0(ℓ, ·) = 0, tr T0 = 0, |T0|² = 2 and ⟨T0, k ⊗ k⟩ =
ν² T0(ℓ, ℓ) = 0. These hold for 𝒵, and that proof applies with 𝒵 in place of T0.

(c) Off the axes let e1 := (−x2, x1, 0, 0)/ρ1, e2 := (0, 0, −x4, x3)/ρ2, and e_ϑ the Euclidean unit vector tangent to
{|x| = r} in the plane spanned by (x1, x2, 0, 0) and (0, 0, x3, x4): a Euclidean orthonormal frame of the tangent space
of {|x| = r}. P_⊥ is the identity on that space and vanishes on x̂; x1 dx2 − x2 dx1 takes the value ρ1 on e1 and vanishes
on e_ϑ, e2 and x̂; and x3 dx4 − x4 dx3 takes the value ρ2 on e2 and vanishes on e_ϑ, e1 and x̂. With ρ1²/r² = (1 + 𝔷)/2
and ρ2²/r² = (1 − 𝔷)/2, 𝒳(x̂, ·) = 0 and 𝒳 is diagonal in the frame, with the entries

    𝔢_ϑ = −(2/√3) cos(π𝔷/3),      𝔢_1 = 𝔢_ϑ + 2 sin(π(1 + 𝔷)/3),      𝔢_2 = 𝔢_ϑ + 2 sin(π(1 − 𝔷)/3).

Since 2 sin(π/3 ± π𝔷/3) = √3 c_𝔷 ± s_𝔷 with c_𝔷 := cos(π𝔷/3) and s_𝔷 := sin(π𝔷/3), these are 𝔢_ϑ = −(2/√3) c_𝔷,
𝔢_1 = (1/√3) c_𝔷 + s_𝔷 and 𝔢_2 = (1/√3) c_𝔷 − s_𝔷. So 𝔢_ϑ + 𝔢_1 + 𝔢_2 = 0 and 𝔢_ϑ² + 𝔢_1² + 𝔢_2² = (4/3 + 1/3 +
1/3) c_𝔷² + 2 s_𝔷² = 2: 𝒳 restricted to the tangent space of {|x| = r} is trace-free for the Euclidean metric, with
Euclidean norm √2, off the axes and, by continuity, on them. 𝒳 is smooth on R × (R⁴ ∖ {0}), since 𝔷, P_⊥ and the forms
(x1 dx2 − x2 dx1)²/r² and (x3 dx4 − x4 dx3)²/r² are and 𝔥 is entire; it has no dτ component; and it is G-invariant,
since the rotations of each plane preserve 𝔷, P_⊥, x1 dx2 − x2 dx1 and x3 dx4 − x4 dx3, and the reflections x2 ↦ −x2
and x4 ↦ −x4 change the sign of one of these 1-forms only.

T𝕊_r = ker dτ ∩ ker dr is spacelike for g0, so 𝔭 and Π are smooth and G-equivariant, and so are 𝒳̊ and 𝒵0, the latter
where |𝒳̊|_Π > 0. By construction 𝒵0 vanishes on the kernel of 𝔭, the g0-orthogonal complement of T𝕊_r. Since u|Σ_τ0 is a
function of r, du vanishes on T𝕊_r, so ℓ lies in that complement and 𝒵0(ℓ, ·) = 0. The g0-trace and the g0-norm of a form
that vanishes on that complement, which is a Lorentzian plane, are its Π-trace and Π-norm on T𝕊_r, so tr_(g0) 𝒵0 = 0
and |𝒵0|² = 2. If g0 is invariant under O(4) with area radius |x|, Π is the Euclidean metric of {|x| = r}, so 𝒳̊ = 𝒳 on
T𝕊_r and |𝒳̊|_Π = √2; and the g0-orthogonal complement of T𝕊_r is span(∂_τ, x̂·∂_x), because the isotropy group of a
point of 𝕊_r acts irreducibly on T𝕊_r and trivially on that span, so that g0(∂_τ, ·) and g0(x̂·∂_x, ·) are invariant
linear forms on T𝕊_r, hence zero; 𝒳 vanishes on that span, so 𝒵0 = 𝒳. The last claim follows by continuity on the compact
set Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω. ∎

The waves of the pair are therefore smooth tensors of the spacetime, with no reference to the orbit space. At axis 2
(𝔷 = 1) the template has the entries (𝔢_ϑ, 𝔢_1, 𝔢_2) = (−1, 2, −1)/√3, equal on e_ϑ and e2 as smoothness at that axis
requires; at axis 1 (𝔷 = −1) they are (−1, −1, 2)/√3. On a round slice its orbit part is 𝔢_ϑ q̂ ⊗ q̂, q̂ the unit
covector of the orbit slice orthogonal to dr, and 𝔢_ϑ ≤ −1/√3 everywhere, the axes included, since cos(π𝔷/3) ≥ ½
where the absolute value of 𝔷 is at most 1: the wave is not torus-polarised at any point, and what removes its term of
order λ⁻¹ in the constraints, which Lemma 52.21 (c) exhibits for a non-radial phase, is that
its phase is radial on Σ_τ0 (Lemma 52.44).

**Lemma 52.44** (Waves tangent to the spheres in the constraints.) Let the data on Σ :=
Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω oscillate as in Lemma 52.21, with families A and γ = γ0 + λ (γ1 + Σ_A W_A) + λ²(…), γ1
slow and G-invariant, κ = κ0 + Σ_A κ1_A + λ(…), the second and mixed harmonics entering at order λ² in γ and λ in κ, γ0
and every profile G-invariant, θ_A = φ_A/λ for the phase φ_A of family A on Σ, and p_A := dφ_A. Put 𝔯 := γ0⁻¹dr. Let each
family be either torus-polarised, as in Lemma 52.21 (b), or *tangent to the spheres*: p_A is a
multiple of dr on Σ, W_A and κ1_A vanish on 𝔯, and tr_(γ0) W_A = tr_(γ0) κ1_A = 0. Then:

(a) for every function α with 1 + α γ0^(rr) > 0 and every k, the terms of Φ(γ + α dr ⊗ dr, κ + k) that carry a second
derivative of some λ W_A or a first derivative of some κ1_A are of order one: λ⁻¹ times λ times a function of the form
[h] of Section 52.6, smooth in α. So the constraint map has no coefficient of order λ⁻¹, and the corrections
of Lemma 7.5 meet none;

(b) the conclusion of Lemma 52.22 holds: p, P, A0, A^B and 𝒮 are of class 𝔓, with parts of order λ⁰
those of (γ0, κ0).

*Proof.* (a) By the proof of Lemma 52.21 (a), these terms are, at order λ⁻¹,

    Σ_A (W_A″(γ_h⁻¹p_A, γ_h⁻¹p_A) − |p_A|²_(γ_h) tr_(γ_h) W_A″)   in ρ,
    2 Σ_A (−κ1_A′(γ_h⁻¹p_A, ·) + p_A tr_(γ_h) κ1_A′)                 in J,

with γ_h := γ + α dr ⊗ dr, W_A″ := ∂²_(θ_A) W_A and κ1_A′ := ∂_(θ_A) κ1_A; every coefficient is a smooth function of x,
the phases, λ and α. The forms γ0, W_B, κ1_B and the profiles are G-invariant, so they have no mixed orbit–torus
components, and neither has γ_h⁻¹; it maps orbit covectors to orbit vectors. For a torus-polarised family, W_A″ and
κ1_A′ vanish on orbit vectors, so the terms with γ_h⁻¹p_A vanish, and the traces are O(λ), as in the proof of
Lemma 52.21 (b). For a family tangent to the spheres, note first that every W_B vanishes on 𝔯:
a torus-polarised one because 𝔯 is an orbit vector, the others by hypothesis. Hence γ_h(𝔯, ·) = (1 + α γ0^(rr)) dr +
O(λ), and γ_h⁻¹dr = (1 + α γ0^(rr))⁻¹ 𝔯 + O(λ); as p_A is a multiple of dr, W_A″(γ_h⁻¹p_A, ·) and κ1_A′(γ_h⁻¹p_A, ·) are
O(λ). Further, with 𝔊 := γ0 + α dr ⊗ dr, 𝔊⁻¹ = γ0⁻¹ − α (1 + α γ0^(rr))⁻¹ 𝔯 ⊗ 𝔯 and γ_h⁻¹ = 𝔊⁻¹ + O(λ), so tr_(γ_h)
W_A″ = tr_(γ0) W_A″ − α (1 + α γ0^(rr))⁻¹ W_A″(𝔯, 𝔯) + O(λ) = O(λ), and likewise tr_(γ_h) κ1_A′ = O(λ). In every case the
coefficient of λ⁻¹ is a smooth function of (x, θ, λ, α) that vanishes at λ = 0, hence λ times such a function, by
Taylor's formula in λ: the term is of order one and of the form [h]. The corrections of Lemma 7.5
change γ by α dr ⊗ dr and κ by terms that enter no term of order λ⁻¹.

(b) The coefficients of the angular second derivatives of α in ρ, those of the first derivatives of (ϖ, q) in J, and 𝒮
involve γ, its inverse, Π and α undifferentiated, so they are of class 𝔓, as in the proof of
Lemma 52.22. That proof writes (γ^(rr))^(3/2) H with H = H̃/ν and H̃ = ½ tr_Π(∂_r Π − 𝓛_σ Π), σ the
shift and ν the lapse of the foliation of Σ by the spheres, σ^B = Π^(BA) γ(∂_r, ∂_A). A derivative costing λ⁻¹ falls on
a term of order λ only in three places. (1) ∂_r of λ W_A in Π gives ∂_r φ_A ∂_(θ_A) W_A restricted to the spheres. (2)
The angular derivatives of λ W_A in σ^C ∂_C Π give σ0^C ∂_C φ_A ∂_(θ_A) W_A restricted to the spheres, σ0 the shift of
γ0. Traced with Π^(AB) = Π0^(AB) + O(λ), (1) and (2) give (∂_r φ_A − σ0^C ∂_C φ_A) ∂_(θ_A) of the Π0-trace of the
restriction of W_A to the spheres, plus O(λ); and that trace is tr_(γ0) W_A = 0 for both kinds, the γ0-trace of a form
that vanishes on 𝔯, the γ0-normal of the spheres, being its Π0-trace. (3) The angular derivatives of the oscillating part
of σ, in 𝓛_σ Π. The part of order λ of σ is Π0⁻¹ applied to (γ1 + Σ_A W_A)(∂_r − σ0, ·) restricted to the spheres, and
∂_r − σ0, being γ0-orthogonal to the spheres, is a multiple of 𝔯, on which every W_A vanishes; so σ has no oscillating
part of order λ (and λ times a profile in θ_A would have angular derivatives O(λ) in any case, the fast one carrying the
factor ∂_C φ_A = 0, since φ_A is a function of r on Σ). The second and mixed harmonics are of order λ² and contribute
O(λ). So H̃ is H̃0 plus λ times a function of the form [h], and, α entering only through ν_U² = ν² + α and γ_U⁻¹,
algebraically, the same holds as functions of α. ∎

**Lemma 52.45** (Invariant functions at an axis.) Near a point of axis 2 with ρ1 > 0 write the chart
as (x′, y), y := (x3, x4), x′ := (τ, x1, x2).

(a) If e(x′, t) is smooth and even in t, then e(x′, |y|) is smooth.

(b) Let f be smooth off the axis near the point and invariant under the rotations of the y-plane, and let f(x′, (t, 0)),
t ≠ 0, extend to a smooth function e(x′, t). Then f extends to a smooth function, f(x′, y) = e(x′, |y|).

(c) Let g be a smooth class metric and u a smooth invariant eikonal of g near the point, with du ≠ 0. Then a_⊥ :=
g(K2, K2)/ρ2², κ2, Θ_h := □_g u − κ1 − κ2 and σ2/ρ2² extend to smooth invariant functions near the point, a_⊥ > 0, and
ρ2² dψ2 extends to a smooth covector field. Here κ_i := g⁻¹(du, dψ_i) are the torus curvatures of
Proposition 51.5 (not the parts κ1_A of a second fundamental form), and σ2 := Θ_h − κ2 is the planar shear of
Proposition 51.21 (not the shift of the spheres).

Near axis 1 the same holds with the two planes exchanged, with σ1 := Θ_h − κ1.

*Proof.* (a) Let 𝔄 be the set of finite sums of functions p(y) e′(x′, |y|), with p a polynomial and e′ smooth and even
in its last variable. Each member of 𝔄 is continuous, on the axis too. For e′ smooth and even, ∂_t e′ is odd, so
∂_t e′(x′, t) = t e″(x′, t) with e″(x′, t) := ∫_0^1 ∂_t² e′(x′, s t) ds, smooth and even. Off the axis,
∂_(x′) (p e′(x′, |y|)) = p (∂_(x′) e′)(x′, |y|) and ∂_(y_i)(p e′(x′, |y|)) = (∂_i p) e′(x′, |y|) + p y_i e″(x′, |y|);
so the first derivatives off the axis of a member of 𝔄 are members of 𝔄. Let f ∈ 𝔄, let z0 be a point of the axis and
L the value at z0 of the continuous extension of the gradient of f. For z near z0 off the axis, the segment from z0 to z
meets the axis only at z0, so

    f(z) − f(z0) − L·(z − z0) = ∫_0^1 (∇f(z0 + s (z − z0)) − L)·(z − z0) ds,

which is at most |z − z0| times the supremum of |∇f − L| off the axis in the ball of radius |z − z0| about z0, hence
o(|z − z0|); by continuity of f the same bound holds for z on the axis. So f is differentiable on the axis with gradient
L, hence C¹, with first derivatives in 𝔄; by induction f is smooth, and e(x′, |y|) ∈ 𝔄.

(b) For y ≠ 0 a rotation maps y to (|y|, 0), so f(x′, y) = e(x′, |y|); the rotation by π gives e(x′, −t) = e(x′, t) for
t ≠ 0, hence for all t, so e is even, and (a) applies.

(c) At the points (x′, (t, 0)), K2 = t ∂_4, so a_⊥ = g(∂_4, ∂_4) there, smooth in (x′, t); by (b) a_⊥ extends smoothly,
and it is positive (Proposition 51.21). Off the axis ψ2 = ½ log a_⊥ + log ρ2, so ρ2² dψ2 = ½ ρ2² da_⊥/a_⊥ + ½ d(ρ2²),
smooth, and κ2 = g⁻¹(du, dψ2) = ½ g⁻¹(du, da_⊥)/a_⊥ + g⁻¹(du, d(ρ2²))/(2ρ2²). At (x′, (t, 0)), d(ρ2²) = 2t dx3, so the
last term is h(x′, t)/t with h := g⁻¹(du, dx3). The rotation by π of the y-plane is an isometry fixing u and changing
the sign of dx3, so h(x′, ·) is odd and h/t = ∫_0^1 ∂_t h(x′, s t) ds is smooth. So κ2 restricted to these points
extends smoothly, and by (b) κ2 extends smoothly. κ1 and □_g u are smooth near the point (g(K1, K1) > 0 there), and so
is Θ_h. Then σ2 is smooth and invariant, its restriction e_σ(x′, t) is even in t, and e_σ(x′, 0) = 0 because σ2 extends
by 0 to the axis (Proposition 51.21 (d)). By Taylor's formula e_σ(x′, t) = t² E_σ(x′, t) with E_σ(x′, t) := ∫_0^1
(1 − s) ∂_t² e_σ(x′, s t) ds, smooth and even, as ∂_t e_σ(x′, 0) = 0. By (a), σ2/ρ2² = E_σ(x′, ρ2) extends smoothly. ∎

**Lemma 52.46** (The commutator up to the axes.) Let g5 be a smooth class metric and u a smooth
invariant eikonal of g5 on a G-invariant open set of {r > 0}, the axes allowed, with du ≠ 0 and ℓ := g5⁻¹du future
directed; put L := ℓ·∂ and H := ∇²u, the Hessian (as in Lemma 52.23). Let 𝔫 be the future unit normal of
the slices, E := −g5(ℓ, 𝔫), ℓ̄ := E⁻¹ 𝔫 − (2E²)⁻¹ ℓ, Θ_h := □5 u − κ1 − κ2 and σ_i := Θ_h − κ_i off the axes, with κ_i
the torus curvatures of Lemma 52.45 (c), 𝔙 := g5⁻¹H(ℓ̄, ·) + H(ℓ̄, ℓ̄) ℓ, and 𝔜 := □5 ℓ +
g5⁻¹Ric(g5)(ℓ, ·), □5 ℓ the wave operator of g5 on the vector field ℓ. Then for every invariant function φ, with
∇φ := g5⁻¹dφ,

    [□5, L] φ = 2 Θ_h □5 φ + 𝔐(L φ) + 𝔑 φ,      𝔐 := 2 H(ℓ̄, ℓ̄) ℓ − 4 𝔙 + 4 Θ_h ℓ̄,
    𝔑 φ := 4 H(𝔙, ∇φ) − 4 Θ_h H(ℓ̄, ∇φ) − 2 Σ_i σ_i g5⁻¹(dψ_i, dφ) + 𝔜(φ),    (52.31)

and Θ_h and the coefficients of 𝔐 and 𝔑 extend smoothly to the whole set, the axes included. Off the axes this is
(52.16), with a = 2 Θ_h = 2 □3 u and 𝔐 = 2𝔐′ for the frame (ℓ, ℓ̄, e) used here. The same holds for
□̃ := g5^(ab) ∂_a∂_b in the chart X, with another 𝔑.

*Proof.* For any metric, [□, ℓ^μ ∇_μ] φ = 2 ⟨∇ℓ, ∇²φ⟩ + 𝔜(φ) (proof of Corollary 52.24), and ∇ℓ is H with an
index raised. E > 0, since ℓ ≠ 0 is null and future directed and 𝔫 is future timelike; and
g5(ℓ̄, ℓ̄) = −E⁻² − 2 E⁻¹ (2E²)⁻¹ g5(𝔫, ℓ) = 0 and g5(ℓ, ℓ̄) = E⁻¹ g5(ℓ, 𝔫) = −1, so ℓ̄ is null with g5(ℓ, ℓ̄) = −1. The
fields 𝔫 and ℓ, hence ℓ̄, are smooth, G-invariant and orthogonal to K1 and K2, as dτ(K_i) = du(K_i) = 0. Off the axes
let e be a unit vector orthogonal to ℓ, ℓ̄, K1 and K2, and e_i := e^(−ψ_i) K_i, so that g5⁻¹ = −ℓ ⊗ ℓ̄ − ℓ̄ ⊗ ℓ + e ⊗ e +
Σ_i e_i ⊗ e_i. By Proposition 51.5 (a) and (b), H(ℓ, ·) = 0, H vanishes on the pairs (e_i, e), (e_i, ℓ̄) and
(e1, e2), and H(e_i, e_i) = κ_i; tracing, □5 u = H(e, e) + κ1 + κ2, so H(e, e) = Θ_h. For a symmetric form S, expanding
both inverse metrics in ⟨H, S⟩,

    ⟨H, S⟩ = H(ℓ̄, ℓ̄) S(ℓ, ℓ) − 2 H(ℓ̄, e) S(ℓ, e) + Θ_h S(e, e) + Σ_i κ_i S(e_i, e_i),

and tr S = −2 S(ℓ, ℓ̄) + S(e, e) + Σ_i S(e_i, e_i). Eliminating S(e, e),

    ⟨H, S⟩ = Θ_h tr S + H(ℓ̄, ℓ̄) S(ℓ, ℓ) − 2 H(ℓ̄, e) S(ℓ, e) + 2 Θ_h S(ℓ, ℓ̄) − Σ_i σ_i S(e_i, e_i).

Take S := ∇²φ. Then tr S = □5 φ; S(ℓ, X) = X(Lφ) − (∇_X ℓ)(φ) = X(Lφ) − H(X, ∇φ); S(e_i, e_i) = g5⁻¹(dψ_i, dφ) by
Proposition 51.5 (a), whose proof uses of the function only its invariance; and H(ℓ̄, e) e = 𝔙, since
g5⁻¹H(ℓ̄, ·) = −H(ℓ̄, ℓ̄) ℓ + H(ℓ̄, e) e, the components along ℓ̄ and e_i vanishing. Inserting these, with H(ℓ, ∇φ) = 0,
gives (52.31) off the axes, and 2(H(ℓ̄, ℓ̄) ℓ − 2𝔙 + 2 Θ_h ℓ̄) is 2𝔐′ of the proof of
Corollary 52.24, whose H is Hess_(g3) u, equal to H on orbit vectors; and Θ_h = □5 u − ⟨du, dψ⟩ = □3 u by
(52.2).

Near a point of axis 2, Θ_h, σ2/ρ2² and ρ2² dψ2 extend smoothly by Lemma 52.45 (c), and κ1, ψ1 are
smooth (g5(K1, K1) > 0 there), so σ1 g5⁻¹(dψ1, dφ) and σ2 g5⁻¹(dψ2, dφ) = (σ2/ρ2²) g5⁻¹(ρ2² dψ2, dφ) are first-order
operators with smooth coefficients; near axis 1 exchange the planes. H(ℓ̄, ℓ̄), 𝔙, ℓ̄ and 𝔜 are smooth everywhere. For
smooth φ both sides of (52.31) are continuous, so the identity holds on the axes as well. For □̃,
□̃φ = □5 φ + H0·∂φ with H0^ρ := g5^(ab) Γ^ρ_ab smooth, and [L, H0·∂] is of first order with smooth coefficients. ∎

So the transport of Corollary 52.24 for Ψ := □̃φ, with ℓ·dφ = f and φ invariant, holds up to the axes with
coefficients that are bounded with all their derivatives on compact sets. On the O(4)-invariant two-dust background
σ_i = 0, the generators being shear-free, and a = 2 Θ_h = 2 L(R)/R is the coefficient of Lemma 50.11.

**Proposition 52.47** (The high-frequency step with a radial pair.) Let Ω be a domain of the type
(2.8), let g0, u_A, F_A and S_A (A = 1, …, n) be as in the setting of Section 52.8, with Ric(g0) =
Σ_A F_A² du_A ⊗ du_A + Σ_𝔨 F_𝔨² dϕ_𝔨 ⊗ dϕ_𝔨 in place of its equation, and let (ϕ_𝔨, F_𝔨), 𝔨 ∈ {in, out}, the *radial
pair*, be two further families: ϕ_𝔨 an eikonal of g0 on the whole of Ω with g0⁻¹dϕ_𝔨 future directed (after the sign
change of Definition 52.5 where needed), F_𝔨 smooth, of either sign, and transported by (52.5), and
S_𝔨 := Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω, so that 𝒱_𝔨 = Ω. Assume (i) for all n + 2 families; (ii′) for every pair among them, with the
frequencies of all n + 2 families in the hierarchy of (ii′); (iii) and (iv) for the n families; (V3) on Σ_τ0; and

- (iii′) the wave of family 𝔨 is the wave of Definition 52.42 at its frequency with a parallel polarisation
  𝒵_𝔨 that vanishes, on Σ_τ0, on every vector g0-orthogonal to the spheres {τ0} × {|x| = const};
- (vi) ϕ_𝔨|Σ_τ0 is a function of r with nonzero derivative on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω.

Then the conclusions of Theorem 52.33, Theorem 52.34 and Theorem 52.36 hold for the
n + 2 families. In particular, as in the proof of Theorem 52.10, for λ ≤ λ0 there is a smooth metric g_λ on Ω,
invariant under T² and both reflections, with Ric(g_λ) = 0, |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ and ∂g_λ − ∂g0 = Σ ν du ⊗ [∂_θ W] +
O(C λ), the sum over the n + 2 families with their phases, frequencies and waves; λ0 and C depend on n.

*Proof.* 𝒱_𝔨 = Ω because, by (i), a past causal curve from a point of Ω meets Σ_τ0 inside Ω, as in the proof of
Lemma 52.13; so (v) of Section 52.8 holds for the pair trivially, its transports being posed on the
whole of Ω. The proofs of the three theorems hold with n + 2 phases and these changes.

(0) *The kernel of the mollifier.* Take the kernel ρ of (5.3) radial, which (M1)–(M6) of Lemma 5.4
allow, since they hold for every ρ ∈ C_c^∞(B_1) with ρ ≥ 0 and ∫ ρ = 1. Then 𝒫 commutes with every R ∈ O(4) acting on
x: the shift map Φ of (5.3) is radial, Φ(Rx) = R Φ(x), so, substituting z = R⁻¹ z′ and using ρ(R⁻¹ z′) =
ρ(z′) and |det R| = 1,

    𝒫(f ∘ R)(x) = ∫ ρ(z) f(R Φ(x) − λ R z) dz = ∫ ρ(z′) f(Φ(Rx) − λ z′) dz′ = (𝒫 f)(Rx).

T² and both reflections act on x by elements of O(4) and fix τ, so 𝒫 commutes with them. In step (1) of the proof of
Theorem 52.34 the phase shifts solve the coupled linear transports ℓ_B·dφ_B = ½ 𝒫 s_B(w − Σ_C φ_C Y_C), with
zero data; the ℓ_B, the Y_C and w = g − g_app are invariant, the solution and the approximant being so, so the system
commutes with T² and both reflections, and by the uniqueness in Picard's theorem every φ_B is invariant, for the
labels and for the pair.

(1) *Stage 0.* By Lemma 52.43 (b), applied on 𝒱_𝔨 = Ω, R^(0)_𝔨 = Ric(g0) − F_𝔨² dϕ_𝔨 ⊗ dϕ_𝔨, with no
oscillating part, the gauge part removing the second harmonic of the quadratic term exactly as for the labels, the
norm |∂_θ W_𝔨|² being 8 ξ_𝔨² sin²θ by |𝒵_𝔨|² = 2. So stage 0 is that of the proof of Theorem 52.33, with
the equation of g0 above. The later stages use of the waves only that each depends on one phase, is annihilated by its
own generator and is trace-free, which holds by Lemma 52.43 (b).

(2) *The uniform estimate.* Step (3) of the proof of Theorem 52.34 uses of G2^B(ℓ_A, ℓ_A) only that it is a
bounded profile in θ_B alone, and of G1^B(ℓ_A, ℓ_A), the coefficient of Ψ_B there, only that it is bounded; for B = 𝔨 the
latter is [−2 ξ_𝔨 sin θ_𝔨 𝒵_𝔨(ℓ_A, ℓ_A) + c_𝔨 cos 2θ_𝔨 ν_𝔨² (dϕ_𝔨(ℓ_A))²]. For B = 𝔨 the former is [−2 ξ_𝔨 cos θ_𝔨
𝒵_𝔨(ℓ_A, ℓ_A) − 2 c_𝔨 sin 2θ_𝔨 ν_𝔨² (dϕ_𝔨(ℓ_A))²], at the phase of family 𝔨: such a profile, here with a polarisation
part besides the gauge part; and for A = 𝔨, G1^𝔨(ℓ_𝔨, ·) = G2^𝔨(ℓ_𝔨, ·) = 0 since W_𝔨(ℓ_𝔨, ·) = 0. In step (4) the
commutator of L_𝔨 is that of Lemma 52.46, which applies since φ_𝔨 is invariant by (0), and whose
coefficients are smooth on Ω, the axes included, hence bounded with all their derivatives on the compact Ω; this is the
only place where that proof uses (iv), and for the n families (iv) holds. Step (5) holds for every family by (i). The
second derivatives of the phase shift of family 𝔨 are handled as in (L6) of Lemma 50.20, the transport field
Z_𝔨 := ℓ_𝔨/ℓ_𝔨(τ) being smooth on Ω, the axes included.

(3) *The data.* In the proof of Theorem 52.36, the gauge parts and the phase corrections vanish on Σ_τ0, the
gauge parts with their θ-derivatives, so on Σ_τ0 family 𝔨 contributes λ W_𝔨 = 2 λ ξ_𝔨 cos θ_𝔨 𝒵_𝔨 to the metric and
its restriction to TΣ_τ0 to γ. Its part κ1_𝔨 of order one in κ is

    κ1_𝔨 = ½ ν_𝔨 dϕ_𝔨(𝔫0) ∂_(θ_𝔨) W_𝔨      on TΣ_τ0,

𝔫0 the future unit normal of Σ_τ0 for g0, κ being ½ 𝓛_𝔫 g on TΣ_τ0, 𝔫 the future unit normal for the metric g of the
approximant (with the opposite sign convention κ1_𝔨 changes sign, which changes nothing below). Indeed, in the chart,
for i and j tangent to Σ_τ0, (𝓛_𝔫 g)_ij = 𝔫^c ∂_c g_ij + g_cj ∂_i 𝔫^c + g_ic ∂_j 𝔫^c, and g = g0 + λ (m_1 + Σ_B W_B) +
λ²(…), m_1 the slow first mean of Theorem 52.33. In the first term the fast derivative of λ W_𝔨 gives ν_𝔨
dϕ_𝔨(𝔫0) ∂_(θ_𝔨) W_𝔨 at order one. In the others, 𝔫 = −(−g⁻¹(dτ, dτ))^(−1/2) g⁻¹dτ, with g⁻¹dτ = g0⁻¹dτ − λ g0⁻¹ (m_1 +
Σ_B W_B)(g0⁻¹dτ, ·) + λ²(…). Each profile W_B(g0⁻¹dτ, ·) vanishes on Σ_τ0 for every value of θ_B: for a label because its
torus part vanishes on the orbit vector g0⁻¹dτ, for the pair by (iii′), g0⁻¹dτ being g0-orthogonal to Σ_τ0, and for both
because the gauge part vanishes there. So its derivatives along Σ_τ0, slow and fast, vanish on Σ_τ0, and likewise for
W_B(g0⁻¹dτ, g0⁻¹dτ) in g⁻¹(dτ, dτ); the slow term λ m_1 and the terms of order λ² contribute O(λ) after one derivative.
Hence ∂_i 𝔫 = ∂_i 𝔫0 + O(λ) on Σ_τ0, and the oscillating part of order one of κ is Σ_B ½ ν_B dϕ_B(𝔫0) ∂_(θ_B) W_B on
TΣ_τ0, with ϕ_B := u_B for a label.

By (iii′), 𝒵_𝔨 vanishes on Σ_τ0 on 𝔫0 and on 𝔯 = γ0⁻¹dr, both g0-orthogonal to the spheres, so W_𝔨 and κ1_𝔨, restricted
to TΣ_τ0, vanish on 𝔯, and they are γ0-trace-free, the g0-trace of a form that vanishes on 𝔫0 being the γ0-trace of
its restriction to TΣ_τ0. By (vi), p_𝔨 = ν_𝔨 d(ϕ_𝔨|Σ_τ0) is a nonzero multiple of dr. So the radial pair is tangent to
the spheres in the sense of Lemma 52.44, the labels are torus-polarised, and that lemma replaces
Lemma 52.21 (b) and Lemma 52.22 in the structure step: f and g̃ are of class
𝔏, and p, P, A0, A^B and 𝒮 are of class 𝔓 with the parts of order λ⁰ of (γ0, κ0). The phases ν_𝔨 ϕ_𝔨|Σ_τ0 are smooth on
Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω, as the phases of Section 52.6 are. The stage data are those of Lemma 7.4 for each of the
n + 2 families, with the polarisation map of each, onto at every point of Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω, the axes included, by the argument
given there, its right inverse commuting with the symmetries. The correction, the r-derivatives and the datum are
unchanged. ∎

*The setting of the corollary.* Let g0 be the two-dust background of Theorem 50.2 on Ω₂, in the chart X of
Lemma 50.8, with the ingoing family (ϕ_in, q_in) := (v, 𝒜/R³) and the outgoing family
(ϕ_out, q_out) := (u, ℬ/R³), u the outgoing phase of Section 50.3 (below, u denotes the labels), and with
the amplitudes F_in := A env(v)/(√3 R^(3/2)) and F_out := A₂ env₂(ϕ_out)/(√3 R^(3/2)), smooth, with F_𝔨² = q_𝔨 (of either
sign, as env and env₂ are). They are transported by (52.5): ℓ_𝔨(ϕ_𝔨) = 0, ℓ_𝔨(R^(−3/2)) = −(3/2)
R^(−5/2) ℓ_𝔨(R), and □5 ϕ_𝔨 = 3 ℓ_𝔨(R)/R by the formula for □_(g0) in the proof of Lemma 50.11, so 2
ℓ_𝔨(F_𝔨) + (□5 ϕ_𝔨) F_𝔨 = 0. Assume that the outgoing packet does not reach the inner sphere, {u1 ≤ ϕ_out ≤ u2} ∩ Ω₂ ∩
{R = a} = ∅, and let η, S_in, S_out, the tubes 𝒯̊_in := {v_start − η ≤ v ≤ v_end + η} ∩ Ω₂ and 𝒯̊_out := {u1 − η ≤ ϕ_out
≤ u2 + η} ∩ Ω₂ and the adapted lateral boundaries be those of Corollary 51.32. A *field for g0* is a smooth
invariant function F ≥ 0 on (Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂) × S¹, labels u, a smooth invariant function on Ω₂ × S¹, and a compact set S ⊂
(Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂) × S¹, each S_α invariant under T² and both reflections, with supp F ⊂ int S, such that (V1) and (V2) hold for
(g0, 0, u) on S, the zero field with these labels (as for the reference of the proof of Proposition 52.40), and

- (V2′) |g0⁻¹(du_α, dϕ_𝔨)| ≥ c_r on D_α(S) ∩ 𝒯̊_𝔨, for 𝔨 ∈ {in, out}, every α and a number c_r > 0.

For ε > 0 the datum D_ε on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂ consists of the densities q_𝔨 and the phases ϕ_𝔨 of g0 restricted to Σ_τ0, the
field εF with the label data u_α|Σ_τ0, and the metric data of g0 corrected by Proposition 52.28, with
λ = 1 and no phases, to satisfy the constraints with the stress of the two dusts and of the field (the τ-components of
dϕ_𝔨 and du_α being the roots of the eikonal equation for the corrected metric near those of g0), completed to Cauchy
data with the lapse and shift of g0 and with the gauge condition D = 0 relative to g0, as in the definition that
precedes Proposition 52.31. Fix a′ with a < a′ < √μ0 and a′ − a < δ0/4, and V′ ∈ (V − δ0/4, V), and put

    Ω₂′ := {p ∈ Ω₂ : R ≥ a′, v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ V′ + 1},

a domain of the type (2.8) in the chart X, with the inner radius a′ and the outer radius b(τ) − (V − V′), which
exceeds a′ + 1 + δ0/2, as b(τ) − a ≥ 1 + δ0 (Lemma 50.8 (f)): its slices satisfy the bound of
Lemma 2.6 (f) with δ0/2 in place of δ0, on which the lemmas of Chapter 5 rest, with (5.1) read
with δ0/2. Fix 𝔡 > 0 with 2𝔡 ≤ min(a′ − a, V − V′), 𝒯̊_out ⊂ {R ≥ a + 2𝔡} (𝒯̊_out is compact and does not meet
{R = a}) and 𝔡 < V + 1 − v_end − η (V + 1 > v_end + η, proof of Corollary 51.32), and put

    Ω₂^𝔡 := {p ∈ Ω₂ : R ≥ a + 𝔡, v + (τ − τ_end) ≤ V − 𝔡 + 1},

so that Ω₂′ ⊂ Ω₂^𝔡 ⊂ Ω₂.

**Remark 52.48** (Labels and the radial pair.) By (52.7), for null covectors
with future-directed generators, |g0⁻¹(du_α, dϕ_𝔨)| = 2 E E′ sin²(δβ/2), δβ the angle between them in the orbit slice,
and the absolute value does not depend on the orientations. So (V2′) holds with c_r = 2 E_* E′_* sin²(β_r/2) when that
angle is at least β_r ∈ (0, π] on D_α(S) ∩ 𝒯̊_𝔨, E_* and E′_* the least energies on these compact sets, and it is empty
where the tubes do not meet. It cannot be dropped: where du_α is parallel to dϕ_𝔨 on the overlap of the supports,
g0⁻¹(du_α, dϕ_𝔨) = 0, and every harmonic j supported on that pair has Q_j = j_A² ν_A² · 0 + 2 j_A j_𝔨 ν_A ν_𝔨
g0⁻¹(du_α, dϕ_𝔨) + j_𝔨² ν_𝔨² · 0 = 0, whatever the frequencies, so that no hierarchy removes the resonance. The pair
itself is separated: g0⁻¹(dv, dϕ_out) is negative and continuous on the compact Ω₂ (Section 50.3), so c_vu :=
min over Ω₂ of |g0⁻¹(dv, dϕ_out)| is positive. So the hierarchy of Lemma 52.15 runs over all n + 2 phases,
with c := min(½ c0 (2π/n)², ½ c_r, ½ c_vu) in the proof of Corollary 52.50.

**Proposition 52.49** (The background with the radial pair.) In the setting above fix m ≥ 6.
There are ε0 > 0 and C, depending on g0, the field, a′ and V′, such that for 0 < ε ≤ ε0 and every k ≥ 2, with constants
n0 and C_k depending also on ε:

(a) D_ε has a smooth development on its adapted domain Ω_ε (Definition 51.30, for Ω₂ and the adapted boundaries of
Corollary 51.32), invariant under T² and both reflections: a metric g_ε; labels u^ε_α, each the eikonal of g_ε
with the data u_α|Σ_τ0 on a neighbourhood in Ω_ε × S¹ of the (x, α) with x in its tube D_α(S), with amplitudes F^ε; and
two dusts (ϕ_𝔨^ε, q_𝔨^ε), ϕ_𝔨^ε an eikonal of g_ε on the whole of Ω_ε with ϕ_𝔨^ε = ϕ_𝔨 on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂, with amplitudes
F_𝔨^ε transported from F_𝔨|Σ_τ0, such that

    Ric(g_ε) = T_V + q_in^ε dϕ_in^ε ⊗ dϕ_in^ε + q_out^ε dϕ_out^ε ⊗ dϕ_out^ε,

with T_V the stress of the field ε F^ε in label form, in the gauge D(g_ε) = 0 relative to g0, and with
‖g_ε − g0‖_(H^(m+1)) ≤ C ε on every slice. Ω_ε contains Ω₂′.

(b) Let D_(ε,n) be the n-dust datum of the data of g_ε on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂^𝔡, in the sense of the definition before
Proposition 52.31, the two radial dusts kept as they are. For n ≥ n0 it has a smooth invariant development
g^(n), in the gauge relative to g_ε, on an adapted domain that contains Ω₂′, with Ric(g^(n)) = Σ_A q_A du_A ⊗ du_A +
Σ_𝔨 q_𝔨^(n) dϕ_𝔨^(n) ⊗ dϕ_𝔨^(n), each u_A an eikonal of g^(n) on its tube 𝒯_A as in Proposition 52.31 and each
ϕ_𝔨^(n) an eikonal of g^(n) on the whole adapted domain, with ϕ_𝔨^(n) = ϕ_𝔨 on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂^𝔡, and on every slice of Ω₂′
the bound (52.26) holds with d(D) = 0, the radial families entering the family norm with weight one. In
particular |g^(n) − g_ε|_(C¹(Ω₂′)) ≤ C_k n^(−k), and the covectors and densities of the families of g^(n) are within
C_k n^(−k) of those of g_ε on the tubes, the labels with the weight of (52.26) and also each alone, as
in the clause of Proposition 52.31 on each family.

*Proof.* (a) The proof of the existence part of Proposition 52.39, with the reference (g0, 0, u) together with the
radial pair of g0, holds with the following changes.

(1) *The n-dust developments.* They are given by the proof of Proposition 52.31 with that reference and k = 2,
run on the adapted domain. The n labels are localised as in parts (i)–(iii) of the proof of
Lemma 52.30: they satisfy (H1′) and (H2′) of that lemma by (V1) and (V2), and they are eikonals of
the developments on their tubes only. The radial pair is not localised, ζ′_𝔨 := 1 and P̃_𝔨 := P_𝔨, so that its
equations are (Aug2)–(Aug4) on the whole domain; it satisfies (H1) of Theorem 51.18, v and ϕ_out
being eikonals of g0 on the whole of Ω₂ (proof of Corollary 51.32), and (H2′) of Theorem 51.31 by the
proof of Corollary 51.32: the tubes of the labels lie at distance at least 2δ from the axes by (V2), so near the
points where the inner boundary meets an axis only the ingoing family has tubes, and near those of the outer boundary at
most the outgoing family. The changes that the proof of Theorem 51.31 makes to that of
Theorem 51.18 are these: for the pair, the right side S^ax_𝔨 of its Raychaudhuri equations near the
axes, the leaves of Lemma 51.28 and Step 10; for the domain, the adapted boundaries and, in Step 9 at
a fixed n, the domain of dependence and the restarts; and, for every family, Step 3 with the tube of T_(τ0,U)(S_A), which
is that of S_A here, T_(τ0,U) being the identity by (2), and Step 6 with the cut-off of each family other than the one to
which a boundary B is adapted vanishing on the sets 𝒰_(r_B), r_B ≤ δ_B ≤ δ/4, about the points where B meets an axis;
here the sets 𝒱_B of Definition 51.30 are taken within δ of the axes and δ_B ≤ δ/4 for the δ of (V2), which that
definition allows, as it fixes both only by conditions of smallness. The cut-offs of the labels, the ζ′_A, vanish within
δ of the axes, so they meet this, and those of the pair meet it by the packet hypothesis, as in Corollary 51.32.
The localisation of the labels does not meet the other changes. Their cut-offs vanish within δ of the axes, and the
adapted boundaries differ from those of Ω₂ only there, the maps T_(τ,U) of Definition 51.30 being the identity off
the sets 𝒱_B, which lie within δ of the axes. Their transport fields, with the cut-offs that the proofs of
Lemma 52.30 and Proposition 52.31 put on them, are transverse to the slices, with P̃_A(τ) ≥
c/2, and satisfy dF(P̃_A) ≥ c′/2 on the lateral boundary of Ω₂; on the adapted boundaries, C¹-close to those of Ω₂ and
spacelike with the domain to their past, the same holds with c′/4. In Step 10 the linear Gronwall inequality runs for the
gauge vector D and the defects of all families together, those of the labels on the tubes 𝒯′_A of part (iii) and those of
the pair on the sets of Step 10 of the proof of Theorem 51.31; so the labels are eikonals on their tubes, by
part (iii), and the phases of the pair are eikonals on the whole adapted domain, by Step 10 of the proof of
Theorem 51.18, that domain being simply connected and every point of it lying on an integral curve of
P_𝔨 that meets Σ_τ0 inside it. The changes (1)–(6) of the proof of Proposition 52.31 concern the labels only: the
weighted family norm, the norm 𝒩^∞ of each label alone, uniformly in n, in the bootstrap, and in Step 9 the scaling of
the unknowns of the labels by (2π/n)^(1/2) with the cut-off on their covectors. The radial pair enters every norm of that
proof with the weight one and is not scaled, as one of a fixed number of families. The labels enter the terms of the pair
only through their part of T(P_𝔨, P_𝔨) = Σ_B q_B g⁻¹(p_𝔨, p_B)², the matter term of the Raychaudhuri equations of the
pair, which vanishes near the axes and is bounded in H^k, as the terms T(P_A, P_A) of (2) of that proof are, by C times
the weighted family norm plus C (𝒩^∞)²; the residual E_n of that proof enters the Raychaudhuri equations of the pair as
E_n(P̊_𝔨, P̊_𝔨), which vanishes within 2δ of the axes and is one of the residuals of (4) there; and the pair enters the
terms of the labels as a fixed number of families. In Step 9, run on the adapted domain, the threshold argument of (6)
there carries over: A^0 is block-diagonal, the transports of the pair being unscaled and having their own cut-off on p_𝔨;
the constant of the Sobolev inequality does not depend on the number of components; the extension 𝔼 of the proof of
Theorem 51.31 acts component by component, with a bound uniform in τ and in the state; the radius within which
the boundary condition holds is set by the wave block; and the states of 𝒟_ρ lie in the balls 𝔅 and 𝔅′ of
Lemma 51.28 near the axes for a ρ independent of n, those balls concerning the metric and the pair
only, which enter the scaled norm with weight one. So the constants are independent of n, and each label is bounded
alone, uniformly in n, as in the statement of Proposition 52.31.

(2) *The data.* Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂ = [a, b(τ0)] × S³, and the radial phases and the label phases of every datum are those of the
reference on Σ_τ0, so the normalisation of the phases by constants is trivial and the normalised radial phases take the
values c_B(τ0) of Corollary 51.32 on {R = a} and on {R = b(τ0)}. So the leaves of the pair on Σ_τ0 are the
spheres, the map T_(τ0,U) of Definition 51.30 is the identity, a datum on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂ suffices, and the condition on
the supports is supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂ ⊂ S_A (the last paragraph of Definition 51.30, the last sentence of
Corollary 51.32). It holds: the radial densities are those of g0, supported in S_in and S_out, and the density of
each label lies in its set S_A := S_(α_A), in which supp F lies, off the axes. The metric data are corrected by
Proposition 52.28 with λ = 1 and no phases. Its 𝔉(0) is minus the constraint stress of the field, of size
ε² in every norm ‖·‖_(j), since the data of g0 satisfy the constraints with the stress of the pair (for the n-dust data,
add the quadrature error of Lemma 52.29); the signs hold by (V3) for the round slice of g0, whose spheres
have positive mean curvature (Lemma 50.25), and by Lemma 52.26. So d(D_ε) ≤ C ε, as in the
proof of Proposition 52.40.

(3) *The limit.* Write U_n for the n-dust development of (1) and Ω_n for its adapted domain, the image of Ω₂ under
Φ_n(τ, x) := (τ, T_(τ,U_n)(x)). For every j the norms of order j of the proof of (1) are bounded uniformly in n, for
n ≥ n0(j), by the clause on m′ of Proposition 52.31; the slices of Ω_n are the images of annuli under maps
whose derivatives are bounded uniformly in τ and n, so the Sobolev inequality holds on them with a uniform constant
(through the extension operator 𝔼 of the proof of Theorem 51.31), and the energy contains the τ-derivatives:
the U_n are bounded in every C^j(Ω_n), uniformly in n. By the bound of Definition 51.30 at every order, and its
form for the τ-derivatives, the Φ_n are bounded in every C^j(Ω₂), with |T_(τ,U_n) − id| ≤ C (sup 𝒩_k + ε) ≤
C (ε + n⁻²), and T_(τ,U_n) = id at distance at least δ from the axes. So the U_n ∘ Φ_n are bounded in every C^j(Ω₂),
and, by the Arzelà–Ascoli theorem and a diagonal argument, along a subsequence Φ_n → Φ = (τ, T_τ) and U_n ∘ Φ_n → U_Φ in
every C^j(Ω₂). The derivative of each T_(τ,U_n) − id is at most ½ in norm (Definition 51.30), and so is that of
T_τ − id; so Φ is a diffeomorphism onto Ω_∞ := Φ(Ω₂), which maps the lateral boundary of Ω₂ onto that of Ω_∞, and
U := U_Φ ∘ Φ⁻¹ is smooth on Ω_∞. For y in a slice and x := T_τ⁻¹(y), the bound |T_(τ,U_n)(x′) − T_(τ,U_n)(x″)| ≥
½ |x′ − x″| gives |T_(τ,U_n)⁻¹(y) − T_τ⁻¹(y)| ≤ 2 |T_(τ,U_n)(x) − T_τ(x)|; so if y_n ∈ Ω_n and y_n → y ∈ Ω_∞, then
Φ_n⁻¹(y_n) → Φ⁻¹(y), and U_n(y_n) → U(y), with all derivatives. In particular a compact subset of Ω_∞ that avoids its
lateral boundary lies in Ω_n for n large, and U_n → U there in every C^j.

Ω_∞ is the adapted domain of U. On the axes near the points where an adapted boundary B meets them, the axis phase of
U_n is the datum's phase, the same for every n, at the point where the integral curve of the transport field of the
family to which B is adapted, in the axis, meets Σ_τ0; these curves converge to those of U, so the points z_B(τ) of the
U_n converge to the point of U at which its axis phase is c_B(τ), the only one near z̊_B(τ) (the monotonicity in
Definition 51.30). The leaves h_B of the U_n over D_B are bounded in every C^j by the bound of Definition 51.30
at every order, and their graphs lie in the lateral boundaries of the Ω_n; along a further subsequence they converge in
every C^j to a function h whose graph lies in the lateral boundary of Ω_∞. The coefficients of (51.24)
for U_n, evaluated on the graph of its leaf, converge to those for U on the graph of h, by the convergence just shown;
so h solves that equation for U, with h(0) the point of U above, for every smooth extension of U across its lateral
boundary, and by the uniqueness in Lemma 51.25 h is the leaf of U through that point. So the whole
subsequence of leaves converges, the d_B of the U_n converge to that of U in every W^(j,∞), Stein's operator and the
average over O(2) being linear and bounded on W^(j,∞), and T_(τ,U_n) → T_(τ,U). Hence T_τ = T_(τ,U), and Ω_∞ is the
adapted domain Ω_ε of U: the limit is on its own adapted domain (the paragraph of Definition 51.30 on the
determination of T_(τ,U) by U on the closure of Ω_U).

The rest of the proof of Proposition 52.39 (the eikonals and amplitudes of the labels, the Riemann sums, the gauge
and the data) is unchanged: the tubes of the labels lie at distance at least δ from the axes, where Ω_n agrees with Ω₂
for every n. The pair of U is the limit of the pairs of the U_n: its covectors are closed and null, as limits of the
dϕ_𝔨^(n), with the spatial parts of d(ϕ_𝔨|Σ_τ0) on Σ_τ0, so they are dϕ_𝔨^ε with ϕ_𝔨^ε an eikonal of g_ε on the simply
connected Ω_ε equal to ϕ_𝔨 on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂; their densities solve (Aug4) with Θ_𝔨 = □ ϕ_𝔨^ε; and the amplitudes F_𝔨^ε,
transported from F_𝔨|Σ_τ0, have squares q_𝔨^ε, both sides solving the same transport with the same data. The limit of
Ric(g^(n)) is T_V plus the stress of the pair, as in Proposition 52.39.

(4) *Containment.* By Definition 51.30, Ω_ε ∩ Σ_τ = T_(τ,U)(Σ_τ ∩ Ω₂) with |T_(τ,U) − id| ≤ C ε. The points of
Σ_τ ∩ Ω₂′ lie at distance at least min(a′ − a, V − V′) from the lateral boundary of Ω₂ in the chart, since the outer
radius of Ω₂′ is b(τ) − (V − V′); and |T_(τ,U)⁻¹(y) − y| ≤ C ε. So for C ε smaller than that distance their preimages
under T_(τ,U) lie in Σ_τ ∩ Ω₂, and Ω₂′ ⊂ Ω_ε.

(b) Lemma 50.8 (a)–(e) hold for g0 on Ω₂^𝔡, of the type of Ω₂ with a + 𝔡 and V − 𝔡 in place of a and V,
(b) because μ ≥ μ0 > (a + 𝔡)² at R = a + 𝔡, as a + 𝔡 < a′ < √μ0. So the proof of Corollary 51.32 applies to
Ω₂^𝔡, with the same η: the outgoing tube does not reach {R = a + 𝔡}, as 𝒯̊_out ⊂ {R ≥ a + 2𝔡}, and the ingoing tube
does not reach the outer boundary, where v = V − 𝔡 + 1 + τ_end − τ ≥ V − 𝔡 + 1 > v_end + η. Let Ω_ε^𝔡 be the adapted
domain of g_ε for Ω₂^𝔡 relative to g0 (Definition 51.30). It lies in Ω_ε at distance at least 𝔡 − C ε from its
lateral boundary, by the bound on the maps T of Definition 51.30, so g_ε is smooth on a neighbourhood of it. In the
sets 𝒰_(2δ_B) about the points where they meet the axes its lateral boundaries are the level sets of ϕ_in^ε and
ϕ_out^ε at the values c_B(τ) (Definition 51.30), so they are adapted to the radial pair of g_ε there, these sets
serving as the 𝒱_B. Ω_ε^𝔡 is admissible for g_ε, being C¹-close to Ω₂^𝔡, which is what the proof of
Proposition 52.31 uses of (Ω), together with the statement on rays, which holds by (c) of
Definition 51.7. By Lemma 52.38, after the replacement of the labels made there, (g_ε, ε F^ε, u^ε)
satisfies (V1) on S with the margins halved and (V2) with δ/2 in place of δ; the proof of that lemma uses the metric
only along the rays of the labels, at distance at least δ from the axes, where Ω_ε agrees with Ω₂. (V3) holds on
Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂^𝔡, an open condition, for ε small. These conditions carry over from Ω_ε to Ω_ε^𝔡, a domain of dependence
for g_ε, with the compact set S ∩ ((Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂^𝔡) × S¹), since a ray of a label from a point of S_α outside Ω₂^𝔡 never
enters Ω_ε^𝔡, and one that leaves Ω_ε^𝔡 never returns. (H2′) of Theorem 51.31 holds for the families of g_ε on
Ω_ε^𝔡 as for those of g0 on Ω₂^𝔡, the tubes moving by at most C ε. The datum D_(ε,n) is corrected on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂^𝔡 by
Proposition 52.28 as in (2), with 𝔉(0) a quadrature error of Lemma 52.29. Its radial phases
are those of g_ε, equal to those of g0 on Σ_τ0, and its label phases are those of g_ε, so its normalised radial phases
take the values c_B(τ0) of the adapted boundaries of Ω₂^𝔡 there, T_(τ0,·) is the identity and the datum on Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂^𝔡
suffices (the last paragraph of Definition 51.30); its densities satisfy supp q_A ∩ Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂^𝔡 ⊂ S_A, the radial
ones being those of g_ε, equal to those of g0 on Σ_τ0, and those of the labels lying in the sets S_(α_A). We apply
Proposition 52.31 with the reference (g_ε, ε F^ε, u^ε), its radial pair and the domain Ω_ε^𝔡, and d = 0, its
proof changed as in (1) of part (a), with g_ε and Ω_ε^𝔡 in place of g0 and Ω₂. It gives the developments g^(n) on their
adapted domains for Ω_ε^𝔡 relative to g_ε, and (52.26) on their slices, the families of g^(n) within C_k
n^(−k) of the sampled families of g_ε. The maps T of these adapted domains differ from the identity by at most C_k
n^(−k), and those of Ω_ε^𝔡 by at most C ε, while the points of Ω₂′ lie at distance at least 𝔡 from the lateral boundary
of Ω₂^𝔡; so for ε small and n ≥ n0 these domains contain Ω₂′, as in (4) of part (a). The slices of Ω₂′ are annuli of
width at least 1 + δ0/2, on which the Sobolev inequality of Lemma 5.1 holds with a constant independent of τ, and
the energy contains the τ-derivatives; with m ≥ 6 this gives the bound in C¹(Ω₂′). ∎

**Corollary 52.50** (The two-dust background with a restricted Vlasov field.) Let g0 be the two-dust
background of Theorem 50.2 on its domain Ω₂, with the outgoing phase ϕ_out, assume that its outgoing packet does
not reach the inner sphere, {u1 ≤ ϕ_out ≤ u2} ∩ Ω₂ ∩ {R = a} = ∅, and replace the lateral boundaries of Ω₂ by the
adapted ones of Corollary 51.32 (Definition 51.30). Let (F, u) be a field for g0 satisfying (V1), (V2) and
(V2′) on S, as in the setting above, and fix a′ and V′ as there. Then there is ε_* > 0 such that for 0 < ε ≤ ε_* the
class Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov solution g_ε of Proposition 52.49 (a), with the two radial
dusts of g0 and the field of amplitude ε F, developed from the data D_ε, exists on its adapted domain, which contains
Ω₂′, and on Ω₂′ it is a weak limit of class vacuum metrics: there are smooth metrics g_i on Ω₂′, invariant under T² and
both reflections, with Ric(g_i) = 0,

    g_i → g_ε uniformly on Ω₂′,      ∂g_i ⇀ ∂g_ε weakly in L²(Ω₂′).

*Proof.* Let ε ≤ ε0 of Proposition 52.49, to be decreased below, and let g_ε and the g^(n) be as there,
restricted to Ω₂′. The solution exists on its adapted domain, which contains Ω₂′, by
Proposition 52.49 (a). We check the hypotheses of Proposition 52.47 for g^(n) on Ω₂′, for odd
n large, and then follow the diagonal of the proof of Theorem 52.10.

*(Ω) and (V3).* For g0 on Ω₂′: Σ_τ is spacelike and {v + τ = const} is spacelike with v + τ increasing along future
causal curves, by Lemma 50.8 (a) and (c); at R = a′, μ ≥ μ0 > a′², so {R = a′} is spacelike with R
decreasing along future causal curves near it, as in Lemma 50.8 (b) with a′ in place of a; so a past causal
curve from a point of Ω₂′ cannot leave Ω₂′ through its lateral boundaries and meets Σ_τ0 inside Ω₂′, as in (d) there.
On Σ_τ0 the slice of g0 is round and its spheres have positive mean curvature (Lemma 50.25). These are
strict inequalities on compact sets, stable under C¹-small changes of the metric. By
Proposition 52.49, g_ε is within C ε of g0 and g^(n) within C_k n^(−k) of g_ε in C² on Ω₂′, with m = 6
there, by Sobolev's inequality on the slices (H⁷ ⊂ C⁴ in dimension four) and the equations for the τ-derivatives; so (Ω)
and (V3) hold for g_ε and for g^(n) on Ω₂′ for ε small and n large, for the generators of every family. So Ω₂′ is a
domain of dependence for each of these metrics: a ray of a label from a point of S_α outside Ω₂′ never enters it, and
one that leaves it never returns. The restriction of each field to Ω₂′ is therefore a field in label form there, with the
compact set S ∩ ((Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂′) × S¹), whose tubes are those of S intersected with Ω₂′, and (V1), (V2) and (V2′) on Ω₂′
follow from the same conditions on Ω₂.

*(ii′).* Two labels: g_ε, after the replacement of the labels made in Lemma 52.38, satisfies (Ω), (V1) and (V2)
on Ω₂′ by that lemma and the preceding paragraph, so Lemma 52.13 holds for g_ε, and the argument of (ii′)
in the proof of Theorem 52.10 gives |g^(n)⁻¹(du_A, du_B)| ≥ ½ c0 (2π/n)² on the overlaps for n large, c0 the constant
of g_ε. A label A and a radial dust 𝔨: fix compact sets S′ and S″ with sections invariant under T² and both reflections,
supp F ⊂ int S″, S″ ⊂ int S′ and S′ ⊂ int S. The rays of a family for two metrics, from the same point of Σ_τ0 with the
future roots over the same spatial covector, and their covectors, differ by at most C times the C¹ distance of the
metrics while both rays are in Ω₂′, by Gronwall's lemma for the geodesic equations; and every point of one in Ω₂′ is
within that distance of a point of the other in Ω₂′, both leaving Ω₂′ transversally through its lateral boundary, as in
the comparison of rays of the proof of Theorem 52.10. Let y ∈ Ω₂′ be a point where the supports of the two families of
g^(n) overlap. It lies on a ray of u_A for g^(n) from a point of S″_(α_A), and on a ray of ϕ_𝔨^(n) from a point of
supp q_𝔨 ∩ Σ_τ0, the data being those of g0. Put C_n := C (ε + C_k n^(−k)), at least C |g^(n) − g0|_(C¹(Ω₂′)). Then
y lies within C_n of a point y′ of D_(α_A)(S″) and of a point y″ of the tube of supp q_𝔨 ∩ Σ_τ0, both for g0, and the
covectors du_A(y) and dϕ_𝔨^(n)(y) lie within C_n of du_(α_A)(y′) and dϕ_𝔨(y″). For g0, u_α is an eikonal on a
neighbourhood of uniform size of D_α(S′) by (V1), so the ray of u_(α_A) for g0 through y, followed to the past, stays in
Ω₂′ and meets Σ_τ0 within C C_n of S″_(α_A); for ε small and n large, y ∈ D_(α_A)(S′) ⊂ D_(α_A)(S). And 𝒯̊_𝔨 contains a
neighbourhood in Ω₂ of the tube for g0 of supp q_𝔨 ∩ Σ_τ0, which lies in {v_start ≤ v ≤ v_end} ∩ Ω₂ for 𝔨 = in and in {u1
≤ ϕ_out ≤ u2} ∩ Ω₂ for 𝔨 = out, so y ∈ 𝒯̊_𝔨 for ε small and n large. By (V2′), |g0⁻¹(du_(α_A), dϕ_𝔨)(y)| ≥ c_r; the
eikonals of g0 being smooth on these neighbourhoods, uniformly in α, |du_(α_A)(y′) − du_(α_A)(y)| and |dϕ_𝔨(y″) −
dϕ_𝔨(y)| are at most C C_n; so |g^(n)⁻¹(du_A, dϕ_𝔨^(n))(y)| ≥ c_r − C C_n ≥ ½ c_r. For the pair, by the same comparison
of rays, the absolute value of g^(n)⁻¹(dϕ_in^(n), dϕ_out^(n)) is at least c_vu − C C_n ≥ ½ c_vu
(Remark 52.48). So (ii′) holds for all n + 2 families with c := min(½ c0 (2π/n)², ½ c_r, ½ c_vu), and
Λ = Λ(n) is chosen as there.

*The setting of Section 52.8, (iii), (iv), (iii′) and (vi).* The setting holds for the labels of g^(n) as in the
proof of Theorem 52.10, with the sets S_A := S″_(α_A) of that proof and u_A extended off its tube by a cut-off, which
changes neither Ric(g^(n)) nor (52.5); their waves are those of that proof, and their sets 𝒱_A lie
within C n^(−k) of D_(α_A)(S) for g_ε, hence at distance at least δ/2 from the axes for n large. For the pair, S_𝔨 :=
Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω₂′ and 𝒱_𝔨 = Ω₂′, ϕ_𝔨^(n) is an eikonal of g^(n) on the whole of Ω₂′ (Proposition 52.49 (b)),
and ϕ_𝔨^(n) = ϕ_𝔨 on Σ_τ0, functions of R = r with nonzero derivative, since dv(∂_R) = 1 and dϕ_out(∂_R) < 0 on Σ_τ0
(proof of Corollary 51.32: dϕ_out(∂_R) = (1 − R_v)/R_u with R_v ≤ ½, and R_u < 0 by
Proposition 50.6 (c)): this is (vi). The metric Π^(n) that g^(n) induces on the spheres of Σ_τ0 is within
C (ε + C_k n^(−k)) in C⁰ of the Euclidean one, which is that of g0; so Lemma 52.43 (c) gives 𝒵0 for g^(n),
and (a) the parallel polarisations 𝒵_𝔨, its transports along the rays of ϕ_𝔨^(n), which vanish on Σ_τ0 on the vectors
g^(n)-orthogonal to the spheres: this is (iii′). The amplitudes F_𝔨^(n) are the solutions of (52.5) with
the data F_𝔨|Σ_τ0, smooth, with (F_𝔨^(n))² = q_𝔨^(n).

So Proposition 52.47 gives, for each odd n ≥ n0 and λ ≤ λ0(n), vacuum metrics g^(n)_λ on Ω₂′, invariant under
T² and both reflections, with |g^(n)_λ − g^(n)| ≤ C(n) λ and ∂g^(n)_λ − ∂g^(n) = Σ ν du ⊗ [∂_θ W] + O(C(n) λ), the sum
over the n + 2 families. For a label, |ν_A ∂_(θ_A) W_A| ≤ C (F_A + F_A²) with C independent of n and A, as in the proof
of Theorem 52.10. For the pair, ν_𝔨 ∂_(θ_𝔨) W_𝔨 = −2 F_𝔨 sin θ_𝔨 𝒵_𝔨 + ν_𝔨³ c_𝔨 cos 2θ_𝔨 dϕ_𝔨 ⊗ dϕ_𝔨, where the
Cartesian components of 𝒵_𝔨 are bounded independently of n (𝒵0 is, and the transport has coefficients bounded by the
C¹ norm of g^(n)), and ν_𝔨³ c_𝔨 ≤ C F_𝔨² as for the labels; so these two terms are bounded independently of n.

*The diagonal.* It is that of the proof of Theorem 52.10, with the n + 2 families and Ω₂′ in place of Ω. The two
