meet {R_u2 < R < R_*}, and it lies in {0.70 ≤ R ≤ R_u2} or in {R ≥ R_*}. ∎

#### 53.10.8 The theorem

**Theorem 53.43** (The background below R_*.) For the background of Section 50.2:

(a) On 𝒞_in, ℓ_v ≥ 0.529 on [u1, u2]; R(u2) ∈ [1.519357, 1.519359]; the mass of region III satisfies μ3 ∈ [0.8220998,
0.8221253] and R(u2)² > μ3.

(b) Region III meets Σ_τ0 ∩ {R ≤ R_*} exactly in 0.70 ≤ R ≤ R_u2, where 1.8614372 ≤ R_u2 ≤ 1.8614410, and contains the
seed region. On the seed region, |ψ_s^(k) − ψ_III^(k)| ≤ 5.1 × 10⁻⁵, 2.6 × 10⁻⁴, 8.7 × 10⁻⁴ for k = 0, 1, 2, and |μ3 −
μ_s| ≤ 1.4 × 10⁻⁵; so the background lies in the tube of Proposition 53.57 (b) and Γ > 0 on the seed region. At the
points of Σ_τ0 with 1.861 ≤ R ≤ R_u2, Γ/E² ≥ 10.40, so Γ > 0 at every point of Σ_τ0 in region III.

(c) On Σ_τ0 for R ≤ R_*: κ > 0, K^l_l < 0, e^ψ f < 1 and κK^l_l ≤ −4.76 × 10⁻³.

*Proof.* (a) is Proposition 53.38, (b) is Proposition 53.40 and Proposition 53.42, (c) is
Proposition 53.41. ∎

**Remark 53.44** (Numerical observation.) The reference quintic ψ_s of Section B.6.2 is the first
piece of a degree-5 smoothing spline fitted to the values of ψ_III on a second-order finite-difference solution of the
characteristic problem on a double-null grid with 160 steps per unit, and μ_s is that solution's mass in region III.
The same grid solution reproduces the six inputs (53.50) at 40 points of the packet on Σ_τ0 to within
2.0 × 10⁻³ (q), 1.1 × 10⁻³ (f), 2.7 × 10⁻³ (ψ_R, of size 0.20), 2.0 × 10⁻³ (ψ_v̂, of size 0.06), 2.8 × 10⁻³ (f_R) and
7.7 × 10⁻⁴ (f_v̂), up to 3 % of the smaller inputs. No proof uses this remark: Proposition 53.40 uses only the printed
coefficients of ψ_s and the number μ_s.

### 53.11 The margins of the angle-localised families

This section proves the inequalities on which Theorem 53.3 and Corollary 53.16 rest, for the
two-dust background of Section 50.2 with the characteristic data of Section 53.10.1, at those data's own
parameters. Three results are proved. Proposition 53.48 and Corollary 53.50 describe the bend of the slice Σ′
and the lens between Σ′ and Σ_τ0. Theorem 53.54 proves that Rácz's split is hyperbolic on Σ′ ∩ {R ≥ R_*}
with an explicit margin, and locates the band of Σ_τ0 where it fails. Proposition 53.57 bounds Γ/E² from below on
the seed region, for a reference profile and for every profile in a tube around it. Each inequality is reduced to a
finite list of rows, printed in Section B.6, and each row is checked by a rule stated here.

*The background.* We recall what is used. The metric is g = −2e^(2σ) du dv + R² dΩ₃² on the quotient by the T² action,
the ingoing dust has profile 𝒜(v) := 3.6 b(v; 3, 4.5) on 𝒞_out := {u = 0}, the outgoing dust has profile ℬ(u) := 1.7 b(u;
5.7, 7.2) on 𝒞_in := {v = 0}, e^(2σ) = 1/2 on both cones, and at the corner R = 5, R_u = −0.47, R_v = 1/2, with mass 3/2.
Here b(x; a, c) := β((2x − a − c)/(c − a)) with the bump β of Section B.6.1. The mass function is μ := R²(1 +
2e^(−2σ) R_u R_v). The time v̂ on 𝒞_out is fixed by v̂ = 0 at the corner and dv̂/dv = −e^(2σ)/R_u on 𝒞_out, and ψ :=
ln(−e^(2σ)/(R_u dv̂/dv)). Then τ := v̂ − R, τ0 := −0.68, and Σ_τ0 = {τ = τ0, 0.70 ≤ R ≤ b(τ0)} is the slice of
Section 53.1. Region I is {u ≤ 5.7}. The proofs use four
identities of the background (Lemma 53.32, (53.44) and the definition of μ):

    (S1)  μ_u = −(2/3) ℬ e^(−2σ) R_v,   μ_v = −(2/3) 𝒜 e^(−2σ) R_u;      (S2)  R_uv = −e^(2σ) μ/R³;
    (S3)  R_vv = −𝒜/(3R²) on 𝒞_out and R_uu = −ℬ/(3R²) on 𝒞_in;                (S4)  ψ_u = ℬ/(3R² R_u),

and R_u < 0 on the domain. We use the time orientation in which u and v increase to the future. Rácz's quantities on a
round slice are κ (the radial extrinsic curvature) and K^l_l (the trace on the spheres), with the sign conventions of
Lemma 53.1. Hyperbolic means first-order symmetrizable hyperbolic, as in
Theorem A.16, by which the split is hyperbolic where κK^l_l < 0. It is not hyperbolic where κK^l_l > 0.
To see this, use the notation of Remark A.17: for a real leaf covector ξ_S = (ξ_K) ≠ 0 put
B(ξ_S) := ξ_K B^(K), k·ξ_S := γ̂^(KL) k_K ξ_L and |ξ_S|² := γ̂^(KL) ξ_K ξ_L > 0, where k is the mixed part of the
extrinsic curvature, and write ξ_n for n̂^i ξ_i. The characteristic polynomial of the split at ξ = (ξ_ρ, ξ_S) is
det(ξ_ρ I + B(ξ_S)), the determinant of its principal symbol, and its essential part, a factor, is the quadratic
[Rac16, (4.22)]

    K^l_l ξ_n² − 2ξ_n (k·ξ_S) + κ|ξ_S|² = 0,   with roots   ξ_n = (k·ξ_S ± √((k·ξ_S)² − κK^l_l|ξ_S|²))/K^l_l.

By [Rac16, (4.23)] a root ξ_n gives the root ξ_ρ = N̂^K ξ_K + N̂ ξ_n of the characteristic polynomial, so −ξ_ρ is an
eigenvalue of B(ξ_S); and since N̂ ≠ 0 (n̂_i = N̂(dρ)_i is a unit covector) and N̂^K ξ_K are real, ξ_ρ is real exactly
when ξ_n is. The leaves are three-dimensional, so we may choose ξ_S with k·ξ_S = 0. Then the discriminant is
−4κK^l_l|ξ_S|² < 0, and the roots ξ_n = ±i|ξ_S|√(κK^l_l)/K^l_l are not real, so B(ξ_S) has an eigenvalue that is not
real. If H were a common symmetrizer, symmetric positive definite with H B^(K) symmetric for every K, then H B(ξ_S) would
be symmetric, so B(ξ_S) would be self-adjoint for the inner product (x, y) ↦ xᵀHy and its eigenvalues would be real. So
the split has no common symmetrizer, and is not hyperbolic, where κK^l_l > 0.

#### 53.11.1 Enclosures and quadrature

**Lemma 53.45** (Enclosures and quadrature.)

(a) Let e be an expression in real variables x_1, …, x_n built from constants, +, −, ×, ÷, positive integer powers, exp
and √, and let I_1, …, I_n be closed bounded intervals. Evaluate e with each x_i replaced by I_i and each operation by
its form on intervals: [a, b] + [c, d] = [a + c, b + d]; [a, b] − [c, d] = [a − d, b − c]; [a, b]·[c, d] is the interval
between the least and the greatest of ac, ad, bc, bd; [a, b]/[c, d] = [a, b]·[1/d, 1/c] when 0 ∉ [c, d]; a power [a, b]ⁿ
is the range of t ↦ tⁿ on [a, b]; exp and √ act on the endpoints. If every step is defined, the resulting interval
contains e(x) for every x ∈ I_1 × ⋯ × I_n. This remains true when the lower end of any intermediate interval is
decreased and its upper end increased.

(b) If f ∈ C²[a, b], h := b − a and 0 ≤ s ≤ 1, then |f(a + sh) − (1 − s) f(a) − s f(b)| ≤ (h²/8) sup|f″|. In particular
f ≥ min(f(a), f(b)) − (h²/8) sup|f″| and f ≤ max(f(a), f(b)) + (h²/8) sup|f″| on [a, b].

(c) If f ∈ C²[a, b], then |∫_a^b f − (h/2)(f(a) + f(b))| ≤ (h³/12) sup|f″|. If f ∈ C⁴[a, b], then

    |∫_a^b f − (h/2)(f(a) + f(b)) + (h²/12)(f′(b) − f′(a))| ≤ (h⁴/384) ∫_a^b |f⁗|.    (53.68)

(d) If ω ≥ 0 is continuous, w ∈ C²[a, b], A0 := ∫_a^b ω and A1 := ∫_a^b (x − a) ω, then

    |∫_a^b ω w − w(a) A0 − (w(b) − w(a)) A1/h| ≤ (h²/8) sup|w″| A0.

*Proof.* (a) By induction on e. Each rule returns exactly the set of values of its operation on the product of its
arguments' intervals: a product is bilinear, so its extreme values on a rectangle are at corners; t ↦ 1/t, exp and √ are
monotone on the intervals where they are applied; the power rule is the definition. Enlarging an intermediate interval
keeps the inclusion. (b) Let L be the linear interpolant of f at a and b. For x ∈ (a, b) choose c with F := f − L − c(t
− a)(t − b) vanishing at x; F vanishes at a, x, b, so F″(ξ) = 0 for some ξ, that is f(x) − L(x) = (f″(ξ)/2)(x − a)(x −
b), and (x − a)(b − x) ≤ h²/4. (c) Two integrations by parts give ∫_a^b f − (h/2)(f(a) + f(b)) = −(1/2) ∫_a^b (x − a)(b
− x) f″(x) dx, and ∫_a^b (x − a)(b − x) dx = h³/6. Four integrations by parts give the left side of
(53.68) without modulus as (1/24) ∫_a^b (x − a)²(b − x)² f⁗(x) dx, and (x − a)²(b − x)² ≤ h⁴/16. (d) The
function w(a) + (w(b) − w(a))(x − a)/h is the linear interpolant of w; integrate (b) against ω ≥ 0. ∎

#### 53.11.2 The bump

**Lemma 53.46** (The bump.) Let z := 1/(1 − y²) for |y| < 1, and

    q3(z) := z³ − 7z² + (21/2) z − 3,     q4(z) := 4z⁵ − 56z⁴ + 232z³ − 348z² + 195z − 30.

(a) On (−1, 1), β′ = −2yz²β, β″ = 2z²(2z² − 6z + 3)β, β‴ = −8yz³ q3(z) β and β⁗ = 4z³ q4(z) β. Every derivative of β
tends to 0 at ±1, so β ∈ C^∞(ℝ). β is even, 0 ≤ β ≤ 1, and β is increasing on [−1, 0].

(b) β″ vanishes on (−1, 1) exactly at ±y_1, y_1 := 3^(−1/4). So β′ is monotone on [−1, −y_1], [−y_1, y_1] and [y_1, 1],
sup|β′| = |β′(y_1)| ≤ 2.17036, and ∫_(−1)^1 |β″| = 4 sup|β′| ≤ 8.6815.

(c) β‴ vanishes on (−1, 1) exactly at 0, ±y_2 and ±y_3, where z(y_2) ∈ (1.594, 1.595) and z(y_3) ∈ (5.031, 5.032), and
β″ is monotone between consecutive points of −1, −y_3, −y_2, 0, y_2, y_3, 1. Further β″(0) = −2, β″(±y_2) ∈ [−4.181,
−4.136] and β″(±y_3) ∈ [21.039, 21.093]; so sup|β″| ≤ 21.093 and ∫_(−1)^1 |β‴| ≤ 97.1.

(d) β⁗ vanishes on (−1, 1) exactly at ±y_4, ±y_5 and ±y_6, where z(y_4) ∈ (1.300, 1.301), z(y_5) ∈ (3.597, 3.598) and
z(y_6) ∈ (8.039, 8.040), and β‴ is monotone between consecutive points of −1, −y_6, −y_5, −y_4, y_4, y_5, y_6, 1. Its
values satisfy β‴(y_4) ∈ [−6.49, −6.24], β‴(y_5) ∈ [216.8, 219.7] and β‴(y_6) ∈ [−507.6, −505.7]; so sup|β‴| ≤ 507.6 and
∫_(−1)^1 |β⁗| ≤ 2936.

*Proof.* (a) Differentiate β = e^(1−z) with z′ = 2yz² and remove even powers of y by y² = 1 − 1/z; for instance β″ =
(4y²z⁴ − 2z² − 8y²z³)β = 2z²(2z² − 6z + 3)β, and the third and fourth derivatives follow in the same way. Each
derivative is a polynomial in y and z times e^(1−z), and z^m e^(1−z) → 0 as z → ∞. Evenness, the bounds and the
monotonicity follow from β = e^(1−z) with z increasing in |y|.

(b) 2z² − 6z + 3 has the roots (3 ± √3)/2, and only (3 + √3)/2 exceeds 1; it gives y² = 1 − 2/(3 + √3) = 3^(−1/2).
There |β′| = 2·3^(−1/4)·((3 + √3)/2)²·e^(−(1+√3)/2) = 2.170357…. On the three pieces β′ runs from 0 to its maximum, from
its maximum to its minimum −sup|β′|, and back to 0; its total variation, which is ∫|β″|, is 4 sup|β′|.

(c) q3(0) = −3, q3(1/2) = 5/8, q3(1.594) = 0.0012406 > 0, q3(1.595) = −0.0029551 < 0, q3(5.031) = −0.0117822 < 0 and
q3(5.032) = 0.0042248 > 0, so the cubic q3 has exactly one root in each of (0, 1/2), (1.594, 1.595) and (5.031, 5.032);
only the last two exceed 1. With y = 0 (the factor y of β‴) these give the zeros. On z ∈ [1.594, 1.595] and z ∈ [5.031,
5.032], Lemma 53.45 (a) applied to 2z²(2z² − 6z + 3)e^(1−z) gives the stated intervals. As β″ is even and
monotone on the pieces, its total variation on [−1, 1] is 2(|β″(y_2) − β″(0)| + |β″(y_3) − β″(y_2)| + |β″(y_3)|) ≤
2(2.181 + 25.274 + 21.093) ≤ 97.1.

(d) q4(0) = −30, q4(1/2) = 49/8, q4(1) = −3, q4(1.300) = −0.00588, q4(1.301) = 0.025631, q4(3.597) = 0.052921,
q4(3.598) = −0.327578, q4(8.039) = −5.84132 and q4(8.040) = 0.897867: five sign changes of a quintic, so exactly one
root in each interval and no other. On the three z-intervals Lemma 53.45 (a) applied to −8yz³q3(z)e^(1−z),
y = (1 − 1/z)^(1/2), gives the stated values. They alternate in sign, and β‴ is odd with β‴(0) = β‴(±1) = 0, so its
total variation on [0, 1] is |e_4| + (|e_4| + |e_5|) + (|e_5| + |e_6|) + |e_6| with e_i := β‴(y_i), at most 2(6.49 +
219.7 + 507.6) ≤ 1467.6, and on [−1, 1] at most 2936. ∎

**Lemma 53.47** (The bump table.) Let C, D, C̃_j and D̃_j be as in Section B.6.1, δ = 1/20, and
K := ∫_(−1)^1 β.

(a) |C(y_j) − C̃_j| ≤ 5 × 10⁻⁵ and |D(y_j) − D̃_j| ≤ 10⁻⁴ for 0 ≤ j ≤ 40; in particular |K − 1.2069048544| ≤ 5 × 10⁻⁵.

(b) For y_j ≤ y ≤ y_(j+1),

    |C(y) − C̃_j − (y − y_j)(β(y_j) + β(y))/2| ≤ 2.7 × 10⁻⁴,
    |D(y) − D̃_j − (y − y_j) C̃_j − (y − y_j)² β(y_j)/2| ≤ 1.5 × 10⁻⁴,

and for y ≥ 1, C(y) = K and D(y) = yK.

(c) Let φ be the bend of Proposition 53.48 and, for its three lobes X with half-width h_X, centre c_X and weight ε_X
(ε = 1 for the central lobe, −l1 and −l2 for the others), y_X := (R − c_X)/h_X. Then φ′(R) = 0.01 Σ_X ε_X h_X C(y_X) and
φ(R) = 0.01 Σ_X ε_X h_X² D(y_X). Evaluating C and D by (b) gives φ′(R) to within 1.7 × 10⁻⁶ and φ(R) to within 10⁻⁶.

*Proof.* (a) The recursion for C̃ applies (53.68) to f = β on each [y_j, y_(j+1)]. Summing, |C(y_j) −
C̃_j| ≤ (δ⁴/384) ∫|β⁗| + 40 × 5 × 10⁻¹¹ ≤ 2936/(384 × 20⁴) + 2 × 10⁻⁹ ≤ 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ by Lemma 53.46 (d), the
second term accounting for the rounding of the printed values. The recursion for D̃ applies (53.68) to
f = C, with f′ = β and f⁗ = β‴, but with C̃ in place of C. So |D(y_j) − D̃_j| is at most (δ⁴/384) ∫|β‴| plus δ times the
sum over i < j of the larger error of C̃ at y_i and y_(i+1), that is at most 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ + 40δ × 4.8 × 10⁻⁵ ≤ 10⁻⁴, using
Lemma 53.46 (c).

(b) By Lemma 53.45 (c), |∫_(y_j)^y β − (y − y_j)(β(y_j) + β(y))/2| ≤ (δ³/12) × 21.093 ≤ 2.2 × 10⁻⁴; add
(a). Next D(y) = D(y_j) + (y − y_j) C(y_j) + ∫_(y_j)^y (y − s) β(s) ds, and |∫_(y_j)^y (y − s)(β(s) − β(y_j)) ds| ≤
sup|β′| ∫_(y_j)^y (y − s)(s − y_j) ds ≤ 2.1704 δ³/6 ≤ 4.6 × 10⁻⁵; add (a) and δ × 5 × 10⁻⁵. For y ≥ 1, C(y) = K, and
D(y) = yK − ∫ sβ(s) ds = yK because β is even. (c) The formulas follow from φ(R) = ∫_(3.5)^R (R − t) φ″(t) dt and the
substitution t = c_X + h_X s. The error in φ′ is at most 0.01 (h_P + l1 h_L + l2 h_R) × 2.7 × 10⁻⁴ ≤ 1.7 × 10⁻⁶. For φ,
a lobe in progress contributes at most 0.01 h_X² × 1.5 × 10⁻⁴ and a completed lobe, where D = y_X K with |y_X| ≤ 7.2, at
most 0.01 h_X² × 7.2 × 5 × 10⁻⁵; in all at most 0.01 (0.09 × 2.3 × 10⁻⁴ + 0.0487 × 3.6 × 10⁻⁴ + 0.05533 × 1.5 × 10⁻⁴) ≤
10⁻⁶. ∎

#### 53.11.3 The bend

**Proposition 53.48** (The bend.) Let l1 := 432/671, l2 := 50/183, and let φ be the function with φ(R) =
0 for R ≤ 3.5 and

    φ″(R) = 0.01 (b(R; 4.1, 4.7) − l1 b(R; 3.5, 4.05) − l2 b(R; 4.85, 5.75)).    (53.69)

(a) The three lobes have half-widths h_L = 11/40, h_P = 3/10, h_R = 9/20 and centres c_L = 151/40, c_P = 22/5, c_R =
53/10. The numbers l1, l2 are the unique ones for which ∫φ″ = ∫ R φ″ dR = 0, namely

    l1 = (h_P/h_L)(c_R − c_P)/(c_R − c_L) = 0.6438152011922503…,
    l2 = (h_P/h_R)(c_P − c_L)/(c_R − c_L) = 0.27322404371584699….

Hence φ = φ′ = 0 outside [3.5, 5.75].

(b) φ ≤ 0. There is x* ∈ (4.415, 4.445) with φ′ < 0 on (3.5, x*) and φ′ > 0 on (x*, 5.75), and

    0.0011590 ≤ max|φ| = −φ(x*) ≤ 0.0011596;

so max|φ| = 0.00116 to three significant figures.

(c) |φ′| ≤ 0.0021370, |φ″| ≤ 0.01, |φ‴| ≤ 0.072346 and |φ⁗| ≤ 2.3437.

*Proof.* (a) Each lobe is a translate and dilate of the even bump β, so ∫ b(R; a, c) dR = hK and ∫ R b(R; a, c) dR =
c′hK for the lobe of half-width h and centre c′. The two conditions read l1 h_L + l2 h_R = h_P and l1 c_L h_L + l2 c_R
h_R = c_P h_P; K cancels. The determinant is h_L h_R (c_R − c_L) ≠ 0, and Cramer's rule gives the formulas: l1 = (12/11)
(9/10)(40/61) = 432/671 and l2 = (2/3)(5/8)(40/61) = 50/183. For R ≥ 5.75, φ′(R) = ∫φ″ = 0 and φ(R) = ∫ (R − t) φ″(t)
dt = R ∫φ″ − ∫ t φ″ = 0.

(b) The lobes have disjoint supports, so φ″ < 0 on (3.5, 4.05) and on (4.85, 5.75), φ″ > 0 on (4.1, 4.7), and φ″ = 0
elsewhere. Hence φ′ falls from 0 to −0.01 l1 h_L K < 0 on [3.5, 4.05], is constant up to 4.1, rises on [4.1, 4.7] to
0.01(h_P − l1 h_L)K = 0.01 h_P (25/61) K > 0, is constant up to 4.85, and falls to φ′(5.75) = 0. So φ′ has a single zero
x* ∈ (4.1, 4.7), φ falls from 0 to φ(x*) and rises back to φ(5.75) = 0, and φ ≤ 0. On [4.1, 4.7] the left lobe is
complete, so

    φ(R) = 0.01 (h_P² D(y_P) − l1 h_L K (R − c_L)),     y_P := (R − c_P)/h_P,

with l1 h_L = 54/305. At R = 4.415, 4.43 and 4.445 (y_P = y_21, y_22, y_23) the table of Section B.6.1 gives, with
K̃ := C̃_40 and rounded to ten decimals,

    0.01 (0.09 D̃_j − (54/305) K̃ (R − c_L)) ≈ −0.0011576361,  −0.0011591651,  −0.0011584676,

and by Lemma 53.47 (a) the true values differ from these printed decimals by at most 0.01(0.09 × 10⁻⁴ +
(54/305) × 0.67 × 5 × 10⁻⁵) + 5 × 10⁻¹¹ ≤ 1.5 × 10⁻⁷. So φ(4.43) < min(φ(4.415), φ(4.445)), and as φ is convex on [4.1,
4.7] its minimum point x* lies in (4.415, 4.445). There Lemma 53.45 (b), with h = 0.015 and sup|φ″| ≤ 0.01,
so that (h²/8) sup|φ″| ≤ 2.82 × 10⁻⁷, gives φ ≥ −0.0011591651 − 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ − 2.82 × 10⁻⁷ = −0.0011595971 ≥ −0.0011596,
while φ(4.43) ≤ −0.0011591651 + 1.5 × 10⁻⁷ ≤ −0.0011590.

(c) By the description of φ′ in (b), |φ′| ≤ 0.01 (54/305) K ≤ 0.0021370 by Lemma 53.47 (a). Since the
lobes are disjoint, |φ^(k)| on the lobe of half-width h and weight c ∈ {1, l1, l2} is at most 0.01 c
sup|β^(k−2)|/h^(k−2); by Lemma 53.46 the largest of these is 0.01 × 2.17036 × (10/3) for k = 3 and 0.01 ×
21.093 × (100/9) for k = 4. ∎

#### 53.11.4 Region I and the data on the shell

**Lemma 53.49** (Region I.)

(a) On region I the background is ingoing Vaidya in the chart (v̂, R):

    g = −f dv̂² + 2 dv̂ dR + R² dΩ₃²,     f := 1 − μ(v̂)/R²,    (53.70)

where μ(v̂) is the mass at the point of 𝒞_out with time v̂. The function μ is nondecreasing; μ = 3/2 for v ≤ 3, μ is
constant for v ≥ 4.5, and μ ≤ 3.6059 everywhere.

(b) Let F(r) := 2r + √(3/2) ln((r − √(3/2))/(r + √(3/2))) and τ_ray(R) := F(R) − F(2.321) − R. Where v̂ ≤ v̂(v = 3) the
null ray u = 5.7 is {τ = τ_ray(R)}. Since τ_ray(3.43718) = −0.68000009 and τ_ray(3.43719) = −0.67998718, it crosses Σ_τ0
at a single radius R_* ∈ (3.43718, 3.43719), with v̂ = τ0 + R_* < 2.7572 < v̂(v = 3) = 3.14533. This R_* is the radius
of Lemma 53.34, which encloses it in [3.43718006, 3.43718007].

(c) Every point with R ≥ R_* and τ ≤ τ0 lies in region I. In particular Σ_τ0 ∩ {R ≥ R_*}, Σ′ ∩ {R ≥ R_*} and every point
with R ≥ R_* between Σ′ and Σ_τ0 do.

*Proof.* (a) In region I, ℬ = 0, so μ_u = 0 by (S1) and ψ_u = 0 by (S4). Thus μ is constant along ingoing rays, equal to
its value on 𝒞_out, and ψ = 0, its value on 𝒞_out. With dv̂ = −(e^(2σ)/R_u) dv (which is ψ = 0) and du = (dR − R_v
dv)/R_u, the quotient metric is −2e^(2σ) du dv = 2 dv̂ dR + 2e^(−2σ) R_u R_v dv̂², and 2e^(−2σ) R_u R_v = μ/R² − 1 by the
definition of μ. On 𝒞_out, μ_v = −(2/3)𝒜 e^(−2σ) R_u ≥ 0 with 𝒜 = 0 outside (3, 4.5); the bound μ ≤ 3.6059 is
Lemma 53.51 (c) at v = 4.5.

(b) For v̂ ≤ v̂(v = 3), μ = 3/2. The ray u = 5.7 starts on 𝒞_in, where v̂ = 0 and, by (S3) with ℬ = 0 for u ≤ 5.7, R = 5
− 0.47 u, so R = 2.321. Outgoing null rays of (53.70) satisfy dv̂/dR = 2/f, and F′(r) = 2r²/(r² − 3/2) is
2/f for μ = 3/2; so v̂ = F(R) − F(2.321) on the ray. The values of τ_ray are direct evaluations, and τ_ray is increasing
by (c) below. Finally v̂(v = 3) is v̂_0 of Section B.6.4.

(c) Along an outgoing null ray of (53.70), dτ/dR = 2/f − 1 > 0 where 0 < f < 2. On the ray u = 5.7 at R ≥
R_*, f ≥ 1 − 3.6059/R_*² > 0 since R_*² > 11.81. So the ray's τ, as a function of R, is increasing on [R_*, ∞) and at
least τ0 there; equivalently its time v̂_ray(R) satisfies v̂_ray(R) ≥ τ0 + R. Let p have R_p ≥ R_* and τ_p ≤ τ0. Then
v̂_ray(R_p) ≥ τ0 + R_p ≥ v̂_p, so the ingoing ray v̂ = v̂_p meets u = 5.7 at a radius R_1 ≤ R_p. Along an ingoing ray u
decreases as R increases (R_u < 0), so u(p) ≤ 5.7. Points of Σ′ have τ = τ0 + φ(R) ≤ τ0 by Proposition 53.48 (b),
and points between the two slices have τ0 + φ(R) ≤ τ ≤ τ0. ∎

**Corollary 53.50** (The lens.) Let Σ′ := {v̂ − R − φ(R) = τ0}. Then Σ′ = Σ_τ0 outside R ∈ [3.5, 5.75],
and Σ′ lies to the past of Σ_τ0 where they differ, at τ-distance at most max|φ| ≤ 0.0011596. Let γ be a causal curve
joining a point p of Σ′ with R_p ≥ R_* to a point q of Σ_τ0. Then γ lies in region I. If γ is not constant, it runs to
the future from p to q, every point of γ other than q has R ∈ (3.5, 5.75), and the angular displacement of γ on the
unit sphere S³ is at most 3.25 × 10⁻⁴. The slice Σ_τ0 is acausal; so a causal curve joining a point p of Σ′ with
R_p < R_*, which lies on Σ_τ0, to a point q of Σ_τ0 is constant, and R_q = R_p < R_*. Hence carrying a domain of
influence from one slice to the other widens its angular support by at most 3.3 × 10⁻⁴ rad.

*Proof.* On Σ′, τ = τ0 + φ(R). By Proposition 53.48, φ = 0 outside [3.5, 5.75], and φ < 0 on (3.5, 5.75), since φ
strictly decreases from φ(3.5) = 0 on [3.5, x*] and strictly increases to φ(5.75) = 0 on [x*, 5.75]. This gives the
first two statements.

*Time functions in region I.* With τ = v̂ − R, (53.70) reads g = −f dτ² + 2(1 − f) dτ dR + (2 − f) dR² +
R² dΩ₃², whose inverse on the (τ, R) plane has g^(ττ) = −(2 − f), g^(τR) = 1 − f and g^(RR) = f. So g⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −(2 −
f) < 0, since f < 1. Where φ′ ≠ 0, R ∈ (3.5, 5.75) and 0 < f < 1 (μ ≤ 3.6059 < 3.5²), so with |φ′| ≤ 0.0022,
g⁻¹(d(τ − φ), d(τ − φ)) = −(2 − f) − 2(1 − f)φ′ + fφ′² ≤ −1 + 2 × 0.0022 + 0.0022² < 0; where φ′ = 0 it is −(2 − f).
So dτ and d(τ − φ) are timelike on region I. The vector −∂_R of the chart (v̂, R) is null and future directed: it is
tangent to an ingoing ray, along which u increases as R decreases, because R_u < 0. On it dτ and d(τ − φ) take the
values 1 and 1 + φ′, both positive. A timelike covector does not vanish on a nonzero causal vector, so it has one sign
on the future causal vectors; hence τ and τ − φ(R) increase strictly along every future causal curve in region I that
is not constant.

*Where γ lies.* Along a future causal curve u and v do not decrease, and v̂ is an increasing function of v (dv̂/dv =
−e^(2σ)/R_u > 0); so v̂ does not decrease. Let γ join p ∈ Σ′, R_p ≥ R_*, to q ∈ Σ_τ0. The point p lies in region I by
Lemma 53.49 (c), which settles a constant γ; suppose γ is not constant. If γ runs to the future from q to
p, then u ≤ u(p) ≤ 5.7 along γ, so γ lies in region I; there τ increases strictly from τ(q) = τ0 to τ(p) = τ0 +
φ(R_p) ≤ τ0, which is impossible. So γ runs to the future from p to q. Then τ0 + R_q = v̂(q) ≥ v̂(p) = τ0 + R_p +
φ(R_p). If R_p ≥ 3.5, this gives R_q ≥ 3.5 − 0.0011596 > R_*; if R_* ≤ R_p < 3.5, then φ(R_p) = 0 and R_q ≥ R_p ≥ R_*.
In either case q lies in region I by Lemma 53.49 (c), so u(q) ≤ 5.7, and u ≤ u(q) along γ: γ lies in
region I. There τ − φ(R) increases strictly from τ0 at p, and τ increases strictly to τ0 at q. So at every point of γ
other than q, φ(R) ≤ τ − τ0 < 0, which forces R ∈ (3.5, 5.75).

*The angular displacement.* A causal vector (τ̇, Ṙ, Ω̇) satisfies

    R²|Ω̇|² ≤ f τ̇² − 2(1 − f) τ̇ Ṙ − (2 − f) Ṙ² ≤ τ̇²/(2 − f),

the right-hand bound being the maximum over Ṙ. At the points of γ other than q, μ ≥ 3/2 and 3.5 < R < 5.75, so
2 − f = 1 + μ/R² ≥ 1 + 1.5/5.75² ≥ 1.045368 and √(2 − f) ≥ 1.02243. Hence |Ω̇| ≤ τ̇/(3.5 × 1.02243) ≤ τ̇/3.5785, and the
angular displacement is at most (τ0 − τ(p))/3.5785 = −φ(R_p)/3.5785 ≤ 0.0011596/3.5785 ≤ 3.25 × 10⁻⁴.

*Σ_τ0 is acausal.* In the chart (53.45), g = −e^(2ψ) f dv̂² + 2e^ψ dv̂ dR + R² dΩ₃², so the induced metric of
Σ_τ0 = {v̂ = τ0 + R, 0.70 ≤ R ≤ b(τ0)} is e^ψ(2 − e^ψ f) dR² + R² dΩ₃². Here e^ψ f < 1 at every point of Σ_τ0: for R ≥
R_* the point lies in region I by Lemma 53.49 (c), where ψ = 0 and f = 1 − μ/R² < 1; for R ≤ R_*, e^ψ f <
1 by Proposition 53.41. Parametrise the quotient curve of Σ_τ0 by R. Along it v̂ = τ0 + R increases, so v increases
strictly, and −2e^(2σ)(du/dR)(dv/dR) = e^ψ(2 − e^ψ f) > 0, so u decreases strictly. Let a future causal curve run from p1
∈ Σ_τ0 to p2 ∈ Σ_τ0. Then v(p2) ≥ v(p1) and u(p2) ≥ u(p1), which give R(p2) ≥ R(p1) and R(p2) ≤ R(p1); so u and v take
the same values at both ends, and as they do not decrease along the curve they are constant on it. Its tangent then has
u̇ = v̇ = 0 and R²|Ω̇|² ≤ 2e^(2σ) u̇ v̇ = 0, so the curve is constant. Finally, a point p of Σ′ with R_p < R_* has
φ(R_p) = 0 and lies on Σ_τ0, so a causal curve joining it to a point q of Σ_τ0 is constant, and R_q = R_p < R_*. ∎

**Lemma 53.51** (The data on the shell.) On 𝒞_out put P := R_v, write ′ for d/dv, and let f_N := 1 −
μ/R², w := f_N/(3P) and g := 2P/f_N along 𝒞_out. For 3 ≤ v ≤ 4.5,

    R′ = P,    P′ = −𝒜/(3R²),    μ′ = 𝒜 w,    v̂′ = g,    (53.71)

with R = 13/2, P = 1/2, μ = 3/2 and v̂ = v̂_0 at v = 3 (v̂_0 as in Section B.6.4). Moreover

    w′ = 2μ/(3R³),    g′ = −4μP²/(f_N² R³),    dμ/dv̂ = (3/2) 𝒜 w².    (53.72)

(a) For 3 ≤ v ≤ 4.5: 0.47428 ≤ P ≤ 1/2, 13/2 ≤ R ≤ 29/4, 3/2 ≤ μ ≤ 3.79034, 0.91028 ≤ f_N ≤ 0.97147 and 0.60685 ≤ w ≤
0.70282.

(b) Let h := 1/80, v_k := 3 + kh, 𝒜_k := 𝒜(v_k), 𝒜′_k := 𝒜′(v_k), and

    Ã0_k := (h/2)(𝒜_k + 𝒜_(k+1)) − (h²/12)(𝒜′_(k+1) − 𝒜′_k),
    Ã1_k := (h²/2) 𝒜_(k+1) − (h²/12)(𝒜_(k+1) − 𝒜_k + h 𝒜′_(k+1)).

The rows (R_k, P_k, μ_k, v̂_k) of Section B.6.4 satisfy

    R_(k+1) = R_k + (h/2)(P_k + P_(k+1)),
    P_(k+1) = P_k − (1/3)(Ã0_k/R_k² + (1/R_(k+1)² − 1/R_k²) Ã1_k/h),
    μ_(k+1) = μ_k + w_k Ã0_k + (w_(k+1) − w_k) Ã1_k/h,    (53.73)
    v̂_(k+1) = v̂_k + (h/2)(g_k + g_(k+1)),

with w_k, g_k evaluated on row k, up to residuals r_k of modulus at most 10⁻⁸ in each line, whose sums over k = 0, …,
119 are at most 5 × 10⁻⁷ in each line.

(c) For every k, |R(v_k) − R_k| ≤ 4 × 10⁻⁶, |P(v_k) − P_k| ≤ 6 × 10⁻⁷, |μ(v_k) − μ_k| ≤ 10⁻⁵ and |v̂(v_k) − v̂_k| ≤ 4 ×
10⁻⁶.

*Proof.* On 𝒞_out, e^(2σ) = 1/2. Then (S3) gives P′ = −𝒜/(3R²); the definition of μ gives μ = R²(1 + 4R_uP), so
R_u = −f_N/(4P); (S1) gives μ′ = −(4/3)𝒜R_u = 𝒜w; and dv̂/dv = −e^(2σ)/R_u = −1/(2R_u) = g. Before the shell 𝒜 = 0,
so R = 5 + v/2, P = 1/2 and μ = 3/2, and v̂(3) = ∫_5^(13/2) 2/f_N dR = F(13/2) − F(5) = v̂_0. Next, f_N′ = −𝒜w/R² +
2μP/R³ gives w′ = (f_N′ P − f_N P′)/(3P²) = −𝒜w/(3PR²) + 2μ/(3R³) + f_N 𝒜/(9P²R²), and the first and last terms cancel
because f_N/(3P) = w. Likewise g′ = 2P′/f_N − 2P f_N′/f_N² = −2𝒜/(3R² f_N) + 2P𝒜w/(R² f_N²) − 4μP²/(R³ f_N²), and
2Pw/f_N² = 2/(3f_N) cancels the first term. Finally dμ/dv̂ = μ′/g = 𝒜w f_N/(2P) = (3/2)𝒜w².

(a) P′ ≤ 0, so P ≤ 1/2, and while P > 0, R ≥ 13/2. Then P ≥ 1/2 − (1/3) ∫𝒜/R² ≥ 1/2 − 2.7K/126.75 ≥ 0.47428, because
∫𝒜 = 3.6 × 0.75 K and K ≤ 1.2069549 by Lemma 53.47 (a). So R ≤ 13/2 + (3/2)(1/2) = 29/4. While f_N > 0,
μ′ ≥ 0 and w ≤ 1/(3 × 0.47428) ≤ 0.70282, so μ ≤ 3/2 + 0.70282 × 3.25878 ≤ 3.79034 and f_N ≥ 1 − 3.79034/42.25 ≥
0.91028 > 0; this closes the argument. The remaining bounds follow from f_N ≤ 1 − 1.5/R² ≤ 1 − 1.5/(29/4)².

(b) is a row-by-row check of Section B.6.4, with 𝒜_k and 𝒜′_k from Lemma 53.46 (a).

(c) For the true solution, let A0_k := ∫ 𝒜 and A1_k := ∫ (v − v_k) 𝒜 over [v_k, v_(k+1)]. By Lemma 53.45
(c) and (d), the true values satisfy the four lines of (53.73) with A0_k, A1_k in place of Ã0_k, Ã1_k, up
to errors τ^R_k, τ^P_k, τ^μ_k, τ^v_k with

    |τ^μ_k| ≤ (h²/8) sup|w″| A0_k,   |τ^v_k| ≤ (h³/12) sup|g″|.

On the box (a), P″ = −𝒜′/(3R²) + 2𝒜P/(3R³) gives |P″| ≤ 10.4178/126.75 + 3.6/823.875 ≤ 0.0866 (sup|𝒜′| = 4.8 sup|β′| ≤
10.4178); (R⁻²)″ = 6P²/R⁴ + 2𝒜/(3R⁵) ≤ 0.00105; w″ = 2𝒜w/(3R³) − 2μP/R⁴ gives |w″| ≤ 0.00827; and differentiating g′
with (53.71) gives |g″| ≤ 4(0.6326 + 0.1077 + 0.1535 + 0.2187)/(0.9102² × 274.625) ≤ 0.0196, the four terms
bounding μ′P², 2μP|P′|, 2μP²|f_N′|/f_N and 3μP³/R. By (53.68) applied to 𝒜 and to (v − v_k)𝒜, |A0_k −
Ã0_k| ≤ (h⁴/384) ∫|𝒜⁗| and |A1_k − Ã1_k| ≤ (h⁴/384)(4 ∫|𝒜‴| + h ∫|𝒜⁗|), integrals over the cell; summed over k, with
∫|𝒜⁗| = 3.6 (4/3)³ ∫|β⁗| ≤ 25054 and ∫|𝒜‴| = 3.6 (4/3)² ∫|β‴| ≤ 622, these are at most 1.6 × 10⁻⁶ and 1.8 × 10⁻⁷. Let
e^X_k be the true value minus the row value, for X = R, P, μ, v̂, so e_0 = 0. On the box (a), which contains the rows,

Ã1_k|. Let E^X be the largest |e^X_k|. Summing from 0 and using Σ_k (|Ã0_k| + 2|Ã1_k|/h) ≤ 6.52 (from the table) and Σ_k

#### 53.11.5 Rácz's quantities in region I

**Lemma 53.52** (Round slices of region I.) In the chart (53.70), let v̂ = V(R) be a round
slice with V′ > 0 and fV′ < 2, write μ̇ := dμ/dv̂, and put

    Ξ := V″ + (μ/R³) V′²(3 − fV′) − μ̇ V′³/(2R²).    (53.74)

Then κ′ = Ξ/(V′(2 − fV′))^(3/2) and K′^l_l = 3(fV′ − 1)/(R (V′(2 − fV′))^(1/2)), so

    κ′ K′^l_l = −c Ξ,     c := 3(1 − fV′)/(R V′² (2 − fV′)²).

On Σ_τ0 (V′ = 1, V″ = 0) this is κ = −N_κ/(2 − f)^(3/2) and K^l_l = 3(f − 1)/(R(2 − f)^(1/2)), with

    N_κ := (μ/R³)(f − 3) + μ̇/(2R²) = −2μ/R³ − μ²/R⁵ + μ̇/(2R²).

*Proof.* With T := V′∂_v̂ + ∂_R tangent to the slice, g(T, T) = V′(2 − fV′) > 0 and the normal covector dv̂ − V′dR has
g⁻¹-norm −V′(2 − fV′); let n be the unit normal with n_♭ = −(dv̂ − V′dR)/(V′(2 − fV′))^(1/2). The Christoffel symbols of
the (v̂, R) part are Γ_(v̂,v̂v̂) = −f_v̂/2, Γ_(v̂,v̂R) = −f_R/2, Γ_(R,v̂v̂) = f_R/2 and zero otherwise (first index
lowered), with f_v̂ = −μ̇/R² and f_R = 2μ/R³. With n^v̂ = V′/(V′(2 − fV′))^(1/2) and n^R = (fV′ − 1)/(V′(2 −
fV′))^(1/2), κ′ := −g(∇_T T, n)/g(T, T) has numerator V″ + f_v̂ V′³/2 + f_R V′² − (fV′ − 1) f_R V′²/2 = Ξ, divided by
(V′(2 − fV′))^(1/2) g(T, T). The trace on the spheres is K′^l_l = 3n^R/R. At V′ = 1, V″ = 0 these are the formulas of
Lemma 53.1 with ψ = 0, which fixes the signs. ∎

On Σ′ the slice is V(R) = τ0 + R + φ(R), so V′ = 1 + φ′ ∈ [0.99786, 1.00149] and V″ = φ″ by
Proposition 53.48, and Ξ = φ″ + (μ/R³)V′²(3 − fV′) − μ̇V′³/(2R²). On Σ′ ∩ {R ≥ R_*}, which lies in region I
by Lemma 53.49 (c), μ ≥ 3/2, so f ≤ 1 − 3/(2R²); with V′ ≤ 1.00149, and V′ = 1 for R ≥ 5.75, this
gives fV′ < 1 on Σ′ ∩ {R ≥ R_*}, so K′^l_l < 0 there, and κ′ > 0 exactly where Ξ > 0.

**Theorem 53.54** (Hyperbolicity margins on R ≥ R_*.) Let R_* ∈ (3.43718, 3.43719) be as in
Lemma 53.49 (b). For the background:

(a) on Σ′, κ′ > 0, K′^l_l < 0 and κ′K′^l_l ≤ −2.96 × 10⁻⁴ for R_* ≤ R ≤ 5.75, and κ′K′^l_l < 0 for R ≥ 5.75;

(b) on Σ_τ0, N_κ < 0 for R ∈ [R_*, 4.2882] ∪ [4.5310, ∞), and N_κ > 0 for R ∈ [4.2955, 4.5258].

So Rácz's split is hyperbolic on all of Σ′ ∩ {R ≥ R_*}; on Σ_τ0 ∩ {R ≥ R_*} it is hyperbolic outside [4.2882, 4.5310]
and is not hyperbolic on [4.2955, 4.5258], and each of the two remaining intervals, of widths 0.0073 and 0.0052,
contains a point where N_κ = 0.

*Proof.* By Lemma 53.49 every point concerned lies in region I, so Lemma 53.52 applies, with μ
and μ̇ those of 𝒞_out at the point's time v̂.

*Σ′ before the shell.* The points of Σ′ with R ≤ R′(3) have v̂ ≤ v̂(3), so μ = 3/2 and μ̇ = 0. Here R′(3) ≈ R′_0 =
3.8254920; by the next paragraph |R′(3) − R′_0| ≤ 5.3 × 10⁻⁶, so R′(3) < 3.82550. On [R_*, 3.5], φ = 0 and Ξ =
(1.5/R³)(2 + 1.5/R²) ≥ 0.074254, while c ≥ 3(1.5/3.5²)/(3.5 (1 + 1.5/R_*²)²) ≥ 0.082639, so κ′K′^l_l ≤ −6.1 × 10⁻³. On
[3.5, 3.82550], φ″ ≥ −0.01 l1 ≥ −0.0064382, V′ ∈ [0.99786, 1] (φ′ ≤ 0 there) and f ∈ [0.877551, 0.897504], so Ξ ≥
−0.0064382 + 0.026793 × 0.995724 × 2.102496 ≥ 0.049653 and c ≥ 0.307488/(3.8255 × 1.124327²) ≥ 0.063585, so κ′K′^l_l ≤
−3.1 × 10⁻³.

*Σ′ over the shell.* For v ∈ [3, 4.5] use Section B.6.6. The map R ↦ R + φ(R) has derivative 1 + φ′ ≥
0.9978; it sends R′(v_k) to v̂(v_k) + 0.68, which is within 4 × 10⁻⁶ of v̂_k + 0.68 by Lemma 53.51 (c),

#### 53.11.7 Γ on the seed region

On a vacuum region of the background, in the chart (v̂, R), g = −e^(2ψ) f dv̂² + 2e^ψ dv̂ dR + R² dΩ₃² with f = 1 −
μ/R², μ constant and ψ = ψ(v̂), the slice Σ_τ0 (v̂ = τ0 + R) has γ = G dR² + R² dΩ₃² with G = e^ψ(2 − e^ψ f), and
N_s√G = 1. Along it write ψ, ψ′ and ψ″ for ψ(τ0 + R) and its derivatives, q := e^ψ, 𝔲 := 1 − q, m := μ/R² and
W := qf = q(1 − m). The quantities ν, β_K, 𝔞, E, P and Γ of Theorem 53.14 are then ν = R³,
β_K = R N_κ/(3(2 − W)(W − 1)) with N_κ = (q f′/2)(W − 3) − ψ′ and f′ = 2μ/R³ (from κ0 and Y0 of
Lemma 53.1; N_κ is the quantity of Lemma 53.52, here with ψ ≠ 0 and μ̇ = 0),
𝔞 = −3(1 − β_K)/R, E = e^(∫𝔞), P = 8νE²R/G − (2νER/√G)′ RE/√G and Γ = 4νE² − P′.

**Lemma 53.55** (Γ/E² in closed form.) On such a region, wherever W < 1,

    Γ/E² = A0 + A1 ψ′ + A2 ψ′² + A3 ψ″,    (53.75)

    A0 := 4R³ n0/(q(2 − W)(1 − W)²),
    n0 := m³ − 2m(2m² − m + 1)𝔲 + (2m + 1)(3m² − 5m + 4)𝔲² − 4m(m − 1)²𝔲³ + (m − 1)³𝔲⁴,
    A1 := 2R⁴ (m(5 − m) − (1 − m)(7 + m)𝔲)/((2 − W)(1 − W)²),
    A2 := 2R⁵ (1 − m)(1 + 2W)/((2 − W)(1 − W)²),     A3 := 2R⁵ (1 − m)/((2 − W)(1 − W)).

Where ψ = 0 this is Γ/E² = 4R³μ/(R² + μ), that is Γ = 4μ/R for the normalisation E = √G/R.

*Proof.* Since E′ = 𝔞E and ν = R³, (2νER/√G)′ = E((2R⁴/√G)′ + 2𝔞R⁴/√G), so P = E²p with p := 8R⁴/G −
R(2R⁴/√G)′/√G − 2𝔞R⁵/G = (R⁵/G)(G′/G − 2𝔞), and Γ/E² = 4R³ − 2𝔞p − p′. Here G′/G = ψ′ − W′/(2 − W) with
W′ = q(ψ′f + f′), and 𝔞 = −3/R + N_κ/((2 − W)(W − 1)). Substituting, p′ contains ψ″ linearly through ψ″ in (G′/G)′
and in N_κ′ = (q/2)(ψ′f′ + f″)(W − 3) + (qf′/2)W′ − ψ″, f″ = −6μ/R⁴. Clearing the common denominator
qR⁶(2 − W)(1 − W)² and collecting the coefficients of 1, ψ′, ψ′² and ψ″, the numerator of the ψ′⁰ term becomes 4R⁹n0
after the substitution q = 1 − 𝔲, m = μ/R², which gives the stated A0, A1, A2, A3. At ψ = 0, 𝔲 = 0 and ψ′ = ψ″ = 0,
so Γ/E² = A0 = 4R³m³/((1 + m)m²) = 4R³μ/(R² + μ). Since E′ = 𝔞E fixes E only up to a constant factor, and Γ scales
with E², the last statement is for the normalisation E = √G/R, which solves E′ = 𝔞E where ψ = 0; there
E² = (R² + μ)/R⁴, and Γ = 4μ/R. ∎

**Lemma 53.56** (The reference profile.) On [0.02, 1.181], ψ_s is increasing, ψ_s′ is positive
and decreasing, and ψ_s″ is negative and increasing.

*Proof.* ψ_s‴(v̂) = 60c_5 v̂² + 24c_4 v̂ + 6c_3 has positive leading coefficient and discriminant (24c_4)² − 4(60c_5)
(6c_3) = 2.6861 × 10⁻⁴ − 3.1207 × 10⁻⁴ < 0, so ψ_s‴ > 0. Hence ψ_s″ increases, and ψ_s″(1.181) = −0.0325045 < 0. So ψ_s′
decreases, and ψ_s′(1.181) = 0.0617566 > 0. So ψ_s increases. ∎

**Proposition 53.57** (Γ on the seed region.) Let (ψ_s, μ_s) be the reference profile of
Section B.6.2 and let Γ/E² be given by (53.75) on R ∈ [0.70, 1.861].

(a) For ψ = ψ_s, ψ′ = ψ_s′, ψ″ = ψ_s″ (at τ0 + R) and μ = μ_s, Γ/E² ≥ 0.4475.

(b) For every μ with |μ − μ_s| ≤ 10⁻⁴ and every (ψ, ψ′, ψ″) with |ψ − ψ_s| ≤ 10⁻³, |ψ′ − ψ_s′| ≤ 10⁻³ and |ψ″ − ψ_s″| ≤
3 × 10⁻² at τ0 + R, Γ/E² ≥ 0.048. In particular Γ > 0 on the seed region for every background whose profile ψ past the
outgoing packet is within (10⁻³, 10⁻³, 3 × 10⁻²) of ψ_s in C² there and whose mass there is within 10⁻⁴ of μ_s.

*Proof.* Cover [0.70, 1.861] by the thirty-two cells of Section B.6.3. On a cell, by
Lemma 53.56, ψ_s, ψ_s′ and ψ_s″ range over the intervals between their values at the ends of the
cell, which lie within 5 × 10⁻⁸ of the printed end values. For (a) take the intervals between the printed end values,
each end moved outward by 5 × 10⁻⁸, and μ = μ_s; for (b) widen these intervals further by 10⁻³, 10⁻³ and 3 × 10⁻², and
take μ ∈ [μ_s − 10⁻⁴, μ_s + 10⁻⁴]. Evaluate (53.75) in the written form by Lemma 53.45
(a), with R the cell, q = e^ψ, 𝔲 = 1 − q, m = μ/R², W = q(1 − m) and 2 − W, 1 − W positive on every cell. The resulting
lower ends are columns (a) and (b); their least values are 0.456 and 0.438, which exceed 0.4475 and 0.048. ∎

By Proposition 53.40 (c), the background itself lies in the tube of (b), which gives Γ > 0 on its seed region; with
Proposition 53.42 it follows that Γ > 0 at every point of Σ_τ0 in region III, {0.70 ≤ R ≤ R_u2}, as
Corollary 53.16 uses.

## 54. The boundary at equality, I: the seed region and the layer

This chapter treats the curvature boundary x_K = 1 of Theorem 3.1 when the seed sits exactly at the threshold, μ0 =
√72 l5². There the margin of Proposition 3.3 vanishes before the shell, and the boundary is the seed's
horizon. We show that g_λ is the seed exactly on {v ≤ v_s}, v_s := inf supp env; that the boundary is spacelike for
g_λ on {v ≥ v_s + η} once λ is small; that a domain within O(λ) of D_T has an inner boundary which no future causal
curve enters; and that the spheres' horizon holds in a form valid at equality. In the layer v_s < v < v_s + η_λ
between, whose width tends to zero with λ, the boundary is not spacelike throughout: Theorem 54.26 shows that on every
column it has points where it is timelike for g_λ, alternating with points where it is spacelike on the scale of the
wavelength, and Corollary 54.27 draws the consequence that future timelike curves cross it into D_T. The mechanism is
the part of g_λ⁻¹(dΦ0, dΦ0) of first degree in the waves: its terms of order λ and λ² vanish identically, and its
term of order λ³ is a first harmonic of the phase that exceeds the margin near the edge of the envelope. The same
holds for the solutions of Theorem 3.7 (Theorem 54.33). The last sections decide the boundary's
character in most of the rest of the layer (Proposition 54.34): for fixed δ ∈ (0, 1/2] and P > 4, where the
level sup_(v′≤v) |env(v′)| is at least λ^(3−δ), near every point where it first reaches a value between λ^P and
λ^(3+δ), and, in the band between, wherever the ratio of the first-degree term to the margin is not within 2λ^(1/10)
of 1. They also give the structure of the expansion in λ (Proposition 54.36) and write the threshold λ_L of
Theorem 54.26 as an explicit formula. The very edge of the layer is the subject of Chapter 55.

Throughout, μ0 = √72 l5², and the notation is that of Chapter 2, Chapter 4, Chapter 5,
Chapter 6 and Chapter 7. The phase is θ and the polar angle of S³ is ϑ.

### 54.1 The setting at equality

In the coordinates (v, r, ϑ, φ1, φ2) of (2.4),

    g0 = −F dv² + 2 dv dr + r² γ,      F := 1 − μ(v)/r²,    (54.1)

F being the function f of (2.4), and μ(v) = μ0 + (2/9) A² ∫_(−∞)^v env², so μ′ = (2/9) A² env² ≥ 0
((2.14)). Since √72 l5² = μ0, the curvature boundary is r = r_q(v) with

    r_q(v) = (μ0 μ(v))^(1/4),      Φ0 := r − r_q(v),

and the boundary is {Φ0 = 0}. Put v_s := inf supp env. Then v_s ≥ v_start and μ = μ0 on {v ≤ v_s}.

*The construction depends on v_start only through the support of env.* The hypotheses of Theorem 3.1 hold with
v_start replaced by v_s: env ∈ C_c^∞([v_s, v_end]), μ = μ0 on {v ≤ v_s}, and v_s − τ0 ≥ v_start − τ0 > √μ0 + 1. The
domain Ω of (2.8) and the constants λ0, C of Theorem 3.1 do not involve v_start. The stage data of
Lemma 7.4 and the correction U of Proposition 7.7 are solved outward in r from zero data at r = a,
with forcing terms that vanish where the earlier stages and the waves vanish, and every stage of the approximant
vanishes on {v ≤ v_s}; both facts are contained in the bounds of Lemma 54.18 below, whose right sides carry a
factor ε_c(v), zero for v ≤ v_s. So the metric g_λ of Theorem 3.1 is the same whether v_start or v_s is used, and λ0,
C and Ω are its constants and domain. Its data on Σ_τ0 ∩ {r < v_s − τ0} are those of the seed, as a metric together
with its first τ-derivative, and not only as Cauchy data: there U = 0 and the approximant is g0, the lapse and shift of
g_λ are those of G(X, u/λ), which is g0 there, and the τ-derivatives of lapse and shift are fixed by D(g) = 0 with
invertible coefficient (Section 7.5), which g0 satisfies.

By items 4 and 5 of Theorem 3.1, |g_λ − g0| ≤ C λ, D(g_λ) = 0 and Ric(g_λ) = 0 on Ω. Since g0⁻¹ is bounded on the
compact Ω and inversion is smooth, after shrinking λ0 so that C λ0 ≤ 1 there is C1 with

    |(g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹)(α, α)| ≤ C1 λ |α|_e²     on Ω, for every covector α,    (54.2)

where |α|_e is the Euclidean norm of the Cartesian components of α. The vector field Y := −g0⁻¹ dτ is uniformly
timelike for g0 on Ω, and, λ0 being shrunk once more, future timelike for g_λ. Put B := 1 + sup |r_q′|, the
supremum over the v-range of D_T. For a covector α = dr − β dv with |β| ≤ B, the Cartesian components are
α = −β dτ + (1 − β) x̂·dx, since dv = dτ + x̂·dx and dr = x̂·dx, so |α|_e² = β² + (1 − β)² ≤ B² + (1 + B)², and by
(54.2)

    |g_λ⁻¹(α, α) − g0⁻¹(α, α)| ≤ C_Φ λ,      C_Φ := C1 (B² + (1 + B)²).    (54.3)

**Lemma 54.1** (g0 at equality.) (a) For Φ = r − ρ(v), on {r = ρ}, g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) = F(ρ) − 2ρ′. For ρ = r_q
this is (3.1), and

    m0(v) := −g0⁻¹(dΦ0, dΦ0) = √(μ/μ0) − 1 + r_q μ′/(2μ),      2 r_q′ = r_q μ′/(2μ).    (54.4)

(b) m0 = 0 on {v ≤ v_s}, m0 > 0 on {v > v_s}, and m0 ≥ δ_η := √(μ(v_s + η)/μ0) − 1 > 0 on {v ≥ v_s + η}, for η > 0.

(c) m0 and all its derivatives vanish at v = v_s.

(d) For every future causal vector X of g0, dv(X) ≥ 0 and dr(X) ≤ (F/2) dv(X).

(e) Y = −g0⁻¹ dτ is future timelike for g0, and for Φ = r − ρ(v), dΦ(Y) = −μ/r² − ρ′; so dΦ(Y) < 0 when ρ′ ≥ 0.

*Proof.* (a) The inverse of (54.1) has g0^(vv) = 0, g0^(vr) = 1 and g0^(rr) = F, so for dΦ = dr − ρ′ dv,
g0⁻¹(dΦ, dΦ) = F − 2ρ′. At equality μ/r_q² = μ/(μ0 μ)^(1/2) = (μ/μ0)^(1/2), so F(r_q) = 1 − √(μ/μ0), and r_q′ =
(1/4)(μ0 μ)^(−3/4) μ0 μ′ = r_q μ′/(4μ).

(b) On {v ≤ v_s}, μ = μ0 and μ′ = 0, so m0 = 0. For v > v_s, env does not vanish identically on (v_s, v): otherwise
env = 0 on the open set (−∞, v), and v_s ∉ supp env. So μ(v) − μ0 = (2/9) A² ∫_(v_s)^v env² > 0. As μ′ ≥ 0, μ is
nondecreasing, and m0(v) ≥ √(μ(v)/μ0) − 1 ≥ δ_η for v ≥ v_s + η.

(c) env vanishes on (−∞, v_s), so env and all its derivatives vanish at v_s; hence so do μ − μ0, μ′ and all their
derivatives, and with them every derivative of m0.

(d) Write X = X^v ∂_v + X^r ∂_r + X_ang. Then g0(X, X) = −F (X^v)² + 2 X^v X^r + r² |X_ang|²_γ ≤ 0, and
dτ(X) = X^v − X^r > 0, since dτ = dv − dr and X is future directed. If X^v = 0, then |X_ang| = 0 and X^r < 0. If
X^v < 0, then X^r < X^v < 0, so 2 X^v X^r > 2 (X^v)² > F (X^v)², as F < 1, and g0(X, X) > 0, a contradiction. So
X^v ≥ 0, with X^v = 0 only for X a positive multiple of −∂_r; and for X^v > 0 the inequality 2 X^v X^r ≤ F (X^v)² gives
X^r ≤ F X^v/2. The bound is attained by the outgoing null direction ∂_v + (F/2) ∂_r.

(e) By Proposition 2.5 (d), g0⁻¹(dτ, dτ) = −1 − μ/r² < 0, so Y is timelike, and dτ(Y) = 1 + μ/r² > 0. With
g0⁻¹(dτ, dr) = μ/r² and g0⁻¹(dτ, dv) = −1 (Lemma 2.6 (c)), dΦ(Y) = −g0⁻¹(dτ, dr) + ρ′ g0⁻¹(dτ, dv) = −μ/r² − ρ′. ∎

### 54.2 The seed region is exact

**Proposition 54.2** (The seed region.) g_λ = g0 on Ω ∩ {v ≤ v_s}. In particular g_λ − g0 and all
its derivatives vanish on Ω ∩ {v = v_s}, and on Ω ∩ {v ≤ v_s} the metric g_λ is the five-dimensional
Schwarzschild–Tangherlini metric of mass μ0, the seed.

*Proof.* Let R := Ω ∩ {v ≤ v_s}, a compact set, and u := g_λ − g0 on R. On R, μ′ = 0, so Ric(g0) = 0, and Ric^H(g0) =
Ric(g0) = 0 since D(g0) = 0 (Section 2.4). D(g_λ) = 0 and Ric(g_λ) = 0 give Ric^H(g_λ) = 0. Subtracting the
equations (2.9) for the two metrics,

    −(1/2) g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b u = (1/2)(g_λ^(ab) − g0^(ab)) ∂_a ∂_b g_λ − Q(X; g_λ)(∂g_λ, ∂g_λ) + Q(X; g0)(∂g0, ∂g0) =: f.

Here g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ = −g_λ⁻¹ u g0⁻¹, and Q is a polynomial in ∂g with coefficients rational in g and smooth in X. Writing
the difference of the Q-terms as ∫_0^1 (d/ds) Q(X; g0 + s u)(∂(g0 + s u), ∂(g0 + s u)) ds, with g0 + s u Lorentzian
and in a compact set for λ ≤ λ0 (|u| ≤ C λ), gives |f| ≤ K_λ (|u| + |∂u|) on R, with K_λ finite for each λ, since ∂²g_λ
is bounded on the compact R.

The data vanish: Σ_τ0 ∩ R = {τ = τ0, a ≤ r ≤ v_s − τ0}, where (g_λ, ∂_τ g_λ) = (g0, ∂_τ g0) for r < v_s − τ0
(Section 54.1) and, by continuity, at r = v_s − τ0. Run the proof of Lemma 5.5 on R in place of Ω, with
g̃ := g0 and the multiplier Y = −g0⁻¹ dτ. The boundary of R ∩ {τ0 ≤ τ′ ≤ τ} consists of Σ_τ0 ∩ R, Σ_τ ∩ R, parts of
∂Ω other than Σ_τ0, which are spacelike with Ω, hence R, to their past (Lemma 2.6), and a part of the hypersurface
{v = v_s}. That part is null for g0 (dv is null, Proposition 2.5 (c)), and R lies to its past, since v does not
decrease along future causal curves (Lemma 54.1 (d)). The flux of the energy current J = T(Y, ·) through it is
∫ T(Y, N) ≥ 0, N its future null generator, by the dominant energy property of T_ab = ∂_a u ∂_b u − (1/2) g0_ab
g0(du, du) for the future causal vectors Y and N; so this flux is dropped, as the fluxes through the spacelike parts
are. The slice R ∩ Σ_τ is {a ≤ r ≤ v_s − τ}, since R does not meet the outer face of Ω, and its outer radius decreases
with τ, so the boundary term in ∂_τ ‖u‖² is at most 0. Hence (5.10) holds on R:

    ‖∂u(τ)‖ + ‖u(τ)‖ ≤ C (‖∂u(τ0)‖ + ‖u(τ0)‖ + ∫_(τ0)^τ ‖f‖) ≤ C K_λ ∫_(τ0)^τ (‖∂u‖ + ‖u‖),

the norms on R ∩ Σ_τ, and Gronwall's inequality gives u = 0 on R. The derivatives of u vanish on Ω ∩ {v = v_s} because
u is smooth on Ω and vanishes on Ω ∩ {v < v_s}, whose closure contains Ω ∩ {v = v_s}. ∎

So g_app = g0 and w = 0 on R. Here the principal part of the difference equation is g0 and the face {v = v_s} is
exactly null for it, so no tilt of that face is needed.

### 54.3 The boundary

**Proposition 54.3** (The boundary at equality.) (a) On {v ≤ v_s} the boundary {Φ0 = 0} is {r = √μ0},
the seed's horizon, null for g_λ. A future causal curve of g_λ that starts in {r ≤ √μ0} stays there while v ≤ v_s:
nothing crosses this portion from inside to outside.

(b) For η > 0 put λ_η := min(λ0, δ_η/(2 C_Φ)). For λ ≤ λ_η the boundary is spacelike for g_λ on {v ≥ v_s + η}, with
g_λ⁻¹(dΦ0, dΦ0) ≤ −δ_η/2, and every future causal curve of g_λ that meets it there leaves D_T there.

(c) For each λ, the portion of the boundary on which these bounds do not decide its causal character lies in the
*layer* v_s < v < v_s + η_λ, where η_λ := inf{η > 0 : δ_η ≥ 2 C_Φ λ}, that is μ(v_s + η_λ) = μ0 (1 + 2 C_Φ λ)²; and
η_λ → 0 as λ → 0.

*Proof.* (a) By Proposition 54.2, g_λ = g0 there; r_q = √μ0 since μ = μ0, and (54.4) gives m0 = 0:
the boundary is null. By Lemma 54.1 (d), along a future causal curve in Ω ∩ {v ≤ v_s}, dr ≤ (F/2) dv with dv ≥ 0
and F = 1 − μ0/r² < 0 for r < √μ0. So where r < √μ0, r does not increase, and a curve from {r < √μ0} stays in {r ≤
r(start)}. From a point with r = √μ0, put f := r − √μ0; where f > 0 and f is small, F ≤ 2f/√μ0, so df ≤ (f/√μ0) dv,
and f₊ e^(−v/√μ0) does not increase along the curve. It starts at 0, so f ≤ 0 while v ≤ v_s.

(b) For v ≥ v_s + η, by (54.3) with β = r_q′ and Lemma 54.1 (b), g_λ⁻¹(dΦ0, dΦ0) ≤ −m0 + C_Φ λ ≤ −δ_η +
δ_η/2. A covector timelike for g_λ has one sign on the future causal cone of g_λ, and the sign is that of dΦ0(Y) < 0
(Lemma 54.1 (e), with ρ′ = r_q′ ≥ 0; Y is future timelike for g_λ). So Φ0 decreases strictly along every future
causal curve near that portion of the boundary, and a future causal curve that meets it there leaves D_T = {Φ0 ≥ 0} ∩
{v ≤ v_end + T}.

(c) δ_η is continuous, nondecreasing in η, and tends to 0 as η ↓ 0, because μ is continuous and nondecreasing with
μ(v_s) = μ0. So η_λ is well defined once 2 C_Φ λ ≤ δ_η at η = v_end − v_s, which λ ≤ λ0 may be assumed to give, and
η_λ → 0 as λ → 0. ∎

**Proposition 54.4** (A domain whose inner boundary nothing enters.) Put κ* := 2 μ(v_end)^(1/4)/μ0^(3/4),
η* := 1/κ*, c_σ := 2 C_Φ, and for λ ≤ λ* := min(λ0, 1/c_σ, δ_(η*)/(6 C_Φ))

    σ_λ(v) := c_σ λ min((v − v_s)₊, η*),      D_T^λ := {v ≤ v_end + T, r ≥ r_q(v) + σ_λ(v)}.    (54.5)

Then D_T^λ ⊂ D_T ⊂ {x_K ≤ 1}, D_T ∖ D_T^λ ⊂ {r_q(v) ≤ r < r_q(v) + c_σ λ η*}, and no future causal curve of g_λ in Ω
enters D_T^λ through its inner boundary {Φ_σ = 0}, Φ_σ := r − r_q(v) − σ_λ(v). The portion of that boundary on {v ≤ v_s}
is the seed's horizon (Proposition 54.3 (a)), and on {v > v_s} it is spacelike for g_λ, uniformly on
{v ≥ v_s + η*}.

*Proof.* Since σ_λ′ ≤ c_σ λ ≤ 1, B bounds |r_q′ + σ_λ′|, so (54.3) applies to dΦ_σ. On the pieces where σ_λ
is smooth, Lemma 54.1 (a) with ρ = r_q + σ, σ := σ_λ, gives at Φ_σ = 0

    g0⁻¹(dΦ_σ, dΦ_σ) = F(ρ) − 2 r_q′ − 2σ′ = −m0(v) + μ (1/r_q² − 1/ρ²) − 2σ′ ≤ −m0(v) + κ* σ − 2σ′.    (54.6)

Indeed 1/r_q² − 1/ρ² = σ(ρ + r_q)/(r_q² ρ²) ≤ 2σ/r_q³, since (ρ + r_q)/ρ² ≤ 2/ρ ≤ 2/r_q; and at equality 2μ/r_q³ =
2μ/(μ0 μ)^(3/4) = 2 μ^(1/4)/μ0^(3/4) ≤ κ*. On v_s < v < v_s + η*: σ′ = c_σ λ and κ* σ ≤ κ* c_σ λ η* = c_σ λ, so
g_λ⁻¹(dΦ_σ, dΦ_σ) ≤ −m0 + c_σ λ − 2 c_σ λ + C_Φ λ = −m0 − C_Φ λ ≤ −C_Φ λ. On v > v_s + η*: σ′ = 0 and κ* σ = c_σ λ, so
g_λ⁻¹(dΦ_σ, dΦ_σ) ≤ −δ_(η*) + 2 C_Φ λ + C_Φ λ ≤ −δ_(η*)/2, by λ ≤ δ_(η*)/(6 C_Φ). On v ≤ v_s, σ = 0 and
Proposition 54.3 (a) applies.

*No entry.* Let γ be a future causal curve of g_λ in Ω with Φ_σ < 0 at its start and Φ_σ ≥ 0 at some later parameter;
let s* be the first such parameter and p := γ(s*), so Φ_σ(p) = 0 and Φ_σ < 0 on γ before s*. Each smooth piece of Φ_σ,
extended a little past its v-interval, keeps a g_λ-timelike differential near p when v(p) > v_s, by continuity of the
margins above, with dΦ(Z) < 0 for future causal Z (the sign of dΦ(Y), Lemma 54.1 (e)). Near the corner v = v_s +
η*, Φ_σ is the larger of its two pieces; near v = v_s, r = √μ0, it is the smaller of Φ0 and Φ1 := Φ0 − c_σ λ (v −
v_s). If v(p) > v_s: the maximum of two functions strictly decreasing along γ near p is strictly decreasing, so
Φ_σ(γ(s)) > 0 for s < s* close to s*, a contradiction. If v(p) < v_s: γ cannot pass from {v > v_s} into {v < v_s},
since on {v ≤ v_s}, where g_λ = g0, v does not decrease (Lemma 54.1 (d)); so γ lies in {v < v_s} on an interval
before s*, where Φ_σ = Φ0 < 0, that is r < √μ0, and r does not increase there (Proposition 54.3 (a)): r(p) < √μ0,
a contradiction. If v(p) = v_s: g_λ⁻¹(dΦ1, dΦ1) = −2 c_σ λ < 0 at p (m0 = 0, σ = 0 and g_λ = g0 there), so Φ1
decreases strictly along γ near p. Points of γ before p with v > v_s would have Φ_σ = Φ1 > Φ1(p) = 0, which is
impossible; so γ approaches p within {v ≤ v_s}, where Φ_σ = Φ0 < 0, that is r < √μ0, and r does not increase there:
r(p) < √μ0, a contradiction. ∎

The statement concerns the inner boundary only; the face {v = v_end + T} of D_T^λ is not treated.

**Remark 54.5** (What the bounds of Theorem 3.1 leave open.) On v_s < v < v_s + η_λ the margin m0 and
the perturbation g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ both vanish to every order at v = v_s (Lemma 54.1 (c), Proposition 54.2).
Theorem 3.1 bounds the perturbation by C λ, uniformly in v, while deciding the sign of g_λ⁻¹(dΦ0, dΦ0) needs a bound by
a fraction of m0, pointwise in v near v_s. The sections from Section 54.5 on obtain the part of the
perturbation of first degree in the waves exactly and bound the rest by the margin's own order.

### 54.4 The spheres' horizon at equality

Let C_θ be the constant C3 of (8.9) in the proof of Proposition 3.4, so that on the columns the
functions θ⁺_λ − θ⁺_0 and ∂_r(θ⁺_λ − θ⁺_0) are at most C_θ λ in absolute value, θ⁺_0 := θ⁺(g0); let R_max be the
largest r on the columns, c_θ := 3/(R_max² + μ(v_end)), and C_h := C_θ/c_θ.

**Proposition 54.6** (The spheres' horizon at equality.) Let K ≥ 6 and λ ≤ λ_H (Proposition 3.4), λ
small.

(a) On every column (v and x̂ fixed, within D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}) θ⁺_λ has at most one zero, positive above it and negative
below; every zero lies within C_h λ of √μ(v); the spheres with r ≥ √μ(v) + C_h λ are untrapped and those with r_q(v)
≤ r ≤ √μ(v) − C_h λ are trapped.

(b) On the columns with v ≤ v_s, θ⁺_λ = θ⁺_0 exactly: its one zero is r = √μ0, the lower end of the column on the
boundary, and every sphere of the column above it is untrapped.

(c) On the columns that reach across √μ(v) + C_h λ and have √μ(v) − r_q(v) ≥ C′ λ, for any C′ > C_θ μ(v_end)/3,
θ⁺_λ has exactly one zero.

*Proof.* By (8.6), θ⁺_0 = 3(r² − μ)/(r(r² + μ)), so |θ⁺_0(r)| = 3 |r − √μ| (r + √μ)/(r(r² + μ)) ≥
c_θ |r − √μ| on the column, as (r + √μ)/r ≥ 1. (a) θ⁺_λ ≥ c_θ (r − √μ) − C_θ λ > 0 for r > √μ + C_h λ, and θ⁺_λ ≤
−c_θ (√μ − r) + C_θ λ < 0 for r < √μ − C_h λ. Near √μ, ∂_r θ⁺_0 = 3/μ at r = √μ, so ∂_r θ⁺_0 ≥ 3/(2μ(v_end)) on a fixed
neighbourhood of √μ, which contains [√μ − C_h λ, √μ + C_h λ] for λ small; there ∂_r θ⁺_λ ≥ 3/(2μ(v_end)) − C_θ λ > 0.
So θ⁺_λ has at most one zero, with the signs stated. Nothing in this uses r_q < √μ. (b) is Proposition 54.2: on
Ω ∩ {v ≤ v_s}, g_λ = g0. (c) With d_h := √μ − r_q ∈ [0, √μ], the identity

    −θ⁺_0(r_q) − 3 d_h/μ = 3 d_h² (μ + √μ r_q + r_q²)/(μ r_q (μ + r_q²))

holds: −θ⁺_0(r_q) = 3 d_h (√μ + r_q)/(r_q (r_q² + μ)), and (√μ + r_q) μ − r_q (r_q² + μ) = μ√μ − r_q³ =
d_h (μ + √μ r_q + r_q²). The right side is nonnegative, so θ⁺_λ(r_q) ≤ −3 d_h/μ + C_θ λ ≤ −3 C′ λ/μ(v_end) + C_θ λ < 0,
while θ⁺_λ > 0 at √μ + C_h λ; the intermediate value theorem and (a) give exactly one zero. ∎

So at equality item 6 of Theorem 3.1 holds in this form: exactly one zero on the columns with v ≤ v_s (at the boundary
itself) and on those with √μ(v) − r_q(v) ≥ C′ λ, a condition that fails only on a set of v whose width tends to 0 with
λ; at most one zero, within C_h λ of √μ(v), everywhere.

### 54.5 The layer: setting

We use the coordinates (v, r, ϑ, φ1, φ2) of (54.1); there ∂_v is the Cartesian ∂_τ (v = τ + r) and ℓ = g0⁻¹ dv =
∂_r (Section 4.4). Put

    Φ0♯ := g0⁻¹ dΦ0 = ∂_v + β_Φ ∂_r,      β_Φ := F(r_q) − r_q′ = 1 − √(μ/μ0) − r_q μ′/(4μ).

The hypersurface {Φ0 = 0} is timelike at a point exactly when dΦ0 is spacelike there, g_λ⁻¹(dΦ0, dΦ0) > 0. The *seed*
is g0° := g0 with μ replaced by μ0, the Schwarzschild–Tangherlini metric of mass μ0; it is vacuum, and g0 = g0° on
{v ≤ v_s}.

The metric g_λ of Theorem 3.1 is g_app + w, with g_app = g0 + λ [g1] + Σ_(j=2)^N λ^j [g_j], N = K + 3, the
fixed-phase form of Theorem 4.11 built with the stage data of Lemma 7.4 (stage N's included). Write
k := g_λ − g0 and, for an integer c ≥ 0,

    E(v) := sup_(v′≤v) |env(v′)|,      ε_c(v) := Σ_(i≤c) sup_(v′≤v) |env^(i)(v′)|,    (54.7)

both continuous, nondecreasing and zero for v ≤ v_s. E is the *level* of the envelope, and E = ε_0; no sign of env is
assumed. A quantity is *of degree at least two* if, with μ − μ0 counted as of degree two, it is a sum of products of at
least two factors of the form A env^(i) times smooth coefficients. A profile H(v, r, ϑ) e^(iθ), H complex, is the
complex form of a first harmonic of the phase, and its real part is meant.
We write ĝ_1 := W = W_TT + χ dv ⊗ dv, so that the oscillating profiles of the ansatz (4.10) are ĝ_1, …, ĝ_(N+1).

**Definition 54.7** (The class 𝔖.) A symmetric 2-tensor h, invariant under T² and both reflections, is
in the class 𝔖 if h_vv = h_vr = h_rr = 0 and γ^(AB) h_AB = 0, A, B running over the angular coordinates. Its remaining
components are h_vϑ, h_rϑ and the γ-traceless angular ones; every h in 𝔖 has tr_(g0) h = 0.

Put v_♯ := v_s + min(1, T). For v ≤ v_♯ let Ω_v := Ω ∩ {v′ ≤ v} and N_v := Ω ∩ {v′ = v}. On Ω ∩ {v ≤ v_♯} the outer
face of Ω is not met, since there v = V + 1 + τ_end − τ ≥ V + 1. N_v is null for g0 (dv is null, Proposition 2.5 (c)),
and Ω_v lies to its past (Lemma 54.1 (d)). For X ∈ Ω let γ_X be the integral curve of ℓ from X: in (v, r, x̂) it
is r ↦ (v(X), r, x̂(X)), r ≥ r(X), and it meets Σ_τ0 at X_Σ := (v(X), v(X) − τ0, x̂(X)) inside Ω (Lemma 2.6 (d)).
Since v is constant along γ_X, every bound weighted by ε_c(v) holds with the same weight along the whole curve.

*Constants.* In this and the following sections C denotes a constant depending on N, the order of differentiation, Ω
(through a, δ0, b(τ0) and τ_end − τ0), μ0, A, finitely many norms sup |env^(i)|, the bounds of the profiles of
Theorem 4.11 and of the stage data of Lemma 7.4 on Ω × S¹ (each smooth with all derivatives bounded
independently of λ), the constants of Theorem 6.1 and of Step 1 of its proof, and C1 of (54.2);
never on λ, v, v1 or the point.

### 54.6 The seed's operators on one harmonic

In (v, r, ϑ, φ1, φ2), with F° := 1 − μ0/r² and Γ̊ the Christoffel symbols of the round metric γ, the Christoffel
symbols of g0° that do not vanish are

    Γ^v_vv = μ0/r³,   Γ^r_vv = F° μ0/r³,   Γ^r_rv = −μ0/r³,   Γ^v_AB = −r γ_AB,   Γ^r_AB = −r F° γ_AB,
    Γ^A_rB = δ^A_B/r,   Γ^A_BC = Γ̊^A_BC;    (54.8)

in particular Γ^A_(av) = 0 for every index a, and Γ^v_(rv) = Γ^v_(rr) = Γ^r_(rr) = 0. Each is read from Γ^σ_ab = (1/2)
g^(σd)(∂_a g_db + ∂_b g_da − ∂_d g_ab) with g_vv = −F°, g_vr = 1, g_rr = 0, g_AB = r² γ_AB and g^vv = 0, g^vr = 1,
g^rr = F°; for instance Γ^r_rv = (1/2) ∂_r g_vv = −μ0/r³ and Γ^v_AB = −(1/2) ∂_r g_AB.

For a symmetric 2-tensor h let

    Pol(h) := h(ℓ, ·) − (1/2) dv tr h,      D_X(h) := div h − (1/2) d tr h,      𝒯 h := −i (∇_ℓ h + (3/(2r)) h),
    R_X(h) := −(1/2) □h + 𝔚(h),      𝔚(h)_mn := −R_m^a_n^b h_ab,    (54.9)

∇, □ = ∇^a ∇_a, div, tr and the Riemann tensor R being those of g0°, indices moved by g0°.

**Lemma 54.8** (The seed's operators.) Let dRic^H and dD be the linearisations at g0° of Ric^H and
D, with the gauge taken relative to g0° (Section 2.4). Let H be a symmetric 2-tensor whose components in (v, r, ϑ,
φ1, φ2) are functions of (v, r, ϑ) and with H_(vφi) = H_(rφi) = H_(ϑφi) = H_(φ1φ2) = 0, and let k ≥ 1 be an integer.

(a) dRic^H(h) = −(1/2) □h + 𝔚(h) and dD(h) = div h − (1/2) d tr h, the latter with its index lowered.

(b) dRic^H(H e^(ikv/λ)) = e^(ikv/λ) (λ⁻¹ k 𝒯H + R_X H) and dD(H e^(ikv/λ)) = e^(ikv/λ) (λ⁻¹ i k Pol(H) + D_X H): there
is no term of order λ⁻².

(c) Componentwise, with Λ := 3/(2r),

    (𝒯H)_vv = −i(∂_r H_vv + Λ H_vv + 2μ0 H_vr/r³),     (𝒯H)_vr = −i(∂_r H_vr + Λ H_vr + μ0 H_rr/r³),
    (𝒯H)_rr = −i(∂_r + Λ) H_rr,      (𝒯H)_vϑ = −i(∂_r H_vϑ + H_vϑ/(2r) + μ0 H_rϑ/r³),
    (𝒯H)_rϑ = −i(∂_r + 1/(2r)) H_rϑ,      (𝒯H)_AB = −i(∂_r − 1/(2r)) H_AB   (A, B angular);
    Pol(H)_v = −(1/2)(F° H_rr + r⁻² γ^(AB) H_AB),   Pol(H)_r = H_rr,   Pol(H)_ϑ = H_rϑ.    (54.10)

(d) If h is in 𝔖, then (dRic^H h)_vv = 0 and tr dRic^H h = 0; the same holds for R_X h.

(e) If h has only angular components, then (□h)_vA = 0 and 𝔚(h)_vA = 0 for every angular A.

*Proof.* (a) At a vacuum metric, with D(g0°) = 0 and the gauge relative to g0°, the variation of the Christoffel symbols
is δΓ^ρ_ab = (1/2)(∇_a h^ρ_b + ∇_b h^ρ_a − ∇^ρ h_ab), so dD^ρ = g0°^(ab) δΓ^ρ_ab = ∇_a h^(aρ) − (1/2) ∇^ρ tr h. The
variation of Ricci is ∇_ρ δΓ^ρ_mn − ∇_n δΓ^ρ_(ρm). Commuting the derivatives in ∇_ρ ∇_m h^ρ_n by the Ricci identity, and
using Ric(g0°) = 0, it equals (1/2)(∇_m dD_n + ∇_n dD_m) − (1/2) □h_mn − R_m^a_n^b h_ab. The variation of the gauge term
of (2.9) at D = 0 is (1/2)(∇_m dD_n + ∇_n dD_m), since ∇̂ = ∇ at g0°. The difference is (a).

(b) For h = H e^(ikv/λ), ∇_a h = (∇_a H + i k λ⁻¹ (∂_a v) H) e^(ikv/λ), and g0°⁻¹(dv, dv) = 0 (Proposition 2.5 (c)) and
□v = 3/r (Section 4.4). Hence

    □(H e^(ikv/λ)) = e^(ikv/λ) (□H + i k λ⁻¹ (2 ∇_ℓ H + (3/r) H)),

with no λ⁻² term, and the zeroth-order term 𝔚 and the first-order dD are expanded in the same way; dD(h) has λ⁻¹ part
i k (H(ℓ, ·) − (1/2) dv tr H). This is (b).

(c) For an angular index A, B, and a, b ∈ {v, r}, (∇_ℓ H)_ab = ∂_r H_ab − Γ^c_(ra) H_cb − Γ^c_(rb) H_ac. By
(54.8) the only symbols with a lower index r are Γ^r_rv = −μ0/r³ and Γ^A_rB = δ^A_B/r. So (∇_ℓ H)_vv =
∂_r H_vv + 2μ0 H_vr/r³, (∇_ℓ H)_vr = ∂_r H_vr + μ0 H_rr/r³, (∇_ℓ H)_rr = ∂_r H_rr, (∇_ℓ H)_vϑ = ∂_r H_vϑ + μ0 H_rϑ/r³ −
H_vϑ/r, (∇_ℓ H)_rϑ = ∂_r H_rϑ − H_rϑ/r and (∇_ℓ H)_AB = ∂_r H_AB − 2 H_AB/r; adding (3/(2r)) H gives the list. For Pol,
H(ℓ, ·) = H(∂_r, ·), and tr H = 2 H_vr + F° H_rr + r⁻² γ^(AB) H_AB, since g0°^(vv) = 0, g0°^(vr) = 1, g0°^(rr) = F°.

(d) The component (𝔚 h)_vv is −R_(vavb) h^(ab). For h in 𝔖 the raised components h^(vv), h^(vr), h^(rr) vanish (they
are built from h_rr, h_vr, h_vv through g^vv = 0), so only h^(vA), h^(rA), h^(AB) remain. g0° is a warped product of
the (v, r) plane with the round S³, invariant under O(4) acting on the spheres; at a point, the isotropy group O(3)
acts on the angular indices, and −1 ∈ O(3) changes the sign of a component with an odd number of angular indices. So
R_(vvvA) = R_(vrvA) = 0, and R_(vAvB) is an O(3)-invariant bilinear form on the tangent space of the sphere, a multiple
of γ_AB. Hence (𝔚 h)_vv = −R_(vAvB) h^(AB) = 0, since h^(AB) is γ-traceless. For □: (∇_b h)_vv = ∂_b h_vv − 2 Γ^c_(bv)
h_cv = −2 Γ^A_(bv) h_Av = 0, and (∇_b h)_rv = −Γ^A_(br) h_Av − Γ^A_(bv) h_rA, which vanishes for b ∈ {v, r}. Then
(∇_a ∇_b h)_vv = −2 Γ^c_(av) (∇_b h)_cv, since (∇h)_vv vanishes identically. The symbols Γ^c_(av) vanish unless a and
c lie in {v, r}, and then g0°^(ab) ≠ 0 forces b ∈ {v, r}, where (∇_b h)_vv = (∇_b h)_rv = 0. So (□h)_vv = 0.
For the trace: g0° is parallel, so tr □h = □ tr h = 0 for h in 𝔖, and tr 𝔚(h) = −Ric(g0°)^(ab) h_ab = 0. These are
statements about every h in 𝔖, so they hold for dRic^H(h) and, applied to H e^(iv/λ) with H in 𝔖, order by order in λ:
for R_X H as well as for 𝒯H.

(e) By the same parity, (𝔚h)_vA = −R_(vBAC) h^(BC) = 0, three of its four indices being angular. For h with only angular
components, (∇_c h)_(vA) = −Γ^E_(cv) h_EA = 0 for every c; (∇_b h)_(vv) = (∇_b h)_(vr) = 0; and (∇_b h)_(rA) =
−Γ^E_(br) h_EA vanishes unless b is angular. In (∇_a ∇_b h)_vA = −Γ^d_(av) (∇_b h)_dA − Γ^d_(aA) (∇_b h)_vd every term
then vanishes after contraction with g0°^(ab): the first because Γ^d_(av) ≠ 0 only for a ∈ {v, r}, where g^(ab) has no
angular b, and the second because (∇_b h)_vd = 0. So (□h)_vA = 0. ∎

Write R_X H also for the λ⁰ part of dRic^H(H e^(iv/λ)) when H depends on v; then ∂_v acts on H, and R_X contains the
derivative ∂_v H through −(1/2) □H (Proposition 54.36 (a)).

**Lemma 54.9** (The Bianchi identity at one harmonic, and propagation of the gauge.) Let H_1, …, H_J be
as in Lemma 54.8, put H_0 := H_(J+1) := 0 and

    Z_j := 𝒯H_j + R_X H_(j−1),      G_j := i Pol(H_(j+1)) + D_X H_j.

(a) For every j ≥ 1, with H_(−1) := 0 and G_(−1) := 0,

    i Pol(Z_j) + div Gt(Z_(j−1)) = −i (∇_ℓ + 3/(2r)) G_(j−1) − (1/2) □G_(j−2),    (54.11)

where Gt(Y) := Y − (1/2)(tr Y) g0° and G_j is a covector.

(b) If Z_j = 0 for j ≤ J and G_j = 0 at Σ_τ0 (at r = v − τ0, on every generator) for j ≤ J − 1, then G_j = 0 on Ω
for j ≤ J − 1.

*Proof.* (a) For every metric, div_g Gt(Ric^H(g)) = −B_g[D(g)] by (7.1). Linearise at g0°, where
Ric^H(g0°) = 0 and D(g0°) = 0: div Gt(dRic^H(h)) = −B_(g0°)[dD(h)], and at g0°, with S(V)_mn = (1/2)(∇_m V_n + ∇_n
V_m), B_(g0°)[V]_n = div Gt(S(V))_n = (1/2) □V_n + (1/2)(∇^m ∇_n V_m − ∇_n ∇^m V_m) = (1/2) □V_n + (1/2) Ric_nm V^m =
(1/2) □V_n. Apply this to h := Σ_(j=1)^J λ^j H_j e^(iv/λ). By Lemma 54.8 (b), dRic^H(h) = e^(iv/λ)
Σ_j λ^(j−1) Z_j and dD(h) = e^(iv/λ) Σ_j λ^(j−1) G_(j−1). For a symmetric Y, div Gt(Y e^(iv/λ)) = e^(iv/λ)(div Gt(Y) +
i λ⁻¹ Pol(Y)), since Gt(Y)(ℓ, ·) = Pol(Y); and □(G e^(iv/λ)) = e^(iv/λ)(□G + i λ⁻¹ (2∇_ℓ + 3/r) G), as in the proof of
Lemma 54.8 (b). Both sides are polynomials in λ⁻¹ and λ with coefficients independent of λ, equal for
every λ > 0; the coefficient of λ^(j−2) is (54.11).

(b) G_0 = i Pol(H_1) + D_X H_0 = i Pol(H_1). Suppose G_(j−2) = 0 with j ≤ J. By (a) and Z_j = Z_(j−1) = 0,
(∇_ℓ + 3/(2r)) G_(j−1) = 0: along every generator γ_X, a linear ordinary differential equation in r, with G_(j−1) = 0 at
X_Σ. So G_(j−1) = 0, and induction from j = 1, where G_(−1) = 0 and G_0 = 0 at Σ_τ0, gives the claim. ∎

**Lemma 54.10** (Pol⁺ at a point.) Let Pol⁺ := Pol^T (Pol Pol^T)⁻¹ be the right inverse of
Lemma 7.4 (i), the transposes taken in the Euclidean structure of the Cartesian components in (τ, x), and let
V = V_v dv + V_r dr + V_ϑ dϑ. Then Y := Pol⁺ V has, in (v, r, ϑ, φ1, φ2),

    Y_vv = V_r/4,   Y_vr = −V_r/2,   Y_rr = V_r,   Y_vϑ = −V_ϑ/2,   Y_rϑ = V_ϑ,
    Y_AB = (1/3)(−F V_r − 2 V_v) r² γ_AB,   tr_(g0) Y = −V_r − 2 V_v,    (54.12)

F := 1 − μ/r² at the point; in particular Pol Y = V, and the γ-traceless angular part of Y vanishes.

*Proof.* Pol is onto (Lemma 7.4 (i)), so Pol Pol^T is invertible, Pol⁺ maps onto the range of Pol^T, and Pol is
injective there. So it suffices to show Pol Y = V and that Y lies in the range of Pol^T. First, by
(54.10) (which hold at g0 as well, with F in place of F°): Pol(Y)_r = Y_rr = V_r, Pol(Y)_ϑ = Y_rϑ = V_ϑ,
and Pol(Y)_v = Y_rv − (1/2) tr Y = −V_r/2 + (V_r + 2 V_v)/2 = V_v, with tr Y = 2 Y_vr + F Y_rr + r⁻² γ^(AB) Y_AB = −V_r +
F V_r − F V_r − 2 V_v. Second, rotate the Cartesian coordinates so that at the point x̂ = e1 and ∂_ϑ = r ∂_(x2); then ℓ =
−∂_τ + ∂_1, dv = dτ + dx1, and g0⁻¹ = η⁻¹ − m L0 ⊗ L0, m := μ/r², L0 = ∂_τ − ∂_1. The Frobenius pairing of Pol(Y) with a
covector ξ is Σ_(a,b) Y_ab ((1/2)(ℓ^a ξ_b + ℓ^b ξ_a) − (1/2)(ξ_0 + ξ_1) g0^(ab)), so the range of Pol^T consists of the
arrays

    Z_00 = −ξ_0 + s(1 + m)/2,   Z_01 = (ξ_0 − ξ_1)/2 − s m/2,   Z_11 = ξ_1 − s(1 − m)/2,
    Z_02 = −ξ_2/2,   Z_12 = ξ_2/2,   Z_22 = Z_33 = Z_44 = −s/2,   Z_0j = −ξ_j/2,  Z_1j = ξ_j/2  (j = 3, 4),

s := ξ_0 + ξ_1, all other entries zero. The Cartesian components of Y follow from ∂_v = ∂_τ, ∂_r = −∂_τ + ∂_1,
∂_ϑ = r ∂_2: Y_00 = V_r/4, Y_01 = −V_r/4, Y_11 = V_r/4, Y_02 = −V_ϑ/(2r), Y_12 = V_ϑ/(2r), Y_22 = Y_33 = Y_44 =
((m − 1) V_r − 2 V_v)/3, and no other entries. This is of the form above with ξ_2 = V_ϑ/r, ξ_3 = ξ_4 = 0, s :=
−2((m − 1) V_r − 2 V_v)/3, ξ_0 := s(1 + m)/2 − V_r/4 and ξ_1 := V_r/4 + s(1 − m)/2, whose sum is s as required; the
entries Z_00, Z_11, Z_22 then hold by construction, and Z_01 = (ξ_0 − ξ_1)/2 − s m/2 = −V_r/4. ∎

### 54.7 The part of first degree

The leading wave is W_TT = Re[A env(v) r^(1/2) T e^(iθ)], with T the angular tensor

    T := −(a + b) dϑ² + c² a dφ1² + s² b dφ2²,      a := (2h/3)(2c² + i s²),      b := −(2h/3)(c² + 2i s²),

c = cos ϑ, s = sin ϑ, h = h(cos 2ϑ) as in (2.11): indeed (2h/3)(2c² cos θ − s² sin θ) = Re[a e^(iθ)] and
(2h/3)(2s² sin θ − c² cos θ) = Re[b e^(iθ)], which with (2.11) gives the claim. T is γ-traceless. Put

    d_1 := (div_γ T)_ϑ = ((a − b) − 3(a + b) cos 2ϑ)/sin 2ϑ − (a + b)′,      d := div_γ div_γ T = (cs)⁻¹ (cs d_1)′,
    (54.13)

′ := d/dϑ; d_1 dϑ is the divergence of T on the round S³ (its φ-components vanish by the symmetries), and d its
divergence, the volume density of γ being cs.

**Definition 54.11** (The first-degree profiles.) H_1 := A env(v) r^(1/2) T, and for j ≥ 1, H_(j+1) is
the solution of

    𝒯 H_(j+1) = −R_X H_j   along ℓ,      H_(j+1) = i Pol⁺(D_X H_j)   on Σ_τ0, at r = r0 := v − τ0,    (54.14)

with the operators of (54.9) at the seed and Pol⁺ of Lemma 54.10 at the seed's F°.

**Proposition 54.12** (The profiles of first degree.) Put a_1 := A env(v) d_1(ϑ), a_2 := A env(v) d(ϑ),
and

    β_2(r) := −1/(2r0) + (μ0/3)(r⁻³ − r0⁻³).

(a) 𝒯H_1 = 0, Pol(H_1) = 0, D_X H_1 = a_1 r^(−3/2) dϑ, and R_X H_1 = a_1 r^(−5/2)(dr ⊗ dϑ + dϑ ⊗ dr) + (a γ-traceless
angular part); in particular R_X H_1 has no vv, vr, rr or vϑ component.

(b) H_2 has the components

    H_2,rϑ = i a_1 r^(−3/2),   H_2,vϑ = i a_1 r^(−1/2) β_2(r),   H_2,AB = −i r^(1/2) ∫_(r0)^r s^(−1/2) (R_X H_1)_AB ds,
    H_2,vv = H_2,vr = H_2,rr = 0,    (54.15)

and H_1, H_2 lie in 𝔖. Moreover i Pol(H_2) + D_X H_1 = 0 on Ω.

(c) D_X H_2 = i a_2 (r^(−5/2) β_2(r) dv + r^(−7/2) dr) + (a dϑ term), and the components vv, vr, rr and the trace of
H_3 are

    tr H_3 = 0,   H_3,rr = −a_2 r^(−7/2),   H_3,vr = −a_2 r^(−5/2) β_2(r),   H_3,vv = −a_2 r^(−3/2) β_2(r)².
    (54.16)

(d) At the horizon r = √μ0, H_3,vv(v, √μ0, ϑ) = A env(v) d(ϑ) ν(r0), where

    ν(r0) := −μ0^(−3/4) β_2(√μ0)² = −μ0^(−7/4) (2ρ³ − 3ρ² − 2)²/(36 ρ⁶),      ρ := r0/√μ0.    (54.17)

ν ≤ 0; it vanishes only at the one real root ρ* ∈ (1.80, 1.81) of 2ρ³ − 3ρ² − 2, where it has a double zero with
d²ν/dρ² ≠ 0; dν/dρ = −μ0^(−7/4) (ρ² + 2)(2ρ³ − 3ρ² − 2)/(6ρ⁷); and ν → −μ0^(−7/4)/9 as ρ → ∞.

*Proof.* (a) H_1 has only angular components, r^(1/2) times functions of (v, ϑ), so (𝒯H_1)_AB = −i(∂_r − 1/(2r))
r^(1/2)(…) = 0, and Pol(H_1) = 0 by (54.10) (H_1,rr = H_1,rϑ = 0, γ^(AB) T_AB = 0). For D_X H_1 =
div H_1 (tr H_1 = 0): in (div h)_n = g0°^(ab)(∂_a h_bn − Γ^d_(ab) h_dn − Γ^d_(an) h_bd) with h angular, the symbols of
(54.8) give (div h)_v = 0, (div h)_r = −r⁻³ γ^(AB) h_AB = 0, and (div h)_ϑ = r⁻² (div_γ h)_ϑ; with
h = H_1 this is a_1 r^(−3/2). For R_X H_1: H_1 is in 𝔖, so (R_X H_1)_vv = 0 and tr R_X H_1 = 0
(Lemma 54.8 (d)), and (R_X H_1)_vϑ = 0 by (e) there. Apply (54.11) at j = 2 to J = 1, H_1
alone: Z_1 = 𝒯H_1 = 0, Z_2 = R_X H_1, G_0 = 0 and G_1 = D_X H_1, so Pol(R_X H_1) = −(∇_ℓ + 3/(2r)) D_X H_1. For the
covector ω := a_1 r^(−3/2) dϑ, (∇_ℓ ω)_ϑ = ∂_r ω_ϑ − ω_ϑ/r and (∇_ℓ ω)_v = (∇_ℓ ω)_r = 0, so −(∇_ℓ + 3/(2r)) ω =
a_1 r^(−5/2) dϑ. Hence (R_X H_1)_rr = 0, (R_X H_1)_rϑ = a_1 r^(−5/2), and (R_X H_1)_rv = (1/2) tr R_X H_1 = 0.

(b) The data: by (a) and (54.12) with V = D_X H_1 = a_1 r0^(−3/2) dϑ, H_2 = i Pol⁺ V has at r0 the
components rϑ = i a_1 r0^(−3/2), vϑ = −(i/2) a_1 r0^(−3/2) = i a_1 r0^(−1/2) β_2(r0), and no other. The transport:
by (a) and (54.10), the vv, vr, rr components of 𝒯H_2 = −R_X H_1 are homogeneous with zero data, so
they vanish; (∂_r + 1/(2r)) H_2,rϑ = −i a_1 r^(−5/2) gives H_2,rϑ = i a_1 r^(−3/2), since (∂_r + 1/(2r)) r^(−3/2) =
−r^(−5/2); (∂_r + 1/(2r)) H_2,vϑ = −μ0 H_2,rϑ/r³ reads i a_1 r^(−1/2) β_2′ = −i μ0 a_1 r^(−9/2), which β_2′ = −μ0 r⁻⁴
satisfies; and (∂_r − 1/(2r)) H_2,AB = −i (R_X H_1)_AB with zero data gives the integral, γ-traceless because (R_X
H_1)_AB is (tr R_X H_1 = 0). So H_2 is in 𝔖. By Lemma 54.9 (b) with J = 2 (Z_1 = Z_2 = 0, G_0 = 0, and
G_1 = 0 at r0 since Pol Pol⁺ = 1), G_1 = i Pol(H_2) + D_X H_1 = 0 on Ω.

(c) For h in 𝔖 the same calculation as in (a) gives (div h)_v = r⁻² div_γ(h_(v·)) and (div h)_r = r⁻² div_γ(h_(r·)),
the divergences on S³ of the covectors h_(vA) and h_(rA): the terms with Γ^A_(·v) vanish, h_vv = h_vr = h_rr = 0, and
the term −Γ^E_(Ar) h_(BE) contracted with g0°^(AB) is a trace. With tr H_2 = 0 and div_γ(d_1 dϑ) = d, this is the
stated form of D_X H_2. By (b) and Lemma 54.8 (d), (R_X H_2)_vv = 0 and tr R_X H_2 = 0. Let H_3 be
given by (54.14). Its data at r0 are, by (54.12) with V_v = i a_2 r0^(−5/2) β_2(r0) and
V_r = i a_2 r0^(−7/2): H_3,vv = i V_r/4 = −a_2 r0^(−7/2)/4 and tr H_3 = i(−V_r − 2 V_v) = 0, since β_2(r0) = −1/(2r0)
gives 2 V_v = −V_r.
The trace of 𝒯H_3 is −i(∂_r + 3/(2r)) tr H_3, as ∇_ℓ commutes with the trace, and equals −tr R_X H_2 = 0; so r^(3/2)
tr H_3 is constant along ℓ, and tr H_3 = 0. By Lemma 54.9 (b) with J = 3, i Pol(H_3) = −D_X H_2 on Ω, that is
H_3,rr = i (D_X H_2)_r = −a_2 r^(−7/2) and H_3,vr − (1/2) tr H_3 = i (D_X H_2)_v = −a_2 r^(−5/2) β_2. The vv component of
𝒯H_3 = −R_X H_2 is ∂_r H_3,vv + (3/(2r)) H_3,vv + 2 μ0 H_3,vr/r³ = 0, that is ∂_r (r^(3/2) H_3,vv) = 2 μ0 a_2 r⁻⁴ β_2.
Since ∂_r(−a_2 β_2²) = −2 a_2 β_2 β_2′ = 2 μ0 a_2 r⁻⁴ β_2 and −a_2 β_2(r0)² = −a_2/(4 r0²) = r0^(3/2) H_3,vv(r0), we get
r^(3/2) H_3,vv = −a_2 β_2² on the whole generator.

(d) At r = √μ0, (c) gives H_3,vv = −a_2 μ0^(−3/4) β_2(√μ0)², and β_2(√μ0) = −1/(2r0) + 1/(3√μ0) − μ0/(3r0³) =
μ0^(−1/2) (2ρ³ − 3ρ² − 2)/(6ρ³), which gives (54.17). Put p(ρ) := 2ρ³ − 3ρ² − 2. Since p′(ρ) = 6ρ(ρ − 1),
p has its local maximum p(0) = −2 < 0 and its local minimum p(1) = −3 < 0, so it has exactly one real root ρ*, in
(1, ∞); p(1.80) = −0.056 < 0 < p(1.81) = 0.031182. ν = −μ0^(−7/4) p²/(36 ρ⁶) has a double zero there, with d²ν/dρ² =
−μ0^(−7/4) p′(ρ*)²/(18 ρ*⁶) ≠ 0 since p′(ρ*) ≠ 0. Differentiating, dν/dρ = −μ0^(−7/4) p (ρ p′ − 3p)/(18 ρ⁷) and ρ p′ −
3p = 3(ρ² + 2). Finally p²/ρ⁶ → 4. ∎

The admissible values are r0 = v − τ0 ≥ v_s − τ0 > √μ0 + 1, that is ρ > 1 + μ0^(−1/2). The coefficient ν depends on τ0,
through r0, and on the Euclidean structure used to define Pol⁺; the one fixed in Lemma 7.4 is used throughout. A
tensor T with d = 0 gives no λ³ term: for instance (a, b) = ((1 + 3 cos 2ϑ)/2, (1 − 3 cos 2ϑ)/2) has d_1 = 0.

**Lemma 54.13** (The angular factor of the waves.) With ζ := cos 2ϑ,

    d_1 = sin 2ϑ · √2 ((3ζ² − 2ζ + 5) + i (3ζ² + 2ζ + 5)) / (3 (1 + ζ²)^(3/2)),
    d = (2√2/3) ((3ζ⁵ + 10ζ³ − 10ζ² + 19ζ + 2) + i (3ζ⁵ + 10ζ³ + 10ζ² + 19ζ − 2)) / (1 + ζ²)^(5/2),    (54.18)

and |d| ≥ 8/3 at every angle, the axes included, with equality only at ζ = 0.

*Proof.* With c² = (1 + ζ)/2, s² = (1 − ζ)/2 and h = √2 (1 + ζ²)^(−1/2),

    a + b = √2 (ζ + 1 + i(ζ − 1)) / (3 √(1 + ζ²)),      a − b = √2 (1 + ζ + i(1 − ζ)) / √(1 + ζ²).

So (a − b) − 3ζ(a + b) = √2 (1 − ζ²)(1 + i)/√(1 + ζ²). With d/dϑ = −2 sin 2ϑ d/dζ and sin 2ϑ = √(1 − ζ²),
−(a + b)′ = 2 sin 2ϑ (d/dζ)(a + b) = (2√2/3) sin 2ϑ ((1 + i) − (1 − i) ζ)/(1 + ζ²)^(3/2). Adding the two terms of
(54.13) gives d_1 = sin 2ϑ · q(ζ) with the q displayed. Then cs d_1 = (1/2)(1 − ζ²) q and d =
(cs)⁻¹ (cs d_1)′ = −2 (d/dζ)((1 − ζ²) q), which is the stated d. For the bound, write the two numerators of d as o + e
and o − e, with the odd part o := 3ζ⁵ + 10ζ³ + 19ζ and the even part e := 2 − 10ζ². Then |d|² = (8/9)((o + e)² + (o −
e)²)/(1 + ζ²)⁵ = (16/9)(o² + e²)/(1 + ζ²)⁵, and with u := ζ²,

    o² + e² − 4 (1 + u)⁵ = 5u⁵ + 40u⁴ + 174u³ + 440u² + 301u ≥ 0,

so |d|² ≥ (16/9) · 4 = 64/9, with equality only at u = 0. ∎

**Lemma 54.14** (The inverse metric on the boundary.) On the boundary,

    g_λ⁻¹(dΦ0, dΦ0) = −m0 − k(Φ0♯, Φ0♯) + q,      |q| ≤ C |k(Φ0♯, ·)| (|k(Φ0♯, ·)| + |k|²),    (54.19)

where C depends on the bounds of g0⁻¹ and g_λ⁻¹ on Ω; here |k| ≤ C λ ≤ 1 on Ω, by item 4 of Theorem 3.1 and the choice
of λ0 in Section 54.1.

*Proof.* From g_λ = g0 + k, g_λ⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ = −g0⁻¹ k g_λ⁻¹, and substituting this once more for g_λ⁻¹ on the right, g_λ⁻¹ =
g0⁻¹ − g0⁻¹ k g0⁻¹ + g0⁻¹ k g0⁻¹ k g_λ⁻¹. Contract with dΦ0 twice: the first two terms give −m0 − k(Φ0♯, Φ0♯), and the
third is q := k(Φ0♯, g0⁻¹ k g_λ⁻¹ dΦ0), so that the absolute value of q is at most C |k(Φ0♯, ·)| times |k(g_λ⁻¹ dΦ0, ·)|.
The same identity applied to g_λ⁻¹ dΦ0 bounds the latter by |k(Φ0♯, ·)| + C |k| |k(Φ0♯, ·)| + C |k|³, which is at
most C (|k(Φ0♯, ·)| + |k|²) since |k| ≤ 1. ∎

### 54.8 Flat-edge bounds

*Two structural facts.* (F1) Every monomial of the forcing term −Π_osc(𝒲(m_m, φ_m) + 𝒴_m) of (4.14) (c),
and of the known part of the data of ĝ_(m+1) in Lemma 7.4 (i), contains an oscillating factor among W, χ and
ĝ_l (l ≤ m), carrying at most two derivatives in the first case and at most one in the second; its other factors are
profiles of Theorem 4.11, bounded globally, or coefficients built from g0. Indeed a monomial without an
oscillating factor does not depend on θ, and Π_osc removes it; and the data of Lemma 7.4 (i) come from the
oscillating part of D, which has one derivative.

(F2) Every monomial of the mean forcing terms (𝒮_m, q_m, ⟨T̂ ĝ_(m+1)⟩ and the coefficient of dφ_m in ⟨𝒲_φ⟩), of the
forcing terms S_m and the coefficient B_m of Lemma 7.4 (iii), of Ric^H(g_app) − Ric(g0) and of the
difference between the constraint map of g_app's data and that of g0's data contains two oscillating factors, or a
factor among the means and phases of earlier stages, μ − μ0 and μ^(k), k ≥ 1. For every oscillating factor has θ-mean
zero, so the θ-mean of a monomial with exactly one oscillating factor and all other factors independent of θ is zero;
and each of these quantities is a polynomial in the profiles and in μ − μ0, μ^(k), with coefficients built from the
seed, whose constant term is the seed's own value, zero (at A = 0 the construction returns the seed). For ⟨T̂ ĝ_(m+1)⟩
more holds: by Lemma 54.8 (b) with k = 1, 2, …, the seed's part T̂_0 of T̂ maps the k-th harmonic to
k 𝒯 of it, an operator in X composed with ∂_θ, of θ-mean zero on every profile; so ⟨T̂ ĝ_(m+1)⟩ = ⟨(T̂ − T̂_0)
ĝ_(m+1)⟩, whose coefficients are built from W, χ, m_1, φ_1 and μ − μ0.

The μ-factors carry the weight at every point: 0 ≤ μ − μ0 ≤ (2/9) A² (v − v_s) ε_0(v)² and |μ^(k)| ≤ C ε_(k−1)(v)².

**Lemma 54.15** (Energy on Ω_v, the null face kept.) Let v ≤ v_♯ and let u, a function or a
Cartesian array, satisfy −(1/2) g0^(ab) ∂_a ∂_b u = f on Ω_v. Put e(τ) := ‖∂u(τ)‖ + ‖u(τ)‖, the flat L² norms on Σ_τ ∩
Ω_v, and F_v(u) := ∫_(N_v) T(L0, Y) r³ dr dω, with T the energy tensor of u for g0, Y = −g0⁻¹ dτ and L0 = −ℓ. Then

    sup_(τ0≤τ≤τ_end) e(τ) + F_v(u)^(1/2) ≤ C_E (e(τ0) + ∫_(τ0)^(τ_end) ‖f‖),    (54.20)

C_E depending on Ω and μ(v_end) only, not on v; and T(L0, Y) = (1/2)(1 + μ/r²)(ℓu)² + |∇̊u|²/(2r²), ∇̊ the gradient on
the unit S³.

*Proof.* Run the proof of Lemma 5.5 on Ω_v ∩ {τ0 ≤ τ′ ≤ τ} with g̃ := g0 and J := T(Y, ·). Its boundary is
Σ_τ0 ∩ Ω_v, Σ_τ ∩ Ω_v, part of {r = a}, spacelike with Ω_v to its past (Lemma 2.6 (b)), whose flux is
nonnegative and dropped, and part of N_v. In (v, r, ω) the volume form of g0 is r³ dv dr dω and the outward conormal of
N_v is dv, so the outward flux through it is ∫ J(dv) r³ dr dω = ∫ T(ℓ, Y) r³ dr dω = −∫ T(L0, Y) r³ dr dω; moved to the
left it is the part of F_v(u) with τ′ ≤ τ. Its density: g0(L0, Y) = −dτ(L0) = −1, Y = ∂_v − (μ/r²) ∂_r, L0 u = −∂_r u,
and g0⁻¹(du, du) = 2 ∂_v u ∂_r u + F (∂_r u)² + r⁻² |∇̊u|², so T(L0, Y) = (L0 u)(Y u) + (1/2) g0⁻¹(du, du) = (1/2)(1 +
μ/r²)(∂_r u)² + |∇̊u|²/(2r²): no transverse derivative ∂_v u enters, and it is nonnegative. The bulk is at most C(e² +
‖f‖ e) as in Lemma 5.5, and ∂_τ ‖u‖² = 2⟨u, ∂_τ u⟩ − ∫_(r=v−τ) |u|² r³ dω, the outer radius v − τ of Σ_τ ∩ Ω_v
decreasing at rate one. Gronwall's inequality, then τ = τ_end for the flux. The constant is that of Lemma 5.5,
which depends on the bounds of g0 and Y on Ω only. ∎

**Lemma 54.16** (Transport on Ω_v and along the generators.) (a) If L0 φ − c φ = f on Ω_v with c
bounded, then ‖φ(τ)‖ ≤ e^(C(τ−τ0)) (‖φ(τ0)‖ + ∫_(τ0)^τ ‖f‖), the norms on Σ_τ ∩ Ω_v. (b) Let Z(X, θ) ∈ ℝ^d solve
−(ℓ·∂_X) Z + 𝓜 Z = F on Ω × S¹, with 𝓜(X) a linear operator on C(S¹; ℝ^d) of norm at most M1. Then for X ∈ Ω

    sup_θ |Z(X, ·)| ≤ e^(M1 L) (sup_θ |Z(X_Σ, ·)| + L sup_(γ_X × S¹) |F|),      L := r(X_Σ) − r(X) ≤ b(τ0) − a.

The derivatives (∂^α_X ∂_θ^p Z)_(|α|+p≤i) solve a system of the same kind (the commutator of ∂_X with ℓ·∂_X is
(∂ℓ)·∂_X, of the same order), with data on Σ_τ0 the tangential derivatives of Z|_(Σ_τ0) and the transverse ones read
from the equation, since dτ(ℓ) = −1.

*Proof.* (a) is the proof of Lemma 5.6 with outer radius b(τ) := v − τ, whose outer boundary term carries the
factor 1 + b′ = 0: L0 is tangent to N_v. (b) In (v, r, ω), ℓ = ∂_r and γ_X is r ↦ (v(X), r, ω(X)), so the equation is a
linear ordinary differential equation in r with values in the Banach space C(S¹; ℝ^d), and Gronwall's inequality gives
the bound. ∎

For the stage transports, 𝓜 := Π_osc ℳ ∂_θ⁻¹ on zero-mean profiles (Lemma 4.8), with ∂_θ⁻¹ the
zero-mean primitive. For a zero-mean continuous Z its zero-mean primitive Y vanishes somewhere, and the integral of Z
over the shorter of the two arcs from that point is at most π sup |Z|, the integral over the whole circle being zero;
so ‖∂_θ⁻¹‖ ≤ π, and ‖Π_osc‖ ≤ 2. Hence ‖𝓜‖ ≤ C by the global bounds of Theorem 4.11.

**Lemma 54.17** (Pointwise bounds from the null face.) For u smooth on Ω_v and Y ∈ N_v,

    |u(Y)| ≤ C_N Σ_(|β|≤2) (sup_(N_v ∩ Σ_τ0) |Ω^β u| + F_v(Ω^β u)^(1/2)),    (54.21)

Ω^β products of the rotations Ω_ab := x_a ∂_b − x_b ∂_a, C_N depending on a and b(τ0) only.

*Proof.* In (v, r, ω), γ_Y runs in N_v from r(Y) ≥ a to r_Σ := v − τ0, and the rotations commute with ℓ = ∂_r. On the
unit S³, |u(r, ·)|_∞ ≤ C Σ_(|β|≤2) ‖Ω^β u(r, ·)‖_(L²(S³)): H² ⊂ L^∞ in dimension three Theorem A.26, the
rotations spanning every tangent space. And ‖Ω^β u(r, ·)‖ ≤ ‖Ω^β u(r_Σ, ·)‖ + ∫_r^(r_Σ) ‖ℓ Ω^β u(r′, ·)‖ dr′ ≤
C sup |Ω^β u|_(r_Σ) + (r_Σ − a)^(1/2) a^(−3/2) (∫∫ (ℓ Ω^β u)² r′³ dr′ dω)^(1/2), and the last double integral is at
most 2 F_v(Ω^β u) by the formula for T(L0, Y). ∎

The flux through N_v controls exactly the derivatives tangent to N_v, which is what an integration along γ_Y and a
Sobolev inequality on the spheres need; the slices Σ_τ ∩ Ω_v = {a ≤ r ≤ v − τ} are arbitrarily thin as v − τ ↓ a,
and no Sobolev inequality on them is used.

**Lemma 54.18** (Flat-edge bounds of the construction.) Let N ≥ 3, and let H_j (1 ≤ j ≤ N + 1) be the
profiles of Definition 54.11. For every X ∈ Ω with v := v(X) ≤ v_♯ and every order i:

(a) *oscillating, degree one:* |∂^i_(X,θ) ĝ_j(X)| ≤ C ε_(i+2j−2)(v), 1 ≤ j ≤ N + 1;

(b) *means and phases, degree two:* |∂^i m_j(X)| + |∂^i φ_j(X)| ≤ C ε_(i+2j+1)(v)² and |∂^i Ψ_j(X)| ≤ C ε_(i+2j+3)(v)²,
1 ≤ j ≤ N, with Ψ_j = □̃φ_j;

(c) *oscillating, the remainder of degree two:* |∂^i_(X,θ)(ĝ_j − Re[H_j e^(iθ)])(X)| ≤ C ε_(i+2j+1)(v)², and |∂^i
H_j(X)| ≤ C ε_(i+2j−2)(v), 1 ≤ j ≤ N + 1;

(d) *residual:* |∂^i Ric^H(g_app)(X)| ≤ C λ^(N−1−i) ε_(i+2N+3)(v);

(e) *slice data:* on Σ_τ0 at radius r with τ0 + r ≤ v_♯, the stage-m data (α_m, ϖ_m, q′_m, ∂_τ (m_m)_(τ·)) of
Lemma 7.4, with their angular derivatives and i radial derivatives, are at most C ε_(i+2m)(τ0 + r)², and the
correction U of Proposition 7.7 obeys sup_(r′≤r) ‖∂_r^j U(r′)‖_(H^s(S³)) ≤ C λ^(N−2−j) ε_(j+2N+3)(τ0 + r) for
j ≤ 3 and the s of Proposition 7.7.

Every cost that Proposition 54.19, Lemma 54.21 and Lemma 54.22 use, at orders
i ≤ 4 and j ≤ 3, is at most 2N + 6 ≤ M* := 2N + 8.

*Proof.* Induction on the stage m = 0, 1, …, N. At stage m the steps run in the order (e) for the stage-m slice data,
(a) for ĝ_(m+1), (b) for (m_m, φ_m, Ψ_m), (c) for ĝ_(m+1); each uses only the global bounds of Theorem 4.11 and
what the earlier steps proved.

*Stage 0.* The Cartesian components of W_TT are A env(v) times smooth functions of (r, x̂, θ) (Lemma 2.9 (a)): cost
i at order i. χ solves (4.9) along ℓ, zero on Σ_τ0; its forcing term F_2 is quadratic in ∂_θ W_TT, with
no slow derivative. So Lemma 54.16 (b) gives |∂^i χ| ≤ C ε_i(v)²: (a) and (c) at j = 1, since ĝ_1 −
Re[H_1 e^(iθ)] = χ dv ⊗ dv.

*Stage m ≥ 1, (e).* The data (α_m, ϖ_m, q′_m) solve the system of Lemma 7.6 on [a, b1] from zero data at
r = a, with forcing S_m. Its restriction to [a, r] solves the same problem on [a, r], whose solution is unique
(Lemma 7.6 on [a, r]), and the bound of Lemma 7.6 holds on [a, r] with its constant for
