truncated domain of dependence that avoids the axes would not give (H1): no such domain contains a region of the form
D_s, since D_s contains the axes. The residual bounds of Section 57.9 hold at points and on boxes of the
region Π of (57.14), which is not of the form D_s, and are not bounds of a norm over a region D_s. So
(H1)–(H3) are established in this paper for no region D with v* > 1/2, and no existence beyond v = 1/2 is claimed.

**Remark 57.45** (Numerical observation.) Write the vacuum equations of the class as three-dimensional
gravity for the rescaled orbit metric of Proposition 2.3 coupled to its two waves, in a null frame of that metric,
and linearise them about a metric of the class. A Grönwall argument for the energies of the linear system on a domain
of dependence truncated to avoid the axes would bound them by F² times the energies of their data and sources, with
F² = exp(2∫a_o du + 2∫a_i dv), where a_o(u) and a_i(v) are the largest, over the unknowns measured on outgoing and on
ingoing cones, of the sums of the absolute values of the coefficients with which each unknown enters. On a computed
solution at the first seed, over |x| ≤ 1/2 on the (u, v)-rectangle of Definition 57.24, where no such truncated
domain exists, so that no such bound applies, this number evaluates to F² ≈ 10^138, and to about 10^66.9 with weights
in the energy norms; toward the axes the coefficients grow like the inverse distance to the axis, and with the band
widened to |x| ≤ 0.95 the figure is about 10^1916. The couplings of the coefficients across a cut in the angular
Chebyshev degree do not depend on the cut beyond the degree of the coefficient, since
T_j T_k = (T_(j+k) + T_(|j−k|))/2, and on the computed coefficients they are of the coefficients' own size, so a Schur
complement estimate on the high angular modes does not lower the constant at any angular resolution. At F² = 10^66.9
the closing condition 4F²G ε_r < 1 asks a residual ε_r of order 10⁻⁶⁸/G, against the bounds 3.73 × 10⁻⁵ at points and
5.0 × 10⁻⁴ on sub-boxes of Proposition 57.39 and Proposition 57.41. No proof uses these observations.

## 58. Scope

This chapter collects what Theorem 3.1, Theorem 3.7, Theorem 3.8 and Theorem 3.9, and the
results of Part X, Part XI and Part XII, claim and what they do not claim; each statement
is followed by the place where it is stated or proved.

### 58.1 The construction and its domain

Theorem 3.1 is made on the compact domain Ω ⊃ D_T ∩ {τ ≥ τ0}, Theorem 3.7 on Ω together with its past
domain, and Theorem 3.8 near past null infinity for the solutions of Theorem 3.7; the inner boundary
r = a of Ω and of the past domain lies a fixed distance inside the curvature boundary x_K = 1, and nothing in the three
theorems is claimed beyond Ω and the past domain (Section 2.3, Section 1.4). Below the inner boundary the
theorems are not silent: the boundary sits at the curvature scale l5, which is arbitrary, and since
r_q(v) = (√72 μ(v) l5²)^(1/4) tends to 0 with l5, a smaller l5 puts every point with r > 0 and v ≤ v_end + T inside
D_T, the constants of Theorem 3.1 then depending on l5 (Section 2.3, Theorem 3.1). At r = 0 the limit itself is
singular, its Kretschmann scalar being 72 μ²/r⁸ (Proposition 2.5). Nothing in the paper involves an inner or Cauchy
horizon (Section 1.4).

The envelope is taken in C_c^∞, and the hypothesis is used as it stands: for a fixed K the estimates use finitely many
derivatives of env, whose number is not determined, an envelope of finite smoothness is not covered, and the profile
sin⁴(π(v − 1/2)/3) on [1/2, 7/2], which is C³ and not C⁴, is covered for no K ≥ 6 (Remark 3.2).

Item 6 of Theorem 3.1 concerns the round family of spheres {v, r = const}: the zero set of their outgoing expansion on
the columns is not a marginally trapped surface (Proposition 3.4, Remark 8.4). Item 7 concerns the Hawking
mass of the spheres of the domain, which is not the angular mean of the mass aspect at past null infinity; that mean is
governed by the mass law of Theorem 3.8 (Proposition 3.5, Remark 8.8). The expansion of
Proposition 10.4, on which Theorem 3.8 rests, claims no uniformity in λ beyond its leading term, and
nothing is claimed about future null infinity or the Bondi mass there, which the domain does not reach
(Remark 10.14).

If μ0 > √72 l5², the boundary x_K = 1 is spacelike for g_λ with a uniform margin once λ is small, and a future causal
curve that meets it leaves D_T there and does not return (Proposition 3.3). At equality, μ0 = √72 l5²,
this fails in a layer at the start of the shell whose width tends to 0 with λ: on every column the boundary has points
where it is timelike for g_λ, and future timelike curves cross it into D_T (Theorem 54.26, Corollary 54.27). That the
domain of Proposition 54.4, whose inner boundary no future causal curve enters, is needed in place of D_T is not shown
(Corollary 54.27). Inside the layer, for δ ∈ (0, 1/2], P > 4 and λ small, the boundary is spacelike above the band
between the levels λ^(3+δ) and λ^(3−δ), and it has points of both characters on every window of length 4πλ that starts
where |env| first reaches a level between λ^P and λ^(3+δ) (Proposition 54.34); on the band its character is decided
up to a factor 1 ± 2λ^(1/10) in the ratio of the first-degree amplitude to the margin (Remark 55.46). For an
envelope increasing at its edge with the hypothesis (H_N) of Definition 55.1 the band is decided by one switch
per column (Theorem 55.33), and the very edge for envelopes with the edge hypotheses, which hold for env_C
(Theorem 55.22, Corollary 55.29). Some regularity of the edge is needed: for an explicit smooth envelope whose
intervals of zeros accumulate at the edge, the boundary is spacelike throughout intervals of length 4πλ below the level
λ^(3+δ), for every small λ (Proposition 55.45), and at a dip of a general envelope the criterion of
Remark 55.46 decides nothing.

### 58.2 The thresholds and the constants

The threshold λ0 and the constant C of Theorem 3.1 are produced by its proof and are not evaluated
(Section 3.1). At the numerical point of Definition 56.1 the threshold that the proof of Theorem 3.1
delivers is below 0.0024433 in the operator norm of the proof, and any λ0 and C with the properties that the proof
gives them satisfy λ0 < 0.0019079 when |·| is read as the Frobenius norm and λ0 < 0.0012228 when it is read as the
largest absolute entry (Proposition 56.8). Of the conditions that the proofs place on λ0 the bound uses only C λ0 ≤ ε1,
and no lower bound for λ0 is given (Section 56.6). The first stage's mean correction M_22 at the point where
the wave is largest would sharpen the three bounds; its value is a numerical observation that no proof uses, no bound
on it is proved, and the bounds proved are those of Proposition 56.8 (Remark 56.9).

The thresholds λ1 and δ of Theorem 3.9 are positive by its proof, and their values are not determined
(Remark 49.114). The proof's formulas give λ1 < δ ≤ 2^(−(32d+9)) and bound the modulus of the initial family
at 2δ by 2^(−(32d+8)), d the loss with which the Nash–Moser theorem is applied (Proposition 49.33). A lower bound for
δ or λ1 would need upper bounds for every constant of the proof that enters them (Section 49.7).

The loss d is at least the loss d_acc that the proof assigns to the tame estimates, and the regularity of the Nash–Moser
step is N_NM = 21d + 6; d_acc is composed of elementary losses in closed form, of the loss of the forward solution
operators, at most 20,180, or 20,183 at the backgrounds h + h_rem(q) + h_tot(p⃗), and of the numbers of steps of the
iterations of the construction (Theorem 49.32 (i)). At the
computational point of Definition 49.1, d > 1.403 × 10²⁰ and N_NM > 2.946 × 10²¹, so that log₁₀ δ < −1.351 × 10²¹
(Theorem 49.32 (ii), Proposition 49.33), and d > 1.2497 × 10²⁴ and N_NM > 2.624 × 10²⁵ at every admissible choice of
the weights, for the index sets as the proofs construct them (Corollary 49.45). These are lower bounds for the
loss that this proof's choices produce, not for the least loss with which the tame estimates hold (Theorem 49.32). At
that point, for those index sets and at one admissible choice of the weights and of the free orders and inner products,
d is at most an integer below 1.57157 × 10⁵⁰ and N_NM at most one below 3.30029 × 10⁵¹ (Theorem 49.59). The
computational point is a point at which the formulas of the proof can be evaluated, and it lies outside the set on which
Theorem 3.9 is proved (Remark 49.2). No result of Chapter 49 is used in the proof of any
theorem outside that chapter; the explicit indices of Proposition 14.40 and Lemma 14.30, which
Proposition 49.21 proves, and the value N′ = 13 of Chapter 16, which rests on Lemma 49.10, are used only in
Chapter 49, whose opening states both.

Explicit values stop upstream of every constant of Theorem 3.9: the proof fixes the gauge and damping parameters
only below thresholds whose existence it proves, and the cut-offs and orders of its function spaces only up to
admissibility; arguments by contradiction, compactness and defect measures give constants without a value; and the
parametrix norms at ι⁺, the tame constants to the order N_NM, the Nash–Moser thresholds of the exterior and slab
problems and the constants of the gluing are not evaluated. This is a limit of the explicit evaluation, not of
Theorem 3.9 (Remark 49.114).

Explicit resolvent bounds are proved for the scalar wave operator on five-dimensional Tangherlini of mass 1, cut off to
{6/5 ≤ r ≤ 4}: for every harmonic and every real 0 < |σ| ≤ 3, and with the constant 11.477 for 3 ≤ |σ| ≤ 384
(Proposition 48.15, Proposition 48.16, Theorem 48.37); the same identities bound the cut-off
resolvent of every master operator of the 1-form wave operator and of the linearised Einstein operator, at every harmonic
and every real σ ≠ 0 (Proposition 48.28). For the scalar wave operator, the smaller values observed
from |σ| = 12 on, and their decay in |σ|, are not proved (Remark 48.39). For the scalar-type blocks of the
linearised gauge-fixed operator at zero energy, an upper bound for the least singular value obstructs a good constant at
a weight next to an indicial root (Lemma 48.53).

The threshold λ_2 of Theorem 44.1, the threshold λ_L of Theorem 54.26 and the thresholds of Theorem 55.22 and
Theorem 55.33 are not evaluated (Theorem 44.1, Remark 54.39, Remark 55.48). λ_L is the
threshold that the proof delivers, not the largest λ for which Theorem 54.26 holds, and for the envelope env_C it is at
most 10^(−430) (Remark 54.39).

### 58.3 After the shell

Theorem 3.9 concerns the exterior of the black hole after the shell, and its rate holds in spatially compact
subsets of the exterior (Theorem 3.9). Its item (i) concerns the development of glued data, which agree with the
data of g_λ on a ball and are continued equivariantly to exact Tangherlini data beyond it; they are not the data of a
continuation of g_λ beyond the ball, and their development is not one (Section 42.3). Its item (ii) is
stated for perturbations in Hintz's own data class, and not for a class of decaying data reached by gluing, since gluing
replaces the data near infinity on which the solution near the hole at late times depends (Remark 41.6). The
perturbations that (ii) reaches, directly or through gluing uniformly in the gluing radius, are exactly those small in
Hintz's class: a perturbation of order of decay a > ℓ0, ℓ0 ∈ (3, 4) being the order of that class's conormal remainder in
the metric (Theorem 3.9), and of small enough size is reached directly, which over the admissible ℓ0 covers every
a > 3 (Corollary 42.8), for 3/2 < a ≤ ℓ0 the rate does not decide, and the statement that (ii) applies up
to the gluing is false for fixed size and large radius at every such a (Theorem 42.21).

With its inner radius taken as half the radius q_end of the curvature boundary after the shell, the development of
Theorem 3.9 (i) is defined on all of {r ≥ q_end} to the future of its initial surface and settles there at the
rate of Theorem 3.9, for every final mass, with λ1, δ and the constants depending on μ_end; the part of its domain
below q_end lies beyond the curvature boundary (Proposition 43.2). For λ small, glued to g_λ along the part of the
initial surface where the two induce the same data, it forms one vacuum spacetime; how far their identification reaches
into the future is not decided, nor whether that part of the initial surface is acausal in all of the domain of g_λ
(Lemma 43.5, Remark 43.6), and nothing in the proof of Theorem 3.9 uses the
identification (Remark 41.5). The interior covered by Proposition 43.2 belongs to a vacuum continuation of g_λ fixed
by the gluing, not to the continuation of g_λ's own data (Remark 43.6). At a fixed λ the data of
either construction of g_λ are available only on a bounded part of Hintz's initial surface, since the proofs give no
threshold uniform in the size of the domain (Remark 43.8).

The development of g_λ's own data on Hintz's initial surface settles, with no gluing and with no exceptional set in λ, in
a data class wider than that of Theorem 3.9 (ii) by half-integer orders (Theorem 44.1). The class of (ii) does
not contain these data: for every amplitude but at most one, the coefficient of r^(−5/2) that g_λ − g0 carries at past
null infinity after the shell is nonzero for every λ ∈ (0, λ_P] off a set with no accumulation point in (0, λ_P], and it
reaches the data at spatial infinity (Chapter 44, Proposition 44.3). The constants ε, d_1 and λ_2 depend on the
class (Theorem 44.1). The continuation of g_λ to the past domain of dependence of the far
part of the initial surface is unique in the wave-map gauge among the continuations within 1/50 of Tangherlini whose
commuted energies of some weight a_0 ∈ (0, 1/2) stay bounded and whose energy tends to 0 toward past null infinity
(Proposition 44.48); existence is not attempted at a weight a_0 ≤ 1/2 (Remark 44.49).

### 58.4 The linear solution in other gauges

The linear statement of Theorem 3.9 is made in the gauge of the stability theory. A linear solution in another
gauge with the same data, given on the whole future of the initial surface outside r = r_♭, differs from it by a
linearised diffeomorphism ℒ_X g, and nothing is asserted there about the size or the decay of X (Corollary 40.13,
Remark 40.14). Two gauges are treated.

In the Regge–Wheeler-type gauge the gauge vector is explicit, and the perturbation settles to the change of mass on each
region r_♭ < r ≤ R′, the horizon included, at the rate of the stability theory with two derivatives lost; the constant
depends on R′, and nothing is claimed uniformly in r (Theorem 45.7). The gauge vector itself decays one power
more slowly, its spherically symmetric part being a time integral, and whether that part decays faster for the solution
of the stability theory is not determined (Theorem 45.7 (c), Remark 45.8). Uniformly in r the statement
fails: the orbit-space components can grow like r^(1/2) on the outgoing part of the leaves of [HKW18]
(Theorem 45.19); with the weight r^(−1/2) on the orbit-space components and r^(1/2) on the angular block they settle
pointwise and uniformly in r, the weights are sharp, and the rates are not claimed sharp (Theorem 45.21,
Theorem 45.22). Compared with the decay of the master quantities proved in [HKW18], the components settle on each
region r ≤ R at the rate τ⁻² in energy once one datum more than [HKW18]'s energies is finite, the second derivative of
the master fields transversal to the horizon, and for the scalar type that datum cannot be dropped (Proposition 45.11,
Lemma 45.17).

In the harmonic gauge every perturbation of the class has a representative on the whole future of the initial surface
outside r = r_♭ that induces the given data and settles on each region r_♭ < r ≤ R′, the horizon included, to
ṁK* + cℒ_(W*)g at the rate t*^(−min(p_0,3/2)+ε), at t*^(−1+ε) when the data differ from a change of mass only on a
ball, and at t*^(−3/2−κ), κ < δ_♯, for data of compact support (Theorem 47.30). The gauge-fixed change of mass
ṁK* grows linearly in v, and the growth cannot be avoided: when the mass changes, no harmonic-gauge solution settles to
a change of mass near the horizon at an integrable rate (Theorem 46.6). Without decay of the data of the spherically
symmetric gauge vector Z′_0, the growth can be traded for a stationary term that does not decay at infinity
(Proposition 46.27 (c)).

### 58.5 Further families

Theorem 50.2 places the outgoing packet on Σ_τ0 between the seed's horizon and the shell. It does not treat a
packet outside the shell, for which the two families do not cross in the future of Σ_τ0, nor one inside the seed's
horizon, a case not examined (Remark 50.3).

The Cauchy stability of the class Einstein–null-dust system, without smallness, constructs the background; the
high-frequency construction over a non-round background needs more: beyond one ingoing and one outgoing family the
further families must have densities vanishing near the axes, and pairwise separation does not suffice when three or
more families are present at a point (Theorem 51.31, Remark 51.33). Its application to the two-dust
background assumes that the outgoing packet does not reach the inner sphere, which the construction of that background
does not decide (Corollary 51.32). On the seed with small non-round families away from the axes the data are
assumed, not constructed (Corollary 51.19).

Theorem 52.10 realises as weak limits of class vacuum metrics, along odd numbers of dusts, the class
Einstein–restricted massless Vlasov solutions whose field is a caustic-free family of dusts labelled by initial
direction and kept off the axes, on domains of the type of Ω whose initial spheres have positive mean curvature; no
smallness is assumed, and the hypotheses hold on a nonempty open set of solutions (Theorem 52.10, Lemma 52.38,
Proposition 52.40). The hypotheses avoid four obstructions proved in Chapter 52, among them that two dusts of
one orientation are not separated at an axis and that a continuous density carried to an axis transversally would
focus there (Remark 52.12). The two radial dusts of Theorem 50.2, which reach the axes, can be added
to a small restricted field when the outgoing packet does not reach the inner sphere; the solution then exists on its
adapted domain and is a weak limit of class vacuum metrics only on narrower domains of the type of Ω inside it, the
high-frequency step not being carried out on the adapted domain itself, and no uniqueness of that solution is stated
(Corollary 52.50, Remark 52.51).

The results on localised data concern the explicit two-dust background of Section 53.10.1, on its slice Σ_τ0 or on a
slice bent from it, and invariant data near the background's data (Chapter 53). Data localised in angle away
from the axes exist on the whole of a slice bent from Σ_τ0 by at most 0.0012, on which Rácz's split is hyperbolic
everywhere; on Σ_τ0 itself the split is hyperbolic off the band 4.2882 ≤ R ≤ 4.5310 inside the shell, and on
4.2955 ≤ R ≤ 4.5258 it is hyperbolic for no foliation (Theorem 53.3, Proposition 53.2). Localisation in angle
and radius at once is decided at second order in the amplitude by the sign of the charge, and it is stated in terms of
the sign of f, nothing using the event horizon: on a vacuum band that meets {f < 0} such vacuum data whose first-order
part is not a gauge perturbation exist for every small amplitude, on a vacuum band where f > 0 they are excluded for
small amplitude when the first-order part is not a gauge perturbation, and on every vacuum band they are excluded for
small amplitude when the first-order part perturbs the extrinsic curvature alone (Theorem 53.30).

### 58.6 At the prescribed wavelength 10 l5

Theorem 3.1 is a statement for small λ; for the smooth envelope of Definition 56.1, whose parameters are those
of the first seed at 10 l5, the threshold that its proof delivers lies below 10 l5 by a factor above 409
(Section 56.6). At λ = 10 l5 there is no separation of scales: the wavelength is 10 times the curvature
length on x_K = 1, and at the horizon more than 2.91 times it at the first seed and more than 0.92 times it at the
second (Proposition 57.2, Theorem 57.18); the statement that the waves are high-frequency on D_T once
λ < l5/10 concerns the approximant, not the threshold λ0 (Section 57.1). The envelope taken there,
sin⁴(π(v − 1/2)/3), is C³ and not C⁴, so Theorem 3.1 does not apply to it at any λ (Remark 3.2).

Posed as a characteristic initial value problem in double-null gauge, the problem at 10 l5 has a solution where the
solution is the seed, v ≤ 1/2 in units of the horizon radius; and wherever a vacuum solution exists in the gauge with the
seed's transverse derivative of R on the seed's cone, its leaves inside the seed's horizon generator are outer trapped,
and its T²-invariant marginally outer trapped sections lie at or outside that generator (Theorem 57.18). No existence is
claimed for v > 1/2: the continuation lemma assumes smooth data and the local existence, uniqueness and continuation of
the characteristic problem in the gauge, which this paper does not establish, the data are not smooth, its a priori
estimate is one on a whole region, the axes included, and the residual bounds proved hold at points and on boxes of a
region not of that form (Theorem 57.18, Lemma 57.43, Remark 57.44). Beyond v = 1/2 the shift on
the outgoing data cone is subject to a constraint that this paper does not treat (Definition 57.17). The size of
the constant of a linear estimate on a numerical solution at the first seed, and with it how far the closing condition of
the continuation lemma lies from the residual bounds proved, is a numerical observation that no proof uses
(Remark 57.45).

### 58.7 Numerical observations

The remarks headed as numerical observations state what was observed, no proof in this paper uses them, and nothing in
them is claimed: among them the value of M_22 (Remark 56.9), the absence of growing modes of the master equations
up to a finite time (Remark 45.23), the solutions at 10 l5 (Remark 57.3, Remark 57.19) and three
further constants of the linear theory at the final black hole (Remark 49.113).

## Appendix A. Results from the literature

The proofs use the published results below as stated; they are not proved here. Five items are consequences of these
results and are proved here: Theorem A.5, Corollary A.30, Theorem A.31,
Corollary A.33 and Corollary A.42; Theorem A.41 (5) and the closing sentences of a few
other items draw short consequences of the quoted statements, each with its reason. Each published result is cited by
its source, with its number and its page where given. Pages are those of the arXiv versions listed in the references;
the arXiv text of [BGP] carries the book's page numbers, [See64] and [MM87] are cited by their journal pages, [Mel93] by
the page of the author's online edition (version 5.0E, 1993), [Hö90], [RS1] and [Tre19] by the pages of the printed
books, and [DLMF] by equation number. Quotation marks enclose the source's own wording, transcribed into this edition's
typography; an ellipsis marks words of the statement left out because no proof here depends on them. Inside each item
the letters are the source's.

### A.1 Linear wave equations on Lorentzian manifolds

**Theorem A.1** ([BGP, Definition 1.3.8, p. 23; Corollary 1.3.12 and Theorem 1.3.13, p. 24;
Corollary A.5.4 and Lemma A.5.6, p. 174; Lemma A.5.9, p. 176].)

(1) Definition 1.3.8: "A connected timeoriented Lorentzian manifold is called globally hyperbolic if it satisfies the
strong causality condition and if for all p, q ∈ M the intersection J^M_+(p) ∩ J^M_−(q) is compact."

(2) Corollary 1.3.12: "On every globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold M there exists a smooth function h : M → ℝ
whose gradient is past directed timelike at every point and all of whose level-sets are spacelike Cauchy
hypersurfaces." Such an h is a Cauchy time-function, and "a Cauchy time-function is strictly monotonically increasing
along any future directed causal curve" (p. 24).

(3) Theorem 1.3.13: "Let M be a globally hyperbolic manifold and S be a spacelike smooth Cauchy hypersurface in M. Then
there exists a Cauchy time-function h : M → ℝ such that S = h⁻¹({0})."

(4) Corollary A.5.4: "Let S be a Cauchy hypersurface in a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold M and let K ⊂ M be
compact. Then J^M_±(K) ∩ S and J^M_±(K) ∩ J^M_∓(S) are compact."

(5) Lemma A.5.6: "Let M be a timeoriented Lorentzian manifold and let S ⊂ M be a spacelike hypersurface. Then for every
point p in S, there exists a basis of open neighborhoods Ω of p in M such that S ∩ Ω is a Cauchy hypersurface in Ω."

(6) Lemma A.5.9 is Theorem A.2.

**Theorem A.2** ([BGP, Lemma A.5.9, p. 176].) "For any acausal hypersurface S in a timeoriented
Lorentzian manifold the Cauchy development D(S) is a causally compatible and globally hyperbolic open subset of M."
Its proof records that "by the definition of D(S), the acausal subset S is a Cauchy hypersurface of D(S)". The Cauchy
development D(S) is the set of points p of M such that every inextendible causal curve through p meets S [BGP,
Definition 1.3.5, p. 22].

**Definition A.3** ([BGP, Section 1.5, p. 33].) Let M be a Lorentzian manifold and E → M a
real or complex vector bundle. "A linear differential operator P : C^∞(M, E) → C^∞(M, E) of second order will be called
normally hyperbolic if its principal symbol is given by the metric, σ_P(ξ) = −⟨ξ, ξ⟩ · id_(E_x)." In local coordinates
and a trivialisation of E,

    P = −Σ g^(ij)(x) ∂²/∂x^i∂x^j + Σ A_j(x) ∂/∂x^j + B_1(x).

**Theorem A.4** ([BGP, Section 1.5, p. 33; Theorem 3.1.1, p. 68; Remark 3.1.3, p. 72;
Corollary 3.2.4, p. 76; Proposition 3.2.5, p. 79; Theorem 3.2.11, p. 85].) Let E be a vector bundle over a Lorentzian
manifold M. Here 𝒟 denotes smooth sections with compact support.

(1) Normally hyperbolic operators are those of Definition A.3 (Section 1.5).

(2) Theorem 3.1.1: "Let M be a connected timeoriented Lorentzian manifold such that (1) the causality condition holds,
i. e., there are no causal loops, (2) the relation '≤' is closed, (3) the time separation function τ is finite and
continuous on M × M. Let P be a normally hyperbolic operator acting on sections in a vector bundle E over M. Then any
distribution u ∈ 𝒟′(M, E) with past or future compact support solving the equation Pu = 0 must vanish identically on
M." By Remark 3.1.3 these assumptions "hold for convex Lorentzian manifolds and for globally hyperbolic manifolds".

(3) Corollary 3.2.4: "Let E be a vector bundle over a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold M. Let ∇ be a connection
on E and let P = □^∇ + B be a normally hyperbolic operator acting on sections in E. Let S be a smooth spacelike Cauchy
hypersurface in M, and let n be the future directed (timelike) unit normal vector field along S. If u ∈ C^∞(M, E)
solves Pu = 0 on M, u = 0 along S, ∇_n u = 0 along S, then u = 0 on M."

(4) Proposition 3.2.5 (local solvability on RCCSV-domains). For each RCCSV-domain Ω ⊂ M such that S ∩ Ω is a
(spacelike) Cauchy hypersurface in Ω, and for each u0, u1 ∈ 𝒟(S ∩ Ω, E) and f ∈ 𝒟(Ω, E), "there exists a unique
u ∈ C^∞(Ω, E) satisfying Pu = f …, u = u0 along S, ∇_n u = u1 along S. Moreover, supp(u) ⊂ J^M(K) where
K = supp(u0) ∪ supp(u1) ∪ supp(f)."

(5) Theorem 3.2.11: "Let M be a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold and let S ⊂ M be a spacelike Cauchy
hypersurface. Let n be the future directed timelike unit normal field along S. Let E be a vector bundle over M and let
P be a normally hyperbolic operator acting on sections in E. Then for each u0, u1 ∈ 𝒟(S, E) and for each f ∈ 𝒟(M, E)
there exists a unique u ∈ C^∞(M, E) satisfying Pu = f, u|_S = u0, and ∇_n u|_S = u1. Moreover, supp(u) ⊂ J^M(K) where
K = supp(u0) ∪ supp(u1) ∪ supp(f)."

In (4) and (5), ∇ is the connection on E with which [BGP, Section 3.2] poses the Cauchy problem. Globally hyperbolic
manifolds are connected, by Theorem A.1 (1).

**Theorem A.5** (The Cauchy problem for wave operators on Minkowski space; proved below from
[BW15, Definition 7 and Theorem 8, p. 13] and [BGP, Definition 3.4.1, pp. 88–89; Corollary 3.4.3, p. 89].) Let
M = ℝ^(1+n) with the Minkowski metric and the Minkowski time t, and write J_±(A) = A + J_±(0) for the causal future and
past of A ⊂ M. Let P be a normally hyperbolic operator (Definition A.3) acting on ℂ^N-valued functions
on M, with smooth coefficients. Let s ∈ ℤ, t0 ∈ ℝ and f ∈ H^(s−1)_loc(M; ℂ^N) with supp f ⊂ {t ≥ t0}. Then there is
exactly one u ∈ 𝒟′(M; ℂ^N) with Pu = f and supp u ⊂ {t ≥ t0}; it lies in H^(s)_loc(M; ℂ^N), and
supp u ⊂ J_+(supp f).

If the principal symbol of a second-order operator Q is the dual metric function times the identity, then Q or −Q is
normally hyperbolic, the sign depending only on the convention for principal symbols, and the theorem applies to Q
with f replaced by ±f.

The proof uses the two results (1) and (2) below and the estimate (3), which is proved from (2). Distributions act on
test functions through the bilinear pairing ∫ φ · u dV, and P^* denotes the formally dual operator,
∫ φ · (Pψ) dV = ∫ (P^*φ) · ψ dV ([BW15, Section 1.4.2, p. 6] writes P† for it). In the coordinates of
Definition A.3, with the constant Minkowski g^(ij),

    P = −Σ g^(ij) ∂²/∂x^i∂x^j + Σ A_j ∂/∂x^j + B_1,    P^*φ = −Σ g^(ij) ∂²φ/∂x^i∂x^j − Σ ∂(A_j^T φ)/∂x^j + B_1^T φ,

T denoting the transpose; so P^* is again normally hyperbolic with smooth coefficients. Here 𝒟 denotes smooth sections
with compact support, and E = M × ℂ^N.

(1) [BGP, Definition 3.4.1, pp. 88–89; Corollary 3.4.3, p. 89]. "A linear map G_+ : 𝒟(M, E) →
C^∞(M, E) satisfying (i) P ∘ G_+ = id_(𝒟(M,E)), (ii) G_+ ∘ P|_(𝒟(M,E)) = id_(𝒟(M,E)), (iii) supp(G_+φ) ⊂
J^M_+(supp(φ)) for all φ ∈ 𝒟(M, E), is called an advanced Green's operator for P. Similarly, a linear map G_− :
𝒟(M, E) → C^∞(M, E) satisfying (i), (ii), and (iii′) supp(G_−φ) ⊂ J^M_−(supp(φ)) for all φ ∈ 𝒟(M, E) instead of
(iii) is called a retarded Green's operator for P." Corollary 3.4.3: "Let M be a globally hyperbolic Lorentzian
manifold. Let P be a normally hyperbolic operator acting on sections in a vector bundle E over M. Then there exist
unique advanced and retarded Green's operators G_± : 𝒟(M, E) → C^∞(M, E) for P." We use (1) for P and for P^*.

(2) [BW15, Definition 7 and Theorem 8, p. 13]. [BW15] considers a wave operator P (a second-order operator whose
principal symbol is given by the metric, P = −Σ g^(ij) ∂²/∂x^i∂x^j + lower order terms, [BW15, Section 1.8, p. 12])
acting on sections of a vector bundle S with a Riemannian or Hermitian metric and a compatible connection ∇, over a
globally hyperbolic manifold with a Cauchy temporal function t, in which the metric is g = −β dt² + g_t (p. 3);
Σ_s := t⁻¹(s), and H^k(Σ_s) is the Sobolev space of [BW15, Section 1.6, pp. 6–8]. Definition 7: "Given a Cauchy
temporal function t, we briefly write

    E_k(u, s) := E_k(u, Σ_s) = ‖u|_(Σ_s)‖²_(H^k(Σ_s)) + ‖β^(−1/2)∇_t u‖²_(H^(k−1)(Σ_s))."

Theorem 8: "Let [T0, T1] ⊂ t(M), let K ⊂ M be compact, and let k ∈ ℝ. Then there exists a constant C > 0 such that

    E_k(u, t1) ≤ E_k(u, t0) · e^(C(t1−t0)) + ∫_(t0)^(t1) e^(C(t1−s)) ‖Pu‖²_(H^(k−1)(Σ_s)) ds      (4)

holds for all t0, t1 ∈ [T0, T1] with t0 < t1 and for all u ∈ FE^(k+1)_sc(M, t; S) with supp(u) ⊂ J(K) and
Pu ∈ C⁰_sc(t(M), H^(k−1)(Σ•))." Here J(K) = J_+(K) ∪ J_−(K) (p. 4), and FE^(k+1)_sc(M, t; S) is the space of finite
(k + 1)-energy sections [BW15, Definition 1, p. 9]; the proof of [BW15, Corollary 12, p. 15] applies (4) to every
smooth u with supp u ⊂ J(K), and so do we. On M = ℝ^(1+n) take S = M × ℂ^N with the standard Hermitian metric and the
trivial connection, and t the Minkowski time: then β = 1, g_t is the Euclidean metric, Σ_s = {s} × ℝⁿ and ∇_t = ∂_t.
Let B ⊂ ℝⁿ be a closed ball and j ≥ 0 an integer. On functions on Σ_s supported in B, ‖·‖_(H^j(Σ_s)) is equivalent,
with constants independent of s, to ‖v‖_(H^j) := (Σ_(|γ|≤j) ‖∂^γ v‖²_(L²(ℝⁿ)))^(1/2): by [BW15, Section 1.6.2, p. 7]
it is the norm of the double of a larger closed ball, the same for every s; by [BW15, Section 1.6.1, p. 7], "for
k ∈ ℕ_0, a norm equivalent to ‖·‖_(H^k(Σ)) is given by ‖u‖² = Σ_(ℓ=0)^k ‖∇^ℓ u‖²_(L²(Σ))"; and for v supported in B
these terms are Euclidean, with |∇^ℓ v|² between Σ_(|γ|=ℓ) |∂^γ v|² and ℓ! times it.

(3) *The slab estimate.* For t0 < t1 let S(t0, t1) := {t0 < t < t1} ⊂ M and, for an integer k ≥ 0,
‖v‖_(k,S(t0,t1)) := (Σ_(|α|≤k) ‖∂^α v‖²_(L²(S(t0,t1))))^(1/2), α ranging over the multi-indices in (t, x). For a
function u on M write u(s) := u(s, ·). Let K ⊂ M be compact, t0 < t1 and k ≥ 1 an integer. There is C such that

    ‖u‖²_(k,S(t0,t1)) ≤ C (‖u(t0)‖²_(H^k) + ‖∂_t u(t0)‖²_(H^(k−1)) + ‖Pu‖²_(k−1,S(t0,t1)))    (A.1)

for every smooth u with supp u ⊂ J(K); and (A.1) also holds with u(t1), ∂_t u(t1) in place of u(t0),
∂_t u(t0).

*Proof of (3).* The set L := J(K) ∩ {t0 ≤ t ≤ t1} is compact, as J_±(K) = K + J_±(0). Let B be a closed ball
containing the projection of L to ℝⁿ, so that u(s) is supported in B for s ∈ [t0, t1]; the coefficients of P and all
their derivatives are bounded on L. Put e(s) := ‖u(s)‖²_(H^k) + ‖∂_t u(s)‖²_(H^(k−1)). By (2), with [T0, T1] := [t0, t1],
applied to the pairs (t0, s), and by the equivalence of norms,

    e(s) ≤ C (e(t0) + ∫_(t0)^(t1) ‖(Pu)(σ)‖²_(H^(k−1)) dσ) ≤ C (e(t0) + ‖Pu‖²_(k−1,S(t0,t1))),      t0 ≤ s ≤ t1,

the second inequality because ‖(Pu)(σ)‖_(H^(k−1)) involves x-derivatives only. For 1 ≤ ℓ ≤ k let N_ℓ be the sum of
‖∂_t^i ∂_x^γ u‖²_(L²(S(t0,t1))) over i ≤ ℓ and i + |γ| ≤ k. Then N_k = ‖u‖²_(k,S(t0,t1)), and N_1 ≤ ∫_(t0)^(t1) e(s) ds.
In the form of P displayed above, ∂_t² u = Pu + Δ_x u − Σ_j A_j ∂u/∂x^j − B_1 u, with x⁰ = t. For 2 ≤ i ≤ k and
i + |γ| ≤ k apply ∂_t^(i−2) ∂_x^γ: the term from Pu is a derivative of Pu of order at most k − 2; the term from Δ_x u
is a sum of derivatives of u of order at most k with at most i − 2 derivatives in t; by Leibniz's rule the remaining
terms are derivatives of u of order at most k − 1 with at most i − 1 derivatives in t, times functions bounded on L.
So N_ℓ ≤ C (N_(ℓ−1) + ‖Pu‖²_(k−1,S(t0,t1))) for 2 ≤ ℓ ≤ k, and

    ‖u‖²_(k,S(t0,t1)) ≤ C (∫_(t0)^(t1) e(s) ds + ‖Pu‖²_(k−1,S(t0,t1))) ≤ C (e(t0) + ‖Pu‖²_(k−1,S(t0,t1))),

which is (A.1). (This is the argument of the proof of [BW15, Corollary 12, p. 15], written for the norm
‖·‖_(k,S(t0,t1)).) For the data at t1, apply this to ũ(t, x) := u(−t, x): it satisfies P̃ũ(t, x) = (Pu)(−t, x) for the
operator P̃ obtained from P by the substitution t ↦ −t, which is normally hyperbolic with smooth coefficients, and
supp ũ ⊂ J(K̃) with K̃ the image of K; the slab S(t0, t1) becomes S(−t1, −t0). ∎

*Proof.* *Uniqueness.* For every p ∈ M the set {t ≥ t0} ∩ J_−(p) is compact, so a distribution supported in
{t ≥ t0} has past compact support; by Theorem A.4 (2), Pu = 0 and supp u ⊂ {t ≥ t0} imply u = 0.

*Reduction to compact support.* Let (χ_j) be a locally finite smooth partition of unity on M by functions with
compact supports, and f_j := χ_j f ∈ H^(s−1)(ℝ^(1+n); ℂ^N). Suppose that for every j there is u_j ∈ H^(s)_loc with
Pu_j = f_j and supp u_j ⊂ J_+(supp f_j). A compact set L meets J_+(supp f_j) only if supp f_j meets the compact set
J_−(L) ∩ {t ≥ t0}, so only finitely many u_j are nonzero near L. Hence u := Σ_j u_j lies in H^(s)_loc, Pu = f, and
supp u ⊂ ⋃_j J_+(supp f_j) ⊂ supp f + J_+(0) ⊂ {t ≥ t0}.

So let g ∈ H^(s−1)(ℝ^(1+n); ℂ^N) have compact support K, and let G_± and G^*_± be the Green's operators of P and of
P^* given by (1).

*The case s ≥ 1.* Let ρ_ε be a standard mollifier and g_k := ρ_(1/k) ∗ g. It is smooth, supported in the closed
(1/k)-neighbourhood K_k of K, and g_k → g in H^(s−1). Put u_k := G_+ g_k: it is smooth, Pu_k = g_k and
supp u_k ⊂ J_+(K_k) ⊂ J_+(K_1). Fix T0 < min_(K_1) t and T1 > T0. The functions u_k − u_l are smooth, supported in
J_+(K_1) ⊂ J(K_1) ∩ {t > T0}, and so vanish with their t-derivatives on {t = T0}. By (A.1) of order s, with
K_1 in place of K and (T0, T1) in place of (t0, t1),

    ‖u_k − u_l‖_(s,S(T0,T1)) ≤ C ‖g_k − g_l‖_(s−1,S(T0,T1)) ≤ C ‖g_k − g_l‖_(H^(s−1)(ℝ^(1+n))),

the last norm being equivalent, for the integer s − 1 ≥ 0, to the sum of the L²-norms of the derivatives of order at
most s − 1, by Plancherel's theorem. As T1 is arbitrary and u_k = 0 for t < T0, (u_k) converges in H^(s)_loc(M) to
some u with Pu = g, and supp u ⊂ ⋂_k (K_k + J_+(0)) = K + J_+(0) = J_+(K).

*The case s ≤ 0.* Put m := 1 − s ≥ 1, so g ∈ H^(−m). Let χ ∈ C_c^∞(M) equal 1 near K. For φ ∈ 𝒟(M; ℂ^N) put

    u(φ) := g(χ G^*_− φ).

If supp φ lies in a compact set L, choose T1 > max_L t and T0 < min_(supp χ) t. Then w := G^*_− φ is smooth,
P^* w = φ, and w is supported in J_−(L) ⊂ J(L) ∩ {t ≤ max_L t}, so w and ∂_t w vanish on {t = T1}. By (A.1)
for P^*, of order m, with the data at T1, with L in place of K and (T0, T1) in place of (t0, t1),
‖w‖_(m,S(T0,T1)) ≤ C ‖φ‖_(m−1,S(T0,T1)) ≤ C ‖φ‖_(H^(m−1)); as χw is supported in {T0 < t < T1},

    |u(φ)| ≤ ‖g‖_(H^(−m)) ‖χw‖_(H^m) ≤ C_L ‖φ‖_(H^(m−1)),      supp φ ⊂ L.

So u is a distribution, and ψu ∈ H^(1−m) for every ψ ∈ C_c^∞(M), that is, u ∈ H^(s)_loc. For φ ∈ 𝒟,
G^*_− P^* φ = φ by (1) (ii), so (Pu)(φ) = u(P^*φ) = g(χφ) = g(φ): Pu = g. If supp φ ∩ J_+(K) = ∅, then
J_−(supp φ) ∩ K = ∅, so χ G^*_− φ vanishes near K and u(φ) = 0; hence supp u ⊂ J_+(K). ∎

### A.2 Quasilinear hyperbolic systems

The setting of [DS23] is the system "∂_t u + A^i(u) ∂_i u = R(u), u(0) = u0, i = 1, 2, …, N" (its (1.1), p. 1) on the
torus 𝕋^N, with A^i : ℝ × 𝕋^N × ℝ^m → ℝ^(m²), R : ℝ × 𝕋^N × ℝ^m → ℝ^m and "N(u)(t, x) = N(t, x, u(t, x)), N ∈ {A^i,
R}" (p. 2). H^r = H^r(𝕋^N), with norm ‖·‖_r, and "I = [−T, T] for some T > 0 and B(I) = C(I; C¹) ∩ C¹(I; C)" (p. 3).
For a non-empty open set U ⊂ ℝ^m, with closure Ū, the hypotheses are, on p. 3:

- (A1) "A^i ∈ C^∞(ℝ × 𝕋^N × Ū; ℝ^(m²)) satisfies that for any multi-indices k ∈ ℕ, α ∈ ℕ^n and β ∈ ℕ^m, there is a
  continuous increasing function f^i_(k,α,β) such that |∂^k_t ∂^α_x ∂^β_ζ A^i(t, x, ζ)| ≤ f^i_(k,α,β)(|ζ|)."
- (A2) The same for R ∈ C^∞(ℝ × 𝕋^N × Ū; ℝ^m), with continuous increasing functions h_(k,α,β).
- (A3) "For any ξ = (ξ_1, …, ξ_N) ∈ ℝ^N ∖ {0} and ζ ∈ Ū, the matrix A = A(t, x, ζ, ξ) = A^i(t, x, ζ) ξ_i is
  diagonalizable and has only real eigenvalues".
- (A4) "The distinct eigenvalues, λ_1 < λ_2 < ⋯ < λ_l, of A satisfy λ_i ∈ C^(1,0,1,0)(ℝ × 𝕋^N × Ū × (ℝ^N ∖ {0})) and
  the λ_i's do not meet each other on ℝ × 𝕋^N × Ū × (ℝ^N ∖ {0})".

The hypotheses do not require R(t, x, 0) = 0.

**Theorem A.6** ([DS23, Theorem 2.4, p. 4].) "Let r > N/2 + 1. Assume that (A1)-(A4) are satisfied
on some U ⊂ ℝ^m open. Then, for any u0 ∈ H^r with M̃ = dist(U^c, Im(u0)) > 0, there exists some T > 0 depending on
‖u0‖_r and M̃ such that (1.1) has a unique solution u ∈ B(I) on I = [−T, T]. Moreover, the solution satisfies u ∈ C(I;
H^r) ∩ C¹(I; H^(r−1)) (2.2)", together with the energy estimates (2.3)–(2.4) of [DS23], "and ⋃_(t∈I) Im(u(t)) ⊂ U
(2.5)."

**Theorem A.7** ([DS23, Theorem 2.6, p. 5].) "Let r > N/2 + 1. Assume that (A1)-(A4) are
satisfied on some U ⊂ ℝ^m open. Given any I = [0, T] for some T > 0, if u ∈ B(I) satisfying (2.5) is a solution to
(1.1) with u0 ∈ H^r, then u satisfies (2.2) and (2.3). Let T* be the supremum times T such that there is a solution u ∈
B(I) to (1.1) on I = [0, T] satisfying (2.5). Then one and only one of the following statements holds. T* = ∞;
inf_(0≤t<T*) dist(U^c, Im u(t)) = 0; lim_(T→T*−) ‖u‖_(B([0,T])) = +∞. Similar results holds on [−T, 0]."

**Remark A.8** ([DS23, Remark 2.3 (i), p. 4].) In the setting above: "Based on (A1) and (A2),
following a standard argument, given any compact interval I ⊂ ℝ and s > N/2, it holds for any u ∈ H^s such that
‖N(u)‖_s ≤ C_I + F_I(‖u‖_∞) ‖u‖_s, N ∈ {A^i, R}; and given any k ∈ ℕ, it holds for any u ∈ C^k that
‖N(u)‖_(k,∞) ≤ F_I(‖u‖_∞) ‖u‖_(k,∞), N ∈ {A^i, R}." Here (p. 3) ℝ_+ = (0, ∞), and "F_I : ℝ_+ → ℝ_+ (C_I, resp.)
denotes a continuous increasing function (a positive constant, resp.) depending on the structure of A^i and R such that
F_(I_1) ≤ F_(I_2) (C_(I_1) ≤ C_(I_2), resp.) whenever I_1 ⊂ I_2."

**Theorem A.9** ([DS23, Theorem 2.5, p. 5].) "Let r > N/2 + 1. Assume that (A1)-(A4) are satisfied
on some U ⊂ ℝ^m open. The solution asserted in Theorem 2.4 depends continuously on the initial data in the following
sense. Assume that u0 ∈ H^r with M̃ = dist(U^c, Im(u0)) > 0 and u is the solution asserted in Theorem 2.4 with initial
datum u0 on the interval I = [−T, T]. If u_(0,n) → u0 in H^r as n → ∞, then for sufficiently large n, the solutions u_n
corresponding to the initial data u_(0,n) also exist on I and u_n → u in C(I, H^r)." Theorem 2.4 of [DS23] is
Theorem A.6.

**Theorem A.10** ([AO14, Theorem 1.1, p. 2, and Remark 1.2, p. 3].) The setting is the initial value
problem (p. 2)

    ∂_μ(A^μν(U) ∂_ν U) = F(U, ∂U) + χ_Ω H(U, ∂U)   in [0, T] × ℝⁿ,      (U, ∂_t U)|_(t=0) = (Ũ0, Ũ1)   in ℝⁿ,

"(1.1)–(1.2)", where "(i) Ω is a bounded open set in ℝⁿ with smooth boundary, (ii) U(x) = (U¹(x), …, U^N(x)) is vector
valued, (iii) A(U) = (A^μν(U)), F = (F^I(U, ∂U)) and H = (H^I(U, ∂U)) (I = 1, …, N) are smooth maps with F(0, 0) = 0,
and (iv) for some γ, κ > 0, A^μν(U) satisfies 1/γ |ξ|² ≤ A^ij(U) ξ_i ξ_j ≤ γ |ξ|² and A^00(U) ≤ −κ (1.3) for all (U,
ξ) ∈ ℝ^N × ℝⁿ", and χ_Ω is the indicator function of Ω. The compatibility conditions (1.5) require the time derivatives
of U at t = 0 generated from the data by the equation to lie in the spaces of [AO14, (1.5)]. "Theorem 1.1. Suppose n ≥
3, s ∈ ℤ_(>n/2) and (Ũ0, Ũ1) ∈ H^(s+1)(ℝⁿ) × H^s(ℝⁿ) satisfy the compatibility conditions (1.5). Then there exist a T >
0 and a map U ∈ CX^(s+1)_T(ℝⁿ) such that U is the unique solution in CX²_T(ℝⁿ) ∩ ⋂_(ℓ=0)^1 C^ℓ([0, T), W^(1−ℓ,∞)(ℝⁿ))
to the initial value problem (1.1)-(1.2). Moreover, if ‖u‖_(W^(1,∞)((0,T)×𝕋ⁿ)) < ∞, then there exists a T* > T such
that the u can be continued uniquely to a solution on [0, T*) × 𝕋ⁿ." In the continuation clause 𝕋ⁿ stands for ℝⁿ: the
proof of that clause, [AO14, Section 4.2, p. 22], assumes ‖U‖_(W^(1,∞)((0,T)×ℝⁿ)) ≤ K. By Remark 1.2 (i)(a) A, F and H
may "depend explicitly on x", and by Remark 1.2 (ii)(b) "Theorem 1.1 is also valid for quasi-linear wave equations
A^μν(U, ∂U) ∂_μ ∂_ν U = F(U, ∂U) + χ_Ω H(U, ∂U) in [0, T] × ℝⁿ, provided that we take s > n/2 + 1 and change the
continuation principle to that of bounding ‖U‖_(W^(2,∞)((0,T)×ℝⁿ))."

**Remark A.11** (The iteration bounded in a high norm and contracting in a low norm.) [AO14, Section 4.1,
p. 19]: "We establish existence and uniqueness of solutions using the well-known strategy, also used by Koch [12], of
setting up an appropriate iterative approximation scheme and showing convergence by establishing boundedness in a high
norm followed by contraction in a low norm." [AG22] names "the boundedness in the high norm and contraction in the low
norm" in its abstract, p. 1; in its Section 9, p. 24, (9.6) is the bound of the iterates in the high norm and (9.7)
the weakly convergent subsequence.

### A.3 The reduced Einstein equations and the gauge

**Theorem A.12** ([CBCM10, (2.7)–(2.9), p. 8].) In n + 1 dimensions, let ĝ be a background metric
with connection D̂ and Christoffel symbols Γ̂, and for a metric g put W^λ := g^(αβ) Γ̂^λ_(αβ) and H^λ := g^(αβ)
Γ^λ_(αβ) − W^λ = g^(αβ)(Γ^λ_(αβ) − Γ̂^λ_(αβ)) (2.7). Then

    "R_(αβ) = R^(H)_(αβ) + 1/2 (g_(αλ) D̂_β H^λ + g_(βλ) D̂_α H^λ)"   (2.8),
    "R^(H)_(αβ) = −1/2 g^(λμ) D̂_λ D̂_μ g_(αβ) + f̂[g, D̂g]_(αβ)"       (2.9),

with f̂ "independent of the second derivatives of g".

**Theorem A.13** ([Hin26a, Proposition 5.1, p. 38].) "Fix any v ∈ (0, 1) and C0 > 0. Fix moreover
α_sf, α_K ∈ ℝ subject to the conditions α_sf < −1/2 and α_K > α_sf + 1/2. Set ρ_sf = r⁻¹ and ρ_K = r/t; put
w := ρ_sf^(α_sf+1) ρ_K^(α_K) and w′ := ρ_sf^(α_sf+1). Then for all sufficiently small e > 0, there exists a 1-form
c ∈ ρ_sf C^∞(M; T*) satisfying the following properties for some r0 > 100m, 0 < δ_r < (4r0)⁻¹, and δ_sf > 0:
- (1) (Basic properties.) c is stationary, i.e., ℒ_(∂_t) c = 0 … Moreover, rc ∈ C^∞(M; T*) is past timelike and
  nowhere vanishing.
- (2) (Explicit regions.) We have c = (1/2) r0^(−2) (r0 dt − v(r − r0) dr) for r0/2 ≤ r ≤ 2r0 (5.1), and
  c = r⁻¹ (dt − v dr) for r ≥ 3r0 (5.2).
- (3) (Interior saddle point …) The endomorphism S_(g,c,e) from Lemma 3.9 is positive definite (with respect to the
  inner product B_(g,c,e) on T* from Lemma 3.3) at all points with |r − r0| ≤ (5/6) r0 √(e/v).
- (4) (Saddle point at ∂𝒦⁺ …) For ρ_sf ≤ 2δ_r and ρ_K ≤ 2δ_r, the endomorphism r²(−ℓ_(g,c,e)(dw/w) + S_(g,c,e)) is
  positive definite.
- (5) (Sink in sf° …) At points where r/t/v ∈ [1 − 2δ_sf, 1 + 2δ_sf] and r⁻¹ ≤ 2δ_r, the endomorphism
  r²(−ℓ_(g,c,e)(dw′/w′) + S_(g,c,e)) is positive definite.
- (6) (Positivity along escape functions …) For m ≤ r ≤ r0 − r0√(e/v), −ℓ_(g,c,e)(−dr) is positive definite. For
  r0 + r0√(e/v) ≤ r < ∞, −ℓ_(g,c,e)(dr) is positive definite. On sf ∩ {r/t ∈ [δ_r, v(1 − δ_sf)]},
  −r² ℓ_(g,c,e)(d(r/t)) is positive definite, and on sf ∩ {r/t ∈ [v(1 + δ_sf), 10]}, −r² ℓ_(g,c,e)(−d(r/t)) is
  positive definite."

The objects S_(g,c,e), B_(g,c,e) and ℓ_(g,c,e) are those of [Hin26a, Lemmas 3.3 and 3.9], and r/t/v in (5) is (r/t)/v.

**Theorem A.14** (Globally hyperbolic developments; [Sbi15, Definitions 2.1, 2.2 and 2.4, p. 11;
Theorems 2.6 and 2.7, p. 12; Theorem 3.4, p. 14; Definition 3.5, p. 15; Theorem 3.13, p. 20; proof of Theorem 2.7,
pp. 20–22].) [Sbi15] works with the vacuum Einstein equations Ric(g) = 0 in any dimension. Its standing assumptions
(p. 10): "we stipulate that all manifolds and tensor fields considered in this paper are smooth, even if this is not
mentioned explicitly"; "We moreover assume that all Lorentzian manifolds we consider are connected and time oriented.
The dimension of the Lorentzian manifolds is denoted by d + 1, where d ≥ 1." "Initial data (𝓜, ḡ, k̄)
for the vacuum Einstein equations consists of a connected d-dimensional Riemannian manifold (𝓜, ḡ) together with a
symmetric 2-covariant tensor field k̄ on 𝓜 that satisfy the constraint equations: R̄ − |k̄|² + (tr k̄)² = 0,
∇̄^i k̄_ij − ∇̄_j tr k̄ = 0" (p. 11).

(1) Definition 2.1: "A globally hyperbolic development (GHD) (M, g, ι) of initial data (𝓜, ḡ, k̄) is a time oriented,
globally hyperbolic Lorentzian manifold (M, g) that satisfies the vacuum Einstein equations, together with an
embedding ι : 𝓜 → M such that 1. ι^*(g) = ḡ 2. ι^*(k) = k̄, where k denotes the second fundamental form of ι(𝓜) in M
with respect to the future normal 3. ι(𝓜) is a Cauchy surface in (M, g)."

(2) Definition 2.2: "Given two GHDs (M, g, ι) and (M′, g′, ι′) of the same initial data, we say that (M′, g′, ι′) is an
extension of (M, g, ι) iff there exists a time orientation preserving isometric embedding ψ : M → M′ that preserves the
initial data, i.e. ψ ∘ ι = ι′." Its footnote 19: "an isometric embedding is an isometric immersion that is a
diffeomorphism onto its image." Definition 2.4: "Given two GHDs (M, g, ι) and (M′, g′, ι′) of initial data
(𝓜, ḡ, k̄), we say that a GHD (U ⊆ M, g|_U, ι) is a common globally hyperbolic development (CGHD) of (M, g, ι) and
(M′, g′, ι′) iff (M′, g′, ι′) is an extension of (U, g_U, ι_U)."

(3) Theorem 2.6: "Given initial data for the vacuum Einstein equations, there exists a GHD, and for any two GHDs of the
same initial data, there exists a CGHD." Theorem 2.7 (Global uniqueness): "Given two GHDs M and M′ of the same initial
data, there exists a GHD M̃ that is an extension of M and M′."

(4) Theorem 3.4 (Existence of MCGHD): "Given two GHDs M and M′ of the same initial data, there exists a unique CGHD U of
M and M′ with the property that if V is another CGHD of M and M′, then U is an extension of V. We call U the maximal
common globally hyperbolic development (MCGHD) of M and M′." In its proof U is the union of all CGHDs of M and M′
contained in M, and "U is open" (p. 14).

(5) Definition 3.5: "Let U be a CGHD of M and M′, and let us denote the isometric embedding of U into M′ with ψ. Two
points p ∈ ∂U ⊆ M and p′ ∈ ∂ψ(U) ⊆ M′ are called corresponding boundary points of U iff for all neighbourhoods V of p
and for all neighbourhoods V′ of p′ one has ψ⁻¹(V′ ∩ ψ(U)) ∩ V ≠ ∅." Theorem 3.13: "Let M and M′ be GHDs of the same
initial data, and let U be the MCGHD of M and M′. Then U does not have corresponding boundary points in M and M′."

(6) The proof of Theorem 2.7 (pp. 20–22) glues M and M′ along U: M̃ := (M ⊔ M′)/∼, where p ∼ ψ(p) for p ∈ U. By
Theorem 3.13 the quotient is Hausdorff (p. 21), and "(M̃, g̃, ι̃) is a GHD of (𝓜, ḡ, k̄) and, moreover, it is an
extension of M and M′, where the isometric embeddings are given by the maps π ∘ j and π ∘ j′" (p. 22), π being the
quotient map and j, j′ the inclusions of M and M′ into M ⊔ M′.

### A.4 The constraint equations

**Theorem A.15** ([CD03, (2.1)–(2.2), p. 4].) "Initial data (g, K) for the vacuum Einstein
equations belong to the zero level set of the constraints map:

    (J, ρ)(K, g) := (2(−∇^j K_ij + ∇_i tr K), R(g) − |K|² + (tr K)²) = (0, 0).   (2.1)

These are the general relativistic constraint equations whatever the space-dimension n." With h = δg and Q = δK, "the
linearisation of the constraints map at (K, g) reads"

    P(Q, h) = ( −K^pq ∇_i h_pq + K^q_i (2∇^j h_qj − ∇_q h^l_l) − 2∇^j Q_ij + 2∇_i tr Q − 2(∇_i K^pq − ∇^q K^p_i) h_pq ,
                −Δ(tr h) + div div h − ⟨h, Ric(g)⟩ + 2 K^pl K^q_l h_pq − 2⟨K, Q⟩ + 2 tr K (−⟨h, K⟩ + tr Q) ).   (2.2)

**Theorem A.16** ([Rac16, (4.20), (4.21) and Lemma 4.1, p. 12; Theorem 4.3, p. 14].) In the
notation of [Rac16, Sections 3–4]: the slice Σ is foliated by the level surfaces S_ρ; κ is given algebraically by
(4.17); and (4.16) and (3.2) are the evolution equations for (k_i, K^l_l) in ρ.

Written as (4.19) (Remark A.17), with u = (k_B, K^E_E)ᵀ, the system has "the coefficients B^(K) of
∂_K, with K = 2, 3, …, n," given by

    B^(K)_ij = −N̂^K δ_ij − N̂ γ̂^(KL) δ_in δ_j(L−1) + (κ N̂/K^E_E) δ_i(K−1) δ_jn
               − 2 (N̂ k_L/K^E_E) γ̂^(LM) δ_i(K−1) δ_(j+1)M,   (4.20)

"where the lowercase and uppercase Latin indices take the value 1, 2, …, n and 2, 3, …, n, respectively"; with a
common symmetrizer as defined in Remark A.17, "It may be verified by a direct calculation that the
matrix of the form

    H_ij = δ_in δ_jn − (2/κ) k_P γ̂^(PQ) [δ_in δ_(j+1)Q + δ_(i+1)Q δ_jn] +
           (1/κ²) [4 (k_P γ̂^(PQ) δ_(i+1)Q) (k_S γ̂^(ST) δ_(j+1)T) − κ · K^E_E γ̂^(PQ) δ_(i+1)P δ_(j+1)Q]   (4.21)

is indeed a common symmetrizer to (4.19) in a subset of Σ where neither κ nor K^l_l vanishes and in which they are of
opposite sign." By footnote 6 (p. 12), "in evaluating a term of the form δ_(j+1)M, here and also in (4.21), one needs
to refer to the (n + 1)-dimensional Kronecker delta"; so u_i = k_(i+1) for i < n and u_n = K^E_E. With a^Q := k_P
γ̂^(PQ), H has the entry 1 at (n, n), the entries −2a^(j+1)/κ elsewhere in the last row and column, and the block
(4a^(i+1)a^(j+1) − κK^E_E γ̂^((i+1)(j+1)))/κ² for i, j < n. Subtracting from that block the product of the last column
with the last row leaves −(K^E_E/κ) γ̂^((i+1)(j+1)), and γ̂ is positive definite; so H is positive definite exactly
where κK^E_E < 0. H is a rational function of k_P, K^E_E, κ and γ̂ whose only denominators are powers of κ.

Lemma 4.1: "Assume that κ · K^l_l < 0 holds in a subset of Σ. Then equations (4.16) and (3.2) comprise a first order
symmetrizable hyperbolic system there."

Theorem 4.3: "Assume that the freely specifiable part of data N̂, N̂^i, γ̂_ij; K̊_ij; e, p_i (4.28) on Σ, and the
initial data (₀k_i, ₀K^l_l) for the system (4.16) and (3.2) on a ρ = ρ0 level surface are chosen such that they are all
smooth on their respective domains, and that the system comprised by (4.16) and (3.2) can be guaranteed to be
symmetrizable hyperbolic in a sufficiently small neighborhood of S_ρ0 in Σ … Then, there exists a unique smooth (local)
solution (k_i, K^l_l) to (4.16) and (3.2) such that k_i|_(S_ρ0) = ₀k_i, K^l_l|_(S_ρ0) = ₀K^l_l. This solution, along
with the freely specifiable data (4.28), uniquely determines κ via (4.17). The fields h_ij and K_ij which can be built
up from the solution to (4.16), (3.2) and (4.17) and from the freely specifiable part of the data do satisfy the full
constraint system (1.1)–(1.2) in the domain of dependence of S_ρ0 in Σ."

**Remark A.17** ([Rac16, (4.19), p. 12; (4.22) and (4.23), p. 13].) In the notation of
Theorem A.16 and [Rac16, (2.1)–(2.6), p. 5]: n̂^i is the unit normal of the leaves S_ρ, γ̂^(KL) is the
inverse of their induced metric in leaf coordinates x^K (K = 2, …, n), κ = n̂^k n̂^l K_kl, k_i = γ̂^k_i n̂^l K_kl is the
mixed part and K^l_l (also written K^E_E) the trace on the leaves of the second fundamental form K_ij of Σ, and N̂, N̂^K
are the lapse and shift of the vector field ρ^i with ρ^i D_i ρ = 1, so that n̂_i = N̂(dρ)_i. On p. 12: "when writing
out (4.16) and (3.2) in local coordinates (ρ, x², …, xⁿ), adopted to the foliation S_ρ and the vector field ρ^i, they
take the form

    ∂_ρ u + B^(K) ∂_K u + C = 0   (4.19)

for the vector valued variable u = (k_B, K^E_E)ᵀ", and "A system of the form of (4.19) is known to be Friedrichs
symmetrizable … if a common symmetrizer of the coefficients B^(K) exists. A bilinear form, H_ij, is called to be a
common symmetrizer to (4.19) if it is positive definite and is such that for any value of K = 2, …, n the product
H_ij B^(K)_jk is symmetric." On p. 13: "It is also informative to inspect the characteristic directions ξ_i = (ξ_ρ,
ξ_2, …, ξ_n) which are the roots of the essential part of the characteristic polynomial

    K^l_l (n̂^i ξ_i)² − 2 (n̂^i ξ_i) (γ̂^(KL) k_K ξ_L) + κ (γ̂^(KL) ξ_K ξ_L) = 0   (4.22)

of (4.19). In virtue of (2.3) and (4.22), for the ρ-component of a characteristic direction the relation

    ξ_ρ = N̂^K ξ_K + (N̂/K^E_E) [(γ̂^(KL) k_K ξ_L) ± √((γ̂^(KL) k_K ξ_L)² − κ · K^E_E (γ̂^(KL) ξ_K ξ_L))]   (4.23)

holds."

**Theorem A.18** ([CD03, Theorem 3.6, p. 13].) "Let k ≥ 0, g0 ∈ W^(k+4,∞)_loc, suppose that (A.2)
holds with 0 ≤ i ≤ 4 + k, that Ric(g0) ∈ φ^(−2) W^(k+2,∞)_φ(g0), K0 ∈ φ^(−1) W^(k+3,∞)_φ(g0), and that the weights φ
and ψ have the scaling property … If there exists a compact set 𝒦 ⊂ M such that for all H̊¹_(φ,ψ)(g0) vector fields Y
and H̊²_(φ,ψ)(g0) functions N, both supported in M ∖ 𝒦, the inequality (3.4) holds, then for all (K, g) close to
(K0, g0) in φ^(−1) W^(k+3,∞)_φ(g0) × W^(k+4,∞)_φ(g0) norm, the map

    π_(𝒦0^(⊥g)) L_(φ,ψ) : 𝒦0^(⊥g) ∩ (H̊^(k+3)_(φ,ψ)(g) × H̊^(k+4)_(φ,ψ)(g))
                         → 𝒦0^(⊥g) ∩ (H̊^(k+1)_(φ,ψ)(g) × H̊^k_(φ,ψ)(g))

is an isomorphism such that the norm of its inverse is bounded independently of (K, g)." Condition (A.2), inequality
(3.4), the scaling property and the operator L_(φ,ψ) are those of [CD03, Section 3 and Appendix A]. 𝒦0 is the kernel
of P* at (K0, g0), with (J, ρ) and P as in Theorem A.15.

**Theorem A.19** ([CD03, Theorem 3.9, p. 14].) "Under the hypotheses of Theorem 3.6, if the map

    (Y, N) ↦ π_(𝒦0^(⊥g)) ψ^(−2) [(J, ρ)((K, g) + ψ² Φ² P*(Y, N)) − (J, ρ)(K, g)]      (3.13)

[from 𝒦0^(⊥g) ∩ (H̊^(k+3)_(φ,ψ)(g) × H̊^(k+4)_(φ,ψ)(g)) to 𝒦0^(⊥g) ∩ (H̊^(k+1)_(φ,ψ)(g) × H̊^k_(φ,ψ)(g))] is
differentiable in a neighborhood of zero, then it is bijective in a (perhaps smaller) neighborhood of zero." The
theorem then states the solvability of (3.14) for small (δJ, δρ). Theorem 3.6 is Theorem A.18.

**Theorem A.20** ([CD03, Proposition G.1, pp. 77–78].) "Let (V_x, ‖·‖_(V_x))_(x∈A) and
(W_x, ‖·‖_(W_x))_(x∈A) be two families of Banach spaces. Let r > 0 and let {f_x : B_(V_x)(0, r) → W_x}_(x∈A) be a
family of differentiable functions such that:
1. Df_x(0) : V_x → W_x has a right inverse for all x ∈ A which is bounded independently of x ∈ A.
2. ‖f_x(v + h) − f_x(v) − Df_x(v)h‖_(W_x)/‖h‖²_(V_x) is bounded independently of x ∈ A, v ∈ B_(V_x)(0, r) and h ∈ V
   such that v + h ∈ B_(V_x)(0, r).
3. ‖Df_x(v + h) − Df_x(v)‖_(L(V_x,W_x))/‖h‖_(V_x) is bounded independently of x ∈ A, v ∈ B_(V_x)(0, r) and h ∈ V
   such that v + h ∈ B_(V_x)(0, r).

Then there exists ε > 0 and C > 0 such that for all x ∈ A and all δf ∈ W_x, ‖δf‖_(W_x) < ε, there exists a solution
δx ∈ V_x of the equation f_x(δx) − f_x(0) = δf, which satisfies ‖δx‖_(V_x) ≤ C ‖δf‖_(W_x)."

**Theorem A.21** ([CD03, Theorem 5.9, p. 25; Proposition 5.10, p. 26; Corollary 5.11, p. 27].)
Theorem 5.9: "Let M be a compact manifold with boundary, let s > 0, k > n/2 and suppose that g0 is a metric on M which
has (W^(k+4,∞)_(x²), k + 4)–behavior at ∂M, with

    x⁴ |Ric(g0)|_(g0) → 0,   x |∇∇x|_(g0) → 0,   K0 ∈ x^(−2) W^(k+3,∞)_(x²)(g0),   x² |K0|_(g0) + x⁴ |∇K0|_(g0) → 0

as x → 0 ((5.10a–c)). There exists ε > 0 such that for all (K, g) in x^(−2) W^(k+3,∞)_(x²)(g0) × W^(k+4,∞)_(x²)(g0)
for which ‖(K − K0, g − g0)‖ < ε, and for all pairs (δJ, δρ) ∈ H^(k+1)_(x²,e^(s/x))(g) × H^k_(x²,e^(s/x))(g)
satisfying ‖(δJ, δρ)‖ < ε, there exists a solution (δK, δg) = e^(−2s/x) Φ² P*(Y, N) ∈
x² H^(k+2)_(x²,e^(s/x))(g) × x⁴ H^(k+2)_(x²,e^(s/x))(g), close to zero, of the equation

    π_(𝒦0^(⊥g)) e^(2s/x) [(J, ρ)(K + δK, g + δg) − (J, ρ)(K, g)] = π_(𝒦0^(⊥g)) e^(2s/x) (δJ, δρ)."      (5.11)

Proposition 5.10 (p. 26) and Corollary 5.11 (p. 27): let k ≥ k0 := ⌊n/2⌋ + 1 and let g0 have
(C^(k+4,α)_(x²,1), k + 5)–behaviour at ∂M, with (5.10). Proposition 5.10 then reads: "there exists ε > 0 such that if
(K, g) in x^(−2) C^(k+3,α)_(x²,1)(g0) × C^(k+4,α)_(x²,1)(g0) with
‖(K − K0, g − g0)‖_(x^(−2) W^(k0+3,∞)_(x²)(g0) × W^(k0+4,∞)_(x²)(g0)) < ε, and if
‖(δJ, δρ)‖_(C^(k0+1,α)_(x²,e^(t/x))(g) × C^(k0,α)_(x²,e^(t/x))(g)) + ‖(δJ, δρ)‖_(H^(k0+1)_(x²,x^(−n)e^(t/x))(g) ×
H^(k0)_(x²,x^(−n)e^(t/x))(g)) < ε with t > 0, then the solution (δK, δg) given by Theorem 5.9 is in
x² C^(k0+2,α)_(x²,e^(t/x))(g) × x⁴ C^(k0+2,α)_(x²,e^(t/x))(g)." Corollary 5.11: "Under the hypotheses of the preceding
proposition, if (δJ, δρ) ∈ C^∞_(x²,e^(s/x))(g) × C^∞_(x²,e^(s/x))(g), and if (K, g) ∈ C^∞(M̄) × C^∞(M̄), then the
solution given by Theorem 5.9 is in x² C^∞_(x²,e^(s/x))(g) × x⁴ C^∞_(x²,e^(s/x))(g) ⊂ C^∞(M̄) × C^∞(M̄). In fact
(δK, δg) can be smoothly extended by zero across ∂M." Corollary 5.11 thus carries both smallness conditions of
Proposition 5.10.

### A.5 The characteristic initial value problem

**Theorem A.22** ([CTG23, Theorem 1.1, pp. 2–3].) "The maximal globally hyperbolic development
of smooth initial data for vacuum Einstein equations with a (possibly zero) cosmological constant Λ ∈ ℝ, on two
characteristic hypersurfaces intersecting transversally, contains a future neighborhood of the initial data
hypersurfaces." The theorem holds in every spacetime dimension. The authors add that "the result remains true in
suitable Sobolev spaces" (p. 3).

### A.6 Higher-dimensional black holes

**Theorem A.23** ([ER08, (14)–(16), p. 10; (31)–(34), p. 14; (42)–(45), p. 16], after [MP86].) The
Myers–Perry black holes are vacuum solutions in every dimension d > 4 [MP86]. In Emparan and Reall's words, "the
solutions belong in the Kerr-Schild class

    g_μν = η_μν + 2H(x^ρ) k_μ k_ν      (31)

where k_μ is a null vector with respect to both g_μν and the Minkowski metric η_μν … Of all known vacuum black holes in
d > 4, only the Myers-Perry solutions seem to have this property" (p. 14).

For odd d, with N = (d − 1)/2 rotation planes, the general solution is

    ds² = −dt² + (r² + a_i²)(dμ_i² + μ_i² dφ_i²) + (μr²/(ΠF)) (dt − a_i μ_i² dφ_i)² + (ΠF/(Π − μr²)) dr²      (42)

summed over i = 1, …, N, with Σ μ_i² = 1 and

    F(r, μ_i) = 1 − Σ a_i² μ_i²/(r² + a_i²),    Π(r) = Π_(i=1)^N (r² + a_i²)      (44).

"The event horizon is again at the largest real root of g^(rr)", which for odd d is Π(r0) − μ r0² = 0 (45). "The
relation between μ and a_i and the mass and angular momenta is the same as (34)":

    M = (d − 2) Ω_(d−2) μ/(16πG),    J = 2Ma/(d − 2).      (34)

Here Ω_(d−2) = 2π^((d−1)/2)/Γ((d − 1)/2). The linearised field of a mass M with angular momentum J_ij is (14)–(16).

**Theorem A.24** ([KI03, (2.7)–(2.8), p. 5; (2.14)–(2.16), p. 6; (3.1)–(3.10), pp. 8–9;
(3.11)–(3.14), pp. 9–10; (5.1)–(5.6), p. 13; (5.7)–(5.15), p. 14; (5.16), p. 15].) The background is

    ds² = −f(r) dt² + dr²/f(r) + r² dσ_n²,    f(r) = K − 2M/r^(n−1) − λr²,    λ = 2Λ/(n(n + 1))      (2.14)–(2.16),

with dσ_n² of constant curvature K. □ and D are the d'Alembertian and covariant derivative of the two-dimensional
orbit space with coordinates (t, r).

(1) Tensor type (p. 13). For harmonics T_ij with (Δ̂_n + k_T²) T_ij = 0, T^i_i = 0, D̂_j T^j_i = 0, and
k_T² = l(l + n − 1) − 2 for K = 1 (5.2): "H_T is gauge-invariant by itself, and in vacuum, it satisfies"

    □H_T + (n/r) Dr · DH_T − ((k_T² + 2K)/r²) H_T = 0.      (5.3)

With Φ = r^(n/2) H_T (5.4), this is □Φ − (V_T/f)Φ = 0 (5.5), where

    V_T(r) = (f/r²) [k_T² + 2K + n(n − 2)K/4 − n(n + 2)λr²/4 + n²M/(2r^(n−1))].      (5.6)

(2) Vector type (p. 14). Here k_V² = l(l + n − 1) − 1 (5.8) and V_ij = −(D̂_i V_j + D̂_j V_i)/(2k_V) (5.9). "For
k² > (n − 1)K,

    F_a = f_a + (r/k_V) D_a H_T      (5.10)

is gauge invariant". In vacuum r^(n−1) F^a = ε^(ab) D_b Ω (5.12), with □Ω − (n/r) Dr · DΩ − ((k_V² − (n − 1)K)/r²)
Ω = 0 (5.11). With Φ = r^(−n/2) Ω (5.13) this is □Φ − (V_V/f)Φ = 0 (5.14), where

    V_V(r) = (f/r²) [k_V² + K + n(n − 2)K/4 − n(n − 2)λr²/4 − 3n²M/(2r^(n−1))].      (5.15)

For l = 1, F_ab = r D_a(f_b/r) − r D_b(f_a/r) (5.16).

(3) Scalar type (pp. 5–10). For k²(k² − nK) ≠ 0 the gauge-invariant variables are

    F = H_L + H_T/n + (1/r) D^a r X_a,   F_ab = f_ab + D_a X_b + D_b X_a,   X_a = (r/k)(f_a + (r/k) D_a H_T)
    ((2.7)–(2.8)).

In terms of X, Y, Z of (2.20) and Z = iωZ̃,

    Φ := (nZ̃ − r(X + Y))/(r^(n/2−1) H),   H = m + n(n + 1)x/2,   m = k² − nK,   x = 2M/r^(n−1)      (3.1)–(3.4),

and (2.24) reduces to

    −f d/dr (f dΦ/dr) + V_S Φ = ω² Φ,    V_S = f Q/(16 r² H²)      (3.5)–(3.6).

With y = λr² (3.8), Q is

    Q(r) = [−n³(n + 2)(n + 1)² x² − 12n²(n + 1)(n − 2) m x + 4(n − 2)(n − 4) m²] y + n⁴(n + 1)² x³
           + n(n + 1)[4(2n² − 3n + 4)m + n(n − 2)(n − 4)(n + 1)K] x²
           − 12n[(n − 4)m + n(n + 1)(n − 2)K] m x + 16m³ + 4Kn(n + 2)m².      (3.7)

The original variables are expressed through Φ by (3.9)–(3.10). In the time domain the equation is □Φ − (V_S/f)Φ = 0
(3.11), and the gauge invariants are given covariantly by (3.12)–(3.14).

**Theorem A.25** ([HKW18, Theorem 2, p. 4; (19)–(20), p. 6; Lemma 11 and Theorem 12 (116), p. 39;
Theorem 18 (130), p. 47].) Let δg be a smooth, symmetric two-tensor on a Schwarzschild–Tangherlini spacetime with orbit
spheres of dimension n, satisfying the linearised Einstein equation. Then [HKW18, Theorem 2]: "there exist
gauge-invariant master quantities satisfying decoupled Regge-Wheeler type equations (134, 149, 153, 174) for the
scalar, co-vector, and two-tensor portions of δg_(ℓ≥2). With further specification of an initial data slice Σ0 and a
decay foliation Σ_τ := φ_τ(Σ0) formed by flowing along the static Killing vector field, a symmetric traceless
two-tensor Ψ solving any one of the equations (134, 149, 153, 174) satisfies the uniform boundedness estimate

    Ě^N_Ψ(Σ_τ) ≤ C(n, M) Ě^N_Ψ(Σ0),      (6)

and, in spacetime dimension six and below, the uniform decay estimate

    Ě^N_Ψ(Σ_τ) ≤ C(n, M) I_Ψ(Σ0)/τ²,      (7)

with Ě^N_Ψ and I_Ψ(Σ0) representing Sobolev data for Ψ on members of the decay foliation Σ_τ and C(n, M) being a
universal constant depending upon the orbit sphere dimension n and the background mass M."

The energies are those of [HKW18, Section 7]: the red-shift energy Ě^N_Ψ is comparable to E^N_Ψ by Lemma 11 (p. 39);
the bounds (6)–(7) are Theorem 12, (116), p. 39, and Theorem 18, (130), p. 47; and I_Ψ(Σ0) is defined after (130). The
horizon is r = r_h := (2M)^(1/(n−1)) (19), and "along the event horizon, the Schwarzschild-Tangherlini solution has
positive surface gravity κ_n := (n − 1)/(2r_h)" (20).

### A.7 Function spaces

In [BH17], s ∈ ℝ and p ∈ (1, ∞) throughout unless stated otherwise (p. 1).

**Theorem A.26** ([BH17, Theorem 7.26, p. 55].) "Let Ω be a nonempty bounded open subset of ℝⁿ with
Lipschitz continuous boundary or Ω = ℝⁿ. If sp > n, then W^(s,p)(Ω) ↪ L^∞(Ω) ∩ C⁰(Ω) and W^(s,p)(Ω) is a Banach
algebra."

**Theorem A.27** ([BH17, Theorem 9.14, p. 85].) "Let Mⁿ be a compact smooth manifold. Let π : E → M be
a smooth vector bundle of rank r over M equipped with fiber metric ⟨·, ·⟩_E (so it is meaningful to talk about
L^∞(M, E)). Suppose s ∈ ℝ and p ∈ (1, ∞) are such that sp > n. Then W^(s,p)(M, E) ↪ L^∞(M, E). Moreover, every element
u in W^(s,p)(M, E) has a continuous version."

**Theorem A.28** ([BH17, Theorem 7.27, p. 56].) "Let Ω be a nonempty bounded open subset of ℝⁿ with
Lipschitz continuous boundary. Suppose 1 ≤ p, q < ∞ (p does not need to be less than or equal to q) and 0 ≤ t ≤ s
satisfy s − n/p ≥ t − n/q. Then W^(s,p)(Ω) ↪ W^(t,q)(Ω). In particular, W^(s,p)(Ω) ↪ W^(t,p)(Ω)." For an integer
k ≥ 0, W^(k,p)(Ω) is the space of u ∈ L^p(Ω) with ‖u‖_(W^(k,p)(Ω)) := Σ_(|ν|≤k) ‖∂^ν u‖_(L^p(Ω)) < ∞ [BH17,
Definition 7.11, p. 50]; W^(0,q)(Ω) = L^q(Ω).

**Theorem A.29** ([GO13, Theorem 1, (2), p. 2].) With J^s := (1 − Δ)^(s/2) on ℝⁿ (p. 1): "Let
1/2 < r < ∞, 1 < p_1, p_2, q_1, q_2 ≤ ∞ satisfy 1/r = 1/p_1 + 1/q_1 = 1/p_2 + 1/q_2. Given s > max(0, n/r − n) or
s ∈ 2ℕ, there exists a constant C = C(n, s, r, p_1, q_1, p_2, q_2) < ∞ such that for all f, g ∈ 𝒮(ℝⁿ) we have …

    ‖J^s(fg)‖_(L^r(ℝⁿ)) ≤ C(s, n) [‖f‖_(L^(p_1)(ℝⁿ)) ‖J^s g‖_(L^(q_1)(ℝⁿ))
                                   + ‖J^s f‖_(L^(p_2)(ℝⁿ)) ‖g‖_(L^(q_2)(ℝⁿ))]      (2)."

For r = 2, p_1 = q_2 = ∞ and q_1 = p_2 = 2 the condition on s is s > 0, and (2) reads, for f, g ∈ 𝒮(ℝⁿ),

    ‖fg‖_(H^s) ≤ C (‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖g‖_(H^s) + ‖f‖_(H^s) ‖g‖_(L^∞)),      ‖u‖_(H^s) := ‖J^s u‖_(L²).    (A.2)

**Corollary A.30** (Moser's product estimate.) Let s ≥ 1 be an integer.

(1) If f, g ∈ H^s(ℝⁿ) ∩ L^∞(ℝⁿ), then fg ∈ H^s(ℝⁿ) and (A.2) holds with the same constant.

(2) Let N be a compact manifold without boundary, of dimension d, with a smooth Riemannian metric, let k ≥ 0, and let
X := ℝ^k × N carry the product metric and its measure. Let W_1, …, W_q be smooth vector fields on N spanning TN at
every point, 𝒱 := {∂_(z_1), …, ∂_(z_k), W_1, …, W_q}, and let H^s(X) be the space of u ∈ L²(X) with V_1 ⋯ V_j u ∈
L²(X) for all V_i ∈ 𝒱 and j ≤ s, normed by the sum of the L²-norms of these derivatives. There is C such that, for
f, g ∈ H^s(X) ∩ L^∞(X), fg ∈ H^s(X) and

    ‖fg‖_(H^s(X)) ≤ C (‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖g‖_(H^s(X)) + ‖f‖_(H^s(X)) ‖g‖_(L^∞)).

(3) Let 0 ≤ χ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝ^k) with Σ_(j∈ℤ^k) χ(z − j) = 1, put χ_j(z, y) := χ(z − j) on X and
‖u‖_(H^s_ul(X)) := sup_j ‖χ_j u‖_(H^s(X)). Then the bound of (2) holds with the uniformly local norms in place of the
H^s(X)-norms, for all f, g ∈ L^∞(X) whose uniformly local norms are finite.

*Proof.* (1) For integer s the norm ‖J^s u‖_(L²) is equivalent to (Σ_(|α|≤s) ‖∂^α u‖²_(L²))^(1/2), by Plancherel's
theorem. Let θ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝⁿ) with 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1 and θ = 1 near 0, let ρ_ε be a standard mollifier, and put
f_ℓ := θ(·/ℓ)(ρ_(1/ℓ) ∗ f) and g_ℓ := θ(·/ℓ)(ρ_(1/ℓ) ∗ g). These are Schwartz functions with ‖f_ℓ‖_(L^∞) ≤ ‖f‖_(L^∞)
and ‖g_ℓ‖_(L^∞) ≤ ‖g‖_(L^∞), and f_ℓ → f, g_ℓ → g in H^s. Indeed, by Leibniz's rule
∂^α(θ(·/ℓ)v) − θ(·/ℓ)∂^α v is a sum of terms ℓ^(−|β|)(∂^β θ)(·/ℓ) ∂^(α−β) v with β ≠ 0; so multiplication by
θ(·/ℓ), ℓ ≥ 1, is bounded on H^s uniformly in ℓ, and θ(·/ℓ)v → v in H^s for each fixed v ∈ H^s, as
θ(·/ℓ)∂^α v → ∂^α v in L² by dominated convergence. Writing f_ℓ − f = θ(·/ℓ)(ρ_(1/ℓ) ∗ f − f) + (θ(·/ℓ)f − f), the
first term tends to 0 in H^s because ρ_(1/ℓ) ∗ f → f in H^s, and the second by the fixed-v case. So the right side
of (A.2) for (f_ℓ, g_ℓ) is at most ‖f‖_(L^∞)‖g_ℓ‖_(H^s) + ‖f_ℓ‖_(H^s)‖g‖_(L^∞), which converges to the
right side for (f, g). Further ‖f_ℓ g_ℓ − fg‖_(L²) ≤ ‖f_ℓ − f‖_(L²) ‖g‖_(L^∞) + ‖f(g_ℓ − g)‖_(L²), and along a
subsequence g_ℓ → g almost everywhere with |f(g_ℓ − g)| ≤ 2‖g‖_(L^∞)|f|, so f_ℓ g_ℓ → fg in L² and
J^s(f_ℓ g_ℓ) → J^s(fg) as tempered distributions. The J^s(f_ℓ g_ℓ) are bounded in L²; a subsequence converges weakly
in L², its limit is J^s(fg), and its norm is at most the limit inferior of the norms.

(2) Choose charts κ_i : U_i → ℝ^d, i = 1, …, I, of N, functions φ_i ∈ C_c^∞(U_i) with Σ_i φ_i² = 1 and ψ_i ∈
C_c^∞(U_i) equal to 1 near supp φ_i. For v on X supported in ℝ^k × supp ψ_i let v^(i) := v ∘ (id × κ_i⁻¹), extended
by zero to ℝ^(k+d). On ℝ^k × supp ψ_i the fields of 𝒱 have, in the coordinates (z, κ_i), coefficients bounded with
all their derivatives, they span the tangent spaces, and the measure has a density bounded above and below; so there
is C with C⁻¹‖v‖_(H^s(X)) ≤ ‖v^(i)‖_(H^s(ℝ^(k+d))) ≤ C‖v‖_(H^s(X)) for such v, and multiplication by φ_i or ψ_i is
bounded on H^s(X). As u = Σ_i φ_i(φ_i u), ‖u‖_(H^s(X)) ≤ C Σ_i ‖(φ_i u)^(i)‖_(H^s). Now (φ_i fg)^(i) =
(ψ_i f)^(i) (φ_i g)^(i) lies in H^s(ℝ^(k+d)) by (1), so φ_i fg ∈ H^s(X) and fg = Σ_i φ_i(φ_i fg) ∈ H^s(X); and (1)
gives

    ‖fg‖_(H^s(X)) ≤ C Σ_i (‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖(φ_i g)^(i)‖_(H^s) + ‖(ψ_i f)^(i)‖_(H^s) ‖g‖_(L^∞))
                  ≤ C (‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖g‖_(H^s(X)) + ‖f‖_(H^s(X)) ‖g‖_(L^∞)).

(3) Let supp χ ⊂ {|z|_∞ ≤ R}, R a positive integer, and χ̃_j := Σ_(|l−j|_∞ ≤ 2R) χ_l. Then χ̃_j = 1 on supp χ_j,
0 ≤ χ̃_j ≤ 1, χ_j fg = (χ̃_j f)(χ_j g), and ‖χ̃_j f‖_(H^s(X)) ≤ (4R + 1)^k ‖f‖_(H^s_ul(X)). Applying (2) to χ̃_j f and
χ_j g and taking the supremum over j gives the bound. ∎

**Theorem A.31** (Products of derivatives.) Let s ≥ 1 be an integer.

(1) There is C, depending only on n and s, such that for f, g ∈ H^s(ℝⁿ) ∩ L^∞(ℝⁿ) and multi-indices α, β
with |α| + |β| ≤ s, ∂^α f ∂^β g ∈ L²(ℝⁿ) and

    ‖∂^α f ∂^β g‖_(L²) ≤ C (‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖g‖_(H^s) + ‖f‖_(H^s) ‖g‖_(L^∞)).    (A.3)

(2) In the setting of Corollary A.30 (2) there is C such that for f, g ∈ H^s(X) ∩ L^∞(X) and V_1, …, V_p,
V′_1, …, V′_q ∈ 𝒱 with p + q ≤ s,

    ‖(V_1 ⋯ V_p f)(V′_1 ⋯ V′_q g)‖_(L²(X)) ≤ C (‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖g‖_(H^s(X)) + ‖f‖_(H^s(X)) ‖g‖_(L^∞)).

*Proof.* (1) We use the norm ‖u‖²_(H^s) := Σ_(|γ|≤s) ‖∂^γ u‖²_(L²), equivalent to that of (A.2) by
Plancherel's theorem. Splitting f and g into real and imaginary parts, which increases neither norm, we may take f
and g real-valued, at the cost of a factor 4 in C. If |α| + |β| = s′ < s, the claim at the order s′ (or, for s′ = 0,
‖fg‖_(L²) ≤ ‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖g‖_(L²)) gives the claim at the order s, as ‖·‖_(H^(s′)) ≤ ‖·‖_(H^s). So let |α| + |β| = s, and
let f and g first be real Schwartz functions.

*An interpolation inequality.* For 0 ≤ j ≤ s put p_j := 2s/j (p_0 := ∞) and a_j := max_(|γ|=j) ‖∂^γ f‖_(L^(p_j)).
Let 1 ≤ j ≤ s − 1 and p := p_j, so 2 < p ≤ 2s. Let |γ| = j, write ∂^γ = ∂_k ∂^(γ′) with |γ′| = j − 1, and put
u := ∂^(γ′) f. The function τ ↦ τ|τ|^(p−2) on ℝ is C¹ with derivative (p − 1)|τ|^(p−2), so integration by parts gives

    ∫ |∂_k u|^p dx = ∫ ∂_k u · ∂_k u |∂_k u|^(p−2) dx = −(p − 1) ∫ u · ∂_k² u · |∂_k u|^(p−2) dx.

Hölder's inequality with the exponents p_(j−1), p_(j+1) and p/(p − 2), whose reciprocals add to
(j − 1)/(2s) + (j + 1)/(2s) + 1 − j/s = 1, gives ‖∂_k u‖^p_(L^p) ≤ (p − 1) ‖u‖_(L^(p_(j−1))) ‖∂_k² u‖_(L^(p_(j+1)))
‖∂_k u‖^(p−2)_(L^p). As ∂_k² u is a derivative of f of order j + 1, this is a_j² ≤ 2s a_(j−1) a_(j+1). If f ≠ 0,
every a_j is positive, since a Schwartz function whose derivatives of order j all vanish is a polynomial, hence 0.
Then d_j := log a_j + ½ j² log(2s) satisfies d_(j−1) + d_(j+1) − 2d_j ≥ 0 for 1 ≤ j ≤ s − 1, so (d_j) is convex on
{0, 1, …, s} and d_j ≤ (1 − j/s) d_0 + (j/s) d_s, that is,

    a_j ≤ (2s)^(j(s−j)/2) a_0^(1−j/s) a_s^(j/s),      0 ≤ j ≤ s,

which holds trivially if f = 0. Here a_0 = ‖f‖_(L^∞) and a_s ≤ ‖f‖_(H^s); the same holds for g.

*The product.* Put σ := |α|/s ∈ [0, 1], so |β|/s = 1 − σ. Hölder's inequality with the exponents p_(|α|) and p_(|β|),
whose reciprocals add to 1/2, and the interpolation inequality for f and for g give

    ‖∂^α f ∂^β g‖_(L²) ≤ ‖∂^α f‖_(L^(p_(|α|))) ‖∂^β g‖_(L^(p_(|β|)))
                       ≤ C (‖f‖_(L^∞)^(1−σ) ‖f‖_(H^s)^σ)(‖g‖_(L^∞)^σ ‖g‖_(H^s)^(1−σ))
                       = C (‖f‖_(H^s) ‖g‖_(L^∞))^σ (‖f‖_(L^∞) ‖g‖_(H^s))^(1−σ),

and x^σ y^(1−σ) ≤ σx + (1 − σ)y for x, y ≥ 0 gives (A.3).

*General f and g.* Let f_ℓ, g_ℓ be the Schwartz functions of the proof of Corollary A.30 (1); they are real
when f and g are, ‖f_ℓ‖_(L^∞) ≤ ‖f‖_(L^∞), ‖g_ℓ‖_(L^∞) ≤ ‖g‖_(L^∞), and f_ℓ → f, g_ℓ → g in H^s. Then ∂^α f_ℓ → ∂^α f
and ∂^β g_ℓ → ∂^β g in L², hence almost everywhere along a subsequence, and Fatou's lemma gives
‖∂^α f ∂^β g‖_(L²) ≤ lim inf ‖∂^α f_ℓ ∂^β g_ℓ‖_(L²), which is at most the right side of (A.3).

(2) Let κ_i, φ_i, ψ_i and v ↦ v^(i) be as in the proof of Corollary A.30 (2), and
Π := (V_1 ⋯ V_p f)(V′_1 ⋯ V′_q g). As Σ_i φ_i² = 1, ‖Π‖²_(L²(X)) = Σ_i ‖φ_i Π‖²_(L²(X)). As ψ_i = 1 near supp φ_i,
on a neighbourhood of supp φ_i we have Π = (V_1 ⋯ V_p(ψ_i f))(V′_1 ⋯ V′_q(ψ_i g)). In the coordinates (z, κ_i) on
ℝ^k × supp ψ_i, V_1 ⋯ V_p = Σ_(|γ|≤p) c_γ ∂^γ and V′_1 ⋯ V′_q = Σ_(|δ|≤q) e_δ ∂^δ with coefficients bounded there,
the fields of 𝒱 having coefficients bounded with all their derivatives. So (φ_i Π)^(i) is a finite sum of terms
b ∂^γ F_i ∂^δ G_i with b bounded, |γ| + |δ| ≤ s, F_i := (ψ_i f)^(i) and G_i := (ψ_i g)^(i). By (1), and as the
measure has a density bounded above and below,

    ‖φ_i Π‖_(L²(X)) ≤ C (‖F_i‖_(L^∞) ‖G_i‖_(H^s) + ‖F_i‖_(H^s) ‖G_i‖_(L^∞)).

Finally ‖F_i‖_(L^∞) ≤ C ‖f‖_(L^∞) and ‖F_i‖_(H^s) ≤ C ‖ψ_i f‖_(H^s(X)) ≤ C ‖f‖_(H^s(X)), by the chart comparison and
the boundedness of multiplication by ψ_i recorded in that proof; likewise for G_i. ∎

**Theorem A.32** ([GO13, p. 1].) Grafakos and Oh recall the commutator estimate of Kato and Ponce
[KP88]: with J^s := (1 − Δ)^(s/2) on ℝⁿ, for Schwartz functions f and g,

    ‖J^s(f g) − f (J^s g)‖_(L^p) ≤ C [‖∇f‖_(L^∞) ‖J^(s−1) g‖_(L^p) + ‖J^s f‖_(L^p) ‖g‖_(L^∞)]

"for 1 < p < ∞ and s > 0", with C a constant depending on n, p and s.

**Corollary A.33** (Kato–Ponce for compactly supported functions.) Let s > 0, and let f, g be compactly
supported on ℝⁿ with ∇f ∈ L^∞, J^s f ∈ L², g ∈ L^∞ and J^(s−1) g ∈ L². Then J^s(f g) − f (J^s g) ∈ L² and the
inequality of Theorem A.32 holds for p = 2 with the same constant.

*Proof.* Let ρ_ε be a standard mollifier and f_ε := ρ_ε ∗ f, g_ε := ρ_ε ∗ g, smooth with compact support, hence
Schwartz functions. Convolution with ρ_ε is a Fourier multiplier of norm at most 1 on L² and on L^∞ and commutes with
J^σ and ∇, so the right side of the inequality for (f_ε, g_ε) is at most the right side for (f, g). As ε → 0, f_ε → f
uniformly, ∇f_ε → ∇f in L², g_ε → g and J^(s−1) g_ε → J^(s−1) g in L². Hence f_ε g_ε → f g in L² and J^s(f_ε g_ε) →
J^s(f g) as tempered distributions. For a test function φ, ⟨f_ε J^s g_ε, φ⟩ = ⟨J^(s−1) g_ε, J(f_ε φ)⟩, and f_ε φ → f φ
in H¹, so J(f_ε φ) → J(f φ) in L² by Plancherel; thus f_ε J^s g_ε → f J^s g as distributions. The left sides for
(f_ε, g_ε) are bounded in L² and converge as distributions; a subsequence converges weakly in L², its limit is J^s(f g)
− f (J^s g), and its norm is at most the limit inferior of the norms. ∎

**Theorem A.34** ([See64, Theorem, p. 625].) For x ∈ ℝⁿ and t ∈ ℝ, let S₊ = ℝⁿ × {t > 0} and
"D₊ = {f : f ∈ C^∞(S₊), f and all its derivatives have continuous limits as t → 0+}". D₊ "has the topology of uniform
convergence of each derivative on compact subsets of the closure of S₊ in ℝ^(n+1), and C^∞(ℝ^(n+1)) has a corresponding
topology". "There is a continuous linear extension operator E : D₊ → C^∞(ℝ^(n+1)) such that Ef(x, t) = f(x, t) for
t > 0."

**Theorem A.35** ([LY22, Theorem 1, pp. 1–2; Theorem 26 and Lemma 27, p. 16].) Theorem 1: "(i)
There exists an extension operator E : C⁰(ℝ̄ⁿ_+) → C⁰(ℝⁿ) that has the form

    Ef(x′, xₙ) = Σ_(j=−∞)^∞ a_j f(x′, −b_j xₙ)  for xₙ < 0,    Ef(x) = f(x)  for xₙ > 0,      (2)

where b_j > 0 such that, for every k ∈ ℤ, Σ_(j=−∞)^∞ a_j (−b_j)^k = 1 and Σ_(j∈ℤ) 2^(δ_k|j|) |a_j| b_j^k < ∞ for some
δ_k > 0 (3). Moreover, when (3) is satisfied, then (2) always defines an extension operator E for functions on ℝⁿ_+,
that has the following boundedness (simultaneously): (ii) … E : W^(k,p)(ℝⁿ_+) → W^(k,p)(ℝⁿ) and
E : C^(k,s)(ℝⁿ_+) → C^(k,s)(ℝⁿ) are defined and bounded for all k ∈ ℤ, 0 < p ≤ ∞ and 0 < s < 1.
E : C^k(ℝⁿ_+) → C^k(ℝⁿ) is bounded for all k = 0, 1, 2, …", one operator for all these spaces at once; its items
(iii)–(iv) give the same for Besov, Triebel–Lizorkin and Morrey-type spaces. Of Seeley's operator
(Theorem A.34) [LY22, p. 1] records that it satisfies "E : C^k(ℝⁿ_+) → C^k(ℝⁿ) for all k = 0, 1, 2, …. In
particular Seeley's extension [preserves] C^∞-smoothness". Theorem 26: "Let Ω ⊂ ℝⁿ be a bounded smooth domain with a
smooth defining function σ, and let U ⊂ ℝⁿ be a bounded neighborhood of Ω̄. Then there exists an extension operator
E : 𝒮′(Ω) → ℰ′(U) that maps extendable distributions in Ω … to compactly supported distributions in U, such that …
(ii) (Universal boundedness) E : W^(k,p)(Ω) → W^(k,p)_c(U) and E : C^(k,s)(Ω) → C^(k,s)_c(U) are defined and bounded
for all k ∈ ℤ, 0 < p ≤ ∞ and 0 < s < 1. In particular E : C^k(Ω) → C^k_c(U) for k ≥ 0." Lemma 27: "Let Φ : ℝⁿ → ℝⁿ be
a bounded diffeomorphism, i.e. Φ is bijective and sup_(x∈ℝⁿ) |∂^α Φ(x)| + |∂^α(Φ⁻¹)(x)| < ∞, ∀ α ∈ ℕⁿ_0 ∖ {0}. Let
χ ∈ C_c^∞(ℝⁿ) be a bounded smooth function. Define a linear map T f := (χ · f) ∘ Φ. (i) T : W^(k,p)(ℝⁿ) → W^(k,p)(ℝⁿ),
T : C^(k,s)(ℝⁿ) → C^(k,s)(ℝⁿ) are both defined and bounded for all k ∈ ℤ, 0 < p ≤ ∞ and 0 < s < 1. In particular
T : C^k(ℝⁿ) → C^k(ℝⁿ) for k ∈ ℕ₀."

**Theorem A.36** ([SY21, Section 1, p. 2; Section 2.1, p. 6].) After Rychkov (p. 2): "for a
Lipschitz domain Ω there exists an operator E = E_Ω that is bounded on Besov spaces E : B^s_pq(Ω) → B^s_pq(ℝⁿ) for all
0 < p, q ≤ ∞, s ∈ ℝ and on Triebel-Lizorkin spaces E : F^s_pq(Ω) → F^s_pq(ℝⁿ) for all 0 < p < ∞, 0 < q ≤ ∞, s ∈ ℝ.
Since E is one single operator which works for all such spaces, we call it an universal extension operator on Ω".
After Stein (p. 6), Ω being a bounded Lipschitz domain and W^(k,p)(Ω) defined in the classical way: Stein "used an
alternative approach to construct an extension operator E^S which is independent of k, such that
E^S : W^(k,p)(Ω) → W^(k,p)(ℝⁿ) is bounded for all k ∈ ℕ and 1 ≤ p ≤ ∞".

### A.8 Microlocal analysis and Fredholm theory

**Theorem A.37** ([HJS, (2.1), Propositions 2.3, 3.7, 3.11, 3.13, 4.9, 4.10, 7.4, 7.5 and 10.1,
Definitions 7.2 and 10.2, Sections 7.5 and 10.1–10.3, Lemma 12.5, pp. 9–95].) The scattering calculus Ψ^(m,l)_sc on
ℝⁿ, n arbitrary, and on scattering manifolds M has the following properties.

(1) Composition [HJS, (2.1), p. 9]: Ψ^(m,l)_sc ∘ Ψ^(m′,l′)_sc ⊂ Ψ^(m+m′,l+l′)_sc.

(2) Ellipticity [HJS, Proposition 2.3, p. 12]: "Every elliptic element of the scattering calculus has a parametrix",
that is, a B ∈ Ψ^(−m,−l)_sc with AB − Id ∈ Ψ^(−∞,−∞)_sc ∋ BA − Id ((2.9)).

(3) Duality [HJS, Proposition 3.7, p. 19]: the L² pairing "extends boundedly to a (conjugate linear) isomorphism
H^(−s,−r)_sc ≅ (H^(s,r)_sc)*".

(4) Boundedness [HJS, Proposition 3.11 and Remark 3.12, p. 20]: "If A ∈ Ψ^(m,l)_sc, then, for all s, r ∈ ℝ, A maps
A : H^(s,r)_sc → H^(s−m,r−l)_sc, and does so boundedly". Moreover "Op(a), viewed as an element of
L(H^(s,r)_sc, H^(s−m,r−l)_sc), depends continuously on a in the sense that if a_1, a_2, ⋯ ∈ S^(m,l)_sc is some
sequence such that a_n → a in S^(m,l)_sc, then Op(a_n) → Op(a) in L(H^(s,r)_sc, H^(s−m,r−l)_sc)".

(5) Compactness [HJS, Proposition 3.13, p. 20]: "For any s, s′, r, r′, with s < s′ and r < r′, the embedding
H^(s′,r′)_sc ↪ H^(s,r)_sc is compact."

(6) Microlocality [HJS, Proposition 4.9, p. 27]: "If A ∈ Ψ^(m,l)_sc and u ∈ 𝒮′, then
WF^(s,r)_sc(Au) ⊆ WF^(s+m,r+l)_sc(u) ∩ WF′_sc(A)."

(7) Microlocal parametrix [HJS, Proposition 4.10, p. 29]: "Suppose that A ∈ Ψ^(m,l)_sc is elliptic at
